Candidate 2, fenofibrate (PPARα agonist; ID 76), while lacking direct dry AMD clinical or late‐stage in vivo data, has a robust safety and PK/PD profile as a systemic drug, extensive preclinical evidence in RPE lipid‐overload and diabetic retinopathy models, and a plausible MoA directly relevant to RPE homeostasis: upregulation of fatty acid oxidation, reduction of lipotoxic by-products (including A2E), mitigation of oxidative stress and inflammation, and potential ancillary benefits (iron chelation, Wnt pathway modulation). Key weaknesses are the need for dedicated dry AMD models to confirm lipofuscin clearance and lysosomal rescue, and ocular delivery optimization, but these are addressable with standard preclinical studies. Relative to eculizumab, fenofibrate offers higher translatability, lower risk, and untapped potential to tackle a core metabolic driver of RPE degeneration in dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab is a recombinant, humanized monoclonal IgG kappa antibody that specifically binds complement component C5 and prevents its proteolytic activation into C5a and C5b, thereby blocking terminal pathway activity and membrane attack complex (MAC; C5b-9) assembly while leaving upstream C3-dependent functions largely intact (for example, opsonization and immune-complex handling) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; West et al., 2024). It was discovered by screening large panels of murine anti-human C5 monoclonals for potent inhibition of C5 activation and terminal complement–mediated hemolysis; the parental murine antibody (5G1.1) was then humanized by CDR grafting into human germline frameworks and engineered to use a hybrid IgG2/IgG4 heavy-chain constant region to minimize Fcγ receptor binding and classical-pathway activation (reducing effector functions that could confound terminal pathway blockade) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009). Eculizumab binds human C5 with very high affinity (Kd approximately 120 pM) and sterically prevents convertase engagement with the MG7 domain of C5; epitope mapping identifies residues in the MG7 domain (including the KSSKC motif around Arg885) critical for binding, and Arg885His/Cys polymorphisms have been linked to clinical non-responsiveness in some patients, consistent with the structural epitope (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

As a drug class, complement inhibitors have been deployed to treat diseases driven by complement dysregulation, with C5 blockade representing a terminal-pathway strategy that ablates C5a signaling and MAC-mediated cytolysis while preserving many proximal complement functions; eculizumab was the first complement inhibitor approved for clinical use and catalyzed broad clinical development of C5, C3, and alternative pathway–targeted agents across hematology, nephrology, neurology, and, more recently, ophthalmology (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Eculizumab is administered intravenously, exhibits a long serum half-life (~272 ± 82 hours), a limited volume of distribution consistent with an intravascularly confined antibody, and shows pharmacodynamic correlation between serum trough concentrations and blockade of hemolytic activity; vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis is required due to increased susceptibility when terminal complement is inhibited (Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Within ophthalmology, complement activation products and MAC deposition have been implicated in AMD pathogenesis, motivating clinical trials of complement inhibitors including C5-directed agents; eculizumab has been formally evaluated in a randomized phase 2 setting for non-exudative AMD (geographic atrophy and drusen cohorts) via systemic administration (Kassa et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Halawa et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
Eculizumab has an extensive clinical record in systemic complement-mediated disorders. It revolutionized therapy for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), where it reduces intravascular hemolysis, decreases transfusion requirements, and improves quality of life; it is also approved for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and for neurologic autoimmune indications including anti–acetylcholine receptor–positive generalized myasthenia gravis and aquaporin-4–positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Early clinical pharmacology in PNH demonstrated that an induction regimen of 600 mg weekly for four weeks followed by 900 mg every other week maintained near-complete terminal pathway blockade and significantly reduced hemolysis and transfusion needs; these dosing principles align with its long half-life and the concentration dependence of hemolytic inhibition (Hillmen et al., 2004; Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012). Despite robust control of intravascular hemolysis, residual extravascular hemolysis can persist because C3 opsonization is not prevented by C5 inhibition, illustrating an important mechanistic limitation of terminal-pathway agents (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; West et al., 2024).

The drug’s safety profile is dominated by infection risk with encapsulated organisms—particularly meningococcal disease—necessitating vaccination; otherwise, eculizumab has shown acceptable tolerability across long-term use, with clinical programs incorporating monitoring of functional complement activity (CH50) to confirm pharmacodynamic blockade and dose adequacy (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009; Eskandary et al., 2016). Mechanistically relevant sources also report pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic complexities: high-affinity binding at acidic endosomal pH encourages recycling of eculizumab:C5 complexes by FcRn, leading to accumulation of total C5 bound to the drug in circulation; next-generation engineering in ravulizumab introduced pH-dependent release to minimize cargo recycling and extend dosing intervals (Schmidt & Smith, 2023).

In ophthalmology, eculizumab has been investigated as a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD. The COMPLETE study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), a single-center, randomized, double-masked phase 2 trial, evaluated intravenous eculizumab in two cohorts: geographic atrophy (GA) and intermediate AMD with high-risk drusen; patients were randomized 2:1 to eculizumab or saline over 24 weeks with follow-up to 52 weeks (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the GA cohort (n = 30 study eyes), eculizumab did not reduce GA enlargement versus placebo at 26 or 52 weeks (square-root–transformed growth 0.19 ± 0.12 mm vs. 0.18 ± 0.15 mm at 26 weeks, P = 0.96; 0.37 ± 0.22 mm vs. 0.37 ± 0.21 mm at 52 weeks, P = 0.93), and no drug-related adverse events were reported (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the drusen cohort (n = 30 total participants; 20 active, 10 placebo), eculizumab failed to meet the prespecified primary endpoint of a ≥ 50% reduction in drusen cube-root volume at 26 weeks; none of 18 treated eyes achieved this threshold, while one placebo eye did (10%; P = 0.36), and there was no detectable difference in mean drusen growth between arms through 26–52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014). Trial conduct included meningococcal vaccination and careful multimodal imaging; retention was high with 28/30 completing 52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). Independent evidence syntheses judged the certainty of evidence as low to very low due to small sample size, imprecision, and some risk of bias; overall, systemic eculizumab “may have made little to no difference” in BCVA and GA lesion growth in the available cohort (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistically similar C5-directed agents have not shown positive phase 2 outcomes in GA when administered systemically or intravitreally (e.g., LFG316 failed in phase 2), whereas intravitreal C5 inhibition with avacincaptad pegol progressed to later-phase testing and regulatory review, suggesting that drug, route, and pharmacology may be important determinants of outcome; by contrast, intravitreal C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) demonstrated efficacy and has been approved for GA, underscoring the translational relevance of target selection and ocular delivery (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024). Multiple reviews conclude that systemic eculizumab is no longer in development for AMD and highlight delivery and mechanistic concerns as likely contributors to the negative results (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, eculizumab targets the MG7 domain of C5 and sterically prevents formation of the C5 convertase–substrate complex, thereby inhibiting the cleavage of C5 into the potent anaphylatoxin C5a and C5b, which nucleates membrane attack complex assembly with C6–C9 (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Rother et al., 2007). Structural analysis of an eculizumab Fab bound to C5 resolved at 4.2 Å shows that five CDRs form the principal interface with MG7; mutational scanning of CDR residues identifies a network of contacts necessary for high-affinity binding, and kinetic assays confirm that these interactions prevent complement-mediated hemolysis in vitro (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016). The epitope includes residues near Arg885, and clinical resistance due to Arg885His/Cys substitutions in C5 provides orthogonal validation of the binding site (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

Pharmacodynamically, eculizumab ablates terminal pathway function: it suppresses CH50 to near zero when trough serum concentrations exceed ~35 μg/mL; however, because proximal C3 activation continues, C3b deposition and downstream opsonins accumulate on surfaces, which can drive extravascular clearance and generate residual pathology even under complete C5 blockade in appropriate disease contexts (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). Additional mechanisms can undermine complete terminal pathway control: (1) during intense proximal activation, densely opsonized surfaces can support C5 activation by convertases in ways that partially bypass classical C5 convertase assembly or even promote conformational C5 activation on surface C3b clusters; such context-dependent activation can manifest as “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” despite apparently adequate free drug levels, and has been reported in clinical settings as residual terminal-pathway activity and elevated sC5b-9 in some patients (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). (2) Eculizumab binds C5 with high affinity at both neutral and mildly acidic pH, allowing FcRn to recycle eculizumab:C5 complexes and potentially alter antigen disposition; ravulizumab’s pH-dependent binding was engineered to release C5 in endosomes and improve pharmacokinetics by avoiding cargo recycling (Schmidt & Smith, 2023). These features are germane to dose selection, monitoring, and potential resistance or escape during strong complement activation.

Rationale for C5 inhibition in AMD rests on abundant mechanistic and histopathological evidence that C5-derived effectors and MAC participate in retinal/choroidal injury. C5a is detected in drusen and acts as a chemotactic and proinflammatory mediator capable of inducing VEGF expression from retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, while C5b initiates MAC assembly; MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris increases with aging and is elevated in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019). Sub-lytic and lytic MAC on choroidal endothelium causes cell injury and can trigger surviving endothelial cells to upregulate VEGF and matrix metalloproteinases, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic injury and pro-angiogenic remodeling; complement regulatory proteins such as CD59 are natural inhibitors of MAC formation and their dysfunction or insufficiency can predispose to damage (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2021). Complement dysregulation in AMD further includes genetic risk (e.g., CFH variants) and evidence of alternative pathway activation in ocular tissues, suggesting both proximal and terminal effector involvement in disease biology (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Importantly, proximal inhibition at C3 has shown the capacity to restore lysosomal function and reduce sub-RPE drusen-like deposits in human iPSC-derived RPE models carrying the high-risk CFH Y402H variant by reducing C3 turnover and lowering downstream MAC (C5b-9) localization at lysosomes; in this system, a compstatin analogue (Cp40) suppressed C3b and MAC deposition and reversed lysosomal abnormalities, whereas direct C5 inhibition has not been shown in this model to rescue lysosomal function, and clinical C5 blockade has failed in GA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). These data reinforce that while terminal pathway effectors are present and likely pathogenic in AMD, distal blockade at C5 does not necessarily address upstream complement turnover that drives intracellular lysosomal stress in RPE, and proximal intervention may be required to normalize cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
The hypothesis proposes that high-affinity C5 blockade with eculizumab will prevent MAC assembly on RPE, thereby reducing sub-RPE deposit–driven lysosomal stress and indirectly supporting photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis in dry AMD. Mechanistically, preventing C5 cleavage would abrogate both C5a signaling and C5b-dependent MAC formation; given the documented presence of C5a in drusen and increased MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane/choriocapillaris with age and AMD, terminal pathway inhibition is expected to reduce MAC-mediated endothelial and RPE injury, dampen MAC-induced VEGF/MMP signaling, and potentially mitigate inflammation (Kassa et al., 2019). In principle, if MAC-driven lysosomal injury contributes to RPE dysfunction, C5 inhibition could reduce new MAC deposition at the RPE surface and limit subsequent endocytosis of MAC into lysosomes, thereby lowering lysosomal burden (Park et al., 2021).

However, two key bodies of evidence temper this expectation. First, clinical testing of systemic eculizumab in GA and intermediate AMD failed to show benefit on primary anatomical endpoints (GA growth and OCT drusen volume) through 26–52 weeks, despite established systemic pharmacodynamic blockade; these negative outcomes argue that either (a) terminal pathway activity at C5 is not the principal driver of lesion growth/drusen regression during the studied disease stages/time horizon, or (b) pharmacokinetic compartmentalization limited ocular target engagement after intravenous dosing (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Filho et al., 2014). Reviews explicitly highlight the compartment barrier problem—systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina or sub-RPE space due to the blood–retina/Bruch’s membrane barriers and large molecular size—and note that eculizumab exposure shorter than six months is unlikely to show benefit in slowly progressive GA, compounding interpretation (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Second, cellular models directly linking complement dysregulation to lysosomal failure in high-risk AMD RPE show that upstream C3 inhibition, not terminal C5 blockade, restores lysosomal function and reduces deposit formation; this suggests that intralysosomal stress is driven by continuous C3 turnover and opsonization rather than MAC alone, and that distal C5 blockade may be insufficient to normalize these processes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Consequently, POS phagocytosis metrics may improve only marginally or not at all if the dominant insult is proximal complement turnover rather than MAC-mediated damage. The clinical failure to slow GA growth or reduce drusen volume with systemic eculizumab supports the inference that target engagement at C5, via the tested route and schedule, did not translate into macroscopic anatomical benefit in human AMD eyes within one year (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).

If eculizumab were to be tested in vitro on human RPE, appropriate readouts would include: surface and intracellular MAC (C5b-9) quantification, lysosomal number/size and membrane integrity (e.g., LAMP2, Galectin-8), Cathepsin D activity, autophagic flux, and POS degradation kinetics; concomitant measurement of upstream C3b/iC3b/C3d deposition would be essential to interpret whether C5 inhibition is affecting the dominant pathogenic pathway in the assay (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In vivo, ocular pharmacokinetic considerations dominate: intravitreal administration delivers drug to the retina and sub-RPE space but is not reported for eculizumab in the provided context and would carry different safety and dosing constraints; systemic dosing faces blood–retina barrier limitations that likely constrained ocular target engagement in COMPLETE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Notably, nearly all complement inhibitors that have shown anatomical effects in GA have been delivered intravitreally, underscoring the importance of route of administration for ocular diseases (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic rationale: C5a and MAC are present in AMD-relevant tissues; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD and can drive endothelial injury, VEGF/MMP upregulation, and potentially RPE dysfunction; blocking C5 should diminish these terminal effector signals (Kassa et al., 2019; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Potent, well-characterized biologic: Eculizumab binds human C5 with picomolar affinity, has a well-defined structural epitope in the MG7 domain, and reliably ablates terminal pathway function systemically with a large clinical safety database outside ophthalmology (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
- Clinical feasibility and tolerability: In AMD trials, intravenous eculizumab was well tolerated without drug-related adverse events and with no clear signal for increased neovascular conversion or ocular infection within one year, supporting general safety of systemic C5 blockade in this population under vaccination protocols (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Negative clinical efficacy in AMD: The randomized phase 2 COMPLETE trial showed no reduction in GA growth and no meaningful reduction in drusen volume through 26–52 weeks; certainty is limited by small sample size but confidence intervals and replication across endpoints argue against a large treatment effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).  
- Compartmentalization barriers for systemic dosing: Blood–retina and Bruch’s membrane barriers likely limit ocular exposure to intravenously administered eculizumab; multiple reviews cite inadequate ocular penetration as a plausible reason for failure, and systemic eculizumab is no longer being pursued in AMD (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
- Target selection may be too distal for RPE lysosomal rescue: Human iPSC-RPE data indicate that complement-driven lysosomal pathology and drusen-like deposits are reversed by C3 inhibition, with concomitant reduction of downstream MAC, while C5 blockade alone has not been shown to restore lysosomal metrics and did not slow GA clinically; this suggests that proximal complement turnover is the dominant driver of RPE lysosomal stress (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Mechanistic escape and incomplete terminal control: Under strong activation, C5 can be activated on dense C3b clusters with features of convertase bypass or conformational priming; stoichiometric C5 inhibitors can form long-lived C5:antibody complexes on surfaces, potentially allowing residual terminal activity, and clinical “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” has been documented (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
- Genetic and biochemical determinants of response: C5 polymorphisms (e.g., R885H/C) can abolish binding and confer resistance; while prevalence in AMD populations is unknown here, such variants are important risk factors for nonresponse (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).  
- Safety/logistics: Terminal complement blockade mandates meningococcal vaccination and vigilance for invasive infections; while acceptable systemically in selected diseases, risk–benefit in a chronic, slowly progressive ocular disorder is less favorable, and the cost and infusion burden are high (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Contextualization with alternative complement strategies  
- C5 vs C3: Clinical success in GA has emerged at the level of C3 (pegcetacoplan), consistent with cellular data showing rescue of lysosomal function by upstream blockade; by contrast, systemic C5 inhibition with eculizumab and other C5-directed agents failed to meet GA endpoints in early trials, and LFG316 also did not demonstrate efficacy in GA (West et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Route of administration: Most agents demonstrating anatomical effects in GA are delivered intravitreally; eculizumab’s large size and systemic administration likely limited ocular penetration in COMPLETE, and no intravitreal eculizumab data are provided here to support local delivery (Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
- Risk of adverse ocular remodeling: Complement modulation has complex, context-dependent effects; in some models, complement inhibition or modulation can alter macrophage polarization and influence CNV formation, underscoring that indiscriminate or poorly targeted complement blockade could have unintended consequences; while the eculizumab AMD trials did not show a neovascular signal, vigilance is warranted when selecting targets and doses (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2021).

Decision Implications  
- As a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD, eculizumab has a low probability of success based on randomized clinical evidence, pharmacokinetic compartment limitations, and mechanistic considerations indicating that distal C5 blockade may not correct the proximal complement turnover driving RPE lysosomal pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- If C5 remains a target of interest, local ocular delivery and alternative molecular formats designed for intravitreal pharmacokinetics (e.g., smaller C5-binding entities, RNAi to intraocular C5 production, or intravitreal C5 inhibitors such as avacincaptad pegol) are more plausible routes; indeed, avacincaptad has advanced in GA, while systemic eculizumab has been discontinued in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019; Nadeem et al., 2023; West et al., 2024).  
- For assays aimed at lysosomal stress and POS phagocytosis, prioritizing proximal complement inhibitors (e.g., C3-targeting) is more aligned with human RPE data and recent clinical experience, whereas C5 inhibition alone is unlikely to fully normalize lysosomal function or confer robust structural benefit (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; West et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
Eculizumab provides a clear mechanistic means to extinguish terminal complement effectors implicated in AMD biology, but the totality of evidence—negative randomized clinical data in GA and drusen, route-of-administration barriers to ocular exposure, mechanistic escape during high activation, and cellular evidence favoring proximal over distal inhibition for lysosomal rescue—argues against further development of systemic eculizumab for dry AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The program should be deprioritized in favor of intraocularly suited agents and proximal complement targets, unless a compelling, testable strategy emerges to achieve effective intraocular C5 blockade with eculizumab (which is not supported by the present context) (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistic Appendix: Biochemical and Pathobiologic Evidence Relevant to the Hypothesis  
- Complement activation and terminal effectors in AMD:  
  - C5a is present in drusen and induces VEGF from RPE; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD; MAC induces endothelial lysis and sub-lytic survival signaling that upregulates VEGF and MMPs (Kassa et al., 2019).  
  - Alternative pathway dysregulation is central in AMD; genetic and experimental data implicate factor H and alternative pathway components in AMD and CNV models; inhibition of C3a, C5a, CFB, MAC or supplementation with CD59/CFH blocks CNV in animals (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Eculizumab structure–function:  
  - Epitope on MG7 with steric convertase blockade; high-affinity binding and resistance polymorphisms at Arg885; CDR function validated by mutational scans (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
  - PK/PD: long half-life, vascular distribution, CH50 suppression threshold, FcRn recycling of C5:eculizumab complexes; ravulizumab engineering to improve recycling and dosing (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
  - Breakthrough mechanisms: convertase bypass and surface-induced conformational activation on dense C3b clusters; residual TP activity despite inhibitors under strong activation (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; Mannes et al., 2021).  
- Clinical AMD trials:  
  - COMPLETE GA cohort: no slowing of GA growth at 26 or 52 weeks; well tolerated (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021).  
  - COMPLETE drusen cohort: no ≥ 50% reduction in drusen volume in treated eyes at 26 weeks; no significant change in drusen growth vs placebo (Filho et al., 2014).  
  - Critical appraisals: small sample, imprecision, risk of bias; systemic delivery may not achieve retinal levels; eculizumab no longer in AMD development (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023).  
- RPE lysosomal biology:  
  - In high-risk Y402H iPSC-RPE, excessive C3 turnover increases MAC internalization and overloads lysosomes; C3 inhibition with Cp40 reduces both C3b and MAC, reverses lysosomal defects, and reduces drusen-like deposits; direct C5 inhibition is not shown to restore lysosomal function in this model (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Operational Recommendation  
- Do not advance systemic eculizumab for dry AMD. If C5 remains a strategic target, consider intravitreal agents designed for ocular PK and evaluate them head-to-head against proximal inhibitors in RPE lysosomal-function assays that quantify both MAC and C3 fragment deposition, with translational go/no-go predicated on alignment with known clinical signals in GA (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibrate originally developed and approved as a lipid‐lowering agent that acts primarily as a peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) agonist. It was discovered through efforts to develop compounds that could enhance fatty acid oxidation and thereby reduce triglyceride levels and improve lipid profiles in patients with dyslipidemia. As a member of the fibrate class of drugs, fenofibrate and its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, have been classically used in cardiometabolic conditions such as hyperlipidemia, where they improve lipid profiles by increasing high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels and lowering triglycerides. The compound available as Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. F6020 is representative of these agents and has been extensively studied in preclinical models of metabolic stress. Its chemical design enables it to bind to PPARα, a nuclear receptor that modulates gene expression of enzymes central to fatty acid β-oxidation and lipid homeostasis. In the context of retinal disorders, fenofibrate has been pursued as a repurposing candidate owing to its robust safety profile and its potential to address the dysregulation of lipid metabolism observed in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. Several studies have suggested that by activating PPARα, fenofibrate may help reduce lipid overload and mitigate the accumulation of toxic by-products such as A2E (a major fluorophore in lipofuscin) that contribute to RPE dysfunction in age-related macular degeneration (Wang et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2022).  

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate has a long clinical history as an antihyperlipidemic agent with a well-established safety profile in patients with cardiovascular risk factors. In addition to its widespread use in metabolic disorders, a significant body of preclinical research has documented the potential benefits of fenofibrate in retinal diseases. Several studies have demonstrated that fenofibrate can ameliorate retinal abnormalities induced by high-fat diets and excessive lipid exposure. For instance, experimental models of fat-induced RPE injury have shown that fenofibrate reduces oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators, thereby protecting RPE integrity through mechanisms such as upregulation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway (Wang et al., 2023). In diabetic retinopathy—a condition that, while distinct from dry AMD, shares underlying processes related to oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and inflammatory cascades—fenofibrate has been explored for its protective effects on the retina, contributing to improvements in vascular permeability and barrier function of the outer blood–retina barrier (Fu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023). Although fenofibrate’s potential use in dry AMD has not been as widely investigated as its role in diabetic retinopathy, the documented protective effects on RPE under conditions of lipid overload, as well as its ability to downregulate markers of oxidative stress (e.g., NOX4 and 3‐nitrotyrosine) and inflammatory cytokines (such as TNFα and ICAM1), support its candidacy for repurposing in dry AMD (Ren et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023). It is noteworthy that while clinical data in diabetic populations (e.g., FIELD study outcomes) have driven considerable interest in fenofibrate’s ocular effects, direct applications to dry AMD remain exploratory and are based largely on preclinical findings that show promise for reducing lipotoxic damage in the RPE.

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate exerts its pharmacological effects primarily through the activation of PPARα, a nuclear receptor that, upon ligand binding, dimerizes with the retinoid X receptor and binds to specific PPAR response elements in promoter regions of target genes. This leads to the transcriptional upregulation of a variety of genes involved in lipid uptake, fatty acid transport, and β-oxidation, ultimately promoting the catabolism of long-chain fatty acids. In RPE cells, robust expression of PPARα is critical for maintaining homeostasis in the face of high lipid loads and oxidative stress. Activation of PPARα by fenofibrate has been shown to enhance mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, thereby reducing intracellular lipid accumulation and possibly the generation of toxic lipid peroxidation products such as A2E, a primary component of the lipofuscin granules that accumulate with age in RPE cells (Ren et al., 2022).

Beyond its classical role in lipid metabolism, fenofibrate has also been reported to engage additional cellular signaling pathways that contribute to its cytoprotective effects. In several preclinical studies, fenofibrate and fenofibric acid have been observed to activate the PI3K/AKT pathway in RPE cells, which is well recognized for its roles in cell survival and stress response. The activation of PI3K/AKT signaling by fenofibrate leads to enhanced cell survival signals, mitigates oxidative damage, and downregulates inflammatory mediators in fatty acid–challenged RPE cells (Wang et al., 2023). Moreover, fenofibrate has been implicated in reducing the expression of pro-oxidant enzymes such as NADPH oxidase 4 (NOX4) and in decreasing levels of markers of oxidative stress like 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) in palmitic acid-treated RPE models (Wang et al., 2023). These actions collectively contribute to mitigation of oxidative injury—a central component of dry AMD pathogenesis.

In addition, some studies have proposed that fenofibrate may exert ancillary effects through mechanisms independent of PPARα activation. For example, evidence suggests that fenofibrate might function as an iron chelator, thereby reducing intracellular free iron levels, which in turn could diminish the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and blunt the aberrant activation of the canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway—a pathway implicated in various ocular pathologies including AMD (Mandala et al., 2020). This suppression of iron-induced oxidative stress and its associated downstream signaling cascades may further contribute to the preservation of RPE cell function under conditions of chronic oxidative insult.

Another mechanism of potential interest is fenofibrate’s impact on inflammatory signaling. Classical anti-inflammatory effects have been verified through its ability to inhibit nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) activity, thereby reducing the transcription of a host of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines that might contribute to retinal degeneration (Garcia-Ramírez et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2020). Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for the repurposing strategy of fenofibrate in dry AMD is that its activation of PPARα in RPE cells—achievable at concentrations with an EC₅₀ of approximately 2 µM—will promote a metabolic shift toward enhanced fatty acid oxidation. This shift is expected to lower the intracellular lipid load and decrease the accumulation of lipofuscin, a complex mixture of lipid-protein aggregates that includes A2E, which is thought to contribute directly to RPE cell dysfunction and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration. In vitro data from models using palmitic acid to induce lipotoxic stress in RPE cells suggest that fenofibrate can restore cellular homeostasis by activating survival pathways such as PI3K/AKT and by suppressing overexpressed stress markers and inflammatory cytokines (Wang et al., 2023).

According to the proposed mechanism, activation of PPARα should lead to the upregulation of genes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, resulting in improved clearance of lipid-rich photoreceptor outer segments. The improvement in lipid processing not only reduces the overall lipid burden within RPE cells but is also expected to restore lysosomal function—specifically, normalizing lysosomal pH and enhancing cathepsin D activity. These changes should facilitate more efficient phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segment debris, thereby mitigating the accumulation of cytotoxic lipofuscin deposits.

Furthermore, by lowering intracellular lipid accumulation and reducing oxidative stress through enhanced PI3K/AKT signaling and potential NF-κB inhibition, fenofibrate is expected to decrease the production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines that contribute to chronic inflammation in the retina. Since inflammation is a driving force behind the progression of dry AMD, such a decrease would synergize with improved autophagy and phagocytosis to stabilize or even improve RPE function. In preclinical models, the application of fenofibrate in conditions simulating high dietary fat has been shown to restore aspects of RPE cell viability and function, lending indirect support to its potential efficacy in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023). Although the precise effects on A2E reduction and lipofuscin clearance have yet to be fully elucidated, the cumulative data on fenofibrate’s capacity to improve lipid metabolism and reduce oxidative and inflammatory stress suggest that the compound could address multiple maladaptive processes that underlie dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
When evaluating fenofibrate as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and potential weaknesses become apparent. On the strengths side, fenofibrate benefits from an extensive clinical safety record, as it is already in widespread use as a lipid-lowering agent in patients with dyslipidemia. This established safety profile, along with known pharmacokinetics, provides an important advantage when considering rapid repurposing for ocular indications. Moreover, its well-documented efficacy in modulating lipid metabolism through PPARα activation is a significant asset, given that dysregulated lipid handling is a central aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis. Preclinical studies have convincingly demonstrated that fenofibrate can attenuate RPE injury induced by fat overload by reducing oxidative stress markers, enhancing protective signaling pathways (e.g., PI3K/AKT), and suppressing inflammatory cytokines (Wang et al., 2023). Additionally, the possibility that fenofibrate might also act through mechanisms independent of PPARα—such as iron chelation and suppression of Wnt/β-catenin signaling—broadens its therapeutic potential in addressing the multifactorial nature of RPE degeneration (Mandala et al., 2020).

Another critical strength is the hypothesized ability of fenofibrate to improve lysosomal function and promote the phagocytosis of lipid-rich photoreceptor outer segments. Although the direct evidence for improvement in autophagy or direct clearance of lipofuscin and A2E is not yet fully established in the context of dry AMD studies, mechanistic insights from fenofibrate’s action in reducing cellular oxidative stress and lipid droplet accumulation provide a plausible basis for such effects (Ren et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023). The EC₅₀ value of roughly 2 µM as suggested in the hypothesis is within a physiologically relevant range based on in vitro findings in other RPE models, and may be achievable in ocular tissues with appropriate drug delivery strategies.

First, while fenofibrate’s benefits have been clearly documented in models of diabetic retinopathy and fat-induced RPE injury, there remains a relative paucity of direct evidence for its efficacy in models that specifically recapitulate the pathophysiological features of dry AMD. Dry AMD is characterized by a complex interplay of factors including drusen formation, chronic inflammation, and impaired phagocytosis, and the literature provided does not offer conclusive data demonstrating that fenofibrate can reduce lipofuscin accumulation or enhance the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments in these contexts (Wang et al., 2023). In other words, while fenofibrate effectively modulates the metabolic state of RPE cells in fat-induced injury models, its impact on the accumulation of A2E and other lipofuscin components remains largely hypothetical at this stage.

Another potential weakness is related to the complexity of AMD pathogenesis. Dry AMD involves not only metabolic and inflammatory dysregulation at the level of the RPE but also changes in Bruch’s membrane, choroidal perfusion, and immune cell infiltration. As such, a therapeutic candidate targeting primarily RPE lipid metabolism and oxidative stress may need to be combined with other interventions or may not be sufficient as a monotherapy to address all pathogenic aspects of the disease. Further, the off-target effects of fenofibrate—such as its potential to act through PPARα-independent pathways—could complicate its clinical profile in the eye, where fine-tuning of multiple overlapping cellular pathways is critical (Mandala et al., 2020; Garcia-Ramírez et al., 2016).

Moreover, although fenofibrate has excellent systemic safety and pharmacokinetics, its ocular penetration, bioavailability in the retina, and long-term effects specifically on the RPE have not been comprehensively evaluated in the context of dry AMD. Optimization of drug delivery to the posterior segment of the eye is a well-known challenge, and while fenofibrate’s lipophilic nature could be advantageous for retinal penetration, formulation and dosing strategies would require careful investigation.

In summary, fenofibrate represents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its ability to activate PPARα and improve lipid metabolism, as well as its demonstrated capacity to reduce oxidative stress and inflammation in RPE cells under conditions of lipid overload. Its long-standing clinical use and excellent safety record provide a strong foundation for further preclinical and eventually clinical studies in the context of ocular degenerative diseases. Nonetheless, a critical gap in the current literature is the direct demonstration that fenofibrate can lower A2E levels and enhance the phagocytosis of lipid-rich photoreceptor outer segments—a key mechanism underlying its hypothesized benefit in dry AMD. Addressing this gap through targeted in vitro and in vivo studies using dry AMD models will be essential. Should these studies confirm that fenofibrate improves lysosomal function, normalizes RPE phagocytosis, and reduces lipofuscin accumulation, it would represent a major advance in the treatment options for dry AMD.

Overall, fenofibrate’s potential lies in its multifaceted mechanisms of action. By combining improved fatty acid oxidation, antioxidant defenses, anti-inflammatory effects, and possibly even modulation of cellular iron levels and aberrant signaling pathways, fenofibrate could serve as a powerful therapeutic to modify the progressive degeneration of the RPE seen in dry AMD. However, additional mechanistic studies and preclinical validations are necessary before this candidate can be confidently advanced in clinical trials for dry AMD. Future research should aim to delineate the concentrations required for ocular efficacy, assess drug delivery methods that maximize retinal bioavailability, and determine whether the cellular effects observed in diabetic retinopathy and fat-induced injury models translate to the unique pathophysiological environment of dry AMD (Fu et al., 2020; Garcia-Ramírez et al., 2016; Mandala et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023).

In conclusion, while fenofibrate is a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD therapy, its ultimate success will depend on the ability to generate robust, direct evidence that supports its hypothesized effects on RPE lipid metabolism, lysosomal function, and phagocytic clearance of toxic lipofuscin components. The existing data on fenofibrate’s systemic and retinal protective effects provide an encouraging starting point; however, the transition from preclinical promise to clinical efficacy in the context of dry AMD remains contingent on focused investigations into these key areas. The strengths of fenofibrate—its established safety profile, multiple beneficial metabolic actions, and evidence from related retinal models—are balanced by the need for more specific, AMD-targeted research to fully validate its repurposing potential (Fu et al., 2020; Garcia-Ramírez et al., 2016; Mandala et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SRT1720 is a synthetic small‐molecule activator of SIRT1 that was originally discovered and optimized by Sirtris Pharmaceuticals through high‐throughput screening and subsequent structural refinement (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018). It belongs to the class of sirtuin‐activating compounds (STACs) that are chemically distinct from natural activators such as resveratrol. Unlike polyphenolic compounds, SRT1720 is based on an imidazothiazole scaffold, incorporating a 2-quinoxaline amidic substituent and a piperazine moiety at the C3 position. This combination of structural features was determined to be optimal for SIRT1 activation, allowing the compound to achieve an EC1.5 value of approximately 0.16 µM with maximal activation levels reported at 781% (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). The compound’s synthetic origins allowed medicinal chemists to overcome many limitations seen with natural compounds, such as poor bioavailability and limited potency, and enabled the generation of a series of analogues ultimately leading to SRT1720. As a representative of third-generation STACs, SRT1720’s well-characterized in vitro profile and documented pharmacokinetic properties position it as a promising candidate for repurposing into new therapeutic areas.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, SRT1720 has been extensively investigated in the context of metabolic disorders, particularly type 2 diabetes and obesity. Preclinical studies in diet-induced obese mice and genetically obese rodent models demonstrated its ability to normalize plasma glucose, enhance insulin sensitivity, and increase mitochondrial capacity without toxicity at proper dosing regimens (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). In these models, SRT1720 was shown not only to mimic the beneficial effects of caloric restriction but also to extend healthspan and, in some paradigms, even lifespan, by improving mitochondrial biogenesis via deacetylation of key transcriptional regulators such as PGC-1α (Feige et al., 2008; Milne et al., 2007). Although SRT1720 has been primarily developed and evaluated for metabolic and cardiovascular indications, its mechanism—centered on the activation of SIRT1 and the subsequent modulation of cellular metabolism, stress response, and anti-inflammatory signaling—has generated interest in its potential applications in other age-related conditions. However, thus far no published studies have specifically addressed its use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or related ocular degenerative conditions. This therapeutic candidate has not been utilized in a clinical or preclinical setting directly targeting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, which is the hallmark of dry AMD, although its known pharmacological profile, good oral bioavailability in rodent models, and the safety profile observed in multiple animal models provide a rationale for its repurposing (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Alcain & Villalba, 2009).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SRT1720 acts as an allosteric activator of SIRT1, an NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase involved in the regulation of energy metabolism, inflammation, autophagy, and other aging-related processes. Its mechanism of action is predicated on binding to the SIRT1-peptide substrate complex rather than the free enzyme. Specifically, SRT1720 has been shown to interact with a site in the N-terminal region of SIRT1, mapped approximately to amino acids 183–225, which is proposed to undergo a conformational change upon binding of acetylated substrates (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). Through this allosteric binding, SRT1720 lowers the Michaelis constant (Km) for the acetylated peptide substrate, thereby increasing the enzyme’s affinity for its substrate and promoting a more productive catalytic conformation. This effect enhances the deacetylation of key substrates, such as PGC-1α, FOXO1, and p53, which are involved in metabolic regulation, stress response, and apoptosis (Feige et al., 2008; Milne et al., 2007). Although initial studies reported a direct activation model analogous to that of resveratrol, subsequent investigations have raised concerns regarding the substrate-dependency of the assay used to measure SIRT1 activity. For instance, certain studies reported that SRT1720 only shows activation when fluorophore-tagged peptides are used, casting doubts on whether the compound directly interacts with SIRT1 under native conditions (Pacholec et al., 2010). Nevertheless, additional kinetic and biophysical studies, including those employing isothermal titration calorimetry and nuclear magnetic resonance, have supported an allosteric activation mechanism that is consistent with a reduction in Km for acetylated substrates (Dittenhafer-Reed et al., 2011; Sanchez-Fidalgo et al., 2012). Moreover, structural and structure-activity relationship studies have confirmed that modifications in the chemical scaffold of SRT1720—particularly adjustments to the piperazine group and quinoxaline moiety—are critically linked to its SIRT1 activating properties (Blum et al., 2011; Granchi & Minutolo, 2018). In summary, despite ongoing debates about the nuances of its mechanism, the prevailing view supports that SRT1720 directly modulates SIRT1 activity via an allosteric mechanism that facilitates deacetylation of substrates, thereby promoting cellular processes that mimic the beneficial aspects of caloric restriction and enhance metabolic health.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
The hypothesis underlying the use of SRT1720 for dry age-related macular degeneration is that SIRT1 activation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells can improve autophagy and cytoskeletal dynamics, thereby enhancing phagocytic cup formation and promoting lysosomal fusion necessary for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). RPE dysfunction—including impaired autophagy and phagocytosis—has been implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In this context, SRT1720’s ability to increase LC3 flux and improve LAMP1 trafficking, as observed in models of oxidative stress, offers a mechanistic rationale for its use. Preclinical findings in non-ocular systems have demonstrated that activation of SIRT1, whether achieved genetically or pharmacologically, augments mitochondrial biogenesis and reduces oxidative stress by increasing the turnover of damaged cellular components (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Mautone et al., 2020). Notably, the EC₅₀ for SIRT1 activation by SRT1720 in some biochemical assays approximates 0.1–0.16 µM, a range that is consistent with the dosing hypothesis proposed for RPE cells (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). Given that the RPE is known to express SIRT1 and other components of the autophagic machinery, the expected result of SRT1720 treatment in the RPE would be deacetylation of key regulators involved in autophagy and cytoskeletal organization. This deacetylation should in turn enhance processes such as phagosome maturation and lysosomal fusion, which are critical for efficient clearance of POS debris (Alcain & Villalba, 2009; Sanchez-Fidalgo et al., 2012). Additionally, SIRT1 activation in RPE cells may mitigate oxidative stress and reduce pro-inflammatory signaling pathways, further contributing to cellular homeostasis and survival in the ocular microenvironment (Dittenhafer-Reed et al., 2011). On a cellular assay level, treatment with SRT1720 is expected to increase markers of autophagic flux (such as LC3-II conversion), promote proper trafficking of lysosomal markers like LAMP1, and enhance the formation of organized phagocytic cups necessary for POS engulfment. These improvements in RPE function could, in theory, translate into better clearance of accumulated debris and ultimately slow or reverse degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD. However, while this hypothesis is supported by data from metabolic and non-ocular cellular studies, it remains essential to validate these effects specifically in RPE cell models and animal models of dry AMD to ensure that the ocular pharmacokinetic profile and tissue-specific responses are favorable (Park et al., 2017; Wan, 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating SRT1720 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the available literature. On the strength side, SRT1720 is one of the most potent synthetic SIRT1 activators reported, with biochemical assays consistently demonstrating activation in the low micromolar to submicromolar range (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). Its synthetic nature and the consequent ability to modify its chemical structure for improved potency and selectivity afford significant advantages over naturally occurring compounds like resveratrol. The extensive preclinical data supporting its beneficial effects in metabolic disorders, including improved mitochondrial function, enhanced autophagy, and anti-inflammatory properties, provide a strong rationale for its potential use in conditions where cellular clearance and stress responses are impaired, such as in the RPE during dry AMD (Milne et al., 2007; Sanchez-Fidalgo et al., 2012). Moreover, the underlying hypothesis that SIRT1 activation can enhance autophagic flux and cytoskeletal dynamics aligns well with the biological challenges faced by the RPE in dry AMD—namely, the accumulation of damaged POS and the ensuing oxidative stress that contributes to disease progression. The documented pharmacokinetic properties, such as good oral bioavailability in rodent models, further suggest that SRT1720 could be optimized for ocular delivery with appropriate formulation strategies (Alcain & Villalba, 2009; Mautone et al., 2020).

On the other hand, notable weaknesses and challenges must be addressed. First, there is ongoing controversy regarding the precise mechanism by which SRT1720 activates SIRT1. Some studies have raised concerns that its observed activity might be an artifact of the assay conditions—particularly its dependence on fluorophore-tagged substrates—which calls for cautious interpretation of its direct effects on native SIRT1 substrates (Pacholec et al., 2010). Such discrepancies underscore the need for additional rigorously controlled biochemical studies using physiological substrates in RPE cells to conclusively establish its mechanism of action in an ocular context. Second, while extensive data exist from metabolic and cardiovascular models, there is a notable paucity of research specifically addressing the use of SRT1720 in ocular tissues or models of retinal degeneration. As dry AMD is characterized by unique aspects of retinal physiology, including a blood–retinal barrier and specific immune responses in the eye, the translational relevance of data from non-ocular models must be carefully validated through targeted preclinical studies (Park et al., 2017). Third, potential off-target effects—such as cross-reactivity with other sirtuin family members like SIRT2—pose additional concerns regarding the specificity and safety profile of SRT1720. Although its selectivity for SIRT1 over SIRT3 appears robust, any unintended modulation of SIRT2 or other enzymes could have unforeseen consequences on RPE cell function and overall retinal health (Milne et al., 2007; Granchi & Minutolo, 2018). Finally, the optimal dosing strategy, route of administration, and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) relationship in the context of ocular delivery remain unexplored, necessitating a series of preclinical ocular pharmacology studies to evaluate whether the effective concentrations observed in vitro can be achieved in the retina without systemic toxicity (Park et al., 2017; Sinclair & Hubbard, 2013).

In conclusion, SRT1720 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well-documented ability to activate SIRT1 and modulate critical cellular processes such as autophagy, mitochondrial biogenesis, and cytoskeletal organization. These properties are particularly relevant given the role of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD, where impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and accumulated cellular debris contribute to disease progression. The compound’s synthetic origins allow for further medicinal chemistry optimization, and its strong in vitro potency (EC₅₀ in the low micromolar range) lends support to the hypothesis that it could achieve meaningful biological effects in the RPE (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). It would be imperative to conduct detailed biochemical studies in primary RPE cell cultures and to establish reliable animal models of dry AMD to evaluate both efficacy and ocular pharmacokinetics. Additional research should also focus on determining whether SRT1720’s modulation of autophagic and cytoskeletal regulators translates into improved POS clearance and enhanced RPE survival under oxidative stress.  

Overall, while SRT1720 demonstrates many characteristics that are theoretically beneficial for treating dry AMD, further targeted research is required to resolve the outstanding controversies and validate its therapeutic potential in the ocular setting. Strengths such as its high potency and favorable metabolic effects are balanced by weaknesses including assay-dependent mechanistic uncertainties and limited direct evidence in retinal systems. Therefore, the recommendation is to pursue rigorous preclinical studies that specifically assess SRT1720’s impact on RPE autophagy, phagocytic cup formation, and lysosomal fusion as well as its in vivo efficacy in relevant dry AMD models before committing substantial resources to later-stage development. This strategy will ensure that the unique challenges of ocular delivery and retinal cellular dynamics are adequately addressed, providing a sound basis for eventual clinical translation if the compound proves efficacious and safe in these specialized assays (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Pacholec et al., 2010; Blum et al., 2011; Alcain & Villalba, 2009).
