Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MCC950 is a synthetic diarylsulfonylurea small molecule originally identified from an IL-1β processing inhibitor chemotype and later defined as a highly potent and selective inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome complex (Coll et al., 2015). Within the inflammasome‐inhibitor landscape, MCC950 is representative of sulfonylurea‐based NLRP3 inhibitors that block canonical and noncanonical NLRP3 activation while sparing other inflammasomes (AIM2, NLRC4, NLRP1) and upstream innate pathways (e.g., TLR-NF-κB priming) (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Mechanistically, MCC950 acts directly on NLRP3 to prevent assembly of the adaptor ASC (apoptosis‐associated speck-like protein containing a CARD) into oligomeric “specks,” thereby preventing caspase-1 activation and maturation of IL-1β and IL-18 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Follow-on mechanistic analyses indicate MCC950 binds the NLRP3 NACHT domain to inhibit its ATPase function and thereby prevent NLRP3 activation; mechanistic models include prevention of ASC oligomerization and disruption of required conformations for NEK7–NLRP3 cooperation during sensor activation (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2023).

This class (selective NLRP3 inhibitors) has been broadly leveraged in preclinical inflammatory disease models to selectively blunt inflammasome‐driven IL-1 family cytokine maturation and pyroptosis without pan‐suppressing innate immune sensing, with documented in vivo efficacy in autoimmune encephalomyelitis, CAPS (NLRP3 gain‐of‐function), spontaneous colitis, atherosclerosis, and myocardial infarction models (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021; Wooff et al., 2020). In ocular biology, several sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950 and chemically related CRID3/IFM compounds—reduce IL-1β secretion and cell lysis in human RPE models and ex vivo mouse RPE/choroid eye cups under diverse AMD‐relevant triggers (lysosomal membrane permeabilization, oxidative/photooxidative stress, and P2X7 activation) (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic and non‐ocular indications. MCC950 has repeatedly shown robust pharmacodynamic suppression of inflammasome outputs and disease modification in vivo. Oral dosing in a spontaneous colitis model suppressed IL-1β/IL-18 production ex vivo and improved clinical/histopathologic indices (Perera et al., 2018). In APC‐driven autoimmune encephalomyelitis and in CAPS, MCC950 reduced IL-1β production and ameliorated disease; in CAPS it rescued neonatal lethality (Coll et al., 2015). In ApoE-deficient mice, MCC950 reduced atherosclerotic plaque burden, intraplaque macrophages, and systemic TNF-α/IL-1β/IL-6/IL-18 (Zeng et al., 2021). Across these studies MCC950 demonstrates in vivo target engagement, cytokine suppression, and disease modification with high selectivity for NLRP3 (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021). However, translational reviews emphasize that many NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950‐class agents—face liabilities for organ penetration (including eye/brain) and potential liver toxicity, underscoring formulation/delivery and safety risks that must be addressed for ocular use (Ortega et al., 2024).

Ocular and retinal contexts. In the ischemic OIR model, MCC950 lowered retinal neovascularization and vascular leakage and shifted an aberrant cytokine balance (decreased IL-1β activity with increased IL-18 activity), with accompanying reductions in angiogenesis‐ and pericyte‐associated signaling molecules (VEGF, VEGFR1/2, MMP2/9, PDGFR-β, Ang2) and evidence of inflammasome activation localized predominantly to macrophages (F4/80+) over endothelium (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Sui et al., 2020c). In a glaucoma model (DBA/2J), MCC950 reduced NLRP3 and cleaved caspase-1 in retina and mitigated retinal ganglion cell loss independently of intraocular pressure, indicating on‐target retinal neuroinflammation suppression (Li, 2020).

By contrast, in a laser‐induced CNV model (wet AMD), short‐course MCC950 lowered IL-1β transcript/protein but paradoxically increased total CNV lesion volume and recruitment of microglia and monocyte‐derived macrophages; ERG a- and b-waves were unchanged, suggesting no gross electrophysiological toxicity under those conditions (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b). This aligns with genetic evidence that inflammasome–IL-1β signaling promotes CNV largely through macrophages/microglia and that non‐NLRP3 inflammasomes also contribute, implying that selectively inhibiting NLRP3 may have complex, context‐dependent effects in neovascular disease (Marneros, 2023a; Marneros, 2023b).

In dry‐AMD–relevant photo‐oxidative damage (PD), intravitreal MCC950 failed to rescue function/structure and high‐dose MCC950 worsened ERG amplitudes: 20 µM showed no functional change versus PBS and did not alter photoreceptor death or IBA-1+ microglia counts; 100 µM significantly reduced ERG function (Wooff et al., 2020b). In the same study, Casp1/11−/− mice exhibited strong protection, whereas Nlrp3−/− mice showed only partial functional preservation, and pharmacologic NLRP3 inhibition or Nlrp3 siRNA provided no benefit (and in some readouts reduced function), leading to the conclusion that downstream caspase-1 is a dominant driver whereas NLRP3 may be neither necessary nor sufficient in this model (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). The authors also highlighted uncertainties about NLRP3 localization (predominantly INL/GCL rather than RPE), protein detection sensitivity, and the absence of ocular pharmacokinetic data for MCC950 (Wooff et al., 2020b).

RPE cell and ex vivo ocular models. In IL-1α–primed ARPE-19 and primary human RPE (pRPE), sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors reduced inflammasome activation and cell injury across diverse triggers relevant to GA, including LMP (Leu-Leu-OMe), oxidative stress (H₂O₂), lipofuscin/photooxidative insult (HNE-POS + blue light), and P2X7 activation (BzATP); in Abca4−/− eye cups, selective NLRP3 inhibitors suppressed IL-1β and LDH release and preserved RPE morphology after blue‐light irradiation (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024). A 2024 synthesis that included MCC950 reports that MCC950, IFM-632, and IFM-514 each decreased IL-1α-primed RPE inflammasome activation independent of the activation trigger, consistent with target class effects in RPE models (Korhonen, 2024). These in vitro/ex vivo data strongly support that NLRP3 activity can be engaged in RPE and that selective, small‐molecule inhibition suppresses canonical outputs (IL-1β, LDH) under multiple AMD‐relevant insults. However, detailed analyses of autophagic flux restoration or lysosomal integrity rescue after MCC950 are not reported in these excerpts (Wang et al., 2019).

Emerging genetics for AMD‐relevant deposits. In a monogenic EFEMP1 R345W knockin model (ML/DHRD) that recapitulates basal laminar deposits (BLamDs), as well as in aged WT mice, whole‐animal deletion of Nlrp3 or Casp1 significantly reduced BLamD size/coverage, normalized proinflammatory retinal cytokine profiles, and reduced microglial activation; these data provide genetic causality linking NLRP3–caspase-1 activity to deposit formation and inflammatory milieu (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). The same preprint cautions that NLRP3 inhibitors frequently suffer inadequate ocular penetration and potential liver toxicity, and emphasizes the need to determine whether ocular‐local versus systemic NLRP3 suppression is required (Ortega et al., 2024b).

Mechanism of Action  
Molecular target and binding mechanism. NLRP3 is a tripartite sensor (PYD–NACHT–LRR) that oligomerizes upon priming and activation to recruit ASC via PYD–PYD interactions, which in turn polymerizes and recruits pro-caspase-1 via CARD–CARD interactions to form an active inflammasome; active caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 and the pore‐forming effector gasdermin D (GSDMD) to elicit cytokine secretion and pyroptosis (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). MCC950 binds NLRP3 and prevents its ATPase activity (NACHT domain), disrupting a conformational step required for oligomerization and ASC speck assembly; in cellular systems, MCC950 suppresses both canonical (e.g., K⁺ efflux, lysosomal rupture, mitochondrial ROS) and noncanonical (caspase-11–triggered) activation pathways (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Notably, MCC950 does not broadly interfere with upstream priming (NF-κB–dependent transcription of NLRP3 and cytokine precursors), K⁺ or Ca²⁺ flux, or NLRP3–ASC direct binding in simple biochemical assays; rather, it functionally prevents ASC oligomerization and caspase-1 processing, reflecting target engagement at the level of sensor activation/oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Selectivity is strong: activity against AIM2, NLRC4, and NLRP1 inflammasomes is not observed, and broad target screening reveals only weak off-target activity (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018).

Cell-context specificity in the retina and RPE. Expression of NLRP3 and caspase-1 in the retina is cell-type and stimulus dependent. In vitro, microglia robustly upregulate Nlrp3, Casp1, and Il1b upon stimulation; Müller cells can increase Nlrp3 and Il1b without matching Casp1 elevation; photoreceptor‐line cells upregulate Nlrp3 while reducing Casp1; ARPE-19 cells often show undetectable NLRP3 protein and variable inflammasome readouts under some conditions (Wooff et al., 2020a). In situ, NLRP3 labeling is minimal in dim-reared mouse retinas but becomes detectable in the INL/GCL after PD, and AMD donor tissue shows NLRP3 in INL/GCL, suggesting inner-retina/microglial inflammasome contributions that complicate direct linkage to outer retina/RPE degeneration (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). Conversely, multiple human and preclinical reports demonstrate NLRP3 upregulation in macular RPE of AMD eyes with strong increases in pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 transcripts, co-localization of NLRP3 with autophagosome-like structures, and mitochondrial damage/autophagy signatures—though the literature is conflicted by antibody specificity and cell line variability (Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b; Marneros, 2023b). Taken together, these data imply that in AMD-relevant contexts, NLRP3 activation can occur in RPE and in inner-retinal microglia/Müller/immune cells; drug effects will be inherently cell-type dependent.

Pathway-level effects in retinal models. In ischemic retinopathy (OIR), NLRP3 activation (NLRP3/ASC/CASP1 upregulation and ASC specks) is observed primarily in macrophages and endothelium, and MCC950 reversal of an increased IL-1β/decreased IL-18 pattern is associated with reduced neovascularization and leakage, implicating vascular-cell responses to inflammasome cytokines as drivers of pathology (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b). In wet AMD CNV, inflammasome activation is localized mainly to infiltrating macrophages and microglia, and IL-1β is a principal driver of lesion growth; however, pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition increased lesion size in one study despite reduced IL-1β, suggesting additional non-NLRP3 inflammasomes and compensatory mechanisms (or cell-intrinsic NLRP3 roles) shape outcomes (Marneros, 2023a; Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b).

Expected Effect  
Proposed assay and mechanism. The proposal posits that MCC950 will specifically inhibit NLRP3 assembly in RPE (IC₅₀ ~7.5 nM), reducing IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, preventing inflammasome-induced lysosomal damage, preserving autophagic flux, and thereby enhancing photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance. Mechanistic underpinnings exist for the first components of this cascade: (i) MCC950 demonstrates nanomolar potency and high selectivity for NLRP3 and suppresses downstream IL-1β/IL-18 (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018); (ii) in IL-1α–primed RPE models (ARPE-19 and pRPE), sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950 in compiled data—suppress IL-1β and LDH release across LMP, oxidative stress, lipofuscin/photooxidative, and P2X7 activation paradigms, and preserve ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology under blue-light irradiation (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024). These findings support the expected reduction of canonical inflammasome outputs in RPE assays under multiple AMD-like stimuli.

Lysosome/autophagy preservation and POS clearance. Autophagy is a key negative regulator of NLRP3 activation: it limits ROS and damaged mitochondria, targets assembled inflammasomes for degradation, and suppresses IL-1β responses; conversely, autophagy suppression increases inflammasome activation and pyroptosis in RPE (Celkova et al., 2015). AMD-relevant triggers—including lipofuscin bisretinoids (e.g., A2E) and oxidative stress—cause lysosomal stress/LMP and NLRP3 activation in RPE, and caspase-1 inhibition can prevent RPE death in LMP contexts (Ildefonso et al., 2016). However, direct evidence that MCC950 restores autophagic flux or lysosomal integrity in RPE is not reported in the cited primary RPE inhibitor studies; the RPE evidence centers on IL-1β and LDH suppression and morphological preservation in ex vivo tissue but does not include autophagy- or lysosome-specific readouts or POS phagocytosis assays (Wang et al., 2019). Therefore, while it is plausible that NLRP3 suppression will indirectly favor autophagy homeostasis in stressed RPE by damping inflammasome-driven pyroptotic signaling (and thereby reduce further lysosomal damage), the proposed “preservation of autophagy and enhanced POS clearance” remains unproven for MCC950 and should be tested explicitly (Celkova et al., 2015).

Disease- and cell-type context expectations. In dry AMD models that feature outer-retinal/RPE degeneration, the translation of RPE in vitro suppression of NLRP3 to in vivo benefit is uncertain. In PD (a dry-AMD–relevant model), intravitreal MCC950 failed to confer protection and at higher dose impaired retinal function; Nlrp3−/− mice showed only partial protection while Casp1/11−/− mice were strongly protected, arguing that downstream caspase-1 and/or other inflammasomes may be the dominant drivers in photoreceptor death (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). In EFEMP1 R345W and aged WT models, genetic inactivation of Nlrp3 or Casp1 reduced basal laminar deposit burden and inflammatory signatures, supporting target pathway relevance for drusen/BLamD biology, but pharmacological MCC950 efficacy in these genetic models has not been reported (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). Importantly, if inflammasome activation in vivo is dominated by subretinal macrophages/microglia in some contexts (e.g., autophagy-impaired RPE signals that activate macrophage inflammasomes), the expected pharmacologic effect of MCC950 may depend more on drug exposure to myeloid cells in the subretinal/choroidal space than on direct RPE engagement (Liu et al., 2016).

Finally, IL-18 biology is context-dependent: while IL-1β is broadly pro-angiogenic and disruptive, IL-18 can be protective/anti-angiogenic in neovascular settings, and AMD-relevant studies have reported discordant roles for IL-18 across disease phenotypes (Celkova et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). Given that NLRP3 blockade reduces both IL-1β and IL-18, net effects on tissue outcomes may vary by disease stage and cell-type source; in OIR, MCC950 “normalized” an inverted IL-1β/IL-18 pattern and improved pathology (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020c), whereas in CNV, MCC950 increased lesion volume—implicating competing effects and non-NLRP3 inflammasomes (Dieckmann et al., 2024a).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- On-target potency/selectivity. MCC950 is among the most potent and selective NLRP3 inhibitors described, blocking canonical and noncanonical activation at nanomolar concentrations and sparing other inflammasomes and upstream pathways; it consistently suppresses IL-1β/IL-18 maturation and caspase-1 activation in primary macrophages and multiple in vivo models (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Perera et al., 2018).  
- RPE-target class activity under AMD-relevant stimuli. Sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors, including MCC950 in compiled datasets, reproducibly suppress IL-1β and LDH in IL-1α–primed ARPE-19 and primary human RPE triggered by LMP, oxidative/photooxidative stress, and P2X7 activation; ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology is preserved by an NLRP3 inhibitor during photooxidative stress (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024).  
- Genetic target validation in AMD-relevant deposit biology. Whole‐body Nlrp3 or Casp1 deletion reduces BLamDs and normalizes inflammatory signatures in EFEMP1 R345W mice and even prevents spontaneous deposits in aged WT, indicating the inflammasome pathway contributes causally to deposit formation and retinal inflammation (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c).  
- Demonstrated retinal efficacy in ischemic models and neuroinflammation. MCC950 improves vascular pathology in OIR (reduced neovascularization and leakage with cytokine-pattern reversal) and rescues retinal ganglion cells in glaucoma, supporting retinal target engagement and functional protection in relevant pathologies (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Li, 2020).

Liabilities and gaps  
- Lack of efficacy and potential toxicity in dry-AMD–relevant PD. Intravitreal MCC950 did not improve functional or structural outcomes in PD and at 100 µM worsened ERG amplitudes; Nlrp3 siRNA similarly failed to protect despite gene knockdown; Casp1/11 deletion was robustly protective while Nlrp3 deletion was only partially protective, arguing sensor-specific inhibition may be insufficient in photoreceptor death contexts (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- Mixed effects in neovascular disease. MCC950 increased CNV lesion volume in LCNV despite lowering IL-1β, and Nlrp3−/− mice displayed larger lesions, raising concern that NLRP3 blockade may remove protective constraints in some inflammatory/angiogenic contexts; non-NLRP3 inflammasomes likely contribute, further complicating pharmacodynamics (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).  
- Uncertain ocular delivery, exposure, and safety margin. Ocular PK for MCC950 is not defined; the PD study underscores unknown intravitreal bioavailability and clearance, and preclinical reviews warn of poor eye penetration and potential liver toxicity with many NLRP3 inhibitors; high intravitreal dose impaired ERG function in PD (Wooff et al., 2020b; Ortega et al., 2024b). While ERGs were unchanged in one CNV study, that does not establish comprehensive ocular safety (Dieckmann et al., 2024a).  
- RPE biology heterogeneity and expression uncertainty. In vivo NLRP3 induction localizes largely to inner retina/microglia rather than RPE in PD; ARPE-19 NLRP3 expression is variable in the literature and some human studies report low/undetectable NLRP3 in RPE, with concerns about antibody specificity, suggesting that direct RPE targeting may not be universally relevant across models or donors (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b; Marneros, 2023b).  
- Unproven restoration of autophagy/lysosomal function by MCC950. Although autophagy restrains inflammasome activation and lysosomal damage is a key trigger in RPE, direct evidence that MCC950 preserves autophagic flux, lysosomal integrity, or POS processing in RPE is absent in the cited studies; current RPE data document IL-1β/LDH suppression and morphology preservation but not autophagy or phagolysosomal kinetics (Celkova et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019).  
- Pathway redundancy suggests downstream targeting may be superior. Strong protection in Casp1/11−/− mice versus weak/absent benefits from NLRP3 inhibition in PD argue for targeting the shared downstream protease (caspase-1) or gasdermin D rather than individual sensors in retinal degeneration (Wooff et al., 2020a).

Risk-adjusted development path and decision inflection points  
- Go/no-go evidence needed in dry-AMD–relevant RPE assays. Establish whether MCC950 preserves lysosomal integrity and autophagic flux in RPE under LMP/photooxidative/P2X7 triggers and whether it restores POS digestion. Required readouts: LC3-II/I and p62 kinetics with and without bafilomycin, lysosomal pH and cathepsin activity, galectin-3 puncta for LMP, ASC speck formation, caspase-1 activity (FLICA), GSDMD cleavage, IL-1β/IL-18 maturation, and POS ingestion/digestion assays in ARPE-19 and pRPE (Celkova et al., 2015; Ranta-aho et al., 2021).  
- Ocular PK/PD and safety. Quantify intravitreal half-life, retinal/RPE/choroid distribution, and exposure–response for inflammasome suppression with MCC950; determine maximum non-toxic intravitreal dose across species. Include ERG, OCT, histopathology, IBA-1/microglial activation, and cytokine profiling. Investigate sustained intravitreal delivery strategies (e.g., silica-based nanoparticles) that have shown extended ocular release and improved anti-inflammatory efficacy for MCC950 in non-AMD contexts, while generating ocular PK and biodegradation data (Sun et al., 2023).  
- Efficacy in chronic dry-AMD models. Test MCC950 in EFEMP1 R345W mice (BLamD) and aging WT (spontaneous BLamD) with local ocular delivery; endpoints: BLamD size and coverage, RPE/Bruch’s integrity, microglial recruitment (Iba1), and cytokine panels. Given PD negative findings, prioritize deposit/atrophy models where genetic Nlrp3/Casp1 loss is protective (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c; Wooff et al., 2020b).  
- Cell-type–specific targeting and biomarkers. Because inflammasome activation is often myeloid-dominant in vivo, delineate whether MCC950’s ocular benefits, if any, require exposure to subretinal macrophages/microglia versus RPE. Use cell-specific pharmacodynamic markers (ASC specks in Iba1+ cells vs RPE65+ cells; IL-1β/IL-18 localization) to define pharmacologic engagement (Liu et al., 2016; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- Comparative strategy. In parallel, benchmark a caspase-1 inhibitor (or GSDMD inhibitor) against MCC950 in the same models, given the superior genetic protection with Casp1/11 deletion and the possibility of non-NLRP3 inflammasome contribution (Wooff et al., 2020a; Marneros, 2023a).

Bottom line  
MCC950 has strong mechanistic rationale, exquisite target selectivity, and reproducible suppression of inflammasome outputs in RPE assays across diverse AMD-like triggers. Genetic data incriminating NLRP3–caspase-1 in deposit biology strengthen the target hypothesis in a subset of dry-AMD phenotypes. However, the most AMD-relevant in vivo pharmacology with MCC950 to date is not supportive: no benefit and possible functional toxicity in PD, and mixed signals in neovascular settings (benefit in OIR, harm in LCNV). The translational path is further complicated by variable NLRP3 expression in RPE in vivo, dominance of myeloid inflammasomes in many retinal contexts, uncertain ocular PK/penetration, and the untested premise that MCC950 restores RPE autophagy/lysosomal function and POS clearance.

Given these data, MCC950 should not advance directly to costly IND-enabling studies for dry AMD without targeted de-risking experiments. The highest-value next steps are (i) mechanistic RPE assays that test autophagy/lysosome rescue and POS processing, (ii) rigorous ocular PK/safety to define a therapeutic index and viable delivery modality, and (iii) efficacy in deposit/atrophy models where the genetic target is validated (EFEMP1 R345W, aged WT). If these studies confirm robust ocular exposure, a favorable safety margin, and disease modification, MCC950—or a chemically optimized ocular NLRP3 inhibitor—could warrant advancement for specific dry-AMD endophenotypes. If not, downstream inflammasome targeting (caspase-1/GSDMD) may represent a more effective and generalizable strategy for retinal degeneration.

Mechanism of Action (detailed)  
NLRP3 activation requires priming (e.g., NF-κB upregulation of NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β/IL-18) and a second signal (e.g., K⁺ efflux via P2X7, lysosomal rupture with cathepsin release, mitochondrial ROS) that promotes sensor oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). NLRP3’s NACHT domain cycles ATP and orchestrates a conformational change enabling PYD-driven nucleation of ASC, which polymerizes into higher-order filaments/specks that template pro-caspase-1 recruitment and activation; activated caspase-1 cleaves GSDMD to induce pyroptotic pore formation and processes IL-1β/IL-18 for secretion (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). MCC950 binds NLRP3 to suppress its ATPase activity (NACHT), preventing the conformational activation needed for ASC oligomerization and caspase-1 activation; in functional assays MCC950 suppresses both canonical and noncanonical pathways and decreases processed caspase-1 p10/p20 in supernatants without altering upstream TNF-α secretion after TLR priming (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Evidence from retinal disease states aligns with these mechanisms: MCC950 reduces NLRP3 and cleaved caspase-1 in glaucomatous retina (DBA/2J), and in OIR normalizes IL-1β/IL-18 signaling and reduces pathologic neovascularization and leakage (Li, 2020; Sui et al., 2020a).

Inflammasome biology in RPE and AMD is multifactorial. AMD-associated triggers—lipofuscin photooxidation, A2E/oxidative stress, drusen lipid adducts (CEP), Alu RNA accumulation from DICER1 deficiency, and lysosomal destabilization—induce NLRP3 activation in RPE or in recruited subretinal macrophages (Ildefonso et al., 2016; Celkova et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016). Autophagy limits NLRP3 activation by removing damaged mitochondria and targeting assembled inflammasomes for autophagosomal degradation; autophagy blockade increases IL-1β production and pyroptotic susceptibility (Celkova et al., 2015). Pharmacologic NLRP3 blockade in RPE reduces IL-1β and LDH release under LMP, oxidative, photooxidative, and P2X7 activation, consistent with suppression of caspase-1 activation and pyroptotic lysis (Wang et al., 2019). Whether these biochemical effects in RPE suffice to modify chronic, multicellular retinal degeneration in vivo depends on drug delivery to relevant compartments (RPE, subretinal macrophages/microglia), on the relative contributions of non-NLRP3 inflammasomes, and on downstream cytokine biology (e.g., IL-18’s context-dependent effects).

Therapeutic History (detailed)  
- Preclinical systemic efficacy and selectivity: MCC950 exhibits nanomolar potency for NLRP3 in human/mouse macrophages, sparing AIM2, NLRC4, NLRP1; suppresses caspase-1 p10 and IL-1β secretion; improves disease in EAE and CAPS; PK characterized; off-targets largely excluded (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018). In atherosclerosis, MCC950 decreased plaques, macrophage content, and circulating cytokines without overt systemic organ toxicity, though cross-indication reviews caution about liver toxicity risk for the class (Zeng et al., 2021; Ortega et al., 2024b).  
- Ocular ischemic/neovascular settings: In OIR, MCC950 reversed an increased IL-1β/decreased IL-18 pattern, reduced neovascularization and leakage, and modulated endothelial/pericyte signaling; inflammasome activity localized more to macrophages than endothelium (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Sui et al., 2020c). In LCNV, MCC950 lowered IL-1β but increased lesion volume; ERG unchanged; genetic Nlrp3 loss also increased lesion size—collectively indicating a complex, possibly protective role of NLRP3 in CNV or compensation by other inflammasomes (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).  
- Dry-AMD–relevant PD and NLRP3 targeting: Intravitreal MCC950 did not protect PD retina; 100 µM reduced ERG amplitudes. Nlrp3 siRNA reduced transcript but not pathology; Nlrp3−/− protected partially; Casp1/11−/− protected robustly, pointing to caspase-1 as the better target (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- RPE in vitro/ex vivo: CRID3/IFM inhibitors (sulfonylureas, same target class as MCC950) reduced IL-1β and LDH across LMP, H₂O₂, lipofuscin/photooxidation, and P2X7 triggers in ARPE-19/pRPE and preserved ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology under photooxidation (Wang et al., 2019). Compiled 2024 data list MCC950 alongside IFM analogs as effective in IL-1α–primed RPE independent of trigger (Korhonen, 2024).  
- Genetic validations in chronic deposit models: Nlrp3 or Casp1 deletion reduces BLamD in EFEMP1 R345W mice and in aged WT, with reduced microglial activation and normalization of cytokine profiles (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). These models offer strong causal support for inflammasome targeting in GA-relevant pathology, albeit via genetic ablation rather than pharmacologic inhibition.

Expected Effect (detailed)  
In ARPE-19/pRPE assays primed with IL-1α, MCC950 should suppress NLRP3 activation triggered by:  
– LMP (Leu-Leu-OMe), where caspase-1 inhibition prevents RPE death and NLRP3 inhibitors reduce IL-1β and LDH release (Ildefonso et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019).  
– Oxidative and lipofuscin/photooxidative stress (H₂O₂, HNE-POS + blue light), where NLRP3 inhibitors significantly lower IL-1β and LDH and preserve RPE morphology ex vivo (Wang et al., 2019).  
– P2X7 activation (BzATP), a canonical AMD-relevant danger signal leading to K⁺ efflux and inflammasome assembly; selective NLRP3 inhibitors attenuate IL-1β and LDH in Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺-free conditions (Wang et al., 2019).

Because autophagy restrains inflammasome activation and removes inflammasome complexes, a reduction in NLRP3 activity may secondarily stabilize autophagic flux under stress. Yet, this remains hypothetical for MCC950 in RPE; explicit autophagy and lysosomal readouts (LC3 flux, p62, LAMP1/2, cathepsin B/D activities, lysosomal pH, galectin-3 LMP puncta) have not been detailed in the RPE inhibitor studies referenced (Celkova et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019). Therefore, while reduction of IL-1β/LDH and preservation of morphology are expected and supported, the proposed enhancement of POS clearance should be considered an untested hypothesis requiring targeted experimentation.

In vivo, efficacy expectations diverge by model:  
– Deposit/atrophy (EFEMP1 R345W, aged WT) are rational choices: genetic deletion of Nlrp3/Casp1 is protective, so MCC950 might reduce BLamD burden and retinal inflammation if adequate ocular exposure is achieved (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c).  
– Photoreceptor acute degeneration (PD) may not respond to NLRP3 inhibition and may be sensitive to dose-related toxicity, favoring downstream caspase-1 inhibition or broader inflammasome suppression (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
– Neovascular models diverge: OIR improved with MCC950; CNV worsened. Dry-AMD-focused development should avoid neovascular endpoints initially, or stratify hypotheses based on IL-1β/IL-18 balance and myeloid contribution (Sui et al., 2020a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).

Overall Evaluation  
MCC950 is a mechanistically compelling, best-in-class NLRP3 inhibitor with credible RPE-target class activity in vitro and strong genetic support for inflammasome involvement in deposit biology. However, the in vivo ocular pharmacology to date is mixed and generally unsupportive for broad dry-AMD application without further de-risking: failure and potential toxicity in PD, context-dependent effects in neovascular models, uncertain RPE expression/engagement in vivo, lack of ocular PK, and unproven restoration of autophagy/lysosomal function in RPE.

On balance, MCC950 merits continued investigation as a mechanistic probe and potential therapeutic lead for specific dry-AMD endophenotypes linked to deposit pathology and chronic inflammasome signaling—provided that the next tranche of studies addresses ocular PK/safety, cell-type exposure, and autophagy/lysosome outcomes. In parallel, downstream targeting (caspase-1) should be benchmarked given superior genetic protection and potential coverage of multiple inflammasome sensors. If MCC950 cannot meet ocular exposure and safety requirements, alternative delivery (e.g., sustained-release nanoparticles) or next-generation NLRP3 inhibitors with better ocular PK and safety profiles may be required (Sun et al., 2023; Ortega et al., 2024b).

In summary, MCC950 has plausible potential for dry AMD if—and only if— its ocular pharmacology can be tuned to the appropriate disease biology: chronic deposit/atrophy with documented inflammasome involvement, sufficient drug exposure at RPE/subretinal myeloid compartments, and a safety margin that avoids the functional liabilities observed at higher intravitreal doses in PD. Without these, the probability of technical success remains low relative to downstream inflammasome targets.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SBI-0206965 is a synthetic small molecule inhibitor that belongs to the class of pyrimidine analogs specifically designed to target the ULK1 (Unc-51-like autophagy-activating kinase 1) enzyme and, to a lesser extent, its paralog ULK2. This compound was developed via a targeted, medicinal chemistry approach using principles of structure–activity relationship (SAR) optimization that originally emerged from modifications of focal adhesion kinase (FAK) inhibitor scaffolds, eventually identifying a pyrimidine core that confers selectivity toward ULK1 kinase activity (Kocak et al., 2022). Commercially available from Sigma-Aldrich (Cat. No. SML1783), SBI-0206965 has been primarily utilized as a tool compound to dissect the roles of ULK1 in autophagy regulation. Compounds of this class have generally been employed in preclinical studies to probe autophagy pathways—in cancer models, for example—to determine the role of autophagy in cellular survival and stress responses. The chemical probe is further characterized by its ability to interfere with autophagy initiation processes, placing it within the emerging category of autophagy modulators intended to refine cellular clearance mechanisms rather than completely abrogate them (Kocak et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
The pharmacological activity of SBI-0206965 has primarily been established in cancer research and neurodegenerative models, where its ability to inhibit ULK1-mediated autophagy is used to sensitize tumor cells to chemotherapy and to protect neurons from acute degenerative stress. For instance, in non–small cell lung cancer cells, SBI-0206965 has been shown to reduce autophagic flux and promote apoptotic cell death when combined with other chemotherapeutic agents (Limpert et al., 2018). Moreover, preclinical studies using retinal ganglion cell models have demonstrated that intravitreal injection of higher concentrations (e.g., 50 µM) of SBI-0206965 can reduce acute axonal degeneration and modify autophagy markers, suggesting that autophagy modulation might translate to neuroprotective outcomes in ocular tissues (Sundermeyer, 2022). Despite these promising results in models of cancer and neuronal injury, there have been no dedicated studies or clinical trials assessing the use of SBI-0206965 specifically for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or related retinal diseases. Nonetheless, foundational evidence supports the concept that autophagy dysregulation, particularly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), contributes to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, providing a rationale for exploring autophagy regulators like SBI-0206965 in this context (Blasiak et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SBI-0206965 functions by competitively inhibiting ULK1 kinase activity, which is a critical initiating event in the canonical autophagy pathway. Under physiological conditions, ULK1 forms a complex with adaptor proteins ATG13, FIP200, and ATG101 to trigger autophagosome formation by promoting the phosphorylation of downstream targets such as Beclin-1 and VPS34; these events are essential for membrane nucleation and the subsequent formation of autophagic vesicles (Intartaglia et al., 2022). SBI-0206965 achieves an inhibitory effect on ULK1 with a biochemical IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range (approximately 108 nM for ULK1 and 711 nM for ULK2), thereby impairing the phosphorylation cascade that would normally lead to the formation of autophagosomes (Kocak et al., 2022). It is noteworthy that the inhibition of ULK1 by SBI-0206965 has been reported to result in decreased phosphorylation of key autophagy regulators, alongside a reduction in LC3-positive puncta and concomitant increases in the autophagic adaptor molecule p62, confirming the compound’s ability to attenuate canonical autophagy (Pinelli et al., 2025; Limpert et al., 2018). Importantly, emerging evidence in RPE cells suggests that, while canonical autophagy is ULK1-dependent, the noncanonical process known as LC3-associated phagocytosis (LAP) is largely independent of ULK1. This mechanistic divergence forms the basis of the hypothesis that low-dose ULK1 inhibition with SBI-0206965 could selectively modulate the balance between bulk autophagy and LAP, favoring the latter—a process known to be integral for the efficient degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in RPE cells (Liton et al., 2023; Jain et al., 2023). However, it is also crucial to mention that the compound exhibits off-target inhibition on kinases such as FAK and AMPK, which could potentially modify additional cellular signaling pathways involved in autophagy and cell survival (Karmacharya & Jung, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis posits that low-dose administration of SBI-0206965 in RPE cells will induce a selective modulation in autophagy initiation. Specifically, the drug is expected to downregulate the canonical autophagy pathway sufficiently to reduce potential overactivation, which may lead to cell stress or death, while simultaneously sparing or even indirectly promoting LC3-associated phagocytosis (LAP)—a noncanonical autophagy process crucial for phagolysosomal fusion and efficient POS degradation. RPE cells naturally exhibit high rates of autophagy due to the daily phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor outer segments; indeed, impaired autophagy in these cells has been directly linked to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, characterized by the accumulation of undigested cellular material and subsequent drusen formation (Pinelli et al., 2023; Blasiak et al., 2025). By partially inhibiting ULK1 activity, SBI-0206965 at submicromolar concentrations is hypothesized to reduce excessive bulk autophagy without compromising the LC3 recruitment to phagosomes—a hallmark of LAP—which is essential for maintaining the continuous renewal of photoreceptor components (Blasiak et al., 2024; Liton et al., 2023). In practical assay systems using cultured RPE cells, one would anticipate observing an increase in markers associated with LAP (such as enhanced LC3 lipidation on phagosomes and improved lysosomal fusion) alongside a controlled, rather than complete, suppression of canonical autophagy markers. Such an outcome would support enhanced POS degradation, ultimately alleviating one of the critical pathogenic processes in dry AMD. It is also expected that preserved or enhanced LAP activity would diminish the accumulation of toxic metabolites and lipofuscin, thereby contributing to improved retinal function and slowed disease progression (Limpert et al., 2018; Pinelli et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
SBI-0206965 presents several compelling advantages as a candidate for modulating autophagy in the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration. Its well-characterized mechanism of action as a ULK1 inhibitor allows for targeted interference with a key early step in canonical autophagy—an approach that has proven valuable in preclinical cancer models and, more recently, in studies addressing neuronal injury in the retina (Kocak et al., 2022; Sundermeyer, 2022). The hypothesis that low-dose SBI-0206965 can shift the cellular autophagy balance toward favoring LC3-associated phagocytosis (LAP) is particularly innovative, given that LAP is instrumental in the efficient degradation of photoreceptor outer segments by RPE cells. This mechanistic nuance, wherein canonical autophagy is dampened while LAP remains active due to its ULK1 independence, holds significant promise for restoring proper phagocytic and degradative functions in RPE cells—a process that is critically disrupted in dry AMD (Pinelli et al., 2023; Liton et al., 2023).

Despite these strengths, several challenges must be acknowledged. First, the off-target effects of SBI-0206965 on kinases such as FAK, AMPK, NUAK1, and MLK1 raise concerns regarding the potential for unintended modulation of other signaling pathways. Such off-target activities could compromise RPE cell viability or alter cellular stress responses that are vital for maintaining retinal homeostasis (Karmacharya & Jung, 2023). Second, while its potency as a ULK1 inhibitor is adequate for investigational use (with an IC₅₀ for ULK1 around 108 nM), newer and more selective ULK1 inhibitors have since been developed, and SBI-0206965 may not represent the most optimal chemical probe in terms of specificity and potency (Martin et al., 2018). Third, most of the existing data on SBI-0206965 derives from cancer cells and neuronal models, and there is a notable lack of direct experimental evidence that confirms its efficacy or safety in RPE cells or animal models of dry AMD. This gap underscores the necessity for carefully designed in vitro studies using RPE lines and subsequent in vivo AMD models to determine the appropriate dosing window that achieves the desired modulation of autophagy without detrimental suppression of essential bulk autophagy processes (Blasiak et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). Additionally, the balance between inhibiting canonical autophagy and preserving LAP is delicately poised; over-inhibition of ULK1 might inadvertently impair necessary degradation pathways, potentially exacerbating cellular dysfunction rather than mitigating it (Pinelli et al., 2025; Si et al., 2023).

Nevertheless, the underlying rationale for repurposing SBI-0206965 in dry AMD is scientifically grounded. Autophagy dysfunction in RPE cells is a well-documented contributor to the progression of dry AMD, and therapeutically modulating this process represents a novel strategy with the potential to alleviate the accumulation of toxic cellular debris and drusen formation. Given that RPE cells face an immense phagocytic burden and are highly sensitive to disruptions in autophagic flux, agents that can fine-tune autophagy—as opposed to completely inhibiting it—are highly desirable. SBI-0206965, when employed at carefully titrated low doses, might provide the necessary modulation to reduce excessive canonical autophagy, thereby preventing the overaccumulation of autophagic vacuoles, while simultaneously preserving or even enhancing LC3-associated phagocytosis that is crucial for processing endogenous waste material (Pinelli et al., 2023; Sundermeyer, 2022; Blasiak et al., 2025).

In summary, SBI-0206965 exhibits considerable promise as an autophagy modulator with potential applications in the treatment of dry AMD due to its targeted inhibition of ULK1, a pathway central to canonical autophagy regulation in RPE cells. The hypothesis that low-dose administration can favorably shift the autophagic balance toward LAP, thereby improving POS degradation while preventing deleterious overactivation of bulk autophagy, is mechanistically sound and aligns with current understandings of RPE cell biology in AMD pathogenesis. However, the candidate’s moderate potency, documented off-target effects, and the paucity of data in ocular models warrant cautious optimism. Further investigation is required, including optimization of dosing strategies and rigorous assessment in preclinical RPE and AMD models, to fully ascertain the therapeutic window and clinical translatability of SBI-0206965 for dry AMD. Overall, while the candidate is not without its limitations, the innovative therapeutic approach it represents—targeted modulation of autophagy to enhance noncanonical phagocytic processes in RPE cells—merits continued exploration and could ultimately contribute to the development of a novel treatment strategy for dry age‐related macular degeneration (Kocak et al., 2022; Karmacharya & Jung, 2023; Sundermeyer, 2022; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin is a naturally derived macrolide initially isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus and belongs to the class of mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) inhibitors. This compound, originally discovered for its immunosuppressive properties, has evolved into a prominent therapeutic candidate across several fields including oncology, immunology, and neurodegeneration. Its chemical derivation and structural complexity allow for potent and selective inhibition of the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1). Rapamycin is widely used in clinical settings as an immunosuppressant following organ transplantation and has been repurposed for other indications based on its ability to modulate intracellular signaling pathways that regulate cellular growth, survival, and autophagy. As such, its potential application in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on a body of work indicating that targeting mTORC1 can restore autophagic and lysosomal function in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—a crucial factor given that RPE dysfunction is central to AMD pathogenesis (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, rapamycin has been extensively used and investigated in various clinical and preclinical settings. Its initial clinical use as an immunosuppressive agent in organ transplant patients laid the groundwork for understanding its mechanisms of action and safety profile in humans. Beyond its immunosuppressive applications, rapamycin has been evaluated for its anti-proliferative effects in several types of cancer and for its capability to extend lifespan in model organisms; these studies underscore the drug’s pleiotropic effects on cellular metabolism and autophagy. Specifically regarding ocular therapeutics, preclinical studies on retinal degenerative diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa and glaucoma have demonstrated that mTOR modulation by rapamycin can exert neuroprotective properties in retinal tissues (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). In the realm of AMD, several investigations have focused on the role of autophagy and lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in RPE cells, where rapamycin has been shown to promote autophagy and decrease the buildup of toxic aggregates, such as lipofuscin (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical studies and safety evaluations—in particular, intravitreal injections in non-human primates—have provided encouraging data regarding the ocular safety profile of rapamycin, thus supporting its further exploration as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, rapamycin exerts its effects by binding to the intracellular receptor FKBP12 (FK506-binding protein 12). This drug–FKBP12 complex then interacts with mTORC1, leading to its allosteric inhibition. Under normal anabolic conditions, active mTORC1 phosphorylates several downstream targets, including the transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is sequestered in the cytosol in its phosphorylated state, thus preventing the transcription of genes associated with lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. When rapamycin inhibits mTORC1, the phosphorylation of TFEB is reduced, permitting its nuclear translocation. Once inside the nucleus, TFEB initiates the transcription of numerous genes involved in autophagy and lysosomal function, thereby enhancing the cell’s capacity to degrade and recycle cellular debris such as accumulated photoreceptor outer segments (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium, mTORC1 normally integrates growth factor signals, nutrient availability, and stress responses to tightly regulate cellular homeostasis. The inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin thus releases the “brake” on autophagy, as evidenced by increased expression of autophagic markers such as LC3-II and lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1. This cascading effect leads to an enhanced intracellular clearance system (phagolysosomal flux), which is particularly critical for RPE cells that are responsible for the daily degradation of shed POS. Several studies have demonstrated that rapamycin-treated RPE cells exhibit improved POS degradation, a reduction in lipofuscin-like granules, and overall restoration of lysosomal function (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, the molecular signatures observed in rapamycin-treated cells mimic those seen under conditions of caloric restriction, further supporting the notion that mTORC1 inhibition can activate protective autophagic pathways (Davis, 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). This advanced understanding of rapamycin’s mechanism of action provides a compelling rationale for its application in dry AMD, where the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and dysregulated autophagy are key pathological features (Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of rapamycin in dry AMD is that its inhibition of mTORC1 will lead to the activation of TFEB by reducing its cytosolic phosphorylation state, thereby promoting nuclear translocation. In iPSC-derived RPE models, this induction of TFEB activity is expected to upregulate a host of autophagy and lysosomal genes, which in turn should enhance the cellular degradation of photoreceptor outer segments—an essential process in maintaining retinal homeostasis (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025). Accordingly, the anticipated in vitro effects upon rapamycin treatment include a robust increase in autophagic flux evidenced by elevated levels of LC3-II and LAMP1, paired with improved processing and clearance of POS debris. This effect is crucial because impaired clearance mechanisms contribute to the accumulation of lipofuscin and other cellular waste materials in RPE cells, both of which are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Falcão et al., 2024).

Supporting this expected outcome are observations from previous studies where rapamycin has been associated with a reduction in autofluorescent granules and a restoration of normal cellular clearance dynamics in RPE cells (Falcão et al., 2024). Additionally, safety assessments performed through intravitreal administration in non-human primates have demonstrated that rapamycin can be delivered to the retina with minimal adverse events, thereby underpinning its feasibility for clinical translation (Falcão et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2022). Importantly, the hypothesis that rapamycin can act at IC₅₀ values as low as approximately 0.1 nM in RPE cells further reinforces the potential sensitivity and efficacy of this candidate in modulating the pathway of interest. Given the expression of mTOR, TFEB, LC3, and LAMP1 in RPE cells—and the established role of these proteins in the autophagic and lysosomal clearance of POS—the expected improvement in autophagic turnover should directly translate into enhanced cell function and potentially mitigate the progression of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2022; Intartaglia et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
Rapamycin emerges as a robust and mechanistically sound therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its established ability to inhibit mTORC1 and consequently activate autophagy and lysosomal gene expression through TFEB nuclear translocation. One of the major strengths of this candidate lies in the well-characterized molecular mechanism that connects mTORC1 inhibition with enhanced clearance of POS debris—a process that is fundamentally disrupted in dry AMD. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence, ranging from biochemical assays that show increased LC3-II and LAMP1 expression in rapamycin-treated RPE cells to preclinical safety data in non-human primates, bolsters confidence in its potential utility (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

Furthermore, the multifaceted benefits of mTORC1 inhibition extend beyond autophagy induction; rapamycin also offers neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects, both of which are advantageous in the treatment of retinal degenerative diseases (Chang et al., 2022). The leverage of TFEB activation not only addresses the aberrant accumulation of toxic cellular debris but may also promote a broader upregulation of lysosomal biogenesis, thereby preempting further functional decline of RPE cells. These properties make rapamycin a strong candidate for mitigating early events in AMD pathogenesis, particularly in the context of experimental iPSC-RPE models where enhanced phagocytic capacity can be directly measured.

Nevertheless, several challenges and potential weaknesses require careful consideration. Despite its promising mechanism and preclinical rationale, clinical trials evaluating rapamycin in the context of ocular diseases have yielded mixed results, with some studies documenting only marginal improvements in visual function and others noting issues related to the drug’s solubility and delivery (Marchesi et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022). In advanced AMD, where the disease pathology is more complex and multifactorial, rapamycin’s efficacy might be limited, and there is a need for precise dosing strategies to balance mTORC1 inhibition with the preservation of physiological mTOR functions that are crucial for RPE cell survival (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). Additionally, the potential for off-target effects or immunosuppressive consequences linked to systemic exposure—although minimized by intravitreal delivery—necessitates further investigation into long-term safety profiles (Wang et al., 2022).

Another potential limitation is the inherent complexity of autophagy regulation in the RPE, which can be influenced by factors such as oxidative stress, metabolic dysfunction, and age-related changes in lysosomal function. While rapamycin is effective in reactivating autophagic pathways under controlled experimental settings, its impact within the pathogenic environment of a diseased retina, particularly if inflammatory processes are simultaneously active, may be less predictable (Davis, 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, the therapeutic window for achieving beneficial rapamycin concentrations without incurring adverse events is not yet fully defined, underscoring the importance of pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic studies specifically tailored to ocular tissues (Falcão et al., 2024).

Taken together, the current body of evidence suggests that rapamycin’s capacity to restore autophagic homeostasis in RPE cells represents a solid mechanistic foundation for its use in dry AMD. Its ability to upregulate autophagy and lysosomal function through TFEB activation directly addresses known defects in the clearance pathways of RPE cells—a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Moreover, the safety data from preclinical intravitreal delivery studies provide additional incentive to advance this candidate further along the translational pipeline. However, given the mixed outcomes observed in some clinical contexts and the challenges related to drug formulation and optimal dosing, further comprehensive studies are warranted to clarify its efficacy in early versus advanced stages of AMD (Mei et al., 2022).

In conclusion, rapamycin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD shows significant promise from both a mechanistic and translational standpoint. Its well-documented ability to inhibit mTORC1, thereby releasing TFEB and ramping up autophagic and lysosomal gene expression, positions it uniquely to tackle the underpinnings of RPE dysfunction characteristic of dry AMD. While preclinical data support its efficacy and safety with intravitreal administration in non-human primates, challenges remain regarding its formulation, potential off-target effects, and the delineation of its therapeutic window in human subjects. Consequently, while rapamycin’s molecular mechanism and early experimental results are highly encouraging, further studies—especially those that integrate pharmacokinetic profiling, dose optimization, and long-term outcome measurements in relevant in vivo models—are essential before definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding its clinical utility for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Si et al., 2023).

Overall, the strengths of rapamycin include its robust and well-characterized action on mTORC1, its downstream activation of autophagic and lysosomal pathways via TFEB, and supportive preclinical safety data in ocular models. In contrast, its weaknesses lie in the variable efficacy observed in clinical studies, formulation challenges due to low solubility, and the need for careful dosing to avoid potential adverse effects related to systemic immunosuppression. These considerations collectively argue for the continued investigation of rapamycin as a therapeutic option for dry AMD with a focus on optimizing delivery strategies and characterizing its long-term impact on retinal structure and function (Wang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Pyrrolidine dithiocarbamate (PDTC) is a synthetic compound that belongs to the dithiocarbamate class, a group of molecules originally derived from the reaction of secondary or tertiary amines with carbon disulfide under alkaline conditions. PDTC is commercially available (for example, from Sigma-Aldrich, Cat. No. 239,804) and has been widely used in experimental research due to its multifunctional properties. Initially, dithiocarbamate compounds were recognized for their potent antioxidant capacities and metal chelation abilities; however, subsequent research identified PDTC as one of the most potent and specific inhibitors of nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), with its inhibitory action shown to be independent of its antioxidant effects (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). The compound’s structure, featuring both a pyrrolidine ring and dithiocarbamate moiety, imbues it with the ability to bind metal ions such as Zn²⁺ and modulate redox signaling pathways. In terms of therapeutic classification, PDTC is considered a research tool and a candidate for repurposing in inflammatory and neoplastic diseases, and its class has been investigated extensively over the past decades for applications in cancer therapy, inflammatory disorders, and experimental models of ocular disease (Kwak et al., 2008; Morais et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
The dithiocarbamate class, and PDTC in particular, has a rich history in biomedical research. PDTC has been employed primarily as an experimental NF-κB inhibitor in various paradigms, ranging from cancer models to inflammatory diseases. In the realm of oncology, PDTC has been shown to induce cell death in multiple cancer cell lines including breast, colon, gastric, and prostate cancers by modulating pathways related to cell survival and apoptosis (Morais et al., 2009). Its ability to chelate metal ions and act as a radical scavenger has also been exploited in studies examining cytoprotective effects in liver injury and neurodegenerative conditions (Shin et al., 2023). Notably, PDTC has been studied in ocular models; for example, its use in experimental endotoxin-induced uveitis in Lewis rats provided evidence of its anti-inflammatory activity and ocular safety profile (Kanai et al., 2010). While there is no record of PDTC having been directly used in clinical trials for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), its application in related ocular inflammatory conditions, such as autoimmune anterior uveitis and retinal neovascularization, offers a promising translational bridge to dry AMD (Morais et al., 2009). In several studies of retinal diseases, PDTC has been shown to modulate angiogenic factors and inflammatory cytokine profiles, indicating its potential utility in conditions where inflammation plays a key pathogenic role (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). Its established use in experimental models, combined with evidence of a favorable safety profile in ocular applications, makes PDTC an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, especially given the emerging understanding of the role of chronic inflammation and NF-κB activation in this degenerative disease (Shin et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
PDTC’s therapeutic potential largely derives from its robust inhibition of NF-κB activation. Under typical conditions, NF-κB is sequestered in the cytoplasm by inhibitory proteins known as IκBs. Upon stimulation by pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α or exposure to oxidative stress, the IκB proteins are phosphorylated, ubiquitinated, and degraded, releasing NF-κB to translocate to the nucleus where it drives the expression of numerous genes involved in inflammatory responses, cell survival, and immune regulation (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). PDTC interferes with this pathway by preventing the phosphorylation and consequent degradation of IκB, thereby keeping NF-κB in its inactive, cytoplasmic state (Kwak et al., 2008). In addition to this canonical inhibition, PDTC is also known to function as a metal ion chelator and a free radical scavenger, and studies have demonstrated that its chelating capability is crucial to its mechanism (Shin et al., 2023). The compound’s ability to chelate zinc ions, which are essential cofactors for the DNA-binding activity of NF-κB, may further contribute to its inhibitory effects on NF-κB-mediated transcription. This property is particularly relevant in the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) physiology; in the hypothesis being considered, PDTC is proposed to chelate Zn²⁺ in RPE cells, thereby impairing NF-κB activation. As NF-κB is known to downregulate genes such as MERTK—a receptor tyrosine kinase critical for the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—and lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, inhibition of NF-κB by PDTC would be expected to restore their expression (Morais et al., 2009). Moreover, beyond simple inhibition of NF-κB nuclear translocation, PDTC has been observed to induce the expression of endogenous antioxidants such as superoxide dismutase and heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) through NF-κB–independent pathways, suggesting that the compound can modulate multiple signaling cascades concurrently (Shin et al., 2023). Collectively, these molecular actions position PDTC as a multifaceted inhibitor of inflammatory signaling, where both the blockade of NF-κB translocation and the chelation of essential metal ions converge to mitigate inflammation-induced cellular dysfunction (Shin et al., 2023; Sui et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed application for dry AMD, the hypothesis is that PDTC will chelate Zn²⁺ and thereby inhibit NF-κB activation in RPE cells. In dry AMD, chronic inflammation is believed to play a crucial role in the downregulation of key proteins involved in phagocytosis and lysosomal function, notably MERTK and cathepsin D. TNF-α—a pro-inflammatory cytokine that robustly activates the NF-κB pathway—is known to downregulate the expression of MERTK and lysosomal genes in ARPE-19 cells, a commonly used model of RPE function (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). By inhibiting NF-κB activation, PDTC is expected to reverse the repressive effects of TNF-α, thereby restoring the normal expression levels of MERTK and cathepsin D. This restoration is anticipated to improve the ingestion and processing of POS, a critical function of RPE cells that is compromised in dry AMD. Improved POS clearance would reduce the accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin, which are hallmarks of RPE dysfunction and contribute to disease progression (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). Additionally, PDTC’s capacity to inhibit NF-κB not only suppresses the transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-6, IL-8, and GM-CSF, but may also promote a shift in the balance of macrophage polarization in the retinal microenvironment. For instance, a reduction in NF-κB–mediated inflammatory signaling has been linked to a decreased abundance of M1-type (pro-inflammatory) macrophages and a corresponding increase in M2-type (anti-inflammatory or tissue repair) macrophages, which would further support retinal homeostasis and repair mechanisms (Sui et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2005). Expression analyses in various studies have confirmed that RPE cells exhibit active NF-κB signaling under inflammatory stress and that inhibition of NF-κB can lead to upregulation of phagocytic receptors and lysosomal enzymes, which are essential for POS turnover (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). Thus, in the described assay using TNF-α–treated ARPE-19 cells, PDTC is expected to counteract the deleterious inflammatory signaling, normalizing the expression of MERTK and cathepsin D, and ultimately improving the functional capacity of the RPE to clear photoreceptor debris (Morais et al., 2009).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of PDTC for dry AMD represents a promising and innovative approach rooted in well-established molecular pharmacology. One of the major strengths of PDTC is its dual mode of action: it is a potent inhibitor of NF-κB, preventing the transcriptional activation of a wide array of pro-inflammatory and cell stress genes, and it also possesses metal chelation properties, which may further enhance its ability to disrupt the pathological signaling cascades in RPE cells (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). The experimental evidence from animal models of ocular inflammation—such as endotoxin-induced uveitis—demonstrates that PDTC can be administered in ocular contexts with a tolerable safety profile, thereby supporting the feasibility of translating these findings to the treatment of dry AMD (Kanai et al., 2010). From a biochemical perspective, the strategy of chelating Zn²⁺ to inhibit NF-κB activation is compelling, particularly in view of the fact that zinc ions are embedded in the structure of NF-κB that is essential for its binding to DNA. In RPE cells, which are subject to continuous oxidative and inflammatory stress in dry AMD, the ability of PDTC to sequester Zn²⁺ may provide a specific molecular intervention point. This intervention could reverse NF-κB–mediated downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D, thereby improving POS uptake and degradation—a critical process that is disrupted in AMD and contributes to the accumulation of toxic debris (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023).

However, there are weaknesses and potential challenges associated with this therapeutic strategy. Although preclinical models of uveitis and retinal neovascularization have shown PDTC’s efficacy in reducing inflammatory markers and preserving tissue structure, there is still a significant gap in direct evidence for its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD. The proposed mechanism—involving restoration of phagocytic receptor and lysosomal gene expression by NF-κB inhibition—has been observed in vitro in ARPE-19 cells, yet extensive in vivo validation in models that recapitulate the complex pathology of dry AMD is lacking (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). Moreover, the specificity of PDTC’s metal chelation in the retinal environment remains uncertain. While Zn²⁺ chelation is a plausible mechanism, other divalent metal ions are present in the retina, and off-target chelation could potentially disrupt essential metalloprotein functions. This necessitates further biochemical studies to dissect the selectivity of PDTC’s chelating action in the RPE (Shin et al., 2023; Morais et al., 2009).

Another potential concern is related to dosing and toxicity. Several studies have indicated that PDTC can exert cytotoxic effects in endothelial cells and other cell types when administered at high concentrations or prolonged exposure periods, even though its anti-inflammatory effects are observed at lower doses (Morais et al., 2009). While ocular models such as those in experimental uveitis have shown acceptable tolerability, the long-term implications of PDTC administration in the context of a chronic condition like dry AMD require careful evaluation. It will be essential to optimize dosing regimens that confer sufficient NF-κB inhibition without incurring cytotoxicity, particularly given that RPE cells are critical for retinal integrity and visual function (Kanai et al., 2010; Morais et al., 2009).

Furthermore, the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD—spanning oxidative stress, inflammation, and impaired lipid metabolism—raises the possibility that a single agent such as PDTC may not be sufficient as a standalone therapy. Combination approaches that integrate PDTC with agents targeting complementary pathways (for example, those modulating complement activation or enhancing endogenous antioxidant defenses) might be necessary to achieve a clinically meaningful impact (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). In addition, while PDTC has been robustly characterized as an NF-κB inhibitor, the literature suggests that its effects on other signaling pathways (such as those involving AP-1 or STAT family members) are less well defined. Unintended modulation of these additional pathways could potentially lead to undesirable effects that need to be accounted for in a comprehensive safety evaluation (Shin et al., 2023; Sui et al., 2020).

In conclusion, PDTC exhibits many attributes that support its consideration as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its well-documented ability to inhibit NF-κB activation—combined with its metal chelation and antioxidant properties—addresses key pathological mechanisms underlying chronic inflammation and impaired phagocytic function in the RPE. Preclinical data from ocular inflammation models lend further credence to its potential translational application. Nevertheless, significant challenges remain, including the need for rigorous in vivo studies to verify restoration of MERTK and lysosomal gene expression, careful titration of dosing to avoid cytotoxicity, and detailed characterization of its chelation selectivity within the intricate retinal milieu. Future investigations should aim to clarify these mechanistic details and evaluate the long-term safety and efficacy of PDTC in relevant animal models of dry AMD before moving toward clinical trials. Overall, PDTC represents a promising candidate with a strong scientific rationale and a history of multifaceted use in experimental settings; however, a cautious and methodical progression through preclinical validation is warranted to fully assess its suitability for addressing the unmet therapeutic needs in dry AMD (Kwak et al., 2008; Kanai et al., 2010; Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023; Sui et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2005).
