Iptacopan (LNP023) is a rationally designed, low–molecular-weight small molecule that selectively inhibits complement factor B (FB), the essential catalytic subunit of the alternative pathway (AP) C3/C5 convertases C3bBb and C3bBbC3b on activating surfaces (including stressed RPE) and within the amplification loop of complement activation (C3 → C3b → C3 convertase) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 4–6). Medicinal-chemistry optimization from an early micromolar FB inhibitor hit (a naphthalene-dihydro-imidazole amine) introduced an indole to occupy the S1 pocket and a piperidine scaffold engaging the S3/non-primed region with a benzoic acid–mediated H-bond network, yielding iptacopan with high potency and selectivity for FB (crystallographically confirmed) (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 10–13; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Iptacopan binds the catalytic serine-protease active site within the Bb subunit of FB—structural analyses show its indole and piperidine moieties seated in S1/S3, forming key hydrogen bonds within the catalytic domain, with the active-site triad (His–Asp–Ser) located in proximity; binding has been explicitly mapped to the catalytic site in Bb and shown to block substrate processing by the AP convertase (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6, 8–10).

Class and precedent: Iptacopan is an oral, proximal complement/AP inhibitor; this class has delivered robust target engagement and clinical benefit in multiple complement-driven diseases (e.g., PNH, C3G, IgAN), establishing translational viability for systemic small-molecule blockade of AP amplification in human disease (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Oral administration achieves rapid systemic exposure (Tmax ≈ 2 hours) with dose-dependent AP suppression and sustained steady-state inhibition at 200 mg twice daily in clinical studies, supporting convenient outpatient dosing with on-target PD (reduced plasma Bb and urinary sC5b-9) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Preclinically, systemic iptacopan potently blocks LPS-induced AP activation in mice in both plasma and eye tissues, indicating ocular target engagement after oral dosing (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). Collectively, synthesis, mechanistic selectivity, and clinical-class performance position iptacopan as a well-characterized, orally bioavailable FB inhibitor suited for indications where local AP amplification contributes to pathology, including dry AMD (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).

Therapeutic History  
- Non-ocular indications and clinical pharmacology. In early-phase clinical studies, iptacopan demonstrated rapid absorption (peak plasma concentration at ~2 hours), favorable tolerability, and dose-dependent inhibition of AP activity; sustained maximal inhibition was reported at 200 mg twice daily, the regimen advanced into multiple phase 2 trials (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Across PNH and AP-driven renal diseases (C3G, IgAN), iptacopan showed robust target engagement and clinical activity: reductions in plasma Bb and urinary sC5b-9, reductions in plasma C3 (in many patients after months), kidney-pathology improvements (reduced glomerular C3 deposition), and meaningful efficacy outcomes (e.g., proteinuria reductions in C3G/IgAN; hemoglobin improvements and transfusion-free status in PNH) with generally favorable safety profiles and no serious infections in the cited trials (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Iptacopan has received regulatory approvals (including an accelerated approval for IgAN) and late-stage development status for multiple indications, validating systemic AP inhibition with this agent (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8).  
- AMD program. A randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial in early/intermediate AMD is ongoing (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022), designed to test whether oral iptacopan prevents conversion to iRORA or late AMD over 24 months, with masked multimodal imaging and planned plasma trough PK by LC–MS; vaccinations for encapsulated organisms are required per complement-inhibition class risk management (no results are available in the excerpt) (“A Masked, Placebo-controlled Study to Assess Iptacopan in Age-related Macular Degeneration,” 2022). Reviews place iptacopan among oral FB inhibitors under evaluation for atrophic AMD as an alternative to intravitreal complement blockade, motivated by the blood–retina barrier and the burden of injections; however, the provided material contains no AMD efficacy outcomes for iptacopan (Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 8–9; Hammadi et al., 2023, pp. 30–31; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
- Ocular-relevant preclinical context. Although iptacopan-specific dry-AMD model data are not provided, two lines of evidence are directly relevant: (1) in the Efemp1 R345W knock-in mouse (an RPE proteostasis model with AMD-like basal deposits), genetic Cfb deletion abolished AP activation and eliminated sub-RPE deposits, while oral pharmacologic FB blockade (with the small molecule DB-82-CB77) reduced deposits by 65% in females and reversed disease-associated pathway perturbations (UPR/inflammation upregulation and mitochondrial repression) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10); (2) systemic iptacopan blocks AP activation in eye tissue in LPS-challenged mice, supporting oral delivery as a viable route to ocular target engagement, though iptacopan-specific AMD-model efficacy is not shown in the provided excerpts (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Complement biology and lysosomal/autophagy pathology in RPE. In CFH Y402H high-risk iPSC-RPE, increased C3 turnover and lysosomal deposition of C5b-9 drive lysosomal swelling, membrane damage, Cathepsin D leakage to sub-RPE deposits, and reduced lysosomal function; blocking C3 with the compstatin analogue Cp40 reverses these phenotypes, restoring lysosomal number/size/function and lowering complement deposition (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13). While these data establish that proximal complement blockade can normalize lysosomal/autophagy dysfunction in high-risk RPE, the excerpts do not directly test FB/AP inhibitors in this RPE system; thus, extrapolation to iptacopan remains mechanistic rather than empirically proven in the provided sources (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 7–13).

Mechanism of Action  
- Biochemical target and binding mode. FB is an abundant plasma glycoprotein (~0.2–0.4 mg/mL; ~2–3 μM) unique to the AP and, upon binding to C3b, is cleaved by factor D into Ba and Bb; Bb contains a VWA domain, MIDAS motif, and a serine-protease domain that provides the catalytic site for AP C3/C5 convertases on C3b-bearing surfaces (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6). Iptacopan binds the catalytic site of Bb in the S1/S3 pockets with a defined hydrogen-bonding network, directly inhibiting the proteolytic activity of the AP convertase and thereby blocking AP-mediated C3/C5 processing (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- Potency, selectivity, and functional inhibition. Iptacopan exhibits an enzymatic IC₅₀ ≈ 0.01 μM against FB and inhibits AP-induced C5b-9 formation in 50% human serum with IC₅₀ ≈ 0.13 μM; it prevents C3 deposition and complement-mediated lysis of PNH erythrocytes with IC₅₀ ≈ 0.4 μM and shows high selectivity over factor D and classical/lectin pathway activity in broad panels (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Alternative affinity reporting (K_D ≈ 0.0079 mM) has been noted in one excerpt, but across structural/functional assays the compound consistently behaves as a highly potent and selective FB catalytic-site inhibitor (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 8–10).  
- Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics relevant to target engagement. Clinically, iptacopan is rapidly absorbed (Tmax ~ 2 hours), with strong steady-state AP inhibition at 200 mg twice daily; pharmacodynamic readouts demonstrate reduced circulating Bb and reduced urinary sC5b-9, consistent with systemic and tissue-level AP suppression (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). While precise human half-life and oral bioavailability values are not provided in the excerpts, iptacopan is described as orally bioavailable with a shorter half-life than antibodies, enabling relatively rapid restoration of AP function after washout—an attribute that informs adherence requirements and infection risk mitigation (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–11). Factor B itself has a long plasma half-life (30–70 h) and high abundance; iptacopan’s high affinity and mechanism allow sustained convertase inhibition because only newly synthesized FB needs to be neutralized at steady state for continued pathway blockade (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- Ocular target engagement. In mice, systemic administration of iptacopan potently blocks LPS-induced complement activation in both plasma and eye tissues, implying that oral dosing can achieve pharmacologically active exposure to ocular compartments, at least under inflammatory conditions (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). In the Efemp1 R345W model, ocular AP activation is local (iC3b and Ba ≈ 2× in eye, not in plasma), aligning with a need for ocular engagement; although iptacopan’s ocular concentration-time profile in humans is not provided, the preclinical PD findings and the AMD phase 2 trial design together support the translational intent to suppress ocular AP activity via oral dosing (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Genetic and disease-mechanism validation. FB is genetically and mechanistically implicated in AMD pathogenesis; protective low-activity variants (e.g., R32Q) associate with reduced AMD risk, and AP dysregulation is a central pathogenic thread in AMD biology (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6). In an RPE proteostasis model (Efemp1 R345W), Cfb deletion abolishes AP activation and prevents sub-RPE deposit formation; pharmacologic FB suppression reduces deposit burden and reverses multiple mutation-associated pathway perturbations (UPR, immune/complement signatures, mitochondrial repression), supporting causal linkage between AP activity and RPE/Bruch’s membrane pathology (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10).  
- Comparison to other complement nodes in AMD models. Complement C3 blockade (Cp40) in CFH Y402H high-risk iPSC-RPE rescues lysosomal structure and function, reduces C3b and C5b-9 deposition (including lysosomal MAC), and diminishes drusen-like phenotypes, demonstrating that proximal complement suppression can reverse RPE degradative defects; this provides a mechanistic bridge to AP/FB inhibition, which is expected to decrease upstream C3 turnover and downstream MAC burden by curtailing the amplification loop, though FB-specific rescue of lysosomal function was not directly tested in that study (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).

Expected Effect  
- In vitro RPE assays and readouts. Based on the AP mechanism and the CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE data with C3 inhibition, iptacopan is expected to reduce AP convertase activity on RPE surfaces, lowering C3b/iC3b deposition and MAC (C5b-9) accrual on and within RPE cells, thereby alleviating lysosomal overburden, improving lysosomal integrity, and facilitating restoration of autophagic flux (e.g., normalized LC3-II/p62 dynamics) and degradative function (e.g., Cathepsin D activity and localization) (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13). The Efemp1 model shows that AP activation is heightened locally and that Cfb deletion or FB inhibition normalizes stress/inflammation (including UPR) and mitochondrial pathways; by analogy, iptacopan should attenuate ER stress/UPR signaling and immune/complement activation signatures in RPE/eyecup proteomes, with secondary benefits for mitochondrial/energy pathways (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2). Although direct demonstration that FB inhibition restores RPE lysosomal function is not presented in the excerpted Efemp1 work, the Cp40 RPE data make a strong mechanistic case that upstream complement suppression reduces complement load on lysosomes and rescues degradative capacity; iptacopan should achieve a similar effect by preventing AP amplification and thus lowering the rate of C3 activation fragment generation and MAC formation at the RPE (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).  
- Ex vivo/animal AMD-relevant endpoints. In female Efemp1 R345W mice, oral FB inhibition (DB-82-CB77) reduced sub-RPE deposits by 65% over 8 weeks, while Cfb deletion completely eliminated deposits and abrogated AP activation in eye, indicating that AP blockade can causally modify a basal laminar–like deposit phenotype; iptacopan, as a potent oral FB inhibitor with demonstrated ocular PD in mice, would be expected to recapitulate these effects on deposits and molecular signatures, subject to dose/exposure parity and sex-dependent biology (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 9–10, 4–6). The Efemp1 eyecup proteomics further suggest that FB blockade rebalances ocular homeostasis, dampening CR3/immune-complement signaling and upstream UPR stress while partially restoring mitochondrial proteins, reinforcing the hypothesis that complement amplification contributes to proteostasis failure and that its inhibition should normalize these axes (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Clinical AMD endpoints. The ongoing phase 2 iptacopan study in AMD is designed to detect prevention of conversion to iRORA or late AMD by SD-/SS-OCT and multimodal imaging over 24 months; systemic trough PK will be monitored. If oral iptacopan meaningfully engages ocular AP in humans, we would anticipate reduced new-onset iRORA and slower disease progression relative to placebo, potentially accompanied by systemic PD markers (Bb suppression), though the trial as described does not include ocular PD sampling (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022). As precedent, intravitreal C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) reduced GA growth in phase 2; conversely, C5 inhibition had mixed results, underscoring the importance of targeting upstream amplification (C3/AP) rather than solely the terminal pathway in AMD (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 7–9). It remains to be shown whether systemic FB inhibition can reproduce these benefits without increasing CNV risk; complement inhibition broadly has been associated with higher rates of new-onset CNV in some trials, a safety signal that must be monitored in FB-targeting programs (Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic and genetic rationale. FB is the essential catalytic subunit of AP convertases, and human genetics supports a causal role of FB activity in AMD (protective low-activity variants) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6). In an RPE-driven mouse model (Efemp1 R345W), Cfb deletion abolishes ocular AP activation and eliminates sub-RPE deposits; pharmacologic FB inhibition reduces deposits and reverses disease-associated pathway dysregulation, linking AP amplification to RPE/proteostasis pathology and basal deposit accumulation (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10).  
- Demonstrated oral target engagement, including ocular PD in mice. Iptacopan is orally bioavailable with rapid absorption and consistent systemic PD (Bb and sC5b-9 suppression) in humans; preclinically, systemic iptacopan blocks AP activation in eye tissue, supporting feasibility of oral ocular target engagement (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Potency/selectivity with favorable clinical precedents. Iptacopan shows nanomolar enzymatic potency, selective FB catalytic-site binding, and clear functional AP inhibition in serum/cell assays; it has delivered convincing efficacy across multiple complement-driven indications with acceptable safety, validating the drug and target class clinically (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14).  
- Convergence with RPE lysosome/autophagy biology. In CFH Y402H high-risk iPSC-RPE, proximal complement blockade (C3 inhibitor Cp40) reverses lysosomal swelling/dysfunction and reduces complement deposition including MAC; these findings mechanistically support the hypothesis that halting AP amplification upstream will relieve lysosomal burden and restore degradative capacity in RPE, a central deficit in dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).

Risks and Gaps  
- Lack of direct iptacopan data in AMD models or RPE lysosome assays. The provided excerpts do not report iptacopan efficacy in AMD-relevant animal models (e.g., Efemp1) or direct rescue of RPE lysosomal/autophagic function; the pharmacologic proof-of-concept in Efemp1 used a different FB inhibitor (DB-82-CB77) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 9–10). Thus, the hypothesis that iptacopan will restore RPE degradative capacity is mechanistically plausible but not yet experimentally demonstrated in the cited AMD models (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 7–13).  
- Ocular PK/PD in humans unproven. The AMD phase 2 protocol measures plasma trough iptacopan but does not include ocular PD; no human ocular PK is provided in the excerpts. Translational dependence on ocular exposure is high because AP activation in Efemp1 is local to the eye (elevated Ba/iC3b in ocular tissue but not plasma) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).  
- Heterogeneity and sex effects in preclinical model. Efemp1 females exhibit ocular AP activation and respond to FB inhibition; males have lower deposits, no ocular AP upregulation, and do not respond, implying biological heterogeneity that may translate to variable clinical responses and may necessitate biomarker-based enrichment (e.g., markers of ocular AP activation) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).  
- Class safety considerations. Complement inhibition increases susceptibility to infections with encapsulated bacteria; vaccination is mandated in the AMD study. Additionally, complement inhibition in GA trials has been associated with increased new-onset CNV versus sham, a signal that must be actively monitored; whether FB inhibition carries a similar CNV liability is unknown from the provided materials (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
- Mixed history of systemic complement inhibitors in AMD. The sole completed RCT of systemic anti-C5 (eculizumab) in AMD failed to show GA benefit, raising delivery and mechanistic questions for systemic approaches, although intravitreal proximal inhibitors (C3) have shown GA-slowing, and the Efemp1 data support AP dependence for basal deposit biology (Hammadi et al., 2023, pp. 17–18; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 7–9).

Program Implications and Next Steps  
- Preclinical toolkit alignment. To directly validate the central hypothesis for iptacopan, run head-to-head studies in AMD-relevant systems:
  - Efemp1 R345W mouse: oral iptacopan dosing matched for AP PD versus DB-82-CB77 benchmark; endpoints: TEM-assessed sub-RPE deposits, ocular Ba/iC3b, eyecup/neural retina proteomics (UPR/complement/mitochondrial modules), and RPE lysosomal/autophagy markers (LAMP1, CTSD activity, LC3-II/p62 flux), stratified by sex (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 9–10, 4–6).  
  - CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE: iptacopan in complement-competent human serum conditions; readouts: C3b/C5b-9 deposition, lysosomal integrity (Lysotracker, Galectin-8), CTSD localization/activity, autophagic flux and POS phagocytosis assays; benchmark to Cp40 rescue (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).  
  - Ocular exposure/PD: quantify iptacopan in ocular compartments (choroid/retina/RPE) and measure ocular AP biomarkers in vivo after oral dosing to confirm exposure–PD matching the LPS PD signal (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Translational biomarker strategy. Incorporate systemic AP markers (Bb, Ba), exploratory ocular biomarkers (e.g., aqueous humor C3 fragments if feasible), and imaging-based deposit/ELM–Bruch’s metrics; in the clinic, deploy multimodal imaging for conversion endpoints as in Novartis Pharmaceuticals (2022), and prospectively monitor CNV incidence (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
- Patient selection. Consider enriching for patients with systemic or local evidence of AP activation (genetics such as CFH risk alleles, complement biomarker profiles) analogous to the female-biased AP activation seen in Efemp1 (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).  
- Dosing rationale and adherence. Target 200 mg twice daily based on human PD experience; given the shorter half-life vs antibodies and the need for sustained AP suppression, emphasize adherence and vaccine prophylaxis; PD sampling should verify on-target AP inhibition longitudinally (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Ricklin, 2024, pp. 7–9; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).

Bottom line. Iptacopan is a mechanistically compelling, clinically validated oral FB inhibitor with demonstrated systemic PD, rapid onset, and preclinical evidence of ocular AP engagement; rigorous AMD-model testing and clinical biomarker integration are now required to close the translational loop from AP biology to RPE lysosomal rescue and clinical protection against atrophy progression (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 8–10; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).

Detailed Assessment Relative to the Stated Hypothesis  
- “Iptacopan will block alternative-pathway C3 convertase assembly on RPE surfaces (IC50 ~50 nM).” Support: Structural and enzymology data indicate direct catalytic-site binding to Bb with enzymatic IC₅₀ ≈ 10 nM against FB and functional inhibition in human serum at ~0.13 μM, consistent with potent AP convertase blockade; the proposed 50 nM figure is within the range bracketed by these assays (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).  
- “Reducing C3b deposition, alleviating lysosomal overburden, indirectly enhancing POS phagocytosis.” Support: In CFH Y402H RPE, proximal complement blockade at C3 reverses lysosomal swelling/fragility and reduces C3b/MAC burden; while FB inhibition was not directly tested, AP inhibition should reduce C3 turnover and MAC burden upstream, plausibly relieving lysosomal stress and enabling degradative function needed for POS processing; direct evidence for iptacopan specifically restoring lysosomal function or POS phagocytosis in RPE is not provided in the excerpts and remains to be shown (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).  
- “Genetic and pharmacologic inhibition of factor B reduces sub-RPE deposits and rescues lysosomal/autophagy dysfunction in CFH high-risk RPE models (Ong et al. Medicina 2024).” Clarification: The provided sources show that FB genetic deletion eliminates deposits and that an oral FB inhibitor reduces deposits and reverses pathway dysregulation in the Efemp1 mouse; rescue of lysosomal/autophagy dysfunction in CFH high-risk RPE is demonstrated with C3 inhibitor Cp40, not with an FB inhibitor in the excerpts provided (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).  
- “Iptacopan has demonstrated oral bioavailability and target engagement in Phase II for AMD, with good ocular tissue penetration.” Clarification: Oral dosing, rapid absorption, and systemic target engagement are established; the AMD phase 2 trial is ongoing with plasma trough PK but no reported results; ocular penetration per se has not been quantified in humans in the provided excerpts, though preclinical iptacopan blocked ocular AP activation in mice (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).

Go/No-Go Considerations for Dry AMD  
- Go signals:  
  - Target validity in AMD pathobiology is strong (genetics, AP dependence of basal deposits, proximal complement benefits in RPE models) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).  
  - Drug is clinically de-risked across multiple indications with robust AP PD and acceptable safety; oral delivery is patient-friendly vs intravitreal regimens (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14).  
  - Ocular PD feasibility is supported in mice for systemic iptacopan; pharmacologic AP blockade reduces deposits in Efemp1 with another orally bioavailable FB inhibitor (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).  
- Caution flags:  
  - No iptacopan AMD-model efficacy in the provided materials; need direct RPE lysosome/autophagy rescue readouts and deposit suppression with iptacopan prior to expensive late-phase commitments (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 7–13).  
  - Macro safety signals observed with complement inhibitors in AMD (CNV incidence) necessitate vigilant monitoring and risk–benefit analyses tailored to FB inhibition (Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
  - Systemic delivery uncertainty—human ocular PK/PD data are lacking; trial design should incorporate robust systemic PD and exploratory ocular biomarkers where feasible (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).

Recommendation  
Advance iptacopan for dry AMD with a focused, staged plan:  
- Preclinical confirmation package: replicate Efemp1 findings with iptacopan (deposits, AP biomarkers, proteomics) and demonstrate RPE lysosomal/autophagy rescue in CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE under complement-competent conditions; quantify ocular exposure–PD after oral dosing (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Biomarker-enriched clinical strategy: leverage systemic AP biomarkers and imaging-based progression metrics from Novartis Pharmaceuticals (2022); consider enrichment by complement genetics/biomarkers reflecting AP activation (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).  
- Safety management: maintain vaccination requirements and active CNV surveillance; implement adherence support given the shorter half-life relative to biologics (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Ricklin, 2024, pp. 7–9; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).

On balance, iptacopan has substantial mechanistic, translational, and clinical-class support to merit continued development in dry AMD, contingent on closing the specific evidence gaps for RPE degradative rescue and direct AMD-model efficacy with this agent (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).

Analysis: Candidate 1, eculizumab (Anti-C5 mAb, ID: 34), benefits from an extensive clinical and mechanistic pedigree as the first‐in‐class C5‐blocking antibody, with well‐characterized binding, pharmacokinetics, safety, and dosing. Preclinical rationale in AMD hinged on complement terminal‐pathway blockade to prevent C5a-driven inflammation and MAC (C5b-9)–mediated injury to RPE and choroidal endothelium. However, systemic and even intravitreal C5 inhibitors have repeatedly failed to show efficacy in geographic atrophy or drusen reduction in randomized trials (e.g., COMPLETE study, LFG316), and reviews attribute these failures to compartmental PK barriers, incomplete rescue of upstream complement turnover, and mechanistic escape. By contrast, Candidate 2, GSK0660 (PPARβ/δ antagonist, ID: 52), is a small‐molecule nuclear-receptor modulator with high receptor selectivity and a dual antagonist/inverse-agonist profile. The repurposing hypothesis is that PPARβ/δ antagonism relieves repression on TFEB and the CLEAR lysosomal gene network in RPE, thereby restoring POS clearance and mitigating A2E/lipofuscin buildup. While GSK0660 has zero direct ocular or AMD data and suffers from poor bioavailability and formulation challenges, its MoA targets a fundamental RPE-intrinsic pathway (lysosomal biogenesis/autophagy) implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis and has strong mechanistic novelty. Eculizumab’s key failings—negative phase 2 results, ocular PK limitations, and mechanistic data favoring proximal (C3) over terminal blockade—argue strongly against further development. In contrast, although GSK0660’s repurposing is speculative, it addresses an unmet mechanism untested clinically, and can be rapidly explored in RPE models for TFEB activation, offering a path to differentiated preclinical proof of concept. Given the extant clinical failures of systemic C5 blockade in dry AMD, GSK0660 represents a higher‐risk but potentially higher‐upward‐mobility hypothesis with a clear set of preclinical experiments and formulation challenges to tackle.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab is a recombinant, humanized monoclonal IgG kappa antibody that specifically binds complement component C5 and prevents its proteolytic activation into C5a and C5b, thereby blocking terminal pathway activity and membrane attack complex (MAC; C5b-9) assembly while leaving upstream C3-dependent functions largely intact (for example, opsonization and immune-complex handling) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; West et al., 2024). It was discovered by screening large panels of murine anti-human C5 monoclonals for potent inhibition of C5 activation and terminal complement–mediated hemolysis; the parental murine antibody (5G1.1) was then humanized by CDR grafting into human germline frameworks and engineered to use a hybrid IgG2/IgG4 heavy-chain constant region to minimize Fcγ receptor binding and classical-pathway activation (reducing effector functions that could confound terminal pathway blockade) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009). Eculizumab binds human C5 with very high affinity (Kd approximately 120 pM) and sterically prevents convertase engagement with the MG7 domain of C5; epitope mapping identifies residues in the MG7 domain (including the KSSKC motif around Arg885) critical for binding, and Arg885His/Cys polymorphisms have been linked to clinical non-responsiveness in some patients, consistent with the structural epitope (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

As a drug class, complement inhibitors have been deployed to treat diseases driven by complement dysregulation, with C5 blockade representing a terminal-pathway strategy that ablates C5a signaling and MAC-mediated cytolysis while preserving many proximal complement functions; eculizumab was the first complement inhibitor approved for clinical use and catalyzed broad clinical development of C5, C3, and alternative pathway–targeted agents across hematology, nephrology, neurology, and, more recently, ophthalmology (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Eculizumab is administered intravenously, exhibits a long serum half-life (~272 ± 82 hours), a limited volume of distribution consistent with an intravascularly confined antibody, and shows pharmacodynamic correlation between serum trough concentrations and blockade of hemolytic activity; vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis is required due to increased susceptibility when terminal complement is inhibited (Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Within ophthalmology, complement activation products and MAC deposition have been implicated in AMD pathogenesis, motivating clinical trials of complement inhibitors including C5-directed agents; eculizumab has been formally evaluated in a randomized phase 2 setting for non-exudative AMD (geographic atrophy and drusen cohorts) via systemic administration (Kassa et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Halawa et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
Eculizumab has an extensive clinical record in systemic complement-mediated disorders. It revolutionized therapy for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), where it reduces intravascular hemolysis, decreases transfusion requirements, and improves quality of life; it is also approved for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and for neurologic autoimmune indications including anti–acetylcholine receptor–positive generalized myasthenia gravis and aquaporin-4–positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Early clinical pharmacology in PNH demonstrated that an induction regimen of 600 mg weekly for four weeks followed by 900 mg every other week maintained near-complete terminal pathway blockade and significantly reduced hemolysis and transfusion needs; these dosing principles align with its long half-life and the concentration dependence of hemolytic inhibition (Hillmen et al., 2004; Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012). Despite robust control of intravascular hemolysis, residual extravascular hemolysis can persist because C3 opsonization is not prevented by C5 inhibition, illustrating an important mechanistic limitation of terminal-pathway agents (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; West et al., 2024).

The drug’s safety profile is dominated by infection risk with encapsulated organisms—particularly meningococcal disease—necessitating vaccination; otherwise, eculizumab has shown acceptable tolerability across long-term use, with clinical programs incorporating monitoring of functional complement activity (CH50) to confirm pharmacodynamic blockade and dose adequacy (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009; Eskandary et al., 2016). Mechanistically relevant sources also report pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic complexities: high-affinity binding at acidic endosomal pH encourages recycling of eculizumab:C5 complexes by FcRn, leading to accumulation of total C5 bound to the drug in circulation; next-generation engineering in ravulizumab introduced pH-dependent release to minimize cargo recycling and extend dosing intervals (Schmidt & Smith, 2023).

In ophthalmology, eculizumab has been investigated as a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD. The COMPLETE study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), a single-center, randomized, double-masked phase 2 trial, evaluated intravenous eculizumab in two cohorts: geographic atrophy (GA) and intermediate AMD with high-risk drusen; patients were randomized 2:1 to eculizumab or saline over 24 weeks with follow-up to 52 weeks (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the GA cohort (n = 30 study eyes), eculizumab did not reduce GA enlargement versus placebo at 26 or 52 weeks (square-root–transformed growth 0.19 ± 0.12 mm vs. 0.18 ± 0.15 mm at 26 weeks, P = 0.96; 0.37 ± 0.22 mm vs. 0.37 ± 0.21 mm at 52 weeks, P = 0.93), and no drug-related adverse events were reported (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the drusen cohort (n = 30 total participants; 20 active, 10 placebo), eculizumab failed to meet the prespecified primary endpoint of a ≥ 50% reduction in drusen cube-root volume at 26 weeks; none of 18 treated eyes achieved this threshold, while one placebo eye did (10%; P = 0.36), and there was no detectable difference in mean drusen growth between arms through 26–52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014). Trial conduct included meningococcal vaccination and careful multimodal imaging; retention was high with 28/30 completing 52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). Independent evidence syntheses judged the certainty of evidence as low to very low due to small sample size, imprecision, and some risk of bias; overall, systemic eculizumab “may have made little to no difference” in BCVA and GA lesion growth in the available cohort (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistically similar C5-directed agents have not shown positive phase 2 outcomes in GA when administered systemically or intravitreally (e.g., LFG316 failed in phase 2), whereas intravitreal C5 inhibition with avacincaptad pegol progressed to later-phase testing and regulatory review, suggesting that drug, route, and pharmacology may be important determinants of outcome; by contrast, intravitreal C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) demonstrated efficacy and has been approved for GA, underscoring the translational relevance of target selection and ocular delivery (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024). Multiple reviews conclude that systemic eculizumab is no longer in development for AMD and highlight delivery and mechanistic concerns as likely contributors to the negative results (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, eculizumab targets the MG7 domain of C5 and sterically prevents formation of the C5 convertase–substrate complex, thereby inhibiting the cleavage of C5 into the potent anaphylatoxin C5a and C5b, which nucleates membrane attack complex assembly with C6–C9 (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Rother et al., 2007). Structural analysis of an eculizumab Fab bound to C5 resolved at 4.2 Å shows that five CDRs form the principal interface with MG7; mutational scanning of CDR residues identifies a network of contacts necessary for high-affinity binding, and kinetic assays confirm that these interactions prevent complement-mediated hemolysis in vitro (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016). The epitope includes residues near Arg885, and clinical resistance due to Arg885His/Cys substitutions in C5 provides orthogonal validation of the binding site (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

Pharmacodynamically, eculizumab ablates terminal pathway function: it suppresses CH50 to near zero when trough serum concentrations exceed ~35 μg/mL; however, because proximal C3 activation continues, C3b deposition and downstream opsonins accumulate on surfaces, which can drive extravascular clearance and generate residual pathology even under complete C5 blockade in appropriate disease contexts (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). Additional mechanisms can undermine complete terminal pathway control: (1) during intense proximal activation, densely opsonized surfaces can support C5 activation by convertases in ways that partially bypass classical C5 convertase assembly or even promote conformational C5 activation on surface C3b clusters; such context-dependent activation can manifest as “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” despite apparently adequate free drug levels, and has been reported in clinical settings as residual terminal-pathway activity and elevated sC5b-9 in some patients (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). (2) Eculizumab binds C5 with high affinity at both neutral and mildly acidic pH, allowing FcRn to recycle eculizumab:C5 complexes and potentially alter antigen disposition; ravulizumab’s pH-dependent binding was engineered to release C5 in endosomes and improve pharmacokinetics by avoiding cargo recycling (Schmidt & Smith, 2023). These features are germane to dose selection, monitoring, and potential resistance or escape during strong complement activation.

Rationale for C5 inhibition in AMD rests on abundant mechanistic and histopathological evidence that C5-derived effectors and MAC participate in retinal/choroidal injury. C5a is detected in drusen and acts as a chemotactic and proinflammatory mediator capable of inducing VEGF expression from retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, while C5b initiates MAC assembly; MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris increases with aging and is elevated in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019). Sub-lytic and lytic MAC on choroidal endothelium causes cell injury and can trigger surviving endothelial cells to upregulate VEGF and matrix metalloproteinases, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic injury and pro-angiogenic remodeling; complement regulatory proteins such as CD59 are natural inhibitors of MAC formation and their dysfunction or insufficiency can predispose to damage (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2021). Complement dysregulation in AMD further includes genetic risk (e.g., CFH variants) and evidence of alternative pathway activation in ocular tissues, suggesting both proximal and terminal effector involvement in disease biology (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Importantly, proximal inhibition at C3 has shown the capacity to restore lysosomal function and reduce sub-RPE drusen-like deposits in human iPSC-derived RPE models carrying the high-risk CFH Y402H variant by reducing C3 turnover and lowering downstream MAC (C5b-9) localization at lysosomes; in this system, a compstatin analogue (Cp40) suppressed C3b and MAC deposition and reversed lysosomal abnormalities, whereas direct C5 inhibition has not been shown in this model to rescue lysosomal function, and clinical C5 blockade has failed in GA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). These data reinforce that while terminal pathway effectors are present and likely pathogenic in AMD, distal blockade at C5 does not necessarily address upstream complement turnover that drives intracellular lysosomal stress in RPE, and proximal intervention may be required to normalize cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
The hypothesis proposes that high-affinity C5 blockade with eculizumab will prevent MAC assembly on RPE, thereby reducing sub-RPE deposit–driven lysosomal stress and indirectly supporting photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis in dry AMD. Mechanistically, preventing C5 cleavage would abrogate both C5a signaling and C5b-dependent MAC formation; given the documented presence of C5a in drusen and increased MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane/choriocapillaris with age and AMD, terminal pathway inhibition is expected to reduce MAC-mediated endothelial and RPE injury, dampen MAC-induced VEGF/MMP signaling, and potentially mitigate inflammation (Kassa et al., 2019). In principle, if MAC-driven lysosomal injury contributes to RPE dysfunction, C5 inhibition could reduce new MAC deposition at the RPE surface and limit subsequent endocytosis of MAC into lysosomes, thereby lowering lysosomal burden (Park et al., 2021).

However, two key bodies of evidence temper this expectation. First, clinical testing of systemic eculizumab in GA and intermediate AMD failed to show benefit on primary anatomical endpoints (GA growth and OCT drusen volume) through 26–52 weeks, despite established systemic pharmacodynamic blockade; these negative outcomes argue that either (a) terminal pathway activity at C5 is not the principal driver of lesion growth/drusen regression during the studied disease stages/time horizon, or (b) pharmacokinetic compartmentalization limited ocular target engagement after intravenous dosing (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Filho et al., 2014). Reviews explicitly highlight the compartment barrier problem—systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina or sub-RPE space due to the blood–retina/Bruch’s membrane barriers and large molecular size—and note that eculizumab exposure shorter than six months is unlikely to show benefit in slowly progressive GA, compounding interpretation (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Second, cellular models directly linking complement dysregulation to lysosomal failure in high-risk AMD RPE show that upstream C3 inhibition, not terminal C5 blockade, restores lysosomal function and reduces deposit formation; this suggests that intralysosomal stress is driven by continuous C3 turnover and opsonization rather than MAC alone, and that distal C5 blockade may be insufficient to normalize these processes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Consequently, POS phagocytosis metrics may improve only marginally or not at all if the dominant insult is proximal complement turnover rather than MAC-mediated damage. The clinical failure to slow GA growth or reduce drusen volume with systemic eculizumab supports the inference that target engagement at C5, via the tested route and schedule, did not translate into macroscopic anatomical benefit in human AMD eyes within one year (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).

If eculizumab were to be tested in vitro on human RPE, appropriate readouts would include: surface and intracellular MAC (C5b-9) quantification, lysosomal number/size and membrane integrity (e.g., LAMP2, Galectin-8), Cathepsin D activity, autophagic flux, and POS degradation kinetics; concomitant measurement of upstream C3b/iC3b/C3d deposition would be essential to interpret whether C5 inhibition is affecting the dominant pathogenic pathway in the assay (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In vivo, ocular pharmacokinetic considerations dominate: intravitreal administration delivers drug to the retina and sub-RPE space but is not reported for eculizumab in the provided context and would carry different safety and dosing constraints; systemic dosing faces blood–retina barrier limitations that likely constrained ocular target engagement in COMPLETE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Notably, nearly all complement inhibitors that have shown anatomical effects in GA have been delivered intravitreally, underscoring the importance of route of administration for ocular diseases (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic rationale: C5a and MAC are present in AMD-relevant tissues; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD and can drive endothelial injury, VEGF/MMP upregulation, and potentially RPE dysfunction; blocking C5 should diminish these terminal effector signals (Kassa et al., 2019; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Potent, well-characterized biologic: Eculizumab binds human C5 with picomolar affinity, has a well-defined structural epitope in the MG7 domain, and reliably ablates terminal pathway function systemically with a large clinical safety database outside ophthalmology (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
- Clinical feasibility and tolerability: In AMD trials, intravenous eculizumab was well tolerated without drug-related adverse events and with no clear signal for increased neovascular conversion or ocular infection within one year, supporting general safety of systemic C5 blockade in this population under vaccination protocols (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Negative clinical efficacy in AMD: The randomized phase 2 COMPLETE trial showed no reduction in GA growth and no meaningful reduction in drusen volume through 26–52 weeks; certainty is limited by small sample size but confidence intervals and replication across endpoints argue against a large treatment effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).  
- Compartmentalization barriers for systemic dosing: Blood–retina and Bruch’s membrane barriers likely limit ocular exposure to intravenously administered eculizumab; multiple reviews cite inadequate ocular penetration as a plausible reason for failure, and systemic eculizumab is no longer being pursued in AMD (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
- Target selection may be too distal for RPE lysosomal rescue: Human iPSC-RPE data indicate that complement-driven lysosomal pathology and drusen-like deposits are reversed by C3 inhibition, with concomitant reduction of downstream MAC, while C5 blockade alone has not been shown to restore lysosomal metrics and did not slow GA clinically; this suggests that proximal complement turnover is the dominant driver of RPE lysosomal stress (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Mechanistic escape and incomplete terminal control: Under strong activation, C5 can be activated on dense C3b clusters with features of convertase bypass or conformational priming; stoichiometric C5 inhibitors can form long-lived C5:antibody complexes on surfaces, potentially allowing residual terminal activity, and clinical “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” has been documented (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
- Genetic and biochemical determinants of response: C5 polymorphisms (e.g., R885H/C) can abolish binding and confer resistance; while prevalence in AMD populations is unknown here, such variants are important risk factors for nonresponse (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).  
- Safety/logistics: Terminal complement blockade mandates meningococcal vaccination and vigilance for invasive infections; while acceptable systemically in selected diseases, risk–benefit in a chronic, slowly progressive ocular disorder is less favorable, and the cost and infusion burden are high (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Contextualization with alternative complement strategies  
- C5 vs C3: Clinical success in GA has emerged at the level of C3 (pegcetacoplan), consistent with cellular data showing rescue of lysosomal function by upstream blockade; by contrast, systemic C5 inhibition with eculizumab and other C5-directed agents failed to meet GA endpoints in early trials, and LFG316 also did not demonstrate efficacy in GA (West et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Route of administration: Most agents demonstrating anatomical effects in GA are delivered intravitreally; eculizumab’s large size and systemic administration likely limited ocular penetration in COMPLETE, and no intravitreal eculizumab data are provided here to support local delivery (Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
- Risk of adverse ocular remodeling: Complement modulation has complex, context-dependent effects; in some models, complement inhibition or modulation can alter macrophage polarization and influence CNV formation, underscoring that indiscriminate or poorly targeted complement blockade could have unintended consequences; while the eculizumab AMD trials did not show a neovascular signal, vigilance is warranted when selecting targets and doses (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2021).

Decision Implications  
- As a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD, eculizumab has a low probability of success based on randomized clinical evidence, pharmacokinetic compartment limitations, and mechanistic considerations indicating that distal C5 blockade may not correct the proximal complement turnover driving RPE lysosomal pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- If C5 remains a target of interest, local ocular delivery and alternative molecular formats designed for intravitreal pharmacokinetics (e.g., smaller C5-binding entities, RNAi to intraocular C5 production, or intravitreal C5 inhibitors such as avacincaptad pegol) are more plausible routes; indeed, avacincaptad has advanced in GA, while systemic eculizumab has been discontinued in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019; Nadeem et al., 2023; West et al., 2024).  
- For assays aimed at lysosomal stress and POS phagocytosis, prioritizing proximal complement inhibitors (e.g., C3-targeting) is more aligned with human RPE data and recent clinical experience, whereas C5 inhibition alone is unlikely to fully normalize lysosomal function or confer robust structural benefit (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; West et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
Eculizumab provides a clear mechanistic means to extinguish terminal complement effectors implicated in AMD biology, but the totality of evidence—negative randomized clinical data in GA and drusen, route-of-administration barriers to ocular exposure, mechanistic escape during high activation, and cellular evidence favoring proximal over distal inhibition for lysosomal rescue—argues against further development of systemic eculizumab for dry AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The program should be deprioritized in favor of intraocularly suited agents and proximal complement targets, unless a compelling, testable strategy emerges to achieve effective intraocular C5 blockade with eculizumab (which is not supported by the present context) (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistic Appendix: Biochemical and Pathobiologic Evidence Relevant to the Hypothesis  
- Complement activation and terminal effectors in AMD:  
  - C5a is present in drusen and induces VEGF from RPE; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD; MAC induces endothelial lysis and sub-lytic survival signaling that upregulates VEGF and MMPs (Kassa et al., 2019).  
  - Alternative pathway dysregulation is central in AMD; genetic and experimental data implicate factor H and alternative pathway components in AMD and CNV models; inhibition of C3a, C5a, CFB, MAC or supplementation with CD59/CFH blocks CNV in animals (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Eculizumab structure–function:  
  - Epitope on MG7 with steric convertase blockade; high-affinity binding and resistance polymorphisms at Arg885; CDR function validated by mutational scans (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
  - PK/PD: long half-life, vascular distribution, CH50 suppression threshold, FcRn recycling of C5:eculizumab complexes; ravulizumab engineering to improve recycling and dosing (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
  - Breakthrough mechanisms: convertase bypass and surface-induced conformational activation on dense C3b clusters; residual TP activity despite inhibitors under strong activation (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; Mannes et al., 2021).  
- Clinical AMD trials:  
  - COMPLETE GA cohort: no slowing of GA growth at 26 or 52 weeks; well tolerated (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021).  
  - COMPLETE drusen cohort: no ≥ 50% reduction in drusen volume in treated eyes at 26 weeks; no significant change in drusen growth vs placebo (Filho et al., 2014).  
  - Critical appraisals: small sample, imprecision, risk of bias; systemic delivery may not achieve retinal levels; eculizumab no longer in AMD development (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023).  
- RPE lysosomal biology:  
  - In high-risk Y402H iPSC-RPE, excessive C3 turnover increases MAC internalization and overloads lysosomes; C3 inhibition with Cp40 reduces both C3b and MAC, reverses lysosomal defects, and reduces drusen-like deposits; direct C5 inhibition is not shown to restore lysosomal function in this model (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Operational Recommendation  
- Do not advance systemic eculizumab for dry AMD. If C5 remains a strategic target, consider intravitreal agents designed for ocular PK and evaluate them head-to-head against proximal inhibitors in RPE lysosomal-function assays that quantify both MAC and C3 fragment deposition, with translational go/no-go predicated on alignment with known clinical signals in GA (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Each section draws on the available literature and data from the provided context.

────────────────────────────────────────  
I. OVERVIEW OF THE THERAPEUTIC CANDIDATE  

GSK0660 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor that gained prominence as the very first PPARβ/δ (peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor beta/delta)–selective inhibitory ligand reported in the scientific literature (Toth et al., 2012). Its design represents a significant breakthrough in the field of nuclear receptor modulation by demonstrating that subtype selectivity within the PPAR family can indeed be achieved with a low molecular weight organic compound. Structurally, GSK0660 belongs to the thiophenecarboxylate chemical class and features a uniquely tailored molecular architecture that includes several key pharmacophores: a methoxy‐substituted 1,4‐diaminobenzene core thought to be essential for receptor binding; a 4′‐aminophenyl substituent that not only contributes to high‐affinity interactions with the receptor’s ligand‐binding domain but also offers a promising site for subsequent chemical modification; and a methyl thiophene carboxylate moiety that helps orient the molecule within the hydrophobic pocket of PPARβ/δ (Toth et al., 2012). Extensive structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies have demonstrated that modifications to portions of the molecule—particularly the 4′‐aminophenyl substituent by introduction of medium‐length n‐alkyl chains—can enhance binding affinity by up to tenfold compared to the original structure (Toth et al., 2012).

GSK0660 was originally synthesized through a multistep organic process that began with commercially available precursors, followed by key transformation steps such as nucleophilic aromatic substitution to install appropriate groups on a benzene ring, catalytic reduction to generate the requisite amine functions, and finally sulfonamidation reactions to yield the final compound (Toth et al., 2012). In essence, this compound was developed primarily as a research tool to dissect the specific biological roles of PPARβ/δ and does not itself originate from a natural product or traditional antibiotic source. Instead, its design and synthesis reflect a targeted medicinal chemistry strategy aimed at obtaining a high degree of receptor selectivity.

Belonging to the broader class of PPAR modulators, GSK0660 occupies a niche that is distinct from the more commonly encountered PPAR agonists. Whereas most efforts historically have focused on the development of agonists for metabolic disorders and anti‐inflammatory indications, GSK0660 and its close analogs are used primarily to achieve receptor inhibition. This selective antagonism is critical for experimental setups in which the contribution of PPARβ/δ to downstream gene regulation and cellular homeostasis is being evaluated (Toth et al., 2012). Furthermore, the structure of GSK0660 aligns with the more general trends in nuclear receptor ligand development, capturing several “drug‐like” properties that, despite known limitations in bioavailability, maintain its status as a high‐quality research compound in proof‐of‐concept investigations.

────────────────────────────────────────  
II. THERAPEUTIC HISTORY  

GSK0660 has been widely used as a chemical probe to examine the biological functions of PPARβ/δ in various preclinical models. In early studies, it served as the first selective antagonist for this receptor subtype and was instrumental in clarifying the roles of PPARβ/δ in lipid metabolism, cell proliferation, and inflammation (Toth et al., 2012). Its experimental applications have spanned a number of research areas. For instance, several investigations in models of neurodegeneration—particularly in Parkinson’s disease—have utilized GSK0660 in both in vitro experiments (using human neuroblastoma cell lines such as SH‐SY5Y) and in vivo rodent models. In these studies, GSK0660 was able to negate the neuroprotective effects of PPARβ/δ agonists by blocking the receptor’s activity, thereby providing compelling evidence for a detrimental role of PPARβ/δ activation under neurodegenerative stress conditions (Antonosante et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023). Such data have contributed to a nuanced understanding of PPAR signaling in the brain, implying that under certain conditions receptor inhibition may be more desirable than activation.

Moreover, GSK0660 has also been evaluated in dermatological applications. In recent studies focusing on psoriasis‐like skin disease, GSK0660—when formulated topically—was shown to mitigate epidermal hyperplasia and reduce inflammatory markers without systemic drug accumulation, thus proving useful for localized treatment strategies (Hack et al., 2012). These dermatological studies not only underscored the compound’s ability to counteract PPARβ/δ‐mediated signaling in inflamed tissues but also highlighted practical challenges associated with its formulation. For example, its inherent chemical instability, manifesting as a tendency to undergo oxidation (where solutions of GSK0660 may turn green upon light exposure at room temperature), underscores issues related to its shelf‐life and stability in clinical formulations (Hack et al., 2012; Lieber, 2015).

Despite its usefulness in these diverse experimental models—ranging from neurodegenerative to inflammatory skin diseases—the therapeutic history of GSK0660 reveals a critical gap: there is no record within the available literature of its application in ocular diseases or in the treatment of dry AMD. A systematic search of clinical trial databases has confirmed that no human clinical investigations have been registered evaluating GSK0660 for indications such as retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, macular degeneration, or related ocular conditions (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). In other words, while the compound has been validated as a tool in non‐ocular systems, its repurposing for dry AMD is entirely uncharted territory. This lack of ocular‐specific data is a limitation that must be considered when assessing its potential for enhancing lysosomal function in RPE cells.

Furthermore, limitations inherent to GSK0660—most notably its poor systemic bioavailability and the requirement for relatively high concentrations to achieve effective antagonism—are recurring themes in its therapeutic history (Toth et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016; Lieber, 2015). Such pharmacokinetic drawbacks have spurred efforts to develop improved derivatives that possess enhanced potency and bioavailability. For instance, SAR studies have evaluated modifications to the 4′‐aminophenyl substituent, yielding analogs with substantially higher binding affinities (Toth et al., 2012). Nonetheless, all available records indicate that GSK0660 itself has remained primarily as a research tool rather than advancing to clinical or even advanced developmental stages in any therapeutic domain beyond the proof‐of‐concept experimental setting.

────────────────────────────────────────  
III. MECHANISM OF ACTION  

At the molecular level, GSK0660 exerts its action by binding selectively to the ligand‐binding domain (LBD) of PPARβ/δ, thereby inhibiting receptor activation. This interaction is competitive in nature; GSK0660 occupies the receptor pocket, effectively blocking binding of endogenous ligands or synthetic agonists (Toth et al., 2012). The molecular determinants of this selective interaction have been elucidated through SAR studies. The methoxy‐substituted 1,4‐diaminobenzene core forms critical hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts with specific residues within the LBD, while the 4′‐aminophenyl group and the methyl thiophene carboxylate moiety contribute additional electrostatic and van der Waals interactions that stabilize the binding complex (Toth et al., 2012).

A notable aspect of GSK0660’s pharmacology is its dual mode of action. In addition to functioning as a competitive antagonist, GSK0660 has been reported in some experimental contexts to act as an inverse agonist. Under basal conditions—where PPARβ/δ exhibits a low level of constitutive transcriptional activity—GSK0660 can further suppress receptor activity beyond mere inhibition by promoting the recruitment of transcriptional corepressors. These corepressors (including members of the NCoR/SMRT family and class I histone deacetylases) bind to the receptor‐corepressor complex, modifying chromatin structure and decreasing transcription of PPARβ/δ target genes (Lieber, 2015; Monsalve et al., 2013). Through these mechanisms, GSK0660 effectively shifts the balance away from gene activation toward transcriptional repression.

The detailed molecular interactions responsible for these phenomena have been characterized using a variety of biochemical assays, including competitive TR‐FRET binding studies and reporter assays in cell‐based systems (Toth et al., 2012). The ability of GSK0660 to inhibit transcriptional activation in response to exogenous agonists has been well demonstrated in several cell models—including skeletal muscle myoblasts where PPARβ/δ activates genes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase‐1A or pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase‐4 (Monsalve et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016). This cellular pharmacology underpins its potential to serve as an experimental “off‐switch” for PPARβ/δ‐mediated transcription.

In the context of the proposed repurposing hypothesis for dry AMD, the mechanistic emphasis shifts toward the regulation of lysosomal biogenesis through transcription factor EB (TFEB). Although direct evidence linking PPARβ/δ antagonism with the modulation of TFEB activity in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells is not yet established, the working hypothesis posits that PPARβ/δ normally exerts a repressive influence on a suite of genes involved in lysosomal function—the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. TFEB is recognized as the master regulator of lysosomal and autophagic gene expression and, upon activation, translocates to the nucleus to drive expression of critical lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1 and proteases such as Cathepsin D (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). By antagonizing PPARβ/δ, GSK0660 is hypothesized to relieve this repressive effect, thereby “releasing the brake” on TFEB activity. This would allow for enhanced transcription of lysosomal genes that are vital for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and the clearance of toxic lipofuscin constituents like A2E.

It is important to note that while the biochemical rationale is compelling, the specific molecular details linking PPARβ/δ inhibition to enhanced TFEB function have yet to be firmly established in ocular models. Nonetheless, the ability of GSK0660 to modulate receptor conformation and corepressor recruitment provides a credible mechanistic basis for the hypothesis, even as further studies must elucidate the crosstalk between PPARβ/δ signaling and the lysosomal gene network in RPE cells (Toth et al., 2012; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Lieber, 2015).

────────────────────────────────────────  
IV. EXPECTED EFFECT IN RPE MODELS  

Dry AMD is characterized by gradual dysfunction and atrophy of the RPE, which plays an essential role in the daily phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). A central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD is the accumulation of undigested POS material and the toxic byproduct A2E, which, in turn, leads to lipofuscin deposition, oxidative stress, and eventual RPE cell death. Critical to the maintenance of RPE homeostasis is the proper function of the lysosomal machinery responsible for cellular clearance. Lysosomal biogenesis, autophagic flux, and the efficient degradation of internalized debris are centrally regulated by transcription factor EB (TFEB), which activates the CLEAR network of genes encoding proteins such as LAMP1 (a lysosomal‐associated membrane protein) and Cathepsin D (a key lysosomal protease) (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Under normal conditions, PPARβ/δ appears to play a role in regulating gene expression through the recruitment of coactivators and corepressors. The hypothesis driving the repurposing of GSK0660 for dry AMD is that activated PPARβ/δ imposes a repressive signal on the CLEAR network genes, thereby limiting TFEB‐mediated lysosomal biogenesis in RPE cells. In an experimental paradigm based on A2E‐loaded RPE cell cultures—a standard in vitro model that mimics the cellular environment of dry AMD—it is anticipated that treatment with GSK0660 at concentrations approximating its receptor inhibition IC₅₀ (~200 nM) will alleviate PPARβ/δ‐mediated repression. This derepression is expected to promote the nuclear translocation of TFEB and upregulate its target genes, culminating in an enhanced lysosomal degradative capacity (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

The expected cellular responses following GSK0660 treatment in RPE models can be summarized as follows. First, by interrupting the ligand‐induced activation of PPARβ/δ, GSK0660 should shift the balance between transcriptional coactivators and corepressors in favor of a transcriptional environment that supports lysosomal gene expression. This would lead to a measurable increase in the mRNA and protein levels of LAMP1 and Cathepsin D, both of which are critical for lysosomal function and for the degradation of POS components (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Second, the enhanced expression of these proteins should translate into an improved capacity for POS degradation—a phenotype that can be monitored using assays that track the clearance of fluorescently labeled POS or the reduction in A2E accumulation. Third, improved lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic clearance are expected to reduce the chronic accumulation of lipofuscin, thereby mitigating oxidative stress and preserving RPE function over time.

In addition to these molecular and cellular endpoints, there is also the expectation that successful derepression of TFEB activity will indirectly contribute to improved cell viability and resistance to stress. The RPE, being highly active in terms of metabolic turnover and phagocytic activity, is particularly vulnerable to the detrimental effects of lysosomal dysfunction. Thus, a treatment that effectively restores lysosomal function is likely to bolster the RPE’s ability to manage accumulated debris and maintain metabolic homeostasis.

It should be acknowledged that one of the primary challenges will be the optimization of the effective dose of GSK0660 in the context of ocular cells. While the compound exhibits potent receptor inhibition in vitro, previous studies have identified limitations with its bioavailability and chemical stability (Toth et al., 2012; Strosznajder et al., 2021). These issues necessitate careful attention to formulation and drug delivery strategies tailored to the ocular environment. For example, controlled‐release formulations or nanoparticle‐based delivery systems might be required to ensure that effective local concentrations of GSK0660 can be maintained in the retina while avoiding systemic exposure and off‐target effects.

Moreover, despite the attractive theoretical framework linking PPARβ/δ antagonism to TFEB activation, direct experimental evidence in RPE cells is currently lacking. As such, the expected effect remains a hypothesis that must be rigorously validated through a series of in vitro assays—including quantitative PCR for lysosomal gene expression, immunoblotting for protein markers, and functional assays to assess the clearance of photoreceptor debris. ────────────────────────────────────────  
V. OVERALL EVALUATION  

GSK0660 stands out as a highly characterized PPARβ/δ antagonist with a well‐documented profile in non‐ocular applications. The compound’s discovery as the first selective ligand for PPARβ/δ established a benchmark in the field and has since made it a prominent research tool in studies of neurodegeneration, inflammation, and even dermatological applications such as psoriasis (Toth et al., 2012; Antonosante et al., 2023; Hack et al., 2012). SAR studies have demonstrated that modifications to these groups can further enhance binding affinity, offering prospects for optimization if needed (Toth et al., 2012).

The principal strength of the compound lies in its receptor selectivity and in its demonstrated capacity to function as both a competitive antagonist and an inverse agonist. This duality is central to the proposed mechanism for reversing PPARβ/δ‐mediated repression of TFEB, which in turn may enhance lysosomal biogenesis and improve the degradative capacity of RPE cells. Considering that lysosomal dysfunction and the resultant accumulation of undegraded POS and toxic byproducts such as A2E are recognized pathological features of dry AMD, the hypothesis that GSK0660 can restore a more robust lysosomal function is innovative and scientifically compelling (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

However, significant caveats temper this optimism. One major limitation is that, to date, GSK0660 has not been studied in the context of retinal diseases or any ocular applications. Although extensive preclinical research has been undertaken in models of Parkinson’s disease and psoriasis, no direct evidence supports its efficacy in modulating RPE cell lysosomal function or in mitigating dry AMD pathology (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Lieber, 2015). This represents a considerable translational gap that would require substantial preclinical work to bridge.

Another critical challenge is the compound’s pharmacokinetic profile. GSK0660 is known to suffer from poor bioavailability, and it frequently requires relatively high concentrations to achieve its intended effects in vitro. Furthermore, the chemical instability of GSK0660—demonstrated by its tendency to oxidize and change color under conditions of light exposure and room temperature storage—poses additional obstacles for formulation development, especially in a sensitive environment such as the eye where prolonged stability and controlled drug release are paramount (Toth et al., 2012; Hack et al., 2012; Strosznajder et al., 2021).

The translation of these findings to an application in dry AMD would also necessitate a careful reexamination of dosing strategies and delivery mechanisms. For instance, while topical formulations have been effective in dermatological models (Hack et al., 2012), the ocular setting will require alternative approaches to bypass obstacles such as the blood‐retinal barrier and to achieve sustained local drug concentrations without systemic spillover. Existing literature on TFEB clearly demonstrates its role as a master regulator of lysosomal genes in retinal cells (Abokyi & Tse, 2025), yet none of the studies directly establish that PPARβ/δ provides a repressive signal to TFEB in this context. Thus, the entire repurposing hypothesis, while attractive, remains speculative until dedicated studies in RPE models confirm that inhibition of PPARβ/δ by GSK0660 indeed results in derepression of TFEB and a subsequent upregulation of lysosomal markers such as LAMP1 and Cathepsin D.

Lastly, while GSK0660 has garnered a robust reputation as a research tool, its historical use in non‐ocular tissues suggests that extensive medicinal chemistry optimization may be required to enhance its physicochemical properties for ocular therapy. In summary, GSK0660 embodies both promise and challenges as a candidate for repurposing to treat dry AMD. Repurposing GSK0660 for dry AMD is underpinned by an innovative hypothesis that bridges nuclear receptor biology with lysosomal regulation—a convergence that is highly relevant given the central role of lysosomal dysfunction in RPE degeneration. The therapeutic history of T0901317 spans preclinical investigations primarily centered on cardiovascular diseases, such as atherosclerosis, where its ability to reduce atherosclerotic lesions by enhancing reverse cholesterol transport was of paramount interest. At the molecular level, T0901317 exerts its biological effects by selectively binding to the ligand-binding domains of LXRα and LXRβ. Upon binding, conformational changes in the receptor facilitate heterodimerization with RXR, leading to recruitment of coactivator proteins and subsequent binding to specific LXR response elements in the promoters of target genes. One of the key effects of this activation is the robust upregulation of ABCA1, a transporter protein that plays a central role in cholesterol efflux by mediating the transfer of cholesterol to extracellular acceptors such as apolipoprotein A-I (apo A-I) and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) particles (Lyssenko et al., 2018). The increase in ABCA1 expression subsequently enhances the reverse cholesterol transport (RCT) pathway, which is essential for preventing the intracellular and sub-RPE accumulation of cholesterol and other lipids—a factor implicated in the formation of drusen-like deposits observed in dry AMD. In addition to its lipid-regulatory activity, T0901317 has been shown to attenuate pro-inflammatory signaling pathways in RPE cells, as evidenced by its ability to modulate NF-κB signaling under conditions of oxidant stress and lipid overload (Wu et al., 2023; Buñay et al., 2021). This dual impact on lipid metabolism and inflammation is particularly relevant in the retinal context, where chronic inflammatory processes and disrupted cholesterol homeostasis converge to promote RPE dysfunction and basal deposit accumulation (Lyssenko et al., 2018). Moreover, studies have illustrated that even under conditions of hypoxia or lipid overload—conditions that normally suppress ABCA1 expression via hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF1)—T0901317 is capable of counteracting these inhibitory effects, thereby reestablishing normal cholesterol efflux in RPE cells (Peters et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022). This detailed mechanistic understanding underscores the drug’s potential to normalize the lipid environment of Bruch’s membrane and restore RPE phagocytic function by mitigating deleterious lipid accumulation (Lyssenko et al., 2018).

The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of T0901317 for dry AMD posits that the compound, when applied at an effective concentration (with an EC₅₀ in the vicinity of 50 nM in RPE cells), will activate LXRs to upregulate ABCA1 and other cholesterol efflux transporters within RPE cells. This molecular cascade is expected to promote a more efficient clearance of excess cholesterol from the RPE and surrounding Bruch’s membrane, thus reducing the formation of drusen-like deposits—a hallmark of early AMD pathology (Lyssenko et al., 2018). Data derived from experiments in ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE models indicate that treatment with T0901317 leads to a significant increase in ABCA1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels, which translates into enhanced cholesterol efflux when proper lipid acceptors such as apoA-I are present in the extracellular milieu (Lyssenko et al., 2018). In preclinical AMD models, enhanced reverse cholesterol transport due to LXR activation has been associated with normalization of the extracellular matrix, reduction of basal deposit thickness, and improved integrin-mediated adhesion—a factor critical for maintaining the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells (Buñay et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2020). A rigorous evaluation of T0901317 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several compelling strengths alongside notable challenges that must be addressed in future research. Among its strengths, T0901317 is a well-characterized LXR agonist with a robust capacity to upregulate ABCA1 and other members of the cholesterol efflux machinery in RPE cells. Another potential challenge lies in the dosing and delivery strategy for T0901317. Considering the collective body of evidence, T0901317 possesses distinct strengths as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD due to its potent LXR agonism that effectively upregulates ABCA1 expression and enhances cholesterol efflux—a critical need in the management of sub-RPE lipid accumulation and basal deposit formation. Future research efforts should focus on optimizing the drug’s delivery to the retina, refining its molecular selectivity, and conducting rigorous in vivo efficacy and safety studies in relevant AMD models. Only through such multifaceted investigations can the full potential of T0901317 be realized as a viable treatment strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration (Lyssenko et al., 2018; Buñay et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2020).

SR1078 is a synthetic ligand originally discovered as the first reported small‐molecule agonist for the orphan nuclear receptors RORα and RORγ. SR1078 has been extensively exploited as a research tool rather than a clinical therapeutic; its major preclinical applications include the characterization of RORα-dependent transcriptional regulation in cell-based systems as well as demonstrating in vivo efficacy by modulating metabolic target genes such as FGF21 and G6Pase in liver tissue (Wang et al., 2010).
