Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Trichostatin A (TSA) is a naturally occurring compound originally isolated from fermentation cultures of Streptomyces species (Grayson et al., 2010). Belonging to the hydroxamate class of histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors, TSA possesses a distinct molecular architecture characterized by three critical structural motifs: a hydroxamic acid moiety, a hydrophobic linker, and a bulky polar cap. These elements cooperate to enable TSA’s high‐affinity binding to the zinc ion within the catalytic site of HDAC enzymes, thereby blocking deacetylation reactions (Grayson et al., 2010). Unlike many newer synthetic compounds, TSA’s discovery dates back several decades, where it was initially identified for its antifungal properties yet quickly found utility as a potent epigenetic modulator in various research fields, including oncology and neurobiology (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). Within this class, HDAC inhibitors are well recognized for their ability to alter chromatin configuration; by preventing the removal of acetyl groups from histone tails, these compounds induce chromatin relaxation and, as a consequence, facilitate robust transcriptional activation of genes that are otherwise epigenetically repressed (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In the context of ocular research, TSA has been exploited primarily as a tool compound to dissect the role of epigenetic modifications in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function and has been applied in studies examining angiogenesis, apoptosis, and inflammatory responses in RPE cells (Hamid et al., 2021). Its availability from commercial suppliers such as Sigma-Aldrich (Cat. No. T1952) underscores its utility as a research-grade standard for HDAC inhibition studies, making it an attractive candidate for drug repurposing efforts aimed at diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where impaired transcription of clearance and autophagy genes plays a pivotal role (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
TSA has garnered extensive attention over the years in the biomedical literature due to its potent HDAC inhibitory function. Originally explored for its antifungal properties, subsequent studies rapidly shifted focus toward its ability to cause histone hyperacetylation, thereby rekindling interest in epigenetic regulation as a therapeutic strategy for various pathologies (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In oncology, for instance, TSA and its synthetic derivatives have been used to induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in cancer cells, ultimately leading to the development of newer, more selective HDAC inhibitors that have reached clinical trials and even regulatory approval for certain hematological malignancies (Grayson et al., 2010). In ocular research, TSA has been employed in experimental models involving retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, such as ARPE-19, where its application has led to notable changes in the transcription of genes involved in inflammation, angiogenesis, and cellular stress responses (Hamid et al., 2021). Although TSA itself has not been approved for clinical use in any ocular disease, its ability to modify gene expression through HDAC inhibition has provided valuable insights into potential interventions for retinal degenerative conditions, including both wet and dry forms of AMD (Hamid et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025). Moreover, preliminary safety studies—such as those performed using topical formulations in animal models for corneal wound healing—have demonstrated that TSA can be applied at low nanomolar concentrations with minimal cytotoxicity, suggesting that careful dose titration could allow its repurposing for RPE-targeted therapies without incurring the severe systemic toxicities observed in some cancer studies (Sharma et al., 2009). However, it is important to note that despite the promising preclinical data in ARPE-19 cells and related ocular models, there remains a significant gap in clinical evidence directly linking TSA treatment with efficacy in dry AMD, meaning that its repurposing for this indication remains experimental and largely hypothesis-driven at this stage (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Hamid et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, TSA is known to inhibit histone deacetylases by binding to the zinc ion in the enzyme’s catalytic pocket, thereby preventing the removal of acetyl groups from lysine residues on histone tails (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In normal physiological conditions, HDACs contribute to the formation of tightly packed chromatin by deacetylating histones, which leads to decreased transcriptional activity at specific gene promoters. TSA’s ability to inhibit this process results in a “relaxed” chromatin structure that is more accessible to transcription factors, leading to enhanced gene expression (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In the context of the RPE, several genes critical for autophagic flux and phagocytic function—such as lysosomal‐associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) and the receptor tyrosine kinase MERTK—are thought to be epigenetically regulated and may be transcriptionally upregulated upon HDAC inhibition (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Importantly, the transcription factor EB (TFEB) is recognized as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy, controlling the expression of a suite of genes organized within the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network (Falcão et al., 2025). In RPE cells, where efficient degradation of phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (POS) is dependent on both lysosomal function and autophagy, the upregulation of TFEB through enhanced chromatin accessibility could theoretically result in improved expression of LAMP1 and, by extension, better phagocytic capacity via receptors such as MERTK (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Moreover, TSA’s inhibition of HDACs also affects non-histone substrates; for example, it increases the acetylation of α-tubulin—a modification that can influence microtubule dynamics and vesicular transport processes (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). However, this action comes with a potential caveat: excessive tubulin acetylation has been reported to impair autophagosome trafficking, which is a critical step in the autophagic clearance pathway (Toops et al., 2015; Tan, 2018). Therefore, while TSA’s global HDAC inhibition can promote the transcription of genes essential for lysosomal biogenesis and POS degradation, careful titration of its concentration is necessary to ensure that the beneficial effects on gene transcription do not get overshadowed by disruptions in cytoskeletal dynamics and autophagosome motility (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). At the same time, TSA has been shown in some studies to downregulate pro-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic mediators such as HIF-1α and IL-1β while upregulating factors like IL-18, which may contribute additional neuroprotective benefits to the RPE (Hamid et al., 2021). Together, these multifaceted actions underline TSA’s potential to reprogram the epigenetic landscape of RPE cells, theoretically reinstating the expression of key genes involved in autophagic and phagocytic function (Boya et al., 2023; Hamid et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the working hypothesis, the expected effect of TSA in RPE cells is twofold. First, by inhibiting HDAC activity, TSA is anticipated to elevate overall chromatin accessibility, thereby stimulating the transcription of genes that are vital for proper lysosomal biogenesis and phagocytosis. In particular, the upregulation of LAMP1, a well-established marker of lysosomal membranes, should lead to an increase in the number and activity of lysosomes. Simultaneously, enhanced expression of MERTK, which plays a central role in mediating the binding and internalization of POS, should result in an improved phagocytic rate of these essential outer segment components (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE cells, where the daily burden of POS phagocytosis is critical for maintaining retinal integrity, such enhancements could potentially mitigate the accumulation of undigested cellular debris—a phenomenon that is closely linked with the progression of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Tan, 2018). Second, TSA is expected to promote the activation and nuclear translocation of TFEB. This transcription factor is normally sequestered in the cytoplasm when phosphorylated by mTORC1, but under conditions of stress or when mTORC1 activity is reduced, TFEB enters the nucleus and drives the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function and autophagy (Falcão et al., 2025). By facilitating an HDAC inhibition–mediated de-repression of the genes governing TFEB activity, TSA may help drive a feed-forward loop that enhances the cellular capacity for lysosomal degradation and autophagy. Given that RPE cells exhibit compromised autophagy and deteriorating lysosomal function in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the net effect of TSA treatment should be an improvement in POS uptake and degradation, leading to better clearance of lipofuscin and other deleterious cellular debris (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025). Furthermore, some studies using ARPE-19 cells have reported TSA-induced changes in the expression of other oxidative stress and inflammatory markers—for example, a decrease in HIF-1α expression and a corresponding increase in antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and GPX3 (Hamid et al., 2021)—which may contribute to an overall protective environment that diminishes the progressive degeneration of RPE cells. The expected cascade of molecular events—from HDAC inhibition through increased histone acetylation, enhanced transcription of TFEB, LAMP1, and MERTK, to improved lysosomal biogenesis and phagocytic function—forms the basis of the therapeutic rationale for repurposing TSA in the context of dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
Evaluating TSA as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD requires an in-depth analysis of both its promising attributes and its inherent limitations. One of the primary strengths of TSA lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action. As a proven, potent pan-HDAC inhibitor, TSA can recast the epigenetic landscape of RPE cells by enforcing hyperacetylation of histone proteins and upregulating transcription of ordinarily silenced genes (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). Considering that dry AMD is marked by severe dysfunction in protein clearance, lysosomal degradation, and autophagic flux, TSA’s capacity to activate TFEB—the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis—and to potentially enhance the expression of key phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and lysosomal markers like LAMP1 offers a compelling pharmacological strategy to restore cellular homeostasis (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). The cascading effect of promoting both lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy could improve the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), thereby mitigating the accumulation of toxic by-products like lipofuscin that contribute significantly to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Tan, 2018).

Furthermore, TSA’s history as a research compound in various cell culture models, including ARPE-19, provides a solid preclinical foundation for its repurposing. Studies have demonstrated that TSA can modulate the expression of inflammatory and apoptotic markers, reduce oxidative stress, and, importantly, alter the expression of genes that control cellular clearance pathways (Hamid et al., 2021). These data support the hypothesis that TSA might improve RPE function, a critical factor given that RPE degeneration is a driving force behind AMD progression. Preliminary ocular safety assessments, particularly in corneal models, indicate that TSA can be administered topically at carefully controlled low doses without significant toxicity (Sharma et al., 2009). Such findings are encouraging in light of the longstanding challenges associated with delivering effective therapeutics to the posterior segment of the eye; however, it must be emphasized that safety profiles established in corneal applications may not fully translate to the intricate microenvironment of the retina and RPE (Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

On the other hand, several weaknesses temper the enthusiasm for TSA as a repurposed treatment for dry AMD. Foremost among these is its broad-spectrum activity; as a pan-HDAC inhibitor, TSA does not differentiate between enzyme isoforms. This lack of selectivity raises the possibility of off-target effects that could disrupt not only histone modifications but also the acetylation status of numerous non-histone proteins, including α-tubulin (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In RPE cells, proper microtubule dynamics are essential for the trafficking of autophagosomes to lysosomes. Excessive tubulin acetylation—an effect that is purportedly enhanced by agents such as TSA, and observed in conditions mimicked by lipofuscin bisretinoids—can impede autophagosome mobility, potentially undermining the very autophagic flux that TSA is intended to improve (Toops et al., 2015; Tan, 2018; Toops et al., 2015). This paradoxical effect suggests that while increasing transcription of lysosomal genes is beneficial, alterations in cytoskeletal regulation might counteract these benefits if not precisely calibrated.

Another concern arises from the conflicting roles of HDAC activity in the context of AMD. Some studies have observed that specific HDAC activities, such as those mediated by HDAC3, are already reduced in the RPE of AMD patients (Chatterjee et al., 2024; Hamid et al., 2021). This raises the possibility that further inhibition of these enzymes might exacerbate a preexisting imbalance rather than re-establish homeostasis. In other words, if the pathological state of AMD is associated with diminished HDAC activity, then TSA’s further suppression could potentially lead to unintended and deleterious transcriptional changes that might compromise cell survival (Chatterjee et al., 2024; Hamid et al., 2021).

Moreover, despite encouraging in vitro data, there remains a paucity of information regarding TSA’s effects on the specific gene targets central to the proposed mechanism—namely, the upregulation of phagocytic receptors like MERTK and lysosomal membrane proteins such as LAMP1. While the rationale is built upon sound principles of epigenetic regulation and the critical role these proteins play in ensuring efficient POS uptake and degradation (Boya et al., 2023), direct evidence linking TSA treatment to enhanced expression of these markers in RPE cells is yet to be conclusively demonstrated. This gap in the literature makes it difficult to fully endorse TSA as having the predicted beneficial impact on RPE phagocytic function and lysosomal biogenesis without further, targeted investigations (Tan, 2018; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

In addressing the translational potential of TSA, one must also consider its pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiles. Although ocular studies—particularly those focusing on corneal wound healing—have suggested that TSA is safe at low nanomolar concentrations (Sharma et al., 2009), its use in chronic conditions such as dry AMD would likely require long-term administration. The potential cumulative toxicity of TSA, given its broad activity and historical association with off-target effects in other tissues, remains a serious concern. The challenge will be to reconcile the need for sufficient HDAC inhibition to achieve therapeutic upregulation of autophagic and phagocytic genes with the imperative to minimize adverse side effects that could compromise either the safety or the efficacy of the treatment (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021).

Overall, TSA is a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its robust epigenetic modulatory effects, which align well with the therapeutic goal of enhancing lysosomal biogenesis and phagocytic clearance in RPE cells. Its ability to interfere with HDAC activity has been demonstrated to affect not only histone acetylation but also the transcription of genes involved in cellular stress responses and degradation pathways. In theory, such modifications could reverse or mitigate several of the pathological features of dry AMD, including the accumulation of undigested POS and subsequent lipofuscin buildup that drive RPE degeneration (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). The elevation of TFEB, a master regulator of lysosomal gene expression, through TSA-mediated chromatin relaxation offers a particularly attractive avenue for restoring the autophagy-lysosome machinery, thereby enhancing both cellular clearance and the overall health of RPE cells (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Nonetheless, the candidate’s broad-spectrum nature and potential to disrupt processes such as microtubule dynamics present significant challenges. The risk of impaired autophagosome trafficking due to aberrant tubulin acetylation (Toops et al., 2015; Tan, 2018) must be weighed against the expected benefits of improved lysosomal function. Moreover, the heterogeneity of HDAC activity in AMD pathology—with some reports indicating already compromised HDAC function in diseased RPE—complicates the prospect of using a pan-HDAC inhibitor without a carefully defined therapeutic window (Chatterjee et al., 2024; Hamid et al., 2021). The absence of definitive data linking TSA treatment to increased expression of MERTK and LAMP1 in RPE cells further underscores the need for additional research to validate the proposed mechanism of action (Tan, 2018; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

In light of these considerations, our evaluation supports the continued exploratory investigation of TSA as a repurposed intervention for dry AMD, with the understanding that several critical questions remain unanswered. Future studies should aim to:  
1. Directly measure the impact of TSA on the expression levels of key phagocytic and lysosomal genes, such as MERTK and LAMP1, in RPE cells using both transcriptional and protein-level assays.  
2. Delineate the dose-response relationship in RPE cells to identify concentrations that achieve optimal activation of the CLEAR network and TFEB-mediated transcription without inducing detrimental levels of tubulin acetylation that could impede autophagosome mobility.  
3. Assess the long-term safety and pharmacokinetics of TSA in ocular tissues, particularly in animal models of dry AMD, to determine whether its beneficial effects on autophagy and phagocytosis can be sustained without incurring off-target toxicity or systemic side effects.  
4. Explore the possibility of developing more selective HDAC inhibitors or targeted delivery systems that concentrate TSA’s effects specifically within the RPE, thereby minimizing the risks associated with its broad-spectrum activity.

Ultimately, while TSA’s established role as an epigenetic modulator makes it an attractive candidate for addressing the underlying cellular dysfunction in dry AMD, careful balancing of its beneficial transcriptional effects against its potential to disrupt critical cellular processes is essential. The data reviewed herein provide a strong mechanistic rationale for TSA’s utility, yet underscore the necessity for rigorously designed preclinical studies to confirm its efficacy and safety in the context of retinal degeneration (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021; Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SHP099 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule allosteric inhibitor of the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP2 (PTPN11) discovered by Novartis through a target-biased screening paradigm that enriched for modulators of full-length, autoinhibited SHP2 and counter-selected catalytic-site binders, followed by structure-based medicinal chemistry optimization to stabilize the closed SHP2 conformation rather than engage the conserved active site (chemical identity: 6-(4-amino-4-methylpiperidin-1-yl)-3-(2,3-dichlorophenyl)pyrazin-2-amine) (PDB: 5EHR) (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kong & Long, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). In the 1.7 Å co-crystal, SHP099 occupies a central “tunnel” at the interface of the N-SH2, C-SH2, and PTP domains present only in the autoinhibited state; its aminopyrazine/amine motif forms hydrogen bonds to Arg111 and Phe113 in the SH2 linker and to Glu250 in the PTP domain, while a 2,3-dichlorophenyl moiety engages hydrophobic residues (Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, Gln495), thereby clamping the interdomain interface and disfavoring opening/activation (ligand volume ~262 Å3; tunnel ~464 Å3) (Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Biochemically, SHP099 is potent and selective (SHP2 enzymatic IC50 ≈ 0.070–0.071 µM; no detectable activity across panels of 21 phosphatases and 66 kinases, including SHP1) and translates to cellular pathway inhibition (p-ERK IC50 ≈ 0.250 µM), with high aqueous solubility, high permeability without efflux, and acceptable mouse oral exposure/bioavailability (~46%) (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kong & Long, 2022). Mechanistically, SHP099 functions as a “molecular glue” that stabilizes the closed, autoinhibited SHP2 conformation via a conformational selection mechanism; affinity is reduced for strongly activating SHP2 mutants (for example, E76K) that bias the open state, although high concentrations can re-close some mutants in vitro and in cells (Meem, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).

SHP099 belongs to the class of SHP2 “tunnel-site” (site 1) allosteric inhibitors that stabilize the autoinhibited state by engaging the N-SH2/C-SH2/PTP interdomain pocket; dual allosteric occupancy (site 1 plus a distal latch, site 2) is structurally and biochemically validated and produces cooperative inhibition when SHP099 is combined with a site-2 ligand (for example SHP244 analogs), underscoring the druggability of multiple noncatalytic surfaces on SHP2 (Fodor et al., 2018; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Discovery and SAR established that the aminopyrazine ring amine is essential (Glu250 H-bond), the 4-amino-4-methylpiperidine motif is favored over piperazines for potency, and an ortho-chlorine on the phenyl ring is critical; a representative synthesis employs Suzuki–Miyaura coupling to install the dichlorophenyl substituent on a pyrazinamine core, followed by SNAr to append the Boc-protected 4-methylpiperidin-4-amine and final acid deprotection to the free base (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-level development moved the SHP099 pharmacophore into diverse chemotypes (for example, pyrimidinones and fused bicyclic pyrazolopyrimidinones) and into clinical candidates (for example, TNO155, RMC-4630, BBP-398), reflecting translational momentum for SHP2 allosteric inhibition (Kerr et al., 2021; Tojjari et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
SHP099 established in vivo proof-of-concept for allosteric SHP2 inhibition in oncology. In an EGFR-amplified esophageal squamous carcinoma xenograft (KYSE-520), oral SHP099 produced dose-dependent pathway suppression (tumor p-ERK), antiproliferative effects, and tumor growth inhibition up to stasis at 100 mg/kg, supported by measurable exposure and oral bioavailability (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Additional preclinical efficacy includes activity in EGFR-driven xenografts and reduction of leukemic burden in FLT3-ITD–positive AML models after oral dosing, with no overt toxicity noted in those studies (Dempke et al., 2018). In glioblastoma models, SHP099 achieved brain exposure after 100 mg/kg oral dosing, reduced tumor growth and vascularity in orthotopic xenografts, and showed activity both as monotherapy and combined with temozolomide, demonstrating CNS penetration and antitumor pharmacology in mice (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-wide, SHP2 allosteric inhibitors have shown single-agent and combination efficacy in RTK/RAS/MAPK-driven tumors, have been advanced into clinical studies across multiple solid tumors, and display mechanism-consistent biomarker modulation (for example, decreased p-ERK) in preclinical models (Kerr et al., 2021; Stanford & Bottini, 2023; Tojjari et al., 2023).

Within the materials provided here, there are no reports of SHP099 (or any SHP2 allosteric inhibitor) being used in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis models, or any ocular indication; multiple reviews focus on oncology/immuno-oncology and either enumerate preclinical tumor evidence or clinical oncology programs, without ocular/retinal data (Kerr et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2020). Consequently, repurposing SHP099 for dry AMD would be a first-in-class application with no precedent in the supplied literature (Yuan et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
SHP2 is maintained in an autoinhibited state by intramolecular engagement of the N-SH2 domain with the PTP catalytic domain; engagement of SH2 domains by bis-phosphotyrosyl motifs on receptors/adaptors relieves autoinhibition, allowing both catalytic and scaffolding functions that couple receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) to RAS activation and downstream MAPK/PI3K signaling (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). SHP099 binds in a tunnel formed by the N-SH2, C-SH2, and PTP domains of autoinhibited SHP2 and locks this closed conformation: crystallography defines hydrogen bonds to Arg111 and Phe113 (SH2 linker) and Glu250 (PTP domain), and hydrophobic contacts to Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, and Gln495 that together stabilize the interface and preclude opening; pre-organization of Arg111 additionally supports a cationic–π interaction with SHP099’s dichlorophenyl ring (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Selectivity over SHP1 is rationalized structurally by differences in SH2-linker/tunnel geometry that preclude analogous Arg/Phe contacts, consistent with lack of SHP1 inhibition in broad profiling (Diop et al., 2022). Binding follows conformational selection, with lowered potency against mutants that favor the open state (for example, E76K, D61Y), though high concentrations or dual-site allosteric occupancy can re-close certain mutants and enhance inhibition (Fodor et al., 2018; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-level medicinal chemistry around SHP099 uncovered both optimization paths (for example, pyrimidinones, fused bicyclic scaffolds) and liabilities such as unexpected hERG inhibition in some derivatives and combination-dosing tolerability issues in mice, underscoring the need for careful safety pharmacology (Meem, 2022).

RPE POS phagocytosis is a ligand-directed, RTK-driven process with defined signaling architecture. Externalized phosphatidylserine on shed POS tips is opsonized (for example, by MFG-E8), engages apical αvβ5 integrin, and triggers a pathway in which MerTK (activated by Gas6 or Protein S) is essential for physiological engulfment in vivo; loss-of-function MERTK mutations in RCS rats or humans abolish POS internalization and cause rapid photoreceptor degeneration (Ghosh et al., 2024; Moran et al., 2022). At the cytoskeletal level, formation of the F-actin phagocytic cup beneath bound POS requires Rac1 activation and a concurrent decrease in RhoA/ROCK-mediated contractility; RhoA elevation blocks cup formation even when Rac1 is active, whereas ROCK inhibition is both necessary and sufficient to enable cup formation and POS internalization and can rescue engulfment and acidification in MerTK-deficient RPE ex vivo (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Mao & Finnemann, 2021). Mechanistically downstream of MerTK, Src is activated and (i) phosphorylates and activates focal adhesion kinase (FAK), recruiting the p130CAS/CRKII/DOCK180 module that activates Rac1, and (ii) phosphorylates GDP-dissociation inhibitor GDI1, promoting dissociation from Rab5 to facilitate Rab cycling needed for cup formation and early phagosome dynamics (Shelby et al., 2015). These pathways define measurable biochemical checkpoints (MerTK/Src/FAK phosphorylation, Rac1-GTP, RhoA/ROCK activity) and functional readouts (cup formation, internalization, phagolysosomal acidification) relevant to any attempt to modulate RPE phagocytosis pharmacologically (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Moran et al., 2022).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis is that SHP099 will inhibit SHP2 in RPE (biochemical IC50 ~70–75 nM), sustain MerTK phosphorylation, maintain Rac1-GTP, and thereby increase POS internalization. The supplied literature confirms that SHP099 potently and selectively inhibits SHP2 by stabilizing the autoinhibited state and blocks RTK→RAS/MAPK signaling in cells, but it does not demonstrate that SHP2 directly dephosphorylates MerTK in RPE or that SHP2 inhibition prolongs MerTK phosphorylation or increases RPE POS uptake (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). Across systems, SHP2 acts as a positive transducer linking activated RTKs to RAS/ERK signaling; SHP2 allosteric inhibition decouples upstream RTKs from RAS activation, lowering RAS-GTP and p-ERK, which is consistent with a broad attenuation of RTK-driven outputs rather than prolonged receptor phosphorylation per se (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). Within the provided ocular literature, the only experimentally demonstrated pharmacologic rescue of RPE POS uptake is acute ROCK inhibition, which operates downstream of MerTK to reduce actomyosin contractility and enable cup formation and internalization—even rescuing MerTK-deficient RPE ex vivo—whereas elevating RhoA blocks phagocytosis despite Rac1 activation (Mao & Finnemann, 2021). Thus, while SHP099 will almost certainly inhibit SHP2 in RPE if exposure is achieved, the predicted increase in POS internalization via prolonged MerTK phosphorylation and sustained Rac1-GTP is speculative and not supported by direct evidence in the materials provided here (Kerr et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2020).

If the assay readout is POS phagocytosis in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE, the mechanistic checkpoints most directly supported by the literature are: phosphorylation kinetics of MerTK and Src/FAK; Rac1-GTP elevation coincident with cup formation; RhoA/ROCK suppression; and functional measures of cup assembly, POS internalization, and phagolysosomal acidification, with a ROCK inhibitor as a validated positive control (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Mao & Finnemann, 2021; Moran et al., 2022). Ocular pharmacokinetics for SHP099 are unknown in the provided corpus; although brain exposure has been documented after oral dosing in mice, retinal/RPE exposure should not be inferred and would need to be measured for systemic or local (for example, intravitreal) dosing paradigms (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths for repurposing consideration  
- Potent, selective, and structurally validated target engagement. SHP099 is characterized at atomic resolution (PDB 5EHR) with a coherent interaction network (Arg111, Phe113, Glu250; Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, Gln495) that rationalizes potency, selectivity versus SHP1, and conformational bias, increasing confidence that SHP2 inhibition will translate biochemically in RPE if drug exposure is achieved (Diop et al., 2022; Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Drug-like properties and in vivo activity. SHP099 exhibits favorable physicochemical properties (high solubility; Caco-2 permeability without efflux), oral bioavailability (~46% in mice), dose-dependent pathway modulation in tumors, and robust xenograft efficacy; CNS exposure after oral dosing has been demonstrated in mice, indicating trans-barrier distribution is feasible with adequate exposure (Fortanet et al., 2016; Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Class-level translational experience. Multiple SHP2 allosteric inhibitors derived from the SHP099 tunnel pharmacophore have entered clinical testing across solid tumors, enabling leverage of class pharmacology, safety learning, and combination strategies if ocular repurposing proceeds (Kerr et al., 2021; Stanford & Bottini, 2023; Tojjari et al., 2023).

Key weaknesses and risks specific to dry AMD/RPE phagocytosis  
- Mechanistic gap in RPE. The premise that SHP2 dephosphorylates MerTK to terminate phagocytic signaling in RPE, and that SHP2 inhibition will prolong MerTK phosphorylation and sustain Rac1 activation, is not supported by the supplied literature; no direct data link SHP2 to MerTK regulation in RPE or demonstrate SHP099-induced increases in POS uptake (Kerr et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2020). In contrast, RhoA/ROCK suppression is a validated, decisive permissive event for cup formation/internalization and can rescue MerTK deficiency, suggesting that targeting ROCK remains a higher-confidence pharmacological route to enhance POS uptake (Mao & Finnemann, 2021).  
- Potential on-target countereffects on trophic RTK signaling. SHP2 broadly transduces RTK signals to RAS/ERK; allosteric SHP2 inhibition reduces RAS-GTP/p-ERK by disconnecting RTKs from downstream pathways, which could dampen beneficial RTK-mediated homeostatic signaling in RPE and choroid (for example, PDGFR, c-MET, IGF1R) even if MerTK phosphorylation were transiently increased, necessitating careful evaluation of RPE viability and stress responses in addition to phagocytosis endpoints (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021).  
- Ocular PK/tissue exposure unknown. There is no reported ocular distribution for SHP099 in the materials provided; CNS penetration does not ensure retinal/RPE exposure, and systemic dosing to achieve ocular levels may be limited by plasma protein binding, efflux, or tolerability, while intravitreal dosing introduces local safety and formulation challenges that would require de novo assessment (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Class liabilities and context-dependent potency. Medicinal chemistry around SHP099 identified derivatives with unexpected hERG activity and tolerability issues in some combination regimens; while not demonstrated specifically for SHP099 here, this flags a class risk requiring prospective cardiac and ocular safety pharmacology. Conformational-selection binding also means potency varies with SHP2 activation state, which is undefined in aging human RPE and could shift under inflammatory or oxidative stress present in dry AMD (Meem, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Lack of precedent in ocular models. No ocular, retinal, or RPE data for SHP099 or related allosteric SHP2 inhibitors are available in the supplied literature, increasing translational uncertainty for this repurposing (Yuan et al., 2020).

Program decision and de-risking experiments  
On the basis of the information provided, SHP099 is not yet a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD without foundational mechanistic validation in RPE. The central claim—that SHP2 inhibition prolongs MerTK phosphorylation and increases POS internalization—remains speculative in the absence of RPE data (Yuan et al., 2020). If the team elects to explore this hypothesis, a gated, mechanism-first workplan is advised:

- Define pathway engagement in RPE. Confirm SHP2 expression and activation state during phagocytosis in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE; assess whether SHP2 associates with MerTK/Src/FAK complexes upon POS challenge by co-immunoprecipitation or proximity assays (Shelby et al., 2015).  
- Biochemical time-courses ± SHP099. Quantify MerTK phosphorylation kinetics, Src and FAK activation, Rac1-GTP, and RhoA/ROCK activity after POS addition with a SHP099 concentration range bracketing its biochemical potency in enzyme assays; benchmark effect sizes against a ROCK inhibitor positive control, which is validated to rescue phagocytosis even in MerTK-deficient contexts (Mao & Finnemann, 2021).  
- Functional phagocytosis assays. Measure POS binding, F-actin cup formation, internalization, and phagolysosomal acidification under the same conditions, using established assays and timepoints aligned to the diurnal phagocytic peak where applicable (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Moran et al., 2022).  
- Ocular PK and safety. Establish retinal/RPE exposure after systemic and (if considered) intravitreal dosing, and perform ocular tolerability assessments (inflammation, ERG, histopathology) to identify potential on- or off-target liabilities early, mindful of class risks noted in optimization campaigns (Meem, 2022; Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).

In summary, SHP099 is a potent, selective, and well-characterized SHP2 allosteric inhibitor with robust oncology pharmacology and drug-like properties, but the case for repurposing to dry AMD by enhancing RPE POS phagocytosis is unsubstantiated in the provided literature and carries meaningful mechanistic and translational risks. Prioritizing direct RPE mechanistic studies and ocular PK/tolerability before any disease-model investment is the appropriate next step; in parallel, ROCK pathway modulation remains the most evidence-backed pharmacologic lever to augment phagocytosis in this system and should serve as a positive control and a benchmark for effect size (Fortanet et al., 2016; Mao & Finnemann, 2021; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
VU0155072 is a synthetic small‐molecule agonist that selectively targets the sphingosine‐1‐phosphate receptor 5 (S1PR5). Although the detailed synthetic route and complete structural characterization for VU0155072 as a University of North Carolina reagent are not fully delineated in the available literature, it belongs to a class of compounds that have been developed to achieve high selectivity for S1PR5. Similar to the structurally characterized S1PR5 agonist A-971432—synthesized via a two‐step process employing reductive amination with azetidine-3-carboxylic acid derivatives (Hobson et al., 2015)—VU0155072 is assumed to incorporate a pharmacophore that confers both high potency and selectivity within the sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor family. Compounds in this class have generally exploited the azetidine or related amino acid framework as a bioisostere to mimic the native lipid ligand, sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), while avoiding the metabolic liabilities of phosphorylated amino alcohols (Hobson et al., 2015). S1P receptor modulators as a group have been widely evaluated in a range of therapeutic areas—from multiple sclerosis and other neurodegenerative disorders to ocular pathologies—due to their ability to modulate immune cell trafficking and endothelial barrier function (Birgbauer, 2024; Hobson et al., 2015). In this context, VU0155072 marks a potential reagent that could be repurposed for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by leveraging its selective activation of S1PR5 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells.

Therapeutic History:  
The broader class of S1P receptor modulators has an extensive therapeutic history, with agents like fingolimod having been approved for multiple sclerosis owing to their immunomodulatory effects; however, these agents generally lack receptor subtype selectivity and consequently trigger side effects related to non-selective S1P receptor engagement (Birgbauer, 2024; Nakamura et al., 2024). More recent efforts have focused on enhancing receptor selectivity, as exemplified by A-971432—which is a selective S1PR5 agonist developed for neurodegenerative conditions—and ASP4058, an S1P1/5-selective agonist that has demonstrated efficacy in ocular vascular pathology models relevant to wet age-related macular degeneration (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024). Despite these advances, none of the compounds described to date have been definitively applied to dry AMD. In contrast to wet AMD therapies, which predominantly target abnormal neovascularization through modulation of VEGF pathways (Nakamura et al., 2024), the potential therapeutic application of S1PR5 agonists in dry AMD lies in their capacity to restore or enhance the phagocytic function of RPE cells. Preliminary evidence suggests that RPE phagocytosis—a critical process for the daily removal of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—may be modulated via S1P receptor signaling. Notably, a human RPE-based screening platform identified compounds capable of enhancing POS phagocytosis, with subsequent transcriptomic analyses revealing that S1PR5 was among the top upregulated genes associated with the enhanced phagocytic response (Schreiter et al., 2020). Moreover, while most of the literature on S1P receptor agonists has focused on neurodegenerative or ocular vascular indications, there is a growing rationale for repurposing these agents for dry AMD, given that RPE dysfunction—including impaired phagosome-lysosome fusion and subsequent accumulation of cellular debris—is a hallmark of the disease (Hobson et al., 2015; Schreiter et al., 2020). Thus, VU0155072, though primarily a research reagent at this stage, stands as a candidate with potential utility for dry AMD based on its receptor selectivity and the emerging role of S1PR5 in RPE phagocytic trafficking.

Mechanism of Action:  
S1PR5 is a member of the G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) family activated by the endogenous ligand sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P). Its activation typically engages downstream signaling cascades that include the modulation of Rho family GTPases, regulation of the actin cytoskeleton, and activation of kinases such as AKT, all of which are crucial for vesicle transport and membrane fusion events (Hobson et al., 2015). In the context of RPE cells, the mechanistic hypothesis for VU0155072 centers on its ability to enhance phagosome-lysosome fusion and the degradation of POS. This is predicated on the observation that modulation of S1P receptor signaling impacts intracellular trafficking pathways. For instance, activation of S1PR5 has been linked to changes in cytoskeletal dynamics that favor efficient vesicular movement and fusion events—a process essential for the clearance of phagosomes containing photoreceptor debris (Schreiter et al., 2020). Additionally, the receptor’s downstream signaling may stimulate pathways involving Rho-associated kinases (ROCK) or PI3K/AKT, both of which facilitate the reorganization of actin filaments and promote the maturation and fusion of phagosomes with lysosomes (Hobson et al., 2015). Importantly, data from a study using a human RPE-based screening platform indicated that pharmacological inhibition of S1PR5 impaired the phagocytic uptake and processing of POS, implying that its activation could restore this cellular function (Schreiter et al., 2020). However, it is noteworthy that several studies examining receptor distribution in RPE cells (using the ARPE-19 cell line as a model) have reported that S1PR5 mRNA expression is very low compared with other S1P receptors such as S1PR3 (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022). This observation raises questions about the sufficiency of endogenous S1PR5 expression in mediating phagocytic processes and whether exogenous activation by a potent agonist like VU0155072 can override such limitations. Nonetheless, the proposed mechanism is coherent with the hypothesis that selective S1PR5 activation leads to enhanced phagosome-lysosome fusion—an effect that would be indirectly mediated by the receptor’s influence on cytoskeletal remodeling and vesicular trafficking proteins.

Expected Effect:  
The primary therapeutic expectation for VU0155072 in dry AMD is that selective activation of S1PR5 in RPE cells will augment the rate and efficiency of phagocytosis, specifically by promoting the fusion of phagosomes with lysosomes and thereby ensuring effective degradation of POS. In dry AMD, one of the pathogenic factors is the defective clearance and subsequent accumulation of photoreceptor debris, which contributes to RPE dysfunction and the formation of drusen. By facilitating robust phagocytic processing, VU0155072 is anticipated to alleviate the cellular stress associated with toxic accumulation, restore RPE homeostasis, and ultimately preserve retinal function (Schreiter et al., 2020). In vitro assays using human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or iPSC-derived RPE) could be employed to assess the efficacy of VU0155072. These assays might measure parameters such as the rate of POS uptake, the kinetics of phagosome-lysosome fusion (potentially using co-localization markers of lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1), and levels of residual POS components after treatment. Given the reported effective concentration (EC₅₀) in the vicinity of 150 nM, one would expect that treatment with VU0155072 at or near this concentration would lead to measurable improvements in phagocytic flux. Moreover, its selectivity may allow the compound to act in a highly targeted fashion, reducing the potential for adverse effects associated with off-target activation of other S1P receptor subtypes—a significant benefit given the pleiotropic roles of other S1P receptors in immune modulation and vascular homeostasis (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024). An additional facet of the expected effect is the possibility that S1PR5 activation may engage MERTK-independent signaling pathways. MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase critical for POS phagocytosis, is often implicated in inherited forms of retinal degeneration when mutated. Should VU0155072 provide an alternate route to stimulate phagosome maturation and clearance, it could be particularly beneficial in cases where MERTK function is compromised (Schreiter et al., 2020). Nonetheless, the low endogenous expression of S1PR5 in commonly used RPE cell lines (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022) may necessitate the use of primary or stem cell-derived RPE models in order to fully capture the therapeutic potential of this approach.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, VU0155072 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD due to its high selectivity for S1PR5 and the compelling hypothesis that S1PR5 activation can restore phagocytic flux in RPE cells. One of the key strengths of this approach is the mechanistic precision: by specifically targeting S1PR5, VU0155072 is expected to modulate intracellular trafficking pathways that are critical for the maintenance and renewal of the RPE’s phagocytic machinery. This stands in contrast to previous S1P receptor modulators that, due to their nonselective binding profiles (such as fingolimod), have demonstrated a range of off-target effects including unwanted immune modulation and vascular dysfunction (Birgbauer, 2024; Nakamura et al., 2024). Moreover, studies on similar S1PR5 agonists like A-971432 have established that selective receptor activation can be achieved with favorable pharmacokinetic profiles, and the precedent set by ASP4058 in addressing ocular pathologies suggests that S1P receptor modulation can be therapeutically beneficial in the retinal context (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024).  

However, the candidate also faces several challenges. A significant potential weakness is the reported low endogenous expression of S1PR5 in RPE cell lines, such as ARPE-19, where expression levels are markedly lower than those of other S1P receptors (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022). This observation raises the question of whether exogenous activation by VU0155072 will be sufficient to elicit a robust phagocytic response in the RPE, or whether receptor upregulation might already be a prerequisite for therapeutic efficacy. Furthermore, while there is evidence that S1PR5 signaling can influence phagocytic processes (Schreiter et al., 2020), most of the existing research has focused on its roles in CNS function and vascular stability rather than in the specific context of RPE-mediated POS degradation. Hence, the proposed mechanism—restoration of phagosome-lysosome fusion and enhancement of POS degradation via S1PR5 activation—remains largely inferential and will require rigorous experimental validation in appropriate in vitro and in vivo models of dry AMD.  

Another consideration is the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic profile of VU0155072, which are described as being favorable in rodents. In theory, such data support its potential translation into clinical settings; however, the degree to which rodent PK accurately predicts human ocular tissue exposure remains uncertain, particularly given the unique microenvironment and barrier properties of the human retina. Additionally, it will be imperative to assess whether VU0155072 exerts any off-target effects on other S1P receptor subtypes, despite its purported selectivity. Off-target binding could complicate the interpretation of preclinical results or introduce safety concerns that have been observed with less selective S1P receptor modulators (Birgbauer, 2024; Nakamura et al., 2024).

From a disease-modifying perspective, the hypothesis that enhancement of phagocytic flux in RPE cells can ameliorate the progression of dry AMD is attractive because it targets a central pathogenic mechanism—namely, the chronic failure of POS clearance that leads to lipofuscin accumulation, drusen formation, and subsequent RPE atrophy. If VU0155072 can indeed stimulate the phagocytic machinery through S1PR5 activation in a meaningful way, it could potentially slow or even reverse some of the degenerative changes associated with dry AMD. This mechanism-driven approach represents a departure from merely symptomatic treatments, addressing the underlying cellular dysfunction that characterizes the disease (Hobson et al., 2015; Schreiter et al., 2020).

In conclusion, while VU0155072 is supported by a mechanistic rationale rooted in S1PR5-mediated regulation of intracellular trafficking and phagocytosis in RPE cells, several factors must be carefully considered before committing to this candidate as a viable therapeutic for dry AMD. The strengths of VU0155072 lie in its receptor specificity, favorable PK in rodent models, and the emerging evidence linking S1PR5 activation with improved phagocytic function in RPE—a critical process compromised in dry AMD. In contrast, the limited endogenous expression of S1PR5 in commonly used RPE models (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022) and the scarce direct evidence of S1PR5 agonism ameliorating dry AMD pathology represent significant challenges. These weaknesses highlight the necessity for further basic research to quantify S1PR5 expression in relevant human RPE cells, to confirm the downstream signaling events triggered by VU0155072, and to validate the beneficial effects of enhanced phagosome-lysosome fusion using both in vitro and in vivo models of dry AMD. Ultimately, while VU0155072 shows promise as a mechanistically precise candidate for restoring phagocytic flux and addressing a key pathological feature of dry AMD, the current literature underscores the need for additional studies to fully establish its therapeutic potential in this context (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024; Qiao et al., 2012; Schreiter et al., 2020; Sorenson et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Astrocyte‐derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a are an innovative, biomimetic class of therapeutic agents that combine the natural properties of extracellular vesicles with the regulatory functions of microRNAs. Exosomes are nano‐sized vesicles (typically 40–160 nm in diameter) generated in the endosomal pathway and released by almost all cell types, including astrocytes, which are a fundamental component of the retinal microenvironment (Heo & Ryu, 2024). In this candidate, exosomes are isolated from retinal astrocytes and selectively engineered to become enriched with miR-146a, a microRNA known for its anti‐inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties. Because astrocytes are intimately involved in neuronal support and retinal homeostasis, their exosomes offer an inherent targeting advantage for diseased retinal regions, particularly in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is compromised (Romero et al., 2024). The enrichment with miR-146a transforms these naturally secreted vesicles into a targeted drug delivery vehicle that can modulate specific intracellular pathways in the RPE. This approach falls within the broader therapeutic class of exosome‐based drug delivery systems, a class that has increasingly attracted attention for its ability to transport nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids with high specificity and minimal immunogenicity (Du & Palczewski, 2022). Exosome therapy has been previously explored in preclinical models for various retinal pathologies using different source cells, such as mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and RPE cells (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2023). Engineering exosomes to carry therapeutic miRNAs like miR-146a exemplifies a precision medicine strategy in which the carrier is not only inert but provides its own biological effects derived from its cell of origin, contributing to the overall therapeutic profile.

Therapeutic History:  
While there is robust literature documenting the application of exosome-based therapies in ocular diseases, the specific use of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched with miR-146a is a relatively novel proposition. In several studies, exosomes isolated from mesenchymal stem cells have been engineered to carry anti-inflammatory microRNAs, including miR-146a, and have shown neuroprotective effects in retinal degeneration models such as retinitis pigmentosa and diabetic retinopathy (Zhang et al., 2022). Moreover, astrocyte-derived exosomes have been explored for their intrinsic neuroprotective and anti‐angiogenic properties. For instance, retinal astrocyte-derived exosomes have been demonstrated to contain multiple anti-angiogenic molecules including endostatin, PEDF, and TIMP-1, which contribute to the suppression of choroidal neovascularization in laser-induced models (Mead & Chow, 2023; Romero et al., 2024). Although these studies primarily target neovascular AMD, their underlying mechanisms emphasize the utility of astrocyte-based exosome therapy in modulating critical retinal pathways. In the context of dry AMD, which is characterized by chronic RPE degeneration, oxidative stress, and complement system dysregulation, the strategy of utilizing exosomal delivery to target RPE dysfunction is supported by evidence that exosome‐mediated miRNA transfer can restore lysosomal function and reduce inflammatory cascades in retinal cells (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Guan et al., 2025). Additionally, complement dysregulation and increased complement factor expression are central features of dry AMD pathology, and prior studies have implicated exosomal cargo in modulating inflammatory and complement pathways (Guan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). Although direct clinical or extensive preclinical experience with astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a in dry AMD is limited, the analogous applications of MSC-derived exosomes carrying miR-146a establish an important precedent and provide a mechanistic rationale for further investigation (Zhang et al., 2022; Berber et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic mechanism of this candidate operates at multiple molecular levels, integrating the known functions of both miR-146a and exosomal delivery systems. miR-146a is recognized as a key negative regulator of inflammation through its ability to target components in the Toll-like receptor (TLR) and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling pathways. Specifically, miR-146a targets interleukin-1 receptor–associated kinase 1 (IRAK1) and TNF receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6), leading to a reduction in NF-κB activation and subsequent downregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Berber et al., 2017; ElShelmani et al., 2021). In the context of dry AMD, complement overactivation has been identified as a pivotal event contributing to RPE degeneration. Complement factor H (CFH) and complement factor B (CFB) play significant roles in regulating the alternative complement pathway, and dysregulation of these factors leads to excessive complement activation, resulting in increased levels of complement fragments such as C3a that promote inflammation and lysosomal stress (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021). The proposed mechanism asserts that miR-146a, delivered via astrocyte-derived exosomes, can penetrate the RPE cell layer and downregulate the transcription and/or translation of complement components such as CFH and CFB. By limiting the production of these factors, miR-146a effectively reduces the downstream formation of the inflammatory anaphylatoxin C3a, alleviating lysosomal overload and preserving the acidic lysosomal environment necessary for optimal activity of degradative enzymes like cathepsin D (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Zhang et al., 2022). This modulation of complement activity is essential because aberrant complement activation in the RPE has been linked to photoreceptor outer segment (POS) accumulation and impaired phagocytosis, which are hallmarks of dry AMD progression (Romero et al., 2024; Sanghani et al., 2022). Furthermore, exosomes themselves possess intrinsic targeting and cell–cell communication properties; their membrane proteins, such as tetraspanins (CD63, CD81) and other surface markers, facilitate uptake by recipient cells and can mediate tissue-specific homing to the RPE (Liu et al., 2023; Romero et al., 2024). The combination of miR-146a’s molecular action on inflammatory and complement pathways with the natural delivery proficiency of astrocyte-derived exosomes creates a synergistic effect that is expected to restore lysosomal integrity and enhance functional POS degradation in high-risk CFH backgrounds (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The expected therapeutic effect in the treatment of dry AMD is multilayered. In vitro studies utilizing RPE cell cultures derived from patient lines with high-risk CFH expression are anticipated to show that treatment with miR-146a-enriched astrocyte exosomes results in a significant downregulation of complement factors, notably CFH and CFB. This downregulation would be reflected in reduced levels of the complement activation fragment C3a, which is known to exacerbate inflammation and lysosomal dysfunction in RPE cells (Romero et al., 2024; Berber et al., 2017). As a direct consequence of complement normalization, lysosomal integrity is expected to be maintained through the preservation of an acidic pH environment and the restoration of cathepsin D activity. Cathepsin D plays a critical role in the degradation of POS material taken up by RPE cells during the daily process of photoreceptor renewal (Liu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022). Enhanced clearance of POS is hypothesized to reduce the accumulation of toxic waste products and drusen formation, a defining characteristic of dry AMD. In addition, the anti-inflammatory action of miR-146a should attenuate the chronic low-grade inflammation observed in the retinal microenvironment, thereby mitigating further RPE and photoreceptor damage (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2020).  
At the molecular level, the treatment is anticipated to modulate intracellular signaling cascades by reducing NF-κB–mediated transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines, which in turn helps to suppress the local inflammatory milieu and prevent further complement activation (Berber et al., 2017; ElShelmani et al., 2021). The exosomal vehicle ensures that miR-146a is delivered in a protected and concentrated form, which maximizes cellular uptake and preserves functional integrity during circulation. Given their natural ability to cross biological barriers, these astrocyte-derived exosomes are expected to efficiently reach the RPE layer, and this targeted delivery is crucial for achieving the desired therapeutic outcomes with minimal off-target effects (Guan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). Furthermore, the experimental assays based on RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD are designed to evaluate both the biological activity of the delivered miR-146a and the restoration of lysosomal function. Expected readouts include a decrease in complement factor mRNA and protein levels, improved lysosomal enzyme activity (especially cathepsin D), reduced accumulation of POS debris, and ultimately, preservation of RPE and photoreceptor viability (Guan et al., 2025; ElShelmani et al., 2021). These effects, if validated, could translate into a slowing of disease progression or even a reversal of certain pathological features in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
The candidate therapeutic of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a holds considerable promise for the treatment of dry AMD due to its innovative design and strong mechanistic rationale. One of the most significant strengths of this approach lies in its biomimetic nature. By harnessing exosomes derived from retinal astrocytes, the therapy benefits from inherent targeting properties that increase the likelihood of efficient delivery to the RPE, a key cell type implicated in dry AMD pathology (Romero et al., 2024; Mead & Chow, 2023). Furthermore, the use of miR-146a—an endogenous regulatory molecule with well-documented anti-inflammatory effects—adds an additional layer of specificity to the treatment by directly modulating the inflammatory milieu and complement dysregulation that are central to dry AMD (Berber et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022). This dual action, combining restoration of lysosomal integrity through improved POS degradation and suppression of complement-mediated inflammation, addresses two critical pathogenic processes simultaneously.  

However, despite its notable strengths, several challenges and uncertainties remain. First, while the therapeutic concept is strongly supported by preclinical studies involving MSC-derived exosomes and by literature demonstrating the beneficial effects of exosomal miRNAs in retinal diseases (Zhang et al., 2022; Du & Palczewski, 2022), the specific application of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched with miR-146a for dry AMD remains to be thoroughly evaluated. There is limited direct evidence in the literature showing that astrocyte-derived exosomes naturally enriched or engineered to carry miR-146a can downregulate complement factor expression in RPE cells in a clinically meaningful way (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023). This represents a gap in knowledge that would need to be addressed through rigorous preclinical investigation, including detailed dose–response studies and assessments of long-term efficacy and safety.  

Another potential weakness lies in the scalability and reproducibility of exosome isolation from astrocytes. Exosome production can vary depending on the source, the culture conditions, and the methods used for enrichment and purification. Manufacturing a consistent and high-quality exosome product that meets clinical grade standards is a well-recognized challenge in the field of exosome therapeutics (Liu et al., 2023; Guan et al., 2025). In addition, while exosomes are known for their low immunogenicity, the possibility of immune reactions, especially when they are over-engineered or when administered repeatedly, cannot be entirely discounted and will require careful evaluation (Romero et al., 2024).  

From a mechanistic standpoint, although the theoretical framework linking miR-146a with the downregulation of complement factors CFH and CFB is compelling, the precise molecular interactions within RPE cells must be validated by robust in vitro and in vivo experiments. Detailed studies are needed to confirm the extent to which miR-146a directly modulates these complement components, and whether additional targets or off-target effects might complicate the therapeutic outcome (Zhang et al., 2022; Berber et al., 2017). Furthermore, while the restoration of lysosomal function and POS degradation is a promising endpoint, the complexity of lysosomal biology in the context of chronic degenerative diseases such as dry AMD means that multifactorial interventions might be necessary. It will be essential to demonstrate that the observed improvements in lysosomal enzyme activity (e.g., cathepsin D) translate into meaningful clinical benefits, such as slowed disease progression or improved visual function (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Romero et al., 2024).  

In summary, the concept of using astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is innovative, leveraging the natural targeting, biocompatibility, and multi-functional capabilities of exosomes along with the potent anti-inflammatory and complement‐modulating properties of miR-146a. The preclinical evidence derived from analogous studies using MSC-derived exosomes and the general literature on exosomal miRNA therapies in retinal diseases provides a solid foundation for this approach (Zhang et al., 2022; Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2023). Nevertheless, the strategy will require comprehensive validation, including optimization of exosome isolation and engineering protocols, detailed mechanistic studies in relevant cellular models, and robust in vivo efficacy assessments in dry AMD animal models before clinical translation can be considered. With targeted efforts to address these challenges, this therapeutic candidate could represent a significant advance in the treatment of dry AMD, offering a precision medicine approach that directly tackles both complement overactivation and lysosomal dysfunction at the cellular level (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Guan et al., 2025; ElShelmani et al., 2021).

Overall, the combination of bioengineered exosomes and miR-146a offers mechanistic specificity and a novel route of administration that may overcome many of the limitations inherent in current dry AMD therapies, particularly those related to anti-VEGF treatments which are primarily indicated for wet AMD. While further preclinical investigations are essential to fully elucidate the pharmacodynamics, safety profile, and therapeutic window of this candidate, the approach holds promise as a next-generation drug candidate for dry AMD that could potentially improve patient outcomes by preserving retinal structure and function through the reestablishment of homeostatic cellular processes (Mead & Chow, 2023; Sanghani et al., 2022; Song et al., 2024).
