Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO‐Me) is a fully synthetic derivative of the naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid oleanolic acid. The parent molecule, oleanolic acid, is widely found in many plants and has been used for centuries in traditional medicine owing to its modest anti‐inflammatory and hepatoprotective properties. However, to overcome its relatively low intrinsic potency and poor pharmacokinetics, medicinal chemists modified oleanolic acid by introducing key structural changes. In particular, the synthesis of CDDO (2-cyano-3,12-dioxoolean-1,9-dien-28-oic acid) involved the installation of a cyano group at the C2 position and oxidation at positions C3 and C12, generating an electrophilic cyanoenone moiety; subsequent esterification at the C28 carboxyl group yielded bardoxolone methyl as the C28 methyl ester. These chemical modifications resulted in a molecule with two electrophilic Michael acceptor sites that are essential for its biological action, notably its ability to react reversibly with cysteine thiols in target proteins. Being part of the synthetic oleanane triterpenoids family, bardoxolone methyl falls into a class of compounds that has been extensively explored for their anti‐inflammatory, antioxidant, anticancer, and cytoprotective activities in various disease models (Borella et al., 2019).

This class of synthetic triterpenoids has historically been pursued to potentiate the natural but modest bioactivities of plant‐derived triterpenes such as oleanolic and ursolic acids. Early research aimed at enhancing anti‐inflammatory activity led to the discovery of potent derivatives such as CDDO, CDDO‐Im (the imidazolide derivative), and ultimately bardoxolone methyl. Their design was motivated by the need to generate highly potent, orally bioavailable agents capable of activating key cytoprotective pathways. The robust preclinical efficacy observed with these compounds in various models of oxidative stress, inflammation, and even tumorigenesis provided proof‐of‐concept for their use as drug candidates (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021). Consequently, bardoxolone methyl has emerged as a leading representative of this chemical class, notable for its finely tuned electrophilic reactivity and its ability to induce a broad spectrum of protective gene products.

Therapeutic History:  
Bardoxolone methyl has a well‐documented history of investigation in both preclinical and clinical settings across various therapeutic indications. Originally developed for its potent anti‐inflammatory and antioxidant properties, it was first investigated in oncology where its pro‐apoptotic and antiproliferative effects were characterized in multiple cancer cell types such as pancreatic, colorectal, ovarian, and breast cancer. Early preclinical studies demonstrated that at nanomolar and low micromolar concentrations, CDDO and its derivatives could exert robust cytoprotective effects via the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2‐related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, as well as induce cell cycle arrest and trigger apoptosis in cancer cells (Borella et al., 2019; Tanase et al., 2022).

Following its anticancer exploration, a serendipitous clinical observation during early oncology trials revealed that patients treated with bardoxolone methyl experienced improved renal function, as measured by an elevation in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). This finding prompted a pivot in therapeutic focus toward kidney diseases, particularly chronic kidney disease (CKD) associated with type 2 diabetes. The promising renoprotective data initially generated in Phase I oncology studies led to Phase II trials (such as the BEAM trial) where bardoxolone methyl displayed remarkable efficacy in increasing eGFR in CKD patients. However, in a subsequent Phase III study (the BEACON trial), concerns were raised after an unexpected increase in cardiovascular events, particularly heart failure, halted the trial. These mixed clinical outcomes have since spurred ongoing efforts to better understand and optimize the safety profile of bardoxolone methyl while leveraging its strong cytoprotective properties (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Sakashita et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).

Notably, while bardoxolone methyl has been extensively investigated in oncology and renal diseases, there is currently no record or published clinical trial data indicating that this compound has been used for treating dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or similar ocular conditions. Nonetheless, its underlying mechanism—primarily Nrf2 activation—is highly relevant to the pathobiology of dry AMD, given that oxidative stress and proteostasis imbalance are central to RPE cell dysfunction. Thus, while previous therapeutic applications have focused on systemic diseases, the repositioning of bardoxolone methyl to an ocular indication represents a scientifically plausible and innovative strategy that builds on its earlier demonstrated biochemical activities in other organ systems (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Bardoxolone methyl’s primary mode of action is its potent and selective activation of the Keap1/Nrf2/ARE (antioxidant response element) pathway. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytoplasm by its inhibitory binding partner Keap1, which targets Nrf2 for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl, owing to its electrophilic cyanoenone structure, covalently modifies reactive cysteine residues on Keap1 (including key sensors such as Cys151), thereby inhibiting its E3 ligase activity. This modification prevents the degradation of Nrf2, allowing it to accumulate and translocate into the nucleus (Hong et al., 2012; Mathis & Cui, 2016).

Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 dimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to ARE sequences in the promoter regions of various cytoprotective genes. This leads to the transcriptional induction of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxification enzymes, including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), glutathione S-transferases, and several molecular chaperones involved in protein folding and proteostasis. Through these gene products, bardoxolone methyl exerts robust antioxidant, anti‐inflammatory, and cytoprotective effects that help mitigate oxidative stress and repair cellular damage (Mathis & Cui, 2020; Tanase et al., 2022).

In addition to Nrf2‐mediated gene induction, bardoxolone methyl has been shown to modulate other signaling pathways that contribute to its anti‐inflammatory profile. For instance, it can inhibit NF-κB signaling, which reduces the transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines, and also affect pathways involving JAK/STAT and PI3K/Akt/mTOR, all of which have been implicated in the control of cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival (Sporn et al., 2011). The dual capacity to both upregulate protective gene networks and downregulate inflammatory signaling is central to the pharmacological action of bardoxolone methyl and underscores its potential to modulate cellular processes that are dysregulated in conditions characterized by oxidative and proteostatic stress (Cores et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014).

Furthermore, crystallographic and proteomic studies have provided molecular‐level evidence for the reversible Michael‐addition interaction between bardoxolone methyl and target cysteine residues on Keap1. This “dock and lock” mechanism ensures that the electrophilic reactivity of the compound is directed preferentially toward specific regulatory cysteines, thereby limiting non‐specific alkylation and supporting its relatively high potency as an Nrf2 activator (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
The hypothesis for repurposing bardoxolone methyl in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is grounded firmly in its ability to activate Nrf2 and thereby bolster the endogenous antioxidant defenses of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). In the RPE, oxidative damage is a pivotal pathomechanism that contributes to the accumulation of lipofuscin, impairment of autophagic flux, and ultimately, decreased phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). As Nrf2 plays a critical role in maintaining redox homeostasis within the RPE, its activation is expected to alleviate oxidative and proteostatic stress, thereby protecting critical functions such as phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation.

At an effective concentration in the submicromolar range (with an EC₅₀ estimated around 0.1 µM), bardoxolone methyl is anticipated to induce the transcription of genes such as HO-1 and NQO1 as well as chaperone proteins that ensure proper protein folding and degradation. The upregulation of these cytoprotective proteins may protect phagocytic receptors from oxidative modifications and preserve lysosomal enzymatic activity, which is essential for the degradation of ingested POS. This action is particularly crucial because impaired phagocytic function contributes to the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin and other debris in RPE cells—a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021).

Moreover, the robust activation of Nrf2 by bardoxolone methyl can help counterbalance the deficit in endogenous antioxidant capacity observed in the RPE of patients with dry AMD, as Nrf2 deficiency has been shown experimentally to exacerbate lipofuscin accumulation and autophagy blockade. Preclinical studies in non‐ocular systems have consistently demonstrated that treatment with CDDO‐Me leads to a marked increase in the expression of antioxidant genes and proteins that are implicated in both oxidative stress management and the maintenance of proteostasis (Hong et al., 2012; Sporn et al., 2011). Extrapolating from these findings, it is reasonable to expect that treatment with bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD cultures would result in a more effective clearance of POS by correcting the underlying oxidative imbalance and restoring lysosomal function. It is also plausible that enhanced expression of chaperones and stress‐response proteins would contribute to improved recycling of degraded photoreceptor material, thereby reducing the burden of intracellular debris (Cores et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014).

Chronic inflammation is increasingly recognized as a contributing factor to AMD progression, and the suppression of pro‐inflammatory mediators would be expected to create a more favorable cellular environment for tissue repair and maintenance of RPE function (Sporn et al., 2011). Collectively, by activating Nrf2 and modulating inflammatory signaling pathways, bardoxolone methyl is expected to restore the cellular homeostasis of RPE cells, leading to enhanced phagocytosis of POS and potentially slowing or even reversing the degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD.

Bardoxolone methyl represents an innovative and promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration, particularly given its well‐characterized ability to activate the Nrf2 pathway and trigger a potent antioxidant and proteostatic response. One clear strength of this compound is its robust preclinical and clinical profile in other indications; extensive studies in oncology and chronic kidney disease have established its capability to induce protective gene networks, coupled with a well‐defined mechanism of action that is directly applicable to combating oxidative stress—one of the central features of dry AMD pathogenesis (Borella et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
P110 is a synthetic, cell‐permeable inhibitory peptide specifically engineered to disrupt the pathological interaction between dynamin‐related protein 1 (Drp1) and its mitochondrial outer membrane receptor fission protein 1 (Fis1). It is synthesized via solid‐phase peptide synthesis methods and rational design strategies that mimic the native binding interface of these two proteins. As such, P110 belongs to the class of peptide-based mitochondrial fission inhibitors, a subclass of compounds that have been previously investigated in a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders, where aberrant mitochondrial fission is implicated in disease pathology. These types of compounds have historically been used experimentally to restore normal mitochondrial morphological dynamics and attenuate excessive fission triggered by oxidative stress. The concept builds upon evidence that an overactive fission process, largely mediated by elevated activity of Drp1 in response to cellular stressors, results in mitochondrial fragmentation, cytochrome c release, and subsequent cell death. In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which bear extremely high energy demands for functions such as photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis, proper mitochondrial network integrity is essential. The peptide’s cell-permeability and selective inhibition of the Drp1/Fis1 binding suggest that P110 can efficiently penetrate ocular tissues and modulate mitochondrial dynamics locally, offering a promising approach to preserve mitochondrial function in the diseased retina (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Numerous preclinical studies have investigated the modulation of mitochondrial dynamics in models of oxidative stress and neurodegeneration, often employing broad-spectrum inhibitors such as mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (Mdivi-1) or genetic silencing approaches using Drp1-specific siRNA. In several in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells—a human RPE cell line—excessive mitochondrial fission triggered by oxidative stress (for example, via hydrogen peroxide exposure) was effectively ameliorated by Drp1 inhibition. This intervention preserved mitochondrial structure, maintained ATP production, and increased cell viability, thereby preventing the morphological transition from tubular to fragmented mitochondria (Yako et al., 2021). Although these investigations have provided robust proof-of-concept evidence that targeting Drp1-mediated fission can be beneficial in preventing RPE dysfunction, most of the studies have not directly tested P110 peptide for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Instead, the literature has explored alternative approaches using compounds like Mdivi-1 and genetic knockdown modalities to decrease Drp1 activity, which indirectly supports the mechanistic rationale for using a targeted inhibitor like P110. The literature also shows that increased expression of mitochondrial fission factor (Mff) and elevated Drp1 levels in AMD donor tissues correlate with impaired mitochondrial homeostasis and defective phagocytosis in the RPE (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022). There remains, however, a gap in direct evidence for P110’s use in AMD despite its clear conceptual alignment with the therapeutic strategy of reducing pathological mitochondrial fission. Clinical trials have emerged that investigate mitochondrial fission inhibitors in ocular conditions, yet the available database queries indicate that while there is clinical interest in Drp1-targeting approaches, specific details on the P110 peptide remain sparse (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Thus, while the broader therapeutic paradigm—targeting aberrant mitochondrial fission—is well supported, P110 itself represents an innovative candidate that requires further preclinical validation in AMD-relevant models.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the pathological process underpinning excessive mitochondrial fission centers on the overactivation of Drp1, a GTPase that orchestrates mitochondrial scission. Under normal physiological conditions, Drp1 exists in the cytosol and is transiently recruited to the mitochondrial outer membrane by receptors such as Fis1, mitochondrial fission factor (Mff), and MiD49/MiD51. In response to oxidative and inflammatory stress—conditions known to be prevalent in the aging RPE and AMD—the interaction between Drp1 and Fis1 is upregulated, leading to excessive fission, mitochondrial fragmentation, and subsequent mitochondrial dysfunction. P110 is designed to selectively inhibit the Drp1/Fis1 binding interface, thereby attenuating the aberrant recruitment of Drp1 to the mitochondria. In doing so, it preserves the elongated and interconnected mitochondrial network, which is essential for optimal mitochondrial bioenergetics and the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Biochemically, inhibition of this interaction prevents the oligomerization of Drp1 on the mitochondrial surface, a process that is otherwise necessary for the formation of constriction rings that facilitate organelle division (Zhao et al., 2025). By blocking Drp1 recruitment, P110 indirectly maintains mitochondrial membrane potential and reduces the likelihood of cytochrome c release—a key event in the apoptosis cascade that is frequently observed in stressed RPE cells (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). Although many of the studies in the context of AMD have focused on Mdivi-1 as a Drp1 inhibitor, the specificity of P110 for the Drp1/Fis1 interaction might offer a distinct pharmacological profile, reducing off-target effects and preserving the physiological fission events necessary for maintaining overall mitochondrial quality control (Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021). Furthermore, the fact that mitochondrial fission and fusion processes are tightly integrated with mitochondrial biogenesis and mitophagy pathways supports the prospect that modulating this specific interaction may lead to a net improvement in mitochondrial dynamics without completely abolishing essential fission events (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Given the underlying hypothesis, the expected effect of P110 in AMD RPE cells would be to restore a balance in mitochondrial dynamics that has been disrupted by chronic oxidative stress. The assay proposed involves exposing cultured RPE cells, such as ARPE-19, to oxidative insults (e.g., H₂O₂) that would otherwise induce excessive Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission. P110’s mode of action is anticipated to specifically block the pathological protein-protein interaction between Drp1 and Fis1, thereby reducing the formation of excessively fragmented mitochondria and promoting the preservation or re-establishment of a tubular mitochondrial network. This intact network is critical for efficient ATP production, which in turn supports high-energy processes such as the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). POS phagocytosis is a metabolically demanding function that is crucial for photoreceptor renewal and overall retinal health. By maintaining ATP supply and preventing the release of pro-apoptotic factors (such as cytochrome c), P110 is expected to protect RPE cells from oxidative damage and improve cellular viability under stress conditions (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). Additionally, studies have demonstrated that mitochondrial fission inhibitors can lead to improved mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and enhanced cell survival under conditions of oxidative insult (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). In RPE cells, these improvements translate into a better capacity for POS uptake and metabolism, which are essential for sustaining the metabolic demands of the outer retina. Given that expression levels of Drp1 and its functional activity are elevated in AMD RPE cells, as evidenced by electron microscopy and proteomic analyses showing reduced mitochondrial numbers, diminished cristae, and defective fusion/fission ratios, the application of P110 is expected to counteract these detrimental changes by stabilizing the mitochondrial network (Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summarizing the overall evaluation of P110 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key points emerge from the literature. First, the mechanistic rationale underpinning P110’s mode of action is robust and well-aligned with current understanding of AMD pathophysiology. Excessive Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission has been implicated as a crucial driver of mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells—a hallmark of dry AMD. Several studies using alternative approaches such as pharmacological inhibition with Mdivi-1 or genetic knockdown via siRNA have consistently demonstrated that mitigating aberrant mitochondrial fission leads to improved mitochondrial integrity, preserved bioenergetic function, and enhanced cell viability in models of oxidative stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). This information directly supports the hypothesis that targeting the Drp1/Fis1 interaction, rather than globally inhibiting all Drp1 activity, could offer a more refined therapeutic approach with potentially fewer side effects. Such specificity is particularly appealing in the context of the retina where finely tuned mitochondrial dynamics are essential for high energy-demand processes like POS phagocytosis (Fisher et al., 2022).

One of the primary strengths of P110 lies in its cell-permeable peptide nature, which facilitates targeted intracellular delivery—a critical characteristic for therapies intended for ocular application. Its design, which specifically disrupts the interaction between Drp1 and Fis1, is predicated on the notion that pathological fission can be selectively blocked without interfering with the physiological fission necessary for regular mitochondrial turnover and repair. This specificity could, in theory, translate to a better safety profile compared to less selective inhibitors such as Mdivi-1 that may have off-target effects, including undesirable impacts on other aspects of mitochondrial function (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2025).

Despite the promising mechanistic rationale and potential for ocular development, there are notable weaknesses and challenges to be considered. The current literature does not yet offer direct preclinical or clinical evidence that P110 peptide itself has been used to treat dry AMD. Most existing studies have extrapolated the benefits of Drp1 inhibition from experiments involving Mdivi-1 or Drp1 knockdown in cellular models of RPE oxidative stress (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Therefore, while the concept of targeting Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission in AMD is well supported, the direct application of P110 remains largely theoretical at this point. This gap in the literature introduces uncertainty regarding the peptide’s pharmacokinetic properties, its stability in ocular tissues, and its potential immunogenic responses upon local administration in the eye.

Another potential limitation is the complex role of mitochondrial dynamics in cellular homeostasis. Although excessive fission in the context of oxidative stress is detrimental, mitochondrial fission is also a necessary process for mitophagy and the removal of damaged organelles. Some studies have indicated that a certain degree of fission may even be beneficial for cellular quality control, as it facilitates the segregation and subsequent removal of malfunctioning mitochondria (Skeie et al., 2021; Yako et al., 2021). The nuanced interplay between reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling and fission means that complete inhibition of fission—even if intended to be only pathological—could potentially have unintended consequences. It will be critical to determine whether P110’s selective inhibition of Drp1/Fis1 interaction can maintain the necessary balance between inhibiting excessive fission while still allowing physiological fission to contribute to normal mitophagy and mitochondrial turnover.

Furthermore, while the peptide’s cell-permeability is an advantage, peptide therapeutics in ocular applications face challenges related to delivery, degradation by ocular proteases, and potential issues with achieving sustained concentrations in the target tissues. Addressing these challenges may require the development of specialized drug delivery systems, such as intravitreal injections with sustained-release formulations or conjugation to nanoparticles, to ensure that adequate therapeutic levels of P110 are maintained at the retinal level over the necessary duration (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Additional practical concerns include the need for rigorous in vivo studies in relevant animal models of dry AMD to assess not only the efficacy in preserving mitochondrial function and POS phagocytosis in RPE cells but also the overall impact on retinal structure and visual function. Currently, many studies have been limited to in vitro models using ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress conditions. Although these models provide valuable mechanistic insights, they do not fully recapitulate the complex interplay of cellular and systemic factors that contribute to AMD in vivo. The therapeutic potential of P110 will need to be evaluated in animal models that mimic the pathophysiological conditions of dry AMD, where factors such as chronic low-grade inflammation, complement activation, and cumulative oxidative damage play significant roles (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

In addition to efficacy and safety concerns, the regulatory landscape for peptide therapeutics in ocular indications should be considered. The development of P110 for dry AMD will require detailed pharmacodynamic and toxicological evaluations to satisfy regulatory requirements. While the peptide’s mechanism—targeting a well-characterized protein-protein interaction—provides a clear scientific rationale, the path toward clinical translation is contingent on demonstrating not only mechanistic efficacy but also an acceptable safety profile in both preclinical toxicology studies and early-phase clinical trials (Fisher et al., 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

In conclusion, the comprehensive literature review supports the notion that targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, specifically through the inhibition of Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission, is a highly promising therapeutic avenue for dry AMD. P110, as a selective inhibitor of the Drp1/Fis1 interaction, is well poised within this framework. The candidate is grounded in a strong mechanistic rationale that links excessive mitochondrial fission to reduced ATP production, impaired POS phagocytosis, and ultimately, RPE cell dysfunction—a cascade of events that underlies the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022).

The inherent advantages of a peptide-based therapeutic, including its specificity and cell-permeability, are particularly attractive for ocular drug development, where targeted delivery and minimal off-target effects are crucial. Nonetheless, notable weaknesses remain that must be addressed before P110 can be considered a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The absence of direct experimental data with P110 in AMD models, the complex nature of mitochondrial dynamics where inhibition of fission must be carefully balanced to avoid impairing critical mitophagy processes, and potential challenges associated with peptide stability and delivery in the ocular environment represent significant hurdles. These challenges underscore the necessity for further preclinical investigations, including in vivo efficacy and safety studies in animal models that recapitulate the chronic oxidative stress and metabolic derangements characteristic of AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).

Ultimately, while the theoretical basis for P110’s use in dry AMD is compelling and supported by a considerable body of literature showing beneficial effects of mitochondrial fission inhibition in RPE cells, advancing this candidate will require a coordinated effort to fill the current gaps in experimental evidence. Future studies should focus on validating the efficacy of P110 in terms of restoring mitochondrial dynamics, preserving ATP production, and ultimately improving POS phagocytosis in both cell culture and animal models of AMD. If these studies yield positive results, P110 has the potential to become an important component of a new generation of therapies aimed at addressing the mitochondrial dysfunction that lies at the heart of dry AMD pathophysiology (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).

Overall, the research direction for P110 is promising given the established relationship between mitochondrial dysfunction and AMD. With its targeted mechanism of action and a strong conceptual basis rooted in the modulation of mitochondrial dynamics, P110 stands as a high-potential candidate. However, careful optimization of dosing, formulation, and delivery, as well as comprehensive preclinical validation, is essential before this therapeutic candidate can be reliably advanced into clinical trials. Should these hurdles be successfully overcome, P110 could not only provide substantial therapeutic benefit by preserving RPE function in dry AMD but also serve as a model for developing other targeted mitochondrial therapies in ocular neurodegeneration (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide, a water‐soluble form of vitamin B3, is a naturally occurring compound that plays a critical role in cellular metabolism by serving as a precursor for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺) synthesis. It is available both through dietary sources and chemical synthesis and has been produced at high purity for research purposes (Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. N4126). Nicotinamide belongs to the vitamin B3 class of compounds, which have been extensively used as nutritional supplements and metabolic regulators; these compounds are well recognized for their role in the salvage pathway that replenishes NAD⁺ levels in cells. The therapeutic candidate under consideration is repurposed with the hypothesis that at a concentration of 10 mM, nicotinamide will boost intracellular NAD⁺ pools and enhance the activity of NAD⁺‐dependent enzymes, such as sirtuins, leading to improved mitochondrial function and increased deacetylation of autophagy regulators. Such effects are expected to restore phagocytic function, specifically the photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation, in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cultures pertinent to dry age‐related macular degeneration (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, nicotinamide has been investigated in various preclinical and clinical settings for its potential neuroprotective effects and its capacity to modulate cellular metabolism. In the context of ocular health, several studies have demonstrated that nicotinamide supplementation can enhance NAD⁺ levels and improve mitochondrial function in retinal cells. Preclinical studies have reported that this vitamin not only supports retinal ganglion cell health in glaucoma models but also shows promise in improving photoreceptor and RPE function in models of age-related macular degeneration (Gemae et al., 2024). Although there remains limited direct clinical experience with nicotinamide in dry AMD, the compound has been a subject of interest in related ocular conditions due to its favorable safety profile and widespread use in other age-related and mitochondrial dysfunction settings (Gemae et al., 2024). More recent investigations have focused on its ability to rescue mitochondrial deficits and restore autophagic flux in RPE cells, with data indicating that in models of CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE, nicotinamide can ameliorate lysosomal processing and POS degradation problems (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). This body of evidence, compounded with its extensive historical use as a nutritional supplement, supports the rationale for repurposing nicotinamide as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, nicotinamide exerts its effects primarily through its role as a key precursor in the NAD⁺ salvage pathway. In this pathway, nicotinamide is converted to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) via the enzyme nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), and subsequently to NAD⁺ by NMN adenylyltransferase. NAD⁺, in turn, is an essential co-factor for numerous enzymes involved in energy metabolism and cellular homeostasis, most notably the sirtuin family of NAD⁺-dependent deacetylases (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Sirtuins, such as SIRT1 and SIRT3, play a pivotal role in mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and regulation of autophagy by deacetylating key transcription factors and enzymes that control metabolic stress responses (Gemae et al., 2024). In RPE cells, increased NAD⁺ levels facilitate the activation of these sirtuins, which then deacetylate a range of targets including histones and autophagy regulators, leading to improved mitochondrial structure and function, enhanced energy production, and the promotion of efficient autophagic and lysosomal degradation pathways (Gemae et al., 2024). Furthermore, the improved mitochondrial function translates into a better cellular energy state, providing the necessary ATP required for high-energy processes such as POS phagocytosis. Experimentally, administration of nicotinamide has been shown to yield a two-fold increase in NAD⁺ levels in ARPE-19 cells, thereby confirming its ability to augment the cellular bioenergetic capacity (Hazim et al., 2022). This mechanism also intersects with the regulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, as enhanced mitochondrial function and sirtuin activity contribute to lower oxidative stress, a known contributor to cellular senescence and dysfunction in the aging retina (Gemae et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the current proposal is that nicotinamide, administered at a concentration of 10 mM in vitro, will significantly increase NAD⁺ levels in RPE cells, thereby enhancing sirtuin activity and downstream mitochondrial function. This boost in NAD⁺ is expected to promote deacetylation of autophagy regulators, which will, in turn, normalize the autophagic flux and facilitate the effective degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE. In models of dry AMD, where phagocytosis deficits and impaired proteostasis are key pathological features, the restoration of autophagy and mitochondrial activity is anticipated to ameliorate cellular senescence and maintain retinal homeostasis (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Data from previous studies suggest that in aging RPE, reduced NAMPT expression is linked to decreased NAD⁺ levels and compromised SIRT1 function, leading to cellular senescence and defective mitochondrial dynamics (Jadeja et al., 2018). By contrast, nicotinamide supplementation helps to reverse these effects, as evidenced by restored NAD⁺ content and reactivation of sirtuins that enable degradation of accumulated defective cellular components, thereby improving lysosomal enzyme processing and phagocytosis (Jadeja et al., 2018). Moreover, enhanced mitochondrial metabolism has been correlated with improved RPE differentiation and the maintenance of a polarized epithelial phenotype, critical factors in ensuring effective POS phagocytosis and overall retinal health (Hazim et al., 2022). Thus, the expected outcome is that nicotinamide treatment will correct metabolic impairments, reduce oxidative stress, and restore phagocytic efficiency in dry AMD cultures, which are all essential for halting or even reversing disease progression (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
Nicotinamide emerges as a highly promising therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on its multi-faceted mechanism of action and extensive preclinical evidence supporting its role in maintaining retinal health. One of the primary strengths of nicotinamide is its excellent safety profile and widespread historical use as a nutritional supplement, which significantly lowers the risk associated with its repurposing (Gemae et al., 2024). Its ability to augment NAD⁺ levels and activate sirtuins directly addresses several key pathological processes in dry AMD, including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and impaired autophagy. Experimental findings have consistently shown that increased NAD⁺ levels, mediated by nicotinamide or its analogues such as NMN, correlate with reduced cellular senescence and improved lysosomal and mitochondrial function in RPE cells (Jadeja et al., 2018).

Moreover, the convergence of multiple lines of evidence—from studies detailing NAMPT decline in aging RPE, to those demonstrating the restoration of NAD⁺ and sirtuin activity by nicotinamide—provides a robust biochemical rationale for its use in combating dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024). The ability of nicotinamide to enhance mitochondrial respiration in ARPE-19 cells and primary human fetal RPE cells further underscores its potential in promoting a healthy, polarized RPE phenotype capable of efficient POS phagocytosis (Hazim et al., 2022). These studies also suggest that improved mitochondrial metabolism is closely linked to enhanced proteostasis and autophagic clearance of damaged cellular components—an outcome that is particularly relevant given the known deficits in autophagy and lysosomal processing observed in dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024).

However, while the preclinical data are encouraging, several challenges must be acknowledged. One potential weakness lies in the translation of in vitro findings to in vivo therapeutic efficacy. The concentration of 10 mM nicotinamide used in cell culture experiments may not directly correspond to achievable or sustainable therapeutic levels in the human retina. Moreover, while nicotinamide is known to boost NAD⁺ synthesis, there is a nuanced balance in its effects on sirtuin activity; in certain contexts, excessive nicotinamide has been reported to inhibit sirtuins, suggesting that dosing and timing will be critical parameters that require careful optimization (Will-Orrego, 2020). There is also the inherent challenge of the multifactorial nature of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired autophagy are only parts of a complex network of pathological events that include inflammatory signaling, extracellular matrix alterations, and genetic predispositions. Thus, while nicotinamide addresses several of these pathways, it may need to be combined with other therapeutic agents to achieve a comprehensive treatment effect (Gemae et al., 2024; Will-Orrego, 2020).

Another important consideration is the need for more extensive clinical studies. Although nicotinamide’s safety profile is well established in the context of dietary supplementation and its use in other neurological and ocular conditions, robust clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD are lacking (Gemae et al., 2024; Lin, 2020). Future research will need to focus not only on the pharmacokinetics and optimal dosing strategies in human subjects but also on precise biomarkers indicating the restoration of NAD⁺ metabolism, mitochondrial function, and POS phagocytosis. Furthermore, mechanistic studies that dissect the interactions between nicotinamide-driven NAD⁺ elevation and the downstream modulation of autophagy regulators will be essential to confirm the proposed mode of action and to identify any potential off-target effects.

Overall, the repurposing of nicotinamide for dry AMD presents several compelling advantages. Its established safety, low cost, and known biochemical mechanisms strongly support its potential as a therapeutic candidate. Preclinical evidence indicates that nicotinamide not only restores NAD⁺ levels but also reactivates sirtuin pathways, thereby mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction and defective autophagy that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. These effects could translate into improved cellular proteostasis and enhanced POS phagocytosis, ultimately preserving retinal integrity and visual function (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Nevertheless, the path forward will require careful dose optimization and rigorous clinical validation to ensure that the in vitro benefits observed translate into meaningful clinical outcomes. In summary, despite the challenges associated with translating cell-based results into human therapy, nicotinamide remains an attractive candidate whose mechanism, historical use, and preclinical successes justify further investigation as a potential treatment for dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Lin, 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB202190 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor belonging to the pyridinyl imidazole class of compounds. Originally discovered through rigorous cell‐based phenotypic screens aimed at identifying agents with anti‐inflammatory properties, SB202190 was developed to selectively inhibit p38 mitogen‐activated protein kinase (MAPK), particularly the α and β isoforms. The molecule was first characterized using radiolabeled ligand binding studies, which confirmed its ability to bind the ATP‐binding pocket of p38 MAPK and suppress its catalytic function (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). Being available commercially (e.g., Sigma‐Aldrich Cat. No. SML0687), SB202190 has been widely used as a biochemical tool to dissect the role of p38 in cellular stress and inflammatory responses. This class of compounds, including SB203580 as a closely related analogue, is recognized for its ability to modulate intracellular signaling cascades under various stress conditions. They have been broadly used in research settings to probe the molecular basis of cytokine production, cell differentiation, apoptosis, and cytoskeletal regulation (Young, 2013; Maugeri et al., 2021). The candidate under discussion is being repurposed with the hypothesis that its high potency against p38α/β—exhibiting an IC₅₀ of approximately 40 nM—can be leveraged to correct stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling defects and improve the phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative stress conditions that mimic the pathophysiology of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Liu et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, SB202190 has been predominantly employed as a research reagent to interrogate the role of p38 MAPK signaling in various cell types and disease models. In the context of ocular studies, SB202190, similar to its analogue SB203580, has been used to examine fibrotic responses, cell migration, and cytokine production in RPE cells. For instance, several in vitro studies have demonstrated that inhibition of p38 MAPK by SB202190 effectively reduces TGF‐β2–induced extracellular matrix (ECM) production (specifically collagen type I and fibronectin synthesis), which serves as an experimental surrogate for fibrotic remodeling observed in retinal degenerative conditions (Saika et al., 2005). Moreover, experiments using ARPE‐19 human RPE cells have revealed that SB202190 can reverse abnormal cell migration and reduce the transformation of RPE cells into fibroblast‐like cells in models of proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) (Saika et al., 2005). Although these models do not directly replicate dry AMD, they capture key aspects of RPE dysfunction, such as cytoskeletal disorganization and aberrant ECM deposition, which are also implicated in the progression of AMD. Beyond ocular research, p38 MAPK inhibitors have been investigated in other pathologies characterized by chronic inflammation and stress‐induced cellular dysfunction, including rheumatoid arthritis and muscular dystrophies (Brennan et al., 2021; Hirosawa et al., 2009). However, to date, clinical applications of SB202190 itself have not been pursued, and its use has remained restricted to preclinical experimental studies, thereby providing both a strong mechanistic rationale and a cautionary note regarding its translational potential (Federspiel et al., 2023; Young, 2013). Importantly, while numerous studies have elucidated p38 MAPK’s involvement in retinal injury and oxidative stress responses, there is limited direct clinical evidence supporting the use of SB202190 for treating dry AMD, and its application in this indication remains strictly hypothetical at this stage (Moustardas et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB202190 is known to selectively target the ATP‐binding pocket of p38 MAPK, thereby inhibiting its enzymatic activity and preventing the phosphorylation of downstream substrates that are pivotal to stress‐induced signaling cascades. Under normal conditions, p38 MAPK becomes activated through dual phosphorylation on specific threonine and tyrosine residues within its activation loop. Once activated, p38 MAPK stimulates various substrates, including transcription factors (e.g., cFos) and regulatory proteins involved in the control of cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and inflammatory mediator production (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). In RPE cells, activation of p38 MAPK has been linked to cytoskeletal rearrangements that lead to stress‐induced cellular defects; these include formation of abnormal actin structures and impaired formation of phagocytic cups necessary for the internalization of POS (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). In the experimental setting, SB202190 has been shown to effectively block the TGF‐β2 mediated phosphorylation of p38, thereby reducing the transcriptional activity of Smad3/4 complexes without impacting the initial receptor‐mediated phosphorylation events of Smads2/3. This mechanism suggests that SB202190 acts downstream of TGF‐β receptor activation, interfering with p38‐dependent enhancement of transcription factor complex formation and nuclear translocation, which in turn can dampen pathological ECM production and abnormal cell migration (Saika et al., 2005). Additionally, literature indicates that stress‐activated p38 signaling contributes to the senescence of RPE cells by regulating the senescence‐associated secretory phenotype (SASP) through modulation of p53 and NF‐κB pathways (Liu et al., 2025). By inhibiting p38 MAPK, SB202190 is hypothesized to replicate the protective effects of endogenous negative regulators such as DUSP4, which dephosphorylate and inactivate p38 MAPK, ultimately reducing RPE cell senescence and maintaining cellular homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025). It is noteworthy that p38 MAPK signaling is intricately intertwined with other MAPK family members, and some studies have reported that SB202190, particularly at higher doses, exhibits a biphasic response where alternative signaling pathways (such as MEK/ERK) may become upregulated, emphasizing the importance of careful dose optimization in any therapeutic application (Wang et al., 2024; Hirosawa et al., 2009). Thus, the mechanism of action of SB202190 involves a highly specific inhibition of p38α/β kinase activity, which is expected to restore normal actin dynamics and cytoskeletal organization in RPE cells, thereby facilitating proper phagosome formation and efficient POS uptake under oxidative stress conditions akin to those found in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The primary hypothesis driving the repurposing of SB202190 for dry AMD is that inhibition of p38α/β in RPE cells will reduce stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling defects and thereby improve the phagocytic internalization of photoreceptor outer segments. Under oxidative stress conditions, such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) in in vitro models using ARPE‐19 cells, activation of p38 MAPK is known to mediate cytoskeletal disorganization and promote aberrant cell migration, processes that are deleterious to the RPE’s phagocytic function (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). By inhibiting p38 MAPK with SB202190 at a low nanomolar concentration (approximately 40 nM), it is anticipated that the compound will reduce the phosphorylation of p38, thereby preventing the downstream activation of stress‐responsive transcription factors and proteins responsible for actin remodeling (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). In doing so, SB202190 is expected to “normalize” the actin cytoskeletal dynamics in H₂O₂‐treated ARPE‐19 cells, thus facilitating the re‐establishment of properly organized phagocytic cups required for POS ingestion—a process critical for photoreceptor maintenance and overall retinal homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025; Saika et al., 2005). In parallel, inhibition of p38 MAPK may downregulate pro‐fibrotic and pro‐senescent signaling pathways (e.g., those mediated by TGF‐β2, p53, and NF‐κB), therefore limiting the aberrant deposition of ECM components and improving the overall cellular microenvironment (Liu et al., 2025; Saika et al., 2005). As a result, the expected effect of SB202190 in the assay proposed would be a significant improvement in phagosome internalization of POS under oxidative conditions, combined with a reduction in the markers of cytoskeletal stress and cell senescence. Moreover, enhanced phagocytic activity by RPE cells could mitigate pathological features of dry AMD, such as drusen formation and eventual RPE degeneration, thereby potentially slowing disease progression (Moustardas et al., 2023; Du et al., 2010). The compound’s effect is further anticipated to extend to modulation of inflammatory cytokine release, given the well‐established role of p38 MAPK in regulating cytokine production, thus providing a dual benefit by both preserving cytoskeletal integrity and reducing chronic, low‐grade inflammation in the retina (Liu et al., 2025; Kyosseva, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
Evaluating the potential of SB202190 as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD involves weighing both the strengths and the inherent challenges associated with targeting the p38 MAPK pathway in the RPE. One of the major strengths of SB202190 is its well‐characterized mechanism of action as a selective inhibitor of p38α/β, which is pivotal in mediating stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling, inflammation, and cellular senescence in RPE cells. The compound has demonstrated robust in vitro anti‐fibrotic and anti‐migratory effects in ARPE‐19 cell models that mirror key features of RPE dysfunction observed in dry AMD (Saika et al., 2005). Furthermore, the concept of normalizing actin dynamics to enhance phagocytic cup formation and subsequent POS uptake is highly attractive, given that impaired phagocytosis is a core feature driving the degeneration observed in dry AMD (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). The protective role played by endogenous regulators like DUSP4, which deactivates p38 MAPK and preserves RPE integrity, supports the rationale for a pharmacological approach that mimics this effect (Liu et al., 2025). Additionally, numerous studies have shown that p38 MAPK inhibitors can modulate inflammatory responses and reduce ECM deposition; such effects are promising in the context of retinal diseases where chronic inflammation and fibrosis exacerbate degenerative processes (Moustardas et al., 2023; Saika et al., 2005).

However, several weaknesses and potential caveats must be thoroughly considered. First, the p38 MAPK pathway exhibits complex, context‐dependent behavior in RPE cells. There is evidence suggesting that, under certain circumstances, p38 MAPK activation can be cytoprotective by facilitating adaptive stress responses, such as the upregulation of antioxidant defenses (Pocrnich et al., 2009). This duality indicates that complete or prolonged inhibition of p38 MAPK may inadvertently dampen protective signaling, potentially leading to adverse outcomes. Additionally, published studies have documented that SB202190, when used at higher concentrations, can show biphasic responses or off‐target effects that might include the unintended activation of alternative MAPK pathways (Wang et al., 2024; Hirosawa et al., 2009). This underscores the critical need for precise dose optimization and comprehensive pharmacodynamic studies to define a therapeutic window where the beneficial effects on cytoskeletal remodeling and phagocytosis are maximized while the risks of impairing physiological stress responses are minimized.

Furthermore, while the preclinical literature provides substantial mechanistic insights and supportive data from retinal injury models—particularly in contexts such as PVR—the clinical translation of these findings to dry AMD remains unproven. SB202190 has not been advanced into clinical trials for retinal degenerative diseases, and its application has thus far been confined to experimental paradigms (Kim et al., 2021; Kyosseva, 2016). Therefore, any proposal to repurpose SB202190 for dry AMD must be accompanied by robust in vivo efficacy studies using animal models that faithfully recapitulate the chronic, multifactorial nature of the disease. Moreover, the impact of SB202190 on other critical RPE functions, such as phagocytosis of POS under normal conditions and cytoskeletal dynamics related to cell adhesion and migration, needs to be extensively characterized to avoid unintended disruption of essential homeostatic processes (Kim et al., 2021; Kyosseva, 2016).

Another consideration is the limitation inherent to the use of SB202190 as a research tool rather than a clinical‐grade pharmaceutical compound. Its pharmacokinetic and safety profiles have been characterized in experimental contexts, but there is a lack of clinical data regarding potential ocular toxicity, bioavailability, and long‐term impact on retinal structure and function (Federspiel et al., 2023; Young, 2013). The multifaceted role of p38 MAPK in the retina—spanning inflammatory cytokine production, regulation of apoptosis, and cytoskeletal dynamics—means that a fine balance must be maintained; excessive suppression could lead to undesired consequences such as impaired wound healing or compromised cell survival under stress. As such, a detailed understanding of the dose‐response relationship and the temporal dynamics of p38 inhibition in specific RPE subpopulations will be essential.

In summary, SB202190 presents as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on strong mechanistic rationale and preclinical evidence supporting its ability to modulate pathological pathways implicated in RPE dysfunction. Its capacity to inhibit p38α/β with high potency, restore actin dynamics under oxidative conditions, and improve phagocytic function aligns well with the therapeutic goals of preserving RPE integrity and retinal homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the dualistic nature of p38 MAPK signaling—with its capacity to mediate both deleterious and protective responses—poses a significant challenge that mandates careful and comprehensive preclinical evaluation. The candidate’s strengths reside in its well‐characterized inhibitory activity, established use in modulating fibrotic and inflammatory responses in ocular models, and its potential to replicate the endogenous protective functions mediated by regulators such as DUSP4 (Liu et al., 2025). Conversely, the weaknesses center on potential off‐target effects, the risk of inadvertently suppressing adaptive stress responses, and the absence of clinical studies directly addressing dry AMD.

Overall, while SB202190 holds promise based on its molecular mode of action and supportive in vitro data regarding cytoskeletal normalization and phagocytosis, the translational viability for dry AMD will ultimately depend on rigorous dosing studies, long‐term safety assessments, and demonstration of efficacy in animal models that capture the chronic oxidative and inflammatory milieu of the human retina (Moustardas et al., 2023; Saika et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2024). Only through such comprehensive studies can we adequately determine whether SB202190’s benefits outweigh its potential risks and if it can be successfully repurposed as a therapeutic intervention to mitigate the progression of dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB431542 is a well‐characterized, synthetic small molecule inhibitor originally developed through medicinal chemistry efforts by researchers at GlaxoSmithKline. Its chemical structure, formally denoted as 4-(5-benzo[1,3]dioxol-5-yl-4-pyridin-2-yl-1H-imidazol-2-yl)-benzamide, incorporates a benzodioxole moiety linked to a pyridyl-imidazol core and terminated by a benzamide group, placing it within the imidazole class of compounds (Laping et al., 2002). SB431542 belongs to the class of transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) type I receptor kinase inhibitors (commonly referred to as ALK5 inhibitors) that inhibit ATP-dependent receptor activation. Initially designed as an improvement over less-selective kinase inhibitors—such as early p38 MAPK inhibitors that exhibited off-target ALK5 inhibition—SB431542 emerged from a rational structure–activity relationship (SAR) campaign aimed at optimizing both potency and selectivity (Laping et al., 2002). Its discovery has been pivotal in establishing a molecular tool for dissecting TGFβ signaling, and its chemical synthesis reflects a focused effort on achieving high-affinity, ATP-competitive inhibition of the TGFβ receptor. This compound has been extensively used in preclinical research to study fibrotic mechanisms and cellular differentiation, thereby marking its reputation as a “gold standard” in TGFβ pathway inhibition (Laping et al., 2002).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SB431542 is primarily rooted in its application as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. In numerous preclinical studies, SB431542 has been consistently used to inhibit TGFβ-induced processes such as extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis, Smad protein activation, and the induction of a fibrotic phenotype in various cell types including renal epithelial cells, fibroblasts, and even certain cancer cell models (Laping et al., 2002). Biochemical studies have shown that SB431542 effectively blocks the phosphorylation of Smad3 with an IC50 of approximately 94 nM, thereby preventing the downstream transcriptional activation of cytokines and matrix proteins (Laping et al., 2002). Its anti-fibrotic effects have been extensively characterized in in vitro assays, where it reduced the expression of collagen I α1, fibronectin, and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) mRNA, thus providing compelling evidence that the compound modulates TGFβ-induced ECM remodeling (Laping et al., 2002).

While SB431542 has been applied in many experimental models to study pathways implicated in fibrotic diseases such as glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, liver cirrhosis, and pulmonary fibrosis, there is scant direct evidence of its historical use in ocular pathologies, particularly dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Akhund et al., 2023; Nyati et al., 2011). However, TGFβ signaling has been implicated in retinal pathologies and in the mesenchymal transition of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells from which some studies have emerged using general TGFβ inhibitors to reverse such pathological changes (Radeke et al., 2015). Although SB431542 itself has not been used in clinical trials for AMD, its mechanistic profile and reported efficacies in other fibrotic and ECM remodeling contexts make it a promising candidate for repurposing to address the abnormal matrix remodeling observed in dry AMD. Preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues have established that targeted inhibition of TGFβ signaling leads to substantial reductions in fibrotic markers, suggesting that similar approaches could mitigate Bruch membrane (BrM) alterations in AMD (Laping et al., 2002).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB431542 functions as an ATP-competitive inhibitor selectively targeting the kinase domain of the TGFβ type I receptor (TGFβRI, also known as ALK5). Its mechanism of action centers on binding to the ATP-binding pocket of TGFβRI, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of key intracellular effectors, primarily the Smad2 and Smad3 proteins (Laping et al., 2002). In normal TGFβ signaling, binding of the ligand (e.g., TGFβ1) to its receptors induces the formation of a heteromeric complex consisting of TGFβRI and TGFβRII, leading to the phosphorylation and activation of Smad2/3. These phosphorylated Smad proteins then form a complex with Smad4, translocate to the nucleus, and activate the transcription of pro-fibrotic genes, including those involved in ECM protein synthesis such as collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002).

Detailed molecular interaction studies have revealed that SB431542 makes critical hydrogen bonding contacts within the ATP-binding site of TGFβRI. For example, the benzodioxol moiety is reported to form a hydrogen bond with the amide nitrogen of His283, while additional interactions with Lys232 and other hydrophobic residues stabilize the inhibitor within the binding pocket (Leonardo-Sousa et al., 2025). This precise molecular engagement confers its high selectivity, as even minor substitutions in the binding region—such as mutations at the gatekeeper residue—can significantly alter inhibitor efficacy (Laping et al., 2002; Leonardo-Sousa et al., 2025). Furthermore, while SB431542 shows potent inhibition against ALK5, it also inhibits closely related receptors such as ALK4 and ALK7 with only modest differences in potency (IC50 for ALK4 is approximately 140 nM), and it exhibits negligible activity against BMP-activated receptors (ALK2, ALK3, and ALK6) (Laping et al., 2002). This selective inhibition ensures that the canonical TGFβ/Smad pathway is targeted without significantly perturbing other pathways that could be essential for cellular homeostasis, such as the BMP signaling cascade (Nyati et al., 2011; Akhund et al., 2023).

In addition to its inhibition of Smad2/3 phosphorylation, SB431542 has been shown to disrupt the subsequent nuclear translocation of these transcription factors, thereby halting the transcription of downstream ECM components. Such inhibition is critical because overactivation of the TGFβ pathway is a central driver in fibrotic diseases and leads to excessive deposition of ECM proteins, which in turn contribute to tissue stiffness and impaired cellular function (Laping et al., 2002). Overall, the molecular mechanism of SB431542 is well-delineated; its high selectivity for TGFβRI and the resulting blockade of Smad-mediated transcription form the foundation for its potential use in addressing aberrant ECM remodeling.

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis for repurposing SB431542 in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is built on the concept that excessive TGFβ signaling within the retinal microenvironment leads to an abnormal accumulation and remodeling of ECM components in the Bruch membrane (BrM). In the context of dry AMD, such ECM changes are believed to increase membrane stiffness and disrupt the diffusion of critical phagocytic ligands—specifically MFGE8 (Milk Fat Globule Epidermal Growth Factor 8) and Gas6—which play key roles in facilitating the integrin αvβ5-mediated binding and uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Radeke et al., 2015).

By inhibiting TGFβRI, SB431542 is expected to block the TGFβ-driven phosphorylation of Smad proteins, thereby directly reducing the transcription of genes that encode for fibrotic and ECM-related proteins such as collagen I α1, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002). In doing so, SB431542 should restore a more balanced ECM composition in the BrM. This normalization of ECM deposition is anticipated to reduce BrM stiffness, thereby enhancing the diffusion of phagocytic ligands like MFGE8 and Gas6 across the membrane. The improved ligand diffusion is expected to restore the optimal microenvironment required for integrin αvβ5 on the RPE surface to effectively bind and internalize POS, a process that is critically impaired in dry AMD (Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011).

Furthermore, by attenuating the fibrotic response within the retina, SB431542 may help preserve the native architecture and function of the RPE layer. This indirect modulation of phagocytosis, achieved through the normalization of ECM characteristics, represents a novel therapeutic angle that bridges the gap between ECM pathology and receptor-mediated cellular processes. In essence, the expected effect of SB431542 is a dual benefit: first, it directly inhibits pathological TGFβ signaling to reduce further fibrotic damage, and second, it indirectly normalizes phagocytic function by restoring the proper presentation of ligands critical for RPE-mediated clearance of POS (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015).

At the cellular and molecular level, the proposed assay is likely to measure a reduction in fibrotic markers (e.g., collagen I α1, fibronectin) and an improvement in assays of POS binding and internalization by RPE cells. Given that RPE cells express integrin αvβ5 and are responsive to TGFβ signaling, the application of SB431542 should result in a shift from a fibrotic, mesenchymal phenotype towards a more differentiated epithelial state that is conducive to normal phagocytic activity (Radeke et al., 2015; Akhund et al., 2023). This outcome would be mechanistically consistent with the known roles of TGFβ in modulating ECM dynamics and cellular differentiation. Consequently, if the hypothesis holds true, SB431542 would not only prevent further ECM deposition and stiffening of the BrM but would also support the resolution of existing pathological ECM alterations, thereby improving the overall homeostasis of the retinal microenvironment.

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of SB431542 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD requires careful consideration of its well-established biochemical profile alongside the translational challenges emerging from its current use primarily as a research tool. On the positive side, SB431542 is a potent and selective inhibitor of TGFβRI, with extensive preclinical evidence demonstrating its capacity to block TGFβ-induced Smad2/3 phosphorylation and consequently reduce the expression of fibrotic markers (Laping et al., 2002). Its high potency (with an IC50 in the low nanomolar range) and favorable selectivity profile—particularly with more than 100-fold selectivity over p38 MAPK and minimal activity against BMP receptors—render it an attractive candidate for targeted modulation of TGFβ signaling in tissues where fibrosis is a major pathogenic factor (Laping et al., 2002). These strengths are of particular relevance in the context of dry AMD, where BrM thickening and ECM remodeling are central features that compromise RPE function.

Moreover, the proposed mechanism underlying the therapeutic hypothesis is compelling. Excessive TGFβ signaling has been implicated in the aberrant remodeling of the BrM, which in turn impairs the presentation of critical phagocytic ligands necessary for efficient POS uptake by the RPE (Radeke et al., 2015). By inhibiting TGFβRI, SB431542 could theoretically restore the balance between collagen and proteoglycan production, thereby normalizing BrM stiffness and improving the diffusion of factors such as MFGE8 and Gas6. In doing so, the drug would indirectly enhance integrin αvβ5-mediated phagocytosis—a process that is essential for the maintenance of photoreceptor health and overall retinal integrity. This innovative indirect approach could represent a significant advancement in the treatment of dry AMD, addressing the disease from both a fibrotic and a functional perspective.

However, several considerable challenges and weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, the bulk of the supporting data for SB431542 comes from studies in non-ocular cell types or animal models of general fibrosis and cancer, with limited direct evidence in ocular systems. Although TGFβ inhibitors have been proposed as therapeutic agents in retinal diseases, there remains a significant gap in data specific to dry AMD or related retinal degenerative conditions (Akhund et al., 2023; Nyati et al., 2011). The absence of ocular pharmacokinetic studies, detailed data on retinal tissue penetration, and long-term safety evaluations in the eye poses a major hurdle for the clinical translation of SB431542 for AMD.

Furthermore, TGFβ signaling is a double-edged sword in many tissues, including the retina. While excessive TGFβ activity drives pathological ECM deposition and fibrosis, TGFβ also participates in immune regulation and cellular homeostasis. Therefore, complete or prolonged inhibition of TGFβ signaling may have unintended consequences, such as impairing normal wound healing or altering the immunological milieu of the retina (Akhund et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023). The delicate balance between therapeutic efficacy and potential adverse effects necessitates that any systemic or even locally delivered TGFβRI inhibitor be subject to rigorous dosing and toxicity studies. In this regard, the narrow therapeutic window often encountered in kinase inhibition therapies could be a limiting factor for SB431542’s adoption in an ophthalmic setting.

Another significant concern is the delivery method. The current literature on SB431542 primarily documents its use in cell culture assays or systemic administration in animal models; however, the ocular environment presents unique challenges due to barriers such as the inner limiting membrane, the blood-retina barrier, and the anatomical constraints of the retina. The pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of SB431542 in ocular tissues remain largely unexplored, which represents a critical gap in current knowledge.

Additionally, although the indirect mechanism of action—namely, the normalization of ECM to facilitate proper ligand–receptor interactions—is scientifically plausible, it is inherently more challenging to measure and validate compared to direct cellular responses. Assays designed to monitor changes in BrM stiffness, ECM composition, and the diffusion characteristics of MFGE8 and Gas6 must be highly sensitive and reproducible, and these endpoints have not been extensively characterized in available preclinical models of AMD. Furthermore, the redundancy within TGFβ signaling pathways raises the possibility that compensatory mechanisms might mitigate the effects of ALK5 inhibition over time, potentially limiting the efficacy of SB431542, particularly in a chronic, slowly progressive disease like dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Akhund et al., 2023).

From an efficacy standpoint, while numerous studies demonstrate that SB431542 effectively reduces TGFβ-induced fibrotic responses in various cell types (Laping et al., 2002), extrapolating these findings to the complex microenvironment of the aged retina is not straightforward. The retina and RPE possess distinct cellular and molecular characteristics that may respond differently to TGFβ signaling modulation. For example, in RPE cells, TGFβ signaling not only regulates ECM deposition but is also involved in the maintenance of epithelial phenotype and may even exert neuroprotective effects under certain conditions. Hence, unspecific inhibition of TGFβ signaling in the retina could conceivably result in a loss of beneficial effects that are essential for retinal homeostasis (Radeke et al., 2015; Akhund et al., 2023).

In summary, while SB431542 exhibits a robust, well-characterized mechanism of action as a TGFβRI inhibitor and has demonstrated potent anti-fibrotic effects in preclinical models of ECM remodeling, its repurposing for dry AMD must overcome several significant challenges. The strengths of SB431542 lie in its high potency, selectivity, and extensive preclinical validation in non-ocular models. Its molecular interactions are well understood, and its ability to inhibit Smad phosphorylation offers a clear mechanistic rationale for reducing pathological ECM deposition. Consequently, if applied to the pathological process associated with dry AMD, SB431542 could, in theory, mitigate the excessive ECM remodeling that impairs ligand diffusion and consequently restores the capacity for integrin αvβ5-mediated POS uptake by RPE cells (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011).

On the other hand, the weaknesses of this approach are substantial. There is limited evidence of SB431542’s efficacy in ocular models, and its pharmacokinetics, ocular tissue penetration, and long-term safety profile have yet to be rigorously evaluated. Additionally, the complexity of TGFβ’s biological roles raises concerns regarding the balance between therapeutic benefit and potential interference with normal retinal physiology. The indirect nature of the hypothesized effect—mediated by ECM normalization—adds further layers of complexity to both preclinical testing and eventual clinical translation. Finally, challenges related to drug delivery to the retina, along with the potential for compensatory signaling pathways to undermine the inhibitor’s efficacy, suggest that significant additional research is warranted before SB431542 can be advanced as a therapeutic candidate in an AMD setting (Akhund et al., 2023; Akhund et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023).

Overall, SB431542 presents a biologically plausible and mechanistically sound candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly given its demonstrated ability to modulate TGFβ-driven fibrotic pathways. However, its successful translation to an ophthalmic therapeutic will hinge on a series of focused preclinical studies that address ocular biodistribution, safety in retinal tissues, and the optimization of dosing regimens tailored to the unique anatomical and physiological challenges of the eye. Only after these critical issues have been resolved can SB431542 be considered a viable strategy to restore ECM homeostasis in the Bruch membrane, normalize phagocytic ligand availability, and ultimately enhance integrin-mediated POS uptake in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011). In conclusion, while SB431542 has strong potential and a compelling mechanistic rationale, further dedicated ocular research is required to fully validate its therapeutic promise in the context of dry AMD before it can be recommended for clinical development.
