Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab is a recombinant, humanized monoclonal IgG kappa antibody that specifically binds complement component C5 and prevents its proteolytic activation into C5a and C5b, thereby blocking terminal pathway activity and membrane attack complex (MAC; C5b-9) assembly while leaving upstream C3-dependent functions largely intact (for example, opsonization and immune-complex handling) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; West et al., 2024). It was discovered by screening large panels of murine anti-human C5 monoclonals for potent inhibition of C5 activation and terminal complement–mediated hemolysis; the parental murine antibody (5G1.1) was then humanized by CDR grafting into human germline frameworks and engineered to use a hybrid IgG2/IgG4 heavy-chain constant region to minimize Fcγ receptor binding and classical-pathway activation (reducing effector functions that could confound terminal pathway blockade) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009). Eculizumab binds human C5 with very high affinity (Kd approximately 120 pM) and sterically prevents convertase engagement with the MG7 domain of C5; epitope mapping identifies residues in the MG7 domain (including the KSSKC motif around Arg885) critical for binding, and Arg885His/Cys polymorphisms have been linked to clinical non-responsiveness in some patients, consistent with the structural epitope (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

As a drug class, complement inhibitors have been deployed to treat diseases driven by complement dysregulation, with C5 blockade representing a terminal-pathway strategy that ablates C5a signaling and MAC-mediated cytolysis while preserving many proximal complement functions; eculizumab was the first complement inhibitor approved for clinical use and catalyzed broad clinical development of C5, C3, and alternative pathway–targeted agents across hematology, nephrology, neurology, and, more recently, ophthalmology (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Eculizumab is administered intravenously, exhibits a long serum half-life (~272 ± 82 hours), a limited volume of distribution consistent with an intravascularly confined antibody, and shows pharmacodynamic correlation between serum trough concentrations and blockade of hemolytic activity; vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis is required due to increased susceptibility when terminal complement is inhibited (Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Within ophthalmology, complement activation products and MAC deposition have been implicated in AMD pathogenesis, motivating clinical trials of complement inhibitors including C5-directed agents; eculizumab has been formally evaluated in a randomized phase 2 setting for non-exudative AMD (geographic atrophy and drusen cohorts) via systemic administration (Kassa et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Halawa et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
Eculizumab has an extensive clinical record in systemic complement-mediated disorders. It revolutionized therapy for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), where it reduces intravascular hemolysis, decreases transfusion requirements, and improves quality of life; it is also approved for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and for neurologic autoimmune indications including anti–acetylcholine receptor–positive generalized myasthenia gravis and aquaporin-4–positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Early clinical pharmacology in PNH demonstrated that an induction regimen of 600 mg weekly for four weeks followed by 900 mg every other week maintained near-complete terminal pathway blockade and significantly reduced hemolysis and transfusion needs; these dosing principles align with its long half-life and the concentration dependence of hemolytic inhibition (Hillmen et al., 2004; Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012). Despite robust control of intravascular hemolysis, residual extravascular hemolysis can persist because C3 opsonization is not prevented by C5 inhibition, illustrating an important mechanistic limitation of terminal-pathway agents (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; West et al., 2024).

The drug’s safety profile is dominated by infection risk with encapsulated organisms—particularly meningococcal disease—necessitating vaccination; otherwise, eculizumab has shown acceptable tolerability across long-term use, with clinical programs incorporating monitoring of functional complement activity (CH50) to confirm pharmacodynamic blockade and dose adequacy (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009; Eskandary et al., 2016). Mechanistically relevant sources also report pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic complexities: high-affinity binding at acidic endosomal pH encourages recycling of eculizumab:C5 complexes by FcRn, leading to accumulation of total C5 bound to the drug in circulation; next-generation engineering in ravulizumab introduced pH-dependent release to minimize cargo recycling and extend dosing intervals (Schmidt & Smith, 2023).

In ophthalmology, eculizumab has been investigated as a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD. The COMPLETE study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), a single-center, randomized, double-masked phase 2 trial, evaluated intravenous eculizumab in two cohorts: geographic atrophy (GA) and intermediate AMD with high-risk drusen; patients were randomized 2:1 to eculizumab or saline over 24 weeks with follow-up to 52 weeks (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the GA cohort (n = 30 study eyes), eculizumab did not reduce GA enlargement versus placebo at 26 or 52 weeks (square-root–transformed growth 0.19 ± 0.12 mm vs. 0.18 ± 0.15 mm at 26 weeks, P = 0.96; 0.37 ± 0.22 mm vs. 0.37 ± 0.21 mm at 52 weeks, P = 0.93), and no drug-related adverse events were reported (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the drusen cohort (n = 30 total participants; 20 active, 10 placebo), eculizumab failed to meet the prespecified primary endpoint of a ≥ 50% reduction in drusen cube-root volume at 26 weeks; none of 18 treated eyes achieved this threshold, while one placebo eye did (10%; P = 0.36), and there was no detectable difference in mean drusen growth between arms through 26–52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014). Trial conduct included meningococcal vaccination and careful multimodal imaging; retention was high with 28/30 completing 52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). Independent evidence syntheses judged the certainty of evidence as low to very low due to small sample size, imprecision, and some risk of bias; overall, systemic eculizumab “may have made little to no difference” in BCVA and GA lesion growth in the available cohort (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistically similar C5-directed agents have not shown positive phase 2 outcomes in GA when administered systemically or intravitreally (e.g., LFG316 failed in phase 2), whereas intravitreal C5 inhibition with avacincaptad pegol progressed to later-phase testing and regulatory review, suggesting that drug, route, and pharmacology may be important determinants of outcome; by contrast, intravitreal C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) demonstrated efficacy and has been approved for GA, underscoring the translational relevance of target selection and ocular delivery (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024). Multiple reviews conclude that systemic eculizumab is no longer in development for AMD and highlight delivery and mechanistic concerns as likely contributors to the negative results (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, eculizumab targets the MG7 domain of C5 and sterically prevents formation of the C5 convertase–substrate complex, thereby inhibiting the cleavage of C5 into the potent anaphylatoxin C5a and C5b, which nucleates membrane attack complex assembly with C6–C9 (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Rother et al., 2007). Structural analysis of an eculizumab Fab bound to C5 resolved at 4.2 Å shows that five CDRs form the principal interface with MG7; mutational scanning of CDR residues identifies a network of contacts necessary for high-affinity binding, and kinetic assays confirm that these interactions prevent complement-mediated hemolysis in vitro (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016). The epitope includes residues near Arg885, and clinical resistance due to Arg885His/Cys substitutions in C5 provides orthogonal validation of the binding site (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

Pharmacodynamically, eculizumab ablates terminal pathway function: it suppresses CH50 to near zero when trough serum concentrations exceed ~35 μg/mL; however, because proximal C3 activation continues, C3b deposition and downstream opsonins accumulate on surfaces, which can drive extravascular clearance and generate residual pathology even under complete C5 blockade in appropriate disease contexts (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). Additional mechanisms can undermine complete terminal pathway control: (1) during intense proximal activation, densely opsonized surfaces can support C5 activation by convertases in ways that partially bypass classical C5 convertase assembly or even promote conformational C5 activation on surface C3b clusters; such context-dependent activation can manifest as “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” despite apparently adequate free drug levels, and has been reported in clinical settings as residual terminal-pathway activity and elevated sC5b-9 in some patients (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). (2) Eculizumab binds C5 with high affinity at both neutral and mildly acidic pH, allowing FcRn to recycle eculizumab:C5 complexes and potentially alter antigen disposition; ravulizumab’s pH-dependent binding was engineered to release C5 in endosomes and improve pharmacokinetics by avoiding cargo recycling (Schmidt & Smith, 2023). These features are germane to dose selection, monitoring, and potential resistance or escape during strong complement activation.

Rationale for C5 inhibition in AMD rests on abundant mechanistic and histopathological evidence that C5-derived effectors and MAC participate in retinal/choroidal injury. C5a is detected in drusen and acts as a chemotactic and proinflammatory mediator capable of inducing VEGF expression from retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, while C5b initiates MAC assembly; MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris increases with aging and is elevated in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019). Sub-lytic and lytic MAC on choroidal endothelium causes cell injury and can trigger surviving endothelial cells to upregulate VEGF and matrix metalloproteinases, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic injury and pro-angiogenic remodeling; complement regulatory proteins such as CD59 are natural inhibitors of MAC formation and their dysfunction or insufficiency can predispose to damage (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2021). Complement dysregulation in AMD further includes genetic risk (e.g., CFH variants) and evidence of alternative pathway activation in ocular tissues, suggesting both proximal and terminal effector involvement in disease biology (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Importantly, proximal inhibition at C3 has shown the capacity to restore lysosomal function and reduce sub-RPE drusen-like deposits in human iPSC-derived RPE models carrying the high-risk CFH Y402H variant by reducing C3 turnover and lowering downstream MAC (C5b-9) localization at lysosomes; in this system, a compstatin analogue (Cp40) suppressed C3b and MAC deposition and reversed lysosomal abnormalities, whereas direct C5 inhibition has not been shown in this model to rescue lysosomal function, and clinical C5 blockade has failed in GA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). These data reinforce that while terminal pathway effectors are present and likely pathogenic in AMD, distal blockade at C5 does not necessarily address upstream complement turnover that drives intracellular lysosomal stress in RPE, and proximal intervention may be required to normalize cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
The hypothesis proposes that high-affinity C5 blockade with eculizumab will prevent MAC assembly on RPE, thereby reducing sub-RPE deposit–driven lysosomal stress and indirectly supporting photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis in dry AMD. Mechanistically, preventing C5 cleavage would abrogate both C5a signaling and C5b-dependent MAC formation; given the documented presence of C5a in drusen and increased MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane/choriocapillaris with age and AMD, terminal pathway inhibition is expected to reduce MAC-mediated endothelial and RPE injury, dampen MAC-induced VEGF/MMP signaling, and potentially mitigate inflammation (Kassa et al., 2019). In principle, if MAC-driven lysosomal injury contributes to RPE dysfunction, C5 inhibition could reduce new MAC deposition at the RPE surface and limit subsequent endocytosis of MAC into lysosomes, thereby lowering lysosomal burden (Park et al., 2021).

However, two key bodies of evidence temper this expectation. First, clinical testing of systemic eculizumab in GA and intermediate AMD failed to show benefit on primary anatomical endpoints (GA growth and OCT drusen volume) through 26–52 weeks, despite established systemic pharmacodynamic blockade; these negative outcomes argue that either (a) terminal pathway activity at C5 is not the principal driver of lesion growth/drusen regression during the studied disease stages/time horizon, or (b) pharmacokinetic compartmentalization limited ocular target engagement after intravenous dosing (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Filho et al., 2014). Reviews explicitly highlight the compartment barrier problem—systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina or sub-RPE space due to the blood–retina/Bruch’s membrane barriers and large molecular size—and note that eculizumab exposure shorter than six months is unlikely to show benefit in slowly progressive GA, compounding interpretation (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Second, cellular models directly linking complement dysregulation to lysosomal failure in high-risk AMD RPE show that upstream C3 inhibition, not terminal C5 blockade, restores lysosomal function and reduces deposit formation; this suggests that intralysosomal stress is driven by continuous C3 turnover and opsonization rather than MAC alone, and that distal C5 blockade may be insufficient to normalize these processes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Consequently, POS phagocytosis metrics may improve only marginally or not at all if the dominant insult is proximal complement turnover rather than MAC-mediated damage. The clinical failure to slow GA growth or reduce drusen volume with systemic eculizumab supports the inference that target engagement at C5, via the tested route and schedule, did not translate into macroscopic anatomical benefit in human AMD eyes within one year (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).

If eculizumab were to be tested in vitro on human RPE, appropriate readouts would include: surface and intracellular MAC (C5b-9) quantification, lysosomal number/size and membrane integrity (e.g., LAMP2, Galectin-8), Cathepsin D activity, autophagic flux, and POS degradation kinetics; concomitant measurement of upstream C3b/iC3b/C3d deposition would be essential to interpret whether C5 inhibition is affecting the dominant pathogenic pathway in the assay (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In vivo, ocular pharmacokinetic considerations dominate: intravitreal administration delivers drug to the retina and sub-RPE space but is not reported for eculizumab in the provided context and would carry different safety and dosing constraints; systemic dosing faces blood–retina barrier limitations that likely constrained ocular target engagement in COMPLETE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Notably, nearly all complement inhibitors that have shown anatomical effects in GA have been delivered intravitreally, underscoring the importance of route of administration for ocular diseases (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic rationale: C5a and MAC are present in AMD-relevant tissues; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD and can drive endothelial injury, VEGF/MMP upregulation, and potentially RPE dysfunction; blocking C5 should diminish these terminal effector signals (Kassa et al., 2019; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Potent, well-characterized biologic: Eculizumab binds human C5 with picomolar affinity, has a well-defined structural epitope in the MG7 domain, and reliably ablates terminal pathway function systemically with a large clinical safety database outside ophthalmology (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
- Clinical feasibility and tolerability: In AMD trials, intravenous eculizumab was well tolerated without drug-related adverse events and with no clear signal for increased neovascular conversion or ocular infection within one year, supporting general safety of systemic C5 blockade in this population under vaccination protocols (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Negative clinical efficacy in AMD: The randomized phase 2 COMPLETE trial showed no reduction in GA growth and no meaningful reduction in drusen volume through 26–52 weeks; certainty is limited by small sample size but confidence intervals and replication across endpoints argue against a large treatment effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).  
- Compartmentalization barriers for systemic dosing: Blood–retina and Bruch’s membrane barriers likely limit ocular exposure to intravenously administered eculizumab; multiple reviews cite inadequate ocular penetration as a plausible reason for failure, and systemic eculizumab is no longer being pursued in AMD (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
- Target selection may be too distal for RPE lysosomal rescue: Human iPSC-RPE data indicate that complement-driven lysosomal pathology and drusen-like deposits are reversed by C3 inhibition, with concomitant reduction of downstream MAC, while C5 blockade alone has not been shown to restore lysosomal metrics and did not slow GA clinically; this suggests that proximal complement turnover is the dominant driver of RPE lysosomal stress (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Mechanistic escape and incomplete terminal control: Under strong activation, C5 can be activated on dense C3b clusters with features of convertase bypass or conformational priming; stoichiometric C5 inhibitors can form long-lived C5:antibody complexes on surfaces, potentially allowing residual terminal activity, and clinical “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” has been documented (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
- Genetic and biochemical determinants of response: C5 polymorphisms (e.g., R885H/C) can abolish binding and confer resistance; while prevalence in AMD populations is unknown here, such variants are important risk factors for nonresponse (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).  
- Safety/logistics: Terminal complement blockade mandates meningococcal vaccination and vigilance for invasive infections; while acceptable systemically in selected diseases, risk–benefit in a chronic, slowly progressive ocular disorder is less favorable, and the cost and infusion burden are high (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Contextualization with alternative complement strategies  
- C5 vs C3: Clinical success in GA has emerged at the level of C3 (pegcetacoplan), consistent with cellular data showing rescue of lysosomal function by upstream blockade; by contrast, systemic C5 inhibition with eculizumab and other C5-directed agents failed to meet GA endpoints in early trials, and LFG316 also did not demonstrate efficacy in GA (West et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Route of administration: Most agents demonstrating anatomical effects in GA are delivered intravitreally; eculizumab’s large size and systemic administration likely limited ocular penetration in COMPLETE, and no intravitreal eculizumab data are provided here to support local delivery (Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
- Risk of adverse ocular remodeling: Complement modulation has complex, context-dependent effects; in some models, complement inhibition or modulation can alter macrophage polarization and influence CNV formation, underscoring that indiscriminate or poorly targeted complement blockade could have unintended consequences; while the eculizumab AMD trials did not show a neovascular signal, vigilance is warranted when selecting targets and doses (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2021).

Decision Implications  
- As a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD, eculizumab has a low probability of success based on randomized clinical evidence, pharmacokinetic compartment limitations, and mechanistic considerations indicating that distal C5 blockade may not correct the proximal complement turnover driving RPE lysosomal pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- If C5 remains a target of interest, local ocular delivery and alternative molecular formats designed for intravitreal pharmacokinetics (e.g., smaller C5-binding entities, RNAi to intraocular C5 production, or intravitreal C5 inhibitors such as avacincaptad pegol) are more plausible routes; indeed, avacincaptad has advanced in GA, while systemic eculizumab has been discontinued in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019; Nadeem et al., 2023; West et al., 2024).  
- For assays aimed at lysosomal stress and POS phagocytosis, prioritizing proximal complement inhibitors (e.g., C3-targeting) is more aligned with human RPE data and recent clinical experience, whereas C5 inhibition alone is unlikely to fully normalize lysosomal function or confer robust structural benefit (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; West et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
Eculizumab provides a clear mechanistic means to extinguish terminal complement effectors implicated in AMD biology, but the totality of evidence—negative randomized clinical data in GA and drusen, route-of-administration barriers to ocular exposure, mechanistic escape during high activation, and cellular evidence favoring proximal over distal inhibition for lysosomal rescue—argues against further development of systemic eculizumab for dry AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The program should be deprioritized in favor of intraocularly suited agents and proximal complement targets, unless a compelling, testable strategy emerges to achieve effective intraocular C5 blockade with eculizumab (which is not supported by the present context) (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistic Appendix: Biochemical and Pathobiologic Evidence Relevant to the Hypothesis  
- Complement activation and terminal effectors in AMD:  
  - C5a is present in drusen and induces VEGF from RPE; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD; MAC induces endothelial lysis and sub-lytic survival signaling that upregulates VEGF and MMPs (Kassa et al., 2019).  
  - Alternative pathway dysregulation is central in AMD; genetic and experimental data implicate factor H and alternative pathway components in AMD and CNV models; inhibition of C3a, C5a, CFB, MAC or supplementation with CD59/CFH blocks CNV in animals (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Eculizumab structure–function:  
  - Epitope on MG7 with steric convertase blockade; high-affinity binding and resistance polymorphisms at Arg885; CDR function validated by mutational scans (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
  - PK/PD: long half-life, vascular distribution, CH50 suppression threshold, FcRn recycling of C5:eculizumab complexes; ravulizumab engineering to improve recycling and dosing (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
  - Breakthrough mechanisms: convertase bypass and surface-induced conformational activation on dense C3b clusters; residual TP activity despite inhibitors under strong activation (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; Mannes et al., 2021).  
- Clinical AMD trials:  
  - COMPLETE GA cohort: no slowing of GA growth at 26 or 52 weeks; well tolerated (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021).  
  - COMPLETE drusen cohort: no ≥ 50% reduction in drusen volume in treated eyes at 26 weeks; no significant change in drusen growth vs placebo (Filho et al., 2014).  
  - Critical appraisals: small sample, imprecision, risk of bias; systemic delivery may not achieve retinal levels; eculizumab no longer in AMD development (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023).  
- RPE lysosomal biology:  
  - In high-risk Y402H iPSC-RPE, excessive C3 turnover increases MAC internalization and overloads lysosomes; C3 inhibition with Cp40 reduces both C3b and MAC, reverses lysosomal defects, and reduces drusen-like deposits; direct C5 inhibition is not shown to restore lysosomal function in this model (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Operational Recommendation  
- Do not advance systemic eculizumab for dry AMD. If C5 remains a strategic target, consider intravitreal agents designed for ocular PK and evaluate them head-to-head against proximal inhibitors in RPE lysosomal-function assays that quantify both MAC and C3 fragment deposition, with translational go/no-go predicated on alignment with known clinical signals in GA (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SU5402 is a small‐molecule inhibitor that belongs to the indolinone, also often described as oxindole, family of compounds designed to target receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), most notably fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs) and platelet‐derived growth factor receptors (PDGFRs) (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Chemically, it is defined as 3-[(3-(2-carboxyethyl)-4-methylpyrrol-2-yl)methylene]-2-indolinone, a structure that features an indolin-2-one nucleus decorated with a propionic acid chain and a methyl substituent on a pyrrole ring; these structural motifs enable the molecule to mimic key interactions commonly found in ATP binding (Prakash et al., 2012; Ho et al., 2014). Originally discovered as one of the first classes of FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors, the compound’s crystal structure in complex with FGFR was resolved as early as 1997, establishing its role as an important lead for further inhibitor design (Liang et al., 2012). SU5402 is therefore categorized as an ATP-competitive inhibitor that occupies a hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the adenine binding site in FGFR, and its design has inspired many subsequent efforts to optimize RTK inhibition for therapeutic purposes (Manetti & Botta, 2003). In addition to its potent activity against FGFR1 (with reported IC₅₀ values around 0.03 μM), SU5402 displays inhibitory effects toward PDGFRβ and even VEGFR2, positioning it as a prototype multi-targeted kinase inhibitor in early-stage drug development programs (Chen et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2014). Its synthesis is rooted in structure-based medicinal chemistry approaches whereby modifications of the indolinone core and side chain functionalities were guided by crystal structure data and structure–activity relationship studies (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Consequently, SU5402 stands as a well-characterized synthetic compound with a clearly delineated pharmacophore, and its molecular interactions with the kinase active site are illustrative of the class’s capacity to serve as lead compounds in various therapeutic areas (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the development and use of SU5402 have been predominantly tied to oncology and anti-angiogenic research. Early investigations demonstrated that by inhibiting FGFR signaling, SU5402 effectively blocked the autophosphorylation of the receptor and downstream proliferative and survival pathways such as RAF-MEK1/2-MAPK and PI3K-AKT—pathways that are essential drivers of tumor growth and angiogenesis (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). These studies established its potency in vitro and in animal models, where it was used as a research tool to interrogate the role of FGFR-related pathways in cancer biology (Manetti & Botta, 2003). In addition, several members of the indolinone inhibitor class, including derivatives related to SU5402, such as SU5416 and SU6668, were developed for anti-tumor and anti-angiogenic applications and were advanced to clinical trials for various malignancies (Ho et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016). Despite its promising biochemical profile, SU5402 itself did not progress further in clinical development for oncology, largely due to issues associated with multi-kinase inhibition and subsequent toxicity profiles observed during broader preclinical studies (Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Notably, there is no published record in the literature, as captured by the provided sources, that SU5402 has ever been intentionally repurposed for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal degenerative diseases (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Its application has remained confined as a tool compound in research settings for understanding FGFR signaling and its role in cellular proliferation and angiogenesis, rather than for modulating processes underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) differentiation and phagocytosis. However, its continued use in ocular safety studies in vitro and in rodent models has provided preliminary evidence of an acceptable safety profile when applied topically or delivered locally in ocular tissues (Chen et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2016). Thus, while SU5402 has a rich history as an FGFR inhibitor in cancer-related research, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding its therapeutic use in dry AMD, an area that remains largely unexplored until now.

Mechanism of Action:  
SU5402 exerts its biological activity as an ATP-competitive inhibitor targeting the tyrosine kinase domain of FGFR1, a member of the receptor tyrosine kinase family implicated in various cellular functions including proliferation, differentiation, and survival. At the molecular level, the indolinone core of SU5402 occupies the ATP-binding site in FGFR1, where it competes with ATP for the binding pocket (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Detailed crystallographic studies have revealed that the oxindole nucleus of the compound forms two or more critical hydrogen bonds with conserved residues in the kinase hinge region, specifically with Glu562 and Ala564, which normally interact with the adenine part of ATP (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017). In addition, the propionic acid group of SU5402 forms a third hydrogen bond with the side chain of Asn568, a residue in the hinge region that further stabilizes the inhibitor-bound conformation of the kinase (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017). This binding pattern not only ensures high potency by blocking the ATP-binding site but also promotes a specific conformational change in the glycine-rich loop of FGFR1, which is integral to the enzyme’s catalytic activity (Mohammadi et al., 1998; Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Beyond its direct interactions with FGFR1, SU5402 has also been reported to interact with other kinases such as VEGFR2 and PDGFRβ, albeit with slightly varying potencies. Its ability to inhibit multiple kinases is attributable to the high degree of structural homology within the ATP-binding regions of these receptor tyrosine kinases and reflects its broad-spectrum activity as an RTK inhibitor (Chen et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2014). Despite this multi-target activity, the molecular determinants for its relative selectivity—particularly the critical hydrogen bond interactions and the spatial orientation of its substituents—have been well characterized, making it a useful tool to dissect kinase-mediated pathways (Pike, 2017; Prakash et al., 2012).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, FGFR signaling is implicated in the regulation of cell polarity, differentiation, and the maintenance of phagocytic receptor expression. The hypothesis under evaluation suggests that inhibition of FGFR by SU5402 may tip the balance of intracellular signaling in favor of differentiation-associated processes, thereby upregulating the surface expression of MERTK and the integrin αvβ5 complex, both of which are essential for the binding and internalization of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). In effect, by interfering with the normal FGFR-driven proliferative and survival signals, SU5402 might foster an environment conducive to RPE maturation and enhanced phagocytic functionality. This molecular action is not only supported by the established biochemistry of SU5402 in cancer models but is also mechanistically plausible in the RPE, where FGFR signaling dynamics play a role in determining cell morphology and receptor trafficking (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Chen et al., 2011).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the central hypothesis, the application of SU5402 in mid-differentiation-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived RPE (iPSC-RPE) is expected to modulate the cell-signaling environment such that differentiation-associated genes, particularly those encoding phagocytic receptors, are upregulated. Specifically, FGFR1 inhibition is postulated to lead to improved cell polarity and receptor localization—a phenomenon that has been documented in related studies where FGFR blockade favorably impacts the maturation state of RPE cells (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). In the system under investigation, the key targets are MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase critical for the clearance of shed POS, and the integrin αvβ5 complex, which is essential for the initial binding of these segments to the RPE surface.

The anticipated outcome is multifaceted. First, by attenuating FGFR signaling, SU5402 would relieve any inhibitory crosstalk that might otherwise suppress the expression or proper trafficking of MERTK and αvβ5 receptors. This hypothesis is built on the concept that during RPE differentiation, FGFR signaling might help maintain a less mature phenotype that is less competent in executing the phagocytic process. Thus, timely pharmacological inhibition is predicted to accelerate or enhance the differentiation process, triggering the upregulation and proper localization of these receptors on the cell membrane (Liang et al., 2012; Pike, 2017).

Second, enhanced receptor expression and correct cellular polarity are expected to translate into an increased capacity for POS binding and uptake. In a functional assay, this would manifest as a measurable increase in the phagocytic index of the treated RPE cells compared to control populations. Since robust phagocytic activity is a hallmark of healthy RPE function, improved receptor availability could, in theory, ameliorate some of the cellular deficits that contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Importantly, while the literature available in the provided context does not directly report the use of SU5402 in dry AMD models, the rationale draws on the broader evidence that modulating FGFR signaling can have beneficial effects on cell differentiation and polarity in other cell types (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Liang et al., 2012).

Additionally, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses in similar cell systems have demonstrated that FGFR signaling influences the expression levels of a variety of genes implicated in the maturation and functional competency of epithelial cells, including those involved in phagocytosis. Therefore, by leveraging SU5402’s known activity profile, the expected effect in the proposed iPSC-RPE system is an improved expression profile of MERTK and αvβ5, leading to enhanced clearance of POS. This effect is of particular interest in the context of dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction and the subsequent accumulation of toxic debris contribute to disease progression (Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, SU5402 presents as a well-characterized, indolinone-based FGFR/PDGFRβ inhibitor with a strong biochemical foundation rooted in detailed structural and mechanistic studies. From a chemical and molecular perspective, its design and mechanism of action are well established; the compound engages the ATP-binding pocket of FGFR1 with high potency primarily through a series of well-defined hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions, which underpins its efficacy as an inhibitor (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003; Prakash et al., 2012). These robust mechanistic features, together with its documented ability to modulate downstream signaling events, constitute significant strengths when considering the repurposing of SU5402 for non-oncological indications such as dry AMD.

A key strength in the context of RPE differentiation is the emerging evidence that modulation of FGFR signaling can enhance cell polarity and receptor localization. This is particularly pertinent for the expression of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and integrin αvβ5, which are vital for POS binding and internalization. By repurposing SU5402, there is a compelling opportunity to improve the functionality of less mature iPSC-derived RPE cells—an effect that could translate into a novel therapeutic strategy to mitigate RPE dysfunction in dry AMD (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Despite these promising aspects, there are several challenges and potential weaknesses that need to be addressed. First, the historical development of SU5402 has been overwhelmingly focused on oncology and anti-angiogenic research, with little to no prior evidence in the literature regarding its efficacy in retinal disorders or dry AMD specifically (Manetti & Botta, 2003). This gap in direct preclinical or clinical data necessitates a cautious approach, with extensive in vitro and in vivo validation required before any definitive conclusions can be drawn about its utility in modulating RPE function.

Moreover, SU5402’s broad-spectrum activity, which includes inhibition of PDGFRβ and VEGFR2 in addition to FGFR1, raises concerns about potential off-target effects. Although multi-kinase inhibition might be advantageous by addressing redundancies in pathological signaling networks, it also carries the risk of unintended consequences in the delicate environment of the retina. The multi-targeted nature of SU5402 might disrupt cellular homeostasis if not dosed carefully or if delivered systemically, emphasizing the need for targeted ocular delivery mechanisms to maximize local efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure (Chen et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2014).

Another limitation is related to the dosing regimen and formulation challenges associated with repurposing a compound originally developed for oncology. Many FGFR inhibitors suffer from issues such as limited solubility, off-target toxicity, and suboptimal pharmacokinetics when used outside their intended systemic applications. For ocular use, the formulation must ensure that therapeutic concentrations are reached at the RPE without causing damage to other retinal cells, a balance that can be particularly challenging given the sensitive and tightly regulated environment of the eye (Zhang et al., 2016; Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Furthermore, while the proposed mechanism of modulating FGFR1 to enhance the expression of MERTK and integrin αvβ5 is scientifically plausible, it remains hypothetical until validated by rigorous experimental data in appropriate models of RPE differentiation. The interplay between FGFR signaling and RPE maturation is complex, and compensatory mechanisms could potentially undermine the desired therapeutic effect. For instance, chronic inhibition of FGFR might inadvertently impair other aspects of RPE function or survival that are essential for long-term retinal health, and the intricacies of these signaling pathways in the RPE context have not been fully elucidated (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Liang et al., 2012).

In addition, while preliminary ocular safety data in vitro and in rodent studies is encouraging, the transition from these models to clinical applications in humans is fraught with challenges. The extrapolation of dosing, efficacy, and safety profiles from rodent models to human retinal physiology is not always straightforward, and significant preclinical work will be needed to optimize the use of SU5402 in a dry AMD setting (Chen et al., 2011; Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Overall, the repurposing of SU5402 for dry AMD represents an innovative and intriguing avenue that leverages a well-understood molecule with a rich background in FGFR inhibition. Its strengths in terms of potency, detailed binding interactions, and the theoretical rationale linking FGFR inhibition to improved RPE differentiation and phagocytic receptor expression provide a solid foundation for further investigation. However, the lack of prior application in retinal disorders, potential off-target effects due to its multi-kinase inhibition profile, and the challenges inherent in repurposing a cancer-targeted agent for ocular use are notable limitations that must be carefully addressed.

In conclusion, while SU5402 is a promising candidate from a mechanistic and chemical standpoint, its utility in the treatment of dry AMD remains speculative at this juncture. The proposed hypothesis that FGFR inhibition during RPE differentiation could elevate the expression of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and integrin αvβ5 is both innovative and scientifically grounded, yet it requires extensive validation using robust iPSC-RPE models and appropriate animal studies before any clinical translation can be justified. A strategic plan involving dose optimization, targeted ocular formulation, and a comprehensive evaluation of off-target effects is imperative to ascertain whether SU5402 can ultimately be repositioned as an effective therapeutic agent for dry AMD (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017).

Its synthesis involves partial substitution of hydroxyl groups on the parent β-cyclodextrin with hydroxypropyl moieties, thus expanding its inclusion complexation repertoire and enabling it to interact with lipophilic substrates such as cholesterol and bisretinoids. This candidate’s prior use in ocular studies, especially those addressing cholesterol dyshomeostasis and lipofuscin clearance, provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD, where abnormal lipid accumulation in the RPE is a core pathology (Nociari, Kiss, & Rodriguez-Boulan, 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
HPβCD, as well as its parent cyclodextrin compounds, have been used extensively in both biomedical research and preclinical studies focused on lipid storage disorders. In Niemann–Pick type C models, for example, cyclodextrins have demonstrated efficacy in reducing cholesterol accumulation in lysosomes by sequestering cholesterol and promoting its efflux from cells. This cholesterol‐removal capability has led to its evaluation in animal models that exhibit retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis. Several studies have provided evidence for HPβCD’s beneficial effects on lysosomal function in various cell types; in fibroblasts from Niemann–Pick patients, for instance, HPβCD treatment restored autophagy and reduced intracellular lipid buildup (Moruno-Manchon et al., 2016; Nixon, 2016). Moreover, in a mouse model of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis, HPβCD treatment produced significant reductions in retinal cholesterol content and reduced pathological deposits at critical interfaces such as the photoreceptor outer segment (POS)–RPE boundary (El-Darzi, Mast, Petrov, & Pikuleva, 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).  
In retinal models more directly related to AMD pathogenesis, cyclodextrins have been shown to decrease A2E, a major bisretinoid that accumulates in the RPE with age, by directly forming inclusion complexes with lipofuscin components (Nociari et al., 2017). Additionally, in cultured human cells and in animal studies, cyclodextrins have demonstrated a capacity to modulate lysosomal acidity and enhance the clearance of aggregated or indigestible material. Some reports, however, caution that cyclodextrins may act predominantly through cholesterol depletion rather than by stimulating lysosomal biogenesis via transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Gaspar, Mathieu, & Alvarez, 2017). Furthermore, studies using patient‐derived iPSC‐RPE cells, particularly in the context of Bietti’s crystalline dystrophy, have shown that cyclodextrin treatment rescues lysosomal pH defects and reinstates autophagic flux, which is directly relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology (Hata et al., 2018). Although HPβCD has not been formally trialed in dry AMD patients to date, its cumulative use in preclinical ocular models suggests that its repurposing for AMD is both a viable and promising strategy (El-Darzi et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular basis for HPβCD’s therapeutic potential in retinal diseases rests on its multifaceted ability to interact with lipid and retinoid components within the RPE’s lysosomal compartment. One of the key pathological features of dry AMD is the accumulation of toxic bisretinoids such as A2E within lysosomes, which contributes to impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and eventual cellular dysfunction (Nociari et al., 2017). HPβCD is thought to ameliorate this situation via several interrelated mechanisms:  

1. Direct Extraction and Complexation of Lipofuscin Precursors:  
HPβCD’s hydrophobic cavity allows it to form inclusion complexes with lipophilic compounds. Several reports have provided computational and experimental evidence that β-cyclodextrins form complexes with A2E and other bisretinoids, effectively “solubilizing” these compounds within their cavity. This extraction mechanism leads to a reduction of lipofuscin accumulation in the lysosomes, which is a critical step since lipofuscin impairs lysosomal enzyme activation such as that of cathepsin D (Nociari et al., 2017). The formation of a 2:1 cyclodextrin–A2E complex has been predicted by in silico models, suggesting that each cyclodextrin can accommodate an arm of the A2E molecule, thereby reducing lipofuscin toxicity (Nociari et al., 2017).  

2. Cholesterol Depletion and Modulation of Lysosomal Lipid Homeostasis:  
HPβCD is well known for its ability to extract free and esterified cholesterol from cellular membranes. In the context of dry AMD, cholesterol accumulation contributes to lysosomal dysfunction by perturbing the activity of the vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), leading to lysosomal alkalinization which in turn reduces cathepsin D activity. By depleting excess cholesterol from the POS and RPE, HPβCD can facilitate the restoration of lysosomal acidity. This cholesterol depletion has been documented in several animal models in which HPβCD treatment led to significant reductions in retinal cholesterol levels and improved ultrastructural characteristics of the RPE (El-Darzi et al., 2021). Additionally, this depletion is likely to relieve the inhibition of v-ATPase activity and promote effective autophagosome–lysosome fusion, thereby enhancing overall lysosomal function (Hata et al., 2018; Gaspar et al., 2017).

3. Activation of Autophagy and TFEB-Mediated Lysosomal Biogenesis:  
In many contexts of lysosomal storage and lipid overload, cellular homeostasis can be restored by triggering autophagy. HPβCD has been shown to induce autophagy by upregulating TFEB, a master transcriptional regulator that governs lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic pathways. Activation of TFEB leads to increased expression of genes involved in lysosome formation, acidification, and function. In experimental models, HPβCD has been reported to promote TFEB translocation to the nucleus, thereby enhancing lysosome-mediated degradation of accumulated substrates such as lipofuscin components (Moruno-Manchon et al., 2016; Nociari et al., 2017). It should be noted that not all studies find TFEB upregulation in all cell types; for instance, some human fibroblast studies have highlighted a cholesterol-mediated mechanism with no direct evidence of TFEB activation (Gaspar et al., 2017). Thus, the net effect of HPβCD may stem from a combination of direct removal of toxic aggregates and improvements in autophagic flux via restored lysosomal pH, rather than relying solely on TFEB-mediated biogenesis.

4. Enhancement of Lysosomal Exocytosis:  
A less widely discussed but complementary mechanism involves the induction of calcium-dependent lysosomal exocytosis. HPβCD has been shown in some studies to promote the exocytosis of lysosomal contents, thereby facilitating the clearance of undegraded material from the cell. This process may help eliminate toxic lipofuscin and other aggregated compounds that accumulate in RPE cells over time (Nociari et al., 2017).  

5. Restoration of Cathepsin D Activity and POS Degradation:  
Cathepsin D is a critical lysosomal protease involved in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) material within RPE cells. Accumulated lipofuscin and cholesterol can raise lysosomal pH and directly interfere with cathepsin D maturation and activity. By extracting excess cholesterol and lipofuscin precursors, HPβCD is expected to normalize lysosomal pH and thereby restore cathepsin D function. This restoration is key to improving POS degradation efficiency, which is compromised in dry AMD and contributes to the progressive degeneration of RPE cells (Gaspar et al., 2017; Nixon, 2016). Although direct measurements of enhanced cathepsin D activity following HPβCD treatment in AMD models are not extensively reported in the current literature, the underlying biochemical interactions support the hypothesis that a more acidic lysosomal environment will favor proper cathepsin D activation (El-Darzi et al., 2023; Nociari et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the integrated mechanisms described above, the expected therapeutic effect of HPβCD in dry AMD models is multifold. First, by forming inclusion complexes with A2E and related lipofuscin precursors, HPβCD is expected to lower the intracellular burden of these toxic compounds in RPE lysosomes. This direct extraction would lead to a decrease in the accumulation of lipofuscin, which is known to exacerbate oxidative stress and inflammation in the RPE (Nociari et al., 2017). Second, through its cholesterol-extracting properties, HPβCD should mitigate lipid overload within the RPE cell membranes and lysosomes. This reduction in cholesterol content is predicted to relieve the inhibition on the lysosomal v-ATPase, thereby restoring the acidic pH necessary for optimal lysosomal enzyme function. Consequently, cathepsin D activity should be reinstated, enhancing the capacity of RPE cells to degrade phagocytosed POS material (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Hata et al., 2018). Third, if HPβCD additionally promotes autophagy via TFEB nuclear translocation and increased lysosome biogenesis, there would be an overall improvement in the turnover of cellular debris and a reinforcement of the cell’s degradative machinery. In turn, these improvements should lead to enhanced clearance of damaged proteins, lipids, and photoreceptor debris, thereby reducing RPE cell stress and dysfunction—a primary drive behind dry AMD pathology (Moruno-Manchon et al., 2016; Nociari et al., 2017).  
Furthermore, because lipofuscin accumulation is directly linked to impaired clearance of POS and chronic inflammation, reducing its burden should indirectly improve the visual cycle. Improvements in RPE function would likely translate to better photoreceptor support and potentially slow the progression of macular degeneration, which is critically important in managing dry AMD. In sum, the expected effect of HPβCD is a synergistic improvement in lysosomal function mediated by both direct chemical extraction of toxic substances and indirect enhancement of cellular clearance pathways (Gaspar et al., 2017; Hata et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
Hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin presents several compelling strengths as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its well-documented ability to extract cholesterol and lipophilic toxins from cells has been validated in several preclinical models, and its potential for restoring lysosomal pH and, consequently, lysosomal enzyme activity is particularly attractive in the context of AMD’s impairment of RPE degradative functions (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Nociari et al., 2017). The multifaceted mechanism of action—ranging from direct complexation with A2E to cholesterol depletion and potential activation of autophagy via TFEB—addresses several interconnected pathological processes that drive dry AMD progression. Moreover, cyclodextrins’ extensive history of use in other lipid storage disorders provides a valuable precedent for their clinical repurposing and supports the feasibility of translating these findings into an ocular application (Hata et al., 2018).  

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. There is some inconsistency in the literature regarding the ability of HPβCD to activate TFEB, with certain studies reporting a predominantly cholesterol-mediated mechanism without marked transcriptional upregulation of lysosomal biogenesis (Gaspar et al., 2017). This indicates that the beneficial effects may depend on the specific cellular context and disease model. Additionally, while preclinical evidence in models of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis and lipofuscin accumulation is promising (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023), there remains a need for more direct studies in AMD models—preferably in vitro studies using primary RPE cells or in vivo studies in well-established dry AMD animal models such as the Abca4−/− or other relevant transgenic lines. The dosing issue is also a consideration; in some studies, effective lipofuscin clearance required higher concentrations of HPβCD, which in turn may introduce off-target effects or toxicity concerns that have been noted in other cyclodextrin applications, such as ototoxicity in systemic administration (Gaspar et al., 2017). Moreover, while its ability to cross blood–retina barriers has been demonstrated in some contexts (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023), ensuring sufficient local concentration in the RPE to achieve the desired lysosomal effects without eliciting adverse systemic effects remains an important translational challenge.

In conclusion, the cumulative evidence from biochemical, cellular, and preclinical studies supports the hypothesis that HPβCD has considerable potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its dual action in directly binding and extracting toxic lipofuscin precursors and in correcting cholesterol-mediated lysosomal dysfunction addresses two key pathogenic pathways in dry AMD. While additional research is needed to optimize dosing, verify the mechanism in AMD-specific models, and fully assess safety profiles in the ocular context, the strengths of HPβCD—derived from its proven track record in modulating lipid metabolism and lysosomal function—make it a promising candidate for further development (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Gaspar et al., 2017). The proposed clinical strategy aiming to lower A2E levels, restore lysosomal pH and cathepsin D activity, and enhance POS degradation is well supported by the current literature, and thus HPβCD merits strong consideration for inclusion in the dry AMD therapeutic pipeline.

Overall, while some mechanistic nuances remain to be elucidated, particularly regarding the relative contributions of TFEB activation versus cholesterol extraction, the convergence of preclinical findings and the candidate’s established utility in lysosomal storage disorders provide a solid foundation for advancing HPβCD toward clinical evaluation in dry AMD. Continued investigation into its pharmacokinetics, local retinal bioavailability, and long-term effects on RPE function, along with careful dose optimization in relevant AMD animal models, will be essential next steps in validating its therapeutic value (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Gaspar et al., 2017).

This comprehensive review indicates that HPβCD stands as a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD with several strengths that are directly aligned with the pathophysiological challenges of the disease, while also highlighting areas that require further investigation to ensure a safe and effective translation from preclinical models to clinical application (Hata et al., 2018; Nociari et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The candidate under evaluation is a synthetic Gla‐domain peptide mimetic of Protein S, designated as a 12‐mer peptide (Peptide 2.0 Cat. No. H‐PS12). In its natural role, Protein S is a vitamin K–dependent protein that contains an N‐terminal gamma‐carboxyglutamic acid (Gla) domain responsible for binding phosphatidylserine (PtdSer) on apoptotic membranes and photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and a C‐terminal region that mediates receptor binding to MerTK. This peptide mimetic is engineered to reproduce the key functional motif of the Gla domain that is critical for MerTK engagement. The synthetic peptide belongs to the class of peptide‐based small molecules designed to mimic native ligand functions and to act as receptor agonists. Peptide mimetics have been explored in several therapeutic contexts – for example, peptides that mimic portions of larger proteins often prove advantageous because of their superior stability, lower immunogenicity, and enhanced tissue penetration relative to full‐length proteins. With respect to the ocular environment, the small size and chemical stability of H‐PS12 favor its application as a locally delivered drug via intravitreal injection or topical administration, particularly in diseases such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where targeting the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is paramount (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Extensive literature supports the pivotal role of native Protein S in mediating MerTK signaling in RPE cells and promoting POS phagocytosis. Several studies demonstrate that Protein S acts as a positive regulator of MerTK‐mediated phagocytosis in the retina and that decreased activity of this pathway contributes to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Parinot et al., 2024). Although native Protein S is known to be a critical ligand for MerTK in RPE cells, its direct application as a therapeutic agent is impeded by its intrinsic lability; indeed, purification challenges and loss of bioactivity in recombinant formats have been reported (Prasad, 2006). By contrast, there is emerging evidence that synthetic peptide mimetics – designed solely from the key Gla domain – can overcome these limitations and reliably stimulate receptor phosphorylation. In macrophage models, such Gla‐domain peptides have been shown to trigger MerTK autophosphorylation within minutes at nanomolar concentrations, suggesting a dose‐responsive mechanism that might be recapitulated in RPE cells (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). To date, while there have been reports on the fundamental biology of Protein S and its role in retinal homeostasis, no synthetic Gla–domain peptide has been commercially developed or clinically evaluated specifically for dry AMD. Nonetheless, the concept of repurposing Protein S’s receptor–binding activity through a stable, small synthetic molecule has been theoretically supported by detailed mechanistic studies in vitro and in animal models (Albert et al., 2015; Nandrot, 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action proposed for H‐PS12 centers on recapitulating the critical interaction between the Gla domain of Protein S and the extracellular binding sites of the receptor tyrosine kinase MerTK. In the native state, Protein S engages MerTK by binding to its Ig‐like extracellular domains through specific gamma‐carboxylated glutamic acid residues. This binding requires calcium ions to stabilize the conformation of the Gla domain and mediate a proper interaction with phosphatidylserine on the target cell surface (Nandrot, 2018; Prasad, 2006). Binding of Protein S initiates receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation, an event which subsequently activates intracellular signaling cascades including PI3K‐ and PLCγ‐dependent pathways—processes that are requisite for cytoskeletal rearrangements and efficient phagocytosis of POS (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006; Albert et al., 2015).

H‐PS12 is designed as a synthetic 12–amino acid peptide that mimics the critical Gla–domain sequence of Protein S, maintaining the γ–carboxylation motif necessary for calcium binding and ensuring the correct spatial orientation for receptor engagement. The hypothesis is that when this peptide is administered to RPE cultures, it will bind to the MerTK extracellular regions in a fashion indistinguishable from that of the native protein, thereby triggering receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation at an effective concentration (EC₅₀) estimated to be around 100 nM (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). This autophosphorylation event then propagates downstream signaling leading to reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton, an essential step for the engulfment of POS. Detailed structure–function analyses have provided evidence that mutations in the Ig–like domains of MerTK (such as G122R and K263I) significantly alter the binding and internalization responses to Protein S and Gas6, thereby establishing the binding specificity that H‐PS12 aims to replicate (Parinot et al., 2024). Additionally, calcium dependency and proper gamma–carboxylation are confirmed as pivotal for TAM receptor activation, emphasizing how H‐PS12’s mimicry of the Gla domain can facilitate stable receptor activation (Nandrot, 2018; Lieffrig et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the failure of RPE cells to effectively phagocytose shed photoreceptor outer segments leads to accumulation of cellular debris and subsequent retinal degeneration. The expected effect of H‐PS12 is to restore or enhance this fundamental phagocytic process by acting as a MerTK agonist. When applied to RPE cell cultures – particularly those derived from CFH–mutant lines, which have been shown to exhibit impaired POS phagocytosis – H‐PS12 is anticipated to bind to MerTK, trigger receptor autophosphorylation, and thereby initiate early phagocytic signaling (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). This activation should, in turn, enhance the uptake and internalization of POS, mimicking the natural role of Protein S in maintaining retinal homeostasis (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006).

At the molecular level, following MerTK activation, downstream signaling cascades that include PI3K and the FAK pathway are activated, leading to actin polymerization and phagosome formation. Such events are crucial for the internalization of POS and are known to be compromised in models of AMD where MerTK signaling is deficient (Prasad, 2006; Lieffrig et al., 2023). Moreover, by restoring efficient phagocytosis, H‐PS12 may reduce the formation of lipofuscin and drusen—hallmarks of dry AMD—and ameliorate inflammatory processes that are secondary to debris accumulation (Albert et al., 2015). Furthermore, the localized expression of both Protein S and MerTK in the RPE, particularly at the apical microvilli interfacing with POS, supports the rationale that direct stimulation of MerTK in these cells will yield the desired therapeutic outcome (Prasad, 2006).

Overall Evaluation:  
The scientific premise underlying H‐PS12 is founded on in–depth mechanistic insights into the biology of Protein S and its regulation of MerTK–mediated phagocytosis in the retina. One of the primary strengths of the candidate lies in its well–defined mechanism of action. By isolating the Gla–domain, which has been shown to be critical for engaging MerTK and initiating receptor autophosphorylation, the synthetic peptide addresses a fundamental defect in dry AMD—the impaired clearance of POS by RPE cells (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018). The small molecular size of the 12–mer peptide not only minimizes potential for immunogenicity but also enhances tissue penetration and stability in the ocular environment, which is a significant advantage over full–length recombinant proteins that have been plagued by stability issues during purification and storage (Prasad, 2006).

Furthermore, the therapeutic rationale is supported by experimental findings in macrophage models, where similar peptides have been demonstrated to stimulate MerTK phosphorylation rapidly, hinting at the translational potential of H‐PS12 from immune cells to RPE cells (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). In addition, evidence from studies using native Protein S in RPE phagocytosis underscores the relevance of the MerTK pathway in retinal degenerative processes, thereby validating MerTK as a promising therapeutic target for AMD (Parinot et al., 2024; Kaarniranta et al., 2018).

On the other hand, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be considered. First, while Protein S has been conclusively shown to stimulate MerTK phosphorylation in biochemical assays, functional studies have revealed that recombinant Protein S can sometimes fail to stimulate phagocytosis in RPE culture systems unless in the presence of serum or additional cofactors (Prasad, 2006). This discrepancy highlights the possibility that the mere activation of MerTK by H‐PS12, as measured by receptor phosphorylation, may not fully recapitulate the complex intracellular processes required for effective phagocytosis in RPE cells.  

Another concern pertains to the delicate balance between the functions of Protein S and Gas6 in modulating retinal phagocytosis. Studies have indicated that while Protein S acts as a stimulatory ligand, Gas6 can exert inhibitory effects at higher concentrations, suggesting that the endogenous ligand stoichiometry is critical for optimal MerTK function (Parinot et al., 2024). Consequently, the introduction of a synthetic peptide might perturb this balance if not properly dosed, potentially leading to unintended modulation of phagocytic activity or downstream signaling cascades. This is particularly important given that the RPE is subject to a finely tuned circadian rhythm in phagocytosis, and any exogenous modulation must be compatible with these natural regulatory cycles (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024).

Moreover, the transition from in vitro assays to in vivo models and ultimately to clinical application is fraught with challenges. Although the EC₅₀ of approximately 100 nM suggests a high potency of H‐PS12 in triggering MerTK activation, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of the peptide in the ocular milieu need to be thoroughly characterized. Issues such as peptide stability in vitreous humor, clearance rates from retinal tissues, and potential off–target effects on other TAM receptors (e.g., TYRO3 and AXL) require detailed investigation (Prasad, 2006). In addition, the efficacy of H‐PS12 in restoring POS phagocytosis must be validated in animal models that closely mimic the human pathophysiology of dry AMD, including models that exhibit CFH mutations where defects in phagocytosis are prominent (Parinot et al., 2024; Palczewska et al., 2016).

A further limitation comes from the fact that dry AMD is a multifactorial disease. Although impaired phagocytosis and resultant debris accumulation at the RPE–photoreceptor interface are central to disease pathogenesis, other pathological mechanisms such as oxidative stress, inflammation, and complement dysregulation also contribute considerably to retinal degeneration (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006; Lieffrig et al., 2023). As such, while H‐PS12 is mechanistically attractive from the standpoint of enhancing phagocytosis via MerTK activation, it may need to be integrated into a broader therapeutic regimen that addresses these additional aspects. The long–term outcome of MerTK activation on retinal inflammation, for instance, has yet to be fully determined, even though some studies suggest that active MerTK signaling is associated with anti–inflammatory effects (Albert et al., 2015).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation of H‐PS12 is positive. The mechanistic rationale is robust and rooted in fundamental observations of Protein S’s role in retinal homeostasis. The potential to restore or enhance RPE phagocytosis, thereby reducing the accumulation of POS debris—a key pathological hallmark of dry AMD—makes this candidate highly promising. In particular, the possibility of correcting phagocytic deficits in CFH–mutant RPE cultures represents a novel approach that can address one of the unmet needs in dry AMD therapy (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

Moreover, the simplicity of a synthetic peptide compared to biologics such as full–length recombinant proteins offers advantages in terms of manufacturing, storage, and cost. The use of a 12–mer peptide also minimizes the risk of unwanted immunogenic reactions, which is especially pertinent in the immune–privileged environment of the eye (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). It is also worth noting that any adverse effects related to off–target activation can be monitored experimentally by assessing not only the phosphorylation status of MerTK but also by profiling the activity of related receptors and inflammatory markers in preclinical models (Albert et al., 2015).

In summary, the H‐PS12 synthetic peptide stands out as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its targeted mechanism of action, favorable biophysical characteristics, and the strong mechanistic data supporting the role of Protein S in RPE phagocytosis. Its development represents an innovative translation of basic mechanistic insights into a potentially viable therapeutic approach. Nevertheless, successful clinical translation of this candidate will depend on overcoming several challenges, including ensuring that receptor activation translates to meaningful functional improvements in POS clearance, optimizing dosing to maintain the physiological ligand balance, and rigorously evaluating the safety and efficacy in appropriate in vivo models. These considerations will be crucial in determining whether H‐PS12 can be advanced beyond the preclinical proof–of–concept stage (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

Overall, while the current data are highly encouraging, further studies are needed to address the following key issues:  
1. Quantitative profiling of MerTK phosphorylation kinetics by H‐PS12 in RPE cells under varying conditions, including chronic exposure and in the presence of competing ligands such as Gas6.  
2. Evaluation of the functional outcomes of MerTK activation by H‐PS12 in RPE phagocytosis assays, particularly the efficacy of POS uptake and clearance in CFH–mutant RPE cultures.  
3. Detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies in ocular models to assess the peptide’s stability, tissue penetration, and potential off–target effects.  
4. Integration of the peptide’s activity with other pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis, such as oxidative stress and complement activation, to ascertain whether a combinatorial therapeutic strategy might be warranted.

Given these considerations, H‐PS12 merits further preclinical investigation as a potential therapeutic for dry AMD. Its development is grounded in well–established mechanistic insights regarding MerTK function and RPE photoreceptor maintenance, and its design as a stable, small peptide offers distinct advantages over native Protein S. With careful optimization and validation, H‐PS12 could represent a significant advance in the treatment of dry AMD, providing a novel means to restore the critical phagocytic function of the RPE, reduce debris accumulation, and ultimately slow the progression of retinal degeneration (Parinot et al., 2024; Parinot et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

In conclusion, the synthetic Gla–domain 12–mer H‐PS12 demonstrates a promising preclinical profile as a repurposed drug candidate for dry age–related macular degeneration. Its ability to specifically bind and activate MerTK through a mechanism that mirrors the native function of Protein S, combined with its enhanced stability and ease of ocular delivery, underscores the potential for a targeted therapeutic approach to correct the underlying phagocytic deficit observed in dry AMD. While challenges remain concerning the translation of in vitro receptor activation to in vivo functional efficacy, the foundational data reviewed here support continued investigation into H‐PS12 as a novel MerTK agonist. Future research addressing dosing, long–term safety, and integration with other therapeutic modalities will be essential in determining the ultimate clinical utility of this synthetic peptide in combating dry AMD (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018; Prasad, 2006; Albert et al., 2015).

Overall, despite the inherent complexities of dry AMD pathogenesis and the potential for variable responses owing to the interplay of multiple ligands at the MerTK receptor, H‐PS12 offers a rational, targeted, and innovative approach to restore RPE phagocytic function. It thereby holds considerable promise as a next–generation therapeutic candidate that addresses a critical, yet hitherto unmet, need in the management of dry AMD (Parinot et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).
