Below is a comprehensive evaluation of the prolyl oligopeptidase inhibitor KYP-2047 as a potential repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). This report is organized into several sections: an overview of the candidate, its therapeutic history, an in‐depth discussion of its mechanism of action, the expected effects in the proposed assay, and an overall evaluation that weighs its strengths and weaknesses.

─────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

KYP-2047 is a synthetic small molecule belonging to the peptidomimetic class of compounds that target the enzyme prolyl oligopeptidase (PREP), also known as prolyl endopeptidase (POP). Chemically designated as 4-phenylbutanoyl-L-prolyl-2(S)-cyanopyrrolidine, this compound was synthesized following methods established by Dr. Elina Jarho at the University of Eastern Finland (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47). Its design represents an evolution from early substrate-like inhibitors, with modifications at specific positions – including a three-carbon aliphatic chain at the P3 position instead of the more commonly used carbamate groups seen in predecessors like ZPP – thereby improving the compound’s overall potency, selectivity, and drug-like properties (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4).

Belonging to a well-known class of PREP inhibitors, KYP-2047 shares common chemical and biophysical properties with analogous peptidomimetic agents that have been primarily designed to interfere with the catalytic activity of a serine protease that cleaves proline-containing peptides. Given its low water solubility, KYP-2047 is typically formulated in saline containing 5% Tween® 80 for experimental studies, which is consistent with formulation challenges observed with many peptidomimetic drug candidates (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47). In recent years, the broader class of PREP inhibitors has been explored for a variety of indications, most notably in neurological conditions as well as in certain cancer models. The research impetus behind this class arises from the enzyme’s presumed role in peptide metabolism, where the inhibition of PREP could alter levels of bioactive peptides that participate in cellular homeostasis. Although these agents were originally developed as anti-amnesic candidates, their biological actions have been found to extend to anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

─────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

The therapeutic exploration of PREP inhibitors dates back to the 1970s when the enzyme was first implicated in the regulation of proline-containing peptides associated with memory formation and synaptic plasticity (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22). Numerous compounds in this class—including S-17092, JTP-4819, and others—were advanced into preclinical studies and even early-phase clinical trials for cognitive enhancement in neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease and senile dementia (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41, 70–72). However, despite initial encouraging in vitro and animal data, these agents failed to progress successfully past phase II clinical trials in humans, most likely due to challenges with efficacy, blood-brain barrier penetration, or the complexity of the enzyme’s in vivo function (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 70–72).

In parallel, PREP inhibitors have been evaluated for other indications. For instance, in a study involving oral squamous cell carcinoma, KYP-2047 demonstrated potent PREP inhibition in the mouse brain along with promising anti-tumor effects, highlighting the compound’s potential utility beyond central nervous system disorders (Scuderi, 2023, pp. 133–135). Furthermore, recent work has begun to explore the ocular applications of PREP inhibition. There is a suggestion in the literature that inhibition of prolyl oligopeptidase may represent “a promising pathway to prevent the progression of age-related macular degeneration” (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13). Notably, recent in vitro studies using human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells with defective proteasomal clearance have shown that KYP-2047 exhibits cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory properties, thereby indirectly supporting its potential use in dry AMD, even though no clinical trials or prior direct therapeutic applications in retinal diseases have yet been reported (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 9–11).

While the primary historical focus of PREP inhibitors has been on neurological and cognitive applications, the body of literature also contains several exploratory studies in inflammatory and cancer contexts (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Thus, even though the bulk of previous applications have not directly targeted dry AMD, the emerging evidence supporting cytoprotection and modulation of proteolytic and autophagy pathways in RPE cells provides a rationale for repurposing KYP-2047 in ocular disease states.

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

The biological target of KYP-2047 is the serine protease prolyl oligopeptidase (PREP), which is responsible for cleaving peptide bonds at the carboxyl side of internal proline residues in small peptides (typically less than ~30 amino acids) (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 22–24, 44–47). PREP is widely expressed in the central nervous system and peripheral tissues and has been implicated in multiple physiological processes including neuropeptide regulation and cell signaling. At the molecular level, the mechanism of action involves the binding of KYP-2047 to the enzyme’s active site, more specifically interacting with the catalytic serine residue. Many PREP inhibitors, including those in the class to which KYP-2047 belongs, are designed as substrate-like pseudopeptides that exploit the structure of the enzyme’s binding pockets (S1, S2, and S3) to achieve selectivity and high-affinity binding (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).

The inhibition by KYP-2047 is characterized as “tight-binding” with slow dissociation, meaning that once the inhibitor occupies the active site of PREP, it remains bound for a significant duration, thereby effectively reducing the enzyme’s catalytic turnover (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 70–72). In neurological models, inhibition of PREP has been associated with enhanced clearance of toxic protein aggregates such as alpha-synuclein, improved autophagic flux, and reduction in oxidative stress (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 85–88; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 9–11). The current therapeutic hypothesis in the context of dry AMD extrapolates these findings to retinal pigment epithelial cells.

In particular, the proposed mechanism posits that elevated PREP activity in RPE cells contributes to an accumulation of proline-rich peptides that, in turn, inhibit the activity of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and lysosomal cathepsin L. These cathepsins are critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and turnover of cellular debris. In dry AMD, defective protein clearance mechanisms, including impaired proteasomal and lysosomal function, result in the buildup of toxic deposits, such as A2E, and contribute to RPE dysfunction. By blocking PREP activity with KYP-2047 (which has an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range, reported to be approximately 30 nM), the proposed effect is to reduce the formation or accumulation of inhibitory peptides, thereby relieving the suppression on cathepsin activity. In addition, KYP-2047-mediated PREP inhibition may trigger downstream intracellular events such as autophagy activation and modulation of MAPK signaling pathways—including p38 and ERK1/2—which have been observed in other cell types and are known to reduce oxidative stress and inflammation (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 85–88).

At the biochemical level, these molecular interactions involve the inhibitor “locking in” the PREP enzyme in a conformational state that either prevents substrate access or alters the dynamics of peptide release once cleavage has occurred. Although the effects on neuropeptide levels (e.g., substance P, neurotensin) have been studied in central nervous system models—with mixed and sometimes counterintuitive outcomes (such as decreased acetylcholine levels) (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 8–16, 70–72)—the rationale for ocular repurposing rests on the idea that the same enzymatic inhibition can counteract the accumulation of cathepsin-inhibiting peptides in RPE cells. Notably, some studies have suggested that PREP inhibition can positively modulate autophagy, a process that is critical for cellular clearance mechanisms. Given that impaired autophagy is a central feature in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, a compound like KYP-2047 that both reduces toxic peptide accumulation and enhances proteolytic pathways presents an attractive, multitargeted strategy (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

The core hypothesis driving the repurposing of KYP-2047 for dry AMD is that inhibition of PREP will reduce the buildup of proline-rich peptides that otherwise impair lysosomal cathepsin activity. In RPE cells, efficient degradation of POS via phagocytosis and lysosomal function is essential for maintaining retinal homeostasis. In the setting of dry AMD, decreased cathepsin D and L activities are implicated in the inefficient clearance of cellular debris, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, ultimately causing RPE dysfunction.

In the proposed assay, RPE cells—typically the ARPE-19 cell line—will be challenged in an environment mimicking AMD pathology; for instance, by loading them with A2E and subjecting the cells to proteasomal stress. Under these conditions, the activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and L is compromised, and POS degradation is impaired. The application of KYP-2047 is expected to inhibit PREP activity with high potency, which theoretically will lead to a reduction in the concentration of peptide substrates that interfere with cathepsin enzymes (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).

The anticipated cascade of events is as follows:  
1. KYP-2047, at concentrations close to its low nanomolar IC₅₀, will effectively bind to and inhibit PREP in RPE cells.  
2. This inhibition will prevent the excessive cleavage of proline-containing peptides, thereby reducing the pool of inhibitory peptides that could otherwise bind to and decrease cathepsin D and L activities.  
3. As a consequence, the restoration of cathepsin activity is expected to improve the degradation of POS components as well as the clearance of other toxic debris, which is a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.  
4. Additionally, the compound’s reported anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects, demonstrated in ARPE-19 cells with defective proteasomal clearance, may further contribute to preserving RPE cell health by curtailing inflammatory cytokine production and oxidative stress (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 4–6).

It is also noteworthy that the mechanistic framework is further supported by the observation that PREP inhibition in other models has led to enhanced autophagy and improved clearance of aggregated proteins. In the context of AMD, effective POS degradation is not only dependent on cathepsin function but also on efficient autophagic flux. By indirectly modulating these pathways, KYP-2047 could offer dual benefits: restoration of lysosomal enzyme activity and bolstering of intracellular clearance mechanisms. Thus, the expected in vitro endpoints would likely include increased cathepsin D/L activity, elevated POS degradation (as detected by uptake assays), reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-6, IL-8, IL-1β), and diminished oxidative stress markers (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 4–6).

Although previous clinical trials in central nervous system indications did not achieve long-term success, the safety data accrued from these studies may lower the translational barrier for ocular applications, provided that proper formulation and localized delivery (or systemic approaches with ocular distribution) can be achieved (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 4–5).

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

The evaluation of KYP-2047 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD involves weighing both its promising aspects and its uncertainties. On the positive side, KYP-2047 is a well-defined, highly potent inhibitor of PREP with an established chemical profile and a strong foundation in preclinical studies. Its synthetic origin as a peptidomimetic compound designed to bind the active site of PREP is well documented (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4), and the compound’s low nanomolar potency provides confidence that even modest drug exposures may achieve effective enzyme inhibition.

The repurposing strategy capitalizes on emerging evidence that PREP inhibitors can exert cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in RPE cells. In vitro studies conducted in ARPE-19 cells with impaired proteasomal clearance have demonstrated that KYP-2047 can reduce inflammatory cytokine production and promote cell viability (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). Given the central role of inflammation and defective lysosomal clearance in dry AMD, these findings provide a mechanistic rationale for testing KYP-2047 in this indication.

Furthermore, the proposed mechanism—whereby inhibition of PREP reduces the formation of inhibitory proline-rich peptides that suppress cathepsin activity—is mechanistically attractive. Restoring the function of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and L could feasibly improve the degradation of POS, a process known to be compromised in dry AMD. This dual-targeted approach (improving both enzyme activity and reducing cell stress) is particularly compelling in the context of a multifactorial disease such as AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

Despite these strengths, several potential weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. First, while extensive preclinical work has been carried out in neurological models—and there exists some early in vitro evidence of benefit in RPE cells—the direct connection between PREP activity and the inhibition of cathepsin function in the context of RPE biology remains largely hypothetical. The literature currently lacks robust in vivo studies in ocular models of dry AMD demonstrating that PREP inhibition translates into measurable improvements in retinal function and morphology. Historical clinical trials of PREP inhibitors for cognitive applications have encountered difficulties due to inconsistent efficacy, which raises concerns about the translation of in vitro findings to clinical benefits (Scuderi, 2023, pp. 133–135; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41).

Second, the formulation challenges associated with KYP-2047 cannot be overlooked. Its low water solubility necessitates specialized carriers (such as saline with 5% Tween® 80), which may complicate delivery to the eye, especially when considering the need for localized administration to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE. Appropriate ocular delivery systems (e.g., intravitreal injections or sustained-release implants) would need to be developed and optimized, which adds a layer of complexity to the overall drug development program (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47).

Another area of concern is the historical inconsistency of PREP inhibitor effects in clinical studies. Although there is evidence of neuroprotective benefits, the fact that several PREP inhibitors failed to advance through the clinical development pipeline for neurological indications suggests that the enzyme’s true physiological role remains incompletely defined. In the absence of a clear and reproducible biomarker for PREP inhibition in vivo, there is a risk that the biochemical benefits seen in cell culture studies may not be recapitulated in the complex environment of the human retina (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 70–72).

Moreover, because PREP is a ubiquitous enzyme expressed in many tissues, systemic administration of KYP-2047 might lead to off-target effects that could limit its therapeutic window. Although the safety profile observed in early neurological trials is encouraging, targeted delivery to the eye (to minimize systemic exposure) will be crucial if KYP-2047 is to be repurposed for dry AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

Finally, while the proposed mechanism that links elevated PREP activity with the inhibition of lysosomal cathepsins is intriguing, it remains to be validated by direct experimental data specifically in RPE cells. The current literature, including the recent study by Toppila and colleagues, primarily focuses on the cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory actions of KYP-2047 in ARPE-19 cells, but detailed biochemical analyses linking PREP inhibition mechanistically to improved cathepsin-mediated degradation of POS are still needed (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 4–6).

─────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

In summary, KYP-2047 is an established prolyl oligopeptidase inhibitor with a well-characterized chemical and pharmacological profile, offering promising features as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its ability to inhibit PREP at low nanomolar concentrations, coupled with demonstrated cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in preclinical RPE models, aligns well with the therapeutic need to restore lysosomal cathepsin activity and improve photoreceptor outer segment degradation in dry AMD (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 12–13).

The strategy to mitigate the accumulation of inhibitory proline-rich peptides and thereby reinstate effective lysosomal function is mechanistically plausible and supported by related studies in neural tissues. Nevertheless, the exact role of PREP in the modulation of cathepsin activity in RPE cells remains to be fully elucidated. In addition, the challenges of achieving appropriate ocular drug delivery and the historical precedents of inconsistent efficacy in PREP inhibitor clinical trials represent significant hurdles that must be addressed in future studies (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41).

Overall, while KYP-2047 brings strengths in terms of potency and a partially validated cytoprotective profile in in vitro models, its repurposing for dry AMD would require further in-depth preclinical studies. These studies should include in vivo efficacy assessments in relevant animal models of AMD, comprehensive pharmacokinetic and ocular distribution evaluations, and mechanistic experiments that clearly link PREP inhibition with improved cathepsin and lysosomal function in the RPE.   - Ocular PD feasibility is supported in mice for systemic iptacopan; pharmacologic AP blockade reduces deposits in Efemp1 with another orally bioavailable FB inhibitor (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).

  - Macro safety signals observed with complement inhibitors in AMD (CNV incidence) necessitate vigilant monitoring and risk–benefit analyses tailored to FB inhibition (Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
  - Systemic delivery uncertainty—human ocular PK/PD data are lacking; trial design should incorporate robust systemic PD and exploratory ocular biomarkers where feasible (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).

Recommendation  
Advance iptacopan for dry AMD with a focused, staged plan:  
- Preclinical confirmation package: replicate Efemp1 findings with iptacopan (deposits, AP biomarkers, proteomics) and demonstrate RPE lysosomal/autophagy rescue in CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE under complement-competent conditions; quantify ocular exposure–PD after oral dosing (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Biomarker-enriched clinical strategy: leverage systemic AP biomarkers and imaging-based progression metrics from Novartis Pharmaceuticals (2022); consider enrichment by complement genetics/biomarkers reflecting AP activation (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).  
- Safety management: maintain vaccination requirements and active CNV surveillance; implement adherence support given the shorter half-life relative to biologics (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Ricklin, 2024, pp. 7–9; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).

On balance, iptacopan has substantial mechanistic, translational, and clinical-class support to merit continued development in dry AMD, contingent on closing the specific evidence gaps for RPE degradative rescue and direct AMD-model efficacy with this agent (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Adalimumab (marketed as Humira) is a fully humanized recombinant IgG1 monoclonal antibody developed using recombinant DNA technology that targets tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNFα). As a member of the anti‐TNFα class of biologics, adalimumab is designed to bind both soluble and membrane‐bound TNFα with high affinity, thereby preventing its interaction with the TNF receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2) on target cells. This antibody was originally discovered and engineered to address systemic inflammatory diseases, and its fully human composition is intended to lower immunogenicity compared to earlier chimeric molecules such as infliximab. In its development, molecular engineering efforts focused on isolating the relevant antibody variable regions that exhibit specificity for TNFα, followed by the construction of a recombinant molecule with human constant regions to improve tolerability and clinical efficacy. Anti‐TNFα antibodies belong to a broader class of therapeutic compounds that have dramatically changed the treatment landscape for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. They have been widely applied in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn’s disease, and ulcerative colitis, and over the past two decades, their use has been extended into ocular inflammatory diseases such as non‐infectious uveitis. Such applications underscore the versatility and translational potential of TNFα inhibition in modulating inflammatory cascades (Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History:  
Adalimumab’s clinical journey began with its approval for systemic autoimmune diseases where TNFα plays a fundamental role in mediating inflammation and tissue damage. Its robust performance in rheumatoid arthritis and related conditions has been well documented in numerous large-scale randomized controlled trials, which demonstrated significant improvement in clinical outcomes and inflammatory markers. These successes provided the foundation for exploring its application in other diseases characterized by inflammatory dysregulation. In recent years, growing evidence from both biochemical studies and clinical observations has highlighted the role of chronic inflammation in the pathogenesis of several retinal degenerative disorders. In particular, studies have shown that TNFα is upregulated in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and may contribute to the degeneration seen in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). For example, preclinical work has demonstrated that inflammation mediated by TNFα can impair the integrity of RPE cells, reduce the expression of proteins critical for RPE function (including visual cycle proteins and complement regulators) and disrupt phagocytic clearance mechanisms; these findings form the basis for hypothesizing that TNFα blockade may preserve RPE function in dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

While the majority of clinical uses of adalimumab have been in the realm of systemic and ocular inflammatory conditions such as non‐infectious uveitis, there has been emerging interest in repurposing anti‐TNFα therapies for retinal degenerations. In the context of ocular disease, several investigators have explored both systemic and local (intravitreal or subconjunctival) routes of administration to modulate intraocular inflammation. Pilot clinical trials and case reports have assessed intravitreal adalimumab in patients with uveitis and even in those with neovascular (“wet”) AMD refractory to anti‐VEGF therapies; these studies reported varying degrees of efficacy and underscored an acceptable local safety profile, though in some instances, higher dosages have been associated with ocular toxicity. In animal studies, intravitreal or subconjunctival administration of adalimumab has been shown to reduce inflammation and offer neuroprotection in models of retinal degeneration, such as in the rd10 mouse model for retinitis pigmentosa, establishing a precedent for local administration to achieve high ocular levels with minimal systemic exposure. Despite these advancements, use of adalimumab specifically for dry AMD has not been established in clinical practice. The proposed approach builds on the mechanistic insights from studies demonstrating that elevated TNFα levels can lead to downregulation of phagocytic receptors and lysosomal enzymes in RPE cells—processes central to dry AMD pathology—and posits that reversing these effects via TNFα neutralization may preserve RPE function (Nashine et al., 2022; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of adalimumab centers on its targeted neutralization of TNFα. TNFα is a proinflammatory cytokine produced by a variety of cell types that include activated T lymphocytes, macrophages, and, importantly, resident cells in the eye such as RPE and Müller glia. When secreted into the extracellular milieu, TNFα binds to its receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2), triggering intracellular signaling cascades that lead to the activation of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and other pathways that promote the expression of additional inflammatory cytokines, adhesion molecules, and matrix metalloproteinases. These processes collectively contribute to a sustained inflammatory response that can result in cellular dysfunction and death. Adalimumab, by virtue of its high affinity binding, sequesters TNFα and prevents receptor engagement. In doing so, it effectively interrupts these downstream proinflammatory signals and halts the amplification of the inflammatory cascade (Wang et al., 2011; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium cells, TNFα-mediated signaling has been implicated in the suppression of genes critical to the maintenance of RPE functions. Specifically, experimental studies have suggested that exposure to TNFα leads to a reduction in the expression of MERTK—a receptor tyrosine kinase essential for the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—as well as cathepsin D, a lysosomal enzyme crucial for the degradation of engulfed material. The decrease in MERTK expression compromises the ability of RPE cells to efficiently phagocytose POS, thereby potentially contributing to the accumulation of cellular debris, drusen formation, and further RPE stress that are characteristic of dry AMD. In parallel, a reduction in cathepsin D would impair lysosomal degradation, exacerbating the intracellular buildup of waste products and further undermining cellular homeostasis in the RPE. By neutralizing TNFα, adalimumab is hypothesized to prevent these detrimental changes, preserving the expression levels of MERTK and cathepsin D and thereby maintaining robust phagocytic and degradative capacity in RPE cells (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021).

At the molecular level, the binding of adalimumab to TNFα is mediated via its antigen-binding (Fab) region, which recognizes specific epitopes on the cytokine. This interaction is characterized by high affinity and specificity, ensuring that even low concentrations of the antibody can effectively neutralize TNFα activity. The blockade prevents TNFα from initiating receptor-mediated signaling that would otherwise promote inflammation and cellular stress. Moreover, because TNFα is known to regulate not only inflammatory cytokine production but also apoptotic processes, its inhibition may confer additional neuroprotective effects in the retina by reducing signals that lead to programmed cell death. The comprehensive inhibition of TNFα by adalimumab therefore stands as a multifaceted intervention, addressing both the inflammatory insult and its secondary effects on critical cellular functions in the RPE (Wang et al., 2011; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Nashine et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for leveraging adalimumab in dry AMD rests on its potential to neutralize elevated TNFα levels in the subretinal microenvironment. Elevated TNFα has been implicated in the pathological downregulation of key proteins involved in RPE function, notably MERTK and cathepsin D. MERTK is a receptor that plays an essential role in the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, a process that is critical for the renewal of photoreceptors and the overall maintenance of retinal health. Cathepsin D, on the other hand, is involved in the lysosomal degradation of the ingested material; together, these proteins ensure that the RPE can effectively clear and recycle photoreceptor debris. In dry AMD, this phagocytic process is compromised, leading to the accumulation of cellular waste products and drusen formation, which further fuels inflammation and RPE degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Administration of adalimumab is expected to interrupt this cascade by neutralizing TNFα, thereby preventing its signaling that leads to the downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D. With TNFα effectively neutralized, RPE cells should experience a more favorable molecular milieu in which the expression of these critical proteins is maintained at functional levels. This preservation would, in turn, support the RPE’s capacity to phagocytose and degrade photoreceptor outer segments, thereby averting the buildup of toxic waste products. Furthermore, since TNFα signaling also contributes to other aspects of cellular stress and inflammation—such as the upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines and the induction of apoptotic pathways—the neutralization of TNFα by adalimumab may also reduce overall cellular stress and promote RPE cell survival and function (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022).

In vitro assays using cultured human RPE cells exposed to TNFα could be employed to test this hypothesis. In these experiments, treatment with adalimumab should result in the normalization or preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression levels when compared to TNFα-treated controls. In addition, functional assays measuring the uptake and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (or surrogate fluorescent particles) would be expected to show improved phagocytic efficiency in RPE cells treated with adalimumab. Such findings would provide robust mechanistic support for the proposed therapeutic strategy. Moreover, preliminary in vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD or models of induced RPE dysfunction could further validate that TNFα blockade leads to preservation of RPE integrity, improved photoreceptor survival, and retardation of retinal degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Considering that the expression of MERTK is well documented in RPE cells and that its function is critical for POS phagocytosis—a process that declines with aging and in the presence of inflammatory mediators—the ability of adalimumab to maintain or restore MERTK expression would be highly relevant in the context of dry AMD. In the proposed strategy, adalimumab may also help to stabilize other RPE functions, such as the regulation of the complement cascade and the visual cycle, both of which have been shown to be adversely affected by TNFα exposure. Thus, the anticipated effect of adalimumab is not limited solely to the preservation of phagocytic machinery; it may also contribute to a broader stabilization of RPE cell health in the face of chronic low-grade inflammation that characterizes dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of adalimumab as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a compelling yet cautiously optimistic perspective. One of the principal strengths of adalimumab lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action; by neutralizing TNFα, it directly addresses a central mediator of inflammation that has been implicated in the dysregulation of RPE functions. The experimental evidence indicating that TNFα exposure can lead to the downregulation of essential proteins such as MERTK and cathepsin D provides a strong rationale for the hypothesis that TNFα inhibition might preserve the RPE’s ability to maintain photoreceptor homeostasis. This mechanistic insight is particularly attractive because it targets one of the fundamental dysfunctions in dry AMD—namely, the failure of the RPE to clear photoreceptor outer segments effectively, which leads to the accumulation of drusen and progressive retinal degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the extensive clinical experience with adalimumab in systemic and ocular inflammatory diseases supports its safety profile. The fact that adalimumab is already approved by regulatory agencies, coupled with several clinical studies demonstrating its localized safety when administered intravitreally or via related routes in ocular conditions such as uveitis, adds to its attractiveness as a candidate for repurposing (Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010; Leal et al., 2018; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. To date, most studies involving adalimumab in the ocular context have focused on inflammatory conditions such as uveitis and neovascular AMD rather than dry AMD specifically. As a result, direct clinical evidence supporting its efficacy in preserving RPE phagocytic function in dry AMD is currently limited. The hypothesis that adalimumab can prevent the TNFα-induced downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D is primarily based on preclinical observations, and further mechanistic studies, both in vitro and in relevant animal models, are necessary to validate this pathway in the context of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Nashine et al., 2022; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Another potential challenge with using adalimumab for dry AMD is related to drug delivery and dosing. While intravitreal administration has shown promise in limited studies, determining the optimal dose that achieves effective TNFα blockade without incurring retinal toxicity remains an unresolved issue. Some animal studies have indicated that higher doses of intravitreal adalimumab can lead to retinal inflammation, reduced electroretinogram responses, or histopathological evidence of toxicity. Given that dry AMD is a chronic condition and would likely require repeated dosing or sustained drug delivery systems, the long-term safety of local TNFα blockade needs to be rigorously evaluated (Manzano et al., 2008; Pascual-Camps et al., 2014).

Moreover, because TNFα plays roles in normal immune surveillance and tissue repair, its complete inhibition—especially in an aged population that may have impaired immune responses—could theoretically predispose patients to infections or other adverse effects. Although the systemic safety profile of adalimumab is well established, the ocular microenvironment has distinct immunological characteristics, and the long-term effects of TNFα inhibition on retinal homeostasis, particularly regarding complement activation and maintenance of the blood–retinal barrier, require further study. There is also the possibility that compensatory inflammatory pathways may become activated in response to TNFα blockade, potentially diminishing the efficacy of the intervention over time (García-Layana et al., 2021; Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Sharma et al., 2009).

Additionally, the magnitude of the contribution of TNFα to the pathogenesis of dry AMD relative to other factors—such as oxidative stress, genetic predispositions (including polymorphisms in complement factors), and lipid metabolism abnormalities—remains to be fully delineated. It is possible that TNFα is one of several drivers of RPE dysfunction, and that its inhibition may need to be combined with other therapeutic strategies (for example, antioxidant supplementation or complement inhibitors) to achieve a meaningful clinical benefit. Therefore, while the rationale for adalimumab is compelling, a monotherapy approach may not be sufficient to halt the multifactorial progression of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nussenblatt et al., 2010).

In summary, adalimumab presents a promising repurposed candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on its potent and specific inhibition of TNFα—a cytokine implicated in the downregulation of crucial RPE proteins such as MERTK and cathepsin D. The drug’s extensive use in other inflammatory settings, along with preliminary evidence supporting its ocular safety, lend credibility to the hypothesis that TNFα blockade can preserve the phagocytic machinery of RPE cells and potentially slow the degenerative process characteristic of dry AMD. Nevertheless, significant challenges remain, including the need for robust preclinical validation in dry AMD models, optimization of ocular dosing regimens, and long-term safety assessments in an elderly population. A carefully designed series of in vitro experiments using human RPE cells—followed by well-controlled animal studies—should be undertaken to establish proof of concept regarding the preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression and function. If these studies yield positive results, subsequent early-phase clinical trials could be justified to evaluate the efficacy of intravitreal adalimumab in patients with dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010).

In light of these considerations, our recommendation is to advance adalimumab into a rigorous preclinical testing pipeline aimed specifically at dry AMD models. This should include studies that measure the expression levels and activity of MERTK and cathepsin D in RPE cells under conditions of TNFα stimulation, both in the presence and absence of adalimumab treatment. Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiling in ocular tissues, along with assessments of retinal structure and function via in vivo imaging and electrophysiological testing, will be critical to determining an appropriate dosing strategy. Finally, integration with complementary therapeutic approaches may be considered to address other facets of dry AMD pathogenesis. While the path to clinical application is fraught with challenges, the potential benefit of preserving RPE phagocytic function—and by extension, photoreceptor survival—in a disease with very limited current treatment options provides a strong impetus for further development of this candidate (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022).

In conclusion, adalimumab’s established molecular profile as a potent TNFα inhibitor, its extensive clinical track record in systemic and ocular inflammatory diseases, and the emerging data linking TNFα to RPE dysfunction collectively support the rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD. Nevertheless, given the complexity of AMD pathogenesis and the potential risks associated with chronic intraocular immunomodulation, a thorough and methodical approach to preclinical investigation is warranted before embarking on large-scale clinical trials. The ultimate goal is to validate that neutralization of TNFα can indeed preserve the phagocytic capabilities of the RPE, thereby maintaining retinal health and preventing the progression of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Strengths of this candidate include its potent and specific inhibition of TNFα, which is a key mediator in inflammatory cascades, its favorable immunogenicity profile stemming from its fully human composition, and its prior demonstration of safety in ocular applications such as uveitis. In addition, the biological rationale is supported by evidence that TNFα negatively impacts the expression of proteins critical for RPE phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation—a process that, when impaired, underlies the pathology of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

On the other hand, weaknesses center on the limited direct evidence for efficacy in dry AMD, potential challenges in achieving precise intraocular dosing without inducing retinal toxicity, and uncertain long-term consequences of sustained TNFα inhibition in the delicate immune environment of the eye. Moreover, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD suggests that a singular focus on TNFα may not fully address the disease’s complex pathophysiology, raising the possibility that combination therapies might eventually be necessary for optimal outcomes (Manzano et al., 2008; Sharma et al., 2009; Nussenblatt et al., 2010).

Given these observations, our evaluation concludes that adalimumab represents a promising and scientifically sound candidate for repurposing to treat dry AMD. Its mechanistic profile aligns well with the goal of preserving RPE phagocytic function by preventing TNFα-mediated downregulation of key proteins like MERTK and cathepsin D. However, to move forward with this candidate, research efforts must focus on resolving the outstanding questions through rigorous preclinical studies, optimization of the drug delivery method, and detailed long-term safety assessments. If successful, these steps could pave the way for early-phase clinical trials designed to test the efficacy of intravitreal adalimumab in stabilizing or improving RPE function in patients with dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010).

In summary, while the current body of literature on adalimumab has primarily focused on its role in systemic inflammatory diseases and ocular inflammatory conditions such as uveitis and neovascular AMD, the underlying mechanistic data provide a persuasive rationale for extending its application to dry AMD. The hypothesis that adalimumab can preserve RPE phagocytic function by neutralizing TNFα—thereby preventing the deleterious downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D—is scientifically plausible and merits further systematic investigation. The potential benefits of repurposing a well-characterized agent with an established safety profile are substantial, especially in a disease area where effective treatments remain elusive (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Overall, our recommendation for the drug development team is to prioritize a series of detailed preclinical studies that examine the effects of adalimumab on RPE cells under TNFα-induced stress conditions, with particular emphasis on the regulation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression and subsequent phagocytic activity. These studies should involve both conventional cell culture models and in vivo models that mimic the chronic inflammatory environment observed in dry AMD. Should these studies yield positive results, a phase I/II clinical trial focusing on safety and early efficacy in patients with dry AMD would be justified. This stepwise approach will ensure that the promising mechanistic rationale is thoroughly vetted before large-scale clinical application (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

In conclusion, the convergence of molecular, biochemical, and clinical evidence supports the further exploration of adalimumab as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to mitigate TNFα-mediated inflammatory cascades could play a critical role in preserving RPE function, maintaining photoreceptor health, and ultimately slowing the progression of a disease that currently lacks effective treatments. Nonetheless, rigorous preclinical validation and careful consideration of dosing and long-term safety will be essential to realize its potential in this new indication (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
AMY-101 is a third-generation compstatin analogue built on the Cp40 scaffold, a cyclic, disulfide-constrained peptide discovered through iterative structure–activity optimization of the original compstatin hit identified by phage display against C3/C3b in 1996 (initial macrocycle I[CVVQDWGHHRC]T) (Lamers et al., 2022). Key potency-improving modifications en route to Cp40 include N-methylation of Trp and insertion of sarcosine, which rigidify the backbone and substantially increase binding affinity to C3; Cp40 (y-I[CV(1Me)WQDWSarAHRC]mI) binds a defined pocket between MG4/MG5 on the β-chain of C3/C3b with subnanomolar affinity and high selectivity for human and nonhuman primate (NHP) C3, while sparing other species, thereby necessitating NHP for translational in vivo work (Lamers et al., 2022). Mechanistically, compstatins are protein–protein interaction inhibitors: they occupy a substrate-binding site on C3 that prevents association with the C3 convertases, blocking convertase-mediated cleavage of native C3, and thereby interrupting the amplification loop and downstream effector generation (C3a, C3b, C5a, and membrane attack complex) independent of the initiating pathway (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Compstatin analogues comprise a class of synthetic macrocyclic peptides that target the central node of complement activation at C3, distinguishing them from terminal-pathway blockers (e.g., C5 antibodies) and alternative-pathway–restricted inhibitors (e.g., factor D), which have shown mixed outcomes in complex complement-driven diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Mastellos et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Clinically, the compstatin platform has matured to produce both a PEGylated bivalent C3 inhibitor (pegcetacoplan/APL-2) approved for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and non-PEGylated Cp40-derived candidates such as AMY-101 in human trials, establishing class translatability and safety management paradigms for chronic C3 inhibition (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

For ophthalmic translation, medicinal chemistry on Cp40 has produced fourth-generation, non-PEGylated lysine-extended derivatives (Cp40-KK, Cp40-KKK) with markedly improved solubility and favorable intraocular retention after intravitreal (IVT) administration in NHPs; these scaffolds maintain subnanomolar C3 affinity and exhibit retinal tissue engagement and co-localization with C3, suggesting target-driven distribution in ocular compartments (Hughes et al., 2020). Within the compstatin clinical lineage, earlier intravitreal compstatin (POT-4) and the PEGylated derivative APL-2/pegcetacoplan provided clinical benchmarks in geographic atrophy (GA), albeit with formulation-dependent considerations (e.g., PEG-associated risks) that motivate PEG-free ocular candidates such as AMY-101 or next-generation Cp40 analogues tailored for ocular delivery (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Compstatin peptides have undergone extensive preclinical characterization and early clinical translation across complement-driven indications. Systemically, Cp40/AMY-101 blocked intravascular hemolysis and C3b opsonization in primate models and attenuated alloimmune responses and downstream B/T cell activation in transplantation models, demonstrating potent complement control and immunomodulatory ripple effects in vivo (Lamers et al., 2022). AMY-101 progressed through a first-in-human phase 1 trial (single and multiple ascending doses; subcutaneous and intravenous) with acceptable safety, no serious adverse events, and pharmacodynamic evidence of complement pathway modulation in healthy volunteers (Amyndas Pharmaceuticals S.A., 2017), and subsequently achieved local-delivery efficacy in a randomized, double-blind, split-mouth Phase IIa study for gingival inflammation with durable anti-inflammatory responses and no drug-induced immunogenicity detected (Hasturk et al., 2021). In the periodontal trial, AMY-101 reduced clinical indices (modified gingival index, bleeding on probing) and decreased matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-8, MMP-9) in gingival crevicular fluid, with effects persisting up to 90 days after the three weekly local injections, supporting local tolerability, biomarker responsiveness, and sustained pharmacodynamic action (Hasturk et al., 2021).

Within ophthalmology and AMD, multiple lines of evidence support the clinical plausibility of C3-directed strategies. Early intravitreal compstatin (POT-4) dosing in a primate model was associated with disappearance of drusen deposits, and PEGylated C3 inhibition (APL-2/pegcetacoplan) reduced GA lesion growth in Phase II and has achieved efficacy signals in Phase III, representing the first successful complement intervention in GA and validating the target class for dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). Conversely, downstream or pathway-restricted modulation disappointed: anti-C5 agents (eculizumab, LFG316) and alternative pathway blockade at factor D (lampalizumab) failed to deliver clinical benefit in GA, bolstering the rationale for upstream C3 control that addresses both opsonization and effector generation (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Although AMY-101 itself has not yet been reported in human ocular trials in the provided context, Cp40-class derivatives have been tailored for ocular use and evaluated in NHPs after single IVT injections, achieving prolonged C3-saturating vitreous concentrations and retinal/choroidal target engagement for over three months—exposure metrics compatible with infrequent intravitreal maintenance regimens (Hughes et al., 2020).

Critically, human iPSC-derived RPE models carrying the common CFH Y402H high-risk variant establish a mechanistic and phenotypic bridge to AMD and provide in vitro evidence that Cp40 reverses disease-relevant pathology, particularly lysosome/autophagy defects and complement-driven lysosomal overburden, thereby directly supporting the translational concept for dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The RPE findings are reinforced by the broader AMD complement literature: complement activation on photoreceptor outer segments drives monocyte-dependent retinal atrophy, factor H genetics (including Y402H) modulates ocular alternative pathway activity, and complement deposition in Bruch’s membrane/sub-RPE space contributes to drusen biogenesis and RPE stress—elements that are mechanistically addressable by C3 blockade (Mastellos et al., 2019).

In sum, compstatin-class agents have an extensive preclinical pedigree and emergent clinical validation. For AMD specifically, the class has ocular proof-of-concept (POT-4) and clinical validation of C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan), and Cp40 analogues demonstrate prolonged ocular PK in NHP; AMY-101 contributes human safety and local-delivery experience that supports translational risk management but requires dedicated ocular development for dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
C3 sits at the convergence of the classical, lectin, and alternative complement pathways; its cleavage by C3 convertases (C4b2b for CP/LP and C3bBb for AP) produces the anaphylatoxin C3a and the opsonin C3b, which seeds an amplification loop by forming additional alternative pathway convertases on activating surfaces (Mastellos et al., 2019). Persistent generation and deposition of C3b (and downstream C5b-9) under dysregulated conditions fuels inflammatory tissue damage and membrane injury; thus, targeting C3 offers initiation-independent suppression of both opsonization and effector generation (C3a, C5a, MAC), addressing multiple pathogenic modalities concurrently (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Compstatins, including Cp40/AMY-101, are substrate-protecting inhibitors that bind to a defined site on C3/C3b (between MG4 and MG5 of the β-chain) and prevent the binding of native C3 to the active convertase, thereby blocking C3 turnover and the AP amplification cycle regardless of initiating pathway (Lamers et al., 2022). This binding mode is supported by co-crystallographic and kinetic analyses, and SAR has established critical roles for N-methylated Trp and charged residues (Asp7, Arg12) in affinity and solubility (Lamers et al., 2022). Unlike some PEGylated bivalent constructs that display altered target preference and weaker affinity to soluble C3, monovalent PEG-free Cp40 binds strongly to both soluble and surface-bound C3/C3b, preserving potency where soluble target is abundant (e.g., in plasma and vitreous), a beneficial profile for local ocular delivery (Lamers et al., 2022).

In human iPSC-RPE carrying CFH Y402H, C3 overactivation and increased C3 turnover correlate with multiple autophagy–lysosome abnormalities: increased expression of autophagosome markers (LC3-II, p62, ATG12–ATG5), expansion and activation of late endosomal/lysosomal/exosomal compartments (LAMP1, CD63; increased Lysotracker), reduced lysosomal functional readouts (decreased Cathepsin D expression/activity), swollen lysosome-like vesicles, lysosomal membrane fragility (elevated galectin-8 recruitment), and extracellular deposition of Cathepsin D in ApoE-positive drusen-like material (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Mechanistic links are twofold: (1) excessive extracellular C3 activation increases surface C5b-9 (MAC) formation, which is internalized to lysosomes and triggers lysosomal membrane permeabilization with cathepsin leakage; (2) intracellular C3–autophagy crosstalk via ATG16L1 and cathepsin-mediated C3 activation may perturb autophagy flux, compounding lysosomal stress (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In this model, Cp40 reduces C3 turnover (biochemical ELISA/MSD readouts) and diminishes C3b and C5b-9 deposition on and within RPE, leading to restoration of lysosomal pH/function and autophagic flux (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Specifically, Cp40 treatment increases Cathepsin D expression/activity, reduces lysosome size and swelling, stabilizes lysosomal membranes (reduced galectin-8/LAMP co-localization), normalizes melanosome content (increased mature type 4 melanosomes), and decreases the volume of drusen-like deposits on transwells—collectively, a reversal of RPE disease phenotypes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Importantly, the RPE data underscore that “tuning” C3 is necessary: stable shRNA knockdown of C3 (~85% reduction) did not restore melanosome/lysosome number and increased stress vacuoles indicative of a detrimental effect, whereas pharmacologic Cp40-mediated control of C3 turnover (not wholesale depletion) was beneficial—consistent with C3’s homeostatic roles in tissue clearance and immune surveillance (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Rapamycin-driven autophagy activation failed to correct lysosomal deficits in the same AMD-RPE model, underscoring that upstream removal of complement burden may be required to re-enable autophagic clearance in complement-dysregulated RPE (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Following a 0.5 mg IVT dose, Cp40-KKK maintained C3-saturating vitreous concentrations over three months (~200 nM during month 1; ~100–120 nM by month 3) and co-localized with C3 in retinal/choroidal tissue, suggesting target-driven retention and possible depot release; intraocular C3 concentrations measured were ~0.1–2 nM, implying inhibitor:target ratios sufficient for sustained pharmacodynamic coverage (Hughes et al., 2020). Only ~0.2% of the initial dose remained unbound in vitreous by day 14, consistent with rapid clearance of free peptide and prolonged persistence of target-bound pools (Hughes et al., 2020). These PK relationships, combined with AMY-101’s subnanomolar C3 affinity and prolonged plasma half-life (>60 h), support the feasibility of durable local complement control via IVT compstatin analogues without PEGylation (Lamers et al., 2022; Hasturk et al., 2021; Lamers et al., 2022).

In the proposed iPSC-RPE assay, AMY-101/Cp40 is expected to bind native C3 in the extracellular milieu and block its convertase-mediated cleavage, thereby suppressing both C3a/C3b generation and downstream terminal-pathway activation, including formation and lysosomal internalization of C5b-9 complexes that exacerbate lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cathepsin leakage in complement-dysregulated RPE (Lamers et al., 2022; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The RPE model provides direct biochemical and cell-biological readouts that respond to C3 inhibition: Cp40 reduced C3 turnover (C3b/iC3b/C3c in supernatants), decreased surface and lysosomal C3b and C5b-9, and restored lysosomal functional markers (Cathepsin D expression and activity), organelle morphology (reduced lysosomal swelling; increased mature melanosomes), and membrane integrity (decreased galectin-8 recruitment), with associated reductions in drusen-like deposit burden—outcomes that would be expected for AMY-101 under similar conditions (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Given the measured RPE complement activity and the presence of C3 in ocular compartments, PD monitoring can include extracellular C3 fragment profiling (e.g., MSD capture for C3a domain detecting C3b; ELISA for C3b/iC3b/C3c), surface and lysosomal C5b-9 immunostaining (e.g., co-localization with LAMP markers), and lysosomal/autophagy endpoints such as LAMP1/CD63 expression, LysoTracker signal, LC3-II and p62 accumulation, Cathepsin D protein/activity, and galectin-8–based lysosomal damage assays (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In the referenced RPE studies, effective Cp40 exposure used 6 µM for seven days with media change mid-course—a regimen that achieved robust biochemical and morphological rescue; potency in cellular systems is governed by high target abundance and convertase dynamics and may not mirror biochemical IC₅₀ values, but AMY-101’s subnanomolar C3 affinity and the low-nanomolar ocular C3 concentrations measured in NHP vitreous suggest that pharmacologically relevant free drug levels in the assay will saturate target (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). We note that no direct IC₅₀ for Cp40/AMY-101 in RPE culture is provided in the cited work; therefore, the proposed IC₅₀ value (~0.5 µM) cannot be confirmed from the current context and dosing should be guided empirically by the established 6 µM exposure used to reverse phenotypes in the Y402H model (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Regarding photoreceptor outer segment (POS) processing, impaired lysosomal function in RPE is causally linked to defective POS degradation; complement activation on POS can drive monocyte-dependent retinal atrophy, providing disease-relevant context for expecting that restoration of lysosomal flux via C3 inhibition would secondarily improve POS handling (Mastellos et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). However, the provided RPE studies did not explicitly report POS uptake/degradation assays in Cp40-treated cells, so POS-specific rescue should be treated as a testable hypothesis rather than an established outcome; lysosomal/autophagy restoration and reduced complement burden provide a mechanistic basis for such improvement (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

For translational extrapolation to IVT dosing paradigms, ocular PK from Cp40-KK/KKK in NHP indicates that non-PEGylated Cp40 analogues can achieve multi-month C3-saturating exposure (retinal/choroidal co-localization with C3), which, combined with AMY-101’s high-affinity binding and absence of PEG (avoiding anti-PEG immunogenicity and PEG-related tissue effects), supports feasibility of infrequent dosing with a favorable mechanistic risk–benefit profile (Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
– Mechanistic centrality and breadth of action at C3: AMY-101 directly blocks the C3 convertase–substrate interaction, upstream of opsonization and effector generation, thereby intercepting multiple pathogenic drivers operative in dry AMD (C3b deposition, C3a/C5a-mediated inflammation, and MAC-mediated membrane injury), in contrast to pathway-restricted or terminal-pathway agents that have underperformed in GA (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). By protecting C3 from cleavage rather than inhibiting a specific convertase assembly, AMY-101 exerts initiation-independent control, appropriate for the complex and mixed complement activation modes present in AMD (Hasturk et al., 2021).  
– Direct human RPE disease-model evidence: In Y402H iPSC-RPE, Cp40 suppressed C3 turnover and downstream C5b-9 deposition, relieved lysosomal overburden and membrane fragility, restored Cathepsin D expression/activity and melanosome maturation, and reduced drusen-like deposits—an unusually comprehensive, mechanistically coherent rescue of AMD-relevant cellular pathology that maps directly onto the hypothesized mode of action for AMY-101 (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Ocular PK/translational feasibility: Single IVT dosing of Cp40 lysine-extended derivatives in NHPs yielded >90 days of C3-saturating intraocular exposure with retinal/choroidal target engagement and co-localization, supporting achievable, infrequent dosing intervals for a PEG-free compstatin platform; methods to quantify ocular drug and C3 (SPR competition; ELISA) and retinal localization are validated and can be deployed for PD monitoring (Hughes et al., 2020).  
– Clinical precedent for the target class in GA and systemic safety: Pegcetacoplan’s efficacy in reducing GA growth validates C3 inhibition in dry AMD; prolonged systemic C3 inhibition has an acceptable safety profile with appropriate vaccination and monitoring, and AMY-101 itself showed favorable safety, lack of anti-drug antibodies, and durable local efficacy in a human local-delivery setting (periodontal disease) (Lamers et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2020; Hasturk et al., 2021).  
– PEG-free design: Non-PEGylated Cp40 analogues avoid PEG-associated liabilities (anti-PEG antibodies, tissue vacuolation, and potential association with CNV conversion observed in a subset of GA patients on PEGylated C3 inhibitors), while maintaining strong affinity for soluble C3—attributes favorable for chronic ocular use (Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
– No human ocular clinical data for AMY-101: Despite compelling RPE in vitro data and NHP ocular PK for related derivatives, AMY-101 lacks reported human ocular PK/safety and clinical efficacy data in AMD in the provided context; bridging studies will be required to confirm ocular tolerability, immunogenicity, and dosing intervals specific to AMY-101 (Lamers et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2020).  
– Species specificity constrains preclinical breadth: Compstatins bind human/NHP C3 with high specificity, precluding meaningful small-animal efficacy studies beyond surrogate approaches; this increases reliance on NHP for ocular PK/PD and toxicity packages and complicates broader in vivo AMD model validation (Lamers et al., 2022).  
– POS degradation not yet demonstrated under Cp40 in RPE: Although lysosomal/autophagy restoration strongly predicts improved POS clearance, the provided RPE studies did not report POS uptake/degradation assays post-Cp40; this is an essential disease-relevant endpoint to include in the next-stage validation (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Need to balance complement suppression: Stable C3 knockdown in the RPE model exacerbated stress phenotypes, underscoring the necessity for controlled pharmacologic inhibition rather than depletion; clinical protocols must monitor for under/over-suppression and preserve homeostatic complement roles in the immunoprivileged ocular environment (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Potential safety/biology caveats with C3 blockade in the eye: Theoretical risks include modulation of macrophage polarization that might favor neovascularization and the necessity to maintain anti-infective surveillance locally; although systemic experience with vaccination mitigates infectious risk, ocular-specific risks and CNV conversion propensity must be assessed prospectively for PEG-free C3 inhibitors (Mastellos et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2020). Patient stratification (“complotype”) and baseline complement activity vary with age/sex and genetics (e.g., CFH), necessitating biomarker-driven inclusion and response frameworks in trials (Mastellos et al., 2019).

Decision-grade Assessment and Development Plan  
– Scientific validity: Strong. The AMD-RPE disease biology is directly addressed by AMY-101’s mechanism, with robust iPSC-RPE rescue data for Cp40 spanning biochemical, organellar, and deposit readouts; the mechanism integrates with known complement–lysosome–autophagy crosstalk and MAC-induced lysosomal permeabilization (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Translational feasibility: Good, with defined tasks. Ocular PK/PD in NHPs for Cp40 derivatives is compelling and suggests IVT dosing intervals of 2–3 months; AMY-101 has favorable systemic/local safety credentials and is PEG-free (Hughes et al., 2020; Hasturk et al., 2021). The absence of human ocular data for AMY-101 is a remediable gap.  
– Comparative landscape: Favorable. Factor D and C5 failures in GA argue for upstream intervention; C3 inhibition has shown clinical benefit (pegcetacoplan), placing AMY-101 in a validated mechanistic class, with potential safety advantages from PEG-free design and strong affinity to soluble C3 (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).  
– Key risks: Ocular safety (immunogenicity, inflammation, CNV conversion), pharmacodynamic over-suppression, and unknowns around long-term retinal tissue distribution with AMY-101 (as distinct from Cp40-KKK). These will be addressed with staged NHP toxicology/PK, dosing optimization, and clinical biomarker surveillance (Hughes et al., 2020; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Recommended studies before IND for dry AMD  
1) In vitro translational package in human iPSC-RPE (Y402H and non-risk): reproduce Cp40 rescue with AMY-101 under identical conditions (6 µM; 7-day dosing), including biochemical C3 turnover (C3b/iC3b/C3c), surface/lysosomal C5b-9, LAMP1/CD63, LysoTracker, LC3-II, p62, galectin-8, Cathepsin D expression and activity, melanosome quantitation, and drusen-like deposit volume (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Add POS feeding assays (pulse–chase of isolated POS) to quantify phagosome–lysosome fusion kinetics and rhodopsin degradation as POS-specific endpoints (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
2) Ocular PK and PD in cynomolgus NHPs with AMY-101: single- and multiple-dose IVT, vitreous/tissue levels by SPR competition assay, vitreous C3 fragments and C3:drug ratios, retinal/choroidal co-localization, and depot behavior versus Cp40-KKK; include dose ranging (≥0.5 mg) and extended sampling to ≥90 days (Hughes et al., 2020).  
3) Ocular safety/toxicology: GLP IVT studies (single and repeat-dose) evaluating inflammation, IOP, ERG, OCT/FAF, histopathology (RPE, choroid, retina), and immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies intraocular/systemic) with correlation to drug levels and C3 suppression; monitor for CNV risk signals (Mastellos et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2020).  
4) Biomarker strategy: translate RPE/animal biomarkers to clinical sampling—aqueous/vitreous C3 fragments, C5a, sC5b-9; imaging biomarkers (FAF for lipofuscin; OCT for outer retinal integrity; autofluorescent deposit quantification) to track pharmacodynamic effects on deposit burden and RPE health (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2020).  
5) Patient stratification plan: incorporate CFH Y402H and broader complotype profiling in trial design, with baseline complement activity and demographic modifiers (age, sex) to enrich for responders and appropriately power efficacy analyses (Mastellos et al., 2019).

Conclusion  
AMY-101 (Cp40) is a mechanistically precise, high-affinity C3 inhibitor whose action is well matched to the complement-driven lysosomal/autophagy pathology observed in dry AMD RPE biology; Cp40 has already demonstrated reversal of Y402H RPE disease phenotypes across orthogonal readouts, and Cp40-class ocular PK in NHPs supports infrequent IVT dosing without PEG, addressing practical treatment constraints (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The class has clinical validation in GA (pegcetacoplan) and an increasingly reassuring safety dossier for chronic C3 inhibition, while AMY-101 itself exhibits favorable human safety and local-delivery performance in non-ocular indications (Lamers et al., 2022; Hasturk et al., 2021). The principal development gaps—human ocular PK/safety for AMY-101 and POS-specific efficacy readouts—are tractable with focused preclinical and early clinical work. Taken together, the weight of mechanistic, cellular, and translational evidence supports advancing AMY-101 into an ophthalmic development path for dry AMD with a high likelihood of mechanistic efficacy and a manageable risk profile under a biomarker-driven, stratified clinical strategy (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).
