Below is a comprehensive evaluation of the prolyl oligopeptidase inhibitor KYP-2047 as a potential repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). This report is organized into several sections: an overview of the candidate, its therapeutic history, an in‐depth discussion of its mechanism of action, the expected effects in the proposed assay, and an overall evaluation that weighs its strengths and weaknesses.

─────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

KYP-2047 is a synthetic small molecule belonging to the peptidomimetic class of compounds that target the enzyme prolyl oligopeptidase (PREP), also known as prolyl endopeptidase (POP). Chemically designated as 4-phenylbutanoyl-L-prolyl-2(S)-cyanopyrrolidine, this compound was synthesized following methods established by Dr. Elina Jarho at the University of Eastern Finland (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47). Its design represents an evolution from early substrate-like inhibitors, with modifications at specific positions – including a three-carbon aliphatic chain at the P3 position instead of the more commonly used carbamate groups seen in predecessors like ZPP – thereby improving the compound’s overall potency, selectivity, and drug-like properties (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4).

Belonging to a well-known class of PREP inhibitors, KYP-2047 shares common chemical and biophysical properties with analogous peptidomimetic agents that have been primarily designed to interfere with the catalytic activity of a serine protease that cleaves proline-containing peptides. Given its low water solubility, KYP-2047 is typically formulated in saline containing 5% Tween® 80 for experimental studies, which is consistent with formulation challenges observed with many peptidomimetic drug candidates (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47). In recent years, the broader class of PREP inhibitors has been explored for a variety of indications, most notably in neurological conditions as well as in certain cancer models. The research impetus behind this class arises from the enzyme’s presumed role in peptide metabolism, where the inhibition of PREP could alter levels of bioactive peptides that participate in cellular homeostasis. Although these agents were originally developed as anti-amnesic candidates, their biological actions have been found to extend to anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

─────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

The therapeutic exploration of PREP inhibitors dates back to the 1970s when the enzyme was first implicated in the regulation of proline-containing peptides associated with memory formation and synaptic plasticity (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22). Numerous compounds in this class—including S-17092, JTP-4819, and others—were advanced into preclinical studies and even early-phase clinical trials for cognitive enhancement in neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease and senile dementia (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41, 70–72). However, despite initial encouraging in vitro and animal data, these agents failed to progress successfully past phase II clinical trials in humans, most likely due to challenges with efficacy, blood-brain barrier penetration, or the complexity of the enzyme’s in vivo function (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 70–72).

In parallel, PREP inhibitors have been evaluated for other indications. For instance, in a study involving oral squamous cell carcinoma, KYP-2047 demonstrated potent PREP inhibition in the mouse brain along with promising anti-tumor effects, highlighting the compound’s potential utility beyond central nervous system disorders (Scuderi, 2023, pp. 133–135). Furthermore, recent work has begun to explore the ocular applications of PREP inhibition. There is a suggestion in the literature that inhibition of prolyl oligopeptidase may represent “a promising pathway to prevent the progression of age-related macular degeneration” (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13). Notably, recent in vitro studies using human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells with defective proteasomal clearance have shown that KYP-2047 exhibits cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory properties, thereby indirectly supporting its potential use in dry AMD, even though no clinical trials or prior direct therapeutic applications in retinal diseases have yet been reported (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 9–11).

While the primary historical focus of PREP inhibitors has been on neurological and cognitive applications, the body of literature also contains several exploratory studies in inflammatory and cancer contexts (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Thus, even though the bulk of previous applications have not directly targeted dry AMD, the emerging evidence supporting cytoprotection and modulation of proteolytic and autophagy pathways in RPE cells provides a rationale for repurposing KYP-2047 in ocular disease states.

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

The biological target of KYP-2047 is the serine protease prolyl oligopeptidase (PREP), which is responsible for cleaving peptide bonds at the carboxyl side of internal proline residues in small peptides (typically less than ~30 amino acids) (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 22–24, 44–47). PREP is widely expressed in the central nervous system and peripheral tissues and has been implicated in multiple physiological processes including neuropeptide regulation and cell signaling. At the molecular level, the mechanism of action involves the binding of KYP-2047 to the enzyme’s active site, more specifically interacting with the catalytic serine residue. Many PREP inhibitors, including those in the class to which KYP-2047 belongs, are designed as substrate-like pseudopeptides that exploit the structure of the enzyme’s binding pockets (S1, S2, and S3) to achieve selectivity and high-affinity binding (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).

The inhibition by KYP-2047 is characterized as “tight-binding” with slow dissociation, meaning that once the inhibitor occupies the active site of PREP, it remains bound for a significant duration, thereby effectively reducing the enzyme’s catalytic turnover (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 70–72). In neurological models, inhibition of PREP has been associated with enhanced clearance of toxic protein aggregates such as alpha-synuclein, improved autophagic flux, and reduction in oxidative stress (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 85–88; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 9–11). The current therapeutic hypothesis in the context of dry AMD extrapolates these findings to retinal pigment epithelial cells.

In particular, the proposed mechanism posits that elevated PREP activity in RPE cells contributes to an accumulation of proline-rich peptides that, in turn, inhibit the activity of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and lysosomal cathepsin L. These cathepsins are critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and turnover of cellular debris. In dry AMD, defective protein clearance mechanisms, including impaired proteasomal and lysosomal function, result in the buildup of toxic deposits, such as A2E, and contribute to RPE dysfunction. By blocking PREP activity with KYP-2047 (which has an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range, reported to be approximately 30 nM), the proposed effect is to reduce the formation or accumulation of inhibitory peptides, thereby relieving the suppression on cathepsin activity. In addition, KYP-2047-mediated PREP inhibition may trigger downstream intracellular events such as autophagy activation and modulation of MAPK signaling pathways—including p38 and ERK1/2—which have been observed in other cell types and are known to reduce oxidative stress and inflammation (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 85–88).

At the biochemical level, these molecular interactions involve the inhibitor “locking in” the PREP enzyme in a conformational state that either prevents substrate access or alters the dynamics of peptide release once cleavage has occurred. Although the effects on neuropeptide levels (e.g., substance P, neurotensin) have been studied in central nervous system models—with mixed and sometimes counterintuitive outcomes (such as decreased acetylcholine levels) (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 8–16, 70–72)—the rationale for ocular repurposing rests on the idea that the same enzymatic inhibition can counteract the accumulation of cathepsin-inhibiting peptides in RPE cells. Notably, some studies have suggested that PREP inhibition can positively modulate autophagy, a process that is critical for cellular clearance mechanisms. Given that impaired autophagy is a central feature in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, a compound like KYP-2047 that both reduces toxic peptide accumulation and enhances proteolytic pathways presents an attractive, multitargeted strategy (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

The core hypothesis driving the repurposing of KYP-2047 for dry AMD is that inhibition of PREP will reduce the buildup of proline-rich peptides that otherwise impair lysosomal cathepsin activity. In RPE cells, efficient degradation of POS via phagocytosis and lysosomal function is essential for maintaining retinal homeostasis. In the setting of dry AMD, decreased cathepsin D and L activities are implicated in the inefficient clearance of cellular debris, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, ultimately causing RPE dysfunction.

In the proposed assay, RPE cells—typically the ARPE-19 cell line—will be challenged in an environment mimicking AMD pathology; for instance, by loading them with A2E and subjecting the cells to proteasomal stress. Under these conditions, the activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and L is compromised, and POS degradation is impaired. The application of KYP-2047 is expected to inhibit PREP activity with high potency, which theoretically will lead to a reduction in the concentration of peptide substrates that interfere with cathepsin enzymes (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).

The anticipated cascade of events is as follows:  
1. KYP-2047, at concentrations close to its low nanomolar IC₅₀, will effectively bind to and inhibit PREP in RPE cells.  
2. This inhibition will prevent the excessive cleavage of proline-containing peptides, thereby reducing the pool of inhibitory peptides that could otherwise bind to and decrease cathepsin D and L activities.  
3. As a consequence, the restoration of cathepsin activity is expected to improve the degradation of POS components as well as the clearance of other toxic debris, which is a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.  
4. Additionally, the compound’s reported anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects, demonstrated in ARPE-19 cells with defective proteasomal clearance, may further contribute to preserving RPE cell health by curtailing inflammatory cytokine production and oxidative stress (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 4–6).

It is also noteworthy that the mechanistic framework is further supported by the observation that PREP inhibition in other models has led to enhanced autophagy and improved clearance of aggregated proteins. In the context of AMD, effective POS degradation is not only dependent on cathepsin function but also on efficient autophagic flux. By indirectly modulating these pathways, KYP-2047 could offer dual benefits: restoration of lysosomal enzyme activity and bolstering of intracellular clearance mechanisms. Thus, the expected in vitro endpoints would likely include increased cathepsin D/L activity, elevated POS degradation (as detected by uptake assays), reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-6, IL-8, IL-1β), and diminished oxidative stress markers (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 4–6).

Moreover, the rationale includes supporting evidence from neurological and cancer research where PREP inhibition by compounds like KYP-2047 improved cell viability and reduced stress responses. Although previous clinical trials in central nervous system indications did not achieve long-term success, the safety data accrued from these studies may lower the translational barrier for ocular applications, provided that proper formulation and localized delivery (or systemic approaches with ocular distribution) can be achieved (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 4–5).

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

The evaluation of KYP-2047 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD involves weighing both its promising aspects and its uncertainties. On the positive side, KYP-2047 is a well-defined, highly potent inhibitor of PREP with an established chemical profile and a strong foundation in preclinical studies. Its synthetic origin as a peptidomimetic compound designed to bind the active site of PREP is well documented (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4), and the compound’s low nanomolar potency provides confidence that even modest drug exposures may achieve effective enzyme inhibition.

The repurposing strategy capitalizes on emerging evidence that PREP inhibitors can exert cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in RPE cells. In vitro studies conducted in ARPE-19 cells with impaired proteasomal clearance have demonstrated that KYP-2047 can reduce inflammatory cytokine production and promote cell viability (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). Given the central role of inflammation and defective lysosomal clearance in dry AMD, these findings provide a mechanistic rationale for testing KYP-2047 in this indication.

Furthermore, the proposed mechanism—whereby inhibition of PREP reduces the formation of inhibitory proline-rich peptides that suppress cathepsin activity—is mechanistically attractive. Restoring the function of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and L could feasibly improve the degradation of POS, a process known to be compromised in dry AMD. This dual-targeted approach (improving both enzyme activity and reducing cell stress) is particularly compelling in the context of a multifactorial disease such as AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

Despite these strengths, several potential weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. First, while extensive preclinical work has been carried out in neurological models—and there exists some early in vitro evidence of benefit in RPE cells—the direct connection between PREP activity and the inhibition of cathepsin function in the context of RPE biology remains largely hypothetical. The literature currently lacks robust in vivo studies in ocular models of dry AMD demonstrating that PREP inhibition translates into measurable improvements in retinal function and morphology. Historical clinical trials of PREP inhibitors for cognitive applications have encountered difficulties due to inconsistent efficacy, which raises concerns about the translation of in vitro findings to clinical benefits (Scuderi, 2023, pp. 133–135; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41).

Second, the formulation challenges associated with KYP-2047 cannot be overlooked. Its low water solubility necessitates specialized carriers (such as saline with 5% Tween® 80), which may complicate delivery to the eye, especially when considering the need for localized administration to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE. Appropriate ocular delivery systems (e.g., intravitreal injections or sustained-release implants) would need to be developed and optimized, which adds a layer of complexity to the overall drug development program (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47).

Another area of concern is the historical inconsistency of PREP inhibitor effects in clinical studies. Although there is evidence of neuroprotective benefits, the fact that several PREP inhibitors failed to advance through the clinical development pipeline for neurological indications suggests that the enzyme’s true physiological role remains incompletely defined. In the absence of a clear and reproducible biomarker for PREP inhibition in vivo, there is a risk that the biochemical benefits seen in cell culture studies may not be recapitulated in the complex environment of the human retina (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 70–72).

Moreover, because PREP is a ubiquitous enzyme expressed in many tissues, systemic administration of KYP-2047 might lead to off-target effects that could limit its therapeutic window. Although the safety profile observed in early neurological trials is encouraging, targeted delivery to the eye (to minimize systemic exposure) will be crucial if KYP-2047 is to be repurposed for dry AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

Finally, while the proposed mechanism that links elevated PREP activity with the inhibition of lysosomal cathepsins is intriguing, it remains to be validated by direct experimental data specifically in RPE cells. The current literature, including the recent study by Toppila and colleagues, primarily focuses on the cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory actions of KYP-2047 in ARPE-19 cells, but detailed biochemical analyses linking PREP inhibition mechanistically to improved cathepsin-mediated degradation of POS are still needed (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 4–6).

─────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

In summary, KYP-2047 is an established prolyl oligopeptidase inhibitor with a well-characterized chemical and pharmacological profile, offering promising features as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its ability to inhibit PREP at low nanomolar concentrations, coupled with demonstrated cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in preclinical RPE models, aligns well with the therapeutic need to restore lysosomal cathepsin activity and improve photoreceptor outer segment degradation in dry AMD (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 12–13).

The strategy to mitigate the accumulation of inhibitory proline-rich peptides and thereby reinstate effective lysosomal function is mechanistically plausible and supported by related studies in neural tissues. Nevertheless, the exact role of PREP in the modulation of cathepsin activity in RPE cells remains to be fully elucidated. In addition, the challenges of achieving appropriate ocular drug delivery and the historical precedents of inconsistent efficacy in PREP inhibitor clinical trials represent significant hurdles that must be addressed in future studies (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41).

Overall, while KYP-2047 brings strengths in terms of potency and a partially validated cytoprotective profile in in vitro models, its repurposing for dry AMD would require further in-depth preclinical studies. These studies should include in vivo efficacy assessments in relevant animal models of AMD, comprehensive pharmacokinetic and ocular distribution evaluations, and mechanistic experiments that clearly link PREP inhibition with improved cathepsin and lysosomal function in the RPE. Should these studies confirm the initial promising results, the favorable safety profile observed in prior neurological trials may indeed support the rapid translation of KYP-2047 into early-phase clinical testing for dry AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

In conclusion, KYP-2047 represents a promising, albeit still exploratory, approach to targeting a novel biochemical pathway in the context of dry AMD. The rationale is supported by a solid foundation of preclinical data in other disease models, yet its success in ocular repurposing will depend on overcoming formulation challenges and further clarifying the mechanistic underpinnings of its action in retinal pigment epithelial cells.

Strengths:  
•  KYP-2047 is a potent, well-characterized PREP inhibitor with a strong synthetic and chemical development history (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4).  
•  Its low nanomolar IC₅₀ provides confidence in its biochemical efficacy, and available preclinical data indicate cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in RPE cell models (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22).  
•  The drug class has been extensively studied in neurological and cancer contexts, offering insights into its safety profile and potential mechanisms such as autophagy activation and reduced oxidative stress (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 70–72, 85–88).  
•  The hypothesis that PREP activity leads to the accumulation of cathepsin-inhibiting peptides is mechanistically plausible, which could lead to restoration of lysosomal enzyme activity in RPE cells (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).  

Weaknesses:  
•  Historically, PREP inhibitors have shown inconsistent efficacy in clinical trials for neurological applications; it remains uncertain whether the benefits will translate to the ocular setting (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 39–41).  
•  Direct evidence linking PREP inhibition with improvements in cathepsin activity and POS degradation in RPE cells is still limited, and further mechanistic studies are required (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
•  The low aqueous solubility of KYP-2047 necessitates complex formulations, which might complicate ocular drug delivery and could require novel delivery systems to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47).  
•  Systemic safety and potential off-target effects remain a concern, given that PREP is widely expressed and the compound’s systemic clearance and ocular bioavailability have yet to be thoroughly characterized in vivo (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

Final Remarks

Based on the current literature and the data available, KYP-2047 exhibits several attractive features for repurposing in dry AMD, especially regarding its potential to restore lysosomal function in the RPE by reducing the inhibitory load on cathepsins. However, while the biochemical rationale is compelling and early in vitro data are promising, significant challenges remain. Translational steps such as in vivo efficacy verification in AMD models, optimization of ocular formulation, and further elucidation of the mechanistic pathway are essential before proceeding to clinical development. Thus, KYP-2047 warrants further preclinical evaluation with a specific focus on its ocular pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics, which will ultimately determine its viability as a novel therapeutic candidate against dry age-related macular degeneration (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

This comprehensive review supports the notion that repurposing KYP-2047 for dry AMD is a promising strategy, but caution must be exercised given the prior challenges encountered with the PREP inhibitor class in other indications. Future studies should be designed to address these gaps and de-risk the development plan before large-scale clinical trials are considered.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Brefeldin A (BFA) is a natural product originally isolated in 1958 from Penicillium decumbens, and its discovery marked the beginning of intensive studies on its unique ability to disrupt intracellular protein trafficking (Hung, 2020). Structurally, BFA is a macrolide characterized by a complex fused system comprising a cyclopentane moiety linked to a 13-membered lactone, and this distinctive architecture has spurred extensive synthetic and medicinal chemistry efforts over the past decades (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015). By targeting the secretory pathway, BFA acts as a Golgi transport inhibitor, primarily through its binding to a protein complex involving a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) and the small G protein Arf1. This binding event results in the rapid disassembly of the Golgi apparatus and redistribution of its components back into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Hung, 2020). BFA is therefore classified among natural product inhibitors of intracellular trafficking, a group that has long served as invaluable research tools in cell biology to dissect the mechanisms of vesicular transport and Golgi-ER dynamics. Its broad bioactivities—as an antiviral, antifungal, and antimitotic agent—have principally been exploited in preclinical research rather than clinical therapeutics (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, BFA has been employed almost exclusively as a biochemical probe to investigate protein processing, secretion, and Golgi morphology in diverse eukaryotic cells. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that BFA’s ability to stall ER-to-Golgi trafficking can modulate various cellular processes including secretion of cytokines, hormones, and growth factors (Hung, 2020). Its documented effects on blocking transport have been leveraged in cancer cell studies where BFA-induced apoptosis and cell cycle arrest were observed, owing to mislocalization of key signaling molecules (Stierle & Stierle, 2015). Despite these promising cellular effects, the clinical development of BFA as a conventional therapeutic agent has been hindered by issues such as poor bioavailability and significant toxicity with prolonged exposure (Seehafer et al., 2013). Importantly, while BFA has not been directly applied in clinical studies for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or any similar degenerative retinal diseases, its mechanistic action on intracellular trafficking, ER stress, and protein secretion renders it an intriguing candidate for repurposing. In the context of AMD, where complement dysregulation and lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells play a critical pathogenic role, BFA could potentially offer a novel means of attenuating the buildup of complement components and misfolded proteins (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). While none of the published literature explicitly documents the use of BFA for AMD therapy, related studies in RPE cellular models have highlighted the importance of complement modulation and lysosomal restoration, establishing a rationale for investigating trafficking inhibitors such as BFA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
On a molecular level, the mechanism of action for Brefeldin A is well characterized. BFA binds to the complex comprising a catalytic GEF and the small GTPase Arf1, inhibiting the exchange of GDP for GTP on Arf1. This inhibition precludes proper recruitment and coat assembly for vesicle budding at the Golgi membranes, leading to a collapse of the Golgi structure and the retrograde redistribution of Golgi proteins to the ER (Hung, 2020). The immediate consequence of this inhibition is a profound disruption in the secretory pathway, which not only halts the export of proteins but also results in an accumulation of proteins within the ER. In cell types where the regulated secretion of proteins is critical for homeostasis, such as in RPE cells, this effect can have dual ramifications. On the one hand, it may help prevent the secretion of misfolded or aberrantly processed proteins, including complement components that are implicated in local inflammation and lysosomal deposition (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). On the other hand, the blockade of Golgi trafficking may transiently lower the secretion of proteins that otherwise contribute to the local pool of complement proteins which, if misfolded or overproduced, could lead to an increase in intracellular complement activation and subsequent deposition of the membrane attack complex (MAC, particularly C5b-9) within lysosomes (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In RPE cells, where robust daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) is essential, the maintenance of lysosomal function is critical; overburdening of lysosomes with complement-derived debris has been implicated in the formation of drusen and lipofuscin accumulation, both of which underlie AMD pathology (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The proposed intervention using BFA therefore leverages its well-established ability to modulate protein trafficking to indirectly reduce the burden of misfolded or overabundant complement proteins on the lysosomal system, thereby potentially restoring cathepsin activity and overall lysosomal function in RPE cells.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing BFA in dry AMD is that brief pulses of BFA administration will selectively inhibit the ER-to-Golgi trafficking route in RPE cells, thereby reducing the processing and secretion of misfolded complement proteins. RPE cells are known to contribute to local complement activation through the production and turnover of various complement components; in AMD, aberrant complement regulation leads to increased turnover, formation of complement split products, and the deposition of terminal complement complexes (C5b-9) in the lysosomes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The expected outcome of BFA treatment would be a reduction in the export of these misfolded or excessively generated complement proteins, ultimately leading to decreased local complement activation and a reduction in lysosomal overload by MAC proteins. Experimental evidence from studies using compstatin analogues (e.g., Cp40) in Y402H-RPE cell models has shown that complement inhibition can restore lysosomal function and cathepsin activity, thereby reducing lysosome size, diminishing drusen-like deposits, and improving the overall cellular phenotype (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015). By analogy, transient BFA treatment is anticipated to produce similar beneficial effects on lysosomal physiology in RPE cells, provided that the inhibition is carefully timed to avoid prolonged exposure which could be deleterious (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Furthermore, because RPE cells are responsible for the daily clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, maintaining an unencumbered lysosomal system is crucial for long-term retinal health. The expected biochemical cascade following BFA administration would therefore include a reduction in ER stress due to diminished protein export, lower secretion of misfolded complement proteins, and a subsequent decrease in complement-mediated lysosomal damage. This in turn should lead to a stabilization or even an improvement in cathepsin levels and activity, promoting a more efficient degradation of cellular debris and restoration of POS clearance (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential repurposing of Brefeldin A as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD is innovative and grounded in a detailed understanding of both its mechanism of action and the pathophysiology of AMD. Several strengths underlie this approach. First, BFA has a well-characterized molecular mechanism that directly affects the secretory pathway by inhibiting ER-to-Golgi trafficking. This offers a mechanistic basis for reducing the secretion of misfolded or aberrantly processed complement proteins—the accumulation of which is a central driver of lysosomal dysfunction and local complement activation in RPE cells (Hung, 2020). Second, preclinical research in AMD models has demonstrated that modulating complement activity, whether through direct inhibition of complement components or by enhancing lysosomal function, can reverse pathological phenotypes associated with the disease (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015). This suggests that a strategy aimed at indirectly reducing complement deposition via interference with protein trafficking holds considerable promise. Third, the idea of using brief pulses of BFA rather than continuous dosing could allow for a transient therapeutic effect that minimizes the known toxicities associated with prolonged BFA exposure—thus potentially overcoming one of the key limitations that has prevented its clinical development in other contexts (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015).

Nonetheless, there are significant challenges and weaknesses that must be addressed before this approach can be advanced. One of the primary concerns relates to the non-selectivity of BFA’s action. Because BFA disrupts a fundamental cellular process, its effects are not confined solely to the trafficking of misfolded complement proteins. It is likely to inhibit the normal secretion of multiple proteins that are essential for RPE cell function, which could inadvertently impair the phagocytosis and processing of photoreceptor outer segments (Hung, 2020; Seehafer et al., 2013). Such disruption could paradoxically exacerbate the very lysosomal dysfunction it is intended to ameliorate, particularly if dosing is not carefully titrated. Furthermore, while transient inhibition may mitigate toxicity, achieving the precise balance between therapeutic efficacy and cellular viability will require rigorous optimization in both in vitro and in vivo models. Another potential drawback is related to pharmacokinetics and delivery. BFA’s poor bioavailability and potential systemic toxicity have long been recognized as obstacles for its use beyond experimental settings (Seehafer et al., 2013). Delivering BFA specifically to the RPE while avoiding off-target effects in other ocular or systemic tissues will demand innovative formulation strategies, such as localized drug delivery systems, which inherently add another layer of complexity to the drug development process. Additionally, while the hypothesis is supported by analogous studies demonstrating that complement modulation can restore lysosomal function in AMD models (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015), there is currently no direct evidence that BFA’s inhibition of ER-to-Golgi trafficking will reproduce these beneficial effects in the delicate environment of the retina. The potential for unforeseen interactions with other components of the RPE’s protein processing machinery or compensatory cellular responses further complicates the translational prospects of this approach.

In summary, as an expert drug development team leader tasked with evaluating promising repurposed drugs for dry AMD, I find the proposal to repurpose Brefeldin A to be both innovative and mechanistically intriguing. The strengths of this candidate lie in its well-characterized molecular target—namely, the inhibition of Arf1-mediated vesicle budding at the Golgi—and its potential to modulate a key pathological feature of AMD, namely the dysregulated secretion and accumulation of complement proteins that leads to lysosomal impairment and MAC deposition (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). However, the inherent risks associated with disrupting a central cellular process cannot be overstated. The lack of selectivity in BFA’s action, potential toxicity from even brief exposures, and challenges in targeting the RPE specifically are serious obstacles that must be systematically addressed. Further preclinical studies are required to delineate the dose-response relationship in RPE cell models, to examine the long-term effects of transient BFA-induced trafficking inhibition on cellular health, and to validate the hypothesis that such intervention can indeed reduce lysosomal MAC deposition and rescue cathepsin activity. Only with convincing evidence from rigorous in vitro and in vivo experiments would it be justified to consider advancing BFA as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. In conclusion, while the proposed use of BFA presents a compelling mechanistic rationale with some supportive preclinical analogies from the literature (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020), significant challenges regarding specificity, delivery, and safety need to be overcome before this approach can be deemed a viable therapeutic option for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Adalimumab (marketed as Humira) is a fully humanized recombinant IgG1 monoclonal antibody developed using recombinant DNA technology that targets tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNFα). As a member of the anti‐TNFα class of biologics, adalimumab is designed to bind both soluble and membrane‐bound TNFα with high affinity, thereby preventing its interaction with the TNF receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2) on target cells. This antibody was originally discovered and engineered to address systemic inflammatory diseases, and its fully human composition is intended to lower immunogenicity compared to earlier chimeric molecules such as infliximab. In its development, molecular engineering efforts focused on isolating the relevant antibody variable regions that exhibit specificity for TNFα, followed by the construction of a recombinant molecule with human constant regions to improve tolerability and clinical efficacy. Anti‐TNFα antibodies belong to a broader class of therapeutic compounds that have dramatically changed the treatment landscape for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. They have been widely applied in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn’s disease, and ulcerative colitis, and over the past two decades, their use has been extended into ocular inflammatory diseases such as non‐infectious uveitis. Such applications underscore the versatility and translational potential of TNFα inhibition in modulating inflammatory cascades (Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History:  
Adalimumab’s clinical journey began with its approval for systemic autoimmune diseases where TNFα plays a fundamental role in mediating inflammation and tissue damage. Its robust performance in rheumatoid arthritis and related conditions has been well documented in numerous large-scale randomized controlled trials, which demonstrated significant improvement in clinical outcomes and inflammatory markers. These successes provided the foundation for exploring its application in other diseases characterized by inflammatory dysregulation. In recent years, growing evidence from both biochemical studies and clinical observations has highlighted the role of chronic inflammation in the pathogenesis of several retinal degenerative disorders. In particular, studies have shown that TNFα is upregulated in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and may contribute to the degeneration seen in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). For example, preclinical work has demonstrated that inflammation mediated by TNFα can impair the integrity of RPE cells, reduce the expression of proteins critical for RPE function (including visual cycle proteins and complement regulators) and disrupt phagocytic clearance mechanisms; these findings form the basis for hypothesizing that TNFα blockade may preserve RPE function in dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

While the majority of clinical uses of adalimumab have been in the realm of systemic and ocular inflammatory conditions such as non‐infectious uveitis, there has been emerging interest in repurposing anti‐TNFα therapies for retinal degenerations. In the context of ocular disease, several investigators have explored both systemic and local (intravitreal or subconjunctival) routes of administration to modulate intraocular inflammation. Pilot clinical trials and case reports have assessed intravitreal adalimumab in patients with uveitis and even in those with neovascular (“wet”) AMD refractory to anti‐VEGF therapies; these studies reported varying degrees of efficacy and underscored an acceptable local safety profile, though in some instances, higher dosages have been associated with ocular toxicity. In animal studies, intravitreal or subconjunctival administration of adalimumab has been shown to reduce inflammation and offer neuroprotection in models of retinal degeneration, such as in the rd10 mouse model for retinitis pigmentosa, establishing a precedent for local administration to achieve high ocular levels with minimal systemic exposure. Despite these advancements, use of adalimumab specifically for dry AMD has not been established in clinical practice. The proposed approach builds on the mechanistic insights from studies demonstrating that elevated TNFα levels can lead to downregulation of phagocytic receptors and lysosomal enzymes in RPE cells—processes central to dry AMD pathology—and posits that reversing these effects via TNFα neutralization may preserve RPE function (Nashine et al., 2022; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of adalimumab centers on its targeted neutralization of TNFα. TNFα is a proinflammatory cytokine produced by a variety of cell types that include activated T lymphocytes, macrophages, and, importantly, resident cells in the eye such as RPE and Müller glia. When secreted into the extracellular milieu, TNFα binds to its receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2), triggering intracellular signaling cascades that lead to the activation of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and other pathways that promote the expression of additional inflammatory cytokines, adhesion molecules, and matrix metalloproteinases. These processes collectively contribute to a sustained inflammatory response that can result in cellular dysfunction and death. Adalimumab, by virtue of its high affinity binding, sequesters TNFα and prevents receptor engagement. In doing so, it effectively interrupts these downstream proinflammatory signals and halts the amplification of the inflammatory cascade (Wang et al., 2011; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium cells, TNFα-mediated signaling has been implicated in the suppression of genes critical to the maintenance of RPE functions. Specifically, experimental studies have suggested that exposure to TNFα leads to a reduction in the expression of MERTK—a receptor tyrosine kinase essential for the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—as well as cathepsin D, a lysosomal enzyme crucial for the degradation of engulfed material. The decrease in MERTK expression compromises the ability of RPE cells to efficiently phagocytose POS, thereby potentially contributing to the accumulation of cellular debris, drusen formation, and further RPE stress that are characteristic of dry AMD. In parallel, a reduction in cathepsin D would impair lysosomal degradation, exacerbating the intracellular buildup of waste products and further undermining cellular homeostasis in the RPE. By neutralizing TNFα, adalimumab is hypothesized to prevent these detrimental changes, preserving the expression levels of MERTK and cathepsin D and thereby maintaining robust phagocytic and degradative capacity in RPE cells (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021).

At the molecular level, the binding of adalimumab to TNFα is mediated via its antigen-binding (Fab) region, which recognizes specific epitopes on the cytokine. This interaction is characterized by high affinity and specificity, ensuring that even low concentrations of the antibody can effectively neutralize TNFα activity. The blockade prevents TNFα from initiating receptor-mediated signaling that would otherwise promote inflammation and cellular stress. Moreover, because TNFα is known to regulate not only inflammatory cytokine production but also apoptotic processes, its inhibition may confer additional neuroprotective effects in the retina by reducing signals that lead to programmed cell death. The comprehensive inhibition of TNFα by adalimumab therefore stands as a multifaceted intervention, addressing both the inflammatory insult and its secondary effects on critical cellular functions in the RPE (Wang et al., 2011; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Nashine et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for leveraging adalimumab in dry AMD rests on its potential to neutralize elevated TNFα levels in the subretinal microenvironment. Elevated TNFα has been implicated in the pathological downregulation of key proteins involved in RPE function, notably MERTK and cathepsin D. MERTK is a receptor that plays an essential role in the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, a process that is critical for the renewal of photoreceptors and the overall maintenance of retinal health. Cathepsin D, on the other hand, is involved in the lysosomal degradation of the ingested material; together, these proteins ensure that the RPE can effectively clear and recycle photoreceptor debris. In dry AMD, this phagocytic process is compromised, leading to the accumulation of cellular waste products and drusen formation, which further fuels inflammation and RPE degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Administration of adalimumab is expected to interrupt this cascade by neutralizing TNFα, thereby preventing its signaling that leads to the downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D. With TNFα effectively neutralized, RPE cells should experience a more favorable molecular milieu in which the expression of these critical proteins is maintained at functional levels. This preservation would, in turn, support the RPE’s capacity to phagocytose and degrade photoreceptor outer segments, thereby averting the buildup of toxic waste products. Furthermore, since TNFα signaling also contributes to other aspects of cellular stress and inflammation—such as the upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines and the induction of apoptotic pathways—the neutralization of TNFα by adalimumab may also reduce overall cellular stress and promote RPE cell survival and function (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022).

In vitro assays using cultured human RPE cells exposed to TNFα could be employed to test this hypothesis. In these experiments, treatment with adalimumab should result in the normalization or preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression levels when compared to TNFα-treated controls. In addition, functional assays measuring the uptake and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (or surrogate fluorescent particles) would be expected to show improved phagocytic efficiency in RPE cells treated with adalimumab. Such findings would provide robust mechanistic support for the proposed therapeutic strategy. Moreover, preliminary in vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD or models of induced RPE dysfunction could further validate that TNFα blockade leads to preservation of RPE integrity, improved photoreceptor survival, and retardation of retinal degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Considering that the expression of MERTK is well documented in RPE cells and that its function is critical for POS phagocytosis—a process that declines with aging and in the presence of inflammatory mediators—the ability of adalimumab to maintain or restore MERTK expression would be highly relevant in the context of dry AMD. In the proposed strategy, adalimumab may also help to stabilize other RPE functions, such as the regulation of the complement cascade and the visual cycle, both of which have been shown to be adversely affected by TNFα exposure. Thus, the anticipated effect of adalimumab is not limited solely to the preservation of phagocytic machinery; it may also contribute to a broader stabilization of RPE cell health in the face of chronic low-grade inflammation that characterizes dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of adalimumab as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a compelling yet cautiously optimistic perspective. One of the principal strengths of adalimumab lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action; by neutralizing TNFα, it directly addresses a central mediator of inflammation that has been implicated in the dysregulation of RPE functions. The experimental evidence indicating that TNFα exposure can lead to the downregulation of essential proteins such as MERTK and cathepsin D provides a strong rationale for the hypothesis that TNFα inhibition might preserve the RPE’s ability to maintain photoreceptor homeostasis. This mechanistic insight is particularly attractive because it targets one of the fundamental dysfunctions in dry AMD—namely, the failure of the RPE to clear photoreceptor outer segments effectively, which leads to the accumulation of drusen and progressive retinal degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the extensive clinical experience with adalimumab in systemic and ocular inflammatory diseases supports its safety profile. The fact that adalimumab is already approved by regulatory agencies, coupled with several clinical studies demonstrating its localized safety when administered intravitreally or via related routes in ocular conditions such as uveitis, adds to its attractiveness as a candidate for repurposing (Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010; Leal et al., 2018; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. To date, most studies involving adalimumab in the ocular context have focused on inflammatory conditions such as uveitis and neovascular AMD rather than dry AMD specifically. As a result, direct clinical evidence supporting its efficacy in preserving RPE phagocytic function in dry AMD is currently limited. The hypothesis that adalimumab can prevent the TNFα-induced downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D is primarily based on preclinical observations, and further mechanistic studies, both in vitro and in relevant animal models, are necessary to validate this pathway in the context of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Nashine et al., 2022; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Another potential challenge with using adalimumab for dry AMD is related to drug delivery and dosing. While intravitreal administration has shown promise in limited studies, determining the optimal dose that achieves effective TNFα blockade without incurring retinal toxicity remains an unresolved issue. Some animal studies have indicated that higher doses of intravitreal adalimumab can lead to retinal inflammation, reduced electroretinogram responses, or histopathological evidence of toxicity. Given that dry AMD is a chronic condition and would likely require repeated dosing or sustained drug delivery systems, the long-term safety of local TNFα blockade needs to be rigorously evaluated (Manzano et al., 2008; Pascual-Camps et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Zinc sulfate (ZnSO₄; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. Z0251) is an inorganic salt that dissociates readily in aqueous solutions to yield zinc ions (Zn²⁺) and sulfate anions. Zinc sulfate is a well‐characterized compound produced via chemical synthesis and has been used for decades as a nutritional supplement to treat zinc deficiency. It belongs to the class of trace mineral supplements, and, more broadly, to inorganic therapeutic agents. In many clinical and veterinary practices, zinc sulfate has been utilized as a dietary supplement to support immune function, antioxidant defenses, and wound healing. Its broad therapeutic use is partly validated by its inclusion in complex formulations—for example, in the Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS) protocol for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where zinc supplementation was associated with a reduction in disease progression risk (Qin, 2007). Zinc sulfate has also found application in ophthalmic preparations due to extensive ocular safety data supporting its use; indeed, zinc sulfate eye drops have been evaluated for ocular safety in early-phase clinical trials (Qin, 2007). This candidate is particularly attractive for repurposing since its manufacturing and formulation are well established, and its molecular properties as a zinc donor could potentially address deficiencies in zinc-dependent enzymatic processes observed in dry AMD.

Therapeutic History  
Historically, the use of zinc in medical treatments dates back to its role as an essential trace element in numerous biological systems. In the context of ocular diseases, mounting evidence has implicated zinc deficiency in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Preclinical studies in animal models have demonstrated that zinc-deficient conditions lead to significant pathological consequences in the RPE, including increased lipofuscin accumulation and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Julien et al., 2011). In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have similarly shown that disruption of zinc homeostasis produces lysosomal dysfunction which contributes to the build-up of toxic metabolic by-products associated with AMD pathology (Rajapakse et al., 2017). Moreover, several investigations have shown that zinc supplementation can rescue lysosomal acidification deficits and restore autophagic flux in RPE cells exposed to toxic compounds such as A2E—a bisretinoid that accumulates abnormally in dry AMD (Choi et al., 2024). Although many of these reports have employed zinc ionophores (e.g., ClioQ, 1H10) to facilitate zinc delivery into cells, they highlight a fundamental therapeutic rationale: zinc is an essential cofactor for proper lysosomal enzyme function, and its supplementation can reverse key features of cellular dysfunction associated with dry AMD (Choi et al., 2024). Clinical approaches, particularly those emerging from the AREDS trials, have also shown that high-dose zinc supplementation (typically delivered as zinc oxide or zinc sulfate) can slow the progression of AMD (Qin, 2007). While these formulations primarily aimed to address generalized zinc deficiency and oxidative stress, they establish a precedent for the repurposing of zinc salts—specifically zinc sulfate—in ocular disorders such as dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, zinc acts as an indispensable cofactor for a multitude of enzymes, including the zinc-dependent cathepsins B and L. Cathepsins are lysosomal proteases critical for the degradation of phagocytosed POS, autophagic cargo, and other intracellular substrates that accumulate over time. In the RPE, the efficient clearance of POS is a daily and metabolically demanding process; thus, any impairment in cathepsin activity can lead to the accumulation of undegraded material, contributing to the formation of lipofuscin and subsequent cellular toxicity (Julien et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2024). Zinc ions contribute structurally and catalytically to the proper folding and activity of these cathepsins. Under conditions of zinc deficiency or altered intracellular zinc distribution—as has been observed in aged RPE and AMD patients—the activity of cathepsin B and L becomes suboptimal, leading to lysosomal dysfunction (Julien et al., 2011; Rajapakse et al., 2017).

Several reports have demonstrated that exposure to bisretinoids such as A2E leads to dose-dependent cell death and lysosomal alkalinization in ARPE-19 cells; this in turn impairs the activity of lysosomal hydrolases that require an acidic environment for optimal function (Choi et al., 2024). Zinc supplementation, when delivered intracellularly via ionophores in these models, restored lysosomal acidification and enabled the reactivation of the degradative machinery, including zinc-dependent enzymes (Choi et al., 2024). This reacidification is crucial because lysosomal proteases, including cathepsin B/L, demonstrate maximal catalytic activity at a pH of approximately 4.5–5.0—a condition that is disrupted in diseased RPE cells (Choi et al., 2024). Moreover, zinc has been shown to influence autophagy dynamics: in models where A2E treatment led to an arrest in autophagic flux (evidenced by increased p62 and LC3-II levels), zinc supplementation was able to reduce p62 levels and partially restore proper autophagic turnover (Choi et al., 2024). The proposal under evaluation extends this line of reasoning by hypothesizing that direct supplementation with Zn²⁺—provided in the form of zinc sulfate—could similarly restore cathepsin B/L activity in RPE cells, thereby improving phagolysosomal enzyme function and photoreceptor outer segment degradation in dry AMD models (Choi et al., 2024).

Based on the aforementioned mechanistic rationale, the expectation is that ZnSO₄ supplementation will elevate intracellular Zn²⁺ concentrations in RPE cells, thereby reconstituting the proper activity of zinc-dependent enzymes. In the context of dry AMD, where lysosomal dysfunction is a key pathological feature, the restoration of cathepsin function is anticipated to improve the degradation of POS. The repurposing of zinc sulfate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on several well-founded observations. First, there is a robust body of preclinical evidence indicating that zinc supplementation can restore lysosomal function in RPE cells challenged with A2E-induced toxicity, which is a well-characterized in vitro model of dry AMD (Choi et al., 2024). Third, mechanistic studies have underlined the pivotal role of zinc as a cofactor for cathepsin B and L, enzymes that are crucial for the phagolysosomal degradation of POS. In the diseased state, reductions in zinc availability or disruptions in zinc homeostasis result in diminished cathepsin activity, impaired clearance of cellular debris, and subsequent lipofuscin accumulation (Julien et al., 2011; Rajapakse et al., 2017).

Despite these strengths, the candidate does have notable limitations. A significant concern is that most of the supportive in vitro studies have used zinc ionophores (such as ClioQ or 1H10) to ensure efficient intracellular delivery of zinc (Choi et al., 2024). Zinc sulfate, being a simple salt, does not possess intrinsic ionophore properties, which may limit its immediate cellular uptake and availability to lysosomal compartments. This suggests that while ZnSO₄ has a favorable safety profile and is easily formulated, its efficacy in rescuing intracellular cathepsin activity may be contingent on formulation strategies that enhance cellular uptake, such as combining it with a permeation enhancer or designing specialized delivery vehicles. Additionally, direct evidence linking zinc sulfate supplementation to the restoration of cathepsin B/L activity in RPE cells is currently inferred from studies using alternative zinc delivery methods rather than from studies employing ZnSO₄ directly (Rajapakse et al., 2017). Another consideration is the multifactorial nature of AMD pathogenesis. While lysosomal dysfunction and cathepsin impairment are certainly central features, AMD is also driven by oxidative stress, inflammation, and complement dysregulation. Zinc exerts broader antioxidant effects partly through its involvement in metallothionein systems and by modulating the activity of antioxidant enzymes (Rajapakse et al., 2017). However, the translational challenges concerning the effective delivery of Zn²⁺—particularly in the absence of an ionophore—must be carefully addressed. S1P receptor modulators as a group have been widely evaluated in a range of therapeutic areas—from multiple sclerosis and other neurodegenerative disorders to ocular pathologies—due to their ability to modulate immune cell trafficking and endothelial barrier function (Birgbauer, 2024; Hobson et al., 2015). Preliminary evidence suggests that RPE phagocytosis—a critical process for the daily removal of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—may be modulated via S1P receptor signaling. Notably, a human RPE-based screening platform identified compounds capable of enhancing POS phagocytosis, with subsequent transcriptomic analyses revealing that S1PR5 was among the top upregulated genes associated with the enhanced phagocytic response (Schreiter et al., 2020). Moreover, while most of the literature on S1P receptor agonists has focused on neurodegenerative or ocular vascular indications, there is a growing rationale for repurposing these agents for dry AMD, given that RPE dysfunction—including impaired phagosome-lysosome fusion and subsequent accumulation of cellular debris—is a hallmark of the disease (Hobson et al., 2015; Schreiter et al., 2020). Thus, VU0155072, though primarily a research reagent at this stage, stands as a candidate with potential utility for dry AMD based on its receptor selectivity and the emerging role of S1PR5 in RPE phagocytic trafficking.

Mechanism of Action:  
S1PR5 is a member of the G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) family activated by the endogenous ligand sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P). Its activation typically engages downstream signaling cascades that include the modulation of Rho family GTPases, regulation of the actin cytoskeleton, and activation of kinases such as AKT, all of which are crucial for vesicle transport and membrane fusion events (Hobson et al., 2015). In the context of RPE cells, the mechanistic hypothesis for VU0155072 centers on its ability to enhance phagosome-lysosome fusion and the degradation of POS. This is predicated on the observation that modulation of S1P receptor signaling impacts intracellular trafficking pathways. For instance, activation of S1PR5 has been linked to changes in cytoskeletal dynamics that favor efficient vesicular movement and fusion events—a process essential for the clearance of phagosomes containing photoreceptor debris (Schreiter et al., 2020). Additionally, the receptor’s downstream signaling may stimulate pathways involving Rho-associated kinases (ROCK) or PI3K/AKT, both of which facilitate the reorganization of actin filaments and promote the maturation and fusion of phagosomes with lysosomes (Hobson et al., 2015). Importantly, data from a study using a human RPE-based screening platform indicated that pharmacological inhibition of S1PR5 impaired the phagocytic uptake and processing of POS, implying that its activation could restore this cellular function (Schreiter et al., 2020). However, it is noteworthy that several studies examining receptor distribution in RPE cells (using the ARPE-19 cell line as a model) have reported that S1PR5 mRNA expression is very low compared with other S1P receptors such as S1PR3 (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022). This observation raises questions about the sufficiency of endogenous S1PR5 expression in mediating phagocytic processes and whether exogenous activation by a potent agonist like VU0155072 can override such limitations. Nonetheless, the proposed mechanism is coherent with the hypothesis that selective S1PR5 activation leads to enhanced phagosome-lysosome fusion—an effect that would be indirectly mediated by the receptor’s influence on cytoskeletal remodeling and vesicular trafficking proteins.

Expected Effect:  
The primary therapeutic expectation for VU0155072 in dry AMD is that selective activation of S1PR5 in RPE cells will augment the rate and efficiency of phagocytosis, specifically by promoting the fusion of phagosomes with lysosomes and thereby ensuring effective degradation of POS. In dry AMD, one of the pathogenic factors is the defective clearance and subsequent accumulation of photoreceptor debris, which contributes to RPE dysfunction and the formation of drusen. By facilitating robust phagocytic processing, VU0155072 is anticipated to alleviate the cellular stress associated with toxic accumulation, restore RPE homeostasis, and ultimately preserve retinal function (Schreiter et al., 2020). In vitro assays using human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or iPSC-derived RPE) could be employed to assess the efficacy of VU0155072. These assays might measure parameters such as the rate of POS uptake, the kinetics of phagosome-lysosome fusion (potentially using co-localization markers of lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1), and levels of residual POS components after treatment. Given the reported effective concentration (EC₅₀) in the vicinity of 150 nM, one would expect that treatment with VU0155072 at or near this concentration would lead to measurable improvements in phagocytic flux. Moreover, its selectivity may allow the compound to act in a highly targeted fashion, reducing the potential for adverse effects associated with off-target activation of other S1P receptor subtypes—a significant benefit given the pleiotropic roles of other S1P receptors in immune modulation and vascular homeostasis (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024). An additional facet of the expected effect is the possibility that S1PR5 activation may engage MERTK-independent signaling pathways. MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase critical for POS phagocytosis, is often implicated in inherited forms of retinal degeneration when mutated. Should VU0155072 provide an alternate route to stimulate phagosome maturation and clearance, it could be particularly beneficial in cases where MERTK function is compromised (Schreiter et al., 2020). Nonetheless, the low endogenous expression of S1PR5 in commonly used RPE cell lines (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022) may necessitate the use of primary or stem cell-derived RPE models in order to fully capture the therapeutic potential of this approach.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, VU0155072 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD due to its high selectivity for S1PR5 and the compelling hypothesis that S1PR5 activation can restore phagocytic flux in RPE cells. One of the key strengths of this approach is the mechanistic precision: by specifically targeting S1PR5, VU0155072 is expected to modulate intracellular trafficking pathways that are critical for the maintenance and renewal of the RPE’s phagocytic machinery. This stands in contrast to previous S1P receptor modulators that, due to their nonselective binding profiles (such as fingolimod), have demonstrated a range of off-target effects including unwanted immune modulation and vascular dysfunction (Birgbauer, 2024; Nakamura et al., 2024). Moreover, studies on similar S1PR5 agonists like A-971432 have established that selective receptor activation can be achieved with favorable pharmacokinetic profiles, and the precedent set by ASP4058 in addressing ocular pathologies suggests that S1P receptor modulation can be therapeutically beneficial in the retinal context (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024).  

However, the candidate also faces several challenges. A significant potential weakness is the reported low endogenous expression of S1PR5 in RPE cell lines, such as ARPE-19, where expression levels are markedly lower than those of other S1P receptors (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022). This observation raises the question of whether exogenous activation by VU0155072 will be sufficient to elicit a robust phagocytic response in the RPE, or whether receptor upregulation might already be a prerequisite for therapeutic efficacy. Furthermore, while there is evidence that S1PR5 signaling can influence phagocytic processes (Schreiter et al., 2020), most of the existing research has focused on its roles in CNS function and vascular stability rather than in the specific context of RPE-mediated POS degradation. Hence, the proposed mechanism—restoration of phagosome-lysosome fusion and enhancement of POS degradation via S1PR5 activation—remains largely inferential and will require rigorous experimental validation in appropriate in vitro and in vivo models of dry AMD.  

Another consideration is the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic profile of VU0155072, which are described as being favorable in rodents. In theory, such data support its potential translation into clinical settings; however, the degree to which rodent PK accurately predicts human ocular tissue exposure remains uncertain, particularly given the unique microenvironment and barrier properties of the human retina. Additionally, it will be imperative to assess whether VU0155072 exerts any off-target effects on other S1P receptor subtypes, despite its purported selectivity. Off-target binding could complicate the interpretation of preclinical results or introduce safety concerns that have been observed with less selective S1P receptor modulators (Birgbauer, 2024; Nakamura et al., 2024).

From a disease-modifying perspective, the hypothesis that enhancement of phagocytic flux in RPE cells can ameliorate the progression of dry AMD is attractive because it targets a central pathogenic mechanism—namely, the chronic failure of POS clearance that leads to lipofuscin accumulation, drusen formation, and subsequent RPE atrophy. If VU0155072 can indeed stimulate the phagocytic machinery through S1PR5 activation in a meaningful way, it could potentially slow or even reverse some of the degenerative changes associated with dry AMD. This mechanism-driven approach represents a departure from merely symptomatic treatments, addressing the underlying cellular dysfunction that characterizes the disease (Hobson et al., 2015; Schreiter et al., 2020).

In conclusion, while VU0155072 is supported by a mechanistic rationale rooted in S1PR5-mediated regulation of intracellular trafficking and phagocytosis in RPE cells, several factors must be carefully considered before committing to this candidate as a viable therapeutic for dry AMD. The strengths of VU0155072 lie in its receptor specificity, favorable PK in rodent models, and the emerging evidence linking S1PR5 activation with improved phagocytic function in RPE—a critical process compromised in dry AMD. In contrast, the limited endogenous expression of S1PR5 in commonly used RPE models (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022) and the scarce direct evidence of S1PR5 agonism ameliorating dry AMD pathology represent significant challenges. These weaknesses highlight the necessity for further basic research to quantify S1PR5 expression in relevant human RPE cells, to confirm the downstream signaling events triggered by VU0155072, and to validate the beneficial effects of enhanced phagosome-lysosome fusion using both in vitro and in vivo models of dry AMD. Ultimately, while VU0155072 shows promise as a mechanistically precise candidate for restoring phagocytic flux and addressing a key pathological feature of dry AMD, the current literature underscores the need for additional studies to fully establish its therapeutic potential in this context (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024; Qiao et al., 2012; Schreiter et al., 2020; Sorenson et al., 2022).
