Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Apocynin is a naturally occurring small-molecule compound originally isolated from the roots of the Himalayan medicinal herb Picrorhiza kurroa. It belongs to the class of methoxy-substituted catechols that have been characterized as NADPH oxidase (NOX) inhibitors capable of modulating reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. The compound, also known as acetovanillone, was discovered through investigations into natural anti‐inflammatory agents and has subsequently been repurposed as a therapeutic candidate in various experimental models of oxidative stress-driven pathology. As a representative of natural antioxidants with the ability to block the assembly of NOX complexes, apocynin has been widely studied in models of cardiovascular, neurological, and ocular diseases to attenuate excessive ROS production and reduce downstream inflammatory cascades (Simonyi et al., 2012). Its chemical synthesis in laboratory settings has mostly focused on replicating the naturally derived molecule while exploring structural analogs that may improve potency or pharmacokinetics. This class of compounds has historically been used both as a tool compound for dissecting NOX-mediated oxidative mechanisms and as an experimental therapeutic agent to counteract the cellular consequences of oxidative damage (Simonyi et al., 2012; Bellezza, 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Extensive preclinical research has demonstrated that apocynin can reduce NOX-dependent ROS production in cell-based systems, particularly in models of inflammation and oxidative stress. Several in vitro studies have documented its ability to ameliorate oxidative damage by inhibiting the activation of NADPH oxidases in various cell types, including vascular endothelial cells, macrophages, and most pertinently, retinal cells. For example, studies have shown that apocynin suppresses NOX4-induced ROS generation in hypoxic human retinal Müller cells and in diabetic rat retinas, suggesting its potential for retinal neuroprotection (Ahmad et al., 2021). Although apocynin has not yet been formally approved for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in clinical settings, its extensive use in ocular inflammation models and retinal degeneration studies underpins its repurposing potential. In addition, the compound has historically been used in various animal models to attenuate exacerbated inflammatory responses linked to NOX-driven oxidative stress, and these studies consistently report improvements in tissue integrity and reductions in oxidative stress markers (Dionysopoulou et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020). Its long history in preclinical ophthalmic applications, when coupled with its excellent safety profile observed in animal studies—indicated by a high LD₅₀ and absence of genotoxicity at effective concentrations—provides further impetus to evaluate its efficacy in dry AMD, a condition characterized by chronic oxidative stress and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction (Kulbay et al., 2024; Rohowetz et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism of action of apocynin lies in its ability to inhibit the assembly and activation of the NADPH oxidase complex, a multi-component enzyme system critically involved in the production of superoxide and other ROS in various cell types. Under physiological conditions, NOX enzymes (including isoforms NOX1, NOX2, and NOX4) contribute to redox signaling; however, their aberrant activation under pathological states such as dry AMD leads to excessive ROS levels that damage cellular lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Mechanistically, apocynin prevents the cytosolic subunits (such as p47^phox) from translocating to the membrane-bound catalytic subunits (such as gp91^phox/NOX2 and NOX4) and forming an active enzyme complex. This inhibition translates into a reduction of ROS generation (Sun et al., 2020; Kulbay et al., 2024). Furthermore, emerging evidence suggests that transcriptional regulators like PU.1/Spi1 serve as master regulators of NOX4-p22^phox complex activation in the RPE during amyloid β–induced injury. Silencing of PU.1 in experimental models resulted in significantly reduced oxidative stress and preserved mitochondrial function; these observations underscore the cascade that apocynin is poised to interrupt by targeting the NADPH oxidase assembly process (Sun et al., 2020; Kulbay et al., 2024). In addition to this primary mode of action, apocynin’s antioxidant properties may also indirectly preserve lysosomal integrity by reducing ROS-mediated peroxidation of lipids in the phagosome–lysosome membranes. This is particularly relevant in RPE cells, which are tasked with daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and are susceptible to lysosomal dysfunction if the autophagic flux is compromised by oxidative damage (Shu et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). The inhibition of NOX-derived ROS in this manner is expected to stabilize cathepsin D activity—a critical lysosomal protease—and maintain the efficient degradation of POS, thereby reducing the accumulation of deleterious lipofuscin deposits that are a hallmark of dry AMD pathology (Sun et al., 2020; Bellezza, 2018).

Expected Effect:  
In the assay system under consideration—where RPE cells are challenged with oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂ exposure) to mimic the pathological conditions of dry AMD—the expected effect of apocynin administration is multifaceted. First, by inhibiting the activation of NADPH oxidase complexes (with an anticipated IC₅₀ in the vicinity of 5 µM), apocynin should significantly reduce the intracellular production of ROS, thereby protecting RPE cells from oxidative damage (Simonyi et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2020). This reduction in ROS is critical, as excessive oxidative stress not only causes direct cellular damage but also impairs the function of lysosomal membranes, leading to decreased cathepsin D activity and inefficient POS degradation. As a result, lipofuscin, which is an autofluorescent pigment composed of undegraded POS remnants and other oxidatively modified cellular components, would accumulate. The hypothesis posits that apocynin’s reduction of ROS will help to maintain the integrity of phagosome–lysosome membranes, thus preserving autophagic flux and ensuring the continuous clearance of POS. This preservation is expected to be measurable via restored cathepsin D activity and increased phagocytic uptake of POS under H₂O₂-challenged conditions (Sun et al., 2020; Ahmad et al., 2021). Additionally, because RPE cells are known to express multiple NOX isoforms (notably NOX2 and NOX4) that contribute to the chronic oxidative stress seen in AMD, the attenuation of their activity by apocynin could lead to reductions in downstream inflammatory signaling mediated by transcription factors such as NF-κB. This, in turn, would be expected to result in improved cellular homeostasis and protection against further degenerative events, including mitochondrial dysfunction and cell death (Kim et al., 2021; Hernández et al., 2025). Ultimately, the expected cumulative effect would be a deceleration of the disease process in dry AMD, as evidenced by improved RPE function, reduced lipofuscin accumulation, and maintenance of photoreceptor viability (Dionysopoulou et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
Evaluating apocynin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several compelling strengths as well as areas that warrant careful consideration. One of the primary strengths of apocynin is its well-documented ability to inhibit NADPH oxidase activity and thereby reduce ROS production—a mechanism that is strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. The extensive body of preclinical literature, which includes studies in ocular inflammation and diabetic retinopathy models, supports the notion that apocynin can restore redox balance and mitigate oxidative cellular damage. This is particularly relevant in the context of RPE cells, where oxidative stress not only contributes directly to cellular dysfunction but also impairs critical processes such as autophagy and POS clearance leading to lipofuscin accumulation (Sun et al., 2020; Ahmad et al., 2021; Ruan et al., 2021). Furthermore, apocynin’s natural origin and favorable safety profile observed in multiple animal studies bolster its attractiveness as a repurposing candidate; its established use in preclinical settings means that a substantial amount of mechanistic and pharmacokinetic data is already available, potentially accelerating its clinical translation (Simonyi et al., 2012; Kulbay et al., 2024).

Nevertheless, there are challenges and potential weaknesses that must be acknowledged. One limitation is the translation of experimental efficacy observed in simplified in vitro models or acute animal studies to the highly complex and multifactorial pathology of dry AMD in humans. Dry AMD involves chronic insults over decades, and while NOX-mediated oxidative stress is a central driver, the disease also involves other processes like chronic inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and dysregulated autophagy that might not be fully addressed by NOX inhibition alone (Shu et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2021). Moreover, apocynin requires metabolic activation by peroxidases—an aspect that could render its effectiveness context-dependent, potentially limiting its efficacy in regions of the retina that do not exhibit sufficiently high levels of activating enzymes. This localized activation may be beneficial by minimizing systemic effects, but it also raises questions regarding the consistency of therapeutic benefit across the heterogeneous RPE microenvironment encountered in dry AMD (Sun et al., 2020; Bellezza, 2018).

Another consideration is the drug delivery challenge. The effective concentration required to achieve NOX inhibition in vitro (in the low micromolar range) may not be easily attainable in retinal tissues with conventional delivery methods. As the RPE is located behind multiple anatomical barriers, ensuring that adequate drug levels reach the target site is critical. Strategies such as intraocular injections, sustained-release formulations, or nanoparticle-based delivery systems might need to be explored and optimized to overcome these pharmacokinetic barriers (Ruan et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2008). Additionally, while apocynin has been reported to preserve lysosomal function and enhance autophagic flux in stressed RPE cells in vitro, robust data from chronic disease models specifically recapitulating dry AMD pathology remain limited. The long-term impact of continuous NOX inhibition on RPE physiology and the potential for off-target effects, especially given the role of low-level ROS in normal cellular signaling, will require careful investigation (Dionysopoulou et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2021).

In summary, the repurposing of apocynin for dry AMD is supported by a solid mechanistic rationale—its inhibition of NOX-mediated ROS production can theoretically interrupt the vicious cycle of oxidative stress, lysosomal dysfunction, and impaired autophagic clearance that underlies RPE degeneration. The strengths of apocynin lie in its natural origin, extensive preclinical use, proven safety profile, and the centrality of its targeted pathway in dry AMD pathology. However, the challenges of ensuring effective and targeted delivery to the retina, verifying its long-term efficacy in chronic disease models, and addressing its context-dependent activation must be thoroughly addressed in future studies. Taken together, these considerations suggest that apocynin is a promising candidate for further preclinical investigation in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to complement other therapeutic strategies targeting oxidative stress and cellular clearance dysfunction (Sun et al., 2020; Ahmad et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025; Simonyi et al., 2012; Rohowetz et al., 2018).

Conclusion:  
Based on the comprehensive review of the current biochemical, clinical, and preclinical literature, apocynin presents as a viable repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its mechanism—centered on the inhibition of NADPH oxidase-driven ROS production—directly addresses critical aspects of RPE dysfunction and lysosomal damage that are central to the disease’s pathogenesis. The evidence from related studies in ocular inflammation models, coupled with its favorable safety profile and natural origin, provides a strong foundation for further investigation. Nonetheless, future research must focus on optimizing delivery systems to overcome ocular barriers, confirming chronic efficacy in models that accurately mimic the slow progression of dry AMD, and delineating the full spectrum of molecular effects in the complex retinal microenvironment before advancing to clinical trials. Despite these challenges, the strengths of apocynin’s targeted action and established preclinical data support its continued exploration as part of a multi-targeted approach to address the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD (Ahmad et al., 2021; Bellezza, 2018; Dionysopoulou et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2021; Simonyi et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Iptacopan (LNP023) is a rationally designed, low–molecular-weight small molecule that selectively inhibits complement factor B (FB), the essential catalytic subunit of the alternative pathway (AP) C3/C5 convertases C3bBb and C3bBbC3b on activating surfaces (including stressed RPE) and within the amplification loop of complement activation (C3 → C3b → C3 convertase) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 4–6). Medicinal-chemistry optimization from an early micromolar FB inhibitor hit (a naphthalene-dihydro-imidazole amine) introduced an indole to occupy the S1 pocket and a piperidine scaffold engaging the S3/non-primed region with a benzoic acid–mediated H-bond network, yielding iptacopan with high potency and selectivity for FB (crystallographically confirmed) (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 10–13; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Iptacopan binds the catalytic serine-protease active site within the Bb subunit of FB—structural analyses show its indole and piperidine moieties seated in S1/S3, forming key hydrogen bonds within the catalytic domain, with the active-site triad (His–Asp–Ser) located in proximity; binding has been explicitly mapped to the catalytic site in Bb and shown to block substrate processing by the AP convertase (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6, 8–10).

Class and precedent: Iptacopan is an oral, proximal complement/AP inhibitor; this class has delivered robust target engagement and clinical benefit in multiple complement-driven diseases (e.g., PNH, C3G, IgAN), establishing translational viability for systemic small-molecule blockade of AP amplification in human disease (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Oral administration achieves rapid systemic exposure (Tmax ≈ 2 hours) with dose-dependent AP suppression and sustained steady-state inhibition at 200 mg twice daily in clinical studies, supporting convenient outpatient dosing with on-target PD (reduced plasma Bb and urinary sC5b-9) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Preclinically, systemic iptacopan potently blocks LPS-induced AP activation in mice in both plasma and eye tissues, indicating ocular target engagement after oral dosing (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). Collectively, synthesis, mechanistic selectivity, and clinical-class performance position iptacopan as a well-characterized, orally bioavailable FB inhibitor suited for indications where local AP amplification contributes to pathology, including dry AMD (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).

Therapeutic History  
- Non-ocular indications and clinical pharmacology. In early-phase clinical studies, iptacopan demonstrated rapid absorption (peak plasma concentration at ~2 hours), favorable tolerability, and dose-dependent inhibition of AP activity; sustained maximal inhibition was reported at 200 mg twice daily, the regimen advanced into multiple phase 2 trials (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Across PNH and AP-driven renal diseases (C3G, IgAN), iptacopan showed robust target engagement and clinical activity: reductions in plasma Bb and urinary sC5b-9, reductions in plasma C3 (in many patients after months), kidney-pathology improvements (reduced glomerular C3 deposition), and meaningful efficacy outcomes (e.g., proteinuria reductions in C3G/IgAN; hemoglobin improvements and transfusion-free status in PNH) with generally favorable safety profiles and no serious infections in the cited trials (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Iptacopan has received regulatory approvals (including an accelerated approval for IgAN) and late-stage development status for multiple indications, validating systemic AP inhibition with this agent (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8).  
- AMD program. A randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial in early/intermediate AMD is ongoing (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022), designed to test whether oral iptacopan prevents conversion to iRORA or late AMD over 24 months, with masked multimodal imaging and planned plasma trough PK by LC–MS; vaccinations for encapsulated organisms are required per complement-inhibition class risk management (no results are available in the excerpt) (“A Masked, Placebo-controlled Study to Assess Iptacopan in Age-related Macular Degeneration,” 2022). Reviews place iptacopan among oral FB inhibitors under evaluation for atrophic AMD as an alternative to intravitreal complement blockade, motivated by the blood–retina barrier and the burden of injections; however, the provided material contains no AMD efficacy outcomes for iptacopan (Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 8–9; Hammadi et al., 2023, pp. 30–31; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
- Ocular-relevant preclinical context. Although iptacopan-specific dry-AMD model data are not provided, two lines of evidence are directly relevant: (1) in the Efemp1 R345W knock-in mouse (an RPE proteostasis model with AMD-like basal deposits), genetic Cfb deletion abolished AP activation and eliminated sub-RPE deposits, while oral pharmacologic FB blockade (with the small molecule DB-82-CB77) reduced deposits by 65% in females and reversed disease-associated pathway perturbations (UPR/inflammation upregulation and mitochondrial repression) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10); (2) systemic iptacopan blocks AP activation in eye tissue in LPS-challenged mice, supporting oral delivery as a viable route to ocular target engagement, though iptacopan-specific AMD-model efficacy is not shown in the provided excerpts (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Complement biology and lysosomal/autophagy pathology in RPE. In CFH Y402H high-risk iPSC-RPE, increased C3 turnover and lysosomal deposition of C5b-9 drive lysosomal swelling, membrane damage, Cathepsin D leakage to sub-RPE deposits, and reduced lysosomal function; blocking C3 with the compstatin analogue Cp40 reverses these phenotypes, restoring lysosomal number/size/function and lowering complement deposition (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13). While these data establish that proximal complement blockade can normalize lysosomal/autophagy dysfunction in high-risk RPE, the excerpts do not directly test FB/AP inhibitors in this RPE system; thus, extrapolation to iptacopan remains mechanistic rather than empirically proven in the provided sources (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 7–13).

Mechanism of Action  
- Biochemical target and binding mode. FB is an abundant plasma glycoprotein (~0.2–0.4 mg/mL; ~2–3 μM) unique to the AP and, upon binding to C3b, is cleaved by factor D into Ba and Bb; Bb contains a VWA domain, MIDAS motif, and a serine-protease domain that provides the catalytic site for AP C3/C5 convertases on C3b-bearing surfaces (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6). Iptacopan binds the catalytic site of Bb in the S1/S3 pockets with a defined hydrogen-bonding network, directly inhibiting the proteolytic activity of the AP convertase and thereby blocking AP-mediated C3/C5 processing (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- Potency, selectivity, and functional inhibition. Iptacopan exhibits an enzymatic IC₅₀ ≈ 0.01 μM against FB and inhibits AP-induced C5b-9 formation in 50% human serum with IC₅₀ ≈ 0.13 μM; it prevents C3 deposition and complement-mediated lysis of PNH erythrocytes with IC₅₀ ≈ 0.4 μM and shows high selectivity over factor D and classical/lectin pathway activity in broad panels (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Alternative affinity reporting (K_D ≈ 0.0079 mM) has been noted in one excerpt, but across structural/functional assays the compound consistently behaves as a highly potent and selective FB catalytic-site inhibitor (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 8–10).  
- Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics relevant to target engagement. Clinically, iptacopan is rapidly absorbed (Tmax ~ 2 hours), with strong steady-state AP inhibition at 200 mg twice daily; pharmacodynamic readouts demonstrate reduced circulating Bb and reduced urinary sC5b-9, consistent with systemic and tissue-level AP suppression (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). While precise human half-life and oral bioavailability values are not provided in the excerpts, iptacopan is described as orally bioavailable with a shorter half-life than antibodies, enabling relatively rapid restoration of AP function after washout—an attribute that informs adherence requirements and infection risk mitigation (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–11). Factor B itself has a long plasma half-life (30–70 h) and high abundance; iptacopan’s high affinity and mechanism allow sustained convertase inhibition because only newly synthesized FB needs to be neutralized at steady state for continued pathway blockade (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- Ocular target engagement. In mice, systemic administration of iptacopan potently blocks LPS-induced complement activation in both plasma and eye tissues, implying that oral dosing can achieve pharmacologically active exposure to ocular compartments, at least under inflammatory conditions (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). In the Efemp1 R345W model, ocular AP activation is local (iC3b and Ba ≈ 2× in eye, not in plasma), aligning with a need for ocular engagement; although iptacopan’s ocular concentration-time profile in humans is not provided, the preclinical PD findings and the AMD phase 2 trial design together support the translational intent to suppress ocular AP activity via oral dosing (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Genetic and disease-mechanism validation. FB is genetically and mechanistically implicated in AMD pathogenesis; protective low-activity variants (e.g., R32Q) associate with reduced AMD risk, and AP dysregulation is a central pathogenic thread in AMD biology (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6). In an RPE proteostasis model (Efemp1 R345W), Cfb deletion abolishes AP activation and prevents sub-RPE deposit formation; pharmacologic FB suppression reduces deposit burden and reverses multiple mutation-associated pathway perturbations (UPR, immune/complement signatures, mitochondrial repression), supporting causal linkage between AP activity and RPE/Bruch’s membrane pathology (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10).  
- Comparison to other complement nodes in AMD models. Complement C3 blockade (Cp40) in CFH Y402H high-risk iPSC-RPE rescues lysosomal structure and function, reduces C3b and C5b-9 deposition (including lysosomal MAC), and diminishes drusen-like phenotypes, demonstrating that proximal complement suppression can reverse RPE degradative defects; this provides a mechanistic bridge to AP/FB inhibition, which is expected to decrease upstream C3 turnover and downstream MAC burden by curtailing the amplification loop, though FB-specific rescue of lysosomal function was not directly tested in that study (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).

Expected Effect  
- In vitro RPE assays and readouts. Based on the AP mechanism and the CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE data with C3 inhibition, iptacopan is expected to reduce AP convertase activity on RPE surfaces, lowering C3b/iC3b deposition and MAC (C5b-9) accrual on and within RPE cells, thereby alleviating lysosomal overburden, improving lysosomal integrity, and facilitating restoration of autophagic flux (e.g., normalized LC3-II/p62 dynamics) and degradative function (e.g., Cathepsin D activity and localization) (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13). The Efemp1 model shows that AP activation is heightened locally and that Cfb deletion or FB inhibition normalizes stress/inflammation (including UPR) and mitochondrial pathways; by analogy, iptacopan should attenuate ER stress/UPR signaling and immune/complement activation signatures in RPE/eyecup proteomes, with secondary benefits for mitochondrial/energy pathways (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2). Although direct demonstration that FB inhibition restores RPE lysosomal function is not presented in the excerpted Efemp1 work, the Cp40 RPE data make a strong mechanistic case that upstream complement suppression reduces complement load on lysosomes and rescues degradative capacity; iptacopan should achieve a similar effect by preventing AP amplification and thus lowering the rate of C3 activation fragment generation and MAC formation at the RPE (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).  
- Ex vivo/animal AMD-relevant endpoints. In female Efemp1 R345W mice, oral FB inhibition (DB-82-CB77) reduced sub-RPE deposits by 65% over 8 weeks, while Cfb deletion completely eliminated deposits and abrogated AP activation in eye, indicating that AP blockade can causally modify a basal laminar–like deposit phenotype; iptacopan, as a potent oral FB inhibitor with demonstrated ocular PD in mice, would be expected to recapitulate these effects on deposits and molecular signatures, subject to dose/exposure parity and sex-dependent biology (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 9–10, 4–6). The Efemp1 eyecup proteomics further suggest that FB blockade rebalances ocular homeostasis, dampening CR3/immune-complement signaling and upstream UPR stress while partially restoring mitochondrial proteins, reinforcing the hypothesis that complement amplification contributes to proteostasis failure and that its inhibition should normalize these axes (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Clinical AMD endpoints. The ongoing phase 2 iptacopan study in AMD is designed to detect prevention of conversion to iRORA or late AMD by SD-/SS-OCT and multimodal imaging over 24 months; systemic trough PK will be monitored. If oral iptacopan meaningfully engages ocular AP in humans, we would anticipate reduced new-onset iRORA and slower disease progression relative to placebo, potentially accompanied by systemic PD markers (Bb suppression), though the trial as described does not include ocular PD sampling (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022). As precedent, intravitreal C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) reduced GA growth in phase 2; conversely, C5 inhibition had mixed results, underscoring the importance of targeting upstream amplification (C3/AP) rather than solely the terminal pathway in AMD (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 7–9). It remains to be shown whether systemic FB inhibition can reproduce these benefits without increasing CNV risk; complement inhibition broadly has been associated with higher rates of new-onset CNV in some trials, a safety signal that must be monitored in FB-targeting programs (Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic and genetic rationale. FB is the essential catalytic subunit of AP convertases, and human genetics supports a causal role of FB activity in AMD (protective low-activity variants) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6). In an RPE-driven mouse model (Efemp1 R345W), Cfb deletion abolishes ocular AP activation and eliminates sub-RPE deposits; pharmacologic FB inhibition reduces deposits and reverses disease-associated pathway dysregulation, linking AP amplification to RPE/proteostasis pathology and basal deposit accumulation (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10).  
- Demonstrated oral target engagement, including ocular PD in mice. Iptacopan is orally bioavailable with rapid absorption and consistent systemic PD (Bb and sC5b-9 suppression) in humans; preclinically, systemic iptacopan blocks AP activation in eye tissue, supporting feasibility of oral ocular target engagement (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Potency/selectivity with favorable clinical precedents. Iptacopan shows nanomolar enzymatic potency, selective FB catalytic-site binding, and clear functional AP inhibition in serum/cell assays; it has delivered convincing efficacy across multiple complement-driven indications with acceptable safety, validating the drug and target class clinically (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14).  
- Convergence with RPE lysosome/autophagy biology. In CFH Y402H high-risk iPSC-RPE, proximal complement blockade (C3 inhibitor Cp40) reverses lysosomal swelling/dysfunction and reduces complement deposition including MAC; these findings mechanistically support the hypothesis that halting AP amplification upstream will relieve lysosomal burden and restore degradative capacity in RPE, a central deficit in dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).

Risks and Gaps  
- Lack of direct iptacopan data in AMD models or RPE lysosome assays. The provided excerpts do not report iptacopan efficacy in AMD-relevant animal models (e.g., Efemp1) or direct rescue of RPE lysosomal/autophagic function; the pharmacologic proof-of-concept in Efemp1 used a different FB inhibitor (DB-82-CB77) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 9–10). Thus, the hypothesis that iptacopan will restore RPE degradative capacity is mechanistically plausible but not yet experimentally demonstrated in the cited AMD models (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 7–13).  
- Ocular PK/PD in humans unproven. The AMD phase 2 protocol measures plasma trough iptacopan but does not include ocular PD; no human ocular PK is provided in the excerpts. Translational dependence on ocular exposure is high because AP activation in Efemp1 is local to the eye (elevated Ba/iC3b in ocular tissue but not plasma) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).  
- Heterogeneity and sex effects in preclinical model. Efemp1 females exhibit ocular AP activation and respond to FB inhibition; males have lower deposits, no ocular AP upregulation, and do not respond, implying biological heterogeneity that may translate to variable clinical responses and may necessitate biomarker-based enrichment (e.g., markers of ocular AP activation) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).  
- Class safety considerations. Complement inhibition increases susceptibility to infections with encapsulated bacteria; vaccination is mandated in the AMD study. Additionally, complement inhibition in GA trials has been associated with increased new-onset CNV versus sham, a signal that must be actively monitored; whether FB inhibition carries a similar CNV liability is unknown from the provided materials (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
- Mixed history of systemic complement inhibitors in AMD. The sole completed RCT of systemic anti-C5 (eculizumab) in AMD failed to show GA benefit, raising delivery and mechanistic questions for systemic approaches, although intravitreal proximal inhibitors (C3) have shown GA-slowing, and the Efemp1 data support AP dependence for basal deposit biology (Hammadi et al., 2023, pp. 17–18; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 7–9).

Program Implications and Next Steps  
- Preclinical toolkit alignment. To directly validate the central hypothesis for iptacopan, run head-to-head studies in AMD-relevant systems:
  - Efemp1 R345W mouse: oral iptacopan dosing matched for AP PD versus DB-82-CB77 benchmark; endpoints: TEM-assessed sub-RPE deposits, ocular Ba/iC3b, eyecup/neural retina proteomics (UPR/complement/mitochondrial modules), and RPE lysosomal/autophagy markers (LAMP1, CTSD activity, LC3-II/p62 flux), stratified by sex (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 9–10, 4–6).  
  - CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE: iptacopan in complement-competent human serum conditions; readouts: C3b/C5b-9 deposition, lysosomal integrity (Lysotracker, Galectin-8), CTSD localization/activity, autophagic flux and POS phagocytosis assays; benchmark to Cp40 rescue (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).  
  - Ocular exposure/PD: quantify iptacopan in ocular compartments (choroid/retina/RPE) and measure ocular AP biomarkers in vivo after oral dosing to confirm exposure–PD matching the LPS PD signal (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Translational biomarker strategy. Incorporate systemic AP markers (Bb, Ba), exploratory ocular biomarkers (e.g., aqueous humor C3 fragments if feasible), and imaging-based deposit/ELM–Bruch’s metrics; in the clinic, deploy multimodal imaging for conversion endpoints as in Novartis Pharmaceuticals (2022), and prospectively monitor CNV incidence (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
- Patient selection. Consider enriching for patients with systemic or local evidence of AP activation (genetics such as CFH risk alleles, complement biomarker profiles) analogous to the female-biased AP activation seen in Efemp1 (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).  
- Dosing rationale and adherence. Target 200 mg twice daily based on human PD experience; given the shorter half-life vs antibodies and the need for sustained AP suppression, emphasize adherence and vaccine prophylaxis; PD sampling should verify on-target AP inhibition longitudinally (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Ricklin, 2024, pp. 7–9; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).

Bottom line. Iptacopan is a mechanistically compelling, clinically validated oral FB inhibitor with demonstrated systemic PD, rapid onset, and preclinical evidence of ocular AP engagement; rigorous AMD-model testing and clinical biomarker integration are now required to close the translational loop from AP biology to RPE lysosomal rescue and clinical protection against atrophy progression (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 8–10; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).

Go/No-Go Considerations for Dry AMD  
- Go signals:  
  - Target validity in AMD pathobiology is strong (genetics, AP dependence of basal deposits, proximal complement benefits in RPE models) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).

  - Ocular PD feasibility is supported in mice for systemic iptacopan; pharmacologic AP blockade reduces deposits in Efemp1 with another orally bioavailable FB inhibitor (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).  
- Caution flags:  
  - No iptacopan AMD-model efficacy in the provided materials; need direct RPE lysosome/autophagy rescue readouts and deposit suppression with iptacopan prior to expensive late-phase commitments (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 7–13).  
  - Macro safety signals observed with complement inhibitors in AMD (CNV incidence) necessitate vigilant monitoring and risk–benefit analyses tailored to FB inhibition (Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
  - Systemic delivery uncertainty—human ocular PK/PD data are lacking; trial design should incorporate robust systemic PD and exploratory ocular biomarkers where feasible (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).

Advance iptacopan for dry AMD with a focused, staged plan:

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AMD3100 (also known as plerixafor) is a small‐molecule, bicyclam compound originally discovered and synthesized as a CXCR4 antagonist. It belongs to a class of compounds designed to block the interaction between the chemokine ligand SDF‐1 (CXCL12) and its receptor CXCR4. This class of compounds was initially developed for their antiviral potential—specifically to inhibit HIV‐1 entry into cells—because CXCR4 serves as a co‐receptor for viral entry. This signaling cascade is known to regulate key cellular processes such as chemotaxis, cell survival, proliferation, and inflammatory gene expression. With its synthetic origin and established profile as a CXCR4 antagonist, AMD3100 has been repurposed beyond its initial anti‐HIV goals to include hematopoietic stem cell mobilization and experimental oncology. Its potential re‐utilization in ocular diseases, particularly in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), capitalizes on its ability to modulate inflammatory signaling pathways implicated in retinal degeneration (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AMD3100 emerged from research aimed at blocking HIV infection, but its clinical development pivoted after it was found to robustly mobilize hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells from the bone marrow. This discovery led to its approval by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as an adjuvant therapy for autologous stem cell transplantation in patients with non‐Hodgkin’s lymphoma and multiple myeloma. Its use in stem cell mobilization has been thoroughly characterized in clinical trials with documented pharmacokinetics and a reasonable safety profile in systemic administration (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019). In addition to these applications, AMD3100 has been investigated in various preclinical models of cancer, where its inhibition of CXCR4-mediated signaling has been linked to reduced tumor cell invasion, decreased angiogenesis, and altered immune cell trafficking (Andtbacka et al., 2022; Cho et al., 2013). In the ocular context, although AMD3100 has not been used directly for treating dry AMD, its effects on CXCR4 signaling have been addressed in studies focusing on glaucomatous models. For example, investigations in trabecular meshwork cells from glaucomatous tissue have demonstrated that AMD3100, when administered at 1 mM concentration, completely abrogates the protective effects of CXCL12 and inadvertently induces apoptosis, highlighting the dual role of CXCR4 signaling in ocular tissues (Denoyer et al., 2012). Moreover, systemic administration studies in non‐ocular models such as the SOD1^G93A ALS mouse model have shown that chronic AMD3100 treatment can yield neuroprotective and anti‐inflammatory benefits (Rabinovich‐Nikitin et al., 2016), which further adds to its therapeutic appeal but also underscores the importance of tissue-specific dosing and context. These historical uses underscore AMD3100’s well-defined pharmacological profile while simultaneously illustrating that translating its benefits to the RPE in dry AMD will require reconciling its established systemic effects with the often finely balanced roles of the CXCR4 axis in retinal tissue repair and inflammation (Cai et al., 2014; Saiman et al., 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, AMD3100 exerts its primary pharmacological action by selectively binding to the CXCR4 receptor and competitively inhibiting the binding of its natural ligand, SDF‐1 (CXCL12). In doing so, it prevents receptor activation and the subsequent engagement of intracellular signaling cascades mediated by G-protein coupled receptor activation. The downstream effects typically include modulation of pathways such as PI3K/Akt, Ras/ERK, and, in many cases, alterations in intracellular calcium fluxes that contribute to chemotaxis and cell survival (Bai et al., 2016; Colasanti et al., 2025). By inhibiting these cascades, AMD3100 hinders not only the migration of cells toward SDF‐1 gradients but also the pro‐inflammatory and pro‐angiogenic gene expression programs that are otherwise activated upon CXCR4 engagement. In cancer models, this mechanism translates into reduced tumor cell invasion and inhibition of angiogenesis, while in immune cells it modulates chemotactic responses and inflammatory cell trafficking (Cho et al., 2013). Importantly, CXCR4 is expressed in multiple ocular cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. In RPE, the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis has been implicated in cellular migration, cytokine secretion, and potentially in the regulation of the phagocytic machinery necessary for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). The hypothesis driving the current proposal suggests that chronic activation of CXCR4 in RPE cells, possibly driven by persistent inflammatory stimuli such as TNF‐α, leads to a pro‐inflammatory state that downregulates key phagocytic receptors like MERTK and compromises lysosomal enzyme activity. By blocking the binding of SDF‐1 to CXCR4, AMD3100 is expected to interrupt this deleterious signaling cascade, resulting in normalization of MERTK expression and lysosomal enzyme levels, and thereby restoring the essential phagocytic function of the RPE (Colasanti et al., 2025). However, the complexity of CXCR4 signaling is underscored by studies in other ocular tissues where its inhibition has led to apoptosis of trabecular cells, suggesting that the outcome of CXCR4 blockade may be highly dependent on the cell type and the local microenvironment (Denoyer et al., 2012). Therefore, while the mechanistic rationale is strong, careful evaluation of AMD3100’s specific molecular interactions in RPE cells will be required to delineate beneficial effects from potential adverse outcomes.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed therapeutic strategy hypothesizes that the blockade of CXCR4 by AMD3100 in RPE cells will lead to two major beneficial outcomes in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration: (1) inhibition of pro-inflammatory signaling that otherwise promotes aberrant cellular migration and deleterious inflammatory gene expression, and (2) restoration of the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells through upregulation of key receptors and enzymes necessary for the efficient clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In dry AMD, a hallmark of disease progression is the accumulation of cellular debris and the failure of RPE cells to effectively clear POS due to impaired phagocytosis—a process that is critical for sustaining photoreceptor health and visual function. Evidence suggests that chronic activation of the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis in the retinal microenvironment can lead to elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines and subsequent downregulation of MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase essential for the recognition and internalization of shed POS (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). In vitro models, such as TNF‐α–treated ARPE-19 cells, have demonstrated that inflammatory stress leads to diminished phagocytic activity, and it is hypothesized that blocking CXCR4 signaling with AMD3100 could counteract this effect by normalizing MERTK levels and restoring lysosomal function. In an ideal scenario, treatment with AMD3100 would reverse the pro-inflammatory signaling cascade by preventing SDF‐1 binding, reduce aberrant RPE migration, and allow the cells to maintain their structural polarity and phagocytic efficiency. Importantly, the RPE expresses CXCR4 receptors on their surface, as demonstrated by immunocytochemical studies, and the receptor’s activation has been linked to altered cellular motility and inflammatory responses (Canonica et al., 2021; Enzmann et al., 2017). The expected pharmacodynamic outcome is that, upon AMD3100 treatment, RPE cells under inflammatory stress conditions would exhibit increased expression of MERTK and lysosomal enzymes, leading to improved clearance of damaged photoreceptor outer segments, which is critical for photoreceptor survival and overall retinal health. While data from other cell types suggest the possibility of safely modulating these pathways, caution is warranted given the evidence from trabecular meshwork cells where CXCR4 antagonism disrupted protective signaling (Denoyer et al., 2012). Hence, the key to success will lie in establishing the proper dosing and delivery mechanisms that provide sufficient blockade of deleterious CXCR4 signaling in RPE without compromising the receptor’s potentially beneficial roles in tissue repair and homeostasis.

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, AMD3100 presents an intriguing candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration given its well-defined mechanism of action, extensive preclinical and clinical history, and a known safety profile in non-ocular indications such as hematopoietic stem cell mobilization and cancer therapy (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019). The central hypothesis—that chronic SDF‐1/CXCR4 signaling in RPE cells contributes to inflammation-driven downregulation of MERTK and consequent impairment of POS phagocytosis—addresses a critical pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD. Blocking this pathway with AMD3100 could, in theory, restore the phagocytic machinery of the RPE, thereby reducing the accumulation of toxic cellular debris and slowing disease progression (Colasanti et al., 2025).

One of the strengths of AMD3100 as a therapeutic candidate lies in its extensive clinical use and established pharmacokinetic profile; its FDA approval for stem cell mobilization means that much is already known about its systemic effects, dosing parameters, and potential toxicities when administered appropriately (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Rabinovich-Nikitin et al., 2016). Moreover, the molecular mechanism—competitive antagonism at the CXCR4 receptor—has been demonstrated across multiple studies and various cell types, providing a robust theoretical framework for its use in modulating pathological signaling cascades in RPE cells (Bai et al., 2016; Colasanti et al., 2025). The concept of repurposing a well-characterized agent such as AMD3100 for dry AMD is attractive from a drug development standpoint because it could potentially shorten the translational timeline and reduce development risks related to novel chemical entities.

However, there are significant challenges and weaknesses that must be addressed before AMD3100 can be considered a promising candidate for dry AMD. First and foremost, the role of SDF‐1/CXCR4 signaling in ocular tissues appears to be multifaceted. While in RPE cells chronic activation may indeed drive a pro-inflammatory and phagocytosis-impairing phenotype, in other ocular tissues such as the trabecular meshwork, CXCR4 signaling has been shown to exert cytoprotective effects. Studies in glaucomatous trabecular cells have demonstrated that blockade of CXCR4 by AMD3100 not only abrogates the beneficial actions of CXCL12 but may also actively induce apoptosis, highlighting a potential risk that the protective aspects of CXCR4 signaling could be compromised (Denoyer et al., 2012). This tissue-specific duality raises concerns that non-selective or systemic inhibition of CXCR4 might lead to unintended adverse effects in the retina and other ocular compartments. Therefore, any consideration of AMD3100 for dry AMD will require extremely careful dosing studies and potentially localized delivery strategies that avoid systemic over-blockade.

Another key consideration is the current lack of direct evidence supporting the efficacy of AMD3100 in restoring MERTK expression or lysosomal enzyme levels in RPE cells, specifically in the context of dry AMD. While preliminary in vitro observations in TNF‐α–treated ARPE-19 cells are promising, these studies remain preliminary, and the translation of these effects into meaningful functional outcomes in vivo has yet to be established. The complexity of dry AMD pathogenesis—which involves not only inflammatory processes but also oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, and altered cellular metabolism—means that targeting a single pathway may not be sufficient to recapitulate the full spectrum of therapeutic benefit required for clinical efficacy (Colasanti et al., 2025).

Furthermore, the potential for AMD3100 to affect cell migration and even cellular differentiation via CXCR4 inhibition might have unpredictable consequences on the RPE’s capacity for repair. For instance, the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis has been implicated in the recruitment of bone marrow–derived progenitor cells to sites of RPE injury, a process that is thought to contribute to endogenous repair mechanisms (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). Inhibiting CXCR4 could inadvertently interfere with these reparative processes if not finely tuned. It is, therefore, imperative that any preclinical evaluation of AMD3100 for dry AMD includes rigorous assessments of not only phagocytic function and inflammatory profile but also the impact on RPE cell survival, differentiation, and regenerative capacity.

In addition to cell-specific concerns, the delivery method for AMD3100 in the context of dry AMD is another critical factor. The compound has been used systemically, but ocular diseases typically require either intravitreal or other localized delivery methods to achieve therapeutic concentrations while minimizing systemic exposure. Prior studies involving AMD3100 in ocular models—mostly in the context of glaucoma—have used subconjunctival injections at relatively high concentrations (e.g., 1 mM), which resulted in localized apoptotic effects (Denoyer et al., 2012). This suggests that the concentration and mode of delivery will need to be carefully optimized for the RPE to ensure that sufficient drug levels are achieved to block aberrant CXCR4 signaling without tipping the balance of protective chemokine functions.

Moreover, while the preclinical data from non-ocular models such as cancer and ALS are encouraging regarding the anti-inflammatory and anti-migratory effects of AMD3100 (Rabinovich-Nikitin et al., 2016; Andtbacka et al., 2022), these contexts differ significantly from the microenvironment of the aging retina. The retinal tissue, particularly in dry AMD, is characterized by complex interactions among the RPE, photoreceptors, Bruch’s membrane, and the choriocapillaris. The interplay of these structures with age-related oxidative stress and immune dysregulation means that any intervention must be evaluated in models that faithfully recapitulate these conditions. There is a paucity of direct literature on the use of AMD3100 in dry AMD models, which suggests that a substantial body of preclinical work is required before a clear signal of benefit can be ascertained.

In summary, AMD3100 has significant strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its well-documented mechanism of competitive antagonism at CXCR4, combined with an established clinical safety profile in systemic applications and a clear rationale for targeting the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis in inflammatory conditions, supports further investigation of its use in the retinal pigment epithelium (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019; Bai et al., 2016). However, key weaknesses include evidence from ocular models that indicate potential cytotoxicity when protective CXCR4 signals are indiscriminately blocked (Denoyer et al., 2012), as well as a lack of direct preclinical data in dry AMD or RPE-specific phagocytic assays. These concerns necessitate a cautious yet exploratory approach, with initial studies focused on establishing the optimal local dosing regimen, confirming that AMD3100 can indeed restore MERTK expression and phagocytic function in ARPE-19 cell models, and ultimately validating these findings in animal models of dry AMD that incorporate stressors such as TNF‐α or oxidative injury.

Overall Evaluation:  
In conclusion, while AMD3100 stands as one of the most thoroughly characterized CXCR4 antagonists with a solid clinical and preclinical background, its application to dry AMD remains largely untested. The theoretical basis—that chronic SDF‐1/CXCR4 activation in RPE drives inflammatory gene expression leading to diminished phagocytic capacity, and that blocking this pathway will restore homeostatic functions—is compelling and addresses a known pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD (Colasanti et al., 2025). The strengths of AMD3100 include its potent CXCR4 binding affinity, the wealth of pharmacological data supporting its mode of action, and its demonstrated ability to modulate inflammatory and migratory responses in various tissues. Moreover, the clinical safety data from its use in hematopoietic stem cell mobilization provide some reassurance regarding its tolerability when used in appropriate dosing regimens (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019).

On the other hand, several significant weaknesses must be acknowledged. Studies in ocular models have shown that CXCR4 blockade can eliminate protective signals that are crucial for cell survival, as evidenced by the induction of apoptosis in trabecular meshwork cells when treated with AMD3100 at high concentrations (Denoyer et al., 2012). In addition, there is a risk that by inhibiting CXCR4 signaling, AMD3100 might interfere with endogenous repair mechanisms mediated by the recruitment of bone marrow–derived progenitor cells, a process that may be beneficial in RPE regeneration (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). The lack of direct data demonstrating restoration of MERTK and improved phagocytosis in RPE cells further complicates the evaluation. Because dry AMD is multifactorial, it is unclear whether modulation of a single pathway—albeit an important one—will be sufficient to yield a meaningful clinical benefit without causing collateral damage to other aspects of RPE function.

Given these considerations, our recommendation is to pursue rigorous preclinical studies specifically tailored to dry AMD. These studies should encompass detailed in vitro analyses using ARPE-19 and primary human RPE cells under inflammatory and oxidative stress conditions to validate whether AMD3100 can reliably restore MERTK expression and lysosomal function, thereby enhancing POS clearance. It will also be critical to establish the appropriate concentration window that achieves therapeutic blockade of deleterious signaling while preserving necessary CXCR4-mediated protective effects. Parallel in vivo studies in animal models of dry AMD should focus on local ocular delivery methods—potentially through intravitreal or controlled-release formulations—to minimize systemic exposure and optimize retinal bioavailability.

In conclusion, AMD3100 represents an exciting and scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its mechanism of CXCR4 antagonism and the hypothesized link between chronic SDF‐1/CXCR4 activation and impaired RPE phagocytosis. However, given the mixed evidence from ocular safety studies and the complexity of CXCR4 signaling in retinal homeostasis, further systematic preclinical evaluation is essential before advancing to clinical trials. The balance between inhibiting pathological inflammation and preserving or even harnessing protective regenerative signals will determine the ultimate viability of AMD3100 as a therapeutic agent for dry age‐related macular degeneration (Denoyer et al., 2012; Rabinovich-Nikitin et al., 2016; Bai et al., 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is a fully synthetic small molecule in the 4-aminoquinoline (4AQ) class, developed in the mid-20th century as a hydroxylated analogue of chloroquine (CQ) to improve tolerability; HCQ differs from CQ by a terminal hydroxyl group on the side chain (HCQ: C18H26ClN3O, 336 g/mol; CQ: C18H26ClN3, 320 g/mol) (Browning, 2014a, 2014b). Industrially, HCQ can be prepared by condensing N1-N-ethyl-N1-β-hydroxyethyl-1,4-pentanediamine with 4,7-dichloroquinoline, paralleling the CQ route from the same quinoline core with an altered aminoalkyl side chain (Rainsford et al., 2015). As a class, HCQ/CQ are alkylated 4-aminoquinolines: weak, amphiphilic bases bearing a flat quinoline nucleus and a basic side chain that traverse membranes in unprotonated form and undergo protonation-dependent sequestration in acidic intracellular compartments (lysosomes, endosomes, Golgi) — a defining pharmacologic property (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Chloroquine’s two basic centers (pKa ≈ 10.2 and 8.1) illustrate the protonation behavior that drives lysosomal trapping; at lysosomal pH (≈ 4–5) these agents become diprotonated and accumulate, with lysosome:plasma distribution ratios measured on the order of ≈ 160 000 and intralysosomal concentrations up to ≈ 2 × 10⁻² M reported for CQ, elevating lysosomal pH toward ≈ 6 (Browning, 2014b, 2014a). Pharmacokinetically, HCQ exhibits high oral bioavailability (≈ 0.7–0.8), an extremely large apparent volume of distribution (> 40 000 L), and a long terminal elimination half-life (≈ 40–60 days), with blood concentrations exceeding plasma due to extensive intracellular partitioning and tissue sequestration (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Melanin-containing ocular tissues are prominent depots; with chronic ingestion, uveal and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) concentrations can reach up to ≈ 10 000× plasma, reflecting lysosomal trapping and melanin binding (Browning, 2014a). Enantiomer-specific disposition has been observed for HCQ, with stereoselective accumulation noted in blood compartments, underscoring complex distribution kinetics (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Clinically, HCQ is commonly administered as the sulfate salt, and CQ as the phosphate salt (Neto et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
HCQ and CQ were developed as antimalarials and subsequently repurposed as disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), with additional uses across dermatology and other immune-mediated conditions; HCQ is generally preferred over CQ for chronic therapy due to a better safety profile while maintaining comparable immunomodulatory efficacy (Rainsford et al., 2015; Neto et al., 2020). Broad clinical applications documented for HCQ/CQ include SLE, RA, primary Sjögren’s syndrome, discoid/cutaneous lupus erythematosus, polymorphous light eruption, solar urticaria, porphyria cutanea tarda, and other inflammatory dermatoses, reflecting lysosomotropic and immune-modulating actions (Rainsford et al., 2015; Rapparini et al., 2025). Mechanistically motivated repurposing has extended to autophagy inhibition in oncology trials, typically at daily doses far exceeding rheumatologic regimens, although HCQ is not approved as an anticancer adjuvant (Yusuf et al., 2023). Over recent decades HCQ prescriptions have increased substantially due to its relative affordability and systemic safety advantages, expanding the exposed population and the need for ocular safety surveillance (Yusuf et al., 2023).

With respect to retinal disease, the literature emphasizes retinotoxic risk and mechanistic links to RPE lysosomal dysfunction rather than therapeutic benefit in degenerative macular disease; authoritative pharmacology and ophthalmology sources do not provide evidence that HCQ/CQ have been used as treatments for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and instead catalogue retinal toxicity mechanisms and monitoring practices associated with long-term systemic use (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). Multiple summaries note that available data do not support therapeutic use of 4AQs for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerations, while documenting ocular accumulation, lysosomal alkalinization, and RPE stress as central safety concerns (Browning, 2014a). Retinopathy, although uncommon at recommended doses, is a recognized dose- and duration-related adverse effect that can be irreversible and may progress after drug cessation, motivating dose caps and structured ophthalmic screening (Rainsford et al., 2015; Ding et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action  
Lysosomotropism and lysosomal alkalinization  
HCQ/CQ are canonical lysosomotropic weak bases that accumulate massively within acidic intracellular organelles and elevate their pH, directly impairing acidity-dependent lysosomal hydrolases, receptor recycling, and degradative pathways including autophagy (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b). In vitro and cell-system studies report that chloroquine exposure increases lysosomal pH from ≈ 4–5 toward ≈ 6, a change sufficient to inhibit cathepsin activities and other acid hydrolases; pharmacologic blockade of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase with bafilomycin A₁ abrogates CQ’s lysosomotropism and toxicity, pinpointing disruption of lysosomal acidification as the proximal driver (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b). In RPE cells specifically, the lysosomotropic alkalinization by 4AQs inhibits lysosomal enzyme activity and autophagic flux, leading to accumulation of undegraded material; experimental inhibition of vacuolar acidification with bafilomycin phenocopies these degradative defects, indicating that pH elevation per se is sufficient to impair RPE lysosomal function (Guha et al., 2014).

Immune modulation and nucleic acid sensing  
Elevation of endolysosomal pH by 4AQs inhibits MHC class II antigen processing and presentation and blocks activation of endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR-3/7/9), thereby reducing MyD88-dependent interferon production and dampening pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion from mononuclear cells and dendritic cells (IL-1, IL-6, TNF, IFN-α/γ, CCL4) (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). The class also interferes with cGAS–STING pathway activation through inhibition of cGAMP synthase and reduces T-cell co-stimulatory signaling (e.g., CD154), a mechanistic constellation that explains DMARD efficacy without significant increases in opportunistic infections (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020; Browning, 2014b). Additional molecular interactions reported for 4AQs include DNA binding/intercalation, kinase pathway modulation (e.g., ERK/MAPK), and diverse enzyme interactions (e.g., cholinesterase), reflecting broad pleiotropy at pharmacologic and suprapharmacologic exposures (Browning, 2014a).

RPE-relevant degradative biology: cathepsins and POS processing  
The RPE depends critically on acidic lysosomes and cathepsin activity to clear the daily phagocytic load of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and maintain autophagic flux; failure of this system yields lipofuscin accumulation and contributes to AMD pathogenesis (Sharif, 2015). Multiple lysosomal proteases are expressed by RPE, including cysteine cathepsins B, L, and S as well as aspartyl cathepsin D; cathepsins are synthesized as pre-proenzymes, processed via the secretory pathway, and activated in the acidic lumen of late endosomes/lysosomes (Sharif, 2015). In human RPE/choroid and RPE cell lines, both inactive and active forms of cathepsin B, L, and S have been detected; functional studies show that broad cysteine protease inhibition or cathepsin S knockdown impairs POS degradation and increases lipofuscin-like inclusions, underscoring their role in RPE proteostasis (Sharif, 2015). Cathepsin D, a major lysosomal aspartyl protease in RPE, is essential for POS processing; its maturation and catalytic efficiency are strongly pH-dependent and occur within the acidic lysosomal lumen (Cardoso et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).

CQ/HCQ disrupt lysosomal proteolysis and lysosome dynamics in RPE  
In RPE models, CQ induces a rapid lysosomal pH increase followed by partial pH recovery, yet produces persistent lysosomal enlargement, accumulation of undegraded endocytic, phagocytic, and autophagic cargos, and a progressive reduction in accessibility of enlarged lysosomes to the endocytic pathway — a phenotype consistent with impaired autolysosome reformation and failure to regenerate a pool of degradatively competent lysosomes (Cardoso et al., 2023). A salient molecular signature of CQ exposure is accumulation of pro-cathepsin D and the lysosomal membrane protein LAMP1 without corresponding mRNA increases, indicating impaired processing/turnover rather than transcriptional upregulation; protease inhibitor treatment phenocopies this pro-cathepsin D accumulation, linking CQ’s effect to reduced proteolytic capacity (Cardoso et al., 2023). Although lysosomotropic agents can activate TFEB-dependent lysosomal gene transcription at high concentrations, the inhibitory effects on cathepsin maturation and lysosome reformation dominate in RPE models at low doses and precede any compensatory changes in gene expression (Cardoso et al., 2023).

HCQ further impairs RPE lysosomes by perturbing cholesterol homeostasis and promoting lysosomal membrane permeability (LMP), with cytosolic release of cathepsin B  
Beyond general autophagy/lysosome inhibition, HCQ suppresses mTORC1-dependent cholesterol biosynthesis, a change that increases lysosomal membrane permeability and allows lysosomal cathepsin B to translocate into the cytosol, where it can activate caspase-dependent apoptosis and drive caspase-independent phosphatidylserine externalization; these effects are mitigated by neutral pH-selective cathepsin B inhibition and exacerbated by pharmacologic cholesterol lowering (simvastatin) or depletion (methyl-β-cyclodextrin) (Wicks et al., 2022). These data in ARPE-19 RPE cells indicate that HCQ-induced lysosomal dysfunction and LMP sensitize RPE to additional stressors (e.g., UV), compounding vulnerability in aging retinal tissue (Wicks et al., 2022).

RPE/retinal stress signatures and storage phenotypes with 4AQ exposure  
Cell and animal studies document that 4AQ exposure produces RPE and retinal stress consistent with impaired lysosomal degradation: multilamellar myeloid bodies in RPE, photoreceptors, and ganglion cells; inhibition of oxidative enzymes in photoreceptors; decreased retinal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and glutathione with increased lipid peroxidation; disruption of the blood–retina barrier; and inhibition of protein synthesis in RPE culture (Browning, 2014a). In RPE cell culture, high concentrations of CQ perturb fusion of autophagic vesicles, increase LC3-II and p62, and can drive cell death, while intravitreal bafilomycin reproduces opsin-loaded phagolysosome accumulation, affirming that alkalinization is sufficient to cause degradative backlog (Guha et al., 2014). Chronic CQ treatment in mice increases mRNA expression of v-H⁺-ATPase and TFEB, consistent with compensatory attempts to reacidify lysosomes and enhance biogenesis, but does not normalize degradative function during exposure (Guha et al., 2014).

Absence of evidence for “low-dose stabilization” of lysosomal pH in RPE  
Across mechanistic summaries and primary RPE studies, there is no evidence that low-dose HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH at an “optimal” value, preserves cathepsin activity, or enhances POS degradation; rather, the consistent effect is lysosomal alkalinization with inhibition of lysosomal enzymes (including cathepsin B) and blockade of autophagic/lysosomal degradation (Browning, 2014a). In fact, low-dose CQ already yields accumulation of pro-cathepsin D and cargo buildup in RPE, indicating that even modest lysosomotropic perturbation degrades proteolytic competence, counter to the hypothesis (Cardoso et al., 2023).

Pharmacokinetic and ocular deposition constraints  
The extreme tissue distribution and ocular melanin binding of 4AQs undermine precise intraocular dose control: uveal/RPE drug levels can markedly exceed plasma during chronic dosing, and the terminal half-life is long, with months-long detectability after discontinuation due to depot release (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). These properties make “titration” to a narrow, hypothetical lysosomal pH window impractical and raise the risk of sustained lysosomal alkalinization even with ostensibly low systemic doses (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis proposes that submicromolar HCQ will “fine-tune” lysosomal pH in RPE to an optimal range for cathepsin activity, thereby preserving cathepsin function and enhancing POS degradation without blocking autophagy. The aggregate evidence contradicts this at mechanistic, cellular, and pharmacokinetic levels.

- Cathepsins in RPE require an acidic lumen for zymogen processing and catalytic function, and multiple cathepsins (B, L, S, D) are expressed and active in RPE lysosomes where they regulate POS degradation and autophagy; broad cysteine protease inhibition or specific cathepsin S knockdown impairs POS clearance and increases lipofuscin-like inclusions, demonstrating the acid-dependent protease requirement (Sharif, 2015). In this context, 4AQs act as lysosomal alkalinizers that inhibit acid hydrolases; CQ/HCQ inhibit cathepsin B and disrupt cathepsin D processing, with CQ causing pro-cathepsin D accumulation and reduced maturation into the active enzyme, a phenotype directly linked to impaired lysosomal proteolysis and cargo clearance (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). Therefore, the expected effect of submicromolar HCQ is not preservation but reduction of cathepsin function in RPE lysosomes, with consequent impairment of POS proteolysis (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023).

- In RPE cells, CQ/HCQ exposure impairs autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, producing enlarged, cargo-laden lysosomes that are progressively less accessible to endocytic inputs; these dynamics deplete the pool of degradatively competent lysosomes needed for daily POS processing, an effect observed even at “low-dose” CQ and preceding transcriptional responses (Cardoso et al., 2023). Thus, in assays measuring POS degradation and lysosomal flux, HCQ is predicted to slow, not enhance, turnover (Cardoso et al., 2023).

- HCQ further increases lysosomal membrane permeability and releases cathepsin B into the cytosol by impairing mTORC1-dependent cholesterol biosynthesis, activating pro-death signaling and phosphatidylserine externalization; pharmacologic cholesterol lowering/depletion magnify these effects, suggesting that HCQ’s action sensitizes RPE to metabolic and environmental stress rather than stabilizing proteolysis (Wicks et al., 2022).

- Beyond lysosomal pH, 4AQs disrupt other RPE functions essential for photoreceptor support: CQ inhibits rod outer segment phagocytosis in human/pig RPE cell lines, and HCQ/CQ inhibit OATP1A2 in human RPE, potentially perturbing all-trans-retinol uptake and the visual cycle — liabilities expected to worsen POS handling and photoreceptor maintenance in AMD models (Yusuf et al., 2023).

- The claim that “over-acidification” in RPE lysosomes needs moderation lacks evidentiary support in this literature corpus; the dominant pathologic signal in RPE aging and AMD models is lysosomal under-acidification/alkalinization and degradative impairment, which 4AQs exacerbate rather than correct (Guha et al., 2014).

- Pharmacokinetically, due to massive ocular accumulation and prolonged tissue persistence, “low systemic dose” does not guarantee low intra-RPE exposure; achieving and maintaining a narrow “optimal pH” window is improbable and unsafe for chronic indications with slowly reversible tissue exposure (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

In sum, in assays of RPE lysosomal function and POS degradation, the most probable outcomes of HCQ at submicromolar concentrations are lysosomal pH elevation, inhibited cathepsin activity/maturation (including cathepsin B inhibition and pro-cathepsin D accumulation), impaired autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, increased LMP with cytosolic cathepsin B release, inhibition of POS phagocytosis, and potential disruption of retinoid transport — all expected to reduce, not enhance, POS degradation (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023; Wicks et al., 2022; Yusuf et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths for development feasibility  
- Extensive clinical pharmacology and systemic experience: HCQ has well-characterized oral pharmacokinetics, metabolism, and drug–drug interactions, with validated immunomodulatory mechanisms (endolysosomal pH elevation, TLR/cGAS–STING inhibition, cytokine suppression) across rheumatology and dermatology; supply chains and clinical dosing paradigms are established, enabling rapid translational work if warranted (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020; Rainsford et al., 2015). The compound’s canonical lysosomotropic action makes it a useful positive control for modeling lysosomal alkalinization and degradative impairment in RPE assays benchmarking alternative, mechanistically restorative strategies (Browning, 2014b).

- Lower ocular toxicity relative to CQ at equipotency: HCQ is generally less retinotoxic than CQ, a difference attributed in part to greater polarity and lower lipophilicity; however, the class risk remains dose- and duration-dependent and clinically significant (Browning, 2014a; Rainsford et al., 2015).

Critical weaknesses for dry AMD  
- Mechanistic conflict with therapeutic goal: RPE catabolism of POS requires acidic lysosomes and intact cathepsin maturation/activity; 4AQs elevate lysosomal pH, inhibit cathepsin activity (including cathepsin B) and maturation (cathepsin D), impair autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, and induce cargo accumulation — a set of changes that predict impaired POS processing and enhanced lipofuscin burden rather than restoration of lysosomal proteolysis (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). No evidence in RPE/AMD models supports the hypothesis that “low-dose” HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH to optimize cathepsin function; the reported outcomes consistently indicate degradative inhibition (Browning, 2014a).

- Ocular tropism and prolonged tissue persistence: The combination of melanin binding and lysosomal trapping produces extreme ocular accumulation and very slow washout, making precise intraocular dose control infeasible and raising the risk of prolonged lysosomal alkalinization even after dose reduction or cessation (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b).

- Added liabilities in RPE and retina: HCQ promotes lysosomal membrane permeability and cytosolic cathepsin B release in RPE, sensitizing cells to UV and cholesterol-lowering stresses; CQ/HCQ also inhibit POS phagocytosis and OATP1A2 in RPE, potentially disrupting retinoid uptake and the visual cycle, and they induce retinal stress signatures (oxidative enzyme inhibition, antioxidant depletion, barrier disruption) — all detrimental in the aging macula (Wicks et al., 2022; Yusuf et al., 2023; Browning, 2014a).

- Absence of supportive precedent in AMD: Comprehensive pharmacologic and ophthalmic reviews provide no evidence that HCQ/CQ have been successfully used to treat dry AMD or analogous retinal degenerations; rather, they underscore retinotoxic risk and mechanisms consistent with RPE lysosomal dysfunction (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

Strategic implications and recommendation  
The central hypothesis — that low-dose HCQ can fine-tune RPE lysosomal pH to preserve cathepsin activity and enhance POS degradation — is at odds with the mechanistic canon and RPE-focused data for 4AQs, which consistently demonstrate lysosomal alkalinization, cathepsin inhibition or maturation block, impaired lysosome reformation and autophagic flux, and accumulation of undegraded cargo (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). No cited evidence shows that HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH or improves POS degradation in RPE or AMD models; on the contrary, RPE studies with CQ/HCQ and mechanistic summaries emphasize inhibited lysosomal enzymes and autophagy as core actions (Browning, 2014a; Guha et al., 2014). Given extreme ocular accumulation and prolonged tissue retention, exploratory dosing aimed at a narrow “optimal” intralysosomal pH is neither controllable nor safe in a chronic neurodegenerative indication; adverse lysosomal effects could persist despite dose adjustments due to depot release (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). If the program goal is to restore RPE lysosomal proteolysis and POS turnover in dry AMD, agents that acidify lysosomes, facilitate cathepsin maturation/activity, or pharmacologically promote lysosome reformation (as suggested by pathways implicated in CQ-induced defects) align mechanistically, whereas HCQ/CQ, as archetypal alkalinizers and autophagy inhibitors, do not (Cardoso et al., 2023).

Conclusion: HCQ (Sigma-Aldrich H0915) is not a suitable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD under the proposed mechanism. The weight of biochemical, cellular, and pharmacokinetic evidence indicates HCQ will alkalinize RPE lysosomes, inhibit cathepsin function and maturation, impair autophagic flux and POS processing, and increase RPE vulnerability to stress, while ocular accumulation and long half-life amplify risk; no supportive evidence exists for benefit in dry AMD (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023; Wicks et al., 2022; Browning, 2014b). I recommend against advancing HCQ for AMD and suggest redirecting efforts toward mechanisms that restore lysosomal acidity, cathepsin activity, and lysosome reformation in RPE (Cardoso et al., 2023).
