Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fasudil is a small‐molecule, synthetic isoquinoline derivative that functions as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil forming kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. Originally discovered and subsequently developed for clinical use in the treatment of cerebral vasospasm following subarachnoid hemorrhage, fasudil represents one of the earliest examples of ROCK inhibitors entering the clinic (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). As a member of the ROCK inhibitor class, it has been synthesized and formulated to target the ATP‐binding pocket of both ROCK isoforms (ROCK1 and ROCK2), thereby effectively competing with ATP and suppressing the kinase activity that is normally responsible for phosphorylating downstream molecular substrates such as the myosin light chain (MLC) and LIM kinase (Catral et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2022). The compound’s synthesis generally follows established medicinal chemistry protocols for heterocyclic compounds and includes derivatization steps that yield a potent inhibitor with an IC₅₀ for ROCK inhibition in the submicromolar range, which in the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function has been postulated to be around 300 nM (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Xiao et al., 2022). Fasudil’s chemical structure and its physicochemical properties allow for formulation into ophthalmic preparations, such as intravitreal injections or potentially sustained-release depot systems, making it an interesting candidate for repurposing in ocular diseases. This class of compounds has historically been used to modulate cytoskeletal dynamics, vascular tone, and cellular contractility in both vascular and neural tissues, and the same properties are being leveraged now to target the pathological stiffening and impaired phagocytic function of RPE cells in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Croze et al., 2014; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Fasudil’s therapeutic history spans multiple clinical and preclinical applications that underscore its broad efficacy in modulating ROCK-mediated pathways. Clinically, fasudil has been approved and widely used in Japan since 1995 for the treatment of cerebral vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage, owing to its vasodilatory and anti-contractile properties (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Its clinical use has expanded into experimental paradigms beyond cerebral applications; for instance, fasudil has shown promise in ocular conditions such as diabetic macular edema, where intravitreal administration in combination with bevacizumab demonstrated feasibility and tolerability, and where its ability to modulate inflammatory responses and vascular permeability were beneficial (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). Furthermore, other members of the ROCK inhibitor class have been investigated for ocular applications, including glaucoma and even experimental models of photoreceptor synapse stabilization following retinal detachment (Townes-Anderson et al., 2017; Yamaguchi et al., 2017). Although fasudil itself has not yet been directly applied in clinical trials for dry AMD, its mechanism of action and safety profile in ocular tissues have been well documented in multiple studies. Animal studies in diabetic retinopathy models have also demonstrated that fasudil can reverse detrimental cytoskeletal changes and restore barrier integrity in RPE cells (Rothschild et al., 2017). Additionally, preclinical data indicate that ROCK inhibitors can improve wound repair responses and prevent epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in RPE cells, which is a hallmark of cellular dysfunction in geographic atrophy – the advanced stage of dry AMD (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Collectively, while fasudil’s historic use has largely focused on vascular and diabetic complications, its repurposing for dry AMD is supported by mechanistic parallels in RPE cytoskeletal plasticity, phagocytosis, and anti-inflammatory modulation (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, fasudil acts by binding to the ATP-binding site of ROCK enzymes, thereby competitively inhibiting their kinase activity (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Under normal cellular conditions, active ROCK phosphorylates several substrates including the myosin light chain (MLC) and myosin phosphatase target subunit 1 (MYPT1), which leads to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stabilization of actin stress fibers, and formation of focal adhesions (Catral et al., 2024; Rothschild et al., 2017). In the context of age-related retinopathies, there is mounting evidence that hyperactivity of the ROCK pathway leads to increased contractile force within the RPE cytoskeleton. This hypercontractility contributes to reduced cellular flexibility and impairs the formation of the phagocytic cups that are critical for the internalization of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) – a process that is essential for retinal homeostasis and visual cycle maintenance (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). Fasudil’s inhibition of ROCK thereby mitigates these cytoskeletal alterations by decreasing the phosphorylation levels of downstream targets, which in turn reduces actomyosin contraction and promotes a more plastic and dynamic actin architecture (Catral et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2022).

Furthermore, ROCK inhibition has been shown to enhance cell adhesion and reduce apoptotic signaling in stressed RPE cells, thereby improving wound repair and the overall cellular microenvironment (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Biochemical experiments have demonstrated that when ROCK activity is suppressed, RPE cells exhibit a reduction in stress fiber formation and an increase in the formation of normal cell–cell junctions, which is crucial for the maintenance of the outer blood-retinal barrier (Rothschild et al., 2017). In addition to its effects on the actin cytoskeleton, fasudil and other ROCK inhibitors have been reported to modulate inflammatory and fibrotic pathways by reducing the phosphorylation of Smad 2/3 in response to TGF-β1 signaling; this effect may further protect RPE cells from deleterious pro-fibrotic and inflammatory cascades that are known to exacerbate dry AMD pathology (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Several studies also indicate that ROCK inhibition promotes RPE differentiation and pigmentation, as evidenced by increased expression of key proteins such as RPE65, which is indispensable for the visual cycle and meso-zeaxanthin biosynthesis (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Given that oxidative stress in the aging retina exacerbates ROCK activation, fasudil’s ability to mitigate these effects through cytoskeletal remodeling and anti-inflammatory actions underlies its proposed mechanism of action in improving POS internalization in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Rothschild et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing fasudil for dry AMD is that inhibition of ROCK in the RPE will lead to normalization of abnormal cytoskeletal tension, thereby enhancing the formation of phagocytic cups required for efficient POS internalization (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). In aged RPE cells from patients with dry AMD, persistent ROCK hyperactivity is thought to cause increased actomyosin contraction; this leads to a “stiff” cytoskeletal state that hinders membrane dynamics essential for phagocytosis (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Rothschild et al., 2017). By reducing ROCK-mediated phosphorylation of MLC and other substrates, fasudil is expected to relieve this contractility, restore a more flexible actin network, and ultimately allow for enhanced phagocytic function. Preclinical studies have already demonstrated that use of ROCK inhibitors like Y-27632 can increase phagocytic activity by RPE cells, leading to improved clearance of POS debris – a key function that deteriorates in dry AMD (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Croze et al., 2014).

In the proposed assay, RPE cells under oxidative stress—an in vitro proxy for the aging microenvironment seen in dry AMD—will be treated with fasudil. The anticipated outcome is that fasudil will enhance cytoskeletal plasticity, thereby facilitating the formation of phagocytic cups and improving the uptake of POS, as measured by quantifiable phagocytosis assays (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). Moreover, fasudil’s reported effects in enhancing cell adhesion and promoting a balanced extracellular matrix deposition are expected to provide additional benefits to RPE cell morphology and barrier integrity, indirectly supporting improved phagocytic function (Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Given that key RPE-specific genes and proteins involved in phagocytosis, including integrin αvβ5 and MFG-E8, are expressed in these cells, normalization of the cytoskeletal machinery via ROCK inhibition is likely to translate into a functional recovery of POS clearance capacity (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Croze et al., 2014). Thus, the overall effect of fasudil treatment is expected to counteract the age-associated impairment in phagocytosis, reduce accumulation of waste material such as drusen, and potentially slow the progression of retinal degeneration in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the repurposing of fasudil for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a substantial mechanistic rationale and a body of preclinical evidence indicating that ROCK inhibition can positively modulate RPE cellular function. The strengths of fasudil as a therapeutic candidate include its well-established clinical safety profile—stemming from decades of use in cerebrovascular conditions in Japan—as well as its robust capacity to modulate actin-cytoskeletal dynamics, reduce excessive cell contraction, and enhance processes such as cell adhesion and phagocytosis among RPE cells (Catral et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). The ability of fasudil to normalize the abnormal, stiff cytoskeletal state present in aged RPE cells is particularly compelling given the central role of impaired POS internalization in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017).

Moreover, similar ROCK inhibitors have demonstrated promising effects in ocular models of retinal degeneration and diabetic retinopathy, where the restoration of RPE function and cytoskeletal composition has correlated with improved retinal architecture and cell survival (Moura-Coelho et al., 2019; Rothschild et al., 2017). Fasudil’s potential to also attenuate inflammatory and fibrotic signaling pathways via downstream effects on TGF-β/Smad signaling may add further benefit by curbing the detrimental microenvironment that exacerbates RPE dysfunction in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). The proposed mechanism—centered on relieving ROCK-induced actomyosin contraction and restoring the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells—addresses a key pathophysiological deficit in dry AMD, namely the impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments that leads to drusen accumulation and subsequent cell degeneration (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017).

However, there are also some weaknesses and challenges associated with using fasudil as a treatment for dry AMD. A major concern is the relatively nonselective nature of fasudil compared to more recently developed ROCK inhibitors that offer isoform specificity (e.g., selective ROCK2 inhibitors) (Alexander, 2017; Yamaguchi et al., 2017). Since ROCK signaling is implicated in multiple cellular processes beyond RPE cytoskeletal dynamics—including vascular regulation, neuronal survival, and immune cell polarization—a nonselective inhibitor may inadvertently affect these other pathways, potentially leading to off-target effects. In particular, the downregulation of thrombospondin 1 (THBS1) observed with some ROCK inhibitors, which is associated with anti-angiogenic processes, could theoretically predispose patients to neovascular complications if not carefully controlled (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Catral et al., 2024).

Another potential limitation is the pharmacokinetic profile of fasudil in ocular tissues. Fasudil is known to have a short plasma half-life (approximately 0.3 hours), although its active metabolite, hydroxyfasudil, has a moderately longer half-life (approximately 2.9 hours) (Futterknecht et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). For effective treatment of dry AMD—where chronic, sustained modulation of ROCK activity may be necessary—injection strategies such as intravitreal administration or depot formulations may be required to maintain therapeutic levels over an extended period. Although intravitreal delivery of fasudil has been demonstrated in diabetic macular edema and other experimental models (Rothschild et al., 2017), further studies will be needed to optimize the dosage, frequency, and formulation for the specific demands of long-term retinal therapy in dry AMD.

Furthermore, while the preclinical evidence regarding the benefits of ROCK inhibition in RPE cells is promising, there remains a lack of direct clinical data demonstrating the efficacy of fasudil in patients with dry AMD. Most studies to date have focused on the use of ROCK inhibitors in models of diabetic retinopathy, neovascular AMD, or other retinal conditions, and the translation of these findings to the dry, atrophic form of AMD is not yet fully established (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Rothschild et al., 2017). This gap underscores the need for focused, well-designed clinical trials and further preclinical studies using models that accurately recapitulate the pathophysiology of dry AMD.

Moreover, it will be essential to monitor whether the positive effects on cytoskeletal plasticity and phagocytosis translate into meaningful clinical endpoints such as improved visual acuity or slowed progression of geographic atrophy. Biomarkers of RPE health, phagocytic activity, and retinal integrity will need to be identified and validated in the context of fasudil treatment (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Croze et al., 2014).

In conclusion, the available literature strongly supports the mechanistic rationale for using fasudil to target ROCK-mediated dysfunction in RPE cells, which is a critical aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis (Catral et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Its established safety profile in other clinical scenarios, coupled with evidence from preclinical models demonstrating improved cytoskeletal regulation, enhanced phagocytic capacity, and attenuated inflammation in retinal cells, makes fasudil a promising therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (Moura-Coelho et al., 2019; Rothschild et al., 2017). Nonetheless, challenges related to drug-specific pharmacokinetics, the risk of off-target effects due to its nonselectivity, and the current lack of direct clinical evidence in dry AMD warrant cautious further investigation. The next steps should involve optimization of ocular delivery methods—potentially through sustained-release formulations—and the initiation of preclinical studies in animal models of dry AMD to assess functional outcomes. If these studies prove successful, they would pave the way for early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of fasudil in patients with dry AMD (Rothschild et al., 2017; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Overall, while significant work remains to be done, the integration of biochemical, cellular, and clinical data from the broader ROCK inhibitor literature provides a compelling argument for further evaluation of fasudil as a potential repurposed treatment for dry AMD. The strategy to inhibit ROCK in RPE cells to restore cytoskeletal dynamics, enhance phagocytosis, and reduce oxidative and inflammatory stress fits well with current understanding of dry AMD pathophysiology and represents an innovative approach that could address a critical unmet need in AMD therapeutics (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Catral et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Brexpiprazole is a synthetic, orally available fifth‐generation antipsychotic developed by Otsuka Pharmaceutical that belongs to the class of serotonin–dopamine activity modulators (SDAMs). It was discovered and developed as an improvement over earlier dopamine partial agonists in order to achieve balanced modulation of neurotransmission. Chemically, brexpiprazole was designed as a dihydrocarbostyril derivative that retains partial agonistic properties at dopamine D₂ receptors while simultaneously exhibiting potent partial agonism at serotonin 5-HT₁A receptors and antagonism at serotonin 5-HT₂A receptors (Das et al., 2016). This balanced receptor profile has been exploited primarily for psychiatric indications, but the receptor distribution of serotonin receptors is not limited to neuronal tissues. In particular, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) expresses several serotonin receptor subtypes, and there is compelling biochemical evidence that serotonergic signaling influences inflammatory gene expression and cellular homeostasis in these cells (Biswal et al., 2015). As such, brexpiprazole’s well‐defined receptor interactions position it as a promising candidate to modulate pathological pathways in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
Brexpiprazole has an established history for its use in central nervous system disorders. It has been approved for the treatment of schizophrenia and as an adjunct therapy in major depressive disorder owing to its favorable safety and tolerability profiles, which include a low risk of extrapyramidal side effects and modest metabolic liabilities (Das et al., 2016; Fabre et al., 2022). To date, however, no clinical trials or preclinical studies have directly examined brexpiprazole for the treatment of retinal degenerative conditions such as dry AMD. Nevertheless, multiple studies have investigated the therapeutic potential of 5-HT₁A receptor agonists in retinal models. For example, research utilizing 8-OH-DPAT—a prototypical 5-HT₁A agonist—demonstrated significant antioxidant protection in RPE cells, reduction in oxidative stress markers, and preservation of retinal architecture under conditions of mitochondrial oxidative stress (Biswal et al., 2015). Other compounds with selective 5-HT₁A agonist properties, such as tandospirone, have been evaluated in retinal models, albeit with mixed clinical outcomes (Buschini et al., 2015). This preclinical precedence establishes an indirect rationale for repurposing brexpiprazole in dry AMD even if direct ocular applications have not been previously explored.

Mechanism of Action:  
Brexpiprazole exerts its pharmacological effects primarily through dual modulation of serotonergic receptors. Its partial agonism at 5-HT₁A receptors, with reported potency in the low nanomolar range (EC₅₀ ~ 5 nM as hypothesized), is thought to trigger intracellular cascades that promote cellular survival and antioxidant defenses. Activation of the 5-HT₁A receptor in other tissues has been associated with upregulation of key antioxidant enzymes—including metallothionein-1 (MT-1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NADPH quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NqO1), catalase, and superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1)—thereby mitigating oxidative stress and reducing mitochondrial damage (Biswal et al., 2015). In RPE cells—the cell type critical for photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance—the 5-HT₁A receptor is endogenously expressed, and its activation has been linked to attenuation of inflammatory signaling. Preclinical studies using other 5-HT₁A agonists in ARPE-19 cells have shown reductions in oxidative stress markers and inflammatory mediators, as well as preservation of tight junction proteins (Biswal et al., 2015).

Simultaneously, brexpiprazole’s antagonism at 5-HT₂A receptors may complement these effects by further modulating inflammatory responses. Blockade of 5-HT₂A receptors has been associated with reduced microglial activation and decreased complement deposition in the outer retina, contributing to neuroprotection in models of retinal degeneration (Biswal et al., 2015; Das et al., 2016). This dual receptor effect is proposed to result in an overall anti-inflammatory microenvironment in the RPE, which is crucial because chronic inflammation is a key pathological feature in dry AMD. Moreover, the compound’s modulation of serotonergic signaling may indirectly support the maintenance of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, which are essential for the normal clearance of POS (Biswal et al., 2015). Although direct studies with brexpiprazole in RPE cells are lacking, these mechanistic insights derived from similar 5-HT₁A agonists underpin the hypothesis that brexpiprazole could reduce production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6 and TNF-α) and restore normal phagocytic and lysosomal function (Biswal et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
In an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells or isolated RPE cells under conditions of complement-induced stress, brexpiprazole is expected to act by modulating serotonergic receptor signaling to yield a multi-faceted protective effect. Specifically, its 5-HT₁A agonism should trigger intracellular survival pathways that result in the upregulation of antioxidant defenses analogous to the responses observed with 8-OH-DPAT in similar models (Biswal et al., 2015). This effect is anticipated to lead to a reduction in oxidative stress markers, such as 8-OH-deoxyguanosine or nitrotyrosine adducts, which are typically elevated in conditions of mitochondrial oxidative injury (Biswal et al., 2015).

Additionally, brexpiprazole is hypothesized to reduce the expression of key pro-inflammatory cytokines—specifically IL-6 and TNF-α—through receptor-mediated modulation of inflammatory signaling cascades. In a cell culture model where RPE cells are exposed to oxidative and complement-mediated insults, a drop in these cytokine levels would be indicative of an amelioration of stress-induced inflammatory responses (Biswal et al., 2015; Wright & Ambati, 2016). This anti-inflammatory effect is critical because uncontrolled inflammation not only perpetuates oxidative damage but also disrupts the barrier and phagocytic functions of the RPE.

Furthermore, the candidate is expected to preserve or restore the expression of MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase crucial for the phagocytosis of POS, as well as cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease necessary for the degradation of internalized material (Biswal et al., 2015; Fischer, 2016). Successful maintenance of these proteins would directly support the clearance functions of RPE cells, an essential element for retinal homeostasis that is compromised in dry AMD. This improved phagocytic capacity, coupled with reduced cytokine production, would likely result in overall preservation of RPE structure and function, as reflected in enhanced visual function in preclinical models (Biswal et al., 2015).

Moreover, although the clinical studies of other serotonergic compounds such as tandospirone have yielded mixed results—with at least one phase III trial for geographic atrophy being discontinued due to lack of efficacy (Buschini et al., 2015)—the favorable pharmacokinetic properties and established safety profile of brexpiprazole in other indications provide a strong rationale for its repurposing, particularly if its ocular penetration can be demonstrated in relevant preclinical models (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation:  
Brexpiprazole offers several attractive strengths as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its dual mechanism—partial agonism at 5-HT₁A receptors paired with antagonism at 5-HT₂A receptors—is well aligned with the emerging understanding of how serotonergic signaling influences retinal cell survival, oxidative stress, and inflammation (Biswal et al., 2015). The wealth of preclinical evidence supporting the role of 5-HT₁A receptor activation in reducing oxidative damage and preserving RPE function under stress conditions provides a sound mechanistic basis for expecting similar protective effects from brexpiprazole. In addition, the targeting of phagocytic receptor expression (i.e., MERTK) and lysosomal enzymes (i.e., cathepsin D) represents a novel strategy to address one of the fundamental dysfunctions in dry AMD: impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (Biswal et al., 2015).

Brexpiprazole’s established safety profile and pharmacokinetics in psychiatric populations further underscore its potential for repurposing. Its high oral bioavailability and documented tolerability in long-term studies, along with evidence that similar compounds can penetrate ocular tissues when administered systemically, add to the candidate’s appeal (Das et al., 2016; Fabre et al., 2022). This is particularly relevant given the chronic nature of dry AMD and the need for therapies that can be safely administered over extended periods.

However, several significant weaknesses and gaps warrant cautious consideration. First, direct evidence linking brexpiprazole to improved RPE function—specifically, its effects on inflammatory signaling markers IL-6 and TNF-α, and on the preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression—remains theoretical and extrapolated from studies using other 5-HT₁A agonists like 8-OH-DPAT (Biswal et al., 2015). This means that while the underlying mechanistic hypothesis is plausible, there is a pressing need for targeted in vitro and in vivo studies focused on brexpiprazole in ocular models. In particular, experiments using ARPE-19 cells under conditions of oxidative or complement-induced stress must be conducted to confirm that brexpiprazole can indeed modulate cytokine levels and restore phagocytic function in these cells.

Another shortcoming is the uncertainty regarding ocular penetration. Although the systemic administration of 5-HT₁A agonists in animal models has led to beneficial retinal outcomes (Biswal et al., 2015), brexpiprazole’s distribution into ocular tissues has not been directly evaluated. It is essential to ascertain the extent to which brexpiprazole reaches the RPE at therapeutically relevant concentrations, particularly given that dosage regimens for psychiatric conditions may not be directly translatable to ocular therapy (Biswal et al., 2015).

Furthermore, while the anti-inflammatory hypothesis is supported by the general role of serotonergic signaling in RPE cells, the direct measurement of inflammatory cytokines and downstream phagocytic markers in response to brexpiprazole treatment remains to be demonstrated. Given that earlier clinical attempts using tandospirone for AMD were unsuccessful (Buschini et al., 2015), there is a need to critically assess whether brexpiprazole’s receptor profile confers advantages that overcome the limitations observed with other 5-HT₁A agonists. Additionally, potential off-target effects in the ocular environment—such as those arising from modulation of other receptor systems—must be thoroughly evaluated.

In summary, brexpiprazole presents a scientifically sound and innovative approach to the treatment of dry AMD by virtue of its serotonergic receptor modulation. Its dual action on 5-HT₁A and 5-HT₂A receptors is supported by a robust body of preclinical evidence indicating that 5-HT₁A receptor activation can reduce oxidative stress and inflammation in RPE cells, while also preserving essential functions like POS clearance (Biswal et al., 2015). The candidate’s excellent safety profile in psychiatric applications and potential for systemic administration further enhance its appeal. Nevertheless, the absence of direct experimental data linking brexpiprazole to improved phagocytosis, reduced IL-6 and TNF-α production, and maintained lysosomal enzyme expression in RPE cells represents a critical gap that must be addressed. As such, while the repurposing of brexpiprazole for dry AMD holds promise, a series of preclinical experiments—encompassing in vitro ARPE-19 cell assays, in vivo ocular pharmacokinetic studies, and efficacy models of retinal degeneration—are required before progressing to clinical trials. Overall, given the mechanistic rationale and the encouraging safety and pharmacological characteristics of brexpiprazole, further research is justified to validate its application in dry AMD, provided that the aforementioned knowledge gaps are systematically addressed (Das et al., 2016; Biswal et al., 2015).

Analysis: Candidate 1 (SB202190) and Candidate 2 (Oncostatin M, OSM) both target RPE dysfunction in dry AMD but differ markedly across the key criteria.  Strength of Evidence: SB202190 has extensive in vitro data in ARPE‐19 cells showing p38α/β inhibition restores cytoskeletal organization, reduces fibrotic markers, and improves POS uptake under oxidative stress. However, no in vivo AMD studies exist and clinical use of SB202190 has not been pursued. OSM has been tested in rat retinal degeneration models with demonstrated photoreceptor protection and precedents from CNTF trials, but direct evidence linking OSM to enhanced RPE phagocytosis in AMD models is lacking.  Mechanism of Action: SB202190’s MoA is crystal‐clear—ATP‐competitive p38α/β inhibition directly targets stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling and inflammatory signaling in RPE. In contrast, OSM acts via gp130/JAK/STAT3 and ERK pathways, a broader, less specific signaling node whose links to phagocytic cup formation in RPE require further proof.  Safety and Risk: Neither candidate has established ocular safety in dry AMD. SB202190 carries p38 inhibitor class risks (off‐target MAPK cross‐reactivity, interference with adaptive stress responses, unknown ocular PK/Toxicity), while OSM poses immunogenicity and pleiotropic cytokine risks (potential EMT, aberrant inflammation).  Feasibility: SB202190, as a small molecule, could be formulated for intravitreal delivery and dose‐titration, but its ADME/PK in the eye remains to be defined. OSM, as a recombinant cytokine, is deliverable intravitreally with existing protein‐drug platforms, yet chronic dosing and control over local cytokine concentrations are challenging.  Novelty: OSM offers greater novelty and translational leverage from CNTF experience; SB202190 repurposing is less novel but grounded in a well‐defined target.  Overall, SB202190 benefits from a precise, direct MoA and robust in vitro RPE data, while OSM’s in vivo retinal protection is compelling but mechanistically indirect and risk‐prone. Given the priority on mechanism specificity, relevance of supporting evidence to RPE phagocytosis, and clear rationale for target engagement, SB202190 scores higher on translatability despite the need for rigorous safety/PK studies.
Reasoning: Between the two, SB202190 is preferred because it offers a highly specific, well‐characterized inhibition of p38α/β—a central mediator of RPE cytoskeletal disruption and inflammation linked to POS phagocytosis defects in dry AMD. Its in vitro data directly demonstrate restoration of phagocytic function under oxidative stress. Although OSM shows in vivo photoreceptor protection, its MoA via broad STAT3/JAK/ERK activation is less directly tied to RPE phagocytosis, and its pleiotropic cytokine effects raise concerns about dosing, EMT, and inflammation. SB202190’s clarity of target engagement, relevance to core pathology, and the feasibility of small‐molecule development outweigh OSM’s advantages in novelty and precedent.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB202190 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor belonging to the pyridinyl imidazole class of compounds. Originally discovered through rigorous cell‐based phenotypic screens aimed at identifying agents with anti‐inflammatory properties, SB202190 was developed to selectively inhibit p38 mitogen‐activated protein kinase (MAPK), particularly the α and β isoforms. The molecule was first characterized using radiolabeled ligand binding studies, which confirmed its ability to bind the ATP‐binding pocket of p38 MAPK and suppress its catalytic function (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). Being available commercially (e.g., Sigma‐Aldrich Cat. No. SML0687), SB202190 has been widely used as a biochemical tool to dissect the role of p38 in cellular stress and inflammatory responses. This class of compounds, including SB203580 as a closely related analogue, is recognized for its ability to modulate intracellular signaling cascades under various stress conditions. They have been broadly used in research settings to probe the molecular basis of cytokine production, cell differentiation, apoptosis, and cytoskeletal regulation (Young, 2013; Maugeri et al., 2021). The candidate under discussion is being repurposed with the hypothesis that its high potency against p38α/β—exhibiting an IC₅₀ of approximately 40 nM—can be leveraged to correct stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling defects and improve the phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative stress conditions that mimic the pathophysiology of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Liu et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, SB202190 has been predominantly employed as a research reagent to interrogate the role of p38 MAPK signaling in various cell types and disease models. In the context of ocular studies, SB202190, similar to its analogue SB203580, has been used to examine fibrotic responses, cell migration, and cytokine production in RPE cells. For instance, several in vitro studies have demonstrated that inhibition of p38 MAPK by SB202190 effectively reduces TGF‐β2–induced extracellular matrix (ECM) production (specifically collagen type I and fibronectin synthesis), which serves as an experimental surrogate for fibrotic remodeling observed in retinal degenerative conditions (Saika et al., 2005). Moreover, experiments using ARPE‐19 human RPE cells have revealed that SB202190 can reverse abnormal cell migration and reduce the transformation of RPE cells into fibroblast‐like cells in models of proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) (Saika et al., 2005). Although these models do not directly replicate dry AMD, they capture key aspects of RPE dysfunction, such as cytoskeletal disorganization and aberrant ECM deposition, which are also implicated in the progression of AMD. Beyond ocular research, p38 MAPK inhibitors have been investigated in other pathologies characterized by chronic inflammation and stress‐induced cellular dysfunction, including rheumatoid arthritis and muscular dystrophies (Brennan et al., 2021; Hirosawa et al., 2009). However, to date, clinical applications of SB202190 itself have not been pursued, and its use has remained restricted to preclinical experimental studies, thereby providing both a strong mechanistic rationale and a cautionary note regarding its translational potential (Federspiel et al., 2023; Young, 2013). Importantly, while numerous studies have elucidated p38 MAPK’s involvement in retinal injury and oxidative stress responses, there is limited direct clinical evidence supporting the use of SB202190 for treating dry AMD, and its application in this indication remains strictly hypothetical at this stage (Moustardas et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB202190 is known to selectively target the ATP‐binding pocket of p38 MAPK, thereby inhibiting its enzymatic activity and preventing the phosphorylation of downstream substrates that are pivotal to stress‐induced signaling cascades. Under normal conditions, p38 MAPK becomes activated through dual phosphorylation on specific threonine and tyrosine residues within its activation loop. Once activated, p38 MAPK stimulates various substrates, including transcription factors (e.g., cFos) and regulatory proteins involved in the control of cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and inflammatory mediator production (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). In RPE cells, activation of p38 MAPK has been linked to cytoskeletal rearrangements that lead to stress‐induced cellular defects; these include formation of abnormal actin structures and impaired formation of phagocytic cups necessary for the internalization of POS (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). In the experimental setting, SB202190 has been shown to effectively block the TGF‐β2 mediated phosphorylation of p38, thereby reducing the transcriptional activity of Smad3/4 complexes without impacting the initial receptor‐mediated phosphorylation events of Smads2/3. This mechanism suggests that SB202190 acts downstream of TGF‐β receptor activation, interfering with p38‐dependent enhancement of transcription factor complex formation and nuclear translocation, which in turn can dampen pathological ECM production and abnormal cell migration (Saika et al., 2005). Additionally, literature indicates that stress‐activated p38 signaling contributes to the senescence of RPE cells by regulating the senescence‐associated secretory phenotype (SASP) through modulation of p53 and NF‐κB pathways (Liu et al., 2025). By inhibiting p38 MAPK, SB202190 is hypothesized to replicate the protective effects of endogenous negative regulators such as DUSP4, which dephosphorylate and inactivate p38 MAPK, ultimately reducing RPE cell senescence and maintaining cellular homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025). It is noteworthy that p38 MAPK signaling is intricately intertwined with other MAPK family members, and some studies have reported that SB202190, particularly at higher doses, exhibits a biphasic response where alternative signaling pathways (such as MEK/ERK) may become upregulated, emphasizing the importance of careful dose optimization in any therapeutic application (Wang et al., 2024; Hirosawa et al., 2009). Thus, the mechanism of action of SB202190 involves a highly specific inhibition of p38α/β kinase activity, which is expected to restore normal actin dynamics and cytoskeletal organization in RPE cells, thereby facilitating proper phagosome formation and efficient POS uptake under oxidative stress conditions akin to those found in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The primary hypothesis driving the repurposing of SB202190 for dry AMD is that inhibition of p38α/β in RPE cells will reduce stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling defects and thereby improve the phagocytic internalization of photoreceptor outer segments. Under oxidative stress conditions, such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) in in vitro models using ARPE‐19 cells, activation of p38 MAPK is known to mediate cytoskeletal disorganization and promote aberrant cell migration, processes that are deleterious to the RPE’s phagocytic function (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). By inhibiting p38 MAPK with SB202190 at a low nanomolar concentration (approximately 40 nM), it is anticipated that the compound will reduce the phosphorylation of p38, thereby preventing the downstream activation of stress‐responsive transcription factors and proteins responsible for actin remodeling (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). In doing so, SB202190 is expected to “normalize” the actin cytoskeletal dynamics in H₂O₂‐treated ARPE‐19 cells, thus facilitating the re‐establishment of properly organized phagocytic cups required for POS ingestion—a process critical for photoreceptor maintenance and overall retinal homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025; Saika et al., 2005). In parallel, inhibition of p38 MAPK may downregulate pro‐fibrotic and pro‐senescent signaling pathways (e.g., those mediated by TGF‐β2, p53, and NF‐κB), therefore limiting the aberrant deposition of ECM components and improving the overall cellular microenvironment (Liu et al., 2025; Saika et al., 2005). As a result, the expected effect of SB202190 in the assay proposed would be a significant improvement in phagosome internalization of POS under oxidative conditions, combined with a reduction in the markers of cytoskeletal stress and cell senescence. Moreover, enhanced phagocytic activity by RPE cells could mitigate pathological features of dry AMD, such as drusen formation and eventual RPE degeneration, thereby potentially slowing disease progression (Moustardas et al., 2023; Du et al., 2010). The compound’s effect is further anticipated to extend to modulation of inflammatory cytokine release, given the well‐established role of p38 MAPK in regulating cytokine production, thus providing a dual benefit by both preserving cytoskeletal integrity and reducing chronic, low‐grade inflammation in the retina (Liu et al., 2025; Kyosseva, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
Evaluating the potential of SB202190 as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD involves weighing both the strengths and the inherent challenges associated with targeting the p38 MAPK pathway in the RPE. One of the major strengths of SB202190 is its well‐characterized mechanism of action as a selective inhibitor of p38α/β, which is pivotal in mediating stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling, inflammation, and cellular senescence in RPE cells. The compound has demonstrated robust in vitro anti‐fibrotic and anti‐migratory effects in ARPE‐19 cell models that mirror key features of RPE dysfunction observed in dry AMD (Saika et al., 2005). Furthermore, the concept of normalizing actin dynamics to enhance phagocytic cup formation and subsequent POS uptake is highly attractive, given that impaired phagocytosis is a core feature driving the degeneration observed in dry AMD (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). The protective role played by endogenous regulators like DUSP4, which deactivates p38 MAPK and preserves RPE integrity, supports the rationale for a pharmacological approach that mimics this effect (Liu et al., 2025). Additionally, numerous studies have shown that p38 MAPK inhibitors can modulate inflammatory responses and reduce ECM deposition; such effects are promising in the context of retinal diseases where chronic inflammation and fibrosis exacerbate degenerative processes (Moustardas et al., 2023; Saika et al., 2005).

However, several weaknesses and potential caveats must be thoroughly considered. First, the p38 MAPK pathway exhibits complex, context‐dependent behavior in RPE cells. There is evidence suggesting that, under certain circumstances, p38 MAPK activation can be cytoprotective by facilitating adaptive stress responses, such as the upregulation of antioxidant defenses (Pocrnich et al., 2009). This duality indicates that complete or prolonged inhibition of p38 MAPK may inadvertently dampen protective signaling, potentially leading to adverse outcomes. Additionally, published studies have documented that SB202190, when used at higher concentrations, can show biphasic responses or off‐target effects that might include the unintended activation of alternative MAPK pathways (Wang et al., 2024; Hirosawa et al., 2009). This underscores the critical need for precise dose optimization and comprehensive pharmacodynamic studies to define a therapeutic window where the beneficial effects on cytoskeletal remodeling and phagocytosis are maximized while the risks of impairing physiological stress responses are minimized.

Furthermore, while the preclinical literature provides substantial mechanistic insights and supportive data from retinal injury models—particularly in contexts such as PVR—the clinical translation of these findings to dry AMD remains unproven. SB202190 has not been advanced into clinical trials for retinal degenerative diseases, and its application has thus far been confined to experimental paradigms (Kim et al., 2021; Kyosseva, 2016). Therefore, any proposal to repurpose SB202190 for dry AMD must be accompanied by robust in vivo efficacy studies using animal models that faithfully recapitulate the chronic, multifactorial nature of the disease. Moreover, the impact of SB202190 on other critical RPE functions, such as phagocytosis of POS under normal conditions and cytoskeletal dynamics related to cell adhesion and migration, needs to be extensively characterized to avoid unintended disruption of essential homeostatic processes (Kim et al., 2021; Kyosseva, 2016).

Another consideration is the limitation inherent to the use of SB202190 as a research tool rather than a clinical‐grade pharmaceutical compound. Its pharmacokinetic and safety profiles have been characterized in experimental contexts, but there is a lack of clinical data regarding potential ocular toxicity, bioavailability, and long‐term impact on retinal structure and function (Federspiel et al., 2023; Young, 2013). The multifaceted role of p38 MAPK in the retina—spanning inflammatory cytokine production, regulation of apoptosis, and cytoskeletal dynamics—means that a fine balance must be maintained; excessive suppression could lead to undesired consequences such as impaired wound healing or compromised cell survival under stress. As such, a detailed understanding of the dose‐response relationship and the temporal dynamics of p38 inhibition in specific RPE subpopulations will be essential.

In summary, SB202190 presents as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on strong mechanistic rationale and preclinical evidence supporting its ability to modulate pathological pathways implicated in RPE dysfunction. Its capacity to inhibit p38α/β with high potency, restore actin dynamics under oxidative conditions, and improve phagocytic function aligns well with the therapeutic goals of preserving RPE integrity and retinal homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the dualistic nature of p38 MAPK signaling—with its capacity to mediate both deleterious and protective responses—poses a significant challenge that mandates careful and comprehensive preclinical evaluation. The candidate’s strengths reside in its well‐characterized inhibitory activity, established use in modulating fibrotic and inflammatory responses in ocular models, and its potential to replicate the endogenous protective functions mediated by regulators such as DUSP4 (Liu et al., 2025). Conversely, the weaknesses center on potential off‐target effects, the risk of inadvertently suppressing adaptive stress responses, and the absence of clinical studies directly addressing dry AMD.

Overall, while SB202190 holds promise based on its molecular mode of action and supportive in vitro data regarding cytoskeletal normalization and phagocytosis, the translational viability for dry AMD will ultimately depend on rigorous dosing studies, long‐term safety assessments, and demonstration of efficacy in animal models that capture the chronic oxidative and inflammatory milieu of the human retina (Moustardas et al., 2023; Saika et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2024). Only through such comprehensive studies can we adequately determine whether SB202190’s benefits outweigh its potential risks and if it can be successfully repurposed as a therapeutic intervention to mitigate the progression of dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Oncostatin M (OSM) is a cytokine originally identified as a member of the interleukin‐6 (IL-6) family and is naturally produced by various immune cells. Recombinant OSM, as provided by R&D Systems (Cat. No. 287-OM), is synthesized using recombinant DNA technology and purified to ensure bioactivity. As a protein therapeutic, OSM belongs to the class of cytokine-based drugs, which have historically been harnessed for their abilities to modulate inflammatory responses, regulate cell differentiation, and promote tissue repair. The recombinant formulation offers high purity and biological consistency, which makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing in ocular diseases. Prior studies have shown that cytokines from the IL-6 family, including OSM, CNTF, and LIF, are capable of inducing cellular protective mechanisms in the retina and may influence inflammatory and repair pathways (Brown, 2015; Pacione, 2004).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, OSM has been investigated in various models of retinal degeneration where its administration was correlated with protection of retinal ganglion cells and photoreceptors. In a rat model of retinal degeneration, OSM injection led to a reduction in photoreceptor loss, suggesting its neuroprotective potential in ocular pathologies (Brown, 2015; Xia et al., 2011). Beyond the retina, evidence indicates that OSM can influence epithelial repair and barrier integrity in tissues affected by inflammation, as seen in studies of airway epithelial cells in diseases such as asthma and allergic rhinitis (Pothoven & Schleimer, 2017). In terms of specific use against dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), there is no direct clinical history of OSM application; however, the body of work on cytokine-based interventions in ocular diseases is promising and supports repurposing efforts. Notably, the success in using CNTF—a cytokine with mechanistic similarities to OSM—in clinical studies to preserve photoreceptors and improve retinal function underscores the potential of this class of agents for treating degenerative retinal disorders (Xia et al., 2011).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of OSM is initiated by its binding to the OSM receptor (OSMR), which forms a heterodimeric complex with the signal-transducing receptor subunit gp130. This receptor engagement prompts the recruitment of Janus kinases (JAKs), including Jak2 and Tyk2, leading to the phosphorylation of specific tyrosine residues on the receptor and subsequent activation of the Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription 3 (STAT3) (Pacione, 2004; Richards, 2013). Once phosphorylated, STAT3 forms homodimers that translocate to the nucleus and bind to STAT-responsive elements in the promoter regions of target genes. Among the genes regulated by STAT3 are those implicated in the acute phase response, such as A2m, as well as genes like Cebpd, which are involved in immune and pro-inflammatory responses (Pacione, 2004).

In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—critical for maintaining photoreceptor health—the activation of STAT3 may have multiple beneficial effects. Studies have shown that OSM not only induces STAT3 phosphorylation in RPE cells, but also phosphorylates ERK1/2 MAP kinase, indicating a broad spectrum of signal transduction modulation that influences cell survival, differentiation, and cytoskeletal organization (Li et al., 2011). Given that cytoskeletal reorganization is essential for the formation of phagocytic cups and subsequent photoreceptor outer segment (POS) internalization, OSM-mediated STAT3 activation is hypothesized to contribute directly to these processes. It is important to note that similar effects have been observed with related IL-6 family cytokines in various epithelial models, supporting the notion that STAT3 signaling plays a pivotal role in establishing and maintaining epithelial barrier integrity (Richards, 2013; Pacione, 2004; Tiffen et al., 2008).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis proposed for repurposing OSM in dry AMD is that when administered at concentrations around the EC₅₀ (~0.1 nM), OSM will robustly activate STAT3 in RPE cells. This activation is expected to drive the transcription of genes that encode tight junction proteins and cytoskeletal elements critical for the morphological and functional integrity of the RPE layer. Enhanced expression of these genes would, in theory, facilitate reorganization of the cytoskeleton, thereby enabling the efficient formation of phagocytic cups. As phagocytosis of shed POS is a central function of the RPE—ensuring the renewal of the photoreceptor layer—improvements in this process may directly translate into enhanced retinal health and slow disease progression in dry AMD (Li et al., 2011; Richards, 2013).

Evidence from the literature suggests that STAT3 activation plays a role in cytoskeletal dynamics and barrier function. For example, in studies with human fetal RPE cells, OSM stimulation led to phosphorylated STAT3 accumulation, which is correlated with modifications in cell shape, inhibition of uncontrolled proliferation, and potentially enhanced phagocytosis (Li et al., 2011). Moreover, the beneficial effects witnessed in similar cytokine treatments, such as with CNTF, reinforce the notion that a shared signaling cascade involving STAT3 not only supports neuroprotection but also augments cellular processes essential for maintaining the RPE’s barrier functions and phagocytic competence (Xia et al., 2011; Mori et al., 2024). However, while the expected induction of tight junction and cytoskeletal gene expression is mechanistically plausible based on the STAT3 pathway, direct evidence linking OSM-induced gene expression specifically to enhanced phagocytic cup formation in RPE cells remains to be conclusively established and would benefit from further in vitro and in vivo validation (Pothoven & Schleimer, 2017; Pacione, 2004).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of Oncostatin M for the treatment of dry AMD is supported by a mechanistic rationale that draws on its established role in STAT3-mediated cellular signaling and its previous demonstrations of neuroprotective effects in retinal degeneration models. One of the key strengths of OSM as a candidate lies in its ability to activate STAT3—a transcription factor that governs a spectrum of genes involved in cell survival, cytoskeletal reorganization, and barrier integrity. This is highly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments contribute to disease progression (Brown, 2015; Pacione, 2004). Additionally, the availability of a high-quality recombinant form, combined with prior research in ocular models showing evidence of photoreceptor protection and potential enhancement of retinal function, renders OSM an attractive prospect for repurposing (Xia et al., 2011; Mori et al., 2024).

Despite these strengths, several challenges and potential weaknesses warrant consideration. First, although OSM-induced STAT3 activation is well documented, its downstream effects on tight junction proteins and the cytoskeletal apparatus within RPE cells have not been conclusively demonstrated in the context of dry AMD. There is some concern that while low to moderate doses of OSM may promote cellular repair and barrier stabilization, higher concentrations—or chronic overexpression—might induce epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and compromise barrier integrity, as seen in other epithelial tissues (Pothoven & Schleimer, 2017). This dual nature of OSM’s action necessitates careful dosing and thorough characterization of its effects on RPE function to avoid adverse outcomes such as enhanced inflammation or unwanted EMT that could exacerbate retinal degeneration.

Furthermore, specific studies in human RPE cells indicate that while OSM robustly activates STAT3 and ERK1/2 pathways, it can also lead to inhibitory effects on cell proliferation and survival, suggesting that its impact on cell dynamics is highly context-dependent (Li et al., 2011; Tiffen et al., 2008). This raises questions regarding the optimal balance between achieving sufficient STAT3 activation to drive cytoskeletal and tight junction gene expression and avoiding potential cytostatic or cytotoxic effects that may impair overall RPE health. There is also a need to determine whether the upregulation of target genes such as A2m and Cebpd—documented in other cellular contexts—translates into functional improvements in POS internalization and maintenance of the RPE barrier in the specific setting of dry AMD (Pacione, 2004).

Moreover, while studies in rat models of retinal degeneration have shown that OSM can reduce photoreceptor loss and promote the regeneration of outer segments (Järgen et al., 2017), these effects have not been directly linked to changes in RPE phagocytic activity or tight junction integrity. Given that dry AMD involves chronic, low-grade inflammation and oxidative stress, it is essential to ascertain whether OSM’s systemic inflammatory modulation would have beneficial or deleterious effects over the longer term. The balance between its regenerative potential and the possibility of promoting inflammatory cascades or pathological angiogenesis (despite some reports of reduced pathological neovascularization) must be rigorously tested in preclinical models that faithfully recapitulate the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathology (Pothoven & Schleimer, 2017; Mori et al., 2024).

Another aspect to consider is the cross-talk between OSM-mediated STAT3 signaling and other cellular pathways that regulate cytoskeletal dynamics and cellular adhesion in the RPE. For instance, the cytokine’s ability to modulate both the ERK1/2 MAP kinase pathway and STAT family proteins suggests that it operates at a nodal point that could influence diverse cellular functions. This complexity, while offering an opportunity to address multiple pathological processes simultaneously, also raises the possibility of off-target effects that could undermine the therapeutic goal. Detailed dose-response studies and time-course experiments will be imperative to delineate the precise window in which OSM functions as a promoter of barrier integrity and efficient phagocytosis, rather than triggering pathological changes detrimental to RPE function (Li et al., 2011; Tiffen et al., 2008).

In terms of translational potential, the strategy of repurposing an existing recombinant cytokine such as OSM offers significant advantages, including the possibility of leveraging existing manufacturing, formulation, and regulatory data. This could expedite the transition from preclinical studies to early-phase clinical trials in patients with dry AMD. Nonetheless, the preclinical evidence specific to dry AMD remains preliminary, and further research is needed to systematically assess OSM’s effects on RPE cell morphology, tight junction formation, cytoskeletal organization, and phagocytic efficiency. It would be beneficial to conduct detailed in vitro experiments using human RPE cell lines or primary RPE cultures, evaluating not only short-term signaling events (e.g., STAT3 phosphorylation kinetics) but also long-term outcomes such as maintenance of the barrier phenotype and resistance to oxidative or inflammatory stress. Such studies could be complemented by in vivo investigations in animal models that mimic the key features of dry AMD, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the balance between beneficial and potentially harmful effects of OSM in the ocular environment (Li et al., 2011; Pacione, 2004).

Overall, Oncostatin M presents as an innovative and mechanistically plausible candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. Its ability to activate STAT3 is intrinsically linked to cytoskeletal reorganization and epithelial barrier maintenance, processes that are critical for proper RPE function and the clearance of shed POS. The preclinical data from retinal degeneration models, along with evidence from related cytokines, lend credence to the hypothesis that OSM could enhance POS internalization and overall retinal health when applied at carefully optimized concentrations (Brown, 2015; Xia et al., 2011). However, the candidate’s dualistic role in modulating epithelial barrier function—including the risk of inducing EMT and compromising cellular integrity at inappropriate doses—necessitates a cautious and methodical approach to further development (Pothoven & Schleimer, 2017).

In conclusion, while the repurposing of Oncostatin M for dry AMD is underpinned by compelling mechanistic insights and supportive data from alternative ocular applications, significant gaps remain in our understanding of its specific effects on RPE cells. Detailed investigations into the optimal dosing regimen, the kinetics of STAT3 activation, and the downstream transcriptional events governing tight junction and cytoskeletal gene expression are crucial. Only through rigorous preclinical evaluation—encompassing both in vitro mechanism-based assays and in vivo efficacy studies—can we validate whether OSM truly possesses the capacity to enhance phagocytic cup formation and POS internalization as hypothesized. The balance between therapeutic benefit and potential adverse effects must be carefully managed to harness the full potential of OSM as a treatment for dry age-related macular degeneration (Pacione, 2004; Li et al., 2011; Richards, 2013).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Geldanamycin is a small-molecule inhibitor of heat shock protein 90 (HSP90) that originally garnered attention as a naturally derived product from Streptomyces species, and it belongs to the benzoquinone ansamycin class of compounds. As a natural product, geldanamycin was first isolated for its antibiotic properties and later found to exert potent effects on cellular protein homeostasis by binding the N-terminal ATP-binding pocket of HSP90. This mode of binding disrupts the chaperone function of HSP90, which is responsible for assisting in the stabilization and maturation of numerous client proteins, including signaling regulators and enzymes. Compounds of this chemical class have historically been investigated for their anticancer potential, given that HSP90 plays a central role in sustaining oncogenic signaling by stabilizing mutated or overexpressed proteins. In the context of ocular research, geldanamycin’s ability to modulate proteostasis and inflammatory cascades has prompted its investigation as a potential therapy for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), where dysregulated protein aggregation, impaired autophagy, and chronic inflammation are key pathological features (Piippo et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, geldanamycin and related HSP90 inhibitors have been used primarily as research tools to interrogate the role of molecular chaperones in cancer, neurodegeneration, and cellular stress responses. In preclinical studies, geldanamycin demonstrated the capacity to induce a robust heat shock response characterized by the upregulation of HSP70 and concomitant modulation of client proteins that depend on HSP90. Its inhibition of HSP90 has been extensively explored in models of protein aggregation diseases and in studies of inflammasome regulation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. For example, several reports have provided direct experimental evidence that HSP90 inhibition by geldanamycin prevents the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in human RPE models—specifically in ARPE-19 cells, human embryonic stem cell-derived RPE, and primary human RPE—by disrupting the protective HSP90–SGT1 complex that stabilizes NLRP3, thereby triggering autophagy-mediated clearance of the receptor (Piippo et al., 2018). In related studies, geldanamycin was also shown to induce an HSP70 response that can modulate proteostasis and reduce cellular inflammatory stress, although its high toxicity has consistently been reported as a barrier to clinical application in humans (Chen et al., 2021). While geldanamycin itself has not been approved for clinical use in dry AMD, its mechanistic insights have spurred research into repurposing HSP90 inhibitors for ocular indications, albeit with a need for derivatives or alternative candidates (Chen et al., 2021; Piippo et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, HSP90 functions as an ATP-dependent molecular chaperone that is critical for the correct folding, stabilization, and activation of a wide range of client proteins, including kinases, transcription factors, and components of the inflammasome complex such as NLRP3. Under basal conditions, HSP90, together with its co-chaperone SGT1, forms a complex with NLRP3 that maintains the receptor in an inactive yet activation-competent state. Geldanamycin binds to the N-terminal ATP-binding pocket of HSP90, thereby competitively inhibiting its ATPase activity and disrupting its chaperone cycle. This inhibition leads to the dissociation of the HSP90–SGT1 complex, releasing NLRP3. Once liberated from the protective chaperone complex, NLRP3 is highly unstable and becomes a substrate for intracellular degradation mechanisms. In the specific context of human RPE cells, experimental evidence has shown that geldanamycin preferentially promotes the autophagic clearance of NLRP3 rather than its proteasomal degradation. Mechanistic experiments that used proteasome inhibition with MG-132 and lysosomal/autophagy inhibition with bafilomycin A₁ or chloroquine revealed that when autophagy is intact, geldanamycin drives the degradation of NLRP3 via the autophagy pathway, resulting in a robust reduction in caspase-1 activity and IL-1β secretion (Piippo et al., 2018). This HSP90-dependent regulation of NLRP3 is particularly significant because inflammasome activation in RPE cells is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In addition, geldanamycin induces the expression of HSP70, a cytoprotective chaperone that further contributes to maintaining proteostasis under stress conditions; however, the increase in HSP70 is a double-edged sword, as it reflects cellular stress responses that could have both beneficial and deleterious effects if dysregulated (Chen et al., 2021; Ryhänen, 2011). Notably, the timing of geldanamycin administration is critical: its inhibitory effect on IL-1β secretion is maximal when added immediately prior to the induction of proteasome or autophagy inhibition, indicating that the HSP90 inhibition must occur before the onset of overwhelming proteostatic stress to be effective (Piippo et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic findings, the expected therapeutic effect of geldanamycin in a dry AMD model is multi-pronged. First, by binding to HSP90 and disrupting its stabilization of NLRP3, geldanamycin is anticipated to accelerate the autophagic clearance of NLRP3 complexes. This clearance is expected to blunt the assembly and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, thereby reducing the cleavage of pro-caspase-1 and ultimately diminishing the production and secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β. In the context of dry AMD, where low-grade chronic inflammation and impaired clearance of damaged cellular proteins contribute to disease progression, the suppression of inflammasome activation is a desirable outcome that could help mitigate retinal inflammation and cell death (Piippo et al., 2018). Second, by reducing the persistent activation of the inflammasome, geldanamycin may help preserve lysosomal function, which is critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE. Lysosomal dysfunction and the resultant accumulation of lipofuscin are hallmark features in the pathogenesis of dry AMD; therefore, maintaining efficient lysosomal degradation is key to restoring RPE homeostasis. Although direct evidence linking geldanamycin to enhanced POS digestion is not comprehensively detailed in the current literature excerpts, there is reasonable mechanistic rationale to suggest that improved autophagic flux and decreased inflammatory burden could promote better phagocytic competence in RPE cells (Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025; Piippo et al., 2018). Finally, given that HSP90 inhibition via geldanamycin has been shown to reduce proteostasis stress and modulate key inflammatory pathways, its application in RPE models of dry AMD could result in improved cellular survival and function, potentially slowing or reversing aspects of the degenerative process. It is important to note that the hypothesized effective concentration (EC₅₀ around 500 nM) is based on in vitro studies in RPE cells, and achieving this efficacy in an in vivo ocular setting via intravitreal administration would require careful dosing and pharmacokinetic optimization to mitigate systemic toxicity (Piippo et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
Geldanamycin represents a promising candidate from a mechanistic perspective for treating dry AMD due to its unique mode of action as an HSP90 inhibitor. The strengths of this therapeutic approach include its ability to directly target a key regulatory protein that stabilizes the NLRP3 inflammasome, leading to downregulation of a major pro-inflammatory pathway implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis. Preclinical research in RPE models, including ARPE-19, hESC-derived RPE, and primary human RPE, has consistently demonstrated that geldanamycin can reduce caspase-1 activity and IL-1β secretion by promoting autophagic degradation of NLRP3, which is central to halting the vicious cycle of chronic inflammation (Piippo et al., 2018). This is further supported by studies indicating that proper timing of HSP90 inhibition is crucial to maximize the clearance of NLRP3 and achieve therapeutic benefits before proteostatic stress overwhelms the cellular degradation machinery (Piippo et al., 2018). Additionally, the induction of HSP70 following geldanamycin treatment may confer additional cytoprotective effects by promoting proper protein folding and assisting in the clearance of misfolded proteins, thus helping preserve lysosomal function and potentially improving photoreceptor outer segment (POS) digestion—a process that is compromised in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2021; Ryhänen, 2011).

However, significant challenges limit the clinical translation of geldanamycin. One of the major weaknesses of this therapeutic candidate is its well-documented toxicity profile. Numerous studies have reported that while geldanamycin is effective in modulating HSP90 and reducing inflammasome activation at low nanomolar doses, its inherent cytotoxicity and off-target effects make it unsuitable for direct clinical application. In several experimental settings, geldanamycin has been described as “too toxic for human administration,” with adverse effects observed in both in vitro and in vivo models (Piippo et al., 2018). Such toxicity is believed to arise in part from the quinone moiety of the molecule, which can engage in redox cycling and generate reactive oxygen species, thereby exacerbating cellular stress and impairing normal proteostasis. Furthermore, while the small-molecule nature of geldanamycin is an advantage in terms of drug delivery—especially for routes such as intravitreal injection—the narrow therapeutic window means that fine-tuning the dose to achieve the desired biological effect without incurring toxicity remains a significant hurdle. There is also the possibility that global inhibition of HSP90 could destabilize multiple client proteins beyond NLRP3, leading to unintended perturbations in vital signaling pathways and cellular homeostasis (Chen et al., 2021).

In addition, despite the promising preclinical data supporting the use of geldanamycin for reducing inflammasome activation in RPE cells, there is a noticeable gap in the literature concerning its impact on other critical aspects of dry AMD pathology—specifically, the direct enhancement of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) digestion. Although it is hypothesized that preserving lysosomal function via inhibition of chronic inflammasome activity should translate into improved phagocytosis of POS by RPE cells, definitive experimental evidence demonstrating that geldanamycin treatment leads to enhanced POS clearance in AMD models is lacking (Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025; Piippo et al., 2018). This represents an area where further targeted studies are required.

Overall, geldanamycin’s mechanism of action is compelling from a proof-of-concept perspective; it elucidates how HSP90 inhibition can modulate the stability of key inflammatory mediators such as NLRP3 and thereby attenuate detrimental inflammatory cascades in RPE cells. The detailed biochemical insights provided by studies using geldanamycin have been invaluable for understanding the interplay between proteostasis, autophagy, and inflammation in the context of dry AMD. However, the clinical translation of geldanamycin as a therapeutic candidate is considerably hampered by its toxicity profile and the potential for off-target effects. Consequently, while geldanamycin offers important mechanistic validation for targeting HSP90 as a strategy to modulate NLRP3 inflammasome activity, repurposing efforts for dry AMD would likely need to focus on less toxic analogues or more selective HSP90 inhibitors (such as TAS-116) that preserve the beneficial effects on proteostasis without incurring significant cytotoxicity (Piippo et al., 2018). In summary, geldanamycin is a scientifically sound candidate from the perspective of modulating key pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD, yet its translational potential is limited by safety concerns that must be addressed either through structural modifications or by identifying alternative inhibitors within the HSP90 inhibitor class that demonstrate improved ocular and systemic tolerability.
