Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Adalimumab (marketed as Humira) is a fully humanized recombinant IgG1 monoclonal antibody developed using recombinant DNA technology that targets tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNFα). As a member of the anti‐TNFα class of biologics, adalimumab is designed to bind both soluble and membrane‐bound TNFα with high affinity, thereby preventing its interaction with the TNF receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2) on target cells. This antibody was originally discovered and engineered to address systemic inflammatory diseases, and its fully human composition is intended to lower immunogenicity compared to earlier chimeric molecules such as infliximab. In its development, molecular engineering efforts focused on isolating the relevant antibody variable regions that exhibit specificity for TNFα, followed by the construction of a recombinant molecule with human constant regions to improve tolerability and clinical efficacy. Anti‐TNFα antibodies belong to a broader class of therapeutic compounds that have dramatically changed the treatment landscape for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. They have been widely applied in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn’s disease, and ulcerative colitis, and over the past two decades, their use has been extended into ocular inflammatory diseases such as non‐infectious uveitis. Such applications underscore the versatility and translational potential of TNFα inhibition in modulating inflammatory cascades (Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History:  
Adalimumab’s clinical journey began with its approval for systemic autoimmune diseases where TNFα plays a fundamental role in mediating inflammation and tissue damage. Its robust performance in rheumatoid arthritis and related conditions has been well documented in numerous large-scale randomized controlled trials, which demonstrated significant improvement in clinical outcomes and inflammatory markers. These successes provided the foundation for exploring its application in other diseases characterized by inflammatory dysregulation. In recent years, growing evidence from both biochemical studies and clinical observations has highlighted the role of chronic inflammation in the pathogenesis of several retinal degenerative disorders. In particular, studies have shown that TNFα is upregulated in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and may contribute to the degeneration seen in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). For example, preclinical work has demonstrated that inflammation mediated by TNFα can impair the integrity of RPE cells, reduce the expression of proteins critical for RPE function (including visual cycle proteins and complement regulators) and disrupt phagocytic clearance mechanisms; these findings form the basis for hypothesizing that TNFα blockade may preserve RPE function in dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

While the majority of clinical uses of adalimumab have been in the realm of systemic and ocular inflammatory conditions such as non‐infectious uveitis, there has been emerging interest in repurposing anti‐TNFα therapies for retinal degenerations. In the context of ocular disease, several investigators have explored both systemic and local (intravitreal or subconjunctival) routes of administration to modulate intraocular inflammation. Pilot clinical trials and case reports have assessed intravitreal adalimumab in patients with uveitis and even in those with neovascular (“wet”) AMD refractory to anti‐VEGF therapies; these studies reported varying degrees of efficacy and underscored an acceptable local safety profile, though in some instances, higher dosages have been associated with ocular toxicity. In animal studies, intravitreal or subconjunctival administration of adalimumab has been shown to reduce inflammation and offer neuroprotection in models of retinal degeneration, such as in the rd10 mouse model for retinitis pigmentosa, establishing a precedent for local administration to achieve high ocular levels with minimal systemic exposure. Despite these advancements, use of adalimumab specifically for dry AMD has not been established in clinical practice. The proposed approach builds on the mechanistic insights from studies demonstrating that elevated TNFα levels can lead to downregulation of phagocytic receptors and lysosomal enzymes in RPE cells—processes central to dry AMD pathology—and posits that reversing these effects via TNFα neutralization may preserve RPE function (Nashine et al., 2022; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of adalimumab centers on its targeted neutralization of TNFα. TNFα is a proinflammatory cytokine produced by a variety of cell types that include activated T lymphocytes, macrophages, and, importantly, resident cells in the eye such as RPE and Müller glia. When secreted into the extracellular milieu, TNFα binds to its receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2), triggering intracellular signaling cascades that lead to the activation of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and other pathways that promote the expression of additional inflammatory cytokines, adhesion molecules, and matrix metalloproteinases. These processes collectively contribute to a sustained inflammatory response that can result in cellular dysfunction and death. Adalimumab, by virtue of its high affinity binding, sequesters TNFα and prevents receptor engagement. In doing so, it effectively interrupts these downstream proinflammatory signals and halts the amplification of the inflammatory cascade (Wang et al., 2011; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium cells, TNFα-mediated signaling has been implicated in the suppression of genes critical to the maintenance of RPE functions. Specifically, experimental studies have suggested that exposure to TNFα leads to a reduction in the expression of MERTK—a receptor tyrosine kinase essential for the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—as well as cathepsin D, a lysosomal enzyme crucial for the degradation of engulfed material. The decrease in MERTK expression compromises the ability of RPE cells to efficiently phagocytose POS, thereby potentially contributing to the accumulation of cellular debris, drusen formation, and further RPE stress that are characteristic of dry AMD. In parallel, a reduction in cathepsin D would impair lysosomal degradation, exacerbating the intracellular buildup of waste products and further undermining cellular homeostasis in the RPE. By neutralizing TNFα, adalimumab is hypothesized to prevent these detrimental changes, preserving the expression levels of MERTK and cathepsin D and thereby maintaining robust phagocytic and degradative capacity in RPE cells (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021).

At the molecular level, the binding of adalimumab to TNFα is mediated via its antigen-binding (Fab) region, which recognizes specific epitopes on the cytokine. This interaction is characterized by high affinity and specificity, ensuring that even low concentrations of the antibody can effectively neutralize TNFα activity. The blockade prevents TNFα from initiating receptor-mediated signaling that would otherwise promote inflammation and cellular stress. Moreover, because TNFα is known to regulate not only inflammatory cytokine production but also apoptotic processes, its inhibition may confer additional neuroprotective effects in the retina by reducing signals that lead to programmed cell death. The comprehensive inhibition of TNFα by adalimumab therefore stands as a multifaceted intervention, addressing both the inflammatory insult and its secondary effects on critical cellular functions in the RPE (Wang et al., 2011; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Nashine et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for leveraging adalimumab in dry AMD rests on its potential to neutralize elevated TNFα levels in the subretinal microenvironment. Elevated TNFα has been implicated in the pathological downregulation of key proteins involved in RPE function, notably MERTK and cathepsin D. MERTK is a receptor that plays an essential role in the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, a process that is critical for the renewal of photoreceptors and the overall maintenance of retinal health. Cathepsin D, on the other hand, is involved in the lysosomal degradation of the ingested material; together, these proteins ensure that the RPE can effectively clear and recycle photoreceptor debris. In dry AMD, this phagocytic process is compromised, leading to the accumulation of cellular waste products and drusen formation, which further fuels inflammation and RPE degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Administration of adalimumab is expected to interrupt this cascade by neutralizing TNFα, thereby preventing its signaling that leads to the downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D. With TNFα effectively neutralized, RPE cells should experience a more favorable molecular milieu in which the expression of these critical proteins is maintained at functional levels. This preservation would, in turn, support the RPE’s capacity to phagocytose and degrade photoreceptor outer segments, thereby averting the buildup of toxic waste products. Furthermore, since TNFα signaling also contributes to other aspects of cellular stress and inflammation—such as the upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines and the induction of apoptotic pathways—the neutralization of TNFα by adalimumab may also reduce overall cellular stress and promote RPE cell survival and function (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022).

In vitro assays using cultured human RPE cells exposed to TNFα could be employed to test this hypothesis. In these experiments, treatment with adalimumab should result in the normalization or preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression levels when compared to TNFα-treated controls. In addition, functional assays measuring the uptake and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (or surrogate fluorescent particles) would be expected to show improved phagocytic efficiency in RPE cells treated with adalimumab. Such findings would provide robust mechanistic support for the proposed therapeutic strategy. Moreover, preliminary in vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD or models of induced RPE dysfunction could further validate that TNFα blockade leads to preservation of RPE integrity, improved photoreceptor survival, and retardation of retinal degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Considering that the expression of MERTK is well documented in RPE cells and that its function is critical for POS phagocytosis—a process that declines with aging and in the presence of inflammatory mediators—the ability of adalimumab to maintain or restore MERTK expression would be highly relevant in the context of dry AMD. In the proposed strategy, adalimumab may also help to stabilize other RPE functions, such as the regulation of the complement cascade and the visual cycle, both of which have been shown to be adversely affected by TNFα exposure. Thus, the anticipated effect of adalimumab is not limited solely to the preservation of phagocytic machinery; it may also contribute to a broader stabilization of RPE cell health in the face of chronic low-grade inflammation that characterizes dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of adalimumab as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a compelling yet cautiously optimistic perspective. One of the principal strengths of adalimumab lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action; by neutralizing TNFα, it directly addresses a central mediator of inflammation that has been implicated in the dysregulation of RPE functions. The experimental evidence indicating that TNFα exposure can lead to the downregulation of essential proteins such as MERTK and cathepsin D provides a strong rationale for the hypothesis that TNFα inhibition might preserve the RPE’s ability to maintain photoreceptor homeostasis. This mechanistic insight is particularly attractive because it targets one of the fundamental dysfunctions in dry AMD—namely, the failure of the RPE to clear photoreceptor outer segments effectively, which leads to the accumulation of drusen and progressive retinal degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the extensive clinical experience with adalimumab in systemic and ocular inflammatory diseases supports its safety profile. The fact that adalimumab is already approved by regulatory agencies, coupled with several clinical studies demonstrating its localized safety when administered intravitreally or via related routes in ocular conditions such as uveitis, adds to its attractiveness as a candidate for repurposing (Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010; Leal et al., 2018; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. To date, most studies involving adalimumab in the ocular context have focused on inflammatory conditions such as uveitis and neovascular AMD rather than dry AMD specifically. As a result, direct clinical evidence supporting its efficacy in preserving RPE phagocytic function in dry AMD is currently limited. The hypothesis that adalimumab can prevent the TNFα-induced downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D is primarily based on preclinical observations, and further mechanistic studies, both in vitro and in relevant animal models, are necessary to validate this pathway in the context of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Nashine et al., 2022; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Another potential challenge with using adalimumab for dry AMD is related to drug delivery and dosing. While intravitreal administration has shown promise in limited studies, determining the optimal dose that achieves effective TNFα blockade without incurring retinal toxicity remains an unresolved issue. Some animal studies have indicated that higher doses of intravitreal adalimumab can lead to retinal inflammation, reduced electroretinogram responses, or histopathological evidence of toxicity. Given that dry AMD is a chronic condition and would likely require repeated dosing or sustained drug delivery systems, the long-term safety of local TNFα blockade needs to be rigorously evaluated (Manzano et al., 2008; Pascual-Camps et al., 2014).

Moreover, because TNFα plays roles in normal immune surveillance and tissue repair, its complete inhibition—especially in an aged population that may have impaired immune responses—could theoretically predispose patients to infections or other adverse effects. Although the systemic safety profile of adalimumab is well established, the ocular microenvironment has distinct immunological characteristics, and the long-term effects of TNFα inhibition on retinal homeostasis, particularly regarding complement activation and maintenance of the blood–retinal barrier, require further study. There is also the possibility that compensatory inflammatory pathways may become activated in response to TNFα blockade, potentially diminishing the efficacy of the intervention over time (García-Layana et al., 2021; Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Sharma et al., 2009).

Additionally, the magnitude of the contribution of TNFα to the pathogenesis of dry AMD relative to other factors—such as oxidative stress, genetic predispositions (including polymorphisms in complement factors), and lipid metabolism abnormalities—remains to be fully delineated. It is possible that TNFα is one of several drivers of RPE dysfunction, and that its inhibition may need to be combined with other therapeutic strategies (for example, antioxidant supplementation or complement inhibitors) to achieve a meaningful clinical benefit. Therefore, while the rationale for adalimumab is compelling, a monotherapy approach may not be sufficient to halt the multifactorial progression of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nussenblatt et al., 2010).

In summary, adalimumab presents a promising repurposed candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on its potent and specific inhibition of TNFα—a cytokine implicated in the downregulation of crucial RPE proteins such as MERTK and cathepsin D. The drug’s extensive use in other inflammatory settings, along with preliminary evidence supporting its ocular safety, lend credibility to the hypothesis that TNFα blockade can preserve the phagocytic machinery of RPE cells and potentially slow the degenerative process characteristic of dry AMD. Nevertheless, significant challenges remain, including the need for robust preclinical validation in dry AMD models, optimization of ocular dosing regimens, and long-term safety assessments in an elderly population. A carefully designed series of in vitro experiments using human RPE cells—followed by well-controlled animal studies—should be undertaken to establish proof of concept regarding the preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression and function. If these studies yield positive results, subsequent early-phase clinical trials could be justified to evaluate the efficacy of intravitreal adalimumab in patients with dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010).

In light of these considerations, our recommendation is to advance adalimumab into a rigorous preclinical testing pipeline aimed specifically at dry AMD models. This should include studies that measure the expression levels and activity of MERTK and cathepsin D in RPE cells under conditions of TNFα stimulation, both in the presence and absence of adalimumab treatment. Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiling in ocular tissues, along with assessments of retinal structure and function via in vivo imaging and electrophysiological testing, will be critical to determining an appropriate dosing strategy. Finally, integration with complementary therapeutic approaches may be considered to address other facets of dry AMD pathogenesis. While the path to clinical application is fraught with challenges, the potential benefit of preserving RPE phagocytic function—and by extension, photoreceptor survival—in a disease with very limited current treatment options provides a strong impetus for further development of this candidate (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022).

In conclusion, adalimumab’s established molecular profile as a potent TNFα inhibitor, its extensive clinical track record in systemic and ocular inflammatory diseases, and the emerging data linking TNFα to RPE dysfunction collectively support the rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD. Nevertheless, given the complexity of AMD pathogenesis and the potential risks associated with chronic intraocular immunomodulation, a thorough and methodical approach to preclinical investigation is warranted before embarking on large-scale clinical trials. The ultimate goal is to validate that neutralization of TNFα can indeed preserve the phagocytic capabilities of the RPE, thereby maintaining retinal health and preventing the progression of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Strengths of this candidate include its potent and specific inhibition of TNFα, which is a key mediator in inflammatory cascades, its favorable immunogenicity profile stemming from its fully human composition, and its prior demonstration of safety in ocular applications such as uveitis. In addition, the biological rationale is supported by evidence that TNFα negatively impacts the expression of proteins critical for RPE phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation—a process that, when impaired, underlies the pathology of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

On the other hand, weaknesses center on the limited direct evidence for efficacy in dry AMD, potential challenges in achieving precise intraocular dosing without inducing retinal toxicity, and uncertain long-term consequences of sustained TNFα inhibition in the delicate immune environment of the eye. Moreover, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD suggests that a singular focus on TNFα may not fully address the disease’s complex pathophysiology, raising the possibility that combination therapies might eventually be necessary for optimal outcomes (Manzano et al., 2008; Sharma et al., 2009; Nussenblatt et al., 2010).

Given these observations, our evaluation concludes that adalimumab represents a promising and scientifically sound candidate for repurposing to treat dry AMD. Its mechanistic profile aligns well with the goal of preserving RPE phagocytic function by preventing TNFα-mediated downregulation of key proteins like MERTK and cathepsin D. However, to move forward with this candidate, research efforts must focus on resolving the outstanding questions through rigorous preclinical studies, optimization of the drug delivery method, and detailed long-term safety assessments. If successful, these steps could pave the way for early-phase clinical trials designed to test the efficacy of intravitreal adalimumab in stabilizing or improving RPE function in patients with dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010).

In summary, while the current body of literature on adalimumab has primarily focused on its role in systemic inflammatory diseases and ocular inflammatory conditions such as uveitis and neovascular AMD, the underlying mechanistic data provide a persuasive rationale for extending its application to dry AMD. The hypothesis that adalimumab can preserve RPE phagocytic function by neutralizing TNFα—thereby preventing the deleterious downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D—is scientifically plausible and merits further systematic investigation. The potential benefits of repurposing a well-characterized agent with an established safety profile are substantial, especially in a disease area where effective treatments remain elusive (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Overall, our recommendation for the drug development team is to prioritize a series of detailed preclinical studies that examine the effects of adalimumab on RPE cells under TNFα-induced stress conditions, with particular emphasis on the regulation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression and subsequent phagocytic activity. These studies should involve both conventional cell culture models and in vivo models that mimic the chronic inflammatory environment observed in dry AMD. Should these studies yield positive results, a phase I/II clinical trial focusing on safety and early efficacy in patients with dry AMD would be justified. This stepwise approach will ensure that the promising mechanistic rationale is thoroughly vetted before large-scale clinical application (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

In conclusion, the convergence of molecular, biochemical, and clinical evidence supports the further exploration of adalimumab as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to mitigate TNFα-mediated inflammatory cascades could play a critical role in preserving RPE function, maintaining photoreceptor health, and ultimately slowing the progression of a disease that currently lacks effective treatments. Nonetheless, rigorous preclinical validation and careful consideration of dosing and long-term safety will be essential to realize its potential in this new indication (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bryostatin‐1 is a naturally derived macrolide originally isolated from marine invertebrates and belongs to a class of compounds collectively known as bryostatins. These compounds exhibit potent modulation of protein kinase C (PKC) activity by binding to the enzyme’s diacylglycerol binding site on the regulatory domain. Bryostatin‐1 has been characterized as a partial agonist of PKC and is noted for its ability to both acutely activate and chronically down‐regulate specific PKC isoforms. The molecular architecture of bryostatin‐1 confers a unique binding profile that distinguishes it from phorbol esters; it induces translocation of target PKC isoforms to membranes without eliciting the full tumor‐promoting effects observed with phorbol esters. The compound is synthetically challenging to produce, yet semisynthetic methodologies have enabled its preparation in sufficient quantities for preclinical and early clinical applications. As a member of the marine natural products family, bryostatin‐1 is frequently investigated for its anticancer and neuroprotective properties, and its chemical structure serves as the basis for designing simplified analogs with improved pharmacological profiles (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).  

Therapeutic History:  
Bryostatin‐1 has a long preclinical history that spans oncology and neurology. In oncology, bryostatin‐1 has been extensively studied for its role in modulating PKC in various tumor types and has been evaluated in numerous clinical trials addressing B‐cell malignancies and renal cancers. Despite promising preclinical results, its cancer‐directed clinical efficacy has been limited by suboptimal outcomes and adverse side effects such as myalgia. More recently, bryostatin‐1 has been repurposed in neurological contexts. Several studies have demonstrated its neuroprotective capabilities in models of Alzheimer’s disease, where it has shown to improve synaptic function, restore dendritic spine morphology, induce synaptogenesis through the upregulation of brain‐derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and enhance cognitive function. Phase II clinical trials in Alzheimer’s patients have provided translational evidence of its ability to modulate PKCε in the central nervous system (Chen et al., 2024; Nelson et al., 2017). However, a search of clinical trial databases has revealed that no formal clinical trials have been registered evaluating bryostatin‐1 in the setting of macular degeneration, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, or Rab7 signaling‐related pathways (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Although there is evidence supporting bryostatin‐1’s capacity to affect cellular pathways—such as inducing autophagy and promoting PKC‐mediated cell survival—in neuronal and cancer cells, its application to ocular diseases like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) remains unexplored in the clinical context (Safarpour, 2009; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).  

Mechanism of Action:  
Bryostatin‐1 functions primarily as a modulator of protein kinase C, a family of serine/threonine kinases that play central roles in regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis, and intracellular trafficking. On a molecular level, bryostatin‐1 binds competitively to the diacylglycerol (DAG) binding site located in the C1 domain of PKC isoforms. This binding event leads to the translocation of PKC from the cytosol to membranous compartments, thereby bringing the kinase into close proximity with its substrates. Unlike potent activators such as phorbol esters, bryostatin‐1 acts as a partial agonist. Short‐term exposure results in the activation of specific PKC isoforms, whereas prolonged exposure leads to their down‐regulation via proteasomal degradation. Structural studies have demonstrated that the complex hydrogen‐bond networks formed by the A- and B-rings of bryostatin‐1 contribute significantly to its isoform selectivity and binding affinity (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).  

In the context of the hypothesized mechanism for dry AMD, it is proposed that bryostatin‐1 can activate atypical PKC isoforms at very low effective concentrations (EC₅₀ ≈ 0.1 nM), potentially including enzymes that are involved in the regulation of Rab7 signalling. Although bryostatin‐1 has been studied predominantly for its activation of classical (e.g., PKCα, PKCβ) and novel PKC isoforms (e.g., PKCδ, PKCε), several experimental reports suggest that PKC activity regulates various aspects of vesicular trafficking, including phagosome maturation. In phagocytic cell lines, enhanced PKC activation has been linked to improved phagolysosomal fusion, which is essential for the degradation of ingested material. This connection is of particular interest in RPE cells, where the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) via the phagosome–lysosome pathway is central to retinal homeostasis. The hypothesis extends this mechanism by proposing that the activation of PKC by bryostatin‐1 may lead to the phosphorylation of Rab7 effector proteins, which are known to control the late stages of phagosome maturation and lysosome fusion. Although direct experimental evidence connecting bryostatin‐1‐mediated PKC activation to Rab7 effector phosphorylation in RPE cells is limited, existing literature has established the importance of PKC in regulating phagocytic processes and intracellular vesicle trafficking (Saddala et al., 2020; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005). Furthermore, mechanistic parallels drawn from studies in neuronal systems—where bryostatin‐1 has been shown to influence autophagic flux and promote synaptic health—support the feasibility of such a cellular response in other highly phagocytic cells like the RPE (Chen et al., 2024).  

Expected Effect:  
Dry AMD is characterized by the dysfunction of RPE cells, which leads to impaired clearance of POS and subsequent accumulation of toxic lipofuscin deposits. RPE dysfunction is associated with disrupted phagosome maturation and lysosomal degradation pathways, contributing to retinal degeneration and vision loss. The therapeutic hypothesis for bryostatin‐1 posits that its administration will enhance the maturation of phagosomes by stimulating PKC isoforms that, in turn, phosphorylate Rab7 effectors. Effective phosphorylation of these effectors is expected to facilitate late phagosome–lysosome fusion, thereby improving the trafficking and degradation of POS. Empirical studies in RPE cells have shown that defects in phagolysosomal fusion lead to the accumulation of nondegradable materials and are closely linked to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Safarpour, 2009; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).  

The candidate mechanism suggests that, upon administration, bryostatin‐1 will rapidly bind to its target PKC isoforms in RPE cells, causing these kinases to translocate to relevant subcellular membranes. This translocation is anticipated to bring PKC in proximity to Rab7 effectors situated on late phagosomes. Activation of these kinases would then promote the phosphorylation of regulatory proteins that control vesicular fusion events. As a result, the impaired phagocytosis observed in dry AMD would be corrected through improved maturation of phagosomes and enhanced fusion with lysosomes. Such a cascade is expected to lead to enhanced clearance of POS debris and, ultimately, a reduction in lipofuscin accumulation, which is central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Although supportive evidence for this cascade exists in the context of non‐ocular phagocytic cells and in neuronal models of autophagy activation, it remains imperative to directly evaluate these effects in primary RPE cell cultures or relevant animal models to solidify the connection between PKC activation by bryostatin‐1 and Rab7‐mediated phagosome maturation (Saddala et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Bryostatin‐1 presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for dry AMD owing to its potent modulation of PKC, a central regulator of intracellular signaling pathways that govern vesicular trafficking, phagocytosis, and autophagy. One of the key strengths of bryostatin‐1 lies in its well‐documented activity in modulating PKC isoforms that are critical in diverse physiological contexts, including neuronal function and cancer cell biology. Its demonstrated neuroprotective efficacy in Alzheimer’s disease clinical studies supports the compound’s translational potential and suggests that its PKC‐modulating effects might be harnessed in alternate tissues such as the retina (Chen et al., 2024). Additionally, the critical role of PKC in promoting phagosome–lysosome fusion has been substantiated in other cell types, which provides a strong theoretical basis for its application in RPE cells where phagocytic clearance is essential for maintaining retinal integrity (Saddala et al., 2020; Safarpour, 2009).

Despite these promising aspects, several challenges and weaknesses must be considered. Foremost, no direct studies to date have evaluated bryostatin‐1 in the context of dry AMD or in RPE cells. Clinical trial databases have not registered any studies for bryostatin‐1 in macular degeneration, underscoring the novelty of this repurposing strategy but also highlighting a significant gap in the literature (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The hypothesis that bryostatin‐1 will stimulate atypical PKC isoforms to phosphorylate Rab7 effectors, although plausible, remains largely speculative. While various studies have linked PKC activity to phagosome maturation and autophagy regulation, the precise isoforms relevant to RPE cell function—and whether these isoforms are the same ones activated by bryostatin‐1 in neuronal or cancer models—have not been comprehensively elucidated. Therefore, it will be crucial to determine, through rigorous in vitro assays and animal models, whether the purported EC₅₀ of approximately 0.1 nM is achievable in RPE cells and whether this concentration effectively modifies the Rab7‐related molecular machinery.

Additional considerations include the potential for off‐target effects and systemic toxicity. Past clinical studies of bryostatin‐1, particularly in oncology, have reported adverse effects such as myalgia and thrombocytopenia. However, the pharmacokinetic profile observed in Alzheimer’s trials suggests that the dosing regimens used for neurological disorders might be translatable to ocular delivery with appropriate formulation strategies. Localized ocular delivery, such as intravitreal injection or controlled‐release implants, may enable targeted modulation of PKC in the retina while mitigating systemic exposure and associated adverse events (Chen et al., 2024; Nelson et al., 2017). Moreover, the challenge of achieving adequate drug penetration to the RPE in vivo is nontrivial. Approaches to enhance ocular bioavailability, including nanoparticle encapsulation or conjugation to targeting ligands, should be explored concurrently with the design of preclinical studies to better validate this therapeutic candidate.

From a mechanistic standpoint, the dual nature of bryostatin‐1—characterized by initial activation followed by downregulation of PKC isoforms—necessitates precise temporal control of its pharmacodynamic effects. In the context of phagosome maturation, transient activation may be beneficial to restore proper lysosomal fusion; however, prolonged downregulation might counteract the desired effect. It is therefore important that future studies carefully delineate the dosing regimen (both concentration and administration frequency) required to achieve an optimal therapeutic window in RPE cells. Additionally, the specificity of bryostatin‐1 for PKC isoforms implicated in Rab7 effector phosphorylation must be confirmed, as the RPE expresses a complex array of PKC isoforms that may play distinct roles in cellular homeostasis and stress responses (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).

The breadth and diversity of bryostatin‐1’s effects in preclinical models have generated considerable interest, yet its repurposing for dry AMD remains at an early stage of conceptual development. Given that disruption of phagosome maturation in RPE cells is a well‐established contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD—and that PKC signaling has been implicated in regulating this process—the rationale for exploring bryostatin‐1 in this indication is scientifically sound. Nonetheless, the transition from a neuroprotective agent in Alzheimer’s disease to an effective modulator of RPE function in dry AMD will depend on new studies that specifically address the cellular context of the retina. In this regard, preliminary investigations using primary RPE cultures or animal models of dry AMD will be critical to validate the hypothesis that PKC activation by bryostatin‐1 can enhance Rab7‐mediated phagolysosomal fusion and improve POS clearance (Saddala et al., 2020; Safarpour, 2009).

In summary, bryostatin‐1 offers both significant promise and notable challenges as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration. Its ability to modulate PKC in a manner that may restore essential phagolysosomal functions in the RPE positions it as an innovative approach to address a major unmet need in ocular therapeutics. The compound’s successful use in Alzheimer’s disease trials provides encouraging translational evidence of its safety and efficacy in modulating neuronal PKC activity. However, the absence of direct evidence in retinal cells, the uncertainty regarding which specific PKC isoforms are most relevant to RPE phagocytosis, and potential issues related to dosing and systemic toxicity form significant hurdles that must be overcome. Moving forward, it will be critical to conduct comprehensive in vitro studies to assess the effects of bryostatin‐1 on RPE phagosome maturation, coupled with robust in vivo experiments in established dry AMD models. Such studies should focus on confirming the expression and role of the putative target proteins, including Rab7 effectors, and determining whether the activation of these pathways can indeed translate into improved clearance of POS and reduced retinal degeneration (Saddala et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Chen et al., 2024; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).

In conclusion, the overall evaluation of bryostatin‐1 as a drug candidate for dry AMD reveals a compound with strong mechanistic rationale and significant translational potential based on its established pharmacological properties in PKC modulation and neuroprotection. The strengths of bryostatin‐1 include its potent activity at nanomolar concentrations, a unique mode of action that distinguishes it from classical PKC activators, and supporting evidence from clinical studies in neurological disorders. Conversely, its weaknesses lie primarily in the absence of direct studies in ocular tissues, uncertainty regarding the specific PKC isoforms involved in RPE phagosome maturation, and potential challenges in achieving localized delivery without systemic side effects. An interdisciplinary approach that integrates detailed molecular studies with innovative drug delivery strategies will be critical in validating bryostatin‐1’s viability for the treatment of dry AMD. Based on the current literature, investing in rigorous preclinical testing to confirm the hypothesized mechanistic link between PKC activation, Rab7 effector phosphorylation, and enhanced phagosome maturation in RPE cells is warranted before progressing to clinical evaluation (Saddala et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Safarpour, 2009; Chen et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The therapeutic candidate under evaluation is a CD82 agonist peptide, marketed as a tetraspanin activator (Peptide Institute Cat. No. K-8202). This candidate is a synthetic peptide designed to interact with the extracellular domain of CD82, a member of the tetraspanin family involved in organizing membrane microdomains and regulating the spatial distribution of various transmembrane proteins such as integrins. Tetraspanins are known to modulate cellular adhesion, migration, and signal transduction by forming dynamic “tetraspanin–enriched microdomains” (TEMs) that include integrins and other proteins; in particular, CD82 has been implicated in the regulation of integrin clustering and function in a range of cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and various immune cells (Lee et al., 2022). The structural design of this peptide likely takes advantage of the sequence and conformational features of the large extracellular loop (LEL) of CD82, which is known to mediate protein–protein interactions through specific binding surfaces and domains. Although similar CD82‐derived peptides have been examined primarily in the context of cancer metastasis suppression, the repurposing of such peptides for retinal applications represents an innovative approach. The rationale is that by binding to CD82 on the RPE cell surface, the peptide may induce a clustering effect that enhances the recruitment and stable assembly of αvβ5 integrin nanodomains, which are critical for the formation of effective phagocytic cups and subsequent photoreceptor outer segment (POS) internalization—a process that is compromised in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Lee et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, tetraspanin proteins such as CD82 have been studied extensively in oncology where they are recognized as metastasis suppressors. In those settings, peptide mimetics of the small extracellular loop (EC1) of CD82 have been developed with the aim of modulating cell adhesion, migration, and invasion. For example, studies have shown that CD82-derived peptides can inhibit tumor cell migration and adhesion by interfering with integrin-mediated signaling pathways, particularly involving integrins such as α5β1, and by attenuating downstream focal adhesion kinase (FAK) signaling (Luan et al., 2018). However, such peptides have primarily been investigated in non-ocular systems, and their actions have been predominantly inhibitory in nature, aimed at suppressing excessive integrin signaling rather than stimulating it. In the specific context of the retina, the use of CD82 or its mimetics has been very limited; one study documented that recombinant human CD82 (rhCD82) can interfere with TGF-β1-mediated epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) in ARPE-19 cells by modulating integrin expression and inhibiting Smad-dependent signaling pathways (Lee et al., 2022). Although that study was conducted within the framework of fibrosis and EMT—processes that are also relevant to AMD—the focus was on anti-fibrotic and anti-migratory properties rather than on enhancing phagocytosis. In addition, indirect evidence from immunological studies indicates that CD82 plays a role in regulating integrin sorting and cytoskeletal reorganization in macrophages and neutrophils, thereby influencing cell migration and adhesion (McGowan et al., 2022). In retinal biology, the αvβ5 integrin is known to be indispensable for efficient POS binding and internalization by RPE cells, and its dysregulation is associated with impaired phagocytosis and consequently with AMD pathogenesis (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). However, there is currently no established history of using a CD82 agonist peptide to specifically enhance αvβ5 integrin clustering or to stimulate phagocytic cup formation in RPE cells, making this candidate both innovative and largely uncharted in preclinical ocular disease models (Lee et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The proposed mechanism of action for the CD82 agonist peptide rests on the capacity of CD82 to orchestrate the lateral organization of integrin receptors in the plasma membrane. Under physiological conditions, CD82 is involved in forming complexes with integrin subunits, including integrin β1 and integrin αv; these interactions have been shown to modulate integrin activation states and can affect downstream signaling pathways (Lee et al., 2022). In the present hypothesis, the agonist peptide is expected to bind to the extracellular domain of CD82 in a manner that promotes its active conformation, thereby enhancing its ability to cluster αvβ5 integrin on the apical surface of RPE cells. The clustering of integrin receptors is a critical step in the initiation of phagocytic cup assembly, as it facilitates the formation of a localized high-density area of signaling and adhesion molecules needed to capture and internalize shed POS particles (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). The biochemistry underlying this process involves the reorganization of membrane microdomains, where CD82, upon binding of the agonist peptide, may recruit additional integrin molecules and potentially interact with adapter proteins that link to the actin cytoskeleton, thereby reinforcing the mechanical stability required for efficient phagocytosis (McGowan et al., 2022). In several cell types, similar tetraspanin activators have been shown to influence cytoskeletal dynamics and cell adhesion by modulating the activity of small GTPases and other signaling intermediates; for example, the inhibition of migration by CD82 in macrophages is associated with decreased filopodia formation (McGowan et al., 2022). By analogy, if the agonist peptide induces a favorable conformational change in CD82 within RPE cells, it could conceivably lead to an optimal reorganization of αvβ5 integrin clusters that promotes the formation and stabilization of phagocytic cups, thereby enhancing the uptake of POS particles. Nonetheless, it is important to note that many of the detailed molecular interactions have been characterized in contexts other than retinal phagocytosis, and extrapolation to RPE cells remains somewhat speculative at this time (Luan et al., 2018). Moreover, while molecular docking analyses have revealed direct interactions between CD82 and integrin subunits (Lee et al., 2022), the specific impact of an agonist peptide on αvβ5 integrin clustering in RPE membranes has not yet been directly demonstrated. This lack of direct evidence underscores the need for rigorous mechanistic studies that investigate the peptide’s binding kinetics, its ability to modulate CD82 conformation, and the subsequent effects on integrin organization and actin remodeling in the specialized environment of RPE cells (Lee et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The anticipated outcome of administering the CD82 agonist peptide in a dry AMD model is an enhancement of RPE function through improved phagocytic activity. In healthy RPE cells, the daily clearance of shed photoreceptor outer segments is mediated primarily by αvβ5 integrin-dependent processes that initiate phagocytic cup assembly and POS internalization. In dry AMD, RPE dysfunction, which may include impaired integrin clustering and reduced phagocytic efficiency, contributes to the accumulation of cellular debris and subsequent retinal degeneration (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). The working hypothesis postulates that the CD82 agonist peptide will bind to CD82, resulting in the clustering and stabilization of αvβ5 integrin microdomains on the apical surface of RPE cells. Enhanced clustering of these integrins is expected to promote a more robust and efficient phagocytic response by facilitating the assembly of actin-rich phagocytic cups that effectively capture and internalize POS particles (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Zihni, 2025). In vitro, this effect would likely be measurable as an increase in the rate and extent of POS uptake in cultured human RPE cells such as ARPE-19, and could be quantified using established phagocytosis assays that utilize fluorescently labeled POS preparations. In vivo, improved phagocytic function could translate into better maintenance of retinal integrity, reduced accumulation of lipofuscin and other intracellular debris, and ultimately a slowdown or reversal of the degenerative changes associated with dry AMD (Ruggiero et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2022). It is also anticipated that by enhancing integrin clustering, the peptide might indirectly influence other signaling pathways involved in RPE homeostasis, potentially mitigating inflammatory or fibrotic processes that exacerbate AMD pathology (McGowan et al., 2022). However, one must exercise caution as the majority of existing literature on CD82 peptide mimetics has focused on modulating cell migration and adhesion in the context of cancer, rather than promoting enhanced phagocytosis (Luan et al., 2018). Therefore, while the expected effect of restored or enhanced POS clearance is theoretically sound, it remains to be validated in the specific cellular and animal models of dry AMD relevant to RPE function.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the proposed CD82 agonist peptide represents an intriguing and innovative candidate for the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration by addressing a fundamental pathological mechanism—impaired RPE phagocytosis. One of the key strengths of this candidate is its novel mechanism of action, which utilizes the concept of targeted receptor organization through the activation of a tetraspanin protein that has been implicated in integrin modulation. The role of αvβ5 integrin in RPE phagocytosis is well established, and its proper clustering is essential for the effective clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, a process that is compromised in aging and AMD (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). The idea of repurposing a CD82 agonist peptide to restore or enhance this process is supported indirectly by the body of literature demonstrating that tetraspanins play critical roles in integrin organization and that modulating tetraspanin function can have significant impacts on cell adhesion and signaling (Lee et al., 2022). Additionally, because current therapeutic strategies for dry AMD remain limited and largely focused on addressing neovascular complications rather than the underlying degenerative process, a candidate that directly improves RPE function and photoreceptor homeostasis offers substantial promise.

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be considered. First, there is a notable gap in the direct experimental evidence linking CD82 agonist peptides to enhanced phagocytic cup assembly or increased POS internalization in RPE cells. Most studies to date that involve CD82 in the context of the retina have concentrated on its role in inhibiting EMT or modulating inflammatory responses in ARPE-19 cells (Lee et al., 2022). In contrast, the majority of the literature on CD82 peptide mimetics in other systems—particularly in cancer—describes inhibitory effects on integrin-mediated signaling and cell migration rather than an agonistic promotion of integrin clustering (Luan et al., 2018). This discrepancy raises concerns regarding whether a peptide designed to activate CD82 will have the desired stimulatory effect on αvβ5 integrin organization in the unique cellular environment of the RPE. Second, the regulatory functions of tetraspanins are inherently complex and highly dependent on the cellular context; while enhanced clustering may be beneficial for phagocytosis, it could also inadvertently alter other CD82-associated pathways, such as TGF-β signaling or immune cell interactions, with potentially unforeseen consequences (McGowan et al., 2022). Third, the preclinical development of peptide-based therapeutics, particularly for ocular applications, poses significant challenges in terms of delivery, stability, and bioavailability. The blood–retinal barrier and the highly specialized microenvironment of the eye may limit the effective concentrations of the peptide that reach the target RPE cells, and any off-target effects due to systemic distribution could further complicate the safety profile.

Moreover, while integrin clustering is a promising target, the evidence linking enhanced αvβ5 organization directly to improved phagocytosis in RPE cells mainly comes from correlative studies in rodent models and in vitro assays (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012; Zihni, 2025). There is a need for more mechanistic studies that specifically dissect how tetraspanin-driven integrin clustering influences the kinetics and efficiency of phagocytic cup assembly in models that faithfully recapitulate the human RPE phenotype. It is also important to confirm that CD82 is expressed and functionally relevant in RPE cells of patients with dry AMD, as variations in tetraspanin expression could impact the efficacy of a peptide-based agonist (Lee et al., 2022). The candidate’s success will depend on rigorous optimization of its pharmacological profile, including its peptide stability, receptor binding affinity, and resistance to proteolytic degradation within ocular tissues.

Despite these challenges, the concept behind the CD82 agonist peptide is compelling. The targeted approach of modulating receptor microdomain architecture represents a departure from more conventional strategies, such as anti-VEGF therapies or broad-spectrum anti-inflammatory agents. If the peptide can selectively promote the clustering of αvβ5 integrins and thereby restore efficient POS clearance, it might not only improve retinal adhesion and photoreceptor survival but also mitigate secondary events such as lipofuscin accumulation and chronic inflammation that drive the progression of dry AMD (McGowan et al., 2022). In theory, such targeted modulation of the RPE microenvironment could offer a disease-modifying strategy rather than merely palliative treatment. Additionally, because tetraspanins like CD82 serve as molecular organizers with relatively high tissue specificity, an agonist peptide could potentially be engineered to have a favorable safety profile with minimal off-target systemic effects.

In weighing the strengths and weaknesses, it becomes clear that while the CD82 agonist peptide holds significant promise as a novel therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, its clinical potential remains largely theoretical at this stage. The mechanism by which tetraspanin activation could enhance αvβ5 integrin clustering is supported by indirect evidence from studies in cancer cells and other non-ocular tissues (Luan et al., 2018). However, the translation of these findings to the RPE, which is both highly polarized and functionally unique, requires additional targeted investigation. Future studies should focus on validating the expression and functional activation of CD82 in RPE cells from both healthy donors and AMD patients, as well as on conducting mechanistic experiments to determine the precise impact of the agonist peptide on integrin clustering and phagocytic cup formation. In vitro assays using cultured RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary human RPE) should be complemented by in vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD to assess whether the peptide can indeed restore or enhance POS clearance and thereby ameliorate retinal degeneration (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012).

An additional aspect to consider is the potential for unexpected off-target effects. Given that CD82 is involved in a variety of cellular processes—including those related to cell adhesion, migration, and even immune modulation—the systemic administration of a CD82 agonist peptide might affect multiple cell types beyond the RPE (McGowan et al., 2022). Therefore, an effective delivery strategy that confines the peptide’s activity to the retina (for example, via intravitreal injection or a controlled-release ocular implant) may be essential for maximizing its therapeutic index. Drug formulation studies, as well as preliminary toxicology assessments, will be crucial in determining whether the peptide achieves the necessary balance between efficacy and safety.

In conclusion, the CD82 agonist peptide (Peptide Institute Cat. No. K-8202) is a novel therapeutic candidate that harnesses the unique properties of tetraspanin CD82 to potentially enhance αvβ5 integrin clustering in RPE membranes. This mechanism is hypothesized to lead to improved phagocytic cup assembly and POS internalization, addressing a key pathogenic process in dry AMD. The candidate belongs to a class of peptide-based modulators that have been historically evaluated for their roles in regulating cell adhesion and migration in cancer, but its application in the context of retinal phagocytosis is largely uncharted. The evidence supporting the role of CD82 in integrin modulation is robust in non-ocular systems (Lee et al., 2022), and there is clear evidence for the importance of αvβ5 integrin in RPE phagocytosis (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). Nonetheless, the direct demonstration that activation of CD82 via an agonist peptide enhances integrin clustering and phagocytic efficiency in RPE cells is currently lacking, and the majority of published studies have demonstrated inhibitory effects of CD82 peptides in different contexts (Luan et al., 2018).

The overall evaluation of this therapeutic candidate is thus twofold. On the one hand, the mechanistic rationale is scientifically intriguing and represents a targeted, innovative approach that aligns with our current understanding of RPE biology and AMD pathogenesis. On the other hand, the candidate’s novelty in the ocular field means that there is a significant gap in the preclinical validation required to confidently predict efficacy in dry AMD. Strengths of the candidate include its potential for receptor-specific modulation, the possibility of restoring natural phagocytic function in the RPE, and the prospect of achieving a disease-modifying effect by targeting a fundamental cellular process. Weaknesses include the lack of direct experimental evidence in RPE models, the possibility that the peptide may exhibit inhibitory rather than stimulatory effects on integrin function as observed in cancer-related studies, and the inherent challenges of peptide-based drug delivery to the retina.

Ultimately, while the CD82 agonist peptide holds considerable promise based on mechanistic reasoning and a growing body of literature that supports the central role of tetraspanins in cellular organization and integrin function (Lee et al., 2022; Bhatwadekar et al., 2020), further rigorous studies are needed. These should include in vitro assays in RPE cell cultures to quantify changes in integrin clustering and phagocytic cup assembly, followed by in vivo evaluations in animal models that recapitulate the pathological features of dry AMD (Lee et al., 2022; McGowan et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human Protein S, also known as Pros1, is a naturally occurring vitamin K–dependent plasma glycoprotein that functions both as an anticoagulant and as a ligand for members of the TAM (Tyro3/Axl/Mer) receptor family. Its biological origins trace back to its purification from human plasma, with early characterizations dating to its discovery in the late 1970s, and over time it has been elucidated to play critical roles not only in blood coagulation but also in efferocytosis and cellular clearance mechanisms. The recombinant form is synthesized using modern expression systems under strict good manufacturing practice (GMP) conditions, ensuring batch‐to‐batch consistency and purity for research and potential clinical applications. Protein S belongs to the therapeutic class of biologics, and like other recombinant proteins, it is designed to mimic the endogenous molecule’s activity. This class of compounds has historically been applied in contexts ranging from coagulation regulation to modulation of immune responses in inflammatory settings, with Protein S specifically recognized for its ability to act as a bridging molecule between apoptotic cells and phagocytes by binding phosphatidylserine via its N‐terminal Gla domain and engaging TAM receptors through its C‐terminal domains (Rothlin et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Protein S has been extensively studied for its role as an anticoagulant in hemostasis, where it potentiates activated protein C to inhibit coagulation factors and maintain vascular homeostasis. In addition to its role in the coagulation cascade, Protein S also exerts non‐coagulation effects through its function as a ligand for TAM receptors, particularly MerTK and Tyro3. Over the past two decades, biochemical and cell-based studies have highlighted its ability to facilitate efferocytosis in macrophages and retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells by bridging phosphatidylserine on apoptotic cell surfaces to MerTK receptors, thereby promoting internalization and clearance (Lumbroso et al., 2018; Lemke, 2015). In the context of retinal biology, several published reports have demonstrated that Protein S stimulates photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis by RPE cells. For instance, studies have shown a dose-dependent stimulatory effect of Protein S on RPE phagocytosis, with evidence that its expression follows a circadian bimodal rhythm matching the peak of phagocytic activity in the retina (Nandrot, 2018). Although the majority of therapeutic uses of Protein S have been traditionally focused on coagulation or its immunomodulatory roles, its involvement in retinal maintenance—particularly the clearance of spent photoreceptor outer segments—has made it an intriguing candidate for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). To date, however, there are no reports of clinical use of recombinant human Protein S in dry AMD or similar retinal diseases, and its potential remains evaluated only in preclinical RPE and in vivo models (Parinot et al., 2024; Lumbroso et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic activity of Protein S in this context hinges on its well-characterized molecular interaction with cell-surface receptors in the TAM family, particularly MerTK. Protein S contains a gamma-carboxylated N-terminal Gla domain that confers Ca²⁺-dependent binding to phosphatidylserine (PtdSer), an “eat-me” signal externalized on apoptotic cells and discarded photoreceptor outer segments. Once bound to PtdSer, Protein S serves as a bridging molecule by engaging with immunoglobulin-like domains on the extracellular portion of the MerTK receptor via its C-terminal SHBG (sex hormone-binding globulin) domains (Lemke, 2015; Lumbroso et al., 2018). This ligand–receptor interaction induces MerTK dimerization and subsequent trans-autophosphorylation of its intracellular kinase domains, thereby triggering downstream signaling cascades essential for phagocytosis. The activated receptor recruits adaptor proteins such as Vav and components of the p130Cas/CrkII/Dock180 complex, which ultimately leads to the activation of the Rho family GTPase Rac. Rac activation triggers the WAVE regulatory complex and subsequent Arp2/3-mediated actin polymerization, ultimately driving the membrane remodeling necessary for engulfing outer segments (Dransfield et al., 2015; Nandrot, 2018).

Importantly, recent mechanistic studies have suggested that Protein S and Gas6, another TAM ligand, can have opposing roles in RPE phagocytosis. Evidence indicates that while Protein S acts as a stimulatory ligand for MerTK-mediated phagocytosis (enhancing binding and internalization of POS), Gas6 may exert inhibitory effects by promoting the cleavage of the extracellular domain of MerTK, thereby generating a soluble receptor (sMerTK) that acts as a decoy (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). Site-directed mutagenesis experiments have further revealed that Protein S and Gas6 recognize distinct amino acid residues on the Ig-like domains of MerTK, supporting the idea that Protein S might preferentially activate MerTK via a unique binding mode that minimizes receptor cleavage and sustains intracellular signaling for effective phagocytosis (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). Additionally, experimental data indicate that Protein S alone may be sufficient to elicit phagocytosis by RPE cells, which is an essential feature given that genetic knockout studies show that mice lacking both ligands exhibit severe retinal degeneration similar to that observed in MerTK-deficient models (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). The differential temporal expression of Protein S relative to Gas6—where Protein S levels increase just before and during the phagocytic peak in the interphotoreceptor matrix—further supports its specialized role in ensuring precise circadian regulation of phagocytosis by RPE cells (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the above mechanistic insights, it is hypothesized that exogenous administration of recombinant human Protein S at a concentration of 5 µg/mL will strongly stimulate MerTK-mediated phagocytosis in RPE cells. In vitro, this therapeutic intervention is expected to enhance both the binding and internalization phases of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake. The anticipated experimental outcome is a robust increase in phagocytic activity in RPE cell culture models, which are typically used to recapitulate the phagocytosis defects observed in dry AMD—where impaired clearance of POS contributes to accumulation of toxic debris and subsequent retinal degeneration (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). Mechanistically, the addition of exogenous Protein S is expected to reduce the cleavage of membrane-bound MerTK, thereby maintaining high levels of active receptor on the RPE surface; this effect is crucial since increased soluble MerTK (sMerTK) has been associated with decreased phagocytic efficiency (Parinot et al., 2024; Lieffrig et al., 2023). In models of MERTK mutation, which mimic aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis, Protein S supplementation has been shown to rescue defective phagocytosis, thus restoring the internalization of outer segments to near-normal levels (Parinot et al., 2024). Since the normal functioning RPE relies on a finely balanced interplay between multiple phagocytic signals—including those mediated by integrins and other bridging molecules such as MFG-E8—the specific targeting of MerTK activation by Protein S is expected to complement these pathways without triggering competing inhibitory signals from Gas6, which has been reported to have higher affinity for MerTK but may paradoxically inhibit phagocytosis through enhanced receptor cleavage (Parinot et al., 2024).

Furthermore, the proposed biological activity is supported by the temporal and spatial expression patterns observed in vivo; Protein S is not only produced by RPE cells but also by photoreceptors themselves, and its rhythmic expression in the interphotoreceptor matrix suggests that it is naturally poised to regulate the daily burst of phagocytosis required for photoreceptor maintenance (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). The anticipated improvement in phagocytic clearance is expected to alleviate the accumulation of POS debris—a key pathogenic feature implicated in the progression of dry AMD—and may also reduce the resultant inflammatory milieu that contributes to RPE atrophy and photoreceptor demise (Nandrot, 2018; Lumbroso et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall potential of recombinant human Protein S as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is promising but not without challenges. One key strength lies in the fundamental and evolutionarily conserved role of Protein S in mediating efferocytosis and phagocytosis through MerTK activation; this function is particularly critical in the RPE, where continuous clearance of photoreceptor outer segments is essential for retinal homeostasis (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). The existing preclinical literature provides strong support that Protein S has a stimulatory effect on POS phagocytosis by RPE cells and that its loss or dysregulation is associated with pathogenic retinal changes that mirror those seen in dry AMD (Lumbroso et al., 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). In addition, the fact that recombinant human Protein S is GMP-manufacturable with favorable pharmacokinetic properties increases its attractiveness as a candidate for intravitreal or subretinal delivery, which allows for highly localized therapeutic effects while minimizing systemic exposure and potential off-target bleeding risks that might be associated with its role in coagulation (Lemke, 2015; Rothlin et al., 2015).

Another significant strength is the mechanistic rationale suggesting that Protein S, unlike Gas6, may preferentially activate MerTK without inducing deleterious receptor cleavage. Studies have demonstrated that while Gas6 can inhibit RPE phagocytosis by augmenting the cleavage of MerTK’s extracellular domain and generating a decoy receptor, Protein S acts to reduce this cleavage and thereby preserve receptor-mediated signaling necessary for efficient phagocytosis (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). Furthermore, protein engineering and mutagenesis studies indicate that the unique binding determinants utilized by Protein S may be exploited to design therapeutic strategies that selectively amplify beneficial signaling cascades in the diseased retina (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024).

Notwithstanding these promising aspects, there are notable weaknesses and uncertainties that must be addressed in further preclinical development. One major concern is the complex interplay between Gas6 and Protein S in modulating MerTK activity. Several studies have indicated that while Protein S is capable of stimulating phagocytosis, Gas6 is expressed at substantially higher levels in retinal tissues and might dominate the receptor activation milieu under certain conditions (Parinot et al., 2024). This raises the question of whether exogenously delivered Protein S can indeed override the inhibitory influence of endogenous Gas6 or if it must be co-administered with other agents to effectively shift the balance toward MerTK activation. Additionally, while the hypothesis is based on in vitro findings in cultured RPE cell models, the translation of these results into an in vivo setting remains uncertain given the heterogeneity and complex microenvironment of the retina in dry AMD, which involves oxidative stress, complement activation, and chronic inflammation (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024).

Another potential downside relates to the multifunctional nature of Protein S. Its well-established anticoagulant activity, while advantageous in managing thrombotic disorders, could pose a risk if systemic leakage occurs following ocular administration. Although intravitreal delivery is likely to confine the drug’s distribution to the eye, careful pharmacokinetic and toxicity studies are essential to ensure that any systemic absorption does not lead to bleeding complications or interfere with hemostasis elsewhere in the body (Lemke, 2015; Rothlin et al., 2015). Moreover, the exact composition and post-translational modifications of the recombinant protein must be meticulously controlled to maintain its intended bioactivity; for instance, the vitamin K–dependent gamma-carboxylation of the Gla domain is critical for its phosphatidylserine binding and subsequent receptor activation, and any perturbation in this process during manufacturing could compromise its therapeutic efficacy (Rothlin et al., 2015; Tasnim, 2020).

There is also the possibility that in the diseased state of dry AMD, RPE cells might have an altered responsiveness to TAM receptor ligands due to chronic oxidative damage or inflammatory insults, thereby diminishing the therapeutic effect of Protein S. Thus, while the restoration of phagocytosis by Protein S appears mechanistically sound in controlled cell culture systems, its real-world impact on rescuing retinal function and halting disease progression will depend on the ability to deliver the protein at effective concentrations and for sustained durations. In addition, optimal dosing studies are needed to determine whether 5 µg/mL is indeed the best concentration for stimulating phagocytosis in damaged RPE cells, as pharmacodynamic variability among patients could require individualized dosing regimens (Parinot et al., 2024).

In summary, recombinant human Protein S represents a novel and highly rational approach for addressing the impaired phagocytosis observed in dry age-related macular degeneration. Its biological function as a MerTK ligand and its ability to rescue phagocytic deficits in RPE models are compelling, and the mechanistic differentiation from Gas6 provides a unique therapeutic avenue that could potentially restore the delicate balance of photoreceptor outer segment turnover in the retina (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024; Lemke, 2015). The strengths of the candidate include its endogenous nature, the availability of robust recombinant production methods, and a solid mechanistic framework that implicates preferential MerTK activation as a means to boost phagocytosis. Conversely, the weaknesses center on the uncertain dominance of Protein S over Gas6 in a complex in vivo environment, potential off-target effects related to its anticoagulant activity, and the challenges inherent in translating in vitro RPE cell model data into effective clinical outcomes in patients with dry AMD.

Given the current literature, further detailed preclinical studies are warranted to assess the efficacy of recombinant human Protein S in appropriate animal models of dry AMD, to optimize dosing strategies, and to address any safety concerns that may arise from its systemic pharmacology. Nonetheless, the mechanistic data supporting its role in promoting the clearance of photoreceptor debris and in potentially mitigating the downstream inflammatory responses that drive RPE degeneration suggest that this candidate holds considerable promise for inclusion in the therapeutic pipeline targeting dry AMD (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). The overall evaluation is that while there is substantial preclinical mechanistic support for the use of recombinant Protein S in stimulating MerTK-mediated POS phagocytosis and rescuing RPE function, careful further experimentation is essential to validate these findings in clinically relevant settings before committing to a full clinical development program.
