Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The anti‐HtrA1 monoclonal antibody under evaluation is a biologic therapeutic candidate developed through advanced recombinant antibody engineering, and its design is predicated on targeting the extracellular serine protease HtrA1, which has been implicated in the pathology of age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). This candidate originates from rational immunization and humanization processes whereby immunized mice (or phage‐display derived libraries) were used to identify and optimize clones that inhibit HtrA1 with high affinity (Kd < 10 nM), thereby ensuring selective binding to its proteolytic domain. The antibody belongs to the class of therapeutic monoclonal antibodies, a group of compounds that have been widely deployed in various inflammatory, oncologic, and degenerative disease states owing to their specificity and ability to modulate cellular microenvironments by neutralizing key mediators; indeed, similar agents have been successfully used to modulate extracellular protease activities in other disorders (Tom et al., 2020). The candidate’s design specifically aims to neutralize excess extracellular HtrA1 activity, thereby preserving the integrity of cell surface receptors such as integrin and CD36 on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Given that the degradation of these receptors impairs the recognition, binding, and subsequent receptor-mediated uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), the antibody is intended to maintain normal phagocytic function in RPE through its targeted blockade of pathological HtrA1 activity (Oura et al., 2018; Tom et al., 2020; Dere et al., 2021). The investigational product, reportedly in clinical evaluation by Novartis in the context of dry AMD and exemplified by its progression into Phase II trial design under the GALLEGO study, exemplifies the translational potential of antibody-based inhibition strategies in ocular degenerative conditions (Asahi et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Anti‐HtrA1 monoclonal antibodies represent a novel therapeutic modality with a unique mechanism relative to classic anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents. Preclinical investigations have provided compelling evidence that aberrant HtrA1 expression contributes to the pathogenesis of AMD through multiple interrelated processes including extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, induction of photoreceptor apoptosis, and interference with receptor function on RPE cells (Oura et al., 2018). Notably, animal models – including zebrafish systems – have demonstrated that HtrA1 overexpression in rod photoreceptors induces retinal morphological changes that recapitulate early AMD features, such as lipofuscin accumulation and photoreceptor structural aberrations; pharmacological inhibition of HtrA1 in these models led to partial rescue of the apoptotic phenotype, thereby validating HtrA1 as a therapeutic target (Oura et al., 2018). In parallel, other preclinical studies have shown that anti‐HtrA1 antibodies, such as the antigen-binding fragment FHTR2163, effectively inhibit HtrA1’s protease activity in in vitro cleavage assays with substrates such as Dickkopf-related protein 3 (DKK3); this observation was further corroborated through in vivo studies in cynomolgus monkeys and rabbits, where intravitreal administration resulted in dose-dependent inhibition of DKK3 cleavage, a phenomenon that served as a robust pharmacodynamic marker (Tom et al., 2020; Khanani et al., 2021). Clinical evaluation of anti-HtrA1 therapy for geographic atrophy (GA), the advanced stage of dry AMD, began with Phase I studies that demonstrated acceptable ocular safety, manageable adverse event profiles, and evidence of target engagement using aqueous humor biomarker assessments (Khanani et al., 2021). However, it is also important to note that emerging literature has raised potential concerns; for example, some studies have reported that in donors with homozygous AMD risk alleles at the chromosome 10q26 locus, HTRA1 mRNA and protein levels in RPE tissue are reduced relative to non-risk donors, suggesting that—at least in some patient subgroups—HtrA1 may be protective rather than purely pathogenic (Williams et al., 2021). Consequently, the therapeutic history of anti-HtrA1 agents for AMD is marked by both promising preclinical and early-phase clinical safety data as well as unresolved controversies regarding patient stratification and the precise role of HtrA1 in disease progression (Tom et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, HtrA1 is a multifunctional serine protease that is secreted into the extracellular space and possesses the capability to degrade multiple ECM proteins and regulatory molecules that are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis. Its proteolytic activity has been implicated in cleaving latent transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) binding proteins, such as latent TGF-β binding protein-1 (LTBP-1), which in turn facilitates dysregulated TGF-β signaling and promotes pro-apoptotic pathways through downstream effectors such as AKT and FOXO (Oura et al., 2018). Additionally, HtrA1’s substrates include proteins involved in the structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane, such as fibronectin, elastin, and other ECM components, and emerging data also suggest that it may cleave cell surface receptors like CD36, thereby directly impairing RPE function in the uptake of lipid-rich photoreceptor outer segments (He et al., 2022; Oura et al., 2018).  
The therapeutic candidate under discussion has been engineered to bind with high affinity to the catalytic domain of HtrA1, forming a “cage-like” inhibition complex that sterically hinders substrate access and completely abrogates its protease activity (Tom et al., 2020). This binding not only prevents the deleterious cleavage of ECM components but also protects important cell surface receptors, including integrin and CD36, from enzymatic degradation. Integrin receptors have been implicated in maintaining the proper adhesion and signaling functions of the RPE, while CD36 plays a crucial role in the recognition and phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments; preserving these receptors is therefore essential to sustaining the normal turnover of POS and preventing photoreceptor degeneration (Oura et al., 2018; Tom et al., 2020). In vitro studies have confirmed that this antibody can effectively inhibit the proteolytic cleavage of DKK3—a known substrate of HtrA1—thus providing a direct measure of target engagement and serving as an important pharmacodynamic biomarker in early clinical assessments (Tom et al., 2020). Moreover, biochemical analyses indicate that the antibody’s binding affinity (with Kd values well below 10 nM) is sufficient to compete with endogenous substrates, ensuring that even low levels of HtrA1 activity are neutralized (Tom et al., 2020). This detailed molecular mode of action underpins the rationale for expecting that inhibition of HtrA1 will restore receptor integrity on RPE cells, thereby normalizing receptor-mediated POS binding and uptake (Oura et al., 2018; Tom et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its mechanism of action, it is anticipated that administration of the anti-HtrA1 monoclonal antibody will result in a cascade of protective effects within the retinal microenvironment that are critical for slowing the progression of dry AMD. The foremost expected outcome is a robust inhibition of HtrA1’s protease activity, as evidenced by a reduction in the proteolytic fragments of key substrates such as DKK3 in the aqueous humor. This reduced substrate cleavage is expected to correlate with enhanced preservation of the structural integrity of extracellular matrix components in Bruch’s membrane and with the maintenance of the cell surface integrity of RPE receptors such as integrin and CD36 (Tom et al., 2020). In preclinical models, inhibition of HtrA1 has been shown to rescue photoreceptor cells from apoptosis and to ameliorate morphological features reminiscent of early AMD, such as lipofuscin accumulation and disorganized photoreceptor outer segments (Oura et al., 2018). The hypothesis underlying the proposed mechanism is that by preventing the degradation of these crucial receptors, the RPE will maintain its natural phagocytic efficiency—specifically, its ability to bind and internalize photoreceptor outer segments, a process essential for the renewal and proper function of the photoreceptor layer (Oura et al., 2018; He et al., 2022).  
In addition, it is expected that the antibody will indirectly modulate pro-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic signaling cascades. HtrA1-mediated ECM breakdown and receptor degradation have been implicated in the activation of inflammatory pathways, which can lead to aberrant VEGF expression and neovascular complications in AMD (Lu et al., 2019). The preservation of integrin and CD36 receptor availability is particularly significant in this context because it ensures the RPE’s ability to perform its routine phagocytic clearance of POS debris, a process that, when compromised, is known to lead to the accumulation of toxic byproducts that exacerbate retinal degeneration (Oura et al., 2018; Tom et al., 2020). Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the anti-HtrA1 monoclonal antibody candidate for dry AMD represents a promising therapeutic strategy, with its strengths rooted in a clear genetic, biochemical, and preclinical rationale. The candidate is supported by compelling evidence that HtrA1 overexpression contributes to RPE dysfunction and photoreceptor cell death via ECM remodeling, receptor cleavage, and dysregulated TGF-β signaling, all of which are critical hallmarks of AMD pathogenesis (Oura et al., 2018; Tom et al., 2020). Its high binding affinity (Kd below 10 nM) ensures potent and specific blockade of HtrA1’s proteolytic activity, and preclinical studies have repeatedly demonstrated that inhibition of HtrA1 can lead to measurable improvements in retinal structure and function, including the preservation of phagocytic receptor integrity on RPE cells (Tom et al., 2020). Early clinical studies have provided encouraging safety and pharmacodynamic data, including the demonstration of dose-dependent reductions in DKK3 cleavage in the ocular compartment, which serves as a reproducible biomarker of target engagement (Khanani et al., 2021).

However, the candidate also faces notable challenges and uncertainties that must be carefully considered as part of the overall development strategy. One significant concern arises from a body of literature which documents that in certain genetically predisposed populations—specifically, those carrying risk alleles at the chromosome 10q26 locus—the expression of HtrA1 in RPE tissues is paradoxically reduced, suggesting that HtrA1 may have a protective or homeostatic role in these contexts (Williams et al., 2021). This dichotomy raises the possibility that a “one-size-fits-all” inhibition strategy may not be appropriate for all patient subgroups, and that detailed molecular phenotyping or patient stratification might be necessary to identify those individuals in whom HtrA1 activity is pathologically elevated rather than diminished. In other words, while anti-HtrA1 inhibition appears beneficial in models characterized by HtrA1 overexpression, it could potentially be detrimental in patients with inherently low HtrA1 levels where further suppression might compromise baseline ECM maintenance and RPE health (Williams et al., 2021; Filliat, 2017).

Furthermore, while the mechanistic rationale involving receptor preservation (integrin and CD36) and the normalization of POS binding is sound and supported by preclinical observations, direct evidence demonstrating improved receptor-mediated phagocytosis in clinical settings remains limited. Although early-phase studies have shown effective neutralization of HtrA1 and corresponding reductions in DKK3 cleavage, it is yet to be definitively established whether these biochemical endpoints translate into meaningful functional improvements in RPE phagocytic capacity and overall retinal health. The preliminary Phase I data are reassuring regarding safety and tolerability; however, efficacy endpoints from larger, longer-term Phase II or Phase III trials will ultimately be needed to validate the clinical benefit of this approach. Moreover, while the current hypothesis specifically targets the preservation of integrin and CD36 receptor integrity, further studies are required to conclusively delineate the interplay between HtrA1 inhibition, receptor restoration, and the normalization of POS binding and uptake (Oura et al., 2018; Tom et al., 2020).

In conclusion, the anti-HtrA1 monoclonal antibody candidate represents one of the most promising repurposed therapeutic strategies for dry AMD currently under investigation. Its design is underpinned by robust scientific rationale and early-phase data that support its potential to mitigate key pathogenic processes—including ECM degradation, receptor cleavage, and inflammation—that are central to AMD progression (Tom et al., 2020; Khanani et al., 2021). The high binding affinity and demonstrated pharmacodynamic effects set a solid foundation for further development. Nonetheless, the conflicting evidence regarding HtrA1 expression in different patient subgroups, along with uncertainties about the direct impact on RPE function and clinical outcomes, highlight the need for rigorous patient selection and further mechanistic studies. Overall, while the candidate shows substantial promise, its ultimate success will depend on confirming that HtrA1 inhibition results in functional benefits for RPE phagocytosis and retinal integrity without adversely affecting the protective aspects of HtrA1 in certain populations (Williams et al., 2021; Tom et al., 2020). Future clinical trials with well-defined inclusion criteria and comprehensive biomarker assessments will be essential to resolve these controversies and to realize the full therapeutic potential of anti-HtrA1 monoclonal antibodies in the treatment of dry AMD.

Historically, rapamycin has been extensively used and investigated in various clinical and preclinical settings. Its initial clinical use as an immunosuppressive agent in organ transplant patients laid the groundwork for understanding its mechanisms of action and safety profile in humans. Beyond its immunosuppressive applications, rapamycin has been evaluated for its anti-proliferative effects in several types of cancer and for its capability to extend lifespan in model organisms; these studies underscore the drug’s pleiotropic effects on cellular metabolism and autophagy. Specifically regarding ocular therapeutics, preclinical studies on retinal degenerative diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa and glaucoma have demonstrated that mTOR modulation by rapamycin can exert neuroprotective properties in retinal tissues (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). In the realm of AMD, several investigations have focused on the role of autophagy and lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in RPE cells, where rapamycin has been shown to promote autophagy and decrease the buildup of toxic aggregates, such as lipofuscin (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical studies and safety evaluations—in particular, intravitreal injections in non-human primates—have provided encouraging data regarding the ocular safety profile of rapamycin, thus supporting its further exploration as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2022).

At the molecular level, rapamycin exerts its effects by binding to the intracellular receptor FKBP12 (FK506-binding protein 12). This drug–FKBP12 complex then interacts with mTORC1, leading to its allosteric inhibition. Under normal anabolic conditions, active mTORC1 phosphorylates several downstream targets, including the transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is sequestered in the cytosol in its phosphorylated state, thus preventing the transcription of genes associated with lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. When rapamycin inhibits mTORC1, the phosphorylation of TFEB is reduced, permitting its nuclear translocation. Once inside the nucleus, TFEB initiates the transcription of numerous genes involved in autophagy and lysosomal function, thereby enhancing the cell’s capacity to degrade and recycle cellular debris such as accumulated photoreceptor outer segments (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium, mTORC1 normally integrates growth factor signals, nutrient availability, and stress responses to tightly regulate cellular homeostasis. The inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin thus releases the “brake” on autophagy, as evidenced by increased expression of autophagic markers such as LC3-II and lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1. This cascading effect leads to an enhanced intracellular clearance system (phagolysosomal flux), which is particularly critical for RPE cells that are responsible for the daily degradation of shed POS. Several studies have demonstrated that rapamycin-treated RPE cells exhibit improved POS degradation, a reduction in lipofuscin-like granules, and overall restoration of lysosomal function (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, the molecular signatures observed in rapamycin-treated cells mimic those seen under conditions of caloric restriction, further supporting the notion that mTORC1 inhibition can activate protective autophagic pathways (Davis, 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). This advanced understanding of rapamycin’s mechanism of action provides a compelling rationale for its application in dry AMD, where the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and dysregulated autophagy are key pathological features (Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of rapamycin in dry AMD is that its inhibition of mTORC1 will lead to the activation of TFEB by reducing its cytosolic phosphorylation state, thereby promoting nuclear translocation. In iPSC-derived RPE models, this induction of TFEB activity is expected to upregulate a host of autophagy and lysosomal genes, which in turn should enhance the cellular degradation of photoreceptor outer segments—an essential process in maintaining retinal homeostasis (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025). Accordingly, the anticipated in vitro effects upon rapamycin treatment include a robust increase in autophagic flux evidenced by elevated levels of LC3-II and LAMP1, paired with improved processing and clearance of POS debris. This effect is crucial because impaired clearance mechanisms contribute to the accumulation of lipofuscin and other cellular waste materials in RPE cells, both of which are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Falcão et al., 2024).

Supporting this expected outcome are observations from previous studies where rapamycin has been associated with a reduction in autofluorescent granules and a restoration of normal cellular clearance dynamics in RPE cells (Falcão et al., 2024). Additionally, safety assessments performed through intravitreal administration in non-human primates have demonstrated that rapamycin can be delivered to the retina with minimal adverse events, thereby underpinning its feasibility for clinical translation (Falcão et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2022). Importantly, the hypothesis that rapamycin can act at IC₅₀ values as low as approximately 0.1 nM in RPE cells further reinforces the potential sensitivity and efficacy of this candidate in modulating the pathway of interest. Given the expression of mTOR, TFEB, LC3, and LAMP1 in RPE cells—and the established role of these proteins in the autophagic and lysosomal clearance of POS—the expected improvement in autophagic turnover should directly translate into enhanced cell function and potentially mitigate the progression of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2022; Intartaglia et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
Rapamycin emerges as a robust and mechanistically sound therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its established ability to inhibit mTORC1 and consequently activate autophagy and lysosomal gene expression through TFEB nuclear translocation. One of the major strengths of this candidate lies in the well-characterized molecular mechanism that connects mTORC1 inhibition with enhanced clearance of POS debris—a process that is fundamentally disrupted in dry AMD. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence, ranging from biochemical assays that show increased LC3-II and LAMP1 expression in rapamycin-treated RPE cells to preclinical safety data in non-human primates, bolsters confidence in its potential utility (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

Furthermore, the multifaceted benefits of mTORC1 inhibition extend beyond autophagy induction; rapamycin also offers neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects, both of which are advantageous in the treatment of retinal degenerative diseases (Chang et al., 2022). The leverage of TFEB activation not only addresses the aberrant accumulation of toxic cellular debris but may also promote a broader upregulation of lysosomal biogenesis, thereby preempting further functional decline of RPE cells. These properties make rapamycin a strong candidate for mitigating early events in AMD pathogenesis, particularly in the context of experimental iPSC-RPE models where enhanced phagocytic capacity can be directly measured.

Nevertheless, several challenges and potential weaknesses require careful consideration. Despite its promising mechanism and preclinical rationale, clinical trials evaluating rapamycin in the context of ocular diseases have yielded mixed results, with some studies documenting only marginal improvements in visual function and others noting issues related to the drug’s solubility and delivery (Marchesi et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022). In advanced AMD, where the disease pathology is more complex and multifactorial, rapamycin’s efficacy might be limited, and there is a need for precise dosing strategies to balance mTORC1 inhibition with the preservation of physiological mTOR functions that are crucial for RPE cell survival (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). Additionally, the potential for off-target effects or immunosuppressive consequences linked to systemic exposure—although minimized by intravitreal delivery—necessitates further investigation into long-term safety profiles (Wang et al., 2022).

Another potential limitation is the inherent complexity of autophagy regulation in the RPE, which can be influenced by factors such as oxidative stress, metabolic dysfunction, and age-related changes in lysosomal function. While rapamycin is effective in reactivating autophagic pathways under controlled experimental settings, its impact within the pathogenic environment of a diseased retina, particularly if inflammatory processes are simultaneously active, may be less predictable (Davis, 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, the therapeutic window for achieving beneficial rapamycin concentrations without incurring adverse events is not yet fully defined, underscoring the importance of pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic studies specifically tailored to ocular tissues (Falcão et al., 2024).

Taken together, the current body of evidence suggests that rapamycin’s capacity to restore autophagic homeostasis in RPE cells represents a solid mechanistic foundation for its use in dry AMD. Its ability to upregulate autophagy and lysosomal function through TFEB activation directly addresses known defects in the clearance pathways of RPE cells—a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Moreover, the safety data from preclinical intravitreal delivery studies provide additional incentive to advance this candidate further along the translational pipeline. However, given the mixed outcomes observed in some clinical contexts and the challenges related to drug formulation and optimal dosing, further comprehensive studies are warranted to clarify its efficacy in early versus advanced stages of AMD (Mei et al., 2022).

In conclusion, rapamycin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD shows significant promise from both a mechanistic and translational standpoint. Its well-documented ability to inhibit mTORC1, thereby releasing TFEB and ramping up autophagic and lysosomal gene expression, positions it uniquely to tackle the underpinnings of RPE dysfunction characteristic of dry AMD. While preclinical data support its efficacy and safety with intravitreal administration in non-human primates, challenges remain regarding its formulation, potential off-target effects, and the delineation of its therapeutic window in human subjects. Consequently, while rapamycin’s molecular mechanism and early experimental results are highly encouraging, further studies—especially those that integrate pharmacokinetic profiling, dose optimization, and long-term outcome measurements in relevant in vivo models—are essential before definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding its clinical utility for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Si et al., 2023).

Overall, the strengths of rapamycin include its robust and well-characterized action on mTORC1, its downstream activation of autophagic and lysosomal pathways via TFEB, and supportive preclinical safety data in ocular models. In contrast, its weaknesses lie in the variable efficacy observed in clinical studies, formulation challenges due to low solubility, and the need for careful dosing to avoid potential adverse effects related to systemic immunosuppression. These considerations collectively argue for the continued investigation of rapamycin as a therapeutic option for dry AMD with a focus on optimizing delivery strategies and characterizing its long-term impact on retinal structure and function (Wang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Axitinib is a synthetic, indazole-based, small-molecule receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor originally discovered via medicinal chemistry optimization for anti-angiogenic oncology indications and subsequently approved as an oral therapy (Inlyta) for advanced renal cell carcinoma, reflecting high potency and selectivity for vascular endothelial growth factor receptors (VEGFR1–3) with additional activity against PDGFR-β and c-KIT (Fei et al., 2024; Tosi et al., 2017). In biochemical and cellular assays relevant to ocular angiogenesis, axitinib demonstrates pan-VEGFR inhibition with substantially greater sensitivity than anti-VEGF monoclonal antibodies in endothelial cells, and it also inhibits PDGFR-β–mediated signaling in pericytes at low nanomolar concentrations, consistent with dual-pathway blockade within the VEGF/PDGF axis (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Pharmacologically, oral axitinib exhibits a short plasma half-life (~2.5–6.1 h) requiring twice-daily systemic dosing in oncology, and class-typical adverse events are dominated by hypertension; these PK/AE features motivated ocular delivery strategies to achieve high intraocular exposure with minimal systemic spillover (Siedlecki et al., 2017). As a class, multi-targeted VEGFR/PDGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have long been deployed systemically for cancer and are being repurposed for ocular neovascular diseases with the goals of broader VEGF-pathway suppression and reduced injection burden via sustained intraocular delivery platforms (suprachoroidal suspensions, intravitreal depot implants, and bioresorbable hydrogel systems) (Fabre et al., 2022; Fei et al., 2024). Axitinib is notable among TKIs for very high VEGFR affinity and measurable inhibition of other angiogenesis-related kinases, including TIE2, which has implications for both efficacy breadth and potential effects on vascular stability in the retina and choroid (Leitch et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical ocular data consistently show axitinib suppresses choroidal and retinal neovascularization across models, with oral dosing at 5 mg/kg reducing laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (L-CNV) in mice, and continuous low-dose systemic infusion (0.875 mg/day for 7 days) decreasing fluorescein leakage and CNV lesion area in rats; in vitro, axitinib suppresses 3D sprouting and inhibits both endothelial and pericyte proliferation/migration at non-toxic concentrations, aligning with dual VEGFR/PDGFR blockade (Fei et al., 2024; Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In a rat L-CNV model, axitinib reduced FA leakage scores and CNV lesion area by approximately one-third versus vehicle, and in co-culture sprouting assays axitinib alone outperformed anti-VEGF and anti-PDGF combinations, reinforcing the mechanistic rationale for dual-pathway inhibition in pathological ocular angiogenesis (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Combinatorial approaches show synergy: co-administration with anti-VEGF antibodies enhanced anti-angiogenic effects in nonclinical studies, consistent with the broader concept that inhibiting pericyte/PDGFR-β support can potentiate VEGF-directed therapy (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Siedlecki et al., 2017).

Multiple ocular delivery strategies for axitinib have entered human investigation in neovascular AMD (nAMD) to address the treatment burden and durability limitations of intravitreal biologics, including a suprachoroidal injectable suspension (CLS-AX) and an intravitreal bioresorbable hydrogel implant (OTX-TKI) designed for 6–9 months of sustained release (Fei et al., 2024). Early clinical and translational signals indicate that suprachoroidal delivery achieves high posterior segment exposure with minimal systemic levels, and initial phase 1/2a experience with CLS-AX in nAMD reported acceptable tolerability and pharmacologic activity at low doses, while OTX-TKI demonstrated favorable safety and durability in early cohorts (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020). Across the TKI class, parallel depot strategies (e.g., vorolanib in Durasert, sunitinib depots) have shown biologic activity and reduced treatment burden in nAMD, although some programs reported visual acuity tradeoffs or required rescue therapy at non-negligible rates, highlighting the need for careful dose, exposure, and target-selectivity optimization (Fei et al., 2024; Leitch et al., 2024).

Topical/eye-drop TKI programs (pazopanib, regorafenib, PAN-90806, acrizanib) underscore translational challenges: although preclinical topical dosing can reduce leakage and CNV thickness, multiple phase II programs failed to meet efficacy endpoints or were terminated due to insufficient posterior segment exposure and ocular safety issues such as reversible corneal haze with acrizanib, indicating that noninvasive delivery often cannot reproducibly attain therapeutic concentrations at the choroid/RPE in humans (Fei et al., 2024). Importantly, the available literature contains no reports of axitinib being tested clinically for dry AMD (geographic atrophy) or for enhancing RPE phagocytosis; the development history for axitinib and related VEGFR/PDGFR TKIs is focused on nAMD and other retinal vascular diseases, and reviews repeatedly note a lack of evidence for dry-AMD applications in this drug class to date (Fei et al., 2024). Furthermore, while localized ocular delivery is being pursued to mitigate systemic exposure, case reports of retinal adverse events during systemic axitinib therapy—including impaired retinal circulation, reversible retinal toxicity, and central retinal vein occlusion—require vigilance and thoughtful PK/PD design in ocular programs (Bakri et al., 2024). More broadly, despite active investigation of small molecules for AMD, reviews emphasize that no clinical success stories for small-molecule drugs in AMD (outside recently approved complement inhibitors for GA) have been established, underscoring translational risk for new mechanisms and reformulations (Fei et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Axitinib is a potent ATP-competitive inhibitor of VEGFR1 (FLT1), VEGFR2 (KDR), and VEGFR3 (FLT4), with additional inhibitory activity against PDGFR-β and c-KIT, thereby interrupting intracellular tyrosine kinase signaling downstream of multiple pro-angiogenic ligands, including VEGF-A/B/C/D and PDGF-B (Tosi et al., 2017; Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In relevant ocular cell types, axitinib inhibits VEGF-driven endothelial proliferation with markedly greater potency than anti-VEGF antibodies and exerts nanomolar inhibition of PDGF-driven pericyte proliferation, supporting the mechanistic premise that simultaneous disruption of endothelial and pericyte signaling can destabilize nascent pathological vessels and reduce neovascular growth (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In 3D co-culture sprouting models that recapitulate endothelial–pericyte interactions, axitinib alone achieves robust inhibition of sprout number and length across low-nanomolar concentrations, matching or exceeding the effect of anti-VEGF plus anti-PDGF combinations, a pattern consistent with multi-receptor inhibition at the level of VEGFR/PDGFR RTKs (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Preclinical studies in retinal endothelial cells further demonstrate axitinib suppression of downstream MAPK/ERK signaling and oxidative stress markers, aligning with direct VEGFR pathway inhibition; limited in vitro reports also suggest reduction of VEGFR1/VEGFR2 and PDGFR-β phosphorylation in RPE or mixed cell models, though these do not extend to functional phagocytosis endpoints (Lazzara et al., 2024).

Mechanistically, axitinib’s kinase profile extends beyond VEGFR/PDGFR to other angiogenesis-modulating targets; notably, among three pan-VEGFR TKIs profiled preclinically (vorolanib, sunitinib, axitinib), only axitinib exhibited strong TIE2 inhibition, a pathway essential for vascular quiescence and stability that could influence choroidal and retinal vascular homeostasis under chronic intraocular exposure (Bakri et al., 2024). In comparative kinase panels and endothelial functional assays, all three TKIs displayed robust pan-VEGFR inhibition and abolished endothelial sprouting at high concentrations, but the TIE2-inhibitory signal was disproportionately strong for axitinib, suggesting type-specific off-target consequences that warrant consideration during dose selection for chronic ocular use (Bakri et al., 2024). While intravitreal biologics neutralize extracellular VEGF ligands, axitinib acts intracellularly to block receptor signaling, potentially addressing compensatory upregulation of VEGF-C/D observed with VEGF-A-only inhibition; however, the breadth of intracellular TKI targeting can also propagate off-target effects in non-endothelial cells if exposures are not carefully controlled (Leitch et al., 2024).

Delivery-route pharmacology is central to ocular mechanism realization: suprachoroidal injection of axitinib has demonstrated posterior-segment targeting with markedly elevated drug levels in the posterior eye cup versus intravitreal injection in rabbits and sustained RPE/choroid exposure with minimal systemic levels, thereby achieving compartmentalized receptor inhibition where angiogenic lesions and the RPE reside (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020). Complementary intravitreal hydrogel implant strategies (OTX-TKI) provide long-acting axitinib delivery (6–9 months), maintaining pharmacologically relevant intraocular concentrations to chronically suppress VEGFR/PDGFR signaling in nAMD; these platforms are designed to mitigate systemic adverse events while sustaining on-target ocular pharmacodynamics (Fei et al., 2024). Importantly, chronic VEGF pathway suppression carries theoretical risks for neurosensory retina and RPE health, and reviews emphasize the need to balance durable angiogenic control with potential adverse effects of continuous VEGF blockade in ocular tissues, particularly for non-neovascular indications (Wolf et al., 2022).

Therapeutic targets in the RPE relevant to the present hypothesis—MerTK and αvβ5 integrin—are core components of the photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytic machinery, with αvβ5 required for synchronized diurnal phagocytosis and MerTK essential for engulfment and internalization; however, the provided literature contains no direct experimental evidence that axitinib upregulates MerTK or αvβ5 expression or function in RPE, nor that PDGFR-β signaling tonically suppresses RPE phagocytic differentiation in vivo (Tosi et al., 2017). Reviews and experimental summaries repeatedly state that available axitinib data focus on endothelial/pericyte targets and CNV models, and that no studies directly link axitinib to enhanced RPE POS uptake, MerTK activation, or αvβ5 integrin upregulation in dry AMD models or RPE cell assays (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). Therefore, while axitinib’s biochemical capacity to inhibit PDGFR-β could, in principle, modulate RPE phenotypes if PDGFR-β were a suppressive node in RPE phagocytic signaling, this mechanistic leap is not supported by direct evidence in the provided literature (Bakri et al., 2024; Fei et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The proposed assay hypothesis is that low-dose axitinib will modulate PDGFR-β signaling in RPE to promote a pro-phagocytic differentiation state, enhancing MerTK and αvβ5 expression and POS uptake; however, the body of evidence provided does not include direct demonstrations of axitinib increasing RPE phagocytosis, MerTK activation, or αvβ5 expression in vitro, ex vivo, or in vivo (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). Available data show that axitinib reduces VEGFR1/VEGFR2 and PDGFR-β phosphorylation in retinal endothelial systems and in limited contexts citing RPE/HUVEC cells, but these findings stop short of connecting PDGFR-β inhibition to increased RPE phagocytic function, and no POS ingestion assays, MerTK phosphorylation readouts, or αvβ5 functional binding assays are reported for axitinib in RPE (Lazzara et al., 2024). By contrast, the canonical RPE phagocytic apparatus depends on αvβ5-mediated POS binding and MerTK-mediated engulfment, with genetic ablation models establishing necessity; the literature here confirms this machinery but does not implicate PDGFR-β overactivation as a hindrance to RPE phagocytic differentiation nor demonstrate that TKIs restore phagocytosis in RPE (Tosi et al., 2017).

If the assay system relies on differentiating human RPE and measures POS uptake alongside MerTK and αvβ5 expression, axitinib’s expected on-target effects would be limited to PDGFR-β kinase inhibition in RPE if PDGFR-β is expressed and active under the assay conditions; nevertheless, there is no provided evidence that such inhibition increases MerTK or αvβ5 levels or POS ingestion, and the hypothesis that PDGFR-β tone suppresses RPE phagocytosis remains unsubstantiated here (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). It is conceivable that low-dose axitinib could indirectly affect RPE phenotype via modulation of growth-factor signaling crosstalk, extracellular matrix deposition, or oxidative stress pathways observed in retinal endothelial cells; however, the provided literature does not extend these effects to RPE phagocytic function, and any expectation of enhanced MerTK/αvβ5 expression is speculative in the absence of direct data (Siedlecki et al., 2017; Lazzara et al., 2024).

Translational pharmacology considerations highlight both opportunity and risk: suprachoroidal axitinib enriches drug at the choroid/RPE with minimal systemic exposure, offering a delivery solution for RPE-targeted modulation if the mechanism were validated; at the same time, axitinib’s TIE2 inhibition and class-level concerns about chronic VEGF pathway suppression in the neurosensory retina argue for caution in non-neovascular indications such as dry AMD (Kaiser et al., 2020; Bakri et al., 2024). Moreover, systemic axitinib has been associated with retinal vascular adverse events in case reports, indicating that even low systemic exposures can affect retinal physiology, so RPE-targeted development would necessitate rigorous intraocular PK/PD mapping and safety margins that preserve vascular stability while testing RPE functional endpoints (Bakri et al., 2024). Given these constraints, the expected effect in an RPE phagocytosis assay is, at present, not evidence-based in the provided materials and should be framed as a hypothesis requiring first-principles validation rather than an anticipated outcome derived from prior literature (Fei et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
- Pharmacologic potency and dual-pathway coverage: Axitinib’s high-affinity pan-VEGFR inhibition with demonstrated PDGFR-β activity enables simultaneous suppression of endothelial and pericyte signaling, a combination that underpins robust anti-angiogenic efficacy in CNV models and may reduce fibrosis-linked extracellular matrix deposition in neovascular settings (Giddabasappa et al., 2016).  
- Validated ocular delivery options: Suprachoroidal suspension (CLS-AX) and intravitreal hydrogel implant (OTX-TKI) platforms have progressed into clinical testing for nAMD with encouraging ocular safety/PK signals, providing translationally relevant routes to expose the RPE/choroid compartment while minimizing systemic exposure (Wolf et al., 2022; Fei et al., 2024).  
- Clinical-stage experience in nAMD: Early-phase trials indicate biological activity and tolerability of axitinib-based intraocular approaches, suggesting a viable path to long-acting ocular therapy development if a new indication such as RPE phagocytosis enhancement is supported by mechanistic data (Leitch et al., 2024).  
- Class learnings and comparator programs: The broader TKI field in nAMD (vorolanib, sunitinib derivatives) offers benchmarks for durability, rescue-free rates, and safety considerations, facilitating rational dose and exposure setting for axitinib formulations (Fei et al., 2024; Leitch et al., 2024).  

Limitations and Critical Gaps  
- No direct evidence for RPE phagocytosis enhancement: Across the provided literature, there are no RPE-specific data showing axitinib increases MerTK or αvβ5 expression, augments POS binding or internalization, or improves phagocytic capacity in differentiating RPE; multiple summaries explicitly state the absence of such evidence and confine axitinib’s demonstrated actions to anti-angiogenic endpoints (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017).  
- Unvalidated mechanistic premise in RPE: While PDGFR-β is central to pericyte biology and vessel stabilization, the assertion that PDGFR-β overactivation hinders RPE differentiation and that its inhibition promotes a pro-phagocytic state is not supported in the provided texts, and the core RPE phagocytic machinery (MerTK, αvβ5) is not linked here to PDGFR-β modulation by TKIs (Tosi et al., 2017; Bakri et al., 2024).

- Delivery constraints for non-neovascular endpoints: Topical TKI programs frequently failed due to inadequate posterior segment exposure and/or ocular surface safety findings, suggesting that any RPE-targeted application of axitinib would require invasive delivery (suprachoroidal/IVT depot) with chronic exposure, elevating the bar for safety and benefit-risk justification in a dry AMD population (Fei et al., 2024).  
- Field precedent: Reviews underscore that, to date, small-molecule success in AMD has been limited, and there are no approved ocular TKIs for either wet or dry AMD, reinforcing translational uncertainty for new mechanism-of-use proposals lacking direct preclinical support (Fei et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).  

Development Recommendations and Go/No-Go Criteria  
- Mechanistic validation in RPE: Before proceeding, perform a staged in vitro program in human iPSC-RPE and primary RPE to test whether axitinib modulates PDGFR-β phosphorylation and secondarily increases MerTK expression, MerTK phosphorylation upon POS challenge, αvβ5 expression/localization, and POS binding/internalization; include dose-response spanning sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar exposures aligned with ocular PK projections from suprachoroidal or depot IVT delivery (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020).  
- Specificity controls and orthogonal readouts: Use chemical and genetic controls to isolate PDGFR-β dependence (e.g., PDGFR-β ligand titrations, selective PDGFR-β inhibitors distinct from axitinib, and PDGFR-β knockdown), and include neutralizing antibodies and MerTK/αvβ5 functional blocking to map pathway causality for any observed phagocytosis changes (Tosi et al., 2017; Siedlecki et al., 2017).  
- Safety pharmacology in pigmented models: Given potential TIE2-related and VEGF-suppression liabilities, include long-term RPE morphology, barrier function (TEER), transcriptomic stress signatures, and photoreceptor/RPE co-culture viability endpoints at projected clinical exposures; extend to pigmented rabbit or NHP pharmacology to define posterior-segment exposure, ocular distribution (RPE/sclera/choroid), and a NOAEL for chronic dosing (Bakri et al., 2024; Kaiser et al., 2020).  
- Translational gating: Advance only if axitinib reproducibly increases POS uptake and MerTK/αvβ5 functional markers in RPE with a therapeutic window that avoids endothelial destabilization signals and preserves neuronal/RPE integrity in chronic exposure models; otherwise, deprioritize axitinib for RPE-targeted dry AMD and refocus efforts on mechanisms directly validated to enhance RPE phagocytosis or survival (Fei et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022).  

Conclusion  
On the strength of available evidence, axitinib is a validated, potent anti-angiogenic TKI with multiple ocular delivery platforms in clinical development for nAMD and robust preclinical efficacy in CNV models; however, the central hypothesis that low-dose axitinib enhances RPE phagocytosis via PDGFR-β modulation and upregulates MerTK/αvβ5 lacks direct support in the provided literature, and multiple sources explicitly state that no such RPE-centric data exist for axitinib at present (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Fei et al., 2024). The translational and safety profiles suggest that invasive ocular delivery could achieve RPE-adjacent exposure, but off-target TIE2 inhibition and class-level VEGF-suppression risks must be weighed carefully in a non-neovascular indication, particularly absent clear preclinical efficacy on RPE phagocytic endpoints (Bakri et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022). Accordingly, while axitinib remains attractive for anti-angiogenic applications, it should not be advanced for dry AMD on a phagocytosis-enhancement rationale without first producing compelling, direct RPE mechanistic data; in the absence of such data, development resources would be better allocated to candidates with demonstrated effects on MerTK/αvβ5 function or on complement-mediated RPE pathology more proximal to dry AMD pathophysiology (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Fei et al., 2024). Pending rigorous in vitro and ex vivo validation as outlined, the current evidence base supports a cautious “mechanism validation required” stance rather than progression to in vivo dry AMD studies or clinical translation for this proposed use (Fei et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human Protein S, also known as Pros1, is a naturally occurring vitamin K–dependent plasma glycoprotein that functions both as an anticoagulant and as a ligand for members of the TAM (Tyro3/Axl/Mer) receptor family. Its biological origins trace back to its purification from human plasma, with early characterizations dating to its discovery in the late 1970s, and over time it has been elucidated to play critical roles not only in blood coagulation but also in efferocytosis and cellular clearance mechanisms. The recombinant form is synthesized using modern expression systems under strict good manufacturing practice (GMP) conditions, ensuring batch‐to‐batch consistency and purity for research and potential clinical applications. Protein S belongs to the therapeutic class of biologics, and like other recombinant proteins, it is designed to mimic the endogenous molecule’s activity. This class of compounds has historically been applied in contexts ranging from coagulation regulation to modulation of immune responses in inflammatory settings, with Protein S specifically recognized for its ability to act as a bridging molecule between apoptotic cells and phagocytes by binding phosphatidylserine via its N‐terminal Gla domain and engaging TAM receptors through its C‐terminal domains (Rothlin et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Protein S has been extensively studied for its role as an anticoagulant in hemostasis, where it potentiates activated protein C to inhibit coagulation factors and maintain vascular homeostasis. In addition to its role in the coagulation cascade, Protein S also exerts non‐coagulation effects through its function as a ligand for TAM receptors, particularly MerTK and Tyro3. Over the past two decades, biochemical and cell-based studies have highlighted its ability to facilitate efferocytosis in macrophages and retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells by bridging phosphatidylserine on apoptotic cell surfaces to MerTK receptors, thereby promoting internalization and clearance (Lumbroso et al., 2018; Lemke, 2015). In the context of retinal biology, several published reports have demonstrated that Protein S stimulates photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis by RPE cells. For instance, studies have shown a dose-dependent stimulatory effect of Protein S on RPE phagocytosis, with evidence that its expression follows a circadian bimodal rhythm matching the peak of phagocytic activity in the retina (Nandrot, 2018). Although the majority of therapeutic uses of Protein S have been traditionally focused on coagulation or its immunomodulatory roles, its involvement in retinal maintenance—particularly the clearance of spent photoreceptor outer segments—has made it an intriguing candidate for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). To date, however, there are no reports of clinical use of recombinant human Protein S in dry AMD or similar retinal diseases, and its potential remains evaluated only in preclinical RPE and in vivo models (Parinot et al., 2024; Lumbroso et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic activity of Protein S in this context hinges on its well-characterized molecular interaction with cell-surface receptors in the TAM family, particularly MerTK. Protein S contains a gamma-carboxylated N-terminal Gla domain that confers Ca²⁺-dependent binding to phosphatidylserine (PtdSer), an “eat-me” signal externalized on apoptotic cells and discarded photoreceptor outer segments. Once bound to PtdSer, Protein S serves as a bridging molecule by engaging with immunoglobulin-like domains on the extracellular portion of the MerTK receptor via its C-terminal SHBG (sex hormone-binding globulin) domains (Lemke, 2015; Lumbroso et al., 2018). This ligand–receptor interaction induces MerTK dimerization and subsequent trans-autophosphorylation of its intracellular kinase domains, thereby triggering downstream signaling cascades essential for phagocytosis. The activated receptor recruits adaptor proteins such as Vav and components of the p130Cas/CrkII/Dock180 complex, which ultimately leads to the activation of the Rho family GTPase Rac. Rac activation triggers the WAVE regulatory complex and subsequent Arp2/3-mediated actin polymerization, ultimately driving the membrane remodeling necessary for engulfing outer segments (Dransfield et al., 2015; Nandrot, 2018).

Importantly, recent mechanistic studies have suggested that Protein S and Gas6, another TAM ligand, can have opposing roles in RPE phagocytosis. Evidence indicates that while Protein S acts as a stimulatory ligand for MerTK-mediated phagocytosis (enhancing binding and internalization of POS), Gas6 may exert inhibitory effects by promoting the cleavage of the extracellular domain of MerTK, thereby generating a soluble receptor (sMerTK) that acts as a decoy (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). Site-directed mutagenesis experiments have further revealed that Protein S and Gas6 recognize distinct amino acid residues on the Ig-like domains of MerTK, supporting the idea that Protein S might preferentially activate MerTK via a unique binding mode that minimizes receptor cleavage and sustains intracellular signaling for effective phagocytosis (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). Additionally, experimental data indicate that Protein S alone may be sufficient to elicit phagocytosis by RPE cells, which is an essential feature given that genetic knockout studies show that mice lacking both ligands exhibit severe retinal degeneration similar to that observed in MerTK-deficient models (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). The differential temporal expression of Protein S relative to Gas6—where Protein S levels increase just before and during the phagocytic peak in the interphotoreceptor matrix—further supports its specialized role in ensuring precise circadian regulation of phagocytosis by RPE cells (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the above mechanistic insights, it is hypothesized that exogenous administration of recombinant human Protein S at a concentration of 5 µg/mL will strongly stimulate MerTK-mediated phagocytosis in RPE cells. In vitro, this therapeutic intervention is expected to enhance both the binding and internalization phases of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake. The anticipated experimental outcome is a robust increase in phagocytic activity in RPE cell culture models, which are typically used to recapitulate the phagocytosis defects observed in dry AMD—where impaired clearance of POS contributes to accumulation of toxic debris and subsequent retinal degeneration (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). Mechanistically, the addition of exogenous Protein S is expected to reduce the cleavage of membrane-bound MerTK, thereby maintaining high levels of active receptor on the RPE surface; this effect is crucial since increased soluble MerTK (sMerTK) has been associated with decreased phagocytic efficiency (Parinot et al., 2024; Lieffrig et al., 2023). In models of MERTK mutation, which mimic aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis, Protein S supplementation has been shown to rescue defective phagocytosis, thus restoring the internalization of outer segments to near-normal levels (Parinot et al., 2024). Since the normal functioning RPE relies on a finely balanced interplay between multiple phagocytic signals—including those mediated by integrins and other bridging molecules such as MFG-E8—the specific targeting of MerTK activation by Protein S is expected to complement these pathways without triggering competing inhibitory signals from Gas6, which has been reported to have higher affinity for MerTK but may paradoxically inhibit phagocytosis through enhanced receptor cleavage (Parinot et al., 2024).

Furthermore, the proposed biological activity is supported by the temporal and spatial expression patterns observed in vivo; Protein S is not only produced by RPE cells but also by photoreceptors themselves, and its rhythmic expression in the interphotoreceptor matrix suggests that it is naturally poised to regulate the daily burst of phagocytosis required for photoreceptor maintenance (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). The anticipated improvement in phagocytic clearance is expected to alleviate the accumulation of POS debris—a key pathogenic feature implicated in the progression of dry AMD—and may also reduce the resultant inflammatory milieu that contributes to RPE atrophy and photoreceptor demise (Nandrot, 2018; Lumbroso et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall potential of recombinant human Protein S as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is promising but not without challenges. One key strength lies in the fundamental and evolutionarily conserved role of Protein S in mediating efferocytosis and phagocytosis through MerTK activation; this function is particularly critical in the RPE, where continuous clearance of photoreceptor outer segments is essential for retinal homeostasis (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). The existing preclinical literature provides strong support that Protein S has a stimulatory effect on POS phagocytosis by RPE cells and that its loss or dysregulation is associated with pathogenic retinal changes that mirror those seen in dry AMD (Lumbroso et al., 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). In addition, the fact that recombinant human Protein S is GMP-manufacturable with favorable pharmacokinetic properties increases its attractiveness as a candidate for intravitreal or subretinal delivery, which allows for highly localized therapeutic effects while minimizing systemic exposure and potential off-target bleeding risks that might be associated with its role in coagulation (Lemke, 2015; Rothlin et al., 2015).

Another significant strength is the mechanistic rationale suggesting that Protein S, unlike Gas6, may preferentially activate MerTK without inducing deleterious receptor cleavage. Studies have demonstrated that while Gas6 can inhibit RPE phagocytosis by augmenting the cleavage of MerTK’s extracellular domain and generating a decoy receptor, Protein S acts to reduce this cleavage and thereby preserve receptor-mediated signaling necessary for efficient phagocytosis (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). Furthermore, protein engineering and mutagenesis studies indicate that the unique binding determinants utilized by Protein S may be exploited to design therapeutic strategies that selectively amplify beneficial signaling cascades in the diseased retina (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024).

Notwithstanding these promising aspects, there are notable weaknesses and uncertainties that must be addressed in further preclinical development. One major concern is the complex interplay between Gas6 and Protein S in modulating MerTK activity. Several studies have indicated that while Protein S is capable of stimulating phagocytosis, Gas6 is expressed at substantially higher levels in retinal tissues and might dominate the receptor activation milieu under certain conditions (Parinot et al., 2024). This raises the question of whether exogenously delivered Protein S can indeed override the inhibitory influence of endogenous Gas6 or if it must be co-administered with other agents to effectively shift the balance toward MerTK activation. Additionally, while the hypothesis is based on in vitro findings in cultured RPE cell models, the translation of these results into an in vivo setting remains uncertain given the heterogeneity and complex microenvironment of the retina in dry AMD, which involves oxidative stress, complement activation, and chronic inflammation (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024).

Another potential downside relates to the multifunctional nature of Protein S. Its well-established anticoagulant activity, while advantageous in managing thrombotic disorders, could pose a risk if systemic leakage occurs following ocular administration. Although intravitreal delivery is likely to confine the drug’s distribution to the eye, careful pharmacokinetic and toxicity studies are essential to ensure that any systemic absorption does not lead to bleeding complications or interfere with hemostasis elsewhere in the body (Lemke, 2015; Rothlin et al., 2015). Moreover, the exact composition and post-translational modifications of the recombinant protein must be meticulously controlled to maintain its intended bioactivity; for instance, the vitamin K–dependent gamma-carboxylation of the Gla domain is critical for its phosphatidylserine binding and subsequent receptor activation, and any perturbation in this process during manufacturing could compromise its therapeutic efficacy (Rothlin et al., 2015; Tasnim, 2020).

There is also the possibility that in the diseased state of dry AMD, RPE cells might have an altered responsiveness to TAM receptor ligands due to chronic oxidative damage or inflammatory insults, thereby diminishing the therapeutic effect of Protein S. Thus, while the restoration of phagocytosis by Protein S appears mechanistically sound in controlled cell culture systems, its real-world impact on rescuing retinal function and halting disease progression will depend on the ability to deliver the protein at effective concentrations and for sustained durations. In addition, optimal dosing studies are needed to determine whether 5 µg/mL is indeed the best concentration for stimulating phagocytosis in damaged RPE cells, as pharmacodynamic variability among patients could require individualized dosing regimens (Parinot et al., 2024).

In summary, recombinant human Protein S represents a novel and highly rational approach for addressing the impaired phagocytosis observed in dry age-related macular degeneration. Its biological function as a MerTK ligand and its ability to rescue phagocytic deficits in RPE models are compelling, and the mechanistic differentiation from Gas6 provides a unique therapeutic avenue that could potentially restore the delicate balance of photoreceptor outer segment turnover in the retina (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024; Lemke, 2015). The strengths of the candidate include its endogenous nature, the availability of robust recombinant production methods, and a solid mechanistic framework that implicates preferential MerTK activation as a means to boost phagocytosis. Conversely, the weaknesses center on the uncertain dominance of Protein S over Gas6 in a complex in vivo environment, potential off-target effects related to its anticoagulant activity, and the challenges inherent in translating in vitro RPE cell model data into effective clinical outcomes in patients with dry AMD.

Given the current literature, further detailed preclinical studies are warranted to assess the efficacy of recombinant human Protein S in appropriate animal models of dry AMD, to optimize dosing strategies, and to address any safety concerns that may arise from its systemic pharmacology. Nonetheless, the mechanistic data supporting its role in promoting the clearance of photoreceptor debris and in potentially mitigating the downstream inflammatory responses that drive RPE degeneration suggest that this candidate holds considerable promise for inclusion in the therapeutic pipeline targeting dry AMD (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024). The overall evaluation is that while there is substantial preclinical mechanistic support for the use of recombinant Protein S in stimulating MerTK-mediated POS phagocytosis and rescuing RPE function, careful further experimentation is essential to validate these findings in clinically relevant settings before committing to a full clinical development program.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Anacetrapib is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor of cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) originally developed by Merck as part of a class of compounds aimed at modulating lipid metabolism. This compound was identified and refined through extensive medicinal chemistry programs designed to target CETP’s lipid transfer function. As a member of the CETP inhibitor class, anacetrapib has been developed primarily for cardiovascular risk reduction by increasing high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL‐C) and lowering low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C), and its chemical structure and binding properties have been designed to disrupt the lipid‐transfer tunnel of the CETP enzyme (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Tall & Rader, 2018). The proposed repurposing for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on the rationale that by inhibiting CETP, the agent could raise local HDL levels in Bruch’s membrane (BrM) and improve reverse cholesterol transport, thereby reducing drusen‐like lipid accumulation and indirectly supporting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) phagocytic capacity—a hypothesis derived from observed associations between CETP activity, local retinal lipid metabolism, and AMD pathogenesis (Betzler et al., 2020; Shughoury et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, CETP inhibitors have been evaluated extensively for their potential to address dyslipidemia and reduce atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Anacetrapib, in particular, has undergone large clinical trials such as the DEFINE and REVEAL studies, where its efficacy in raising HDL‐C by approximately 138% and reducing LDL‐C by 37–40% compared to placebo was demonstrated (Cheung et al., 2017; Tall & Rader, 2018). The class of CETP inhibitors also includes compounds such as torcetrapib, dalcetrapib, and evacetrapib—with torcetrapib’s development being terminated due to off‐target effects including blood pressure elevations, while anacetrapib and evacetrapib showed more favorable profiles in subsequent trials (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Sirtori, 2011). Although these compounds were developed to address cardiovascular pathologies, genetic and mechanistic studies have implicated CETP and HDL metabolism in the ocular environment as well. Several genome‐wide association studies and Mendelian randomization studies have demonstrated a relationship between CETP gene variants, HDL levels, and AMD risk (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020). Despite this, no CETP inhibitor has previously been used in a clinical setting for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular diseases, and the repurposing of anacetrapib for dry AMD represents a novel therapeutic direction inspired by preclinical studies in murine models that suggest potential benefits in the retinal context (Cheung et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
Anacetrapib functions by binding to CETP, thereby preventing the transfer of cholesteryl esters from HDL to apolipoprotein B‐containing lipoproteins (i.e., LDL, very‐low‐density lipoprotein [VLDL]) and the subsequent exchange of triglycerides in the opposite direction. At the molecular level, CETP normally operates via a tunnel‐mechanism or shuttle mechanism to facilitate the bidirectional lipid transfer between lipoproteins. Inhibition of CETP by anacetrapib results in the accumulation of cholesterol-rich, enlarged HDL particles and a concomitant reduction in the levels of atherogenic LDL particles (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Sirtori, 2011). In the context of the retina, emerging evidence suggests that CETP is expressed not only systemically but also locally—in the retinal pigment epithelium, photoreceptor outer segments, and interphotoreceptor matrix (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). The rationale is that CETP activity in Bruch’s membrane may normally lower HDL levels, thereby impairing the capacity for reverse cholesterol transport in this specialized extracellular matrix, which can lead to the accumulation of lipids and the formation of drusen. By inhibiting CETP, anacetrapib may restore or increase local HDL levels, improving the efflux of accumulated cholesterol and other lipids from the RPE and neighboring structures (Fan et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2022). Moreover, the resulting HDL particles may gain enhanced cholesterol efflux capacity, as evidenced by preclinical studies that show increased cholesterol removal from macrophages via ABCA1- and ABCG1-mediated pathways (Sirtori, 2011; Page et al., 2016). In addition, proper HDL particle composition under CETP inhibition could influence key inflammatory regulatory mechanisms through the carriage of complement factors, which are linked to AMD pathogenesis (Tricorache et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assay, treatment with anacetrapib is expected to increase HDL levels locally in Bruch’s membrane, thereby enhancing reverse cholesterol transport across the retinal layers. The improved cholesterol efflux from the RPE is postulated to mitigate the accumulation of drusen-like lipid deposits—a hallmark of dry AMD—and potentially restore critical cellular functions such as integrin localization and associated phagocytic receptor activity (Cheung et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020). This restoration of lipid homeostasis is anticipated to reduce the build-up of oxidized lipids and other debris beneath the RPE, ultimately alleviating RPE dysfunction—a central component in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). The mechanism relies on the observation that HDL not only serves as a cholesterol acceptor but also carries important complement regulatory proteins and inflammatory mediators; thus, its normalization in Bruch’s membrane could indirectly support the phagocytic activity of RPE cells and improve tissue homeostasis (Lin et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). Gene expression studies have identified CETP expression in ocular tissues, reinforcing the notion that local CETP inhibition may directly influence lipid handling in the retina (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). Ultimately, the expected outcomes in preclinical models—and, by extension, in clinical trials—are a measurable reduction in drusen burden, improvement in RPE functionality, and a potential delay or attenuation in the progression of dry AMD (Schmidt et al., 2020; Cheung et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of anacetrapib for the treatment of dry AMD presents a compelling opportunity, supported by a solid mechanistic hypothesis and a favorable human safety profile established in cardiovascular trials. Among the clear strengths is the extensive biochemical and clinical data on CETP inhibitors in the context of dyslipidemia; anacetrapib has demonstrated robust HDL‐C raising and LDL‐C lowering effects, with a tolerability profile superior to earlier CETP inhibitors such as torcetrapib (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Tall & Rader, 2018). Furthermore, emerging evidence of CETP expression in ocular tissues and its potential role in modulating local lipid metabolism—combined with findings that suggest dysfunctional HDL composition may contribute to drusen formation—lends strong support to the therapeutic rationale (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017).

However, there are important weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed. First, the genetic and epidemiological data linking HDL cholesterol and AMD have been paradoxical; several Mendelian randomization studies have implicated HDL‐raising alleles, particularly those related to CETP modulation, with an increased risk for AMD (Betzler et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2017). This counterintuitive observation raises concerns that simply increasing HDL levels may not guarantee improved RPE function unless the quality and functionality of HDL particles are also enhanced (Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022). Second, while the cardiovascular applications of anacetrapib provide a strong safety signal, the ocular-specific pharmacodynamics and tissue distribution of the drug remain largely unexplored. It is conceivable that the systemic modulation of HDL might not translate into the desired local changes in Bruch’s membrane, particularly given the unique lipid microenvironment of the retina (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Third, preclinical data demonstrating that anacetrapib can reduce BrM lipid burden and restore integrin localization in murine models, although promising, have yet to be validated extensively, and species differences in CETP expression and lipid metabolism could limit translatability to human patients (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Lastly, the long-term consequences of altering CETP activity in the retina are unknown, and there exists a potential risk that chronic CETP inhibition could inadvertently disrupt local complement regulation or other aspects of retinal homeostasis, given the tight interplay between lipid metabolism and inflammation in AMD pathogenesis (Tricorache et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2015).

Overall, while the conceptual framework underlying the repurposing of anacetrapib for dry AMD is scientifically intriguing and supported by a convergence of genetic, biochemical, and preclinical mechanistic data, further investigation is needed to reconcile the paradoxical relationships observed in human genetic studies, to precisely characterize the local retinal pharmacokinetics of the drug, and to validate its effects on reverse cholesterol transport in the specific context of the retina. In summary, anacetrapib holds potential as a novel therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but its ultimate success will depend on carefully designed preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials that specifically address its ocular efficacy and safety profile (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022).
