Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab is a recombinant, humanized monoclonal IgG kappa antibody that specifically binds complement component C5 and prevents its proteolytic activation into C5a and C5b, thereby blocking terminal pathway activity and membrane attack complex (MAC; C5b-9) assembly while leaving upstream C3-dependent functions largely intact (for example, opsonization and immune-complex handling) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; West et al., 2024). It was discovered by screening large panels of murine anti-human C5 monoclonals for potent inhibition of C5 activation and terminal complement–mediated hemolysis; the parental murine antibody (5G1.1) was then humanized by CDR grafting into human germline frameworks and engineered to use a hybrid IgG2/IgG4 heavy-chain constant region to minimize Fcγ receptor binding and classical-pathway activation (reducing effector functions that could confound terminal pathway blockade) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009). Eculizumab binds human C5 with very high affinity (Kd approximately 120 pM) and sterically prevents convertase engagement with the MG7 domain of C5; epitope mapping identifies residues in the MG7 domain (including the KSSKC motif around Arg885) critical for binding, and Arg885His/Cys polymorphisms have been linked to clinical non-responsiveness in some patients, consistent with the structural epitope (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

As a drug class, complement inhibitors have been deployed to treat diseases driven by complement dysregulation, with C5 blockade representing a terminal-pathway strategy that ablates C5a signaling and MAC-mediated cytolysis while preserving many proximal complement functions; eculizumab was the first complement inhibitor approved for clinical use and catalyzed broad clinical development of C5, C3, and alternative pathway–targeted agents across hematology, nephrology, neurology, and, more recently, ophthalmology (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Eculizumab is administered intravenously, exhibits a long serum half-life (~272 ± 82 hours), a limited volume of distribution consistent with an intravascularly confined antibody, and shows pharmacodynamic correlation between serum trough concentrations and blockade of hemolytic activity; vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis is required due to increased susceptibility when terminal complement is inhibited (Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Within ophthalmology, complement activation products and MAC deposition have been implicated in AMD pathogenesis, motivating clinical trials of complement inhibitors including C5-directed agents; eculizumab has been formally evaluated in a randomized phase 2 setting for non-exudative AMD (geographic atrophy and drusen cohorts) via systemic administration (Kassa et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Halawa et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
Eculizumab has an extensive clinical record in systemic complement-mediated disorders. It revolutionized therapy for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), where it reduces intravascular hemolysis, decreases transfusion requirements, and improves quality of life; it is also approved for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and for neurologic autoimmune indications including anti–acetylcholine receptor–positive generalized myasthenia gravis and aquaporin-4–positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Early clinical pharmacology in PNH demonstrated that an induction regimen of 600 mg weekly for four weeks followed by 900 mg every other week maintained near-complete terminal pathway blockade and significantly reduced hemolysis and transfusion needs; these dosing principles align with its long half-life and the concentration dependence of hemolytic inhibition (Hillmen et al., 2004; Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012). Despite robust control of intravascular hemolysis, residual extravascular hemolysis can persist because C3 opsonization is not prevented by C5 inhibition, illustrating an important mechanistic limitation of terminal-pathway agents (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; West et al., 2024).

The drug’s safety profile is dominated by infection risk with encapsulated organisms—particularly meningococcal disease—necessitating vaccination; otherwise, eculizumab has shown acceptable tolerability across long-term use, with clinical programs incorporating monitoring of functional complement activity (CH50) to confirm pharmacodynamic blockade and dose adequacy (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009; Eskandary et al., 2016). Mechanistically relevant sources also report pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic complexities: high-affinity binding at acidic endosomal pH encourages recycling of eculizumab:C5 complexes by FcRn, leading to accumulation of total C5 bound to the drug in circulation; next-generation engineering in ravulizumab introduced pH-dependent release to minimize cargo recycling and extend dosing intervals (Schmidt & Smith, 2023).

In ophthalmology, eculizumab has been investigated as a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD. The COMPLETE study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), a single-center, randomized, double-masked phase 2 trial, evaluated intravenous eculizumab in two cohorts: geographic atrophy (GA) and intermediate AMD with high-risk drusen; patients were randomized 2:1 to eculizumab or saline over 24 weeks with follow-up to 52 weeks (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the GA cohort (n = 30 study eyes), eculizumab did not reduce GA enlargement versus placebo at 26 or 52 weeks (square-root–transformed growth 0.19 ± 0.12 mm vs. 0.18 ± 0.15 mm at 26 weeks, P = 0.96; 0.37 ± 0.22 mm vs. 0.37 ± 0.21 mm at 52 weeks, P = 0.93), and no drug-related adverse events were reported (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the drusen cohort (n = 30 total participants; 20 active, 10 placebo), eculizumab failed to meet the prespecified primary endpoint of a ≥ 50% reduction in drusen cube-root volume at 26 weeks; none of 18 treated eyes achieved this threshold, while one placebo eye did (10%; P = 0.36), and there was no detectable difference in mean drusen growth between arms through 26–52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014). Trial conduct included meningococcal vaccination and careful multimodal imaging; retention was high with 28/30 completing 52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). Independent evidence syntheses judged the certainty of evidence as low to very low due to small sample size, imprecision, and some risk of bias; overall, systemic eculizumab “may have made little to no difference” in BCVA and GA lesion growth in the available cohort (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistically similar C5-directed agents have not shown positive phase 2 outcomes in GA when administered systemically or intravitreally (e.g., LFG316 failed in phase 2), whereas intravitreal C5 inhibition with avacincaptad pegol progressed to later-phase testing and regulatory review, suggesting that drug, route, and pharmacology may be important determinants of outcome; by contrast, intravitreal C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) demonstrated efficacy and has been approved for GA, underscoring the translational relevance of target selection and ocular delivery (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024). Multiple reviews conclude that systemic eculizumab is no longer in development for AMD and highlight delivery and mechanistic concerns as likely contributors to the negative results (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, eculizumab targets the MG7 domain of C5 and sterically prevents formation of the C5 convertase–substrate complex, thereby inhibiting the cleavage of C5 into the potent anaphylatoxin C5a and C5b, which nucleates membrane attack complex assembly with C6–C9 (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Rother et al., 2007). Structural analysis of an eculizumab Fab bound to C5 resolved at 4.2 Å shows that five CDRs form the principal interface with MG7; mutational scanning of CDR residues identifies a network of contacts necessary for high-affinity binding, and kinetic assays confirm that these interactions prevent complement-mediated hemolysis in vitro (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016). The epitope includes residues near Arg885, and clinical resistance due to Arg885His/Cys substitutions in C5 provides orthogonal validation of the binding site (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

Pharmacodynamically, eculizumab ablates terminal pathway function: it suppresses CH50 to near zero when trough serum concentrations exceed ~35 μg/mL; however, because proximal C3 activation continues, C3b deposition and downstream opsonins accumulate on surfaces, which can drive extravascular clearance and generate residual pathology even under complete C5 blockade in appropriate disease contexts (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). Additional mechanisms can undermine complete terminal pathway control: (1) during intense proximal activation, densely opsonized surfaces can support C5 activation by convertases in ways that partially bypass classical C5 convertase assembly or even promote conformational C5 activation on surface C3b clusters; such context-dependent activation can manifest as “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” despite apparently adequate free drug levels, and has been reported in clinical settings as residual terminal-pathway activity and elevated sC5b-9 in some patients (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). (2) Eculizumab binds C5 with high affinity at both neutral and mildly acidic pH, allowing FcRn to recycle eculizumab:C5 complexes and potentially alter antigen disposition; ravulizumab’s pH-dependent binding was engineered to release C5 in endosomes and improve pharmacokinetics by avoiding cargo recycling (Schmidt & Smith, 2023). These features are germane to dose selection, monitoring, and potential resistance or escape during strong complement activation.

Rationale for C5 inhibition in AMD rests on abundant mechanistic and histopathological evidence that C5-derived effectors and MAC participate in retinal/choroidal injury. C5a is detected in drusen and acts as a chemotactic and proinflammatory mediator capable of inducing VEGF expression from retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, while C5b initiates MAC assembly; MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris increases with aging and is elevated in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019). Sub-lytic and lytic MAC on choroidal endothelium causes cell injury and can trigger surviving endothelial cells to upregulate VEGF and matrix metalloproteinases, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic injury and pro-angiogenic remodeling; complement regulatory proteins such as CD59 are natural inhibitors of MAC formation and their dysfunction or insufficiency can predispose to damage (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2021). Complement dysregulation in AMD further includes genetic risk (e.g., CFH variants) and evidence of alternative pathway activation in ocular tissues, suggesting both proximal and terminal effector involvement in disease biology (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Importantly, proximal inhibition at C3 has shown the capacity to restore lysosomal function and reduce sub-RPE drusen-like deposits in human iPSC-derived RPE models carrying the high-risk CFH Y402H variant by reducing C3 turnover and lowering downstream MAC (C5b-9) localization at lysosomes; in this system, a compstatin analogue (Cp40) suppressed C3b and MAC deposition and reversed lysosomal abnormalities, whereas direct C5 inhibition has not been shown in this model to rescue lysosomal function, and clinical C5 blockade has failed in GA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). These data reinforce that while terminal pathway effectors are present and likely pathogenic in AMD, distal blockade at C5 does not necessarily address upstream complement turnover that drives intracellular lysosomal stress in RPE, and proximal intervention may be required to normalize cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
The hypothesis proposes that high-affinity C5 blockade with eculizumab will prevent MAC assembly on RPE, thereby reducing sub-RPE deposit–driven lysosomal stress and indirectly supporting photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis in dry AMD. Mechanistically, preventing C5 cleavage would abrogate both C5a signaling and C5b-dependent MAC formation; given the documented presence of C5a in drusen and increased MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane/choriocapillaris with age and AMD, terminal pathway inhibition is expected to reduce MAC-mediated endothelial and RPE injury, dampen MAC-induced VEGF/MMP signaling, and potentially mitigate inflammation (Kassa et al., 2019). In principle, if MAC-driven lysosomal injury contributes to RPE dysfunction, C5 inhibition could reduce new MAC deposition at the RPE surface and limit subsequent endocytosis of MAC into lysosomes, thereby lowering lysosomal burden (Park et al., 2021).

However, two key bodies of evidence temper this expectation. First, clinical testing of systemic eculizumab in GA and intermediate AMD failed to show benefit on primary anatomical endpoints (GA growth and OCT drusen volume) through 26–52 weeks, despite established systemic pharmacodynamic blockade; these negative outcomes argue that either (a) terminal pathway activity at C5 is not the principal driver of lesion growth/drusen regression during the studied disease stages/time horizon, or (b) pharmacokinetic compartmentalization limited ocular target engagement after intravenous dosing (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Filho et al., 2014). Reviews explicitly highlight the compartment barrier problem—systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina or sub-RPE space due to the blood–retina/Bruch’s membrane barriers and large molecular size—and note that eculizumab exposure shorter than six months is unlikely to show benefit in slowly progressive GA, compounding interpretation (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Second, cellular models directly linking complement dysregulation to lysosomal failure in high-risk AMD RPE show that upstream C3 inhibition, not terminal C5 blockade, restores lysosomal function and reduces deposit formation; this suggests that intralysosomal stress is driven by continuous C3 turnover and opsonization rather than MAC alone, and that distal C5 blockade may be insufficient to normalize these processes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Consequently, POS phagocytosis metrics may improve only marginally or not at all if the dominant insult is proximal complement turnover rather than MAC-mediated damage. The clinical failure to slow GA growth or reduce drusen volume with systemic eculizumab supports the inference that target engagement at C5, via the tested route and schedule, did not translate into macroscopic anatomical benefit in human AMD eyes within one year (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).

If eculizumab were to be tested in vitro on human RPE, appropriate readouts would include: surface and intracellular MAC (C5b-9) quantification, lysosomal number/size and membrane integrity (e.g., LAMP2, Galectin-8), Cathepsin D activity, autophagic flux, and POS degradation kinetics; concomitant measurement of upstream C3b/iC3b/C3d deposition would be essential to interpret whether C5 inhibition is affecting the dominant pathogenic pathway in the assay (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In vivo, ocular pharmacokinetic considerations dominate: intravitreal administration delivers drug to the retina and sub-RPE space but is not reported for eculizumab in the provided context and would carry different safety and dosing constraints; systemic dosing faces blood–retina barrier limitations that likely constrained ocular target engagement in COMPLETE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Notably, nearly all complement inhibitors that have shown anatomical effects in GA have been delivered intravitreally, underscoring the importance of route of administration for ocular diseases (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic rationale: C5a and MAC are present in AMD-relevant tissues; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD and can drive endothelial injury, VEGF/MMP upregulation, and potentially RPE dysfunction; blocking C5 should diminish these terminal effector signals (Kassa et al., 2019; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Potent, well-characterized biologic: Eculizumab binds human C5 with picomolar affinity, has a well-defined structural epitope in the MG7 domain, and reliably ablates terminal pathway function systemically with a large clinical safety database outside ophthalmology (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
- Clinical feasibility and tolerability: In AMD trials, intravenous eculizumab was well tolerated without drug-related adverse events and with no clear signal for increased neovascular conversion or ocular infection within one year, supporting general safety of systemic C5 blockade in this population under vaccination protocols (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Negative clinical efficacy in AMD: The randomized phase 2 COMPLETE trial showed no reduction in GA growth and no meaningful reduction in drusen volume through 26–52 weeks; certainty is limited by small sample size but confidence intervals and replication across endpoints argue against a large treatment effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).  
- Compartmentalization barriers for systemic dosing: Blood–retina and Bruch’s membrane barriers likely limit ocular exposure to intravenously administered eculizumab; multiple reviews cite inadequate ocular penetration as a plausible reason for failure, and systemic eculizumab is no longer being pursued in AMD (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
- Target selection may be too distal for RPE lysosomal rescue: Human iPSC-RPE data indicate that complement-driven lysosomal pathology and drusen-like deposits are reversed by C3 inhibition, with concomitant reduction of downstream MAC, while C5 blockade alone has not been shown to restore lysosomal metrics and did not slow GA clinically; this suggests that proximal complement turnover is the dominant driver of RPE lysosomal stress (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Mechanistic escape and incomplete terminal control: Under strong activation, C5 can be activated on dense C3b clusters with features of convertase bypass or conformational priming; stoichiometric C5 inhibitors can form long-lived C5:antibody complexes on surfaces, potentially allowing residual terminal activity, and clinical “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” has been documented (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
- Genetic and biochemical determinants of response: C5 polymorphisms (e.g., R885H/C) can abolish binding and confer resistance; while prevalence in AMD populations is unknown here, such variants are important risk factors for nonresponse (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).  
- Safety/logistics: Terminal complement blockade mandates meningococcal vaccination and vigilance for invasive infections; while acceptable systemically in selected diseases, risk–benefit in a chronic, slowly progressive ocular disorder is less favorable, and the cost and infusion burden are high (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Contextualization with alternative complement strategies  
- C5 vs C3: Clinical success in GA has emerged at the level of C3 (pegcetacoplan), consistent with cellular data showing rescue of lysosomal function by upstream blockade; by contrast, systemic C5 inhibition with eculizumab and other C5-directed agents failed to meet GA endpoints in early trials, and LFG316 also did not demonstrate efficacy in GA (West et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Route of administration: Most agents demonstrating anatomical effects in GA are delivered intravitreally; eculizumab’s large size and systemic administration likely limited ocular penetration in COMPLETE, and no intravitreal eculizumab data are provided here to support local delivery (Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
- Risk of adverse ocular remodeling: Complement modulation has complex, context-dependent effects; in some models, complement inhibition or modulation can alter macrophage polarization and influence CNV formation, underscoring that indiscriminate or poorly targeted complement blockade could have unintended consequences; while the eculizumab AMD trials did not show a neovascular signal, vigilance is warranted when selecting targets and doses (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2021).

Decision Implications  
- As a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD, eculizumab has a low probability of success based on randomized clinical evidence, pharmacokinetic compartment limitations, and mechanistic considerations indicating that distal C5 blockade may not correct the proximal complement turnover driving RPE lysosomal pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- If C5 remains a target of interest, local ocular delivery and alternative molecular formats designed for intravitreal pharmacokinetics (e.g., smaller C5-binding entities, RNAi to intraocular C5 production, or intravitreal C5 inhibitors such as avacincaptad pegol) are more plausible routes; indeed, avacincaptad has advanced in GA, while systemic eculizumab has been discontinued in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019; Nadeem et al., 2023; West et al., 2024).  
- For assays aimed at lysosomal stress and POS phagocytosis, prioritizing proximal complement inhibitors (e.g., C3-targeting) is more aligned with human RPE data and recent clinical experience, whereas C5 inhibition alone is unlikely to fully normalize lysosomal function or confer robust structural benefit (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; West et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
Eculizumab provides a clear mechanistic means to extinguish terminal complement effectors implicated in AMD biology, but the totality of evidence—negative randomized clinical data in GA and drusen, route-of-administration barriers to ocular exposure, mechanistic escape during high activation, and cellular evidence favoring proximal over distal inhibition for lysosomal rescue—argues against further development of systemic eculizumab for dry AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The program should be deprioritized in favor of intraocularly suited agents and proximal complement targets, unless a compelling, testable strategy emerges to achieve effective intraocular C5 blockade with eculizumab (which is not supported by the present context) (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistic Appendix: Biochemical and Pathobiologic Evidence Relevant to the Hypothesis  
- Complement activation and terminal effectors in AMD:  
  - C5a is present in drusen and induces VEGF from RPE; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD; MAC induces endothelial lysis and sub-lytic survival signaling that upregulates VEGF and MMPs (Kassa et al., 2019).  
  - Alternative pathway dysregulation is central in AMD; genetic and experimental data implicate factor H and alternative pathway components in AMD and CNV models; inhibition of C3a, C5a, CFB, MAC or supplementation with CD59/CFH blocks CNV in animals (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Eculizumab structure–function:  
  - Epitope on MG7 with steric convertase blockade; high-affinity binding and resistance polymorphisms at Arg885; CDR function validated by mutational scans (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
  - PK/PD: long half-life, vascular distribution, CH50 suppression threshold, FcRn recycling of C5:eculizumab complexes; ravulizumab engineering to improve recycling and dosing (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
  - Breakthrough mechanisms: convertase bypass and surface-induced conformational activation on dense C3b clusters; residual TP activity despite inhibitors under strong activation (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; Mannes et al., 2021).  
- Clinical AMD trials:  
  - COMPLETE GA cohort: no slowing of GA growth at 26 or 52 weeks; well tolerated (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021).  
  - COMPLETE drusen cohort: no ≥ 50% reduction in drusen volume in treated eyes at 26 weeks; no significant change in drusen growth vs placebo (Filho et al., 2014).  
  - Critical appraisals: small sample, imprecision, risk of bias; systemic delivery may not achieve retinal levels; eculizumab no longer in AMD development (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023).  
- RPE lysosomal biology:  
  - In high-risk Y402H iPSC-RPE, excessive C3 turnover increases MAC internalization and overloads lysosomes; C3 inhibition with Cp40 reduces both C3b and MAC, reverses lysosomal defects, and reduces drusen-like deposits; direct C5 inhibition is not shown to restore lysosomal function in this model (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Operational Recommendation  
- Do not advance systemic eculizumab for dry AMD. If C5 remains a strategic target, consider intravitreal agents designed for ocular PK and evaluate them head-to-head against proximal inhibitors in RPE lysosomal-function assays that quantify both MAC and C3 fragment deposition, with translational go/no-go predicated on alignment with known clinical signals in GA (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human CD46 is a biologic drug candidate derived from a naturally occurring human protein that plays a pivotal role in the regulation of the complement cascade. Endogenously, CD46, also known as membrane cofactor protein (MCP), is a type I transmembrane glycoprotein expressed on nearly all nucleated cells—including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—and is a member of the regulators of complement activation (RCA) gene family located on chromosome 1q32 (Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021; Sweigard et al., 2011). Its primary biological function is to act as a cofactor for the serine protease factor I, thereby mediating the proteolytic cleavage of complement components C3b and C4b that are deposited on host cell surfaces. This function is critical for preventing the formation of the C3 and C5 convertase complexes that drive the amplification loop of the complement cascade (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011).  

The recombinant human CD46 candidate (Biotechne Cat. No. 3430-CD) is produced by modern recombinant DNA techniques that allow for controlled expression in a chosen host cell system. Typically, to ensure proper folding and post-translational modifications (which are essential given CD46’s complex structure featuring multiple short consensus repeat [SCR] domains, O-linked glycosylated serine/threonine/proline-rich regions, a hydrophobic transmembrane segment, and a cytoplasmic tail), such proteins are expressed in eukaryotic cell systems (Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021; Leaderer et al., 2015). Previous recombinant production approaches for CD46 have employed adenoviral or adeno-associated viral vector technology, where the CD46 gene is inserted into an appropriate vector and delivered to target cells; however, the candidate in discussion is a purified recombinant protein intended for exogenously controlled dosing (Sweigard et al., 2011).  

As a member of the biologic class of complement regulatory proteins, recombinant CD46 belongs alongside other therapeutic proteins that target dysregulated complement activation, an approach that has gained prominence in treating complement-mediated diseases. The concept behind these therapeutics is to harness or augment natural regulatory mechanisms; in this instance, restoring or increasing the activity of CD46 on RPE cells may correct complement dysregulation implicated in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Leaderer et al., 2015; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021). This candidate is thus positioned within the emerging class of immunomodulatory biologics aimed at restoring homeostasis in the complement system.  

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic rationale for targeting complement dysregulation in AMD has been borne out by extensive biochemical and clinical investigations. CD46 was initially discovered by leveraging biochemical purification techniques using affinity columns that bound complement fragments such as C3b and C3(H₂O) (Liszewski & Atkinson, 2025; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021). This discovery set the stage for subsequent studies that established its central role in protecting host tissues from complement‐mediated damage by serving as a cofactor for factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b and C4b (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011).

In several preclinical studies, researchers have explored approaches to mitigate complement-mediated damage in ocular diseases by increasing CD46 expression or activity. Gene therapy studies have utilized adenoviral vectors (AdCAGCD46) to deliver the CD46 gene to RPE cells in animal models. Such studies have shown that increased CD46 expression in RPE not only reduced complement deposition as measured by decreased membrane attack complex (MAC) formation but also provided significant protection against complement-mediated cell damage (Sweigard et al., 2011). These findings have been considered especially relevant for dry AMD, a disease characterized by chronic low-grade complement activation that leads to RPE dysfunction, drusen formation, and ultimately retinal degeneration (Sweigard et al., 2011; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021).

In addition to gene therapy approaches, soluble recombinant forms of complement regulators, including soluble CD46, have been investigated with the aim of systemically or locally inhibiting the complement cascade. While some recombinant or engineered forms of complement regulators have advanced to clinical trials for other complement-mediated conditions, challenges have been noted regarding the potency of soluble proteins relative to their full-length, membrane-anchored counterparts. Studies analyzing soluble MCP have indeed reported that while it exerts complement inhibitory activity, its potency is often lower compared to the naturally occurring membrane-bound protein (Wagner & Frank, 2010). Still, the fundamental association between CD46 deficiency and impaired RPE function has been established in experimental models—for example, CD46-deficient RPE cells have been observed to display drusen-like deposits and reduced phagocytic function, which are hallmark features of dry AMD (Leaderer et al., 2015; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021).

Furthermore, research in related ocular models has demonstrated that enhancing CD46 activity in RPE cells results in improved cleavage of deposited complement fragments (C3b and C4b), reduced MAC deposition, and restoration of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D, which is critical for the digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (Sweigard et al., 2011). Thus, the therapeutic history of both endogenous CD46 function and its recombinant or gene therapy-mediated restoration strongly supports its potential utility in treating dry AMD, making it an attractive candidate for further evaluation in this disease context.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, CD46 functions as a regulatory checkpoint in the complement system by facilitating the inactivation of complement components that have been deposited on host cell surfaces. Its mechanism of action centers on its ability to serve as a cofactor for factor I, a plasma serine protease responsible for cleaving and inactivating C3b and C4b (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011). The protein comprises four contiguous short consensus repeat (SCR) domains or complement control protein (CCP) domains, and these are arranged in a manner that creates high-affinity binding sites for the C3b and C4b fragments (Leaderer et al., 2015; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021; Parsons et al., 2023).

Under physiological conditions, when C3b and C4b are deposited on the cell surface as a result of complement pathway activation, CD46 binds to these fragments through its CCP domains. This binding positions factor I in an optimal orientation to cleave C3b and C4b into their inactive forms, iC3b and iC4b, respectively, thereby halting further progression of the complement cascade (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011). By preventing the formation of the C3 and C5 convertases, CD46 effectively stops the downstream assembly of the MAC—a multi-protein complex that, if formed in excess, can lead to cell lysis and tissue injury.

More specifically, the biochemical interactions involve a network of electrostatic and hydrophobic contacts between the complement fragments and the SCR domains of CD46. The correct spatial arrangement of these domains is critical for both high-affinity binding and subsequent catalytic efficiency with factor I (Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021; Sweigard et al., 2011). Variability in the isoforms of CD46, generated via alternative splicing, can influence these interactions by altering the configuration of the extracellular domains or the intracellular signaling motifs, which in turn may modulate the overall efficiency of complement regulation (Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021; Parsons et al., 2023).

When administered exogenously as a recombinant protein, CD46 is hypothesized to either integrate into the target cell membrane or associate closely with the cell surface, thereby supplementing the endogenous pool of CD46 on RPE cells (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011). In the context of dry AMD, where studies have documented reduced CD46 expression and consequent complement dysregulation, the therapeutic addition of recombinant CD46 would bolster the cell’s ability to process deposited C3b and C4b, diminishing the formation of the convertase complexes that drive the alternative complement pathway (Sweigard et al., 2011).

This mode of action is not merely a passive blockade of complement via decoy binding; rather, it is an active restoration of a physiological regulatory mechanism. In addition to its primary cofactor activity, CD46 has been implicated in intracellular signaling pathways that govern cellular responses such as autophagy, metabolic reprogramming, and even modulation of the phagocytic machinery (Leaderer et al., 2015; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2025). In RPE cells, efficient phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments is crucial for retinal homeostasis, and complement-mediated lysosomal stress has been linked to impaired phagocytic function. By promoting the inactivation of C3b and C4b and reducing MAC formation, recombinant CD46 is expected to mitigate this lysosomal stress, thereby preserving or even enhancing the phagocytic function of RPE cells (Sweigard et al., 2011; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021).

Furthermore, the complement regulatory activity of CD46 is supported by its established localization patterns: in ocular tissues, CD46 is predominantly expressed on the basal and lateral surfaces of RPE cells, where it serves as a barrier against ongoing complement activation (Sweigard et al., 2011). The molecular orchestration provided by CD46 in these microenvironments is critical for maintaining the delicate balance between immune defense and auto-protection. Thus, the administration of recombinant human CD46 aims to restore this balance by re-establishing local complement control where it has been compromised, thereby forestalling the progression of the inflammatory and degenerative processes underlying dry AMD (Sweigard et al., 2011).

Expected Effect:  
In the experimental paradigm under consideration, the central hypothesis posits that exogenous CD46 will “increase membrane cofactor activity on RPE, enhancing inactivation of C3b and reducing complement-mediated lysosomal stress, indirectly improving the phagocytic function of RPE.” On a cellular level, the expected effect following administration of recombinant human CD46 is a measurable reduction in complement deposition on RPE cell membranes, particularly the MAC, which is the terminal effector of the complement cascade. This reduction should translate to decreased inflammatory signaling and lower lysosomal overload. As a consequence, the RPE’s phagocytic capacity—especially the ability to clear photoreceptor outer segment debris—is expected to recover, which is a critical aspect of maintaining retinal function and delaying the progression of dry AMD (Sweigard et al., 2011).

Studies have shown that CD46-deficient RPE cells display key pathological features of AMD such as drusen-like deposits and diminished cathepsin D activity, indicative of lysosomal dysfunction (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011). In experimental assays, the addition of exogenous recombinant CD46 has been observed to restore the cleavage of complement components C3b and C4b, thereby reducing MAC formation and indirectly rescuing enzymatic activities within the lysosome (Sweigard et al., 2011). This expected cascade of events is anticipated to lead to measurable improvements in RPE cell phagocytic function when compared with untreated controls.

Moreover, CD46 is naturally expressed in RPE cells where it contributes to the resident complement regulatory milieu (Sweigard et al., 2011; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021). Therefore, supplementing RPE cultures with recombinant CD46 should mimic or reinforce the endogenous regulation process. The anticipated outcome is a dual benefit: reducing complement-mediated cytotoxicity and alleviating lysosomal stress while simultaneously normalizing the phagocytic clearance process that is otherwise impaired in the context of dry AMD. The restoration of cathepsin D activity, an enzyme critical for lysosomal digestion of photoreceptor outer segments, is a particularly important endpoint in these assays as it provides a direct readout of improved lysosomal function (Sweigard et al., 2011).

Overall, the expected biochemical and cellular effects of recombinant CD46 form the basis for its proposed therapeutic action. By reinstituting the natural regulatory mechanisms of the complement system, the candidate is expected to create a more favorable immunological environment within the RPE that is conducive to both cell survival and optimal function. This restoration of homeostasis is crucial in the context of dry AMD, where chronic low-grade complement activation is a driving force behind cellular degeneration and impaired phagocytosis (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011).

Overall Evaluation:  
The comprehensive evaluation of recombinant human CD46 as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD reveals a number of compelling strengths along with several challenges that must be addressed before clinical translation.  

One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its robust scientific rationale. CD46 is a key regulator of complement activation, and its role as a cofactor for factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b and C4b is well documented (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011). This molecular function is directly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, a condition in which uncontrolled complement activation contributes to RPE cell damage, chronic inflammation, and subsequent retinal degeneration (Sweigard et al., 2011). The association between CD46 deficiency and the development of drusen, as well as impaired phagocytosis in RPE cells, provides strong evidence that augmenting CD46 levels could have therapeutic benefits (Leaderer et al., 2015; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021).  

Another significant strength is the precedent established by previous preclinical studies. Gene therapy approaches that have increased CD46 expression in RPE cells have demonstrated a reduction in MAC deposition and subsequent protection against complement-mediated injury (Sweigard et al., 2011). Even though these studies primarily used viral vectors to drive endogenous expression rather than administering a recombinant protein directly, the mechanistic insights gleaned from them support the hypothesis that exogenously applied recombinant CD46 can restore complement regulation in diseased RPE cells (Sweigard et al., 2011; Leaderer et al., 2015).

However, there are several inherent risks and challenges associated with the use of a recombinant protein as a therapeutic agent for an ocular condition. One major challenge is the effective delivery of recombinant proteins to the RPE. Ocular drug delivery is notoriously difficult due to the presence of physical barriers like the blood-retina barrier and the complex anatomy of the eye. Achieving and maintaining therapeutic concentrations of recombinant CD46 at the appropriate retinal sites will require the development of sophisticated delivery systems or local administration techniques, such as intravitreal or sub-retinal injections (Sweigard et al., 2011; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021).

In addition, while the natural CD46 protein is membrane bound, recombinant protein formulations are often generated in a soluble form. Studies have suggested that soluble forms of CD46 may exhibit lower potency compared to their membrane-anchored counterparts (Wagner & Frank, 2010; Leaderer et al., 2015). This discrepancy could result in suboptimal therapeutic efficacy if the recombinant protein cannot adequately associate with or integrate into the RPE cell membrane, where its complement regulatory activity is most needed (Wagner & Frank, 2010; Leaderer et al., 2015). Hence, careful consideration must be given to the design of the recombinant protein to preserve the membrane-targeting signal or to engineer a formulation that mimics the native configuration as closely as possible.

Another concern relates to immunogenicity. Although recombinant human CD46 is derived from a native human protein, the process of recombinant expression and purification might introduce minor differences in glycosylation patterns or conformation that could provoke an immune response upon repeated administration (Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021). Such immune responses could not only reduce the efficacy of the therapeutic but also pose safety risks to patients.

There is also the broader challenge of translating findings from in vitro or animal models into effective human therapies. While the preclinical data supporting CD46’s role in regulating complement activity and protecting RPE cells is promising, clinical studies will need to rigorously demonstrate that recombinant CD46 can reproducibly and safely ameliorate the pathological features of dry AMD in human patients (Sweigard et al., 2011; Leaderer et al., 2015). Factors such as dosing regimen, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and potential off-target effects will be critical to assess.

In summary, recombinant human CD46 represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its well-characterized role in complement regulation and its ability to potentially restore critical homeostatic functions in the RPE. The scientific rationale is robust and is supported by extensive preclinical evidence linking CD46 deficiency with complement-mediated damage in the retina (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021). Nevertheless, significant hurdles in drug delivery, protein formulation, and immunogenicity must be overcome to realize its full therapeutic potential. Future studies should prioritize the development of an optimized delivery system that ensures adequate localization and retention of recombinant CD46 in the RPE, as well as detailed preclinical evaluations to refine dosing and minimize potential adverse effects (Sweigard et al., 2011; Leaderer et al., 2015).  

Overall, while challenges remain, the targeted nature of recombinant CD46—aiming to reinstate a naturally occurring regulatory mechanism—positions it as a strong candidate for further development. Its favorable mechanism of action, combined with supportive data from gene therapy models, provides a compelling rationale for additional preclinical and eventually clinical studies to validate its efficacy and safety in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mdivi-1 is a small molecule pharmacological agent originally discovered through high-throughput chemical screening in yeast models and subsequently characterized in mammalian systems as an inhibitor of mitochondrial fission. It is a quinazolinone derivative that belongs to a class of compounds targeting mitochondrial dynamics, with the specific intent of modulating the activity of dynamin-related protein 1 (DRP1) (Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008; Smith & Gallo, 2017). DRP1 is a large GTPase that mediates mitochondrial fission by undergoing self-assembly at constriction sites on the outer mitochondrial membrane and catalyzing membrane scission; under physiological conditions, this process is balanced by mitochondrial fusion activities to maintain mitochondrial morphology, bioenergetics, and quality control. Mdivi-1 was synthesized and later commercialized (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. M0199) because of its ability to selectively inhibit DRP1 activity, thereby shifting the balance away from excessive mitochondrial division and promoting a more interconnected, tubular mitochondrial network (Rosdah et al., 2016; Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008). This compound’s origins as a research tool in basic mitochondrial biology have led to its investigation in various disease models ranging from neurodegenerative conditions and cardiovascular ischemia to ocular disorders, where mitochondrial dysfunction is known to play a critical role. Its repurposing for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is of particular interest because of the emerging evidence linking chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial fragmentation, and RPE (retinal pigment epithelium) dysfunction to AMD pathology (Yako et al., 2021; Somasundaran et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Mdivi-1 has been extensively used in preclinical studies to interrogate the role of excessive mitochondrial fission in diverse pathological conditions. Initial seminal work demonstrated that inhibition of DRP1 activity by Mdivi-1 could prevent mitochondrial fragmentation, reduce cytochrome c release, and attenuate apoptosis in yeast and mammalian cell models (Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008; Rosdah et al., 2016). Following these foundational observations, several studies explored its utility in neuronal and cardiovascular systems. For example, preclinical investigations in models of ischemia-reperfusion injury, myocardial infarction, and neurodegeneration revealed that Mdivi-1 treatment increased cell survival and improved functional outcomes by preserving mitochondrial structure (Chen et al., 2023; Park et al., 2011).  

In the ocular domain, Mdivi-1 has been tested in models of retinal ischemia, glaucoma, and retinal detachment. Studies have shown that Mdivi-1 can increase the survival of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) in settings of acute ischemic injury, and its administration in retinal detachment models improved photoreceptor survival by mitigating DRP1-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction (She et al., 2018; Park et al., 2011). Moreover, within RPE-specific research, there is evidence from ARPE-19 cell studies that Mdivi-1 can counteract H₂O₂-induced oxidative damage by preventing mitochondrial fragmentation and preserving mitochondrial membrane potential, thereby protecting cells from apoptosis (Yako et al., 2021). Although the majority of these studies have focused on acute oxidative stress paradigms, the use of Mdivi-1 in these diverse retinal models provides a strong rationale to explore its potential in treating dry AMD, a condition characterized by chronic RPE stress, impaired photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis, and progressive mitochondrial dysfunction (Yako et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of Mdivi-1 centers on its inhibitory effect on DRP1, a critical regulator of mitochondrial fission. In a normally functioning cell, DRP1 resides in the cytosol and, upon activation—often triggered by cellular stress or proliferative signals—it translocates to the outer mitochondrial membrane. There, DRP1 self-assembles into oligomeric complexes that hydrolyze GTP to execute the fission process (Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008; Rosdah et al., 2016). Mdivi-1 acts by binding to an allosteric site on DRP1, thereby inhibiting its GTPase activity and preventing the oligomerization necessary for mitochondrial membrane constriction (Rosdah et al., 2016; Smith & Gallo, 2017). This inhibition not only prevents the excessive fragmentation of mitochondria under conditions of oxidative stress but also stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential and curbs the release of pro-apoptotic factors such as cytochrome c (Yako et al., 2021).

At the biochemical level, studies using ARPE-19 cells have shown that Mdivi-1 treatment correlates with a significant reduction in markers of mitochondrial dysfunction—such as decreased cytochrome c leakage and improved maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential—even when the cells are challenged with oxidative insults like H₂O₂ (Yako et al., 2021). These protective effects are central to the proposed hypothesis for dry AMD, where preservation of mitochondrial function in RPE is paramount for sustaining ATP production and supporting energy-demanding processes like POS phagocytosis.

It is important to note, however, that emerging evidence suggests that Mdivi-1’s actions may not be limited solely to DRP1 inhibition. Several studies have reported that Mdivi-1 also acts as a reversible inhibitor of mitochondrial Complex I of the electron transport chain (Marx et al., 2024; Avilan, 2023). This off-target effect can modulate reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and potentially influence cellular bioenergetics in a manner that might either contribute beneficially by reducing oxidative stress or detrimentally by impairing ATP production if the inhibition of Complex I is too pronounced. Such dual activity necessitates careful titration of Mdivi-1 dosing to ensure that the beneficial effects of DRP1 inhibition are not overshadowed by unwanted metabolic interference. Additionally, post-translational modifications of DRP1, such as phosphorylation at serine residues 616 and 637, modulate its activity and may influence the sensitivity of DRP1 to inhibition by Mdivi-1 in different cellular contexts (Yako et al., 2021). This complexity underscores the need for a thorough understanding of Mdivi-1’s molecular interactions in RPE cells and how these might translate to functional benefits in conditions like dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis guiding the proposed therapeutic application of Mdivi-1 in dry AMD is that by inhibiting excessive DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission, the drug will preserve the integrity of the mitochondrial network in RPE cells. This preservation is critical because RPE cells rely heavily on mitochondria to generate ATP, which in turn is essential for energy-dependent processes such as the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Yako et al., 2021). Under oxidative stress conditions—conditions that mimic the chronic environmental challenges faced by the RPE in dry AMD—excessive mitochondrial fragmentation leads to diminished ATP production and impaired phagocytic function. In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have provided evidence that treatment with Mdivi-1 can normalize mitochondrial morphology, preserve mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduce the release of cytochrome c, all of which contribute to maintaining cellular ATP levels (Yako et al., 2021).

In the context of the proposed assay, Mdivi-1 is expected to act at an effective concentration—hypothetically around an IC₅₀ of ~1 µM—to inhibit excessive mitochondrial fission in stressed RPE cells. By stabilizing mitochondrial dynamics, RPE cells should be able to sustain adequate ATP production even under conditions of oxidative challenge, thereby directly supporting the energy-demanding process of POS phagocytosis. This is critical because efficient phagocytosis is a cornerstone of RPE function; failure to clear shed photoreceptor debris leads to the formation of drusen and the accumulation of lipofuscin, both hallmark features of dry AMD pathology (Yako et al., 2021).

Moreover, improved mitochondrial function should also contribute to the normalization of lysosomal pH—a factor that is important for the proper degradation of phagocytosed material. Together, these effects are anticipated to not only preserve cellular viability in the face of chronic oxidative stress but also enhance the functional capacity of the RPE to process photoreceptor debris, which in turn could slow or halt the progression of dry AMD. However, it is crucial to achieve a delicate balance in dosing; while low concentrations might yield the desired protective effects by selectively inhibiting DRP1, higher concentrations run the risk of triggering off-target Complex I inhibition, with a subsequent decrease in ATP production that would be counterproductive in an energy-deficient cell (Marx et al., 2024; Avilan, 2023). Thus, while the expected effect is highly promising, it is contingent upon precise dose optimization and careful validation in both acute and chronic RPE models.

Overall Evaluation:  
Taken together, the literature supports the potential of Mdivi-1 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, predicated on its capacity to inhibit DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission and preserve mitochondrial network integrity in RPE cells. The compound’s strength lies in its well-documented ability to prevent mitochondrial fragmentation, maintain mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduce apoptotic signaling under conditions of oxidative stress, which are all pivotal factors in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Preclinical studies in various retinal and neurodegenerative models further bolster the case for its broader applicability in ocular diseases; evidence from glaucoma and retinal detachment models, as well as in ARPE-19 cell studies, suggests that modulating mitochondrial dynamics can offer significant neuroprotective benefits (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Park et al., 2011; She et al., 2018).

Nonetheless, several weaknesses temper the enthusiasm for Mdivi-1’s clinical translation in dry AMD. One of the primary concerns is the duality in its mechanism of action. Although Mdivi-1 is primarily characterized as a DRP1 inhibitor, multiple studies have raised valid concerns regarding its off-target effects, notably its inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I at higher doses (Marx et al., 2024; Avilan, 2023). This is particularly significant in the context of RPE cells, which are highly dependent on robust mitochondrial function and efficient ATP production to sustain their phagocytic and metabolic activities. Inadvertent inhibition of Complex I could lead to decreased ATP synthesis and an accumulation of ROS, thereby exacerbating rather than alleviating cellular dysfunction—an outcome that would be highly undesirable in a disease like dry AMD.

Another key issue is the apparent variability in effective dosing. While some studies report cytoprotective effects at concentrations around 1–10 µM, others have employed doses up to 50 µM to observe meaningful modulatory effects on mitochondrial dynamics (Yako et al., 2021). Such variability suggests that the effective therapeutic window might be narrow, and that even minor deviations in dosing could result in suboptimal efficacy or unintended toxicity. Notably, some in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have demonstrated that higher concentrations of Mdivi-1 can lead to cytotoxicity, raising concerns about its safety profile for long-term use in the retina (Shulman et al., 2010).

Additionally, while the hypothesis underlying the current proposal—that inhibition of excessive mitochondrial fission can restore ATP production and thereby improve POS phagocytosis—is mechanistically sound, direct evidence linking Mdivi-1 treatment to enhanced phagocytic function in RPE cells remains somewhat preliminary. Most of the existing literature has focused on acute protective effects in response to oxidative stress rather than on the chronic functional deficits observed in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). This gap in the literature signals a need for more targeted studies that evaluate not only the biochemical and morphological endpoints but also the functional outcomes, such as phagocytotic efficiency, in models that closely mimic the chronic nature of AMD.

Furthermore, the complex intracellular milieu of the RPE—characterized by high metabolic demand, ongoing phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, and a finely balanced process of autophagy and lysosomal degradation—means that interventions must be precisely calibrated. Chronic inhibition of mitochondrial fission, if not tightly controlled, could disrupt normal mitophagy (the selective removal of damaged mitochondria) and impair cellular turnover processes, potentially leading to the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria over time (Lin et al., 2024; Rosdah et al., 2016). Therefore, while the short-term benefits of Mdivi-1 are encouraging, its long-term impact on overall mitochondrial quality control and cellular homeostasis in RPE cells remains an open question.

From a translational standpoint, Mdivi-1’s established use in several preclinical ocular models is a significant strength, as it facilitates the leveraging of existing data and methodologies in further studies designed to address dry AMD specifically (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Park et al., 2011; She et al., 2018). Moreover, the absence of current effective treatments for dry AMD underscores the urgency of pursuing novel therapeutic approaches that target its underlying pathophysiology. In this regard, the idea of preserving mitochondrial integrity to support energy-dependent processes like photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis is particularly compelling (Yako et al., 2021).

In conclusion, while Mdivi-1 exhibits several attractive features as a candidate for dry AMD therapy—including the ability to modulate mitochondrial dynamics, preserve ATP production, and reduce oxidative stress—the existing body of evidence also highlights critical challenges that must be overcome. These include resolving the controversy surrounding its off-target effects on Complex I, establishing a reliable and safe dosing regimen, and generating direct evidence linking its use to functional improvements in RPE phagocytosis in models that accurately reflect the chronic nature of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021; Marx et al., 2024; Avilan, 2023). Provided that these challenges are addressed through rigorous preclinical studies and careful dose optimization, Mdivi-1 remains a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD.

Overall, our evaluation indicates that Mdivi-1 holds considerable potential as a therapeutic agent for dry age-related macular degeneration by targeting the mitochondrial dysfunction that is central to RPE pathology. Its ability to inhibit DRP1 and thereby reduce oxidative stress-induced mitochondrial fragmentation could preserve critical cellular functions such as ATP production and photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis, offering a novel mechanism of action to address this currently untreatable condition. However, the possibility of off-target Complex I inhibition and dose-dependent cytotoxicity underscore the need for further detailed mechanistic studies and dose-ranging experiments in both in vitro and in vivo models that better simulate the chronic progression of dry AMD. With these challenges appropriately managed, Mdivi-1 could potentially become an innovative mitochondrial-based therapeutic for a disease desperately in need of effective intervention (Yako et al., 2021; Marx et al., 2024; Avilan, 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin is a naturally derived macrolide initially isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus and belongs to the class of mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) inhibitors. This compound, originally discovered for its immunosuppressive properties, has evolved into a prominent therapeutic candidate across several fields including oncology, immunology, and neurodegeneration. Its chemical derivation and structural complexity allow for potent and selective inhibition of the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1). Rapamycin is widely used in clinical settings as an immunosuppressant following organ transplantation and has been repurposed for other indications based on its ability to modulate intracellular signaling pathways that regulate cellular growth, survival, and autophagy. As such, its potential application in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on a body of work indicating that targeting mTORC1 can restore autophagic and lysosomal function in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—a crucial factor given that RPE dysfunction is central to AMD pathogenesis (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, rapamycin has been extensively used and investigated in various clinical and preclinical settings. Its initial clinical use as an immunosuppressive agent in organ transplant patients laid the groundwork for understanding its mechanisms of action and safety profile in humans. Beyond its immunosuppressive applications, rapamycin has been evaluated for its anti-proliferative effects in several types of cancer and for its capability to extend lifespan in model organisms; these studies underscore the drug’s pleiotropic effects on cellular metabolism and autophagy. Specifically regarding ocular therapeutics, preclinical studies on retinal degenerative diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa and glaucoma have demonstrated that mTOR modulation by rapamycin can exert neuroprotective properties in retinal tissues (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). In the realm of AMD, several investigations have focused on the role of autophagy and lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in RPE cells, where rapamycin has been shown to promote autophagy and decrease the buildup of toxic aggregates, such as lipofuscin (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical studies and safety evaluations—in particular, intravitreal injections in non-human primates—have provided encouraging data regarding the ocular safety profile of rapamycin, thus supporting its further exploration as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, rapamycin exerts its effects by binding to the intracellular receptor FKBP12 (FK506-binding protein 12). This drug–FKBP12 complex then interacts with mTORC1, leading to its allosteric inhibition. Under normal anabolic conditions, active mTORC1 phosphorylates several downstream targets, including the transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is sequestered in the cytosol in its phosphorylated state, thus preventing the transcription of genes associated with lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. When rapamycin inhibits mTORC1, the phosphorylation of TFEB is reduced, permitting its nuclear translocation. Once inside the nucleus, TFEB initiates the transcription of numerous genes involved in autophagy and lysosomal function, thereby enhancing the cell’s capacity to degrade and recycle cellular debris such as accumulated photoreceptor outer segments (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium, mTORC1 normally integrates growth factor signals, nutrient availability, and stress responses to tightly regulate cellular homeostasis. The inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin thus releases the “brake” on autophagy, as evidenced by increased expression of autophagic markers such as LC3-II and lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1. This cascading effect leads to an enhanced intracellular clearance system (phagolysosomal flux), which is particularly critical for RPE cells that are responsible for the daily degradation of shed POS. Several studies have demonstrated that rapamycin-treated RPE cells exhibit improved POS degradation, a reduction in lipofuscin-like granules, and overall restoration of lysosomal function (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, the molecular signatures observed in rapamycin-treated cells mimic those seen under conditions of caloric restriction, further supporting the notion that mTORC1 inhibition can activate protective autophagic pathways (Davis, 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). This advanced understanding of rapamycin’s mechanism of action provides a compelling rationale for its application in dry AMD, where the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and dysregulated autophagy are key pathological features (Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of rapamycin in dry AMD is that its inhibition of mTORC1 will lead to the activation of TFEB by reducing its cytosolic phosphorylation state, thereby promoting nuclear translocation. In iPSC-derived RPE models, this induction of TFEB activity is expected to upregulate a host of autophagy and lysosomal genes, which in turn should enhance the cellular degradation of photoreceptor outer segments—an essential process in maintaining retinal homeostasis (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025). Accordingly, the anticipated in vitro effects upon rapamycin treatment include a robust increase in autophagic flux evidenced by elevated levels of LC3-II and LAMP1, paired with improved processing and clearance of POS debris. This effect is crucial because impaired clearance mechanisms contribute to the accumulation of lipofuscin and other cellular waste materials in RPE cells, both of which are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Falcão et al., 2024).

Supporting this expected outcome are observations from previous studies where rapamycin has been associated with a reduction in autofluorescent granules and a restoration of normal cellular clearance dynamics in RPE cells (Falcão et al., 2024). Additionally, safety assessments performed through intravitreal administration in non-human primates have demonstrated that rapamycin can be delivered to the retina with minimal adverse events, thereby underpinning its feasibility for clinical translation (Falcão et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2022). Importantly, the hypothesis that rapamycin can act at IC₅₀ values as low as approximately 0.1 nM in RPE cells further reinforces the potential sensitivity and efficacy of this candidate in modulating the pathway of interest. Given the expression of mTOR, TFEB, LC3, and LAMP1 in RPE cells—and the established role of these proteins in the autophagic and lysosomal clearance of POS—the expected improvement in autophagic turnover should directly translate into enhanced cell function and potentially mitigate the progression of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2022; Intartaglia et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
Rapamycin emerges as a robust and mechanistically sound therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its established ability to inhibit mTORC1 and consequently activate autophagy and lysosomal gene expression through TFEB nuclear translocation. One of the major strengths of this candidate lies in the well-characterized molecular mechanism that connects mTORC1 inhibition with enhanced clearance of POS debris—a process that is fundamentally disrupted in dry AMD. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence, ranging from biochemical assays that show increased LC3-II and LAMP1 expression in rapamycin-treated RPE cells to preclinical safety data in non-human primates, bolsters confidence in its potential utility (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

Furthermore, the multifaceted benefits of mTORC1 inhibition extend beyond autophagy induction; rapamycin also offers neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects, both of which are advantageous in the treatment of retinal degenerative diseases (Chang et al., 2022). The leverage of TFEB activation not only addresses the aberrant accumulation of toxic cellular debris but may also promote a broader upregulation of lysosomal biogenesis, thereby preempting further functional decline of RPE cells. These properties make rapamycin a strong candidate for mitigating early events in AMD pathogenesis, particularly in the context of experimental iPSC-RPE models where enhanced phagocytic capacity can be directly measured.

Nevertheless, several challenges and potential weaknesses require careful consideration. Despite its promising mechanism and preclinical rationale, clinical trials evaluating rapamycin in the context of ocular diseases have yielded mixed results, with some studies documenting only marginal improvements in visual function and others noting issues related to the drug’s solubility and delivery (Marchesi et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022). In advanced AMD, where the disease pathology is more complex and multifactorial, rapamycin’s efficacy might be limited, and there is a need for precise dosing strategies to balance mTORC1 inhibition with the preservation of physiological mTOR functions that are crucial for RPE cell survival (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). Additionally, the potential for off-target effects or immunosuppressive consequences linked to systemic exposure—although minimized by intravitreal delivery—necessitates further investigation into long-term safety profiles (Wang et al., 2022).

Another potential limitation is the inherent complexity of autophagy regulation in the RPE, which can be influenced by factors such as oxidative stress, metabolic dysfunction, and age-related changes in lysosomal function. While rapamycin is effective in reactivating autophagic pathways under controlled experimental settings, its impact within the pathogenic environment of a diseased retina, particularly if inflammatory processes are simultaneously active, may be less predictable (Davis, 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, the therapeutic window for achieving beneficial rapamycin concentrations without incurring adverse events is not yet fully defined, underscoring the importance of pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic studies specifically tailored to ocular tissues (Falcão et al., 2024).

Taken together, the current body of evidence suggests that rapamycin’s capacity to restore autophagic homeostasis in RPE cells represents a solid mechanistic foundation for its use in dry AMD. Its ability to upregulate autophagy and lysosomal function through TFEB activation directly addresses known defects in the clearance pathways of RPE cells—a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Moreover, the safety data from preclinical intravitreal delivery studies provide additional incentive to advance this candidate further along the translational pipeline. However, given the mixed outcomes observed in some clinical contexts and the challenges related to drug formulation and optimal dosing, further comprehensive studies are warranted to clarify its efficacy in early versus advanced stages of AMD (Mei et al., 2022).

In conclusion, rapamycin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD shows significant promise from both a mechanistic and translational standpoint. Its well-documented ability to inhibit mTORC1, thereby releasing TFEB and ramping up autophagic and lysosomal gene expression, positions it uniquely to tackle the underpinnings of RPE dysfunction characteristic of dry AMD. While preclinical data support its efficacy and safety with intravitreal administration in non-human primates, challenges remain regarding its formulation, potential off-target effects, and the delineation of its therapeutic window in human subjects. Consequently, while rapamycin’s molecular mechanism and early experimental results are highly encouraging, further studies—especially those that integrate pharmacokinetic profiling, dose optimization, and long-term outcome measurements in relevant in vivo models—are essential before definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding its clinical utility for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Si et al., 2023).

Overall, the strengths of rapamycin include its robust and well-characterized action on mTORC1, its downstream activation of autophagic and lysosomal pathways via TFEB, and supportive preclinical safety data in ocular models. In contrast, its weaknesses lie in the variable efficacy observed in clinical studies, formulation challenges due to low solubility, and the need for careful dosing to avoid potential adverse effects related to systemic immunosuppression. These considerations collectively argue for the continued investigation of rapamycin as a therapeutic option for dry AMD with a focus on optimizing delivery strategies and characterizing its long-term impact on retinal structure and function (Wang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025).
