Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SU5402 is a small‐molecule inhibitor that belongs to the indolinone, also often described as oxindole, family of compounds designed to target receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), most notably fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs) and platelet‐derived growth factor receptors (PDGFRs) (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Chemically, it is defined as 3-[(3-(2-carboxyethyl)-4-methylpyrrol-2-yl)methylene]-2-indolinone, a structure that features an indolin-2-one nucleus decorated with a propionic acid chain and a methyl substituent on a pyrrole ring; these structural motifs enable the molecule to mimic key interactions commonly found in ATP binding (Prakash et al., 2012; Ho et al., 2014). Originally discovered as one of the first classes of FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors, the compound’s crystal structure in complex with FGFR was resolved as early as 1997, establishing its role as an important lead for further inhibitor design (Liang et al., 2012). SU5402 is therefore categorized as an ATP-competitive inhibitor that occupies a hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the adenine binding site in FGFR, and its design has inspired many subsequent efforts to optimize RTK inhibition for therapeutic purposes (Manetti & Botta, 2003). In addition to its potent activity against FGFR1 (with reported IC₅₀ values around 0.03 μM), SU5402 displays inhibitory effects toward PDGFRβ and even VEGFR2, positioning it as a prototype multi-targeted kinase inhibitor in early-stage drug development programs (Chen et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2014). Its synthesis is rooted in structure-based medicinal chemistry approaches whereby modifications of the indolinone core and side chain functionalities were guided by crystal structure data and structure–activity relationship studies (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Consequently, SU5402 stands as a well-characterized synthetic compound with a clearly delineated pharmacophore, and its molecular interactions with the kinase active site are illustrative of the class’s capacity to serve as lead compounds in various therapeutic areas (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the development and use of SU5402 have been predominantly tied to oncology and anti-angiogenic research. Early investigations demonstrated that by inhibiting FGFR signaling, SU5402 effectively blocked the autophosphorylation of the receptor and downstream proliferative and survival pathways such as RAF-MEK1/2-MAPK and PI3K-AKT—pathways that are essential drivers of tumor growth and angiogenesis (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). GSK2606414 is a small‐molecule, synthetic inhibitor of PERK (protein kinase R‐like endoplasmic reticulum kinase) originally developed by GlaxoSmithKline. The compound was designed to target the unfolded protein response (UPR) and integrated stress response (ISR) by binding in the ATP pocket of PERK, thereby blocking its autophosphorylation and subsequent phosphorylation of its downstream target, eIF2α. This family of inhibitors has historically been used as a research tool to dissect the role of PERK in diverse contexts, including cancer, neurodegeneration, and other stress‐related diseases, owing to their ability to modulate protein synthesis under conditions of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (Chu et al., 2021; Kalinin et al., 2025). The high biochemical potency (with reported PERK IC₅₀ values in the sub-nanomolar range in enzymatic assays) contrasts with the micromolar concentrations sometimes needed to achieve cellular effects, as demonstrated in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell studies where IC₅₀ values in the low micromolar range have been observed (Jiang et al., 2017). Through its capacity to inhibit the PERK-eIF2α axis, GSK2606414 has become an important tool compound when exploring how ER stress contributes to cellular dysfunction and death, while its chemical scaffold has inspired the development of further optimized analogues for more selective targeting (Jiang et al., 2017; Axten, 2017).

GSK2606414 has been extensively studied across multiple preclinical disease models, most notably in neurodegeneration and cancer. In the field of neurodegenerative diseases, it has been shown to provide neuroprotection in models of prion disease and tauopathy by alleviating chronic translational repression and restoring synaptic protein synthesis (Hetz et al., 2019; Mercado et al., 2018). In oncology, GSK2606414 has been used both as a monotherapy and in combination with other agents, where it demonstrated modest antitumor effects in pancreatic xenografts and synergized with chemotherapeutic approaches (Axten, 2017; Agalakova, 2025). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ibrutinib is a fully synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally developed as an irreversible inhibitor of Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK). It achieves inhibition by covalently binding to the conserved Cys481 residue located within the ATP‐binding pocket of BTK, a key member of the TEC family of kinases. This irreversible binding results in permanent inactivation of BTK, thereby interrupting B‐cell receptor signaling as well as other downstream pathways that are critical for cell survival and proliferation (Xie et al., 2021). As a member of the broader class of tyrosine kinase inhibitors, ibrutinib is designed through refined organic synthesis strategies that optimize its selectivity and potency. Compounds of this chemical class have been extensively utilized in oncology, particularly for the treatment of B‐cell malignancies, where they serve to disrupt aberrant oncogenic signaling pathways. Ibrutinib is available commercially (e.g., SelleckChem Cat. No. S2680) and has been subject to rigorous clinical evaluation, ensuring that its chemical properties, including its irreversible binding mechanism and cell penetration capabilities, are well established in the literature (Xie et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, ibrutinib was developed and advanced clinically for hematologic cancers such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia (WM), and other B‐cell malignancies. Its success in these domains is attributed to its effective inhibition of BTK, a kinase that is critical for B‐cell receptor signaling and survival (Xie et al., 2021). Once approved by the U.S. FDA in 2013, it rapidly became a standard of care in oncology. Outside of its oncologic use, ibrutinib has been recognized for its immunomodulatory effects that extend to innate immune cells such as macrophages, dendritic cells, and, notably, microglia. Although the primary application of ibrutinib is in cancer therapy, there is emerging evidence and growing scientific interest suggesting that BTK plays a role in innate immune signaling pathways that contribute to chronic inflammatory states, including those implicated in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Brandli et al., 2024). In pharmacovigilance studies, ocular adverse events—including uveitis, cataracts, and retinal disorders—have been identified among patients treated with ibrutinib, which indicates that the molecule penetrates ocular compartments and exerts biological effects there (Allouchery et al., 2021). However, despite these observations, ibrutinib has not been previously developed or marketed for the treatment of dry AMD or similar degenerative retinal diseases. Instead, its potential repurposing arises from the hypothesis that by modulating BTK-dependent inflammatory pathways in microglia and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, ibrutinib might reduce deleterious inflammasome priming and cytokine production that contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ibrutinib exerts its primary action by binding irreversibly to BTK, thereby preventing autophosphorylation and subsequent transmission of intracellular signals that lead to inflammation and cell survival. BTK is not only a critical mediator of B‐cell receptor signaling but is also expressed in cells of the innate immune system including microglia and RPE cells. Its activation is linked to the regulation of the NLRP3 inflammasome—a multiprotein complex that senses cellular stress, leading to the activation of caspase-1 and the maturation and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Brandli et al., 2024). There is accumulating evidence that BTK facilitates the priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome in response to various stimuli, including oxidative stress and the accumulation of deleterious protein aggregates, both of which are implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis. Experimental data suggest that inhibition of BTK by ibrutinib can lead to a reduction in IL-1β release, which in turn may lower downstream pro-inflammatory signals such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) (Far et al., 2022; Allouchery et al., 2021). Moreover, the preservation of lysosomal cathepsin activity observed in ARPE-19 cells under inflammasome-stimulating conditions implies that BTK inhibition may also support the maintenance of RPE lysosomal integrity and phagocytic function. Such actions are critical for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and prevention of drusen accumulation—a hallmark of dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). In summary, by covalently binding to BTK, ibrutinib not only halts aberrant immune cell signaling but also indirectly modulates inflammasome activity and associated inflammatory cytokine release in retinal cells (Xie et al., 2021; Brandli et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for the repurposing of ibrutinib in dry AMD revolves around its ability to inhibit BTK activity within microglia and RPE cells, thereby suppressing inflammasome priming and limiting the production of inflammatory mediators such as IL-1β and TNFα. In the context of an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells, it is anticipated that the application of ibrutinib (IC₅₀ ~0.5 nM) will result in a marked attenuation of inflammasome activation, as evidenced by reduced secretion of IL-1β and preserved lysosomal cathepsin activity (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). The proposed mechanism by which ibrutinib exerts its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD is multifaceted. First, by inhibiting BTK, the compound is expected to downregulate the overactive NLRP3 inflammasome that plays a central role in the inflammatory cascade within the retinal pigment epithelium (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024). Second, by reducing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines—especially TNFα—which have been shown to negatively impact the phagocytic ability of RPE cells, ibrutinib may help to maintain the clearance of photoreceptor outer segment debris. This is particularly important because impaired clearance mechanisms contribute to the accumulation of drusen and subsequent RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024). Moreover, animal and clinical pharmacovigilance studies have provided evidence that ibrutinib is capable of crossing the blood-brain and blood-retinal barriers, suggesting that it can reach retinal tissues at therapeutically relevant concentrations. Although there is documented evidence of ocular adverse events in patients treated with ibrutinib for hematologic malignancies—including instances of uveitis and cystoid macular edema—such effects have been largely reported as unintended consequences rather than engineered therapeutic outcomes. In the current repurposing framework, the premise is that controlled intravitreal or local administration, possibly as a modified formulation, could harness the anti-inflammatory properties of ibrutinib while minimizing systemic exposure and the risk of ocular adverse events (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022). Ultimately, the expected effect is a preserved RPE function with enhanced ability to clear POS debris, thereby mitigating the degenerative progression typically observed in dry AMD (Korhonen, 2024; Brandli et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
Ibrutinib presents as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to its well-characterized molecular mechanism and its established clinical profile in oncology. One of the major strengths of ibrutinib lies in its potent and selective irreversible inhibition of BTK, a kinase implicated not only in B-cell malignancies but also in the pathogenesis of inflammatory retinal diseases through its role in NLRP3 inflammasome priming (Xie et al., 2021). The scientific rationale for its repurposing is supported by preclinical observations indicating that BTK inhibition leads to reduced IL-1β secretion and preservation of lysosomal function in RPE cells, which are essential for maintaining photoreceptor homeostasis and preventing drusen accumulation in dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). Furthermore, the demonstration that ibrutinib crosses the blood-retinal barrier underscores its potential utility in directly targeting retinal tissues, especially when administered via routes that ensure localized high concentrations with limited systemic exposure (Xie et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022).

However, there are several challenges and weaknesses associated with this therapeutic candidate. First, the ocular safety profile of ibrutinib is a matter of concern, as pharmacovigilance data have linked ibrutinib to a spectrum of adverse ocular events including cataracts, uveitis, and retinal disorders (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022). While these effects have so far been observed in the context of systemic cancer therapy, they raise important safety questions when considering chronic administration for a disease such as dry AMD that often requires long-term treatment. Second, the dosages and formulation required to achieve an anti-inflammatory effect in the retina, while concurrently minimizing cytotoxicity and other off-target effects, remain uncertain. Ibrutinib’s off-target inhibitory effects, such as its activity against VEGFR2, may impart vascular side effects that could further complicate its use in the delicate retinal environment (Allouchery et al., 2021). Third, the repurposing strategy relies heavily on the extrapolation of cellular and animal model data—such as the observed reduction of inflammasome activation and preservation of cathepsin activity in ARPE-19 cells—to the complex pathophysiology of human dry AMD. The heterogeneity of dry AMD pathogenesis, driven by a confluence of genetic, environmental, and age-related factors, means that successful translation from preclinical models to effective clinical outcomes is not guaranteed (Korhonen, 2024; Brandli et al., 2024). Additionally, while there is a robust theoretical framework underpinning BTK’s involvement in inflamed retinal microenvironments, direct evidence of ibrutinib’s efficacy in modulating microglial or RPE function specifically in the setting of dry AMD remains limited.

Despite these challenges, the mechanistic rationale for using a BTK inhibitor in dry AMD is compelling. The interplay between NLRP3 inflammasome activation, chronic low-grade inflammation, and RPE dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a pivotal driver of dry AMD progression (Brandli et al., 2024). If ibrutinib can effectively attenuate these inflammatory processes without incurring prohibitive adverse events, it may offer a novel therapeutic avenue for a disease area currently lacking effective treatment options. However, this necessitates a series of rigorous preclinical studies to characterize the dose-response relationship, evaluate retinal safety, and define the pharmacokinetic profile of ibrutinib when delivered via ocular routes. Moreover, any proposed clinical trial must incorporate comprehensive ophthalmologic monitoring given the known spectrum of ibrutinib-induced ocular side effects (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022).

In summary, while ibrutinib is primarily an approved oncologic agent, its underlying mechanism of inhibiting BTK—the kinase that modulates inflammasome priming in microglia and RPE cells—provides a strong scientific basis for its repurposing in dry AMD. The expected effects of reduced IL-1β and TNFα production, coupled with preserved lysosomal cathepsin activity and improved phagocytic function, align well with the therapeutic goals of mitigating chronic inflammation and preserving retinal integrity in dry AMD. Nevertheless, the potential ocular adverse effects and the challenges related to achieving a favorable therapeutic index in the retinal environment are significant concerns that must be addressed through further rigorous preclinical and clinical evaluations (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). Overall, ibrutinib represents an intriguing candidate with a solid mechanistic rationale for dry AMD treatment; however, careful attention to formulation, dosing, and safety testing is warranted before advancing this repurposing strategy to later-stage clinical trials (Xie et al., 2021; Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bryostatin‐1 is a naturally derived macrolide originally isolated from marine invertebrates and belongs to a class of compounds collectively known as bryostatins. These compounds exhibit potent modulation of protein kinase C (PKC) activity by binding to the enzyme’s diacylglycerol binding site on the regulatory domain. Bryostatin‐1 has been characterized as a partial agonist of PKC and is noted for its ability to both acutely activate and chronically down‐regulate specific PKC isoforms. The molecular architecture of bryostatin‐1 confers a unique binding profile that distinguishes it from phorbol esters; it induces translocation of target PKC isoforms to membranes without eliciting the full tumor‐promoting effects observed with phorbol esters. The compound is synthetically challenging to produce, yet semisynthetic methodologies have enabled its preparation in sufficient quantities for preclinical and early clinical applications. As a member of the marine natural products family, bryostatin‐1 is frequently investigated for its anticancer and neuroprotective properties, and its chemical structure serves as the basis for designing simplified analogs with improved pharmacological profiles (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).  

Therapeutic History:  
Bryostatin‐1 has a long preclinical history that spans oncology and neurology. In oncology, bryostatin‐1 has been extensively studied for its role in modulating PKC in various tumor types and has been evaluated in numerous clinical trials addressing B‐cell malignancies and renal cancers. Despite promising preclinical results, its cancer‐directed clinical efficacy has been limited by suboptimal outcomes and adverse side effects such as myalgia. More recently, bryostatin‐1 has been repurposed in neurological contexts. Several studies have demonstrated its neuroprotective capabilities in models of Alzheimer’s disease, where it has shown to improve synaptic function, restore dendritic spine morphology, induce synaptogenesis through the upregulation of brain‐derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and enhance cognitive function. Phase II clinical trials in Alzheimer’s patients have provided translational evidence of its ability to modulate PKCε in the central nervous system (Chen et al., 2024; Nelson et al., 2017). However, a search of clinical trial databases has revealed that no formal clinical trials have been registered evaluating bryostatin‐1 in the setting of macular degeneration, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, or Rab7 signaling‐related pathways (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Although there is evidence supporting bryostatin‐1’s capacity to affect cellular pathways—such as inducing autophagy and promoting PKC‐mediated cell survival—in neuronal and cancer cells, its application to ocular diseases like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) remains unexplored in the clinical context (Safarpour, 2009; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).  

Mechanism of Action:  
Bryostatin‐1 functions primarily as a modulator of protein kinase C, a family of serine/threonine kinases that play central roles in regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis, and intracellular trafficking. On a molecular level, bryostatin‐1 binds competitively to the diacylglycerol (DAG) binding site located in the C1 domain of PKC isoforms. This binding event leads to the translocation of PKC from the cytosol to membranous compartments, thereby bringing the kinase into close proximity with its substrates. Unlike potent activators such as phorbol esters, bryostatin‐1 acts as a partial agonist. Short‐term exposure results in the activation of specific PKC isoforms, whereas prolonged exposure leads to their down‐regulation via proteasomal degradation. Structural studies have demonstrated that the complex hydrogen‐bond networks formed by the A- and B-rings of bryostatin‐1 contribute significantly to its isoform selectivity and binding affinity (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).  

In the context of the hypothesized mechanism for dry AMD, it is proposed that bryostatin‐1 can activate atypical PKC isoforms at very low effective concentrations (EC₅₀ ≈ 0.1 nM), potentially including enzymes that are involved in the regulation of Rab7 signalling. Although bryostatin‐1 has been studied predominantly for its activation of classical (e.g., PKCα, PKCβ) and novel PKC isoforms (e.g., PKCδ, PKCε), several experimental reports suggest that PKC activity regulates various aspects of vesicular trafficking, including phagosome maturation. In phagocytic cell lines, enhanced PKC activation has been linked to improved phagolysosomal fusion, which is essential for the degradation of ingested material. This connection is of particular interest in RPE cells, where the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) via the phagosome–lysosome pathway is central to retinal homeostasis. The hypothesis extends this mechanism by proposing that the activation of PKC by bryostatin‐1 may lead to the phosphorylation of Rab7 effector proteins, which are known to control the late stages of phagosome maturation and lysosome fusion. Although direct experimental evidence connecting bryostatin‐1‐mediated PKC activation to Rab7 effector phosphorylation in RPE cells is limited, existing literature has established the importance of PKC in regulating phagocytic processes and intracellular vesicle trafficking (Saddala et al., 2020; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005). Furthermore, mechanistic parallels drawn from studies in neuronal systems—where bryostatin‐1 has been shown to influence autophagic flux and promote synaptic health—support the feasibility of such a cellular response in other highly phagocytic cells like the RPE (Chen et al., 2024).  

Expected Effect:  
Dry AMD is characterized by the dysfunction of RPE cells, which leads to impaired clearance of POS and subsequent accumulation of toxic lipofuscin deposits. RPE dysfunction is associated with disrupted phagosome maturation and lysosomal degradation pathways, contributing to retinal degeneration and vision loss. The therapeutic hypothesis for bryostatin‐1 posits that its administration will enhance the maturation of phagosomes by stimulating PKC isoforms that, in turn, phosphorylate Rab7 effectors. Effective phosphorylation of these effectors is expected to facilitate late phagosome–lysosome fusion, thereby improving the trafficking and degradation of POS. Empirical studies in RPE cells have shown that defects in phagolysosomal fusion lead to the accumulation of nondegradable materials and are closely linked to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Safarpour, 2009; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).  

The candidate mechanism suggests that, upon administration, bryostatin‐1 will rapidly bind to its target PKC isoforms in RPE cells, causing these kinases to translocate to relevant subcellular membranes. This translocation is anticipated to bring PKC in proximity to Rab7 effectors situated on late phagosomes. Activation of these kinases would then promote the phosphorylation of regulatory proteins that control vesicular fusion events. As a result, the impaired phagocytosis observed in dry AMD would be corrected through improved maturation of phagosomes and enhanced fusion with lysosomes. Such a cascade is expected to lead to enhanced clearance of POS debris and, ultimately, a reduction in lipofuscin accumulation, which is central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Although supportive evidence for this cascade exists in the context of non‐ocular phagocytic cells and in neuronal models of autophagy activation, it remains imperative to directly evaluate these effects in primary RPE cell cultures or relevant animal models to solidify the connection between PKC activation by bryostatin‐1 and Rab7‐mediated phagosome maturation (Saddala et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Bryostatin‐1 presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for dry AMD owing to its potent modulation of PKC, a central regulator of intracellular signaling pathways that govern vesicular trafficking, phagocytosis, and autophagy. One of the key strengths of bryostatin‐1 lies in its well‐documented activity in modulating PKC isoforms that are critical in diverse physiological contexts, including neuronal function and cancer cell biology. Its demonstrated neuroprotective efficacy in Alzheimer’s disease clinical studies supports the compound’s translational potential and suggests that its PKC‐modulating effects might be harnessed in alternate tissues such as the retina (Chen et al., 2024). Additionally, the critical role of PKC in promoting phagosome–lysosome fusion has been substantiated in other cell types, which provides a strong theoretical basis for its application in RPE cells where phagocytic clearance is essential for maintaining retinal integrity (Saddala et al., 2020; Safarpour, 2009).

Despite these promising aspects, several challenges and weaknesses must be considered. Foremost, no direct studies to date have evaluated bryostatin‐1 in the context of dry AMD or in RPE cells. Clinical trial databases have not registered any studies for bryostatin‐1 in macular degeneration, underscoring the novelty of this repurposing strategy but also highlighting a significant gap in the literature (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The hypothesis that bryostatin‐1 will stimulate atypical PKC isoforms to phosphorylate Rab7 effectors, although plausible, remains largely speculative. While various studies have linked PKC activity to phagosome maturation and autophagy regulation, the precise isoforms relevant to RPE cell function—and whether these isoforms are the same ones activated by bryostatin‐1 in neuronal or cancer models—have not been comprehensively elucidated. Therefore, it will be crucial to determine, through rigorous in vitro assays and animal models, whether the purported EC₅₀ of approximately 0.1 nM is achievable in RPE cells and whether this concentration effectively modifies the Rab7‐related molecular machinery.

Additional considerations include the potential for off‐target effects and systemic toxicity. Past clinical studies of bryostatin‐1, particularly in oncology, have reported adverse effects such as myalgia and thrombocytopenia. However, the pharmacokinetic profile observed in Alzheimer’s trials suggests that the dosing regimens used for neurological disorders might be translatable to ocular delivery with appropriate formulation strategies. Localized ocular delivery, such as intravitreal injection or controlled‐release implants, may enable targeted modulation of PKC in the retina while mitigating systemic exposure and associated adverse events (Chen et al., 2024; Nelson et al., 2017). Moreover, the challenge of achieving adequate drug penetration to the RPE in vivo is nontrivial. Approaches to enhance ocular bioavailability, including nanoparticle encapsulation or conjugation to targeting ligands, should be explored concurrently with the design of preclinical studies to better validate this therapeutic candidate.

From a mechanistic standpoint, the dual nature of bryostatin‐1—characterized by initial activation followed by downregulation of PKC isoforms—necessitates precise temporal control of its pharmacodynamic effects. In the context of phagosome maturation, transient activation may be beneficial to restore proper lysosomal fusion; however, prolonged downregulation might counteract the desired effect. It is therefore important that future studies carefully delineate the dosing regimen (both concentration and administration frequency) required to achieve an optimal therapeutic window in RPE cells. Additionally, the specificity of bryostatin‐1 for PKC isoforms implicated in Rab7 effector phosphorylation must be confirmed, as the RPE expresses a complex array of PKC isoforms that may play distinct roles in cellular homeostasis and stress responses (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).

The breadth and diversity of bryostatin‐1’s effects in preclinical models have generated considerable interest, yet its repurposing for dry AMD remains at an early stage of conceptual development. Given that disruption of phagosome maturation in RPE cells is a well‐established contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD—and that PKC signaling has been implicated in regulating this process—the rationale for exploring bryostatin‐1 in this indication is scientifically sound. Nonetheless, the transition from a neuroprotective agent in Alzheimer’s disease to an effective modulator of RPE function in dry AMD will depend on new studies that specifically address the cellular context of the retina. In this regard, preliminary investigations using primary RPE cultures or animal models of dry AMD will be critical to validate the hypothesis that PKC activation by bryostatin‐1 can enhance Rab7‐mediated phagolysosomal fusion and improve POS clearance (Saddala et al., 2020; Safarpour, 2009).

In summary, bryostatin‐1 offers both significant promise and notable challenges as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration. Its ability to modulate PKC in a manner that may restore essential phagolysosomal functions in the RPE positions it as an innovative approach to address a major unmet need in ocular therapeutics. The compound’s successful use in Alzheimer’s disease trials provides encouraging translational evidence of its safety and efficacy in modulating neuronal PKC activity. However, the absence of direct evidence in retinal cells, the uncertainty regarding which specific PKC isoforms are most relevant to RPE phagocytosis, and potential issues related to dosing and systemic toxicity form significant hurdles that must be overcome. Moving forward, it will be critical to conduct comprehensive in vitro studies to assess the effects of bryostatin‐1 on RPE phagosome maturation, coupled with robust in vivo experiments in established dry AMD models. Such studies should focus on confirming the expression and role of the putative target proteins, including Rab7 effectors, and determining whether the activation of these pathways can indeed translate into improved clearance of POS and reduced retinal degeneration (Saddala et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Chen et al., 2024; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).

In conclusion, the overall evaluation of bryostatin‐1 as a drug candidate for dry AMD reveals a compound with strong mechanistic rationale and significant translational potential based on its established pharmacological properties in PKC modulation and neuroprotection. The strengths of bryostatin‐1 include its potent activity at nanomolar concentrations, a unique mode of action that distinguishes it from classical PKC activators, and supporting evidence from clinical studies in neurological disorders. Conversely, its weaknesses lie primarily in the absence of direct studies in ocular tissues, uncertainty regarding the specific PKC isoforms involved in RPE phagosome maturation, and potential challenges in achieving localized delivery without systemic side effects. An interdisciplinary approach that integrates detailed molecular studies with innovative drug delivery strategies will be critical in validating bryostatin‐1’s viability for the treatment of dry AMD. Based on the current literature, investing in rigorous preclinical testing to confirm the hypothesized mechanistic link between PKC activation, Rab7 effector phosphorylation, and enhanced phagosome maturation in RPE cells is warranted before progressing to clinical evaluation (Saddala et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Safarpour, 2009; Chen et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ceapin-A7 is a small molecule inhibitor that belongs to the pyrazole amide class of compounds. It was originally discovered through high‐throughput cell‐based screening assays designed to identify modulators of the unfolded protein response (UPR), with an emphasis on selectively targeting the ATF6α signaling branch (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Hetz et al., 2019). Structural optimization through structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies led to the development of Ceapin-A7 as a potent derivative with submicromolar inhibitory activity against ATF6α (Hetz et al., 2019). The molecule’s chemical origins are purely synthetic; its pyrazole amide core is complemented by additional substituents that optimize its binding affinity and selectivity. Traditionally, compounds in this chemical class have been explored as research tools to dissect the UPR pathways and have shown promise in modulating ER stress signaling in various cellular contexts (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). The compound’s design exploits the unique structure–function relationships of ATF6α, aiming to interfere with its normal intracellular trafficking rather than block downstream proteolysis directly, which marks a novel approach compared with many enzyme inhibitors developed for other targets.

Therapeutic History:  
To date, Ceapin-A7 has been mainly used as an investigative tool in cellular models to study mechanisms underlying ER stress and the UPR. Its ability to selectively inhibit ATF6α activation has been characterized in multiple cell lines, including human osteosarcoma U2-OS cells and HEK293 cells engineered to express tagged ATF6α constructs (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Hetz et al., 2019). Although there is extensive preclinical evidence supporting its utility in modulating UPR signaling—all of which has been generated in the context of studies on cancer cells, neurodegeneration, and endothelial dysfunction—there is no historically established clinical or veterinary usage for Ceapin-A7 specifically in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal degenerative diseases. However, the mechanistic insights gained from its application in other cell types have spurred investigations into repurposing Ceapin-A7 as a potential therapeutic candidate for correcting maladaptive ER stress responses in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which plays a pivotal role in diseases such as dry AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Torres et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
Ceapin-A7 exerts its pharmacological action by selectively inhibiting the ATF6α branch of the UPR. Under normal ER stress conditions, ATF6α, a 90-kDa transmembrane protein located in the endoplasmic reticulum, undergoes a stress-induced conformational change that facilitates its packaging into COPII vesicles and subsequent trafficking to the Golgi apparatus. Once in the Golgi, ATF6α is cleaved sequentially by site-1 (S1P) and site-2 (S2P) proteases to release its N-terminal transcription factor domain, which then translocates to the nucleus to upregulate several chaperone and ER stress-related genes (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Ceapin-A7 intervenes at this critical transport step. Rather than inhibiting the proteolytic machinery directly, Ceapin-A7 selectively prevents the ER-to-Golgi trafficking of ATF6α. Mechanistic studies have demonstrated that upon treatment with Ceapin-A7, ATF6α is sequestered within the ER where it accumulates in discrete foci. Fluorescence microscopy analyses have shown that these foci do not colocalize with ER exit site markers such as SEC16 or SEC31A, indicating that the compound disrupts the selection of ATF6α into COPII vesicles (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

One particularly novel aspect of Ceapin-A7’s mechanism is its induction of a neomorphic inter-organelle tether. Detailed proteomic and genome-wide CRISPR interference screening studies have revealed that Ceapin-A7 induces a physical interaction between the cytosolic domain of ATF6α and the peroxisomal transporter protein ABCD3 (Torres et al., 2019). This newly formed tether effectively anchors ATF6α within the ER and precludes its normal traffic to the Golgi. In addition, Ceapin-A7 appears to stabilize ATF6α in its oligomeric state, rather than allowing it to convert to the transport-competent monomeric form (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). The fact that these mechanistic events are reversible upon compound washout further indicates that Ceapin-A7 provides a transient yet highly specific method for modulating ATF6α activity without causing permanent alterations to the protein structure or its eventual capacity to function when the inhibitor is removed (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Such high selectivity distinguishes Ceapin-A7 from broader ER stress inhibitors that often affect multiple UPR signaling branches.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the hypothesized role of Ceapin-A7 is to inhibit chronic ATF6α overactivation in RPE cells, thereby rebalancing the UPR toward adaptive rather than pro-apoptotic responses. Chronic or overwhelming ER stress in RPE cells, as observed in AMD, is associated with decreased expression of genes critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis, including those linked to autophagy, lysosomal function, and the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Because RPE cells are responsible for daily phagocytosis of POS, maintaining efficient lysosomal clearance is crucial for retinal health. In dry AMD, impaired phagocytosis leads to the buildup of toxic byproducts such as lipofuscin, which further exacerbates cellular dysfunction (Kubra et al., 2022; Benedetti et al., 2024).

The therapeutic hypothesis for Ceapin-A7 centers on its capacity to inhibit ATF6α at an IC₅₀ in the low micromolar range (approximately 2 µM, as proposed), thus reducing maladaptive UPR signaling. By preventing ATF6α from trafficking and undergoing proteolytic activation, Ceapin-A7 is expected to alleviate the chronic ER stress that drives RPE dysfunction. In a proposed assay—using ARPE-19 cells in conditions of induced ER stress (for instance, via tunicamycin treatment)—Ceapin-A7 should reduce the levels of cleaved, active ATF6α. This in turn is expected to restore the gene expression patterns associated with lysosomal enzyme production and phagocytic receptor synthesis, thereby enhancing the clearance of POS components (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Furthermore, because the ATF6 branch of the UPR is associated with the upregulation of chaperones like BiP/Grp78, persistent activation can lead to resource exhaustion and an imbalance that favors apoptotic signaling under chronic ER stress conditions (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). By selectively inhibiting this pathway, Ceapin-A7 might reduce excessive chaperone induction and allow cellular systems to shift toward a more balanced, adaptive stress response that promotes autophagy and lysosomal function. Importantly, RPE cells express ATF6, as evidenced by studies utilizing ARPE-19 and primary RPE cultures, making these cells appropriate targets for ATF6 modulation (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Thus, the expected effect is a reestablishment of normal proteostasis in RPE cells via the restoration of adaptive autophagy, improved lysosomal enzyme activity, and enhanced phagocytic receptor expression, all of which are critical for the sustained clearance of photoreceptor outer segment debris and prevention of cytotoxic accumulation in dry AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
Ceapin-A7 represents an innovative therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration due to its unique and selective mechanism of action targeting the ATF6α branch of the UPR. One of the main strengths of this compound is its ability to modulate a very specific aspect of cellular stress signaling. By preventing the ER-to-Golgi trafficking of ATF6α and thereby inhibiting its proteolytic activation, Ceapin-A7 offers a promising strategy for shifting the balance of UPR signaling toward adaptive autophagy instead of chronic, detrimental ER stress (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). This is particularly relevant in the context of RPE cells, which require efficient protein quality control and robust lysosomal function to maintain photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance and overall retinal integrity.

In vitro studies have validated the mechanism of Ceapin-A7, with data showing that the compound induces the formation of discrete ATF6α-positive foci in the ER (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Moreover, the reversible nature of its action implies that Ceapin-A7 may offer a controllable therapeutic window, enabling fine-tuning of UPR modulation in a clinical setting (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). The involvement of peroxisomal protein ABCD3 in a neomorphic tethering mechanism further differentiates Ceapin-A7 from other UPR modulators by introducing a novel means of sequestering ATF6α (Torres et al., 2019). Such specificity is particularly compelling because it suggests that Ceapin-A7 can mitigate the chronic ER stress observed in dry AMD without interfering with other UPR branches (such as IRE1 or PERK), which are essential for normal cellular adaptation to transient stress.

However, there are notable limitations and challenges that warrant careful evaluation. First, despite the extensive preclinical work in cell lines and non-retinal systems, Ceapin-A7 has yet to be thoroughly evaluated in RPE-specific models or in vivo systems relevant to AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Second, the full spectrum of off-target effects is not yet fully characterized. While Ceapin-A7 shows selectivity for ATF6α, the influence of its induced neomorphic tether between ATF6α and ABCD3 on peroxisome function remains to be fully elucidated. Although available evidence suggests that Ceapin-A7 does not interfere significantly with ABCD3’s normal transporter function (Torres et al., 2019), the robustness of these findings in the retinal context remains an open question.

Another potential caveat is the dual role that ATF6α may play in various tissues. Although chronic activation of ATF6α is thought to contribute to maladaptive ER stress and consequent cellular dysfunction in AMD, ATF6α also participates in adaptive responses by upregulating crucial ER chaperones that preserve proteostasis (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Therefore, complete inhibition of ATF6α activity might have unintended consequences if not properly dosed or if the timing of inhibition is not carefully managed. An optimal therapeutic strategy might require a fine balance between sufficient ATF6α inhibition to restore lysosomal and phagocytic function in RPE cells and preserving enough ATF6α activity to maintain overall cellular homeostasis, particularly in tissues under variable stress dynamics.

Moreover, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of Ceapin-A7 in the ocular environment have not been established. For a drug candidate to be viable in treating dry AMD, it must be effectively delivered to the RPE with minimal systemic exposure, maintain a stable concentration over time, and be cleared without inducing local toxicity. The formulation challenges of ocular drug delivery, including crossing the blood-retinal barrier and achieving sustained release in the subretinal space, remain critical hurdles that must be addressed in future studies (Hetz et al., 2019; Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Finally, long-term safety studies are essential. The reversible nature of Ceapin-A7’s effects is promising; however, chronic treatment in a degenerative condition like dry AMD necessitates an in-depth understanding of the potential cumulative effects or chronic alterations in ER stress responses over time. Safety profiles in animal models, particularly those that recapitulate the chronic oxidative stress and proteostasis defects seen in AMD, will be crucial for advancing Ceapin-A7 into clinical trials.

In summary, Ceapin-A7 holds significant promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its precise mechanism—selectively inhibiting ATF6α activation by preventing its ER-to-Golgi trafficking and inducing a novel tether with ABCD3—positions it as a unique tool for rebalancing maladaptive UPR signaling (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Torres et al., 2019). The expected therapeutic benefit in RPE cells is the restoration of adaptive autophagy, maintenance of lysosomal function, and enhanced phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, all of which are critical to slowing or halting the progression of dry AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Nevertheless, the lack of extensive in vivo data in retinal models and the potential for off-target effects or unintended suppression of adaptive ER stress responses are significant concerns that must be addressed before clinical translation (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Rigorous investigation in RPE-specific systems, careful dose–response studies, pharmacokinetic profiling, and long-term safety evaluations are essential next steps. Overall, Ceapin-A7 is a mechanistically innovative candidate that merits further preclinical development as a novel intervention for dry AMD, provided that its complex interplay with ER stress, autophagy, and lysosomal function is thoroughly characterized in ocular tissues (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Cerulenin is a natural product originally isolated from the filamentous fungus Cephalosporium caerulens and was the first discovered fatty acid synthase (FAS) inhibitor (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; López & Diéguez, 2007). Chemically, this compound is classified as an epoxy-keto fatty acid analogue; it contains a reactive epoxide ring conjugated to a diene/amidic structure that mimics fatty acid substrates. This reactive epoxide is key to its mechanism because it enables cerulenin to irreversibly bind to its target enzyme via covalent modification. As such, cerulenin belongs to the class of FAS inhibitors that historically have been used as biochemical probes to investigate lipid metabolism and, subsequently, as lead compounds in the development of antineoplastic agents, given the upregulation of de novo lipogenesis in many cancers (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; López & Diéguez, 2007; Abramson, 2011). The molecule’s natural origin, combined with its potent inhibitory activity, has made it a valuable tool in studies of metabolic regulation and lipogenesis over several decades.

Therapeutic History:  
In the past, cerulenin was primarily developed and investigated as an antimicrobial and antifungal antibiotic due to its capacity to irreversibly inhibit fatty acid synthesis in both bacterial and eukaryotic systems (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Subsequent research in the fields of oncology and metabolic regulation revealed that several tumor types exhibit elevated expression of FAS, making FAS inhibitors promising candidates for anticancer therapy. Preclinical studies demonstrated that cerulenin could induce apoptosis in tumor cells, delay disease progression in xenograft models, and even affect systemic metabolic parameters such as food intake and body weight in rodent models (López & Diéguez, 2007; Heath, White, & Rock, 2002; Goodman & McFadden, 2007). Despite these promising results, its clinical utility has been constrained by poor chemical stability—primarily due to its reactive epoxide moiety—and significant toxicity stemming from irreversibility and off-target interactions with other cysteine-containing proteins (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Furthermore, while modifications have led to second-generation analogues like C75, designed to improve stability and selectivity, there are no records of cerulenin being specifically applied to ophthalmologic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal lipotoxicity diseases (Menendez & Lupu, 2017; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999). Although cerulenin has been explored in other in vivo models (for example, for retinitis pigmentosa in preclinical studies), no clinical trials have been registered for its use in AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, cerulenin exerts its biological effects by targeting the fatty acid synthase complex. Its mechanism involves the formation of an irreversible covalent adduct with an active-site cysteine residue (specifically, Cys1305) within the ketosynthase (KS) domain of type I FAS. This is achieved by an epoxide ring-opening reaction at the C-2 position of cerulenin, leading to the nucleophilic attack by the thiol (-SH) group of the catalytic cysteine residue (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008). Crystallographic studies have provided precise structural insights into this interaction, showing that such covalent modification not only blocks the initial acyl-transfer step but also induces conformational changes—such as the flipping of key residues like F1646 and the rotation of M1251—that ultimately disrupt the hydrophobic acyl-binding tunnel required for fatty acid chain elongation (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008; Fhu & Ali, 2020). In addition to inhibiting FAS directly, cerulenin has also been shown to impair protein palmitoylation, a post-translational modification that plays an important role in regulating membrane association and signaling functions of numerous proteins including Ras oncoproteins (Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999). This dual mechanism—targeting both de novo fatty acid synthesis and protein acylation—underscores the broad-spectrum bioactivity of cerulenin and its potential impact on multiple cellular pathways that are dysregulated in disease states (Menendez & Lupu, 2017; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis underpinning the proposed repurposing of cerulenin for dry AMD centers on its ability to attenuate de novo lipogenesis in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. In the context of dry AMD, pathologic accumulation of lipofuscin and toxic bisretinoid compounds such as A2E is thought to result from excessive lipid synthesis and impaired degradation of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) material. Excess levels of intracellular fatty acids, often derived from hyperactive FAS, contribute to the generation of these lipofuscin precursors—ultimately impairing lysosomal function and leading to RPE dysfunction (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). By inhibiting FAS activity in the RPE, cerulenin is expected to reduce the synthesis of fatty acids that serve as precursors for lipofuscin components. This reduced lipogenesis should, in theory, alleviate the accumulation of lipofuscin, restore optimal levels of lysosomal pH, and enhance the activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D—thereby improving the degradation and turnover of POS material (Radka & Rock, 2022; Troudi, Pagès, & Brunel, 2021). Furthermore, since oxidative stress is a key driver of abnormal lipid metabolism in RPE cells, the ability of cerulenin to lower fatty acid synthesis may concurrently reduce the burden of oxidative damage and improve cellular homeostasis (Vázquez et al., 2008; Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007). It is also noteworthy that FAS expression has been detected and functionally characterized in various extrahepatic tissues; while direct evidence of its expression in RPE cells is less extensively documented in the provided citations, the extrapolation from other cellular models supports the likelihood that modulating FAS activity in RPE would confer benefits in lipid turnover and lysosomal efficiency (Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999; Johansson et al., 2008). Thus, within the proposed assay—where RPE cells are subjected to oxidative stress that mimics the environment of dry AMD—cerulenin is anticipated to lower intracellular lipid levels, minimize the generation of lipofuscin precursors, and ultimately restore RPE functional capacity.

Overall Evaluation:  
Cerulenin presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD owing to its well-documented ability to inhibit fatty acid synthase through a unique irreversible, covalent mechanism. Its molecular footprint, characterized by a reactive epoxide ring, has been exploited in multiple studies to evaluate cellular lipid synthesis and, by extension, to modulate metabolic pathways that underpin several disease processes (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Abramson, 2011). Mechanistically, its capacity to bind to a crucial cysteine residue in the FAS enzyme and to interfere with lipid assembly positions it as a potentially valuable agent to counter the lipid-driven pathogenesis implicated in RPE dysfunction and lipofuscin accumulation in dry AMD (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008).

The strengths of cerulenin as a candidate include its small-molecule profile, which facilitates cellular entry; its established use as a research tool in in vitro and in vivo models; and its dual activity profile that not only curtails de novo lipogenesis but may also impede aberrant protein palmitoylation. Such multifaceted activity could be beneficial in a complex tissue environment like the retina, where multiple overlapping metabolic dysfunctions contribute to disease progression (Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999). In particular, by reducing the synthesis of fatty acids in RPE cells, cerulenin could deplete one of the key substrates for the formation of lipofuscin precursors such as A2E, thereby potentially improving lysosomal degradation of shed POS and arresting a vicious cycle of intracellular lipid accumulation and oxidative stress (Radka & Rock, 2022; Troudi, Pagès, & Brunel, 2021).

However, several weaknesses must be carefully considered. Cerulenin’s inherent chemical instability, attributed to its reactive epoxide ring, raises significant concerns regarding its pharmacokinetic profile and overall toxicity, especially in a sensitive tissue like the retina where off-target effects may exacerbate cellular stress rather than alleviate it (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Heath, White, & Rock, 2002). The irreversible nature of its enzyme inhibition—while beneficial for ensuring sustained suppression of FAS—may lead to collateral damage in non-target tissues, and the narrow therapeutic window observed in other preclinical studies suggests that dose optimization could be challenging (Fhu & Ali, 2020; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Moreover, although the hypothesis posits that inhibition of de novo lipogenesis in the RPE will mitigate lipid accumulation and improve lysosomal function, there is a paucity of direct evidence linking cerulenin or similar FAS inhibitors to improved outcomes in dry AMD models specifically. The documented applications of cerulenin are primarily in the realms of oncology and metabolic regulation, with little precedent for its use in ocular conditions (Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). This suggests that while the mechanistic rationale is sound, the translational leap to an ocular indication will require additional supportive data both from in vitro RPE assays and from appropriate animal models of AMD.

Another point of concern is that cerulenin’s nonselective inhibition of fatty acid synthase may also impair essential lipid synthesis in cells that require robust regenerative capacity, potentially leading to unintended cytotoxicity or impaired cell membrane maintenance. In the context of the RPE, where cellular health is paramount for photoreceptor support, any off-target lipid synthesis inhibition must be tightly controlled (Goodman & McFadden, 2007; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Furthermore, its use in vivo has been historically hampered by issues such as poor aqueous solubility—it often requires solvents like DMSO for administration—and its propensity for rapid degradation in protic environments, all of which represent substantial formulation challenges that must be overcome for ocular delivery (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Vázquez et al., 2008).

Given these considerations, while cerulenin offers a compelling proof-of-concept relating to the modulation of lipogenesis and lysosomal function, its practical development as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD would likely necessitate further chemical modifications. The precedent set by the development of derivatives such as C75—which were specifically engineered to overcome the limitations of cerulenin by removing the problematic epoxide group and enhancing stability—suggests that optimization is both possible and necessary (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Optimized analogues with improved pharmacokinetic and safety profiles may hold greater promise in the ocular setting than the parent compound.

In summary, cerulenin’s capacity to inhibit fatty acid synthase at the molecular level through irreversible covalent binding is well-established and aligns with the proposed therapeutic mechanism of reducing RPE lipid accumulation and lipofuscin precursor formation. However, its historical limitations in terms of chemical stability, toxicity, and nonselectivity present significant hurdles for its repurposing in dry AMD. The compound’s extensive use in metabolic and oncologic research provides a strong foundation for understanding its biochemical actions, but the absence of direct evidence in retinal models and the challenges associated with its delivery to ocular tissues temper enthusiasm for immediate clinical translation (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Therefore, while there is sufficient mechanistic rationale to pursue further preclinical investigations—potentially in parallel with the development of more stable derivatives—the current state of evidence suggests that cerulenin itself may not be ideal as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD without significant further optimization. More comprehensive in vitro studies using RPE cell models and targeted in vivo studies in AMD-relevant animal models are needed to validate whether the inhibition of de novo lipogenesis by cerulenin can indeed translate into restored lysosomal function and improved photoreceptor outer segment degradation in this disease context (Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007; Radka & Rock, 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Sulforaphane is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate that is principally derived from cruciferous vegetables, notably broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and cabbage (Dutta et al., 2023; Lagunas-Rangel, 2024). In its natural state, sulforaphane is present as its glucosinolate precursor, glucoraphanin, which is enzymatically converted to the active form upon tissue disruption by the enzyme myrosinase (Habtemariam, 2024; Mangla et al., 2021). This conversion is a well‐established biochemical process that occurs during food processing or mastication, and it provides the basis for sulforaphane’s identification as a nutraceutical with significant potential in various disease contexts (Houghton, 2019; Lagunas-Rangel, 2024). Sulforaphane belongs to the isothiocyanate class of compounds, a group known for their prominent antioxidant, anti‐inflammatory, and anticancer activities (Dutta et al., 2023; Habtemariam, 2024). Its discovery and subsequent characterization have positioned it as a compound of interest not only in cancer chemoprevention but also in other chronic disease models including neurodegenerative conditions and ocular pathologies (Ordonez et al., 2021; Habtemariam, 2024). The current therapeutic candidate—in this case, Sulforaphane (Nrf2 activator; LKT Laboratories Cat. No. S8044)—is being evaluated for its potential to modulate specific cellular pathways implicated in the pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly its ability to activate the Nrf2 transcription factor in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells at a proposed concentration of 5 µM (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Sulforaphane’s therapeutic history is extensive and spans multiple domains, primarily due to its ability to induce phase II detoxification enzymes and to modulate oxidative stress responses at the cellular level. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its efficacy in inducing apoptosis and mitigating cancer cell proliferation through the modulation of key signaling pathways (Dutta et al., 2023; Tortorella et al., 2015). In addition to its anticancer properties, sulforaphane has been evaluated in models of neurodegeneration, where it has been shown to confer neuroprotection by alleviating oxidative stress and inflammation—a property that is particularly relevant to retinal diseases such as AMD (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024). In ocular research, various investigations using in vitro and in vivo models have highlighted sulforaphane’s capacity to activate the Nrf2 pathway in retinal cells, leading to enhanced antioxidant enzyme expression and reduced oxidative damage (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). Notably, studies employing retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, such as ARPE-19 cells, have documented protective effects of sulforaphane against oxidative insult, where enhanced expression of genes such as heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), glutathione peroxidase (GPX), and glutamate-cysteine ligase modulatory subunit (GCLM) has been observed (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Kubo et al., 2017). Although sulforaphane has been predominantly explored in the context of cancer chemoprevention and neuroprotection, its application in treating ocular conditions such as dry AMD is emerging. Early studies suggest that sulforaphane might reduce lipofuscin accumulation and rescue lysosomal pH abnormalities in A2E-loaded RPE cells, which are hallmark features of dry AMD pathogenesis (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). Safety profiles established through both in vitro studies and limited clinical trials indicate that sulforaphane is generally well-tolerated, with few adverse effects even upon oral administration, thereby rendering it a promising agent for repurposing in ocular disorders (Ordonez et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic actions of sulforaphane are mediated primarily through the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, a central regulator of antioxidant defense mechanisms. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytosol by its inhibitory partner, Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1), which facilitates its ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Mangla et al., 2021). Sulforaphane exerts its effect by covalently modifying critical cysteine residues on KEAP1, thereby disrupting the KEAP1-Nrf2 complex. This modification impedes Nrf2 degradation and permits its rapid translocation into the nucleus (Habtemariam, 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small musculoaponeurotic fibrosarcoma (sMaf) proteins and binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoter regions of a multitude of genes, culminating in the transcriptional activation of phase II detoxification enzymes such as HO-1, GPX, and GCLM (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2024; Hyttinen et al., 2019). In addition to enhancing the antioxidant capacity of the cell, activation of Nrf2 by sulforaphane has been associated with the upregulation of genes implicated in the regulation of autophagy and lysosomal function (Chang et al., 2020; Bergandi et al., 2024). This is particularly salient in the context of RPE biology, where proper lysosomal function is critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and the prevention of lipofuscin accumulation. Impaired degradation pathways in RPE cells lead to cellular stress and contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). Moreover, sulforaphane’s ability to reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine production through suppression of mediators like intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) further supports its cytoprotective role in the retina (Habtemariam, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). The proposed concentration of 5 µM in vitro is supported by studies indicating that such a dose is sufficient to robustly activate Nrf2, thereby inducing an antioxidant response without eliciting toxicity in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). This multifaceted mechanism—encompassing enhanced transcription of antioxidant defense genes, promotion of autophagy, and attenuation of inflammatory signaling—underpins the rationale for deploying sulforaphane as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Expected Effect:  
Within the iPSC-derived RPE model of dry AMD, the administration of sulforaphane at 5 µM is hypothesized to yield several beneficial outcomes. First, by engaging the Nrf2 signaling pathway, sulforaphane is expected to increase the transcription of key antioxidant genes such as GCLM, GPX, and HO-1 (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Kubo et al., 2017). This upregulation will enhance the cellular capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS), thereby mitigating oxidative stress—a well-known contributor to RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2024). Second, the improved activation of Nrf2 is anticipated to restore autophagy processes and lysosomal enzyme function within RPE cells, facilitating more efficient degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and the removal of toxic byproducts such as lipofuscin (Chang et al., 2020; Bergandi et al., 2024). A2E, a major bisretinoid component of lipofuscin, has been implicated in the disruption of lysosomal pH and function; therefore, by rescuing lysosomal acidity and enhancing enzymatic activity, sulforaphane could support the clearance of A2E aggregates and related debris (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Third, given its anti-inflammatory attributes, sulforaphane is expected to downregulate cytokine expression and other inflammatory mediators, thus reducing the chronic inflammatory state that exacerbates RPE damage in dry AMD (Habtemariam, 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). On a molecular level, the improved phagocytic function of RPE cells, achieved through the normalization of lysosomal and autophagic pathways, is critical for maintaining retinal integrity and function since efficient POS degradation is necessary for visual cycle homeostasis (Chang et al., 2020; Kubo et al., 2017). Furthermore, the favorable safety profile observed in preclinical studies—coupled with evidence of minimal toxicity even at higher concentrations—supports the use of sulforaphane at the proposed dose, making it a mechanistically specific strategy to alleviate oxidative and lysosomal stress in dry AMD models (Ordonez et al., 2021; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Collectively, the expected effects at the molecular, cellular, and functional levels converge on the hypothesis that sulforaphane will both preserve RPE cell viability and enhance cellular clearance mechanisms, thereby countering key pathological features of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Sulforaphane represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its multifaceted mechanism of action, which directly targets key pathological processes involved in retinal degeneration. One of its primary strengths lies in its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway; this leads to a comprehensive antioxidant response by upregulating detoxification and cytoprotective genes that are essential for neutralizing ROS and ameliorating oxidative stress in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Kubo et al., 2017). The capacity to rescue lysosomal function and promote autophagy is another major advantage, as it addresses the abnormal accumulation of lipofuscin—a hallmark of dry AMD—by restoring the degradation and recycling of photoreceptor outer segments (Chang et al., 2020; Bergandi et al., 2024). Additionally, sulforaphane’s documented anti-inflammatory effects further enhance its therapeutic potential by reducing the expression of inflammatory cytokines that contribute to retinal damage (Habtemariam, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). The favorable safety profile noted in various studies reinforces the viability of repurposing sulforaphane, particularly since clinical trials in other indications have demonstrated minimal systemic toxicity and good tolerability (Ordonez et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

Despite these strengths, several challenges must be acknowledged. A key limitation associated with sulforaphane is its inherently low water solubility and bioavailability, which pose significant obstacles for achieving therapeutic concentrations at the target site, especially in ocular tissues where the blood–ocular barriers prevent easy drug penetration (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Current formulations may result in a high first-pass effect and limited tissue penetration upon systemic administration. This challenge necessitates the exploration of novel delivery systems—such as nanoformulations, liposomes, or other topical ocular delivery strategies—that can enhance the stability and bioavailability of sulforaphane (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Furthermore, while preclinical data in cell culture models and animal studies are promising, there remains an evidence gap regarding the efficacy of sulforaphane in human subjects with dry AMD. Robust clinical trials designed to establish dose-response relationships, optimal administration routes, and long-term safety profiles are essential before the compound can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic intervention for dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2024).

Another area of concern is the scalability and reproducibility of the effect. Variability in bioactivity may arise due to differences in the extraction or synthesis of sulforaphane, as the compound’s activity greatly depends on its purity, the presence of specific enantiomers, and the method of formulation (Lagunas-Rangel, 2024; Tortorella et al., 2015). This variability could potentially influence both the efficacy and safety outcomes in clinical applications. The current hypothesis proposes that a 5 µM concentration is effective for activating Nrf2 in RPE cells; however, translating this concentration from an in vitro model to an in vivo setting presents additional challenges. The effective dose in the retina might differ substantially due to differences in drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion, which must be carefully optimized through pharmacokinetic studies (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Kubo et al., 2017).

In summary, sulforaphane holds compelling potential as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD owing to its well-defined mechanism of action, which encompasses antioxidant activation via Nrf2, restoration of lysosomal and autophagic function, and anti-inflammatory effects. These mechanisms directly target the cellular dysfunctions that underlie dry AMD pathology—including oxidative damage, impaired POS degradation, and chronic inflammation—and thus position sulforaphane as a mechanistically specific strategy to ameliorate disease progression (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). The primary strengths of sulforaphane are its natural origin, its extensive preclinical validation across various disease models, and its capacity to modulate multiple cellular protective pathways simultaneously. However, weaknesses such as poor bioavailability, formulation challenges, and a current lack of definitive clinical data in the context of AMD temper its immediate translational readiness (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024).

To optimize the clinical translation of sulforaphane for dry AMD, future research directions should include:  
1. The development and validation of advanced drug delivery systems tailored for ocular tissues that can overcome the limitations posed by the blood–ocular barrier and enhance the drug’s bioavailability.  
2. Comprehensive pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies in animal models and early-phase clinical trials to determine the optimal dosing regimen that achieves therapeutic efficacy in the retina without compromising safety.  
3. Detailed investigations into the long-term effects of sulforaphane on retinal structure and function, including its impact on photoreceptor survival, RPE cell integrity, and overall visual performance.  
4. Comparative studies to evaluate sulforaphane’s efficacy relative to existing antioxidant and anti-inflammatory therapies in dry AMD, in order to establish its potential niche within the therapeutic landscape.  

Overall, while significant work remains to be done, sulforaphane exhibits a compelling mechanistic rationale and a promising preclinical profile that justify further investigation as a repurposed therapeutic agent for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its ability to activate Nrf2, boost antioxidant defenses, restore autophagy and lysosomal function, and reduce inflammatory mediators provides a multi-pronged approach to address the complex pathology of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). If formulation and delivery challenges can be effectively overcome, sulforaphane may well represent a viable and innovative strategy to preserve retinal health and counteract the progressive degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Habtemariam, 2024).

In conclusion, the current body of evidence from biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical studies supports the hypothesis that sulforaphane can enhance Nrf2 activation in RPE cells and improve antioxidant and lysosomal function, thereby potentially alleviating key pathological features of dry AMD. Given its extensive therapeutic history, well-characterized mechanism of action, and favorable safety profile, sulforaphane is a strong candidate deserving further rigorous evaluation and development. Nonetheless, targeted efforts to address its formulation and bioavailability limitations will be critical in shaping its future as a clinically effective treatment for dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).
