Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
NBDHEX (6-(7-nitro-2,1,3-benzoxadiazol-4-ylthio)hexanol) is a fully synthetic small molecule that belongs to the class of nitrobenzoxadiazole (NBD) derivatives. This compound was originally developed for its robust activity as a glutathione S-transferase (GST) inhibitor, and its synthesis follows methodologies previously reported (Pasello et al., 2011). As a GST inhibitor, NBDHEX is categorized as a “suicide inhibitor” because it covalently binds to the enzyme’s substrate binding site (the H-site) where it reacts with glutathione in the G-site to form a stable complex that inactivates the target enzyme (Filomeni et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2014). In traditional applications, members of this therapeutic class have been predominantly explored as anticancer agents; they have been used to counteract tumor chemoresistance by inhibiting GST isoenzymes that metabolize and neutralize cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents (Pasello et al., 2011; Filomeni et al., 2008). The compound’s design, structure, and biochemical properties have been extensively characterized within an oncology context, with numerous studies documenting its structure–activity relationships and its capacity to overcome multidrug resistance in cell lines from various cancer types (Filomeni et al., 2008; Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, NBDHEX has been investigated almost exclusively within the realm of cancer research. Preclinical studies have applied NBDHEX against musculoskeletal sarcomas, including osteosarcoma, Ewing’s sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma, as well as in small cell lung cancer and melanoma models (Pasello et al., 2011; Filomeni et al., 2008). In these studies, it demonstrated cytostatic and cytotoxic effects with effective concentrations typically in the low micromolar to submicromolar range, even in drug-resistant cancer cell lines (Pasello et al., 2011). Its anticancer activity has been attributed to both the direct inhibition of GST catalytic function and the disruption of GSTP1 interactions with key signaling proteins such as JNK and TRAF2, which are known to modulate apoptosis and stress signaling pathways (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Pasello et al., 2011). In contrast, there is currently no recorded history of NBDHEX having been used in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or any similar ocular degenerative disease. However, several studies have emphasized the importance of GSTP1 in ocular tissues, particularly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where it plays a critical role in detoxification and cellular defense against oxidative stress (Lee et al., 2014). These observations lend indirect support to the hypothesis that modulating GSTP1 activity—even through inhibition—might have therapeutic implications in the context of AMD. Nonetheless, while the anticancer literature provides extensive data on the pharmacology and safety of NBDHEX in oncology, its potential for ocular application remains largely uncharted and would necessitate rigorous preclinical investigation (Lee et al., 2014).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which NBDHEX exerts its biological effects is well delineated in the published literature. As a suicide inhibitor, NBDHEX anchors itself to the active site of GST enzymes, particularly GSTP1, by binding to the hydrophobic substrate binding (H-site) region; once bound, it reacts in the presence of reduced glutathione to produce a stable, inactive complex (Filomeni et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2014). This covalent modification effectively prevents GSTP1 from catalyzing the detoxification reactions normally necessary to neutralize electrophilic and oxidative species. In addition, GSTP1 is known not only for its detoxification role but also for its involvement in protein–protein interactions, most notably with components of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway including c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and TNF receptor-associated factor 2 (TRAF2) (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Pasello et al., 2011). Under basal conditions, GSTP1 binds to JNK and TRAF2, suppressing their downstream pro-apoptotic signaling. By inhibiting GSTP1, NBDHEX disrupts these interactions, thereby relieving the inhibitory constraints and enabling the activation of stress response pathways mediated by JNK (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Pasello et al., 2011).  
In the context of the RPE, GSTP1 has been documented as a zeaxanthin-binding protein and a critical detoxification enzyme whose levels are reduced in AMD-affected retinas (Lee et al., 2014). This loss of GSTP1 is associated with a diminished capacity of RPE cells to counteract reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated by light exposure, leading to impaired cellular homeostasis and increased risk of retinal degeneration. The hypothesis underlying the use of NBDHEX in dry AMD is that its inhibition of GSTP1 may, in a carefully titrated fashion, increase ROS levels sufficiently to trigger cytoprotective pathways such as autophagy without overwhelming the cell’s defense mechanisms. Indeed, experimental evidence from cancer models has shown that treatment with NBDHEX leads to an accumulation of autophagy markers, including p62 (SQSTM1) and LC3-II, suggesting that the compound can modulate autophagic flux (Sciarretta et al., 2019). It is postulated that the elevation of ROS following GSTP1 inhibition may stimulate the autophagy machinery, thereby improving lysosomal degradation of damaged photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and alleviating one of the pathological hallmarks of dry AMD (Lee et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed experimental scenario—where RPE cells are exposed to oxidative stress—the administration of NBDHEX is expected to inhibit GSTP1 activity at an IC₅₀ in the vicinity of 0.1 µM. This inhibition would lead to a modest and controlled increase in ROS levels. In RPE cells, which normally express GSTP1 as part of their intrinsic antioxidant defense (and where GSTP1 expression is known to be developmentally regulated and inducible by light exposure), an increase in intracellular ROS may serve as a signal to activate cytoprotective autophagy pathways (Lee et al., 2014). As autophagy is crucial for the clearance of damaged proteins and cellular debris—including the phagocytosis and degradation of POS—the induction of autophagy via upregulation of p62 and LC3-II is anticipated to enhance the lysosomal clearance capacity of RPE cells. This could potentially counteract the lipofuscin accumulation and impaired phagocytosis that are characteristic of the dry AMD phenotype (Lee et al., 2014).  
Moreover, literature in cancer cells has documented that treatment with NBDHEX results in a dose-dependent accumulation of LC3-II and p62, markers which are indicative of autophagosome build-up, and—if coupled with improved lysosomal flux—may correspond to functional autophagy (Sciarretta et al., 2019; Pasello et al., 2011). If a similar mechanism operates in RPE cells, the net result could be an improvement in POS degradation under oxidative conditions. Such a response would be particularly beneficial in dry AMD, where defective autophagy and dysregulated oxidative stress are believed to contribute to RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration. Thus, the expected outcome is that NBDHEX, at concentrations that achieve partial GSTP1 inhibition without causing overt toxicity, would restore a more favorable balance between ROS generation and autophagic clearance, leading to enhanced POS degradation and improved cell survival under oxidative stress (Lee et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation:  
NBDHEX represents a promising repurposing candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well‐characterized inhibitory activity against GSTP1 and its documented ability to modulate autophagy in other cellular models. One of the key strengths of this candidate is its robust mechanistic rationale: GSTP1 is known to play a dual role in detoxifying ROS and in suppressing pro-autophagic signaling via sequestration of proteins like p62. In RPE cells—where GSTP1 not only contributes to managing oxidative stress but also interacts with protective pigments such as zeaxanthin—the reduction in GSTP1 function observed in AMD patients implies that further controlled modulation of this enzyme might recalibrate cellular stress responses (Sciarretta et al., 2019; Filomeni et al., 2008). The ability of NBDHEX to disrupt GSTP1’s interactions with JNK and TRAF2 adds another layer of therapeutic potential, as the resultant activation of stress-responsive signaling pathways could further promote cell survival mechanisms. Additionally, evidence from cancer models showing increased levels of autophagy markers such as p62 and LC3-II following NBDHEX treatment supports the concept that this compound can induce autophagic flux, which is of paramount importance in RPE cells for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (Sciarretta et al., 2019; Filomeni et al., 2008).

Despite its promise, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. First, the bulk of the extant literature on NBDHEX pertains to its use as an anticancer agent with applications in solid tumors; there is a notable lack of direct preclinical or clinical studies assessing its efficacy and safety in ocular models or specifically in the context of dry AMD (Pasello et al., 2011; Filomeni et al., 2008). The unique environment of the retina, with its high oxygen consumption, photoreceptor interactions, and specialized blood-retinal barriers, poses distinct pharmacokinetic and toxicity challenges that may not be evident in cancer studies. Second, while the hypothesis relies on a controlled increase in ROS to stimulate autophagy, GSTP1 is an essential component of the antioxidant defense system, and its inhibition could theoretically precipitate excessive oxidative damage if the dosage is not meticulously controlled (Lee et al., 2014; Pasello et al., 2011). Furthermore, some studies indicate that NBDHEX may exhibit limited specificity for GSTP1, with a higher affinity for other GST isoenzymes such as GSTM2-2, which could lead to off-target effects and complicate the therapeutic profile of the compound in non-oncologic tissues (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Filomeni et al., 2008). Finally, ocular drug delivery represents a further hurdle; the ability of NBDHEX to penetrate retinal tissues and safely reach RPE cells within the complex structure of the eye has not been demonstrated and would require rigorous formulation and pharmacokinetic optimization.

In summary, NBDHEX exhibits a compelling mechanism of action that aligns well with the pathophysiology of dry AMD—in particular, its potential to re-establish redox balance and promote autophagy in RPE cells by modulating GSTP1 activity. The strengths of this approach lie in both the detailed molecular insights available from cancer research and the established role of GSTP1 in retinal health. Nonetheless, significant gaps in the literature remain with respect to ocular safety, effective dosing, and the specific cellular context of the RPE. As such, while NBDHEX is a scientifically attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, its translation from oncology to ophthalmology must be approached with caution. Preclinical studies using ex vivo RPE models and appropriate animal models of AMD are essential to validate the hypothesized benefits and to address potential off-target effects. Should these studies demonstrate favorable outcomes—particularly in improving lysosomal flux and POS degradation without eliciting detrimental oxidative damage—then NBDHEX could emerge as a novel therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, addressing a significant unmet medical need in retinal degenerative disease (Lee et al., 2014; Filomeni et al., 2008; Sciarretta et al., 2019).

Overall, the candidate’s repurposing for dry AMD shows promise from a mechanistic standpoint, particularly in enhancing the intrinsic capacity of RPE cells to clear photoreceptor debris and mitigate oxidative stress through autophagy. However, further research is clearly warranted to rigorously evaluate both its efficacy and ocular safety profile before advancing toward clinical application. This comprehensive literature review supports cautious optimism while underscoring the critical need for detailed preclinical validation in the specific context of retinal degeneration (Lee et al., 2014).

While these models provide valuable insights into the molecular and cellular effects of IFM-514, the translation to in vivo efficacy—especially in complex models of dry AMD—requires further investigation. Detailed ocular pharmacokinetics, biodistribution studies, and long-term safety evaluations in animal models of dry AMD are critical to establish that IFM-514 successfully reaches the retina at therapeutic concentrations and does so without eliciting adverse effects (Wang et al., 2019).

• Translational and Clinical Uncertainty:  
There is currently no clinical data for IFM-514 in patients with dry AMD. Although the preclinical profile is promising, the transition from cell-based/in vitro models to human disease entails numerous challenges, including potential differences in drug metabolism, off-target impacts in the human eye, and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathology. Clinical trials will ultimately be necessary to validate the therapeutic potential and safety of IFM-514 in a human setting (Wang et al., 2019).

Overall, IFM-514 represents a promising candidate for the treatment of dry AMD by virtue of its selective inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome, its potent anti-inflammatory effects in RPE models, and its rational design aimed at overcoming the limitations of earlier compounds. The preclinical literature provides substantial evidence that targeting NLRP3-driven inflammation can ameliorate key pathological processes in RPE cells, such as cytokine overproduction, pyroptosis, and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments—all of which contribute to the progression of dry AMD. However, to advance IFM-514 confidently into clinical development, several critical gaps must be addressed. These include obtaining detailed molecular binding and selectivity data, conducting comprehensive ocular pharmacokinetic studies in relevant in vivo models, and performing robust comparisons with established NLRP3 inhibitors. Additionally, while the in vitro and ex vivo data are encouraging, in vivo efficacy studies in animal models that recapitulate the chronic nature of dry AMD will be essential to confirm that the promising effects observed in simpler systems translate into meaningful clinical benefits.  

In summary, IFM-514’s strong preclinical efficacy—demonstrated by its ability to reduce IL-1β secretion and cell lysis, maintain lysosomal stability, and potentially enhance POS phagocytosis—combined with its optimized chemical design and favorable safety profile, make it a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. The strengths of this approach lie in its molecular precision to intercept a key inflammatory pathway implicated in RPE injury. Nevertheless, the candidate’s overall success will depend on rigorous further investigation into its in vivo behavior, long-term safety, and efficacy in animal models that closely mimic human dry AMD pathology. If these studies yield positive results, IFM-514 could offer a novel, mechanism-based therapeutic option for a disease that currently has very limited treatment alternatives (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024).

Given the comprehensive preclinical data suggesting that selective NLRP3 inhibition can protect RPE cells from inflammasome-mediated injury and improve key functional outcomes relevant to dry AMD, IFM-514 is a highly promising therapeutic candidate. The proposed mechanism—coupling allosteric inhibition of NLRP3 with downstream prevention of caspase-1 activation and cytokine maturation—directly addresses the inflammatory pathology underlying RPE degeneration in dry AMD. The evidence supports a rationale for further development, including in vivo efficacy studies, detailed ocular pharmacokinetic analyses, and ultimately early-phase clinical trials to evaluate safety and preliminary clinical benefit in patients with dry AMD (Wang et al., 2019).

In conclusion, the therapeutic candidate IFM-514 possesses a favorable design and biological rationale for use in dry AMD. Its development as a selective NLRP3 antagonist derived from the sulfonylurea class, its demonstrated efficacy in reducing key inflammatory and cell death markers in RPE models, and its potential for superior ocular PK and tolerability collectively make a strong case for advancing IFM-514 into further preclinical and clinical testing. However, to fully validate its potential, additional data—especially in vivo and mechanistic binding studies—are required to ensure that this promising candidate will provide a safe and effective treatment for patients suffering from dry AMD (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab is a recombinant, humanized monoclonal IgG kappa antibody that specifically binds complement component C5 and prevents its proteolytic activation into C5a and C5b, thereby blocking terminal pathway activity and membrane attack complex (MAC; C5b-9) assembly while leaving upstream C3-dependent functions largely intact (for example, opsonization and immune-complex handling) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; West et al., 2024). It was discovered by screening large panels of murine anti-human C5 monoclonals for potent inhibition of C5 activation and terminal complement–mediated hemolysis; the parental murine antibody (5G1.1) was then humanized by CDR grafting into human germline frameworks and engineered to use a hybrid IgG2/IgG4 heavy-chain constant region to minimize Fcγ receptor binding and classical-pathway activation (reducing effector functions that could confound terminal pathway blockade) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009). Eculizumab binds human C5 with very high affinity (Kd approximately 120 pM) and sterically prevents convertase engagement with the MG7 domain of C5; epitope mapping identifies residues in the MG7 domain (including the KSSKC motif around Arg885) critical for binding, and Arg885His/Cys polymorphisms have been linked to clinical non-responsiveness in some patients, consistent with the structural epitope (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

As a drug class, complement inhibitors have been deployed to treat diseases driven by complement dysregulation, with C5 blockade representing a terminal-pathway strategy that ablates C5a signaling and MAC-mediated cytolysis while preserving many proximal complement functions; eculizumab was the first complement inhibitor approved for clinical use and catalyzed broad clinical development of C5, C3, and alternative pathway–targeted agents across hematology, nephrology, neurology, and, more recently, ophthalmology (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Eculizumab is administered intravenously, exhibits a long serum half-life (~272 ± 82 hours), a limited volume of distribution consistent with an intravascularly confined antibody, and shows pharmacodynamic correlation between serum trough concentrations and blockade of hemolytic activity; vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis is required due to increased susceptibility when terminal complement is inhibited (Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Within ophthalmology, complement activation products and MAC deposition have been implicated in AMD pathogenesis, motivating clinical trials of complement inhibitors including C5-directed agents; eculizumab has been formally evaluated in a randomized phase 2 setting for non-exudative AMD (geographic atrophy and drusen cohorts) via systemic administration (Kassa et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Halawa et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
Eculizumab has an extensive clinical record in systemic complement-mediated disorders. It revolutionized therapy for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), where it reduces intravascular hemolysis, decreases transfusion requirements, and improves quality of life; it is also approved for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and for neurologic autoimmune indications including anti–acetylcholine receptor–positive generalized myasthenia gravis and aquaporin-4–positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Early clinical pharmacology in PNH demonstrated that an induction regimen of 600 mg weekly for four weeks followed by 900 mg every other week maintained near-complete terminal pathway blockade and significantly reduced hemolysis and transfusion needs; these dosing principles align with its long half-life and the concentration dependence of hemolytic inhibition (Hillmen et al., 2004; Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012). Despite robust control of intravascular hemolysis, residual extravascular hemolysis can persist because C3 opsonization is not prevented by C5 inhibition, illustrating an important mechanistic limitation of terminal-pathway agents (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; West et al., 2024).

The drug’s safety profile is dominated by infection risk with encapsulated organisms—particularly meningococcal disease—necessitating vaccination; otherwise, eculizumab has shown acceptable tolerability across long-term use, with clinical programs incorporating monitoring of functional complement activity (CH50) to confirm pharmacodynamic blockade and dose adequacy (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009; Eskandary et al., 2016). Mechanistically relevant sources also report pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic complexities: high-affinity binding at acidic endosomal pH encourages recycling of eculizumab:C5 complexes by FcRn, leading to accumulation of total C5 bound to the drug in circulation; next-generation engineering in ravulizumab introduced pH-dependent release to minimize cargo recycling and extend dosing intervals (Schmidt & Smith, 2023).

In ophthalmology, eculizumab has been investigated as a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD. The COMPLETE study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), a single-center, randomized, double-masked phase 2 trial, evaluated intravenous eculizumab in two cohorts: geographic atrophy (GA) and intermediate AMD with high-risk drusen; patients were randomized 2:1 to eculizumab or saline over 24 weeks with follow-up to 52 weeks (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the GA cohort (n = 30 study eyes), eculizumab did not reduce GA enlargement versus placebo at 26 or 52 weeks (square-root–transformed growth 0.19 ± 0.12 mm vs. 0.18 ± 0.15 mm at 26 weeks, P = 0.96; 0.37 ± 0.22 mm vs. 0.37 ± 0.21 mm at 52 weeks, P = 0.93), and no drug-related adverse events were reported (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the drusen cohort (n = 30 total participants; 20 active, 10 placebo), eculizumab failed to meet the prespecified primary endpoint of a ≥ 50% reduction in drusen cube-root volume at 26 weeks; none of 18 treated eyes achieved this threshold, while one placebo eye did (10%; P = 0.36), and there was no detectable difference in mean drusen growth between arms through 26–52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014). Trial conduct included meningococcal vaccination and careful multimodal imaging; retention was high with 28/30 completing 52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). Independent evidence syntheses judged the certainty of evidence as low to very low due to small sample size, imprecision, and some risk of bias; overall, systemic eculizumab “may have made little to no difference” in BCVA and GA lesion growth in the available cohort (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistically similar C5-directed agents have not shown positive phase 2 outcomes in GA when administered systemically or intravitreally (e.g., LFG316 failed in phase 2), whereas intravitreal C5 inhibition with avacincaptad pegol progressed to later-phase testing and regulatory review, suggesting that drug, route, and pharmacology may be important determinants of outcome; by contrast, intravitreal C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) demonstrated efficacy and has been approved for GA, underscoring the translational relevance of target selection and ocular delivery (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024). Multiple reviews conclude that systemic eculizumab is no longer in development for AMD and highlight delivery and mechanistic concerns as likely contributors to the negative results (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, eculizumab targets the MG7 domain of C5 and sterically prevents formation of the C5 convertase–substrate complex, thereby inhibiting the cleavage of C5 into the potent anaphylatoxin C5a and C5b, which nucleates membrane attack complex assembly with C6–C9 (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Rother et al., 2007). Structural analysis of an eculizumab Fab bound to C5 resolved at 4.2 Å shows that five CDRs form the principal interface with MG7; mutational scanning of CDR residues identifies a network of contacts necessary for high-affinity binding, and kinetic assays confirm that these interactions prevent complement-mediated hemolysis in vitro (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016). The epitope includes residues near Arg885, and clinical resistance due to Arg885His/Cys substitutions in C5 provides orthogonal validation of the binding site (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

Pharmacodynamically, eculizumab ablates terminal pathway function: it suppresses CH50 to near zero when trough serum concentrations exceed ~35 μg/mL; however, because proximal C3 activation continues, C3b deposition and downstream opsonins accumulate on surfaces, which can drive extravascular clearance and generate residual pathology even under complete C5 blockade in appropriate disease contexts (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). Additional mechanisms can undermine complete terminal pathway control: (1) during intense proximal activation, densely opsonized surfaces can support C5 activation by convertases in ways that partially bypass classical C5 convertase assembly or even promote conformational C5 activation on surface C3b clusters; such context-dependent activation can manifest as “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” despite apparently adequate free drug levels, and has been reported in clinical settings as residual terminal-pathway activity and elevated sC5b-9 in some patients (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). (2) Eculizumab binds C5 with high affinity at both neutral and mildly acidic pH, allowing FcRn to recycle eculizumab:C5 complexes and potentially alter antigen disposition; ravulizumab’s pH-dependent binding was engineered to release C5 in endosomes and improve pharmacokinetics by avoiding cargo recycling (Schmidt & Smith, 2023). These features are germane to dose selection, monitoring, and potential resistance or escape during strong complement activation.

Rationale for C5 inhibition in AMD rests on abundant mechanistic and histopathological evidence that C5-derived effectors and MAC participate in retinal/choroidal injury. C5a is detected in drusen and acts as a chemotactic and proinflammatory mediator capable of inducing VEGF expression from retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, while C5b initiates MAC assembly; MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris increases with aging and is elevated in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019). Sub-lytic and lytic MAC on choroidal endothelium causes cell injury and can trigger surviving endothelial cells to upregulate VEGF and matrix metalloproteinases, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic injury and pro-angiogenic remodeling; complement regulatory proteins such as CD59 are natural inhibitors of MAC formation and their dysfunction or insufficiency can predispose to damage (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2021). Complement dysregulation in AMD further includes genetic risk (e.g., CFH variants) and evidence of alternative pathway activation in ocular tissues, suggesting both proximal and terminal effector involvement in disease biology (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Importantly, proximal inhibition at C3 has shown the capacity to restore lysosomal function and reduce sub-RPE drusen-like deposits in human iPSC-derived RPE models carrying the high-risk CFH Y402H variant by reducing C3 turnover and lowering downstream MAC (C5b-9) localization at lysosomes; in this system, a compstatin analogue (Cp40) suppressed C3b and MAC deposition and reversed lysosomal abnormalities, whereas direct C5 inhibition has not been shown in this model to rescue lysosomal function, and clinical C5 blockade has failed in GA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). These data reinforce that while terminal pathway effectors are present and likely pathogenic in AMD, distal blockade at C5 does not necessarily address upstream complement turnover that drives intracellular lysosomal stress in RPE, and proximal intervention may be required to normalize cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
The hypothesis proposes that high-affinity C5 blockade with eculizumab will prevent MAC assembly on RPE, thereby reducing sub-RPE deposit–driven lysosomal stress and indirectly supporting photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis in dry AMD. Mechanistically, preventing C5 cleavage would abrogate both C5a signaling and C5b-dependent MAC formation; given the documented presence of C5a in drusen and increased MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane/choriocapillaris with age and AMD, terminal pathway inhibition is expected to reduce MAC-mediated endothelial and RPE injury, dampen MAC-induced VEGF/MMP signaling, and potentially mitigate inflammation (Kassa et al., 2019). In principle, if MAC-driven lysosomal injury contributes to RPE dysfunction, C5 inhibition could reduce new MAC deposition at the RPE surface and limit subsequent endocytosis of MAC into lysosomes, thereby lowering lysosomal burden (Park et al., 2021).

However, two key bodies of evidence temper this expectation. First, clinical testing of systemic eculizumab in GA and intermediate AMD failed to show benefit on primary anatomical endpoints (GA growth and OCT drusen volume) through 26–52 weeks, despite established systemic pharmacodynamic blockade; these negative outcomes argue that either (a) terminal pathway activity at C5 is not the principal driver of lesion growth/drusen regression during the studied disease stages/time horizon, or (b) pharmacokinetic compartmentalization limited ocular target engagement after intravenous dosing (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Filho et al., 2014). Reviews explicitly highlight the compartment barrier problem—systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina or sub-RPE space due to the blood–retina/Bruch’s membrane barriers and large molecular size—and note that eculizumab exposure shorter than six months is unlikely to show benefit in slowly progressive GA, compounding interpretation (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Second, cellular models directly linking complement dysregulation to lysosomal failure in high-risk AMD RPE show that upstream C3 inhibition, not terminal C5 blockade, restores lysosomal function and reduces deposit formation; this suggests that intralysosomal stress is driven by continuous C3 turnover and opsonization rather than MAC alone, and that distal C5 blockade may be insufficient to normalize these processes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Consequently, POS phagocytosis metrics may improve only marginally or not at all if the dominant insult is proximal complement turnover rather than MAC-mediated damage. The clinical failure to slow GA growth or reduce drusen volume with systemic eculizumab supports the inference that target engagement at C5, via the tested route and schedule, did not translate into macroscopic anatomical benefit in human AMD eyes within one year (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).

If eculizumab were to be tested in vitro on human RPE, appropriate readouts would include: surface and intracellular MAC (C5b-9) quantification, lysosomal number/size and membrane integrity (e.g., LAMP2, Galectin-8), Cathepsin D activity, autophagic flux, and POS degradation kinetics; concomitant measurement of upstream C3b/iC3b/C3d deposition would be essential to interpret whether C5 inhibition is affecting the dominant pathogenic pathway in the assay (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In vivo, ocular pharmacokinetic considerations dominate: intravitreal administration delivers drug to the retina and sub-RPE space but is not reported for eculizumab in the provided context and would carry different safety and dosing constraints; systemic dosing faces blood–retina barrier limitations that likely constrained ocular target engagement in COMPLETE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Notably, nearly all complement inhibitors that have shown anatomical effects in GA have been delivered intravitreally, underscoring the importance of route of administration for ocular diseases (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic rationale: C5a and MAC are present in AMD-relevant tissues; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD and can drive endothelial injury, VEGF/MMP upregulation, and potentially RPE dysfunction; blocking C5 should diminish these terminal effector signals (Kassa et al., 2019; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Potent, well-characterized biologic: Eculizumab binds human C5 with picomolar affinity, has a well-defined structural epitope in the MG7 domain, and reliably ablates terminal pathway function systemically with a large clinical safety database outside ophthalmology (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
- Clinical feasibility and tolerability: In AMD trials, intravenous eculizumab was well tolerated without drug-related adverse events and with no clear signal for increased neovascular conversion or ocular infection within one year, supporting general safety of systemic C5 blockade in this population under vaccination protocols (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Negative clinical efficacy in AMD: The randomized phase 2 COMPLETE trial showed no reduction in GA growth and no meaningful reduction in drusen volume through 26–52 weeks; certainty is limited by small sample size but confidence intervals and replication across endpoints argue against a large treatment effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).  
- Compartmentalization barriers for systemic dosing: Blood–retina and Bruch’s membrane barriers likely limit ocular exposure to intravenously administered eculizumab; multiple reviews cite inadequate ocular penetration as a plausible reason for failure, and systemic eculizumab is no longer being pursued in AMD (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
- Target selection may be too distal for RPE lysosomal rescue: Human iPSC-RPE data indicate that complement-driven lysosomal pathology and drusen-like deposits are reversed by C3 inhibition, with concomitant reduction of downstream MAC, while C5 blockade alone has not been shown to restore lysosomal metrics and did not slow GA clinically; this suggests that proximal complement turnover is the dominant driver of RPE lysosomal stress (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Mechanistic escape and incomplete terminal control: Under strong activation, C5 can be activated on dense C3b clusters with features of convertase bypass or conformational priming; stoichiometric C5 inhibitors can form long-lived C5:antibody complexes on surfaces, potentially allowing residual terminal activity, and clinical “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” has been documented (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
- Genetic and biochemical determinants of response: C5 polymorphisms (e.g., R885H/C) can abolish binding and confer resistance; while prevalence in AMD populations is unknown here, such variants are important risk factors for nonresponse (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).  
- Safety/logistics: Terminal complement blockade mandates meningococcal vaccination and vigilance for invasive infections; while acceptable systemically in selected diseases, risk–benefit in a chronic, slowly progressive ocular disorder is less favorable, and the cost and infusion burden are high (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Contextualization with alternative complement strategies  
- C5 vs C3: Clinical success in GA has emerged at the level of C3 (pegcetacoplan), consistent with cellular data showing rescue of lysosomal function by upstream blockade; by contrast, systemic C5 inhibition with eculizumab and other C5-directed agents failed to meet GA endpoints in early trials, and LFG316 also did not demonstrate efficacy in GA (West et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Route of administration: Most agents demonstrating anatomical effects in GA are delivered intravitreally; eculizumab’s large size and systemic administration likely limited ocular penetration in COMPLETE, and no intravitreal eculizumab data are provided here to support local delivery (Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
- Risk of adverse ocular remodeling: Complement modulation has complex, context-dependent effects; in some models, complement inhibition or modulation can alter macrophage polarization and influence CNV formation, underscoring that indiscriminate or poorly targeted complement blockade could have unintended consequences; while the eculizumab AMD trials did not show a neovascular signal, vigilance is warranted when selecting targets and doses (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2021).

Decision Implications  
- As a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD, eculizumab has a low probability of success based on randomized clinical evidence, pharmacokinetic compartment limitations, and mechanistic considerations indicating that distal C5 blockade may not correct the proximal complement turnover driving RPE lysosomal pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- If C5 remains a target of interest, local ocular delivery and alternative molecular formats designed for intravitreal pharmacokinetics (e.g., smaller C5-binding entities, RNAi to intraocular C5 production, or intravitreal C5 inhibitors such as avacincaptad pegol) are more plausible routes; indeed, avacincaptad has advanced in GA, while systemic eculizumab has been discontinued in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019; Nadeem et al., 2023; West et al., 2024).  
- For assays aimed at lysosomal stress and POS phagocytosis, prioritizing proximal complement inhibitors (e.g., C3-targeting) is more aligned with human RPE data and recent clinical experience, whereas C5 inhibition alone is unlikely to fully normalize lysosomal function or confer robust structural benefit (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; West et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
Eculizumab provides a clear mechanistic means to extinguish terminal complement effectors implicated in AMD biology, but the totality of evidence—negative randomized clinical data in GA and drusen, route-of-administration barriers to ocular exposure, mechanistic escape during high activation, and cellular evidence favoring proximal over distal inhibition for lysosomal rescue—argues against further development of systemic eculizumab for dry AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The program should be deprioritized in favor of intraocularly suited agents and proximal complement targets, unless a compelling, testable strategy emerges to achieve effective intraocular C5 blockade with eculizumab (which is not supported by the present context) (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistic Appendix: Biochemical and Pathobiologic Evidence Relevant to the Hypothesis  
- Complement activation and terminal effectors in AMD:  
  - C5a is present in drusen and induces VEGF from RPE; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD; MAC induces endothelial lysis and sub-lytic survival signaling that upregulates VEGF and MMPs (Kassa et al., 2019).  
  - Alternative pathway dysregulation is central in AMD; genetic and experimental data implicate factor H and alternative pathway components in AMD and CNV models; inhibition of C3a, C5a, CFB, MAC or supplementation with CD59/CFH blocks CNV in animals (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Eculizumab structure–function:  
  - Epitope on MG7 with steric convertase blockade; high-affinity binding and resistance polymorphisms at Arg885; CDR function validated by mutational scans (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
  - PK/PD: long half-life, vascular distribution, CH50 suppression threshold, FcRn recycling of C5:eculizumab complexes; ravulizumab engineering to improve recycling and dosing (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
  - Breakthrough mechanisms: convertase bypass and surface-induced conformational activation on dense C3b clusters; residual TP activity despite inhibitors under strong activation (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; Mannes et al., 2021).  
- Clinical AMD trials:  
  - COMPLETE GA cohort: no slowing of GA growth at 26 or 52 weeks; well tolerated (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021).  
  - COMPLETE drusen cohort: no ≥ 50% reduction in drusen volume in treated eyes at 26 weeks; no significant change in drusen growth vs placebo (Filho et al., 2014).  
  - Critical appraisals: small sample, imprecision, risk of bias; systemic delivery may not achieve retinal levels; eculizumab no longer in AMD development (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023).  
- RPE lysosomal biology:  
  - In high-risk Y402H iPSC-RPE, excessive C3 turnover increases MAC internalization and overloads lysosomes; C3 inhibition with Cp40 reduces both C3b and MAC, reverses lysosomal defects, and reduces drusen-like deposits; direct C5 inhibition is not shown to restore lysosomal function in this model (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Operational Recommendation  
- Do not advance systemic eculizumab for dry AMD. If C5 remains a strategic target, consider intravitreal agents designed for ocular PK and evaluate them head-to-head against proximal inhibitors in RPE lysosomal-function assays that quantify both MAC and C3 fragment deposition, with translational go/no-go predicated on alignment with known clinical signals in GA (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mini‐FH is a rationally engineered, recombinant protein therapeutic derived from human complement factor H (FH) by selectively fusing its N-terminal complement control protein (CCP) modules 1–4 with its C-terminal CCP modules 19–20 (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). This minimal construct is synthesized through recombinant DNA methodologies that allow for expression in suitable heterologous systems such as yeast, insect cells, or mammalian cell lines; its design takes full advantage of recent advances in protein engineering guided by high‐resolution structural data (Dobo et al., 2018; Makou et al., 2013). Belonging to the class of engineered biologics—or “modular complement regulators”—Mini‐FH represents a more manufacturable, compact alternative to full‐length FH (≈155 kDa), reducing the molecular weight to roughly 40–45 kDa, which is expected to facilitate improved tissue and cellular penetration (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). This therapeutic candidate is designed to recapitulate the dual functionality of native FH: the CCP1–4 region provides regulatory activity through decay‐accelerating and cofactor functions against the alternative pathway (AP) C3 convertase, while the CCP19–20 region confers selective binding to surface‐associated ligands, including C3b/C3d and glycosaminoglycans, thereby anchoring the inhibitor to host membranes (Merle et al., 2015; Biggs et al., 2022). In essence, Mini‐FH is synthesized as a fusion protein that retains critical complement regulatory activities in a smaller, more agile molecule; this design underscores a broader trend in drug development toward developing “miniaturized,” high‐potency biologics that can overcome limitations of full‐length proteins in terms of tissue distribution and immunogenicity (Dobo et al., 2018; Makou et al., 2013).

Therapeutic History:  
The use of complement regulators as therapeutic agents has a long history in clinical research, particularly for diseases driven by dysregulation of the AP of complement. Engineered FH fragments like Mini‐FH have been the subject of extensive biochemical and preclinical evaluation, with studies demonstrating that constructs consisting of CCP1–4/19–20 exhibit enhanced binding to C3 fragments and improved decay‐accelerating activity compared to native FH on a per‐molecule basis (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). Preclinical in vitro assays, such as surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and hemolytic assays, have confirmed that Mini‐FH binds C3b with high affinity and competitively inhibits AP convertase formation by both displacing factor B and accelerating convertase decay (Dobo et al., 2018; Biggs et al., 2022). Moreover, animal studies, including those involving FH‐deficient mice, have provided compelling evidence for the in vivo activity of such engineered constructs, wherein administration of Mini‐FH or homodimeric variants (e.g., HDM-FH) reduced complement deposition and ameliorated tissue pathology in models of complement‐mediated kidney disease (de Boer et al., 2020; Kamala et al., 2021). Although direct clinical trials of Mini‐FH specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) have not yet been reported, related compounds such as full‐length recombinant FH (GEM103) have entered phase-2 clinical testing for AMD, thereby validating the concept of using FH‐based molecules to restore complement homeostasis in ocular diseases (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Additionally, engineered versions of FH, including dimerized variants designed to enhance serum half-life and tissue binding, have shown promising preclinical efficacy in non-ocular models such as paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and C3 glomerulopathy, further suggesting that the underlying mechanism is broadly applicable to complement‐mediated disorders (de Boer et al., 2020; Biggs et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of Mini‐FH relies on its ability to simultaneously exploit the dual functionalities of FH through its modular design. The N-terminal CCP1–4 domain comprises the core regulatory region that mediates AP control by binding directly to C3b. This interaction competitively prevents the binding of factor B (FB), thereby inhibiting the formation of the pro-convertase C3bB complex and effectively blocking the assembly of the C3 convertase (C3bBb) (Merle et al., 2015; Kamala et al., 2021). In addition, CCP1–4 exerts decay-accelerating activity by accelerating the dissociation of Bb from the C3bBb complex; it also provides a binding platform for factor I (FI), thereby functioning as a cofactor that promotes the proteolytic cleavage of C3b to inactive iC3b (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). Complementing this, the C-terminal CCP19–20 domains of Mini‐FH are involved in high-affinity ligand recognition. These domains bind to the thioester-containing domain (TED) of C3b as well as to C3d fragments, which are present at sites of previous complement activation, and they interact with glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) and sialic acid residues on host cell surfaces (Merle et al., 2015; Biggs et al., 2022). This binding not only increases the overall avidity of the interaction by engaging multiple sites on a single C3b molecule but also serves to target the regulatory activity specifically to host surfaces that are decorated with complement activation products—a critical factor in distinguishing self from non-self (Dobo et al., 2018; Makou et al., 2013). Furthermore, by engaging in a dual binding mode, Mini‐FH effectively “bridges” the regulatory and recognition functions that in full-length FH are partially masked by the intervening CCP modules, thus resulting in a higher potency per molecule (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Structural studies, including crystallographic analysis of complexes such as C3b:Mini-FH:FI, substantiate that Mini-FH engages two spatially distinct sites on C3b and even recruits FI through additional contacts involving CCP2–3, which further enhances its complement inhibitory function (Biggs et al., 2022). The overall consequence of these molecular interactions is the efficient disruption of the AP amplification loop, thereby reducing the cascade of complement activation products and ultimately limiting tissue damage driven by uncontrolled complement activity (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the hypothesis posits that Mini-FH will competitively bind to C3b deposited on the surfaces of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and within Bruch’s membrane, specifically restoring local complement regulation by the alternative pathway (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). The expected mechanism is that, upon intravitreal administration, Mini-FH will localize to the subretinal space where excessive complement activation is known to occur as a result of FH deficiency or dysfunction associated with the Y402H polymorphism. Once there, the CCP1–4 segment of Mini-FH is anticipated to exert decay-accelerating and cofactor activities that promote the inactivation of C3b—inhibiting the formation and persistence of the C3 convertase (C3bBb) and thereby interrupting the amplification of the cascade (de Boer et al., 2020; Dobo et al., 2018). This biochemical activity is expected to result in a reduction of downstream complement components such as C5b–9 (the membrane attack complex) and inflammatory mediators like C3a and C5a, which are implicated in the chronic inflammation observed in dry AMD (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

From a cellular perspective, by limiting complement activation on RPE surfaces, Mini-FH is expected to reduce the formation and accumulation of drusen-like deposits—extracellular aggregates that have been associated with inappropriate complement activity and are a hallmark of AMD pathology (Dobo et al., 2018; Makou et al., 2013). In addition, the engagement of CCP19–20 with surface-bound C3b/C3d and GAGs should enhance the targeted accumulation of Mini-FH on the RPE and in Bruch’s membrane, areas that are known hotspots for complement dysregulation in AMD (Merle et al., 2015; Biggs et al., 2022). This targeted binding not only localizes the regulatory function where it is most needed but may also facilitate secondary beneficial effects; for example, by mitigating complement-mediated cytotoxicity, Mini-FH may indirectly improve the phagocytic function of the RPE. Efficient post-phagocytosis is critical for the daily clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and disruption of this process is a contributing factor in the progression of AMD (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Preclinical experiments in RPE explant models or murine AMD models that have been exposed to Mini-FH are thus expected to demonstrate a decrease in C3 deposition and complement activation markers, accompanied by restoration of normal RPE phagocytic capacity (de Boer et al., 2020; Dobo et al., 2018). Moreover, due to its relatively small size when compared to full-length FH, Mini-FH is predicted to have superior tissue penetration, which is essential for reaching the deeper layers of Bruch’s membrane and the subretinal space, where the pathological complement activation predominantly occurs (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating the potential of Mini-FH (Recombinant FH CCP1–4/19–20) as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key strengths and challenges emerge. One of the primary strengths of Mini-FH is its rational design based on a deep understanding of FH architecture and function. By incorporating the most critical regulatory and recognition domains into a single, compact molecule, Mini-FH offers enhanced potency on a per-molecule basis and efficient competitive binding to C3b. The enhanced decay-accelerating activity and ability to serve as a cofactor for FI-mediated C3b inactivation have been well documented in preclinical assays, including SPR and hemolysis studies (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). These features are especially promising given that dysregulated complement activation is a central element of AMD pathogenesis. Furthermore, Mini-FH’s smaller size relative to full-length FH suggests improved penetration into ocular tissues such as Bruch’s membrane and the subretinal space, where therapeutic intervention is most needed (Dobo et al., 2018; de Boer et al., 2020).

Another significant strength is the translational rationale supported by biochemical and preclinical animal studies. Engineered FH fragments, including Mini-FH variants, have demonstrated efficacy in reducing complement activity in murine models of complement dysregulation, such as C3 glomerulopathy and PNH, which supports the concept that restoring control over the AP can ameliorate tissue damage (Kamala et al., 2021; Biggs et al., 2022). The fact that full-length recombinant FH (GEM103) is already being evaluated clinically for AMD further bolsters the therapeutic validity of targeting the complement cascade in ocular diseases (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Moreover, the diverse strategies employed in the development of similar biologics (e.g., dimerized forms of Mini-FH or fusion constructs with additional targeting domains) point to an active area of research and innovation that is likely to yield clinically effective solutions (Makou et al., 2013; Dobo et al., 2018).

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges warrant careful consideration. Although Mini-FH has demonstrated robust in vitro complement regulatory activity, its reduced size relative to the full-length molecule may also come with a trade-off, such as a potential reduction in FI cofactor activity under certain conditions (de Boer et al., 2020; Kamala et al., 2021). This diminished cofactor activity might necessitate higher dosing to achieve complete complement inhibition, which in turn could impact the safety profile and overall therapeutic index in the delicate ocular environment. Immunogenicity remains another concern; engineered proteins can sometimes elicit anti-drug antibodies (ADAs), and although intravitreal delivery benefits from the eye’s relative immune privilege, long-term administration in a chronic disease like AMD may eventually overcome this barrier (Kamala et al., 2021; Biggs et al., 2022). In addition, while animal model data in non-ocular systems are promising, the unique anatomy and microenvironment of the retina—especially the dynamics of RPE function, Bruch’s membrane characteristics, and POS phagocytosis—present additional layers of complexity that have not yet been fully addressed by preclinical studies specific to this application (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

There is also the challenge of ensuring consistent manufacturing and high-yield recombinant production of a complex, multi-domain protein like Mini-FH. Although advances in recombinant expression systems have made it feasible to produce such proteins at scale, the retention of full activity, appropriate post-translational modifications, and proper folding is critical for therapeutic efficacy and must be established within a robust quality control framework (Makou et al., 2013). Furthermore, the pharmacokinetic profile of Mini-FH, including its half-life on ocular tissues and systemic clearance if any, requires detailed investigation; alterations in inter-domain linker length or structural flexibility could impact tissue distribution and drug retention at the target site (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

From a mechanistic standpoint, while Mini-FH is designed to restore regulation by competitively binding to C3b and facilitating its inactivation, the downstream consequences of complement repression in the retina are multifaceted. In dry AMD, chronic complement dysregulation not only drives inflammation but also contributes to impaired phagocytosis of POS by the RPE. Although preclinical evidence suggests that restoring complementary control can indirectly improve RPE function (Kamala et al., 2021), the exact molecular pathways linking complement inhibition to improved POS clearance have not been fully elucidated, necessitating further mechanistic studies in retinal model systems (Dobo et al., 2018).

In summary, Mini‐FH represents a highly promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its engineered dual functionality—providing both potent AP convertase regulatory activity and targeted binding to complement‐deposited surfaces—as well as its potential for superior tissue penetration given its compact molecular size (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). Its mechanism of action is well supported by structural, biochemical, and preclinical data, and the conceptual framework is further validated by ongoing clinical evaluations of full‐length recombinant FH in AMD. However, while the biochemical rationale and preclinical models lend strong support to the therapeutic strategy, challenges remain in translating these findings to the complex ocular environment; these include ensuring sufficient FI cofactor activity, managing potential immunogenicity, optimizing intravitreal delivery parameters, and confirming that the beneficial effects observed in kidney or systemic models are recapitulated in retinal tissues (de Boer et al., 2020; Dobo et al., 2018).

However, several critical issues must be addressed before advancing Mini‐FH as a clinical candidate for dry AMD. First, direct evidence from retinal model systems is required to confirm that the biochemical potency of Mini‐FH translates into meaningful therapeutic outcomes in the context of RPE integrity, Bruch’s membrane function, and POS phagocytosis (de Boer et al., 2020; Dobo et al., 2018). Second, while the immune privileged status of the eye may mitigate ADA risk, long-term intravitreal delivery studies need to be conducted to establish both safety and sustained efficacy over the chronic course of AMD (Kamala et al., 2021; Biggs et al., 2022). Third, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles in the ocular milieu must be rigorously characterized to determine the optimal dosing regimen, ensuring that Mini‐FH reaches and remains active at the target site without eliciting off-target effects (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Finally, manufacturing consistency and scalability remain practical challenges for any complex recombinant protein therapeutic, and these aspects must be optimized early in the development process to facilitate clinical translation (Makou et al., 2013).

In conclusion, Mini‐FH (Recombinant FH CCP1–4/19–20) is a state-of-the-art, mechanistically driven therapeutic candidate that harnesses the targeted complement inhibitory potential of engineered FH fragments for the treatment of dry AMD. Its design leverages the strengths of both the N-terminal regulatory and C-terminal recognition domains, offering a potent means to counteract the dysregulated complement activation underlying AMD pathology. While the preclinical data from non-ocular models are very promising, targeted studies in retinal systems are necessary to confirm its efficacy and safety in the context of dry AMD. Based on the comprehensive literature review, Mini‐FH represents a compelling candidate with strong scientific rationale and significant translational potential, but further preclinical work specifically focused on retinal endpoints is essential before progressing to clinical trials. The balance between enhanced C3b binding and potential trade-offs in FI cofactor activity, along with considerations of immunogenicity and optimal delivery strategies, will be critical determinants of its ultimate clinical success in alleviating the burden of dry AMD (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018; de Boer et al., 2020; Biggs et al., 2022).
