I. Introduction  
Age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) remains one of the foremost causes of irreversible vision loss in the elderly population. In particular, the dry form of AMD is characterized by the progressive decline of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function, accumulation of extracellular deposits, and eventual photoreceptor loss. Over recent years, a growing body of research has implicated epigenetic dysregulation—especially aberrant histone modifications—and impaired autophagy as central features contributing to AMD pathogenesis (Campello et al., 2021). With these insights, a novel therapeutic direction has emerged that involves modulating the epigenomic landscape of RPE cells to restore homeostatic mechanisms. This report evaluates the drug candidate Methylstat—a JmjC-domain histone demethylase inhibitor—as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The central hypothesis under investigation posits that Methylstat, by inhibiting histone demethylases in RPE cells, will enhance the transcription of autophagy and phagocytosis genes (e.g., TFEB and MERTK). Such a transcriptional upregulation is expected to promote the uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and improve lysosomal function, thereby ameliorating the cellular damage associated with oxidative stress in AMD (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

II. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Methylstat is a small molecule inhibitor originally synthesized for its potent activity against the Jumonji C (JmjC) domain-containing family of histone demethylases. These enzymes catalyze the removal of methyl groups from lysine residues on histone proteins, a process that modulates chromatin structure and thereby influences gene transcription. As a synthetic compound, Methylstat was developed to interrogate the functional roles of histone demethylases in various cellular contexts and disease states. It belongs to a class of epigenetic modulators that have been broadly investigated in oncology and other diseases where epigenetic misregulation plays a critical role (Campello et al., 2021). Although the majority of research in retinal diseases has focused on inhibitors of histone deacetylases or activating lysosomal biogenesis via mTOR modulation (Kaštelan et al., 2024; Sinha et al., 2016), there is promising rationale to consider histone demethylase inhibitors as well. The candidate’s chemical structure and mechanism of enzyme inhibition suggest that it may increase levels of activating histone marks such as H3K4me3 at key gene promoters, ultimately facilitating a transcriptionally active chromatin state in RPE cells.

Importantly, repurposing Methylstat for ocular use leverages its established preclinical profile. In rodent models, preliminary ocular safety data suggest tolerability, providing an impetus to explore its potential application in diseases such as dry AMD (Campello et al., 2021; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). By virtue of its synthetic origin and the ability to fine-tune its dosage and delivery, Methylstat offers a strategic advantage over compounds that require extensive de novo safety profiling. This advantage is complemented by its mechanistic promise: by altering the epigenetic landscape, Methylstat may restore proper regulation of genes critical for autophagy, phagocytosis, and lysosomal clearance that are known to be compromised in aging RPE cells (Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

III. Therapeutic History  
Prior to its consideration in the context of AMD, Methylstat has primarily been utilized as a chemical probe in studies aimed at understanding the biological function of the JmjC family of histone demethylases in several cellular systems. Traditionally, this class of compounds has been investigated for their antitumor properties due to their capacity to alter gene expression profiles that govern cell proliferation and apoptosis (Campello et al., 2021). In contrast, interventions in age-related retinal diseases have so far concentrated on modifying chromatin accessibility through histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi) and acetyltransferase modulators, with several groups reporting that targeting these epigenetic enzymes may mitigate retinal damage and slow functional decline (Campello et al., 2021).

The literature regarding histone demethylases—especially those within the JmjC family—indicates that their role in retinal pathophysiology is less well-defined. Notably, the Open Targets platform data provide only limited support for the implication of histone demethylases such as KDM4A and KDM4C in AMD (Buniello et al., 2025). Furthermore, current evidence suggests that these particular demethylases have low association scores with AMD phenotypes and a dearth of mechanistic studies validating their function in RPE health (Buniello et al., 2025). In light of these factors, the therapeutic exploration of Methylstat represents an innovative, albeit higher-risk, strategy. It aims to extend the paradigm of epigenetic therapy to a class of enzymes that has not been rigorously evaluated in the context of AMD, thereby potentially uncovering new biological insights and therapeutic windows (Campello et al., 2021).

IV. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, Methylstat functions by inhibiting the catalytic activity of JmjC domain-containing histone demethylases. These enzymes are responsible for demethylating lysine residues on histone tails—a modification that can either activate or repress gene transcription depending on the residue involved and the degree of methylation. For instance, trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4me3) is generally associated with open chromatin and active transcription, particularly at gene promoter regions. Under normal physiological conditions, a dynamic equilibrium between methylation and demethylation controls chromatin accessibility and the transcriptional potential of a cell (Campello et al., 2021).

Methylstat’s inhibition of these enzymes is expected to lead to an accumulation of methylation marks such as H3K4me3. This buildup can render the chromatin more accessible to transcription factors and the transcriptional machinery, thereby upregulating the expression of genes involved in cellular homeostasis. Specifically, the hypothesis driving the use of Methylstat in dry AMD is that this drug will increase H3K4me3 levels at the promoters of key regulatory genes involved in autophagy and phagocytosis—most notably transcription factor EB (TFEB) and MER tyrosine kinase (MERTK) (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. When its expression is upregulated, there is an increased transcription of a suite of genes that coordinate the formation of autophagosomes, lysosomal fusion, and the processing of intracellular debris (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). In parallel, MERTK is critically involved in the phagocytic function of RPE cells, particularly in the uptake and clearance of POS, which are regularly shed by photoreceptors as part of their normal renewal process. By enhancing the transcription of such genes, Methylstat may ultimately promote more efficient autophagic flux and phagocytic clearance, mitigating the accumulation of damaged proteins and debris that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Sinha et al., 2016).

At a biochemical level, the inhibition mechanism most likely involves Methylstat binding to the active site of the demethylase where essential cofactors such as Fe(II) and α-ketoglutarate are coordinated. By chelating or otherwise interfering with these cofactors, Methylstat prevents the oxidative demethylation reaction that would normally remove methyl groups from histone substrates. The net consequence is an epigenetic shift toward transcriptional activation of autophagy and phagocytosis genes (Grigoryan & Markitantova, 2025). Moreover, in the oxidative environment typical of stressed RPE cells, maintaining an active autophagic response is critical to counterbalancing the accumulation of cellular damage. The literature underscores that impaired autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are pivotal to the progression of AMD, as these pathways are central to the degradation of oxidized proteins and other cellular waste products (Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

An additional layer of complexity in this mechanism is the interplay between histone methylation and the broader network of epigenetic modifications. Dysregulation of histone deacetylases (HDACs) in AMD has been well documented (Campello et al., 2021; Kaštelan et al., 2024), and it often results in a transcriptionally repressive chromatin state. By contrast, Methylstat’s action is aimed at promoting a transcriptionally permissive configuration through the sustained presence of methyl marks. Thus, combining Methylstat’s mechanism with insights into HDAC regulation could eventually lead to combination therapies that more comprehensively restore the epigenetic balance in damaged RPE cells (Zibetti, 2025).

V. Expected Effect  
In vitro assays utilizing cultured RPE cells exposed to oxidative stress are expected to provide the first line of evidence regarding the efficacy of Methylstat. Under conditions that mimic the stress encountered in the aging retina, RPE cells experience an overload of damaged proteins and dysfunctional organelles. This is typically exacerbated by impaired autophagy—a process that is essential not only for recycling cellular components but also for mitigating apoptotic signals and inflammatory responses associated with chronic stress (Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

It is anticipated that treatment with Methylstat will yield several measurable outcomes in these assays. First, there should be an observable increase in global levels of H3K4me3, particularly at promoters of autophagy- and phagocytosis-related genes. Chromatin immunoprecipitation studies could verify this epigenetic shift, providing direct evidence that the histone demethylase activity is being successfully inhibited (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Second, such an epigenetic change should correspond to upregulated transcription of TFEB, MERTK, and potentially other downstream effectors vital for lysosomal function and autophagosome formation (Sinha et al., 2016). Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and RNA sequencing approaches would likely reveal increased messenger RNA levels for these genes, reinforcing the expected mechanism of action.

Functionally, RPE cells exposed to Methylstat may exhibit enhanced clearance of photoreceptor outer segments. In the healthy eye, efficient phagocytosis of these outer segments by RPE cells is essential to maintain photoreceptor function and overall retinal integrity. Under oxidative stress conditions, compromised phagocytosis leads to the accumulation of debris, formation of lipofuscin, and subsequent cellular senescence (Campello et al., 2021; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). By promoting the expression of genes directly involved in phagocytic uptake and lysosomal degradation, Methylstat is hypothesized to boost the cells’ capacity to remove POS cargo effectively. This enhanced clearance could not only improve retinal function but also potentially slow or reverse the progression of dry AMD.

Furthermore, the expected increase in TFEB activity would likely lead to improved lysosomal biogenesis and function. Given that lysosomal fusion and clearance are critical to mitigating cellular damage within the RPE, enhanced TFEB-driven gene expression offers a compelling mechanistic rationale. In fact, several studies have indicated that restoration of autophagic processes and lysosomal function represents a promising therapeutic strategy to counteract the accumulation of cellular waste and the ensuing inflammatory cascade seen in AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). The net result of these effects would be the preservation of cellular homeostasis and prevention of premature senescence in RPE cells, which is a critical upstream event in the development of AMD pathology (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Campello et al., 2021).

In summary, the expected effect of Methylstat in cell-based assays is twofold: (1) an epigenetic reprogramming event characterized by increased H3K4me3 levels and upregulation of key autophagy and phagocytosis genes, and (2) a physiological enhancement of POS uptake and lysosomal degradation processes, thereby potentially mitigating the deleterious sequelae of oxidative stress in the aging retina (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

VI. Overall Evaluation  
The assessment of Methylstat as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD involves a careful weighing of the theoretical strengths against practical challenges and gaps in current evidence. On the strength side, the concept of epigenetic modulation in restoring retinal cellular homeostasis is supported by a growing body of evidence. Studies have demonstrated that targeting chromatin modifiers—such as HDACs and acetylases—can confer therapeutic benefits in models of retinal degeneration (Campello et al., 2021). Methylstat extends this approach by specifically targeting JmjC histone demethylases, thereby offering a novel mechanism that could upregulate genes crucial for autophagy and phagocytosis. The proposed increase in H3K4me3 levels at promoters of TFEB and MERTK is especially attractive because these genes are central to maintaining the lysosomal integrity and phagocytic function of RPE cells, functions that are critically compromised in AMD (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Another significant strength lies in the practical aspects of drug development. Methylstat has already been characterized in other contexts, and preliminary rodent ocular safety data add a level of confidence regarding its tolerability (Campello et al., 2021; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Given that drug repurposing can greatly accelerate the timeline from preclinical validation to clinical application, Methylstat represents an appealing candidate from a strategic standpoint. Additionally, its small molecular size and synthetic origins provide opportunities for chemical optimization that may improve its specificity for retinal targets while minimizing systemic toxicity (Campello et al., 2021).

However, there are notable weaknesses and challenges associated with this therapeutic strategy. Foremost among these is the limited evidence linking JmjC histone demethylases—specifically the ones targeted by Methylstat—with AMD pathology. The Open Targets data indicate that potential targets such as KDM4A and KDM4C have low association scores with AMD, and there is scant evidence of their expression changes or pathogenic involvement in the retinal pigment epithelium during disease progression (Buniello et al., 2025). This suggests that while the theoretical underpinning is sound, the direct relevance of these enzymes to the disease phenotype remains to be conclusively demonstrated. As such, there is a significant risk that inhibition of these targets may not yield the expected therapeutic benefits.

Furthermore, the complexity of epigenetic regulation in the retina cannot be understated. RPE cells are subject to a tightly coordinated network of epigenetic modifications that interact dynamically. Whereas histone demethylation plays an important role, it is but one component of a broader regulatory milieu that includes histone acetylation, methylation at different residues, and DNA methylation. Consequently, the inhibition of one enzyme class may lead to compensatory changes in others, potentially diluting or even reversing the intended outcome. For instance, while Methylstat may increase H3K4 trimethylation, other repressive histone marks might persist or even become upregulated in response, thereby limiting the net transcriptional activation of autophagy and phagocytosis genes (Kaštelan et al., 2024; Zibetti, 2025; Sinha et al., 2016).

There is also the challenge of off-target effects. Histone demethylases are broadly expressed and are involved in numerous cellular processes beyond autophagy and phagocytosis. Inhibition of these enzymes in non-target cells could lead to unforeseen side effects, potentially compromising tissue integrity or inducing aberrant gene expression profiles that might exacerbate inflammation or other deleterious processes. Given that the retina is a highly specialized tissue with a fine balance of metabolic and oxidative stresses, any off-target effects resulting from systemic exposure to Methylstat will need to be carefully evaluated in preclinical studies (Buniello et al., 2025).

Another practical consideration is whether the epigenetic modulation achieved by Methylstat will be of sufficient magnitude and duration to effect functional improvements in RPE cells. Upregulation of TFEB and MERTK is an attractive proposition; however, the transcriptional responses in cells under chronic oxidative stress may differ from those in controlled in vitro environments. Additionally, the kinetics of chromatin modifications can be highly cell context-dependent, and there remains uncertainty regarding how quickly and sustainably Methylstat-mediated chromatin changes will translate into improved autophagic flux. This is particularly relevant given that AMD is a chronic disease and any therapeutic intervention must yield long-term benefits to justify clinical use (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

In light of these considerations, a phased and incremental research strategy is advisable. Initial studies should focus on establishing robust links between histone demethylase activity, H3K4me3 levels, and the transcriptional status of autophagy and phagocytosis genes in RPE cells. Advanced genomic techniques, such as ChIP-seq and RNA-seq, should be employed to detail the chromatin landscape before and after Methylstat treatment. Such studies will help to determine whether the predicted epigenetic changes are indeed occurring at the necessary target loci, and whether these changes correlate with improved cellular function.

Additionally, in vivo models of dry AMD should be used to validate the therapeutic effect of Methylstat in a physiologically relevant context. Rodent models that recapitulate key features of RPE dysfunction and oxidative stress are particularly valuable in this regard. Evaluations should include histological assessments of RPE integrity, measurements of lysosomal enzyme activity, and functional assays of photoreceptor viability. It will also be important to monitor potential systemic effects, given the widespread expression of histone demethylases throughout the body (Campello et al., 2021; Sinha et al., 2016).

Finally, combination therapies that target multiple aspects of the epigenetic network may be warranted. Given that other chromatin modifiers, such as histone deacetylases, have already shown therapeutic potential in AMD (Campello et al., 2021; Kaštelan et al., 2024), a synergistic approach that includes Methylstat along with HDAC inhibitors or mTOR modulators might provide a broader restoration of the epigenetic landscape in RPE cells. Such combinations would need to be carefully optimized to balance efficacy with safety, but they could ultimately offer a more comprehensive strategy to counteract the multifactorial etiology of AMD (Zibetti, 2025; Sinha et al., 2016).

VII. Conclusion  
In summary, Methylstat presents an intriguing candidate for repurposing as a therapy for dry age-related macular degeneration. The theoretical basis for its use rests on its ability to inhibit JmjC histone demethylases, leading to an accumulation of activating histone marks such as H3K4me3. This epigenetic reprogramming is hypothesized to enhance the expression of critical autophagy and phagocytosis genes—including TFEB and MERTK—in RPE cells, thereby improving the uptake and lysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments. Should these cellular processes be successfully augmented, the downstream effect would be a reduction in oxidative stress–induced damage, preservation of RPE function, and ultimately a slowdown or reversal of AMD progression (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

The strengths of this approach include its innovative mechanism that builds on the established relevance of epigenetic dysregulation in retinal degeneration, as well as the practical advantages associated with drug repurposing. Methylstat’s synthetic nature, existing preclinical safety data, and capacity for chemical modification all contribute to its potential as a versatile therapeutic tool. Moreover, the focus on restoring autophagic and phagocytic pathways aligns well with current insights into AMD pathophysiology, which repeatedly highlight the importance of efficient waste clearance in maintaining retinal cell homeostasis (Campello et al., 2021; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Nevertheless, challenges remain. The current evidence directly linking JmjC histone demethylases to AMD pathogenesis is limited. Open Targets analyses indicate a low association of enzymes such as KDM4A and KDM4C with the disease phenotype, raising concerns about whether their inhibition will yield significant clinical benefits (Buniello et al., 2025). Moreover, the complexity of epigenetic regulation—and the potential for compensatory mechanisms among various chromatin modifiers—necessitates a cautious approach. Off-target effects, the kinetics of transcriptional changes, and the chronic nature of AMD all underscore the need for comprehensive preclinical evaluation before advancing Methylstat into clinical trials.

In conclusion, while Methylstat exhibits several compelling features that justify its further investigation as a therapy for dry AMD, it is clear that significant gaps in our understanding of the role of histone demethylases in retinal aging must be addressed. Rigorous in vitro studies, supported by in vivo animal model data, are essential to validate the proposed mechanism of action and to optimize dosage and delivery strategies. Only through such a multifaceted approach can the full therapeutic potential of Methylstat be properly ascertained. If these initial studies demonstrate robust, reproducible benefits in restoring autophagic, phagocytic, and lysosomal functions in RPE cells, then Methylstat may emerge as a valuable addition to the currently limited therapeutic arsenal for dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Overall, the proposal to repurpose Methylstat for dry AMD treatment is scientifically intriguing and mechanistically plausible. However, the journey from hypothesis to clinical efficacy will require careful validation of the compound’s epigenetic impact in the pathological context of AMD. With concerted efforts combined with stratified preclinical studies, this candidate may open new avenues for precision pharmacotherapy in age-related retinal diseases (Campello et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Cp40‐Peg is a PEGylated analog derived from the original compstatin peptide, a cyclic peptide identified through phage display technology and subsequently optimized for high‐affinity binding to complement component C3. The parent molecule, Cp40, binds specifically to C3 with nanomolar potency (IC₅₀ ~ 1 nM) and was engineered to interrupt the complement cascade by preventing the cleavage of C3 into its active fragments. To improve upon the pharmacokinetic limitations of unmodified compstatin peptides, Cp40 was chemically modified by conjugation with polyethylene glycol (PEG), a strategy known as PEGylation, which is designed to substantially extend systemic and, in this case, intraocular half‐life. This molecular modification confers several advantages, including enhanced aqueous solubility, reduced proteolytic degradation, and diminished renal clearance, all of which contribute to sustaining therapeutic concentrations for extended durations within ocular tissues. As a member of the compstatin class of complement inhibitors, Cp40‐Peg belongs to a novel class of therapeutics that have been explored for their capacity to modulate complement activation in various inflammatory and degenerative conditions, including ocular diseases. The design of Cp40‐Peg is grounded in decades of biochemical research that have progressively refined the structure–activity relationship (SAR) of compstatin peptides to achieve not only improved potency but also desirable pharmacokinetic properties for chronic indications such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
The evolution of compstatin-based therapies can be traced back to initial studies that harnessed the cyclic peptide’s ability to inhibit complement activation, a finding that spurred interest in targeting complement-mediated pathology. Early compstatin analogs were investigated in the context of systemic complement dysregulation disorders such as paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and sepsis, with subsequent research extending these findings to ocular indications where complement-mediated inflammation plays a critical role in disease progression. Multiple compstatin derivatives have undergone rigorous preclinical testing in animal models, including cynomolgus monkeys, where the peptides demonstrated significant efficacy in suppressing drusen formation and restoring retinal health by mitigating complement overactivation (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2015). More recently, compounds in this class have been repurposed for the treatment of dry AMD. For example, pegcetacoplan, a PEGylated compstatin analog distinct from Cp40‐Peg but conceptually similar, has been advanced into Phase III clinical trials and has shown promising results in reducing geographic atrophy (GA) lesion growth in dry AMD patients (Ong et al., 2024; Patel et al., 2022). Cp40‐Peg, the candidate under review, builds upon this established therapeutic framework by combining the potent and selective C3 inhibition of Cp40 with a PEGylation strategy designed to extend the intraocular residence time to greater than three months, as demonstrated in non‐human primate studies (Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). Although Cp40‐Peg is in earlier stages of development relative to some other compounds in the class, its preclinical profile—marked by sustained C3-saturating levels and restoration of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function—is highly encouraging for further advancement in dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of Cp40‐Peg is centered on its targeted inhibition of the complement cascade at the level of C3, an essential component that converges all three complement activation pathways (classical, lectin, and alternative). Cp40, a cyclic peptide with a refined amino acid sequence, binds to a critical region on the C3 molecule—specifically, the MG4/MG5 domains—thereby sterically hindering the formation of the C3 convertase enzyme complexes (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2015). This targeted binding effectively prevents the cleavage of native C3 into its active fragments including C3a, a potent anaphylatoxin, and C3b, which participates in opsonization and subsequent formation of the C5 convertase. Through this inhibition, Cp40‐Peg interrupts the propagation of the cascade that ordinarily leads to the formation of pro-inflammatory mediators and the assembly of the membrane attack complex. Importantly, the PEGylation of the Cp40 moiety does not compromise its binding affinity; rather, it stabilizes the molecule in the vitreous humor and ensures that sustained levels of the inhibitor are maintained over a prolonged period. This combination of high affinity (IC₅₀ ~ 1 nM) with extended residence time means that Cp40‐Peg is capable of providing continuous complement suppression on the RPE surface. Consequently, by averting chronic complement activation, the compound mitigates the inflammatory damage that contributes to the degeneration of photoreceptor cells and RPE dysfunction, an aspect that is further linked to impaired lysosomal and autophagic processing in dry AMD (Lamers et al., 2022; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The detailed structural interactions—illustrated by compstatin’s binding to critical loops on C3—help ensure that while complement is inhibited in a pathological context, essential immune functions that rely on regulated complement activity are preserved to some extent, highlighting the therapeutic precision achieved with this class of inhibitors (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2015; Hughes et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Dry AMD is characterized by the progressive degeneration of the macula due in part to chronic inflammation, drusen accumulation, and impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE. The hypothesis underlying the use of Cp40‐Peg in dry AMD is that sustained blockade of C3 will result in significant reductions in local complement-mediated inflammation that drive RPE dysfunction. By preventing the cleavage of C3, Cp40‐Peg is expected to reduce the production of complement activation fragments that contribute to an inflammatory microenvironment, thereby alleviating the deposition of complement components on RPE cells. This continuous inhibition of complement activity is projected to restore lysosomal and autophagic functionality within the RPE, improving the cells’ ability to process and clear POS debris—a process that is critically impaired in dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The expected pharmacodynamic effect is a decrease in the accumulation of drusen-like deposits and a concomitant improvement in the structural and functional integrity of the RPE. Preclinical studies in non-human primate models have demonstrated that prolonged intraocular exposure to Cp40-based inhibitors leads to a reduction in complement deposition and an improvement in lysosomal clearance markers, supporting the proposed mechanism by which Cp40‐Peg may exert its therapeutic benefits (Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). Moreover, the high target specificity and sustained inhibition translate into a pharmacological profile that could potentially reduce treatment frequency and improve patient compliance. Data from in vitro assays using high-risk RPE cells have shown that treatment with Cp40 analogs not only curtails complement activation but also promotes morphological and functional recovery of lysosomal compartments, thereby enhancing autophagy—a process critical for the clearance of photoreceptor debris and overall cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). This dual action of dampening inflammation and restoring RPE phagocytic function is expected to slow or even halt the progressive degenerative changes seen in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
In assessing the potential of Cp40‐Peg as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several critical strengths and potential limitations emerge. One of the major strengths of Cp40‐Peg is its potent and selective inhibition of C3 at extremely low nanomolar concentrations, which has been well established in biochemical studies. This high degree of potency ensures that even low concentrations of the inhibitor can achieve significant blockade of the complement cascade, a feature that is particularly important in the context of chronic diseases where sustained inhibition is required (Lamers et al., 2022; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Another key advantage is the PEGylation strategy that confers an extended intraocular residence time, with preclinical studies suggesting that a single intravitreal injection may maintain C3-saturating levels for more than three months. This long-acting pharmacokinetic profile is highly advantageous in reducing the treatment burden on patients and improving adherence in a chronic condition like AMD (Mastellos et al., 2015; Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

From a mechanistic perspective, Cp40‐Peg directly addresses the core pathogenic processes underlying dry AMD by targeting an essential mediator of inflammation. By inhibiting C3 activation, the drug not only blocks the generation of inflammatory anaphylatoxins and opsonins but also facilitates the restoration of critical RPE functions, including lysosomal degradation and autophagic processing vital for POS clearance. Such restoration is fundamental to re-establishing cellular homeostasis and mitigating the degenerative progression seen in dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Furthermore, the specificity of the compstatin-based approach minimizes the risk of widespread immune suppression, as it selectively targets one pivotal node in the complement cascade rather than broadly inhibiting immune function. This precision could potentially translate into a favorable safety profile, although vigilance regarding complement inhibition–related adverse effects must be maintained.

Despite these significant strengths, there are important challenges and potential weaknesses associated with Cp40‐Peg that must be considered. Long-term inhibition of the complement system, even if targeted and partial, can theoretically predispose patients to an increased risk of infections, particularly in the context of ocular immunity where defense against pathogens is crucial. Clinical trials of related agents, such as pegcetacoplan, have reported adverse events including increased incidences of neovascular complications, which underscore the need for careful safety evaluation in future studies (Ong et al., 2024; Mastellos et al., 2015). Moreover, while PEGylation offers extended residence time, it also introduces potential complications such as the development of anti-PEG antibodies. Such immunogenic responses could potentially alter the pharmacokinetics and efficacy of the drug over time, necessitating dose adjustments or alternative strategies in the long-term management of dry AMD (Mastellos et al., 2015; Park et al., 2019). Another consideration is the challenge of translating preclinical efficacy into clinical success. Although non-human primate models have provided promising data on the restoration of RPE homeostasis and prolonged complement suppression, the complexity of human AMD pathobiology demands rigorous clinical investigations to confirm these effects in patients with diverse genetic and environmental backgrounds (Lamers et al., 2022; Yu & Wykoff, 2021).

When comparing Cp40‐Peg with other therapeutic candidates within the compstatin family, its prolonged intraocular residence and potent C3 inhibition distinguish it as a particularly attractive candidate for dry AMD. However, the balance between achieving sufficient complement inhibition to confer therapeutic benefit and avoiding excessive blockade that could compromise host defense mechanisms remains a critical aspect of its clinical development. The continued progression of related agents into advanced clinical trial phases lends credence to the overall strategy, yet also highlights the necessity for comprehensive long-term safety and efficacy studies specifically tailored to the dry AMD patient population (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2022).

In summary, Cp40‐Peg exhibits a compelling combination of molecular potency, extended pharmacokinetic properties, and a mechanistically sound approach to addressing the pathological features of dry AMD—namely, chronic complement-mediated inflammation and RPE dysfunction. Its ability to sustain C3 inhibition over extended periods holds promise for improved dosing regimens and better patient adherence. Nonetheless, the risk of complement inhibition–related adverse effects, challenges associated with PEGylation such as immunogenicity, and the inherent complexities of translating preclinical findings to clinical efficacy represent important hurdles that will need to be overcome in future studies. Overall, while further detailed preclinical and early-phase clinical trials are warranted, the current evidence supports the continued development of Cp40‐Peg as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, with the potential to significantly restore RPE function and retard disease progression by re-establishing lysosomal and autophagic balance (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2015; Hughes et al., 2020; Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Ong et al., 2024).

Anacetrapib is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor of cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) originally developed by Merck as part of a class of compounds aimed at modulating lipid metabolism. This compound was identified and refined through extensive medicinal chemistry programs designed to target CETP’s lipid transfer function. As a member of the CETP inhibitor class, anacetrapib has been developed primarily for cardiovascular risk reduction by increasing high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL‐C) and lowering low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C), and its chemical structure and binding properties have been designed to disrupt the lipid‐transfer tunnel of the CETP enzyme (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Tall & Rader, 2018). The proposed repurposing for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on the rationale that by inhibiting CETP, the agent could raise local HDL levels in Bruch’s membrane (BrM) and improve reverse cholesterol transport, thereby reducing drusen‐like lipid accumulation and indirectly supporting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) phagocytic capacity—a hypothesis derived from observed associations between CETP activity, local retinal lipid metabolism, and AMD pathogenesis (Betzler et al., 2020; Shughoury et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, CETP inhibitors have been evaluated extensively for their potential to address dyslipidemia and reduce atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Anacetrapib, in particular, has undergone large clinical trials such as the DEFINE and REVEAL studies, where its efficacy in raising HDL‐C by approximately 138% and reducing LDL‐C by 37–40% compared to placebo was demonstrated (Cheung et al., 2017; Tall & Rader, 2018). The class of CETP inhibitors also includes compounds such as torcetrapib, dalcetrapib, and evacetrapib—with torcetrapib’s development being terminated due to off‐target effects including blood pressure elevations, while anacetrapib and evacetrapib showed more favorable profiles in subsequent trials (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Sirtori, 2011). Although these compounds were developed to address cardiovascular pathologies, genetic and mechanistic studies have implicated CETP and HDL metabolism in the ocular environment as well. Several genome‐wide association studies and Mendelian randomization studies have demonstrated a relationship between CETP gene variants, HDL levels, and AMD risk (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020). Despite this, no CETP inhibitor has previously been used in a clinical setting for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular diseases, and the repurposing of anacetrapib for dry AMD represents a novel therapeutic direction inspired by preclinical studies in murine models that suggest potential benefits in the retinal context (Cheung et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
Anacetrapib functions by binding to CETP, thereby preventing the transfer of cholesteryl esters from HDL to apolipoprotein B‐containing lipoproteins (i.e., LDL, very‐low‐density lipoprotein [VLDL]) and the subsequent exchange of triglycerides in the opposite direction. At the molecular level, CETP normally operates via a tunnel‐mechanism or shuttle mechanism to facilitate the bidirectional lipid transfer between lipoproteins. Inhibition of CETP by anacetrapib results in the accumulation of cholesterol-rich, enlarged HDL particles and a concomitant reduction in the levels of atherogenic LDL particles (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Sirtori, 2011). In the context of the retina, emerging evidence suggests that CETP is expressed not only systemically but also locally—in the retinal pigment epithelium, photoreceptor outer segments, and interphotoreceptor matrix (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). The rationale is that CETP activity in Bruch’s membrane may normally lower HDL levels, thereby impairing the capacity for reverse cholesterol transport in this specialized extracellular matrix, which can lead to the accumulation of lipids and the formation of drusen. By inhibiting CETP, anacetrapib may restore or increase local HDL levels, improving the efflux of accumulated cholesterol and other lipids from the RPE and neighboring structures (Fan et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2022). Moreover, the resulting HDL particles may gain enhanced cholesterol efflux capacity, as evidenced by preclinical studies that show increased cholesterol removal from macrophages via ABCA1- and ABCG1-mediated pathways (Sirtori, 2011; Page et al., 2016). In addition, proper HDL particle composition under CETP inhibition could influence key inflammatory regulatory mechanisms through the carriage of complement factors, which are linked to AMD pathogenesis (Tricorache et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assay, treatment with anacetrapib is expected to increase HDL levels locally in Bruch’s membrane, thereby enhancing reverse cholesterol transport across the retinal layers. The improved cholesterol efflux from the RPE is postulated to mitigate the accumulation of drusen-like lipid deposits—a hallmark of dry AMD—and potentially restore critical cellular functions such as integrin localization and associated phagocytic receptor activity (Cheung et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020). This restoration of lipid homeostasis is anticipated to reduce the build-up of oxidized lipids and other debris beneath the RPE, ultimately alleviating RPE dysfunction—a central component in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). The mechanism relies on the observation that HDL not only serves as a cholesterol acceptor but also carries important complement regulatory proteins and inflammatory mediators; thus, its normalization in Bruch’s membrane could indirectly support the phagocytic activity of RPE cells and improve tissue homeostasis (Lin et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). Gene expression studies have identified CETP expression in ocular tissues, reinforcing the notion that local CETP inhibition may directly influence lipid handling in the retina (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). Ultimately, the expected outcomes in preclinical models—and, by extension, in clinical trials—are a measurable reduction in drusen burden, improvement in RPE functionality, and a potential delay or attenuation in the progression of dry AMD (Schmidt et al., 2020; Cheung et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of anacetrapib for the treatment of dry AMD presents a compelling opportunity, supported by a solid mechanistic hypothesis and a favorable human safety profile established in cardiovascular trials. Among the clear strengths is the extensive biochemical and clinical data on CETP inhibitors in the context of dyslipidemia; anacetrapib has demonstrated robust HDL‐C raising and LDL‐C lowering effects, with a tolerability profile superior to earlier CETP inhibitors such as torcetrapib (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Tall & Rader, 2018). Furthermore, emerging evidence of CETP expression in ocular tissues and its potential role in modulating local lipid metabolism—combined with findings that suggest dysfunctional HDL composition may contribute to drusen formation—lends strong support to the therapeutic rationale (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017).

However, there are important weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed. First, the genetic and epidemiological data linking HDL cholesterol and AMD have been paradoxical; several Mendelian randomization studies have implicated HDL‐raising alleles, particularly those related to CETP modulation, with an increased risk for AMD (Betzler et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2017). This counterintuitive observation raises concerns that simply increasing HDL levels may not guarantee improved RPE function unless the quality and functionality of HDL particles are also enhanced (Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022). Second, while the cardiovascular applications of anacetrapib provide a strong safety signal, the ocular-specific pharmacodynamics and tissue distribution of the drug remain largely unexplored. It is conceivable that the systemic modulation of HDL might not translate into the desired local changes in Bruch’s membrane, particularly given the unique lipid microenvironment of the retina (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Third, preclinical data demonstrating that anacetrapib can reduce BrM lipid burden and restore integrin localization in murine models, although promising, have yet to be validated extensively, and species differences in CETP expression and lipid metabolism could limit translatability to human patients (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Lastly, the long-term consequences of altering CETP activity in the retina are unknown, and there exists a potential risk that chronic CETP inhibition could inadvertently disrupt local complement regulation or other aspects of retinal homeostasis, given the tight interplay between lipid metabolism and inflammation in AMD pathogenesis (Tricorache et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2015).

Overall, while the conceptual framework underlying the repurposing of anacetrapib for dry AMD is scientifically intriguing and supported by a convergence of genetic, biochemical, and preclinical mechanistic data, further investigation is needed to reconcile the paradoxical relationships observed in human genetic studies, to precisely characterize the local retinal pharmacokinetics of the drug, and to validate its effects on reverse cholesterol transport in the specific context of the retina. In summary, anacetrapib holds potential as a novel therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but its ultimate success will depend on carefully designed preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials that specifically address its ocular efficacy and safety profile (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of the prolyl oligopeptidase inhibitor KYP-2047 as a potential repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). This report is organized into several sections: an overview of the candidate, its therapeutic history, an in‐depth discussion of its mechanism of action, the expected effects in the proposed assay, and an overall evaluation that weighs its strengths and weaknesses.

─────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

KYP-2047 is a synthetic small molecule belonging to the peptidomimetic class of compounds that target the enzyme prolyl oligopeptidase (PREP), also known as prolyl endopeptidase (POP). Chemically designated as 4-phenylbutanoyl-L-prolyl-2(S)-cyanopyrrolidine, this compound was synthesized following methods established by Dr. Elina Jarho at the University of Eastern Finland (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47). Its design represents an evolution from early substrate-like inhibitors, with modifications at specific positions – including a three-carbon aliphatic chain at the P3 position instead of the more commonly used carbamate groups seen in predecessors like ZPP – thereby improving the compound’s overall potency, selectivity, and drug-like properties (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4).

Belonging to a well-known class of PREP inhibitors, KYP-2047 shares common chemical and biophysical properties with analogous peptidomimetic agents that have been primarily designed to interfere with the catalytic activity of a serine protease that cleaves proline-containing peptides. Given its low water solubility, KYP-2047 is typically formulated in saline containing 5% Tween® 80 for experimental studies, which is consistent with formulation challenges observed with many peptidomimetic drug candidates (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47). In recent years, the broader class of PREP inhibitors has been explored for a variety of indications, most notably in neurological conditions as well as in certain cancer models. The research impetus behind this class arises from the enzyme’s presumed role in peptide metabolism, where the inhibition of PREP could alter levels of bioactive peptides that participate in cellular homeostasis. Although these agents were originally developed as anti-amnesic candidates, their biological actions have been found to extend to anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

─────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

The therapeutic exploration of PREP inhibitors dates back to the 1970s when the enzyme was first implicated in the regulation of proline-containing peptides associated with memory formation and synaptic plasticity (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22). Numerous compounds in this class—including S-17092, JTP-4819, and others—were advanced into preclinical studies and even early-phase clinical trials for cognitive enhancement in neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease and senile dementia (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41, 70–72). However, despite initial encouraging in vitro and animal data, these agents failed to progress successfully past phase II clinical trials in humans, most likely due to challenges with efficacy, blood-brain barrier penetration, or the complexity of the enzyme’s in vivo function (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 70–72).

In parallel, PREP inhibitors have been evaluated for other indications. For instance, in a study involving oral squamous cell carcinoma, KYP-2047 demonstrated potent PREP inhibition in the mouse brain along with promising anti-tumor effects, highlighting the compound’s potential utility beyond central nervous system disorders (Scuderi, 2023, pp. 133–135). Furthermore, recent work has begun to explore the ocular applications of PREP inhibition. There is a suggestion in the literature that inhibition of prolyl oligopeptidase may represent “a promising pathway to prevent the progression of age-related macular degeneration” (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13). Notably, recent in vitro studies using human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells with defective proteasomal clearance have shown that KYP-2047 exhibits cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory properties, thereby indirectly supporting its potential use in dry AMD, even though no clinical trials or prior direct therapeutic applications in retinal diseases have yet been reported (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 9–11).

While the primary historical focus of PREP inhibitors has been on neurological and cognitive applications, the body of literature also contains several exploratory studies in inflammatory and cancer contexts (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Thus, even though the bulk of previous applications have not directly targeted dry AMD, the emerging evidence supporting cytoprotection and modulation of proteolytic and autophagy pathways in RPE cells provides a rationale for repurposing KYP-2047 in ocular disease states.

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

The biological target of KYP-2047 is the serine protease prolyl oligopeptidase (PREP), which is responsible for cleaving peptide bonds at the carboxyl side of internal proline residues in small peptides (typically less than ~30 amino acids) (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 22–24, 44–47). PREP is widely expressed in the central nervous system and peripheral tissues and has been implicated in multiple physiological processes including neuropeptide regulation and cell signaling. At the molecular level, the mechanism of action involves the binding of KYP-2047 to the enzyme’s active site, more specifically interacting with the catalytic serine residue. Many PREP inhibitors, including those in the class to which KYP-2047 belongs, are designed as substrate-like pseudopeptides that exploit the structure of the enzyme’s binding pockets (S1, S2, and S3) to achieve selectivity and high-affinity binding (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).

The inhibition by KYP-2047 is characterized as “tight-binding” with slow dissociation, meaning that once the inhibitor occupies the active site of PREP, it remains bound for a significant duration, thereby effectively reducing the enzyme’s catalytic turnover (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 70–72). In neurological models, inhibition of PREP has been associated with enhanced clearance of toxic protein aggregates such as alpha-synuclein, improved autophagic flux, and reduction in oxidative stress (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 85–88; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 9–11). The current therapeutic hypothesis in the context of dry AMD extrapolates these findings to retinal pigment epithelial cells.

In particular, the proposed mechanism posits that elevated PREP activity in RPE cells contributes to an accumulation of proline-rich peptides that, in turn, inhibit the activity of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and lysosomal cathepsin L. These cathepsins are critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and turnover of cellular debris. In dry AMD, defective protein clearance mechanisms, including impaired proteasomal and lysosomal function, result in the buildup of toxic deposits, such as A2E, and contribute to RPE dysfunction. By blocking PREP activity with KYP-2047 (which has an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range, reported to be approximately 30 nM), the proposed effect is to reduce the formation or accumulation of inhibitory peptides, thereby relieving the suppression on cathepsin activity. In addition, KYP-2047-mediated PREP inhibition may trigger downstream intracellular events such as autophagy activation and modulation of MAPK signaling pathways—including p38 and ERK1/2—which have been observed in other cell types and are known to reduce oxidative stress and inflammation (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 85–88).

At the biochemical level, these molecular interactions involve the inhibitor “locking in” the PREP enzyme in a conformational state that either prevents substrate access or alters the dynamics of peptide release once cleavage has occurred. Although the effects on neuropeptide levels (e.g., substance P, neurotensin) have been studied in central nervous system models—with mixed and sometimes counterintuitive outcomes (such as decreased acetylcholine levels) (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 8–16, 70–72)—the rationale for ocular repurposing rests on the idea that the same enzymatic inhibition can counteract the accumulation of cathepsin-inhibiting peptides in RPE cells. Notably, some studies have suggested that PREP inhibition can positively modulate autophagy, a process that is critical for cellular clearance mechanisms. Given that impaired autophagy is a central feature in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, a compound like KYP-2047 that both reduces toxic peptide accumulation and enhances proteolytic pathways presents an attractive, multitargeted strategy (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

The core hypothesis driving the repurposing of KYP-2047 for dry AMD is that inhibition of PREP will reduce the buildup of proline-rich peptides that otherwise impair lysosomal cathepsin activity. In RPE cells, efficient degradation of POS via phagocytosis and lysosomal function is essential for maintaining retinal homeostasis. In the setting of dry AMD, decreased cathepsin D and L activities are implicated in the inefficient clearance of cellular debris, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, ultimately causing RPE dysfunction.

In the proposed assay, RPE cells—typically the ARPE-19 cell line—will be challenged in an environment mimicking AMD pathology; for instance, by loading them with A2E and subjecting the cells to proteasomal stress. Under these conditions, the activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and L is compromised, and POS degradation is impaired. The application of KYP-2047 is expected to inhibit PREP activity with high potency, which theoretically will lead to a reduction in the concentration of peptide substrates that interfere with cathepsin enzymes (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).

The anticipated cascade of events is as follows:  
1. KYP-2047, at concentrations close to its low nanomolar IC₅₀, will effectively bind to and inhibit PREP in RPE cells.  
2. This inhibition will prevent the excessive cleavage of proline-containing peptides, thereby reducing the pool of inhibitory peptides that could otherwise bind to and decrease cathepsin D and L activities.  
3. As a consequence, the restoration of cathepsin activity is expected to improve the degradation of POS components as well as the clearance of other toxic debris, which is a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.  
4. Additionally, the compound’s reported anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects, demonstrated in ARPE-19 cells with defective proteasomal clearance, may further contribute to preserving RPE cell health by curtailing inflammatory cytokine production and oxidative stress (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 4–6).

It is also noteworthy that the mechanistic framework is further supported by the observation that PREP inhibition in other models has led to enhanced autophagy and improved clearance of aggregated proteins. In the context of AMD, effective POS degradation is not only dependent on cathepsin function but also on efficient autophagic flux. By indirectly modulating these pathways, KYP-2047 could offer dual benefits: restoration of lysosomal enzyme activity and bolstering of intracellular clearance mechanisms. Thus, the expected in vitro endpoints would likely include increased cathepsin D/L activity, elevated POS degradation (as detected by uptake assays), reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-6, IL-8, IL-1β), and diminished oxidative stress markers (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 4–6).

Moreover, the rationale includes supporting evidence from neurological and cancer research where PREP inhibition by compounds like KYP-2047 improved cell viability and reduced stress responses. Although previous clinical trials in central nervous system indications did not achieve long-term success, the safety data accrued from these studies may lower the translational barrier for ocular applications, provided that proper formulation and localized delivery (or systemic approaches with ocular distribution) can be achieved (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 4–5).

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

The evaluation of KYP-2047 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD involves weighing both its promising aspects and its uncertainties. On the positive side, KYP-2047 is a well-defined, highly potent inhibitor of PREP with an established chemical profile and a strong foundation in preclinical studies. Its synthetic origin as a peptidomimetic compound designed to bind the active site of PREP is well documented (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4), and the compound’s low nanomolar potency provides confidence that even modest drug exposures may achieve effective enzyme inhibition.

The repurposing strategy capitalizes on emerging evidence that PREP inhibitors can exert cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in RPE cells. In vitro studies conducted in ARPE-19 cells with impaired proteasomal clearance have demonstrated that KYP-2047 can reduce inflammatory cytokine production and promote cell viability (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). Given the central role of inflammation and defective lysosomal clearance in dry AMD, these findings provide a mechanistic rationale for testing KYP-2047 in this indication.

Furthermore, the proposed mechanism—whereby inhibition of PREP reduces the formation of inhibitory proline-rich peptides that suppress cathepsin activity—is mechanistically attractive. Restoring the function of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and L could feasibly improve the degradation of POS, a process known to be compromised in dry AMD. This dual-targeted approach (improving both enzyme activity and reducing cell stress) is particularly compelling in the context of a multifactorial disease such as AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

Despite these strengths, several potential weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. First, while extensive preclinical work has been carried out in neurological models—and there exists some early in vitro evidence of benefit in RPE cells—the direct connection between PREP activity and the inhibition of cathepsin function in the context of RPE biology remains largely hypothetical. The literature currently lacks robust in vivo studies in ocular models of dry AMD demonstrating that PREP inhibition translates into measurable improvements in retinal function and morphology. Historical clinical trials of PREP inhibitors for cognitive applications have encountered difficulties due to inconsistent efficacy, which raises concerns about the translation of in vitro findings to clinical benefits (Scuderi, 2023, pp. 133–135; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41).

Second, the formulation challenges associated with KYP-2047 cannot be overlooked. Its low water solubility necessitates specialized carriers (such as saline with 5% Tween® 80), which may complicate delivery to the eye, especially when considering the need for localized administration to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE. Appropriate ocular delivery systems (e.g., intravitreal injections or sustained-release implants) would need to be developed and optimized, which adds a layer of complexity to the overall drug development program (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47).

Another area of concern is the historical inconsistency of PREP inhibitor effects in clinical studies. Although there is evidence of neuroprotective benefits, the fact that several PREP inhibitors failed to advance through the clinical development pipeline for neurological indications suggests that the enzyme’s true physiological role remains incompletely defined. In the absence of a clear and reproducible biomarker for PREP inhibition in vivo, there is a risk that the biochemical benefits seen in cell culture studies may not be recapitulated in the complex environment of the human retina (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 70–72).

Moreover, because PREP is a ubiquitous enzyme expressed in many tissues, systemic administration of KYP-2047 might lead to off-target effects that could limit its therapeutic window. Although the safety profile observed in early neurological trials is encouraging, targeted delivery to the eye (to minimize systemic exposure) will be crucial if KYP-2047 is to be repurposed for dry AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

Finally, while the proposed mechanism that links elevated PREP activity with the inhibition of lysosomal cathepsins is intriguing, it remains to be validated by direct experimental data specifically in RPE cells. The current literature, including the recent study by Toppila and colleagues, primarily focuses on the cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory actions of KYP-2047 in ARPE-19 cells, but detailed biochemical analyses linking PREP inhibition mechanistically to improved cathepsin-mediated degradation of POS are still needed (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 4–6).

─────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

In summary, KYP-2047 is an established prolyl oligopeptidase inhibitor with a well-characterized chemical and pharmacological profile, offering promising features as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its ability to inhibit PREP at low nanomolar concentrations, coupled with demonstrated cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in preclinical RPE models, aligns well with the therapeutic need to restore lysosomal cathepsin activity and improve photoreceptor outer segment degradation in dry AMD (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 12–13).

The strategy to mitigate the accumulation of inhibitory proline-rich peptides and thereby reinstate effective lysosomal function is mechanistically plausible and supported by related studies in neural tissues. Nevertheless, the exact role of PREP in the modulation of cathepsin activity in RPE cells remains to be fully elucidated. In addition, the challenges of achieving appropriate ocular drug delivery and the historical precedents of inconsistent efficacy in PREP inhibitor clinical trials represent significant hurdles that must be addressed in future studies (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41).

Overall, while KYP-2047 brings strengths in terms of potency and a partially validated cytoprotective profile in in vitro models, its repurposing for dry AMD would require further in-depth preclinical studies. These studies should include in vivo efficacy assessments in relevant animal models of AMD, comprehensive pharmacokinetic and ocular distribution evaluations, and mechanistic experiments that clearly link PREP inhibition with improved cathepsin and lysosomal function in the RPE. Should these studies confirm the initial promising results, the favorable safety profile observed in prior neurological trials may indeed support the rapid translation of KYP-2047 into early-phase clinical testing for dry AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

In conclusion, KYP-2047 represents a promising, albeit still exploratory, approach to targeting a novel biochemical pathway in the context of dry AMD. The rationale is supported by a solid foundation of preclinical data in other disease models, yet its success in ocular repurposing will depend on overcoming formulation challenges and further clarifying the mechanistic underpinnings of its action in retinal pigment epithelial cells.

─────────────────────────────  
Strengths and Weaknesses Summary

Strengths:  
•  KYP-2047 is a potent, well-characterized PREP inhibitor with a strong synthetic and chemical development history (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4).  
•  Its low nanomolar IC₅₀ provides confidence in its biochemical efficacy, and available preclinical data indicate cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in RPE cell models (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22).  
•  The drug class has been extensively studied in neurological and cancer contexts, offering insights into its safety profile and potential mechanisms such as autophagy activation and reduced oxidative stress (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 70–72, 85–88).

SB203580 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally developed as a research tool designed to selectively target the α and β isoforms of p38 MAPK, a serine/threonine protein kinase implicated in the cellular response to oxidative and inflammatory stress. Its commercial availability (for example, via Sigma-Aldrich, Cat. No. S8307) underscores its utility as a standard pharmacological reagent in preclinical research. SB203580 is structurally characterized by a core imidazole ring fused to a pyridine moiety, and its mechanism of action involves competitive binding to the ATP‐binding pocket of p38 MAPK, effectively preventing subsequent substrate phosphorylation. This compound has been critical in delineating the role of p38 MAPK in various pathophysiological conditions, including inflammatory responses, cellular senescence, and stress‐induced cytoskeletal rearrangements, all of which are relevant to the pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration (Marin-Castaño, 2013; Roduit & Schorderet, 2008).

Historically, SB203580 has been employed predominantly as an investigative tool to dissect the molecular underpinnings of the p38 MAPK signaling cascade rather than as a therapeutic agent per se. In the context of ocular research, numerous studies have utilized SB203580 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models to elucidate the contributions of p38 MAPK to oxidative stress responses and cellular senescence—phenomena that underpin the progression of dry AMD. At the molecular level, SB203580 exerts its effects predominantly through the inhibition of p38 MAPK activity. Under normal conditions, p38 MAPK becomes activated in response to various extracellular stress signals—such as oxidative stress, UV irradiation, and pro-inflammatory cytokines—via dual phosphorylation on its Thr and Tyr residues located in the activation loop. Once activated, p38 phosphorylates several downstream targets, including Heat shock protein 27 (Hsp27), which has a pivotal role in modulating actin dynamics and cytoskeletal organization. Phosphorylated Hsp27 facilitates cytoskeletal reorganization, contributing to cell shape changes, membrane blebbing, and potentially impaired receptor recycling. SB203580 binds competitively to the ATP-binding site of p38 MAPK, thereby preventing its kinase activity and effectively blocking phosphorylation of substrates like Hsp27 (Marin-Castaño, 2013). In ARPE-19 cells exposed to oxidative stressors, SB203580’s inhibition of p38 MAPK abrogates stress-induced phosphorylation events, hence stabilizing the actin cytoskeleton and curtailing the formation of pathological cellular structures that are often seen in senescent or apoptotic cells (Roduit & Schorderet, 2008). Additionally, in models of BMP4-mediated senescence, p38 inhibition by SB203580 prevents the activation of the p53/p21Cip1/WAF1 pathway while preserving the phosphorylation state of the retinoblastoma protein (Rb), thereby contributing to the maintenance of a proliferative or quiescent—but non-senescent—cellular phenotype (Zhu et al., 2009).
