Below is a comprehensive evaluation of the prolyl oligopeptidase inhibitor KYP-2047 as a potential repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). This report is organized into several sections: an overview of the candidate, its therapeutic history, an in‐depth discussion of its mechanism of action, the expected effects in the proposed assay, and an overall evaluation that weighs its strengths and weaknesses.

─────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

KYP-2047 is a synthetic small molecule belonging to the peptidomimetic class of compounds that target the enzyme prolyl oligopeptidase (PREP), also known as prolyl endopeptidase (POP). Chemically designated as 4-phenylbutanoyl-L-prolyl-2(S)-cyanopyrrolidine, this compound was synthesized following methods established by Dr. Elina Jarho at the University of Eastern Finland (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47). Its design represents an evolution from early substrate-like inhibitors, with modifications at specific positions – including a three-carbon aliphatic chain at the P3 position instead of the more commonly used carbamate groups seen in predecessors like ZPP – thereby improving the compound’s overall potency, selectivity, and drug-like properties (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4).

Belonging to a well-known class of PREP inhibitors, KYP-2047 shares common chemical and biophysical properties with analogous peptidomimetic agents that have been primarily designed to interfere with the catalytic activity of a serine protease that cleaves proline-containing peptides. Given its low water solubility, KYP-2047 is typically formulated in saline containing 5% Tween® 80 for experimental studies, which is consistent with formulation challenges observed with many peptidomimetic drug candidates (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47). In recent years, the broader class of PREP inhibitors has been explored for a variety of indications, most notably in neurological conditions as well as in certain cancer models. The research impetus behind this class arises from the enzyme’s presumed role in peptide metabolism, where the inhibition of PREP could alter levels of bioactive peptides that participate in cellular homeostasis. Although these agents were originally developed as anti-amnesic candidates, their biological actions have been found to extend to anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

─────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

The therapeutic exploration of PREP inhibitors dates back to the 1970s when the enzyme was first implicated in the regulation of proline-containing peptides associated with memory formation and synaptic plasticity (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22). Numerous compounds in this class—including S-17092, JTP-4819, and others—were advanced into preclinical studies and even early-phase clinical trials for cognitive enhancement in neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease and senile dementia (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41, 70–72). However, despite initial encouraging in vitro and animal data, these agents failed to progress successfully past phase II clinical trials in humans, most likely due to challenges with efficacy, blood-brain barrier penetration, or the complexity of the enzyme’s in vivo function (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 70–72).

In parallel, PREP inhibitors have been evaluated for other indications. For instance, in a study involving oral squamous cell carcinoma, KYP-2047 demonstrated potent PREP inhibition in the mouse brain along with promising anti-tumor effects, highlighting the compound’s potential utility beyond central nervous system disorders (Scuderi, 2023, pp. 133–135). Furthermore, recent work has begun to explore the ocular applications of PREP inhibition. There is a suggestion in the literature that inhibition of prolyl oligopeptidase may represent “a promising pathway to prevent the progression of age-related macular degeneration” (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13). Notably, recent in vitro studies using human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells with defective proteasomal clearance have shown that KYP-2047 exhibits cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory properties, thereby indirectly supporting its potential use in dry AMD, even though no clinical trials or prior direct therapeutic applications in retinal diseases have yet been reported (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 9–11).

While the primary historical focus of PREP inhibitors has been on neurological and cognitive applications, the body of literature also contains several exploratory studies in inflammatory and cancer contexts (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Thus, even though the bulk of previous applications have not directly targeted dry AMD, the emerging evidence supporting cytoprotection and modulation of proteolytic and autophagy pathways in RPE cells provides a rationale for repurposing KYP-2047 in ocular disease states.

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

The biological target of KYP-2047 is the serine protease prolyl oligopeptidase (PREP), which is responsible for cleaving peptide bonds at the carboxyl side of internal proline residues in small peptides (typically less than ~30 amino acids) (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 22–24, 44–47). PREP is widely expressed in the central nervous system and peripheral tissues and has been implicated in multiple physiological processes including neuropeptide regulation and cell signaling. At the molecular level, the mechanism of action involves the binding of KYP-2047 to the enzyme’s active site, more specifically interacting with the catalytic serine residue. Many PREP inhibitors, including those in the class to which KYP-2047 belongs, are designed as substrate-like pseudopeptides that exploit the structure of the enzyme’s binding pockets (S1, S2, and S3) to achieve selectivity and high-affinity binding (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).

The inhibition by KYP-2047 is characterized as “tight-binding” with slow dissociation, meaning that once the inhibitor occupies the active site of PREP, it remains bound for a significant duration, thereby effectively reducing the enzyme’s catalytic turnover (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 70–72). In neurological models, inhibition of PREP has been associated with enhanced clearance of toxic protein aggregates such as alpha-synuclein, improved autophagic flux, and reduction in oxidative stress (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 85–88; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 9–11). The current therapeutic hypothesis in the context of dry AMD extrapolates these findings to retinal pigment epithelial cells.

In particular, the proposed mechanism posits that elevated PREP activity in RPE cells contributes to an accumulation of proline-rich peptides that, in turn, inhibit the activity of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and lysosomal cathepsin L. These cathepsins are critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and turnover of cellular debris. In dry AMD, defective protein clearance mechanisms, including impaired proteasomal and lysosomal function, result in the buildup of toxic deposits, such as A2E, and contribute to RPE dysfunction. By blocking PREP activity with KYP-2047 (which has an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range, reported to be approximately 30 nM), the proposed effect is to reduce the formation or accumulation of inhibitory peptides, thereby relieving the suppression on cathepsin activity. In addition, KYP-2047-mediated PREP inhibition may trigger downstream intracellular events such as autophagy activation and modulation of MAPK signaling pathways—including p38 and ERK1/2—which have been observed in other cell types and are known to reduce oxidative stress and inflammation (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 85–88).

At the biochemical level, these molecular interactions involve the inhibitor “locking in” the PREP enzyme in a conformational state that either prevents substrate access or alters the dynamics of peptide release once cleavage has occurred. Although the effects on neuropeptide levels (e.g., substance P, neurotensin) have been studied in central nervous system models—with mixed and sometimes counterintuitive outcomes (such as decreased acetylcholine levels) (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 8–16, 70–72)—the rationale for ocular repurposing rests on the idea that the same enzymatic inhibition can counteract the accumulation of cathepsin-inhibiting peptides in RPE cells. Notably, some studies have suggested that PREP inhibition can positively modulate autophagy, a process that is critical for cellular clearance mechanisms. Given that impaired autophagy is a central feature in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, a compound like KYP-2047 that both reduces toxic peptide accumulation and enhances proteolytic pathways presents an attractive, multitargeted strategy (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

The core hypothesis driving the repurposing of KYP-2047 for dry AMD is that inhibition of PREP will reduce the buildup of proline-rich peptides that otherwise impair lysosomal cathepsin activity. In RPE cells, efficient degradation of POS via phagocytosis and lysosomal function is essential for maintaining retinal homeostasis. In the setting of dry AMD, decreased cathepsin D and L activities are implicated in the inefficient clearance of cellular debris, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, ultimately causing RPE dysfunction.

In the proposed assay, RPE cells—typically the ARPE-19 cell line—will be challenged in an environment mimicking AMD pathology; for instance, by loading them with A2E and subjecting the cells to proteasomal stress. Under these conditions, the activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and L is compromised, and POS degradation is impaired. The application of KYP-2047 is expected to inhibit PREP activity with high potency, which theoretically will lead to a reduction in the concentration of peptide substrates that interfere with cathepsin enzymes (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).

The anticipated cascade of events is as follows:  
1. KYP-2047, at concentrations close to its low nanomolar IC₅₀, will effectively bind to and inhibit PREP in RPE cells.  
2. This inhibition will prevent the excessive cleavage of proline-containing peptides, thereby reducing the pool of inhibitory peptides that could otherwise bind to and decrease cathepsin D and L activities.  
3. As a consequence, the restoration of cathepsin activity is expected to improve the degradation of POS components as well as the clearance of other toxic debris, which is a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.  
4. Additionally, the compound’s reported anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects, demonstrated in ARPE-19 cells with defective proteasomal clearance, may further contribute to preserving RPE cell health by curtailing inflammatory cytokine production and oxidative stress (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 4–6).

It is also noteworthy that the mechanistic framework is further supported by the observation that PREP inhibition in other models has led to enhanced autophagy and improved clearance of aggregated proteins. In the context of AMD, effective POS degradation is not only dependent on cathepsin function but also on efficient autophagic flux. By indirectly modulating these pathways, KYP-2047 could offer dual benefits: restoration of lysosomal enzyme activity and bolstering of intracellular clearance mechanisms. Thus, the expected in vitro endpoints would likely include increased cathepsin D/L activity, elevated POS degradation (as detected by uptake assays), reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-6, IL-8, IL-1β), and diminished oxidative stress markers (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 4–6).

Moreover, the rationale includes supporting evidence from neurological and cancer research where PREP inhibition by compounds like KYP-2047 improved cell viability and reduced stress responses. Although previous clinical trials in central nervous system indications did not achieve long-term success, the safety data accrued from these studies may lower the translational barrier for ocular applications, provided that proper formulation and localized delivery (or systemic approaches with ocular distribution) can be achieved (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 4–5).

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

The evaluation of KYP-2047 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD involves weighing both its promising aspects and its uncertainties. On the positive side, KYP-2047 is a well-defined, highly potent inhibitor of PREP with an established chemical profile and a strong foundation in preclinical studies. Its synthetic origin as a peptidomimetic compound designed to bind the active site of PREP is well documented (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4), and the compound’s low nanomolar potency provides confidence that even modest drug exposures may achieve effective enzyme inhibition.

The repurposing strategy capitalizes on emerging evidence that PREP inhibitors can exert cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in RPE cells. In vitro studies conducted in ARPE-19 cells with impaired proteasomal clearance have demonstrated that KYP-2047 can reduce inflammatory cytokine production and promote cell viability (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). Given the central role of inflammation and defective lysosomal clearance in dry AMD, these findings provide a mechanistic rationale for testing KYP-2047 in this indication.

Furthermore, the proposed mechanism—whereby inhibition of PREP reduces the formation of inhibitory proline-rich peptides that suppress cathepsin activity—is mechanistically attractive. Restoring the function of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and L could feasibly improve the degradation of POS, a process known to be compromised in dry AMD. This dual-targeted approach (improving both enzyme activity and reducing cell stress) is particularly compelling in the context of a multifactorial disease such as AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

Despite these strengths, several potential weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. First, while extensive preclinical work has been carried out in neurological models—and there exists some early in vitro evidence of benefit in RPE cells—the direct connection between PREP activity and the inhibition of cathepsin function in the context of RPE biology remains largely hypothetical. The literature currently lacks robust in vivo studies in ocular models of dry AMD demonstrating that PREP inhibition translates into measurable improvements in retinal function and morphology. Historical clinical trials of PREP inhibitors for cognitive applications have encountered difficulties due to inconsistent efficacy, which raises concerns about the translation of in vitro findings to clinical benefits (Scuderi, 2023, pp. 133–135; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41).

Second, the formulation challenges associated with KYP-2047 cannot be overlooked. Its low water solubility necessitates specialized carriers (such as saline with 5% Tween® 80), which may complicate delivery to the eye, especially when considering the need for localized administration to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE. Appropriate ocular delivery systems (e.g., intravitreal injections or sustained-release implants) would need to be developed and optimized, which adds a layer of complexity to the overall drug development program (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47).

Another area of concern is the historical inconsistency of PREP inhibitor effects in clinical studies. Although there is evidence of neuroprotective benefits, the fact that several PREP inhibitors failed to advance through the clinical development pipeline for neurological indications suggests that the enzyme’s true physiological role remains incompletely defined. In the absence of a clear and reproducible biomarker for PREP inhibition in vivo, there is a risk that the biochemical benefits seen in cell culture studies may not be recapitulated in the complex environment of the human retina (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 70–72).

Moreover, because PREP is a ubiquitous enzyme expressed in many tissues, systemic administration of KYP-2047 might lead to off-target effects that could limit its therapeutic window. Although the safety profile observed in early neurological trials is encouraging, targeted delivery to the eye (to minimize systemic exposure) will be crucial if KYP-2047 is to be repurposed for dry AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

Finally, while the proposed mechanism that links elevated PREP activity with the inhibition of lysosomal cathepsins is intriguing, it remains to be validated by direct experimental data specifically in RPE cells. The current literature, including the recent study by Toppila and colleagues, primarily focuses on the cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory actions of KYP-2047 in ARPE-19 cells, but detailed biochemical analyses linking PREP inhibition mechanistically to improved cathepsin-mediated degradation of POS are still needed (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 4–6).

─────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

In summary, KYP-2047 is an established prolyl oligopeptidase inhibitor with a well-characterized chemical and pharmacological profile, offering promising features as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its ability to inhibit PREP at low nanomolar concentrations, coupled with demonstrated cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in preclinical RPE models, aligns well with the therapeutic need to restore lysosomal cathepsin activity and improve photoreceptor outer segment degradation in dry AMD (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 12–13).

The strategy to mitigate the accumulation of inhibitory proline-rich peptides and thereby reinstate effective lysosomal function is mechanistically plausible and supported by related studies in neural tissues. Nevertheless, the exact role of PREP in the modulation of cathepsin activity in RPE cells remains to be fully elucidated. In addition, the challenges of achieving appropriate ocular drug delivery and the historical precedents of inconsistent efficacy in PREP inhibitor clinical trials represent significant hurdles that must be addressed in future studies (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41).

Overall, while KYP-2047 brings strengths in terms of potency and a partially validated cytoprotective profile in in vitro models, its repurposing for dry AMD would require further in-depth preclinical studies. These studies should include in vivo efficacy assessments in relevant animal models of AMD, comprehensive pharmacokinetic and ocular distribution evaluations, and mechanistic experiments that clearly link PREP inhibition with improved cathepsin and lysosomal function in the RPE. Should these studies confirm the initial promising results, the favorable safety profile observed in prior neurological trials may indeed support the rapid translation of KYP-2047 into early-phase clinical testing for dry AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

In conclusion, KYP-2047 represents a promising, albeit still exploratory, approach to targeting a novel biochemical pathway in the context of dry AMD. The rationale is supported by a solid foundation of preclinical data in other disease models, yet its success in ocular repurposing will depend on overcoming formulation challenges and further clarifying the mechanistic underpinnings of its action in retinal pigment epithelial cells.

─────────────────────────────  
Strengths and Weaknesses Summary

Strengths:  
•  KYP-2047 is a potent, well-characterized PREP inhibitor with a strong synthetic and chemical development history (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4).  
•  Its low nanomolar IC₅₀ provides confidence in its biochemical efficacy, and available preclinical data indicate cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in RPE cell models (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22).  
•  The drug class has been extensively studied in neurological and cancer contexts, offering insights into its safety profile and potential mechanisms such as autophagy activation and reduced oxidative stress (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 70–72, 85–88).  
•  The hypothesis that PREP activity leads to the accumulation of cathepsin-inhibiting peptides is mechanistically plausible, which could lead to restoration of lysosomal enzyme activity in RPE cells (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).  

Weaknesses:  
•  Historically, PREP inhibitors have shown inconsistent efficacy in clinical trials for neurological applications; it remains uncertain whether the benefits will translate to the ocular setting (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 39–41).  
•  Direct evidence linking PREP inhibition with improvements in cathepsin activity and POS degradation in RPE cells is still limited, and further mechanistic studies are required (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
•  The low aqueous solubility of KYP-2047 necessitates complex formulations, which might complicate ocular drug delivery and could require novel delivery systems to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47).  
•  Systemic safety and potential off-target effects remain a concern, given that PREP is widely expressed and the compound’s systemic clearance and ocular bioavailability have yet to be thoroughly characterized in vivo (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

─────────────────────────────  
Final Remarks

Based on the current literature and the data available, KYP-2047 exhibits several attractive features for repurposing in dry AMD, especially regarding its potential to restore lysosomal function in the RPE by reducing the inhibitory load on cathepsins. However, while the biochemical rationale is compelling and early in vitro data are promising, significant challenges remain. Translational steps such as in vivo efficacy verification in AMD models, optimization of ocular formulation, and further elucidation of the mechanistic pathway are essential before proceeding to clinical development. Thus, KYP-2047 warrants further preclinical evaluation with a specific focus on its ocular pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics, which will ultimately determine its viability as a novel therapeutic candidate against dry age-related macular degeneration (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

This comprehensive review supports the notion that repurposing KYP-2047 for dry AMD is a promising strategy, but caution must be exercised given the prior challenges encountered with the PREP inhibitor class in other indications. Future studies should be designed to address these gaps and de-risk the development plan before large-scale clinical trials are considered.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab is a recombinant, humanized monoclonal IgG kappa antibody that specifically binds complement component C5 and prevents its proteolytic activation into C5a and C5b, thereby blocking terminal pathway activity and membrane attack complex (MAC; C5b-9) assembly while leaving upstream C3-dependent functions largely intact (for example, opsonization and immune-complex handling) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; West et al., 2024). It was discovered by screening large panels of murine anti-human C5 monoclonals for potent inhibition of C5 activation and terminal complement–mediated hemolysis; the parental murine antibody (5G1.1) was then humanized by CDR grafting into human germline frameworks and engineered to use a hybrid IgG2/IgG4 heavy-chain constant region to minimize Fcγ receptor binding and classical-pathway activation (reducing effector functions that could confound terminal pathway blockade) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009). Eculizumab binds human C5 with very high affinity (Kd approximately 120 pM) and sterically prevents convertase engagement with the MG7 domain of C5; epitope mapping identifies residues in the MG7 domain (including the KSSKC motif around Arg885) critical for binding, and Arg885His/Cys polymorphisms have been linked to clinical non-responsiveness in some patients, consistent with the structural epitope (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

As a drug class, complement inhibitors have been deployed to treat diseases driven by complement dysregulation, with C5 blockade representing a terminal-pathway strategy that ablates C5a signaling and MAC-mediated cytolysis while preserving many proximal complement functions; eculizumab was the first complement inhibitor approved for clinical use and catalyzed broad clinical development of C5, C3, and alternative pathway–targeted agents across hematology, nephrology, neurology, and, more recently, ophthalmology (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Eculizumab is administered intravenously, exhibits a long serum half-life (~272 ± 82 hours), a limited volume of distribution consistent with an intravascularly confined antibody, and shows pharmacodynamic correlation between serum trough concentrations and blockade of hemolytic activity; vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis is required due to increased susceptibility when terminal complement is inhibited (Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Within ophthalmology, complement activation products and MAC deposition have been implicated in AMD pathogenesis, motivating clinical trials of complement inhibitors including C5-directed agents; eculizumab has been formally evaluated in a randomized phase 2 setting for non-exudative AMD (geographic atrophy and drusen cohorts) via systemic administration (Kassa et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Halawa et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
Eculizumab has an extensive clinical record in systemic complement-mediated disorders. It revolutionized therapy for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), where it reduces intravascular hemolysis, decreases transfusion requirements, and improves quality of life; it is also approved for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and for neurologic autoimmune indications including anti–acetylcholine receptor–positive generalized myasthenia gravis and aquaporin-4–positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Early clinical pharmacology in PNH demonstrated that an induction regimen of 600 mg weekly for four weeks followed by 900 mg every other week maintained near-complete terminal pathway blockade and significantly reduced hemolysis and transfusion needs; these dosing principles align with its long half-life and the concentration dependence of hemolytic inhibition (Hillmen et al., 2004; Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012). Despite robust control of intravascular hemolysis, residual extravascular hemolysis can persist because C3 opsonization is not prevented by C5 inhibition, illustrating an important mechanistic limitation of terminal-pathway agents (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; West et al., 2024).

The drug’s safety profile is dominated by infection risk with encapsulated organisms—particularly meningococcal disease—necessitating vaccination; otherwise, eculizumab has shown acceptable tolerability across long-term use, with clinical programs incorporating monitoring of functional complement activity (CH50) to confirm pharmacodynamic blockade and dose adequacy (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009; Eskandary et al., 2016). Mechanistically relevant sources also report pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic complexities: high-affinity binding at acidic endosomal pH encourages recycling of eculizumab:C5 complexes by FcRn, leading to accumulation of total C5 bound to the drug in circulation; next-generation engineering in ravulizumab introduced pH-dependent release to minimize cargo recycling and extend dosing intervals (Schmidt & Smith, 2023).

In ophthalmology, eculizumab has been investigated as a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD. The COMPLETE study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), a single-center, randomized, double-masked phase 2 trial, evaluated intravenous eculizumab in two cohorts: geographic atrophy (GA) and intermediate AMD with high-risk drusen; patients were randomized 2:1 to eculizumab or saline over 24 weeks with follow-up to 52 weeks (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the GA cohort (n = 30 study eyes), eculizumab did not reduce GA enlargement versus placebo at 26 or 52 weeks (square-root–transformed growth 0.19 ± 0.12 mm vs. 0.18 ± 0.15 mm at 26 weeks, P = 0.96; 0.37 ± 0.22 mm vs. 0.37 ± 0.21 mm at 52 weeks, P = 0.93), and no drug-related adverse events were reported (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the drusen cohort (n = 30 total participants; 20 active, 10 placebo), eculizumab failed to meet the prespecified primary endpoint of a ≥ 50% reduction in drusen cube-root volume at 26 weeks; none of 18 treated eyes achieved this threshold, while one placebo eye did (10%; P = 0.36), and there was no detectable difference in mean drusen growth between arms through 26–52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014). Trial conduct included meningococcal vaccination and careful multimodal imaging; retention was high with 28/30 completing 52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). Independent evidence syntheses judged the certainty of evidence as low to very low due to small sample size, imprecision, and some risk of bias; overall, systemic eculizumab “may have made little to no difference” in BCVA and GA lesion growth in the available cohort (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistically similar C5-directed agents have not shown positive phase 2 outcomes in GA when administered systemically or intravitreally (e.g., LFG316 failed in phase 2), whereas intravitreal C5 inhibition with avacincaptad pegol progressed to later-phase testing and regulatory review, suggesting that drug, route, and pharmacology may be important determinants of outcome; by contrast, intravitreal C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) demonstrated efficacy and has been approved for GA, underscoring the translational relevance of target selection and ocular delivery (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024). Multiple reviews conclude that systemic eculizumab is no longer in development for AMD and highlight delivery and mechanistic concerns as likely contributors to the negative results (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, eculizumab targets the MG7 domain of C5 and sterically prevents formation of the C5 convertase–substrate complex, thereby inhibiting the cleavage of C5 into the potent anaphylatoxin C5a and C5b, which nucleates membrane attack complex assembly with C6–C9 (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Rother et al., 2007). Structural analysis of an eculizumab Fab bound to C5 resolved at 4.2 Å shows that five CDRs form the principal interface with MG7; mutational scanning of CDR residues identifies a network of contacts necessary for high-affinity binding, and kinetic assays confirm that these interactions prevent complement-mediated hemolysis in vitro (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016). The epitope includes residues near Arg885, and clinical resistance due to Arg885His/Cys substitutions in C5 provides orthogonal validation of the binding site (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

Pharmacodynamically, eculizumab ablates terminal pathway function: it suppresses CH50 to near zero when trough serum concentrations exceed ~35 μg/mL; however, because proximal C3 activation continues, C3b deposition and downstream opsonins accumulate on surfaces, which can drive extravascular clearance and generate residual pathology even under complete C5 blockade in appropriate disease contexts (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). Additional mechanisms can undermine complete terminal pathway control: (1) during intense proximal activation, densely opsonized surfaces can support C5 activation by convertases in ways that partially bypass classical C5 convertase assembly or even promote conformational C5 activation on surface C3b clusters; such context-dependent activation can manifest as “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” despite apparently adequate free drug levels, and has been reported in clinical settings as residual terminal-pathway activity and elevated sC5b-9 in some patients (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). (2) Eculizumab binds C5 with high affinity at both neutral and mildly acidic pH, allowing FcRn to recycle eculizumab:C5 complexes and potentially alter antigen disposition; ravulizumab’s pH-dependent binding was engineered to release C5 in endosomes and improve pharmacokinetics by avoiding cargo recycling (Schmidt & Smith, 2023). These features are germane to dose selection, monitoring, and potential resistance or escape during strong complement activation.

Rationale for C5 inhibition in AMD rests on abundant mechanistic and histopathological evidence that C5-derived effectors and MAC participate in retinal/choroidal injury. C5a is detected in drusen and acts as a chemotactic and proinflammatory mediator capable of inducing VEGF expression from retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, while C5b initiates MAC assembly; MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris increases with aging and is elevated in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019). Sub-lytic and lytic MAC on choroidal endothelium causes cell injury and can trigger surviving endothelial cells to upregulate VEGF and matrix metalloproteinases, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic injury and pro-angiogenic remodeling; complement regulatory proteins such as CD59 are natural inhibitors of MAC formation and their dysfunction or insufficiency can predispose to damage (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2021). Complement dysregulation in AMD further includes genetic risk (e.g., CFH variants) and evidence of alternative pathway activation in ocular tissues, suggesting both proximal and terminal effector involvement in disease biology (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Importantly, proximal inhibition at C3 has shown the capacity to restore lysosomal function and reduce sub-RPE drusen-like deposits in human iPSC-derived RPE models carrying the high-risk CFH Y402H variant by reducing C3 turnover and lowering downstream MAC (C5b-9) localization at lysosomes; in this system, a compstatin analogue (Cp40) suppressed C3b and MAC deposition and reversed lysosomal abnormalities, whereas direct C5 inhibition has not been shown in this model to rescue lysosomal function, and clinical C5 blockade has failed in GA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). These data reinforce that while terminal pathway effectors are present and likely pathogenic in AMD, distal blockade at C5 does not necessarily address upstream complement turnover that drives intracellular lysosomal stress in RPE, and proximal intervention may be required to normalize cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
The hypothesis proposes that high-affinity C5 blockade with eculizumab will prevent MAC assembly on RPE, thereby reducing sub-RPE deposit–driven lysosomal stress and indirectly supporting photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis in dry AMD. Mechanistically, preventing C5 cleavage would abrogate both C5a signaling and C5b-dependent MAC formation; given the documented presence of C5a in drusen and increased MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane/choriocapillaris with age and AMD, terminal pathway inhibition is expected to reduce MAC-mediated endothelial and RPE injury, dampen MAC-induced VEGF/MMP signaling, and potentially mitigate inflammation (Kassa et al., 2019). In principle, if MAC-driven lysosomal injury contributes to RPE dysfunction, C5 inhibition could reduce new MAC deposition at the RPE surface and limit subsequent endocytosis of MAC into lysosomes, thereby lowering lysosomal burden (Park et al., 2021).

However, two key bodies of evidence temper this expectation. First, clinical testing of systemic eculizumab in GA and intermediate AMD failed to show benefit on primary anatomical endpoints (GA growth and OCT drusen volume) through 26–52 weeks, despite established systemic pharmacodynamic blockade; these negative outcomes argue that either (a) terminal pathway activity at C5 is not the principal driver of lesion growth/drusen regression during the studied disease stages/time horizon, or (b) pharmacokinetic compartmentalization limited ocular target engagement after intravenous dosing (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Filho et al., 2014). Reviews explicitly highlight the compartment barrier problem—systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina or sub-RPE space due to the blood–retina/Bruch’s membrane barriers and large molecular size—and note that eculizumab exposure shorter than six months is unlikely to show benefit in slowly progressive GA, compounding interpretation (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Second, cellular models directly linking complement dysregulation to lysosomal failure in high-risk AMD RPE show that upstream C3 inhibition, not terminal C5 blockade, restores lysosomal function and reduces deposit formation; this suggests that intralysosomal stress is driven by continuous C3 turnover and opsonization rather than MAC alone, and that distal C5 blockade may be insufficient to normalize these processes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Consequently, POS phagocytosis metrics may improve only marginally or not at all if the dominant insult is proximal complement turnover rather than MAC-mediated damage. The clinical failure to slow GA growth or reduce drusen volume with systemic eculizumab supports the inference that target engagement at C5, via the tested route and schedule, did not translate into macroscopic anatomical benefit in human AMD eyes within one year (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).

If eculizumab were to be tested in vitro on human RPE, appropriate readouts would include: surface and intracellular MAC (C5b-9) quantification, lysosomal number/size and membrane integrity (e.g., LAMP2, Galectin-8), Cathepsin D activity, autophagic flux, and POS degradation kinetics; concomitant measurement of upstream C3b/iC3b/C3d deposition would be essential to interpret whether C5 inhibition is affecting the dominant pathogenic pathway in the assay (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In vivo, ocular pharmacokinetic considerations dominate: intravitreal administration delivers drug to the retina and sub-RPE space but is not reported for eculizumab in the provided context and would carry different safety and dosing constraints; systemic dosing faces blood–retina barrier limitations that likely constrained ocular target engagement in COMPLETE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Notably, nearly all complement inhibitors that have shown anatomical effects in GA have been delivered intravitreally, underscoring the importance of route of administration for ocular diseases (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic rationale: C5a and MAC are present in AMD-relevant tissues; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD and can drive endothelial injury, VEGF/MMP upregulation, and potentially RPE dysfunction; blocking C5 should diminish these terminal effector signals (Kassa et al., 2019; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Potent, well-characterized biologic: Eculizumab binds human C5 with picomolar affinity, has a well-defined structural epitope in the MG7 domain, and reliably ablates terminal pathway function systemically with a large clinical safety database outside ophthalmology (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
- Clinical feasibility and tolerability: In AMD trials, intravenous eculizumab was well tolerated without drug-related adverse events and with no clear signal for increased neovascular conversion or ocular infection within one year, supporting general safety of systemic C5 blockade in this population under vaccination protocols (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Negative clinical efficacy in AMD: The randomized phase 2 COMPLETE trial showed no reduction in GA growth and no meaningful reduction in drusen volume through 26–52 weeks; certainty is limited by small sample size but confidence intervals and replication across endpoints argue against a large treatment effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).  
- Compartmentalization barriers for systemic dosing: Blood–retina and Bruch’s membrane barriers likely limit ocular exposure to intravenously administered eculizumab; multiple reviews cite inadequate ocular penetration as a plausible reason for failure, and systemic eculizumab is no longer being pursued in AMD (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
- Target selection may be too distal for RPE lysosomal rescue: Human iPSC-RPE data indicate that complement-driven lysosomal pathology and drusen-like deposits are reversed by C3 inhibition, with concomitant reduction of downstream MAC, while C5 blockade alone has not been shown to restore lysosomal metrics and did not slow GA clinically; this suggests that proximal complement turnover is the dominant driver of RPE lysosomal stress (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Mechanistic escape and incomplete terminal control: Under strong activation, C5 can be activated on dense C3b clusters with features of convertase bypass or conformational priming; stoichiometric C5 inhibitors can form long-lived C5:antibody complexes on surfaces, potentially allowing residual terminal activity, and clinical “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” has been documented (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
- Genetic and biochemical determinants of response: C5 polymorphisms (e.g., R885H/C) can abolish binding and confer resistance; while prevalence in AMD populations is unknown here, such variants are important risk factors for nonresponse (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).  
- Safety/logistics: Terminal complement blockade mandates meningococcal vaccination and vigilance for invasive infections; while acceptable systemically in selected diseases, risk–benefit in a chronic, slowly progressive ocular disorder is less favorable, and the cost and infusion burden are high (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Contextualization with alternative complement strategies  
- C5 vs C3: Clinical success in GA has emerged at the level of C3 (pegcetacoplan), consistent with cellular data showing rescue of lysosomal function by upstream blockade; by contrast, systemic C5 inhibition with eculizumab and other C5-directed agents failed to meet GA endpoints in early trials, and LFG316 also did not demonstrate efficacy in GA (West et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Route of administration: Most agents demonstrating anatomical effects in GA are delivered intravitreally; eculizumab’s large size and systemic administration likely limited ocular penetration in COMPLETE, and no intravitreal eculizumab data are provided here to support local delivery (Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
- Risk of adverse ocular remodeling: Complement modulation has complex, context-dependent effects; in some models, complement inhibition or modulation can alter macrophage polarization and influence CNV formation, underscoring that indiscriminate or poorly targeted complement blockade could have unintended consequences; while the eculizumab AMD trials did not show a neovascular signal, vigilance is warranted when selecting targets and doses (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2021).

Decision Implications  
- As a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD, eculizumab has a low probability of success based on randomized clinical evidence, pharmacokinetic compartment limitations, and mechanistic considerations indicating that distal C5 blockade may not correct the proximal complement turnover driving RPE lysosomal pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- If C5 remains a target of interest, local ocular delivery and alternative molecular formats designed for intravitreal pharmacokinetics (e.g., smaller C5-binding entities, RNAi to intraocular C5 production, or intravitreal C5 inhibitors such as avacincaptad pegol) are more plausible routes; indeed, avacincaptad has advanced in GA, while systemic eculizumab has been discontinued in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019; Nadeem et al., 2023; West et al., 2024).  
- For assays aimed at lysosomal stress and POS phagocytosis, prioritizing proximal complement inhibitors (e.g., C3-targeting) is more aligned with human RPE data and recent clinical experience, whereas C5 inhibition alone is unlikely to fully normalize lysosomal function or confer robust structural benefit (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; West et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
Eculizumab provides a clear mechanistic means to extinguish terminal complement effectors implicated in AMD biology, but the totality of evidence—negative randomized clinical data in GA and drusen, route-of-administration barriers to ocular exposure, mechanistic escape during high activation, and cellular evidence favoring proximal over distal inhibition for lysosomal rescue—argues against further development of systemic eculizumab for dry AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The program should be deprioritized in favor of intraocularly suited agents and proximal complement targets, unless a compelling, testable strategy emerges to achieve effective intraocular C5 blockade with eculizumab (which is not supported by the present context) (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistic Appendix: Biochemical and Pathobiologic Evidence Relevant to the Hypothesis  
- Complement activation and terminal effectors in AMD:  
  - C5a is present in drusen and induces VEGF from RPE; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD; MAC induces endothelial lysis and sub-lytic survival signaling that upregulates VEGF and MMPs (Kassa et al., 2019).  
  - Alternative pathway dysregulation is central in AMD; genetic and experimental data implicate factor H and alternative pathway components in AMD and CNV models; inhibition of C3a, C5a, CFB, MAC or supplementation with CD59/CFH blocks CNV in animals (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Eculizumab structure–function:  
  - Epitope on MG7 with steric convertase blockade; high-affinity binding and resistance polymorphisms at Arg885; CDR function validated by mutational scans (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
  - PK/PD: long half-life, vascular distribution, CH50 suppression threshold, FcRn recycling of C5:eculizumab complexes; ravulizumab engineering to improve recycling and dosing (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB 290157 (N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine) is a synthetic, low–molecular-weight, nonpeptide ligand originally discovered in a SmithKline Beecham high-throughput radioligand displacement screen (~240,000 compounds) for inhibitors of human C3a binding to membranes from RBL-2H3 cells stably expressing C3aR; subsequent medicinal chemistry optimization of the initial hit (SKF 63649) yielded SB 290157 with markedly improved potency and cross-species activity at C3aR (human, mouse, guinea pig) (Ames et al., 2001). The compound is typically supplied as a trifluoroacetate salt by commercial vendors and has been used extensively as a pharmacological tool compound in vitro and in vivo, including ocular and non-ocular models (Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Chemically, SB 290157 is an arginine derivative bearing a 2,2-diphenylethoxyacetyl N2-acyl substituent; synthetic steps reported by the discovery group used Fmoc/Boc protection of arginine on Wang resin, coupling of tert-butyl(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetate via carbodiimide/DMAP, and final deprotection with TFA to give the target amide (Ames et al., 2001). In the original pharmacological characterization, SB 290157 behaved as a competitive C3aR antagonist in radioligand binding and functional assays in recombinant cells and primary neutrophils, with reported low-nanomolar functional potency in Ca2+-mobilization and platelet ATP-release assays; selectivity was claimed versus C5aR and other neutrophil chemoattractant GPCRs in those systems (Ames et al., 2001). The class of nonpeptide C3aR-directed small molecules has been pursued largely as research tools and preclinical probes of anaphylatoxin biology; SB 290157 is the prototypical representative and has been used across diverse inflammatory models to interrogate complement C3a–C3aR signaling (Ames et al., 2001).

Therapeutic History  
- Foundational pharmacology and in vivo anti-inflammatory activity: SB 290157 was reported in 2001 to inhibit C3a-induced responses in multiple cell systems and to reduce inflammation in rodent models, including decreased neutrophil accumulation in a guinea pig LPS-induced airway neutrophilia model and attenuation of paw edema in a rat adjuvant-induced arthritis (AIA) model when dosed intraperitoneally twice daily (b.i.d.) at up to 30 mg/kg (Ames et al., 2001). Pharmacokinetics in guinea pigs after a single 30 mg/kg i.p. dose showed high Cmax (~7000 ng/ml), sustained plasma levels (>100 ng/ml at 8 h), and a short apparent half-life (~0.9 h) (Ames et al., 2001). In ex vivo vascular assays, SB 290157 blocked C3a-induced increases in perfused rat caudal artery pressure and prevented receptor internalization in neutrophils, supporting functional antagonism in those readouts (Ames et al., 2001).  
- Ocular/retinal relevance: In an in vitro human fetal retinal pigment epithelium (hfRPE) transwell model, chronic recombinant human C3a exposure for two weeks drove sub-RPE extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation and wide-spaced collagen deposition, which were prevented by co-treatment with SB 290157 at 10 µM (trifluoroacetate salt); the antagonist did not impair transepithelial resistance or monolayer morphology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Mechanistically in the same hfRPE system, C3a impaired ubiquitin–proteasome pathway (UPP) activity and selectively elevated basal MMP-2 activity without changing proteasome-subunit mRNA, while promoting deposition of collagens IV and VI; these C3a-driven effects were reported to be abrogated by a C3aR antagonist, consistent with C3aR-mediated pathology in RPE (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In vivo, SB 290157 was used in a laser-induced retinal vein occlusion (RVO) mouse model where pharmacologic blockade of C3a/C3aR reduced fluorescein leakage, retinal thickness abnormalities, disorganization of inner retinal layers (DRIL), and serous detachment height, improved ERG b-wave and oscillatory potentials, and suppressed inflammatory gene programs (DEGs enriched for chemokine/NF-κB/IL-17 pathways); the authors explicitly note known pharmacological limitations of SB 290157 including potential off-target and agonist actions (Zhao et al., 2025). Genetic evidence relevant to ocular disease includes partial protection in light-damage models: global C3aR deletion decelerated retinal thinning after light insult, although photoreceptor apoptosis levels (TUNEL) were not significantly altered, suggesting C3aR contributes to retinal structural change but not necessarily acute photoreceptor death in that model (Behnke et al., 2025).  
- Broader in vivo applications and cautions: SB 290157 has been used to probe complement biology in diverse indications, with reported benefits in models of lupus nephritis, antibody-induced arthritis, thromboembolic stroke, and AD-related cognition; however, many of these reports predate or did not control for later-recognized pharmacology (partial agonism, off-targets), which complicates interpretation (Li et al., 2021; Coulthard & Woodruff, 2015). In a mouse cuprizone demyelination model, intraperitoneal SB 290157 at 1 mg/kg every other day modulated astrocyte reactivity (GFAP), TNF-α dynamics, and complement deposition (C3d), with the dosing choice explicitly motivated to minimize off-target C5aR engagement; nevertheless, the authors caution about SB 290157’s weak C5aR agonism and interpretability of systemic dosing (Frankle, 2023). In neuropathic pain (spared nerve injury), SB 290157 acutely reversed mechanical hypersensitivity but is limited by a short half-life (~1.5 h) and known off-target/agonist properties (Cook, 2019).  
- Pharmacological controversies and off-target receptor activity: Soon after its introduction, independent groups reported that SB 290157 exhibits C3aR agonist/partial-agonist activity in multiple cell systems, with potency dependent on receptor density and assay context; examples include near-maximal Ca2+ mobilization in transfected RBL cells, NAG release in differentiated U-937 cells, and ATP release in guinea pig platelets, whereas it appeared antagonistic in other systems (e.g., guinea pig platelets with very low receptor expression) (Mathieu et al., 2005). More recently, SB 290157 was shown to be a partial agonist at C5aR2 (β-arrestin recruitment EC50 ~16 µM; partial efficacy vs C5a) and to dampen C5a-induced ERK signaling in macrophages, introducing a mechanistically plausible anti-inflammatory off-target pathway at commonly used concentrations (Li et al., 2021). Practical dosing analyses indicate that in vivo exposures at commonly used doses (>10 mg/kg i.p. or >0.3 mg/kg i.v.) will engage both C3aR and C5aR2, and high-dose use has been associated with adverse effects in animals (neutropenia, transient hypertension, weight gain, hematopoietic effects, tachycardia) (Li et al., 2021). Finally, modern C3aR signaling work demonstrates SB 290157 is a potent C3aR agonist that drives Gi/o/z activation and strong β-arrestin–dependent internalization, which can masquerade as “antagonism” in Ca2+ flux assays by depleting surface receptors and calcium stores; this β-arrestin–driven internalization explains many prior contradictory results (Rodriguez et al., 2024).  

Importantly, no published animal model of drusen or geographic atrophy using SB 290157 is identified in the provided context; evidence for drusen/sub-RPE deposit modulation by SB 290157 is restricted to in vitro hfRPE systems, while in vivo ocular use has been reported in RVO, which is a vascular occlusive disease and mechanistically distinct from dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Zhao et al., 2025).  

Mechanism of Action  
- Target and signaling context: C3aR (C3aR1) is a class A GPCR canonically activated by the complement anaphylatoxin C3a; it couples preferentially to Gi/o/z to inhibit cAMP, mobilize Ca2+, and recruit β-arrestins to mediate receptor internalization and signaling bias, with expression across immune and stromal cells, including microglia/macrophages, neutrophils, mast cells, and ocular cells (Müller cells, microglia, macrophages, vascular endothelium), and on human RPE in vitro (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). C3a/C3aR signaling has been implicated in RPE dysfunction and retinal pathologies through both pro-inflammatory outputs (e.g., VEGF upregulation, leukocyte recruitment) and tissue remodeling (ECM deposition) (Kleinman & Ambati, 2016; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- SB 290157 at C3aR: Original reports characterized SB 290157 as a competitive C3aR antagonist in binding and functional assays, demonstrating inhibition of C3a-induced Ca2+ mobilization (IC50 ~27.7 nM in human RBL-C3aR cells; low-nanomolar potency across species) and blockade of receptor internalization and smooth muscle contractile responses (Ames et al., 2001). Later work showed that SB 290157 can behave as a partial/full agonist in multiple expression systems, with potency strongly influenced by receptor density; in overexpression models (CHO-C3aR), SB 290157 induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation with an EC50 ~0.46 nM and near-maximal efficacy relative to C3a, while in some primary systems (e.g., HMDMs) it did not exhibit agonism up to 100 µM yet inhibited C3a-induced ERK with an IC50 ~236 nM (Li et al., 2021). Orthogonal signaling profiling confirmed that SB 290157 is a potent C3aR agonist across Gi/o/z subtypes and is highly efficacious at β-arrestin recruitment/internalization; antagonism observed in Ca2+ assays can arise from this strong internalization blocking subsequent G-protein signaling (effects unmasked by barbadin or Pitstop-2), i.e., SB 290157 acts as a biased agonist with dominant β-arrestin/internalization bias in many contexts (Rodriguez et al., 2024).  
- SB 290157 at other complement receptors: Counter-screening revealed no activation of C5aR1 in the tested ERK readout, but consistent partial agonism at C5aR2 (β-arrestin2 recruitment EC50 ~16.1 µM; ~31% efficacy vs C5a), with functional consequences including attenuation of C5a-induced ERK signaling in human and mouse macrophages; thus, SB 290157 can engage anti-inflammatory C5aR2 pathways at micromolar concentrations (Li et al., 2021). Importantly, in vivo exposures at common doses are predicted to co-engage both C3aR and C5aR2, complicating mechanistic attribution (Li et al., 2021).  
- RPE-specific pathomechanisms and C3aR blockade: In primary hfRPE, C3a binds basolateral C3aR and triggers a cascade leading to sub-RPE ECM accumulation: (i) decreased proteasome (UPP) activity without changes in proteasome-subunit mRNA, indicating post-transcriptional downregulation; (ii) dysregulation of ECM turnover via increased basal MMP-2 activity and reduced TIMP-3 (markedly reduced TIMP-3 with proteasome inhibitor MG-132), consistent with enhanced collagenase activity; and (iii) increased deposition of collagen IV and VI beneath the RPE monolayer (dose- and time-dependent), without changes in collagen I or EFEMP1 (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). C3a exposure increased C3aR expression/localization on RPE basolateral membranes, while a C3aR antagonist prevented the C3a-driven proteasome impairment, MMP-2 elevation, and accumulation of basal deposits in this model (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Notably, C3a did not acutely alter intracellular calcium in these RPE cultures, suggesting RPE-specific signaling architecture differs from classic immune cell paradigms; the antagonist’s protective effects in RPE thus map to UPP/ECM modulation rather than Ca2+-dependent degranulation (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- Potency considerations: Reported SB 290157 binding affinity to C3aR is in the low-hundreds of nanomolar range (competition IC50 ~500 ± 250 nM; Ki ~210 ± 90 nM in membrane binding), whereas functional potencies span 7–30 nM in many GPCR Ca2+ or platelet assays; in HMDMs, C3a-ERK inhibition IC50 ~236 nM has been reported, and in hfRPE studies the antagonist was used at 10 µM without a defined IC50 in that context (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001; Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). These disparities emphasize system-specific pharmacodynamics and the need for concentration–response characterization in RPE.  

Expected Effect  
The proposed hypothesis is that SB 290157 will competitively inhibit C3aR on RPE (IC50 ~500 nM), thereby preventing C3a-driven proteasome dysregulation and sub-RPE deposit formation, restoring proteostasis and improving photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake and degradation in dry AMD RPE cultures. Available data from the hfRPE system strongly support the first two mechanistic links—C3a promotes basal deposit formation via UPP inhibition and MMP-2/TIMP-3 imbalance, and C3aR blockade with SB 290157 (10 µM) prevents those ECM/proteostasis changes and associated sub-RPE deposit formation without damaging the RPE monolayer (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Specifically, in multi-week C3a exposures, antagonist co-treatment normalized ECM ultrastructure (SEM/TEM), blocked accumulation of collagens IV and VI beneath the RPE, prevented C3a-induced upregulation of C3aR expression, and preserved proteasome functional readouts, which together map to restoration of RPE proteostasis and ECM turnover in this model (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). These observations are consistent with the broader mechanistic framework that C3a–C3aR signaling at RPE can drive early AMD-like basal deposit formation and that C3aR antagonism can reverse the key biochemical drivers (UPP impairment and MMP-2/TIMP-3 dysregulation) underlying deposit accumulation (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
However, the “IC50 ~500 nM” statement matches binding competition in recombinant systems rather than functional antagonism in RPE; hfRPE studies used 10 µM without a reported potency or binding occupancy analysis in this cell type, and inhibitory potencies vary substantially across cell systems (7–30 nM in Ca2+ mobilization and platelet ATP-release assays, ~236 nM for ERK blockade in HMDMs) (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001; Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). For the intended RPE assay, an empirical concentration–response curve is needed to establish the minimal effective concentration that prevents C3a-driven UPP and ECM changes, ideally bracketed below concentrations known to partially activate C5aR2 to avoid confounded anti-inflammatory signaling (Li et al., 2021). The claim that SB 290157 will improve POS uptake/degradation is not supported by the provided literature; neither the hfRPE work nor the broader SB 290157 pharmacology summarizes RPE phagocytosis or POS processing endpoints, and the signaling work documenting SB 290157 effects on phagocytosis pertains to microglia, not RPE (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Thus, while restoration of proteasome function may secondarily benefit proteostasis pathways relevant to POS degradation, this remains to be demonstrated in RPE and should be considered an untested hypothesis rather than an evidence-based expectation at this time (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
Expression of the pharmacological target in the assay system is established in vitro: C3aR is present on hfRPE basolateral membranes, is upregulated by C3a challenge, and mediates the proteasome/ECM phenotypes that are reversed by antagonist co-treatment (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Complement-responsive cell types within the retina (e.g., Müller cells, microglia, macrophages, vascular endothelium) also express C3aR, providing mechanistic plausibility for in vivo effects of C3aR blockade in retinal disease models, although RVO pathobiology differs fundamentally from dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2025).  

Overall Evaluation  
SB 290157 engages a biologically compelling axis (C3a–C3aR) with direct mechanistic links to early dry AMD pathogenesis in RPE, but its complex and context-dependent pharmacology imposes significant risks for both interpretation and translational development. The totality of evidence supports continued use of C3aR antagonism as a mechanistic strategy in RPE, while casting doubt on SB 290157 as a development-grade candidate without substantial de-risking.  

Strengths  
- Disease-mechanism alignment in RPE: Chronic C3a exposure in hfRPE is sufficient to recapitulate sub-RPE ECM changes typical of early AMD (collagen IV/VI deposition, wide-spaced collagen, impaired UPP, elevated basal MMP-2), and C3aR antagonism with SB 290157 prevents these changes with preservation of barrier integrity, directly linking the pharmacological target to a core pathophysiology in dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). This is among the strongest mechanistic anchors for any complement-modulatory strategy specifically at the RPE level in vitro.  
- Ocular in vivo proof-of-concept for C3aR blockade: In an RVO model (distinct from dry AMD), SB 290157 reduced clinical, imaging, and functional pathology and dampened retinal inflammatory transcriptional programs, supporting ocular efficacy when the C3a/C3aR axis is pathologically active in vivo (Zhao et al., 2025). Although RVO is not dry AMD, these data imply that C3aR antagonism can be delivered in vivo to the eye with measurable therapeutic impact on inflammation-driven retinal pathology.  
- Established discovery provenance and extensive preclinical use: The origin, synthesis, and extensive cross-species pharmacology of SB 290157 are well documented, facilitating procurement and standardized use as a pharmacologic probe in RPE assays; the compound is commercially available as a TFA salt and has been broadly applied in complementary models, enabling rapid head-to-head comparisons and orthogonal validation strategies (Ames et al., 2001; Li et al., 2021).  

Limitations and risks  
- Intrinsic pharmacology is not a clean “antagonist”: SB 290157 is a potent, biased C3aR agonist that robustly recruits β-arrestin and internalizes the receptor, and it partially activates C5aR2 at micromolar concentrations; both properties confound interpretation of putative antagonism and introduce off-target anti-inflammatory mechanisms at concentrations commonly used in vitro and in vivo (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In particular, the 10 µM concentration effective in hfRPE lies in the range that can engage C5aR2, so anti-inflammatory effects may not be solely attributable to C3aR blockade (Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- System-dependent behavior: SB 290157 displays agonism at C3aR in overexpression systems and certain endogenously expressing cells, but antagonizes readouts in others (e.g., human macrophages, guinea pig platelets), a pattern explained by receptor density and signaling bias; this variability raises concerns that RPE outcomes could depend on culture conditions (e.g., receptor upregulation by C3a) and surface expression levels in ways that shift net pharmacology (Mathieu et al., 2005; Rodriguez et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- Dosing and translational exposure liabilities: In vivo, commonly used doses achieve plasma concentrations predicted to co-activate C5aR2 and/or trigger undesired systemic effects (neutropenia, cardiovascular changes); short half-life complicates chronic dosing paradigms, and ocular tissue exposure metrics are not defined for SB 290157 (Li et al., 2021; Ames et al., 2001; Mathieu et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2025). While the RVO study demonstrates functional benefit, it also acknowledges SB 290157’s pharmacological limitations, emphasizing the need for sham controls and target validation beyond a single tool compound (Zhao et al., 2025).  
- Lack of in vivo dry AMD/drusen data: No in vivo evidence in the provided context demonstrates that SB 290157 reduces drusen or geographic atrophy in animal models; the in vitro hfRPE data are compelling but represent a reductionist system that does not capture subretinal immune cell interactions, Bruch’s membrane transport, or choriocapillaris alterations central to dry AMD pathogenesis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- POS uptake/degradation claim is unsubstantiated: The assertion that SB 290157 will improve RPE POS phagocytosis and degradation is not supported by the cited literature; no presented data quantify SB 290157 effects on RPE phagolysosomal function, and extrapolation from proteasome restoration to POS handling remains hypothetical (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  

Recommendations for a decision path  
- Near-term, SB 290157 is suitable as a positive-control pharmacological tool for target validation in RPE culture under stringent controls, not as a development candidate. In hfRPE, reproduce and extend published findings under defined C3a challenges by:  
  • Determining a full concentration–response for SB 290157 (e.g., 30 nM to 10 µM) on UPP activity, basal MMP-2, TIMP-3 expression, and collagen IV/VI deposition, with parallel assessment of C3aR surface expression, to establish minimally effective concentrations and exclude pro-inflammatory or agonist-like effects at lower doses (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
  • Incorporating orthogonal target validation: C3aR knockdown/knockout in RPE (if feasible), and pharmacological controls to test C5aR2 involvement (e.g., C5aR2-selective agonism as a counter model, acknowledging that RPE C5aR2 expression is not defined here), plus use of alternative C3aR reagents (e.g., anti-C3aR antibodies) where practical (Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
  • Adding phagocytosis endpoints (POS uptake, lysosomal degradation kinetics) to directly test the hypothesis that proteasome restoration by C3aR blockade enhances POS processing; these endpoints are currently unsupported (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
  • Monitoring off-target and cytotoxicity signals, including β-arrestin–dependent internalization (if assayable) to correlate with functional outcomes and to avoid misinterpreting biased agonism as antagonism (Rodriguez et al., 2024).  
- For in vivo exploration, given the interpretability risks with SB 290157, de-emphasize systemic dosing and consider localized delivery paradigms and/or more selective C3aR agents if available. If SB 290157 must be used, constrain intraperitoneal dosing to ≤1 mg/kg to minimize C5aR2 engagement and track pharmacodynamic readouts consistent with RPE-centric mechanisms (e.g., basal laminar deposit markers, MMP-2/TIMP-3 balance) in AMD-relevant models, recognizing that no such drusen/GA mitigation data are currently available for SB 290157 (Li et al., 2021). Genetic models (C3aR deletion) provide partial support for retinal structural preservation after injury, but differ in mechanism and context from RPE-intrinsic deposit biology (Behnke et al., 2025).  
- Strategically, prioritize identification or design of true C3aR antagonists devoid of agonist/β-arrestin bias and C5aR2 activity, or evaluate upstream C3 blockade where ocular delivery and safety allow, as parallel development tracks. The need for improved C3aR ligands is highlighted repeatedly in the pharmacology literature due to SB 290157’s liabilities (Mathieu et al., 2005; Coulthard & Woodruff, 2015; Rodriguez et al., 2024).  

Conclusion  
On balance, C3aR antagonism remains an attractive target mechanism for early dry AMD based on robust RPE-centric in vitro data linking C3a–C3aR signaling to proteasome impairment, ECM dysregulation, and sub-RPE deposit formation, with SB 290157 acting as an effective tool compound to prevent these changes in hfRPE (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). However, SB 290157’s complex pharmacology—potent biased C3aR agonism and partial C5aR2 agonism—creates substantial risks for misattributing mechanism and for translation, particularly at micromolar concentrations or systemic in vivo exposures where off-target signaling is likely (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Li et al., 2021). There is no in vivo evidence here that SB 290157 reduces drusen/geographic atrophy, and the claimed benefits for POS phagocytosis are unproven (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Zhao et al., 2025). As a result, I recommend using SB 290157 only as a controlled, short-term pharmacologic probe to (a) mechanistically validate the role of C3aR in RPE proteostasis/ECM biology and (b) set pharmacodynamic benchmarks for target engagement in RPE; in parallel, we should invest in sourcing or developing next-generation, selective C3aR antagonists with confirmed lack of agonism and C5aR2 activity for any advancement toward dry AMD models and, ultimately, clinical translation (Mathieu et al., 2005; Rodriguez et al., 2024; Coulthard & Woodruff, 2015).
