Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB431542 is a well‐characterized, synthetic small molecule inhibitor originally developed through medicinal chemistry efforts by researchers at GlaxoSmithKline. Its chemical structure, formally denoted as 4-(5-benzo[1,3]dioxol-5-yl-4-pyridin-2-yl-1H-imidazol-2-yl)-benzamide, incorporates a benzodioxole moiety linked to a pyridyl-imidazol core and terminated by a benzamide group, placing it within the imidazole class of compounds (Laping et al., 2002). SB431542 belongs to the class of transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) type I receptor kinase inhibitors (commonly referred to as ALK5 inhibitors) that inhibit ATP-dependent receptor activation. Initially designed as an improvement over less-selective kinase inhibitors—such as early p38 MAPK inhibitors that exhibited off-target ALK5 inhibition—SB431542 emerged from a rational structure–activity relationship (SAR) campaign aimed at optimizing both potency and selectivity (Laping et al., 2002). Its discovery has been pivotal in establishing a molecular tool for dissecting TGFβ signaling, and its chemical synthesis reflects a focused effort on achieving high-affinity, ATP-competitive inhibition of the TGFβ receptor. This compound has been extensively used in preclinical research to study fibrotic mechanisms and cellular differentiation, thereby marking its reputation as a “gold standard” in TGFβ pathway inhibition (Laping et al., 2002).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SB431542 is primarily rooted in its application as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. In numerous preclinical studies, SB431542 has been consistently used to inhibit TGFβ-induced processes such as extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis, Smad protein activation, and the induction of a fibrotic phenotype in various cell types including renal epithelial cells, fibroblasts, and even certain cancer cell models (Laping et al., 2002). Biochemical studies have shown that SB431542 effectively blocks the phosphorylation of Smad3 with an IC50 of approximately 94 nM, thereby preventing the downstream transcriptional activation of cytokines and matrix proteins (Laping et al., 2002). Its anti-fibrotic effects have been extensively characterized in in vitro assays, where it reduced the expression of collagen I α1, fibronectin, and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) mRNA, thus providing compelling evidence that the compound modulates TGFβ-induced ECM remodeling (Laping et al., 2002).

While SB431542 has been applied in many experimental models to study pathways implicated in fibrotic diseases such as glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, liver cirrhosis, and pulmonary fibrosis, there is scant direct evidence of its historical use in ocular pathologies, particularly dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Akhund et al., 2023; Nyati et al., 2011). However, TGFβ signaling has been implicated in retinal pathologies and in the mesenchymal transition of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells from which some studies have emerged using general TGFβ inhibitors to reverse such pathological changes (Radeke et al., 2015). Although SB431542 itself has not been used in clinical trials for AMD, its mechanistic profile and reported efficacies in other fibrotic and ECM remodeling contexts make it a promising candidate for repurposing to address the abnormal matrix remodeling observed in dry AMD. Preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues have established that targeted inhibition of TGFβ signaling leads to substantial reductions in fibrotic markers, suggesting that similar approaches could mitigate Bruch membrane (BrM) alterations in AMD (Laping et al., 2002).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB431542 functions as an ATP-competitive inhibitor selectively targeting the kinase domain of the TGFβ type I receptor (TGFβRI, also known as ALK5). Its mechanism of action centers on binding to the ATP-binding pocket of TGFβRI, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of key intracellular effectors, primarily the Smad2 and Smad3 proteins (Laping et al., 2002). In normal TGFβ signaling, binding of the ligand (e.g., TGFβ1) to its receptors induces the formation of a heteromeric complex consisting of TGFβRI and TGFβRII, leading to the phosphorylation and activation of Smad2/3. These phosphorylated Smad proteins then form a complex with Smad4, translocate to the nucleus, and activate the transcription of pro-fibrotic genes, including those involved in ECM protein synthesis such as collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002).

Detailed molecular interaction studies have revealed that SB431542 makes critical hydrogen bonding contacts within the ATP-binding site of TGFβRI. For example, the benzodioxol moiety is reported to form a hydrogen bond with the amide nitrogen of His283, while additional interactions with Lys232 and other hydrophobic residues stabilize the inhibitor within the binding pocket (Leonardo-Sousa et al., 2025). This precise molecular engagement confers its high selectivity, as even minor substitutions in the binding region—such as mutations at the gatekeeper residue—can significantly alter inhibitor efficacy (Laping et al., 2002; Leonardo-Sousa et al., 2025). Furthermore, while SB431542 shows potent inhibition against ALK5, it also inhibits closely related receptors such as ALK4 and ALK7 with only modest differences in potency (IC50 for ALK4 is approximately 140 nM), and it exhibits negligible activity against BMP-activated receptors (ALK2, ALK3, and ALK6) (Laping et al., 2002). This selective inhibition ensures that the canonical TGFβ/Smad pathway is targeted without significantly perturbing other pathways that could be essential for cellular homeostasis, such as the BMP signaling cascade (Nyati et al., 2011; Akhund et al., 2023).

In addition to its inhibition of Smad2/3 phosphorylation, SB431542 has been shown to disrupt the subsequent nuclear translocation of these transcription factors, thereby halting the transcription of downstream ECM components. Such inhibition is critical because overactivation of the TGFβ pathway is a central driver in fibrotic diseases and leads to excessive deposition of ECM proteins, which in turn contribute to tissue stiffness and impaired cellular function (Laping et al., 2002). Overall, the molecular mechanism of SB431542 is well-delineated; its high selectivity for TGFβRI and the resulting blockade of Smad-mediated transcription form the foundation for its potential use in addressing aberrant ECM remodeling.

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis for repurposing SB431542 in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is built on the concept that excessive TGFβ signaling within the retinal microenvironment leads to an abnormal accumulation and remodeling of ECM components in the Bruch membrane (BrM). In the context of dry AMD, such ECM changes are believed to increase membrane stiffness and disrupt the diffusion of critical phagocytic ligands—specifically MFGE8 (Milk Fat Globule Epidermal Growth Factor 8) and Gas6—which play key roles in facilitating the integrin αvβ5-mediated binding and uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Radeke et al., 2015).

By inhibiting TGFβRI, SB431542 is expected to block the TGFβ-driven phosphorylation of Smad proteins, thereby directly reducing the transcription of genes that encode for fibrotic and ECM-related proteins such as collagen I α1, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002). In doing so, SB431542 should restore a more balanced ECM composition in the BrM. This normalization of ECM deposition is anticipated to reduce BrM stiffness, thereby enhancing the diffusion of phagocytic ligands like MFGE8 and Gas6 across the membrane. The improved ligand diffusion is expected to restore the optimal microenvironment required for integrin αvβ5 on the RPE surface to effectively bind and internalize POS, a process that is critically impaired in dry AMD (Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011).

Furthermore, by attenuating the fibrotic response within the retina, SB431542 may help preserve the native architecture and function of the RPE layer. This indirect modulation of phagocytosis, achieved through the normalization of ECM characteristics, represents a novel therapeutic angle that bridges the gap between ECM pathology and receptor-mediated cellular processes. In essence, the expected effect of SB431542 is a dual benefit: first, it directly inhibits pathological TGFβ signaling to reduce further fibrotic damage, and second, it indirectly normalizes phagocytic function by restoring the proper presentation of ligands critical for RPE-mediated clearance of POS (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015).

At the cellular and molecular level, the proposed assay is likely to measure a reduction in fibrotic markers (e.g., collagen I α1, fibronectin) and an improvement in assays of POS binding and internalization by RPE cells. Given that RPE cells express integrin αvβ5 and are responsive to TGFβ signaling, the application of SB431542 should result in a shift from a fibrotic, mesenchymal phenotype towards a more differentiated epithelial state that is conducive to normal phagocytic activity (Radeke et al., 2015; Akhund et al., 2023). This outcome would be mechanistically consistent with the known roles of TGFβ in modulating ECM dynamics and cellular differentiation. Consequently, if the hypothesis holds true, SB431542 would not only prevent further ECM deposition and stiffening of the BrM but would also support the resolution of existing pathological ECM alterations, thereby improving the overall homeostasis of the retinal microenvironment.

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of SB431542 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD requires careful consideration of its well-established biochemical profile alongside the translational challenges emerging from its current use primarily as a research tool. On the positive side, SB431542 is a potent and selective inhibitor of TGFβRI, with extensive preclinical evidence demonstrating its capacity to block TGFβ-induced Smad2/3 phosphorylation and consequently reduce the expression of fibrotic markers (Laping et al., 2002). Its high potency (with an IC50 in the low nanomolar range) and favorable selectivity profile—particularly with more than 100-fold selectivity over p38 MAPK and minimal activity against BMP receptors—render it an attractive candidate for targeted modulation of TGFβ signaling in tissues where fibrosis is a major pathogenic factor (Laping et al., 2002). These strengths are of particular relevance in the context of dry AMD, where BrM thickening and ECM remodeling are central features that compromise RPE function.

Moreover, the proposed mechanism underlying the therapeutic hypothesis is compelling. Excessive TGFβ signaling has been implicated in the aberrant remodeling of the BrM, which in turn impairs the presentation of critical phagocytic ligands necessary for efficient POS uptake by the RPE (Radeke et al., 2015). By inhibiting TGFβRI, SB431542 could theoretically restore the balance between collagen and proteoglycan production, thereby normalizing BrM stiffness and improving the diffusion of factors such as MFGE8 and Gas6. In doing so, the drug would indirectly enhance integrin αvβ5-mediated phagocytosis—a process that is essential for the maintenance of photoreceptor health and overall retinal integrity. This innovative indirect approach could represent a significant advancement in the treatment of dry AMD, addressing the disease from both a fibrotic and a functional perspective.

However, several considerable challenges and weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, the bulk of the supporting data for SB431542 comes from studies in non-ocular cell types or animal models of general fibrosis and cancer, with limited direct evidence in ocular systems. Although TGFβ inhibitors have been proposed as therapeutic agents in retinal diseases, there remains a significant gap in data specific to dry AMD or related retinal degenerative conditions (Akhund et al., 2023; Nyati et al., 2011). The absence of ocular pharmacokinetic studies, detailed data on retinal tissue penetration, and long-term safety evaluations in the eye poses a major hurdle for the clinical translation of SB431542 for AMD.

Furthermore, TGFβ signaling is a double-edged sword in many tissues, including the retina. While excessive TGFβ activity drives pathological ECM deposition and fibrosis, TGFβ also participates in immune regulation and cellular homeostasis. Therefore, complete or prolonged inhibition of TGFβ signaling may have unintended consequences, such as impairing normal wound healing or altering the immunological milieu of the retina (Akhund et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023). The delicate balance between therapeutic efficacy and potential adverse effects necessitates that any systemic or even locally delivered TGFβRI inhibitor be subject to rigorous dosing and toxicity studies. In this regard, the narrow therapeutic window often encountered in kinase inhibition therapies could be a limiting factor for SB431542’s adoption in an ophthalmic setting.

Another significant concern is the delivery method. The current literature on SB431542 primarily documents its use in cell culture assays or systemic administration in animal models; however, the ocular environment presents unique challenges due to barriers such as the inner limiting membrane, the blood-retina barrier, and the anatomical constraints of the retina. To achieve therapeutically relevant concentrations in the sub-retinal space or at the level of the BrM, innovative delivery strategies—such as topical formulations, intravitreal injections, or sustained-release devices—must be developed and validated (Hachana & Larrivée, 2022; Radeke et al., 2015). The pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of SB431542 in ocular tissues remain largely unexplored, which represents a critical gap in current knowledge.

Additionally, although the indirect mechanism of action—namely, the normalization of ECM to facilitate proper ligand–receptor interactions—is scientifically plausible, it is inherently more challenging to measure and validate compared to direct cellular responses. Assays designed to monitor changes in BrM stiffness, ECM composition, and the diffusion characteristics of MFGE8 and Gas6 must be highly sensitive and reproducible, and these endpoints have not been extensively characterized in available preclinical models of AMD. Furthermore, the redundancy within TGFβ signaling pathways raises the possibility that compensatory mechanisms might mitigate the effects of ALK5 inhibition over time, potentially limiting the efficacy of SB431542, particularly in a chronic, slowly progressive disease like dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Akhund et al., 2023).

From an efficacy standpoint, while numerous studies demonstrate that SB431542 effectively reduces TGFβ-induced fibrotic responses in various cell types (Laping et al., 2002), extrapolating these findings to the complex microenvironment of the aged retina is not straightforward. The retina and RPE possess distinct cellular and molecular characteristics that may respond differently to TGFβ signaling modulation. For example, in RPE cells, TGFβ signaling not only regulates ECM deposition but is also involved in the maintenance of epithelial phenotype and may even exert neuroprotective effects under certain conditions. Hence, unspecific inhibition of TGFβ signaling in the retina could conceivably result in a loss of beneficial effects that are essential for retinal homeostasis (Radeke et al., 2015; Akhund et al., 2023).

In summary, while SB431542 exhibits a robust, well-characterized mechanism of action as a TGFβRI inhibitor and has demonstrated potent anti-fibrotic effects in preclinical models of ECM remodeling, its repurposing for dry AMD must overcome several significant challenges. The strengths of SB431542 lie in its high potency, selectivity, and extensive preclinical validation in non-ocular models. Its molecular interactions are well understood, and its ability to inhibit Smad phosphorylation offers a clear mechanistic rationale for reducing pathological ECM deposition. Consequently, if applied to the pathological process associated with dry AMD, SB431542 could, in theory, mitigate the excessive ECM remodeling that impairs ligand diffusion and consequently restores the capacity for integrin αvβ5-mediated POS uptake by RPE cells (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011).

On the other hand, the weaknesses of this approach are substantial. There is limited evidence of SB431542’s efficacy in ocular models, and its pharmacokinetics, ocular tissue penetration, and long-term safety profile have yet to be rigorously evaluated. Additionally, the complexity of TGFβ’s biological roles raises concerns regarding the balance between therapeutic benefit and potential interference with normal retinal physiology. The indirect nature of the hypothesized effect—mediated by ECM normalization—adds further layers of complexity to both preclinical testing and eventual clinical translation. Finally, challenges related to drug delivery to the retina, along with the potential for compensatory signaling pathways to undermine the inhibitor’s efficacy, suggest that significant additional research is warranted before SB431542 can be advanced as a therapeutic candidate in an AMD setting (Akhund et al., 2023; Akhund et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023).

Overall, SB431542 presents a biologically plausible and mechanistically sound candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly given its demonstrated ability to modulate TGFβ-driven fibrotic pathways. However, its successful translation to an ophthalmic therapeutic will hinge on a series of focused preclinical studies that address ocular biodistribution, safety in retinal tissues, and the optimization of dosing regimens tailored to the unique anatomical and physiological challenges of the eye. Only after these critical issues have been resolved can SB431542 be considered a viable strategy to restore ECM homeostasis in the Bruch membrane, normalize phagocytic ligand availability, and ultimately enhance integrin-mediated POS uptake in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011). In conclusion, while SB431542 has strong potential and a compelling mechanistic rationale, further dedicated ocular research is required to fully validate its therapeutic promise in the context of dry AMD before it can be recommended for clinical development.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ibrutinib is a fully synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally developed as an irreversible inhibitor of Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK). It achieves inhibition by covalently binding to the conserved Cys481 residue located within the ATP‐binding pocket of BTK, a key member of the TEC family of kinases. This irreversible binding results in permanent inactivation of BTK, thereby interrupting B‐cell receptor signaling as well as other downstream pathways that are critical for cell survival and proliferation (Xie et al., 2021). As a member of the broader class of tyrosine kinase inhibitors, ibrutinib is designed through refined organic synthesis strategies that optimize its selectivity and potency. Compounds of this chemical class have been extensively utilized in oncology, particularly for the treatment of B‐cell malignancies, where they serve to disrupt aberrant oncogenic signaling pathways. Ibrutinib is available commercially (e.g., SelleckChem Cat. No. S2680) and has been subject to rigorous clinical evaluation, ensuring that its chemical properties, including its irreversible binding mechanism and cell penetration capabilities, are well established in the literature (Xie et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, ibrutinib was developed and advanced clinically for hematologic cancers such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia (WM), and other B‐cell malignancies. Its success in these domains is attributed to its effective inhibition of BTK, a kinase that is critical for B‐cell receptor signaling and survival (Xie et al., 2021). Once approved by the U.S. FDA in 2013, it rapidly became a standard of care in oncology. Outside of its oncologic use, ibrutinib has been recognized for its immunomodulatory effects that extend to innate immune cells such as macrophages, dendritic cells, and, notably, microglia. Although the primary application of ibrutinib is in cancer therapy, there is emerging evidence and growing scientific interest suggesting that BTK plays a role in innate immune signaling pathways that contribute to chronic inflammatory states, including those implicated in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Brandli et al., 2024). In pharmacovigilance studies, ocular adverse events—including uveitis, cataracts, and retinal disorders—have been identified among patients treated with ibrutinib, which indicates that the molecule penetrates ocular compartments and exerts biological effects there (Allouchery et al., 2021). However, despite these observations, ibrutinib has not been previously developed or marketed for the treatment of dry AMD or similar degenerative retinal diseases. Instead, its potential repurposing arises from the hypothesis that by modulating BTK-dependent inflammatory pathways in microglia and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, ibrutinib might reduce deleterious inflammasome priming and cytokine production that contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ibrutinib exerts its primary action by binding irreversibly to BTK, thereby preventing autophosphorylation and subsequent transmission of intracellular signals that lead to inflammation and cell survival. BTK is not only a critical mediator of B‐cell receptor signaling but is also expressed in cells of the innate immune system including microglia and RPE cells. Its activation is linked to the regulation of the NLRP3 inflammasome—a multiprotein complex that senses cellular stress, leading to the activation of caspase-1 and the maturation and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Brandli et al., 2024). There is accumulating evidence that BTK facilitates the priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome in response to various stimuli, including oxidative stress and the accumulation of deleterious protein aggregates, both of which are implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis. Experimental data suggest that inhibition of BTK by ibrutinib can lead to a reduction in IL-1β release, which in turn may lower downstream pro-inflammatory signals such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) (Far et al., 2022; Allouchery et al., 2021). Moreover, the preservation of lysosomal cathepsin activity observed in ARPE-19 cells under inflammasome-stimulating conditions implies that BTK inhibition may also support the maintenance of RPE lysosomal integrity and phagocytic function. Such actions are critical for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and prevention of drusen accumulation—a hallmark of dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). In summary, by covalently binding to BTK, ibrutinib not only halts aberrant immune cell signaling but also indirectly modulates inflammasome activity and associated inflammatory cytokine release in retinal cells (Xie et al., 2021; Brandli et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for the repurposing of ibrutinib in dry AMD revolves around its ability to inhibit BTK activity within microglia and RPE cells, thereby suppressing inflammasome priming and limiting the production of inflammatory mediators such as IL-1β and TNFα. In the context of an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells, it is anticipated that the application of ibrutinib (IC₅₀ ~0.5 nM) will result in a marked attenuation of inflammasome activation, as evidenced by reduced secretion of IL-1β and preserved lysosomal cathepsin activity (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). The proposed mechanism by which ibrutinib exerts its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD is multifaceted. First, by inhibiting BTK, the compound is expected to downregulate the overactive NLRP3 inflammasome that plays a central role in the inflammatory cascade within the retinal pigment epithelium (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024). Second, by reducing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines—especially TNFα—which have been shown to negatively impact the phagocytic ability of RPE cells, ibrutinib may help to maintain the clearance of photoreceptor outer segment debris. This is particularly important because impaired clearance mechanisms contribute to the accumulation of drusen and subsequent RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024). Moreover, animal and clinical pharmacovigilance studies have provided evidence that ibrutinib is capable of crossing the blood-brain and blood-retinal barriers, suggesting that it can reach retinal tissues at therapeutically relevant concentrations. Although there is documented evidence of ocular adverse events in patients treated with ibrutinib for hematologic malignancies—including instances of uveitis and cystoid macular edema—such effects have been largely reported as unintended consequences rather than engineered therapeutic outcomes. In the current repurposing framework, the premise is that controlled intravitreal or local administration, possibly as a modified formulation, could harness the anti-inflammatory properties of ibrutinib while minimizing systemic exposure and the risk of ocular adverse events (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022). Ultimately, the expected effect is a preserved RPE function with enhanced ability to clear POS debris, thereby mitigating the degenerative progression typically observed in dry AMD (Korhonen, 2024; Brandli et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
Ibrutinib presents as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to its well-characterized molecular mechanism and its established clinical profile in oncology. One of the major strengths of ibrutinib lies in its potent and selective irreversible inhibition of BTK, a kinase implicated not only in B-cell malignancies but also in the pathogenesis of inflammatory retinal diseases through its role in NLRP3 inflammasome priming (Xie et al., 2021). The scientific rationale for its repurposing is supported by preclinical observations indicating that BTK inhibition leads to reduced IL-1β secretion and preservation of lysosomal function in RPE cells, which are essential for maintaining photoreceptor homeostasis and preventing drusen accumulation in dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). Furthermore, the demonstration that ibrutinib crosses the blood-retinal barrier underscores its potential utility in directly targeting retinal tissues, especially when administered via routes that ensure localized high concentrations with limited systemic exposure (Xie et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022).

However, there are several challenges and weaknesses associated with this therapeutic candidate. First, the ocular safety profile of ibrutinib is a matter of concern, as pharmacovigilance data have linked ibrutinib to a spectrum of adverse ocular events including cataracts, uveitis, and retinal disorders (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022). While these effects have so far been observed in the context of systemic cancer therapy, they raise important safety questions when considering chronic administration for a disease such as dry AMD that often requires long-term treatment. Second, the dosages and formulation required to achieve an anti-inflammatory effect in the retina, while concurrently minimizing cytotoxicity and other off-target effects, remain uncertain. Ibrutinib’s off-target inhibitory effects, such as its activity against VEGFR2, may impart vascular side effects that could further complicate its use in the delicate retinal environment (Allouchery et al., 2021). Third, the repurposing strategy relies heavily on the extrapolation of cellular and animal model data—such as the observed reduction of inflammasome activation and preservation of cathepsin activity in ARPE-19 cells—to the complex pathophysiology of human dry AMD. The heterogeneity of dry AMD pathogenesis, driven by a confluence of genetic, environmental, and age-related factors, means that successful translation from preclinical models to effective clinical outcomes is not guaranteed (Korhonen, 2024; Brandli et al., 2024). Additionally, while there is a robust theoretical framework underpinning BTK’s involvement in inflamed retinal microenvironments, direct evidence of ibrutinib’s efficacy in modulating microglial or RPE function specifically in the setting of dry AMD remains limited.

Despite these challenges, the mechanistic rationale for using a BTK inhibitor in dry AMD is compelling. The interplay between NLRP3 inflammasome activation, chronic low-grade inflammation, and RPE dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a pivotal driver of dry AMD progression (Brandli et al., 2024). If ibrutinib can effectively attenuate these inflammatory processes without incurring prohibitive adverse events, it may offer a novel therapeutic avenue for a disease area currently lacking effective treatment options. However, this necessitates a series of rigorous preclinical studies to characterize the dose-response relationship, evaluate retinal safety, and define the pharmacokinetic profile of ibrutinib when delivered via ocular routes. Moreover, any proposed clinical trial must incorporate comprehensive ophthalmologic monitoring given the known spectrum of ibrutinib-induced ocular side effects (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022).

In summary, while ibrutinib is primarily an approved oncologic agent, its underlying mechanism of inhibiting BTK—the kinase that modulates inflammasome priming in microglia and RPE cells—provides a strong scientific basis for its repurposing in dry AMD. The expected effects of reduced IL-1β and TNFα production, coupled with preserved lysosomal cathepsin activity and improved phagocytic function, align well with the therapeutic goals of mitigating chronic inflammation and preserving retinal integrity in dry AMD. Nevertheless, the potential ocular adverse effects and the challenges related to achieving a favorable therapeutic index in the retinal environment are significant concerns that must be addressed through further rigorous preclinical and clinical evaluations (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). Overall, ibrutinib represents an intriguing candidate with a solid mechanistic rationale for dry AMD treatment; however, careful attention to formulation, dosing, and safety testing is warranted before advancing this repurposing strategy to later-stage clinical trials (Xie et al., 2021; Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AMD3100 (also known as plerixafor) is a small‐molecule, bicyclam compound originally discovered and synthesized as a CXCR4 antagonist. It belongs to a class of compounds designed to block the interaction between the chemokine ligand SDF‐1 (CXCL12) and its receptor CXCR4. This class of compounds was initially developed for their antiviral potential—specifically to inhibit HIV‐1 entry into cells—because CXCR4 serves as a co‐receptor for viral entry. Subsequent studies showed that through its high affinity for CXCR4 (with IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range, and our current hypothesis citing ~20 nM in RPE cells), AMD3100 can effectively block the downstream signaling of the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis. This signaling cascade is known to regulate key cellular processes such as chemotaxis, cell survival, proliferation, and inflammatory gene expression. With its synthetic origin and established profile as a CXCR4 antagonist, AMD3100 has been repurposed beyond its initial anti‐HIV goals to include hematopoietic stem cell mobilization and experimental oncology. Its potential re‐utilization in ocular diseases, particularly in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), capitalizes on its ability to modulate inflammatory signaling pathways implicated in retinal degeneration (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AMD3100 emerged from research aimed at blocking HIV infection, but its clinical development pivoted after it was found to robustly mobilize hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells from the bone marrow. This discovery led to its approval by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as an adjuvant therapy for autologous stem cell transplantation in patients with non‐Hodgkin’s lymphoma and multiple myeloma. Its use in stem cell mobilization has been thoroughly characterized in clinical trials with documented pharmacokinetics and a reasonable safety profile in systemic administration (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019). In addition to these applications, AMD3100 has been investigated in various preclinical models of cancer, where its inhibition of CXCR4-mediated signaling has been linked to reduced tumor cell invasion, decreased angiogenesis, and altered immune cell trafficking (Andtbacka et al., 2022; Cho et al., 2013). In the ocular context, although AMD3100 has not been used directly for treating dry AMD, its effects on CXCR4 signaling have been addressed in studies focusing on glaucomatous models. For example, investigations in trabecular meshwork cells from glaucomatous tissue have demonstrated that AMD3100, when administered at 1 mM concentration, completely abrogates the protective effects of CXCL12 and inadvertently induces apoptosis, highlighting the dual role of CXCR4 signaling in ocular tissues (Denoyer et al., 2012). Moreover, systemic administration studies in non‐ocular models such as the SOD1^G93A ALS mouse model have shown that chronic AMD3100 treatment can yield neuroprotective and anti‐inflammatory benefits (Rabinovich‐Nikitin et al., 2016), which further adds to its therapeutic appeal but also underscores the importance of tissue-specific dosing and context. These historical uses underscore AMD3100’s well-defined pharmacological profile while simultaneously illustrating that translating its benefits to the RPE in dry AMD will require reconciling its established systemic effects with the often finely balanced roles of the CXCR4 axis in retinal tissue repair and inflammation (Cai et al., 2014; Saiman et al., 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, AMD3100 exerts its primary pharmacological action by selectively binding to the CXCR4 receptor and competitively inhibiting the binding of its natural ligand, SDF‐1 (CXCL12). In doing so, it prevents receptor activation and the subsequent engagement of intracellular signaling cascades mediated by G-protein coupled receptor activation. The downstream effects typically include modulation of pathways such as PI3K/Akt, Ras/ERK, and, in many cases, alterations in intracellular calcium fluxes that contribute to chemotaxis and cell survival (Bai et al., 2016; Colasanti et al., 2025). By inhibiting these cascades, AMD3100 hinders not only the migration of cells toward SDF‐1 gradients but also the pro‐inflammatory and pro‐angiogenic gene expression programs that are otherwise activated upon CXCR4 engagement. In cancer models, this mechanism translates into reduced tumor cell invasion and inhibition of angiogenesis, while in immune cells it modulates chemotactic responses and inflammatory cell trafficking (Cho et al., 2013). Importantly, CXCR4 is expressed in multiple ocular cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. In RPE, the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis has been implicated in cellular migration, cytokine secretion, and potentially in the regulation of the phagocytic machinery necessary for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). The hypothesis driving the current proposal suggests that chronic activation of CXCR4 in RPE cells, possibly driven by persistent inflammatory stimuli such as TNF‐α, leads to a pro‐inflammatory state that downregulates key phagocytic receptors like MERTK and compromises lysosomal enzyme activity. By blocking the binding of SDF‐1 to CXCR4, AMD3100 is expected to interrupt this deleterious signaling cascade, resulting in normalization of MERTK expression and lysosomal enzyme levels, and thereby restoring the essential phagocytic function of the RPE (Colasanti et al., 2025). However, the complexity of CXCR4 signaling is underscored by studies in other ocular tissues where its inhibition has led to apoptosis of trabecular cells, suggesting that the outcome of CXCR4 blockade may be highly dependent on the cell type and the local microenvironment (Denoyer et al., 2012). Therefore, while the mechanistic rationale is strong, careful evaluation of AMD3100’s specific molecular interactions in RPE cells will be required to delineate beneficial effects from potential adverse outcomes.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed therapeutic strategy hypothesizes that the blockade of CXCR4 by AMD3100 in RPE cells will lead to two major beneficial outcomes in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration: (1) inhibition of pro-inflammatory signaling that otherwise promotes aberrant cellular migration and deleterious inflammatory gene expression, and (2) restoration of the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells through upregulation of key receptors and enzymes necessary for the efficient clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In dry AMD, a hallmark of disease progression is the accumulation of cellular debris and the failure of RPE cells to effectively clear POS due to impaired phagocytosis—a process that is critical for sustaining photoreceptor health and visual function. Evidence suggests that chronic activation of the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis in the retinal microenvironment can lead to elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines and subsequent downregulation of MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase essential for the recognition and internalization of shed POS (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). In vitro models, such as TNF‐α–treated ARPE-19 cells, have demonstrated that inflammatory stress leads to diminished phagocytic activity, and it is hypothesized that blocking CXCR4 signaling with AMD3100 could counteract this effect by normalizing MERTK levels and restoring lysosomal function. In an ideal scenario, treatment with AMD3100 would reverse the pro-inflammatory signaling cascade by preventing SDF‐1 binding, reduce aberrant RPE migration, and allow the cells to maintain their structural polarity and phagocytic efficiency. Importantly, the RPE expresses CXCR4 receptors on their surface, as demonstrated by immunocytochemical studies, and the receptor’s activation has been linked to altered cellular motility and inflammatory responses (Canonica et al., 2021; Enzmann et al., 2017). The expected pharmacodynamic outcome is that, upon AMD3100 treatment, RPE cells under inflammatory stress conditions would exhibit increased expression of MERTK and lysosomal enzymes, leading to improved clearance of damaged photoreceptor outer segments, which is critical for photoreceptor survival and overall retinal health. While data from other cell types suggest the possibility of safely modulating these pathways, caution is warranted given the evidence from trabecular meshwork cells where CXCR4 antagonism disrupted protective signaling (Denoyer et al., 2012). Hence, the key to success will lie in establishing the proper dosing and delivery mechanisms that provide sufficient blockade of deleterious CXCR4 signaling in RPE without compromising the receptor’s potentially beneficial roles in tissue repair and homeostasis.

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, AMD3100 presents an intriguing candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration given its well-defined mechanism of action, extensive preclinical and clinical history, and a known safety profile in non-ocular indications such as hematopoietic stem cell mobilization and cancer therapy (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019). The central hypothesis—that chronic SDF‐1/CXCR4 signaling in RPE cells contributes to inflammation-driven downregulation of MERTK and consequent impairment of POS phagocytosis—addresses a critical pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD. Blocking this pathway with AMD3100 could, in theory, restore the phagocytic machinery of the RPE, thereby reducing the accumulation of toxic cellular debris and slowing disease progression (Colasanti et al., 2025).

One of the strengths of AMD3100 as a therapeutic candidate lies in its extensive clinical use and established pharmacokinetic profile; its FDA approval for stem cell mobilization means that much is already known about its systemic effects, dosing parameters, and potential toxicities when administered appropriately (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Rabinovich-Nikitin et al., 2016). Moreover, the molecular mechanism—competitive antagonism at the CXCR4 receptor—has been demonstrated across multiple studies and various cell types, providing a robust theoretical framework for its use in modulating pathological signaling cascades in RPE cells (Bai et al., 2016; Colasanti et al., 2025). The concept of repurposing a well-characterized agent such as AMD3100 for dry AMD is attractive from a drug development standpoint because it could potentially shorten the translational timeline and reduce development risks related to novel chemical entities.

However, there are significant challenges and weaknesses that must be addressed before AMD3100 can be considered a promising candidate for dry AMD. First and foremost, the role of SDF‐1/CXCR4 signaling in ocular tissues appears to be multifaceted. While in RPE cells chronic activation may indeed drive a pro-inflammatory and phagocytosis-impairing phenotype, in other ocular tissues such as the trabecular meshwork, CXCR4 signaling has been shown to exert cytoprotective effects. Studies in glaucomatous trabecular cells have demonstrated that blockade of CXCR4 by AMD3100 not only abrogates the beneficial actions of CXCL12 but may also actively induce apoptosis, highlighting a potential risk that the protective aspects of CXCR4 signaling could be compromised (Denoyer et al., 2012). This tissue-specific duality raises concerns that non-selective or systemic inhibition of CXCR4 might lead to unintended adverse effects in the retina and other ocular compartments. Therefore, any consideration of AMD3100 for dry AMD will require extremely careful dosing studies and potentially localized delivery strategies that avoid systemic over-blockade.

Another key consideration is the current lack of direct evidence supporting the efficacy of AMD3100 in restoring MERTK expression or lysosomal enzyme levels in RPE cells, specifically in the context of dry AMD. While preliminary in vitro observations in TNF‐α–treated ARPE-19 cells are promising, these studies remain preliminary, and the translation of these effects into meaningful functional outcomes in vivo has yet to be established. The complexity of dry AMD pathogenesis—which involves not only inflammatory processes but also oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, and altered cellular metabolism—means that targeting a single pathway may not be sufficient to recapitulate the full spectrum of therapeutic benefit required for clinical efficacy (Colasanti et al., 2025).

Furthermore, the potential for AMD3100 to affect cell migration and even cellular differentiation via CXCR4 inhibition might have unpredictable consequences on the RPE’s capacity for repair. For instance, the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis has been implicated in the recruitment of bone marrow–derived progenitor cells to sites of RPE injury, a process that is thought to contribute to endogenous repair mechanisms (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). Inhibiting CXCR4 could inadvertently interfere with these reparative processes if not finely tuned. It is, therefore, imperative that any preclinical evaluation of AMD3100 for dry AMD includes rigorous assessments of not only phagocytic function and inflammatory profile but also the impact on RPE cell survival, differentiation, and regenerative capacity.

In addition to cell-specific concerns, the delivery method for AMD3100 in the context of dry AMD is another critical factor. The compound has been used systemically, but ocular diseases typically require either intravitreal or other localized delivery methods to achieve therapeutic concentrations while minimizing systemic exposure. Prior studies involving AMD3100 in ocular models—mostly in the context of glaucoma—have used subconjunctival injections at relatively high concentrations (e.g., 1 mM), which resulted in localized apoptotic effects (Denoyer et al., 2012). This suggests that the concentration and mode of delivery will need to be carefully optimized for the RPE to ensure that sufficient drug levels are achieved to block aberrant CXCR4 signaling without tipping the balance of protective chemokine functions.

Moreover, while the preclinical data from non-ocular models such as cancer and ALS are encouraging regarding the anti-inflammatory and anti-migratory effects of AMD3100 (Rabinovich-Nikitin et al., 2016; Andtbacka et al., 2022), these contexts differ significantly from the microenvironment of the aging retina. The retinal tissue, particularly in dry AMD, is characterized by complex interactions among the RPE, photoreceptors, Bruch’s membrane, and the choriocapillaris. The interplay of these structures with age-related oxidative stress and immune dysregulation means that any intervention must be evaluated in models that faithfully recapitulate these conditions. There is a paucity of direct literature on the use of AMD3100 in dry AMD models, which suggests that a substantial body of preclinical work is required before a clear signal of benefit can be ascertained.

In summary, AMD3100 has significant strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its well-documented mechanism of competitive antagonism at CXCR4, combined with an established clinical safety profile in systemic applications and a clear rationale for targeting the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis in inflammatory conditions, supports further investigation of its use in the retinal pigment epithelium (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019; Bai et al., 2016). However, key weaknesses include evidence from ocular models that indicate potential cytotoxicity when protective CXCR4 signals are indiscriminately blocked (Denoyer et al., 2012), as well as a lack of direct preclinical data in dry AMD or RPE-specific phagocytic assays. These concerns necessitate a cautious yet exploratory approach, with initial studies focused on establishing the optimal local dosing regimen, confirming that AMD3100 can indeed restore MERTK expression and phagocytic function in ARPE-19 cell models, and ultimately validating these findings in animal models of dry AMD that incorporate stressors such as TNF‐α or oxidative injury.

Overall Evaluation:  
In conclusion, while AMD3100 stands as one of the most thoroughly characterized CXCR4 antagonists with a solid clinical and preclinical background, its application to dry AMD remains largely untested. The theoretical basis—that chronic SDF‐1/CXCR4 activation in RPE drives inflammatory gene expression leading to diminished phagocytic capacity, and that blocking this pathway will restore homeostatic functions—is compelling and addresses a known pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD (Colasanti et al., 2025). The strengths of AMD3100 include its potent CXCR4 binding affinity, the wealth of pharmacological data supporting its mode of action, and its demonstrated ability to modulate inflammatory and migratory responses in various tissues. Moreover, the clinical safety data from its use in hematopoietic stem cell mobilization provide some reassurance regarding its tolerability when used in appropriate dosing regimens (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019).

On the other hand, several significant weaknesses must be acknowledged. Studies in ocular models have shown that CXCR4 blockade can eliminate protective signals that are crucial for cell survival, as evidenced by the induction of apoptosis in trabecular meshwork cells when treated with AMD3100 at high concentrations (Denoyer et al., 2012). In addition, there is a risk that by inhibiting CXCR4 signaling, AMD3100 might interfere with endogenous repair mechanisms mediated by the recruitment of bone marrow–derived progenitor cells, a process that may be beneficial in RPE regeneration (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). The lack of direct data demonstrating restoration of MERTK and improved phagocytosis in RPE cells further complicates the evaluation. Because dry AMD is multifactorial, it is unclear whether modulation of a single pathway—albeit an important one—will be sufficient to yield a meaningful clinical benefit without causing collateral damage to other aspects of RPE function.

Given these considerations, our recommendation is to pursue rigorous preclinical studies specifically tailored to dry AMD. These studies should encompass detailed in vitro analyses using ARPE-19 and primary human RPE cells under inflammatory and oxidative stress conditions to validate whether AMD3100 can reliably restore MERTK expression and lysosomal function, thereby enhancing POS clearance. It will also be critical to establish the appropriate concentration window that achieves therapeutic blockade of deleterious signaling while preserving necessary CXCR4-mediated protective effects. Parallel in vivo studies in animal models of dry AMD should focus on local ocular delivery methods—potentially through intravitreal or controlled-release formulations—to minimize systemic exposure and optimize retinal bioavailability.

In conclusion, AMD3100 represents an exciting and scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its mechanism of CXCR4 antagonism and the hypothesized link between chronic SDF‐1/CXCR4 activation and impaired RPE phagocytosis. However, given the mixed evidence from ocular safety studies and the complexity of CXCR4 signaling in retinal homeostasis, further systematic preclinical evaluation is essential before advancing to clinical trials. The balance between inhibiting pathological inflammation and preserving or even harnessing protective regenerative signals will determine the ultimate viability of AMD3100 as a therapeutic agent for dry age‐related macular degeneration (Denoyer et al., 2012; Rabinovich-Nikitin et al., 2016; Bai et al., 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin is a naturally derived macrolide initially isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus and belongs to the class of mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) inhibitors. This compound, originally discovered for its immunosuppressive properties, has evolved into a prominent therapeutic candidate across several fields including oncology, immunology, and neurodegeneration. Its chemical derivation and structural complexity allow for potent and selective inhibition of the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1). Rapamycin is widely used in clinical settings as an immunosuppressant following organ transplantation and has been repurposed for other indications based on its ability to modulate intracellular signaling pathways that regulate cellular growth, survival, and autophagy. As such, its potential application in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on a body of work indicating that targeting mTORC1 can restore autophagic and lysosomal function in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—a crucial factor given that RPE dysfunction is central to AMD pathogenesis (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, rapamycin has been extensively used and investigated in various clinical and preclinical settings. Its initial clinical use as an immunosuppressive agent in organ transplant patients laid the groundwork for understanding its mechanisms of action and safety profile in humans. Beyond its immunosuppressive applications, rapamycin has been evaluated for its anti-proliferative effects in several types of cancer and for its capability to extend lifespan in model organisms; these studies underscore the drug’s pleiotropic effects on cellular metabolism and autophagy. Specifically regarding ocular therapeutics, preclinical studies on retinal degenerative diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa and glaucoma have demonstrated that mTOR modulation by rapamycin can exert neuroprotective properties in retinal tissues (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). In the realm of AMD, several investigations have focused on the role of autophagy and lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in RPE cells, where rapamycin has been shown to promote autophagy and decrease the buildup of toxic aggregates, such as lipofuscin (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical studies and safety evaluations—in particular, intravitreal injections in non-human primates—have provided encouraging data regarding the ocular safety profile of rapamycin, thus supporting its further exploration as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, rapamycin exerts its effects by binding to the intracellular receptor FKBP12 (FK506-binding protein 12). This drug–FKBP12 complex then interacts with mTORC1, leading to its allosteric inhibition. Under normal anabolic conditions, active mTORC1 phosphorylates several downstream targets, including the transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is sequestered in the cytosol in its phosphorylated state, thus preventing the transcription of genes associated with lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. When rapamycin inhibits mTORC1, the phosphorylation of TFEB is reduced, permitting its nuclear translocation. Once inside the nucleus, TFEB initiates the transcription of numerous genes involved in autophagy and lysosomal function, thereby enhancing the cell’s capacity to degrade and recycle cellular debris such as accumulated photoreceptor outer segments (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium, mTORC1 normally integrates growth factor signals, nutrient availability, and stress responses to tightly regulate cellular homeostasis. The inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin thus releases the “brake” on autophagy, as evidenced by increased expression of autophagic markers such as LC3-II and lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1. This cascading effect leads to an enhanced intracellular clearance system (phagolysosomal flux), which is particularly critical for RPE cells that are responsible for the daily degradation of shed POS. Several studies have demonstrated that rapamycin-treated RPE cells exhibit improved POS degradation, a reduction in lipofuscin-like granules, and overall restoration of lysosomal function (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, the molecular signatures observed in rapamycin-treated cells mimic those seen under conditions of caloric restriction, further supporting the notion that mTORC1 inhibition can activate protective autophagic pathways (Davis, 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). This advanced understanding of rapamycin’s mechanism of action provides a compelling rationale for its application in dry AMD, where the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and dysregulated autophagy are key pathological features (Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of rapamycin in dry AMD is that its inhibition of mTORC1 will lead to the activation of TFEB by reducing its cytosolic phosphorylation state, thereby promoting nuclear translocation. In iPSC-derived RPE models, this induction of TFEB activity is expected to upregulate a host of autophagy and lysosomal genes, which in turn should enhance the cellular degradation of photoreceptor outer segments—an essential process in maintaining retinal homeostasis (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025). Accordingly, the anticipated in vitro effects upon rapamycin treatment include a robust increase in autophagic flux evidenced by elevated levels of LC3-II and LAMP1, paired with improved processing and clearance of POS debris. This effect is crucial because impaired clearance mechanisms contribute to the accumulation of lipofuscin and other cellular waste materials in RPE cells, both of which are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Falcão et al., 2024).

Supporting this expected outcome are observations from previous studies where rapamycin has been associated with a reduction in autofluorescent granules and a restoration of normal cellular clearance dynamics in RPE cells (Falcão et al., 2024). Additionally, safety assessments performed through intravitreal administration in non-human primates have demonstrated that rapamycin can be delivered to the retina with minimal adverse events, thereby underpinning its feasibility for clinical translation (Falcão et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2022). Importantly, the hypothesis that rapamycin can act at IC₅₀ values as low as approximately 0.1 nM in RPE cells further reinforces the potential sensitivity and efficacy of this candidate in modulating the pathway of interest. Given the expression of mTOR, TFEB, LC3, and LAMP1 in RPE cells—and the established role of these proteins in the autophagic and lysosomal clearance of POS—the expected improvement in autophagic turnover should directly translate into enhanced cell function and potentially mitigate the progression of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2022; Intartaglia et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
Rapamycin emerges as a robust and mechanistically sound therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its established ability to inhibit mTORC1 and consequently activate autophagy and lysosomal gene expression through TFEB nuclear translocation. One of the major strengths of this candidate lies in the well-characterized molecular mechanism that connects mTORC1 inhibition with enhanced clearance of POS debris—a process that is fundamentally disrupted in dry AMD. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence, ranging from biochemical assays that show increased LC3-II and LAMP1 expression in rapamycin-treated RPE cells to preclinical safety data in non-human primates, bolsters confidence in its potential utility (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

Furthermore, the multifaceted benefits of mTORC1 inhibition extend beyond autophagy induction; rapamycin also offers neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects, both of which are advantageous in the treatment of retinal degenerative diseases (Chang et al., 2022). The leverage of TFEB activation not only addresses the aberrant accumulation of toxic cellular debris but may also promote a broader upregulation of lysosomal biogenesis, thereby preempting further functional decline of RPE cells. These properties make rapamycin a strong candidate for mitigating early events in AMD pathogenesis, particularly in the context of experimental iPSC-RPE models where enhanced phagocytic capacity can be directly measured.

Nevertheless, several challenges and potential weaknesses require careful consideration. Despite its promising mechanism and preclinical rationale, clinical trials evaluating rapamycin in the context of ocular diseases have yielded mixed results, with some studies documenting only marginal improvements in visual function and others noting issues related to the drug’s solubility and delivery (Marchesi et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022). In advanced AMD, where the disease pathology is more complex and multifactorial, rapamycin’s efficacy might be limited, and there is a need for precise dosing strategies to balance mTORC1 inhibition with the preservation of physiological mTOR functions that are crucial for RPE cell survival (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). Additionally, the potential for off-target effects or immunosuppressive consequences linked to systemic exposure—although minimized by intravitreal delivery—necessitates further investigation into long-term safety profiles (Wang et al., 2022).

Another potential limitation is the inherent complexity of autophagy regulation in the RPE, which can be influenced by factors such as oxidative stress, metabolic dysfunction, and age-related changes in lysosomal function. While rapamycin is effective in reactivating autophagic pathways under controlled experimental settings, its impact within the pathogenic environment of a diseased retina, particularly if inflammatory processes are simultaneously active, may be less predictable (Davis, 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, the therapeutic window for achieving beneficial rapamycin concentrations without incurring adverse events is not yet fully defined, underscoring the importance of pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic studies specifically tailored to ocular tissues (Falcão et al., 2024).

Taken together, the current body of evidence suggests that rapamycin’s capacity to restore autophagic homeostasis in RPE cells represents a solid mechanistic foundation for its use in dry AMD. Its ability to upregulate autophagy and lysosomal function through TFEB activation directly addresses known defects in the clearance pathways of RPE cells—a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Moreover, the safety data from preclinical intravitreal delivery studies provide additional incentive to advance this candidate further along the translational pipeline. However, given the mixed outcomes observed in some clinical contexts and the challenges related to drug formulation and optimal dosing, further comprehensive studies are warranted to clarify its efficacy in early versus advanced stages of AMD (Mei et al., 2022).

In conclusion, rapamycin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD shows significant promise from both a mechanistic and translational standpoint. Its well-documented ability to inhibit mTORC1, thereby releasing TFEB and ramping up autophagic and lysosomal gene expression, positions it uniquely to tackle the underpinnings of RPE dysfunction characteristic of dry AMD. While preclinical data support its efficacy and safety with intravitreal administration in non-human primates, challenges remain regarding its formulation, potential off-target effects, and the delineation of its therapeutic window in human subjects. Consequently, while rapamycin’s molecular mechanism and early experimental results are highly encouraging, further studies—especially those that integrate pharmacokinetic profiling, dose optimization, and long-term outcome measurements in relevant in vivo models—are essential before definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding its clinical utility for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Si et al., 2023).

Overall, the strengths of rapamycin include its robust and well-characterized action on mTORC1, its downstream activation of autophagic and lysosomal pathways via TFEB, and supportive preclinical safety data in ocular models. In contrast, its weaknesses lie in the variable efficacy observed in clinical studies, formulation challenges due to low solubility, and the need for careful dosing to avoid potential adverse effects related to systemic immunosuppression. These considerations collectively argue for the continued investigation of rapamycin as a therapeutic option for dry AMD with a focus on optimizing delivery strategies and characterizing its long-term impact on retinal structure and function (Wang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AM580 is a fully synthetic retinoid compound designed as a highly selective agonist for the retinoic acid receptor α (RARα). Its chemical structure—a derivative of naphthalene and benzoic acid—was rationally engineered to confer two key properties: a more rigid molecular architecture compared with the natural ligand all‐trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and a marked preferential binding to RARα over other retinoid receptor subtypes (RARβ and RARγ) (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992). The molecule’s chemical name, 4-(5,6,7,8-tetrahydro-5,5,8,8-tetramethyl-2-naphthalenyl)carboxamido]benzoic acid, reflects its derivation from a series of modifications intended to enhance receptor selectivity and bioactivity (Martin et al., 1992). AM580 belongs to the broader class of retinoids—compounds that are either natural derivatives of vitamin A or synthetically modified analogues—which function as ligands for nuclear hormone receptors. Retinoids have been exploited in various fields of medicine due to their ability to modulate cellular differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis by activating retinoic acid receptor (RAR) and retinoid X receptor (RXR) pathways (Cras et al., 2010; Martin et al., 1992). In the case of AM580, its design emphasizes selective RARα activation, as demonstrated by its 30-fold higher binding affinity for RARα compared to RARβ and RARγ (Teng et al., 1996; Martin et al., 1992), making it an excellent molecular tool for dissection of RARα-specific biological responses.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, retinoids have been at the forefront of differentiation therapy, with ATRA being successfully employed in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) (Garattini et al., 2007; Garattini et al., 1997). However, the clinical use of natural retinoids like ATRA has been limited by drawbacks such as isomerization, rapid metabolism, and broad receptor engagement leading to unnecessary side effects (Drowley et al., 2020; Cras et al., 2010). These limitations spurred the development of receptor subtype–selective ligands, among which AM580 emerged as a leading RARα-selective agonist (Martin et al., 1992). Beyond oncology, synthetic retinoids have been investigated in a variety of contexts including dermatology and even cardiovascular applications (Nagy et al., 2012; Petrukhin, 2013); however, more recent studies have explored the potential ocular applications of retinoid receptor agonists. In particular, a growing body of literature has begun to examine the effects of RAR agonists on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that activation of RARα in RPE cells by compounds such as AM580 can modulate epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and improve cellular functions relevant to retinal homeostasis (Kobayashi et al., 2021). Although not previously approved as an ocular therapeutic, the compound’s use in research settings—including those investigating phagocytic processes in the RPE—provides a promising precedent for repurposing it for conditions like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of AM580 is well delineated at the molecular level. As an RARα agonist, it binds with high affinity to the ligand-binding domain of RARα, a nuclear receptor that functions as a ligand-dependent transcription factor. Upon ligand binding, the receptor undergoes a conformational change that results in the dissociation of co-repressor complexes and the recruitment of co-activators and other transcriptional machinery. This ligand-induced activation facilitates the heterodimerization of RARα with retinoid X receptor (RXR), followed by binding to retinoic acid response elements (RAREs) in the promoter regions of target genes (Garattini et al., 2007; Teng et al., 1996).  
Notably, AM580’s structural modification—featuring a polar amide linkage—enhances its selectivity for RARα by promoting specific hydrogen bonding interactions within the receptor’s binding pocket that are not available in RARβ or RARγ (Teng et al., 1996). Once activated, RARα modulates a variety of downstream genes. Among these, studies have recently indicated that selective RARα activation can lead to the upregulation of milk fat globule epidermal growth factor 8 (MFGE8) in RPE cells (Unknown Reference). MFGE8 plays a critical role in facilitating the bridging of phosphatidylserine (exposed on the shed photoreceptor outer segments (POS)) to integrin receptors—specifically αvβ5—which are expressed on the RPE, thereby promoting efficient phagocytosis (Drowley et al., 2020; Kobayashi et al., 2021). Consequently, AM580’s engagement of RARα is expected to not only drive transcriptional changes related to RPE differentiation and anti-fibrotic responses but also directly enhance phagocytic clearance mechanisms essential for retinal health (Kobayashi et al., 2021). In additional preclinical settings, RARα agonism via AM580 has been implicated in modulating transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling pathways, which further supports its capacity to inhibit aberrant EMT—a process implicated in retinal scarring and progression of dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis under evaluation posits that AM580, by selectively activating RARα at an effective concentration (EC₅₀ ~50 nM as observed in RPE cell assays), will stimulate the transcription of the MFGE8 gene. Upregulation of MFGE8 is crucial because this glycoprotein acts as a “molecular bridge” by binding to phosphatidylserine on POS and to integrin receptors such as αvβ5 on the RPE. Under normal conditions, MFGE8 is an essential mediator of RPE phagocytosis, facilitating the daily clearance of spent outer segments—a process that is impaired in dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2012). Evidence from preclinical studies, including those using Mertk-deficient RPE models, suggests that AM580 treatment can lead to increased MFGE8 levels and a concomitant improvement in POS uptake (Kobayashi et al., 2021). Thus, in the assay proposed by the team, AM580 is expected to restore or enhance the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells by boosting MFGE8 expression. This improved clearance mechanism would help reduce the accumulation of POS debris and lipofuscin—a buildup known to contribute to RPE dysfunction and the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Furthermore, secondary effects such as the inhibition of deleterious EMT processes—which are associated with fibrosis and the progression of dry AMD—may also be realized, thereby preserving or restoring a more differentiated, functional RPE phenotype (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

AM580 represents a compelling therapeutic candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, based on several lines of evidence gathered from the literature. Its primary strength lies in its high degree of selectivity for RARα. This receptor selectivity is critical because it allows for target‐specific modulation of gene expression, potentially reducing the broad side effects observed with natural retinoids like ATRA that activate multiple receptor subtypes (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992; Teng et al., 1996). The structural optimization of AM580 not only confers potent agonistic activity but also provides a pharmacological tool for dissecting the specific roles of RARα in retinal biology, particularly within the RPE. Preclinical studies have underscored the utility of RARα activation in modulating key processes such as cellular differentiation, inhibition of EMT, and enhancement of phagocytic function in RPE cells (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2012).  
However, several potential challenges must also be acknowledged. Retinoid compounds are notorious for their complex pharmacokinetics and potential for off-target effects, including teratogenicity, as evidenced by prior studies of AM580 in teratogenicity models (Elmazar et al., 2001). The delicate balance between efficacy and safety remains a critical issue, particularly for a condition such as dry AMD where long-term treatment is anticipated. Clinical validation in human subjects is still lacking, and the translation of dose levels, tissue penetration, and metabolic stability from the laboratory to the clinic remains an open question (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Another concern is that AM580, while selective, does retain some activity at RARβ and RARγ at higher concentrations (Teng et al., 1996), an effect that may have unpredictable consequences on cell signaling in the complex microenvironment of the RPE. Moreover, the retinoid system is intricately linked with multiple signaling pathways, and long-term modulation may lead to compensatory mechanisms or unforeseen adverse outcomes.  
In summary, the repurposing of AM580 for dry AMD is supported by a robust molecular rationale—its ability to selectively activate RARα is directly linked to the upregulation of MFGE8 and, consequently, the enhancement of POS phagocytosis in RPE cells. This mechanism directly addresses a critical defect in dry AMD pathology, namely the impaired clearance of photoreceptor debris, which is a central driver of retinal degeneration (Garattini et al., 2007; Kobayashi et al., 2021). The preclinical literature offers promising evidence that selective RARα modulation can exert beneficial effects on RPE physiology, including the prevention of EMT and restoration of phagocytic function (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Despite these strengths, the transition from preclinical studies to clinical application will require careful attention to pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic factors, as well as rigorous safety assessments to mitigate risks typical of retinoid therapies. Overall, while challenges remain, AM580’s unique properties render it a promising candidate that merits further investigation in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to fill a significant therapeutic gap in the management of this debilitating condition (Martin et al., 1992; Teng et al., 1996; Kobayashi et al., 2021).
