Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Adalimumab (marketed as Humira) is a fully humanized recombinant IgG1 monoclonal antibody developed using recombinant DNA technology that targets tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNFα). As a member of the anti‐TNFα class of biologics, adalimumab is designed to bind both soluble and membrane‐bound TNFα with high affinity, thereby preventing its interaction with the TNF receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2) on target cells. This antibody was originally discovered and engineered to address systemic inflammatory diseases, and its fully human composition is intended to lower immunogenicity compared to earlier chimeric molecules such as infliximab. In its development, molecular engineering efforts focused on isolating the relevant antibody variable regions that exhibit specificity for TNFα, followed by the construction of a recombinant molecule with human constant regions to improve tolerability and clinical efficacy. Anti‐TNFα antibodies belong to a broader class of therapeutic compounds that have dramatically changed the treatment landscape for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. They have been widely applied in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn’s disease, and ulcerative colitis, and over the past two decades, their use has been extended into ocular inflammatory diseases such as non‐infectious uveitis. Such applications underscore the versatility and translational potential of TNFα inhibition in modulating inflammatory cascades (Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History:  
Adalimumab’s clinical journey began with its approval for systemic autoimmune diseases where TNFα plays a fundamental role in mediating inflammation and tissue damage. Its robust performance in rheumatoid arthritis and related conditions has been well documented in numerous large-scale randomized controlled trials, which demonstrated significant improvement in clinical outcomes and inflammatory markers. These successes provided the foundation for exploring its application in other diseases characterized by inflammatory dysregulation. In recent years, growing evidence from both biochemical studies and clinical observations has highlighted the role of chronic inflammation in the pathogenesis of several retinal degenerative disorders. In particular, studies have shown that TNFα is upregulated in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and may contribute to the degeneration seen in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). For example, preclinical work has demonstrated that inflammation mediated by TNFα can impair the integrity of RPE cells, reduce the expression of proteins critical for RPE function (including visual cycle proteins and complement regulators) and disrupt phagocytic clearance mechanisms; these findings form the basis for hypothesizing that TNFα blockade may preserve RPE function in dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

While the majority of clinical uses of adalimumab have been in the realm of systemic and ocular inflammatory conditions such as non‐infectious uveitis, there has been emerging interest in repurposing anti‐TNFα therapies for retinal degenerations. In the context of ocular disease, several investigators have explored both systemic and local (intravitreal or subconjunctival) routes of administration to modulate intraocular inflammation. Pilot clinical trials and case reports have assessed intravitreal adalimumab in patients with uveitis and even in those with neovascular (“wet”) AMD refractory to anti‐VEGF therapies; these studies reported varying degrees of efficacy and underscored an acceptable local safety profile, though in some instances, higher dosages have been associated with ocular toxicity. In animal studies, intravitreal or subconjunctival administration of adalimumab has been shown to reduce inflammation and offer neuroprotection in models of retinal degeneration, such as in the rd10 mouse model for retinitis pigmentosa, establishing a precedent for local administration to achieve high ocular levels with minimal systemic exposure. Despite these advancements, use of adalimumab specifically for dry AMD has not been established in clinical practice. The proposed approach builds on the mechanistic insights from studies demonstrating that elevated TNFα levels can lead to downregulation of phagocytic receptors and lysosomal enzymes in RPE cells—processes central to dry AMD pathology—and posits that reversing these effects via TNFα neutralization may preserve RPE function (Nashine et al., 2022; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of adalimumab centers on its targeted neutralization of TNFα. TNFα is a proinflammatory cytokine produced by a variety of cell types that include activated T lymphocytes, macrophages, and, importantly, resident cells in the eye such as RPE and Müller glia. When secreted into the extracellular milieu, TNFα binds to its receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2), triggering intracellular signaling cascades that lead to the activation of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and other pathways that promote the expression of additional inflammatory cytokines, adhesion molecules, and matrix metalloproteinases. These processes collectively contribute to a sustained inflammatory response that can result in cellular dysfunction and death. Adalimumab, by virtue of its high affinity binding, sequesters TNFα and prevents receptor engagement. In doing so, it effectively interrupts these downstream proinflammatory signals and halts the amplification of the inflammatory cascade (Wang et al., 2011; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium cells, TNFα-mediated signaling has been implicated in the suppression of genes critical to the maintenance of RPE functions. Specifically, experimental studies have suggested that exposure to TNFα leads to a reduction in the expression of MERTK—a receptor tyrosine kinase essential for the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—as well as cathepsin D, a lysosomal enzyme crucial for the degradation of engulfed material. The decrease in MERTK expression compromises the ability of RPE cells to efficiently phagocytose POS, thereby potentially contributing to the accumulation of cellular debris, drusen formation, and further RPE stress that are characteristic of dry AMD. In parallel, a reduction in cathepsin D would impair lysosomal degradation, exacerbating the intracellular buildup of waste products and further undermining cellular homeostasis in the RPE. By neutralizing TNFα, adalimumab is hypothesized to prevent these detrimental changes, preserving the expression levels of MERTK and cathepsin D and thereby maintaining robust phagocytic and degradative capacity in RPE cells (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021).

At the molecular level, the binding of adalimumab to TNFα is mediated via its antigen-binding (Fab) region, which recognizes specific epitopes on the cytokine. This interaction is characterized by high affinity and specificity, ensuring that even low concentrations of the antibody can effectively neutralize TNFα activity. The blockade prevents TNFα from initiating receptor-mediated signaling that would otherwise promote inflammation and cellular stress. Moreover, because TNFα is known to regulate not only inflammatory cytokine production but also apoptotic processes, its inhibition may confer additional neuroprotective effects in the retina by reducing signals that lead to programmed cell death. The comprehensive inhibition of TNFα by adalimumab therefore stands as a multifaceted intervention, addressing both the inflammatory insult and its secondary effects on critical cellular functions in the RPE (Wang et al., 2011; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Nashine et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for leveraging adalimumab in dry AMD rests on its potential to neutralize elevated TNFα levels in the subretinal microenvironment. Elevated TNFα has been implicated in the pathological downregulation of key proteins involved in RPE function, notably MERTK and cathepsin D. MERTK is a receptor that plays an essential role in the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, a process that is critical for the renewal of photoreceptors and the overall maintenance of retinal health. Cathepsin D, on the other hand, is involved in the lysosomal degradation of the ingested material; together, these proteins ensure that the RPE can effectively clear and recycle photoreceptor debris. In dry AMD, this phagocytic process is compromised, leading to the accumulation of cellular waste products and drusen formation, which further fuels inflammation and RPE degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Administration of adalimumab is expected to interrupt this cascade by neutralizing TNFα, thereby preventing its signaling that leads to the downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D. With TNFα effectively neutralized, RPE cells should experience a more favorable molecular milieu in which the expression of these critical proteins is maintained at functional levels. This preservation would, in turn, support the RPE’s capacity to phagocytose and degrade photoreceptor outer segments, thereby averting the buildup of toxic waste products. Furthermore, since TNFα signaling also contributes to other aspects of cellular stress and inflammation—such as the upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines and the induction of apoptotic pathways—the neutralization of TNFα by adalimumab may also reduce overall cellular stress and promote RPE cell survival and function (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022).

In vitro assays using cultured human RPE cells exposed to TNFα could be employed to test this hypothesis. In these experiments, treatment with adalimumab should result in the normalization or preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression levels when compared to TNFα-treated controls. In addition, functional assays measuring the uptake and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (or surrogate fluorescent particles) would be expected to show improved phagocytic efficiency in RPE cells treated with adalimumab. Such findings would provide robust mechanistic support for the proposed therapeutic strategy. Moreover, preliminary in vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD or models of induced RPE dysfunction could further validate that TNFα blockade leads to preservation of RPE integrity, improved photoreceptor survival, and retardation of retinal degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Considering that the expression of MERTK is well documented in RPE cells and that its function is critical for POS phagocytosis—a process that declines with aging and in the presence of inflammatory mediators—the ability of adalimumab to maintain or restore MERTK expression would be highly relevant in the context of dry AMD. In the proposed strategy, adalimumab may also help to stabilize other RPE functions, such as the regulation of the complement cascade and the visual cycle, both of which have been shown to be adversely affected by TNFα exposure. Thus, the anticipated effect of adalimumab is not limited solely to the preservation of phagocytic machinery; it may also contribute to a broader stabilization of RPE cell health in the face of chronic low-grade inflammation that characterizes dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of adalimumab as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a compelling yet cautiously optimistic perspective. One of the principal strengths of adalimumab lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action; by neutralizing TNFα, it directly addresses a central mediator of inflammation that has been implicated in the dysregulation of RPE functions. The experimental evidence indicating that TNFα exposure can lead to the downregulation of essential proteins such as MERTK and cathepsin D provides a strong rationale for the hypothesis that TNFα inhibition might preserve the RPE’s ability to maintain photoreceptor homeostasis. This mechanistic insight is particularly attractive because it targets one of the fundamental dysfunctions in dry AMD—namely, the failure of the RPE to clear photoreceptor outer segments effectively, which leads to the accumulation of drusen and progressive retinal degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the extensive clinical experience with adalimumab in systemic and ocular inflammatory diseases supports its safety profile. The fact that adalimumab is already approved by regulatory agencies, coupled with several clinical studies demonstrating its localized safety when administered intravitreally or via related routes in ocular conditions such as uveitis, adds to its attractiveness as a candidate for repurposing (Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010; Leal et al., 2018; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. To date, most studies involving adalimumab in the ocular context have focused on inflammatory conditions such as uveitis and neovascular AMD rather than dry AMD specifically. As a result, direct clinical evidence supporting its efficacy in preserving RPE phagocytic function in dry AMD is currently limited. The hypothesis that adalimumab can prevent the TNFα-induced downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D is primarily based on preclinical observations, and further mechanistic studies, both in vitro and in relevant animal models, are necessary to validate this pathway in the context of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Nashine et al., 2022; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Another potential challenge with using adalimumab for dry AMD is related to drug delivery and dosing. While intravitreal administration has shown promise in limited studies, determining the optimal dose that achieves effective TNFα blockade without incurring retinal toxicity remains an unresolved issue. Some animal studies have indicated that higher doses of intravitreal adalimumab can lead to retinal inflammation, reduced electroretinogram responses, or histopathological evidence of toxicity. Given that dry AMD is a chronic condition and would likely require repeated dosing or sustained drug delivery systems, the long-term safety of local TNFα blockade needs to be rigorously evaluated (Manzano et al., 2008; Pascual-Camps et al., 2014).

Moreover, because TNFα plays roles in normal immune surveillance and tissue repair, its complete inhibition—especially in an aged population that may have impaired immune responses—could theoretically predispose patients to infections or other adverse effects. Although the systemic safety profile of adalimumab is well established, the ocular microenvironment has distinct immunological characteristics, and the long-term effects of TNFα inhibition on retinal homeostasis, particularly regarding complement activation and maintenance of the blood–retinal barrier, require further study. There is also the possibility that compensatory inflammatory pathways may become activated in response to TNFα blockade, potentially diminishing the efficacy of the intervention over time (García-Layana et al., 2021; Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Sharma et al., 2009).

Additionally, the magnitude of the contribution of TNFα to the pathogenesis of dry AMD relative to other factors—such as oxidative stress, genetic predispositions (including polymorphisms in complement factors), and lipid metabolism abnormalities—remains to be fully delineated. It is possible that TNFα is one of several drivers of RPE dysfunction, and that its inhibition may need to be combined with other therapeutic strategies (for example, antioxidant supplementation or complement inhibitors) to achieve a meaningful clinical benefit. Therefore, while the rationale for adalimumab is compelling, a monotherapy approach may not be sufficient to halt the multifactorial progression of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nussenblatt et al., 2010).

In summary, adalimumab presents a promising repurposed candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on its potent and specific inhibition of TNFα—a cytokine implicated in the downregulation of crucial RPE proteins such as MERTK and cathepsin D. The drug’s extensive use in other inflammatory settings, along with preliminary evidence supporting its ocular safety, lend credibility to the hypothesis that TNFα blockade can preserve the phagocytic machinery of RPE cells and potentially slow the degenerative process characteristic of dry AMD. Nevertheless, significant challenges remain, including the need for robust preclinical validation in dry AMD models, optimization of ocular dosing regimens, and long-term safety assessments in an elderly population. A carefully designed series of in vitro experiments using human RPE cells—followed by well-controlled animal studies—should be undertaken to establish proof of concept regarding the preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression and function. If these studies yield positive results, subsequent early-phase clinical trials could be justified to evaluate the efficacy of intravitreal adalimumab in patients with dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010).

In light of these considerations, our recommendation is to advance adalimumab into a rigorous preclinical testing pipeline aimed specifically at dry AMD models. This should include studies that measure the expression levels and activity of MERTK and cathepsin D in RPE cells under conditions of TNFα stimulation, both in the presence and absence of adalimumab treatment. Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiling in ocular tissues, along with assessments of retinal structure and function via in vivo imaging and electrophysiological testing, will be critical to determining an appropriate dosing strategy. Finally, integration with complementary therapeutic approaches may be considered to address other facets of dry AMD pathogenesis. While the path to clinical application is fraught with challenges, the potential benefit of preserving RPE phagocytic function—and by extension, photoreceptor survival—in a disease with very limited current treatment options provides a strong impetus for further development of this candidate (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022).

In conclusion, adalimumab’s established molecular profile as a potent TNFα inhibitor, its extensive clinical track record in systemic and ocular inflammatory diseases, and the emerging data linking TNFα to RPE dysfunction collectively support the rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD. Nevertheless, given the complexity of AMD pathogenesis and the potential risks associated with chronic intraocular immunomodulation, a thorough and methodical approach to preclinical investigation is warranted before embarking on large-scale clinical trials. The ultimate goal is to validate that neutralization of TNFα can indeed preserve the phagocytic capabilities of the RPE, thereby maintaining retinal health and preventing the progression of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Strengths of this candidate include its potent and specific inhibition of TNFα, which is a key mediator in inflammatory cascades, its favorable immunogenicity profile stemming from its fully human composition, and its prior demonstration of safety in ocular applications such as uveitis. In addition, the biological rationale is supported by evidence that TNFα negatively impacts the expression of proteins critical for RPE phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation—a process that, when impaired, underlies the pathology of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

On the other hand, weaknesses center on the limited direct evidence for efficacy in dry AMD, potential challenges in achieving precise intraocular dosing without inducing retinal toxicity, and uncertain long-term consequences of sustained TNFα inhibition in the delicate immune environment of the eye. Moreover, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD suggests that a singular focus on TNFα may not fully address the disease’s complex pathophysiology, raising the possibility that combination therapies might eventually be necessary for optimal outcomes (Manzano et al., 2008; Sharma et al., 2009; Nussenblatt et al., 2010).

Given these observations, our evaluation concludes that adalimumab represents a promising and scientifically sound candidate for repurposing to treat dry AMD. Its mechanistic profile aligns well with the goal of preserving RPE phagocytic function by preventing TNFα-mediated downregulation of key proteins like MERTK and cathepsin D. However, to move forward with this candidate, research efforts must focus on resolving the outstanding questions through rigorous preclinical studies, optimization of the drug delivery method, and detailed long-term safety assessments. If successful, these steps could pave the way for early-phase clinical trials designed to test the efficacy of intravitreal adalimumab in stabilizing or improving RPE function in patients with dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010).

In summary, while the current body of literature on adalimumab has primarily focused on its role in systemic inflammatory diseases and ocular inflammatory conditions such as uveitis and neovascular AMD, the underlying mechanistic data provide a persuasive rationale for extending its application to dry AMD. The hypothesis that adalimumab can preserve RPE phagocytic function by neutralizing TNFα—thereby preventing the deleterious downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D—is scientifically plausible and merits further systematic investigation. The potential benefits of repurposing a well-characterized agent with an established safety profile are substantial, especially in a disease area where effective treatments remain elusive (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Overall, our recommendation for the drug development team is to prioritize a series of detailed preclinical studies that examine the effects of adalimumab on RPE cells under TNFα-induced stress conditions, with particular emphasis on the regulation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression and subsequent phagocytic activity. These studies should involve both conventional cell culture models and in vivo models that mimic the chronic inflammatory environment observed in dry AMD. Should these studies yield positive results, a phase I/II clinical trial focusing on safety and early efficacy in patients with dry AMD would be justified. This stepwise approach will ensure that the promising mechanistic rationale is thoroughly vetted before large-scale clinical application (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

In conclusion, the convergence of molecular, biochemical, and clinical evidence supports the further exploration of adalimumab as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to mitigate TNFα-mediated inflammatory cascades could play a critical role in preserving RPE function, maintaining photoreceptor health, and ultimately slowing the progression of a disease that currently lacks effective treatments. Nonetheless, rigorous preclinical validation and careful consideration of dosing and long-term safety will be essential to realize its potential in this new indication (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SHP099 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule allosteric inhibitor of the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP2 (PTPN11) discovered by Novartis through a target-biased screening paradigm that enriched for modulators of full-length, autoinhibited SHP2 and counter-selected catalytic-site binders, followed by structure-based medicinal chemistry optimization to stabilize the closed SHP2 conformation rather than engage the conserved active site (chemical identity: 6-(4-amino-4-methylpiperidin-1-yl)-3-(2,3-dichlorophenyl)pyrazin-2-amine) (PDB: 5EHR) (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kong & Long, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). In the 1.7 Å co-crystal, SHP099 occupies a central “tunnel” at the interface of the N-SH2, C-SH2, and PTP domains present only in the autoinhibited state; its aminopyrazine/amine motif forms hydrogen bonds to Arg111 and Phe113 in the SH2 linker and to Glu250 in the PTP domain, while a 2,3-dichlorophenyl moiety engages hydrophobic residues (Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, Gln495), thereby clamping the interdomain interface and disfavoring opening/activation (ligand volume ~262 Å3; tunnel ~464 Å3) (Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Biochemically, SHP099 is potent and selective (SHP2 enzymatic IC50 ≈ 0.070–0.071 µM; no detectable activity across panels of 21 phosphatases and 66 kinases, including SHP1) and translates to cellular pathway inhibition (p-ERK IC50 ≈ 0.250 µM), with high aqueous solubility, high permeability without efflux, and acceptable mouse oral exposure/bioavailability (~46%) (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kong & Long, 2022). Mechanistically, SHP099 functions as a “molecular glue” that stabilizes the closed, autoinhibited SHP2 conformation via a conformational selection mechanism; affinity is reduced for strongly activating SHP2 mutants (for example, E76K) that bias the open state, although high concentrations can re-close some mutants in vitro and in cells (Meem, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).

SHP099 belongs to the class of SHP2 “tunnel-site” (site 1) allosteric inhibitors that stabilize the autoinhibited state by engaging the N-SH2/C-SH2/PTP interdomain pocket; dual allosteric occupancy (site 1 plus a distal latch, site 2) is structurally and biochemically validated and produces cooperative inhibition when SHP099 is combined with a site-2 ligand (for example SHP244 analogs), underscoring the druggability of multiple noncatalytic surfaces on SHP2 (Fodor et al., 2018; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Discovery and SAR established that the aminopyrazine ring amine is essential (Glu250 H-bond), the 4-amino-4-methylpiperidine motif is favored over piperazines for potency, and an ortho-chlorine on the phenyl ring is critical; a representative synthesis employs Suzuki–Miyaura coupling to install the dichlorophenyl substituent on a pyrazinamine core, followed by SNAr to append the Boc-protected 4-methylpiperidin-4-amine and final acid deprotection to the free base (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-level development moved the SHP099 pharmacophore into diverse chemotypes (for example, pyrimidinones and fused bicyclic pyrazolopyrimidinones) and into clinical candidates (for example, TNO155, RMC-4630, BBP-398), reflecting translational momentum for SHP2 allosteric inhibition (Kerr et al., 2021; Tojjari et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
SHP099 established in vivo proof-of-concept for allosteric SHP2 inhibition in oncology. In an EGFR-amplified esophageal squamous carcinoma xenograft (KYSE-520), oral SHP099 produced dose-dependent pathway suppression (tumor p-ERK), antiproliferative effects, and tumor growth inhibition up to stasis at 100 mg/kg, supported by measurable exposure and oral bioavailability (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Additional preclinical efficacy includes activity in EGFR-driven xenografts and reduction of leukemic burden in FLT3-ITD–positive AML models after oral dosing, with no overt toxicity noted in those studies (Dempke et al., 2018). In glioblastoma models, SHP099 achieved brain exposure after 100 mg/kg oral dosing, reduced tumor growth and vascularity in orthotopic xenografts, and showed activity both as monotherapy and combined with temozolomide, demonstrating CNS penetration and antitumor pharmacology in mice (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-wide, SHP2 allosteric inhibitors have shown single-agent and combination efficacy in RTK/RAS/MAPK-driven tumors, have been advanced into clinical studies across multiple solid tumors, and display mechanism-consistent biomarker modulation (for example, decreased p-ERK) in preclinical models (Kerr et al., 2021; Stanford & Bottini, 2023; Tojjari et al., 2023).

Within the materials provided here, there are no reports of SHP099 (or any SHP2 allosteric inhibitor) being used in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis models, or any ocular indication; multiple reviews focus on oncology/immuno-oncology and either enumerate preclinical tumor evidence or clinical oncology programs, without ocular/retinal data (Kerr et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2020). Consequently, repurposing SHP099 for dry AMD would be a first-in-class application with no precedent in the supplied literature (Yuan et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
SHP2 is maintained in an autoinhibited state by intramolecular engagement of the N-SH2 domain with the PTP catalytic domain; engagement of SH2 domains by bis-phosphotyrosyl motifs on receptors/adaptors relieves autoinhibition, allowing both catalytic and scaffolding functions that couple receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) to RAS activation and downstream MAPK/PI3K signaling (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). SHP099 binds in a tunnel formed by the N-SH2, C-SH2, and PTP domains of autoinhibited SHP2 and locks this closed conformation: crystallography defines hydrogen bonds to Arg111 and Phe113 (SH2 linker) and Glu250 (PTP domain), and hydrophobic contacts to Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, and Gln495 that together stabilize the interface and preclude opening; pre-organization of Arg111 additionally supports a cationic–π interaction with SHP099’s dichlorophenyl ring (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Selectivity over SHP1 is rationalized structurally by differences in SH2-linker/tunnel geometry that preclude analogous Arg/Phe contacts, consistent with lack of SHP1 inhibition in broad profiling (Diop et al., 2022). Binding follows conformational selection, with lowered potency against mutants that favor the open state (for example, E76K, D61Y), though high concentrations or dual-site allosteric occupancy can re-close certain mutants and enhance inhibition (Fodor et al., 2018; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-level medicinal chemistry around SHP099 uncovered both optimization paths (for example, pyrimidinones, fused bicyclic scaffolds) and liabilities such as unexpected hERG inhibition in some derivatives and combination-dosing tolerability issues in mice, underscoring the need for careful safety pharmacology (Meem, 2022).

RPE POS phagocytosis is a ligand-directed, RTK-driven process with defined signaling architecture. Externalized phosphatidylserine on shed POS tips is opsonized (for example, by MFG-E8), engages apical αvβ5 integrin, and triggers a pathway in which MerTK (activated by Gas6 or Protein S) is essential for physiological engulfment in vivo; loss-of-function MERTK mutations in RCS rats or humans abolish POS internalization and cause rapid photoreceptor degeneration (Ghosh et al., 2024; Moran et al., 2022). At the cytoskeletal level, formation of the F-actin phagocytic cup beneath bound POS requires Rac1 activation and a concurrent decrease in RhoA/ROCK-mediated contractility; RhoA elevation blocks cup formation even when Rac1 is active, whereas ROCK inhibition is both necessary and sufficient to enable cup formation and POS internalization and can rescue engulfment and acidification in MerTK-deficient RPE ex vivo (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Mao & Finnemann, 2021). Mechanistically downstream of MerTK, Src is activated and (i) phosphorylates and activates focal adhesion kinase (FAK), recruiting the p130CAS/CRKII/DOCK180 module that activates Rac1, and (ii) phosphorylates GDP-dissociation inhibitor GDI1, promoting dissociation from Rab5 to facilitate Rab cycling needed for cup formation and early phagosome dynamics (Shelby et al., 2015). These pathways define measurable biochemical checkpoints (MerTK/Src/FAK phosphorylation, Rac1-GTP, RhoA/ROCK activity) and functional readouts (cup formation, internalization, phagolysosomal acidification) relevant to any attempt to modulate RPE phagocytosis pharmacologically (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Moran et al., 2022).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis is that SHP099 will inhibit SHP2 in RPE (biochemical IC50 ~70–75 nM), sustain MerTK phosphorylation, maintain Rac1-GTP, and thereby increase POS internalization. The supplied literature confirms that SHP099 potently and selectively inhibits SHP2 by stabilizing the autoinhibited state and blocks RTK→RAS/MAPK signaling in cells, but it does not demonstrate that SHP2 directly dephosphorylates MerTK in RPE or that SHP2 inhibition prolongs MerTK phosphorylation or increases RPE POS uptake (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). Across systems, SHP2 acts as a positive transducer linking activated RTKs to RAS/ERK signaling; SHP2 allosteric inhibition decouples upstream RTKs from RAS activation, lowering RAS-GTP and p-ERK, which is consistent with a broad attenuation of RTK-driven outputs rather than prolonged receptor phosphorylation per se (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). Within the provided ocular literature, the only experimentally demonstrated pharmacologic rescue of RPE POS uptake is acute ROCK inhibition, which operates downstream of MerTK to reduce actomyosin contractility and enable cup formation and internalization—even rescuing MerTK-deficient RPE ex vivo—whereas elevating RhoA blocks phagocytosis despite Rac1 activation (Mao & Finnemann, 2021). Thus, while SHP099 will almost certainly inhibit SHP2 in RPE if exposure is achieved, the predicted increase in POS internalization via prolonged MerTK phosphorylation and sustained Rac1-GTP is speculative and not supported by direct evidence in the materials provided here (Kerr et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2020).

If the assay readout is POS phagocytosis in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE, the mechanistic checkpoints most directly supported by the literature are: phosphorylation kinetics of MerTK and Src/FAK; Rac1-GTP elevation coincident with cup formation; RhoA/ROCK suppression; and functional measures of cup assembly, POS internalization, and phagolysosomal acidification, with a ROCK inhibitor as a validated positive control (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Mao & Finnemann, 2021; Moran et al., 2022). Ocular pharmacokinetics for SHP099 are unknown in the provided corpus; although brain exposure has been documented after oral dosing in mice, retinal/RPE exposure should not be inferred and would need to be measured for systemic or local (for example, intravitreal) dosing paradigms (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths for repurposing consideration  
- Potent, selective, and structurally validated target engagement. SHP099 is characterized at atomic resolution (PDB 5EHR) with a coherent interaction network (Arg111, Phe113, Glu250; Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, Gln495) that rationalizes potency, selectivity versus SHP1, and conformational bias, increasing confidence that SHP2 inhibition will translate biochemically in RPE if drug exposure is achieved (Diop et al., 2022; Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Drug-like properties and in vivo activity. SHP099 exhibits favorable physicochemical properties (high solubility; Caco-2 permeability without efflux), oral bioavailability (~46% in mice), dose-dependent pathway modulation in tumors, and robust xenograft efficacy; CNS exposure after oral dosing has been demonstrated in mice, indicating trans-barrier distribution is feasible with adequate exposure (Fortanet et al., 2016; Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Class-level translational experience. Multiple SHP2 allosteric inhibitors derived from the SHP099 tunnel pharmacophore have entered clinical testing across solid tumors, enabling leverage of class pharmacology, safety learning, and combination strategies if ocular repurposing proceeds (Kerr et al., 2021; Stanford & Bottini, 2023; Tojjari et al., 2023).

Key weaknesses and risks specific to dry AMD/RPE phagocytosis  
- Mechanistic gap in RPE. The premise that SHP2 dephosphorylates MerTK to terminate phagocytic signaling in RPE, and that SHP2 inhibition will prolong MerTK phosphorylation and sustain Rac1 activation, is not supported by the supplied literature; no direct data link SHP2 to MerTK regulation in RPE or demonstrate SHP099-induced increases in POS uptake (Kerr et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2020). In contrast, RhoA/ROCK suppression is a validated, decisive permissive event for cup formation/internalization and can rescue MerTK deficiency, suggesting that targeting ROCK remains a higher-confidence pharmacological route to enhance POS uptake (Mao & Finnemann, 2021).  
- Potential on-target countereffects on trophic RTK signaling. SHP2 broadly transduces RTK signals to RAS/ERK; allosteric SHP2 inhibition reduces RAS-GTP/p-ERK by disconnecting RTKs from downstream pathways, which could dampen beneficial RTK-mediated homeostatic signaling in RPE and choroid (for example, PDGFR, c-MET, IGF1R) even if MerTK phosphorylation were transiently increased, necessitating careful evaluation of RPE viability and stress responses in addition to phagocytosis endpoints (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021).  
- Ocular PK/tissue exposure unknown. There is no reported ocular distribution for SHP099 in the materials provided; CNS penetration does not ensure retinal/RPE exposure, and systemic dosing to achieve ocular levels may be limited by plasma protein binding, efflux, or tolerability, while intravitreal dosing introduces local safety and formulation challenges that would require de novo assessment (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Class liabilities and context-dependent potency. Medicinal chemistry around SHP099 identified derivatives with unexpected hERG activity and tolerability issues in some combination regimens; while not demonstrated specifically for SHP099 here, this flags a class risk requiring prospective cardiac and ocular safety pharmacology. Conformational-selection binding also means potency varies with SHP2 activation state, which is undefined in aging human RPE and could shift under inflammatory or oxidative stress present in dry AMD (Meem, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Lack of precedent in ocular models. No ocular, retinal, or RPE data for SHP099 or related allosteric SHP2 inhibitors are available in the supplied literature, increasing translational uncertainty for this repurposing (Yuan et al., 2020).

Program decision and de-risking experiments  
On the basis of the information provided, SHP099 is not yet a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD without foundational mechanistic validation in RPE. The central claim—that SHP2 inhibition prolongs MerTK phosphorylation and increases POS internalization—remains speculative in the absence of RPE data (Yuan et al., 2020). If the team elects to explore this hypothesis, a gated, mechanism-first workplan is advised:

- Define pathway engagement in RPE. Confirm SHP2 expression and activation state during phagocytosis in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE; assess whether SHP2 associates with MerTK/Src/FAK complexes upon POS challenge by co-immunoprecipitation or proximity assays (Shelby et al., 2015).  
- Biochemical time-courses ± SHP099. Quantify MerTK phosphorylation kinetics, Src and FAK activation, Rac1-GTP, and RhoA/ROCK activity after POS addition with a SHP099 concentration range bracketing its biochemical potency in enzyme assays; benchmark effect sizes against a ROCK inhibitor positive control, which is validated to rescue phagocytosis even in MerTK-deficient contexts (Mao & Finnemann, 2021).  
- Functional phagocytosis assays. Measure POS binding, F-actin cup formation, internalization, and phagolysosomal acidification under the same conditions, using established assays and timepoints aligned to the diurnal phagocytic peak where applicable (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Moran et al., 2022).  
- Ocular PK and safety. Establish retinal/RPE exposure after systemic and (if considered) intravitreal dosing, and perform ocular tolerability assessments (inflammation, ERG, histopathology) to identify potential on- or off-target liabilities early, mindful of class risks noted in optimization campaigns (Meem, 2022; Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).

In summary, SHP099 is a potent, selective, and well-characterized SHP2 allosteric inhibitor with robust oncology pharmacology and drug-like properties, but the case for repurposing to dry AMD by enhancing RPE POS phagocytosis is unsubstantiated in the provided literature and carries meaningful mechanistic and translational risks. Prioritizing direct RPE mechanistic studies and ocular PK/tolerability before any disease-model investment is the appropriate next step; in parallel, ROCK pathway modulation remains the most evidence-backed pharmacologic lever to augment phagocytosis in this system and should serve as a positive control and a benchmark for effect size (Fortanet et al., 2016; Mao & Finnemann, 2021; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SRT1720 is a synthetic small‐molecule activator of SIRT1 that was originally discovered and optimized by Sirtris Pharmaceuticals through high‐throughput screening and subsequent structural refinement (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018). It belongs to the class of sirtuin‐activating compounds (STACs) that are chemically distinct from natural activators such as resveratrol. Unlike polyphenolic compounds, SRT1720 is based on an imidazothiazole scaffold, incorporating a 2-quinoxaline amidic substituent and a piperazine moiety at the C3 position. This combination of structural features was determined to be optimal for SIRT1 activation, allowing the compound to achieve an EC1.5 value of approximately 0.16 µM with maximal activation levels reported at 781% (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). The compound’s synthetic origins allowed medicinal chemists to overcome many limitations seen with natural compounds, such as poor bioavailability and limited potency, and enabled the generation of a series of analogues ultimately leading to SRT1720. As a representative of third-generation STACs, SRT1720’s well-characterized in vitro profile and documented pharmacokinetic properties position it as a promising candidate for repurposing into new therapeutic areas.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, SRT1720 has been extensively investigated in the context of metabolic disorders, particularly type 2 diabetes and obesity. Preclinical studies in diet-induced obese mice and genetically obese rodent models demonstrated its ability to normalize plasma glucose, enhance insulin sensitivity, and increase mitochondrial capacity without toxicity at proper dosing regimens (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). In these models, SRT1720 was shown not only to mimic the beneficial effects of caloric restriction but also to extend healthspan and, in some paradigms, even lifespan, by improving mitochondrial biogenesis via deacetylation of key transcriptional regulators such as PGC-1α (Feige et al., 2008; Milne et al., 2007). Although SRT1720 has been primarily developed and evaluated for metabolic and cardiovascular indications, its mechanism—centered on the activation of SIRT1 and the subsequent modulation of cellular metabolism, stress response, and anti-inflammatory signaling—has generated interest in its potential applications in other age-related conditions. However, thus far no published studies have specifically addressed its use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or related ocular degenerative conditions. This therapeutic candidate has not been utilized in a clinical or preclinical setting directly targeting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, which is the hallmark of dry AMD, although its known pharmacological profile, good oral bioavailability in rodent models, and the safety profile observed in multiple animal models provide a rationale for its repurposing (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Alcain & Villalba, 2009).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SRT1720 acts as an allosteric activator of SIRT1, an NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase involved in the regulation of energy metabolism, inflammation, autophagy, and other aging-related processes. Its mechanism of action is predicated on binding to the SIRT1-peptide substrate complex rather than the free enzyme. Specifically, SRT1720 has been shown to interact with a site in the N-terminal region of SIRT1, mapped approximately to amino acids 183–225, which is proposed to undergo a conformational change upon binding of acetylated substrates (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). Through this allosteric binding, SRT1720 lowers the Michaelis constant (Km) for the acetylated peptide substrate, thereby increasing the enzyme’s affinity for its substrate and promoting a more productive catalytic conformation. This effect enhances the deacetylation of key substrates, such as PGC-1α, FOXO1, and p53, which are involved in metabolic regulation, stress response, and apoptosis (Feige et al., 2008; Milne et al., 2007). Although initial studies reported a direct activation model analogous to that of resveratrol, subsequent investigations have raised concerns regarding the substrate-dependency of the assay used to measure SIRT1 activity. For instance, certain studies reported that SRT1720 only shows activation when fluorophore-tagged peptides are used, casting doubts on whether the compound directly interacts with SIRT1 under native conditions (Pacholec et al., 2010). Nevertheless, additional kinetic and biophysical studies, including those employing isothermal titration calorimetry and nuclear magnetic resonance, have supported an allosteric activation mechanism that is consistent with a reduction in Km for acetylated substrates (Dittenhafer-Reed et al., 2011; Sanchez-Fidalgo et al., 2012). Moreover, structural and structure-activity relationship studies have confirmed that modifications in the chemical scaffold of SRT1720—particularly adjustments to the piperazine group and quinoxaline moiety—are critically linked to its SIRT1 activating properties (Blum et al., 2011; Granchi & Minutolo, 2018). In summary, despite ongoing debates about the nuances of its mechanism, the prevailing view supports that SRT1720 directly modulates SIRT1 activity via an allosteric mechanism that facilitates deacetylation of substrates, thereby promoting cellular processes that mimic the beneficial aspects of caloric restriction and enhance metabolic health.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
The hypothesis underlying the use of SRT1720 for dry age-related macular degeneration is that SIRT1 activation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells can improve autophagy and cytoskeletal dynamics, thereby enhancing phagocytic cup formation and promoting lysosomal fusion necessary for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). RPE dysfunction—including impaired autophagy and phagocytosis—has been implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In this context, SRT1720’s ability to increase LC3 flux and improve LAMP1 trafficking, as observed in models of oxidative stress, offers a mechanistic rationale for its use. Preclinical findings in non-ocular systems have demonstrated that activation of SIRT1, whether achieved genetically or pharmacologically, augments mitochondrial biogenesis and reduces oxidative stress by increasing the turnover of damaged cellular components (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Mautone et al., 2020). Notably, the EC₅₀ for SIRT1 activation by SRT1720 in some biochemical assays approximates 0.1–0.16 µM, a range that is consistent with the dosing hypothesis proposed for RPE cells (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). Given that the RPE is known to express SIRT1 and other components of the autophagic machinery, the expected result of SRT1720 treatment in the RPE would be deacetylation of key regulators involved in autophagy and cytoskeletal organization. This deacetylation should in turn enhance processes such as phagosome maturation and lysosomal fusion, which are critical for efficient clearance of POS debris (Alcain & Villalba, 2009; Sanchez-Fidalgo et al., 2012). Additionally, SIRT1 activation in RPE cells may mitigate oxidative stress and reduce pro-inflammatory signaling pathways, further contributing to cellular homeostasis and survival in the ocular microenvironment (Dittenhafer-Reed et al., 2011). On a cellular assay level, treatment with SRT1720 is expected to increase markers of autophagic flux (such as LC3-II conversion), promote proper trafficking of lysosomal markers like LAMP1, and enhance the formation of organized phagocytic cups necessary for POS engulfment. These improvements in RPE function could, in theory, translate into better clearance of accumulated debris and ultimately slow or reverse degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD. Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating SRT1720 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the available literature. On the strength side, SRT1720 is one of the most potent synthetic SIRT1 activators reported, with biochemical assays consistently demonstrating activation in the low micromolar to submicromolar range (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). Its synthetic nature and the consequent ability to modify its chemical structure for improved potency and selectivity afford significant advantages over naturally occurring compounds like resveratrol. The extensive preclinical data supporting its beneficial effects in metabolic disorders, including improved mitochondrial function, enhanced autophagy, and anti-inflammatory properties, provide a strong rationale for its potential use in conditions where cellular clearance and stress responses are impaired, such as in the RPE during dry AMD (Milne et al., 2007; Sanchez-Fidalgo et al., 2012). Moreover, the underlying hypothesis that SIRT1 activation can enhance autophagic flux and cytoskeletal dynamics aligns well with the biological challenges faced by the RPE in dry AMD—namely, the accumulation of damaged POS and the ensuing oxidative stress that contributes to disease progression. The documented pharmacokinetic properties, such as good oral bioavailability in rodent models, further suggest that SRT1720 could be optimized for ocular delivery with appropriate formulation strategies (Alcain & Villalba, 2009; Mautone et al., 2020).

On the other hand, notable weaknesses and challenges must be addressed. First, there is ongoing controversy regarding the precise mechanism by which SRT1720 activates SIRT1. Some studies have raised concerns that its observed activity might be an artifact of the assay conditions—particularly its dependence on fluorophore-tagged substrates—which calls for cautious interpretation of its direct effects on native SIRT1 substrates (Pacholec et al., 2010). Such discrepancies underscore the need for additional rigorously controlled biochemical studies using physiological substrates in RPE cells to conclusively establish its mechanism of action in an ocular context. Second, while extensive data exist from metabolic and cardiovascular models, there is a notable paucity of research specifically addressing the use of SRT1720 in ocular tissues or models of retinal degeneration. As dry AMD is characterized by unique aspects of retinal physiology, including a blood–retinal barrier and specific immune responses in the eye, the translational relevance of data from non-ocular models must be carefully validated through targeted preclinical studies (Park et al., 2017). Third, potential off-target effects—such as cross-reactivity with other sirtuin family members like SIRT2—pose additional concerns regarding the specificity and safety profile of SRT1720. Although its selectivity for SIRT1 over SIRT3 appears robust, any unintended modulation of SIRT2 or other enzymes could have unforeseen consequences on RPE cell function and overall retinal health (Milne et al., 2007; Granchi & Minutolo, 2018). Finally, the optimal dosing strategy, route of administration, and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) relationship in the context of ocular delivery remain unexplored, necessitating a series of preclinical ocular pharmacology studies to evaluate whether the effective concentrations observed in vitro can be achieved in the retina without systemic toxicity (Park et al., 2017; Sinclair & Hubbard, 2013).

In conclusion, SRT1720 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well-documented ability to activate SIRT1 and modulate critical cellular processes such as autophagy, mitochondrial biogenesis, and cytoskeletal organization. These properties are particularly relevant given the role of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD, where impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and accumulated cellular debris contribute to disease progression. The compound’s synthetic origins allow for further medicinal chemistry optimization, and its strong in vitro potency (EC₅₀ in the low micromolar range) lends support to the hypothesis that it could achieve meaningful biological effects in the RPE (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). However, the controversies surrounding its mechanism of action—as well as the lack of direct evidence in ocular models—highlight significant gaps that must be addressed before advancing SRT1720 into ophthalmologic applications. It would be imperative to conduct detailed biochemical studies in primary RPE cell cultures and to establish reliable animal models of dry AMD to evaluate both efficacy and ocular pharmacokinetics. Additional research should also focus on determining whether SRT1720’s modulation of autophagic and cytoskeletal regulators translates into improved POS clearance and enhanced RPE survival under oxidative stress.  

Overall, while SRT1720 demonstrates many characteristics that are theoretically beneficial for treating dry AMD, further targeted research is required to resolve the outstanding controversies and validate its therapeutic potential in the ocular setting. Strengths such as its high potency and favorable metabolic effects are balanced by weaknesses including assay-dependent mechanistic uncertainties and limited direct evidence in retinal systems. Therefore, the recommendation is to pursue rigorous preclinical studies that specifically assess SRT1720’s impact on RPE autophagy, phagocytic cup formation, and lysosomal fusion as well as its in vivo efficacy in relevant dry AMD models before committing substantial resources to later-stage development. This strategy will ensure that the unique challenges of ocular delivery and retinal cellular dynamics are adequately addressed, providing a sound basis for eventual clinical translation if the compound proves efficacious and safe in these specialized assays (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Pacholec et al., 2010; Blum et al., 2011; Alcain & Villalba, 2009).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
P110 is a synthetic, cell‐permeable inhibitory peptide specifically engineered to disrupt the pathological interaction between dynamin‐related protein 1 (Drp1) and its mitochondrial outer membrane receptor fission protein 1 (Fis1). It is synthesized via solid‐phase peptide synthesis methods and rational design strategies that mimic the native binding interface of these two proteins. As such, P110 belongs to the class of peptide-based mitochondrial fission inhibitors, a subclass of compounds that have been previously investigated in a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders, where aberrant mitochondrial fission is implicated in disease pathology. These types of compounds have historically been used experimentally to restore normal mitochondrial morphological dynamics and attenuate excessive fission triggered by oxidative stress. The concept builds upon evidence that an overactive fission process, largely mediated by elevated activity of Drp1 in response to cellular stressors, results in mitochondrial fragmentation, cytochrome c release, and subsequent cell death. In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which bear extremely high energy demands for functions such as photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis, proper mitochondrial network integrity is essential. The peptide’s cell-permeability and selective inhibition of the Drp1/Fis1 binding suggest that P110 can efficiently penetrate ocular tissues and modulate mitochondrial dynamics locally, offering a promising approach to preserve mitochondrial function in the diseased retina (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Numerous preclinical studies have investigated the modulation of mitochondrial dynamics in models of oxidative stress and neurodegeneration, often employing broad-spectrum inhibitors such as mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (Mdivi-1) or genetic silencing approaches using Drp1-specific siRNA. In several in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells—a human RPE cell line—excessive mitochondrial fission triggered by oxidative stress (for example, via hydrogen peroxide exposure) was effectively ameliorated by Drp1 inhibition. This intervention preserved mitochondrial structure, maintained ATP production, and increased cell viability, thereby preventing the morphological transition from tubular to fragmented mitochondria (Yako et al., 2021). Although these investigations have provided robust proof-of-concept evidence that targeting Drp1-mediated fission can be beneficial in preventing RPE dysfunction, most of the studies have not directly tested P110 peptide for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Instead, the literature has explored alternative approaches using compounds like Mdivi-1 and genetic knockdown modalities to decrease Drp1 activity, which indirectly supports the mechanistic rationale for using a targeted inhibitor like P110. The literature also shows that increased expression of mitochondrial fission factor (Mff) and elevated Drp1 levels in AMD donor tissues correlate with impaired mitochondrial homeostasis and defective phagocytosis in the RPE (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022). There remains, however, a gap in direct evidence for P110’s use in AMD despite its clear conceptual alignment with the therapeutic strategy of reducing pathological mitochondrial fission. Clinical trials have emerged that investigate mitochondrial fission inhibitors in ocular conditions, yet the available database queries indicate that while there is clinical interest in Drp1-targeting approaches, specific details on the P110 peptide remain sparse (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Thus, while the broader therapeutic paradigm—targeting aberrant mitochondrial fission—is well supported, P110 itself represents an innovative candidate that requires further preclinical validation in AMD-relevant models.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the pathological process underpinning excessive mitochondrial fission centers on the overactivation of Drp1, a GTPase that orchestrates mitochondrial scission. Under normal physiological conditions, Drp1 exists in the cytosol and is transiently recruited to the mitochondrial outer membrane by receptors such as Fis1, mitochondrial fission factor (Mff), and MiD49/MiD51. In response to oxidative and inflammatory stress—conditions known to be prevalent in the aging RPE and AMD—the interaction between Drp1 and Fis1 is upregulated, leading to excessive fission, mitochondrial fragmentation, and subsequent mitochondrial dysfunction. P110 is designed to selectively inhibit the Drp1/Fis1 binding interface, thereby attenuating the aberrant recruitment of Drp1 to the mitochondria. In doing so, it preserves the elongated and interconnected mitochondrial network, which is essential for optimal mitochondrial bioenergetics and the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Biochemically, inhibition of this interaction prevents the oligomerization of Drp1 on the mitochondrial surface, a process that is otherwise necessary for the formation of constriction rings that facilitate organelle division (Zhao et al., 2025). By blocking Drp1 recruitment, P110 indirectly maintains mitochondrial membrane potential and reduces the likelihood of cytochrome c release—a key event in the apoptosis cascade that is frequently observed in stressed RPE cells (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). Although many of the studies in the context of AMD have focused on Mdivi-1 as a Drp1 inhibitor, the specificity of P110 for the Drp1/Fis1 interaction might offer a distinct pharmacological profile, reducing off-target effects and preserving the physiological fission events necessary for maintaining overall mitochondrial quality control (Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021). Furthermore, the fact that mitochondrial fission and fusion processes are tightly integrated with mitochondrial biogenesis and mitophagy pathways supports the prospect that modulating this specific interaction may lead to a net improvement in mitochondrial dynamics without completely abolishing essential fission events (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Given the underlying hypothesis, the expected effect of P110 in AMD RPE cells would be to restore a balance in mitochondrial dynamics that has been disrupted by chronic oxidative stress. The assay proposed involves exposing cultured RPE cells, such as ARPE-19, to oxidative insults (e.g., H₂O₂) that would otherwise induce excessive Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission. P110’s mode of action is anticipated to specifically block the pathological protein-protein interaction between Drp1 and Fis1, thereby reducing the formation of excessively fragmented mitochondria and promoting the preservation or re-establishment of a tubular mitochondrial network. This intact network is critical for efficient ATP production, which in turn supports high-energy processes such as the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). POS phagocytosis is a metabolically demanding function that is crucial for photoreceptor renewal and overall retinal health. By maintaining ATP supply and preventing the release of pro-apoptotic factors (such as cytochrome c), P110 is expected to protect RPE cells from oxidative damage and improve cellular viability under stress conditions (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). Additionally, studies have demonstrated that mitochondrial fission inhibitors can lead to improved mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and enhanced cell survival under conditions of oxidative insult (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). In RPE cells, these improvements translate into a better capacity for POS uptake and metabolism, which are essential for sustaining the metabolic demands of the outer retina. Given that expression levels of Drp1 and its functional activity are elevated in AMD RPE cells, as evidenced by electron microscopy and proteomic analyses showing reduced mitochondrial numbers, diminished cristae, and defective fusion/fission ratios, the application of P110 is expected to counteract these detrimental changes by stabilizing the mitochondrial network (Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summarizing the overall evaluation of P110 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key points emerge from the literature. First, the mechanistic rationale underpinning P110’s mode of action is robust and well-aligned with current understanding of AMD pathophysiology. Excessive Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission has been implicated as a crucial driver of mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells—a hallmark of dry AMD. Several studies using alternative approaches such as pharmacological inhibition with Mdivi-1 or genetic knockdown via siRNA have consistently demonstrated that mitigating aberrant mitochondrial fission leads to improved mitochondrial integrity, preserved bioenergetic function, and enhanced cell viability in models of oxidative stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). This information directly supports the hypothesis that targeting the Drp1/Fis1 interaction, rather than globally inhibiting all Drp1 activity, could offer a more refined therapeutic approach with potentially fewer side effects. Such specificity is particularly appealing in the context of the retina where finely tuned mitochondrial dynamics are essential for high energy-demand processes like POS phagocytosis (Fisher et al., 2022).

One of the primary strengths of P110 lies in its cell-permeable peptide nature, which facilitates targeted intracellular delivery—a critical characteristic for therapies intended for ocular application. Its design, which specifically disrupts the interaction between Drp1 and Fis1, is predicated on the notion that pathological fission can be selectively blocked without interfering with the physiological fission necessary for regular mitochondrial turnover and repair. This specificity could, in theory, translate to a better safety profile compared to less selective inhibitors such as Mdivi-1 that may have off-target effects, including undesirable impacts on other aspects of mitochondrial function (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2025).

Despite the promising mechanistic rationale and potential for ocular development, there are notable weaknesses and challenges to be considered. The current literature does not yet offer direct preclinical or clinical evidence that P110 peptide itself has been used to treat dry AMD. Most existing studies have extrapolated the benefits of Drp1 inhibition from experiments involving Mdivi-1 or Drp1 knockdown in cellular models of RPE oxidative stress (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Therefore, while the concept of targeting Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission in AMD is well supported, the direct application of P110 remains largely theoretical at this point. This gap in the literature introduces uncertainty regarding the peptide’s pharmacokinetic properties, its stability in ocular tissues, and its potential immunogenic responses upon local administration in the eye.

Another potential limitation is the complex role of mitochondrial dynamics in cellular homeostasis. Although excessive fission in the context of oxidative stress is detrimental, mitochondrial fission is also a necessary process for mitophagy and the removal of damaged organelles. Some studies have indicated that a certain degree of fission may even be beneficial for cellular quality control, as it facilitates the segregation and subsequent removal of malfunctioning mitochondria (Skeie et al., 2021; Yako et al., 2021). The nuanced interplay between reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling and fission means that complete inhibition of fission—even if intended to be only pathological—could potentially have unintended consequences. It will be critical to determine whether P110’s selective inhibition of Drp1/Fis1 interaction can maintain the necessary balance between inhibiting excessive fission while still allowing physiological fission to contribute to normal mitophagy and mitochondrial turnover.

Furthermore, while the peptide’s cell-permeability is an advantage, peptide therapeutics in ocular applications face challenges related to delivery, degradation by ocular proteases, and potential issues with achieving sustained concentrations in the target tissues. Addressing these challenges may require the development of specialized drug delivery systems, such as intravitreal injections with sustained-release formulations or conjugation to nanoparticles, to ensure that adequate therapeutic levels of P110 are maintained at the retinal level over the necessary duration (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Currently, many studies have been limited to in vitro models using ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress conditions. Although these models provide valuable mechanistic insights, they do not fully recapitulate the complex interplay of cellular and systemic factors that contribute to AMD in vivo. The therapeutic potential of P110 will need to be evaluated in animal models that mimic the pathophysiological conditions of dry AMD, where factors such as chronic low-grade inflammation, complement activation, and cumulative oxidative damage play significant roles (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

In addition to efficacy and safety concerns, the regulatory landscape for peptide therapeutics in ocular indications should be considered. The development of P110 for dry AMD will require detailed pharmacodynamic and toxicological evaluations to satisfy regulatory requirements. While the peptide’s mechanism—targeting a well-characterized protein-protein interaction—provides a clear scientific rationale, the path toward clinical translation is contingent on demonstrating not only mechanistic efficacy but also an acceptable safety profile in both preclinical toxicology studies and early-phase clinical trials (Fisher et al., 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

In conclusion, the comprehensive literature review supports the notion that targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, specifically through the inhibition of Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission, is a highly promising therapeutic avenue for dry AMD. P110, as a selective inhibitor of the Drp1/Fis1 interaction, is well poised within this framework. The candidate is grounded in a strong mechanistic rationale that links excessive mitochondrial fission to reduced ATP production, impaired POS phagocytosis, and ultimately, RPE cell dysfunction—a cascade of events that underlies the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
NBDHEX (6-(7-nitro-2,1,3-benzoxadiazol-4-ylthio)hexanol) is a fully synthetic small molecule that belongs to the class of nitrobenzoxadiazole (NBD) derivatives. This compound was originally developed for its robust activity as a glutathione S-transferase (GST) inhibitor, and its synthesis follows methodologies previously reported (Pasello et al., 2011). As a GST inhibitor, NBDHEX is categorized as a “suicide inhibitor” because it covalently binds to the enzyme’s substrate binding site (the H-site) where it reacts with glutathione in the G-site to form a stable complex that inactivates the target enzyme (Filomeni et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2014). In traditional applications, members of this therapeutic class have been predominantly explored as anticancer agents; they have been used to counteract tumor chemoresistance by inhibiting GST isoenzymes that metabolize and neutralize cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents (Pasello et al., 2011; Filomeni et al., 2008). The compound’s design, structure, and biochemical properties have been extensively characterized within an oncology context, with numerous studies documenting its structure–activity relationships and its capacity to overcome multidrug resistance in cell lines from various cancer types (Filomeni et al., 2008; Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, NBDHEX has been investigated almost exclusively within the realm of cancer research. Preclinical studies have applied NBDHEX against musculoskeletal sarcomas, including osteosarcoma, Ewing’s sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma, as well as in small cell lung cancer and melanoma models (Pasello et al., 2011; Filomeni et al., 2008). In these studies, it demonstrated cytostatic and cytotoxic effects with effective concentrations typically in the low micromolar to submicromolar range, even in drug-resistant cancer cell lines (Pasello et al., 2011). Its anticancer activity has been attributed to both the direct inhibition of GST catalytic function and the disruption of GSTP1 interactions with key signaling proteins such as JNK and TRAF2, which are known to modulate apoptosis and stress signaling pathways (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Pasello et al., 2011). However, several studies have emphasized the importance of GSTP1 in ocular tissues, particularly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where it plays a critical role in detoxification and cellular defense against oxidative stress (Lee et al., 2014). These observations lend indirect support to the hypothesis that modulating GSTP1 activity—even through inhibition—might have therapeutic implications in the context of AMD. The molecular mechanism by which NBDHEX exerts its biological effects is well delineated in the published literature. As a suicide inhibitor, NBDHEX anchors itself to the active site of GST enzymes, particularly GSTP1, by binding to the hydrophobic substrate binding (H-site) region; once bound, it reacts in the presence of reduced glutathione to produce a stable, inactive complex (Filomeni et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2014). This covalent modification effectively prevents GSTP1 from catalyzing the detoxification reactions normally necessary to neutralize electrophilic and oxidative species. In addition, GSTP1 is known not only for its detoxification role but also for its involvement in protein–protein interactions, most notably with components of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway including c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and TNF receptor-associated factor 2 (TRAF2) (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Pasello et al., 2011). Under basal conditions, GSTP1 binds to JNK and TRAF2, suppressing their downstream pro-apoptotic signaling. By inhibiting GSTP1, NBDHEX disrupts these interactions, thereby relieving the inhibitory constraints and enabling the activation of stress response pathways mediated by JNK (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Pasello et al., 2011).  
In the context of the RPE, GSTP1 has been documented as a zeaxanthin-binding protein and a critical detoxification enzyme whose levels are reduced in AMD-affected retinas (Lee et al., 2014). This loss of GSTP1 is associated with a diminished capacity of RPE cells to counteract reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated by light exposure, leading to impaired cellular homeostasis and increased risk of retinal degeneration. In RPE cells, which normally express GSTP1 as part of their intrinsic antioxidant defense (and where GSTP1 expression is known to be developmentally regulated and inducible by light exposure), an increase in intracellular ROS may serve as a signal to activate cytoprotective autophagy pathways (Lee et al., 2014). As autophagy is crucial for the clearance of damaged proteins and cellular debris—including the phagocytosis and degradation of POS—the induction of autophagy via upregulation of p62 and LC3-II is anticipated to enhance the lysosomal clearance capacity of RPE cells. NBDHEX represents a promising repurposing candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well‐characterized inhibitory activity against GSTP1 and its documented ability to modulate autophagy in other cellular models. The ability of NBDHEX to disrupt GSTP1’s interactions with JNK and TRAF2 adds another layer of therapeutic potential, as the resultant activation of stress-responsive signaling pathways could further promote cell survival mechanisms. Additionally, evidence from cancer models showing increased levels of autophagy markers such as p62 and LC3-II following NBDHEX treatment supports the concept that this compound can induce autophagic flux, which is of paramount importance in RPE cells for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (Sciarretta et al., 2019; Filomeni et al., 2008).

Despite its promise, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. First, the bulk of the extant literature on NBDHEX pertains to its use as an anticancer agent with applications in solid tumors; there is a notable lack of direct preclinical or clinical studies assessing its efficacy and safety in ocular models or specifically in the context of dry AMD (Pasello et al., 2011; Filomeni et al., 2008). Second, while the hypothesis relies on a controlled increase in ROS to stimulate autophagy, GSTP1 is an essential component of the antioxidant defense system, and its inhibition could theoretically precipitate excessive oxidative damage if the dosage is not meticulously controlled (Lee et al., 2014; Pasello et al., 2011). Nonetheless, significant gaps in the literature remain with respect to ocular safety, effective dosing, and the specific cellular context of the RPE. As such, while NBDHEX is a scientifically attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, its translation from oncology to ophthalmology must be approached with caution.
