Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Astrocyte‐derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a are an innovative, biomimetic class of therapeutic agents that combine the natural properties of extracellular vesicles with the regulatory functions of microRNAs. Exosomes are nano‐sized vesicles (typically 40–160 nm in diameter) generated in the endosomal pathway and released by almost all cell types, including astrocytes, which are a fundamental component of the retinal microenvironment (Heo & Ryu, 2024). In this candidate, exosomes are isolated from retinal astrocytes and selectively engineered to become enriched with miR-146a, a microRNA known for its anti‐inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties. Because astrocytes are intimately involved in neuronal support and retinal homeostasis, their exosomes offer an inherent targeting advantage for diseased retinal regions, particularly in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is compromised (Romero et al., 2024). The enrichment with miR-146a transforms these naturally secreted vesicles into a targeted drug delivery vehicle that can modulate specific intracellular pathways in the RPE. This approach falls within the broader therapeutic class of exosome‐based drug delivery systems, a class that has increasingly attracted attention for its ability to transport nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids with high specificity and minimal immunogenicity (Du & Palczewski, 2022). Exosome therapy has been previously explored in preclinical models for various retinal pathologies using different source cells, such as mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and RPE cells (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2023). Engineering exosomes to carry therapeutic miRNAs like miR-146a exemplifies a precision medicine strategy in which the carrier is not only inert but provides its own biological effects derived from its cell of origin, contributing to the overall therapeutic profile.

Therapeutic History:  
While there is robust literature documenting the application of exosome-based therapies in ocular diseases, the specific use of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched with miR-146a is a relatively novel proposition. In several studies, exosomes isolated from mesenchymal stem cells have been engineered to carry anti-inflammatory microRNAs, including miR-146a, and have shown neuroprotective effects in retinal degeneration models such as retinitis pigmentosa and diabetic retinopathy (Zhang et al., 2022). Moreover, astrocyte-derived exosomes have been explored for their intrinsic neuroprotective and anti‐angiogenic properties. For instance, retinal astrocyte-derived exosomes have been demonstrated to contain multiple anti-angiogenic molecules including endostatin, PEDF, and TIMP-1, which contribute to the suppression of choroidal neovascularization in laser-induced models (Mead & Chow, 2023; Romero et al., 2024). Although these studies primarily target neovascular AMD, their underlying mechanisms emphasize the utility of astrocyte-based exosome therapy in modulating critical retinal pathways. In the context of dry AMD, which is characterized by chronic RPE degeneration, oxidative stress, and complement system dysregulation, the strategy of utilizing exosomal delivery to target RPE dysfunction is supported by evidence that exosome‐mediated miRNA transfer can restore lysosomal function and reduce inflammatory cascades in retinal cells (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Guan et al., 2025). Additionally, complement dysregulation and increased complement factor expression are central features of dry AMD pathology, and prior studies have implicated exosomal cargo in modulating inflammatory and complement pathways (Guan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). Although direct clinical or extensive preclinical experience with astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a in dry AMD is limited, the analogous applications of MSC-derived exosomes carrying miR-146a establish an important precedent and provide a mechanistic rationale for further investigation (Zhang et al., 2022; Berber et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic mechanism of this candidate operates at multiple molecular levels, integrating the known functions of both miR-146a and exosomal delivery systems. miR-146a is recognized as a key negative regulator of inflammation through its ability to target components in the Toll-like receptor (TLR) and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling pathways. Specifically, miR-146a targets interleukin-1 receptor–associated kinase 1 (IRAK1) and TNF receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6), leading to a reduction in NF-κB activation and subsequent downregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Berber et al., 2017; ElShelmani et al., 2021). In the context of dry AMD, complement overactivation has been identified as a pivotal event contributing to RPE degeneration. Complement factor H (CFH) and complement factor B (CFB) play significant roles in regulating the alternative complement pathway, and dysregulation of these factors leads to excessive complement activation, resulting in increased levels of complement fragments such as C3a that promote inflammation and lysosomal stress (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021). The proposed mechanism asserts that miR-146a, delivered via astrocyte-derived exosomes, can penetrate the RPE cell layer and downregulate the transcription and/or translation of complement components such as CFH and CFB. By limiting the production of these factors, miR-146a effectively reduces the downstream formation of the inflammatory anaphylatoxin C3a, alleviating lysosomal overload and preserving the acidic lysosomal environment necessary for optimal activity of degradative enzymes like cathepsin D (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Zhang et al., 2022). This modulation of complement activity is essential because aberrant complement activation in the RPE has been linked to photoreceptor outer segment (POS) accumulation and impaired phagocytosis, which are hallmarks of dry AMD progression (Romero et al., 2024; Sanghani et al., 2022). Furthermore, exosomes themselves possess intrinsic targeting and cell–cell communication properties; their membrane proteins, such as tetraspanins (CD63, CD81) and other surface markers, facilitate uptake by recipient cells and can mediate tissue-specific homing to the RPE (Liu et al., 2023; Romero et al., 2024). The combination of miR-146a’s molecular action on inflammatory and complement pathways with the natural delivery proficiency of astrocyte-derived exosomes creates a synergistic effect that is expected to restore lysosomal integrity and enhance functional POS degradation in high-risk CFH backgrounds (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The expected therapeutic effect in the treatment of dry AMD is multilayered. In vitro studies utilizing RPE cell cultures derived from patient lines with high-risk CFH expression are anticipated to show that treatment with miR-146a-enriched astrocyte exosomes results in a significant downregulation of complement factors, notably CFH and CFB. This downregulation would be reflected in reduced levels of the complement activation fragment C3a, which is known to exacerbate inflammation and lysosomal dysfunction in RPE cells (Romero et al., 2024; Berber et al., 2017). As a direct consequence of complement normalization, lysosomal integrity is expected to be maintained through the preservation of an acidic pH environment and the restoration of cathepsin D activity. Cathepsin D plays a critical role in the degradation of POS material taken up by RPE cells during the daily process of photoreceptor renewal (Liu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022). Enhanced clearance of POS is hypothesized to reduce the accumulation of toxic waste products and drusen formation, a defining characteristic of dry AMD. In addition, the anti-inflammatory action of miR-146a should attenuate the chronic low-grade inflammation observed in the retinal microenvironment, thereby mitigating further RPE and photoreceptor damage (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2020).  
At the molecular level, the treatment is anticipated to modulate intracellular signaling cascades by reducing NF-κB–mediated transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines, which in turn helps to suppress the local inflammatory milieu and prevent further complement activation (Berber et al., 2017; ElShelmani et al., 2021). The exosomal vehicle ensures that miR-146a is delivered in a protected and concentrated form, which maximizes cellular uptake and preserves functional integrity during circulation. Given their natural ability to cross biological barriers, these astrocyte-derived exosomes are expected to efficiently reach the RPE layer, and this targeted delivery is crucial for achieving the desired therapeutic outcomes with minimal off-target effects (Guan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). Furthermore, the experimental assays based on RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD are designed to evaluate both the biological activity of the delivered miR-146a and the restoration of lysosomal function. Expected readouts include a decrease in complement factor mRNA and protein levels, improved lysosomal enzyme activity (especially cathepsin D), reduced accumulation of POS debris, and ultimately, preservation of RPE and photoreceptor viability (Guan et al., 2025; ElShelmani et al., 2021). These effects, if validated, could translate into a slowing of disease progression or even a reversal of certain pathological features in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
The candidate therapeutic of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a holds considerable promise for the treatment of dry AMD due to its innovative design and strong mechanistic rationale. One of the most significant strengths of this approach lies in its biomimetic nature. By harnessing exosomes derived from retinal astrocytes, the therapy benefits from inherent targeting properties that increase the likelihood of efficient delivery to the RPE, a key cell type implicated in dry AMD pathology (Romero et al., 2024; Mead & Chow, 2023). Furthermore, the use of miR-146a—an endogenous regulatory molecule with well-documented anti-inflammatory effects—adds an additional layer of specificity to the treatment by directly modulating the inflammatory milieu and complement dysregulation that are central to dry AMD (Berber et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022). This dual action, combining restoration of lysosomal integrity through improved POS degradation and suppression of complement-mediated inflammation, addresses two critical pathogenic processes simultaneously.  

However, despite its notable strengths, several challenges and uncertainties remain. First, while the therapeutic concept is strongly supported by preclinical studies involving MSC-derived exosomes and by literature demonstrating the beneficial effects of exosomal miRNAs in retinal diseases (Zhang et al., 2022; Du & Palczewski, 2022), the specific application of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched with miR-146a for dry AMD remains to be thoroughly evaluated. There is limited direct evidence in the literature showing that astrocyte-derived exosomes naturally enriched or engineered to carry miR-146a can downregulate complement factor expression in RPE cells in a clinically meaningful way (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023). This represents a gap in knowledge that would need to be addressed through rigorous preclinical investigation, including detailed dose–response studies and assessments of long-term efficacy and safety.  

Another potential weakness lies in the scalability and reproducibility of exosome isolation from astrocytes. Exosome production can vary depending on the source, the culture conditions, and the methods used for enrichment and purification. Manufacturing a consistent and high-quality exosome product that meets clinical grade standards is a well-recognized challenge in the field of exosome therapeutics (Liu et al., 2023; Guan et al., 2025). In addition, while exosomes are known for their low immunogenicity, the possibility of immune reactions, especially when they are over-engineered or when administered repeatedly, cannot be entirely discounted and will require careful evaluation (Romero et al., 2024).  

From a mechanistic standpoint, although the theoretical framework linking miR-146a with the downregulation of complement factors CFH and CFB is compelling, the precise molecular interactions within RPE cells must be validated by robust in vitro and in vivo experiments. Detailed studies are needed to confirm the extent to which miR-146a directly modulates these complement components, and whether additional targets or off-target effects might complicate the therapeutic outcome (Zhang et al., 2022; Berber et al., 2017). Furthermore, while the restoration of lysosomal function and POS degradation is a promising endpoint, the complexity of lysosomal biology in the context of chronic degenerative diseases such as dry AMD means that multifactorial interventions might be necessary. It will be essential to demonstrate that the observed improvements in lysosomal enzyme activity (e.g., cathepsin D) translate into meaningful clinical benefits, such as slowed disease progression or improved visual function (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Romero et al., 2024).  

In summary, the concept of using astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is innovative, leveraging the natural targeting, biocompatibility, and multi-functional capabilities of exosomes along with the potent anti-inflammatory and complement‐modulating properties of miR-146a. The preclinical evidence derived from analogous studies using MSC-derived exosomes and the general literature on exosomal miRNA therapies in retinal diseases provides a solid foundation for this approach (Zhang et al., 2022; Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2023). Nevertheless, the strategy will require comprehensive validation, including optimization of exosome isolation and engineering protocols, detailed mechanistic studies in relevant cellular models, and robust in vivo efficacy assessments in dry AMD animal models before clinical translation can be considered. With targeted efforts to address these challenges, this therapeutic candidate could represent a significant advance in the treatment of dry AMD, offering a precision medicine approach that directly tackles both complement overactivation and lysosomal dysfunction at the cellular level (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Guan et al., 2025; ElShelmani et al., 2021).

Overall, the combination of bioengineered exosomes and miR-146a offers mechanistic specificity and a novel route of administration that may overcome many of the limitations inherent in current dry AMD therapies, particularly those related to anti-VEGF treatments which are primarily indicated for wet AMD. While further preclinical investigations are essential to fully elucidate the pharmacodynamics, safety profile, and therapeutic window of this candidate, the approach holds promise as a next-generation drug candidate for dry AMD that could potentially improve patient outcomes by preserving retinal structure and function through the reestablishment of homeostatic cellular processes (Mead & Chow, 2023; Sanghani et al., 2022; Song et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Metformin is a well‐established biguanide originally derived from the natural compound galegine found in Galega officinalis. Over decades of development, it has been chemically optimized and synthesized into its modern, orally administrable form. Today, metformin is classified within the antidiabetic drug class and is routinely used to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus. Its discovery as an antihyperglycemic agent was serendipitous, and subsequent structural modifications have resulted in a drug with an excellent safety profile and pleiotropic effects beyond blood glucose regulation. As a small synthetic molecule available from reputable suppliers such as Sigma‐Aldrich (Cat. No. D150959), metformin has been repurposed in recent years for potential applications outside of metabolic diseases, including neurodegeneration and retinal degenerative disorders. This candidate belongs to a class of compounds that have historically been used for systemic metabolic control, but emerging evidence also suggests that their ability to activate AMPK—a critical cellular energy sensor—can be exploited to modulate autophagy and mitochondrial function in non‐metabolic tissues, including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhao et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, metformin has long been the first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes due to its robust glucose-lowering capability and favorable long-term risk profile. The extensive clinical use of metformin in diabetic populations has allowed researchers to retrospectively observe its pleiotropic effects on other organ systems. Notably, retrospective epidemiological studies have demonstrated that diabetic patients treated with metformin exhibit a lower incidence of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) compared to non-users, suggesting potential protective effects in the retina (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Huang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Furthermore, preclinical studies investigating metformin in vitro have shown that it protects human RPE cells against oxidative stress-induced damage, largely mediated by stimulation of the AMPK pathway (Zhao et al., 2020). In addition, in vivo models employing metformin have provided evidence of its ability to mitigate light-induced photoreceptor loss and retinal degeneration, supporting the hypothesis that its molecular targets in the RPE could be leveraged against dry AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Miyagishima et al., 2021). Although metformin has not been established as a conventional treatment for AMD, its proven use in modulating metabolic pathways, along with demonstrable effects on autophagy, mitochondrial function, and inflammation in retinal cells, provides the rationale for repurposing it in the context of dry AMD (Vessey et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, metformin exerts its primary pharmacological effects by inhibiting mitochondrial electron transport chain complex I, which leads to a reduction in ATP production and a concomitant increase in the AMP/ATP ratio. This energetic shift results in the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a master regulator of cellular metabolism and autophagy (Zhao et al., 2020). Activated AMPK phosphorylates several downstream targets that collectively restore energy homeostasis; among these targets are key regulators of autophagy, including the inhibition of mTOR and the direct phosphorylation of ULK1, which initiates autophagosome formation (Zhao et al., 2020; Dang et al., 2021). One important biochemical hallmark of this autophagy induction is the conversion of cytosolic LC3-I to its lipidated, membrane-bound form LC3-II, which has been used extensively as a marker to assess autophagy flux in RPE cell studies (Zhao et al., 2020). Additionally, metformin’s activation of AMPK influences mitochondrial biogenesis through upregulation of transcription co-activators such as PGC-1α, thereby promoting the generation of new, functionally active mitochondria (Dang et al., 2021; Sekar et al., 2023). These mechanisms are particularly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where RPE metabolic dysfunction is a key pathological feature. Moreover, metformin has been shown to modulate lipid metabolism, notably by enhancing cholesterol efflux via the AMPK/LXR pathway, which can reduce intracellular lipid accumulation—a contributor to drusen formation in AMD (Dang et al., 2021). Additional anti-inflammatory effects are mediated through suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation and modulation of VEGF signaling, further contributing to the overall cytoprotective profile of metformin in the retina (Dang et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed hypothesis and existing evidence, it is expected that metformin will activate AMPK in RPE cells, thereby promoting autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis. In practical terms, treatment with metformin is anticipated to lead to a measurable increase in LC3-II formation, a reduction in intracellular lipid accumulation, and restoration of ATP levels in RPE cells—specifically in models employing CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE cells, which serve as a relevant in vitro model of AMD (Zhao et al., 2020). The enhanced autophagic flux, as indicated by increased LC3-II levels and decreased p62 levels, will facilitate the clearance of damaged organelles, including dysfunctional mitochondria. This process of mitophagy is expected to improve overall mitochondrial homeostasis, thereby restoring the energetic capacity required for efficient phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Given that efficient POS degradation by RPE cells is critical for photoreceptor renewal and retinal health, the metformin-induced restoration of energy balance and autophagic function could lead to improved visual function. Importantly, AMPK is expressed in RPE cells and has been shown to be a crucial mediator of autophagy and mitochondrial quality control in these cells, ensuring that metformin’s mechanism of action is well-targeted to the cellular environment affected in dry AMD (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Furthermore, several in vivo studies support the notion that metformin can rescue mitochondrial function and enhance cellular clearance mechanisms, which are expected outcomes of its use in dry AMD models (Sekar et al., 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating metformin as a drug candidate for treating dry age-related macular degeneration, there are several notable strengths. First, metformin’s well-established safety profile from decades of clinical use for type 2 diabetes offers an advantageous starting point for repurposing—its known pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties facilitate its potential translation to ophthalmic indications (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Second, robust preclinical data support metformin’s ability to activate AMPK and promote autophagy, two pathways intimately involved in the maintenance of RPE health. Activation of AMPK has been repeatedly shown to enhance LC3-II formation, reduce oxidative stress, restore mitochondrial membrane potential, and upregulate mitochondrial biogenesis, all of which are critical to counteracting the metabolic deficits seen in AMD (Zhao et al., 2020; Dang et al., 2021; Sekar et al., 2023). Third, epidemiological studies have suggested that metformin use correlates with a reduced incidence of AMD, lending clinical relevance to its potential protective effects in the retina (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Huang et al., 2023). Fourth, the ability of metformin to modulate lipid metabolism, particularly by promoting cholesterol efflux and thereby reducing drusen-associated lipid accumulation, represents another beneficial mechanism targeting a fundamental aspect of AMD pathology (Dang et al., 2021).

However, several weaknesses and challenges must also be considered. Although many preclinical and retrospective clinical studies point toward a beneficial role of metformin in retinal health, direct prospective evidence in dry AMD patients remains limited. Some of the data originate from studies published in journals of variable quality, and there exists heterogeneity in the responses observed across different model systems, including patient-derived RPE cells where metformin’s effects may vary (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Moreover, while metformin is effective in activating AMPK systemically at standard doses used for diabetes, the optimal dosing regimen, route of administration, and tissue-targeting strategies necessary to achieve effective concentrations in the retinal tissue remain to be determined. The possibility that metformin’s efficacy may depend on specific genetic or metabolic backgrounds of patients—such as differences in CFH status or other AMD-related risk factors—also raises concerns about patient heterogeneity in clinical trials (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Additionally, while the expected restoration of autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis is promising, the precise quantitative changes in LC3-II, ATP levels, lipid accumulation, and POS degradation need rigorous validation under controlled experimental conditions before definitive conclusions can be drawn (Zhao et al., 2020; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Finally, potential systemic side effects such as gastrointestinal disturbances, rare occurrences of lactic acidosis, and vitamin B12 deficiency, albeit infrequent, may need consideration when repurposing metformin for chronic ocular use, especially in non-diabetic populations (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Brown et al., 2019).

Overall, metformin represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its multifaceted effects on enhancing autophagy, improving mitochondrial biogenesis, and restoring cellular energy metabolism in RPE cells. Its safety profile and broad availability further support its potential for rapid clinical translation. Nonetheless, the candidate’s ultimate success will depend on careful dose optimization, robust clinical trial designs that account for inter-patient variability, and further mechanistic studies to precisely delineate the quantitative biochemical improvements—such as LC3-II increase, lipid clearance, ATP restoration, and enhanced POS degradation—in preclinical AMD models (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhao et al., 2020). The convergence of epidemiological, biochemical, and preclinical data thus supports proceeding with further validation studies, while also highlighting the need to address remaining uncertainties regarding tissue-specific drug delivery and long-term outcomes in the context of dry AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Vessey et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The candidate under evaluation is an anti‐Tyro3 agonist monoclonal antibody (mAb), a protein‐based therapeutic engineered to specifically bind and activate the Tyro3 receptor. Tyro3 is one of the three members of the TAM receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) family—comprising Tyro3, Axl, and MerTK—that modulate key cellular functions in different tissues. In the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), both MerTK and Tyro3 are expressed; however, MerTK is traditionally recognized as the primary driver of phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), while Tyro3 has emerged as a compensatory receptor with a crucial anti‐inflammatory signal in MerTK‐deficient settings (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Palczewska et al., 2016). This candidate antibody is presumed to be of research grade, synthesized using recombinant antibody technology. It is generated by isolating B cells that produce an antibody directed against the extracellular domain of Tyro3; through hybridoma technology or phage display methods, a specific mAb is cloned and further optimized for high binding affinity and agonistic activity with an effective concentration (EC₅₀) on the order of approximately 20 nM. Monoclonal antibodies, by virtue of their proteinaceous nature and high specificity, have long served as therapeutics in a wide range of indications including oncology, autoimmunity, and inflammatory diseases. In this particular case, the therapeutic candidate belongs to the class of receptor agonists rather than the more common inhibitory antibodies. Receptor agonist antibodies are designed to cross‐link target receptors, thereby inducing conformational changes that stimulate receptor dimerization and activation of downstream signaling cascades. Although the majority of previous antibody therapeutics have been developed as receptor antagonists to block signaling (as is often the case with oncogenic targets), the approach of receptor activation via agonist antibodies is emerging as a promising strategy in diseases where deficiency in receptor function contributes to pathology (Palczewska et al., 2016).  

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic use of monoclonal antibodies targeting the TAM RTK family has primarily been explored in oncology. In cancer, for example, anti‐TYRO3 antibodies have been predominantly investigated as inhibitors intended to block tumorigenic signaling pathways (Hsu et al., 2019). However, the narrative differs considerably when one considers ocular diseases such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). Dry AMD is characterized by RPE dysfunction, accumulation of photoreceptor debris, and a resultant chronic inflammatory milieu that drives retinal degeneration. Although MerTK is well documented as being critically involved in the phagocytosis of POS—with deficiencies in its function directly linked to retinal degeneration in models such as the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) rat—recent genetic and biochemical studies have indicated that Tyro3, despite historically receiving less attention than MerTK, can functionally compensate in aspects of anti‐inflammatory signaling when MerTK is absent (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Akalu et al., 2017). In MerTK‐deficient RPE cells, the compensatory actions of Tyro3 have been demonstrated to preserve anti‐inflammatory gene expression profiles and maintain retinal viability, suggesting the therapeutic potential of harnessing Tyro3 agonism to ameliorate inflammation‐mediated retinal degeneration in dry AMD (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Palczewska et al., 2016). Despite this promising genetic evidence, there is little precedent in the literature for the clinical or preclinical use of an anti‐Tyro3 agonist antibody explicitly for dry AMD or similar retinal diseases. The majority of TAM receptor–targeted therapeutic approaches developed to date have focused on receptor inhibition for cancer therapy (Hsu et al., 2019). As such, the repurposing of an agonist antibody against Tyro3 to enhance RPE phagocytosis represents a novel direction that capitalizes on emerging insights into compensatory TAM signaling in the retina (Lieffrig et al., 2023). While there are no reports of prior successful application of anti‐Tyro3 agonist antibodies in either clinical or veterinary practice specifically for dry AMD, the genetic suppression of photoreceptor degeneration in MerTK‐deficient models by Tyro3 signals a strong preclinical rationale worthy of further investigation (Akalu et al., 2017; Palczewska et al., 2016).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The proposed mechanism of action for the anti‐Tyro3 agonist antibody revolves around its ability to engage and activate Tyro3 in RPE cells where MerTK function is compromised. Under normal conditions, MerTK activation in RPE cells triggers a cascade of intracellular events that lead to phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor outer segments. This process is mediated by the recruitment of signaling molecules that activate regulators of the actin cytoskeleton, chiefly through pathways involving the small GTPase Rac1. Specifically, upon ligand binding, MerTK undergoes dimerization and trans‐autophosphorylation, generating docking sites for signal transduction proteins such as Vav and the p130Cas/CrkII/Dock180 complex; these effectors then catalyze Rac1 activation, which in turn promotes the actin polymerization necessary for the formation of phagocytic cups around POS (Kwon & Freeman, 2020). In the context of MerTK deficiency, however, RPE cells exhibit a marked disruption in phagocytosis, even though compensatory pathways involving Tyro3 are partially active. Experimental observations indicate that in mertk−/− RPE cells that retain Tyro3 expression, while anti‐inflammatory gene expression is preserved, the phagocytic uptake of POS remains severely impaired, suggesting that Tyro3’s natural activation level is suboptimal for driving effective phagocytosis under these conditions (Lieffrig et al., 2023).  

The agonist mAb candidate is designed to overcome this limitation by binding specifically to the extracellular domain of Tyro3 and triggering receptor activation through induced dimerization. This antibody binding is expected to mimic the natural ligand-induced conformational changes and stimulate the intracellular kinase activity of Tyro3. Upon receptor activation, Tyro3 should phosphorylate its own intracellular tyrosine residues, creating docking sites for various adaptor proteins that propagate downstream signaling cascades. Although the precise molecular details of Tyro3 signaling in RPE cells are not as well characterized as those for MerTK, it is anticipated that downstream effectors such as the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) and Rac1 will become activated. PI3K activation leads to the generation of phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP₃), which in turn recruits Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) to the plasma membrane, thereby catalyzing the conversion of Rac1 to its active GTP-bound form. Active Rac1 is critical for orchestrating rearrangements of the actin cytoskeleton, a key step in phagocytic cup formation and subsequent internalization of POS (Palczewska et al., 2016; Lieffrig et al., 2023).  

Furthermore, evidence suggests that Tyro3 signaling may be linked to the regulation of αvβ5 integrin, another receptor complex highly expressed in RPE cells that plays an important role during POS phagocytosis. In wild-type RPE cells, αvβ5 integrin engages with bridging molecules such as MFG-E8 to facilitate the physical attachment of POS to the RPE cell surface. Although MerTK is instrumental in transducing signals required for the downstream internalization process, it is the coordinated activity between MerTK and αvβ5 integrin that ensures a successful phagocytic event (Kwon & Freeman, 2020; Palczewska et al., 2016). The hypothesis underlying this therapeutic candidate is that, in the absence or dysfunction of MerTK, an agonist mAb stimulating Tyro3 can activate a compensatory signaling cascade that establishes convergence with αvβ5 integrin-mediated pathways. This cross-talk is believed to enhance Rac1 activation and promote cytoskeletal reorganization necessary for POS internalization even under compromised conditions (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Palczewska et al., 2016). In summary, the antibody-driven activation of Tyro3 is anticipated to increase intracellular PI3K and Rac1 signaling, consequently supporting not only anti-inflammatory responses but also promoting the assembly of phagocytic structures in MerTK-impaired RPE cells.  

Expected Effect:  
In the in vitro and in vivo assays proposed for dry AMD, the administration of the anti‐Tyro3 agonist mAb is expected to yield several beneficial effects on RPE cell function. First, by binding to and activating Tyro3, the antibody is anticipated to trigger a cascade of intracellular signals that primarily enhance the downstream activity of PI3K and Rac1, which are critical mediators in remodeling the actin cytoskeleton for phagocytosis (Palczewska et al., 2016; Lieffrig et al., 2023). Given that MerTK-deficient RPE cells have been shown to retain anti-inflammatory signaling via Tyro3 yet suffer from diminished phagocytic uptake of POS, the agonist is postulated to at least partially restore the phagocytic capacity. The expected increase in active Rac1 will promote pseudopod formation and stabilization of the phagocytic cup around bound photoreceptor debris, thereby facilitating the internalization process.  

Moreover, αvβ5 integrin complexes, which are essential for the initial binding of POS to the RPE surface, are expected to be functionally engaged in the presence of enhanced Tyro3 signaling. The hypothesized cross-regulation between Tyro3 and these integrin complexes should result in improved phagocytic efficiency. Recent experimental evidence suggests that wild-type RPE cells, which naturally co-express MerTK and Tyro3, maintain a robust anti-inflammatory gene expression profile and efficient POS clearance; conversely, in mertk−/− models, the intact expression of Tyro3 is sufficient to sustain retinal viability despite markedly impaired phagocytosis (Lieffrig et al., 2023). Thus, an anti‐Tyro3 agonist mAb could potentially tip the balance toward enhanced phagocytic performance in diseased states by elevating Tyro3 signaling from its basal compensatory level to one that more effectively drives phagocytosis.  

The proposed expected effect in the assay includes an increase in the phagocytic index of RPE cells, as measured by the uptake of fluorescently labeled POS, and a reduction in markers of retinal inflammation. In mechanistic experiments, activation of Tyro3 should correlate with increased phosphorylation levels of pivotal signaling intermediates such as PI3K and Akt, and a subsequent rise in GTP-bound Rac1 levels, which can be detected via pull-down assays. In addition, the impact on αvβ5 integrin function may be assessed by examining the recruitment of cytoskeletal adaptor proteins that have established roles in integrin-mediated phagocytosis. Furthermore, given that Tyro3’s activation may also support anti-inflammatory gene expression, treatment with the antibody might reduce levels of inflammatory cytokines in RPE cultures under oxidative or inflammatory stress conditions—conditions that mimic dry AMD pathogenesis (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Palczewska et al., 2016).  

It is important to note that although Tyro3 agonism is projected to enhance intracellular signaling events associated with phagocytosis, previous studies have indicated that in MerTK-deficient RPE cells the restoration of phagocytic function is only partially achievable through Tyro3 activation alone (Lieffrig et al., 2023). Therefore, while an increase in Rac1 and PI3K signaling levels is anticipated with the anti‐Tyro3 agonist, it might not fully recapitulate the robust phagocytic response observed in fully functional RPE cells. Nonetheless, the profound anti-inflammatory effects observed in Tyro3-expressing RPE cells could contribute to preserving retinal structure and function over time, thereby delaying the progression of dry AMD. In addition, gene expression studies have documented that Tyro3 is naturally expressed in the RPE, albeit at levels comparable to those in the rodent and human retina (Palczewska et al., 2016), thereby providing a cellular substrate for the agonist mAb to exert its effects.  

Overall Evaluation:  
In assessing the potential of an anti‐Tyro3 agonist antibody as a therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration, several points of strength and limitation emerge from the available literature.  

Strengths:  
One of the foremost strengths of this therapeutic candidate lies in its receptor specificity. Tyro3 is highly expressed in RPE cells and is demonstrated to participate in anti‐inflammatory signaling; importantly, genetic studies have revealed that Tyro3 acts as a suppressor of photoreceptor degeneration in MerTK-deficient models (Akalu et al., 2017; Palczewska et al., 2016). This genetic evidence suggests that enhancement of Tyro3 signaling could counteract some of the detrimental consequences associated with MerTK deficiency that are known to contribute to dry AMD pathology (Lieffrig et al., 2023). The approach leverages the inherent compensatory potential of Tyro3 and could offer an innovative strategy to bypass the limitations imposed by non-functional MerTK. Additionally, the design of an agonist mAb allows for targeted activation of the receptor, theoretically minimizing off-target effects that might occur with less specific small-molecule agonists. Given that monoclonal antibodies can be engineered to display high binding affinity (targeting an EC₅₀ in the vicinity of 20 nM) and long half-lives in situ, the intrinsic pharmacokinetic properties of an antibody therapeutic could be advantageous in the ocular environment, where sustained receptor activation may be necessary (Palczewska et al., 2016).  

Furthermore, the mechanism by which Tyro3 activation is proposed to enhance phagocytosis involves well-characterized intracellular cascades—including the PI3K and Rac1 signaling pathways—that are known to be essential for actin cytoskeleton reorganization and phagocytic cup formation (Palczewska et al., 2016; Lieffrig et al., 2023). The interplay between Tyro3 and αvβ5 integrin complexes represents an attractive target because αvβ5 integrin is already implicated in POS binding and is a critical component of the RPE’s phagocytic machinery (Kwon & Freeman, 2020). Thus, the strategy of boosting Tyro3 activity may not only revitalize phagocytic signaling in MerTK-impaired cells but could also reinforce the integrin-mediated aspects of the phagocytic process. These mechanistic attributes confer a rational basis for pursuing an agonist-based approach in dry AMD, a field where current treatment options remain largely palliative (Lieffrig et al., 2023).  

Weaknesses:  
On the other hand, there are several challenges and uncertainties that temper enthusiasm for the candidate. Notably, while Tyro3 activation has been demonstrated to preserve anti-inflammatory signaling in RPE cells, the literature consistently reports that phagocytosis remains significantly impaired in MerTK-deficient models even when Tyro3 is intact (Lieffrig et al., 2023). This suggests that although agonizing Tyro3 may mitigate inflammation—which is instrumental in curtailing further retinal damage—it does not necessarily normalize the essential phagocytic clearance of POS. Consequently, the anticipated improvement in phagocytosis through Tyro3 agonism might be only partial in nature, thereby limiting the therapeutic impact on a key aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis.  

Another major limitation stems from the fact that the detailed molecular mechanisms underlying Tyro3-specific signaling in the RPE remain less well characterized relative to MerTK. With much of the established research focusing on MerTK’s role in phagocytosis (Kwon & Freeman, 2020; Si et al., 2023), there exists a significant knowledge gap regarding the full spectrum of Tyro3’s downstream signaling cascades, potential cross-talk with αvβ5 integrin, and the modulatory control of Rac1/PI3K activity. This incomplete mechanistic understanding introduces uncertainties into how robustly Tyro3 agonism can be translated into effective POS internalization. In addition, the structural homology among the TAM receptors poses a potential challenge in developing antibodies that can selectively activate Tyro3 without unintended cross-reactivity with MerTK or Axl—a challenge that has been encountered in the development of TAM receptor inhibitors in oncology (Hsu et al., 2019; Myers et al., 2019).  

Furthermore, prior therapeutic approaches targeting TAM receptors in other disease areas have predominantly involved receptor inhibition rather than activation. In cancer, for example, the focus on developing inhibitors for TYRO3 has yielded several small molecule compounds and antibody-based antagonists (Hsu et al., 2019). The shift from inhibition to activation for therapeutic gain in dry AMD is conceptually innovative but also uncharted territory with limited preclinical validation. The delivery of antibody therapeutics to the retina presents additional hurdles, including issues related to ocular penetration, stability, and dosing regimen—factors that must be rigorously optimized in subsequent preclinical studies. Finally, while expression analyses confirm that Tyro3 is present in the retina and RPE, quantitative differences in receptor density between in vitro cell cultures and in vivo retinal tissue may influence the efficacy and dosing of the candidate mAb (Palczewska et al., 2016).  

Overall, the anti‐Tyro3 agonist antibody candidate presents a compelling and innovative therapeutic strategy for dry AMD by aiming to leverage Tyro3’s compensatory signaling capacity in the RPE to overcome deficits in MerTK. Its strengths lie in the high specificity of an agonist mAb approach, the solid genetic rationale provided by models showing retinal protection via Tyro3, and the potential to modulate key intracellular pathways such as PI3K and Rac1 that are essential for phagocytosis and anti-inflammatory responses (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Akalu et al., 2017). However, significant weaknesses remain, including the incomplete capacity of Tyro3 signaling to fully restore phagocytic activity in MerTK-deficient settings, the comparatively limited mechanistic insight into Tyro3’s actions in RPE cells, and the challenges associated with achieving high specificity among structurally similar TAM receptors. Moreover, whereas robust preclinical data exist supporting the concept of Tyro3 acting as a genetic suppressor of photoreceptor degeneration, the translation of these findings into a receptor-specific agonist antibody therapy for dry AMD is largely uncharted and will require extensive validation in both in vitro models and animal studies (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Palczewska et al., 2016).  

From an overall perspective, the candidate shows promise by addressing an unmet need in dry AMD, particularly through its potential to modulate inflammatory and phagocytic pathways compromised in the disease. The strategy of using receptor-specific agonism to bypass defects in MerTK signaling is innovative and supported by genetic evidence, yet its success hinges on the ability to induce sufficient downstream activation of PI3K/Rac1 and to engage integrin-mediated mechanisms to boost phagocytosis. Given that prior studies indicate that Tyro3 alone does not fully complement the loss of MerTK in terms of POS clearance—leading primarily to anti-inflammatory maintenance rather than complete phagocytic restoration—further studies are needed to determine whether antibody-mediated activation can overcome this limitation or whether combination therapies might be warranted (Lieffrig et al., 2023).  

In conclusion, while the anti‐Tyro3 agonist antibody candidate is built upon a robust scientific hypothesis with promising preclinical genetic support, its therapeutic viability for dry AMD will depend on resolving several key issues: confirming that elevated Tyro3 signaling can indeed significantly enhance POS phagocytosis, ensuring that the designed antibody is both highly selective and potent in the complex ocular environment, and establishing favorable pharmacokinetic and safety profiles in relevant preclinical models. The current body of evidence indicates that Tyro3 can partially compensate for MerTK deficiency in terms of anti-inflammatory signaling and retinal preservation, which bodes well for its potential application in dry AMD (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Akalu et al., 2017). However, the incomplete restoration of phagocytosis observed in MerTK-deficient models even when Tyro3 is active suggests that this approach, while promising, may need to be part of a broader strategy to fully rescue RPE function. Thus, the candidate merits further investigation, with a recommendation to pursue detailed preclinical studies to refine the antibody design, evaluate downstream signaling and biological effects in RPE cells, and ultimately determine whether this approach can translate into a clinically meaningful therapy for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ML‐SA1 is a fully synthetic small molecule designed as an agonist of the transient receptor potential mucolipin 1 (TRPML1) channel. It belongs to the class of mucolipin synthetic agonists, which were initially derived as analogs of earlier lead compounds such as SF‐51 and SF‐22. These compounds were discovered using high‐throughput screening approaches aimed at identifying activators of TRPML channels, and ML‐SA1 was subsequently optimized for improved potency and selectivity in mammalian systems (Feng et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2012). As a synthetic compound, ML‐SA1 exemplifies a rational drug design strategy in which the molecule is engineered to mimic the action of the endogenous lipid agonist phosphatidylinositol 3,5‐bisphosphate [PI(3,5)P₂] by directly binding to the channel’s pore region. This binding stabilizes TRPML1 in its open conformation, thereby facilitating lysosomal Ca²⁺ release. The chemical class represented by ML‐SA1 has historically been employed as a research tool to interrogate lysosomal physiology and calcium homeostasis in diverse cell types, including neuronal and retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Therapeutic History:  
Previous studies have demonstrated that ML‐SA1 robustly elevates cytosolic calcium levels in several cellular models by activating TRPML1 channels. In particular, ML‐SA1 has been applied to multiple RPE cell models—including mouse RPE, human embryonic stem cell‐derived RPE, and the ARPE‐19 cell line—to assess its ability to restore lysosomal calcium signaling and normalize lysosomal function (Gómez et al., 2018). In these experiments, ML‐SA1 elicited rapid, robust, and reversible Ca²⁺ signals that were completely absent in TRPML1 knockout cells, thereby confirming target engagement and specificity (Gómez et al., 2018). Beyond RPE biology, ML‐SA1 has been evaluated in neuronal models of lysosomal dysfunction, including experimental systems relevant to Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease, where it mediated correction of defective lysosomal acidification and improved autophagic flux (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022). Although no clinical trials have yet investigated ML‐SA1 directly in patients with dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), its demonstrated efficacy in rescuing lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling—in conditions that share underlying pathophysiological features with dry AMD such as lysosomal storage and autophagy blockade—suggests that its repurposing may yield therapeutic benefits in this disease context (Open Targets Platform, 2025). To date, the use of ML‐SA1 has predominantly been within experimental research settings rather than in clinical practice or veterinary medicine, and its repurposing for dry AMD represents an innovative and rationale‐driven approach rooted in the overlap between TRPML1 dysfunction and RPE pathology (Feng et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2017).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic action of ML‐SA1 is centered upon its ability to directly activate TRPML1 channels located on lysosomal membranes. TRPML1 plays a critical role in regulating lysosomal calcium homeostasis by mediating Ca²⁺ efflux from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol. ML‐SA1 binds directly to TRPML1—likely within a hydrophobic pocket formed at the S5–S6 transmembrane domain interface—and stabilizes the channel’s open state (Feng et al., 2014). This activation occurs independently of exogenous PI(3,5)P₂ in mammalian cells, setting ML‐SA1 apart from the endogenous regulatory mechanisms that otherwise depend on dynamic fluctuations in phosphoinositide levels (Feng et al., 2014; Gómez et al., 2018). As a result of channel activation, lysosomal Ca²⁺ is released into the cytosol, triggering a cascade of calcium‐dependent signaling pathways. One critical downstream effect is the promotion of lysosomal membrane fission and fusion events, processes that are essential for proper lysosomal trafficking and the maturation of autophagosomes into autolysosomes (Cao et al., 2017; Li & Li, 2022).  

Beyond its immediate role in calcium mobilization, ML‐SA1‐mediated activation of TRPML1 also facilitates the activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Increased cytosolic Ca²⁺ can activate calcineurin, which in turn dephosphorylates TFEB, enabling its translocation to the nucleus where it upregulates the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function and autophagy (Pollmanns et al., 2022). In some models, ML‐SA1 treatment has been shown to improve the processing and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D, thereby contributing to normalization of lysosomal pH and enhanced protein degradation (Hui et al., 2019). Importantly, the ability of ML‐SA1 to restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling directly targets the pathological cascade observed when TRPML1 is deficient or inhibited—a scenario that is reminiscent of the lysosomal storage, impaired autophagy, and stalled phagolysosomal degradation evident in dry AMD RPE cells (Gómez et al., 2018; Pamonag, 2021).  

Expected Effect:  
Based on the observed mechanisms in diverse cellular models, it is expected that ML‐SA1 will re‐establish normal lysosomal function in RPE cells afflicted by dry AMD. In the proposed assay, the activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 at concentrations near its EC₅₀ (approximately 5 µM) should restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ efflux, thereby driving several beneficial downstream effects. First, the induced calcium release is anticipated to promote lysosomal membrane dynamics that favor fission and fusion events, ultimately leading to improved lysosomal trafficking and an enhanced capacity for phagolysosomal degradation. This is particularly relevant for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), the routine phagocytic burden of RPE cells that, when inadequately processed, contributes to lipofuscin accumulation and retinal degeneration (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Second, by normalizing Ca²⁺ signaling, ML‐SA1 is expected to reinstate proper lysosomal acidification. Acidification is crucial for the optimal activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D; ML‐SA1 has been shown in various models to restore cathepsin D processing, thereby resetting the enzymatic degradation cascade necessary for POS turnover (Hui et al., 2019). Such restoration of acidification and enzyme activity would directly counteract the pathological accumulation of undegraded material—a hallmark of dry AMD.  

Third, the downstream activation of TFEB induced by ML‐SA1’s modulation of lysosomal calcium may trigger an upregulation of the entire lysosomal-autophagy gene network. This transcriptional reprogramming is vital for augmenting both the number and function of lysosomes, thereby enhancing the overall cellular clearance capacity in RPE cells. Because ample evidence suggests that TRPML1 is expressed in RPE cells and that its dysfunction contributes directly to the autophagy block observed in dry AMD (Pamonag, 2021; Gómez et al., 2018), the activation of this pathway by ML‐SA1 is expected to result in a net improvement in POS degradation and a reduction in toxic debris accumulation. Ultimately, the integrated effects of improved lysosomal trafficking, normalized pH, enhanced enzymatic processing, and boosted autophagic flux are hypothesized to alleviate key pathological features of dry AMD, potentially slowing or even reversing degenerative changes in the retinal pigment epithelium (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Our comprehensive literature review indicates that ML‐SA1 is a scientifically compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration. One of its principal strengths lies in its well‐defined mechanism of action: by directly activating TRPML1 channels, ML‐SA1 has been shown to restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ homeostasis—a central defect in several models of lysosomal storage and autophagy dysfunction (Gómez et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2014). The robust experimental data obtained in RPE cell models and other relevant systems supports the hypothesis that ML‐SA1 can reverse deficits in lysosomal trafficking, acidification, and autophagosome maturation. The compound’s ability to elicit rapid, reproducible, and reversible Ca²⁺ signals is particularly encouraging, as it suggests that pharmacological modulation of TRPML1 can be finely tuned through dosing adjustments (Gómez et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2017).  

Furthermore, the extensive research demonstrating ML‐SA1’s effects in cellular models of lysosomal storage diseases—including those markers that mimic the pathological lipid accumulation and autophagy impairment found in dry AMD—provides additional rationale for its application in RPE cells (Feng et al., 2014; Pollmanns et al., 2022; Hui et al., 2019). The fact that ML‐SA1 has also been evaluated in non-ocular contexts (such as neuronal models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s diseases) where it facilitated autophagic clearance and improved lysosomal functions underscores the versatility of its mechanism and hints at broader therapeutic utility (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022).  

Nonetheless, several challenges must be acknowledged. One notable weakness is that ML‐SA1’s efficacy can be compromised by lysosomal lipid accumulation—a common feature of advanced dry AMD. Studies suggest that in cells with significant lipid deposition, such as those accumulating sphingomyelin or other inhibitory lipids, the activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 is attenuated (Gómez et al., 2018). This raises concerns that in patients with advanced dry AMD, the therapeutic window may be narrower or may require combination strategies to first reduce lipid burden. Additionally, while the in vitro EC₅₀ is promising (around 5 µM), there remains uncertainty regarding the pharmacokinetic profile, bioavailability, tissue penetration (particularly across the blood‐retina barrier), and potential off-target effects of ML‐SA1 when administered in vivo (Li & Li, 2022).  

Another area of concern is the current lack of direct clinical data pertaining to ML‐SA1 in dry AMD. Although preclinical studies in RPE cell models provide a solid foundation, translation to in vivo models of AMD—and eventually to human clinical trials—will require additional investigation. The absence of any reported clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD with TRPML1 agonists (as confirmed by database searches such as those reflected in the Open Targets Platform) indicates that this is still a largely uncharted therapeutic area requiring further validation (Open Targets Platform, 2025). Moreover, chronic activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 may have unforeseen consequences related to intracellular calcium homeostasis and autophagic balance, which warrant careful evaluation in long-term studies (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022).  

In summary, ML‐SA1 represents a highly promising candidate for the repurposing in dry AMD based on its ability to rescue lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling, enhance autophagic clearance, and restore normal lysosomal pH and trafficking in RPE cells. Its synthetic origin and well‐characterized mechanism provide a strong mechanistic rationale for its use. However, issues related to lipid-mediated inhibition of TRPML1, pharmacokinetic considerations, and the current lack of in vivo data in AMD models must be addressed. Overall, the candidate shows significant potential, but a focused program of preclinical validation—including animal models of dry AMD, detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiling, and exploration of strategies to mitigate lysosomal lipid accumulation—is essential before advancing ML‐SA1 to clinical trials for dry AMD (Gómez et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
T0901317 is a synthetic small‐molecule ligand originally developed as a full agonist for the liver X receptors (LXRs), a class of nuclear receptors that govern lipid and cholesterol homeostasis. This compound belongs to the nonsteroidal LXR agonists, and its development was initially driven by the need to probe the mechanisms underlying reverse cholesterol transport and lipid metabolism in various tissues. T0901317 was designed to potently activate both LXRα and LXRβ isoforms, thereby upregulating a suite of genes that mediate cholesterol efflux, including ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) and ABCG1. The synthetic origins of T0901317 can be traced back to efforts to create tool compounds that efficiently modulate LXR signaling, with its chemical structure optimized to bind within the ligand-binding domain of LXRs and induce a conformational change that facilitates heterodimerization with retinoid X receptors (RXRs). In diverse studies, including those involving retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells of the eye, T0901317 has been shown to enhance cholesterol efflux mechanisms that are crucial for maintaining cellular lipid balance and extracellular matrix composition (Lyssenko et al., 2018; Choudhary et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of T0901317 spans preclinical investigations primarily centered on cardiovascular diseases, such as atherosclerosis, where its ability to reduce atherosclerotic lesions by enhancing reverse cholesterol transport was of paramount interest. In rodent models, particularly in LDL receptor–deficient mice, T0901317 administration resulted in meaningful reductions in plaque area and plasma cholesterol levels, while concomitantly increasing the expression of ABCA1 in target tissues (Welch et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2017). These studies established the compound’s potent lipid‐modulatory activity, albeit with an accompanying induction of hepatic lipogenesis and elevated plasma triglycerides that raised safety concerns for systemic use. More recently, the focus has shifted to exploring the potential application of T0901317 in ocular diseases, specifically dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In preclinical investigations using ARPE-19 cells and other RPE models, T0901317 has emerged as a promising agent due to its ability to stimulate LXR-mediated pathways that regulate cholesterol efflux and modulate inflammatory responses in the retina (Lyssenko et al., 2018; Choudhary et al., 2020). Although T0901317 was not originally developed with AMD in mind, the identification of dysregulated lipid metabolism and sub-RPE deposit formation as key features in the pathobiology of dry AMD has led to hypothesis-driven studies that repurpose LXR agonists for restoring lipid homeostasis in the retina (Buñay et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2020). Furthermore, the compound’s established pharmacokinetic profile in rodent models offers a degree of translational reassurance regarding its use as a tool for modulating extracellular matrix composition and RPE function, thereby rendering it a viable candidate for further preclinical validation in AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, T0901317 exerts its biological effects by selectively binding to the ligand-binding domains of LXRα and LXRβ. Upon binding, conformational changes in the receptor facilitate heterodimerization with RXR, leading to recruitment of coactivator proteins and subsequent binding to specific LXR response elements in the promoters of target genes. One of the key effects of this activation is the robust upregulation of ABCA1, a transporter protein that plays a central role in cholesterol efflux by mediating the transfer of cholesterol to extracellular acceptors such as apolipoprotein A-I (apo A-I) and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) particles (Lyssenko et al., 2018). The increase in ABCA1 expression subsequently enhances the reverse cholesterol transport (RCT) pathway, which is essential for preventing the intracellular and sub-RPE accumulation of cholesterol and other lipids—a factor implicated in the formation of drusen-like deposits observed in dry AMD. In addition to its lipid-regulatory activity, T0901317 has been shown to attenuate pro-inflammatory signaling pathways in RPE cells, as evidenced by its ability to modulate NF-κB signaling under conditions of oxidant stress and lipid overload (Wu et al., 2023; Buñay et al., 2021). This dual impact on lipid metabolism and inflammation is particularly relevant in the retinal context, where chronic inflammatory processes and disrupted cholesterol homeostasis converge to promote RPE dysfunction and basal deposit accumulation (Lyssenko et al., 2018). Moreover, studies have illustrated that even under conditions of hypoxia or lipid overload—conditions that normally suppress ABCA1 expression via hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF1)—T0901317 is capable of counteracting these inhibitory effects, thereby reestablishing normal cholesterol efflux in RPE cells (Peters et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022). This detailed mechanistic understanding underscores the drug’s potential to normalize the lipid environment of Bruch’s membrane and restore RPE phagocytic function by mitigating deleterious lipid accumulation (Lyssenko et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of T0901317 for dry AMD posits that the compound, when applied at an effective concentration (with an EC₅₀ in the vicinity of 50 nM in RPE cells), will activate LXRs to upregulate ABCA1 and other cholesterol efflux transporters within RPE cells. This molecular cascade is expected to promote a more efficient clearance of excess cholesterol from the RPE and surrounding Bruch’s membrane, thus reducing the formation of drusen-like deposits—a hallmark of early AMD pathology (Lyssenko et al., 2018). Data derived from experiments in ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE models indicate that treatment with T0901317 leads to a significant increase in ABCA1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels, which translates into enhanced cholesterol efflux when proper lipid acceptors such as apoA-I are present in the extracellular milieu (Lyssenko et al., 2018). In preclinical AMD models, enhanced reverse cholesterol transport due to LXR activation has been associated with normalization of the extracellular matrix, reduction of basal deposit thickness, and improved integrin-mediated adhesion—a factor critical for maintaining the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells (Buñay et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2020). Additionally, the compound is hypothesized to indirectly facilitate RPE phagocytic function by restoring proper localization of phagocytic receptors through improved integrin-mediated adhesion mechanisms, thereby supporting the efficient uptake and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Buñay et al., 2021; Peters et al., 2022). In summary, treatment with T0901317 is expected to exert a multifaceted beneficial effect in the context of dry AMD by both reducing sub-RPE lipid deposition and enhancing the intrinsic capacity of RPE cells to clear photoreceptor debris, all of which are pivotal to preserving retinal structure and function (Choudhary et al., 2020; Rao & Fliesler, 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
A rigorous evaluation of T0901317 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several compelling strengths alongside notable challenges that must be addressed in future research. Among its strengths, T0901317 is a well-characterized LXR agonist with a robust capacity to upregulate ABCA1 and other members of the cholesterol efflux machinery in RPE cells. Its mechanism of action has been extensively validated across multiple preclinical studies, with evidence demonstrating that enhanced reverse cholesterol transport can lead to normalization of Bruch’s membrane lipid composition and reduction of drusen-like deposits, factors that are directly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Lyssenko et al., 2018). Furthermore, the pharmacokinetic data available in rodent models, combined with efficacy studies in ARPE-19 cells, provide a degree of translational optimism that localized administration of T0901317—potentially via intravitreal or sustained-release ocular formulations—could mitigate systemic exposure, thereby circumventing some of the deleterious metabolic effects observed with systemic dosing (Choudhary et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2017).

Despite these promising attributes, the therapeutic application of T0901317 for dry AMD is not without its weaknesses. Chief among these are the well-documented metabolic liabilities associated with systemic LXR activation. Multiple studies have reported that T0901317 can induce hepatic de novo lipogenesis, elevate plasma levels of triglycerides, and promote hepatic steatosis—a profile that raises significant concerns regarding its safety for long-term systemic use (Welch et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2023; Kirchgessner et al., 2016). Given that AMD predominantly affects older individuals who may also have coexistent metabolic disorders, the risk of exacerbating systemic lipid dysregulation is a critical barrier to clinical translation. Moreover, the promiscuity of T0901317 in interacting with other nuclear receptors, including potential dual agonist activity for FXR, further complicates its safety profile and may lead to off-target effects that are difficult to predict from preclinical models (Choudhary et al., 2020; Loren et al., 2013). Additionally, while preclinical data support the concept that LXR activation can ameliorate features of AMD, there remains a substantial gap between these experimental findings and clinical efficacy in human patients; the precise impact of T0901317 on drusen composition, integrin-mediated adhesion, and RPE phagocytosis in vivo requires further elucidation through rigorous translational studies (Buñay et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2020).

Another potential challenge lies in the dosing and delivery strategy for T0901317. The compound has demonstrated an effective EC₅₀ around 50 nM in RPE cellular models, yet achieving and maintaining such therapeutic concentrations in the subretinal space in vivo—while avoiding systemic exposure—represents a formidable formulation challenge. Advancements in targeted drug delivery platforms, such as nanoparticle-based intravitreal injections or biodegradable implants, may offer viable solutions; however, these technologies will need to be integrated into the development strategy to minimize the systemic adverse effects that have hampered previous efforts involving T0901317 (Wu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023).

On the other hand, the mechanism by which T0901317 exerts its effects—namely, the stimulation of cholesterol efflux via ABCA1 and the modulation of inflammatory pathways—aligns well with the emerging understanding of dry AMD pathobiology. Research over the past decade has increasingly implicated disrupted cholesterol homeostasis, lipid accumulation in Bruch’s membrane, and chronic low-grade inflammation as key drivers of RPE dysfunction and photoreceptor degeneration (Choudhary et al., 2020). By directly targeting these processes, T0901317 could potentially reverse or at least halt the progression of pathological changes in the retina. Importantly, there is evidence that LXR activation can restore integrin-mediated cell adhesion and phagocytic receptor localization in RPE cells, which is critical for the regular clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and maintenance of retinal integrity (Buñay et al., 2021; Peters et al., 2022). This mechanistic synergy offers a compelling rationale for further exploration of T0901317 as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, provided that its administration can be optimized to limit systemic exposure and maximize localized retinal effects (Choudhary et al., 2020; Rao & Fliesler, 2021).

In summation, T0901317 exhibits a well-defined mechanism of action that is directly relevant to the pathophysiological underpinnings of dry AMD. Its ability to activate LXRs and induce key cholesterol efflux transporters such as ABCA1 offers significant promise in normalizing lipid composition in the sub-RPE environment and reducing drusen-like deposits, while concurrently enhancing the phagocytic function of RPE cells. Nonetheless, the compound’s established profile of metabolic disturbances—characterized by increased hepatic lipogenesis, hypertriglyceridemia, and potential off-target nuclear receptor activation—represents significant hurdles that must be mitigated before clinical application. The prospect of localized ocular delivery holds some promise in this regard, but further preclinical work is essential to optimize formulation, dosing, and safety profiles in eye-specific models of AMD (Lyssenko et al., 2018; Loren et al., 2013; Welch et al., 2022). Given the current state of evidence, T0901317 stands as a promising candidate from a mechanistic perspective; however, its translational potential will ultimately depend on developing strategies to minimize its systemic toxicity while harnessing its beneficial effects on retinal lipid metabolism and RPE function (Buñay et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2020; Lyssenko et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation and Future Directions:  
Considering the collective body of evidence, T0901317 possesses distinct strengths as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD due to its potent LXR agonism that effectively upregulates ABCA1 expression and enhances cholesterol efflux—a critical need in the management of sub-RPE lipid accumulation and basal deposit formation. Its robust preclinical data in RPE models and its documented pharmacodynamic properties in the context of lipid metabolism underscore its potential utility in restoring retinal homeostasis. The compound’s capacity to alleviate inflammation, improve integrin-mediated adhesion, and potentially enhance RPE phagocytosis provides an additional mechanistic basis for its application in dry AMD (Lyssenko et al., 2018; Buñay et al., 2021).

Nevertheless, the translational road map for T0901317 is marred by significant challenges. The adverse metabolic effects reported in systemic studies—namely hepatic steatosis, elevated plasma triglycerides, and off-target receptor activation—represent major concerns that have thus far limited the clinical advancement of this molecule in other therapeutic areas, including atherosclerosis (Welch et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2023; Kirchgessner et al., 2016). These safety liabilities necessitate a re-evaluation of the delivery strategy for T0901317. One potential approach is the development of localized ocular delivery systems that concentrate the therapeutic effect in the retina while minimizing systemic absorption. Advances in drug delivery technologies, such as intravitreal implants or nanoparticle carriers, may offer a viable solution to this conundrum by enabling sustained, localized release of T0901317 directly to the RPE and Bruch’s membrane (Wu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023).

Furthermore, the dual agonist nature of T0901317—implicating both LXR and potentially FXR pathways—raises additional questions regarding the spectrum of its biological effects. While dual receptor activation may provide additive or synergistic benefits in some contexts, there is also the risk of unintended crosstalk and off-target activity that could complicate the clinical picture, especially in a delicate tissue such as the retina. Addressing these issues may require structural modifications to enhance LXR selectivity or the development of second-generation compounds that retain the beneficial actions on cholesterol efflux while mitigating the adverse lipogenic effects (Choudhary et al., 2020; Loren et al., 2013).

Moreover, although there is promising evidence from in vitro studies indicating that T0901317 can upregulate ABCA1 in RPE cells and promote cholesterol efflux, comprehensive in vivo studies in animal models of dry AMD are warranted to definitively establish its efficacy in reducing drusen formation, restoring RPE phagocytic function, and ultimately preserving visual function. The heterogeneity of AMD pathophysiology also suggests that T0901317 may be most effective as part of a combinatorial therapy, potentially in combination with other agents targeting complementary pathways such as oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, or angiogenesis (Buñay et al., 2021; Storti et al., 2019).

In conclusion, T0901317 represents a promising yet challenging therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. Its well-documented mechanism of activating LXR-mediated cholesterol efflux and modulating inflammatory responses aligns closely with the pathological features of AMD, namely disrupted lipid homeostasis and chronic inflammation in the RPE and Bruch’s membrane. However, the compound’s established systemic metabolic liabilities and broad nuclear receptor activation profile introduce significant hurdles that must be overcome before clinical translation can be realized. Future research efforts should focus on optimizing the drug’s delivery to the retina, refining its molecular selectivity, and conducting rigorous in vivo efficacy and safety studies in relevant AMD models. Only through such multifaceted investigations can the full potential of T0901317 be realized as a viable treatment strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration (Lyssenko et al., 2018; Buñay et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2020).
