Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB 290157 (N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine) is a synthetic, low–molecular-weight, nonpeptide ligand originally discovered in a SmithKline Beecham high-throughput radioligand displacement screen (~240,000 compounds) for inhibitors of human C3a binding to membranes from RBL-2H3 cells stably expressing C3aR; subsequent medicinal chemistry optimization of the initial hit (SKF 63649) yielded SB 290157 with markedly improved potency and cross-species activity at C3aR (human, mouse, guinea pig) (Ames et al., 2001). The compound is typically supplied as a trifluoroacetate salt by commercial vendors and has been used extensively as a pharmacological tool compound in vitro and in vivo, including ocular and non-ocular models (Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Chemically, SB 290157 is an arginine derivative bearing a 2,2-diphenylethoxyacetyl N2-acyl substituent; synthetic steps reported by the discovery group used Fmoc/Boc protection of arginine on Wang resin, coupling of tert-butyl(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetate via carbodiimide/DMAP, and final deprotection with TFA to give the target amide (Ames et al., 2001). In the original pharmacological characterization, SB 290157 behaved as a competitive C3aR antagonist in radioligand binding and functional assays in recombinant cells and primary neutrophils, with reported low-nanomolar functional potency in Ca2+-mobilization and platelet ATP-release assays; selectivity was claimed versus C5aR and other neutrophil chemoattractant GPCRs in those systems (Ames et al., 2001). The class of nonpeptide C3aR-directed small molecules has been pursued largely as research tools and preclinical probes of anaphylatoxin biology; SB 290157 is the prototypical representative and has been used across diverse inflammatory models to interrogate complement C3a–C3aR signaling (Ames et al., 2001).

Therapeutic History  
- Foundational pharmacology and in vivo anti-inflammatory activity: SB 290157 was reported in 2001 to inhibit C3a-induced responses in multiple cell systems and to reduce inflammation in rodent models, including decreased neutrophil accumulation in a guinea pig LPS-induced airway neutrophilia model and attenuation of paw edema in a rat adjuvant-induced arthritis (AIA) model when dosed intraperitoneally twice daily (b.i.d.) at up to 30 mg/kg (Ames et al., 2001). Pharmacokinetics in guinea pigs after a single 30 mg/kg i.p. dose showed high Cmax (~7000 ng/ml), sustained plasma levels (>100 ng/ml at 8 h), and a short apparent half-life (~0.9 h) (Ames et al., 2001). In ex vivo vascular assays, SB 290157 blocked C3a-induced increases in perfused rat caudal artery pressure and prevented receptor internalization in neutrophils, supporting functional antagonism in those readouts (Ames et al., 2001).  
- Ocular/retinal relevance: In an in vitro human fetal retinal pigment epithelium (hfRPE) transwell model, chronic recombinant human C3a exposure for two weeks drove sub-RPE extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation and wide-spaced collagen deposition, which were prevented by co-treatment with SB 290157 at 10 µM (trifluoroacetate salt); the antagonist did not impair transepithelial resistance or monolayer morphology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Mechanistically in the same hfRPE system, C3a impaired ubiquitin–proteasome pathway (UPP) activity and selectively elevated basal MMP-2 activity without changing proteasome-subunit mRNA, while promoting deposition of collagens IV and VI; these C3a-driven effects were reported to be abrogated by a C3aR antagonist, consistent with C3aR-mediated pathology in RPE (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In vivo, SB 290157 was used in a laser-induced retinal vein occlusion (RVO) mouse model where pharmacologic blockade of C3a/C3aR reduced fluorescein leakage, retinal thickness abnormalities, disorganization of inner retinal layers (DRIL), and serous detachment height, improved ERG b-wave and oscillatory potentials, and suppressed inflammatory gene programs (DEGs enriched for chemokine/NF-κB/IL-17 pathways); the authors explicitly note known pharmacological limitations of SB 290157 including potential off-target and agonist actions (Zhao et al., 2025). Genetic evidence relevant to ocular disease includes partial protection in light-damage models: global C3aR deletion decelerated retinal thinning after light insult, although photoreceptor apoptosis levels (TUNEL) were not significantly altered, suggesting C3aR contributes to retinal structural change but not necessarily acute photoreceptor death in that model (Behnke et al., 2025).  
- Broader in vivo applications and cautions: SB 290157 has been used to probe complement biology in diverse indications, with reported benefits in models of lupus nephritis, antibody-induced arthritis, thromboembolic stroke, and AD-related cognition; however, many of these reports predate or did not control for later-recognized pharmacology (partial agonism, off-targets), which complicates interpretation (Li et al., 2021; Coulthard & Woodruff, 2015). In a mouse cuprizone demyelination model, intraperitoneal SB 290157 at 1 mg/kg every other day modulated astrocyte reactivity (GFAP), TNF-α dynamics, and complement deposition (C3d), with the dosing choice explicitly motivated to minimize off-target C5aR engagement; nevertheless, the authors caution about SB 290157’s weak C5aR agonism and interpretability of systemic dosing (Frankle, 2023). In neuropathic pain (spared nerve injury), SB 290157 acutely reversed mechanical hypersensitivity but is limited by a short half-life (~1.5 h) and known off-target/agonist properties (Cook, 2019).  
- Pharmacological controversies and off-target receptor activity: Soon after its introduction, independent groups reported that SB 290157 exhibits C3aR agonist/partial-agonist activity in multiple cell systems, with potency dependent on receptor density and assay context; examples include near-maximal Ca2+ mobilization in transfected RBL cells, NAG release in differentiated U-937 cells, and ATP release in guinea pig platelets, whereas it appeared antagonistic in other systems (e.g., guinea pig platelets with very low receptor expression) (Mathieu et al., 2005). More recently, SB 290157 was shown to be a partial agonist at C5aR2 (β-arrestin recruitment EC50 ~16 µM; partial efficacy vs C5a) and to dampen C5a-induced ERK signaling in macrophages, introducing a mechanistically plausible anti-inflammatory off-target pathway at commonly used concentrations (Li et al., 2021). Practical dosing analyses indicate that in vivo exposures at commonly used doses (>10 mg/kg i.p. or >0.3 mg/kg i.v.) will engage both C3aR and C5aR2, and high-dose use has been associated with adverse effects in animals (neutropenia, transient hypertension, weight gain, hematopoietic effects, tachycardia) (Li et al., 2021). Finally, modern C3aR signaling work demonstrates SB 290157 is a potent C3aR agonist that drives Gi/o/z activation and strong β-arrestin–dependent internalization, which can masquerade as “antagonism” in Ca2+ flux assays by depleting surface receptors and calcium stores; this β-arrestin–driven internalization explains many prior contradictory results (Rodriguez et al., 2024).  

Importantly, no published animal model of drusen or geographic atrophy using SB 290157 is identified in the provided context; evidence for drusen/sub-RPE deposit modulation by SB 290157 is restricted to in vitro hfRPE systems, while in vivo ocular use has been reported in RVO, which is a vascular occlusive disease and mechanistically distinct from dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Zhao et al., 2025).  

Mechanism of Action  
- Target and signaling context: C3aR (C3aR1) is a class A GPCR canonically activated by the complement anaphylatoxin C3a; it couples preferentially to Gi/o/z to inhibit cAMP, mobilize Ca2+, and recruit β-arrestins to mediate receptor internalization and signaling bias, with expression across immune and stromal cells, including microglia/macrophages, neutrophils, mast cells, and ocular cells (Müller cells, microglia, macrophages, vascular endothelium), and on human RPE in vitro (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). C3a/C3aR signaling has been implicated in RPE dysfunction and retinal pathologies through both pro-inflammatory outputs (e.g., VEGF upregulation, leukocyte recruitment) and tissue remodeling (ECM deposition) (Kleinman & Ambati, 2016; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- SB 290157 at C3aR: Original reports characterized SB 290157 as a competitive C3aR antagonist in binding and functional assays, demonstrating inhibition of C3a-induced Ca2+ mobilization (IC50 ~27.7 nM in human RBL-C3aR cells; low-nanomolar potency across species) and blockade of receptor internalization and smooth muscle contractile responses (Ames et al., 2001). Later work showed that SB 290157 can behave as a partial/full agonist in multiple expression systems, with potency strongly influenced by receptor density; in overexpression models (CHO-C3aR), SB 290157 induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation with an EC50 ~0.46 nM and near-maximal efficacy relative to C3a, while in some primary systems (e.g., HMDMs) it did not exhibit agonism up to 100 µM yet inhibited C3a-induced ERK with an IC50 ~236 nM (Li et al., 2021). Orthogonal signaling profiling confirmed that SB 290157 is a potent C3aR agonist across Gi/o/z subtypes and is highly efficacious at β-arrestin recruitment/internalization; antagonism observed in Ca2+ assays can arise from this strong internalization blocking subsequent G-protein signaling (effects unmasked by barbadin or Pitstop-2), i.e., SB 290157 acts as a biased agonist with dominant β-arrestin/internalization bias in many contexts (Rodriguez et al., 2024).  
- SB 290157 at other complement receptors: Counter-screening revealed no activation of C5aR1 in the tested ERK readout, but consistent partial agonism at C5aR2 (β-arrestin2 recruitment EC50 ~16.1 µM; ~31% efficacy vs C5a), with functional consequences including attenuation of C5a-induced ERK signaling in human and mouse macrophages; thus, SB 290157 can engage anti-inflammatory C5aR2 pathways at micromolar concentrations (Li et al., 2021). Importantly, in vivo exposures at common doses are predicted to co-engage both C3aR and C5aR2, complicating mechanistic attribution (Li et al., 2021).  
- RPE-specific pathomechanisms and C3aR blockade: In primary hfRPE, C3a binds basolateral C3aR and triggers a cascade leading to sub-RPE ECM accumulation: (i) decreased proteasome (UPP) activity without changes in proteasome-subunit mRNA, indicating post-transcriptional downregulation; (ii) dysregulation of ECM turnover via increased basal MMP-2 activity and reduced TIMP-3 (markedly reduced TIMP-3 with proteasome inhibitor MG-132), consistent with enhanced collagenase activity; and (iii) increased deposition of collagen IV and VI beneath the RPE monolayer (dose- and time-dependent), without changes in collagen I or EFEMP1 (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). C3a exposure increased C3aR expression/localization on RPE basolateral membranes, while a C3aR antagonist prevented the C3a-driven proteasome impairment, MMP-2 elevation, and accumulation of basal deposits in this model (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Notably, C3a did not acutely alter intracellular calcium in these RPE cultures, suggesting RPE-specific signaling architecture differs from classic immune cell paradigms; the antagonist’s protective effects in RPE thus map to UPP/ECM modulation rather than Ca2+-dependent degranulation (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- Potency considerations: Reported SB 290157 binding affinity to C3aR is in the low-hundreds of nanomolar range (competition IC50 ~500 ± 250 nM; Ki ~210 ± 90 nM in membrane binding), whereas functional potencies span 7–30 nM in many GPCR Ca2+ or platelet assays; in HMDMs, C3a-ERK inhibition IC50 ~236 nM has been reported, and in hfRPE studies the antagonist was used at 10 µM without a defined IC50 in that context (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001; Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). These disparities emphasize system-specific pharmacodynamics and the need for concentration–response characterization in RPE.  

Expected Effect  
The proposed hypothesis is that SB 290157 will competitively inhibit C3aR on RPE (IC50 ~500 nM), thereby preventing C3a-driven proteasome dysregulation and sub-RPE deposit formation, restoring proteostasis and improving photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake and degradation in dry AMD RPE cultures. Available data from the hfRPE system strongly support the first two mechanistic links—C3a promotes basal deposit formation via UPP inhibition and MMP-2/TIMP-3 imbalance, and C3aR blockade with SB 290157 (10 µM) prevents those ECM/proteostasis changes and associated sub-RPE deposit formation without damaging the RPE monolayer (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Specifically, in multi-week C3a exposures, antagonist co-treatment normalized ECM ultrastructure (SEM/TEM), blocked accumulation of collagens IV and VI beneath the RPE, prevented C3a-induced upregulation of C3aR expression, and preserved proteasome functional readouts, which together map to restoration of RPE proteostasis and ECM turnover in this model (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). These observations are consistent with the broader mechanistic framework that C3a–C3aR signaling at RPE can drive early AMD-like basal deposit formation and that C3aR antagonism can reverse the key biochemical drivers (UPP impairment and MMP-2/TIMP-3 dysregulation) underlying deposit accumulation (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
However, the “IC50 ~500 nM” statement matches binding competition in recombinant systems rather than functional antagonism in RPE; hfRPE studies used 10 µM without a reported potency or binding occupancy analysis in this cell type, and inhibitory potencies vary substantially across cell systems (7–30 nM in Ca2+ mobilization and platelet ATP-release assays, ~236 nM for ERK blockade in HMDMs) (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001; Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). For the intended RPE assay, an empirical concentration–response curve is needed to establish the minimal effective concentration that prevents C3a-driven UPP and ECM changes, ideally bracketed below concentrations known to partially activate C5aR2 to avoid confounded anti-inflammatory signaling (Li et al., 2021). The claim that SB 290157 will improve POS uptake/degradation is not supported by the provided literature; neither the hfRPE work nor the broader SB 290157 pharmacology summarizes RPE phagocytosis or POS processing endpoints, and the signaling work documenting SB 290157 effects on phagocytosis pertains to microglia, not RPE (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Thus, while restoration of proteasome function may secondarily benefit proteostasis pathways relevant to POS degradation, this remains to be demonstrated in RPE and should be considered an untested hypothesis rather than an evidence-based expectation at this time (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
Expression of the pharmacological target in the assay system is established in vitro: C3aR is present on hfRPE basolateral membranes, is upregulated by C3a challenge, and mediates the proteasome/ECM phenotypes that are reversed by antagonist co-treatment (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Complement-responsive cell types within the retina (e.g., Müller cells, microglia, macrophages, vascular endothelium) also express C3aR, providing mechanistic plausibility for in vivo effects of C3aR blockade in retinal disease models, although RVO pathobiology differs fundamentally from dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2025).  

Overall Evaluation  
SB 290157 engages a biologically compelling axis (C3a–C3aR) with direct mechanistic links to early dry AMD pathogenesis in RPE, but its complex and context-dependent pharmacology imposes significant risks for both interpretation and translational development. The totality of evidence supports continued use of C3aR antagonism as a mechanistic strategy in RPE, while casting doubt on SB 290157 as a development-grade candidate without substantial de-risking.  

Strengths  
- Disease-mechanism alignment in RPE: Chronic C3a exposure in hfRPE is sufficient to recapitulate sub-RPE ECM changes typical of early AMD (collagen IV/VI deposition, wide-spaced collagen, impaired UPP, elevated basal MMP-2), and C3aR antagonism with SB 290157 prevents these changes with preservation of barrier integrity, directly linking the pharmacological target to a core pathophysiology in dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). This is among the strongest mechanistic anchors for any complement-modulatory strategy specifically at the RPE level in vitro.  
- Ocular in vivo proof-of-concept for C3aR blockade: In an RVO model (distinct from dry AMD), SB 290157 reduced clinical, imaging, and functional pathology and dampened retinal inflammatory transcriptional programs, supporting ocular efficacy when the C3a/C3aR axis is pathologically active in vivo (Zhao et al., 2025). Although RVO is not dry AMD, these data imply that C3aR antagonism can be delivered in vivo to the eye with measurable therapeutic impact on inflammation-driven retinal pathology.  
- Established discovery provenance and extensive preclinical use: The origin, synthesis, and extensive cross-species pharmacology of SB 290157 are well documented, facilitating procurement and standardized use as a pharmacologic probe in RPE assays; the compound is commercially available as a TFA salt and has been broadly applied in complementary models, enabling rapid head-to-head comparisons and orthogonal validation strategies (Ames et al., 2001; Li et al., 2021).  

Limitations and risks  
- Intrinsic pharmacology is not a clean “antagonist”: SB 290157 is a potent, biased C3aR agonist that robustly recruits β-arrestin and internalizes the receptor, and it partially activates C5aR2 at micromolar concentrations; both properties confound interpretation of putative antagonism and introduce off-target anti-inflammatory mechanisms at concentrations commonly used in vitro and in vivo (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In particular, the 10 µM concentration effective in hfRPE lies in the range that can engage C5aR2, so anti-inflammatory effects may not be solely attributable to C3aR blockade (Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- System-dependent behavior: SB 290157 displays agonism at C3aR in overexpression systems and certain endogenously expressing cells, but antagonizes readouts in others (e.g., human macrophages, guinea pig platelets), a pattern explained by receptor density and signaling bias; this variability raises concerns that RPE outcomes could depend on culture conditions (e.g., receptor upregulation by C3a) and surface expression levels in ways that shift net pharmacology (Mathieu et al., 2005; Rodriguez et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- Dosing and translational exposure liabilities: In vivo, commonly used doses achieve plasma concentrations predicted to co-activate C5aR2 and/or trigger undesired systemic effects (neutropenia, cardiovascular changes); short half-life complicates chronic dosing paradigms, and ocular tissue exposure metrics are not defined for SB 290157 (Li et al., 2021; Ames et al., 2001; Mathieu et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2025). While the RVO study demonstrates functional benefit, it also acknowledges SB 290157’s pharmacological limitations, emphasizing the need for sham controls and target validation beyond a single tool compound (Zhao et al., 2025).  
- Lack of in vivo dry AMD/drusen data: No in vivo evidence in the provided context demonstrates that SB 290157 reduces drusen or geographic atrophy in animal models; the in vitro hfRPE data are compelling but represent a reductionist system that does not capture subretinal immune cell interactions, Bruch’s membrane transport, or choriocapillaris alterations central to dry AMD pathogenesis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- POS uptake/degradation claim is unsubstantiated: The assertion that SB 290157 will improve RPE POS phagocytosis and degradation is not supported by the cited literature; no presented data quantify SB 290157 effects on RPE phagolysosomal function, and extrapolation from proteasome restoration to POS handling remains hypothetical (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  

Recommendations for a decision path  
- Near-term, SB 290157 is suitable as a positive-control pharmacological tool for target validation in RPE culture under stringent controls, not as a development candidate. In hfRPE, reproduce and extend published findings under defined C3a challenges by:  
  • Determining a full concentration–response for SB 290157 (e.g., 30 nM to 10 µM) on UPP activity, basal MMP-2, TIMP-3 expression, and collagen IV/VI deposition, with parallel assessment of C3aR surface expression, to establish minimally effective concentrations and exclude pro-inflammatory or agonist-like effects at lower doses (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
  • Incorporating orthogonal target validation: C3aR knockdown/knockout in RPE (if feasible), and pharmacological controls to test C5aR2 involvement (e.g., C5aR2-selective agonism as a counter model, acknowledging that RPE C5aR2 expression is not defined here), plus use of alternative C3aR reagents (e.g., anti-C3aR antibodies) where practical (Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
  • Adding phagocytosis endpoints (POS uptake, lysosomal degradation kinetics) to directly test the hypothesis that proteasome restoration by C3aR blockade enhances POS processing; these endpoints are currently unsupported (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
  • Monitoring off-target and cytotoxicity signals, including β-arrestin–dependent internalization (if assayable) to correlate with functional outcomes and to avoid misinterpreting biased agonism as antagonism (Rodriguez et al., 2024).  
- For in vivo exploration, given the interpretability risks with SB 290157, de-emphasize systemic dosing and consider localized delivery paradigms and/or more selective C3aR agents if available. If SB 290157 must be used, constrain intraperitoneal dosing to ≤1 mg/kg to minimize C5aR2 engagement and track pharmacodynamic readouts consistent with RPE-centric mechanisms (e.g., basal laminar deposit markers, MMP-2/TIMP-3 balance) in AMD-relevant models, recognizing that no such drusen/GA mitigation data are currently available for SB 290157 (Li et al., 2021). Genetic models (C3aR deletion) provide partial support for retinal structural preservation after injury, but differ in mechanism and context from RPE-intrinsic deposit biology (Behnke et al., 2025).  
- Strategically, prioritize identification or design of true C3aR antagonists devoid of agonist/β-arrestin bias and C5aR2 activity, or evaluate upstream C3 blockade where ocular delivery and safety allow, as parallel development tracks. The need for improved C3aR ligands is highlighted repeatedly in the pharmacology literature due to SB 290157’s liabilities (Mathieu et al., 2005; Coulthard & Woodruff, 2015; Rodriguez et al., 2024).  

Conclusion  
On balance, C3aR antagonism remains an attractive target mechanism for early dry AMD based on robust RPE-centric in vitro data linking C3a–C3aR signaling to proteasome impairment, ECM dysregulation, and sub-RPE deposit formation, with SB 290157 acting as an effective tool compound to prevent these changes in hfRPE (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). However, SB 290157’s complex pharmacology—potent biased C3aR agonism and partial C5aR2 agonism—creates substantial risks for misattributing mechanism and for translation, particularly at micromolar concentrations or systemic in vivo exposures where off-target signaling is likely (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Li et al., 2021). There is no in vivo evidence here that SB 290157 reduces drusen/geographic atrophy, and the claimed benefits for POS phagocytosis are unproven (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Zhao et al., 2025). As a result, I recommend using SB 290157 only as a controlled, short-term pharmacologic probe to (a) mechanistically validate the role of C3aR in RPE proteostasis/ECM biology and (b) set pharmacodynamic benchmarks for target engagement in RPE; in parallel, we should invest in sourcing or developing next-generation, selective C3aR antagonists with confirmed lack of agonism and C5aR2 activity for any advancement toward dry AMD models and, ultimately, clinical translation (Mathieu et al., 2005; Rodriguez et al., 2024; Coulthard & Woodruff, 2015).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is a fully synthetic small molecule in the 4-aminoquinoline (4AQ) class, developed in the mid-20th century as a hydroxylated analogue of chloroquine (CQ) to improve tolerability; HCQ differs from CQ by a terminal hydroxyl group on the side chain (HCQ: C18H26ClN3O, 336 g/mol; CQ: C18H26ClN3, 320 g/mol) (Browning, 2014a, 2014b). Industrially, HCQ can be prepared by condensing N1-N-ethyl-N1-β-hydroxyethyl-1,4-pentanediamine with 4,7-dichloroquinoline, paralleling the CQ route from the same quinoline core with an altered aminoalkyl side chain (Rainsford et al., 2015). As a class, HCQ/CQ are alkylated 4-aminoquinolines: weak, amphiphilic bases bearing a flat quinoline nucleus and a basic side chain that traverse membranes in unprotonated form and undergo protonation-dependent sequestration in acidic intracellular compartments (lysosomes, endosomes, Golgi) — a defining pharmacologic property (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Chloroquine’s two basic centers (pKa ≈ 10.2 and 8.1) illustrate the protonation behavior that drives lysosomal trapping; at lysosomal pH (≈ 4–5) these agents become diprotonated and accumulate, with lysosome:plasma distribution ratios measured on the order of ≈ 160 000 and intralysosomal concentrations up to ≈ 2 × 10⁻² M reported for CQ, elevating lysosomal pH toward ≈ 6 (Browning, 2014b, 2014a). Pharmacokinetically, HCQ exhibits high oral bioavailability (≈ 0.7–0.8), an extremely large apparent volume of distribution (> 40 000 L), and a long terminal elimination half-life (≈ 40–60 days), with blood concentrations exceeding plasma due to extensive intracellular partitioning and tissue sequestration (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Melanin-containing ocular tissues are prominent depots; with chronic ingestion, uveal and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) concentrations can reach up to ≈ 10 000× plasma, reflecting lysosomal trapping and melanin binding (Browning, 2014a). Enantiomer-specific disposition has been observed for HCQ, with stereoselective accumulation noted in blood compartments, underscoring complex distribution kinetics (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Clinically, HCQ is commonly administered as the sulfate salt, and CQ as the phosphate salt (Neto et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
HCQ and CQ were developed as antimalarials and subsequently repurposed as disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), with additional uses across dermatology and other immune-mediated conditions; HCQ is generally preferred over CQ for chronic therapy due to a better safety profile while maintaining comparable immunomodulatory efficacy (Rainsford et al., 2015; Neto et al., 2020). Broad clinical applications documented for HCQ/CQ include SLE, RA, primary Sjögren’s syndrome, discoid/cutaneous lupus erythematosus, polymorphous light eruption, solar urticaria, porphyria cutanea tarda, and other inflammatory dermatoses, reflecting lysosomotropic and immune-modulating actions (Rainsford et al., 2015; Rapparini et al., 2025). Mechanistically motivated repurposing has extended to autophagy inhibition in oncology trials, typically at daily doses far exceeding rheumatologic regimens, although HCQ is not approved as an anticancer adjuvant (Yusuf et al., 2023). Over recent decades HCQ prescriptions have increased substantially due to its relative affordability and systemic safety advantages, expanding the exposed population and the need for ocular safety surveillance (Yusuf et al., 2023).

With respect to retinal disease, the literature emphasizes retinotoxic risk and mechanistic links to RPE lysosomal dysfunction rather than therapeutic benefit in degenerative macular disease; authoritative pharmacology and ophthalmology sources do not provide evidence that HCQ/CQ have been used as treatments for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and instead catalogue retinal toxicity mechanisms and monitoring practices associated with long-term systemic use (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). Multiple summaries note that available data do not support therapeutic use of 4AQs for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerations, while documenting ocular accumulation, lysosomal alkalinization, and RPE stress as central safety concerns (Browning, 2014a). Retinopathy, although uncommon at recommended doses, is a recognized dose- and duration-related adverse effect that can be irreversible and may progress after drug cessation, motivating dose caps and structured ophthalmic screening (Rainsford et al., 2015; Ding et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action  
Lysosomotropism and lysosomal alkalinization  
HCQ/CQ are canonical lysosomotropic weak bases that accumulate massively within acidic intracellular organelles and elevate their pH, directly impairing acidity-dependent lysosomal hydrolases, receptor recycling, and degradative pathways including autophagy (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b). In vitro and cell-system studies report that chloroquine exposure increases lysosomal pH from ≈ 4–5 toward ≈ 6, a change sufficient to inhibit cathepsin activities and other acid hydrolases; pharmacologic blockade of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase with bafilomycin A₁ abrogates CQ’s lysosomotropism and toxicity, pinpointing disruption of lysosomal acidification as the proximal driver (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b). In RPE cells specifically, the lysosomotropic alkalinization by 4AQs inhibits lysosomal enzyme activity and autophagic flux, leading to accumulation of undegraded material; experimental inhibition of vacuolar acidification with bafilomycin phenocopies these degradative defects, indicating that pH elevation per se is sufficient to impair RPE lysosomal function (Guha et al., 2014).

Immune modulation and nucleic acid sensing  
Elevation of endolysosomal pH by 4AQs inhibits MHC class II antigen processing and presentation and blocks activation of endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR-3/7/9), thereby reducing MyD88-dependent interferon production and dampening pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion from mononuclear cells and dendritic cells (IL-1, IL-6, TNF, IFN-α/γ, CCL4) (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). The class also interferes with cGAS–STING pathway activation through inhibition of cGAMP synthase and reduces T-cell co-stimulatory signaling (e.g., CD154), a mechanistic constellation that explains DMARD efficacy without significant increases in opportunistic infections (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020; Browning, 2014b). Additional molecular interactions reported for 4AQs include DNA binding/intercalation, kinase pathway modulation (e.g., ERK/MAPK), and diverse enzyme interactions (e.g., cholinesterase), reflecting broad pleiotropy at pharmacologic and suprapharmacologic exposures (Browning, 2014a).

RPE-relevant degradative biology: cathepsins and POS processing  
The RPE depends critically on acidic lysosomes and cathepsin activity to clear the daily phagocytic load of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and maintain autophagic flux; failure of this system yields lipofuscin accumulation and contributes to AMD pathogenesis (Sharif, 2015). Multiple lysosomal proteases are expressed by RPE, including cysteine cathepsins B, L, and S as well as aspartyl cathepsin D; cathepsins are synthesized as pre-proenzymes, processed via the secretory pathway, and activated in the acidic lumen of late endosomes/lysosomes (Sharif, 2015). In human RPE/choroid and RPE cell lines, both inactive and active forms of cathepsin B, L, and S have been detected; functional studies show that broad cysteine protease inhibition or cathepsin S knockdown impairs POS degradation and increases lipofuscin-like inclusions, underscoring their role in RPE proteostasis (Sharif, 2015). Cathepsin D, a major lysosomal aspartyl protease in RPE, is essential for POS processing; its maturation and catalytic efficiency are strongly pH-dependent and occur within the acidic lysosomal lumen (Cardoso et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).

CQ/HCQ disrupt lysosomal proteolysis and lysosome dynamics in RPE  
In RPE models, CQ induces a rapid lysosomal pH increase followed by partial pH recovery, yet produces persistent lysosomal enlargement, accumulation of undegraded endocytic, phagocytic, and autophagic cargos, and a progressive reduction in accessibility of enlarged lysosomes to the endocytic pathway — a phenotype consistent with impaired autolysosome reformation and failure to regenerate a pool of degradatively competent lysosomes (Cardoso et al., 2023). A salient molecular signature of CQ exposure is accumulation of pro-cathepsin D and the lysosomal membrane protein LAMP1 without corresponding mRNA increases, indicating impaired processing/turnover rather than transcriptional upregulation; protease inhibitor treatment phenocopies this pro-cathepsin D accumulation, linking CQ’s effect to reduced proteolytic capacity (Cardoso et al., 2023). Although lysosomotropic agents can activate TFEB-dependent lysosomal gene transcription at high concentrations, the inhibitory effects on cathepsin maturation and lysosome reformation dominate in RPE models at low doses and precede any compensatory changes in gene expression (Cardoso et al., 2023).

HCQ further impairs RPE lysosomes by perturbing cholesterol homeostasis and promoting lysosomal membrane permeability (LMP), with cytosolic release of cathepsin B  
Beyond general autophagy/lysosome inhibition, HCQ suppresses mTORC1-dependent cholesterol biosynthesis, a change that increases lysosomal membrane permeability and allows lysosomal cathepsin B to translocate into the cytosol, where it can activate caspase-dependent apoptosis and drive caspase-independent phosphatidylserine externalization; these effects are mitigated by neutral pH-selective cathepsin B inhibition and exacerbated by pharmacologic cholesterol lowering (simvastatin) or depletion (methyl-β-cyclodextrin) (Wicks et al., 2022). These data in ARPE-19 RPE cells indicate that HCQ-induced lysosomal dysfunction and LMP sensitize RPE to additional stressors (e.g., UV), compounding vulnerability in aging retinal tissue (Wicks et al., 2022).

RPE/retinal stress signatures and storage phenotypes with 4AQ exposure  
Cell and animal studies document that 4AQ exposure produces RPE and retinal stress consistent with impaired lysosomal degradation: multilamellar myeloid bodies in RPE, photoreceptors, and ganglion cells; inhibition of oxidative enzymes in photoreceptors; decreased retinal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and glutathione with increased lipid peroxidation; disruption of the blood–retina barrier; and inhibition of protein synthesis in RPE culture (Browning, 2014a). In RPE cell culture, high concentrations of CQ perturb fusion of autophagic vesicles, increase LC3-II and p62, and can drive cell death, while intravitreal bafilomycin reproduces opsin-loaded phagolysosome accumulation, affirming that alkalinization is sufficient to cause degradative backlog (Guha et al., 2014). Chronic CQ treatment in mice increases mRNA expression of v-H⁺-ATPase and TFEB, consistent with compensatory attempts to reacidify lysosomes and enhance biogenesis, but does not normalize degradative function during exposure (Guha et al., 2014).

Absence of evidence for “low-dose stabilization” of lysosomal pH in RPE  
Across mechanistic summaries and primary RPE studies, there is no evidence that low-dose HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH at an “optimal” value, preserves cathepsin activity, or enhances POS degradation; rather, the consistent effect is lysosomal alkalinization with inhibition of lysosomal enzymes (including cathepsin B) and blockade of autophagic/lysosomal degradation (Browning, 2014a). In fact, low-dose CQ already yields accumulation of pro-cathepsin D and cargo buildup in RPE, indicating that even modest lysosomotropic perturbation degrades proteolytic competence, counter to the hypothesis (Cardoso et al., 2023).

Pharmacokinetic and ocular deposition constraints  
The extreme tissue distribution and ocular melanin binding of 4AQs undermine precise intraocular dose control: uveal/RPE drug levels can markedly exceed plasma during chronic dosing, and the terminal half-life is long, with months-long detectability after discontinuation due to depot release (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). These properties make “titration” to a narrow, hypothetical lysosomal pH window impractical and raise the risk of sustained lysosomal alkalinization even with ostensibly low systemic doses (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis proposes that submicromolar HCQ will “fine-tune” lysosomal pH in RPE to an optimal range for cathepsin activity, thereby preserving cathepsin function and enhancing POS degradation without blocking autophagy. The aggregate evidence contradicts this at mechanistic, cellular, and pharmacokinetic levels.

- Cathepsins in RPE require an acidic lumen for zymogen processing and catalytic function, and multiple cathepsins (B, L, S, D) are expressed and active in RPE lysosomes where they regulate POS degradation and autophagy; broad cysteine protease inhibition or specific cathepsin S knockdown impairs POS clearance and increases lipofuscin-like inclusions, demonstrating the acid-dependent protease requirement (Sharif, 2015). In this context, 4AQs act as lysosomal alkalinizers that inhibit acid hydrolases; CQ/HCQ inhibit cathepsin B and disrupt cathepsin D processing, with CQ causing pro-cathepsin D accumulation and reduced maturation into the active enzyme, a phenotype directly linked to impaired lysosomal proteolysis and cargo clearance (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). Therefore, the expected effect of submicromolar HCQ is not preservation but reduction of cathepsin function in RPE lysosomes, with consequent impairment of POS proteolysis (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023).

- In RPE cells, CQ/HCQ exposure impairs autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, producing enlarged, cargo-laden lysosomes that are progressively less accessible to endocytic inputs; these dynamics deplete the pool of degradatively competent lysosomes needed for daily POS processing, an effect observed even at “low-dose” CQ and preceding transcriptional responses (Cardoso et al., 2023). Thus, in assays measuring POS degradation and lysosomal flux, HCQ is predicted to slow, not enhance, turnover (Cardoso et al., 2023).

- HCQ further increases lysosomal membrane permeability and releases cathepsin B into the cytosol by impairing mTORC1-dependent cholesterol biosynthesis, activating pro-death signaling and phosphatidylserine externalization; pharmacologic cholesterol lowering/depletion magnify these effects, suggesting that HCQ’s action sensitizes RPE to metabolic and environmental stress rather than stabilizing proteolysis (Wicks et al., 2022).

- Beyond lysosomal pH, 4AQs disrupt other RPE functions essential for photoreceptor support: CQ inhibits rod outer segment phagocytosis in human/pig RPE cell lines, and HCQ/CQ inhibit OATP1A2 in human RPE, potentially perturbing all-trans-retinol uptake and the visual cycle — liabilities expected to worsen POS handling and photoreceptor maintenance in AMD models (Yusuf et al., 2023).

- The claim that “over-acidification” in RPE lysosomes needs moderation lacks evidentiary support in this literature corpus; the dominant pathologic signal in RPE aging and AMD models is lysosomal under-acidification/alkalinization and degradative impairment, which 4AQs exacerbate rather than correct (Guha et al., 2014).

- Pharmacokinetically, due to massive ocular accumulation and prolonged tissue persistence, “low systemic dose” does not guarantee low intra-RPE exposure; achieving and maintaining a narrow “optimal pH” window is improbable and unsafe for chronic indications with slowly reversible tissue exposure (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

In sum, in assays of RPE lysosomal function and POS degradation, the most probable outcomes of HCQ at submicromolar concentrations are lysosomal pH elevation, inhibited cathepsin activity/maturation (including cathepsin B inhibition and pro-cathepsin D accumulation), impaired autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, increased LMP with cytosolic cathepsin B release, inhibition of POS phagocytosis, and potential disruption of retinoid transport — all expected to reduce, not enhance, POS degradation (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023; Wicks et al., 2022; Yusuf et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths for development feasibility  
- Extensive clinical pharmacology and systemic experience: HCQ has well-characterized oral pharmacokinetics, metabolism, and drug–drug interactions, with validated immunomodulatory mechanisms (endolysosomal pH elevation, TLR/cGAS–STING inhibition, cytokine suppression) across rheumatology and dermatology; supply chains and clinical dosing paradigms are established, enabling rapid translational work if warranted (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020; Rainsford et al., 2015). The compound’s canonical lysosomotropic action makes it a useful positive control for modeling lysosomal alkalinization and degradative impairment in RPE assays benchmarking alternative, mechanistically restorative strategies (Browning, 2014b).

- Lower ocular toxicity relative to CQ at equipotency: HCQ is generally less retinotoxic than CQ, a difference attributed in part to greater polarity and lower lipophilicity; however, the class risk remains dose- and duration-dependent and clinically significant (Browning, 2014a; Rainsford et al., 2015).

Critical weaknesses for dry AMD  
- Mechanistic conflict with therapeutic goal: RPE catabolism of POS requires acidic lysosomes and intact cathepsin maturation/activity; 4AQs elevate lysosomal pH, inhibit cathepsin activity (including cathepsin B) and maturation (cathepsin D), impair autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, and induce cargo accumulation — a set of changes that predict impaired POS processing and enhanced lipofuscin burden rather than restoration of lysosomal proteolysis (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). No evidence in RPE/AMD models supports the hypothesis that “low-dose” HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH to optimize cathepsin function; the reported outcomes consistently indicate degradative inhibition (Browning, 2014a).

- Ocular tropism and prolonged tissue persistence: The combination of melanin binding and lysosomal trapping produces extreme ocular accumulation and very slow washout, making precise intraocular dose control infeasible and raising the risk of prolonged lysosomal alkalinization even after dose reduction or cessation (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b).

- Added liabilities in RPE and retina: HCQ promotes lysosomal membrane permeability and cytosolic cathepsin B release in RPE, sensitizing cells to UV and cholesterol-lowering stresses; CQ/HCQ also inhibit POS phagocytosis and OATP1A2 in RPE, potentially disrupting retinoid uptake and the visual cycle, and they induce retinal stress signatures (oxidative enzyme inhibition, antioxidant depletion, barrier disruption) — all detrimental in the aging macula (Wicks et al., 2022; Yusuf et al., 2023; Browning, 2014a).

- Absence of supportive precedent in AMD: Comprehensive pharmacologic and ophthalmic reviews provide no evidence that HCQ/CQ have been successfully used to treat dry AMD or analogous retinal degenerations; rather, they underscore retinotoxic risk and mechanisms consistent with RPE lysosomal dysfunction (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

Strategic implications and recommendation  
The central hypothesis — that low-dose HCQ can fine-tune RPE lysosomal pH to preserve cathepsin activity and enhance POS degradation — is at odds with the mechanistic canon and RPE-focused data for 4AQs, which consistently demonstrate lysosomal alkalinization, cathepsin inhibition or maturation block, impaired lysosome reformation and autophagic flux, and accumulation of undegraded cargo (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). No cited evidence shows that HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH or improves POS degradation in RPE or AMD models; on the contrary, RPE studies with CQ/HCQ and mechanistic summaries emphasize inhibited lysosomal enzymes and autophagy as core actions (Browning, 2014a; Guha et al., 2014). Given extreme ocular accumulation and prolonged tissue retention, exploratory dosing aimed at a narrow “optimal” intralysosomal pH is neither controllable nor safe in a chronic neurodegenerative indication; adverse lysosomal effects could persist despite dose adjustments due to depot release (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). If the program goal is to restore RPE lysosomal proteolysis and POS turnover in dry AMD, agents that acidify lysosomes, facilitate cathepsin maturation/activity, or pharmacologically promote lysosome reformation (as suggested by pathways implicated in CQ-induced defects) align mechanistically, whereas HCQ/CQ, as archetypal alkalinizers and autophagy inhibitors, do not (Cardoso et al., 2023).

Conclusion: HCQ (Sigma-Aldrich H0915) is not a suitable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD under the proposed mechanism. The weight of biochemical, cellular, and pharmacokinetic evidence indicates HCQ will alkalinize RPE lysosomes, inhibit cathepsin function and maturation, impair autophagic flux and POS processing, and increase RPE vulnerability to stress, while ocular accumulation and long half-life amplify risk; no supportive evidence exists for benefit in dry AMD (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023; Wicks et al., 2022; Browning, 2014b). I recommend against advancing HCQ for AMD and suggest redirecting efforts toward mechanisms that restore lysosomal acidity, cathepsin activity, and lysosome reformation in RPE (Cardoso et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Brexpiprazole is a synthetic, orally available fifth‐generation antipsychotic developed by Otsuka Pharmaceutical that belongs to the class of serotonin–dopamine activity modulators (SDAMs). It was discovered and developed as an improvement over earlier dopamine partial agonists in order to achieve balanced modulation of neurotransmission. Chemically, brexpiprazole was designed as a dihydrocarbostyril derivative that retains partial agonistic properties at dopamine D₂ receptors while simultaneously exhibiting potent partial agonism at serotonin 5-HT₁A receptors and antagonism at serotonin 5-HT₂A receptors (Das et al., 2016). This balanced receptor profile has been exploited primarily for psychiatric indications, but the receptor distribution of serotonin receptors is not limited to neuronal tissues. In particular, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) expresses several serotonin receptor subtypes, and there is compelling biochemical evidence that serotonergic signaling influences inflammatory gene expression and cellular homeostasis in these cells (Biswal et al., 2015). As such, brexpiprazole’s well‐defined receptor interactions position it as a promising candidate to modulate pathological pathways in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
Brexpiprazole has an established history for its use in central nervous system disorders. It has been approved for the treatment of schizophrenia and as an adjunct therapy in major depressive disorder owing to its favorable safety and tolerability profiles, which include a low risk of extrapyramidal side effects and modest metabolic liabilities (Das et al., 2016; Fabre et al., 2022). To date, however, no clinical trials or preclinical studies have directly examined brexpiprazole for the treatment of retinal degenerative conditions such as dry AMD. Nevertheless, multiple studies have investigated the therapeutic potential of 5-HT₁A receptor agonists in retinal models. For example, research utilizing 8-OH-DPAT—a prototypical 5-HT₁A agonist—demonstrated significant antioxidant protection in RPE cells, reduction in oxidative stress markers, and preservation of retinal architecture under conditions of mitochondrial oxidative stress (Biswal et al., 2015). Other compounds with selective 5-HT₁A agonist properties, such as tandospirone, have been evaluated in retinal models, albeit with mixed clinical outcomes (Buschini et al., 2015). This preclinical precedence establishes an indirect rationale for repurposing brexpiprazole in dry AMD even if direct ocular applications have not been previously explored.

Mechanism of Action:  
Brexpiprazole exerts its pharmacological effects primarily through dual modulation of serotonergic receptors. Its partial agonism at 5-HT₁A receptors, with reported potency in the low nanomolar range (EC₅₀ ~ 5 nM as hypothesized), is thought to trigger intracellular cascades that promote cellular survival and antioxidant defenses. Activation of the 5-HT₁A receptor in other tissues has been associated with upregulation of key antioxidant enzymes—including metallothionein-1 (MT-1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NADPH quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NqO1), catalase, and superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1)—thereby mitigating oxidative stress and reducing mitochondrial damage (Biswal et al., 2015). In RPE cells—the cell type critical for photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance—the 5-HT₁A receptor is endogenously expressed, and its activation has been linked to attenuation of inflammatory signaling. Preclinical studies using other 5-HT₁A agonists in ARPE-19 cells have shown reductions in oxidative stress markers and inflammatory mediators, as well as preservation of tight junction proteins (Biswal et al., 2015).

Simultaneously, brexpiprazole’s antagonism at 5-HT₂A receptors may complement these effects by further modulating inflammatory responses. Blockade of 5-HT₂A receptors has been associated with reduced microglial activation and decreased complement deposition in the outer retina, contributing to neuroprotection in models of retinal degeneration (Biswal et al., 2015; Das et al., 2016). This dual receptor effect is proposed to result in an overall anti-inflammatory microenvironment in the RPE, which is crucial because chronic inflammation is a key pathological feature in dry AMD. Moreover, the compound’s modulation of serotonergic signaling may indirectly support the maintenance of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, which are essential for the normal clearance of POS (Biswal et al., 2015). Although direct studies with brexpiprazole in RPE cells are lacking, these mechanistic insights derived from similar 5-HT₁A agonists underpin the hypothesis that brexpiprazole could reduce production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6 and TNF-α) and restore normal phagocytic and lysosomal function (Biswal et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
In an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells or isolated RPE cells under conditions of complement-induced stress, brexpiprazole is expected to act by modulating serotonergic receptor signaling to yield a multi-faceted protective effect. Specifically, its 5-HT₁A agonism should trigger intracellular survival pathways that result in the upregulation of antioxidant defenses analogous to the responses observed with 8-OH-DPAT in similar models (Biswal et al., 2015). This effect is anticipated to lead to a reduction in oxidative stress markers, such as 8-OH-deoxyguanosine or nitrotyrosine adducts, which are typically elevated in conditions of mitochondrial oxidative injury (Biswal et al., 2015).

Additionally, brexpiprazole is hypothesized to reduce the expression of key pro-inflammatory cytokines—specifically IL-6 and TNF-α—through receptor-mediated modulation of inflammatory signaling cascades. In a cell culture model where RPE cells are exposed to oxidative and complement-mediated insults, a drop in these cytokine levels would be indicative of an amelioration of stress-induced inflammatory responses (Biswal et al., 2015; Wright & Ambati, 2016). This anti-inflammatory effect is critical because uncontrolled inflammation not only perpetuates oxidative damage but also disrupts the barrier and phagocytic functions of the RPE.

Furthermore, the candidate is expected to preserve or restore the expression of MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase crucial for the phagocytosis of POS, as well as cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease necessary for the degradation of internalized material (Biswal et al., 2015; Fischer, 2016). Successful maintenance of these proteins would directly support the clearance functions of RPE cells, an essential element for retinal homeostasis that is compromised in dry AMD. This improved phagocytic capacity, coupled with reduced cytokine production, would likely result in overall preservation of RPE structure and function, as reflected in enhanced visual function in preclinical models (Biswal et al., 2015).

Moreover, although the clinical studies of other serotonergic compounds such as tandospirone have yielded mixed results—with at least one phase III trial for geographic atrophy being discontinued due to lack of efficacy (Buschini et al., 2015)—the favorable pharmacokinetic properties and established safety profile of brexpiprazole in other indications provide a strong rationale for its repurposing, particularly if its ocular penetration can be demonstrated in relevant preclinical models (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation:  
Brexpiprazole offers several attractive strengths as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its dual mechanism—partial agonism at 5-HT₁A receptors paired with antagonism at 5-HT₂A receptors—is well aligned with the emerging understanding of how serotonergic signaling influences retinal cell survival, oxidative stress, and inflammation (Biswal et al., 2015). The wealth of preclinical evidence supporting the role of 5-HT₁A receptor activation in reducing oxidative damage and preserving RPE function under stress conditions provides a sound mechanistic basis for expecting similar protective effects from brexpiprazole. In addition, the targeting of phagocytic receptor expression (i.e., MERTK) and lysosomal enzymes (i.e., cathepsin D) represents a novel strategy to address one of the fundamental dysfunctions in dry AMD: impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (Biswal et al., 2015).

Brexpiprazole’s established safety profile and pharmacokinetics in psychiatric populations further underscore its potential for repurposing. Its high oral bioavailability and documented tolerability in long-term studies, along with evidence that similar compounds can penetrate ocular tissues when administered systemically, add to the candidate’s appeal (Das et al., 2016; Fabre et al., 2022). This is particularly relevant given the chronic nature of dry AMD and the need for therapies that can be safely administered over extended periods.

However, several significant weaknesses and gaps warrant cautious consideration. First, direct evidence linking brexpiprazole to improved RPE function—specifically, its effects on inflammatory signaling markers IL-6 and TNF-α, and on the preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression—remains theoretical and extrapolated from studies using other 5-HT₁A agonists like 8-OH-DPAT (Biswal et al., 2015). This means that while the underlying mechanistic hypothesis is plausible, there is a pressing need for targeted in vitro and in vivo studies focused on brexpiprazole in ocular models. In particular, experiments using ARPE-19 cells under conditions of oxidative or complement-induced stress must be conducted to confirm that brexpiprazole can indeed modulate cytokine levels and restore phagocytic function in these cells.

Another shortcoming is the uncertainty regarding ocular penetration. Although the systemic administration of 5-HT₁A agonists in animal models has led to beneficial retinal outcomes (Biswal et al., 2015), brexpiprazole’s distribution into ocular tissues has not been directly evaluated. It is essential to ascertain the extent to which brexpiprazole reaches the RPE at therapeutically relevant concentrations, particularly given that dosage regimens for psychiatric conditions may not be directly translatable to ocular therapy (Biswal et al., 2015).

Furthermore, while the anti-inflammatory hypothesis is supported by the general role of serotonergic signaling in RPE cells, the direct measurement of inflammatory cytokines and downstream phagocytic markers in response to brexpiprazole treatment remains to be demonstrated. Given that earlier clinical attempts using tandospirone for AMD were unsuccessful (Buschini et al., 2015), there is a need to critically assess whether brexpiprazole’s receptor profile confers advantages that overcome the limitations observed with other 5-HT₁A agonists. Additionally, potential off-target effects in the ocular environment—such as those arising from modulation of other receptor systems—must be thoroughly evaluated.

In summary, brexpiprazole presents a scientifically sound and innovative approach to the treatment of dry AMD by virtue of its serotonergic receptor modulation. Its dual action on 5-HT₁A and 5-HT₂A receptors is supported by a robust body of preclinical evidence indicating that 5-HT₁A receptor activation can reduce oxidative stress and inflammation in RPE cells, while also preserving essential functions like POS clearance (Biswal et al., 2015). The candidate’s excellent safety profile in psychiatric applications and potential for systemic administration further enhance its appeal. Nevertheless, the absence of direct experimental data linking brexpiprazole to improved phagocytosis, reduced IL-6 and TNF-α production, and maintained lysosomal enzyme expression in RPE cells represents a critical gap that must be addressed. As such, while the repurposing of brexpiprazole for dry AMD holds promise, a series of preclinical experiments—encompassing in vitro ARPE-19 cell assays, in vivo ocular pharmacokinetic studies, and efficacy models of retinal degeneration—are required before progressing to clinical trials. Overall, given the mechanistic rationale and the encouraging safety and pharmacological characteristics of brexpiprazole, further research is justified to validate its application in dry AMD, provided that the aforementioned knowledge gaps are systematically addressed (Das et al., 2016; Biswal et al., 2015).

AM580 is a highly selective RARα agonist with demonstration of direct effects on RPE biology: it upregulates MFGE8, enhances phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, and inhibits EMT in RPE cells. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AM580 is a fully synthetic retinoid compound designed as a highly selective agonist for the retinoic acid receptor α (RARα). Its chemical structure—a derivative of naphthalene and benzoic acid—was rationally engineered to confer two key properties: a more rigid molecular architecture compared with the natural ligand all‐trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and a marked preferential binding to RARα over other retinoid receptor subtypes (RARβ and RARγ) (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992). The molecule’s chemical name, 4-(5,6,7,8-tetrahydro-5,5,8,8-tetramethyl-2-naphthalenyl)carboxamido]benzoic acid, reflects its derivation from a series of modifications intended to enhance receptor selectivity and bioactivity (Martin et al., 1992). AM580 belongs to the broader class of retinoids—compounds that are either natural derivatives of vitamin A or synthetically modified analogues—which function as ligands for nuclear hormone receptors. Retinoids have been exploited in various fields of medicine due to their ability to modulate cellular differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis by activating retinoic acid receptor (RAR) and retinoid X receptor (RXR) pathways (Cras et al., 2010; Martin et al., 1992). In the case of AM580, its design emphasizes selective RARα activation, as demonstrated by its 30-fold higher binding affinity for RARα compared to RARβ and RARγ (Teng et al., 1996; Martin et al., 1992), making it an excellent molecular tool for dissection of RARα-specific biological responses.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, retinoids have been at the forefront of differentiation therapy, with ATRA being successfully employed in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) (Garattini et al., 2007; Garattini et al., 1997). However, the clinical use of natural retinoids like ATRA has been limited by drawbacks such as isomerization, rapid metabolism, and broad receptor engagement leading to unnecessary side effects (Drowley et al., 2020; Cras et al., 2010). These limitations spurred the development of receptor subtype–selective ligands, among which AM580 emerged as a leading RARα-selective agonist (Martin et al., 1992). Beyond oncology, synthetic retinoids have been investigated in a variety of contexts including dermatology and even cardiovascular applications (Nagy et al., 2012; Petrukhin, 2013); however, more recent studies have explored the potential ocular applications of retinoid receptor agonists. In particular, a growing body of literature has begun to examine the effects of RAR agonists on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that activation of RARα in RPE cells by compounds such as AM580 can modulate epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and improve cellular functions relevant to retinal homeostasis (Kobayashi et al., 2021). Although not previously approved as an ocular therapeutic, the compound’s use in research settings—including those investigating phagocytic processes in the RPE—provides a promising precedent for repurposing it for conditions like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of AM580 is well delineated at the molecular level. As an RARα agonist, it binds with high affinity to the ligand-binding domain of RARα, a nuclear receptor that functions as a ligand-dependent transcription factor. Upon ligand binding, the receptor undergoes a conformational change that results in the dissociation of co-repressor complexes and the recruitment of co-activators and other transcriptional machinery. This ligand-induced activation facilitates the heterodimerization of RARα with retinoid X receptor (RXR), followed by binding to retinoic acid response elements (RAREs) in the promoter regions of target genes (Garattini et al., 2007; Teng et al., 1996).  
Notably, AM580’s structural modification—featuring a polar amide linkage—enhances its selectivity for RARα by promoting specific hydrogen bonding interactions within the receptor’s binding pocket that are not available in RARβ or RARγ (Teng et al., 1996). Once activated, RARα modulates a variety of downstream genes. Among these, studies have recently indicated that selective RARα activation can lead to the upregulation of milk fat globule epidermal growth factor 8 (MFGE8) in RPE cells (Unknown Reference). MFGE8 plays a critical role in facilitating the bridging of phosphatidylserine (exposed on the shed photoreceptor outer segments (POS)) to integrin receptors—specifically αvβ5—which are expressed on the RPE, thereby promoting efficient phagocytosis (Drowley et al., 2020; Kobayashi et al., 2021). Consequently, AM580’s engagement of RARα is expected to not only drive transcriptional changes related to RPE differentiation and anti-fibrotic responses but also directly enhance phagocytic clearance mechanisms essential for retinal health (Kobayashi et al., 2021). In additional preclinical settings, RARα agonism via AM580 has been implicated in modulating transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling pathways, which further supports its capacity to inhibit aberrant EMT—a process implicated in retinal scarring and progression of dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis under evaluation posits that AM580, by selectively activating RARα at an effective concentration (EC₅₀ ~50 nM as observed in RPE cell assays), will stimulate the transcription of the MFGE8 gene. Upregulation of MFGE8 is crucial because this glycoprotein acts as a “molecular bridge” by binding to phosphatidylserine on POS and to integrin receptors such as αvβ5 on the RPE. Under normal conditions, MFGE8 is an essential mediator of RPE phagocytosis, facilitating the daily clearance of spent outer segments—a process that is impaired in dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2012). Evidence from preclinical studies, including those using Mertk-deficient RPE models, suggests that AM580 treatment can lead to increased MFGE8 levels and a concomitant improvement in POS uptake (Kobayashi et al., 2021). Thus, in the assay proposed by the team, AM580 is expected to restore or enhance the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells by boosting MFGE8 expression. This improved clearance mechanism would help reduce the accumulation of POS debris and lipofuscin—a buildup known to contribute to RPE dysfunction and the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Furthermore, secondary effects such as the inhibition of deleterious EMT processes—which are associated with fibrosis and the progression of dry AMD—may also be realized, thereby preserving or restoring a more differentiated, functional RPE phenotype (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
AM580 represents a compelling therapeutic candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, based on several lines of evidence gathered from the literature. Its primary strength lies in its high degree of selectivity for RARα. This receptor selectivity is critical because it allows for target‐specific modulation of gene expression, potentially reducing the broad side effects observed with natural retinoids like ATRA that activate multiple receptor subtypes (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992; Teng et al., 1996). The structural optimization of AM580 not only confers potent agonistic activity but also provides a pharmacological tool for dissecting the specific roles of RARα in retinal biology, particularly within the RPE. Preclinical studies have underscored the utility of RARα activation in modulating key processes such as cellular differentiation, inhibition of EMT, and enhancement of phagocytic function in RPE cells (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2012).  
However, several potential challenges must also be acknowledged. Retinoid compounds are notorious for their complex pharmacokinetics and potential for off-target effects, including teratogenicity, as evidenced by prior studies of AM580 in teratogenicity models (Elmazar et al., 2001). The delicate balance between efficacy and safety remains a critical issue, particularly for a condition such as dry AMD where long-term treatment is anticipated. Furthermore, while the preclinical evidence supporting the induction of MFGE8 by RARα activation is promising, the available data remain largely confined to in vitro studies and select animal models. Clinical validation in human subjects is still lacking, and the translation of dose levels, tissue penetration, and metabolic stability from the laboratory to the clinic remains an open question (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Another concern is that AM580, while selective, does retain some activity at RARβ and RARγ at higher concentrations (Teng et al., 1996), an effect that may have unpredictable consequences on cell signaling in the complex microenvironment of the RPE. Moreover, the retinoid system is intricately linked with multiple signaling pathways, and long-term modulation may lead to compensatory mechanisms or unforeseen adverse outcomes.  
In summary, the repurposing of AM580 for dry AMD is supported by a robust molecular rationale—its ability to selectively activate RARα is directly linked to the upregulation of MFGE8 and, consequently, the enhancement of POS phagocytosis in RPE cells. This mechanism directly addresses a critical defect in dry AMD pathology, namely the impaired clearance of photoreceptor debris, which is a central driver of retinal degeneration (Garattini et al., 2007; Kobayashi et al., 2021). The preclinical literature offers promising evidence that selective RARα modulation can exert beneficial effects on RPE physiology, including the prevention of EMT and restoration of phagocytic function (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Despite these strengths, the transition from preclinical studies to clinical application will require careful attention to pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic factors, as well as rigorous safety assessments to mitigate risks typical of retinoid therapies. Overall, while challenges remain, AM580’s unique properties render it a promising candidate that merits further investigation in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to fill a significant therapeutic gap in the management of this debilitating condition (Martin et al., 1992; Teng et al., 1996; Kobayashi et al., 2021).
