Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SHP099 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule allosteric inhibitor of the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP2 (PTPN11) discovered by Novartis through a target-biased screening paradigm that enriched for modulators of full-length, autoinhibited SHP2 and counter-selected catalytic-site binders, followed by structure-based medicinal chemistry optimization to stabilize the closed SHP2 conformation rather than engage the conserved active site (chemical identity: 6-(4-amino-4-methylpiperidin-1-yl)-3-(2,3-dichlorophenyl)pyrazin-2-amine) (PDB: 5EHR) (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kong & Long, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). In the 1.7 Å co-crystal, SHP099 occupies a central “tunnel” at the interface of the N-SH2, C-SH2, and PTP domains present only in the autoinhibited state; its aminopyrazine/amine motif forms hydrogen bonds to Arg111 and Phe113 in the SH2 linker and to Glu250 in the PTP domain, while a 2,3-dichlorophenyl moiety engages hydrophobic residues (Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, Gln495), thereby clamping the interdomain interface and disfavoring opening/activation (ligand volume ~262 Å3; tunnel ~464 Å3) (Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Biochemically, SHP099 is potent and selective (SHP2 enzymatic IC50 ≈ 0.070–0.071 µM; no detectable activity across panels of 21 phosphatases and 66 kinases, including SHP1) and translates to cellular pathway inhibition (p-ERK IC50 ≈ 0.250 µM), with high aqueous solubility, high permeability without efflux, and acceptable mouse oral exposure/bioavailability (~46%) (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kong & Long, 2022). Mechanistically, SHP099 functions as a “molecular glue” that stabilizes the closed, autoinhibited SHP2 conformation via a conformational selection mechanism; affinity is reduced for strongly activating SHP2 mutants (for example, E76K) that bias the open state, although high concentrations can re-close some mutants in vitro and in cells (Meem, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).

SHP099 belongs to the class of SHP2 “tunnel-site” (site 1) allosteric inhibitors that stabilize the autoinhibited state by engaging the N-SH2/C-SH2/PTP interdomain pocket; dual allosteric occupancy (site 1 plus a distal latch, site 2) is structurally and biochemically validated and produces cooperative inhibition when SHP099 is combined with a site-2 ligand (for example SHP244 analogs), underscoring the druggability of multiple noncatalytic surfaces on SHP2 (Fodor et al., 2018; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Discovery and SAR established that the aminopyrazine ring amine is essential (Glu250 H-bond), the 4-amino-4-methylpiperidine motif is favored over piperazines for potency, and an ortho-chlorine on the phenyl ring is critical; a representative synthesis employs Suzuki–Miyaura coupling to install the dichlorophenyl substituent on a pyrazinamine core, followed by SNAr to append the Boc-protected 4-methylpiperidin-4-amine and final acid deprotection to the free base (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-level development moved the SHP099 pharmacophore into diverse chemotypes (for example, pyrimidinones and fused bicyclic pyrazolopyrimidinones) and into clinical candidates (for example, TNO155, RMC-4630, BBP-398), reflecting translational momentum for SHP2 allosteric inhibition (Kerr et al., 2021; Tojjari et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
SHP099 established in vivo proof-of-concept for allosteric SHP2 inhibition in oncology. In an EGFR-amplified esophageal squamous carcinoma xenograft (KYSE-520), oral SHP099 produced dose-dependent pathway suppression (tumor p-ERK), antiproliferative effects, and tumor growth inhibition up to stasis at 100 mg/kg, supported by measurable exposure and oral bioavailability (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Additional preclinical efficacy includes activity in EGFR-driven xenografts and reduction of leukemic burden in FLT3-ITD–positive AML models after oral dosing, with no overt toxicity noted in those studies (Dempke et al., 2018). In glioblastoma models, SHP099 achieved brain exposure after 100 mg/kg oral dosing, reduced tumor growth and vascularity in orthotopic xenografts, and showed activity both as monotherapy and combined with temozolomide, demonstrating CNS penetration and antitumor pharmacology in mice (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-wide, SHP2 allosteric inhibitors have shown single-agent and combination efficacy in RTK/RAS/MAPK-driven tumors, have been advanced into clinical studies across multiple solid tumors, and display mechanism-consistent biomarker modulation (for example, decreased p-ERK) in preclinical models (Kerr et al., 2021; Stanford & Bottini, 2023; Tojjari et al., 2023).

Within the materials provided here, there are no reports of SHP099 (or any SHP2 allosteric inhibitor) being used in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis models, or any ocular indication; multiple reviews focus on oncology/immuno-oncology and either enumerate preclinical tumor evidence or clinical oncology programs, without ocular/retinal data (Kerr et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2020). Consequently, repurposing SHP099 for dry AMD would be a first-in-class application with no precedent in the supplied literature (Yuan et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
SHP2 is maintained in an autoinhibited state by intramolecular engagement of the N-SH2 domain with the PTP catalytic domain; engagement of SH2 domains by bis-phosphotyrosyl motifs on receptors/adaptors relieves autoinhibition, allowing both catalytic and scaffolding functions that couple receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) to RAS activation and downstream MAPK/PI3K signaling (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). SHP099 binds in a tunnel formed by the N-SH2, C-SH2, and PTP domains of autoinhibited SHP2 and locks this closed conformation: crystallography defines hydrogen bonds to Arg111 and Phe113 (SH2 linker) and Glu250 (PTP domain), and hydrophobic contacts to Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, and Gln495 that together stabilize the interface and preclude opening; pre-organization of Arg111 additionally supports a cationic–π interaction with SHP099’s dichlorophenyl ring (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Selectivity over SHP1 is rationalized structurally by differences in SH2-linker/tunnel geometry that preclude analogous Arg/Phe contacts, consistent with lack of SHP1 inhibition in broad profiling (Diop et al., 2022). Binding follows conformational selection, with lowered potency against mutants that favor the open state (for example, E76K, D61Y), though high concentrations or dual-site allosteric occupancy can re-close certain mutants and enhance inhibition (Fodor et al., 2018; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-level medicinal chemistry around SHP099 uncovered both optimization paths (for example, pyrimidinones, fused bicyclic scaffolds) and liabilities such as unexpected hERG inhibition in some derivatives and combination-dosing tolerability issues in mice, underscoring the need for careful safety pharmacology (Meem, 2022).

RPE POS phagocytosis is a ligand-directed, RTK-driven process with defined signaling architecture. Externalized phosphatidylserine on shed POS tips is opsonized (for example, by MFG-E8), engages apical αvβ5 integrin, and triggers a pathway in which MerTK (activated by Gas6 or Protein S) is essential for physiological engulfment in vivo; loss-of-function MERTK mutations in RCS rats or humans abolish POS internalization and cause rapid photoreceptor degeneration (Ghosh et al., 2024; Moran et al., 2022). At the cytoskeletal level, formation of the F-actin phagocytic cup beneath bound POS requires Rac1 activation and a concurrent decrease in RhoA/ROCK-mediated contractility; RhoA elevation blocks cup formation even when Rac1 is active, whereas ROCK inhibition is both necessary and sufficient to enable cup formation and POS internalization and can rescue engulfment and acidification in MerTK-deficient RPE ex vivo (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Mao & Finnemann, 2021). Mechanistically downstream of MerTK, Src is activated and (i) phosphorylates and activates focal adhesion kinase (FAK), recruiting the p130CAS/CRKII/DOCK180 module that activates Rac1, and (ii) phosphorylates GDP-dissociation inhibitor GDI1, promoting dissociation from Rab5 to facilitate Rab cycling needed for cup formation and early phagosome dynamics (Shelby et al., 2015). These pathways define measurable biochemical checkpoints (MerTK/Src/FAK phosphorylation, Rac1-GTP, RhoA/ROCK activity) and functional readouts (cup formation, internalization, phagolysosomal acidification) relevant to any attempt to modulate RPE phagocytosis pharmacologically (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Moran et al., 2022).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis is that SHP099 will inhibit SHP2 in RPE (biochemical IC50 ~70–75 nM), sustain MerTK phosphorylation, maintain Rac1-GTP, and thereby increase POS internalization. The supplied literature confirms that SHP099 potently and selectively inhibits SHP2 by stabilizing the autoinhibited state and blocks RTK→RAS/MAPK signaling in cells, but it does not demonstrate that SHP2 directly dephosphorylates MerTK in RPE or that SHP2 inhibition prolongs MerTK phosphorylation or increases RPE POS uptake (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). Across systems, SHP2 acts as a positive transducer linking activated RTKs to RAS/ERK signaling; SHP2 allosteric inhibition decouples upstream RTKs from RAS activation, lowering RAS-GTP and p-ERK, which is consistent with a broad attenuation of RTK-driven outputs rather than prolonged receptor phosphorylation per se (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). Within the provided ocular literature, the only experimentally demonstrated pharmacologic rescue of RPE POS uptake is acute ROCK inhibition, which operates downstream of MerTK to reduce actomyosin contractility and enable cup formation and internalization—even rescuing MerTK-deficient RPE ex vivo—whereas elevating RhoA blocks phagocytosis despite Rac1 activation (Mao & Finnemann, 2021). Thus, while SHP099 will almost certainly inhibit SHP2 in RPE if exposure is achieved, the predicted increase in POS internalization via prolonged MerTK phosphorylation and sustained Rac1-GTP is speculative and not supported by direct evidence in the materials provided here (Kerr et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2020).

If the assay readout is POS phagocytosis in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE, the mechanistic checkpoints most directly supported by the literature are: phosphorylation kinetics of MerTK and Src/FAK; Rac1-GTP elevation coincident with cup formation; RhoA/ROCK suppression; and functional measures of cup assembly, POS internalization, and phagolysosomal acidification, with a ROCK inhibitor as a validated positive control (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Mao & Finnemann, 2021; Moran et al., 2022). Ocular pharmacokinetics for SHP099 are unknown in the provided corpus; although brain exposure has been documented after oral dosing in mice, retinal/RPE exposure should not be inferred and would need to be measured for systemic or local (for example, intravitreal) dosing paradigms (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths for repurposing consideration  
- Potent, selective, and structurally validated target engagement. SHP099 is characterized at atomic resolution (PDB 5EHR) with a coherent interaction network (Arg111, Phe113, Glu250; Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, Gln495) that rationalizes potency, selectivity versus SHP1, and conformational bias, increasing confidence that SHP2 inhibition will translate biochemically in RPE if drug exposure is achieved (Diop et al., 2022; Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Drug-like properties and in vivo activity. SHP099 exhibits favorable physicochemical properties (high solubility; Caco-2 permeability without efflux), oral bioavailability (~46% in mice), dose-dependent pathway modulation in tumors, and robust xenograft efficacy; CNS exposure after oral dosing has been demonstrated in mice, indicating trans-barrier distribution is feasible with adequate exposure (Fortanet et al., 2016; Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Class-level translational experience. Multiple SHP2 allosteric inhibitors derived from the SHP099 tunnel pharmacophore have entered clinical testing across solid tumors, enabling leverage of class pharmacology, safety learning, and combination strategies if ocular repurposing proceeds (Kerr et al., 2021; Stanford & Bottini, 2023; Tojjari et al., 2023).

Key weaknesses and risks specific to dry AMD/RPE phagocytosis  
- Mechanistic gap in RPE. The premise that SHP2 dephosphorylates MerTK to terminate phagocytic signaling in RPE, and that SHP2 inhibition will prolong MerTK phosphorylation and sustain Rac1 activation, is not supported by the supplied literature; no direct data link SHP2 to MerTK regulation in RPE or demonstrate SHP099-induced increases in POS uptake (Kerr et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2020). In contrast, RhoA/ROCK suppression is a validated, decisive permissive event for cup formation/internalization and can rescue MerTK deficiency, suggesting that targeting ROCK remains a higher-confidence pharmacological route to enhance POS uptake (Mao & Finnemann, 2021).  
- Potential on-target countereffects on trophic RTK signaling. SHP2 broadly transduces RTK signals to RAS/ERK; allosteric SHP2 inhibition reduces RAS-GTP/p-ERK by disconnecting RTKs from downstream pathways, which could dampen beneficial RTK-mediated homeostatic signaling in RPE and choroid (for example, PDGFR, c-MET, IGF1R) even if MerTK phosphorylation were transiently increased, necessitating careful evaluation of RPE viability and stress responses in addition to phagocytosis endpoints (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021).  
- Ocular PK/tissue exposure unknown. There is no reported ocular distribution for SHP099 in the materials provided; CNS penetration does not ensure retinal/RPE exposure, and systemic dosing to achieve ocular levels may be limited by plasma protein binding, efflux, or tolerability, while intravitreal dosing introduces local safety and formulation challenges that would require de novo assessment (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Class liabilities and context-dependent potency. Medicinal chemistry around SHP099 identified derivatives with unexpected hERG activity and tolerability issues in some combination regimens; while not demonstrated specifically for SHP099 here, this flags a class risk requiring prospective cardiac and ocular safety pharmacology. Conformational-selection binding also means potency varies with SHP2 activation state, which is undefined in aging human RPE and could shift under inflammatory or oxidative stress present in dry AMD (Meem, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Lack of precedent in ocular models. No ocular, retinal, or RPE data for SHP099 or related allosteric SHP2 inhibitors are available in the supplied literature, increasing translational uncertainty for this repurposing (Yuan et al., 2020).

Program decision and de-risking experiments  
On the basis of the information provided, SHP099 is not yet a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD without foundational mechanistic validation in RPE. The central claim—that SHP2 inhibition prolongs MerTK phosphorylation and increases POS internalization—remains speculative in the absence of RPE data (Yuan et al., 2020). If the team elects to explore this hypothesis, a gated, mechanism-first workplan is advised:

- Define pathway engagement in RPE. Confirm SHP2 expression and activation state during phagocytosis in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE; assess whether SHP2 associates with MerTK/Src/FAK complexes upon POS challenge by co-immunoprecipitation or proximity assays (Shelby et al., 2015).  
- Biochemical time-courses ± SHP099. Quantify MerTK phosphorylation kinetics, Src and FAK activation, Rac1-GTP, and RhoA/ROCK activity after POS addition with a SHP099 concentration range bracketing its biochemical potency in enzyme assays; benchmark effect sizes against a ROCK inhibitor positive control, which is validated to rescue phagocytosis even in MerTK-deficient contexts (Mao & Finnemann, 2021).  
- Functional phagocytosis assays. Measure POS binding, F-actin cup formation, internalization, and phagolysosomal acidification under the same conditions, using established assays and timepoints aligned to the diurnal phagocytic peak where applicable (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Moran et al., 2022).  
- Ocular PK and safety. Establish retinal/RPE exposure after systemic and (if considered) intravitreal dosing, and perform ocular tolerability assessments (inflammation, ERG, histopathology) to identify potential on- or off-target liabilities early, mindful of class risks noted in optimization campaigns (Meem, 2022; Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).

In summary, SHP099 is a potent, selective, and well-characterized SHP2 allosteric inhibitor with robust oncology pharmacology and drug-like properties, but the case for repurposing to dry AMD by enhancing RPE POS phagocytosis is unsubstantiated in the provided literature and carries meaningful mechanistic and translational risks. Prioritizing direct RPE mechanistic studies and ocular PK/tolerability before any disease-model investment is the appropriate next step; in parallel, ROCK pathway modulation remains the most evidence-backed pharmacologic lever to augment phagocytosis in this system and should serve as a positive control and a benchmark for effect size (Fortanet et al., 2016; Mao & Finnemann, 2021; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
P110 is a synthetic, cell‐permeable inhibitory peptide specifically engineered to disrupt the pathological interaction between dynamin‐related protein 1 (Drp1) and its mitochondrial outer membrane receptor fission protein 1 (Fis1). It is synthesized via solid‐phase peptide synthesis methods and rational design strategies that mimic the native binding interface of these two proteins. As such, P110 belongs to the class of peptide-based mitochondrial fission inhibitors, a subclass of compounds that have been previously investigated in a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders, where aberrant mitochondrial fission is implicated in disease pathology. These types of compounds have historically been used experimentally to restore normal mitochondrial morphological dynamics and attenuate excessive fission triggered by oxidative stress. The concept builds upon evidence that an overactive fission process, largely mediated by elevated activity of Drp1 in response to cellular stressors, results in mitochondrial fragmentation, cytochrome c release, and subsequent cell death. In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which bear extremely high energy demands for functions such as photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis, proper mitochondrial network integrity is essential. The peptide’s cell-permeability and selective inhibition of the Drp1/Fis1 binding suggest that P110 can efficiently penetrate ocular tissues and modulate mitochondrial dynamics locally, offering a promising approach to preserve mitochondrial function in the diseased retina (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Numerous preclinical studies have investigated the modulation of mitochondrial dynamics in models of oxidative stress and neurodegeneration, often employing broad-spectrum inhibitors such as mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (Mdivi-1) or genetic silencing approaches using Drp1-specific siRNA. In several in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells—a human RPE cell line—excessive mitochondrial fission triggered by oxidative stress (for example, via hydrogen peroxide exposure) was effectively ameliorated by Drp1 inhibition. This intervention preserved mitochondrial structure, maintained ATP production, and increased cell viability, thereby preventing the morphological transition from tubular to fragmented mitochondria (Yako et al., 2021). Although these investigations have provided robust proof-of-concept evidence that targeting Drp1-mediated fission can be beneficial in preventing RPE dysfunction, most of the studies have not directly tested P110 peptide for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Instead, the literature has explored alternative approaches using compounds like Mdivi-1 and genetic knockdown modalities to decrease Drp1 activity, which indirectly supports the mechanistic rationale for using a targeted inhibitor like P110. The literature also shows that increased expression of mitochondrial fission factor (Mff) and elevated Drp1 levels in AMD donor tissues correlate with impaired mitochondrial homeostasis and defective phagocytosis in the RPE (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022). There remains, however, a gap in direct evidence for P110’s use in AMD despite its clear conceptual alignment with the therapeutic strategy of reducing pathological mitochondrial fission. Clinical trials have emerged that investigate mitochondrial fission inhibitors in ocular conditions, yet the available database queries indicate that while there is clinical interest in Drp1-targeting approaches, specific details on the P110 peptide remain sparse (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Thus, while the broader therapeutic paradigm—targeting aberrant mitochondrial fission—is well supported, P110 itself represents an innovative candidate that requires further preclinical validation in AMD-relevant models.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the pathological process underpinning excessive mitochondrial fission centers on the overactivation of Drp1, a GTPase that orchestrates mitochondrial scission. Under normal physiological conditions, Drp1 exists in the cytosol and is transiently recruited to the mitochondrial outer membrane by receptors such as Fis1, mitochondrial fission factor (Mff), and MiD49/MiD51. In response to oxidative and inflammatory stress—conditions known to be prevalent in the aging RPE and AMD—the interaction between Drp1 and Fis1 is upregulated, leading to excessive fission, mitochondrial fragmentation, and subsequent mitochondrial dysfunction. P110 is designed to selectively inhibit the Drp1/Fis1 binding interface, thereby attenuating the aberrant recruitment of Drp1 to the mitochondria. In doing so, it preserves the elongated and interconnected mitochondrial network, which is essential for optimal mitochondrial bioenergetics and the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Biochemically, inhibition of this interaction prevents the oligomerization of Drp1 on the mitochondrial surface, a process that is otherwise necessary for the formation of constriction rings that facilitate organelle division (Zhao et al., 2025). By blocking Drp1 recruitment, P110 indirectly maintains mitochondrial membrane potential and reduces the likelihood of cytochrome c release—a key event in the apoptosis cascade that is frequently observed in stressed RPE cells (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). Although many of the studies in the context of AMD have focused on Mdivi-1 as a Drp1 inhibitor, the specificity of P110 for the Drp1/Fis1 interaction might offer a distinct pharmacological profile, reducing off-target effects and preserving the physiological fission events necessary for maintaining overall mitochondrial quality control (Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021). Furthermore, the fact that mitochondrial fission and fusion processes are tightly integrated with mitochondrial biogenesis and mitophagy pathways supports the prospect that modulating this specific interaction may lead to a net improvement in mitochondrial dynamics without completely abolishing essential fission events (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Given the underlying hypothesis, the expected effect of P110 in AMD RPE cells would be to restore a balance in mitochondrial dynamics that has been disrupted by chronic oxidative stress. The assay proposed involves exposing cultured RPE cells, such as ARPE-19, to oxidative insults (e.g., H₂O₂) that would otherwise induce excessive Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission. P110’s mode of action is anticipated to specifically block the pathological protein-protein interaction between Drp1 and Fis1, thereby reducing the formation of excessively fragmented mitochondria and promoting the preservation or re-establishment of a tubular mitochondrial network. This intact network is critical for efficient ATP production, which in turn supports high-energy processes such as the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). POS phagocytosis is a metabolically demanding function that is crucial for photoreceptor renewal and overall retinal health. By maintaining ATP supply and preventing the release of pro-apoptotic factors (such as cytochrome c), P110 is expected to protect RPE cells from oxidative damage and improve cellular viability under stress conditions (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). Additionally, studies have demonstrated that mitochondrial fission inhibitors can lead to improved mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and enhanced cell survival under conditions of oxidative insult (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). In RPE cells, these improvements translate into a better capacity for POS uptake and metabolism, which are essential for sustaining the metabolic demands of the outer retina. Given that expression levels of Drp1 and its functional activity are elevated in AMD RPE cells, as evidenced by electron microscopy and proteomic analyses showing reduced mitochondrial numbers, diminished cristae, and defective fusion/fission ratios, the application of P110 is expected to counteract these detrimental changes by stabilizing the mitochondrial network (Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summarizing the overall evaluation of P110 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key points emerge from the literature. First, the mechanistic rationale underpinning P110’s mode of action is robust and well-aligned with current understanding of AMD pathophysiology. Excessive Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission has been implicated as a crucial driver of mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells—a hallmark of dry AMD. Several studies using alternative approaches such as pharmacological inhibition with Mdivi-1 or genetic knockdown via siRNA have consistently demonstrated that mitigating aberrant mitochondrial fission leads to improved mitochondrial integrity, preserved bioenergetic function, and enhanced cell viability in models of oxidative stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). This information directly supports the hypothesis that targeting the Drp1/Fis1 interaction, rather than globally inhibiting all Drp1 activity, could offer a more refined therapeutic approach with potentially fewer side effects. Such specificity is particularly appealing in the context of the retina where finely tuned mitochondrial dynamics are essential for high energy-demand processes like POS phagocytosis (Fisher et al., 2022).

One of the primary strengths of P110 lies in its cell-permeable peptide nature, which facilitates targeted intracellular delivery—a critical characteristic for therapies intended for ocular application. Its design, which specifically disrupts the interaction between Drp1 and Fis1, is predicated on the notion that pathological fission can be selectively blocked without interfering with the physiological fission necessary for regular mitochondrial turnover and repair. This specificity could, in theory, translate to a better safety profile compared to less selective inhibitors such as Mdivi-1 that may have off-target effects, including undesirable impacts on other aspects of mitochondrial function (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2025).

Despite the promising mechanistic rationale and potential for ocular development, there are notable weaknesses and challenges to be considered. The current literature does not yet offer direct preclinical or clinical evidence that P110 peptide itself has been used to treat dry AMD. Most existing studies have extrapolated the benefits of Drp1 inhibition from experiments involving Mdivi-1 or Drp1 knockdown in cellular models of RPE oxidative stress (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Therefore, while the concept of targeting Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission in AMD is well supported, the direct application of P110 remains largely theoretical at this point. This gap in the literature introduces uncertainty regarding the peptide’s pharmacokinetic properties, its stability in ocular tissues, and its potential immunogenic responses upon local administration in the eye.

Another potential limitation is the complex role of mitochondrial dynamics in cellular homeostasis. Although excessive fission in the context of oxidative stress is detrimental, mitochondrial fission is also a necessary process for mitophagy and the removal of damaged organelles. Some studies have indicated that a certain degree of fission may even be beneficial for cellular quality control, as it facilitates the segregation and subsequent removal of malfunctioning mitochondria (Skeie et al., 2021; Yako et al., 2021). The nuanced interplay between reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling and fission means that complete inhibition of fission—even if intended to be only pathological—could potentially have unintended consequences. It will be critical to determine whether P110’s selective inhibition of Drp1/Fis1 interaction can maintain the necessary balance between inhibiting excessive fission while still allowing physiological fission to contribute to normal mitophagy and mitochondrial turnover.

Furthermore, while the peptide’s cell-permeability is an advantage, peptide therapeutics in ocular applications face challenges related to delivery, degradation by ocular proteases, and potential issues with achieving sustained concentrations in the target tissues. Addressing these challenges may require the development of specialized drug delivery systems, such as intravitreal injections with sustained-release formulations or conjugation to nanoparticles, to ensure that adequate therapeutic levels of P110 are maintained at the retinal level over the necessary duration (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Additional practical concerns include the need for rigorous in vivo studies in relevant animal models of dry AMD to assess not only the efficacy in preserving mitochondrial function and POS phagocytosis in RPE cells but also the overall impact on retinal structure and visual function. Currently, many studies have been limited to in vitro models using ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress conditions. Although these models provide valuable mechanistic insights, they do not fully recapitulate the complex interplay of cellular and systemic factors that contribute to AMD in vivo. The therapeutic potential of P110 will need to be evaluated in animal models that mimic the pathophysiological conditions of dry AMD, where factors such as chronic low-grade inflammation, complement activation, and cumulative oxidative damage play significant roles (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

In addition to efficacy and safety concerns, the regulatory landscape for peptide therapeutics in ocular indications should be considered. The development of P110 for dry AMD will require detailed pharmacodynamic and toxicological evaluations to satisfy regulatory requirements. While the peptide’s mechanism—targeting a well-characterized protein-protein interaction—provides a clear scientific rationale, the path toward clinical translation is contingent on demonstrating not only mechanistic efficacy but also an acceptable safety profile in both preclinical toxicology studies and early-phase clinical trials (Fisher et al., 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

In conclusion, the comprehensive literature review supports the notion that targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, specifically through the inhibition of Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission, is a highly promising therapeutic avenue for dry AMD. P110, as a selective inhibitor of the Drp1/Fis1 interaction, is well poised within this framework. The candidate is grounded in a strong mechanistic rationale that links excessive mitochondrial fission to reduced ATP production, impaired POS phagocytosis, and ultimately, RPE cell dysfunction—a cascade of events that underlies the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022).

The inherent advantages of a peptide-based therapeutic, including its specificity and cell-permeability, are particularly attractive for ocular drug development, where targeted delivery and minimal off-target effects are crucial. Nonetheless, notable weaknesses remain that must be addressed before P110 can be considered a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The absence of direct experimental data with P110 in AMD models, the complex nature of mitochondrial dynamics where inhibition of fission must be carefully balanced to avoid impairing critical mitophagy processes, and potential challenges associated with peptide stability and delivery in the ocular environment represent significant hurdles. These challenges underscore the necessity for further preclinical investigations, including in vivo efficacy and safety studies in animal models that recapitulate the chronic oxidative stress and metabolic derangements characteristic of AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).

Ultimately, while the theoretical basis for P110’s use in dry AMD is compelling and supported by a considerable body of literature showing beneficial effects of mitochondrial fission inhibition in RPE cells, advancing this candidate will require a coordinated effort to fill the current gaps in experimental evidence. Future studies should focus on validating the efficacy of P110 in terms of restoring mitochondrial dynamics, preserving ATP production, and ultimately improving POS phagocytosis in both cell culture and animal models of AMD. If these studies yield positive results, P110 has the potential to become an important component of a new generation of therapies aimed at addressing the mitochondrial dysfunction that lies at the heart of dry AMD pathophysiology (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).

Overall, the research direction for P110 is promising given the established relationship between mitochondrial dysfunction and AMD. With its targeted mechanism of action and a strong conceptual basis rooted in the modulation of mitochondrial dynamics, P110 stands as a high-potential candidate. However, careful optimization of dosing, formulation, and delivery, as well as comprehensive preclinical validation, is essential before this therapeutic candidate can be reliably advanced into clinical trials. Should these hurdles be successfully overcome, P110 could not only provide substantial therapeutic benefit by preserving RPE function in dry AMD but also serve as a model for developing other targeted mitochondrial therapies in ocular neurodegeneration (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Celastrol is a naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid compound originally isolated from the root extracts of Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F, commonly known as the “Thunder God Vine” (Gu et al., 2018; Cascao et al., 2017). This compound belongs to the quinone methide triterpenoid class, a group of bioactive natural products that have been used in traditional Chinese medicine for centuries to alleviate inflammatory, autoimmune, and neurodegenerative disorders (Law, 2022; Chan et al., 2024). Celastrol’s unique chemical structure, characterized by electrophilic centers that enable covalent interactions with nucleophilic cysteine residues on target proteins, confers upon it a multi-targeted mechanism of action. Its triterpenoid nature places it among a class of compounds known for their broad anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anticancer properties, which have been applied in diverse preclinical settings ranging from rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease to neurodegenerative conditions such as Parkinson’s disease (Bian et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2019). The candidate under consideration, provided by Santa Cruz Biotech (Cat. No. sc-204268), is being evaluated for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a disease characterized by chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and impairment in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function (Zhang et al., 2019; Du et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Celastrol’s therapeutic history spans several decades and includes extensive preclinical research across multiple disease models. Historically, extracts from Tripterygium wilfordii have been utilized in traditional medicine for conditions marked by inflammation and autoimmunity. Modern biochemical investigations have validated celastrol’s anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions, particularly through its ability to suppress proinflammatory cytokine production by inhibiting the NF-κB pathway (Zhang et al., 2019). In ocular research, celastrol has been shown to provide significant protection in models of retinal injury. For example, in studies using human ARPE-19 cells—a widely accepted in vitro model for RPE—the compound has demonstrated cytoprotective effects against hydrogen peroxide-induced oxidative stress, reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, autophagy, and apoptosis while enhancing cell survival (Du et al., 2019). Additionally, preclinical animal studies have demonstrated that celastrol can protect retinal ganglion cells from optic nerve crush–induced degeneration, underscoring its neuroprotective potential within ocular tissues (Kyung et al., 2015; Law, 2022). Although direct clinical evaluations in dry AMD are few, the compound’s efficacy in analogous retinal degenerative conditions, including its ability to modulate inflammatory responses and oxidative stress in retinal cells, provides a compelling rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2018). Moreover, its application in other chronic inflammatory diseases and early-phase clinical investigations in rheumatoid arthritis have established proof-of-concept that celastrol can be used safely at carefully controlled dosages, although challenges with bioavailability and systemic toxicity have been repeatedly noted (Cascao et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
Celastrol exerts its cellular effects through a dual mechanism that targets two critical signaling pathways implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis: the nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) pathway and the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. On the inflammatory front, celastrol inhibits the NF-κB signaling cascade. Under normal conditions, NF-κB is held inactive in the cytoplasm by inhibitory proteins (IκBs). Upon inflammatory stimulation, IκBs are phosphorylated and degraded, allowing NF-κB to translocate to the nucleus and induce transcription of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 (IL-6), interleukin-8 (IL-8), and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) (Zhang et al., 2019). Celastrol has been shown to block the phosphorylation of key regulatory proteins such as IKKα/β and IκBα, thereby preventing nuclear translocation of the p65 subunit and subsequent activation of inflammatory gene transcription in RPE cells (Zhang et al., 2019). This results in a marked reduction in cytokine secretion—a finding that is crucial for attenuating the chronic inflammatory milieu present in dry AMD. Simultaneously, celastrol activates the Nrf2 signaling pathway. Under oxidative stress conditions, Nrf2 dissociates from its cytoplasmic chaperone Keap1 and translocates to the nucleus, where it binds to antioxidant response elements (ARE) and promotes the transcription of a battery of antioxidant enzymes such as heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), and glutamate-cysteine ligase catalysis (Catanzaro et al., 2020; Du et al., 2019). Activation of Nrf2 not only enhances the antioxidant capacity of RPE cells but also supports cellular defense mechanisms against oxidative insults, which are central to the progression of dry AMD. Further contributing to its protective profile, celastrol has been implicated in modulating SIRT3 expression—a mitochondrial sirtuin involved in the regulation of metabolic and oxidative stress responses—and in promoting autophagy by upregulating markers such as LC3II/LC3I ratio and Beclin-1 (Du et al., 2019). The compound’s electrophilic properties permit it to form covalent adducts with target proteins, thereby impairing the activity of key proinflammatory mediators while simultaneously bolstering the cell’s intrinsic antioxidant machinery (Venkatesha & Moudgil, 2016; Law, 2022). This comprehensive modulation of both inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways underpins celastrol’s potential utility in preserving RPE function under the duress of chronic stressors typical of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The primary hypothesis driving the repurposing of celastrol for dry AMD is that, at an effective concentration (approximately EC₅₀ ~1 µM), the compound will exert a dual molecular effect in RPE cells by inhibiting NF-κB and activating Nrf2. In an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells, celastrol is expected to reduce the expression and secretion of proinflammatory cytokines—such as IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α—by interfering with the phosphorylation events necessary for NF-κB activation (Zhang et al., 2019). This reduction in cytokine levels is crucial given that inflammatory mediators are known to downregulate the expression of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK, which are essential for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Impaired POS clearance leads to the accumulation of toxic cellular debris and lipofuscin, contributing significantly to RPE dysfunction and progression of dry AMD (Venkatesha & Moudgil, 2016; Zhang et al., 2019). Concurrently, the activation of the Nrf2 pathway by celastrol will upregulate antioxidant enzymes including HO-1, thereby enhancing the cell’s ability to neutralize ROS and mitigate oxidative damage (Catanzaro et al., 2020; Du et al., 2019). Enhanced antioxidant defenses contribute to the maintenance of mitochondrial integrity and facilitate proper lysosomal function and autophagic flux in the RPE. This is critical not only for cellular survival under oxidative stress but also for the preservation of proper phagocytic functions necessary for efficient POS clearance (Du et al., 2019). Additionally, studies indicate that improvements in mitochondrial function via SIRT3 upregulation—in part mediated by celastrol—may further support the energy-dependent processes underlying phagocytosis and intracellular recycling (Du et al., 2019). As a result, the expected outcomes in the proposed assay are multi-fold: a decrease in inflammatory signaling, an increase in cellular antioxidant capacity, preservation or restoration of phagocytic receptor expression (such as MERTK), and overall enhanced clearance of POS debris by RPE cells. Taken together, these effects would slow or even halt the degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD, thereby preserving retinal structure and function.

Overall Evaluation:  
Celastrol represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its multi-targeted mechanisms that directly address the disease’s central pathophysiological processes—namely, chronic inflammation and oxidative stress. One of the fundamental strengths of celastrol is its dual modulatory action. By inhibiting the NF-κB pathway, celastrol effectively lowers the production of proinflammatory cytokines that are linked to the downregulation of MERTK and disruption of RPE phagocytic function (Zhang et al., 2019). This mechanism is particularly relevant for AMD, where uncontrolled inflammation contributes not only to RPE degeneration but also to subsequent retinal dysfunction. Simultaneously, the activation of the Nrf2 pathway and upregulation of antioxidant enzymes such as HO-1 play a pivotal role in neutralizing the excessive oxidative stress that drives RPE cell damage in dry AMD (Catanzaro et al., 2020; Du et al., 2019). Additionally, the ability of celastrol to modulate SIRT3 expression and enhance autophagic processes provides further mechanistic support for its potential to restore the balance between cellular degradation pathways and survival, thereby supporting the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and maintenance of retinal health (Du et al., 2019).  

From a therapeutic history perspective, celastrol has been extensively studied in preclinical models of inflammation, oxidative stress, and ocular diseases. Its protective effects in ARPE-19 cells, including reduced ROS production, decreased apoptosis, and improved autophagy, are particularly encouraging for its repurposing in dry AMD (Du et al., 2019). Moreover, in vivo studies demonstrating neuroprotective effects in retinal ganglion cell models and protection against light-induced retinal degeneration further underscore its potential ocular benefits (Kyung et al., 2015; Law, 2022). These data collectively suggest that celastrol’s mechanisms of action intersect effectively with the molecular dysfunctions observed in dry AMD, making it a candidate with strong scientific rationale for further investigation.

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. A primary limitation of celastrol is its poor water solubility and low bioavailability, which have been highlighted as significant hurdles in its clinical development (Cascao et al., 2017; Chan et al., 2024). The narrow therapeutic window and potential systemic toxicity observed at higher doses necessitate careful dose optimization and the development of advanced drug delivery systems—such as nanocarriers or liposomal formulations—that could improve its ocular bioavailability and target specificity (Cascao et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2021). Additionally, while there is a substantial body of data supporting celastrol’s anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, most of these studies have been conducted in vitro or in non-AMD-specific animal models. Therefore, direct evidence of its efficacy in dry AMD models—particularly those that recapitulate the complex interplay between oxidative stress, inflammation, and impaired phagocytic function in the RPE—is still limited (Zhao et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2018).  

The hypothesis underlying the proposed research is compelling: by inhibiting NF-κB signaling and activating Nrf2-mediated antioxidant responses, celastrol could restore the balance between inflammation and cellular defense mechanisms in RPE cells, ultimately preserving the expression of phagocytic receptors like MERTK and enhancing lysosomal function. This restoration is expected to improve the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, a process critically impaired in dry AMD (Venkatesha & Moudgil, 2016; Du et al., 2019). However, it is important to note that the actual in vitro and in vivo efficacy of celastrol in improving POS clearance and maintaining RPE function must be rigorously demonstrated through additional experiments. Furthermore, while there are encouraging indications regarding ocular safety from rodent models, the translation of these findings to human clinical settings involves further validation regarding pharmacokinetic properties, dosing regimens, and long-term safety profiles (Kyung et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2018).

In summary, celastrol offers a robust mechanistic rationale for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD by simultaneously targeting key pathological processes—chronic inflammation mediated by NF-κB and oxidative stress mitigated by Nrf2. The compound’s ability to enhance antioxidant defenses while suppressing deleterious inflammatory cascades holds considerable promise for preserving RPE function, maintaining photoreceptor outer segment clearance, and ultimately slowing the progression of retinal degeneration. Nonetheless, challenges related to its formulation, delivery, and potential systemic toxicity are significant and must be addressed through advanced drug development strategies and further preclinical testing in AMD-specific models. Given these considerations, celastrol stands as an attractive but complex candidate for dry AMD therapy, warranting a comprehensive research program to optimize its clinical potential while mitigating associated risks (Cascao et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).

Overall, the evidence supports continued investigation into celastrol’s application in dry AMD, particularly focusing on detailed pharmacodynamic studies in RPE systems, optimization of ocular delivery methods, and rigorous safety and efficacy evaluations in well-established dry AMD animal models. If these hurdles can be successfully overcome, celastrol may emerge as a valuable addition to the currently limited therapeutic arsenal available for the treatment of dry AMD, offering hope for addressing a significant unmet medical need in age-related retinal degeneration (Zhang et al., 2019; Du et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
VX-765, also known as Belnacasan, is a synthetic, orally available caspase-1 inhibitor originally developed by Vertex Pharmaceuticals as part of their research into anti-inflammatory therapeutics (Dhani et al., 2021; Kallinich, 2015). This drug is a peptidomimetic compound designed to mimic the substrate recognition sequence of caspase-1 – a feature that traces its molecular design to early peptide-based inhibitors based on the tetrapeptide motif YVAD (Kudelova et al., 2015; Doyle et al., 2015). VX-765 is administered as an inactive prodrug that is rapidly cleaved by plasma and liver esterases into its active metabolite, VRT-043198, which then exerts inhibitory effects on caspase-1 (Liang et al., 2022; Kallinich, 2015). As a member of the caspase inhibitor class, VX-765 represents a second‐generation approach compared to its predecessor pralnacasan (VX-740), seeking improved oral bioavailability, enhanced selectivity, and a more favorable pharmacokinetic profile (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015). The drug belongs to the broader class of inflammasome inhibitors that target IL-1β and IL-18 releasing cascades, which have been extensively explored for inflammatory, autoimmune, and neurological disorders (Kallinich, 2015; Kudelova et al., 2015). The synthetic origin and deliberate design emphasizes a precision targeting of caspase-1’s catalytic cysteine, a critical residue in the enzyme’s active site, thereby inhibiting its proteolytic function; this is particularly important given the role of caspase-1 in mediating pyroptosis and inflammatory cytokine maturation (Kallinich, 2015; Kudelova et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, VX-765 has been evaluated in preclinical studies and early-phase human trials mainly for systemic inflammatory and neurological conditions. Early investigations demonstrated that VX-765 robustly reduced plasma cytokine levels in dose-dependent manners in Phase I studies, and subsequent Phase II trials in psoriasis provided evidence of both safety and clinical activity (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015; Maroso et al., 2011). Its predecessor pralnacasan showed efficacy in rheumatoid arthritis clinical trials, although long-term use in animal models eventually raised concerns about potential hepatotoxicity, leading to its withdrawal despite promising initial results (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015). VX-765 was later repurposed for neurological conditions; it has been tested in partial epilepsy where, despite a good safety profile, its efficacy was less than anticipated (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015; Kallinich, 2015). In addition, VX-765 has demonstrated anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects in preclinical models of Alzheimer’s disease by reducing IL-1β production in the brain and preserving synaptic function (Liang et al., 2022; Flores et al., 2018). Importantly, although the clinical and preclinical development history of VX-765 spans a variety of inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases, it has not been extensively evaluated for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or retinal diseases per se (Dhani et al., 2021; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020; Kallinich, 2015). Nevertheless, a search in clinical trial databases has uncovered a limited number of studies investigating caspase-1 inhibitors in the context of macular degeneration, reinforcing the notion that the therapeutic paradigm may be extended to ocular disorders (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
Caspase-1 is a cysteine-dependent aspartate-directed protease that plays a central role in the activation of inflammatory cytokines by cleaving pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature, biologically active forms; these cytokines are major mediators of inflammatory cascades and pyroptotic cell death (Kallinich, 2015; Kudelova et al., 2015). VX-765 functions by inhibiting caspase-1 through a competitive mechanism that involves binding to the catalytic cysteine residue; structural studies have indicated that its peptidomimetic scaffold effectively occupies the substrate-binding pocket, thereby preventing substrate access (Kudelova et al., 2015; Kallinich, 2015). Although the hypothesis for repurposing VX-765 in dry AMD posits an irreversible inhibition of caspase-1, the bulk of the literature supports that VX-765 is, in fact, a reversible inhibitor (Dhani et al., 2021; Kallinich, 2015). Activation of VX-765 in vivo produces VRT-043198, which exhibits low nanomolar inhibitory potency against human caspase-1 (IC₅₀ ~3.68–9.91 nM) and comparable activity in murine models (IC₅₀ ~18–52.1 nM), rendering it suitable for precise modulation of caspase-1 activity (Flores et al., 2018; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020). By inhibiting caspase-1, VX-765 effectively prevents the maturation and secretion of IL-1β and IL-18, thereby disrupting the propagation of inflammatory signals that can lead to dysfunctional cellular responses such as pyroptosis—a lytic form of programmed cell death triggered by inflammasome activation (Kallinich, 2015; Younus & Reddy, 2018). In RPE cells, where caspase-1 expression has been documented as a component of inflammasome signaling especially during stress conditions, inhibition of caspase-1 is anticipated to preserve lysosomal integrity by reducing cytokine-induced lysosomal destabilization and preventing the cleavage of substrates that contribute to cell death pathways (Gao et al., 2019; Kudelova et al., 2015). Moreover, evidence suggests that caspase-1 activation leads to gasdermin D cleavage, which forms membrane pores and facilitates pyroptotic cell death; therefore, blockade by VX-765 could mitigate this deleterious cascade (Kallinich, 2015; Flores et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is a critical cell type responsible for maintaining photoreceptor health through the daily phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Under pathological conditions, chronic low-grade inflammation driven by the inflammasome can lead to caspase-1 activation in RPE cells, resulting in IL-1β maturation and subsequent pyroptotic signaling that compromises lysosomal integrity (Gao et al., 2019; Marneros, 2023). The proposed therapeutic hypothesis is that VX-765, by inhibiting caspase-1 at an IC₅₀ value of approximately 10 nM in RPE cell assays (for example, in the ARPE-19 cell line), will significantly reduce IL-1β production and attenuate subsequent inflammatory cascades (Kallinich, 2015; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020). This preservation of lysosomal function is clinically significant because it is expected to stabilize LAMP1-positive lysosomal structures within the RPE, thereby maintaining efficient clearance of POS and preventing the accumulation of toxic debris—a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis (Kudelova et al., 2015). Preclinical evidence from studies using caspase-1 inhibitors indicates that such intervention leads to a reduction in inflammatory cytokine release and improves cellular homeostasis in contexts similar to those observed in AMD (Kudelova et al., 2015). Although the majority of previous studies have focused on systemic inflammatory or neurological disorders, the underlying mechanisms—namely, the inhibition of the caspase-1/IL-1β axis—are directly relevant to RPE dysfunction and can feasibly be repurposed for the treatment of dry AMD (Marneros, 2023). The ultimate expected outcome would be the preservation of RPE phagocytic pathways, ensuring proper degradation of POS, reducing chronic inflammation, and thereby potentially slowing or halting the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Gao et al., 2019; Marneros, 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of VX-765 for dry AMD represents a compelling strategy, driven by a strong mechanistic rationale and bolstered by its demonstrated efficacy in other inflammatory models. One of the primary strengths of VX-765 is its potent and selective inhibition of caspase-1, with low nanomolar IC₅₀ values ensuring that only minimal concentrations are required to achieve therapeutic effects (Flores et al., 2018; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020). This level of potency is crucial given the sensitivity of RPE cells to inflammatory mediators and the need for high selectivity in ocular tissues where off-target effects could be particularly damaging (Dhani et al., 2021; Kallinich, 2015). Moreover, the fact that VX-765 has already undergone Phase II clinical evaluation for indications such as psoriasis and epilepsy provides an established safety profile and foundational pharmacokinetic data that may be extrapolated to ocular applications, albeit with necessary adjustments for local delivery (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015).

Despite these strengths, several challenges persist. A critical point of concern is the discrepancy between the working hypothesis, which posits irreversible inhibition of caspase-1, and the well-documented reversible mode of action of VX-765 (Dhani et al., 2021; Kallinich, 2015). This difference in mechanism may influence both the duration of drug action and the frequency of dosing required to maintain therapeutic inhibition in vivo. Furthermore, while the anti-inflammatory effects have been established in systemic and neuronal contexts, direct evidence supporting the efficacy of VX-765 in preserving RPE lysosomal integrity and phagocytic function in dry AMD remains limited. Specific in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have indicated a reduction in IL-1β release and preservation of LAMP1-positive lysosomes upon caspase-1 inhibition (Kudelova et al., 2015), yet these findings need to be replicated and further validated in dry AMD models to ascertain translational potential.

Another potential weakness arises from safety considerations observed in the development history of related compounds. Pralnacasan (VX-740), a predecessor of VX-765, was associated with dose-limiting hepatotoxicity in long-term animal studies despite initial safety in human trials (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015). Although VX-765 has demonstrated a better safety profile in early clinical testing, caution must be exercised when repurposing the drug for chronic ocular use, particularly given the possibility of systemic absorption from an ocular delivery formulation (Dhani et al., 2021; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020). Additionally, while systemic administration of VX-765 has been explored, the optimal method for targeting the retina—whether through intravitreal injection, sustained-release implants, or other localized delivery systems—remains to be determined. Such considerations are paramount given the unique anatomy of the eye and the necessity of achieving pharmacologically active concentrations in the retina while minimizing exposure to off-target tissues (Kallinich, 2015; Gao et al., 2019).

From a biochemical perspective, the proposed mechanism of action offers a robust framework for the therapeutic intervention in dry AMD. Inhibition of caspase-1 directly limits the maturation of IL-1β and IL-18, inflammatory cytokines that have been implicated in the disruption of lysosomal function and phagocytic degradation of POS in RPE cells (Kallinich, 2015; Flores et al., 2018). Given that chronic inflammation and impaired degradation of photoreceptor debris are central to the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD, targeting this pathway could have a disease-modifying effect (Gao et al., 2019; Marneros, 2023). Furthermore, preventing the activation of gasdermin D by caspase-1 could reduce pyroptotic cell death, thereby preserving RPE cell viability—a critical factor in maintaining the outer blood-retina barrier and overall retinal function (Kallinich, 2015; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020).

Although much of the focus has been on the neovascular form of AMD—with interventions targeting VEGF signaling—the underlying inflammatory processes are shared with the dry form, particularly in the progression of geographic atrophy. The fact that caspase-1 activation has been demonstrated in activated macrophages and retinal microglia in the context of choroidal neovascularization (Marneros, 2023) further supports the notion that modulating this pathway could yield benefits in dry AMD in which inflammatory stress on the RPE is a prominent feature.

In the event that future preclinical work confirms the preservation of lysosomal function and improved POS clearance in RPE models, VX-765 could represent a viable candidate to slow the progression of dry AMD—a condition for which there are currently no approved disease-modifying treatments (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Marneros, 2023).

The extensive development history of VX-765 in other indications provides valuable insights into the dosing, safety, and pharmacodynamics of the compound, thereby reducing some of the risks traditionally associated with early-stage drug development (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015).

Nevertheless, several critical hurdles remain. First, the discrepancy between the hypothesized irreversible inhibition and the documented reversible inhibition necessitates a re-evaluation of dosing strategies to achieve sustained caspase-1 suppression in the retinal environment (Dhani et al., 2021; Kallinich, 2015). Second, the translation of systemic safety data to ocular applications is not straightforward; the unique microenvironment of the eye, coupled with the challenges of achieving adequate intraocular concentrations, calls for rigorous preclinical studies using relevant animal models of dry AMD (Gao et al., 2019; Marneros, 2023). Additionally, given the potential for off-target effects and the historical context of hepatotoxicity observed with related compounds, investigators must prioritize the development of formulations that maximize local efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015).

Finally, it is important to recognize that while the anti-inflammatory approach targeting the caspase-1 pathway is scientifically sound, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease with a complex pathogenesis that includes oxidative stress, genetic predispositions, and metabolic dysregulation. Therefore, combination therapies that target multiple pathways may ultimately prove more effective than monotherapy with a single agent (Gao et al., 2019; Marneros, 2023). In this light, VX-765 could be considered as a component of a broader therapeutic strategy, potentially in conjunction with agents that address other aspects of RPE dysfunction and retinal degeneration.

In conclusion, the repurposing of VX-765 for dry AMD is supported by a robust body of preclinical and clinical data that demonstrate its ability to inhibit caspase-1 and attenuate inflammatory cascades. The candidate’s prior clinical evaluation in other indications offers a promising starting point, yet the leap to treating a chronic ocular disease will require careful, systematic investigation.
