Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human MCP-1 (monocyte chemoattractant protein-1), also known as CCL2, is a biologically active recombinant cytokine derived using modern recombinant protein production techniques under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) conditions (Ramkumar et al., 2010). This molecule belongs to the CC chemokine family and is naturally secreted in response to tissue injury and inflammatory stimuli, where it functions primarily to recruit monocytes, memory T cells, and dendritic cells via binding to its cognate receptor CCR2 (Chen & Xu, 2015). Its synthesis involves expression in appropriate host cells (commonly mammalian or bacterial expression systems) followed by purification and rigorous quality control measures, such that its physicochemical properties and pharmacokinetics are well characterized for ocular administration (Tolentino et al., 2023; Wong et al., 2022). As a therapeutic candidate, recombinant human MCP-1 represents a protein biologic aiming to restore a natural homeostatic mechanism that appears to be compromised in age-related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly in models where a deficiency in CCL2 drives drusen-like lesions through impaired recruitment and function of phagocytic cells (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the biological role of MCP-1 has been extensively characterized in both experimental and genetic models of inflammatory and degenerative diseases. In murine models of AMD, genetic knockout studies have demonstrated that deficiency in Ccl2 (the murine homolog) results in the development of AMD-like retinal changes including drusen-like deposits, thickening and fragmentation of Bruch’s membrane, disrupted collagen and elastin layers, and eventual retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009). These findings have provided substantial preclinical evidence that the CCL2/CCR2 axis is critical for the recruitment of monocytes to the subretinal space, thus facilitating debris clearance and maintenance of retinal homeostasis (Chen & Xu, 2015; DaCosta, 2015). In contrast, some studies have also indicated that improper or excessive recruitment of CCR2⁺ cells may lead to pathological states, including amplified inflammatory cytokine production (Chen & Xu, 2015) and even contribute to angiogenic responses under certain conditions (Hu et al., 2016; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). While recombinant MCP-1 has been used in basic research to probe the role of chemokine signaling in immune cell trafficking and inflammation in various diseases, its direct therapeutic application for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative conditions has not been previously established in clinical or formal veterinary studies (Marin-Castaño, 2013). The unique proposition in the current candidate is to administer low doses of recombinant MCP-1 directly into the subretinal space in order to restore the regulated recruitment of monocytes and thereby improve clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris—a strategy that has been hypothesized based on earlier experimental findings (Luhmann et al., 2009; Chen & Xu, 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
MCP-1 functions as a chemoattractant by binding with high affinity to the CCR2 receptor expressed on inflammatory monocytes and certain subsets of macrophages. Once the ligand binds, it initiates a cascade of intracellular signaling events mediated by G-proteins that result in actin cytoskeleton reorganization, cell polarization, and directed migration towards higher concentrations of MCP-1 (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Chen & Xu, 2015). In the context of ocular physiology, RPE cells under stress conditions or oxidative insult have been shown to secrete MCP-1 as part of an endogenous mechanism intended to attract CCR2⁺ monocytes to areas of debris accumulation (Marin-Castaño, 2013). These recruited monocytes are expected to differentiate into macrophages capable of phagocytosing shed POS debris and other cellular waste products that accumulate with aging and contribute to drusen formation (Luhmann et al., 2009). At the molecular level, binding of MCP-1 to CCR2 results in receptor dimerization and the activation of downstream effectors such as phospholipase C, MAP kinases, and small GTPases that collectively drive cytoskeletal changes and cell motility (Chen & Xu, 2015). It is important to note that the MCP-1/CCR2 axis is tightly regulated, and its function is context dependent; in some models, an overactive response can lead to exacerbated inflammation, while in others the signaling is critical for normal tissue repair and debris clearance (Luhmann et al., 2009; DaCosta, 2015). The hypothesis under evaluation contends that a carefully titrated, low-dose supplementation of recombinant MCP-1 in a dry AMD setting—characterized by Ccl2 deficiency—is capable of reinstating physiologic levels of monocyte recruitment to the subretinal space, thereby bolstering the phagocytic capacity of these cells and normalizing RPE function in terms of outer segment processing (Tolentino et al., 2023; Luhmann et al., 2009).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed mechanism, the expected outcome of administering low-dose recombinant human MCP-1 is an enhancement in the homing behavior of CCR2⁺ monocytes toward the subretinal space. In experimental models where Ccl2 deficiency leads to an accumulation of drusen-like deposits, the rationale is that MCP-1 supplementation will counter the defect in chemotactic signaling, allowing monocytes to effectively transmigrate through the choriocapillaris and accumulate at sites in the retina where depot of POS debris occurs (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009). In these settings, recruited monocytes are anticipated to engage in active phagocytosis of lipofuscin-laden debris, thus alleviating the burden on the RPE cells which are responsible for digesting and recycling photoreceptor outer segments (Chen & Xu, 2015; Marin-Castaño, 2013). Improvement in the RPE’s phagocytic index is hypothesized to lead to several beneficial downstream effects; these include reduced drusen formation, preservation of the structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane, and ultimately a deceleration in the progression of dry AMD pathology (Luhmann et al., 2009). Furthermore, because recombinant MCP-1 is provided in a controlled low-dose fashion, the intended effect is to mimic the physiological signaling observed in the nonpathological state, thereby avoiding overactivation of inflammatory pathways that could otherwise potentiate a deleterious chronic inflammatory milieu (Marin-Castaño, 2013). It should be emphasized that while the concept is theoretically sound, there remains an inherent risk that the recruited monocytes, if not adequately polarized into a reparative (or M2) phenotype, might adopt a pro-inflammatory (or M1) profile that could exacerbate local tissue damage (Chen & Xu, 2015; Elbaz-Hayoun et al., 2023). Thus, the assay’s success will hinge on demonstrating that low-dose MCP-1 can selectively enhance beneficial debris clearance while avoiding unintended inflammatory side effects—a balance that must be meticulously evaluated in preclinical models before any translation to clinical settings (DaCosta, 2015; Tolentino et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
A comprehensive evaluation of recombinant human MCP-1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a candidate with a strong biological rationale based on its central role in monocyte recruitment and tissue repair. The primary strength of this candidate lies in its capacity to restore a key homeostatic function that is compromised in Ccl2 deficiency models of AMD, as evidenced by robust preclinical data showing that diminished MCP-1 signaling correlates with drusen accumulation and RPE dysfunction (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009). Moreover, the fact that recombinant MCP-1 is available as GMP-grade material with known ocular pharmacokinetic properties lends a degree of translational feasibility to the proposed studies (Wong et al., 2022; Tolentino et al., 2023). The hypothesis that subretinal injection of low-dose MCP-1 can ameliorate debris accumulation by recruiting CCR2⁺ monocytes is supported by the well-established molecular interactions between MCP-1 and CCR2, which have been validated in several inflammatory and degenerative models (Chen & Xu, 2015; Marin-Castaño, 2013).

However, several critical weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, the literature presents conflicting roles for the MCP-1/CCR2 axis in AMD pathogenesis. While genetic deficiencies in CCL2 lead to drusen-like lesions, other studies have shown that blocking MCP-1/CCR2 signaling can yield protective effects by reducing inflammatory monocyte recruitment and subsequent tissue damage (Hu et al., 2016; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Elbaz-Hayoun et al., 2023). This dichotomy underscores the delicate balance between debris clearance and inflammation; excessive or misdirected monocyte recruitment may inadvertently exacerbate retinal degeneration rather than ameliorate it (Marin-Castaño, 2013; Tolentino et al., 2023). Second, there is a substantial risk that exogenously administered MCP-1—even at low doses—could stimulate an overzealous inflammatory response if it fails to promote the desired anti-inflammatory, reparative monocyte phenotype. Given that monocyte polarization is highly context dependent, additional studies would be required to ensure that the recruited cells adopt a phenotype conducive to tissue repair rather than one that contributes to chronic inflammation or neovascular complications (Chen & Xu, 2015; Elbaz-Hayoun et al., 2023). Third, while the candidate hypothesis is partly based on observations from knockout models, these models have inherent limitations; some studies indicate that the majority of AMD-related morphological changes in Ccl2- and Ccr2-deficient mice may actually represent accelerated aging rather than true disease pathology (Luhmann et al., 2009; Tolentino et al., 2023). Thus, extrapolating these findings to a therapeutic scenario in human dry AMD requires careful validation in models that more accurately recapitulate the human disease phenotype.

In summary, recombinant human MCP-1 holds promise as a novel therapeutic strategy for dry AMD by potentially restoring a physiologic mechanism for debris clearance through the recruitment of CCR2⁺ monocytes. Its strengths include its well-characterized molecular mechanism, availability as a GMP-grade product with defined ocular pharmacokinetics, and a solid preclinical rationale based on studies showing that CCL2 deficiency leads to AMD-like pathology (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009). Conversely, its weaknesses stem from the complex and sometimes contradictory roles of the MCP-1/CCR2 axis in retinal inflammation and degeneration, the risk of inadvertently triggering detrimental inflammatory responses, and the challenge of translating findings from knockout models to a clinical setting (Hu et al., 2016; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Elbaz-Hayoun et al., 2023). Given these considerations, while the candidate is scientifically intriguing, further rigorous preclinical research is essential to define the appropriate dosing regimen, confirm the beneficial polarization of recruited monocytes, and rule out any potential exacerbation of inflammatory pathology before advancing to clinical trials. This balanced approach will ultimately determine whether recombinant MCP-1 can be viably repurposed as a therapeutic agent to mitigate the progression of dry AMD by enhancing RPE function and debris clearance (Marin-Castaño, 2013; DaCosta, 2015).

Below is our comprehensive evaluation of BTB06584 as a repurposed drug candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BTB06584 is described as a V‐ATPase inhibitor available commercially (e.g., Tocris Cat. No. 5208) that is purported to act by selectively targeting the V₀ subunit of the vacuolar proton pump. V‐ATPase is a large multisubunit enzyme complex consisting of a cytosolic V₁ domain (responsible for ATP hydrolysis) and a membrane‐embedded V₀ domain (which translocates protons) that together acidify intracellular compartments such as lysosomes. BTB06584 appears to belong to the class of small molecules developed to modulate lysosomal acidification and, by extension, lysosome‐dependent degradative processes. Although several classes of V‐ATPase inhibitors (for example, the plecomacrolides bafilomycin A₁ and concanamycin A, as well as benzolactone enamides and others) have been extensively characterized as experimental probes, BTB06584 is postulated to be unique in its relatively selective action on the V₀ sector. This selectivity is important because it offers the theoretical possibility of “partial” inhibition rather than the broad, complete blockade observed with classical inhibitors that are often associated with high toxicity (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7; Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 21–23). In many published studies, V‐ATPase inhibitors have served as critical biochemical tools to dissect lysosomal pH regulation and phagosome degradation, especially in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, where impaired acidification is linked to cellular dysfunction in AMD (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7). No detailed synthesis or discovery history has been provided in the existing context, but BTB06584 is assumed to be a synthetic agent designed in line with modern small‐molecule drug development paradigms targeting the V₀ domain.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, V‐ATPase inhibitors have been widely used as experimental probes to study lysosomal acidification and related cellular processes. Classical inhibitors such as bafilomycin A₁ and concanamycin A have been employed in many in vitro and in vivo studies to raise lysosomal pH, alter autophagy and phagocytosis, and to trigger apoptosis in sensitive cell types (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7). In ocular research, V‐ATPase inhibition—albeit through these broader agents—has been demonstrated to impair photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation in RPE cells, which serves as an experimental proxy for early AMD‐related pathology (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7; Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 4–6). Moreover, genetic models in zebrafish and mice further underscore the importance of proper V‐ATPase function in retinal homeostasis (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 4–6; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–5). However, to date, the literature available in our context does not report any prior clinical or preclinical use of BTB06584 specifically for treating dry AMD or for modulating lysosomal pH in RPE cells; indeed, several excerpts explicitly note that BTB06584 is not mentioned by name in the primary‐literature reports on V‐ATPase inhibitors (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 23–24; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). In other words, while the class of V‐ATPase inhibitors has been widely explored—primarily in cancer and osteoporosis research (Holliday, 2017, pp. 4–6; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11)—there is no direct record that BTB06584 has been used clinically or in animal models related to macular degeneration. This gap in the therapeutic history means that any proposed repurposing effort must contend with a virtual absence of detailed preclinical data in AMD‐relevant systems.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, V‐ATPase functions as an ATP‐driven proton pump essential for maintaining the acidic pH of endolysosomal compartments. Lysosomal enzymes, including cathepsin D, require an optimal acidic environment (typically around pH 4.5) for their catalytic function (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7). Disruption of V‐ATPase activity, whether pharmacologically by agents such as bafilomycin A₁ or via genetic manipulation (for example, loss of βA3/A1‐crystallin, which is known to modulate V‐ATPase function), leads to a rise in lysosomal pH, reduced activity of acid‐dependent proteases, and impaired degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 4–6; Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–4). In contrast to complete inhibition—which often results in a strong, detrimental rise in pH—the hypothesis for BTB06584 is that it will “partially” inhibit the V‐ATPase. The goal would be to fine‐tune the activity of the enzyme so that instead of producing a supraphysiologic pH (as with full inhibition), the lysosomal environment is restored to an optimal acidic set point (around pH 4.5) that promotes maximal cathepsin D activity and efficient POS clearance (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–5). Structural studies of V‐ATPase have shown that selective targeting of subunit isoforms, particularly those within the V₀ sector, can influence not only proton pumping but also other functions such as membrane fusion during phagosome–lysosome fusion events (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 21–23; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). If BTB06584 indeed exhibits specificity for the V₀ subunit—and perhaps even for particular isoforms expressed in RPE—it might exert a modulatory effect that differs from the broad and often toxic inhibition seen with compounds like bafilomycin A₁. However, as noted in the literature summaries, there is currently no detailed primary data regarding the binding kinetics, structural interaction, or precise molecular pharmacology of BTB06584 (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 23–24; Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 26–28). In other words, while the proposed mechanism is logically consistent with our understanding of V‐ATPase biology, it remains unsubstantiated by direct experimental evidence for this particular compound.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, RPE dysfunction is characterized, in part, by altered lysosomal pH and impaired degradation of POS, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and subsequent oxidative stress and cellular demise (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7; Valapala et al., 2014, pp. 16–17). The central hypothesis is that dysregulated V‐ATPase activity in AMD RPE leads to lysosomal pH drift—either excessive alkalinization due to inhibition by A2E or a failure to maintain optimal acidity—and that this pH imbalance impacts cathepsin D activity. Cathepsin D is optimally active at a pH of around 4.5, and even a modest deviation toward alkalinity (for example, pH 5.0) can reduce its activity by up to 80% (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–4; Shine et al., 2014, p. 7). BTB06584 is expected to “partially” inhibit V‐ATPase in a manner that normalizes lysosomal pH without “shutting off” the proton pump entirely. In RPE cells, particularly in A2E-treated ARPE-19 assays, such a fine-tuning effect could restore an optimal acidic environment, thereby reactivating cathepsin D and other hydrolases; this, in turn, would facilitate proper degradation of ingested photoreceptor outer segments and reduce the buildup of undigested material and associated autofluorescence (Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–5; Valapala et al., 2014, pp. 16–17). Importantly, the candidate’s hypothesized selective action on the V₀ subunit—if proven—aligns with evidence that manipulating particular V‐ATPase subunit isoforms can affect not only proton pumping but also membrane fusion events that are essential for proper lysosomal function (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 21–23; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7). Given that the RPE expresses specific V‐ATPase isoforms (for example, different V₀ a isoforms) and that genetic studies have linked loss of V‐ATPase activity to defects in POS degradation (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 4–6; Shine et al., 2014, p. 7), the restoration of lysosomal homeostasis through a “partial inhibitor” like BTB06584 could theoretically improve the clearance of POS. However, it must be emphasized that the expected effect of normalizing pH from a suboptimal or variable level to precisely 4.5 is a very delicate modulation – one that must be demonstrated through rigorous in vitro assays in ARPE-19 cells (or better yet, in iPSC-derived RPE models) followed by in vivo animal studies.

Overall Evaluation:  
The proposed strategy of repurposing BTB06584 for dry AMD is innovative in that it aims to address a central pathological feature—lysosomal dysfunction—by modulating, rather than completely inhibiting, the V‐ATPase. The strength of the candidate lies in its potential for selective inhibition of the V₀ subunit, which is critical given that generalized inhibition via broad-spectrum compounds (like bafilomycin A₁) has been associated with significant toxicity and dysfunction in multiple cell types (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). Furthermore, the concept of “fine-tuning” lysosomal pH to optimize cathepsin D activity is appealing because it targets the underlying mechanism that controls the degradation of POS in RPE cells—a process known to be perturbed in AMD (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7; Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–4).  

Nonetheless, there are notable weaknesses. Chief among these is the absence of direct experimental evidence supporting the efficacy of BTB06584 in RPE models or animal models of dry AMD. None of the available literature excerpts provide primary data regarding its chemical characterization, mechanism of action in retinal cells, or any preclinical studies using BTB06584 (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 23–24; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). Consequently, while the hypothesis is congruent with the general concept that selective modulation of V‐ATPase can restore lysosomal function, the candidate remains largely unvalidated in the context of ocular therapeutics. In addition, there is an inherent risk associated with modulating a central enzyme such as V-ATPase: even partial inhibition might affect other vital cellular processes, including autophagy, phagosome–lysosome fusion, and even neurotransmitter release in neural tissues (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 21–23; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). Moreover, the narrow therapeutic window required to normalize acidification (without overshooting into detrimental alkalinization) poses significant challenges; this alone necessitates careful dose-response profiling in multiple models before any clinical translation can be considered.  

Overall, while the theoretical framework supporting BTB06584 is robust in terms of targeting a mechanism that is central to RPE pathology in dry AMD, the lack of direct data leaves critical gaps. At this stage, BTB06584 represents a promising but highly speculative candidate. To advance its development, we recommend that rigorous in vitro studies (using ARPE-19 cells and iPSC-derived RPE under A2E/lipofuscin stress) be undertaken to characterize its effect on lysosomal pH, cathepsin D activity, and POS degradation. These should be complemented by mechanistic assays—such as assessments of lysosomal fusion events and measurements of autophagic flux—to fully delineate its mode of action. If favorable, subsequent in vivo studies in appropriate AMD models will be essential to evaluate efficacy and systemic toxicity.  

In summary, our overall evaluation is that while the candidate BTB06584 is conceptually attractive because it promises selective modulation of V‐ATPase activity—potentially correcting the lysosomal pH imbalance that underlies defects in POS clearance in dry AMD—the current literature does not supply direct supportive evidence for its use in retinal disease, and its safety/efficacy profile remains unproven. Further preclinical investigation is therefore necessary before considering BTB06584 as a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7; Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 23–24; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Sulforaphane is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate that is principally derived from cruciferous vegetables, notably broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and cabbage (Dutta et al., 2023; Lagunas-Rangel, 2024). In its natural state, sulforaphane is present as its glucosinolate precursor, glucoraphanin, which is enzymatically converted to the active form upon tissue disruption by the enzyme myrosinase (Habtemariam, 2024; Mangla et al., 2021). This conversion is a well‐established biochemical process that occurs during food processing or mastication, and it provides the basis for sulforaphane’s identification as a nutraceutical with significant potential in various disease contexts (Houghton, 2019; Lagunas-Rangel, 2024). Sulforaphane belongs to the isothiocyanate class of compounds, a group known for their prominent antioxidant, anti‐inflammatory, and anticancer activities (Dutta et al., 2023; Habtemariam, 2024). Its discovery and subsequent characterization have positioned it as a compound of interest not only in cancer chemoprevention but also in other chronic disease models including neurodegenerative conditions and ocular pathologies (Ordonez et al., 2021; Habtemariam, 2024). The current therapeutic candidate—in this case, Sulforaphane (Nrf2 activator; LKT Laboratories Cat. No. S8044)—is being evaluated for its potential to modulate specific cellular pathways implicated in the pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly its ability to activate the Nrf2 transcription factor in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells at a proposed concentration of 5 µM (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Sulforaphane’s therapeutic history is extensive and spans multiple domains, primarily due to its ability to induce phase II detoxification enzymes and to modulate oxidative stress responses at the cellular level. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its efficacy in inducing apoptosis and mitigating cancer cell proliferation through the modulation of key signaling pathways (Dutta et al., 2023; Tortorella et al., 2015). In addition to its anticancer properties, sulforaphane has been evaluated in models of neurodegeneration, where it has been shown to confer neuroprotection by alleviating oxidative stress and inflammation—a property that is particularly relevant to retinal diseases such as AMD (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024). In ocular research, various investigations using in vitro and in vivo models have highlighted sulforaphane’s capacity to activate the Nrf2 pathway in retinal cells, leading to enhanced antioxidant enzyme expression and reduced oxidative damage (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). Notably, studies employing retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, such as ARPE-19 cells, have documented protective effects of sulforaphane against oxidative insult, where enhanced expression of genes such as heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), glutathione peroxidase (GPX), and glutamate-cysteine ligase modulatory subunit (GCLM) has been observed (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Kubo et al., 2017). Although sulforaphane has been predominantly explored in the context of cancer chemoprevention and neuroprotection, its application in treating ocular conditions such as dry AMD is emerging. Early studies suggest that sulforaphane might reduce lipofuscin accumulation and rescue lysosomal pH abnormalities in A2E-loaded RPE cells, which are hallmark features of dry AMD pathogenesis (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). Safety profiles established through both in vitro studies and limited clinical trials indicate that sulforaphane is generally well-tolerated, with few adverse effects even upon oral administration, thereby rendering it a promising agent for repurposing in ocular disorders (Ordonez et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic actions of sulforaphane are mediated primarily through the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, a central regulator of antioxidant defense mechanisms. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytosol by its inhibitory partner, Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1), which facilitates its ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Mangla et al., 2021). Sulforaphane exerts its effect by covalently modifying critical cysteine residues on KEAP1, thereby disrupting the KEAP1-Nrf2 complex. This modification impedes Nrf2 degradation and permits its rapid translocation into the nucleus (Habtemariam, 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small musculoaponeurotic fibrosarcoma (sMaf) proteins and binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoter regions of a multitude of genes, culminating in the transcriptional activation of phase II detoxification enzymes such as HO-1, GPX, and GCLM (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2024; Hyttinen et al., 2019). In addition to enhancing the antioxidant capacity of the cell, activation of Nrf2 by sulforaphane has been associated with the upregulation of genes implicated in the regulation of autophagy and lysosomal function (Chang et al., 2020; Bergandi et al., 2024). This is particularly salient in the context of RPE biology, where proper lysosomal function is critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and the prevention of lipofuscin accumulation. Impaired degradation pathways in RPE cells lead to cellular stress and contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). Moreover, sulforaphane’s ability to reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine production through suppression of mediators like intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) further supports its cytoprotective role in the retina (Habtemariam, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). The proposed concentration of 5 µM in vitro is supported by studies indicating that such a dose is sufficient to robustly activate Nrf2, thereby inducing an antioxidant response without eliciting toxicity in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). This multifaceted mechanism—encompassing enhanced transcription of antioxidant defense genes, promotion of autophagy, and attenuation of inflammatory signaling—underpins the rationale for deploying sulforaphane as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Expected Effect:  
Within the iPSC-derived RPE model of dry AMD, the administration of sulforaphane at 5 µM is hypothesized to yield several beneficial outcomes. First, by engaging the Nrf2 signaling pathway, sulforaphane is expected to increase the transcription of key antioxidant genes such as GCLM, GPX, and HO-1 (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Kubo et al., 2017). This upregulation will enhance the cellular capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS), thereby mitigating oxidative stress—a well-known contributor to RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2024). Second, the improved activation of Nrf2 is anticipated to restore autophagy processes and lysosomal enzyme function within RPE cells, facilitating more efficient degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and the removal of toxic byproducts such as lipofuscin (Chang et al., 2020; Bergandi et al., 2024). A2E, a major bisretinoid component of lipofuscin, has been implicated in the disruption of lysosomal pH and function; therefore, by rescuing lysosomal acidity and enhancing enzymatic activity, sulforaphane could support the clearance of A2E aggregates and related debris (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Third, given its anti-inflammatory attributes, sulforaphane is expected to downregulate cytokine expression and other inflammatory mediators, thus reducing the chronic inflammatory state that exacerbates RPE damage in dry AMD (Habtemariam, 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). On a molecular level, the improved phagocytic function of RPE cells, achieved through the normalization of lysosomal and autophagic pathways, is critical for maintaining retinal integrity and function since efficient POS degradation is necessary for visual cycle homeostasis (Chang et al., 2020; Kubo et al., 2017). Furthermore, the favorable safety profile observed in preclinical studies—coupled with evidence of minimal toxicity even at higher concentrations—supports the use of sulforaphane at the proposed dose, making it a mechanistically specific strategy to alleviate oxidative and lysosomal stress in dry AMD models (Ordonez et al., 2021; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Collectively, the expected effects at the molecular, cellular, and functional levels converge on the hypothesis that sulforaphane will both preserve RPE cell viability and enhance cellular clearance mechanisms, thereby countering key pathological features of dry AMD.

Sulforaphane represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its multifaceted mechanism of action, which directly targets key pathological processes involved in retinal degeneration. One of its primary strengths lies in its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway; this leads to a comprehensive antioxidant response by upregulating detoxification and cytoprotective genes that are essential for neutralizing ROS and ameliorating oxidative stress in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Kubo et al., 2017). The capacity to rescue lysosomal function and promote autophagy is another major advantage, as it addresses the abnormal accumulation of lipofuscin—a hallmark of dry AMD—by restoring the degradation and recycling of photoreceptor outer segments (Chang et al., 2020; Bergandi et al., 2024). Additionally, sulforaphane’s documented anti-inflammatory effects further enhance its therapeutic potential by reducing the expression of inflammatory cytokines that contribute to retinal damage (Habtemariam, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). The favorable safety profile noted in various studies reinforces the viability of repurposing sulforaphane, particularly since clinical trials in other indications have demonstrated minimal systemic toxicity and good tolerability (Ordonez et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

Despite these strengths, several challenges must be acknowledged. A key limitation associated with sulforaphane is its inherently low water solubility and bioavailability, which pose significant obstacles for achieving therapeutic concentrations at the target site, especially in ocular tissues where the blood–ocular barriers prevent easy drug penetration (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Current formulations may result in a high first-pass effect and limited tissue penetration upon systemic administration. This challenge necessitates the exploration of novel delivery systems—such as nanoformulations, liposomes, or other topical ocular delivery strategies—that can enhance the stability and bioavailability of sulforaphane (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Furthermore, while preclinical data in cell culture models and animal studies are promising, there remains an evidence gap regarding the efficacy of sulforaphane in human subjects with dry AMD. 4. Comparative studies to evaluate sulforaphane’s efficacy relative to existing antioxidant and anti-inflammatory therapies in dry AMD, in order to establish its potential niche within the therapeutic landscape.

If formulation and delivery challenges can be effectively overcome, sulforaphane may well represent a viable and innovative strategy to preserve retinal health and counteract the progressive degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Habtemariam, 2024).

In conclusion, the current body of evidence from biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical studies supports the hypothesis that sulforaphane can enhance Nrf2 activation in RPE cells and improve antioxidant and lysosomal function, thereby potentially alleviating key pathological features of dry AMD. Given its extensive therapeutic history, well-characterized mechanism of action, and favorable safety profile, sulforaphane is a strong candidate deserving further rigorous evaluation and development. More recent investigations have focused on its ability to rescue mitochondrial deficits and restore autophagic flux in RPE cells, with data indicating that in models of CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE, nicotinamide can ameliorate lysosomal processing and POS degradation problems (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). This body of evidence, compounded with its extensive historical use as a nutritional supplement, supports the rationale for repurposing nicotinamide as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, nicotinamide exerts its effects primarily through its role as a key precursor in the NAD⁺ salvage pathway. In this pathway, nicotinamide is converted to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) via the enzyme nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), and subsequently to NAD⁺ by NMN adenylyltransferase. NAD⁺, in turn, is an essential co-factor for numerous enzymes involved in energy metabolism and cellular homeostasis, most notably the sirtuin family of NAD⁺-dependent deacetylases (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Sirtuins, such as SIRT1 and SIRT3, play a pivotal role in mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and regulation of autophagy by deacetylating key transcription factors and enzymes that control metabolic stress responses (Gemae et al., 2024). In RPE cells, increased NAD⁺ levels facilitate the activation of these sirtuins, which then deacetylate a range of targets including histones and autophagy regulators, leading to improved mitochondrial structure and function, enhanced energy production, and the promotion of efficient autophagic and lysosomal degradation pathways (Gemae et al., 2024). Furthermore, the improved mitochondrial function translates into a better cellular energy state, providing the necessary ATP required for high-energy processes such as POS phagocytosis. Experimentally, administration of nicotinamide has been shown to yield a two-fold increase in NAD⁺ levels in ARPE-19 cells, thereby confirming its ability to augment the cellular bioenergetic capacity (Hazim et al., 2022). This mechanism also intersects with the regulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, as enhanced mitochondrial function and sirtuin activity contribute to lower oxidative stress, a known contributor to cellular senescence and dysfunction in the aging retina (Gemae et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the current proposal is that nicotinamide, administered at a concentration of 10 mM in vitro, will significantly increase NAD⁺ levels in RPE cells, thereby enhancing sirtuin activity and downstream mitochondrial function. This boost in NAD⁺ is expected to promote deacetylation of autophagy regulators, which will, in turn, normalize the autophagic flux and facilitate the effective degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE. In models of dry AMD, where phagocytosis deficits and impaired proteostasis are key pathological features, the restoration of autophagy and mitochondrial activity is anticipated to ameliorate cellular senescence and maintain retinal homeostasis (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Data from previous studies suggest that in aging RPE, reduced NAMPT expression is linked to decreased NAD⁺ levels and compromised SIRT1 function, leading to cellular senescence and defective mitochondrial dynamics (Jadeja et al., 2018). By contrast, nicotinamide supplementation helps to reverse these effects, as evidenced by restored NAD⁺ content and reactivation of sirtuins that enable degradation of accumulated defective cellular components, thereby improving lysosomal enzyme processing and phagocytosis (Jadeja et al., 2018). Moreover, enhanced mitochondrial metabolism has been correlated with improved RPE differentiation and the maintenance of a polarized epithelial phenotype, critical factors in ensuring effective POS phagocytosis and overall retinal health (Hazim et al., 2022). Thus, the expected outcome is that nicotinamide treatment will correct metabolic impairments, reduce oxidative stress, and restore phagocytic efficiency in dry AMD cultures, which are all essential for halting or even reversing disease progression (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
Nicotinamide emerges as a highly promising therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on its multi-faceted mechanism of action and extensive preclinical evidence supporting its role in maintaining retinal health. One of the primary strengths of nicotinamide is its excellent safety profile and widespread historical use as a nutritional supplement, which significantly lowers the risk associated with its repurposing (Gemae et al., 2024). Its ability to augment NAD⁺ levels and activate sirtuins directly addresses several key pathological processes in dry AMD, including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and impaired autophagy. Experimental findings have consistently shown that increased NAD⁺ levels, mediated by nicotinamide or its analogues such as NMN, correlate with reduced cellular senescence and improved lysosomal and mitochondrial function in RPE cells (Jadeja et al., 2018).

Moreover, the convergence of multiple lines of evidence—from studies detailing NAMPT decline in aging RPE, to those demonstrating the restoration of NAD⁺ and sirtuin activity by nicotinamide—provides a robust biochemical rationale for its use in combating dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024). The ability of nicotinamide to enhance mitochondrial respiration in ARPE-19 cells and primary human fetal RPE cells further underscores its potential in promoting a healthy, polarized RPE phenotype capable of efficient POS phagocytosis (Hazim et al., 2022). These studies also suggest that improved mitochondrial metabolism is closely linked to enhanced proteostasis and autophagic clearance of damaged cellular components—an outcome that is particularly relevant given the known deficits in autophagy and lysosomal processing observed in dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024).

However, while the preclinical data are encouraging, several challenges must be acknowledged. One potential weakness lies in the translation of in vitro findings to in vivo therapeutic efficacy. The concentration of 10 mM nicotinamide used in cell culture experiments may not directly correspond to achievable or sustainable therapeutic levels in the human retina. Moreover, while nicotinamide is known to boost NAD⁺ synthesis, there is a nuanced balance in its effects on sirtuin activity; in certain contexts, excessive nicotinamide has been reported to inhibit sirtuins, suggesting that dosing and timing will be critical parameters that require careful optimization (Will-Orrego, 2020). There is also the inherent challenge of the multifactorial nature of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired autophagy are only parts of a complex network of pathological events that include inflammatory signaling, extracellular matrix alterations, and genetic predispositions. Thus, while nicotinamide addresses several of these pathways, it may need to be combined with other therapeutic agents to achieve a comprehensive treatment effect (Gemae et al., 2024; Will-Orrego, 2020).

Another important consideration is the need for more extensive clinical studies. Although nicotinamide’s safety profile is well established in the context of dietary supplementation and its use in other neurological and ocular conditions, robust clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD are lacking (Gemae et al., 2024; Lin, 2020). Future research will need to focus not only on the pharmacokinetics and optimal dosing strategies in human subjects but also on precise biomarkers indicating the restoration of NAD⁺ metabolism, mitochondrial function, and POS phagocytosis. Furthermore, mechanistic studies that dissect the interactions between nicotinamide-driven NAD⁺ elevation and the downstream modulation of autophagy regulators will be essential to confirm the proposed mode of action and to identify any potential off-target effects.

Overall, the repurposing of nicotinamide for dry AMD presents several compelling advantages. Its established safety, low cost, and known biochemical mechanisms strongly support its potential as a therapeutic candidate. Preclinical evidence indicates that nicotinamide not only restores NAD⁺ levels but also reactivates sirtuin pathways, thereby mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction and defective autophagy that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. These effects could translate into improved cellular proteostasis and enhanced POS phagocytosis, ultimately preserving retinal integrity and visual function (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Nevertheless, the path forward will require careful dose optimization and rigorous clinical validation to ensure that the in vitro benefits observed translate into meaningful clinical outcomes. In summary, despite the challenges associated with translating cell-based results into human therapy, nicotinamide remains an attractive candidate whose mechanism, historical use, and preclinical successes justify further investigation as a potential treatment for dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Lin, 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Probenecid is an old, small‐molecule drug originally developed in the mid‐20th century as a uricosuric agent for the treatment of gout. It is a benzoic acid derivative that gained clinical utility by inhibiting renal tubular organic anion transporters (OATs), thereby reducing the excretion of uric acid and concomitantly increasing the plasma levels of antibiotics when co‐administered. As a member of the OAT inhibitor class, probenecid has the unique property of modulating membrane transport processes by binding to and inhibiting transport proteins that mediate the efflux of diverse anionic compounds. Its chemical properties, including high lipophilicity and significant plasma protein binding, have led to its usage not only in gout and antibiotic “boosting” regimens but also in experimental settings within the central nervous system and the ocular compartment, where it modulates the activity of transporters critical for drug bioavailability. The candidate proposed for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is envisioned to leverage the drug’s capacity to inhibit organic anion transporters expressed in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby modifying intracellular signaling cascades. In particular, by inhibiting OATs and related transporters on the apical RPE membrane—a compartment known to display probenecid‐sensitive transport activities—there is a hypothesis that intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) could be augmented, leading to activation of protein kinase A (PKA). This falls in line with the broader therapeutic strategy of repurposing well‐characterized OAT inhibitors for their potential to modulate intracellular signaling and cellular functions beyond their classical renal roles (García-Rodríguez et al., 2023; Schlosshauer & Steuer, 2005).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, probenecid has had a long and well-documented clinical history. Since its advent as a treatment for gout, probenecid has been utilized to inhibit renal excretion of antibiotics and other compounds, capitalizing on its ability to block OATs such as OAT1 and OAT3, as evidenced by its measured inhibitory concentrations (IC₅₀ values in the low micromolar range) (García-Rodríguez et al., 2023). Over the years, its usage has expanded into preclinical studies within the central nervous system, where its inhibition of organic anion transporters and pannexin 1 (Panx1) channels has been explored as a means to modulate neuroinflammation and enhance drug delivery across blood–brain barrier-like structures (García-Rodríguez et al., 2023; Silverman et al., 2008). In the ocular arena, several studies have employed probenecid to probe its capabilities as a transporter modulator—demonstrating effects on ocular drug disposition, retinal electrophysiologic function in light-damage models, and reductions in inflammatory markers in acute animal models (Nor et al., 2021). Despite these encouraging preclinical findings, it is important to note that there are no direct or published clinical studies employing probenecid for the treatment of dry AMD or diseases with similar pathophysiology. Although the literature includes a variety of therapeutic investigations involving retinal cell lines, light-damage models, and studies on ocular transporter expression, none have yet formally evaluated a protocol wherein probenecid is used specifically to enhance photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake in the RPE via modulation of intracellular cAMP signaling. Thus, while the drug’s history lends it safety and a rich background of transporter pharmacology, its application in chronic degenerative retinal diseases such as dry AMD remains unvalidated (Mannermaa et al., 2009; Hass et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, probenecid is classically known to inhibit organic anion transporters (OATs) and members of the organic anion transporting polypeptides (OATPs). Experimental studies have demonstrated that probenecid binds to and inhibits OAT1 and OAT3, with IC₅₀ values reported at approximately 12.3 μM for OAT1 and 4.93 μM for OAT3 (García-Rodríguez et al., 2023). Moreover, in retinal cells, evidence indicates that there exists a probenecid-inhibitable organic anion transporter on the apical membrane of RPE cells, implicating its potential to modulate substrate transport in this tissue (Schlosshauer & Steuer, 2005). The candidate hypothesis proposes that inhibition of these transporters will lead to intracellular accumulation of cyclic nucleotides, specifically cAMP, since proteins such as MRP4 and MRP5—which are expressed in ARPE-19 and primary human RPE cells—have been implicated in the homeostasis of cAMP and cGMP (Mannermaa et al., 2009). These transporters, sensitive to probenecid, normally export cyclic nucleotides and other substrates; thus, their inhibition could potentially lead to an elevation in intracellular cAMP levels. Increased cAMP is well known to activate PKA, which in turn phosphorylates a host of downstream targets involved in cytoskeletal dynamics, including actin remodeling factors. Such cytoskeletal remodeling is thought to be critical for the formation of the phagocytic cup during the process of POS uptake by the RPE—a process that is impaired in dry AMD. 

Notably, some literature has documented that organic anion transport inhibitors can suppress certain cAMP-induced responses. For instance, García and Burnside (Hass et al., 2024) reported that suppression of a cAMP-induced pigment granule aggregation in RPE by organic anion transport inhibitors occurs, suggesting that blocking these transporters may not always lead to a straightforward increase in all cAMP-mediated cytoskeletal effects. The intricate balance between cAMP’s multiple downstream effects must therefore be considered. Additionally, probenecid is also known to block pannexin-1 channels, which are involved in ATP release and subsequent inflammatory signaling (Silverman et al., 2008; Yang, 2017). While inhibition of pannexin channels could contribute to reduced inflammation—a desirable outcome in retinal degenerations—the direct link between pannexin blockade and augmented cAMP/PKA signaling in the context of RPE phagocytosis remains speculative. Experimental evidence from ARPE-19 cells also shows that probenecid can inhibit P2X7 receptor/pannexin-1-dependent membrane pore formation induced by oxysterols, though this has been more closely associated with modulation of cell death pathways and inflammatory responses rather than enhancement of phagocytosis (Olivier et al., 2016). Moreover, work demonstrating that probenecid can block the uptake of Firsocostat—a drug that requires an OATP for cellular entry—provides direct evidence of its ability to inhibit transporter-mediated processes in RPE cells (Hass et al., 2023). However, these studies do not directly address the impact on intracellular cAMP levels, PKA activation, actin dynamics, or phagocytic cup formation. In summary, while the mechanistic rationale for utilizing probenecid to modulate RPE cell physiology is grounded in its well-described inhibitory effects on organic anion transporters and its potential to influence cyclic nucleotide homeostasis, the literature does not yet provide a definitive demonstration that these effects translate into enhanced PKA activation or improved phagocytic uptake of POS in the RPE (Mannermaa et al., 2009; Lee & Pelis, 2016; Hass et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The proposed therapeutic hypothesis is that treatment with probenecid will inhibit OATs (and possibly OATPs and MRPs) expressed on the apical surface of RPE cells, resulting in an elevation of intracellular cAMP levels. This, in turn, is expected to augment PKA activity within the cell. Elevated PKA activity is known to drive a range of cellular processes including the modulation of actin cytoskeletal architecture, which is crucial for the formation of phagocytic cups during the process of POS internalization. In the RPE, daily phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor outer segments is essential for photoreceptor maintenance, and dysregulation of this process is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Conceptually, probenecid is hypothesized to “boost” the phagocytic capability of RPE cells by pharmacologically inducing conditions that favor actin polymerization and cytoskeletal rearrangements associated with efficient formation of the phagocytic cup. 

Further support for the relevance of cAMP in RPE lysosomal and phagocytic functions comes from studies with other compounds; for example, P2Y12 receptor antagonism (as seen with ticagrelor) leads to lowered lysosomal pH and improved clearance of autofluorescent material in RPE cells from ABCA4−/− models (Lu et al., 2018). Such work underscores the link between cAMP elevation and improved catabolic function in RPE cells, providing a proof-of-concept that activation of cAMP/PKA signaling pathways can be beneficial. However, to date there is no published data directly demonstrating that probenecid increases cAMP levels or PKA activity in ARPE-19 cells, nor is there evidence that treatment with probenecid improves the efficiency of phagocytic cup formation or enhances POS uptake in these cells (Hass et al., 2024; Hass et al., 2023). The expected effect, therefore, remains a theoretical extension of the known pharmacology of probenecid based on its ability to interact with RPE-expressed organic anion transporters. While the anatomical evidence supports the presence of probenecid-sensitive transporters in RPE (Schlosshauer & Steuer, 2005; Mannermaa et al., 2009) and the broader pharmacologic literature confirms probenecid’s ability to modulate transporter-mediated processes (García-Rodríguez et al., 2023; Silverman et al., 2008), there is a gap in direct experimental research linking these events to enhanced cAMP-driven cytoskeletal remodeling and increased PR phagocytosis. As such, while the expected effect is mechanistically attractive, it currently relies on an extrapolation from fundamental transporter biology and indirect studies of cyclic nucleotide regulation rather than on direct proof-of-concept experiments in RPE phagocytic assays.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating probenecid as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, there are several strengths and weaknesses that emerge from a comprehensive literature review. On the strengths side, probenecid is a well-characterized, clinically approved drug with an extensive safety history. Its ability to inhibit organic anion transporters, including OATs, OATPs, and even certain multidrug resistance-associated proteins like MRP4 and MRP5, is well documented (García-Rodríguez et al., 2023; Schlosshauer & Steuer, 2005; Mannermaa et al., 2009). The documented presence of probenecid-sensitive transporters in the RPE supports the notion that the drug could modulate RPE intracellular homeostasis. Furthermore, preclinical studies in ocular models—including light-damage and oxygen-induced retinopathy models—suggest that probenecid can exert neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in the retina, with improvements in retinal architecture and electrophysiological parameters (Nor et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2021). Such findings bolster the case that probenecid, via modulation of transporter activity and potentially via additional actions on pannexin channels, can yield beneficial biological responses in retinal tissues, which may be relevant for the treatment of degenerative conditions like dry AMD.

However, the candidate’s weaknesses are significant from the perspective of the specific therapeutic hypothesis under consideration. The central hypothesis posits that probenecid will increase intracellular cAMP and thereby activate PKA to promote cytoskeletal rearrangements that enhance the phagocytic uptake of POS by RPE cells. The literature does provide evidence for probenecid’s inhibition of organic anion transporters in ocular tissues (Hass et al., 2023; Schlosshauer & Steuer, 2005), but there is no direct experimental data linking probenecid treatment to increased intracellular cAMP levels in RPE cells or to enhanced PKA activity. In fact, one study suggests that organic anion transport inhibitors may suppress a cAMP-dependent response (e.g., pigment granule aggregation in RPE) (Hass et al., 2024), which could be interpreted as counter to the proposed mechanism. Additionally, while other compounds such as ticagrelor have been shown to influence lysosomal pH and phagocytic processing via cAMP/PKA pathways (Lu et al., 2018), these effects have not been recapitulated with probenecid in any published work. This leaves a critical gap: the central premise—that inhibiting organic anion transport in RPE will necessarily elevate cAMP and induce the desired cytoskeletal and phagocytic changes—remains unproven in the context of probenecid.

Further complicating the picture is probenecid’s known activity as a pannexin-1 channel inhibitor (Silverman et al., 2008; Yang, 2017). While inhibition of Panx1 can mitigate pathological ATP release and reduce inflammatory signaling—effects that could be beneficial in a neurodegenerative retinal setting—this mechanism is distinct from the modulation of cAMP/PKA signaling that underpins the current therapeutic hypothesis. The potential for off-target effects also raises concerns: if probenecid primarily acts by blocking pannexin channels or by interfering with other transporters not directly related to cAMP homeostasis, its administration could lead to side effects or fail to deliver the anticipated enhancement in phagocytosis. Moreover, the literature does not define the precise dosing regimens or pharmacokinetic profiles in RPE cells that would be required to achieve the proposed biochemical changes. For example, experiments showing inhibition of transporter-mediated uptake in RPE have employed concentrations on the order of 100 μM to 1 mM (Hass et al., 2023; Olivier et al., 2016), raising questions about the feasibility of translating such concentrations in vivo without off-target toxicity or interference with other critical cellular processes.

In terms of translational potential, while probenecid’s long clinical history is a favorable aspect, its application in a chronic disease such as dry AMD requires clear demonstration of sustained modulation of RPE function over time. The evidence from acute light-damage or oxygen-induced retinopathy models (Nor et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2021) suggests that probenecid may improve retinal integrity and reduce neuroinflammation; however, these models do not replicate the slow degenerative progression and complex pathophysiology of dry AMD, where chronic dysfunction in POS phagocytosis and RPE metabolism play central roles. Without explicit studies showing that probenecid can enhance phagocytic cup formation and POS uptake in RPE cells—and thereby ameliorate dry AMD-like pathology in animal models—the candidate remains only a theoretical possibility for this indication.

Thus, while the concept of repurposing probenecid for dry AMD is innovative and leverages a drug with robust safety credentials and a well-understood mechanism as an OAT inhibitor, the current state of the literature presents significant gaps. There is compelling evidence for the presence of probenecid-sensitive organic anion transporters in RPE and for the drug’s efficacy in modulating ocular transporter activity (Schlosshauer & Steuer, 2005; Hass et al., 2023), yet critical downstream assays linking this modulation to increased intracellular cAMP, PKA activation, actin cytoskeletal remodeling, and enhanced POS phagocytosis are lacking. Given that some studies even indicate potential suppression of cAMP-dependent processes by organic anion transport inhibitors (Hass et al., 2024), it is imperative to conduct focused biochemical and cellular experiments in ARPE-19 or primary RPE models that assay cAMP levels, PKA activity, and cytoskeletal changes under probenecid treatment. Additionally, in vivo studies in animal models that more closely mimic the chronic pathology of dry AMD would be necessary to determine whether these in vitro effects translate into meaningful therapeutic benefits.

Overall, the repurposing strategy for probenecid aimed at enhancing phagocytic signaling in RPE cells by modulating organic anion transporter activity is mechanistically plausible yet remains unproven. Its established inhibitory action on OATs and related transporters provides a strong foundation, and its additional anti-inflammatory effects via pannexin blockade further underscore its potential in ocular applications. However, the absence of direct evidence linking probenecid to increased cAMP and PKA activation in RPE, coupled with conflicting indications from studies on cAMP-mediated responses, represents a major weakness in the current proposal. Before proceeding further along the translational pathway, it is critical to perform targeted preclinical studies that (i) quantify changes in intracellular cAMP and PKA activity in RPE following probenecid administration, (ii) assess the resultant impact on actin cytoskeleton dynamics and phagocytic cup formation, and (iii) evaluate whether these cellular alterations lead to improved POS uptake and reduced features of dry AMD in appropriate animal models (Mannermaa et al., 2009; Hass et al., 2023; Hass et al., 2024).

In summary, while probenecid offers several attractive features—including clinical familiarity, a well-characterized pharmacological profile, and documented inhibitory effects on ocular transporters—the current body of evidence does not sufficiently demonstrate that its mechanism of action will result in the intracellular signaling changes necessary to enhance RPE phagocytosis in the context of dry AMD. The hypothesis that increasing intracellular cAMP via OAT inhibition will drive PKA-mediated cytoskeletal remodeling and improved POS clearance in RPE remains speculative until validated by further biomechanical, cellular, and in vivo studies. The overall evaluation of probenecid as a candidate for dry AMD is therefore cautiously optimistic but underscores the need for additional targeted research to bridge the gap between transporter inhibition and the desired modulation of phagocytic signaling (García-Rodríguez et al., 2023; Silverman et al., 2008; Olivier et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
The pharmacological activity of SBI-0206965 has primarily been established in cancer research and neurodegenerative models, where its ability to inhibit ULK1-mediated autophagy is used to sensitize tumor cells to chemotherapy and to protect neurons from acute degenerative stress. For instance, in non–small cell lung cancer cells, SBI-0206965 has been shown to reduce autophagic flux and promote apoptotic cell death when combined with other chemotherapeutic agents (Limpert et al., 2018). Moreover, preclinical studies using retinal ganglion cell models have demonstrated that intravitreal injection of higher concentrations (e.g., 50 µM) of SBI-0206965 can reduce acute axonal degeneration and modify autophagy markers, suggesting that autophagy modulation might translate to neuroprotective outcomes in ocular tissues (Sundermeyer, 2022). Despite these promising results in models of cancer and neuronal injury, there have been no dedicated studies or clinical trials assessing the use of SBI-0206965 specifically for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or related retinal diseases. Nonetheless, foundational evidence supports the concept that autophagy dysregulation, particularly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), contributes to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, providing a rationale for exploring autophagy regulators like SBI-0206965 in this context (Blasiak et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SBI-0206965 functions by competitively inhibiting ULK1 kinase activity, which is a critical initiating event in the canonical autophagy pathway. Under physiological conditions, ULK1 forms a complex with adaptor proteins ATG13, FIP200, and ATG101 to trigger autophagosome formation by promoting the phosphorylation of downstream targets such as Beclin-1 and VPS34; these events are essential for membrane nucleation and the subsequent formation of autophagic vesicles (Intartaglia et al., 2022). SBI-0206965 achieves an inhibitory effect on ULK1 with a biochemical IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range (approximately 108 nM for ULK1 and 711 nM for ULK2), thereby impairing the phosphorylation cascade that would normally lead to the formation of autophagosomes (Kocak et al., 2022). It is noteworthy that the inhibition of ULK1 by SBI-0206965 has been reported to result in decreased phosphorylation of key autophagy regulators, alongside a reduction in LC3-positive puncta and concomitant increases in the autophagic adaptor molecule p62, confirming the compound’s ability to attenuate canonical autophagy (Pinelli et al., 2025; Limpert et al., 2018). Importantly, emerging evidence in RPE cells suggests that, while canonical autophagy is ULK1-dependent, the noncanonical process known as LC3-associated phagocytosis (LAP) is largely independent of ULK1. This mechanistic divergence forms the basis of the hypothesis that low-dose ULK1 inhibition with SBI-0206965 could selectively modulate the balance between bulk autophagy and LAP, favoring the latter—a process known to be integral for the efficient degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in RPE cells (Liton et al., 2023; Jain et al., 2023). However, it is also crucial to mention that the compound exhibits off-target inhibition on kinases such as FAK and AMPK, which could potentially modify additional cellular signaling pathways involved in autophagy and cell survival (Karmacharya & Jung, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis posits that low-dose administration of SBI-0206965 in RPE cells will induce a selective modulation in autophagy initiation. Specifically, the drug is expected to downregulate the canonical autophagy pathway sufficiently to reduce potential overactivation, which may lead to cell stress or death, while simultaneously sparing or even indirectly promoting LC3-associated phagocytosis (LAP)—a noncanonical autophagy process crucial for phagolysosomal fusion and efficient POS degradation. RPE cells naturally exhibit high rates of autophagy due to the daily phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor outer segments; indeed, impaired autophagy in these cells has been directly linked to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, characterized by the accumulation of undigested cellular material and subsequent drusen formation (Pinelli et al., 2023; Blasiak et al., 2025). By partially inhibiting ULK1 activity, SBI-0206965 at submicromolar concentrations is hypothesized to reduce excessive bulk autophagy without compromising the LC3 recruitment to phagosomes—a hallmark of LAP—which is essential for maintaining the continuous renewal of photoreceptor components (Blasiak et al., 2024; Liton et al., 2023). In practical assay systems using cultured RPE cells, one would anticipate observing an increase in markers associated with LAP (such as enhanced LC3 lipidation on phagosomes and improved lysosomal fusion) alongside a controlled, rather than complete, suppression of canonical autophagy markers. Such an outcome would support enhanced POS degradation, ultimately alleviating one of the critical pathogenic processes in dry AMD. It is also expected that preserved or enhanced LAP activity would diminish the accumulation of toxic metabolites and lipofuscin, thereby contributing to improved retinal function and slowed disease progression (Limpert et al., 2018; Pinelli et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
SBI-0206965 presents several compelling advantages as a candidate for modulating autophagy in the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration. Its well-characterized mechanism of action as a ULK1 inhibitor allows for targeted interference with a key early step in canonical autophagy—an approach that has proven valuable in preclinical cancer models and, more recently, in studies addressing neuronal injury in the retina (Kocak et al., 2022; Sundermeyer, 2022). The hypothesis that low-dose SBI-0206965 can shift the cellular autophagy balance toward favoring LC3-associated phagocytosis (LAP) is particularly innovative, given that LAP is instrumental in the efficient degradation of photoreceptor outer segments by RPE cells. This mechanistic nuance, wherein canonical autophagy is dampened while LAP remains active due to its ULK1 independence, holds significant promise for restoring proper phagocytic and degradative functions in RPE cells—a process that is critically disrupted in dry AMD (Pinelli et al., 2023; Liton et al., 2023).

Despite these strengths, several challenges must be acknowledged. First, the off-target effects of SBI-0206965 on kinases such as FAK, AMPK, NUAK1, and MLK1 raise concerns regarding the potential for unintended modulation of other signaling pathways. Such off-target activities could compromise RPE cell viability or alter cellular stress responses that are vital for maintaining retinal homeostasis (Karmacharya & Jung, 2023). Second, while its potency as a ULK1 inhibitor is adequate for investigational use (with an IC₅₀ for ULK1 around 108 nM), newer and more selective ULK1 inhibitors have since been developed, and SBI-0206965 may not represent the most optimal chemical probe in terms of specificity and potency (Martin et al., 2018). Third, most of the existing data on SBI-0206965 derives from cancer cells and neuronal models, and there is a notable lack of direct experimental evidence that confirms its efficacy or safety in RPE cells or animal models of dry AMD. This gap underscores the necessity for carefully designed in vitro studies using RPE lines and subsequent in vivo AMD models to determine the appropriate dosing window that achieves the desired modulation of autophagy without detrimental suppression of essential bulk autophagy processes (Blasiak et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). Additionally, the balance between inhibiting canonical autophagy and preserving LAP is delicately poised; over-inhibition of ULK1 might inadvertently impair necessary degradation pathways, potentially exacerbating cellular dysfunction rather than mitigating it (Pinelli et al., 2025; Si et al., 2023).

Nevertheless, the underlying rationale for repurposing SBI-0206965 in dry AMD is scientifically grounded. Autophagy dysfunction in RPE cells is a well-documented contributor to the progression of dry AMD, and therapeutically modulating this process represents a novel strategy with the potential to alleviate the accumulation of toxic cellular debris and drusen formation. Given that RPE cells face an immense phagocytic burden and are highly sensitive to disruptions in autophagic flux, agents that can fine-tune autophagy—as opposed to completely inhibiting it—are highly desirable. SBI-0206965, when employed at carefully titrated low doses, might provide the necessary modulation to reduce excessive canonical autophagy, thereby preventing the overaccumulation of autophagic vacuoles, while simultaneously preserving or even enhancing LC3-associated phagocytosis that is crucial for processing endogenous waste material (Pinelli et al., 2023; Sundermeyer, 2022; Blasiak et al., 2025).

In summary, SBI-0206965 exhibits considerable promise as an autophagy modulator with potential applications in the treatment of dry AMD due to its targeted inhibition of ULK1, a pathway central to canonical autophagy regulation in RPE cells. The hypothesis that low-dose administration can favorably shift the autophagic balance toward LAP, thereby improving POS degradation while preventing deleterious overactivation of bulk autophagy, is mechanistically sound and aligns with current understandings of RPE cell biology in AMD pathogenesis. However, the candidate’s moderate potency, documented off-target effects, and the paucity of data in ocular models warrant cautious optimism. Further investigation is required, including optimization of dosing strategies and rigorous assessment in preclinical RPE and AMD models, to fully ascertain the therapeutic window and clinical translatability of SBI-0206965 for dry AMD. Overall, while the candidate is not without its limitations, the innovative therapeutic approach it represents—targeted modulation of autophagy to enhance noncanonical phagocytic processes in RPE cells—merits continued exploration and could ultimately contribute to the development of a novel treatment strategy for dry age‐related macular degeneration (Kocak et al., 2022; Karmacharya & Jung, 2023; Sundermeyer, 2022; Blasiak et al., 2025).
