Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Trehalose is a naturally occurring, nonreducing disaccharide composed of two D‐glucose units (MW = 342.3 Da) that is not synthesized endogenously in mammals but is abundant in other organisms such as fungi, plants, and invertebrates (Cox et al., 2025). It was originally discovered as a cellular protectant and osmolyte that stabilizes proteins and membranes under conditions of stress, and its unique chemical stability and protein‐protective properties have led to its use in cryopreservation and organ transplant protocols (Lotfi et al., 2018). As a small-molecule therapeutic candidate, trehalose belongs to a class of compounds known as osmolytes and molecular chaperones; this category has been extensively explored for its capacity to stabilize proteins, prevent aggregation, and enhance cellular resilience in the face of diverse environmental and metabolic stresses (Abokyi et al., 2020; Cox et al., 2025). In drug development contexts, its repurposing for dry age-related macular degeneration (dAMD) is driven by its capacity to activate TFEB—a master transcription factor regulating the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network—and thereby boost autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ghosh et al., 2023). Trehalose has been formulated for ocular use, most notably as an ingredient in tear substitutes for dry eye, and its safety profile in such formulations provides ancillary support for its potential repurposing to target RPE dysfunction in dAMD (Cox et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Trehalose has a well-documented history in biochemical and preclinical research due to its potent protein-stabilizing and osmoprotectant actions. It has been widely used in non-ophthalmic applications, most notably in cryopreservation protocols, where its ability to preserve protein structure and cellular integrity under desiccating and freezing conditions is exploited (Cox et al., 2025; Lotfi et al., 2018). In the ocular field, trehalose has been evaluated primarily for anterior segment indications such as dry eye disease; several randomized clinical trials have demonstrated its tolerability and efficacy as a tear substitute when combined with hyaluronic acid, with improvements in tear film break-up time (TBUT) and ocular surface symptoms (Chiambaretta et al., 2017).  
More importantly for dAMD, multiple in vitro studies using human RPE cell models—including ARPE-19 and iPSC-derived RPE from patients with genetic risk factors like CFH mutations—have shown that trehalose rescues autophagy deficits and lysosomal dysfunction, especially under oxidative-stress conditions induced by agents such as hydroquinone (Abokyi et al., 2020). These studies report that trehalose treatment upregulates key autophagy regulators (e.g., ATG5, ATG7) and lysosomal markers (e.g., LAMP2, cathepsin D) while enhancing autophagic flux, thereby improving the degradative capacity of RPE cells—a fundamental defect implicated in the accumulation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and lipofuscin in dAMD (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). Additionally, in murine models of retinal degeneration—whether induced by light exposure or by genetic interventions—trehalose has been shown to protect against retinal cell loss and preserve outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness, offering further preclinical evidence of its neuroprotective potential (Cox et al., 2025). Thus, while trehalose has an established record in non-ocular uses and in the treatment of anterior ocular surface disorders, emerging data now support its repurposing for dAMD by virtue of its ability to modulate autophagy and lysosomal degradation in RPE cells (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central mechanism by which trehalose is hypothesized to benefit dry AMD involves its capacity to activate the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of the CLEAR network. TFEB controls the transcription of a whole battery of genes required for autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and metabolic adaptation (Abokyi et al., 2020). Typically, TFEB resides in the cytoplasm in an inactive, phosphorylated state under nutrient-rich or stress-depleted conditions; its translocation to the nucleus is tightly regulated by mTORC1-dependent and mTORC1-independent signaling pathways (Ghosh et al., 2023; Karim et al., 2020). Trehalose has been shown to induce TFEB nuclear translocation independently of mTOR inhibition, potentially through mechanisms involving Akt signaling modulation and AMPK activation (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Upon nuclear entry, TFEB binds to CLEAR elements in the promoter regions of target genes, thereby upregulating autophagy mediators such as ATG5 and ATG7, enhancing the expression of lysosomal proteins like LAMP2, and increasing the levels of protein markers such as LC3B and p62 that are involved in autophagosome formation and maturation (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Several biochemical studies in human RPE cells have demonstrated that trehalose treatment leads to increased TFEB mRNA and protein levels with concomitant upregulation of CLEAR network gene expression. For instance, in ARPE-19 cells exposed to hydroquinone—a model for oxidative stress relevant to dAMD—it was observed that trehalose not only increased LC3-II levels and GFP-LC3 puncta formation but also enhanced the degradation of autophagic substrates, indicating that trehalose facilitates effective autophagic flux rather than merely blocking lysosomal degradation (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Mechanistically, trehalose is thought to penetrate mammalian cells via fluid-phase endocytosis and possibly through the SLC2A8 (GLUT8) transporter, which facilitates its intracellular accumulation at millimolar concentrations (Cox et al., 2025). Once inside the cell, trehalose appears to modulate several key pathways: by inhibiting Akt signaling, it reduces the phosphorylation of TFEB at specific residues (such as S467) that normally prevent its nuclear import; concurrently, trehalose may activate AMPK, which further supports autophagy induction (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020). Moreover, although trehalose transiently upregulates NRF2 under basal conditions—thereby enhancing antioxidant defenses—its primary protective effect in oxidative stress models of the RPE appears to be mediated by restored autophagy, as demonstrated by loss of cytoprotection when autophagy is genetically disrupted via ATG5 knockdown (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Beyond its role in autophagy, trehalose has been implicated in promoting chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) through stimulation of LAMP2 expression, which is essential for CMA substrate recognition and lysosomal import (Abokyi et al., 2020). In this way, trehalose may offer a dual benefit: boosting canonical macroautophagy while also enhancing CMA, collectively leading to improved clearance of damaged organelles, aggregated proteins, and undigested POS in the RPE—a critical function given the strong association between defective POS clearance and the pathogenesis of dAMD (Abokyi et al., 2020). Furthermore, in CFH-mutant iPSC-derived RPE cells, trehalose has been shown to rescue the diminished activity of lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D and to restore other proteostasis markers, establishing a direct molecular link between trehalose-induced TFEB activation and functional improvements in the degradative capacity of RPE cells (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
Collectively, the mechanistic data suggest that trehalose exerts its beneficial effects through a complex interplay of intracellular signaling pathways that converge on the activation of TFEB, thereby re-establishing efficient autophagic clearance processes that are impaired in the aging and oxidative-stressed RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020; Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic insights outlined above, the hypothesis posits that treatment with trehalose at a concentration of 5 mM in an in vitro assay using iPSC-derived RPE cells from dry AMD patients will lead to robust TFEB nuclear translocation. This nuclear translocation is expected to result in the transcriptional upregulation of CLEAR network genes, thereby increasing the expression of autophagy regulators such as ATG5 and ATG7 and promoting the biogenesis of lysosomes, as evidenced by increased levels of lysosomal markers like LAMP2 and cathepsin D (Abokyi et al., 2020). In an environment of oxidative stress—for example, when the iPSC-RPE cells are challenged with hydroquinone to mimic cigarette smoke-induced damage or other oxidative insults commonly associated with AMD—the activation of TFEB by trehalose is anticipated to restore impaired autophagic flux. This restoration would be reflected in the accumulation of LC3-II upon inhibition of lysosomal function (e.g., in the presence of chloroquine) and decreased levels of autophagy substrate p62 (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Crucially, by enhancing autophagic and lysosomal function in the RPE, trehalose is expected to improve POS degradation. Efficient degradation of POS is vital for photoreceptor health, and its impairment has been implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD through the accumulation of toxic byproducts and lipofuscin (Abokyi et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025). Thus, the expected phenotype in the in vitro assay would include not only molecular signatures of enhanced autophagy (e.g., increased LC3B puncta, upregulated ATG gene expression) but also functional improvements such as reduced oxidative stress (lower reactive oxygen species levels) and improved cell viability under stress conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Moreover, previous studies have shown that trehalose’s cytoprotective effects are autophagy-dependent because genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of autophagy (e.g., via ATG5 knockdown) abolishes the otherwise protective effects of trehalose, thereby reinforcing the notion that the expected improvement in POS degradation and overall cellular homeostasis is tightly linked to the restoration of autophagy and lysosomal competence (Abokyi et al., 2020). In essence, the application of 5 mM trehalose to oxidative-stressed iPSC-RPE cells is anticipated to reverse the autophagic deficits that are characteristic of dry AMD, ultimately leading to enhanced clearance of POS, reduced accumulation of cytotoxic aggregates, and improved cellular survival and function in an in vitro model that recapitulates key aspects of the disease (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
Trehalose represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its multifaceted capacity to modulate intracellular degradation pathways that are critically impaired in the disease state. One of the primary strengths of trehalose is its robust preclinical evidence base. Multiple studies have demonstrated that trehalose can induce TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE models, resulting in the transcriptional activation of an array of autophagy and lysosomal genes (Abokyi et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2023; Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020). This mechanistic property directly addresses a key pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD, where the accumulation of undegraded photoreceptor outer segments and lipofuscin due to defective autophagy plays a contributory role in RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration (Abokyi et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025). The ability of trehalose to enhance both macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy augments its therapeutic appeal, as it suggests an overall improvement in cellular proteostasis, which is imperative in aged or stressed RPE cells (Abokyi et al., 2020; Cox et al., 2025).  
Another notable strength is the established safety profile of trehalose. It is a naturally occurring compound with a long history of use in various medical and industrial applications, including as an ingredient in ocular surface formulations for dry eye disease (Chiambaretta et al., 2017; Cox et al., 2025). Furthermore, the preclinical data showing that trehalose can protect against oxidative stress and preserve retinal function in animal models lend credibility to the hypothesis that it may exert similar protective effects in human RPE cells (Cox et al., 2025).  
However, several weaknesses and gaps must be acknowledged as well. First, the majority of the compelling evidence for trehalose’s efficacy in modulating TFEB and enhancing autophagy comes from in vitro studies using immortalized RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19) or rodent models, with only limited data available from human iPSC-derived RPE models specifically derived from AMD patients (Abokyi et al., 2020). Second, there are ongoing debates in the literature regarding the precise molecular mechanisms by which trehalose exerts its autophagy-enhancing effects, with some reports disputing its ability to induce autophagy under certain conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).  
Another potential challenge lies in the delivery of trehalose to the RPE in a clinically meaningful manner. Although trehalose is orally bioavailable and has been successfully formulated for topical ocular use in dry eye applications, the posterior segment of the eye presents unique drug delivery hurdles. Penetration through the cornea and subsequent distribution to the RPE and retina often require specialized formulations, and while there are preclinical reports of trehalose reaching posterior ocular tissues (Cox et al., 2025), comprehensive pharmacokinetic and ocular bioavailability data for trehalose in the context of dAMD remain sparse.  
Furthermore, while the repurposing of trehalose is attractive due to its established safety and low cost, intellectual property issues and regulatory challenges associated with drug repurposing may complicate clinical development. Despite these concerns, the overall body of evidence supports further investigation into trehalose as a potential modulator of TFEB and autophagy in the RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cox et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).  
In summary, trehalose offers several strong advantages as a candidate therapeutic for dry AMD. Its ability to activate TFEB and upregulate a broad spectrum of autophagy and lysosomal genes addresses a fundamental defect in RPE cells implicated in the disease. Robust preclinical evidence in both in vitro and animal models suggests that trehalose enhances autophagic flux, improves POS clearance, and confers cytoprotective effects against oxidative stress. Its favorable safety profile and prior use in ocular formulations further support its translational potential. However, critical gaps remain in terms of validating its efficacy in human-derived RPE models, optimizing its dosing and delivery to the posterior segment, and resolving discrepancies regarding its mechanism of action in different experimental contexts. Given these considerations, trehalose represents a promising candidate that merits further investigation—particularly through rigorous dose-response studies, advanced formulation development to enhance retinal delivery, and robust clinical trials in patient populations at risk for dry AMD—to fully establish its therapeutic value (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cox et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
T0901317 is a synthetic small‐molecule ligand originally developed as a full agonist for the liver X receptors (LXRs), a class of nuclear receptors that govern lipid and cholesterol homeostasis. The therapeutic history of T0901317 spans preclinical investigations primarily centered on cardiovascular diseases, such as atherosclerosis, where its ability to reduce atherosclerotic lesions by enhancing reverse cholesterol transport was of paramount interest. In rodent models, particularly in LDL receptor–deficient mice, T0901317 administration resulted in meaningful reductions in plaque area and plasma cholesterol levels, while concomitantly increasing the expression of ABCA1 in target tissues (Welch et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2017). These studies established the compound’s potent lipid‐modulatory activity, albeit with an accompanying induction of hepatic lipogenesis and elevated plasma triglycerides that raised safety concerns for systemic use. More recently, the focus has shifted to exploring the potential application of T0901317 in ocular diseases, specifically dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In preclinical investigations using ARPE-19 cells and other RPE models, T0901317 has emerged as a promising agent due to its ability to stimulate LXR-mediated pathways that regulate cholesterol efflux and modulate inflammatory responses in the retina (Lyssenko et al., 2018; Choudhary et al., 2020). Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, T0901317 exerts its biological effects by selectively binding to the ligand-binding domains of LXRα and LXRβ. Upon binding, conformational changes in the receptor facilitate heterodimerization with RXR, leading to recruitment of coactivator proteins and subsequent binding to specific LXR response elements in the promoters of target genes. One of the key effects of this activation is the robust upregulation of ABCA1, a transporter protein that plays a central role in cholesterol efflux by mediating the transfer of cholesterol to extracellular acceptors such as apolipoprotein A-I (apo A-I) and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) particles (Lyssenko et al., 2018). The increase in ABCA1 expression subsequently enhances the reverse cholesterol transport (RCT) pathway, which is essential for preventing the intracellular and sub-RPE accumulation of cholesterol and other lipids—a factor implicated in the formation of drusen-like deposits observed in dry AMD. In addition to its lipid-regulatory activity, T0901317 has been shown to attenuate pro-inflammatory signaling pathways in RPE cells, as evidenced by its ability to modulate NF-κB signaling under conditions of oxidant stress and lipid overload (Wu et al., 2023; Buñay et al., 2021). This dual impact on lipid metabolism and inflammation is particularly relevant in the retinal context, where chronic inflammatory processes and disrupted cholesterol homeostasis converge to promote RPE dysfunction and basal deposit accumulation (Lyssenko et al., 2018). Moreover, studies have illustrated that even under conditions of hypoxia or lipid overload—conditions that normally suppress ABCA1 expression via hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF1)—T0901317 is capable of counteracting these inhibitory effects, thereby reestablishing normal cholesterol efflux in RPE cells (Peters et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022). This molecular cascade is expected to promote a more efficient clearance of excess cholesterol from the RPE and surrounding Bruch’s membrane, thus reducing the formation of drusen-like deposits—a hallmark of early AMD pathology (Lyssenko et al., 2018). Data derived from experiments in ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE models indicate that treatment with T0901317 leads to a significant increase in ABCA1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels, which translates into enhanced cholesterol efflux when proper lipid acceptors such as apoA-I are present in the extracellular milieu (Lyssenko et al., 2018). A rigorous evaluation of T0901317 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several compelling strengths alongside notable challenges that must be addressed in future research. Considering the collective body of evidence, T0901317 possesses distinct strengths as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD due to its potent LXR agonism that effectively upregulates ABCA1 expression and enhances cholesterol efflux—a critical need in the management of sub-RPE lipid accumulation and basal deposit formation. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Adalimumab (marketed as Humira) is a fully humanized recombinant IgG1 monoclonal antibody developed using recombinant DNA technology that targets tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNFα). As a member of the anti‐TNFα class of biologics, adalimumab is designed to bind both soluble and membrane‐bound TNFα with high affinity, thereby preventing its interaction with the TNF receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2) on target cells. This antibody was originally discovered and engineered to address systemic inflammatory diseases, and its fully human composition is intended to lower immunogenicity compared to earlier chimeric molecules such as infliximab. In its development, molecular engineering efforts focused on isolating the relevant antibody variable regions that exhibit specificity for TNFα, followed by the construction of a recombinant molecule with human constant regions to improve tolerability and clinical efficacy. Anti‐TNFα antibodies belong to a broader class of therapeutic compounds that have dramatically changed the treatment landscape for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. They have been widely applied in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn’s disease, and ulcerative colitis, and over the past two decades, their use has been extended into ocular inflammatory diseases such as non‐infectious uveitis. Such applications underscore the versatility and translational potential of TNFα inhibition in modulating inflammatory cascades (Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History:  
Adalimumab’s clinical journey began with its approval for systemic autoimmune diseases where TNFα plays a fundamental role in mediating inflammation and tissue damage. Its robust performance in rheumatoid arthritis and related conditions has been well documented in numerous large-scale randomized controlled trials, which demonstrated significant improvement in clinical outcomes and inflammatory markers. These successes provided the foundation for exploring its application in other diseases characterized by inflammatory dysregulation. In recent years, growing evidence from both biochemical studies and clinical observations has highlighted the role of chronic inflammation in the pathogenesis of several retinal degenerative disorders. In particular, studies have shown that TNFα is upregulated in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and may contribute to the degeneration seen in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). For example, preclinical work has demonstrated that inflammation mediated by TNFα can impair the integrity of RPE cells, reduce the expression of proteins critical for RPE function (including visual cycle proteins and complement regulators) and disrupt phagocytic clearance mechanisms; these findings form the basis for hypothesizing that TNFα blockade may preserve RPE function in dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

While the majority of clinical uses of adalimumab have been in the realm of systemic and ocular inflammatory conditions such as non‐infectious uveitis, there has been emerging interest in repurposing anti‐TNFα therapies for retinal degenerations. In the context of ocular disease, several investigators have explored both systemic and local (intravitreal or subconjunctival) routes of administration to modulate intraocular inflammation. Pilot clinical trials and case reports have assessed intravitreal adalimumab in patients with uveitis and even in those with neovascular (“wet”) AMD refractory to anti‐VEGF therapies; these studies reported varying degrees of efficacy and underscored an acceptable local safety profile, though in some instances, higher dosages have been associated with ocular toxicity. In animal studies, intravitreal or subconjunctival administration of adalimumab has been shown to reduce inflammation and offer neuroprotection in models of retinal degeneration, such as in the rd10 mouse model for retinitis pigmentosa, establishing a precedent for local administration to achieve high ocular levels with minimal systemic exposure. Despite these advancements, use of adalimumab specifically for dry AMD has not been established in clinical practice. The proposed approach builds on the mechanistic insights from studies demonstrating that elevated TNFα levels can lead to downregulation of phagocytic receptors and lysosomal enzymes in RPE cells—processes central to dry AMD pathology—and posits that reversing these effects via TNFα neutralization may preserve RPE function (Nashine et al., 2022; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of adalimumab centers on its targeted neutralization of TNFα. TNFα is a proinflammatory cytokine produced by a variety of cell types that include activated T lymphocytes, macrophages, and, importantly, resident cells in the eye such as RPE and Müller glia. When secreted into the extracellular milieu, TNFα binds to its receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2), triggering intracellular signaling cascades that lead to the activation of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and other pathways that promote the expression of additional inflammatory cytokines, adhesion molecules, and matrix metalloproteinases. These processes collectively contribute to a sustained inflammatory response that can result in cellular dysfunction and death. Adalimumab, by virtue of its high affinity binding, sequesters TNFα and prevents receptor engagement. In doing so, it effectively interrupts these downstream proinflammatory signals and halts the amplification of the inflammatory cascade (Wang et al., 2011; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium cells, TNFα-mediated signaling has been implicated in the suppression of genes critical to the maintenance of RPE functions. Specifically, experimental studies have suggested that exposure to TNFα leads to a reduction in the expression of MERTK—a receptor tyrosine kinase essential for the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—as well as cathepsin D, a lysosomal enzyme crucial for the degradation of engulfed material. The decrease in MERTK expression compromises the ability of RPE cells to efficiently phagocytose POS, thereby potentially contributing to the accumulation of cellular debris, drusen formation, and further RPE stress that are characteristic of dry AMD. In parallel, a reduction in cathepsin D would impair lysosomal degradation, exacerbating the intracellular buildup of waste products and further undermining cellular homeostasis in the RPE. By neutralizing TNFα, adalimumab is hypothesized to prevent these detrimental changes, preserving the expression levels of MERTK and cathepsin D and thereby maintaining robust phagocytic and degradative capacity in RPE cells (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021).

At the molecular level, the binding of adalimumab to TNFα is mediated via its antigen-binding (Fab) region, which recognizes specific epitopes on the cytokine. This interaction is characterized by high affinity and specificity, ensuring that even low concentrations of the antibody can effectively neutralize TNFα activity. The blockade prevents TNFα from initiating receptor-mediated signaling that would otherwise promote inflammation and cellular stress. Moreover, because TNFα is known to regulate not only inflammatory cytokine production but also apoptotic processes, its inhibition may confer additional neuroprotective effects in the retina by reducing signals that lead to programmed cell death. The comprehensive inhibition of TNFα by adalimumab therefore stands as a multifaceted intervention, addressing both the inflammatory insult and its secondary effects on critical cellular functions in the RPE (Wang et al., 2011; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Nashine et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for leveraging adalimumab in dry AMD rests on its potential to neutralize elevated TNFα levels in the subretinal microenvironment. Elevated TNFα has been implicated in the pathological downregulation of key proteins involved in RPE function, notably MERTK and cathepsin D. MERTK is a receptor that plays an essential role in the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, a process that is critical for the renewal of photoreceptors and the overall maintenance of retinal health. Cathepsin D, on the other hand, is involved in the lysosomal degradation of the ingested material; together, these proteins ensure that the RPE can effectively clear and recycle photoreceptor debris. In dry AMD, this phagocytic process is compromised, leading to the accumulation of cellular waste products and drusen formation, which further fuels inflammation and RPE degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Administration of adalimumab is expected to interrupt this cascade by neutralizing TNFα, thereby preventing its signaling that leads to the downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D. With TNFα effectively neutralized, RPE cells should experience a more favorable molecular milieu in which the expression of these critical proteins is maintained at functional levels. This preservation would, in turn, support the RPE’s capacity to phagocytose and degrade photoreceptor outer segments, thereby averting the buildup of toxic waste products. Furthermore, since TNFα signaling also contributes to other aspects of cellular stress and inflammation—such as the upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines and the induction of apoptotic pathways—the neutralization of TNFα by adalimumab may also reduce overall cellular stress and promote RPE cell survival and function (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022).

In vitro assays using cultured human RPE cells exposed to TNFα could be employed to test this hypothesis. In these experiments, treatment with adalimumab should result in the normalization or preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression levels when compared to TNFα-treated controls. In addition, functional assays measuring the uptake and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (or surrogate fluorescent particles) would be expected to show improved phagocytic efficiency in RPE cells treated with adalimumab. Such findings would provide robust mechanistic support for the proposed therapeutic strategy. Moreover, preliminary in vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD or models of induced RPE dysfunction could further validate that TNFα blockade leads to preservation of RPE integrity, improved photoreceptor survival, and retardation of retinal degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Considering that the expression of MERTK is well documented in RPE cells and that its function is critical for POS phagocytosis—a process that declines with aging and in the presence of inflammatory mediators—the ability of adalimumab to maintain or restore MERTK expression would be highly relevant in the context of dry AMD. In the proposed strategy, adalimumab may also help to stabilize other RPE functions, such as the regulation of the complement cascade and the visual cycle, both of which have been shown to be adversely affected by TNFα exposure. Thus, the anticipated effect of adalimumab is not limited solely to the preservation of phagocytic machinery; it may also contribute to a broader stabilization of RPE cell health in the face of chronic low-grade inflammation that characterizes dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of adalimumab as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a compelling yet cautiously optimistic perspective. One of the principal strengths of adalimumab lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action; by neutralizing TNFα, it directly addresses a central mediator of inflammation that has been implicated in the dysregulation of RPE functions. The experimental evidence indicating that TNFα exposure can lead to the downregulation of essential proteins such as MERTK and cathepsin D provides a strong rationale for the hypothesis that TNFα inhibition might preserve the RPE’s ability to maintain photoreceptor homeostasis. This mechanistic insight is particularly attractive because it targets one of the fundamental dysfunctions in dry AMD—namely, the failure of the RPE to clear photoreceptor outer segments effectively, which leads to the accumulation of drusen and progressive retinal degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the extensive clinical experience with adalimumab in systemic and ocular inflammatory diseases supports its safety profile. The fact that adalimumab is already approved by regulatory agencies, coupled with several clinical studies demonstrating its localized safety when administered intravitreally or via related routes in ocular conditions such as uveitis, adds to its attractiveness as a candidate for repurposing (Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010; Leal et al., 2018; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. To date, most studies involving adalimumab in the ocular context have focused on inflammatory conditions such as uveitis and neovascular AMD rather than dry AMD specifically. As a result, direct clinical evidence supporting its efficacy in preserving RPE phagocytic function in dry AMD is currently limited. The hypothesis that adalimumab can prevent the TNFα-induced downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D is primarily based on preclinical observations, and further mechanistic studies, both in vitro and in relevant animal models, are necessary to validate this pathway in the context of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Nashine et al., 2022; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Another potential challenge with using adalimumab for dry AMD is related to drug delivery and dosing. While intravitreal administration has shown promise in limited studies, determining the optimal dose that achieves effective TNFα blockade without incurring retinal toxicity remains an unresolved issue. Some animal studies have indicated that higher doses of intravitreal adalimumab can lead to retinal inflammation, reduced electroretinogram responses, or histopathological evidence of toxicity. Given that dry AMD is a chronic condition and would likely require repeated dosing or sustained drug delivery systems, the long-term safety of local TNFα blockade needs to be rigorously evaluated (Manzano et al., 2008; Pascual-Camps et al., 2014).

Moreover, because TNFα plays roles in normal immune surveillance and tissue repair, its complete inhibition—especially in an aged population that may have impaired immune responses—could theoretically predispose patients to infections or other adverse effects. Although the systemic safety profile of adalimumab is well established, the ocular microenvironment has distinct immunological characteristics, and the long-term effects of TNFα inhibition on retinal homeostasis, particularly regarding complement activation and maintenance of the blood–retinal barrier, require further study. There is also the possibility that compensatory inflammatory pathways may become activated in response to TNFα blockade, potentially diminishing the efficacy of the intervention over time (García-Layana et al., 2021; Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Sharma et al., 2009).

Additionally, the magnitude of the contribution of TNFα to the pathogenesis of dry AMD relative to other factors—such as oxidative stress, genetic predispositions (including polymorphisms in complement factors), and lipid metabolism abnormalities—remains to be fully delineated. It is possible that TNFα is one of several drivers of RPE dysfunction, and that its inhibition may need to be combined with other therapeutic strategies (for example, antioxidant supplementation or complement inhibitors) to achieve a meaningful clinical benefit. Therefore, while the rationale for adalimumab is compelling, a monotherapy approach may not be sufficient to halt the multifactorial progression of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nussenblatt et al., 2010).

In summary, adalimumab presents a promising repurposed candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on its potent and specific inhibition of TNFα—a cytokine implicated in the downregulation of crucial RPE proteins such as MERTK and cathepsin D. The drug’s extensive use in other inflammatory settings, along with preliminary evidence supporting its ocular safety, lend credibility to the hypothesis that TNFα blockade can preserve the phagocytic machinery of RPE cells and potentially slow the degenerative process characteristic of dry AMD. Nevertheless, significant challenges remain, including the need for robust preclinical validation in dry AMD models, optimization of ocular dosing regimens, and long-term safety assessments in an elderly population. A carefully designed series of in vitro experiments using human RPE cells—followed by well-controlled animal studies—should be undertaken to establish proof of concept regarding the preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression and function. If these studies yield positive results, subsequent early-phase clinical trials could be justified to evaluate the efficacy of intravitreal adalimumab in patients with dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010).

In light of these considerations, our recommendation is to advance adalimumab into a rigorous preclinical testing pipeline aimed specifically at dry AMD models. This should include studies that measure the expression levels and activity of MERTK and cathepsin D in RPE cells under conditions of TNFα stimulation, both in the presence and absence of adalimumab treatment. Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiling in ocular tissues, along with assessments of retinal structure and function via in vivo imaging and electrophysiological testing, will be critical to determining an appropriate dosing strategy. Finally, integration with complementary therapeutic approaches may be considered to address other facets of dry AMD pathogenesis. While the path to clinical application is fraught with challenges, the potential benefit of preserving RPE phagocytic function—and by extension, photoreceptor survival—in a disease with very limited current treatment options provides a strong impetus for further development of this candidate (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022).

In conclusion, adalimumab’s established molecular profile as a potent TNFα inhibitor, its extensive clinical track record in systemic and ocular inflammatory diseases, and the emerging data linking TNFα to RPE dysfunction collectively support the rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD. Nevertheless, given the complexity of AMD pathogenesis and the potential risks associated with chronic intraocular immunomodulation, a thorough and methodical approach to preclinical investigation is warranted before embarking on large-scale clinical trials. The ultimate goal is to validate that neutralization of TNFα can indeed preserve the phagocytic capabilities of the RPE, thereby maintaining retinal health and preventing the progression of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Strengths of this candidate include its potent and specific inhibition of TNFα, which is a key mediator in inflammatory cascades, its favorable immunogenicity profile stemming from its fully human composition, and its prior demonstration of safety in ocular applications such as uveitis. In addition, the biological rationale is supported by evidence that TNFα negatively impacts the expression of proteins critical for RPE phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation—a process that, when impaired, underlies the pathology of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

On the other hand, weaknesses center on the limited direct evidence for efficacy in dry AMD, potential challenges in achieving precise intraocular dosing without inducing retinal toxicity, and uncertain long-term consequences of sustained TNFα inhibition in the delicate immune environment of the eye. Moreover, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD suggests that a singular focus on TNFα may not fully address the disease’s complex pathophysiology, raising the possibility that combination therapies might eventually be necessary for optimal outcomes (Manzano et al., 2008; Sharma et al., 2009; Nussenblatt et al., 2010).

Given these observations, our evaluation concludes that adalimumab represents a promising and scientifically sound candidate for repurposing to treat dry AMD. Its mechanistic profile aligns well with the goal of preserving RPE phagocytic function by preventing TNFα-mediated downregulation of key proteins like MERTK and cathepsin D. However, to move forward with this candidate, research efforts must focus on resolving the outstanding questions through rigorous preclinical studies, optimization of the drug delivery method, and detailed long-term safety assessments. If successful, these steps could pave the way for early-phase clinical trials designed to test the efficacy of intravitreal adalimumab in stabilizing or improving RPE function in patients with dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010).

In summary, while the current body of literature on adalimumab has primarily focused on its role in systemic inflammatory diseases and ocular inflammatory conditions such as uveitis and neovascular AMD, the underlying mechanistic data provide a persuasive rationale for extending its application to dry AMD. The hypothesis that adalimumab can preserve RPE phagocytic function by neutralizing TNFα—thereby preventing the deleterious downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D—is scientifically plausible and merits further systematic investigation. The potential benefits of repurposing a well-characterized agent with an established safety profile are substantial, especially in a disease area where effective treatments remain elusive (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Overall, our recommendation for the drug development team is to prioritize a series of detailed preclinical studies that examine the effects of adalimumab on RPE cells under TNFα-induced stress conditions, with particular emphasis on the regulation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression and subsequent phagocytic activity. These studies should involve both conventional cell culture models and in vivo models that mimic the chronic inflammatory environment observed in dry AMD. Should these studies yield positive results, a phase I/II clinical trial focusing on safety and early efficacy in patients with dry AMD would be justified. This stepwise approach will ensure that the promising mechanistic rationale is thoroughly vetted before large-scale clinical application (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

In conclusion, the convergence of molecular, biochemical, and clinical evidence supports the further exploration of adalimumab as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to mitigate TNFα-mediated inflammatory cascades could play a critical role in preserving RPE function, maintaining photoreceptor health, and ultimately slowing the progression of a disease that currently lacks effective treatments. Nonetheless, rigorous preclinical validation and careful consideration of dosing and long-term safety will be essential to realize its potential in this new indication (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Homotaurine is a small-molecule GABA analogue that was originally investigated for its potential neuroprotective properties in Alzheimer’s disease due to its ability to interact with inhibitory neurotransmitter receptors. Although originally isolated from marine algae as a natural sulfonated amino acid derivative, the synthetic production of homotaurine has allowed for its repurposing and pharmacological refinement for various clinical indications. As a member of the GABAergic modulator class, it is designed to mimic the activity of the endogenous neurotransmitter γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), thereby affecting neuronal excitability and cellular homeostasis. In particular, homotaurine is postulated to activate GABAA receptors, which are ligand-gated chloride channels that normally contribute to membrane hyperpolarization and dampening of excitatory input. This class of compounds has been widely explored for neuroprotective purposes and has been utilized in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease, where an acceptable safety profile was established. The fact that homotaurine has progressed to advanced clinical stages in Alzheimer’s research supports its tolerability and widespread bioactivity, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in ocular diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Carullo et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, homotaurine has been primarily evaluated in the context of Alzheimer’s disease, where its anti-aggregation properties and potential to interfere with amyloid-β deposition were of paramount interest. Its prior clinical examination, which concluded with a favorable safety record, provides a solid foundation for its repurposing in other neurodegenerative conditions. Although there is no direct record of homotaurine being used to treat dry AMD, other compounds that modulate GABAergic signaling have been investigated in retinal degenerative models. For example, several studies have documented the expression of GABA receptor subunits, including those of the GABAA family, in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, suggesting that pharmacological targeting of these receptors may have therapeutic implications in diseases associated with retinal dysfunction (Arellano et al., 2025). Furthermore, inhibitory neurotransmitters such as GABA have been implicated in maintaining proper cellular excitability and synaptic balance in the retina; alterations in their regulation are associated with excitotoxicity and neurodegeneration in retinal conditions including macular degeneration (Pavan & Dalpiaz, 2018; Schur et al., 2018). In a similar vein, preclinical studies have used GABA modulators to rescue or protect RPE and photoreceptor function in models of retinal degeneration and light-induced injury (Schur et al., 2018). Thus, while direct clinical evidence for homotaurine in dry AMD is lacking, its antecedents in the GABAergic drug class and the known vulnerability of RPE cells to excitotoxic calcium overload position it as a promising candidate for therapeutic repurposing.

Mechanism of Action:  
The hypothesized mechanism of action of homotaurine in dry AMD rests on its ability to activate GABAA receptors expressed on RPE cells. Under physiological conditions, GABAA receptors are heteropentameric chloride channels that, upon binding GABA, permit chloride influx and hyperpolarize the cell membrane. This hyperpolarization ordinarily serves to counteract excessive excitation and limit voltage-gated calcium channel opening. In the context of RPE function, maintaining a tight regulation of intracellular calcium is paramount because calcium levels directly influence cytoskeletal reorganization, phagosome trafficking, and lysosomal fusion events necessary for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Nagymihaly et al., 2021). Several studies have documented that RPE cells not only express GABAA receptor subunits, such as GABAAα1, but that receptor activation in these cells can modify intracellular calcium concentrations, thereby modulating a host of calcium-dependent cellular processes—including phagocytosis (Arellano et al., 2025).

In dry AMD, the RPE’s phagocytic capacity is compromised, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and other toxic by-products, which in turn further disrupt cellular function and promote oxidative stress (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018). Homotaurine’s binding to GABAA receptors is expected to stabilize the membrane potential and reduce the abnormal Ca²⁺ influx that occurs during excitotoxic stress. This reduction in calcium entry is anticipated to alleviate downstream effects such as dysregulated cytoskeletal dynamics and impaired lysosomal trafficking. Cytoskeletal reorganization is essential for phagosome motility; proper F-actin dynamics direct the trafficking of phagosomes toward lysosomal compartments where degradation occurs (Inana et al., 2018; Nagymihaly et al., 2021). Moreover, studies have demonstrated that inflammatory mediators present in AMD, including TNF-α and interleukin-1β, modulate GABAA receptor expression and function, suggesting that modulation of these receptors could be a viable strategy to counteract inflammation-driven excitotoxicity (Arellano et al., 2025). In addition, the excitotoxic environment generated by imbalanced glutamate/GABA signaling in the retina can be mitigated by restoring the inhibitory tone through GABAA receptor activation. The specific EC₅₀ of approximately 10 µM for homotaurine indicates that it has the potential to achieve receptor activation within a therapeutic window that is plausible in an ocular formulation (Carullo et al., 2020; Arellano et al., 2025). Taken together, the combined modulation of calcium influx, along with the stabilization of cytoskeletal and lysosomal pathways, constitutes a comprehensive molecular strategy that homotaurine may employ to rescue impaired POS degradation in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed assay in ARPE-19 cells—a well-established in vitro model for RPE function—aims to evaluate whether homotaurine, via activation of GABAA receptors, can restore impaired photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis under conditions of glutamate-induced stress. RPE cell dysfunction in dry AMD is characterized by diminished phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation of POS, leading to the pathological accumulation of lipofuscin, which further impedes cellular function (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018). By engaging GABAA receptors, homotaurine is expected to “rescue” this vital phagocytic process by normalizing intracellular Ca²⁺ dynamics—thus preventing excitotoxicity—and by ensuring the proper reorganization of actin filaments or other cytoskeletal elements that are essential for efficient phagosome motility (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).

Experimental evidence in related studies supports that compounds with similar mechanisms (i.e., GABA modulators and taurine-related molecules) are capable of influencing intracellular calcium signaling and can enhance the uptake and processing of POS in RPE cells (Arellano et al., 2025; López-Colomé et al., 1994). Under normo-physiological conditions, RPE cells efficiently internalize shed POS through receptor-mediated pathways involving CD36, MerTK, and αVβ5 integrin, initiating a cascade that is dependent on well-regulated intracellular Ca²⁺ fluctuations (Nagymihaly et al., 2021). In a stress state, glutamate excess drives excitotoxic Ca²⁺ entry that may dysregulate these processes. By antagonizing this excitotoxic cascade, homotaurine is anticipated to reduce the aberrant Ca²⁺ load, thereby restoring the dynamic equilibrium that supports both cytoskeletal integrity and lysosomal trafficking. This mechanism is supported by studies showing that dysregulation of Ca²⁺ not only impairs phagosome motility but also has deleterious effects on downstream lysosomal fusion and degradation, ultimately impacting cellular clearance mechanisms (Si et al., 2023; Nowak et al., 2025). Thus, the expected effect is a measurable enhancement in POS uptake as well as improved degradation kinetics in RPE cells subjected to glutamate-induced stress, which would correlate with potential therapeutic efficacy in dry AMD. Furthermore, since the underlying pathology of dry AMD involves chronic oxidative stress and accumulation of metabolic by-products, a pharmacological intervention that can restore intracellular homeostasis has far-reaching implications for halting or even reversing disease progression (Arellano et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating homotaurine for dry age-related macular degeneration, several critical observations emerge. One of the key strengths of homotaurine is its well-documented safety profile from Alzheimer’s clinical trials, which lowers the translational hurdles when repurposing the compound for ocular administration. The fact that homotaurine is a GABA analogue that activates GABAA receptors—a receptor class that is expressed on RPE cells and critically involved in regulating intracellular Ca²⁺—provides a strong mechanistic rationale for its application in dry AMD (Arellano et al., 2025). By potentially mitigating excitotoxic Ca²⁺ influx, homotaurine could restore normal cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal trafficking, both of which are indispensable for the effective degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).

Among the strengths, the following points are notable:  
1. The candidate’s mechanism directly addresses a central pathology of dry AMD—namely, impaired RPE phagocytosis and lysosomal dysfunction—which leads to toxic lipofuscin accumulation (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018).  
2. Activation of GABAA receptors by homotaurine could normalize Ca²⁺ handling within RPE cells, thereby alleviating the excitotoxic stress that is linked to altered cytoskeletal assembly and defective phagosome trafficking (Arellano et al., 2025; Inana et al., 2018).  
3. The compound’s history in Alzheimer’s trials suggests a favorable safety margin and known pharmacokinetic properties that may be adapted for ocular use, thus enhancing its potential for rapid clinical translation (Carullo et al., 2020).  
4. Preclinical evidence from other studies involving GABA modulators and related compounds shows that interfering with aberrant neurotransmitter signaling in the retina can elicit neuroprotective and phagocytosis-enhancing effects (Schur et al., 2018).

Conversely, some weaknesses and uncertainties remain that necessitate further investigation:  
1. Although the proposed EC₅₀ of approximately 10 µM for homotaurine is within a plausible therapeutic window for GABAA receptor activation, the actual pharmacodynamic response in RPE cells—especially in the diseased microenvironment of dry AMD—remains to be rigorously quantified (Arellano et al., 2025).  
2. The retinal microenvironment in dry AMD is complex, characterized not only by excitotoxic stress but also by chronic oxidative stress, inflammation, and altered expression of multiple receptor types. In such a context, GABAA receptor activation could be affected by altered ionic gradients, potentially leading to reversed or atypical receptor responses as has been documented in other retinal degenerations (Arellano et al., 2025; Telegina et al., 2022).  
3. While indirect evidence supports the role of GABAergic modulation in restoring phagocytic function, there is a paucity of direct data demonstrating that homotaurine can specifically enhance POS uptake in ARPE-19 cells under injurious conditions. This gap necessitates additional in vitro studies to detail its effects on cytoskeletal reorganization, vesicular trafficking, and lysosomal fusion dynamics (Si et al., 2023; Nagymihaly et al., 2021).  
4. The exact downstream signaling pathways that link GABAA receptor activation to the observed improvements in phagocytic function must be delineated further. For example, the interplay between calcium channel deactivation, actin cytoskeleton stabilization, and the regulation of key phagocytic receptors (e.g., MerTK, αvβ5 integrin) remains incompletely characterized in the context of GABAergic modulation (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).  
5. Finally, the translational leap from in vitro findings in ARPE-19 cells to a robust therapeutic effect in human dry AMD patients is non-trivial. Aging RPE cells in vivo exhibit additional layers of complexity, including altered gene expression profiles, metabolic imbalances, and possible shifts in receptor isoforms, all of which might influence the responsiveness to homotaurine (Nowak et al., 2025; Si et al., 2023).

Overall, homotaurine represents a scientifically sound and mechanistically plausible candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its potential to activate GABAA receptors on RPE cells, thereby reducing excitotoxic calcium influx and normalizing the intracellular processes that govern cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal trafficking, aligns well with the pathophysiological underpinnings of AMD (Arellano et al., 2025). Given the favorable safety data from Alzheimer’s trials and the breadth of preclinical evidence supporting the neuroprotective effects of GABAergic modulation in retinal contexts, homotaurine merits further exploration. Prior to clinical application, however, detailed mechanistic studies using ARPE-19 cells and appropriate animal models of dry AMD must be conducted. These studies should focus on quantifying calcium flux, cytoskeletal dynamics, phagosome motility, and lysosomal fusion efficiency upon homotaurine treatment under pathologically relevant conditions. Additionally, it will be important to investigate potential off-target effects and to determine whether combinatorial therapies that address oxidative stress and inflammation might synergize with homotaurine’s mechanism. In summary, while challenges remain, the repurposing of homotaurine for dry AMD offers a promising therapeutic avenue worthy of investment and further preclinical validation (Arellano et al., 2025; Si et al., 2023; Carullo et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Axitinib is a synthetic, indazole-based, small-molecule receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor originally discovered via medicinal chemistry optimization for anti-angiogenic oncology indications and subsequently approved as an oral therapy (Inlyta) for advanced renal cell carcinoma, reflecting high potency and selectivity for vascular endothelial growth factor receptors (VEGFR1–3) with additional activity against PDGFR-β and c-KIT (Fei et al., 2024; Tosi et al., 2017). In biochemical and cellular assays relevant to ocular angiogenesis, axitinib demonstrates pan-VEGFR inhibition with substantially greater sensitivity than anti-VEGF monoclonal antibodies in endothelial cells, and it also inhibits PDGFR-β–mediated signaling in pericytes at low nanomolar concentrations, consistent with dual-pathway blockade within the VEGF/PDGF axis (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Pharmacologically, oral axitinib exhibits a short plasma half-life (~2.5–6.1 h) requiring twice-daily systemic dosing in oncology, and class-typical adverse events are dominated by hypertension; these PK/AE features motivated ocular delivery strategies to achieve high intraocular exposure with minimal systemic spillover (Siedlecki et al., 2017). As a class, multi-targeted VEGFR/PDGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have long been deployed systemically for cancer and are being repurposed for ocular neovascular diseases with the goals of broader VEGF-pathway suppression and reduced injection burden via sustained intraocular delivery platforms (suprachoroidal suspensions, intravitreal depot implants, and bioresorbable hydrogel systems) (Fabre et al., 2022; Fei et al., 2024). Axitinib is notable among TKIs for very high VEGFR affinity and measurable inhibition of other angiogenesis-related kinases, including TIE2, which has implications for both efficacy breadth and potential effects on vascular stability in the retina and choroid (Leitch et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical ocular data consistently show axitinib suppresses choroidal and retinal neovascularization across models, with oral dosing at 5 mg/kg reducing laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (L-CNV) in mice, and continuous low-dose systemic infusion (0.875 mg/day for 7 days) decreasing fluorescein leakage and CNV lesion area in rats; in vitro, axitinib suppresses 3D sprouting and inhibits both endothelial and pericyte proliferation/migration at non-toxic concentrations, aligning with dual VEGFR/PDGFR blockade (Fei et al., 2024; Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In a rat L-CNV model, axitinib reduced FA leakage scores and CNV lesion area by approximately one-third versus vehicle, and in co-culture sprouting assays axitinib alone outperformed anti-VEGF and anti-PDGF combinations, reinforcing the mechanistic rationale for dual-pathway inhibition in pathological ocular angiogenesis (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Combinatorial approaches show synergy: co-administration with anti-VEGF antibodies enhanced anti-angiogenic effects in nonclinical studies, consistent with the broader concept that inhibiting pericyte/PDGFR-β support can potentiate VEGF-directed therapy (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Siedlecki et al., 2017).

Multiple ocular delivery strategies for axitinib have entered human investigation in neovascular AMD (nAMD) to address the treatment burden and durability limitations of intravitreal biologics, including a suprachoroidal injectable suspension (CLS-AX) and an intravitreal bioresorbable hydrogel implant (OTX-TKI) designed for 6–9 months of sustained release (Fei et al., 2024). Early clinical and translational signals indicate that suprachoroidal delivery achieves high posterior segment exposure with minimal systemic levels, and initial phase 1/2a experience with CLS-AX in nAMD reported acceptable tolerability and pharmacologic activity at low doses, while OTX-TKI demonstrated favorable safety and durability in early cohorts (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020). Across the TKI class, parallel depot strategies (e.g., vorolanib in Durasert, sunitinib depots) have shown biologic activity and reduced treatment burden in nAMD, although some programs reported visual acuity tradeoffs or required rescue therapy at non-negligible rates, highlighting the need for careful dose, exposure, and target-selectivity optimization (Fei et al., 2024; Leitch et al., 2024).

Topical/eye-drop TKI programs (pazopanib, regorafenib, PAN-90806, acrizanib) underscore translational challenges: although preclinical topical dosing can reduce leakage and CNV thickness, multiple phase II programs failed to meet efficacy endpoints or were terminated due to insufficient posterior segment exposure and ocular safety issues such as reversible corneal haze with acrizanib, indicating that noninvasive delivery often cannot reproducibly attain therapeutic concentrations at the choroid/RPE in humans (Fei et al., 2024). Importantly, the available literature contains no reports of axitinib being tested clinically for dry AMD (geographic atrophy) or for enhancing RPE phagocytosis; the development history for axitinib and related VEGFR/PDGFR TKIs is focused on nAMD and other retinal vascular diseases, and reviews repeatedly note a lack of evidence for dry-AMD applications in this drug class to date (Fei et al., 2024). Furthermore, while localized ocular delivery is being pursued to mitigate systemic exposure, case reports of retinal adverse events during systemic axitinib therapy—including impaired retinal circulation, reversible retinal toxicity, and central retinal vein occlusion—require vigilance and thoughtful PK/PD design in ocular programs (Bakri et al., 2024). More broadly, despite active investigation of small molecules for AMD, reviews emphasize that no clinical success stories for small-molecule drugs in AMD (outside recently approved complement inhibitors for GA) have been established, underscoring translational risk for new mechanisms and reformulations (Fei et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Axitinib is a potent ATP-competitive inhibitor of VEGFR1 (FLT1), VEGFR2 (KDR), and VEGFR3 (FLT4), with additional inhibitory activity against PDGFR-β and c-KIT, thereby interrupting intracellular tyrosine kinase signaling downstream of multiple pro-angiogenic ligands, including VEGF-A/B/C/D and PDGF-B (Tosi et al., 2017; Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In relevant ocular cell types, axitinib inhibits VEGF-driven endothelial proliferation with markedly greater potency than anti-VEGF antibodies and exerts nanomolar inhibition of PDGF-driven pericyte proliferation, supporting the mechanistic premise that simultaneous disruption of endothelial and pericyte signaling can destabilize nascent pathological vessels and reduce neovascular growth (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In 3D co-culture sprouting models that recapitulate endothelial–pericyte interactions, axitinib alone achieves robust inhibition of sprout number and length across low-nanomolar concentrations, matching or exceeding the effect of anti-VEGF plus anti-PDGF combinations, a pattern consistent with multi-receptor inhibition at the level of VEGFR/PDGFR RTKs (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Preclinical studies in retinal endothelial cells further demonstrate axitinib suppression of downstream MAPK/ERK signaling and oxidative stress markers, aligning with direct VEGFR pathway inhibition; limited in vitro reports also suggest reduction of VEGFR1/VEGFR2 and PDGFR-β phosphorylation in RPE or mixed cell models, though these do not extend to functional phagocytosis endpoints (Lazzara et al., 2024).

Mechanistically, axitinib’s kinase profile extends beyond VEGFR/PDGFR to other angiogenesis-modulating targets; notably, among three pan-VEGFR TKIs profiled preclinically (vorolanib, sunitinib, axitinib), only axitinib exhibited strong TIE2 inhibition, a pathway essential for vascular quiescence and stability that could influence choroidal and retinal vascular homeostasis under chronic intraocular exposure (Bakri et al., 2024). In comparative kinase panels and endothelial functional assays, all three TKIs displayed robust pan-VEGFR inhibition and abolished endothelial sprouting at high concentrations, but the TIE2-inhibitory signal was disproportionately strong for axitinib, suggesting type-specific off-target consequences that warrant consideration during dose selection for chronic ocular use (Bakri et al., 2024). While intravitreal biologics neutralize extracellular VEGF ligands, axitinib acts intracellularly to block receptor signaling, potentially addressing compensatory upregulation of VEGF-C/D observed with VEGF-A-only inhibition; however, the breadth of intracellular TKI targeting can also propagate off-target effects in non-endothelial cells if exposures are not carefully controlled (Leitch et al., 2024).

Delivery-route pharmacology is central to ocular mechanism realization: suprachoroidal injection of axitinib has demonstrated posterior-segment targeting with markedly elevated drug levels in the posterior eye cup versus intravitreal injection in rabbits and sustained RPE/choroid exposure with minimal systemic levels, thereby achieving compartmentalized receptor inhibition where angiogenic lesions and the RPE reside (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020). Complementary intravitreal hydrogel implant strategies (OTX-TKI) provide long-acting axitinib delivery (6–9 months), maintaining pharmacologically relevant intraocular concentrations to chronically suppress VEGFR/PDGFR signaling in nAMD; these platforms are designed to mitigate systemic adverse events while sustaining on-target ocular pharmacodynamics (Fei et al., 2024). Importantly, chronic VEGF pathway suppression carries theoretical risks for neurosensory retina and RPE health, and reviews emphasize the need to balance durable angiogenic control with potential adverse effects of continuous VEGF blockade in ocular tissues, particularly for non-neovascular indications (Wolf et al., 2022).

Therapeutic targets in the RPE relevant to the present hypothesis—MerTK and αvβ5 integrin—are core components of the photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytic machinery, with αvβ5 required for synchronized diurnal phagocytosis and MerTK essential for engulfment and internalization; however, the provided literature contains no direct experimental evidence that axitinib upregulates MerTK or αvβ5 expression or function in RPE, nor that PDGFR-β signaling tonically suppresses RPE phagocytic differentiation in vivo (Tosi et al., 2017). Reviews and experimental summaries repeatedly state that available axitinib data focus on endothelial/pericyte targets and CNV models, and that no studies directly link axitinib to enhanced RPE POS uptake, MerTK activation, or αvβ5 integrin upregulation in dry AMD models or RPE cell assays (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). Therefore, while axitinib’s biochemical capacity to inhibit PDGFR-β could, in principle, modulate RPE phenotypes if PDGFR-β were a suppressive node in RPE phagocytic signaling, this mechanistic leap is not supported by direct evidence in the provided literature (Bakri et al., 2024; Fei et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The proposed assay hypothesis is that low-dose axitinib will modulate PDGFR-β signaling in RPE to promote a pro-phagocytic differentiation state, enhancing MerTK and αvβ5 expression and POS uptake; however, the body of evidence provided does not include direct demonstrations of axitinib increasing RPE phagocytosis, MerTK activation, or αvβ5 expression in vitro, ex vivo, or in vivo (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). If the assay system relies on differentiating human RPE and measures POS uptake alongside MerTK and αvβ5 expression, axitinib’s expected on-target effects would be limited to PDGFR-β kinase inhibition in RPE if PDGFR-β is expressed and active under the assay conditions; nevertheless, there is no provided evidence that such inhibition increases MerTK or αvβ5 levels or POS ingestion, and the hypothesis that PDGFR-β tone suppresses RPE phagocytosis remains unsubstantiated here (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). Translational pharmacology considerations highlight both opportunity and risk: suprachoroidal axitinib enriches drug at the choroid/RPE with minimal systemic exposure, offering a delivery solution for RPE-targeted modulation if the mechanism were validated; at the same time, axitinib’s TIE2 inhibition and class-level concerns about chronic VEGF pathway suppression in the neurosensory retina argue for caution in non-neovascular indications such as dry AMD (Kaiser et al., 2020; Bakri et al., 2024). Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
- Pharmacologic potency and dual-pathway coverage: Axitinib’s high-affinity pan-VEGFR inhibition with demonstrated PDGFR-β activity enables simultaneous suppression of endothelial and pericyte signaling, a combination that underpins robust anti-angiogenic efficacy in CNV models and may reduce fibrosis-linked extracellular matrix deposition in neovascular settings (Giddabasappa et al., 2016).  
- Validated ocular delivery options: Suprachoroidal suspension (CLS-AX) and intravitreal hydrogel implant (OTX-TKI) platforms have progressed into clinical testing for nAMD with encouraging ocular safety/PK signals, providing translationally relevant routes to expose the RPE/choroid compartment while minimizing systemic exposure (Wolf et al., 2022; Fei et al., 2024).  
- Clinical-stage experience in nAMD: Early-phase trials indicate biological activity and tolerability of axitinib-based intraocular approaches, suggesting a viable path to long-acting ocular therapy development if a new indication such as RPE phagocytosis enhancement is supported by mechanistic data (Leitch et al., 2024).  
- Class learnings and comparator programs: The broader TKI field in nAMD (vorolanib, sunitinib derivatives) offers benchmarks for durability, rescue-free rates, and safety considerations, facilitating rational dose and exposure setting for axitinib formulations (Fei et al., 2024; Leitch et al., 2024).  

Limitations and Critical Gaps  
- No direct evidence for RPE phagocytosis enhancement: Across the provided literature, there are no RPE-specific data showing axitinib increases MerTK or αvβ5 expression, augments POS binding or internalization, or improves phagocytic capacity in differentiating RPE; multiple summaries explicitly state the absence of such evidence and confine axitinib’s demonstrated actions to anti-angiogenic endpoints (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017).  
- Unvalidated mechanistic premise in RPE: While PDGFR-β is central to pericyte biology and vessel stabilization, the assertion that PDGFR-β overactivation hinders RPE differentiation and that its inhibition promotes a pro-phagocytic state is not supported in the provided texts, and the core RPE phagocytic machinery (MerTK, αvβ5) is not linked here to PDGFR-β modulation by TKIs (Tosi et al., 2017; Bakri et al., 2024).  
- Safety liabilities and target selectivity: Axitinib’s strong TIE2 inhibition could perturb vascular stability with chronic intraocular exposure, and class-level concerns exist for continuous VEGF pathway suppression affecting neurosensory retina and RPE; rare but notable retinal vascular AEs reported with systemic axitinib further mandate conservative exposure design and careful safety pharmacology tailored to non-neovascular indications (Bakri et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022).  
- Delivery constraints for non-neovascular endpoints: Topical TKI programs frequently failed due to inadequate posterior segment exposure and/or ocular surface safety findings, suggesting that any RPE-targeted application of axitinib would require invasive delivery (suprachoroidal/IVT depot) with chronic exposure, elevating the bar for safety and benefit-risk justification in a dry AMD population (Fei et al., 2024).  
- Field precedent: Reviews underscore that, to date, small-molecule success in AMD has been limited, and there are no approved ocular TKIs for either wet or dry AMD, reinforcing translational uncertainty for new mechanism-of-use proposals lacking direct preclinical support (Fei et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).  

Development Recommendations and Go/No-Go Criteria  
- Mechanistic validation in RPE: Before proceeding, perform a staged in vitro program in human iPSC-RPE and primary RPE to test whether axitinib modulates PDGFR-β phosphorylation and secondarily increases MerTK expression, MerTK phosphorylation upon POS challenge, αvβ5 expression/localization, and POS binding/internalization; include dose-response spanning sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar exposures aligned with ocular PK projections from suprachoroidal or depot IVT delivery (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020).  
- Specificity controls and orthogonal readouts: Use chemical and genetic controls to isolate PDGFR-β dependence (e.g., PDGFR-β ligand titrations, selective PDGFR-β inhibitors distinct from axitinib, and PDGFR-β knockdown), and include neutralizing antibodies and MerTK/αvβ5 functional blocking to map pathway causality for any observed phagocytosis changes (Tosi et al., 2017; Siedlecki et al., 2017).  
- Safety pharmacology in pigmented models: Given potential TIE2-related and VEGF-suppression liabilities, include long-term RPE morphology, barrier function (TEER), transcriptomic stress signatures, and photoreceptor/RPE co-culture viability endpoints at projected clinical exposures; extend to pigmented rabbit or NHP pharmacology to define posterior-segment exposure, ocular distribution (RPE/sclera/choroid), and a NOAEL for chronic dosing (Bakri et al., 2024; Kaiser et al., 2020).  
- Translational gating: Advance only if axitinib reproducibly increases POS uptake and MerTK/αvβ5 functional markers in RPE with a therapeutic window that avoids endothelial destabilization signals and preserves neuronal/RPE integrity in chronic exposure models; otherwise, deprioritize axitinib for RPE-targeted dry AMD and refocus efforts on mechanisms directly validated to enhance RPE phagocytosis or survival (Fei et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022).  

Conclusion  
On the strength of available evidence, axitinib is a validated, potent anti-angiogenic TKI with multiple ocular delivery platforms in clinical development for nAMD and robust preclinical efficacy in CNV models; however, the central hypothesis that low-dose axitinib enhances RPE phagocytosis via PDGFR-β modulation and upregulates MerTK/αvβ5 lacks direct support in the provided literature, and multiple sources explicitly state that no such RPE-centric data exist for axitinib at present (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Fei et al., 2024). The translational and safety profiles suggest that invasive ocular delivery could achieve RPE-adjacent exposure, but off-target TIE2 inhibition and class-level VEGF-suppression risks must be weighed carefully in a non-neovascular indication, particularly absent clear preclinical efficacy on RPE phagocytic endpoints (Bakri et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022). Accordingly, while axitinib remains attractive for anti-angiogenic applications, it should not be advanced for dry AMD on a phagocytosis-enhancement rationale without first producing compelling, direct RPE mechanistic data; in the absence of such data, development resources would be better allocated to candidates with demonstrated effects on MerTK/αvβ5 function or on complement-mediated RPE pathology more proximal to dry AMD pathophysiology (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Fei et al., 2024). Pending rigorous in vitro and ex vivo validation as outlined, the current evidence base supports a cautious “mechanism validation required” stance rather than progression to in vivo dry AMD studies or clinical translation for this proposed use (Fei et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).
