Below is a detailed evaluation of the candidate, AGI-1067, for potential repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AGI-1067 is a synthetic, small‐molecule derivative developed as an analog of probucol—a well‐known phenolic antioxidant originally discovered for its lipid‐lowering and antiatherosclerotic properties. Chemically, AGI-1067 is the monosuccinic acid ester of probucol. In its synthesis, the parent molecule probucol is modified using a reaction with succinic anhydride under basic conditions (typically in a solvent such as tetrahydrofuran with sodium hydride) to yield the monosubstituted ester derivative (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007). This chemical alteration is key: by substituting one of the two phenolic hydroxyl groups with a succinate moiety, the molecule retains one essential antioxidant phenol while significantly enhancing its water solubility, cell permeability, and overall pharmacokinetic properties. Such modifications have been shown to mitigate the drawbacks of the parent compound—namely, its poor bioavailability, cardiotoxicity via QT interval prolongation, and unwanted HDL cholesterol lowering—while keeping the desirable antioxidant and lipid-modulating activities intact (Meng et al., 2002).

AGI-1067 belongs to the class of phenolic antioxidants, a group of compounds known for their ability to scavenge free radicals and interrupt the chain reactions that govern lipid peroxidation. Historically, phenolic antioxidants—including probucol itself—have been employed to counteract oxidative stress in cardiovascular disease, largely based on their capacity to protect low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles from oxidative modification. More recently, AGI-1067 has been classified under the emerging category of “vascular protectants” as it additionally exhibits anti-inflammatory actions, such as the inhibition of VCAM-1 and MCP-1, which are central to inflammatory signaling within vascular tissues (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007; Stix, 2003). The chemical design of AGI-1067 was informed by detailed structure-activity relationship studies—demonstrating that modification of the probucol scaffold can yield a compound with enhanced therapeutic indices—that is, with potency comparable to probucol in antioxidant assays, yet with a safer profile in vivo (Tardif, 2005; Meng et al., 2002).

The origins of AGI-1067 are rooted in medicinal chemistry strategies aimed at overcoming the known liabilities of probucol through targeted chemical modifications. In doing so, not only is the inherent bioactivity maintained, but delivery characteristics are improved substantially. AGI-1067 has been advanced through preclinical development and early-phase clinical trials in cardiovascular diseases, suggesting that the molecule has been thoroughly vetted for systemic safety and efficacy (Serebruany et al., 2007; Sundell et al., 2003). As a compound with robust antioxidant and anti-inflammatory capabilities, AGI-1067 is now being considered for applications beyond its original indication, with dry AMD emerging as a plausible target given the shared mechanisms of oxidative and inflammatory stress in both vascular and retinal degenerative diseases (Tardif et al., 2003a; Tardif, 2005).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic lineage of AGI-1067 is intrinsically linked to that of probucol, a lipid‐soluble phenolic antioxidant first discovered in the 1960s. Probucol was initially explored and later used primarily for its cholesterol-lowering effects and its ability to protect LDL particles against oxidation. Its clinical use, however, was compromised by significant side effects, including marked reductions in HDL cholesterol and adverse cardiac electrophysiological effects (notably QT interval prolongation). Recognizing these clinical limitations, researchers embarked on a drug development program to modify the structure of probucol, thereby retaining its beneficial antioxidant properties while eliminating or reducing its untoward effects. AGI-1067 emerged from this program as a promising candidate due to its modified structure—specifically, the introduction of a succinic acid ester group—that confers improved pharmacokinetic and safety profiles (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007).

In a series of preclinical studies, AGI-1067 demonstrated equipotent antioxidant effects compared to probucol, as measured by its ability to inhibit copper-induced oxidation of linoleic acid and to scavenge free radicals. More importantly, however, AGI-1067 showed enhanced anti-inflammatory properties in vitro: it potently inhibited TNF-α–inducible expression of VCAM-1 in endothelial cells with an IC₅₀ around 6 µM—a dramatic improvement relative to probucol, which shows minimal activity at concentrations greater than 50 µM (Meng et al., 2002). These encouraging preclinical findings spurred the progression of AGI-1067 into Phase II clinical studies for the treatment of cardiovascular diseases such as atherosclerosis, where its efficacy was not solely limited to antioxidant protection but extended to lipid modulation and inhibition of inflammatory gene expression (Serebruany et al., 2007; Sundell et al., 2003; Tardif, 2005).

Despite these developments, no prior studies have directly applied AGI-1067 to ocular diseases such as dry AMD. However, the key pathophysiological processes—in particular, chronic oxidative stress and inflammation—are central to both atherosclerosis and dry AMD. In dry AMD, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is subjected to chronic oxidative damage from light exposure, metabolic activity, and the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin byproducts like A2E. The success of AGI-1067 in inhibiting oxidative stress and inflammatory responses in vascular tissues thus provides a compelling rationale for investigating its utility in the RPE, where similar stressors contribute to cellular dysfunction and the consequent impairment of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007; Siu, 2010).

Further supporting its therapeutic repurposing is the fact that AGI-1067, as an orally bioavailable agent with a well-established safety record in Phase II clinical trials, offers a distinct advantage over many novel drug candidates that often struggle with systemic toxicity or poor pharmacokinetics. The clinical history of AGI-1067 in cardiovascular trials demonstrates that its metabolic stability allows it to reach therapeutic plasma concentrations rapidly (in less than two weeks), a feature that might be beneficial when considering dosing strategies for chronic conditions like dry AMD (Tardif, 2005; Serebruany et al., 2007). Although the translation from cardiovascular disease to retinal degeneration represents a significant leap, the underlying mechanistic overlap—centered on oxidative and inflammatory damage—positions AGI-1067 as an attractive candidate for further exploration in ocular applications (Tardif et al., 2003a).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, AGI-1067 acts through a multitiered mechanism that combines robust antioxidant activity with selective anti-inflammatory signaling modulation. The phenolic structure, inherited from probucol, facilitates free radical scavenging by donating hydrogen atoms to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS). This chain-breaking antioxidant mechanism interferes directly with lipid peroxidation, a process known to damage cellular membranes and macromolecules. Importantly, the conservation of one phenolic group is critical; it provides the necessary redox chemistry without overwhelming the system with potentially toxic metabolites. The strategic conversion of the second phenolic group into a succinic acid ester not only reduces lipophilicity—thus enhancing aqueous solubility—but also increases cellular uptake, as this modification improves passage across cell membranes (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007).

In vascular and inflammatory cell models, AGI-1067 has demonstrated an ability to suppress the expression of key inflammatory proteins. One of its most notable effects is the inhibition of vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1) expression upon stimulation by TNF-α. VCAM-1 is a critical mediator of leukocyte adhesion and transmigration, and its upregulation is a hallmark of inflammatory vascular injury. AGI-1067 achieves this inhibition at low micromolar concentrations (IC₅₀ ≈ 6 µM), far surpassing the potency of probucol, which fails to significantly inhibit VCAM-1 even at concentrations as high as 100 µM (Meng et al., 2002). Similarly, agents in this class inhibit monocyte chemotactic protein-1 (MCP-1) expression, a chemokine that further perpetuates inflammation by recruiting monocytes to sites of tissue damage (Tardif, 2006; Tardif, 2005).

While some studies suggest that AGI-1067 may interfere with NF-κB activation—a central transcription factor that regulates a host of inflammatory genes—the exact interplay remains complex. There is evidence to suggest that the compound’s ability to inhibit the expression of adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1 is at least partially independent of traditional NF-κB nuclear translocation pathways. Nonetheless, the net result is a dampening of the inflammatory cascade that typically follows oxidative stimuli (Tardif, 2006; Sundell et al., 2003). In addition to these anti-inflammatory actions, AGI-1067 exerts mild antiplatelet effects. By modulating the expression and function of platelet surface receptors and decreasing the synthesis of pro-aggregation signals such as thromboxane, the compound helps to reduce platelet activation—a property that, while primarily beneficial for cardiovascular disease, may also contribute to a systemic reduction in inflammatory tone (Muldrew & Franks, 2009; Serebruany et al., 2007).

This comprehensive mode of action—combining free radical scavenging with the selective suppression of inflammation—makes AGI-1067 a prototypical multifunctional antioxidant. In many preclinical models, the compound’s capacity to block redox-sensitive signaling has been linked to decreased vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, reduced inflammatory cell recruitment, and overall protection against tissue injury induced by oxidative stress. These molecular interactions are mediated through its phenolic backbone and are further enhanced by the succinic acid moiety, which allows for a more favorable distribution in aqueous environments and within the intracellular milieu (Meng et al., 2002; Tardif, 2005; Muldrew & Franks, 2009).

In the specific context of cellular metabolism, AGI-1067’s actions have been correlated with a down-regulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, at least in vascular endothelial cells. While such studies have largely been conducted in non-ocular tissues, the ubiquitous nature of these signaling pathways suggests that similar molecular interactions would occur in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, which are known to be highly sensitive to oxidative and inflammatory stress (Siu, 2010; Sundell et al., 2003). Thus, the compound’s multifactorial mechanism positions it not only as an effective scavenger of ROS but also as a modulatory agent that disrupts the cycle of chronic inflammation—a critical pathogenic driver in both atherosclerosis and dry AMD.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
Dry AMD is characterized by a gradual degeneration of the RPE and subsequent photoreceptor dysfunction, largely driven by chronic oxidative stress and low-grade inflammation. In the RPE, the continuous phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) leads to the accumulation of lipofuscin pigments such as A2E, which in turn disrupt lysosomal function by inducing pH changes and impairing the activity of degradative enzymes like cathepsins. Over time, these alterations diminish the cell’s ability to clear damaged POS, exacerbating oxidative damage and activating inflammatory cascades that further compromise retinal integrity.

Based on the known pharmacological profile of AGI-1067, it is hypothesized that the compound will exert a protective effect on RPE cells through several convergent mechanisms. First, by activating antioxidant pathways, AGI-1067 is expected to reduce intracellular ROS levels. Its potent free radical scavenging ability should directly counteract oxidative damage to cellular lipids and proteins, thereby preserving the integrity of the membranes that are essential for normal phagocytic and lysosomal function (Sundell et al., 2003; Meng et al., 2002). In vitro experiments in non-ocular cell models have demonstrated that AGI-1067 can safeguard cells from oxidative insults even at concentrations as low as 2 µM, suggesting that a similar effective concentration might be achieved in RPE cells (Meng et al., 2002; Tardif, 2005).

Second, AGI-1067 is postulated to inhibit NF-κB signaling in RPE cells. NF-κB is a key transcription factor that becomes activated in response to oxidative stress and drives the expression of numerous pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. In the RPE, such activation would lead to an inflammatory milieu that not only damages the cells themselves but also disrupts the regulation of phagocytic receptors necessary for efficient POS uptake. By mitigating NF-κB activation, AGI-1067 may lower the production of cytokines like TNF-α and IL-1β, thus breaking the cycle of inflammation and oxidative stress (Tardif, 2006; Tardif et al., 2008). This anti-inflammatory effect would be critical for preserving lysosomal integrity, as excessive inflammation has been shown to interfere with lysosome acidification and enzyme activity—two processes that are essential for proper POS degradation.

Moreover, the compound’s ability to rescue cathepsin activity is of particular interest. In RPE cells, cathepsins are responsible for the breakdown of POS, and their inactivation (often due to lysosomal pH elevation induced by A2E accumulation) is a hallmark of dry AMD. The hypothesis, supported by recent in vitro data (Si et al. Biomolecules 2023), is that AGI-1067 can prevent A2E-induced increases in lysosomal pH, thereby maintaining cathepsin activity and ensuring the continued clearance of POS. This preservation of lysosomal function is expected to not only slow down the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin pigments but also maintain overall cellular health, reducing the propensity for RPE cell death (Sundell et al., 2003; Tardif, 2005).

In addition to these direct effects on oxidative stress and inflammation, AGI-1067 may also exert beneficial systemic effects that are indirectly relevant to dry AMD. For instance, its lipid-modulating properties could result in a more favorable systemic lipid profile, which has been associated with reduced risk of AMD progression in epidemiological studies. Although the primary focus in dry AMD is on local oxidative and inflammatory processes, a more balanced systemic lipid environment might lessen the burden of inflammatory lipids that can accumulate in the retina (Sundell et al., 2003).

Importantly, RPE cells express a range of receptors and intracellular signaling molecules that are sensitive to both oxidative and inflammatory cues. Studies in vascular endothelial cells have shown that AGI-1067 modulates the expression of adhesion molecules and inflammatory mediators; given the shared signaling pathways between endothelial and RPE cells, similar downstream effects can be expected in the retina (Siu, 2010; Sundell et al., 2003). Therefore, the anticipated effect of AGI-1067 in the context of dry AMD is multifactorial: reduction of ROS levels, normalization of lysosomal pH, preservation of cathepsin activity, and attenuation of inflammatory cytokine production. Together, these actions should promote better POS phagocytosis and degradation, slow RPE degeneration, and ultimately help maintain photoreceptor health.

Overall Evaluation:  
Taking into account the extensive body of preclinical and clinical data available for AGI-1067 in cardiovascular applications, along with its well-characterized multifaceted mechanism of action, the repurposing of AGI-1067 for dry AMD has considerable appeal. One of the strongest points in favor of this candidate is its dual functionality. Unlike conventional antioxidants that merely scavenge free radicals, AGI-1067 has been shown to simultaneously suppress inflammatory signaling—particularly by inhibiting the expression of adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1 and chemokines like MCP-1—in a highly selective manner (Meng et al., 2002). In the context of dry AMD, where chronic inflammation and oxidative stress interlace to drive RPE dysfunction and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration, such dual activity is likely to be highly beneficial. The preservation of lysosomal function and, by extension, the maintenance of effective POS degradation are especially critical endpoints given that impaired phagocytosis is a key pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD (Sundell et al., 2003; Tardif, 2005).

Another compelling aspect of AGI-1067 is its improved pharmacokinetic profile relative to its parent compound. Its enhanced water solubility and cell permeability mean that it achieves steady-state plasma levels more rapidly—a factor that could translate to more predictable and effective dosing regimens in a chronic condition like dry AMD (Serebruany et al., 2007; Stix, 2003). Moreover, the Phase II clinical data supporting its safety in applications for cardiovascular disease, where it was not associated with dangerous QT interval prolongation or significant adverse lipid profile alterations, reduces the translational risk when considering an alternative indication (Sundell et al., 2003; Tardif et al., 2003b).

Nonetheless, there are notable challenges that must be addressed before advancing AGI-1067 as a treatment for dry AMD. First, the bulk of the published work on AGI-1067 has been in vascular contexts; as such, direct evidence for its efficacy in ocular tissues, and specifically in RPE cells, is limited. The cellular environment of the retina is markedly different from that of vascular endothelium, and it will be essential to establish that the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties of AGI-1067 translate effectively within RPE cells. Detailed in vitro studies using RPE cell lines or primary RPE cultures that examine key endpoints—such as ROS production, NF-κB activation, lysosomal pH regulation, and cathepsin activity—are crucial (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007).

Second, the ability of AGI-1067 to penetrate the blood-retinal barrier remains an open question. While its enhanced water solubility is an advantage over probucol, the compound must still be demonstrated to reach therapeutic concentrations in the retina following systemic administration or via alternative routes, such as intravitreal injection. Pharmacokinetic studies in ocular models will be vital to define dosing parameters and ensure that the drug can exert its effects in situ without off-target toxicity (Tardif, 2005; Serebruany et al., 2007).

The signaling pathways leading to NF-κB activation—although similar in many cell types—may have unique regulatory mechanisms in the RPE. As such, targeted studies evaluating the modulation of NF-κB and related inflammatory mediators in RPE cells treated with AGI-1067 will help clarify this aspect of its mechanism in the context of dry AMD (Tardif, 2006; Sundell et al., 2003).

Furthermore, while the systemic safety profile of AGI-1067 is relatively well established, the possibility of ocular-specific adverse effects cannot be dismissed. Retinal tissues have a unique sensitivity to certain pharmacological agents, and what is safe in the cardiovascular system might necessitate additional scrutiny in the context of the eye. Preclinical toxicology studies using relevant animal models of retinal degeneration would be required to assess any potential retinal toxicity, inflammation, or interference with normal RPE function (Serebruany et al., 2007; Tardif et al., 2003a).

In addition, the chronic nature of dry AMD implies that long-term dosing will be essential. AGI-1067’s ability to maintain efficacy over prolonged treatment periods without inducing tolerance or unexpected metabolic alterations will need to be carefully evaluated. Although the compound has demonstrated metabolic stability in cardiovascular trials, this must be validated in the long-term context of an ocular application (Tardif, 2005; Sundell et al., 2003).

In conclusion, AGI-1067 exhibits several properties that are highly attractive for the treatment of dry AMD. Its design as a repurposed probucol analog—with enhanced water solubility, improved cellular uptake, and an integrated antioxidant/anti-inflammatory mechanism—is well aligned with the pathogenic underpinnings of dry AMD, where oxidative stress and chronic inflammation play pivotal roles in RPE dysfunction. The molecular mechanisms by which AGI-1067 acts—inhibiting redox-sensitive signaling pathways, preserving cathepsin activity, and reducing inflammatory mediator expression—offer a sound scientific basis for the hypothesis that it could protect RPE cells and preserve the critical process of POS phagocytosis (Meng et al., 2002; Meng et al., 2002; Siu, 2010).

However, the current body of work on AGI-1067 has focused predominantly on its cardiovascular applications, meaning that substantial additional research is required to evaluate its efficacy in ocular models. Key next steps would include (1) in vitro studies using RPE cell cultures to confirm its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects at the proposed EC₅₀ of approximately 2 µM; (2) assessment of its ability to preserve lysosomal pH and cathepsin activity in the face of A2E exposure; (3) pharmacokinetic studies to ensure effective retinal penetration; and (4) in vivo efficacy and safety studies in animal models of dry AMD.

Overall, the multifaceted biological activities of AGI-1067—ranging from free radical scavenging and inhibition of inflammatory cytokine production to improved lipid handling and platelet inhibition—provide a compelling rationale for its repurposing. Its established clinical safety in Phase II trials for cardiovascular indications further diminishes the risk associated with translational development. Nevertheless, the absence of direct data in the context of the eye and the potential challenges posed by the unique microenvironment of the retina underscore the need for a rigorous preclinical evaluation before progressing to clinical trials in dry AMD patients (Tardif et al., 2003b; Serebruany et al., 2007; Tardif et al., 2008).

In summary, AGI-1067 stands out as a promising candidate for dry AMD therapy based on its robust antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, optimized chemical design, and favorable safety profile. While there are clear challenges associated with adapting a cardiovascular drug for an ocular application—especially regarding retinal drug delivery and ensuring efficacy in RPE cells—the mechanistic rationale and preclinical success in related fields justify further investigation. Given the devastating impact that dry AMD has on quality of life and the limited therapeutic options currently available, repurposing a compound such as AGI-1067 could represent a significant advancement in the management of this complex degenerative disease (Meng et al., 2002; Tardif et al., 2002; Sundell et al., 2003).

On balance, the strengths of AGI-1067—including its multifunctional mode of action, established clinical safety, and enhanced pharmacological properties over its precursor—strongly support its evaluation in the context of dry AMD. Simultaneously, the potential weaknesses related to ocular bioavailability, direct effects on RPE-specific pathways, and the need for comprehensive retinal safety data warrant careful, targeted preclinical investigations. It is recommended that the drug development team pursue further in vitro and in vivo studies in models of retinal degeneration to clarify these points before proceeding to early-phase clinical trials. Such a stepwise approach would ensure that the promising attributes of AGI-1067 are fully leveraged while minimizing the risks associated with repurposing an agent developed for a different therapeutic domain (Serebruany et al., 2007; Tardif, 2005; Tardif et al., 2008).

In conclusion, based on the comprehensive review of the biomedical, clinical, and biochemical literature available through our current sources, AGI-1067 shows considerable potential as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD. Its capacity to reduce oxidative stress, inhibit key inflammatory mediators, and preserve the phagocytic and lysosomal function of RPE cells provides a strong scientific foundation for further exploration. Should subsequent studies confirm its efficacy in ocular models and demonstrate adequate retinal bioavailability and safety, AGI-1067 may ultimately serve as a valuable therapeutic option for patients suffering from dry AMD, a condition in urgent need of novel treatment strategies (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007; Siu, 2010; Serebruany et al., 2007).

Each of these observations is supported by multiple studies in related fields, and while direct evidence in RPE cells remains to be generated, the mechanistic overlap between atherosclerotic and retinal degenerative processes encourages this promising translational pursuit.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB202190 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor belonging to the pyridinyl imidazole class of compounds. Originally discovered through rigorous cell‐based phenotypic screens aimed at identifying agents with anti‐inflammatory properties, SB202190 was developed to selectively inhibit p38 mitogen‐activated protein kinase (MAPK), particularly the α and β isoforms. The molecule was first characterized using radiolabeled ligand binding studies, which confirmed its ability to bind the ATP‐binding pocket of p38 MAPK and suppress its catalytic function (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). Being available commercially (e.g., Sigma‐Aldrich Cat. No. SML0687), SB202190 has been widely used as a biochemical tool to dissect the role of p38 in cellular stress and inflammatory responses. This class of compounds, including SB203580 as a closely related analogue, is recognized for its ability to modulate intracellular signaling cascades under various stress conditions. They have been broadly used in research settings to probe the molecular basis of cytokine production, cell differentiation, apoptosis, and cytoskeletal regulation (Young, 2013; Maugeri et al., 2021). The candidate under discussion is being repurposed with the hypothesis that its high potency against p38α/β—exhibiting an IC₅₀ of approximately 40 nM—can be leveraged to correct stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling defects and improve the phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative stress conditions that mimic the pathophysiology of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Liu et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, SB202190 has been predominantly employed as a research reagent to interrogate the role of p38 MAPK signaling in various cell types and disease models. In the context of ocular studies, SB202190, similar to its analogue SB203580, has been used to examine fibrotic responses, cell migration, and cytokine production in RPE cells. For instance, several in vitro studies have demonstrated that inhibition of p38 MAPK by SB202190 effectively reduces TGF‐β2–induced extracellular matrix (ECM) production (specifically collagen type I and fibronectin synthesis), which serves as an experimental surrogate for fibrotic remodeling observed in retinal degenerative conditions (Saika et al., 2005). Moreover, experiments using ARPE‐19 human RPE cells have revealed that SB202190 can reverse abnormal cell migration and reduce the transformation of RPE cells into fibroblast‐like cells in models of proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) (Saika et al., 2005). Although these models do not directly replicate dry AMD, they capture key aspects of RPE dysfunction, such as cytoskeletal disorganization and aberrant ECM deposition, which are also implicated in the progression of AMD. Beyond ocular research, p38 MAPK inhibitors have been investigated in other pathologies characterized by chronic inflammation and stress‐induced cellular dysfunction, including rheumatoid arthritis and muscular dystrophies (Brennan et al., 2021; Hirosawa et al., 2009). However, to date, clinical applications of SB202190 itself have not been pursued, and its use has remained restricted to preclinical experimental studies, thereby providing both a strong mechanistic rationale and a cautionary note regarding its translational potential (Federspiel et al., 2023; Young, 2013). Importantly, while numerous studies have elucidated p38 MAPK’s involvement in retinal injury and oxidative stress responses, there is limited direct clinical evidence supporting the use of SB202190 for treating dry AMD, and its application in this indication remains strictly hypothetical at this stage (Moustardas et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB202190 is known to selectively target the ATP‐binding pocket of p38 MAPK, thereby inhibiting its enzymatic activity and preventing the phosphorylation of downstream substrates that are pivotal to stress‐induced signaling cascades. Under normal conditions, p38 MAPK becomes activated through dual phosphorylation on specific threonine and tyrosine residues within its activation loop. Once activated, p38 MAPK stimulates various substrates, including transcription factors (e.g., cFos) and regulatory proteins involved in the control of cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and inflammatory mediator production (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). In RPE cells, activation of p38 MAPK has been linked to cytoskeletal rearrangements that lead to stress‐induced cellular defects; these include formation of abnormal actin structures and impaired formation of phagocytic cups necessary for the internalization of POS (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). In the experimental setting, SB202190 has been shown to effectively block the TGF‐β2 mediated phosphorylation of p38, thereby reducing the transcriptional activity of Smad3/4 complexes without impacting the initial receptor‐mediated phosphorylation events of Smads2/3. This mechanism suggests that SB202190 acts downstream of TGF‐β receptor activation, interfering with p38‐dependent enhancement of transcription factor complex formation and nuclear translocation, which in turn can dampen pathological ECM production and abnormal cell migration (Saika et al., 2005). Additionally, literature indicates that stress‐activated p38 signaling contributes to the senescence of RPE cells by regulating the senescence‐associated secretory phenotype (SASP) through modulation of p53 and NF‐κB pathways (Liu et al., 2025). By inhibiting p38 MAPK, SB202190 is hypothesized to replicate the protective effects of endogenous negative regulators such as DUSP4, which dephosphorylate and inactivate p38 MAPK, ultimately reducing RPE cell senescence and maintaining cellular homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025). It is noteworthy that p38 MAPK signaling is intricately intertwined with other MAPK family members, and some studies have reported that SB202190, particularly at higher doses, exhibits a biphasic response where alternative signaling pathways (such as MEK/ERK) may become upregulated, emphasizing the importance of careful dose optimization in any therapeutic application (Wang et al., 2024; Hirosawa et al., 2009). Thus, the mechanism of action of SB202190 involves a highly specific inhibition of p38α/β kinase activity, which is expected to restore normal actin dynamics and cytoskeletal organization in RPE cells, thereby facilitating proper phagosome formation and efficient POS uptake under oxidative stress conditions akin to those found in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The primary hypothesis driving the repurposing of SB202190 for dry AMD is that inhibition of p38α/β in RPE cells will reduce stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling defects and thereby improve the phagocytic internalization of photoreceptor outer segments. Under oxidative stress conditions, such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) in in vitro models using ARPE‐19 cells, activation of p38 MAPK is known to mediate cytoskeletal disorganization and promote aberrant cell migration, processes that are deleterious to the RPE’s phagocytic function (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). By inhibiting p38 MAPK with SB202190 at a low nanomolar concentration (approximately 40 nM), it is anticipated that the compound will reduce the phosphorylation of p38, thereby preventing the downstream activation of stress‐responsive transcription factors and proteins responsible for actin remodeling (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). In doing so, SB202190 is expected to “normalize” the actin cytoskeletal dynamics in H₂O₂‐treated ARPE‐19 cells, thus facilitating the re‐establishment of properly organized phagocytic cups required for POS ingestion—a process critical for photoreceptor maintenance and overall retinal homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025; Saika et al., 2005). In parallel, inhibition of p38 MAPK may downregulate pro‐fibrotic and pro‐senescent signaling pathways (e.g., those mediated by TGF‐β2, p53, and NF‐κB), therefore limiting the aberrant deposition of ECM components and improving the overall cellular microenvironment (Liu et al., 2025; Saika et al., 2005). As a result, the expected effect of SB202190 in the assay proposed would be a significant improvement in phagosome internalization of POS under oxidative conditions, combined with a reduction in the markers of cytoskeletal stress and cell senescence. Moreover, enhanced phagocytic activity by RPE cells could mitigate pathological features of dry AMD, such as drusen formation and eventual RPE degeneration, thereby potentially slowing disease progression (Moustardas et al., 2023; Du et al., 2010). The compound’s effect is further anticipated to extend to modulation of inflammatory cytokine release, given the well‐established role of p38 MAPK in regulating cytokine production, thus providing a dual benefit by both preserving cytoskeletal integrity and reducing chronic, low‐grade inflammation in the retina (Liu et al., 2025; Kyosseva, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
Evaluating the potential of SB202190 as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD involves weighing both the strengths and the inherent challenges associated with targeting the p38 MAPK pathway in the RPE. One of the major strengths of SB202190 is its well‐characterized mechanism of action as a selective inhibitor of p38α/β, which is pivotal in mediating stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling, inflammation, and cellular senescence in RPE cells. The compound has demonstrated robust in vitro anti‐fibrotic and anti‐migratory effects in ARPE‐19 cell models that mirror key features of RPE dysfunction observed in dry AMD (Saika et al., 2005). Furthermore, the concept of normalizing actin dynamics to enhance phagocytic cup formation and subsequent POS uptake is highly attractive, given that impaired phagocytosis is a core feature driving the degeneration observed in dry AMD (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). The protective role played by endogenous regulators like DUSP4, which deactivates p38 MAPK and preserves RPE integrity, supports the rationale for a pharmacological approach that mimics this effect (Liu et al., 2025). Additionally, numerous studies have shown that p38 MAPK inhibitors can modulate inflammatory responses and reduce ECM deposition; such effects are promising in the context of retinal diseases where chronic inflammation and fibrosis exacerbate degenerative processes (Moustardas et al., 2023; Saika et al., 2005).

However, several weaknesses and potential caveats must be thoroughly considered. First, the p38 MAPK pathway exhibits complex, context‐dependent behavior in RPE cells. There is evidence suggesting that, under certain circumstances, p38 MAPK activation can be cytoprotective by facilitating adaptive stress responses, such as the upregulation of antioxidant defenses (Pocrnich et al., 2009). This duality indicates that complete or prolonged inhibition of p38 MAPK may inadvertently dampen protective signaling, potentially leading to adverse outcomes. Additionally, published studies have documented that SB202190, when used at higher concentrations, can show biphasic responses or off‐target effects that might include the unintended activation of alternative MAPK pathways (Wang et al., 2024; Hirosawa et al., 2009). This underscores the critical need for precise dose optimization and comprehensive pharmacodynamic studies to define a therapeutic window where the beneficial effects on cytoskeletal remodeling and phagocytosis are maximized while the risks of impairing physiological stress responses are minimized.

Furthermore, while the preclinical literature provides substantial mechanistic insights and supportive data from retinal injury models—particularly in contexts such as PVR—the clinical translation of these findings to dry AMD remains unproven. SB202190 has not been advanced into clinical trials for retinal degenerative diseases, and its application has thus far been confined to experimental paradigms (Kim et al., 2021; Kyosseva, 2016). Therefore, any proposal to repurpose SB202190 for dry AMD must be accompanied by robust in vivo efficacy studies using animal models that faithfully recapitulate the chronic, multifactorial nature of the disease. Moreover, the impact of SB202190 on other critical RPE functions, such as phagocytosis of POS under normal conditions and cytoskeletal dynamics related to cell adhesion and migration, needs to be extensively characterized to avoid unintended disruption of essential homeostatic processes (Kim et al., 2021; Kyosseva, 2016).

Another consideration is the limitation inherent to the use of SB202190 as a research tool rather than a clinical‐grade pharmaceutical compound. Its pharmacokinetic and safety profiles have been characterized in experimental contexts, but there is a lack of clinical data regarding potential ocular toxicity, bioavailability, and long‐term impact on retinal structure and function (Federspiel et al., 2023; Young, 2013). The multifaceted role of p38 MAPK in the retina—spanning inflammatory cytokine production, regulation of apoptosis, and cytoskeletal dynamics—means that a fine balance must be maintained; excessive suppression could lead to undesired consequences such as impaired wound healing or compromised cell survival under stress. As such, a detailed understanding of the dose‐response relationship and the temporal dynamics of p38 inhibition in specific RPE subpopulations will be essential.

In summary, SB202190 presents as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on strong mechanistic rationale and preclinical evidence supporting its ability to modulate pathological pathways implicated in RPE dysfunction. Its capacity to inhibit p38α/β with high potency, restore actin dynamics under oxidative conditions, and improve phagocytic function aligns well with the therapeutic goals of preserving RPE integrity and retinal homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the dualistic nature of p38 MAPK signaling—with its capacity to mediate both deleterious and protective responses—poses a significant challenge that mandates careful and comprehensive preclinical evaluation. The candidate’s strengths reside in its well‐characterized inhibitory activity, established use in modulating fibrotic and inflammatory responses in ocular models, and its potential to replicate the endogenous protective functions mediated by regulators such as DUSP4 (Liu et al., 2025). Conversely, the weaknesses center on potential off‐target effects, the risk of inadvertently suppressing adaptive stress responses, and the absence of clinical studies directly addressing dry AMD.

Overall, while SB202190 holds promise based on its molecular mode of action and supportive in vitro data regarding cytoskeletal normalization and phagocytosis, the translational viability for dry AMD will ultimately depend on rigorous dosing studies, long‐term safety assessments, and demonstration of efficacy in animal models that capture the chronic oxidative and inflammatory milieu of the human retina (Moustardas et al., 2023; Saika et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2024). Only through such comprehensive studies can we adequately determine whether SB202190’s benefits outweigh its potential risks and if it can be successfully repurposed as a therapeutic intervention to mitigate the progression of dry AMD.

Under normal conditions, p38 MAPK becomes activated in response to various extracellular stress signals—such as oxidative stress, UV irradiation, and pro-inflammatory cytokines—via dual phosphorylation on its Thr and Tyr residues located in the activation loop. Once activated, p38 phosphorylates several downstream targets, including Heat shock protein 27 (Hsp27), which has a pivotal role in modulating actin dynamics and cytoskeletal organization. Phosphorylated Hsp27 facilitates cytoskeletal reorganization, contributing to cell shape changes, membrane blebbing, and potentially impaired receptor recycling. SB203580 binds competitively to the ATP-binding site of p38 MAPK, thereby preventing its kinase activity and effectively blocking phosphorylation of substrates like Hsp27 (Marin-Castaño, 2013). In ARPE-19 cells exposed to oxidative stressors, SB203580’s inhibition of p38 MAPK abrogates stress-induced phosphorylation events, hence stabilizing the actin cytoskeleton and curtailing the formation of pathological cellular structures that are often seen in senescent or apoptotic cells (Roduit & Schorderet, 2008). Moreover, p38 MAPK is known to cooperate with other signaling molecules such as the AP-1 complex to propagate pro-apoptotic and pro-senescence signaling; blockade of p38 by SB203580 has been shown to reduce the downstream transcriptional responses that exacerbate cell death and inflammatory cytokine release. Furthermore, the inhibition of p38 also seems to counteract pro-inflammatory signaling cascades implicated in AMD by reducing the secretion of cytokines such as IL-8 in response to various stimuli (Qiao et al., 2012). Thus, by targeting the p38 MAPK pathway, SB203580 interrupts a cascade of events—ranging from oxidative stress signaling to inflammation, apoptosis, and senescence—that collectively contribute to RPE dysfunction and the progression of dry AMD (Marin-Castaño, 2013; Roduit & Schorderet, 2008; Zhu et al., 2009).

It is anticipated that the inhibition of these deleterious pathways will allow RPE cells to regain a more physiological state, including the restoration of proper integrin β5 recycling dynamics (Marin-Castaño, 2013). Although direct measurements of integrin β5 recycling following SB203580 treatment are limited in the published literature, the compound’s ability to reverse actin cytoskeletal disorganization suggests that it could indeed normalize the trafficking and cell surface presentation of integrin receptors. Enhanced availability of integrin β5 on the RPE cell membrane is expected to improve the phagocytic recycling of POS, thereby restoring a critical functionality of RPE cells that is compromised in dry AMD (Roduit & Schorderet, 2008; Zhu et al., 2009; Marin-Castaño, 2013).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating SB203580 as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, several compelling strengths as well as notable limitations must be considered. On the strength side, SB203580 is one of the most well-characterized inhibitors of p38 MAPK, with a robust body of preclinical evidence supporting its ability to mitigate the cellular consequences of oxidative stress in RPE cells. Multiple independent studies have demonstrated that SB203580 can effectively block UV-induced apoptosis and oxidative stress-induced senescence in ARPE-19 cells by inhibiting key phosphorylation events—including those of Hsp27—which in turn stabilize the actin cytoskeleton and prevent deleterious morphological changes (Marin-Castaño, 2013; Roduit & Schorderet, 2008). Furthermore, by interfering with the p38 MAPK pathway, SB203580 may additionally reduce the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, thereby mitigating local inflammatory responses that exacerbate retinal degeneration (Qiao et al., 2012). These biochemical actions provide a strong rationale for expecting that SB203580 could restore the dysfunctional recycling of key integrin receptors—particularly integrin β5—on RPE cells, which is crucial for the phagocytosis of POS and ultimately for retinal health.

However, several challenges and weaknesses must also be acknowledged. First, despite the promising in vitro evidence, SB203580 has not yet undergone rigorous in vivo evaluation or clinical testing specifically for dry AMD. Much of the existing data derives from experiments in the ARPE-19 cell line—a robust but simplified model of RPE physiology. The translation of these findings to the more complex in vivo environment of the human retina remains uncertain, particularly given the unique challenges of achieving appropriate drug delivery, dosing, and sustained therapeutic activity within ocular tissues (Zhu et al., 2009). Second, p38 MAPK is not solely a mediator of pathological processes; it also fulfills essential roles in normal cellular homeostasis, including the regulation of baseline VEGF expression and other survival pathways. Therefore, broad inhibition of p38 may carry the risk of unintended interference with physiological functions that are vital for retinal maintenance, thereby necessitating carefully calibrated dosing regimens and targeted delivery systems to mitigate potential adverse effects (Moustardas et al., 2023). In summary, SB203580 holds considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its well-documented ability to inhibit p38 MAPK and thereby attenuate several key pathological processes in RPE cells. Its capacity to block Hsp27 phosphorylation, reduce cytoskeletal disruptions, mitigate apoptosis and senescence, and potentially restore integrin receptor recycling offers a multifaceted approach to correcting RPE dysfunction—a central feature in the progression of dry AMD (Marin-Castaño, 2013; Roduit & Schorderet, 2008; Zhu et al., 2009). Nonetheless, the transition from compelling in vitro data to a viable clinical therapy entails overcoming significant hurdles, including confirming the effect on integrin β5 recycling and POS binding in more physiologically relevant models, establishing an acceptable safety profile in the sensitive ocular environment, and determining effective delivery modalities. Given the current evidence, further preclinical studies—including in vivo animal models and detailed mechanistic investigations—are warranted to validate the proposed hypothesis and to assess the translational potential of SB203580 for dry AMD treatment. In the meantime, its established role in inflammatory ocular models provides a promising foundation upon which future research can build, with the ultimate goal of developing an effective therapeutic intervention for dry AMD, a condition that remains a significant unmet medical need.

Historically, VX-765 has been evaluated in preclinical studies and early-phase human trials mainly for systemic inflammatory and neurological conditions. Caspase-1 is a cysteine-dependent aspartate-directed protease that plays a central role in the activation of inflammatory cytokines by cleaving pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature, biologically active forms; these cytokines are major mediators of inflammatory cascades and pyroptotic cell death (Kallinich, 2015; Kudelova et al., 2015). The repurposing of VX-765 for dry AMD represents a compelling strategy, driven by a strong mechanistic rationale and bolstered by its demonstrated efficacy in other inflammatory models. NR has a robust preclinical and early clinical history as a nutritional supplement with demonstrated efficacy in boosting NAD⁺ levels systemically. Prior biochemical studies have documented that oral NR supplementation raises circulating NAD⁺ and associated metabolites in both murine and human subjects, with repeated dosing regimens showing increases in NAD⁺ of up to 100% above baseline without causing adverse events such as flushing or liver toxicity—side effects that have been problematic with other niacin derivatives (Airhart et al., 2017; Conze et al., 2019). Furthermore, NR has been shown to ameliorate metabolic deficits in various disease models, including mouse models of diet-induced obesity, neurodegeneration, peripheral neuropathy, and even light-induced retinal degeneration, where systemic treatment with NR improved retinal outcomes in mice (Zhang et al., 2020; Biţă et al., 2023). Although NR has not been directly tested in clinical trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in dedicated experiments on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) phagocytosis, the accumulated evidence from related ocular studies and from the broader literature on NAD⁺ restoration suggests that its application in retinal degenerative conditions is plausible (Jadeja et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, NR is rapidly taken up by cells and phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRK1 and NRK2) to produce nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), which is subsequently converted to NAD⁺ by NMN adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) (Zhang et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). NAD⁺ is a key metabolic hub that is required for essential cellular processes, including fueling mitochondrial ATP production via glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation, while also serving as a critical substrate for sirtuin deacetylases (notably SIRT1 and SIRT3) and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs) that mediate DNA repair and stress responses (Braidy et al., 2019; Biţă et al., 2023). In the context of the RPE, diminished NAD⁺ availability is linked to compromised mitochondrial bioenergetics, impaired autophagy/mitophagy, increased oxidative stress, and defective phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), all of which contribute to the etiology of dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2020). NR supplementation is proposed to elevate intracellular NAD⁺ levels above the physiological threshold, thereby stimulating sirtuin activity (particularly SIRT3 in mitochondria), stabilizing mitochondrial membrane potential, promoting efficient mitophagy, and reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Biţă et al., 2023). Additionally, by restoring the NAD⁺/NADH balance, NR may directly support energy-dependent processes such as phagocytosis in RPE cells, where the clearance of aged POS is critically energy demanding (Zhang et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed hypothesis for dry AMD, exogenous NR supplementation is expected to boost NAD⁺ levels in RPE cells, an effect that should be observable at an effective concentration (EC₅₀) in the range of approximately 100 µM in vitro (Zhang et al., 2020). This increase in NAD⁺ is anticipated to enhance mitochondrial respiration and activate sirtuin-dependent pathways that promote mitochondrial biogenesis and repair. In turn, improved mitochondrial function provides the necessary ATP for energy-dependent cellular functions, particularly the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), which is impaired in dry AMD. Preclinical studies have indicated that NAD⁺ precursors, including nicotinamide and NMN, can correct defects in mitochondrial respiration and restore normal phagocytic activity in RPE models; NR, being an orally bioavailable NAD⁺ precursor with favorable safety profiles, is predicted to act similarly by reducing oxidative stress–induced damage to the phagocytic machinery and enhancing mitophagy to clear damaged mitochondria (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020; Hawkins et al., 2024). In animal models of retinal degeneration, NR supplementation has been linked to improved functional outcomes, supporting the notion that similar mechanisms may be relevant in the context of dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction underlies photoreceptor degeneration (Zhang et al., 2020). Thus, the expected effect is a dual benefit in RPE cells: increased energy production to drive POS phagocytosis and enhanced resistance to oxidative damage through improved mitochondrial quality control, ultimately helping to preserve RPE function and slow dry AMD progression (Conze et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
NR is an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its unique combination of advantages. Among its strengths is its origin as a naturally occurring, orally bioavailable NAD⁺ precursor that has a long record of safe use in human nutritional studies; clinical trials have repeatedly demonstrated its ability to significantly elevate systemic NAD⁺ levels without dose-limiting adverse effects such as flushing or hepatotoxicity, which are common to other niacin derivatives (Airhart et al., 2017; Conze et al., 2019). Its mechanism of action is well understood at the biochemical level: by feeding into the NAD⁺ salvage pathway, NR supports key cellular functions including mitochondrial respiration, DNA repair, and stress signaling via sirtuins and PARPs—pathways that are critically compromised in the aging RPE and in dry AMD (Braidy et al., 2019; Biţă et al., 2023). Additionally, preclinical data have shown that NAD⁺ restoration via NR or related precursors can ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction and improve phagocytic activity in retinal tissues, providing a plausible molecular rationale for its use in maintaining RPE health (Zhang et al., 2020).

On the other hand, there are significant challenges that must be acknowledged. Despite promising preclinical evidence in various models of retinal degeneration, direct application of NR in the context of dry AMD has not yet been rigorously evaluated in dedicated clinical trials, leaving a gap between the compelling mechanistic rationale and the demonstration of clinical efficacy (Jadeja et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2024). The concentration required (EC₅₀ ≈ 100 µM) and the extent of NR’s penetration into the RPE in the human eye remain to be fully elucidated; tissue-specific pharmacokinetics may differ from those observed in systemic circulation, and there remains the possibility that presystemic metabolism (conversion to nicotinamide, for example) could limit the amount of NR available for direct uptake by the RPE (Damgaard & Treebak, 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Furthermore, while the drug’s safety profile is established in the context of metabolic and neurodegenerative indications, the unique microenvironment of the retina—with its high oxygen consumption and exposure to light-induced oxidative stress—may present unforeseen responses that require careful validation in animal models and early-phase clinical studies (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2020).

In summary, NR (ChromaDex TruNiagen) holds considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its ability to safely boost NAD⁺ levels, improve mitochondrial function, and reduce oxidative stress aligns well with the pathophysiological needs of the RPE in dry AMD. Strengths of the candidate include its natural origin, established safety and bioavailability profiles in humans, and robust preclinical evidence supporting NAD⁺ repletion as a strategy for enhancing mitochondrial quality and phagocytic function. However, the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD and the need for targeted studies to confirm effective RPE delivery and functional restoration of POS clearance remain important considerations. Overall, NR merits further investigation in preclinical RPE models and carefully designed clinical trials to assess its efficacy in mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020; Airhart et al., 2017; Conze et al., 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AMD3100 (also known as plerixafor) is a small‐molecule, bicyclam compound originally discovered and synthesized as a CXCR4 antagonist. It belongs to a class of compounds designed to block the interaction between the chemokine ligand SDF‐1 (CXCL12) and its receptor CXCR4. This class of compounds was initially developed for their antiviral potential—specifically to inhibit HIV‐1 entry into cells—because CXCR4 serves as a co‐receptor for viral entry. Subsequent studies showed that through its high affinity for CXCR4 (with IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range, and our current hypothesis citing ~20 nM in RPE cells), AMD3100 can effectively block the downstream signaling of the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis. This signaling cascade is known to regulate key cellular processes such as chemotaxis, cell survival, proliferation, and inflammatory gene expression. With its synthetic origin and established profile as a CXCR4 antagonist, AMD3100 has been repurposed beyond its initial anti‐HIV goals to include hematopoietic stem cell mobilization and experimental oncology. Its potential re‐utilization in ocular diseases, particularly in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), capitalizes on its ability to modulate inflammatory signaling pathways implicated in retinal degeneration (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AMD3100 emerged from research aimed at blocking HIV infection, but its clinical development pivoted after it was found to robustly mobilize hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells from the bone marrow. This discovery led to its approval by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as an adjuvant therapy for autologous stem cell transplantation in patients with non‐Hodgkin’s lymphoma and multiple myeloma. Its use in stem cell mobilization has been thoroughly characterized in clinical trials with documented pharmacokinetics and a reasonable safety profile in systemic administration (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019). In addition to these applications, AMD3100 has been investigated in various preclinical models of cancer, where its inhibition of CXCR4-mediated signaling has been linked to reduced tumor cell invasion, decreased angiogenesis, and altered immune cell trafficking (Andtbacka et al., 2022; Cho et al., 2013). In the ocular context, although AMD3100 has not been used directly for treating dry AMD, its effects on CXCR4 signaling have been addressed in studies focusing on glaucomatous models. For example, investigations in trabecular meshwork cells from glaucomatous tissue have demonstrated that AMD3100, when administered at 1 mM concentration, completely abrogates the protective effects of CXCL12 and inadvertently induces apoptosis, highlighting the dual role of CXCR4 signaling in ocular tissues (Denoyer et al., 2012). Moreover, systemic administration studies in non‐ocular models such as the SOD1^G93A ALS mouse model have shown that chronic AMD3100 treatment can yield neuroprotective and anti‐inflammatory benefits (Rabinovich‐Nikitin et al., 2016), which further adds to its therapeutic appeal but also underscores the importance of tissue-specific dosing and context. These historical uses underscore AMD3100’s well-defined pharmacological profile while simultaneously illustrating that translating its benefits to the RPE in dry AMD will require reconciling its established systemic effects with the often finely balanced roles of the CXCR4 axis in retinal tissue repair and inflammation (Cai et al., 2014; Saiman et al., 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, AMD3100 exerts its primary pharmacological action by selectively binding to the CXCR4 receptor and competitively inhibiting the binding of its natural ligand, SDF‐1 (CXCL12). In doing so, it prevents receptor activation and the subsequent engagement of intracellular signaling cascades mediated by G-protein coupled receptor activation. The downstream effects typically include modulation of pathways such as PI3K/Akt, Ras/ERK, and, in many cases, alterations in intracellular calcium fluxes that contribute to chemotaxis and cell survival (Bai et al., 2016; Colasanti et al., 2025). By inhibiting these cascades, AMD3100 hinders not only the migration of cells toward SDF‐1 gradients but also the pro‐inflammatory and pro‐angiogenic gene expression programs that are otherwise activated upon CXCR4 engagement. In cancer models, this mechanism translates into reduced tumor cell invasion and inhibition of angiogenesis, while in immune cells it modulates chemotactic responses and inflammatory cell trafficking (Cho et al., 2013). Importantly, CXCR4 is expressed in multiple ocular cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. In RPE, the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis has been implicated in cellular migration, cytokine secretion, and potentially in the regulation of the phagocytic machinery necessary for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). The hypothesis driving the current proposal suggests that chronic activation of CXCR4 in RPE cells, possibly driven by persistent inflammatory stimuli such as TNF‐α, leads to a pro‐inflammatory state that downregulates key phagocytic receptors like MERTK and compromises lysosomal enzyme activity. By blocking the binding of SDF‐1 to CXCR4, AMD3100 is expected to interrupt this deleterious signaling cascade, resulting in normalization of MERTK expression and lysosomal enzyme levels, and thereby restoring the essential phagocytic function of the RPE (Colasanti et al., 2025). However, the complexity of CXCR4 signaling is underscored by studies in other ocular tissues where its inhibition has led to apoptosis of trabecular cells, suggesting that the outcome of CXCR4 blockade may be highly dependent on the cell type and the local microenvironment (Denoyer et al., 2012). Therefore, while the mechanistic rationale is strong, careful evaluation of AMD3100’s specific molecular interactions in RPE cells will be required to delineate beneficial effects from potential adverse outcomes.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed therapeutic strategy hypothesizes that the blockade of CXCR4 by AMD3100 in RPE cells will lead to two major beneficial outcomes in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration: (1) inhibition of pro-inflammatory signaling that otherwise promotes aberrant cellular migration and deleterious inflammatory gene expression, and (2) restoration of the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells through upregulation of key receptors and enzymes necessary for the efficient clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In dry AMD, a hallmark of disease progression is the accumulation of cellular debris and the failure of RPE cells to effectively clear POS due to impaired phagocytosis—a process that is critical for sustaining photoreceptor health and visual function. Evidence suggests that chronic activation of the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis in the retinal microenvironment can lead to elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines and subsequent downregulation of MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase essential for the recognition and internalization of shed POS (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). In vitro models, such as TNF‐α–treated ARPE-19 cells, have demonstrated that inflammatory stress leads to diminished phagocytic activity, and it is hypothesized that blocking CXCR4 signaling with AMD3100 could counteract this effect by normalizing MERTK levels and restoring lysosomal function. In an ideal scenario, treatment with AMD3100 would reverse the pro-inflammatory signaling cascade by preventing SDF‐1 binding, reduce aberrant RPE migration, and allow the cells to maintain their structural polarity and phagocytic efficiency. Importantly, the RPE expresses CXCR4 receptors on their surface, as demonstrated by immunocytochemical studies, and the receptor’s activation has been linked to altered cellular motility and inflammatory responses (Canonica et al., 2021; Enzmann et al., 2017). The expected pharmacodynamic outcome is that, upon AMD3100 treatment, RPE cells under inflammatory stress conditions would exhibit increased expression of MERTK and lysosomal enzymes, leading to improved clearance of damaged photoreceptor outer segments, which is critical for photoreceptor survival and overall retinal health. While data from other cell types suggest the possibility of safely modulating these pathways, caution is warranted given the evidence from trabecular meshwork cells where CXCR4 antagonism disrupted protective signaling (Denoyer et al., 2012). Hence, the key to success will lie in establishing the proper dosing and delivery mechanisms that provide sufficient blockade of deleterious CXCR4 signaling in RPE without compromising the receptor’s potentially beneficial roles in tissue repair and homeostasis.

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, AMD3100 presents an intriguing candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration given its well-defined mechanism of action, extensive preclinical and clinical history, and a known safety profile in non-ocular indications such as hematopoietic stem cell mobilization and cancer therapy (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019). The central hypothesis—that chronic SDF‐1/CXCR4 signaling in RPE cells contributes to inflammation-driven downregulation of MERTK and consequent impairment of POS phagocytosis—addresses a critical pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD. Blocking this pathway with AMD3100 could, in theory, restore the phagocytic machinery of the RPE, thereby reducing the accumulation of toxic cellular debris and slowing disease progression (Colasanti et al., 2025).

One of the strengths of AMD3100 as a therapeutic candidate lies in its extensive clinical use and established pharmacokinetic profile; its FDA approval for stem cell mobilization means that much is already known about its systemic effects, dosing parameters, and potential toxicities when administered appropriately (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Rabinovich-Nikitin et al., 2016). Moreover, the molecular mechanism—competitive antagonism at the CXCR4 receptor—has been demonstrated across multiple studies and various cell types, providing a robust theoretical framework for its use in modulating pathological signaling cascades in RPE cells (Bai et al., 2016; Colasanti et al., 2025). The concept of repurposing a well-characterized agent such as AMD3100 for dry AMD is attractive from a drug development standpoint because it could potentially shorten the translational timeline and reduce development risks related to novel chemical entities.

However, there are significant challenges and weaknesses that must be addressed before AMD3100 can be considered a promising candidate for dry AMD. First and foremost, the role of SDF‐1/CXCR4 signaling in ocular tissues appears to be multifaceted. While in RPE cells chronic activation may indeed drive a pro-inflammatory and phagocytosis-impairing phenotype, in other ocular tissues such as the trabecular meshwork, CXCR4 signaling has been shown to exert cytoprotective effects. Studies in glaucomatous trabecular cells have demonstrated that blockade of CXCR4 by AMD3100 not only abrogates the beneficial actions of CXCL12 but may also actively induce apoptosis, highlighting a potential risk that the protective aspects of CXCR4 signaling could be compromised (Denoyer et al., 2012). This tissue-specific duality raises concerns that non-selective or systemic inhibition of CXCR4 might lead to unintended adverse effects in the retina and other ocular compartments. Therefore, any consideration of AMD3100 for dry AMD will require extremely careful dosing studies and potentially localized delivery strategies that avoid systemic over-blockade.

Another key consideration is the current lack of direct evidence supporting the efficacy of AMD3100 in restoring MERTK expression or lysosomal enzyme levels in RPE cells, specifically in the context of dry AMD. While preliminary in vitro observations in TNF‐α–treated ARPE-19 cells are promising, these studies remain preliminary, and the translation of these effects into meaningful functional outcomes in vivo has yet to be established. The complexity of dry AMD pathogenesis—which involves not only inflammatory processes but also oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, and altered cellular metabolism—means that targeting a single pathway may not be sufficient to recapitulate the full spectrum of therapeutic benefit required for clinical efficacy (Colasanti et al., 2025).

Furthermore, the potential for AMD3100 to affect cell migration and even cellular differentiation via CXCR4 inhibition might have unpredictable consequences on the RPE’s capacity for repair. For instance, the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis has been implicated in the recruitment of bone marrow–derived progenitor cells to sites of RPE injury, a process that is thought to contribute to endogenous repair mechanisms (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). Inhibiting CXCR4 could inadvertently interfere with these reparative processes if not finely tuned. It is, therefore, imperative that any preclinical evaluation of AMD3100 for dry AMD includes rigorous assessments of not only phagocytic function and inflammatory profile but also the impact on RPE cell survival, differentiation, and regenerative capacity.

In addition to cell-specific concerns, the delivery method for AMD3100 in the context of dry AMD is another critical factor. The compound has been used systemically, but ocular diseases typically require either intravitreal or other localized delivery methods to achieve therapeutic concentrations while minimizing systemic exposure. Prior studies involving AMD3100 in ocular models—mostly in the context of glaucoma—have used subconjunctival injections at relatively high concentrations (e.g., 1 mM), which resulted in localized apoptotic effects (Denoyer et al., 2012). This suggests that the concentration and mode of delivery will need to be carefully optimized for the RPE to ensure that sufficient drug levels are achieved to block aberrant CXCR4 signaling without tipping the balance of protective chemokine functions.

Moreover, while the preclinical data from non-ocular models such as cancer and ALS are encouraging regarding the anti-inflammatory and anti-migratory effects of AMD3100 (Rabinovich-Nikitin et al., 2016; Andtbacka et al., 2022), these contexts differ significantly from the microenvironment of the aging retina. The retinal tissue, particularly in dry AMD, is characterized by complex interactions among the RPE, photoreceptors, Bruch’s membrane, and the choriocapillaris. The interplay of these structures with age-related oxidative stress and immune dysregulation means that any intervention must be evaluated in models that faithfully recapitulate these conditions. There is a paucity of direct literature on the use of AMD3100 in dry AMD models, which suggests that a substantial body of preclinical work is required before a clear signal of benefit can be ascertained.

In summary, AMD3100 has significant strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its well-documented mechanism of competitive antagonism at CXCR4, combined with an established clinical safety profile in systemic applications and a clear rationale for targeting the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis in inflammatory conditions, supports further investigation of its use in the retinal pigment epithelium (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019; Bai et al., 2016). However, key weaknesses include evidence from ocular models that indicate potential cytotoxicity when protective CXCR4 signals are indiscriminately blocked (Denoyer et al., 2012), as well as a lack of direct preclinical data in dry AMD or RPE-specific phagocytic assays. These concerns necessitate a cautious yet exploratory approach, with initial studies focused on establishing the optimal local dosing regimen, confirming that AMD3100 can indeed restore MERTK expression and phagocytic function in ARPE-19 cell models, and ultimately validating these findings in animal models of dry AMD that incorporate stressors such as TNF‐α or oxidative injury.

Overall Evaluation:  
In conclusion, while AMD3100 stands as one of the most thoroughly characterized CXCR4 antagonists with a solid clinical and preclinical background, its application to dry AMD remains largely untested. The theoretical basis—that chronic SDF‐1/CXCR4 activation in RPE drives inflammatory gene expression leading to diminished phagocytic capacity, and that blocking this pathway will restore homeostatic functions—is compelling and addresses a known pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD (Colasanti et al., 2025). The strengths of AMD3100 include its potent CXCR4 binding affinity, the wealth of pharmacological data supporting its mode of action, and its demonstrated ability to modulate inflammatory and migratory responses in various tissues. Moreover, the clinical safety data from its use in hematopoietic stem cell mobilization provide some reassurance regarding its tolerability when used in appropriate dosing regimens (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019).

On the other hand, several significant weaknesses must be acknowledged. Studies in ocular models have shown that CXCR4 blockade can eliminate protective signals that are crucial for cell survival, as evidenced by the induction of apoptosis in trabecular meshwork cells when treated with AMD3100 at high concentrations (Denoyer et al., 2012). In addition, there is a risk that by inhibiting CXCR4 signaling, AMD3100 might interfere with endogenous repair mechanisms mediated by the recruitment of bone marrow–derived progenitor cells, a process that may be beneficial in RPE regeneration (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). The lack of direct data demonstrating restoration of MERTK and improved phagocytosis in RPE cells further complicates the evaluation. Because dry AMD is multifactorial, it is unclear whether modulation of a single pathway—albeit an important one—will be sufficient to yield a meaningful clinical benefit without causing collateral damage to other aspects of RPE function.

Given these considerations, our recommendation is to pursue rigorous preclinical studies specifically tailored to dry AMD. These studies should encompass detailed in vitro analyses using ARPE-19 and primary human RPE cells under inflammatory and oxidative stress conditions to validate whether AMD3100 can reliably restore MERTK expression and lysosomal function, thereby enhancing POS clearance. It will also be critical to establish the appropriate concentration window that achieves therapeutic blockade of deleterious signaling while preserving necessary CXCR4-mediated protective effects. Parallel in vivo studies in animal models of dry AMD should focus on local ocular delivery methods—potentially through intravitreal or controlled-release formulations—to minimize systemic exposure and optimize retinal bioavailability.

In conclusion, AMD3100 represents an exciting and scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its mechanism of CXCR4 antagonism and the hypothesized link between chronic SDF‐1/CXCR4 activation and impaired RPE phagocytosis. However, given the mixed evidence from ocular safety studies and the complexity of CXCR4 signaling in retinal homeostasis, further systematic preclinical evaluation is essential before advancing to clinical trials. The balance between inhibiting pathological inflammation and preserving or even harnessing protective regenerative signals will determine the ultimate viability of AMD3100 as a therapeutic agent for dry age‐related macular degeneration (Denoyer et al., 2012; Rabinovich-Nikitin et al., 2016; Bai et al., 2016).
