Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is a fully synthetic small molecule in the 4-aminoquinoline (4AQ) class, developed in the mid-20th century as a hydroxylated analogue of chloroquine (CQ) to improve tolerability; HCQ differs from CQ by a terminal hydroxyl group on the side chain (HCQ: C18H26ClN3O, 336 g/mol; CQ: C18H26ClN3, 320 g/mol) (Browning, 2014a, 2014b). Industrially, HCQ can be prepared by condensing N1-N-ethyl-N1-β-hydroxyethyl-1,4-pentanediamine with 4,7-dichloroquinoline, paralleling the CQ route from the same quinoline core with an altered aminoalkyl side chain (Rainsford et al., 2015). As a class, HCQ/CQ are alkylated 4-aminoquinolines: weak, amphiphilic bases bearing a flat quinoline nucleus and a basic side chain that traverse membranes in unprotonated form and undergo protonation-dependent sequestration in acidic intracellular compartments (lysosomes, endosomes, Golgi) — a defining pharmacologic property (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Chloroquine’s two basic centers (pKa ≈ 10.2 and 8.1) illustrate the protonation behavior that drives lysosomal trapping; at lysosomal pH (≈ 4–5) these agents become diprotonated and accumulate, with lysosome:plasma distribution ratios measured on the order of ≈ 160 000 and intralysosomal concentrations up to ≈ 2 × 10⁻² M reported for CQ, elevating lysosomal pH toward ≈ 6 (Browning, 2014b, 2014a). Pharmacokinetically, HCQ exhibits high oral bioavailability (≈ 0.7–0.8), an extremely large apparent volume of distribution (> 40 000 L), and a long terminal elimination half-life (≈ 40–60 days), with blood concentrations exceeding plasma due to extensive intracellular partitioning and tissue sequestration (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Melanin-containing ocular tissues are prominent depots; with chronic ingestion, uveal and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) concentrations can reach up to ≈ 10 000× plasma, reflecting lysosomal trapping and melanin binding (Browning, 2014a). Enantiomer-specific disposition has been observed for HCQ, with stereoselective accumulation noted in blood compartments, underscoring complex distribution kinetics (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Clinically, HCQ is commonly administered as the sulfate salt, and CQ as the phosphate salt (Neto et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
HCQ and CQ were developed as antimalarials and subsequently repurposed as disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), with additional uses across dermatology and other immune-mediated conditions; HCQ is generally preferred over CQ for chronic therapy due to a better safety profile while maintaining comparable immunomodulatory efficacy (Rainsford et al., 2015; Neto et al., 2020). Broad clinical applications documented for HCQ/CQ include SLE, RA, primary Sjögren’s syndrome, discoid/cutaneous lupus erythematosus, polymorphous light eruption, solar urticaria, porphyria cutanea tarda, and other inflammatory dermatoses, reflecting lysosomotropic and immune-modulating actions (Rainsford et al., 2015; Rapparini et al., 2025). Mechanistically motivated repurposing has extended to autophagy inhibition in oncology trials, typically at daily doses far exceeding rheumatologic regimens, although HCQ is not approved as an anticancer adjuvant (Yusuf et al., 2023). Over recent decades HCQ prescriptions have increased substantially due to its relative affordability and systemic safety advantages, expanding the exposed population and the need for ocular safety surveillance (Yusuf et al., 2023).

With respect to retinal disease, the literature emphasizes retinotoxic risk and mechanistic links to RPE lysosomal dysfunction rather than therapeutic benefit in degenerative macular disease; authoritative pharmacology and ophthalmology sources do not provide evidence that HCQ/CQ have been used as treatments for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and instead catalogue retinal toxicity mechanisms and monitoring practices associated with long-term systemic use (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). Multiple summaries note that available data do not support therapeutic use of 4AQs for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerations, while documenting ocular accumulation, lysosomal alkalinization, and RPE stress as central safety concerns (Browning, 2014a). Retinopathy, although uncommon at recommended doses, is a recognized dose- and duration-related adverse effect that can be irreversible and may progress after drug cessation, motivating dose caps and structured ophthalmic screening (Rainsford et al., 2015; Ding et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action  
Lysosomotropism and lysosomal alkalinization  
HCQ/CQ are canonical lysosomotropic weak bases that accumulate massively within acidic intracellular organelles and elevate their pH, directly impairing acidity-dependent lysosomal hydrolases, receptor recycling, and degradative pathways including autophagy (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b). In vitro and cell-system studies report that chloroquine exposure increases lysosomal pH from ≈ 4–5 toward ≈ 6, a change sufficient to inhibit cathepsin activities and other acid hydrolases; pharmacologic blockade of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase with bafilomycin A₁ abrogates CQ’s lysosomotropism and toxicity, pinpointing disruption of lysosomal acidification as the proximal driver (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b). In RPE cells specifically, the lysosomotropic alkalinization by 4AQs inhibits lysosomal enzyme activity and autophagic flux, leading to accumulation of undegraded material; experimental inhibition of vacuolar acidification with bafilomycin phenocopies these degradative defects, indicating that pH elevation per se is sufficient to impair RPE lysosomal function (Guha et al., 2014).

Immune modulation and nucleic acid sensing  
Elevation of endolysosomal pH by 4AQs inhibits MHC class II antigen processing and presentation and blocks activation of endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR-3/7/9), thereby reducing MyD88-dependent interferon production and dampening pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion from mononuclear cells and dendritic cells (IL-1, IL-6, TNF, IFN-α/γ, CCL4) (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). The class also interferes with cGAS–STING pathway activation through inhibition of cGAMP synthase and reduces T-cell co-stimulatory signaling (e.g., CD154), a mechanistic constellation that explains DMARD efficacy without significant increases in opportunistic infections (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020; Browning, 2014b). Additional molecular interactions reported for 4AQs include DNA binding/intercalation, kinase pathway modulation (e.g., ERK/MAPK), and diverse enzyme interactions (e.g., cholinesterase), reflecting broad pleiotropy at pharmacologic and suprapharmacologic exposures (Browning, 2014a).

RPE-relevant degradative biology: cathepsins and POS processing  
The RPE depends critically on acidic lysosomes and cathepsin activity to clear the daily phagocytic load of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and maintain autophagic flux; failure of this system yields lipofuscin accumulation and contributes to AMD pathogenesis (Sharif, 2015). Multiple lysosomal proteases are expressed by RPE, including cysteine cathepsins B, L, and S as well as aspartyl cathepsin D; cathepsins are synthesized as pre-proenzymes, processed via the secretory pathway, and activated in the acidic lumen of late endosomes/lysosomes (Sharif, 2015). In human RPE/choroid and RPE cell lines, both inactive and active forms of cathepsin B, L, and S have been detected; functional studies show that broad cysteine protease inhibition or cathepsin S knockdown impairs POS degradation and increases lipofuscin-like inclusions, underscoring their role in RPE proteostasis (Sharif, 2015). Cathepsin D, a major lysosomal aspartyl protease in RPE, is essential for POS processing; its maturation and catalytic efficiency are strongly pH-dependent and occur within the acidic lysosomal lumen (Cardoso et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).

CQ/HCQ disrupt lysosomal proteolysis and lysosome dynamics in RPE  
In RPE models, CQ induces a rapid lysosomal pH increase followed by partial pH recovery, yet produces persistent lysosomal enlargement, accumulation of undegraded endocytic, phagocytic, and autophagic cargos, and a progressive reduction in accessibility of enlarged lysosomes to the endocytic pathway — a phenotype consistent with impaired autolysosome reformation and failure to regenerate a pool of degradatively competent lysosomes (Cardoso et al., 2023). A salient molecular signature of CQ exposure is accumulation of pro-cathepsin D and the lysosomal membrane protein LAMP1 without corresponding mRNA increases, indicating impaired processing/turnover rather than transcriptional upregulation; protease inhibitor treatment phenocopies this pro-cathepsin D accumulation, linking CQ’s effect to reduced proteolytic capacity (Cardoso et al., 2023). Although lysosomotropic agents can activate TFEB-dependent lysosomal gene transcription at high concentrations, the inhibitory effects on cathepsin maturation and lysosome reformation dominate in RPE models at low doses and precede any compensatory changes in gene expression (Cardoso et al., 2023).

HCQ further impairs RPE lysosomes by perturbing cholesterol homeostasis and promoting lysosomal membrane permeability (LMP), with cytosolic release of cathepsin B  
Beyond general autophagy/lysosome inhibition, HCQ suppresses mTORC1-dependent cholesterol biosynthesis, a change that increases lysosomal membrane permeability and allows lysosomal cathepsin B to translocate into the cytosol, where it can activate caspase-dependent apoptosis and drive caspase-independent phosphatidylserine externalization; these effects are mitigated by neutral pH-selective cathepsin B inhibition and exacerbated by pharmacologic cholesterol lowering (simvastatin) or depletion (methyl-β-cyclodextrin) (Wicks et al., 2022). These data in ARPE-19 RPE cells indicate that HCQ-induced lysosomal dysfunction and LMP sensitize RPE to additional stressors (e.g., UV), compounding vulnerability in aging retinal tissue (Wicks et al., 2022).

RPE/retinal stress signatures and storage phenotypes with 4AQ exposure  
Cell and animal studies document that 4AQ exposure produces RPE and retinal stress consistent with impaired lysosomal degradation: multilamellar myeloid bodies in RPE, photoreceptors, and ganglion cells; inhibition of oxidative enzymes in photoreceptors; decreased retinal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and glutathione with increased lipid peroxidation; disruption of the blood–retina barrier; and inhibition of protein synthesis in RPE culture (Browning, 2014a). In RPE cell culture, high concentrations of CQ perturb fusion of autophagic vesicles, increase LC3-II and p62, and can drive cell death, while intravitreal bafilomycin reproduces opsin-loaded phagolysosome accumulation, affirming that alkalinization is sufficient to cause degradative backlog (Guha et al., 2014). Chronic CQ treatment in mice increases mRNA expression of v-H⁺-ATPase and TFEB, consistent with compensatory attempts to reacidify lysosomes and enhance biogenesis, but does not normalize degradative function during exposure (Guha et al., 2014).

Absence of evidence for “low-dose stabilization” of lysosomal pH in RPE  
Across mechanistic summaries and primary RPE studies, there is no evidence that low-dose HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH at an “optimal” value, preserves cathepsin activity, or enhances POS degradation; rather, the consistent effect is lysosomal alkalinization with inhibition of lysosomal enzymes (including cathepsin B) and blockade of autophagic/lysosomal degradation (Browning, 2014a). In fact, low-dose CQ already yields accumulation of pro-cathepsin D and cargo buildup in RPE, indicating that even modest lysosomotropic perturbation degrades proteolytic competence, counter to the hypothesis (Cardoso et al., 2023).

Pharmacokinetic and ocular deposition constraints  
The extreme tissue distribution and ocular melanin binding of 4AQs undermine precise intraocular dose control: uveal/RPE drug levels can markedly exceed plasma during chronic dosing, and the terminal half-life is long, with months-long detectability after discontinuation due to depot release (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). These properties make “titration” to a narrow, hypothetical lysosomal pH window impractical and raise the risk of sustained lysosomal alkalinization even with ostensibly low systemic doses (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis proposes that submicromolar HCQ will “fine-tune” lysosomal pH in RPE to an optimal range for cathepsin activity, thereby preserving cathepsin function and enhancing POS degradation without blocking autophagy. The aggregate evidence contradicts this at mechanistic, cellular, and pharmacokinetic levels.

- Cathepsins in RPE require an acidic lumen for zymogen processing and catalytic function, and multiple cathepsins (B, L, S, D) are expressed and active in RPE lysosomes where they regulate POS degradation and autophagy; broad cysteine protease inhibition or specific cathepsin S knockdown impairs POS clearance and increases lipofuscin-like inclusions, demonstrating the acid-dependent protease requirement (Sharif, 2015). In this context, 4AQs act as lysosomal alkalinizers that inhibit acid hydrolases; CQ/HCQ inhibit cathepsin B and disrupt cathepsin D processing, with CQ causing pro-cathepsin D accumulation and reduced maturation into the active enzyme, a phenotype directly linked to impaired lysosomal proteolysis and cargo clearance (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). Therefore, the expected effect of submicromolar HCQ is not preservation but reduction of cathepsin function in RPE lysosomes, with consequent impairment of POS proteolysis (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023).

- In RPE cells, CQ/HCQ exposure impairs autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, producing enlarged, cargo-laden lysosomes that are progressively less accessible to endocytic inputs; these dynamics deplete the pool of degradatively competent lysosomes needed for daily POS processing, an effect observed even at “low-dose” CQ and preceding transcriptional responses (Cardoso et al., 2023). Thus, in assays measuring POS degradation and lysosomal flux, HCQ is predicted to slow, not enhance, turnover (Cardoso et al., 2023).

- HCQ further increases lysosomal membrane permeability and releases cathepsin B into the cytosol by impairing mTORC1-dependent cholesterol biosynthesis, activating pro-death signaling and phosphatidylserine externalization; pharmacologic cholesterol lowering/depletion magnify these effects, suggesting that HCQ’s action sensitizes RPE to metabolic and environmental stress rather than stabilizing proteolysis (Wicks et al., 2022).

- Beyond lysosomal pH, 4AQs disrupt other RPE functions essential for photoreceptor support: CQ inhibits rod outer segment phagocytosis in human/pig RPE cell lines, and HCQ/CQ inhibit OATP1A2 in human RPE, potentially perturbing all-trans-retinol uptake and the visual cycle — liabilities expected to worsen POS handling and photoreceptor maintenance in AMD models (Yusuf et al., 2023).

- The claim that “over-acidification” in RPE lysosomes needs moderation lacks evidentiary support in this literature corpus; the dominant pathologic signal in RPE aging and AMD models is lysosomal under-acidification/alkalinization and degradative impairment, which 4AQs exacerbate rather than correct (Guha et al., 2014).

- Pharmacokinetically, due to massive ocular accumulation and prolonged tissue persistence, “low systemic dose” does not guarantee low intra-RPE exposure; achieving and maintaining a narrow “optimal pH” window is improbable and unsafe for chronic indications with slowly reversible tissue exposure (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

In sum, in assays of RPE lysosomal function and POS degradation, the most probable outcomes of HCQ at submicromolar concentrations are lysosomal pH elevation, inhibited cathepsin activity/maturation (including cathepsin B inhibition and pro-cathepsin D accumulation), impaired autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, increased LMP with cytosolic cathepsin B release, inhibition of POS phagocytosis, and potential disruption of retinoid transport — all expected to reduce, not enhance, POS degradation (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023; Wicks et al., 2022; Yusuf et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths for development feasibility  
- Extensive clinical pharmacology and systemic experience: HCQ has well-characterized oral pharmacokinetics, metabolism, and drug–drug interactions, with validated immunomodulatory mechanisms (endolysosomal pH elevation, TLR/cGAS–STING inhibition, cytokine suppression) across rheumatology and dermatology; supply chains and clinical dosing paradigms are established, enabling rapid translational work if warranted (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020; Rainsford et al., 2015). The compound’s canonical lysosomotropic action makes it a useful positive control for modeling lysosomal alkalinization and degradative impairment in RPE assays benchmarking alternative, mechanistically restorative strategies (Browning, 2014b).

- Lower ocular toxicity relative to CQ at equipotency: HCQ is generally less retinotoxic than CQ, a difference attributed in part to greater polarity and lower lipophilicity; however, the class risk remains dose- and duration-dependent and clinically significant (Browning, 2014a; Rainsford et al., 2015).

Critical weaknesses for dry AMD  
- Mechanistic conflict with therapeutic goal: RPE catabolism of POS requires acidic lysosomes and intact cathepsin maturation/activity; 4AQs elevate lysosomal pH, inhibit cathepsin activity (including cathepsin B) and maturation (cathepsin D), impair autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, and induce cargo accumulation — a set of changes that predict impaired POS processing and enhanced lipofuscin burden rather than restoration of lysosomal proteolysis (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). No evidence in RPE/AMD models supports the hypothesis that “low-dose” HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH to optimize cathepsin function; the reported outcomes consistently indicate degradative inhibition (Browning, 2014a).

- Ocular tropism and prolonged tissue persistence: The combination of melanin binding and lysosomal trapping produces extreme ocular accumulation and very slow washout, making precise intraocular dose control infeasible and raising the risk of prolonged lysosomal alkalinization even after dose reduction or cessation (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b).

- Added liabilities in RPE and retina: HCQ promotes lysosomal membrane permeability and cytosolic cathepsin B release in RPE, sensitizing cells to UV and cholesterol-lowering stresses; CQ/HCQ also inhibit POS phagocytosis and OATP1A2 in RPE, potentially disrupting retinoid uptake and the visual cycle, and they induce retinal stress signatures (oxidative enzyme inhibition, antioxidant depletion, barrier disruption) — all detrimental in the aging macula (Wicks et al., 2022; Yusuf et al., 2023; Browning, 2014a).

- Absence of supportive precedent in AMD: Comprehensive pharmacologic and ophthalmic reviews provide no evidence that HCQ/CQ have been successfully used to treat dry AMD or analogous retinal degenerations; rather, they underscore retinotoxic risk and mechanisms consistent with RPE lysosomal dysfunction (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

Strategic implications and recommendation  
The central hypothesis — that low-dose HCQ can fine-tune RPE lysosomal pH to preserve cathepsin activity and enhance POS degradation — is at odds with the mechanistic canon and RPE-focused data for 4AQs, which consistently demonstrate lysosomal alkalinization, cathepsin inhibition or maturation block, impaired lysosome reformation and autophagic flux, and accumulation of undegraded cargo (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). No cited evidence shows that HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH or improves POS degradation in RPE or AMD models; on the contrary, RPE studies with CQ/HCQ and mechanistic summaries emphasize inhibited lysosomal enzymes and autophagy as core actions (Browning, 2014a; Guha et al., 2014). Given extreme ocular accumulation and prolonged tissue retention, exploratory dosing aimed at a narrow “optimal” intralysosomal pH is neither controllable nor safe in a chronic neurodegenerative indication; adverse lysosomal effects could persist despite dose adjustments due to depot release (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). If the program goal is to restore RPE lysosomal proteolysis and POS turnover in dry AMD, agents that acidify lysosomes, facilitate cathepsin maturation/activity, or pharmacologically promote lysosome reformation (as suggested by pathways implicated in CQ-induced defects) align mechanistically, whereas HCQ/CQ, as archetypal alkalinizers and autophagy inhibitors, do not (Cardoso et al., 2023).

Conclusion: HCQ (Sigma-Aldrich H0915) is not a suitable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD under the proposed mechanism. The weight of biochemical, cellular, and pharmacokinetic evidence indicates HCQ will alkalinize RPE lysosomes, inhibit cathepsin function and maturation, impair autophagic flux and POS processing, and increase RPE vulnerability to stress, while ocular accumulation and long half-life amplify risk; no supportive evidence exists for benefit in dry AMD (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023; Wicks et al., 2022; Browning, 2014b). I recommend against advancing HCQ for AMD and suggest redirecting efforts toward mechanisms that restore lysosomal acidity, cathepsin activity, and lysosome reformation in RPE (Cardoso et al., 2023).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of MitoQ as a therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD) based on its chemical origins, therapeutic history, mechanism of action, expected effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and an overall assessment of its potential.

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

MitoQ is a synthetically derived mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant that was developed by chemically conjugating a redox‐active ubiquinone (a structural analogue of the endogenous coenzyme Q10) to a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation via a decyl (approximately 10‐carbon) alkyl linker (Gueven et al., 2017; Rocha et al., 2014). The TPP⁺ moiety is chosen because its positive charge and high lipophilicity enable it to readily traverse biological membranes and to exploit the large, negative mitochondrial membrane potential for selective accumulation in the mitochondrial matrix (Lukashev et al., 2014; Kim & Han, 2017). The synthesis of MitoQ involves standard organic conjugation chemistry where the ubiquinone scaffold is covalently linked to the TPP⁺ unit, thereby converting a relatively non–mitochondria‐selective antioxidant into a compound that is “targeted” to mitochondria in a membrane‐potential–dependent manner (Gueven et al., 2017).

MitoQ belongs to a broader class of compounds known as mitochondria‐targeted antioxidants (MTAs). These compounds are designed to overcome the limitations of conventional antioxidants whose systemic distribution rarely leads to sufficient concentrations in mitochondria—the primary site of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Over the past decades, TPP⁺–conjugated antioxidants (including MitoQ, MitoVit E, SkQ1, and MitoTEMPO) have been actively developed and studied in various preclinical and clinical contexts with the aim of mitigating oxidative stress in a range of disorders (Gueven et al., 2017; Fields et al., 2023). Unlike natural antioxidants that occur endogenously (e.g., coenzyme Q10 in the mitochondrial inner membrane), MitoQ is a synthetic molecule whose design is entirely based on medicinal-chemistry principles that link a potent antioxidant moiety with a mitochondrial targeting domain. This chemical class of compounds has been used in multiple experimental paradigms—including cardiovascular, metabolic, neurodegenerative, hepatic, and inflammatory diseases—where oxidative damage is key to the pathological process (Lukashev et al., 2014; Apostolova & Victor, 2015). In summary, MitoQ’s design confers it high mitochondrial uptake and a redox-cycling ability that is central to its biochemical activities.

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

MitoQ has been extensively evaluated in numerous preclinical disease models because of its capacity to concentrate in mitochondria and scavenge ROS. Numerous animal studies have demonstrated its protective effects in models of neurodegeneration, cardiovascular injury (e.g., ischemia–reperfusion injury), metabolic syndrome, and hepatic toxicity (Gueven et al., 2017; Apostolova & Victor, 2015). For example, preclinical animal models have shown that oral administration of MitoQ can reduce lipid peroxidation, improve mitochondrial respiration, and restore ATP production in tissues compromised by oxidative stress (Kim & Han, 2017; Apostolova & Victor, 2015). Moreover, MitoQ has reached the clinical arena; double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials have been conducted in conditions such as Parkinson’s disease and chronic hepatitis C to assess its efficacy and safety in humans (Gueven et al., 2017; Apostolova & Victor, 2015). In these studies, MitoQ exhibited a favorable pharmacokinetic profile with evidence of oral bioavailability and rapid tissue uptake driven by mitochondrial membrane potential (Gueven et al., 2017; Forini et al., 2020).

Notably, while the broader class of mitochondria-targeted antioxidants has been extensively investigated, the evidence for MitoQ’s use specifically in ocular contexts such as dry age–related macular degeneration is limited. In one animal study of inherited photoreceptor degeneration related to elevated ROS, MitoQ failed to restore retinal complex I activity, glutathione (GSH) levels, or prevent photoreceptor degeneration (Gueven et al., 2017). This result suggests that MitoQ’s efficacy in ocular settings, particularly for retinal degenerative processes, might not be as robust as observed in systemic or neurological diseases. In contrast, other mitochondria-targeted compounds such as SkQ1 have shown promising preclinical outcomes in ocular and age-related conditions (Lukashev et al., 2014; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). Thus, while the therapeutic history of MitoQ in general oxidative stress–related conditions is well documented—with several positive outcomes in cardiometabolic and neurodegenerative models—the evidence supporting its repurposing for dry AMD remains mixed and requires further investigation.

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

MitoQ’s mechanism of action is intricately tied to its structural design and mitochondrial targeting capabilities. Once administered, the TPP⁺ moiety propels MitoQ across biological membranes and into the mitochondrial matrix, where the large negative membrane potential (approximately –150 to –180 mV) ensures that MitoQ accumulates up to several hundred times above cytosolic concentrations (Gueven et al., 2017; Rocha et al., 2014). After mitochondrial entry, the ubiquinone moiety of MitoQ is enzymatically reduced—primarily by Complex II (and potentially by Complex I in some contexts)—to generate its active antioxidant form, mitoquinol (MitoQH₂) (Lukashev et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2014). This reduction is a key step because only the reduced form is effective in scavenging harmful free radicals.

The active mitoquinol acts as an electron donor, neutralizing reactive oxygen species such as superoxide (O₂⁻·) and peroxynitrite (ONOO⁻) (Kim & Han, 2017; Subramanian et al., 2010). In doing so, it interrupts lipid peroxidation chains within the mitochondrial inner membrane—a process that can lead to damage of critical mitochondrial proteins, lipids, and enzymes essential for ATP production. The antioxidant action of MitoQ is not a one-off event; rather, mitoquinol, upon donating an electron, is oxidized back to its quinone form, where it can then be re-reduced by the mitochondrial respiratory chain to continue the cycle (Gueven et al., 2017; Rocha et al., 2014). This rechargeable, redox-cycling behavior is what underpins its classification as a “rechargeable mitochondria-targeted antioxidant.”

At the molecular level, MitoQ is thought to provide protection by directly intercepting lipid peroxyl radicals before they can propagate membrane damage. The proximity of MitoQ’s quinone moiety to the phospholipid bilayer of the inner mitochondrial membrane, thanks to its hydrophobic decyl chain, is critical to its function (Gueven et al., 2017). The compound’s localization is highly dependent on mitochondrial membrane potential; experimental studies have demonstrated that dissipating the membrane potential with uncouplers such as FCCP significantly reduces MitoQ uptake and thereby its subsequent antioxidant effects (Gueven et al., 2017; Kim & Han, 2017).

Beyond its direct ROS-scavenging activity, MitoQ has been shown in several studies to contribute to the preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics. By preventing oxidative damage to components of the electron transport chain, it aids in maintaining mitochondrial ATP production, which is crucial for cellular functions including the energy-intensive process of phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation in RPE cells (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). In addition, there is emerging evidence that targeting mitochondrial ROS not only mitigates damage at the level of the membrane but may also normalize the expression of autophagy markers and improve the overall turnover of damaged organelles (Gueven et al., 2017; Kim & Han, 2017). Such cellular housekeeping functions are intimately linked to the health and function of retinal pigment epithelium, particularly in the context of age-related degeneration where mitochondrial dysfunction and lysosomal impairment have been implicated.

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD Models

Dry AMD is characterized by the progressive dysfunction of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which is essential for the phagocytosis, degradation, and recycling of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Oxidative stress, particularly to the mitochondria within RPE cells, has been implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Accumulating evidence suggests that mitochondrial ROS can impair cytoskeletal remodeling, disrupt lysosomal function, and lead to the accumulation of toxic waste products—all contributing to RPE dysfunction (Gueven et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014).

Based on its mechanism of action, the hypothesis is that MitoQ will concentrate within the mitochondria of RPE cells, where its redox-cycling and ROS-scavenging properties will help to mitigate the deleterious effects of oxidative stress. Specifically, by reducing mitochondrial ROS, MitoQ is expected to prevent oxidative damage to the phagosome–lysosome system. This, in turn, should preserve the efficient uptake and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments, a process that is intimately related to the maintenance of RPE health and function (Gueven et al., 2017; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Experimental assays designed to test this hypothesis would likely involve subjecting cultured RPE cells to oxidative stress (using agents such as H₂O₂ or cigarette smoke extract) and assessing the impact of MitoQ on several key parameters. These parameters include:

1. Mitochondrial ROS levels, as measured by specific fluorescent indicators. A decrease following MitoQ treatment would confirm its ROS scavenging activity (Kim & Han, 2017; Gueven et al., 2017).

2. ATP production within RPE cells, restoring normal energy levels essential for phagocytosis. Effective MitoQ treatment should help normalize ATP levels that are typically depressed under oxidative stress conditions (Gueven et al., 2017; Fields et al., 2023).

3. Lysosomal function and autophagy markers, such as LC3-II, p62, and cathepsin activity, which serve as proxies for the proper degradation and turnover of cellular components. Normalization of these markers in the presence of MitoQ would suggest that its protective actions extend to maintaining phagosome–lysosome integrity (Gueven et al., 2017; Kim & Han, 2017).

4. Photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake and degradation assays in RPE cells. Improved efficiency in these assays following MitoQ treatment would support the hypothesis that MitoQ helps preserve RPE function in the face of oxidative stress (Gueven et al., 2017; Rocha et al., 2014). Although direct published studies of MitoQ in this context are not abundant, analogies can be drawn from its ability to restore autophagic flux in other disease models (Amorim et al., 2018; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Moreover, because mitochondrial ROS has been implicated in impairing cytoskeletal remodeling—a process crucial for the proper formation and movement of phagosomes—the normalization of such cellular dynamics through MitoQ may further contribute to the restoration of POS phagocytosis (Lukashev et al., 2014; Gueven et al., 2017). Given the favorable pharmacokinetic profile of MitoQ already demonstrated in human studies (including rapid tissue uptake and oral bioavailability) (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Forini et al., 2020), it is reasonable to expect that, upon targeted delivery in preclinical models of oxidative-stress–induced dry AMD, MitoQ would attenuate mitochondrial oxidative damage and consequently preserve RPE functional capacity.

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

In summary, MitoQ exemplifies a highly engineered mitochondria-targeted antioxidant with a well-understood chemical structure and mechanism of action. The strength of MitoQ lies in its design: by conjugating a potent antioxidant moiety to a TPP⁺ carrier, it achieves selective accumulation in mitochondria where oxidative stress is most deleterious. This design has been validated in numerous preclinical studies across a broad spectrum of diseases, with several reports of improved mitochondrial bioenergetics, reduced lipid peroxidation, and restoration of redox balance in tissues under oxidative pressure (Gueven et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014; Rocha et al., 2014). Its favorable pharmacokinetic and safety profiles in human trials for other indications further support its potential as a drug candidate (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Forini et al., 2020).

For the treatment of dry AMD, the proposed hypothesis that MitoQ will accumulate in RPE mitochondria and thereby preserve the phagosome–lysosome machinery is mechanistically sound. There is ample biochemical rationale suggesting that mitigating mitochondrial ROS can restore cellular functions such as ATP production and autophagy, both of which are critical in the RPE’s handling of photoreceptor outer segments (Gueven et al., 2017; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). Moreover, the overall reduction in oxidative damage could conceivably stabilize the cytoskeletal dynamics necessary for efficient phagocytosis (Lukashev et al., 2014).

However, several important challenges and weaknesses remain. First, although MitoQ has demonstrated robust effects in many systemic and neuronal models, its efficacy in ocular models, particularly those relevant to dry AMD, remains underexplored. In fact, some preclinical studies have shown that MitoQ failed to restore mitochondrial complex I activity or prevent photoreceptor degeneration in mouse models with elevated ROS (Gueven et al., 2017). In contrast, other mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (such as SkQ1) have shown more promising ophthalmic outcomes, including in phase II clinical trials for ocular surface disease (Lukashev et al., 2014; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). This mixed evidence raises concerns about whether MitoQ’s pharmacodynamics in the retina will meet the requisite therapeutic thresholds needed to prevent or slow dry AMD progression.

A second potential weakness is related to tissue-specific biodistribution. Although MitoQ is designed to concentrate in mitochondria via the TPP⁺ mechanism, the specificity with which it targets RPE cells versus other retinal cell types or non-ocular tissues is not well established. There is a concern that the compound’s systemic administration might lead to underdosing in the RPE, which is critical for its hypothesized mechanism in dry AMD. Furthermore, in neurodegenerative trials—such as those for Parkinson’s disease—MitoQ did not show clinical efficacy, possibly due to limitations in crossing the blood–brain barrier or other tissue-specific factors (Gueven et al., 2017).

Moreover, while MitoQ is effective at scavenging certain ROS, its antioxidant efficacy may also be limited by its own redox cycling; at high concentrations, some studies have suggested that TPP⁺–linked antioxidants might act as pro-oxidants, potentially causing additional mitochondrial stress (Gueven et al., 2017; Kim & Han, 2017). Therefore, determining the optimal therapeutic window will be critical to avoid potential off-target toxicity, especially in a delicate tissue like the retina.

Another consideration is the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD. Beyond mitochondrial oxidative stress, factors such as inflammation, complement dysregulation, and genetic predispositions (e.g., in complement factor H) contribute to its development. While MitoQ’s targeted action on mitochondria may address only one facet of this complex disease, combination therapies might ultimately be required to achieve meaningful clinical benefit.

Strengths of MitoQ include its well-documented mechanism of action, the robust body of preclinical work supporting its ability to restore mitochondrial bioenergetics and reduce oxidative damage in a variety of cell types, and its relatively safe profile in earlier human trials. The synthetic nature of MitoQ allows for reproducible manufacturing and potential chemical modifications to optimize its ocular delivery. Additionally, the concept of directly mitigating mitochondrial ROS is highly relevant in the context of the RPE, where oxidative damage is recognized as a key event in the progression of dry AMD (Gueven et al., 2017; Rocha et al., 2014).

In conclusion, while MitoQ is a promising candidate from the standpoint of its chemical design and systemic antioxidant efficacy, its translation to the treatment of dry AMD remains an area that requires careful and focused investigation. The hypothesis that MitoQ can ameliorate RPE dysfunction via preservation of mitochondrial and lysosomal integrity is plausible, yet the preclinical evidence in ocular models is limited and in some cases mixed. Future studies should involve dedicated ocular pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic assessments, evaluation in relevant RPE cell culture models and animal models of oxidative-stress–induced dry AMD, and careful titration of dosing to avoid potential pro-oxidant effects.

Overall, the candidate exhibits significant promise due to its targeted antioxidant mechanism and favorable safety profile; however, the lack of robust ocular-specific evidence represents a notable weakness. Continued research into its retinal uptake, the effect on phagosome–lysosome dynamics in RPE cells, and comparison with other ophthalmic mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (such as SkQ1 or peptide-based approaches) will be critical for validating its potential in dry AMD. This evaluation suggests that MitoQ is a viable candidate meriting further preclinical investigation, though alternative mitochondria-targeted compounds with more directly demonstrable ocular benefits may also need to be considered in parallel (Gueven et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014; Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Rocha et al., 2014; Kim & Han, 2017; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2014; Sheu et al., 2006).

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
Final Remarks

In summary, MitoQ represents a sophisticated example of mitochondria-targeted drug development with an established scientific rationale and a strong background in combating oxidative stress. Its structural design as a TPP⁺-conjugated ubiquinone analogue makes it particularly suited to accumulate within mitochondria and neutralize ROS—a mechanism that is highly relevant to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. Although preclinical and clinical studies outside the eye have shown promise, evidence specific to retinal diseases is either lacking or inconclusive. Therefore, while the candidate is scientifically sound, further focused research involving ocular-specific models and functional assessments in RPE cells is imperative before advancing to clinical trials for dry AMD. The strengths lie in its well-established mitochondrial targeting strategy, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and systemic safety data, whereas the primary weaknesses involve insufficient ocular efficacy data, potential dosing challenges, and the need to address the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. Based on the literature, MitoQ remains a promising repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD—but further preclinical studies focusing directly on RPE function under oxidative stress and assessing the preservation of phagosome–lysosome integrity are warranted to definitively validate its efficacy.

Preclinical studies in diet-induced obese mice and genetically obese rodent models demonstrated its ability to normalize plasma glucose, enhance insulin sensitivity, and increase mitochondrial capacity without toxicity at proper dosing regimens (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). In these models, SRT1720 was shown not only to mimic the beneficial effects of caloric restriction but also to extend healthspan and, in some paradigms, even lifespan, by improving mitochondrial biogenesis via deacetylation of key transcriptional regulators such as PGC-1α (Feige et al., 2008; Milne et al., 2007). Although SRT1720 has been primarily developed and evaluated for metabolic and cardiovascular indications, its mechanism—centered on the activation of SIRT1 and the subsequent modulation of cellular metabolism, stress response, and anti-inflammatory signaling—has generated interest in its potential applications in other age-related conditions. Specifically, SRT1720 has been shown to interact with a site in the N-terminal region of SIRT1, mapped approximately to amino acids 183–225, which is proposed to undergo a conformational change upon binding of acetylated substrates (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). This effect enhances the deacetylation of key substrates, such as PGC-1α, FOXO1, and p53, which are involved in metabolic regulation, stress response, and apoptosis (Feige et al., 2008; Milne et al., 2007). SU5402 is a small‐molecule inhibitor that belongs to the indolinone, also often described as oxindole, family of compounds designed to target receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), most notably fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs) and platelet‐derived growth factor receptors (PDGFRs) (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). SU5402 is therefore categorized as an ATP-competitive inhibitor that occupies a hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the adenine binding site in FGFR, and its design has inspired many subsequent efforts to optimize RTK inhibition for therapeutic purposes (Manetti & Botta, 2003). In addition to its potent activity against FGFR1 (with reported IC₅₀ values around 0.03 μM), SU5402 displays inhibitory effects toward PDGFRβ and even VEGFR2, positioning it as a prototype multi-targeted kinase inhibitor in early-stage drug development programs (Chen et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2014). Its synthesis is rooted in structure-based medicinal chemistry approaches whereby modifications of the indolinone core and side chain functionalities were guided by crystal structure data and structure–activity relationship studies (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Consequently, SU5402 stands as a well-characterized synthetic compound with a clearly delineated pharmacophore, and its molecular interactions with the kinase active site are illustrative of the class’s capacity to serve as lead compounds in various therapeutic areas (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017).

Historically, the development and use of SU5402 have been predominantly tied to oncology and anti-angiogenic research. Early investigations demonstrated that by inhibiting FGFR signaling, SU5402 effectively blocked the autophosphorylation of the receptor and downstream proliferative and survival pathways such as RAF-MEK1/2-MAPK and PI3K-AKT—pathways that are essential drivers of tumor growth and angiogenesis (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). These studies established its potency in vitro and in animal models, where it was used as a research tool to interrogate the role of FGFR-related pathways in cancer biology (Manetti & Botta, 2003). In addition, several members of the indolinone inhibitor class, including derivatives related to SU5402, such as SU5416 and SU6668, were developed for anti-tumor and anti-angiogenic applications and were advanced to clinical trials for various malignancies (Ho et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016). Despite its promising biochemical profile, SU5402 itself did not progress further in clinical development for oncology, largely due to issues associated with multi-kinase inhibition and subsequent toxicity profiles observed during broader preclinical studies (Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Notably, there is no published record in the literature, as captured by the provided sources, that SU5402 has ever been intentionally repurposed for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal degenerative diseases (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Its application has remained confined as a tool compound in research settings for understanding FGFR signaling and its role in cellular proliferation and angiogenesis, rather than for modulating processes underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) differentiation and phagocytosis. However, its continued use in ocular safety studies in vitro and in rodent models has provided preliminary evidence of an acceptable safety profile when applied topically or delivered locally in ocular tissues (Chen et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2016). Thus, while SU5402 has a rich history as an FGFR inhibitor in cancer-related research, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding its therapeutic use in dry AMD, an area that remains largely unexplored until now.

Mechanism of Action:  
SU5402 exerts its biological activity as an ATP-competitive inhibitor targeting the tyrosine kinase domain of FGFR1, a member of the receptor tyrosine kinase family implicated in various cellular functions including proliferation, differentiation, and survival. At the molecular level, the indolinone core of SU5402 occupies the ATP-binding site in FGFR1, where it competes with ATP for the binding pocket (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Overall, the repurposing of SU5402 for dry AMD represents an innovative and intriguing avenue that leverages a well-understood molecule with a rich background in FGFR inhibition. Its strengths in terms of potency, detailed binding interactions, and the theoretical rationale linking FGFR inhibition to improved RPE differentiation and phagocytic receptor expression provide a solid foundation for further investigation. However, the lack of prior application in retinal disorders, potential off-target effects due to its multi-kinase inhibition profile, and the challenges inherent in repurposing a cancer-targeted agent for ocular use are notable limitations that must be carefully addressed.

In conclusion, while SU5402 is a promising candidate from a mechanistic and chemical standpoint, its utility in the treatment of dry AMD remains speculative at this juncture. The proposed hypothesis that FGFR inhibition during RPE differentiation could elevate the expression of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and integrin αvβ5 is both innovative and scientifically grounded, yet it requires extensive validation using robust iPSC-RPE models and appropriate animal studies before any clinical translation can be justified. A strategic plan involving dose optimization, targeted ocular formulation, and a comprehensive evaluation of off-target effects is imperative to ascertain whether SU5402 can ultimately be repositioned as an effective therapeutic agent for dry AMD (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Auranofin is an orally bioavailable gold(I) complex that was first synthesized as a candidate to treat rheumatoid arthritis and is historically considered the first orally administered gold drug. Chemically, it is composed of a water‐soluble aurothioglucose moiety linked to a lipophilic triethylphosphine ligand, and, upon metabolism, it yields active gold species such as a triethylphosphine–gold(I) cation and gold–thioglucose derivatives (Abdalbari, 2025). Auranofin belongs to the class of organogold compounds, which have long been recognized for their anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties. In general, this class of compounds has been used primarily in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis due to their ability to modulate immune cell activity, interfere with inflammatory cytokine production, and target redox-sensitive enzymes. Although originally developed and clinically validated for rheumatic diseases, research over the past decades has repurposed auranofin for anticancer, antiparasitic, antimicrobial, and more recently, for potential neuroprotective indications (Madeira, 2012; Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a).  

Therapeutic History:  
Auranofin has an established therapeutic history as an anti-rheumatic agent with a clinical safety profile characterized over several decades of use. In the 1980s it was approved by regulatory agencies for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis where it demonstrated comparable efficacy with fewer severe side effects relative to parenteral gold salts, while its oral delivery provided a significant improvement in patient compliance (Abdalbari, 2025). In addition to its use in rheumatology, auranofin has been studied for its anticancer properties, with investigations demonstrating its ability to induce reactive oxygen species (ROS), inhibit cell proliferation, and trigger apoptosis in various cancer models including ovarian, lung, and mesothelioma cells (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a; Mertens et al., 2023). Despite its broad repurposing interest in oncology and infectious diseases, auranofin has not been directly used for treating dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, the cellular mechanisms implicated in its pharmacological actions—particularly its effects on redox homeostasis and anti-inflammatory pathways—provide a compelling rationale for exploring its potential in dry AMD, a disease known to involve chronic oxidative stress, lysosomal dysfunction, and inflammation in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021b; Chen et al., 2023).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary molecular target of auranofin is thioredoxin reductase (TrxR), a critical selenoenzyme involved in maintaining cellular redox balance. Auranofin interacts with TrxR by binding preferentially to its redox-active selenocysteine residue, thereby irreversibly inhibiting its NADPH-dependent catalytic activity (Abdalbari, 2025). Inhibition of TrxR disrupts the thioredoxin (Trx) system leading to an accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and oxidative stress within the cell. This increase in ROS, while potentially cytotoxic at high levels, can also serve as a signal to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, a master regulator of antioxidant responses. Under conditions of elevated oxidative stress, Nrf2 translocates to the nucleus and binds to antioxidant response elements (ARE) in the regulatory regions of target genes, inducing the expression of several cytoprotective enzymes, including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) and enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis and regeneration (Chen et al., 2016; Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a).  

In addition to its redox-modulatory function, auranofin has been reported to affect lysosomal pathways. Preclinical studies in RPE-derived cells (ARPE-19) have shown that auranofin can attenuate lysosomal alkalinization and thereby improve lysosomal function, an effect that may translate into enhanced degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) under oxidative stress conditions (Chen et al., 2016). This effect on lysosomal preservation is particularly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where the accumulation of undigested POS debris contributes to the formation of drusen and lipofuscin, leading to RPE dysfunction over time. Auranofin’s dual impact—disrupting redox homeostasis via TrxR inhibition while simultaneously triggering a compensatory Nrf2-mediated antioxidant response and preserving lysosomal function—constitutes an attractive mechanistic rationale for its repurposing into ocular indications (Abdalbari, 2025).  

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesized mechanism, when applied to RPE cells, auranofin is expected to inhibit TrxR activity, thus initially promoting an increase in ROS production. This controlled elevation in ROS is anticipated to serve as a secondary signal for the activation of Nrf2, which in turn drives the transcription of antioxidant genes such as HO-1 and genes involved in glutathione synthesis, thereby restoring intracellular redox balance (Madeira, 2012; Abdalbari, 2025). In ARPE-19 cell assays, this cascade should lead to a measurable increase in cellular antioxidant capacity, as well as a reduction in oxidative damage markers. Furthermore, by preserving or even restoring lysosomal acidity and function, auranofin is expected to boost the degradation of POS, particularly in cells challenged with lipofuscin components such as A2E that are known to disrupt lysosomal function (Chen et al., 2016). The enhanced clearance of POS should, in theory, mitigate the accumulation of toxic byproducts that contribute to RPE senescence and the progression of dry AMD (Chen et al., 2023; Brodzka et al., 2024). Moreover, the improvement in lysosomal function may also translate into better maintenance of the RPE’s barrier function and phagocytic capacity, both of which are vital for retinal homeostasis. The oral safety profile established in rheumatoid arthritis supports the notion that, with proper dosing and perhaps targeted ocular delivery strategies, auranofin could be repurposed safely for ocular use, though detailed pharmacokinetic studies in ocular tissues would be required to confirm this (Abdalbari, 2025).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Auranofin presents several compelling strengths as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its well-documented history as an orally administered anti-rheumatic agent with an established human safety profile allows for rapid progression into clinical testing if preliminary ocular efficacy is demonstrated. The mechanistic rationale is robust: by inhibiting TrxR, auranofin triggers an increase in ROS that activates the Nrf2 pathway, culminating in the upregulation of cytoprotective antioxidant genes, restoration of glutathione levels, and the preservation of lysosomal function—all of which are key factors in countering the pathogenic processes in dry AMD (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a; Mertens et al., 2023). In addition, preclinical evidence in RPE models indicates that auranofin can modulate signaling pathways such as EGFR/MAPK and that its effects are ROS-dependent, as demonstrated by the mitigation of toxicity with the antioxidant N-acetyl cysteine (Chen et al., 2016).  

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges remain. Although the mechanistic data derived from cancer and non-ocular studies are promising, direct in vivo evidence of auranofin’s efficacy in AMD or related RPE dysfunction models is currently lacking. The cytotoxic nature of auranofin at higher concentrations observed in ARPE-19 cells necessitates careful determination of a dosing window that maximizes the beneficial activation of Nrf2 and lysosomal preservation without exacerbating oxidative damage or inducing cell death (Chen et al., 2016; Madeira, 2012). Furthermore, while the systemic safety of auranofin in rheumatic diseases is relatively well established, the specific requirements for ocular drug delivery—such as achieving sufficient retinal bioavailability while minimizing off-target effects—pose additional challenges that must be addressed through formulation innovation and rigorous preclinical testing (Abdalbari, 2025). Finally, because the pathogenesis of dry AMD is multifactorial, involving not only oxidative stress and lysosomal dysfunction but also inflammatory and complement-mediated processes, it is possible that auranofin alone may not be sufficiently efficacious in a clinical setting without combination with other therapeutic modalities designed to address these complementary pathways (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a; Chen et al., 2016).  

In summary, auranofin holds potential as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD due to its ability to modulate critical redox pathways via TrxR inhibition and subsequent Nrf2 activation, along with its potential to restore lysosomal function and improve the clearance of POS-related debris. Its established safety record in rheumatoid arthritis, combined with promising mechanistic underpinnings observed in both non-ocular and limited ocular cell models, supports further investigation into its use for dry AMD. However, given the current gaps in direct ocular evidence and the challenges of ocular drug delivery, additional preclinical studies specifically in AMD-relevant models (including detailed ARPE-19 studies, in vivo AMD models, and pharmacokinetic assessments in retinal tissue) are warranted to fully validate its therapeutic potential and safety for eventual clinical application (Chen et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2016; Madeira, 2012; Abdalbari, 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The candidate under evaluation is a synthetic Gla‐domain peptide mimetic of Protein S, designated as a 12‐mer peptide (Peptide 2.0 Cat. No. H‐PS12). In its natural role, Protein S is a vitamin K–dependent protein that contains an N‐terminal gamma‐carboxyglutamic acid (Gla) domain responsible for binding phosphatidylserine (PtdSer) on apoptotic membranes and photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and a C‐terminal region that mediates receptor binding to MerTK. This peptide mimetic is engineered to reproduce the key functional motif of the Gla domain that is critical for MerTK engagement. The synthetic peptide belongs to the class of peptide‐based small molecules designed to mimic native ligand functions and to act as receptor agonists. Peptide mimetics have been explored in several therapeutic contexts – for example, peptides that mimic portions of larger proteins often prove advantageous because of their superior stability, lower immunogenicity, and enhanced tissue penetration relative to full‐length proteins. With respect to the ocular environment, the small size and chemical stability of H‐PS12 favor its application as a locally delivered drug via intravitreal injection or topical administration, particularly in diseases such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where targeting the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is paramount (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Extensive literature supports the pivotal role of native Protein S in mediating MerTK signaling in RPE cells and promoting POS phagocytosis. Several studies demonstrate that Protein S acts as a positive regulator of MerTK‐mediated phagocytosis in the retina and that decreased activity of this pathway contributes to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Parinot et al., 2024). Although native Protein S is known to be a critical ligand for MerTK in RPE cells, its direct application as a therapeutic agent is impeded by its intrinsic lability; indeed, purification challenges and loss of bioactivity in recombinant formats have been reported (Prasad, 2006). By contrast, there is emerging evidence that synthetic peptide mimetics – designed solely from the key Gla domain – can overcome these limitations and reliably stimulate receptor phosphorylation. In macrophage models, such Gla‐domain peptides have been shown to trigger MerTK autophosphorylation within minutes at nanomolar concentrations, suggesting a dose‐responsive mechanism that might be recapitulated in RPE cells (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). To date, while there have been reports on the fundamental biology of Protein S and its role in retinal homeostasis, no synthetic Gla–domain peptide has been commercially developed or clinically evaluated specifically for dry AMD. Nonetheless, the concept of repurposing Protein S’s receptor–binding activity through a stable, small synthetic molecule has been theoretically supported by detailed mechanistic studies in vitro and in animal models (Albert et al., 2015; Nandrot, 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action proposed for H‐PS12 centers on recapitulating the critical interaction between the Gla domain of Protein S and the extracellular binding sites of the receptor tyrosine kinase MerTK. In the native state, Protein S engages MerTK by binding to its Ig‐like extracellular domains through specific gamma‐carboxylated glutamic acid residues. This binding requires calcium ions to stabilize the conformation of the Gla domain and mediate a proper interaction with phosphatidylserine on the target cell surface (Nandrot, 2018; Prasad, 2006). Binding of Protein S initiates receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation, an event which subsequently activates intracellular signaling cascades including PI3K‐ and PLCγ‐dependent pathways—processes that are requisite for cytoskeletal rearrangements and efficient phagocytosis of POS (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006; Albert et al., 2015).

H‐PS12 is designed as a synthetic 12–amino acid peptide that mimics the critical Gla–domain sequence of Protein S, maintaining the γ–carboxylation motif necessary for calcium binding and ensuring the correct spatial orientation for receptor engagement. The hypothesis is that when this peptide is administered to RPE cultures, it will bind to the MerTK extracellular regions in a fashion indistinguishable from that of the native protein, thereby triggering receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation at an effective concentration (EC₅₀) estimated to be around 100 nM (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). This autophosphorylation event then propagates downstream signaling leading to reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton, an essential step for the engulfment of POS. Detailed structure–function analyses have provided evidence that mutations in the Ig–like domains of MerTK (such as G122R and K263I) significantly alter the binding and internalization responses to Protein S and Gas6, thereby establishing the binding specificity that H‐PS12 aims to replicate (Parinot et al., 2024). Additionally, calcium dependency and proper gamma–carboxylation are confirmed as pivotal for TAM receptor activation, emphasizing how H‐PS12’s mimicry of the Gla domain can facilitate stable receptor activation (Nandrot, 2018; Lieffrig et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the failure of RPE cells to effectively phagocytose shed photoreceptor outer segments leads to accumulation of cellular debris and subsequent retinal degeneration. The expected effect of H‐PS12 is to restore or enhance this fundamental phagocytic process by acting as a MerTK agonist. When applied to RPE cell cultures – particularly those derived from CFH–mutant lines, which have been shown to exhibit impaired POS phagocytosis – H‐PS12 is anticipated to bind to MerTK, trigger receptor autophosphorylation, and thereby initiate early phagocytic signaling (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). This activation should, in turn, enhance the uptake and internalization of POS, mimicking the natural role of Protein S in maintaining retinal homeostasis (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006).

At the molecular level, following MerTK activation, downstream signaling cascades that include PI3K and the FAK pathway are activated, leading to actin polymerization and phagosome formation. Such events are crucial for the internalization of POS and are known to be compromised in models of AMD where MerTK signaling is deficient (Prasad, 2006; Lieffrig et al., 2023). Moreover, by restoring efficient phagocytosis, H‐PS12 may reduce the formation of lipofuscin and drusen—hallmarks of dry AMD—and ameliorate inflammatory processes that are secondary to debris accumulation (Albert et al., 2015). Furthermore, the localized expression of both Protein S and MerTK in the RPE, particularly at the apical microvilli interfacing with POS, supports the rationale that direct stimulation of MerTK in these cells will yield the desired therapeutic outcome (Prasad, 2006).

Overall Evaluation:  
The scientific premise underlying H‐PS12 is founded on in–depth mechanistic insights into the biology of Protein S and its regulation of MerTK–mediated phagocytosis in the retina. One of the primary strengths of the candidate lies in its well–defined mechanism of action. By isolating the Gla–domain, which has been shown to be critical for engaging MerTK and initiating receptor autophosphorylation, the synthetic peptide addresses a fundamental defect in dry AMD—the impaired clearance of POS by RPE cells (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018). The small molecular size of the 12–mer peptide not only minimizes potential for immunogenicity but also enhances tissue penetration and stability in the ocular environment, which is a significant advantage over full–length recombinant proteins that have been plagued by stability issues during purification and storage (Prasad, 2006).

Furthermore, the therapeutic rationale is supported by experimental findings in macrophage models, where similar peptides have been demonstrated to stimulate MerTK phosphorylation rapidly, hinting at the translational potential of H‐PS12 from immune cells to RPE cells (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). In addition, evidence from studies using native Protein S in RPE phagocytosis underscores the relevance of the MerTK pathway in retinal degenerative processes, thereby validating MerTK as a promising therapeutic target for AMD (Parinot et al., 2024; Kaarniranta et al., 2018).

On the other hand, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be considered. First, while Protein S has been conclusively shown to stimulate MerTK phosphorylation in biochemical assays, functional studies have revealed that recombinant Protein S can sometimes fail to stimulate phagocytosis in RPE culture systems unless in the presence of serum or additional cofactors (Prasad, 2006). This discrepancy highlights the possibility that the mere activation of MerTK by H‐PS12, as measured by receptor phosphorylation, may not fully recapitulate the complex intracellular processes required for effective phagocytosis in RPE cells.  

Another concern pertains to the delicate balance between the functions of Protein S and Gas6 in modulating retinal phagocytosis. Studies have indicated that while Protein S acts as a stimulatory ligand, Gas6 can exert inhibitory effects at higher concentrations, suggesting that the endogenous ligand stoichiometry is critical for optimal MerTK function (Parinot et al., 2024). Consequently, the introduction of a synthetic peptide might perturb this balance if not properly dosed, potentially leading to unintended modulation of phagocytic activity or downstream signaling cascades. This is particularly important given that the RPE is subject to a finely tuned circadian rhythm in phagocytosis, and any exogenous modulation must be compatible with these natural regulatory cycles (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024).

Moreover, the transition from in vitro assays to in vivo models and ultimately to clinical application is fraught with challenges. Although the EC₅₀ of approximately 100 nM suggests a high potency of H‐PS12 in triggering MerTK activation, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of the peptide in the ocular milieu need to be thoroughly characterized. Issues such as peptide stability in vitreous humor, clearance rates from retinal tissues, and potential off–target effects on other TAM receptors (e.g., TYRO3 and AXL) require detailed investigation (Prasad, 2006). In addition, the efficacy of H‐PS12 in restoring POS phagocytosis must be validated in animal models that closely mimic the human pathophysiology of dry AMD, including models that exhibit CFH mutations where defects in phagocytosis are prominent (Parinot et al., 2024; Palczewska et al., 2016).

A further limitation comes from the fact that dry AMD is a multifactorial disease. Although impaired phagocytosis and resultant debris accumulation at the RPE–photoreceptor interface are central to disease pathogenesis, other pathological mechanisms such as oxidative stress, inflammation, and complement dysregulation also contribute considerably to retinal degeneration (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006; Lieffrig et al., 2023). As such, while H‐PS12 is mechanistically attractive from the standpoint of enhancing phagocytosis via MerTK activation, it may need to be integrated into a broader therapeutic regimen that addresses these additional aspects. The long–term outcome of MerTK activation on retinal inflammation, for instance, has yet to be fully determined, even though some studies suggest that active MerTK signaling is associated with anti–inflammatory effects (Albert et al., 2015).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation of H‐PS12 is positive. The mechanistic rationale is robust and rooted in fundamental observations of Protein S’s role in retinal homeostasis. The potential to restore or enhance RPE phagocytosis, thereby reducing the accumulation of POS debris—a key pathological hallmark of dry AMD—makes this candidate highly promising. In particular, the possibility of correcting phagocytic deficits in CFH–mutant RPE cultures represents a novel approach that can address one of the unmet needs in dry AMD therapy (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

Moreover, the simplicity of a synthetic peptide compared to biologics such as full–length recombinant proteins offers advantages in terms of manufacturing, storage, and cost. The use of a 12–mer peptide also minimizes the risk of unwanted immunogenic reactions, which is especially pertinent in the immune–privileged environment of the eye (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). It is also worth noting that any adverse effects related to off–target activation can be monitored experimentally by assessing not only the phosphorylation status of MerTK but also by profiling the activity of related receptors and inflammatory markers in preclinical models (Albert et al., 2015).

In summary, the H‐PS12 synthetic peptide stands out as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its targeted mechanism of action, favorable biophysical characteristics, and the strong mechanistic data supporting the role of Protein S in RPE phagocytosis. Its development represents an innovative translation of basic mechanistic insights into a potentially viable therapeutic approach. Nevertheless, successful clinical translation of this candidate will depend on overcoming several challenges, including ensuring that receptor activation translates to meaningful functional improvements in POS clearance, optimizing dosing to maintain the physiological ligand balance, and rigorously evaluating the safety and efficacy in appropriate in vivo models. These considerations will be crucial in determining whether H‐PS12 can be advanced beyond the preclinical proof–of–concept stage (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

Overall, while the current data are highly encouraging, further studies are needed to address the following key issues:  
1. Quantitative profiling of MerTK phosphorylation kinetics by H‐PS12 in RPE cells under varying conditions, including chronic exposure and in the presence of competing ligands such as Gas6.  
2. Evaluation of the functional outcomes of MerTK activation by H‐PS12 in RPE phagocytosis assays, particularly the efficacy of POS uptake and clearance in CFH–mutant RPE cultures.  
3. Detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies in ocular models to assess the peptide’s stability, tissue penetration, and potential off–target effects.  
4. Integration of the peptide’s activity with other pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis, such as oxidative stress and complement activation, to ascertain whether a combinatorial therapeutic strategy might be warranted.

Given these considerations, H‐PS12 merits further preclinical investigation as a potential therapeutic for dry AMD. Its development is grounded in well–established mechanistic insights regarding MerTK function and RPE photoreceptor maintenance, and its design as a stable, small peptide offers distinct advantages over native Protein S. With careful optimization and validation, H‐PS12 could represent a significant advance in the treatment of dry AMD, providing a novel means to restore the critical phagocytic function of the RPE, reduce debris accumulation, and ultimately slow the progression of retinal degeneration (Parinot et al., 2024; Parinot et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

In conclusion, the synthetic Gla–domain 12–mer H‐PS12 demonstrates a promising preclinical profile as a repurposed drug candidate for dry age–related macular degeneration. Its ability to specifically bind and activate MerTK through a mechanism that mirrors the native function of Protein S, combined with its enhanced stability and ease of ocular delivery, underscores the potential for a targeted therapeutic approach to correct the underlying phagocytic deficit observed in dry AMD. While challenges remain concerning the translation of in vitro receptor activation to in vivo functional efficacy, the foundational data reviewed here support continued investigation into H‐PS12 as a novel MerTK agonist. Future research addressing dosing, long–term safety, and integration with other therapeutic modalities will be essential in determining the ultimate clinical utility of this synthetic peptide in combating dry AMD (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018; Prasad, 2006; Albert et al., 2015).

Overall, despite the inherent complexities of dry AMD pathogenesis and the potential for variable responses owing to the interplay of multiple ligands at the MerTK receptor, H‐PS12 offers a rational, targeted, and innovative approach to restore RPE phagocytic function.
