Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Axitinib is a synthetic, indazole-based, small-molecule receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor originally discovered via medicinal chemistry optimization for anti-angiogenic oncology indications and subsequently approved as an oral therapy (Inlyta) for advanced renal cell carcinoma, reflecting high potency and selectivity for vascular endothelial growth factor receptors (VEGFR1–3) with additional activity against PDGFR-β and c-KIT (Fei et al., 2024; Tosi et al., 2017). In biochemical and cellular assays relevant to ocular angiogenesis, axitinib demonstrates pan-VEGFR inhibition with substantially greater sensitivity than anti-VEGF monoclonal antibodies in endothelial cells, and it also inhibits PDGFR-β–mediated signaling in pericytes at low nanomolar concentrations, consistent with dual-pathway blockade within the VEGF/PDGF axis (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Pharmacologically, oral axitinib exhibits a short plasma half-life (~2.5–6.1 h) requiring twice-daily systemic dosing in oncology, and class-typical adverse events are dominated by hypertension; these PK/AE features motivated ocular delivery strategies to achieve high intraocular exposure with minimal systemic spillover (Siedlecki et al., 2017). As a class, multi-targeted VEGFR/PDGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have long been deployed systemically for cancer and are being repurposed for ocular neovascular diseases with the goals of broader VEGF-pathway suppression and reduced injection burden via sustained intraocular delivery platforms (suprachoroidal suspensions, intravitreal depot implants, and bioresorbable hydrogel systems) (Fabre et al., 2022; Fei et al., 2024). Axitinib is notable among TKIs for very high VEGFR affinity and measurable inhibition of other angiogenesis-related kinases, including TIE2, which has implications for both efficacy breadth and potential effects on vascular stability in the retina and choroid (Leitch et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical ocular data consistently show axitinib suppresses choroidal and retinal neovascularization across models, with oral dosing at 5 mg/kg reducing laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (L-CNV) in mice, and continuous low-dose systemic infusion (0.875 mg/day for 7 days) decreasing fluorescein leakage and CNV lesion area in rats; in vitro, axitinib suppresses 3D sprouting and inhibits both endothelial and pericyte proliferation/migration at non-toxic concentrations, aligning with dual VEGFR/PDGFR blockade (Fei et al., 2024; Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In a rat L-CNV model, axitinib reduced FA leakage scores and CNV lesion area by approximately one-third versus vehicle, and in co-culture sprouting assays axitinib alone outperformed anti-VEGF and anti-PDGF combinations, reinforcing the mechanistic rationale for dual-pathway inhibition in pathological ocular angiogenesis (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Combinatorial approaches show synergy: co-administration with anti-VEGF antibodies enhanced anti-angiogenic effects in nonclinical studies, consistent with the broader concept that inhibiting pericyte/PDGFR-β support can potentiate VEGF-directed therapy (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Siedlecki et al., 2017).

Multiple ocular delivery strategies for axitinib have entered human investigation in neovascular AMD (nAMD) to address the treatment burden and durability limitations of intravitreal biologics, including a suprachoroidal injectable suspension (CLS-AX) and an intravitreal bioresorbable hydrogel implant (OTX-TKI) designed for 6–9 months of sustained release (Fei et al., 2024). Early clinical and translational signals indicate that suprachoroidal delivery achieves high posterior segment exposure with minimal systemic levels, and initial phase 1/2a experience with CLS-AX in nAMD reported acceptable tolerability and pharmacologic activity at low doses, while OTX-TKI demonstrated favorable safety and durability in early cohorts (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020). Across the TKI class, parallel depot strategies (e.g., vorolanib in Durasert, sunitinib depots) have shown biologic activity and reduced treatment burden in nAMD, although some programs reported visual acuity tradeoffs or required rescue therapy at non-negligible rates, highlighting the need for careful dose, exposure, and target-selectivity optimization (Fei et al., 2024; Leitch et al., 2024).

Topical/eye-drop TKI programs (pazopanib, regorafenib, PAN-90806, acrizanib) underscore translational challenges: although preclinical topical dosing can reduce leakage and CNV thickness, multiple phase II programs failed to meet efficacy endpoints or were terminated due to insufficient posterior segment exposure and ocular safety issues such as reversible corneal haze with acrizanib, indicating that noninvasive delivery often cannot reproducibly attain therapeutic concentrations at the choroid/RPE in humans (Fei et al., 2024). Importantly, the available literature contains no reports of axitinib being tested clinically for dry AMD (geographic atrophy) or for enhancing RPE phagocytosis; the development history for axitinib and related VEGFR/PDGFR TKIs is focused on nAMD and other retinal vascular diseases, and reviews repeatedly note a lack of evidence for dry-AMD applications in this drug class to date (Fei et al., 2024). Furthermore, while localized ocular delivery is being pursued to mitigate systemic exposure, case reports of retinal adverse events during systemic axitinib therapy—including impaired retinal circulation, reversible retinal toxicity, and central retinal vein occlusion—require vigilance and thoughtful PK/PD design in ocular programs (Bakri et al., 2024). More broadly, despite active investigation of small molecules for AMD, reviews emphasize that no clinical success stories for small-molecule drugs in AMD (outside recently approved complement inhibitors for GA) have been established, underscoring translational risk for new mechanisms and reformulations (Fei et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Axitinib is a potent ATP-competitive inhibitor of VEGFR1 (FLT1), VEGFR2 (KDR), and VEGFR3 (FLT4), with additional inhibitory activity against PDGFR-β and c-KIT, thereby interrupting intracellular tyrosine kinase signaling downstream of multiple pro-angiogenic ligands, including VEGF-A/B/C/D and PDGF-B (Tosi et al., 2017; Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In relevant ocular cell types, axitinib inhibits VEGF-driven endothelial proliferation with markedly greater potency than anti-VEGF antibodies and exerts nanomolar inhibition of PDGF-driven pericyte proliferation, supporting the mechanistic premise that simultaneous disruption of endothelial and pericyte signaling can destabilize nascent pathological vessels and reduce neovascular growth (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In 3D co-culture sprouting models that recapitulate endothelial–pericyte interactions, axitinib alone achieves robust inhibition of sprout number and length across low-nanomolar concentrations, matching or exceeding the effect of anti-VEGF plus anti-PDGF combinations, a pattern consistent with multi-receptor inhibition at the level of VEGFR/PDGFR RTKs (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Preclinical studies in retinal endothelial cells further demonstrate axitinib suppression of downstream MAPK/ERK signaling and oxidative stress markers, aligning with direct VEGFR pathway inhibition; limited in vitro reports also suggest reduction of VEGFR1/VEGFR2 and PDGFR-β phosphorylation in RPE or mixed cell models, though these do not extend to functional phagocytosis endpoints (Lazzara et al., 2024).

Mechanistically, axitinib’s kinase profile extends beyond VEGFR/PDGFR to other angiogenesis-modulating targets; notably, among three pan-VEGFR TKIs profiled preclinically (vorolanib, sunitinib, axitinib), only axitinib exhibited strong TIE2 inhibition, a pathway essential for vascular quiescence and stability that could influence choroidal and retinal vascular homeostasis under chronic intraocular exposure (Bakri et al., 2024). In comparative kinase panels and endothelial functional assays, all three TKIs displayed robust pan-VEGFR inhibition and abolished endothelial sprouting at high concentrations, but the TIE2-inhibitory signal was disproportionately strong for axitinib, suggesting type-specific off-target consequences that warrant consideration during dose selection for chronic ocular use (Bakri et al., 2024). While intravitreal biologics neutralize extracellular VEGF ligands, axitinib acts intracellularly to block receptor signaling, potentially addressing compensatory upregulation of VEGF-C/D observed with VEGF-A-only inhibition; however, the breadth of intracellular TKI targeting can also propagate off-target effects in non-endothelial cells if exposures are not carefully controlled (Leitch et al., 2024).

Delivery-route pharmacology is central to ocular mechanism realization: suprachoroidal injection of axitinib has demonstrated posterior-segment targeting with markedly elevated drug levels in the posterior eye cup versus intravitreal injection in rabbits and sustained RPE/choroid exposure with minimal systemic levels, thereby achieving compartmentalized receptor inhibition where angiogenic lesions and the RPE reside (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020). Complementary intravitreal hydrogel implant strategies (OTX-TKI) provide long-acting axitinib delivery (6–9 months), maintaining pharmacologically relevant intraocular concentrations to chronically suppress VEGFR/PDGFR signaling in nAMD; these platforms are designed to mitigate systemic adverse events while sustaining on-target ocular pharmacodynamics (Fei et al., 2024). Importantly, chronic VEGF pathway suppression carries theoretical risks for neurosensory retina and RPE health, and reviews emphasize the need to balance durable angiogenic control with potential adverse effects of continuous VEGF blockade in ocular tissues, particularly for non-neovascular indications (Wolf et al., 2022).

Therapeutic targets in the RPE relevant to the present hypothesis—MerTK and αvβ5 integrin—are core components of the photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytic machinery, with αvβ5 required for synchronized diurnal phagocytosis and MerTK essential for engulfment and internalization; however, the provided literature contains no direct experimental evidence that axitinib upregulates MerTK or αvβ5 expression or function in RPE, nor that PDGFR-β signaling tonically suppresses RPE phagocytic differentiation in vivo (Tosi et al., 2017). Reviews and experimental summaries repeatedly state that available axitinib data focus on endothelial/pericyte targets and CNV models, and that no studies directly link axitinib to enhanced RPE POS uptake, MerTK activation, or αvβ5 integrin upregulation in dry AMD models or RPE cell assays (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). Therefore, while axitinib’s biochemical capacity to inhibit PDGFR-β could, in principle, modulate RPE phenotypes if PDGFR-β were a suppressive node in RPE phagocytic signaling, this mechanistic leap is not supported by direct evidence in the provided literature (Bakri et al., 2024; Fei et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The proposed assay hypothesis is that low-dose axitinib will modulate PDGFR-β signaling in RPE to promote a pro-phagocytic differentiation state, enhancing MerTK and αvβ5 expression and POS uptake; however, the body of evidence provided does not include direct demonstrations of axitinib increasing RPE phagocytosis, MerTK activation, or αvβ5 expression in vitro, ex vivo, or in vivo (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). Available data show that axitinib reduces VEGFR1/VEGFR2 and PDGFR-β phosphorylation in retinal endothelial systems and in limited contexts citing RPE/HUVEC cells, but these findings stop short of connecting PDGFR-β inhibition to increased RPE phagocytic function, and no POS ingestion assays, MerTK phosphorylation readouts, or αvβ5 functional binding assays are reported for axitinib in RPE (Lazzara et al., 2024). By contrast, the canonical RPE phagocytic apparatus depends on αvβ5-mediated POS binding and MerTK-mediated engulfment, with genetic ablation models establishing necessity; the literature here confirms this machinery but does not implicate PDGFR-β overactivation as a hindrance to RPE phagocytic differentiation nor demonstrate that TKIs restore phagocytosis in RPE (Tosi et al., 2017).

If the assay system relies on differentiating human RPE and measures POS uptake alongside MerTK and αvβ5 expression, axitinib’s expected on-target effects would be limited to PDGFR-β kinase inhibition in RPE if PDGFR-β is expressed and active under the assay conditions; nevertheless, there is no provided evidence that such inhibition increases MerTK or αvβ5 levels or POS ingestion, and the hypothesis that PDGFR-β tone suppresses RPE phagocytosis remains unsubstantiated here (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). It is conceivable that low-dose axitinib could indirectly affect RPE phenotype via modulation of growth-factor signaling crosstalk, extracellular matrix deposition, or oxidative stress pathways observed in retinal endothelial cells; however, the provided literature does not extend these effects to RPE phagocytic function, and any expectation of enhanced MerTK/αvβ5 expression is speculative in the absence of direct data (Siedlecki et al., 2017; Lazzara et al., 2024).

Translational pharmacology considerations highlight both opportunity and risk: suprachoroidal axitinib enriches drug at the choroid/RPE with minimal systemic exposure, offering a delivery solution for RPE-targeted modulation if the mechanism were validated; at the same time, axitinib’s TIE2 inhibition and class-level concerns about chronic VEGF pathway suppression in the neurosensory retina argue for caution in non-neovascular indications such as dry AMD (Kaiser et al., 2020; Bakri et al., 2024). Moreover, systemic axitinib has been associated with retinal vascular adverse events in case reports, indicating that even low systemic exposures can affect retinal physiology, so RPE-targeted development would necessitate rigorous intraocular PK/PD mapping and safety margins that preserve vascular stability while testing RPE functional endpoints (Bakri et al., 2024). Given these constraints, the expected effect in an RPE phagocytosis assay is, at present, not evidence-based in the provided materials and should be framed as a hypothesis requiring first-principles validation rather than an anticipated outcome derived from prior literature (Fei et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
- Pharmacologic potency and dual-pathway coverage: Axitinib’s high-affinity pan-VEGFR inhibition with demonstrated PDGFR-β activity enables simultaneous suppression of endothelial and pericyte signaling, a combination that underpins robust anti-angiogenic efficacy in CNV models and may reduce fibrosis-linked extracellular matrix deposition in neovascular settings (Giddabasappa et al., 2016).  
- Validated ocular delivery options: Suprachoroidal suspension (CLS-AX) and intravitreal hydrogel implant (OTX-TKI) platforms have progressed into clinical testing for nAMD with encouraging ocular safety/PK signals, providing translationally relevant routes to expose the RPE/choroid compartment while minimizing systemic exposure (Wolf et al., 2022; Fei et al., 2024).  
- Clinical-stage experience in nAMD: Early-phase trials indicate biological activity and tolerability of axitinib-based intraocular approaches, suggesting a viable path to long-acting ocular therapy development if a new indication such as RPE phagocytosis enhancement is supported by mechanistic data (Leitch et al., 2024).  
- Class learnings and comparator programs: The broader TKI field in nAMD (vorolanib, sunitinib derivatives) offers benchmarks for durability, rescue-free rates, and safety considerations, facilitating rational dose and exposure setting for axitinib formulations (Fei et al., 2024; Leitch et al., 2024).  

Limitations and Critical Gaps  
- No direct evidence for RPE phagocytosis enhancement: Across the provided literature, there are no RPE-specific data showing axitinib increases MerTK or αvβ5 expression, augments POS binding or internalization, or improves phagocytic capacity in differentiating RPE; multiple summaries explicitly state the absence of such evidence and confine axitinib’s demonstrated actions to anti-angiogenic endpoints (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017).  
- Unvalidated mechanistic premise in RPE: While PDGFR-β is central to pericyte biology and vessel stabilization, the assertion that PDGFR-β overactivation hinders RPE differentiation and that its inhibition promotes a pro-phagocytic state is not supported in the provided texts, and the core RPE phagocytic machinery (MerTK, αvβ5) is not linked here to PDGFR-β modulation by TKIs (Tosi et al., 2017; Bakri et al., 2024).  
- Safety liabilities and target selectivity: Axitinib’s strong TIE2 inhibition could perturb vascular stability with chronic intraocular exposure, and class-level concerns exist for continuous VEGF pathway suppression affecting neurosensory retina and RPE; rare but notable retinal vascular AEs reported with systemic axitinib further mandate conservative exposure design and careful safety pharmacology tailored to non-neovascular indications (Bakri et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022).  
- Delivery constraints for non-neovascular endpoints: Topical TKI programs frequently failed due to inadequate posterior segment exposure and/or ocular surface safety findings, suggesting that any RPE-targeted application of axitinib would require invasive delivery (suprachoroidal/IVT depot) with chronic exposure, elevating the bar for safety and benefit-risk justification in a dry AMD population (Fei et al., 2024).  
- Field precedent: Reviews underscore that, to date, small-molecule success in AMD has been limited, and there are no approved ocular TKIs for either wet or dry AMD, reinforcing translational uncertainty for new mechanism-of-use proposals lacking direct preclinical support (Fei et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).  

Development Recommendations and Go/No-Go Criteria  
- Mechanistic validation in RPE: Before proceeding, perform a staged in vitro program in human iPSC-RPE and primary RPE to test whether axitinib modulates PDGFR-β phosphorylation and secondarily increases MerTK expression, MerTK phosphorylation upon POS challenge, αvβ5 expression/localization, and POS binding/internalization; include dose-response spanning sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar exposures aligned with ocular PK projections from suprachoroidal or depot IVT delivery (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020).  
- Specificity controls and orthogonal readouts: Use chemical and genetic controls to isolate PDGFR-β dependence (e.g., PDGFR-β ligand titrations, selective PDGFR-β inhibitors distinct from axitinib, and PDGFR-β knockdown), and include neutralizing antibodies and MerTK/αvβ5 functional blocking to map pathway causality for any observed phagocytosis changes (Tosi et al., 2017; Siedlecki et al., 2017).  
- Safety pharmacology in pigmented models: Given potential TIE2-related and VEGF-suppression liabilities, include long-term RPE morphology, barrier function (TEER), transcriptomic stress signatures, and photoreceptor/RPE co-culture viability endpoints at projected clinical exposures; extend to pigmented rabbit or NHP pharmacology to define posterior-segment exposure, ocular distribution (RPE/sclera/choroid), and a NOAEL for chronic dosing (Bakri et al., 2024; Kaiser et al., 2020).  
- Translational gating: Advance only if axitinib reproducibly increases POS uptake and MerTK/αvβ5 functional markers in RPE with a therapeutic window that avoids endothelial destabilization signals and preserves neuronal/RPE integrity in chronic exposure models; otherwise, deprioritize axitinib for RPE-targeted dry AMD and refocus efforts on mechanisms directly validated to enhance RPE phagocytosis or survival (Fei et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022).  

Conclusion  
On the strength of available evidence, axitinib is a validated, potent anti-angiogenic TKI with multiple ocular delivery platforms in clinical development for nAMD and robust preclinical efficacy in CNV models; however, the central hypothesis that low-dose axitinib enhances RPE phagocytosis via PDGFR-β modulation and upregulates MerTK/αvβ5 lacks direct support in the provided literature, and multiple sources explicitly state that no such RPE-centric data exist for axitinib at present (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Fei et al., 2024). The translational and safety profiles suggest that invasive ocular delivery could achieve RPE-adjacent exposure, but off-target TIE2 inhibition and class-level VEGF-suppression risks must be weighed carefully in a non-neovascular indication, particularly absent clear preclinical efficacy on RPE phagocytic endpoints (Bakri et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022). Accordingly, while axitinib remains attractive for anti-angiogenic applications, it should not be advanced for dry AMD on a phagocytosis-enhancement rationale without first producing compelling, direct RPE mechanistic data; in the absence of such data, development resources would be better allocated to candidates with demonstrated effects on MerTK/αvβ5 function or on complement-mediated RPE pathology more proximal to dry AMD pathophysiology (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Fei et al., 2024). Pending rigorous in vitro and ex vivo validation as outlined, the current evidence base supports a cautious “mechanism validation required” stance rather than progression to in vivo dry AMD studies or clinical translation for this proposed use (Fei et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
NBDHEX (6-(7-nitro-2,1,3-benzoxadiazol-4-ylthio)hexanol) is a fully synthetic small molecule that belongs to the class of nitrobenzoxadiazole (NBD) derivatives. This compound was originally developed for its robust activity as a glutathione S-transferase (GST) inhibitor, and its synthesis follows methodologies previously reported (Pasello et al., 2011). As a GST inhibitor, NBDHEX is categorized as a “suicide inhibitor” because it covalently binds to the enzyme’s substrate binding site (the H-site) where it reacts with glutathione in the G-site to form a stable complex that inactivates the target enzyme (Filomeni et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2014). In traditional applications, members of this therapeutic class have been predominantly explored as anticancer agents; they have been used to counteract tumor chemoresistance by inhibiting GST isoenzymes that metabolize and neutralize cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents (Pasello et al., 2011; Filomeni et al., 2008). The compound’s design, structure, and biochemical properties have been extensively characterized within an oncology context, with numerous studies documenting its structure–activity relationships and its capacity to overcome multidrug resistance in cell lines from various cancer types (Filomeni et al., 2008; Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, NBDHEX has been investigated almost exclusively within the realm of cancer research. Preclinical studies have applied NBDHEX against musculoskeletal sarcomas, including osteosarcoma, Ewing’s sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma, as well as in small cell lung cancer and melanoma models (Pasello et al., 2011; Filomeni et al., 2008). In these studies, it demonstrated cytostatic and cytotoxic effects with effective concentrations typically in the low micromolar to submicromolar range, even in drug-resistant cancer cell lines (Pasello et al., 2011). Its anticancer activity has been attributed to both the direct inhibition of GST catalytic function and the disruption of GSTP1 interactions with key signaling proteins such as JNK and TRAF2, which are known to modulate apoptosis and stress signaling pathways (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Pasello et al., 2011). In contrast, there is currently no recorded history of NBDHEX having been used in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or any similar ocular degenerative disease. However, several studies have emphasized the importance of GSTP1 in ocular tissues, particularly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where it plays a critical role in detoxification and cellular defense against oxidative stress (Lee et al., 2014). These observations lend indirect support to the hypothesis that modulating GSTP1 activity—even through inhibition—might have therapeutic implications in the context of AMD. Nonetheless, while the anticancer literature provides extensive data on the pharmacology and safety of NBDHEX in oncology, its potential for ocular application remains largely uncharted and would necessitate rigorous preclinical investigation (Lee et al., 2014).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which NBDHEX exerts its biological effects is well delineated in the published literature. As a suicide inhibitor, NBDHEX anchors itself to the active site of GST enzymes, particularly GSTP1, by binding to the hydrophobic substrate binding (H-site) region; once bound, it reacts in the presence of reduced glutathione to produce a stable, inactive complex (Filomeni et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2014). This covalent modification effectively prevents GSTP1 from catalyzing the detoxification reactions normally necessary to neutralize electrophilic and oxidative species. In addition, GSTP1 is known not only for its detoxification role but also for its involvement in protein–protein interactions, most notably with components of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway including c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and TNF receptor-associated factor 2 (TRAF2) (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Pasello et al., 2011). Under basal conditions, GSTP1 binds to JNK and TRAF2, suppressing their downstream pro-apoptotic signaling. By inhibiting GSTP1, NBDHEX disrupts these interactions, thereby relieving the inhibitory constraints and enabling the activation of stress response pathways mediated by JNK (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Pasello et al., 2011).  
In the context of the RPE, GSTP1 has been documented as a zeaxanthin-binding protein and a critical detoxification enzyme whose levels are reduced in AMD-affected retinas (Lee et al., 2014). This loss of GSTP1 is associated with a diminished capacity of RPE cells to counteract reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated by light exposure, leading to impaired cellular homeostasis and increased risk of retinal degeneration. The hypothesis underlying the use of NBDHEX in dry AMD is that its inhibition of GSTP1 may, in a carefully titrated fashion, increase ROS levels sufficiently to trigger cytoprotective pathways such as autophagy without overwhelming the cell’s defense mechanisms. Indeed, experimental evidence from cancer models has shown that treatment with NBDHEX leads to an accumulation of autophagy markers, including p62 (SQSTM1) and LC3-II, suggesting that the compound can modulate autophagic flux (Sciarretta et al., 2019). It is postulated that the elevation of ROS following GSTP1 inhibition may stimulate the autophagy machinery, thereby improving lysosomal degradation of damaged photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and alleviating one of the pathological hallmarks of dry AMD (Lee et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed experimental scenario—where RPE cells are exposed to oxidative stress—the administration of NBDHEX is expected to inhibit GSTP1 activity at an IC₅₀ in the vicinity of 0.1 µM. This inhibition would lead to a modest and controlled increase in ROS levels. In RPE cells, which normally express GSTP1 as part of their intrinsic antioxidant defense (and where GSTP1 expression is known to be developmentally regulated and inducible by light exposure), an increase in intracellular ROS may serve as a signal to activate cytoprotective autophagy pathways (Lee et al., 2014). As autophagy is crucial for the clearance of damaged proteins and cellular debris—including the phagocytosis and degradation of POS—the induction of autophagy via upregulation of p62 and LC3-II is anticipated to enhance the lysosomal clearance capacity of RPE cells. This could potentially counteract the lipofuscin accumulation and impaired phagocytosis that are characteristic of the dry AMD phenotype (Lee et al., 2014).  
Moreover, literature in cancer cells has documented that treatment with NBDHEX results in a dose-dependent accumulation of LC3-II and p62, markers which are indicative of autophagosome build-up, and—if coupled with improved lysosomal flux—may correspond to functional autophagy (Sciarretta et al., 2019; Pasello et al., 2011). If a similar mechanism operates in RPE cells, the net result could be an improvement in POS degradation under oxidative conditions. Such a response would be particularly beneficial in dry AMD, where defective autophagy and dysregulated oxidative stress are believed to contribute to RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration. Thus, the expected outcome is that NBDHEX, at concentrations that achieve partial GSTP1 inhibition without causing overt toxicity, would restore a more favorable balance between ROS generation and autophagic clearance, leading to enhanced POS degradation and improved cell survival under oxidative stress (Lee et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation:  
NBDHEX represents a promising repurposing candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well‐characterized inhibitory activity against GSTP1 and its documented ability to modulate autophagy in other cellular models. One of the key strengths of this candidate is its robust mechanistic rationale: GSTP1 is known to play a dual role in detoxifying ROS and in suppressing pro-autophagic signaling via sequestration of proteins like p62. In RPE cells—where GSTP1 not only contributes to managing oxidative stress but also interacts with protective pigments such as zeaxanthin—the reduction in GSTP1 function observed in AMD patients implies that further controlled modulation of this enzyme might recalibrate cellular stress responses (Sciarretta et al., 2019; Filomeni et al., 2008). The ability of NBDHEX to disrupt GSTP1’s interactions with JNK and TRAF2 adds another layer of therapeutic potential, as the resultant activation of stress-responsive signaling pathways could further promote cell survival mechanisms. Additionally, evidence from cancer models showing increased levels of autophagy markers such as p62 and LC3-II following NBDHEX treatment supports the concept that this compound can induce autophagic flux, which is of paramount importance in RPE cells for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (Sciarretta et al., 2019; Filomeni et al., 2008).

Despite its promise, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. First, the bulk of the extant literature on NBDHEX pertains to its use as an anticancer agent with applications in solid tumors; there is a notable lack of direct preclinical or clinical studies assessing its efficacy and safety in ocular models or specifically in the context of dry AMD (Pasello et al., 2011; Filomeni et al., 2008). The unique environment of the retina, with its high oxygen consumption, photoreceptor interactions, and specialized blood-retinal barriers, poses distinct pharmacokinetic and toxicity challenges that may not be evident in cancer studies. Second, while the hypothesis relies on a controlled increase in ROS to stimulate autophagy, GSTP1 is an essential component of the antioxidant defense system, and its inhibition could theoretically precipitate excessive oxidative damage if the dosage is not meticulously controlled (Lee et al., 2014; Pasello et al., 2011). Furthermore, some studies indicate that NBDHEX may exhibit limited specificity for GSTP1, with a higher affinity for other GST isoenzymes such as GSTM2-2, which could lead to off-target effects and complicate the therapeutic profile of the compound in non-oncologic tissues (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Filomeni et al., 2008). Finally, ocular drug delivery represents a further hurdle; the ability of NBDHEX to penetrate retinal tissues and safely reach RPE cells within the complex structure of the eye has not been demonstrated and would require rigorous formulation and pharmacokinetic optimization.

In summary, NBDHEX exhibits a compelling mechanism of action that aligns well with the pathophysiology of dry AMD—in particular, its potential to re-establish redox balance and promote autophagy in RPE cells by modulating GSTP1 activity. The strengths of this approach lie in both the detailed molecular insights available from cancer research and the established role of GSTP1 in retinal health. Nonetheless, significant gaps in the literature remain with respect to ocular safety, effective dosing, and the specific cellular context of the RPE. As such, while NBDHEX is a scientifically attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, its translation from oncology to ophthalmology must be approached with caution. Preclinical studies using ex vivo RPE models and appropriate animal models of AMD are essential to validate the hypothesized benefits and to address potential off-target effects. Should these studies demonstrate favorable outcomes—particularly in improving lysosomal flux and POS degradation without eliciting detrimental oxidative damage—then NBDHEX could emerge as a novel therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, addressing a significant unmet medical need in retinal degenerative disease (Lee et al., 2014; Filomeni et al., 2008; Sciarretta et al., 2019).

Overall, the candidate’s repurposing for dry AMD shows promise from a mechanistic standpoint, particularly in enhancing the intrinsic capacity of RPE cells to clear photoreceptor debris and mitigate oxidative stress through autophagy. However, further research is clearly warranted to rigorously evaluate both its efficacy and ocular safety profile before advancing toward clinical application. This comprehensive literature review supports cautious optimism while underscoring the critical need for detailed preclinical validation in the specific context of retinal degeneration (Lee et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SR-3029 is a synthetic small molecule designed to specifically inhibit casein kinase 1 delta (CK1δ) and epsilon (CK1ε). Originally developed in the context of oncology, this compound (catalog number Tocris Cat. No. 6401) belongs to the class of CK1 inhibitors, which have been widely investigated for their role in modulating circadian rhythms and cell cycle regulation. Chemically, SR-3029 has been optimized for high potency with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range (approximately 10 nM) in various cell systems. The compound’s molecular design focuses on targeting the catalytic domain of CK1 isoforms, thereby interfering with their ability to phosphorylate downstream substrates. Historically, CK1 inhibitors have been used to interrogate the biology of circadian processes and have demonstrated promising anti-proliferative effects in certain cancer cell lines, particularly in melanoma models (Battaglin et al., 2021, pp. 9–11). The underlying rationale for its repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) hinges on the well-documented role of CK1 in regulating the stability of circadian clock proteins, specifically PERIOD 2 (PER2), which is a crucial mediator of circadian regulation. Although SR-3029 was initially synthesized with oncological applications in mind, the chemical properties that confer potent inhibition of CK1δ/ε have now been hypothesized to be beneficial in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, where robust circadian timing is essential for maintaining phagocytic rhythms necessary for retinal homeostasis (Battaglin et al., 2021, pp. 9–11).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past decade, the research community has leveraged CK1 inhibitors to explore diverse cellular functions through their impact on circadian and cell cycle-related pathways. SR-3029, along with related analogs such as SR-2890, has been extensively characterized in preclinical cancer models where inhibition of CK1δ/ε resulted in anti-proliferative activity. For instance, studies conducted in melanoma cell lines, including A375, have consistently demonstrated that SR-3029 exhibits robust activity in suppressing tumor cell proliferation by modulating circadian proteins that also play roles in cell cycle control (Battaglin et al., 2021, pp. 9–11). Despite these promising anti-cancer properties, the candidate has not been previously investigated for ocular indications. A comprehensive search of biomedical and clinical literature reveals that neither the CK1 isoforms nor inhibitors such as SR-3029 have been robustly associated with the treatment of dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative conditions. This lack of direct evidence is underscored by data from the Open Targets Platform, which indicates no significant target–disease associations for CSNK1D or CSNK1E in age-related macular degeneration (Buniello et al., 2025). In effect, while the historical therapeutic applications of SR-3029 have been concentrated in oncology, there remains a significant knowledge gap and an unmet opportunity in exploring its potential to normalize circadian regulation in the RPE of dry AMD patients.

Mechanism of Action:  
The fundamental mechanism of action of SR-3029 stems from its ability to inhibit CK1δ/ε activity. CK1δ is a pivotal regulator of biological rhythms, in part by phosphorylating key sites on the circadian regulator PER2. Specific phosphorylation events, particularly at residues such as T347, have been demonstrated to dictate the stability and subsequent degradation of PER2, thereby influencing the periodicity of the circadian clock (Eng et al., 2017, pp. 2–4). Under normal conditions, CK1-mediated phosphorylation tags PER2 for ubiquitin-driven proteasomal degradation, ensuring a timely turnover that is essential for maintaining a robust circadian rhythm. Pharmacological inhibition of CK1δ/ε provided by agents like SR-3029 is expected to reduce such phosphorylation events, thereby stabilizing PER2 and allowing it to accumulate within the cell. This stabilization is theorized to provide a more consistent and regulated circadian signal, which is particularly relevant in tissues reliant on synchronized timing mechanisms.

In retinal pigment epithelium cells, the circadian clock plays an integral role in regulating the phagocytic clearing of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), a process intrinsically linked to the diurnal cycle. The proper timing of phagocytosis in the RPE is essential to nutritive and metabolic homeostasis in the retina, as the RPE is responsible for the daily clearance of shed POS. Experimental evidence from non-ocular systems underscores that CK1 inhibition can lead to enhanced PER2 stability, a critical factor in rhythmic cellular activities (Eng et al., 2017, pp. 2–4, 16–17). Additionally, studies have reported that CK1δ and CK1ε not only affect PER2 stability but also interact in a broader regulatory network that includes proline-directed kinases, such as cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), as well as light-responsive signaling pathways that further entrench the circadian control of cellular functions (Eng et al., 2017, pp. 12–14).

Given these mechanistic insights, SR-3029’s inhibition of CK1δ/ε is expected to directly impact the circadian machinery within the RPE. By stabilizing PER2, the compound may restore circadian phase coherence and improve the timing of daily photoreceptor debris clearance. While the biochemical evidence for SR-3029’s action is robust in non-ocular tissue, the permissiveness of these pathways within the RPE microenvironment remains to be fully documented. Nonetheless, the extrapolation from studies in circadian regulation suggests that the proposed intervention in the context of dry AMD is biochemically plausible (Eng et al., 2017, pp. 2–4, 12–14, 16–17).

Expected Effect:  
The working hypothesis for repurposing SR-3029 in the treatment of dry AMD is predicated on its ability to modulate circadian rhythms in retinal pigment epithelium cells. Specifically, the expectation is that SR-3029 will inhibit the catalytic activity of CK1δ/ε in the RPE at an IC₅₀ of roughly 10 nM, resulting in the stabilization of PER2. The enhancement of PER2 stability is anticipated to restore the circadian timing of phagocytic bursts—a process critical to the timely ingestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by RPE cells. In dry AMD, impaired or misaligned phagocytic rhythms can lead to the accumulation of cellular debris and subsequent retinal degeneration. By reestablishing the diurnal cycle of phagocytosis, SR-3029 holds the potential to improve the clearance of POS debris and sustain retinal homeostasis over time (Eng et al., 2017, pp. 16–17).

In vitro studies with the ARPE-19 cell line have suggested that disruption of circadian cues can be at least partially rectified by targeting CK1 activity, thereby restoring the correct peak timing and magnitude of phagocytic activity. Although these observations derive from limited datasets, they serve as a conceptual proof-of-principle that the circadian machinery—when appropriately modulated—can influence phagocytic outcomes. With SR-3029, the expected sequence of events is as follows: (1) Inhibition of CK1δ/ε leads to a reduction in PER2 phosphorylation; (2) PER2 becomes stabilized and accumulates in a controlled, rhythmic fashion; (3) Enhanced PER2 levels reset or reinforce the intrinsic circadian clock of the RPE; (4) A reestablished diurnal rhythm drives the timely initiation of phagocytosis, thereby ensuring that photoreceptor outer segments are ingested during the optimal time window. The overall outcome of this mechanism should be an improvement in the clearance of POS debris, which is a critical factor in mitigating the progression of retinal degeneration in dry AMD (Eng et al., 2017, pp. 2–4, 12–14, 16–17).

On a molecular level, several markers are anticipated in an effective experimental model: a measurable increase in PER2 protein levels, a synchronized restoration of downstream circadian gene expression, and an improvement in the amplitude and timing of phagocytic bursts as quantified in vitro. Furthermore, if SR-3029 can exert its pharmacological effects specifically within the RPE without significant off-target activities, it may offer a dual benefit by not only modulating circadian rhythms but also potentially ameliorating any concurrent cellular stress responses linked to dysregulated CK1 activity. However, it is important to note that while the proposed mechanism is supported by mechanistic studies in non-ocular tissues, direct in vivo evidence in retinal models of dry AMD remains sparse. The data from the Open Targets Platform reveal an absence of direct associations between CK1 isoforms and AMD, suggesting that while the biochemical rationale is strong, further targeted studies are needed to corroborate these expected physiological outcomes in the eye (Buniello et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, SR-3029 presents as a promising therapeutic candidate by virtue of its potent inhibition of CK1δ/ε and its well-characterized biochemical mechanism that involves the stabilization of PER2 protein. The strengths of this candidate are manifold. First, its high potency at low nanomolar concentrations translates to a favorable pharmacodynamic profile, which has been confirmed in oncology models (Battaglin et al., 2021, pp. 9–11). The ability of SR-3029 to modulate the circadian clock through stabilization of PER2 positions it as an attractive candidate for diseases where dysregulated circadian rhythms play a pivotal role, such as in the daily phagocytic activity of the RPE. The theoretical framework underpinning its repurposing for dry AMD is built upon robust circadian biology, wherein proper clock function is essential for mediating temporal processes like phagocytosis (Eng et al., 2017, pp. 2–4, 16–17). This mechanistic link is particularly relevant given that the maintenance of retinal homeostasis depends critically on the precise timing of photoreceptor debris clearance—a process that is compromised in dry AMD.

Despite the promising mechanistic rationale, there are significant challenges and weaknesses that must be addressed before SR-3029 can be considered a validated therapeutic for dry AMD. A key limitation is the absence of direct evidence linking CK1δ/ε inhibition to improved retinal outcomes in preclinical models of dry AMD. Data from the Open Targets Platform clearly show an absence of target–disease associations between CSNK1D/CSNK1E and AMD, suggesting that the role of CK1 isoforms in retinal degeneration remains underexplored (Buniello et al., 2025). This gap in the literature highlights the necessity for dedicated in vitro and in vivo studies to determine whether SR-3029 can elicit the expected beneficial effects on RPE phagocytosis and overall retinal function.

Another potential concern is the translatability of findings from cancer cell systems to non-transformed, terminally differentiated cells such as those found in the RPE. The anti-proliferative activity of SR-3029, while advantageous in the context of oncology, raises questions regarding its safety profile when applied to ocular tissues. Off-target effects, particularly those that might interfere with the normal physiological functions of non-dividing retinal cells, must be rigorously evaluated. Additionally, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties established in oncological studies may not directly mirror the behavior of the drug in the ocular microenvironment. Issues such as drug delivery to the RPE, potential retinal toxicity, and the compound’s ability to traverse the blood–retinal barrier will need thorough investigation in preclinical models.

From a mechanistic perspective, while the hypothesis that SR-3029 will stabilize PER2 and thereby enhance circadian regulation in the RPE is compelling, it remains a largely theoretical proposition at this point. The published literature underscores the importance of CK1-mediated phosphorylation in determining PER2 stability, but direct evidence for such mechanisms in ocular tissues—particularly in the context of phagocytic function—is limited (Eng et al., 2017, pp. 2–4, 12–14, 16–17). It is critical to recognize that even if PER2 stabilization is achieved, the downstream impact on phagocytic burst timing may be influenced by a complex interplay of additional regulatory factors present in the RPE. Therefore, the expected effect of SR-3029 on diurnal POS ingestion, although plausible, remains to be empirically validated.

A further point of evaluation concerns the broader pharmacological profile of SR-3029. Studies in oncology have demonstrated that SR-3029, along with its analogs, possesses favorable pharmacokinetic properties, such as stability and interactions with cytochrome P450 enzymes, which are indicative of good metabolic profiles (Battaglin et al., 2021, pp. 9–11). These characteristics are beneficial from a drug development standpoint, as they suggest that the compound could be administered with a predictable safety profile and efficacious dosing regimen. Nonetheless, the ocular application of such compounds often requires re-optimization of dosing strategies and formulation development to ensure adequate drug levels reach the target tissue without eliciting off-target toxicities.

In weighing the overall evidence, SR-3029 stands out as a candidate with a strong biochemical rationale, particularly when viewed through the lens of circadian biology. The compound’s ability to modulate kinase activity that governs the stability of the circadian regulator PER2 ties directly into the hypothesis that reestablishing a proper circadian rhythm in RPE cells will lead to improved phagocytosis. Given that impaired phagocytic clearance is a significant pathogenic contributor in dry AMD, this approach represents an innovative therapeutic strategy that moves beyond conventional anti-inflammatory or vascular-targeted therapies. The repurposing of a compound originally developed for cancer therapy to address retinal degeneration is a novel and potentially transformative idea that leverages the deep mechanistic insights gained from circadian biology research (Battaglin et al., 2021, pp. 9–11; Buniello et al., 2025; Eng et al., 2017, pp. 2–4, 12–14, 16–17).

Conversely, the most notable weakness of the proposal lies in the current disconnect between the known pharmacodynamic actions of CK1 inhibitors and their demonstrated efficacy in retinal models of dry AMD. The lack of pre-existing data specifically linking CK1δ/ε inhibition with improvements in RPE phagocytosis, coupled with the Open Targets Platform’s indication of no known target–disease link between these kinases and AMD, raises concerns about the translational relevance of this approach (Buniello et al., 2025). Moreover, even though the anti-proliferative effects of SR-3029 are well documented in melanoma and related cancer models (Battaglin et al., 2021, pp. 9–11), these effects may not necessarily translate into clinical benefits in the context of retinal diseases, where the cellular landscape and treatment paradigms differ substantially.

In addition, the intricate balance of kinase signaling in the RPE must be considered. CK1 isoforms are involved in a myriad of cellular processes beyond circadian regulation, including cell survival, metabolism, and stress responses. Therefore, global inhibition of CK1δ/ε could theoretically disrupt other homeostatic processes, potentially leading to unintended consequences. Such off-target or pleiotropic effects, while possibly tolerable in cancer treatment—where the therapeutic window is often broader—could be more problematic in the delicate environment of the retina, where precise regulation is paramount.

It is also important to consider the broader landscape of AMD research. Many current therapeutic efforts in AMD focus on anti-angiogenic agents and complement pathway inhibitors; targeting the circadian machinery represents a relatively unexplored avenue. This novelty, while offering the potential for breakthroughs, also entails increased risk, as the underlying biology connecting circadian dysfunction to AMD pathology is not yet fully understood. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Homotaurine is a small-molecule GABA analogue that was originally investigated for its potential neuroprotective properties in Alzheimer’s disease due to its ability to interact with inhibitory neurotransmitter receptors. Although originally isolated from marine algae as a natural sulfonated amino acid derivative, the synthetic production of homotaurine has allowed for its repurposing and pharmacological refinement for various clinical indications. As a member of the GABAergic modulator class, it is designed to mimic the activity of the endogenous neurotransmitter γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), thereby affecting neuronal excitability and cellular homeostasis. In particular, homotaurine is postulated to activate GABAA receptors, which are ligand-gated chloride channels that normally contribute to membrane hyperpolarization and dampening of excitatory input. This class of compounds has been widely explored for neuroprotective purposes and has been utilized in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease, where an acceptable safety profile was established. The fact that homotaurine has progressed to advanced clinical stages in Alzheimer’s research supports its tolerability and widespread bioactivity, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in ocular diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Carullo et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, homotaurine has been primarily evaluated in the context of Alzheimer’s disease, where its anti-aggregation properties and potential to interfere with amyloid-β deposition were of paramount interest. Its prior clinical examination, which concluded with a favorable safety record, provides a solid foundation for its repurposing in other neurodegenerative conditions. Although there is no direct record of homotaurine being used to treat dry AMD, other compounds that modulate GABAergic signaling have been investigated in retinal degenerative models. For example, several studies have documented the expression of GABA receptor subunits, including those of the GABAA family, in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, suggesting that pharmacological targeting of these receptors may have therapeutic implications in diseases associated with retinal dysfunction (Arellano et al., 2025). Furthermore, inhibitory neurotransmitters such as GABA have been implicated in maintaining proper cellular excitability and synaptic balance in the retina; alterations in their regulation are associated with excitotoxicity and neurodegeneration in retinal conditions including macular degeneration (Pavan & Dalpiaz, 2018; Schur et al., 2018). In a similar vein, preclinical studies have used GABA modulators to rescue or protect RPE and photoreceptor function in models of retinal degeneration and light-induced injury (Schur et al., 2018). Thus, while direct clinical evidence for homotaurine in dry AMD is lacking, its antecedents in the GABAergic drug class and the known vulnerability of RPE cells to excitotoxic calcium overload position it as a promising candidate for therapeutic repurposing.

Mechanism of Action:  
The hypothesized mechanism of action of homotaurine in dry AMD rests on its ability to activate GABAA receptors expressed on RPE cells. Under physiological conditions, GABAA receptors are heteropentameric chloride channels that, upon binding GABA, permit chloride influx and hyperpolarize the cell membrane. This hyperpolarization ordinarily serves to counteract excessive excitation and limit voltage-gated calcium channel opening. In the context of RPE function, maintaining a tight regulation of intracellular calcium is paramount because calcium levels directly influence cytoskeletal reorganization, phagosome trafficking, and lysosomal fusion events necessary for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Nagymihaly et al., 2021). Several studies have documented that RPE cells not only express GABAA receptor subunits, such as GABAAα1, but that receptor activation in these cells can modify intracellular calcium concentrations, thereby modulating a host of calcium-dependent cellular processes—including phagocytosis (Arellano et al., 2025).

In dry AMD, the RPE’s phagocytic capacity is compromised, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and other toxic by-products, which in turn further disrupt cellular function and promote oxidative stress (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018). Homotaurine’s binding to GABAA receptors is expected to stabilize the membrane potential and reduce the abnormal Ca²⁺ influx that occurs during excitotoxic stress. This reduction in calcium entry is anticipated to alleviate downstream effects such as dysregulated cytoskeletal dynamics and impaired lysosomal trafficking. Cytoskeletal reorganization is essential for phagosome motility; proper F-actin dynamics direct the trafficking of phagosomes toward lysosomal compartments where degradation occurs (Inana et al., 2018; Nagymihaly et al., 2021). Moreover, studies have demonstrated that inflammatory mediators present in AMD, including TNF-α and interleukin-1β, modulate GABAA receptor expression and function, suggesting that modulation of these receptors could be a viable strategy to counteract inflammation-driven excitotoxicity (Arellano et al., 2025). In addition, the excitotoxic environment generated by imbalanced glutamate/GABA signaling in the retina can be mitigated by restoring the inhibitory tone through GABAA receptor activation. The specific EC₅₀ of approximately 10 µM for homotaurine indicates that it has the potential to achieve receptor activation within a therapeutic window that is plausible in an ocular formulation (Carullo et al., 2020; Arellano et al., 2025). Taken together, the combined modulation of calcium influx, along with the stabilization of cytoskeletal and lysosomal pathways, constitutes a comprehensive molecular strategy that homotaurine may employ to rescue impaired POS degradation in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed assay in ARPE-19 cells—a well-established in vitro model for RPE function—aims to evaluate whether homotaurine, via activation of GABAA receptors, can restore impaired photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis under conditions of glutamate-induced stress. RPE cell dysfunction in dry AMD is characterized by diminished phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation of POS, leading to the pathological accumulation of lipofuscin, which further impedes cellular function (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018). By engaging GABAA receptors, homotaurine is expected to “rescue” this vital phagocytic process by normalizing intracellular Ca²⁺ dynamics—thus preventing excitotoxicity—and by ensuring the proper reorganization of actin filaments or other cytoskeletal elements that are essential for efficient phagosome motility (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).

Experimental evidence in related studies supports that compounds with similar mechanisms (i.e., GABA modulators and taurine-related molecules) are capable of influencing intracellular calcium signaling and can enhance the uptake and processing of POS in RPE cells (Arellano et al., 2025; López-Colomé et al., 1994). Under normo-physiological conditions, RPE cells efficiently internalize shed POS through receptor-mediated pathways involving CD36, MerTK, and αVβ5 integrin, initiating a cascade that is dependent on well-regulated intracellular Ca²⁺ fluctuations (Nagymihaly et al., 2021). In a stress state, glutamate excess drives excitotoxic Ca²⁺ entry that may dysregulate these processes. By antagonizing this excitotoxic cascade, homotaurine is anticipated to reduce the aberrant Ca²⁺ load, thereby restoring the dynamic equilibrium that supports both cytoskeletal integrity and lysosomal trafficking. This mechanism is supported by studies showing that dysregulation of Ca²⁺ not only impairs phagosome motility but also has deleterious effects on downstream lysosomal fusion and degradation, ultimately impacting cellular clearance mechanisms (Si et al., 2023; Nowak et al., 2025). Thus, the expected effect is a measurable enhancement in POS uptake as well as improved degradation kinetics in RPE cells subjected to glutamate-induced stress, which would correlate with potential therapeutic efficacy in dry AMD. Furthermore, since the underlying pathology of dry AMD involves chronic oxidative stress and accumulation of metabolic by-products, a pharmacological intervention that can restore intracellular homeostasis has far-reaching implications for halting or even reversing disease progression (Arellano et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating homotaurine for dry age-related macular degeneration, several critical observations emerge. One of the key strengths of homotaurine is its well-documented safety profile from Alzheimer’s clinical trials, which lowers the translational hurdles when repurposing the compound for ocular administration. The fact that homotaurine is a GABA analogue that activates GABAA receptors—a receptor class that is expressed on RPE cells and critically involved in regulating intracellular Ca²⁺—provides a strong mechanistic rationale for its application in dry AMD (Arellano et al., 2025). By potentially mitigating excitotoxic Ca²⁺ influx, homotaurine could restore normal cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal trafficking, both of which are indispensable for the effective degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).

Among the strengths, the following points are notable:  
1. The candidate’s mechanism directly addresses a central pathology of dry AMD—namely, impaired RPE phagocytosis and lysosomal dysfunction—which leads to toxic lipofuscin accumulation (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018).  
2. Activation of GABAA receptors by homotaurine could normalize Ca²⁺ handling within RPE cells, thereby alleviating the excitotoxic stress that is linked to altered cytoskeletal assembly and defective phagosome trafficking (Arellano et al., 2025; Inana et al., 2018).  
3. The compound’s history in Alzheimer’s trials suggests a favorable safety margin and known pharmacokinetic properties that may be adapted for ocular use, thus enhancing its potential for rapid clinical translation (Carullo et al., 2020).  
4. Preclinical evidence from other studies involving GABA modulators and related compounds shows that interfering with aberrant neurotransmitter signaling in the retina can elicit neuroprotective and phagocytosis-enhancing effects (Schur et al., 2018).

Conversely, some weaknesses and uncertainties remain that necessitate further investigation:  
1. Although the proposed EC₅₀ of approximately 10 µM for homotaurine is within a plausible therapeutic window for GABAA receptor activation, the actual pharmacodynamic response in RPE cells—especially in the diseased microenvironment of dry AMD—remains to be rigorously quantified (Arellano et al., 2025).  
2. The retinal microenvironment in dry AMD is complex, characterized not only by excitotoxic stress but also by chronic oxidative stress, inflammation, and altered expression of multiple receptor types. In such a context, GABAA receptor activation could be affected by altered ionic gradients, potentially leading to reversed or atypical receptor responses as has been documented in other retinal degenerations (Arellano et al., 2025; Telegina et al., 2022).  
3. While indirect evidence supports the role of GABAergic modulation in restoring phagocytic function, there is a paucity of direct data demonstrating that homotaurine can specifically enhance POS uptake in ARPE-19 cells under injurious conditions. This gap necessitates additional in vitro studies to detail its effects on cytoskeletal reorganization, vesicular trafficking, and lysosomal fusion dynamics (Si et al., 2023; Nagymihaly et al., 2021).  
4. The exact downstream signaling pathways that link GABAA receptor activation to the observed improvements in phagocytic function must be delineated further. For example, the interplay between calcium channel deactivation, actin cytoskeleton stabilization, and the regulation of key phagocytic receptors (e.g., MerTK, αvβ5 integrin) remains incompletely characterized in the context of GABAergic modulation (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).  
5. Finally, the translational leap from in vitro findings in ARPE-19 cells to a robust therapeutic effect in human dry AMD patients is non-trivial. Aging RPE cells in vivo exhibit additional layers of complexity, including altered gene expression profiles, metabolic imbalances, and possible shifts in receptor isoforms, all of which might influence the responsiveness to homotaurine (Nowak et al., 2025; Si et al., 2023).

Overall, homotaurine represents a scientifically sound and mechanistically plausible candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its potential to activate GABAA receptors on RPE cells, thereby reducing excitotoxic calcium influx and normalizing the intracellular processes that govern cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal trafficking, aligns well with the pathophysiological underpinnings of AMD (Arellano et al., 2025). Given the favorable safety data from Alzheimer’s trials and the breadth of preclinical evidence supporting the neuroprotective effects of GABAergic modulation in retinal contexts, homotaurine merits further exploration. Prior to clinical application, however, detailed mechanistic studies using ARPE-19 cells and appropriate animal models of dry AMD must be conducted. These studies should focus on quantifying calcium flux, cytoskeletal dynamics, phagosome motility, and lysosomal fusion efficiency upon homotaurine treatment under pathologically relevant conditions. Additionally, it will be important to investigate potential off-target effects and to determine whether combinatorial therapies that address oxidative stress and inflammation might synergize with homotaurine’s mechanism. In summary, while challenges remain, the repurposing of homotaurine for dry AMD offers a promising therapeutic avenue worthy of investment and further preclinical validation (Arellano et al., 2025; Si et al., 2023; Carullo et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human MCP-1 (monocyte chemoattractant protein-1), also known as CCL2, is a biologically active recombinant cytokine derived using modern recombinant protein production techniques under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) conditions (Ramkumar et al., 2010). This molecule belongs to the CC chemokine family and is naturally secreted in response to tissue injury and inflammatory stimuli, where it functions primarily to recruit monocytes, memory T cells, and dendritic cells via binding to its cognate receptor CCR2 (Chen & Xu, 2015). Its synthesis involves expression in appropriate host cells (commonly mammalian or bacterial expression systems) followed by purification and rigorous quality control measures, such that its physicochemical properties and pharmacokinetics are well characterized for ocular administration (Tolentino et al., 2023; Wong et al., 2022). As a therapeutic candidate, recombinant human MCP-1 represents a protein biologic aiming to restore a natural homeostatic mechanism that appears to be compromised in age-related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly in models where a deficiency in CCL2 drives drusen-like lesions through impaired recruitment and function of phagocytic cells (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the biological role of MCP-1 has been extensively characterized in both experimental and genetic models of inflammatory and degenerative diseases. In murine models of AMD, genetic knockout studies have demonstrated that deficiency in Ccl2 (the murine homolog) results in the development of AMD-like retinal changes including drusen-like deposits, thickening and fragmentation of Bruch’s membrane, disrupted collagen and elastin layers, and eventual retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009). These findings have provided substantial preclinical evidence that the CCL2/CCR2 axis is critical for the recruitment of monocytes to the subretinal space, thus facilitating debris clearance and maintenance of retinal homeostasis (Chen & Xu, 2015; DaCosta, 2015). In contrast, some studies have also indicated that improper or excessive recruitment of CCR2⁺ cells may lead to pathological states, including amplified inflammatory cytokine production (Chen & Xu, 2015) and even contribute to angiogenic responses under certain conditions (Hu et al., 2016; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). While recombinant MCP-1 has been used in basic research to probe the role of chemokine signaling in immune cell trafficking and inflammation in various diseases, its direct therapeutic application for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative conditions has not been previously established in clinical or formal veterinary studies (Marin-Castaño, 2013). The unique proposition in the current candidate is to administer low doses of recombinant MCP-1 directly into the subretinal space in order to restore the regulated recruitment of monocytes and thereby improve clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris—a strategy that has been hypothesized based on earlier experimental findings (Luhmann et al., 2009; Chen & Xu, 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
MCP-1 functions as a chemoattractant by binding with high affinity to the CCR2 receptor expressed on inflammatory monocytes and certain subsets of macrophages. Once the ligand binds, it initiates a cascade of intracellular signaling events mediated by G-proteins that result in actin cytoskeleton reorganization, cell polarization, and directed migration towards higher concentrations of MCP-1 (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Chen & Xu, 2015). In the context of ocular physiology, RPE cells under stress conditions or oxidative insult have been shown to secrete MCP-1 as part of an endogenous mechanism intended to attract CCR2⁺ monocytes to areas of debris accumulation (Marin-Castaño, 2013). These recruited monocytes are expected to differentiate into macrophages capable of phagocytosing shed POS debris and other cellular waste products that accumulate with aging and contribute to drusen formation (Luhmann et al., 2009). At the molecular level, binding of MCP-1 to CCR2 results in receptor dimerization and the activation of downstream effectors such as phospholipase C, MAP kinases, and small GTPases that collectively drive cytoskeletal changes and cell motility (Chen & Xu, 2015). It is important to note that the MCP-1/CCR2 axis is tightly regulated, and its function is context dependent; in some models, an overactive response can lead to exacerbated inflammation, while in others the signaling is critical for normal tissue repair and debris clearance (Luhmann et al., 2009; DaCosta, 2015). The hypothesis under evaluation contends that a carefully titrated, low-dose supplementation of recombinant MCP-1 in a dry AMD setting—characterized by Ccl2 deficiency—is capable of reinstating physiologic levels of monocyte recruitment to the subretinal space, thereby bolstering the phagocytic capacity of these cells and normalizing RPE function in terms of outer segment processing (Tolentino et al., 2023; Luhmann et al., 2009).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed mechanism, the expected outcome of administering low-dose recombinant human MCP-1 is an enhancement in the homing behavior of CCR2⁺ monocytes toward the subretinal space. In experimental models where Ccl2 deficiency leads to an accumulation of drusen-like deposits, the rationale is that MCP-1 supplementation will counter the defect in chemotactic signaling, allowing monocytes to effectively transmigrate through the choriocapillaris and accumulate at sites in the retina where depot of POS debris occurs (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009). In these settings, recruited monocytes are anticipated to engage in active phagocytosis of lipofuscin-laden debris, thus alleviating the burden on the RPE cells which are responsible for digesting and recycling photoreceptor outer segments (Chen & Xu, 2015; Marin-Castaño, 2013). Improvement in the RPE’s phagocytic index is hypothesized to lead to several beneficial downstream effects; these include reduced drusen formation, preservation of the structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane, and ultimately a deceleration in the progression of dry AMD pathology (Luhmann et al., 2009). Furthermore, because recombinant MCP-1 is provided in a controlled low-dose fashion, the intended effect is to mimic the physiological signaling observed in the nonpathological state, thereby avoiding overactivation of inflammatory pathways that could otherwise potentiate a deleterious chronic inflammatory milieu (Marin-Castaño, 2013). It should be emphasized that while the concept is theoretically sound, there remains an inherent risk that the recruited monocytes, if not adequately polarized into a reparative (or M2) phenotype, might adopt a pro-inflammatory (or M1) profile that could exacerbate local tissue damage (Chen & Xu, 2015; Elbaz-Hayoun et al., 2023). Thus, the assay’s success will hinge on demonstrating that low-dose MCP-1 can selectively enhance beneficial debris clearance while avoiding unintended inflammatory side effects—a balance that must be meticulously evaluated in preclinical models before any translation to clinical settings (DaCosta, 2015; Tolentino et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
A comprehensive evaluation of recombinant human MCP-1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a candidate with a strong biological rationale based on its central role in monocyte recruitment and tissue repair. The primary strength of this candidate lies in its capacity to restore a key homeostatic function that is compromised in Ccl2 deficiency models of AMD, as evidenced by robust preclinical data showing that diminished MCP-1 signaling correlates with drusen accumulation and RPE dysfunction (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009). Moreover, the fact that recombinant MCP-1 is available as GMP-grade material with known ocular pharmacokinetic properties lends a degree of translational feasibility to the proposed studies (Wong et al., 2022; Tolentino et al., 2023). The hypothesis that subretinal injection of low-dose MCP-1 can ameliorate debris accumulation by recruiting CCR2⁺ monocytes is supported by the well-established molecular interactions between MCP-1 and CCR2, which have been validated in several inflammatory and degenerative models (Chen & Xu, 2015; Marin-Castaño, 2013).

However, several critical weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, the literature presents conflicting roles for the MCP-1/CCR2 axis in AMD pathogenesis. While genetic deficiencies in CCL2 lead to drusen-like lesions, other studies have shown that blocking MCP-1/CCR2 signaling can yield protective effects by reducing inflammatory monocyte recruitment and subsequent tissue damage (Hu et al., 2016; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Elbaz-Hayoun et al., 2023). This dichotomy underscores the delicate balance between debris clearance and inflammation; excessive or misdirected monocyte recruitment may inadvertently exacerbate retinal degeneration rather than ameliorate it (Marin-Castaño, 2013; Tolentino et al., 2023). Second, there is a substantial risk that exogenously administered MCP-1—even at low doses—could stimulate an overzealous inflammatory response if it fails to promote the desired anti-inflammatory, reparative monocyte phenotype. Given that monocyte polarization is highly context dependent, additional studies would be required to ensure that the recruited cells adopt a phenotype conducive to tissue repair rather than one that contributes to chronic inflammation or neovascular complications (Chen & Xu, 2015; Elbaz-Hayoun et al., 2023). Third, while the candidate hypothesis is partly based on observations from knockout models, these models have inherent limitations; some studies indicate that the majority of AMD-related morphological changes in Ccl2- and Ccr2-deficient mice may actually represent accelerated aging rather than true disease pathology (Luhmann et al., 2009; Tolentino et al., 2023). Thus, extrapolating these findings to a therapeutic scenario in human dry AMD requires careful validation in models that more accurately recapitulate the human disease phenotype.

In summary, recombinant human MCP-1 holds promise as a novel therapeutic strategy for dry AMD by potentially restoring a physiologic mechanism for debris clearance through the recruitment of CCR2⁺ monocytes. Its strengths include its well-characterized molecular mechanism, availability as a GMP-grade product with defined ocular pharmacokinetics, and a solid preclinical rationale based on studies showing that CCL2 deficiency leads to AMD-like pathology (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009). Conversely, its weaknesses stem from the complex and sometimes contradictory roles of the MCP-1/CCR2 axis in retinal inflammation and degeneration, the risk of inadvertently triggering detrimental inflammatory responses, and the challenge of translating findings from knockout models to a clinical setting (Hu et al., 2016; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Elbaz-Hayoun et al., 2023). Given these considerations, while the candidate is scientifically intriguing, further rigorous preclinical research is essential to define the appropriate dosing regimen, confirm the beneficial polarization of recruited monocytes, and rule out any potential exacerbation of inflammatory pathology before advancing to clinical trials. This balanced approach will ultimately determine whether recombinant MCP-1 can be viably repurposed as a therapeutic agent to mitigate the progression of dry AMD by enhancing RPE function and debris clearance (Marin-Castaño, 2013; DaCosta, 2015).
