Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
D609, chemically known as tricyclodecan-9-yl xanthogenate, is a synthetic small‐molecule compound belonging to the xanthate class. It was originally synthesized through classical organic‐chemical methods involving the reaction of diastereomeric tricyclic alcohols with carbon disulfide in the presence of a strong base such as potassium tert‐butoxide, yielding a mixture of eight stereoisomers due to its three asymmetric centers (Bhat et al., 2022; Eurtivong et al., 2023). As a member of the xanthate family, D609 has been extensively studied for its diverse biological activities that include antiviral, antitumoral, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective effects (Bhat et al., 2022). Its mechanism of competitive inhibition of phosphatidylcholine-specific phospholipase C (PC-PLC) was discovered during the evaluation of lipid signaling pathways, and it is commercially available (for example, Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. D0209) as a research-grade compound (Wang et al., 2020). This chemical class has traditionally been investigated in various biomedical contexts, with early work focusing on its antiviral properties dating back to the 1980s and subsequent studies extending its uses into oncology and neurology (Bhat et al., 2022). Its water solubility and relatively low molecular weight make it an attractive candidate for repurposing into ocular applications where intracellular signaling and oxidative stress play key roles.

Therapeutic History:  
D609 has been the subject of more than 700 published reports over the last three decades and has been explored in preclinical studies ranging from antiviral and anticancer applications to neuroprotection and inflammation modulation (Bhat et al., 2022). One of the most compelling lines of evidence for repurposing D609 concerns its potential in treating ocular conditions, particularly dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In several studies, D609 has been directly evaluated for its ability to protect retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) cells from oxidative damage using in vitro cell models such as the widely used ARPE-19 cell line and primary human RPE cells (Wang et al., 2020). For instance, one study employing a high-content screening strategy on 814 protective compounds identified D609 as a lead candidate that maintained RPE cell viability above 95% under severe oxidative stress induced by sodium iodate—a condition used to model dry AMD (Wang et al., 2020). Furthermore, in vivo animal models, including sodium iodate-induced AMD mouse models, have confirmed that D609 can protect the RPE layer, preserve retinal structure and function, and prevent geographic atrophy—findings that underscore its translational potential for dry AMD therapy (Wang et al., 2020). Outside the field of ophthalmology, D609 has been evaluated in oncology, where it affected cell proliferation and induced apoptosis in certain tumor cell lines, and in neuroscience for its neuroprotective effects against amyloid-beta toxicity and oxidative stress in neuronal cultures (Bhat et al., 2022). Although no clinical trials have yet been reported that specifically target dry AMD with D609, the preclinical data generated in ocular, cancer, and neurodegenerative studies provide a robust therapeutic history that supports depth of investigation into its ocular application (Wang et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At its core, D609 is a competitive inhibitor of PC-PLC. PC-PLC is an enzyme that hydrolyzes phosphatidylcholine (PC) into phosphorylcholine and diacylglycerol (DAG). In RPE cells, overactivation of this enzyme under oxidative stress conditions may lead to excessive DAG production that, in turn, drives hyperactivation of protein kinase C (PKC) and downstream signaling events deleteriously affecting cytoskeletal dynamics and phagocytosis (Wang et al., 2020). D609 exerts its inhibitory activity by mimicking parts of the natural substrate, competitively binding to the active site of PC-PLC—in part through its dithiocarbonate group, which can chelate zinc ions that are critical for enzyme function (Wang et al., 2020; González-Roura et al., 2002). In addition to its direct inhibition of PC-PLC, D609 has been reported to exert antioxidative effects indirectly via upregulation of metallothionein proteins—an antioxidative protein family that plays a protective role against reactive oxygen species (ROS) and metal-induced damage (Wang et al., 2020). This dual mechanism—direct enzyme inhibition and indirect antioxidant protection—suggests that D609 may help stabilize the lipid signaling environment of the RPE, normalizing DAG levels and mitigating PKC-mediated perturbations in actin cytoskeletal dynamics that are essential for the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Wang et al., 2020). Some studies even propose that the beneficial effects observed in RPE cells may derive more from the metallothionein upregulation than from pure PC-PLC inhibition, raising the possibility that D609’s mode of action is multifactorial rather than strictly enzyme-targeted (Wang et al., 2020). However, in the context of the current hypothesis—where the goal is to inhibit the DAG-PKC axis to restore cytoskeletal dynamics and phagocytosis—the competitive inhibition of PC-PLC by D609 remains a key molecular mechanism (Bhat et al., 2022). It should be noted that D609 is not entirely selective; it also inhibits other enzymes in lipid metabolism such as sphingomyelin synthase (SMS) and possibly phospholipase D (PLD), which could contribute to both its therapeutic efficacy and its off-target effects (Eurtivong et al., 2023; González-Roura et al., 2002). The compound’s broad-spectrum inhibition profile, while advantageous in some settings, raises concerns regarding precise modulation of the PC-PLC–DAG–PKC pathway in the specialized setting of RPE biology (Zhao et al., 2020; Bhat et al., 2022). Nevertheless, the downstream reduction in DAG levels is expected to temper PKC activation, which is crucial since PKC hyperactivation is known to impair actin polymerization and therefore phagocytosis—a critical function of RPE cells in maintaining photoreceptor health (Wang et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
The working hypothesis for repurposing D609 for dry AMD is that its inhibition of PC-PLC in RPE cells will lead to reduced DAG formation, thereby limiting DAG-driven PKC hyperactivation. This in turn is expected to stabilize cytoskeletal dynamics by restoring normal actin polymerization, thus improving the phagocytic capacity of the RPE to internalize and process POS. In experimental assays, ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxidative insult (e.g., hydroquinone treatment) typically display disrupted actin architecture and impaired POS uptake. Treatment with D609 is hypothesized to counteract these effects by balancing the intracellular signaling milieu—specifically by reducing the aberrant activation of the DAG-PKC axis—and by promoting the antioxidant metallothionein pathway, which further preserves cellular homeostasis (Wang et al., 2020). Expression of PC-PLC and related signaling components in RPE cells has been indirectly verified by the cellular responses observed upon oxidative challenge, and the reversal of these effects by D609 supports the notion that this enzyme is active and pathophysiologically relevant in RPE cells (Wang et al., 2020). The expected phenotypic outcomes in the assay include a restoration of actin polymerization, as evidenced by improved F-actin staining patterns, increased phagocytosis of labeled POS, and decreased levels of oxidative markers such as ROS. Indeed, previous studies demonstrated that when ARPE-19 cells were pretreated with D609, they exhibited markedly reduced necrotic and apoptotic markers, along with preserved mitochondrial mass and function under oxidative stress conditions induced by sodium iodate (Wang et al., 2020). These outcomes directly support the hypothesis that normalization of PC-PLC activity via D609 not only mitigates the immediate oxidative insult but also restores the critical cellular function of POS internalization—a process that, when dysfunctional, is a hallmark of dry AMD pathology (Wang et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
D609 presents as an intriguing and promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly because of its ability to modulate lipid signaling pathways that are disrupted by oxidative stress and contribute to RPE dysfunction. One of the principal strengths of D609 is its well-documented protective effect on RPE cells both in vitro and in vivo. Studies have shown that D609 maintains high levels of cell viability in RPE models under conditions of severe oxidative stress, and its administration in animal models of AMD has led to significant preservation of retinal structure and function (Wang et al., 2020). Moreover, its water solubility and low molecular weight facilitate ocular delivery and reduce formulation challenges, making it suitable for local administration to the retina (Wang et al., 2020). The dual-action mechanism—combining inhibition of PC-PLC with upregulation of metallothionein—provides both a direct reduction in deleterious DAG-PKC signaling and an indirect bolster to the cell’s antioxidant defenses, which is crucial in the context of dry AMD where oxidative stress is a primary driver of pathology (Wang et al., 2020).

However, several weaknesses must be noted. First, D609 is a non-selective inhibitor; while it effectively targets PC-PLC, it also inhibits other enzymes such as sphingomyelin synthase and phospholipase D, which may introduce off-target effects that could complicate its clinical use (Eurtivong et al., 2023; González-Roura et al., 2002). This lack of selectivity may lead to unpredictable interactions in the intricate lipid signaling networks present in the retina. Second, the compound exists as a mixture of eight stereoisomers, and the differential activity among these isomers is not well understood. Variability in stereoisomeric composition could result in inconsistent pharmacodynamic outcomes and present challenges in the regulatory approval process (Eurtivong et al., 2023; Bhat et al., 2022). Third, the anticipated IC₅₀ of approximately 35 µM for PC-PLC inhibition in RPE cells is relatively high, suggesting that effective biological activity may require high local concentrations that may be difficult to achieve or maintain in vivo without risking toxicity (Wang et al., 2020; Bhat et al., 2022). Although ocular safety studies in rabbits have been favorable, further pharmacokinetic and toxicological investigations will be essential to confirm the therapeutic window for chronic treatment in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2020; Bhat et al., 2022).

From a mechanism-of-action standpoint, while the hypothesis that reducing DAG-mediated PKC hyperactivation will normalize actin dynamics and improve phagocytosis is biologically plausible, much of the existing literature on D609’s protective effects in RPE cells emphasizes its ability to upregulate metallothionein expression and confer antioxidant protection rather than solely modulating the DAG-PKC axis (Wang et al., 2020). Thus, it remains to be clarified whether the beneficial outcomes in RPE phagocytosis are driven primarily by alterations in the DAG-PKC pathway or by a broader restoration of cellular redox balance. This mechanistic ambiguity, while not diminishing the overall therapeutic promise, suggests that future studies should incorporate detailed pathway analyses to dissect the relative contributions of each mechanism.

In summary, D609 is well supported by preclinical evidence as a compound that can protect RPE cells from oxidative damage and has potential applications in dry AMD therapy (Wang et al., 2020). Its established safety profile in ocular studies, combined with a mechanistic basis that addresses both lipid signaling dysregulation and oxidative stress, offers significant advantages for repurposing in this context. Nonetheless, challenges related to off-target effects, stereochemical variability, and the need for high effective concentrations must be rigorously addressed in subsequent studies. Overall, D609 merits further investigative efforts in translational research focused on dry AMD, with particular emphasis on optimizing its pharmacodynamics, ensuring reproducible stereoisomeric composition, and validating its efficacy in restoring RPE phagocytic function under physiologically relevant oxidative stress conditions (Eurtivong et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The therapeutic candidate under evaluation is a CD82 agonist peptide, marketed as a tetraspanin activator (Peptide Institute Cat. No. K-8202). This candidate is a synthetic peptide designed to interact with the extracellular domain of CD82, a member of the tetraspanin family involved in organizing membrane microdomains and regulating the spatial distribution of various transmembrane proteins such as integrins. Tetraspanins are known to modulate cellular adhesion, migration, and signal transduction by forming dynamic “tetraspanin–enriched microdomains” (TEMs) that include integrins and other proteins; in particular, CD82 has been implicated in the regulation of integrin clustering and function in a range of cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and various immune cells (Lee et al., 2022). The structural design of this peptide likely takes advantage of the sequence and conformational features of the large extracellular loop (LEL) of CD82, which is known to mediate protein–protein interactions through specific binding surfaces and domains. Although similar CD82‐derived peptides have been examined primarily in the context of cancer metastasis suppression, the repurposing of such peptides for retinal applications represents an innovative approach. The rationale is that by binding to CD82 on the RPE cell surface, the peptide may induce a clustering effect that enhances the recruitment and stable assembly of αvβ5 integrin nanodomains, which are critical for the formation of effective phagocytic cups and subsequent photoreceptor outer segment (POS) internalization—a process that is compromised in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Lee et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, tetraspanin proteins such as CD82 have been studied extensively in oncology where they are recognized as metastasis suppressors. In those settings, peptide mimetics of the small extracellular loop (EC1) of CD82 have been developed with the aim of modulating cell adhesion, migration, and invasion. For example, studies have shown that CD82-derived peptides can inhibit tumor cell migration and adhesion by interfering with integrin-mediated signaling pathways, particularly involving integrins such as α5β1, and by attenuating downstream focal adhesion kinase (FAK) signaling (Luan et al., 2018). However, such peptides have primarily been investigated in non-ocular systems, and their actions have been predominantly inhibitory in nature, aimed at suppressing excessive integrin signaling rather than stimulating it. In the specific context of the retina, the use of CD82 or its mimetics has been very limited; one study documented that recombinant human CD82 (rhCD82) can interfere with TGF-β1-mediated epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) in ARPE-19 cells by modulating integrin expression and inhibiting Smad-dependent signaling pathways (Lee et al., 2022). Although that study was conducted within the framework of fibrosis and EMT—processes that are also relevant to AMD—the focus was on anti-fibrotic and anti-migratory properties rather than on enhancing phagocytosis. In addition, indirect evidence from immunological studies indicates that CD82 plays a role in regulating integrin sorting and cytoskeletal reorganization in macrophages and neutrophils, thereby influencing cell migration and adhesion (McGowan et al., 2022). In retinal biology, the αvβ5 integrin is known to be indispensable for efficient POS binding and internalization by RPE cells, and its dysregulation is associated with impaired phagocytosis and consequently with AMD pathogenesis (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). However, there is currently no established history of using a CD82 agonist peptide to specifically enhance αvβ5 integrin clustering or to stimulate phagocytic cup formation in RPE cells, making this candidate both innovative and largely uncharted in preclinical ocular disease models (Lee et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The proposed mechanism of action for the CD82 agonist peptide rests on the capacity of CD82 to orchestrate the lateral organization of integrin receptors in the plasma membrane. Under physiological conditions, CD82 is involved in forming complexes with integrin subunits, including integrin β1 and integrin αv; these interactions have been shown to modulate integrin activation states and can affect downstream signaling pathways (Lee et al., 2022). In the present hypothesis, the agonist peptide is expected to bind to the extracellular domain of CD82 in a manner that promotes its active conformation, thereby enhancing its ability to cluster αvβ5 integrin on the apical surface of RPE cells. The clustering of integrin receptors is a critical step in the initiation of phagocytic cup assembly, as it facilitates the formation of a localized high-density area of signaling and adhesion molecules needed to capture and internalize shed POS particles (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). The biochemistry underlying this process involves the reorganization of membrane microdomains, where CD82, upon binding of the agonist peptide, may recruit additional integrin molecules and potentially interact with adapter proteins that link to the actin cytoskeleton, thereby reinforcing the mechanical stability required for efficient phagocytosis (McGowan et al., 2022). In several cell types, similar tetraspanin activators have been shown to influence cytoskeletal dynamics and cell adhesion by modulating the activity of small GTPases and other signaling intermediates; for example, the inhibition of migration by CD82 in macrophages is associated with decreased filopodia formation (McGowan et al., 2022). By analogy, if the agonist peptide induces a favorable conformational change in CD82 within RPE cells, it could conceivably lead to an optimal reorganization of αvβ5 integrin clusters that promotes the formation and stabilization of phagocytic cups, thereby enhancing the uptake of POS particles. Nonetheless, it is important to note that many of the detailed molecular interactions have been characterized in contexts other than retinal phagocytosis, and extrapolation to RPE cells remains somewhat speculative at this time (Luan et al., 2018). Moreover, while molecular docking analyses have revealed direct interactions between CD82 and integrin subunits (Lee et al., 2022), the specific impact of an agonist peptide on αvβ5 integrin clustering in RPE membranes has not yet been directly demonstrated. This lack of direct evidence underscores the need for rigorous mechanistic studies that investigate the peptide’s binding kinetics, its ability to modulate CD82 conformation, and the subsequent effects on integrin organization and actin remodeling in the specialized environment of RPE cells (Lee et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The anticipated outcome of administering the CD82 agonist peptide in a dry AMD model is an enhancement of RPE function through improved phagocytic activity. In healthy RPE cells, the daily clearance of shed photoreceptor outer segments is mediated primarily by αvβ5 integrin-dependent processes that initiate phagocytic cup assembly and POS internalization. In dry AMD, RPE dysfunction, which may include impaired integrin clustering and reduced phagocytic efficiency, contributes to the accumulation of cellular debris and subsequent retinal degeneration (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). The working hypothesis postulates that the CD82 agonist peptide will bind to CD82, resulting in the clustering and stabilization of αvβ5 integrin microdomains on the apical surface of RPE cells. Enhanced clustering of these integrins is expected to promote a more robust and efficient phagocytic response by facilitating the assembly of actin-rich phagocytic cups that effectively capture and internalize POS particles (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Zihni, 2025). In vitro, this effect would likely be measurable as an increase in the rate and extent of POS uptake in cultured human RPE cells such as ARPE-19, and could be quantified using established phagocytosis assays that utilize fluorescently labeled POS preparations. In vivo, improved phagocytic function could translate into better maintenance of retinal integrity, reduced accumulation of lipofuscin and other intracellular debris, and ultimately a slowdown or reversal of the degenerative changes associated with dry AMD (Ruggiero et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2022). It is also anticipated that by enhancing integrin clustering, the peptide might indirectly influence other signaling pathways involved in RPE homeostasis, potentially mitigating inflammatory or fibrotic processes that exacerbate AMD pathology (McGowan et al., 2022). However, one must exercise caution as the majority of existing literature on CD82 peptide mimetics has focused on modulating cell migration and adhesion in the context of cancer, rather than promoting enhanced phagocytosis (Luan et al., 2018). Therefore, while the expected effect of restored or enhanced POS clearance is theoretically sound, it remains to be validated in the specific cellular and animal models of dry AMD relevant to RPE function.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the proposed CD82 agonist peptide represents an intriguing and innovative candidate for the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration by addressing a fundamental pathological mechanism—impaired RPE phagocytosis. One of the key strengths of this candidate is its novel mechanism of action, which utilizes the concept of targeted receptor organization through the activation of a tetraspanin protein that has been implicated in integrin modulation. The role of αvβ5 integrin in RPE phagocytosis is well established, and its proper clustering is essential for the effective clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, a process that is compromised in aging and AMD (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). The idea of repurposing a CD82 agonist peptide to restore or enhance this process is supported indirectly by the body of literature demonstrating that tetraspanins play critical roles in integrin organization and that modulating tetraspanin function can have significant impacts on cell adhesion and signaling (Lee et al., 2022). Additionally, because current therapeutic strategies for dry AMD remain limited and largely focused on addressing neovascular complications rather than the underlying degenerative process, a candidate that directly improves RPE function and photoreceptor homeostasis offers substantial promise.

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be considered. First, there is a notable gap in the direct experimental evidence linking CD82 agonist peptides to enhanced phagocytic cup assembly or increased POS internalization in RPE cells. Most studies to date that involve CD82 in the context of the retina have concentrated on its role in inhibiting EMT or modulating inflammatory responses in ARPE-19 cells (Lee et al., 2022). In contrast, the majority of the literature on CD82 peptide mimetics in other systems—particularly in cancer—describes inhibitory effects on integrin-mediated signaling and cell migration rather than an agonistic promotion of integrin clustering (Luan et al., 2018). This discrepancy raises concerns regarding whether a peptide designed to activate CD82 will have the desired stimulatory effect on αvβ5 integrin organization in the unique cellular environment of the RPE. Second, the regulatory functions of tetraspanins are inherently complex and highly dependent on the cellular context; while enhanced clustering may be beneficial for phagocytosis, it could also inadvertently alter other CD82-associated pathways, such as TGF-β signaling or immune cell interactions, with potentially unforeseen consequences (McGowan et al., 2022). Third, the preclinical development of peptide-based therapeutics, particularly for ocular applications, poses significant challenges in terms of delivery, stability, and bioavailability. The blood–retinal barrier and the highly specialized microenvironment of the eye may limit the effective concentrations of the peptide that reach the target RPE cells, and any off-target effects due to systemic distribution could further complicate the safety profile.

Moreover, while integrin clustering is a promising target, the evidence linking enhanced αvβ5 organization directly to improved phagocytosis in RPE cells mainly comes from correlative studies in rodent models and in vitro assays (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012; Zihni, 2025). There is a need for more mechanistic studies that specifically dissect how tetraspanin-driven integrin clustering influences the kinetics and efficiency of phagocytic cup assembly in models that faithfully recapitulate the human RPE phenotype. It is also important to confirm that CD82 is expressed and functionally relevant in RPE cells of patients with dry AMD, as variations in tetraspanin expression could impact the efficacy of a peptide-based agonist (Lee et al., 2022). The candidate’s success will depend on rigorous optimization of its pharmacological profile, including its peptide stability, receptor binding affinity, and resistance to proteolytic degradation within ocular tissues.

Despite these challenges, the concept behind the CD82 agonist peptide is compelling. The targeted approach of modulating receptor microdomain architecture represents a departure from more conventional strategies, such as anti-VEGF therapies or broad-spectrum anti-inflammatory agents. If the peptide can selectively promote the clustering of αvβ5 integrins and thereby restore efficient POS clearance, it might not only improve retinal adhesion and photoreceptor survival but also mitigate secondary events such as lipofuscin accumulation and chronic inflammation that drive the progression of dry AMD (McGowan et al., 2022). In theory, such targeted modulation of the RPE microenvironment could offer a disease-modifying strategy rather than merely palliative treatment. Additionally, because tetraspanins like CD82 serve as molecular organizers with relatively high tissue specificity, an agonist peptide could potentially be engineered to have a favorable safety profile with minimal off-target systemic effects.

In weighing the strengths and weaknesses, it becomes clear that while the CD82 agonist peptide holds significant promise as a novel therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, its clinical potential remains largely theoretical at this stage. The mechanism by which tetraspanin activation could enhance αvβ5 integrin clustering is supported by indirect evidence from studies in cancer cells and other non-ocular tissues (Luan et al., 2018). However, the translation of these findings to the RPE, which is both highly polarized and functionally unique, requires additional targeted investigation. Future studies should focus on validating the expression and functional activation of CD82 in RPE cells from both healthy donors and AMD patients, as well as on conducting mechanistic experiments to determine the precise impact of the agonist peptide on integrin clustering and phagocytic cup formation. In vitro assays using cultured RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary human RPE) should be complemented by in vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD to assess whether the peptide can indeed restore or enhance POS clearance and thereby ameliorate retinal degeneration (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012).

An additional aspect to consider is the potential for unexpected off-target effects. Given that CD82 is involved in a variety of cellular processes—including those related to cell adhesion, migration, and even immune modulation—the systemic administration of a CD82 agonist peptide might affect multiple cell types beyond the RPE (McGowan et al., 2022). Therefore, an effective delivery strategy that confines the peptide’s activity to the retina (for example, via intravitreal injection or a controlled-release ocular implant) may be essential for maximizing its therapeutic index. Drug formulation studies, as well as preliminary toxicology assessments, will be crucial in determining whether the peptide achieves the necessary balance between efficacy and safety.

In conclusion, the CD82 agonist peptide (Peptide Institute Cat. No. K-8202) is a novel therapeutic candidate that harnesses the unique properties of tetraspanin CD82 to potentially enhance αvβ5 integrin clustering in RPE membranes. This mechanism is hypothesized to lead to improved phagocytic cup assembly and POS internalization, addressing a key pathogenic process in dry AMD. The candidate belongs to a class of peptide-based modulators that have been historically evaluated for their roles in regulating cell adhesion and migration in cancer, but its application in the context of retinal phagocytosis is largely uncharted. The evidence supporting the role of CD82 in integrin modulation is robust in non-ocular systems (Lee et al., 2022), and there is clear evidence for the importance of αvβ5 integrin in RPE phagocytosis (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). Nonetheless, the direct demonstration that activation of CD82 via an agonist peptide enhances integrin clustering and phagocytic efficiency in RPE cells is currently lacking, and the majority of published studies have demonstrated inhibitory effects of CD82 peptides in different contexts (Luan et al., 2018).

The overall evaluation of this therapeutic candidate is thus twofold. On the one hand, the mechanistic rationale is scientifically intriguing and represents a targeted, innovative approach that aligns with our current understanding of RPE biology and AMD pathogenesis. On the other hand, the candidate’s novelty in the ocular field means that there is a significant gap in the preclinical validation required to confidently predict efficacy in dry AMD. Strengths of the candidate include its potential for receptor-specific modulation, the possibility of restoring natural phagocytic function in the RPE, and the prospect of achieving a disease-modifying effect by targeting a fundamental cellular process. Weaknesses include the lack of direct experimental evidence in RPE models, the possibility that the peptide may exhibit inhibitory rather than stimulatory effects on integrin function as observed in cancer-related studies, and the inherent challenges of peptide-based drug delivery to the retina.

Ultimately, while the CD82 agonist peptide holds considerable promise based on mechanistic reasoning and a growing body of literature that supports the central role of tetraspanins in cellular organization and integrin function (Lee et al., 2022; Bhatwadekar et al., 2020), further rigorous studies are needed. These should include in vitro assays in RPE cell cultures to quantify changes in integrin clustering and phagocytic cup assembly, followed by in vivo evaluations in animal models that recapitulate the pathological features of dry AMD (Lee et al., 2022; McGowan et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
VU0155072 is a synthetic small‐molecule agonist that selectively targets the sphingosine‐1‐phosphate receptor 5 (S1PR5). Although the detailed synthetic route and complete structural characterization for VU0155072 as a University of North Carolina reagent are not fully delineated in the available literature, it belongs to a class of compounds that have been developed to achieve high selectivity for S1PR5. Similar to the structurally characterized S1PR5 agonist A-971432—synthesized via a two‐step process employing reductive amination with azetidine-3-carboxylic acid derivatives (Hobson et al., 2015)—VU0155072 is assumed to incorporate a pharmacophore that confers both high potency and selectivity within the sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor family. Compounds in this class have generally exploited the azetidine or related amino acid framework as a bioisostere to mimic the native lipid ligand, sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), while avoiding the metabolic liabilities of phosphorylated amino alcohols (Hobson et al., 2015). S1P receptor modulators as a group have been widely evaluated in a range of therapeutic areas—from multiple sclerosis and other neurodegenerative disorders to ocular pathologies—due to their ability to modulate immune cell trafficking and endothelial barrier function (Birgbauer, 2024; Hobson et al., 2015). In this context, VU0155072 marks a potential reagent that could be repurposed for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by leveraging its selective activation of S1PR5 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells.

Therapeutic History:  
The broader class of S1P receptor modulators has an extensive therapeutic history, with agents like fingolimod having been approved for multiple sclerosis owing to their immunomodulatory effects; however, these agents generally lack receptor subtype selectivity and consequently trigger side effects related to non-selective S1P receptor engagement (Birgbauer, 2024; Nakamura et al., 2024). More recent efforts have focused on enhancing receptor selectivity, as exemplified by A-971432—which is a selective S1PR5 agonist developed for neurodegenerative conditions—and ASP4058, an S1P1/5-selective agonist that has demonstrated efficacy in ocular vascular pathology models relevant to wet age-related macular degeneration (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024). Despite these advances, none of the compounds described to date have been definitively applied to dry AMD. In contrast to wet AMD therapies, which predominantly target abnormal neovascularization through modulation of VEGF pathways (Nakamura et al., 2024), the potential therapeutic application of S1PR5 agonists in dry AMD lies in their capacity to restore or enhance the phagocytic function of RPE cells. Preliminary evidence suggests that RPE phagocytosis—a critical process for the daily removal of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—may be modulated via S1P receptor signaling. Notably, a human RPE-based screening platform identified compounds capable of enhancing POS phagocytosis, with subsequent transcriptomic analyses revealing that S1PR5 was among the top upregulated genes associated with the enhanced phagocytic response (Schreiter et al., 2020). Moreover, while most of the literature on S1P receptor agonists has focused on neurodegenerative or ocular vascular indications, there is a growing rationale for repurposing these agents for dry AMD, given that RPE dysfunction—including impaired phagosome-lysosome fusion and subsequent accumulation of cellular debris—is a hallmark of the disease (Hobson et al., 2015; Schreiter et al., 2020). Thus, VU0155072, though primarily a research reagent at this stage, stands as a candidate with potential utility for dry AMD based on its receptor selectivity and the emerging role of S1PR5 in RPE phagocytic trafficking.

Mechanism of Action:  
S1PR5 is a member of the G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) family activated by the endogenous ligand sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P). Its activation typically engages downstream signaling cascades that include the modulation of Rho family GTPases, regulation of the actin cytoskeleton, and activation of kinases such as AKT, all of which are crucial for vesicle transport and membrane fusion events (Hobson et al., 2015). In the context of RPE cells, the mechanistic hypothesis for VU0155072 centers on its ability to enhance phagosome-lysosome fusion and the degradation of POS. This is predicated on the observation that modulation of S1P receptor signaling impacts intracellular trafficking pathways. For instance, activation of S1PR5 has been linked to changes in cytoskeletal dynamics that favor efficient vesicular movement and fusion events—a process essential for the clearance of phagosomes containing photoreceptor debris (Schreiter et al., 2020). Additionally, the receptor’s downstream signaling may stimulate pathways involving Rho-associated kinases (ROCK) or PI3K/AKT, both of which facilitate the reorganization of actin filaments and promote the maturation and fusion of phagosomes with lysosomes (Hobson et al., 2015). Importantly, data from a study using a human RPE-based screening platform indicated that pharmacological inhibition of S1PR5 impaired the phagocytic uptake and processing of POS, implying that its activation could restore this cellular function (Schreiter et al., 2020). However, it is noteworthy that several studies examining receptor distribution in RPE cells (using the ARPE-19 cell line as a model) have reported that S1PR5 mRNA expression is very low compared with other S1P receptors such as S1PR3 (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022). This observation raises questions about the sufficiency of endogenous S1PR5 expression in mediating phagocytic processes and whether exogenous activation by a potent agonist like VU0155072 can override such limitations. Nonetheless, the proposed mechanism is coherent with the hypothesis that selective S1PR5 activation leads to enhanced phagosome-lysosome fusion—an effect that would be indirectly mediated by the receptor’s influence on cytoskeletal remodeling and vesicular trafficking proteins.

Expected Effect:  
The primary therapeutic expectation for VU0155072 in dry AMD is that selective activation of S1PR5 in RPE cells will augment the rate and efficiency of phagocytosis, specifically by promoting the fusion of phagosomes with lysosomes and thereby ensuring effective degradation of POS. In dry AMD, one of the pathogenic factors is the defective clearance and subsequent accumulation of photoreceptor debris, which contributes to RPE dysfunction and the formation of drusen. By facilitating robust phagocytic processing, VU0155072 is anticipated to alleviate the cellular stress associated with toxic accumulation, restore RPE homeostasis, and ultimately preserve retinal function (Schreiter et al., 2020). In vitro assays using human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or iPSC-derived RPE) could be employed to assess the efficacy of VU0155072. These assays might measure parameters such as the rate of POS uptake, the kinetics of phagosome-lysosome fusion (potentially using co-localization markers of lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1), and levels of residual POS components after treatment. Given the reported effective concentration (EC₅₀) in the vicinity of 150 nM, one would expect that treatment with VU0155072 at or near this concentration would lead to measurable improvements in phagocytic flux. Moreover, its selectivity may allow the compound to act in a highly targeted fashion, reducing the potential for adverse effects associated with off-target activation of other S1P receptor subtypes—a significant benefit given the pleiotropic roles of other S1P receptors in immune modulation and vascular homeostasis (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024). An additional facet of the expected effect is the possibility that S1PR5 activation may engage MERTK-independent signaling pathways. MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase critical for POS phagocytosis, is often implicated in inherited forms of retinal degeneration when mutated. Should VU0155072 provide an alternate route to stimulate phagosome maturation and clearance, it could be particularly beneficial in cases where MERTK function is compromised (Schreiter et al., 2020). Nonetheless, the low endogenous expression of S1PR5 in commonly used RPE cell lines (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022) may necessitate the use of primary or stem cell-derived RPE models in order to fully capture the therapeutic potential of this approach.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, VU0155072 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD due to its high selectivity for S1PR5 and the compelling hypothesis that S1PR5 activation can restore phagocytic flux in RPE cells. One of the key strengths of this approach is the mechanistic precision: by specifically targeting S1PR5, VU0155072 is expected to modulate intracellular trafficking pathways that are critical for the maintenance and renewal of the RPE’s phagocytic machinery. This stands in contrast to previous S1P receptor modulators that, due to their nonselective binding profiles (such as fingolimod), have demonstrated a range of off-target effects including unwanted immune modulation and vascular dysfunction (Birgbauer, 2024; Nakamura et al., 2024). Moreover, studies on similar S1PR5 agonists like A-971432 have established that selective receptor activation can be achieved with favorable pharmacokinetic profiles, and the precedent set by ASP4058 in addressing ocular pathologies suggests that S1P receptor modulation can be therapeutically beneficial in the retinal context (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024).  

However, the candidate also faces several challenges. A significant potential weakness is the reported low endogenous expression of S1PR5 in RPE cell lines, such as ARPE-19, where expression levels are markedly lower than those of other S1P receptors (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022). This observation raises the question of whether exogenous activation by VU0155072 will be sufficient to elicit a robust phagocytic response in the RPE, or whether receptor upregulation might already be a prerequisite for therapeutic efficacy. Furthermore, while there is evidence that S1PR5 signaling can influence phagocytic processes (Schreiter et al., 2020), most of the existing research has focused on its roles in CNS function and vascular stability rather than in the specific context of RPE-mediated POS degradation. Hence, the proposed mechanism—restoration of phagosome-lysosome fusion and enhancement of POS degradation via S1PR5 activation—remains largely inferential and will require rigorous experimental validation in appropriate in vitro and in vivo models of dry AMD.  

Another consideration is the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic profile of VU0155072, which are described as being favorable in rodents. In theory, such data support its potential translation into clinical settings; however, the degree to which rodent PK accurately predicts human ocular tissue exposure remains uncertain, particularly given the unique microenvironment and barrier properties of the human retina. Additionally, it will be imperative to assess whether VU0155072 exerts any off-target effects on other S1P receptor subtypes, despite its purported selectivity. Off-target binding could complicate the interpretation of preclinical results or introduce safety concerns that have been observed with less selective S1P receptor modulators (Birgbauer, 2024; Nakamura et al., 2024).

From a disease-modifying perspective, the hypothesis that enhancement of phagocytic flux in RPE cells can ameliorate the progression of dry AMD is attractive because it targets a central pathogenic mechanism—namely, the chronic failure of POS clearance that leads to lipofuscin accumulation, drusen formation, and subsequent RPE atrophy. If VU0155072 can indeed stimulate the phagocytic machinery through S1PR5 activation in a meaningful way, it could potentially slow or even reverse some of the degenerative changes associated with dry AMD. This mechanism-driven approach represents a departure from merely symptomatic treatments, addressing the underlying cellular dysfunction that characterizes the disease (Hobson et al., 2015; Schreiter et al., 2020).

In conclusion, while VU0155072 is supported by a mechanistic rationale rooted in S1PR5-mediated regulation of intracellular trafficking and phagocytosis in RPE cells, several factors must be carefully considered before committing to this candidate as a viable therapeutic for dry AMD. The strengths of VU0155072 lie in its receptor specificity, favorable PK in rodent models, and the emerging evidence linking S1PR5 activation with improved phagocytic function in RPE—a critical process compromised in dry AMD. In contrast, the limited endogenous expression of S1PR5 in commonly used RPE models (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022) and the scarce direct evidence of S1PR5 agonism ameliorating dry AMD pathology represent significant challenges. These weaknesses highlight the necessity for further basic research to quantify S1PR5 expression in relevant human RPE cells, to confirm the downstream signaling events triggered by VU0155072, and to validate the beneficial effects of enhanced phagosome-lysosome fusion using both in vitro and in vivo models of dry AMD. Ultimately, while VU0155072 shows promise as a mechanistically precise candidate for restoring phagocytic flux and addressing a key pathological feature of dry AMD, the current literature underscores the need for additional studies to fully establish its therapeutic potential in this context (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024; Qiao et al., 2012; Schreiter et al., 2020; Sorenson et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Anacetrapib is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor of cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) originally developed by Merck as part of a class of compounds aimed at modulating lipid metabolism. This compound was identified and refined through extensive medicinal chemistry programs designed to target CETP’s lipid transfer function. As a member of the CETP inhibitor class, anacetrapib has been developed primarily for cardiovascular risk reduction by increasing high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL‐C) and lowering low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C), and its chemical structure and binding properties have been designed to disrupt the lipid‐transfer tunnel of the CETP enzyme (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Tall & Rader, 2018). The proposed repurposing for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on the rationale that by inhibiting CETP, the agent could raise local HDL levels in Bruch’s membrane (BrM) and improve reverse cholesterol transport, thereby reducing drusen‐like lipid accumulation and indirectly supporting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) phagocytic capacity—a hypothesis derived from observed associations between CETP activity, local retinal lipid metabolism, and AMD pathogenesis (Betzler et al., 2020; Shughoury et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, CETP inhibitors have been evaluated extensively for their potential to address dyslipidemia and reduce atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Anacetrapib, in particular, has undergone large clinical trials such as the DEFINE and REVEAL studies, where its efficacy in raising HDL‐C by approximately 138% and reducing LDL‐C by 37–40% compared to placebo was demonstrated (Cheung et al., 2017; Tall & Rader, 2018). The class of CETP inhibitors also includes compounds such as torcetrapib, dalcetrapib, and evacetrapib—with torcetrapib’s development being terminated due to off‐target effects including blood pressure elevations, while anacetrapib and evacetrapib showed more favorable profiles in subsequent trials (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Sirtori, 2011). Although these compounds were developed to address cardiovascular pathologies, genetic and mechanistic studies have implicated CETP and HDL metabolism in the ocular environment as well. Several genome‐wide association studies and Mendelian randomization studies have demonstrated a relationship between CETP gene variants, HDL levels, and AMD risk (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020). Despite this, no CETP inhibitor has previously been used in a clinical setting for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular diseases, and the repurposing of anacetrapib for dry AMD represents a novel therapeutic direction inspired by preclinical studies in murine models that suggest potential benefits in the retinal context (Cheung et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
Anacetrapib functions by binding to CETP, thereby preventing the transfer of cholesteryl esters from HDL to apolipoprotein B‐containing lipoproteins (i.e., LDL, very‐low‐density lipoprotein [VLDL]) and the subsequent exchange of triglycerides in the opposite direction. At the molecular level, CETP normally operates via a tunnel‐mechanism or shuttle mechanism to facilitate the bidirectional lipid transfer between lipoproteins. Inhibition of CETP by anacetrapib results in the accumulation of cholesterol-rich, enlarged HDL particles and a concomitant reduction in the levels of atherogenic LDL particles (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Sirtori, 2011). In the context of the retina, emerging evidence suggests that CETP is expressed not only systemically but also locally—in the retinal pigment epithelium, photoreceptor outer segments, and interphotoreceptor matrix (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). The rationale is that CETP activity in Bruch’s membrane may normally lower HDL levels, thereby impairing the capacity for reverse cholesterol transport in this specialized extracellular matrix, which can lead to the accumulation of lipids and the formation of drusen. By inhibiting CETP, anacetrapib may restore or increase local HDL levels, improving the efflux of accumulated cholesterol and other lipids from the RPE and neighboring structures (Fan et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2022). Moreover, the resulting HDL particles may gain enhanced cholesterol efflux capacity, as evidenced by preclinical studies that show increased cholesterol removal from macrophages via ABCA1- and ABCG1-mediated pathways (Sirtori, 2011; Page et al., 2016). In addition, proper HDL particle composition under CETP inhibition could influence key inflammatory regulatory mechanisms through the carriage of complement factors, which are linked to AMD pathogenesis (Tricorache et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assay, treatment with anacetrapib is expected to increase HDL levels locally in Bruch’s membrane, thereby enhancing reverse cholesterol transport across the retinal layers. The improved cholesterol efflux from the RPE is postulated to mitigate the accumulation of drusen-like lipid deposits—a hallmark of dry AMD—and potentially restore critical cellular functions such as integrin localization and associated phagocytic receptor activity (Cheung et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020). This restoration of lipid homeostasis is anticipated to reduce the build-up of oxidized lipids and other debris beneath the RPE, ultimately alleviating RPE dysfunction—a central component in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). The mechanism relies on the observation that HDL not only serves as a cholesterol acceptor but also carries important complement regulatory proteins and inflammatory mediators; thus, its normalization in Bruch’s membrane could indirectly support the phagocytic activity of RPE cells and improve tissue homeostasis (Lin et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). Gene expression studies have identified CETP expression in ocular tissues, reinforcing the notion that local CETP inhibition may directly influence lipid handling in the retina (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). Ultimately, the expected outcomes in preclinical models—and, by extension, in clinical trials—are a measurable reduction in drusen burden, improvement in RPE functionality, and a potential delay or attenuation in the progression of dry AMD (Schmidt et al., 2020; Cheung et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of anacetrapib for the treatment of dry AMD presents a compelling opportunity, supported by a solid mechanistic hypothesis and a favorable human safety profile established in cardiovascular trials. Among the clear strengths is the extensive biochemical and clinical data on CETP inhibitors in the context of dyslipidemia; anacetrapib has demonstrated robust HDL‐C raising and LDL‐C lowering effects, with a tolerability profile superior to earlier CETP inhibitors such as torcetrapib (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Tall & Rader, 2018). Furthermore, emerging evidence of CETP expression in ocular tissues and its potential role in modulating local lipid metabolism—combined with findings that suggest dysfunctional HDL composition may contribute to drusen formation—lends strong support to the therapeutic rationale (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017).

However, there are important weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed. First, the genetic and epidemiological data linking HDL cholesterol and AMD have been paradoxical; several Mendelian randomization studies have implicated HDL‐raising alleles, particularly those related to CETP modulation, with an increased risk for AMD (Betzler et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2017). This counterintuitive observation raises concerns that simply increasing HDL levels may not guarantee improved RPE function unless the quality and functionality of HDL particles are also enhanced (Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022). Second, while the cardiovascular applications of anacetrapib provide a strong safety signal, the ocular-specific pharmacodynamics and tissue distribution of the drug remain largely unexplored. It is conceivable that the systemic modulation of HDL might not translate into the desired local changes in Bruch’s membrane, particularly given the unique lipid microenvironment of the retina (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Third, preclinical data demonstrating that anacetrapib can reduce BrM lipid burden and restore integrin localization in murine models, although promising, have yet to be validated extensively, and species differences in CETP expression and lipid metabolism could limit translatability to human patients (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Lastly, the long-term consequences of altering CETP activity in the retina are unknown, and there exists a potential risk that chronic CETP inhibition could inadvertently disrupt local complement regulation or other aspects of retinal homeostasis, given the tight interplay between lipid metabolism and inflammation in AMD pathogenesis (Tricorache et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2015).

Overall, while the conceptual framework underlying the repurposing of anacetrapib for dry AMD is scientifically intriguing and supported by a convergence of genetic, biochemical, and preclinical mechanistic data, further investigation is needed to reconcile the paradoxical relationships observed in human genetic studies, to precisely characterize the local retinal pharmacokinetics of the drug, and to validate its effects on reverse cholesterol transport in the specific context of the retina. In summary, anacetrapib holds potential as a novel therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but its ultimate success will depend on carefully designed preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials that specifically address its ocular efficacy and safety profile (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022).

At the molecular level, the CD59-Fc fusion protein acts by binding specifically to the complement components C8 and/or C9, which is critical during the final assembly phase of the MAC; normally, native CD59 prevents the recruitment of C9 to the C5b-8 complex, thereby effectively halting pore formation on the target cell membrane, which would otherwise lead to uncontrolled ion fluxes, cell lysis, or sub-lytic MAC deposition that can trigger pro-inflammatory and pro-apoptotic signaling cascades (Tan et al., 2016). Analysis: Candidate 1 (CCT128930) and Candidate 2 (PDTC) each present repurposing strategies for dry AMD, but differ markedly in evidence relevance, mechanism specificity, and safety profiles.  Strength of Supporting Evidence:  CCT128930 has robust preclinical characterization as an AKT2 inhibitor with low nM potency and emerging RPE‐specific data (Ghosh et al. 2024) linking AKT2 hyperactivity to TFEB sequestration, lysosomal dysfunction, and drusen formation in dry AMD models. PDTC, while widely used in inflammatory paradigms and showing ocular safety in uveitis models, has no direct dry AMD efficacy data and relies on indirect downstream modulation of phagocytic receptor expression via NF-κB inhibition.  Mechanism of Action:  CCT128930 targets a core upstream node (AKT2/TFEB axis) directly restoring lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy in RPE cells—a central pathological mechanism of dry AMD. PDTC’s MoA is broader, inhibiting NF-κB and chelating Zn²⁺, with less specificity to autophagic clearance, potentially leaving other disease drivers unaddressed.  Safety and Tolerability:  CCT128930 carries known off-target and systemic toxicities from Phase I oncology work; however, intravitreal delivery could localize exposure but mandates detailed ocular toxicology. PDTC has demonstrated tolerability in ocular inflammation models but carries risks of nonselective metal chelation and potential cytotoxicity at higher doses over chronic treatment.  Feasibility:  Both require formulation for intravitreal delivery. CCT128930’s synthetic tractability allows development of sustained‐release nanoparticles; PDTC is commercially available but needs optimization of ocular delivery and dosing to avoid off-target chelation.  Novelty:  CCT128930 offers an innovative, disease‐modifying strategy by reactivating TFEB and autophagy, whereas PDTC rehashes general anti-inflammatory approaches with uncertain efficacy in dry AMD.
Reasoning: While PDTC benefits from some ocular safety data and general anti-inflammatory effects, its indirect MoA and lack of direct AMD efficacy data reduce its translational appeal. CCT128930, despite requiring thorough ocular safety and PK studies, directly addresses lysosomal/autophagy deficits central to RPE degeneration in dry AMD. Its high selectivity for AKT2 and low nM potency offer a precise, disease-modifying mechanism not paralleled by PDTC. Therefore, CCT128930 (ID 30) has the higher probability of successful preclinical validation and eventual clinical translation in dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
CCT128930 is a synthetic small molecule that belongs to the pyrrolopyrimidine class and was initially discovered and optimized for its potent ATP‐competitive inhibition of AKT kinases, particularly targeting the AKT2 isoform (Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 9–11; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8). Its discovery was achieved through a combination of fragment-based screening and structure-based drug design strategies, which allowed researchers to identify and refine a scaffold capable of binding within the ATP pocket of kinases such as AKT and PDK1 (Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 7–9). The molecular design of CCT128930 incorporates a substituted 2-anilino-7H-pyrrolopyrimidine core that confers high affinity and selectivity, as evidenced by its low nanomolar IC₅₀ value—the reported potency for AKT inhibition is around 6–10 nM (Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5). Originally developed for oncology purposes, where aberrant AKT signaling drives uncontrolled cell proliferation, the compound demonstrated significant antiproliferative effects in multiple tumor cell lines with some studies noting efficacy comparable to established inhibitors such as Erlotinib (Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 9–11; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 8–9). The synthetic origins and chemical tractability of the pyrrolopyrimidine scaffold have historically permitted further chemical modifications to optimize pharmacokinetics and minimize off-target activity, traits that are now valuable in the context of repurposing efforts. In summary, CCT128930 is a robustly characterized ATP-competitive inhibitor with a synthetic pedigree grounded in modern medicinal chemistry, which originally found application in cancer therapy yet holds promise for other diseases where AKT2-mediated signaling is implicated (Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, CCT128930 was developed within an oncology paradigm as researchers sought to inhibit aberrant AKT signaling—a driver of cell survival, proliferation, and metabolism—in various cancer models (Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 9–11; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8). Preclinical studies demonstrated that by inhibiting the phosphorylation of key downstream targets such as PRAS40 and FOXO3a, CCT128930 could induce cell cycle arrest and reduce tumor growth in vitro and in xenograft models (Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 9–11; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8). Its antiproliferative efficacy was further underpinned by its ability to compete effectively with ATP for binding to the kinase domain of AKT, a mode of action that led to promising results in early-phase oncology trials. Despite these encouraging effects, further clinical development was halted during phase I studies primarily because of concerns regarding off-target activity and toxicities that limited its therapeutic window (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8). Notably, before the current repurposing hypothesis was proposed, CCT128930 had not been utilized for any ocular indications, including dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), nor had it been evaluated in veterinary settings for similar degenerative diseases. Emerging literature on the role of AKT2 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, particularly through its phosphorylation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), now provides a mechanistic basis for repurposing this compound. Previous studies have linked AKT2 activity with impaired lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy in RPE cells—a critical pathological mechanism in dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). Thus, while the therapeutic history of CCT128930 is rooted in oncology, its well-documented pharmacology, including preclinical pharmacokinetics, tissue penetration (notably CNS penetration), and kinase selectivity, supports its potential application in ocular conditions through localized delivery approaches such as intravitreal injection (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6).  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, CCT128930 exerts its effects primarily by acting as an ATP-competitive inhibitor of AKT kinases, binding to the ATP-binding site within the kinase domain to block the phosphorylation of downstream targets (Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5; Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 7–9). Its mode of action is underscored by its high degree of selectivity for AKT2 over other kinases such as protein kinase A (PKA), which is critical given the need to minimize off-target effects in sensitive tissues like the retina (Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5; Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 7–9). In normal cellular physiology, AKT2 phosphorylates a variety of substrates, including regulatory proteins that modulate cell survival, metabolism, and growth. One particularly important substrate is transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Under standard conditions, TFEB translocates from the cytosol to the nucleus where it drives the expression of numerous genes involved in lysosome formation and the autophagic process. However, in the setting of chronic AKT2 activation—a scenario evident in RPE cells in dry AMD—TFEB becomes phosphorylated at specific serine residues (for example, Ser467), which results in its retention in the cytosol and subsequent inactivation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 1–5). This aberrant phosphorylation leads to reduced autophagic flux and lysosomal dysfunction, impairing the RPE’s capacity to degrade photoreceptor outer segments (POS) effectively (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 8–10).  

By selectively inhibiting AKT2, CCT128930 is hypothesized to reduce the phosphorylation of TFEB, thereby liberating it from its cytosolic sequestration and allowing its translocation into the nucleus (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 2–4). Once in the nucleus, TFEB can stimulate the transcription of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes, enhancing the degradative capacity of RPE cells through increased lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Karim et al., 2020, pp. 10–12). Structural studies of pyrrolopyrimidine inhibitors reveal that the binding of CCT128930 involves specific hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions with key amino acid residues in the ATP-binding pocket of AKT2, leading to its functional inactivation (Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5). This interaction ensures that even at low concentrations, the compound can effectively disrupt AKT2-mediated signaling cascades. The interruption of this signaling cascade is particularly important in the RPE context, where sustained AKT2 activation contributes to the accumulation of cellular debris and the formation of drusen—hallmark features of dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6). Consequently, the molecular events set in motion by CCT128930—namely, the reduction of TFEB phosphorylation and the subsequent activation of lysosomal and autophagy genes—provide a coherent therapeutic rationale for its repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD.  

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed experimental and therapeutic setting, the central expectation is that CCT128930 will inhibit AKT2-mediated TFEB phosphorylation in RPE cells, thus alleviating the cytosolic retention of TFEB and promoting its nuclear translocation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). This mechanistic modulation is anticipated to reinvigorate the transcription of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic genes that are critical for the degradation of POS—a continuous and essential process in the maintenance of retinal health. In dry AMD, the inability of RPE cells to effectively process and clear accumulated photoreceptor debris leads to the formation of drusen and subsequent retinal degeneration. By restoring TFEB activity, treatment with CCT128930 is expected to enhance lysosomal function and lead to improved clearance of these cellular wastes, thereby potentially halting or reversing the progression of disease pathology (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  

Experimental assays to confirm this expected effect would involve measuring the levels of nuclear TFEB through immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation, alongside quantitative PCR assessments for the expression of lysosome-associated genes. Enhanced autophagic flux could be monitored by evaluating markers such as LC3-II conversion and p62 degradation. Given the compound’s IC₅₀ of approximately 6–10 nM, it is anticipated that effective concentrations can be achieved in vitro at low nanomolar doses, with further adjustments made for optimized intravitreal formulations (Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, since RPE cells derived from CFH mutant models have been shown to exhibit greater dysregulation of the AKT2/TFEB signaling pathway, efficacious treatment with CCT128930 should yield measurable improvements in surrogate endpoints such as restored lysosomal enzyme activity and reduced accumulation of POS debris (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). Such outcomes would not only validate the underlying hypothesis but also establish critical proof-of-concept data to support the transition of CCT128930 into further preclinical and, eventually, clinical studies for dry AMD.  

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of CCT128930 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic, informed by a combination of robust mechanistic rationale and a well-characterized pharmacological profile derived from prior oncology research. Strengths of the candidate include its potent ATP-competitive inhibition of AKT2, evidenced by its low nanomolar IC₅₀, and its demonstrated selectivity over other kinases such as PKA, which is critical in reducing the risk of off-target effects (Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5). The molecular rationale for its use in dry AMD hinges on the role of AKT2 in promoting the phosphorylation and cytosolic retention of TFEB—a transcription factor that, when activated, orchestrates lysosomal biogenesis and the autophagic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). By reversing this phosphorylation, CCT128930 is expected to restore TFEB nuclear translocation and thereby rejuvenate the intrinsic degradation pathways within RPE cells, which are compromised in dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 2–4; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).  

However, there are notable challenges and weaknesses that warrant careful consideration. Chief among these is the historical context of CCT128930’s clinical development in oncology, where its advancement was ultimately discontinued due to off-target toxicity and suboptimal safety profiles (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40). Although intravitreal delivery is proposed to localize the drug’s effects and minimize systemic exposure, the unique architecture and sensitivity of the retina demand that comprehensive ocular toxicology studies be undertaken before clinical application. In addition, the extrapolation from cancer cell line models to RPE physiology is not trivial; the intracellular signaling milieu and compensatory mechanisms in RPE cells may differ significantly from those in proliferative tumor cells, potentially affecting the efficacy and safety of AKT2 inhibition in this new context (Yap et al., 2011, pp. 1–2; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8).  

Moreover, the efficiency of CCT128930 in achieving the desired pharmacodynamic outcome in RPE cells will depend heavily on its ability to penetrate the retinal layers and persist at effective concentrations for a sufficient duration. Although available preclinical pharmacokinetics suggest favorable CNS penetration, detailed studies focused specifically on ocular distribution, metabolic stability in vitreous humor, and clearance mechanisms are critical (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Guo et al., 2021, pp. 9–11). Additionally, inter-individual variability in disease pathology—particularly in patients with genetic predispositions such as the CFH Y402H variant—may necessitate personalized approaches or combination therapies to fully harness the compound’s therapeutic potential (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  

In the context of overall therapeutic strategy, the repurposing of CCT128930 offers a novel and mechanistically targeted approach to dry AMD—a disease area where current therapeutic options are limited. The focus on restoring autophagic and lysosomal function addresses a key pathological hallmark of dry AMD, potentially offering a disease-modifying rather than merely symptomatic intervention (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6). Nonetheless, the transition from preclinical promise to clinical reality will require a dedicated effort to optimize drug delivery, thoroughly assess safety in the ocular setting, and define the most responsive patient populations. If these challenges can be overcome, CCT128930 has the potential to be a transformative therapy for dry AMD, representing both a smart and targeted application of existing pharmacological knowledge as well as an innovative shift in treatment paradigms (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2).  

Potential Developments and Future Directions:  
A critical next step involves designing robust preclinical studies that closely mimic the clinical scenarios encountered in dry AMD. Studies should begin with in vitro investigations using primary RPE cells and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE models, particularly those harboring CFH mutations known to accentuate the dysregulation of the AKT2/TFEB pathway (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). These experiments will need to quantify key parameters such as nuclear translocation of TFEB, lysosomal gene expression, and autophagic flux using standard biomarkers (Karim et al., 2020, pp. 10–12; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). In parallel, it will be essential to develop in vivo animal models of dry AMD to assess the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of CCT128930 following intravitreal injection. Parameters such as drug retention in the vitreous, retinal penetration, and clearance rates must be rigorously evaluated to establish an optimal dosing regimen that balances efficacy with safety (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Guo et al., 2021, pp. 9–11).  

Innovative drug delivery approaches should also be explored. For example, encapsulating CCT128930 in biodegradable nanoparticles or liposomal carriers could facilitate a sustained release profile, reducing the frequency of intravitreal injections and minimizing peak-related toxicity. Such delivery systems have shown promise in improving the local bioavailability of other ocular drugs and may similarly enhance the therapeutic index of CCT128930 in the retinal environment (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Guo et al., 2021, pp. 9–11).  

Rigorously addressing the potential for off-target toxicity is another priority. Detailed in vitro and in vivo toxicity studies should monitor retinal structure and function using imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT), fundus autofluorescence, and electrophysiological evaluations (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 9–10). These evaluations will be critical to ensuring that prolonged inhibition of AKT2 does not inadvertently compromise other essential signaling pathways within the retina.  

Furthermore, the development of validated biomarkers for target engagement is crucial. Such biomarkers could include quantifiable metrics of TFEB nuclear localization, lysosomal enzyme activity, or even specific transcriptomic changes associated with enhanced autophagy. These surrogate endpoints would not only help in the preclinical assessment of drug efficacy but could also serve as early indicators of therapeutic response in clinical trials (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8).  

Translational Potential and Risk Mitigation:  
The repurposing strategy for CCT128930 necessitates a comprehensive risk mitigation framework that leverages its strong pharmacological attributes while addressing potential safety concerns. Localized intravitreal delivery offers a means to concentrate the drug’s action within the eye while minimizing systemic exposure—a critical consideration given the adverse events observed in earlier oncology trials (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). At the same time, continued medicinal chemistry efforts may yield derivatives with an improved safety profile that are even more suited to the ocular environment. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies can identify chemical modifications that retain the desired potency in AKT2 inhibition while reducing potential off-target interactions, thereby refining the therapeutic index for chronic ocular use (Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5).  

In parallel, integrating robust pharmacodynamic biomarkers into preclinical and clinical studies will allow for the fine-tuning of dosing regimens and early detection of potential adverse effects. Such biomarkers could include imaging findings related to retinal morphology changes or molecular indicators of restored autophagic function in RPE cells, all of which would contribute to ensuring that the efficacy of CCT128930 is achieved without compromising retinal integrity (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6).  

Collaboration across disciplines—bringing together experts in pharmacology, ophthalmology, and drug delivery science—will be paramount for addressing the unique challenges posed by repurposing an oncology drug for ocular conditions. These interdisciplinary efforts will help design and implement the necessary preclinical studies to evaluate not only drug efficacy but also long-term safety in the delicate retinal environment.  

Regulatory Considerations:  
Repurposing CCT128930 for dry AMD will require comprehensive preclinical data that address the compound’s ocular pharmacokinetics, toxicity profiles, and immunogenicity following repeated intravitreal dosing. Given its previous clinical history in oncology, regulators will likely demand additional evidence to ensure that the risks observed in systemic administration do not extend to the ocular context (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). Early engagement with regulatory agencies is recommended to outline the repurposing strategy, propose appropriate endpoints for clinical trials, and define acceptable risk thresholds. The integration of validated biomarkers for therapeutic response and the use of advanced drug delivery platforms could also help streamline the regulatory pathway by providing robust, multidimensional evidence of both efficacy and safety (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6).
