D609 presents as an intriguing and promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly because of its ability to modulate lipid signaling pathways that are disrupted by oxidative stress and contribute to RPE dysfunction. One of the principal strengths of D609 is its well-documented protective effect on RPE cells both in vitro and in vivo. Studies have shown that D609 maintains high levels of cell viability in RPE models under conditions of severe oxidative stress, and its administration in animal models of AMD has led to significant preservation of retinal structure and function (Wang et al., 2020). Moreover, its water solubility and low molecular weight facilitate ocular delivery and reduce formulation challenges, making it suitable for local administration to the retina (Wang et al., 2020). The dual-action mechanism—combining inhibition of PC-PLC with upregulation of metallothionein—provides both a direct reduction in deleterious DAG-PKC signaling and an indirect bolster to the cell’s antioxidant defenses, which is crucial in the context of dry AMD where oxidative stress is a primary driver of pathology (Wang et al., 2020).

However, several weaknesses must be noted. First, D609 is a non-selective inhibitor; while it effectively targets PC-PLC, it also inhibits other enzymes such as sphingomyelin synthase and phospholipase D, which may introduce off-target effects that could complicate its clinical use (Eurtivong et al., 2023; González-Roura et al., 2002). This lack of selectivity may lead to unpredictable interactions in the intricate lipid signaling networks present in the retina. Second, the compound exists as a mixture of eight stereoisomers, and the differential activity among these isomers is not well understood. Variability in stereoisomeric composition could result in inconsistent pharmacodynamic outcomes and present challenges in the regulatory approval process (Eurtivong et al., 2023; Bhat et al., 2022). Third, the anticipated IC₅₀ of approximately 35 µM for PC-PLC inhibition in RPE cells is relatively high, suggesting that effective biological activity may require high local concentrations that may be difficult to achieve or maintain in vivo without risking toxicity (Wang et al., 2020; Bhat et al., 2022). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nintedanib is a synthetic small‐molecule drug originally discovered and developed by Boehringer Ingelheim through an extensive lead optimization program that began in the late 1990s. Its design emerged during early cancer drug discovery efforts focused on angiogenesis inhibition, inspired in part by Judah Folkman’s pioneering work. The compound belongs to the indolinone chemical class – more precisely, it is a 6‐methoxycarbonyl‐substituted indolinone derivative – and was identified after systematic structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies that evaluated numerous six‐substituted indolinone analogues. In particular, modifications such as moving an amido group on the oxindole scaffold were shown to eliminate unwanted CDK4 inhibition while retaining potent VEGFR inhibition, and these insights eventually led to the convergence on the lead compound now known as nintedanib (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 1–8). The synthetic strategy employed a convergent approach that involved classical malonic ester addition reactions, followed by hydrogenation under acidic conditions that induced decarboxylative cyclization, and concluded with condensation steps and salt formation (resulting in the monoethanesulfonate form) to yield a highly crystalline final product (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 5–10, 39–43). As an indolinone derivative, nintedanib exemplifies a well‐studied class of therapeutic compounds that modulate receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs). Similar compounds in this class have been widely used in antiangiogenic and antifibrotic therapies in oncology and pulmonary medicine, and their ability to simultaneously inhibit multiple RTK pathways has been key to overcoming resistance mechanisms frequently encountered with single‐target inhibitors (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 1–5; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 22–25).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, nintedanib was developed with an emphasis on its anticancer potential. Its original targeting of the vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR) and subsequent demonstration of triple angiokinase inhibition – simultaneously inhibiting VEGFR, platelet‐derived growth factor receptors (PDGFR), and fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFR) – made it a candidate for addressing tumor angiogenesis. Early preclinical studies confirmed that nintedanib potently inhibited endothelial cell proliferation and in vivo tumor growth, leading to its progression into numerous Phase I through III clinical trials for non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), ovarian cancer, and other malignancies (Azuma et al., 2015, pp. 3–5; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 20–22). In addition, the compound’s remarkable specificity, as evidenced by low nanomolar inhibition of PDGFR and VEGFR family members (with IC₅₀ values in the range of 13–65 nM for different targets), underscored its potential as a broad‐spectrum antiangiogenic agent (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 10–15; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 12–14).  

Beyond its oncology applications, accumulating clinical evidence revealed that nintedanib also exhibits strong antifibrotic properties. Its efficacy in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) – with demonstrated improvements in forced vital capacity decline and overall clinical outcomes – led to its regulatory approval for IPF treatment in regions such as Europe and the United States (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 36–39; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 20–22). These diverse therapeutic indications illustrate that while nintedanib was originally intended as an anticancer agent, its mechanism of inhibiting multiple RTK‐mediated pathways allowed its repurposing for fibrotic diseases. Although nintedanib has not yet been extensively used in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), recent preclinical evidence in ocular models has suggested that its kinase inhibition profile could be exploited to modulate dysfunctional signaling in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17). Notably, studies in retinal models have demonstrated that nintedanib can suppress VEGF secretion and reduce neovascularization, both of which provide indirect evidence supporting its ocular tolerability and hint at potential utility in diseases such as dry AMD.  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, nintedanib exerts its pharmacological effect by acting as a competitive inhibitor of the ATP‐binding site located within the catalytic domain of receptor tyrosine kinases. Structural studies, including co‐crystallization and high‐resolution X‐ray diffraction analyses, have revealed that its indolinone core is critical for binding; the molecule forms two canonical hydrogen bonds with key residues within the kinase “hinge” region – for example, interactions with the nitrogen of a conserved cysteine residue (such as Cys919 in VEGFR2) and with a carbonyl oxygen (such as Glu917) – thereby stabilizing its association with the enzyme (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12). The presence of a methyl carboxylate substituent on the indolinone core further extends into the kinase specificity pocket to reinforce binding, and a methyl piperazinyl side chain interacts with solvent‐exposed portions of the protein, contributing both to the agent’s selectivity and to its sustained inhibitory profile (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 39–43; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12).  

Functionally, nintedanib displays potent inhibition of multiple RTKs. Its IC₅₀ values have been reported to be in the low nanomolar range for VEGFR subtypes (e.g., approximately 21 nM for VEGFR2 and 13 nM for VEGFR3), as well as for PDGFR isoforms (roughly 41–58 nM) and FGFR family members (with values ranging from 37 nM for FGFR2 to higher values for other FGFRs) (Azuma et al., 2015, pp. 3–5; Roth et al., 2015, pp. 10–15; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 12–14). By competitively occupying the ATP‐binding pocket, nintedanib prevents receptor autophosphorylation, thereby blocking subsequent activation of downstream signaling cascades, including the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and protein kinase B (Akt) pathways (Reck, 2015, pp. 2–3; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12). This broad inhibition interrupts not only angiogenic signaling in endothelial cells and pericytes but also fibrotic signaling in fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. An additional key feature of nintedanib’s mode of action is the sustained duration of receptor blockade; experimental studies have shown that even after a short 1-hour exposure, inhibition of VEGFR2 phosphorylation can persist for at least 32 hours, suggesting a relatively slow dissociation rate from the kinase active site (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 10–15; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12).  

In the specific context of retinal pigment epithelial cells, PDGFRβ and FGFR1 are among the RTKs implicated in maintaining cellular differentiation, regulating cytoskeletal organization, and modulating phagocytic activity. Dysregulation of these signaling pathways in RPE cells may lead to a decrease in the effective expression of key phagocytic receptors such as integrin αvβ5 and MERTK – receptors that are vital for the ingestion and clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Although much of the detailed mechanistic work in RPE cells remains in the early stages, the existing experimental evidence supports the notion that balanced RTK signaling is necessary for optimal RPE function. By inhibiting overactive signaling through PDGFRβ and FGFR1, nintedanib could restore a more physiologic phosphorylation state that permits proper receptor recycling and expression at the cell surface, thereby supporting phagocytosis and maintaining cellular integrity (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17). Additionally, by modulating these upstream kinases, downstream events that regulate cytoskeletal dynamics – potentially including reorganization of actin filaments and stabilization of focal adhesions – could be favorably altered. Although direct evidence in RPE cells is still emerging, analogous effects in other cell types have been observed when RTK signaling is normalized by multi-target inhibitors such as nintedanib (Hilberg et al., 2018, pp. 14–15, 19–20).  

Expected Effect:  
Within the RPE, efficient phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments is fundamental to retinal homeostasis, and failure of this process is believed to contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. The hypothesis proposes that dysregulated PDGFRβ and FGFR1 signaling in RPE cells impairs the expression and functional activity of phagocytic receptors, notably integrin αvβ5 and MERTK, which are responsible for recognizing and internalizing shed POS. Under normal conditions, these receptors are tightly regulated by extracellular signals, many of which are modulated by RTK activity. In the diseased state, abnormal RTK phosphorylation – perhaps via overactivation of PDGFR and FGFR pathways – could lead to a decrease in phagocytic receptor levels and result in defective POS clearance, contributing to the accumulation of cellular debris, chronic inflammation, and eventual geographic atrophy observed in dry AMD.  

By virtue of its potent inhibitory properties, nintedanib is expected to act by normalizing the aberrantly high RTK signaling in RPE cells. Its inhibition of PDGFRβ, in particular, would be anticipated to reduce excessive downstream signaling that might otherwise lead to a suppression of phagocytic receptor synthesis or recycling. In parallel, FGFR1 inhibition could correct imbalances in signaling that contribute to impaired cytoskeletal remodeling. The cytoskeleton is intimately involved in the process of phagocytosis, not only by providing the structural basis for membrane extension during engulfment but also by facilitating receptor clustering and the formation of phagocytic cups. Therefore, it is plausible to expect that the use of nintedanib would lead to enhanced expression of integrin αvβ5 and MERTK at the RPE cell surface as normal feedback loops are reinstated, thereby promoting increased rates of POS ingestion in assays of RPE differentiation (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17).  

Furthermore, preclinical studies have shown that in settings where RPE cells are exposed to pathological stimuli (such as necrotic cell lysates, which serve as a surrogate for sterile inflammatory conditions seen in retinal diseases), treatment with nintedanib results in a concentration-dependent suppression of aberrant VEGF secretion. This observation suggests that nintedanib is not only capable of regulating angiogenic processes in the retina but may also normalize other aspects of RPE cell function that rely on balanced RTK signaling (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13). In the context of the proposed assays, one would expect that treatment with nintedanib will restore proper receptor tyrosine kinase activity, result in the upregulation of phagocytic receptor expression, and enhance the mechanical and structural reorganization required for efficient POS uptake. These outcomes could be measured both biochemically – through assays of receptor expression and phosphorylation levels – and functionally, via quantification of POS ingestion in differentiated RPE cultures (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12; Rashdan & Hanna, 2014, pp. 2–3).  

In addition to its direct impact on RTK signaling, nintedanib’s inhibition is anticipated to indirectly influence other cytoskeleton-regulating pathways that are governed by MAPK and Akt cascades. Thus, normalization of these signaling pathways may foster an environment in RPE cells where cytoskeletal remodeling is optimized, ultimately leading to improved structural integrity and function—key factors in maintaining retinal health in the face of degenerative processes (Reck, 2015, pp. 2–3; Hilberg et al., 2018, pp. 19–20).

In summary, nintedanib presents a compelling profile as a therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration. One of its primary strengths is its well‐documented ability to inhibit multiple receptor tyrosine kinases simultaneously. This triple angiokinase inhibition—encompassing VEGFR, PDGFR, and FGFR—has been extensively characterized in both in vitro and in vivo models, resulting in robust antitumor and antifibrotic effects in clinical studies for cancer and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 36–39; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 20–22). The compound’s chemical structure, based on its indolinone core, not only permits tight binding and competitive inhibition at the ATP‐binding site but also provides the necessary selectivity that minimizes off-target effects, a critical feature when considering repurposing for a delicate tissue such as the retina (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12; Roth et al., 2015, pp. 39–43).  

From a therapeutic history perspective, the extensive clinical experience with nintedanib in non‐small cell lung cancer and IPF engenders a level of confidence in its pharmacokinetic profile and tolerability when administered systemically. Although its use in ocular applications remains experimental, preliminary preclinical findings provide encouraging data. For instance, studies have demonstrated that nintedanib can inhibit VEGF secretion from retinal pigment epithelial cells exposed to pathological stimuli and can reduce retinal and choroidal neovascularization in animal models. These findings support the notion that, with appropriate reformulation or local delivery (e.g., intravitreal injection), nintedanib could achieve therapeutic levels in the retina without incurring unacceptable toxicity (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17).  

The mechanistic basis for considering nintedanib in dry AMD is particularly appealing. Dry AMD is characterized in part by the dysfunction of RPE cells, including impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments—a process tightly regulated by surface receptors such as integrin αvβ5 and MERTK. Dysregulation of upstream receptor tyrosine kinases, notably PDGFRβ and FGFR1, is hypothesized to contribute to the diminished expression or function of these phagocytic receptors. Nintedanib, by virtue of its potent inhibition of these kinases, holds the potential to recalibrate RTK signaling networks toward a more balanced state. This recalibration may not only restore proper levels of phagocytic receptors on RPE cells but also promote cytoskeletal remodeling necessary for the engulfment and processing of POS (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17). The downstream effects of such restoration could conceivably slow or even reverse aspects of RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration in dry AMD.  

Nonetheless, there are important considerations and potential weaknesses. One significant challenge lies in the delivery of nintedanib to the retina at therapeutic concentrations. Systemic administration of nintedanib is associated with low oral bioavailability and extensive first-pass metabolism (as observed in its use for IPF), which implies that direct ocular administration, likely via intravitreal injection, would be necessary for effective treatment of dry AMD. Although preclinical studies have demonstrated tolerability in ocular models, comprehensive toxicology studies specific to the retinal environment are required to ensure that the compound does not adversely affect other critical retinal cell types, including photoreceptors and inner retinal neurons (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 15–19; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 12–14).  

Another potential limitation is the broad scope of kinase inhibition exerted by nintedanib. While its ability to simultaneously target VEGFR, PDGFR, and FGFR is a strength in terms of overcoming compensatory mechanisms, it also raises the possibility of off-target effects that may disrupt other cellular processes in the retina. The retina is a highly specialized and tightly regulated tissue, and even subtle perturbations in signaling networks can lead to unintended consequences. Therefore, it will be critical to establish that nintedanib’s inhibition of RTKs in RPE cells does not interfere with other essential pathways—especially those involved in retinal development and neuroprotection (Hilberg et al., 2018, pp. 14–15; Hilberg et al., 2018, pp. 19–20).  

In addition, while the hypothesis that nintedanib can enhance phagocytic receptor expression (e.g., upregulating integrin αvβ5 and MERTK) is supported by the general principle that RTK signaling modulates these receptors, direct evidence linking nintedanib treatment to increased phagocytosis in RPE cells is still at an early, hypothesis‐driven stage. Furthermore, while the ocular tolerability of nintedanib has been indirectly inferred from its use in non‐small cell lung cancer and preclinical models of choroidal neovascularization, comprehensive studies specifically designed to evaluate its safety profile in the context of dry AMD are lacking. Given that dry AMD is a chronic condition that would likely require long‐term treatment, issues of sustained drug exposure, potential cumulative toxicity, and the risk of eliciting off‐target effects must be thoroughly investigated (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13; Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 16–17).  

Overall, nintedanib’s established preclinical and clinical data in oncology and fibrosis, combined with its potent multi-targeted inhibition of key receptor tyrosine kinases, provides a strong foundation for its consideration as a repurposed therapeutic candidate in dry AMD. The molecular rationale—that abnormal PDGFRβ and FGFR1 signaling impair the expression and function of essential phagocytic receptors in RPE cells—is both biologically plausible and supported by insights from related pathologies. The anticipated restoration of phagocytic capacity via improved expression of integrin αvβ5 and MERTK, along with enhanced cytoskeletal remodeling conducive to POS uptake, represents an attractive therapeutic mechanism that could address a central defect in dry AMD pathogenesis (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17).  

In conclusion, while the repurposing of nintedanib for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic framework and encouraging early preclinical findings, significant gaps remain that must be addressed before further clinical development is warranted. Critical next steps include:  
1. Detailed in vitro studies using differentiated human RPE cells to measure the impact of nintedanib on PDGFRβ and FGFR1 phosphorylation status, the expression levels of integrin αvβ5 and MERTK, and functional phagocytic assays assessing POS uptake.  
2. In vivo investigations in relevant animal models of dry AMD to evaluate retinal pharmacokinetics, tissue distribution, and the long-term safety profile following local ocular administration.  
3. Exploration of optimal delivery strategies to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic absorption and potential off-target effects.  
4. Further mechanistic studies to elucidate the downstream signaling pathways – including MAPK and Akt cascades – that may be modulated by nintedanib in the RPE and contribute to cytoskeletal remodeling.  

By addressing these areas, it should be possible to rigorously validate whether nintedanib can indeed “normalize” RTK signaling in the RPE and restore the phagocytic function that is compromised in dry AMD. The strengths of nintedanib lie in its potent, well-characterized kinase inhibition and its established clinical safety record in other disease indications. However, challenges remain in adapting its pharmacologic profile to the unique requirements of retinal therapy and ensuring that its broad RTK profile does not inadvertently disrupt other critical ocular functions. If these challenges can be overcome through careful preclinical and translational research, nintedanib may represent a transformative therapeutic option for addressing an unmet need in dry AMD (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 1–5, 20–22; Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13).  

Overall, our evaluation suggests that while caution must be exercised due to potential pharmacokinetic and off-target concerns, the available biochemical and clinical evidence provides sufficient justification for further investigation. The detailed molecular insights into nintedanib’s action, its demonstrated efficacy in modulating kinase pathways central to angiogenesis and fibrosis, and preliminary data in ocular models collectively support its candidacy for repurposing in dry AMD. Rigorous further studies will determine its ultimate utility, but current data indicate that nintedanib is a promising candidate worthy of additional mechanistic and translational evaluation (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12; Reck, 2015, pp. 2–3; Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bryostatin‐1 is a naturally derived macrolide originally isolated from marine invertebrates and belongs to a class of compounds collectively known as bryostatins. These compounds exhibit potent modulation of protein kinase C (PKC) activity by binding to the enzyme’s diacylglycerol binding site on the regulatory domain. Bryostatin‐1 has been characterized as a partial agonist of PKC and is noted for its ability to both acutely activate and chronically down‐regulate specific PKC isoforms. The molecular architecture of bryostatin‐1 confers a unique binding profile that distinguishes it from phorbol esters; it induces translocation of target PKC isoforms to membranes without eliciting the full tumor‐promoting effects observed with phorbol esters. The compound is synthetically challenging to produce, yet semisynthetic methodologies have enabled its preparation in sufficient quantities for preclinical and early clinical applications. As a member of the marine natural products family, bryostatin‐1 is frequently investigated for its anticancer and neuroprotective properties, and its chemical structure serves as the basis for designing simplified analogs with improved pharmacological profiles (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).  

Therapeutic History:  
Bryostatin‐1 has a long preclinical history that spans oncology and neurology. In oncology, bryostatin‐1 has been extensively studied for its role in modulating PKC in various tumor types and has been evaluated in numerous clinical trials addressing B‐cell malignancies and renal cancers. Despite promising preclinical results, its cancer‐directed clinical efficacy has been limited by suboptimal outcomes and adverse side effects such as myalgia. More recently, bryostatin‐1 has been repurposed in neurological contexts. Several studies have demonstrated its neuroprotective capabilities in models of Alzheimer’s disease, where it has shown to improve synaptic function, restore dendritic spine morphology, induce synaptogenesis through the upregulation of brain‐derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and enhance cognitive function. Phase II clinical trials in Alzheimer’s patients have provided translational evidence of its ability to modulate PKCε in the central nervous system (Chen et al., 2024; Nelson et al., 2017). However, a search of clinical trial databases has revealed that no formal clinical trials have been registered evaluating bryostatin‐1 in the setting of macular degeneration, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, or Rab7 signaling‐related pathways (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Although there is evidence supporting bryostatin‐1’s capacity to affect cellular pathways—such as inducing autophagy and promoting PKC‐mediated cell survival—in neuronal and cancer cells, its application to ocular diseases like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) remains unexplored in the clinical context (Safarpour, 2009; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).  

Mechanism of Action:  
Bryostatin‐1 functions primarily as a modulator of protein kinase C, a family of serine/threonine kinases that play central roles in regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis, and intracellular trafficking. On a molecular level, bryostatin‐1 binds competitively to the diacylglycerol (DAG) binding site located in the C1 domain of PKC isoforms. This binding event leads to the translocation of PKC from the cytosol to membranous compartments, thereby bringing the kinase into close proximity with its substrates. Unlike potent activators such as phorbol esters, bryostatin‐1 acts as a partial agonist. Short‐term exposure results in the activation of specific PKC isoforms, whereas prolonged exposure leads to their down‐regulation via proteasomal degradation. Structural studies have demonstrated that the complex hydrogen‐bond networks formed by the A- and B-rings of bryostatin‐1 contribute significantly to its isoform selectivity and binding affinity (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).  

In the context of the hypothesized mechanism for dry AMD, it is proposed that bryostatin‐1 can activate atypical PKC isoforms at very low effective concentrations (EC₅₀ ≈ 0.1 nM), potentially including enzymes that are involved in the regulation of Rab7 signalling. Although bryostatin‐1 has been studied predominantly for its activation of classical (e.g., PKCα, PKCβ) and novel PKC isoforms (e.g., PKCδ, PKCε), several experimental reports suggest that PKC activity regulates various aspects of vesicular trafficking, including phagosome maturation. In phagocytic cell lines, enhanced PKC activation has been linked to improved phagolysosomal fusion, which is essential for the degradation of ingested material. This connection is of particular interest in RPE cells, where the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) via the phagosome–lysosome pathway is central to retinal homeostasis. The hypothesis extends this mechanism by proposing that the activation of PKC by bryostatin‐1 may lead to the phosphorylation of Rab7 effector proteins, which are known to control the late stages of phagosome maturation and lysosome fusion. Although direct experimental evidence connecting bryostatin‐1‐mediated PKC activation to Rab7 effector phosphorylation in RPE cells is limited, existing literature has established the importance of PKC in regulating phagocytic processes and intracellular vesicle trafficking (Saddala et al., 2020; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005). Dry AMD is characterized by the dysfunction of RPE cells, which leads to impaired clearance of POS and subsequent accumulation of toxic lipofuscin deposits. RPE dysfunction is associated with disrupted phagosome maturation and lysosomal degradation pathways, contributing to retinal degeneration and vision loss. The therapeutic hypothesis for bryostatin‐1 posits that its administration will enhance the maturation of phagosomes by stimulating PKC isoforms that, in turn, phosphorylate Rab7 effectors. Effective phosphorylation of these effectors is expected to facilitate late phagosome–lysosome fusion, thereby improving the trafficking and degradation of POS. Empirical studies in RPE cells have shown that defects in phagolysosomal fusion lead to the accumulation of nondegradable materials and are closely linked to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Safarpour, 2009; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).  

The candidate mechanism suggests that, upon administration, bryostatin‐1 will rapidly bind to its target PKC isoforms in RPE cells, causing these kinases to translocate to relevant subcellular membranes. This translocation is anticipated to bring PKC in proximity to Rab7 effectors situated on late phagosomes. Activation of these kinases would then promote the phosphorylation of regulatory proteins that control vesicular fusion events. As a result, the impaired phagocytosis observed in dry AMD would be corrected through improved maturation of phagosomes and enhanced fusion with lysosomes. Such a cascade is expected to lead to enhanced clearance of POS debris and, ultimately, a reduction in lipofuscin accumulation, which is central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Bryostatin‐1 presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for dry AMD owing to its potent modulation of PKC, a central regulator of intracellular signaling pathways that govern vesicular trafficking, phagocytosis, and autophagy. One of the key strengths of bryostatin‐1 lies in its well‐documented activity in modulating PKC isoforms that are critical in diverse physiological contexts, including neuronal function and cancer cell biology. Its demonstrated neuroprotective efficacy in Alzheimer’s disease clinical studies supports the compound’s translational potential and suggests that its PKC‐modulating effects might be harnessed in alternate tissues such as the retina (Chen et al., 2024). Additionally, the critical role of PKC in promoting phagosome–lysosome fusion has been substantiated in other cell types, which provides a strong theoretical basis for its application in RPE cells where phagocytic clearance is essential for maintaining retinal integrity (Saddala et al., 2020; Safarpour, 2009).

Despite these promising aspects, several challenges and weaknesses must be considered. Foremost, no direct studies to date have evaluated bryostatin‐1 in the context of dry AMD or in RPE cells. Clinical trial databases have not registered any studies for bryostatin‐1 in macular degeneration, underscoring the novelty of this repurposing strategy but also highlighting a significant gap in the literature (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The hypothesis that bryostatin‐1 will stimulate atypical PKC isoforms to phosphorylate Rab7 effectors, although plausible, remains largely speculative. While various studies have linked PKC activity to phagosome maturation and autophagy regulation, the precise isoforms relevant to RPE cell function—and whether these isoforms are the same ones activated by bryostatin‐1 in neuronal or cancer models—have not been comprehensively elucidated. Therefore, it will be crucial to determine, through rigorous in vitro assays and animal models, whether the purported EC₅₀ of approximately 0.1 nM is achievable in RPE cells and whether this concentration effectively modifies the Rab7‐related molecular machinery.

Additional considerations include the potential for off‐target effects and systemic toxicity. Past clinical studies of bryostatin‐1, particularly in oncology, have reported adverse effects such as myalgia and thrombocytopenia. However, the pharmacokinetic profile observed in Alzheimer’s trials suggests that the dosing regimens used for neurological disorders might be translatable to ocular delivery with appropriate formulation strategies. Localized ocular delivery, such as intravitreal injection or controlled‐release implants, may enable targeted modulation of PKC in the retina while mitigating systemic exposure and associated adverse events (Chen et al., 2024; Nelson et al., 2017). Moreover, the challenge of achieving adequate drug penetration to the RPE in vivo is nontrivial. Approaches to enhance ocular bioavailability, including nanoparticle encapsulation or conjugation to targeting ligands, should be explored concurrently with the design of preclinical studies to better validate this therapeutic candidate.

From a mechanistic standpoint, the dual nature of bryostatin‐1—characterized by initial activation followed by downregulation of PKC isoforms—necessitates precise temporal control of its pharmacodynamic effects. In the context of phagosome maturation, transient activation may be beneficial to restore proper lysosomal fusion; however, prolonged downregulation might counteract the desired effect. It is therefore important that future studies carefully delineate the dosing regimen (both concentration and administration frequency) required to achieve an optimal therapeutic window in RPE cells. Additionally, the specificity of bryostatin‐1 for PKC isoforms implicated in Rab7 effector phosphorylation must be confirmed, as the RPE expresses a complex array of PKC isoforms that may play distinct roles in cellular homeostasis and stress responses (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).

The breadth and diversity of bryostatin‐1’s effects in preclinical models have generated considerable interest, yet its repurposing for dry AMD remains at an early stage of conceptual development. Given that disruption of phagosome maturation in RPE cells is a well‐established contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD—and that PKC signaling has been implicated in regulating this process—the rationale for exploring bryostatin‐1 in this indication is scientifically sound. Nonetheless, the transition from a neuroprotective agent in Alzheimer’s disease to an effective modulator of RPE function in dry AMD will depend on new studies that specifically address the cellular context of the retina. In this regard, preliminary investigations using primary RPE cultures or animal models of dry AMD will be critical to validate the hypothesis that PKC activation by bryostatin‐1 can enhance Rab7‐mediated phagolysosomal fusion and improve POS clearance (Saddala et al., 2020; Safarpour, 2009).

In summary, bryostatin‐1 offers both significant promise and notable challenges as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration. Its ability to modulate PKC in a manner that may restore essential phagolysosomal functions in the RPE positions it as an innovative approach to address a major unmet need in ocular therapeutics. The compound’s successful use in Alzheimer’s disease trials provides encouraging translational evidence of its safety and efficacy in modulating neuronal PKC activity. However, the absence of direct evidence in retinal cells, the uncertainty regarding which specific PKC isoforms are most relevant to RPE phagocytosis, and potential issues related to dosing and systemic toxicity form significant hurdles that must be overcome. Moving forward, it will be critical to conduct comprehensive in vitro studies to assess the effects of bryostatin‐1 on RPE phagosome maturation, coupled with robust in vivo experiments in established dry AMD models. Such studies should focus on confirming the expression and role of the putative target proteins, including Rab7 effectors, and determining whether the activation of these pathways can indeed translate into improved clearance of POS and reduced retinal degeneration (Saddala et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Chen et al., 2024; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).

In conclusion, the overall evaluation of bryostatin‐1 as a drug candidate for dry AMD reveals a compound with strong mechanistic rationale and significant translational potential based on its established pharmacological properties in PKC modulation and neuroprotection. The strengths of bryostatin‐1 include its potent activity at nanomolar concentrations, a unique mode of action that distinguishes it from classical PKC activators, and supporting evidence from clinical studies in neurological disorders. Conversely, its weaknesses lie primarily in the absence of direct studies in ocular tissues, uncertainty regarding the specific PKC isoforms involved in RPE phagosome maturation, and potential challenges in achieving localized delivery without systemic side effects. An interdisciplinary approach that integrates detailed molecular studies with innovative drug delivery strategies will be critical in validating bryostatin‐1’s viability for the treatment of dry AMD. Based on the current literature, investing in rigorous preclinical testing to confirm the hypothesized mechanistic link between PKC activation, Rab7 effector phosphorylation, and enhanced phagosome maturation in RPE cells is warranted before progressing to clinical evaluation (Saddala et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Safarpour, 2009; Chen et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Trehalose is a naturally occurring, nonreducing disaccharide composed of two D‐glucose units (MW = 342.3 Da) that is not synthesized endogenously in mammals but is abundant in other organisms such as fungi, plants, and invertebrates (Cox et al., 2025). It was originally discovered as a cellular protectant and osmolyte that stabilizes proteins and membranes under conditions of stress, and its unique chemical stability and protein‐protective properties have led to its use in cryopreservation and organ transplant protocols (Lotfi et al., 2018). As a small-molecule therapeutic candidate, trehalose belongs to a class of compounds known as osmolytes and molecular chaperones; this category has been extensively explored for its capacity to stabilize proteins, prevent aggregation, and enhance cellular resilience in the face of diverse environmental and metabolic stresses (Abokyi et al., 2020; Cox et al., 2025). In drug development contexts, its repurposing for dry age-related macular degeneration (dAMD) is driven by its capacity to activate TFEB—a master transcription factor regulating the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network—and thereby boost autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ghosh et al., 2023). Trehalose has been formulated for ocular use, most notably as an ingredient in tear substitutes for dry eye, and its safety profile in such formulations provides ancillary support for its potential repurposing to target RPE dysfunction in dAMD (Cox et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Trehalose has a well-documented history in biochemical and preclinical research due to its potent protein-stabilizing and osmoprotectant actions. It has been widely used in non-ophthalmic applications, most notably in cryopreservation protocols, where its ability to preserve protein structure and cellular integrity under desiccating and freezing conditions is exploited (Cox et al., 2025; Lotfi et al., 2018). In the ocular field, trehalose has been evaluated primarily for anterior segment indications such as dry eye disease; several randomized clinical trials have demonstrated its tolerability and efficacy as a tear substitute when combined with hyaluronic acid, with improvements in tear film break-up time (TBUT) and ocular surface symptoms (Chiambaretta et al., 2017).  
More importantly for dAMD, multiple in vitro studies using human RPE cell models—including ARPE-19 and iPSC-derived RPE from patients with genetic risk factors like CFH mutations—have shown that trehalose rescues autophagy deficits and lysosomal dysfunction, especially under oxidative-stress conditions induced by agents such as hydroquinone (Abokyi et al., 2020). These studies report that trehalose treatment upregulates key autophagy regulators (e.g., ATG5, ATG7) and lysosomal markers (e.g., LAMP2, cathepsin D) while enhancing autophagic flux, thereby improving the degradative capacity of RPE cells—a fundamental defect implicated in the accumulation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and lipofuscin in dAMD (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). Additionally, in murine models of retinal degeneration—whether induced by light exposure or by genetic interventions—trehalose has been shown to protect against retinal cell loss and preserve outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness, offering further preclinical evidence of its neuroprotective potential (Cox et al., 2025). Thus, while trehalose has an established record in non-ocular uses and in the treatment of anterior ocular surface disorders, emerging data now support its repurposing for dAMD by virtue of its ability to modulate autophagy and lysosomal degradation in RPE cells (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central mechanism by which trehalose is hypothesized to benefit dry AMD involves its capacity to activate the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of the CLEAR network. TFEB controls the transcription of a whole battery of genes required for autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and metabolic adaptation (Abokyi et al., 2020). Typically, TFEB resides in the cytoplasm in an inactive, phosphorylated state under nutrient-rich or stress-depleted conditions; its translocation to the nucleus is tightly regulated by mTORC1-dependent and mTORC1-independent signaling pathways (Ghosh et al., 2023; Karim et al., 2020). Trehalose has been shown to induce TFEB nuclear translocation independently of mTOR inhibition, potentially through mechanisms involving Akt signaling modulation and AMPK activation (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Upon nuclear entry, TFEB binds to CLEAR elements in the promoter regions of target genes, thereby upregulating autophagy mediators such as ATG5 and ATG7, enhancing the expression of lysosomal proteins like LAMP2, and increasing the levels of protein markers such as LC3B and p62 that are involved in autophagosome formation and maturation (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Several biochemical studies in human RPE cells have demonstrated that trehalose treatment leads to increased TFEB mRNA and protein levels with concomitant upregulation of CLEAR network gene expression. For instance, in ARPE-19 cells exposed to hydroquinone—a model for oxidative stress relevant to dAMD—it was observed that trehalose not only increased LC3-II levels and GFP-LC3 puncta formation but also enhanced the degradation of autophagic substrates, indicating that trehalose facilitates effective autophagic flux rather than merely blocking lysosomal degradation (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Mechanistically, trehalose is thought to penetrate mammalian cells via fluid-phase endocytosis and possibly through the SLC2A8 (GLUT8) transporter, which facilitates its intracellular accumulation at millimolar concentrations (Cox et al., 2025). Once inside the cell, trehalose appears to modulate several key pathways: by inhibiting Akt signaling, it reduces the phosphorylation of TFEB at specific residues (such as S467) that normally prevent its nuclear import; concurrently, trehalose may activate AMPK, which further supports autophagy induction (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020). Moreover, although trehalose transiently upregulates NRF2 under basal conditions—thereby enhancing antioxidant defenses—its primary protective effect in oxidative stress models of the RPE appears to be mediated by restored autophagy, as demonstrated by loss of cytoprotection when autophagy is genetically disrupted via ATG5 knockdown (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Beyond its role in autophagy, trehalose has been implicated in promoting chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) through stimulation of LAMP2 expression, which is essential for CMA substrate recognition and lysosomal import (Abokyi et al., 2020). In this way, trehalose may offer a dual benefit: boosting canonical macroautophagy while also enhancing CMA, collectively leading to improved clearance of damaged organelles, aggregated proteins, and undigested POS in the RPE—a critical function given the strong association between defective POS clearance and the pathogenesis of dAMD (Abokyi et al., 2020). Furthermore, in CFH-mutant iPSC-derived RPE cells, trehalose has been shown to rescue the diminished activity of lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D and to restore other proteostasis markers, establishing a direct molecular link between trehalose-induced TFEB activation and functional improvements in the degradative capacity of RPE cells (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
Collectively, the mechanistic data suggest that trehalose exerts its beneficial effects through a complex interplay of intracellular signaling pathways that converge on the activation of TFEB, thereby re-establishing efficient autophagic clearance processes that are impaired in the aging and oxidative-stressed RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020; Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic insights outlined above, the hypothesis posits that treatment with trehalose at a concentration of 5 mM in an in vitro assay using iPSC-derived RPE cells from dry AMD patients will lead to robust TFEB nuclear translocation. This nuclear translocation is expected to result in the transcriptional upregulation of CLEAR network genes, thereby increasing the expression of autophagy regulators such as ATG5 and ATG7 and promoting the biogenesis of lysosomes, as evidenced by increased levels of lysosomal markers like LAMP2 and cathepsin D (Abokyi et al., 2020). In an environment of oxidative stress—for example, when the iPSC-RPE cells are challenged with hydroquinone to mimic cigarette smoke-induced damage or other oxidative insults commonly associated with AMD—the activation of TFEB by trehalose is anticipated to restore impaired autophagic flux. This restoration would be reflected in the accumulation of LC3-II upon inhibition of lysosomal function (e.g., in the presence of chloroquine) and decreased levels of autophagy substrate p62 (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Crucially, by enhancing autophagic and lysosomal function in the RPE, trehalose is expected to improve POS degradation. Efficient degradation of POS is vital for photoreceptor health, and its impairment has been implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD through the accumulation of toxic byproducts and lipofuscin (Abokyi et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025). Thus, the expected phenotype in the in vitro assay would include not only molecular signatures of enhanced autophagy (e.g., increased LC3B puncta, upregulated ATG gene expression) but also functional improvements such as reduced oxidative stress (lower reactive oxygen species levels) and improved cell viability under stress conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Moreover, previous studies have shown that trehalose’s cytoprotective effects are autophagy-dependent because genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of autophagy (e.g., via ATG5 knockdown) abolishes the otherwise protective effects of trehalose, thereby reinforcing the notion that the expected improvement in POS degradation and overall cellular homeostasis is tightly linked to the restoration of autophagy and lysosomal competence (Abokyi et al., 2020). In essence, the application of 5 mM trehalose to oxidative-stressed iPSC-RPE cells is anticipated to reverse the autophagic deficits that are characteristic of dry AMD, ultimately leading to enhanced clearance of POS, reduced accumulation of cytotoxic aggregates, and improved cellular survival and function in an in vitro model that recapitulates key aspects of the disease (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
Trehalose represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its multifaceted capacity to modulate intracellular degradation pathways that are critically impaired in the disease state. One of the primary strengths of trehalose is its robust preclinical evidence base. Multiple studies have demonstrated that trehalose can induce TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE models, resulting in the transcriptional activation of an array of autophagy and lysosomal genes (Abokyi et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2023; Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020). This mechanistic property directly addresses a key pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD, where the accumulation of undegraded photoreceptor outer segments and lipofuscin due to defective autophagy plays a contributory role in RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration (Abokyi et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025). The ability of trehalose to enhance both macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy augments its therapeutic appeal, as it suggests an overall improvement in cellular proteostasis, which is imperative in aged or stressed RPE cells (Abokyi et al., 2020; Cox et al., 2025).  
Another notable strength is the established safety profile of trehalose. It is a naturally occurring compound with a long history of use in various medical and industrial applications, including as an ingredient in ocular surface formulations for dry eye disease (Chiambaretta et al., 2017; Cox et al., 2025). Furthermore, the preclinical data showing that trehalose can protect against oxidative stress and preserve retinal function in animal models lend credibility to the hypothesis that it may exert similar protective effects in human RPE cells (Cox et al., 2025).  
However, several weaknesses and gaps must be acknowledged as well. First, the majority of the compelling evidence for trehalose’s efficacy in modulating TFEB and enhancing autophagy comes from in vitro studies using immortalized RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19) or rodent models, with only limited data available from human iPSC-derived RPE models specifically derived from AMD patients (Abokyi et al., 2020). Second, there are ongoing debates in the literature regarding the precise molecular mechanisms by which trehalose exerts its autophagy-enhancing effects, with some reports disputing its ability to induce autophagy under certain conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).  
Another potential challenge lies in the delivery of trehalose to the RPE in a clinically meaningful manner. Although trehalose is orally bioavailable and has been successfully formulated for topical ocular use in dry eye applications, the posterior segment of the eye presents unique drug delivery hurdles. Penetration through the cornea and subsequent distribution to the RPE and retina often require specialized formulations, and while there are preclinical reports of trehalose reaching posterior ocular tissues (Cox et al., 2025), comprehensive pharmacokinetic and ocular bioavailability data for trehalose in the context of dAMD remain sparse.  
Furthermore, while the repurposing of trehalose is attractive due to its established safety and low cost, intellectual property issues and regulatory challenges associated with drug repurposing may complicate clinical development. Despite these concerns, the overall body of evidence supports further investigation into trehalose as a potential modulator of TFEB and autophagy in the RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cox et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).  
In summary, trehalose offers several strong advantages as a candidate therapeutic for dry AMD. Its ability to activate TFEB and upregulate a broad spectrum of autophagy and lysosomal genes addresses a fundamental defect in RPE cells implicated in the disease. Robust preclinical evidence in both in vitro and animal models suggests that trehalose enhances autophagic flux, improves POS clearance, and confers cytoprotective effects against oxidative stress. Its favorable safety profile and prior use in ocular formulations further support its translational potential. However, critical gaps remain in terms of validating its efficacy in human-derived RPE models, optimizing its dosing and delivery to the posterior segment, and resolving discrepancies regarding its mechanism of action in different experimental contexts. Given these considerations, trehalose represents a promising candidate that merits further investigation—particularly through rigorous dose-response studies, advanced formulation development to enhance retinal delivery, and robust clinical trials in patient populations at risk for dry AMD—to fully establish its therapeutic value (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cox et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Historically, CCT128930 was developed within an oncology paradigm as researchers sought to inhibit aberrant AKT signaling—a driver of cell survival, proliferation, and metabolism—in various cancer models (Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 9–11; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8). Preclinical studies demonstrated that by inhibiting the phosphorylation of key downstream targets such as PRAS40 and FOXO3a, CCT128930 could induce cell cycle arrest and reduce tumor growth in vitro and in xenograft models (Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 9–11; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8). Its antiproliferative efficacy was further underpinned by its ability to compete effectively with ATP for binding to the kinase domain of AKT, a mode of action that led to promising results in early-phase oncology trials. Despite these encouraging effects, further clinical development was halted during phase I studies primarily because of concerns regarding off-target activity and toxicities that limited its therapeutic window (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8). Notably, before the current repurposing hypothesis was proposed, CCT128930 had not been utilized for any ocular indications, including dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), nor had it been evaluated in veterinary settings for similar degenerative diseases. Emerging literature on the role of AKT2 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, particularly through its phosphorylation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), now provides a mechanistic basis for repurposing this compound. Previous studies have linked AKT2 activity with impaired lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy in RPE cells—a critical pathological mechanism in dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). Thus, while the therapeutic history of CCT128930 is rooted in oncology, its well-documented pharmacology, including preclinical pharmacokinetics, tissue penetration (notably CNS penetration), and kinase selectivity, supports its potential application in ocular conditions through localized delivery approaches such as intravitreal injection (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6).  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, CCT128930 exerts its effects primarily by acting as an ATP-competitive inhibitor of AKT kinases, binding to the ATP-binding site within the kinase domain to block the phosphorylation of downstream targets (Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5; Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 7–9). Its mode of action is underscored by its high degree of selectivity for AKT2 over other kinases such as protein kinase A (PKA), which is critical given the need to minimize off-target effects in sensitive tissues like the retina (Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5; Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 7–9). In normal cellular physiology, AKT2 phosphorylates a variety of substrates, including regulatory proteins that modulate cell survival, metabolism, and growth. One particularly important substrate is transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Under standard conditions, TFEB translocates from the cytosol to the nucleus where it drives the expression of numerous genes involved in lysosome formation and the autophagic process. However, in the setting of chronic AKT2 activation—a scenario evident in RPE cells in dry AMD—TFEB becomes phosphorylated at specific serine residues (for example, Ser467), which results in its retention in the cytosol and subsequent inactivation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 1–5). This aberrant phosphorylation leads to reduced autophagic flux and lysosomal dysfunction, impairing the RPE’s capacity to degrade photoreceptor outer segments (POS) effectively (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 8–10).  

By selectively inhibiting AKT2, CCT128930 is hypothesized to reduce the phosphorylation of TFEB, thereby liberating it from its cytosolic sequestration and allowing its translocation into the nucleus (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 2–4). Once in the nucleus, TFEB can stimulate the transcription of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes, enhancing the degradative capacity of RPE cells through increased lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Karim et al., 2020, pp. 10–12). Structural studies of pyrrolopyrimidine inhibitors reveal that the binding of CCT128930 involves specific hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions with key amino acid residues in the ATP-binding pocket of AKT2, leading to its functional inactivation (Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5). This interaction ensures that even at low concentrations, the compound can effectively disrupt AKT2-mediated signaling cascades. The interruption of this signaling cascade is particularly important in the RPE context, where sustained AKT2 activation contributes to the accumulation of cellular debris and the formation of drusen—hallmark features of dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6). Consequently, the molecular events set in motion by CCT128930—namely, the reduction of TFEB phosphorylation and the subsequent activation of lysosomal and autophagy genes—provide a coherent therapeutic rationale for its repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD.  

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed experimental and therapeutic setting, the central expectation is that CCT128930 will inhibit AKT2-mediated TFEB phosphorylation in RPE cells, thus alleviating the cytosolic retention of TFEB and promoting its nuclear translocation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). This mechanistic modulation is anticipated to reinvigorate the transcription of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic genes that are critical for the degradation of POS—a continuous and essential process in the maintenance of retinal health. In dry AMD, the inability of RPE cells to effectively process and clear accumulated photoreceptor debris leads to the formation of drusen and subsequent retinal degeneration. By restoring TFEB activity, treatment with CCT128930 is expected to enhance lysosomal function and lead to improved clearance of these cellular wastes, thereby potentially halting or reversing the progression of disease pathology (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  

Experimental assays to confirm this expected effect would involve measuring the levels of nuclear TFEB through immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation, alongside quantitative PCR assessments for the expression of lysosome-associated genes. Enhanced autophagic flux could be monitored by evaluating markers such as LC3-II conversion and p62 degradation. Given the compound’s IC₅₀ of approximately 6–10 nM, it is anticipated that effective concentrations can be achieved in vitro at low nanomolar doses, with further adjustments made for optimized intravitreal formulations (Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, since RPE cells derived from CFH mutant models have been shown to exhibit greater dysregulation of the AKT2/TFEB signaling pathway, efficacious treatment with CCT128930 should yield measurable improvements in surrogate endpoints such as restored lysosomal enzyme activity and reduced accumulation of POS debris (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). Such outcomes would not only validate the underlying hypothesis but also establish critical proof-of-concept data to support the transition of CCT128930 into further preclinical and, eventually, clinical studies for dry AMD.  

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of CCT128930 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic, informed by a combination of robust mechanistic rationale and a well-characterized pharmacological profile derived from prior oncology research. Strengths of the candidate include its potent ATP-competitive inhibition of AKT2, evidenced by its low nanomolar IC₅₀, and its demonstrated selectivity over other kinases such as PKA, which is critical in reducing the risk of off-target effects (Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5). The molecular rationale for its use in dry AMD hinges on the role of AKT2 in promoting the phosphorylation and cytosolic retention of TFEB—a transcription factor that, when activated, orchestrates lysosomal biogenesis and the autophagic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). By reversing this phosphorylation, CCT128930 is expected to restore TFEB nuclear translocation and thereby rejuvenate the intrinsic degradation pathways within RPE cells, which are compromised in dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 2–4; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).  

However, there are notable challenges and weaknesses that warrant careful consideration. Chief among these is the historical context of CCT128930’s clinical development in oncology, where its advancement was ultimately discontinued due to off-target toxicity and suboptimal safety profiles (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40). Although intravitreal delivery is proposed to localize the drug’s effects and minimize systemic exposure, the unique architecture and sensitivity of the retina demand that comprehensive ocular toxicology studies be undertaken before clinical application. In addition, the extrapolation from cancer cell line models to RPE physiology is not trivial; the intracellular signaling milieu and compensatory mechanisms in RPE cells may differ significantly from those in proliferative tumor cells, potentially affecting the efficacy and safety of AKT2 inhibition in this new context (Yap et al., 2011, pp. 1–2; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8).  

Moreover, the efficiency of CCT128930 in achieving the desired pharmacodynamic outcome in RPE cells will depend heavily on its ability to penetrate the retinal layers and persist at effective concentrations for a sufficient duration. Although available preclinical pharmacokinetics suggest favorable CNS penetration, detailed studies focused specifically on ocular distribution, metabolic stability in vitreous humor, and clearance mechanisms are critical (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Guo et al., 2021, pp. 9–11). Additionally, inter-individual variability in disease pathology—particularly in patients with genetic predispositions such as the CFH Y402H variant—may necessitate personalized approaches or combination therapies to fully harness the compound’s therapeutic potential (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  

In the context of overall therapeutic strategy, the repurposing of CCT128930 offers a novel and mechanistically targeted approach to dry AMD—a disease area where current therapeutic options are limited. The focus on restoring autophagic and lysosomal function addresses a key pathological hallmark of dry AMD, potentially offering a disease-modifying rather than merely symptomatic intervention (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6). Nonetheless, the transition from preclinical promise to clinical reality will require a dedicated effort to optimize drug delivery, thoroughly assess safety in the ocular setting, and define the most responsive patient populations. If these challenges can be overcome, CCT128930 has the potential to be a transformative therapy for dry AMD, representing both a smart and targeted application of existing pharmacological knowledge as well as an innovative shift in treatment paradigms (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2).  

Potential Developments and Future Directions:  
A critical next step involves designing robust preclinical studies that closely mimic the clinical scenarios encountered in dry AMD. Studies should begin with in vitro investigations using primary RPE cells and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE models, particularly those harboring CFH mutations known to accentuate the dysregulation of the AKT2/TFEB pathway (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). These experiments will need to quantify key parameters such as nuclear translocation of TFEB, lysosomal gene expression, and autophagic flux using standard biomarkers (Karim et al., 2020, pp. 10–12; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). In parallel, it will be essential to develop in vivo animal models of dry AMD to assess the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of CCT128930 following intravitreal injection. Parameters such as drug retention in the vitreous, retinal penetration, and clearance rates must be rigorously evaluated to establish an optimal dosing regimen that balances efficacy with safety (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Guo et al., 2021, pp. 9–11).  

Innovative drug delivery approaches should also be explored. For example, encapsulating CCT128930 in biodegradable nanoparticles or liposomal carriers could facilitate a sustained release profile, reducing the frequency of intravitreal injections and minimizing peak-related toxicity. Such delivery systems have shown promise in improving the local bioavailability of other ocular drugs and may similarly enhance the therapeutic index of CCT128930 in the retinal environment (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Guo et al., 2021, pp. 9–11).  

Rigorously addressing the potential for off-target toxicity is another priority. Detailed in vitro and in vivo toxicity studies should monitor retinal structure and function using imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT), fundus autofluorescence, and electrophysiological evaluations (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 9–10). These evaluations will be critical to ensuring that prolonged inhibition of AKT2 does not inadvertently compromise other essential signaling pathways within the retina.  

Furthermore, the development of validated biomarkers for target engagement is crucial. Such biomarkers could include quantifiable metrics of TFEB nuclear localization, lysosomal enzyme activity, or even specific transcriptomic changes associated with enhanced autophagy. These surrogate endpoints would not only help in the preclinical assessment of drug efficacy but could also serve as early indicators of therapeutic response in clinical trials (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8).  

Translational Potential and Risk Mitigation:  
The repurposing strategy for CCT128930 necessitates a comprehensive risk mitigation framework that leverages its strong pharmacological attributes while addressing potential safety concerns. Localized intravitreal delivery offers a means to concentrate the drug’s action within the eye while minimizing systemic exposure—a critical consideration given the adverse events observed in earlier oncology trials (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). At the same time, continued medicinal chemistry efforts may yield derivatives with an improved safety profile that are even more suited to the ocular environment. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies can identify chemical modifications that retain the desired potency in AKT2 inhibition while reducing potential off-target interactions, thereby refining the therapeutic index for chronic ocular use (Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5).  

In parallel, integrating robust pharmacodynamic biomarkers into preclinical and clinical studies will allow for the fine-tuning of dosing regimens and early detection of potential adverse effects. Such biomarkers could include imaging findings related to retinal morphology changes or molecular indicators of restored autophagic function in RPE cells, all of which would contribute to ensuring that the efficacy of CCT128930 is achieved without compromising retinal integrity (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6).  

Collaboration across disciplines—bringing together experts in pharmacology, ophthalmology, and drug delivery science—will be paramount for addressing the unique challenges posed by repurposing an oncology drug for ocular conditions. These interdisciplinary efforts will help design and implement the necessary preclinical studies to evaluate not only drug efficacy but also long-term safety in the delicate retinal environment.  

Regulatory Considerations:  
Repurposing CCT128930 for dry AMD will require comprehensive preclinical data that address the compound’s ocular pharmacokinetics, toxicity profiles, and immunogenicity following repeated intravitreal dosing. Given its previous clinical history in oncology, regulators will likely demand additional evidence to ensure that the risks observed in systemic administration do not extend to the ocular context (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). Early engagement with regulatory agencies is recommended to outline the repurposing strategy, propose appropriate endpoints for clinical trials, and define acceptable risk thresholds. The integration of validated biomarkers for therapeutic response and the use of advanced drug delivery platforms could also help streamline the regulatory pathway by providing robust, multidimensional evidence of both efficacy and safety (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6).  

Comparative Analysis with Other Therapeutics:  
In the landscape of treatments for age-related macular degeneration, particularly the dry form, current strategies predominantly focus on mitigating inflammation, oxidative stress, or neovascularization in the case of wet AMD. However, few therapies directly target the underlying cellular clearance deficits that characterize dry AMD. The mechanism of action of CCT128930, which centers on the inhibition of AKT2 to restore TFEB function and enhance autophagy, represents a novel approach that directly addresses the impaired lysosomal degradation essential for RPE health (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). While other candidates have been evaluated for their ability to modulate autophagy, the precise targeting of the AKT2/TFEB axis distinguishes CCT128930 from these agents and offers the possibility of a more durable, disease-modifying effect. In light of the limited efficacy of current treatments for dry AMD, a drug candidate that can substantially improve the intrinsic degradative capacity of the RPE would represent a significant advancement over existing modalities (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  

Integration with Current Treatment Paradigms and Future Research Directions:  
Given the unmet need in dry AMD—where available treatments are largely supportive rather than restorative—the integration of a molecule like CCT128930 into the clinical armamentarium holds considerable appeal. Its repurposing would represent a shift toward targeting the core pathology of RPE degradation and lysosomal dysfunction, rather than simply addressing downstream outcomes. Future research should prioritize studies that confirm the beneficial effects of AKT2 inhibition on TFEB activation in RPE cells, particularly using models that recapitulate the genetic and metabolic nuances of dry AMD. Investigations should extend from cell culture systems to animal models, examining functional endpoints such as retinal morphology, visual acuity, and markers of photoreceptor outer segment turnover (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6). Additionally, research into advanced drug delivery methods—such as encapsulation in biodegradable nanoparticles—to sustain intravitreal drug levels over time will be critical for translating the strong in vitro effects of CCT128930 into meaningful clinical outcomes (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Guo et al., 2021, pp. 9–11).  

Considerations for Dosing and Patient Selection:  
A particularly important aspect in the potential repurposing of CCT128930 is the need to define an optimal dosing regimen that achieves sustained AKT2 inhibition in the retina without compromising cellular viability. The compound’s low nanomolar potency suggests that effective concentrations may be achievable with limited drug exposure, thereby reducing the likelihood of toxicity. However, the unique pharmacokinetic properties of the eye, including the barriers to drug diffusion and the turnover rates of the vitreous humor, necessitate careful dose optimization studies in animal models. Furthermore, patient selection may play a critical role in therapeutic success. For example, individuals with genetic predispositions—such as those carrying the CFH Y402H variant—may exhibit more pronounced dysregulation of the AKT2/TFEB pathway and could therefore derive greater benefit from treatment with CCT128930. Stratifying patients based on genetic and molecular markers may help in tailoring therapies to achieve maximal therapeutic benefit (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6).  

Assessment of Potential Adverse Events:  
While the inhibition of AKT2 holds promise for restoring lysosomal function in RPE cells, it is imperative to assess potential adverse events associated with CCT128930. The compound’s history in oncology, where off-target toxicity and systemic adverse effects led to discontinuation, underscores the need for a careful reevaluation of its safety profile in an ocular setting (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 9–10). The specific effects of sustained AKT2 inhibition on various retinal cell types—including photoreceptors, ganglion cells, and Müller glia—must be systematically investigated using both histological and functional assays. Electroretinography, imaging modalities, and molecular assessments of cellular stress markers will be essential components of any comprehensive preclinical safety evaluation. These studies will help ensure that the benefits of improved autophagic clearance are not overshadowed by unwanted disruptions of retinal homeostasis.  

Integration with Ongoing Research in the Field:  
The contemporary research focus on autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis as therapeutic targets in dry AMD aligns well with the proposed mechanism underlying CCT128930’s repurposing. Emerging studies have consistently shown that restoring lysosomal function through modulation of TFEB activity can ameliorate RPE dysfunction and reduce the progression of retinal degeneration. In this context, the targeted inhibition of AKT2 to relieve TFEB phosphorylation represents a novel and highly specific strategy that addresses a key pathological node in AMD. Collaboration between research groups working on molecular pathways in RPE cells and experts in drug delivery and clinical ophthalmology will be crucial for the successful translation of this approach. The convergence of insights from multiple disciplines serves to reinforce the potential impact of CCT128930 and encourages further exploration through well-designed preclinical studies (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 2–4).  

Conclusion and Strategic Recommendations:  
In conclusion, the repurposing of CCT128930 for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is underpinned by a robust mechanistic rationale and a comprehensive body of preclinical data derived from oncology research. Its potent and selective inhibition of AKT2—with consequent reduction in TFEB phosphorylation—offers a novel therapeutic strategy to restore lysosomal function and autophagic clearance in RPE cells, addressing a fundamental pathological mechanism in dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). While the compound’s chemical and pharmacological attributes are well documented, several challenges remain, including the need to optimize ocular delivery, establish a favorable safety profile, and verify efficacy in relevant preclinical models. A comprehensive research strategy that includes in vitro validation using genetically representative RPE models, in vivo pharmacokinetic and toxicological assessments, and the development of advanced sustained-release formulations is recommended to mitigate risks and maximize therapeutic potential (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6).  

Moreover, given the limited treatment options currently available for dry AMD, a condition where restoring RPE function could profoundly impact disease progression, advancing CCT128930 into a dedicated preclinical development program is both scientifically and clinically justified. Early-phase clinical studies, designed with a strong emphasis on biomarker-driven endpoints and safety, will be critical to establishing whether the encouraging in vitro and preclinical findings can be reproduced in patients. By carefully addressing the challenges of drug delivery and off-target toxicity, and by harnessing innovative approaches to patient stratification and treatment monitoring, CCT128930 could ultimately evolve into a transformative therapy for dry AMD. As such, its inclusion in the drug development pipeline is recommended, pending further rigorous investigation and validation of its ocular efficacy and safety profile (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8).  

Ultimately, the repurposing of CCT128930 embodies a forward-thinking strategy in drug development, leveraging established pharmacological principles and preexisting safety data from oncology to address a pressing unmet need in ophthalmology. Through a multidisciplinary approach that integrates advanced drug formulation, precise molecular targeting, and patient-specific strategies, this therapeutic candidate has the potential to restore impaired autophagic and lysosomal processes in the RPE, thereby offering a novel modality for the treatment of dry AMD. The translational journey for CCT128930 will require meticulous preclinical characterization, careful clinical trial planning, and close collaboration with regulatory agencies, but the promise of a mechanism-based intervention that targets the root cause of RPE degeneration provides a compelling impetus for further exploration (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8).
