Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Sulforaphane is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate that is principally derived from cruciferous vegetables, notably broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and cabbage (Dutta et al., 2023; Lagunas-Rangel, 2024). In its natural state, sulforaphane is present as its glucosinolate precursor, glucoraphanin, which is enzymatically converted to the active form upon tissue disruption by the enzyme myrosinase (Habtemariam, 2024; Mangla et al., 2021). This conversion is a well‐established biochemical process that occurs during food processing or mastication, and it provides the basis for sulforaphane’s identification as a nutraceutical with significant potential in various disease contexts (Houghton, 2019; Lagunas-Rangel, 2024). Sulforaphane belongs to the isothiocyanate class of compounds, a group known for their prominent antioxidant, anti‐inflammatory, and anticancer activities (Dutta et al., 2023; Habtemariam, 2024). Its discovery and subsequent characterization have positioned it as a compound of interest not only in cancer chemoprevention but also in other chronic disease models including neurodegenerative conditions and ocular pathologies (Ordonez et al., 2021; Habtemariam, 2024). The current therapeutic candidate—in this case, Sulforaphane (Nrf2 activator; LKT Laboratories Cat. No. S8044)—is being evaluated for its potential to modulate specific cellular pathways implicated in the pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly its ability to activate the Nrf2 transcription factor in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells at a proposed concentration of 5 µM (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Sulforaphane’s therapeutic history is extensive and spans multiple domains, primarily due to its ability to induce phase II detoxification enzymes and to modulate oxidative stress responses at the cellular level. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its efficacy in inducing apoptosis and mitigating cancer cell proliferation through the modulation of key signaling pathways (Dutta et al., 2023; Tortorella et al., 2015). In addition to its anticancer properties, sulforaphane has been evaluated in models of neurodegeneration, where it has been shown to confer neuroprotection by alleviating oxidative stress and inflammation—a property that is particularly relevant to retinal diseases such as AMD (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024). In ocular research, various investigations using in vitro and in vivo models have highlighted sulforaphane’s capacity to activate the Nrf2 pathway in retinal cells, leading to enhanced antioxidant enzyme expression and reduced oxidative damage (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). Notably, studies employing retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, such as ARPE-19 cells, have documented protective effects of sulforaphane against oxidative insult, where enhanced expression of genes such as heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), glutathione peroxidase (GPX), and glutamate-cysteine ligase modulatory subunit (GCLM) has been observed (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Kubo et al., 2017). Although sulforaphane has been predominantly explored in the context of cancer chemoprevention and neuroprotection, its application in treating ocular conditions such as dry AMD is emerging. Early studies suggest that sulforaphane might reduce lipofuscin accumulation and rescue lysosomal pH abnormalities in A2E-loaded RPE cells, which are hallmark features of dry AMD pathogenesis (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). Safety profiles established through both in vitro studies and limited clinical trials indicate that sulforaphane is generally well-tolerated, with few adverse effects even upon oral administration, thereby rendering it a promising agent for repurposing in ocular disorders (Ordonez et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic actions of sulforaphane are mediated primarily through the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, a central regulator of antioxidant defense mechanisms. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytosol by its inhibitory partner, Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1), which facilitates its ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Mangla et al., 2021). Sulforaphane exerts its effect by covalently modifying critical cysteine residues on KEAP1, thereby disrupting the KEAP1-Nrf2 complex. This modification impedes Nrf2 degradation and permits its rapid translocation into the nucleus (Habtemariam, 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small musculoaponeurotic fibrosarcoma (sMaf) proteins and binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoter regions of a multitude of genes, culminating in the transcriptional activation of phase II detoxification enzymes such as HO-1, GPX, and GCLM (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2024; Hyttinen et al., 2019). In addition to enhancing the antioxidant capacity of the cell, activation of Nrf2 by sulforaphane has been associated with the upregulation of genes implicated in the regulation of autophagy and lysosomal function (Chang et al., 2020; Bergandi et al., 2024). This is particularly salient in the context of RPE biology, where proper lysosomal function is critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and the prevention of lipofuscin accumulation. Impaired degradation pathways in RPE cells lead to cellular stress and contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). Moreover, sulforaphane’s ability to reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine production through suppression of mediators like intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) further supports its cytoprotective role in the retina (Habtemariam, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). The proposed concentration of 5 µM in vitro is supported by studies indicating that such a dose is sufficient to robustly activate Nrf2, thereby inducing an antioxidant response without eliciting toxicity in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). This multifaceted mechanism—encompassing enhanced transcription of antioxidant defense genes, promotion of autophagy, and attenuation of inflammatory signaling—underpins the rationale for deploying sulforaphane as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Within the iPSC-derived RPE model of dry AMD, the administration of sulforaphane at 5 µM is hypothesized to yield several beneficial outcomes. These elements cooperate to enable TSA’s high‐affinity binding to the zinc ion within the catalytic site of HDAC enzymes, thereby blocking deacetylation reactions (Grayson et al., 2010). Unlike many newer synthetic compounds, TSA’s discovery dates back several decades, where it was initially identified for its antifungal properties yet quickly found utility as a potent epigenetic modulator in various research fields, including oncology and neurobiology (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). Within this class, HDAC inhibitors are well recognized for their ability to alter chromatin configuration; by preventing the removal of acetyl groups from histone tails, these compounds induce chromatin relaxation and, as a consequence, facilitate robust transcriptional activation of genes that are otherwise epigenetically repressed (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In the context of ocular research, TSA has been exploited primarily as a tool compound to dissect the role of epigenetic modifications in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function and has been applied in studies examining angiogenesis, apoptosis, and inflammatory responses in RPE cells (Hamid et al., 2021). Its availability from commercial suppliers such as Sigma-Aldrich (Cat. No. T1952) underscores its utility as a research-grade standard for HDAC inhibition studies, making it an attractive candidate for drug repurposing efforts aimed at diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where impaired transcription of clearance and autophagy genes plays a pivotal role (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
TSA has garnered extensive attention over the years in the biomedical literature due to its potent HDAC inhibitory function. Originally explored for its antifungal properties, subsequent studies rapidly shifted focus toward its ability to cause histone hyperacetylation, thereby rekindling interest in epigenetic regulation as a therapeutic strategy for various pathologies (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In oncology, for instance, TSA and its synthetic derivatives have been used to induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in cancer cells, ultimately leading to the development of newer, more selective HDAC inhibitors that have reached clinical trials and even regulatory approval for certain hematological malignancies (Grayson et al., 2010). In ocular research, TSA has been employed in experimental models involving retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, such as ARPE-19, where its application has led to notable changes in the transcription of genes involved in inflammation, angiogenesis, and cellular stress responses (Hamid et al., 2021). Although TSA itself has not been approved for clinical use in any ocular disease, its ability to modify gene expression through HDAC inhibition has provided valuable insights into potential interventions for retinal degenerative conditions, including both wet and dry forms of AMD (Hamid et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025). Moreover, preliminary safety studies—such as those performed using topical formulations in animal models for corneal wound healing—have demonstrated that TSA can be applied at low nanomolar concentrations with minimal cytotoxicity, suggesting that careful dose titration could allow its repurposing for RPE-targeted therapies without incurring the severe systemic toxicities observed in some cancer studies (Sharma et al., 2009). However, it is important to note that despite the promising preclinical data in ARPE-19 cells and related ocular models, there remains a significant gap in clinical evidence directly linking TSA treatment with efficacy in dry AMD, meaning that its repurposing for this indication remains experimental and largely hypothesis-driven at this stage (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Hamid et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, TSA is known to inhibit histone deacetylases by binding to the zinc ion in the enzyme’s catalytic pocket, thereby preventing the removal of acetyl groups from lysine residues on histone tails (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In normal physiological conditions, HDACs contribute to the formation of tightly packed chromatin by deacetylating histones, which leads to decreased transcriptional activity at specific gene promoters. TSA’s ability to inhibit this process results in a “relaxed” chromatin structure that is more accessible to transcription factors, leading to enhanced gene expression (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In the context of the RPE, several genes critical for autophagic flux and phagocytic function—such as lysosomal‐associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) and the receptor tyrosine kinase MERTK—are thought to be epigenetically regulated and may be transcriptionally upregulated upon HDAC inhibition (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Importantly, the transcription factor EB (TFEB) is recognized as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy, controlling the expression of a suite of genes organized within the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network (Falcão et al., 2025). In RPE cells, where efficient degradation of phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (POS) is dependent on both lysosomal function and autophagy, the upregulation of TFEB through enhanced chromatin accessibility could theoretically result in improved expression of LAMP1 and, by extension, better phagocytic capacity via receptors such as MERTK (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Moreover, TSA’s inhibition of HDACs also affects non-histone substrates; for example, it increases the acetylation of α-tubulin—a modification that can influence microtubule dynamics and vesicular transport processes (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). However, this action comes with a potential caveat: excessive tubulin acetylation has been reported to impair autophagosome trafficking, which is a critical step in the autophagic clearance pathway (Toops et al., 2015; Tan, 2018). Therefore, while TSA’s global HDAC inhibition can promote the transcription of genes essential for lysosomal biogenesis and POS degradation, careful titration of its concentration is necessary to ensure that the beneficial effects on gene transcription do not get overshadowed by disruptions in cytoskeletal dynamics and autophagosome motility (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). At the same time, TSA has been shown in some studies to downregulate pro-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic mediators such as HIF-1α and IL-1β while upregulating factors like IL-18, which may contribute additional neuroprotective benefits to the RPE (Hamid et al., 2021). Together, these multifaceted actions underline TSA’s potential to reprogram the epigenetic landscape of RPE cells, theoretically reinstating the expression of key genes involved in autophagic and phagocytic function (Boya et al., 2023; Hamid et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the working hypothesis, the expected effect of TSA in RPE cells is twofold. First, by inhibiting HDAC activity, TSA is anticipated to elevate overall chromatin accessibility, thereby stimulating the transcription of genes that are vital for proper lysosomal biogenesis and phagocytosis. In particular, the upregulation of LAMP1, a well-established marker of lysosomal membranes, should lead to an increase in the number and activity of lysosomes. Simultaneously, enhanced expression of MERTK, which plays a central role in mediating the binding and internalization of POS, should result in an improved phagocytic rate of these essential outer segment components (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE cells, where the daily burden of POS phagocytosis is critical for maintaining retinal integrity, such enhancements could potentially mitigate the accumulation of undigested cellular debris—a phenomenon that is closely linked with the progression of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Tan, 2018). Second, TSA is expected to promote the activation and nuclear translocation of TFEB. This transcription factor is normally sequestered in the cytoplasm when phosphorylated by mTORC1, but under conditions of stress or when mTORC1 activity is reduced, TFEB enters the nucleus and drives the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function and autophagy (Falcão et al., 2025). By facilitating an HDAC inhibition–mediated de-repression of the genes governing TFEB activity, TSA may help drive a feed-forward loop that enhances the cellular capacity for lysosomal degradation and autophagy. Given that RPE cells exhibit compromised autophagy and deteriorating lysosomal function in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the net effect of TSA treatment should be an improvement in POS uptake and degradation, leading to better clearance of lipofuscin and other deleterious cellular debris (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025). Furthermore, some studies using ARPE-19 cells have reported TSA-induced changes in the expression of other oxidative stress and inflammatory markers—for example, a decrease in HIF-1α expression and a corresponding increase in antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and GPX3 (Hamid et al., 2021)—which may contribute to an overall protective environment that diminishes the progressive degeneration of RPE cells. The expected cascade of molecular events—from HDAC inhibition through increased histone acetylation, enhanced transcription of TFEB, LAMP1, and MERTK, to improved lysosomal biogenesis and phagocytic function—forms the basis of the therapeutic rationale for repurposing TSA in the context of dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
Evaluating TSA as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD requires an in-depth analysis of both its promising attributes and its inherent limitations. One of the primary strengths of TSA lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action. As a proven, potent pan-HDAC inhibitor, TSA can recast the epigenetic landscape of RPE cells by enforcing hyperacetylation of histone proteins and upregulating transcription of ordinarily silenced genes (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). Considering that dry AMD is marked by severe dysfunction in protein clearance, lysosomal degradation, and autophagic flux, TSA’s capacity to activate TFEB—the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis—and to potentially enhance the expression of key phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and lysosomal markers like LAMP1 offers a compelling pharmacological strategy to restore cellular homeostasis (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). The cascading effect of promoting both lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy could improve the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), thereby mitigating the accumulation of toxic by-products like lipofuscin that contribute significantly to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Tan, 2018).

Furthermore, TSA’s history as a research compound in various cell culture models, including ARPE-19, provides a solid preclinical foundation for its repurposing. Studies have demonstrated that TSA can modulate the expression of inflammatory and apoptotic markers, reduce oxidative stress, and, importantly, alter the expression of genes that control cellular clearance pathways (Hamid et al., 2021). These data support the hypothesis that TSA might improve RPE function, a critical factor given that RPE degeneration is a driving force behind AMD progression. Preliminary ocular safety assessments, particularly in corneal models, indicate that TSA can be administered topically at carefully controlled low doses without significant toxicity (Sharma et al., 2009). Such findings are encouraging in light of the longstanding challenges associated with delivering effective therapeutics to the posterior segment of the eye; however, it must be emphasized that safety profiles established in corneal applications may not fully translate to the intricate microenvironment of the retina and RPE (Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

On the other hand, several weaknesses temper the enthusiasm for TSA as a repurposed treatment for dry AMD. Foremost among these is its broad-spectrum activity; as a pan-HDAC inhibitor, TSA does not differentiate between enzyme isoforms. This lack of selectivity raises the possibility of off-target effects that could disrupt not only histone modifications but also the acetylation status of numerous non-histone proteins, including α-tubulin (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In RPE cells, proper microtubule dynamics are essential for the trafficking of autophagosomes to lysosomes. Excessive tubulin acetylation—an effect that is purportedly enhanced by agents such as TSA, and observed in conditions mimicked by lipofuscin bisretinoids—can impede autophagosome mobility, potentially undermining the very autophagic flux that TSA is intended to improve (Toops et al., 2015; Tan, 2018; Toops et al., 2015). This paradoxical effect suggests that while increasing transcription of lysosomal genes is beneficial, alterations in cytoskeletal regulation might counteract these benefits if not precisely calibrated.

Another concern arises from the conflicting roles of HDAC activity in the context of AMD. Some studies have observed that specific HDAC activities, such as those mediated by HDAC3, are already reduced in the RPE of AMD patients (Chatterjee et al., 2024; Hamid et al., 2021). This raises the possibility that further inhibition of these enzymes might exacerbate a preexisting imbalance rather than re-establish homeostasis. In other words, if the pathological state of AMD is associated with diminished HDAC activity, then TSA’s further suppression could potentially lead to unintended and deleterious transcriptional changes that might compromise cell survival (Chatterjee et al., 2024; Hamid et al., 2021).

Moreover, despite encouraging in vitro data, there remains a paucity of information regarding TSA’s effects on the specific gene targets central to the proposed mechanism—namely, the upregulation of phagocytic receptors like MERTK and lysosomal membrane proteins such as LAMP1. While the rationale is built upon sound principles of epigenetic regulation and the critical role these proteins play in ensuring efficient POS uptake and degradation (Boya et al., 2023), direct evidence linking TSA treatment to enhanced expression of these markers in RPE cells is yet to be conclusively demonstrated. This gap in the literature makes it difficult to fully endorse TSA as having the predicted beneficial impact on RPE phagocytic function and lysosomal biogenesis without further, targeted investigations (Tan, 2018; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

In addressing the translational potential of TSA, one must also consider its pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiles. Although ocular studies—particularly those focusing on corneal wound healing—have suggested that TSA is safe at low nanomolar concentrations (Sharma et al., 2009), its use in chronic conditions such as dry AMD would likely require long-term administration. The potential cumulative toxicity of TSA, given its broad activity and historical association with off-target effects in other tissues, remains a serious concern. The challenge will be to reconcile the need for sufficient HDAC inhibition to achieve therapeutic upregulation of autophagic and phagocytic genes with the imperative to minimize adverse side effects that could compromise either the safety or the efficacy of the treatment (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021).

Overall, TSA is a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its robust epigenetic modulatory effects, which align well with the therapeutic goal of enhancing lysosomal biogenesis and phagocytic clearance in RPE cells. Its ability to interfere with HDAC activity has been demonstrated to affect not only histone acetylation but also the transcription of genes involved in cellular stress responses and degradation pathways. In theory, such modifications could reverse or mitigate several of the pathological features of dry AMD, including the accumulation of undigested POS and subsequent lipofuscin buildup that drive RPE degeneration (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). The elevation of TFEB, a master regulator of lysosomal gene expression, through TSA-mediated chromatin relaxation offers a particularly attractive avenue for restoring the autophagy-lysosome machinery, thereby enhancing both cellular clearance and the overall health of RPE cells (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Nonetheless, the candidate’s broad-spectrum nature and potential to disrupt processes such as microtubule dynamics present significant challenges. The risk of impaired autophagosome trafficking due to aberrant tubulin acetylation (Toops et al., 2015; Tan, 2018) must be weighed against the expected benefits of improved lysosomal function. Moreover, the heterogeneity of HDAC activity in AMD pathology—with some reports indicating already compromised HDAC function in diseased RPE—complicates the prospect of using a pan-HDAC inhibitor without a carefully defined therapeutic window (Chatterjee et al., 2024; Hamid et al., 2021). The absence of definitive data linking TSA treatment to increased expression of MERTK and LAMP1 in RPE cells further underscores the need for additional research to validate the proposed mechanism of action (Tan, 2018; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

In light of these considerations, our evaluation supports the continued exploratory investigation of TSA as a repurposed intervention for dry AMD, with the understanding that several critical questions remain unanswered. Future studies should aim to:  
1. Directly measure the impact of TSA on the expression levels of key phagocytic and lysosomal genes, such as MERTK and LAMP1, in RPE cells using both transcriptional and protein-level assays.  
2. Delineate the dose-response relationship in RPE cells to identify concentrations that achieve optimal activation of the CLEAR network and TFEB-mediated transcription without inducing detrimental levels of tubulin acetylation that could impede autophagosome mobility.  
3. Assess the long-term safety and pharmacokinetics of TSA in ocular tissues, particularly in animal models of dry AMD, to determine whether its beneficial effects on autophagy and phagocytosis can be sustained without incurring off-target toxicity or systemic side effects.  
4. Explore the possibility of developing more selective HDAC inhibitors or targeted delivery systems that concentrate TSA’s effects specifically within the RPE, thereby minimizing the risks associated with its broad-spectrum activity.

Ultimately, while TSA’s established role as an epigenetic modulator makes it an attractive candidate for addressing the underlying cellular dysfunction in dry AMD, careful balancing of its beneficial transcriptional effects against its potential to disrupt critical cellular processes is essential. The data reviewed herein provide a strong mechanistic rationale for TSA’s utility, yet underscore the necessity for rigorously designed preclinical studies to confirm its efficacy and safety in the context of retinal degeneration (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021; Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Astrocyte‐derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a are an innovative, biomimetic class of therapeutic agents that combine the natural properties of extracellular vesicles with the regulatory functions of microRNAs. Exosomes are nano‐sized vesicles (typically 40–160 nm in diameter) generated in the endosomal pathway and released by almost all cell types, including astrocytes, which are a fundamental component of the retinal microenvironment (Heo & Ryu, 2024). In this candidate, exosomes are isolated from retinal astrocytes and selectively engineered to become enriched with miR-146a, a microRNA known for its anti‐inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties. Because astrocytes are intimately involved in neuronal support and retinal homeostasis, their exosomes offer an inherent targeting advantage for diseased retinal regions, particularly in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is compromised (Romero et al., 2024). The enrichment with miR-146a transforms these naturally secreted vesicles into a targeted drug delivery vehicle that can modulate specific intracellular pathways in the RPE. This approach falls within the broader therapeutic class of exosome‐based drug delivery systems, a class that has increasingly attracted attention for its ability to transport nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids with high specificity and minimal immunogenicity (Du & Palczewski, 2022). Exosome therapy has been previously explored in preclinical models for various retinal pathologies using different source cells, such as mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and RPE cells (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2023). Engineering exosomes to carry therapeutic miRNAs like miR-146a exemplifies a precision medicine strategy in which the carrier is not only inert but provides its own biological effects derived from its cell of origin, contributing to the overall therapeutic profile.

Therapeutic History:  
While there is robust literature documenting the application of exosome-based therapies in ocular diseases, the specific use of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched with miR-146a is a relatively novel proposition. In several studies, exosomes isolated from mesenchymal stem cells have been engineered to carry anti-inflammatory microRNAs, including miR-146a, and have shown neuroprotective effects in retinal degeneration models such as retinitis pigmentosa and diabetic retinopathy (Zhang et al., 2022). Moreover, astrocyte-derived exosomes have been explored for their intrinsic neuroprotective and anti‐angiogenic properties. For instance, retinal astrocyte-derived exosomes have been demonstrated to contain multiple anti-angiogenic molecules including endostatin, PEDF, and TIMP-1, which contribute to the suppression of choroidal neovascularization in laser-induced models (Mead & Chow, 2023; Romero et al., 2024). Although these studies primarily target neovascular AMD, their underlying mechanisms emphasize the utility of astrocyte-based exosome therapy in modulating critical retinal pathways. In the context of dry AMD, which is characterized by chronic RPE degeneration, oxidative stress, and complement system dysregulation, the strategy of utilizing exosomal delivery to target RPE dysfunction is supported by evidence that exosome‐mediated miRNA transfer can restore lysosomal function and reduce inflammatory cascades in retinal cells (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Guan et al., 2025). Additionally, complement dysregulation and increased complement factor expression are central features of dry AMD pathology, and prior studies have implicated exosomal cargo in modulating inflammatory and complement pathways (Guan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). Although direct clinical or extensive preclinical experience with astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a in dry AMD is limited, the analogous applications of MSC-derived exosomes carrying miR-146a establish an important precedent and provide a mechanistic rationale for further investigation (Zhang et al., 2022; Berber et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic mechanism of this candidate operates at multiple molecular levels, integrating the known functions of both miR-146a and exosomal delivery systems. miR-146a is recognized as a key negative regulator of inflammation through its ability to target components in the Toll-like receptor (TLR) and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling pathways. Specifically, miR-146a targets interleukin-1 receptor–associated kinase 1 (IRAK1) and TNF receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6), leading to a reduction in NF-κB activation and subsequent downregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Berber et al., 2017; ElShelmani et al., 2021). In the context of dry AMD, complement overactivation has been identified as a pivotal event contributing to RPE degeneration. Complement factor H (CFH) and complement factor B (CFB) play significant roles in regulating the alternative complement pathway, and dysregulation of these factors leads to excessive complement activation, resulting in increased levels of complement fragments such as C3a that promote inflammation and lysosomal stress (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021). The proposed mechanism asserts that miR-146a, delivered via astrocyte-derived exosomes, can penetrate the RPE cell layer and downregulate the transcription and/or translation of complement components such as CFH and CFB. By limiting the production of these factors, miR-146a effectively reduces the downstream formation of the inflammatory anaphylatoxin C3a, alleviating lysosomal overload and preserving the acidic lysosomal environment necessary for optimal activity of degradative enzymes like cathepsin D (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Zhang et al., 2022). This modulation of complement activity is essential because aberrant complement activation in the RPE has been linked to photoreceptor outer segment (POS) accumulation and impaired phagocytosis, which are hallmarks of dry AMD progression (Romero et al., 2024; Sanghani et al., 2022). Furthermore, exosomes themselves possess intrinsic targeting and cell–cell communication properties; their membrane proteins, such as tetraspanins (CD63, CD81) and other surface markers, facilitate uptake by recipient cells and can mediate tissue-specific homing to the RPE (Liu et al., 2023; Romero et al., 2024). The combination of miR-146a’s molecular action on inflammatory and complement pathways with the natural delivery proficiency of astrocyte-derived exosomes creates a synergistic effect that is expected to restore lysosomal integrity and enhance functional POS degradation in high-risk CFH backgrounds (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The expected therapeutic effect in the treatment of dry AMD is multilayered. In vitro studies utilizing RPE cell cultures derived from patient lines with high-risk CFH expression are anticipated to show that treatment with miR-146a-enriched astrocyte exosomes results in a significant downregulation of complement factors, notably CFH and CFB. This downregulation would be reflected in reduced levels of the complement activation fragment C3a, which is known to exacerbate inflammation and lysosomal dysfunction in RPE cells (Romero et al., 2024; Berber et al., 2017). As a direct consequence of complement normalization, lysosomal integrity is expected to be maintained through the preservation of an acidic pH environment and the restoration of cathepsin D activity. Cathepsin D plays a critical role in the degradation of POS material taken up by RPE cells during the daily process of photoreceptor renewal (Liu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022). Enhanced clearance of POS is hypothesized to reduce the accumulation of toxic waste products and drusen formation, a defining characteristic of dry AMD. In addition, the anti-inflammatory action of miR-146a should attenuate the chronic low-grade inflammation observed in the retinal microenvironment, thereby mitigating further RPE and photoreceptor damage (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2020).  
At the molecular level, the treatment is anticipated to modulate intracellular signaling cascades by reducing NF-κB–mediated transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines, which in turn helps to suppress the local inflammatory milieu and prevent further complement activation (Berber et al., 2017; ElShelmani et al., 2021). The exosomal vehicle ensures that miR-146a is delivered in a protected and concentrated form, which maximizes cellular uptake and preserves functional integrity during circulation. Given their natural ability to cross biological barriers, these astrocyte-derived exosomes are expected to efficiently reach the RPE layer, and this targeted delivery is crucial for achieving the desired therapeutic outcomes with minimal off-target effects (Guan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). Furthermore, the experimental assays based on RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD are designed to evaluate both the biological activity of the delivered miR-146a and the restoration of lysosomal function. Expected readouts include a decrease in complement factor mRNA and protein levels, improved lysosomal enzyme activity (especially cathepsin D), reduced accumulation of POS debris, and ultimately, preservation of RPE and photoreceptor viability (Guan et al., 2025; ElShelmani et al., 2021). These effects, if validated, could translate into a slowing of disease progression or even a reversal of certain pathological features in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
The candidate therapeutic of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a holds considerable promise for the treatment of dry AMD due to its innovative design and strong mechanistic rationale. One of the most significant strengths of this approach lies in its biomimetic nature. By harnessing exosomes derived from retinal astrocytes, the therapy benefits from inherent targeting properties that increase the likelihood of efficient delivery to the RPE, a key cell type implicated in dry AMD pathology (Romero et al., 2024; Mead & Chow, 2023). Furthermore, the use of miR-146a—an endogenous regulatory molecule with well-documented anti-inflammatory effects—adds an additional layer of specificity to the treatment by directly modulating the inflammatory milieu and complement dysregulation that are central to dry AMD (Berber et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022). This dual action, combining restoration of lysosomal integrity through improved POS degradation and suppression of complement-mediated inflammation, addresses two critical pathogenic processes simultaneously.  

However, despite its notable strengths, several challenges and uncertainties remain. First, while the therapeutic concept is strongly supported by preclinical studies involving MSC-derived exosomes and by literature demonstrating the beneficial effects of exosomal miRNAs in retinal diseases (Zhang et al., 2022; Du & Palczewski, 2022), the specific application of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched with miR-146a for dry AMD remains to be thoroughly evaluated. There is limited direct evidence in the literature showing that astrocyte-derived exosomes naturally enriched or engineered to carry miR-146a can downregulate complement factor expression in RPE cells in a clinically meaningful way (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023). This represents a gap in knowledge that would need to be addressed through rigorous preclinical investigation, including detailed dose–response studies and assessments of long-term efficacy and safety.  

Another potential weakness lies in the scalability and reproducibility of exosome isolation from astrocytes. Exosome production can vary depending on the source, the culture conditions, and the methods used for enrichment and purification. Manufacturing a consistent and high-quality exosome product that meets clinical grade standards is a well-recognized challenge in the field of exosome therapeutics (Liu et al., 2023; Guan et al., 2025). In addition, while exosomes are known for their low immunogenicity, the possibility of immune reactions, especially when they are over-engineered or when administered repeatedly, cannot be entirely discounted and will require careful evaluation (Romero et al., 2024).  

From a mechanistic standpoint, although the theoretical framework linking miR-146a with the downregulation of complement factors CFH and CFB is compelling, the precise molecular interactions within RPE cells must be validated by robust in vitro and in vivo experiments. Detailed studies are needed to confirm the extent to which miR-146a directly modulates these complement components, and whether additional targets or off-target effects might complicate the therapeutic outcome (Zhang et al., 2022; Berber et al., 2017). Furthermore, while the restoration of lysosomal function and POS degradation is a promising endpoint, the complexity of lysosomal biology in the context of chronic degenerative diseases such as dry AMD means that multifactorial interventions might be necessary. It will be essential to demonstrate that the observed improvements in lysosomal enzyme activity (e.g., cathepsin D) translate into meaningful clinical benefits, such as slowed disease progression or improved visual function (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Romero et al., 2024).  

In summary, the concept of using astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is innovative, leveraging the natural targeting, biocompatibility, and multi-functional capabilities of exosomes along with the potent anti-inflammatory and complement‐modulating properties of miR-146a. The preclinical evidence derived from analogous studies using MSC-derived exosomes and the general literature on exosomal miRNA therapies in retinal diseases provides a solid foundation for this approach (Zhang et al., 2022; Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2023). Nevertheless, the strategy will require comprehensive validation, including optimization of exosome isolation and engineering protocols, detailed mechanistic studies in relevant cellular models, and robust in vivo efficacy assessments in dry AMD animal models before clinical translation can be considered. With targeted efforts to address these challenges, this therapeutic candidate could represent a significant advance in the treatment of dry AMD, offering a precision medicine approach that directly tackles both complement overactivation and lysosomal dysfunction at the cellular level (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Guan et al., 2025; ElShelmani et al., 2021).

Overall, the combination of bioengineered exosomes and miR-146a offers mechanistic specificity and a novel route of administration that may overcome many of the limitations inherent in current dry AMD therapies, particularly those related to anti-VEGF treatments which are primarily indicated for wet AMD. While further preclinical investigations are essential to fully elucidate the pharmacodynamics, safety profile, and therapeutic window of this candidate, the approach holds promise as a next-generation drug candidate for dry AMD that could potentially improve patient outcomes by preserving retinal structure and function through the reestablishment of homeostatic cellular processes (Mead & Chow, 2023; Sanghani et al., 2022; Song et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB431542 is a well‐characterized, synthetic small molecule inhibitor originally developed through medicinal chemistry efforts by researchers at GlaxoSmithKline. Its chemical structure, formally denoted as 4-(5-benzo[1,3]dioxol-5-yl-4-pyridin-2-yl-1H-imidazol-2-yl)-benzamide, incorporates a benzodioxole moiety linked to a pyridyl-imidazol core and terminated by a benzamide group, placing it within the imidazole class of compounds (Laping et al., 2002). SB431542 belongs to the class of transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) type I receptor kinase inhibitors (commonly referred to as ALK5 inhibitors) that inhibit ATP-dependent receptor activation. Initially designed as an improvement over less-selective kinase inhibitors—such as early p38 MAPK inhibitors that exhibited off-target ALK5 inhibition—SB431542 emerged from a rational structure–activity relationship (SAR) campaign aimed at optimizing both potency and selectivity (Laping et al., 2002). Its discovery has been pivotal in establishing a molecular tool for dissecting TGFβ signaling, and its chemical synthesis reflects a focused effort on achieving high-affinity, ATP-competitive inhibition of the TGFβ receptor. This compound has been extensively used in preclinical research to study fibrotic mechanisms and cellular differentiation, thereby marking its reputation as a “gold standard” in TGFβ pathway inhibition (Laping et al., 2002).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SB431542 is primarily rooted in its application as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. In numerous preclinical studies, SB431542 has been consistently used to inhibit TGFβ-induced processes such as extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis, Smad protein activation, and the induction of a fibrotic phenotype in various cell types including renal epithelial cells, fibroblasts, and even certain cancer cell models (Laping et al., 2002). Biochemical studies have shown that SB431542 effectively blocks the phosphorylation of Smad3 with an IC50 of approximately 94 nM, thereby preventing the downstream transcriptional activation of cytokines and matrix proteins (Laping et al., 2002). Its anti-fibrotic effects have been extensively characterized in in vitro assays, where it reduced the expression of collagen I α1, fibronectin, and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) mRNA, thus providing compelling evidence that the compound modulates TGFβ-induced ECM remodeling (Laping et al., 2002).

While SB431542 has been applied in many experimental models to study pathways implicated in fibrotic diseases such as glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, liver cirrhosis, and pulmonary fibrosis, there is scant direct evidence of its historical use in ocular pathologies, particularly dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Akhund et al., 2023; Nyati et al., 2011). However, TGFβ signaling has been implicated in retinal pathologies and in the mesenchymal transition of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells from which some studies have emerged using general TGFβ inhibitors to reverse such pathological changes (Radeke et al., 2015). Although SB431542 itself has not been used in clinical trials for AMD, its mechanistic profile and reported efficacies in other fibrotic and ECM remodeling contexts make it a promising candidate for repurposing to address the abnormal matrix remodeling observed in dry AMD. Preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues have established that targeted inhibition of TGFβ signaling leads to substantial reductions in fibrotic markers, suggesting that similar approaches could mitigate Bruch membrane (BrM) alterations in AMD (Laping et al., 2002).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB431542 functions as an ATP-competitive inhibitor selectively targeting the kinase domain of the TGFβ type I receptor (TGFβRI, also known as ALK5). Its mechanism of action centers on binding to the ATP-binding pocket of TGFβRI, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of key intracellular effectors, primarily the Smad2 and Smad3 proteins (Laping et al., 2002). In normal TGFβ signaling, binding of the ligand (e.g., TGFβ1) to its receptors induces the formation of a heteromeric complex consisting of TGFβRI and TGFβRII, leading to the phosphorylation and activation of Smad2/3. These phosphorylated Smad proteins then form a complex with Smad4, translocate to the nucleus, and activate the transcription of pro-fibrotic genes, including those involved in ECM protein synthesis such as collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002).

Detailed molecular interaction studies have revealed that SB431542 makes critical hydrogen bonding contacts within the ATP-binding site of TGFβRI. For example, the benzodioxol moiety is reported to form a hydrogen bond with the amide nitrogen of His283, while additional interactions with Lys232 and other hydrophobic residues stabilize the inhibitor within the binding pocket (Leonardo-Sousa et al., 2025). This precise molecular engagement confers its high selectivity, as even minor substitutions in the binding region—such as mutations at the gatekeeper residue—can significantly alter inhibitor efficacy (Laping et al., 2002; Leonardo-Sousa et al., 2025). Furthermore, while SB431542 shows potent inhibition against ALK5, it also inhibits closely related receptors such as ALK4 and ALK7 with only modest differences in potency (IC50 for ALK4 is approximately 140 nM), and it exhibits negligible activity against BMP-activated receptors (ALK2, ALK3, and ALK6) (Laping et al., 2002). This selective inhibition ensures that the canonical TGFβ/Smad pathway is targeted without significantly perturbing other pathways that could be essential for cellular homeostasis, such as the BMP signaling cascade (Nyati et al., 2011; Akhund et al., 2023).

In addition to its inhibition of Smad2/3 phosphorylation, SB431542 has been shown to disrupt the subsequent nuclear translocation of these transcription factors, thereby halting the transcription of downstream ECM components. Such inhibition is critical because overactivation of the TGFβ pathway is a central driver in fibrotic diseases and leads to excessive deposition of ECM proteins, which in turn contribute to tissue stiffness and impaired cellular function (Laping et al., 2002). Overall, the molecular mechanism of SB431542 is well-delineated; its high selectivity for TGFβRI and the resulting blockade of Smad-mediated transcription form the foundation for its potential use in addressing aberrant ECM remodeling.

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis for repurposing SB431542 in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is built on the concept that excessive TGFβ signaling within the retinal microenvironment leads to an abnormal accumulation and remodeling of ECM components in the Bruch membrane (BrM). In the context of dry AMD, such ECM changes are believed to increase membrane stiffness and disrupt the diffusion of critical phagocytic ligands—specifically MFGE8 (Milk Fat Globule Epidermal Growth Factor 8) and Gas6—which play key roles in facilitating the integrin αvβ5-mediated binding and uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Radeke et al., 2015).

By inhibiting TGFβRI, SB431542 is expected to block the TGFβ-driven phosphorylation of Smad proteins, thereby directly reducing the transcription of genes that encode for fibrotic and ECM-related proteins such as collagen I α1, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002). In doing so, SB431542 should restore a more balanced ECM composition in the BrM. This normalization of ECM deposition is anticipated to reduce BrM stiffness, thereby enhancing the diffusion of phagocytic ligands like MFGE8 and Gas6 across the membrane. The improved ligand diffusion is expected to restore the optimal microenvironment required for integrin αvβ5 on the RPE surface to effectively bind and internalize POS, a process that is critically impaired in dry AMD (Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011).

Furthermore, by attenuating the fibrotic response within the retina, SB431542 may help preserve the native architecture and function of the RPE layer. This indirect modulation of phagocytosis, achieved through the normalization of ECM characteristics, represents a novel therapeutic angle that bridges the gap between ECM pathology and receptor-mediated cellular processes. In essence, the expected effect of SB431542 is a dual benefit: first, it directly inhibits pathological TGFβ signaling to reduce further fibrotic damage, and second, it indirectly normalizes phagocytic function by restoring the proper presentation of ligands critical for RPE-mediated clearance of POS (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015).

At the cellular and molecular level, the proposed assay is likely to measure a reduction in fibrotic markers (e.g., collagen I α1, fibronectin) and an improvement in assays of POS binding and internalization by RPE cells. Given that RPE cells express integrin αvβ5 and are responsive to TGFβ signaling, the application of SB431542 should result in a shift from a fibrotic, mesenchymal phenotype towards a more differentiated epithelial state that is conducive to normal phagocytic activity (Radeke et al., 2015; Akhund et al., 2023). This outcome would be mechanistically consistent with the known roles of TGFβ in modulating ECM dynamics and cellular differentiation. Consequently, if the hypothesis holds true, SB431542 would not only prevent further ECM deposition and stiffening of the BrM but would also support the resolution of existing pathological ECM alterations, thereby improving the overall homeostasis of the retinal microenvironment.

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of SB431542 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD requires careful consideration of its well-established biochemical profile alongside the translational challenges emerging from its current use primarily as a research tool. On the positive side, SB431542 is a potent and selective inhibitor of TGFβRI, with extensive preclinical evidence demonstrating its capacity to block TGFβ-induced Smad2/3 phosphorylation and consequently reduce the expression of fibrotic markers (Laping et al., 2002). Its high potency (with an IC50 in the low nanomolar range) and favorable selectivity profile—particularly with more than 100-fold selectivity over p38 MAPK and minimal activity against BMP receptors—render it an attractive candidate for targeted modulation of TGFβ signaling in tissues where fibrosis is a major pathogenic factor (Laping et al., 2002). These strengths are of particular relevance in the context of dry AMD, where BrM thickening and ECM remodeling are central features that compromise RPE function.

Moreover, the proposed mechanism underlying the therapeutic hypothesis is compelling. Excessive TGFβ signaling has been implicated in the aberrant remodeling of the BrM, which in turn impairs the presentation of critical phagocytic ligands necessary for efficient POS uptake by the RPE (Radeke et al., 2015). By inhibiting TGFβRI, SB431542 could theoretically restore the balance between collagen and proteoglycan production, thereby normalizing BrM stiffness and improving the diffusion of factors such as MFGE8 and Gas6. In doing so, the drug would indirectly enhance integrin αvβ5-mediated phagocytosis—a process that is essential for the maintenance of photoreceptor health and overall retinal integrity. This innovative indirect approach could represent a significant advancement in the treatment of dry AMD, addressing the disease from both a fibrotic and a functional perspective.

However, several considerable challenges and weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, the bulk of the supporting data for SB431542 comes from studies in non-ocular cell types or animal models of general fibrosis and cancer, with limited direct evidence in ocular systems. Although TGFβ inhibitors have been proposed as therapeutic agents in retinal diseases, there remains a significant gap in data specific to dry AMD or related retinal degenerative conditions (Akhund et al., 2023; Nyati et al., 2011). The absence of ocular pharmacokinetic studies, detailed data on retinal tissue penetration, and long-term safety evaluations in the eye poses a major hurdle for the clinical translation of SB431542 for AMD.

Furthermore, TGFβ signaling is a double-edged sword in many tissues, including the retina. While excessive TGFβ activity drives pathological ECM deposition and fibrosis, TGFβ also participates in immune regulation and cellular homeostasis. Therefore, complete or prolonged inhibition of TGFβ signaling may have unintended consequences, such as impairing normal wound healing or altering the immunological milieu of the retina (Akhund et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023). The delicate balance between therapeutic efficacy and potential adverse effects necessitates that any systemic or even locally delivered TGFβRI inhibitor be subject to rigorous dosing and toxicity studies. In this regard, the narrow therapeutic window often encountered in kinase inhibition therapies could be a limiting factor for SB431542’s adoption in an ophthalmic setting.

Another significant concern is the delivery method. The current literature on SB431542 primarily documents its use in cell culture assays or systemic administration in animal models; however, the ocular environment presents unique challenges due to barriers such as the inner limiting membrane, the blood-retina barrier, and the anatomical constraints of the retina. To achieve therapeutically relevant concentrations in the sub-retinal space or at the level of the BrM, innovative delivery strategies—such as topical formulations, intravitreal injections, or sustained-release devices—must be developed and validated (Hachana & Larrivée, 2022; Radeke et al., 2015). The pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of SB431542 in ocular tissues remain largely unexplored, which represents a critical gap in current knowledge.

Additionally, although the indirect mechanism of action—namely, the normalization of ECM to facilitate proper ligand–receptor interactions—is scientifically plausible, it is inherently more challenging to measure and validate compared to direct cellular responses. Assays designed to monitor changes in BrM stiffness, ECM composition, and the diffusion characteristics of MFGE8 and Gas6 must be highly sensitive and reproducible, and these endpoints have not been extensively characterized in available preclinical models of AMD. Furthermore, the redundancy within TGFβ signaling pathways raises the possibility that compensatory mechanisms might mitigate the effects of ALK5 inhibition over time, potentially limiting the efficacy of SB431542, particularly in a chronic, slowly progressive disease like dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Akhund et al., 2023).

From an efficacy standpoint, while numerous studies demonstrate that SB431542 effectively reduces TGFβ-induced fibrotic responses in various cell types (Laping et al., 2002), extrapolating these findings to the complex microenvironment of the aged retina is not straightforward. The retina and RPE possess distinct cellular and molecular characteristics that may respond differently to TGFβ signaling modulation. For example, in RPE cells, TGFβ signaling not only regulates ECM deposition but is also involved in the maintenance of epithelial phenotype and may even exert neuroprotective effects under certain conditions. Hence, unspecific inhibition of TGFβ signaling in the retina could conceivably result in a loss of beneficial effects that are essential for retinal homeostasis (Radeke et al., 2015; Akhund et al., 2023).

In summary, while SB431542 exhibits a robust, well-characterized mechanism of action as a TGFβRI inhibitor and has demonstrated potent anti-fibrotic effects in preclinical models of ECM remodeling, its repurposing for dry AMD must overcome several significant challenges. The strengths of SB431542 lie in its high potency, selectivity, and extensive preclinical validation in non-ocular models. Its molecular interactions are well understood, and its ability to inhibit Smad phosphorylation offers a clear mechanistic rationale for reducing pathological ECM deposition. Consequently, if applied to the pathological process associated with dry AMD, SB431542 could, in theory, mitigate the excessive ECM remodeling that impairs ligand diffusion and consequently restores the capacity for integrin αvβ5-mediated POS uptake by RPE cells (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011).

On the other hand, the weaknesses of this approach are substantial. There is limited evidence of SB431542’s efficacy in ocular models, and its pharmacokinetics, ocular tissue penetration, and long-term safety profile have yet to be rigorously evaluated. Additionally, the complexity of TGFβ’s biological roles raises concerns regarding the balance between therapeutic benefit and potential interference with normal retinal physiology. The indirect nature of the hypothesized effect—mediated by ECM normalization—adds further layers of complexity to both preclinical testing and eventual clinical translation. Finally, challenges related to drug delivery to the retina, along with the potential for compensatory signaling pathways to undermine the inhibitor’s efficacy, suggest that significant additional research is warranted before SB431542 can be advanced as a therapeutic candidate in an AMD setting (Akhund et al., 2023; Akhund et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023).

Overall, SB431542 presents a biologically plausible and mechanistically sound candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly given its demonstrated ability to modulate TGFβ-driven fibrotic pathways. However, its successful translation to an ophthalmic therapeutic will hinge on a series of focused preclinical studies that address ocular biodistribution, safety in retinal tissues, and the optimization of dosing regimens tailored to the unique anatomical and physiological challenges of the eye. Only after these critical issues have been resolved can SB431542 be considered a viable strategy to restore ECM homeostasis in the Bruch membrane, normalize phagocytic ligand availability, and ultimately enhance integrin-mediated POS uptake in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011). In conclusion, while SB431542 has strong potential and a compelling mechanistic rationale, further dedicated ocular research is required to fully validate its therapeutic promise in the context of dry AMD before it can be recommended for clinical development.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
VX-765, also known as Belnacasan, is a synthetic, orally available caspase-1 inhibitor originally developed by Vertex Pharmaceuticals as part of their research into anti-inflammatory therapeutics (Dhani et al., 2021; Kallinich, 2015). This drug is a peptidomimetic compound designed to mimic the substrate recognition sequence of caspase-1 – a feature that traces its molecular design to early peptide-based inhibitors based on the tetrapeptide motif YVAD (Kudelova et al., 2015; Doyle et al., 2015). VX-765 is administered as an inactive prodrug that is rapidly cleaved by plasma and liver esterases into its active metabolite, VRT-043198, which then exerts inhibitory effects on caspase-1 (Liang et al., 2022; Kallinich, 2015). As a member of the caspase inhibitor class, VX-765 represents a second‐generation approach compared to its predecessor pralnacasan (VX-740), seeking improved oral bioavailability, enhanced selectivity, and a more favorable pharmacokinetic profile (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015). The drug belongs to the broader class of inflammasome inhibitors that target IL-1β and IL-18 releasing cascades, which have been extensively explored for inflammatory, autoimmune, and neurological disorders (Kallinich, 2015; Kudelova et al., 2015). The synthetic origin and deliberate design emphasizes a precision targeting of caspase-1’s catalytic cysteine, a critical residue in the enzyme’s active site, thereby inhibiting its proteolytic function; this is particularly important given the role of caspase-1 in mediating pyroptosis and inflammatory cytokine maturation (Kallinich, 2015; Kudelova et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, VX-765 has been evaluated in preclinical studies and early-phase human trials mainly for systemic inflammatory and neurological conditions. Early investigations demonstrated that VX-765 robustly reduced plasma cytokine levels in dose-dependent manners in Phase I studies, and subsequent Phase II trials in psoriasis provided evidence of both safety and clinical activity (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015; Maroso et al., 2011). Its predecessor pralnacasan showed efficacy in rheumatoid arthritis clinical trials, although long-term use in animal models eventually raised concerns about potential hepatotoxicity, leading to its withdrawal despite promising initial results (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015). VX-765 was later repurposed for neurological conditions; it has been tested in partial epilepsy where, despite a good safety profile, its efficacy was less than anticipated (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015; Kallinich, 2015). In addition, VX-765 has demonstrated anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects in preclinical models of Alzheimer’s disease by reducing IL-1β production in the brain and preserving synaptic function (Liang et al., 2022; Flores et al., 2018). Importantly, although the clinical and preclinical development history of VX-765 spans a variety of inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases, it has not been extensively evaluated for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or retinal diseases per se (Dhani et al., 2021; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020; Kallinich, 2015). Nevertheless, a search in clinical trial databases has uncovered a limited number of studies investigating caspase-1 inhibitors in the context of macular degeneration, reinforcing the notion that the therapeutic paradigm may be extended to ocular disorders (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
Caspase-1 is a cysteine-dependent aspartate-directed protease that plays a central role in the activation of inflammatory cytokines by cleaving pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature, biologically active forms; these cytokines are major mediators of inflammatory cascades and pyroptotic cell death (Kallinich, 2015; Kudelova et al., 2015). VX-765 functions by inhibiting caspase-1 through a competitive mechanism that involves binding to the catalytic cysteine residue; structural studies have indicated that its peptidomimetic scaffold effectively occupies the substrate-binding pocket, thereby preventing substrate access (Kudelova et al., 2015; Kallinich, 2015). Although the hypothesis for repurposing VX-765 in dry AMD posits an irreversible inhibition of caspase-1, the bulk of the literature supports that VX-765 is, in fact, a reversible inhibitor (Dhani et al., 2021; Kallinich, 2015). Activation of VX-765 in vivo produces VRT-043198, which exhibits low nanomolar inhibitory potency against human caspase-1 (IC₅₀ ~3.68–9.91 nM) and comparable activity in murine models (IC₅₀ ~18–52.1 nM), rendering it suitable for precise modulation of caspase-1 activity (Flores et al., 2018; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020). By inhibiting caspase-1, VX-765 effectively prevents the maturation and secretion of IL-1β and IL-18, thereby disrupting the propagation of inflammatory signals that can lead to dysfunctional cellular responses such as pyroptosis—a lytic form of programmed cell death triggered by inflammasome activation (Kallinich, 2015; Younus & Reddy, 2018). In RPE cells, where caspase-1 expression has been documented as a component of inflammasome signaling especially during stress conditions, inhibition of caspase-1 is anticipated to preserve lysosomal integrity by reducing cytokine-induced lysosomal destabilization and preventing the cleavage of substrates that contribute to cell death pathways (Gao et al., 2019; Kudelova et al., 2015). Moreover, evidence suggests that caspase-1 activation leads to gasdermin D cleavage, which forms membrane pores and facilitates pyroptotic cell death; therefore, blockade by VX-765 could mitigate this deleterious cascade (Kallinich, 2015; Flores et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is a critical cell type responsible for maintaining photoreceptor health through the daily phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Under pathological conditions, chronic low-grade inflammation driven by the inflammasome can lead to caspase-1 activation in RPE cells, resulting in IL-1β maturation and subsequent pyroptotic signaling that compromises lysosomal integrity (Gao et al., 2019; Marneros, 2023). The proposed therapeutic hypothesis is that VX-765, by inhibiting caspase-1 at an IC₅₀ value of approximately 10 nM in RPE cell assays (for example, in the ARPE-19 cell line), will significantly reduce IL-1β production and attenuate subsequent inflammatory cascades (Kallinich, 2015; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020). This preservation of lysosomal function is clinically significant because it is expected to stabilize LAMP1-positive lysosomal structures within the RPE, thereby maintaining efficient clearance of POS and preventing the accumulation of toxic debris—a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis (Kudelova et al., 2015). Preclinical evidence from studies using caspase-1 inhibitors indicates that such intervention leads to a reduction in inflammatory cytokine release and improves cellular homeostasis in contexts similar to those observed in AMD (Kudelova et al., 2015). Although the majority of previous studies have focused on systemic inflammatory or neurological disorders, the underlying mechanisms—namely, the inhibition of the caspase-1/IL-1β axis—are directly relevant to RPE dysfunction and can feasibly be repurposed for the treatment of dry AMD (Marneros, 2023). The ultimate expected outcome would be the preservation of RPE phagocytic pathways, ensuring proper degradation of POS, reducing chronic inflammation, and thereby potentially slowing or halting the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Gao et al., 2019; Marneros, 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of VX-765 for dry AMD represents a compelling strategy, driven by a strong mechanistic rationale and bolstered by its demonstrated efficacy in other inflammatory models. One of the primary strengths of VX-765 is its potent and selective inhibition of caspase-1, with low nanomolar IC₅₀ values ensuring that only minimal concentrations are required to achieve therapeutic effects (Flores et al., 2018; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020). This level of potency is crucial given the sensitivity of RPE cells to inflammatory mediators and the need for high selectivity in ocular tissues where off-target effects could be particularly damaging (Dhani et al., 2021; Kallinich, 2015). Moreover, the fact that VX-765 has already undergone Phase II clinical evaluation for indications such as psoriasis and epilepsy provides an established safety profile and foundational pharmacokinetic data that may be extrapolated to ocular applications, albeit with necessary adjustments for local delivery (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015).

Despite these strengths, several challenges persist. A critical point of concern is the discrepancy between the working hypothesis, which posits irreversible inhibition of caspase-1, and the well-documented reversible mode of action of VX-765 (Dhani et al., 2021; Kallinich, 2015). This difference in mechanism may influence both the duration of drug action and the frequency of dosing required to maintain therapeutic inhibition in vivo. Furthermore, while the anti-inflammatory effects have been established in systemic and neuronal contexts, direct evidence supporting the efficacy of VX-765 in preserving RPE lysosomal integrity and phagocytic function in dry AMD remains limited. Specific in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have indicated a reduction in IL-1β release and preservation of LAMP1-positive lysosomes upon caspase-1 inhibition (Kudelova et al., 2015), yet these findings need to be replicated and further validated in dry AMD models to ascertain translational potential.

Another potential weakness arises from safety considerations observed in the development history of related compounds. Pralnacasan (VX-740), a predecessor of VX-765, was associated with dose-limiting hepatotoxicity in long-term animal studies despite initial safety in human trials (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015). Although VX-765 has demonstrated a better safety profile in early clinical testing, caution must be exercised when repurposing the drug for chronic ocular use, particularly given the possibility of systemic absorption from an ocular delivery formulation (Dhani et al., 2021; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020). Additionally, while systemic administration of VX-765 has been explored, the optimal method for targeting the retina—whether through intravitreal injection, sustained-release implants, or other localized delivery systems—remains to be determined. Such considerations are paramount given the unique anatomy of the eye and the necessity of achieving pharmacologically active concentrations in the retina while minimizing exposure to off-target tissues (Kallinich, 2015; Gao et al., 2019).

From a biochemical perspective, the proposed mechanism of action offers a robust framework for the therapeutic intervention in dry AMD. Inhibition of caspase-1 directly limits the maturation of IL-1β and IL-18, inflammatory cytokines that have been implicated in the disruption of lysosomal function and phagocytic degradation of POS in RPE cells (Kallinich, 2015; Flores et al., 2018). Given that chronic inflammation and impaired degradation of photoreceptor debris are central to the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD, targeting this pathway could have a disease-modifying effect (Gao et al., 2019; Marneros, 2023). Furthermore, preventing the activation of gasdermin D by caspase-1 could reduce pyroptotic cell death, thereby preserving RPE cell viability—a critical factor in maintaining the outer blood-retina barrier and overall retinal function (Kallinich, 2015; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020).

Another area of promise lies in the potential for repurposing VX-765 based on emerging evidence that links inflammasome activity to ocular disease pathogenesis. Several recent studies have highlighted the role of caspase-1 and its downstream effects in models of retinal degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, and even neovascular AMD (Gao et al., 2019; Bian et al., 2011). Although much of the focus has been on the neovascular form of AMD—with interventions targeting VEGF signaling—the underlying inflammatory processes are shared with the dry form, particularly in the progression of geographic atrophy. The fact that caspase-1 activation has been demonstrated in activated macrophages and retinal microglia in the context of choroidal neovascularization (Marneros, 2023) further supports the notion that modulating this pathway could yield benefits in dry AMD in which inflammatory stress on the RPE is a prominent feature.

On the translational front, the existing clinical data for VX-765 suggest that its safety and tolerability profile is adequate for further investigation in ocular indications (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Marneros, 2023). The challenges associated with systemic toxicity observed in some preclinical contexts must be carefully balanced against the potential benefits of localized ocular delivery, which may allow lower doses and reduced systemic exposure. In the event that future preclinical work confirms the preservation of lysosomal function and improved POS clearance in RPE models, VX-765 could represent a viable candidate to slow the progression of dry AMD—a condition for which there are currently no approved disease-modifying treatments (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Marneros, 2023).

Overall, the strategy of repurposing VX-765 for dry AMD is supported by a coherent mechanistic rationale: by attenuating the caspase-1/IL-1β axis, the compound is expected to reduce inflammasome-mediated lysosomal damage, a key pathological event in RPE dysfunction and photoreceptor degeneration (Kallinich, 2015; Gao et al., 2019). Preclinical studies in other models have demonstrated that caspase-1 inhibition can reduce inflammatory cytokine secretion and preserve cell viability; extending these findings to RPE cells is a logical progression that could address unmet needs in dry AMD therapy (Kallinich, 2015; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020). The extensive development history of VX-765 in other indications provides valuable insights into the dosing, safety, and pharmacodynamics of the compound, thereby reducing some of the risks traditionally associated with early-stage drug development (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015).

Nevertheless, several critical hurdles remain. First, the discrepancy between the hypothesized irreversible inhibition and the documented reversible inhibition necessitates a re-evaluation of dosing strategies to achieve sustained caspase-1 suppression in the retinal environment (Dhani et al., 2021; Kallinich, 2015). Second, the translation of systemic safety data to ocular applications is not straightforward; the unique microenvironment of the eye, coupled with the challenges of achieving adequate intraocular concentrations, calls for rigorous preclinical studies using relevant animal models of dry AMD (Gao et al., 2019; Marneros, 2023). Additionally, given the potential for off-target effects and the historical context of hepatotoxicity observed with related compounds, investigators must prioritize the development of formulations that maximize local efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015).

Finally, it is important to recognize that while the anti-inflammatory approach targeting the caspase-1 pathway is scientifically sound, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease with a complex pathogenesis that includes oxidative stress, genetic predispositions, and metabolic dysregulation. Therefore, combination therapies that target multiple pathways may ultimately prove more effective than monotherapy with a single agent (Gao et al., 2019; Marneros, 2023). In this light, VX-765 could be considered as a component of a broader therapeutic strategy, potentially in conjunction with agents that address other aspects of RPE dysfunction and retinal degeneration.

In conclusion, the repurposing of VX-765 for dry AMD is supported by a robust body of preclinical and clinical data that demonstrate its ability to inhibit caspase-1 and attenuate inflammatory cascades. The compound’s synthetic origins, its established role as a reversible peptidomimetic caspase-1 inhibitor, and its demonstrated efficacy in reducing IL-1β maturation collectively form a strong foundation for its potential use in preserving lysosomal integrity and sustaining POS clearance in RPE cells (Dhani et al., 2021; Kallinich, 2015). However, further targeted studies in ocular models are imperative to validate these effects in the context of dry AMD, to optimize dosing regimens that account for its reversible mechanism, and to develop delivery strategies that ensure localized efficacy with minimal systemic risk. The candidate’s prior clinical evaluation in other indications offers a promising starting point, yet the leap to treating a chronic ocular disease will require careful, systematic investigation. Overall, VX-765 holds promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but its ultimate success will depend on overcoming formulation challenges, confirming its mechanism in RPE cells, and integrating its use into a multifaceted therapeutic regimen tailored to the complex pathogenesis of dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Marneros, 2023; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020).
