Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO‐Me) is a fully synthetic derivative of the naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid oleanolic acid. The parent molecule, oleanolic acid, is widely found in many plants and has been used for centuries in traditional medicine owing to its modest anti‐inflammatory and hepatoprotective properties. However, to overcome its relatively low intrinsic potency and poor pharmacokinetics, medicinal chemists modified oleanolic acid by introducing key structural changes. In particular, the synthesis of CDDO (2-cyano-3,12-dioxoolean-1,9-dien-28-oic acid) involved the installation of a cyano group at the C2 position and oxidation at positions C3 and C12, generating an electrophilic cyanoenone moiety; subsequent esterification at the C28 carboxyl group yielded bardoxolone methyl as the C28 methyl ester. These chemical modifications resulted in a molecule with two electrophilic Michael acceptor sites that are essential for its biological action, notably its ability to react reversibly with cysteine thiols in target proteins. Being part of the synthetic oleanane triterpenoids family, bardoxolone methyl falls into a class of compounds that has been extensively explored for their anti‐inflammatory, antioxidant, anticancer, and cytoprotective activities in various disease models (Borella et al., 2019).

This class of synthetic triterpenoids has historically been pursued to potentiate the natural but modest bioactivities of plant‐derived triterpenes such as oleanolic and ursolic acids. Early research aimed at enhancing anti‐inflammatory activity led to the discovery of potent derivatives such as CDDO, CDDO‐Im (the imidazolide derivative), and ultimately bardoxolone methyl. Their design was motivated by the need to generate highly potent, orally bioavailable agents capable of activating key cytoprotective pathways. The robust preclinical efficacy observed with these compounds in various models of oxidative stress, inflammation, and even tumorigenesis provided proof‐of‐concept for their use as drug candidates (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021). Consequently, bardoxolone methyl has emerged as a leading representative of this chemical class, notable for its finely tuned electrophilic reactivity and its ability to induce a broad spectrum of protective gene products.

Therapeutic History:  
Bardoxolone methyl has a well‐documented history of investigation in both preclinical and clinical settings across various therapeutic indications. Originally developed for its potent anti‐inflammatory and antioxidant properties, it was first investigated in oncology where its pro‐apoptotic and antiproliferative effects were characterized in multiple cancer cell types such as pancreatic, colorectal, ovarian, and breast cancer. Early preclinical studies demonstrated that at nanomolar and low micromolar concentrations, CDDO and its derivatives could exert robust cytoprotective effects via the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2‐related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, as well as induce cell cycle arrest and trigger apoptosis in cancer cells (Borella et al., 2019; Tanase et al., 2022).

Following its anticancer exploration, a serendipitous clinical observation during early oncology trials revealed that patients treated with bardoxolone methyl experienced improved renal function, as measured by an elevation in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). This finding prompted a pivot in therapeutic focus toward kidney diseases, particularly chronic kidney disease (CKD) associated with type 2 diabetes. The promising renoprotective data initially generated in Phase I oncology studies led to Phase II trials (such as the BEAM trial) where bardoxolone methyl displayed remarkable efficacy in increasing eGFR in CKD patients. However, in a subsequent Phase III study (the BEACON trial), concerns were raised after an unexpected increase in cardiovascular events, particularly heart failure, halted the trial. These mixed clinical outcomes have since spurred ongoing efforts to better understand and optimize the safety profile of bardoxolone methyl while leveraging its strong cytoprotective properties (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Sakashita et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).

Notably, while bardoxolone methyl has been extensively investigated in oncology and renal diseases, there is currently no record or published clinical trial data indicating that this compound has been used for treating dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or similar ocular conditions. Nonetheless, its underlying mechanism—primarily Nrf2 activation—is highly relevant to the pathobiology of dry AMD, given that oxidative stress and proteostasis imbalance are central to RPE cell dysfunction. Thus, while previous therapeutic applications have focused on systemic diseases, the repositioning of bardoxolone methyl to an ocular indication represents a scientifically plausible and innovative strategy that builds on its earlier demonstrated biochemical activities in other organ systems (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Bardoxolone methyl’s primary mode of action is its potent and selective activation of the Keap1/Nrf2/ARE (antioxidant response element) pathway. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytoplasm by its inhibitory binding partner Keap1, which targets Nrf2 for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl, owing to its electrophilic cyanoenone structure, covalently modifies reactive cysteine residues on Keap1 (including key sensors such as Cys151), thereby inhibiting its E3 ligase activity. This modification prevents the degradation of Nrf2, allowing it to accumulate and translocate into the nucleus (Hong et al., 2012; Mathis & Cui, 2016).

Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 dimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to ARE sequences in the promoter regions of various cytoprotective genes. This leads to the transcriptional induction of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxification enzymes, including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), glutathione S-transferases, and several molecular chaperones involved in protein folding and proteostasis. Through these gene products, bardoxolone methyl exerts robust antioxidant, anti‐inflammatory, and cytoprotective effects that help mitigate oxidative stress and repair cellular damage (Mathis & Cui, 2020; Tanase et al., 2022).

In addition to Nrf2‐mediated gene induction, bardoxolone methyl has been shown to modulate other signaling pathways that contribute to its anti‐inflammatory profile. For instance, it can inhibit NF-κB signaling, which reduces the transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines, and also affect pathways involving JAK/STAT and PI3K/Akt/mTOR, all of which have been implicated in the control of cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival (Sporn et al., 2011). The dual capacity to both upregulate protective gene networks and downregulate inflammatory signaling is central to the pharmacological action of bardoxolone methyl and underscores its potential to modulate cellular processes that are dysregulated in conditions characterized by oxidative and proteostatic stress (Cores et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014).

Furthermore, crystallographic and proteomic studies have provided molecular‐level evidence for the reversible Michael‐addition interaction between bardoxolone methyl and target cysteine residues on Keap1. This “dock and lock” mechanism ensures that the electrophilic reactivity of the compound is directed preferentially toward specific regulatory cysteines, thereby limiting non‐specific alkylation and supporting its relatively high potency as an Nrf2 activator (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
The hypothesis for repurposing bardoxolone methyl in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is grounded firmly in its ability to activate Nrf2 and thereby bolster the endogenous antioxidant defenses of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). In the RPE, oxidative damage is a pivotal pathomechanism that contributes to the accumulation of lipofuscin, impairment of autophagic flux, and ultimately, decreased phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). As Nrf2 plays a critical role in maintaining redox homeostasis within the RPE, its activation is expected to alleviate oxidative and proteostatic stress, thereby protecting critical functions such as phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation.

At an effective concentration in the submicromolar range (with an EC₅₀ estimated around 0.1 µM), bardoxolone methyl is anticipated to induce the transcription of genes such as HO-1 and NQO1 as well as chaperone proteins that ensure proper protein folding and degradation. The upregulation of these cytoprotective proteins may protect phagocytic receptors from oxidative modifications and preserve lysosomal enzymatic activity, which is essential for the degradation of ingested POS. This action is particularly crucial because impaired phagocytic function contributes to the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin and other debris in RPE cells—a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021).

Moreover, the robust activation of Nrf2 by bardoxolone methyl can help counterbalance the deficit in endogenous antioxidant capacity observed in the RPE of patients with dry AMD, as Nrf2 deficiency has been shown experimentally to exacerbate lipofuscin accumulation and autophagy blockade. Preclinical studies in non‐ocular systems have consistently demonstrated that treatment with CDDO‐Me leads to a marked increase in the expression of antioxidant genes and proteins that are implicated in both oxidative stress management and the maintenance of proteostasis (Hong et al., 2012; Sporn et al., 2011). Extrapolating from these findings, it is reasonable to expect that treatment with bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD cultures would result in a more effective clearance of POS by correcting the underlying oxidative imbalance and restoring lysosomal function. It is also plausible that enhanced expression of chaperones and stress‐response proteins would contribute to improved recycling of degraded photoreceptor material, thereby reducing the burden of intracellular debris (Cores et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014).

In addition, the effects of bardoxolone methyl on other signaling cascades—such as its inhibitory impact on NF-κB—could further reduce inflammatory responses within the RPE. Chronic inflammation is increasingly recognized as a contributing factor to AMD progression, and the suppression of pro‐inflammatory mediators would be expected to create a more favorable cellular environment for tissue repair and maintenance of RPE function (Sporn et al., 2011). Collectively, by activating Nrf2 and modulating inflammatory signaling pathways, bardoxolone methyl is expected to restore the cellular homeostasis of RPE cells, leading to enhanced phagocytosis of POS and potentially slowing or even reversing the degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Bardoxolone methyl represents an innovative and promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration, particularly given its well‐characterized ability to activate the Nrf2 pathway and trigger a potent antioxidant and proteostatic response. One clear strength of this compound is its robust preclinical and clinical profile in other indications; extensive studies in oncology and chronic kidney disease have established its capability to induce protective gene networks, coupled with a well‐defined mechanism of action that is directly applicable to combating oxidative stress—one of the central features of dry AMD pathogenesis (Borella et al., 2019).

From a mechanistic standpoint, bardoxolone methyl’s electrophilic structure enables it to interact in a highly regulated manner with the Keap1 protein. This interaction leads to the stabilization and nuclear translocation of Nrf2, culminating in the transcriptional activation of a spectrum of cytoprotective genes, including HO-1, NQO1, and various chaperones. These genes are known to be expressed in RPE cells and are essential for maintaining the integrity of phagocytic receptors and lysosomal enzymes that mediate POS clearance. Thus, the molecular rationale for its use in dry AMD is strong, as it addresses a fundamental aspect of RPE cell dysfunction (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Hong et al., 2012).

In terms of therapeutic history, while bardoxolone methyl has not previously been applied to ocular indications, its repositioning for dry AMD is scientifically warranted by the extensive evidence linking Nrf2 deficiency to the progression of RPE degeneration and lipofuscin accumulation. The previously observed benefits in non‐ocular systems, such as improvements in renal function via Nrf2 activation, support the idea that similar cytoprotective processes could be beneficial in the eye, particularly if local delivery or ocular formulation approaches can be developed to maximize efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure (Sakashita et al., 2021; Tanase et al., 2022).

Nevertheless, there are several challenges and weaknesses that must be carefully considered. First, the systemic use of bardoxolone methyl has been marred by significant cardiovascular safety concerns, as evidenced by the terminated BEACON trial in CKD patients. Although these adverse events were observed in a systemic context and might be mitigated by localized (for example, intravitreal) administration in the eye, they nonetheless raise caution regarding the compound’s off‐target effects and overall safety profile. The intrinsic electrophilicity that underlies its mechanism also bears the potential risk of non‐specific protein modification and cytotoxicity if not carefully controlled, particularly in a delicate tissue such as the retina (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014).

Second, while preclinical ocular safety data are being cited as supportive evidence for repositioning, robust and comprehensive studies specific to retinal tissues and RPE cell models must be undertaken to confirm that the drug does not induce unintended damage or disrupt other vital functions of the retina. Pharmacokinetic challenges—such as achieving and maintaining an effective therapeutic concentration in the RPE without eliciting systemic exposure—will also need to be addressed. The EC₅₀ for Nrf2 activation in RPE is hypothesized to be approximately 0.1 µM, and this level must be reliably achieved in an ocular setting, ideally through controlled‐release formulations or targeted delivery systems (Cores et al., 2020).

An additional consideration is the complexity of dry AMD itself, which is influenced not only by oxidative stress and impaired autophagy but also by chronic low‐grade inflammation, complement dysregulation, and extracellular matrix alterations in Bruch’s membrane. Although bardoxolone methyl’s anti‐inflammatory effects via NF-κB inhibition are a potential asset, it remains to be determined how these multiple pathways will interact within the unique microenvironment of the retina. Tailored preclinical studies that specifically evaluate the compound’s impact on POS clearance, RPE phagocytosis, and lysosomal function in models of dry AMD are essential to validate the underlying hypothesis (Sporn et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2014).

On the strength side, the repositioning of bardoxolone methyl is supported by its extensive clinical investigation in other indications. The existence of Phase I and II human data provides a valuable foundation regarding dosing, pharmacokinetics, and some aspects of safety, which can significantly de‐risk early translational studies in the ocular domain. The compound’s well‐documented capacity to activate Nrf2—a pathway known to be highly relevant in the aging RPE and in the pathogenesis of dry AMD—further underscores its potential utility. Moreover, the synthetic nature of bardoxolone methyl facilitates the possibility of further chemical optimization and the development of novel formulations (such as nanoparticle‐ or liposome‐based ocular delivery systems) that may enhance its safety and efficacy profile when administered locally (Borella et al., 2019; Borella et al., 2019; Sporn et al., 2011).

In summary, bardoxolone methyl appears to be a promising candidate for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration based on its potent Nrf2‐activating properties and its capacity to upregulate antioxidant and proteostasis genes. These effects could theoretically restore and enhance the phagocytic function of RPE cells, thereby improving the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and reducing lipofuscin accumulation—a central pathogenic feature of dry AMD. However, significant challenges remain, including addressing the compound’s systemic safety concerns, ensuring specific ocular delivery, and confirming efficacy and safety in relevant RPE and retinal models. Rigorous preclinical studies focusing on ocular pharmacodynamics, toxicity, and long‐term effects in models of dry AMD are warranted before advancing to clinical trials for this indication. While the repurposing hypothesis is scientifically sound and mechanistically compelling, the unique challenges of ocular drug development must be navigated cautiously (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2014; Thomas, 2012; Dao et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
Bardoxolone methyl’s robust mechanistic action as an Nrf2 activator—coupled with its documented preclinical and early clinical efficacy in other indications—positions it as a highly attractive repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its molecular design, derived from oleanolic acid and enhanced through strategic electrophilic modifications, underpins a powerful ability to upregulate antioxidant defenses and restore proteostasis. These actions directly address the cellular deficits observed in dry AMD, namely the accumulation of oxidative damage, impaired autophagy, and subsequent dysfunction of the RPE.  

Strengths of the candidate include:  
• A well‐characterized synthetic origin with clearly defined structure–activity relationships, ensuring potent Nrf2 activation at low concentrations (Borella et al., 2019).  
• Substantial preclinical data indicating its ability to induce cytoprotective gene networks such as HO-1, NQO1, and molecular chaperones that are crucial for maintaining RPE function (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Hong et al., 2012).  
• An extensive history in clinical testing in systemic diseases (oncology and CKD), which provides valuable information regarding dosing and pharmacokinetics that could inform ocular application (Zhou et al., 2014; Sakashita et al., 2021).  
• The underlying hypothesis is supported by evidence that Nrf2 deficiency exacerbates RPE dysfunction and lipofuscin accumulation, suggesting that restoring Nrf2 activity could ameliorate key pathological features of dry AMD.

Weaknesses and challenges include:  
• The previous systemic administration of bardoxolone methyl was associated with significant cardiovascular adverse events, and while local delivery to the eye may mitigate this risk, careful ocular safety studies are essential (Tanase et al., 2022; Mathis & Cui, 2016).  
• There is a paucity of data on the compound’s effects in retinal tissues specifically; it has not been previously tested in dry AMD or similar ocular models, necessitating robust preclinical validation in RPE cells and animal models (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021).  
• The inherent electrophilic reactivity of bardoxolone methyl, while central to its mechanism, poses a risk of off‐target protein modification and possible cytotoxicity, particularly in the sensitive environment of the retina (Zhou et al., 2014; Cores et al., 2020).  
• Achieving the optimal therapeutic window in the eye may require innovative formulation strategies to ensure sustained, localized exposure at the low nanomolar range that is effective for Nrf2 activation without provoking adverse effects.  
• Given the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis—encompassing oxidative stress, inflammation, and extracellular matrix alterations—it is critical to consider that Nrf2 activation alone may not fully address all aspects of the disease, implying that combination therapies or adjunctive treatments might ultimately be necessary (Sporn et al., 2011).

In conclusion, the repurposing of bardoxolone methyl for dry AMD is a scientifically sound and potentially transformative strategy, especially if its potent Nrf2 activation can be harnessed safely within the ocular milieu. Its capacity to induce elegant cytoprotective responses aligns well with the need to mitigate oxidative damage and restore autophagy in stressed RPE cells. Nonetheless, before committing significant resources to clinical trials in this indication, it is imperative to undertake thorough preclinical studies focused on ocular pharmacokinetics, toxicity, and efficacy in relevant models of dry AMD. These investigations will not only validate the underlying hypothesis but also inform the development of appropriate delivery systems to maximize local efficacy and minimize systemic risk. With these considerations addressed, bardoxolone methyl holds considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate that could significantly improve outcomes for patients suffering from dry age‐related macular degeneration (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2014; Dao et al., 2015; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AM580 is a fully synthetic retinoid compound designed as a highly selective agonist for the retinoic acid receptor α (RARα). Its chemical structure—a derivative of naphthalene and benzoic acid—was rationally engineered to confer two key properties: a more rigid molecular architecture compared with the natural ligand all‐trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and a marked preferential binding to RARα over other retinoid receptor subtypes (RARβ and RARγ) (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992). The molecule’s chemical name, 4-(5,6,7,8-tetrahydro-5,5,8,8-tetramethyl-2-naphthalenyl)carboxamido]benzoic acid, reflects its derivation from a series of modifications intended to enhance receptor selectivity and bioactivity (Martin et al., 1992). AM580 belongs to the broader class of retinoids—compounds that are either natural derivatives of vitamin A or synthetically modified analogues—which function as ligands for nuclear hormone receptors. Retinoids have been exploited in various fields of medicine due to their ability to modulate cellular differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis by activating retinoic acid receptor (RAR) and retinoid X receptor (RXR) pathways (Cras et al., 2010; Martin et al., 1992). In the case of AM580, its design emphasizes selective RARα activation, as demonstrated by its 30-fold higher binding affinity for RARα compared to RARβ and RARγ (Teng et al., 1996; Martin et al., 1992), making it an excellent molecular tool for dissection of RARα-specific biological responses.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, retinoids have been at the forefront of differentiation therapy, with ATRA being successfully employed in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) (Garattini et al., 2007; Garattini et al., 1997). However, the clinical use of natural retinoids like ATRA has been limited by drawbacks such as isomerization, rapid metabolism, and broad receptor engagement leading to unnecessary side effects (Drowley et al., 2020; Cras et al., 2010). These limitations spurred the development of receptor subtype–selective ligands, among which AM580 emerged as a leading RARα-selective agonist (Martin et al., 1992). Beyond oncology, synthetic retinoids have been investigated in a variety of contexts including dermatology and even cardiovascular applications (Nagy et al., 2012; Petrukhin, 2013); however, more recent studies have explored the potential ocular applications of retinoid receptor agonists. In particular, a growing body of literature has begun to examine the effects of RAR agonists on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that activation of RARα in RPE cells by compounds such as AM580 can modulate epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and improve cellular functions relevant to retinal homeostasis (Kobayashi et al., 2021). Although not previously approved as an ocular therapeutic, the compound’s use in research settings—including those investigating phagocytic processes in the RPE—provides a promising precedent for repurposing it for conditions like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of AM580 is well delineated at the molecular level. As an RARα agonist, it binds with high affinity to the ligand-binding domain of RARα, a nuclear receptor that functions as a ligand-dependent transcription factor. Upon ligand binding, the receptor undergoes a conformational change that results in the dissociation of co-repressor complexes and the recruitment of co-activators and other transcriptional machinery. This ligand-induced activation facilitates the heterodimerization of RARα with retinoid X receptor (RXR), followed by binding to retinoic acid response elements (RAREs) in the promoter regions of target genes (Garattini et al., 2007; Teng et al., 1996).  
Notably, AM580’s structural modification—featuring a polar amide linkage—enhances its selectivity for RARα by promoting specific hydrogen bonding interactions within the receptor’s binding pocket that are not available in RARβ or RARγ (Teng et al., 1996). Once activated, RARα modulates a variety of downstream genes. Among these, studies have recently indicated that selective RARα activation can lead to the upregulation of milk fat globule epidermal growth factor 8 (MFGE8) in RPE cells (Unknown Reference). MFGE8 plays a critical role in facilitating the bridging of phosphatidylserine (exposed on the shed photoreceptor outer segments (POS)) to integrin receptors—specifically αvβ5—which are expressed on the RPE, thereby promoting efficient phagocytosis (Drowley et al., 2020; Kobayashi et al., 2021). Consequently, AM580’s engagement of RARα is expected to not only drive transcriptional changes related to RPE differentiation and anti-fibrotic responses but also directly enhance phagocytic clearance mechanisms essential for retinal health (Kobayashi et al., 2021). In additional preclinical settings, RARα agonism via AM580 has been implicated in modulating transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling pathways, which further supports its capacity to inhibit aberrant EMT—a process implicated in retinal scarring and progression of dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis under evaluation posits that AM580, by selectively activating RARα at an effective concentration (EC₅₀ ~50 nM as observed in RPE cell assays), will stimulate the transcription of the MFGE8 gene. Upregulation of MFGE8 is crucial because this glycoprotein acts as a “molecular bridge” by binding to phosphatidylserine on POS and to integrin receptors such as αvβ5 on the RPE. Under normal conditions, MFGE8 is an essential mediator of RPE phagocytosis, facilitating the daily clearance of spent outer segments—a process that is impaired in dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2012). Evidence from preclinical studies, including those using Mertk-deficient RPE models, suggests that AM580 treatment can lead to increased MFGE8 levels and a concomitant improvement in POS uptake (Kobayashi et al., 2021). Thus, in the assay proposed by the team, AM580 is expected to restore or enhance the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells by boosting MFGE8 expression. This improved clearance mechanism would help reduce the accumulation of POS debris and lipofuscin—a buildup known to contribute to RPE dysfunction and the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Furthermore, secondary effects such as the inhibition of deleterious EMT processes—which are associated with fibrosis and the progression of dry AMD—may also be realized, thereby preserving or restoring a more differentiated, functional RPE phenotype (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
AM580 represents a compelling therapeutic candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, based on several lines of evidence gathered from the literature. Its primary strength lies in its high degree of selectivity for RARα. This receptor selectivity is critical because it allows for target‐specific modulation of gene expression, potentially reducing the broad side effects observed with natural retinoids like ATRA that activate multiple receptor subtypes (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992; Teng et al., 1996). The structural optimization of AM580 not only confers potent agonistic activity but also provides a pharmacological tool for dissecting the specific roles of RARα in retinal biology, particularly within the RPE. Preclinical studies have underscored the utility of RARα activation in modulating key processes such as cellular differentiation, inhibition of EMT, and enhancement of phagocytic function in RPE cells (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2012).  
However, several potential challenges must also be acknowledged. Retinoid compounds are notorious for their complex pharmacokinetics and potential for off-target effects, including teratogenicity, as evidenced by prior studies of AM580 in teratogenicity models (Elmazar et al., 2001). The delicate balance between efficacy and safety remains a critical issue, particularly for a condition such as dry AMD where long-term treatment is anticipated. Furthermore, while the preclinical evidence supporting the induction of MFGE8 by RARα activation is promising, the available data remain largely confined to in vitro studies and select animal models. Clinical validation in human subjects is still lacking, and the translation of dose levels, tissue penetration, and metabolic stability from the laboratory to the clinic remains an open question (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Another concern is that AM580, while selective, does retain some activity at RARβ and RARγ at higher concentrations (Teng et al., 1996), an effect that may have unpredictable consequences on cell signaling in the complex microenvironment of the RPE. Moreover, the retinoid system is intricately linked with multiple signaling pathways, and long-term modulation may lead to compensatory mechanisms or unforeseen adverse outcomes.  
In summary, the repurposing of AM580 for dry AMD is supported by a robust molecular rationale—its ability to selectively activate RARα is directly linked to the upregulation of MFGE8 and, consequently, the enhancement of POS phagocytosis in RPE cells. This mechanism directly addresses a critical defect in dry AMD pathology, namely the impaired clearance of photoreceptor debris, which is a central driver of retinal degeneration (Garattini et al., 2007; Kobayashi et al., 2021). The preclinical literature offers promising evidence that selective RARα modulation can exert beneficial effects on RPE physiology, including the prevention of EMT and restoration of phagocytic function (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Despite these strengths, the transition from preclinical studies to clinical application will require careful attention to pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic factors, as well as rigorous safety assessments to mitigate risks typical of retinoid therapies. Overall, while challenges remain, AM580’s unique properties render it a promising candidate that merits further investigation in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to fill a significant therapeutic gap in the management of this debilitating condition (Martin et al., 1992; Teng et al., 1996; Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide, a water‐soluble form of vitamin B3, is a naturally occurring compound that plays a critical role in cellular metabolism by serving as a precursor for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺) synthesis. It is available both through dietary sources and chemical synthesis and has been produced at high purity for research purposes (Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. N4126). Nicotinamide belongs to the vitamin B3 class of compounds, which have been extensively used as nutritional supplements and metabolic regulators; these compounds are well recognized for their role in the salvage pathway that replenishes NAD⁺ levels in cells. The therapeutic candidate under consideration is repurposed with the hypothesis that at a concentration of 10 mM, nicotinamide will boost intracellular NAD⁺ pools and enhance the activity of NAD⁺‐dependent enzymes, such as sirtuins, leading to improved mitochondrial function and increased deacetylation of autophagy regulators. Such effects are expected to restore phagocytic function, specifically the photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation, in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cultures pertinent to dry age‐related macular degeneration (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, nicotinamide has been investigated in various preclinical and clinical settings for its potential neuroprotective effects and its capacity to modulate cellular metabolism. In the context of ocular health, several studies have demonstrated that nicotinamide supplementation can enhance NAD⁺ levels and improve mitochondrial function in retinal cells. Preclinical studies have reported that this vitamin not only supports retinal ganglion cell health in glaucoma models but also shows promise in improving photoreceptor and RPE function in models of age-related macular degeneration (Gemae et al., 2024). Although there remains limited direct clinical experience with nicotinamide in dry AMD, the compound has been a subject of interest in related ocular conditions due to its favorable safety profile and widespread use in other age-related and mitochondrial dysfunction settings (Gemae et al., 2024). More recent investigations have focused on its ability to rescue mitochondrial deficits and restore autophagic flux in RPE cells, with data indicating that in models of CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE, nicotinamide can ameliorate lysosomal processing and POS degradation problems (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). This body of evidence, compounded with its extensive historical use as a nutritional supplement, supports the rationale for repurposing nicotinamide as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, nicotinamide exerts its effects primarily through its role as a key precursor in the NAD⁺ salvage pathway. In this pathway, nicotinamide is converted to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) via the enzyme nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), and subsequently to NAD⁺ by NMN adenylyltransferase. NAD⁺, in turn, is an essential co-factor for numerous enzymes involved in energy metabolism and cellular homeostasis, most notably the sirtuin family of NAD⁺-dependent deacetylases (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Sirtuins, such as SIRT1 and SIRT3, play a pivotal role in mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and regulation of autophagy by deacetylating key transcription factors and enzymes that control metabolic stress responses (Gemae et al., 2024). In RPE cells, increased NAD⁺ levels facilitate the activation of these sirtuins, which then deacetylate a range of targets including histones and autophagy regulators, leading to improved mitochondrial structure and function, enhanced energy production, and the promotion of efficient autophagic and lysosomal degradation pathways (Gemae et al., 2024). Furthermore, the improved mitochondrial function translates into a better cellular energy state, providing the necessary ATP required for high-energy processes such as POS phagocytosis. Experimentally, administration of nicotinamide has been shown to yield a two-fold increase in NAD⁺ levels in ARPE-19 cells, thereby confirming its ability to augment the cellular bioenergetic capacity (Hazim et al., 2022). This mechanism also intersects with the regulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, as enhanced mitochondrial function and sirtuin activity contribute to lower oxidative stress, a known contributor to cellular senescence and dysfunction in the aging retina (Gemae et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the current proposal is that nicotinamide, administered at a concentration of 10 mM in vitro, will significantly increase NAD⁺ levels in RPE cells, thereby enhancing sirtuin activity and downstream mitochondrial function. This boost in NAD⁺ is expected to promote deacetylation of autophagy regulators, which will, in turn, normalize the autophagic flux and facilitate the effective degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE. In models of dry AMD, where phagocytosis deficits and impaired proteostasis are key pathological features, the restoration of autophagy and mitochondrial activity is anticipated to ameliorate cellular senescence and maintain retinal homeostasis (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Data from previous studies suggest that in aging RPE, reduced NAMPT expression is linked to decreased NAD⁺ levels and compromised SIRT1 function, leading to cellular senescence and defective mitochondrial dynamics (Jadeja et al., 2018). By contrast, nicotinamide supplementation helps to reverse these effects, as evidenced by restored NAD⁺ content and reactivation of sirtuins that enable degradation of accumulated defective cellular components, thereby improving lysosomal enzyme processing and phagocytosis (Jadeja et al., 2018). Moreover, enhanced mitochondrial metabolism has been correlated with improved RPE differentiation and the maintenance of a polarized epithelial phenotype, critical factors in ensuring effective POS phagocytosis and overall retinal health (Hazim et al., 2022). Thus, the expected outcome is that nicotinamide treatment will correct metabolic impairments, reduce oxidative stress, and restore phagocytic efficiency in dry AMD cultures, which are all essential for halting or even reversing disease progression (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
Nicotinamide emerges as a highly promising therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on its multi-faceted mechanism of action and extensive preclinical evidence supporting its role in maintaining retinal health. One of the primary strengths of nicotinamide is its excellent safety profile and widespread historical use as a nutritional supplement, which significantly lowers the risk associated with its repurposing (Gemae et al., 2024). Its ability to augment NAD⁺ levels and activate sirtuins directly addresses several key pathological processes in dry AMD, including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and impaired autophagy. Experimental findings have consistently shown that increased NAD⁺ levels, mediated by nicotinamide or its analogues such as NMN, correlate with reduced cellular senescence and improved lysosomal and mitochondrial function in RPE cells (Jadeja et al., 2018).

Moreover, the convergence of multiple lines of evidence—from studies detailing NAMPT decline in aging RPE, to those demonstrating the restoration of NAD⁺ and sirtuin activity by nicotinamide—provides a robust biochemical rationale for its use in combating dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024). The ability of nicotinamide to enhance mitochondrial respiration in ARPE-19 cells and primary human fetal RPE cells further underscores its potential in promoting a healthy, polarized RPE phenotype capable of efficient POS phagocytosis (Hazim et al., 2022). These studies also suggest that improved mitochondrial metabolism is closely linked to enhanced proteostasis and autophagic clearance of damaged cellular components—an outcome that is particularly relevant given the known deficits in autophagy and lysosomal processing observed in dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024).

However, while the preclinical data are encouraging, several challenges must be acknowledged. One potential weakness lies in the translation of in vitro findings to in vivo therapeutic efficacy. The concentration of 10 mM nicotinamide used in cell culture experiments may not directly correspond to achievable or sustainable therapeutic levels in the human retina. Moreover, while nicotinamide is known to boost NAD⁺ synthesis, there is a nuanced balance in its effects on sirtuin activity; in certain contexts, excessive nicotinamide has been reported to inhibit sirtuins, suggesting that dosing and timing will be critical parameters that require careful optimization (Will-Orrego, 2020). There is also the inherent challenge of the multifactorial nature of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired autophagy are only parts of a complex network of pathological events that include inflammatory signaling, extracellular matrix alterations, and genetic predispositions. Thus, while nicotinamide addresses several of these pathways, it may need to be combined with other therapeutic agents to achieve a comprehensive treatment effect (Gemae et al., 2024; Will-Orrego, 2020).

Another important consideration is the need for more extensive clinical studies. Although nicotinamide’s safety profile is well established in the context of dietary supplementation and its use in other neurological and ocular conditions, robust clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD are lacking (Gemae et al., 2024; Lin, 2020). Future research will need to focus not only on the pharmacokinetics and optimal dosing strategies in human subjects but also on precise biomarkers indicating the restoration of NAD⁺ metabolism, mitochondrial function, and POS phagocytosis. Furthermore, mechanistic studies that dissect the interactions between nicotinamide-driven NAD⁺ elevation and the downstream modulation of autophagy regulators will be essential to confirm the proposed mode of action and to identify any potential off-target effects.

Overall, the repurposing of nicotinamide for dry AMD presents several compelling advantages. Its established safety, low cost, and known biochemical mechanisms strongly support its potential as a therapeutic candidate. Preclinical evidence indicates that nicotinamide not only restores NAD⁺ levels but also reactivates sirtuin pathways, thereby mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction and defective autophagy that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. These effects could translate into improved cellular proteostasis and enhanced POS phagocytosis, ultimately preserving retinal integrity and visual function (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Nevertheless, the path forward will require careful dose optimization and rigorous clinical validation to ensure that the in vitro benefits observed translate into meaningful clinical outcomes. In summary, despite the challenges associated with translating cell-based results into human therapy, nicotinamide remains an attractive candidate whose mechanism, historical use, and preclinical successes justify further investigation as a potential treatment for dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Lin, 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Brefeldin A (BFA) is a natural product originally isolated in 1958 from Penicillium decumbens, and its discovery marked the beginning of intensive studies on its unique ability to disrupt intracellular protein trafficking (Hung, 2020). Structurally, BFA is a macrolide characterized by a complex fused system comprising a cyclopentane moiety linked to a 13-membered lactone, and this distinctive architecture has spurred extensive synthetic and medicinal chemistry efforts over the past decades (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015). By targeting the secretory pathway, BFA acts as a Golgi transport inhibitor, primarily through its binding to a protein complex involving a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) and the small G protein Arf1. This binding event results in the rapid disassembly of the Golgi apparatus and redistribution of its components back into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Hung, 2020). BFA is therefore classified among natural product inhibitors of intracellular trafficking, a group that has long served as invaluable research tools in cell biology to dissect the mechanisms of vesicular transport and Golgi-ER dynamics. Its broad bioactivities—as an antiviral, antifungal, and antimitotic agent—have principally been exploited in preclinical research rather than clinical therapeutics (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, BFA has been employed almost exclusively as a biochemical probe to investigate protein processing, secretion, and Golgi morphology in diverse eukaryotic cells. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that BFA’s ability to stall ER-to-Golgi trafficking can modulate various cellular processes including secretion of cytokines, hormones, and growth factors (Hung, 2020). Its documented effects on blocking transport have been leveraged in cancer cell studies where BFA-induced apoptosis and cell cycle arrest were observed, owing to mislocalization of key signaling molecules (Stierle & Stierle, 2015). Despite these promising cellular effects, the clinical development of BFA as a conventional therapeutic agent has been hindered by issues such as poor bioavailability and significant toxicity with prolonged exposure (Seehafer et al., 2013). Importantly, while BFA has not been directly applied in clinical studies for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or any similar degenerative retinal diseases, its mechanistic action on intracellular trafficking, ER stress, and protein secretion renders it an intriguing candidate for repurposing. In the context of AMD, where complement dysregulation and lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells play a critical pathogenic role, BFA could potentially offer a novel means of attenuating the buildup of complement components and misfolded proteins (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). While none of the published literature explicitly documents the use of BFA for AMD therapy, related studies in RPE cellular models have highlighted the importance of complement modulation and lysosomal restoration, establishing a rationale for investigating trafficking inhibitors such as BFA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
On a molecular level, the mechanism of action for Brefeldin A is well characterized. BFA binds to the complex comprising a catalytic GEF and the small GTPase Arf1, inhibiting the exchange of GDP for GTP on Arf1. This inhibition precludes proper recruitment and coat assembly for vesicle budding at the Golgi membranes, leading to a collapse of the Golgi structure and the retrograde redistribution of Golgi proteins to the ER (Hung, 2020). The immediate consequence of this inhibition is a profound disruption in the secretory pathway, which not only halts the export of proteins but also results in an accumulation of proteins within the ER. In cell types where the regulated secretion of proteins is critical for homeostasis, such as in RPE cells, this effect can have dual ramifications. On the one hand, it may help prevent the secretion of misfolded or aberrantly processed proteins, including complement components that are implicated in local inflammation and lysosomal deposition (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). On the other hand, the blockade of Golgi trafficking may transiently lower the secretion of proteins that otherwise contribute to the local pool of complement proteins which, if misfolded or overproduced, could lead to an increase in intracellular complement activation and subsequent deposition of the membrane attack complex (MAC, particularly C5b-9) within lysosomes (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In RPE cells, where robust daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) is essential, the maintenance of lysosomal function is critical; overburdening of lysosomes with complement-derived debris has been implicated in the formation of drusen and lipofuscin accumulation, both of which underlie AMD pathology (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The proposed intervention using BFA therefore leverages its well-established ability to modulate protein trafficking to indirectly reduce the burden of misfolded or overabundant complement proteins on the lysosomal system, thereby potentially restoring cathepsin activity and overall lysosomal function in RPE cells.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing BFA in dry AMD is that brief pulses of BFA administration will selectively inhibit the ER-to-Golgi trafficking route in RPE cells, thereby reducing the processing and secretion of misfolded complement proteins. RPE cells are known to contribute to local complement activation through the production and turnover of various complement components; in AMD, aberrant complement regulation leads to increased turnover, formation of complement split products, and the deposition of terminal complement complexes (C5b-9) in the lysosomes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The expected outcome of BFA treatment would be a reduction in the export of these misfolded or excessively generated complement proteins, ultimately leading to decreased local complement activation and a reduction in lysosomal overload by MAC proteins. Experimental evidence from studies using compstatin analogues (e.g., Cp40) in Y402H-RPE cell models has shown that complement inhibition can restore lysosomal function and cathepsin activity, thereby reducing lysosome size, diminishing drusen-like deposits, and improving the overall cellular phenotype (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015). By analogy, transient BFA treatment is anticipated to produce similar beneficial effects on lysosomal physiology in RPE cells, provided that the inhibition is carefully timed to avoid prolonged exposure which could be deleterious (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Furthermore, because RPE cells are responsible for the daily clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, maintaining an unencumbered lysosomal system is crucial for long-term retinal health. The expected biochemical cascade following BFA administration would therefore include a reduction in ER stress due to diminished protein export, lower secretion of misfolded complement proteins, and a subsequent decrease in complement-mediated lysosomal damage. This in turn should lead to a stabilization or even an improvement in cathepsin levels and activity, promoting a more efficient degradation of cellular debris and restoration of POS clearance (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential repurposing of Brefeldin A as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD is innovative and grounded in a detailed understanding of both its mechanism of action and the pathophysiology of AMD. Several strengths underlie this approach. First, BFA has a well-characterized molecular mechanism that directly affects the secretory pathway by inhibiting ER-to-Golgi trafficking. This offers a mechanistic basis for reducing the secretion of misfolded or aberrantly processed complement proteins—the accumulation of which is a central driver of lysosomal dysfunction and local complement activation in RPE cells (Hung, 2020). Second, preclinical research in AMD models has demonstrated that modulating complement activity, whether through direct inhibition of complement components or by enhancing lysosomal function, can reverse pathological phenotypes associated with the disease (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015). This suggests that a strategy aimed at indirectly reducing complement deposition via interference with protein trafficking holds considerable promise. Third, the idea of using brief pulses of BFA rather than continuous dosing could allow for a transient therapeutic effect that minimizes the known toxicities associated with prolonged BFA exposure—thus potentially overcoming one of the key limitations that has prevented its clinical development in other contexts (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015).

Nonetheless, there are significant challenges and weaknesses that must be addressed before this approach can be advanced. One of the primary concerns relates to the non-selectivity of BFA’s action. Because BFA disrupts a fundamental cellular process, its effects are not confined solely to the trafficking of misfolded complement proteins. It is likely to inhibit the normal secretion of multiple proteins that are essential for RPE cell function, which could inadvertently impair the phagocytosis and processing of photoreceptor outer segments (Hung, 2020; Seehafer et al., 2013). Such disruption could paradoxically exacerbate the very lysosomal dysfunction it is intended to ameliorate, particularly if dosing is not carefully titrated. Furthermore, while transient inhibition may mitigate toxicity, achieving the precise balance between therapeutic efficacy and cellular viability will require rigorous optimization in both in vitro and in vivo models. Another potential drawback is related to pharmacokinetics and delivery. BFA’s poor bioavailability and potential systemic toxicity have long been recognized as obstacles for its use beyond experimental settings (Seehafer et al., 2013). Delivering BFA specifically to the RPE while avoiding off-target effects in other ocular or systemic tissues will demand innovative formulation strategies, such as localized drug delivery systems, which inherently add another layer of complexity to the drug development process. Additionally, while the hypothesis is supported by analogous studies demonstrating that complement modulation can restore lysosomal function in AMD models (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015), there is currently no direct evidence that BFA’s inhibition of ER-to-Golgi trafficking will reproduce these beneficial effects in the delicate environment of the retina. The potential for unforeseen interactions with other components of the RPE’s protein processing machinery or compensatory cellular responses further complicates the translational prospects of this approach.

In summary, as an expert drug development team leader tasked with evaluating promising repurposed drugs for dry AMD, I find the proposal to repurpose Brefeldin A to be both innovative and mechanistically intriguing. The strengths of this candidate lie in its well-characterized molecular target—namely, the inhibition of Arf1-mediated vesicle budding at the Golgi—and its potential to modulate a key pathological feature of AMD, namely the dysregulated secretion and accumulation of complement proteins that leads to lysosomal impairment and MAC deposition (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). However, the inherent risks associated with disrupting a central cellular process cannot be overstated. The lack of selectivity in BFA’s action, potential toxicity from even brief exposures, and challenges in targeting the RPE specifically are serious obstacles that must be systematically addressed. Further preclinical studies are required to delineate the dose-response relationship in RPE cell models, to examine the long-term effects of transient BFA-induced trafficking inhibition on cellular health, and to validate the hypothesis that such intervention can indeed reduce lysosomal MAC deposition and rescue cathepsin activity. Only with convincing evidence from rigorous in vitro and in vivo experiments would it be justified to consider advancing BFA as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. In conclusion, while the proposed use of BFA presents a compelling mechanistic rationale with some supportive preclinical analogies from the literature (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020), significant challenges regarding specificity, delivery, and safety need to be overcome before this approach can be deemed a viable therapeutic option for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO‐Me) is a fully synthetic derivative of the naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid oleanolic acid. The parent molecule, oleanolic acid, is widely found in many plants and has been used for centuries in traditional medicine owing to its modest anti‐inflammatory and hepatoprotective properties. However, to overcome its relatively low intrinsic potency and poor pharmacokinetics, medicinal chemists modified oleanolic acid by introducing key structural changes. In particular, the synthesis of CDDO (2-cyano-3,12-dioxoolean-1,9-dien-28-oic acid) involved the installation of a cyano group at the C2 position and oxidation at positions C3 and C12, generating an electrophilic cyanoenone moiety; subsequent esterification at the C28 carboxyl group yielded bardoxolone methyl as the C28 methyl ester. These chemical modifications resulted in a molecule with two electrophilic Michael acceptor sites that are essential for its biological action, notably its ability to react reversibly with cysteine thiols in target proteins. Being part of the synthetic oleanane triterpenoids family, bardoxolone methyl falls into a class of compounds that has been extensively explored for their anti‐inflammatory, antioxidant, anticancer, and cytoprotective activities in various disease models (Borella et al., 2019).

This class of synthetic triterpenoids has historically been pursued to potentiate the natural but modest bioactivities of plant‐derived triterpenes such as oleanolic and ursolic acids. Early research aimed at enhancing anti‐inflammatory activity led to the discovery of potent derivatives such as CDDO, CDDO‐Im (the imidazolide derivative), and ultimately bardoxolone methyl. Their design was motivated by the need to generate highly potent, orally bioavailable agents capable of activating key cytoprotective pathways. The robust preclinical efficacy observed with these compounds in various models of oxidative stress, inflammation, and even tumorigenesis provided proof‐of‐concept for their use as drug candidates (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021). Consequently, bardoxolone methyl has emerged as a leading representative of this chemical class, notable for its finely tuned electrophilic reactivity and its ability to induce a broad spectrum of protective gene products.

Therapeutic History:  
Bardoxolone methyl has a well‐documented history of investigation in both preclinical and clinical settings across various therapeutic indications. Originally developed for its potent anti‐inflammatory and antioxidant properties, it was first investigated in oncology where its pro‐apoptotic and antiproliferative effects were characterized in multiple cancer cell types such as pancreatic, colorectal, ovarian, and breast cancer. Early preclinical studies demonstrated that at nanomolar and low micromolar concentrations, CDDO and its derivatives could exert robust cytoprotective effects via the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2‐related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, as well as induce cell cycle arrest and trigger apoptosis in cancer cells (Borella et al., 2019; Tanase et al., 2022).

Following its anticancer exploration, a serendipitous clinical observation during early oncology trials revealed that patients treated with bardoxolone methyl experienced improved renal function, as measured by an elevation in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). This finding prompted a pivot in therapeutic focus toward kidney diseases, particularly chronic kidney disease (CKD) associated with type 2 diabetes. The promising renoprotective data initially generated in Phase I oncology studies led to Phase II trials (such as the BEAM trial) where bardoxolone methyl displayed remarkable efficacy in increasing eGFR in CKD patients. However, in a subsequent Phase III study (the BEACON trial), concerns were raised after an unexpected increase in cardiovascular events, particularly heart failure, halted the trial. These mixed clinical outcomes have since spurred ongoing efforts to better understand and optimize the safety profile of bardoxolone methyl while leveraging its strong cytoprotective properties (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Sakashita et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).

Notably, while bardoxolone methyl has been extensively investigated in oncology and renal diseases, there is currently no record or published clinical trial data indicating that this compound has been used for treating dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or similar ocular conditions. Nonetheless, its underlying mechanism—primarily Nrf2 activation—is highly relevant to the pathobiology of dry AMD, given that oxidative stress and proteostasis imbalance are central to RPE cell dysfunction. Thus, while previous therapeutic applications have focused on systemic diseases, the repositioning of bardoxolone methyl to an ocular indication represents a scientifically plausible and innovative strategy that builds on its earlier demonstrated biochemical activities in other organ systems (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Bardoxolone methyl’s primary mode of action is its potent and selective activation of the Keap1/Nrf2/ARE (antioxidant response element) pathway. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytoplasm by its inhibitory binding partner Keap1, which targets Nrf2 for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl, owing to its electrophilic cyanoenone structure, covalently modifies reactive cysteine residues on Keap1 (including key sensors such as Cys151), thereby inhibiting its E3 ligase activity. This modification prevents the degradation of Nrf2, allowing it to accumulate and translocate into the nucleus (Hong et al., 2012; Mathis & Cui, 2016).

Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 dimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to ARE sequences in the promoter regions of various cytoprotective genes. This leads to the transcriptional induction of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxification enzymes, including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), glutathione S-transferases, and several molecular chaperones involved in protein folding and proteostasis. Through these gene products, bardoxolone methyl exerts robust antioxidant, anti‐inflammatory, and cytoprotective effects that help mitigate oxidative stress and repair cellular damage (Mathis & Cui, 2020; Tanase et al., 2022).

In addition to Nrf2‐mediated gene induction, bardoxolone methyl has been shown to modulate other signaling pathways that contribute to its anti‐inflammatory profile. For instance, it can inhibit NF-κB signaling, which reduces the transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines, and also affect pathways involving JAK/STAT and PI3K/Akt/mTOR, all of which have been implicated in the control of cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival (Sporn et al., 2011). The dual capacity to both upregulate protective gene networks and downregulate inflammatory signaling is central to the pharmacological action of bardoxolone methyl and underscores its potential to modulate cellular processes that are dysregulated in conditions characterized by oxidative and proteostatic stress (Cores et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014).

Furthermore, crystallographic and proteomic studies have provided molecular‐level evidence for the reversible Michael‐addition interaction between bardoxolone methyl and target cysteine residues on Keap1. This “dock and lock” mechanism ensures that the electrophilic reactivity of the compound is directed preferentially toward specific regulatory cysteines, thereby limiting non‐specific alkylation and supporting its relatively high potency as an Nrf2 activator (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
The hypothesis for repurposing bardoxolone methyl in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is grounded firmly in its ability to activate Nrf2 and thereby bolster the endogenous antioxidant defenses of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). In the RPE, oxidative damage is a pivotal pathomechanism that contributes to the accumulation of lipofuscin, impairment of autophagic flux, and ultimately, decreased phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). As Nrf2 plays a critical role in maintaining redox homeostasis within the RPE, its activation is expected to alleviate oxidative and proteostatic stress, thereby protecting critical functions such as phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation.

At an effective concentration in the submicromolar range (with an EC₅₀ estimated around 0.1 µM), bardoxolone methyl is anticipated to induce the transcription of genes such as HO-1 and NQO1 as well as chaperone proteins that ensure proper protein folding and degradation. The upregulation of these cytoprotective proteins may protect phagocytic receptors from oxidative modifications and preserve lysosomal enzymatic activity, which is essential for the degradation of ingested POS. This action is particularly crucial because impaired phagocytic function contributes to the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin and other debris in RPE cells—a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021).

Moreover, the robust activation of Nrf2 by bardoxolone methyl can help counterbalance the deficit in endogenous antioxidant capacity observed in the RPE of patients with dry AMD, as Nrf2 deficiency has been shown experimentally to exacerbate lipofuscin accumulation and autophagy blockade. Preclinical studies in non‐ocular systems have consistently demonstrated that treatment with CDDO‐Me leads to a marked increase in the expression of antioxidant genes and proteins that are implicated in both oxidative stress management and the maintenance of proteostasis (Hong et al., 2012; Sporn et al., 2011). Extrapolating from these findings, it is reasonable to expect that treatment with bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD cultures would result in a more effective clearance of POS by correcting the underlying oxidative imbalance and restoring lysosomal function. It is also plausible that enhanced expression of chaperones and stress‐response proteins would contribute to improved recycling of degraded photoreceptor material, thereby reducing the burden of intracellular debris (Cores et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014).

In addition, the effects of bardoxolone methyl on other signaling cascades—such as its inhibitory impact on NF-κB—could further reduce inflammatory responses within the RPE. Chronic inflammation is increasingly recognized as a contributing factor to AMD progression, and the suppression of pro‐inflammatory mediators would be expected to create a more favorable cellular environment for tissue repair and maintenance of RPE function (Sporn et al., 2011). Collectively, by activating Nrf2 and modulating inflammatory signaling pathways, bardoxolone methyl is expected to restore the cellular homeostasis of RPE cells, leading to enhanced phagocytosis of POS and potentially slowing or even reversing the degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Bardoxolone methyl represents an innovative and promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration, particularly given its well‐characterized ability to activate the Nrf2 pathway and trigger a potent antioxidant and proteostatic response. One clear strength of this compound is its robust preclinical and clinical profile in other indications; extensive studies in oncology and chronic kidney disease have established its capability to induce protective gene networks, coupled with a well‐defined mechanism of action that is directly applicable to combating oxidative stress—one of the central features of dry AMD pathogenesis (Borella et al., 2019).

From a mechanistic standpoint, bardoxolone methyl’s electrophilic structure enables it to interact in a highly regulated manner with the Keap1 protein. This interaction leads to the stabilization and nuclear translocation of Nrf2, culminating in the transcriptional activation of a spectrum of cytoprotective genes, including HO-1, NQO1, and various chaperones. These genes are known to be expressed in RPE cells and are essential for maintaining the integrity of phagocytic receptors and lysosomal enzymes that mediate POS clearance. Thus, the molecular rationale for its use in dry AMD is strong, as it addresses a fundamental aspect of RPE cell dysfunction (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Hong et al., 2012).

In terms of therapeutic history, while bardoxolone methyl has not previously been applied to ocular indications, its repositioning for dry AMD is scientifically warranted by the extensive evidence linking Nrf2 deficiency to the progression of RPE degeneration and lipofuscin accumulation. The previously observed benefits in non‐ocular systems, such as improvements in renal function via Nrf2 activation, support the idea that similar cytoprotective processes could be beneficial in the eye, particularly if local delivery or ocular formulation approaches can be developed to maximize efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure (Sakashita et al., 2021; Tanase et al., 2022).

Nevertheless, there are several challenges and weaknesses that must be carefully considered. First, the systemic use of bardoxolone methyl has been marred by significant cardiovascular safety concerns, as evidenced by the terminated BEACON trial in CKD patients. Although these adverse events were observed in a systemic context and might be mitigated by localized (for example, intravitreal) administration in the eye, they nonetheless raise caution regarding the compound’s off‐target effects and overall safety profile. The intrinsic electrophilicity that underlies its mechanism also bears the potential risk of non‐specific protein modification and cytotoxicity if not carefully controlled, particularly in a delicate tissue such as the retina (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014).

Second, while preclinical ocular safety data are being cited as supportive evidence for repositioning, robust and comprehensive studies specific to retinal tissues and RPE cell models must be undertaken to confirm that the drug does not induce unintended damage or disrupt other vital functions of the retina. Pharmacokinetic challenges—such as achieving and maintaining an effective therapeutic concentration in the RPE without eliciting systemic exposure—will also need to be addressed. The EC₅₀ for Nrf2 activation in RPE is hypothesized to be approximately 0.1 µM, and this level must be reliably achieved in an ocular setting, ideally through controlled‐release formulations or targeted delivery systems (Cores et al., 2020).

An additional consideration is the complexity of dry AMD itself, which is influenced not only by oxidative stress and impaired autophagy but also by chronic low‐grade inflammation, complement dysregulation, and extracellular matrix alterations in Bruch’s membrane. Although bardoxolone methyl’s anti‐inflammatory effects via NF-κB inhibition are a potential asset, it remains to be determined how these multiple pathways will interact within the unique microenvironment of the retina. Tailored preclinical studies that specifically evaluate the compound’s impact on POS clearance, RPE phagocytosis, and lysosomal function in models of dry AMD are essential to validate the underlying hypothesis (Sporn et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2014).

On the strength side, the repositioning of bardoxolone methyl is supported by its extensive clinical investigation in other indications. The existence of Phase I and II human data provides a valuable foundation regarding dosing, pharmacokinetics, and some aspects of safety, which can significantly de‐risk early translational studies in the ocular domain. The compound’s well‐documented capacity to activate Nrf2—a pathway known to be highly relevant in the aging RPE and in the pathogenesis of dry AMD—further underscores its potential utility. Moreover, the synthetic nature of bardoxolone methyl facilitates the possibility of further chemical optimization and the development of novel formulations (such as nanoparticle‐ or liposome‐based ocular delivery systems) that may enhance its safety and efficacy profile when administered locally (Borella et al., 2019; Borella et al., 2019; Sporn et al., 2011).

In summary, bardoxolone methyl appears to be a promising candidate for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration based on its potent Nrf2‐activating properties and its capacity to upregulate antioxidant and proteostasis genes. These effects could theoretically restore and enhance the phagocytic function of RPE cells, thereby improving the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and reducing lipofuscin accumulation—a central pathogenic feature of dry AMD. However, significant challenges remain, including addressing the compound’s systemic safety concerns, ensuring specific ocular delivery, and confirming efficacy and safety in relevant RPE and retinal models. Rigorous preclinical studies focusing on ocular pharmacodynamics, toxicity, and long‐term effects in models of dry AMD are warranted before advancing to clinical trials for this indication. While the repurposing hypothesis is scientifically sound and mechanistically compelling, the unique challenges of ocular drug development must be navigated cautiously (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2014; Thomas, 2012; Dao et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
Bardoxolone methyl’s robust mechanistic action as an Nrf2 activator—coupled with its documented preclinical and early clinical efficacy in other indications—positions it as a highly attractive repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its molecular design, derived from oleanolic acid and enhanced through strategic electrophilic modifications, underpins a powerful ability to upregulate antioxidant defenses and restore proteostasis. These actions directly address the cellular deficits observed in dry AMD, namely the accumulation of oxidative damage, impaired autophagy, and subsequent dysfunction of the RPE.  

Strengths of the candidate include:  
• A well‐characterized synthetic origin with clearly defined structure–activity relationships, ensuring potent Nrf2 activation at low concentrations (Borella et al., 2019).  
• Substantial preclinical data indicating its ability to induce cytoprotective gene networks such as HO-1, NQO1, and molecular chaperones that are crucial for maintaining RPE function (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Hong et al., 2012).  
• An extensive history in clinical testing in systemic diseases (oncology and CKD), which provides valuable information regarding dosing and pharmacokinetics that could inform ocular application (Zhou et al., 2014; Sakashita et al., 2021).  
• The underlying hypothesis is supported by evidence that Nrf2 deficiency exacerbates RPE dysfunction and lipofuscin accumulation, suggesting that restoring Nrf2 activity could ameliorate key pathological features of dry AMD.

Weaknesses and challenges include:  
• The previous systemic administration of bardoxolone methyl was associated with significant cardiovascular adverse events, and while local delivery to the eye may mitigate this risk, careful ocular safety studies are essential (Tanase et al., 2022; Mathis & Cui, 2016).  
• There is a paucity of data on the compound’s effects in retinal tissues specifically; it has not been previously tested in dry AMD or similar ocular models, necessitating robust preclinical validation in RPE cells and animal models (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021).  
• The inherent electrophilic reactivity of bardoxolone methyl, while central to its mechanism, poses a risk of off‐target protein modification and possible cytotoxicity, particularly in the sensitive environment of the retina (Zhou et al., 2014; Cores et al., 2020).  
• Achieving the optimal therapeutic window in the eye may require innovative formulation strategies to ensure sustained, localized exposure at the low nanomolar range that is effective for Nrf2 activation without provoking adverse effects.  
• Given the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis—encompassing oxidative stress, inflammation, and extracellular matrix alterations—it is critical to consider that Nrf2 activation alone may not fully address all aspects of the disease, implying that combination therapies or adjunctive treatments might ultimately be necessary (Sporn et al., 2011).

In conclusion, the repurposing of bardoxolone methyl for dry AMD is a scientifically sound and potentially transformative strategy, especially if its potent Nrf2 activation can be harnessed safely within the ocular milieu. Its capacity to induce elegant cytoprotective responses aligns well with the need to mitigate oxidative damage and restore autophagy in stressed RPE cells. Nonetheless, before committing significant resources to clinical trials in this indication, it is imperative to undertake thorough preclinical studies focused on ocular pharmacokinetics, toxicity, and efficacy in relevant models of dry AMD. These investigations will not only validate the underlying hypothesis but also inform the development of appropriate delivery systems to maximize local efficacy and minimize systemic risk. With these considerations addressed, bardoxolone methyl holds considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate that could significantly improve outcomes for patients suffering from dry age‐related macular degeneration (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2014; Dao et al., 2015; Cuadrado et al., 2019).
