Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ML‐SA1 is a fully synthetic small molecule designed as an agonist of the transient receptor potential mucolipin 1 (TRPML1) channel. It belongs to the class of mucolipin synthetic agonists, which were initially derived as analogs of earlier lead compounds such as SF‐51 and SF‐22. These compounds were discovered using high‐throughput screening approaches aimed at identifying activators of TRPML channels, and ML‐SA1 was subsequently optimized for improved potency and selectivity in mammalian systems (Feng et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2012). As a synthetic compound, ML‐SA1 exemplifies a rational drug design strategy in which the molecule is engineered to mimic the action of the endogenous lipid agonist phosphatidylinositol 3,5‐bisphosphate [PI(3,5)P₂] by directly binding to the channel’s pore region. This binding stabilizes TRPML1 in its open conformation, thereby facilitating lysosomal Ca²⁺ release. The chemical class represented by ML‐SA1 has historically been employed as a research tool to interrogate lysosomal physiology and calcium homeostasis in diverse cell types, including neuronal and retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Therapeutic History:  
Previous studies have demonstrated that ML‐SA1 robustly elevates cytosolic calcium levels in several cellular models by activating TRPML1 channels. In particular, ML‐SA1 has been applied to multiple RPE cell models—including mouse RPE, human embryonic stem cell‐derived RPE, and the ARPE‐19 cell line—to assess its ability to restore lysosomal calcium signaling and normalize lysosomal function (Gómez et al., 2018). In these experiments, ML‐SA1 elicited rapid, robust, and reversible Ca²⁺ signals that were completely absent in TRPML1 knockout cells, thereby confirming target engagement and specificity (Gómez et al., 2018). Beyond RPE biology, ML‐SA1 has been evaluated in neuronal models of lysosomal dysfunction, including experimental systems relevant to Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease, where it mediated correction of defective lysosomal acidification and improved autophagic flux (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022). Although no clinical trials have yet investigated ML‐SA1 directly in patients with dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), its demonstrated efficacy in rescuing lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling—in conditions that share underlying pathophysiological features with dry AMD such as lysosomal storage and autophagy blockade—suggests that its repurposing may yield therapeutic benefits in this disease context (Open Targets Platform, 2025). To date, the use of ML‐SA1 has predominantly been within experimental research settings rather than in clinical practice or veterinary medicine, and its repurposing for dry AMD represents an innovative and rationale‐driven approach rooted in the overlap between TRPML1 dysfunction and RPE pathology (Feng et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2017).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic action of ML‐SA1 is centered upon its ability to directly activate TRPML1 channels located on lysosomal membranes. TRPML1 plays a critical role in regulating lysosomal calcium homeostasis by mediating Ca²⁺ efflux from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol. ML‐SA1 binds directly to TRPML1—likely within a hydrophobic pocket formed at the S5–S6 transmembrane domain interface—and stabilizes the channel’s open state (Feng et al., 2014). This activation occurs independently of exogenous PI(3,5)P₂ in mammalian cells, setting ML‐SA1 apart from the endogenous regulatory mechanisms that otherwise depend on dynamic fluctuations in phosphoinositide levels (Feng et al., 2014; Gómez et al., 2018). As a result of channel activation, lysosomal Ca²⁺ is released into the cytosol, triggering a cascade of calcium‐dependent signaling pathways. One critical downstream effect is the promotion of lysosomal membrane fission and fusion events, processes that are essential for proper lysosomal trafficking and the maturation of autophagosomes into autolysosomes (Cao et al., 2017; Li & Li, 2022).  

Beyond its immediate role in calcium mobilization, ML‐SA1‐mediated activation of TRPML1 also facilitates the activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Increased cytosolic Ca²⁺ can activate calcineurin, which in turn dephosphorylates TFEB, enabling its translocation to the nucleus where it upregulates the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function and autophagy (Pollmanns et al., 2022). In some models, ML‐SA1 treatment has been shown to improve the processing and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D, thereby contributing to normalization of lysosomal pH and enhanced protein degradation (Hui et al., 2019). Importantly, the ability of ML‐SA1 to restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling directly targets the pathological cascade observed when TRPML1 is deficient or inhibited—a scenario that is reminiscent of the lysosomal storage, impaired autophagy, and stalled phagolysosomal degradation evident in dry AMD RPE cells (Gómez et al., 2018; Pamonag, 2021).  

Expected Effect:  
Based on the observed mechanisms in diverse cellular models, it is expected that ML‐SA1 will re‐establish normal lysosomal function in RPE cells afflicted by dry AMD. In the proposed assay, the activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 at concentrations near its EC₅₀ (approximately 5 µM) should restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ efflux, thereby driving several beneficial downstream effects. First, the induced calcium release is anticipated to promote lysosomal membrane dynamics that favor fission and fusion events, ultimately leading to improved lysosomal trafficking and an enhanced capacity for phagolysosomal degradation. This is particularly relevant for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), the routine phagocytic burden of RPE cells that, when inadequately processed, contributes to lipofuscin accumulation and retinal degeneration (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Second, by normalizing Ca²⁺ signaling, ML‐SA1 is expected to reinstate proper lysosomal acidification. Acidification is crucial for the optimal activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D; ML‐SA1 has been shown in various models to restore cathepsin D processing, thereby resetting the enzymatic degradation cascade necessary for POS turnover (Hui et al., 2019). Such restoration of acidification and enzyme activity would directly counteract the pathological accumulation of undegraded material—a hallmark of dry AMD.  

Third, the downstream activation of TFEB induced by ML‐SA1’s modulation of lysosomal calcium may trigger an upregulation of the entire lysosomal-autophagy gene network. This transcriptional reprogramming is vital for augmenting both the number and function of lysosomes, thereby enhancing the overall cellular clearance capacity in RPE cells. Because ample evidence suggests that TRPML1 is expressed in RPE cells and that its dysfunction contributes directly to the autophagy block observed in dry AMD (Pamonag, 2021; Gómez et al., 2018), the activation of this pathway by ML‐SA1 is expected to result in a net improvement in POS degradation and a reduction in toxic debris accumulation. Ultimately, the integrated effects of improved lysosomal trafficking, normalized pH, enhanced enzymatic processing, and boosted autophagic flux are hypothesized to alleviate key pathological features of dry AMD, potentially slowing or even reversing degenerative changes in the retinal pigment epithelium (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Our comprehensive literature review indicates that ML‐SA1 is a scientifically compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration. One of its principal strengths lies in its well‐defined mechanism of action: by directly activating TRPML1 channels, ML‐SA1 has been shown to restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ homeostasis—a central defect in several models of lysosomal storage and autophagy dysfunction (Gómez et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2014). The robust experimental data obtained in RPE cell models and other relevant systems supports the hypothesis that ML‐SA1 can reverse deficits in lysosomal trafficking, acidification, and autophagosome maturation. The compound’s ability to elicit rapid, reproducible, and reversible Ca²⁺ signals is particularly encouraging, as it suggests that pharmacological modulation of TRPML1 can be finely tuned through dosing adjustments (Gómez et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2017).  

Furthermore, the extensive research demonstrating ML‐SA1’s effects in cellular models of lysosomal storage diseases—including those markers that mimic the pathological lipid accumulation and autophagy impairment found in dry AMD—provides additional rationale for its application in RPE cells (Feng et al., 2014; Pollmanns et al., 2022; Hui et al., 2019). The fact that ML‐SA1 has also been evaluated in non-ocular contexts (such as neuronal models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s diseases) where it facilitated autophagic clearance and improved lysosomal functions underscores the versatility of its mechanism and hints at broader therapeutic utility (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022).  

Nonetheless, several challenges must be acknowledged. One notable weakness is that ML‐SA1’s efficacy can be compromised by lysosomal lipid accumulation—a common feature of advanced dry AMD. Studies suggest that in cells with significant lipid deposition, such as those accumulating sphingomyelin or other inhibitory lipids, the activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 is attenuated (Gómez et al., 2018). This raises concerns that in patients with advanced dry AMD, the therapeutic window may be narrower or may require combination strategies to first reduce lipid burden. Additionally, while the in vitro EC₅₀ is promising (around 5 µM), there remains uncertainty regarding the pharmacokinetic profile, bioavailability, tissue penetration (particularly across the blood‐retina barrier), and potential off-target effects of ML‐SA1 when administered in vivo (Li & Li, 2022).  

Another area of concern is the current lack of direct clinical data pertaining to ML‐SA1 in dry AMD. Although preclinical studies in RPE cell models provide a solid foundation, translation to in vivo models of AMD—and eventually to human clinical trials—will require additional investigation. The absence of any reported clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD with TRPML1 agonists (as confirmed by database searches such as those reflected in the Open Targets Platform) indicates that this is still a largely uncharted therapeutic area requiring further validation (Open Targets Platform, 2025). Moreover, chronic activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 may have unforeseen consequences related to intracellular calcium homeostasis and autophagic balance, which warrant careful evaluation in long-term studies (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022).  

In summary, ML‐SA1 represents a highly promising candidate for the repurposing in dry AMD based on its ability to rescue lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling, enhance autophagic clearance, and restore normal lysosomal pH and trafficking in RPE cells. Its synthetic origin and well‐characterized mechanism provide a strong mechanistic rationale for its use. However, issues related to lipid-mediated inhibition of TRPML1, pharmacokinetic considerations, and the current lack of in vivo data in AMD models must be addressed. Overall, the candidate shows significant potential, but a focused program of preclinical validation—including animal models of dry AMD, detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiling, and exploration of strategies to mitigate lysosomal lipid accumulation—is essential before advancing ML‐SA1 to clinical trials for dry AMD (Gómez et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nintedanib is a synthetic small‐molecule drug originally discovered and developed by Boehringer Ingelheim through an extensive lead optimization program that began in the late 1990s. Its design emerged during early cancer drug discovery efforts focused on angiogenesis inhibition, inspired in part by Judah Folkman’s pioneering work. The compound belongs to the indolinone chemical class – more precisely, it is a 6‐methoxycarbonyl‐substituted indolinone derivative – and was identified after systematic structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies that evaluated numerous six‐substituted indolinone analogues. In particular, modifications such as moving an amido group on the oxindole scaffold were shown to eliminate unwanted CDK4 inhibition while retaining potent VEGFR inhibition, and these insights eventually led to the convergence on the lead compound now known as nintedanib (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 1–8). The synthetic strategy employed a convergent approach that involved classical malonic ester addition reactions, followed by hydrogenation under acidic conditions that induced decarboxylative cyclization, and concluded with condensation steps and salt formation (resulting in the monoethanesulfonate form) to yield a highly crystalline final product (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 5–10, 39–43). As an indolinone derivative, nintedanib exemplifies a well‐studied class of therapeutic compounds that modulate receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs). Similar compounds in this class have been widely used in antiangiogenic and antifibrotic therapies in oncology and pulmonary medicine, and their ability to simultaneously inhibit multiple RTK pathways has been key to overcoming resistance mechanisms frequently encountered with single‐target inhibitors (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 1–5; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 22–25).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, nintedanib was developed with an emphasis on its anticancer potential. Its original targeting of the vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR) and subsequent demonstration of triple angiokinase inhibition – simultaneously inhibiting VEGFR, platelet‐derived growth factor receptors (PDGFR), and fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFR) – made it a candidate for addressing tumor angiogenesis. Early preclinical studies confirmed that nintedanib potently inhibited endothelial cell proliferation and in vivo tumor growth, leading to its progression into numerous Phase I through III clinical trials for non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), ovarian cancer, and other malignancies (Azuma et al., 2015, pp. 3–5; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 20–22). In addition, the compound’s remarkable specificity, as evidenced by low nanomolar inhibition of PDGFR and VEGFR family members (with IC₅₀ values in the range of 13–65 nM for different targets), underscored its potential as a broad‐spectrum antiangiogenic agent (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 10–15; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 12–14).  

Beyond its oncology applications, accumulating clinical evidence revealed that nintedanib also exhibits strong antifibrotic properties. Its efficacy in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) – with demonstrated improvements in forced vital capacity decline and overall clinical outcomes – led to its regulatory approval for IPF treatment in regions such as Europe and the United States (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 36–39; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 20–22). These diverse therapeutic indications illustrate that while nintedanib was originally intended as an anticancer agent, its mechanism of inhibiting multiple RTK‐mediated pathways allowed its repurposing for fibrotic diseases. Although nintedanib has not yet been extensively used in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), recent preclinical evidence in ocular models has suggested that its kinase inhibition profile could be exploited to modulate dysfunctional signaling in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17). Notably, studies in retinal models have demonstrated that nintedanib can suppress VEGF secretion and reduce neovascularization, both of which provide indirect evidence supporting its ocular tolerability and hint at potential utility in diseases such as dry AMD.  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, nintedanib exerts its pharmacological effect by acting as a competitive inhibitor of the ATP‐binding site located within the catalytic domain of receptor tyrosine kinases. Structural studies, including co‐crystallization and high‐resolution X‐ray diffraction analyses, have revealed that its indolinone core is critical for binding; the molecule forms two canonical hydrogen bonds with key residues within the kinase “hinge” region – for example, interactions with the nitrogen of a conserved cysteine residue (such as Cys919 in VEGFR2) and with a carbonyl oxygen (such as Glu917) – thereby stabilizing its association with the enzyme (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12). The presence of a methyl carboxylate substituent on the indolinone core further extends into the kinase specificity pocket to reinforce binding, and a methyl piperazinyl side chain interacts with solvent‐exposed portions of the protein, contributing both to the agent’s selectivity and to its sustained inhibitory profile (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 39–43; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12).  

Functionally, nintedanib displays potent inhibition of multiple RTKs. Its IC₅₀ values have been reported to be in the low nanomolar range for VEGFR subtypes (e.g., approximately 21 nM for VEGFR2 and 13 nM for VEGFR3), as well as for PDGFR isoforms (roughly 41–58 nM) and FGFR family members (with values ranging from 37 nM for FGFR2 to higher values for other FGFRs) (Azuma et al., 2015, pp. 3–5; Roth et al., 2015, pp. 10–15; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 12–14). By competitively occupying the ATP‐binding pocket, nintedanib prevents receptor autophosphorylation, thereby blocking subsequent activation of downstream signaling cascades, including the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and protein kinase B (Akt) pathways (Reck, 2015, pp. 2–3; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12). This broad inhibition interrupts not only angiogenic signaling in endothelial cells and pericytes but also fibrotic signaling in fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. An additional key feature of nintedanib’s mode of action is the sustained duration of receptor blockade; experimental studies have shown that even after a short 1-hour exposure, inhibition of VEGFR2 phosphorylation can persist for at least 32 hours, suggesting a relatively slow dissociation rate from the kinase active site (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 10–15; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12).  

In the specific context of retinal pigment epithelial cells, PDGFRβ and FGFR1 are among the RTKs implicated in maintaining cellular differentiation, regulating cytoskeletal organization, and modulating phagocytic activity. Dysregulation of these signaling pathways in RPE cells may lead to a decrease in the effective expression of key phagocytic receptors such as integrin αvβ5 and MERTK – receptors that are vital for the ingestion and clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Although much of the detailed mechanistic work in RPE cells remains in the early stages, the existing experimental evidence supports the notion that balanced RTK signaling is necessary for optimal RPE function. By inhibiting overactive signaling through PDGFRβ and FGFR1, nintedanib could restore a more physiologic phosphorylation state that permits proper receptor recycling and expression at the cell surface, thereby supporting phagocytosis and maintaining cellular integrity (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17). Additionally, by modulating these upstream kinases, downstream events that regulate cytoskeletal dynamics – potentially including reorganization of actin filaments and stabilization of focal adhesions – could be favorably altered. Although direct evidence in RPE cells is still emerging, analogous effects in other cell types have been observed when RTK signaling is normalized by multi-target inhibitors such as nintedanib (Hilberg et al., 2018, pp. 14–15, 19–20).  

Expected Effect:  
Within the RPE, efficient phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments is fundamental to retinal homeostasis, and failure of this process is believed to contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. The hypothesis proposes that dysregulated PDGFRβ and FGFR1 signaling in RPE cells impairs the expression and functional activity of phagocytic receptors, notably integrin αvβ5 and MERTK, which are responsible for recognizing and internalizing shed POS. Under normal conditions, these receptors are tightly regulated by extracellular signals, many of which are modulated by RTK activity. In the diseased state, abnormal RTK phosphorylation – perhaps via overactivation of PDGFR and FGFR pathways – could lead to a decrease in phagocytic receptor levels and result in defective POS clearance, contributing to the accumulation of cellular debris, chronic inflammation, and eventual geographic atrophy observed in dry AMD.  

By virtue of its potent inhibitory properties, nintedanib is expected to act by normalizing the aberrantly high RTK signaling in RPE cells. Its inhibition of PDGFRβ, in particular, would be anticipated to reduce excessive downstream signaling that might otherwise lead to a suppression of phagocytic receptor synthesis or recycling. In parallel, FGFR1 inhibition could correct imbalances in signaling that contribute to impaired cytoskeletal remodeling. The cytoskeleton is intimately involved in the process of phagocytosis, not only by providing the structural basis for membrane extension during engulfment but also by facilitating receptor clustering and the formation of phagocytic cups. Therefore, it is plausible to expect that the use of nintedanib would lead to enhanced expression of integrin αvβ5 and MERTK at the RPE cell surface as normal feedback loops are reinstated, thereby promoting increased rates of POS ingestion in assays of RPE differentiation (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17).  

Furthermore, preclinical studies have shown that in settings where RPE cells are exposed to pathological stimuli (such as necrotic cell lysates, which serve as a surrogate for sterile inflammatory conditions seen in retinal diseases), treatment with nintedanib results in a concentration-dependent suppression of aberrant VEGF secretion. This observation suggests that nintedanib is not only capable of regulating angiogenic processes in the retina but may also normalize other aspects of RPE cell function that rely on balanced RTK signaling (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13). In the context of the proposed assays, one would expect that treatment with nintedanib will restore proper receptor tyrosine kinase activity, result in the upregulation of phagocytic receptor expression, and enhance the mechanical and structural reorganization required for efficient POS uptake. These outcomes could be measured both biochemically – through assays of receptor expression and phosphorylation levels – and functionally, via quantification of POS ingestion in differentiated RPE cultures (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12; Rashdan & Hanna, 2014, pp. 2–3).  

In addition to its direct impact on RTK signaling, nintedanib’s inhibition is anticipated to indirectly influence other cytoskeleton-regulating pathways that are governed by MAPK and Akt cascades. These pathways have been associated with the regulation of actin dynamics and the assembly of focal adhesions, both of which are essential for robust phagocytic activity. Thus, normalization of these signaling pathways may foster an environment in RPE cells where cytoskeletal remodeling is optimized, ultimately leading to improved structural integrity and function—key factors in maintaining retinal health in the face of degenerative processes (Reck, 2015, pp. 2–3; Hilberg et al., 2018, pp. 19–20).  

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, nintedanib presents a compelling profile as a therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration. One of its primary strengths is its well‐documented ability to inhibit multiple receptor tyrosine kinases simultaneously. This triple angiokinase inhibition—encompassing VEGFR, PDGFR, and FGFR—has been extensively characterized in both in vitro and in vivo models, resulting in robust antitumor and antifibrotic effects in clinical studies for cancer and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 36–39; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 20–22). The compound’s chemical structure, based on its indolinone core, not only permits tight binding and competitive inhibition at the ATP‐binding site but also provides the necessary selectivity that minimizes off-target effects, a critical feature when considering repurposing for a delicate tissue such as the retina (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12; Roth et al., 2015, pp. 39–43).  

From a therapeutic history perspective, the extensive clinical experience with nintedanib in non‐small cell lung cancer and IPF engenders a level of confidence in its pharmacokinetic profile and tolerability when administered systemically. Although its use in ocular applications remains experimental, preliminary preclinical findings provide encouraging data. For instance, studies have demonstrated that nintedanib can inhibit VEGF secretion from retinal pigment epithelial cells exposed to pathological stimuli and can reduce retinal and choroidal neovascularization in animal models. These findings support the notion that, with appropriate reformulation or local delivery (e.g., intravitreal injection), nintedanib could achieve therapeutic levels in the retina without incurring unacceptable toxicity (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17).  

The mechanistic basis for considering nintedanib in dry AMD is particularly appealing. Dry AMD is characterized in part by the dysfunction of RPE cells, including impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments—a process tightly regulated by surface receptors such as integrin αvβ5 and MERTK. Dysregulation of upstream receptor tyrosine kinases, notably PDGFRβ and FGFR1, is hypothesized to contribute to the diminished expression or function of these phagocytic receptors. Nintedanib, by virtue of its potent inhibition of these kinases, holds the potential to recalibrate RTK signaling networks toward a more balanced state. This recalibration may not only restore proper levels of phagocytic receptors on RPE cells but also promote cytoskeletal remodeling necessary for the engulfment and processing of POS (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17). The downstream effects of such restoration could conceivably slow or even reverse aspects of RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration in dry AMD.  

Nonetheless, there are important considerations and potential weaknesses. One significant challenge lies in the delivery of nintedanib to the retina at therapeutic concentrations. Systemic administration of nintedanib is associated with low oral bioavailability and extensive first-pass metabolism (as observed in its use for IPF), which implies that direct ocular administration, likely via intravitreal injection, would be necessary for effective treatment of dry AMD. Although preclinical studies have demonstrated tolerability in ocular models, comprehensive toxicology studies specific to the retinal environment are required to ensure that the compound does not adversely affect other critical retinal cell types, including photoreceptors and inner retinal neurons (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 15–19; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 12–14).  

Another potential limitation is the broad scope of kinase inhibition exerted by nintedanib. While its ability to simultaneously target VEGFR, PDGFR, and FGFR is a strength in terms of overcoming compensatory mechanisms, it also raises the possibility of off-target effects that may disrupt other cellular processes in the retina. The retina is a highly specialized and tightly regulated tissue, and even subtle perturbations in signaling networks can lead to unintended consequences. Therefore, it will be critical to establish that nintedanib’s inhibition of RTKs in RPE cells does not interfere with other essential pathways—especially those involved in retinal development and neuroprotection (Hilberg et al., 2018, pp. 14–15; Hilberg et al., 2018, pp. 19–20).  

In addition, while the hypothesis that nintedanib can enhance phagocytic receptor expression (e.g., upregulating integrin αvβ5 and MERTK) is supported by the general principle that RTK signaling modulates these receptors, direct evidence linking nintedanib treatment to increased phagocytosis in RPE cells is still at an early, hypothesis‐driven stage. Rigorous experimental validation will be needed, potentially involving detailed biochemical assays to measure receptor expression and functional assays to assess POS ingestion rates in differentiated RPE cultures as well as in relevant animal models of dry AMD (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12; Rashdan & Hanna, 2014, pp. 2–3).  

Furthermore, while the ocular tolerability of nintedanib has been indirectly inferred from its use in non‐small cell lung cancer and preclinical models of choroidal neovascularization, comprehensive studies specifically designed to evaluate its safety profile in the context of dry AMD are lacking. Given that dry AMD is a chronic condition that would likely require long‐term treatment, issues of sustained drug exposure, potential cumulative toxicity, and the risk of eliciting off‐target effects must be thoroughly investigated (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13; Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 16–17).  

Overall, nintedanib’s established preclinical and clinical data in oncology and fibrosis, combined with its potent multi-targeted inhibition of key receptor tyrosine kinases, provides a strong foundation for its consideration as a repurposed therapeutic candidate in dry AMD. The molecular rationale—that abnormal PDGFRβ and FGFR1 signaling impair the expression and function of essential phagocytic receptors in RPE cells—is both biologically plausible and supported by insights from related pathologies. The anticipated restoration of phagocytic capacity via improved expression of integrin αvβ5 and MERTK, along with enhanced cytoskeletal remodeling conducive to POS uptake, represents an attractive therapeutic mechanism that could address a central defect in dry AMD pathogenesis (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17).  

In conclusion, while the repurposing of nintedanib for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic framework and encouraging early preclinical findings, significant gaps remain that must be addressed before further clinical development is warranted. Critical next steps include:  
1. Detailed in vitro studies using differentiated human RPE cells to measure the impact of nintedanib on PDGFRβ and FGFR1 phosphorylation status, the expression levels of integrin αvβ5 and MERTK, and functional phagocytic assays assessing POS uptake.  
2. In vivo investigations in relevant animal models of dry AMD to evaluate retinal pharmacokinetics, tissue distribution, and the long-term safety profile following local ocular administration.  
3. Exploration of optimal delivery strategies to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic absorption and potential off-target effects.  
4. Further mechanistic studies to elucidate the downstream signaling pathways – including MAPK and Akt cascades – that may be modulated by nintedanib in the RPE and contribute to cytoskeletal remodeling.  

By addressing these areas, it should be possible to rigorously validate whether nintedanib can indeed “normalize” RTK signaling in the RPE and restore the phagocytic function that is compromised in dry AMD. The strengths of nintedanib lie in its potent, well-characterized kinase inhibition and its established clinical safety record in other disease indications. However, challenges remain in adapting its pharmacologic profile to the unique requirements of retinal therapy and ensuring that its broad RTK profile does not inadvertently disrupt other critical ocular functions. If these challenges can be overcome through careful preclinical and translational research, nintedanib may represent a transformative therapeutic option for addressing an unmet need in dry AMD (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 1–5, 20–22; Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13).  

Overall, our evaluation suggests that while caution must be exercised due to potential pharmacokinetic and off-target concerns, the available biochemical and clinical evidence provides sufficient justification for further investigation. The detailed molecular insights into nintedanib’s action, its demonstrated efficacy in modulating kinase pathways central to angiogenesis and fibrosis, and preliminary data in ocular models collectively support its candidacy for repurposing in dry AMD. Rigorous further studies will determine its ultimate utility, but current data indicate that nintedanib is a promising candidate worthy of additional mechanistic and translational evaluation (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12; Reck, 2015, pp. 2–3; Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Iptacopan (LNP023) is a rationally designed, low–molecular-weight small molecule that selectively inhibits complement factor B (FB), the essential catalytic subunit of the alternative pathway (AP) C3/C5 convertases C3bBb and C3bBbC3b on activating surfaces (including stressed RPE) and within the amplification loop of complement activation (C3 → C3b → C3 convertase) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 4–6). Medicinal-chemistry optimization from an early micromolar FB inhibitor hit (a naphthalene-dihydro-imidazole amine) introduced an indole to occupy the S1 pocket and a piperidine scaffold engaging the S3/non-primed region with a benzoic acid–mediated H-bond network, yielding iptacopan with high potency and selectivity for FB (crystallographically confirmed) (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 10–13; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Iptacopan binds the catalytic serine-protease active site within the Bb subunit of FB—structural analyses show its indole and piperidine moieties seated in S1/S3, forming key hydrogen bonds within the catalytic domain, with the active-site triad (His–Asp–Ser) located in proximity; binding has been explicitly mapped to the catalytic site in Bb and shown to block substrate processing by the AP convertase (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6, 8–10).

Class and precedent: Iptacopan is an oral, proximal complement/AP inhibitor; this class has delivered robust target engagement and clinical benefit in multiple complement-driven diseases (e.g., PNH, C3G, IgAN), establishing translational viability for systemic small-molecule blockade of AP amplification in human disease (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Oral administration achieves rapid systemic exposure (Tmax ≈ 2 hours) with dose-dependent AP suppression and sustained steady-state inhibition at 200 mg twice daily in clinical studies, supporting convenient outpatient dosing with on-target PD (reduced plasma Bb and urinary sC5b-9) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Preclinically, systemic iptacopan potently blocks LPS-induced AP activation in mice in both plasma and eye tissues, indicating ocular target engagement after oral dosing (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). Collectively, synthesis, mechanistic selectivity, and clinical-class performance position iptacopan as a well-characterized, orally bioavailable FB inhibitor suited for indications where local AP amplification contributes to pathology, including dry AMD (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).

Therapeutic History  
- Non-ocular indications and clinical pharmacology. In early-phase clinical studies, iptacopan demonstrated rapid absorption (peak plasma concentration at ~2 hours), favorable tolerability, and dose-dependent inhibition of AP activity; sustained maximal inhibition was reported at 200 mg twice daily, the regimen advanced into multiple phase 2 trials (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Across PNH and AP-driven renal diseases (C3G, IgAN), iptacopan showed robust target engagement and clinical activity: reductions in plasma Bb and urinary sC5b-9, reductions in plasma C3 (in many patients after months), kidney-pathology improvements (reduced glomerular C3 deposition), and meaningful efficacy outcomes (e.g., proteinuria reductions in C3G/IgAN; hemoglobin improvements and transfusion-free status in PNH) with generally favorable safety profiles and no serious infections in the cited trials (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Iptacopan has received regulatory approvals (including an accelerated approval for IgAN) and late-stage development status for multiple indications, validating systemic AP inhibition with this agent (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8).  
- AMD program. A randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial in early/intermediate AMD is ongoing (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022), designed to test whether oral iptacopan prevents conversion to iRORA or late AMD over 24 months, with masked multimodal imaging and planned plasma trough PK by LC–MS; vaccinations for encapsulated organisms are required per complement-inhibition class risk management (no results are available in the excerpt) (“A Masked, Placebo-controlled Study to Assess Iptacopan in Age-related Macular Degeneration,” 2022). Reviews place iptacopan among oral FB inhibitors under evaluation for atrophic AMD as an alternative to intravitreal complement blockade, motivated by the blood–retina barrier and the burden of injections; however, the provided material contains no AMD efficacy outcomes for iptacopan (Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 8–9; Hammadi et al., 2023, pp. 30–31; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
- Ocular-relevant preclinical context. Although iptacopan-specific dry-AMD model data are not provided, two lines of evidence are directly relevant: (1) in the Efemp1 R345W knock-in mouse (an RPE proteostasis model with AMD-like basal deposits), genetic Cfb deletion abolished AP activation and eliminated sub-RPE deposits, while oral pharmacologic FB blockade (with the small molecule DB-82-CB77) reduced deposits by 65% in females and reversed disease-associated pathway perturbations (UPR/inflammation upregulation and mitochondrial repression) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10); (2) systemic iptacopan blocks AP activation in eye tissue in LPS-challenged mice, supporting oral delivery as a viable route to ocular target engagement, though iptacopan-specific AMD-model efficacy is not shown in the provided excerpts (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Complement biology and lysosomal/autophagy pathology in RPE. In CFH Y402H high-risk iPSC-RPE, increased C3 turnover and lysosomal deposition of C5b-9 drive lysosomal swelling, membrane damage, Cathepsin D leakage to sub-RPE deposits, and reduced lysosomal function; blocking C3 with the compstatin analogue Cp40 reverses these phenotypes, restoring lysosomal number/size/function and lowering complement deposition (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13). While these data establish that proximal complement blockade can normalize lysosomal/autophagy dysfunction in high-risk RPE, the excerpts do not directly test FB/AP inhibitors in this RPE system; thus, extrapolation to iptacopan remains mechanistic rather than empirically proven in the provided sources (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 7–13).

Mechanism of Action  
- Biochemical target and binding mode. FB is an abundant plasma glycoprotein (~0.2–0.4 mg/mL; ~2–3 μM) unique to the AP and, upon binding to C3b, is cleaved by factor D into Ba and Bb; Bb contains a VWA domain, MIDAS motif, and a serine-protease domain that provides the catalytic site for AP C3/C5 convertases on C3b-bearing surfaces (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6). Iptacopan binds the catalytic site of Bb in the S1/S3 pockets with a defined hydrogen-bonding network, directly inhibiting the proteolytic activity of the AP convertase and thereby blocking AP-mediated C3/C5 processing (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- Potency, selectivity, and functional inhibition. Iptacopan exhibits an enzymatic IC₅₀ ≈ 0.01 μM against FB and inhibits AP-induced C5b-9 formation in 50% human serum with IC₅₀ ≈ 0.13 μM; it prevents C3 deposition and complement-mediated lysis of PNH erythrocytes with IC₅₀ ≈ 0.4 μM and shows high selectivity over factor D and classical/lectin pathway activity in broad panels (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Alternative affinity reporting (K_D ≈ 0.0079 mM) has been noted in one excerpt, but across structural/functional assays the compound consistently behaves as a highly potent and selective FB catalytic-site inhibitor (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 8–10).  
- Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics relevant to target engagement. Clinically, iptacopan is rapidly absorbed (Tmax ~ 2 hours), with strong steady-state AP inhibition at 200 mg twice daily; pharmacodynamic readouts demonstrate reduced circulating Bb and reduced urinary sC5b-9, consistent with systemic and tissue-level AP suppression (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). While precise human half-life and oral bioavailability values are not provided in the excerpts, iptacopan is described as orally bioavailable with a shorter half-life than antibodies, enabling relatively rapid restoration of AP function after washout—an attribute that informs adherence requirements and infection risk mitigation (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–11). Factor B itself has a long plasma half-life (30–70 h) and high abundance; iptacopan’s high affinity and mechanism allow sustained convertase inhibition because only newly synthesized FB needs to be neutralized at steady state for continued pathway blockade (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- Ocular target engagement. In mice, systemic administration of iptacopan potently blocks LPS-induced complement activation in both plasma and eye tissues, implying that oral dosing can achieve pharmacologically active exposure to ocular compartments, at least under inflammatory conditions (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). In the Efemp1 R345W model, ocular AP activation is local (iC3b and Ba ≈ 2× in eye, not in plasma), aligning with a need for ocular engagement; although iptacopan’s ocular concentration-time profile in humans is not provided, the preclinical PD findings and the AMD phase 2 trial design together support the translational intent to suppress ocular AP activity via oral dosing (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Genetic and disease-mechanism validation. FB is genetically and mechanistically implicated in AMD pathogenesis; protective low-activity variants (e.g., R32Q) associate with reduced AMD risk, and AP dysregulation is a central pathogenic thread in AMD biology (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6). In an RPE proteostasis model (Efemp1 R345W), Cfb deletion abolishes AP activation and prevents sub-RPE deposit formation; pharmacologic FB suppression reduces deposit burden and reverses multiple mutation-associated pathway perturbations (UPR, immune/complement signatures, mitochondrial repression), supporting causal linkage between AP activity and RPE/Bruch’s membrane pathology (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10).  
- Comparison to other complement nodes in AMD models. Complement C3 blockade (Cp40) in CFH Y402H high-risk iPSC-RPE rescues lysosomal structure and function, reduces C3b and C5b-9 deposition (including lysosomal MAC), and diminishes drusen-like phenotypes, demonstrating that proximal complement suppression can reverse RPE degradative defects; this provides a mechanistic bridge to AP/FB inhibition, which is expected to decrease upstream C3 turnover and downstream MAC burden by curtailing the amplification loop, though FB-specific rescue of lysosomal function was not directly tested in that study (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).

Expected Effect  
- In vitro RPE assays and readouts. Based on the AP mechanism and the CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE data with C3 inhibition, iptacopan is expected to reduce AP convertase activity on RPE surfaces, lowering C3b/iC3b deposition and MAC (C5b-9) accrual on and within RPE cells, thereby alleviating lysosomal overburden, improving lysosomal integrity, and facilitating restoration of autophagic flux (e.g., normalized LC3-II/p62 dynamics) and degradative function (e.g., Cathepsin D activity and localization) (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13). The Efemp1 model shows that AP activation is heightened locally and that Cfb deletion or FB inhibition normalizes stress/inflammation (including UPR) and mitochondrial pathways; by analogy, iptacopan should attenuate ER stress/UPR signaling and immune/complement activation signatures in RPE/eyecup proteomes, with secondary benefits for mitochondrial/energy pathways (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2). Although direct demonstration that FB inhibition restores RPE lysosomal function is not presented in the excerpted Efemp1 work, the Cp40 RPE data make a strong mechanistic case that upstream complement suppression reduces complement load on lysosomes and rescues degradative capacity; iptacopan should achieve a similar effect by preventing AP amplification and thus lowering the rate of C3 activation fragment generation and MAC formation at the RPE (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).  
- Ex vivo/animal AMD-relevant endpoints. In female Efemp1 R345W mice, oral FB inhibition (DB-82-CB77) reduced sub-RPE deposits by 65% over 8 weeks, while Cfb deletion completely eliminated deposits and abrogated AP activation in eye, indicating that AP blockade can causally modify a basal laminar–like deposit phenotype; iptacopan, as a potent oral FB inhibitor with demonstrated ocular PD in mice, would be expected to recapitulate these effects on deposits and molecular signatures, subject to dose/exposure parity and sex-dependent biology (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 9–10, 4–6). The Efemp1 eyecup proteomics further suggest that FB blockade rebalances ocular homeostasis, dampening CR3/immune-complement signaling and upstream UPR stress while partially restoring mitochondrial proteins, reinforcing the hypothesis that complement amplification contributes to proteostasis failure and that its inhibition should normalize these axes (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Clinical AMD endpoints. The ongoing phase 2 iptacopan study in AMD is designed to detect prevention of conversion to iRORA or late AMD by SD-/SS-OCT and multimodal imaging over 24 months; systemic trough PK will be monitored. If oral iptacopan meaningfully engages ocular AP in humans, we would anticipate reduced new-onset iRORA and slower disease progression relative to placebo, potentially accompanied by systemic PD markers (Bb suppression), though the trial as described does not include ocular PD sampling (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022). As precedent, intravitreal C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) reduced GA growth in phase 2; conversely, C5 inhibition had mixed results, underscoring the importance of targeting upstream amplification (C3/AP) rather than solely the terminal pathway in AMD (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 7–9). It remains to be shown whether systemic FB inhibition can reproduce these benefits without increasing CNV risk; complement inhibition broadly has been associated with higher rates of new-onset CNV in some trials, a safety signal that must be monitored in FB-targeting programs (Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic and genetic rationale. FB is the essential catalytic subunit of AP convertases, and human genetics supports a causal role of FB activity in AMD (protective low-activity variants) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6). In an RPE-driven mouse model (Efemp1 R345W), Cfb deletion abolishes ocular AP activation and eliminates sub-RPE deposits; pharmacologic FB inhibition reduces deposits and reverses disease-associated pathway dysregulation, linking AP amplification to RPE/proteostasis pathology and basal deposit accumulation (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10).  
- Demonstrated oral target engagement, including ocular PD in mice. Iptacopan is orally bioavailable with rapid absorption and consistent systemic PD (Bb and sC5b-9 suppression) in humans; preclinically, systemic iptacopan blocks AP activation in eye tissue, supporting feasibility of oral ocular target engagement (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Potency/selectivity with favorable clinical precedents. Iptacopan shows nanomolar enzymatic potency, selective FB catalytic-site binding, and clear functional AP inhibition in serum/cell assays; it has delivered convincing efficacy across multiple complement-driven indications with acceptable safety, validating the drug and target class clinically (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14).  
- Convergence with RPE lysosome/autophagy biology. In CFH Y402H high-risk iPSC-RPE, proximal complement blockade (C3 inhibitor Cp40) reverses lysosomal swelling/dysfunction and reduces complement deposition including MAC; these findings mechanistically support the hypothesis that halting AP amplification upstream will relieve lysosomal burden and restore degradative capacity in RPE, a central deficit in dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).

Risks and Gaps  
- Lack of direct iptacopan data in AMD models or RPE lysosome assays. The provided excerpts do not report iptacopan efficacy in AMD-relevant animal models (e.g., Efemp1) or direct rescue of RPE lysosomal/autophagic function; the pharmacologic proof-of-concept in Efemp1 used a different FB inhibitor (DB-82-CB77) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 9–10). Thus, the hypothesis that iptacopan will restore RPE degradative capacity is mechanistically plausible but not yet experimentally demonstrated in the cited AMD models (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 7–13).  
- Ocular PK/PD in humans unproven. The AMD phase 2 protocol measures plasma trough iptacopan but does not include ocular PD; no human ocular PK is provided in the excerpts. Translational dependence on ocular exposure is high because AP activation in Efemp1 is local to the eye (elevated Ba/iC3b in ocular tissue but not plasma) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).  
- Heterogeneity and sex effects in preclinical model. Efemp1 females exhibit ocular AP activation and respond to FB inhibition; males have lower deposits, no ocular AP upregulation, and do not respond, implying biological heterogeneity that may translate to variable clinical responses and may necessitate biomarker-based enrichment (e.g., markers of ocular AP activation) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).  
- Class safety considerations. Complement inhibition increases susceptibility to infections with encapsulated bacteria; vaccination is mandated in the AMD study. Additionally, complement inhibition in GA trials has been associated with increased new-onset CNV versus sham, a signal that must be actively monitored; whether FB inhibition carries a similar CNV liability is unknown from the provided materials (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
- Mixed history of systemic complement inhibitors in AMD. The sole completed RCT of systemic anti-C5 (eculizumab) in AMD failed to show GA benefit, raising delivery and mechanistic questions for systemic approaches, although intravitreal proximal inhibitors (C3) have shown GA-slowing, and the Efemp1 data support AP dependence for basal deposit biology (Hammadi et al., 2023, pp. 17–18; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 7–9).

Program Implications and Next Steps  
- Preclinical toolkit alignment. To directly validate the central hypothesis for iptacopan, run head-to-head studies in AMD-relevant systems:
  - Efemp1 R345W mouse: oral iptacopan dosing matched for AP PD versus DB-82-CB77 benchmark; endpoints: TEM-assessed sub-RPE deposits, ocular Ba/iC3b, eyecup/neural retina proteomics (UPR/complement/mitochondrial modules), and RPE lysosomal/autophagy markers (LAMP1, CTSD activity, LC3-II/p62 flux), stratified by sex (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 9–10, 4–6).  
  - CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE: iptacopan in complement-competent human serum conditions; readouts: C3b/C5b-9 deposition, lysosomal integrity (Lysotracker, Galectin-8), CTSD localization/activity, autophagic flux and POS phagocytosis assays; benchmark to Cp40 rescue (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).  
  - Ocular exposure/PD: quantify iptacopan in ocular compartments (choroid/retina/RPE) and measure ocular AP biomarkers in vivo after oral dosing to confirm exposure–PD matching the LPS PD signal (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Translational biomarker strategy. Incorporate systemic AP markers (Bb, Ba), exploratory ocular biomarkers (e.g., aqueous humor C3 fragments if feasible), and imaging-based deposit/ELM–Bruch’s metrics; in the clinic, deploy multimodal imaging for conversion endpoints as in Novartis Pharmaceuticals (2022), and prospectively monitor CNV incidence (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
- Patient selection. Consider enriching for patients with systemic or local evidence of AP activation (genetics such as CFH risk alleles, complement biomarker profiles) analogous to the female-biased AP activation seen in Efemp1 (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).  
- Dosing rationale and adherence. Target 200 mg twice daily based on human PD experience; given the shorter half-life vs antibodies and the need for sustained AP suppression, emphasize adherence and vaccine prophylaxis; PD sampling should verify on-target AP inhibition longitudinally (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Ricklin, 2024, pp. 7–9; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).

Bottom line. Iptacopan is a mechanistically compelling, clinically validated oral FB inhibitor with demonstrated systemic PD, rapid onset, and preclinical evidence of ocular AP engagement; rigorous AMD-model testing and clinical biomarker integration are now required to close the translational loop from AP biology to RPE lysosomal rescue and clinical protection against atrophy progression (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 8–10; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).

Detailed Assessment Relative to the Stated Hypothesis

Medicina 2024).” Clarification: The provided sources show that FB genetic deletion eliminates deposits and that an oral FB inhibitor reduces deposits and reverses pathway dysregulation in the Efemp1 mouse; rescue of lysosomal/autophagy dysfunction in CFH high-risk RPE is demonstrated with C3 inhibitor Cp40, not with an FB inhibitor in the excerpts provided (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).

Go/No-Go Considerations for Dry AMD  
- Go signals:  
  - Target validity in AMD pathobiology is strong (genetics, AP dependence of basal deposits, proximal complement benefits in RPE models) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).  
  - Drug is clinically de-risked across multiple indications with robust AP PD and acceptable safety; oral delivery is patient-friendly vs intravitreal regimens (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14).  
  - Ocular PD feasibility is supported in mice for systemic iptacopan; pharmacologic AP blockade reduces deposits in Efemp1 with another orally bioavailable FB inhibitor (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).  
- Caution flags:  
  - No iptacopan AMD-model efficacy in the provided materials; need direct RPE lysosome/autophagy rescue readouts and deposit suppression with iptacopan prior to expensive late-phase commitments (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 7–13).  
  - Macro safety signals observed with complement inhibitors in AMD (CNV incidence) necessitate vigilant monitoring and risk–benefit analyses tailored to FB inhibition (Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
  - Systemic delivery uncertainty—human ocular PK/PD data are lacking; trial design should incorporate robust systemic PD and exploratory ocular biomarkers where feasible (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).

Recommendation  
Advance iptacopan for dry AMD with a focused, staged plan:  
- Preclinical confirmation package: replicate Efemp1 findings with iptacopan (deposits, AP biomarkers, proteomics) and demonstrate RPE lysosomal/autophagy rescue in CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE under complement-competent conditions; quantify ocular exposure–PD after oral dosing (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Biomarker-enriched clinical strategy: leverage systemic AP biomarkers and imaging-based progression metrics from Novartis Pharmaceuticals (2022); consider enrichment by complement genetics/biomarkers reflecting AP activation (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).  
- Safety management: maintain vaccination requirements and active CNV surveillance; implement adherence support given the shorter half-life relative to biologics (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Ricklin, 2024, pp. 7–9; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).

On balance, iptacopan has substantial mechanistic, translational, and clinical-class support to merit continued development in dry AMD, contingent on closing the specific evidence gaps for RPE degradative rescue and direct AMD-model efficacy with this agent (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).

Below is our comprehensive evaluation of BTB06584 as a repurposed drug candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BTB06584 is described as a V‐ATPase inhibitor available commercially (e.g., Tocris Cat. No. 5208) that is purported to act by selectively targeting the V₀ subunit of the vacuolar proton pump. V‐ATPase is a large multisubunit enzyme complex consisting of a cytosolic V₁ domain (responsible for ATP hydrolysis) and a membrane‐embedded V₀ domain (which translocates protons) that together acidify intracellular compartments such as lysosomes. BTB06584 appears to belong to the class of small molecules developed to modulate lysosomal acidification and, by extension, lysosome‐dependent degradative processes. Although several classes of V‐ATPase inhibitors (for example, the plecomacrolides bafilomycin A₁ and concanamycin A, as well as benzolactone enamides and others) have been extensively characterized as experimental probes, BTB06584 is postulated to be unique in its relatively selective action on the V₀ sector. This selectivity is important because it offers the theoretical possibility of “partial” inhibition rather than the broad, complete blockade observed with classical inhibitors that are often associated with high toxicity (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7; Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 21–23). In many published studies, V‐ATPase inhibitors have served as critical biochemical tools to dissect lysosomal pH regulation and phagosome degradation, especially in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, where impaired acidification is linked to cellular dysfunction in AMD (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7). No detailed synthesis or discovery history has been provided in the existing context, but BTB06584 is assumed to be a synthetic agent designed in line with modern small‐molecule drug development paradigms targeting the V₀ domain.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, V‐ATPase inhibitors have been widely used as experimental probes to study lysosomal acidification and related cellular processes. Classical inhibitors such as bafilomycin A₁ and concanamycin A have been employed in many in vitro and in vivo studies to raise lysosomal pH, alter autophagy and phagocytosis, and to trigger apoptosis in sensitive cell types (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7). In ocular research, V‐ATPase inhibition—albeit through these broader agents—has been demonstrated to impair photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation in RPE cells, which serves as an experimental proxy for early AMD‐related pathology (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7; Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 4–6). Moreover, genetic models in zebrafish and mice further underscore the importance of proper V‐ATPase function in retinal homeostasis (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 4–6; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–5). However, to date, the literature available in our context does not report any prior clinical or preclinical use of BTB06584 specifically for treating dry AMD or for modulating lysosomal pH in RPE cells; indeed, several excerpts explicitly note that BTB06584 is not mentioned by name in the primary‐literature reports on V‐ATPase inhibitors (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 23–24; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). In other words, while the class of V‐ATPase inhibitors has been widely explored—primarily in cancer and osteoporosis research (Holliday, 2017, pp. 4–6; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11)—there is no direct record that BTB06584 has been used clinically or in animal models related to macular degeneration. This gap in the therapeutic history means that any proposed repurposing effort must contend with a virtual absence of detailed preclinical data in AMD‐relevant systems.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, V‐ATPase functions as an ATP‐driven proton pump essential for maintaining the acidic pH of endolysosomal compartments. Lysosomal enzymes, including cathepsin D, require an optimal acidic environment (typically around pH 4.5) for their catalytic function (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7). Disruption of V‐ATPase activity, whether pharmacologically by agents such as bafilomycin A₁ or via genetic manipulation (for example, loss of βA3/A1‐crystallin, which is known to modulate V‐ATPase function), leads to a rise in lysosomal pH, reduced activity of acid‐dependent proteases, and impaired degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 4–6; Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–4). In contrast to complete inhibition—which often results in a strong, detrimental rise in pH—the hypothesis for BTB06584 is that it will “partially” inhibit the V‐ATPase. The goal would be to fine‐tune the activity of the enzyme so that instead of producing a supraphysiologic pH (as with full inhibition), the lysosomal environment is restored to an optimal acidic set point (around pH 4.5) that promotes maximal cathepsin D activity and efficient POS clearance (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–5). Structural studies of V‐ATPase have shown that selective targeting of subunit isoforms, particularly those within the V₀ sector, can influence not only proton pumping but also other functions such as membrane fusion during phagosome–lysosome fusion events (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 21–23; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). If BTB06584 indeed exhibits specificity for the V₀ subunit—and perhaps even for particular isoforms expressed in RPE—it might exert a modulatory effect that differs from the broad and often toxic inhibition seen with compounds like bafilomycin A₁. However, as noted in the literature summaries, there is currently no detailed primary data regarding the binding kinetics, structural interaction, or precise molecular pharmacology of BTB06584 (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 23–24; Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 26–28). In other words, while the proposed mechanism is logically consistent with our understanding of V‐ATPase biology, it remains unsubstantiated by direct experimental evidence for this particular compound.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, RPE dysfunction is characterized, in part, by altered lysosomal pH and impaired degradation of POS, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and subsequent oxidative stress and cellular demise (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7; Valapala et al., 2014, pp. 16–17). The central hypothesis is that dysregulated V‐ATPase activity in AMD RPE leads to lysosomal pH drift—either excessive alkalinization due to inhibition by A2E or a failure to maintain optimal acidity—and that this pH imbalance impacts cathepsin D activity. Cathepsin D is optimally active at a pH of around 4.5, and even a modest deviation toward alkalinity (for example, pH 5.0) can reduce its activity by up to 80% (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–4; Shine et al., 2014, p. 7). BTB06584 is expected to “partially” inhibit V‐ATPase in a manner that normalizes lysosomal pH without “shutting off” the proton pump entirely. In RPE cells, particularly in A2E-treated ARPE-19 assays, such a fine-tuning effect could restore an optimal acidic environment, thereby reactivating cathepsin D and other hydrolases; this, in turn, would facilitate proper degradation of ingested photoreceptor outer segments and reduce the buildup of undigested material and associated autofluorescence (Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–5; Valapala et al., 2014, pp. 16–17). Importantly, the candidate’s hypothesized selective action on the V₀ subunit—if proven—aligns with evidence that manipulating particular V‐ATPase subunit isoforms can affect not only proton pumping but also membrane fusion events that are essential for proper lysosomal function (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 21–23; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7). Given that the RPE expresses specific V‐ATPase isoforms (for example, different V₀ a isoforms) and that genetic studies have linked loss of V‐ATPase activity to defects in POS degradation (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 4–6; Shine et al., 2014, p. 7), the restoration of lysosomal homeostasis through a “partial inhibitor” like BTB06584 could theoretically improve the clearance of POS. However, it must be emphasized that the expected effect of normalizing pH from a suboptimal or variable level to precisely 4.5 is a very delicate modulation – one that must be demonstrated through rigorous in vitro assays in ARPE-19 cells (or better yet, in iPSC-derived RPE models) followed by in vivo animal studies.

Overall Evaluation:  
The proposed strategy of repurposing BTB06584 for dry AMD is innovative in that it aims to address a central pathological feature—lysosomal dysfunction—by modulating, rather than completely inhibiting, the V‐ATPase. The strength of the candidate lies in its potential for selective inhibition of the V₀ subunit, which is critical given that generalized inhibition via broad-spectrum compounds (like bafilomycin A₁) has been associated with significant toxicity and dysfunction in multiple cell types (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). Furthermore, the concept of “fine-tuning” lysosomal pH to optimize cathepsin D activity is appealing because it targets the underlying mechanism that controls the degradation of POS in RPE cells—a process known to be perturbed in AMD (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7; Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–4).  

Nonetheless, there are notable weaknesses. Chief among these is the absence of direct experimental evidence supporting the efficacy of BTB06584 in RPE models or animal models of dry AMD. None of the available literature excerpts provide primary data regarding its chemical characterization, mechanism of action in retinal cells, or any preclinical studies using BTB06584 (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 23–24; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). Consequently, while the hypothesis is congruent with the general concept that selective modulation of V‐ATPase can restore lysosomal function, the candidate remains largely unvalidated in the context of ocular therapeutics. In addition, there is an inherent risk associated with modulating a central enzyme such as V-ATPase: even partial inhibition might affect other vital cellular processes, including autophagy, phagosome–lysosome fusion, and even neurotransmitter release in neural tissues (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 21–23; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). Moreover, the narrow therapeutic window required to normalize acidification (without overshooting into detrimental alkalinization) poses significant challenges; this alone necessitates careful dose-response profiling in multiple models before any clinical translation can be considered.  

Overall, while the theoretical framework supporting BTB06584 is robust in terms of targeting a mechanism that is central to RPE pathology in dry AMD, the lack of direct data leaves critical gaps. At this stage, BTB06584 represents a promising but highly speculative candidate. To advance its development, we recommend that rigorous in vitro studies (using ARPE-19 cells and iPSC-derived RPE under A2E/lipofuscin stress) be undertaken to characterize its effect on lysosomal pH, cathepsin D activity, and POS degradation. These should be complemented by mechanistic assays—such as assessments of lysosomal fusion events and measurements of autophagic flux—to fully delineate its mode of action. If favorable, subsequent in vivo studies in appropriate AMD models will be essential to evaluate efficacy and systemic toxicity.  

In summary, our overall evaluation is that while the candidate BTB06584 is conceptually attractive because it promises selective modulation of V‐ATPase activity—potentially correcting the lysosomal pH imbalance that underlies defects in POS clearance in dry AMD—the current literature does not supply direct supportive evidence for its use in retinal disease, and its safety/efficacy profile remains unproven. Further preclinical investigation is therefore necessary before considering BTB06584 as a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7; Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 23–24; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4).
