Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
FX-68 is a synthetic small‐molecule agonist developed from a chemical library (ChemBridge Cat. No. 6789012) and represents an emerging member of a class of chemokine receptor modulators that selectively target CX3CR1. This compound is designed to mimic the natural ligand, fractalkine (CX3CL1), and has been optimized for potency with an EC₅₀ of approximately 100 nM, which suggests that it is capable of activating CX3CR1 at pharmacologically achievable concentrations (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–5, 6–7). The candidate belongs to the broader category of small-molecule GPCR agonists, a class that has been successfully employed in various inflammatory and neurodegenerative indications because of their favorable oral bioavailability and capacity to cross biological barriers; such compounds have a long history in modulating immune cell behavior and attenuating aberrant inflammation (Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 2–4; Chinnery et al., 2012, pp. 7–8). In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), FX-68 is proposed to restore appropriate signaling in the CX3CL1–CX3CR1 axis—a pathway that is critically involved in the regulation of microglial migration, phagocytosis and, indirectly, the trophic support provided to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6). Its synthetic origin coupled with repurposing potential makes FX-68 an attractive candidate for conditions in which deficient microglial clearance and disrupted RPE–microglia crosstalk contribute to disease progression (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3, 4–5).

Therapeutic History:  
The link between CX3CR1 function and retinal health was established through extensive genetic and preclinical studies, in which loss-of-function mutations or deficiencies in CX3CR1 were found to produce a constellation of AMD-like features, including the accumulation of subretinal microglia, formation of drusen-like deposits, and secondary photoreceptor degeneration (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7; Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 4–5). Historically, research in this area has focused on genetic knock-out models and human polymorphism analyses rather than on the administration of direct pharmacologic agonists; for example, CX3CR1-deficient mice consistently exhibit abnormal subretinal microglial behavior and accompanying retinal pathology, which has been used as a rationale for targeting this signaling pathway therapeutically (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–6). Although exogenous delivery of CX3CL1 has been explored in certain experimental paradigms, no small-molecule CX3CR1 agonist has yet been advanced in clinical or veterinary practice for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerations (Chinnery et al., 2012, pp. 7–8; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3). Instead, the therapeutic potential in this space has largely emerged indirectly from studies that demonstrate that disrupted CX3CR1 signaling is deleterious to retinal homeostasis, thereby suggesting that its appropriate stimulation could restore normal microglial behavior (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7). As a repurposed candidate, FX-68 aims to fill this translational gap by reactivating a pathway that is both genetically implicated in AMD and mechanistically understood in other contexts of neuroinflammation (Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 2–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
The CX3CL1–CX3CR1 axis is a pivotal mediator of neuron–microglia communication in the retina and broader central nervous system, where fractalkine (CX3CL1) exists in both membrane-bound and soluble forms and interacts exclusively with CX3CR1, a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) expressed predominantly by microglia (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–5, 6–7). Under physiological conditions, tonic signaling through CX3CR1 serves to restrain microglial activation, regulate their migratory behavior, and facilitate their efficient surveillance and debris clearance functions (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6). In the diseased retina—such as in dry AMD—loss or dysfunction of CX3CR1 impairs these regulatory mechanisms, leading to chronic accumulation of lipid-laden microglia in the subretinal space, excessive phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and subsequent RPE stress and degeneration, a sequence that contributes to the formation of drusen-like deposits and ultimately to photoreceptor cell death (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3, 6–7).

FX-68 is designed as a CX3CR1 agonist that binds to and activates this receptor, mimicking the natural action of CX3CL1. Upon binding, it is expected to trigger downstream signaling cascades typical of GPCR activation, including modulation of adenylate cyclase activity and activation of MAP kinase pathways, which in turn alter cytoskeletal dynamics essential for microglial migration and phagocytosis (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–6). At a molecular level, proper CX3CR1 activation is theorized to correct the aberrant microglial behavior seen in CX3CR1 deficiency: it should promote the egression or apoptotic clearance of subretinal microglia that have phagocytosed excessive amounts of POS debris and prevent their transformation into foam cells laden with intracellular lipids (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7; Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4). Moreover, by reestablishing a functional microglia–RPE communication axis, FX-68 may help restore the RPE’s inherent phagocytic capacity to clear POS effectively, ultimately leading to improved outer retinal homeostasis (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). With CX3CR1 activation, signaling may also suppress the production of proangiogenic factors such as VEGF, thereby limiting pathological neovascularization—a secondary complication sometimes observed in the context of AMD (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). This mechanism is further supported by studies in which exogenous CX3CL1 reduced microglial phagocytosis and inflammatory activation in models of retinal degeneration, albeit in genetic loss-of-function contexts rather than using a pharmacologic agonist (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Zabel et al., 2016, pp. 10–12). The overall molecular interaction profile of FX-68, therefore, hinges on reinstating the anti-inflammatory, pro-homeostatic functions of CX3CR1 in retinal microglia, with the intended effect of reducing deleterious phagocytosis and enhancing trophic support for the RPE (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assays and in preclinical models—particularly in the challenging Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mouse model, which recapitulates many aspects of dry AMD—the expected effect of FX-68 is multifaceted. First, by binding and activating CX3CR1 on retinal microglia, FX-68 is anticipated to restore regulated cell migration and proper phagocytic clearance, thereby reducing the abnormal accumulation of subretinal microglia that is observed in CX3CR1-deficient models (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). Such restoration is expected to lead to a normalization of the phagocytic process, where instead of over-ingesting POS debris and becoming lipid-laden foam cells, microglia will clear debris efficiently and then either return to a surveillant state or undergo timely apoptosis or emigration away from the subretinal space (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6).

Second, FX-68 is proposed to facilitate enhanced trophic support for RPE cells. Evidence suggests that proper microglial signaling is critically involved in modulating RPE phagocytosis of POS, partly through the secretion of growth factors and early inflammatory mediators that prime RPE cells for efficient clearance functions (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). In co-culture assays involving microglia and RPE cells, treatment with FX-68 is expected to lead to an increase in the efficiency of POS turnover, as microglial activation is reined in and redirected toward beneficial debris clearance rather than deleterious inflammatory activation (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). This effect, in theory, would reduce the buildup of toxic debris in the subretinal region, limit the formation of drusen-like deposits and diminish secondary inflammatory and proangiogenic signaling, such as excessive VEGF release, that further compromise retinal integrity (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3; Rashid et al., 2019, p. 14).

Moreover, in animal models like the Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mice—where the dual deficiency exacerbates retinal degeneration and drusen-like pathology—FX-68 is expected to mitigate these phenotypes by reactivating the CX3CR1 pathway. The hypothesis posits that restoration of CX3CR1 signaling will not only lower subretinal microglial accumulation but also re-establish a crosstalk with the RPE that is essential for maintaining the delicate balance between debris clearance and inflammation (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). In this way, the compound may indirectly improve photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance, thereby preserving overall photoreceptor function and slowing the progression of dry AMD (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6; Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4).

An important aspect of the expected effect is the modulation of microglial cytokine production. CX3CR1 signaling has been linked to the suppression of proinflammatory pathways—in particular, the reduction of IL-1β and VEGF expression, which are key mediators of chronic inflammation and pathological angiogenesis (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). FX-68, by serving as a CX3CR1 agonist, would clarify whether the attenuation of these proinflammatory signals could indeed translate to structural and functional retinal preservation in vivo. This result would be highly significant given that chronic inflammation is a critical driver of dry AMD progression (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3; Rashid et al., 2019, p. 14).

Furthermore, the expected effect extends to the normalization of microglial morphology and dispersal. In healthy retinas, microglia are characterized by a ramified morphology that is conducive to efficient surveillance, whereas in CX3CR1-deficient retinas, microglia become amoeboid, exhibit excessive adhesion, and accumulate in the subretinal space (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). FX-68 is anticipated to promote a return to the ramified, homeostatic phenotype, thereby reducing the deleterious impact of microglial hyperactivation and aberrant phagocytosis on both photoreceptors and RPE cells (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6). Altogether, these expected effects form the basis of the hypothesis that FX-68 may improve outer retinal homeostasis by enhancing POS turnover and supporting the RPE via finely tuned microglial regulation (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7; Rashid et al., 2019, p. 14).

The overall evaluation of FX-68 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD must balance a compelling mechanistic rationale against significant preclinical gaps and potential safety concerns. On the one hand, there is robust and convergent evidence from genetic and experimental studies that impaired CX3CR1 signaling leads to pathological subretinal microglial accumulation, excessive phagocytosis of photoreceptor debris, and subsequent RPE and photoreceptor damage—as seen in various mouse models and human genetic association studies (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7; Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 4–5; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–5). This evidence strongly supports the notion that reactivating CX3CR1 signaling could normalize microglial behavior, improve debris clearance, limit drusen formation, and ultimately slow the progression of retinal degeneration (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6).

A key strength of FX-68 is its small-molecule nature, which provides advantages in terms of potential administration routes (oral or topical), manufacturability, and the possibility for fine-tuning its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties. With an EC₅₀ of approximately 100 nM, FX-68 appears to be a potent agonist, meaning that it could achieve therapeutic concentrations without off-target effects if the dosing regimen is carefully optimized (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). Furthermore, the therapeutic strategy targeting CX3CR1 is innovative because it leverages an endogenous regulatory pathway known to modulate microglial behavior—a cell type that is increasingly recognized as playing a central role in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3).

However, there are several weaknesses and uncertainties that must be addressed before this candidate can be confidently advanced. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Trichostatin A (TSA) is a naturally occurring compound originally isolated from fermentation cultures of Streptomyces species (Grayson et al., 2010). Belonging to the hydroxamate class of histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors, TSA possesses a distinct molecular architecture characterized by three critical structural motifs: a hydroxamic acid moiety, a hydrophobic linker, and a bulky polar cap. These elements cooperate to enable TSA’s high‐affinity binding to the zinc ion within the catalytic site of HDAC enzymes, thereby blocking deacetylation reactions (Grayson et al., 2010). Unlike many newer synthetic compounds, TSA’s discovery dates back several decades, where it was initially identified for its antifungal properties yet quickly found utility as a potent epigenetic modulator in various research fields, including oncology and neurobiology (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). Within this class, HDAC inhibitors are well recognized for their ability to alter chromatin configuration; by preventing the removal of acetyl groups from histone tails, these compounds induce chromatin relaxation and, as a consequence, facilitate robust transcriptional activation of genes that are otherwise epigenetically repressed (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In the context of ocular research, TSA has been exploited primarily as a tool compound to dissect the role of epigenetic modifications in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function and has been applied in studies examining angiogenesis, apoptosis, and inflammatory responses in RPE cells (Hamid et al., 2021). Its availability from commercial suppliers such as Sigma-Aldrich (Cat. No. T1952) underscores its utility as a research-grade standard for HDAC inhibition studies, making it an attractive candidate for drug repurposing efforts aimed at diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where impaired transcription of clearance and autophagy genes plays a pivotal role (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
TSA has garnered extensive attention over the years in the biomedical literature due to its potent HDAC inhibitory function. Originally explored for its antifungal properties, subsequent studies rapidly shifted focus toward its ability to cause histone hyperacetylation, thereby rekindling interest in epigenetic regulation as a therapeutic strategy for various pathologies (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In oncology, for instance, TSA and its synthetic derivatives have been used to induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in cancer cells, ultimately leading to the development of newer, more selective HDAC inhibitors that have reached clinical trials and even regulatory approval for certain hematological malignancies (Grayson et al., 2010). In ocular research, TSA has been employed in experimental models involving retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, such as ARPE-19, where its application has led to notable changes in the transcription of genes involved in inflammation, angiogenesis, and cellular stress responses (Hamid et al., 2021). Although TSA itself has not been approved for clinical use in any ocular disease, its ability to modify gene expression through HDAC inhibition has provided valuable insights into potential interventions for retinal degenerative conditions, including both wet and dry forms of AMD (Hamid et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025). Moreover, preliminary safety studies—such as those performed using topical formulations in animal models for corneal wound healing—have demonstrated that TSA can be applied at low nanomolar concentrations with minimal cytotoxicity, suggesting that careful dose titration could allow its repurposing for RPE-targeted therapies without incurring the severe systemic toxicities observed in some cancer studies (Sharma et al., 2009). However, it is important to note that despite the promising preclinical data in ARPE-19 cells and related ocular models, there remains a significant gap in clinical evidence directly linking TSA treatment with efficacy in dry AMD, meaning that its repurposing for this indication remains experimental and largely hypothesis-driven at this stage (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Hamid et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, TSA is known to inhibit histone deacetylases by binding to the zinc ion in the enzyme’s catalytic pocket, thereby preventing the removal of acetyl groups from lysine residues on histone tails (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In normal physiological conditions, HDACs contribute to the formation of tightly packed chromatin by deacetylating histones, which leads to decreased transcriptional activity at specific gene promoters. TSA’s ability to inhibit this process results in a “relaxed” chromatin structure that is more accessible to transcription factors, leading to enhanced gene expression (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In the context of the RPE, several genes critical for autophagic flux and phagocytic function—such as lysosomal‐associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) and the receptor tyrosine kinase MERTK—are thought to be epigenetically regulated and may be transcriptionally upregulated upon HDAC inhibition (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Importantly, the transcription factor EB (TFEB) is recognized as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy, controlling the expression of a suite of genes organized within the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network (Falcão et al., 2025). In RPE cells, where efficient degradation of phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (POS) is dependent on both lysosomal function and autophagy, the upregulation of TFEB through enhanced chromatin accessibility could theoretically result in improved expression of LAMP1 and, by extension, better phagocytic capacity via receptors such as MERTK (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Moreover, TSA’s inhibition of HDACs also affects non-histone substrates; for example, it increases the acetylation of α-tubulin—a modification that can influence microtubule dynamics and vesicular transport processes (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). However, this action comes with a potential caveat: excessive tubulin acetylation has been reported to impair autophagosome trafficking, which is a critical step in the autophagic clearance pathway (Toops et al., 2015; Tan, 2018). Therefore, while TSA’s global HDAC inhibition can promote the transcription of genes essential for lysosomal biogenesis and POS degradation, careful titration of its concentration is necessary to ensure that the beneficial effects on gene transcription do not get overshadowed by disruptions in cytoskeletal dynamics and autophagosome motility (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). At the same time, TSA has been shown in some studies to downregulate pro-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic mediators such as HIF-1α and IL-1β while upregulating factors like IL-18, which may contribute additional neuroprotective benefits to the RPE (Hamid et al., 2021). Together, these multifaceted actions underline TSA’s potential to reprogram the epigenetic landscape of RPE cells, theoretically reinstating the expression of key genes involved in autophagic and phagocytic function (Boya et al., 2023; Hamid et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the working hypothesis, the expected effect of TSA in RPE cells is twofold. First, by inhibiting HDAC activity, TSA is anticipated to elevate overall chromatin accessibility, thereby stimulating the transcription of genes that are vital for proper lysosomal biogenesis and phagocytosis. In particular, the upregulation of LAMP1, a well-established marker of lysosomal membranes, should lead to an increase in the number and activity of lysosomes. Simultaneously, enhanced expression of MERTK, which plays a central role in mediating the binding and internalization of POS, should result in an improved phagocytic rate of these essential outer segment components (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE cells, where the daily burden of POS phagocytosis is critical for maintaining retinal integrity, such enhancements could potentially mitigate the accumulation of undigested cellular debris—a phenomenon that is closely linked with the progression of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Tan, 2018). Second, TSA is expected to promote the activation and nuclear translocation of TFEB. This transcription factor is normally sequestered in the cytoplasm when phosphorylated by mTORC1, but under conditions of stress or when mTORC1 activity is reduced, TFEB enters the nucleus and drives the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function and autophagy (Falcão et al., 2025). By facilitating an HDAC inhibition–mediated de-repression of the genes governing TFEB activity, TSA may help drive a feed-forward loop that enhances the cellular capacity for lysosomal degradation and autophagy. Given that RPE cells exhibit compromised autophagy and deteriorating lysosomal function in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the net effect of TSA treatment should be an improvement in POS uptake and degradation, leading to better clearance of lipofuscin and other deleterious cellular debris (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025). Furthermore, some studies using ARPE-19 cells have reported TSA-induced changes in the expression of other oxidative stress and inflammatory markers—for example, a decrease in HIF-1α expression and a corresponding increase in antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and GPX3 (Hamid et al., 2021)—which may contribute to an overall protective environment that diminishes the progressive degeneration of RPE cells. The expected cascade of molecular events—from HDAC inhibition through increased histone acetylation, enhanced transcription of TFEB, LAMP1, and MERTK, to improved lysosomal biogenesis and phagocytic function—forms the basis of the therapeutic rationale for repurposing TSA in the context of dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
Evaluating TSA as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD requires an in-depth analysis of both its promising attributes and its inherent limitations. One of the primary strengths of TSA lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action. As a proven, potent pan-HDAC inhibitor, TSA can recast the epigenetic landscape of RPE cells by enforcing hyperacetylation of histone proteins and upregulating transcription of ordinarily silenced genes (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). Considering that dry AMD is marked by severe dysfunction in protein clearance, lysosomal degradation, and autophagic flux, TSA’s capacity to activate TFEB—the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis—and to potentially enhance the expression of key phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and lysosomal markers like LAMP1 offers a compelling pharmacological strategy to restore cellular homeostasis (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). The cascading effect of promoting both lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy could improve the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), thereby mitigating the accumulation of toxic by-products like lipofuscin that contribute significantly to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Tan, 2018).

Furthermore, TSA’s history as a research compound in various cell culture models, including ARPE-19, provides a solid preclinical foundation for its repurposing. Studies have demonstrated that TSA can modulate the expression of inflammatory and apoptotic markers, reduce oxidative stress, and, importantly, alter the expression of genes that control cellular clearance pathways (Hamid et al., 2021). These data support the hypothesis that TSA might improve RPE function, a critical factor given that RPE degeneration is a driving force behind AMD progression. Preliminary ocular safety assessments, particularly in corneal models, indicate that TSA can be administered topically at carefully controlled low doses without significant toxicity (Sharma et al., 2009). Such findings are encouraging in light of the longstanding challenges associated with delivering effective therapeutics to the posterior segment of the eye; however, it must be emphasized that safety profiles established in corneal applications may not fully translate to the intricate microenvironment of the retina and RPE (Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

On the other hand, several weaknesses temper the enthusiasm for TSA as a repurposed treatment for dry AMD. Foremost among these is its broad-spectrum activity; as a pan-HDAC inhibitor, TSA does not differentiate between enzyme isoforms. This lack of selectivity raises the possibility of off-target effects that could disrupt not only histone modifications but also the acetylation status of numerous non-histone proteins, including α-tubulin (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In RPE cells, proper microtubule dynamics are essential for the trafficking of autophagosomes to lysosomes. Excessive tubulin acetylation—an effect that is purportedly enhanced by agents such as TSA, and observed in conditions mimicked by lipofuscin bisretinoids—can impede autophagosome mobility, potentially undermining the very autophagic flux that TSA is intended to improve (Toops et al., 2015; Tan, 2018; Toops et al., 2015). This paradoxical effect suggests that while increasing transcription of lysosomal genes is beneficial, alterations in cytoskeletal regulation might counteract these benefits if not precisely calibrated.

Another concern arises from the conflicting roles of HDAC activity in the context of AMD. Some studies have observed that specific HDAC activities, such as those mediated by HDAC3, are already reduced in the RPE of AMD patients (Chatterjee et al., 2024; Hamid et al., 2021). This raises the possibility that further inhibition of these enzymes might exacerbate a preexisting imbalance rather than re-establish homeostasis. In other words, if the pathological state of AMD is associated with diminished HDAC activity, then TSA’s further suppression could potentially lead to unintended and deleterious transcriptional changes that might compromise cell survival (Chatterjee et al., 2024; Hamid et al., 2021).

Moreover, despite encouraging in vitro data, there remains a paucity of information regarding TSA’s effects on the specific gene targets central to the proposed mechanism—namely, the upregulation of phagocytic receptors like MERTK and lysosomal membrane proteins such as LAMP1. While the rationale is built upon sound principles of epigenetic regulation and the critical role these proteins play in ensuring efficient POS uptake and degradation (Boya et al., 2023), direct evidence linking TSA treatment to enhanced expression of these markers in RPE cells is yet to be conclusively demonstrated. This gap in the literature makes it difficult to fully endorse TSA as having the predicted beneficial impact on RPE phagocytic function and lysosomal biogenesis without further, targeted investigations (Tan, 2018; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

In addressing the translational potential of TSA, one must also consider its pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiles. Although ocular studies—particularly those focusing on corneal wound healing—have suggested that TSA is safe at low nanomolar concentrations (Sharma et al., 2009), its use in chronic conditions such as dry AMD would likely require long-term administration. The potential cumulative toxicity of TSA, given its broad activity and historical association with off-target effects in other tissues, remains a serious concern. The challenge will be to reconcile the need for sufficient HDAC inhibition to achieve therapeutic upregulation of autophagic and phagocytic genes with the imperative to minimize adverse side effects that could compromise either the safety or the efficacy of the treatment (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021).

Overall, TSA is a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its robust epigenetic modulatory effects, which align well with the therapeutic goal of enhancing lysosomal biogenesis and phagocytic clearance in RPE cells. Its ability to interfere with HDAC activity has been demonstrated to affect not only histone acetylation but also the transcription of genes involved in cellular stress responses and degradation pathways. In theory, such modifications could reverse or mitigate several of the pathological features of dry AMD, including the accumulation of undigested POS and subsequent lipofuscin buildup that drive RPE degeneration (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). The elevation of TFEB, a master regulator of lysosomal gene expression, through TSA-mediated chromatin relaxation offers a particularly attractive avenue for restoring the autophagy-lysosome machinery, thereby enhancing both cellular clearance and the overall health of RPE cells (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Nonetheless, the candidate’s broad-spectrum nature and potential to disrupt processes such as microtubule dynamics present significant challenges. The risk of impaired autophagosome trafficking due to aberrant tubulin acetylation (Toops et al., 2015; Tan, 2018) must be weighed against the expected benefits of improved lysosomal function. Moreover, the heterogeneity of HDAC activity in AMD pathology—with some reports indicating already compromised HDAC function in diseased RPE—complicates the prospect of using a pan-HDAC inhibitor without a carefully defined therapeutic window (Chatterjee et al., 2024; Hamid et al., 2021). The absence of definitive data linking TSA treatment to increased expression of MERTK and LAMP1 in RPE cells further underscores the need for additional research to validate the proposed mechanism of action (Tan, 2018; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

In light of these considerations, our evaluation supports the continued exploratory investigation of TSA as a repurposed intervention for dry AMD, with the understanding that several critical questions remain unanswered. Future studies should aim to:  
1. Directly measure the impact of TSA on the expression levels of key phagocytic and lysosomal genes, such as MERTK and LAMP1, in RPE cells using both transcriptional and protein-level assays.  
2. Delineate the dose-response relationship in RPE cells to identify concentrations that achieve optimal activation of the CLEAR network and TFEB-mediated transcription without inducing detrimental levels of tubulin acetylation that could impede autophagosome mobility.  
3. Assess the long-term safety and pharmacokinetics of TSA in ocular tissues, particularly in animal models of dry AMD, to determine whether its beneficial effects on autophagy and phagocytosis can be sustained without incurring off-target toxicity or systemic side effects.  
4. Explore the possibility of developing more selective HDAC inhibitors or targeted delivery systems that concentrate TSA’s effects specifically within the RPE, thereby minimizing the risks associated with its broad-spectrum activity.

Ultimately, while TSA’s established role as an epigenetic modulator makes it an attractive candidate for addressing the underlying cellular dysfunction in dry AMD, careful balancing of its beneficial transcriptional effects against its potential to disrupt critical cellular processes is essential. The data reviewed herein provide a strong mechanistic rationale for TSA’s utility, yet underscore the necessity for rigorously designed preclinical studies to confirm its efficacy and safety in the context of retinal degeneration (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021; Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Divanillin is a naturally occurring oxidative dimer of vanillin that belongs to the class of phenolic dimers. Its synthesis is based on the oxidative coupling of monomeric vanillin—a well‐known flavor and fragrance molecule—using either chemical oxidants or, more efficiently, enzymatic methods. For instance, studies have demonstrated that fungal laccases, in particular, those derived from white-rot fungi such as Funalia trogii, can oxidize vanillin to form divanillin with near-quantitative yields under controlled reaction conditions (Esparan, 2015; Tai et al., 2011). Historically, divanillin was first noted for its presence in cured vanilla beans and has subsequently been developed for applications in the flavor and fragrance industries owing to its potent taste-enhancing properties, including its well-documented bitterness masking effects and its very low sensory threshold (Esparan, 2015; Krings et al., 2015; Torres-Zamudio et al., 2025). Its chemical profile, with lower water solubility compared to vanillin, also sets it apart as a candidate in formulations where controlled bioavailability is desired. As a low-molecular-weight compound, divanillin is amenable to formulation for ocular applications, and its repurposing as a modulator of intracellular signaling pathways, specifically in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), is a novel extension of its traditional roles.  

Therapeutic History:  
Divanillin’s historical usage has been largely in the realm of food and cosmetic applications. It has been known since the late 19th century and has been subject to extensive chemical characterization and synthesis studies through the early to mid-20th century (Esparan, 2015; Krings et al., 2015). In these fields, it is typically employed as a taste enhancer and bitterness masking agent, with its generation via enzymatic oxidation contributing to its characterization as a stable, bioactive phenolic dimer (Esparan, 2015; Torres-Zamudio et al., 2025). Over the years, the antioxidant properties of vanillin and its derivatives have been a major focus, with research demonstrating that multi-vanillin moieties can yield compounds with dramatically enhanced antioxidant activity compared to vanillin alone (Scipioni et al., 2018). Although these studies have primarily concentrated on neuroprotection, DNA damage protection, and cellular antioxidant capacities—such as those observed in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells—the literature does not currently report any direct clinical or preclinical application of divanillin for retinal diseases, including dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Scipioni et al., 2018; Tai et al., 2011). In parallel, a number of small-molecule SIRT1 activators, such as resveratrol and other natural polyphenols, have been explored in various ocular models and have shown promise in protecting RPE cells from oxidative damage and in modulating inflammatory pathways (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Ishida et al., 2017; Taurone et al., 2022). Thus, while divanillin itself has not been previously used for treating dry AMD or similar retinal conditions, its structural relationship to vanillin combined with emerging evidence regarding the benefits of vanillin derivatives suggests that repurposing divanillin for ocular use is a feasible and promising strategy.

Mechanism of Action:  
The central hypothesis proposed for divanillin is that it can function as a small molecule activator of SIRT1 in retinal pigment epithelial cells by achieving an effective concentration (EC₅₀) of approximately 1 µM. SIRT1 is a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)-dependent deacetylase that has critical roles in cellular metabolism, stress responses, and longevity. One of its well-established functions is the deacetylation of key cytoskeletal regulatory proteins, including cortactin and cofilin, which govern actin assembly and remodeling (Shentu et al., 2016). Cortactin, for instance, is a scaffold protein that binds to filamentous actin (F-actin) and the Arp2/3 complex and is involved in the formation of cell protrusions and phagocytic cups, whereas cofilin facilitates actin filament severing and turnover. In endothelial cells, it has been shown that AMPK phosphorylates cortactin at a critical threonine residue, priming it for SIRT1-mediated deacetylation; this sequential modification is essential for cortactin’s proper localization at the cell periphery and for dynamic actin remodeling (Shentu et al., 2016). Although this mechanism has been elucidated mainly in endothelial and other cell types, it is highly plausible that a similar pathway operates in RPE cells, where robust cytoskeletal dynamics are needed to support the daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Tarau et al., 2019; Cabrera, 2018).  

In RPE cells, phagocytosis is not a mere housekeeping task but a highly regulated process that demands rapid and targeted rearrangement of the actin cytoskeleton to form phagocytic cups that engulf the shed POS. Emerging studies have demonstrated that oxidative stress—a feature central to dry AMD pathology—can cause significant disruptions in the actin cytoskeleton, which contribute to impaired POS uptake and cellular degeneration (Tarau et al., 2019). SIRT1 activation, by deacetylating substrates such as cortactin and possibly cofilin, may restore or enhance the dynamic assembly of F-actin, thereby promoting more efficient phagocytic cup formation and POS internalization. In parallel, activation of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis in RPE cells has been linked with improved mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant responses, offering a dual mode of cytoprotection—a mechanism that is particularly attractive in the context of chronic oxidative stress typical of dry AMD (Ishida et al., 2017; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Furthermore, other small-molecule SIRT1 activators have already demonstrated the capacity to modulate oxidative stress and confer cellular protection in ocular models (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Taurone et al., 2022), lending additional credence to the hypothesis that divanillin may exert similar beneficial effects. In summary, the proposed mechanism of action for divanillin involves its SIRT1 activation properties leading to enhanced deacetylation of cytoskeletal regulatory proteins, which in turn promotes actin reorganization necessary for efficient phagocytosis by RPE cells under conditions of oxidative stress.

Expected Effect:  
Under the experimental conditions outlined in the proposal, treatment of RPE cells with divanillin at concentrations around its EC₅₀ of 1 µM is expected to result in the activation of SIRT1, a response that could be measured using biochemical assays indicative of its deacetylase activity. This SIRT1 activation is anticipated to lead to the deacetylation of its substrates, notably cortactin and cofilin, which are critical to the regulation of F-actin polymerization and reorganization (Shentu et al., 2016). At the molecular level, enhanced deacetylation of cortactin should facilitate its translocation to the cell periphery, where it can interact more effectively with the actin cytoskeleton, thereby promoting the formation of phagocytic cups, structures that are essential for the ingestion of POS (Tarau et al., 2019; Cabrera, 2018). The resulting improvement in cytoskeletal dynamics is projected to augment the ability of RPE cells to internalize shed photoreceptor outer segments—a process that is compromised in dry AMD due to cumulative oxidative damage and cytoskeletal disruption (Scipioni et al., 2018; Tarau et al., 2019).

Furthermore, activation of SIRT1 is expected to simultaneously confer additional cytoprotective benefits, including the enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis and function through the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis. This effect is highly relevant in RPE cells because their high metabolic demand and constant exposure to oxidative stress make them particularly vulnerable to mitochondrial dysfunction (Ishida et al., 2017; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). The improved mitochondrial function coupled with enhanced phagocytic efficiency would likely reduce the accumulation of oxidative damage and cellular debris, thereby mitigating key pathological features of dry AMD. Based on analogous studies employing other SIRT1 activators—such as resveratrol, which has been shown to protect RPE cells from oxidative stress and improve their phagocytic capability—the anticipated outcomes with divanillin include a measurable increase in POS uptake and improved cellular resilience under stress conditions (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Taurone et al., 2022). Consequently, these translational effects would be expected to translate into overall improved cellular homeostasis and a potential retardation of the degenerative processes observed in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
In assessing divanillin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several compelling strengths emerge. First and foremost, divanillin is a small-molecule agent that can be synthesized via well-established enzymatic processes from vanillin, a compound with a long history of safe use in food and cosmetic applications (Esparan, 2015). This favorable tolerability profile, combined with its robust antioxidant properties, provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in the ocular setting. The preclinical literature on vanillin derivatives indicates that incorporating multiple vanillin moieties into a single molecule can lead to a dramatic increase in antioxidant and cytoprotective activities (Scipioni et al., 2018), suggesting that divanillin may confer similar benefits in the context of retinal degeneration.  

Moreover, the innovative hypothesis that divanillin can activate SIRT1 in RPE cells is supported by a broader body of work demonstrating that SIRT1 plays a critical role in modulating oxidative stress, mitochondrial biogenesis, and cytoskeletal dynamics. There is substantial literature illustrating that SIRT1 activation leads to the deacetylation of key regulatory proteins such as cortactin, thereby promoting actin cytoskeleton remodeling—a process essential for phagocytic cup formation and efficient photoreceptor outer segment internalization (Shentu et al., 2016; Tarau et al., 2019). In this regard, targeting the SIRT1 pathway is a sound strategy, given that other natural SIRT1 activators, including resveratrol, have exhibited beneficial effects in RPE models under oxidative stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Taurone et al., 2022). This dual action—not only providing antioxidant protection but also enhancing the structural functionality of RPE cells—addresses two critical components of dry AMD pathogenesis: oxidative damage and impaired phagocytosis.

Despite these promising attributes, several weaknesses and uncertainties remain. Foremost among these is the lack of direct experimental evidence linking divanillin with SIRT1 activation in RPE cells. The proposed effective concentration (EC₅₀ ~ 1 µM) is based on extrapolations from studies with other vanillin derivatives and SIRT1 activators; however, no published data currently validate this specific potency for divanillin in ocular cells. In addition, while the mechanism by which SIRT1 deacetylates cortactin and potentially cofilin is well established in endothelial cells and other models (Shentu et al., 2016), it remains an assumption that RPE cells will respond identically, given their unique metabolic demands and specialized phagocytic functions (Tarau et al., 2019; Cabrera, 2018).  

There is also a significant gap concerning the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of divanillin in the context of ocular delivery. Although its small-molecule status and prior applications in non-ocular formulations suggest that it may have acceptable ocular tolerability and penetration, dedicated studies in retinal models or in vivo eye preparations are necessary to confirm its bioavailability and efficacy at the site of action. Furthermore, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD—with contributions from chronic inflammation, complement system dysregulation, and extracellular deposit formation—means that targeting SIRT1 and cytoskeletal dynamics may represent only one aspect of a comprehensive therapeutic approach (Crooke et al., 2017; Taurone et al., 2022). It will be important to consider whether divanillin’s purported mechanism can effectively address these other pathogenic mechanisms either alone or in combination with other treatments.

Another limitation is that, while divanillin’s antioxidant and cytoprotective properties have been indirectly demonstrated in studies examining vanillin and its derivatives (Scipioni et al., 2018; Tai et al., 2011), the direct link between these properties and improved phagocytic performance in RPE cells is yet to be established. Given that RPE phagocytosis is a highly specialized function that relies on precise spatial and temporal coordination of cytoskeletal activity (Tarau et al., 2019; Cabrera, 2018), even modest discrepancies in the modulation of actin dynamics could have substantial downstream effects on cellular homeostasis.  

Taken together, the overall evaluation of divanillin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. On the strength side, divanillin’s natural origin, ease of synthesis, and demonstrated antioxidant activity support its potential repurposing as a SIRT1 activator in the RPE. Its ability to modulate SIRT1—if validated experimentally—could translate into improved deacetylation of cytoskeletal regulatory proteins, enhanced F-actin remodeling, and more efficient phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments. These effects, in turn, could mitigate key aspects of dry AMD pathology, including the accumulation of oxidative damage and the gradual loss of RPE function. Such a dual mechanism of action—combining antioxidant protection with improved cellular architecture—is particularly attractive given the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD (Scipioni et al., 2018; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Shentu et al., 2016).  

However, the proposal is not without its challenges. The absence of direct evidence for divanillin’s SIRT1 activation in RPE cells, an unvalidated EC₅₀, and potential differences in the response of RPE cells compared to other cell types mean that significant preclinical work remains to be done. Rigorous in vitro studies using primary RPE cultures or established RPE cell lines will be necessary to confirm that divanillin can indeed enhance SIRT1 activity, deacetylate key substrates like cortactin and cofilin, and ultimately improve phagocytic cup formation and POS uptake. Additionally, in vivo studies using animal models of dry AMD will be critical to evaluate the compound’s pharmacokinetics, ocular bioavailability, and long-term safety and efficacy.  

In conclusion, divanillin represents a promising novel candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its potential to activate SIRT1 and thereby enhance actin cytoskeleton remodeling and phagocytosis addresses two critical pathological aspects of dry AMD—oxidative stress and impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments. Nonetheless, the current body of literature provides only indirect support for this mechanism, and several key areas require further investigation. If subsequent experimental studies confirm the proposed SIRT1 activation and cytoskeletal effects in RPE cells, divanillin could emerge as a valuable addition to the therapeutic arsenal against dry AMD, either as a monotherapy or as part of a combinatory treatment regimen. This candidate, therefore, warrants immediate prioritization in preclinical screening assays with a focus on verifying its molecular mechanism, efficacy in enhancing phagocytosis, and its overall impact on RPE cell function under oxidative stress conditions (Scipioni et al., 2018; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Shentu et al., 2016; Cabrera, 2018; Ishida et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Cerulenin is a natural product originally isolated from the filamentous fungus Cephalosporium caerulens and was the first discovered fatty acid synthase (FAS) inhibitor (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; López & Diéguez, 2007). Chemically, this compound is classified as an epoxy-keto fatty acid analogue; it contains a reactive epoxide ring conjugated to a diene/amidic structure that mimics fatty acid substrates. This reactive epoxide is key to its mechanism because it enables cerulenin to irreversibly bind to its target enzyme via covalent modification. As such, cerulenin belongs to the class of FAS inhibitors that historically have been used as biochemical probes to investigate lipid metabolism and, subsequently, as lead compounds in the development of antineoplastic agents, given the upregulation of de novo lipogenesis in many cancers (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; López & Diéguez, 2007; Abramson, 2011). The molecule’s natural origin, combined with its potent inhibitory activity, has made it a valuable tool in studies of metabolic regulation and lipogenesis over several decades.

Therapeutic History:  
In the past, cerulenin was primarily developed and investigated as an antimicrobial and antifungal antibiotic due to its capacity to irreversibly inhibit fatty acid synthesis in both bacterial and eukaryotic systems (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Subsequent research in the fields of oncology and metabolic regulation revealed that several tumor types exhibit elevated expression of FAS, making FAS inhibitors promising candidates for anticancer therapy. Preclinical studies demonstrated that cerulenin could induce apoptosis in tumor cells, delay disease progression in xenograft models, and even affect systemic metabolic parameters such as food intake and body weight in rodent models (López & Diéguez, 2007; Heath, White, & Rock, 2002; Goodman & McFadden, 2007). Despite these promising results, its clinical utility has been constrained by poor chemical stability—primarily due to its reactive epoxide moiety—and significant toxicity stemming from irreversibility and off-target interactions with other cysteine-containing proteins (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Furthermore, while modifications have led to second-generation analogues like C75, designed to improve stability and selectivity, there are no records of cerulenin being specifically applied to ophthalmologic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal lipotoxicity diseases (Menendez & Lupu, 2017; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999). At the molecular level, cerulenin exerts its biological effects by targeting the fatty acid synthase complex. Its mechanism involves the formation of an irreversible covalent adduct with an active-site cysteine residue (specifically, Cys1305) within the ketosynthase (KS) domain of type I FAS. This is achieved by an epoxide ring-opening reaction at the C-2 position of cerulenin, leading to the nucleophilic attack by the thiol (-SH) group of the catalytic cysteine residue (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008). This dual mechanism—targeting both de novo fatty acid synthesis and protein acylation—underscores the broad-spectrum bioactivity of cerulenin and its potential impact on multiple cellular pathways that are dysregulated in disease states (Menendez & Lupu, 2017; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999).

Thus, within the proposed assay—where RPE cells are subjected to oxidative stress that mimics the environment of dry AMD—cerulenin is anticipated to lower intracellular lipid levels, minimize the generation of lipofuscin precursors, and ultimately restore RPE functional capacity.

Cerulenin presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD owing to its well-documented ability to inhibit fatty acid synthase through a unique irreversible, covalent mechanism. Its molecular footprint, characterized by a reactive epoxide ring, has been exploited in multiple studies to evaluate cellular lipid synthesis and, by extension, to modulate metabolic pathways that underpin several disease processes (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Abramson, 2011). Mechanistically, its capacity to bind to a crucial cysteine residue in the FAS enzyme and to interfere with lipid assembly positions it as a potentially valuable agent to counter the lipid-driven pathogenesis implicated in RPE dysfunction and lipofuscin accumulation in dry AMD (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008).

The strengths of cerulenin as a candidate include its small-molecule profile, which facilitates cellular entry; its established use as a research tool in in vitro and in vivo models; and its dual activity profile that not only curtails de novo lipogenesis but may also impede aberrant protein palmitoylation. The documented applications of cerulenin are primarily in the realms of oncology and metabolic regulation, with little precedent for its use in ocular conditions (Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Another point of concern is that cerulenin’s nonselective inhibition of fatty acid synthase may also impair essential lipid synthesis in cells that require robust regenerative capacity, potentially leading to unintended cytotoxicity or impaired cell membrane maintenance. In the context of the RPE, where cellular health is paramount for photoreceptor support, any off-target lipid synthesis inhibition must be tightly controlled (Goodman & McFadden, 2007; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Furthermore, its use in vivo has been historically hampered by issues such as poor aqueous solubility—it often requires solvents like DMSO for administration—and its propensity for rapid degradation in protic environments, all of which represent substantial formulation challenges that must be overcome for ocular delivery (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Vázquez et al., 2008).

Given these considerations, while cerulenin offers a compelling proof-of-concept relating to the modulation of lipogenesis and lysosomal function, its practical development as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD would likely necessitate further chemical modifications. The precedent set by the development of derivatives such as C75—which were specifically engineered to overcome the limitations of cerulenin by removing the problematic epoxide group and enhancing stability—suggests that optimization is both possible and necessary (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Optimized analogues with improved pharmacokinetic and safety profiles may hold greater promise in the ocular setting than the parent compound.

In summary, cerulenin’s capacity to inhibit fatty acid synthase at the molecular level through irreversible covalent binding is well-established and aligns with the proposed therapeutic mechanism of reducing RPE lipid accumulation and lipofuscin precursor formation. However, its historical limitations in terms of chemical stability, toxicity, and nonselectivity present significant hurdles for its repurposing in dry AMD. The compound’s extensive use in metabolic and oncologic research provides a strong foundation for understanding its biochemical actions, but the absence of direct evidence in retinal models and the challenges associated with its delivery to ocular tissues temper enthusiasm for immediate clinical translation (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Therefore, while there is sufficient mechanistic rationale to pursue further preclinical investigations—potentially in parallel with the development of more stable derivatives—the current state of evidence suggests that cerulenin itself may not be ideal as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD without significant further optimization. More comprehensive in vitro studies using RPE cell models and targeted in vivo studies in AMD-relevant animal models are needed to validate whether the inhibition of de novo lipogenesis by cerulenin can indeed translate into restored lysosomal function and improved photoreceptor outer segment degradation in this disease context (Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007; Radka & Rock, 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ML‐SA1 is a fully synthetic small molecule designed as an agonist of the transient receptor potential mucolipin 1 (TRPML1) channel. It belongs to the class of mucolipin synthetic agonists, which were initially derived as analogs of earlier lead compounds such as SF‐51 and SF‐22. These compounds were discovered using high‐throughput screening approaches aimed at identifying activators of TRPML channels, and ML‐SA1 was subsequently optimized for improved potency and selectivity in mammalian systems (Feng et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2012). As a synthetic compound, ML‐SA1 exemplifies a rational drug design strategy in which the molecule is engineered to mimic the action of the endogenous lipid agonist phosphatidylinositol 3,5‐bisphosphate [PI(3,5)P₂] by directly binding to the channel’s pore region. This binding stabilizes TRPML1 in its open conformation, thereby facilitating lysosomal Ca²⁺ release. The chemical class represented by ML‐SA1 has historically been employed as a research tool to interrogate lysosomal physiology and calcium homeostasis in diverse cell types, including neuronal and retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Therapeutic History:  
Previous studies have demonstrated that ML‐SA1 robustly elevates cytosolic calcium levels in several cellular models by activating TRPML1 channels. In particular, ML‐SA1 has been applied to multiple RPE cell models—including mouse RPE, human embryonic stem cell‐derived RPE, and the ARPE‐19 cell line—to assess its ability to restore lysosomal calcium signaling and normalize lysosomal function (Gómez et al., 2018). In these experiments, ML‐SA1 elicited rapid, robust, and reversible Ca²⁺ signals that were completely absent in TRPML1 knockout cells, thereby confirming target engagement and specificity (Gómez et al., 2018). Beyond RPE biology, ML‐SA1 has been evaluated in neuronal models of lysosomal dysfunction, including experimental systems relevant to Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease, where it mediated correction of defective lysosomal acidification and improved autophagic flux (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022). Although no clinical trials have yet investigated ML‐SA1 directly in patients with dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), its demonstrated efficacy in rescuing lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling—in conditions that share underlying pathophysiological features with dry AMD such as lysosomal storage and autophagy blockade—suggests that its repurposing may yield therapeutic benefits in this disease context (Open Targets Platform, 2025). To date, the use of ML‐SA1 has predominantly been within experimental research settings rather than in clinical practice or veterinary medicine, and its repurposing for dry AMD represents an innovative and rationale‐driven approach rooted in the overlap between TRPML1 dysfunction and RPE pathology (Feng et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2017).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic action of ML‐SA1 is centered upon its ability to directly activate TRPML1 channels located on lysosomal membranes. TRPML1 plays a critical role in regulating lysosomal calcium homeostasis by mediating Ca²⁺ efflux from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol. ML‐SA1 binds directly to TRPML1—likely within a hydrophobic pocket formed at the S5–S6 transmembrane domain interface—and stabilizes the channel’s open state (Feng et al., 2014). This activation occurs independently of exogenous PI(3,5)P₂ in mammalian cells, setting ML‐SA1 apart from the endogenous regulatory mechanisms that otherwise depend on dynamic fluctuations in phosphoinositide levels (Feng et al., 2014; Gómez et al., 2018). As a result of channel activation, lysosomal Ca²⁺ is released into the cytosol, triggering a cascade of calcium‐dependent signaling pathways. One critical downstream effect is the promotion of lysosomal membrane fission and fusion events, processes that are essential for proper lysosomal trafficking and the maturation of autophagosomes into autolysosomes (Cao et al., 2017; Li & Li, 2022).  

Beyond its immediate role in calcium mobilization, ML‐SA1‐mediated activation of TRPML1 also facilitates the activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Increased cytosolic Ca²⁺ can activate calcineurin, which in turn dephosphorylates TFEB, enabling its translocation to the nucleus where it upregulates the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function and autophagy (Pollmanns et al., 2022). In some models, ML‐SA1 treatment has been shown to improve the processing and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D, thereby contributing to normalization of lysosomal pH and enhanced protein degradation (Hui et al., 2019). Importantly, the ability of ML‐SA1 to restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling directly targets the pathological cascade observed when TRPML1 is deficient or inhibited—a scenario that is reminiscent of the lysosomal storage, impaired autophagy, and stalled phagolysosomal degradation evident in dry AMD RPE cells (Gómez et al., 2018; Pamonag, 2021).  

Expected Effect:  
Based on the observed mechanisms in diverse cellular models, it is expected that ML‐SA1 will re‐establish normal lysosomal function in RPE cells afflicted by dry AMD. In the proposed assay, the activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 at concentrations near its EC₅₀ (approximately 5 µM) should restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ efflux, thereby driving several beneficial downstream effects. First, the induced calcium release is anticipated to promote lysosomal membrane dynamics that favor fission and fusion events, ultimately leading to improved lysosomal trafficking and an enhanced capacity for phagolysosomal degradation. This is particularly relevant for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), the routine phagocytic burden of RPE cells that, when inadequately processed, contributes to lipofuscin accumulation and retinal degeneration (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Second, by normalizing Ca²⁺ signaling, ML‐SA1 is expected to reinstate proper lysosomal acidification. Acidification is crucial for the optimal activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D; ML‐SA1 has been shown in various models to restore cathepsin D processing, thereby resetting the enzymatic degradation cascade necessary for POS turnover (Hui et al., 2019). Such restoration of acidification and enzyme activity would directly counteract the pathological accumulation of undegraded material—a hallmark of dry AMD.  

Third, the downstream activation of TFEB induced by ML‐SA1’s modulation of lysosomal calcium may trigger an upregulation of the entire lysosomal-autophagy gene network. This transcriptional reprogramming is vital for augmenting both the number and function of lysosomes, thereby enhancing the overall cellular clearance capacity in RPE cells. Because ample evidence suggests that TRPML1 is expressed in RPE cells and that its dysfunction contributes directly to the autophagy block observed in dry AMD (Pamonag, 2021; Gómez et al., 2018), the activation of this pathway by ML‐SA1 is expected to result in a net improvement in POS degradation and a reduction in toxic debris accumulation. Ultimately, the integrated effects of improved lysosomal trafficking, normalized pH, enhanced enzymatic processing, and boosted autophagic flux are hypothesized to alleviate key pathological features of dry AMD, potentially slowing or even reversing degenerative changes in the retinal pigment epithelium (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Our comprehensive literature review indicates that ML‐SA1 is a scientifically compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration. One of its principal strengths lies in its well‐defined mechanism of action: by directly activating TRPML1 channels, ML‐SA1 has been shown to restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ homeostasis—a central defect in several models of lysosomal storage and autophagy dysfunction (Gómez et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2014). The robust experimental data obtained in RPE cell models and other relevant systems supports the hypothesis that ML‐SA1 can reverse deficits in lysosomal trafficking, acidification, and autophagosome maturation. The compound’s ability to elicit rapid, reproducible, and reversible Ca²⁺ signals is particularly encouraging, as it suggests that pharmacological modulation of TRPML1 can be finely tuned through dosing adjustments (Gómez et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2017).  

Furthermore, the extensive research demonstrating ML‐SA1’s effects in cellular models of lysosomal storage diseases—including those markers that mimic the pathological lipid accumulation and autophagy impairment found in dry AMD—provides additional rationale for its application in RPE cells (Feng et al., 2014; Pollmanns et al., 2022; Hui et al., 2019). The fact that ML‐SA1 has also been evaluated in non-ocular contexts (such as neuronal models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s diseases) where it facilitated autophagic clearance and improved lysosomal functions underscores the versatility of its mechanism and hints at broader therapeutic utility (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022).  

Nonetheless, several challenges must be acknowledged. One notable weakness is that ML‐SA1’s efficacy can be compromised by lysosomal lipid accumulation—a common feature of advanced dry AMD. Studies suggest that in cells with significant lipid deposition, such as those accumulating sphingomyelin or other inhibitory lipids, the activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 is attenuated (Gómez et al., 2018). This raises concerns that in patients with advanced dry AMD, the therapeutic window may be narrower or may require combination strategies to first reduce lipid burden. Additionally, while the in vitro EC₅₀ is promising (around 5 µM), there remains uncertainty regarding the pharmacokinetic profile, bioavailability, tissue penetration (particularly across the blood‐retina barrier), and potential off-target effects of ML‐SA1 when administered in vivo (Li & Li, 2022).  

Another area of concern is the current lack of direct clinical data pertaining to ML‐SA1 in dry AMD. Although preclinical studies in RPE cell models provide a solid foundation, translation to in vivo models of AMD—and eventually to human clinical trials—will require additional investigation. The absence of any reported clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD with TRPML1 agonists (as confirmed by database searches such as those reflected in the Open Targets Platform) indicates that this is still a largely uncharted therapeutic area requiring further validation (Open Targets Platform, 2025). Moreover, chronic activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 may have unforeseen consequences related to intracellular calcium homeostasis and autophagic balance, which warrant careful evaluation in long-term studies (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022).  

In summary, ML‐SA1 represents a highly promising candidate for the repurposing in dry AMD based on its ability to rescue lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling, enhance autophagic clearance, and restore normal lysosomal pH and trafficking in RPE cells. Its synthetic origin and well‐characterized mechanism provide a strong mechanistic rationale for its use. However, issues related to lipid-mediated inhibition of TRPML1, pharmacokinetic considerations, and the current lack of in vivo data in AMD models must be addressed. Overall, the candidate shows significant potential, but a focused program of preclinical validation—including animal models of dry AMD, detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiling, and exploration of strategies to mitigate lysosomal lipid accumulation—is essential before advancing ML‐SA1 to clinical trials for dry AMD (Gómez et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2014).
