Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Trehalose is a naturally occurring, nonreducing disaccharide composed of two D‐glucose units (MW = 342.3 Da) that is not synthesized endogenously in mammals but is abundant in other organisms such as fungi, plants, and invertebrates (Cox et al., 2025). It was originally discovered as a cellular protectant and osmolyte that stabilizes proteins and membranes under conditions of stress, and its unique chemical stability and protein‐protective properties have led to its use in cryopreservation and organ transplant protocols (Lotfi et al., 2018). As a small-molecule therapeutic candidate, trehalose belongs to a class of compounds known as osmolytes and molecular chaperones; this category has been extensively explored for its capacity to stabilize proteins, prevent aggregation, and enhance cellular resilience in the face of diverse environmental and metabolic stresses (Abokyi et al., 2020; Cox et al., 2025). In drug development contexts, its repurposing for dry age-related macular degeneration (dAMD) is driven by its capacity to activate TFEB—a master transcription factor regulating the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network—and thereby boost autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ghosh et al., 2023). Trehalose has been formulated for ocular use, most notably as an ingredient in tear substitutes for dry eye, and its safety profile in such formulations provides ancillary support for its potential repurposing to target RPE dysfunction in dAMD (Cox et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Trehalose has a well-documented history in biochemical and preclinical research due to its potent protein-stabilizing and osmoprotectant actions. It has been widely used in non-ophthalmic applications, most notably in cryopreservation protocols, where its ability to preserve protein structure and cellular integrity under desiccating and freezing conditions is exploited (Cox et al., 2025; Lotfi et al., 2018). In the ocular field, trehalose has been evaluated primarily for anterior segment indications such as dry eye disease; several randomized clinical trials have demonstrated its tolerability and efficacy as a tear substitute when combined with hyaluronic acid, with improvements in tear film break-up time (TBUT) and ocular surface symptoms (Chiambaretta et al., 2017).  
More importantly for dAMD, multiple in vitro studies using human RPE cell models—including ARPE-19 and iPSC-derived RPE from patients with genetic risk factors like CFH mutations—have shown that trehalose rescues autophagy deficits and lysosomal dysfunction, especially under oxidative-stress conditions induced by agents such as hydroquinone (Abokyi et al., 2020). These studies report that trehalose treatment upregulates key autophagy regulators (e.g., ATG5, ATG7) and lysosomal markers (e.g., LAMP2, cathepsin D) while enhancing autophagic flux, thereby improving the degradative capacity of RPE cells—a fundamental defect implicated in the accumulation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and lipofuscin in dAMD (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). Additionally, in murine models of retinal degeneration—whether induced by light exposure or by genetic interventions—trehalose has been shown to protect against retinal cell loss and preserve outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness, offering further preclinical evidence of its neuroprotective potential (Cox et al., 2025). Thus, while trehalose has an established record in non-ocular uses and in the treatment of anterior ocular surface disorders, emerging data now support its repurposing for dAMD by virtue of its ability to modulate autophagy and lysosomal degradation in RPE cells (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central mechanism by which trehalose is hypothesized to benefit dry AMD involves its capacity to activate the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of the CLEAR network. TFEB controls the transcription of a whole battery of genes required for autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and metabolic adaptation (Abokyi et al., 2020). Typically, TFEB resides in the cytoplasm in an inactive, phosphorylated state under nutrient-rich or stress-depleted conditions; its translocation to the nucleus is tightly regulated by mTORC1-dependent and mTORC1-independent signaling pathways (Ghosh et al., 2023; Karim et al., 2020). Trehalose has been shown to induce TFEB nuclear translocation independently of mTOR inhibition, potentially through mechanisms involving Akt signaling modulation and AMPK activation (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Upon nuclear entry, TFEB binds to CLEAR elements in the promoter regions of target genes, thereby upregulating autophagy mediators such as ATG5 and ATG7, enhancing the expression of lysosomal proteins like LAMP2, and increasing the levels of protein markers such as LC3B and p62 that are involved in autophagosome formation and maturation (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Several biochemical studies in human RPE cells have demonstrated that trehalose treatment leads to increased TFEB mRNA and protein levels with concomitant upregulation of CLEAR network gene expression. For instance, in ARPE-19 cells exposed to hydroquinone—a model for oxidative stress relevant to dAMD—it was observed that trehalose not only increased LC3-II levels and GFP-LC3 puncta formation but also enhanced the degradation of autophagic substrates, indicating that trehalose facilitates effective autophagic flux rather than merely blocking lysosomal degradation (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Mechanistically, trehalose is thought to penetrate mammalian cells via fluid-phase endocytosis and possibly through the SLC2A8 (GLUT8) transporter, which facilitates its intracellular accumulation at millimolar concentrations (Cox et al., 2025). Once inside the cell, trehalose appears to modulate several key pathways: by inhibiting Akt signaling, it reduces the phosphorylation of TFEB at specific residues (such as S467) that normally prevent its nuclear import; concurrently, trehalose may activate AMPK, which further supports autophagy induction (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020). Moreover, although trehalose transiently upregulates NRF2 under basal conditions—thereby enhancing antioxidant defenses—its primary protective effect in oxidative stress models of the RPE appears to be mediated by restored autophagy, as demonstrated by loss of cytoprotection when autophagy is genetically disrupted via ATG5 knockdown (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Beyond its role in autophagy, trehalose has been implicated in promoting chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) through stimulation of LAMP2 expression, which is essential for CMA substrate recognition and lysosomal import (Abokyi et al., 2020). In this way, trehalose may offer a dual benefit: boosting canonical macroautophagy while also enhancing CMA, collectively leading to improved clearance of damaged organelles, aggregated proteins, and undigested POS in the RPE—a critical function given the strong association between defective POS clearance and the pathogenesis of dAMD (Abokyi et al., 2020). Furthermore, in CFH-mutant iPSC-derived RPE cells, trehalose has been shown to rescue the diminished activity of lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D and to restore other proteostasis markers, establishing a direct molecular link between trehalose-induced TFEB activation and functional improvements in the degradative capacity of RPE cells (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
Collectively, the mechanistic data suggest that trehalose exerts its beneficial effects through a complex interplay of intracellular signaling pathways that converge on the activation of TFEB, thereby re-establishing efficient autophagic clearance processes that are impaired in the aging and oxidative-stressed RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020; Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic insights outlined above, the hypothesis posits that treatment with trehalose at a concentration of 5 mM in an in vitro assay using iPSC-derived RPE cells from dry AMD patients will lead to robust TFEB nuclear translocation. This nuclear translocation is expected to result in the transcriptional upregulation of CLEAR network genes, thereby increasing the expression of autophagy regulators such as ATG5 and ATG7 and promoting the biogenesis of lysosomes, as evidenced by increased levels of lysosomal markers like LAMP2 and cathepsin D (Abokyi et al., 2020). In an environment of oxidative stress—for example, when the iPSC-RPE cells are challenged with hydroquinone to mimic cigarette smoke-induced damage or other oxidative insults commonly associated with AMD—the activation of TFEB by trehalose is anticipated to restore impaired autophagic flux. This restoration would be reflected in the accumulation of LC3-II upon inhibition of lysosomal function (e.g., in the presence of chloroquine) and decreased levels of autophagy substrate p62 (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Crucially, by enhancing autophagic and lysosomal function in the RPE, trehalose is expected to improve POS degradation. Efficient degradation of POS is vital for photoreceptor health, and its impairment has been implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD through the accumulation of toxic byproducts and lipofuscin (Abokyi et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025). Thus, the expected phenotype in the in vitro assay would include not only molecular signatures of enhanced autophagy (e.g., increased LC3B puncta, upregulated ATG gene expression) but also functional improvements such as reduced oxidative stress (lower reactive oxygen species levels) and improved cell viability under stress conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Moreover, previous studies have shown that trehalose’s cytoprotective effects are autophagy-dependent because genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of autophagy (e.g., via ATG5 knockdown) abolishes the otherwise protective effects of trehalose, thereby reinforcing the notion that the expected improvement in POS degradation and overall cellular homeostasis is tightly linked to the restoration of autophagy and lysosomal competence (Abokyi et al., 2020). In essence, the application of 5 mM trehalose to oxidative-stressed iPSC-RPE cells is anticipated to reverse the autophagic deficits that are characteristic of dry AMD, ultimately leading to enhanced clearance of POS, reduced accumulation of cytotoxic aggregates, and improved cellular survival and function in an in vitro model that recapitulates key aspects of the disease (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
Trehalose represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its multifaceted capacity to modulate intracellular degradation pathways that are critically impaired in the disease state. One of the primary strengths of trehalose is its robust preclinical evidence base. Multiple studies have demonstrated that trehalose can induce TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE models, resulting in the transcriptional activation of an array of autophagy and lysosomal genes (Abokyi et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2023; Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020). This mechanistic property directly addresses a key pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD, where the accumulation of undegraded photoreceptor outer segments and lipofuscin due to defective autophagy plays a contributory role in RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration (Abokyi et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025). The ability of trehalose to enhance both macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy augments its therapeutic appeal, as it suggests an overall improvement in cellular proteostasis, which is imperative in aged or stressed RPE cells (Abokyi et al., 2020; Cox et al., 2025).  
Another notable strength is the established safety profile of trehalose. It is a naturally occurring compound with a long history of use in various medical and industrial applications, including as an ingredient in ocular surface formulations for dry eye disease (Chiambaretta et al., 2017; Cox et al., 2025). Furthermore, the preclinical data showing that trehalose can protect against oxidative stress and preserve retinal function in animal models lend credibility to the hypothesis that it may exert similar protective effects in human RPE cells (Cox et al., 2025).  
However, several weaknesses and gaps must be acknowledged as well. First, the majority of the compelling evidence for trehalose’s efficacy in modulating TFEB and enhancing autophagy comes from in vitro studies using immortalized RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19) or rodent models, with only limited data available from human iPSC-derived RPE models specifically derived from AMD patients (Abokyi et al., 2020). Second, there are ongoing debates in the literature regarding the precise molecular mechanisms by which trehalose exerts its autophagy-enhancing effects, with some reports disputing its ability to induce autophagy under certain conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).  
Another potential challenge lies in the delivery of trehalose to the RPE in a clinically meaningful manner. Although trehalose is orally bioavailable and has been successfully formulated for topical ocular use in dry eye applications, the posterior segment of the eye presents unique drug delivery hurdles. Penetration through the cornea and subsequent distribution to the RPE and retina often require specialized formulations, and while there are preclinical reports of trehalose reaching posterior ocular tissues (Cox et al., 2025), comprehensive pharmacokinetic and ocular bioavailability data for trehalose in the context of dAMD remain sparse.  
Furthermore, while the repurposing of trehalose is attractive due to its established safety and low cost, intellectual property issues and regulatory challenges associated with drug repurposing may complicate clinical development. Despite these concerns, the overall body of evidence supports further investigation into trehalose as a potential modulator of TFEB and autophagy in the RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cox et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).  
In summary, trehalose offers several strong advantages as a candidate therapeutic for dry AMD. Its ability to activate TFEB and upregulate a broad spectrum of autophagy and lysosomal genes addresses a fundamental defect in RPE cells implicated in the disease. Robust preclinical evidence in both in vitro and animal models suggests that trehalose enhances autophagic flux, improves POS clearance, and confers cytoprotective effects against oxidative stress. Its favorable safety profile and prior use in ocular formulations further support its translational potential. However, critical gaps remain in terms of validating its efficacy in human-derived RPE models, optimizing its dosing and delivery to the posterior segment, and resolving discrepancies regarding its mechanism of action in different experimental contexts. Given these considerations, trehalose represents a promising candidate that merits further investigation—particularly through rigorous dose-response studies, advanced formulation development to enhance retinal delivery, and robust clinical trials in patient populations at risk for dry AMD—to fully establish its therapeutic value (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cox et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of 2‐hydroxypropyl‐β‐cyclodextrin (HPβCD; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. C0926) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
HPβCD is a chemically modified cyclic oligosaccharide belonging to the cyclodextrin drug class, which consists of cyclic arrangements of glucopyranose units. In the case of HPβCD, hydroxypropyl groups are substituted on the β-cyclodextrin ring, thereby increasing its water solubility and overall biocompatibility while maintaining the inherent toroidal structure with a hydrophobic inner cavity and hydrophilic exterior. This unique architecture allows HPβCD to encapsulate lipophilic compounds such as cholesterol, forming stable inclusion complexes that enhance the solubilization, mobilization, or extraction of these molecules from biological membranes or intracellular compartments (Braga, 2023; Davidson et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020). Originally discovered and adapted as an excipient to improve the solubility and delivery of hydrophobic drugs, cyclodextrins have more recently gained attention as active pharmaceutical ingredients due to their capacity to modulate lipid metabolism. In particular, HPβCD is being repurposed as a therapeutic candidate because of its established ability to reduce cholesterol accumulation in tissues—an effect that is central to its potential role in addressing dry AMD pathology (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, HPβCD has been widely utilized as a pharmaceutical excipient and delivery system with a strong safety record, as evidenced by its FDA-approved use in various formulations. More notably, its cholesterol-binding and mobilizing activity has driven its repurposing for treatment of cholesterol storage disorders, most prominently Niemann–Pick Type C (NPC) disease. In NPC, HPβCD has been administered by various routes—including systemic, intrathecal, and subcutaneous injections—to solubilize and extract unesterified cholesterol from lysosomal compartments, thereby ameliorating the pathological accumulation of lipids in neuronal and peripheral tissues (Davidson et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Kfoury et al., 2025; Rao & Fliesler, 2021). Preclinical studies in NPC models have consistently demonstrated that HPβCD can normalize cholesterol trafficking and extend lifespan in affected animals. Additional biochemical and clinical studies in related fields such as atherosclerosis further underscore the compound’s potency as a cholesterol-mobilizing agent (Braga, 2023; Coisne et al., 2016; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020). Although HPβCD has not been used explicitly in clinical trials for dry AMD to date, the mechanistic rationale for its application is compelling since retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells in dry AMD exhibit lysosomal cholesterol accumulation and associated dysfunction similar to the cellular defects observed in NPC and atherosclerotic conditions (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023). Moreover, retinal studies in mouse models have shown that HPβCD can reduce cholesterol levels in the retina and restore aspects of cellular homeostasis, thereby laying the groundwork for the proposed repurposing in dry AMD (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, HPβCD functions primarily by exploiting its unique cyclic structure, which provides a hydrophobic cavity designed to accommodate cholesterol molecules. The hydrophobic interactions between the cyclodextrin cavity and the sterol ring system of cholesterol enable HPβCD to form a reversible inclusion complex with both free and esterified cholesterol. This process shifts the equilibrium of intracellular cholesterol pools and promotes a net efflux of cholesterol from cellular membranes and lysosomal compartments (El-Darzi et al., 2023; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020).

In cells burdened by cholesterol accumulation—such as RPE cells in the context of drusen formation—the excess cholesterol impairs the fluidity of membranes and disrupts the acidification and enzymatic activity within lysosomes. HPβCD is hypothesized to extract this excess cholesterol from the lysosomal membrane, thereby restoring proper membrane fluidity and normalizing the pH within the lysosome. This in turn is expected to reactivate lysosomal enzymes, such as cathepsins, and restore proper autophagic flux and phagocytic turnover of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Coisne et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

On a biochemical level, studies have shown that HPβCD can upregulate proteins related to cholesterol efflux. For instance, the compound has been observed to modulate the expression of ATP-binding cassette transporters, such as ABCA1 and ABCG1, via liver X receptor (LXR)-dependent pathways. Additionally, HPβCD treatment can alter the cellular distribution of cholesterol by promoting trafficking from the lysosome to other cellular compartments such as the endoplasmic reticulum, where it is enzymatically esterified and eventually excreted (Cougnoux et al., 2023; El-Darzi et al., 2021; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020).

Another important mechanistic aspect is the compound’s influence on lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. HPβCD has been shown to increase the abundance of lysosome-associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) and to activate the transcription factor EB (TFEB), which is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic processes. Such activation contributes to maintaining cellular clearance pathways that are essential for RPE cell health, especially in the face of chronic insult from photoreceptor outer segments and accumulated lipofuscin bisretinoids (Braga, 2023; Brown et al., 2016). Through these molecular interactions, HPβCD may counteract the cellular stress induced by disrupted cholesterol homeostasis, thereby mitigating the dual impact of both lipid accumulation and impaired lysosomal degradation that is central to dry AMD pathogenesis. However, it is noteworthy that some studies have reported that prolonged exposure to HPβCD can induce pro-inflammatory responses and even ototoxicity in animal models, underscoring the importance of optimizing dosing regimens (Houben et al., 2021a, 2021b; Yamada et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis driving the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is that by extracting the excess cholesterol accumulated in the lysosomes of RPE cells, the compound will restore normal cellular functions. The primary expected effect is multifold. First, the removal of cholesterol is anticipated to restore lysosomal pH to its optimal acidic range. An appropriate pH is crucial for the full activation of lysosomal hydrolases, such as cathepsins, which are necessary for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments that normally enter the RPE through phagocytosis (Braga, 2023; El-Darzi et al., 2023). Second, by normalizing membrane fluidity, HPβCD would improve the trafficking and fusion of lysosomes, thus enhancing the clearance of cellular waste. This improved clearance capacity may help resolve drusen-like deposits and prevent inflammatory activation of retinal microglia and macrophages—a process that has been implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Brown et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Houben et al., 2021b).

From a molecular perspective, RPE cells express key proteins involved in cholesterol handling, including NPC1, ABCA1, and LXR. The activation of these pathways after HPβCD application could lead to improved reverse cholesterol transport, where the excess cholesterol is removed from RPE cells and delivered to extracellular acceptors for clearance (Davidson et al., 2016; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020). This facilitated removal is expected to lower intracellular levels of unesterified cholesterol, reduce cholesterol crystal formation, and subsequently attenuate the pro-inflammatory milieu that contributes to RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Braga, 2023; Houben et al., 2021b).

In experimental assays, one might expect to observe a decrease in the levels of cholesterol and cholesterol crystals by biochemical analyses or imaging of RPE cells treated with HPβCD, alongside a normalization of lysosomal pH values measured via pH-sensitive dyes. Enzyme assays should reveal a restoration of cathepsin activity, and phagocytosis assays would ideally demonstrate an increased turnover of POS. Taken together, these effects would not only preserve RPE cell function but also potentially slow the progression of the disease and improve retinal structure and function (Coisne et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, HPβCD represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its well-documented ability to modulate cholesterol homeostasis and improve lysosomal function. The compound’s favorable physicochemical properties—stemming from its cyclic oligosaccharide structure and enhanced solubility due to hydroxypropylation—make it an attractive candidate for drug repurposing. The extensive preclinical evidence in lysosomal cholesterol storage disorders, including NPC disease and atherosclerosis models, provides a solid foundation that supports its potential efficacy in conditions characterized by intracellular cholesterol dysregulation, such as dry AMD (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

One of the major strengths of HPβCD is its multifaceted mechanism of action. It not only physically extracts cholesterol by forming inclusion complexes but also appears to modulate key cellular pathways that govern cholesterol efflux, lysosomal biogenesis, and autophagic clearance. This combined activity has the potential to address several pathological features of dry AMD simultaneously: restoring lysosomal pH, normalizing the activity of pH-dependent enzymes like cathepsins, and enhancing the degradation of deposited photoreceptor outer segments. Additionally, the evidence that HPβCD can reduce inflammatory activation by preventing cholesterol crystal formation and macrophage recruitment further supports its application in a disease state where chronic inflammation is a well-known driver of progression (Brown et al., 2016; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020).

However, there are also notable weaknesses and concerns that must be carefully considered. First, while HPβCD’s safety profile is well-established for its role as an excipient and, to some extent, in NPC clinical trials, significant safety issues have been reported in the context of systemic and even local administration. Ototoxicity has emerged as a recurrent concern in multiple preclinical studies and some clinical observations, which could be particularly problematic if similar toxicities are encountered when used in the delicate tissues of the eye (Braga, 2023; Calias, 2018; Yamada et al., 2021). Moreover, some studies have reported dose-dependent pro-inflammatory effects upon chronic exposure to HPβCD, underscoring the necessity for optimizing dosing regimens and careful monitoring of inflammatory markers (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Hoque et al., 2020).

Another potential challenge is the delivery route. Given that the eye is a compartment with unique barriers and an immunoprivileged status, determining the optimal method of administration (e.g., intravitreal injection, topical eye drops, or systemic administration with targeted delivery) will be critical. The compound’s ability to cross the blood-retina barrier has been demonstrated in preclinical models, but achieving sufficient retinal concentration without systemic toxicity may require advanced formulation strategies, such as encapsulation in polymer-based nanoparticles or the development of polyrotaxane-based delivery systems (Coisne et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

The overall evaluation is therefore cautiously optimistic. On the one hand, the strong mechanistic rationale for using HPβCD to address the underlying cholesterol dysregulation and lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD is supported by a robust body of literature from related fields (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020). The compound benefits from established use in other cholesterol accumulation disorders and has clearly defined biochemical activities that could be translated into therapeutic benefits in the context of AMD. On the other hand, significant challenges remain in terms of safety—especially related to ototoxicity and potential inflammatory side effects—and in the optimization of delivery methods that can achieve effective retinal concentrations without off-target toxicity (Braga, 2023; Houben et al., 2021a; Yamada et al., 2021).

Given these considerations, it is recommended that the next phases of drug development focus on detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicity studies specific to ocular tissues, along with the exploration of novel delivery formulations that may mitigate systemic and local adverse effects. Further preclinical validation using AMD-relevant models is warranted to assess functional outcomes such as restoration of lysosomal pH, increased cathepsin activity, improved phagocytic efficiency of POS, and ultimately, preservation of retinal structure and function (Coisne et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

In conclusion, while HPβCD demonstrates considerable potential as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its cholesterol-extracting capabilities and beneficial effects on lysosomal function, the balance between efficacy and safety remains a critical area for further investigation. The strengths—mechanistic depth, prior clinical use in related disorders, and robust preclinical data—are compelling; however, the weaknesses, notably regarding ototoxicity and the need for optimized delivery, must be addressed before moving to clinical trials in AMD patients (Braga, 2023; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020; Yamada et al., 2021). Continued research with targeted formulations, dosing studies, and AMD-specific preclinical models will be essential to determine whether HPβCD can be safely and effectively repurposed to improve outcomes in patients with dry age‐related macular degeneration.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
D609, chemically known as tricyclodecan-9-yl xanthogenate, is a synthetic small‐molecule compound belonging to the xanthate class. It was originally synthesized through classical organic‐chemical methods involving the reaction of diastereomeric tricyclic alcohols with carbon disulfide in the presence of a strong base such as potassium tert‐butoxide, yielding a mixture of eight stereoisomers due to its three asymmetric centers (Bhat et al., 2022; Eurtivong et al., 2023). As a member of the xanthate family, D609 has been extensively studied for its diverse biological activities that include antiviral, antitumoral, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective effects (Bhat et al., 2022). Its mechanism of competitive inhibition of phosphatidylcholine-specific phospholipase C (PC-PLC) was discovered during the evaluation of lipid signaling pathways, and it is commercially available (for example, Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. D0209) as a research-grade compound (Wang et al., 2020). This chemical class has traditionally been investigated in various biomedical contexts, with early work focusing on its antiviral properties dating back to the 1980s and subsequent studies extending its uses into oncology and neurology (Bhat et al., 2022). Its water solubility and relatively low molecular weight make it an attractive candidate for repurposing into ocular applications where intracellular signaling and oxidative stress play key roles.

Therapeutic History:  
D609 has been the subject of more than 700 published reports over the last three decades and has been explored in preclinical studies ranging from antiviral and anticancer applications to neuroprotection and inflammation modulation (Bhat et al., 2022). One of the most compelling lines of evidence for repurposing D609 concerns its potential in treating ocular conditions, particularly dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In several studies, D609 has been directly evaluated for its ability to protect retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) cells from oxidative damage using in vitro cell models such as the widely used ARPE-19 cell line and primary human RPE cells (Wang et al., 2020). For instance, one study employing a high-content screening strategy on 814 protective compounds identified D609 as a lead candidate that maintained RPE cell viability above 95% under severe oxidative stress induced by sodium iodate—a condition used to model dry AMD (Wang et al., 2020). Furthermore, in vivo animal models, including sodium iodate-induced AMD mouse models, have confirmed that D609 can protect the RPE layer, preserve retinal structure and function, and prevent geographic atrophy—findings that underscore its translational potential for dry AMD therapy (Wang et al., 2020). Outside the field of ophthalmology, D609 has been evaluated in oncology, where it affected cell proliferation and induced apoptosis in certain tumor cell lines, and in neuroscience for its neuroprotective effects against amyloid-beta toxicity and oxidative stress in neuronal cultures (Bhat et al., 2022). Although no clinical trials have yet been reported that specifically target dry AMD with D609, the preclinical data generated in ocular, cancer, and neurodegenerative studies provide a robust therapeutic history that supports depth of investigation into its ocular application (Wang et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At its core, D609 is a competitive inhibitor of PC-PLC. PC-PLC is an enzyme that hydrolyzes phosphatidylcholine (PC) into phosphorylcholine and diacylglycerol (DAG). In RPE cells, overactivation of this enzyme under oxidative stress conditions may lead to excessive DAG production that, in turn, drives hyperactivation of protein kinase C (PKC) and downstream signaling events deleteriously affecting cytoskeletal dynamics and phagocytosis (Wang et al., 2020). D609 exerts its inhibitory activity by mimicking parts of the natural substrate, competitively binding to the active site of PC-PLC—in part through its dithiocarbonate group, which can chelate zinc ions that are critical for enzyme function (Wang et al., 2020; González-Roura et al., 2002). In addition to its direct inhibition of PC-PLC, D609 has been reported to exert antioxidative effects indirectly via upregulation of metallothionein proteins—an antioxidative protein family that plays a protective role against reactive oxygen species (ROS) and metal-induced damage (Wang et al., 2020). This dual mechanism—direct enzyme inhibition and indirect antioxidant protection—suggests that D609 may help stabilize the lipid signaling environment of the RPE, normalizing DAG levels and mitigating PKC-mediated perturbations in actin cytoskeletal dynamics that are essential for the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Wang et al., 2020). Some studies even propose that the beneficial effects observed in RPE cells may derive more from the metallothionein upregulation than from pure PC-PLC inhibition, raising the possibility that D609’s mode of action is multifactorial rather than strictly enzyme-targeted (Wang et al., 2020). However, in the context of the current hypothesis—where the goal is to inhibit the DAG-PKC axis to restore cytoskeletal dynamics and phagocytosis—the competitive inhibition of PC-PLC by D609 remains a key molecular mechanism (Bhat et al., 2022). It should be noted that D609 is not entirely selective; it also inhibits other enzymes in lipid metabolism such as sphingomyelin synthase (SMS) and possibly phospholipase D (PLD), which could contribute to both its therapeutic efficacy and its off-target effects (Eurtivong et al., 2023; González-Roura et al., 2002). The compound’s broad-spectrum inhibition profile, while advantageous in some settings, raises concerns regarding precise modulation of the PC-PLC–DAG–PKC pathway in the specialized setting of RPE biology (Zhao et al., 2020; Bhat et al., 2022). Nevertheless, the downstream reduction in DAG levels is expected to temper PKC activation, which is crucial since PKC hyperactivation is known to impair actin polymerization and therefore phagocytosis—a critical function of RPE cells in maintaining photoreceptor health (Wang et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
The working hypothesis for repurposing D609 for dry AMD is that its inhibition of PC-PLC in RPE cells will lead to reduced DAG formation, thereby limiting DAG-driven PKC hyperactivation. This in turn is expected to stabilize cytoskeletal dynamics by restoring normal actin polymerization, thus improving the phagocytic capacity of the RPE to internalize and process POS. In experimental assays, ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxidative insult (e.g., hydroquinone treatment) typically display disrupted actin architecture and impaired POS uptake. Treatment with D609 is hypothesized to counteract these effects by balancing the intracellular signaling milieu—specifically by reducing the aberrant activation of the DAG-PKC axis—and by promoting the antioxidant metallothionein pathway, which further preserves cellular homeostasis (Wang et al., 2020). Expression of PC-PLC and related signaling components in RPE cells has been indirectly verified by the cellular responses observed upon oxidative challenge, and the reversal of these effects by D609 supports the notion that this enzyme is active and pathophysiologically relevant in RPE cells (Wang et al., 2020). The expected phenotypic outcomes in the assay include a restoration of actin polymerization, as evidenced by improved F-actin staining patterns, increased phagocytosis of labeled POS, and decreased levels of oxidative markers such as ROS. Indeed, previous studies demonstrated that when ARPE-19 cells were pretreated with D609, they exhibited markedly reduced necrotic and apoptotic markers, along with preserved mitochondrial mass and function under oxidative stress conditions induced by sodium iodate (Wang et al., 2020). These outcomes directly support the hypothesis that normalization of PC-PLC activity via D609 not only mitigates the immediate oxidative insult but also restores the critical cellular function of POS internalization—a process that, when dysfunctional, is a hallmark of dry AMD pathology (Wang et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
D609 presents as an intriguing and promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly because of its ability to modulate lipid signaling pathways that are disrupted by oxidative stress and contribute to RPE dysfunction. One of the principal strengths of D609 is its well-documented protective effect on RPE cells both in vitro and in vivo. Studies have shown that D609 maintains high levels of cell viability in RPE models under conditions of severe oxidative stress, and its administration in animal models of AMD has led to significant preservation of retinal structure and function (Wang et al., 2020). Moreover, its water solubility and low molecular weight facilitate ocular delivery and reduce formulation challenges, making it suitable for local administration to the retina (Wang et al., 2020). The dual-action mechanism—combining inhibition of PC-PLC with upregulation of metallothionein—provides both a direct reduction in deleterious DAG-PKC signaling and an indirect bolster to the cell’s antioxidant defenses, which is crucial in the context of dry AMD where oxidative stress is a primary driver of pathology (Wang et al., 2020).

However, several weaknesses must be noted. First, D609 is a non-selective inhibitor; while it effectively targets PC-PLC, it also inhibits other enzymes such as sphingomyelin synthase and phospholipase D, which may introduce off-target effects that could complicate its clinical use (Eurtivong et al., 2023; González-Roura et al., 2002). This lack of selectivity may lead to unpredictable interactions in the intricate lipid signaling networks present in the retina. Second, the compound exists as a mixture of eight stereoisomers, and the differential activity among these isomers is not well understood. Variability in stereoisomeric composition could result in inconsistent pharmacodynamic outcomes and present challenges in the regulatory approval process (Eurtivong et al., 2023; Bhat et al., 2022). Third, the anticipated IC₅₀ of approximately 35 µM for PC-PLC inhibition in RPE cells is relatively high, suggesting that effective biological activity may require high local concentrations that may be difficult to achieve or maintain in vivo without risking toxicity (Wang et al., 2020; Bhat et al., 2022). Although ocular safety studies in rabbits have been favorable, further pharmacokinetic and toxicological investigations will be essential to confirm the therapeutic window for chronic treatment in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2020; Bhat et al., 2022).

From a mechanism-of-action standpoint, while the hypothesis that reducing DAG-mediated PKC hyperactivation will normalize actin dynamics and improve phagocytosis is biologically plausible, much of the existing literature on D609’s protective effects in RPE cells emphasizes its ability to upregulate metallothionein expression and confer antioxidant protection rather than solely modulating the DAG-PKC axis (Wang et al., 2020). Thus, it remains to be clarified whether the beneficial outcomes in RPE phagocytosis are driven primarily by alterations in the DAG-PKC pathway or by a broader restoration of cellular redox balance. This mechanistic ambiguity, while not diminishing the overall therapeutic promise, suggests that future studies should incorporate detailed pathway analyses to dissect the relative contributions of each mechanism.

In summary, D609 is well supported by preclinical evidence as a compound that can protect RPE cells from oxidative damage and has potential applications in dry AMD therapy (Wang et al., 2020). Its established safety profile in ocular studies, combined with a mechanistic basis that addresses both lipid signaling dysregulation and oxidative stress, offers significant advantages for repurposing in this context. Nonetheless, challenges related to off-target effects, stereochemical variability, and the need for high effective concentrations must be rigorously addressed in subsequent studies. Overall, D609 merits further investigative efforts in translational research focused on dry AMD, with particular emphasis on optimizing its pharmacodynamics, ensuring reproducible stereoisomeric composition, and validating its efficacy in restoring RPE phagocytic function under physiologically relevant oxidative stress conditions (Eurtivong et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2020).

This report is organized into several sections: an overview of the candidate, its therapeutic history, an in‐depth discussion of its mechanism of action, the expected effects in the proposed assay, and an overall evaluation that weighs its strengths and weaknesses.

─────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

KYP-2047 is a synthetic small molecule belonging to the peptidomimetic class of compounds that target the enzyme prolyl oligopeptidase (PREP), also known as prolyl endopeptidase (POP). Chemically designated as 4-phenylbutanoyl-L-prolyl-2(S)-cyanopyrrolidine, this compound was synthesized following methods established by Dr. Elina Jarho at the University of Eastern Finland (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47). Its design represents an evolution from early substrate-like inhibitors, with modifications at specific positions – including a three-carbon aliphatic chain at the P3 position instead of the more commonly used carbamate groups seen in predecessors like ZPP – thereby improving the compound’s overall potency, selectivity, and drug-like properties (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4).

Belonging to a well-known class of PREP inhibitors, KYP-2047 shares common chemical and biophysical properties with analogous peptidomimetic agents that have been primarily designed to interfere with the catalytic activity of a serine protease that cleaves proline-containing peptides. Given its low water solubility, KYP-2047 is typically formulated in saline containing 5% Tween® 80 for experimental studies, which is consistent with formulation challenges observed with many peptidomimetic drug candidates (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47). In recent years, the broader class of PREP inhibitors has been explored for a variety of indications, most notably in neurological conditions as well as in certain cancer models. The research impetus behind this class arises from the enzyme’s presumed role in peptide metabolism, where the inhibition of PREP could alter levels of bioactive peptides that participate in cellular homeostasis. Although these agents were originally developed as anti-amnesic candidates, their biological actions have been found to extend to anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

─────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

The therapeutic exploration of PREP inhibitors dates back to the 1970s when the enzyme was first implicated in the regulation of proline-containing peptides associated with memory formation and synaptic plasticity (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22). Numerous compounds in this class—including S-17092, JTP-4819, and others—were advanced into preclinical studies and even early-phase clinical trials for cognitive enhancement in neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease and senile dementia (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41, 70–72). However, despite initial encouraging in vitro and animal data, these agents failed to progress successfully past phase II clinical trials in humans, most likely due to challenges with efficacy, blood-brain barrier penetration, or the complexity of the enzyme’s in vivo function (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 70–72).

In parallel, PREP inhibitors have been evaluated for other indications. For instance, in a study involving oral squamous cell carcinoma, KYP-2047 demonstrated potent PREP inhibition in the mouse brain along with promising anti-tumor effects, highlighting the compound’s potential utility beyond central nervous system disorders (Scuderi, 2023, pp. 133–135). Furthermore, recent work has begun to explore the ocular applications of PREP inhibition. There is a suggestion in the literature that inhibition of prolyl oligopeptidase may represent “a promising pathway to prevent the progression of age-related macular degeneration” (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13). Notably, recent in vitro studies using human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells with defective proteasomal clearance have shown that KYP-2047 exhibits cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory properties, thereby indirectly supporting its potential use in dry AMD, even though no clinical trials or prior direct therapeutic applications in retinal diseases have yet been reported (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 9–11).

While the primary historical focus of PREP inhibitors has been on neurological and cognitive applications, the body of literature also contains several exploratory studies in inflammatory and cancer contexts (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Thus, even though the bulk of previous applications have not directly targeted dry AMD, the emerging evidence supporting cytoprotection and modulation of proteolytic and autophagy pathways in RPE cells provides a rationale for repurposing KYP-2047 in ocular disease states.

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

The biological target of KYP-2047 is the serine protease prolyl oligopeptidase (PREP), which is responsible for cleaving peptide bonds at the carboxyl side of internal proline residues in small peptides (typically less than ~30 amino acids) (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 22–24, 44–47). PREP is widely expressed in the central nervous system and peripheral tissues and has been implicated in multiple physiological processes including neuropeptide regulation and cell signaling. At the molecular level, the mechanism of action involves the binding of KYP-2047 to the enzyme’s active site, more specifically interacting with the catalytic serine residue. Many PREP inhibitors, including those in the class to which KYP-2047 belongs, are designed as substrate-like pseudopeptides that exploit the structure of the enzyme’s binding pockets (S1, S2, and S3) to achieve selectivity and high-affinity binding (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).

The inhibition by KYP-2047 is characterized as “tight-binding” with slow dissociation, meaning that once the inhibitor occupies the active site of PREP, it remains bound for a significant duration, thereby effectively reducing the enzyme’s catalytic turnover (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 70–72). In neurological models, inhibition of PREP has been associated with enhanced clearance of toxic protein aggregates such as alpha-synuclein, improved autophagic flux, and reduction in oxidative stress (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 85–88; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 9–11). The current therapeutic hypothesis in the context of dry AMD extrapolates these findings to retinal pigment epithelial cells.

In particular, the proposed mechanism posits that elevated PREP activity in RPE cells contributes to an accumulation of proline-rich peptides that, in turn, inhibit the activity of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and lysosomal cathepsin L. These cathepsins are critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and turnover of cellular debris. In dry AMD, defective protein clearance mechanisms, including impaired proteasomal and lysosomal function, result in the buildup of toxic deposits, such as A2E, and contribute to RPE dysfunction. By blocking PREP activity with KYP-2047 (which has an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range, reported to be approximately 30 nM), the proposed effect is to reduce the formation or accumulation of inhibitory peptides, thereby relieving the suppression on cathepsin activity. In addition, KYP-2047-mediated PREP inhibition may trigger downstream intracellular events such as autophagy activation and modulation of MAPK signaling pathways—including p38 and ERK1/2—which have been observed in other cell types and are known to reduce oxidative stress and inflammation (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 85–88).

At the biochemical level, these molecular interactions involve the inhibitor “locking in” the PREP enzyme in a conformational state that either prevents substrate access or alters the dynamics of peptide release once cleavage has occurred. Although the effects on neuropeptide levels (e.g., substance P, neurotensin) have been studied in central nervous system models—with mixed and sometimes counterintuitive outcomes (such as decreased acetylcholine levels) (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 8–16, 70–72)—the rationale for ocular repurposing rests on the idea that the same enzymatic inhibition can counteract the accumulation of cathepsin-inhibiting peptides in RPE cells. Notably, some studies have suggested that PREP inhibition can positively modulate autophagy, a process that is critical for cellular clearance mechanisms. Given that impaired autophagy is a central feature in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, a compound like KYP-2047 that both reduces toxic peptide accumulation and enhances proteolytic pathways presents an attractive, multitargeted strategy (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

The core hypothesis driving the repurposing of KYP-2047 for dry AMD is that inhibition of PREP will reduce the buildup of proline-rich peptides that otherwise impair lysosomal cathepsin activity. In RPE cells, efficient degradation of POS via phagocytosis and lysosomal function is essential for maintaining retinal homeostasis. In the setting of dry AMD, decreased cathepsin D and L activities are implicated in the inefficient clearance of cellular debris, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, ultimately causing RPE dysfunction.

In the proposed assay, RPE cells—typically the ARPE-19 cell line—will be challenged in an environment mimicking AMD pathology; for instance, by loading them with A2E and subjecting the cells to proteasomal stress. Under these conditions, the activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and L is compromised, and POS degradation is impaired. The application of KYP-2047 is expected to inhibit PREP activity with high potency, which theoretically will lead to a reduction in the concentration of peptide substrates that interfere with cathepsin enzymes (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).

The anticipated cascade of events is as follows:  
1. KYP-2047, at concentrations close to its low nanomolar IC₅₀, will effectively bind to and inhibit PREP in RPE cells.  
2. This inhibition will prevent the excessive cleavage of proline-containing peptides, thereby reducing the pool of inhibitory peptides that could otherwise bind to and decrease cathepsin D and L activities.  
3. As a consequence, the restoration of cathepsin activity is expected to improve the degradation of POS components as well as the clearance of other toxic debris, which is a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.  
4. Additionally, the compound’s reported anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects, demonstrated in ARPE-19 cells with defective proteasomal clearance, may further contribute to preserving RPE cell health by curtailing inflammatory cytokine production and oxidative stress (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 4–6).

It is also noteworthy that the mechanistic framework is further supported by the observation that PREP inhibition in other models has led to enhanced autophagy and improved clearance of aggregated proteins. In the context of AMD, effective POS degradation is not only dependent on cathepsin function but also on efficient autophagic flux. By indirectly modulating these pathways, KYP-2047 could offer dual benefits: restoration of lysosomal enzyme activity and bolstering of intracellular clearance mechanisms. Thus, the expected in vitro endpoints would likely include increased cathepsin D/L activity, elevated POS degradation (as detected by uptake assays), reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-6, IL-8, IL-1β), and diminished oxidative stress markers (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 4–6).

Moreover, the rationale includes supporting evidence from neurological and cancer research where PREP inhibition by compounds like KYP-2047 improved cell viability and reduced stress responses. Although previous clinical trials in central nervous system indications did not achieve long-term success, the safety data accrued from these studies may lower the translational barrier for ocular applications, provided that proper formulation and localized delivery (or systemic approaches with ocular distribution) can be achieved (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 4–5).

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

The evaluation of KYP-2047 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD involves weighing both its promising aspects and its uncertainties. On the positive side, KYP-2047 is a well-defined, highly potent inhibitor of PREP with an established chemical profile and a strong foundation in preclinical studies. Its synthetic origin as a peptidomimetic compound designed to bind the active site of PREP is well documented (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4), and the compound’s low nanomolar potency provides confidence that even modest drug exposures may achieve effective enzyme inhibition.

The repurposing strategy capitalizes on emerging evidence that PREP inhibitors can exert cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in RPE cells. In vitro studies conducted in ARPE-19 cells with impaired proteasomal clearance have demonstrated that KYP-2047 can reduce inflammatory cytokine production and promote cell viability (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). Given the central role of inflammation and defective lysosomal clearance in dry AMD, these findings provide a mechanistic rationale for testing KYP-2047 in this indication.

Furthermore, the proposed mechanism—whereby inhibition of PREP reduces the formation of inhibitory proline-rich peptides that suppress cathepsin activity—is mechanistically attractive. Restoring the function of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and L could feasibly improve the degradation of POS, a process known to be compromised in dry AMD. This dual-targeted approach (improving both enzyme activity and reducing cell stress) is particularly compelling in the context of a multifactorial disease such as AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

Despite these strengths, several potential weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. First, while extensive preclinical work has been carried out in neurological models—and there exists some early in vitro evidence of benefit in RPE cells—the direct connection between PREP activity and the inhibition of cathepsin function in the context of RPE biology remains largely hypothetical. The literature currently lacks robust in vivo studies in ocular models of dry AMD demonstrating that PREP inhibition translates into measurable improvements in retinal function and morphology. Historical clinical trials of PREP inhibitors for cognitive applications have encountered difficulties due to inconsistent efficacy, which raises concerns about the translation of in vitro findings to clinical benefits (Scuderi, 2023, pp. 133–135; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41).

Second, the formulation challenges associated with KYP-2047 cannot be overlooked. Its low water solubility necessitates specialized carriers (such as saline with 5% Tween® 80), which may complicate delivery to the eye, especially when considering the need for localized administration to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE. Appropriate ocular delivery systems (e.g., intravitreal injections or sustained-release implants) would need to be developed and optimized, which adds a layer of complexity to the overall drug development program (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47).

Another area of concern is the historical inconsistency of PREP inhibitor effects in clinical studies. Although there is evidence of neuroprotective benefits, the fact that several PREP inhibitors failed to advance through the clinical development pipeline for neurological indications suggests that the enzyme’s true physiological role remains incompletely defined. In the absence of a clear and reproducible biomarker for PREP inhibition in vivo, there is a risk that the biochemical benefits seen in cell culture studies may not be recapitulated in the complex environment of the human retina (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 70–72).

Moreover, because PREP is a ubiquitous enzyme expressed in many tissues, systemic administration of KYP-2047 might lead to off-target effects that could limit its therapeutic window. Although the safety profile observed in early neurological trials is encouraging, targeted delivery to the eye (to minimize systemic exposure) will be crucial if KYP-2047 is to be repurposed for dry AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

Finally, while the proposed mechanism that links elevated PREP activity with the inhibition of lysosomal cathepsins is intriguing, it remains to be validated by direct experimental data specifically in RPE cells. The current literature, including the recent study by Toppila and colleagues, primarily focuses on the cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory actions of KYP-2047 in ARPE-19 cells, but detailed biochemical analyses linking PREP inhibition mechanistically to improved cathepsin-mediated degradation of POS are still needed (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 4–6).

─────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

In summary, KYP-2047 is an established prolyl oligopeptidase inhibitor with a well-characterized chemical and pharmacological profile, offering promising features as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its ability to inhibit PREP at low nanomolar concentrations, coupled with demonstrated cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in preclinical RPE models, aligns well with the therapeutic need to restore lysosomal cathepsin activity and improve photoreceptor outer segment degradation in dry AMD (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 12–13).

The strategy to mitigate the accumulation of inhibitory proline-rich peptides and thereby reinstate effective lysosomal function is mechanistically plausible and supported by related studies in neural tissues. Nevertheless, the exact role of PREP in the modulation of cathepsin activity in RPE cells remains to be fully elucidated. In addition, the challenges of achieving appropriate ocular drug delivery and the historical precedents of inconsistent efficacy in PREP inhibitor clinical trials represent significant hurdles that must be addressed in future studies (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41).

Overall, while KYP-2047 brings strengths in terms of potency and a partially validated cytoprotective profile in in vitro models, its repurposing for dry AMD would require further in-depth preclinical studies. These studies should include in vivo efficacy assessments in relevant animal models of AMD, comprehensive pharmacokinetic and ocular distribution evaluations, and mechanistic experiments that clearly link PREP inhibition with improved cathepsin and lysosomal function in the RPE. Should these studies confirm the initial promising results, the favorable safety profile observed in prior neurological trials may indeed support the rapid translation of KYP-2047 into early-phase clinical testing for dry AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

In conclusion, KYP-2047 represents a promising, albeit still exploratory, approach to targeting a novel biochemical pathway in the context of dry AMD. The rationale is supported by a solid foundation of preclinical data in other disease models, yet its success in ocular repurposing will depend on overcoming formulation challenges and further clarifying the mechanistic underpinnings of its action in retinal pigment epithelial cells.

─────────────────────────────  
Strengths and Weaknesses Summary

Strengths:  
•  KYP-2047 is a potent, well-characterized PREP inhibitor with a strong synthetic and chemical development history (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4).  
•  Its low nanomolar IC₅₀ provides confidence in its biochemical efficacy, and available preclinical data indicate cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in RPE cell models (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22).  
•  The drug class has been extensively studied in neurological and cancer contexts, offering insights into its safety profile and potential mechanisms such as autophagy activation and reduced oxidative stress (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 70–72, 85–88).  
•  The hypothesis that PREP activity leads to the accumulation of cathepsin-inhibiting peptides is mechanistically plausible, which could lead to restoration of lysosomal enzyme activity in RPE cells (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).  

Weaknesses:  
•  Historically, PREP inhibitors have shown inconsistent efficacy in clinical trials for neurological applications; it remains uncertain whether the benefits will translate to the ocular setting (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 39–41).  
•  Direct evidence linking PREP inhibition with improvements in cathepsin activity and POS degradation in RPE cells is still limited, and further mechanistic studies are required (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
•  The low aqueous solubility of KYP-2047 necessitates complex formulations, which might complicate ocular drug delivery and could require novel delivery systems to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47).  
•  Systemic safety and potential off-target effects remain a concern, given that PREP is widely expressed and the compound’s systemic clearance and ocular bioavailability have yet to be thoroughly characterized in vivo (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

─────────────────────────────  
Final Remarks

Based on the current literature and the data available, KYP-2047 exhibits several attractive features for repurposing in dry AMD, especially regarding its potential to restore lysosomal function in the RPE by reducing the inhibitory load on cathepsins. However, while the biochemical rationale is compelling and early in vitro data are promising, significant challenges remain. Translational steps such as in vivo efficacy verification in AMD models, optimization of ocular formulation, and further elucidation of the mechanistic pathway are essential before proceeding to clinical development. Thus, KYP-2047 warrants further preclinical evaluation with a specific focus on its ocular pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics, which will ultimately determine its viability as a novel therapeutic candidate against dry age-related macular degeneration (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

This comprehensive review supports the notion that repurposing KYP-2047 for dry AMD is a promising strategy, but caution must be exercised given the prior challenges encountered with the PREP inhibitor class in other indications. Future studies should be designed to address these gaps and de-risk the development plan before large-scale clinical trials are considered.

Early studies demonstrated that inhibition of GSK-3β with compounds like SB415286 could protect neurons from intracellular stresses by moderately suppressing pro-apoptotic signals (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In the ocular field, GSK-3β inhibitors have been explored in the context of diabetic retinopathy, where their use was associated with improved retinal ganglion cell survival and mitigation of neurodegenerative processes induced by oxidative stress (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20). Furthermore, related compounds such as SB216763—sharing similar mechanisms—with evidence of restoring Nrf2 levels in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) under oxidative stress supports the hypothesis that GSK-3β inhibition is beneficial in ocular settings (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6; Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 10–12). Despite these promising findings, the clinical evidence directly linking GSK-3β inhibition to the treatment of dry AMD remains sparse. In fact, comprehensive analyses such as those performed using the Open Targets Platform have revealed only a very weak association between GSK3B and AMD with minimal literature evidence, suggesting that while the concept is scientifically sound and mechanistically plausible, direct translational studies in dry AMD are still in an early stage (Buniello et al., 2025). Nevertheless, the preclinical use of SB415286 in retinal models of diabetic retinopathy and its documented capacity to modulate pathways relevant to oxidative stress and autophagy imply that repurposing this candidate for dry AMD merits further investigation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, GSK-3β is a serine/threonine kinase that is constitutively active in many cells and functions as a pivotal regulator of several intracellular signaling cascades. Under basal conditions, GSK-3β phosphorylates its substrates—including β-catenin—thereby marking them for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. In the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, the inhibition of GSK-3β (either through upstream signals such as Wnt ligand binding or via pharmacological inhibitors like SB415286) prevents the phosphorylation of β-catenin, allowing it to accumulate in the cytoplasm and eventually translocate into the nucleus (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Once in the nucleus, β-catenin forms complexes with TCF/LEF transcription factors to drive the transcription of genes involved in cell proliferation, differentiation, and cytoskeletal remodeling. In the context of RPE cells, this activation is critical because it is believed to upregulate lysosomal proteins, such as LAMP1, and phagocytic receptors, like MERTK, that are essential for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17; Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).  

Moreover, GSK-3β also exerts a negative regulatory influence on the Nrf2/NRF2 antioxidant pathway. Under oxidative stress, Nrf2 typically transactivates a battery of cytoprotective genes; however, GSK-3β phosphorylates Nrf2 at specific motifs within its Neh6 domain, facilitating recognition by the β-TrCP E3 ubiquitin ligase and leading to its degradation (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6). Hence, inhibition of GSK-3β with SB415286 can stabilize Nrf2, thereby reinforcing the cellular antioxidant capacity—a particularly attractive mechanism given the elevated oxidative stress encountered in aging RPE cells in dry AMD.  

In addition to these signaling events, inhibition of GSK-3β modulates autophagy. Research indicates that proper autophagic flux is necessary for the turnover of damaged cellular components, including the disposal of POS debris, and that impaired autophagy is a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 10–12, 32–34). By inhibiting GSK-3β, SB415286 is hypothesized to promote the autophagy/Nrf2 axis, thereby enhancing lysosomal function and improving the clearance of accumulated waste products in RPE cells. It is also important to note that GSK-3β is implicated in the regulation of the cytoskeletal machinery; its inhibition may lead to reorganization of actin and other cytoskeletal elements, which is critical for the phagocytic process in RPE cells (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). However, caution is warranted because GSK-3β not only modulates beneficial pathways but also participates in processes such as epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), where excessive or inappropriate inhibition has been associated with fibrotic changes in the RPE (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 14–18). Thus, while the inhibition of GSK-3β by SB415286 is expected to elevate β-catenin levels and trigger downstream transcription of lysosomal and cytoskeletal genes, the balance of these signaling events must be carefully modulated to avoid adverse outcomes.

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis proposes that SB415286 will act directly on RPE cells by inhibiting GSK-3β, thereby releasing the inhibition on β-catenin. The resultant accumulation and nuclear translocation of β-catenin are expected to drive the transcription of a subset of genes critical for maintaining RPE function, including those involved in lysosome biogenesis (e.g., LAMP1) and the phagocytic machinery (e.g., MERTK). In dry AMD, a deficiency in the clearance of POS is a contributing factor to RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration, so enhancing gene expression that supports these processes is of significant therapeutic interest (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17).  

In cell-based assays—particularly flow cytometry-based phagocytosis assays—it is anticipated that treatment with SB415286 will result in an increased rate of POS uptake by RPE cells. This improvement in phagocytic efficiency is thought to arise from the upregulation of cytoskeletal genes that govern actin dynamics, which in turn facilitate the formation of phagocytic cups and subsequent internalization of photoreceptor debris (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5; Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 32–34). Additionally, by relieving the negative regulation on Nrf2, SB415286 is expected to bolster the antioxidant defense mechanisms in RPE cells. The stabilization of Nrf2 not only aids in the upregulation of detoxification and radical-scavenging enzymes but also indirectly supports autophagy—a process crucial for the degradation of cellular waste and maintenance of cellular homeostasis in the aging RPE (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6).  

Furthermore, emerging data from ocular models of diabetic retinopathy provide supporting evidence that GSK-3β inhibitors can improve retinal cell survival and function. Although diabetic retinopathy and dry AMD are distinct conditions, both involve significant oxidative stress, inflammation, and RPE dysfunction. The translational potential observed in these models suggests that SB415286 may similarly ameliorate pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD by enhancing the phagocytic and lysosomal capacity of RPE cells (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20). Nevertheless, the dualistic nature of GSK-3β’s roles necessitates a cautious interpretation; while promoting β-catenin signaling is advantageous for lysosomal and cytoskeletal gene expression, overactivation of Wnt signaling has been implicated in unwanted cellular phenotypes such as EMT, which could potentiate fibrotic responses if not carefully controlled (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 14–18). Therefore, the expected beneficial effects of SB415286 on POS clearance must be weighed against the risk of activating other deleterious pathways.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating SB415286 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key aspects emerge from the literature review. On one hand, the compound’s potent inhibition of GSK-3β, a kinase centrally involved in multiple signaling pathways, offers a mechanistically coherent strategy for addressing several pathological features of dry AMD. By targeting GSK-3β, SB415286 is designed to simultaneously activate Wnt/β-catenin signaling and stabilize Nrf2, thereby promoting the transcription of genes such as LAMP1 and MERTK that are essential for effective lysosomal function and phagocytosis in RPE cells (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17). The induction of lysosomal and cytoskeletal genes is expected to enhance the phagocytic clearance of POS, a critical function that is often compromised in the diseased RPE, ultimately helping to mitigate the progression of dry AMD. Additionally, supportive evidence from diabetic retinopathy models and other retinal degeneration studies suggests that modulating GSK-3β activity can exert beneficial effects in ocular tissues (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20).  

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be considered. First, GSK-3β is a multifunctional kinase that plays roles in a wide array of cellular processes; it is involved not only in the regulation of the Wnt/β-catenin and Nrf2 pathways but also in the control of apoptosis, glucose homeostasis, and even inflammatory responses. The broad distribution and pleiotropic functions of GSK-3β raise concerns about off-target effects and unwanted side effects when its activity is pharmacologically inhibited. For instance, unchecked activation of β-catenin signaling could inadvertently promote epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in RPE cells—a process that has been linked to fibrotic changes and worsening of retinal pathology (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 14–18). The risk of such adverse outcomes underscores the importance of fine-tuning the dosage and exposure duration of SB415286 to achieve a therapeutic window that maximizes benefits while minimizing collateral activation of harmful signaling cascades.  

Another notable limitation is the relatively weak overall association between GSK3B and AMD as evidenced by integrative platforms, which point to only a minimal body of literature linking GSK-3β directly to the pathogenesis of AMD (Buniello et al., 2025). This weak association suggests that, although the mechanistic rationale for employing GSK-3β inhibitors is compelling at a biochemical level, direct evidence from AMD models remains limited. Consequently, while preclinical data in related retinal conditions are encouraging, additional research using dry AMD-specific models is required to establish the efficacy, safety, and dosing regimens for SB415286 in this context.  

Furthermore, the dual role of GSK-3β in both apoptosis and survival presents another layer of complexity. On one hand, inhibition of GSK-3β may protect RPE cells from intrinsic apoptotic stimuli by preventing the activation of mitochondrial death pathways; on the other hand, it may also inadvertently increase sensitivity to extrinsic apoptotic signals, thereby complicating the overall cellular response (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–5). This paradoxical effect, combined with the potential for overlap with other kinases given the structural similarity among kinase domains, necessitates rigorous pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic investigations to ensure that SB415286 can be administered safely without compromising RPE cell viability or function.  

In summary, SB415286 stands out as a promising repurposed drug candidate with a strong mechanistic foundation for the treatment of dry AMD. Its targeted inhibition of GSK-3β is expected to unleash β-catenin–driven transcriptional programs that upregulate lysosomal, cytoskeletal, and phagocytic genes, thereby enhancing the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments—a critical deficit in dry AMD pathology (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17). The compound’s track record in preclinical ocular models, particularly in contexts where oxidative stress and autophagic impairment are prominent, supports its potential translational value (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20). Nevertheless, the complexity of GSK-3β’s role in cellular signaling, the modest association between GSK3B and AMD observed in broader datasets, and the possibility of off-target effects, especially the unintended activation of fibrotic pathways, represent significant challenges that need to be addressed through comprehensive preclinical studies. Careful evaluation of dose, duration, and cell-type specificity will be critical in harnessing the therapeutic benefits of SB415286 while avoiding its potential pitfalls. Overall, while SB415286 is a promising candidate for dry AMD, its further development will require a balanced approach characterized by detailed mechanistic studies, robust in vitro and in vivo evaluations, and a clear understanding of the trade-offs inherent in modulating a kinase as pleiotropic as GSK-3β (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–3, 16–17; Buniello et al., 2025).
