Each section draws on the available literature and data from the provided context.

────────────────────────────────────────  
I. OVERVIEW OF THE THERAPEUTIC CANDIDATE  

GSK0660 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor that gained prominence as the very first PPARβ/δ (peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor beta/delta)–selective inhibitory ligand reported in the scientific literature (Toth et al., 2012). Its design represents a significant breakthrough in the field of nuclear receptor modulation by demonstrating that subtype selectivity within the PPAR family can indeed be achieved with a low molecular weight organic compound. Structurally, GSK0660 belongs to the thiophenecarboxylate chemical class and features a uniquely tailored molecular architecture that includes several key pharmacophores: a methoxy‐substituted 1,4‐diaminobenzene core thought to be essential for receptor binding; a 4′‐aminophenyl substituent that not only contributes to high‐affinity interactions with the receptor’s ligand‐binding domain but also offers a promising site for subsequent chemical modification; and a methyl thiophene carboxylate moiety that helps orient the molecule within the hydrophobic pocket of PPARβ/δ (Toth et al., 2012). Extensive structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies have demonstrated that modifications to portions of the molecule—particularly the 4′‐aminophenyl substituent by introduction of medium‐length n‐alkyl chains—can enhance binding affinity by up to tenfold compared to the original structure (Toth et al., 2012).

GSK0660 was originally synthesized through a multistep organic process that began with commercially available precursors, followed by key transformation steps such as nucleophilic aromatic substitution to install appropriate groups on a benzene ring, catalytic reduction to generate the requisite amine functions, and finally sulfonamidation reactions to yield the final compound (Toth et al., 2012). In essence, this compound was developed primarily as a research tool to dissect the specific biological roles of PPARβ/δ and does not itself originate from a natural product or traditional antibiotic source. Instead, its design and synthesis reflect a targeted medicinal chemistry strategy aimed at obtaining a high degree of receptor selectivity.

Belonging to the broader class of PPAR modulators, GSK0660 occupies a niche that is distinct from the more commonly encountered PPAR agonists. Whereas most efforts historically have focused on the development of agonists for metabolic disorders and anti‐inflammatory indications, GSK0660 and its close analogs are used primarily to achieve receptor inhibition. This selective antagonism is critical for experimental setups in which the contribution of PPARβ/δ to downstream gene regulation and cellular homeostasis is being evaluated (Toth et al., 2012). Furthermore, the structure of GSK0660 aligns with the more general trends in nuclear receptor ligand development, capturing several “drug‐like” properties that, despite known limitations in bioavailability, maintain its status as a high‐quality research compound in proof‐of‐concept investigations.

────────────────────────────────────────  
II. THERAPEUTIC HISTORY  

GSK0660 has been widely used as a chemical probe to examine the biological functions of PPARβ/δ in various preclinical models. In early studies, it served as the first selective antagonist for this receptor subtype and was instrumental in clarifying the roles of PPARβ/δ in lipid metabolism, cell proliferation, and inflammation (Toth et al., 2012). Its experimental applications have spanned a number of research areas. For instance, several investigations in models of neurodegeneration—particularly in Parkinson’s disease—have utilized GSK0660 in both in vitro experiments (using human neuroblastoma cell lines such as SH‐SY5Y) and in vivo rodent models. In these studies, GSK0660 was able to negate the neuroprotective effects of PPARβ/δ agonists by blocking the receptor’s activity, thereby providing compelling evidence for a detrimental role of PPARβ/δ activation under neurodegenerative stress conditions (Antonosante et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023). Such data have contributed to a nuanced understanding of PPAR signaling in the brain, implying that under certain conditions receptor inhibition may be more desirable than activation.

Moreover, GSK0660 has also been evaluated in dermatological applications. In recent studies focusing on psoriasis‐like skin disease, GSK0660—when formulated topically—was shown to mitigate epidermal hyperplasia and reduce inflammatory markers without systemic drug accumulation, thus proving useful for localized treatment strategies (Hack et al., 2012). These dermatological studies not only underscored the compound’s ability to counteract PPARβ/δ‐mediated signaling in inflamed tissues but also highlighted practical challenges associated with its formulation. For example, its inherent chemical instability, manifesting as a tendency to undergo oxidation (where solutions of GSK0660 may turn green upon light exposure at room temperature), underscores issues related to its shelf‐life and stability in clinical formulations (Hack et al., 2012; Lieber, 2015).

Despite its usefulness in these diverse experimental models—ranging from neurodegenerative to inflammatory skin diseases—the therapeutic history of GSK0660 reveals a critical gap: there is no record within the available literature of its application in ocular diseases or in the treatment of dry AMD. A systematic search of clinical trial databases has confirmed that no human clinical investigations have been registered evaluating GSK0660 for indications such as retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, macular degeneration, or related ocular conditions (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). In other words, while the compound has been validated as a tool in non‐ocular systems, its repurposing for dry AMD is entirely uncharted territory. This lack of ocular‐specific data is a limitation that must be considered when assessing its potential for enhancing lysosomal function in RPE cells.

Furthermore, limitations inherent to GSK0660—most notably its poor systemic bioavailability and the requirement for relatively high concentrations to achieve effective antagonism—are recurring themes in its therapeutic history (Toth et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016; Lieber, 2015). Such pharmacokinetic drawbacks have spurred efforts to develop improved derivatives that possess enhanced potency and bioavailability. For instance, SAR studies have evaluated modifications to the 4′‐aminophenyl substituent, yielding analogs with substantially higher binding affinities (Toth et al., 2012). Nonetheless, all available records indicate that GSK0660 itself has remained primarily as a research tool rather than advancing to clinical or even advanced developmental stages in any therapeutic domain beyond the proof‐of‐concept experimental setting.

────────────────────────────────────────  
III. MECHANISM OF ACTION  

At the molecular level, GSK0660 exerts its action by binding selectively to the ligand‐binding domain (LBD) of PPARβ/δ, thereby inhibiting receptor activation. This interaction is competitive in nature; GSK0660 occupies the receptor pocket, effectively blocking binding of endogenous ligands or synthetic agonists (Toth et al., 2012). The molecular determinants of this selective interaction have been elucidated through SAR studies. The methoxy‐substituted 1,4‐diaminobenzene core forms critical hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts with specific residues within the LBD, while the 4′‐aminophenyl group and the methyl thiophene carboxylate moiety contribute additional electrostatic and van der Waals interactions that stabilize the binding complex (Toth et al., 2012).

A notable aspect of GSK0660’s pharmacology is its dual mode of action. In addition to functioning as a competitive antagonist, GSK0660 has been reported in some experimental contexts to act as an inverse agonist. Under basal conditions—where PPARβ/δ exhibits a low level of constitutive transcriptional activity—GSK0660 can further suppress receptor activity beyond mere inhibition by promoting the recruitment of transcriptional corepressors. These corepressors (including members of the NCoR/SMRT family and class I histone deacetylases) bind to the receptor‐corepressor complex, modifying chromatin structure and decreasing transcription of PPARβ/δ target genes (Lieber, 2015; Monsalve et al., 2013). Through these mechanisms, GSK0660 effectively shifts the balance away from gene activation toward transcriptional repression.

The detailed molecular interactions responsible for these phenomena have been characterized using a variety of biochemical assays, including competitive TR‐FRET binding studies and reporter assays in cell‐based systems (Toth et al., 2012). The ability of GSK0660 to inhibit transcriptional activation in response to exogenous agonists has been well demonstrated in several cell models—including skeletal muscle myoblasts where PPARβ/δ activates genes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase‐1A or pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase‐4 (Monsalve et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016). This cellular pharmacology underpins its potential to serve as an experimental “off‐switch” for PPARβ/δ‐mediated transcription.

In the context of the proposed repurposing hypothesis for dry AMD, the mechanistic emphasis shifts toward the regulation of lysosomal biogenesis through transcription factor EB (TFEB). Although direct evidence linking PPARβ/δ antagonism with the modulation of TFEB activity in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells is not yet established, the working hypothesis posits that PPARβ/δ normally exerts a repressive influence on a suite of genes involved in lysosomal function—the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. TFEB is recognized as the master regulator of lysosomal and autophagic gene expression and, upon activation, translocates to the nucleus to drive expression of critical lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1 and proteases such as Cathepsin D (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). By antagonizing PPARβ/δ, GSK0660 is hypothesized to relieve this repressive effect, thereby “releasing the brake” on TFEB activity. This would allow for enhanced transcription of lysosomal genes that are vital for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and the clearance of toxic lipofuscin constituents like A2E.

It is important to note that while the biochemical rationale is compelling, the specific molecular details linking PPARβ/δ inhibition to enhanced TFEB function have yet to be firmly established in ocular models. Nonetheless, the ability of GSK0660 to modulate receptor conformation and corepressor recruitment provides a credible mechanistic basis for the hypothesis, even as further studies must elucidate the crosstalk between PPARβ/δ signaling and the lysosomal gene network in RPE cells (Toth et al., 2012; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Lieber, 2015).

────────────────────────────────────────  
IV. EXPECTED EFFECT IN RPE MODELS  

Dry AMD is characterized by gradual dysfunction and atrophy of the RPE, which plays an essential role in the daily phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). A central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD is the accumulation of undigested POS material and the toxic byproduct A2E, which, in turn, leads to lipofuscin deposition, oxidative stress, and eventual RPE cell death. Critical to the maintenance of RPE homeostasis is the proper function of the lysosomal machinery responsible for cellular clearance. Lysosomal biogenesis, autophagic flux, and the efficient degradation of internalized debris are centrally regulated by transcription factor EB (TFEB), which activates the CLEAR network of genes encoding proteins such as LAMP1 (a lysosomal‐associated membrane protein) and Cathepsin D (a key lysosomal protease) (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Under normal conditions, PPARβ/δ appears to play a role in regulating gene expression through the recruitment of coactivators and corepressors. The hypothesis driving the repurposing of GSK0660 for dry AMD is that activated PPARβ/δ imposes a repressive signal on the CLEAR network genes, thereby limiting TFEB‐mediated lysosomal biogenesis in RPE cells. In an experimental paradigm based on A2E‐loaded RPE cell cultures—a standard in vitro model that mimics the cellular environment of dry AMD—it is anticipated that treatment with GSK0660 at concentrations approximating its receptor inhibition IC₅₀ (~200 nM) will alleviate PPARβ/δ‐mediated repression. This derepression is expected to promote the nuclear translocation of TFEB and upregulate its target genes, culminating in an enhanced lysosomal degradative capacity (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

The expected cellular responses following GSK0660 treatment in RPE models can be summarized as follows. First, by interrupting the ligand‐induced activation of PPARβ/δ, GSK0660 should shift the balance between transcriptional coactivators and corepressors in favor of a transcriptional environment that supports lysosomal gene expression. This would lead to a measurable increase in the mRNA and protein levels of LAMP1 and Cathepsin D, both of which are critical for lysosomal function and for the degradation of POS components (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Second, the enhanced expression of these proteins should translate into an improved capacity for POS degradation—a phenotype that can be monitored using assays that track the clearance of fluorescently labeled POS or the reduction in A2E accumulation. Third, improved lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic clearance are expected to reduce the chronic accumulation of lipofuscin, thereby mitigating oxidative stress and preserving RPE function over time.

In addition to these molecular and cellular endpoints, there is also the expectation that successful derepression of TFEB activity will indirectly contribute to improved cell viability and resistance to stress. The RPE, being highly active in terms of metabolic turnover and phagocytic activity, is particularly vulnerable to the detrimental effects of lysosomal dysfunction. Thus, a treatment that effectively restores lysosomal function is likely to bolster the RPE’s ability to manage accumulated debris and maintain metabolic homeostasis.

It should be acknowledged that one of the primary challenges will be the optimization of the effective dose of GSK0660 in the context of ocular cells. While the compound exhibits potent receptor inhibition in vitro, previous studies have identified limitations with its bioavailability and chemical stability (Toth et al., 2012; Strosznajder et al., 2021). These issues necessitate careful attention to formulation and drug delivery strategies tailored to the ocular environment. For example, controlled‐release formulations or nanoparticle‐based delivery systems might be required to ensure that effective local concentrations of GSK0660 can be maintained in the retina while avoiding systemic exposure and off‐target effects.

Moreover, despite the attractive theoretical framework linking PPARβ/δ antagonism to TFEB activation, direct experimental evidence in RPE cells is currently lacking. As such, the expected effect remains a hypothesis that must be rigorously validated through a series of in vitro assays—including quantitative PCR for lysosomal gene expression, immunoblotting for protein markers, and functional assays to assess the clearance of photoreceptor debris. Additional studies might also involve monitoring autophagic flux using established markers such as LC3-II and p62 to provide a more comprehensive picture of the compound’s impact on RPE cell homeostasis.

────────────────────────────────────────  
V. OVERALL EVALUATION  

GSK0660 stands out as a highly characterized PPARβ/δ antagonist with a well‐documented profile in non‐ocular applications. The compound’s discovery as the first selective ligand for PPARβ/δ established a benchmark in the field and has since made it a prominent research tool in studies of neurodegeneration, inflammation, and even dermatological applications such as psoriasis (Toth et al., 2012; Antonosante et al., 2023; Hack et al., 2012). From a medicinal chemistry perspective, the structural features of GSK0660—the methoxy‐substituted 1,4‐diaminobenzene core, the 4′‐aminophenyl substituent, and the methyl thiophene carboxylate moiety—endow the molecule with high selectivity for the receptor. SAR studies have demonstrated that modifications to these groups can further enhance binding affinity, offering prospects for optimization if needed (Toth et al., 2012).

The principal strength of the compound lies in its receptor selectivity and in its demonstrated capacity to function as both a competitive antagonist and an inverse agonist. This duality is central to the proposed mechanism for reversing PPARβ/δ‐mediated repression of TFEB, which in turn may enhance lysosomal biogenesis and improve the degradative capacity of RPE cells. Considering that lysosomal dysfunction and the resultant accumulation of undegraded POS and toxic byproducts such as A2E are recognized pathological features of dry AMD, the hypothesis that GSK0660 can restore a more robust lysosomal function is innovative and scientifically compelling (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

However, significant caveats temper this optimism. One major limitation is that, to date, GSK0660 has not been studied in the context of retinal diseases or any ocular applications. Although extensive preclinical research has been undertaken in models of Parkinson’s disease and psoriasis, no direct evidence supports its efficacy in modulating RPE cell lysosomal function or in mitigating dry AMD pathology (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Lieber, 2015). This represents a considerable translational gap that would require substantial preclinical work to bridge.

Another critical challenge is the compound’s pharmacokinetic profile. GSK0660 is known to suffer from poor bioavailability, and it frequently requires relatively high concentrations to achieve its intended effects in vitro. Furthermore, the chemical instability of GSK0660—demonstrated by its tendency to oxidize and change color under conditions of light exposure and room temperature storage—poses additional obstacles for formulation development, especially in a sensitive environment such as the eye where prolonged stability and controlled drug release are paramount (Toth et al., 2012; Hack et al., 2012; Strosznajder et al., 2021).

The translation of these findings to an application in dry AMD would also necessitate a careful reexamination of dosing strategies and delivery mechanisms. For instance, while topical formulations have been effective in dermatological models (Hack et al., 2012), the ocular setting will require alternative approaches to bypass obstacles such as the blood‐retinal barrier and to achieve sustained local drug concentrations without systemic spillover. Innovative drug delivery platforms—perhaps involving biodegradable implants, nanoparticles, or hydrogels—will likely need to be developed to turn the promising molecular mechanism of GSK0660 into a clinically viable treatment option.

Furthermore, although the mechanistic rationale linking PPARβ/δ antagonism with the activation of TFEB is theoretically sound, the direct evidence supporting this specific link in RPE cells is limited. Existing literature on TFEB clearly demonstrates its role as a master regulator of lysosomal genes in retinal cells (Abokyi & Tse, 2025), yet none of the studies directly establish that PPARβ/δ provides a repressive signal to TFEB in this context. Thus, the entire repurposing hypothesis, while attractive, remains speculative until dedicated studies in RPE models confirm that inhibition of PPARβ/δ by GSK0660 indeed results in derepression of TFEB and a subsequent upregulation of lysosomal markers such as LAMP1 and Cathepsin D.

Lastly, while GSK0660 has garnered a robust reputation as a research tool, its historical use in non‐ocular tissues suggests that extensive medicinal chemistry optimization may be required to enhance its physicochemical properties for ocular therapy. In essence, the compound may serve as an excellent lead structure, but modifications that improve its bioavailability, chemical stability, and potency in the ocular microenvironment will be essential steps before considering any clinical translation.

In summary, GSK0660 embodies both promise and challenges as a candidate for repurposing to treat dry AMD. On the one hand, its well‐defined receptor selectivity and dual mode of inhibition provide a solid mechanistic foundation to hypothesize that, by antagonizing PPARβ/δ, it may relieve repression of TFEB and thereby restore lysosomal function in RPE cells. On the other hand, the lack of any direct ocular data, coupled with severe limitations in bioavailability and chemical stability, underscores that significant preclinical validation and formulation optimization will be required before GSK0660 can be considered a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Toth et al., 2012; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Zhang et al., 2016; Hack et al., 2012).

────────────────────────────────────────  
VI. CONCLUDING REMARKS  

Repurposing GSK0660 for dry AMD is underpinned by an innovative hypothesis that bridges nuclear receptor biology with lysosomal regulation—a convergence that is highly relevant given the central role of lysosomal dysfunction in RPE degeneration. The expected therapeutic mechanism is clear: by blocking PPARβ/δ activity, GSK0660 may relieve a repressive influence on the CLEAR network, thereby enabling TFEB to drive lysosomal biogenesis and enhance the clearance of toxic photoreceptor debris. Such a therapeutic approach would address a key pathogenic process behind the progressive accumulation of lipofuscin and other deleterious cellular materials in the RPE, which are hallmarks of dry AMD (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Nonetheless, several hurdles must be overcome for this conceptual strategy to move forward. First, the absence of any preexisting data linking GSK0660 to ocular applications necessitates a comprehensive set of in vitro experiments targeting RPE cells—including assays for gene expression, lysosomal function, and POS degradation. Second, the known limitations of GSK0660—poor bioavailability, chemical instability, and the requirement for high concentrations—must be addressed via improved drug formulations or through the development of optimized analogs. Third, it will be critical to investigate whether the proposed crosstalk between PPARβ/δ signaling and TFEB‐mediated lysosomal regulation holds true in the RPE microenvironment, potentially involving studies using animal models of dry AMD. Finally, given the highly specialized nature of ocular drug delivery, translational efforts may need to incorporate modern delivery strategies such as implantable controlled‐release devices, nanoparticles, or hydrogels to ensure sustained local efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure.

In its current form, GSK0660 remains a highly informative research tool with excellent selectivity for PPARβ/δ, yet its direct translation into an ocular therapeutic faces significant challenges. The compound’s historical utility in preclinical models of Parkinson’s disease and psoriasis attests to its potential to modulate critical signaling pathways; however, the leap from these systems to effective treatment of dry AMD will require concerted efforts in medicinal chemistry, formulation science, and rigorous preclinical testing (Antonosante et al., 2023; Hack et al., 2012; Boya et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The proposed therapeutic candidate is a bivalent agonist anti-MerTK antibody (Merestinib-like; R&D Systems Cat. No. MAB8916) designed to target the extracellular domain of the Mer tyrosine kinase (MerTK) receptor. MerTK is a receptor tyrosine kinase expressed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells that plays a critical role in the daily clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). The antibody is engineered to mimic the binding of natural ligands, such as Growth Arrest–Specific 6 (Gas6), by binding with high affinity (EC₅₀ ~ 10 nM as hypothesized) and promoting receptor dimerization, which is essential for activating downstream signaling cascades involved in phagocytosis. As a monoclonal antibody, it falls within a class of biologics that have been used successfully in oncology, autoimmune disorders, and other degenerative diseases. Historically, therapeutic antibodies have been harnessed not only for neutralizing targets but also for agonizing receptors to restore deficient signaling. Here, the candidate is repurposed for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) based on extensive preclinical evidence demonstrating that MerTK activation enhances actin-mediated phagocytic cup formation and promotes the efficient uptake of POS debris—a function that becomes compromised in aging RPE (Albert et al., 2015).

The synthesis of such an antibody typically involves recombinant DNA techniques wherein the variable regions, optimized for high-affinity binding to the MerTK extracellular domain, are fused to constant regions of immunoglobulins to generate a full-length IgG. The bivalency inherent to IgG molecules is particularly advantageous because it promotes receptor cross-linking, a prerequisite for MerTK autophosphorylation and full activation of its signaling functions (Ghosh et al., 2024; Artero-Castro et al., 2021). In this context, the candidate can be considered a repurposed biologic with a new application in the modulation of RPE function in dry AMD—a disease for which few effective treatments currently exist.  

Therapeutic History:  
The significance of MerTK in retinal pigment epithelium physiology has been firmly established in both preclinical and ex vivo studies. Pioneering work has shown that MerTK is essential for POS phagocytosis, as evidenced by experiments in which MerTK deficiency in animal models such as the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) rat leads to the accumulation of photoreceptor debris and subsequent retinal degeneration (Albert et al., 2015; Lew et al., 2020). In addition, studies using human embryonic stem cell–derived RPE and gene-corrected patient-derived hiPSC-RPE have demonstrated that restoring MerTK expression correlates with a significant recovery of phagocytic capacity, with phagocytosis rates in corrected cells approaching those seen in healthy controls (Almedawar et al., 2020; Artero-Castro et al., 2021).  

While many prior studies have investigated the use of natural ligands, such as Gas6 or Protein S, to stimulate MerTK-mediated phagocytosis (Albert et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2016), there is comparatively little clinical or preclinical data evaluating an antibody-based agonist approach to directly activate MerTK in the context of dry AMD. Research employing small molecule modulators—for example, the use of tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) that can restore MerTK phosphorylation in RPE cells (Murase et al., 2015)—provides additional evidence that pharmacological activation of MerTK can reverse phagocytic deficits. However, antibody-mediated receptor agonism represents a unique modality that offers the potential for high specificity and controlled activation, with a dosing regimen that could be similar to intravitreal injections already common in retinal therapeutics. Despite a strong theoretical rationale, direct clinical or veterinary application of MerTK agonists for dry AMD remains to be established, making this candidate an innovative repurposing strategy targeting a well-validated mechanism in RPE homeostasis (Albert et al., 2015; Ghosh et al., 2024; Li, 2013).

Mechanism of Action:  
MerTK is a member of the TAM (Tyro3, Axl, MerTK) receptor family and is integral to the phagocytic clearance of POS debris—a daily task required to maintain retinal homeostasis and photoreceptor health. Under physiological conditions, MerTK is activated when its extracellular domain binds to its natural ligands (e.g., Gas6), which leads to receptor dimerization and subsequent autophosphorylation on key tyrosine residues (such as Tyr-867). This phosphorylation event creates docking sites for intracellular adaptor proteins and kinases, including GRB2, phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), and focal adhesion kinase (FAK). Downstream of these interactions, small GTPases such as Rac1 are activated, triggering actin cytoskeletal reorganization necessary for the formation of the phagocytic cup that physically engulfs the POS (Albert et al., 2015; Ghosh et al., 2024; Szatmári-Tóth, 2016).  

The candidate antibody is designed to bind to the MerTK extracellular domain in a bivalent manner, effectively mimicking the natural ligand’s mode of receptor engagement. By cross-linking MerTK molecules on the surface of RPE cells, the antibody induces receptor dimerization, leading to robust autophosphorylation. This activation is expected to enhance intracellular signaling pathways that govern both phagocytosis and the anti-inflammatory functions of MerTK, a dual role critical for maintaining retinal integrity (Ghosh et al., 2024; Murase et al., 2015). Notably, studies have demonstrated that when MerTK is activated—either through natural ligand engagement or by compounds that promote its phosphorylation—RPE cells display increased uptake of photoreceptor outer segments, thereby preventing the toxic accumulation of cellular debris that is characteristic of dry AMD (Albert et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2016).  

At the molecular level, the cross-linking effect is central to the candidate’s mechanism of action; the bivalent antibody not only occupies the ligand binding site but also forces an active dimer configuration that is necessary to initiate downstream signaling. This mechanism is analogous to how engineered agonist antibodies have been employed in other receptor systems to restore deficient signaling pathways. Furthermore, MerTK activation has been linked to the modulation of anti-inflammatory cascades, which contributes to cell survival and tissue homeostasis—a particularly relevant benefit in the context of retinal degeneration where secondary inflammation plays a major causative role (Murase et al., 2015; Albert et al., 2015).  

Expected Effect:  
In in vitro assays employing human RPE cells, including primary cultures and hiPSC-derived RPE, the expected outcome following treatment with the agonist anti-MerTK antibody is multifaceted. First, engagement of the antibody with MerTK should result in a dose-dependent increase in receptor autophosphorylation, which can be measured using phospho-specific antibodies against key tyrosine residues (e.g., Tyr-867). This biochemical readout will serve as a direct indicator of receptor activation. Second, the activation of MerTK is anticipated to stimulate downstream signaling pathways that culminate in the reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton via Rac1 activation. This cytoskeletal remodeling is critical for the formation of the phagocytic cup—a dynamic structure that facilitates the engulfment and internalization of photoreceptor outer segments (Albert et al., 2015; Ghosh et al., 2024; Szatmári-Tóth, 2016).  

Functionally, enhanced MerTK signaling is predicted to lead to increased phagocytic activity in RPE cells. This improvement could be quantified using established phagocytosis assays that involve adding labeled photoreceptor outer segments (or surrogate particles such as pHrodo-conjugated substrates) to cultured cells. For example, studies have shown that restoring MerTK expression in MERTK-deficient cells via gene correction can recover phagocytosis rates to approximately 73% of those observed in healthy cells (Artero-Castro et al., 2021). By directly stimulating MerTK with the candidate antibody, one would expect to see a similarly significant enhancement of POS clearance in RPE cells, potentially mitigating the buildup of lipofuscin and other toxic debris that drive the degenerative process in dry AMD (Artero-Castro et al., 2021; Albert et al., 2015).  

Moreover, given MerTK’s known anti-inflammatory roles, antibody-mediated activation might also suppress the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and limit microglial activation—a secondary benefit that could help stabilize the retinal environment. The combination of improved debris clearance and reduced inflammation is particularly appealing in dry AMD, where the failure of RPE phagocytosis initiates a cascade of cellular stress and immune activation (Ghosh et al., 2024; Lieffrig et al., 2023). The overall expected effect is not only the enhancement of phagocytic activity but also the restoration of a more homeostatic and anti-inflammatory state in the RPE, potentially delaying or even reversing the progression of retinal degeneration.  

The effect is anticipated to be measurable at multiple levels: biochemical activation of MerTK (through increased phosphorylation levels), morphological changes in RPE cells (such as enhanced formation of actin-rich phagocytic cups), and functional recovery of phagocytic ability as demonstrated by quantitative in vitro POS uptake assays. In preclinical animal models, it is conceivable that such improvements in RPE function would translate to decreased subretinal debris accumulation, preservation of photoreceptor integrity, and ultimately improved visual function.

The overall evaluation of the agonist anti-MerTK antibody candidate—MAB8916—reveals a promising yet challenging therapeutic approach for dry AMD. One of the foremost strengths of this candidate is the robust preclinical evidence supporting the central role of MerTK in RPE cell physiology and its critical involvement in the daily clearance of photoreceptor outer segments. Data from multiple studies have firmly established that compromised MerTK function, whether due to genetic mutations, reduced expression, or receptor cleavage, leads to the accumulation of cellular debris, the formation of toxic lipofuscin, and subsequent retinal degeneration (Albert et al., 2015; Puddu et al., 2022). Restoring or enhancing MerTK activity, therefore, represents a highly attractive intervention point in the context of dry AMD.  

The candidate’s mechanism—using a bivalent antibody to mimic the natural agonist Gas6—offers several advantages. It promises a high degree of specificity, as the antibody is designed to bind exclusively to the MerTK extracellular domain, thereby reducing the likelihood of off-target effects. The bivalent nature facilitates receptor dimerization, a prerequisite for effective signaling, and may provide a more sustained activation compared to monovalent ligands or small molecules that could be rapidly cleared from the vitreous (Ghosh et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015). Moreover, antibody-based therapies have a well-established clinical track record in ophthalmology, as exemplified by anti-VEGF agents used in neovascular AMD; this precedent suggests that intravitreal delivery of a MerTK agonist could be feasible from both a formulation and safety perspective.

However, the candidate is not without potential weaknesses and challenges. One significant concern is the inherent complexity of MerTK signaling, which plays dual roles in promoting phagocytosis and suppressing inflammation. While activation of MerTK is beneficial for enhancing POS uptake, there is a risk that excessive or prolonged stimulation could lead to receptor desensitization or dysregulation of downstream pathways. For instance, unrestrained MerTK activity might alter the delicate balance between phagocytosis and anti-inflammatory signaling, potentially resulting in unexpected cellular stress or adverse immune reactions (Hamm et al., 2022; Law et al., 2015). Preclinical studies using MerTK inhibitors have demonstrated that inhibition of this receptor causes severe retinal toxicity due to the blockade of essential phagocytic processes (Hamm et al., 2022; Law et al., 2015). Although the proposed strategy is the converse—seeking to enhance MerTK activity—the fine line separating therapeutic activation from potential overstimulation must be carefully navigated. The dosing regimen, duration of exposure, and biodistribution of the antibody will all need to be rigorously optimized in appropriate animal models before progressing to clinical trials. Immunogenicity is another potential drawback; as with all biologics, the possibility of eliciting an immune response, particularly in the immune-privileged environment of the eye, cannot be discounted and will require thorough investigation.

From a translational perspective, the relative novelty of employing an agonist antibody for MerTK activation in dry AMD implies that there is limited historical data on which to base dosing strategies or predict long-term outcomes (Albert et al., 2015; Murase et al., 2015; Li, 2013). Although analogous approaches in other therapeutic areas provide a useful framework, the unique biology of the retina and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD necessitate careful and comprehensive preclinical validation. This includes detailed pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic studies, assessment of retinal structure and function in animal models (such as the RCS rat or other models of AMD), and exploration of potential synergistic or antagonistic interactions with other retinal cell signaling pathways.

Despite these challenges, the targeted approach of using an agonist anti-MerTK antibody is highly attractive. The preclinical evidence underscores that even modest enhancements in MerTK-mediated phagocytosis can lead to significant improvements in RPE function and potentially slow the progression of AMD. For instance, studies in which MerTK expression was restored or augmented in deficient models resulted in a significant recovery of phagocytic capacity and a reduction in the accumulation of toxic debris (Artero-Castro et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2016). Such findings provide a strong mechanistic rationale for the therapeutic hypothesis being tested here. Moreover, by directly addressing a primary pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD—namely, the failure of RPE cells to clear shed photoreceptor outer segments—the candidate offers a targeted intervention that could complement or even surpass currently available treatments, which largely focus on managing neovascular complications rather than halting the underlying degenerative process.

In summary, the agonist anti-MerTK antibody candidate (MAB8916) presents a novel, mechanism-based therapeutic strategy for dry AMD. Its design to mimic the natural ligand Gas6 and directly stimulate MerTK signaling aligns well with the extensive body of preclinical evidence highlighting the central role of MerTK in RPE phagocytosis and retinal homeostasis (Albert et al., 2015; Ghosh et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015). The anticipated outcomes include increased MerTK phosphorylation, enhanced actin-cup formation, and improved POS uptake, which together would address the defective clearance mechanism that underlies progressive retinal degeneration in dry AMD. While there are challenges associated with ensuring a balanced activation of MerTK without triggering adverse effects, the strategy benefits from a strong scientific rationale and the potential for high specificity. Further investigation in advanced in vitro models (such as primary human RPE cultures and hiPSC-derived RPE systems) and in vivo studies in animal models of retinal degeneration will be crucial to establish the safety, dosing, and efficacy profile of this candidate before it can be considered for clinical development.

Overall, the candidate’s strengths lie in its targeted mechanism of action, its potential to restore a key physiological process in the RPE, and the promising preclinical data that underscore the importance of MerTK in retinal health (Ghosh et al., 2024; Artero-Castro et al., 2021; Albert et al., 2015). Conversely, weaknesses include the limited direct evidence for antibody-mediated MerTK agonism in AMD, the potential for off-target or excessive activation effects, and the need for thorough safety and immunogenicity assessments. Given these factors, the agonist anti-MerTK antibody represents a compelling and innovative therapeutic avenue that warrants further comprehensive investigation as a candidate for treating dry age-related macular degeneration (Murase et al., 2015; Hamm et al., 2022; Law et al., 2015; Artero-Castro et al., 2021).

In biochemical and cellular assays relevant to ocular angiogenesis, axitinib demonstrates pan-VEGFR inhibition with substantially greater sensitivity than anti-VEGF monoclonal antibodies in endothelial cells, and it also inhibits PDGFR-β–mediated signaling in pericytes at low nanomolar concentrations, consistent with dual-pathway blockade within the VEGF/PDGF axis (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Pharmacologically, oral axitinib exhibits a short plasma half-life (~2.5–6.1 h) requiring twice-daily systemic dosing in oncology, and class-typical adverse events are dominated by hypertension; these PK/AE features motivated ocular delivery strategies to achieve high intraocular exposure with minimal systemic spillover (Siedlecki et al., 2017). As a class, multi-targeted VEGFR/PDGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have long been deployed systemically for cancer and are being repurposed for ocular neovascular diseases with the goals of broader VEGF-pathway suppression and reduced injection burden via sustained intraocular delivery platforms (suprachoroidal suspensions, intravitreal depot implants, and bioresorbable hydrogel systems) (Fabre et al., 2022; Fei et al., 2024). Axitinib is notable among TKIs for very high VEGFR affinity and measurable inhibition of other angiogenesis-related kinases, including TIE2, which has implications for both efficacy breadth and potential effects on vascular stability in the retina and choroid (Leitch et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical ocular data consistently show axitinib suppresses choroidal and retinal neovascularization across models, with oral dosing at 5 mg/kg reducing laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (L-CNV) in mice, and continuous low-dose systemic infusion (0.875 mg/day for 7 days) decreasing fluorescein leakage and CNV lesion area in rats; in vitro, axitinib suppresses 3D sprouting and inhibits both endothelial and pericyte proliferation/migration at non-toxic concentrations, aligning with dual VEGFR/PDGFR blockade (Fei et al., 2024; Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In a rat L-CNV model, axitinib reduced FA leakage scores and CNV lesion area by approximately one-third versus vehicle, and in co-culture sprouting assays axitinib alone outperformed anti-VEGF and anti-PDGF combinations, reinforcing the mechanistic rationale for dual-pathway inhibition in pathological ocular angiogenesis (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Combinatorial approaches show synergy: co-administration with anti-VEGF antibodies enhanced anti-angiogenic effects in nonclinical studies, consistent with the broader concept that inhibiting pericyte/PDGFR-β support can potentiate VEGF-directed therapy (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Siedlecki et al., 2017).

Multiple ocular delivery strategies for axitinib have entered human investigation in neovascular AMD (nAMD) to address the treatment burden and durability limitations of intravitreal biologics, including a suprachoroidal injectable suspension (CLS-AX) and an intravitreal bioresorbable hydrogel implant (OTX-TKI) designed for 6–9 months of sustained release (Fei et al., 2024). Early clinical and translational signals indicate that suprachoroidal delivery achieves high posterior segment exposure with minimal systemic levels, and initial phase 1/2a experience with CLS-AX in nAMD reported acceptable tolerability and pharmacologic activity at low doses, while OTX-TKI demonstrated favorable safety and durability in early cohorts (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020). Across the TKI class, parallel depot strategies (e.g., vorolanib in Durasert, sunitinib depots) have shown biologic activity and reduced treatment burden in nAMD, although some programs reported visual acuity tradeoffs or required rescue therapy at non-negligible rates, highlighting the need for careful dose, exposure, and target-selectivity optimization (Fei et al., 2024; Leitch et al., 2024).

Topical/eye-drop TKI programs (pazopanib, regorafenib, PAN-90806, acrizanib) underscore translational challenges: although preclinical topical dosing can reduce leakage and CNV thickness, multiple phase II programs failed to meet efficacy endpoints or were terminated due to insufficient posterior segment exposure and ocular safety issues such as reversible corneal haze with acrizanib, indicating that noninvasive delivery often cannot reproducibly attain therapeutic concentrations at the choroid/RPE in humans (Fei et al., 2024). Importantly, the available literature contains no reports of axitinib being tested clinically for dry AMD (geographic atrophy) or for enhancing RPE phagocytosis; the development history for axitinib and related VEGFR/PDGFR TKIs is focused on nAMD and other retinal vascular diseases, and reviews repeatedly note a lack of evidence for dry-AMD applications in this drug class to date (Fei et al., 2024). Furthermore, while localized ocular delivery is being pursued to mitigate systemic exposure, case reports of retinal adverse events during systemic axitinib therapy—including impaired retinal circulation, reversible retinal toxicity, and central retinal vein occlusion—require vigilance and thoughtful PK/PD design in ocular programs (Bakri et al., 2024). More broadly, despite active investigation of small molecules for AMD, reviews emphasize that no clinical success stories for small-molecule drugs in AMD (outside recently approved complement inhibitors for GA) have been established, underscoring translational risk for new mechanisms and reformulations (Fei et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Axitinib is a potent ATP-competitive inhibitor of VEGFR1 (FLT1), VEGFR2 (KDR), and VEGFR3 (FLT4), with additional inhibitory activity against PDGFR-β and c-KIT, thereby interrupting intracellular tyrosine kinase signaling downstream of multiple pro-angiogenic ligands, including VEGF-A/B/C/D and PDGF-B (Tosi et al., 2017; Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In relevant ocular cell types, axitinib inhibits VEGF-driven endothelial proliferation with markedly greater potency than anti-VEGF antibodies and exerts nanomolar inhibition of PDGF-driven pericyte proliferation, supporting the mechanistic premise that simultaneous disruption of endothelial and pericyte signaling can destabilize nascent pathological vessels and reduce neovascular growth (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In 3D co-culture sprouting models that recapitulate endothelial–pericyte interactions, axitinib alone achieves robust inhibition of sprout number and length across low-nanomolar concentrations, matching or exceeding the effect of anti-VEGF plus anti-PDGF combinations, a pattern consistent with multi-receptor inhibition at the level of VEGFR/PDGFR RTKs (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Preclinical studies in retinal endothelial cells further demonstrate axitinib suppression of downstream MAPK/ERK signaling and oxidative stress markers, aligning with direct VEGFR pathway inhibition; limited in vitro reports also suggest reduction of VEGFR1/VEGFR2 and PDGFR-β phosphorylation in RPE or mixed cell models, though these do not extend to functional phagocytosis endpoints (Lazzara et al., 2024).

Mechanistically, axitinib’s kinase profile extends beyond VEGFR/PDGFR to other angiogenesis-modulating targets; notably, among three pan-VEGFR TKIs profiled preclinically (vorolanib, sunitinib, axitinib), only axitinib exhibited strong TIE2 inhibition, a pathway essential for vascular quiescence and stability that could influence choroidal and retinal vascular homeostasis under chronic intraocular exposure (Bakri et al., 2024). In comparative kinase panels and endothelial functional assays, all three TKIs displayed robust pan-VEGFR inhibition and abolished endothelial sprouting at high concentrations, but the TIE2-inhibitory signal was disproportionately strong for axitinib, suggesting type-specific off-target consequences that warrant consideration during dose selection for chronic ocular use (Bakri et al., 2024). While intravitreal biologics neutralize extracellular VEGF ligands, axitinib acts intracellularly to block receptor signaling, potentially addressing compensatory upregulation of VEGF-C/D observed with VEGF-A-only inhibition; however, the breadth of intracellular TKI targeting can also propagate off-target effects in non-endothelial cells if exposures are not carefully controlled (Leitch et al., 2024).

Delivery-route pharmacology is central to ocular mechanism realization: suprachoroidal injection of axitinib has demonstrated posterior-segment targeting with markedly elevated drug levels in the posterior eye cup versus intravitreal injection in rabbits and sustained RPE/choroid exposure with minimal systemic levels, thereby achieving compartmentalized receptor inhibition where angiogenic lesions and the RPE reside (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020). Complementary intravitreal hydrogel implant strategies (OTX-TKI) provide long-acting axitinib delivery (6–9 months), maintaining pharmacologically relevant intraocular concentrations to chronically suppress VEGFR/PDGFR signaling in nAMD; these platforms are designed to mitigate systemic adverse events while sustaining on-target ocular pharmacodynamics (Fei et al., 2024). Importantly, chronic VEGF pathway suppression carries theoretical risks for neurosensory retina and RPE health, and reviews emphasize the need to balance durable angiogenic control with potential adverse effects of continuous VEGF blockade in ocular tissues, particularly for non-neovascular indications (Wolf et al., 2022).

Therapeutic targets in the RPE relevant to the present hypothesis—MerTK and αvβ5 integrin—are core components of the photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytic machinery, with αvβ5 required for synchronized diurnal phagocytosis and MerTK essential for engulfment and internalization; however, the provided literature contains no direct experimental evidence that axitinib upregulates MerTK or αvβ5 expression or function in RPE, nor that PDGFR-β signaling tonically suppresses RPE phagocytic differentiation in vivo (Tosi et al., 2017). Reviews and experimental summaries repeatedly state that available axitinib data focus on endothelial/pericyte targets and CNV models, and that no studies directly link axitinib to enhanced RPE POS uptake, MerTK activation, or αvβ5 integrin upregulation in dry AMD models or RPE cell assays (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). Therefore, while axitinib’s biochemical capacity to inhibit PDGFR-β could, in principle, modulate RPE phenotypes if PDGFR-β were a suppressive node in RPE phagocytic signaling, this mechanistic leap is not supported by direct evidence in the provided literature (Bakri et al., 2024; Fei et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The proposed assay hypothesis is that low-dose axitinib will modulate PDGFR-β signaling in RPE to promote a pro-phagocytic differentiation state, enhancing MerTK and αvβ5 expression and POS uptake; however, the body of evidence provided does not include direct demonstrations of axitinib increasing RPE phagocytosis, MerTK activation, or αvβ5 expression in vitro, ex vivo, or in vivo (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). Available data show that axitinib reduces VEGFR1/VEGFR2 and PDGFR-β phosphorylation in retinal endothelial systems and in limited contexts citing RPE/HUVEC cells, but these findings stop short of connecting PDGFR-β inhibition to increased RPE phagocytic function, and no POS ingestion assays, MerTK phosphorylation readouts, or αvβ5 functional binding assays are reported for axitinib in RPE (Lazzara et al., 2024). By contrast, the canonical RPE phagocytic apparatus depends on αvβ5-mediated POS binding and MerTK-mediated engulfment, with genetic ablation models establishing necessity; the literature here confirms this machinery but does not implicate PDGFR-β overactivation as a hindrance to RPE phagocytic differentiation nor demonstrate that TKIs restore phagocytosis in RPE (Tosi et al., 2017).

If the assay system relies on differentiating human RPE and measures POS uptake alongside MerTK and αvβ5 expression, axitinib’s expected on-target effects would be limited to PDGFR-β kinase inhibition in RPE if PDGFR-β is expressed and active under the assay conditions; nevertheless, there is no provided evidence that such inhibition increases MerTK or αvβ5 levels or POS ingestion, and the hypothesis that PDGFR-β tone suppresses RPE phagocytosis remains unsubstantiated here (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). It is conceivable that low-dose axitinib could indirectly affect RPE phenotype via modulation of growth-factor signaling crosstalk, extracellular matrix deposition, or oxidative stress pathways observed in retinal endothelial cells; however, the provided literature does not extend these effects to RPE phagocytic function, and any expectation of enhanced MerTK/αvβ5 expression is speculative in the absence of direct data (Siedlecki et al., 2017; Lazzara et al., 2024).

Translational pharmacology considerations highlight both opportunity and risk: suprachoroidal axitinib enriches drug at the choroid/RPE with minimal systemic exposure, offering a delivery solution for RPE-targeted modulation if the mechanism were validated; at the same time, axitinib’s TIE2 inhibition and class-level concerns about chronic VEGF pathway suppression in the neurosensory retina argue for caution in non-neovascular indications such as dry AMD (Kaiser et al., 2020; Bakri et al., 2024). Moreover, systemic axitinib has been associated with retinal vascular adverse events in case reports, indicating that even low systemic exposures can affect retinal physiology, so RPE-targeted development would necessitate rigorous intraocular PK/PD mapping and safety margins that preserve vascular stability while testing RPE functional endpoints (Bakri et al., 2024). Given these constraints, the expected effect in an RPE phagocytosis assay is, at present, not evidence-based in the provided materials and should be framed as a hypothesis requiring first-principles validation rather than an anticipated outcome derived from prior literature (Fei et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
- Pharmacologic potency and dual-pathway coverage: Axitinib’s high-affinity pan-VEGFR inhibition with demonstrated PDGFR-β activity enables simultaneous suppression of endothelial and pericyte signaling, a combination that underpins robust anti-angiogenic efficacy in CNV models and may reduce fibrosis-linked extracellular matrix deposition in neovascular settings (Giddabasappa et al., 2016).  
- Validated ocular delivery options: Suprachoroidal suspension (CLS-AX) and intravitreal hydrogel implant (OTX-TKI) platforms have progressed into clinical testing for nAMD with encouraging ocular safety/PK signals, providing translationally relevant routes to expose the RPE/choroid compartment while minimizing systemic exposure (Wolf et al., 2022; Fei et al., 2024).  
- Clinical-stage experience in nAMD: Early-phase trials indicate biological activity and tolerability of axitinib-based intraocular approaches, suggesting a viable path to long-acting ocular therapy development if a new indication such as RPE phagocytosis enhancement is supported by mechanistic data (Leitch et al., 2024).  
- Class learnings and comparator programs: The broader TKI field in nAMD (vorolanib, sunitinib derivatives) offers benchmarks for durability, rescue-free rates, and safety considerations, facilitating rational dose and exposure setting for axitinib formulations (Fei et al., 2024; Leitch et al., 2024).  

Limitations and Critical Gaps  
- No direct evidence for RPE phagocytosis enhancement: Across the provided literature, there are no RPE-specific data showing axitinib increases MerTK or αvβ5 expression, augments POS binding or internalization, or improves phagocytic capacity in differentiating RPE; multiple summaries explicitly state the absence of such evidence and confine axitinib’s demonstrated actions to anti-angiogenic endpoints (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017).  
- Unvalidated mechanistic premise in RPE: While PDGFR-β is central to pericyte biology and vessel stabilization, the assertion that PDGFR-β overactivation hinders RPE differentiation and that its inhibition promotes a pro-phagocytic state is not supported in the provided texts, and the core RPE phagocytic machinery (MerTK, αvβ5) is not linked here to PDGFR-β modulation by TKIs (Tosi et al., 2017; Bakri et al., 2024).  
- Safety liabilities and target selectivity: Axitinib’s strong TIE2 inhibition could perturb vascular stability with chronic intraocular exposure, and class-level concerns exist for continuous VEGF pathway suppression affecting neurosensory retina and RPE; rare but notable retinal vascular AEs reported with systemic axitinib further mandate conservative exposure design and careful safety pharmacology tailored to non-neovascular indications (Bakri et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022).  
- Delivery constraints for non-neovascular endpoints: Topical TKI programs frequently failed due to inadequate posterior segment exposure and/or ocular surface safety findings, suggesting that any RPE-targeted application of axitinib would require invasive delivery (suprachoroidal/IVT depot) with chronic exposure, elevating the bar for safety and benefit-risk justification in a dry AMD population (Fei et al., 2024).  
- Field precedent: Reviews underscore that, to date, small-molecule success in AMD has been limited, and there are no approved ocular TKIs for either wet or dry AMD, reinforcing translational uncertainty for new mechanism-of-use proposals lacking direct preclinical support (Fei et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).  

Development Recommendations and Go/No-Go Criteria  
- Mechanistic validation in RPE: Before proceeding, perform a staged in vitro program in human iPSC-RPE and primary RPE to test whether axitinib modulates PDGFR-β phosphorylation and secondarily increases MerTK expression, MerTK phosphorylation upon POS challenge, αvβ5 expression/localization, and POS binding/internalization; include dose-response spanning sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar exposures aligned with ocular PK projections from suprachoroidal or depot IVT delivery (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020).  
- Specificity controls and orthogonal readouts: Use chemical and genetic controls to isolate PDGFR-β dependence (e.g., PDGFR-β ligand titrations, selective PDGFR-β inhibitors distinct from axitinib, and PDGFR-β knockdown), and include neutralizing antibodies and MerTK/αvβ5 functional blocking to map pathway causality for any observed phagocytosis changes (Tosi et al., 2017; Siedlecki et al., 2017).  
- Safety pharmacology in pigmented models: Given potential TIE2-related and VEGF-suppression liabilities, include long-term RPE morphology, barrier function (TEER), transcriptomic stress signatures, and photoreceptor/RPE co-culture viability endpoints at projected clinical exposures; extend to pigmented rabbit or NHP pharmacology to define posterior-segment exposure, ocular distribution (RPE/sclera/choroid), and a NOAEL for chronic dosing (Bakri et al., 2024; Kaiser et al., 2020).  
- Translational gating: Advance only if axitinib reproducibly increases POS uptake and MerTK/αvβ5 functional markers in RPE with a therapeutic window that avoids endothelial destabilization signals and preserves neuronal/RPE integrity in chronic exposure models; otherwise, deprioritize axitinib for RPE-targeted dry AMD and refocus efforts on mechanisms directly validated to enhance RPE phagocytosis or survival (Fei et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022).  

Conclusion  
On the strength of available evidence, axitinib is a validated, potent anti-angiogenic TKI with multiple ocular delivery platforms in clinical development for nAMD and robust preclinical efficacy in CNV models; however, the central hypothesis that low-dose axitinib enhances RPE phagocytosis via PDGFR-β modulation and upregulates MerTK/αvβ5 lacks direct support in the provided literature, and multiple sources explicitly state that no such RPE-centric data exist for axitinib at present (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Fei et al., 2024). The translational and safety profiles suggest that invasive ocular delivery could achieve RPE-adjacent exposure, but off-target TIE2 inhibition and class-level VEGF-suppression risks must be weighed carefully in a non-neovascular indication, particularly absent clear preclinical efficacy on RPE phagocytic endpoints (Bakri et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022). Accordingly, while axitinib remains attractive for anti-angiogenic applications, it should not be advanced for dry AMD on a phagocytosis-enhancement rationale without first producing compelling, direct RPE mechanistic data; in the absence of such data, development resources would be better allocated to candidates with demonstrated effects on MerTK/αvβ5 function or on complement-mediated RPE pathology more proximal to dry AMD pathophysiology (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Fei et al., 2024). Pending rigorous in vitro and ex vivo validation as outlined, the current evidence base supports a cautious “mechanism validation required” stance rather than progression to in vivo dry AMD studies or clinical translation for this proposed use (Fei et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring derivative of vitamin B3 that was originally isolated from milk and later recognized for its role as an NAD⁺ precursor. NR belongs to the class of NAD⁺‐boosting compounds and is structurally a pyridine riboside with a glycosidic bond linking nicotinamide to ribose; this bond has proven to be chemically labile, which has driven innovations in its synthesis and stabilization (Zhang et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). Recent advances in synthetic methods have enabled the production of purer, more thermally and chemically stable forms, such as borate-stabilized NR, although commercial formulations like NR chloride (ChromaDex TruNiagen) are widely used owing to their proven oral bioavailability (Biţă et al., 2023). As a member of the NAD⁺ precursor family that also includes nicotinamide and nicotinic acid, NR has been repurposed for its potential to restore intracellular NAD⁺ levels, a vital coenzyme in redox reactions and as a substrate for enzymes such as sirtuins and PARPs; these properties have been harnessed in research aimed at improving mitochondrial function and addressing age-related degeneration (Zhang et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
NR has a robust preclinical and early clinical history as a nutritional supplement with demonstrated efficacy in boosting NAD⁺ levels systemically. Prior biochemical studies have documented that oral NR supplementation raises circulating NAD⁺ and associated metabolites in both murine and human subjects, with repeated dosing regimens showing increases in NAD⁺ of up to 100% above baseline without causing adverse events such as flushing or liver toxicity—side effects that have been problematic with other niacin derivatives (Airhart et al., 2017; Conze et al., 2019). Furthermore, NR has been shown to ameliorate metabolic deficits in various disease models, including mouse models of diet-induced obesity, neurodegeneration, peripheral neuropathy, and even light-induced retinal degeneration, where systemic treatment with NR improved retinal outcomes in mice (Zhang et al., 2020; Biţă et al., 2023). Although NR has not been directly tested in clinical trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in dedicated experiments on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) phagocytosis, the accumulated evidence from related ocular studies and from the broader literature on NAD⁺ restoration suggests that its application in retinal degenerative conditions is plausible (Jadeja et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, NR is rapidly taken up by cells and phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRK1 and NRK2) to produce nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), which is subsequently converted to NAD⁺ by NMN adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) (Zhang et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). NAD⁺ is a key metabolic hub that is required for essential cellular processes, including fueling mitochondrial ATP production via glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation, while also serving as a critical substrate for sirtuin deacetylases (notably SIRT1 and SIRT3) and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs) that mediate DNA repair and stress responses (Braidy et al., 2019; Biţă et al., 2023). In the context of the RPE, diminished NAD⁺ availability is linked to compromised mitochondrial bioenergetics, impaired autophagy/mitophagy, increased oxidative stress, and defective phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), all of which contribute to the etiology of dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2020). NR supplementation is proposed to elevate intracellular NAD⁺ levels above the physiological threshold, thereby stimulating sirtuin activity (particularly SIRT3 in mitochondria), stabilizing mitochondrial membrane potential, promoting efficient mitophagy, and reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Biţă et al., 2023). Additionally, by restoring the NAD⁺/NADH balance, NR may directly support energy-dependent processes such as phagocytosis in RPE cells, where the clearance of aged POS is critically energy demanding (Zhang et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed hypothesis for dry AMD, exogenous NR supplementation is expected to boost NAD⁺ levels in RPE cells, an effect that should be observable at an effective concentration (EC₅₀) in the range of approximately 100 µM in vitro (Zhang et al., 2020). This increase in NAD⁺ is anticipated to enhance mitochondrial respiration and activate sirtuin-dependent pathways that promote mitochondrial biogenesis and repair. In turn, improved mitochondrial function provides the necessary ATP for energy-dependent cellular functions, particularly the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), which is impaired in dry AMD. Preclinical studies have indicated that NAD⁺ precursors, including nicotinamide and NMN, can correct defects in mitochondrial respiration and restore normal phagocytic activity in RPE models; NR, being an orally bioavailable NAD⁺ precursor with favorable safety profiles, is predicted to act similarly by reducing oxidative stress–induced damage to the phagocytic machinery and enhancing mitophagy to clear damaged mitochondria (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020; Hawkins et al., 2024). In animal models of retinal degeneration, NR supplementation has been linked to improved functional outcomes, supporting the notion that similar mechanisms may be relevant in the context of dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction underlies photoreceptor degeneration (Zhang et al., 2020). Thus, the expected effect is a dual benefit in RPE cells: increased energy production to drive POS phagocytosis and enhanced resistance to oxidative damage through improved mitochondrial quality control, ultimately helping to preserve RPE function and slow dry AMD progression (Conze et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
NR is an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its unique combination of advantages. Among its strengths is its origin as a naturally occurring, orally bioavailable NAD⁺ precursor that has a long record of safe use in human nutritional studies; clinical trials have repeatedly demonstrated its ability to significantly elevate systemic NAD⁺ levels without dose-limiting adverse effects such as flushing or hepatotoxicity, which are common to other niacin derivatives (Airhart et al., 2017; Conze et al., 2019). Its mechanism of action is well understood at the biochemical level: by feeding into the NAD⁺ salvage pathway, NR supports key cellular functions including mitochondrial respiration, DNA repair, and stress signaling via sirtuins and PARPs—pathways that are critically compromised in the aging RPE and in dry AMD (Braidy et al., 2019; Biţă et al., 2023). Additionally, preclinical data have shown that NAD⁺ restoration via NR or related precursors can ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction and improve phagocytic activity in retinal tissues, providing a plausible molecular rationale for its use in maintaining RPE health (Zhang et al., 2020).

On the other hand, there are significant challenges that must be acknowledged. Despite promising preclinical evidence in various models of retinal degeneration, direct application of NR in the context of dry AMD has not yet been rigorously evaluated in dedicated clinical trials, leaving a gap between the compelling mechanistic rationale and the demonstration of clinical efficacy (Jadeja et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2024). The concentration required (EC₅₀ ≈ 100 µM) and the extent of NR’s penetration into the RPE in the human eye remain to be fully elucidated; tissue-specific pharmacokinetics may differ from those observed in systemic circulation, and there remains the possibility that presystemic metabolism (conversion to nicotinamide, for example) could limit the amount of NR available for direct uptake by the RPE (Damgaard & Treebak, 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Furthermore, while the drug’s safety profile is established in the context of metabolic and neurodegenerative indications, the unique microenvironment of the retina—with its high oxygen consumption and exposure to light-induced oxidative stress—may present unforeseen responses that require careful validation in animal models and early-phase clinical studies (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2020).

In summary, NR (ChromaDex TruNiagen) holds considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its ability to safely boost NAD⁺ levels, improve mitochondrial function, and reduce oxidative stress aligns well with the pathophysiological needs of the RPE in dry AMD. Strengths of the candidate include its natural origin, established safety and bioavailability profiles in humans, and robust preclinical evidence supporting NAD⁺ repletion as a strategy for enhancing mitochondrial quality and phagocytic function. However, the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD and the need for targeted studies to confirm effective RPE delivery and functional restoration of POS clearance remain important considerations. Overall, NR merits further investigation in preclinical RPE models and carefully designed clinical trials to assess its efficacy in mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020; Airhart et al., 2017; Conze et al., 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020).
