Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB431542 is a well‐characterized, synthetic small molecule inhibitor originally developed through medicinal chemistry efforts by researchers at GlaxoSmithKline. Its chemical structure, formally denoted as 4-(5-benzo[1,3]dioxol-5-yl-4-pyridin-2-yl-1H-imidazol-2-yl)-benzamide, incorporates a benzodioxole moiety linked to a pyridyl-imidazol core and terminated by a benzamide group, placing it within the imidazole class of compounds (Laping et al., 2002). SB431542 belongs to the class of transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) type I receptor kinase inhibitors (commonly referred to as ALK5 inhibitors) that inhibit ATP-dependent receptor activation. Initially designed as an improvement over less-selective kinase inhibitors—such as early p38 MAPK inhibitors that exhibited off-target ALK5 inhibition—SB431542 emerged from a rational structure–activity relationship (SAR) campaign aimed at optimizing both potency and selectivity (Laping et al., 2002). Its discovery has been pivotal in establishing a molecular tool for dissecting TGFβ signaling, and its chemical synthesis reflects a focused effort on achieving high-affinity, ATP-competitive inhibition of the TGFβ receptor. This compound has been extensively used in preclinical research to study fibrotic mechanisms and cellular differentiation, thereby marking its reputation as a “gold standard” in TGFβ pathway inhibition (Laping et al., 2002).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SB431542 is primarily rooted in its application as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. In numerous preclinical studies, SB431542 has been consistently used to inhibit TGFβ-induced processes such as extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis, Smad protein activation, and the induction of a fibrotic phenotype in various cell types including renal epithelial cells, fibroblasts, and even certain cancer cell models (Laping et al., 2002). Biochemical studies have shown that SB431542 effectively blocks the phosphorylation of Smad3 with an IC50 of approximately 94 nM, thereby preventing the downstream transcriptional activation of cytokines and matrix proteins (Laping et al., 2002). Its anti-fibrotic effects have been extensively characterized in in vitro assays, where it reduced the expression of collagen I α1, fibronectin, and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) mRNA, thus providing compelling evidence that the compound modulates TGFβ-induced ECM remodeling (Laping et al., 2002).

While SB431542 has been applied in many experimental models to study pathways implicated in fibrotic diseases such as glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, liver cirrhosis, and pulmonary fibrosis, there is scant direct evidence of its historical use in ocular pathologies, particularly dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Akhund et al., 2023; Nyati et al., 2011). However, TGFβ signaling has been implicated in retinal pathologies and in the mesenchymal transition of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells from which some studies have emerged using general TGFβ inhibitors to reverse such pathological changes (Radeke et al., 2015). Although SB431542 itself has not been used in clinical trials for AMD, its mechanistic profile and reported efficacies in other fibrotic and ECM remodeling contexts make it a promising candidate for repurposing to address the abnormal matrix remodeling observed in dry AMD. Preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues have established that targeted inhibition of TGFβ signaling leads to substantial reductions in fibrotic markers, suggesting that similar approaches could mitigate Bruch membrane (BrM) alterations in AMD (Laping et al., 2002).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB431542 functions as an ATP-competitive inhibitor selectively targeting the kinase domain of the TGFβ type I receptor (TGFβRI, also known as ALK5). Its mechanism of action centers on binding to the ATP-binding pocket of TGFβRI, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of key intracellular effectors, primarily the Smad2 and Smad3 proteins (Laping et al., 2002). In normal TGFβ signaling, binding of the ligand (e.g., TGFβ1) to its receptors induces the formation of a heteromeric complex consisting of TGFβRI and TGFβRII, leading to the phosphorylation and activation of Smad2/3. These phosphorylated Smad proteins then form a complex with Smad4, translocate to the nucleus, and activate the transcription of pro-fibrotic genes, including those involved in ECM protein synthesis such as collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002).

Detailed molecular interaction studies have revealed that SB431542 makes critical hydrogen bonding contacts within the ATP-binding site of TGFβRI. For example, the benzodioxol moiety is reported to form a hydrogen bond with the amide nitrogen of His283, while additional interactions with Lys232 and other hydrophobic residues stabilize the inhibitor within the binding pocket (Leonardo-Sousa et al., 2025). This precise molecular engagement confers its high selectivity, as even minor substitutions in the binding region—such as mutations at the gatekeeper residue—can significantly alter inhibitor efficacy (Laping et al., 2002; Leonardo-Sousa et al., 2025). Furthermore, while SB431542 shows potent inhibition against ALK5, it also inhibits closely related receptors such as ALK4 and ALK7 with only modest differences in potency (IC50 for ALK4 is approximately 140 nM), and it exhibits negligible activity against BMP-activated receptors (ALK2, ALK3, and ALK6) (Laping et al., 2002). This selective inhibition ensures that the canonical TGFβ/Smad pathway is targeted without significantly perturbing other pathways that could be essential for cellular homeostasis, such as the BMP signaling cascade (Nyati et al., 2011; Akhund et al., 2023).

In addition to its inhibition of Smad2/3 phosphorylation, SB431542 has been shown to disrupt the subsequent nuclear translocation of these transcription factors, thereby halting the transcription of downstream ECM components. Such inhibition is critical because overactivation of the TGFβ pathway is a central driver in fibrotic diseases and leads to excessive deposition of ECM proteins, which in turn contribute to tissue stiffness and impaired cellular function (Laping et al., 2002). Overall, the molecular mechanism of SB431542 is well-delineated; its high selectivity for TGFβRI and the resulting blockade of Smad-mediated transcription form the foundation for its potential use in addressing aberrant ECM remodeling.

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis for repurposing SB431542 in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is built on the concept that excessive TGFβ signaling within the retinal microenvironment leads to an abnormal accumulation and remodeling of ECM components in the Bruch membrane (BrM). In the context of dry AMD, such ECM changes are believed to increase membrane stiffness and disrupt the diffusion of critical phagocytic ligands—specifically MFGE8 (Milk Fat Globule Epidermal Growth Factor 8) and Gas6—which play key roles in facilitating the integrin αvβ5-mediated binding and uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Radeke et al., 2015).

By inhibiting TGFβRI, SB431542 is expected to block the TGFβ-driven phosphorylation of Smad proteins, thereby directly reducing the transcription of genes that encode for fibrotic and ECM-related proteins such as collagen I α1, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002). In doing so, SB431542 should restore a more balanced ECM composition in the BrM. This normalization of ECM deposition is anticipated to reduce BrM stiffness, thereby enhancing the diffusion of phagocytic ligands like MFGE8 and Gas6 across the membrane. The improved ligand diffusion is expected to restore the optimal microenvironment required for integrin αvβ5 on the RPE surface to effectively bind and internalize POS, a process that is critically impaired in dry AMD (Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011).

Furthermore, by attenuating the fibrotic response within the retina, SB431542 may help preserve the native architecture and function of the RPE layer. This indirect modulation of phagocytosis, achieved through the normalization of ECM characteristics, represents a novel therapeutic angle that bridges the gap between ECM pathology and receptor-mediated cellular processes. In essence, the expected effect of SB431542 is a dual benefit: first, it directly inhibits pathological TGFβ signaling to reduce further fibrotic damage, and second, it indirectly normalizes phagocytic function by restoring the proper presentation of ligands critical for RPE-mediated clearance of POS (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015).

At the cellular and molecular level, the proposed assay is likely to measure a reduction in fibrotic markers (e.g., collagen I α1, fibronectin) and an improvement in assays of POS binding and internalization by RPE cells. Given that RPE cells express integrin αvβ5 and are responsive to TGFβ signaling, the application of SB431542 should result in a shift from a fibrotic, mesenchymal phenotype towards a more differentiated epithelial state that is conducive to normal phagocytic activity (Radeke et al., 2015; Akhund et al., 2023). This outcome would be mechanistically consistent with the known roles of TGFβ in modulating ECM dynamics and cellular differentiation. Consequently, if the hypothesis holds true, SB431542 would not only prevent further ECM deposition and stiffening of the BrM but would also support the resolution of existing pathological ECM alterations, thereby improving the overall homeostasis of the retinal microenvironment.

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of SB431542 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD requires careful consideration of its well-established biochemical profile alongside the translational challenges emerging from its current use primarily as a research tool. On the positive side, SB431542 is a potent and selective inhibitor of TGFβRI, with extensive preclinical evidence demonstrating its capacity to block TGFβ-induced Smad2/3 phosphorylation and consequently reduce the expression of fibrotic markers (Laping et al., 2002). Its high potency (with an IC50 in the low nanomolar range) and favorable selectivity profile—particularly with more than 100-fold selectivity over p38 MAPK and minimal activity against BMP receptors—render it an attractive candidate for targeted modulation of TGFβ signaling in tissues where fibrosis is a major pathogenic factor (Laping et al., 2002). These strengths are of particular relevance in the context of dry AMD, where BrM thickening and ECM remodeling are central features that compromise RPE function.

Moreover, the proposed mechanism underlying the therapeutic hypothesis is compelling. Excessive TGFβ signaling has been implicated in the aberrant remodeling of the BrM, which in turn impairs the presentation of critical phagocytic ligands necessary for efficient POS uptake by the RPE (Radeke et al., 2015). By inhibiting TGFβRI, SB431542 could theoretically restore the balance between collagen and proteoglycan production, thereby normalizing BrM stiffness and improving the diffusion of factors such as MFGE8 and Gas6. In doing so, the drug would indirectly enhance integrin αvβ5-mediated phagocytosis—a process that is essential for the maintenance of photoreceptor health and overall retinal integrity. This innovative indirect approach could represent a significant advancement in the treatment of dry AMD, addressing the disease from both a fibrotic and a functional perspective.

However, several considerable challenges and weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, the bulk of the supporting data for SB431542 comes from studies in non-ocular cell types or animal models of general fibrosis and cancer, with limited direct evidence in ocular systems. Although TGFβ inhibitors have been proposed as therapeutic agents in retinal diseases, there remains a significant gap in data specific to dry AMD or related retinal degenerative conditions (Akhund et al., 2023; Nyati et al., 2011). The absence of ocular pharmacokinetic studies, detailed data on retinal tissue penetration, and long-term safety evaluations in the eye poses a major hurdle for the clinical translation of SB431542 for AMD.

Furthermore, TGFβ signaling is a double-edged sword in many tissues, including the retina. While excessive TGFβ activity drives pathological ECM deposition and fibrosis, TGFβ also participates in immune regulation and cellular homeostasis. Therefore, complete or prolonged inhibition of TGFβ signaling may have unintended consequences, such as impairing normal wound healing or altering the immunological milieu of the retina (Akhund et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023). The delicate balance between therapeutic efficacy and potential adverse effects necessitates that any systemic or even locally delivered TGFβRI inhibitor be subject to rigorous dosing and toxicity studies. In this regard, the narrow therapeutic window often encountered in kinase inhibition therapies could be a limiting factor for SB431542’s adoption in an ophthalmic setting.

Another significant concern is the delivery method. The current literature on SB431542 primarily documents its use in cell culture assays or systemic administration in animal models; however, the ocular environment presents unique challenges due to barriers such as the inner limiting membrane, the blood-retina barrier, and the anatomical constraints of the retina. To achieve therapeutically relevant concentrations in the sub-retinal space or at the level of the BrM, innovative delivery strategies—such as topical formulations, intravitreal injections, or sustained-release devices—must be developed and validated (Hachana & Larrivée, 2022; Radeke et al., 2015). The pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of SB431542 in ocular tissues remain largely unexplored, which represents a critical gap in current knowledge.

Additionally, although the indirect mechanism of action—namely, the normalization of ECM to facilitate proper ligand–receptor interactions—is scientifically plausible, it is inherently more challenging to measure and validate compared to direct cellular responses. Assays designed to monitor changes in BrM stiffness, ECM composition, and the diffusion characteristics of MFGE8 and Gas6 must be highly sensitive and reproducible, and these endpoints have not been extensively characterized in available preclinical models of AMD. Furthermore, the redundancy within TGFβ signaling pathways raises the possibility that compensatory mechanisms might mitigate the effects of ALK5 inhibition over time, potentially limiting the efficacy of SB431542, particularly in a chronic, slowly progressive disease like dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Akhund et al., 2023).

From an efficacy standpoint, while numerous studies demonstrate that SB431542 effectively reduces TGFβ-induced fibrotic responses in various cell types (Laping et al., 2002), extrapolating these findings to the complex microenvironment of the aged retina is not straightforward. The retina and RPE possess distinct cellular and molecular characteristics that may respond differently to TGFβ signaling modulation. For example, in RPE cells, TGFβ signaling not only regulates ECM deposition but is also involved in the maintenance of epithelial phenotype and may even exert neuroprotective effects under certain conditions. Hence, unspecific inhibition of TGFβ signaling in the retina could conceivably result in a loss of beneficial effects that are essential for retinal homeostasis (Radeke et al., 2015; Akhund et al., 2023).

In summary, while SB431542 exhibits a robust, well-characterized mechanism of action as a TGFβRI inhibitor and has demonstrated potent anti-fibrotic effects in preclinical models of ECM remodeling, its repurposing for dry AMD must overcome several significant challenges. The strengths of SB431542 lie in its high potency, selectivity, and extensive preclinical validation in non-ocular models. Its molecular interactions are well understood, and its ability to inhibit Smad phosphorylation offers a clear mechanistic rationale for reducing pathological ECM deposition. Consequently, if applied to the pathological process associated with dry AMD, SB431542 could, in theory, mitigate the excessive ECM remodeling that impairs ligand diffusion and consequently restores the capacity for integrin αvβ5-mediated POS uptake by RPE cells (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011).

On the other hand, the weaknesses of this approach are substantial. There is limited evidence of SB431542’s efficacy in ocular models, and its pharmacokinetics, ocular tissue penetration, and long-term safety profile have yet to be rigorously evaluated. Additionally, the complexity of TGFβ’s biological roles raises concerns regarding the balance between therapeutic benefit and potential interference with normal retinal physiology. The indirect nature of the hypothesized effect—mediated by ECM normalization—adds further layers of complexity to both preclinical testing and eventual clinical translation. Finally, challenges related to drug delivery to the retina, along with the potential for compensatory signaling pathways to undermine the inhibitor’s efficacy, suggest that significant additional research is warranted before SB431542 can be advanced as a therapeutic candidate in an AMD setting (Akhund et al., 2023; Akhund et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023).

Overall, SB431542 presents a biologically plausible and mechanistically sound candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly given its demonstrated ability to modulate TGFβ-driven fibrotic pathways. However, its successful translation to an ophthalmic therapeutic will hinge on a series of focused preclinical studies that address ocular biodistribution, safety in retinal tissues, and the optimization of dosing regimens tailored to the unique anatomical and physiological challenges of the eye. Only after these critical issues have been resolved can SB431542 be considered a viable strategy to restore ECM homeostasis in the Bruch membrane, normalize phagocytic ligand availability, and ultimately enhance integrin-mediated POS uptake in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011). In conclusion, while SB431542 has strong potential and a compelling mechanistic rationale, further dedicated ocular research is required to fully validate its therapeutic promise in the context of dry AMD before it can be recommended for clinical development.

Its mechanism—SIRT1‐mediated deacetylation of cortactin/cofilin to enhance actin remodeling and phagocytosis under oxidative stress—is biologically plausible and addresses core dry AMD pathologies (impaired POS clearance, mitochondrial dysfunction). The experimental plan is conceptual, with key gaps in potency, target engagement, and delivery. Compared to SB 290157, divanillin presents fewer off-target risks and a clearer safety path, but requires de-risking of its MoA and ocular delivery. SB 290157’s interpretability and safety liabilities make it unsuitable as a development candidate despite strong in vitro efficacy.
Reasoning: While SB 290157 demonstrates direct in vitro and in vivo modulation of complement-driven RPE pathology, its biased agonism, off-target C5aR2 activity, short half-life, and systemic toxicities severely limit its translational potential. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Divanillin is a naturally occurring oxidative dimer of vanillin that belongs to the class of phenolic dimers. Its synthesis is based on the oxidative coupling of monomeric vanillin—a well‐known flavor and fragrance molecule—using either chemical oxidants or, more efficiently, enzymatic methods. For instance, studies have demonstrated that fungal laccases, in particular, those derived from white-rot fungi such as Funalia trogii, can oxidize vanillin to form divanillin with near-quantitative yields under controlled reaction conditions (Esparan, 2015; Tai et al., 2011). Historically, divanillin was first noted for its presence in cured vanilla beans and has subsequently been developed for applications in the flavor and fragrance industries owing to its potent taste-enhancing properties, including its well-documented bitterness masking effects and its very low sensory threshold (Esparan, 2015; Krings et al., 2015; Torres-Zamudio et al., 2025). Its chemical profile, with lower water solubility compared to vanillin, also sets it apart as a candidate in formulations where controlled bioavailability is desired. As a low-molecular-weight compound, divanillin is amenable to formulation for ocular applications, and its repurposing as a modulator of intracellular signaling pathways, specifically in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), is a novel extension of its traditional roles.  

Therapeutic History:  
Divanillin’s historical usage has been largely in the realm of food and cosmetic applications. It has been known since the late 19th century and has been subject to extensive chemical characterization and synthesis studies through the early to mid-20th century (Esparan, 2015; Krings et al., 2015). In these fields, it is typically employed as a taste enhancer and bitterness masking agent, with its generation via enzymatic oxidation contributing to its characterization as a stable, bioactive phenolic dimer (Esparan, 2015; Torres-Zamudio et al., 2025). Over the years, the antioxidant properties of vanillin and its derivatives have been a major focus, with research demonstrating that multi-vanillin moieties can yield compounds with dramatically enhanced antioxidant activity compared to vanillin alone (Scipioni et al., 2018). Although these studies have primarily concentrated on neuroprotection, DNA damage protection, and cellular antioxidant capacities—such as those observed in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells—the literature does not currently report any direct clinical or preclinical application of divanillin for retinal diseases, including dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Scipioni et al., 2018; Tai et al., 2011). In parallel, a number of small-molecule SIRT1 activators, such as resveratrol and other natural polyphenols, have been explored in various ocular models and have shown promise in protecting RPE cells from oxidative damage and in modulating inflammatory pathways (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Ishida et al., 2017; Taurone et al., 2022). Thus, while divanillin itself has not been previously used for treating dry AMD or similar retinal conditions, its structural relationship to vanillin combined with emerging evidence regarding the benefits of vanillin derivatives suggests that repurposing divanillin for ocular use is a feasible and promising strategy.

Mechanism of Action:  
The central hypothesis proposed for divanillin is that it can function as a small molecule activator of SIRT1 in retinal pigment epithelial cells by achieving an effective concentration (EC₅₀) of approximately 1 µM. SIRT1 is a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)-dependent deacetylase that has critical roles in cellular metabolism, stress responses, and longevity. One of its well-established functions is the deacetylation of key cytoskeletal regulatory proteins, including cortactin and cofilin, which govern actin assembly and remodeling (Shentu et al., 2016). Cortactin, for instance, is a scaffold protein that binds to filamentous actin (F-actin) and the Arp2/3 complex and is involved in the formation of cell protrusions and phagocytic cups, whereas cofilin facilitates actin filament severing and turnover. In endothelial cells, it has been shown that AMPK phosphorylates cortactin at a critical threonine residue, priming it for SIRT1-mediated deacetylation; this sequential modification is essential for cortactin’s proper localization at the cell periphery and for dynamic actin remodeling (Shentu et al., 2016). Although this mechanism has been elucidated mainly in endothelial and other cell types, it is highly plausible that a similar pathway operates in RPE cells, where robust cytoskeletal dynamics are needed to support the daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Tarau et al., 2019; Cabrera, 2018).  

In RPE cells, phagocytosis is not a mere housekeeping task but a highly regulated process that demands rapid and targeted rearrangement of the actin cytoskeleton to form phagocytic cups that engulf the shed POS. Emerging studies have demonstrated that oxidative stress—a feature central to dry AMD pathology—can cause significant disruptions in the actin cytoskeleton, which contribute to impaired POS uptake and cellular degeneration (Tarau et al., 2019). SIRT1 activation, by deacetylating substrates such as cortactin and possibly cofilin, may restore or enhance the dynamic assembly of F-actin, thereby promoting more efficient phagocytic cup formation and POS internalization. In parallel, activation of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis in RPE cells has been linked with improved mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant responses, offering a dual mode of cytoprotection—a mechanism that is particularly attractive in the context of chronic oxidative stress typical of dry AMD (Ishida et al., 2017; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Furthermore, other small-molecule SIRT1 activators have already demonstrated the capacity to modulate oxidative stress and confer cellular protection in ocular models (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Taurone et al., 2022), lending additional credence to the hypothesis that divanillin may exert similar beneficial effects. In summary, the proposed mechanism of action for divanillin involves its SIRT1 activation properties leading to enhanced deacetylation of cytoskeletal regulatory proteins, which in turn promotes actin reorganization necessary for efficient phagocytosis by RPE cells under conditions of oxidative stress.

Expected Effect:  
Under the experimental conditions outlined in the proposal, treatment of RPE cells with divanillin at concentrations around its EC₅₀ of 1 µM is expected to result in the activation of SIRT1, a response that could be measured using biochemical assays indicative of its deacetylase activity. This SIRT1 activation is anticipated to lead to the deacetylation of its substrates, notably cortactin and cofilin, which are critical to the regulation of F-actin polymerization and reorganization (Shentu et al., 2016). At the molecular level, enhanced deacetylation of cortactin should facilitate its translocation to the cell periphery, where it can interact more effectively with the actin cytoskeleton, thereby promoting the formation of phagocytic cups, structures that are essential for the ingestion of POS (Tarau et al., 2019; Cabrera, 2018). The resulting improvement in cytoskeletal dynamics is projected to augment the ability of RPE cells to internalize shed photoreceptor outer segments—a process that is compromised in dry AMD due to cumulative oxidative damage and cytoskeletal disruption (Scipioni et al., 2018; Tarau et al., 2019).

Furthermore, activation of SIRT1 is expected to simultaneously confer additional cytoprotective benefits, including the enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis and function through the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis. This effect is highly relevant in RPE cells because their high metabolic demand and constant exposure to oxidative stress make them particularly vulnerable to mitochondrial dysfunction (Ishida et al., 2017; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). The improved mitochondrial function coupled with enhanced phagocytic efficiency would likely reduce the accumulation of oxidative damage and cellular debris, thereby mitigating key pathological features of dry AMD. Based on analogous studies employing other SIRT1 activators—such as resveratrol, which has been shown to protect RPE cells from oxidative stress and improve their phagocytic capability—the anticipated outcomes with divanillin include a measurable increase in POS uptake and improved cellular resilience under stress conditions (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Taurone et al., 2022). Consequently, these translational effects would be expected to translate into overall improved cellular homeostasis and a potential retardation of the degenerative processes observed in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
In assessing divanillin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several compelling strengths emerge. First and foremost, divanillin is a small-molecule agent that can be synthesized via well-established enzymatic processes from vanillin, a compound with a long history of safe use in food and cosmetic applications (Esparan, 2015). This favorable tolerability profile, combined with its robust antioxidant properties, provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in the ocular setting. The preclinical literature on vanillin derivatives indicates that incorporating multiple vanillin moieties into a single molecule can lead to a dramatic increase in antioxidant and cytoprotective activities (Scipioni et al., 2018), suggesting that divanillin may confer similar benefits in the context of retinal degeneration.  

Moreover, the innovative hypothesis that divanillin can activate SIRT1 in RPE cells is supported by a broader body of work demonstrating that SIRT1 plays a critical role in modulating oxidative stress, mitochondrial biogenesis, and cytoskeletal dynamics. There is substantial literature illustrating that SIRT1 activation leads to the deacetylation of key regulatory proteins such as cortactin, thereby promoting actin cytoskeleton remodeling—a process essential for phagocytic cup formation and efficient photoreceptor outer segment internalization (Shentu et al., 2016; Tarau et al., 2019). In this regard, targeting the SIRT1 pathway is a sound strategy, given that other natural SIRT1 activators, including resveratrol, have exhibited beneficial effects in RPE models under oxidative stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Taurone et al., 2022). This dual action—not only providing antioxidant protection but also enhancing the structural functionality of RPE cells—addresses two critical components of dry AMD pathogenesis: oxidative damage and impaired phagocytosis.

Despite these promising attributes, several weaknesses and uncertainties remain. Foremost among these is the lack of direct experimental evidence linking divanillin with SIRT1 activation in RPE cells. The proposed effective concentration (EC₅₀ ~ 1 µM) is based on extrapolations from studies with other vanillin derivatives and SIRT1 activators; however, no published data currently validate this specific potency for divanillin in ocular cells. In addition, while the mechanism by which SIRT1 deacetylates cortactin and potentially cofilin is well established in endothelial cells and other models (Shentu et al., 2016), it remains an assumption that RPE cells will respond identically, given their unique metabolic demands and specialized phagocytic functions (Tarau et al., 2019; Cabrera, 2018).  

There is also a significant gap concerning the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of divanillin in the context of ocular delivery. Although its small-molecule status and prior applications in non-ocular formulations suggest that it may have acceptable ocular tolerability and penetration, dedicated studies in retinal models or in vivo eye preparations are necessary to confirm its bioavailability and efficacy at the site of action. Furthermore, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD—with contributions from chronic inflammation, complement system dysregulation, and extracellular deposit formation—means that targeting SIRT1 and cytoskeletal dynamics may represent only one aspect of a comprehensive therapeutic approach (Crooke et al., 2017; Taurone et al., 2022). It will be important to consider whether divanillin’s purported mechanism can effectively address these other pathogenic mechanisms either alone or in combination with other treatments.

Another limitation is that, while divanillin’s antioxidant and cytoprotective properties have been indirectly demonstrated in studies examining vanillin and its derivatives (Scipioni et al., 2018; Tai et al., 2011), the direct link between these properties and improved phagocytic performance in RPE cells is yet to be established. Given that RPE phagocytosis is a highly specialized function that relies on precise spatial and temporal coordination of cytoskeletal activity (Tarau et al., 2019; Cabrera, 2018), even modest discrepancies in the modulation of actin dynamics could have substantial downstream effects on cellular homeostasis.  

Taken together, the overall evaluation of divanillin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. On the strength side, divanillin’s natural origin, ease of synthesis, and demonstrated antioxidant activity support its potential repurposing as a SIRT1 activator in the RPE. Its ability to modulate SIRT1—if validated experimentally—could translate into improved deacetylation of cytoskeletal regulatory proteins, enhanced F-actin remodeling, and more efficient phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments. These effects, in turn, could mitigate key aspects of dry AMD pathology, including the accumulation of oxidative damage and the gradual loss of RPE function. Such a dual mechanism of action—combining antioxidant protection with improved cellular architecture—is particularly attractive given the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD (Scipioni et al., 2018; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Shentu et al., 2016).  

However, the proposal is not without its challenges. The absence of direct evidence for divanillin’s SIRT1 activation in RPE cells, an unvalidated EC₅₀, and potential differences in the response of RPE cells compared to other cell types mean that significant preclinical work remains to be done. Rigorous in vitro studies using primary RPE cultures or established RPE cell lines will be necessary to confirm that divanillin can indeed enhance SIRT1 activity, deacetylate key substrates like cortactin and cofilin, and ultimately improve phagocytic cup formation and POS uptake. Additionally, in vivo studies using animal models of dry AMD will be critical to evaluate the compound’s pharmacokinetics, ocular bioavailability, and long-term safety and efficacy.  

In conclusion, divanillin represents a promising novel candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its potential to activate SIRT1 and thereby enhance actin cytoskeleton remodeling and phagocytosis addresses two critical pathological aspects of dry AMD—oxidative stress and impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments. Nonetheless, the current body of literature provides only indirect support for this mechanism, and several key areas require further investigation. If subsequent experimental studies confirm the proposed SIRT1 activation and cytoskeletal effects in RPE cells, divanillin could emerge as a valuable addition to the therapeutic arsenal against dry AMD, either as a monotherapy or as part of a combinatory treatment regimen. This candidate, therefore, warrants immediate prioritization in preclinical screening assays with a focus on verifying its molecular mechanism, efficacy in enhancing phagocytosis, and its overall impact on RPE cell function under oxidative stress conditions (Scipioni et al., 2018; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Shentu et al., 2016; Cabrera, 2018; Ishida et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB 290157 (N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine) is a synthetic, low–molecular-weight, nonpeptide ligand originally discovered in a SmithKline Beecham high-throughput radioligand displacement screen (~240,000 compounds) for inhibitors of human C3a binding to membranes from RBL-2H3 cells stably expressing C3aR; subsequent medicinal chemistry optimization of the initial hit (SKF 63649) yielded SB 290157 with markedly improved potency and cross-species activity at C3aR (human, mouse, guinea pig) (Ames et al., 2001). The compound is typically supplied as a trifluoroacetate salt by commercial vendors and has been used extensively as a pharmacological tool compound in vitro and in vivo, including ocular and non-ocular models (Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Chemically, SB 290157 is an arginine derivative bearing a 2,2-diphenylethoxyacetyl N2-acyl substituent; synthetic steps reported by the discovery group used Fmoc/Boc protection of arginine on Wang resin, coupling of tert-butyl(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetate via carbodiimide/DMAP, and final deprotection with TFA to give the target amide (Ames et al., 2001). In the original pharmacological characterization, SB 290157 behaved as a competitive C3aR antagonist in radioligand binding and functional assays in recombinant cells and primary neutrophils, with reported low-nanomolar functional potency in Ca2+-mobilization and platelet ATP-release assays; selectivity was claimed versus C5aR and other neutrophil chemoattractant GPCRs in those systems (Ames et al., 2001). The class of nonpeptide C3aR-directed small molecules has been pursued largely as research tools and preclinical probes of anaphylatoxin biology; SB 290157 is the prototypical representative and has been used across diverse inflammatory models to interrogate complement C3a–C3aR signaling (Ames et al., 2001).

Therapeutic History  
- Foundational pharmacology and in vivo anti-inflammatory activity: SB 290157 was reported in 2001 to inhibit C3a-induced responses in multiple cell systems and to reduce inflammation in rodent models, including decreased neutrophil accumulation in a guinea pig LPS-induced airway neutrophilia model and attenuation of paw edema in a rat adjuvant-induced arthritis (AIA) model when dosed intraperitoneally twice daily (b.i.d.) at up to 30 mg/kg (Ames et al., 2001). Pharmacokinetics in guinea pigs after a single 30 mg/kg i.p. dose showed high Cmax (~7000 ng/ml), sustained plasma levels (>100 ng/ml at 8 h), and a short apparent half-life (~0.9 h) (Ames et al., 2001). In ex vivo vascular assays, SB 290157 blocked C3a-induced increases in perfused rat caudal artery pressure and prevented receptor internalization in neutrophils, supporting functional antagonism in those readouts (Ames et al., 2001).  
- Ocular/retinal relevance: In an in vitro human fetal retinal pigment epithelium (hfRPE) transwell model, chronic recombinant human C3a exposure for two weeks drove sub-RPE extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation and wide-spaced collagen deposition, which were prevented by co-treatment with SB 290157 at 10 µM (trifluoroacetate salt); the antagonist did not impair transepithelial resistance or monolayer morphology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Mechanistically in the same hfRPE system, C3a impaired ubiquitin–proteasome pathway (UPP) activity and selectively elevated basal MMP-2 activity without changing proteasome-subunit mRNA, while promoting deposition of collagens IV and VI; these C3a-driven effects were reported to be abrogated by a C3aR antagonist, consistent with C3aR-mediated pathology in RPE (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In vivo, SB 290157 was used in a laser-induced retinal vein occlusion (RVO) mouse model where pharmacologic blockade of C3a/C3aR reduced fluorescein leakage, retinal thickness abnormalities, disorganization of inner retinal layers (DRIL), and serous detachment height, improved ERG b-wave and oscillatory potentials, and suppressed inflammatory gene programs (DEGs enriched for chemokine/NF-κB/IL-17 pathways); the authors explicitly note known pharmacological limitations of SB 290157 including potential off-target and agonist actions (Zhao et al., 2025). Genetic evidence relevant to ocular disease includes partial protection in light-damage models: global C3aR deletion decelerated retinal thinning after light insult, although photoreceptor apoptosis levels (TUNEL) were not significantly altered, suggesting C3aR contributes to retinal structural change but not necessarily acute photoreceptor death in that model (Behnke et al., 2025).  
- Broader in vivo applications and cautions: SB 290157 has been used to probe complement biology in diverse indications, with reported benefits in models of lupus nephritis, antibody-induced arthritis, thromboembolic stroke, and AD-related cognition; however, many of these reports predate or did not control for later-recognized pharmacology (partial agonism, off-targets), which complicates interpretation (Li et al., 2021; Coulthard & Woodruff, 2015). In a mouse cuprizone demyelination model, intraperitoneal SB 290157 at 1 mg/kg every other day modulated astrocyte reactivity (GFAP), TNF-α dynamics, and complement deposition (C3d), with the dosing choice explicitly motivated to minimize off-target C5aR engagement; nevertheless, the authors caution about SB 290157’s weak C5aR agonism and interpretability of systemic dosing (Frankle, 2023). In neuropathic pain (spared nerve injury), SB 290157 acutely reversed mechanical hypersensitivity but is limited by a short half-life (~1.5 h) and known off-target/agonist properties (Cook, 2019).  
- Pharmacological controversies and off-target receptor activity: Soon after its introduction, independent groups reported that SB 290157 exhibits C3aR agonist/partial-agonist activity in multiple cell systems, with potency dependent on receptor density and assay context; examples include near-maximal Ca2+ mobilization in transfected RBL cells, NAG release in differentiated U-937 cells, and ATP release in guinea pig platelets, whereas it appeared antagonistic in other systems (e.g., guinea pig platelets with very low receptor expression) (Mathieu et al., 2005). More recently, SB 290157 was shown to be a partial agonist at C5aR2 (β-arrestin recruitment EC50 ~16 µM; partial efficacy vs C5a) and to dampen C5a-induced ERK signaling in macrophages, introducing a mechanistically plausible anti-inflammatory off-target pathway at commonly used concentrations (Li et al., 2021). Practical dosing analyses indicate that in vivo exposures at commonly used doses (>10 mg/kg i.p. or >0.3 mg/kg i.v.) will engage both C3aR and C5aR2, and high-dose use has been associated with adverse effects in animals (neutropenia, transient hypertension, weight gain, hematopoietic effects, tachycardia) (Li et al., 2021). Finally, modern C3aR signaling work demonstrates SB 290157 is a potent C3aR agonist that drives Gi/o/z activation and strong β-arrestin–dependent internalization, which can masquerade as “antagonism” in Ca2+ flux assays by depleting surface receptors and calcium stores; this β-arrestin–driven internalization explains many prior contradictory results (Rodriguez et al., 2024).  

Importantly, no published animal model of drusen or geographic atrophy using SB 290157 is identified in the provided context; evidence for drusen/sub-RPE deposit modulation by SB 290157 is restricted to in vitro hfRPE systems, while in vivo ocular use has been reported in RVO, which is a vascular occlusive disease and mechanistically distinct from dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Zhao et al., 2025).  

Mechanism of Action  
- Target and signaling context: C3aR (C3aR1) is a class A GPCR canonically activated by the complement anaphylatoxin C3a; it couples preferentially to Gi/o/z to inhibit cAMP, mobilize Ca2+, and recruit β-arrestins to mediate receptor internalization and signaling bias, with expression across immune and stromal cells, including microglia/macrophages, neutrophils, mast cells, and ocular cells (Müller cells, microglia, macrophages, vascular endothelium), and on human RPE in vitro (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). C3a/C3aR signaling has been implicated in RPE dysfunction and retinal pathologies through both pro-inflammatory outputs (e.g., VEGF upregulation, leukocyte recruitment) and tissue remodeling (ECM deposition) (Kleinman & Ambati, 2016; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- SB 290157 at C3aR: Original reports characterized SB 290157 as a competitive C3aR antagonist in binding and functional assays, demonstrating inhibition of C3a-induced Ca2+ mobilization (IC50 ~27.7 nM in human RBL-C3aR cells; low-nanomolar potency across species) and blockade of receptor internalization and smooth muscle contractile responses (Ames et al., 2001). Later work showed that SB 290157 can behave as a partial/full agonist in multiple expression systems, with potency strongly influenced by receptor density; in overexpression models (CHO-C3aR), SB 290157 induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation with an EC50 ~0.46 nM and near-maximal efficacy relative to C3a, while in some primary systems (e.g., HMDMs) it did not exhibit agonism up to 100 µM yet inhibited C3a-induced ERK with an IC50 ~236 nM (Li et al., 2021). Orthogonal signaling profiling confirmed that SB 290157 is a potent C3aR agonist across Gi/o/z subtypes and is highly efficacious at β-arrestin recruitment/internalization; antagonism observed in Ca2+ assays can arise from this strong internalization blocking subsequent G-protein signaling (effects unmasked by barbadin or Pitstop-2), i.e., SB 290157 acts as a biased agonist with dominant β-arrestin/internalization bias in many contexts (Rodriguez et al., 2024).  
- SB 290157 at other complement receptors: Counter-screening revealed no activation of C5aR1 in the tested ERK readout, but consistent partial agonism at C5aR2 (β-arrestin2 recruitment EC50 ~16.1 µM; ~31% efficacy vs C5a), with functional consequences including attenuation of C5a-induced ERK signaling in human and mouse macrophages; thus, SB 290157 can engage anti-inflammatory C5aR2 pathways at micromolar concentrations (Li et al., 2021). Importantly, in vivo exposures at common doses are predicted to co-engage both C3aR and C5aR2, complicating mechanistic attribution (Li et al., 2021).  
- RPE-specific pathomechanisms and C3aR blockade: In primary hfRPE, C3a binds basolateral C3aR and triggers a cascade leading to sub-RPE ECM accumulation: (i) decreased proteasome (UPP) activity without changes in proteasome-subunit mRNA, indicating post-transcriptional downregulation; (ii) dysregulation of ECM turnover via increased basal MMP-2 activity and reduced TIMP-3 (markedly reduced TIMP-3 with proteasome inhibitor MG-132), consistent with enhanced collagenase activity; and (iii) increased deposition of collagen IV and VI beneath the RPE monolayer (dose- and time-dependent), without changes in collagen I or EFEMP1 (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). C3a exposure increased C3aR expression/localization on RPE basolateral membranes, while a C3aR antagonist prevented the C3a-driven proteasome impairment, MMP-2 elevation, and accumulation of basal deposits in this model (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Notably, C3a did not acutely alter intracellular calcium in these RPE cultures, suggesting RPE-specific signaling architecture differs from classic immune cell paradigms; the antagonist’s protective effects in RPE thus map to UPP/ECM modulation rather than Ca2+-dependent degranulation (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- Potency considerations: Reported SB 290157 binding affinity to C3aR is in the low-hundreds of nanomolar range (competition IC50 ~500 ± 250 nM; Ki ~210 ± 90 nM in membrane binding), whereas functional potencies span 7–30 nM in many GPCR Ca2+ or platelet assays; in HMDMs, C3a-ERK inhibition IC50 ~236 nM has been reported, and in hfRPE studies the antagonist was used at 10 µM without a defined IC50 in that context (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001; Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). These disparities emphasize system-specific pharmacodynamics and the need for concentration–response characterization in RPE.  

Expected Effect  
The proposed hypothesis is that SB 290157 will competitively inhibit C3aR on RPE (IC50 ~500 nM), thereby preventing C3a-driven proteasome dysregulation and sub-RPE deposit formation, restoring proteostasis and improving photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake and degradation in dry AMD RPE cultures. Available data from the hfRPE system strongly support the first two mechanistic links—C3a promotes basal deposit formation via UPP inhibition and MMP-2/TIMP-3 imbalance, and C3aR blockade with SB 290157 (10 µM) prevents those ECM/proteostasis changes and associated sub-RPE deposit formation without damaging the RPE monolayer (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Specifically, in multi-week C3a exposures, antagonist co-treatment normalized ECM ultrastructure (SEM/TEM), blocked accumulation of collagens IV and VI beneath the RPE, prevented C3a-induced upregulation of C3aR expression, and preserved proteasome functional readouts, which together map to restoration of RPE proteostasis and ECM turnover in this model (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). These observations are consistent with the broader mechanistic framework that C3a–C3aR signaling at RPE can drive early AMD-like basal deposit formation and that C3aR antagonism can reverse the key biochemical drivers (UPP impairment and MMP-2/TIMP-3 dysregulation) underlying deposit accumulation (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
However, the “IC50 ~500 nM” statement matches binding competition in recombinant systems rather than functional antagonism in RPE; hfRPE studies used 10 µM without a reported potency or binding occupancy analysis in this cell type, and inhibitory potencies vary substantially across cell systems (7–30 nM in Ca2+ mobilization and platelet ATP-release assays, ~236 nM for ERK blockade in HMDMs) (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001; Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). For the intended RPE assay, an empirical concentration–response curve is needed to establish the minimal effective concentration that prevents C3a-driven UPP and ECM changes, ideally bracketed below concentrations known to partially activate C5aR2 to avoid confounded anti-inflammatory signaling (Li et al., 2021). The claim that SB 290157 will improve POS uptake/degradation is not supported by the provided literature; neither the hfRPE work nor the broader SB 290157 pharmacology summarizes RPE phagocytosis or POS processing endpoints, and the signaling work documenting SB 290157 effects on phagocytosis pertains to microglia, not RPE (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Thus, while restoration of proteasome function may secondarily benefit proteostasis pathways relevant to POS degradation, this remains to be demonstrated in RPE and should be considered an untested hypothesis rather than an evidence-based expectation at this time (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
Expression of the pharmacological target in the assay system is established in vitro: C3aR is present on hfRPE basolateral membranes, is upregulated by C3a challenge, and mediates the proteasome/ECM phenotypes that are reversed by antagonist co-treatment (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Complement-responsive cell types within the retina (e.g., Müller cells, microglia, macrophages, vascular endothelium) also express C3aR, providing mechanistic plausibility for in vivo effects of C3aR blockade in retinal disease models, although RVO pathobiology differs fundamentally from dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2025).  

Overall Evaluation  
SB 290157 engages a biologically compelling axis (C3a–C3aR) with direct mechanistic links to early dry AMD pathogenesis in RPE, but its complex and context-dependent pharmacology imposes significant risks for both interpretation and translational development. The totality of evidence supports continued use of C3aR antagonism as a mechanistic strategy in RPE, while casting doubt on SB 290157 as a development-grade candidate without substantial de-risking.  

Strengths  
- Disease-mechanism alignment in RPE: Chronic C3a exposure in hfRPE is sufficient to recapitulate sub-RPE ECM changes typical of early AMD (collagen IV/VI deposition, wide-spaced collagen, impaired UPP, elevated basal MMP-2), and C3aR antagonism with SB 290157 prevents these changes with preservation of barrier integrity, directly linking the pharmacological target to a core pathophysiology in dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). This is among the strongest mechanistic anchors for any complement-modulatory strategy specifically at the RPE level in vitro.  
- Ocular in vivo proof-of-concept for C3aR blockade: In an RVO model (distinct from dry AMD), SB 290157 reduced clinical, imaging, and functional pathology and dampened retinal inflammatory transcriptional programs, supporting ocular efficacy when the C3a/C3aR axis is pathologically active in vivo (Zhao et al., 2025). Although RVO is not dry AMD, these data imply that C3aR antagonism can be delivered in vivo to the eye with measurable therapeutic impact on inflammation-driven retinal pathology.  
- Established discovery provenance and extensive preclinical use: The origin, synthesis, and extensive cross-species pharmacology of SB 290157 are well documented, facilitating procurement and standardized use as a pharmacologic probe in RPE assays; the compound is commercially available as a TFA salt and has been broadly applied in complementary models, enabling rapid head-to-head comparisons and orthogonal validation strategies (Ames et al., 2001; Li et al., 2021).  

Limitations and risks  
- Intrinsic pharmacology is not a clean “antagonist”: SB 290157 is a potent, biased C3aR agonist that robustly recruits β-arrestin and internalizes the receptor, and it partially activates C5aR2 at micromolar concentrations; both properties confound interpretation of putative antagonism and introduce off-target anti-inflammatory mechanisms at concentrations commonly used in vitro and in vivo (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In particular, the 10 µM concentration effective in hfRPE lies in the range that can engage C5aR2, so anti-inflammatory effects may not be solely attributable to C3aR blockade (Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- System-dependent behavior: SB 290157 displays agonism at C3aR in overexpression systems and certain endogenously expressing cells, but antagonizes readouts in others (e.g., human macrophages, guinea pig platelets), a pattern explained by receptor density and signaling bias; this variability raises concerns that RPE outcomes could depend on culture conditions (e.g., receptor upregulation by C3a) and surface expression levels in ways that shift net pharmacology (Mathieu et al., 2005; Rodriguez et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- Dosing and translational exposure liabilities: In vivo, commonly used doses achieve plasma concentrations predicted to co-activate C5aR2 and/or trigger undesired systemic effects (neutropenia, cardiovascular changes); short half-life complicates chronic dosing paradigms, and ocular tissue exposure metrics are not defined for SB 290157 (Li et al., 2021; Ames et al., 2001; Mathieu et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2025). While the RVO study demonstrates functional benefit, it also acknowledges SB 290157’s pharmacological limitations, emphasizing the need for sham controls and target validation beyond a single tool compound (Zhao et al., 2025).  
- Lack of in vivo dry AMD/drusen data: No in vivo evidence in the provided context demonstrates that SB 290157 reduces drusen or geographic atrophy in animal models; the in vitro hfRPE data are compelling but represent a reductionist system that does not capture subretinal immune cell interactions, Bruch’s membrane transport, or choriocapillaris alterations central to dry AMD pathogenesis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- POS uptake/degradation claim is unsubstantiated: The assertion that SB 290157 will improve RPE POS phagocytosis and degradation is not supported by the cited literature; no presented data quantify SB 290157 effects on RPE phagolysosomal function, and extrapolation from proteasome restoration to POS handling remains hypothetical (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  

Recommendations for a decision path  
- Near-term, SB 290157 is suitable as a positive-control pharmacological tool for target validation in RPE culture under stringent controls, not as a development candidate. In hfRPE, reproduce and extend published findings under defined C3a challenges by:  
  • Determining a full concentration–response for SB 290157 (e.g., 30 nM to 10 µM) on UPP activity, basal MMP-2, TIMP-3 expression, and collagen IV/VI deposition, with parallel assessment of C3aR surface expression, to establish minimally effective concentrations and exclude pro-inflammatory or agonist-like effects at lower doses (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
  • Incorporating orthogonal target validation: C3aR knockdown/knockout in RPE (if feasible), and pharmacological controls to test C5aR2 involvement (e.g., C5aR2-selective agonism as a counter model, acknowledging that RPE C5aR2 expression is not defined here), plus use of alternative C3aR reagents (e.g., anti-C3aR antibodies) where practical (Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
  • Adding phagocytosis endpoints (POS uptake, lysosomal degradation kinetics) to directly test the hypothesis that proteasome restoration by C3aR blockade enhances POS processing; these endpoints are currently unsupported (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
  • Monitoring off-target and cytotoxicity signals, including β-arrestin–dependent internalization (if assayable) to correlate with functional outcomes and to avoid misinterpreting biased agonism as antagonism (Rodriguez et al., 2024).  
- For in vivo exploration, given the interpretability risks with SB 290157, de-emphasize systemic dosing and consider localized delivery paradigms and/or more selective C3aR agents if available. If SB 290157 must be used, constrain intraperitoneal dosing to ≤1 mg/kg to minimize C5aR2 engagement and track pharmacodynamic readouts consistent with RPE-centric mechanisms (e.g., basal laminar deposit markers, MMP-2/TIMP-3 balance) in AMD-relevant models, recognizing that no such drusen/GA mitigation data are currently available for SB 290157 (Li et al., 2021). Genetic models (C3aR deletion) provide partial support for retinal structural preservation after injury, but differ in mechanism and context from RPE-intrinsic deposit biology (Behnke et al., 2025).

The need for improved C3aR ligands is highlighted repeatedly in the pharmacology literature due to SB 290157’s liabilities (Mathieu et al., 2005; Coulthard & Woodruff, 2015; Rodriguez et al., 2024).  

Conclusion  
On balance, C3aR antagonism remains an attractive target mechanism for early dry AMD based on robust RPE-centric in vitro data linking C3a–C3aR signaling to proteasome impairment, ECM dysregulation, and sub-RPE deposit formation, with SB 290157 acting as an effective tool compound to prevent these changes in hfRPE (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). However, SB 290157’s complex pharmacology—potent biased C3aR agonism and partial C5aR2 agonism—creates substantial risks for misattributing mechanism and for translation, particularly at micromolar concentrations or systemic in vivo exposures where off-target signaling is likely (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Li et al., 2021). There is no in vivo evidence here that SB 290157 reduces drusen/geographic atrophy, and the claimed benefits for POS phagocytosis are unproven (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Zhao et al., 2025). As a result, I recommend using SB 290157 only as a controlled, short-term pharmacologic probe to (a) mechanistically validate the role of C3aR in RPE proteostasis/ECM biology and (b) set pharmacodynamic benchmarks for target engagement in RPE; in parallel, we should invest in sourcing or developing next-generation, selective C3aR antagonists with confirmed lack of agonism and C5aR2 activity for any advancement toward dry AMD models and, ultimately, clinical translation (Mathieu et al., 2005; Rodriguez et al., 2024; Coulthard & Woodruff, 2015).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Auranofin is an orally bioavailable gold(I) complex that was first synthesized as a candidate to treat rheumatoid arthritis and is historically considered the first orally administered gold drug. Chemically, it is composed of a water‐soluble aurothioglucose moiety linked to a lipophilic triethylphosphine ligand, and, upon metabolism, it yields active gold species such as a triethylphosphine–gold(I) cation and gold–thioglucose derivatives (Abdalbari, 2025). Auranofin belongs to the class of organogold compounds, which have long been recognized for their anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties. In general, this class of compounds has been used primarily in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis due to their ability to modulate immune cell activity, interfere with inflammatory cytokine production, and target redox-sensitive enzymes. Although originally developed and clinically validated for rheumatic diseases, research over the past decades has repurposed auranofin for anticancer, antiparasitic, antimicrobial, and more recently, for potential neuroprotective indications (Madeira, 2012; Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a).  

Therapeutic History:  
Auranofin has an established therapeutic history as an anti-rheumatic agent with a clinical safety profile characterized over several decades of use. In the 1980s it was approved by regulatory agencies for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis where it demonstrated comparable efficacy with fewer severe side effects relative to parenteral gold salts, while its oral delivery provided a significant improvement in patient compliance (Abdalbari, 2025). In addition to its use in rheumatology, auranofin has been studied for its anticancer properties, with investigations demonstrating its ability to induce reactive oxygen species (ROS), inhibit cell proliferation, and trigger apoptosis in various cancer models including ovarian, lung, and mesothelioma cells (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a; Mertens et al., 2023). Despite its broad repurposing interest in oncology and infectious diseases, auranofin has not been directly used for treating dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, the cellular mechanisms implicated in its pharmacological actions—particularly its effects on redox homeostasis and anti-inflammatory pathways—provide a compelling rationale for exploring its potential in dry AMD, a disease known to involve chronic oxidative stress, lysosomal dysfunction, and inflammation in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021b; Chen et al., 2023).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary molecular target of auranofin is thioredoxin reductase (TrxR), a critical selenoenzyme involved in maintaining cellular redox balance. Auranofin interacts with TrxR by binding preferentially to its redox-active selenocysteine residue, thereby irreversibly inhibiting its NADPH-dependent catalytic activity (Abdalbari, 2025). Inhibition of TrxR disrupts the thioredoxin (Trx) system leading to an accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and oxidative stress within the cell. This increase in ROS, while potentially cytotoxic at high levels, can also serve as a signal to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, a master regulator of antioxidant responses. Under conditions of elevated oxidative stress, Nrf2 translocates to the nucleus and binds to antioxidant response elements (ARE) in the regulatory regions of target genes, inducing the expression of several cytoprotective enzymes, including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) and enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis and regeneration (Chen et al., 2016; Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a).  

In addition to its redox-modulatory function, auranofin has been reported to affect lysosomal pathways. Preclinical studies in RPE-derived cells (ARPE-19) have shown that auranofin can attenuate lysosomal alkalinization and thereby improve lysosomal function, an effect that may translate into enhanced degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) under oxidative stress conditions (Chen et al., 2016). This effect on lysosomal preservation is particularly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where the accumulation of undigested POS debris contributes to the formation of drusen and lipofuscin, leading to RPE dysfunction over time. Auranofin’s dual impact—disrupting redox homeostasis via TrxR inhibition while simultaneously triggering a compensatory Nrf2-mediated antioxidant response and preserving lysosomal function—constitutes an attractive mechanistic rationale for its repurposing into ocular indications (Abdalbari, 2025).  

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesized mechanism, when applied to RPE cells, auranofin is expected to inhibit TrxR activity, thus initially promoting an increase in ROS production. This controlled elevation in ROS is anticipated to serve as a secondary signal for the activation of Nrf2, which in turn drives the transcription of antioxidant genes such as HO-1 and genes involved in glutathione synthesis, thereby restoring intracellular redox balance (Madeira, 2012; Abdalbari, 2025). In ARPE-19 cell assays, this cascade should lead to a measurable increase in cellular antioxidant capacity, as well as a reduction in oxidative damage markers. Furthermore, by preserving or even restoring lysosomal acidity and function, auranofin is expected to boost the degradation of POS, particularly in cells challenged with lipofuscin components such as A2E that are known to disrupt lysosomal function (Chen et al., 2016). The enhanced clearance of POS should, in theory, mitigate the accumulation of toxic byproducts that contribute to RPE senescence and the progression of dry AMD (Chen et al., 2023; Brodzka et al., 2024). Moreover, the improvement in lysosomal function may also translate into better maintenance of the RPE’s barrier function and phagocytic capacity, both of which are vital for retinal homeostasis. The oral safety profile established in rheumatoid arthritis supports the notion that, with proper dosing and perhaps targeted ocular delivery strategies, auranofin could be repurposed safely for ocular use, though detailed pharmacokinetic studies in ocular tissues would be required to confirm this (Abdalbari, 2025).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Auranofin presents several compelling strengths as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its well-documented history as an orally administered anti-rheumatic agent with an established human safety profile allows for rapid progression into clinical testing if preliminary ocular efficacy is demonstrated. The mechanistic rationale is robust: by inhibiting TrxR, auranofin triggers an increase in ROS that activates the Nrf2 pathway, culminating in the upregulation of cytoprotective antioxidant genes, restoration of glutathione levels, and the preservation of lysosomal function—all of which are key factors in countering the pathogenic processes in dry AMD (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a; Mertens et al., 2023). In addition, preclinical evidence in RPE models indicates that auranofin can modulate signaling pathways such as EGFR/MAPK and that its effects are ROS-dependent, as demonstrated by the mitigation of toxicity with the antioxidant N-acetyl cysteine (Chen et al., 2016).  

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges remain. Although the mechanistic data derived from cancer and non-ocular studies are promising, direct in vivo evidence of auranofin’s efficacy in AMD or related RPE dysfunction models is currently lacking. The cytotoxic nature of auranofin at higher concentrations observed in ARPE-19 cells necessitates careful determination of a dosing window that maximizes the beneficial activation of Nrf2 and lysosomal preservation without exacerbating oxidative damage or inducing cell death (Chen et al., 2016; Madeira, 2012). Furthermore, while the systemic safety of auranofin in rheumatic diseases is relatively well established, the specific requirements for ocular drug delivery—such as achieving sufficient retinal bioavailability while minimizing off-target effects—pose additional challenges that must be addressed through formulation innovation and rigorous preclinical testing (Abdalbari, 2025). Finally, because the pathogenesis of dry AMD is multifactorial, involving not only oxidative stress and lysosomal dysfunction but also inflammatory and complement-mediated processes, it is possible that auranofin alone may not be sufficiently efficacious in a clinical setting without combination with other therapeutic modalities designed to address these complementary pathways (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a; Chen et al., 2016).  

In summary, auranofin holds potential as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD due to its ability to modulate critical redox pathways via TrxR inhibition and subsequent Nrf2 activation, along with its potential to restore lysosomal function and improve the clearance of POS-related debris. Its established safety record in rheumatoid arthritis, combined with promising mechanistic underpinnings observed in both non-ocular and limited ocular cell models, supports further investigation into its use for dry AMD. However, given the current gaps in direct ocular evidence and the challenges of ocular drug delivery, additional preclinical studies specifically in AMD-relevant models (including detailed ARPE-19 studies, in vivo AMD models, and pharmacokinetic assessments in retinal tissue) are warranted to fully validate its therapeutic potential and safety for eventual clinical application (Chen et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2016; Madeira, 2012; Abdalbari, 2025).
