Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mdivi-1 is a small molecule pharmacological agent originally discovered through high-throughput chemical screening in yeast models and subsequently characterized in mammalian systems as an inhibitor of mitochondrial fission. It is a quinazolinone derivative that belongs to a class of compounds targeting mitochondrial dynamics, with the specific intent of modulating the activity of dynamin-related protein 1 (DRP1) (Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008; Smith & Gallo, 2017). DRP1 is a large GTPase that mediates mitochondrial fission by undergoing self-assembly at constriction sites on the outer mitochondrial membrane and catalyzing membrane scission; under physiological conditions, this process is balanced by mitochondrial fusion activities to maintain mitochondrial morphology, bioenergetics, and quality control. Mdivi-1 was synthesized and later commercialized (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. M0199) because of its ability to selectively inhibit DRP1 activity, thereby shifting the balance away from excessive mitochondrial division and promoting a more interconnected, tubular mitochondrial network (Rosdah et al., 2016; Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008). This compound’s origins as a research tool in basic mitochondrial biology have led to its investigation in various disease models ranging from neurodegenerative conditions and cardiovascular ischemia to ocular disorders, where mitochondrial dysfunction is known to play a critical role. Its repurposing for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is of particular interest because of the emerging evidence linking chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial fragmentation, and RPE (retinal pigment epithelium) dysfunction to AMD pathology (Yako et al., 2021; Somasundaran et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Mdivi-1 has been extensively used in preclinical studies to interrogate the role of excessive mitochondrial fission in diverse pathological conditions. Initial seminal work demonstrated that inhibition of DRP1 activity by Mdivi-1 could prevent mitochondrial fragmentation, reduce cytochrome c release, and attenuate apoptosis in yeast and mammalian cell models (Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008; Rosdah et al., 2016). Following these foundational observations, several studies explored its utility in neuronal and cardiovascular systems. For example, preclinical investigations in models of ischemia-reperfusion injury, myocardial infarction, and neurodegeneration revealed that Mdivi-1 treatment increased cell survival and improved functional outcomes by preserving mitochondrial structure (Chen et al., 2023; Park et al., 2011).  

In the ocular domain, Mdivi-1 has been tested in models of retinal ischemia, glaucoma, and retinal detachment. Studies have shown that Mdivi-1 can increase the survival of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) in settings of acute ischemic injury, and its administration in retinal detachment models improved photoreceptor survival by mitigating DRP1-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction (She et al., 2018; Park et al., 2011). Moreover, within RPE-specific research, there is evidence from ARPE-19 cell studies that Mdivi-1 can counteract H₂O₂-induced oxidative damage by preventing mitochondrial fragmentation and preserving mitochondrial membrane potential, thereby protecting cells from apoptosis (Yako et al., 2021). Although the majority of these studies have focused on acute oxidative stress paradigms, the use of Mdivi-1 in these diverse retinal models provides a strong rationale to explore its potential in treating dry AMD, a condition characterized by chronic RPE stress, impaired photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis, and progressive mitochondrial dysfunction (Yako et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of Mdivi-1 centers on its inhibitory effect on DRP1, a critical regulator of mitochondrial fission. In a normally functioning cell, DRP1 resides in the cytosol and, upon activation—often triggered by cellular stress or proliferative signals—it translocates to the outer mitochondrial membrane. There, DRP1 self-assembles into oligomeric complexes that hydrolyze GTP to execute the fission process (Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008; Rosdah et al., 2016). Mdivi-1 acts by binding to an allosteric site on DRP1, thereby inhibiting its GTPase activity and preventing the oligomerization necessary for mitochondrial membrane constriction (Rosdah et al., 2016; Smith & Gallo, 2017). This inhibition not only prevents the excessive fragmentation of mitochondria under conditions of oxidative stress but also stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential and curbs the release of pro-apoptotic factors such as cytochrome c (Yako et al., 2021).

At the biochemical level, studies using ARPE-19 cells have shown that Mdivi-1 treatment correlates with a significant reduction in markers of mitochondrial dysfunction—such as decreased cytochrome c leakage and improved maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential—even when the cells are challenged with oxidative insults like H₂O₂ (Yako et al., 2021). These protective effects are central to the proposed hypothesis for dry AMD, where preservation of mitochondrial function in RPE is paramount for sustaining ATP production and supporting energy-demanding processes like POS phagocytosis.

Several studies have reported that Mdivi-1 also acts as a reversible inhibitor of mitochondrial Complex I of the electron transport chain (Marx et al., 2024; Avilan, 2023). This off-target effect can modulate reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and potentially influence cellular bioenergetics in a manner that might either contribute beneficially by reducing oxidative stress or detrimentally by impairing ATP production if the inhibition of Complex I is too pronounced. Such dual activity necessitates careful titration of Mdivi-1 dosing to ensure that the beneficial effects of DRP1 inhibition are not overshadowed by unwanted metabolic interference. Additionally, post-translational modifications of DRP1, such as phosphorylation at serine residues 616 and 637, modulate its activity and may influence the sensitivity of DRP1 to inhibition by Mdivi-1 in different cellular contexts (Yako et al., 2021). This complexity underscores the need for a thorough understanding of Mdivi-1’s molecular interactions in RPE cells and how these might translate to functional benefits in conditions like dry AMD.

The central hypothesis guiding the proposed therapeutic application of Mdivi-1 in dry AMD is that by inhibiting excessive DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission, the drug will preserve the integrity of the mitochondrial network in RPE cells. Under oxidative stress conditions—conditions that mimic the chronic environmental challenges faced by the RPE in dry AMD—excessive mitochondrial fragmentation leads to diminished ATP production and impaired phagocytic function. In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have provided evidence that treatment with Mdivi-1 can normalize mitochondrial morphology, preserve mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduce the release of cytochrome c, all of which contribute to maintaining cellular ATP levels (Yako et al., 2021).

By stabilizing mitochondrial dynamics, RPE cells should be able to sustain adequate ATP production even under conditions of oxidative challenge, thereby directly supporting the energy-demanding process of POS phagocytosis. This is critical because efficient phagocytosis is a cornerstone of RPE function; failure to clear shed photoreceptor debris leads to the formation of drusen and the accumulation of lipofuscin, both hallmark features of dry AMD pathology (Yako et al., 2021).

Moreover, improved mitochondrial function should also contribute to the normalization of lysosomal pH—a factor that is important for the proper degradation of phagocytosed material. Together, these effects are anticipated to not only preserve cellular viability in the face of chronic oxidative stress but also enhance the functional capacity of the RPE to process photoreceptor debris, which in turn could slow or halt the progression of dry AMD. Thus, while the expected effect is highly promising, it is contingent upon precise dose optimization and careful validation in both acute and chronic RPE models.

Taken together, the literature supports the potential of Mdivi-1 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, predicated on its capacity to inhibit DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission and preserve mitochondrial network integrity in RPE cells. The compound’s strength lies in its well-documented ability to prevent mitochondrial fragmentation, maintain mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduce apoptotic signaling under conditions of oxidative stress, which are all pivotal factors in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Preclinical studies in various retinal and neurodegenerative models further bolster the case for its broader applicability in ocular diseases; evidence from glaucoma and retinal detachment models, as well as in ARPE-19 cell studies, suggests that modulating mitochondrial dynamics can offer significant neuroprotective benefits (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Park et al., 2011; She et al., 2018).

Nonetheless, several weaknesses temper the enthusiasm for Mdivi-1’s clinical translation in dry AMD. One of the primary concerns is the duality in its mechanism of action. Although Mdivi-1 is primarily characterized as a DRP1 inhibitor, multiple studies have raised valid concerns regarding its off-target effects, notably its inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I at higher doses (Marx et al., 2024; Avilan, 2023). This is particularly significant in the context of RPE cells, which are highly dependent on robust mitochondrial function and efficient ATP production to sustain their phagocytic and metabolic activities. Inadvertent inhibition of Complex I could lead to decreased ATP synthesis and an accumulation of ROS, thereby exacerbating rather than alleviating cellular dysfunction—an outcome that would be highly undesirable in a disease like dry AMD.

Another key issue is the apparent variability in effective dosing. While some studies report cytoprotective effects at concentrations around 1–10 µM, others have employed doses up to 50 µM to observe meaningful modulatory effects on mitochondrial dynamics (Yako et al., 2021). Such variability suggests that the effective therapeutic window might be narrow, and that even minor deviations in dosing could result in suboptimal efficacy or unintended toxicity. Provided that these challenges are addressed through rigorous preclinical studies and careful dose optimization, Mdivi-1 remains a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD.

Overall, our evaluation indicates that Mdivi-1 holds considerable potential as a therapeutic agent for dry age-related macular degeneration by targeting the mitochondrial dysfunction that is central to RPE pathology. Its ability to inhibit DRP1 and thereby reduce oxidative stress-induced mitochondrial fragmentation could preserve critical cellular functions such as ATP production and photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis, offering a novel mechanism of action to address this currently untreatable condition. However, the possibility of off-target Complex I inhibition and dose-dependent cytotoxicity underscore the need for further detailed mechanistic studies and dose-ranging experiments in both in vitro and in vivo models that better simulate the chronic progression of dry AMD. With these challenges appropriately managed, Mdivi-1 could potentially become an innovative mitochondrial-based therapeutic for a disease desperately in need of effective intervention (Yako et al., 2021; Marx et al., 2024; Avilan, 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Axitinib is a synthetic, indazole-based, small-molecule receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor originally discovered via medicinal chemistry optimization for anti-angiogenic oncology indications and subsequently approved as an oral therapy (Inlyta) for advanced renal cell carcinoma, reflecting high potency and selectivity for vascular endothelial growth factor receptors (VEGFR1–3) with additional activity against PDGFR-β and c-KIT (Fei et al., 2024; Tosi et al., 2017). In biochemical and cellular assays relevant to ocular angiogenesis, axitinib demonstrates pan-VEGFR inhibition with substantially greater sensitivity than anti-VEGF monoclonal antibodies in endothelial cells, and it also inhibits PDGFR-β–mediated signaling in pericytes at low nanomolar concentrations, consistent with dual-pathway blockade within the VEGF/PDGF axis (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Pharmacologically, oral axitinib exhibits a short plasma half-life (~2.5–6.1 h) requiring twice-daily systemic dosing in oncology, and class-typical adverse events are dominated by hypertension; these PK/AE features motivated ocular delivery strategies to achieve high intraocular exposure with minimal systemic spillover (Siedlecki et al., 2017). As a class, multi-targeted VEGFR/PDGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have long been deployed systemically for cancer and are being repurposed for ocular neovascular diseases with the goals of broader VEGF-pathway suppression and reduced injection burden via sustained intraocular delivery platforms (suprachoroidal suspensions, intravitreal depot implants, and bioresorbable hydrogel systems) (Fabre et al., 2022; Fei et al., 2024). Axitinib is notable among TKIs for very high VEGFR affinity and measurable inhibition of other angiogenesis-related kinases, including TIE2, which has implications for both efficacy breadth and potential effects on vascular stability in the retina and choroid (Leitch et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical ocular data consistently show axitinib suppresses choroidal and retinal neovascularization across models, with oral dosing at 5 mg/kg reducing laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (L-CNV) in mice, and continuous low-dose systemic infusion (0.875 mg/day for 7 days) decreasing fluorescein leakage and CNV lesion area in rats; in vitro, axitinib suppresses 3D sprouting and inhibits both endothelial and pericyte proliferation/migration at non-toxic concentrations, aligning with dual VEGFR/PDGFR blockade (Fei et al., 2024; Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In a rat L-CNV model, axitinib reduced FA leakage scores and CNV lesion area by approximately one-third versus vehicle, and in co-culture sprouting assays axitinib alone outperformed anti-VEGF and anti-PDGF combinations, reinforcing the mechanistic rationale for dual-pathway inhibition in pathological ocular angiogenesis (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Combinatorial approaches show synergy: co-administration with anti-VEGF antibodies enhanced anti-angiogenic effects in nonclinical studies, consistent with the broader concept that inhibiting pericyte/PDGFR-β support can potentiate VEGF-directed therapy (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Siedlecki et al., 2017).

Multiple ocular delivery strategies for axitinib have entered human investigation in neovascular AMD (nAMD) to address the treatment burden and durability limitations of intravitreal biologics, including a suprachoroidal injectable suspension (CLS-AX) and an intravitreal bioresorbable hydrogel implant (OTX-TKI) designed for 6–9 months of sustained release (Fei et al., 2024). Early clinical and translational signals indicate that suprachoroidal delivery achieves high posterior segment exposure with minimal systemic levels, and initial phase 1/2a experience with CLS-AX in nAMD reported acceptable tolerability and pharmacologic activity at low doses, while OTX-TKI demonstrated favorable safety and durability in early cohorts (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020). Across the TKI class, parallel depot strategies (e.g., vorolanib in Durasert, sunitinib depots) have shown biologic activity and reduced treatment burden in nAMD, although some programs reported visual acuity tradeoffs or required rescue therapy at non-negligible rates, highlighting the need for careful dose, exposure, and target-selectivity optimization (Fei et al., 2024; Leitch et al., 2024).

Topical/eye-drop TKI programs (pazopanib, regorafenib, PAN-90806, acrizanib) underscore translational challenges: although preclinical topical dosing can reduce leakage and CNV thickness, multiple phase II programs failed to meet efficacy endpoints or were terminated due to insufficient posterior segment exposure and ocular safety issues such as reversible corneal haze with acrizanib, indicating that noninvasive delivery often cannot reproducibly attain therapeutic concentrations at the choroid/RPE in humans (Fei et al., 2024). Importantly, the available literature contains no reports of axitinib being tested clinically for dry AMD (geographic atrophy) or for enhancing RPE phagocytosis; the development history for axitinib and related VEGFR/PDGFR TKIs is focused on nAMD and other retinal vascular diseases, and reviews repeatedly note a lack of evidence for dry-AMD applications in this drug class to date (Fei et al., 2024). Furthermore, while localized ocular delivery is being pursued to mitigate systemic exposure, case reports of retinal adverse events during systemic axitinib therapy—including impaired retinal circulation, reversible retinal toxicity, and central retinal vein occlusion—require vigilance and thoughtful PK/PD design in ocular programs (Bakri et al., 2024). More broadly, despite active investigation of small molecules for AMD, reviews emphasize that no clinical success stories for small-molecule drugs in AMD (outside recently approved complement inhibitors for GA) have been established, underscoring translational risk for new mechanisms and reformulations (Fei et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Axitinib is a potent ATP-competitive inhibitor of VEGFR1 (FLT1), VEGFR2 (KDR), and VEGFR3 (FLT4), with additional inhibitory activity against PDGFR-β and c-KIT, thereby interrupting intracellular tyrosine kinase signaling downstream of multiple pro-angiogenic ligands, including VEGF-A/B/C/D and PDGF-B (Tosi et al., 2017; Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In relevant ocular cell types, axitinib inhibits VEGF-driven endothelial proliferation with markedly greater potency than anti-VEGF antibodies and exerts nanomolar inhibition of PDGF-driven pericyte proliferation, supporting the mechanistic premise that simultaneous disruption of endothelial and pericyte signaling can destabilize nascent pathological vessels and reduce neovascular growth (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In 3D co-culture sprouting models that recapitulate endothelial–pericyte interactions, axitinib alone achieves robust inhibition of sprout number and length across low-nanomolar concentrations, matching or exceeding the effect of anti-VEGF plus anti-PDGF combinations, a pattern consistent with multi-receptor inhibition at the level of VEGFR/PDGFR RTKs (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Preclinical studies in retinal endothelial cells further demonstrate axitinib suppression of downstream MAPK/ERK signaling and oxidative stress markers, aligning with direct VEGFR pathway inhibition; limited in vitro reports also suggest reduction of VEGFR1/VEGFR2 and PDGFR-β phosphorylation in RPE or mixed cell models, though these do not extend to functional phagocytosis endpoints (Lazzara et al., 2024).

Mechanistically, axitinib’s kinase profile extends beyond VEGFR/PDGFR to other angiogenesis-modulating targets; notably, among three pan-VEGFR TKIs profiled preclinically (vorolanib, sunitinib, axitinib), only axitinib exhibited strong TIE2 inhibition, a pathway essential for vascular quiescence and stability that could influence choroidal and retinal vascular homeostasis under chronic intraocular exposure (Bakri et al., 2024). In comparative kinase panels and endothelial functional assays, all three TKIs displayed robust pan-VEGFR inhibition and abolished endothelial sprouting at high concentrations, but the TIE2-inhibitory signal was disproportionately strong for axitinib, suggesting type-specific off-target consequences that warrant consideration during dose selection for chronic ocular use (Bakri et al., 2024). While intravitreal biologics neutralize extracellular VEGF ligands, axitinib acts intracellularly to block receptor signaling, potentially addressing compensatory upregulation of VEGF-C/D observed with VEGF-A-only inhibition; however, the breadth of intracellular TKI targeting can also propagate off-target effects in non-endothelial cells if exposures are not carefully controlled (Leitch et al., 2024).

Delivery-route pharmacology is central to ocular mechanism realization: suprachoroidal injection of axitinib has demonstrated posterior-segment targeting with markedly elevated drug levels in the posterior eye cup versus intravitreal injection in rabbits and sustained RPE/choroid exposure with minimal systemic levels, thereby achieving compartmentalized receptor inhibition where angiogenic lesions and the RPE reside (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020). Complementary intravitreal hydrogel implant strategies (OTX-TKI) provide long-acting axitinib delivery (6–9 months), maintaining pharmacologically relevant intraocular concentrations to chronically suppress VEGFR/PDGFR signaling in nAMD; these platforms are designed to mitigate systemic adverse events while sustaining on-target ocular pharmacodynamics (Fei et al., 2024). Importantly, chronic VEGF pathway suppression carries theoretical risks for neurosensory retina and RPE health, and reviews emphasize the need to balance durable angiogenic control with potential adverse effects of continuous VEGF blockade in ocular tissues, particularly for non-neovascular indications (Wolf et al., 2022).

Therapeutic targets in the RPE relevant to the present hypothesis—MerTK and αvβ5 integrin—are core components of the photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytic machinery, with αvβ5 required for synchronized diurnal phagocytosis and MerTK essential for engulfment and internalization; however, the provided literature contains no direct experimental evidence that axitinib upregulates MerTK or αvβ5 expression or function in RPE, nor that PDGFR-β signaling tonically suppresses RPE phagocytic differentiation in vivo (Tosi et al., 2017). Reviews and experimental summaries repeatedly state that available axitinib data focus on endothelial/pericyte targets and CNV models, and that no studies directly link axitinib to enhanced RPE POS uptake, MerTK activation, or αvβ5 integrin upregulation in dry AMD models or RPE cell assays (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). Therefore, while axitinib’s biochemical capacity to inhibit PDGFR-β could, in principle, modulate RPE phenotypes if PDGFR-β were a suppressive node in RPE phagocytic signaling, this mechanistic leap is not supported by direct evidence in the provided literature (Bakri et al., 2024; Fei et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The proposed assay hypothesis is that low-dose axitinib will modulate PDGFR-β signaling in RPE to promote a pro-phagocytic differentiation state, enhancing MerTK and αvβ5 expression and POS uptake; however, the body of evidence provided does not include direct demonstrations of axitinib increasing RPE phagocytosis, MerTK activation, or αvβ5 expression in vitro, ex vivo, or in vivo (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). Available data show that axitinib reduces VEGFR1/VEGFR2 and PDGFR-β phosphorylation in retinal endothelial systems and in limited contexts citing RPE/HUVEC cells, but these findings stop short of connecting PDGFR-β inhibition to increased RPE phagocytic function, and no POS ingestion assays, MerTK phosphorylation readouts, or αvβ5 functional binding assays are reported for axitinib in RPE (Lazzara et al., 2024). By contrast, the canonical RPE phagocytic apparatus depends on αvβ5-mediated POS binding and MerTK-mediated engulfment, with genetic ablation models establishing necessity; the literature here confirms this machinery but does not implicate PDGFR-β overactivation as a hindrance to RPE phagocytic differentiation nor demonstrate that TKIs restore phagocytosis in RPE (Tosi et al., 2017).

If the assay system relies on differentiating human RPE and measures POS uptake alongside MerTK and αvβ5 expression, axitinib’s expected on-target effects would be limited to PDGFR-β kinase inhibition in RPE if PDGFR-β is expressed and active under the assay conditions; nevertheless, there is no provided evidence that such inhibition increases MerTK or αvβ5 levels or POS ingestion, and the hypothesis that PDGFR-β tone suppresses RPE phagocytosis remains unsubstantiated here (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). It is conceivable that low-dose axitinib could indirectly affect RPE phenotype via modulation of growth-factor signaling crosstalk, extracellular matrix deposition, or oxidative stress pathways observed in retinal endothelial cells; however, the provided literature does not extend these effects to RPE phagocytic function, and any expectation of enhanced MerTK/αvβ5 expression is speculative in the absence of direct data (Siedlecki et al., 2017; Lazzara et al., 2024).

Translational pharmacology considerations highlight both opportunity and risk: suprachoroidal axitinib enriches drug at the choroid/RPE with minimal systemic exposure, offering a delivery solution for RPE-targeted modulation if the mechanism were validated; at the same time, axitinib’s TIE2 inhibition and class-level concerns about chronic VEGF pathway suppression in the neurosensory retina argue for caution in non-neovascular indications such as dry AMD (Kaiser et al., 2020; Bakri et al., 2024). Moreover, systemic axitinib has been associated with retinal vascular adverse events in case reports, indicating that even low systemic exposures can affect retinal physiology, so RPE-targeted development would necessitate rigorous intraocular PK/PD mapping and safety margins that preserve vascular stability while testing RPE functional endpoints (Bakri et al., 2024). Given these constraints, the expected effect in an RPE phagocytosis assay is, at present, not evidence-based in the provided materials and should be framed as a hypothesis requiring first-principles validation rather than an anticipated outcome derived from prior literature (Fei et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
- Pharmacologic potency and dual-pathway coverage: Axitinib’s high-affinity pan-VEGFR inhibition with demonstrated PDGFR-β activity enables simultaneous suppression of endothelial and pericyte signaling, a combination that underpins robust anti-angiogenic efficacy in CNV models and may reduce fibrosis-linked extracellular matrix deposition in neovascular settings (Giddabasappa et al., 2016).  
- Validated ocular delivery options: Suprachoroidal suspension (CLS-AX) and intravitreal hydrogel implant (OTX-TKI) platforms have progressed into clinical testing for nAMD with encouraging ocular safety/PK signals, providing translationally relevant routes to expose the RPE/choroid compartment while minimizing systemic exposure (Wolf et al., 2022; Fei et al., 2024).  
- Clinical-stage experience in nAMD: Early-phase trials indicate biological activity and tolerability of axitinib-based intraocular approaches, suggesting a viable path to long-acting ocular therapy development if a new indication such as RPE phagocytosis enhancement is supported by mechanistic data (Leitch et al., 2024).  
- Class learnings and comparator programs: The broader TKI field in nAMD (vorolanib, sunitinib derivatives) offers benchmarks for durability, rescue-free rates, and safety considerations, facilitating rational dose and exposure setting for axitinib formulations (Fei et al., 2024; Leitch et al., 2024).  

Limitations and Critical Gaps  
- No direct evidence for RPE phagocytosis enhancement: Across the provided literature, there are no RPE-specific data showing axitinib increases MerTK or αvβ5 expression, augments POS binding or internalization, or improves phagocytic capacity in differentiating RPE; multiple summaries explicitly state the absence of such evidence and confine axitinib’s demonstrated actions to anti-angiogenic endpoints (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017).  
- Unvalidated mechanistic premise in RPE: While PDGFR-β is central to pericyte biology and vessel stabilization, the assertion that PDGFR-β overactivation hinders RPE differentiation and that its inhibition promotes a pro-phagocytic state is not supported in the provided texts, and the core RPE phagocytic machinery (MerTK, αvβ5) is not linked here to PDGFR-β modulation by TKIs (Tosi et al., 2017; Bakri et al., 2024).  
- Safety liabilities and target selectivity: Axitinib’s strong TIE2 inhibition could perturb vascular stability with chronic intraocular exposure, and class-level concerns exist for continuous VEGF pathway suppression affecting neurosensory retina and RPE; rare but notable retinal vascular AEs reported with systemic axitinib further mandate conservative exposure design and careful safety pharmacology tailored to non-neovascular indications (Bakri et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022).  
- Delivery constraints for non-neovascular endpoints: Topical TKI programs frequently failed due to inadequate posterior segment exposure and/or ocular surface safety findings, suggesting that any RPE-targeted application of axitinib would require invasive delivery (suprachoroidal/IVT depot) with chronic exposure, elevating the bar for safety and benefit-risk justification in a dry AMD population (Fei et al., 2024).  
- Field precedent: Reviews underscore that, to date, small-molecule success in AMD has been limited, and there are no approved ocular TKIs for either wet or dry AMD, reinforcing translational uncertainty for new mechanism-of-use proposals lacking direct preclinical support (Fei et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).  

Development Recommendations and Go/No-Go Criteria  
- Mechanistic validation in RPE: Before proceeding, perform a staged in vitro program in human iPSC-RPE and primary RPE to test whether axitinib modulates PDGFR-β phosphorylation and secondarily increases MerTK expression, MerTK phosphorylation upon POS challenge, αvβ5 expression/localization, and POS binding/internalization; include dose-response spanning sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar exposures aligned with ocular PK projections from suprachoroidal or depot IVT delivery (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020).  
- Specificity controls and orthogonal readouts: Use chemical and genetic controls to isolate PDGFR-β dependence (e.g., PDGFR-β ligand titrations, selective PDGFR-β inhibitors distinct from axitinib, and PDGFR-β knockdown), and include neutralizing antibodies and MerTK/αvβ5 functional blocking to map pathway causality for any observed phagocytosis changes (Tosi et al., 2017; Siedlecki et al., 2017).  
- Safety pharmacology in pigmented models: Given potential TIE2-related and VEGF-suppression liabilities, include long-term RPE morphology, barrier function (TEER), transcriptomic stress signatures, and photoreceptor/RPE co-culture viability endpoints at projected clinical exposures; extend to pigmented rabbit or NHP pharmacology to define posterior-segment exposure, ocular distribution (RPE/sclera/choroid), and a NOAEL for chronic dosing (Bakri et al., 2024; Kaiser et al., 2020).  
- Translational gating: Advance only if axitinib reproducibly increases POS uptake and MerTK/αvβ5 functional markers in RPE with a therapeutic window that avoids endothelial destabilization signals and preserves neuronal/RPE integrity in chronic exposure models; otherwise, deprioritize axitinib for RPE-targeted dry AMD and refocus efforts on mechanisms directly validated to enhance RPE phagocytosis or survival (Fei et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022).  

Conclusion  
On the strength of available evidence, axitinib is a validated, potent anti-angiogenic TKI with multiple ocular delivery platforms in clinical development for nAMD and robust preclinical efficacy in CNV models; however, the central hypothesis that low-dose axitinib enhances RPE phagocytosis via PDGFR-β modulation and upregulates MerTK/αvβ5 lacks direct support in the provided literature, and multiple sources explicitly state that no such RPE-centric data exist for axitinib at present (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Fei et al., 2024). The translational and safety profiles suggest that invasive ocular delivery could achieve RPE-adjacent exposure, but off-target TIE2 inhibition and class-level VEGF-suppression risks must be weighed carefully in a non-neovascular indication, particularly absent clear preclinical efficacy on RPE phagocytic endpoints (Bakri et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022). Accordingly, while axitinib remains attractive for anti-angiogenic applications, it should not be advanced for dry AMD on a phagocytosis-enhancement rationale without first producing compelling, direct RPE mechanistic data; in the absence of such data, development resources would be better allocated to candidates with demonstrated effects on MerTK/αvβ5 function or on complement-mediated RPE pathology more proximal to dry AMD pathophysiology (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Fei et al., 2024). Pending rigorous in vitro and ex vivo validation as outlined, the current evidence base supports a cautious “mechanism validation required” stance rather than progression to in vivo dry AMD studies or clinical translation for this proposed use (Fei et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).

The therapeutic candidate under evaluation is a CD82 agonist peptide, marketed as a tetraspanin activator (Peptide Institute Cat. No. K-8202). Tetraspanins are known to modulate cellular adhesion, migration, and signal transduction by forming dynamic “tetraspanin–enriched microdomains” (TEMs) that include integrins and other proteins; in particular, CD82 has been implicated in the regulation of integrin clustering and function in a range of cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and various immune cells (Lee et al., 2022). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB415286 is a synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK-3β) that belongs to the class of anilinomaleimide derivatives. It was discovered through high-throughput screening approaches using compound libraries such as that of SmithKline Beecham, where its ability to inhibit GSK-3β activity was identified in vitro with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range (approximately 20 nM) (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). As a representative of GSK-3β inhibitors, SB415286 has been widely used as a research tool to interrogate the role of GSK-3β in multiple biological processes including Wnt/β-catenin signaling, apoptosis, oxidative stress regulation, and autophagy. The chemical optimization of these compounds was driven by the need for greater potency and specificity in modulating complex kinase networks associated with neurodegenerative and ocular pathologies. SB415286 is commercially available (Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. SML0787) and exhibits properties that make it suitable for cell-based assays as well as animal studies targeting retinal cell functions (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In general, compounds in this class have been used in preclinical models to activate Wnt signaling by preventing β-catenin degradation, thereby enhancing transcription of genes involved in cell survival, differentiation, and tissue regeneration. This approach has been applied primarily in neurological research as well as in studies focusing on retinal degeneration, making SB415286 a candidate of interest for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
GSK-3β inhibitors as a class have a long history of preclinical exploration in various disease models, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and other neurodegenerative disorders where excessive kinase activity contributes to neuronal cell death. SB415286, in particular, has been used in primary neuronal cultures to elucidate the role of GSK-3β in mediating apoptotic pathways. Early studies demonstrated that inhibition of GSK-3β with compounds like SB415286 could protect neurons from intracellular stresses by moderately suppressing pro-apoptotic signals (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In the ocular field, GSK-3β inhibitors have been explored in the context of diabetic retinopathy, where their use was associated with improved retinal ganglion cell survival and mitigation of neurodegenerative processes induced by oxidative stress (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20). Furthermore, related compounds such as SB216763—sharing similar mechanisms—with evidence of restoring Nrf2 levels in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) under oxidative stress supports the hypothesis that GSK-3β inhibition is beneficial in ocular settings (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6; Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 10–12). Despite these promising findings, the clinical evidence directly linking GSK-3β inhibition to the treatment of dry AMD remains sparse. In fact, comprehensive analyses such as those performed using the Open Targets Platform have revealed only a very weak association between GSK3B and AMD with minimal literature evidence, suggesting that while the concept is scientifically sound and mechanistically plausible, direct translational studies in dry AMD are still in an early stage (Buniello et al., 2025). Nevertheless, the preclinical use of SB415286 in retinal models of diabetic retinopathy and its documented capacity to modulate pathways relevant to oxidative stress and autophagy imply that repurposing this candidate for dry AMD merits further investigation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, GSK-3β is a serine/threonine kinase that is constitutively active in many cells and functions as a pivotal regulator of several intracellular signaling cascades. Under basal conditions, GSK-3β phosphorylates its substrates—including β-catenin—thereby marking them for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. In the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, the inhibition of GSK-3β (either through upstream signals such as Wnt ligand binding or via pharmacological inhibitors like SB415286) prevents the phosphorylation of β-catenin, allowing it to accumulate in the cytoplasm and eventually translocate into the nucleus (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Once in the nucleus, β-catenin forms complexes with TCF/LEF transcription factors to drive the transcription of genes involved in cell proliferation, differentiation, and cytoskeletal remodeling. In the context of RPE cells, this activation is critical because it is believed to upregulate lysosomal proteins, such as LAMP1, and phagocytic receptors, like MERTK, that are essential for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17; Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).  

Moreover, GSK-3β also exerts a negative regulatory influence on the Nrf2/NRF2 antioxidant pathway. Under oxidative stress, Nrf2 typically transactivates a battery of cytoprotective genes; however, GSK-3β phosphorylates Nrf2 at specific motifs within its Neh6 domain, facilitating recognition by the β-TrCP E3 ubiquitin ligase and leading to its degradation (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6). Hence, inhibition of GSK-3β with SB415286 can stabilize Nrf2, thereby reinforcing the cellular antioxidant capacity—a particularly attractive mechanism given the elevated oxidative stress encountered in aging RPE cells in dry AMD.  

In addition to these signaling events, inhibition of GSK-3β modulates autophagy. Research indicates that proper autophagic flux is necessary for the turnover of damaged cellular components, including the disposal of POS debris, and that impaired autophagy is a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 10–12, 32–34). It is also important to note that GSK-3β is implicated in the regulation of the cytoskeletal machinery; its inhibition may lead to reorganization of actin and other cytoskeletal elements, which is critical for the phagocytic process in RPE cells (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). However, caution is warranted because GSK-3β not only modulates beneficial pathways but also participates in processes such as epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), where excessive or inappropriate inhibition has been associated with fibrotic changes in the RPE (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 14–18). Thus, while the inhibition of GSK-3β by SB415286 is expected to elevate β-catenin levels and trigger downstream transcription of lysosomal and cytoskeletal genes, the balance of these signaling events must be carefully modulated to avoid adverse outcomes.

The resultant accumulation and nuclear translocation of β-catenin are expected to drive the transcription of a subset of genes critical for maintaining RPE function, including those involved in lysosome biogenesis (e.g., LAMP1) and the phagocytic machinery (e.g., MERTK). In evaluating SB415286 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key aspects emerge from the literature review. First, GSK-3β is a multifunctional kinase that plays roles in a wide array of cellular processes; it is involved not only in the regulation of the Wnt/β-catenin and Nrf2 pathways but also in the control of apoptosis, glucose homeostasis, and even inflammatory responses. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Trehalose is a naturally occurring, nonreducing disaccharide composed of two D‐glucose units (MW = 342.3 Da) that is not synthesized endogenously in mammals but is abundant in other organisms such as fungi, plants, and invertebrates (Cox et al., 2025). It was originally discovered as a cellular protectant and osmolyte that stabilizes proteins and membranes under conditions of stress, and its unique chemical stability and protein‐protective properties have led to its use in cryopreservation and organ transplant protocols (Lotfi et al., 2018). As a small-molecule therapeutic candidate, trehalose belongs to a class of compounds known as osmolytes and molecular chaperones; this category has been extensively explored for its capacity to stabilize proteins, prevent aggregation, and enhance cellular resilience in the face of diverse environmental and metabolic stresses (Abokyi et al., 2020; Cox et al., 2025). In drug development contexts, its repurposing for dry age-related macular degeneration (dAMD) is driven by its capacity to activate TFEB—a master transcription factor regulating the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network—and thereby boost autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ghosh et al., 2023). Trehalose has been formulated for ocular use, most notably as an ingredient in tear substitutes for dry eye, and its safety profile in such formulations provides ancillary support for its potential repurposing to target RPE dysfunction in dAMD (Cox et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Trehalose has a well-documented history in biochemical and preclinical research due to its potent protein-stabilizing and osmoprotectant actions. It has been widely used in non-ophthalmic applications, most notably in cryopreservation protocols, where its ability to preserve protein structure and cellular integrity under desiccating and freezing conditions is exploited (Cox et al., 2025; Lotfi et al., 2018). In the ocular field, trehalose has been evaluated primarily for anterior segment indications such as dry eye disease; several randomized clinical trials have demonstrated its tolerability and efficacy as a tear substitute when combined with hyaluronic acid, with improvements in tear film break-up time (TBUT) and ocular surface symptoms (Chiambaretta et al., 2017).  
More importantly for dAMD, multiple in vitro studies using human RPE cell models—including ARPE-19 and iPSC-derived RPE from patients with genetic risk factors like CFH mutations—have shown that trehalose rescues autophagy deficits and lysosomal dysfunction, especially under oxidative-stress conditions induced by agents such as hydroquinone (Abokyi et al., 2020). These studies report that trehalose treatment upregulates key autophagy regulators (e.g., ATG5, ATG7) and lysosomal markers (e.g., LAMP2, cathepsin D) while enhancing autophagic flux, thereby improving the degradative capacity of RPE cells—a fundamental defect implicated in the accumulation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and lipofuscin in dAMD (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). Additionally, in murine models of retinal degeneration—whether induced by light exposure or by genetic interventions—trehalose has been shown to protect against retinal cell loss and preserve outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness, offering further preclinical evidence of its neuroprotective potential (Cox et al., 2025). Thus, while trehalose has an established record in non-ocular uses and in the treatment of anterior ocular surface disorders, emerging data now support its repurposing for dAMD by virtue of its ability to modulate autophagy and lysosomal degradation in RPE cells (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central mechanism by which trehalose is hypothesized to benefit dry AMD involves its capacity to activate the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of the CLEAR network. TFEB controls the transcription of a whole battery of genes required for autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and metabolic adaptation (Abokyi et al., 2020). Typically, TFEB resides in the cytoplasm in an inactive, phosphorylated state under nutrient-rich or stress-depleted conditions; its translocation to the nucleus is tightly regulated by mTORC1-dependent and mTORC1-independent signaling pathways (Ghosh et al., 2023; Karim et al., 2020). Trehalose has been shown to induce TFEB nuclear translocation independently of mTOR inhibition, potentially through mechanisms involving Akt signaling modulation and AMPK activation (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Upon nuclear entry, TFEB binds to CLEAR elements in the promoter regions of target genes, thereby upregulating autophagy mediators such as ATG5 and ATG7, enhancing the expression of lysosomal proteins like LAMP2, and increasing the levels of protein markers such as LC3B and p62 that are involved in autophagosome formation and maturation (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Several biochemical studies in human RPE cells have demonstrated that trehalose treatment leads to increased TFEB mRNA and protein levels with concomitant upregulation of CLEAR network gene expression. For instance, in ARPE-19 cells exposed to hydroquinone—a model for oxidative stress relevant to dAMD—it was observed that trehalose not only increased LC3-II levels and GFP-LC3 puncta formation but also enhanced the degradation of autophagic substrates, indicating that trehalose facilitates effective autophagic flux rather than merely blocking lysosomal degradation (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Mechanistically, trehalose is thought to penetrate mammalian cells via fluid-phase endocytosis and possibly through the SLC2A8 (GLUT8) transporter, which facilitates its intracellular accumulation at millimolar concentrations (Cox et al., 2025). Once inside the cell, trehalose appears to modulate several key pathways: by inhibiting Akt signaling, it reduces the phosphorylation of TFEB at specific residues (such as S467) that normally prevent its nuclear import; concurrently, trehalose may activate AMPK, which further supports autophagy induction (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020). Moreover, although trehalose transiently upregulates NRF2 under basal conditions—thereby enhancing antioxidant defenses—its primary protective effect in oxidative stress models of the RPE appears to be mediated by restored autophagy, as demonstrated by loss of cytoprotection when autophagy is genetically disrupted via ATG5 knockdown (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Beyond its role in autophagy, trehalose has been implicated in promoting chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) through stimulation of LAMP2 expression, which is essential for CMA substrate recognition and lysosomal import (Abokyi et al., 2020). In this way, trehalose may offer a dual benefit: boosting canonical macroautophagy while also enhancing CMA, collectively leading to improved clearance of damaged organelles, aggregated proteins, and undigested POS in the RPE—a critical function given the strong association between defective POS clearance and the pathogenesis of dAMD (Abokyi et al., 2020). Furthermore, in CFH-mutant iPSC-derived RPE cells, trehalose has been shown to rescue the diminished activity of lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D and to restore other proteostasis markers, establishing a direct molecular link between trehalose-induced TFEB activation and functional improvements in the degradative capacity of RPE cells (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
Collectively, the mechanistic data suggest that trehalose exerts its beneficial effects through a complex interplay of intracellular signaling pathways that converge on the activation of TFEB, thereby re-establishing efficient autophagic clearance processes that are impaired in the aging and oxidative-stressed RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020; Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic insights outlined above, the hypothesis posits that treatment with trehalose at a concentration of 5 mM in an in vitro assay using iPSC-derived RPE cells from dry AMD patients will lead to robust TFEB nuclear translocation. This nuclear translocation is expected to result in the transcriptional upregulation of CLEAR network genes, thereby increasing the expression of autophagy regulators such as ATG5 and ATG7 and promoting the biogenesis of lysosomes, as evidenced by increased levels of lysosomal markers like LAMP2 and cathepsin D (Abokyi et al., 2020). In an environment of oxidative stress—for example, when the iPSC-RPE cells are challenged with hydroquinone to mimic cigarette smoke-induced damage or other oxidative insults commonly associated with AMD—the activation of TFEB by trehalose is anticipated to restore impaired autophagic flux. This restoration would be reflected in the accumulation of LC3-II upon inhibition of lysosomal function (e.g., in the presence of chloroquine) and decreased levels of autophagy substrate p62 (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Crucially, by enhancing autophagic and lysosomal function in the RPE, trehalose is expected to improve POS degradation. Efficient degradation of POS is vital for photoreceptor health, and its impairment has been implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD through the accumulation of toxic byproducts and lipofuscin (Abokyi et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025). Thus, the expected phenotype in the in vitro assay would include not only molecular signatures of enhanced autophagy (e.g., increased LC3B puncta, upregulated ATG gene expression) but also functional improvements such as reduced oxidative stress (lower reactive oxygen species levels) and improved cell viability under stress conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Moreover, previous studies have shown that trehalose’s cytoprotective effects are autophagy-dependent because genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of autophagy (e.g., via ATG5 knockdown) abolishes the otherwise protective effects of trehalose, thereby reinforcing the notion that the expected improvement in POS degradation and overall cellular homeostasis is tightly linked to the restoration of autophagy and lysosomal competence (Abokyi et al., 2020). In essence, the application of 5 mM trehalose to oxidative-stressed iPSC-RPE cells is anticipated to reverse the autophagic deficits that are characteristic of dry AMD, ultimately leading to enhanced clearance of POS, reduced accumulation of cytotoxic aggregates, and improved cellular survival and function in an in vitro model that recapitulates key aspects of the disease (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
Trehalose represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its multifaceted capacity to modulate intracellular degradation pathways that are critically impaired in the disease state. One of the primary strengths of trehalose is its robust preclinical evidence base. Multiple studies have demonstrated that trehalose can induce TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE models, resulting in the transcriptional activation of an array of autophagy and lysosomal genes (Abokyi et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2023; Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020). This mechanistic property directly addresses a key pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD, where the accumulation of undegraded photoreceptor outer segments and lipofuscin due to defective autophagy plays a contributory role in RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration (Abokyi et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025). The ability of trehalose to enhance both macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy augments its therapeutic appeal, as it suggests an overall improvement in cellular proteostasis, which is imperative in aged or stressed RPE cells (Abokyi et al., 2020; Cox et al., 2025).  
Another notable strength is the established safety profile of trehalose. It is a naturally occurring compound with a long history of use in various medical and industrial applications, including as an ingredient in ocular surface formulations for dry eye disease (Chiambaretta et al., 2017; Cox et al., 2025). Furthermore, the preclinical data showing that trehalose can protect against oxidative stress and preserve retinal function in animal models lend credibility to the hypothesis that it may exert similar protective effects in human RPE cells (Cox et al., 2025).  
However, several weaknesses and gaps must be acknowledged as well. First, the majority of the compelling evidence for trehalose’s efficacy in modulating TFEB and enhancing autophagy comes from in vitro studies using immortalized RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19) or rodent models, with only limited data available from human iPSC-derived RPE models specifically derived from AMD patients (Abokyi et al., 2020). Second, there are ongoing debates in the literature regarding the precise molecular mechanisms by which trehalose exerts its autophagy-enhancing effects, with some reports disputing its ability to induce autophagy under certain conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).  
Another potential challenge lies in the delivery of trehalose to the RPE in a clinically meaningful manner. Although trehalose is orally bioavailable and has been successfully formulated for topical ocular use in dry eye applications, the posterior segment of the eye presents unique drug delivery hurdles. Penetration through the cornea and subsequent distribution to the RPE and retina often require specialized formulations, and while there are preclinical reports of trehalose reaching posterior ocular tissues (Cox et al., 2025), comprehensive pharmacokinetic and ocular bioavailability data for trehalose in the context of dAMD remain sparse.  
Furthermore, while the repurposing of trehalose is attractive due to its established safety and low cost, intellectual property issues and regulatory challenges associated with drug repurposing may complicate clinical development. Despite these concerns, the overall body of evidence supports further investigation into trehalose as a potential modulator of TFEB and autophagy in the RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cox et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).  
In summary, trehalose offers several strong advantages as a candidate therapeutic for dry AMD. Its ability to activate TFEB and upregulate a broad spectrum of autophagy and lysosomal genes addresses a fundamental defect in RPE cells implicated in the disease. Robust preclinical evidence in both in vitro and animal models suggests that trehalose enhances autophagic flux, improves POS clearance, and confers cytoprotective effects against oxidative stress. Its favorable safety profile and prior use in ocular formulations further support its translational potential. However, critical gaps remain in terms of validating its efficacy in human-derived RPE models, optimizing its dosing and delivery to the posterior segment, and resolving discrepancies regarding its mechanism of action in different experimental contexts. Given these considerations, trehalose represents a promising candidate that merits further investigation—particularly through rigorous dose-response studies, advanced formulation development to enhance retinal delivery, and robust clinical trials in patient populations at risk for dry AMD—to fully establish its therapeutic value (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cox et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Pyrrolidine dithiocarbamate (PDTC) is a synthetic compound that belongs to the dithiocarbamate class, a group of molecules originally derived from the reaction of secondary or tertiary amines with carbon disulfide under alkaline conditions. PDTC is commercially available (for example, from Sigma-Aldrich, Cat. No. 239,804) and has been widely used in experimental research due to its multifunctional properties. Initially, dithiocarbamate compounds were recognized for their potent antioxidant capacities and metal chelation abilities; however, subsequent research identified PDTC as one of the most potent and specific inhibitors of nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), with its inhibitory action shown to be independent of its antioxidant effects (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). The compound’s structure, featuring both a pyrrolidine ring and dithiocarbamate moiety, imbues it with the ability to bind metal ions such as Zn²⁺ and modulate redox signaling pathways. In terms of therapeutic classification, PDTC is considered a research tool and a candidate for repurposing in inflammatory and neoplastic diseases, and its class has been investigated extensively over the past decades for applications in cancer therapy, inflammatory disorders, and experimental models of ocular disease (Kwak et al., 2008; Morais et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
The dithiocarbamate class, and PDTC in particular, has a rich history in biomedical research. PDTC has been employed primarily as an experimental NF-κB inhibitor in various paradigms, ranging from cancer models to inflammatory diseases. In the realm of oncology, PDTC has been shown to induce cell death in multiple cancer cell lines including breast, colon, gastric, and prostate cancers by modulating pathways related to cell survival and apoptosis (Morais et al., 2009). Its ability to chelate metal ions and act as a radical scavenger has also been exploited in studies examining cytoprotective effects in liver injury and neurodegenerative conditions (Shin et al., 2023). Notably, PDTC has been studied in ocular models; for example, its use in experimental endotoxin-induced uveitis in Lewis rats provided evidence of its anti-inflammatory activity and ocular safety profile (Kanai et al., 2010). While there is no record of PDTC having been directly used in clinical trials for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), its application in related ocular inflammatory conditions, such as autoimmune anterior uveitis and retinal neovascularization, offers a promising translational bridge to dry AMD (Morais et al., 2009). In several studies of retinal diseases, PDTC has been shown to modulate angiogenic factors and inflammatory cytokine profiles, indicating its potential utility in conditions where inflammation plays a key pathogenic role (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). Its established use in experimental models, combined with evidence of a favorable safety profile in ocular applications, makes PDTC an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, especially given the emerging understanding of the role of chronic inflammation and NF-κB activation in this degenerative disease (Shin et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
PDTC’s therapeutic potential largely derives from its robust inhibition of NF-κB activation. Under typical conditions, NF-κB is sequestered in the cytoplasm by inhibitory proteins known as IκBs. Upon stimulation by pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α or exposure to oxidative stress, the IκB proteins are phosphorylated, ubiquitinated, and degraded, releasing NF-κB to translocate to the nucleus where it drives the expression of numerous genes involved in inflammatory responses, cell survival, and immune regulation (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). PDTC interferes with this pathway by preventing the phosphorylation and consequent degradation of IκB, thereby keeping NF-κB in its inactive, cytoplasmic state (Kwak et al., 2008). In addition to this canonical inhibition, PDTC is also known to function as a metal ion chelator and a free radical scavenger, and studies have demonstrated that its chelating capability is crucial to its mechanism (Shin et al., 2023). The compound’s ability to chelate zinc ions, which are essential cofactors for the DNA-binding activity of NF-κB, may further contribute to its inhibitory effects on NF-κB-mediated transcription. This property is particularly relevant in the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) physiology; in the hypothesis being considered, PDTC is proposed to chelate Zn²⁺ in RPE cells, thereby impairing NF-κB activation. As NF-κB is known to downregulate genes such as MERTK—a receptor tyrosine kinase critical for the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—and lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, inhibition of NF-κB by PDTC would be expected to restore their expression (Morais et al., 2009). Moreover, beyond simple inhibition of NF-κB nuclear translocation, PDTC has been observed to induce the expression of endogenous antioxidants such as superoxide dismutase and heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) through NF-κB–independent pathways, suggesting that the compound can modulate multiple signaling cascades concurrently (Shin et al., 2023). Collectively, these molecular actions position PDTC as a multifaceted inhibitor of inflammatory signaling, where both the blockade of NF-κB translocation and the chelation of essential metal ions converge to mitigate inflammation-induced cellular dysfunction (Shin et al., 2023; Sui et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed application for dry AMD, the hypothesis is that PDTC will chelate Zn²⁺ and thereby inhibit NF-κB activation in RPE cells. In dry AMD, chronic inflammation is believed to play a crucial role in the downregulation of key proteins involved in phagocytosis and lysosomal function, notably MERTK and cathepsin D. TNF-α—a pro-inflammatory cytokine that robustly activates the NF-κB pathway—is known to downregulate the expression of MERTK and lysosomal genes in ARPE-19 cells, a commonly used model of RPE function (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). By inhibiting NF-κB activation, PDTC is expected to reverse the repressive effects of TNF-α, thereby restoring the normal expression levels of MERTK and cathepsin D. This restoration is anticipated to improve the ingestion and processing of POS, a critical function of RPE cells that is compromised in dry AMD. Improved POS clearance would reduce the accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin, which are hallmarks of RPE dysfunction and contribute to disease progression (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). Additionally, PDTC’s capacity to inhibit NF-κB not only suppresses the transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-6, IL-8, and GM-CSF, but may also promote a shift in the balance of macrophage polarization in the retinal microenvironment. For instance, a reduction in NF-κB–mediated inflammatory signaling has been linked to a decreased abundance of M1-type (pro-inflammatory) macrophages and a corresponding increase in M2-type (anti-inflammatory or tissue repair) macrophages, which would further support retinal homeostasis and repair mechanisms (Sui et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2005). Expression analyses in various studies have confirmed that RPE cells exhibit active NF-κB signaling under inflammatory stress and that inhibition of NF-κB can lead to upregulation of phagocytic receptors and lysosomal enzymes, which are essential for POS turnover (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). Thus, in the described assay using TNF-α–treated ARPE-19 cells, PDTC is expected to counteract the deleterious inflammatory signaling, normalizing the expression of MERTK and cathepsin D, and ultimately improving the functional capacity of the RPE to clear photoreceptor debris (Morais et al., 2009).

The repurposing of PDTC for dry AMD represents a promising and innovative approach rooted in well-established molecular pharmacology. One of the major strengths of PDTC is its dual mode of action: it is a potent inhibitor of NF-κB, preventing the transcriptional activation of a wide array of pro-inflammatory and cell stress genes, and it also possesses metal chelation properties, which may further enhance its ability to disrupt the pathological signaling cascades in RPE cells (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). The experimental evidence from animal models of ocular inflammation—such as endotoxin-induced uveitis—demonstrates that PDTC can be administered in ocular contexts with a tolerable safety profile, thereby supporting the feasibility of translating these findings to the treatment of dry AMD (Kanai et al., 2010). From a biochemical perspective, the strategy of chelating Zn²⁺ to inhibit NF-κB activation is compelling, particularly in view of the fact that zinc ions are embedded in the structure of NF-κB that is essential for its binding to DNA. In RPE cells, which are subject to continuous oxidative and inflammatory stress in dry AMD, the ability of PDTC to sequester Zn²⁺ may provide a specific molecular intervention point. This intervention could reverse NF-κB–mediated downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D, thereby improving POS uptake and degradation—a critical process that is disrupted in AMD and contributes to the accumulation of toxic debris (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023).

However, there are weaknesses and potential challenges associated with this therapeutic strategy. Although preclinical models of uveitis and retinal neovascularization have shown PDTC’s efficacy in reducing inflammatory markers and preserving tissue structure, there is still a significant gap in direct evidence for its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD. The proposed mechanism—involving restoration of phagocytic receptor and lysosomal gene expression by NF-κB inhibition—has been observed in vitro in ARPE-19 cells, yet extensive in vivo validation in models that recapitulate the complex pathology of dry AMD is lacking (Morais et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2023). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ibrutinib is a fully synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally developed as an irreversible inhibitor of Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK). It achieves inhibition by covalently binding to the conserved Cys481 residue located within the ATP‐binding pocket of BTK, a key member of the TEC family of kinases. This irreversible binding results in permanent inactivation of BTK, thereby interrupting B‐cell receptor signaling as well as other downstream pathways that are critical for cell survival and proliferation (Xie et al., 2021). As a member of the broader class of tyrosine kinase inhibitors, ibrutinib is designed through refined organic synthesis strategies that optimize its selectivity and potency. Compounds of this chemical class have been extensively utilized in oncology, particularly for the treatment of B‐cell malignancies, where they serve to disrupt aberrant oncogenic signaling pathways. Ibrutinib is available commercially (e.g., SelleckChem Cat. Therapeutic History:  
Historically, ibrutinib was developed and advanced clinically for hematologic cancers such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia (WM), and other B‐cell malignancies. Its success in these domains is attributed to its effective inhibition of BTK, a kinase that is critical for B‐cell receptor signaling and survival (Xie et al., 2021). Once approved by the U.S. FDA in 2013, it rapidly became a standard of care in oncology. Outside of its oncologic use, ibrutinib has been recognized for its immunomodulatory effects that extend to innate immune cells such as macrophages, dendritic cells, and, notably, microglia. In pharmacovigilance studies, ocular adverse events—including uveitis, cataracts, and retinal disorders—have been identified among patients treated with ibrutinib, which indicates that the molecule penetrates ocular compartments and exerts biological effects there (Allouchery et al., 2021). Instead, its potential repurposing arises from the hypothesis that by modulating BTK-dependent inflammatory pathways in microglia and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, ibrutinib might reduce deleterious inflammasome priming and cytokine production that contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024).

T0901317 is a synthetic small‐molecule ligand originally developed as a full agonist for the liver X receptors (LXRs), a class of nuclear receptors that govern lipid and cholesterol homeostasis. This compound belongs to the nonsteroidal LXR agonists, and its development was initially driven by the need to probe the mechanisms underlying reverse cholesterol transport and lipid metabolism in various tissues. T0901317 was designed to potently activate both LXRα and LXRβ isoforms, thereby upregulating a suite of genes that mediate cholesterol efflux, including ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) and ABCG1. The synthetic origins of T0901317 can be traced back to efforts to create tool compounds that efficiently modulate LXR signaling, with its chemical structure optimized to bind within the ligand-binding domain of LXRs and induce a conformational change that facilitates heterodimerization with retinoid X receptors (RXRs). In diverse studies, including those involving retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells of the eye, T0901317 has been shown to enhance cholesterol efflux mechanisms that are crucial for maintaining cellular lipid balance and extracellular matrix composition (Lyssenko et al., 2018; Choudhary et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of T0901317 spans preclinical investigations primarily centered on cardiovascular diseases, such as atherosclerosis, where its ability to reduce atherosclerotic lesions by enhancing reverse cholesterol transport was of paramount interest. In rodent models, particularly in LDL receptor–deficient mice, T0901317 administration resulted in meaningful reductions in plaque area and plasma cholesterol levels, while concomitantly increasing the expression of ABCA1 in target tissues (Welch et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2017). These studies established the compound’s potent lipid‐modulatory activity, albeit with an accompanying induction of hepatic lipogenesis and elevated plasma triglycerides that raised safety concerns for systemic use. More recently, the focus has shifted to exploring the potential application of T0901317 in ocular diseases, specifically dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In preclinical investigations using ARPE-19 cells and other RPE models, T0901317 has emerged as a promising agent due to its ability to stimulate LXR-mediated pathways that regulate cholesterol efflux and modulate inflammatory responses in the retina (Lyssenko et al., 2018; Choudhary et al., 2020). Although T0901317 was not originally developed with AMD in mind, the identification of dysregulated lipid metabolism and sub-RPE deposit formation as key features in the pathobiology of dry AMD has led to hypothesis-driven studies that repurpose LXR agonists for restoring lipid homeostasis in the retina (Buñay et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2020). Furthermore, the compound’s established pharmacokinetic profile in rodent models offers a degree of translational reassurance regarding its use as a tool for modulating extracellular matrix composition and RPE function, thereby rendering it a viable candidate for further preclinical validation in AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, T0901317 exerts its biological effects by selectively binding to the ligand-binding domains of LXRα and LXRβ. Upon binding, conformational changes in the receptor facilitate heterodimerization with RXR, leading to recruitment of coactivator proteins and subsequent binding to specific LXR response elements in the promoters of target genes. One of the key effects of this activation is the robust upregulation of ABCA1, a transporter protein that plays a central role in cholesterol efflux by mediating the transfer of cholesterol to extracellular acceptors such as apolipoprotein A-I (apo A-I) and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) particles (Lyssenko et al., 2018). The increase in ABCA1 expression subsequently enhances the reverse cholesterol transport (RCT) pathway, which is essential for preventing the intracellular and sub-RPE accumulation of cholesterol and other lipids—a factor implicated in the formation of drusen-like deposits observed in dry AMD. In addition to its lipid-regulatory activity, T0901317 has been shown to attenuate pro-inflammatory signaling pathways in RPE cells, as evidenced by its ability to modulate NF-κB signaling under conditions of oxidant stress and lipid overload (Wu et al., 2023; Buñay et al., 2021). This dual impact on lipid metabolism and inflammation is particularly relevant in the retinal context, where chronic inflammatory processes and disrupted cholesterol homeostasis converge to promote RPE dysfunction and basal deposit accumulation (Lyssenko et al., 2018). Moreover, studies have illustrated that even under conditions of hypoxia or lipid overload—conditions that normally suppress ABCA1 expression via hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF1)—T0901317 is capable of counteracting these inhibitory effects, thereby reestablishing normal cholesterol efflux in RPE cells (Peters et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022). This detailed mechanistic understanding underscores the drug’s potential to normalize the lipid environment of Bruch’s membrane and restore RPE phagocytic function by mitigating deleterious lipid accumulation (Lyssenko et al., 2018).

The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of T0901317 for dry AMD posits that the compound, when applied at an effective concentration (with an EC₅₀ in the vicinity of 50 nM in RPE cells), will activate LXRs to upregulate ABCA1 and other cholesterol efflux transporters within RPE cells. This molecular cascade is expected to promote a more efficient clearance of excess cholesterol from the RPE and surrounding Bruch’s membrane, thus reducing the formation of drusen-like deposits—a hallmark of early AMD pathology (Lyssenko et al., 2018). Data derived from experiments in ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE models indicate that treatment with T0901317 leads to a significant increase in ABCA1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels, which translates into enhanced cholesterol efflux when proper lipid acceptors such as apoA-I are present in the extracellular milieu (Lyssenko et al., 2018). In preclinical AMD models, enhanced reverse cholesterol transport due to LXR activation has been associated with normalization of the extracellular matrix, reduction of basal deposit thickness, and improved integrin-mediated adhesion—a factor critical for maintaining the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells (Buñay et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2020). A rigorous evaluation of T0901317 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several compelling strengths alongside notable challenges that must be addressed in future research. Among its strengths, T0901317 is a well-characterized LXR agonist with a robust capacity to upregulate ABCA1 and other members of the cholesterol efflux machinery in RPE cells. These safety liabilities necessitate a re-evaluation of the delivery strategy for T0901317. One potential approach is the development of localized ocular delivery systems that concentrate the therapeutic effect in the retina while minimizing systemic absorption. Advances in drug delivery technologies, such as intravitreal implants or nanoparticle carriers, may offer a viable solution to this conundrum by enabling sustained, localized release of T0901317 directly to the RPE and Bruch’s membrane (Wu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023).

Furthermore, the dual agonist nature of T0901317—implicating both LXR and potentially FXR pathways—raises additional questions regarding the spectrum of its biological effects. While dual receptor activation may provide additive or synergistic benefits in some contexts, there is also the risk of unintended crosstalk and off-target activity that could complicate the clinical picture, especially in a delicate tissue such as the retina. Addressing these issues may require structural modifications to enhance LXR selectivity or the development of second-generation compounds that retain the beneficial actions on cholesterol efflux while mitigating the adverse lipogenic effects (Choudhary et al., 2020; Loren et al., 2013).

Moreover, although there is promising evidence from in vitro studies indicating that T0901317 can upregulate ABCA1 in RPE cells and promote cholesterol efflux, comprehensive in vivo studies in animal models of dry AMD are warranted to definitively establish its efficacy in reducing drusen formation, restoring RPE phagocytic function, and ultimately preserving visual function. The heterogeneity of AMD pathophysiology also suggests that T0901317 may be most effective as part of a combinatorial therapy, potentially in combination with other agents targeting complementary pathways such as oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, or angiogenesis (Buñay et al., 2021; Storti et al., 2019).

In conclusion, T0901317 represents a promising yet challenging therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. Its well-documented mechanism of activating LXR-mediated cholesterol efflux and modulating inflammatory responses aligns closely with the pathological features of AMD, namely disrupted lipid homeostasis and chronic inflammation in the RPE and Bruch’s membrane. However, the compound’s established systemic metabolic liabilities and broad nuclear receptor activation profile introduce significant hurdles that must be overcome before clinical translation can be realized. Future research efforts should focus on optimizing the drug’s delivery to the retina, refining its molecular selectivity, and conducting rigorous in vivo efficacy and safety studies in relevant AMD models. Only through such multifaceted investigations can the full potential of T0901317 be realized as a viable treatment strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration (Lyssenko et al., 2018; Buñay et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2020).
