Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fasudil is a small‐molecule, synthetic isoquinoline derivative that functions as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil forming kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. Originally discovered and subsequently developed for clinical use in the treatment of cerebral vasospasm following subarachnoid hemorrhage, fasudil represents one of the earliest examples of ROCK inhibitors entering the clinic (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). As a member of the ROCK inhibitor class, it has been synthesized and formulated to target the ATP‐binding pocket of both ROCK isoforms (ROCK1 and ROCK2), thereby effectively competing with ATP and suppressing the kinase activity that is normally responsible for phosphorylating downstream molecular substrates such as the myosin light chain (MLC) and LIM kinase (Catral et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2022). The compound’s synthesis generally follows established medicinal chemistry protocols for heterocyclic compounds and includes derivatization steps that yield a potent inhibitor with an IC₅₀ for ROCK inhibition in the submicromolar range, which in the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function has been postulated to be around 300 nM (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Xiao et al., 2022). Fasudil’s chemical structure and its physicochemical properties allow for formulation into ophthalmic preparations, such as intravitreal injections or potentially sustained-release depot systems, making it an interesting candidate for repurposing in ocular diseases. This class of compounds has historically been used to modulate cytoskeletal dynamics, vascular tone, and cellular contractility in both vascular and neural tissues, and the same properties are being leveraged now to target the pathological stiffening and impaired phagocytic function of RPE cells in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Croze et al., 2014; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Fasudil’s therapeutic history spans multiple clinical and preclinical applications that underscore its broad efficacy in modulating ROCK-mediated pathways. Clinically, fasudil has been approved and widely used in Japan since 1995 for the treatment of cerebral vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage, owing to its vasodilatory and anti-contractile properties (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Its clinical use has expanded into experimental paradigms beyond cerebral applications; for instance, fasudil has shown promise in ocular conditions such as diabetic macular edema, where intravitreal administration in combination with bevacizumab demonstrated feasibility and tolerability, and where its ability to modulate inflammatory responses and vascular permeability were beneficial (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). Furthermore, other members of the ROCK inhibitor class have been investigated for ocular applications, including glaucoma and even experimental models of photoreceptor synapse stabilization following retinal detachment (Townes-Anderson et al., 2017; Yamaguchi et al., 2017). Although fasudil itself has not yet been directly applied in clinical trials for dry AMD, its mechanism of action and safety profile in ocular tissues have been well documented in multiple studies. Animal studies in diabetic retinopathy models have also demonstrated that fasudil can reverse detrimental cytoskeletal changes and restore barrier integrity in RPE cells (Rothschild et al., 2017). Additionally, preclinical data indicate that ROCK inhibitors can improve wound repair responses and prevent epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in RPE cells, which is a hallmark of cellular dysfunction in geographic atrophy – the advanced stage of dry AMD (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Collectively, while fasudil’s historic use has largely focused on vascular and diabetic complications, its repurposing for dry AMD is supported by mechanistic parallels in RPE cytoskeletal plasticity, phagocytosis, and anti-inflammatory modulation (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, fasudil acts by binding to the ATP-binding site of ROCK enzymes, thereby competitively inhibiting their kinase activity (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Under normal cellular conditions, active ROCK phosphorylates several substrates including the myosin light chain (MLC) and myosin phosphatase target subunit 1 (MYPT1), which leads to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stabilization of actin stress fibers, and formation of focal adhesions (Catral et al., 2024; Rothschild et al., 2017). In the context of age-related retinopathies, there is mounting evidence that hyperactivity of the ROCK pathway leads to increased contractile force within the RPE cytoskeleton. This hypercontractility contributes to reduced cellular flexibility and impairs the formation of the phagocytic cups that are critical for the internalization of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) – a process that is essential for retinal homeostasis and visual cycle maintenance (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). Fasudil’s inhibition of ROCK thereby mitigates these cytoskeletal alterations by decreasing the phosphorylation levels of downstream targets, which in turn reduces actomyosin contraction and promotes a more plastic and dynamic actin architecture (Catral et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2022).

Furthermore, ROCK inhibition has been shown to enhance cell adhesion and reduce apoptotic signaling in stressed RPE cells, thereby improving wound repair and the overall cellular microenvironment (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Biochemical experiments have demonstrated that when ROCK activity is suppressed, RPE cells exhibit a reduction in stress fiber formation and an increase in the formation of normal cell–cell junctions, which is crucial for the maintenance of the outer blood-retinal barrier (Rothschild et al., 2017). In addition to its effects on the actin cytoskeleton, fasudil and other ROCK inhibitors have been reported to modulate inflammatory and fibrotic pathways by reducing the phosphorylation of Smad 2/3 in response to TGF-β1 signaling; this effect may further protect RPE cells from deleterious pro-fibrotic and inflammatory cascades that are known to exacerbate dry AMD pathology (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Several studies also indicate that ROCK inhibition promotes RPE differentiation and pigmentation, as evidenced by increased expression of key proteins such as RPE65, which is indispensable for the visual cycle and meso-zeaxanthin biosynthesis (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Given that oxidative stress in the aging retina exacerbates ROCK activation, fasudil’s ability to mitigate these effects through cytoskeletal remodeling and anti-inflammatory actions underlies its proposed mechanism of action in improving POS internalization in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Rothschild et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing fasudil for dry AMD is that inhibition of ROCK in the RPE will lead to normalization of abnormal cytoskeletal tension, thereby enhancing the formation of phagocytic cups required for efficient POS internalization (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). In aged RPE cells from patients with dry AMD, persistent ROCK hyperactivity is thought to cause increased actomyosin contraction; this leads to a “stiff” cytoskeletal state that hinders membrane dynamics essential for phagocytosis (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Rothschild et al., 2017). By reducing ROCK-mediated phosphorylation of MLC and other substrates, fasudil is expected to relieve this contractility, restore a more flexible actin network, and ultimately allow for enhanced phagocytic function. Preclinical studies have already demonstrated that use of ROCK inhibitors like Y-27632 can increase phagocytic activity by RPE cells, leading to improved clearance of POS debris – a key function that deteriorates in dry AMD (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Croze et al., 2014).

In the proposed assay, RPE cells under oxidative stress—an in vitro proxy for the aging microenvironment seen in dry AMD—will be treated with fasudil. The anticipated outcome is that fasudil will enhance cytoskeletal plasticity, thereby facilitating the formation of phagocytic cups and improving the uptake of POS, as measured by quantifiable phagocytosis assays (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). Moreover, fasudil’s reported effects in enhancing cell adhesion and promoting a balanced extracellular matrix deposition are expected to provide additional benefits to RPE cell morphology and barrier integrity, indirectly supporting improved phagocytic function (Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Given that key RPE-specific genes and proteins involved in phagocytosis, including integrin αvβ5 and MFG-E8, are expressed in these cells, normalization of the cytoskeletal machinery via ROCK inhibition is likely to translate into a functional recovery of POS clearance capacity (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Croze et al., 2014). Thus, the overall effect of fasudil treatment is expected to counteract the age-associated impairment in phagocytosis, reduce accumulation of waste material such as drusen, and potentially slow the progression of retinal degeneration in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the repurposing of fasudil for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a substantial mechanistic rationale and a body of preclinical evidence indicating that ROCK inhibition can positively modulate RPE cellular function. The strengths of fasudil as a therapeutic candidate include its well-established clinical safety profile—stemming from decades of use in cerebrovascular conditions in Japan—as well as its robust capacity to modulate actin-cytoskeletal dynamics, reduce excessive cell contraction, and enhance processes such as cell adhesion and phagocytosis among RPE cells (Catral et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). The ability of fasudil to normalize the abnormal, stiff cytoskeletal state present in aged RPE cells is particularly compelling given the central role of impaired POS internalization in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017).

Moreover, similar ROCK inhibitors have demonstrated promising effects in ocular models of retinal degeneration and diabetic retinopathy, where the restoration of RPE function and cytoskeletal composition has correlated with improved retinal architecture and cell survival (Moura-Coelho et al., 2019; Rothschild et al., 2017). Fasudil’s potential to also attenuate inflammatory and fibrotic signaling pathways via downstream effects on TGF-β/Smad signaling may add further benefit by curbing the detrimental microenvironment that exacerbates RPE dysfunction in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). The proposed mechanism—centered on relieving ROCK-induced actomyosin contraction and restoring the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells—addresses a key pathophysiological deficit in dry AMD, namely the impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments that leads to drusen accumulation and subsequent cell degeneration (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017).

However, there are also some weaknesses and challenges associated with using fasudil as a treatment for dry AMD. A major concern is the relatively nonselective nature of fasudil compared to more recently developed ROCK inhibitors that offer isoform specificity (e.g., selective ROCK2 inhibitors) (Alexander, 2017; Yamaguchi et al., 2017). Since ROCK signaling is implicated in multiple cellular processes beyond RPE cytoskeletal dynamics—including vascular regulation, neuronal survival, and immune cell polarization—a nonselective inhibitor may inadvertently affect these other pathways, potentially leading to off-target effects. In particular, the downregulation of thrombospondin 1 (THBS1) observed with some ROCK inhibitors, which is associated with anti-angiogenic processes, could theoretically predispose patients to neovascular complications if not carefully controlled (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Catral et al., 2024).

Another potential limitation is the pharmacokinetic profile of fasudil in ocular tissues. Fasudil is known to have a short plasma half-life (approximately 0.3 hours), although its active metabolite, hydroxyfasudil, has a moderately longer half-life (approximately 2.9 hours) (Futterknecht et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). For effective treatment of dry AMD—where chronic, sustained modulation of ROCK activity may be necessary—injection strategies such as intravitreal administration or depot formulations may be required to maintain therapeutic levels over an extended period. Although intravitreal delivery of fasudil has been demonstrated in diabetic macular edema and other experimental models (Rothschild et al., 2017), further studies will be needed to optimize the dosage, frequency, and formulation for the specific demands of long-term retinal therapy in dry AMD.

Furthermore, while the preclinical evidence regarding the benefits of ROCK inhibition in RPE cells is promising, there remains a lack of direct clinical data demonstrating the efficacy of fasudil in patients with dry AMD. Most studies to date have focused on the use of ROCK inhibitors in models of diabetic retinopathy, neovascular AMD, or other retinal conditions, and the translation of these findings to the dry, atrophic form of AMD is not yet fully established (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Rothschild et al., 2017). This gap underscores the need for focused, well-designed clinical trials and further preclinical studies using models that accurately recapitulate the pathophysiology of dry AMD.

Moreover, it will be essential to monitor whether the positive effects on cytoskeletal plasticity and phagocytosis translate into meaningful clinical endpoints such as improved visual acuity or slowed progression of geographic atrophy. Biomarkers of RPE health, phagocytic activity, and retinal integrity will need to be identified and validated in the context of fasudil treatment (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Croze et al., 2014).

In conclusion, the available literature strongly supports the mechanistic rationale for using fasudil to target ROCK-mediated dysfunction in RPE cells, which is a critical aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis (Catral et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Its established safety profile in other clinical scenarios, coupled with evidence from preclinical models demonstrating improved cytoskeletal regulation, enhanced phagocytic capacity, and attenuated inflammation in retinal cells, makes fasudil a promising therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (Moura-Coelho et al., 2019; Rothschild et al., 2017). Nonetheless, challenges related to drug-specific pharmacokinetics, the risk of off-target effects due to its nonselectivity, and the current lack of direct clinical evidence in dry AMD warrant cautious further investigation. The next steps should involve optimization of ocular delivery methods—potentially through sustained-release formulations—and the initiation of preclinical studies in animal models of dry AMD to assess functional outcomes. If these studies prove successful, they would pave the way for early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of fasudil in patients with dry AMD (Rothschild et al., 2017; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Overall, while significant work remains to be done, the integration of biochemical, cellular, and clinical data from the broader ROCK inhibitor literature provides a compelling argument for further evaluation of fasudil as a potential repurposed treatment for dry AMD. The strategy to inhibit ROCK in RPE cells to restore cytoskeletal dynamics, enhance phagocytosis, and reduce oxidative and inflammatory stress fits well with current understanding of dry AMD pathophysiology and represents an innovative approach that could address a critical unmet need in AMD therapeutics (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Catral et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Iptacopan (LNP023) is a rationally designed, low–molecular-weight small molecule that selectively inhibits complement factor B (FB), the essential catalytic subunit of the alternative pathway (AP) C3/C5 convertases C3bBb and C3bBbC3b on activating surfaces (including stressed RPE) and within the amplification loop of complement activation (C3 → C3b → C3 convertase) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 4–6). Medicinal-chemistry optimization from an early micromolar FB inhibitor hit (a naphthalene-dihydro-imidazole amine) introduced an indole to occupy the S1 pocket and a piperidine scaffold engaging the S3/non-primed region with a benzoic acid–mediated H-bond network, yielding iptacopan with high potency and selectivity for FB (crystallographically confirmed) (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 10–13; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Iptacopan binds the catalytic serine-protease active site within the Bb subunit of FB—structural analyses show its indole and piperidine moieties seated in S1/S3, forming key hydrogen bonds within the catalytic domain, with the active-site triad (His–Asp–Ser) located in proximity; binding has been explicitly mapped to the catalytic site in Bb and shown to block substrate processing by the AP convertase (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6, 8–10).

Class and precedent: Iptacopan is an oral, proximal complement/AP inhibitor; this class has delivered robust target engagement and clinical benefit in multiple complement-driven diseases (e.g., PNH, C3G, IgAN), establishing translational viability for systemic small-molecule blockade of AP amplification in human disease (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Oral administration achieves rapid systemic exposure (Tmax ≈ 2 hours) with dose-dependent AP suppression and sustained steady-state inhibition at 200 mg twice daily in clinical studies, supporting convenient outpatient dosing with on-target PD (reduced plasma Bb and urinary sC5b-9) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Preclinically, systemic iptacopan potently blocks LPS-induced AP activation in mice in both plasma and eye tissues, indicating ocular target engagement after oral dosing (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). Collectively, synthesis, mechanistic selectivity, and clinical-class performance position iptacopan as a well-characterized, orally bioavailable FB inhibitor suited for indications where local AP amplification contributes to pathology, including dry AMD (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).

Therapeutic History  
- Non-ocular indications and clinical pharmacology. In early-phase clinical studies, iptacopan demonstrated rapid absorption (peak plasma concentration at ~2 hours), favorable tolerability, and dose-dependent inhibition of AP activity; sustained maximal inhibition was reported at 200 mg twice daily, the regimen advanced into multiple phase 2 trials (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Across PNH and AP-driven renal diseases (C3G, IgAN), iptacopan showed robust target engagement and clinical activity: reductions in plasma Bb and urinary sC5b-9, reductions in plasma C3 (in many patients after months), kidney-pathology improvements (reduced glomerular C3 deposition), and meaningful efficacy outcomes (e.g., proteinuria reductions in C3G/IgAN; hemoglobin improvements and transfusion-free status in PNH) with generally favorable safety profiles and no serious infections in the cited trials (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Iptacopan has received regulatory approvals (including an accelerated approval for IgAN) and late-stage development status for multiple indications, validating systemic AP inhibition with this agent (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8).  
- AMD program. A randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial in early/intermediate AMD is ongoing (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022), designed to test whether oral iptacopan prevents conversion to iRORA or late AMD over 24 months, with masked multimodal imaging and planned plasma trough PK by LC–MS; vaccinations for encapsulated organisms are required per complement-inhibition class risk management (no results are available in the excerpt) (“A Masked, Placebo-controlled Study to Assess Iptacopan in Age-related Macular Degeneration,” 2022). Reviews place iptacopan among oral FB inhibitors under evaluation for atrophic AMD as an alternative to intravitreal complement blockade, motivated by the blood–retina barrier and the burden of injections; however, the provided material contains no AMD efficacy outcomes for iptacopan (Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 8–9; Hammadi et al., 2023, pp. 30–31; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
- Ocular-relevant preclinical context. Although iptacopan-specific dry-AMD model data are not provided, two lines of evidence are directly relevant: (1) in the Efemp1 R345W knock-in mouse (an RPE proteostasis model with AMD-like basal deposits), genetic Cfb deletion abolished AP activation and eliminated sub-RPE deposits, while oral pharmacologic FB blockade (with the small molecule DB-82-CB77) reduced deposits by 65% in females and reversed disease-associated pathway perturbations (UPR/inflammation upregulation and mitochondrial repression) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10); (2) systemic iptacopan blocks AP activation in eye tissue in LPS-challenged mice, supporting oral delivery as a viable route to ocular target engagement, though iptacopan-specific AMD-model efficacy is not shown in the provided excerpts (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Complement biology and lysosomal/autophagy pathology in RPE. In CFH Y402H high-risk iPSC-RPE, increased C3 turnover and lysosomal deposition of C5b-9 drive lysosomal swelling, membrane damage, Cathepsin D leakage to sub-RPE deposits, and reduced lysosomal function; blocking C3 with the compstatin analogue Cp40 reverses these phenotypes, restoring lysosomal number/size/function and lowering complement deposition (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13). While these data establish that proximal complement blockade can normalize lysosomal/autophagy dysfunction in high-risk RPE, the excerpts do not directly test FB/AP inhibitors in this RPE system; thus, extrapolation to iptacopan remains mechanistic rather than empirically proven in the provided sources (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 7–13).

Mechanism of Action  
- Biochemical target and binding mode. FB is an abundant plasma glycoprotein (~0.2–0.4 mg/mL; ~2–3 μM) unique to the AP and, upon binding to C3b, is cleaved by factor D into Ba and Bb; Bb contains a VWA domain, MIDAS motif, and a serine-protease domain that provides the catalytic site for AP C3/C5 convertases on C3b-bearing surfaces (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6). Iptacopan binds the catalytic site of Bb in the S1/S3 pockets with a defined hydrogen-bonding network, directly inhibiting the proteolytic activity of the AP convertase and thereby blocking AP-mediated C3/C5 processing (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- Potency, selectivity, and functional inhibition. Iptacopan exhibits an enzymatic IC₅₀ ≈ 0.01 μM against FB and inhibits AP-induced C5b-9 formation in 50% human serum with IC₅₀ ≈ 0.13 μM; it prevents C3 deposition and complement-mediated lysis of PNH erythrocytes with IC₅₀ ≈ 0.4 μM and shows high selectivity over factor D and classical/lectin pathway activity in broad panels (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Alternative affinity reporting (K_D ≈ 0.0079 mM) has been noted in one excerpt, but across structural/functional assays the compound consistently behaves as a highly potent and selective FB catalytic-site inhibitor (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 8–10).  
- Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics relevant to target engagement. Clinically, iptacopan is rapidly absorbed (Tmax ~ 2 hours), with strong steady-state AP inhibition at 200 mg twice daily; pharmacodynamic readouts demonstrate reduced circulating Bb and reduced urinary sC5b-9, consistent with systemic and tissue-level AP suppression (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). While precise human half-life and oral bioavailability values are not provided in the excerpts, iptacopan is described as orally bioavailable with a shorter half-life than antibodies, enabling relatively rapid restoration of AP function after washout—an attribute that informs adherence requirements and infection risk mitigation (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–11). Factor B itself has a long plasma half-life (30–70 h) and high abundance; iptacopan’s high affinity and mechanism allow sustained convertase inhibition because only newly synthesized FB needs to be neutralized at steady state for continued pathway blockade (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- Ocular target engagement. In mice, systemic administration of iptacopan potently blocks LPS-induced complement activation in both plasma and eye tissues, implying that oral dosing can achieve pharmacologically active exposure to ocular compartments, at least under inflammatory conditions (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). In the Efemp1 R345W model, ocular AP activation is local (iC3b and Ba ≈ 2× in eye, not in plasma), aligning with a need for ocular engagement; although iptacopan’s ocular concentration-time profile in humans is not provided, the preclinical PD findings and the AMD phase 2 trial design together support the translational intent to suppress ocular AP activity via oral dosing (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Genetic and disease-mechanism validation. FB is genetically and mechanistically implicated in AMD pathogenesis; protective low-activity variants (e.g., R32Q) associate with reduced AMD risk, and AP dysregulation is a central pathogenic thread in AMD biology (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6). In an RPE proteostasis model (Efemp1 R345W), Cfb deletion abolishes AP activation and prevents sub-RPE deposit formation; pharmacologic FB suppression reduces deposit burden and reverses multiple mutation-associated pathway perturbations (UPR, immune/complement signatures, mitochondrial repression), supporting causal linkage between AP activity and RPE/Bruch’s membrane pathology (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10).  
- Comparison to other complement nodes in AMD models. Complement C3 blockade (Cp40) in CFH Y402H high-risk iPSC-RPE rescues lysosomal structure and function, reduces C3b and C5b-9 deposition (including lysosomal MAC), and diminishes drusen-like phenotypes, demonstrating that proximal complement suppression can reverse RPE degradative defects; this provides a mechanistic bridge to AP/FB inhibition, which is expected to decrease upstream C3 turnover and downstream MAC burden by curtailing the amplification loop, though FB-specific rescue of lysosomal function was not directly tested in that study (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).

Expected Effect  
- In vitro RPE assays and readouts. Based on the AP mechanism and the CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE data with C3 inhibition, iptacopan is expected to reduce AP convertase activity on RPE surfaces, lowering C3b/iC3b deposition and MAC (C5b-9) accrual on and within RPE cells, thereby alleviating lysosomal overburden, improving lysosomal integrity, and facilitating restoration of autophagic flux (e.g., normalized LC3-II/p62 dynamics) and degradative function (e.g., Cathepsin D activity and localization) (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13). The Efemp1 model shows that AP activation is heightened locally and that Cfb deletion or FB inhibition normalizes stress/inflammation (including UPR) and mitochondrial pathways; by analogy, iptacopan should attenuate ER stress/UPR signaling and immune/complement activation signatures in RPE/eyecup proteomes, with secondary benefits for mitochondrial/energy pathways (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2). Although direct demonstration that FB inhibition restores RPE lysosomal function is not presented in the excerpted Efemp1 work, the Cp40 RPE data make a strong mechanistic case that upstream complement suppression reduces complement load on lysosomes and rescues degradative capacity; iptacopan should achieve a similar effect by preventing AP amplification and thus lowering the rate of C3 activation fragment generation and MAC formation at the RPE (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).  
- Ex vivo/animal AMD-relevant endpoints. In female Efemp1 R345W mice, oral FB inhibition (DB-82-CB77) reduced sub-RPE deposits by 65% over 8 weeks, while Cfb deletion completely eliminated deposits and abrogated AP activation in eye, indicating that AP blockade can causally modify a basal laminar–like deposit phenotype; iptacopan, as a potent oral FB inhibitor with demonstrated ocular PD in mice, would be expected to recapitulate these effects on deposits and molecular signatures, subject to dose/exposure parity and sex-dependent biology (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 9–10, 4–6). The Efemp1 eyecup proteomics further suggest that FB blockade rebalances ocular homeostasis, dampening CR3/immune-complement signaling and upstream UPR stress while partially restoring mitochondrial proteins, reinforcing the hypothesis that complement amplification contributes to proteostasis failure and that its inhibition should normalize these axes (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Clinical AMD endpoints. The ongoing phase 2 iptacopan study in AMD is designed to detect prevention of conversion to iRORA or late AMD by SD-/SS-OCT and multimodal imaging over 24 months; systemic trough PK will be monitored. If oral iptacopan meaningfully engages ocular AP in humans, we would anticipate reduced new-onset iRORA and slower disease progression relative to placebo, potentially accompanied by systemic PD markers (Bb suppression), though the trial as described does not include ocular PD sampling (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022). As precedent, intravitreal C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) reduced GA growth in phase 2; conversely, C5 inhibition had mixed results, underscoring the importance of targeting upstream amplification (C3/AP) rather than solely the terminal pathway in AMD (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 7–9). It remains to be shown whether systemic FB inhibition can reproduce these benefits without increasing CNV risk; complement inhibition broadly has been associated with higher rates of new-onset CNV in some trials, a safety signal that must be monitored in FB-targeting programs (Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic and genetic rationale. FB is the essential catalytic subunit of AP convertases, and human genetics supports a causal role of FB activity in AMD (protective low-activity variants) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6). In an RPE-driven mouse model (Efemp1 R345W), Cfb deletion abolishes ocular AP activation and eliminates sub-RPE deposits; pharmacologic FB inhibition reduces deposits and reverses disease-associated pathway dysregulation, linking AP amplification to RPE/proteostasis pathology and basal deposit accumulation (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2, 9–10).  
- Demonstrated oral target engagement, including ocular PD in mice. Iptacopan is orally bioavailable with rapid absorption and consistent systemic PD (Bb and sC5b-9 suppression) in humans; preclinically, systemic iptacopan blocks AP activation in eye tissue, supporting feasibility of oral ocular target engagement (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Potency/selectivity with favorable clinical precedents. Iptacopan shows nanomolar enzymatic potency, selective FB catalytic-site binding, and clear functional AP inhibition in serum/cell assays; it has delivered convincing efficacy across multiple complement-driven indications with acceptable safety, validating the drug and target class clinically (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14).  
- Convergence with RPE lysosome/autophagy biology. In CFH Y402H high-risk iPSC-RPE, proximal complement blockade (C3 inhibitor Cp40) reverses lysosomal swelling/dysfunction and reduces complement deposition including MAC; these findings mechanistically support the hypothesis that halting AP amplification upstream will relieve lysosomal burden and restore degradative capacity in RPE, a central deficit in dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).

Risks and Gaps  
- Lack of direct iptacopan data in AMD models or RPE lysosome assays. The provided excerpts do not report iptacopan efficacy in AMD-relevant animal models (e.g., Efemp1) or direct rescue of RPE lysosomal/autophagic function; the pharmacologic proof-of-concept in Efemp1 used a different FB inhibitor (DB-82-CB77) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 9–10). Thus, the hypothesis that iptacopan will restore RPE degradative capacity is mechanistically plausible but not yet experimentally demonstrated in the cited AMD models (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 7–13).  
- Ocular PK/PD in humans unproven. The AMD phase 2 protocol measures plasma trough iptacopan but does not include ocular PD; no human ocular PK is provided in the excerpts. Translational dependence on ocular exposure is high because AP activation in Efemp1 is local to the eye (elevated Ba/iC3b in ocular tissue but not plasma) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).  
- Heterogeneity and sex effects in preclinical model. Efemp1 females exhibit ocular AP activation and respond to FB inhibition; males have lower deposits, no ocular AP upregulation, and do not respond, implying biological heterogeneity that may translate to variable clinical responses and may necessitate biomarker-based enrichment (e.g., markers of ocular AP activation) (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).  
- Class safety considerations. Complement inhibition increases susceptibility to infections with encapsulated bacteria; vaccination is mandated in the AMD study. Additionally, complement inhibition in GA trials has been associated with increased new-onset CNV versus sham, a signal that must be actively monitored; whether FB inhibition carries a similar CNV liability is unknown from the provided materials (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
- Mixed history of systemic complement inhibitors in AMD. The sole completed RCT of systemic anti-C5 (eculizumab) in AMD failed to show GA benefit, raising delivery and mechanistic questions for systemic approaches, although intravitreal proximal inhibitors (C3) have shown GA-slowing, and the Efemp1 data support AP dependence for basal deposit biology (Hammadi et al., 2023, pp. 17–18; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 7–9).

Program Implications and Next Steps  
- Preclinical toolkit alignment. To directly validate the central hypothesis for iptacopan, run head-to-head studies in AMD-relevant systems:
  - Efemp1 R345W mouse: oral iptacopan dosing matched for AP PD versus DB-82-CB77 benchmark; endpoints: TEM-assessed sub-RPE deposits, ocular Ba/iC3b, eyecup/neural retina proteomics (UPR/complement/mitochondrial modules), and RPE lysosomal/autophagy markers (LAMP1, CTSD activity, LC3-II/p62 flux), stratified by sex (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 9–10, 4–6).  
  - CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE: iptacopan in complement-competent human serum conditions; readouts: C3b/C5b-9 deposition, lysosomal integrity (Lysotracker, Galectin-8), CTSD localization/activity, autophagic flux and POS phagocytosis assays; benchmark to Cp40 rescue (Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 2–4, 7–13).  
  - Ocular exposure/PD: quantify iptacopan in ocular compartments (choroid/retina/RPE) and measure ocular AP biomarkers in vivo after oral dosing to confirm exposure–PD matching the LPS PD signal (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Translational biomarker strategy. Incorporate systemic AP markers (Bb, Ba), exploratory ocular biomarkers (e.g., aqueous humor C3 fragments if feasible), and imaging-based deposit/ELM–Bruch’s metrics; in the clinic, deploy multimodal imaging for conversion endpoints as in Novartis Pharmaceuticals (2022), and prospectively monitor CNV incidence (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
- Patient selection. Consider enriching for patients with systemic or local evidence of AP activation (genetics such as CFH risk alleles, complement biomarker profiles) analogous to the female-biased AP activation seen in Efemp1 (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).  
- Dosing rationale and adherence. Target 200 mg twice daily based on human PD experience; given the shorter half-life vs antibodies and the need for sustained AP suppression, emphasize adherence and vaccine prophylaxis; PD sampling should verify on-target AP inhibition longitudinally (Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14; Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Ricklin, 2024, pp. 7–9; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).

Bottom line. Iptacopan is a mechanistically compelling, clinically validated oral FB inhibitor with demonstrated systemic PD, rapid onset, and preclinical evidence of ocular AP engagement; rigorous AMD-model testing and clinical biomarker integration are now required to close the translational loop from AP biology to RPE lysosomal rescue and clinical protection against atrophy progression (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 8–10; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).

Go/No-Go Considerations for Dry AMD  
- Go signals:  
  - Target validity in AMD pathobiology is strong (genetics, AP dependence of basal deposits, proximal complement benefits in RPE models) (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 4–6; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).  
  - Drug is clinically de-risked across multiple indications with robust AP PD and acceptable safety; oral delivery is patient-friendly vs intravitreal regimens (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 7–8; Schubart et al., 2023, pp. 13–14).  
  - Ocular PD feasibility is supported in mice for systemic iptacopan; pharmacologic AP blockade reduces deposits in Efemp1 with another orally bioavailable FB inhibitor (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).  
- Caution flags:  
  - No iptacopan AMD-model efficacy in the provided materials; need direct RPE lysosome/autophagy rescue readouts and deposit suppression with iptacopan prior to expensive late-phase commitments (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 7–13).  
  - Macro safety signals observed with complement inhibitors in AMD (CNV incidence) necessitate vigilant monitoring and risk–benefit analyses tailored to FB inhibition (Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).  
  - Systemic delivery uncertainty—human ocular PK/PD data are lacking; trial design should incorporate robust systemic PD and exploratory ocular biomarkers where feasible (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).

Recommendation  
Advance iptacopan for dry AMD with a focused, staged plan:  
- Preclinical confirmation package: replicate Efemp1 findings with iptacopan (deposits, AP biomarkers, proteomics) and demonstrate RPE lysosomal/autophagy rescue in CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE under complement-competent conditions; quantify ocular exposure–PD after oral dosing (Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
- Biomarker-enriched clinical strategy: leverage systemic AP biomarkers and imaging-based progression metrics from Novartis Pharmaceuticals (2022); consider enrichment by complement genetics/biomarkers reflecting AP activation (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022).  
- Safety management: maintain vaccination requirements and active CNV surveillance; implement adherence support given the shorter half-life relative to biologics (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2022; Ricklin, 2024, pp. 7–9; Wilke & Apte, 2024, pp. 7–8).

On balance, iptacopan has substantial mechanistic, translational, and clinical-class support to merit continued development in dry AMD, contingent on closing the specific evidence gaps for RPE degradative rescue and direct AMD-model efficacy with this agent (Kavanagh et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Crowley et al., 2023, pp. 1–2; Cerniauskas et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The therapeutic candidate under evaluation is a CD59-Fc fusion protein, a recombinant biologic that combines the extracellular functional domain of CD59—a naturally occurring complement regulatory protein—with the Fc portion of an immunoglobulin (typically IgG1) to extend its ocular half‐life and improve tissue penetration. This fusion protein is synthesized using recombinant DNA technology in mammalian cell expression systems to ensure proper post‐translational modifications and folding, which are critical for retaining high binding affinity (with a reported dissociation constant, Kd, of <1 nM) toward its targets, the complement components C8 and C9, on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) surfaces (Qin et al., 2021; Tan, 2018). The compound belongs to the class of complement inhibitors—a group of therapeutic agents that have been developed to modulate the immune complement cascade, thereby mitigating complement-mediated tissue damage; historically, this class has been primarily investigated for inflammatory and degenerative conditions, including paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, and more recently age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The rationale behind harnessing a CD59-based approach is based on the well-established physiological role of native CD59 in inhibiting the terminal pathway of complement activation by blocking the incorporation of C9 into the C5b-8 complex to form the membrane attack complex (MAC), thus preventing cell lysis and downstream inflammatory cascades (Tan et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
CD59, as a natural complement regulatory protein, has been a focus of research for several years due to its intrinsic ability to safeguard host tissues from complement-mediated injury; multiple studies have demonstrated that impaired CD59 recycling or decreased CD59 surface expression is associated with increased MAC deposition on RPE cells in AMD models, ultimately leading to lysosomal dysfunction and cellular injury (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Although the CD59-Fc fusion protein itself has not been extensively tested in clinical settings, analogous therapeutic approaches—including gene therapy strategies such as AAVCAGsCD59, which deliver soluble forms of CD59 to the retina—have been evaluated preclinically and in early-phase clinical trials, with evidence suggesting that enhancement of CD59 function can reduce complement-mediated damage in the eye (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2021). In addition, complementary studies using other classes of complement inhibitors (for example, compstatin analogs like Cp40 that act upstream at the C3 convertase level) have demonstrated reversal of pathological phenotypes in AMD models by protecting lysosomal integrity and restoring RPE cellular function (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). While most of the clinical research in dry AMD has focused on C3- and C5-targeting agents (such as pegcetacoplan and avacincaptad pegol, respectively) with mixed outcomes, these data collectively support the strategy of terminal pathway inhibition as a viable approach; however, the CD59-Fc candidate distinguishes itself by directly recapitulating the naturally evolved mechanism of MAC inhibition (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022). Notably, while the clinical history of CD59-based therapies in AMD is still in its early stages, preclinical models strongly implicate the loss of CD59 function in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, thereby making CD59 enhancement a rational repurposing strategy in this context (Tan et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the CD59-Fc fusion protein acts by binding specifically to the complement components C8 and/or C9, which is critical during the final assembly phase of the MAC; normally, native CD59 prevents the recruitment of C9 to the C5b-8 complex, thereby effectively halting pore formation on the target cell membrane, which would otherwise lead to uncontrolled ion fluxes, cell lysis, or sub-lytic MAC deposition that can trigger pro-inflammatory and pro-apoptotic signaling cascades (Tan et al., 2016). The high affinity binding (Kd < 1 nM) is expected to allow the fusion protein to effectively compete with endogenous CD59, thereby providing robust inhibition even in the milieu of heightened complement activation as observed in AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In addition to its direct inhibition of MAC assembly, the Fc fragment confers several pharmacokinetic advantages: it enhances the protein’s stability, increases its half-life through neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)-mediated recycling, and may facilitate localized retention within the ocular environment upon intravitreal injection, ensuring sustained therapeutic levels over prolonged treatment intervals (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2021). Moreover, by preventing MAC deposition on RPE cells, the candidate is anticipated to safeguard the integrity of lysosomal membranes—a process crucial for proper autophagic function and the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS); lysosomal damage through MAC-induced membrane permeabilization has been implicated in RPE dysfunction and the subsequent progression of dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). On a cellular level, experimental models have shown that complement attack leads to lysosomal swelling, membrane fragility, and eventual mitochondrial dysfunction due to leakage of lysosomal enzymes (such as Cathepsin D) into the cytosol or drusen-like deposits; by mitigating MAC formation, CD59-Fc is expected to interrupt this deleterious cascade and restore cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
The expected pharmacodynamic effect of the CD59-Fc fusion protein centers on its capacity to prevent MAC deposition on the cell surface of RPE cells; this is hypothesized to occur through the high-affinity binding of the fusion protein to complement components C8 and C9, thereby precluding the insertion of the complete MAC pore into the plasma or lysosomal membranes of these cells (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). By averting MAC formation, the candidate helps maintain lysosomal membrane integrity, which in turn supports normal autophagic degradation and proper phagocytic processing of POS—a process that is critically impaired in AMD and is associated with lipofuscin accumulation and further complement activation (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In functional assays, treatment with CD59-Fc is expected to result in a significant reduction of intracellular MAC deposition, as evidenced by decreased staining of markers associated with complement activation, and to preserve lysosomal structure, as reflected by normalized lysosome size and reduced markers of lysosomal membrane permeability (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). This preservation of lysosomal function is central to ensuring that the RPE retains its ability to efficiently phagocytose and degrade POS, thereby sustaining the retinal microenvironment and potentially slowing or reversing the progression of geographic atrophy—the late stage of dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Moreover, by protecting mitochondrial integrity indirectly through the maintenance of lysosomal function, CD59-Fc may also reduce oxidative stress and apoptotic signaling within RPE cells, contributing further to cell survival and retinal health (Tan et al., 2016). The candidate’s mechanism is supported by data from ex vivo experiments in complement-challenged explants, where application of complement inhibitors similar to CD59-based agents reduced MAC deposition and preserved lysosomal morphology (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2021). Additionally, studies where cholesterol accumulation or the presence of oxidized lipoproteins disrupts CD59 recycling correlate with enhanced MAC deposition and lysosomal dysfunction, reinforcing the notion that restoring CD59 activity through a fusion protein could have broad protective effects on the RPE (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
In assessing the potential of the CD59-Fc fusion protein as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses become apparent. On the positive side, the candidate leverages the body’s natural defense mechanism against complement-mediated injury by directly targeting a key step in the formation of the membrane attack complex, a process that has been strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of AMD. Numerous preclinical studies have established that excessive MAC deposition on RPE cells leads to lysosomal dysfunction, impaired autophagy, and subsequent RPE cell death, all of which are critical factors in the progression of geographic atrophy (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The CD59-Fc fusion protein is therefore expected to interrupt this pathological cascade by preserving lysosomal integrity and promoting the maintenance of cellular homeostasis, with potential downstream benefits including the restoration of normal POS phagocytosis and improved metabolic health of RPE cells (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Another strength is the inclusion of the Fc moiety, which not only extends the protein’s half-life, ensuring sustained therapeutic exposure in the eye, but may also aid in achieving effective localized concentrations following intravitreal administration (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2021). This pharmacokinetic advantage is particularly significant in ocular therapies, where frequent dosing and short half-life of drugs have historically challenged the long-term management of chronic conditions such as dry AMD. Moreover, the concept of using a recombinant fusion protein to mimic or enhance endogenous regulatory mechanisms has precedence in other therapeutic areas, providing a solid scientific foundation for this approach (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Tan et al., 2016).

However, there are also notable challenges and potential weaknesses that warrant careful consideration. One primary concern is that, while preclinical models and ex vivo explant studies provide promising evidence for the efficacy of complement inhibitors in halting or reversing complement-mediated damage, the translation of these findings into clinical success in dry AMD has been fraught with mixed results. Several complement inhibitors, particularly those targeting upstream components like C3 and C5 (e.g., pegcetacoplan, avacincaptad pegol), have shown significant anatomical benefits such as reduced geographic atrophy lesion growth but have failed to reliably improve visual acuity, and in some instances have been associated with adverse events such as conversion to neovascular AMD (Tzoumas et al., 2023). Although CD59-Fc acts at a different point in the complement cascade, the complexity of the complement system in the ocular microenvironment and the possibility of compensatory mechanisms remain a potential hurdle that could limit therapeutic efficacy (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Another consideration is that the CD59-Fc fusion protein has yet to be tested extensively in in vivo models of AMD, and its pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics in the human eye are largely unknown. Challenges such as achieving sufficient tissue penetration, avoiding systemic immune activation, and mitigating any unforeseen off-target effects will need to be addressed in rigorous preclinical studies before any clinical trial can be contemplated (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022). Additionally, there is always the risk associated with biologics that their large molecular size or Fc-mediated effector functions might lead to immunogenicity or unexpected interactions with other components of the immune system, potentially triggering inflammatory responses—this is particularly critical in the immune-privileged ocular environment where preserving immune homeostasis is essential (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Finally, while the hypothesis postulates that by protecting lysosomal membranes CD59-Fc will indirectly improve POS phagocytic and degradative function, the relationship between complement suppression and restoration of complex RPE cell functions remains to be conclusively established in AMD pathology. Although there is compelling evidence that complement-mediated MAC deposition is deleterious to lysosomal function and that complement inhibition can restore cellular homeostasis, the multifactorial nature of AMD pathogenesis—which includes oxidative stress, lipid dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and genetic predispositions—means that CD59-Fc may need to be used in combination with other therapeutic strategies to achieve clinically meaningful outcomes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2016).

In summary, the CD59-Fc fusion protein represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its profound mechanistic rationale, which is anchored in the prevention of MAC formation and the subsequent protection of lysosomal membranes in RPE cells. Its design to mimic and potentiate a natural protective pathway, combined with the pharmacokinetic benefits conferred by the Fc fusion, positions it favorably among complement-based therapeutic strategies. However, the challenges of translating preclinical successes into reliable clinical outcomes in the heterogeneous and multifactorial landscape of AMD cannot be understated. A focused program of further preclinical studies—including detailed pharmacodynamic assessments, tissue distribution, efficacy in robust in vivo models of dry AMD, and safety evaluations—will be essential to validate the therapeutic potential of CD59-Fc prior to embarking on human clinical trials. Overall, while the strengths of the candidate are compelling, its ultimate success will depend on resolving the inherent complexities of complement regulation in the retinal microenvironment and ensuring that the beneficial effects on lysosomal preservation translate into meaningful improvements in visual function and disease progression in patients with dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2016; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
P110 is a synthetic, cell‐permeable inhibitory peptide specifically engineered to disrupt the pathological interaction between dynamin‐related protein 1 (Drp1) and its mitochondrial outer membrane receptor fission protein 1 (Fis1). It is synthesized via solid‐phase peptide synthesis methods and rational design strategies that mimic the native binding interface of these two proteins. As such, P110 belongs to the class of peptide-based mitochondrial fission inhibitors, a subclass of compounds that have been previously investigated in a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders, where aberrant mitochondrial fission is implicated in disease pathology. These types of compounds have historically been used experimentally to restore normal mitochondrial morphological dynamics and attenuate excessive fission triggered by oxidative stress. The concept builds upon evidence that an overactive fission process, largely mediated by elevated activity of Drp1 in response to cellular stressors, results in mitochondrial fragmentation, cytochrome c release, and subsequent cell death. In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which bear extremely high energy demands for functions such as photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis, proper mitochondrial network integrity is essential. The peptide’s cell-permeability and selective inhibition of the Drp1/Fis1 binding suggest that P110 can efficiently penetrate ocular tissues and modulate mitochondrial dynamics locally, offering a promising approach to preserve mitochondrial function in the diseased retina (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Numerous preclinical studies have investigated the modulation of mitochondrial dynamics in models of oxidative stress and neurodegeneration, often employing broad-spectrum inhibitors such as mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (Mdivi-1) or genetic silencing approaches using Drp1-specific siRNA. In several in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells—a human RPE cell line—excessive mitochondrial fission triggered by oxidative stress (for example, via hydrogen peroxide exposure) was effectively ameliorated by Drp1 inhibition. This intervention preserved mitochondrial structure, maintained ATP production, and increased cell viability, thereby preventing the morphological transition from tubular to fragmented mitochondria (Yako et al., 2021). Although these investigations have provided robust proof-of-concept evidence that targeting Drp1-mediated fission can be beneficial in preventing RPE dysfunction, most of the studies have not directly tested P110 peptide for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Instead, the literature has explored alternative approaches using compounds like Mdivi-1 and genetic knockdown modalities to decrease Drp1 activity, which indirectly supports the mechanistic rationale for using a targeted inhibitor like P110. The literature also shows that increased expression of mitochondrial fission factor (Mff) and elevated Drp1 levels in AMD donor tissues correlate with impaired mitochondrial homeostasis and defective phagocytosis in the RPE (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022). There remains, however, a gap in direct evidence for P110’s use in AMD despite its clear conceptual alignment with the therapeutic strategy of reducing pathological mitochondrial fission. Clinical trials have emerged that investigate mitochondrial fission inhibitors in ocular conditions, yet the available database queries indicate that while there is clinical interest in Drp1-targeting approaches, specific details on the P110 peptide remain sparse (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Thus, while the broader therapeutic paradigm—targeting aberrant mitochondrial fission—is well supported, P110 itself represents an innovative candidate that requires further preclinical validation in AMD-relevant models.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the pathological process underpinning excessive mitochondrial fission centers on the overactivation of Drp1, a GTPase that orchestrates mitochondrial scission. Under normal physiological conditions, Drp1 exists in the cytosol and is transiently recruited to the mitochondrial outer membrane by receptors such as Fis1, mitochondrial fission factor (Mff), and MiD49/MiD51. In response to oxidative and inflammatory stress—conditions known to be prevalent in the aging RPE and AMD—the interaction between Drp1 and Fis1 is upregulated, leading to excessive fission, mitochondrial fragmentation, and subsequent mitochondrial dysfunction. P110 is designed to selectively inhibit the Drp1/Fis1 binding interface, thereby attenuating the aberrant recruitment of Drp1 to the mitochondria. In doing so, it preserves the elongated and interconnected mitochondrial network, which is essential for optimal mitochondrial bioenergetics and the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Biochemically, inhibition of this interaction prevents the oligomerization of Drp1 on the mitochondrial surface, a process that is otherwise necessary for the formation of constriction rings that facilitate organelle division (Zhao et al., 2025). By blocking Drp1 recruitment, P110 indirectly maintains mitochondrial membrane potential and reduces the likelihood of cytochrome c release—a key event in the apoptosis cascade that is frequently observed in stressed RPE cells (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). Although many of the studies in the context of AMD have focused on Mdivi-1 as a Drp1 inhibitor, the specificity of P110 for the Drp1/Fis1 interaction might offer a distinct pharmacological profile, reducing off-target effects and preserving the physiological fission events necessary for maintaining overall mitochondrial quality control (Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021). Furthermore, the fact that mitochondrial fission and fusion processes are tightly integrated with mitochondrial biogenesis and mitophagy pathways supports the prospect that modulating this specific interaction may lead to a net improvement in mitochondrial dynamics without completely abolishing essential fission events (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Given the underlying hypothesis, the expected effect of P110 in AMD RPE cells would be to restore a balance in mitochondrial dynamics that has been disrupted by chronic oxidative stress. The assay proposed involves exposing cultured RPE cells, such as ARPE-19, to oxidative insults (e.g., H₂O₂) that would otherwise induce excessive Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission. P110’s mode of action is anticipated to specifically block the pathological protein-protein interaction between Drp1 and Fis1, thereby reducing the formation of excessively fragmented mitochondria and promoting the preservation or re-establishment of a tubular mitochondrial network. This intact network is critical for efficient ATP production, which in turn supports high-energy processes such as the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). POS phagocytosis is a metabolically demanding function that is crucial for photoreceptor renewal and overall retinal health. By maintaining ATP supply and preventing the release of pro-apoptotic factors (such as cytochrome c), P110 is expected to protect RPE cells from oxidative damage and improve cellular viability under stress conditions (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). Additionally, studies have demonstrated that mitochondrial fission inhibitors can lead to improved mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and enhanced cell survival under conditions of oxidative insult (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). In RPE cells, these improvements translate into a better capacity for POS uptake and metabolism, which are essential for sustaining the metabolic demands of the outer retina. Given that expression levels of Drp1 and its functional activity are elevated in AMD RPE cells, as evidenced by electron microscopy and proteomic analyses showing reduced mitochondrial numbers, diminished cristae, and defective fusion/fission ratios, the application of P110 is expected to counteract these detrimental changes by stabilizing the mitochondrial network (Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summarizing the overall evaluation of P110 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key points emerge from the literature. First, the mechanistic rationale underpinning P110’s mode of action is robust and well-aligned with current understanding of AMD pathophysiology. Excessive Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission has been implicated as a crucial driver of mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells—a hallmark of dry AMD. Several studies using alternative approaches such as pharmacological inhibition with Mdivi-1 or genetic knockdown via siRNA have consistently demonstrated that mitigating aberrant mitochondrial fission leads to improved mitochondrial integrity, preserved bioenergetic function, and enhanced cell viability in models of oxidative stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). This information directly supports the hypothesis that targeting the Drp1/Fis1 interaction, rather than globally inhibiting all Drp1 activity, could offer a more refined therapeutic approach with potentially fewer side effects. Such specificity is particularly appealing in the context of the retina where finely tuned mitochondrial dynamics are essential for high energy-demand processes like POS phagocytosis (Fisher et al., 2022).

One of the primary strengths of P110 lies in its cell-permeable peptide nature, which facilitates targeted intracellular delivery—a critical characteristic for therapies intended for ocular application. Its design, which specifically disrupts the interaction between Drp1 and Fis1, is predicated on the notion that pathological fission can be selectively blocked without interfering with the physiological fission necessary for regular mitochondrial turnover and repair. This specificity could, in theory, translate to a better safety profile compared to less selective inhibitors such as Mdivi-1 that may have off-target effects, including undesirable impacts on other aspects of mitochondrial function (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2025).

Despite the promising mechanistic rationale and potential for ocular development, there are notable weaknesses and challenges to be considered. The current literature does not yet offer direct preclinical or clinical evidence that P110 peptide itself has been used to treat dry AMD. Most existing studies have extrapolated the benefits of Drp1 inhibition from experiments involving Mdivi-1 or Drp1 knockdown in cellular models of RPE oxidative stress (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Therefore, while the concept of targeting Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission in AMD is well supported, the direct application of P110 remains largely theoretical at this point. This gap in the literature introduces uncertainty regarding the peptide’s pharmacokinetic properties, its stability in ocular tissues, and its potential immunogenic responses upon local administration in the eye.

Another potential limitation is the complex role of mitochondrial dynamics in cellular homeostasis. Although excessive fission in the context of oxidative stress is detrimental, mitochondrial fission is also a necessary process for mitophagy and the removal of damaged organelles. Some studies have indicated that a certain degree of fission may even be beneficial for cellular quality control, as it facilitates the segregation and subsequent removal of malfunctioning mitochondria (Skeie et al., 2021; Yako et al., 2021). The nuanced interplay between reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling and fission means that complete inhibition of fission—even if intended to be only pathological—could potentially have unintended consequences. It will be critical to determine whether P110’s selective inhibition of Drp1/Fis1 interaction can maintain the necessary balance between inhibiting excessive fission while still allowing physiological fission to contribute to normal mitophagy and mitochondrial turnover.

Furthermore, while the peptide’s cell-permeability is an advantage, peptide therapeutics in ocular applications face challenges related to delivery, degradation by ocular proteases, and potential issues with achieving sustained concentrations in the target tissues. Addressing these challenges may require the development of specialized drug delivery systems, such as intravitreal injections with sustained-release formulations or conjugation to nanoparticles, to ensure that adequate therapeutic levels of P110 are maintained at the retinal level over the necessary duration (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Additional practical concerns include the need for rigorous in vivo studies in relevant animal models of dry AMD to assess not only the efficacy in preserving mitochondrial function and POS phagocytosis in RPE cells but also the overall impact on retinal structure and visual function. Currently, many studies have been limited to in vitro models using ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress conditions. Although these models provide valuable mechanistic insights, they do not fully recapitulate the complex interplay of cellular and systemic factors that contribute to AMD in vivo. The therapeutic potential of P110 will need to be evaluated in animal models that mimic the pathophysiological conditions of dry AMD, where factors such as chronic low-grade inflammation, complement activation, and cumulative oxidative damage play significant roles (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

In addition to efficacy and safety concerns, the regulatory landscape for peptide therapeutics in ocular indications should be considered. The development of P110 for dry AMD will require detailed pharmacodynamic and toxicological evaluations to satisfy regulatory requirements. While the peptide’s mechanism—targeting a well-characterized protein-protein interaction—provides a clear scientific rationale, the path toward clinical translation is contingent on demonstrating not only mechanistic efficacy but also an acceptable safety profile in both preclinical toxicology studies and early-phase clinical trials (Fisher et al., 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

In conclusion, the comprehensive literature review supports the notion that targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, specifically through the inhibition of Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission, is a highly promising therapeutic avenue for dry AMD. P110, as a selective inhibitor of the Drp1/Fis1 interaction, is well poised within this framework. The candidate is grounded in a strong mechanistic rationale that links excessive mitochondrial fission to reduced ATP production, impaired POS phagocytosis, and ultimately, RPE cell dysfunction—a cascade of events that underlies the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022).

The inherent advantages of a peptide-based therapeutic, including its specificity and cell-permeability, are particularly attractive for ocular drug development, where targeted delivery and minimal off-target effects are crucial. Nonetheless, notable weaknesses remain that must be addressed before P110 can be considered a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The absence of direct experimental data with P110 in AMD models, the complex nature of mitochondrial dynamics where inhibition of fission must be carefully balanced to avoid impairing critical mitophagy processes, and potential challenges associated with peptide stability and delivery in the ocular environment represent significant hurdles. These challenges underscore the necessity for further preclinical investigations, including in vivo efficacy and safety studies in animal models that recapitulate the chronic oxidative stress and metabolic derangements characteristic of AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).

Ultimately, while the theoretical basis for P110’s use in dry AMD is compelling and supported by a considerable body of literature showing beneficial effects of mitochondrial fission inhibition in RPE cells, advancing this candidate will require a coordinated effort to fill the current gaps in experimental evidence. Future studies should focus on validating the efficacy of P110 in terms of restoring mitochondrial dynamics, preserving ATP production, and ultimately improving POS phagocytosis in both cell culture and animal models of AMD. If these studies yield positive results, P110 has the potential to become an important component of a new generation of therapies aimed at addressing the mitochondrial dysfunction that lies at the heart of dry AMD pathophysiology (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).

Overall, the research direction for P110 is promising given the established relationship between mitochondrial dysfunction and AMD. With its targeted mechanism of action and a strong conceptual basis rooted in the modulation of mitochondrial dynamics, P110 stands as a high-potential candidate. However, careful optimization of dosing, formulation, and delivery, as well as comprehensive preclinical validation, is essential before this therapeutic candidate can be reliably advanced into clinical trials. Should these hurdles be successfully overcome, P110 could not only provide substantial therapeutic benefit by preserving RPE function in dry AMD but also serve as a model for developing other targeted mitochondrial therapies in ocular neurodegeneration (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).
