Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ezetimibe (SCH-58235) is a synthetic small molecule developed as a specific inhibitor of intestinal sterol absorption and clinically positioned as an LDL-cholesterol–lowering agent and as therapy for rare sterol storage disorders such as sitosterolemia (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, 2001). Ezetimibe’s pharmacological class is “cholesterol absorption inhibitor,” a class characterized by selective action at the intestinal epithelium to reduce uptake of dietary and biliary cholesterol, thereby decreasing hepatic delivery of chylomicron-derived cholesterol, upregulating LDL receptor–mediated clearance, and lowering plasma LDL-C; in human and animal studies, agents in this class also increase fecal neutral sterol excretion and augment reverse cholesterol transport (RCT) from plasma to feces (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, 2001; Radiant Research, 2008; Ostlund, 2014; Bujold, 2012). Mechanistically, this class targets the Niemann–Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) protein at the apical surface of intestinal enterocytes, the principal protein-mediated pathway for sterol influx from mixed micelles; inhibition of NPC1L1 decreases absorption efficiency and increases fecal sterol output (Guo et al., 2024; Murillo, 2016; Bujold, 2012). Within ophthalmology, ezetimibe has been proposed in preclinical AMD literature as a systemic modulator of cholesterol handling that could mitigate diet-induced lipoprotein stress and downstream retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/Bruch’s membrane (BrM) pathology, but published ocular outcome data are not yet available (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). In short, ezetimibe is a clinically established synthetic NPC1L1 inhibitor designed to reduce intestinal sterol uptake and circulating atherogenic lipoproteins; its repurposing to dry AMD rests on the hypothesis that systemic lipid lowering will secondarily ameliorate RPE lipid burden and associated lysosomal/autophagy dysfunction (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Clinical use and systemic metabolic effects. Ezetimibe is an approved LDL-lowering therapy for hypercholesterolemia and sitosterolemia, typically dosed at 10 mg daily, and is widely used in combination with statins to achieve LDL targets with improved tolerability compared with high-intensity statin monotherapy in cardiovascular populations (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, 2001; Cho, 2023). Human metabolic studies using stable isotope tracers demonstrate that ezetimibe increases endogenous fecal neutral sterol excretion and reduces intestinal cholesterol absorption as expected for an NPC1L1 inhibitor; crossover and parallel-arm trials confirm effects on absorption efficiency and synthesis compensation, particularly when combined with statins (Radiant Research, 2008; Ostlund, 2014; Organon and Co., 2003). In randomized human feeding studies, ezetimibe reduces cholesterol absorption and lowers LDL-C; combined with phytosterols, effects on fecal sterols and LDL are additive, consistent with distinct yet complementary intestinal mechanisms (Washington University School of Medicine, 2009). In atherosclerosis-prone mice, ezetimibe reduces plaque burden; genetic deficiency of NPC1L1 similarly prevents atherosclerosis, and these intestinal manipulations enhance macrophage-to-feces RCT, implicating transintestinal cholesterol efflux (TICE) as a significant route for whole-body cholesterol disposal (Bujold, 2012).

Non-ocular lipid disease contexts. Beyond hypercholesterolemia, ezetimibe has been clinically evaluated in sitosterolemia (inherited sterol transport disorder), producing reductions in plasma plant sterols and LDL-C consistent with intestinal absorption blockade; protocols emphasize its role as a specific cholesterol absorption inhibitor in these patients (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, 2001). Multiple cardiovascular trials have examined ezetimibe’s LDL-lowering efficacy alone and in combination, and protocol summaries and meta-trials reiterate its intestinal mechanism and complementarity with statins (Organon and Co., 2003; Cho, 2023).

Ophthalmic/retinal disease history. The AMD preclinical literature reviewed by Landowski and Bowes Rickman identifies dietary cholesterol as a modifiable driver of AMD-like pathology in aged complement factor H (CFH) transgenic mice: high-fat, cholesterol-enriched (HFC) diets increase circulating lipoproteins, and aged CFH-H/H mice on HFC or high-cholesterol diets exhibit decreased scotopic ERG b-wave amplitudes; based on these observations, the authors propose that therapeutics reducing intestinal cholesterol uptake (citing ezetimibe) “may prevent visual loss in aged CFH-H/H HFC mice,” with ongoing studies to test whether ezetimibe can mimic dietary modulation and influence eyecup ApoB48 and ApoA-1 (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). However, those reports explicitly note that these are investigational questions; no completed preclinical data on retinal function, RPE lipid endpoints, autophagy, or lysosomal indices under ezetimibe treatment are presented in the cited excerpts (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). Reviews of lipid-lowering therapies in diabetic retinopathy (DR) list ezetimibe among LDL-lowering agents of interest but underscore the absence of large randomized controlled trials with DR endpoints and provide no ocular pharmacokinetic or safety data for ezetimibe; the text highlights that intraocular delivery can dramatically alter retinal exposure relative to systemic administration, underscoring a translational gap for systemically delivered LDL-modifying agents in ocular disease (Jenkins et al., 2022). Across the provided literature, there are no reports of ezetimibe being used to treat dry AMD or direct analogs (e.g., Stargardt disease) in humans, and no completed preclinical animal studies demonstrating ezetimibe-induced improvements in RPE lipofuscin, lysosome/autophagy function, photoreceptor survival, or drusen-like deposits (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary molecular target and tissue of action. The canonical molecular target for ezetimibe is NPC1L1, a sterol influx transporter localized to the apical membrane of small-intestinal enterocytes, which mediates uptake of dietary and biliary cholesterol from mixed micelles; blocking NPC1L1 reduces intestinal absorption and lowers delivery of cholesterol to the liver via chylomicrons, thus decreasing hepatic VLDL production and circulating LDL levels (Guo et al., 2024; Murillo, 2016). The LDL-lowering and fecal sterol-raising effects of ezetimibe in humans and mice, together with similar outcomes observed in NPC1L1 deficiency, support on-target action at the intestinal epithelium (Bujold, 2012; Radiant Research, 2008; Ostlund, 2014; Organon and Co., 2003). Ezetimibe’s systemic metabolic effects—reduced LDL-C and enhanced RCT/TICE—are therefore downstream consequences of intestinal NPC1L1 inhibition rather than direct hepatic or peripheral tissue binding (Bujold, 2012; Radiant Research, 2008).

Systemic lipid fluxes relevant to the eye. After intestinal absorption, cholesterol is packaged into chylomicrons (ApoB48-containing) that deliver dietary lipid to the liver; hepatic secretion of VLDL (ApoB100-containing) and intravascular remodeling generate LDL, which distributes cholesterol systemically, including to the eye; cellular uptake of LDL occurs via the LDL receptor (LDLR) on peripheral cells (including RPE), while HDL mediates reverse cholesterol transport from tissues back to the liver through ABCA1/ABCG1-dependent efflux (Unknown Reference). The RPE has LDL and scavenger receptor activity and participates in receptor-mediated uptake of lipoprotein-bound cholesterol; this receptor-mediated uptake is proposed to be a major route for retinal cholesterol acquisition from systemic circulation, complementing local synthesis (Zekavat et al., 2017). Thus, ezetimibe can plausibly modulate ocular lipid influx indirectly by lowering plasma LDL and chylomicron-remnant delivery to the outer retina, which may reduce lipoprotein deposition in Bruch’s membrane and sub-RPE basal deposits in models where circulating lipoproteins contribute materially to the ocular lipid burden (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Retinal cholesterol homeostasis and AMD-relevant pathobiology. Retina and RPE cholesterol derive largely from in situ synthesis behind the blood–retinal barrier, stringently controlled by transcriptional networks (SREBP2, LXR/RXR) and efflux transporters (ABCA1/ABCG1); age-related dysfunction in these pathways, along with mitochondrial decline, is implicated in AMD (Guo et al., 2024; Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). Lipids constitute a large fraction of drusen volume (~40%), and oxidized cholesterol species—notably 7-ketocholesterol (7KCh)—accumulate in the outer retina and RPE, where they inhibit autophagic flux (elevated p62), promote lipofuscin accumulation within lysosomes, activate NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasomes, and trigger apoptosis, collectively linking cholesterol dysregulation to lysosomal dysfunction and inflammation in AMD (Guo et al., 2024). These pathogenic cascades are exacerbated by inefficiencies in photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis and degradation by the RPE, processes that can be impaired by lipofuscin bisretinoids such as A2E and cholesterol crystal-driven inflammasome activation (Nociari et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2024). Independent preclinical work shows that enhancing cholesterol efflux (e.g., via LXR agonism) and inducing autophagy can normalize endosomal/lysosomal morphology and reduce RPE lipid accumulation in disease models such as Abca4-/-, and that RPE-specific ablation of ABCA1/ABCG1 produces lipid accumulation, RPE/photoreceptor degeneration, and vision loss—highlighting the centrality of cholesterol handling to retinal health (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). These data provide a mechanistic framework in which interventions that reduce retinal lipid influx, promote efflux, or restore lysosomal/autophagic capacity could beneficially modulate AMD-relevant endpoints.

Distinguishing NPC1L1 (intestinal) from NPC1 (lysosomal). It is important to differentiate the intestinal sterol influx transporter NPC1L1 (targeted by ezetimibe) from the lysosomal cholesterol egress protein NPC1; loss or inhibition of NPC1 traps cholesterol in late endosomes/lysosomes, whereas modulation of NPC1L1 affects apical enterocyte uptake (Schmiedt, 2012). In human RPE, palmitoylation of NPC1 governs cholesterol export from late endosomes; mutation of key cysteines increases lysosomal cholesterol accumulation without altering gross NPC1 localization, underscoring that RPE cholesterol trafficking depends on NPC1 and intracellular sorting mechanisms, not on NPC1L1 (Li et al., 2022). The provided literature does not demonstrate expression or functional roles for NPC1L1 in RPE, and no direct ocular actions of ezetimibe on RPE cholesterol uptake or lysosomal function are reported (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024).

AMD-relevant systemic–ocular linkage in CFH models. In aged CFH-transgenic mice, high-fat/high-cholesterol diets increase circulating chylomicron/VLDL/LDL and are associated with decreased scotopic ERG responses and sub-RPE deposit phenotypes; these findings motivate testing whether decreasing intestinal cholesterol absorption (e.g., ezetimibe) can mimic dietary cholesterol restriction and preserve visual function (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). The same review emphasizes RPE-derived lipoprotein accumulation in BrM and proposes that reducing intestinal cholesterol could reduce ocular ApoB48/ApoA-1 signals in the eyecup, consistent with lower lipoprotein flux to or from RPE/BrM (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). However, these are prospective hypotheses; experimental results were not reported in the excerpts (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Expected Effect  
Proposed hypothesis and assay context. The working hypothesis asserts that ezetimibe will “block cholesterol uptake in RPE (IC50 ~0.5 µM), reducing cholesterol-driven lysosomal dysfunction and lipofuscin, thereby improving POS degradation in dry AMD models,” and claims that ezetimibe “reduces cholesterol content in RPE, normalizes lysosomal pH, and enhances POS clearance in high-cholesterol culture,” with supportive statements about oral safety and ocular penetration in animals. The provided literature does not support these specific assertions: there are no data in the excerpts demonstrating NPC1L1 expression in RPE, ezetimibe binding or potency against an RPE target, direct effects on RPE cholesterol content, lysosomal pH normalization, lipofuscin reduction, or POS degradation, and no ocular penetration measurements are reported (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024; Jenkins et al., 2022). Therefore, a direct RPE-cell autonomous mechanism for ezetimibe is currently unsubstantiated by the cited literature.

Mechanistically grounded expectations in vitro (RPE systems). Given the lack of evidence that RPE expresses NPC1L1, the expected direct effect of ezetimibe in RPE culture under high-cholesterol conditions is uncertain. RPE cholesterol uptake from the extracellular milieu is thought to be mediated predominantly by LDLR and scavenger receptors acting on lipoprotein particles, not by NPC1L1-mediated micellar uptake as in enterocytes (Zekavat et al., 2017). Moreover, intracellular lysosomal cholesterol egress in RPE depends on NPC1/NPC2 and is modulated by protein palmitoylation and other lysosomal trafficking determinants, not by NPC1L1 (Li et al., 2022; Schmiedt, 2012). Consequently, unless ezetimibe has unidentified off-target activity relevant to RPE cholesterol uptake or lysosomal function, one would not anticipate robust correction of lysosomal cholesterol storage, lysosomal pH, autophagic flux, lipofuscin accumulation, or POS digestion kinetics in RPE culture solely from ezetimibe exposure; the provided literature does not document such off-target activities (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024). In contrast, other interventions have demonstrated RPE-directed effects in vitro and in vivo: autophagy inducers reduce intracellular RPE lipid burden, and LXR agonism can normalize endosomal size and reduce complement activation in Abca4-/- RPE—establishing precedents for lipid/autophagy-targeted corrections in RPE models (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). Additionally, β-cyclodextrins directly deplete lysosomal cholesterol and reduce lipofuscin bisretinoids in RPE models, highlighting an approach that directly targets the lysosome rather than systemic lipid flux (Nociari et al., 2017).

Mechanistically grounded expectations in vivo (mouse AMD-relevant models). In systems where circulating lipoproteins contribute substantially to outer-retinal lipid burden—e.g., aged CFH-transgenic mice exposed to HFC diets—reducing intestinal cholesterol absorption with ezetimibe should lower plasma chylomicron remnants/VLDL/LDL, reduce delivery of cholesterol to the outer retina via lipoprotein receptors, and potentially decrease RPE/BrM lipoprotein deposition and sequelae such as ERG attenuation and sub-RPE basal deposit accumulation; the CFH literature explicitly proposes this test and notes ongoing studies (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). Mechanistically, this would be a systemic route: ezetimibe acts in the intestine, lowers circulating atherogenic lipoproteins, and thereby diminishes receptor-mediated uptake into RPE; it would not require NPC1L1 expression in the eye (Guo et al., 2024; Zekavat et al., 2017). If successful, ancillary effects could include downstream reductions in oxidized cholesterol species such as 7KCh in the outer retina, potentially normalizing autophagic flux and reducing inflammasome activation driven by lipid peroxidation, although such cascading benefits remain hypothetical in the absence of reported in vivo data (Guo et al., 2024). It should be noted that mice differ from humans in plasma lipoprotein distribution due to the absence of CETP (mouse plasma is HDL-dominant), which can alter the plasma lipid response to intestinal absorption blockade and complicate extrapolation of systemic lipid changes to ocular endpoints; diet manipulations can partially humanize lipoprotein profiles but introduce other confounders (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). These interspecies differences emphasize the need for careful readouts of ocular lipid and function rather than reliance on plasma LDL changes alone.

Target expression and pathway linkage. The hypothesis’s protein target for direct ocular action is NPC1L1; however, the provided literature does not demonstrate NPC1L1 expression in human or mouse RPE, nor does it provide functional evidence for an NPC1L1-dependent uptake pathway in RPE cells (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024). In contrast, multiple sources document LDLR/scavenger receptor–mediated lipoprotein uptake in RPE and predominant local retinal cholesterol synthesis behind the blood–retinal barrier, suggesting that systemic LDL flux and local biosynthesis/efflux determine RPE lipid load (Zekavat et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2024). Within lysosomes, cholesterol egress uses NPC1/NPC2, and manipulation of these pathways (e.g., via palmitoylation state) alters lysosomal cholesterol burden in RPE (Li et al., 2022). Therefore, if ezetimibe were to produce benefits in AMD models, the most parsimonious mechanism would be indirect and systemic (reducing lipoprotein delivery to the eye) rather than a direct RPE NPC1L1-dependent effect (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Safety and ocular exposure considerations. The clinical literature presented confirms extensive systemic use of ezetimibe, including long-duration combination therapy trials, supporting a favorable systemic safety profile; however, the provided excerpts contain no eye-specific pharmacokinetic or safety data and emphasize that systemic LDL-lowering agents generally lack large ocular endpoint trials and that ocular delivery can alter tissue exposure relative to systemic administration (Cho, 2023; Jenkins et al., 2022). Consequently, the assumption that orally dosed ezetimibe achieves pharmacologically relevant concentrations in ocular tissues is not substantiated by the cited material (Jenkins et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong systemic pharmacology and safety foundation. Ezetimibe is a clinically validated oral NPC1L1 inhibitor with robust human and animal data demonstrating reduced intestinal cholesterol absorption, increased fecal neutral sterol excretion, augmented reverse cholesterol transport, and lowered circulating LDL-C; these systemic effects are precisely the inputs one would manipulate to test lipid-driven outer-retinal pathology in diet-sensitive AMD models (Radiant Research, 2008; Ostlund, 2014; Organon and Co., 2003; Bujold, 2012).  
- Mechanistic plausibility via systemic–ocular linkage in selected models. Aged CFH-transgenic mice demonstrate diet-induced increases in circulating chylomicron/VLDL/LDL, sub-RPE lipid deposition, and ERG decrements; authors of a leading AMD lipid review specifically propose ezetimibe as a test agent to mimic dietary cholesterol restriction and potentially prevent visual loss in these mice, with ongoing studies to evaluate effects on ocular lipoprotein markers (ApoB48, ApoA-1) (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
- Meaningful disease biology linkage. Independent lines of evidence implicate cholesterol and its oxidized derivatives (7KCh) in autophagy blockade, lysosomal lipofuscin accumulation, inflammasome activation, and RPE/photoreceptor cell death—key pathologies in dry AMD—supporting the concept that reducing retinal lipid influx or burden could yield functional benefit (Guo et al., 2024). Preclinical manipulations that increase efflux (LXR agonism) or induce autophagy normalize endosome/lysosome phenotypes in RPE models, further strengthening the causal pathway between lipid load and degradative capacity (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
- Practical development advantages. Ezetimibe is already formulated for oral use, with known human dosing, tolerability, and pharmacodynamic biomarkers (fecal sterols, cholesterol absorption efficiency), enabling rapid, biomarker-driven translational studies if ocular efficacy can be shown in animals (Radiant Research, 2008; Organon and Co., 2003).

Weaknesses and key gaps  
- No evidence for direct RPE NPC1L1 expression or action. The provided literature does not document NPC1L1 expression in RPE or other ocular tissues, nor any cellular data showing ezetimibe reduces RPE cholesterol content, normalizes lysosomal pH, augments autophagic flux, lowers lipofuscin, or improves POS degradation; the specific potency claim (IC50 ~0.5 µM in RPE) is unsupported by the cited sources (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024). This undermines the core in vitro arm of the proposed hypothesis.  
- Retinal cholesterol is primarily locally synthesized. Due to the blood–retinal barrier, retinal cholesterol pools arise chiefly from in situ synthesis; modulating intestinal absorption may have limited impact on retinal cholesterol content unless circulating lipoproteins contribute substantially to outer-retinal lipid influx in the specific model under study (Guo et al., 2024). While RPE does possess LDL/scavenger receptor activity and can take up systemic lipoproteins, the quantitative contribution relative to local synthesis remains uncertain and likely context-dependent (Zekavat et al., 2017).  
- Lack of ocular pharmacokinetic and clinical endpoint data. There are no reported data on ezetimibe ocular penetration or exposure in animals or humans, and reviews emphasize the absence of large randomized retinal endpoint trials for LDL-lowering drugs, including ezetimibe; ocular efficacy with systemic dosing therefore remains speculative (Jenkins et al., 2022).  
- Species and model translation caveats. Mice lack CETP and are HDL-dominant, which affects systemic lipid responses to intestinal absorption inhibition and complicates extrapolation to human lipoprotein physiology; diet manipulations can humanize lipoproteins but introduce confounding metabolic changes that could independently influence RPE lysosomal/autophagy function (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). In addition, anatomical differences between mouse and human retinas (rod-dominance, RPE density, POS phagocytic load) can alter lysosomal stress and degradative capacity, further complicating translation (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
- Comparative mechanistic alternatives are more direct. Other interventions with demonstrated RPE-centric mechanisms—LXR agonists to increase ABCA1/ABCG1-mediated efflux, autophagy inducers, and β-cyclodextrins that directly solubilize lysosomal cholesterol and bind bisretinoids—have shown positive effects on RPE endosomal/lysosomal phenotypes or lipofuscin burden in preclinical models, suggesting more direct levers on the implicated pathogenic nodes than systemic intestinal absorption blockade (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Nociari et al., 2017).

Decision-oriented recommendations  
- Do not proceed on the assumption of a direct RPE target for ezetimibe. Before committing to RPE-centric in vitro efficacy claims, establish whether NPC1L1 is expressed in primary human RPE/iPSC-RPE and at what level; the provided literature indicates this is unknown, and NPC1L1 is classically enterocyte-restricted (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024; Murillo, 2016). In parallel, verify that ezetimibe has no off-target effects on LDLR- or scavenger receptor-mediated lipoprotein uptake in RPE and no direct impact on NPC1-dependent lysosomal cholesterol egress; current RPE mechanistic data implicate NPC1 palmitoylation in lysosomal cholesterol egress, not NPC1L1 activity (Li et al., 2022; Schmiedt, 2012).  
- Prioritize an in vivo, systemic-mechanism proof-of-concept study in a diet-sensitized AMD model. The strongest rationale for ezetimibe in AMD resides in aged CFH-transgenic mice where HFC diet increases circulating lipoproteins and impairs retinal function; test whether ezetimibe prevents ERG decline and reduces ocular ApoB48/ApoA-1 and sub-RPE lipid deposition under HFC challenge, as proposed in ongoing preclinical work (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). Include endpoints that index RPE lysosome/autophagy status and lipid oxidation (e.g., p62/LC3 flux, lysosomal pH, A2E/7KCh, NLRP3 activation) to probe whether systemic lipid lowering secondarily normalizes degradative pathways (Guo et al., 2024; Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
- Incorporate lipid handling comparators that act directly at the RPE. To de-risk mechanism, include a positive-control arm with an LXR agonist (to increase ABCA1/ABCG1) or an autophagy inducer known to reduce RPE lipid burdens, and consider a β-cyclodextrin arm to directly test whether lowering lysosomal cholesterol and bisretinoids rescues degradative function; these comparators will benchmark the magnitude of effect achievable with RPE-centric strategies (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Nociari et al., 2017).  
- Use plasma and fecal sterol biomarkers to confirm on-target intestinal action. Quantify fecal neutral sterol excretion and cholesterol absorption efficiency to verify effective NPC1L1 inhibition in vivo; these human-validated biomarkers have a mechanistic link to ezetimibe action and can anchor ocular outcome interpretations to on-target pharmacodynamics (Radiant Research, 2008; Ostlund, 2014; Organon and Co., 2003).  
- Plan for translational risks tied to retinal cholesterol sources. Given the primacy of local retinal cholesterol synthesis, negative results in models with minor circulating lipoprotein contributions to RPE lipid load would not falsify all systemic lipid-lowering hypotheses but would argue against ezetimibe’s utility except in specific lipid-sensitized genetic/dietary contexts (Guo et al., 2024; Zekavat et al., 2017). Selection of models should therefore be driven by evidence of systemic lipid influx effects on RPE/BrM biology (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Bottom line. On current evidence, ezetimibe has credible potential to test the systemic lipid-influx axis of AMD pathogenesis in select diet-sensitized genetic models (e.g., aged CFH-H/H on HFC diets), with a plausible mechanism to reduce plasma lipoproteins and secondarily lower RPE/BrM lipid deposition; however, there is no substantiation for direct RPE action via NPC1L1, no reported ocular pharmacokinetics, and no preclinical efficacy data published on RPE lysosome/autophagy endpoints or lipofuscin under ezetimibe treatment. For dry AMD, ezetimibe should be considered a hypothesis-generating, low-to-moderate probability repurposing candidate with high translational uncertainty; it merits a focused, biomarker-anchored in vivo proof-of-concept in an appropriate model, but should not displace more direct RPE-targeting lipid/autophagy strategies in the near-term pipeline (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Nociari et al., 2017; Jenkins et al., 2022).

Detailed appraisal of disease biology and how ezetimibe might intersect  
- Cholesterol exposure and RPE degradative failure. Excess cholesterol in the outer retina oxidizes to 7KCh and other oxysterols that directly inhibit autophagic flux (p62 accumulation), acidify/injure mitochondria, and promote polymerization of oxidation products that become lipofuscin within lysosomes; lipofuscin accumulation impairs lysosomal phagocytosis and autophagy, reducing POS clearance—a core function of RPE (Guo et al., 2024). These processes activate NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling and lead to RPE and photoreceptor apoptosis in rodent models, reproducing elements of dry AMD pathophysiology (Guo et al., 2024). Although ezetimibe does not directly target RPE degradative machinery, a systemic reduction in lipoprotein-delivered cholesterol could attenuate upstream substrate pressure for these oxidative and degradative stress pathways in models where systemic influx is important (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
- RPE lipid handling machinery points to more proximal targets. ABCA1/ABCG1 are critical for RPE cholesterol efflux; their loss in RPE leads to lipid accumulation, degeneration, and vision loss, while pharmacologic LXR activation mimics endosomal normalization seen with acid sphingomyelinase inhibition in Abca4-/- RPE, illustrating the benefit of directly boosting efflux pathways (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). Such direct manipulation of RPE lipid handling may offer a higher likelihood of efficacy than systemic manipulations in models where local synthesis dominates retinal cholesterol pools (Guo et al., 2024).  
- Lipoprotein biology and CFH genetic risk. CFH variants modulate RPE-derived lipoprotein accumulation in BrM, and HFC diets exacerbate ocular phenotypes in CFH-transgenic mice, positioning systemic lipoprotein burden as a modifiable driver in these contexts; ezetimibe is explicitly proposed in this literature as a candidate to reduce intestinal cholesterol uptake and test whether lowering circulating lipoproteins rescues visual function (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Programmatic risk–benefit and go/no-go criteria  
- Go criteria for advancing to animal efficacy testing:  
  • Demonstration of on-target intestinal pharmacodynamics in the chosen species/diet (increased fecal neutral sterols; reduced fractional cholesterol absorption) at a clinically relevant dose (Radiant Research, 2008; Organon and Co., 2003).  
  • Aged CFH-transgenic mice on HFC diet with documented elevation of plasma chylomicron/VLDL/LDL and ERG decrements at baseline, to ensure model sensitivity to circulating lipoprotein changes (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
  • Predefined ocular endpoints that read out RPE lipid and degradative status (ApoB48/ApoA-1 eyecup content, RPE/BrM lipid histology, LC3/p62 flux, lysosomal pH, A2E/7KCh levels, complement activation, ERG b-wave amplitude) (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024).  

- No-go criteria prior to significant resource commitment:  
  • Failure to demonstrate on-target intestinal pharmacodynamics at tolerated doses in the selected model (Radiant Research, 2008).  
  • Lack of effect on ocular lipoprotein readouts (ApoB48/ApoA-1) or ERG despite robust plasma LDL lowering and fecal sterol increase, suggesting that circulating lipoprotein flux is not rate-limiting for the ocular phenotypes in that model (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
  • Evidence from expression analyses that NPC1L1 is not expressed in RPE (which would deprioritize direct cellular assays) and that systemic LDL reductions do not translate to reduced RPE lipid load (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Zekavat et al., 2017).

Summary conclusions  
- The overarching mechanistic thesis that cholesterol-driven lysosomal/autophagy dysfunction underlies key dry AMD phenotypes is well supported by preclinical data (7KCh-driven autophagy inhibition, lipofuscin accumulation, inflammasome activation, and apoptosis), and interventions that improve RPE lipid handling and degradative capacity show benefit in relevant models (Guo et al., 2024).  
- Ezetimibe’s capacity to reduce intestinal cholesterol absorption and lower circulating atherogenic lipoproteins is firmly established; translationally, this provides a credible lever to test whether systemic lipoprotein pressure influences RPE/BrM lipid deposition and function in susceptible genotypes/diets (Bujold, 2012; Radiant Research, 2008; Ostlund, 2014; Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
- However, the specific claim that ezetimibe directly blocks RPE cholesterol uptake with sub-micromolar potency, normalizes lysosomal pH, reduces lipofuscin, and enhances POS degradation lacks support in the provided literature; moreover, NPC1L1 expression in RPE has not been demonstrated in these sources, and the intestine-restricted action of ezetimibe argues that any ocular benefits would be indirect via systemic lipid lowering (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024).  
- Given the lack of ocular PK data and the primacy of local retinal cholesterol synthesis, the prior probability of large clinical benefit in unselected dry AMD populations is modest; nonetheless, in CFH-sensitized, diet-exacerbated models the hypothesis is testable and may yield meaningful insights about the contribution of systemic lipoproteins to outer-retinal pathology (Guo et al., 2024; Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Recommendation: Advance ezetimibe to a focused, biomarker-rich preclinical proof-of-concept in aged CFH-H/H mice under HFC diet, with stringent ocular endpoints and on-target intestinal PD confirmation. In parallel, deprioritize RPE-centric in vitro efficacy claims pending demonstration of NPC1L1 expression in RPE and direct cellular activity; maintain higher prioritization for agents with demonstrated RPE-direct mechanisms (LXR agonists, autophagy inducers, β-cyclodextrins) as nearer-term AMD therapeutics (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Nociari et al., 2017).

CCT128930 is a synthetic small molecule that belongs to the pyrrolopyrimidine class and was initially discovered and optimized for its potent ATP‐competitive inhibition of AKT kinases, particularly targeting the AKT2 isoform (Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 9–11; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8). Its discovery was achieved through a combination of fragment-based screening and structure-based drug design strategies, which allowed researchers to identify and refine a scaffold capable of binding within the ATP pocket of kinases such as AKT and PDK1 (Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 7–9). The molecular design of CCT128930 incorporates a substituted 2-anilino-7H-pyrrolopyrimidine core that confers high affinity and selectivity, as evidenced by its low nanomolar IC₅₀ value—the reported potency for AKT inhibition is around 6–10 nM (Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5). Originally developed for oncology purposes, where aberrant AKT signaling drives uncontrolled cell proliferation, the compound demonstrated significant antiproliferative effects in multiple tumor cell lines with some studies noting efficacy comparable to established inhibitors such as Erlotinib (Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 9–11; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 8–9). The synthetic origins and chemical tractability of the pyrrolopyrimidine scaffold have historically permitted further chemical modifications to optimize pharmacokinetics and minimize off-target activity, traits that are now valuable in the context of repurposing efforts. In summary, CCT128930 is a robustly characterized ATP-competitive inhibitor with a synthetic pedigree grounded in modern medicinal chemistry, which originally found application in cancer therapy yet holds promise for other diseases where AKT2-mediated signaling is implicated (Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, CCT128930 was developed within an oncology paradigm as researchers sought to inhibit aberrant AKT signaling—a driver of cell survival, proliferation, and metabolism—in various cancer models (Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 9–11; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8). Preclinical studies demonstrated that by inhibiting the phosphorylation of key downstream targets such as PRAS40 and FOXO3a, CCT128930 could induce cell cycle arrest and reduce tumor growth in vitro and in xenograft models (Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 9–11; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8). Its antiproliferative efficacy was further underpinned by its ability to compete effectively with ATP for binding to the kinase domain of AKT, a mode of action that led to promising results in early-phase oncology trials. Despite these encouraging effects, further clinical development was halted during phase I studies primarily because of concerns regarding off-target activity and toxicities that limited its therapeutic window (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8). Notably, before the current repurposing hypothesis was proposed, CCT128930 had not been utilized for any ocular indications, including dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), nor had it been evaluated in veterinary settings for similar degenerative diseases. Emerging literature on the role of AKT2 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, particularly through its phosphorylation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), now provides a mechanistic basis for repurposing this compound. Previous studies have linked AKT2 activity with impaired lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy in RPE cells—a critical pathological mechanism in dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). Thus, while the therapeutic history of CCT128930 is rooted in oncology, its well-documented pharmacology, including preclinical pharmacokinetics, tissue penetration (notably CNS penetration), and kinase selectivity, supports its potential application in ocular conditions through localized delivery approaches such as intravitreal injection (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6).  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, CCT128930 exerts its effects primarily by acting as an ATP-competitive inhibitor of AKT kinases, binding to the ATP-binding site within the kinase domain to block the phosphorylation of downstream targets (Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5; Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 7–9). Its mode of action is underscored by its high degree of selectivity for AKT2 over other kinases such as protein kinase A (PKA), which is critical given the need to minimize off-target effects in sensitive tissues like the retina (Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5; Adel et al., 2018a, pp. 7–9). In normal cellular physiology, AKT2 phosphorylates a variety of substrates, including regulatory proteins that modulate cell survival, metabolism, and growth. One particularly important substrate is transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Under standard conditions, TFEB translocates from the cytosol to the nucleus where it drives the expression of numerous genes involved in lysosome formation and the autophagic process. However, in the setting of chronic AKT2 activation—a scenario evident in RPE cells in dry AMD—TFEB becomes phosphorylated at specific serine residues (for example, Ser467), which results in its retention in the cytosol and subsequent inactivation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 1–5). This aberrant phosphorylation leads to reduced autophagic flux and lysosomal dysfunction, impairing the RPE’s capacity to degrade photoreceptor outer segments (POS) effectively (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 8–10).  

By selectively inhibiting AKT2, CCT128930 is hypothesized to reduce the phosphorylation of TFEB, thereby liberating it from its cytosolic sequestration and allowing its translocation into the nucleus (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 2–4). Once in the nucleus, TFEB can stimulate the transcription of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes, enhancing the degradative capacity of RPE cells through increased lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Karim et al., 2020, pp. 10–12). Structural studies of pyrrolopyrimidine inhibitors reveal that the binding of CCT128930 involves specific hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions with key amino acid residues in the ATP-binding pocket of AKT2, leading to its functional inactivation (Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5). This interaction ensures that even at low concentrations, the compound can effectively disrupt AKT2-mediated signaling cascades. The interruption of this signaling cascade is particularly important in the RPE context, where sustained AKT2 activation contributes to the accumulation of cellular debris and the formation of drusen—hallmark features of dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6). Consequently, the molecular events set in motion by CCT128930—namely, the reduction of TFEB phosphorylation and the subsequent activation of lysosomal and autophagy genes—provide a coherent therapeutic rationale for its repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD.  

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed experimental and therapeutic setting, the central expectation is that CCT128930 will inhibit AKT2-mediated TFEB phosphorylation in RPE cells, thus alleviating the cytosolic retention of TFEB and promoting its nuclear translocation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). This mechanistic modulation is anticipated to reinvigorate the transcription of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic genes that are critical for the degradation of POS—a continuous and essential process in the maintenance of retinal health. In dry AMD, the inability of RPE cells to effectively process and clear accumulated photoreceptor debris leads to the formation of drusen and subsequent retinal degeneration. By restoring TFEB activity, treatment with CCT128930 is expected to enhance lysosomal function and lead to improved clearance of these cellular wastes, thereby potentially halting or reversing the progression of disease pathology (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  

Experimental assays to confirm this expected effect would involve measuring the levels of nuclear TFEB through immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation, alongside quantitative PCR assessments for the expression of lysosome-associated genes. Enhanced autophagic flux could be monitored by evaluating markers such as LC3-II conversion and p62 degradation. Given the compound’s IC₅₀ of approximately 6–10 nM, it is anticipated that effective concentrations can be achieved in vitro at low nanomolar doses, with further adjustments made for optimized intravitreal formulations (Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, since RPE cells derived from CFH mutant models have been shown to exhibit greater dysregulation of the AKT2/TFEB signaling pathway, efficacious treatment with CCT128930 should yield measurable improvements in surrogate endpoints such as restored lysosomal enzyme activity and reduced accumulation of POS debris (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). Such outcomes would not only validate the underlying hypothesis but also establish critical proof-of-concept data to support the transition of CCT128930 into further preclinical and, eventually, clinical studies for dry AMD.  

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of CCT128930 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic, informed by a combination of robust mechanistic rationale and a well-characterized pharmacological profile derived from prior oncology research. Strengths of the candidate include its potent ATP-competitive inhibition of AKT2, evidenced by its low nanomolar IC₅₀, and its demonstrated selectivity over other kinases such as PKA, which is critical in reducing the risk of off-target effects (Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5). The molecular rationale for its use in dry AMD hinges on the role of AKT2 in promoting the phosphorylation and cytosolic retention of TFEB—a transcription factor that, when activated, orchestrates lysosomal biogenesis and the autophagic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). By reversing this phosphorylation, CCT128930 is expected to restore TFEB nuclear translocation and thereby rejuvenate the intrinsic degradation pathways within RPE cells, which are compromised in dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 2–4; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).  

However, there are notable challenges and weaknesses that warrant careful consideration. Chief among these is the historical context of CCT128930’s clinical development in oncology, where its advancement was ultimately discontinued due to off-target toxicity and suboptimal safety profiles (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40). Although intravitreal delivery is proposed to localize the drug’s effects and minimize systemic exposure, the unique architecture and sensitivity of the retina demand that comprehensive ocular toxicology studies be undertaken before clinical application. In addition, the extrapolation from cancer cell line models to RPE physiology is not trivial; the intracellular signaling milieu and compensatory mechanisms in RPE cells may differ significantly from those in proliferative tumor cells, potentially affecting the efficacy and safety of AKT2 inhibition in this new context (Yap et al., 2011, pp. 1–2; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8).  

Moreover, the efficiency of CCT128930 in achieving the desired pharmacodynamic outcome in RPE cells will depend heavily on its ability to penetrate the retinal layers and persist at effective concentrations for a sufficient duration. Although available preclinical pharmacokinetics suggest favorable CNS penetration, detailed studies focused specifically on ocular distribution, metabolic stability in vitreous humor, and clearance mechanisms are critical (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Guo et al., 2021, pp. 9–11). Additionally, inter-individual variability in disease pathology—particularly in patients with genetic predispositions such as the CFH Y402H variant—may necessitate personalized approaches or combination therapies to fully harness the compound’s therapeutic potential (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  

In the context of overall therapeutic strategy, the repurposing of CCT128930 offers a novel and mechanistically targeted approach to dry AMD—a disease area where current therapeutic options are limited. The focus on restoring autophagic and lysosomal function addresses a key pathological hallmark of dry AMD, potentially offering a disease-modifying rather than merely symptomatic intervention (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6). Nonetheless, the transition from preclinical promise to clinical reality will require a dedicated effort to optimize drug delivery, thoroughly assess safety in the ocular setting, and define the most responsive patient populations. If these challenges can be overcome, CCT128930 has the potential to be a transformative therapy for dry AMD, representing both a smart and targeted application of existing pharmacological knowledge as well as an innovative shift in treatment paradigms (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2).  

Potential Developments and Future Directions:  
A critical next step involves designing robust preclinical studies that closely mimic the clinical scenarios encountered in dry AMD. Studies should begin with in vitro investigations using primary RPE cells and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE models, particularly those harboring CFH mutations known to accentuate the dysregulation of the AKT2/TFEB pathway (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). These experiments will need to quantify key parameters such as nuclear translocation of TFEB, lysosomal gene expression, and autophagic flux using standard biomarkers (Karim et al., 2020, pp. 10–12; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). In parallel, it will be essential to develop in vivo animal models of dry AMD to assess the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of CCT128930 following intravitreal injection. Parameters such as drug retention in the vitreous, retinal penetration, and clearance rates must be rigorously evaluated to establish an optimal dosing regimen that balances efficacy with safety (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Guo et al., 2021, pp. 9–11).  

Innovative drug delivery approaches should also be explored. For example, encapsulating CCT128930 in biodegradable nanoparticles or liposomal carriers could facilitate a sustained release profile, reducing the frequency of intravitreal injections and minimizing peak-related toxicity. Such delivery systems have shown promise in improving the local bioavailability of other ocular drugs and may similarly enhance the therapeutic index of CCT128930 in the retinal environment (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Guo et al., 2021, pp. 9–11).  

Rigorously addressing the potential for off-target toxicity is another priority. Detailed in vitro and in vivo toxicity studies should monitor retinal structure and function using imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT), fundus autofluorescence, and electrophysiological evaluations (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 9–10). These evaluations will be critical to ensuring that prolonged inhibition of AKT2 does not inadvertently compromise other essential signaling pathways within the retina.  

Furthermore, the development of validated biomarkers for target engagement is crucial. Such biomarkers could include quantifiable metrics of TFEB nuclear localization, lysosomal enzyme activity, or even specific transcriptomic changes associated with enhanced autophagy. These surrogate endpoints would not only help in the preclinical assessment of drug efficacy but could also serve as early indicators of therapeutic response in clinical trials (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8).  

Translational Potential and Risk Mitigation:  
The repurposing strategy for CCT128930 necessitates a comprehensive risk mitigation framework that leverages its strong pharmacological attributes while addressing potential safety concerns. Localized intravitreal delivery offers a means to concentrate the drug’s action within the eye while minimizing systemic exposure—a critical consideration given the adverse events observed in earlier oncology trials (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). At the same time, continued medicinal chemistry efforts may yield derivatives with an improved safety profile that are even more suited to the ocular environment. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies can identify chemical modifications that retain the desired potency in AKT2 inhibition while reducing potential off-target interactions, thereby refining the therapeutic index for chronic ocular use (Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 3–5).  

In parallel, integrating robust pharmacodynamic biomarkers into preclinical and clinical studies will allow for the fine-tuning of dosing regimens and early detection of potential adverse effects. Such biomarkers could include imaging findings related to retinal morphology changes or molecular indicators of restored autophagic function in RPE cells, all of which would contribute to ensuring that the efficacy of CCT128930 is achieved without compromising retinal integrity (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6).  

Collaboration across disciplines—bringing together experts in pharmacology, ophthalmology, and drug delivery science—will be paramount for addressing the unique challenges posed by repurposing an oncology drug for ocular conditions. These interdisciplinary efforts will help design and implement the necessary preclinical studies to evaluate not only drug efficacy but also long-term safety in the delicate retinal environment.  

Regulatory Considerations:  
Repurposing CCT128930 for dry AMD will require comprehensive preclinical data that address the compound’s ocular pharmacokinetics, toxicity profiles, and immunogenicity following repeated intravitreal dosing. Given its previous clinical history in oncology, regulators will likely demand additional evidence to ensure that the risks observed in systemic administration do not extend to the ocular context (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). Early engagement with regulatory agencies is recommended to outline the repurposing strategy, propose appropriate endpoints for clinical trials, and define acceptable risk thresholds. The integration of validated biomarkers for therapeutic response and the use of advanced drug delivery platforms could also help streamline the regulatory pathway by providing robust, multidimensional evidence of both efficacy and safety (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6).  

Comparative Analysis with Other Therapeutics:  
In the landscape of treatments for age-related macular degeneration, particularly the dry form, current strategies predominantly focus on mitigating inflammation, oxidative stress, or neovascularization in the case of wet AMD. However, few therapies directly target the underlying cellular clearance deficits that characterize dry AMD. The mechanism of action of CCT128930, which centers on the inhibition of AKT2 to restore TFEB function and enhance autophagy, represents a novel approach that directly addresses the impaired lysosomal degradation essential for RPE health (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). While other candidates have been evaluated for their ability to modulate autophagy, the precise targeting of the AKT2/TFEB axis distinguishes CCT128930 from these agents and offers the possibility of a more durable, disease-modifying effect. In light of the limited efficacy of current treatments for dry AMD, a drug candidate that can substantially improve the intrinsic degradative capacity of the RPE would represent a significant advancement over existing modalities (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  

Integration with Current Treatment Paradigms and Future Research Directions:  
Given the unmet need in dry AMD—where available treatments are largely supportive rather than restorative—the integration of a molecule like CCT128930 into the clinical armamentarium holds considerable appeal. Its repurposing would represent a shift toward targeting the core pathology of RPE degradation and lysosomal dysfunction, rather than simply addressing downstream outcomes. Future research should prioritize studies that confirm the beneficial effects of AKT2 inhibition on TFEB activation in RPE cells, particularly using models that recapitulate the genetic and metabolic nuances of dry AMD. Investigations should extend from cell culture systems to animal models, examining functional endpoints such as retinal morphology, visual acuity, and markers of photoreceptor outer segment turnover (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6). Additionally, research into advanced drug delivery methods—such as encapsulation in biodegradable nanoparticles—to sustain intravitreal drug levels over time will be critical for translating the strong in vitro effects of CCT128930 into meaningful clinical outcomes (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Guo et al., 2021, pp. 9–11).  

Considerations for Dosing and Patient Selection:  
A particularly important aspect in the potential repurposing of CCT128930 is the need to define an optimal dosing regimen that achieves sustained AKT2 inhibition in the retina without compromising cellular viability. The compound’s low nanomolar potency suggests that effective concentrations may be achievable with limited drug exposure, thereby reducing the likelihood of toxicity. However, the unique pharmacokinetic properties of the eye, including the barriers to drug diffusion and the turnover rates of the vitreous humor, necessitate careful dose optimization studies in animal models. Furthermore, patient selection may play a critical role in therapeutic success. For example, individuals with genetic predispositions—such as those carrying the CFH Y402H variant—may exhibit more pronounced dysregulation of the AKT2/TFEB pathway and could therefore derive greater benefit from treatment with CCT128930. Stratifying patients based on genetic and molecular markers may help in tailoring therapies to achieve maximal therapeutic benefit (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6).  

Assessment of Potential Adverse Events:  
While the inhibition of AKT2 holds promise for restoring lysosomal function in RPE cells, it is imperative to assess potential adverse events associated with CCT128930. The compound’s history in oncology, where off-target toxicity and systemic adverse effects led to discontinuation, underscores the need for a careful reevaluation of its safety profile in an ocular setting (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Yap et al., 2011, pp. 9–10). The specific effects of sustained AKT2 inhibition on various retinal cell types—including photoreceptors, ganglion cells, and Müller glia—must be systematically investigated using both histological and functional assays. Electroretinography, imaging modalities, and molecular assessments of cellular stress markers will be essential components of any comprehensive preclinical safety evaluation. These studies will help ensure that the benefits of improved autophagic clearance are not overshadowed by unwanted disruptions of retinal homeostasis.  

Integration with Ongoing Research in the Field:  
The contemporary research focus on autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis as therapeutic targets in dry AMD aligns well with the proposed mechanism underlying CCT128930’s repurposing. Emerging studies have consistently shown that restoring lysosomal function through modulation of TFEB activity can ameliorate RPE dysfunction and reduce the progression of retinal degeneration. In this context, the targeted inhibition of AKT2 to relieve TFEB phosphorylation represents a novel and highly specific strategy that addresses a key pathological node in AMD. Collaboration between research groups working on molecular pathways in RPE cells and experts in drug delivery and clinical ophthalmology will be crucial for the successful translation of this approach. The convergence of insights from multiple disciplines serves to reinforce the potential impact of CCT128930 and encourages further exploration through well-designed preclinical studies (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 2–4).  

Conclusion and Strategic Recommendations:  
In conclusion, the repurposing of CCT128930 for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is underpinned by a robust mechanistic rationale and a comprehensive body of preclinical data derived from oncology research. Its potent and selective inhibition of AKT2—with consequent reduction in TFEB phosphorylation—offers a novel therapeutic strategy to restore lysosomal function and autophagic clearance in RPE cells, addressing a fundamental pathological mechanism in dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). While the compound’s chemical and pharmacological attributes are well documented, several challenges remain, including the need to optimize ocular delivery, establish a favorable safety profile, and verify efficacy in relevant preclinical models. A comprehensive research strategy that includes in vitro validation using genetically representative RPE models, in vivo pharmacokinetic and toxicological assessments, and the development of advanced sustained-release formulations is recommended to mitigate risks and maximize therapeutic potential (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6).  

Moreover, given the limited treatment options currently available for dry AMD, a condition where restoring RPE function could profoundly impact disease progression, advancing CCT128930 into a dedicated preclinical development program is both scientifically and clinically justified. Early-phase clinical studies, designed with a strong emphasis on biomarker-driven endpoints and safety, will be critical to establishing whether the encouraging in vitro and preclinical findings can be reproduced in patients. By carefully addressing the challenges of drug delivery and off-target toxicity, and by harnessing innovative approaches to patient stratification and treatment monitoring, CCT128930 could ultimately evolve into a transformative therapy for dry AMD. As such, its inclusion in the drug development pipeline is recommended, pending further rigorous investigation and validation of its ocular efficacy and safety profile (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8).  

Ultimately, the repurposing of CCT128930 embodies a forward-thinking strategy in drug development, leveraging established pharmacological principles and preexisting safety data from oncology to address a pressing unmet need in ophthalmology. Through a multidisciplinary approach that integrates advanced drug formulation, precise molecular targeting, and patient-specific strategies, this therapeutic candidate has the potential to restore impaired autophagic and lysosomal processes in the RPE, thereby offering a novel modality for the treatment of dry AMD. The translational journey for CCT128930 will require meticulous preclinical characterization, careful clinical trial planning, and close collaboration with regulatory agencies, but the promise of a mechanism-based intervention that targets the root cause of RPE degeneration provides a compelling impetus for further exploration (Fang et al., 2013, pp. 36–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 4–6; Adel et al., 2018b, pp. 6–8).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SHP099 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule allosteric inhibitor of the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP2 (PTPN11) discovered by Novartis through a target-biased screening paradigm that enriched for modulators of full-length, autoinhibited SHP2 and counter-selected catalytic-site binders, followed by structure-based medicinal chemistry optimization to stabilize the closed SHP2 conformation rather than engage the conserved active site (chemical identity: 6-(4-amino-4-methylpiperidin-1-yl)-3-(2,3-dichlorophenyl)pyrazin-2-amine) (PDB: 5EHR) (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kong & Long, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). In the 1.7 Å co-crystal, SHP099 occupies a central “tunnel” at the interface of the N-SH2, C-SH2, and PTP domains present only in the autoinhibited state; its aminopyrazine/amine motif forms hydrogen bonds to Arg111 and Phe113 in the SH2 linker and to Glu250 in the PTP domain, while a 2,3-dichlorophenyl moiety engages hydrophobic residues (Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, Gln495), thereby clamping the interdomain interface and disfavoring opening/activation (ligand volume ~262 Å3; tunnel ~464 Å3) (Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Biochemically, SHP099 is potent and selective (SHP2 enzymatic IC50 ≈ 0.070–0.071 µM; no detectable activity across panels of 21 phosphatases and 66 kinases, including SHP1) and translates to cellular pathway inhibition (p-ERK IC50 ≈ 0.250 µM), with high aqueous solubility, high permeability without efflux, and acceptable mouse oral exposure/bioavailability (~46%) (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kong & Long, 2022). Mechanistically, SHP099 functions as a “molecular glue” that stabilizes the closed, autoinhibited SHP2 conformation via a conformational selection mechanism; affinity is reduced for strongly activating SHP2 mutants (for example, E76K) that bias the open state, although high concentrations can re-close some mutants in vitro and in cells (Meem, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).

SHP099 belongs to the class of SHP2 “tunnel-site” (site 1) allosteric inhibitors that stabilize the autoinhibited state by engaging the N-SH2/C-SH2/PTP interdomain pocket; dual allosteric occupancy (site 1 plus a distal latch, site 2) is structurally and biochemically validated and produces cooperative inhibition when SHP099 is combined with a site-2 ligand (for example SHP244 analogs), underscoring the druggability of multiple noncatalytic surfaces on SHP2 (Fodor et al., 2018; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Discovery and SAR established that the aminopyrazine ring amine is essential (Glu250 H-bond), the 4-amino-4-methylpiperidine motif is favored over piperazines for potency, and an ortho-chlorine on the phenyl ring is critical; a representative synthesis employs Suzuki–Miyaura coupling to install the dichlorophenyl substituent on a pyrazinamine core, followed by SNAr to append the Boc-protected 4-methylpiperidin-4-amine and final acid deprotection to the free base (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-level development moved the SHP099 pharmacophore into diverse chemotypes (for example, pyrimidinones and fused bicyclic pyrazolopyrimidinones) and into clinical candidates (for example, TNO155, RMC-4630, BBP-398), reflecting translational momentum for SHP2 allosteric inhibition (Kerr et al., 2021; Tojjari et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
SHP099 established in vivo proof-of-concept for allosteric SHP2 inhibition in oncology. In an EGFR-amplified esophageal squamous carcinoma xenograft (KYSE-520), oral SHP099 produced dose-dependent pathway suppression (tumor p-ERK), antiproliferative effects, and tumor growth inhibition up to stasis at 100 mg/kg, supported by measurable exposure and oral bioavailability (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Additional preclinical efficacy includes activity in EGFR-driven xenografts and reduction of leukemic burden in FLT3-ITD–positive AML models after oral dosing, with no overt toxicity noted in those studies (Dempke et al., 2018). In glioblastoma models, SHP099 achieved brain exposure after 100 mg/kg oral dosing, reduced tumor growth and vascularity in orthotopic xenografts, and showed activity both as monotherapy and combined with temozolomide, demonstrating CNS penetration and antitumor pharmacology in mice (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-wide, SHP2 allosteric inhibitors have shown single-agent and combination efficacy in RTK/RAS/MAPK-driven tumors, have been advanced into clinical studies across multiple solid tumors, and display mechanism-consistent biomarker modulation (for example, decreased p-ERK) in preclinical models (Kerr et al., 2021; Stanford & Bottini, 2023; Tojjari et al., 2023).

Within the materials provided here, there are no reports of SHP099 (or any SHP2 allosteric inhibitor) being used in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis models, or any ocular indication; multiple reviews focus on oncology/immuno-oncology and either enumerate preclinical tumor evidence or clinical oncology programs, without ocular/retinal data (Kerr et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2020). Consequently, repurposing SHP099 for dry AMD would be a first-in-class application with no precedent in the supplied literature (Yuan et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
SHP2 is maintained in an autoinhibited state by intramolecular engagement of the N-SH2 domain with the PTP catalytic domain; engagement of SH2 domains by bis-phosphotyrosyl motifs on receptors/adaptors relieves autoinhibition, allowing both catalytic and scaffolding functions that couple receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) to RAS activation and downstream MAPK/PI3K signaling (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). SHP099 binds in a tunnel formed by the N-SH2, C-SH2, and PTP domains of autoinhibited SHP2 and locks this closed conformation: crystallography defines hydrogen bonds to Arg111 and Phe113 (SH2 linker) and Glu250 (PTP domain), and hydrophobic contacts to Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, and Gln495 that together stabilize the interface and preclude opening; pre-organization of Arg111 additionally supports a cationic–π interaction with SHP099’s dichlorophenyl ring (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Selectivity over SHP1 is rationalized structurally by differences in SH2-linker/tunnel geometry that preclude analogous Arg/Phe contacts, consistent with lack of SHP1 inhibition in broad profiling (Diop et al., 2022). Binding follows conformational selection, with lowered potency against mutants that favor the open state (for example, E76K, D61Y), though high concentrations or dual-site allosteric occupancy can re-close certain mutants and enhance inhibition (Fodor et al., 2018; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-level medicinal chemistry around SHP099 uncovered both optimization paths (for example, pyrimidinones, fused bicyclic scaffolds) and liabilities such as unexpected hERG inhibition in some derivatives and combination-dosing tolerability issues in mice, underscoring the need for careful safety pharmacology (Meem, 2022).

RPE POS phagocytosis is a ligand-directed, RTK-driven process with defined signaling architecture. Externalized phosphatidylserine on shed POS tips is opsonized (for example, by MFG-E8), engages apical αvβ5 integrin, and triggers a pathway in which MerTK (activated by Gas6 or Protein S) is essential for physiological engulfment in vivo; loss-of-function MERTK mutations in RCS rats or humans abolish POS internalization and cause rapid photoreceptor degeneration (Ghosh et al., 2024; Moran et al., 2022). At the cytoskeletal level, formation of the F-actin phagocytic cup beneath bound POS requires Rac1 activation and a concurrent decrease in RhoA/ROCK-mediated contractility; RhoA elevation blocks cup formation even when Rac1 is active, whereas ROCK inhibition is both necessary and sufficient to enable cup formation and POS internalization and can rescue engulfment and acidification in MerTK-deficient RPE ex vivo (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Mao & Finnemann, 2021). Mechanistically downstream of MerTK, Src is activated and (i) phosphorylates and activates focal adhesion kinase (FAK), recruiting the p130CAS/CRKII/DOCK180 module that activates Rac1, and (ii) phosphorylates GDP-dissociation inhibitor GDI1, promoting dissociation from Rab5 to facilitate Rab cycling needed for cup formation and early phagosome dynamics (Shelby et al., 2015). These pathways define measurable biochemical checkpoints (MerTK/Src/FAK phosphorylation, Rac1-GTP, RhoA/ROCK activity) and functional readouts (cup formation, internalization, phagolysosomal acidification) relevant to any attempt to modulate RPE phagocytosis pharmacologically (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Moran et al., 2022).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis is that SHP099 will inhibit SHP2 in RPE (biochemical IC50 ~70–75 nM), sustain MerTK phosphorylation, maintain Rac1-GTP, and thereby increase POS internalization. The supplied literature confirms that SHP099 potently and selectively inhibits SHP2 by stabilizing the autoinhibited state and blocks RTK→RAS/MAPK signaling in cells, but it does not demonstrate that SHP2 directly dephosphorylates MerTK in RPE or that SHP2 inhibition prolongs MerTK phosphorylation or increases RPE POS uptake (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). Across systems, SHP2 acts as a positive transducer linking activated RTKs to RAS/ERK signaling; SHP2 allosteric inhibition decouples upstream RTKs from RAS activation, lowering RAS-GTP and p-ERK, which is consistent with a broad attenuation of RTK-driven outputs rather than prolonged receptor phosphorylation per se (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). Within the provided ocular literature, the only experimentally demonstrated pharmacologic rescue of RPE POS uptake is acute ROCK inhibition, which operates downstream of MerTK to reduce actomyosin contractility and enable cup formation and internalization—even rescuing MerTK-deficient RPE ex vivo—whereas elevating RhoA blocks phagocytosis despite Rac1 activation (Mao & Finnemann, 2021). Thus, while SHP099 will almost certainly inhibit SHP2 in RPE if exposure is achieved, the predicted increase in POS internalization via prolonged MerTK phosphorylation and sustained Rac1-GTP is speculative and not supported by direct evidence in the materials provided here (Kerr et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2020).

If the assay readout is POS phagocytosis in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE, the mechanistic checkpoints most directly supported by the literature are: phosphorylation kinetics of MerTK and Src/FAK; Rac1-GTP elevation coincident with cup formation; RhoA/ROCK suppression; and functional measures of cup assembly, POS internalization, and phagolysosomal acidification, with a ROCK inhibitor as a validated positive control (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Mao & Finnemann, 2021; Moran et al., 2022). Ocular pharmacokinetics for SHP099 are unknown in the provided corpus; although brain exposure has been documented after oral dosing in mice, retinal/RPE exposure should not be inferred and would need to be measured for systemic or local (for example, intravitreal) dosing paradigms (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths for repurposing consideration  
- Potent, selective, and structurally validated target engagement. SHP099 is characterized at atomic resolution (PDB 5EHR) with a coherent interaction network (Arg111, Phe113, Glu250; Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, Gln495) that rationalizes potency, selectivity versus SHP1, and conformational bias, increasing confidence that SHP2 inhibition will translate biochemically in RPE if drug exposure is achieved (Diop et al., 2022; Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Drug-like properties and in vivo activity. SHP099 exhibits favorable physicochemical properties (high solubility; Caco-2 permeability without efflux), oral bioavailability (~46% in mice), dose-dependent pathway modulation in tumors, and robust xenograft efficacy; CNS exposure after oral dosing has been demonstrated in mice, indicating trans-barrier distribution is feasible with adequate exposure (Fortanet et al., 2016; Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Class-level translational experience. Multiple SHP2 allosteric inhibitors derived from the SHP099 tunnel pharmacophore have entered clinical testing across solid tumors, enabling leverage of class pharmacology, safety learning, and combination strategies if ocular repurposing proceeds (Kerr et al., 2021; Stanford & Bottini, 2023; Tojjari et al., 2023).

Key weaknesses and risks specific to dry AMD/RPE phagocytosis  
- Mechanistic gap in RPE. The premise that SHP2 dephosphorylates MerTK to terminate phagocytic signaling in RPE, and that SHP2 inhibition will prolong MerTK phosphorylation and sustain Rac1 activation, is not supported by the supplied literature; no direct data link SHP2 to MerTK regulation in RPE or demonstrate SHP099-induced increases in POS uptake (Kerr et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2020). In contrast, RhoA/ROCK suppression is a validated, decisive permissive event for cup formation/internalization and can rescue MerTK deficiency, suggesting that targeting ROCK remains a higher-confidence pharmacological route to enhance POS uptake (Mao & Finnemann, 2021).  
- Potential on-target countereffects on trophic RTK signaling. SHP2 broadly transduces RTK signals to RAS/ERK; allosteric SHP2 inhibition reduces RAS-GTP/p-ERK by disconnecting RTKs from downstream pathways, which could dampen beneficial RTK-mediated homeostatic signaling in RPE and choroid (for example, PDGFR, c-MET, IGF1R) even if MerTK phosphorylation were transiently increased, necessitating careful evaluation of RPE viability and stress responses in addition to phagocytosis endpoints (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021).  
- Ocular PK/tissue exposure unknown. There is no reported ocular distribution for SHP099 in the materials provided; CNS penetration does not ensure retinal/RPE exposure, and systemic dosing to achieve ocular levels may be limited by plasma protein binding, efflux, or tolerability, while intravitreal dosing introduces local safety and formulation challenges that would require de novo assessment (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Class liabilities and context-dependent potency. Medicinal chemistry around SHP099 identified derivatives with unexpected hERG activity and tolerability issues in some combination regimens; while not demonstrated specifically for SHP099 here, this flags a class risk requiring prospective cardiac and ocular safety pharmacology. Conformational-selection binding also means potency varies with SHP2 activation state, which is undefined in aging human RPE and could shift under inflammatory or oxidative stress present in dry AMD (Meem, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Lack of precedent in ocular models. No ocular, retinal, or RPE data for SHP099 or related allosteric SHP2 inhibitors are available in the supplied literature, increasing translational uncertainty for this repurposing (Yuan et al., 2020).

Program decision and de-risking experiments  
On the basis of the information provided, SHP099 is not yet a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD without foundational mechanistic validation in RPE. The central claim—that SHP2 inhibition prolongs MerTK phosphorylation and increases POS internalization—remains speculative in the absence of RPE data (Yuan et al., 2020). If the team elects to explore this hypothesis, a gated, mechanism-first workplan is advised:

- Define pathway engagement in RPE. Confirm SHP2 expression and activation state during phagocytosis in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE; assess whether SHP2 associates with MerTK/Src/FAK complexes upon POS challenge by co-immunoprecipitation or proximity assays (Shelby et al., 2015).  
- Biochemical time-courses ± SHP099. Quantify MerTK phosphorylation kinetics, Src and FAK activation, Rac1-GTP, and RhoA/ROCK activity after POS addition with a SHP099 concentration range bracketing its biochemical potency in enzyme assays; benchmark effect sizes against a ROCK inhibitor positive control, which is validated to rescue phagocytosis even in MerTK-deficient contexts (Mao & Finnemann, 2021).  
- Functional phagocytosis assays. Measure POS binding, F-actin cup formation, internalization, and phagolysosomal acidification under the same conditions, using established assays and timepoints aligned to the diurnal phagocytic peak where applicable (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Moran et al., 2022).  
- Ocular PK and safety. Establish retinal/RPE exposure after systemic and (if considered) intravitreal dosing, and perform ocular tolerability assessments (inflammation, ERG, histopathology) to identify potential on- or off-target liabilities early, mindful of class risks noted in optimization campaigns (Meem, 2022; Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).

In summary, SHP099 is a potent, selective, and well-characterized SHP2 allosteric inhibitor with robust oncology pharmacology and drug-like properties, but the case for repurposing to dry AMD by enhancing RPE POS phagocytosis is unsubstantiated in the provided literature and carries meaningful mechanistic and translational risks. Prioritizing direct RPE mechanistic studies and ocular PK/tolerability before any disease-model investment is the appropriate next step; in parallel, ROCK pathway modulation remains the most evidence-backed pharmacologic lever to augment phagocytosis in this system and should serve as a positive control and a benchmark for effect size (Fortanet et al., 2016; Mao & Finnemann, 2021; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).
