Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Brexpiprazole is a synthetic, orally available fifth‐generation antipsychotic developed by Otsuka Pharmaceutical that belongs to the class of serotonin–dopamine activity modulators (SDAMs). It was discovered and developed as an improvement over earlier dopamine partial agonists in order to achieve balanced modulation of neurotransmission. Chemically, brexpiprazole was designed as a dihydrocarbostyril derivative that retains partial agonistic properties at dopamine D₂ receptors while simultaneously exhibiting potent partial agonism at serotonin 5-HT₁A receptors and antagonism at serotonin 5-HT₂A receptors (Das et al., 2016). This balanced receptor profile has been exploited primarily for psychiatric indications, but the receptor distribution of serotonin receptors is not limited to neuronal tissues. In particular, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) expresses several serotonin receptor subtypes, and there is compelling biochemical evidence that serotonergic signaling influences inflammatory gene expression and cellular homeostasis in these cells (Biswal et al., 2015). As such, brexpiprazole’s well‐defined receptor interactions position it as a promising candidate to modulate pathological pathways in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
Brexpiprazole has an established history for its use in central nervous system disorders. It has been approved for the treatment of schizophrenia and as an adjunct therapy in major depressive disorder owing to its favorable safety and tolerability profiles, which include a low risk of extrapyramidal side effects and modest metabolic liabilities (Das et al., 2016; Fabre et al., 2022). To date, however, no clinical trials or preclinical studies have directly examined brexpiprazole for the treatment of retinal degenerative conditions such as dry AMD. Nevertheless, multiple studies have investigated the therapeutic potential of 5-HT₁A receptor agonists in retinal models. For example, research utilizing 8-OH-DPAT—a prototypical 5-HT₁A agonist—demonstrated significant antioxidant protection in RPE cells, reduction in oxidative stress markers, and preservation of retinal architecture under conditions of mitochondrial oxidative stress (Biswal et al., 2015). Other compounds with selective 5-HT₁A agonist properties, such as tandospirone, have been evaluated in retinal models, albeit with mixed clinical outcomes (Buschini et al., 2015). This preclinical precedence establishes an indirect rationale for repurposing brexpiprazole in dry AMD even if direct ocular applications have not been previously explored.

Mechanism of Action:  
Brexpiprazole exerts its pharmacological effects primarily through dual modulation of serotonergic receptors. Its partial agonism at 5-HT₁A receptors, with reported potency in the low nanomolar range (EC₅₀ ~ 5 nM as hypothesized), is thought to trigger intracellular cascades that promote cellular survival and antioxidant defenses. Activation of the 5-HT₁A receptor in other tissues has been associated with upregulation of key antioxidant enzymes—including metallothionein-1 (MT-1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NADPH quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NqO1), catalase, and superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1)—thereby mitigating oxidative stress and reducing mitochondrial damage (Biswal et al., 2015). In RPE cells—the cell type critical for photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance—the 5-HT₁A receptor is endogenously expressed, and its activation has been linked to attenuation of inflammatory signaling. Preclinical studies using other 5-HT₁A agonists in ARPE-19 cells have shown reductions in oxidative stress markers and inflammatory mediators, as well as preservation of tight junction proteins (Biswal et al., 2015).

Simultaneously, brexpiprazole’s antagonism at 5-HT₂A receptors may complement these effects by further modulating inflammatory responses. Blockade of 5-HT₂A receptors has been associated with reduced microglial activation and decreased complement deposition in the outer retina, contributing to neuroprotection in models of retinal degeneration (Biswal et al., 2015; Das et al., 2016). This dual receptor effect is proposed to result in an overall anti-inflammatory microenvironment in the RPE, which is crucial because chronic inflammation is a key pathological feature in dry AMD. Moreover, the compound’s modulation of serotonergic signaling may indirectly support the maintenance of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, which are essential for the normal clearance of POS (Biswal et al., 2015). Although direct studies with brexpiprazole in RPE cells are lacking, these mechanistic insights derived from similar 5-HT₁A agonists underpin the hypothesis that brexpiprazole could reduce production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6 and TNF-α) and restore normal phagocytic and lysosomal function (Biswal et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
In an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells or isolated RPE cells under conditions of complement-induced stress, brexpiprazole is expected to act by modulating serotonergic receptor signaling to yield a multi-faceted protective effect. Specifically, its 5-HT₁A agonism should trigger intracellular survival pathways that result in the upregulation of antioxidant defenses analogous to the responses observed with 8-OH-DPAT in similar models (Biswal et al., 2015). This effect is anticipated to lead to a reduction in oxidative stress markers, such as 8-OH-deoxyguanosine or nitrotyrosine adducts, which are typically elevated in conditions of mitochondrial oxidative injury (Biswal et al., 2015).

Additionally, brexpiprazole is hypothesized to reduce the expression of key pro-inflammatory cytokines—specifically IL-6 and TNF-α—through receptor-mediated modulation of inflammatory signaling cascades. In a cell culture model where RPE cells are exposed to oxidative and complement-mediated insults, a drop in these cytokine levels would be indicative of an amelioration of stress-induced inflammatory responses (Biswal et al., 2015; Wright & Ambati, 2016). This anti-inflammatory effect is critical because uncontrolled inflammation not only perpetuates oxidative damage but also disrupts the barrier and phagocytic functions of the RPE.

Furthermore, the candidate is expected to preserve or restore the expression of MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase crucial for the phagocytosis of POS, as well as cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease necessary for the degradation of internalized material (Biswal et al., 2015; Fischer, 2016). Successful maintenance of these proteins would directly support the clearance functions of RPE cells, an essential element for retinal homeostasis that is compromised in dry AMD. This improved phagocytic capacity, coupled with reduced cytokine production, would likely result in overall preservation of RPE structure and function, as reflected in enhanced visual function in preclinical models (Biswal et al., 2015).

Moreover, although the clinical studies of other serotonergic compounds such as tandospirone have yielded mixed results—with at least one phase III trial for geographic atrophy being discontinued due to lack of efficacy (Buschini et al., 2015)—the favorable pharmacokinetic properties and established safety profile of brexpiprazole in other indications provide a strong rationale for its repurposing, particularly if its ocular penetration can be demonstrated in relevant preclinical models (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation:  
Brexpiprazole offers several attractive strengths as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its dual mechanism—partial agonism at 5-HT₁A receptors paired with antagonism at 5-HT₂A receptors—is well aligned with the emerging understanding of how serotonergic signaling influences retinal cell survival, oxidative stress, and inflammation (Biswal et al., 2015). The wealth of preclinical evidence supporting the role of 5-HT₁A receptor activation in reducing oxidative damage and preserving RPE function under stress conditions provides a sound mechanistic basis for expecting similar protective effects from brexpiprazole. In addition, the targeting of phagocytic receptor expression (i.e., MERTK) and lysosomal enzymes (i.e., cathepsin D) represents a novel strategy to address one of the fundamental dysfunctions in dry AMD: impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (Biswal et al., 2015).

Brexpiprazole’s established safety profile and pharmacokinetics in psychiatric populations further underscore its potential for repurposing. Its high oral bioavailability and documented tolerability in long-term studies, along with evidence that similar compounds can penetrate ocular tissues when administered systemically, add to the candidate’s appeal (Das et al., 2016; Fabre et al., 2022). This is particularly relevant given the chronic nature of dry AMD and the need for therapies that can be safely administered over extended periods.

However, several significant weaknesses and gaps warrant cautious consideration. First, direct evidence linking brexpiprazole to improved RPE function—specifically, its effects on inflammatory signaling markers IL-6 and TNF-α, and on the preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression—remains theoretical and extrapolated from studies using other 5-HT₁A agonists like 8-OH-DPAT (Biswal et al., 2015). This means that while the underlying mechanistic hypothesis is plausible, there is a pressing need for targeted in vitro and in vivo studies focused on brexpiprazole in ocular models. In particular, experiments using ARPE-19 cells under conditions of oxidative or complement-induced stress must be conducted to confirm that brexpiprazole can indeed modulate cytokine levels and restore phagocytic function in these cells.

Another shortcoming is the uncertainty regarding ocular penetration. Although the systemic administration of 5-HT₁A agonists in animal models has led to beneficial retinal outcomes (Biswal et al., 2015), brexpiprazole’s distribution into ocular tissues has not been directly evaluated. It is essential to ascertain the extent to which brexpiprazole reaches the RPE at therapeutically relevant concentrations, particularly given that dosage regimens for psychiatric conditions may not be directly translatable to ocular therapy (Biswal et al., 2015).

Furthermore, while the anti-inflammatory hypothesis is supported by the general role of serotonergic signaling in RPE cells, the direct measurement of inflammatory cytokines and downstream phagocytic markers in response to brexpiprazole treatment remains to be demonstrated. Given that earlier clinical attempts using tandospirone for AMD were unsuccessful (Buschini et al., 2015), there is a need to critically assess whether brexpiprazole’s receptor profile confers advantages that overcome the limitations observed with other 5-HT₁A agonists. Additionally, potential off-target effects in the ocular environment—such as those arising from modulation of other receptor systems—must be thoroughly evaluated.

In summary, brexpiprazole presents a scientifically sound and innovative approach to the treatment of dry AMD by virtue of its serotonergic receptor modulation. Its dual action on 5-HT₁A and 5-HT₂A receptors is supported by a robust body of preclinical evidence indicating that 5-HT₁A receptor activation can reduce oxidative stress and inflammation in RPE cells, while also preserving essential functions like POS clearance (Biswal et al., 2015). The candidate’s excellent safety profile in psychiatric applications and potential for systemic administration further enhance its appeal. Nevertheless, the absence of direct experimental data linking brexpiprazole to improved phagocytosis, reduced IL-6 and TNF-α production, and maintained lysosomal enzyme expression in RPE cells represents a critical gap that must be addressed. As such, while the repurposing of brexpiprazole for dry AMD holds promise, a series of preclinical experiments—encompassing in vitro ARPE-19 cell assays, in vivo ocular pharmacokinetic studies, and efficacy models of retinal degeneration—are required before progressing to clinical trials. Overall, given the mechanistic rationale and the encouraging safety and pharmacological characteristics of brexpiprazole, further research is justified to validate its application in dry AMD, provided that the aforementioned knowledge gaps are systematically addressed (Das et al., 2016; Biswal et al., 2015).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Sulforaphane is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate that is principally derived from cruciferous vegetables, notably broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and cabbage (Dutta et al., 2023; Lagunas-Rangel, 2024). In its natural state, sulforaphane is present as its glucosinolate precursor, glucoraphanin, which is enzymatically converted to the active form upon tissue disruption by the enzyme myrosinase (Habtemariam, 2024; Mangla et al., 2021). This conversion is a well‐established biochemical process that occurs during food processing or mastication, and it provides the basis for sulforaphane’s identification as a nutraceutical with significant potential in various disease contexts (Houghton, 2019; Lagunas-Rangel, 2024). Sulforaphane belongs to the isothiocyanate class of compounds, a group known for their prominent antioxidant, anti‐inflammatory, and anticancer activities (Dutta et al., 2023; Habtemariam, 2024). Its discovery and subsequent characterization have positioned it as a compound of interest not only in cancer chemoprevention but also in other chronic disease models including neurodegenerative conditions and ocular pathologies (Ordonez et al., 2021; Habtemariam, 2024). The current therapeutic candidate—in this case, Sulforaphane (Nrf2 activator; LKT Laboratories Cat. No. S8044)—is being evaluated for its potential to modulate specific cellular pathways implicated in the pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly its ability to activate the Nrf2 transcription factor in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells at a proposed concentration of 5 µM (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Sulforaphane’s therapeutic history is extensive and spans multiple domains, primarily due to its ability to induce phase II detoxification enzymes and to modulate oxidative stress responses at the cellular level. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its efficacy in inducing apoptosis and mitigating cancer cell proliferation through the modulation of key signaling pathways (Dutta et al., 2023; Tortorella et al., 2015). In addition to its anticancer properties, sulforaphane has been evaluated in models of neurodegeneration, where it has been shown to confer neuroprotection by alleviating oxidative stress and inflammation—a property that is particularly relevant to retinal diseases such as AMD (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024). In ocular research, various investigations using in vitro and in vivo models have highlighted sulforaphane’s capacity to activate the Nrf2 pathway in retinal cells, leading to enhanced antioxidant enzyme expression and reduced oxidative damage (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). Notably, studies employing retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, such as ARPE-19 cells, have documented protective effects of sulforaphane against oxidative insult, where enhanced expression of genes such as heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), glutathione peroxidase (GPX), and glutamate-cysteine ligase modulatory subunit (GCLM) has been observed (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Kubo et al., 2017). Although sulforaphane has been predominantly explored in the context of cancer chemoprevention and neuroprotection, its application in treating ocular conditions such as dry AMD is emerging. Early studies suggest that sulforaphane might reduce lipofuscin accumulation and rescue lysosomal pH abnormalities in A2E-loaded RPE cells, which are hallmark features of dry AMD pathogenesis (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). Safety profiles established through both in vitro studies and limited clinical trials indicate that sulforaphane is generally well-tolerated, with few adverse effects even upon oral administration, thereby rendering it a promising agent for repurposing in ocular disorders (Ordonez et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic actions of sulforaphane are mediated primarily through the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, a central regulator of antioxidant defense mechanisms. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytosol by its inhibitory partner, Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1), which facilitates its ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Mangla et al., 2021). Sulforaphane exerts its effect by covalently modifying critical cysteine residues on KEAP1, thereby disrupting the KEAP1-Nrf2 complex. This modification impedes Nrf2 degradation and permits its rapid translocation into the nucleus (Habtemariam, 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small musculoaponeurotic fibrosarcoma (sMaf) proteins and binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoter regions of a multitude of genes, culminating in the transcriptional activation of phase II detoxification enzymes such as HO-1, GPX, and GCLM (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2024; Hyttinen et al., 2019). In addition to enhancing the antioxidant capacity of the cell, activation of Nrf2 by sulforaphane has been associated with the upregulation of genes implicated in the regulation of autophagy and lysosomal function (Chang et al., 2020; Bergandi et al., 2024). This is particularly salient in the context of RPE biology, where proper lysosomal function is critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and the prevention of lipofuscin accumulation. Impaired degradation pathways in RPE cells lead to cellular stress and contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). Moreover, sulforaphane’s ability to reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine production through suppression of mediators like intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) further supports its cytoprotective role in the retina (Habtemariam, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). The proposed concentration of 5 µM in vitro is supported by studies indicating that such a dose is sufficient to robustly activate Nrf2, thereby inducing an antioxidant response without eliciting toxicity in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). This multifaceted mechanism—encompassing enhanced transcription of antioxidant defense genes, promotion of autophagy, and attenuation of inflammatory signaling—underpins the rationale for deploying sulforaphane as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Expected Effect:  
Within the iPSC-derived RPE model of dry AMD, the administration of sulforaphane at 5 µM is hypothesized to yield several beneficial outcomes. First, by engaging the Nrf2 signaling pathway, sulforaphane is expected to increase the transcription of key antioxidant genes such as GCLM, GPX, and HO-1 (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Kubo et al., 2017). This upregulation will enhance the cellular capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS), thereby mitigating oxidative stress—a well-known contributor to RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2024). Second, the improved activation of Nrf2 is anticipated to restore autophagy processes and lysosomal enzyme function within RPE cells, facilitating more efficient degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and the removal of toxic byproducts such as lipofuscin (Chang et al., 2020; Bergandi et al., 2024). A2E, a major bisretinoid component of lipofuscin, has been implicated in the disruption of lysosomal pH and function; therefore, by rescuing lysosomal acidity and enhancing enzymatic activity, sulforaphane could support the clearance of A2E aggregates and related debris (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Third, given its anti-inflammatory attributes, sulforaphane is expected to downregulate cytokine expression and other inflammatory mediators, thus reducing the chronic inflammatory state that exacerbates RPE damage in dry AMD (Habtemariam, 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). On a molecular level, the improved phagocytic function of RPE cells, achieved through the normalization of lysosomal and autophagic pathways, is critical for maintaining retinal integrity and function since efficient POS degradation is necessary for visual cycle homeostasis (Chang et al., 2020; Kubo et al., 2017). Furthermore, the favorable safety profile observed in preclinical studies—coupled with evidence of minimal toxicity even at higher concentrations—supports the use of sulforaphane at the proposed dose, making it a mechanistically specific strategy to alleviate oxidative and lysosomal stress in dry AMD models (Ordonez et al., 2021; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Collectively, the expected effects at the molecular, cellular, and functional levels converge on the hypothesis that sulforaphane will both preserve RPE cell viability and enhance cellular clearance mechanisms, thereby countering key pathological features of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Sulforaphane represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its multifaceted mechanism of action, which directly targets key pathological processes involved in retinal degeneration. One of its primary strengths lies in its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway; this leads to a comprehensive antioxidant response by upregulating detoxification and cytoprotective genes that are essential for neutralizing ROS and ameliorating oxidative stress in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Kubo et al., 2017). The capacity to rescue lysosomal function and promote autophagy is another major advantage, as it addresses the abnormal accumulation of lipofuscin—a hallmark of dry AMD—by restoring the degradation and recycling of photoreceptor outer segments (Chang et al., 2020; Bergandi et al., 2024). Additionally, sulforaphane’s documented anti-inflammatory effects further enhance its therapeutic potential by reducing the expression of inflammatory cytokines that contribute to retinal damage (Habtemariam, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). The favorable safety profile noted in various studies reinforces the viability of repurposing sulforaphane, particularly since clinical trials in other indications have demonstrated minimal systemic toxicity and good tolerability (Ordonez et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

Despite these strengths, several challenges must be acknowledged. A key limitation associated with sulforaphane is its inherently low water solubility and bioavailability, which pose significant obstacles for achieving therapeutic concentrations at the target site, especially in ocular tissues where the blood–ocular barriers prevent easy drug penetration (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Current formulations may result in a high first-pass effect and limited tissue penetration upon systemic administration. This challenge necessitates the exploration of novel delivery systems—such as nanoformulations, liposomes, or other topical ocular delivery strategies—that can enhance the stability and bioavailability of sulforaphane (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Furthermore, while preclinical data in cell culture models and animal studies are promising, there remains an evidence gap regarding the efficacy of sulforaphane in human subjects with dry AMD. Robust clinical trials designed to establish dose-response relationships, optimal administration routes, and long-term safety profiles are essential before the compound can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic intervention for dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2024).

Another area of concern is the scalability and reproducibility of the effect. Variability in bioactivity may arise due to differences in the extraction or synthesis of sulforaphane, as the compound’s activity greatly depends on its purity, the presence of specific enantiomers, and the method of formulation (Lagunas-Rangel, 2024; Tortorella et al., 2015). This variability could potentially influence both the efficacy and safety outcomes in clinical applications. The current hypothesis proposes that a 5 µM concentration is effective for activating Nrf2 in RPE cells; however, translating this concentration from an in vitro model to an in vivo setting presents additional challenges. The effective dose in the retina might differ substantially due to differences in drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion, which must be carefully optimized through pharmacokinetic studies (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Kubo et al., 2017).

In summary, sulforaphane holds compelling potential as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD owing to its well-defined mechanism of action, which encompasses antioxidant activation via Nrf2, restoration of lysosomal and autophagic function, and anti-inflammatory effects. These mechanisms directly target the cellular dysfunctions that underlie dry AMD pathology—including oxidative damage, impaired POS degradation, and chronic inflammation—and thus position sulforaphane as a mechanistically specific strategy to ameliorate disease progression (Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). The primary strengths of sulforaphane are its natural origin, its extensive preclinical validation across various disease models, and its capacity to modulate multiple cellular protective pathways simultaneously. However, weaknesses such as poor bioavailability, formulation challenges, and a current lack of definitive clinical data in the context of AMD temper its immediate translational readiness (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024).

To optimize the clinical translation of sulforaphane for dry AMD, future research directions should include:  
1. The development and validation of advanced drug delivery systems tailored for ocular tissues that can overcome the limitations posed by the blood–ocular barrier and enhance the drug’s bioavailability.  
2. Comprehensive pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies in animal models and early-phase clinical trials to determine the optimal dosing regimen that achieves therapeutic efficacy in the retina without compromising safety.  
3. Detailed investigations into the long-term effects of sulforaphane on retinal structure and function, including its impact on photoreceptor survival, RPE cell integrity, and overall visual performance.  
4. Comparative studies to evaluate sulforaphane’s efficacy relative to existing antioxidant and anti-inflammatory therapies in dry AMD, in order to establish its potential niche within the therapeutic landscape.  

Overall, while significant work remains to be done, sulforaphane exhibits a compelling mechanistic rationale and a promising preclinical profile that justify further investigation as a repurposed therapeutic agent for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its ability to activate Nrf2, boost antioxidant defenses, restore autophagy and lysosomal function, and reduce inflammatory mediators provides a multi-pronged approach to address the complex pathology of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). If formulation and delivery challenges can be effectively overcome, sulforaphane may well represent a viable and innovative strategy to preserve retinal health and counteract the progressive degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Habtemariam, 2024).

In conclusion, the current body of evidence from biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical studies supports the hypothesis that sulforaphane can enhance Nrf2 activation in RPE cells and improve antioxidant and lysosomal function, thereby potentially alleviating key pathological features of dry AMD. Given its extensive therapeutic history, well-characterized mechanism of action, and favorable safety profile, sulforaphane is a strong candidate deserving further rigorous evaluation and development. Nonetheless, targeted efforts to address its formulation and bioavailability limitations will be critical in shaping its future as a clinically effective treatment for dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab is a recombinant, humanized monoclonal IgG kappa antibody that specifically binds complement component C5 and prevents its proteolytic activation into C5a and C5b, thereby blocking terminal pathway activity and membrane attack complex (MAC; C5b-9) assembly while leaving upstream C3-dependent functions largely intact (for example, opsonization and immune-complex handling) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; West et al., 2024). It was discovered by screening large panels of murine anti-human C5 monoclonals for potent inhibition of C5 activation and terminal complement–mediated hemolysis; the parental murine antibody (5G1.1) was then humanized by CDR grafting into human germline frameworks and engineered to use a hybrid IgG2/IgG4 heavy-chain constant region to minimize Fcγ receptor binding and classical-pathway activation (reducing effector functions that could confound terminal pathway blockade) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009). Eculizumab binds human C5 with very high affinity (Kd approximately 120 pM) and sterically prevents convertase engagement with the MG7 domain of C5; epitope mapping identifies residues in the MG7 domain (including the KSSKC motif around Arg885) critical for binding, and Arg885His/Cys polymorphisms have been linked to clinical non-responsiveness in some patients, consistent with the structural epitope (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

As a drug class, complement inhibitors have been deployed to treat diseases driven by complement dysregulation, with C5 blockade representing a terminal-pathway strategy that ablates C5a signaling and MAC-mediated cytolysis while preserving many proximal complement functions; eculizumab was the first complement inhibitor approved for clinical use and catalyzed broad clinical development of C5, C3, and alternative pathway–targeted agents across hematology, nephrology, neurology, and, more recently, ophthalmology (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Eculizumab is administered intravenously, exhibits a long serum half-life (~272 ± 82 hours), a limited volume of distribution consistent with an intravascularly confined antibody, and shows pharmacodynamic correlation between serum trough concentrations and blockade of hemolytic activity; vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis is required due to increased susceptibility when terminal complement is inhibited (Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Within ophthalmology, complement activation products and MAC deposition have been implicated in AMD pathogenesis, motivating clinical trials of complement inhibitors including C5-directed agents; eculizumab has been formally evaluated in a randomized phase 2 setting for non-exudative AMD (geographic atrophy and drusen cohorts) via systemic administration (Kassa et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Halawa et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
Eculizumab has an extensive clinical record in systemic complement-mediated disorders. It revolutionized therapy for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), where it reduces intravascular hemolysis, decreases transfusion requirements, and improves quality of life; it is also approved for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and for neurologic autoimmune indications including anti–acetylcholine receptor–positive generalized myasthenia gravis and aquaporin-4–positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Early clinical pharmacology in PNH demonstrated that an induction regimen of 600 mg weekly for four weeks followed by 900 mg every other week maintained near-complete terminal pathway blockade and significantly reduced hemolysis and transfusion needs; these dosing principles align with its long half-life and the concentration dependence of hemolytic inhibition (Hillmen et al., 2004; Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012). Despite robust control of intravascular hemolysis, residual extravascular hemolysis can persist because C3 opsonization is not prevented by C5 inhibition, illustrating an important mechanistic limitation of terminal-pathway agents (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; West et al., 2024).

The drug’s safety profile is dominated by infection risk with encapsulated organisms—particularly meningococcal disease—necessitating vaccination; otherwise, eculizumab has shown acceptable tolerability across long-term use, with clinical programs incorporating monitoring of functional complement activity (CH50) to confirm pharmacodynamic blockade and dose adequacy (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009; Eskandary et al., 2016). Mechanistically relevant sources also report pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic complexities: high-affinity binding at acidic endosomal pH encourages recycling of eculizumab:C5 complexes by FcRn, leading to accumulation of total C5 bound to the drug in circulation; next-generation engineering in ravulizumab introduced pH-dependent release to minimize cargo recycling and extend dosing intervals (Schmidt & Smith, 2023).

In ophthalmology, eculizumab has been investigated as a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD. The COMPLETE study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), a single-center, randomized, double-masked phase 2 trial, evaluated intravenous eculizumab in two cohorts: geographic atrophy (GA) and intermediate AMD with high-risk drusen; patients were randomized 2:1 to eculizumab or saline over 24 weeks with follow-up to 52 weeks (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the GA cohort (n = 30 study eyes), eculizumab did not reduce GA enlargement versus placebo at 26 or 52 weeks (square-root–transformed growth 0.19 ± 0.12 mm vs. 0.18 ± 0.15 mm at 26 weeks, P = 0.96; 0.37 ± 0.22 mm vs. 0.37 ± 0.21 mm at 52 weeks, P = 0.93), and no drug-related adverse events were reported (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the drusen cohort (n = 30 total participants; 20 active, 10 placebo), eculizumab failed to meet the prespecified primary endpoint of a ≥ 50% reduction in drusen cube-root volume at 26 weeks; none of 18 treated eyes achieved this threshold, while one placebo eye did (10%; P = 0.36), and there was no detectable difference in mean drusen growth between arms through 26–52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014). Trial conduct included meningococcal vaccination and careful multimodal imaging; retention was high with 28/30 completing 52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). Independent evidence syntheses judged the certainty of evidence as low to very low due to small sample size, imprecision, and some risk of bias; overall, systemic eculizumab “may have made little to no difference” in BCVA and GA lesion growth in the available cohort (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistically similar C5-directed agents have not shown positive phase 2 outcomes in GA when administered systemically or intravitreally (e.g., LFG316 failed in phase 2), whereas intravitreal C5 inhibition with avacincaptad pegol progressed to later-phase testing and regulatory review, suggesting that drug, route, and pharmacology may be important determinants of outcome; by contrast, intravitreal C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) demonstrated efficacy and has been approved for GA, underscoring the translational relevance of target selection and ocular delivery (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024). Multiple reviews conclude that systemic eculizumab is no longer in development for AMD and highlight delivery and mechanistic concerns as likely contributors to the negative results (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, eculizumab targets the MG7 domain of C5 and sterically prevents formation of the C5 convertase–substrate complex, thereby inhibiting the cleavage of C5 into the potent anaphylatoxin C5a and C5b, which nucleates membrane attack complex assembly with C6–C9 (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Rother et al., 2007). Structural analysis of an eculizumab Fab bound to C5 resolved at 4.2 Å shows that five CDRs form the principal interface with MG7; mutational scanning of CDR residues identifies a network of contacts necessary for high-affinity binding, and kinetic assays confirm that these interactions prevent complement-mediated hemolysis in vitro (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016). The epitope includes residues near Arg885, and clinical resistance due to Arg885His/Cys substitutions in C5 provides orthogonal validation of the binding site (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

Pharmacodynamically, eculizumab ablates terminal pathway function: it suppresses CH50 to near zero when trough serum concentrations exceed ~35 μg/mL; however, because proximal C3 activation continues, C3b deposition and downstream opsonins accumulate on surfaces, which can drive extravascular clearance and generate residual pathology even under complete C5 blockade in appropriate disease contexts (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). Additional mechanisms can undermine complete terminal pathway control: (1) during intense proximal activation, densely opsonized surfaces can support C5 activation by convertases in ways that partially bypass classical C5 convertase assembly or even promote conformational C5 activation on surface C3b clusters; such context-dependent activation can manifest as “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” despite apparently adequate free drug levels, and has been reported in clinical settings as residual terminal-pathway activity and elevated sC5b-9 in some patients (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). (2) Eculizumab binds C5 with high affinity at both neutral and mildly acidic pH, allowing FcRn to recycle eculizumab:C5 complexes and potentially alter antigen disposition; ravulizumab’s pH-dependent binding was engineered to release C5 in endosomes and improve pharmacokinetics by avoiding cargo recycling (Schmidt & Smith, 2023). These features are germane to dose selection, monitoring, and potential resistance or escape during strong complement activation.

Rationale for C5 inhibition in AMD rests on abundant mechanistic and histopathological evidence that C5-derived effectors and MAC participate in retinal/choroidal injury. C5a is detected in drusen and acts as a chemotactic and proinflammatory mediator capable of inducing VEGF expression from retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, while C5b initiates MAC assembly; MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris increases with aging and is elevated in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019). Sub-lytic and lytic MAC on choroidal endothelium causes cell injury and can trigger surviving endothelial cells to upregulate VEGF and matrix metalloproteinases, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic injury and pro-angiogenic remodeling; complement regulatory proteins such as CD59 are natural inhibitors of MAC formation and their dysfunction or insufficiency can predispose to damage (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2021). Complement dysregulation in AMD further includes genetic risk (e.g., CFH variants) and evidence of alternative pathway activation in ocular tissues, suggesting both proximal and terminal effector involvement in disease biology (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Importantly, proximal inhibition at C3 has shown the capacity to restore lysosomal function and reduce sub-RPE drusen-like deposits in human iPSC-derived RPE models carrying the high-risk CFH Y402H variant by reducing C3 turnover and lowering downstream MAC (C5b-9) localization at lysosomes; in this system, a compstatin analogue (Cp40) suppressed C3b and MAC deposition and reversed lysosomal abnormalities, whereas direct C5 inhibition has not been shown in this model to rescue lysosomal function, and clinical C5 blockade has failed in GA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). These data reinforce that while terminal pathway effectors are present and likely pathogenic in AMD, distal blockade at C5 does not necessarily address upstream complement turnover that drives intracellular lysosomal stress in RPE, and proximal intervention may be required to normalize cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
The hypothesis proposes that high-affinity C5 blockade with eculizumab will prevent MAC assembly on RPE, thereby reducing sub-RPE deposit–driven lysosomal stress and indirectly supporting photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis in dry AMD. Mechanistically, preventing C5 cleavage would abrogate both C5a signaling and C5b-dependent MAC formation; given the documented presence of C5a in drusen and increased MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane/choriocapillaris with age and AMD, terminal pathway inhibition is expected to reduce MAC-mediated endothelial and RPE injury, dampen MAC-induced VEGF/MMP signaling, and potentially mitigate inflammation (Kassa et al., 2019). In principle, if MAC-driven lysosomal injury contributes to RPE dysfunction, C5 inhibition could reduce new MAC deposition at the RPE surface and limit subsequent endocytosis of MAC into lysosomes, thereby lowering lysosomal burden (Park et al., 2021).

However, two key bodies of evidence temper this expectation. First, clinical testing of systemic eculizumab in GA and intermediate AMD failed to show benefit on primary anatomical endpoints (GA growth and OCT drusen volume) through 26–52 weeks, despite established systemic pharmacodynamic blockade; these negative outcomes argue that either (a) terminal pathway activity at C5 is not the principal driver of lesion growth/drusen regression during the studied disease stages/time horizon, or (b) pharmacokinetic compartmentalization limited ocular target engagement after intravenous dosing (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Filho et al., 2014). Reviews explicitly highlight the compartment barrier problem—systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina or sub-RPE space due to the blood–retina/Bruch’s membrane barriers and large molecular size—and note that eculizumab exposure shorter than six months is unlikely to show benefit in slowly progressive GA, compounding interpretation (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Second, cellular models directly linking complement dysregulation to lysosomal failure in high-risk AMD RPE show that upstream C3 inhibition, not terminal C5 blockade, restores lysosomal function and reduces deposit formation; this suggests that intralysosomal stress is driven by continuous C3 turnover and opsonization rather than MAC alone, and that distal C5 blockade may be insufficient to normalize these processes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Consequently, POS phagocytosis metrics may improve only marginally or not at all if the dominant insult is proximal complement turnover rather than MAC-mediated damage. The clinical failure to slow GA growth or reduce drusen volume with systemic eculizumab supports the inference that target engagement at C5, via the tested route and schedule, did not translate into macroscopic anatomical benefit in human AMD eyes within one year (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).

If eculizumab were to be tested in vitro on human RPE, appropriate readouts would include: surface and intracellular MAC (C5b-9) quantification, lysosomal number/size and membrane integrity (e.g., LAMP2, Galectin-8), Cathepsin D activity, autophagic flux, and POS degradation kinetics; concomitant measurement of upstream C3b/iC3b/C3d deposition would be essential to interpret whether C5 inhibition is affecting the dominant pathogenic pathway in the assay (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In vivo, ocular pharmacokinetic considerations dominate: intravitreal administration delivers drug to the retina and sub-RPE space but is not reported for eculizumab in the provided context and would carry different safety and dosing constraints; systemic dosing faces blood–retina barrier limitations that likely constrained ocular target engagement in COMPLETE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Notably, nearly all complement inhibitors that have shown anatomical effects in GA have been delivered intravitreally, underscoring the importance of route of administration for ocular diseases (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic rationale: C5a and MAC are present in AMD-relevant tissues; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD and can drive endothelial injury, VEGF/MMP upregulation, and potentially RPE dysfunction; blocking C5 should diminish these terminal effector signals (Kassa et al., 2019; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Potent, well-characterized biologic: Eculizumab binds human C5 with picomolar affinity, has a well-defined structural epitope in the MG7 domain, and reliably ablates terminal pathway function systemically with a large clinical safety database outside ophthalmology (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
- Clinical feasibility and tolerability: In AMD trials, intravenous eculizumab was well tolerated without drug-related adverse events and with no clear signal for increased neovascular conversion or ocular infection within one year, supporting general safety of systemic C5 blockade in this population under vaccination protocols (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Negative clinical efficacy in AMD: The randomized phase 2 COMPLETE trial showed no reduction in GA growth and no meaningful reduction in drusen volume through 26–52 weeks; certainty is limited by small sample size but confidence intervals and replication across endpoints argue against a large treatment effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).  
- Compartmentalization barriers for systemic dosing: Blood–retina and Bruch’s membrane barriers likely limit ocular exposure to intravenously administered eculizumab; multiple reviews cite inadequate ocular penetration as a plausible reason for failure, and systemic eculizumab is no longer being pursued in AMD (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
- Target selection may be too distal for RPE lysosomal rescue: Human iPSC-RPE data indicate that complement-driven lysosomal pathology and drusen-like deposits are reversed by C3 inhibition, with concomitant reduction of downstream MAC, while C5 blockade alone has not been shown to restore lysosomal metrics and did not slow GA clinically; this suggests that proximal complement turnover is the dominant driver of RPE lysosomal stress (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Mechanistic escape and incomplete terminal control: Under strong activation, C5 can be activated on dense C3b clusters with features of convertase bypass or conformational priming; stoichiometric C5 inhibitors can form long-lived C5:antibody complexes on surfaces, potentially allowing residual terminal activity, and clinical “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” has been documented (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
- Genetic and biochemical determinants of response: C5 polymorphisms (e.g., R885H/C) can abolish binding and confer resistance; while prevalence in AMD populations is unknown here, such variants are important risk factors for nonresponse (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).  
- Safety/logistics: Terminal complement blockade mandates meningococcal vaccination and vigilance for invasive infections; while acceptable systemically in selected diseases, risk–benefit in a chronic, slowly progressive ocular disorder is less favorable, and the cost and infusion burden are high (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Contextualization with alternative complement strategies  
- C5 vs C3: Clinical success in GA has emerged at the level of C3 (pegcetacoplan), consistent with cellular data showing rescue of lysosomal function by upstream blockade; by contrast, systemic C5 inhibition with eculizumab and other C5-directed agents failed to meet GA endpoints in early trials, and LFG316 also did not demonstrate efficacy in GA (West et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Route of administration: Most agents demonstrating anatomical effects in GA are delivered intravitreally; eculizumab’s large size and systemic administration likely limited ocular penetration in COMPLETE, and no intravitreal eculizumab data are provided here to support local delivery (Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
- Risk of adverse ocular remodeling: Complement modulation has complex, context-dependent effects; in some models, complement inhibition or modulation can alter macrophage polarization and influence CNV formation, underscoring that indiscriminate or poorly targeted complement blockade could have unintended consequences; while the eculizumab AMD trials did not show a neovascular signal, vigilance is warranted when selecting targets and doses (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2021).

Decision Implications  
- As a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD, eculizumab has a low probability of success based on randomized clinical evidence, pharmacokinetic compartment limitations, and mechanistic considerations indicating that distal C5 blockade may not correct the proximal complement turnover driving RPE lysosomal pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- If C5 remains a target of interest, local ocular delivery and alternative molecular formats designed for intravitreal pharmacokinetics (e.g., smaller C5-binding entities, RNAi to intraocular C5 production, or intravitreal C5 inhibitors such as avacincaptad pegol) are more plausible routes; indeed, avacincaptad has advanced in GA, while systemic eculizumab has been discontinued in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019; Nadeem et al., 2023; West et al., 2024).  
- For assays aimed at lysosomal stress and POS phagocytosis, prioritizing proximal complement inhibitors (e.g., C3-targeting) is more aligned with human RPE data and recent clinical experience, whereas C5 inhibition alone is unlikely to fully normalize lysosomal function or confer robust structural benefit (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; West et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
Eculizumab provides a clear mechanistic means to extinguish terminal complement effectors implicated in AMD biology, but the totality of evidence—negative randomized clinical data in GA and drusen, route-of-administration barriers to ocular exposure, mechanistic escape during high activation, and cellular evidence favoring proximal over distal inhibition for lysosomal rescue—argues against further development of systemic eculizumab for dry AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The program should be deprioritized in favor of intraocularly suited agents and proximal complement targets, unless a compelling, testable strategy emerges to achieve effective intraocular C5 blockade with eculizumab (which is not supported by the present context) (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistic Appendix: Biochemical and Pathobiologic Evidence Relevant to the Hypothesis  
- Complement activation and terminal effectors in AMD:  
  - C5a is present in drusen and induces VEGF from RPE; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD; MAC induces endothelial lysis and sub-lytic survival signaling that upregulates VEGF and MMPs (Kassa et al., 2019).  
  - Alternative pathway dysregulation is central in AMD; genetic and experimental data implicate factor H and alternative pathway components in AMD and CNV models; inhibition of C3a, C5a, CFB, MAC or supplementation with CD59/CFH blocks CNV in animals (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Eculizumab structure–function:  
  - Epitope on MG7 with steric convertase blockade; high-affinity binding and resistance polymorphisms at Arg885; CDR function validated by mutational scans (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
  - PK/PD: long half-life, vascular distribution, CH50 suppression threshold, FcRn recycling of C5:eculizumab complexes; ravulizumab engineering to improve recycling and dosing (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
  - Breakthrough mechanisms: convertase bypass and surface-induced conformational activation on dense C3b clusters; residual TP activity despite inhibitors under strong activation (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; Mannes et al., 2021).  
- Clinical AMD trials:  
  - COMPLETE GA cohort: no slowing of GA growth at 26 or 52 weeks; well tolerated (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021).  
  - COMPLETE drusen cohort: no ≥ 50% reduction in drusen volume in treated eyes at 26 weeks; no significant change in drusen growth vs placebo (Filho et al., 2014).  
  - Critical appraisals: small sample, imprecision, risk of bias; systemic delivery may not achieve retinal levels; eculizumab no longer in AMD development (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023).  
- RPE lysosomal biology:  
  - In high-risk Y402H iPSC-RPE, excessive C3 turnover increases MAC internalization and overloads lysosomes; C3 inhibition with Cp40 reduces both C3b and MAC, reverses lysosomal defects, and reduces drusen-like deposits; direct C5 inhibition is not shown to restore lysosomal function in this model (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Operational Recommendation  
- Do not advance systemic eculizumab for dry AMD. If C5 remains a strategic target, consider intravitreal agents designed for ocular PK and evaluate them head-to-head against proximal inhibitors in RPE lysosomal-function assays that quantify both MAC and C3 fragment deposition, with translational go/no-go predicated on alignment with known clinical signals in GA (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
TTP-488, also known as Azeliragon, is a small-molecule synthetic RAGE antagonist originally discovered in the context of Alzheimer’s disease research. It belongs to the class of compounds designed to block the receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) by preventing the interaction between RAGE and its ligands – such as advanced glycation end products (AGEs), amyloid-β peptides, and S100 proteins – that trigger downstream inflammatory signaling cascades. The synthetic origin of TTP-488 stems from medicinal chemistry efforts targeting neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress pathways, and members of this compound class have been investigated for their anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative, and anti-fibrotic properties in multiple disease settings. Its chemical design focused on achieving high binding potency to the extracellular ligand binding domain of RAGE, with an IC₅₀ in the nanomolar range (approximately 100 nM as hypothesized) for inhibition of ligand engagement. This class of RAGE antagonists, including TTP-488, has been predominantly studied in the context of neurodegenerative diseases where aberrant RAGE signaling contributes to pathology, supporting their potential repurposing for diseases characterized by chronic inflammation and oxidative stress, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2, 5–6).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, TTP-488 has been evaluated in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease, where its ability to block RAGE-mediated amyloid-β interactions provided a sound mechanistic rationale for attenuating neuroinflammation and oxidative damage. In these trials, TTP-488 demonstrated an acceptable oral safety profile and favorable pharmacokinetics that make systemic administration feasible—a key consideration when repurposing drugs for alternative indications. While the use of TTP-488 specifically for dry AMD has not been clinically evaluated, a growing body of preclinical evidence has implicated RAGE signaling as a central mediator in AMD pathogenesis. For instance, studies have reported that RAGE expression is significantly upregulated in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells in AMD and that advanced glycation end products accumulate in the drusen deposits characteristic of the disease (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2, 7–8). Moreover, animal models using RAGE-deficient mice have shown reduced choroidal neovascularization and attenuated retinal fibrosis, suggesting that RAGE inhibition could also be beneficial in conditions with similar underlying pathology such as dry AMD (Park, 2017, pp. 157–163, 163–168). Although RAGE antagonists were originally developed with neurodegenerative conditions in mind, the convergence of pathogenic mechanisms such as oxidative stress, lysosomal dysfunction, and inflammation in both Alzheimer’s disease and AMD provides a strong basis for considering TTP-488’s repurposing for retinal degenerative disorders (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 5–6; Barile & Schmidt, 2007, pp. 3–4).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, TTP-488 functions by competitively inhibiting the binding of multiple pathological ligands to the RAGE receptor. Under normal or stressed conditions, AGEs accumulate on extracellular matrices and within drusen deposits, where they interact with RAGE on RPE cells to trigger the activation of several downstream signaling cascades. Activation of RAGE results in the induction of nuclear factor-kappaB (NF-κB), p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), and TGF-β/Smad2 signaling pathways, which collectively contribute to increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, chronic inflammation, and the promotion of fibrotic responses (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2; Barile & Schmidt, 2007, pp. 3–4). Specifically, in the retinal pigment epithelium—cells that are responsible for the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—RAGE activation has been shown to impair lysosomal function, cause lysosomal alkalinization, and disrupt tight junction integrity. This aberrant signaling causes a vicious cycle of increased oxidative stress and inflammation, leading to further accumulation of deleterious metabolic byproducts and progression of dry AMD pathology (Julius & Renuka, 2023, pp. 1–2; Dahrouj et al., 2015, pp. 1–3). TTP-488, by binding to RAGE with high affinity, prevents AGE-RAGE interactions and thereby interrupts this cycle. Moreover, preclinical studies have demonstrated that the inhibition of RAGE through agents such as TTP-488 can attenuate TGF-β2-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in RPE cells, reduce mitochondrial ROS production, and diminish the expression of fibrotic markers like α-smooth muscle actin (αSMA) and collagen I (Sreekumar et al., 2025, pp. 7–10). Blocking these signaling cascades is anticipated to lead to a normalization of lysosomal pH, enhanced clearance of extracellular debris, and ultimately improved phagocytosis of POS, thereby supporting retinal homeostasis (Barile & Schmidt, 2007, pp. 3–4; Park, 2017, pp. 163–168).

Expected Effect:  
The expected therapeutic effect of TTP-488 in the context of dry AMD is based on its ability to restore normal RPE function by mitigating the harmful consequences of AGE-induced RAGE activation. In a typical assay, when cultured RPE cells are exposed to excessive AGEs, the interaction with RAGE triggers oxidative stress and lysosomal dysfunction, leading to impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments—a critical physiological process required for retinal renewal. Treatment with TTP-488 is hypothesized to competitively block these interactions, thus reducing the ensuing ROS production and normalizing lysosomal pH. This normalization is expected to re-establish efficient activation of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway, leading to increased phagocytic uptake and degradation of POS as well as clearance of accumulated debris that may contribute to drusen formation (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4). Additionally, because RAGE signaling also promotes the upregulation of pro-angiogenic factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), its inhibition by TTP-488 is anticipated to reduce aberrant VEGF expression, thereby potentially mitigating secondary pathological features associated with neovascularization, even though dry AMD is predominantly characterized by atrophic processes rather than neovascular ones (Dahrouj et al., 2015, pp. 1–3; Park, 2017, pp. 163–168). Furthermore, RPE cells have been shown to express high levels of RAGE especially in regions adjacent to drusen deposits, indicating that the drug target is well-represented in the critical cellular compartment for treating dry AMD (Park et al., 2015, pp. 1–2; Ruan et al., 2020, pp. 9–11). Ultimately, the net outcome of TTP-488 administration in preclinical models is expected to be a reduction in oxidative damage, an improvement in lysosomal function, and a restoration of RPE-mediated phagocytic capacity, which together could slow or potentially reverse the progression of RPE degeneration observed in dry AMD (Sreekumar et al., 2025, pp. 7–10).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating TTP-488 as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses become apparent. One of the key strengths is the robust molecular rationale underpinning its application in AMD. Numerous studies have implicated the AGE-RAGE axis in the initiation and progression of dry AMD, with evidence of AGE accumulation in drusen, increased RAGE expression in compromised RPE cells, and the subsequent triggering of inflammatory, oxidative, and fibrotic signaling pathways that drive retinal degeneration (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2, 7–8; Julius & Renuka, 2023, pp. 1–2). The fact that TTP-488 has already been evaluated in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease provides a significant advantage in terms of pre-established oral safety data, which could accelerate its repurposing for ocular indications. Preclinical studies have also shown that RAGE antagonism via TTP-488 can reduce key pathological processes – such as EMT, ROS production, and fibrotic marker expression in RPE cells – which directly translates to the primary pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD (Sreekumar et al., 2025, pp. 7–10; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4).

Another strength lies in the multifaceted mechanism of action of TTP-488. By targeting a common upstream mediator (RAGE) that links several deleterious pathways, there is potential to simultaneously impact oxidative stress, inflammation, and lysosomal dysfunction, all of which are critical in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. This multipronged effect is particularly valuable in complex diseases like dry AMD that do not succumb to single-target therapies. Moreover, the hypothesis that TTP-488 can restore POS phagocytosis in RPE cells is supported by mechanistic evidence demonstrating that RAGE activation disrupts the autophagy-lysosomal system—a cornerstone of RPE cell maintenance (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4; Kivinen, 2018, pp. 9–10). Therefore, the expected improvement in the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments indirectly supports the maintenance of retinal integrity over time.

However, there are also several challenges that temper the optimism regarding TTP-488’s repurposing for dry AMD. First, although the safety profile in Alzheimer’s disease is encouraging, it remains uncertain whether systemic administration of TTP-488 will achieve adequate ocular tissue penetration given the presence of blood-retinal barriers. It may be necessary to develop alternative delivery formulations (for example, localized ocular delivery systems) to bypass these pharmacokinetic hurdles without compromising the well-tolerated systemic profile observed in Alzheimer’s trials (Tang et al., 2024, pp. 12–13; Park, 2017, pp. 99–106). Another potential weakness is the translational gap between the preclinical models explored so far—many of which focus on retinal fibrosis and subretinal neovascularization—and the specific pathology of dry AMD, which is characterized predominantly by atrophic changes rather than overt neovascular events (Park, 2017, pp. 157–163, 163–168). This underscores the need for dedicated preclinical studies in models that more closely recapitulate the slow progression and specific cellular dysfunction seen in dry AMD.

VX-765, also known as Belnacasan, is a synthetic, orally available caspase-1 inhibitor originally developed by Vertex Pharmaceuticals as part of their research into anti-inflammatory therapeutics (Dhani et al., 2021; Kallinich, 2015). As a member of the caspase inhibitor class, VX-765 represents a second‐generation approach compared to its predecessor pralnacasan (VX-740), seeking improved oral bioavailability, enhanced selectivity, and a more favorable pharmacokinetic profile (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015). The synthetic origin and deliberate design emphasizes a precision targeting of caspase-1’s catalytic cysteine, a critical residue in the enzyme’s active site, thereby inhibiting its proteolytic function; this is particularly important given the role of caspase-1 in mediating pyroptosis and inflammatory cytokine maturation (Kallinich, 2015; Kudelova et al., 2015).

Historically, VX-765 has been evaluated in preclinical studies and early-phase human trials mainly for systemic inflammatory and neurological conditions. Early investigations demonstrated that VX-765 robustly reduced plasma cytokine levels in dose-dependent manners in Phase I studies, and subsequent Phase II trials in psoriasis provided evidence of both safety and clinical activity (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015; Maroso et al., 2011). Its predecessor pralnacasan showed efficacy in rheumatoid arthritis clinical trials, although long-term use in animal models eventually raised concerns about potential hepatotoxicity, leading to its withdrawal despite promising initial results (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015). VX-765 was later repurposed for neurological conditions; it has been tested in partial epilepsy where, despite a good safety profile, its efficacy was less than anticipated (Dhani et al., 2021; Kudelova et al., 2015; Kallinich, 2015). In addition, VX-765 has demonstrated anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects in preclinical models of Alzheimer’s disease by reducing IL-1β production in the brain and preserving synaptic function (Liang et al., 2022; Flores et al., 2018). Importantly, although the clinical and preclinical development history of VX-765 spans a variety of inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases, it has not been extensively evaluated for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or retinal diseases per se (Dhani et al., 2021; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020; Kallinich, 2015). Nevertheless, a search in clinical trial databases has uncovered a limited number of studies investigating caspase-1 inhibitors in the context of macular degeneration, reinforcing the notion that the therapeutic paradigm may be extended to ocular disorders (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
Caspase-1 is a cysteine-dependent aspartate-directed protease that plays a central role in the activation of inflammatory cytokines by cleaving pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature, biologically active forms; these cytokines are major mediators of inflammatory cascades and pyroptotic cell death (Kallinich, 2015; Kudelova et al., 2015). VX-765 functions by inhibiting caspase-1 through a competitive mechanism that involves binding to the catalytic cysteine residue; structural studies have indicated that its peptidomimetic scaffold effectively occupies the substrate-binding pocket, thereby preventing substrate access (Kudelova et al., 2015; Kallinich, 2015). Although the hypothesis for repurposing VX-765 in dry AMD posits an irreversible inhibition of caspase-1, the bulk of the literature supports that VX-765 is, in fact, a reversible inhibitor (Dhani et al., 2021; Kallinich, 2015). Activation of VX-765 in vivo produces VRT-043198, which exhibits low nanomolar inhibitory potency against human caspase-1 (IC₅₀ ~3.68–9.91 nM) and comparable activity in murine models (IC₅₀ ~18–52.1 nM), rendering it suitable for precise modulation of caspase-1 activity (Flores et al., 2018; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020). By inhibiting caspase-1, VX-765 effectively prevents the maturation and secretion of IL-1β and IL-18, thereby disrupting the propagation of inflammatory signals that can lead to dysfunctional cellular responses such as pyroptosis—a lytic form of programmed cell death triggered by inflammasome activation (Kallinich, 2015; Younus & Reddy, 2018). In RPE cells, where caspase-1 expression has been documented as a component of inflammasome signaling especially during stress conditions, inhibition of caspase-1 is anticipated to preserve lysosomal integrity by reducing cytokine-induced lysosomal destabilization and preventing the cleavage of substrates that contribute to cell death pathways (Gao et al., 2019; Kudelova et al., 2015). Moreover, evidence suggests that caspase-1 activation leads to gasdermin D cleavage, which forms membrane pores and facilitates pyroptotic cell death; therefore, blockade by VX-765 could mitigate this deleterious cascade (Kallinich, 2015; Flores et al., 2018).

In the context of dry AMD, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is a critical cell type responsible for maintaining photoreceptor health through the daily phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor outer segments (POS). The repurposing of VX-765 for dry AMD represents a compelling strategy, driven by a strong mechanistic rationale and bolstered by its demonstrated efficacy in other inflammatory models. One of the primary strengths of VX-765 is its potent and selective inhibition of caspase-1, with low nanomolar IC₅₀ values ensuring that only minimal concentrations are required to achieve therapeutic effects (Flores et al., 2018; Rasoulinejad et al., 2020).
