Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Trehalose is a naturally occurring, nonreducing disaccharide composed of two D‐glucose units (MW = 342.3 Da) that is not synthesized endogenously in mammals but is abundant in other organisms such as fungi, plants, and invertebrates (Cox et al., 2025). It was originally discovered as a cellular protectant and osmolyte that stabilizes proteins and membranes under conditions of stress, and its unique chemical stability and protein‐protective properties have led to its use in cryopreservation and organ transplant protocols (Lotfi et al., 2018). As a small-molecule therapeutic candidate, trehalose belongs to a class of compounds known as osmolytes and molecular chaperones; this category has been extensively explored for its capacity to stabilize proteins, prevent aggregation, and enhance cellular resilience in the face of diverse environmental and metabolic stresses (Abokyi et al., 2020; Cox et al., 2025). In drug development contexts, its repurposing for dry age-related macular degeneration (dAMD) is driven by its capacity to activate TFEB—a master transcription factor regulating the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network—and thereby boost autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ghosh et al., 2023). Trehalose has been formulated for ocular use, most notably as an ingredient in tear substitutes for dry eye, and its safety profile in such formulations provides ancillary support for its potential repurposing to target RPE dysfunction in dAMD (Cox et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Trehalose has a well-documented history in biochemical and preclinical research due to its potent protein-stabilizing and osmoprotectant actions. It has been widely used in non-ophthalmic applications, most notably in cryopreservation protocols, where its ability to preserve protein structure and cellular integrity under desiccating and freezing conditions is exploited (Cox et al., 2025; Lotfi et al., 2018). In the ocular field, trehalose has been evaluated primarily for anterior segment indications such as dry eye disease; several randomized clinical trials have demonstrated its tolerability and efficacy as a tear substitute when combined with hyaluronic acid, with improvements in tear film break-up time (TBUT) and ocular surface symptoms (Chiambaretta et al., 2017).  
More importantly for dAMD, multiple in vitro studies using human RPE cell models—including ARPE-19 and iPSC-derived RPE from patients with genetic risk factors like CFH mutations—have shown that trehalose rescues autophagy deficits and lysosomal dysfunction, especially under oxidative-stress conditions induced by agents such as hydroquinone (Abokyi et al., 2020). These studies report that trehalose treatment upregulates key autophagy regulators (e.g., ATG5, ATG7) and lysosomal markers (e.g., LAMP2, cathepsin D) while enhancing autophagic flux, thereby improving the degradative capacity of RPE cells—a fundamental defect implicated in the accumulation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and lipofuscin in dAMD (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). Additionally, in murine models of retinal degeneration—whether induced by light exposure or by genetic interventions—trehalose has been shown to protect against retinal cell loss and preserve outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness, offering further preclinical evidence of its neuroprotective potential (Cox et al., 2025). Thus, while trehalose has an established record in non-ocular uses and in the treatment of anterior ocular surface disorders, emerging data now support its repurposing for dAMD by virtue of its ability to modulate autophagy and lysosomal degradation in RPE cells (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central mechanism by which trehalose is hypothesized to benefit dry AMD involves its capacity to activate the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of the CLEAR network. TFEB controls the transcription of a whole battery of genes required for autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and metabolic adaptation (Abokyi et al., 2020). Typically, TFEB resides in the cytoplasm in an inactive, phosphorylated state under nutrient-rich or stress-depleted conditions; its translocation to the nucleus is tightly regulated by mTORC1-dependent and mTORC1-independent signaling pathways (Ghosh et al., 2023; Karim et al., 2020). Trehalose has been shown to induce TFEB nuclear translocation independently of mTOR inhibition, potentially through mechanisms involving Akt signaling modulation and AMPK activation (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Upon nuclear entry, TFEB binds to CLEAR elements in the promoter regions of target genes, thereby upregulating autophagy mediators such as ATG5 and ATG7, enhancing the expression of lysosomal proteins like LAMP2, and increasing the levels of protein markers such as LC3B and p62 that are involved in autophagosome formation and maturation (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Several biochemical studies in human RPE cells have demonstrated that trehalose treatment leads to increased TFEB mRNA and protein levels with concomitant upregulation of CLEAR network gene expression. For instance, in ARPE-19 cells exposed to hydroquinone—a model for oxidative stress relevant to dAMD—it was observed that trehalose not only increased LC3-II levels and GFP-LC3 puncta formation but also enhanced the degradation of autophagic substrates, indicating that trehalose facilitates effective autophagic flux rather than merely blocking lysosomal degradation (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Mechanistically, trehalose is thought to penetrate mammalian cells via fluid-phase endocytosis and possibly through the SLC2A8 (GLUT8) transporter, which facilitates its intracellular accumulation at millimolar concentrations (Cox et al., 2025). Once inside the cell, trehalose appears to modulate several key pathways: by inhibiting Akt signaling, it reduces the phosphorylation of TFEB at specific residues (such as S467) that normally prevent its nuclear import; concurrently, trehalose may activate AMPK, which further supports autophagy induction (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020). Moreover, although trehalose transiently upregulates NRF2 under basal conditions—thereby enhancing antioxidant defenses—its primary protective effect in oxidative stress models of the RPE appears to be mediated by restored autophagy, as demonstrated by loss of cytoprotection when autophagy is genetically disrupted via ATG5 knockdown (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Beyond its role in autophagy, trehalose has been implicated in promoting chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) through stimulation of LAMP2 expression, which is essential for CMA substrate recognition and lysosomal import (Abokyi et al., 2020). In this way, trehalose may offer a dual benefit: boosting canonical macroautophagy while also enhancing CMA, collectively leading to improved clearance of damaged organelles, aggregated proteins, and undigested POS in the RPE—a critical function given the strong association between defective POS clearance and the pathogenesis of dAMD (Abokyi et al., 2020). Furthermore, in CFH-mutant iPSC-derived RPE cells, trehalose has been shown to rescue the diminished activity of lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D and to restore other proteostasis markers, establishing a direct molecular link between trehalose-induced TFEB activation and functional improvements in the degradative capacity of RPE cells (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
Collectively, the mechanistic data suggest that trehalose exerts its beneficial effects through a complex interplay of intracellular signaling pathways that converge on the activation of TFEB, thereby re-establishing efficient autophagic clearance processes that are impaired in the aging and oxidative-stressed RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020; Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic insights outlined above, the hypothesis posits that treatment with trehalose at a concentration of 5 mM in an in vitro assay using iPSC-derived RPE cells from dry AMD patients will lead to robust TFEB nuclear translocation. This nuclear translocation is expected to result in the transcriptional upregulation of CLEAR network genes, thereby increasing the expression of autophagy regulators such as ATG5 and ATG7 and promoting the biogenesis of lysosomes, as evidenced by increased levels of lysosomal markers like LAMP2 and cathepsin D (Abokyi et al., 2020). In an environment of oxidative stress—for example, when the iPSC-RPE cells are challenged with hydroquinone to mimic cigarette smoke-induced damage or other oxidative insults commonly associated with AMD—the activation of TFEB by trehalose is anticipated to restore impaired autophagic flux. This restoration would be reflected in the accumulation of LC3-II upon inhibition of lysosomal function (e.g., in the presence of chloroquine) and decreased levels of autophagy substrate p62 (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Crucially, by enhancing autophagic and lysosomal function in the RPE, trehalose is expected to improve POS degradation. Efficient degradation of POS is vital for photoreceptor health, and its impairment has been implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD through the accumulation of toxic byproducts and lipofuscin (Abokyi et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025). Thus, the expected phenotype in the in vitro assay would include not only molecular signatures of enhanced autophagy (e.g., increased LC3B puncta, upregulated ATG gene expression) but also functional improvements such as reduced oxidative stress (lower reactive oxygen species levels) and improved cell viability under stress conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020).  
Moreover, previous studies have shown that trehalose’s cytoprotective effects are autophagy-dependent because genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of autophagy (e.g., via ATG5 knockdown) abolishes the otherwise protective effects of trehalose, thereby reinforcing the notion that the expected improvement in POS degradation and overall cellular homeostasis is tightly linked to the restoration of autophagy and lysosomal competence (Abokyi et al., 2020). In essence, the application of 5 mM trehalose to oxidative-stressed iPSC-RPE cells is anticipated to reverse the autophagic deficits that are characteristic of dry AMD, ultimately leading to enhanced clearance of POS, reduced accumulation of cytotoxic aggregates, and improved cellular survival and function in an in vitro model that recapitulates key aspects of the disease (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
Trehalose represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its multifaceted capacity to modulate intracellular degradation pathways that are critically impaired in the disease state. One of the primary strengths of trehalose is its robust preclinical evidence base. Multiple studies have demonstrated that trehalose can induce TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE models, resulting in the transcriptional activation of an array of autophagy and lysosomal genes (Abokyi et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2023; Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020). This mechanistic property directly addresses a key pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD, where the accumulation of undegraded photoreceptor outer segments and lipofuscin due to defective autophagy plays a contributory role in RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration (Abokyi et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025). The ability of trehalose to enhance both macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy augments its therapeutic appeal, as it suggests an overall improvement in cellular proteostasis, which is imperative in aged or stressed RPE cells (Abokyi et al., 2020; Cox et al., 2025).  
Another notable strength is the established safety profile of trehalose. It is a naturally occurring compound with a long history of use in various medical and industrial applications, including as an ingredient in ocular surface formulations for dry eye disease (Chiambaretta et al., 2017; Cox et al., 2025). Furthermore, the preclinical data showing that trehalose can protect against oxidative stress and preserve retinal function in animal models lend credibility to the hypothesis that it may exert similar protective effects in human RPE cells (Cox et al., 2025).  
However, several weaknesses and gaps must be acknowledged as well. First, the majority of the compelling evidence for trehalose’s efficacy in modulating TFEB and enhancing autophagy comes from in vitro studies using immortalized RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19) or rodent models, with only limited data available from human iPSC-derived RPE models specifically derived from AMD patients (Abokyi et al., 2020). Second, there are ongoing debates in the literature regarding the precise molecular mechanisms by which trehalose exerts its autophagy-enhancing effects, with some reports disputing its ability to induce autophagy under certain conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).  
Another potential challenge lies in the delivery of trehalose to the RPE in a clinically meaningful manner. Although trehalose is orally bioavailable and has been successfully formulated for topical ocular use in dry eye applications, the posterior segment of the eye presents unique drug delivery hurdles. Penetration through the cornea and subsequent distribution to the RPE and retina often require specialized formulations, and while there are preclinical reports of trehalose reaching posterior ocular tissues (Cox et al., 2025), comprehensive pharmacokinetic and ocular bioavailability data for trehalose in the context of dAMD remain sparse.  
Furthermore, while the repurposing of trehalose is attractive due to its established safety and low cost, intellectual property issues and regulatory challenges associated with drug repurposing may complicate clinical development. Despite these concerns, the overall body of evidence supports further investigation into trehalose as a potential modulator of TFEB and autophagy in the RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cox et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).  
In summary, trehalose offers several strong advantages as a candidate therapeutic for dry AMD. Its ability to activate TFEB and upregulate a broad spectrum of autophagy and lysosomal genes addresses a fundamental defect in RPE cells implicated in the disease. Robust preclinical evidence in both in vitro and animal models suggests that trehalose enhances autophagic flux, improves POS clearance, and confers cytoprotective effects against oxidative stress. Its favorable safety profile and prior use in ocular formulations further support its translational potential. However, critical gaps remain in terms of validating its efficacy in human-derived RPE models, optimizing its dosing and delivery to the posterior segment, and resolving discrepancies regarding its mechanism of action in different experimental contexts. Given these considerations, trehalose represents a promising candidate that merits further investigation—particularly through rigorous dose-response studies, advanced formulation development to enhance retinal delivery, and robust clinical trials in patient populations at risk for dry AMD—to fully establish its therapeutic value (Abokyi et al., 2020; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cox et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
FX-68 is a synthetic small‐molecule agonist developed from a chemical library (ChemBridge Cat. No. 6789012) and represents an emerging member of a class of chemokine receptor modulators that selectively target CX3CR1. This compound is designed to mimic the natural ligand, fractalkine (CX3CL1), and has been optimized for potency with an EC₅₀ of approximately 100 nM, which suggests that it is capable of activating CX3CR1 at pharmacologically achievable concentrations (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–5, 6–7). The candidate belongs to the broader category of small-molecule GPCR agonists, a class that has been successfully employed in various inflammatory and neurodegenerative indications because of their favorable oral bioavailability and capacity to cross biological barriers; such compounds have a long history in modulating immune cell behavior and attenuating aberrant inflammation (Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 2–4; Chinnery et al., 2012, pp. 7–8). In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), FX-68 is proposed to restore appropriate signaling in the CX3CL1–CX3CR1 axis—a pathway that is critically involved in the regulation of microglial migration, phagocytosis and, indirectly, the trophic support provided to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6). Its synthetic origin coupled with repurposing potential makes FX-68 an attractive candidate for conditions in which deficient microglial clearance and disrupted RPE–microglia crosstalk contribute to disease progression (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3, 4–5).

Therapeutic History:  
The link between CX3CR1 function and retinal health was established through extensive genetic and preclinical studies, in which loss-of-function mutations or deficiencies in CX3CR1 were found to produce a constellation of AMD-like features, including the accumulation of subretinal microglia, formation of drusen-like deposits, and secondary photoreceptor degeneration (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7; Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 4–5). Historically, research in this area has focused on genetic knock-out models and human polymorphism analyses rather than on the administration of direct pharmacologic agonists; for example, CX3CR1-deficient mice consistently exhibit abnormal subretinal microglial behavior and accompanying retinal pathology, which has been used as a rationale for targeting this signaling pathway therapeutically (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–6). Although exogenous delivery of CX3CL1 has been explored in certain experimental paradigms, no small-molecule CX3CR1 agonist has yet been advanced in clinical or veterinary practice for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerations (Chinnery et al., 2012, pp. 7–8; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3). Instead, the therapeutic potential in this space has largely emerged indirectly from studies that demonstrate that disrupted CX3CR1 signaling is deleterious to retinal homeostasis, thereby suggesting that its appropriate stimulation could restore normal microglial behavior (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7). As a repurposed candidate, FX-68 aims to fill this translational gap by reactivating a pathway that is both genetically implicated in AMD and mechanistically understood in other contexts of neuroinflammation (Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 2–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
The CX3CL1–CX3CR1 axis is a pivotal mediator of neuron–microglia communication in the retina and broader central nervous system, where fractalkine (CX3CL1) exists in both membrane-bound and soluble forms and interacts exclusively with CX3CR1, a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) expressed predominantly by microglia (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–5, 6–7). Under physiological conditions, tonic signaling through CX3CR1 serves to restrain microglial activation, regulate their migratory behavior, and facilitate their efficient surveillance and debris clearance functions (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6). In the diseased retina—such as in dry AMD—loss or dysfunction of CX3CR1 impairs these regulatory mechanisms, leading to chronic accumulation of lipid-laden microglia in the subretinal space, excessive phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and subsequent RPE stress and degeneration, a sequence that contributes to the formation of drusen-like deposits and ultimately to photoreceptor cell death (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3, 6–7).

FX-68 is designed as a CX3CR1 agonist that binds to and activates this receptor, mimicking the natural action of CX3CL1. Upon binding, it is expected to trigger downstream signaling cascades typical of GPCR activation, including modulation of adenylate cyclase activity and activation of MAP kinase pathways, which in turn alter cytoskeletal dynamics essential for microglial migration and phagocytosis (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–6). At a molecular level, proper CX3CR1 activation is theorized to correct the aberrant microglial behavior seen in CX3CR1 deficiency: it should promote the egression or apoptotic clearance of subretinal microglia that have phagocytosed excessive amounts of POS debris and prevent their transformation into foam cells laden with intracellular lipids (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7; Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4). Moreover, by reestablishing a functional microglia–RPE communication axis, FX-68 may help restore the RPE’s inherent phagocytic capacity to clear POS effectively, ultimately leading to improved outer retinal homeostasis (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). With CX3CR1 activation, signaling may also suppress the production of proangiogenic factors such as VEGF, thereby limiting pathological neovascularization—a secondary complication sometimes observed in the context of AMD (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). This mechanism is further supported by studies in which exogenous CX3CL1 reduced microglial phagocytosis and inflammatory activation in models of retinal degeneration, albeit in genetic loss-of-function contexts rather than using a pharmacologic agonist (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Zabel et al., 2016, pp. 10–12). The overall molecular interaction profile of FX-68, therefore, hinges on reinstating the anti-inflammatory, pro-homeostatic functions of CX3CR1 in retinal microglia, with the intended effect of reducing deleterious phagocytosis and enhancing trophic support for the RPE (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assays and in preclinical models—particularly in the challenging Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mouse model, which recapitulates many aspects of dry AMD—the expected effect of FX-68 is multifaceted. First, by binding and activating CX3CR1 on retinal microglia, FX-68 is anticipated to restore regulated cell migration and proper phagocytic clearance, thereby reducing the abnormal accumulation of subretinal microglia that is observed in CX3CR1-deficient models (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). Such restoration is expected to lead to a normalization of the phagocytic process, where instead of over-ingesting POS debris and becoming lipid-laden foam cells, microglia will clear debris efficiently and then either return to a surveillant state or undergo timely apoptosis or emigration away from the subretinal space (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6).

Second, FX-68 is proposed to facilitate enhanced trophic support for RPE cells. Evidence suggests that proper microglial signaling is critically involved in modulating RPE phagocytosis of POS, partly through the secretion of growth factors and early inflammatory mediators that prime RPE cells for efficient clearance functions (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). In co-culture assays involving microglia and RPE cells, treatment with FX-68 is expected to lead to an increase in the efficiency of POS turnover, as microglial activation is reined in and redirected toward beneficial debris clearance rather than deleterious inflammatory activation (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). This effect, in theory, would reduce the buildup of toxic debris in the subretinal region, limit the formation of drusen-like deposits and diminish secondary inflammatory and proangiogenic signaling, such as excessive VEGF release, that further compromise retinal integrity (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3; Rashid et al., 2019, p. 14).

Moreover, in animal models like the Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mice—where the dual deficiency exacerbates retinal degeneration and drusen-like pathology—FX-68 is expected to mitigate these phenotypes by reactivating the CX3CR1 pathway. The hypothesis posits that restoration of CX3CR1 signaling will not only lower subretinal microglial accumulation but also re-establish a crosstalk with the RPE that is essential for maintaining the delicate balance between debris clearance and inflammation (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). In this way, the compound may indirectly improve photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance, thereby preserving overall photoreceptor function and slowing the progression of dry AMD (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6; Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4).

An important aspect of the expected effect is the modulation of microglial cytokine production. CX3CR1 signaling has been linked to the suppression of proinflammatory pathways—in particular, the reduction of IL-1β and VEGF expression, which are key mediators of chronic inflammation and pathological angiogenesis (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). FX-68, by serving as a CX3CR1 agonist, would clarify whether the attenuation of these proinflammatory signals could indeed translate to structural and functional retinal preservation in vivo. This result would be highly significant given that chronic inflammation is a critical driver of dry AMD progression (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3; Rashid et al., 2019, p. 14).

Furthermore, the expected effect extends to the normalization of microglial morphology and dispersal. In healthy retinas, microglia are characterized by a ramified morphology that is conducive to efficient surveillance, whereas in CX3CR1-deficient retinas, microglia become amoeboid, exhibit excessive adhesion, and accumulate in the subretinal space (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). FX-68 is anticipated to promote a return to the ramified, homeostatic phenotype, thereby reducing the deleterious impact of microglial hyperactivation and aberrant phagocytosis on both photoreceptors and RPE cells (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6). Altogether, these expected effects form the basis of the hypothesis that FX-68 may improve outer retinal homeostasis by enhancing POS turnover and supporting the RPE via finely tuned microglial regulation (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7; Rashid et al., 2019, p. 14).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of FX-68 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD must balance a compelling mechanistic rationale against significant preclinical gaps and potential safety concerns. On the one hand, there is robust and convergent evidence from genetic and experimental studies that impaired CX3CR1 signaling leads to pathological subretinal microglial accumulation, excessive phagocytosis of photoreceptor debris, and subsequent RPE and photoreceptor damage—as seen in various mouse models and human genetic association studies (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7; Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 4–5; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–5). This evidence strongly supports the notion that reactivating CX3CR1 signaling could normalize microglial behavior, improve debris clearance, limit drusen formation, and ultimately slow the progression of retinal degeneration (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6).

A key strength of FX-68 is its small-molecule nature, which provides advantages in terms of potential administration routes (oral or topical), manufacturability, and the possibility for fine-tuning its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties. With an EC₅₀ of approximately 100 nM, FX-68 appears to be a potent agonist, meaning that it could achieve therapeutic concentrations without off-target effects if the dosing regimen is carefully optimized (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). Furthermore, the therapeutic strategy targeting CX3CR1 is innovative because it leverages an endogenous regulatory pathway known to modulate microglial behavior—a cell type that is increasingly recognized as playing a central role in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) is the taurine-conjugated form of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), a hydrophilic secondary bile acid generated by microbial metabolism and hepatic conjugation, and long used in hepatobiliary disease pharmacotherapy as a cytoprotective bile salt scaffold (class: bile acids; subclass: hydrophilic ursane bile acids/taurine conjugates) (Cabrera et al., 2019). As a small amphipathic molecule, TUDCA exhibits chemical-chaperone activity that stabilizes nascent polypeptides, reduces protein misfolding/aggregation burden, and modulates unfolded protein response (UPR) signaling, thereby lowering endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress across cell types (e.g., hepatocytes, epithelial cells, neurons) (Kusaczuk, 2019). In vitro and in vivo ocular studies identify TUDCA as a broadly neuroprotective agent that rescues photoreceptors and retinal cells in multiple injury paradigms, consistent with multimodal actions that include mitigation of ER stress, inhibition of mitochondrial pathway apoptosis, reduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and anti-inflammatory effects (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Win et al., 2021). In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, TUDCA directly promotes phagocytosis via Mer tyrosine kinase (MerTK) activation and restores phagocytic function under oxidative stress, implicating a direct action on the canonical RPE phagocytic machinery (Murase et al., 2015). Delivery to ocular tissues is feasible with systemic dosing and local routes; related UDCA crosses the human blood–retinal barrier, and TUDCA tissue distribution has been quantified after intravitreal, systemic, and suprachoroidal administration in large animals (Daruich et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
Clinically, the UDCA/TUDCA class is established in hepatology; mechanistic reviews document antiapoptotic activity via inhibition of mitochondrial cytochrome c release, stabilization of mitochondrial membranes, attenuation of ER stress via chaperone actions, increases in glutathione pools, and activation of survival kinases (p38/ERK/MAPK/PI3K), with a translational safety track record that has motivated evaluation in neurodegenerative disorders (Cabrera et al., 2019). In ophthalmology, preclinical data repeatedly show that systemic or local TUDCA protects retina across models: it preserves photoreceptors in genetic (rd10, P23H, Rpgr knockout) and injury models (retinal detachment, light damage), decreases ER stress and apoptosis markers (e.g., caspase-3), and improves electroretinography (ERG) function (Win et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). In diabetic retinopathy–like models and vascular stress paradigms, TUDCA or UDCA reduces vascular permeability, inflammation, and ER stress, and in retinal endothelial cells these effects require the bile acid receptor TGR5, supporting receptor-mediated protection in the retina (Lenin et al., 2023). In RPE models (ARPE-19 and primary human RPE), TUDCA protects against H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury and thapsigargin-induced ER stress, improves viability, suppresses apoptosis, and activates antioxidant defenses, while also reversing oxidative-stress–induced phagocytic dysfunction via MerTK/FAK signaling (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Although these mechanistic actions align with pathogenic axes in dry age-related macular degeneration (dAMD), no clinical trials in dAMD are referenced in the supplied context; the current evidence base is preclinical and translational (e.g., drug distribution and barrier penetration) rather than RPE/dAMD clinical efficacy (Olsen et al., 2020; Daruich et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
ER proteostasis and unfolded protein response modulation  
- Chemical chaperoning: TUDCA stabilizes folding intermediates, reduces aberrant protein–protein interactions, promotes ATF6-driven folding capacity, and prevents UPR malfunction, thereby attenuating ER stress signaling (downregulating BiP/GRP78, ATF4/eIF2α, XBP1 splicing, and CHOP in multiple models) (Kusaczuk, 2019). In ARPE-19 cells, TUDCA reduces thapsigargin-induced CHOP expression and spliced XBP1, with parallel decreases in apoptosis and improved survival, linking chaperone action to UPR attenuation in RPE (Alhasani et al., 2020). Across retinal systems, TUDCA repeatedly lowers ER stress signatures, and the retina-relevant pathophysiology of UPR–mitochondrial crosstalk (IRE1/JNK pro-apoptotic routing, CHOP-mediated death, PERK’s protective vs. maladaptive bifurcation) underscores why ER stress relief is mechanistically central in RPE and photoreceptors (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).

Mitochondrial membrane stabilization and anti-apoptotic signaling  
- Intrinsic apoptosis blockade: TUDCA inhibits Bax translocation, preserves mitochondrial outer membrane integrity, prevents cytochrome c release, and suppresses caspase activation (caspase-3/7), thereby interrupting the mitochondrial execution cascade and preserving oxidative phosphorylation capacity (Alhasani et al., 2020; Cabrera et al., 2019). In neuronal and isolated mitochondrial systems, co-incubation with TUDCA prevents amyloid-β–induced mitochondrial membrane perturbation, preserves redox state and protein conformation of the outer membrane, and limits cytochrome c release—convergent evidence for direct mitochondrial membrane stabilization and preservation of electron transport chain function under proteotoxic/oxidative stress (Khalaf et al., 2022). TUDCA upregulates survival signaling (PI3K/Akt → Bad phosphorylation; ERK/MAPK) and inhibits stress kinases (JNK/c-Jun), further shifting the balance away from mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) and toward survival (Cabrera et al., 2019; Win et al., 2021).

Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory reprogramming  
- NRF2 axis and redox control: In RPE oxidative injury models, TUDCA reduces intracellular ROS and malondialdehyde (MDA), restores NRF2 expression, upregulates antioxidant enzymes (SOD1, catalase, GPX1, NQO1, GCLM), elevates reduced glutathione (GSH), and rescues SOD/catalase activities—features of a robust antioxidant response that stabilizes mitochondrial redox homeostasis (Alhasani et al., 2020). Suppression of inflammatory signaling (decreased IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α transcription and secretion) further reduces secondary mitochondrial injury and death receptor cross-talk (Alhasani et al., 2020). Such antioxidant/anti-inflammatory shifts are consistent with TUDCA-induced NRF2 pathway enhancement reported across tissues and with the known linkage between persistent UPR activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine induction in RPE (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

RPE phagocytic machinery activation  
- MerTK/FAK signaling and POS uptake: TUDCA increases MerTK phosphorylation in a concentration-dependent manner, maintains FAK phosphorylation under oxidative stress, and restores H₂O₂-impaired RPE phagocytosis in both ARPE-19 and primary human RPE, supporting a direct effect on RPE’s canonical POS ingestion machinery (MerTK–FAK–integrin axis) (Murase et al., 2015). Functional assays demonstrate increased uptake and lysosomal digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (pHrodo® and FITC readouts), indicating rescue of both recognition/engulfment and downstream processing (Murase et al., 2015). Notably, in the MerTK rescue paradigm GRP78 was not altered by TUDCA, implying that the pro-phagocytic effect can occur independently of a measurable reduction in ER stress under those specific conditions and may involve upstream integrin/FAK/Src signaling that converges on MerTK (Murase et al., 2015).

Bile acid receptors and signaling in the retina  
- TGR5-dependent protection: In diabetic and inflammatory retinal models, TUDCA reduces ER stress markers (GRP78, IRE1α, sXBP1, CHOP), inflammation, and vascular permeability; these endothelial barrier and anti-inflammatory effects require TGR5 expression in retinal endothelial cells and correlate with functional rescue in vivo (ERG, optokinetic responses), suggesting a receptor-mediated component that is present in the retina (Lenin et al., 2023). Although FXR appears less relevant in retina, additional candidate receptors (TGR5, α5β1 integrin, S1PR2, PXR, GR/mineralocorticoid receptor) have been implicated at the transcript/protein level in ocular tissues, providing plausible upstream routes for TUDCA’s signaling (Daruich et al., 2022; Win et al., 2021).

Mechanistic integration in AMD biology  
- In RPE, ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction reinforce each other: UPR activation (IRE1/JNK, ATF4–CHOP) promotes mitochondrial apoptosis and ATP decline; mitochondrial impairment (Δψm loss, ROS) feeds back to exacerbate ER stress and can drive epithelial–mesenchymal transition seen in early dAMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020). TUDCA’s combined actions—chemical chaperoning of ER proteostasis, MOMP blockade/cytochrome c retention, redox control via NRF2, and restoration of MerTK/FAK-dependent phagocytosis—directly map onto these intersecting failure modes and therefore represent a coherent, biologically grounded therapeutic hypothesis for dAMD (Alhasani et al., 2020; Cabrera et al., 2019; Murase et al., 2015).

Important mechanistic gaps for dAMD  
- Despite strong plausibility, direct RPE bioenergetics readouts (ATP levels, oxygen consumption rate, mitochondrial membrane potential) after TUDCA in dAMD-relevant stress paradigms are not reported in the provided RPE studies and remain a central evidentiary gap for this indication (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Likewise, while TUDCA rescues phagocytosis and activates MerTK, there are no data here on cathepsin transcription, maturation, or activity in RPE phagolysosomes after TUDCA, precluding claims about normalization of lysosomal proteases in dAMD RPE (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Murase et al., 2015).

Expected Effect  
In a dAMD-relevant RPE assay comprising oxidative and/or ER stress with phagocytosis readouts, the following effects are expected based on the compiled evidence:

- ER stress attenuation and reduced UPR-driven apoptosis: TUDCA should lower CHOP and spliced XBP1 levels and decrease TUNEL/caspase-3/7 activation, improving viability under thapsigargin or oxidative stress, consistent with chemical chaperone–mediated UPR modulation (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- Mitochondrial preservation and anti-apoptosis: TUDCA should suppress Bax translocation/cytochrome c release and maintain mitochondrial membrane integrity, thereby reducing mitochondrial pathway apoptosis and preserving the proton motive force needed for oxidative phosphorylation; while these endpoints have not yet been quantified in RPE with Seahorse or JC-1 in the supplied reports, they are supported mechanistically in retina/neuronal systems and hepatocyte models (Cabrera et al., 2019; Khalaf et al., 2022).  
- Antioxidant reset via NRF2: TUDCA should reduce ROS/MDA, restore NRF2 expression, increase GSH, and upregulate antioxidant enzymes (SOD, CAT, GPX1, NQO1, GCLM), consistent with lower oxidative injury to mitochondrial lipids/proteins and stabilized respiratory capacity (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- Restoration of RPE phagocytosis via MerTK/FAK: Under oxidative stress (H₂O₂), TUDCA is expected to restore POS ingestion/digestion as measured by pHrodo®/FITC assays, accompanied by increased MerTK phosphorylation and maintenance of FAK signaling, potentially via upstream integrin activation; this rescues both recognition/engulfment and lysosomal processing phases (Murase et al., 2015).  
- Anti-inflammatory effects: TUDCA should reduce IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α at mRNA/protein levels in RPE challenged by H₂O₂, limiting cytokine-driven mitochondrial impairment and secondary UPR activation (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- Putative receptor mediation: In endothelial/retinal contexts, TUDCA’s ER-stress and barrier benefits require TGR5; although RPE-specific TGR5 dependency is not demonstrated in the supplied texts, receptor-mediated contributions in the retinal environment are plausible and testable (Lenin et al., 2023).  

Expression and pathway presence in RPE are well established for MerTK, integrins (e.g., αvβ5), and FAK—core components of the POS phagocytosis cascade targeted by TUDCA in RPE cells (Murase et al., 2015).  

Dosing and assay considerations:  
- In ARPE-19, 100 µM TUDCA improved survival under 750 µM H₂O₂; higher concentrations (200–500 µM) impaired viability, indicating a window for benefit (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- In phagocytosis assays, TUDCA increased MerTK phosphorylation at high concentration (1 mM) and improved phagocytosis at lower concentrations (≥ 0.1 µM) under non-H₂O₂ conditions, suggesting multiple dose-dependent mechanisms (direct vs. upstream integrin-mediated pathways) (Murase et al., 2015).  

Endpoints to include for hypothesis validation:  
- ER stress/UPR: GRP78/BiP, sXBP1, CHOP, ATF4, eIF2α-P, ATF6 targets (Alhasani et al., 2020; Kusaczuk, 2019).  
- Mitochondrial bioenergetics: Δψm (JC-1/TMRM), oxygen consumption rate and extracellular acidification rate (Seahorse), cellular ATP (luminescent readout), cytochrome c release/Bax translocation (Cabrera et al., 2019; Khalaf et al., 2022).  
- Redox/inflammation: ROS (DCFH-DA), MDA (TBARS), GSH, NRF2 targets, cytokine ELISAs (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- Phagocytosis: MerTK/FAK phosphorylation, POS binding/engulfment/digestion (pHrodo®/FITC), and key lysosomal proteolysis markers; importantly, add cathepsin D/B/L maturation/activity assays to address the specific lysosomal arm of the hypothesis, which remains untested in the provided literature (Murase et al., 2015; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Overall Evaluation  
Summary judgment  
TUDCA is a mechanistically coherent, repurposable candidate for dAMD that targets central RPE failure modes—ER proteostasis breakdown, mitochondrial injury/apoptosis, oxidative and inflammatory stress—and functionally restores a defining RPE task (POS phagocytosis) via MerTK/FAK signaling under oxidative insult (strengths: convergent mechanistic breadth and direct RPE function rescue) (Alhasani et al., 2020; Cabrera et al., 2019; Murase et al., 2015). However, two critical evidence gaps must be addressed to de-risk the program for dAMD: (1) lack of direct demonstration that TUDCA preserves RPE mitochondrial bioenergetics and ATP production under dAMD-relevant stress, and (2) absence of data that TUDCA normalizes lysosomal cathepsin expression/maturation/activity downstream of phagosome–lysosome fusion (weaknesses: missing bioenergetic and lysosomal endpoints underpinning the hypothesis) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit to dAMD pathophysiology: TUDCA reduces ER stress/UPR effectors (CHOP, sXBP1), blocks mitochondrial pathway apoptosis (Bax/cytochrome c/caspase-3), induces NRF2-driven antioxidant programs, and suppresses inflammatory cytokines—all directly relevant to the ER–mitochondria redox loop that destabilizes RPE in early AMD (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  
- Direct RPE functional efficacy: Restoration of POS phagocytosis via MerTK activation and FAK stabilization under oxidative stress offers a clear, disease-relevant mechanism to preserve outer segment turnover and RPE homeostasis (Murase et al., 2015).  
- Mitochondrial stabilization plausibility: Strong cross-system evidence shows TUDCA preserves mitochondrial membrane structure, limits cytochrome c release, and blocks permeability transition–like events, which would support ATP maintenance under stress (albeit not yet measured in RPE) (Khalaf et al., 2022; Cabrera et al., 2019).  
- Retinal in vivo activity and barrier access: Systemic TUDCA protects photoreceptors and retinal function in multiple rodent disease models; related UDCA crosses the human blood–retinal barrier, and ocular delivery platforms achieve retinal distribution in large animals, supporting translational feasibility (Win et al., 2021; Daruich et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2020).  
- Receptor-mediated tractability: TGR5 dependency for retinal endothelial barrier/inflammation effects offers a defined receptor axis for pharmacodynamic biomarkers in vivo, complementing MerTK/FAK functional readouts in RPE (Lenin et al., 2023).  

Weaknesses and risks  
- Mitochondrial bioenergetics unproven in RPE: No ATP, OCR/ECAR, or Δψm data in stressed RPE after TUDCA are provided; this is a pivotal gap because preservation of energy production is central to the proposed disease-modifying effect in dAMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  
- Lysosomal protease (cathepsin) claims unsupported: While TUDCA rescues phagocytosis and MerTK signaling, there are no data here that TUDCA restores cathepsin expression/maturation/activity in RPE; the stated hypothesis reference to “alleviates ER stress–induced downregulation of MERTK and cathepsins” is not substantiated in the supplied sources and should be considered unverified for RPE/dAMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Murase et al., 2015).  
- Dose–mechanism tension: In RPE phagocytosis assays, MerTK phosphorylation was robust at 1 mM, whereas phagocytosis enhancement occurred at ≥ 0.1 µM, suggesting indirect upstream mechanisms at low doses and raising questions about clinically relevant concentrations for direct MerTK phosphorylation (Murase et al., 2015).  
- Heterogeneity of mechanistic readouts: In one RPE phagocytosis study, GRP78 was not changed by TUDCA during rescue, indicating ER stress reduction is not required for the pro-phagocytic effect in that setting; mechanism may differ across contexts (Murase et al., 2015).  
- Evidence quality and generalizability: Several RPE-focused studies are from lower-tier journals, and many mechanistic claims derive from non-RPE systems; rigorous replication with polarized primary human RPE and in dAMD-relevant in vivo models is needed (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Decision framework and next experiments  
Given the favorable mechanistic alignment and preclinical retinal efficacy, TUDCA merits advancement to a focused preclinical validation plan tailored to dAMD, gated by resolution of the bioenergetics and lysosomal gaps:  

- Bioenergetics/mitochondria (must-have): In human primary, polarized RPE under defined oxidative and ER stress (e.g., low-dose H₂O₂, tunicamycin/thapsigargin), quantify Δψm (TMRM), OCR/ECAR (Seahorse), cellular ATP, cytochrome c release, and Bax translocation with and without TUDCA; include NRF2 dependency (siRNA) to map antioxidant mediation (Alhasani et al., 2020; Cabrera et al., 2019).  
- Phagolysosomal proteolysis (must-have): In POS ingestion assays, measure cathepsin D/B/L maturation (pro-/mature forms), activity (fluorogenic substrates), lysosomal pH and degradative capacity; test whether TUDCA normalizes these under ER/oxidative stress and whether effects require MerTK or integrin/FAK signaling (Murase et al., 2015).  
- ER–mitochondria crosstalk mapping (should-have): Track UPR arms (IRE1/JNK, PERK/eIF2α/ATF4, ATF6) alongside mitochondrial readouts to define causal sequence; test whether TUDCA biases PERK toward pro-survival signaling and reduces CHOP/TRB3 induction (Alhasani et al., 2020; Kusaczuk, 2019).  
- In vivo dAMD-relevant model (should-have): In RPE mitochondrial/oxidative stress models (e.g., sodium iodate low-dose; cigarette-smoke–derived oxidants), test systemic and local TUDCA dosing for RPE structure/function (autofluorescence, OCT, ERG) and RPE phagocytosis biomarkers, plus mitochondrial/UPR markers (Win et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2020).  
- Pharmacology/PK/PD (must-have): Link ocular exposure (vitreous/choroid/RPE) to effect using delivery modalities with translational potential (oral UDCA as a proxy crossing BRB; suprachoroidal implant pharmacokinetics); incorporate PD markers (retinal ER stress proteins, NRF2 targets) (Daruich et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2020; Lenin et al., 2023).  

Positioning in dAMD  
If the above gaps are closed positively, TUDCA would be positioned as a proteostasis–mitochondria stabilizer that preserves RPE phagocytic function and metabolic sufficiency—an upstream, disease-modifying approach complementary to complement modulation and to anti-angiogenic strategies (the latter relevant if geographic atrophy coexists with incipient neovascularization) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). The MerTK/FAK rescue of phagocytosis provides a strong functional anchor for mechanism-based biomarkers, while the antioxidant/UPR signatures support PD tracking in early-phase clinical translation (Murase et al., 2015; Alhasani et al., 2020).

Go/no-go conclusion  
- Go for preclinical dAMD validation with a clear focus on mitochondrial bioenergetics and lysosomal protease function in RPE, using polarized human RPE and in vivo oxidative/ER-stress models that recapitulate early dAMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  
- No-go for cathepsin-centered claims until direct RPE evidence is generated; likewise, refrain from asserting ATP rescue in RPE until OCR/ATP/Δψm data are obtained (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

On balance, TUDCA is a high-priority repurposing candidate with strong mechanistic plausibility and supportive retinal efficacy, but it requires targeted, RPE-centric bioenergetics and lysosomal validation to meet decision-grade standards for a dAMD program (Cabrera et al., 2019; Win et al., 2021; Murase et al., 2015; Alhasani et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is a fully synthetic small molecule in the 4-aminoquinoline (4AQ) class, developed in the mid-20th century as a hydroxylated analogue of chloroquine (CQ) to improve tolerability; HCQ differs from CQ by a terminal hydroxyl group on the side chain (HCQ: C18H26ClN3O, 336 g/mol; CQ: C18H26ClN3, 320 g/mol) (Browning, 2014a, 2014b). Industrially, HCQ can be prepared by condensing N1-N-ethyl-N1-β-hydroxyethyl-1,4-pentanediamine with 4,7-dichloroquinoline, paralleling the CQ route from the same quinoline core with an altered aminoalkyl side chain (Rainsford et al., 2015). As a class, HCQ/CQ are alkylated 4-aminoquinolines: weak, amphiphilic bases bearing a flat quinoline nucleus and a basic side chain that traverse membranes in unprotonated form and undergo protonation-dependent sequestration in acidic intracellular compartments (lysosomes, endosomes, Golgi) — a defining pharmacologic property (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Chloroquine’s two basic centers (pKa ≈ 10.2 and 8.1) illustrate the protonation behavior that drives lysosomal trapping; at lysosomal pH (≈ 4–5) these agents become diprotonated and accumulate, with lysosome:plasma distribution ratios measured on the order of ≈ 160 000 and intralysosomal concentrations up to ≈ 2 × 10⁻² M reported for CQ, elevating lysosomal pH toward ≈ 6 (Browning, 2014b, 2014a). Pharmacokinetically, HCQ exhibits high oral bioavailability (≈ 0.7–0.8), an extremely large apparent volume of distribution (> 40 000 L), and a long terminal elimination half-life (≈ 40–60 days), with blood concentrations exceeding plasma due to extensive intracellular partitioning and tissue sequestration (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Melanin-containing ocular tissues are prominent depots; with chronic ingestion, uveal and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) concentrations can reach up to ≈ 10 000× plasma, reflecting lysosomal trapping and melanin binding (Browning, 2014a). Enantiomer-specific disposition has been observed for HCQ, with stereoselective accumulation noted in blood compartments, underscoring complex distribution kinetics (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Clinically, HCQ is commonly administered as the sulfate salt, and CQ as the phosphate salt (Neto et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
HCQ and CQ were developed as antimalarials and subsequently repurposed as disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), with additional uses across dermatology and other immune-mediated conditions; HCQ is generally preferred over CQ for chronic therapy due to a better safety profile while maintaining comparable immunomodulatory efficacy (Rainsford et al., 2015; Neto et al., 2020). Broad clinical applications documented for HCQ/CQ include SLE, RA, primary Sjögren’s syndrome, discoid/cutaneous lupus erythematosus, polymorphous light eruption, solar urticaria, porphyria cutanea tarda, and other inflammatory dermatoses, reflecting lysosomotropic and immune-modulating actions (Rainsford et al., 2015; Rapparini et al., 2025). Mechanistically motivated repurposing has extended to autophagy inhibition in oncology trials, typically at daily doses far exceeding rheumatologic regimens, although HCQ is not approved as an anticancer adjuvant (Yusuf et al., 2023). Over recent decades HCQ prescriptions have increased substantially due to its relative affordability and systemic safety advantages, expanding the exposed population and the need for ocular safety surveillance (Yusuf et al., 2023).

With respect to retinal disease, the literature emphasizes retinotoxic risk and mechanistic links to RPE lysosomal dysfunction rather than therapeutic benefit in degenerative macular disease; authoritative pharmacology and ophthalmology sources do not provide evidence that HCQ/CQ have been used as treatments for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and instead catalogue retinal toxicity mechanisms and monitoring practices associated with long-term systemic use (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). Multiple summaries note that available data do not support therapeutic use of 4AQs for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerations, while documenting ocular accumulation, lysosomal alkalinization, and RPE stress as central safety concerns (Browning, 2014a). Retinopathy, although uncommon at recommended doses, is a recognized dose- and duration-related adverse effect that can be irreversible and may progress after drug cessation, motivating dose caps and structured ophthalmic screening (Rainsford et al., 2015; Ding et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action  
Lysosomotropism and lysosomal alkalinization  
HCQ/CQ are canonical lysosomotropic weak bases that accumulate massively within acidic intracellular organelles and elevate their pH, directly impairing acidity-dependent lysosomal hydrolases, receptor recycling, and degradative pathways including autophagy (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b). In vitro and cell-system studies report that chloroquine exposure increases lysosomal pH from ≈ 4–5 toward ≈ 6, a change sufficient to inhibit cathepsin activities and other acid hydrolases; pharmacologic blockade of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase with bafilomycin A₁ abrogates CQ’s lysosomotropism and toxicity, pinpointing disruption of lysosomal acidification as the proximal driver (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b). In RPE cells specifically, the lysosomotropic alkalinization by 4AQs inhibits lysosomal enzyme activity and autophagic flux, leading to accumulation of undegraded material; experimental inhibition of vacuolar acidification with bafilomycin phenocopies these degradative defects, indicating that pH elevation per se is sufficient to impair RPE lysosomal function (Guha et al., 2014).

Immune modulation and nucleic acid sensing  
Elevation of endolysosomal pH by 4AQs inhibits MHC class II antigen processing and presentation and blocks activation of endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR-3/7/9), thereby reducing MyD88-dependent interferon production and dampening pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion from mononuclear cells and dendritic cells (IL-1, IL-6, TNF, IFN-α/γ, CCL4) (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). The class also interferes with cGAS–STING pathway activation through inhibition of cGAMP synthase and reduces T-cell co-stimulatory signaling (e.g., CD154), a mechanistic constellation that explains DMARD efficacy without significant increases in opportunistic infections (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020; Browning, 2014b). Additional molecular interactions reported for 4AQs include DNA binding/intercalation, kinase pathway modulation (e.g., ERK/MAPK), and diverse enzyme interactions (e.g., cholinesterase), reflecting broad pleiotropy at pharmacologic and suprapharmacologic exposures (Browning, 2014a).

RPE-relevant degradative biology: cathepsins and POS processing  
The RPE depends critically on acidic lysosomes and cathepsin activity to clear the daily phagocytic load of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and maintain autophagic flux; failure of this system yields lipofuscin accumulation and contributes to AMD pathogenesis (Sharif, 2015). Multiple lysosomal proteases are expressed by RPE, including cysteine cathepsins B, L, and S as well as aspartyl cathepsin D; cathepsins are synthesized as pre-proenzymes, processed via the secretory pathway, and activated in the acidic lumen of late endosomes/lysosomes (Sharif, 2015). In human RPE/choroid and RPE cell lines, both inactive and active forms of cathepsin B, L, and S have been detected; functional studies show that broad cysteine protease inhibition or cathepsin S knockdown impairs POS degradation and increases lipofuscin-like inclusions, underscoring their role in RPE proteostasis (Sharif, 2015). Cathepsin D, a major lysosomal aspartyl protease in RPE, is essential for POS processing; its maturation and catalytic efficiency are strongly pH-dependent and occur within the acidic lysosomal lumen (Cardoso et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).

CQ/HCQ disrupt lysosomal proteolysis and lysosome dynamics in RPE  
In RPE models, CQ induces a rapid lysosomal pH increase followed by partial pH recovery, yet produces persistent lysosomal enlargement, accumulation of undegraded endocytic, phagocytic, and autophagic cargos, and a progressive reduction in accessibility of enlarged lysosomes to the endocytic pathway — a phenotype consistent with impaired autolysosome reformation and failure to regenerate a pool of degradatively competent lysosomes (Cardoso et al., 2023). A salient molecular signature of CQ exposure is accumulation of pro-cathepsin D and the lysosomal membrane protein LAMP1 without corresponding mRNA increases, indicating impaired processing/turnover rather than transcriptional upregulation; protease inhibitor treatment phenocopies this pro-cathepsin D accumulation, linking CQ’s effect to reduced proteolytic capacity (Cardoso et al., 2023). Although lysosomotropic agents can activate TFEB-dependent lysosomal gene transcription at high concentrations, the inhibitory effects on cathepsin maturation and lysosome reformation dominate in RPE models at low doses and precede any compensatory changes in gene expression (Cardoso et al., 2023).

HCQ further impairs RPE lysosomes by perturbing cholesterol homeostasis and promoting lysosomal membrane permeability (LMP), with cytosolic release of cathepsin B  
Beyond general autophagy/lysosome inhibition, HCQ suppresses mTORC1-dependent cholesterol biosynthesis, a change that increases lysosomal membrane permeability and allows lysosomal cathepsin B to translocate into the cytosol, where it can activate caspase-dependent apoptosis and drive caspase-independent phosphatidylserine externalization; these effects are mitigated by neutral pH-selective cathepsin B inhibition and exacerbated by pharmacologic cholesterol lowering (simvastatin) or depletion (methyl-β-cyclodextrin) (Wicks et al., 2022). These data in ARPE-19 RPE cells indicate that HCQ-induced lysosomal dysfunction and LMP sensitize RPE to additional stressors (e.g., UV), compounding vulnerability in aging retinal tissue (Wicks et al., 2022).

RPE/retinal stress signatures and storage phenotypes with 4AQ exposure  
Cell and animal studies document that 4AQ exposure produces RPE and retinal stress consistent with impaired lysosomal degradation: multilamellar myeloid bodies in RPE, photoreceptors, and ganglion cells; inhibition of oxidative enzymes in photoreceptors; decreased retinal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and glutathione with increased lipid peroxidation; disruption of the blood–retina barrier; and inhibition of protein synthesis in RPE culture (Browning, 2014a). In RPE cell culture, high concentrations of CQ perturb fusion of autophagic vesicles, increase LC3-II and p62, and can drive cell death, while intravitreal bafilomycin reproduces opsin-loaded phagolysosome accumulation, affirming that alkalinization is sufficient to cause degradative backlog (Guha et al., 2014). Chronic CQ treatment in mice increases mRNA expression of v-H⁺-ATPase and TFEB, consistent with compensatory attempts to reacidify lysosomes and enhance biogenesis, but does not normalize degradative function during exposure (Guha et al., 2014).

Absence of evidence for “low-dose stabilization” of lysosomal pH in RPE  
Across mechanistic summaries and primary RPE studies, there is no evidence that low-dose HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH at an “optimal” value, preserves cathepsin activity, or enhances POS degradation; rather, the consistent effect is lysosomal alkalinization with inhibition of lysosomal enzymes (including cathepsin B) and blockade of autophagic/lysosomal degradation (Browning, 2014a). In fact, low-dose CQ already yields accumulation of pro-cathepsin D and cargo buildup in RPE, indicating that even modest lysosomotropic perturbation degrades proteolytic competence, counter to the hypothesis (Cardoso et al., 2023).

Pharmacokinetic and ocular deposition constraints  
The extreme tissue distribution and ocular melanin binding of 4AQs undermine precise intraocular dose control: uveal/RPE drug levels can markedly exceed plasma during chronic dosing, and the terminal half-life is long, with months-long detectability after discontinuation due to depot release (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). These properties make “titration” to a narrow, hypothetical lysosomal pH window impractical and raise the risk of sustained lysosomal alkalinization even with ostensibly low systemic doses (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis proposes that submicromolar HCQ will “fine-tune” lysosomal pH in RPE to an optimal range for cathepsin activity, thereby preserving cathepsin function and enhancing POS degradation without blocking autophagy. The aggregate evidence contradicts this at mechanistic, cellular, and pharmacokinetic levels.

- Cathepsins in RPE require an acidic lumen for zymogen processing and catalytic function, and multiple cathepsins (B, L, S, D) are expressed and active in RPE lysosomes where they regulate POS degradation and autophagy; broad cysteine protease inhibition or specific cathepsin S knockdown impairs POS clearance and increases lipofuscin-like inclusions, demonstrating the acid-dependent protease requirement (Sharif, 2015). In this context, 4AQs act as lysosomal alkalinizers that inhibit acid hydrolases; CQ/HCQ inhibit cathepsin B and disrupt cathepsin D processing, with CQ causing pro-cathepsin D accumulation and reduced maturation into the active enzyme, a phenotype directly linked to impaired lysosomal proteolysis and cargo clearance (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). Therefore, the expected effect of submicromolar HCQ is not preservation but reduction of cathepsin function in RPE lysosomes, with consequent impairment of POS proteolysis (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023).

- In RPE cells, CQ/HCQ exposure impairs autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, producing enlarged, cargo-laden lysosomes that are progressively less accessible to endocytic inputs; these dynamics deplete the pool of degradatively competent lysosomes needed for daily POS processing, an effect observed even at “low-dose” CQ and preceding transcriptional responses (Cardoso et al., 2023). Thus, in assays measuring POS degradation and lysosomal flux, HCQ is predicted to slow, not enhance, turnover (Cardoso et al., 2023).

- HCQ further increases lysosomal membrane permeability and releases cathepsin B into the cytosol by impairing mTORC1-dependent cholesterol biosynthesis, activating pro-death signaling and phosphatidylserine externalization; pharmacologic cholesterol lowering/depletion magnify these effects, suggesting that HCQ’s action sensitizes RPE to metabolic and environmental stress rather than stabilizing proteolysis (Wicks et al., 2022).

- Beyond lysosomal pH, 4AQs disrupt other RPE functions essential for photoreceptor support: CQ inhibits rod outer segment phagocytosis in human/pig RPE cell lines, and HCQ/CQ inhibit OATP1A2 in human RPE, potentially perturbing all-trans-retinol uptake and the visual cycle — liabilities expected to worsen POS handling and photoreceptor maintenance in AMD models (Yusuf et al., 2023).

- The claim that “over-acidification” in RPE lysosomes needs moderation lacks evidentiary support in this literature corpus; the dominant pathologic signal in RPE aging and AMD models is lysosomal under-acidification/alkalinization and degradative impairment, which 4AQs exacerbate rather than correct (Guha et al., 2014).

- Pharmacokinetically, due to massive ocular accumulation and prolonged tissue persistence, “low systemic dose” does not guarantee low intra-RPE exposure; achieving and maintaining a narrow “optimal pH” window is improbable and unsafe for chronic indications with slowly reversible tissue exposure (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

In sum, in assays of RPE lysosomal function and POS degradation, the most probable outcomes of HCQ at submicromolar concentrations are lysosomal pH elevation, inhibited cathepsin activity/maturation (including cathepsin B inhibition and pro-cathepsin D accumulation), impaired autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, increased LMP with cytosolic cathepsin B release, inhibition of POS phagocytosis, and potential disruption of retinoid transport — all expected to reduce, not enhance, POS degradation (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023; Wicks et al., 2022; Yusuf et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths for development feasibility  
- Extensive clinical pharmacology and systemic experience: HCQ has well-characterized oral pharmacokinetics, metabolism, and drug–drug interactions, with validated immunomodulatory mechanisms (endolysosomal pH elevation, TLR/cGAS–STING inhibition, cytokine suppression) across rheumatology and dermatology; supply chains and clinical dosing paradigms are established, enabling rapid translational work if warranted (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020; Rainsford et al., 2015). The compound’s canonical lysosomotropic action makes it a useful positive control for modeling lysosomal alkalinization and degradative impairment in RPE assays benchmarking alternative, mechanistically restorative strategies (Browning, 2014b).

- Lower ocular toxicity relative to CQ at equipotency: HCQ is generally less retinotoxic than CQ, a difference attributed in part to greater polarity and lower lipophilicity; however, the class risk remains dose- and duration-dependent and clinically significant (Browning, 2014a; Rainsford et al., 2015).

Critical weaknesses for dry AMD  
- Mechanistic conflict with therapeutic goal: RPE catabolism of POS requires acidic lysosomes and intact cathepsin maturation/activity; 4AQs elevate lysosomal pH, inhibit cathepsin activity (including cathepsin B) and maturation (cathepsin D), impair autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, and induce cargo accumulation — a set of changes that predict impaired POS processing and enhanced lipofuscin burden rather than restoration of lysosomal proteolysis (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). No evidence in RPE/AMD models supports the hypothesis that “low-dose” HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH to optimize cathepsin function; the reported outcomes consistently indicate degradative inhibition (Browning, 2014a).

- Ocular tropism and prolonged tissue persistence: The combination of melanin binding and lysosomal trapping produces extreme ocular accumulation and very slow washout, making precise intraocular dose control infeasible and raising the risk of prolonged lysosomal alkalinization even after dose reduction or cessation (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b).

- Added liabilities in RPE and retina: HCQ promotes lysosomal membrane permeability and cytosolic cathepsin B release in RPE, sensitizing cells to UV and cholesterol-lowering stresses; CQ/HCQ also inhibit POS phagocytosis and OATP1A2 in RPE, potentially disrupting retinoid uptake and the visual cycle, and they induce retinal stress signatures (oxidative enzyme inhibition, antioxidant depletion, barrier disruption) — all detrimental in the aging macula (Wicks et al., 2022; Yusuf et al., 2023; Browning, 2014a).

- Absence of supportive precedent in AMD: Comprehensive pharmacologic and ophthalmic reviews provide no evidence that HCQ/CQ have been successfully used to treat dry AMD or analogous retinal degenerations; rather, they underscore retinotoxic risk and mechanisms consistent with RPE lysosomal dysfunction (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

Strategic implications and recommendation  
The central hypothesis — that low-dose HCQ can fine-tune RPE lysosomal pH to preserve cathepsin activity and enhance POS degradation — is at odds with the mechanistic canon and RPE-focused data for 4AQs, which consistently demonstrate lysosomal alkalinization, cathepsin inhibition or maturation block, impaired lysosome reformation and autophagic flux, and accumulation of undegraded cargo (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). No cited evidence shows that HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH or improves POS degradation in RPE or AMD models; on the contrary, RPE studies with CQ/HCQ and mechanistic summaries emphasize inhibited lysosomal enzymes and autophagy as core actions (Browning, 2014a; Guha et al., 2014). Given extreme ocular accumulation and prolonged tissue retention, exploratory dosing aimed at a narrow “optimal” intralysosomal pH is neither controllable nor safe in a chronic neurodegenerative indication; adverse lysosomal effects could persist despite dose adjustments due to depot release (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). If the program goal is to restore RPE lysosomal proteolysis and POS turnover in dry AMD, agents that acidify lysosomes, facilitate cathepsin maturation/activity, or pharmacologically promote lysosome reformation (as suggested by pathways implicated in CQ-induced defects) align mechanistically, whereas HCQ/CQ, as archetypal alkalinizers and autophagy inhibitors, do not (Cardoso et al., 2023).

Conclusion: HCQ (Sigma-Aldrich H0915) is not a suitable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD under the proposed mechanism. The weight of biochemical, cellular, and pharmacokinetic evidence indicates HCQ will alkalinize RPE lysosomes, inhibit cathepsin function and maturation, impair autophagic flux and POS processing, and increase RPE vulnerability to stress, while ocular accumulation and long half-life amplify risk; no supportive evidence exists for benefit in dry AMD (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023; Wicks et al., 2022; Browning, 2014b). I recommend against advancing HCQ for AMD and suggest redirecting efforts toward mechanisms that restore lysosomal acidity, cathepsin activity, and lysosome reformation in RPE (Cardoso et al., 2023).
