Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Brefeldin A (BFA) is a natural product originally isolated in 1958 from Penicillium decumbens, and its discovery marked the beginning of intensive studies on its unique ability to disrupt intracellular protein trafficking (Hung, 2020). Structurally, BFA is a macrolide characterized by a complex fused system comprising a cyclopentane moiety linked to a 13-membered lactone, and this distinctive architecture has spurred extensive synthetic and medicinal chemistry efforts over the past decades (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015). By targeting the secretory pathway, BFA acts as a Golgi transport inhibitor, primarily through its binding to a protein complex involving a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) and the small G protein Arf1. This binding event results in the rapid disassembly of the Golgi apparatus and redistribution of its components back into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Hung, 2020). BFA is therefore classified among natural product inhibitors of intracellular trafficking, a group that has long served as invaluable research tools in cell biology to dissect the mechanisms of vesicular transport and Golgi-ER dynamics. Its broad bioactivities—as an antiviral, antifungal, and antimitotic agent—have principally been exploited in preclinical research rather than clinical therapeutics (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, BFA has been employed almost exclusively as a biochemical probe to investigate protein processing, secretion, and Golgi morphology in diverse eukaryotic cells. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that BFA’s ability to stall ER-to-Golgi trafficking can modulate various cellular processes including secretion of cytokines, hormones, and growth factors (Hung, 2020). Its documented effects on blocking transport have been leveraged in cancer cell studies where BFA-induced apoptosis and cell cycle arrest were observed, owing to mislocalization of key signaling molecules (Stierle & Stierle, 2015). Despite these promising cellular effects, the clinical development of BFA as a conventional therapeutic agent has been hindered by issues such as poor bioavailability and significant toxicity with prolonged exposure (Seehafer et al., 2013). Importantly, while BFA has not been directly applied in clinical studies for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or any similar degenerative retinal diseases, its mechanistic action on intracellular trafficking, ER stress, and protein secretion renders it an intriguing candidate for repurposing. In the context of AMD, where complement dysregulation and lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells play a critical pathogenic role, BFA could potentially offer a novel means of attenuating the buildup of complement components and misfolded proteins (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). While none of the published literature explicitly documents the use of BFA for AMD therapy, related studies in RPE cellular models have highlighted the importance of complement modulation and lysosomal restoration, establishing a rationale for investigating trafficking inhibitors such as BFA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
On a molecular level, the mechanism of action for Brefeldin A is well characterized. BFA binds to the complex comprising a catalytic GEF and the small GTPase Arf1, inhibiting the exchange of GDP for GTP on Arf1. This inhibition precludes proper recruitment and coat assembly for vesicle budding at the Golgi membranes, leading to a collapse of the Golgi structure and the retrograde redistribution of Golgi proteins to the ER (Hung, 2020). The immediate consequence of this inhibition is a profound disruption in the secretory pathway, which not only halts the export of proteins but also results in an accumulation of proteins within the ER. In cell types where the regulated secretion of proteins is critical for homeostasis, such as in RPE cells, this effect can have dual ramifications. On the one hand, it may help prevent the secretion of misfolded or aberrantly processed proteins, including complement components that are implicated in local inflammation and lysosomal deposition (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). On the other hand, the blockade of Golgi trafficking may transiently lower the secretion of proteins that otherwise contribute to the local pool of complement proteins which, if misfolded or overproduced, could lead to an increase in intracellular complement activation and subsequent deposition of the membrane attack complex (MAC, particularly C5b-9) within lysosomes (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In RPE cells, where robust daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) is essential, the maintenance of lysosomal function is critical; overburdening of lysosomes with complement-derived debris has been implicated in the formation of drusen and lipofuscin accumulation, both of which underlie AMD pathology (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The proposed intervention using BFA therefore leverages its well-established ability to modulate protein trafficking to indirectly reduce the burden of misfolded or overabundant complement proteins on the lysosomal system, thereby potentially restoring cathepsin activity and overall lysosomal function in RPE cells.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing BFA in dry AMD is that brief pulses of BFA administration will selectively inhibit the ER-to-Golgi trafficking route in RPE cells, thereby reducing the processing and secretion of misfolded complement proteins. RPE cells are known to contribute to local complement activation through the production and turnover of various complement components; in AMD, aberrant complement regulation leads to increased turnover, formation of complement split products, and the deposition of terminal complement complexes (C5b-9) in the lysosomes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The expected outcome of BFA treatment would be a reduction in the export of these misfolded or excessively generated complement proteins, ultimately leading to decreased local complement activation and a reduction in lysosomal overload by MAC proteins. Experimental evidence from studies using compstatin analogues (e.g., Cp40) in Y402H-RPE cell models has shown that complement inhibition can restore lysosomal function and cathepsin activity, thereby reducing lysosome size, diminishing drusen-like deposits, and improving the overall cellular phenotype (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015). By analogy, transient BFA treatment is anticipated to produce similar beneficial effects on lysosomal physiology in RPE cells, provided that the inhibition is carefully timed to avoid prolonged exposure which could be deleterious (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Furthermore, because RPE cells are responsible for the daily clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, maintaining an unencumbered lysosomal system is crucial for long-term retinal health. The expected biochemical cascade following BFA administration would therefore include a reduction in ER stress due to diminished protein export, lower secretion of misfolded complement proteins, and a subsequent decrease in complement-mediated lysosomal damage. This in turn should lead to a stabilization or even an improvement in cathepsin levels and activity, promoting a more efficient degradation of cellular debris and restoration of POS clearance (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential repurposing of Brefeldin A as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD is innovative and grounded in a detailed understanding of both its mechanism of action and the pathophysiology of AMD. Several strengths underlie this approach. First, BFA has a well-characterized molecular mechanism that directly affects the secretory pathway by inhibiting ER-to-Golgi trafficking. This offers a mechanistic basis for reducing the secretion of misfolded or aberrantly processed complement proteins—the accumulation of which is a central driver of lysosomal dysfunction and local complement activation in RPE cells (Hung, 2020). Second, preclinical research in AMD models has demonstrated that modulating complement activity, whether through direct inhibition of complement components or by enhancing lysosomal function, can reverse pathological phenotypes associated with the disease (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015). This suggests that a strategy aimed at indirectly reducing complement deposition via interference with protein trafficking holds considerable promise. Third, the idea of using brief pulses of BFA rather than continuous dosing could allow for a transient therapeutic effect that minimizes the known toxicities associated with prolonged BFA exposure—thus potentially overcoming one of the key limitations that has prevented its clinical development in other contexts (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015).

Nonetheless, there are significant challenges and weaknesses that must be addressed before this approach can be advanced. One of the primary concerns relates to the non-selectivity of BFA’s action. Because BFA disrupts a fundamental cellular process, its effects are not confined solely to the trafficking of misfolded complement proteins. It is likely to inhibit the normal secretion of multiple proteins that are essential for RPE cell function, which could inadvertently impair the phagocytosis and processing of photoreceptor outer segments (Hung, 2020; Seehafer et al., 2013). Such disruption could paradoxically exacerbate the very lysosomal dysfunction it is intended to ameliorate, particularly if dosing is not carefully titrated. Furthermore, while transient inhibition may mitigate toxicity, achieving the precise balance between therapeutic efficacy and cellular viability will require rigorous optimization in both in vitro and in vivo models. Another potential drawback is related to pharmacokinetics and delivery. BFA’s poor bioavailability and potential systemic toxicity have long been recognized as obstacles for its use beyond experimental settings (Seehafer et al., 2013). Delivering BFA specifically to the RPE while avoiding off-target effects in other ocular or systemic tissues will demand innovative formulation strategies, such as localized drug delivery systems, which inherently add another layer of complexity to the drug development process. Additionally, while the hypothesis is supported by analogous studies demonstrating that complement modulation can restore lysosomal function in AMD models (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015), there is currently no direct evidence that BFA’s inhibition of ER-to-Golgi trafficking will reproduce these beneficial effects in the delicate environment of the retina. The potential for unforeseen interactions with other components of the RPE’s protein processing machinery or compensatory cellular responses further complicates the translational prospects of this approach.

In summary, as an expert drug development team leader tasked with evaluating promising repurposed drugs for dry AMD, I find the proposal to repurpose Brefeldin A to be both innovative and mechanistically intriguing. The strengths of this candidate lie in its well-characterized molecular target—namely, the inhibition of Arf1-mediated vesicle budding at the Golgi—and its potential to modulate a key pathological feature of AMD, namely the dysregulated secretion and accumulation of complement proteins that leads to lysosomal impairment and MAC deposition (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). However, the inherent risks associated with disrupting a central cellular process cannot be overstated. The lack of selectivity in BFA’s action, potential toxicity from even brief exposures, and challenges in targeting the RPE specifically are serious obstacles that must be systematically addressed. Further preclinical studies are required to delineate the dose-response relationship in RPE cell models, to examine the long-term effects of transient BFA-induced trafficking inhibition on cellular health, and to validate the hypothesis that such intervention can indeed reduce lysosomal MAC deposition and rescue cathepsin activity. Only with convincing evidence from rigorous in vitro and in vivo experiments would it be justified to consider advancing BFA as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. In conclusion, while the proposed use of BFA presents a compelling mechanistic rationale with some supportive preclinical analogies from the literature (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020), significant challenges regarding specificity, delivery, and safety need to be overcome before this approach can be deemed a viable therapeutic option for dry AMD.

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of 2‐hydroxypropyl‐β‐cyclodextrin (HPβCD; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. C0926) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
HPβCD is a chemically modified cyclic oligosaccharide belonging to the cyclodextrin drug class, which consists of cyclic arrangements of glucopyranose units. In the case of HPβCD, hydroxypropyl groups are substituted on the β-cyclodextrin ring, thereby increasing its water solubility and overall biocompatibility while maintaining the inherent toroidal structure with a hydrophobic inner cavity and hydrophilic exterior. This unique architecture allows HPβCD to encapsulate lipophilic compounds such as cholesterol, forming stable inclusion complexes that enhance the solubilization, mobilization, or extraction of these molecules from biological membranes or intracellular compartments (Braga, 2023; Davidson et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020). Originally discovered and adapted as an excipient to improve the solubility and delivery of hydrophobic drugs, cyclodextrins have more recently gained attention as active pharmaceutical ingredients due to their capacity to modulate lipid metabolism. In particular, HPβCD is being repurposed as a therapeutic candidate because of its established ability to reduce cholesterol accumulation in tissues—an effect that is central to its potential role in addressing dry AMD pathology (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, HPβCD has been widely utilized as a pharmaceutical excipient and delivery system with a strong safety record, as evidenced by its FDA-approved use in various formulations. More notably, its cholesterol-binding and mobilizing activity has driven its repurposing for treatment of cholesterol storage disorders, most prominently Niemann–Pick Type C (NPC) disease. In NPC, HPβCD has been administered by various routes—including systemic, intrathecal, and subcutaneous injections—to solubilize and extract unesterified cholesterol from lysosomal compartments, thereby ameliorating the pathological accumulation of lipids in neuronal and peripheral tissues (Davidson et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Kfoury et al., 2025; Rao & Fliesler, 2021). Preclinical studies in NPC models have consistently demonstrated that HPβCD can normalize cholesterol trafficking and extend lifespan in affected animals. Additional biochemical and clinical studies in related fields such as atherosclerosis further underscore the compound’s potency as a cholesterol-mobilizing agent (Braga, 2023; Coisne et al., 2016; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020). Although HPβCD has not been used explicitly in clinical trials for dry AMD to date, the mechanistic rationale for its application is compelling since retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells in dry AMD exhibit lysosomal cholesterol accumulation and associated dysfunction similar to the cellular defects observed in NPC and atherosclerotic conditions (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023). Moreover, retinal studies in mouse models have shown that HPβCD can reduce cholesterol levels in the retina and restore aspects of cellular homeostasis, thereby laying the groundwork for the proposed repurposing in dry AMD (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, HPβCD functions primarily by exploiting its unique cyclic structure, which provides a hydrophobic cavity designed to accommodate cholesterol molecules. The hydrophobic interactions between the cyclodextrin cavity and the sterol ring system of cholesterol enable HPβCD to form a reversible inclusion complex with both free and esterified cholesterol. This process shifts the equilibrium of intracellular cholesterol pools and promotes a net efflux of cholesterol from cellular membranes and lysosomal compartments (El-Darzi et al., 2023; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020).

In cells burdened by cholesterol accumulation—such as RPE cells in the context of drusen formation—the excess cholesterol impairs the fluidity of membranes and disrupts the acidification and enzymatic activity within lysosomes. HPβCD is hypothesized to extract this excess cholesterol from the lysosomal membrane, thereby restoring proper membrane fluidity and normalizing the pH within the lysosome. This in turn is expected to reactivate lysosomal enzymes, such as cathepsins, and restore proper autophagic flux and phagocytic turnover of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Coisne et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

On a biochemical level, studies have shown that HPβCD can upregulate proteins related to cholesterol efflux. For instance, the compound has been observed to modulate the expression of ATP-binding cassette transporters, such as ABCA1 and ABCG1, via liver X receptor (LXR)-dependent pathways. Additionally, HPβCD treatment can alter the cellular distribution of cholesterol by promoting trafficking from the lysosome to other cellular compartments such as the endoplasmic reticulum, where it is enzymatically esterified and eventually excreted (Cougnoux et al., 2023; El-Darzi et al., 2021; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020).

Another important mechanistic aspect is the compound’s influence on lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. HPβCD has been shown to increase the abundance of lysosome-associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) and to activate the transcription factor EB (TFEB), which is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic processes. Such activation contributes to maintaining cellular clearance pathways that are essential for RPE cell health, especially in the face of chronic insult from photoreceptor outer segments and accumulated lipofuscin bisretinoids (Braga, 2023; Brown et al., 2016). Through these molecular interactions, HPβCD may counteract the cellular stress induced by disrupted cholesterol homeostasis, thereby mitigating the dual impact of both lipid accumulation and impaired lysosomal degradation that is central to dry AMD pathogenesis. However, it is noteworthy that some studies have reported that prolonged exposure to HPβCD can induce pro-inflammatory responses and even ototoxicity in animal models, underscoring the importance of optimizing dosing regimens (Houben et al., 2021a, 2021b; Yamada et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis driving the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is that by extracting the excess cholesterol accumulated in the lysosomes of RPE cells, the compound will restore normal cellular functions. The primary expected effect is multifold. First, the removal of cholesterol is anticipated to restore lysosomal pH to its optimal acidic range. An appropriate pH is crucial for the full activation of lysosomal hydrolases, such as cathepsins, which are necessary for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments that normally enter the RPE through phagocytosis (Braga, 2023; El-Darzi et al., 2023). Second, by normalizing membrane fluidity, HPβCD would improve the trafficking and fusion of lysosomes, thus enhancing the clearance of cellular waste. This improved clearance capacity may help resolve drusen-like deposits and prevent inflammatory activation of retinal microglia and macrophages—a process that has been implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Brown et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Houben et al., 2021b).

From a molecular perspective, RPE cells express key proteins involved in cholesterol handling, including NPC1, ABCA1, and LXR. The activation of these pathways after HPβCD application could lead to improved reverse cholesterol transport, where the excess cholesterol is removed from RPE cells and delivered to extracellular acceptors for clearance (Davidson et al., 2016; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020). This facilitated removal is expected to lower intracellular levels of unesterified cholesterol, reduce cholesterol crystal formation, and subsequently attenuate the pro-inflammatory milieu that contributes to RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Braga, 2023; Houben et al., 2021b).

In experimental assays, one might expect to observe a decrease in the levels of cholesterol and cholesterol crystals by biochemical analyses or imaging of RPE cells treated with HPβCD, alongside a normalization of lysosomal pH values measured via pH-sensitive dyes. Enzyme assays should reveal a restoration of cathepsin activity, and phagocytosis assays would ideally demonstrate an increased turnover of POS. Taken together, these effects would not only preserve RPE cell function but also potentially slow the progression of the disease and improve retinal structure and function (Coisne et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, HPβCD represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its well-documented ability to modulate cholesterol homeostasis and improve lysosomal function. The compound’s favorable physicochemical properties—stemming from its cyclic oligosaccharide structure and enhanced solubility due to hydroxypropylation—make it an attractive candidate for drug repurposing. The extensive preclinical evidence in lysosomal cholesterol storage disorders, including NPC disease and atherosclerosis models, provides a solid foundation that supports its potential efficacy in conditions characterized by intracellular cholesterol dysregulation, such as dry AMD (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

One of the major strengths of HPβCD is its multifaceted mechanism of action. It not only physically extracts cholesterol by forming inclusion complexes but also appears to modulate key cellular pathways that govern cholesterol efflux, lysosomal biogenesis, and autophagic clearance. This combined activity has the potential to address several pathological features of dry AMD simultaneously: restoring lysosomal pH, normalizing the activity of pH-dependent enzymes like cathepsins, and enhancing the degradation of deposited photoreceptor outer segments. Additionally, the evidence that HPβCD can reduce inflammatory activation by preventing cholesterol crystal formation and macrophage recruitment further supports its application in a disease state where chronic inflammation is a well-known driver of progression (Brown et al., 2016; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020).

However, there are also notable weaknesses and concerns that must be carefully considered. First, while HPβCD’s safety profile is well-established for its role as an excipient and, to some extent, in NPC clinical trials, significant safety issues have been reported in the context of systemic and even local administration. Ototoxicity has emerged as a recurrent concern in multiple preclinical studies and some clinical observations, which could be particularly problematic if similar toxicities are encountered when used in the delicate tissues of the eye (Braga, 2023; Calias, 2018; Yamada et al., 2021). Moreover, some studies have reported dose-dependent pro-inflammatory effects upon chronic exposure to HPβCD, underscoring the necessity for optimizing dosing regimens and careful monitoring of inflammatory markers (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Hoque et al., 2020).

Another potential challenge is the delivery route. Given that the eye is a compartment with unique barriers and an immunoprivileged status, determining the optimal method of administration (e.g., intravitreal injection, topical eye drops, or systemic administration with targeted delivery) will be critical. The compound’s ability to cross the blood-retina barrier has been demonstrated in preclinical models, but achieving sufficient retinal concentration without systemic toxicity may require advanced formulation strategies, such as encapsulation in polymer-based nanoparticles or the development of polyrotaxane-based delivery systems (Coisne et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

The overall evaluation is therefore cautiously optimistic. On the one hand, the strong mechanistic rationale for using HPβCD to address the underlying cholesterol dysregulation and lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD is supported by a robust body of literature from related fields (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020). The compound benefits from established use in other cholesterol accumulation disorders and has clearly defined biochemical activities that could be translated into therapeutic benefits in the context of AMD. On the other hand, significant challenges remain in terms of safety—especially related to ototoxicity and potential inflammatory side effects—and in the optimization of delivery methods that can achieve effective retinal concentrations without off-target toxicity (Braga, 2023; Houben et al., 2021a; Yamada et al., 2021).

Given these considerations, it is recommended that the next phases of drug development focus on detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicity studies specific to ocular tissues, along with the exploration of novel delivery formulations that may mitigate systemic and local adverse effects. Further preclinical validation using AMD-relevant models is warranted to assess functional outcomes such as restoration of lysosomal pH, increased cathepsin activity, improved phagocytic efficiency of POS, and ultimately, preservation of retinal structure and function (Coisne et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

In conclusion, while HPβCD demonstrates considerable potential as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its cholesterol-extracting capabilities and beneficial effects on lysosomal function, the balance between efficacy and safety remains a critical area for further investigation. The strengths—mechanistic depth, prior clinical use in related disorders, and robust preclinical data—are compelling; however, the weaknesses, notably regarding ototoxicity and the need for optimized delivery, must be addressed before moving to clinical trials in AMD patients (Braga, 2023; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020; Yamada et al., 2021). Continued research with targeted formulations, dosing studies, and AMD-specific preclinical models will be essential to determine whether HPβCD can be safely and effectively repurposed to improve outcomes in patients with dry age‐related macular degeneration.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AM580 is a fully synthetic retinoid compound designed as a highly selective agonist for the retinoic acid receptor α (RARα). Its chemical structure—a derivative of naphthalene and benzoic acid—was rationally engineered to confer two key properties: a more rigid molecular architecture compared with the natural ligand all‐trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and a marked preferential binding to RARα over other retinoid receptor subtypes (RARβ and RARγ) (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992). The molecule’s chemical name, 4-(5,6,7,8-tetrahydro-5,5,8,8-tetramethyl-2-naphthalenyl)carboxamido]benzoic acid, reflects its derivation from a series of modifications intended to enhance receptor selectivity and bioactivity (Martin et al., 1992). AM580 belongs to the broader class of retinoids—compounds that are either natural derivatives of vitamin A or synthetically modified analogues—which function as ligands for nuclear hormone receptors. Retinoids have been exploited in various fields of medicine due to their ability to modulate cellular differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis by activating retinoic acid receptor (RAR) and retinoid X receptor (RXR) pathways (Cras et al., 2010; Martin et al., 1992). In the case of AM580, its design emphasizes selective RARα activation, as demonstrated by its 30-fold higher binding affinity for RARα compared to RARβ and RARγ (Teng et al., 1996; Martin et al., 1992), making it an excellent molecular tool for dissection of RARα-specific biological responses.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, retinoids have been at the forefront of differentiation therapy, with ATRA being successfully employed in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) (Garattini et al., 2007; Garattini et al., 1997). However, the clinical use of natural retinoids like ATRA has been limited by drawbacks such as isomerization, rapid metabolism, and broad receptor engagement leading to unnecessary side effects (Drowley et al., 2020; Cras et al., 2010). These limitations spurred the development of receptor subtype–selective ligands, among which AM580 emerged as a leading RARα-selective agonist (Martin et al., 1992). Beyond oncology, synthetic retinoids have been investigated in a variety of contexts including dermatology and even cardiovascular applications (Nagy et al., 2012; Petrukhin, 2013); however, more recent studies have explored the potential ocular applications of retinoid receptor agonists. In particular, a growing body of literature has begun to examine the effects of RAR agonists on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that activation of RARα in RPE cells by compounds such as AM580 can modulate epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and improve cellular functions relevant to retinal homeostasis (Kobayashi et al., 2021). Although not previously approved as an ocular therapeutic, the compound’s use in research settings—including those investigating phagocytic processes in the RPE—provides a promising precedent for repurposing it for conditions like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of AM580 is well delineated at the molecular level. As an RARα agonist, it binds with high affinity to the ligand-binding domain of RARα, a nuclear receptor that functions as a ligand-dependent transcription factor. Upon ligand binding, the receptor undergoes a conformational change that results in the dissociation of co-repressor complexes and the recruitment of co-activators and other transcriptional machinery. This ligand-induced activation facilitates the heterodimerization of RARα with retinoid X receptor (RXR), followed by binding to retinoic acid response elements (RAREs) in the promoter regions of target genes (Garattini et al., 2007; Teng et al., 1996).  
Notably, AM580’s structural modification—featuring a polar amide linkage—enhances its selectivity for RARα by promoting specific hydrogen bonding interactions within the receptor’s binding pocket that are not available in RARβ or RARγ (Teng et al., 1996). Once activated, RARα modulates a variety of downstream genes. Among these, studies have recently indicated that selective RARα activation can lead to the upregulation of milk fat globule epidermal growth factor 8 (MFGE8) in RPE cells (Unknown Reference). MFGE8 plays a critical role in facilitating the bridging of phosphatidylserine (exposed on the shed photoreceptor outer segments (POS)) to integrin receptors—specifically αvβ5—which are expressed on the RPE, thereby promoting efficient phagocytosis (Drowley et al., 2020; Kobayashi et al., 2021). Consequently, AM580’s engagement of RARα is expected to not only drive transcriptional changes related to RPE differentiation and anti-fibrotic responses but also directly enhance phagocytic clearance mechanisms essential for retinal health (Kobayashi et al., 2021). In additional preclinical settings, RARα agonism via AM580 has been implicated in modulating transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling pathways, which further supports its capacity to inhibit aberrant EMT—a process implicated in retinal scarring and progression of dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis under evaluation posits that AM580, by selectively activating RARα at an effective concentration (EC₅₀ ~50 nM as observed in RPE cell assays), will stimulate the transcription of the MFGE8 gene. Upregulation of MFGE8 is crucial because this glycoprotein acts as a “molecular bridge” by binding to phosphatidylserine on POS and to integrin receptors such as αvβ5 on the RPE. Under normal conditions, MFGE8 is an essential mediator of RPE phagocytosis, facilitating the daily clearance of spent outer segments—a process that is impaired in dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2012). Evidence from preclinical studies, including those using Mertk-deficient RPE models, suggests that AM580 treatment can lead to increased MFGE8 levels and a concomitant improvement in POS uptake (Kobayashi et al., 2021). Thus, in the assay proposed by the team, AM580 is expected to restore or enhance the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells by boosting MFGE8 expression. This improved clearance mechanism would help reduce the accumulation of POS debris and lipofuscin—a buildup known to contribute to RPE dysfunction and the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Furthermore, secondary effects such as the inhibition of deleterious EMT processes—which are associated with fibrosis and the progression of dry AMD—may also be realized, thereby preserving or restoring a more differentiated, functional RPE phenotype (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
AM580 represents a compelling therapeutic candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, based on several lines of evidence gathered from the literature. Its primary strength lies in its high degree of selectivity for RARα. This receptor selectivity is critical because it allows for target‐specific modulation of gene expression, potentially reducing the broad side effects observed with natural retinoids like ATRA that activate multiple receptor subtypes (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992; Teng et al., 1996). The structural optimization of AM580 not only confers potent agonistic activity but also provides a pharmacological tool for dissecting the specific roles of RARα in retinal biology, particularly within the RPE. Preclinical studies have underscored the utility of RARα activation in modulating key processes such as cellular differentiation, inhibition of EMT, and enhancement of phagocytic function in RPE cells (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2012).  
However, several potential challenges must also be acknowledged. Retinoid compounds are notorious for their complex pharmacokinetics and potential for off-target effects, including teratogenicity, as evidenced by prior studies of AM580 in teratogenicity models (Elmazar et al., 2001). The delicate balance between efficacy and safety remains a critical issue, particularly for a condition such as dry AMD where long-term treatment is anticipated. Furthermore, while the preclinical evidence supporting the induction of MFGE8 by RARα activation is promising, the available data remain largely confined to in vitro studies and select animal models. Clinical validation in human subjects is still lacking, and the translation of dose levels, tissue penetration, and metabolic stability from the laboratory to the clinic remains an open question (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Another concern is that AM580, while selective, does retain some activity at RARβ and RARγ at higher concentrations (Teng et al., 1996), an effect that may have unpredictable consequences on cell signaling in the complex microenvironment of the RPE. Moreover, the retinoid system is intricately linked with multiple signaling pathways, and long-term modulation may lead to compensatory mechanisms or unforeseen adverse outcomes.  
In summary, the repurposing of AM580 for dry AMD is supported by a robust molecular rationale—its ability to selectively activate RARα is directly linked to the upregulation of MFGE8 and, consequently, the enhancement of POS phagocytosis in RPE cells. This mechanism directly addresses a critical defect in dry AMD pathology, namely the impaired clearance of photoreceptor debris, which is a central driver of retinal degeneration (Garattini et al., 2007; Kobayashi et al., 2021). The preclinical literature offers promising evidence that selective RARα modulation can exert beneficial effects on RPE physiology, including the prevention of EMT and restoration of phagocytic function (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Despite these strengths, the transition from preclinical studies to clinical application will require careful attention to pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic factors, as well as rigorous safety assessments to mitigate risks typical of retinoid therapies. Overall, while challenges remain, AM580’s unique properties render it a promising candidate that merits further investigation in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to fill a significant therapeutic gap in the management of this debilitating condition (Martin et al., 1992; Teng et al., 1996; Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Geldanamycin is a small-molecule inhibitor of heat shock protein 90 (HSP90) that originally garnered attention as a naturally derived product from Streptomyces species, and it belongs to the benzoquinone ansamycin class of compounds. As a natural product, geldanamycin was first isolated for its antibiotic properties and later found to exert potent effects on cellular protein homeostasis by binding the N-terminal ATP-binding pocket of HSP90. This mode of binding disrupts the chaperone function of HSP90, which is responsible for assisting in the stabilization and maturation of numerous client proteins, including signaling regulators and enzymes. Compounds of this chemical class have historically been investigated for their anticancer potential, given that HSP90 plays a central role in sustaining oncogenic signaling by stabilizing mutated or overexpressed proteins. In the context of ocular research, geldanamycin’s ability to modulate proteostasis and inflammatory cascades has prompted its investigation as a potential therapy for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), where dysregulated protein aggregation, impaired autophagy, and chronic inflammation are key pathological features (Piippo et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, geldanamycin and related HSP90 inhibitors have been used primarily as research tools to interrogate the role of molecular chaperones in cancer, neurodegeneration, and cellular stress responses. In preclinical studies, geldanamycin demonstrated the capacity to induce a robust heat shock response characterized by the upregulation of HSP70 and concomitant modulation of client proteins that depend on HSP90. Its inhibition of HSP90 has been extensively explored in models of protein aggregation diseases and in studies of inflammasome regulation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. For example, several reports have provided direct experimental evidence that HSP90 inhibition by geldanamycin prevents the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in human RPE models—specifically in ARPE-19 cells, human embryonic stem cell-derived RPE, and primary human RPE—by disrupting the protective HSP90–SGT1 complex that stabilizes NLRP3, thereby triggering autophagy-mediated clearance of the receptor (Piippo et al., 2018). In related studies, geldanamycin was also shown to induce an HSP70 response that can modulate proteostasis and reduce cellular inflammatory stress, although its high toxicity has consistently been reported as a barrier to clinical application in humans (Chen et al., 2021). While geldanamycin itself has not been approved for clinical use in dry AMD, its mechanistic insights have spurred research into repurposing HSP90 inhibitors for ocular indications, albeit with a need for derivatives or alternative candidates (Chen et al., 2021; Piippo et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, HSP90 functions as an ATP-dependent molecular chaperone that is critical for the correct folding, stabilization, and activation of a wide range of client proteins, including kinases, transcription factors, and components of the inflammasome complex such as NLRP3. Under basal conditions, HSP90, together with its co-chaperone SGT1, forms a complex with NLRP3 that maintains the receptor in an inactive yet activation-competent state. Geldanamycin binds to the N-terminal ATP-binding pocket of HSP90, thereby competitively inhibiting its ATPase activity and disrupting its chaperone cycle. This inhibition leads to the dissociation of the HSP90–SGT1 complex, releasing NLRP3. Once liberated from the protective chaperone complex, NLRP3 is highly unstable and becomes a substrate for intracellular degradation mechanisms. In the specific context of human RPE cells, experimental evidence has shown that geldanamycin preferentially promotes the autophagic clearance of NLRP3 rather than its proteasomal degradation. Mechanistic experiments that used proteasome inhibition with MG-132 and lysosomal/autophagy inhibition with bafilomycin A₁ or chloroquine revealed that when autophagy is intact, geldanamycin drives the degradation of NLRP3 via the autophagy pathway, resulting in a robust reduction in caspase-1 activity and IL-1β secretion (Piippo et al., 2018). This HSP90-dependent regulation of NLRP3 is particularly significant because inflammasome activation in RPE cells is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In addition, geldanamycin induces the expression of HSP70, a cytoprotective chaperone that further contributes to maintaining proteostasis under stress conditions; however, the increase in HSP70 is a double-edged sword, as it reflects cellular stress responses that could have both beneficial and deleterious effects if dysregulated (Chen et al., 2021; Ryhänen, 2011). Notably, the timing of geldanamycin administration is critical: its inhibitory effect on IL-1β secretion is maximal when added immediately prior to the induction of proteasome or autophagy inhibition, indicating that the HSP90 inhibition must occur before the onset of overwhelming proteostatic stress to be effective (Piippo et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic findings, the expected therapeutic effect of geldanamycin in a dry AMD model is multi-pronged. First, by binding to HSP90 and disrupting its stabilization of NLRP3, geldanamycin is anticipated to accelerate the autophagic clearance of NLRP3 complexes. This clearance is expected to blunt the assembly and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, thereby reducing the cleavage of pro-caspase-1 and ultimately diminishing the production and secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β. In the context of dry AMD, where low-grade chronic inflammation and impaired clearance of damaged cellular proteins contribute to disease progression, the suppression of inflammasome activation is a desirable outcome that could help mitigate retinal inflammation and cell death (Piippo et al., 2018). Second, by reducing the persistent activation of the inflammasome, geldanamycin may help preserve lysosomal function, which is critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE. Lysosomal dysfunction and the resultant accumulation of lipofuscin are hallmark features in the pathogenesis of dry AMD; therefore, maintaining efficient lysosomal degradation is key to restoring RPE homeostasis. Although direct evidence linking geldanamycin to enhanced POS digestion is not comprehensively detailed in the current literature excerpts, there is reasonable mechanistic rationale to suggest that improved autophagic flux and decreased inflammatory burden could promote better phagocytic competence in RPE cells (Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025; Piippo et al., 2018). Finally, given that HSP90 inhibition via geldanamycin has been shown to reduce proteostasis stress and modulate key inflammatory pathways, its application in RPE models of dry AMD could result in improved cellular survival and function, potentially slowing or reversing aspects of the degenerative process. It is important to note that the hypothesized effective concentration (EC₅₀ around 500 nM) is based on in vitro studies in RPE cells, and achieving this efficacy in an in vivo ocular setting via intravitreal administration would require careful dosing and pharmacokinetic optimization to mitigate systemic toxicity (Piippo et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
Geldanamycin represents a promising candidate from a mechanistic perspective for treating dry AMD due to its unique mode of action as an HSP90 inhibitor. The strengths of this therapeutic approach include its ability to directly target a key regulatory protein that stabilizes the NLRP3 inflammasome, leading to downregulation of a major pro-inflammatory pathway implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis. Preclinical research in RPE models, including ARPE-19, hESC-derived RPE, and primary human RPE, has consistently demonstrated that geldanamycin can reduce caspase-1 activity and IL-1β secretion by promoting autophagic degradation of NLRP3, which is central to halting the vicious cycle of chronic inflammation (Piippo et al., 2018). This is further supported by studies indicating that proper timing of HSP90 inhibition is crucial to maximize the clearance of NLRP3 and achieve therapeutic benefits before proteostatic stress overwhelms the cellular degradation machinery (Piippo et al., 2018). Additionally, the induction of HSP70 following geldanamycin treatment may confer additional cytoprotective effects by promoting proper protein folding and assisting in the clearance of misfolded proteins, thus helping preserve lysosomal function and potentially improving photoreceptor outer segment (POS) digestion—a process that is compromised in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2021; Ryhänen, 2011).

However, significant challenges limit the clinical translation of geldanamycin. One of the major weaknesses of this therapeutic candidate is its well-documented toxicity profile. Numerous studies have reported that while geldanamycin is effective in modulating HSP90 and reducing inflammasome activation at low nanomolar doses, its inherent cytotoxicity and off-target effects make it unsuitable for direct clinical application. In several experimental settings, geldanamycin has been described as “too toxic for human administration,” with adverse effects observed in both in vitro and in vivo models (Piippo et al., 2018). Such toxicity is believed to arise in part from the quinone moiety of the molecule, which can engage in redox cycling and generate reactive oxygen species, thereby exacerbating cellular stress and impairing normal proteostasis. Furthermore, while the small-molecule nature of geldanamycin is an advantage in terms of drug delivery—especially for routes such as intravitreal injection—the narrow therapeutic window means that fine-tuning the dose to achieve the desired biological effect without incurring toxicity remains a significant hurdle. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
NBDHEX (6-(7-nitro-2,1,3-benzoxadiazol-4-ylthio)hexanol) is a fully synthetic small molecule that belongs to the class of nitrobenzoxadiazole (NBD) derivatives. This compound was originally developed for its robust activity as a glutathione S-transferase (GST) inhibitor, and its synthesis follows methodologies previously reported (Pasello et al., 2011). As a GST inhibitor, NBDHEX is categorized as a “suicide inhibitor” because it covalently binds to the enzyme’s substrate binding site (the H-site) where it reacts with glutathione in the G-site to form a stable complex that inactivates the target enzyme (Filomeni et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2014). In traditional applications, members of this therapeutic class have been predominantly explored as anticancer agents; they have been used to counteract tumor chemoresistance by inhibiting GST isoenzymes that metabolize and neutralize cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents (Pasello et al., 2011; Filomeni et al., 2008). The compound’s design, structure, and biochemical properties have been extensively characterized within an oncology context, with numerous studies documenting its structure–activity relationships and its capacity to overcome multidrug resistance in cell lines from various cancer types (Filomeni et al., 2008; Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, NBDHEX has been investigated almost exclusively within the realm of cancer research. Preclinical studies have applied NBDHEX against musculoskeletal sarcomas, including osteosarcoma, Ewing’s sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma, as well as in small cell lung cancer and melanoma models (Pasello et al., 2011; Filomeni et al., 2008). In these studies, it demonstrated cytostatic and cytotoxic effects with effective concentrations typically in the low micromolar to submicromolar range, even in drug-resistant cancer cell lines (Pasello et al., 2011). Its anticancer activity has been attributed to both the direct inhibition of GST catalytic function and the disruption of GSTP1 interactions with key signaling proteins such as JNK and TRAF2, which are known to modulate apoptosis and stress signaling pathways (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Pasello et al., 2011). In contrast, there is currently no recorded history of NBDHEX having been used in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or any similar ocular degenerative disease. However, several studies have emphasized the importance of GSTP1 in ocular tissues, particularly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where it plays a critical role in detoxification and cellular defense against oxidative stress (Lee et al., 2014). These observations lend indirect support to the hypothesis that modulating GSTP1 activity—even through inhibition—might have therapeutic implications in the context of AMD. Nonetheless, while the anticancer literature provides extensive data on the pharmacology and safety of NBDHEX in oncology, its potential for ocular application remains largely uncharted and would necessitate rigorous preclinical investigation (Lee et al., 2014).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which NBDHEX exerts its biological effects is well delineated in the published literature. As a suicide inhibitor, NBDHEX anchors itself to the active site of GST enzymes, particularly GSTP1, by binding to the hydrophobic substrate binding (H-site) region; once bound, it reacts in the presence of reduced glutathione to produce a stable, inactive complex (Filomeni et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2014). This covalent modification effectively prevents GSTP1 from catalyzing the detoxification reactions normally necessary to neutralize electrophilic and oxidative species. In addition, GSTP1 is known not only for its detoxification role but also for its involvement in protein–protein interactions, most notably with components of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway including c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and TNF receptor-associated factor 2 (TRAF2) (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Pasello et al., 2011). Under basal conditions, GSTP1 binds to JNK and TRAF2, suppressing their downstream pro-apoptotic signaling. By inhibiting GSTP1, NBDHEX disrupts these interactions, thereby relieving the inhibitory constraints and enabling the activation of stress response pathways mediated by JNK (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Pasello et al., 2011).  
In the context of the RPE, GSTP1 has been documented as a zeaxanthin-binding protein and a critical detoxification enzyme whose levels are reduced in AMD-affected retinas (Lee et al., 2014). Indeed, experimental evidence from cancer models has shown that treatment with NBDHEX leads to an accumulation of autophagy markers, including p62 (SQSTM1) and LC3-II, suggesting that the compound can modulate autophagic flux (Sciarretta et al., 2019). In RPE cells, which normally express GSTP1 as part of their intrinsic antioxidant defense (and where GSTP1 expression is known to be developmentally regulated and inducible by light exposure), an increase in intracellular ROS may serve as a signal to activate cytoprotective autophagy pathways (Lee et al., 2014). As autophagy is crucial for the clearance of damaged proteins and cellular debris—including the phagocytosis and degradation of POS—the induction of autophagy via upregulation of p62 and LC3-II is anticipated to enhance the lysosomal clearance capacity of RPE cells. This could potentially counteract the lipofuscin accumulation and impaired phagocytosis that are characteristic of the dry AMD phenotype (Lee et al., 2014).

Such a response would be particularly beneficial in dry AMD, where defective autophagy and dysregulated oxidative stress are believed to contribute to RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration. NBDHEX represents a promising repurposing candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well‐characterized inhibitory activity against GSTP1 and its documented ability to modulate autophagy in other cellular models. One of the key strengths of this candidate is its robust mechanistic rationale: GSTP1 is known to play a dual role in detoxifying ROS and in suppressing pro-autophagic signaling via sequestration of proteins like p62. In RPE cells—where GSTP1 not only contributes to managing oxidative stress but also interacts with protective pigments such as zeaxanthin—the reduction in GSTP1 function observed in AMD patients implies that further controlled modulation of this enzyme might recalibrate cellular stress responses (Sciarretta et al., 2019; Filomeni et al., 2008). The ability of NBDHEX to disrupt GSTP1’s interactions with JNK and TRAF2 adds another layer of therapeutic potential, as the resultant activation of stress-responsive signaling pathways could further promote cell survival mechanisms. Additionally, evidence from cancer models showing increased levels of autophagy markers such as p62 and LC3-II following NBDHEX treatment supports the concept that this compound can induce autophagic flux, which is of paramount importance in RPE cells for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (Sciarretta et al., 2019; Filomeni et al., 2008).

Despite its promise, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. First, the bulk of the extant literature on NBDHEX pertains to its use as an anticancer agent with applications in solid tumors; there is a notable lack of direct preclinical or clinical studies assessing its efficacy and safety in ocular models or specifically in the context of dry AMD (Pasello et al., 2011; Filomeni et al., 2008). The unique environment of the retina, with its high oxygen consumption, photoreceptor interactions, and specialized blood-retinal barriers, poses distinct pharmacokinetic and toxicity challenges that may not be evident in cancer studies. Second, while the hypothesis relies on a controlled increase in ROS to stimulate autophagy, GSTP1 is an essential component of the antioxidant defense system, and its inhibition could theoretically precipitate excessive oxidative damage if the dosage is not meticulously controlled (Lee et al., 2014; Pasello et al., 2011). Furthermore, some studies indicate that NBDHEX may exhibit limited specificity for GSTP1, with a higher affinity for other GST isoenzymes such as GSTM2-2, which could lead to off-target effects and complicate the therapeutic profile of the compound in non-oncologic tissues (Pljesa-Ercegovac et al., 2018; Filomeni et al., 2008). Finally, ocular drug delivery represents a further hurdle; the ability of NBDHEX to penetrate retinal tissues and safely reach RPE cells within the complex structure of the eye has not been demonstrated and would require rigorous formulation and pharmacokinetic optimization.

In summary, NBDHEX exhibits a compelling mechanism of action that aligns well with the pathophysiology of dry AMD—in particular, its potential to re-establish redox balance and promote autophagy in RPE cells by modulating GSTP1 activity. The strengths of this approach lie in both the detailed molecular insights available from cancer research and the established role of GSTP1 in retinal health. Nonetheless, significant gaps in the literature remain with respect to ocular safety, effective dosing, and the specific cellular context of the RPE. As such, while NBDHEX is a scientifically attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, its translation from oncology to ophthalmology must be approached with caution. Preclinical studies using ex vivo RPE models and appropriate animal models of AMD are essential to validate the hypothesized benefits and to address potential off-target effects. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fasudil is a small‐molecule, synthetic isoquinoline derivative that functions as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil forming kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. Originally discovered and subsequently developed for clinical use in the treatment of cerebral vasospasm following subarachnoid hemorrhage, fasudil represents one of the earliest examples of ROCK inhibitors entering the clinic (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). As a member of the ROCK inhibitor class, it has been synthesized and formulated to target the ATP‐binding pocket of both ROCK isoforms (ROCK1 and ROCK2), thereby effectively competing with ATP and suppressing the kinase activity that is normally responsible for phosphorylating downstream molecular substrates such as the myosin light chain (MLC) and LIM kinase (Catral et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2022). The compound’s synthesis generally follows established medicinal chemistry protocols for heterocyclic compounds and includes derivatization steps that yield a potent inhibitor with an IC₅₀ for ROCK inhibition in the submicromolar range, which in the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function has been postulated to be around 300 nM (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Xiao et al., 2022). Fasudil’s chemical structure and its physicochemical properties allow for formulation into ophthalmic preparations, such as intravitreal injections or potentially sustained-release depot systems, making it an interesting candidate for repurposing in ocular diseases. This class of compounds has historically been used to modulate cytoskeletal dynamics, vascular tone, and cellular contractility in both vascular and neural tissues, and the same properties are being leveraged now to target the pathological stiffening and impaired phagocytic function of RPE cells in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Croze et al., 2014; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Fasudil’s therapeutic history spans multiple clinical and preclinical applications that underscore its broad efficacy in modulating ROCK-mediated pathways. Clinically, fasudil has been approved and widely used in Japan since 1995 for the treatment of cerebral vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage, owing to its vasodilatory and anti-contractile properties (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Its clinical use has expanded into experimental paradigms beyond cerebral applications; for instance, fasudil has shown promise in ocular conditions such as diabetic macular edema, where intravitreal administration in combination with bevacizumab demonstrated feasibility and tolerability, and where its ability to modulate inflammatory responses and vascular permeability were beneficial (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). Furthermore, other members of the ROCK inhibitor class have been investigated for ocular applications, including glaucoma and even experimental models of photoreceptor synapse stabilization following retinal detachment (Townes-Anderson et al., 2017; Yamaguchi et al., 2017). Although fasudil itself has not yet been directly applied in clinical trials for dry AMD, its mechanism of action and safety profile in ocular tissues have been well documented in multiple studies. Animal studies in diabetic retinopathy models have also demonstrated that fasudil can reverse detrimental cytoskeletal changes and restore barrier integrity in RPE cells (Rothschild et al., 2017). Additionally, preclinical data indicate that ROCK inhibitors can improve wound repair responses and prevent epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in RPE cells, which is a hallmark of cellular dysfunction in geographic atrophy – the advanced stage of dry AMD (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Collectively, while fasudil’s historic use has largely focused on vascular and diabetic complications, its repurposing for dry AMD is supported by mechanistic parallels in RPE cytoskeletal plasticity, phagocytosis, and anti-inflammatory modulation (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, fasudil acts by binding to the ATP-binding site of ROCK enzymes, thereby competitively inhibiting their kinase activity (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Under normal cellular conditions, active ROCK phosphorylates several substrates including the myosin light chain (MLC) and myosin phosphatase target subunit 1 (MYPT1), which leads to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stabilization of actin stress fibers, and formation of focal adhesions (Catral et al., 2024; Rothschild et al., 2017). In the context of age-related retinopathies, there is mounting evidence that hyperactivity of the ROCK pathway leads to increased contractile force within the RPE cytoskeleton. This hypercontractility contributes to reduced cellular flexibility and impairs the formation of the phagocytic cups that are critical for the internalization of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) – a process that is essential for retinal homeostasis and visual cycle maintenance (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). Fasudil’s inhibition of ROCK thereby mitigates these cytoskeletal alterations by decreasing the phosphorylation levels of downstream targets, which in turn reduces actomyosin contraction and promotes a more plastic and dynamic actin architecture (Catral et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2022).

Furthermore, ROCK inhibition has been shown to enhance cell adhesion and reduce apoptotic signaling in stressed RPE cells, thereby improving wound repair and the overall cellular microenvironment (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Biochemical experiments have demonstrated that when ROCK activity is suppressed, RPE cells exhibit a reduction in stress fiber formation and an increase in the formation of normal cell–cell junctions, which is crucial for the maintenance of the outer blood-retinal barrier (Rothschild et al., 2017). In addition to its effects on the actin cytoskeleton, fasudil and other ROCK inhibitors have been reported to modulate inflammatory and fibrotic pathways by reducing the phosphorylation of Smad 2/3 in response to TGF-β1 signaling; this effect may further protect RPE cells from deleterious pro-fibrotic and inflammatory cascades that are known to exacerbate dry AMD pathology (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Several studies also indicate that ROCK inhibition promotes RPE differentiation and pigmentation, as evidenced by increased expression of key proteins such as RPE65, which is indispensable for the visual cycle and meso-zeaxanthin biosynthesis (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Given that oxidative stress in the aging retina exacerbates ROCK activation, fasudil’s ability to mitigate these effects through cytoskeletal remodeling and anti-inflammatory actions underlies its proposed mechanism of action in improving POS internalization in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Rothschild et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing fasudil for dry AMD is that inhibition of ROCK in the RPE will lead to normalization of abnormal cytoskeletal tension, thereby enhancing the formation of phagocytic cups required for efficient POS internalization (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). In aged RPE cells from patients with dry AMD, persistent ROCK hyperactivity is thought to cause increased actomyosin contraction; this leads to a “stiff” cytoskeletal state that hinders membrane dynamics essential for phagocytosis (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Rothschild et al., 2017). By reducing ROCK-mediated phosphorylation of MLC and other substrates, fasudil is expected to relieve this contractility, restore a more flexible actin network, and ultimately allow for enhanced phagocytic function. Preclinical studies have already demonstrated that use of ROCK inhibitors like Y-27632 can increase phagocytic activity by RPE cells, leading to improved clearance of POS debris – a key function that deteriorates in dry AMD (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Croze et al., 2014).

In the proposed assay, RPE cells under oxidative stress—an in vitro proxy for the aging microenvironment seen in dry AMD—will be treated with fasudil. The anticipated outcome is that fasudil will enhance cytoskeletal plasticity, thereby facilitating the formation of phagocytic cups and improving the uptake of POS, as measured by quantifiable phagocytosis assays (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). Moreover, fasudil’s reported effects in enhancing cell adhesion and promoting a balanced extracellular matrix deposition are expected to provide additional benefits to RPE cell morphology and barrier integrity, indirectly supporting improved phagocytic function (Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Given that key RPE-specific genes and proteins involved in phagocytosis, including integrin αvβ5 and MFG-E8, are expressed in these cells, normalization of the cytoskeletal machinery via ROCK inhibition is likely to translate into a functional recovery of POS clearance capacity (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Croze et al., 2014). Thus, the overall effect of fasudil treatment is expected to counteract the age-associated impairment in phagocytosis, reduce accumulation of waste material such as drusen, and potentially slow the progression of retinal degeneration in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the repurposing of fasudil for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a substantial mechanistic rationale and a body of preclinical evidence indicating that ROCK inhibition can positively modulate RPE cellular function. The strengths of fasudil as a therapeutic candidate include its well-established clinical safety profile—stemming from decades of use in cerebrovascular conditions in Japan—as well as its robust capacity to modulate actin-cytoskeletal dynamics, reduce excessive cell contraction, and enhance processes such as cell adhesion and phagocytosis among RPE cells (Catral et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). The ability of fasudil to normalize the abnormal, stiff cytoskeletal state present in aged RPE cells is particularly compelling given the central role of impaired POS internalization in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017).

Moreover, similar ROCK inhibitors have demonstrated promising effects in ocular models of retinal degeneration and diabetic retinopathy, where the restoration of RPE function and cytoskeletal composition has correlated with improved retinal architecture and cell survival (Moura-Coelho et al., 2019; Rothschild et al., 2017). Fasudil’s potential to also attenuate inflammatory and fibrotic signaling pathways via downstream effects on TGF-β/Smad signaling may add further benefit by curbing the detrimental microenvironment that exacerbates RPE dysfunction in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). The proposed mechanism—centered on relieving ROCK-induced actomyosin contraction and restoring the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells—addresses a key pathophysiological deficit in dry AMD, namely the impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments that leads to drusen accumulation and subsequent cell degeneration (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017).

However, there are also some weaknesses and challenges associated with using fasudil as a treatment for dry AMD. A major concern is the relatively nonselective nature of fasudil compared to more recently developed ROCK inhibitors that offer isoform specificity (e.g., selective ROCK2 inhibitors) (Alexander, 2017; Yamaguchi et al., 2017). Since ROCK signaling is implicated in multiple cellular processes beyond RPE cytoskeletal dynamics—including vascular regulation, neuronal survival, and immune cell polarization—a nonselective inhibitor may inadvertently affect these other pathways, potentially leading to off-target effects. In particular, the downregulation of thrombospondin 1 (THBS1) observed with some ROCK inhibitors, which is associated with anti-angiogenic processes, could theoretically predispose patients to neovascular complications if not carefully controlled (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Catral et al., 2024).

Another potential limitation is the pharmacokinetic profile of fasudil in ocular tissues. Fasudil is known to have a short plasma half-life (approximately 0.3 hours), although its active metabolite, hydroxyfasudil, has a moderately longer half-life (approximately 2.9 hours) (Futterknecht et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). For effective treatment of dry AMD—where chronic, sustained modulation of ROCK activity may be necessary—injection strategies such as intravitreal administration or depot formulations may be required to maintain therapeutic levels over an extended period. Although intravitreal delivery of fasudil has been demonstrated in diabetic macular edema and other experimental models (Rothschild et al., 2017), further studies will be needed to optimize the dosage, frequency, and formulation for the specific demands of long-term retinal therapy in dry AMD.

Furthermore, while the preclinical evidence regarding the benefits of ROCK inhibition in RPE cells is promising, there remains a lack of direct clinical data demonstrating the efficacy of fasudil in patients with dry AMD. Most studies to date have focused on the use of ROCK inhibitors in models of diabetic retinopathy, neovascular AMD, or other retinal conditions, and the translation of these findings to the dry, atrophic form of AMD is not yet fully established (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Rothschild et al., 2017). This gap underscores the need for focused, well-designed clinical trials and further preclinical studies using models that accurately recapitulate the pathophysiology of dry AMD.

Moreover, it will be essential to monitor whether the positive effects on cytoskeletal plasticity and phagocytosis translate into meaningful clinical endpoints such as improved visual acuity or slowed progression of geographic atrophy. Biomarkers of RPE health, phagocytic activity, and retinal integrity will need to be identified and validated in the context of fasudil treatment (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Croze et al., 2014).

In conclusion, the available literature strongly supports the mechanistic rationale for using fasudil to target ROCK-mediated dysfunction in RPE cells, which is a critical aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis (Catral et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Its established safety profile in other clinical scenarios, coupled with evidence from preclinical models demonstrating improved cytoskeletal regulation, enhanced phagocytic capacity, and attenuated inflammation in retinal cells, makes fasudil a promising therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (Moura-Coelho et al., 2019; Rothschild et al., 2017). Nonetheless, challenges related to drug-specific pharmacokinetics, the risk of off-target effects due to its nonselectivity, and the current lack of direct clinical evidence in dry AMD warrant cautious further investigation. The next steps should involve optimization of ocular delivery methods—potentially through sustained-release formulations—and the initiation of preclinical studies in animal models of dry AMD to assess functional outcomes. If these studies prove successful, they would pave the way for early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of fasudil in patients with dry AMD (Rothschild et al., 2017; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Overall, while significant work remains to be done, the integration of biochemical, cellular, and clinical data from the broader ROCK inhibitor literature provides a compelling argument for further evaluation of fasudil as a potential repurposed treatment for dry AMD.
