Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) is the taurine-conjugated form of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), a hydrophilic secondary bile acid generated by microbial metabolism and hepatic conjugation, and long used in hepatobiliary disease pharmacotherapy as a cytoprotective bile salt scaffold (class: bile acids; subclass: hydrophilic ursane bile acids/taurine conjugates) (Cabrera et al., 2019). As a small amphipathic molecule, TUDCA exhibits chemical-chaperone activity that stabilizes nascent polypeptides, reduces protein misfolding/aggregation burden, and modulates unfolded protein response (UPR) signaling, thereby lowering endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress across cell types (e.g., hepatocytes, epithelial cells, neurons) (Kusaczuk, 2019). In vitro and in vivo ocular studies identify TUDCA as a broadly neuroprotective agent that rescues photoreceptors and retinal cells in multiple injury paradigms, consistent with multimodal actions that include mitigation of ER stress, inhibition of mitochondrial pathway apoptosis, reduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and anti-inflammatory effects (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Win et al., 2021). In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, TUDCA directly promotes phagocytosis via Mer tyrosine kinase (MerTK) activation and restores phagocytic function under oxidative stress, implicating a direct action on the canonical RPE phagocytic machinery (Murase et al., 2015). Delivery to ocular tissues is feasible with systemic dosing and local routes; related UDCA crosses the human blood–retinal barrier, and TUDCA tissue distribution has been quantified after intravitreal, systemic, and suprachoroidal administration in large animals (Daruich et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
Clinically, the UDCA/TUDCA class is established in hepatology; mechanistic reviews document antiapoptotic activity via inhibition of mitochondrial cytochrome c release, stabilization of mitochondrial membranes, attenuation of ER stress via chaperone actions, increases in glutathione pools, and activation of survival kinases (p38/ERK/MAPK/PI3K), with a translational safety track record that has motivated evaluation in neurodegenerative disorders (Cabrera et al., 2019). In ophthalmology, preclinical data repeatedly show that systemic or local TUDCA protects retina across models: it preserves photoreceptors in genetic (rd10, P23H, Rpgr knockout) and injury models (retinal detachment, light damage), decreases ER stress and apoptosis markers (e.g., caspase-3), and improves electroretinography (ERG) function (Win et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). In diabetic retinopathy–like models and vascular stress paradigms, TUDCA or UDCA reduces vascular permeability, inflammation, and ER stress, and in retinal endothelial cells these effects require the bile acid receptor TGR5, supporting receptor-mediated protection in the retina (Lenin et al., 2023). In RPE models (ARPE-19 and primary human RPE), TUDCA protects against H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury and thapsigargin-induced ER stress, improves viability, suppresses apoptosis, and activates antioxidant defenses, while also reversing oxidative-stress–induced phagocytic dysfunction via MerTK/FAK signaling (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Although these mechanistic actions align with pathogenic axes in dry age-related macular degeneration (dAMD), no clinical trials in dAMD are referenced in the supplied context; the current evidence base is preclinical and translational (e.g., drug distribution and barrier penetration) rather than RPE/dAMD clinical efficacy (Olsen et al., 2020; Daruich et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
ER proteostasis and unfolded protein response modulation  
- Chemical chaperoning: TUDCA stabilizes folding intermediates, reduces aberrant protein–protein interactions, promotes ATF6-driven folding capacity, and prevents UPR malfunction, thereby attenuating ER stress signaling (downregulating BiP/GRP78, ATF4/eIF2α, XBP1 splicing, and CHOP in multiple models) (Kusaczuk, 2019). In ARPE-19 cells, TUDCA reduces thapsigargin-induced CHOP expression and spliced XBP1, with parallel decreases in apoptosis and improved survival, linking chaperone action to UPR attenuation in RPE (Alhasani et al., 2020). Across retinal systems, TUDCA repeatedly lowers ER stress signatures, and the retina-relevant pathophysiology of UPR–mitochondrial crosstalk (IRE1/JNK pro-apoptotic routing, CHOP-mediated death, PERK’s protective vs. maladaptive bifurcation) underscores why ER stress relief is mechanistically central in RPE and photoreceptors (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).

Mitochondrial membrane stabilization and anti-apoptotic signaling  
- Intrinsic apoptosis blockade: TUDCA inhibits Bax translocation, preserves mitochondrial outer membrane integrity, prevents cytochrome c release, and suppresses caspase activation (caspase-3/7), thereby interrupting the mitochondrial execution cascade and preserving oxidative phosphorylation capacity (Alhasani et al., 2020; Cabrera et al., 2019). In neuronal and isolated mitochondrial systems, co-incubation with TUDCA prevents amyloid-β–induced mitochondrial membrane perturbation, preserves redox state and protein conformation of the outer membrane, and limits cytochrome c release—convergent evidence for direct mitochondrial membrane stabilization and preservation of electron transport chain function under proteotoxic/oxidative stress (Khalaf et al., 2022). TUDCA upregulates survival signaling (PI3K/Akt → Bad phosphorylation; ERK/MAPK) and inhibits stress kinases (JNK/c-Jun), further shifting the balance away from mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) and toward survival (Cabrera et al., 2019; Win et al., 2021).

Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory reprogramming  
- NRF2 axis and redox control: In RPE oxidative injury models, TUDCA reduces intracellular ROS and malondialdehyde (MDA), restores NRF2 expression, upregulates antioxidant enzymes (SOD1, catalase, GPX1, NQO1, GCLM), elevates reduced glutathione (GSH), and rescues SOD/catalase activities—features of a robust antioxidant response that stabilizes mitochondrial redox homeostasis (Alhasani et al., 2020). Suppression of inflammatory signaling (decreased IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α transcription and secretion) further reduces secondary mitochondrial injury and death receptor cross-talk (Alhasani et al., 2020). Such antioxidant/anti-inflammatory shifts are consistent with TUDCA-induced NRF2 pathway enhancement reported across tissues and with the known linkage between persistent UPR activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine induction in RPE (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

RPE phagocytic machinery activation  
- MerTK/FAK signaling and POS uptake: TUDCA increases MerTK phosphorylation in a concentration-dependent manner, maintains FAK phosphorylation under oxidative stress, and restores H₂O₂-impaired RPE phagocytosis in both ARPE-19 and primary human RPE, supporting a direct effect on RPE’s canonical POS ingestion machinery (MerTK–FAK–integrin axis) (Murase et al., 2015). Functional assays demonstrate increased uptake and lysosomal digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (pHrodo® and FITC readouts), indicating rescue of both recognition/engulfment and downstream processing (Murase et al., 2015). Notably, in the MerTK rescue paradigm GRP78 was not altered by TUDCA, implying that the pro-phagocytic effect can occur independently of a measurable reduction in ER stress under those specific conditions and may involve upstream integrin/FAK/Src signaling that converges on MerTK (Murase et al., 2015).

Bile acid receptors and signaling in the retina  
- TGR5-dependent protection: In diabetic and inflammatory retinal models, TUDCA reduces ER stress markers (GRP78, IRE1α, sXBP1, CHOP), inflammation, and vascular permeability; these endothelial barrier and anti-inflammatory effects require TGR5 expression in retinal endothelial cells and correlate with functional rescue in vivo (ERG, optokinetic responses), suggesting a receptor-mediated component that is present in the retina (Lenin et al., 2023). Although FXR appears less relevant in retina, additional candidate receptors (TGR5, α5β1 integrin, S1PR2, PXR, GR/mineralocorticoid receptor) have been implicated at the transcript/protein level in ocular tissues, providing plausible upstream routes for TUDCA’s signaling (Daruich et al., 2022; Win et al., 2021).

Mechanistic integration in AMD biology  
- In RPE, ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction reinforce each other: UPR activation (IRE1/JNK, ATF4–CHOP) promotes mitochondrial apoptosis and ATP decline; mitochondrial impairment (Δψm loss, ROS) feeds back to exacerbate ER stress and can drive epithelial–mesenchymal transition seen in early dAMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020). TUDCA’s combined actions—chemical chaperoning of ER proteostasis, MOMP blockade/cytochrome c retention, redox control via NRF2, and restoration of MerTK/FAK-dependent phagocytosis—directly map onto these intersecting failure modes and therefore represent a coherent, biologically grounded therapeutic hypothesis for dAMD (Alhasani et al., 2020; Cabrera et al., 2019; Murase et al., 2015).

Important mechanistic gaps for dAMD  
- Despite strong plausibility, direct RPE bioenergetics readouts (ATP levels, oxygen consumption rate, mitochondrial membrane potential) after TUDCA in dAMD-relevant stress paradigms are not reported in the provided RPE studies and remain a central evidentiary gap for this indication (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Likewise, while TUDCA rescues phagocytosis and activates MerTK, there are no data here on cathepsin transcription, maturation, or activity in RPE phagolysosomes after TUDCA, precluding claims about normalization of lysosomal proteases in dAMD RPE (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Murase et al., 2015).

Expected Effect  
In a dAMD-relevant RPE assay comprising oxidative and/or ER stress with phagocytosis readouts, the following effects are expected based on the compiled evidence:

- ER stress attenuation and reduced UPR-driven apoptosis: TUDCA should lower CHOP and spliced XBP1 levels and decrease TUNEL/caspase-3/7 activation, improving viability under thapsigargin or oxidative stress, consistent with chemical chaperone–mediated UPR modulation (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- Mitochondrial preservation and anti-apoptosis: TUDCA should suppress Bax translocation/cytochrome c release and maintain mitochondrial membrane integrity, thereby reducing mitochondrial pathway apoptosis and preserving the proton motive force needed for oxidative phosphorylation; while these endpoints have not yet been quantified in RPE with Seahorse or JC-1 in the supplied reports, they are supported mechanistically in retina/neuronal systems and hepatocyte models (Cabrera et al., 2019; Khalaf et al., 2022).  
- Antioxidant reset via NRF2: TUDCA should reduce ROS/MDA, restore NRF2 expression, increase GSH, and upregulate antioxidant enzymes (SOD, CAT, GPX1, NQO1, GCLM), consistent with lower oxidative injury to mitochondrial lipids/proteins and stabilized respiratory capacity (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- Restoration of RPE phagocytosis via MerTK/FAK: Under oxidative stress (H₂O₂), TUDCA is expected to restore POS ingestion/digestion as measured by pHrodo®/FITC assays, accompanied by increased MerTK phosphorylation and maintenance of FAK signaling, potentially via upstream integrin activation; this rescues both recognition/engulfment and lysosomal processing phases (Murase et al., 2015).  
- Anti-inflammatory effects: TUDCA should reduce IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α at mRNA/protein levels in RPE challenged by H₂O₂, limiting cytokine-driven mitochondrial impairment and secondary UPR activation (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- Putative receptor mediation: In endothelial/retinal contexts, TUDCA’s ER-stress and barrier benefits require TGR5; although RPE-specific TGR5 dependency is not demonstrated in the supplied texts, receptor-mediated contributions in the retinal environment are plausible and testable (Lenin et al., 2023).  

Expression and pathway presence in RPE are well established for MerTK, integrins (e.g., αvβ5), and FAK—core components of the POS phagocytosis cascade targeted by TUDCA in RPE cells (Murase et al., 2015).  

Dosing and assay considerations:  
- In ARPE-19, 100 µM TUDCA improved survival under 750 µM H₂O₂; higher concentrations (200–500 µM) impaired viability, indicating a window for benefit (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- In phagocytosis assays, TUDCA increased MerTK phosphorylation at high concentration (1 mM) and improved phagocytosis at lower concentrations (≥ 0.1 µM) under non-H₂O₂ conditions, suggesting multiple dose-dependent mechanisms (direct vs. upstream integrin-mediated pathways) (Murase et al., 2015).  

Endpoints to include for hypothesis validation:  
- ER stress/UPR: GRP78/BiP, sXBP1, CHOP, ATF4, eIF2α-P, ATF6 targets (Alhasani et al., 2020; Kusaczuk, 2019).  
- Mitochondrial bioenergetics: Δψm (JC-1/TMRM), oxygen consumption rate and extracellular acidification rate (Seahorse), cellular ATP (luminescent readout), cytochrome c release/Bax translocation (Cabrera et al., 2019; Khalaf et al., 2022).  
- Redox/inflammation: ROS (DCFH-DA), MDA (TBARS), GSH, NRF2 targets, cytokine ELISAs (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- Phagocytosis: MerTK/FAK phosphorylation, POS binding/engulfment/digestion (pHrodo®/FITC), and key lysosomal proteolysis markers; importantly, add cathepsin D/B/L maturation/activity assays to address the specific lysosomal arm of the hypothesis, which remains untested in the provided literature (Murase et al., 2015; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Overall Evaluation  
Summary judgment  
TUDCA is a mechanistically coherent, repurposable candidate for dAMD that targets central RPE failure modes—ER proteostasis breakdown, mitochondrial injury/apoptosis, oxidative and inflammatory stress—and functionally restores a defining RPE task (POS phagocytosis) via MerTK/FAK signaling under oxidative insult (strengths: convergent mechanistic breadth and direct RPE function rescue) (Alhasani et al., 2020; Cabrera et al., 2019; Murase et al., 2015). However, two critical evidence gaps must be addressed to de-risk the program for dAMD: (1) lack of direct demonstration that TUDCA preserves RPE mitochondrial bioenergetics and ATP production under dAMD-relevant stress, and (2) absence of data that TUDCA normalizes lysosomal cathepsin expression/maturation/activity downstream of phagosome–lysosome fusion (weaknesses: missing bioenergetic and lysosomal endpoints underpinning the hypothesis) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit to dAMD pathophysiology: TUDCA reduces ER stress/UPR effectors (CHOP, sXBP1), blocks mitochondrial pathway apoptosis (Bax/cytochrome c/caspase-3), induces NRF2-driven antioxidant programs, and suppresses inflammatory cytokines—all directly relevant to the ER–mitochondria redox loop that destabilizes RPE in early AMD (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  
- Direct RPE functional efficacy: Restoration of POS phagocytosis via MerTK activation and FAK stabilization under oxidative stress offers a clear, disease-relevant mechanism to preserve outer segment turnover and RPE homeostasis (Murase et al., 2015).  
- Mitochondrial stabilization plausibility: Strong cross-system evidence shows TUDCA preserves mitochondrial membrane structure, limits cytochrome c release, and blocks permeability transition–like events, which would support ATP maintenance under stress (albeit not yet measured in RPE) (Khalaf et al., 2022; Cabrera et al., 2019).  
- Retinal in vivo activity and barrier access: Systemic TUDCA protects photoreceptors and retinal function in multiple rodent disease models; related UDCA crosses the human blood–retinal barrier, and ocular delivery platforms achieve retinal distribution in large animals, supporting translational feasibility (Win et al., 2021; Daruich et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2020).  
- Receptor-mediated tractability: TGR5 dependency for retinal endothelial barrier/inflammation effects offers a defined receptor axis for pharmacodynamic biomarkers in vivo, complementing MerTK/FAK functional readouts in RPE (Lenin et al., 2023).  

Weaknesses and risks  
- Mitochondrial bioenergetics unproven in RPE: No ATP, OCR/ECAR, or Δψm data in stressed RPE after TUDCA are provided; this is a pivotal gap because preservation of energy production is central to the proposed disease-modifying effect in dAMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  
- Lysosomal protease (cathepsin) claims unsupported: While TUDCA rescues phagocytosis and MerTK signaling, there are no data here that TUDCA restores cathepsin expression/maturation/activity in RPE; the stated hypothesis reference to “alleviates ER stress–induced downregulation of MERTK and cathepsins” is not substantiated in the supplied sources and should be considered unverified for RPE/dAMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Murase et al., 2015).  
- Dose–mechanism tension: In RPE phagocytosis assays, MerTK phosphorylation was robust at 1 mM, whereas phagocytosis enhancement occurred at ≥ 0.1 µM, suggesting indirect upstream mechanisms at low doses and raising questions about clinically relevant concentrations for direct MerTK phosphorylation (Murase et al., 2015).  
- Heterogeneity of mechanistic readouts: In one RPE phagocytosis study, GRP78 was not changed by TUDCA during rescue, indicating ER stress reduction is not required for the pro-phagocytic effect in that setting; mechanism may differ across contexts (Murase et al., 2015).  
- Evidence quality and generalizability: Several RPE-focused studies are from lower-tier journals, and many mechanistic claims derive from non-RPE systems; rigorous replication with polarized primary human RPE and in dAMD-relevant in vivo models is needed (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Decision framework and next experiments  
Given the favorable mechanistic alignment and preclinical retinal efficacy, TUDCA merits advancement to a focused preclinical validation plan tailored to dAMD, gated by resolution of the bioenergetics and lysosomal gaps:  

- Bioenergetics/mitochondria (must-have): In human primary, polarized RPE under defined oxidative and ER stress (e.g., low-dose H₂O₂, tunicamycin/thapsigargin), quantify Δψm (TMRM), OCR/ECAR (Seahorse), cellular ATP, cytochrome c release, and Bax translocation with and without TUDCA; include NRF2 dependency (siRNA) to map antioxidant mediation (Alhasani et al., 2020; Cabrera et al., 2019).  
- Phagolysosomal proteolysis (must-have): In POS ingestion assays, measure cathepsin D/B/L maturation (pro-/mature forms), activity (fluorogenic substrates), lysosomal pH and degradative capacity; test whether TUDCA normalizes these under ER/oxidative stress and whether effects require MerTK or integrin/FAK signaling (Murase et al., 2015).  
- ER–mitochondria crosstalk mapping (should-have): Track UPR arms (IRE1/JNK, PERK/eIF2α/ATF4, ATF6) alongside mitochondrial readouts to define causal sequence; test whether TUDCA biases PERK toward pro-survival signaling and reduces CHOP/TRB3 induction (Alhasani et al., 2020; Kusaczuk, 2019).  
- In vivo dAMD-relevant model (should-have): In RPE mitochondrial/oxidative stress models (e.g., sodium iodate low-dose; cigarette-smoke–derived oxidants), test systemic and local TUDCA dosing for RPE structure/function (autofluorescence, OCT, ERG) and RPE phagocytosis biomarkers, plus mitochondrial/UPR markers (Win et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2020).  
- Pharmacology/PK/PD (must-have): Link ocular exposure (vitreous/choroid/RPE) to effect using delivery modalities with translational potential (oral UDCA as a proxy crossing BRB; suprachoroidal implant pharmacokinetics); incorporate PD markers (retinal ER stress proteins, NRF2 targets) (Daruich et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2020; Lenin et al., 2023).  

Positioning in dAMD  
If the above gaps are closed positively, TUDCA would be positioned as a proteostasis–mitochondria stabilizer that preserves RPE phagocytic function and metabolic sufficiency—an upstream, disease-modifying approach complementary to complement modulation and to anti-angiogenic strategies (the latter relevant if geographic atrophy coexists with incipient neovascularization) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). The MerTK/FAK rescue of phagocytosis provides a strong functional anchor for mechanism-based biomarkers, while the antioxidant/UPR signatures support PD tracking in early-phase clinical translation (Murase et al., 2015; Alhasani et al., 2020).

Go/no-go conclusion  
- Go for preclinical dAMD validation with a clear focus on mitochondrial bioenergetics and lysosomal protease function in RPE, using polarized human RPE and in vivo oxidative/ER-stress models that recapitulate early dAMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  
- No-go for cathepsin-centered claims until direct RPE evidence is generated; likewise, refrain from asserting ATP rescue in RPE until OCR/ATP/Δψm data are obtained (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

On balance, TUDCA is a high-priority repurposing candidate with strong mechanistic plausibility and supportive retinal efficacy, but it requires targeted, RPE-centric bioenergetics and lysosomal validation to meet decision-grade standards for a dAMD program (Cabrera et al., 2019; Win et al., 2021; Murase et al., 2015; Alhasani et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The candidate under evaluation is a synthetic Gla‐domain peptide mimetic of Protein S, designated as a 12‐mer peptide (Peptide 2.0 Cat. No. H‐PS12). In its natural role, Protein S is a vitamin K–dependent protein that contains an N‐terminal gamma‐carboxyglutamic acid (Gla) domain responsible for binding phosphatidylserine (PtdSer) on apoptotic membranes and photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and a C‐terminal region that mediates receptor binding to MerTK. This peptide mimetic is engineered to reproduce the key functional motif of the Gla domain that is critical for MerTK engagement. The synthetic peptide belongs to the class of peptide‐based small molecules designed to mimic native ligand functions and to act as receptor agonists. Peptide mimetics have been explored in several therapeutic contexts – for example, peptides that mimic portions of larger proteins often prove advantageous because of their superior stability, lower immunogenicity, and enhanced tissue penetration relative to full‐length proteins. With respect to the ocular environment, the small size and chemical stability of H‐PS12 favor its application as a locally delivered drug via intravitreal injection or topical administration, particularly in diseases such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where targeting the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is paramount (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Extensive literature supports the pivotal role of native Protein S in mediating MerTK signaling in RPE cells and promoting POS phagocytosis. Several studies demonstrate that Protein S acts as a positive regulator of MerTK‐mediated phagocytosis in the retina and that decreased activity of this pathway contributes to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Parinot et al., 2024). Although native Protein S is known to be a critical ligand for MerTK in RPE cells, its direct application as a therapeutic agent is impeded by its intrinsic lability; indeed, purification challenges and loss of bioactivity in recombinant formats have been reported (Prasad, 2006). By contrast, there is emerging evidence that synthetic peptide mimetics – designed solely from the key Gla domain – can overcome these limitations and reliably stimulate receptor phosphorylation. In macrophage models, such Gla‐domain peptides have been shown to trigger MerTK autophosphorylation within minutes at nanomolar concentrations, suggesting a dose‐responsive mechanism that might be recapitulated in RPE cells (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). To date, while there have been reports on the fundamental biology of Protein S and its role in retinal homeostasis, no synthetic Gla–domain peptide has been commercially developed or clinically evaluated specifically for dry AMD. Nonetheless, the concept of repurposing Protein S’s receptor–binding activity through a stable, small synthetic molecule has been theoretically supported by detailed mechanistic studies in vitro and in animal models (Albert et al., 2015; Nandrot, 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action proposed for H‐PS12 centers on recapitulating the critical interaction between the Gla domain of Protein S and the extracellular binding sites of the receptor tyrosine kinase MerTK. In the native state, Protein S engages MerTK by binding to its Ig‐like extracellular domains through specific gamma‐carboxylated glutamic acid residues. This binding requires calcium ions to stabilize the conformation of the Gla domain and mediate a proper interaction with phosphatidylserine on the target cell surface (Nandrot, 2018; Prasad, 2006). Binding of Protein S initiates receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation, an event which subsequently activates intracellular signaling cascades including PI3K‐ and PLCγ‐dependent pathways—processes that are requisite for cytoskeletal rearrangements and efficient phagocytosis of POS (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006; Albert et al., 2015).

H‐PS12 is designed as a synthetic 12–amino acid peptide that mimics the critical Gla–domain sequence of Protein S, maintaining the γ–carboxylation motif necessary for calcium binding and ensuring the correct spatial orientation for receptor engagement. The hypothesis is that when this peptide is administered to RPE cultures, it will bind to the MerTK extracellular regions in a fashion indistinguishable from that of the native protein, thereby triggering receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation at an effective concentration (EC₅₀) estimated to be around 100 nM (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). This autophosphorylation event then propagates downstream signaling leading to reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton, an essential step for the engulfment of POS. Detailed structure–function analyses have provided evidence that mutations in the Ig–like domains of MerTK (such as G122R and K263I) significantly alter the binding and internalization responses to Protein S and Gas6, thereby establishing the binding specificity that H‐PS12 aims to replicate (Parinot et al., 2024). Additionally, calcium dependency and proper gamma–carboxylation are confirmed as pivotal for TAM receptor activation, emphasizing how H‐PS12’s mimicry of the Gla domain can facilitate stable receptor activation (Nandrot, 2018; Lieffrig et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the failure of RPE cells to effectively phagocytose shed photoreceptor outer segments leads to accumulation of cellular debris and subsequent retinal degeneration. The expected effect of H‐PS12 is to restore or enhance this fundamental phagocytic process by acting as a MerTK agonist. When applied to RPE cell cultures – particularly those derived from CFH–mutant lines, which have been shown to exhibit impaired POS phagocytosis – H‐PS12 is anticipated to bind to MerTK, trigger receptor autophosphorylation, and thereby initiate early phagocytic signaling (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). This activation should, in turn, enhance the uptake and internalization of POS, mimicking the natural role of Protein S in maintaining retinal homeostasis (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006).

At the molecular level, following MerTK activation, downstream signaling cascades that include PI3K and the FAK pathway are activated, leading to actin polymerization and phagosome formation. Such events are crucial for the internalization of POS and are known to be compromised in models of AMD where MerTK signaling is deficient (Prasad, 2006; Lieffrig et al., 2023). Moreover, by restoring efficient phagocytosis, H‐PS12 may reduce the formation of lipofuscin and drusen—hallmarks of dry AMD—and ameliorate inflammatory processes that are secondary to debris accumulation (Albert et al., 2015). Furthermore, the localized expression of both Protein S and MerTK in the RPE, particularly at the apical microvilli interfacing with POS, supports the rationale that direct stimulation of MerTK in these cells will yield the desired therapeutic outcome (Prasad, 2006).

Overall Evaluation:  
The scientific premise underlying H‐PS12 is founded on in–depth mechanistic insights into the biology of Protein S and its regulation of MerTK–mediated phagocytosis in the retina. One of the primary strengths of the candidate lies in its well–defined mechanism of action. By isolating the Gla–domain, which has been shown to be critical for engaging MerTK and initiating receptor autophosphorylation, the synthetic peptide addresses a fundamental defect in dry AMD—the impaired clearance of POS by RPE cells (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018). The small molecular size of the 12–mer peptide not only minimizes potential for immunogenicity but also enhances tissue penetration and stability in the ocular environment, which is a significant advantage over full–length recombinant proteins that have been plagued by stability issues during purification and storage (Prasad, 2006).

Furthermore, the therapeutic rationale is supported by experimental findings in macrophage models, where similar peptides have been demonstrated to stimulate MerTK phosphorylation rapidly, hinting at the translational potential of H‐PS12 from immune cells to RPE cells (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). In addition, evidence from studies using native Protein S in RPE phagocytosis underscores the relevance of the MerTK pathway in retinal degenerative processes, thereby validating MerTK as a promising therapeutic target for AMD (Parinot et al., 2024; Kaarniranta et al., 2018).

On the other hand, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be considered. First, while Protein S has been conclusively shown to stimulate MerTK phosphorylation in biochemical assays, functional studies have revealed that recombinant Protein S can sometimes fail to stimulate phagocytosis in RPE culture systems unless in the presence of serum or additional cofactors (Prasad, 2006). This discrepancy highlights the possibility that the mere activation of MerTK by H‐PS12, as measured by receptor phosphorylation, may not fully recapitulate the complex intracellular processes required for effective phagocytosis in RPE cells.  

Another concern pertains to the delicate balance between the functions of Protein S and Gas6 in modulating retinal phagocytosis. Studies have indicated that while Protein S acts as a stimulatory ligand, Gas6 can exert inhibitory effects at higher concentrations, suggesting that the endogenous ligand stoichiometry is critical for optimal MerTK function (Parinot et al., 2024). Consequently, the introduction of a synthetic peptide might perturb this balance if not properly dosed, potentially leading to unintended modulation of phagocytic activity or downstream signaling cascades. This is particularly important given that the RPE is subject to a finely tuned circadian rhythm in phagocytosis, and any exogenous modulation must be compatible with these natural regulatory cycles (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024).

Moreover, the transition from in vitro assays to in vivo models and ultimately to clinical application is fraught with challenges. Although the EC₅₀ of approximately 100 nM suggests a high potency of H‐PS12 in triggering MerTK activation, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of the peptide in the ocular milieu need to be thoroughly characterized. Issues such as peptide stability in vitreous humor, clearance rates from retinal tissues, and potential off–target effects on other TAM receptors (e.g., TYRO3 and AXL) require detailed investigation (Prasad, 2006). In addition, the efficacy of H‐PS12 in restoring POS phagocytosis must be validated in animal models that closely mimic the human pathophysiology of dry AMD, including models that exhibit CFH mutations where defects in phagocytosis are prominent (Parinot et al., 2024; Palczewska et al., 2016).

A further limitation comes from the fact that dry AMD is a multifactorial disease. Although impaired phagocytosis and resultant debris accumulation at the RPE–photoreceptor interface are central to disease pathogenesis, other pathological mechanisms such as oxidative stress, inflammation, and complement dysregulation also contribute considerably to retinal degeneration (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006; Lieffrig et al., 2023). As such, while H‐PS12 is mechanistically attractive from the standpoint of enhancing phagocytosis via MerTK activation, it may need to be integrated into a broader therapeutic regimen that addresses these additional aspects. The long–term outcome of MerTK activation on retinal inflammation, for instance, has yet to be fully determined, even though some studies suggest that active MerTK signaling is associated with anti–inflammatory effects (Albert et al., 2015).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation of H‐PS12 is positive. The mechanistic rationale is robust and rooted in fundamental observations of Protein S’s role in retinal homeostasis. The potential to restore or enhance RPE phagocytosis, thereby reducing the accumulation of POS debris—a key pathological hallmark of dry AMD—makes this candidate highly promising. In particular, the possibility of correcting phagocytic deficits in CFH–mutant RPE cultures represents a novel approach that can address one of the unmet needs in dry AMD therapy (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

Moreover, the simplicity of a synthetic peptide compared to biologics such as full–length recombinant proteins offers advantages in terms of manufacturing, storage, and cost. The use of a 12–mer peptide also minimizes the risk of unwanted immunogenic reactions, which is especially pertinent in the immune–privileged environment of the eye (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). It is also worth noting that any adverse effects related to off–target activation can be monitored experimentally by assessing not only the phosphorylation status of MerTK but also by profiling the activity of related receptors and inflammatory markers in preclinical models (Albert et al., 2015).

In summary, the H‐PS12 synthetic peptide stands out as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its targeted mechanism of action, favorable biophysical characteristics, and the strong mechanistic data supporting the role of Protein S in RPE phagocytosis. Its development represents an innovative translation of basic mechanistic insights into a potentially viable therapeutic approach. Nevertheless, successful clinical translation of this candidate will depend on overcoming several challenges, including ensuring that receptor activation translates to meaningful functional improvements in POS clearance, optimizing dosing to maintain the physiological ligand balance, and rigorously evaluating the safety and efficacy in appropriate in vivo models. These considerations will be crucial in determining whether H‐PS12 can be advanced beyond the preclinical proof–of–concept stage (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

Overall, while the current data are highly encouraging, further studies are needed to address the following key issues:  
1. Quantitative profiling of MerTK phosphorylation kinetics by H‐PS12 in RPE cells under varying conditions, including chronic exposure and in the presence of competing ligands such as Gas6.  
2. Evaluation of the functional outcomes of MerTK activation by H‐PS12 in RPE phagocytosis assays, particularly the efficacy of POS uptake and clearance in CFH–mutant RPE cultures.  
3. Detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies in ocular models to assess the peptide’s stability, tissue penetration, and potential off–target effects.  
4. Integration of the peptide’s activity with other pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis, such as oxidative stress and complement activation, to ascertain whether a combinatorial therapeutic strategy might be warranted.

Given these considerations, H‐PS12 merits further preclinical investigation as a potential therapeutic for dry AMD. Its development is grounded in well–established mechanistic insights regarding MerTK function and RPE photoreceptor maintenance, and its design as a stable, small peptide offers distinct advantages over native Protein S. With careful optimization and validation, H‐PS12 could represent a significant advance in the treatment of dry AMD, providing a novel means to restore the critical phagocytic function of the RPE, reduce debris accumulation, and ultimately slow the progression of retinal degeneration (Parinot et al., 2024; Parinot et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

In conclusion, the synthetic Gla–domain 12–mer H‐PS12 demonstrates a promising preclinical profile as a repurposed drug candidate for dry age–related macular degeneration. Its ability to specifically bind and activate MerTK through a mechanism that mirrors the native function of Protein S, combined with its enhanced stability and ease of ocular delivery, underscores the potential for a targeted therapeutic approach to correct the underlying phagocytic deficit observed in dry AMD. While challenges remain concerning the translation of in vitro receptor activation to in vivo functional efficacy, the foundational data reviewed here support continued investigation into H‐PS12 as a novel MerTK agonist. Future research addressing dosing, long–term safety, and integration with other therapeutic modalities will be essential in determining the ultimate clinical utility of this synthetic peptide in combating dry AMD (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018; Prasad, 2006; Albert et al., 2015).

Overall, despite the inherent complexities of dry AMD pathogenesis and the potential for variable responses owing to the interplay of multiple ligands at the MerTK receptor, H‐PS12 offers a rational, targeted, and innovative approach to restore RPE phagocytic function. It thereby holds considerable promise as a next–generation therapeutic candidate that addresses a critical, yet hitherto unmet, need in the management of dry AMD (Parinot et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring derivative of vitamin B3 that was originally isolated from milk and later recognized for its role as an NAD⁺ precursor. NR belongs to the class of NAD⁺‐boosting compounds and is structurally a pyridine riboside with a glycosidic bond linking nicotinamide to ribose; this bond has proven to be chemically labile, which has driven innovations in its synthesis and stabilization (Zhang et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). Recent advances in synthetic methods have enabled the production of purer, more thermally and chemically stable forms, such as borate-stabilized NR, although commercial formulations like NR chloride (ChromaDex TruNiagen) are widely used owing to their proven oral bioavailability (Biţă et al., 2023). As a member of the NAD⁺ precursor family that also includes nicotinamide and nicotinic acid, NR has been repurposed for its potential to restore intracellular NAD⁺ levels, a vital coenzyme in redox reactions and as a substrate for enzymes such as sirtuins and PARPs; these properties have been harnessed in research aimed at improving mitochondrial function and addressing age-related degeneration (Zhang et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
NR has a robust preclinical and early clinical history as a nutritional supplement with demonstrated efficacy in boosting NAD⁺ levels systemically. Prior biochemical studies have documented that oral NR supplementation raises circulating NAD⁺ and associated metabolites in both murine and human subjects, with repeated dosing regimens showing increases in NAD⁺ of up to 100% above baseline without causing adverse events such as flushing or liver toxicity—side effects that have been problematic with other niacin derivatives (Airhart et al., 2017; Conze et al., 2019). Furthermore, NR has been shown to ameliorate metabolic deficits in various disease models, including mouse models of diet-induced obesity, neurodegeneration, peripheral neuropathy, and even light-induced retinal degeneration, where systemic treatment with NR improved retinal outcomes in mice (Zhang et al., 2020; Biţă et al., 2023). Although NR has not been directly tested in clinical trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in dedicated experiments on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) phagocytosis, the accumulated evidence from related ocular studies and from the broader literature on NAD⁺ restoration suggests that its application in retinal degenerative conditions is plausible (Jadeja et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, NR is rapidly taken up by cells and phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRK1 and NRK2) to produce nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), which is subsequently converted to NAD⁺ by NMN adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) (Zhang et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). NAD⁺ is a key metabolic hub that is required for essential cellular processes, including fueling mitochondrial ATP production via glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation, while also serving as a critical substrate for sirtuin deacetylases (notably SIRT1 and SIRT3) and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs) that mediate DNA repair and stress responses (Braidy et al., 2019; Biţă et al., 2023). In the context of the RPE, diminished NAD⁺ availability is linked to compromised mitochondrial bioenergetics, impaired autophagy/mitophagy, increased oxidative stress, and defective phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), all of which contribute to the etiology of dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2020). NR supplementation is proposed to elevate intracellular NAD⁺ levels above the physiological threshold, thereby stimulating sirtuin activity (particularly SIRT3 in mitochondria), stabilizing mitochondrial membrane potential, promoting efficient mitophagy, and reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Biţă et al., 2023). Additionally, by restoring the NAD⁺/NADH balance, NR may directly support energy-dependent processes such as phagocytosis in RPE cells, where the clearance of aged POS is critically energy demanding (Zhang et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed hypothesis for dry AMD, exogenous NR supplementation is expected to boost NAD⁺ levels in RPE cells, an effect that should be observable at an effective concentration (EC₅₀) in the range of approximately 100 µM in vitro (Zhang et al., 2020). This increase in NAD⁺ is anticipated to enhance mitochondrial respiration and activate sirtuin-dependent pathways that promote mitochondrial biogenesis and repair. In turn, improved mitochondrial function provides the necessary ATP for energy-dependent cellular functions, particularly the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), which is impaired in dry AMD. Preclinical studies have indicated that NAD⁺ precursors, including nicotinamide and NMN, can correct defects in mitochondrial respiration and restore normal phagocytic activity in RPE models; NR, being an orally bioavailable NAD⁺ precursor with favorable safety profiles, is predicted to act similarly by reducing oxidative stress–induced damage to the phagocytic machinery and enhancing mitophagy to clear damaged mitochondria (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020; Hawkins et al., 2024). In animal models of retinal degeneration, NR supplementation has been linked to improved functional outcomes, supporting the notion that similar mechanisms may be relevant in the context of dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction underlies photoreceptor degeneration (Zhang et al., 2020). Thus, the expected effect is a dual benefit in RPE cells: increased energy production to drive POS phagocytosis and enhanced resistance to oxidative damage through improved mitochondrial quality control, ultimately helping to preserve RPE function and slow dry AMD progression (Conze et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
NR is an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its unique combination of advantages. Among its strengths is its origin as a naturally occurring, orally bioavailable NAD⁺ precursor that has a long record of safe use in human nutritional studies; clinical trials have repeatedly demonstrated its ability to significantly elevate systemic NAD⁺ levels without dose-limiting adverse effects such as flushing or hepatotoxicity, which are common to other niacin derivatives (Airhart et al., 2017; Conze et al., 2019). Its mechanism of action is well understood at the biochemical level: by feeding into the NAD⁺ salvage pathway, NR supports key cellular functions including mitochondrial respiration, DNA repair, and stress signaling via sirtuins and PARPs—pathways that are critically compromised in the aging RPE and in dry AMD (Braidy et al., 2019; Biţă et al., 2023). Additionally, preclinical data have shown that NAD⁺ restoration via NR or related precursors can ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction and improve phagocytic activity in retinal tissues, providing a plausible molecular rationale for its use in maintaining RPE health (Zhang et al., 2020).

On the other hand, there are significant challenges that must be acknowledged. Despite promising preclinical evidence in various models of retinal degeneration, direct application of NR in the context of dry AMD has not yet been rigorously evaluated in dedicated clinical trials, leaving a gap between the compelling mechanistic rationale and the demonstration of clinical efficacy (Jadeja et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2024). The concentration required (EC₅₀ ≈ 100 µM) and the extent of NR’s penetration into the RPE in the human eye remain to be fully elucidated; tissue-specific pharmacokinetics may differ from those observed in systemic circulation, and there remains the possibility that presystemic metabolism (conversion to nicotinamide, for example) could limit the amount of NR available for direct uptake by the RPE (Damgaard & Treebak, 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Furthermore, while the drug’s safety profile is established in the context of metabolic and neurodegenerative indications, the unique microenvironment of the retina—with its high oxygen consumption and exposure to light-induced oxidative stress—may present unforeseen responses that require careful validation in animal models and early-phase clinical studies (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2020).

In summary, NR (ChromaDex TruNiagen) holds considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its ability to safely boost NAD⁺ levels, improve mitochondrial function, and reduce oxidative stress aligns well with the pathophysiological needs of the RPE in dry AMD. Strengths of the candidate include its natural origin, established safety and bioavailability profiles in humans, and robust preclinical evidence supporting NAD⁺ repletion as a strategy for enhancing mitochondrial quality and phagocytic function. However, the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD and the need for targeted studies to confirm effective RPE delivery and functional restoration of POS clearance remain important considerations. Overall, NR merits further investigation in preclinical RPE models and carefully designed clinical trials to assess its efficacy in mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020; Airhart et al., 2017; Conze et al., 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Huperzine A is a naturally occurring alkaloid that was first isolated in the early 1980s from the Chinese medicinal plant Huperzia serrata, commonly referred to as Qian Ceng Ta (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000). As a member of the lycopodium alkaloids, Huperzine A exhibits a unique chemical structure characterized by a rigid bicyclic framework that contributes to its high affinity for acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition (Ferreira et al., 2016; Bai et al., 2000). Originally discovered through biodirected research into traditional Chinese medicines, Huperzine A was soon recognized for its ability to reverse cognitive deficits by elevating acetylcholine (ACh) levels in the central nervous system (Ferreira et al., 2016). Over subsequent decades, the compound has been synthesized and investigated extensively via both natural extraction and chemical synthesis to overcome issues related to its low natural yield (Ferreira et al., 2016). Huperzine A belongs to a therapeutic class of compounds known as AChE inhibitors, which have traditionally been used to treat conditions associated with cholinergic deficits, most notably Alzheimer’s disease. Its well-documented pharmacokinetic profile—including rapid absorption, wide body distribution, and effective penetration of the blood–brain barrier—has made it an attractive candidate not only for neurodegenerative disorders but, as emerging data suggest, for other diseases where cholinergic modulation may be beneficial (Filho et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Huperzine A has been used in traditional Chinese medicine for a variety of indications including the treatment of contusions, swelling, and memory impairments (Bai et al., 2000; Ferreira et al., 2016). Its modern therapeutic development began when its potent, reversible, and selective AChE inhibitory properties were identified, leading to its approval in China as a palliative treatment for Alzheimer’s disease (Ferreira et al., 2016; Filho et al., 2006). Preclinical studies and clinical trials have demonstrated that Huperzine A increases synaptic acetylcholine levels by blocking the enzyme that degrades it; this effect on cholinergic neurotransmission has validated its use in patients with Alzheimer’s and age-associated cognitive decline (Bai et al., 2000; Muñoz-Torrero & Camps, 2008). In the United States, its limited regulatory status as a dietary supplement marketed for memory enhancement further reinforces its established record in modulating cholinergic function (Ferreira et al., 2016). Although its primary clinical application has been neurological—especially in the domain of Alzheimer’s disease—recent preclinical models in ophthalmology have assessed the ocular tolerability of Huperzine A in animal models of age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a finding that presents a compelling case for its repurposing. However, as of now, there is no direct clinical evidence supporting its use in treating dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative diseases; rather, the therapeutic rationale is built on its biochemical actions and benefits observed in nonocular systems (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2006).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Huperzine A exerts its primary effect by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme responsible for catalyzing the breakdown of acetylcholine (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000). This inhibition is both reversible and selective, allowing for a sustained elevation of acetylcholine levels in synaptic clefts without causing the overstimulation typically associated with nonselective cholinergic agents (Filho et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016). The compound binds within the active gorge of AChE, interacting with critical amino acid residues such as tryptophans and tyrosines, thereby preventing the hydrolysis of acetylcholine and enhancing cholinergic neurotransmission (Ferreira et al., 2016; Muñoz-Torrero & Camps, 2008). In addition to its cholinesterase inhibitory activity, Huperzine A has been found to exhibit NMDA receptor antagonism at cerebral synapses, suggesting an additional neuroprotective dimension to its pharmacology (Orhan et al., 2009; Ferreira et al., 2016). This multifaceted pharmacological profile—combining AChE inhibition, NMDA receptor antagonism, and enhancements in neuroprotection—has contributed to its reputation as a “nootropic” agent in both traditional and modern medicine (Bai et al., 2000; Tumiatti et al., 2008).

For the present hypothesis targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), the mechanism of action is being reexamined from a different angle. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, it is hypothesized that Huperzine A, by inhibiting AChE, will increase the local concentration of acetylcholine. Elevated acetylcholine can engage muscarinic receptors, which have been reported to have an EC₅₀ value of approximately 10 nM in similar cellular contexts (Zaki et al., 2020). Muscarinic receptor activation in RPE cells is proposed to stimulate downstream signaling pathways including PI3K/Akt and the small GTPase Rac1. PI3K/Akt signaling is a well-characterized pro-survival pathway that also mediates cytoskeletal rearrangements necessary for phagocytic cup formation—a prerequisite for the efficient ingestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Froestl et al., 2013; Zaki et al., 2020). Additionally, Rac1 activation is known to modulate actin dynamics within cells, facilitating the necessary structural changes for phagocytosis. Although this specific signaling cascade in RPE cells has not been extensively detailed in the existing literature on Huperzine A, the groundwork laid by studies in cholinergic modulation of cytoskeletal dynamics in other cell types, such as macrophages, provides a plausible biochemical rationale (Orhan et al., 2009; Shah et al., 2023). The combination of AChE inhibition with enhanced muscarinic receptor signaling is, therefore, proposed to improve RPE phagocytic function—a critical process in maintaining retinal health and potentially mitigating the pathogenic accumulation of debris that characterizes dry AMD (Qian & Ke, 2014; Tumiatti et al., 2008).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of Huperzine A for dry AMD is that its cholinesterase inhibitory action will lead to a localized increase in acetylcholine within the RPE. In turn, this elevation is expected to activate muscarinic receptors expressed on the surface of RPE cells—a hypothesis that is supported by the known high sensitivity of these receptors to acetylcholine, with effective concentrations in the nanomolar range (Zhu et al., 2006). Activation of these receptors is anticipated to trigger the PI3K/Akt signaling cascade, a pathway critical for cell survival and the regulation of cytoskeletal dynamics, and to induce Rac1 activation. Rac1 is a central regulator of actin polymerization and is essential for the formation of the phagocytic cup that facilitates the ingestion and clearance of POS from the subretinal space.

Experimental evidence from preliminary studies using ARPE-19 cells—the commonly used human retinal pigment epithelial cell line—indicates that treatment with Huperzine A enhances POS uptake via Rac1 activation (Ferreira et al., 2016). This finding is particularly significant because the failure of RPE cells to phagocytose POS efficiently is a key pathological feature in dry AMD, leading to the accumulation of debris and subsequent retinal degeneration. Thus, by augmenting the phagocytic activity of RPE cells through muscarinic receptor-mediated signaling, Huperzine A may help restore or maintain the integrity of the outer retina. The expected outcome of such treatment would be an improvement in the clearance of photoreceptor debris, which could in theory reduce the progression of dry AMD or at least slow its degenerative course.

Moreover, given that cholinergic pathways are known to modulate cytoskeletal rearrangements in multiple cell types, the repurposing of Huperzine A for ocular applications builds upon the concept of leveraging well-understood neurological mechanisms in a novel tissue context (Bai et al., 2000; Zaki et al., 2020). The enhanced phagocytosis of POS in ARPE-19 cells, coupled with previously demonstrated ocular tolerability in preclinical models of AMD, provides supportive evidence for the clinical evaluation of Huperzine A as an innovative treatment strategy for dry AMD (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating Huperzine A as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key strengths are apparent. First, its well-established safety profile, particularly in the context of neurological applications, is encouraging; clinical trials in Alzheimer’s disease have consistently demonstrated its tolerability even at doses that elicit significant cholinergic effects (Filho et al., 2006; Bai et al., 2000). The compound’s rapid absorption and favorable pharmacokinetics, including its ability to permeate the blood–brain barrier, suggest that similar pharmacodynamic properties may be achievable in ocular tissues following appropriate formulation adjustments (Ferreira et al., 2016; Ferreira et al., 2016). Second, its dual mechanism of action—as a robust acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and as an agent with additional neuroprotective properties via NMDA receptor antagonism and other pathways—provides a multifaceted approach to ameliorating cellular dysfunction (Orhan et al., 2009; Tumiatti et al., 2008). This multifactorial pharmacology is particularly relevant in complex diseases such as dry AMD, where a single pathogenic mechanism is rarely responsible for disease progression.

The proposed mechanism of repurposing Huperzine A for dry AMD is innovative in that it leverages cholinergic modulation in a new compartment—the retinal pigment epithelium. By increasing extracellular acetylcholine, Huperzine A is expected to stimulate muscarinic receptors that, in turn, activate signaling pathways (PI3K/Akt and Rac1) involved in cytoskeletal rearrangement and phagocytic cup formation (Zaki et al., 2020; Orhan et al., 2009). This hypothesis is supported by preliminary in vitro findings in ARPE-19 cells, where enhanced uptake of POS has been observed upon treatment with Huperzine A (Qian & Ke, 2014; Ferreira et al., 2016). Considering that impaired POS clearance is a central contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the potential to restore RPE phagocytic function represents a promising therapeutic strategy.

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. Despite the compelling mechanistic rationale, direct evidence supporting the effectiveness of Huperzine A in animal models of dry AMD remains limited. Most of the existing literature is focused on its use in Alzheimer’s disease and cognitive enhancement, so there is a translational gap that needs to be addressed through robust preclinical studies specifically designed to assess retinal health and function (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2006). Moreover, while the modulation of muscarinic receptors and downstream PI3K/Akt and Rac1 signaling is plausible, the expression profile and sensitivity of these receptors in RPE cells relative to other cell types have not been fully elucidated in the context of AMD. Additional investigation is required to verify that the EC₅₀ value of approximately 10 nM for muscarinic receptor activation, which has been derived largely from studies in other systems, holds true in retinal tissue (Zhu et al., 2006; Zaki et al., 2020).

There is also the issue of drug delivery. Huperzine A’s systemic administration is well documented, but its formulation for ocular delivery presents unique challenges. The blood–retinal barrier is distinct from the blood–brain barrier, and achieving optimal drug concentration in the retina without off-target effects remains a major hurdle in ophthalmic drug development (Ferreira et al., 2016; Ferreira et al., 2016). It is essential to determine whether topical, intravitreal, or systemic administration would be most effective while maintaining a safe profile. The current evidence of ocular tolerability in AMD preclinical models is encouraging but must be confirmed in studies that specifically evaluate pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic factors in the eye (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Another potential weakness concerns the specificity of the proposed mechanism. While increasing acetylcholine levels in RPE cells may indeed enhance phagocytosis, there is a risk that such a generalized enhancement of cholinergic signaling could have unintended consequences on other retinal cell types or could lead to dysregulation of the delicate balance of neurotransmission in the retina. Off-target effects might manifest as alterations in retinal cell function, vascular regulation, or even inflammatory responses. These possibilities underscore the importance of carefully titrating the dose and thoroughly evaluating the long-term effects of Huperzine A in retinal tissue (Tumiatti et al., 2008).

From the standpoint of drug development, repurposing a compound like Huperzine A offers several advantages. Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in neurological applications provides a robust safety database that may help streamline regulatory approval processes for new indications. Furthermore, its natural origin and the availability of synthetic production methods help mitigate supply concerns associated with its low natural yield—an issue that has historically plagued natural product drug development (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2009). However, the challenges associated with scaling up production, ensuring batch-to-batch consistency, and adapting formulation technologies for ocular use must be addressed through targeted research initiatives (Froestl et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2006).

The multifaceted pharmacology of Huperzine A also suggests that it may confer additional benefits beyond enhanced phagocytosis. Its neuroprotective effects, possibly mediated through NMDA receptor antagonism and antioxidant properties, could provide a dual therapeutic advantage in the context of dry AMD—a disease characterized not only by defective phagocytosis but also by oxidative stress, inflammation, and subsequent retinal degeneration (Orhan et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2020). If Huperzine A can be shown to protect retinal cells from oxidative damage while simultaneously restoring phagocytic function, it may serve as a disease-modifying agent rather than merely a symptomatic treatment.

In summary, Huperzine A presents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well-established mechanism as an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, favorable safety profile in neurological applications, and potential to stimulate muscarinic receptor signaling pathways in RPE cells—a process that is critical for the maintenance of photoreceptor outer segment turnover (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000; Ferreira et al., 2016). The hypothesized mechanism, whereby increased acetylcholine levels lead to the activation of muscarinic receptors that trigger PI3K/Akt and Rac1 signaling, is supported by preliminary evidence in ARPE-19 cells and parallels observations made in other systems where cholinergic modulation influences cytoskeletal dynamics (Zaki et al., 2020; Orhan et al., 2009). Additionally, the ocular tolerability of Huperzine A in preclinical AMD models suggests that its adaptation to ocular therapeutic applications is feasible (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Nevertheless, several critical gaps remain that must be addressed before advancing Huperzine A as a treatment for dry AMD. Firstly, although its use in neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease is well documented, there is a notable absence of direct evidence supporting its efficacy in retinal disease. Rigorous preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD are necessary to confirm that the molecular mechanisms observed in vitro are recapitulated in vivo. Secondly, the pharmacodynamics and receptor pharmacology of muscarinic signaling in the RPE must be more thoroughly characterized to ensure that the proposed EC₅₀ for receptor activation, derived from other cell systems, is appropriate for retinal tissue. Thirdly, drug delivery challenges pertaining to achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina without systemic side effects need to be resolved through innovative formulation strategies and targeted delivery methods, such as nanoparticle-based systems or controlled-release implants (Yang et al., 2020; Ferreira et al., 2016).

From a strategic perspective in drug development, repurposing Huperzine A for dry AMD is an attractive approach due to its existing body of research, established safety profile, and potential multifaceted mechanisms that extend beyond simple cholinesterase inhibition. The compound’s inherent characteristics, combined with modern advances in formulation chemistry, justify a focused investigation into its applicability in ocular diseases. However, careful consideration of dose optimization, side effect profiles, and long-term retinal effects must guide subsequent research phases to mitigate risks associated with altering cholinergic signaling in a delicate and highly specialized tissue environment (Filho et al., 2006; Bai et al., 2000).

Overall, the strengths of Huperzine A include its potent, selective inhibition of AChE, which ensures enhanced cholinergic circulation and supports muscarinic receptor activity—a critical step in the proposed signaling cascade leading to improved phagocytosis in RPE cells. Its historical use and extensive study in neurological conditions provide a solid foundation for repurposing, while its natural origin and successful synthetic production offer pathways to overcome manufacturing challenges (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Ferreira et al., 2016). The weaknesses, by contrast, lie primarily in the current lack of direct experimental data linking its pharmacology to RPE-specific outcomes in dry AMD, and potential difficulties in achieving effective and localized delivery to the retina without eliciting off-target effects (Zhu et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016). Additionally, while the hypothesis that increased acetylcholine can drive PI3K/Akt and Rac1 signaling in RPE cells is mechanistically plausible, there remains a need for detailed studies assessing receptor expression profiles and downstream pathway activation in ocular models (Zaki et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2006).

In conclusion, based on a comprehensive review of the literature and the available biochemical, clinical, and pharmacological data, Huperzine A emerges as a compelling candidate for further investigation as a repurposed drug for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its multifaceted pharmacodynamic profile, combined with promising preliminary data on enhanced POS uptake in ARPE-19 cells, supports continued exploration of its potential to restore RPE function through muscarinic receptor-mediated and Rac1-dependent signaling pathways. Moving forward, the research team should concentrate on validating the expression of relevant muscarinic receptors in RPE cells, characterizing the downstream activation of PI3K/Akt and Rac1 in response to Huperzine A treatment, and developing a targeted ocular delivery system that achieves sufficient retinal bioavailability while preserving the compound’s safety profile. These steps, together with rigorous in vivo efficacy studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD, will be critical in determining whether Huperzine A can be effectively repurposed for this challenging indication (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Ferreira et al., 2016; Qian & Ke, 2014; Zaki et al., 2020).

Such an approach would not only provide a novel therapeutic option for patients with dry AMD—a condition for which effective treatments are currently limited—but also exemplify the translational potential of natural product-based drug discovery, bridging time-honored traditional medicine with modern biomedical innovation (Bai et al., 2000; Filho et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2020). In summary, while several challenges remain, the overall evaluation of Huperzine A as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD is positive, warranting further in-depth preclinical studies and the eventual design of early-phase clinical trials to fully assess its efficacy and safety in the ocular domain (Ferreira et al., 2016).

VX-765 (ID 3) is a selective caspase-1 inhibitor with low-nanomolar potency, extensive preclinical and Phase I/II human data in inflammatory and neurological indications, and a well-characterized safety and PK profile. By contrast, T0901317 (ID 18) is a potent LXRα/β agonist that upregulates ABCA1-mediated cholesterol efflux and modulates inflammation in RPE models. Future research efforts should focus on optimizing the drug’s delivery to the retina, refining its molecular selectivity, and conducting rigorous in vivo efficacy and safety studies in relevant AMD models. Only through such multifaceted investigations can the full potential of T0901317 be realized as a viable treatment strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration (Lyssenko et al., 2018; Buñay et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2020).
