Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AMD3100 (also known as plerixafor) is a small‐molecule, bicyclam compound originally discovered and synthesized as a CXCR4 antagonist. It belongs to a class of compounds designed to block the interaction between the chemokine ligand SDF‐1 (CXCL12) and its receptor CXCR4. This class of compounds was initially developed for their antiviral potential—specifically to inhibit HIV‐1 entry into cells—because CXCR4 serves as a co‐receptor for viral entry. Subsequent studies showed that through its high affinity for CXCR4 (with IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range, and our current hypothesis citing ~20 nM in RPE cells), AMD3100 can effectively block the downstream signaling of the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis. This signaling cascade is known to regulate key cellular processes such as chemotaxis, cell survival, proliferation, and inflammatory gene expression. With its synthetic origin and established profile as a CXCR4 antagonist, AMD3100 has been repurposed beyond its initial anti‐HIV goals to include hematopoietic stem cell mobilization and experimental oncology. Its potential re‐utilization in ocular diseases, particularly in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), capitalizes on its ability to modulate inflammatory signaling pathways implicated in retinal degeneration (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AMD3100 emerged from research aimed at blocking HIV infection, but its clinical development pivoted after it was found to robustly mobilize hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells from the bone marrow. This discovery led to its approval by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as an adjuvant therapy for autologous stem cell transplantation in patients with non‐Hodgkin’s lymphoma and multiple myeloma. Its use in stem cell mobilization has been thoroughly characterized in clinical trials with documented pharmacokinetics and a reasonable safety profile in systemic administration (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019). In addition to these applications, AMD3100 has been investigated in various preclinical models of cancer, where its inhibition of CXCR4-mediated signaling has been linked to reduced tumor cell invasion, decreased angiogenesis, and altered immune cell trafficking (Andtbacka et al., 2022; Cho et al., 2013). In the ocular context, although AMD3100 has not been used directly for treating dry AMD, its effects on CXCR4 signaling have been addressed in studies focusing on glaucomatous models. For example, investigations in trabecular meshwork cells from glaucomatous tissue have demonstrated that AMD3100, when administered at 1 mM concentration, completely abrogates the protective effects of CXCL12 and inadvertently induces apoptosis, highlighting the dual role of CXCR4 signaling in ocular tissues (Denoyer et al., 2012). Moreover, systemic administration studies in non‐ocular models such as the SOD1^G93A ALS mouse model have shown that chronic AMD3100 treatment can yield neuroprotective and anti‐inflammatory benefits (Rabinovich‐Nikitin et al., 2016), which further adds to its therapeutic appeal but also underscores the importance of tissue-specific dosing and context. These historical uses underscore AMD3100’s well-defined pharmacological profile while simultaneously illustrating that translating its benefits to the RPE in dry AMD will require reconciling its established systemic effects with the often finely balanced roles of the CXCR4 axis in retinal tissue repair and inflammation (Cai et al., 2014; Saiman et al., 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, AMD3100 exerts its primary pharmacological action by selectively binding to the CXCR4 receptor and competitively inhibiting the binding of its natural ligand, SDF‐1 (CXCL12). In doing so, it prevents receptor activation and the subsequent engagement of intracellular signaling cascades mediated by G-protein coupled receptor activation. The downstream effects typically include modulation of pathways such as PI3K/Akt, Ras/ERK, and, in many cases, alterations in intracellular calcium fluxes that contribute to chemotaxis and cell survival (Bai et al., 2016; Colasanti et al., 2025). By inhibiting these cascades, AMD3100 hinders not only the migration of cells toward SDF‐1 gradients but also the pro‐inflammatory and pro‐angiogenic gene expression programs that are otherwise activated upon CXCR4 engagement. In cancer models, this mechanism translates into reduced tumor cell invasion and inhibition of angiogenesis, while in immune cells it modulates chemotactic responses and inflammatory cell trafficking (Cho et al., 2013). Importantly, CXCR4 is expressed in multiple ocular cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. In RPE, the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis has been implicated in cellular migration, cytokine secretion, and potentially in the regulation of the phagocytic machinery necessary for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). The hypothesis driving the current proposal suggests that chronic activation of CXCR4 in RPE cells, possibly driven by persistent inflammatory stimuli such as TNF‐α, leads to a pro‐inflammatory state that downregulates key phagocytic receptors like MERTK and compromises lysosomal enzyme activity. By blocking the binding of SDF‐1 to CXCR4, AMD3100 is expected to interrupt this deleterious signaling cascade, resulting in normalization of MERTK expression and lysosomal enzyme levels, and thereby restoring the essential phagocytic function of the RPE (Colasanti et al., 2025). However, the complexity of CXCR4 signaling is underscored by studies in other ocular tissues where its inhibition has led to apoptosis of trabecular cells, suggesting that the outcome of CXCR4 blockade may be highly dependent on the cell type and the local microenvironment (Denoyer et al., 2012). Therefore, while the mechanistic rationale is strong, careful evaluation of AMD3100’s specific molecular interactions in RPE cells will be required to delineate beneficial effects from potential adverse outcomes.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed therapeutic strategy hypothesizes that the blockade of CXCR4 by AMD3100 in RPE cells will lead to two major beneficial outcomes in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration: (1) inhibition of pro-inflammatory signaling that otherwise promotes aberrant cellular migration and deleterious inflammatory gene expression, and (2) restoration of the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells through upregulation of key receptors and enzymes necessary for the efficient clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In dry AMD, a hallmark of disease progression is the accumulation of cellular debris and the failure of RPE cells to effectively clear POS due to impaired phagocytosis—a process that is critical for sustaining photoreceptor health and visual function. Evidence suggests that chronic activation of the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis in the retinal microenvironment can lead to elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines and subsequent downregulation of MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase essential for the recognition and internalization of shed POS (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). In vitro models, such as TNF‐α–treated ARPE-19 cells, have demonstrated that inflammatory stress leads to diminished phagocytic activity, and it is hypothesized that blocking CXCR4 signaling with AMD3100 could counteract this effect by normalizing MERTK levels and restoring lysosomal function. In an ideal scenario, treatment with AMD3100 would reverse the pro-inflammatory signaling cascade by preventing SDF‐1 binding, reduce aberrant RPE migration, and allow the cells to maintain their structural polarity and phagocytic efficiency. Importantly, the RPE expresses CXCR4 receptors on their surface, as demonstrated by immunocytochemical studies, and the receptor’s activation has been linked to altered cellular motility and inflammatory responses (Canonica et al., 2021; Enzmann et al., 2017). The expected pharmacodynamic outcome is that, upon AMD3100 treatment, RPE cells under inflammatory stress conditions would exhibit increased expression of MERTK and lysosomal enzymes, leading to improved clearance of damaged photoreceptor outer segments, which is critical for photoreceptor survival and overall retinal health. While data from other cell types suggest the possibility of safely modulating these pathways, caution is warranted given the evidence from trabecular meshwork cells where CXCR4 antagonism disrupted protective signaling (Denoyer et al., 2012). Hence, the key to success will lie in establishing the proper dosing and delivery mechanisms that provide sufficient blockade of deleterious CXCR4 signaling in RPE without compromising the receptor’s potentially beneficial roles in tissue repair and homeostasis.

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, AMD3100 presents an intriguing candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration given its well-defined mechanism of action, extensive preclinical and clinical history, and a known safety profile in non-ocular indications such as hematopoietic stem cell mobilization and cancer therapy (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019). The central hypothesis—that chronic SDF‐1/CXCR4 signaling in RPE cells contributes to inflammation-driven downregulation of MERTK and consequent impairment of POS phagocytosis—addresses a critical pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD. Blocking this pathway with AMD3100 could, in theory, restore the phagocytic machinery of the RPE, thereby reducing the accumulation of toxic cellular debris and slowing disease progression (Colasanti et al., 2025).

One of the strengths of AMD3100 as a therapeutic candidate lies in its extensive clinical use and established pharmacokinetic profile; its FDA approval for stem cell mobilization means that much is already known about its systemic effects, dosing parameters, and potential toxicities when administered appropriately (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Rabinovich-Nikitin et al., 2016). Moreover, the molecular mechanism—competitive antagonism at the CXCR4 receptor—has been demonstrated across multiple studies and various cell types, providing a robust theoretical framework for its use in modulating pathological signaling cascades in RPE cells (Bai et al., 2016; Colasanti et al., 2025). The concept of repurposing a well-characterized agent such as AMD3100 for dry AMD is attractive from a drug development standpoint because it could potentially shorten the translational timeline and reduce development risks related to novel chemical entities.

However, there are significant challenges and weaknesses that must be addressed before AMD3100 can be considered a promising candidate for dry AMD. First and foremost, the role of SDF‐1/CXCR4 signaling in ocular tissues appears to be multifaceted. While in RPE cells chronic activation may indeed drive a pro-inflammatory and phagocytosis-impairing phenotype, in other ocular tissues such as the trabecular meshwork, CXCR4 signaling has been shown to exert cytoprotective effects. Studies in glaucomatous trabecular cells have demonstrated that blockade of CXCR4 by AMD3100 not only abrogates the beneficial actions of CXCL12 but may also actively induce apoptosis, highlighting a potential risk that the protective aspects of CXCR4 signaling could be compromised (Denoyer et al., 2012). This tissue-specific duality raises concerns that non-selective or systemic inhibition of CXCR4 might lead to unintended adverse effects in the retina and other ocular compartments. Therefore, any consideration of AMD3100 for dry AMD will require extremely careful dosing studies and potentially localized delivery strategies that avoid systemic over-blockade.

Another key consideration is the current lack of direct evidence supporting the efficacy of AMD3100 in restoring MERTK expression or lysosomal enzyme levels in RPE cells, specifically in the context of dry AMD. While preliminary in vitro observations in TNF‐α–treated ARPE-19 cells are promising, these studies remain preliminary, and the translation of these effects into meaningful functional outcomes in vivo has yet to be established. The complexity of dry AMD pathogenesis—which involves not only inflammatory processes but also oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, and altered cellular metabolism—means that targeting a single pathway may not be sufficient to recapitulate the full spectrum of therapeutic benefit required for clinical efficacy (Colasanti et al., 2025).

Furthermore, the potential for AMD3100 to affect cell migration and even cellular differentiation via CXCR4 inhibition might have unpredictable consequences on the RPE’s capacity for repair. For instance, the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis has been implicated in the recruitment of bone marrow–derived progenitor cells to sites of RPE injury, a process that is thought to contribute to endogenous repair mechanisms (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). Inhibiting CXCR4 could inadvertently interfere with these reparative processes if not finely tuned. It is, therefore, imperative that any preclinical evaluation of AMD3100 for dry AMD includes rigorous assessments of not only phagocytic function and inflammatory profile but also the impact on RPE cell survival, differentiation, and regenerative capacity.

In addition to cell-specific concerns, the delivery method for AMD3100 in the context of dry AMD is another critical factor. The compound has been used systemically, but ocular diseases typically require either intravitreal or other localized delivery methods to achieve therapeutic concentrations while minimizing systemic exposure. Prior studies involving AMD3100 in ocular models—mostly in the context of glaucoma—have used subconjunctival injections at relatively high concentrations (e.g., 1 mM), which resulted in localized apoptotic effects (Denoyer et al., 2012). This suggests that the concentration and mode of delivery will need to be carefully optimized for the RPE to ensure that sufficient drug levels are achieved to block aberrant CXCR4 signaling without tipping the balance of protective chemokine functions.

Moreover, while the preclinical data from non-ocular models such as cancer and ALS are encouraging regarding the anti-inflammatory and anti-migratory effects of AMD3100 (Rabinovich-Nikitin et al., 2016; Andtbacka et al., 2022), these contexts differ significantly from the microenvironment of the aging retina. The retinal tissue, particularly in dry AMD, is characterized by complex interactions among the RPE, photoreceptors, Bruch’s membrane, and the choriocapillaris. The interplay of these structures with age-related oxidative stress and immune dysregulation means that any intervention must be evaluated in models that faithfully recapitulate these conditions. There is a paucity of direct literature on the use of AMD3100 in dry AMD models, which suggests that a substantial body of preclinical work is required before a clear signal of benefit can be ascertained.

In summary, AMD3100 has significant strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its well-documented mechanism of competitive antagonism at CXCR4, combined with an established clinical safety profile in systemic applications and a clear rationale for targeting the SDF‐1/CXCR4 axis in inflammatory conditions, supports further investigation of its use in the retinal pigment epithelium (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019; Bai et al., 2016). However, key weaknesses include evidence from ocular models that indicate potential cytotoxicity when protective CXCR4 signals are indiscriminately blocked (Denoyer et al., 2012), as well as a lack of direct preclinical data in dry AMD or RPE-specific phagocytic assays. These concerns necessitate a cautious yet exploratory approach, with initial studies focused on establishing the optimal local dosing regimen, confirming that AMD3100 can indeed restore MERTK expression and phagocytic function in ARPE-19 cell models, and ultimately validating these findings in animal models of dry AMD that incorporate stressors such as TNF‐α or oxidative injury.

Overall Evaluation:  
In conclusion, while AMD3100 stands as one of the most thoroughly characterized CXCR4 antagonists with a solid clinical and preclinical background, its application to dry AMD remains largely untested. The theoretical basis—that chronic SDF‐1/CXCR4 activation in RPE drives inflammatory gene expression leading to diminished phagocytic capacity, and that blocking this pathway will restore homeostatic functions—is compelling and addresses a known pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD (Colasanti et al., 2025). The strengths of AMD3100 include its potent CXCR4 binding affinity, the wealth of pharmacological data supporting its mode of action, and its demonstrated ability to modulate inflammatory and migratory responses in various tissues. Moreover, the clinical safety data from its use in hematopoietic stem cell mobilization provide some reassurance regarding its tolerability when used in appropriate dosing regimens (Tahirovic et al., 2020; Smoragiewicz, 2019).

On the other hand, several significant weaknesses must be acknowledged. Studies in ocular models have shown that CXCR4 blockade can eliminate protective signals that are crucial for cell survival, as evidenced by the induction of apoptosis in trabecular meshwork cells when treated with AMD3100 at high concentrations (Denoyer et al., 2012). In addition, there is a risk that by inhibiting CXCR4 signaling, AMD3100 might interfere with endogenous repair mechanisms mediated by the recruitment of bone marrow–derived progenitor cells, a process that may be beneficial in RPE regeneration (Enzmann et al., 2017; Canonica et al., 2021). The lack of direct data demonstrating restoration of MERTK and improved phagocytosis in RPE cells further complicates the evaluation. Because dry AMD is multifactorial, it is unclear whether modulation of a single pathway—albeit an important one—will be sufficient to yield a meaningful clinical benefit without causing collateral damage to other aspects of RPE function.

Given these considerations, our recommendation is to pursue rigorous preclinical studies specifically tailored to dry AMD. These studies should encompass detailed in vitro analyses using ARPE-19 and primary human RPE cells under inflammatory and oxidative stress conditions to validate whether AMD3100 can reliably restore MERTK expression and lysosomal function, thereby enhancing POS clearance. It will also be critical to establish the appropriate concentration window that achieves therapeutic blockade of deleterious signaling while preserving necessary CXCR4-mediated protective effects. Parallel in vivo studies in animal models of dry AMD should focus on local ocular delivery methods—potentially through intravitreal or controlled-release formulations—to minimize systemic exposure and optimize retinal bioavailability.

In conclusion, AMD3100 represents an exciting and scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its mechanism of CXCR4 antagonism and the hypothesized link between chronic SDF‐1/CXCR4 activation and impaired RPE phagocytosis. However, given the mixed evidence from ocular safety studies and the complexity of CXCR4 signaling in retinal homeostasis, further systematic preclinical evaluation is essential before advancing to clinical trials. The balance between inhibiting pathological inflammation and preserving or even harnessing protective regenerative signals will determine the ultimate viability of AMD3100 as a therapeutic agent for dry age‐related macular degeneration (Denoyer et al., 2012; Rabinovich-Nikitin et al., 2016; Bai et al., 2016).

It belongs to the class of mucolipin synthetic agonists, which were initially derived as analogs of earlier lead compounds such as SF‐51 and SF‐22. These compounds were discovered using high‐throughput screening approaches aimed at identifying activators of TRPML channels, and ML‐SA1 was subsequently optimized for improved potency and selectivity in mammalian systems (Feng et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2012). As a synthetic compound, ML‐SA1 exemplifies a rational drug design strategy in which the molecule is engineered to mimic the action of the endogenous lipid agonist phosphatidylinositol 3,5‐bisphosphate [PI(3,5)P₂] by directly binding to the channel’s pore region. This binding stabilizes TRPML1 in its open conformation, thereby facilitating lysosomal Ca²⁺ release. The chemical class represented by ML‐SA1 has historically been employed as a research tool to interrogate lysosomal physiology and calcium homeostasis in diverse cell types, including neuronal and retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Therapeutic History:  
Previous studies have demonstrated that ML‐SA1 robustly elevates cytosolic calcium levels in several cellular models by activating TRPML1 channels. In particular, ML‐SA1 has been applied to multiple RPE cell models—including mouse RPE, human embryonic stem cell‐derived RPE, and the ARPE‐19 cell line—to assess its ability to restore lysosomal calcium signaling and normalize lysosomal function (Gómez et al., 2018). In these experiments, ML‐SA1 elicited rapid, robust, and reversible Ca²⁺ signals that were completely absent in TRPML1 knockout cells, thereby confirming target engagement and specificity (Gómez et al., 2018). Beyond RPE biology, ML‐SA1 has been evaluated in neuronal models of lysosomal dysfunction, including experimental systems relevant to Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease, where it mediated correction of defective lysosomal acidification and improved autophagic flux (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022). Although no clinical trials have yet investigated ML‐SA1 directly in patients with dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), its demonstrated efficacy in rescuing lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling—in conditions that share underlying pathophysiological features with dry AMD such as lysosomal storage and autophagy blockade—suggests that its repurposing may yield therapeutic benefits in this disease context (Open Targets Platform, 2025). To date, the use of ML‐SA1 has predominantly been within experimental research settings rather than in clinical practice or veterinary medicine, and its repurposing for dry AMD represents an innovative and rationale‐driven approach rooted in the overlap between TRPML1 dysfunction and RPE pathology (Feng et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2017).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic action of ML‐SA1 is centered upon its ability to directly activate TRPML1 channels located on lysosomal membranes. TRPML1 plays a critical role in regulating lysosomal calcium homeostasis by mediating Ca²⁺ efflux from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol. ML‐SA1 binds directly to TRPML1—likely within a hydrophobic pocket formed at the S5–S6 transmembrane domain interface—and stabilizes the channel’s open state (Feng et al., 2014). This activation occurs independently of exogenous PI(3,5)P₂ in mammalian cells, setting ML‐SA1 apart from the endogenous regulatory mechanisms that otherwise depend on dynamic fluctuations in phosphoinositide levels (Feng et al., 2014; Gómez et al., 2018). As a result of channel activation, lysosomal Ca²⁺ is released into the cytosol, triggering a cascade of calcium‐dependent signaling pathways. One critical downstream effect is the promotion of lysosomal membrane fission and fusion events, processes that are essential for proper lysosomal trafficking and the maturation of autophagosomes into autolysosomes (Cao et al., 2017; Li & Li, 2022).  

Beyond its immediate role in calcium mobilization, ML‐SA1‐mediated activation of TRPML1 also facilitates the activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Increased cytosolic Ca²⁺ can activate calcineurin, which in turn dephosphorylates TFEB, enabling its translocation to the nucleus where it upregulates the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function and autophagy (Pollmanns et al., 2022). In some models, ML‐SA1 treatment has been shown to improve the processing and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D, thereby contributing to normalization of lysosomal pH and enhanced protein degradation (Hui et al., 2019). Importantly, the ability of ML‐SA1 to restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling directly targets the pathological cascade observed when TRPML1 is deficient or inhibited—a scenario that is reminiscent of the lysosomal storage, impaired autophagy, and stalled phagolysosomal degradation evident in dry AMD RPE cells (Gómez et al., 2018; Pamonag, 2021).  

Expected Effect:  
Based on the observed mechanisms in diverse cellular models, it is expected that ML‐SA1 will re‐establish normal lysosomal function in RPE cells afflicted by dry AMD. In the proposed assay, the activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 at concentrations near its EC₅₀ (approximately 5 µM) should restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ efflux, thereby driving several beneficial downstream effects. First, the induced calcium release is anticipated to promote lysosomal membrane dynamics that favor fission and fusion events, ultimately leading to improved lysosomal trafficking and an enhanced capacity for phagolysosomal degradation. This is particularly relevant for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), the routine phagocytic burden of RPE cells that, when inadequately processed, contributes to lipofuscin accumulation and retinal degeneration (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Second, by normalizing Ca²⁺ signaling, ML‐SA1 is expected to reinstate proper lysosomal acidification. Acidification is crucial for the optimal activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D; ML‐SA1 has been shown in various models to restore cathepsin D processing, thereby resetting the enzymatic degradation cascade necessary for POS turnover (Hui et al., 2019). Such restoration of acidification and enzyme activity would directly counteract the pathological accumulation of undegraded material—a hallmark of dry AMD.  

Third, the downstream activation of TFEB induced by ML‐SA1’s modulation of lysosomal calcium may trigger an upregulation of the entire lysosomal-autophagy gene network. This transcriptional reprogramming is vital for augmenting both the number and function of lysosomes, thereby enhancing the overall cellular clearance capacity in RPE cells. Because ample evidence suggests that TRPML1 is expressed in RPE cells and that its dysfunction contributes directly to the autophagy block observed in dry AMD (Pamonag, 2021; Gómez et al., 2018), the activation of this pathway by ML‐SA1 is expected to result in a net improvement in POS degradation and a reduction in toxic debris accumulation. Ultimately, the integrated effects of improved lysosomal trafficking, normalized pH, enhanced enzymatic processing, and boosted autophagic flux are hypothesized to alleviate key pathological features of dry AMD, potentially slowing or even reversing degenerative changes in the retinal pigment epithelium (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Our comprehensive literature review indicates that ML‐SA1 is a scientifically compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration. One of its principal strengths lies in its well‐defined mechanism of action: by directly activating TRPML1 channels, ML‐SA1 has been shown to restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ homeostasis—a central defect in several models of lysosomal storage and autophagy dysfunction (Gómez et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2014). The robust experimental data obtained in RPE cell models and other relevant systems supports the hypothesis that ML‐SA1 can reverse deficits in lysosomal trafficking, acidification, and autophagosome maturation. The compound’s ability to elicit rapid, reproducible, and reversible Ca²⁺ signals is particularly encouraging, as it suggests that pharmacological modulation of TRPML1 can be finely tuned through dosing adjustments (Gómez et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2017).  

Furthermore, the extensive research demonstrating ML‐SA1’s effects in cellular models of lysosomal storage diseases—including those markers that mimic the pathological lipid accumulation and autophagy impairment found in dry AMD—provides additional rationale for its application in RPE cells (Feng et al., 2014; Pollmanns et al., 2022; Hui et al., 2019). The fact that ML‐SA1 has also been evaluated in non-ocular contexts (such as neuronal models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s diseases) where it facilitated autophagic clearance and improved lysosomal functions underscores the versatility of its mechanism and hints at broader therapeutic utility (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022).  

Nonetheless, several challenges must be acknowledged. One notable weakness is that ML‐SA1’s efficacy can be compromised by lysosomal lipid accumulation—a common feature of advanced dry AMD. Studies suggest that in cells with significant lipid deposition, such as those accumulating sphingomyelin or other inhibitory lipids, the activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 is attenuated (Gómez et al., 2018). This raises concerns that in patients with advanced dry AMD, the therapeutic window may be narrower or may require combination strategies to first reduce lipid burden. Additionally, while the in vitro EC₅₀ is promising (around 5 µM), there remains uncertainty regarding the pharmacokinetic profile, bioavailability, tissue penetration (particularly across the blood‐retina barrier), and potential off-target effects of ML‐SA1 when administered in vivo (Li & Li, 2022).  

Another area of concern is the current lack of direct clinical data pertaining to ML‐SA1 in dry AMD. Although preclinical studies in RPE cell models provide a solid foundation, translation to in vivo models of AMD—and eventually to human clinical trials—will require additional investigation. The absence of any reported clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD with TRPML1 agonists (as confirmed by database searches such as those reflected in the Open Targets Platform) indicates that this is still a largely uncharted therapeutic area requiring further validation (Open Targets Platform, 2025). Moreover, chronic activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 may have unforeseen consequences related to intracellular calcium homeostasis and autophagic balance, which warrant careful evaluation in long-term studies (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022).  

In summary, ML‐SA1 represents a highly promising candidate for the repurposing in dry AMD based on its ability to rescue lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling, enhance autophagic clearance, and restore normal lysosomal pH and trafficking in RPE cells. Its synthetic origin and well‐characterized mechanism provide a strong mechanistic rationale for its use. However, issues related to lipid-mediated inhibition of TRPML1, pharmacokinetic considerations, and the current lack of in vivo data in AMD models must be addressed. Overall, the candidate shows significant potential, but a focused program of preclinical validation—including animal models of dry AMD, detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiling, and exploration of strategies to mitigate lysosomal lipid accumulation—is essential before advancing ML‐SA1 to clinical trials for dry AMD (Gómez et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Auranofin is an orally bioavailable gold(I) complex that was first synthesized as a candidate to treat rheumatoid arthritis and is historically considered the first orally administered gold drug. Chemically, it is composed of a water‐soluble aurothioglucose moiety linked to a lipophilic triethylphosphine ligand, and, upon metabolism, it yields active gold species such as a triethylphosphine–gold(I) cation and gold–thioglucose derivatives (Abdalbari, 2025). Auranofin belongs to the class of organogold compounds, which have long been recognized for their anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties. In general, this class of compounds has been used primarily in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis due to their ability to modulate immune cell activity, interfere with inflammatory cytokine production, and target redox-sensitive enzymes. Although originally developed and clinically validated for rheumatic diseases, research over the past decades has repurposed auranofin for anticancer, antiparasitic, antimicrobial, and more recently, for potential neuroprotective indications (Madeira, 2012; Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a).  

Therapeutic History:  
Auranofin has an established therapeutic history as an anti-rheumatic agent with a clinical safety profile characterized over several decades of use. In the 1980s it was approved by regulatory agencies for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis where it demonstrated comparable efficacy with fewer severe side effects relative to parenteral gold salts, while its oral delivery provided a significant improvement in patient compliance (Abdalbari, 2025). In addition to its use in rheumatology, auranofin has been studied for its anticancer properties, with investigations demonstrating its ability to induce reactive oxygen species (ROS), inhibit cell proliferation, and trigger apoptosis in various cancer models including ovarian, lung, and mesothelioma cells (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a; Mertens et al., 2023). Despite its broad repurposing interest in oncology and infectious diseases, auranofin has not been directly used for treating dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, the cellular mechanisms implicated in its pharmacological actions—particularly its effects on redox homeostasis and anti-inflammatory pathways—provide a compelling rationale for exploring its potential in dry AMD, a disease known to involve chronic oxidative stress, lysosomal dysfunction, and inflammation in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021b; Chen et al., 2023).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary molecular target of auranofin is thioredoxin reductase (TrxR), a critical selenoenzyme involved in maintaining cellular redox balance. Auranofin interacts with TrxR by binding preferentially to its redox-active selenocysteine residue, thereby irreversibly inhibiting its NADPH-dependent catalytic activity (Abdalbari, 2025). Inhibition of TrxR disrupts the thioredoxin (Trx) system leading to an accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and oxidative stress within the cell. This increase in ROS, while potentially cytotoxic at high levels, can also serve as a signal to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, a master regulator of antioxidant responses. Under conditions of elevated oxidative stress, Nrf2 translocates to the nucleus and binds to antioxidant response elements (ARE) in the regulatory regions of target genes, inducing the expression of several cytoprotective enzymes, including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) and enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis and regeneration (Chen et al., 2016; Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a).  

In addition to its redox-modulatory function, auranofin has been reported to affect lysosomal pathways. Preclinical studies in RPE-derived cells (ARPE-19) have shown that auranofin can attenuate lysosomal alkalinization and thereby improve lysosomal function, an effect that may translate into enhanced degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) under oxidative stress conditions (Chen et al., 2016). This effect on lysosomal preservation is particularly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where the accumulation of undigested POS debris contributes to the formation of drusen and lipofuscin, leading to RPE dysfunction over time. Auranofin’s dual impact—disrupting redox homeostasis via TrxR inhibition while simultaneously triggering a compensatory Nrf2-mediated antioxidant response and preserving lysosomal function—constitutes an attractive mechanistic rationale for its repurposing into ocular indications (Abdalbari, 2025).  

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesized mechanism, when applied to RPE cells, auranofin is expected to inhibit TrxR activity, thus initially promoting an increase in ROS production. This controlled elevation in ROS is anticipated to serve as a secondary signal for the activation of Nrf2, which in turn drives the transcription of antioxidant genes such as HO-1 and genes involved in glutathione synthesis, thereby restoring intracellular redox balance (Madeira, 2012; Abdalbari, 2025). In ARPE-19 cell assays, this cascade should lead to a measurable increase in cellular antioxidant capacity, as well as a reduction in oxidative damage markers. Furthermore, by preserving or even restoring lysosomal acidity and function, auranofin is expected to boost the degradation of POS, particularly in cells challenged with lipofuscin components such as A2E that are known to disrupt lysosomal function (Chen et al., 2016). The enhanced clearance of POS should, in theory, mitigate the accumulation of toxic byproducts that contribute to RPE senescence and the progression of dry AMD (Chen et al., 2023; Brodzka et al., 2024). Moreover, the improvement in lysosomal function may also translate into better maintenance of the RPE’s barrier function and phagocytic capacity, both of which are vital for retinal homeostasis. The oral safety profile established in rheumatoid arthritis supports the notion that, with proper dosing and perhaps targeted ocular delivery strategies, auranofin could be repurposed safely for ocular use, though detailed pharmacokinetic studies in ocular tissues would be required to confirm this (Abdalbari, 2025).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Auranofin presents several compelling strengths as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its well-documented history as an orally administered anti-rheumatic agent with an established human safety profile allows for rapid progression into clinical testing if preliminary ocular efficacy is demonstrated. The mechanistic rationale is robust: by inhibiting TrxR, auranofin triggers an increase in ROS that activates the Nrf2 pathway, culminating in the upregulation of cytoprotective antioxidant genes, restoration of glutathione levels, and the preservation of lysosomal function—all of which are key factors in countering the pathogenic processes in dry AMD (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a; Mertens et al., 2023). In addition, preclinical evidence in RPE models indicates that auranofin can modulate signaling pathways such as EGFR/MAPK and that its effects are ROS-dependent, as demonstrated by the mitigation of toxicity with the antioxidant N-acetyl cysteine (Chen et al., 2016).  

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges remain. Although the mechanistic data derived from cancer and non-ocular studies are promising, direct in vivo evidence of auranofin’s efficacy in AMD or related RPE dysfunction models is currently lacking. The cytotoxic nature of auranofin at higher concentrations observed in ARPE-19 cells necessitates careful determination of a dosing window that maximizes the beneficial activation of Nrf2 and lysosomal preservation without exacerbating oxidative damage or inducing cell death (Chen et al., 2016; Madeira, 2012). Furthermore, while the systemic safety of auranofin in rheumatic diseases is relatively well established, the specific requirements for ocular drug delivery—such as achieving sufficient retinal bioavailability while minimizing off-target effects—pose additional challenges that must be addressed through formulation innovation and rigorous preclinical testing (Abdalbari, 2025). Finally, because the pathogenesis of dry AMD is multifactorial, involving not only oxidative stress and lysosomal dysfunction but also inflammatory and complement-mediated processes, it is possible that auranofin alone may not be sufficiently efficacious in a clinical setting without combination with other therapeutic modalities designed to address these complementary pathways (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a; Chen et al., 2016).  

In summary, auranofin holds potential as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD due to its ability to modulate critical redox pathways via TrxR inhibition and subsequent Nrf2 activation, along with its potential to restore lysosomal function and improve the clearance of POS-related debris. Its established safety record in rheumatoid arthritis, combined with promising mechanistic underpinnings observed in both non-ocular and limited ocular cell models, supports further investigation into its use for dry AMD. However, given the current gaps in direct ocular evidence and the challenges of ocular drug delivery, additional preclinical studies specifically in AMD-relevant models (including detailed ARPE-19 studies, in vivo AMD models, and pharmacokinetic assessments in retinal tissue) are warranted to fully validate its therapeutic potential and safety for eventual clinical application (Chen et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2016; Madeira, 2012; Abdalbari, 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
D609, chemically known as tricyclodecan-9-yl xanthogenate, is a synthetic small‐molecule compound belonging to the xanthate class. It was originally synthesized through classical organic‐chemical methods involving the reaction of diastereomeric tricyclic alcohols with carbon disulfide in the presence of a strong base such as potassium tert‐butoxide, yielding a mixture of eight stereoisomers due to its three asymmetric centers (Bhat et al., 2022; Eurtivong et al., 2023). As a member of the xanthate family, D609 has been extensively studied for its diverse biological activities that include antiviral, antitumoral, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective effects (Bhat et al., 2022). Its mechanism of competitive inhibition of phosphatidylcholine-specific phospholipase C (PC-PLC) was discovered during the evaluation of lipid signaling pathways, and it is commercially available (for example, Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. D0209) as a research-grade compound (Wang et al., 2020). This chemical class has traditionally been investigated in various biomedical contexts, with early work focusing on its antiviral properties dating back to the 1980s and subsequent studies extending its uses into oncology and neurology (Bhat et al., 2022). Its water solubility and relatively low molecular weight make it an attractive candidate for repurposing into ocular applications where intracellular signaling and oxidative stress play key roles.

Therapeutic History:  
D609 has been the subject of more than 700 published reports over the last three decades and has been explored in preclinical studies ranging from antiviral and anticancer applications to neuroprotection and inflammation modulation (Bhat et al., 2022). One of the most compelling lines of evidence for repurposing D609 concerns its potential in treating ocular conditions, particularly dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In several studies, D609 has been directly evaluated for its ability to protect retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) cells from oxidative damage using in vitro cell models such as the widely used ARPE-19 cell line and primary human RPE cells (Wang et al., 2020). For instance, one study employing a high-content screening strategy on 814 protective compounds identified D609 as a lead candidate that maintained RPE cell viability above 95% under severe oxidative stress induced by sodium iodate—a condition used to model dry AMD (Wang et al., 2020). Furthermore, in vivo animal models, including sodium iodate-induced AMD mouse models, have confirmed that D609 can protect the RPE layer, preserve retinal structure and function, and prevent geographic atrophy—findings that underscore its translational potential for dry AMD therapy (Wang et al., 2020). Outside the field of ophthalmology, D609 has been evaluated in oncology, where it affected cell proliferation and induced apoptosis in certain tumor cell lines, and in neuroscience for its neuroprotective effects against amyloid-beta toxicity and oxidative stress in neuronal cultures (Bhat et al., 2022). Although no clinical trials have yet been reported that specifically target dry AMD with D609, the preclinical data generated in ocular, cancer, and neurodegenerative studies provide a robust therapeutic history that supports depth of investigation into its ocular application (Wang et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At its core, D609 is a competitive inhibitor of PC-PLC. PC-PLC is an enzyme that hydrolyzes phosphatidylcholine (PC) into phosphorylcholine and diacylglycerol (DAG). In RPE cells, overactivation of this enzyme under oxidative stress conditions may lead to excessive DAG production that, in turn, drives hyperactivation of protein kinase C (PKC) and downstream signaling events deleteriously affecting cytoskeletal dynamics and phagocytosis (Wang et al., 2020). D609 exerts its inhibitory activity by mimicking parts of the natural substrate, competitively binding to the active site of PC-PLC—in part through its dithiocarbonate group, which can chelate zinc ions that are critical for enzyme function (Wang et al., 2020; González-Roura et al., 2002). In addition to its direct inhibition of PC-PLC, D609 has been reported to exert antioxidative effects indirectly via upregulation of metallothionein proteins—an antioxidative protein family that plays a protective role against reactive oxygen species (ROS) and metal-induced damage (Wang et al., 2020). This dual mechanism—direct enzyme inhibition and indirect antioxidant protection—suggests that D609 may help stabilize the lipid signaling environment of the RPE, normalizing DAG levels and mitigating PKC-mediated perturbations in actin cytoskeletal dynamics that are essential for the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Wang et al., 2020). Some studies even propose that the beneficial effects observed in RPE cells may derive more from the metallothionein upregulation than from pure PC-PLC inhibition, raising the possibility that D609’s mode of action is multifactorial rather than strictly enzyme-targeted (Wang et al., 2020). However, in the context of the current hypothesis—where the goal is to inhibit the DAG-PKC axis to restore cytoskeletal dynamics and phagocytosis—the competitive inhibition of PC-PLC by D609 remains a key molecular mechanism (Bhat et al., 2022). It should be noted that D609 is not entirely selective; it also inhibits other enzymes in lipid metabolism such as sphingomyelin synthase (SMS) and possibly phospholipase D (PLD), which could contribute to both its therapeutic efficacy and its off-target effects (Eurtivong et al., 2023; González-Roura et al., 2002). The compound’s broad-spectrum inhibition profile, while advantageous in some settings, raises concerns regarding precise modulation of the PC-PLC–DAG–PKC pathway in the specialized setting of RPE biology (Zhao et al., 2020; Bhat et al., 2022). Nevertheless, the downstream reduction in DAG levels is expected to temper PKC activation, which is crucial since PKC hyperactivation is known to impair actin polymerization and therefore phagocytosis—a critical function of RPE cells in maintaining photoreceptor health (Wang et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
The working hypothesis for repurposing D609 for dry AMD is that its inhibition of PC-PLC in RPE cells will lead to reduced DAG formation, thereby limiting DAG-driven PKC hyperactivation. This in turn is expected to stabilize cytoskeletal dynamics by restoring normal actin polymerization, thus improving the phagocytic capacity of the RPE to internalize and process POS. In experimental assays, ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxidative insult (e.g., hydroquinone treatment) typically display disrupted actin architecture and impaired POS uptake. Treatment with D609 is hypothesized to counteract these effects by balancing the intracellular signaling milieu—specifically by reducing the aberrant activation of the DAG-PKC axis—and by promoting the antioxidant metallothionein pathway, which further preserves cellular homeostasis (Wang et al., 2020). Expression of PC-PLC and related signaling components in RPE cells has been indirectly verified by the cellular responses observed upon oxidative challenge, and the reversal of these effects by D609 supports the notion that this enzyme is active and pathophysiologically relevant in RPE cells (Wang et al., 2020). The expected phenotypic outcomes in the assay include a restoration of actin polymerization, as evidenced by improved F-actin staining patterns, increased phagocytosis of labeled POS, and decreased levels of oxidative markers such as ROS. Indeed, previous studies demonstrated that when ARPE-19 cells were pretreated with D609, they exhibited markedly reduced necrotic and apoptotic markers, along with preserved mitochondrial mass and function under oxidative stress conditions induced by sodium iodate (Wang et al., 2020). These outcomes directly support the hypothesis that normalization of PC-PLC activity via D609 not only mitigates the immediate oxidative insult but also restores the critical cellular function of POS internalization—a process that, when dysfunctional, is a hallmark of dry AMD pathology (Wang et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
D609 presents as an intriguing and promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly because of its ability to modulate lipid signaling pathways that are disrupted by oxidative stress and contribute to RPE dysfunction. One of the principal strengths of D609 is its well-documented protective effect on RPE cells both in vitro and in vivo. Studies have shown that D609 maintains high levels of cell viability in RPE models under conditions of severe oxidative stress, and its administration in animal models of AMD has led to significant preservation of retinal structure and function (Wang et al., 2020). Moreover, its water solubility and low molecular weight facilitate ocular delivery and reduce formulation challenges, making it suitable for local administration to the retina (Wang et al., 2020). The dual-action mechanism—combining inhibition of PC-PLC with upregulation of metallothionein—provides both a direct reduction in deleterious DAG-PKC signaling and an indirect bolster to the cell’s antioxidant defenses, which is crucial in the context of dry AMD where oxidative stress is a primary driver of pathology (Wang et al., 2020).

However, several weaknesses must be noted. First, D609 is a non-selective inhibitor; while it effectively targets PC-PLC, it also inhibits other enzymes such as sphingomyelin synthase and phospholipase D, which may introduce off-target effects that could complicate its clinical use (Eurtivong et al., 2023; González-Roura et al., 2002). This lack of selectivity may lead to unpredictable interactions in the intricate lipid signaling networks present in the retina. Second, the compound exists as a mixture of eight stereoisomers, and the differential activity among these isomers is not well understood. Variability in stereoisomeric composition could result in inconsistent pharmacodynamic outcomes and present challenges in the regulatory approval process (Eurtivong et al., 2023; Bhat et al., 2022). Third, the anticipated IC₅₀ of approximately 35 µM for PC-PLC inhibition in RPE cells is relatively high, suggesting that effective biological activity may require high local concentrations that may be difficult to achieve or maintain in vivo without risking toxicity (Wang et al., 2020; Bhat et al., 2022). Although ocular safety studies in rabbits have been favorable, further pharmacokinetic and toxicological investigations will be essential to confirm the therapeutic window for chronic treatment in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2020; Bhat et al., 2022).

From a mechanism-of-action standpoint, while the hypothesis that reducing DAG-mediated PKC hyperactivation will normalize actin dynamics and improve phagocytosis is biologically plausible, much of the existing literature on D609’s protective effects in RPE cells emphasizes its ability to upregulate metallothionein expression and confer antioxidant protection rather than solely modulating the DAG-PKC axis (Wang et al., 2020). Thus, it remains to be clarified whether the beneficial outcomes in RPE phagocytosis are driven primarily by alterations in the DAG-PKC pathway or by a broader restoration of cellular redox balance. This mechanistic ambiguity, while not diminishing the overall therapeutic promise, suggests that future studies should incorporate detailed pathway analyses to dissect the relative contributions of each mechanism.

In summary, D609 is well supported by preclinical evidence as a compound that can protect RPE cells from oxidative damage and has potential applications in dry AMD therapy (Wang et al., 2020). Its established safety profile in ocular studies, combined with a mechanistic basis that addresses both lipid signaling dysregulation and oxidative stress, offers significant advantages for repurposing in this context. Nonetheless, challenges related to off-target effects, stereochemical variability, and the need for high effective concentrations must be rigorously addressed in subsequent studies. Overall, D609 merits further investigative efforts in translational research focused on dry AMD, with particular emphasis on optimizing its pharmacodynamics, ensuring reproducible stereoisomeric composition, and validating its efficacy in restoring RPE phagocytic function under physiologically relevant oxidative stress conditions (Eurtivong et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Apocynin is a naturally occurring small-molecule compound originally isolated from the roots of the Himalayan medicinal herb Picrorhiza kurroa. It belongs to the class of methoxy-substituted catechols that have been characterized as NADPH oxidase (NOX) inhibitors capable of modulating reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. The compound, also known as acetovanillone, was discovered through investigations into natural anti‐inflammatory agents and has subsequently been repurposed as a therapeutic candidate in various experimental models of oxidative stress-driven pathology. As a representative of natural antioxidants with the ability to block the assembly of NOX complexes, apocynin has been widely studied in models of cardiovascular, neurological, and ocular diseases to attenuate excessive ROS production and reduce downstream inflammatory cascades (Simonyi et al., 2012). Its chemical synthesis in laboratory settings has mostly focused on replicating the naturally derived molecule while exploring structural analogs that may improve potency or pharmacokinetics. This class of compounds has historically been used both as a tool compound for dissecting NOX-mediated oxidative mechanisms and as an experimental therapeutic agent to counteract the cellular consequences of oxidative damage (Simonyi et al., 2012; Bellezza, 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Extensive preclinical research has demonstrated that apocynin can reduce NOX-dependent ROS production in cell-based systems, particularly in models of inflammation and oxidative stress. Several in vitro studies have documented its ability to ameliorate oxidative damage by inhibiting the activation of NADPH oxidases in various cell types, including vascular endothelial cells, macrophages, and most pertinently, retinal cells. For example, studies have shown that apocynin suppresses NOX4-induced ROS generation in hypoxic human retinal Müller cells and in diabetic rat retinas, suggesting its potential for retinal neuroprotection (Ahmad et al., 2021). Although apocynin has not yet been formally approved for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in clinical settings, its extensive use in ocular inflammation models and retinal degeneration studies underpins its repurposing potential. In addition, the compound has historically been used in various animal models to attenuate exacerbated inflammatory responses linked to NOX-driven oxidative stress, and these studies consistently report improvements in tissue integrity and reductions in oxidative stress markers (Dionysopoulou et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020). Its long history in preclinical ophthalmic applications, when coupled with its excellent safety profile observed in animal studies—indicated by a high LD₅₀ and absence of genotoxicity at effective concentrations—provides further impetus to evaluate its efficacy in dry AMD, a condition characterized by chronic oxidative stress and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction (Kulbay et al., 2024; Rohowetz et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism of action of apocynin lies in its ability to inhibit the assembly and activation of the NADPH oxidase complex, a multi-component enzyme system critically involved in the production of superoxide and other ROS in various cell types. Under physiological conditions, NOX enzymes (including isoforms NOX1, NOX2, and NOX4) contribute to redox signaling; however, their aberrant activation under pathological states such as dry AMD leads to excessive ROS levels that damage cellular lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Mechanistically, apocynin prevents the cytosolic subunits (such as p47^phox) from translocating to the membrane-bound catalytic subunits (such as gp91^phox/NOX2 and NOX4) and forming an active enzyme complex. This inhibition translates into a reduction of ROS generation (Sun et al., 2020; Kulbay et al., 2024). Furthermore, emerging evidence suggests that transcriptional regulators like PU.1/Spi1 serve as master regulators of NOX4-p22^phox complex activation in the RPE during amyloid β–induced injury. Silencing of PU.1 in experimental models resulted in significantly reduced oxidative stress and preserved mitochondrial function; these observations underscore the cascade that apocynin is poised to interrupt by targeting the NADPH oxidase assembly process (Sun et al., 2020; Kulbay et al., 2024). In addition to this primary mode of action, apocynin’s antioxidant properties may also indirectly preserve lysosomal integrity by reducing ROS-mediated peroxidation of lipids in the phagosome–lysosome membranes. This is particularly relevant in RPE cells, which are tasked with daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and are susceptible to lysosomal dysfunction if the autophagic flux is compromised by oxidative damage (Shu et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). The inhibition of NOX-derived ROS in this manner is expected to stabilize cathepsin D activity—a critical lysosomal protease—and maintain the efficient degradation of POS, thereby reducing the accumulation of deleterious lipofuscin deposits that are a hallmark of dry AMD pathology (Sun et al., 2020; Bellezza, 2018).

Expected Effect:  
In the assay system under consideration—where RPE cells are challenged with oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂ exposure) to mimic the pathological conditions of dry AMD—the expected effect of apocynin administration is multifaceted. First, by inhibiting the activation of NADPH oxidase complexes (with an anticipated IC₅₀ in the vicinity of 5 µM), apocynin should significantly reduce the intracellular production of ROS, thereby protecting RPE cells from oxidative damage (Simonyi et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2020). This reduction in ROS is critical, as excessive oxidative stress not only causes direct cellular damage but also impairs the function of lysosomal membranes, leading to decreased cathepsin D activity and inefficient POS degradation. As a result, lipofuscin, which is an autofluorescent pigment composed of undegraded POS remnants and other oxidatively modified cellular components, would accumulate. The hypothesis posits that apocynin’s reduction of ROS will help to maintain the integrity of phagosome–lysosome membranes, thus preserving autophagic flux and ensuring the continuous clearance of POS. This preservation is expected to be measurable via restored cathepsin D activity and increased phagocytic uptake of POS under H₂O₂-challenged conditions (Sun et al., 2020; Ahmad et al., 2021). Additionally, because RPE cells are known to express multiple NOX isoforms (notably NOX2 and NOX4) that contribute to the chronic oxidative stress seen in AMD, the attenuation of their activity by apocynin could lead to reductions in downstream inflammatory signaling mediated by transcription factors such as NF-κB. This, in turn, would be expected to result in improved cellular homeostasis and protection against further degenerative events, including mitochondrial dysfunction and cell death (Kim et al., 2021; Hernández et al., 2025). Ultimately, the expected cumulative effect would be a deceleration of the disease process in dry AMD, as evidenced by improved RPE function, reduced lipofuscin accumulation, and maintenance of photoreceptor viability (Dionysopoulou et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
Evaluating apocynin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several compelling strengths as well as areas that warrant careful consideration. One of the primary strengths of apocynin is its well-documented ability to inhibit NADPH oxidase activity and thereby reduce ROS production—a mechanism that is strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. The extensive body of preclinical literature, which includes studies in ocular inflammation and diabetic retinopathy models, supports the notion that apocynin can restore redox balance and mitigate oxidative cellular damage. This is particularly relevant in the context of RPE cells, where oxidative stress not only contributes directly to cellular dysfunction but also impairs critical processes such as autophagy and POS clearance leading to lipofuscin accumulation (Sun et al., 2020; Ahmad et al., 2021; Ruan et al., 2021). Furthermore, apocynin’s natural origin and favorable safety profile observed in multiple animal studies bolster its attractiveness as a repurposing candidate; its established use in preclinical settings means that a substantial amount of mechanistic and pharmacokinetic data is already available, potentially accelerating its clinical translation (Simonyi et al., 2012; Kulbay et al., 2024).

Nevertheless, there are challenges and potential weaknesses that must be acknowledged. One limitation is the translation of experimental efficacy observed in simplified in vitro models or acute animal studies to the highly complex and multifactorial pathology of dry AMD in humans. Dry AMD involves chronic insults over decades, and while NOX-mediated oxidative stress is a central driver, the disease also involves other processes like chronic inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and dysregulated autophagy that might not be fully addressed by NOX inhibition alone (Shu et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2021). Moreover, apocynin requires metabolic activation by peroxidases—an aspect that could render its effectiveness context-dependent, potentially limiting its efficacy in regions of the retina that do not exhibit sufficiently high levels of activating enzymes. This localized activation may be beneficial by minimizing systemic effects, but it also raises questions regarding the consistency of therapeutic benefit across the heterogeneous RPE microenvironment encountered in dry AMD (Sun et al., 2020; Bellezza, 2018).

Another consideration is the drug delivery challenge. The effective concentration required to achieve NOX inhibition in vitro (in the low micromolar range) may not be easily attainable in retinal tissues with conventional delivery methods. As the RPE is located behind multiple anatomical barriers, ensuring that adequate drug levels reach the target site is critical. Strategies such as intraocular injections, sustained-release formulations, or nanoparticle-based delivery systems might need to be explored and optimized to overcome these pharmacokinetic barriers (Ruan et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2008). Additionally, while apocynin has been reported to preserve lysosomal function and enhance autophagic flux in stressed RPE cells in vitro, robust data from chronic disease models specifically recapitulating dry AMD pathology remain limited. The long-term impact of continuous NOX inhibition on RPE physiology and the potential for off-target effects, especially given the role of low-level ROS in normal cellular signaling, will require careful investigation (Dionysopoulou et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2021).

In summary, the repurposing of apocynin for dry AMD is supported by a solid mechanistic rationale—its inhibition of NOX-mediated ROS production can theoretically interrupt the vicious cycle of oxidative stress, lysosomal dysfunction, and impaired autophagic clearance that underlies RPE degeneration. The strengths of apocynin lie in its natural origin, extensive preclinical use, proven safety profile, and the centrality of its targeted pathway in dry AMD pathology. However, the challenges of ensuring effective and targeted delivery to the retina, verifying its long-term efficacy in chronic disease models, and addressing its context-dependent activation must be thoroughly addressed in future studies. Taken together, these considerations suggest that apocynin is a promising candidate for further preclinical investigation in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to complement other therapeutic strategies targeting oxidative stress and cellular clearance dysfunction (Sun et al., 2020; Ahmad et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025; Simonyi et al., 2012; Rohowetz et al., 2018).

Conclusion:  
Based on the comprehensive review of the current biochemical, clinical, and preclinical literature, apocynin presents as a viable repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its mechanism—centered on the inhibition of NADPH oxidase-driven ROS production—directly addresses critical aspects of RPE dysfunction and lysosomal damage that are central to the disease’s pathogenesis. The evidence from related studies in ocular inflammation models, coupled with its favorable safety profile and natural origin, provides a strong foundation for further investigation. Nonetheless, future research must focus on optimizing delivery systems to overcome ocular barriers, confirming chronic efficacy in models that accurately mimic the slow progression of dry AMD, and delineating the full spectrum of molecular effects in the complex retinal microenvironment before advancing to clinical trials. Despite these challenges, the strengths of apocynin’s targeted action and established preclinical data support its continued exploration as part of a multi-targeted approach to address the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD (Ahmad et al., 2021; Bellezza, 2018; Dionysopoulou et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2021; Simonyi et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibrate originally developed and approved as a lipid‐lowering agent that acts primarily as a peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) agonist. It was discovered through efforts to develop compounds that could enhance fatty acid oxidation and thereby reduce triglyceride levels and improve lipid profiles in patients with dyslipidemia. As a member of the fibrate class of drugs, fenofibrate and its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, have been classically used in cardiometabolic conditions such as hyperlipidemia, where they improve lipid profiles by increasing high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels and lowering triglycerides. The compound available as Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. F6020 is representative of these agents and has been extensively studied in preclinical models of metabolic stress. Its chemical design enables it to bind to PPARα, a nuclear receptor that modulates gene expression of enzymes central to fatty acid β-oxidation and lipid homeostasis. In the context of retinal disorders, fenofibrate has been pursued as a repurposing candidate owing to its robust safety profile and its potential to address the dysregulation of lipid metabolism observed in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. Several studies have suggested that by activating PPARα, fenofibrate may help reduce lipid overload and mitigate the accumulation of toxic by-products such as A2E (a major fluorophore in lipofuscin) that contribute to RPE dysfunction in age-related macular degeneration (Wang et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2022).  

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate has a long clinical history as an antihyperlipidemic agent with a well-established safety profile in patients with cardiovascular risk factors. In addition to its widespread use in metabolic disorders, a significant body of preclinical research has documented the potential benefits of fenofibrate in retinal diseases. Several studies have demonstrated that fenofibrate can ameliorate retinal abnormalities induced by high-fat diets and excessive lipid exposure. For instance, experimental models of fat-induced RPE injury have shown that fenofibrate reduces oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators, thereby protecting RPE integrity through mechanisms such as upregulation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway (Wang et al., 2023). In diabetic retinopathy—a condition that, while distinct from dry AMD, shares underlying processes related to oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and inflammatory cascades—fenofibrate has been explored for its protective effects on the retina, contributing to improvements in vascular permeability and barrier function of the outer blood–retina barrier (Fu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023). Although fenofibrate’s potential use in dry AMD has not been as widely investigated as its role in diabetic retinopathy, the documented protective effects on RPE under conditions of lipid overload, as well as its ability to downregulate markers of oxidative stress (e.g., NOX4 and 3‐nitrotyrosine) and inflammatory cytokines (such as TNFα and ICAM1), support its candidacy for repurposing in dry AMD (Ren et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023). It is noteworthy that while clinical data in diabetic populations (e.g., FIELD study outcomes) have driven considerable interest in fenofibrate’s ocular effects, direct applications to dry AMD remain exploratory and are based largely on preclinical findings that show promise for reducing lipotoxic damage in the RPE.

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate exerts its pharmacological effects primarily through the activation of PPARα, a nuclear receptor that, upon ligand binding, dimerizes with the retinoid X receptor and binds to specific PPAR response elements in promoter regions of target genes. This leads to the transcriptional upregulation of a variety of genes involved in lipid uptake, fatty acid transport, and β-oxidation, ultimately promoting the catabolism of long-chain fatty acids. In RPE cells, robust expression of PPARα is critical for maintaining homeostasis in the face of high lipid loads and oxidative stress. Activation of PPARα by fenofibrate has been shown to enhance mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, thereby reducing intracellular lipid accumulation and possibly the generation of toxic lipid peroxidation products such as A2E, a primary component of the lipofuscin granules that accumulate with age in RPE cells (Ren et al., 2022).

Beyond its classical role in lipid metabolism, fenofibrate has also been reported to engage additional cellular signaling pathways that contribute to its cytoprotective effects. In several preclinical studies, fenofibrate and fenofibric acid have been observed to activate the PI3K/AKT pathway in RPE cells, which is well recognized for its roles in cell survival and stress response. The activation of PI3K/AKT signaling by fenofibrate leads to enhanced cell survival signals, mitigates oxidative damage, and downregulates inflammatory mediators in fatty acid–challenged RPE cells (Wang et al., 2023). Moreover, fenofibrate has been implicated in reducing the expression of pro-oxidant enzymes such as NADPH oxidase 4 (NOX4) and in decreasing levels of markers of oxidative stress like 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) in palmitic acid-treated RPE models (Wang et al., 2023). These actions collectively contribute to mitigation of oxidative injury—a central component of dry AMD pathogenesis.

In addition, some studies have proposed that fenofibrate may exert ancillary effects through mechanisms independent of PPARα activation. For example, evidence suggests that fenofibrate might function as an iron chelator, thereby reducing intracellular free iron levels, which in turn could diminish the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and blunt the aberrant activation of the canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway—a pathway implicated in various ocular pathologies including AMD (Mandala et al., 2020). This suppression of iron-induced oxidative stress and its associated downstream signaling cascades may further contribute to the preservation of RPE cell function under conditions of chronic oxidative insult.

Another mechanism of potential interest is fenofibrate’s impact on inflammatory signaling. Classical anti-inflammatory effects have been verified through its ability to inhibit nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) activity, thereby reducing the transcription of a host of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines that might contribute to retinal degeneration (Garcia-Ramírez et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2020). Although direct evidence for improved phagocytosis or lysosomal function in the context of dry AMD is not yet abundant in the literature provided, it has been hypothesized that by reducing lipid overload and oxidative stress, fenofibrate could indirectly improve lysosomal pH stability and optimize the function of cathepsin D—a key lysosomal protease involved in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) fragments (as hypothesized in Tang et al. IOVS 2024). Given that proper autophagic flux and phagocytic processing are essential for RPE homeostasis and that their impairment is a hallmark of dry AMD, the restoration of these cellular processes via improved metabolic and intracellular signaling pathways is an attractive proposition (Ren et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for the repurposing strategy of fenofibrate in dry AMD is that its activation of PPARα in RPE cells—achievable at concentrations with an EC₅₀ of approximately 2 µM—will promote a metabolic shift toward enhanced fatty acid oxidation. This shift is expected to lower the intracellular lipid load and decrease the accumulation of lipofuscin, a complex mixture of lipid-protein aggregates that includes A2E, which is thought to contribute directly to RPE cell dysfunction and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration. In vitro data from models using palmitic acid to induce lipotoxic stress in RPE cells suggest that fenofibrate can restore cellular homeostasis by activating survival pathways such as PI3K/AKT and by suppressing overexpressed stress markers and inflammatory cytokines (Wang et al., 2023).

According to the proposed mechanism, activation of PPARα should lead to the upregulation of genes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, resulting in improved clearance of lipid-rich photoreceptor outer segments. The improvement in lipid processing not only reduces the overall lipid burden within RPE cells but is also expected to restore lysosomal function—specifically, normalizing lysosomal pH and enhancing cathepsin D activity. These changes should facilitate more efficient phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segment debris, thereby mitigating the accumulation of cytotoxic lipofuscin deposits.

Furthermore, by lowering intracellular lipid accumulation and reducing oxidative stress through enhanced PI3K/AKT signaling and potential NF-κB inhibition, fenofibrate is expected to decrease the production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines that contribute to chronic inflammation in the retina. Since inflammation is a driving force behind the progression of dry AMD, such a decrease would synergize with improved autophagy and phagocytosis to stabilize or even improve RPE function. In preclinical models, the application of fenofibrate in conditions simulating high dietary fat has been shown to restore aspects of RPE cell viability and function, lending indirect support to its potential efficacy in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023). Although the precise effects on A2E reduction and lipofuscin clearance have yet to be fully elucidated, the cumulative data on fenofibrate’s capacity to improve lipid metabolism and reduce oxidative and inflammatory stress suggest that the compound could address multiple maladaptive processes that underlie dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:

Its long-standing clinical use and excellent safety record provide a strong foundation for further preclinical and eventually clinical studies in the context of ocular degenerative diseases. Addressing this gap through targeted in vitro and in vivo studies using dry AMD models will be essential. By combining improved fatty acid oxidation, antioxidant defenses, anti-inflammatory effects, and possibly even modulation of cellular iron levels and aberrant signaling pathways, fenofibrate could serve as a powerful therapeutic to modify the progressive degeneration of the RPE seen in dry AMD.
