Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Cerulenin is a natural product originally isolated from the filamentous fungus Cephalosporium caerulens and was the first discovered fatty acid synthase (FAS) inhibitor (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; López & Diéguez, 2007). Chemically, this compound is classified as an epoxy-keto fatty acid analogue; it contains a reactive epoxide ring conjugated to a diene/amidic structure that mimics fatty acid substrates. This reactive epoxide is key to its mechanism because it enables cerulenin to irreversibly bind to its target enzyme via covalent modification. As such, cerulenin belongs to the class of FAS inhibitors that historically have been used as biochemical probes to investigate lipid metabolism and, subsequently, as lead compounds in the development of antineoplastic agents, given the upregulation of de novo lipogenesis in many cancers (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; López & Diéguez, 2007; Abramson, 2011). The molecule’s natural origin, combined with its potent inhibitory activity, has made it a valuable tool in studies of metabolic regulation and lipogenesis over several decades.

Therapeutic History:  
In the past, cerulenin was primarily developed and investigated as an antimicrobial and antifungal antibiotic due to its capacity to irreversibly inhibit fatty acid synthesis in both bacterial and eukaryotic systems (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Subsequent research in the fields of oncology and metabolic regulation revealed that several tumor types exhibit elevated expression of FAS, making FAS inhibitors promising candidates for anticancer therapy. Preclinical studies demonstrated that cerulenin could induce apoptosis in tumor cells, delay disease progression in xenograft models, and even affect systemic metabolic parameters such as food intake and body weight in rodent models (López & Diéguez, 2007; Heath, White, & Rock, 2002; Goodman & McFadden, 2007). Despite these promising results, its clinical utility has been constrained by poor chemical stability—primarily due to its reactive epoxide moiety—and significant toxicity stemming from irreversibility and off-target interactions with other cysteine-containing proteins (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Furthermore, while modifications have led to second-generation analogues like C75, designed to improve stability and selectivity, there are no records of cerulenin being specifically applied to ophthalmologic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal lipotoxicity diseases (Menendez & Lupu, 2017; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999). Although cerulenin has been explored in other in vivo models (for example, for retinitis pigmentosa in preclinical studies), no clinical trials have been registered for its use in AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, cerulenin exerts its biological effects by targeting the fatty acid synthase complex. Its mechanism involves the formation of an irreversible covalent adduct with an active-site cysteine residue (specifically, Cys1305) within the ketosynthase (KS) domain of type I FAS. This is achieved by an epoxide ring-opening reaction at the C-2 position of cerulenin, leading to the nucleophilic attack by the thiol (-SH) group of the catalytic cysteine residue (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008). Crystallographic studies have provided precise structural insights into this interaction, showing that such covalent modification not only blocks the initial acyl-transfer step but also induces conformational changes—such as the flipping of key residues like F1646 and the rotation of M1251—that ultimately disrupt the hydrophobic acyl-binding tunnel required for fatty acid chain elongation (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008; Fhu & Ali, 2020). In addition to inhibiting FAS directly, cerulenin has also been shown to impair protein palmitoylation, a post-translational modification that plays an important role in regulating membrane association and signaling functions of numerous proteins including Ras oncoproteins (Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999). This dual mechanism—targeting both de novo fatty acid synthesis and protein acylation—underscores the broad-spectrum bioactivity of cerulenin and its potential impact on multiple cellular pathways that are dysregulated in disease states (Menendez & Lupu, 2017; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis underpinning the proposed repurposing of cerulenin for dry AMD centers on its ability to attenuate de novo lipogenesis in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. In the context of dry AMD, pathologic accumulation of lipofuscin and toxic bisretinoid compounds such as A2E is thought to result from excessive lipid synthesis and impaired degradation of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) material. Excess levels of intracellular fatty acids, often derived from hyperactive FAS, contribute to the generation of these lipofuscin precursors—ultimately impairing lysosomal function and leading to RPE dysfunction (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). By inhibiting FAS activity in the RPE, cerulenin is expected to reduce the synthesis of fatty acids that serve as precursors for lipofuscin components. This reduced lipogenesis should, in theory, alleviate the accumulation of lipofuscin, restore optimal levels of lysosomal pH, and enhance the activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D—thereby improving the degradation and turnover of POS material (Radka & Rock, 2022; Troudi, Pagès, & Brunel, 2021). Furthermore, since oxidative stress is a key driver of abnormal lipid metabolism in RPE cells, the ability of cerulenin to lower fatty acid synthesis may concurrently reduce the burden of oxidative damage and improve cellular homeostasis (Vázquez et al., 2008; Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007). It is also noteworthy that FAS expression has been detected and functionally characterized in various extrahepatic tissues; while direct evidence of its expression in RPE cells is less extensively documented in the provided citations, the extrapolation from other cellular models supports the likelihood that modulating FAS activity in RPE would confer benefits in lipid turnover and lysosomal efficiency (Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999; Johansson et al., 2008). Thus, within the proposed assay—where RPE cells are subjected to oxidative stress that mimics the environment of dry AMD—cerulenin is anticipated to lower intracellular lipid levels, minimize the generation of lipofuscin precursors, and ultimately restore RPE functional capacity.

Overall Evaluation:  
Cerulenin presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD owing to its well-documented ability to inhibit fatty acid synthase through a unique irreversible, covalent mechanism. Its molecular footprint, characterized by a reactive epoxide ring, has been exploited in multiple studies to evaluate cellular lipid synthesis and, by extension, to modulate metabolic pathways that underpin several disease processes (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Abramson, 2011). Mechanistically, its capacity to bind to a crucial cysteine residue in the FAS enzyme and to interfere with lipid assembly positions it as a potentially valuable agent to counter the lipid-driven pathogenesis implicated in RPE dysfunction and lipofuscin accumulation in dry AMD (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008).

The strengths of cerulenin as a candidate include its small-molecule profile, which facilitates cellular entry; its established use as a research tool in in vitro and in vivo models; and its dual activity profile that not only curtails de novo lipogenesis but may also impede aberrant protein palmitoylation. Such multifaceted activity could be beneficial in a complex tissue environment like the retina, where multiple overlapping metabolic dysfunctions contribute to disease progression (Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999). In particular, by reducing the synthesis of fatty acids in RPE cells, cerulenin could deplete one of the key substrates for the formation of lipofuscin precursors such as A2E, thereby potentially improving lysosomal degradation of shed POS and arresting a vicious cycle of intracellular lipid accumulation and oxidative stress (Radka & Rock, 2022; Troudi, Pagès, & Brunel, 2021).

However, several weaknesses must be carefully considered. Cerulenin’s inherent chemical instability, attributed to its reactive epoxide ring, raises significant concerns regarding its pharmacokinetic profile and overall toxicity, especially in a sensitive tissue like the retina where off-target effects may exacerbate cellular stress rather than alleviate it (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Heath, White, & Rock, 2002). The irreversible nature of its enzyme inhibition—while beneficial for ensuring sustained suppression of FAS—may lead to collateral damage in non-target tissues, and the narrow therapeutic window observed in other preclinical studies suggests that dose optimization could be challenging (Fhu & Ali, 2020; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Moreover, although the hypothesis posits that inhibition of de novo lipogenesis in the RPE will mitigate lipid accumulation and improve lysosomal function, there is a paucity of direct evidence linking cerulenin or similar FAS inhibitors to improved outcomes in dry AMD models specifically. The documented applications of cerulenin are primarily in the realms of oncology and metabolic regulation, with little precedent for its use in ocular conditions (Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). This suggests that while the mechanistic rationale is sound, the translational leap to an ocular indication will require additional supportive data both from in vitro RPE assays and from appropriate animal models of AMD.

Another point of concern is that cerulenin’s nonselective inhibition of fatty acid synthase may also impair essential lipid synthesis in cells that require robust regenerative capacity, potentially leading to unintended cytotoxicity or impaired cell membrane maintenance. In the context of the RPE, where cellular health is paramount for photoreceptor support, any off-target lipid synthesis inhibition must be tightly controlled (Goodman & McFadden, 2007; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Furthermore, its use in vivo has been historically hampered by issues such as poor aqueous solubility—it often requires solvents like DMSO for administration—and its propensity for rapid degradation in protic environments, all of which represent substantial formulation challenges that must be overcome for ocular delivery (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Vázquez et al., 2008).

Given these considerations, while cerulenin offers a compelling proof-of-concept relating to the modulation of lipogenesis and lysosomal function, its practical development as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD would likely necessitate further chemical modifications. The precedent set by the development of derivatives such as C75—which were specifically engineered to overcome the limitations of cerulenin by removing the problematic epoxide group and enhancing stability—suggests that optimization is both possible and necessary (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Optimized analogues with improved pharmacokinetic and safety profiles may hold greater promise in the ocular setting than the parent compound.

In summary, cerulenin’s capacity to inhibit fatty acid synthase at the molecular level through irreversible covalent binding is well-established and aligns with the proposed therapeutic mechanism of reducing RPE lipid accumulation and lipofuscin precursor formation. However, its historical limitations in terms of chemical stability, toxicity, and nonselectivity present significant hurdles for its repurposing in dry AMD. The compound’s extensive use in metabolic and oncologic research provides a strong foundation for understanding its biochemical actions, but the absence of direct evidence in retinal models and the challenges associated with its delivery to ocular tissues temper enthusiasm for immediate clinical translation (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Therefore, while there is sufficient mechanistic rationale to pursue further preclinical investigations—potentially in parallel with the development of more stable derivatives—the current state of evidence suggests that cerulenin itself may not be ideal as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD without significant further optimization. More comprehensive in vitro studies using RPE cell models and targeted in vivo studies in AMD-relevant animal models are needed to validate whether the inhibition of de novo lipogenesis by cerulenin can indeed translate into restored lysosomal function and improved photoreceptor outer segment degradation in this disease context (Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007; Radka & Rock, 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ML‐SA1 is a fully synthetic small molecule designed as an agonist of the transient receptor potential mucolipin 1 (TRPML1) channel. It belongs to the class of mucolipin synthetic agonists, which were initially derived as analogs of earlier lead compounds such as SF‐51 and SF‐22. These compounds were discovered using high‐throughput screening approaches aimed at identifying activators of TRPML channels, and ML‐SA1 was subsequently optimized for improved potency and selectivity in mammalian systems (Feng et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2012). As a synthetic compound, ML‐SA1 exemplifies a rational drug design strategy in which the molecule is engineered to mimic the action of the endogenous lipid agonist phosphatidylinositol 3,5‐bisphosphate [PI(3,5)P₂] by directly binding to the channel’s pore region. This binding stabilizes TRPML1 in its open conformation, thereby facilitating lysosomal Ca²⁺ release. The chemical class represented by ML‐SA1 has historically been employed as a research tool to interrogate lysosomal physiology and calcium homeostasis in diverse cell types, including neuronal and retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Therapeutic History:  
Previous studies have demonstrated that ML‐SA1 robustly elevates cytosolic calcium levels in several cellular models by activating TRPML1 channels. In particular, ML‐SA1 has been applied to multiple RPE cell models—including mouse RPE, human embryonic stem cell‐derived RPE, and the ARPE‐19 cell line—to assess its ability to restore lysosomal calcium signaling and normalize lysosomal function (Gómez et al., 2018). In these experiments, ML‐SA1 elicited rapid, robust, and reversible Ca²⁺ signals that were completely absent in TRPML1 knockout cells, thereby confirming target engagement and specificity (Gómez et al., 2018). Beyond RPE biology, ML‐SA1 has been evaluated in neuronal models of lysosomal dysfunction, including experimental systems relevant to Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease, where it mediated correction of defective lysosomal acidification and improved autophagic flux (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022). Although no clinical trials have yet investigated ML‐SA1 directly in patients with dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), its demonstrated efficacy in rescuing lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling—in conditions that share underlying pathophysiological features with dry AMD such as lysosomal storage and autophagy blockade—suggests that its repurposing may yield therapeutic benefits in this disease context (Open Targets Platform, 2025). To date, the use of ML‐SA1 has predominantly been within experimental research settings rather than in clinical practice or veterinary medicine, and its repurposing for dry AMD represents an innovative and rationale‐driven approach rooted in the overlap between TRPML1 dysfunction and RPE pathology (Feng et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2017).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic action of ML‐SA1 is centered upon its ability to directly activate TRPML1 channels located on lysosomal membranes. TRPML1 plays a critical role in regulating lysosomal calcium homeostasis by mediating Ca²⁺ efflux from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol. ML‐SA1 binds directly to TRPML1—likely within a hydrophobic pocket formed at the S5–S6 transmembrane domain interface—and stabilizes the channel’s open state (Feng et al., 2014). This activation occurs independently of exogenous PI(3,5)P₂ in mammalian cells, setting ML‐SA1 apart from the endogenous regulatory mechanisms that otherwise depend on dynamic fluctuations in phosphoinositide levels (Feng et al., 2014; Gómez et al., 2018). As a result of channel activation, lysosomal Ca²⁺ is released into the cytosol, triggering a cascade of calcium‐dependent signaling pathways. One critical downstream effect is the promotion of lysosomal membrane fission and fusion events, processes that are essential for proper lysosomal trafficking and the maturation of autophagosomes into autolysosomes (Cao et al., 2017; Li & Li, 2022).  

Beyond its immediate role in calcium mobilization, ML‐SA1‐mediated activation of TRPML1 also facilitates the activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Increased cytosolic Ca²⁺ can activate calcineurin, which in turn dephosphorylates TFEB, enabling its translocation to the nucleus where it upregulates the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function and autophagy (Pollmanns et al., 2022). In some models, ML‐SA1 treatment has been shown to improve the processing and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D, thereby contributing to normalization of lysosomal pH and enhanced protein degradation (Hui et al., 2019). Importantly, the ability of ML‐SA1 to restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling directly targets the pathological cascade observed when TRPML1 is deficient or inhibited—a scenario that is reminiscent of the lysosomal storage, impaired autophagy, and stalled phagolysosomal degradation evident in dry AMD RPE cells (Gómez et al., 2018; Pamonag, 2021).  

Expected Effect:  
Based on the observed mechanisms in diverse cellular models, it is expected that ML‐SA1 will re‐establish normal lysosomal function in RPE cells afflicted by dry AMD. In the proposed assay, the activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 at concentrations near its EC₅₀ (approximately 5 µM) should restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ efflux, thereby driving several beneficial downstream effects. First, the induced calcium release is anticipated to promote lysosomal membrane dynamics that favor fission and fusion events, ultimately leading to improved lysosomal trafficking and an enhanced capacity for phagolysosomal degradation. This is particularly relevant for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), the routine phagocytic burden of RPE cells that, when inadequately processed, contributes to lipofuscin accumulation and retinal degeneration (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Second, by normalizing Ca²⁺ signaling, ML‐SA1 is expected to reinstate proper lysosomal acidification. Acidification is crucial for the optimal activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D; ML‐SA1 has been shown in various models to restore cathepsin D processing, thereby resetting the enzymatic degradation cascade necessary for POS turnover (Hui et al., 2019). Such restoration of acidification and enzyme activity would directly counteract the pathological accumulation of undegraded material—a hallmark of dry AMD.  

Third, the downstream activation of TFEB induced by ML‐SA1’s modulation of lysosomal calcium may trigger an upregulation of the entire lysosomal-autophagy gene network. This transcriptional reprogramming is vital for augmenting both the number and function of lysosomes, thereby enhancing the overall cellular clearance capacity in RPE cells. Because ample evidence suggests that TRPML1 is expressed in RPE cells and that its dysfunction contributes directly to the autophagy block observed in dry AMD (Pamonag, 2021; Gómez et al., 2018), the activation of this pathway by ML‐SA1 is expected to result in a net improvement in POS degradation and a reduction in toxic debris accumulation. Ultimately, the integrated effects of improved lysosomal trafficking, normalized pH, enhanced enzymatic processing, and boosted autophagic flux are hypothesized to alleviate key pathological features of dry AMD, potentially slowing or even reversing degenerative changes in the retinal pigment epithelium (Gómez et al., 2018).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Our comprehensive literature review indicates that ML‐SA1 is a scientifically compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration. One of its principal strengths lies in its well‐defined mechanism of action: by directly activating TRPML1 channels, ML‐SA1 has been shown to restore lysosomal Ca²⁺ homeostasis—a central defect in several models of lysosomal storage and autophagy dysfunction (Gómez et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2014). Additionally, while the in vitro EC₅₀ is promising (around 5 µM), there remains uncertainty regarding the pharmacokinetic profile, bioavailability, tissue penetration (particularly across the blood‐retina barrier), and potential off-target effects of ML‐SA1 when administered in vivo (Li & Li, 2022).  

Another area of concern is the current lack of direct clinical data pertaining to ML‐SA1 in dry AMD. Although preclinical studies in RPE cell models provide a solid foundation, translation to in vivo models of AMD—and eventually to human clinical trials—will require additional investigation. The absence of any reported clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD with TRPML1 agonists (as confirmed by database searches such as those reflected in the Open Targets Platform) indicates that this is still a largely uncharted therapeutic area requiring further validation (Open Targets Platform, 2025). Moreover, chronic activation of TRPML1 by ML‐SA1 may have unforeseen consequences related to intracellular calcium homeostasis and autophagic balance, which warrant careful evaluation in long-term studies (Hui et al., 2019; Pollmanns et al., 2022).  

In summary, ML‐SA1 represents a highly promising candidate for the repurposing in dry AMD based on its ability to rescue lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling, enhance autophagic clearance, and restore normal lysosomal pH and trafficking in RPE cells. Its synthetic origin and well‐characterized mechanism provide a strong mechanistic rationale for its use. However, issues related to lipid-mediated inhibition of TRPML1, pharmacokinetic considerations, and the current lack of in vivo data in AMD models must be addressed. Overall, the candidate shows significant potential, but a focused program of preclinical validation—including animal models of dry AMD, detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiling, and exploration of strategies to mitigate lysosomal lipid accumulation—is essential before advancing ML‐SA1 to clinical trials for dry AMD (Gómez et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2014).

The chemical optimization of these compounds was driven by the need for greater potency and specificity in modulating complex kinase networks associated with neurodegenerative and ocular pathologies. SB415286 is commercially available (Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. SML0787) and exhibits properties that make it suitable for cell-based assays as well as animal studies targeting retinal cell functions (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In general, compounds in this class have been used in preclinical models to activate Wnt signaling by preventing β-catenin degradation, thereby enhancing transcription of genes involved in cell survival, differentiation, and tissue regeneration. This approach has been applied primarily in neurological research as well as in studies focusing on retinal degeneration, making SB415286 a candidate of interest for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
GSK-3β inhibitors as a class have a long history of preclinical exploration in various disease models, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and other neurodegenerative disorders where excessive kinase activity contributes to neuronal cell death. SB415286, in particular, has been used in primary neuronal cultures to elucidate the role of GSK-3β in mediating apoptotic pathways. Early studies demonstrated that inhibition of GSK-3β with compounds like SB415286 could protect neurons from intracellular stresses by moderately suppressing pro-apoptotic signals (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In the ocular field, GSK-3β inhibitors have been explored in the context of diabetic retinopathy, where their use was associated with improved retinal ganglion cell survival and mitigation of neurodegenerative processes induced by oxidative stress (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20). Furthermore, related compounds such as SB216763—sharing similar mechanisms—with evidence of restoring Nrf2 levels in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) under oxidative stress supports the hypothesis that GSK-3β inhibition is beneficial in ocular settings (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6; Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 10–12). Despite these promising findings, the clinical evidence directly linking GSK-3β inhibition to the treatment of dry AMD remains sparse. In fact, comprehensive analyses such as those performed using the Open Targets Platform have revealed only a very weak association between GSK3B and AMD with minimal literature evidence, suggesting that while the concept is scientifically sound and mechanistically plausible, direct translational studies in dry AMD are still in an early stage (Buniello et al., 2025). Nevertheless, the preclinical use of SB415286 in retinal models of diabetic retinopathy and its documented capacity to modulate pathways relevant to oxidative stress and autophagy imply that repurposing this candidate for dry AMD merits further investigation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, GSK-3β is a serine/threonine kinase that is constitutively active in many cells and functions as a pivotal regulator of several intracellular signaling cascades. Under basal conditions, GSK-3β phosphorylates its substrates—including β-catenin—thereby marking them for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. In the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, the inhibition of GSK-3β (either through upstream signals such as Wnt ligand binding or via pharmacological inhibitors like SB415286) prevents the phosphorylation of β-catenin, allowing it to accumulate in the cytoplasm and eventually translocate into the nucleus (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Once in the nucleus, β-catenin forms complexes with TCF/LEF transcription factors to drive the transcription of genes involved in cell proliferation, differentiation, and cytoskeletal remodeling. In the context of RPE cells, this activation is critical because it is believed to upregulate lysosomal proteins, such as LAMP1, and phagocytic receptors, like MERTK, that are essential for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17; Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).  

Moreover, GSK-3β also exerts a negative regulatory influence on the Nrf2/NRF2 antioxidant pathway. Under oxidative stress, Nrf2 typically transactivates a battery of cytoprotective genes; however, GSK-3β phosphorylates Nrf2 at specific motifs within its Neh6 domain, facilitating recognition by the β-TrCP E3 ubiquitin ligase and leading to its degradation (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6). In addition to these signaling events, inhibition of GSK-3β modulates autophagy. Research indicates that proper autophagic flux is necessary for the turnover of damaged cellular components, including the disposal of POS debris, and that impaired autophagy is a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 10–12, 32–34). It is also important to note that GSK-3β is implicated in the regulation of the cytoskeletal machinery; its inhibition may lead to reorganization of actin and other cytoskeletal elements, which is critical for the phagocytic process in RPE cells (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Thus, while the inhibition of GSK-3β by SB415286 is expected to elevate β-catenin levels and trigger downstream transcription of lysosomal and cytoskeletal genes, the balance of these signaling events must be carefully modulated to avoid adverse outcomes.

The therapeutic hypothesis proposes that SB415286 will act directly on RPE cells by inhibiting GSK-3β, thereby releasing the inhibition on β-catenin. The resultant accumulation and nuclear translocation of β-catenin are expected to drive the transcription of a subset of genes critical for maintaining RPE function, including those involved in lysosome biogenesis (e.g., LAMP1) and the phagocytic machinery (e.g., MERTK). In dry AMD, a deficiency in the clearance of POS is a contributing factor to RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration, so enhancing gene expression that supports these processes is of significant therapeutic interest (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17).  

In cell-based assays—particularly flow cytometry-based phagocytosis assays—it is anticipated that treatment with SB415286 will result in an increased rate of POS uptake by RPE cells. Additionally, by relieving the negative regulation on Nrf2, SB415286 is expected to bolster the antioxidant defense mechanisms in RPE cells. The stabilization of Nrf2 not only aids in the upregulation of detoxification and radical-scavenging enzymes but also indirectly supports autophagy—a process crucial for the degradation of cellular waste and maintenance of cellular homeostasis in the aging RPE (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6).

Although diabetic retinopathy and dry AMD are distinct conditions, both involve significant oxidative stress, inflammation, and RPE dysfunction. The translational potential observed in these models suggests that SB415286 may similarly ameliorate pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD by enhancing the phagocytic and lysosomal capacity of RPE cells (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20). Nevertheless, the dualistic nature of GSK-3β’s roles necessitates a cautious interpretation; while promoting β-catenin signaling is advantageous for lysosomal and cytoskeletal gene expression, overactivation of Wnt signaling has been implicated in unwanted cellular phenotypes such as EMT, which could potentiate fibrotic responses if not carefully controlled (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 14–18). Therefore, the expected beneficial effects of SB415286 on POS clearance must be weighed against the risk of activating other deleterious pathways.

In evaluating SB415286 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key aspects emerge from the literature review. On one hand, the compound’s potent inhibition of GSK-3β, a kinase centrally involved in multiple signaling pathways, offers a mechanistically coherent strategy for addressing several pathological features of dry AMD. By targeting GSK-3β, SB415286 is designed to simultaneously activate Wnt/β-catenin signaling and stabilize Nrf2, thereby promoting the transcription of genes such as LAMP1 and MERTK that are essential for effective lysosomal function and phagocytosis in RPE cells (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17). The induction of lysosomal and cytoskeletal genes is expected to enhance the phagocytic clearance of POS, a critical function that is often compromised in the diseased RPE, ultimately helping to mitigate the progression of dry AMD. Additionally, supportive evidence from diabetic retinopathy models and other retinal degeneration studies suggests that modulating GSK-3β activity can exert beneficial effects in ocular tissues (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20).  

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be considered. First, GSK-3β is a multifunctional kinase that plays roles in a wide array of cellular processes; it is involved not only in the regulation of the Wnt/β-catenin and Nrf2 pathways but also in the control of apoptosis, glucose homeostasis, and even inflammatory responses. The broad distribution and pleiotropic functions of GSK-3β raise concerns about off-target effects and unwanted side effects when its activity is pharmacologically inhibited. For instance, unchecked activation of β-catenin signaling could inadvertently promote epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in RPE cells—a process that has been linked to fibrotic changes and worsening of retinal pathology (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 14–18). This weak association suggests that, although the mechanistic rationale for employing GSK-3β inhibitors is compelling at a biochemical level, direct evidence from AMD models remains limited. Consequently, while preclinical data in related retinal conditions are encouraging, additional research using dry AMD-specific models is required to establish the efficacy, safety, and dosing regimens for SB415286 in this context.  

Furthermore, the dual role of GSK-3β in both apoptosis and survival presents another layer of complexity. Its targeted inhibition of GSK-3β is expected to unleash β-catenin–driven transcriptional programs that upregulate lysosomal, cytoskeletal, and phagocytic genes, thereby enhancing the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments—a critical deficit in dry AMD pathology (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17). Nevertheless, the complexity of GSK-3β’s role in cellular signaling, the modest association between GSK3B and AMD observed in broader datasets, and the possibility of off-target effects, especially the unintended activation of fibrotic pathways, represent significant challenges that need to be addressed through comprehensive preclinical studies. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Homotaurine is a small-molecule GABA analogue that was originally investigated for its potential neuroprotective properties in Alzheimer’s disease due to its ability to interact with inhibitory neurotransmitter receptors. Although originally isolated from marine algae as a natural sulfonated amino acid derivative, the synthetic production of homotaurine has allowed for its repurposing and pharmacological refinement for various clinical indications. As a member of the GABAergic modulator class, it is designed to mimic the activity of the endogenous neurotransmitter γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), thereby affecting neuronal excitability and cellular homeostasis. In particular, homotaurine is postulated to activate GABAA receptors, which are ligand-gated chloride channels that normally contribute to membrane hyperpolarization and dampening of excitatory input. This class of compounds has been widely explored for neuroprotective purposes and has been utilized in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease, where an acceptable safety profile was established. The fact that homotaurine has progressed to advanced clinical stages in Alzheimer’s research supports its tolerability and widespread bioactivity, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in ocular diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Carullo et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, homotaurine has been primarily evaluated in the context of Alzheimer’s disease, where its anti-aggregation properties and potential to interfere with amyloid-β deposition were of paramount interest. Its prior clinical examination, which concluded with a favorable safety record, provides a solid foundation for its repurposing in other neurodegenerative conditions. Although there is no direct record of homotaurine being used to treat dry AMD, other compounds that modulate GABAergic signaling have been investigated in retinal degenerative models. For example, several studies have documented the expression of GABA receptor subunits, including those of the GABAA family, in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, suggesting that pharmacological targeting of these receptors may have therapeutic implications in diseases associated with retinal dysfunction (Arellano et al., 2025). Furthermore, inhibitory neurotransmitters such as GABA have been implicated in maintaining proper cellular excitability and synaptic balance in the retina; alterations in their regulation are associated with excitotoxicity and neurodegeneration in retinal conditions including macular degeneration (Pavan & Dalpiaz, 2018; Schur et al., 2018). In a similar vein, preclinical studies have used GABA modulators to rescue or protect RPE and photoreceptor function in models of retinal degeneration and light-induced injury (Schur et al., 2018). Thus, while direct clinical evidence for homotaurine in dry AMD is lacking, its antecedents in the GABAergic drug class and the known vulnerability of RPE cells to excitotoxic calcium overload position it as a promising candidate for therapeutic repurposing.

Mechanism of Action:  
The hypothesized mechanism of action of homotaurine in dry AMD rests on its ability to activate GABAA receptors expressed on RPE cells. Under physiological conditions, GABAA receptors are heteropentameric chloride channels that, upon binding GABA, permit chloride influx and hyperpolarize the cell membrane. This hyperpolarization ordinarily serves to counteract excessive excitation and limit voltage-gated calcium channel opening. In the context of RPE function, maintaining a tight regulation of intracellular calcium is paramount because calcium levels directly influence cytoskeletal reorganization, phagosome trafficking, and lysosomal fusion events necessary for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Nagymihaly et al., 2021). Several studies have documented that RPE cells not only express GABAA receptor subunits, such as GABAAα1, but that receptor activation in these cells can modify intracellular calcium concentrations, thereby modulating a host of calcium-dependent cellular processes—including phagocytosis (Arellano et al., 2025).

In dry AMD, the RPE’s phagocytic capacity is compromised, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and other toxic by-products, which in turn further disrupt cellular function and promote oxidative stress (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018). Homotaurine’s binding to GABAA receptors is expected to stabilize the membrane potential and reduce the abnormal Ca²⁺ influx that occurs during excitotoxic stress. This reduction in calcium entry is anticipated to alleviate downstream effects such as dysregulated cytoskeletal dynamics and impaired lysosomal trafficking. Cytoskeletal reorganization is essential for phagosome motility; proper F-actin dynamics direct the trafficking of phagosomes toward lysosomal compartments where degradation occurs (Inana et al., 2018; Nagymihaly et al., 2021). Moreover, studies have demonstrated that inflammatory mediators present in AMD, including TNF-α and interleukin-1β, modulate GABAA receptor expression and function, suggesting that modulation of these receptors could be a viable strategy to counteract inflammation-driven excitotoxicity (Arellano et al., 2025). In addition, the excitotoxic environment generated by imbalanced glutamate/GABA signaling in the retina can be mitigated by restoring the inhibitory tone through GABAA receptor activation. The specific EC₅₀ of approximately 10 µM for homotaurine indicates that it has the potential to achieve receptor activation within a therapeutic window that is plausible in an ocular formulation (Carullo et al., 2020; Arellano et al., 2025). Taken together, the combined modulation of calcium influx, along with the stabilization of cytoskeletal and lysosomal pathways, constitutes a comprehensive molecular strategy that homotaurine may employ to rescue impaired POS degradation in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed assay in ARPE-19 cells—a well-established in vitro model for RPE function—aims to evaluate whether homotaurine, via activation of GABAA receptors, can restore impaired photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis under conditions of glutamate-induced stress. RPE cell dysfunction in dry AMD is characterized by diminished phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation of POS, leading to the pathological accumulation of lipofuscin, which further impedes cellular function (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018). By engaging GABAA receptors, homotaurine is expected to “rescue” this vital phagocytic process by normalizing intracellular Ca²⁺ dynamics—thus preventing excitotoxicity—and by ensuring the proper reorganization of actin filaments or other cytoskeletal elements that are essential for efficient phagosome motility (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).

Experimental evidence in related studies supports that compounds with similar mechanisms (i.e., GABA modulators and taurine-related molecules) are capable of influencing intracellular calcium signaling and can enhance the uptake and processing of POS in RPE cells (Arellano et al., 2025; López-Colomé et al., 1994). Under normo-physiological conditions, RPE cells efficiently internalize shed POS through receptor-mediated pathways involving CD36, MerTK, and αVβ5 integrin, initiating a cascade that is dependent on well-regulated intracellular Ca²⁺ fluctuations (Nagymihaly et al., 2021). In a stress state, glutamate excess drives excitotoxic Ca²⁺ entry that may dysregulate these processes. By antagonizing this excitotoxic cascade, homotaurine is anticipated to reduce the aberrant Ca²⁺ load, thereby restoring the dynamic equilibrium that supports both cytoskeletal integrity and lysosomal trafficking. This mechanism is supported by studies showing that dysregulation of Ca²⁺ not only impairs phagosome motility but also has deleterious effects on downstream lysosomal fusion and degradation, ultimately impacting cellular clearance mechanisms (Si et al., 2023; Nowak et al., 2025). Thus, the expected effect is a measurable enhancement in POS uptake as well as improved degradation kinetics in RPE cells subjected to glutamate-induced stress, which would correlate with potential therapeutic efficacy in dry AMD. Furthermore, since the underlying pathology of dry AMD involves chronic oxidative stress and accumulation of metabolic by-products, a pharmacological intervention that can restore intracellular homeostasis has far-reaching implications for halting or even reversing disease progression (Arellano et al., 2025).

In evaluating homotaurine for dry age-related macular degeneration, several critical observations emerge. One of the key strengths of homotaurine is its well-documented safety profile from Alzheimer’s clinical trials, which lowers the translational hurdles when repurposing the compound for ocular administration. The fact that homotaurine is a GABA analogue that activates GABAA receptors—a receptor class that is expressed on RPE cells and critically involved in regulating intracellular Ca²⁺—provides a strong mechanistic rationale for its application in dry AMD (Arellano et al., 2025). By potentially mitigating excitotoxic Ca²⁺ influx, homotaurine could restore normal cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal trafficking, both of which are indispensable for the effective degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).

Among the strengths, the following points are notable:  
1. The candidate’s mechanism directly addresses a central pathology of dry AMD—namely, impaired RPE phagocytosis and lysosomal dysfunction—which leads to toxic lipofuscin accumulation (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018).  
2. Activation of GABAA receptors by homotaurine could normalize Ca²⁺ handling within RPE cells, thereby alleviating the excitotoxic stress that is linked to altered cytoskeletal assembly and defective phagosome trafficking (Arellano et al., 2025; Inana et al., 2018).  
3. The compound’s history in Alzheimer’s trials suggests a favorable safety margin and known pharmacokinetic properties that may be adapted for ocular use, thus enhancing its potential for rapid clinical translation (Carullo et al., 2020).  
4. Preclinical evidence from other studies involving GABA modulators and related compounds shows that interfering with aberrant neurotransmitter signaling in the retina can elicit neuroprotective and phagocytosis-enhancing effects (Schur et al., 2018).

Conversely, some weaknesses and uncertainties remain that necessitate further investigation:  
1. Although the proposed EC₅₀ of approximately 10 µM for homotaurine is within a plausible therapeutic window for GABAA receptor activation, the actual pharmacodynamic response in RPE cells—especially in the diseased microenvironment of dry AMD—remains to be rigorously quantified (Arellano et al., 2025).  
2. The retinal microenvironment in dry AMD is complex, characterized not only by excitotoxic stress but also by chronic oxidative stress, inflammation, and altered expression of multiple receptor types. In such a context, GABAA receptor activation could be affected by altered ionic gradients, potentially leading to reversed or atypical receptor responses as has been documented in other retinal degenerations (Arellano et al., 2025; Telegina et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Edaravone (3-methyl-1-phenyl-2-pyrazolin-5-one, also known as MCI-186 or Radicut) is a synthetic small-molecule free radical scavenger that was originally discovered and developed for its neuroprotective properties. Developed by Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma, edaravone belongs to the class of pyrazolone derivatives that have potent antioxidant activities. Its design allows it to function in both aqueous and lipid environments by donating electrons to a range of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and converting these free radicals into an inactive metabolite (2-oxo-3-(phenylhydrazono)-butanoic acid). The chemical structure of edaravone confers low molecular weight and high diffusibility, making it well-suited for rapid cellular uptake and efficient interaction with intracellular free radicals. This property has been exploited in its established clinical use in acute ischemic stroke, and its physicochemical characteristics have also encouraged exploration in other CNS and ocular conditions. The free radical scavenger class of compounds has a long history of use in protecting tissues from oxidative damage, and edaravone, in particular, has been shown to mitigate the destructive effects of excessive ROS generation—a process implicated in numerous degenerative conditions (Masuda et al., 2017; Imai et al., 2010).

Therapeutic History:  
Edaravone has a well-documented clinical history primarily in the management of acute ischemic stroke in Japan, where it was approved in 2001 based on its ability to reduce infarct size and improve neurological outcomes. Its established safety profile in human neurological diseases, including modern trials in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), underlines its potential for systemic administration. Over the years, extensive preclinical investigations have demonstrated that edaravone confers significant neuroprotection by lowering ROS levels, preventing lipid peroxidation, and inhibiting apoptosis in stressed tissue. Although edaravone’s approved indications do not include dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), its neuroprotective and antioxidant properties have been tested in various retinal disease models. For example, studies in animal models of light-induced photoreceptor degeneration, retinal detachment, and even laser-induced choroidal neovascularization have consistently shown that edaravone can reduce oxidative damage, suppress inflammatory cascades, and protect retinal neurons (Imai et al., 2010; Roh et al., 2011). While these models are not direct representations of dry AMD, they share key pathophysiological features with dry AMD, such as high oxidative stress in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor degeneration. Additionally, evidence from in vitro studies using RPE cells supports the idea that edaravone can lower intracellular ROS and thereby improve cell survival under oxidative challenge (Abokyi et al., 2020; Masuda et al., 2017). This history of broad-based use in conditions where excessive ROS plays a central role forms the rationale for repurposing edaravone for dry AMD, a disease in which chronic oxidative stress is a central pathogenic factor.

Mechanism of Action:  
Edaravone exerts its protective effects primarily through its potent antioxidant activity. At the molecular level, it scavenges a variety of ROS—including hydroxyl radicals, superoxide anions, and hydrogen peroxide—by donating an electron to these reactive species. This electron donation converts active free radicals into less harmful molecules and leads to the formation of an inactive end‐product, thereby interrupting the self‐propagating chain reactions of lipid peroxidation (Imai et al., 2010; Masuda et al., 2017). Such oxidative reactions are known to damage cellular components including lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.

In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium, which is characterized by a high rate of oxidative metabolism and exposure to intense light, ROS accumulation has several deleterious consequences. One key aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis is the oxidative inactivation of lysosomal enzymes, particularly cathepsin D, which is essential for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Under conditions of excessive ROS, lysosomal membranes become compromised by lipid peroxidation, resulting in increased lysosomal pH and subsequent inactivation of cathepsin D. This inefficiency in lysosomal digestion leads to the accumulation of undigested POS and lipofuscin—a process that further exacerbates cellular dysfunction in the RPE (Klettner et al., 2013).

Edaravone’s capacity to scavenge ROS is therefore hypothesized to maintain the functional integrity of lysosomes in RPE cells. By reducing the oxidative burden, edaravone can help preserve the acidic environment (low pH) required for optimal cathepsin D activity. Additionally, oxidative stress is known to impair autophagic flux in RPE cells, as evidenced by alterations in the conversion of LC3-I to its lipidated form LC3-II, which is a marker for autophagosome formation. Enhanced LC3-II flux is associated with efficient autophagy—a process crucial for the clearance of damaged proteins and organelles. By mitigating ROS, edaravone is expected to promote proper LC3-II flux and autophagic activity, further contributing to the clearance of POS debris and damaged organelles in RPE cells (Masuda et al., 2017; Pinelli et al., 2023).

Moreover, several studies have indicated that edaravone can modulate intracellular signaling pathways associated with oxidative stress. For instance, it has been shown to reduce the phosphorylation of stress-activated kinases such as p38 and JNK, both of which are activated in response to elevated ROS levels. Inhibition of these pathways may contribute not only to decreased apoptotic signaling but also to the stabilization of lysosomal function and autophagic processes (Imai et al., 2010; Roh et al., 2011). Overall, the molecular interactions of edaravone—scavenging of free radicals, preservation of lysosomal pH, protection of critical proteases like cathepsin D, and restoration of autophagic flux—form the basis for its proposed repurposing in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The primary expected effect of edaravone in the context of dry AMD is a reduction of oxidative stress within the RPE, thereby preventing the cascade of events that lead to lysosomal dysfunction and defective POS digestion. RPE cells are responsible for the cyclic phagocytosis of POS, and this process is heavily reliant on intact lysosomal function. Under oxidative stress, the lysosomal pH can drift toward alkalinity, which inactivates cathepsin D and impairs the degradation of phagocytosed material. By scavenging ROS, edaravone is anticipated to maintain the acidic environment of lysosomes, thus preserving the enzymatic activity of cathepsin D. This restoration of lysosomal function should translate into improved clearance of POS and reduce the buildup of lipofuscin and drusen—hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Klettner et al., 2013).

Experimental evidence suggests that excessive ROS impairs this flux, leading to the accumulation of dysfunctional autophagosomes and cellular debris. Furthermore, Western blot analysis might reveal a normalization of LC3-II levels, indicating improved autophagic flux. The overall effect would be increased phagocytic capacity of the RPE cells and a reduction in cellular stress markers, ultimately leading to enhanced retinal cell survival and function (Abokyi et al., 2020; Pinelli et al., 2023).

Intravitreal formulations—either as free drug or best yet, as encapsulated in liposomal vehicles—have been shown to achieve therapeutic antioxidant levels in the retina, ensuring that effective concentrations of edaravone reach the RPE. Edaravone emerges as a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on a strong mechanistic rationale and an established track record in oxidative stress mitigation. Among its primary strengths is its potent free radical scavenging activity, which underpins its ability to counteract the oxidative stress that is central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Its chemical properties—and the fact that it has been used safely in the treatment of acute ischemic stroke and ALS—lend significant weight to its potential for repurposing in retinal diseases (Imai et al., 2010; Masuda et al., 2017).

A notable strength is the dual benefit edaravone is expected to offer: not only does it reduce ROS levels, but it also helps to preserve critical lysosomal functions by maintaining an optimal acidic pH, thereby securing cathepsin D activity. This is particularly important because lysosomal degradation of POS is an essential process in RPE cells, and its disruption is a key driver of dry AMD progression (Klettner et al., 2013). Similarly, by promoting normal LC3-II flux, edaravone supports the autophagic machinery required for cellular clearance, further protecting the RPE from the accumulation of toxic waste products (Pinelli et al., 2023).

The preclinical literature provides substantive evidence of edaravone’s efficacy in various models of retinal degeneration. Studies in animal models of retinal detachment, photoreceptor cell death, and experimentally induced oxidative damage all report protective effects following edaravone treatment, including reductions in markers of apoptosis and oxidative stress, as well as improvements in cell survival and retinal morphology (Imai et al., 2010; Roh et al., 2011). In several of these studies, the protective effects of edaravone were enhanced when delivered via liposomal formulations, suggesting that optimized ocular delivery systems can overcome inherent pharmacokinetic challenges and achieve sustained retinal protection (Hironaka et al., 2011).

However, several potential weaknesses must be considered. First, while the underlying rationale for edaravone’s use in dry AMD is robust, direct evidence demonstrating its efficacy in dry AMD models is still limited. Most existing studies have focused on acute retinal damage models such as light-induced degeneration or retinal detachment rather than on the chronic degenerative process observed in dry AMD. Although oxidative stress is a driving force in the disease, the pathogenesis of dry AMD is also influenced by dysregulated complement activation, chronic inflammation, genetic predispositions, and metabolic disturbances. The compound’s extensive preclinical evidence in retinal models and established systemic safety profile further support its potential utility. However, the transition from acute retinal injury models to the chronic, multifaceted pathology of dry AMD requires additional focused studies. Specifically, further research is needed to validate its effects on cathepsin D activity, lysosomal pH regulation, and LC3-II flux within the context of RPE and to define the optimal dosing and delivery methods for sustained ocular protection. Given these considerations, edaravone merits further preclinical evaluation in dry AMD models and, if promising, could progress into clinical trials as an adjunct or combination therapy for this major cause of vision loss in the elderly (Abokyi et al., 2020; Imai et al., 2010; Masuda et al., 2017; Pinelli et al., 2023; Roh et al., 2011).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human CD46 is a biologic drug candidate derived from a naturally occurring human protein that plays a pivotal role in the regulation of the complement cascade. Endogenously, CD46, also known as membrane cofactor protein (MCP), is a type I transmembrane glycoprotein expressed on nearly all nucleated cells—including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—and is a member of the regulators of complement activation (RCA) gene family located on chromosome 1q32 (Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021; Sweigard et al., 2011). Its primary biological function is to act as a cofactor for the serine protease factor I, thereby mediating the proteolytic cleavage of complement components C3b and C4b that are deposited on host cell surfaces. This function is critical for preventing the formation of the C3 and C5 convertase complexes that drive the amplification loop of the complement cascade (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011).  

The recombinant human CD46 candidate (Biotechne Cat. No. 3430-CD) is produced by modern recombinant DNA techniques that allow for controlled expression in a chosen host cell system. Typically, to ensure proper folding and post-translational modifications (which are essential given CD46’s complex structure featuring multiple short consensus repeat [SCR] domains, O-linked glycosylated serine/threonine/proline-rich regions, a hydrophobic transmembrane segment, and a cytoplasmic tail), such proteins are expressed in eukaryotic cell systems (Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021; Leaderer et al., 2015). Previous recombinant production approaches for CD46 have employed adenoviral or adeno-associated viral vector technology, where the CD46 gene is inserted into an appropriate vector and delivered to target cells; however, the candidate in discussion is a purified recombinant protein intended for exogenously controlled dosing (Sweigard et al., 2011).  

As a member of the biologic class of complement regulatory proteins, recombinant CD46 belongs alongside other therapeutic proteins that target dysregulated complement activation, an approach that has gained prominence in treating complement-mediated diseases. The concept behind these therapeutics is to harness or augment natural regulatory mechanisms; in this instance, restoring or increasing the activity of CD46 on RPE cells may correct complement dysregulation implicated in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Leaderer et al., 2015; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021). This candidate is thus positioned within the emerging class of immunomodulatory biologics aimed at restoring homeostasis in the complement system.  

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic rationale for targeting complement dysregulation in AMD has been borne out by extensive biochemical and clinical investigations. CD46 was initially discovered by leveraging biochemical purification techniques using affinity columns that bound complement fragments such as C3b and C3(H₂O) (Liszewski & Atkinson, 2025; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021). This discovery set the stage for subsequent studies that established its central role in protecting host tissues from complement‐mediated damage by serving as a cofactor for factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b and C4b (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011).

In several preclinical studies, researchers have explored approaches to mitigate complement-mediated damage in ocular diseases by increasing CD46 expression or activity. Gene therapy studies have utilized adenoviral vectors (AdCAGCD46) to deliver the CD46 gene to RPE cells in animal models. Such studies have shown that increased CD46 expression in RPE not only reduced complement deposition as measured by decreased membrane attack complex (MAC) formation but also provided significant protection against complement-mediated cell damage (Sweigard et al., 2011). These findings have been considered especially relevant for dry AMD, a disease characterized by chronic low-grade complement activation that leads to RPE dysfunction, drusen formation, and ultimately retinal degeneration (Sweigard et al., 2011; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021).

In addition to gene therapy approaches, soluble recombinant forms of complement regulators, including soluble CD46, have been investigated with the aim of systemically or locally inhibiting the complement cascade. While some recombinant or engineered forms of complement regulators have advanced to clinical trials for other complement-mediated conditions, challenges have been noted regarding the potency of soluble proteins relative to their full-length, membrane-anchored counterparts. Studies analyzing soluble MCP have indeed reported that while it exerts complement inhibitory activity, its potency is often lower compared to the naturally occurring membrane-bound protein (Wagner & Frank, 2010). Still, the fundamental association between CD46 deficiency and impaired RPE function has been established in experimental models—for example, CD46-deficient RPE cells have been observed to display drusen-like deposits and reduced phagocytic function, which are hallmark features of dry AMD (Leaderer et al., 2015; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021).

Furthermore, research in related ocular models has demonstrated that enhancing CD46 activity in RPE cells results in improved cleavage of deposited complement fragments (C3b and C4b), reduced MAC deposition, and restoration of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D, which is critical for the digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (Sweigard et al., 2011). Thus, the therapeutic history of both endogenous CD46 function and its recombinant or gene therapy-mediated restoration strongly supports its potential utility in treating dry AMD, making it an attractive candidate for further evaluation in this disease context.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, CD46 functions as a regulatory checkpoint in the complement system by facilitating the inactivation of complement components that have been deposited on host cell surfaces. Its mechanism of action centers on its ability to serve as a cofactor for factor I, a plasma serine protease responsible for cleaving and inactivating C3b and C4b (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011). The protein comprises four contiguous short consensus repeat (SCR) domains or complement control protein (CCP) domains, and these are arranged in a manner that creates high-affinity binding sites for the C3b and C4b fragments (Leaderer et al., 2015; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021; Parsons et al., 2023).

Under physiological conditions, when C3b and C4b are deposited on the cell surface as a result of complement pathway activation, CD46 binds to these fragments through its CCP domains. This binding positions factor I in an optimal orientation to cleave C3b and C4b into their inactive forms, iC3b and iC4b, respectively, thereby halting further progression of the complement cascade (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011). By preventing the formation of the C3 and C5 convertases, CD46 effectively stops the downstream assembly of the MAC—a multi-protein complex that, if formed in excess, can lead to cell lysis and tissue injury.

More specifically, the biochemical interactions involve a network of electrostatic and hydrophobic contacts between the complement fragments and the SCR domains of CD46. The correct spatial arrangement of these domains is critical for both high-affinity binding and subsequent catalytic efficiency with factor I (Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021; Sweigard et al., 2011). Variability in the isoforms of CD46, generated via alternative splicing, can influence these interactions by altering the configuration of the extracellular domains or the intracellular signaling motifs, which in turn may modulate the overall efficiency of complement regulation (Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021; Parsons et al., 2023).

When administered exogenously as a recombinant protein, CD46 is hypothesized to either integrate into the target cell membrane or associate closely with the cell surface, thereby supplementing the endogenous pool of CD46 on RPE cells (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011). In the context of dry AMD, where studies have documented reduced CD46 expression and consequent complement dysregulation, the therapeutic addition of recombinant CD46 would bolster the cell’s ability to process deposited C3b and C4b, diminishing the formation of the convertase complexes that drive the alternative complement pathway (Sweigard et al., 2011).

This mode of action is not merely a passive blockade of complement via decoy binding; rather, it is an active restoration of a physiological regulatory mechanism. In addition to its primary cofactor activity, CD46 has been implicated in intracellular signaling pathways that govern cellular responses such as autophagy, metabolic reprogramming, and even modulation of the phagocytic machinery (Leaderer et al., 2015; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2025). In RPE cells, efficient phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments is crucial for retinal homeostasis, and complement-mediated lysosomal stress has been linked to impaired phagocytic function. By promoting the inactivation of C3b and C4b and reducing MAC formation, recombinant CD46 is expected to mitigate this lysosomal stress, thereby preserving or even enhancing the phagocytic function of RPE cells (Sweigard et al., 2011; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021).

Furthermore, the complement regulatory activity of CD46 is supported by its established localization patterns: in ocular tissues, CD46 is predominantly expressed on the basal and lateral surfaces of RPE cells, where it serves as a barrier against ongoing complement activation (Sweigard et al., 2011). The molecular orchestration provided by CD46 in these microenvironments is critical for maintaining the delicate balance between immune defense and auto-protection. Thus, the administration of recombinant human CD46 aims to restore this balance by re-establishing local complement control where it has been compromised, thereby forestalling the progression of the inflammatory and degenerative processes underlying dry AMD (Sweigard et al., 2011).

Expected Effect:  
In the experimental paradigm under consideration, the central hypothesis posits that exogenous CD46 will “increase membrane cofactor activity on RPE, enhancing inactivation of C3b and reducing complement-mediated lysosomal stress, indirectly improving the phagocytic function of RPE.” On a cellular level, the expected effect following administration of recombinant human CD46 is a measurable reduction in complement deposition on RPE cell membranes, particularly the MAC, which is the terminal effector of the complement cascade. This reduction should translate to decreased inflammatory signaling and lower lysosomal overload. As a consequence, the RPE’s phagocytic capacity—especially the ability to clear photoreceptor outer segment debris—is expected to recover, which is a critical aspect of maintaining retinal function and delaying the progression of dry AMD (Sweigard et al., 2011).

Studies have shown that CD46-deficient RPE cells display key pathological features of AMD such as drusen-like deposits and diminished cathepsin D activity, indicative of lysosomal dysfunction (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011). In experimental assays, the addition of exogenous recombinant CD46 has been observed to restore the cleavage of complement components C3b and C4b, thereby reducing MAC formation and indirectly rescuing enzymatic activities within the lysosome (Sweigard et al., 2011). This expected cascade of events is anticipated to lead to measurable improvements in RPE cell phagocytic function when compared with untreated controls.

Moreover, CD46 is naturally expressed in RPE cells where it contributes to the resident complement regulatory milieu (Sweigard et al., 2011; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021). Therefore, supplementing RPE cultures with recombinant CD46 should mimic or reinforce the endogenous regulation process. The anticipated outcome is a dual benefit: reducing complement-mediated cytotoxicity and alleviating lysosomal stress while simultaneously normalizing the phagocytic clearance process that is otherwise impaired in the context of dry AMD. The restoration of cathepsin D activity, an enzyme critical for lysosomal digestion of photoreceptor outer segments, is a particularly important endpoint in these assays as it provides a direct readout of improved lysosomal function (Sweigard et al., 2011).

Overall, the expected biochemical and cellular effects of recombinant CD46 form the basis for its proposed therapeutic action. By reinstituting the natural regulatory mechanisms of the complement system, the candidate is expected to create a more favorable immunological environment within the RPE that is conducive to both cell survival and optimal function. This restoration of homeostasis is crucial in the context of dry AMD, where chronic low-grade complement activation is a driving force behind cellular degeneration and impaired phagocytosis (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011).

Overall Evaluation:  
The comprehensive evaluation of recombinant human CD46 as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD reveals a number of compelling strengths along with several challenges that must be addressed before clinical translation.  

One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its robust scientific rationale. CD46 is a key regulator of complement activation, and its role as a cofactor for factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b and C4b is well documented (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011). This molecular function is directly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, a condition in which uncontrolled complement activation contributes to RPE cell damage, chronic inflammation, and subsequent retinal degeneration (Sweigard et al., 2011). The association between CD46 deficiency and the development of drusen, as well as impaired phagocytosis in RPE cells, provides strong evidence that augmenting CD46 levels could have therapeutic benefits (Leaderer et al., 2015; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021).  

Another significant strength is the precedent established by previous preclinical studies. Gene therapy approaches that have increased CD46 expression in RPE cells have demonstrated a reduction in MAC deposition and subsequent protection against complement-mediated injury (Sweigard et al., 2011). Even though these studies primarily used viral vectors to drive endogenous expression rather than administering a recombinant protein directly, the mechanistic insights gleaned from them support the hypothesis that exogenously applied recombinant CD46 can restore complement regulation in diseased RPE cells (Sweigard et al., 2011; Leaderer et al., 2015).

However, there are several inherent risks and challenges associated with the use of a recombinant protein as a therapeutic agent for an ocular condition. One major challenge is the effective delivery of recombinant proteins to the RPE. Ocular drug delivery is notoriously difficult due to the presence of physical barriers like the blood-retina barrier and the complex anatomy of the eye. Achieving and maintaining therapeutic concentrations of recombinant CD46 at the appropriate retinal sites will require the development of sophisticated delivery systems or local administration techniques, such as intravitreal or sub-retinal injections (Sweigard et al., 2011; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021).

In addition, while the natural CD46 protein is membrane bound, recombinant protein formulations are often generated in a soluble form. Studies have suggested that soluble forms of CD46 may exhibit lower potency compared to their membrane-anchored counterparts (Wagner & Frank, 2010; Leaderer et al., 2015). This discrepancy could result in suboptimal therapeutic efficacy if the recombinant protein cannot adequately associate with or integrate into the RPE cell membrane, where its complement regulatory activity is most needed (Wagner & Frank, 2010; Leaderer et al., 2015). Hence, careful consideration must be given to the design of the recombinant protein to preserve the membrane-targeting signal or to engineer a formulation that mimics the native configuration as closely as possible.

Another concern relates to immunogenicity. Although recombinant human CD46 is derived from a native human protein, the process of recombinant expression and purification might introduce minor differences in glycosylation patterns or conformation that could provoke an immune response upon repeated administration (Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021). Such immune responses could not only reduce the efficacy of the therapeutic but also pose safety risks to patients.

There is also the broader challenge of translating findings from in vitro or animal models into effective human therapies. While the preclinical data supporting CD46’s role in regulating complement activity and protecting RPE cells is promising, clinical studies will need to rigorously demonstrate that recombinant CD46 can reproducibly and safely ameliorate the pathological features of dry AMD in human patients (Sweigard et al., 2011; Leaderer et al., 2015). Factors such as dosing regimen, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and potential off-target effects will be critical to assess.

In summary, recombinant human CD46 represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its well-characterized role in complement regulation and its ability to potentially restore critical homeostatic functions in the RPE. The scientific rationale is robust and is supported by extensive preclinical evidence linking CD46 deficiency with complement-mediated damage in the retina (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021). Nevertheless, significant hurdles in drug delivery, protein formulation, and immunogenicity must be overcome to realize its full therapeutic potential. Future studies should prioritize the development of an optimized delivery system that ensures adequate localization and retention of recombinant CD46 in the RPE, as well as detailed preclinical evaluations to refine dosing and minimize potential adverse effects (Sweigard et al., 2011; Leaderer et al., 2015).  

Overall, while challenges remain, the targeted nature of recombinant CD46—aiming to reinstate a naturally occurring regulatory mechanism—positions it as a strong candidate for further development. Its favorable mechanism of action, combined with supportive data from gene therapy models, provides a compelling rationale for additional preclinical and eventually clinical studies to validate its efficacy and safety in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021).
