Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SRT1720 is a synthetic small‐molecule activator of SIRT1 that was originally discovered and optimized by Sirtris Pharmaceuticals through high‐throughput screening and subsequent structural refinement (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018). It belongs to the class of sirtuin‐activating compounds (STACs) that are chemically distinct from natural activators such as resveratrol. Unlike polyphenolic compounds, SRT1720 is based on an imidazothiazole scaffold, incorporating a 2-quinoxaline amidic substituent and a piperazine moiety at the C3 position. This combination of structural features was determined to be optimal for SIRT1 activation, allowing the compound to achieve an EC1.5 value of approximately 0.16 µM with maximal activation levels reported at 781% (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). The compound’s synthetic origins allowed medicinal chemists to overcome many limitations seen with natural compounds, such as poor bioavailability and limited potency, and enabled the generation of a series of analogues ultimately leading to SRT1720. As a representative of third-generation STACs, SRT1720’s well-characterized in vitro profile and documented pharmacokinetic properties position it as a promising candidate for repurposing into new therapeutic areas.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, SRT1720 has been extensively investigated in the context of metabolic disorders, particularly type 2 diabetes and obesity. Preclinical studies in diet-induced obese mice and genetically obese rodent models demonstrated its ability to normalize plasma glucose, enhance insulin sensitivity, and increase mitochondrial capacity without toxicity at proper dosing regimens (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). In these models, SRT1720 was shown not only to mimic the beneficial effects of caloric restriction but also to extend healthspan and, in some paradigms, even lifespan, by improving mitochondrial biogenesis via deacetylation of key transcriptional regulators such as PGC-1α (Feige et al., 2008; Milne et al., 2007). Although SRT1720 has been primarily developed and evaluated for metabolic and cardiovascular indications, its mechanism—centered on the activation of SIRT1 and the subsequent modulation of cellular metabolism, stress response, and anti-inflammatory signaling—has generated interest in its potential applications in other age-related conditions. However, thus far no published studies have specifically addressed its use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or related ocular degenerative conditions. This therapeutic candidate has not been utilized in a clinical or preclinical setting directly targeting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, which is the hallmark of dry AMD, although its known pharmacological profile, good oral bioavailability in rodent models, and the safety profile observed in multiple animal models provide a rationale for its repurposing (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Alcain & Villalba, 2009).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SRT1720 acts as an allosteric activator of SIRT1, an NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase involved in the regulation of energy metabolism, inflammation, autophagy, and other aging-related processes. Its mechanism of action is predicated on binding to the SIRT1-peptide substrate complex rather than the free enzyme. Specifically, SRT1720 has been shown to interact with a site in the N-terminal region of SIRT1, mapped approximately to amino acids 183–225, which is proposed to undergo a conformational change upon binding of acetylated substrates (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). Through this allosteric binding, SRT1720 lowers the Michaelis constant (Km) for the acetylated peptide substrate, thereby increasing the enzyme’s affinity for its substrate and promoting a more productive catalytic conformation. This effect enhances the deacetylation of key substrates, such as PGC-1α, FOXO1, and p53, which are involved in metabolic regulation, stress response, and apoptosis (Feige et al., 2008; Milne et al., 2007). Although initial studies reported a direct activation model analogous to that of resveratrol, subsequent investigations have raised concerns regarding the substrate-dependency of the assay used to measure SIRT1 activity. For instance, certain studies reported that SRT1720 only shows activation when fluorophore-tagged peptides are used, casting doubts on whether the compound directly interacts with SIRT1 under native conditions (Pacholec et al., 2010). Nevertheless, additional kinetic and biophysical studies, including those employing isothermal titration calorimetry and nuclear magnetic resonance, have supported an allosteric activation mechanism that is consistent with a reduction in Km for acetylated substrates (Dittenhafer-Reed et al., 2011; Sanchez-Fidalgo et al., 2012). Moreover, structural and structure-activity relationship studies have confirmed that modifications in the chemical scaffold of SRT1720—particularly adjustments to the piperazine group and quinoxaline moiety—are critically linked to its SIRT1 activating properties (Blum et al., 2011; Granchi & Minutolo, 2018). In summary, despite ongoing debates about the nuances of its mechanism, the prevailing view supports that SRT1720 directly modulates SIRT1 activity via an allosteric mechanism that facilitates deacetylation of substrates, thereby promoting cellular processes that mimic the beneficial aspects of caloric restriction and enhance metabolic health.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
The hypothesis underlying the use of SRT1720 for dry age-related macular degeneration is that SIRT1 activation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells can improve autophagy and cytoskeletal dynamics, thereby enhancing phagocytic cup formation and promoting lysosomal fusion necessary for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). RPE dysfunction—including impaired autophagy and phagocytosis—has been implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In this context, SRT1720’s ability to increase LC3 flux and improve LAMP1 trafficking, as observed in models of oxidative stress, offers a mechanistic rationale for its use. Preclinical findings in non-ocular systems have demonstrated that activation of SIRT1, whether achieved genetically or pharmacologically, augments mitochondrial biogenesis and reduces oxidative stress by increasing the turnover of damaged cellular components (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Mautone et al., 2020). Notably, the EC₅₀ for SIRT1 activation by SRT1720 in some biochemical assays approximates 0.1–0.16 µM, a range that is consistent with the dosing hypothesis proposed for RPE cells (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). Given that the RPE is known to express SIRT1 and other components of the autophagic machinery, the expected result of SRT1720 treatment in the RPE would be deacetylation of key regulators involved in autophagy and cytoskeletal organization. This deacetylation should in turn enhance processes such as phagosome maturation and lysosomal fusion, which are critical for efficient clearance of POS debris (Alcain & Villalba, 2009; Sanchez-Fidalgo et al., 2012). Additionally, SIRT1 activation in RPE cells may mitigate oxidative stress and reduce pro-inflammatory signaling pathways, further contributing to cellular homeostasis and survival in the ocular microenvironment (Dittenhafer-Reed et al., 2011). On a cellular assay level, treatment with SRT1720 is expected to increase markers of autophagic flux (such as LC3-II conversion), promote proper trafficking of lysosomal markers like LAMP1, and enhance the formation of organized phagocytic cups necessary for POS engulfment. These improvements in RPE function could, in theory, translate into better clearance of accumulated debris and ultimately slow or reverse degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD. However, while this hypothesis is supported by data from metabolic and non-ocular cellular studies, it remains essential to validate these effects specifically in RPE cell models and animal models of dry AMD to ensure that the ocular pharmacokinetic profile and tissue-specific responses are favorable (Park et al., 2017; Wan, 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating SRT1720 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the available literature. On the strength side, SRT1720 is one of the most potent synthetic SIRT1 activators reported, with biochemical assays consistently demonstrating activation in the low micromolar to submicromolar range (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). Its synthetic nature and the consequent ability to modify its chemical structure for improved potency and selectivity afford significant advantages over naturally occurring compounds like resveratrol. The extensive preclinical data supporting its beneficial effects in metabolic disorders, including improved mitochondrial function, enhanced autophagy, and anti-inflammatory properties, provide a strong rationale for its potential use in conditions where cellular clearance and stress responses are impaired, such as in the RPE during dry AMD (Milne et al., 2007; Sanchez-Fidalgo et al., 2012). Moreover, the underlying hypothesis that SIRT1 activation can enhance autophagic flux and cytoskeletal dynamics aligns well with the biological challenges faced by the RPE in dry AMD—namely, the accumulation of damaged POS and the ensuing oxidative stress that contributes to disease progression. The documented pharmacokinetic properties, such as good oral bioavailability in rodent models, further suggest that SRT1720 could be optimized for ocular delivery with appropriate formulation strategies (Alcain & Villalba, 2009; Mautone et al., 2020).

On the other hand, notable weaknesses and challenges must be addressed. First, there is ongoing controversy regarding the precise mechanism by which SRT1720 activates SIRT1. Some studies have raised concerns that its observed activity might be an artifact of the assay conditions—particularly its dependence on fluorophore-tagged substrates—which calls for cautious interpretation of its direct effects on native SIRT1 substrates (Pacholec et al., 2010). Such discrepancies underscore the need for additional rigorously controlled biochemical studies using physiological substrates in RPE cells to conclusively establish its mechanism of action in an ocular context. Second, while extensive data exist from metabolic and cardiovascular models, there is a notable paucity of research specifically addressing the use of SRT1720 in ocular tissues or models of retinal degeneration. As dry AMD is characterized by unique aspects of retinal physiology, including a blood–retinal barrier and specific immune responses in the eye, the translational relevance of data from non-ocular models must be carefully validated through targeted preclinical studies (Park et al., 2017). Third, potential off-target effects—such as cross-reactivity with other sirtuin family members like SIRT2—pose additional concerns regarding the specificity and safety profile of SRT1720. Although its selectivity for SIRT1 over SIRT3 appears robust, any unintended modulation of SIRT2 or other enzymes could have unforeseen consequences on RPE cell function and overall retinal health (Milne et al., 2007; Granchi & Minutolo, 2018). Finally, the optimal dosing strategy, route of administration, and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) relationship in the context of ocular delivery remain unexplored, necessitating a series of preclinical ocular pharmacology studies to evaluate whether the effective concentrations observed in vitro can be achieved in the retina without systemic toxicity (Park et al., 2017; Sinclair & Hubbard, 2013).

In conclusion, SRT1720 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well-documented ability to activate SIRT1 and modulate critical cellular processes such as autophagy, mitochondrial biogenesis, and cytoskeletal organization. These properties are particularly relevant given the role of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD, where impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and accumulated cellular debris contribute to disease progression. The compound’s synthetic origins allow for further medicinal chemistry optimization, and its strong in vitro potency (EC₅₀ in the low micromolar range) lends support to the hypothesis that it could achieve meaningful biological effects in the RPE (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Milne et al., 2007). However, the controversies surrounding its mechanism of action—as well as the lack of direct evidence in ocular models—highlight significant gaps that must be addressed before advancing SRT1720 into ophthalmologic applications. It would be imperative to conduct detailed biochemical studies in primary RPE cell cultures and to establish reliable animal models of dry AMD to evaluate both efficacy and ocular pharmacokinetics. Additional research should also focus on determining whether SRT1720’s modulation of autophagic and cytoskeletal regulators translates into improved POS clearance and enhanced RPE survival under oxidative stress.  

Overall, while SRT1720 demonstrates many characteristics that are theoretically beneficial for treating dry AMD, further targeted research is required to resolve the outstanding controversies and validate its therapeutic potential in the ocular setting. Strengths such as its high potency and favorable metabolic effects are balanced by weaknesses including assay-dependent mechanistic uncertainties and limited direct evidence in retinal systems. Therefore, the recommendation is to pursue rigorous preclinical studies that specifically assess SRT1720’s impact on RPE autophagy, phagocytic cup formation, and lysosomal fusion as well as its in vivo efficacy in relevant dry AMD models before committing substantial resources to later-stage development. This strategy will ensure that the unique challenges of ocular delivery and retinal cellular dynamics are adequately addressed, providing a sound basis for eventual clinical translation if the compound proves efficacious and safe in these specialized assays (Granchi & Minutolo, 2018; Pacholec et al., 2010; Blum et al., 2011; Alcain & Villalba, 2009).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The therapeutic candidate under evaluation is a CD82 agonist peptide, marketed as a tetraspanin activator (Peptide Institute Cat. No. K-8202). This candidate is a synthetic peptide designed to interact with the extracellular domain of CD82, a member of the tetraspanin family involved in organizing membrane microdomains and regulating the spatial distribution of various transmembrane proteins such as integrins. Tetraspanins are known to modulate cellular adhesion, migration, and signal transduction by forming dynamic “tetraspanin–enriched microdomains” (TEMs) that include integrins and other proteins; in particular, CD82 has been implicated in the regulation of integrin clustering and function in a range of cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and various immune cells (Lee et al., 2022). The structural design of this peptide likely takes advantage of the sequence and conformational features of the large extracellular loop (LEL) of CD82, which is known to mediate protein–protein interactions through specific binding surfaces and domains. Although similar CD82‐derived peptides have been examined primarily in the context of cancer metastasis suppression, the repurposing of such peptides for retinal applications represents an innovative approach. The rationale is that by binding to CD82 on the RPE cell surface, the peptide may induce a clustering effect that enhances the recruitment and stable assembly of αvβ5 integrin nanodomains, which are critical for the formation of effective phagocytic cups and subsequent photoreceptor outer segment (POS) internalization—a process that is compromised in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Lee et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, tetraspanin proteins such as CD82 have been studied extensively in oncology where they are recognized as metastasis suppressors. In those settings, peptide mimetics of the small extracellular loop (EC1) of CD82 have been developed with the aim of modulating cell adhesion, migration, and invasion. For example, studies have shown that CD82-derived peptides can inhibit tumor cell migration and adhesion by interfering with integrin-mediated signaling pathways, particularly involving integrins such as α5β1, and by attenuating downstream focal adhesion kinase (FAK) signaling (Luan et al., 2018). However, such peptides have primarily been investigated in non-ocular systems, and their actions have been predominantly inhibitory in nature, aimed at suppressing excessive integrin signaling rather than stimulating it. In the specific context of the retina, the use of CD82 or its mimetics has been very limited; one study documented that recombinant human CD82 (rhCD82) can interfere with TGF-β1-mediated epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) in ARPE-19 cells by modulating integrin expression and inhibiting Smad-dependent signaling pathways (Lee et al., 2022). Although that study was conducted within the framework of fibrosis and EMT—processes that are also relevant to AMD—the focus was on anti-fibrotic and anti-migratory properties rather than on enhancing phagocytosis. In addition, indirect evidence from immunological studies indicates that CD82 plays a role in regulating integrin sorting and cytoskeletal reorganization in macrophages and neutrophils, thereby influencing cell migration and adhesion (McGowan et al., 2022). In retinal biology, the αvβ5 integrin is known to be indispensable for efficient POS binding and internalization by RPE cells, and its dysregulation is associated with impaired phagocytosis and consequently with AMD pathogenesis (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). However, there is currently no established history of using a CD82 agonist peptide to specifically enhance αvβ5 integrin clustering or to stimulate phagocytic cup formation in RPE cells, making this candidate both innovative and largely uncharted in preclinical ocular disease models (Lee et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The proposed mechanism of action for the CD82 agonist peptide rests on the capacity of CD82 to orchestrate the lateral organization of integrin receptors in the plasma membrane. Under physiological conditions, CD82 is involved in forming complexes with integrin subunits, including integrin β1 and integrin αv; these interactions have been shown to modulate integrin activation states and can affect downstream signaling pathways (Lee et al., 2022). In the present hypothesis, the agonist peptide is expected to bind to the extracellular domain of CD82 in a manner that promotes its active conformation, thereby enhancing its ability to cluster αvβ5 integrin on the apical surface of RPE cells. The clustering of integrin receptors is a critical step in the initiation of phagocytic cup assembly, as it facilitates the formation of a localized high-density area of signaling and adhesion molecules needed to capture and internalize shed POS particles (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). The biochemistry underlying this process involves the reorganization of membrane microdomains, where CD82, upon binding of the agonist peptide, may recruit additional integrin molecules and potentially interact with adapter proteins that link to the actin cytoskeleton, thereby reinforcing the mechanical stability required for efficient phagocytosis (McGowan et al., 2022). In several cell types, similar tetraspanin activators have been shown to influence cytoskeletal dynamics and cell adhesion by modulating the activity of small GTPases and other signaling intermediates; for example, the inhibition of migration by CD82 in macrophages is associated with decreased filopodia formation (McGowan et al., 2022). By analogy, if the agonist peptide induces a favorable conformational change in CD82 within RPE cells, it could conceivably lead to an optimal reorganization of αvβ5 integrin clusters that promotes the formation and stabilization of phagocytic cups, thereby enhancing the uptake of POS particles. Nonetheless, it is important to note that many of the detailed molecular interactions have been characterized in contexts other than retinal phagocytosis, and extrapolation to RPE cells remains somewhat speculative at this time (Luan et al., 2018). Moreover, while molecular docking analyses have revealed direct interactions between CD82 and integrin subunits (Lee et al., 2022), the specific impact of an agonist peptide on αvβ5 integrin clustering in RPE membranes has not yet been directly demonstrated. This lack of direct evidence underscores the need for rigorous mechanistic studies that investigate the peptide’s binding kinetics, its ability to modulate CD82 conformation, and the subsequent effects on integrin organization and actin remodeling in the specialized environment of RPE cells (Lee et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The anticipated outcome of administering the CD82 agonist peptide in a dry AMD model is an enhancement of RPE function through improved phagocytic activity. In healthy RPE cells, the daily clearance of shed photoreceptor outer segments is mediated primarily by αvβ5 integrin-dependent processes that initiate phagocytic cup assembly and POS internalization. In dry AMD, RPE dysfunction, which may include impaired integrin clustering and reduced phagocytic efficiency, contributes to the accumulation of cellular debris and subsequent retinal degeneration (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). The working hypothesis postulates that the CD82 agonist peptide will bind to CD82, resulting in the clustering and stabilization of αvβ5 integrin microdomains on the apical surface of RPE cells. Enhanced clustering of these integrins is expected to promote a more robust and efficient phagocytic response by facilitating the assembly of actin-rich phagocytic cups that effectively capture and internalize POS particles (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Zihni, 2025). In vitro, this effect would likely be measurable as an increase in the rate and extent of POS uptake in cultured human RPE cells such as ARPE-19, and could be quantified using established phagocytosis assays that utilize fluorescently labeled POS preparations. In vivo, improved phagocytic function could translate into better maintenance of retinal integrity, reduced accumulation of lipofuscin and other intracellular debris, and ultimately a slowdown or reversal of the degenerative changes associated with dry AMD (Ruggiero et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2022). It is also anticipated that by enhancing integrin clustering, the peptide might indirectly influence other signaling pathways involved in RPE homeostasis, potentially mitigating inflammatory or fibrotic processes that exacerbate AMD pathology (McGowan et al., 2022). However, one must exercise caution as the majority of existing literature on CD82 peptide mimetics has focused on modulating cell migration and adhesion in the context of cancer, rather than promoting enhanced phagocytosis (Luan et al., 2018). Therefore, while the expected effect of restored or enhanced POS clearance is theoretically sound, it remains to be validated in the specific cellular and animal models of dry AMD relevant to RPE function.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the proposed CD82 agonist peptide represents an intriguing and innovative candidate for the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration by addressing a fundamental pathological mechanism—impaired RPE phagocytosis. One of the key strengths of this candidate is its novel mechanism of action, which utilizes the concept of targeted receptor organization through the activation of a tetraspanin protein that has been implicated in integrin modulation. The role of αvβ5 integrin in RPE phagocytosis is well established, and its proper clustering is essential for the effective clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, a process that is compromised in aging and AMD (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). The idea of repurposing a CD82 agonist peptide to restore or enhance this process is supported indirectly by the body of literature demonstrating that tetraspanins play critical roles in integrin organization and that modulating tetraspanin function can have significant impacts on cell adhesion and signaling (Lee et al., 2022). Additionally, because current therapeutic strategies for dry AMD remain limited and largely focused on addressing neovascular complications rather than the underlying degenerative process, a candidate that directly improves RPE function and photoreceptor homeostasis offers substantial promise.

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be considered. First, there is a notable gap in the direct experimental evidence linking CD82 agonist peptides to enhanced phagocytic cup assembly or increased POS internalization in RPE cells. Most studies to date that involve CD82 in the context of the retina have concentrated on its role in inhibiting EMT or modulating inflammatory responses in ARPE-19 cells (Lee et al., 2022). In contrast, the majority of the literature on CD82 peptide mimetics in other systems—particularly in cancer—describes inhibitory effects on integrin-mediated signaling and cell migration rather than an agonistic promotion of integrin clustering (Luan et al., 2018). This discrepancy raises concerns regarding whether a peptide designed to activate CD82 will have the desired stimulatory effect on αvβ5 integrin organization in the unique cellular environment of the RPE. Second, the regulatory functions of tetraspanins are inherently complex and highly dependent on the cellular context; while enhanced clustering may be beneficial for phagocytosis, it could also inadvertently alter other CD82-associated pathways, such as TGF-β signaling or immune cell interactions, with potentially unforeseen consequences (McGowan et al., 2022). Third, the preclinical development of peptide-based therapeutics, particularly for ocular applications, poses significant challenges in terms of delivery, stability, and bioavailability. The blood–retinal barrier and the highly specialized microenvironment of the eye may limit the effective concentrations of the peptide that reach the target RPE cells, and any off-target effects due to systemic distribution could further complicate the safety profile.

Moreover, while integrin clustering is a promising target, the evidence linking enhanced αvβ5 organization directly to improved phagocytosis in RPE cells mainly comes from correlative studies in rodent models and in vitro assays (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012; Zihni, 2025). There is a need for more mechanistic studies that specifically dissect how tetraspanin-driven integrin clustering influences the kinetics and efficiency of phagocytic cup assembly in models that faithfully recapitulate the human RPE phenotype. It is also important to confirm that CD82 is expressed and functionally relevant in RPE cells of patients with dry AMD, as variations in tetraspanin expression could impact the efficacy of a peptide-based agonist (Lee et al., 2022). The candidate’s success will depend on rigorous optimization of its pharmacological profile, including its peptide stability, receptor binding affinity, and resistance to proteolytic degradation within ocular tissues.

Despite these challenges, the concept behind the CD82 agonist peptide is compelling. The targeted approach of modulating receptor microdomain architecture represents a departure from more conventional strategies, such as anti-VEGF therapies or broad-spectrum anti-inflammatory agents. If the peptide can selectively promote the clustering of αvβ5 integrins and thereby restore efficient POS clearance, it might not only improve retinal adhesion and photoreceptor survival but also mitigate secondary events such as lipofuscin accumulation and chronic inflammation that drive the progression of dry AMD (McGowan et al., 2022). In theory, such targeted modulation of the RPE microenvironment could offer a disease-modifying strategy rather than merely palliative treatment. Additionally, because tetraspanins like CD82 serve as molecular organizers with relatively high tissue specificity, an agonist peptide could potentially be engineered to have a favorable safety profile with minimal off-target systemic effects.

In weighing the strengths and weaknesses, it becomes clear that while the CD82 agonist peptide holds significant promise as a novel therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, its clinical potential remains largely theoretical at this stage. The mechanism by which tetraspanin activation could enhance αvβ5 integrin clustering is supported by indirect evidence from studies in cancer cells and other non-ocular tissues (Luan et al., 2018). However, the translation of these findings to the RPE, which is both highly polarized and functionally unique, requires additional targeted investigation. Future studies should focus on validating the expression and functional activation of CD82 in RPE cells from both healthy donors and AMD patients, as well as on conducting mechanistic experiments to determine the precise impact of the agonist peptide on integrin clustering and phagocytic cup formation. In vitro assays using cultured RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary human RPE) should be complemented by in vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD to assess whether the peptide can indeed restore or enhance POS clearance and thereby ameliorate retinal degeneration (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012).

An additional aspect to consider is the potential for unexpected off-target effects. Given that CD82 is involved in a variety of cellular processes—including those related to cell adhesion, migration, and even immune modulation—the systemic administration of a CD82 agonist peptide might affect multiple cell types beyond the RPE (McGowan et al., 2022). Therefore, an effective delivery strategy that confines the peptide’s activity to the retina (for example, via intravitreal injection or a controlled-release ocular implant) may be essential for maximizing its therapeutic index. Drug formulation studies, as well as preliminary toxicology assessments, will be crucial in determining whether the peptide achieves the necessary balance between efficacy and safety.

In conclusion, the CD82 agonist peptide (Peptide Institute Cat. No. K-8202) is a novel therapeutic candidate that harnesses the unique properties of tetraspanin CD82 to potentially enhance αvβ5 integrin clustering in RPE membranes. This mechanism is hypothesized to lead to improved phagocytic cup assembly and POS internalization, addressing a key pathogenic process in dry AMD. The candidate belongs to a class of peptide-based modulators that have been historically evaluated for their roles in regulating cell adhesion and migration in cancer, but its application in the context of retinal phagocytosis is largely uncharted. The evidence supporting the role of CD82 in integrin modulation is robust in non-ocular systems (Lee et al., 2022), and there is clear evidence for the importance of αvβ5 integrin in RPE phagocytosis (Bhatwadekar et al., 2020; Ruggiero et al., 2012). Nonetheless, the direct demonstration that activation of CD82 via an agonist peptide enhances integrin clustering and phagocytic efficiency in RPE cells is currently lacking, and the majority of published studies have demonstrated inhibitory effects of CD82 peptides in different contexts (Luan et al., 2018).

The overall evaluation of this therapeutic candidate is thus twofold. On the one hand, the mechanistic rationale is scientifically intriguing and represents a targeted, innovative approach that aligns with our current understanding of RPE biology and AMD pathogenesis. On the other hand, the candidate’s novelty in the ocular field means that there is a significant gap in the preclinical validation required to confidently predict efficacy in dry AMD. Strengths of the candidate include its potential for receptor-specific modulation, the possibility of restoring natural phagocytic function in the RPE, and the prospect of achieving a disease-modifying effect by targeting a fundamental cellular process. Weaknesses include the lack of direct experimental evidence in RPE models, the possibility that the peptide may exhibit inhibitory rather than stimulatory effects on integrin function as observed in cancer-related studies, and the inherent challenges of peptide-based drug delivery to the retina.

Ultimately, while the CD82 agonist peptide holds considerable promise based on mechanistic reasoning and a growing body of literature that supports the central role of tetraspanins in cellular organization and integrin function (Lee et al., 2022; Bhatwadekar et al., 2020), further rigorous studies are needed. These should include in vitro assays in RPE cell cultures to quantify changes in integrin clustering and phagocytic cup assembly, followed by in vivo evaluations in animal models that recapitulate the pathological features of dry AMD (Lee et al., 2022; McGowan et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB202190 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor belonging to the pyridinyl imidazole class of compounds. Originally discovered through rigorous cell‐based phenotypic screens aimed at identifying agents with anti‐inflammatory properties, SB202190 was developed to selectively inhibit p38 mitogen‐activated protein kinase (MAPK), particularly the α and β isoforms. The molecule was first characterized using radiolabeled ligand binding studies, which confirmed its ability to bind the ATP‐binding pocket of p38 MAPK and suppress its catalytic function (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). Being available commercially (e.g., Sigma‐Aldrich Cat. No. SML0687), SB202190 has been widely used as a biochemical tool to dissect the role of p38 in cellular stress and inflammatory responses. This class of compounds, including SB203580 as a closely related analogue, is recognized for its ability to modulate intracellular signaling cascades under various stress conditions. They have been broadly used in research settings to probe the molecular basis of cytokine production, cell differentiation, apoptosis, and cytoskeletal regulation (Young, 2013; Maugeri et al., 2021). The candidate under discussion is being repurposed with the hypothesis that its high potency against p38α/β—exhibiting an IC₅₀ of approximately 40 nM—can be leveraged to correct stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling defects and improve the phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative stress conditions that mimic the pathophysiology of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Liu et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, SB202190 has been predominantly employed as a research reagent to interrogate the role of p38 MAPK signaling in various cell types and disease models. In the context of ocular studies, SB202190, similar to its analogue SB203580, has been used to examine fibrotic responses, cell migration, and cytokine production in RPE cells. For instance, several in vitro studies have demonstrated that inhibition of p38 MAPK by SB202190 effectively reduces TGF‐β2–induced extracellular matrix (ECM) production (specifically collagen type I and fibronectin synthesis), which serves as an experimental surrogate for fibrotic remodeling observed in retinal degenerative conditions (Saika et al., 2005). Moreover, experiments using ARPE‐19 human RPE cells have revealed that SB202190 can reverse abnormal cell migration and reduce the transformation of RPE cells into fibroblast‐like cells in models of proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) (Saika et al., 2005). Although these models do not directly replicate dry AMD, they capture key aspects of RPE dysfunction, such as cytoskeletal disorganization and aberrant ECM deposition, which are also implicated in the progression of AMD. Beyond ocular research, p38 MAPK inhibitors have been investigated in other pathologies characterized by chronic inflammation and stress‐induced cellular dysfunction, including rheumatoid arthritis and muscular dystrophies (Brennan et al., 2021; Hirosawa et al., 2009). However, to date, clinical applications of SB202190 itself have not been pursued, and its use has remained restricted to preclinical experimental studies, thereby providing both a strong mechanistic rationale and a cautionary note regarding its translational potential (Federspiel et al., 2023; Young, 2013). Importantly, while numerous studies have elucidated p38 MAPK’s involvement in retinal injury and oxidative stress responses, there is limited direct clinical evidence supporting the use of SB202190 for treating dry AMD, and its application in this indication remains strictly hypothetical at this stage (Moustardas et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB202190 is known to selectively target the ATP‐binding pocket of p38 MAPK, thereby inhibiting its enzymatic activity and preventing the phosphorylation of downstream substrates that are pivotal to stress‐induced signaling cascades. Under normal conditions, p38 MAPK becomes activated through dual phosphorylation on specific threonine and tyrosine residues within its activation loop. Once activated, p38 MAPK stimulates various substrates, including transcription factors (e.g., cFos) and regulatory proteins involved in the control of cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and inflammatory mediator production (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). In RPE cells, activation of p38 MAPK has been linked to cytoskeletal rearrangements that lead to stress‐induced cellular defects; these include formation of abnormal actin structures and impaired formation of phagocytic cups necessary for the internalization of POS (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). In the experimental setting, SB202190 has been shown to effectively block the TGF‐β2 mediated phosphorylation of p38, thereby reducing the transcriptional activity of Smad3/4 complexes without impacting the initial receptor‐mediated phosphorylation events of Smads2/3. This mechanism suggests that SB202190 acts downstream of TGF‐β receptor activation, interfering with p38‐dependent enhancement of transcription factor complex formation and nuclear translocation, which in turn can dampen pathological ECM production and abnormal cell migration (Saika et al., 2005). Additionally, literature indicates that stress‐activated p38 signaling contributes to the senescence of RPE cells by regulating the senescence‐associated secretory phenotype (SASP) through modulation of p53 and NF‐κB pathways (Liu et al., 2025). By inhibiting p38 MAPK, SB202190 is hypothesized to replicate the protective effects of endogenous negative regulators such as DUSP4, which dephosphorylate and inactivate p38 MAPK, ultimately reducing RPE cell senescence and maintaining cellular homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025). It is noteworthy that p38 MAPK signaling is intricately intertwined with other MAPK family members, and some studies have reported that SB202190, particularly at higher doses, exhibits a biphasic response where alternative signaling pathways (such as MEK/ERK) may become upregulated, emphasizing the importance of careful dose optimization in any therapeutic application (Wang et al., 2024; Hirosawa et al., 2009). Thus, the mechanism of action of SB202190 involves a highly specific inhibition of p38α/β kinase activity, which is expected to restore normal actin dynamics and cytoskeletal organization in RPE cells, thereby facilitating proper phagosome formation and efficient POS uptake under oxidative stress conditions akin to those found in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The primary hypothesis driving the repurposing of SB202190 for dry AMD is that inhibition of p38α/β in RPE cells will reduce stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling defects and thereby improve the phagocytic internalization of photoreceptor outer segments. Under oxidative stress conditions, such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) in in vitro models using ARPE‐19 cells, activation of p38 MAPK is known to mediate cytoskeletal disorganization and promote aberrant cell migration, processes that are deleterious to the RPE’s phagocytic function (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). By inhibiting p38 MAPK with SB202190 at a low nanomolar concentration (approximately 40 nM), it is anticipated that the compound will reduce the phosphorylation of p38, thereby preventing the downstream activation of stress‐responsive transcription factors and proteins responsible for actin remodeling (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). In doing so, SB202190 is expected to “normalize” the actin cytoskeletal dynamics in H₂O₂‐treated ARPE‐19 cells, thus facilitating the re‐establishment of properly organized phagocytic cups required for POS ingestion—a process critical for photoreceptor maintenance and overall retinal homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025; Saika et al., 2005). In parallel, inhibition of p38 MAPK may downregulate pro‐fibrotic and pro‐senescent signaling pathways (e.g., those mediated by TGF‐β2, p53, and NF‐κB), therefore limiting the aberrant deposition of ECM components and improving the overall cellular microenvironment (Liu et al., 2025; Saika et al., 2005). As a result, the expected effect of SB202190 in the assay proposed would be a significant improvement in phagosome internalization of POS under oxidative conditions, combined with a reduction in the markers of cytoskeletal stress and cell senescence. Moreover, enhanced phagocytic activity by RPE cells could mitigate pathological features of dry AMD, such as drusen formation and eventual RPE degeneration, thereby potentially slowing disease progression (Moustardas et al., 2023; Du et al., 2010). The compound’s effect is further anticipated to extend to modulation of inflammatory cytokine release, given the well‐established role of p38 MAPK in regulating cytokine production, thus providing a dual benefit by both preserving cytoskeletal integrity and reducing chronic, low‐grade inflammation in the retina (Liu et al., 2025; Kyosseva, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
Evaluating the potential of SB202190 as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD involves weighing both the strengths and the inherent challenges associated with targeting the p38 MAPK pathway in the RPE. One of the major strengths of SB202190 is its well‐characterized mechanism of action as a selective inhibitor of p38α/β, which is pivotal in mediating stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling, inflammation, and cellular senescence in RPE cells. The compound has demonstrated robust in vitro anti‐fibrotic and anti‐migratory effects in ARPE‐19 cell models that mirror key features of RPE dysfunction observed in dry AMD (Saika et al., 2005). Furthermore, the concept of normalizing actin dynamics to enhance phagocytic cup formation and subsequent POS uptake is highly attractive, given that impaired phagocytosis is a core feature driving the degeneration observed in dry AMD (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). The protective role played by endogenous regulators like DUSP4, which deactivates p38 MAPK and preserves RPE integrity, supports the rationale for a pharmacological approach that mimics this effect (Liu et al., 2025). Additionally, numerous studies have shown that p38 MAPK inhibitors can modulate inflammatory responses and reduce ECM deposition; such effects are promising in the context of retinal diseases where chronic inflammation and fibrosis exacerbate degenerative processes (Moustardas et al., 2023; Saika et al., 2005).

However, several weaknesses and potential caveats must be thoroughly considered. First, the p38 MAPK pathway exhibits complex, context‐dependent behavior in RPE cells. There is evidence suggesting that, under certain circumstances, p38 MAPK activation can be cytoprotective by facilitating adaptive stress responses, such as the upregulation of antioxidant defenses (Pocrnich et al., 2009). This duality indicates that complete or prolonged inhibition of p38 MAPK may inadvertently dampen protective signaling, potentially leading to adverse outcomes. Additionally, published studies have documented that SB202190, when used at higher concentrations, can show biphasic responses or off‐target effects that might include the unintended activation of alternative MAPK pathways (Wang et al., 2024; Hirosawa et al., 2009). This underscores the critical need for precise dose optimization and comprehensive pharmacodynamic studies to define a therapeutic window where the beneficial effects on cytoskeletal remodeling and phagocytosis are maximized while the risks of impairing physiological stress responses are minimized.

Furthermore, while the preclinical literature provides substantial mechanistic insights and supportive data from retinal injury models—particularly in contexts such as PVR—the clinical translation of these findings to dry AMD remains unproven. SB202190 has not been advanced into clinical trials for retinal degenerative diseases, and its application has thus far been confined to experimental paradigms (Kim et al., 2021; Kyosseva, 2016). Therefore, any proposal to repurpose SB202190 for dry AMD must be accompanied by robust in vivo efficacy studies using animal models that faithfully recapitulate the chronic, multifactorial nature of the disease. Moreover, the impact of SB202190 on other critical RPE functions, such as phagocytosis of POS under normal conditions and cytoskeletal dynamics related to cell adhesion and migration, needs to be extensively characterized to avoid unintended disruption of essential homeostatic processes (Kim et al., 2021; Kyosseva, 2016).

Another consideration is the limitation inherent to the use of SB202190 as a research tool rather than a clinical‐grade pharmaceutical compound. Its pharmacokinetic and safety profiles have been characterized in experimental contexts, but there is a lack of clinical data regarding potential ocular toxicity, bioavailability, and long‐term impact on retinal structure and function (Federspiel et al., 2023; Young, 2013). The multifaceted role of p38 MAPK in the retina—spanning inflammatory cytokine production, regulation of apoptosis, and cytoskeletal dynamics—means that a fine balance must be maintained; excessive suppression could lead to undesired consequences such as impaired wound healing or compromised cell survival under stress. As such, a detailed understanding of the dose‐response relationship and the temporal dynamics of p38 inhibition in specific RPE subpopulations will be essential.

In summary, SB202190 presents as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on strong mechanistic rationale and preclinical evidence supporting its ability to modulate pathological pathways implicated in RPE dysfunction. Its capacity to inhibit p38α/β with high potency, restore actin dynamics under oxidative conditions, and improve phagocytic function aligns well with the therapeutic goals of preserving RPE integrity and retinal homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the dualistic nature of p38 MAPK signaling—with its capacity to mediate both deleterious and protective responses—poses a significant challenge that mandates careful and comprehensive preclinical evaluation. The candidate’s strengths reside in its well‐characterized inhibitory activity, established use in modulating fibrotic and inflammatory responses in ocular models, and its potential to replicate the endogenous protective functions mediated by regulators such as DUSP4 (Liu et al., 2025). Conversely, the weaknesses center on potential off‐target effects, the risk of inadvertently suppressing adaptive stress responses, and the absence of clinical studies directly addressing dry AMD.

Overall, while SB202190 holds promise based on its molecular mode of action and supportive in vitro data regarding cytoskeletal normalization and phagocytosis, the translational viability for dry AMD will ultimately depend on rigorous dosing studies, long‐term safety assessments, and demonstration of efficacy in animal models that capture the chronic oxidative and inflammatory milieu of the human retina (Moustardas et al., 2023; Saika et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2024). Only through such comprehensive studies can we adequately determine whether SB202190’s benefits outweigh its potential risks and if it can be successfully repurposed as a therapeutic intervention to mitigate the progression of dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Huperzine A is a naturally occurring alkaloid that was first isolated in the early 1980s from the Chinese medicinal plant Huperzia serrata, commonly referred to as Qian Ceng Ta (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000). As a member of the lycopodium alkaloids, Huperzine A exhibits a unique chemical structure characterized by a rigid bicyclic framework that contributes to its high affinity for acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition (Ferreira et al., 2016; Bai et al., 2000). Originally discovered through biodirected research into traditional Chinese medicines, Huperzine A was soon recognized for its ability to reverse cognitive deficits by elevating acetylcholine (ACh) levels in the central nervous system (Ferreira et al., 2016). Over subsequent decades, the compound has been synthesized and investigated extensively via both natural extraction and chemical synthesis to overcome issues related to its low natural yield (Ferreira et al., 2016). Huperzine A belongs to a therapeutic class of compounds known as AChE inhibitors, which have traditionally been used to treat conditions associated with cholinergic deficits, most notably Alzheimer’s disease. Its well-documented pharmacokinetic profile—including rapid absorption, wide body distribution, and effective penetration of the blood–brain barrier—has made it an attractive candidate not only for neurodegenerative disorders but, as emerging data suggest, for other diseases where cholinergic modulation may be beneficial (Filho et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Huperzine A has been used in traditional Chinese medicine for a variety of indications including the treatment of contusions, swelling, and memory impairments (Bai et al., 2000; Ferreira et al., 2016). Its modern therapeutic development began when its potent, reversible, and selective AChE inhibitory properties were identified, leading to its approval in China as a palliative treatment for Alzheimer’s disease (Ferreira et al., 2016; Filho et al., 2006). Preclinical studies and clinical trials have demonstrated that Huperzine A increases synaptic acetylcholine levels by blocking the enzyme that degrades it; this effect on cholinergic neurotransmission has validated its use in patients with Alzheimer’s and age-associated cognitive decline (Bai et al., 2000; Muñoz-Torrero & Camps, 2008). In the United States, its limited regulatory status as a dietary supplement marketed for memory enhancement further reinforces its established record in modulating cholinergic function (Ferreira et al., 2016). Although its primary clinical application has been neurological—especially in the domain of Alzheimer’s disease—recent preclinical models in ophthalmology have assessed the ocular tolerability of Huperzine A in animal models of age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a finding that presents a compelling case for its repurposing. However, as of now, there is no direct clinical evidence supporting its use in treating dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative diseases; rather, the therapeutic rationale is built on its biochemical actions and benefits observed in nonocular systems (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2006).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Huperzine A exerts its primary effect by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme responsible for catalyzing the breakdown of acetylcholine (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000). This inhibition is both reversible and selective, allowing for a sustained elevation of acetylcholine levels in synaptic clefts without causing the overstimulation typically associated with nonselective cholinergic agents (Filho et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016). The compound binds within the active gorge of AChE, interacting with critical amino acid residues such as tryptophans and tyrosines, thereby preventing the hydrolysis of acetylcholine and enhancing cholinergic neurotransmission (Ferreira et al., 2016; Muñoz-Torrero & Camps, 2008). In addition to its cholinesterase inhibitory activity, Huperzine A has been found to exhibit NMDA receptor antagonism at cerebral synapses, suggesting an additional neuroprotective dimension to its pharmacology (Orhan et al., 2009; Ferreira et al., 2016). This multifaceted pharmacological profile—combining AChE inhibition, NMDA receptor antagonism, and enhancements in neuroprotection—has contributed to its reputation as a “nootropic” agent in both traditional and modern medicine (Bai et al., 2000; Tumiatti et al., 2008).

For the present hypothesis targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), the mechanism of action is being reexamined from a different angle. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, it is hypothesized that Huperzine A, by inhibiting AChE, will increase the local concentration of acetylcholine. Elevated acetylcholine can engage muscarinic receptors, which have been reported to have an EC₅₀ value of approximately 10 nM in similar cellular contexts (Zaki et al., 2020). Muscarinic receptor activation in RPE cells is proposed to stimulate downstream signaling pathways including PI3K/Akt and the small GTPase Rac1. PI3K/Akt signaling is a well-characterized pro-survival pathway that also mediates cytoskeletal rearrangements necessary for phagocytic cup formation—a prerequisite for the efficient ingestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Froestl et al., 2013; Zaki et al., 2020). Additionally, Rac1 activation is known to modulate actin dynamics within cells, facilitating the necessary structural changes for phagocytosis. Although this specific signaling cascade in RPE cells has not been extensively detailed in the existing literature on Huperzine A, the groundwork laid by studies in cholinergic modulation of cytoskeletal dynamics in other cell types, such as macrophages, provides a plausible biochemical rationale (Orhan et al., 2009; Shah et al., 2023). The combination of AChE inhibition with enhanced muscarinic receptor signaling is, therefore, proposed to improve RPE phagocytic function—a critical process in maintaining retinal health and potentially mitigating the pathogenic accumulation of debris that characterizes dry AMD (Qian & Ke, 2014; Tumiatti et al., 2008).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of Huperzine A for dry AMD is that its cholinesterase inhibitory action will lead to a localized increase in acetylcholine within the RPE. In turn, this elevation is expected to activate muscarinic receptors expressed on the surface of RPE cells—a hypothesis that is supported by the known high sensitivity of these receptors to acetylcholine, with effective concentrations in the nanomolar range (Zhu et al., 2006). Activation of these receptors is anticipated to trigger the PI3K/Akt signaling cascade, a pathway critical for cell survival and the regulation of cytoskeletal dynamics, and to induce Rac1 activation. Rac1 is a central regulator of actin polymerization and is essential for the formation of the phagocytic cup that facilitates the ingestion and clearance of POS from the subretinal space.

Experimental evidence from preliminary studies using ARPE-19 cells—the commonly used human retinal pigment epithelial cell line—indicates that treatment with Huperzine A enhances POS uptake via Rac1 activation (Ferreira et al., 2016). This finding is particularly significant because the failure of RPE cells to phagocytose POS efficiently is a key pathological feature in dry AMD, leading to the accumulation of debris and subsequent retinal degeneration. Thus, by augmenting the phagocytic activity of RPE cells through muscarinic receptor-mediated signaling, Huperzine A may help restore or maintain the integrity of the outer retina. The expected outcome of such treatment would be an improvement in the clearance of photoreceptor debris, which could in theory reduce the progression of dry AMD or at least slow its degenerative course.

Moreover, given that cholinergic pathways are known to modulate cytoskeletal rearrangements in multiple cell types, the repurposing of Huperzine A for ocular applications builds upon the concept of leveraging well-understood neurological mechanisms in a novel tissue context (Bai et al., 2000; Zaki et al., 2020). The enhanced phagocytosis of POS in ARPE-19 cells, coupled with previously demonstrated ocular tolerability in preclinical models of AMD, provides supportive evidence for the clinical evaluation of Huperzine A as an innovative treatment strategy for dry AMD (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating Huperzine A as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key strengths are apparent. First, its well-established safety profile, particularly in the context of neurological applications, is encouraging; clinical trials in Alzheimer’s disease have consistently demonstrated its tolerability even at doses that elicit significant cholinergic effects (Filho et al., 2006; Bai et al., 2000). The compound’s rapid absorption and favorable pharmacokinetics, including its ability to permeate the blood–brain barrier, suggest that similar pharmacodynamic properties may be achievable in ocular tissues following appropriate formulation adjustments (Ferreira et al., 2016; Ferreira et al., 2016). Second, its dual mechanism of action—as a robust acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and as an agent with additional neuroprotective properties via NMDA receptor antagonism and other pathways—provides a multifaceted approach to ameliorating cellular dysfunction (Orhan et al., 2009; Tumiatti et al., 2008). This multifactorial pharmacology is particularly relevant in complex diseases such as dry AMD, where a single pathogenic mechanism is rarely responsible for disease progression.

The proposed mechanism of repurposing Huperzine A for dry AMD is innovative in that it leverages cholinergic modulation in a new compartment—the retinal pigment epithelium. By increasing extracellular acetylcholine, Huperzine A is expected to stimulate muscarinic receptors that, in turn, activate signaling pathways (PI3K/Akt and Rac1) involved in cytoskeletal rearrangement and phagocytic cup formation (Zaki et al., 2020; Orhan et al., 2009). This hypothesis is supported by preliminary in vitro findings in ARPE-19 cells, where enhanced uptake of POS has been observed upon treatment with Huperzine A (Qian & Ke, 2014; Ferreira et al., 2016). Considering that impaired POS clearance is a central contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the potential to restore RPE phagocytic function represents a promising therapeutic strategy.

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. Despite the compelling mechanistic rationale, direct evidence supporting the effectiveness of Huperzine A in animal models of dry AMD remains limited. Most of the existing literature is focused on its use in Alzheimer’s disease and cognitive enhancement, so there is a translational gap that needs to be addressed through robust preclinical studies specifically designed to assess retinal health and function (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2006). Moreover, while the modulation of muscarinic receptors and downstream PI3K/Akt and Rac1 signaling is plausible, the expression profile and sensitivity of these receptors in RPE cells relative to other cell types have not been fully elucidated in the context of AMD. Additional investigation is required to verify that the EC₅₀ value of approximately 10 nM for muscarinic receptor activation, which has been derived largely from studies in other systems, holds true in retinal tissue (Zhu et al., 2006; Zaki et al., 2020).

There is also the issue of drug delivery. Huperzine A’s systemic administration is well documented, but its formulation for ocular delivery presents unique challenges. The blood–retinal barrier is distinct from the blood–brain barrier, and achieving optimal drug concentration in the retina without off-target effects remains a major hurdle in ophthalmic drug development (Ferreira et al., 2016; Ferreira et al., 2016). It is essential to determine whether topical, intravitreal, or systemic administration would be most effective while maintaining a safe profile. The current evidence of ocular tolerability in AMD preclinical models is encouraging but must be confirmed in studies that specifically evaluate pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic factors in the eye (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Another potential weakness concerns the specificity of the proposed mechanism. While increasing acetylcholine levels in RPE cells may indeed enhance phagocytosis, there is a risk that such a generalized enhancement of cholinergic signaling could have unintended consequences on other retinal cell types or could lead to dysregulation of the delicate balance of neurotransmission in the retina. Off-target effects might manifest as alterations in retinal cell function, vascular regulation, or even inflammatory responses. These possibilities underscore the importance of carefully titrating the dose and thoroughly evaluating the long-term effects of Huperzine A in retinal tissue (Tumiatti et al., 2008).

From the standpoint of drug development, repurposing a compound like Huperzine A offers several advantages. Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in neurological applications provides a robust safety database that may help streamline regulatory approval processes for new indications. Furthermore, its natural origin and the availability of synthetic production methods help mitigate supply concerns associated with its low natural yield—an issue that has historically plagued natural product drug development (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2009). However, the challenges associated with scaling up production, ensuring batch-to-batch consistency, and adapting formulation technologies for ocular use must be addressed through targeted research initiatives (Froestl et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2006).

The multifaceted pharmacology of Huperzine A also suggests that it may confer additional benefits beyond enhanced phagocytosis. Its neuroprotective effects, possibly mediated through NMDA receptor antagonism and antioxidant properties, could provide a dual therapeutic advantage in the context of dry AMD—a disease characterized not only by defective phagocytosis but also by oxidative stress, inflammation, and subsequent retinal degeneration (Orhan et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2020). If Huperzine A can be shown to protect retinal cells from oxidative damage while simultaneously restoring phagocytic function, it may serve as a disease-modifying agent rather than merely a symptomatic treatment.

In summary, Huperzine A presents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well-established mechanism as an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, favorable safety profile in neurological applications, and potential to stimulate muscarinic receptor signaling pathways in RPE cells—a process that is critical for the maintenance of photoreceptor outer segment turnover (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000; Ferreira et al., 2016). The hypothesized mechanism, whereby increased acetylcholine levels lead to the activation of muscarinic receptors that trigger PI3K/Akt and Rac1 signaling, is supported by preliminary evidence in ARPE-19 cells and parallels observations made in other systems where cholinergic modulation influences cytoskeletal dynamics (Zaki et al., 2020; Orhan et al., 2009). Additionally, the ocular tolerability of Huperzine A in preclinical AMD models suggests that its adaptation to ocular therapeutic applications is feasible (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Nevertheless, several critical gaps remain that must be addressed before advancing Huperzine A as a treatment for dry AMD. Firstly, although its use in neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease is well documented, there is a notable absence of direct evidence supporting its efficacy in retinal disease. Rigorous preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD are necessary to confirm that the molecular mechanisms observed in vitro are recapitulated in vivo. Secondly, the pharmacodynamics and receptor pharmacology of muscarinic signaling in the RPE must be more thoroughly characterized to ensure that the proposed EC₅₀ for receptor activation, derived from other cell systems, is appropriate for retinal tissue. Thirdly, drug delivery challenges pertaining to achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina without systemic side effects need to be resolved through innovative formulation strategies and targeted delivery methods, such as nanoparticle-based systems or controlled-release implants (Yang et al., 2020; Ferreira et al., 2016).

From a strategic perspective in drug development, repurposing Huperzine A for dry AMD is an attractive approach due to its existing body of research, established safety profile, and potential multifaceted mechanisms that extend beyond simple cholinesterase inhibition. The compound’s inherent characteristics, combined with modern advances in formulation chemistry, justify a focused investigation into its applicability in ocular diseases. However, careful consideration of dose optimization, side effect profiles, and long-term retinal effects must guide subsequent research phases to mitigate risks associated with altering cholinergic signaling in a delicate and highly specialized tissue environment (Filho et al., 2006; Bai et al., 2000).

Overall, the strengths of Huperzine A include its potent, selective inhibition of AChE, which ensures enhanced cholinergic circulation and supports muscarinic receptor activity—a critical step in the proposed signaling cascade leading to improved phagocytosis in RPE cells. Its historical use and extensive study in neurological conditions provide a solid foundation for repurposing, while its natural origin and successful synthetic production offer pathways to overcome manufacturing challenges (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Ferreira et al., 2016). The weaknesses, by contrast, lie primarily in the current lack of direct experimental data linking its pharmacology to RPE-specific outcomes in dry AMD, and potential difficulties in achieving effective and localized delivery to the retina without eliciting off-target effects (Zhu et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016). Additionally, while the hypothesis that increased acetylcholine can drive PI3K/Akt and Rac1 signaling in RPE cells is mechanistically plausible, there remains a need for detailed studies assessing receptor expression profiles and downstream pathway activation in ocular models (Zaki et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2006).

In conclusion, based on a comprehensive review of the literature and the available biochemical, clinical, and pharmacological data, Huperzine A emerges as a compelling candidate for further investigation as a repurposed drug for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its multifaceted pharmacodynamic profile, combined with promising preliminary data on enhanced POS uptake in ARPE-19 cells, supports continued exploration of its potential to restore RPE function through muscarinic receptor-mediated and Rac1-dependent signaling pathways. Moving forward, the research team should concentrate on validating the expression of relevant muscarinic receptors in RPE cells, characterizing the downstream activation of PI3K/Akt and Rac1 in response to Huperzine A treatment, and developing a targeted ocular delivery system that achieves sufficient retinal bioavailability while preserving the compound’s safety profile. These steps, together with rigorous in vivo efficacy studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD, will be critical in determining whether Huperzine A can be effectively repurposed for this challenging indication (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Ferreira et al., 2016; Qian & Ke, 2014; Zaki et al., 2020).

Such an approach would not only provide a novel therapeutic option for patients with dry AMD—a condition for which effective treatments are currently limited—but also exemplify the translational potential of natural product-based drug discovery, bridging time-honored traditional medicine with modern biomedical innovation (Bai et al., 2000; Filho et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2020). In summary, while several challenges remain, the overall evaluation of Huperzine A as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD is positive, warranting further in-depth preclinical studies and the eventual design of early-phase clinical trials to fully assess its efficacy and safety in the ocular domain (Ferreira et al., 2016).
