Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Apelin-13 is an endogenous peptide derived from the apelin gene product and is one of several bioactive fragments generated from a larger 77–amino acid preproapelin precursor. Initially discovered in bovine stomach extracts by Tatemoto and colleagues in 1998 (Davenport et al., 2019), apelin peptides belong to a class of naturally occurring vasoactive peptide hormones that activate the apelin receptor (APJ), a G protein–coupled receptor. The peptide is synthesized naturally in various tissues, including the central nervous system, heart, and retina, and undergoes posttranslational processing to yield distinct isoforms such as apelin-36, apelin-17, and the shorter apelin-13. The focus on apelin-13 is due in part to structure–activity relationship studies that have identified a core pharmacophoric region, including a critical C-terminal phenylalanine residue, that is essential for receptor activation (Davenport et al., 2019). Being a member of the bioactive peptide class, apelin-13 has been previously studied in cardiovascular, metabolic, and certain retinal contexts, with distinct advantages offered by its relatively small peptide size, which enables intravitreal delivery and minimizes immunogenicity. This candidate, available commercially (Bachem Cat. No. H-3705), represents a repurposing opportunity that leverages its endogenous origin, excellent receptor specificity, and established ability to modulate intracellular signaling cascades relevant for cellular homeostasis in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Davenport et al., 2019; Enders, 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, apelin peptides have been primarily explored for their cardiovascular and metabolic effects. In cardiovascular studies, apelin-13 has been shown to exert potent inotropic and vasodilatory responses, reduce cardiac fibrosis, and improve cardiac output in heart failure models, thus demonstrating its multifunctional role as an endogenous regulator in the cardiovascular system (Davenport et al., 2019). In metabolic research, apelin has been documented to influence insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism, while also functioning as an adipokine, linking it to obesity-related pathways (Davenport et al., 2019). Within the context of ophthalmology, several preclinical studies have investigated the role of apelin peptides, particularly apelin-13, in retinal disease models. Notably, apelin-13 has been demonstrated to promote proliferation, migration, and enhanced expression of cytoskeletal and tight junction proteins in human RPE cells, mediated through activation of the PI3K/Akt and MAPK/Erk signaling pathways (Li et al., 2017). Though most clinical and preclinical research in retinal settings has predominantly focused on diabetic retinopathy and related retinal vascular pathologies, where apelin expression is altered and exogenous supplementation can restore normal cellular function (Li et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018), there is emerging interest in extrapolating these findings to other conditions of RPE dysfunction. Dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) is characterized by impaired RPE phagocytosis and accumulation of toxic photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris, making it plausible that a drug candidate capable of enhancing RPE phagocytosis could benefit these patients. Although direct studies evaluating apelin-13 in dry AMD are limited, its demonstrated ability to improve RPE cell survival and actin dynamics under stress conditions in vitro presents a compelling rationale for repurposing (Li et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism underlying the therapeutic potential of apelin-13 centers on its binding to the APJ receptor, which is robustly expressed in RPE cells and other retinal cell types. Upon receptor engagement, apelin-13 activates downstream G protein–mediated signaling cascades, notably the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt pathway and the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK)/Erk pathway (Li et al., 2017; Chiang et al., 2017). Activation of PI3K/Akt signaling is of particular interest because it plays a critical role in the regulation of actin cytoskeletal reorganization—a process essential for the formation of phagocytic cups required for the internalization of POS. This pathway additionally modulates intracellular trafficking events that culminate in improved clearance of outer segment debris by RPE cells (Chiang et al., 2017). Biochemical investigations reveal that pharmacological inhibition of PI3K or downstream Akt phosphorylation dramatically reduces RPE phagocytosis, underscoring the necessity of this signaling module in maintaining RPE homeostasis (Chiang et al., 2017). Moreover, apelin-13’s EC₅₀ in stimulating PI3K/Akt signaling in RPE cells is reported to be approximately 0.5 nM, suggesting high potency in activating this pathway (Li et al., 2017). In the context of oxidative stress, which is heavily implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis, activation of PI3K/Akt also confers cytoprotective effects by enhancing cell survival pathways and promoting anti-apoptotic signaling. Structural evidence and receptor–ligand interaction studies further validate that apelin-13 engages critical residues at the receptor interface, leading to effective downstream signal transduction that may drive cytoskeletal remodeling and facilitate phagosome maturation and trafficking (Davenport et al., 2019). Thus, apelin-13’s mode of action is characterized by its dual ability to stimulate RPE phagocytic function while concurrently enhancing cell survival under stress conditions.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed therapeutic hypothesis for apelin-13 in dry AMD hinges on its capacity to enhance RPE function by activating the APJ receptor and triggering PI3K/Akt signaling. In an assay designed to evaluate phagocytosis of POS, administration of apelin-13 is expected to increase the internalization and subsequent clearance of shed POS by RPE cells. This response is anticipated to result from enhanced actin reorganization and improved phagosome trafficking, driven by the activation of PI3K/Akt signaling—a pathway that is well known to be essential for cytoskeletal dynamics during phagocytosis (Chiang et al., 2017). In vitro, human RPE cell studies have shown that apelin-13 treatment leads to increased expression of cytoskeletal proteins and tight junction proteins, which are integral to maintaining the cellular architecture necessary for effective phagocytic activity (Li et al., 2017). Additionally, because dry AMD involves an accumulation of lipofuscin and impaired clearance of degradative byproducts from POS, enhancing this clearance mechanism could prevent or slow the progression of RPE dysfunction. Given the reported EC₅₀ near 0.5 nM for activation of PI3K/Akt signaling in RPE cells by apelin-13, the anticipated effect in vivo would be a dose-dependent improvement in phagocytosis that could translate to preservation of RPE integrity and retinal function. Furthermore, since apelin-13 has been described as having a favorable safety profile in other ocular studies—including those addressing glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy—there is strong support for the feasibility of intravitreal application, which is a standard mode of delivery in the treatment of many retinal diseases (Lu et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017). The expected outcome is not only an enhancement of POS clearance but also overall improvement in RPE cell survival under chronic oxidative stress conditions, a critical component in the pathogenesis of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Apelin-13 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on its endogenous nature, well-characterized mechanism of action, and preclinical evidence supporting its beneficial effects on RPE cellular functions. One significant strength of this candidate is its high potency in activating the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway in RPE cells, a pathway that is crucial for cytoskeletal remodeling and phagocytosis of POS (Chiang et al., 2017). The safety profile of apelin-13, as established by studies involving intravitreal injection in various retinal models, further supports its potential, especially given the routine use of intravitreal therapies in ophthalmology (Lu et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017). In addition, the dual action of apelin-13—promoting both phagocytic clearance and cell survival under oxidative stress—addresses two primary pathological features of dry AMD: accumulation of toxic debris and RPE cell degeneration.

However, there are challenges and weaknesses to consider. Most of the existing data on apelin-13 in ocular applications come from models of diabetic retinopathy rather than from direct studies in dry AMD. While the underlying mechanisms of impaired phagocytosis and oxidative stress are common to both conditions, the pathology of dry AMD is multifactorial and includes additional components such as complement dysregulation and chronic inflammation, which may not be directly addressed by apelin-13 therapy (Li et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017). Furthermore, the biphasic nature of Akt involvement in phagocytosis—as evidenced by studies showing variable effects at early versus later time points—underscores the complexity of modulating this pathway therapeutically (Chiang et al., 2017). There is also a potential for unwanted off-target effects if apelin-13 were to inadvertently stimulate angiogenic pathways under certain conditions; however, given that dry AMD is characterized by atrophic rather than neovascular pathology, careful dosing and patient selection could mitigate such risks (Wu et al., 2017). Finally, while intravitreal delivery is a proven route for ocular therapies, peptide-based drugs often face challenges related to stability, degradation, and the need for repeated dosing, which may necessitate formulation modifications such as PEGylation or cyclization to prolong half-life (Davenport et al., 2019).

In conclusion, the overall evaluation of apelin-13 as a candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. The strong mechanistic rationale—centered on the activation of the APJ receptor and subsequent PI3K/Akt signaling to improve cytoskeletal remodeling and POS clearance—coupled with existing evidence in retinal models, supports further investigation. Preclinical studies specifically tailored to dry AMD models are warranted, including evaluations of efficacy in improving RPE phagocytosis, protection against oxidative stress, and overall retinal function. Additionally, pharmacokinetic and formulation studies should be conducted to optimize intravitreal delivery and stability. If these studies confirm target engagement and therapeutic benefit, apelin-13 could offer a novel approach for restoring RPE function and slowing the progression of dry AMD, thereby addressing an unmet clinical need in a field where current therapeutic options remain limited (Li et al., 2017; Chiang et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
D609, chemically known as tricyclodecan-9-yl xanthogenate, is a synthetic small‐molecule compound belonging to the xanthate class. It was originally synthesized through classical organic‐chemical methods involving the reaction of diastereomeric tricyclic alcohols with carbon disulfide in the presence of a strong base such as potassium tert‐butoxide, yielding a mixture of eight stereoisomers due to its three asymmetric centers (Bhat et al., 2022; Eurtivong et al., 2023). As a member of the xanthate family, D609 has been extensively studied for its diverse biological activities that include antiviral, antitumoral, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective effects (Bhat et al., 2022). Its mechanism of competitive inhibition of phosphatidylcholine-specific phospholipase C (PC-PLC) was discovered during the evaluation of lipid signaling pathways, and it is commercially available (for example, Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. D0209) as a research-grade compound (Wang et al., 2020). This chemical class has traditionally been investigated in various biomedical contexts, with early work focusing on its antiviral properties dating back to the 1980s and subsequent studies extending its uses into oncology and neurology (Bhat et al., 2022). Its water solubility and relatively low molecular weight make it an attractive candidate for repurposing into ocular applications where intracellular signaling and oxidative stress play key roles.

Therapeutic History:  
D609 has been the subject of more than 700 published reports over the last three decades and has been explored in preclinical studies ranging from antiviral and anticancer applications to neuroprotection and inflammation modulation (Bhat et al., 2022). One of the most compelling lines of evidence for repurposing D609 concerns its potential in treating ocular conditions, particularly dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In several studies, D609 has been directly evaluated for its ability to protect retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) cells from oxidative damage using in vitro cell models such as the widely used ARPE-19 cell line and primary human RPE cells (Wang et al., 2020). For instance, one study employing a high-content screening strategy on 814 protective compounds identified D609 as a lead candidate that maintained RPE cell viability above 95% under severe oxidative stress induced by sodium iodate—a condition used to model dry AMD (Wang et al., 2020). Furthermore, in vivo animal models, including sodium iodate-induced AMD mouse models, have confirmed that D609 can protect the RPE layer, preserve retinal structure and function, and prevent geographic atrophy—findings that underscore its translational potential for dry AMD therapy (Wang et al., 2020). Outside the field of ophthalmology, D609 has been evaluated in oncology, where it affected cell proliferation and induced apoptosis in certain tumor cell lines, and in neuroscience for its neuroprotective effects against amyloid-beta toxicity and oxidative stress in neuronal cultures (Bhat et al., 2022). Although no clinical trials have yet been reported that specifically target dry AMD with D609, the preclinical data generated in ocular, cancer, and neurodegenerative studies provide a robust therapeutic history that supports depth of investigation into its ocular application (Wang et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At its core, D609 is a competitive inhibitor of PC-PLC. PC-PLC is an enzyme that hydrolyzes phosphatidylcholine (PC) into phosphorylcholine and diacylglycerol (DAG). In RPE cells, overactivation of this enzyme under oxidative stress conditions may lead to excessive DAG production that, in turn, drives hyperactivation of protein kinase C (PKC) and downstream signaling events deleteriously affecting cytoskeletal dynamics and phagocytosis (Wang et al., 2020). D609 exerts its inhibitory activity by mimicking parts of the natural substrate, competitively binding to the active site of PC-PLC—in part through its dithiocarbonate group, which can chelate zinc ions that are critical for enzyme function (Wang et al., 2020; González-Roura et al., 2002). In addition to its direct inhibition of PC-PLC, D609 has been reported to exert antioxidative effects indirectly via upregulation of metallothionein proteins—an antioxidative protein family that plays a protective role against reactive oxygen species (ROS) and metal-induced damage (Wang et al., 2020). This dual mechanism—direct enzyme inhibition and indirect antioxidant protection—suggests that D609 may help stabilize the lipid signaling environment of the RPE, normalizing DAG levels and mitigating PKC-mediated perturbations in actin cytoskeletal dynamics that are essential for the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Wang et al., 2020). Some studies even propose that the beneficial effects observed in RPE cells may derive more from the metallothionein upregulation than from pure PC-PLC inhibition, raising the possibility that D609’s mode of action is multifactorial rather than strictly enzyme-targeted (Wang et al., 2020). However, in the context of the current hypothesis—where the goal is to inhibit the DAG-PKC axis to restore cytoskeletal dynamics and phagocytosis—the competitive inhibition of PC-PLC by D609 remains a key molecular mechanism (Bhat et al., 2022). It should be noted that D609 is not entirely selective; it also inhibits other enzymes in lipid metabolism such as sphingomyelin synthase (SMS) and possibly phospholipase D (PLD), which could contribute to both its therapeutic efficacy and its off-target effects (Eurtivong et al., 2023; González-Roura et al., 2002). The working hypothesis for repurposing D609 for dry AMD is that its inhibition of PC-PLC in RPE cells will lead to reduced DAG formation, thereby limiting DAG-driven PKC hyperactivation. Treatment with D609 is hypothesized to counteract these effects by balancing the intracellular signaling milieu—specifically by reducing the aberrant activation of the DAG-PKC axis—and by promoting the antioxidant metallothionein pathway, which further preserves cellular homeostasis (Wang et al., 2020). Expression of PC-PLC and related signaling components in RPE cells has been indirectly verified by the cellular responses observed upon oxidative challenge, and the reversal of these effects by D609 supports the notion that this enzyme is active and pathophysiologically relevant in RPE cells (Wang et al., 2020). D609 presents as an intriguing and promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly because of its ability to modulate lipid signaling pathways that are disrupted by oxidative stress and contribute to RPE dysfunction. First, D609 is a non-selective inhibitor; while it effectively targets PC-PLC, it also inhibits other enzymes such as sphingomyelin synthase and phospholipase D, which may introduce off-target effects that could complicate its clinical use (Eurtivong et al., 2023; González-Roura et al., 2002). This mechanistic ambiguity, while not diminishing the overall therapeutic promise, suggests that future studies should incorporate detailed pathway analyses to dissect the relative contributions of each mechanism.

In summary, D609 is well supported by preclinical evidence as a compound that can protect RPE cells from oxidative damage and has potential applications in dry AMD therapy (Wang et al., 2020). Its established safety profile in ocular studies, combined with a mechanistic basis that addresses both lipid signaling dysregulation and oxidative stress, offers significant advantages for repurposing in this context. Nonetheless, challenges related to off-target effects, stereochemical variability, and the need for high effective concentrations must be rigorously addressed in subsequent studies. Overall, D609 merits further investigative efforts in translational research focused on dry AMD, with particular emphasis on optimizing its pharmacodynamics, ensuring reproducible stereoisomeric composition, and validating its efficacy in restoring RPE phagocytic function under physiologically relevant oxidative stress conditions (Eurtivong et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2020).

The candidate under evaluation is an anti‐Tyro3 agonist monoclonal antibody (mAb), a protein‐based therapeutic engineered to specifically bind and activate the Tyro3 receptor. Tyro3 is one of the three members of the TAM receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) family—comprising Tyro3, Axl, and MerTK—that modulate key cellular functions in different tissues. In the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), both MerTK and Tyro3 are expressed; however, MerTK is traditionally recognized as the primary driver of phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), while Tyro3 has emerged as a compensatory receptor with a crucial anti‐inflammatory signal in MerTK‐deficient settings (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Palczewska et al., 2016). This candidate antibody is presumed to be of research grade, synthesized using recombinant antibody technology. It is generated by isolating B cells that produce an antibody directed against the extracellular domain of Tyro3; through hybridoma technology or phage display methods, a specific mAb is cloned and further optimized for high binding affinity and agonistic activity with an effective concentration (EC₅₀) on the order of approximately 20 nM. Monoclonal antibodies, by virtue of their proteinaceous nature and high specificity, have long served as therapeutics in a wide range of indications including oncology, autoimmunity, and inflammatory diseases. In this particular case, the therapeutic candidate belongs to the class of receptor agonists rather than the more common inhibitory antibodies. Receptor agonist antibodies are designed to cross‐link target receptors, thereby inducing conformational changes that stimulate receptor dimerization and activation of downstream signaling cascades. Although the majority of previous antibody therapeutics have been developed as receptor antagonists to block signaling (as is often the case with oncogenic targets), the approach of receptor activation via agonist antibodies is emerging as a promising strategy in diseases where deficiency in receptor function contributes to pathology (Palczewska et al., 2016).  

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic use of monoclonal antibodies targeting the TAM RTK family has primarily been explored in oncology. In cancer, for example, anti‐TYRO3 antibodies have been predominantly investigated as inhibitors intended to block tumorigenic signaling pathways (Hsu et al., 2019). However, the narrative differs considerably when one considers ocular diseases such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). Dry AMD is characterized by RPE dysfunction, accumulation of photoreceptor debris, and a resultant chronic inflammatory milieu that drives retinal degeneration. Although MerTK is well documented as being critically involved in the phagocytosis of POS—with deficiencies in its function directly linked to retinal degeneration in models such as the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) rat—recent genetic and biochemical studies have indicated that Tyro3, despite historically receiving less attention than MerTK, can functionally compensate in aspects of anti‐inflammatory signaling when MerTK is absent (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Akalu et al., 2017). In MerTK‐deficient RPE cells, the compensatory actions of Tyro3 have been demonstrated to preserve anti‐inflammatory gene expression profiles and maintain retinal viability, suggesting the therapeutic potential of harnessing Tyro3 agonism to ameliorate inflammation‐mediated retinal degeneration in dry AMD (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Palczewska et al., 2016). Despite this promising genetic evidence, there is little precedent in the literature for the clinical or preclinical use of an anti‐Tyro3 agonist antibody explicitly for dry AMD or similar retinal diseases. The majority of TAM receptor–targeted therapeutic approaches developed to date have focused on receptor inhibition for cancer therapy (Hsu et al., 2019). As such, the repurposing of an agonist antibody against Tyro3 to enhance RPE phagocytosis represents a novel direction that capitalizes on emerging insights into compensatory TAM signaling in the retina (Lieffrig et al., 2023). While there are no reports of prior successful application of anti‐Tyro3 agonist antibodies in either clinical or veterinary practice specifically for dry AMD, the genetic suppression of photoreceptor degeneration in MerTK‐deficient models by Tyro3 signals a strong preclinical rationale worthy of further investigation (Akalu et al., 2017; Palczewska et al., 2016).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The proposed mechanism of action for the anti‐Tyro3 agonist antibody revolves around its ability to engage and activate Tyro3 in RPE cells where MerTK function is compromised. Under normal conditions, MerTK activation in RPE cells triggers a cascade of intracellular events that lead to phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor outer segments. This process is mediated by the recruitment of signaling molecules that activate regulators of the actin cytoskeleton, chiefly through pathways involving the small GTPase Rac1. Specifically, upon ligand binding, MerTK undergoes dimerization and trans‐autophosphorylation, generating docking sites for signal transduction proteins such as Vav and the p130Cas/CrkII/Dock180 complex; these effectors then catalyze Rac1 activation, which in turn promotes the actin polymerization necessary for the formation of phagocytic cups around POS (Kwon & Freeman, 2020). In the context of MerTK deficiency, however, RPE cells exhibit a marked disruption in phagocytosis, even though compensatory pathways involving Tyro3 are partially active. Experimental observations indicate that in mertk−/− RPE cells that retain Tyro3 expression, while anti‐inflammatory gene expression is preserved, the phagocytic uptake of POS remains severely impaired, suggesting that Tyro3’s natural activation level is suboptimal for driving effective phagocytosis under these conditions (Lieffrig et al., 2023).  

The agonist mAb candidate is designed to overcome this limitation by binding specifically to the extracellular domain of Tyro3 and triggering receptor activation through induced dimerization. This antibody binding is expected to mimic the natural ligand-induced conformational changes and stimulate the intracellular kinase activity of Tyro3. Upon receptor activation, Tyro3 should phosphorylate its own intracellular tyrosine residues, creating docking sites for various adaptor proteins that propagate downstream signaling cascades. Although the precise molecular details of Tyro3 signaling in RPE cells are not as well characterized as those for MerTK, it is anticipated that downstream effectors such as the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) and Rac1 will become activated. PI3K activation leads to the generation of phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP₃), which in turn recruits Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) to the plasma membrane, thereby catalyzing the conversion of Rac1 to its active GTP-bound form. Active Rac1 is critical for orchestrating rearrangements of the actin cytoskeleton, a key step in phagocytic cup formation and subsequent internalization of POS (Palczewska et al., 2016; Lieffrig et al., 2023).  

Furthermore, evidence suggests that Tyro3 signaling may be linked to the regulation of αvβ5 integrin, another receptor complex highly expressed in RPE cells that plays an important role during POS phagocytosis. In wild-type RPE cells, αvβ5 integrin engages with bridging molecules such as MFG-E8 to facilitate the physical attachment of POS to the RPE cell surface. Although MerTK is instrumental in transducing signals required for the downstream internalization process, it is the coordinated activity between MerTK and αvβ5 integrin that ensures a successful phagocytic event (Kwon & Freeman, 2020; Palczewska et al., 2016). The hypothesis underlying this therapeutic candidate is that, in the absence or dysfunction of MerTK, an agonist mAb stimulating Tyro3 can activate a compensatory signaling cascade that establishes convergence with αvβ5 integrin-mediated pathways. This cross-talk is believed to enhance Rac1 activation and promote cytoskeletal reorganization necessary for POS internalization even under compromised conditions (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Palczewska et al., 2016). In summary, the antibody-driven activation of Tyro3 is anticipated to increase intracellular PI3K and Rac1 signaling, consequently supporting not only anti-inflammatory responses but also promoting the assembly of phagocytic structures in MerTK-impaired RPE cells.  

Expected Effect:  
In the in vitro and in vivo assays proposed for dry AMD, the administration of the anti‐Tyro3 agonist mAb is expected to yield several beneficial effects on RPE cell function. First, by binding to and activating Tyro3, the antibody is anticipated to trigger a cascade of intracellular signals that primarily enhance the downstream activity of PI3K and Rac1, which are critical mediators in remodeling the actin cytoskeleton for phagocytosis (Palczewska et al., 2016; Lieffrig et al., 2023). Given that MerTK-deficient RPE cells have been shown to retain anti-inflammatory signaling via Tyro3 yet suffer from diminished phagocytic uptake of POS, the agonist is postulated to at least partially restore the phagocytic capacity. The expected increase in active Rac1 will promote pseudopod formation and stabilization of the phagocytic cup around bound photoreceptor debris, thereby facilitating the internalization process.  

Moreover, αvβ5 integrin complexes, which are essential for the initial binding of POS to the RPE surface, are expected to be functionally engaged in the presence of enhanced Tyro3 signaling. The hypothesized cross-regulation between Tyro3 and these integrin complexes should result in improved phagocytic efficiency. Recent experimental evidence suggests that wild-type RPE cells, which naturally co-express MerTK and Tyro3, maintain a robust anti-inflammatory gene expression profile and efficient POS clearance; conversely, in mertk−/− models, the intact expression of Tyro3 is sufficient to sustain retinal viability despite markedly impaired phagocytosis (Lieffrig et al., 2023). Thus, an anti‐Tyro3 agonist mAb could potentially tip the balance toward enhanced phagocytic performance in diseased states by elevating Tyro3 signaling from its basal compensatory level to one that more effectively drives phagocytosis.  

The proposed expected effect in the assay includes an increase in the phagocytic index of RPE cells, as measured by the uptake of fluorescently labeled POS, and a reduction in markers of retinal inflammation. In mechanistic experiments, activation of Tyro3 should correlate with increased phosphorylation levels of pivotal signaling intermediates such as PI3K and Akt, and a subsequent rise in GTP-bound Rac1 levels, which can be detected via pull-down assays. In addition, the impact on αvβ5 integrin function may be assessed by examining the recruitment of cytoskeletal adaptor proteins that have established roles in integrin-mediated phagocytosis. Furthermore, given that Tyro3’s activation may also support anti-inflammatory gene expression, treatment with the antibody might reduce levels of inflammatory cytokines in RPE cultures under oxidative or inflammatory stress conditions—conditions that mimic dry AMD pathogenesis (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Palczewska et al., 2016).  

It is important to note that although Tyro3 agonism is projected to enhance intracellular signaling events associated with phagocytosis, previous studies have indicated that in MerTK-deficient RPE cells the restoration of phagocytic function is only partially achievable through Tyro3 activation alone (Lieffrig et al., 2023). Therefore, while an increase in Rac1 and PI3K signaling levels is anticipated with the anti‐Tyro3 agonist, it might not fully recapitulate the robust phagocytic response observed in fully functional RPE cells. Nonetheless, the profound anti-inflammatory effects observed in Tyro3-expressing RPE cells could contribute to preserving retinal structure and function over time, thereby delaying the progression of dry AMD. In addition, gene expression studies have documented that Tyro3 is naturally expressed in the RPE, albeit at levels comparable to those in the rodent and human retina (Palczewska et al., 2016), thereby providing a cellular substrate for the agonist mAb to exert its effects.  

Overall Evaluation:  
In assessing the potential of an anti‐Tyro3 agonist antibody as a therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration, several points of strength and limitation emerge from the available literature.  

Strengths:  
One of the foremost strengths of this therapeutic candidate lies in its receptor specificity. Tyro3 is highly expressed in RPE cells and is demonstrated to participate in anti‐inflammatory signaling; importantly, genetic studies have revealed that Tyro3 acts as a suppressor of photoreceptor degeneration in MerTK-deficient models (Akalu et al., 2017; Palczewska et al., 2016). This genetic evidence suggests that enhancement of Tyro3 signaling could counteract some of the detrimental consequences associated with MerTK deficiency that are known to contribute to dry AMD pathology (Lieffrig et al., 2023). The approach leverages the inherent compensatory potential of Tyro3 and could offer an innovative strategy to bypass the limitations imposed by non-functional MerTK. Additionally, the design of an agonist mAb allows for targeted activation of the receptor, theoretically minimizing off-target effects that might occur with less specific small-molecule agonists. Given that monoclonal antibodies can be engineered to display high binding affinity (targeting an EC₅₀ in the vicinity of 20 nM) and long half-lives in situ, the intrinsic pharmacokinetic properties of an antibody therapeutic could be advantageous in the ocular environment, where sustained receptor activation may be necessary (Palczewska et al., 2016).  

Furthermore, the mechanism by which Tyro3 activation is proposed to enhance phagocytosis involves well-characterized intracellular cascades—including the PI3K and Rac1 signaling pathways—that are known to be essential for actin cytoskeleton reorganization and phagocytic cup formation (Palczewska et al., 2016; Lieffrig et al., 2023). The interplay between Tyro3 and αvβ5 integrin complexes represents an attractive target because αvβ5 integrin is already implicated in POS binding and is a critical component of the RPE’s phagocytic machinery (Kwon & Freeman, 2020). Thus, the strategy of boosting Tyro3 activity may not only revitalize phagocytic signaling in MerTK-impaired cells but could also reinforce the integrin-mediated aspects of the phagocytic process. These mechanistic attributes confer a rational basis for pursuing an agonist-based approach in dry AMD, a field where current treatment options remain largely palliative (Lieffrig et al., 2023).  

Weaknesses:  
On the other hand, there are several challenges and uncertainties that temper enthusiasm for the candidate. Notably, while Tyro3 activation has been demonstrated to preserve anti-inflammatory signaling in RPE cells, the literature consistently reports that phagocytosis remains significantly impaired in MerTK-deficient models even when Tyro3 is intact (Lieffrig et al., 2023). This suggests that although agonizing Tyro3 may mitigate inflammation—which is instrumental in curtailing further retinal damage—it does not necessarily normalize the essential phagocytic clearance of POS. Consequently, the anticipated improvement in phagocytosis through Tyro3 agonism might be only partial in nature, thereby limiting the therapeutic impact on a key aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis.  

Another major limitation stems from the fact that the detailed molecular mechanisms underlying Tyro3-specific signaling in the RPE remain less well characterized relative to MerTK. With much of the established research focusing on MerTK’s role in phagocytosis (Kwon & Freeman, 2020; Si et al., 2023), there exists a significant knowledge gap regarding the full spectrum of Tyro3’s downstream signaling cascades, potential cross-talk with αvβ5 integrin, and the modulatory control of Rac1/PI3K activity. This incomplete mechanistic understanding introduces uncertainties into how robustly Tyro3 agonism can be translated into effective POS internalization. In addition, the structural homology among the TAM receptors poses a potential challenge in developing antibodies that can selectively activate Tyro3 without unintended cross-reactivity with MerTK or Axl—a challenge that has been encountered in the development of TAM receptor inhibitors in oncology (Hsu et al., 2019; Myers et al., 2019).  

Furthermore, prior therapeutic approaches targeting TAM receptors in other disease areas have predominantly involved receptor inhibition rather than activation. In cancer, for example, the focus on developing inhibitors for TYRO3 has yielded several small molecule compounds and antibody-based antagonists (Hsu et al., 2019). The shift from inhibition to activation for therapeutic gain in dry AMD is conceptually innovative but also uncharted territory with limited preclinical validation. The delivery of antibody therapeutics to the retina presents additional hurdles, including issues related to ocular penetration, stability, and dosing regimen—factors that must be rigorously optimized in subsequent preclinical studies. Finally, while expression analyses confirm that Tyro3 is present in the retina and RPE, quantitative differences in receptor density between in vitro cell cultures and in vivo retinal tissue may influence the efficacy and dosing of the candidate mAb (Palczewska et al., 2016).  

Overall, the anti‐Tyro3 agonist antibody candidate presents a compelling and innovative therapeutic strategy for dry AMD by aiming to leverage Tyro3’s compensatory signaling capacity in the RPE to overcome deficits in MerTK. Its strengths lie in the high specificity of an agonist mAb approach, the solid genetic rationale provided by models showing retinal protection via Tyro3, and the potential to modulate key intracellular pathways such as PI3K and Rac1 that are essential for phagocytosis and anti-inflammatory responses (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Akalu et al., 2017). However, significant weaknesses remain, including the incomplete capacity of Tyro3 signaling to fully restore phagocytic activity in MerTK-deficient settings, the comparatively limited mechanistic insight into Tyro3’s actions in RPE cells, and the challenges associated with achieving high specificity among structurally similar TAM receptors. Moreover, whereas robust preclinical data exist supporting the concept of Tyro3 acting as a genetic suppressor of photoreceptor degeneration, the translation of these findings into a receptor-specific agonist antibody therapy for dry AMD is largely uncharted and will require extensive validation in both in vitro models and animal studies (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Palczewska et al., 2016).  

From an overall perspective, the candidate shows promise by addressing an unmet need in dry AMD, particularly through its potential to modulate inflammatory and phagocytic pathways compromised in the disease. The strategy of using receptor-specific agonism to bypass defects in MerTK signaling is innovative and supported by genetic evidence, yet its success hinges on the ability to induce sufficient downstream activation of PI3K/Rac1 and to engage integrin-mediated mechanisms to boost phagocytosis. Given that prior studies indicate that Tyro3 alone does not fully complement the loss of MerTK in terms of POS clearance—leading primarily to anti-inflammatory maintenance rather than complete phagocytic restoration—further studies are needed to determine whether antibody-mediated activation can overcome this limitation or whether combination therapies might be warranted (Lieffrig et al., 2023).  

In conclusion, while the anti‐Tyro3 agonist antibody candidate is built upon a robust scientific hypothesis with promising preclinical genetic support, its therapeutic viability for dry AMD will depend on resolving several key issues: confirming that elevated Tyro3 signaling can indeed significantly enhance POS phagocytosis, ensuring that the designed antibody is both highly selective and potent in the complex ocular environment, and establishing favorable pharmacokinetic and safety profiles in relevant preclinical models. The current body of evidence indicates that Tyro3 can partially compensate for MerTK deficiency in terms of anti-inflammatory signaling and retinal preservation, which bodes well for its potential application in dry AMD (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Akalu et al., 2017). However, the incomplete restoration of phagocytosis observed in MerTK-deficient models even when Tyro3 is active suggests that this approach, while promising, may need to be part of a broader strategy to fully rescue RPE function. Thus, the candidate merits further investigation, with a recommendation to pursue detailed preclinical studies to refine the antibody design, evaluate downstream signaling and biological effects in RPE cells, and ultimately determine whether this approach can translate into a clinically meaningful therapy for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin is a naturally derived macrolide initially isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus and belongs to the class of mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) inhibitors. This compound, originally discovered for its immunosuppressive properties, has evolved into a prominent therapeutic candidate across several fields including oncology, immunology, and neurodegeneration. Its chemical derivation and structural complexity allow for potent and selective inhibition of the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1). Rapamycin is widely used in clinical settings as an immunosuppressant following organ transplantation and has been repurposed for other indications based on its ability to modulate intracellular signaling pathways that regulate cellular growth, survival, and autophagy. As such, its potential application in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on a body of work indicating that targeting mTORC1 can restore autophagic and lysosomal function in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—a crucial factor given that RPE dysfunction is central to AMD pathogenesis (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, rapamycin has been extensively used and investigated in various clinical and preclinical settings. Its initial clinical use as an immunosuppressive agent in organ transplant patients laid the groundwork for understanding its mechanisms of action and safety profile in humans. Beyond its immunosuppressive applications, rapamycin has been evaluated for its anti-proliferative effects in several types of cancer and for its capability to extend lifespan in model organisms; these studies underscore the drug’s pleiotropic effects on cellular metabolism and autophagy. Specifically regarding ocular therapeutics, preclinical studies on retinal degenerative diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa and glaucoma have demonstrated that mTOR modulation by rapamycin can exert neuroprotective properties in retinal tissues (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). In the realm of AMD, several investigations have focused on the role of autophagy and lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in RPE cells, where rapamycin has been shown to promote autophagy and decrease the buildup of toxic aggregates, such as lipofuscin (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical studies and safety evaluations—in particular, intravitreal injections in non-human primates—have provided encouraging data regarding the ocular safety profile of rapamycin, thus supporting its further exploration as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, rapamycin exerts its effects by binding to the intracellular receptor FKBP12 (FK506-binding protein 12). This drug–FKBP12 complex then interacts with mTORC1, leading to its allosteric inhibition. Under normal anabolic conditions, active mTORC1 phosphorylates several downstream targets, including the transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is sequestered in the cytosol in its phosphorylated state, thus preventing the transcription of genes associated with lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. When rapamycin inhibits mTORC1, the phosphorylation of TFEB is reduced, permitting its nuclear translocation. Once inside the nucleus, TFEB initiates the transcription of numerous genes involved in autophagy and lysosomal function, thereby enhancing the cell’s capacity to degrade and recycle cellular debris such as accumulated photoreceptor outer segments (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium, mTORC1 normally integrates growth factor signals, nutrient availability, and stress responses to tightly regulate cellular homeostasis. The inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin thus releases the “brake” on autophagy, as evidenced by increased expression of autophagic markers such as LC3-II and lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1. This cascading effect leads to an enhanced intracellular clearance system (phagolysosomal flux), which is particularly critical for RPE cells that are responsible for the daily degradation of shed POS. Several studies have demonstrated that rapamycin-treated RPE cells exhibit improved POS degradation, a reduction in lipofuscin-like granules, and overall restoration of lysosomal function (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, the molecular signatures observed in rapamycin-treated cells mimic those seen under conditions of caloric restriction, further supporting the notion that mTORC1 inhibition can activate protective autophagic pathways (Davis, 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). This advanced understanding of rapamycin’s mechanism of action provides a compelling rationale for its application in dry AMD, where the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and dysregulated autophagy are key pathological features (Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of rapamycin in dry AMD is that its inhibition of mTORC1 will lead to the activation of TFEB by reducing its cytosolic phosphorylation state, thereby promoting nuclear translocation. In iPSC-derived RPE models, this induction of TFEB activity is expected to upregulate a host of autophagy and lysosomal genes, which in turn should enhance the cellular degradation of photoreceptor outer segments—an essential process in maintaining retinal homeostasis (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025). Accordingly, the anticipated in vitro effects upon rapamycin treatment include a robust increase in autophagic flux evidenced by elevated levels of LC3-II and LAMP1, paired with improved processing and clearance of POS debris. This effect is crucial because impaired clearance mechanisms contribute to the accumulation of lipofuscin and other cellular waste materials in RPE cells, both of which are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Falcão et al., 2024).

Supporting this expected outcome are observations from previous studies where rapamycin has been associated with a reduction in autofluorescent granules and a restoration of normal cellular clearance dynamics in RPE cells (Falcão et al., 2024). Additionally, safety assessments performed through intravitreal administration in non-human primates have demonstrated that rapamycin can be delivered to the retina with minimal adverse events, thereby underpinning its feasibility for clinical translation (Falcão et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2022). Importantly, the hypothesis that rapamycin can act at IC₅₀ values as low as approximately 0.1 nM in RPE cells further reinforces the potential sensitivity and efficacy of this candidate in modulating the pathway of interest. Given the expression of mTOR, TFEB, LC3, and LAMP1 in RPE cells—and the established role of these proteins in the autophagic and lysosomal clearance of POS—the expected improvement in autophagic turnover should directly translate into enhanced cell function and potentially mitigate the progression of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2022; Intartaglia et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
Rapamycin emerges as a robust and mechanistically sound therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its established ability to inhibit mTORC1 and consequently activate autophagy and lysosomal gene expression through TFEB nuclear translocation. One of the major strengths of this candidate lies in the well-characterized molecular mechanism that connects mTORC1 inhibition with enhanced clearance of POS debris—a process that is fundamentally disrupted in dry AMD. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence, ranging from biochemical assays that show increased LC3-II and LAMP1 expression in rapamycin-treated RPE cells to preclinical safety data in non-human primates, bolsters confidence in its potential utility (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

Furthermore, the multifaceted benefits of mTORC1 inhibition extend beyond autophagy induction; rapamycin also offers neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects, both of which are advantageous in the treatment of retinal degenerative diseases (Chang et al., 2022). The leverage of TFEB activation not only addresses the aberrant accumulation of toxic cellular debris but may also promote a broader upregulation of lysosomal biogenesis, thereby preempting further functional decline of RPE cells. These properties make rapamycin a strong candidate for mitigating early events in AMD pathogenesis, particularly in the context of experimental iPSC-RPE models where enhanced phagocytic capacity can be directly measured.

Nevertheless, several challenges and potential weaknesses require careful consideration. Despite its promising mechanism and preclinical rationale, clinical trials evaluating rapamycin in the context of ocular diseases have yielded mixed results, with some studies documenting only marginal improvements in visual function and others noting issues related to the drug’s solubility and delivery (Marchesi et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022). In advanced AMD, where the disease pathology is more complex and multifactorial, rapamycin’s efficacy might be limited, and there is a need for precise dosing strategies to balance mTORC1 inhibition with the preservation of physiological mTOR functions that are crucial for RPE cell survival (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). Additionally, the potential for off-target effects or immunosuppressive consequences linked to systemic exposure—although minimized by intravitreal delivery—necessitates further investigation into long-term safety profiles (Wang et al., 2022).

Another potential limitation is the inherent complexity of autophagy regulation in the RPE, which can be influenced by factors such as oxidative stress, metabolic dysfunction, and age-related changes in lysosomal function. While rapamycin is effective in reactivating autophagic pathways under controlled experimental settings, its impact within the pathogenic environment of a diseased retina, particularly if inflammatory processes are simultaneously active, may be less predictable (Davis, 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, the therapeutic window for achieving beneficial rapamycin concentrations without incurring adverse events is not yet fully defined, underscoring the importance of pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic studies specifically tailored to ocular tissues (Falcão et al., 2024).

Taken together, the current body of evidence suggests that rapamycin’s capacity to restore autophagic homeostasis in RPE cells represents a solid mechanistic foundation for its use in dry AMD. Its ability to upregulate autophagy and lysosomal function through TFEB activation directly addresses known defects in the clearance pathways of RPE cells—a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Moreover, the safety data from preclinical intravitreal delivery studies provide additional incentive to advance this candidate further along the translational pipeline. However, given the mixed outcomes observed in some clinical contexts and the challenges related to drug formulation and optimal dosing, further comprehensive studies are warranted to clarify its efficacy in early versus advanced stages of AMD (Mei et al., 2022).

In conclusion, rapamycin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD shows significant promise from both a mechanistic and translational standpoint. Its well-documented ability to inhibit mTORC1, thereby releasing TFEB and ramping up autophagic and lysosomal gene expression, positions it uniquely to tackle the underpinnings of RPE dysfunction characteristic of dry AMD. While preclinical data support its efficacy and safety with intravitreal administration in non-human primates, challenges remain regarding its formulation, potential off-target effects, and the delineation of its therapeutic window in human subjects. Consequently, while rapamycin’s molecular mechanism and early experimental results are highly encouraging, further studies—especially those that integrate pharmacokinetic profiling, dose optimization, and long-term outcome measurements in relevant in vivo models—are essential before definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding its clinical utility for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Si et al., 2023).

Overall, the strengths of rapamycin include its robust and well-characterized action on mTORC1, its downstream activation of autophagic and lysosomal pathways via TFEB, and supportive preclinical safety data in ocular models. In contrast, its weaknesses lie in the variable efficacy observed in clinical studies, formulation challenges due to low solubility, and the need for careful dosing to avoid potential adverse effects related to systemic immunosuppression. These considerations collectively argue for the continued investigation of rapamycin as a therapeutic option for dry AMD with a focus on optimizing delivery strategies and characterizing its long-term impact on retinal structure and function (Wang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AM580 is a fully synthetic retinoid compound designed as a highly selective agonist for the retinoic acid receptor α (RARα). Its chemical structure—a derivative of naphthalene and benzoic acid—was rationally engineered to confer two key properties: a more rigid molecular architecture compared with the natural ligand all‐trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and a marked preferential binding to RARα over other retinoid receptor subtypes (RARβ and RARγ) (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992). The molecule’s chemical name, 4-(5,6,7,8-tetrahydro-5,5,8,8-tetramethyl-2-naphthalenyl)carboxamido]benzoic acid, reflects its derivation from a series of modifications intended to enhance receptor selectivity and bioactivity (Martin et al., 1992). AM580 belongs to the broader class of retinoids—compounds that are either natural derivatives of vitamin A or synthetically modified analogues—which function as ligands for nuclear hormone receptors. Retinoids have been exploited in various fields of medicine due to their ability to modulate cellular differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis by activating retinoic acid receptor (RAR) and retinoid X receptor (RXR) pathways (Cras et al., 2010; Martin et al., 1992). In the case of AM580, its design emphasizes selective RARα activation, as demonstrated by its 30-fold higher binding affinity for RARα compared to RARβ and RARγ (Teng et al., 1996; Martin et al., 1992), making it an excellent molecular tool for dissection of RARα-specific biological responses.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, retinoids have been at the forefront of differentiation therapy, with ATRA being successfully employed in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) (Garattini et al., 2007; Garattini et al., 1997). The mechanism of action of AM580 is well delineated at the molecular level. The central hypothesis under evaluation posits that AM580, by selectively activating RARα at an effective concentration (EC₅₀ ~50 nM as observed in RPE cell assays), will stimulate the transcription of the MFGE8 gene. AM580 represents a compelling therapeutic candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, based on several lines of evidence gathered from the literature. This receptor selectivity is critical because it allows for target‐specific modulation of gene expression, potentially reducing the broad side effects observed with natural retinoids like ATRA that activate multiple receptor subtypes (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992; Teng et al., 1996). Preclinical studies have underscored the utility of RARα activation in modulating key processes such as cellular differentiation, inhibition of EMT, and enhancement of phagocytic function in RPE cells (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2012).

Retinoid compounds are notorious for their complex pharmacokinetics and potential for off-target effects, including teratogenicity, as evidenced by prior studies of AM580 in teratogenicity models (Elmazar et al., 2001). The delicate balance between efficacy and safety remains a critical issue, particularly for a condition such as dry AMD where long-term treatment is anticipated. Clinical validation in human subjects is still lacking, and the translation of dose levels, tissue penetration, and metabolic stability from the laboratory to the clinic remains an open question (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Another concern is that AM580, while selective, does retain some activity at RARβ and RARγ at higher concentrations (Teng et al., 1996), an effect that may have unpredictable consequences on cell signaling in the complex microenvironment of the RPE. This mechanism directly addresses a critical defect in dry AMD pathology, namely the impaired clearance of photoreceptor debris, which is a central driver of retinal degeneration (Garattini et al., 2007; Kobayashi et al., 2021). The preclinical literature offers promising evidence that selective RARα modulation can exert beneficial effects on RPE physiology, including the prevention of EMT and restoration of phagocytic function (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Despite these strengths, the transition from preclinical studies to clinical application will require careful attention to pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic factors, as well as rigorous safety assessments to mitigate risks typical of retinoid therapies. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Anacetrapib is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor of cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) originally developed by Merck as part of a class of compounds aimed at modulating lipid metabolism. This compound was identified and refined through extensive medicinal chemistry programs designed to target CETP’s lipid transfer function. As a member of the CETP inhibitor class, anacetrapib has been developed primarily for cardiovascular risk reduction by increasing high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL‐C) and lowering low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C), and its chemical structure and binding properties have been designed to disrupt the lipid‐transfer tunnel of the CETP enzyme (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Tall & Rader, 2018). The proposed repurposing for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on the rationale that by inhibiting CETP, the agent could raise local HDL levels in Bruch’s membrane (BrM) and improve reverse cholesterol transport, thereby reducing drusen‐like lipid accumulation and indirectly supporting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) phagocytic capacity—a hypothesis derived from observed associations between CETP activity, local retinal lipid metabolism, and AMD pathogenesis (Betzler et al., 2020; Shughoury et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, CETP inhibitors have been evaluated extensively for their potential to address dyslipidemia and reduce atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Anacetrapib, in particular, has undergone large clinical trials such as the DEFINE and REVEAL studies, where its efficacy in raising HDL‐C by approximately 138% and reducing LDL‐C by 37–40% compared to placebo was demonstrated (Cheung et al., 2017; Tall & Rader, 2018). The class of CETP inhibitors also includes compounds such as torcetrapib, dalcetrapib, and evacetrapib—with torcetrapib’s development being terminated due to off‐target effects including blood pressure elevations, while anacetrapib and evacetrapib showed more favorable profiles in subsequent trials (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Sirtori, 2011). Although these compounds were developed to address cardiovascular pathologies, genetic and mechanistic studies have implicated CETP and HDL metabolism in the ocular environment as well. Several genome‐wide association studies and Mendelian randomization studies have demonstrated a relationship between CETP gene variants, HDL levels, and AMD risk (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020). Despite this, no CETP inhibitor has previously been used in a clinical setting for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular diseases, and the repurposing of anacetrapib for dry AMD represents a novel therapeutic direction inspired by preclinical studies in murine models that suggest potential benefits in the retinal context (Cheung et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
Anacetrapib functions by binding to CETP, thereby preventing the transfer of cholesteryl esters from HDL to apolipoprotein B‐containing lipoproteins (i.e., LDL, very‐low‐density lipoprotein [VLDL]) and the subsequent exchange of triglycerides in the opposite direction. At the molecular level, CETP normally operates via a tunnel‐mechanism or shuttle mechanism to facilitate the bidirectional lipid transfer between lipoproteins. Inhibition of CETP by anacetrapib results in the accumulation of cholesterol-rich, enlarged HDL particles and a concomitant reduction in the levels of atherogenic LDL particles (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Sirtori, 2011). In the context of the retina, emerging evidence suggests that CETP is expressed not only systemically but also locally—in the retinal pigment epithelium, photoreceptor outer segments, and interphotoreceptor matrix (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). The rationale is that CETP activity in Bruch’s membrane may normally lower HDL levels, thereby impairing the capacity for reverse cholesterol transport in this specialized extracellular matrix, which can lead to the accumulation of lipids and the formation of drusen. By inhibiting CETP, anacetrapib may restore or increase local HDL levels, improving the efflux of accumulated cholesterol and other lipids from the RPE and neighboring structures (Fan et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2022). Moreover, the resulting HDL particles may gain enhanced cholesterol efflux capacity, as evidenced by preclinical studies that show increased cholesterol removal from macrophages via ABCA1- and ABCG1-mediated pathways (Sirtori, 2011; Page et al., 2016). In addition, proper HDL particle composition under CETP inhibition could influence key inflammatory regulatory mechanisms through the carriage of complement factors, which are linked to AMD pathogenesis (Tricorache et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assay, treatment with anacetrapib is expected to increase HDL levels locally in Bruch’s membrane, thereby enhancing reverse cholesterol transport across the retinal layers. The improved cholesterol efflux from the RPE is postulated to mitigate the accumulation of drusen-like lipid deposits—a hallmark of dry AMD—and potentially restore critical cellular functions such as integrin localization and associated phagocytic receptor activity (Cheung et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020). This restoration of lipid homeostasis is anticipated to reduce the build-up of oxidized lipids and other debris beneath the RPE, ultimately alleviating RPE dysfunction—a central component in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). The mechanism relies on the observation that HDL not only serves as a cholesterol acceptor but also carries important complement regulatory proteins and inflammatory mediators; thus, its normalization in Bruch’s membrane could indirectly support the phagocytic activity of RPE cells and improve tissue homeostasis (Lin et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). Gene expression studies have identified CETP expression in ocular tissues, reinforcing the notion that local CETP inhibition may directly influence lipid handling in the retina (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). Ultimately, the expected outcomes in preclinical models—and, by extension, in clinical trials—are a measurable reduction in drusen burden, improvement in RPE functionality, and a potential delay or attenuation in the progression of dry AMD (Schmidt et al., 2020; Cheung et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of anacetrapib for the treatment of dry AMD presents a compelling opportunity, supported by a solid mechanistic hypothesis and a favorable human safety profile established in cardiovascular trials. Among the clear strengths is the extensive biochemical and clinical data on CETP inhibitors in the context of dyslipidemia; anacetrapib has demonstrated robust HDL‐C raising and LDL‐C lowering effects, with a tolerability profile superior to earlier CETP inhibitors such as torcetrapib (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Tall & Rader, 2018). Furthermore, emerging evidence of CETP expression in ocular tissues and its potential role in modulating local lipid metabolism—combined with findings that suggest dysfunctional HDL composition may contribute to drusen formation—lends strong support to the therapeutic rationale (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017).

However, there are important weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed. First, the genetic and epidemiological data linking HDL cholesterol and AMD have been paradoxical; several Mendelian randomization studies have implicated HDL‐raising alleles, particularly those related to CETP modulation, with an increased risk for AMD (Betzler et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2017). This counterintuitive observation raises concerns that simply increasing HDL levels may not guarantee improved RPE function unless the quality and functionality of HDL particles are also enhanced (Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022). Second, while the cardiovascular applications of anacetrapib provide a strong safety signal, the ocular-specific pharmacodynamics and tissue distribution of the drug remain largely unexplored. It is conceivable that the systemic modulation of HDL might not translate into the desired local changes in Bruch’s membrane, particularly given the unique lipid microenvironment of the retina (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Third, preclinical data demonstrating that anacetrapib can reduce BrM lipid burden and restore integrin localization in murine models, although promising, have yet to be validated extensively, and species differences in CETP expression and lipid metabolism could limit translatability to human patients (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Lastly, the long-term consequences of altering CETP activity in the retina are unknown, and there exists a potential risk that chronic CETP inhibition could inadvertently disrupt local complement regulation or other aspects of retinal homeostasis, given the tight interplay between lipid metabolism and inflammation in AMD pathogenesis (Tricorache et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2015).

Overall, while the conceptual framework underlying the repurposing of anacetrapib for dry AMD is scientifically intriguing and supported by a convergence of genetic, biochemical, and preclinical mechanistic data, further investigation is needed to reconcile the paradoxical relationships observed in human genetic studies, to precisely characterize the local retinal pharmacokinetics of the drug, and to validate its effects on reverse cholesterol transport in the specific context of the retina. In summary, anacetrapib holds potential as a novel therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but its ultimate success will depend on carefully designed preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials that specifically address its ocular efficacy and safety profile (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022).

The repurposing of anacetrapib for the treatment of dry AMD presents a compelling opportunity, supported by a solid mechanistic hypothesis and a favorable human safety profile established in cardiovascular trials. Among the clear strengths is the extensive biochemical and clinical data on CETP inhibitors in the context of dyslipidemia; anacetrapib has demonstrated robust HDL‐C raising and LDL‐C lowering effects, with a tolerability profile superior to earlier CETP inhibitors such as torcetrapib (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Tall & Rader, 2018). Furthermore, emerging evidence of CETP expression in ocular tissues and its potential role in modulating local lipid metabolism—combined with findings that suggest dysfunctional HDL composition may contribute to drusen formation—lends strong support to the therapeutic rationale (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017).

However, there are important weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed. First, the genetic and epidemiological data linking HDL cholesterol and AMD have been paradoxical; several Mendelian randomization studies have implicated HDL‐raising alleles, particularly those related to CETP modulation, with an increased risk for AMD (Betzler et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2017). This counterintuitive observation raises concerns that simply increasing HDL levels may not guarantee improved RPE function unless the quality and functionality of HDL particles are also enhanced (Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022). Second, while the cardiovascular applications of anacetrapib provide a strong safety signal, the ocular-specific pharmacodynamics and tissue distribution of the drug remain largely unexplored. It is conceivable that the systemic modulation of HDL might not translate into the desired local changes in Bruch’s membrane, particularly given the unique lipid microenvironment of the retina (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Third, preclinical data demonstrating that anacetrapib can reduce BrM lipid burden and restore integrin localization in murine models, although promising, have yet to be validated extensively, and species differences in CETP expression and lipid metabolism could limit translatability to human patients (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Lastly, the long-term consequences of altering CETP activity in the retina are unknown, and there exists a potential risk that chronic CETP inhibition could inadvertently disrupt local complement regulation or other aspects of retinal homeostasis, given the tight interplay between lipid metabolism and inflammation in AMD pathogenesis (Tricorache et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2015).

Overall, while the conceptual framework underlying the repurposing of anacetrapib for dry AMD is scientifically intriguing and supported by a convergence of genetic, biochemical, and preclinical mechanistic data, further investigation is needed to reconcile the paradoxical relationships observed in human genetic studies, to precisely characterize the local retinal pharmacokinetics of the drug, and to validate its effects on reverse cholesterol transport in the specific context of the retina. In summary, anacetrapib holds potential as a novel therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but its ultimate success will depend on carefully designed preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials that specifically address its ocular efficacy and safety profile (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022).
