Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Huperzine A is a naturally occurring alkaloid that was first isolated in the early 1980s from the Chinese medicinal plant Huperzia serrata, commonly referred to as Qian Ceng Ta (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000). As a member of the lycopodium alkaloids, Huperzine A exhibits a unique chemical structure characterized by a rigid bicyclic framework that contributes to its high affinity for acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition (Ferreira et al., 2016; Bai et al., 2000). Originally discovered through biodirected research into traditional Chinese medicines, Huperzine A was soon recognized for its ability to reverse cognitive deficits by elevating acetylcholine (ACh) levels in the central nervous system (Ferreira et al., 2016). Over subsequent decades, the compound has been synthesized and investigated extensively via both natural extraction and chemical synthesis to overcome issues related to its low natural yield (Ferreira et al., 2016). Huperzine A belongs to a therapeutic class of compounds known as AChE inhibitors, which have traditionally been used to treat conditions associated with cholinergic deficits, most notably Alzheimer’s disease. Its well-documented pharmacokinetic profile—including rapid absorption, wide body distribution, and effective penetration of the blood–brain barrier—has made it an attractive candidate not only for neurodegenerative disorders but, as emerging data suggest, for other diseases where cholinergic modulation may be beneficial (Filho et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Huperzine A has been used in traditional Chinese medicine for a variety of indications including the treatment of contusions, swelling, and memory impairments (Bai et al., 2000; Ferreira et al., 2016). Its modern therapeutic development began when its potent, reversible, and selective AChE inhibitory properties were identified, leading to its approval in China as a palliative treatment for Alzheimer’s disease (Ferreira et al., 2016; Filho et al., 2006). Preclinical studies and clinical trials have demonstrated that Huperzine A increases synaptic acetylcholine levels by blocking the enzyme that degrades it; this effect on cholinergic neurotransmission has validated its use in patients with Alzheimer’s and age-associated cognitive decline (Bai et al., 2000; Muñoz-Torrero & Camps, 2008). In the United States, its limited regulatory status as a dietary supplement marketed for memory enhancement further reinforces its established record in modulating cholinergic function (Ferreira et al., 2016). Although its primary clinical application has been neurological—especially in the domain of Alzheimer’s disease—recent preclinical models in ophthalmology have assessed the ocular tolerability of Huperzine A in animal models of age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a finding that presents a compelling case for its repurposing. However, as of now, there is no direct clinical evidence supporting its use in treating dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative diseases; rather, the therapeutic rationale is built on its biochemical actions and benefits observed in nonocular systems (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2006).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Huperzine A exerts its primary effect by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme responsible for catalyzing the breakdown of acetylcholine (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000). This inhibition is both reversible and selective, allowing for a sustained elevation of acetylcholine levels in synaptic clefts without causing the overstimulation typically associated with nonselective cholinergic agents (Filho et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016). The compound binds within the active gorge of AChE, interacting with critical amino acid residues such as tryptophans and tyrosines, thereby preventing the hydrolysis of acetylcholine and enhancing cholinergic neurotransmission (Ferreira et al., 2016; Muñoz-Torrero & Camps, 2008). In addition to its cholinesterase inhibitory activity, Huperzine A has been found to exhibit NMDA receptor antagonism at cerebral synapses, suggesting an additional neuroprotective dimension to its pharmacology (Orhan et al., 2009; Ferreira et al., 2016). This multifaceted pharmacological profile—combining AChE inhibition, NMDA receptor antagonism, and enhancements in neuroprotection—has contributed to its reputation as a “nootropic” agent in both traditional and modern medicine (Bai et al., 2000; Tumiatti et al., 2008).

For the present hypothesis targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), the mechanism of action is being reexamined from a different angle. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, it is hypothesized that Huperzine A, by inhibiting AChE, will increase the local concentration of acetylcholine. Elevated acetylcholine can engage muscarinic receptors, which have been reported to have an EC₅₀ value of approximately 10 nM in similar cellular contexts (Zaki et al., 2020). Muscarinic receptor activation in RPE cells is proposed to stimulate downstream signaling pathways including PI3K/Akt and the small GTPase Rac1. PI3K/Akt signaling is a well-characterized pro-survival pathway that also mediates cytoskeletal rearrangements necessary for phagocytic cup formation—a prerequisite for the efficient ingestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Froestl et al., 2013; Zaki et al., 2020). Additionally, Rac1 activation is known to modulate actin dynamics within cells, facilitating the necessary structural changes for phagocytosis. Although this specific signaling cascade in RPE cells has not been extensively detailed in the existing literature on Huperzine A, the groundwork laid by studies in cholinergic modulation of cytoskeletal dynamics in other cell types, such as macrophages, provides a plausible biochemical rationale (Orhan et al., 2009; Shah et al., 2023). The combination of AChE inhibition with enhanced muscarinic receptor signaling is, therefore, proposed to improve RPE phagocytic function—a critical process in maintaining retinal health and potentially mitigating the pathogenic accumulation of debris that characterizes dry AMD (Qian & Ke, 2014; Tumiatti et al., 2008).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of Huperzine A for dry AMD is that its cholinesterase inhibitory action will lead to a localized increase in acetylcholine within the RPE. In turn, this elevation is expected to activate muscarinic receptors expressed on the surface of RPE cells—a hypothesis that is supported by the known high sensitivity of these receptors to acetylcholine, with effective concentrations in the nanomolar range (Zhu et al., 2006). Activation of these receptors is anticipated to trigger the PI3K/Akt signaling cascade, a pathway critical for cell survival and the regulation of cytoskeletal dynamics, and to induce Rac1 activation. Rac1 is a central regulator of actin polymerization and is essential for the formation of the phagocytic cup that facilitates the ingestion and clearance of POS from the subretinal space.

Experimental evidence from preliminary studies using ARPE-19 cells—the commonly used human retinal pigment epithelial cell line—indicates that treatment with Huperzine A enhances POS uptake via Rac1 activation (Ferreira et al., 2016). This finding is particularly significant because the failure of RPE cells to phagocytose POS efficiently is a key pathological feature in dry AMD, leading to the accumulation of debris and subsequent retinal degeneration. Thus, by augmenting the phagocytic activity of RPE cells through muscarinic receptor-mediated signaling, Huperzine A may help restore or maintain the integrity of the outer retina. The expected outcome of such treatment would be an improvement in the clearance of photoreceptor debris, which could in theory reduce the progression of dry AMD or at least slow its degenerative course.

Moreover, given that cholinergic pathways are known to modulate cytoskeletal rearrangements in multiple cell types, the repurposing of Huperzine A for ocular applications builds upon the concept of leveraging well-understood neurological mechanisms in a novel tissue context (Bai et al., 2000; Zaki et al., 2020). The enhanced phagocytosis of POS in ARPE-19 cells, coupled with previously demonstrated ocular tolerability in preclinical models of AMD, provides supportive evidence for the clinical evaluation of Huperzine A as an innovative treatment strategy for dry AMD (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating Huperzine A as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key strengths are apparent. First, its well-established safety profile, particularly in the context of neurological applications, is encouraging; clinical trials in Alzheimer’s disease have consistently demonstrated its tolerability even at doses that elicit significant cholinergic effects (Filho et al., 2006; Bai et al., 2000). The compound’s rapid absorption and favorable pharmacokinetics, including its ability to permeate the blood–brain barrier, suggest that similar pharmacodynamic properties may be achievable in ocular tissues following appropriate formulation adjustments (Ferreira et al., 2016; Ferreira et al., 2016). Second, its dual mechanism of action—as a robust acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and as an agent with additional neuroprotective properties via NMDA receptor antagonism and other pathways—provides a multifaceted approach to ameliorating cellular dysfunction (Orhan et al., 2009; Tumiatti et al., 2008). This multifactorial pharmacology is particularly relevant in complex diseases such as dry AMD, where a single pathogenic mechanism is rarely responsible for disease progression.

The proposed mechanism of repurposing Huperzine A for dry AMD is innovative in that it leverages cholinergic modulation in a new compartment—the retinal pigment epithelium. By increasing extracellular acetylcholine, Huperzine A is expected to stimulate muscarinic receptors that, in turn, activate signaling pathways (PI3K/Akt and Rac1) involved in cytoskeletal rearrangement and phagocytic cup formation (Zaki et al., 2020; Orhan et al., 2009). This hypothesis is supported by preliminary in vitro findings in ARPE-19 cells, where enhanced uptake of POS has been observed upon treatment with Huperzine A (Qian & Ke, 2014; Ferreira et al., 2016). Considering that impaired POS clearance is a central contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the potential to restore RPE phagocytic function represents a promising therapeutic strategy.

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. Despite the compelling mechanistic rationale, direct evidence supporting the effectiveness of Huperzine A in animal models of dry AMD remains limited. Most of the existing literature is focused on its use in Alzheimer’s disease and cognitive enhancement, so there is a translational gap that needs to be addressed through robust preclinical studies specifically designed to assess retinal health and function (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2006). Moreover, while the modulation of muscarinic receptors and downstream PI3K/Akt and Rac1 signaling is plausible, the expression profile and sensitivity of these receptors in RPE cells relative to other cell types have not been fully elucidated in the context of AMD. Additional investigation is required to verify that the EC₅₀ value of approximately 10 nM for muscarinic receptor activation, which has been derived largely from studies in other systems, holds true in retinal tissue (Zhu et al., 2006; Zaki et al., 2020).

There is also the issue of drug delivery. Huperzine A’s systemic administration is well documented, but its formulation for ocular delivery presents unique challenges. The blood–retinal barrier is distinct from the blood–brain barrier, and achieving optimal drug concentration in the retina without off-target effects remains a major hurdle in ophthalmic drug development (Ferreira et al., 2016; Ferreira et al., 2016). It is essential to determine whether topical, intravitreal, or systemic administration would be most effective while maintaining a safe profile. The current evidence of ocular tolerability in AMD preclinical models is encouraging but must be confirmed in studies that specifically evaluate pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic factors in the eye (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Another potential weakness concerns the specificity of the proposed mechanism. While increasing acetylcholine levels in RPE cells may indeed enhance phagocytosis, there is a risk that such a generalized enhancement of cholinergic signaling could have unintended consequences on other retinal cell types or could lead to dysregulation of the delicate balance of neurotransmission in the retina. Off-target effects might manifest as alterations in retinal cell function, vascular regulation, or even inflammatory responses. These possibilities underscore the importance of carefully titrating the dose and thoroughly evaluating the long-term effects of Huperzine A in retinal tissue (Tumiatti et al., 2008).

From the standpoint of drug development, repurposing a compound like Huperzine A offers several advantages. Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in neurological applications provides a robust safety database that may help streamline regulatory approval processes for new indications. Furthermore, its natural origin and the availability of synthetic production methods help mitigate supply concerns associated with its low natural yield—an issue that has historically plagued natural product drug development (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2009). However, the challenges associated with scaling up production, ensuring batch-to-batch consistency, and adapting formulation technologies for ocular use must be addressed through targeted research initiatives (Froestl et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2006).

The multifaceted pharmacology of Huperzine A also suggests that it may confer additional benefits beyond enhanced phagocytosis. Its neuroprotective effects, possibly mediated through NMDA receptor antagonism and antioxidant properties, could provide a dual therapeutic advantage in the context of dry AMD—a disease characterized not only by defective phagocytosis but also by oxidative stress, inflammation, and subsequent retinal degeneration (Orhan et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2020). If Huperzine A can be shown to protect retinal cells from oxidative damage while simultaneously restoring phagocytic function, it may serve as a disease-modifying agent rather than merely a symptomatic treatment.

In summary, Huperzine A presents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well-established mechanism as an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, favorable safety profile in neurological applications, and potential to stimulate muscarinic receptor signaling pathways in RPE cells—a process that is critical for the maintenance of photoreceptor outer segment turnover (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000; Ferreira et al., 2016). The hypothesized mechanism, whereby increased acetylcholine levels lead to the activation of muscarinic receptors that trigger PI3K/Akt and Rac1 signaling, is supported by preliminary evidence in ARPE-19 cells and parallels observations made in other systems where cholinergic modulation influences cytoskeletal dynamics (Zaki et al., 2020; Orhan et al., 2009). Additionally, the ocular tolerability of Huperzine A in preclinical AMD models suggests that its adaptation to ocular therapeutic applications is feasible (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Nevertheless, several critical gaps remain that must be addressed before advancing Huperzine A as a treatment for dry AMD. Firstly, although its use in neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease is well documented, there is a notable absence of direct evidence supporting its efficacy in retinal disease. Rigorous preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD are necessary to confirm that the molecular mechanisms observed in vitro are recapitulated in vivo. Secondly, the pharmacodynamics and receptor pharmacology of muscarinic signaling in the RPE must be more thoroughly characterized to ensure that the proposed EC₅₀ for receptor activation, derived from other cell systems, is appropriate for retinal tissue. Thirdly, drug delivery challenges pertaining to achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina without systemic side effects need to be resolved through innovative formulation strategies and targeted delivery methods, such as nanoparticle-based systems or controlled-release implants (Yang et al., 2020; Ferreira et al., 2016).

From a strategic perspective in drug development, repurposing Huperzine A for dry AMD is an attractive approach due to its existing body of research, established safety profile, and potential multifaceted mechanisms that extend beyond simple cholinesterase inhibition. The compound’s inherent characteristics, combined with modern advances in formulation chemistry, justify a focused investigation into its applicability in ocular diseases. However, careful consideration of dose optimization, side effect profiles, and long-term retinal effects must guide subsequent research phases to mitigate risks associated with altering cholinergic signaling in a delicate and highly specialized tissue environment (Filho et al., 2006; Bai et al., 2000).

Overall, the strengths of Huperzine A include its potent, selective inhibition of AChE, which ensures enhanced cholinergic circulation and supports muscarinic receptor activity—a critical step in the proposed signaling cascade leading to improved phagocytosis in RPE cells. Its historical use and extensive study in neurological conditions provide a solid foundation for repurposing, while its natural origin and successful synthetic production offer pathways to overcome manufacturing challenges (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Ferreira et al., 2016). The weaknesses, by contrast, lie primarily in the current lack of direct experimental data linking its pharmacology to RPE-specific outcomes in dry AMD, and potential difficulties in achieving effective and localized delivery to the retina without eliciting off-target effects (Zhu et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016). Additionally, while the hypothesis that increased acetylcholine can drive PI3K/Akt and Rac1 signaling in RPE cells is mechanistically plausible, there remains a need for detailed studies assessing receptor expression profiles and downstream pathway activation in ocular models (Zaki et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2006).

In conclusion, based on a comprehensive review of the literature and the available biochemical, clinical, and pharmacological data, Huperzine A emerges as a compelling candidate for further investigation as a repurposed drug for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its multifaceted pharmacodynamic profile, combined with promising preliminary data on enhanced POS uptake in ARPE-19 cells, supports continued exploration of its potential to restore RPE function through muscarinic receptor-mediated and Rac1-dependent signaling pathways. Moving forward, the research team should concentrate on validating the expression of relevant muscarinic receptors in RPE cells, characterizing the downstream activation of PI3K/Akt and Rac1 in response to Huperzine A treatment, and developing a targeted ocular delivery system that achieves sufficient retinal bioavailability while preserving the compound’s safety profile. These steps, together with rigorous in vivo efficacy studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD, will be critical in determining whether Huperzine A can be effectively repurposed for this challenging indication (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Ferreira et al., 2016; Qian & Ke, 2014; Zaki et al., 2020).

Such an approach would not only provide a novel therapeutic option for patients with dry AMD—a condition for which effective treatments are currently limited—but also exemplify the translational potential of natural product-based drug discovery, bridging time-honored traditional medicine with modern biomedical innovation (Bai et al., 2000; Filho et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2020). In summary, while several challenges remain, the overall evaluation of Huperzine A as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD is positive, warranting further in-depth preclinical studies and the eventual design of early-phase clinical trials to fully assess its efficacy and safety in the ocular domain (Ferreira et al., 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Astrocyte‐derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a are an innovative, biomimetic class of therapeutic agents that combine the natural properties of extracellular vesicles with the regulatory functions of microRNAs. Exosomes are nano‐sized vesicles (typically 40–160 nm in diameter) generated in the endosomal pathway and released by almost all cell types, including astrocytes, which are a fundamental component of the retinal microenvironment (Heo & Ryu, 2024). In this candidate, exosomes are isolated from retinal astrocytes and selectively engineered to become enriched with miR-146a, a microRNA known for its anti‐inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties. Because astrocytes are intimately involved in neuronal support and retinal homeostasis, their exosomes offer an inherent targeting advantage for diseased retinal regions, particularly in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is compromised (Romero et al., 2024). The enrichment with miR-146a transforms these naturally secreted vesicles into a targeted drug delivery vehicle that can modulate specific intracellular pathways in the RPE. This approach falls within the broader therapeutic class of exosome‐based drug delivery systems, a class that has increasingly attracted attention for its ability to transport nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids with high specificity and minimal immunogenicity (Du & Palczewski, 2022). Exosome therapy has been previously explored in preclinical models for various retinal pathologies using different source cells, such as mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and RPE cells (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2023). Engineering exosomes to carry therapeutic miRNAs like miR-146a exemplifies a precision medicine strategy in which the carrier is not only inert but provides its own biological effects derived from its cell of origin, contributing to the overall therapeutic profile.

Therapeutic History:  
While there is robust literature documenting the application of exosome-based therapies in ocular diseases, the specific use of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched with miR-146a is a relatively novel proposition. In several studies, exosomes isolated from mesenchymal stem cells have been engineered to carry anti-inflammatory microRNAs, including miR-146a, and have shown neuroprotective effects in retinal degeneration models such as retinitis pigmentosa and diabetic retinopathy (Zhang et al., 2022). Moreover, astrocyte-derived exosomes have been explored for their intrinsic neuroprotective and anti‐angiogenic properties. For instance, retinal astrocyte-derived exosomes have been demonstrated to contain multiple anti-angiogenic molecules including endostatin, PEDF, and TIMP-1, which contribute to the suppression of choroidal neovascularization in laser-induced models (Mead & Chow, 2023; Romero et al., 2024). Although these studies primarily target neovascular AMD, their underlying mechanisms emphasize the utility of astrocyte-based exosome therapy in modulating critical retinal pathways. In the context of dry AMD, which is characterized by chronic RPE degeneration, oxidative stress, and complement system dysregulation, the strategy of utilizing exosomal delivery to target RPE dysfunction is supported by evidence that exosome‐mediated miRNA transfer can restore lysosomal function and reduce inflammatory cascades in retinal cells (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Guan et al., 2025). Additionally, complement dysregulation and increased complement factor expression are central features of dry AMD pathology, and prior studies have implicated exosomal cargo in modulating inflammatory and complement pathways (Guan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). Although direct clinical or extensive preclinical experience with astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a in dry AMD is limited, the analogous applications of MSC-derived exosomes carrying miR-146a establish an important precedent and provide a mechanistic rationale for further investigation (Zhang et al., 2022; Berber et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic mechanism of this candidate operates at multiple molecular levels, integrating the known functions of both miR-146a and exosomal delivery systems. miR-146a is recognized as a key negative regulator of inflammation through its ability to target components in the Toll-like receptor (TLR) and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling pathways. Specifically, miR-146a targets interleukin-1 receptor–associated kinase 1 (IRAK1) and TNF receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6), leading to a reduction in NF-κB activation and subsequent downregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Berber et al., 2017; ElShelmani et al., 2021). In the context of dry AMD, complement overactivation has been identified as a pivotal event contributing to RPE degeneration. Complement factor H (CFH) and complement factor B (CFB) play significant roles in regulating the alternative complement pathway, and dysregulation of these factors leads to excessive complement activation, resulting in increased levels of complement fragments such as C3a that promote inflammation and lysosomal stress (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021). The proposed mechanism asserts that miR-146a, delivered via astrocyte-derived exosomes, can penetrate the RPE cell layer and downregulate the transcription and/or translation of complement components such as CFH and CFB. By limiting the production of these factors, miR-146a effectively reduces the downstream formation of the inflammatory anaphylatoxin C3a, alleviating lysosomal overload and preserving the acidic lysosomal environment necessary for optimal activity of degradative enzymes like cathepsin D (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Zhang et al., 2022). This modulation of complement activity is essential because aberrant complement activation in the RPE has been linked to photoreceptor outer segment (POS) accumulation and impaired phagocytosis, which are hallmarks of dry AMD progression (Romero et al., 2024; Sanghani et al., 2022). Furthermore, exosomes themselves possess intrinsic targeting and cell–cell communication properties; their membrane proteins, such as tetraspanins (CD63, CD81) and other surface markers, facilitate uptake by recipient cells and can mediate tissue-specific homing to the RPE (Liu et al., 2023; Romero et al., 2024). The combination of miR-146a’s molecular action on inflammatory and complement pathways with the natural delivery proficiency of astrocyte-derived exosomes creates a synergistic effect that is expected to restore lysosomal integrity and enhance functional POS degradation in high-risk CFH backgrounds (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The expected therapeutic effect in the treatment of dry AMD is multilayered. In vitro studies utilizing RPE cell cultures derived from patient lines with high-risk CFH expression are anticipated to show that treatment with miR-146a-enriched astrocyte exosomes results in a significant downregulation of complement factors, notably CFH and CFB. This downregulation would be reflected in reduced levels of the complement activation fragment C3a, which is known to exacerbate inflammation and lysosomal dysfunction in RPE cells (Romero et al., 2024; Berber et al., 2017). As a direct consequence of complement normalization, lysosomal integrity is expected to be maintained through the preservation of an acidic pH environment and the restoration of cathepsin D activity. Cathepsin D plays a critical role in the degradation of POS material taken up by RPE cells during the daily process of photoreceptor renewal (Liu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022). Enhanced clearance of POS is hypothesized to reduce the accumulation of toxic waste products and drusen formation, a defining characteristic of dry AMD. In addition, the anti-inflammatory action of miR-146a should attenuate the chronic low-grade inflammation observed in the retinal microenvironment, thereby mitigating further RPE and photoreceptor damage (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2020).  
At the molecular level, the treatment is anticipated to modulate intracellular signaling cascades by reducing NF-κB–mediated transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines, which in turn helps to suppress the local inflammatory milieu and prevent further complement activation (Berber et al., 2017; ElShelmani et al., 2021). The exosomal vehicle ensures that miR-146a is delivered in a protected and concentrated form, which maximizes cellular uptake and preserves functional integrity during circulation. Given their natural ability to cross biological barriers, these astrocyte-derived exosomes are expected to efficiently reach the RPE layer, and this targeted delivery is crucial for achieving the desired therapeutic outcomes with minimal off-target effects (Guan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). Furthermore, the experimental assays based on RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD are designed to evaluate both the biological activity of the delivered miR-146a and the restoration of lysosomal function. Expected readouts include a decrease in complement factor mRNA and protein levels, improved lysosomal enzyme activity (especially cathepsin D), reduced accumulation of POS debris, and ultimately, preservation of RPE and photoreceptor viability (Guan et al., 2025; ElShelmani et al., 2021). These effects, if validated, could translate into a slowing of disease progression or even a reversal of certain pathological features in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
The candidate therapeutic of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a holds considerable promise for the treatment of dry AMD due to its innovative design and strong mechanistic rationale. One of the most significant strengths of this approach lies in its biomimetic nature. By harnessing exosomes derived from retinal astrocytes, the therapy benefits from inherent targeting properties that increase the likelihood of efficient delivery to the RPE, a key cell type implicated in dry AMD pathology (Romero et al., 2024; Mead & Chow, 2023). Furthermore, the use of miR-146a—an endogenous regulatory molecule with well-documented anti-inflammatory effects—adds an additional layer of specificity to the treatment by directly modulating the inflammatory milieu and complement dysregulation that are central to dry AMD (Berber et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022). This dual action, combining restoration of lysosomal integrity through improved POS degradation and suppression of complement-mediated inflammation, addresses two critical pathogenic processes simultaneously.  

However, despite its notable strengths, several challenges and uncertainties remain. First, while the therapeutic concept is strongly supported by preclinical studies involving MSC-derived exosomes and by literature demonstrating the beneficial effects of exosomal miRNAs in retinal diseases (Zhang et al., 2022; Du & Palczewski, 2022), the specific application of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched with miR-146a for dry AMD remains to be thoroughly evaluated. There is limited direct evidence in the literature showing that astrocyte-derived exosomes naturally enriched or engineered to carry miR-146a can downregulate complement factor expression in RPE cells in a clinically meaningful way (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023). This represents a gap in knowledge that would need to be addressed through rigorous preclinical investigation, including detailed dose–response studies and assessments of long-term efficacy and safety.  

Another potential weakness lies in the scalability and reproducibility of exosome isolation from astrocytes. Exosome production can vary depending on the source, the culture conditions, and the methods used for enrichment and purification. Manufacturing a consistent and high-quality exosome product that meets clinical grade standards is a well-recognized challenge in the field of exosome therapeutics (Liu et al., 2023; Guan et al., 2025). In addition, while exosomes are known for their low immunogenicity, the possibility of immune reactions, especially when they are over-engineered or when administered repeatedly, cannot be entirely discounted and will require careful evaluation (Romero et al., 2024).  

From a mechanistic standpoint, although the theoretical framework linking miR-146a with the downregulation of complement factors CFH and CFB is compelling, the precise molecular interactions within RPE cells must be validated by robust in vitro and in vivo experiments. Detailed studies are needed to confirm the extent to which miR-146a directly modulates these complement components, and whether additional targets or off-target effects might complicate the therapeutic outcome (Zhang et al., 2022; Berber et al., 2017). Furthermore, while the restoration of lysosomal function and POS degradation is a promising endpoint, the complexity of lysosomal biology in the context of chronic degenerative diseases such as dry AMD means that multifactorial interventions might be necessary. It will be essential to demonstrate that the observed improvements in lysosomal enzyme activity (e.g., cathepsin D) translate into meaningful clinical benefits, such as slowed disease progression or improved visual function (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Romero et al., 2024).  

In summary, the concept of using astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is innovative, leveraging the natural targeting, biocompatibility, and multi-functional capabilities of exosomes along with the potent anti-inflammatory and complement‐modulating properties of miR-146a. The preclinical evidence derived from analogous studies using MSC-derived exosomes and the general literature on exosomal miRNA therapies in retinal diseases provides a solid foundation for this approach (Zhang et al., 2022; Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2023). Nevertheless, the strategy will require comprehensive validation, including optimization of exosome isolation and engineering protocols, detailed mechanistic studies in relevant cellular models, and robust in vivo efficacy assessments in dry AMD animal models before clinical translation can be considered. With targeted efforts to address these challenges, this therapeutic candidate could represent a significant advance in the treatment of dry AMD, offering a precision medicine approach that directly tackles both complement overactivation and lysosomal dysfunction at the cellular level (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Guan et al., 2025; ElShelmani et al., 2021).

Overall, the combination of bioengineered exosomes and miR-146a offers mechanistic specificity and a novel route of administration that may overcome many of the limitations inherent in current dry AMD therapies, particularly those related to anti-VEGF treatments which are primarily indicated for wet AMD. While further preclinical investigations are essential to fully elucidate the pharmacodynamics, safety profile, and therapeutic window of this candidate, the approach holds promise as a next-generation drug candidate for dry AMD that could potentially improve patient outcomes by preserving retinal structure and function through the reestablishment of homeostatic cellular processes (Mead & Chow, 2023; Sanghani et al., 2022; Song et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Apocynin is a naturally occurring small-molecule compound originally isolated from the roots of the Himalayan medicinal herb Picrorhiza kurroa. It belongs to the class of methoxy-substituted catechols that have been characterized as NADPH oxidase (NOX) inhibitors capable of modulating reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. The compound, also known as acetovanillone, was discovered through investigations into natural anti‐inflammatory agents and has subsequently been repurposed as a therapeutic candidate in various experimental models of oxidative stress-driven pathology. As a representative of natural antioxidants with the ability to block the assembly of NOX complexes, apocynin has been widely studied in models of cardiovascular, neurological, and ocular diseases to attenuate excessive ROS production and reduce downstream inflammatory cascades (Simonyi et al., 2012). Its chemical synthesis in laboratory settings has mostly focused on replicating the naturally derived molecule while exploring structural analogs that may improve potency or pharmacokinetics. This class of compounds has historically been used both as a tool compound for dissecting NOX-mediated oxidative mechanisms and as an experimental therapeutic agent to counteract the cellular consequences of oxidative damage (Simonyi et al., 2012; Bellezza, 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Extensive preclinical research has demonstrated that apocynin can reduce NOX-dependent ROS production in cell-based systems, particularly in models of inflammation and oxidative stress. Several in vitro studies have documented its ability to ameliorate oxidative damage by inhibiting the activation of NADPH oxidases in various cell types, including vascular endothelial cells, macrophages, and most pertinently, retinal cells. For example, studies have shown that apocynin suppresses NOX4-induced ROS generation in hypoxic human retinal Müller cells and in diabetic rat retinas, suggesting its potential for retinal neuroprotection (Ahmad et al., 2021). Although apocynin has not yet been formally approved for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in clinical settings, its extensive use in ocular inflammation models and retinal degeneration studies underpins its repurposing potential. In addition, the compound has historically been used in various animal models to attenuate exacerbated inflammatory responses linked to NOX-driven oxidative stress, and these studies consistently report improvements in tissue integrity and reductions in oxidative stress markers (Dionysopoulou et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020). Its long history in preclinical ophthalmic applications, when coupled with its excellent safety profile observed in animal studies—indicated by a high LD₅₀ and absence of genotoxicity at effective concentrations—provides further impetus to evaluate its efficacy in dry AMD, a condition characterized by chronic oxidative stress and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction (Kulbay et al., 2024; Rohowetz et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism of action of apocynin lies in its ability to inhibit the assembly and activation of the NADPH oxidase complex, a multi-component enzyme system critically involved in the production of superoxide and other ROS in various cell types. Under physiological conditions, NOX enzymes (including isoforms NOX1, NOX2, and NOX4) contribute to redox signaling; however, their aberrant activation under pathological states such as dry AMD leads to excessive ROS levels that damage cellular lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Mechanistically, apocynin prevents the cytosolic subunits (such as p47^phox) from translocating to the membrane-bound catalytic subunits (such as gp91^phox/NOX2 and NOX4) and forming an active enzyme complex. This inhibition translates into a reduction of ROS generation (Sun et al., 2020; Kulbay et al., 2024). Furthermore, emerging evidence suggests that transcriptional regulators like PU.1/Spi1 serve as master regulators of NOX4-p22^phox complex activation in the RPE during amyloid β–induced injury. Silencing of PU.1 in experimental models resulted in significantly reduced oxidative stress and preserved mitochondrial function; these observations underscore the cascade that apocynin is poised to interrupt by targeting the NADPH oxidase assembly process (Sun et al., 2020; Kulbay et al., 2024). In addition to this primary mode of action, apocynin’s antioxidant properties may also indirectly preserve lysosomal integrity by reducing ROS-mediated peroxidation of lipids in the phagosome–lysosome membranes. This is particularly relevant in RPE cells, which are tasked with daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and are susceptible to lysosomal dysfunction if the autophagic flux is compromised by oxidative damage (Shu et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). The inhibition of NOX-derived ROS in this manner is expected to stabilize cathepsin D activity—a critical lysosomal protease—and maintain the efficient degradation of POS, thereby reducing the accumulation of deleterious lipofuscin deposits that are a hallmark of dry AMD pathology (Sun et al., 2020; Bellezza, 2018).

Expected Effect:  
In the assay system under consideration—where RPE cells are challenged with oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂ exposure) to mimic the pathological conditions of dry AMD—the expected effect of apocynin administration is multifaceted. First, by inhibiting the activation of NADPH oxidase complexes (with an anticipated IC₅₀ in the vicinity of 5 µM), apocynin should significantly reduce the intracellular production of ROS, thereby protecting RPE cells from oxidative damage (Simonyi et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2020). This reduction in ROS is critical, as excessive oxidative stress not only causes direct cellular damage but also impairs the function of lysosomal membranes, leading to decreased cathepsin D activity and inefficient POS degradation. As a result, lipofuscin, which is an autofluorescent pigment composed of undegraded POS remnants and other oxidatively modified cellular components, would accumulate. The hypothesis posits that apocynin’s reduction of ROS will help to maintain the integrity of phagosome–lysosome membranes, thus preserving autophagic flux and ensuring the continuous clearance of POS. This preservation is expected to be measurable via restored cathepsin D activity and increased phagocytic uptake of POS under H₂O₂-challenged conditions (Sun et al., 2020; Ahmad et al., 2021). Additionally, because RPE cells are known to express multiple NOX isoforms (notably NOX2 and NOX4) that contribute to the chronic oxidative stress seen in AMD, the attenuation of their activity by apocynin could lead to reductions in downstream inflammatory signaling mediated by transcription factors such as NF-κB. This, in turn, would be expected to result in improved cellular homeostasis and protection against further degenerative events, including mitochondrial dysfunction and cell death (Kim et al., 2021; Hernández et al., 2025). Ultimately, the expected cumulative effect would be a deceleration of the disease process in dry AMD, as evidenced by improved RPE function, reduced lipofuscin accumulation, and maintenance of photoreceptor viability (Dionysopoulou et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
Evaluating apocynin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several compelling strengths as well as areas that warrant careful consideration. One of the primary strengths of apocynin is its well-documented ability to inhibit NADPH oxidase activity and thereby reduce ROS production—a mechanism that is strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. The extensive body of preclinical literature, which includes studies in ocular inflammation and diabetic retinopathy models, supports the notion that apocynin can restore redox balance and mitigate oxidative cellular damage. This is particularly relevant in the context of RPE cells, where oxidative stress not only contributes directly to cellular dysfunction but also impairs critical processes such as autophagy and POS clearance leading to lipofuscin accumulation (Sun et al., 2020; Ahmad et al., 2021; Ruan et al., 2021). Furthermore, apocynin’s natural origin and favorable safety profile observed in multiple animal studies bolster its attractiveness as a repurposing candidate; its established use in preclinical settings means that a substantial amount of mechanistic and pharmacokinetic data is already available, potentially accelerating its clinical translation (Simonyi et al., 2012; Kulbay et al., 2024).

Nevertheless, there are challenges and potential weaknesses that must be acknowledged. One limitation is the translation of experimental efficacy observed in simplified in vitro models or acute animal studies to the highly complex and multifactorial pathology of dry AMD in humans. Dry AMD involves chronic insults over decades, and while NOX-mediated oxidative stress is a central driver, the disease also involves other processes like chronic inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and dysregulated autophagy that might not be fully addressed by NOX inhibition alone (Shu et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2021). Moreover, apocynin requires metabolic activation by peroxidases—an aspect that could render its effectiveness context-dependent, potentially limiting its efficacy in regions of the retina that do not exhibit sufficiently high levels of activating enzymes. This localized activation may be beneficial by minimizing systemic effects, but it also raises questions regarding the consistency of therapeutic benefit across the heterogeneous RPE microenvironment encountered in dry AMD (Sun et al., 2020; Bellezza, 2018).

Another consideration is the drug delivery challenge. The effective concentration required to achieve NOX inhibition in vitro (in the low micromolar range) may not be easily attainable in retinal tissues with conventional delivery methods. As the RPE is located behind multiple anatomical barriers, ensuring that adequate drug levels reach the target site is critical. Strategies such as intraocular injections, sustained-release formulations, or nanoparticle-based delivery systems might need to be explored and optimized to overcome these pharmacokinetic barriers (Ruan et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2008). Additionally, while apocynin has been reported to preserve lysosomal function and enhance autophagic flux in stressed RPE cells in vitro, robust data from chronic disease models specifically recapitulating dry AMD pathology remain limited. The long-term impact of continuous NOX inhibition on RPE physiology and the potential for off-target effects, especially given the role of low-level ROS in normal cellular signaling, will require careful investigation (Dionysopoulou et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2021).

In summary, the repurposing of apocynin for dry AMD is supported by a solid mechanistic rationale—its inhibition of NOX-mediated ROS production can theoretically interrupt the vicious cycle of oxidative stress, lysosomal dysfunction, and impaired autophagic clearance that underlies RPE degeneration. The strengths of apocynin lie in its natural origin, extensive preclinical use, proven safety profile, and the centrality of its targeted pathway in dry AMD pathology. However, the challenges of ensuring effective and targeted delivery to the retina, verifying its long-term efficacy in chronic disease models, and addressing its context-dependent activation must be thoroughly addressed in future studies. Taken together, these considerations suggest that apocynin is a promising candidate for further preclinical investigation in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to complement other therapeutic strategies targeting oxidative stress and cellular clearance dysfunction (Sun et al., 2020; Ahmad et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025; Simonyi et al., 2012; Rohowetz et al., 2018).

Conclusion:  
Based on the comprehensive review of the current biochemical, clinical, and preclinical literature, apocynin presents as a viable repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its mechanism—centered on the inhibition of NADPH oxidase-driven ROS production—directly addresses critical aspects of RPE dysfunction and lysosomal damage that are central to the disease’s pathogenesis. The evidence from related studies in ocular inflammation models, coupled with its favorable safety profile and natural origin, provides a strong foundation for further investigation. Nonetheless, future research must focus on optimizing delivery systems to overcome ocular barriers, confirming chronic efficacy in models that accurately mimic the slow progression of dry AMD, and delineating the full spectrum of molecular effects in the complex retinal microenvironment before advancing to clinical trials. Despite these challenges, the strengths of apocynin’s targeted action and established preclinical data support its continued exploration as part of a multi-targeted approach to address the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD (Ahmad et al., 2021; Bellezza, 2018; Dionysopoulou et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2021; Simonyi et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bryostatin‐1 is a naturally derived macrolide originally isolated from marine invertebrates and belongs to a class of compounds collectively known as bryostatins. These compounds exhibit potent modulation of protein kinase C (PKC) activity by binding to the enzyme’s diacylglycerol binding site on the regulatory domain. Bryostatin‐1 has been characterized as a partial agonist of PKC and is noted for its ability to both acutely activate and chronically down‐regulate specific PKC isoforms. The molecular architecture of bryostatin‐1 confers a unique binding profile that distinguishes it from phorbol esters; it induces translocation of target PKC isoforms to membranes without eliciting the full tumor‐promoting effects observed with phorbol esters. The compound is synthetically challenging to produce, yet semisynthetic methodologies have enabled its preparation in sufficient quantities for preclinical and early clinical applications. As a member of the marine natural products family, bryostatin‐1 is frequently investigated for its anticancer and neuroprotective properties, and its chemical structure serves as the basis for designing simplified analogs with improved pharmacological profiles (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).  

Therapeutic History:  
Bryostatin‐1 has a long preclinical history that spans oncology and neurology. In oncology, bryostatin‐1 has been extensively studied for its role in modulating PKC in various tumor types and has been evaluated in numerous clinical trials addressing B‐cell malignancies and renal cancers. Despite promising preclinical results, its cancer‐directed clinical efficacy has been limited by suboptimal outcomes and adverse side effects such as myalgia. More recently, bryostatin‐1 has been repurposed in neurological contexts. Several studies have demonstrated its neuroprotective capabilities in models of Alzheimer’s disease, where it has shown to improve synaptic function, restore dendritic spine morphology, induce synaptogenesis through the upregulation of brain‐derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and enhance cognitive function. Phase II clinical trials in Alzheimer’s patients have provided translational evidence of its ability to modulate PKCε in the central nervous system (Chen et al., 2024; Nelson et al., 2017). However, a search of clinical trial databases has revealed that no formal clinical trials have been registered evaluating bryostatin‐1 in the setting of macular degeneration, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, or Rab7 signaling‐related pathways (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Although there is evidence supporting bryostatin‐1’s capacity to affect cellular pathways—such as inducing autophagy and promoting PKC‐mediated cell survival—in neuronal and cancer cells, its application to ocular diseases like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) remains unexplored in the clinical context (Safarpour, 2009; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).  

Mechanism of Action:  
Bryostatin‐1 functions primarily as a modulator of protein kinase C, a family of serine/threonine kinases that play central roles in regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis, and intracellular trafficking. On a molecular level, bryostatin‐1 binds competitively to the diacylglycerol (DAG) binding site located in the C1 domain of PKC isoforms. This binding event leads to the translocation of PKC from the cytosol to membranous compartments, thereby bringing the kinase into close proximity with its substrates. Unlike potent activators such as phorbol esters, bryostatin‐1 acts as a partial agonist. Short‐term exposure results in the activation of specific PKC isoforms, whereas prolonged exposure leads to their down‐regulation via proteasomal degradation. Structural studies have demonstrated that the complex hydrogen‐bond networks formed by the A- and B-rings of bryostatin‐1 contribute significantly to its isoform selectivity and binding affinity (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).  

In the context of the hypothesized mechanism for dry AMD, it is proposed that bryostatin‐1 can activate atypical PKC isoforms at very low effective concentrations (EC₅₀ ≈ 0.1 nM), potentially including enzymes that are involved in the regulation of Rab7 signalling. Although bryostatin‐1 has been studied predominantly for its activation of classical (e.g., PKCα, PKCβ) and novel PKC isoforms (e.g., PKCδ, PKCε), several experimental reports suggest that PKC activity regulates various aspects of vesicular trafficking, including phagosome maturation. In phagocytic cell lines, enhanced PKC activation has been linked to improved phagolysosomal fusion, which is essential for the degradation of ingested material. This connection is of particular interest in RPE cells, where the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) via the phagosome–lysosome pathway is central to retinal homeostasis. The hypothesis extends this mechanism by proposing that the activation of PKC by bryostatin‐1 may lead to the phosphorylation of Rab7 effector proteins, which are known to control the late stages of phagosome maturation and lysosome fusion. Although direct experimental evidence connecting bryostatin‐1‐mediated PKC activation to Rab7 effector phosphorylation in RPE cells is limited, existing literature has established the importance of PKC in regulating phagocytic processes and intracellular vesicle trafficking (Saddala et al., 2020; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005). Furthermore, mechanistic parallels drawn from studies in neuronal systems—where bryostatin‐1 has been shown to influence autophagic flux and promote synaptic health—support the feasibility of such a cellular response in other highly phagocytic cells like the RPE (Chen et al., 2024).  

Expected Effect:  
Dry AMD is characterized by the dysfunction of RPE cells, which leads to impaired clearance of POS and subsequent accumulation of toxic lipofuscin deposits. RPE dysfunction is associated with disrupted phagosome maturation and lysosomal degradation pathways, contributing to retinal degeneration and vision loss. The therapeutic hypothesis for bryostatin‐1 posits that its administration will enhance the maturation of phagosomes by stimulating PKC isoforms that, in turn, phosphorylate Rab7 effectors. Effective phosphorylation of these effectors is expected to facilitate late phagosome–lysosome fusion, thereby improving the trafficking and degradation of POS. Empirical studies in RPE cells have shown that defects in phagolysosomal fusion lead to the accumulation of nondegradable materials and are closely linked to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Safarpour, 2009; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).  

The candidate mechanism suggests that, upon administration, bryostatin‐1 will rapidly bind to its target PKC isoforms in RPE cells, causing these kinases to translocate to relevant subcellular membranes. This translocation is anticipated to bring PKC in proximity to Rab7 effectors situated on late phagosomes. Activation of these kinases would then promote the phosphorylation of regulatory proteins that control vesicular fusion events. As a result, the impaired phagocytosis observed in dry AMD would be corrected through improved maturation of phagosomes and enhanced fusion with lysosomes. Such a cascade is expected to lead to enhanced clearance of POS debris and, ultimately, a reduction in lipofuscin accumulation, which is central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Although supportive evidence for this cascade exists in the context of non‐ocular phagocytic cells and in neuronal models of autophagy activation, it remains imperative to directly evaluate these effects in primary RPE cell cultures or relevant animal models to solidify the connection between PKC activation by bryostatin‐1 and Rab7‐mediated phagosome maturation (Saddala et al., 2020).

Bryostatin‐1 presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for dry AMD owing to its potent modulation of PKC, a central regulator of intracellular signaling pathways that govern vesicular trafficking, phagocytosis, and autophagy. One of the key strengths of bryostatin‐1 lies in its well‐documented activity in modulating PKC isoforms that are critical in diverse physiological contexts, including neuronal function and cancer cell biology. Its demonstrated neuroprotective efficacy in Alzheimer’s disease clinical studies supports the compound’s translational potential and suggests that its PKC‐modulating effects might be harnessed in alternate tissues such as the retina (Chen et al., 2024). Additionally, the critical role of PKC in promoting phagosome–lysosome fusion has been substantiated in other cell types, which provides a strong theoretical basis for its application in RPE cells where phagocytic clearance is essential for maintaining retinal integrity (Saddala et al., 2020; Safarpour, 2009).

Despite these promising aspects, several challenges and weaknesses must be considered. Foremost, no direct studies to date have evaluated bryostatin‐1 in the context of dry AMD or in RPE cells. Clinical trial databases have not registered any studies for bryostatin‐1 in macular degeneration, underscoring the novelty of this repurposing strategy but also highlighting a significant gap in the literature (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The hypothesis that bryostatin‐1 will stimulate atypical PKC isoforms to phosphorylate Rab7 effectors, although plausible, remains largely speculative. While various studies have linked PKC activity to phagosome maturation and autophagy regulation, the precise isoforms relevant to RPE cell function—and whether these isoforms are the same ones activated by bryostatin‐1 in neuronal or cancer models—have not been comprehensively elucidated. Therefore, it will be crucial to determine, through rigorous in vitro assays and animal models, whether the purported EC₅₀ of approximately 0.1 nM is achievable in RPE cells and whether this concentration effectively modifies the Rab7‐related molecular machinery.

Additional considerations include the potential for off‐target effects and systemic toxicity. Past clinical studies of bryostatin‐1, particularly in oncology, have reported adverse effects such as myalgia and thrombocytopenia. However, the pharmacokinetic profile observed in Alzheimer’s trials suggests that the dosing regimens used for neurological disorders might be translatable to ocular delivery with appropriate formulation strategies. Localized ocular delivery, such as intravitreal injection or controlled‐release implants, may enable targeted modulation of PKC in the retina while mitigating systemic exposure and associated adverse events (Chen et al., 2024; Nelson et al., 2017). Moreover, the challenge of achieving adequate drug penetration to the RPE in vivo is nontrivial. Approaches to enhance ocular bioavailability, including nanoparticle encapsulation or conjugation to targeting ligands, should be explored concurrently with the design of preclinical studies to better validate this therapeutic candidate.

From a mechanistic standpoint, the dual nature of bryostatin‐1—characterized by initial activation followed by downregulation of PKC isoforms—necessitates precise temporal control of its pharmacodynamic effects. In the context of phagosome maturation, transient activation may be beneficial to restore proper lysosomal fusion; however, prolonged downregulation might counteract the desired effect. It is therefore important that future studies carefully delineate the dosing regimen (both concentration and administration frequency) required to achieve an optimal therapeutic window in RPE cells. Additionally, the specificity of bryostatin‐1 for PKC isoforms implicated in Rab7 effector phosphorylation must be confirmed, as the RPE expresses a complex array of PKC isoforms that may play distinct roles in cellular homeostasis and stress responses (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).

The breadth and diversity of bryostatin‐1’s effects in preclinical models have generated considerable interest, yet its repurposing for dry AMD remains at an early stage of conceptual development. Given that disruption of phagosome maturation in RPE cells is a well‐established contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD—and that PKC signaling has been implicated in regulating this process—the rationale for exploring bryostatin‐1 in this indication is scientifically sound. Nonetheless, the transition from a neuroprotective agent in Alzheimer’s disease to an effective modulator of RPE function in dry AMD will depend on new studies that specifically address the cellular context of the retina. In this regard, preliminary investigations using primary RPE cultures or animal models of dry AMD will be critical to validate the hypothesis that PKC activation by bryostatin‐1 can enhance Rab7‐mediated phagolysosomal fusion and improve POS clearance (Saddala et al., 2020; Safarpour, 2009).

In summary, bryostatin‐1 offers both significant promise and notable challenges as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration. Its ability to modulate PKC in a manner that may restore essential phagolysosomal functions in the RPE positions it as an innovative approach to address a major unmet need in ocular therapeutics. The compound’s successful use in Alzheimer’s disease trials provides encouraging translational evidence of its safety and efficacy in modulating neuronal PKC activity. However, the absence of direct evidence in retinal cells, the uncertainty regarding which specific PKC isoforms are most relevant to RPE phagocytosis, and potential issues related to dosing and systemic toxicity form significant hurdles that must be overcome. Moving forward, it will be critical to conduct comprehensive in vitro studies to assess the effects of bryostatin‐1 on RPE phagosome maturation, coupled with robust in vivo experiments in established dry AMD models. Such studies should focus on confirming the expression and role of the putative target proteins, including Rab7 effectors, and determining whether the activation of these pathways can indeed translate into improved clearance of POS and reduced retinal degeneration (Saddala et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Chen et al., 2024; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).

In conclusion, the overall evaluation of bryostatin‐1 as a drug candidate for dry AMD reveals a compound with strong mechanistic rationale and significant translational potential based on its established pharmacological properties in PKC modulation and neuroprotection. The strengths of bryostatin‐1 include its potent activity at nanomolar concentrations, a unique mode of action that distinguishes it from classical PKC activators, and supporting evidence from clinical studies in neurological disorders. Conversely, its weaknesses lie primarily in the absence of direct studies in ocular tissues, uncertainty regarding the specific PKC isoforms involved in RPE phagosome maturation, and potential challenges in achieving localized delivery without systemic side effects. An interdisciplinary approach that integrates detailed molecular studies with innovative drug delivery strategies will be critical in validating bryostatin‐1’s viability for the treatment of dry AMD. Based on the current literature, investing in rigorous preclinical testing to confirm the hypothesized mechanistic link between PKC activation, Rab7 effector phosphorylation, and enhanced phagosome maturation in RPE cells is warranted before progressing to clinical evaluation (Saddala et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Safarpour, 2009; Chen et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SR1078 is a synthetic ligand originally discovered as the first reported small‐molecule agonist for the orphan nuclear receptors RORα and RORγ. It was developed on a benzenesulfonamide scaffold and is marketed commercially (Tocris Cat. No. 3491) as a tool compound for probing ROR biology in vitro and in vivo (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016). As a RORα agonist, SR1078 belongs to the nuclear receptor modulator class of compounds, a family of therapeutics that have historically been used to orchestrate transcriptional programs related to metabolism, inflammation, and circadian regulation across various tissues (Solt & Burris, 2012). The synthetic origins of SR1078 trace back to programs that sought to optimize ligand interactions within the ROR ligand binding domain; detailed chemical characterization studies have shown that SR1078 binds and stabilizes the receptor’s active conformation, particularly by engaging critical residues that allow proper positioning of helix 12 for subsequent coactivator recruitment (Wang et al., 2010). This class of compounds has previously been employed primarily as a chemical biology probe in preclinical research, addressing metabolic dysregulation in liver and immunomodulatory effects in macrophages, and sometimes even in contexts such as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and autoimmune models (Matsuoka & Michihara, 2021; Wang et al., 2010).

Therapeutic History:  
SR1078 has been extensively exploited as a research tool rather than a clinical therapeutic; its major preclinical applications include the characterization of RORα-dependent transcriptional regulation in cell-based systems as well as demonstrating in vivo efficacy by modulating metabolic target genes such as FGF21 and G6Pase in liver tissue (Wang et al., 2010). In multiple studies, a single 10 mg/kg intraperitoneal (i.p.) dose of SR1078 in mice produced measurable plasma exposures in the low micromolar range—specifically approximately 3.6 μM at 1 hour post-dose—indicating that the compound has appreciable systemic bioavailability when administered in vivo (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016; Wang et al., 2010). Despite these promising pharmacokinetic data in non-ocular models, there are no registered clinical trials or preclinical studies in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal degenerative diseases on public repositories such as ClinicalTrials.gov (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.); indeed, the literature does not document any previous therapeutic use of SR1078 for treating dry AMD or analogous retinal conditions (Wang et al., 2010). Moreover, while several studies have harnessed SR1078 to explore ROR-dependent transcriptional mechanisms in liver and immune cells, the compound’s utility in ocular pathologies has not been established, which means that its repurposing for AMD remains a novel and uncharted application at this time (Solt & Burris, 2012; Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SR1078 exerts its pharmacological effects by binding directly to the ligand binding domains (LBDs) of the retinoic acid receptor–related orphan receptors, with particular emphasis on RORα. Binding of SR1078 induces a conformational change in the receptor that leads to stabilization of helix 12 (H12), a structural event that is critical for the recruitment of LXXLL-containing coactivator proteins (Wang et al., 2010). This ligand-dependent stabilization promotes enhanced transcription of canonical ROR target genes including metabolic regulators such as fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) and glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase), as demonstrated in liver-based assays in HepG2 cells and in vivo in murine models (Wang et al., 2010). Additionally, in immunological contexts, RORα activation by SR1078 has been associated with shifts in macrophage polarization toward an M2 phenotype via upregulation of the Krüppel-like factor 4 (KLF4) gene, showcasing the versatility of RORα signaling in modulating inflammatory states (Matsuoka & Michihara, 2021). Despite these well-characterized mechanisms, it must be noted that the current literature does not provide any direct evidence that SR1078 modulates the transcription of phagocytic receptors—particularly S1PR5—in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) or that it enhances the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016; Solt & Burris, 2012). The hypothesis under consideration extends the established mechanism of SR1078’s action into a novel pathway linked to RPE physiology by proposing that SR1078 activation of RORα will lead to upregulation of S1PR5, a receptor that is implicated in phagosome maturation and may offer MERTK-independent enhancement of POS uptake and trafficking (Buniello et al., 2025). However, while SR1078 is well characterized for its ROR-dependent transcriptional effects in other cell types, detailed biochemical data connecting its activity to the expression of S1PR5 in RPE remain absent in the current literature corpus (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016; Solt & Burris, 2012). Furthermore, studies investigating RORα in retinal contexts have primarily focused on inflammatory and angiogenic processes, with limited discussion of phagocytic receptor dynamics and POS handling (Buniello et al., 2025; Lew, Mazzoni, & Finnemann, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing SR1078 for dry AMD is that activation of RORα in RPE cells by SR1078 will drive transcriptional upregulation of S1PR5, thereby enhancing the availability or function of phagocytic receptors required for the efficient uptake, trafficking, and eventual degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). This is especially relevant for MERTK-mutant iPSC-RPE models, where defective MERTK-dependent phagocytosis has been well-documented as a key pathological mechanism leading to accumulations of POS debris and subsequent retinal degeneration (Ramsden et al., 2017; Lukovic et al., 2015). In these models, MERTK deficiency abolishes the normal internalization of POS, leading to functional deficits in the RPE (Ramsden et al., 2017). The expected therapeutic effect of SR1078, as posited, would be the restoration of phagocytic capacity through a bypass mechanism; by activating RORα, it is anticipated that SR1078 may upregulate S1PR5 expression, which in turn is hypothesized to support phagosome maturation and a pathway of POS uptake that does not solely rely on MERTK signaling (Buniello et al., 2025). This effect is bolstered by mechanistic reasoning suggesting that S1P receptor signaling plays a role in phagosome dynamics, as demonstrated in studies highlighting sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) mediated regulatory pathways in the RPE (Lee et al., 2025); however, it is important to emphasize that these studies have primarily implicated S1PR3 rather than S1PR5, and the evidence for S1PR5’s involvement in RPE phagocytosis is comparatively limited (Buniello et al., 2025). Additionally, a follow-up reference (Unknown Reference) has been mentioned in internal discussions to indicate that SR1078 induces S1PR5 transcription in RPE, although this publication is not directly available in the current context. Therefore, if the hypothesis holds true, treatment with SR1078 would be expected to mitigate the phagocytic deficits observed in MERTK-mutant iPSC-RPE by increasing the transcriptional output of S1PR5 and possibly other RORα-dependent genes linked to membrane trafficking and lipid handling, thereby normalizing POS processing and ultimately slowing the progression of dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025). However, any such expected effect remains largely hypothetical at this stage, given the absence of direct experimental data linking SR1078-mediated RORα activation to enhanced POS uptake in RPE cells (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016; Solt & Burris, 2012).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating SR1078 as a therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses need to be considered. One of the major strengths is that SR1078 is a well-characterized synthetic agonist with robust biochemical evidence supporting its ability to modulate RORα activity. Its pharmacological profile includes demonstrable in vivo exposure, with measurable plasma concentrations following i.p. dosing, and it has been shown to activate canonical ROR target genes in hepatic and immune cell contexts (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016; Wang et al., 2010). Its established use as a chemical biology tool provides a solid foundation regarding its mechanism of action, including the ligand-induced stabilization of helix 12 within the receptor’s ligand binding domain, a critical determinant for coactivator recruitment and transcriptional activation (Wang et al., 2010). Moreover, SR1078’s potential brain penetrance is cited in internal discussions, which could be advantageous for targeting tissues behind biological barriers such as the blood–retina barrier, although detailed ocular pharmacokinetic data are not available in the current literature (Wang et al., 2010). This systemic exposure and preclinical PK profile may allow for eventual ocular delivery if its safety and efficacy in retinal cells can be established.

Despite these strengths, there are notable weaknesses and gaps in the evidence supporting the repurposing of SR1078 for dry AMD. First, while SR1078 is a proven RORα agonist in other tissue systems, there is no direct experimental data demonstrating that RORα activation by SR1078 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) leads to upregulation of S1PR5 or enhancement of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake. The proposed mechanism—that RORα activation will upregulate S1PR5, which in turn supports phagosome maturation and MERTK-independent POS uptake—is conceptually plausible, but it remains speculative in the absence of specific studies connecting these dots (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016; Solt & Burris, 2012). In fact, available open-target data suggest that while RORA (and by extension, its modulators) has some animal-model support in retinal diseases, both RORA and S1PR5 display minimal recorded evidence linking them directly to age-related macular degeneration (Buniello et al., 2025).

Another concern is the potential for adverse effects. One excerpt has indicated that activation of RORα by SR1078 in certain cellular contexts can result in elevated p53 levels and apoptosis (Solt & Burris, 2012). Such pro-apoptotic effects in RPE cells would be counterproductive in any therapy aimed at rescuing or preserving photoreceptor function, since the health of the RPE is critical for maintaining retinal integrity (Solt & Burris, 2012).

Furthermore, while several preclinical studies document the efficacy of SR1078 in modulating metabolic and immune pathways in liver and macrophage models (Wang et al., 2010; Matsuoka & Michihara, 2021), none of these studies have extended their investigations into RPE cell biology or directly measured outcomes such as POS phagocytosis. Given that alternative strategies—such as translational readthrough inducing drugs (TRIDs) and AAV-mediated gene therapies—are already in development to address MERTK deficiency (Ramsden et al., 2017; Lukovic et al., 2015), the rationale for pursuing a strategy based on RORα agonism hinges critically on demonstrating that SR1078 can effect a meaningful rescue of phagocytic function in these specialized cellular models. At present, the literature does not provide such evidence; thus, the anticipated beneficial effect in the RPE remains hypothetical.

Moreover, the clinical and translational track record of drugs targeting nuclear receptors is mixed. While some compounds in this class have advanced to clinical use in metabolic and inflammatory disorders, many have faced issues related to off-target effects or an unfavorable safety profile due to the broad physiological roles of nuclear receptors (Solt & Burris, 2012). In the specific case of SR1078, the absence of any clinical trial data for retinal indications—as evidenced by a negative search on ClinicalTrials.gov—further underscores the need for caution as we consider its potential repurposing for dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

On the other hand, the conceptual framework behind the hypothesis—that modulating alternative phagocytic pathways might bypass MERTK-dependent defects—is compelling. MERTK mutations are well documented in models of retinitis pigmentosa and have been linked to defective POS internalization in RPE cells (Ramsden et al., 2017; Lukovic et al., 2015). If SR1078 can indeed stimulate an alternative route for POS clearance via upregulation of S1PR5, this could represent a novel therapeutic angle for a subset of dry AMD patients whose disease is driven by phagocytic insufficiency. S1PR5 has been implicated in phagosome maturation, and although its expression levels in RPE are reported to be low (Buniello et al., 2025), even a modest upregulation might yield functional benefits in the context of otherwise compromised clearance mechanisms. Nevertheless, the primary gap remains the absence of direct evidence; key experiments—such as validating S1PR5 upregulation upon SR1078 treatment in iPSC-derived RPE, demonstrating enhancements in POS uptake in MERTK-mutant models, and confirming the lack of deleterious pro-apoptotic effects in retinal cells—are urgently needed before this approach can be considered promising for clinical translation (Buniello et al., 2025; Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016).

In summary, SR1078 emerges as an intriguing candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its well-established mechanism as a RORα agonist, its favorable pharmacokinetic exposure in preclinical models, and its use as a robust tool compound in nuclear receptor biology. Its potential to influence cellular metabolism and inflammatory responses might theoretically be harnessed to modulate alternative pathways of phagocytosis in RPE, particularly in cases where MERTK mutations compromise the canonical clearance of photoreceptor outer segments. The direct relationship between RORα activation by SR1078 and the upregulation of S1PR5 in RPE is not substantiated by existing literature, and the evidentiary link connecting this pathway to enhanced photoreceptor outer segment processing remains highly speculative (Buniello et al., 2025; Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016).
