Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
FX-68 is a synthetic small‐molecule agonist developed from a chemical library (ChemBridge Cat. No. 6789012) and represents an emerging member of a class of chemokine receptor modulators that selectively target CX3CR1. This compound is designed to mimic the natural ligand, fractalkine (CX3CL1), and has been optimized for potency with an EC₅₀ of approximately 100 nM, which suggests that it is capable of activating CX3CR1 at pharmacologically achievable concentrations (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–5, 6–7). The candidate belongs to the broader category of small-molecule GPCR agonists, a class that has been successfully employed in various inflammatory and neurodegenerative indications because of their favorable oral bioavailability and capacity to cross biological barriers; such compounds have a long history in modulating immune cell behavior and attenuating aberrant inflammation (Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 2–4; Chinnery et al., 2012, pp. 7–8). In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), FX-68 is proposed to restore appropriate signaling in the CX3CL1–CX3CR1 axis—a pathway that is critically involved in the regulation of microglial migration, phagocytosis and, indirectly, the trophic support provided to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6). Its synthetic origin coupled with repurposing potential makes FX-68 an attractive candidate for conditions in which deficient microglial clearance and disrupted RPE–microglia crosstalk contribute to disease progression (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3, 4–5).

Therapeutic History:  
The link between CX3CR1 function and retinal health was established through extensive genetic and preclinical studies, in which loss-of-function mutations or deficiencies in CX3CR1 were found to produce a constellation of AMD-like features, including the accumulation of subretinal microglia, formation of drusen-like deposits, and secondary photoreceptor degeneration (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7; Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 4–5). Historically, research in this area has focused on genetic knock-out models and human polymorphism analyses rather than on the administration of direct pharmacologic agonists; for example, CX3CR1-deficient mice consistently exhibit abnormal subretinal microglial behavior and accompanying retinal pathology, which has been used as a rationale for targeting this signaling pathway therapeutically (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–6). Although exogenous delivery of CX3CL1 has been explored in certain experimental paradigms, no small-molecule CX3CR1 agonist has yet been advanced in clinical or veterinary practice for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerations (Chinnery et al., 2012, pp. 7–8; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3). Instead, the therapeutic potential in this space has largely emerged indirectly from studies that demonstrate that disrupted CX3CR1 signaling is deleterious to retinal homeostasis, thereby suggesting that its appropriate stimulation could restore normal microglial behavior (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7). As a repurposed candidate, FX-68 aims to fill this translational gap by reactivating a pathway that is both genetically implicated in AMD and mechanistically understood in other contexts of neuroinflammation (Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 2–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
The CX3CL1–CX3CR1 axis is a pivotal mediator of neuron–microglia communication in the retina and broader central nervous system, where fractalkine (CX3CL1) exists in both membrane-bound and soluble forms and interacts exclusively with CX3CR1, a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) expressed predominantly by microglia (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–5, 6–7). Under physiological conditions, tonic signaling through CX3CR1 serves to restrain microglial activation, regulate their migratory behavior, and facilitate their efficient surveillance and debris clearance functions (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6). In the diseased retina—such as in dry AMD—loss or dysfunction of CX3CR1 impairs these regulatory mechanisms, leading to chronic accumulation of lipid-laden microglia in the subretinal space, excessive phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and subsequent RPE stress and degeneration, a sequence that contributes to the formation of drusen-like deposits and ultimately to photoreceptor cell death (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3, 6–7).

FX-68 is designed as a CX3CR1 agonist that binds to and activates this receptor, mimicking the natural action of CX3CL1. Upon binding, it is expected to trigger downstream signaling cascades typical of GPCR activation, including modulation of adenylate cyclase activity and activation of MAP kinase pathways, which in turn alter cytoskeletal dynamics essential for microglial migration and phagocytosis (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–6). At a molecular level, proper CX3CR1 activation is theorized to correct the aberrant microglial behavior seen in CX3CR1 deficiency: it should promote the egression or apoptotic clearance of subretinal microglia that have phagocytosed excessive amounts of POS debris and prevent their transformation into foam cells laden with intracellular lipids (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7; Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4). Moreover, by reestablishing a functional microglia–RPE communication axis, FX-68 may help restore the RPE’s inherent phagocytic capacity to clear POS effectively, ultimately leading to improved outer retinal homeostasis (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). With CX3CR1 activation, signaling may also suppress the production of proangiogenic factors such as VEGF, thereby limiting pathological neovascularization—a secondary complication sometimes observed in the context of AMD (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). This mechanism is further supported by studies in which exogenous CX3CL1 reduced microglial phagocytosis and inflammatory activation in models of retinal degeneration, albeit in genetic loss-of-function contexts rather than using a pharmacologic agonist (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Zabel et al., 2016, pp. 10–12). The overall molecular interaction profile of FX-68, therefore, hinges on reinstating the anti-inflammatory, pro-homeostatic functions of CX3CR1 in retinal microglia, with the intended effect of reducing deleterious phagocytosis and enhancing trophic support for the RPE (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assays and in preclinical models—particularly in the challenging Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mouse model, which recapitulates many aspects of dry AMD—the expected effect of FX-68 is multifaceted. First, by binding and activating CX3CR1 on retinal microglia, FX-68 is anticipated to restore regulated cell migration and proper phagocytic clearance, thereby reducing the abnormal accumulation of subretinal microglia that is observed in CX3CR1-deficient models (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). Such restoration is expected to lead to a normalization of the phagocytic process, where instead of over-ingesting POS debris and becoming lipid-laden foam cells, microglia will clear debris efficiently and then either return to a surveillant state or undergo timely apoptosis or emigration away from the subretinal space (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6).

Second, FX-68 is proposed to facilitate enhanced trophic support for RPE cells. Evidence suggests that proper microglial signaling is critically involved in modulating RPE phagocytosis of POS, partly through the secretion of growth factors and early inflammatory mediators that prime RPE cells for efficient clearance functions (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). In co-culture assays involving microglia and RPE cells, treatment with FX-68 is expected to lead to an increase in the efficiency of POS turnover, as microglial activation is reined in and redirected toward beneficial debris clearance rather than deleterious inflammatory activation (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). This effect, in theory, would reduce the buildup of toxic debris in the subretinal region, limit the formation of drusen-like deposits and diminish secondary inflammatory and proangiogenic signaling, such as excessive VEGF release, that further compromise retinal integrity (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3; Rashid et al., 2019, p. 14).

Moreover, in animal models like the Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mice—where the dual deficiency exacerbates retinal degeneration and drusen-like pathology—FX-68 is expected to mitigate these phenotypes by reactivating the CX3CR1 pathway. The hypothesis posits that restoration of CX3CR1 signaling will not only lower subretinal microglial accumulation but also re-establish a crosstalk with the RPE that is essential for maintaining the delicate balance between debris clearance and inflammation (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). In this way, the compound may indirectly improve photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance, thereby preserving overall photoreceptor function and slowing the progression of dry AMD (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6; Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4).

An important aspect of the expected effect is the modulation of microglial cytokine production. CX3CR1 signaling has been linked to the suppression of proinflammatory pathways—in particular, the reduction of IL-1β and VEGF expression, which are key mediators of chronic inflammation and pathological angiogenesis (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). FX-68, by serving as a CX3CR1 agonist, would clarify whether the attenuation of these proinflammatory signals could indeed translate to structural and functional retinal preservation in vivo. This result would be highly significant given that chronic inflammation is a critical driver of dry AMD progression (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3; Rashid et al., 2019, p. 14).

Furthermore, the expected effect extends to the normalization of microglial morphology and dispersal. In healthy retinas, microglia are characterized by a ramified morphology that is conducive to efficient surveillance, whereas in CX3CR1-deficient retinas, microglia become amoeboid, exhibit excessive adhesion, and accumulate in the subretinal space (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Homotaurine is a small-molecule GABA analogue that was originally investigated for its potential neuroprotective properties in Alzheimer’s disease due to its ability to interact with inhibitory neurotransmitter receptors. Although originally isolated from marine algae as a natural sulfonated amino acid derivative, the synthetic production of homotaurine has allowed for its repurposing and pharmacological refinement for various clinical indications. As a member of the GABAergic modulator class, it is designed to mimic the activity of the endogenous neurotransmitter γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), thereby affecting neuronal excitability and cellular homeostasis. In particular, homotaurine is postulated to activate GABAA receptors, which are ligand-gated chloride channels that normally contribute to membrane hyperpolarization and dampening of excitatory input. This class of compounds has been widely explored for neuroprotective purposes and has been utilized in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease, where an acceptable safety profile was established. The fact that homotaurine has progressed to advanced clinical stages in Alzheimer’s research supports its tolerability and widespread bioactivity, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in ocular diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Carullo et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, homotaurine has been primarily evaluated in the context of Alzheimer’s disease, where its anti-aggregation properties and potential to interfere with amyloid-β deposition were of paramount interest. Its prior clinical examination, which concluded with a favorable safety record, provides a solid foundation for its repurposing in other neurodegenerative conditions. Although there is no direct record of homotaurine being used to treat dry AMD, other compounds that modulate GABAergic signaling have been investigated in retinal degenerative models. For example, several studies have documented the expression of GABA receptor subunits, including those of the GABAA family, in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, suggesting that pharmacological targeting of these receptors may have therapeutic implications in diseases associated with retinal dysfunction (Arellano et al., 2025). Furthermore, inhibitory neurotransmitters such as GABA have been implicated in maintaining proper cellular excitability and synaptic balance in the retina; alterations in their regulation are associated with excitotoxicity and neurodegeneration in retinal conditions including macular degeneration (Pavan & Dalpiaz, 2018; Schur et al., 2018). In a similar vein, preclinical studies have used GABA modulators to rescue or protect RPE and photoreceptor function in models of retinal degeneration and light-induced injury (Schur et al., 2018). Thus, while direct clinical evidence for homotaurine in dry AMD is lacking, its antecedents in the GABAergic drug class and the known vulnerability of RPE cells to excitotoxic calcium overload position it as a promising candidate for therapeutic repurposing.

Mechanism of Action:  
The hypothesized mechanism of action of homotaurine in dry AMD rests on its ability to activate GABAA receptors expressed on RPE cells. Under physiological conditions, GABAA receptors are heteropentameric chloride channels that, upon binding GABA, permit chloride influx and hyperpolarize the cell membrane. This hyperpolarization ordinarily serves to counteract excessive excitation and limit voltage-gated calcium channel opening. In the context of RPE function, maintaining a tight regulation of intracellular calcium is paramount because calcium levels directly influence cytoskeletal reorganization, phagosome trafficking, and lysosomal fusion events necessary for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Nagymihaly et al., 2021). Several studies have documented that RPE cells not only express GABAA receptor subunits, such as GABAAα1, but that receptor activation in these cells can modify intracellular calcium concentrations, thereby modulating a host of calcium-dependent cellular processes—including phagocytosis (Arellano et al., 2025).

In dry AMD, the RPE’s phagocytic capacity is compromised, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and other toxic by-products, which in turn further disrupt cellular function and promote oxidative stress (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018). Homotaurine’s binding to GABAA receptors is expected to stabilize the membrane potential and reduce the abnormal Ca²⁺ influx that occurs during excitotoxic stress. This reduction in calcium entry is anticipated to alleviate downstream effects such as dysregulated cytoskeletal dynamics and impaired lysosomal trafficking. Cytoskeletal reorganization is essential for phagosome motility; proper F-actin dynamics direct the trafficking of phagosomes toward lysosomal compartments where degradation occurs (Inana et al., 2018; Nagymihaly et al., 2021). Moreover, studies have demonstrated that inflammatory mediators present in AMD, including TNF-α and interleukin-1β, modulate GABAA receptor expression and function, suggesting that modulation of these receptors could be a viable strategy to counteract inflammation-driven excitotoxicity (Arellano et al., 2025). In addition, the excitotoxic environment generated by imbalanced glutamate/GABA signaling in the retina can be mitigated by restoring the inhibitory tone through GABAA receptor activation. The specific EC₅₀ of approximately 10 µM for homotaurine indicates that it has the potential to achieve receptor activation within a therapeutic window that is plausible in an ocular formulation (Carullo et al., 2020; Arellano et al., 2025). Taken together, the combined modulation of calcium influx, along with the stabilization of cytoskeletal and lysosomal pathways, constitutes a comprehensive molecular strategy that homotaurine may employ to rescue impaired POS degradation in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed assay in ARPE-19 cells—a well-established in vitro model for RPE function—aims to evaluate whether homotaurine, via activation of GABAA receptors, can restore impaired photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis under conditions of glutamate-induced stress. RPE cell dysfunction in dry AMD is characterized by diminished phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation of POS, leading to the pathological accumulation of lipofuscin, which further impedes cellular function (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018). By engaging GABAA receptors, homotaurine is expected to “rescue” this vital phagocytic process by normalizing intracellular Ca²⁺ dynamics—thus preventing excitotoxicity—and by ensuring the proper reorganization of actin filaments or other cytoskeletal elements that are essential for efficient phagosome motility (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).

Experimental evidence in related studies supports that compounds with similar mechanisms (i.e., GABA modulators and taurine-related molecules) are capable of influencing intracellular calcium signaling and can enhance the uptake and processing of POS in RPE cells (Arellano et al., 2025; López-Colomé et al., 1994). Under normo-physiological conditions, RPE cells efficiently internalize shed POS through receptor-mediated pathways involving CD36, MerTK, and αVβ5 integrin, initiating a cascade that is dependent on well-regulated intracellular Ca²⁺ fluctuations (Nagymihaly et al., 2021). In a stress state, glutamate excess drives excitotoxic Ca²⁺ entry that may dysregulate these processes. By antagonizing this excitotoxic cascade, homotaurine is anticipated to reduce the aberrant Ca²⁺ load, thereby restoring the dynamic equilibrium that supports both cytoskeletal integrity and lysosomal trafficking. This mechanism is supported by studies showing that dysregulation of Ca²⁺ not only impairs phagosome motility but also has deleterious effects on downstream lysosomal fusion and degradation, ultimately impacting cellular clearance mechanisms (Si et al., 2023; Nowak et al., 2025). Thus, the expected effect is a measurable enhancement in POS uptake as well as improved degradation kinetics in RPE cells subjected to glutamate-induced stress, which would correlate with potential therapeutic efficacy in dry AMD. Furthermore, since the underlying pathology of dry AMD involves chronic oxidative stress and accumulation of metabolic by-products, a pharmacological intervention that can restore intracellular homeostasis has far-reaching implications for halting or even reversing disease progression (Arellano et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating homotaurine for dry age-related macular degeneration, several critical observations emerge. One of the key strengths of homotaurine is its well-documented safety profile from Alzheimer’s clinical trials, which lowers the translational hurdles when repurposing the compound for ocular administration. The fact that homotaurine is a GABA analogue that activates GABAA receptors—a receptor class that is expressed on RPE cells and critically involved in regulating intracellular Ca²⁺—provides a strong mechanistic rationale for its application in dry AMD (Arellano et al., 2025). By potentially mitigating excitotoxic Ca²⁺ influx, homotaurine could restore normal cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal trafficking, both of which are indispensable for the effective degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).

Among the strengths, the following points are notable:  
1. The candidate’s mechanism directly addresses a central pathology of dry AMD—namely, impaired RPE phagocytosis and lysosomal dysfunction—which leads to toxic lipofuscin accumulation (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018).  
2. Activation of GABAA receptors by homotaurine could normalize Ca²⁺ handling within RPE cells, thereby alleviating the excitotoxic stress that is linked to altered cytoskeletal assembly and defective phagosome trafficking (Arellano et al., 2025; Inana et al., 2018).  
3. The compound’s history in Alzheimer’s trials suggests a favorable safety margin and known pharmacokinetic properties that may be adapted for ocular use, thus enhancing its potential for rapid clinical translation (Carullo et al., 2020).  
4. Preclinical evidence from other studies involving GABA modulators and related compounds shows that interfering with aberrant neurotransmitter signaling in the retina can elicit neuroprotective and phagocytosis-enhancing effects (Schur et al., 2018).

Conversely, some weaknesses and uncertainties remain that necessitate further investigation:  
1. Although the proposed EC₅₀ of approximately 10 µM for homotaurine is within a plausible therapeutic window for GABAA receptor activation, the actual pharmacodynamic response in RPE cells—especially in the diseased microenvironment of dry AMD—remains to be rigorously quantified (Arellano et al., 2025).  
2. The retinal microenvironment in dry AMD is complex, characterized not only by excitotoxic stress but also by chronic oxidative stress, inflammation, and altered expression of multiple receptor types. In such a context, GABAA receptor activation could be affected by altered ionic gradients, potentially leading to reversed or atypical receptor responses as has been documented in other retinal degenerations (Arellano et al., 2025; Telegina et al., 2022).  
3. While indirect evidence supports the role of GABAergic modulation in restoring phagocytic function, there is a paucity of direct data demonstrating that homotaurine can specifically enhance POS uptake in ARPE-19 cells under injurious conditions. This gap necessitates additional in vitro studies to detail its effects on cytoskeletal reorganization, vesicular trafficking, and lysosomal fusion dynamics (Si et al., 2023; Nagymihaly et al., 2021).  
4. The exact downstream signaling pathways that link GABAA receptor activation to the observed improvements in phagocytic function must be delineated further. For example, the interplay between calcium channel deactivation, actin cytoskeleton stabilization, and the regulation of key phagocytic receptors (e.g., MerTK, αvβ5 integrin) remains incompletely characterized in the context of GABAergic modulation (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).  
5. Finally, the translational leap from in vitro findings in ARPE-19 cells to a robust therapeutic effect in human dry AMD patients is non-trivial. Aging RPE cells in vivo exhibit additional layers of complexity, including altered gene expression profiles, metabolic imbalances, and possible shifts in receptor isoforms, all of which might influence the responsiveness to homotaurine (Nowak et al., 2025; Si et al., 2023).

Overall, homotaurine represents a scientifically sound and mechanistically plausible candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its potential to activate GABAA receptors on RPE cells, thereby reducing excitotoxic calcium influx and normalizing the intracellular processes that govern cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal trafficking, aligns well with the pathophysiological underpinnings of AMD (Arellano et al., 2025). Given the favorable safety data from Alzheimer’s trials and the breadth of preclinical evidence supporting the neuroprotective effects of GABAergic modulation in retinal contexts, homotaurine merits further exploration. Prior to clinical application, however, detailed mechanistic studies using ARPE-19 cells and appropriate animal models of dry AMD must be conducted. These studies should focus on quantifying calcium flux, cytoskeletal dynamics, phagosome motility, and lysosomal fusion efficiency upon homotaurine treatment under pathologically relevant conditions. Additionally, it will be important to investigate potential off-target effects and to determine whether combinatorial therapies that address oxidative stress and inflammation might synergize with homotaurine’s mechanism. In summary, while challenges remain, the repurposing of homotaurine for dry AMD offers a promising therapeutic avenue worthy of investment and further preclinical validation (Arellano et al., 2025; Si et al., 2023; Carullo et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bryostatin‐1 is a naturally derived macrolide originally isolated from marine invertebrates and belongs to a class of compounds collectively known as bryostatins. These compounds exhibit potent modulation of protein kinase C (PKC) activity by binding to the enzyme’s diacylglycerol binding site on the regulatory domain. Bryostatin‐1 has been characterized as a partial agonist of PKC and is noted for its ability to both acutely activate and chronically down‐regulate specific PKC isoforms. The molecular architecture of bryostatin‐1 confers a unique binding profile that distinguishes it from phorbol esters; it induces translocation of target PKC isoforms to membranes without eliciting the full tumor‐promoting effects observed with phorbol esters. The compound is synthetically challenging to produce, yet semisynthetic methodologies have enabled its preparation in sufficient quantities for preclinical and early clinical applications. As a member of the marine natural products family, bryostatin‐1 is frequently investigated for its anticancer and neuroprotective properties, and its chemical structure serves as the basis for designing simplified analogs with improved pharmacological profiles (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).  

Therapeutic History:  
Bryostatin‐1 has a long preclinical history that spans oncology and neurology. In oncology, bryostatin‐1 has been extensively studied for its role in modulating PKC in various tumor types and has been evaluated in numerous clinical trials addressing B‐cell malignancies and renal cancers. Despite promising preclinical results, its cancer‐directed clinical efficacy has been limited by suboptimal outcomes and adverse side effects such as myalgia. More recently, bryostatin‐1 has been repurposed in neurological contexts. Several studies have demonstrated its neuroprotective capabilities in models of Alzheimer’s disease, where it has shown to improve synaptic function, restore dendritic spine morphology, induce synaptogenesis through the upregulation of brain‐derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and enhance cognitive function. Phase II clinical trials in Alzheimer’s patients have provided translational evidence of its ability to modulate PKCε in the central nervous system (Chen et al., 2024; Nelson et al., 2017). However, a search of clinical trial databases has revealed that no formal clinical trials have been registered evaluating bryostatin‐1 in the setting of macular degeneration, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, or Rab7 signaling‐related pathways (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Although there is evidence supporting bryostatin‐1’s capacity to affect cellular pathways—such as inducing autophagy and promoting PKC‐mediated cell survival—in neuronal and cancer cells, its application to ocular diseases like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) remains unexplored in the clinical context (Safarpour, 2009; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).  

Mechanism of Action:  
Bryostatin‐1 functions primarily as a modulator of protein kinase C, a family of serine/threonine kinases that play central roles in regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis, and intracellular trafficking. On a molecular level, bryostatin‐1 binds competitively to the diacylglycerol (DAG) binding site located in the C1 domain of PKC isoforms. This binding event leads to the translocation of PKC from the cytosol to membranous compartments, thereby bringing the kinase into close proximity with its substrates. Unlike potent activators such as phorbol esters, bryostatin‐1 acts as a partial agonist. Short‐term exposure results in the activation of specific PKC isoforms, whereas prolonged exposure leads to their down‐regulation via proteasomal degradation. Structural studies have demonstrated that the complex hydrogen‐bond networks formed by the A- and B-rings of bryostatin‐1 contribute significantly to its isoform selectivity and binding affinity (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).  

In the context of the hypothesized mechanism for dry AMD, it is proposed that bryostatin‐1 can activate atypical PKC isoforms at very low effective concentrations (EC₅₀ ≈ 0.1 nM), potentially including enzymes that are involved in the regulation of Rab7 signalling. Although bryostatin‐1 has been studied predominantly for its activation of classical (e.g., PKCα, PKCβ) and novel PKC isoforms (e.g., PKCδ, PKCε), several experimental reports suggest that PKC activity regulates various aspects of vesicular trafficking, including phagosome maturation. In phagocytic cell lines, enhanced PKC activation has been linked to improved phagolysosomal fusion, which is essential for the degradation of ingested material. This connection is of particular interest in RPE cells, where the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) via the phagosome–lysosome pathway is central to retinal homeostasis. The hypothesis extends this mechanism by proposing that the activation of PKC by bryostatin‐1 may lead to the phosphorylation of Rab7 effector proteins, which are known to control the late stages of phagosome maturation and lysosome fusion. Although direct experimental evidence connecting bryostatin‐1‐mediated PKC activation to Rab7 effector phosphorylation in RPE cells is limited, existing literature has established the importance of PKC in regulating phagocytic processes and intracellular vesicle trafficking (Saddala et al., 2020; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005). Furthermore, mechanistic parallels drawn from studies in neuronal systems—where bryostatin‐1 has been shown to influence autophagic flux and promote synaptic health—support the feasibility of such a cellular response in other highly phagocytic cells like the RPE (Chen et al., 2024).  

Expected Effect:  
Dry AMD is characterized by the dysfunction of RPE cells, which leads to impaired clearance of POS and subsequent accumulation of toxic lipofuscin deposits. RPE dysfunction is associated with disrupted phagosome maturation and lysosomal degradation pathways, contributing to retinal degeneration and vision loss. The therapeutic hypothesis for bryostatin‐1 posits that its administration will enhance the maturation of phagosomes by stimulating PKC isoforms that, in turn, phosphorylate Rab7 effectors. Effective phosphorylation of these effectors is expected to facilitate late phagosome–lysosome fusion, thereby improving the trafficking and degradation of POS. Empirical studies in RPE cells have shown that defects in phagolysosomal fusion lead to the accumulation of nondegradable materials and are closely linked to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Safarpour, 2009; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).  

The candidate mechanism suggests that, upon administration, bryostatin‐1 will rapidly bind to its target PKC isoforms in RPE cells, causing these kinases to translocate to relevant subcellular membranes. This translocation is anticipated to bring PKC in proximity to Rab7 effectors situated on late phagosomes. Activation of these kinases would then promote the phosphorylation of regulatory proteins that control vesicular fusion events. As a result, the impaired phagocytosis observed in dry AMD would be corrected through improved maturation of phagosomes and enhanced fusion with lysosomes. Such a cascade is expected to lead to enhanced clearance of POS debris and, ultimately, a reduction in lipofuscin accumulation, which is central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Although supportive evidence for this cascade exists in the context of non‐ocular phagocytic cells and in neuronal models of autophagy activation, it remains imperative to directly evaluate these effects in primary RPE cell cultures or relevant animal models to solidify the connection between PKC activation by bryostatin‐1 and Rab7‐mediated phagosome maturation (Saddala et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Bryostatin‐1 presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for dry AMD owing to its potent modulation of PKC, a central regulator of intracellular signaling pathways that govern vesicular trafficking, phagocytosis, and autophagy. One of the key strengths of bryostatin‐1 lies in its well‐documented activity in modulating PKC isoforms that are critical in diverse physiological contexts, including neuronal function and cancer cell biology. Its demonstrated neuroprotective efficacy in Alzheimer’s disease clinical studies supports the compound’s translational potential and suggests that its PKC‐modulating effects might be harnessed in alternate tissues such as the retina (Chen et al., 2024). Additionally, the critical role of PKC in promoting phagosome–lysosome fusion has been substantiated in other cell types, which provides a strong theoretical basis for its application in RPE cells where phagocytic clearance is essential for maintaining retinal integrity (Saddala et al., 2020; Safarpour, 2009).

Despite these promising aspects, several challenges and weaknesses must be considered. Foremost, no direct studies to date have evaluated bryostatin‐1 in the context of dry AMD or in RPE cells. Clinical trial databases have not registered any studies for bryostatin‐1 in macular degeneration, underscoring the novelty of this repurposing strategy but also highlighting a significant gap in the literature (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The hypothesis that bryostatin‐1 will stimulate atypical PKC isoforms to phosphorylate Rab7 effectors, although plausible, remains largely speculative. While various studies have linked PKC activity to phagosome maturation and autophagy regulation, the precise isoforms relevant to RPE cell function—and whether these isoforms are the same ones activated by bryostatin‐1 in neuronal or cancer models—have not been comprehensively elucidated. Therefore, it will be crucial to determine, through rigorous in vitro assays and animal models, whether the purported EC₅₀ of approximately 0.1 nM is achievable in RPE cells and whether this concentration effectively modifies the Rab7‐related molecular machinery.

Additional considerations include the potential for off‐target effects and systemic toxicity. Past clinical studies of bryostatin‐1, particularly in oncology, have reported adverse effects such as myalgia and thrombocytopenia. However, the pharmacokinetic profile observed in Alzheimer’s trials suggests that the dosing regimens used for neurological disorders might be translatable to ocular delivery with appropriate formulation strategies. Localized ocular delivery, such as intravitreal injection or controlled‐release implants, may enable targeted modulation of PKC in the retina while mitigating systemic exposure and associated adverse events (Chen et al., 2024; Nelson et al., 2017). Moreover, the challenge of achieving adequate drug penetration to the RPE in vivo is nontrivial. Approaches to enhance ocular bioavailability, including nanoparticle encapsulation or conjugation to targeting ligands, should be explored concurrently with the design of preclinical studies to better validate this therapeutic candidate.

From a mechanistic standpoint, the dual nature of bryostatin‐1—characterized by initial activation followed by downregulation of PKC isoforms—necessitates precise temporal control of its pharmacodynamic effects. In the context of phagosome maturation, transient activation may be beneficial to restore proper lysosomal fusion; however, prolonged downregulation might counteract the desired effect. It is therefore important that future studies carefully delineate the dosing regimen (both concentration and administration frequency) required to achieve an optimal therapeutic window in RPE cells. Additionally, the specificity of bryostatin‐1 for PKC isoforms implicated in Rab7 effector phosphorylation must be confirmed, as the RPE expresses a complex array of PKC isoforms that may play distinct roles in cellular homeostasis and stress responses (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).

The breadth and diversity of bryostatin‐1’s effects in preclinical models have generated considerable interest, yet its repurposing for dry AMD remains at an early stage of conceptual development. Given that disruption of phagosome maturation in RPE cells is a well‐established contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD—and that PKC signaling has been implicated in regulating this process—the rationale for exploring bryostatin‐1 in this indication is scientifically sound. Nonetheless, the transition from a neuroprotective agent in Alzheimer’s disease to an effective modulator of RPE function in dry AMD will depend on new studies that specifically address the cellular context of the retina. In this regard, preliminary investigations using primary RPE cultures or animal models of dry AMD will be critical to validate the hypothesis that PKC activation by bryostatin‐1 can enhance Rab7‐mediated phagolysosomal fusion and improve POS clearance (Saddala et al., 2020; Safarpour, 2009).

In summary, bryostatin‐1 offers both significant promise and notable challenges as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration. Its ability to modulate PKC in a manner that may restore essential phagolysosomal functions in the RPE positions it as an innovative approach to address a major unmet need in ocular therapeutics. The compound’s successful use in Alzheimer’s disease trials provides encouraging translational evidence of its safety and efficacy in modulating neuronal PKC activity. However, the absence of direct evidence in retinal cells, the uncertainty regarding which specific PKC isoforms are most relevant to RPE phagocytosis, and potential issues related to dosing and systemic toxicity form significant hurdles that must be overcome. Moving forward, it will be critical to conduct comprehensive in vitro studies to assess the effects of bryostatin‐1 on RPE phagosome maturation, coupled with robust in vivo experiments in established dry AMD models. Such studies should focus on confirming the expression and role of the putative target proteins, including Rab7 effectors, and determining whether the activation of these pathways can indeed translate into improved clearance of POS and reduced retinal degeneration (Saddala et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Chen et al., 2024; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).

In conclusion, the overall evaluation of bryostatin‐1 as a drug candidate for dry AMD reveals a compound with strong mechanistic rationale and significant translational potential based on its established pharmacological properties in PKC modulation and neuroprotection. The strengths of bryostatin‐1 include its potent activity at nanomolar concentrations, a unique mode of action that distinguishes it from classical PKC activators, and supporting evidence from clinical studies in neurological disorders. Conversely, its weaknesses lie primarily in the absence of direct studies in ocular tissues, uncertainty regarding the specific PKC isoforms involved in RPE phagosome maturation, and potential challenges in achieving localized delivery without systemic side effects. An interdisciplinary approach that integrates detailed molecular studies with innovative drug delivery strategies will be critical in validating bryostatin‐1’s viability for the treatment of dry AMD. Based on the current literature, investing in rigorous preclinical testing to confirm the hypothesized mechanistic link between PKC activation, Rab7 effector phosphorylation, and enhanced phagosome maturation in RPE cells is warranted before progressing to clinical evaluation (Saddala et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Safarpour, 2009; Chen et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB415286 is a synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK-3β) that belongs to the class of anilinomaleimide derivatives. It was discovered through high-throughput screening approaches using compound libraries such as that of SmithKline Beecham, where its ability to inhibit GSK-3β activity was identified in vitro with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range (approximately 20 nM) (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). As a representative of GSK-3β inhibitors, SB415286 has been widely used as a research tool to interrogate the role of GSK-3β in multiple biological processes including Wnt/β-catenin signaling, apoptosis, oxidative stress regulation, and autophagy. The chemical optimization of these compounds was driven by the need for greater potency and specificity in modulating complex kinase networks associated with neurodegenerative and ocular pathologies. SB415286 is commercially available (Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. SML0787) and exhibits properties that make it suitable for cell-based assays as well as animal studies targeting retinal cell functions (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In general, compounds in this class have been used in preclinical models to activate Wnt signaling by preventing β-catenin degradation, thereby enhancing transcription of genes involved in cell survival, differentiation, and tissue regeneration. This approach has been applied primarily in neurological research as well as in studies focusing on retinal degeneration, making SB415286 a candidate of interest for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
GSK-3β inhibitors as a class have a long history of preclinical exploration in various disease models, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and other neurodegenerative disorders where excessive kinase activity contributes to neuronal cell death. SB415286, in particular, has been used in primary neuronal cultures to elucidate the role of GSK-3β in mediating apoptotic pathways. Early studies demonstrated that inhibition of GSK-3β with compounds like SB415286 could protect neurons from intracellular stresses by moderately suppressing pro-apoptotic signals (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In the ocular field, GSK-3β inhibitors have been explored in the context of diabetic retinopathy, where their use was associated with improved retinal ganglion cell survival and mitigation of neurodegenerative processes induced by oxidative stress (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20). Furthermore, related compounds such as SB216763—sharing similar mechanisms—with evidence of restoring Nrf2 levels in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) under oxidative stress supports the hypothesis that GSK-3β inhibition is beneficial in ocular settings (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6; Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 10–12). Despite these promising findings, the clinical evidence directly linking GSK-3β inhibition to the treatment of dry AMD remains sparse. In fact, comprehensive analyses such as those performed using the Open Targets Platform have revealed only a very weak association between GSK3B and AMD with minimal literature evidence, suggesting that while the concept is scientifically sound and mechanistically plausible, direct translational studies in dry AMD are still in an early stage (Buniello et al., 2025). Nevertheless, the preclinical use of SB415286 in retinal models of diabetic retinopathy and its documented capacity to modulate pathways relevant to oxidative stress and autophagy imply that repurposing this candidate for dry AMD merits further investigation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, GSK-3β is a serine/threonine kinase that is constitutively active in many cells and functions as a pivotal regulator of several intracellular signaling cascades. Under basal conditions, GSK-3β phosphorylates its substrates—including β-catenin—thereby marking them for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. In the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, the inhibition of GSK-3β (either through upstream signals such as Wnt ligand binding or via pharmacological inhibitors like SB415286) prevents the phosphorylation of β-catenin, allowing it to accumulate in the cytoplasm and eventually translocate into the nucleus (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Once in the nucleus, β-catenin forms complexes with TCF/LEF transcription factors to drive the transcription of genes involved in cell proliferation, differentiation, and cytoskeletal remodeling. In the context of RPE cells, this activation is critical because it is believed to upregulate lysosomal proteins, such as LAMP1, and phagocytic receptors, like MERTK, that are essential for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17; Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).  

Moreover, GSK-3β also exerts a negative regulatory influence on the Nrf2/NRF2 antioxidant pathway. Under oxidative stress, Nrf2 typically transactivates a battery of cytoprotective genes; however, GSK-3β phosphorylates Nrf2 at specific motifs within its Neh6 domain, facilitating recognition by the β-TrCP E3 ubiquitin ligase and leading to its degradation (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6). Hence, inhibition of GSK-3β with SB415286 can stabilize Nrf2, thereby reinforcing the cellular antioxidant capacity—a particularly attractive mechanism given the elevated oxidative stress encountered in aging RPE cells in dry AMD.  

In addition to these signaling events, inhibition of GSK-3β modulates autophagy. Research indicates that proper autophagic flux is necessary for the turnover of damaged cellular components, including the disposal of POS debris, and that impaired autophagy is a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 10–12, 32–34). By inhibiting GSK-3β, SB415286 is hypothesized to promote the autophagy/Nrf2 axis, thereby enhancing lysosomal function and improving the clearance of accumulated waste products in RPE cells. It is also important to note that GSK-3β is implicated in the regulation of the cytoskeletal machinery; its inhibition may lead to reorganization of actin and other cytoskeletal elements, which is critical for the phagocytic process in RPE cells (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). However, caution is warranted because GSK-3β not only modulates beneficial pathways but also participates in processes such as epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), where excessive or inappropriate inhibition has been associated with fibrotic changes in the RPE (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 14–18). Thus, while the inhibition of GSK-3β by SB415286 is expected to elevate β-catenin levels and trigger downstream transcription of lysosomal and cytoskeletal genes, the balance of these signaling events must be carefully modulated to avoid adverse outcomes.

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis proposes that SB415286 will act directly on RPE cells by inhibiting GSK-3β, thereby releasing the inhibition on β-catenin. The resultant accumulation and nuclear translocation of β-catenin are expected to drive the transcription of a subset of genes critical for maintaining RPE function, including those involved in lysosome biogenesis (e.g., LAMP1) and the phagocytic machinery (e.g., MERTK). In dry AMD, a deficiency in the clearance of POS is a contributing factor to RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration, so enhancing gene expression that supports these processes is of significant therapeutic interest (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17).  

In cell-based assays—particularly flow cytometry-based phagocytosis assays—it is anticipated that treatment with SB415286 will result in an increased rate of POS uptake by RPE cells. This improvement in phagocytic efficiency is thought to arise from the upregulation of cytoskeletal genes that govern actin dynamics, which in turn facilitate the formation of phagocytic cups and subsequent internalization of photoreceptor debris (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5; Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 32–34). Additionally, by relieving the negative regulation on Nrf2, SB415286 is expected to bolster the antioxidant defense mechanisms in RPE cells. The stabilization of Nrf2 not only aids in the upregulation of detoxification and radical-scavenging enzymes but also indirectly supports autophagy—a process crucial for the degradation of cellular waste and maintenance of cellular homeostasis in the aging RPE (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6).  

Furthermore, emerging data from ocular models of diabetic retinopathy provide supporting evidence that GSK-3β inhibitors can improve retinal cell survival and function. Although diabetic retinopathy and dry AMD are distinct conditions, both involve significant oxidative stress, inflammation, and RPE dysfunction. The translational potential observed in these models suggests that SB415286 may similarly ameliorate pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD by enhancing the phagocytic and lysosomal capacity of RPE cells (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20). Nevertheless, the dualistic nature of GSK-3β’s roles necessitates a cautious interpretation; while promoting β-catenin signaling is advantageous for lysosomal and cytoskeletal gene expression, overactivation of Wnt signaling has been implicated in unwanted cellular phenotypes such as EMT, which could potentiate fibrotic responses if not carefully controlled (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 14–18). Therefore, the expected beneficial effects of SB415286 on POS clearance must be weighed against the risk of activating other deleterious pathways.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating SB415286 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key aspects emerge from the literature review. On one hand, the compound’s potent inhibition of GSK-3β, a kinase centrally involved in multiple signaling pathways, offers a mechanistically coherent strategy for addressing several pathological features of dry AMD. By targeting GSK-3β, SB415286 is designed to simultaneously activate Wnt/β-catenin signaling and stabilize Nrf2, thereby promoting the transcription of genes such as LAMP1 and MERTK that are essential for effective lysosomal function and phagocytosis in RPE cells (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17). The induction of lysosomal and cytoskeletal genes is expected to enhance the phagocytic clearance of POS, a critical function that is often compromised in the diseased RPE, ultimately helping to mitigate the progression of dry AMD. Additionally, supportive evidence from diabetic retinopathy models and other retinal degeneration studies suggests that modulating GSK-3β activity can exert beneficial effects in ocular tissues (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20).  

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be considered. First, GSK-3β is a multifunctional kinase that plays roles in a wide array of cellular processes; it is involved not only in the regulation of the Wnt/β-catenin and Nrf2 pathways but also in the control of apoptosis, glucose homeostasis, and even inflammatory responses. The broad distribution and pleiotropic functions of GSK-3β raise concerns about off-target effects and unwanted side effects when its activity is pharmacologically inhibited. For instance, unchecked activation of β-catenin signaling could inadvertently promote epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in RPE cells—a process that has been linked to fibrotic changes and worsening of retinal pathology (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 14–18). The risk of such adverse outcomes underscores the importance of fine-tuning the dosage and exposure duration of SB415286 to achieve a therapeutic window that maximizes benefits while minimizing collateral activation of harmful signaling cascades.  

Another notable limitation is the relatively weak overall association between GSK3B and AMD as evidenced by integrative platforms, which point to only a minimal body of literature linking GSK-3β directly to the pathogenesis of AMD (Buniello et al., 2025). This weak association suggests that, although the mechanistic rationale for employing GSK-3β inhibitors is compelling at a biochemical level, direct evidence from AMD models remains limited. Consequently, while preclinical data in related retinal conditions are encouraging, additional research using dry AMD-specific models is required to establish the efficacy, safety, and dosing regimens for SB415286 in this context.  

Furthermore, the dual role of GSK-3β in both apoptosis and survival presents another layer of complexity. On one hand, inhibition of GSK-3β may protect RPE cells from intrinsic apoptotic stimuli by preventing the activation of mitochondrial death pathways; on the other hand, it may also inadvertently increase sensitivity to extrinsic apoptotic signals, thereby complicating the overall cellular response (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–5). This paradoxical effect, combined with the potential for overlap with other kinases given the structural similarity among kinase domains, necessitates rigorous pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic investigations to ensure that SB415286 can be administered safely without compromising RPE cell viability or function.  

In summary, SB415286 stands out as a promising repurposed drug candidate with a strong mechanistic foundation for the treatment of dry AMD. Its targeted inhibition of GSK-3β is expected to unleash β-catenin–driven transcriptional programs that upregulate lysosomal, cytoskeletal, and phagocytic genes, thereby enhancing the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments—a critical deficit in dry AMD pathology (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17). The compound’s track record in preclinical ocular models, particularly in contexts where oxidative stress and autophagic impairment are prominent, supports its potential translational value (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20). Nevertheless, the complexity of GSK-3β’s role in cellular signaling, the modest association between GSK3B and AMD observed in broader datasets, and the possibility of off-target effects, especially the unintended activation of fibrotic pathways, represent significant challenges that need to be addressed through comprehensive preclinical studies. Careful evaluation of dose, duration, and cell-type specificity will be critical in harnessing the therapeutic benefits of SB415286 while avoiding its potential pitfalls. Overall, while SB415286 is a promising candidate for dry AMD, its further development will require a balanced approach characterized by detailed mechanistic studies, robust in vitro and in vivo evaluations, and a clear understanding of the trade-offs inherent in modulating a kinase as pleiotropic as GSK-3β (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–3, 16–17; Buniello et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Metformin is a well‐established biguanide originally derived from the natural compound galegine found in Galega officinalis. Over decades of development, it has been chemically optimized and synthesized into its modern, orally administrable form. Today, metformin is classified within the antidiabetic drug class and is routinely used to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus. Its discovery as an antihyperglycemic agent was serendipitous, and subsequent structural modifications have resulted in a drug with an excellent safety profile and pleiotropic effects beyond blood glucose regulation. As a small synthetic molecule available from reputable suppliers such as Sigma‐Aldrich (Cat. No. D150959), metformin has been repurposed in recent years for potential applications outside of metabolic diseases, including neurodegeneration and retinal degenerative disorders. This candidate belongs to a class of compounds that have historically been used for systemic metabolic control, but emerging evidence also suggests that their ability to activate AMPK—a critical cellular energy sensor—can be exploited to modulate autophagy and mitochondrial function in non‐metabolic tissues, including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhao et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, metformin has long been the first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes due to its robust glucose-lowering capability and favorable long-term risk profile. The extensive clinical use of metformin in diabetic populations has allowed researchers to retrospectively observe its pleiotropic effects on other organ systems. Notably, retrospective epidemiological studies have demonstrated that diabetic patients treated with metformin exhibit a lower incidence of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) compared to non-users, suggesting potential protective effects in the retina (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Huang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Furthermore, preclinical studies investigating metformin in vitro have shown that it protects human RPE cells against oxidative stress-induced damage, largely mediated by stimulation of the AMPK pathway (Zhao et al., 2020). In addition, in vivo models employing metformin have provided evidence of its ability to mitigate light-induced photoreceptor loss and retinal degeneration, supporting the hypothesis that its molecular targets in the RPE could be leveraged against dry AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Miyagishima et al., 2021). Although metformin has not been established as a conventional treatment for AMD, its proven use in modulating metabolic pathways, along with demonstrable effects on autophagy, mitochondrial function, and inflammation in retinal cells, provides the rationale for repurposing it in the context of dry AMD (Vessey et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, metformin exerts its primary pharmacological effects by inhibiting mitochondrial electron transport chain complex I, which leads to a reduction in ATP production and a concomitant increase in the AMP/ATP ratio. This energetic shift results in the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a master regulator of cellular metabolism and autophagy (Zhao et al., 2020). Activated AMPK phosphorylates several downstream targets that collectively restore energy homeostasis; among these targets are key regulators of autophagy, including the inhibition of mTOR and the direct phosphorylation of ULK1, which initiates autophagosome formation (Zhao et al., 2020; Dang et al., 2021). One important biochemical hallmark of this autophagy induction is the conversion of cytosolic LC3-I to its lipidated, membrane-bound form LC3-II, which has been used extensively as a marker to assess autophagy flux in RPE cell studies (Zhao et al., 2020). Additionally, metformin’s activation of AMPK influences mitochondrial biogenesis through upregulation of transcription co-activators such as PGC-1α, thereby promoting the generation of new, functionally active mitochondria (Dang et al., 2021; Sekar et al., 2023). These mechanisms are particularly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where RPE metabolic dysfunction is a key pathological feature. Moreover, metformin has been shown to modulate lipid metabolism, notably by enhancing cholesterol efflux via the AMPK/LXR pathway, which can reduce intracellular lipid accumulation—a contributor to drusen formation in AMD (Dang et al., 2021). Additional anti-inflammatory effects are mediated through suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation and modulation of VEGF signaling, further contributing to the overall cytoprotective profile of metformin in the retina (Dang et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed hypothesis and existing evidence, it is expected that metformin will activate AMPK in RPE cells, thereby promoting autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis. In practical terms, treatment with metformin is anticipated to lead to a measurable increase in LC3-II formation, a reduction in intracellular lipid accumulation, and restoration of ATP levels in RPE cells—specifically in models employing CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE cells, which serve as a relevant in vitro model of AMD (Zhao et al., 2020). The enhanced autophagic flux, as indicated by increased LC3-II levels and decreased p62 levels, will facilitate the clearance of damaged organelles, including dysfunctional mitochondria. This process of mitophagy is expected to improve overall mitochondrial homeostasis, thereby restoring the energetic capacity required for efficient phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Given that efficient POS degradation by RPE cells is critical for photoreceptor renewal and retinal health, the metformin-induced restoration of energy balance and autophagic function could lead to improved visual function. Importantly, AMPK is expressed in RPE cells and has been shown to be a crucial mediator of autophagy and mitochondrial quality control in these cells, ensuring that metformin’s mechanism of action is well-targeted to the cellular environment affected in dry AMD (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Furthermore, several in vivo studies support the notion that metformin can rescue mitochondrial function and enhance cellular clearance mechanisms, which are expected outcomes of its use in dry AMD models (Sekar et al., 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating metformin as a drug candidate for treating dry age-related macular degeneration, there are several notable strengths. First, metformin’s well-established safety profile from decades of clinical use for type 2 diabetes offers an advantageous starting point for repurposing—its known pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties facilitate its potential translation to ophthalmic indications (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Second, robust preclinical data support metformin’s ability to activate AMPK and promote autophagy, two pathways intimately involved in the maintenance of RPE health. Activation of AMPK has been repeatedly shown to enhance LC3-II formation, reduce oxidative stress, restore mitochondrial membrane potential, and upregulate mitochondrial biogenesis, all of which are critical to counteracting the metabolic deficits seen in AMD (Zhao et al., 2020; Dang et al., 2021; Sekar et al., 2023). Third, epidemiological studies have suggested that metformin use correlates with a reduced incidence of AMD, lending clinical relevance to its potential protective effects in the retina (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Huang et al., 2023). Fourth, the ability of metformin to modulate lipid metabolism, particularly by promoting cholesterol efflux and thereby reducing drusen-associated lipid accumulation, represents another beneficial mechanism targeting a fundamental aspect of AMD pathology (Dang et al., 2021).

However, several weaknesses and challenges must also be considered. Although many preclinical and retrospective clinical studies point toward a beneficial role of metformin in retinal health, direct prospective evidence in dry AMD patients remains limited. Some of the data originate from studies published in journals of variable quality, and there exists heterogeneity in the responses observed across different model systems, including patient-derived RPE cells where metformin’s effects may vary (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Moreover, while metformin is effective in activating AMPK systemically at standard doses used for diabetes, the optimal dosing regimen, route of administration, and tissue-targeting strategies necessary to achieve effective concentrations in the retinal tissue remain to be determined. The possibility that metformin’s efficacy may depend on specific genetic or metabolic backgrounds of patients—such as differences in CFH status or other AMD-related risk factors—also raises concerns about patient heterogeneity in clinical trials (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Additionally, while the expected restoration of autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis is promising, the precise quantitative changes in LC3-II, ATP levels, lipid accumulation, and POS degradation need rigorous validation under controlled experimental conditions before definitive conclusions can be drawn (Zhao et al., 2020; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Finally, potential systemic side effects such as gastrointestinal disturbances, rare occurrences of lactic acidosis, and vitamin B12 deficiency, albeit infrequent, may need consideration when repurposing metformin for chronic ocular use, especially in non-diabetic populations (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Brown et al., 2019).

Overall, metformin represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its multifaceted effects on enhancing autophagy, improving mitochondrial biogenesis, and restoring cellular energy metabolism in RPE cells. Its safety profile and broad availability further support its potential for rapid clinical translation. Nonetheless, the candidate’s ultimate success will depend on careful dose optimization, robust clinical trial designs that account for inter-patient variability, and further mechanistic studies to precisely delineate the quantitative biochemical improvements—such as LC3-II increase, lipid clearance, ATP restoration, and enhanced POS degradation—in preclinical AMD models (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhao et al., 2020). The convergence of epidemiological, biochemical, and preclinical data thus supports proceeding with further validation studies, while also highlighting the need to address remaining uncertainties regarding tissue-specific drug delivery and long-term outcomes in the context of dry AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Vessey et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2020).
