Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MCC950 is a synthetic diarylsulfonylurea small molecule originally identified from an IL-1β processing inhibitor chemotype and later defined as a highly potent and selective inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome complex (Coll et al., 2015). Within the inflammasome‐inhibitor landscape, MCC950 is representative of sulfonylurea‐based NLRP3 inhibitors that block canonical and noncanonical NLRP3 activation while sparing other inflammasomes (AIM2, NLRC4, NLRP1) and upstream innate pathways (e.g., TLR-NF-κB priming) (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Mechanistically, MCC950 acts directly on NLRP3 to prevent assembly of the adaptor ASC (apoptosis‐associated speck-like protein containing a CARD) into oligomeric “specks,” thereby preventing caspase-1 activation and maturation of IL-1β and IL-18 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Follow-on mechanistic analyses indicate MCC950 binds the NLRP3 NACHT domain to inhibit its ATPase function and thereby prevent NLRP3 activation; mechanistic models include prevention of ASC oligomerization and disruption of required conformations for NEK7–NLRP3 cooperation during sensor activation (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2023).

This class (selective NLRP3 inhibitors) has been broadly leveraged in preclinical inflammatory disease models to selectively blunt inflammasome‐driven IL-1 family cytokine maturation and pyroptosis without pan‐suppressing innate immune sensing, with documented in vivo efficacy in autoimmune encephalomyelitis, CAPS (NLRP3 gain‐of‐function), spontaneous colitis, atherosclerosis, and myocardial infarction models (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021; Wooff et al., 2020). In ocular biology, several sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950 and chemically related CRID3/IFM compounds—reduce IL-1β secretion and cell lysis in human RPE models and ex vivo mouse RPE/choroid eye cups under diverse AMD‐relevant triggers (lysosomal membrane permeabilization, oxidative/photooxidative stress, and P2X7 activation) (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic and non‐ocular indications. MCC950 has repeatedly shown robust pharmacodynamic suppression of inflammasome outputs and disease modification in vivo. Oral dosing in a spontaneous colitis model suppressed IL-1β/IL-18 production ex vivo and improved clinical/histopathologic indices (Perera et al., 2018). In APC‐driven autoimmune encephalomyelitis and in CAPS, MCC950 reduced IL-1β production and ameliorated disease; in CAPS it rescued neonatal lethality (Coll et al., 2015). In ApoE-deficient mice, MCC950 reduced atherosclerotic plaque burden, intraplaque macrophages, and systemic TNF-α/IL-1β/IL-6/IL-18 (Zeng et al., 2021). Across these studies MCC950 demonstrates in vivo target engagement, cytokine suppression, and disease modification with high selectivity for NLRP3 (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021). However, translational reviews emphasize that many NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950‐class agents—face liabilities for organ penetration (including eye/brain) and potential liver toxicity, underscoring formulation/delivery and safety risks that must be addressed for ocular use (Ortega et al., 2024).

Ocular and retinal contexts. In the ischemic OIR model, MCC950 lowered retinal neovascularization and vascular leakage and shifted an aberrant cytokine balance (decreased IL-1β activity with increased IL-18 activity), with accompanying reductions in angiogenesis‐ and pericyte‐associated signaling molecules (VEGF, VEGFR1/2, MMP2/9, PDGFR-β, Ang2) and evidence of inflammasome activation localized predominantly to macrophages (F4/80+) over endothelium (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Sui et al., 2020c). In a glaucoma model (DBA/2J), MCC950 reduced NLRP3 and cleaved caspase-1 in retina and mitigated retinal ganglion cell loss independently of intraocular pressure, indicating on‐target retinal neuroinflammation suppression (Li, 2020).

By contrast, in a laser‐induced CNV model (wet AMD), short‐course MCC950 lowered IL-1β transcript/protein but paradoxically increased total CNV lesion volume and recruitment of microglia and monocyte‐derived macrophages; ERG a- and b-waves were unchanged, suggesting no gross electrophysiological toxicity under those conditions (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b). This aligns with genetic evidence that inflammasome–IL-1β signaling promotes CNV largely through macrophages/microglia and that non‐NLRP3 inflammasomes also contribute, implying that selectively inhibiting NLRP3 may have complex, context‐dependent effects in neovascular disease (Marneros, 2023a; Marneros, 2023b).

In dry‐AMD–relevant photo‐oxidative damage (PD), intravitreal MCC950 failed to rescue function/structure and high‐dose MCC950 worsened ERG amplitudes: 20 µM showed no functional change versus PBS and did not alter photoreceptor death or IBA-1+ microglia counts; 100 µM significantly reduced ERG function (Wooff et al., 2020b). In the same study, Casp1/11−/− mice exhibited strong protection, whereas Nlrp3−/− mice showed only partial functional preservation, and pharmacologic NLRP3 inhibition or Nlrp3 siRNA provided no benefit (and in some readouts reduced function), leading to the conclusion that downstream caspase-1 is a dominant driver whereas NLRP3 may be neither necessary nor sufficient in this model (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). The authors also highlighted uncertainties about NLRP3 localization (predominantly INL/GCL rather than RPE), protein detection sensitivity, and the absence of ocular pharmacokinetic data for MCC950 (Wooff et al., 2020b).

RPE cell and ex vivo ocular models. In IL-1α–primed ARPE-19 and primary human RPE (pRPE), sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors reduced inflammasome activation and cell injury across diverse triggers relevant to GA, including LMP (Leu-Leu-OMe), oxidative stress (H₂O₂), lipofuscin/photooxidative insult (HNE-POS + blue light), and P2X7 activation (BzATP); in Abca4−/− eye cups, selective NLRP3 inhibitors suppressed IL-1β and LDH release and preserved RPE morphology after blue‐light irradiation (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024). A 2024 synthesis that included MCC950 reports that MCC950, IFM-632, and IFM-514 each decreased IL-1α-primed RPE inflammasome activation independent of the activation trigger, consistent with target class effects in RPE models (Korhonen, 2024). These in vitro/ex vivo data strongly support that NLRP3 activity can be engaged in RPE and that selective, small‐molecule inhibition suppresses canonical outputs (IL-1β, LDH) under multiple AMD‐relevant insults. However, detailed analyses of autophagic flux restoration or lysosomal integrity rescue after MCC950 are not reported in these excerpts (Wang et al., 2019).

Emerging genetics for AMD‐relevant deposits. In a monogenic EFEMP1 R345W knockin model (ML/DHRD) that recapitulates basal laminar deposits (BLamDs), as well as in aged WT mice, whole‐animal deletion of Nlrp3 or Casp1 significantly reduced BLamD size/coverage, normalized proinflammatory retinal cytokine profiles, and reduced microglial activation; these data provide genetic causality linking NLRP3–caspase-1 activity to deposit formation and inflammatory milieu (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). The same preprint cautions that NLRP3 inhibitors frequently suffer inadequate ocular penetration and potential liver toxicity, and emphasizes the need to determine whether ocular‐local versus systemic NLRP3 suppression is required (Ortega et al., 2024b).

Mechanism of Action  
Molecular target and binding mechanism. NLRP3 is a tripartite sensor (PYD–NACHT–LRR) that oligomerizes upon priming and activation to recruit ASC via PYD–PYD interactions, which in turn polymerizes and recruits pro-caspase-1 via CARD–CARD interactions to form an active inflammasome; active caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 and the pore‐forming effector gasdermin D (GSDMD) to elicit cytokine secretion and pyroptosis (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). MCC950 binds NLRP3 and prevents its ATPase activity (NACHT domain), disrupting a conformational step required for oligomerization and ASC speck assembly; in cellular systems, MCC950 suppresses both canonical (e.g., K⁺ efflux, lysosomal rupture, mitochondrial ROS) and noncanonical (caspase-11–triggered) activation pathways (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Notably, MCC950 does not broadly interfere with upstream priming (NF-κB–dependent transcription of NLRP3 and cytokine precursors), K⁺ or Ca²⁺ flux, or NLRP3–ASC direct binding in simple biochemical assays; rather, it functionally prevents ASC oligomerization and caspase-1 processing, reflecting target engagement at the level of sensor activation/oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Selectivity is strong: activity against AIM2, NLRC4, and NLRP1 inflammasomes is not observed, and broad target screening reveals only weak off-target activity (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018).

Cell-context specificity in the retina and RPE. Expression of NLRP3 and caspase-1 in the retina is cell-type and stimulus dependent. In vitro, microglia robustly upregulate Nlrp3, Casp1, and Il1b upon stimulation; Müller cells can increase Nlrp3 and Il1b without matching Casp1 elevation; photoreceptor‐line cells upregulate Nlrp3 while reducing Casp1; ARPE-19 cells often show undetectable NLRP3 protein and variable inflammasome readouts under some conditions (Wooff et al., 2020a). In situ, NLRP3 labeling is minimal in dim-reared mouse retinas but becomes detectable in the INL/GCL after PD, and AMD donor tissue shows NLRP3 in INL/GCL, suggesting inner-retina/microglial inflammasome contributions that complicate direct linkage to outer retina/RPE degeneration (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). Conversely, multiple human and preclinical reports demonstrate NLRP3 upregulation in macular RPE of AMD eyes with strong increases in pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 transcripts, co-localization of NLRP3 with autophagosome-like structures, and mitochondrial damage/autophagy signatures—though the literature is conflicted by antibody specificity and cell line variability (Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b; Marneros, 2023b). Taken together, these data imply that in AMD-relevant contexts, NLRP3 activation can occur in RPE and in inner-retinal microglia/Müller/immune cells; drug effects will be inherently cell-type dependent.

Pathway-level effects in retinal models. In ischemic retinopathy (OIR), NLRP3 activation (NLRP3/ASC/CASP1 upregulation and ASC specks) is observed primarily in macrophages and endothelium, and MCC950 reversal of an increased IL-1β/decreased IL-18 pattern is associated with reduced neovascularization and leakage, implicating vascular-cell responses to inflammasome cytokines as drivers of pathology (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b). In wet AMD CNV, inflammasome activation is localized mainly to infiltrating macrophages and microglia, and IL-1β is a principal driver of lesion growth; however, pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition increased lesion size in one study despite reduced IL-1β, suggesting additional non-NLRP3 inflammasomes and compensatory mechanisms (or cell-intrinsic NLRP3 roles) shape outcomes (Marneros, 2023a; Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b).

Expected Effect  
Proposed assay and mechanism. The proposal posits that MCC950 will specifically inhibit NLRP3 assembly in RPE (IC₅₀ ~7.5 nM), reducing IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, preventing inflammasome-induced lysosomal damage, preserving autophagic flux, and thereby enhancing photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance. Mechanistic underpinnings exist for the first components of this cascade: (i) MCC950 demonstrates nanomolar potency and high selectivity for NLRP3 and suppresses downstream IL-1β/IL-18 (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018); (ii) in IL-1α–primed RPE models (ARPE-19 and pRPE), sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950 in compiled data—suppress IL-1β and LDH release across LMP, oxidative stress, lipofuscin/photooxidative, and P2X7 activation paradigms, and preserve ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology under blue-light irradiation (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024). These findings support the expected reduction of canonical inflammasome outputs in RPE assays under multiple AMD-like stimuli.

Lysosome/autophagy preservation and POS clearance. Autophagy is a key negative regulator of NLRP3 activation: it limits ROS and damaged mitochondria, targets assembled inflammasomes for degradation, and suppresses IL-1β responses; conversely, autophagy suppression increases inflammasome activation and pyroptosis in RPE (Celkova et al., 2015). AMD-relevant triggers—including lipofuscin bisretinoids (e.g., A2E) and oxidative stress—cause lysosomal stress/LMP and NLRP3 activation in RPE, and caspase-1 inhibition can prevent RPE death in LMP contexts (Ildefonso et al., 2016). However, direct evidence that MCC950 restores autophagic flux or lysosomal integrity in RPE is not reported in the cited primary RPE inhibitor studies; the RPE evidence centers on IL-1β and LDH suppression and morphological preservation in ex vivo tissue but does not include autophagy- or lysosome-specific readouts or POS phagocytosis assays (Wang et al., 2019). Therefore, while it is plausible that NLRP3 suppression will indirectly favor autophagy homeostasis in stressed RPE by damping inflammasome-driven pyroptotic signaling (and thereby reduce further lysosomal damage), the proposed “preservation of autophagy and enhanced POS clearance” remains unproven for MCC950 and should be tested explicitly (Celkova et al., 2015).

Disease- and cell-type context expectations. In dry AMD models that feature outer-retinal/RPE degeneration, the translation of RPE in vitro suppression of NLRP3 to in vivo benefit is uncertain. In PD (a dry-AMD–relevant model), intravitreal MCC950 failed to confer protection and at higher dose impaired retinal function; Nlrp3−/− mice showed only partial protection while Casp1/11−/− mice were strongly protected, arguing that downstream caspase-1 and/or other inflammasomes may be the dominant drivers in photoreceptor death (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). In EFEMP1 R345W and aged WT models, genetic inactivation of Nlrp3 or Casp1 reduced basal laminar deposit burden and inflammatory signatures, supporting target pathway relevance for drusen/BLamD biology, but pharmacological MCC950 efficacy in these genetic models has not been reported (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). Importantly, if inflammasome activation in vivo is dominated by subretinal macrophages/microglia in some contexts (e.g., autophagy-impaired RPE signals that activate macrophage inflammasomes), the expected pharmacologic effect of MCC950 may depend more on drug exposure to myeloid cells in the subretinal/choroidal space than on direct RPE engagement (Liu et al., 2016).

Finally, IL-18 biology is context-dependent: while IL-1β is broadly pro-angiogenic and disruptive, IL-18 can be protective/anti-angiogenic in neovascular settings, and AMD-relevant studies have reported discordant roles for IL-18 across disease phenotypes (Celkova et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). Given that NLRP3 blockade reduces both IL-1β and IL-18, net effects on tissue outcomes may vary by disease stage and cell-type source; in OIR, MCC950 “normalized” an inverted IL-1β/IL-18 pattern and improved pathology (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020c), whereas in CNV, MCC950 increased lesion volume—implicating competing effects and non-NLRP3 inflammasomes (Dieckmann et al., 2024a).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- On-target potency/selectivity. MCC950 is among the most potent and selective NLRP3 inhibitors described, blocking canonical and noncanonical activation at nanomolar concentrations and sparing other inflammasomes and upstream pathways; it consistently suppresses IL-1β/IL-18 maturation and caspase-1 activation in primary macrophages and multiple in vivo models (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Perera et al., 2018).  
- RPE-target class activity under AMD-relevant stimuli. Sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors, including MCC950 in compiled datasets, reproducibly suppress IL-1β and LDH in IL-1α–primed ARPE-19 and primary human RPE triggered by LMP, oxidative/photooxidative stress, and P2X7 activation; ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology is preserved by an NLRP3 inhibitor during photooxidative stress (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024).  
- Genetic target validation in AMD-relevant deposit biology. Whole‐body Nlrp3 or Casp1 deletion reduces BLamDs and normalizes inflammatory signatures in EFEMP1 R345W mice and even prevents spontaneous deposits in aged WT, indicating the inflammasome pathway contributes causally to deposit formation and retinal inflammation (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c).  
- Demonstrated retinal efficacy in ischemic models and neuroinflammation. MCC950 improves vascular pathology in OIR (reduced neovascularization and leakage with cytokine-pattern reversal) and rescues retinal ganglion cells in glaucoma, supporting retinal target engagement and functional protection in relevant pathologies (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Li, 2020).

Liabilities and gaps  
- Lack of efficacy and potential toxicity in dry-AMD–relevant PD. Intravitreal MCC950 did not improve functional or structural outcomes in PD and at 100 µM worsened ERG amplitudes; Nlrp3 siRNA similarly failed to protect despite gene knockdown; Casp1/11 deletion was robustly protective while Nlrp3 deletion was only partially protective, arguing sensor-specific inhibition may be insufficient in photoreceptor death contexts (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- Mixed effects in neovascular disease. MCC950 increased CNV lesion volume in LCNV despite lowering IL-1β, and Nlrp3−/− mice displayed larger lesions, raising concern that NLRP3 blockade may remove protective constraints in some inflammatory/angiogenic contexts; non-NLRP3 inflammasomes likely contribute, further complicating pharmacodynamics (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).  
- Uncertain ocular delivery, exposure, and safety margin. Ocular PK for MCC950 is not defined; the PD study underscores unknown intravitreal bioavailability and clearance, and preclinical reviews warn of poor eye penetration and potential liver toxicity with many NLRP3 inhibitors; high intravitreal dose impaired ERG function in PD (Wooff et al., 2020b; Ortega et al., 2024b). While ERGs were unchanged in one CNV study, that does not establish comprehensive ocular safety (Dieckmann et al., 2024a).  
- RPE biology heterogeneity and expression uncertainty. In vivo NLRP3 induction localizes largely to inner retina/microglia rather than RPE in PD; ARPE-19 NLRP3 expression is variable in the literature and some human studies report low/undetectable NLRP3 in RPE, with concerns about antibody specificity, suggesting that direct RPE targeting may not be universally relevant across models or donors (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b; Marneros, 2023b).  
- Unproven restoration of autophagy/lysosomal function by MCC950. Although autophagy restrains inflammasome activation and lysosomal damage is a key trigger in RPE, direct evidence that MCC950 preserves autophagic flux, lysosomal integrity, or POS processing in RPE is absent in the cited studies; current RPE data document IL-1β/LDH suppression and morphology preservation but not autophagy or phagolysosomal kinetics (Celkova et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019).  
- Pathway redundancy suggests downstream targeting may be superior. Strong protection in Casp1/11−/− mice versus weak/absent benefits from NLRP3 inhibition in PD argue for targeting the shared downstream protease (caspase-1) or gasdermin D rather than individual sensors in retinal degeneration (Wooff et al., 2020a).

Risk-adjusted development path and decision inflection points  
- Go/no-go evidence needed in dry-AMD–relevant RPE assays. Establish whether MCC950 preserves lysosomal integrity and autophagic flux in RPE under LMP/photooxidative/P2X7 triggers and whether it restores POS digestion. Required readouts: LC3-II/I and p62 kinetics with and without bafilomycin, lysosomal pH and cathepsin activity, galectin-3 puncta for LMP, ASC speck formation, caspase-1 activity (FLICA), GSDMD cleavage, IL-1β/IL-18 maturation, and POS ingestion/digestion assays in ARPE-19 and pRPE (Celkova et al., 2015; Ranta-aho et al., 2021).  
- Ocular PK/PD and safety. Quantify intravitreal half-life, retinal/RPE/choroid distribution, and exposure–response for inflammasome suppression with MCC950; determine maximum non-toxic intravitreal dose across species. Include ERG, OCT, histopathology, IBA-1/microglial activation, and cytokine profiling. Investigate sustained intravitreal delivery strategies (e.g., silica-based nanoparticles) that have shown extended ocular release and improved anti-inflammatory efficacy for MCC950 in non-AMD contexts, while generating ocular PK and biodegradation data (Sun et al., 2023).  
- Efficacy in chronic dry-AMD models. Test MCC950 in EFEMP1 R345W mice (BLamD) and aging WT (spontaneous BLamD) with local ocular delivery; endpoints: BLamD size and coverage, RPE/Bruch’s integrity, microglial recruitment (Iba1), and cytokine panels. Given PD negative findings, prioritize deposit/atrophy models where genetic Nlrp3/Casp1 loss is protective (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c; Wooff et al., 2020b).  
- Cell-type–specific targeting and biomarkers. Because inflammasome activation is often myeloid-dominant in vivo, delineate whether MCC950’s ocular benefits, if any, require exposure to subretinal macrophages/microglia versus RPE. Use cell-specific pharmacodynamic markers (ASC specks in Iba1+ cells vs RPE65+ cells; IL-1β/IL-18 localization) to define pharmacologic engagement (Liu et al., 2016; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- Comparative strategy. In parallel, benchmark a caspase-1 inhibitor (or GSDMD inhibitor) against MCC950 in the same models, given the superior genetic protection with Casp1/11 deletion and the possibility of non-NLRP3 inflammasome contribution (Wooff et al., 2020a; Marneros, 2023a).

Bottom line  
MCC950 has strong mechanistic rationale, exquisite target selectivity, and reproducible suppression of inflammasome outputs in RPE assays across diverse AMD-like triggers. Genetic data incriminating NLRP3–caspase-1 in deposit biology strengthen the target hypothesis in a subset of dry-AMD phenotypes. However, the most AMD-relevant in vivo pharmacology with MCC950 to date is not supportive: no benefit and possible functional toxicity in PD, and mixed signals in neovascular settings (benefit in OIR, harm in LCNV). The translational path is further complicated by variable NLRP3 expression in RPE in vivo, dominance of myeloid inflammasomes in many retinal contexts, uncertain ocular PK/penetration, and the untested premise that MCC950 restores RPE autophagy/lysosomal function and POS clearance.

Given these data, MCC950 should not advance directly to costly IND-enabling studies for dry AMD without targeted de-risking experiments. The highest-value next steps are (i) mechanistic RPE assays that test autophagy/lysosome rescue and POS processing, (ii) rigorous ocular PK/safety to define a therapeutic index and viable delivery modality, and (iii) efficacy in deposit/atrophy models where the genetic target is validated (EFEMP1 R345W, aged WT). If these studies confirm robust ocular exposure, a favorable safety margin, and disease modification, MCC950—or a chemically optimized ocular NLRP3 inhibitor—could warrant advancement for specific dry-AMD endophenotypes. If not, downstream inflammasome targeting (caspase-1/GSDMD) may represent a more effective and generalizable strategy for retinal degeneration.

Mechanism of Action (detailed)  
NLRP3 activation requires priming (e.g., NF-κB upregulation of NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β/IL-18) and a second signal (e.g., K⁺ efflux via P2X7, lysosomal rupture with cathepsin release, mitochondrial ROS) that promotes sensor oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). NLRP3’s NACHT domain cycles ATP and orchestrates a conformational change enabling PYD-driven nucleation of ASC, which polymerizes into higher-order filaments/specks that template pro-caspase-1 recruitment and activation; activated caspase-1 cleaves GSDMD to induce pyroptotic pore formation and processes IL-1β/IL-18 for secretion (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). MCC950 binds NLRP3 to suppress its ATPase activity (NACHT), preventing the conformational activation needed for ASC oligomerization and caspase-1 activation; in functional assays MCC950 suppresses both canonical and noncanonical pathways and decreases processed caspase-1 p10/p20 in supernatants without altering upstream TNF-α secretion after TLR priming (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Evidence from retinal disease states aligns with these mechanisms: MCC950 reduces NLRP3 and cleaved caspase-1 in glaucomatous retina (DBA/2J), and in OIR normalizes IL-1β/IL-18 signaling and reduces pathologic neovascularization and leakage (Li, 2020; Sui et al., 2020a).

Inflammasome biology in RPE and AMD is multifactorial. AMD-associated triggers—lipofuscin photooxidation, A2E/oxidative stress, drusen lipid adducts (CEP), Alu RNA accumulation from DICER1 deficiency, and lysosomal destabilization—induce NLRP3 activation in RPE or in recruited subretinal macrophages (Ildefonso et al., 2016; Celkova et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016). Autophagy limits NLRP3 activation by removing damaged mitochondria and targeting assembled inflammasomes for autophagosomal degradation; autophagy blockade increases IL-1β production and pyroptotic susceptibility (Celkova et al., 2015). Pharmacologic NLRP3 blockade in RPE reduces IL-1β and LDH release under LMP, oxidative, photooxidative, and P2X7 activation, consistent with suppression of caspase-1 activation and pyroptotic lysis (Wang et al., 2019). Whether these biochemical effects in RPE suffice to modify chronic, multicellular retinal degeneration in vivo depends on drug delivery to relevant compartments (RPE, subretinal macrophages/microglia), on the relative contributions of non-NLRP3 inflammasomes, and on downstream cytokine biology (e.g., IL-18’s context-dependent effects).

Therapeutic History (detailed)  
- Preclinical systemic efficacy and selectivity: MCC950 exhibits nanomolar potency for NLRP3 in human/mouse macrophages, sparing AIM2, NLRC4, NLRP1; suppresses caspase-1 p10 and IL-1β secretion; improves disease in EAE and CAPS; PK characterized; off-targets largely excluded (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018). In atherosclerosis, MCC950 decreased plaques, macrophage content, and circulating cytokines without overt systemic organ toxicity, though cross-indication reviews caution about liver toxicity risk for the class (Zeng et al., 2021; Ortega et al., 2024b).  
- Ocular ischemic/neovascular settings: In OIR, MCC950 reversed an increased IL-1β/decreased IL-18 pattern, reduced neovascularization and leakage, and modulated endothelial/pericyte signaling; inflammasome activity localized more to macrophages than endothelium (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Sui et al., 2020c). In LCNV, MCC950 lowered IL-1β but increased lesion volume; ERG unchanged; genetic Nlrp3 loss also increased lesion size—collectively indicating a complex, possibly protective role of NLRP3 in CNV or compensation by other inflammasomes (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).  
- Dry-AMD–relevant PD and NLRP3 targeting: Intravitreal MCC950 did not protect PD retina; 100 µM reduced ERG amplitudes. Nlrp3 siRNA reduced transcript but not pathology; Nlrp3−/− protected partially; Casp1/11−/− protected robustly, pointing to caspase-1 as the better target (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- RPE in vitro/ex vivo: CRID3/IFM inhibitors (sulfonylureas, same target class as MCC950) reduced IL-1β and LDH across LMP, H₂O₂, lipofuscin/photooxidation, and P2X7 triggers in ARPE-19/pRPE and preserved ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology under photooxidation (Wang et al., 2019). Compiled 2024 data list MCC950 alongside IFM analogs as effective in IL-1α–primed RPE independent of trigger (Korhonen, 2024).  
- Genetic validations in chronic deposit models: Nlrp3 or Casp1 deletion reduces BLamD in EFEMP1 R345W mice and in aged WT, with reduced microglial activation and normalization of cytokine profiles (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). These models offer strong causal support for inflammasome targeting in GA-relevant pathology, albeit via genetic ablation rather than pharmacologic inhibition.

Expected Effect (detailed)  
In ARPE-19/pRPE assays primed with IL-1α, MCC950 should suppress NLRP3 activation triggered by:  
– LMP (Leu-Leu-OMe), where caspase-1 inhibition prevents RPE death and NLRP3 inhibitors reduce IL-1β and LDH release (Ildefonso et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019).  
– Oxidative and lipofuscin/photooxidative stress (H₂O₂, HNE-POS + blue light), where NLRP3 inhibitors significantly lower IL-1β and LDH and preserve RPE morphology ex vivo (Wang et al., 2019).  
– P2X7 activation (BzATP), a canonical AMD-relevant danger signal leading to K⁺ efflux and inflammasome assembly; selective NLRP3 inhibitors attenuate IL-1β and LDH in Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺-free conditions (Wang et al., 2019).

Because autophagy restrains inflammasome activation and removes inflammasome complexes, a reduction in NLRP3 activity may secondarily stabilize autophagic flux under stress. Yet, this remains hypothetical for MCC950 in RPE; explicit autophagy and lysosomal readouts (LC3 flux, p62, LAMP1/2, cathepsin B/D activities, lysosomal pH, galectin-3 LMP puncta) have not been detailed in the RPE inhibitor studies referenced (Celkova et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019). Therefore, while reduction of IL-1β/LDH and preservation of morphology are expected and supported, the proposed enhancement of POS clearance should be considered an untested hypothesis requiring targeted experimentation.

In vivo, efficacy expectations diverge by model:  
– Deposit/atrophy (EFEMP1 R345W, aged WT) are rational choices: genetic deletion of Nlrp3/Casp1 is protective, so MCC950 might reduce BLamD burden and retinal inflammation if adequate ocular exposure is achieved (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c).  
– Photoreceptor acute degeneration (PD) may not respond to NLRP3 inhibition and may be sensitive to dose-related toxicity, favoring downstream caspase-1 inhibition or broader inflammasome suppression (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
– Neovascular models diverge: OIR improved with MCC950; CNV worsened. Dry-AMD-focused development should avoid neovascular endpoints initially, or stratify hypotheses based on IL-1β/IL-18 balance and myeloid contribution (Sui et al., 2020a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).

Overall Evaluation  
MCC950 is a mechanistically compelling, best-in-class NLRP3 inhibitor with credible RPE-target class activity in vitro and strong genetic support for inflammasome involvement in deposit biology. However, the in vivo ocular pharmacology to date is mixed and generally unsupportive for broad dry-AMD application without further de-risking: failure and potential toxicity in PD, context-dependent effects in neovascular models, uncertain RPE expression/engagement in vivo, lack of ocular PK, and unproven restoration of autophagy/lysosomal function in RPE.

On balance, MCC950 merits continued investigation as a mechanistic probe and potential therapeutic lead for specific dry-AMD endophenotypes linked to deposit pathology and chronic inflammasome signaling—provided that the next tranche of studies addresses ocular PK/safety, cell-type exposure, and autophagy/lysosome outcomes. In parallel, downstream targeting (caspase-1) should be benchmarked given superior genetic protection and potential coverage of multiple inflammasome sensors. If MCC950 cannot meet ocular exposure and safety requirements, alternative delivery (e.g., sustained-release nanoparticles) or next-generation NLRP3 inhibitors with better ocular PK and safety profiles may be required (Sun et al., 2023; Ortega et al., 2024b).

In summary, MCC950 has plausible potential for dry AMD if—and only if— its ocular pharmacology can be tuned to the appropriate disease biology: chronic deposit/atrophy with documented inflammasome involvement, sufficient drug exposure at RPE/subretinal myeloid compartments, and a safety margin that avoids the functional liabilities observed at higher intravitreal doses in PD. Without these, the probability of technical success remains low relative to downstream inflammasome targets.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Cerulenin is a natural product originally isolated from the filamentous fungus Cephalosporium caerulens and was the first discovered fatty acid synthase (FAS) inhibitor (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; López & Diéguez, 2007). Chemically, this compound is classified as an epoxy-keto fatty acid analogue; it contains a reactive epoxide ring conjugated to a diene/amidic structure that mimics fatty acid substrates. This reactive epoxide is key to its mechanism because it enables cerulenin to irreversibly bind to its target enzyme via covalent modification. As such, cerulenin belongs to the class of FAS inhibitors that historically have been used as biochemical probes to investigate lipid metabolism and, subsequently, as lead compounds in the development of antineoplastic agents, given the upregulation of de novo lipogenesis in many cancers (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; López & Diéguez, 2007; Abramson, 2011). The molecule’s natural origin, combined with its potent inhibitory activity, has made it a valuable tool in studies of metabolic regulation and lipogenesis over several decades.

Therapeutic History:  
In the past, cerulenin was primarily developed and investigated as an antimicrobial and antifungal antibiotic due to its capacity to irreversibly inhibit fatty acid synthesis in both bacterial and eukaryotic systems (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Subsequent research in the fields of oncology and metabolic regulation revealed that several tumor types exhibit elevated expression of FAS, making FAS inhibitors promising candidates for anticancer therapy. Preclinical studies demonstrated that cerulenin could induce apoptosis in tumor cells, delay disease progression in xenograft models, and even affect systemic metabolic parameters such as food intake and body weight in rodent models (López & Diéguez, 2007; Heath, White, & Rock, 2002; Goodman & McFadden, 2007). Despite these promising results, its clinical utility has been constrained by poor chemical stability—primarily due to its reactive epoxide moiety—and significant toxicity stemming from irreversibility and off-target interactions with other cysteine-containing proteins (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Furthermore, while modifications have led to second-generation analogues like C75, designed to improve stability and selectivity, there are no records of cerulenin being specifically applied to ophthalmologic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal lipotoxicity diseases (Menendez & Lupu, 2017; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999). Although cerulenin has been explored in other in vivo models (for example, for retinitis pigmentosa in preclinical studies), no clinical trials have been registered for its use in AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, cerulenin exerts its biological effects by targeting the fatty acid synthase complex. Its mechanism involves the formation of an irreversible covalent adduct with an active-site cysteine residue (specifically, Cys1305) within the ketosynthase (KS) domain of type I FAS. This is achieved by an epoxide ring-opening reaction at the C-2 position of cerulenin, leading to the nucleophilic attack by the thiol (-SH) group of the catalytic cysteine residue (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008). Crystallographic studies have provided precise structural insights into this interaction, showing that such covalent modification not only blocks the initial acyl-transfer step but also induces conformational changes—such as the flipping of key residues like F1646 and the rotation of M1251—that ultimately disrupt the hydrophobic acyl-binding tunnel required for fatty acid chain elongation (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008; Fhu & Ali, 2020). In addition to inhibiting FAS directly, cerulenin has also been shown to impair protein palmitoylation, a post-translational modification that plays an important role in regulating membrane association and signaling functions of numerous proteins including Ras oncoproteins (Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999). This dual mechanism—targeting both de novo fatty acid synthesis and protein acylation—underscores the broad-spectrum bioactivity of cerulenin and its potential impact on multiple cellular pathways that are dysregulated in disease states (Menendez & Lupu, 2017; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis underpinning the proposed repurposing of cerulenin for dry AMD centers on its ability to attenuate de novo lipogenesis in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. In the context of dry AMD, pathologic accumulation of lipofuscin and toxic bisretinoid compounds such as A2E is thought to result from excessive lipid synthesis and impaired degradation of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) material. Excess levels of intracellular fatty acids, often derived from hyperactive FAS, contribute to the generation of these lipofuscin precursors—ultimately impairing lysosomal function and leading to RPE dysfunction (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). By inhibiting FAS activity in the RPE, cerulenin is expected to reduce the synthesis of fatty acids that serve as precursors for lipofuscin components. This reduced lipogenesis should, in theory, alleviate the accumulation of lipofuscin, restore optimal levels of lysosomal pH, and enhance the activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D—thereby improving the degradation and turnover of POS material (Radka & Rock, 2022; Troudi, Pagès, & Brunel, 2021). Furthermore, since oxidative stress is a key driver of abnormal lipid metabolism in RPE cells, the ability of cerulenin to lower fatty acid synthesis may concurrently reduce the burden of oxidative damage and improve cellular homeostasis (Vázquez et al., 2008; Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007). It is also noteworthy that FAS expression has been detected and functionally characterized in various extrahepatic tissues; while direct evidence of its expression in RPE cells is less extensively documented in the provided citations, the extrapolation from other cellular models supports the likelihood that modulating FAS activity in RPE would confer benefits in lipid turnover and lysosomal efficiency (Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999; Johansson et al., 2008). Thus, within the proposed assay—where RPE cells are subjected to oxidative stress that mimics the environment of dry AMD—cerulenin is anticipated to lower intracellular lipid levels, minimize the generation of lipofuscin precursors, and ultimately restore RPE functional capacity.

Overall Evaluation:  
Cerulenin presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD owing to its well-documented ability to inhibit fatty acid synthase through a unique irreversible, covalent mechanism. Its molecular footprint, characterized by a reactive epoxide ring, has been exploited in multiple studies to evaluate cellular lipid synthesis and, by extension, to modulate metabolic pathways that underpin several disease processes (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Abramson, 2011). Mechanistically, its capacity to bind to a crucial cysteine residue in the FAS enzyme and to interfere with lipid assembly positions it as a potentially valuable agent to counter the lipid-driven pathogenesis implicated in RPE dysfunction and lipofuscin accumulation in dry AMD (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008).

The strengths of cerulenin as a candidate include its small-molecule profile, which facilitates cellular entry; its established use as a research tool in in vitro and in vivo models; and its dual activity profile that not only curtails de novo lipogenesis but may also impede aberrant protein palmitoylation. Such multifaceted activity could be beneficial in a complex tissue environment like the retina, where multiple overlapping metabolic dysfunctions contribute to disease progression (Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999). In particular, by reducing the synthesis of fatty acids in RPE cells, cerulenin could deplete one of the key substrates for the formation of lipofuscin precursors such as A2E, thereby potentially improving lysosomal degradation of shed POS and arresting a vicious cycle of intracellular lipid accumulation and oxidative stress (Radka & Rock, 2022; Troudi, Pagès, & Brunel, 2021).

However, several weaknesses must be carefully considered. Cerulenin’s inherent chemical instability, attributed to its reactive epoxide ring, raises significant concerns regarding its pharmacokinetic profile and overall toxicity, especially in a sensitive tissue like the retina where off-target effects may exacerbate cellular stress rather than alleviate it (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Heath, White, & Rock, 2002). The irreversible nature of its enzyme inhibition—while beneficial for ensuring sustained suppression of FAS—may lead to collateral damage in non-target tissues, and the narrow therapeutic window observed in other preclinical studies suggests that dose optimization could be challenging (Fhu & Ali, 2020; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Moreover, although the hypothesis posits that inhibition of de novo lipogenesis in the RPE will mitigate lipid accumulation and improve lysosomal function, there is a paucity of direct evidence linking cerulenin or similar FAS inhibitors to improved outcomes in dry AMD models specifically. The documented applications of cerulenin are primarily in the realms of oncology and metabolic regulation, with little precedent for its use in ocular conditions (Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). This suggests that while the mechanistic rationale is sound, the translational leap to an ocular indication will require additional supportive data both from in vitro RPE assays and from appropriate animal models of AMD.

Another point of concern is that cerulenin’s nonselective inhibition of fatty acid synthase may also impair essential lipid synthesis in cells that require robust regenerative capacity, potentially leading to unintended cytotoxicity or impaired cell membrane maintenance. In the context of the RPE, where cellular health is paramount for photoreceptor support, any off-target lipid synthesis inhibition must be tightly controlled (Goodman & McFadden, 2007; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Furthermore, its use in vivo has been historically hampered by issues such as poor aqueous solubility—it often requires solvents like DMSO for administration—and its propensity for rapid degradation in protic environments, all of which represent substantial formulation challenges that must be overcome for ocular delivery (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Vázquez et al., 2008).

Given these considerations, while cerulenin offers a compelling proof-of-concept relating to the modulation of lipogenesis and lysosomal function, its practical development as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD would likely necessitate further chemical modifications. The precedent set by the development of derivatives such as C75—which were specifically engineered to overcome the limitations of cerulenin by removing the problematic epoxide group and enhancing stability—suggests that optimization is both possible and necessary (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Optimized analogues with improved pharmacokinetic and safety profiles may hold greater promise in the ocular setting than the parent compound.

In summary, cerulenin’s capacity to inhibit fatty acid synthase at the molecular level through irreversible covalent binding is well-established and aligns with the proposed therapeutic mechanism of reducing RPE lipid accumulation and lipofuscin precursor formation. However, its historical limitations in terms of chemical stability, toxicity, and nonselectivity present significant hurdles for its repurposing in dry AMD. The compound’s extensive use in metabolic and oncologic research provides a strong foundation for understanding its biochemical actions, but the absence of direct evidence in retinal models and the challenges associated with its delivery to ocular tissues temper enthusiasm for immediate clinical translation (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Therefore, while there is sufficient mechanistic rationale to pursue further preclinical investigations—potentially in parallel with the development of more stable derivatives—the current state of evidence suggests that cerulenin itself may not be ideal as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD without significant further optimization. More comprehensive in vitro studies using RPE cell models and targeted in vivo studies in AMD-relevant animal models are needed to validate whether the inhibition of de novo lipogenesis by cerulenin can indeed translate into restored lysosomal function and improved photoreceptor outer segment degradation in this disease context (Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007; Radka & Rock, 2022).

This report is organized into several sections: an overview of the candidate, its therapeutic history, an in‐depth discussion of its mechanism of action, the expected effects in the proposed assay, and an overall evaluation that weighs its strengths and weaknesses.

─────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

KYP-2047 is a synthetic small molecule belonging to the peptidomimetic class of compounds that target the enzyme prolyl oligopeptidase (PREP), also known as prolyl endopeptidase (POP). Chemically designated as 4-phenylbutanoyl-L-prolyl-2(S)-cyanopyrrolidine, this compound was synthesized following methods established by Dr. Elina Jarho at the University of Eastern Finland (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47). Its design represents an evolution from early substrate-like inhibitors, with modifications at specific positions – including a three-carbon aliphatic chain at the P3 position instead of the more commonly used carbamate groups seen in predecessors like ZPP – thereby improving the compound’s overall potency, selectivity, and drug-like properties (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4).

Belonging to a well-known class of PREP inhibitors, KYP-2047 shares common chemical and biophysical properties with analogous peptidomimetic agents that have been primarily designed to interfere with the catalytic activity of a serine protease that cleaves proline-containing peptides. Given its low water solubility, KYP-2047 is typically formulated in saline containing 5% Tween® 80 for experimental studies, which is consistent with formulation challenges observed with many peptidomimetic drug candidates (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47). In recent years, the broader class of PREP inhibitors has been explored for a variety of indications, most notably in neurological conditions as well as in certain cancer models. The research impetus behind this class arises from the enzyme’s presumed role in peptide metabolism, where the inhibition of PREP could alter levels of bioactive peptides that participate in cellular homeostasis. Although these agents were originally developed as anti-amnesic candidates, their biological actions have been found to extend to anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

─────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

The therapeutic exploration of PREP inhibitors dates back to the 1970s when the enzyme was first implicated in the regulation of proline-containing peptides associated with memory formation and synaptic plasticity (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22). Numerous compounds in this class—including S-17092, JTP-4819, and others—were advanced into preclinical studies and even early-phase clinical trials for cognitive enhancement in neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease and senile dementia (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41, 70–72). However, despite initial encouraging in vitro and animal data, these agents failed to progress successfully past phase II clinical trials in humans, most likely due to challenges with efficacy, blood-brain barrier penetration, or the complexity of the enzyme’s in vivo function (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 70–72).

In parallel, PREP inhibitors have been evaluated for other indications. For instance, in a study involving oral squamous cell carcinoma, KYP-2047 demonstrated potent PREP inhibition in the mouse brain along with promising anti-tumor effects, highlighting the compound’s potential utility beyond central nervous system disorders (Scuderi, 2023, pp. 133–135). Furthermore, recent work has begun to explore the ocular applications of PREP inhibition. There is a suggestion in the literature that inhibition of prolyl oligopeptidase may represent “a promising pathway to prevent the progression of age-related macular degeneration” (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13). Notably, recent in vitro studies using human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells with defective proteasomal clearance have shown that KYP-2047 exhibits cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory properties, thereby indirectly supporting its potential use in dry AMD, even though no clinical trials or prior direct therapeutic applications in retinal diseases have yet been reported (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 9–11).

While the primary historical focus of PREP inhibitors has been on neurological and cognitive applications, the body of literature also contains several exploratory studies in inflammatory and cancer contexts (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 13–14). Thus, even though the bulk of previous applications have not directly targeted dry AMD, the emerging evidence supporting cytoprotection and modulation of proteolytic and autophagy pathways in RPE cells provides a rationale for repurposing KYP-2047 in ocular disease states.

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

The biological target of KYP-2047 is the serine protease prolyl oligopeptidase (PREP), which is responsible for cleaving peptide bonds at the carboxyl side of internal proline residues in small peptides (typically less than ~30 amino acids) (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 22–24, 44–47). PREP is widely expressed in the central nervous system and peripheral tissues and has been implicated in multiple physiological processes including neuropeptide regulation and cell signaling. At the molecular level, the mechanism of action involves the binding of KYP-2047 to the enzyme’s active site, more specifically interacting with the catalytic serine residue. Many PREP inhibitors, including those in the class to which KYP-2047 belongs, are designed as substrate-like pseudopeptides that exploit the structure of the enzyme’s binding pockets (S1, S2, and S3) to achieve selectivity and high-affinity binding (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).

The inhibition by KYP-2047 is characterized as “tight-binding” with slow dissociation, meaning that once the inhibitor occupies the active site of PREP, it remains bound for a significant duration, thereby effectively reducing the enzyme’s catalytic turnover (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 70–72). In neurological models, inhibition of PREP has been associated with enhanced clearance of toxic protein aggregates such as alpha-synuclein, improved autophagic flux, and reduction in oxidative stress (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 85–88; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 9–11). The current therapeutic hypothesis in the context of dry AMD extrapolates these findings to retinal pigment epithelial cells.

In particular, the proposed mechanism posits that elevated PREP activity in RPE cells contributes to an accumulation of proline-rich peptides that, in turn, inhibit the activity of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and lysosomal cathepsin L. These cathepsins are critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and turnover of cellular debris. In dry AMD, defective protein clearance mechanisms, including impaired proteasomal and lysosomal function, result in the buildup of toxic deposits, such as A2E, and contribute to RPE dysfunction. By blocking PREP activity with KYP-2047 (which has an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range, reported to be approximately 30 nM), the proposed effect is to reduce the formation or accumulation of inhibitory peptides, thereby relieving the suppression on cathepsin activity. In addition, KYP-2047-mediated PREP inhibition may trigger downstream intracellular events such as autophagy activation and modulation of MAPK signaling pathways—including p38 and ERK1/2—which have been observed in other cell types and are known to reduce oxidative stress and inflammation (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 85–88).

At the biochemical level, these molecular interactions involve the inhibitor “locking in” the PREP enzyme in a conformational state that either prevents substrate access or alters the dynamics of peptide release once cleavage has occurred. Although the effects on neuropeptide levels (e.g., substance P, neurotensin) have been studied in central nervous system models—with mixed and sometimes counterintuitive outcomes (such as decreased acetylcholine levels) (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 8–16, 70–72)—the rationale for ocular repurposing rests on the idea that the same enzymatic inhibition can counteract the accumulation of cathepsin-inhibiting peptides in RPE cells. Notably, some studies have suggested that PREP inhibition can positively modulate autophagy, a process that is critical for cellular clearance mechanisms. Given that impaired autophagy is a central feature in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, a compound like KYP-2047 that both reduces toxic peptide accumulation and enhances proteolytic pathways presents an attractive, multitargeted strategy (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

The core hypothesis driving the repurposing of KYP-2047 for dry AMD is that inhibition of PREP will reduce the buildup of proline-rich peptides that otherwise impair lysosomal cathepsin activity. In RPE cells, efficient degradation of POS via phagocytosis and lysosomal function is essential for maintaining retinal homeostasis. In the setting of dry AMD, decreased cathepsin D and L activities are implicated in the inefficient clearance of cellular debris, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, ultimately causing RPE dysfunction.

In the proposed assay, RPE cells—typically the ARPE-19 cell line—will be challenged in an environment mimicking AMD pathology; for instance, by loading them with A2E and subjecting the cells to proteasomal stress. Under these conditions, the activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and L is compromised, and POS degradation is impaired. The application of KYP-2047 is expected to inhibit PREP activity with high potency, which theoretically will lead to a reduction in the concentration of peptide substrates that interfere with cathepsin enzymes (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).

The anticipated cascade of events is as follows:  
1. KYP-2047, at concentrations close to its low nanomolar IC₅₀, will effectively bind to and inhibit PREP in RPE cells.  
2. This inhibition will prevent the excessive cleavage of proline-containing peptides, thereby reducing the pool of inhibitory peptides that could otherwise bind to and decrease cathepsin D and L activities.  
3. As a consequence, the restoration of cathepsin activity is expected to improve the degradation of POS components as well as the clearance of other toxic debris, which is a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.  
4. Additionally, the compound’s reported anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects, demonstrated in ARPE-19 cells with defective proteasomal clearance, may further contribute to preserving RPE cell health by curtailing inflammatory cytokine production and oxidative stress (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 4–6).

It is also noteworthy that the mechanistic framework is further supported by the observation that PREP inhibition in other models has led to enhanced autophagy and improved clearance of aggregated proteins. In the context of AMD, effective POS degradation is not only dependent on cathepsin function but also on efficient autophagic flux. By indirectly modulating these pathways, KYP-2047 could offer dual benefits: restoration of lysosomal enzyme activity and bolstering of intracellular clearance mechanisms. Thus, the expected in vitro endpoints would likely include increased cathepsin D/L activity, elevated POS degradation (as detected by uptake assays), reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-6, IL-8, IL-1β), and diminished oxidative stress markers (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 4–6).

Moreover, the rationale includes supporting evidence from neurological and cancer research where PREP inhibition by compounds like KYP-2047 improved cell viability and reduced stress responses. Although previous clinical trials in central nervous system indications did not achieve long-term success, the safety data accrued from these studies may lower the translational barrier for ocular applications, provided that proper formulation and localized delivery (or systemic approaches with ocular distribution) can be achieved (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 4–5).

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

The evaluation of KYP-2047 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD involves weighing both its promising aspects and its uncertainties. On the positive side, KYP-2047 is a well-defined, highly potent inhibitor of PREP with an established chemical profile and a strong foundation in preclinical studies. Its synthetic origin as a peptidomimetic compound designed to bind the active site of PREP is well documented (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4), and the compound’s low nanomolar potency provides confidence that even modest drug exposures may achieve effective enzyme inhibition.

The repurposing strategy capitalizes on emerging evidence that PREP inhibitors can exert cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in RPE cells. In vitro studies conducted in ARPE-19 cells with impaired proteasomal clearance have demonstrated that KYP-2047 can reduce inflammatory cytokine production and promote cell viability (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). Given the central role of inflammation and defective lysosomal clearance in dry AMD, these findings provide a mechanistic rationale for testing KYP-2047 in this indication.

Furthermore, the proposed mechanism—whereby inhibition of PREP reduces the formation of inhibitory proline-rich peptides that suppress cathepsin activity—is mechanistically attractive. Restoring the function of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and L could feasibly improve the degradation of POS, a process known to be compromised in dry AMD. This dual-targeted approach (improving both enzyme activity and reducing cell stress) is particularly compelling in the context of a multifactorial disease such as AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

Despite these strengths, several potential weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. First, while extensive preclinical work has been carried out in neurological models—and there exists some early in vitro evidence of benefit in RPE cells—the direct connection between PREP activity and the inhibition of cathepsin function in the context of RPE biology remains largely hypothetical. The literature currently lacks robust in vivo studies in ocular models of dry AMD demonstrating that PREP inhibition translates into measurable improvements in retinal function and morphology. Historical clinical trials of PREP inhibitors for cognitive applications have encountered difficulties due to inconsistent efficacy, which raises concerns about the translation of in vitro findings to clinical benefits (Scuderi, 2023, pp. 133–135; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41).

Second, the formulation challenges associated with KYP-2047 cannot be overlooked. Its low water solubility necessitates specialized carriers (such as saline with 5% Tween® 80), which may complicate delivery to the eye, especially when considering the need for localized administration to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE. Appropriate ocular delivery systems (e.g., intravitreal injections or sustained-release implants) would need to be developed and optimized, which adds a layer of complexity to the overall drug development program (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47).

Another area of concern is the historical inconsistency of PREP inhibitor effects in clinical studies. Although there is evidence of neuroprotective benefits, the fact that several PREP inhibitors failed to advance through the clinical development pipeline for neurological indications suggests that the enzyme’s true physiological role remains incompletely defined. In the absence of a clear and reproducible biomarker for PREP inhibition in vivo, there is a risk that the biochemical benefits seen in cell culture studies may not be recapitulated in the complex environment of the human retina (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 70–72).

Moreover, because PREP is a ubiquitous enzyme expressed in many tissues, systemic administration of KYP-2047 might lead to off-target effects that could limit its therapeutic window. Although the safety profile observed in early neurological trials is encouraging, targeted delivery to the eye (to minimize systemic exposure) will be crucial if KYP-2047 is to be repurposed for dry AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

Finally, while the proposed mechanism that links elevated PREP activity with the inhibition of lysosomal cathepsins is intriguing, it remains to be validated by direct experimental data specifically in RPE cells. The current literature, including the recent study by Toppila and colleagues, primarily focuses on the cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory actions of KYP-2047 in ARPE-19 cells, but detailed biochemical analyses linking PREP inhibition mechanistically to improved cathepsin-mediated degradation of POS are still needed (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 4–6).

─────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

In summary, KYP-2047 is an established prolyl oligopeptidase inhibitor with a well-characterized chemical and pharmacological profile, offering promising features as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its ability to inhibit PREP at low nanomolar concentrations, coupled with demonstrated cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in preclinical RPE models, aligns well with the therapeutic need to restore lysosomal cathepsin activity and improve photoreceptor outer segment degradation in dry AMD (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 12–13).

The strategy to mitigate the accumulation of inhibitory proline-rich peptides and thereby reinstate effective lysosomal function is mechanistically plausible and supported by related studies in neural tissues. Nevertheless, the exact role of PREP in the modulation of cathepsin activity in RPE cells remains to be fully elucidated. In addition, the challenges of achieving appropriate ocular drug delivery and the historical precedents of inconsistent efficacy in PREP inhibitor clinical trials represent significant hurdles that must be addressed in future studies (Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 39–41).

Overall, while KYP-2047 brings strengths in terms of potency and a partially validated cytoprotective profile in in vitro models, its repurposing for dry AMD would require further in-depth preclinical studies. These studies should include in vivo efficacy assessments in relevant animal models of AMD, comprehensive pharmacokinetic and ocular distribution evaluations, and mechanistic experiments that clearly link PREP inhibition with improved cathepsin and lysosomal function in the RPE. Should these studies confirm the initial promising results, the favorable safety profile observed in prior neurological trials may indeed support the rapid translation of KYP-2047 into early-phase clinical testing for dry AMD (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

In conclusion, KYP-2047 represents a promising, albeit still exploratory, approach to targeting a novel biochemical pathway in the context of dry AMD. The rationale is supported by a solid foundation of preclinical data in other disease models, yet its success in ocular repurposing will depend on overcoming formulation challenges and further clarifying the mechanistic underpinnings of its action in retinal pigment epithelial cells.

─────────────────────────────  
Strengths and Weaknesses Summary

Strengths:  
•  KYP-2047 is a potent, well-characterized PREP inhibitor with a strong synthetic and chemical development history (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Guardiola et al., 2018, pp. 3–4).  
•  Its low nanomolar IC₅₀ provides confidence in its biochemical efficacy, and available preclinical data indicate cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in RPE cell models (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22).  
•  The drug class has been extensively studied in neurological and cancer contexts, offering insights into its safety profile and potential mechanisms such as autophagy activation and reduced oxidative stress (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 70–72, 85–88).  
•  The hypothesis that PREP activity leads to the accumulation of cathepsin-inhibiting peptides is mechanistically plausible, which could lead to restoration of lysosomal enzyme activity in RPE cells (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).  

Weaknesses:  
•  Historically, PREP inhibitors have shown inconsistent efficacy in clinical trials for neurological applications; it remains uncertain whether the benefits will translate to the ocular setting (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 18–22, 39–41).  
•  Direct evidence linking PREP inhibition with improvements in cathepsin activity and POS degradation in RPE cells is still limited, and further mechanistic studies are required (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47; Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
•  The low aqueous solubility of KYP-2047 necessitates complex formulations, which might complicate ocular drug delivery and could require novel delivery systems to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 44–47).  
•  Systemic safety and potential off-target effects remain a concern, given that PREP is widely expressed and the compound’s systemic clearance and ocular bioavailability have yet to be thoroughly characterized in vivo (Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

─────────────────────────────  
Final Remarks

Based on the current literature and the data available, KYP-2047 exhibits several attractive features for repurposing in dry AMD, especially regarding its potential to restore lysosomal function in the RPE by reducing the inhibitory load on cathepsins. However, while the biochemical rationale is compelling and early in vitro data are promising, significant challenges remain. Translational steps such as in vivo efficacy verification in AMD models, optimization of ocular formulation, and further elucidation of the mechanistic pathway are essential before proceeding to clinical development. Thus, KYP-2047 warrants further preclinical evaluation with a specific focus on its ocular pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics, which will ultimately determine its viability as a novel therapeutic candidate against dry age-related macular degeneration (Toppila et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 12–13; Jalkanen, 2012, pp. 66–68).

This comprehensive review supports the notion that repurposing KYP-2047 for dry AMD is a promising strategy, but caution must be exercised given the prior challenges encountered with the PREP inhibitor class in other indications. Future studies should be designed to address these gaps and de-risk the development plan before large-scale clinical trials are considered.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AM580 is a fully synthetic retinoid compound designed as a highly selective agonist for the retinoic acid receptor α (RARα). Its chemical structure—a derivative of naphthalene and benzoic acid—was rationally engineered to confer two key properties: a more rigid molecular architecture compared with the natural ligand all‐trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and a marked preferential binding to RARα over other retinoid receptor subtypes (RARβ and RARγ) (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992). AM580 belongs to the broader class of retinoids—compounds that are either natural derivatives of vitamin A or synthetically modified analogues—which function as ligands for nuclear hormone receptors. Retinoids have been exploited in various fields of medicine due to their ability to modulate cellular differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis by activating retinoic acid receptor (RAR) and retinoid X receptor (RXR) pathways (Cras et al., 2010; Martin et al., 1992). In the case of AM580, its design emphasizes selective RARα activation, as demonstrated by its 30-fold higher binding affinity for RARα compared to RARβ and RARγ (Teng et al., 1996; Martin et al., 1992), making it an excellent molecular tool for dissection of RARα-specific biological responses.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, retinoids have been at the forefront of differentiation therapy, with ATRA being successfully employed in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) (Garattini et al., 2007; Garattini et al., 1997). However, the clinical use of natural retinoids like ATRA has been limited by drawbacks such as isomerization, rapid metabolism, and broad receptor engagement leading to unnecessary side effects (Drowley et al., 2020; Cras et al., 2010). These limitations spurred the development of receptor subtype–selective ligands, among which AM580 emerged as a leading RARα-selective agonist (Martin et al., 1992). Beyond oncology, synthetic retinoids have been investigated in a variety of contexts including dermatology and even cardiovascular applications (Nagy et al., 2012; Petrukhin, 2013); however, more recent studies have explored the potential ocular applications of retinoid receptor agonists. In particular, a growing body of literature has begun to examine the effects of RAR agonists on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that activation of RARα in RPE cells by compounds such as AM580 can modulate epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and improve cellular functions relevant to retinal homeostasis (Kobayashi et al., 2021). Although not previously approved as an ocular therapeutic, the compound’s use in research settings—including those investigating phagocytic processes in the RPE—provides a promising precedent for repurposing it for conditions like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of AM580 is well delineated at the molecular level. As an RARα agonist, it binds with high affinity to the ligand-binding domain of RARα, a nuclear receptor that functions as a ligand-dependent transcription factor. Upon ligand binding, the receptor undergoes a conformational change that results in the dissociation of co-repressor complexes and the recruitment of co-activators and other transcriptional machinery. This ligand-induced activation facilitates the heterodimerization of RARα with retinoid X receptor (RXR), followed by binding to retinoic acid response elements (RAREs) in the promoter regions of target genes (Garattini et al., 2007; Teng et al., 1996).  
Notably, AM580’s structural modification—featuring a polar amide linkage—enhances its selectivity for RARα by promoting specific hydrogen bonding interactions within the receptor’s binding pocket that are not available in RARβ or RARγ (Teng et al., 1996). Once activated, RARα modulates a variety of downstream genes. Among these, studies have recently indicated that selective RARα activation can lead to the upregulation of milk fat globule epidermal growth factor 8 (MFGE8) in RPE cells (Unknown Reference). MFGE8 plays a critical role in facilitating the bridging of phosphatidylserine (exposed on the shed photoreceptor outer segments (POS)) to integrin receptors—specifically αvβ5—which are expressed on the RPE, thereby promoting efficient phagocytosis (Drowley et al., 2020; Kobayashi et al., 2021). Consequently, AM580’s engagement of RARα is expected to not only drive transcriptional changes related to RPE differentiation and anti-fibrotic responses but also directly enhance phagocytic clearance mechanisms essential for retinal health (Kobayashi et al., 2021). In additional preclinical settings, RARα agonism via AM580 has been implicated in modulating transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling pathways, which further supports its capacity to inhibit aberrant EMT—a process implicated in retinal scarring and progression of dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

The central hypothesis under evaluation posits that AM580, by selectively activating RARα at an effective concentration (EC₅₀ ~50 nM as observed in RPE cell assays), will stimulate the transcription of the MFGE8 gene. AM580 represents a compelling therapeutic candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, based on several lines of evidence gathered from the literature. Its primary strength lies in its high degree of selectivity for RARα. This receptor selectivity is critical because it allows for target‐specific modulation of gene expression, potentially reducing the broad side effects observed with natural retinoids like ATRA that activate multiple receptor subtypes (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992; Teng et al., 1996). Another concern is that AM580, while selective, does retain some activity at RARβ and RARγ at higher concentrations (Teng et al., 1996), an effect that may have unpredictable consequences on cell signaling in the complex microenvironment of the RPE. Despite these strengths, the transition from preclinical studies to clinical application will require careful attention to pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic factors, as well as rigorous safety assessments to mitigate risks typical of retinoid therapies. Overall, while challenges remain, AM580’s unique properties render it a promising candidate that merits further investigation in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to fill a significant therapeutic gap in the management of this debilitating condition (Martin et al., 1992; Teng et al., 1996; Kobayashi et al., 2021).
