Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
AMY-101 is a third-generation compstatin analogue built on the Cp40 scaffold, a cyclic, disulfide-constrained peptide discovered through iterative structure–activity optimization of the original compstatin hit identified by phage display against C3/C3b in 1996 (initial macrocycle I[CVVQDWGHHRC]T) (Lamers et al., 2022). Key potency-improving modifications en route to Cp40 include N-methylation of Trp and insertion of sarcosine, which rigidify the backbone and substantially increase binding affinity to C3; Cp40 (y-I[CV(1Me)WQDWSarAHRC]mI) binds a defined pocket between MG4/MG5 on the β-chain of C3/C3b with subnanomolar affinity and high selectivity for human and nonhuman primate (NHP) C3, while sparing other species, thereby necessitating NHP for translational in vivo work (Lamers et al., 2022). Mechanistically, compstatins are protein–protein interaction inhibitors: they occupy a substrate-binding site on C3 that prevents association with the C3 convertases, blocking convertase-mediated cleavage of native C3, and thereby interrupting the amplification loop and downstream effector generation (C3a, C3b, C5a, and membrane attack complex) independent of the initiating pathway (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Compstatin analogues comprise a class of synthetic macrocyclic peptides that target the central node of complement activation at C3, distinguishing them from terminal-pathway blockers (e.g., C5 antibodies) and alternative-pathway–restricted inhibitors (e.g., factor D), which have shown mixed outcomes in complex complement-driven diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Mastellos et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Clinically, the compstatin platform has matured to produce both a PEGylated bivalent C3 inhibitor (pegcetacoplan/APL-2) approved for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and non-PEGylated Cp40-derived candidates such as AMY-101 in human trials, establishing class translatability and safety management paradigms for chronic C3 inhibition (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

For ophthalmic translation, medicinal chemistry on Cp40 has produced fourth-generation, non-PEGylated lysine-extended derivatives (Cp40-KK, Cp40-KKK) with markedly improved solubility and favorable intraocular retention after intravitreal (IVT) administration in NHPs; these scaffolds maintain subnanomolar C3 affinity and exhibit retinal tissue engagement and co-localization with C3, suggesting target-driven distribution in ocular compartments (Hughes et al., 2020). Within the compstatin clinical lineage, earlier intravitreal compstatin (POT-4) and the PEGylated derivative APL-2/pegcetacoplan provided clinical benchmarks in geographic atrophy (GA), albeit with formulation-dependent considerations (e.g., PEG-associated risks) that motivate PEG-free ocular candidates such as AMY-101 or next-generation Cp40 analogues tailored for ocular delivery (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Compstatin peptides have undergone extensive preclinical characterization and early clinical translation across complement-driven indications. Systemically, Cp40/AMY-101 blocked intravascular hemolysis and C3b opsonization in primate models and attenuated alloimmune responses and downstream B/T cell activation in transplantation models, demonstrating potent complement control and immunomodulatory ripple effects in vivo (Lamers et al., 2022). AMY-101 progressed through a first-in-human phase 1 trial (single and multiple ascending doses; subcutaneous and intravenous) with acceptable safety, no serious adverse events, and pharmacodynamic evidence of complement pathway modulation in healthy volunteers (Amyndas Pharmaceuticals S.A., 2017), and subsequently achieved local-delivery efficacy in a randomized, double-blind, split-mouth Phase IIa study for gingival inflammation with durable anti-inflammatory responses and no drug-induced immunogenicity detected (Hasturk et al., 2021). In the periodontal trial, AMY-101 reduced clinical indices (modified gingival index, bleeding on probing) and decreased matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-8, MMP-9) in gingival crevicular fluid, with effects persisting up to 90 days after the three weekly local injections, supporting local tolerability, biomarker responsiveness, and sustained pharmacodynamic action (Hasturk et al., 2021).

Within ophthalmology and AMD, multiple lines of evidence support the clinical plausibility of C3-directed strategies. Early intravitreal compstatin (POT-4) dosing in a primate model was associated with disappearance of drusen deposits, and PEGylated C3 inhibition (APL-2/pegcetacoplan) reduced GA lesion growth in Phase II and has achieved efficacy signals in Phase III, representing the first successful complement intervention in GA and validating the target class for dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). Conversely, downstream or pathway-restricted modulation disappointed: anti-C5 agents (eculizumab, LFG316) and alternative pathway blockade at factor D (lampalizumab) failed to deliver clinical benefit in GA, bolstering the rationale for upstream C3 control that addresses both opsonization and effector generation (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Although AMY-101 itself has not yet been reported in human ocular trials in the provided context, Cp40-class derivatives have been tailored for ocular use and evaluated in NHPs after single IVT injections, achieving prolonged C3-saturating vitreous concentrations and retinal/choroidal target engagement for over three months—exposure metrics compatible with infrequent intravitreal maintenance regimens (Hughes et al., 2020).

Critically, human iPSC-derived RPE models carrying the common CFH Y402H high-risk variant establish a mechanistic and phenotypic bridge to AMD and provide in vitro evidence that Cp40 reverses disease-relevant pathology, particularly lysosome/autophagy defects and complement-driven lysosomal overburden, thereby directly supporting the translational concept for dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The RPE findings are reinforced by the broader AMD complement literature: complement activation on photoreceptor outer segments drives monocyte-dependent retinal atrophy, factor H genetics (including Y402H) modulates ocular alternative pathway activity, and complement deposition in Bruch’s membrane/sub-RPE space contributes to drusen biogenesis and RPE stress—elements that are mechanistically addressable by C3 blockade (Mastellos et al., 2019).

In sum, compstatin-class agents have an extensive preclinical pedigree and emergent clinical validation. For AMD specifically, the class has ocular proof-of-concept (POT-4) and clinical validation of C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan), and Cp40 analogues demonstrate prolonged ocular PK in NHP; AMY-101 contributes human safety and local-delivery experience that supports translational risk management but requires dedicated ocular development for dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
C3 sits at the convergence of the classical, lectin, and alternative complement pathways; its cleavage by C3 convertases (C4b2b for CP/LP and C3bBb for AP) produces the anaphylatoxin C3a and the opsonin C3b, which seeds an amplification loop by forming additional alternative pathway convertases on activating surfaces (Mastellos et al., 2019). Persistent generation and deposition of C3b (and downstream C5b-9) under dysregulated conditions fuels inflammatory tissue damage and membrane injury; thus, targeting C3 offers initiation-independent suppression of both opsonization and effector generation (C3a, C5a, MAC), addressing multiple pathogenic modalities concurrently (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Compstatins, including Cp40/AMY-101, are substrate-protecting inhibitors that bind to a defined site on C3/C3b (between MG4 and MG5 of the β-chain) and prevent the binding of native C3 to the active convertase, thereby blocking C3 turnover and the AP amplification cycle regardless of initiating pathway (Lamers et al., 2022). This binding mode is supported by co-crystallographic and kinetic analyses, and SAR has established critical roles for N-methylated Trp and charged residues (Asp7, Arg12) in affinity and solubility (Lamers et al., 2022). Unlike some PEGylated bivalent constructs that display altered target preference and weaker affinity to soluble C3, monovalent PEG-free Cp40 binds strongly to both soluble and surface-bound C3/C3b, preserving potency where soluble target is abundant (e.g., in plasma and vitreous), a beneficial profile for local ocular delivery (Lamers et al., 2022).

In human iPSC-RPE carrying CFH Y402H, C3 overactivation and increased C3 turnover correlate with multiple autophagy–lysosome abnormalities: increased expression of autophagosome markers (LC3-II, p62, ATG12–ATG5), expansion and activation of late endosomal/lysosomal/exosomal compartments (LAMP1, CD63; increased Lysotracker), reduced lysosomal functional readouts (decreased Cathepsin D expression/activity), swollen lysosome-like vesicles, lysosomal membrane fragility (elevated galectin-8 recruitment), and extracellular deposition of Cathepsin D in ApoE-positive drusen-like material (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Mechanistic links are twofold: (1) excessive extracellular C3 activation increases surface C5b-9 (MAC) formation, which is internalized to lysosomes and triggers lysosomal membrane permeabilization with cathepsin leakage; (2) intracellular C3–autophagy crosstalk via ATG16L1 and cathepsin-mediated C3 activation may perturb autophagy flux, compounding lysosomal stress (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In this model, Cp40 reduces C3 turnover (biochemical ELISA/MSD readouts) and diminishes C3b and C5b-9 deposition on and within RPE, leading to restoration of lysosomal pH/function and autophagic flux (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Specifically, Cp40 treatment increases Cathepsin D expression/activity, reduces lysosome size and swelling, stabilizes lysosomal membranes (reduced galectin-8/LAMP co-localization), normalizes melanosome content (increased mature type 4 melanosomes), and decreases the volume of drusen-like deposits on transwells—collectively, a reversal of RPE disease phenotypes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Importantly, the RPE data underscore that “tuning” C3 is necessary: stable shRNA knockdown of C3 (~85% reduction) did not restore melanosome/lysosome number and increased stress vacuoles indicative of a detrimental effect, whereas pharmacologic Cp40-mediated control of C3 turnover (not wholesale depletion) was beneficial—consistent with C3’s homeostatic roles in tissue clearance and immune surveillance (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Rapamycin-driven autophagy activation failed to correct lysosomal deficits in the same AMD-RPE model, underscoring that upstream removal of complement burden may be required to re-enable autophagic clearance in complement-dysregulated RPE (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

For ophthalmic PK/PD, next-generation Cp40 derivatives (Cp40-KK, Cp40-KKK) demonstrate prolonged vitreous residence and target engagement after single IVT injection in cynomolgus NHPs, measured by a sensitive SPR-based competition assay that recovers peptide from C3 complexes by heat dissociation and quantifies active inhibitor; ocular C3 levels were assayed in parallel (Hughes et al., 2020). Following a 0.5 mg IVT dose, Cp40-KKK maintained C3-saturating vitreous concentrations over three months (~200 nM during month 1; ~100–120 nM by month 3) and co-localized with C3 in retinal/choroidal tissue, suggesting target-driven retention and possible depot release; intraocular C3 concentrations measured were ~0.1–2 nM, implying inhibitor:target ratios sufficient for sustained pharmacodynamic coverage (Hughes et al., 2020). Only ~0.2% of the initial dose remained unbound in vitreous by day 14, consistent with rapid clearance of free peptide and prolonged persistence of target-bound pools (Hughes et al., 2020). These PK relationships, combined with AMY-101’s subnanomolar C3 affinity and prolonged plasma half-life (>60 h), support the feasibility of durable local complement control via IVT compstatin analogues without PEGylation (Lamers et al., 2022; Hasturk et al., 2021; Lamers et al., 2022).

Expected Effect  
In the proposed iPSC-RPE assay, AMY-101/Cp40 is expected to bind native C3 in the extracellular milieu and block its convertase-mediated cleavage, thereby suppressing both C3a/C3b generation and downstream terminal-pathway activation, including formation and lysosomal internalization of C5b-9 complexes that exacerbate lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cathepsin leakage in complement-dysregulated RPE (Lamers et al., 2022; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The RPE model provides direct biochemical and cell-biological readouts that respond to C3 inhibition: Cp40 reduced C3 turnover (C3b/iC3b/C3c in supernatants), decreased surface and lysosomal C3b and C5b-9, and restored lysosomal functional markers (Cathepsin D expression and activity), organelle morphology (reduced lysosomal swelling; increased mature melanosomes), and membrane integrity (decreased galectin-8 recruitment), with associated reductions in drusen-like deposit burden—outcomes that would be expected for AMY-101 under similar conditions (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Given the measured RPE complement activity and the presence of C3 in ocular compartments, PD monitoring can include extracellular C3 fragment profiling (e.g., MSD capture for C3a domain detecting C3b; ELISA for C3b/iC3b/C3c), surface and lysosomal C5b-9 immunostaining (e.g., co-localization with LAMP markers), and lysosomal/autophagy endpoints such as LAMP1/CD63 expression, LysoTracker signal, LC3-II and p62 accumulation, Cathepsin D protein/activity, and galectin-8–based lysosomal damage assays (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In the referenced RPE studies, effective Cp40 exposure used 6 µM for seven days with media change mid-course—a regimen that achieved robust biochemical and morphological rescue; potency in cellular systems is governed by high target abundance and convertase dynamics and may not mirror biochemical IC₅₀ values, but AMY-101’s subnanomolar C3 affinity and the low-nanomolar ocular C3 concentrations measured in NHP vitreous suggest that pharmacologically relevant free drug levels in the assay will saturate target (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). We note that no direct IC₅₀ for Cp40/AMY-101 in RPE culture is provided in the cited work; therefore, the proposed IC₅₀ value (~0.5 µM) cannot be confirmed from the current context and dosing should be guided empirically by the established 6 µM exposure used to reverse phenotypes in the Y402H model (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Regarding photoreceptor outer segment (POS) processing, impaired lysosomal function in RPE is causally linked to defective POS degradation; complement activation on POS can drive monocyte-dependent retinal atrophy, providing disease-relevant context for expecting that restoration of lysosomal flux via C3 inhibition would secondarily improve POS handling (Mastellos et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). However, the provided RPE studies did not explicitly report POS uptake/degradation assays in Cp40-treated cells, so POS-specific rescue should be treated as a testable hypothesis rather than an established outcome; lysosomal/autophagy restoration and reduced complement burden provide a mechanistic basis for such improvement (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

For translational extrapolation to IVT dosing paradigms, ocular PK from Cp40-KK/KKK in NHP indicates that non-PEGylated Cp40 analogues can achieve multi-month C3-saturating exposure (retinal/choroidal co-localization with C3), which, combined with AMY-101’s high-affinity binding and absence of PEG (avoiding anti-PEG immunogenicity and PEG-related tissue effects), supports feasibility of infrequent dosing with a favorable mechanistic risk–benefit profile (Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
– Mechanistic centrality and breadth of action at C3: AMY-101 directly blocks the C3 convertase–substrate interaction, upstream of opsonization and effector generation, thereby intercepting multiple pathogenic drivers operative in dry AMD (C3b deposition, C3a/C5a-mediated inflammation, and MAC-mediated membrane injury), in contrast to pathway-restricted or terminal-pathway agents that have underperformed in GA (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). By protecting C3 from cleavage rather than inhibiting a specific convertase assembly, AMY-101 exerts initiation-independent control, appropriate for the complex and mixed complement activation modes present in AMD (Hasturk et al., 2021).  
– Direct human RPE disease-model evidence: In Y402H iPSC-RPE, Cp40 suppressed C3 turnover and downstream C5b-9 deposition, relieved lysosomal overburden and membrane fragility, restored Cathepsin D expression/activity and melanosome maturation, and reduced drusen-like deposits—an unusually comprehensive, mechanistically coherent rescue of AMD-relevant cellular pathology that maps directly onto the hypothesized mode of action for AMY-101 (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Ocular PK/translational feasibility: Single IVT dosing of Cp40 lysine-extended derivatives in NHPs yielded >90 days of C3-saturating intraocular exposure with retinal/choroidal target engagement and co-localization, supporting achievable, infrequent dosing intervals for a PEG-free compstatin platform; methods to quantify ocular drug and C3 (SPR competition; ELISA) and retinal localization are validated and can be deployed for PD monitoring (Hughes et al., 2020).  
– Clinical precedent for the target class in GA and systemic safety: Pegcetacoplan’s efficacy in reducing GA growth validates C3 inhibition in dry AMD; prolonged systemic C3 inhibition has an acceptable safety profile with appropriate vaccination and monitoring, and AMY-101 itself showed favorable safety, lack of anti-drug antibodies, and durable local efficacy in a human local-delivery setting (periodontal disease) (Lamers et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2020; Hasturk et al., 2021).  
– PEG-free design: Non-PEGylated Cp40 analogues avoid PEG-associated liabilities (anti-PEG antibodies, tissue vacuolation, and potential association with CNV conversion observed in a subset of GA patients on PEGylated C3 inhibitors), while maintaining strong affinity for soluble C3—attributes favorable for chronic ocular use (Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
– No human ocular clinical data for AMY-101: Despite compelling RPE in vitro data and NHP ocular PK for related derivatives, AMY-101 lacks reported human ocular PK/safety and clinical efficacy data in AMD in the provided context; bridging studies will be required to confirm ocular tolerability, immunogenicity, and dosing intervals specific to AMY-101 (Lamers et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2020).  
– Species specificity constrains preclinical breadth: Compstatins bind human/NHP C3 with high specificity, precluding meaningful small-animal efficacy studies beyond surrogate approaches; this increases reliance on NHP for ocular PK/PD and toxicity packages and complicates broader in vivo AMD model validation (Lamers et al., 2022).  
– POS degradation not yet demonstrated under Cp40 in RPE: Although lysosomal/autophagy restoration strongly predicts improved POS clearance, the provided RPE studies did not report POS uptake/degradation assays post-Cp40; this is an essential disease-relevant endpoint to include in the next-stage validation (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Need to balance complement suppression: Stable C3 knockdown in the RPE model exacerbated stress phenotypes, underscoring the necessity for controlled pharmacologic inhibition rather than depletion; clinical protocols must monitor for under/over-suppression and preserve homeostatic complement roles in the immunoprivileged ocular environment (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Potential safety/biology caveats with C3 blockade in the eye: Theoretical risks include modulation of macrophage polarization that might favor neovascularization and the necessity to maintain anti-infective surveillance locally; although systemic experience with vaccination mitigates infectious risk, ocular-specific risks and CNV conversion propensity must be assessed prospectively for PEG-free C3 inhibitors (Mastellos et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2020). Patient stratification (“complotype”) and baseline complement activity vary with age/sex and genetics (e.g., CFH), necessitating biomarker-driven inclusion and response frameworks in trials (Mastellos et al., 2019).

Decision-grade Assessment and Development Plan  
– Scientific validity: Strong. The AMD-RPE disease biology is directly addressed by AMY-101’s mechanism, with robust iPSC-RPE rescue data for Cp40 spanning biochemical, organellar, and deposit readouts; the mechanism integrates with known complement–lysosome–autophagy crosstalk and MAC-induced lysosomal permeabilization (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Translational feasibility: Good, with defined tasks. Ocular PK/PD in NHPs for Cp40 derivatives is compelling and suggests IVT dosing intervals of 2–3 months; AMY-101 has favorable systemic/local safety credentials and is PEG-free (Hughes et al., 2020; Hasturk et al., 2021). The absence of human ocular data for AMY-101 is a remediable gap.  
– Comparative landscape: Favorable. Factor D and C5 failures in GA argue for upstream intervention; C3 inhibition has shown clinical benefit (pegcetacoplan), placing AMY-101 in a validated mechanistic class, with potential safety advantages from PEG-free design and strong affinity to soluble C3 (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).  
– Key risks: Ocular safety (immunogenicity, inflammation, CNV conversion), pharmacodynamic over-suppression, and unknowns around long-term retinal tissue distribution with AMY-101 (as distinct from Cp40-KKK). These will be addressed with staged NHP toxicology/PK, dosing optimization, and clinical biomarker surveillance (Hughes et al., 2020; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Recommended studies before IND for dry AMD  
1) In vitro translational package in human iPSC-RPE (Y402H and non-risk): reproduce Cp40 rescue with AMY-101 under identical conditions (6 µM; 7-day dosing), including biochemical C3 turnover (C3b/iC3b/C3c), surface/lysosomal C5b-9, LAMP1/CD63, LysoTracker, LC3-II, p62, galectin-8, Cathepsin D expression and activity, melanosome quantitation, and drusen-like deposit volume (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Add POS feeding assays (pulse–chase of isolated POS) to quantify phagosome–lysosome fusion kinetics and rhodopsin degradation as POS-specific endpoints (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
2) Ocular PK and PD in cynomolgus NHPs with AMY-101: single- and multiple-dose IVT, vitreous/tissue levels by SPR competition assay, vitreous C3 fragments and C3:drug ratios, retinal/choroidal co-localization, and depot behavior versus Cp40-KKK; include dose ranging (≥0.5 mg) and extended sampling to ≥90 days (Hughes et al., 2020).  
3) Ocular safety/toxicology: GLP IVT studies (single and repeat-dose) evaluating inflammation, IOP, ERG, OCT/FAF, histopathology (RPE, choroid, retina), and immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies intraocular/systemic) with correlation to drug levels and C3 suppression; monitor for CNV risk signals (Mastellos et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2020).  
4) Biomarker strategy: translate RPE/animal biomarkers to clinical sampling—aqueous/vitreous C3 fragments, C5a, sC5b-9; imaging biomarkers (FAF for lipofuscin; OCT for outer retinal integrity; autofluorescent deposit quantification) to track pharmacodynamic effects on deposit burden and RPE health (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2020).  
5) Patient stratification plan: incorporate CFH Y402H and broader complotype profiling in trial design, with baseline complement activity and demographic modifiers (age, sex) to enrich for responders and appropriately power efficacy analyses (Mastellos et al., 2019).

Conclusion  
AMY-101 (Cp40) is a mechanistically precise, high-affinity C3 inhibitor whose action is well matched to the complement-driven lysosomal/autophagy pathology observed in dry AMD RPE biology; Cp40 has already demonstrated reversal of Y402H RPE disease phenotypes across orthogonal readouts, and Cp40-class ocular PK in NHPs supports infrequent IVT dosing without PEG, addressing practical treatment constraints (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The class has clinical validation in GA (pegcetacoplan) and an increasingly reassuring safety dossier for chronic C3 inhibition, while AMY-101 itself exhibits favorable human safety and local-delivery performance in non-ocular indications (Lamers et al., 2022; Hasturk et al., 2021). The principal development gaps—human ocular PK/safety for AMY-101 and POS-specific efficacy readouts—are tractable with focused preclinical and early clinical work. Taken together, the weight of mechanistic, cellular, and translational evidence supports advancing AMY-101 into an ophthalmic development path for dry AMD with a high likelihood of mechanistic efficacy and a manageable risk profile under a biomarker-driven, stratified clinical strategy (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Edaravone (3-methyl-1-phenyl-2-pyrazolin-5-one, also known as MCI-186 or Radicut) is a synthetic small-molecule free radical scavenger that was originally discovered and developed for its neuroprotective properties. Developed by Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma, edaravone belongs to the class of pyrazolone derivatives that have potent antioxidant activities. Its design allows it to function in both aqueous and lipid environments by donating electrons to a range of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and converting these free radicals into an inactive metabolite (2-oxo-3-(phenylhydrazono)-butanoic acid). The chemical structure of edaravone confers low molecular weight and high diffusibility, making it well-suited for rapid cellular uptake and efficient interaction with intracellular free radicals. This property has been exploited in its established clinical use in acute ischemic stroke, and its physicochemical characteristics have also encouraged exploration in other CNS and ocular conditions. The free radical scavenger class of compounds has a long history of use in protecting tissues from oxidative damage, and edaravone, in particular, has been shown to mitigate the destructive effects of excessive ROS generation—a process implicated in numerous degenerative conditions (Masuda et al., 2017; Imai et al., 2010).

Therapeutic History:  
Edaravone has a well-documented clinical history primarily in the management of acute ischemic stroke in Japan, where it was approved in 2001 based on its ability to reduce infarct size and improve neurological outcomes. Its established safety profile in human neurological diseases, including modern trials in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), underlines its potential for systemic administration. Over the years, extensive preclinical investigations have demonstrated that edaravone confers significant neuroprotection by lowering ROS levels, preventing lipid peroxidation, and inhibiting apoptosis in stressed tissue. Although edaravone’s approved indications do not include dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), its neuroprotective and antioxidant properties have been tested in various retinal disease models. For example, studies in animal models of light-induced photoreceptor degeneration, retinal detachment, and even laser-induced choroidal neovascularization have consistently shown that edaravone can reduce oxidative damage, suppress inflammatory cascades, and protect retinal neurons (Imai et al., 2010; Roh et al., 2011). While these models are not direct representations of dry AMD, they share key pathophysiological features with dry AMD, such as high oxidative stress in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor degeneration. Additionally, evidence from in vitro studies using RPE cells supports the idea that edaravone can lower intracellular ROS and thereby improve cell survival under oxidative challenge (Abokyi et al., 2020; Masuda et al., 2017). This history of broad-based use in conditions where excessive ROS plays a central role forms the rationale for repurposing edaravone for dry AMD, a disease in which chronic oxidative stress is a central pathogenic factor.

Mechanism of Action:  
Edaravone exerts its protective effects primarily through its potent antioxidant activity. At the molecular level, it scavenges a variety of ROS—including hydroxyl radicals, superoxide anions, and hydrogen peroxide—by donating an electron to these reactive species. This electron donation converts active free radicals into less harmful molecules and leads to the formation of an inactive end‐product, thereby interrupting the self‐propagating chain reactions of lipid peroxidation (Imai et al., 2010; Masuda et al., 2017). Such oxidative reactions are known to damage cellular components including lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.

In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium, which is characterized by a high rate of oxidative metabolism and exposure to intense light, ROS accumulation has several deleterious consequences. One key aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis is the oxidative inactivation of lysosomal enzymes, particularly cathepsin D, which is essential for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Under conditions of excessive ROS, lysosomal membranes become compromised by lipid peroxidation, resulting in increased lysosomal pH and subsequent inactivation of cathepsin D. This inefficiency in lysosomal digestion leads to the accumulation of undigested POS and lipofuscin—a process that further exacerbates cellular dysfunction in the RPE (Klettner et al., 2013).

Edaravone’s capacity to scavenge ROS is therefore hypothesized to maintain the functional integrity of lysosomes in RPE cells. By reducing the oxidative burden, edaravone can help preserve the acidic environment (low pH) required for optimal cathepsin D activity. Additionally, oxidative stress is known to impair autophagic flux in RPE cells, as evidenced by alterations in the conversion of LC3-I to its lipidated form LC3-II, which is a marker for autophagosome formation. Enhanced LC3-II flux is associated with efficient autophagy—a process crucial for the clearance of damaged proteins and organelles. By mitigating ROS, edaravone is expected to promote proper LC3-II flux and autophagic activity, further contributing to the clearance of POS debris and damaged organelles in RPE cells (Masuda et al., 2017; Pinelli et al., 2023).

Moreover, several studies have indicated that edaravone can modulate intracellular signaling pathways associated with oxidative stress. For instance, it has been shown to reduce the phosphorylation of stress-activated kinases such as p38 and JNK, both of which are activated in response to elevated ROS levels. Inhibition of these pathways may contribute not only to decreased apoptotic signaling but also to the stabilization of lysosomal function and autophagic processes (Imai et al., 2010; Roh et al., 2011). Overall, the molecular interactions of edaravone—scavenging of free radicals, preservation of lysosomal pH, protection of critical proteases like cathepsin D, and restoration of autophagic flux—form the basis for its proposed repurposing in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The primary expected effect of edaravone in the context of dry AMD is a reduction of oxidative stress within the RPE, thereby preventing the cascade of events that lead to lysosomal dysfunction and defective POS digestion. RPE cells are responsible for the cyclic phagocytosis of POS, and this process is heavily reliant on intact lysosomal function. Under oxidative stress, the lysosomal pH can drift toward alkalinity, which inactivates cathepsin D and impairs the degradation of phagocytosed material. By scavenging ROS, edaravone is anticipated to maintain the acidic environment of lysosomes, thus preserving the enzymatic activity of cathepsin D. This restoration of lysosomal function should translate into improved clearance of POS and reduce the buildup of lipofuscin and drusen—hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Klettner et al., 2013).

The conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II is an essential step in autophagosome formation, and efficient autophagic flux is critical for the removal of damaged organelles and protein aggregates. Experimental evidence suggests that excessive ROS impairs this flux, leading to the accumulation of dysfunctional autophagosomes and cellular debris. Edaravone emerges as a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on a strong mechanistic rationale and an established track record in oxidative stress mitigation. Among its primary strengths is its potent free radical scavenging activity, which underpins its ability to counteract the oxidative stress that is central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. The preclinical literature provides substantive evidence of edaravone’s efficacy in various models of retinal degeneration. The compound’s extensive preclinical evidence in retinal models and established systemic safety profile further support its potential utility. However, the transition from acute retinal injury models to the chronic, multifaceted pathology of dry AMD requires additional focused studies. Specifically, further research is needed to validate its effects on cathepsin D activity, lysosomal pH regulation, and LC3-II flux within the context of RPE and to define the optimal dosing and delivery methods for sustained ocular protection. Given these considerations, edaravone merits further preclinical evaluation in dry AMD models and, if promising, could progress into clinical trials as an adjunct or combination therapy for this major cause of vision loss in the elderly (Abokyi et al., 2020; Imai et al., 2010; Masuda et al., 2017; Pinelli et al., 2023; Roh et al., 2011).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SU5402 is a small‐molecule inhibitor that belongs to the indolinone, also often described as oxindole, family of compounds designed to target receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), most notably fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs) and platelet‐derived growth factor receptors (PDGFRs) (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Chemically, it is defined as 3-[(3-(2-carboxyethyl)-4-methylpyrrol-2-yl)methylene]-2-indolinone, a structure that features an indolin-2-one nucleus decorated with a propionic acid chain and a methyl substituent on a pyrrole ring; these structural motifs enable the molecule to mimic key interactions commonly found in ATP binding (Prakash et al., 2012; Ho et al., 2014). Originally discovered as one of the first classes of FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors, the compound’s crystal structure in complex with FGFR was resolved as early as 1997, establishing its role as an important lead for further inhibitor design (Liang et al., 2012). SU5402 is therefore categorized as an ATP-competitive inhibitor that occupies a hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the adenine binding site in FGFR, and its design has inspired many subsequent efforts to optimize RTK inhibition for therapeutic purposes (Manetti & Botta, 2003). In addition to its potent activity against FGFR1 (with reported IC₅₀ values around 0.03 μM), SU5402 displays inhibitory effects toward PDGFRβ and even VEGFR2, positioning it as a prototype multi-targeted kinase inhibitor in early-stage drug development programs (Chen et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2014). Its synthesis is rooted in structure-based medicinal chemistry approaches whereby modifications of the indolinone core and side chain functionalities were guided by crystal structure data and structure–activity relationship studies (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Consequently, SU5402 stands as a well-characterized synthetic compound with a clearly delineated pharmacophore, and its molecular interactions with the kinase active site are illustrative of the class’s capacity to serve as lead compounds in various therapeutic areas (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the development and use of SU5402 have been predominantly tied to oncology and anti-angiogenic research. Early investigations demonstrated that by inhibiting FGFR signaling, SU5402 effectively blocked the autophosphorylation of the receptor and downstream proliferative and survival pathways such as RAF-MEK1/2-MAPK and PI3K-AKT—pathways that are essential drivers of tumor growth and angiogenesis (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). These studies established its potency in vitro and in animal models, where it was used as a research tool to interrogate the role of FGFR-related pathways in cancer biology (Manetti & Botta, 2003). In addition, several members of the indolinone inhibitor class, including derivatives related to SU5402, such as SU5416 and SU6668, were developed for anti-tumor and anti-angiogenic applications and were advanced to clinical trials for various malignancies (Ho et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016). Despite its promising biochemical profile, SU5402 itself did not progress further in clinical development for oncology, largely due to issues associated with multi-kinase inhibition and subsequent toxicity profiles observed during broader preclinical studies (Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Notably, there is no published record in the literature, as captured by the provided sources, that SU5402 has ever been intentionally repurposed for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal degenerative diseases (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Its application has remained confined as a tool compound in research settings for understanding FGFR signaling and its role in cellular proliferation and angiogenesis, rather than for modulating processes underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) differentiation and phagocytosis. However, its continued use in ocular safety studies in vitro and in rodent models has provided preliminary evidence of an acceptable safety profile when applied topically or delivered locally in ocular tissues (Chen et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2016). Thus, while SU5402 has a rich history as an FGFR inhibitor in cancer-related research, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding its therapeutic use in dry AMD, an area that remains largely unexplored until now.

Mechanism of Action:  
SU5402 exerts its biological activity as an ATP-competitive inhibitor targeting the tyrosine kinase domain of FGFR1, a member of the receptor tyrosine kinase family implicated in various cellular functions including proliferation, differentiation, and survival. At the molecular level, the indolinone core of SU5402 occupies the ATP-binding site in FGFR1, where it competes with ATP for the binding pocket (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Detailed crystallographic studies have revealed that the oxindole nucleus of the compound forms two or more critical hydrogen bonds with conserved residues in the kinase hinge region, specifically with Glu562 and Ala564, which normally interact with the adenine part of ATP (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017). In addition, the propionic acid group of SU5402 forms a third hydrogen bond with the side chain of Asn568, a residue in the hinge region that further stabilizes the inhibitor-bound conformation of the kinase (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017). This binding pattern not only ensures high potency by blocking the ATP-binding site but also promotes a specific conformational change in the glycine-rich loop of FGFR1, which is integral to the enzyme’s catalytic activity (Mohammadi et al., 1998; Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Beyond its direct interactions with FGFR1, SU5402 has also been reported to interact with other kinases such as VEGFR2 and PDGFRβ, albeit with slightly varying potencies. Its ability to inhibit multiple kinases is attributable to the high degree of structural homology within the ATP-binding regions of these receptor tyrosine kinases and reflects its broad-spectrum activity as an RTK inhibitor (Chen et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2014). Despite this multi-target activity, the molecular determinants for its relative selectivity—particularly the critical hydrogen bond interactions and the spatial orientation of its substituents—have been well characterized, making it a useful tool to dissect kinase-mediated pathways (Pike, 2017; Prakash et al., 2012).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, FGFR signaling is implicated in the regulation of cell polarity, differentiation, and the maintenance of phagocytic receptor expression. The hypothesis under evaluation suggests that inhibition of FGFR by SU5402 may tip the balance of intracellular signaling in favor of differentiation-associated processes, thereby upregulating the surface expression of MERTK and the integrin αvβ5 complex, both of which are essential for the binding and internalization of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). In effect, by interfering with the normal FGFR-driven proliferative and survival signals, SU5402 might foster an environment conducive to RPE maturation and enhanced phagocytic functionality. This molecular action is not only supported by the established biochemistry of SU5402 in cancer models but is also mechanistically plausible in the RPE, where FGFR signaling dynamics play a role in determining cell morphology and receptor trafficking (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Chen et al., 2011).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the central hypothesis, the application of SU5402 in mid-differentiation-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived RPE (iPSC-RPE) is expected to modulate the cell-signaling environment such that differentiation-associated genes, particularly those encoding phagocytic receptors, are upregulated. Specifically, FGFR1 inhibition is postulated to lead to improved cell polarity and receptor localization—a phenomenon that has been documented in related studies where FGFR blockade favorably impacts the maturation state of RPE cells (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). In the system under investigation, the key targets are MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase critical for the clearance of shed POS, and the integrin αvβ5 complex, which is essential for the initial binding of these segments to the RPE surface.

The anticipated outcome is multifaceted. First, by attenuating FGFR signaling, SU5402 would relieve any inhibitory crosstalk that might otherwise suppress the expression or proper trafficking of MERTK and αvβ5 receptors. This hypothesis is built on the concept that during RPE differentiation, FGFR signaling might help maintain a less mature phenotype that is less competent in executing the phagocytic process. Thus, timely pharmacological inhibition is predicted to accelerate or enhance the differentiation process, triggering the upregulation and proper localization of these receptors on the cell membrane (Liang et al., 2012; Pike, 2017).

Second, enhanced receptor expression and correct cellular polarity are expected to translate into an increased capacity for POS binding and uptake. In a functional assay, this would manifest as a measurable increase in the phagocytic index of the treated RPE cells compared to control populations. Since robust phagocytic activity is a hallmark of healthy RPE function, improved receptor availability could, in theory, ameliorate some of the cellular deficits that contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Importantly, while the literature available in the provided context does not directly report the use of SU5402 in dry AMD models, the rationale draws on the broader evidence that modulating FGFR signaling can have beneficial effects on cell differentiation and polarity in other cell types (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Liang et al., 2012).

Additionally, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses in similar cell systems have demonstrated that FGFR signaling influences the expression levels of a variety of genes implicated in the maturation and functional competency of epithelial cells, including those involved in phagocytosis. Therefore, by leveraging SU5402’s known activity profile, the expected effect in the proposed iPSC-RPE system is an improved expression profile of MERTK and αvβ5, leading to enhanced clearance of POS. This effect is of particular interest in the context of dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction and the subsequent accumulation of toxic debris contribute to disease progression (Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, SU5402 presents as a well-characterized, indolinone-based FGFR/PDGFRβ inhibitor with a strong biochemical foundation rooted in detailed structural and mechanistic studies. From a chemical and molecular perspective, its design and mechanism of action are well established; the compound engages the ATP-binding pocket of FGFR1 with high potency primarily through a series of well-defined hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions, which underpins its efficacy as an inhibitor (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003; Prakash et al., 2012). These robust mechanistic features, together with its documented ability to modulate downstream signaling events, constitute significant strengths when considering the repurposing of SU5402 for non-oncological indications such as dry AMD.

A key strength in the context of RPE differentiation is the emerging evidence that modulation of FGFR signaling can enhance cell polarity and receptor localization. This is particularly pertinent for the expression of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and integrin αvβ5, which are vital for POS binding and internalization. By repurposing SU5402, there is a compelling opportunity to improve the functionality of less mature iPSC-derived RPE cells—an effect that could translate into a novel therapeutic strategy to mitigate RPE dysfunction in dry AMD (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Despite these promising aspects, there are several challenges and potential weaknesses that need to be addressed. First, the historical development of SU5402 has been overwhelmingly focused on oncology and anti-angiogenic research, with little to no prior evidence in the literature regarding its efficacy in retinal disorders or dry AMD specifically (Manetti & Botta, 2003). Although multi-kinase inhibition might be advantageous by addressing redundancies in pathological signaling networks, it also carries the risk of unintended consequences in the delicate environment of the retina. The multi-targeted nature of SU5402 might disrupt cellular homeostasis if not dosed carefully or if delivered systemically, emphasizing the need for targeted ocular delivery mechanisms to maximize local efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure (Chen et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2014).

Another limitation is related to the dosing regimen and formulation challenges associated with repurposing a compound originally developed for oncology. Many FGFR inhibitors suffer from issues such as limited solubility, off-target toxicity, and suboptimal pharmacokinetics when used outside their intended systemic applications. For ocular use, the formulation must ensure that therapeutic concentrations are reached at the RPE without causing damage to other retinal cells, a balance that can be particularly challenging given the sensitive and tightly regulated environment of the eye (Zhang et al., 2016; Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Furthermore, while the proposed mechanism of modulating FGFR1 to enhance the expression of MERTK and integrin αvβ5 is scientifically plausible, it remains hypothetical until validated by rigorous experimental data in appropriate models of RPE differentiation. The interplay between FGFR signaling and RPE maturation is complex, and compensatory mechanisms could potentially undermine the desired therapeutic effect. For instance, chronic inhibition of FGFR might inadvertently impair other aspects of RPE function or survival that are essential for long-term retinal health, and the intricacies of these signaling pathways in the RPE context have not been fully elucidated (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Liang et al., 2012).

In addition, while preliminary ocular safety data in vitro and in rodent studies is encouraging, the transition from these models to clinical applications in humans is fraught with challenges. The extrapolation of dosing, efficacy, and safety profiles from rodent models to human retinal physiology is not always straightforward, and significant preclinical work will be needed to optimize the use of SU5402 in a dry AMD setting (Chen et al., 2011; Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Overall, the repurposing of SU5402 for dry AMD represents an innovative and intriguing avenue that leverages a well-understood molecule with a rich background in FGFR inhibition. Its strengths in terms of potency, detailed binding interactions, and the theoretical rationale linking FGFR inhibition to improved RPE differentiation and phagocytic receptor expression provide a solid foundation for further investigation. However, the lack of prior application in retinal disorders, potential off-target effects due to its multi-kinase inhibition profile, and the challenges inherent in repurposing a cancer-targeted agent for ocular use are notable limitations that must be carefully addressed.

In conclusion, while SU5402 is a promising candidate from a mechanistic and chemical standpoint, its utility in the treatment of dry AMD remains speculative at this juncture. The proposed hypothesis that FGFR inhibition during RPE differentiation could elevate the expression of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and integrin αvβ5 is both innovative and scientifically grounded, yet it requires extensive validation using robust iPSC-RPE models and appropriate animal studies before any clinical translation can be justified. A strategic plan involving dose optimization, targeted ocular formulation, and a comprehensive evaluation of off-target effects is imperative to ascertain whether SU5402 can ultimately be repositioned as an effective therapeutic agent for dry AMD (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017).

The report is organized into several sections that describe the candidate’s origin, therapeutic history, molecular mechanism, expected effects in the context of RPE (retinal pigment epithelium) pathology, and an overall evaluation of its potential utility in dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Hydroxypropyl‐β‐cyclodextrin (HPβCD) is a chemically modified derivative of β-cyclodextrin, a cyclic oligosaccharide originally discovered as a naturally occurring compound that forms toroidal structures with a hydrophilic exterior and a hydrophobic interior. The modification with hydroxypropyl groups improves its aqueous solubility and reduces toxicity, making it more suitable for biomedical applications. HPβCD belongs to the cyclodextrin family, which has been widely used as drug carriers and excipients due to their ability to form inclusion complexes with a range of lipophilic molecules. The development of HPβCD was driven by the need to improve the solubility and stability of lipophilic drugs, and its ability to modulate cholesterol homeostasis has led to its investigation in several disorders characterized by lipid accumulation. Notably, HPβCD has been studied in the context of cholesterol‐storage diseases such as Niemann–Pick type C disease by virtue of its capacity to extract cholesterol from intracellular membranes. Its synthesis involves partial substitution of hydroxyl groups on the parent β-cyclodextrin with hydroxypropyl moieties, thus expanding its inclusion complexation repertoire and enabling it to interact with lipophilic substrates such as cholesterol and bisretinoids. This candidate’s prior use in ocular studies, especially those addressing cholesterol dyshomeostasis and lipofuscin clearance, provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD, where abnormal lipid accumulation in the RPE is a core pathology (Nociari, Kiss, & Rodriguez-Boulan, 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
HPβCD, as well as its parent cyclodextrin compounds, have been used extensively in both biomedical research and preclinical studies focused on lipid storage disorders. In Niemann–Pick type C models, for example, cyclodextrins have demonstrated efficacy in reducing cholesterol accumulation in lysosomes by sequestering cholesterol and promoting its efflux from cells. This cholesterol‐removal capability has led to its evaluation in animal models that exhibit retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis. Several studies have provided evidence for HPβCD’s beneficial effects on lysosomal function in various cell types; in fibroblasts from Niemann–Pick patients, for instance, HPβCD treatment restored autophagy and reduced intracellular lipid buildup (Moruno-Manchon et al., 2016; Nixon, 2016). Moreover, in a mouse model of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis, HPβCD treatment produced significant reductions in retinal cholesterol content and reduced pathological deposits at critical interfaces such as the photoreceptor outer segment (POS)–RPE boundary (El-Darzi, Mast, Petrov, & Pikuleva, 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).  
In retinal models more directly related to AMD pathogenesis, cyclodextrins have been shown to decrease A2E, a major bisretinoid that accumulates in the RPE with age, by directly forming inclusion complexes with lipofuscin components (Nociari et al., 2017). Additionally, in cultured human cells and in animal studies, cyclodextrins have demonstrated a capacity to modulate lysosomal acidity and enhance the clearance of aggregated or indigestible material. Some reports, however, caution that cyclodextrins may act predominantly through cholesterol depletion rather than by stimulating lysosomal biogenesis via transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Gaspar, Mathieu, & Alvarez, 2017). Furthermore, studies using patient‐derived iPSC‐RPE cells, particularly in the context of Bietti’s crystalline dystrophy, have shown that cyclodextrin treatment rescues lysosomal pH defects and reinstates autophagic flux, which is directly relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology (Hata et al., 2018). Although HPβCD has not been formally trialed in dry AMD patients to date, its cumulative use in preclinical ocular models suggests that its repurposing for AMD is both a viable and promising strategy (El-Darzi et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular basis for HPβCD’s therapeutic potential in retinal diseases rests on its multifaceted ability to interact with lipid and retinoid components within the RPE’s lysosomal compartment. One of the key pathological features of dry AMD is the accumulation of toxic bisretinoids such as A2E within lysosomes, which contributes to impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and eventual cellular dysfunction (Nociari et al., 2017). HPβCD is thought to ameliorate this situation via several interrelated mechanisms:  

1. Direct Extraction and Complexation of Lipofuscin Precursors:  
HPβCD’s hydrophobic cavity allows it to form inclusion complexes with lipophilic compounds. Several reports have provided computational and experimental evidence that β-cyclodextrins form complexes with A2E and other bisretinoids, effectively “solubilizing” these compounds within their cavity. This extraction mechanism leads to a reduction of lipofuscin accumulation in the lysosomes, which is a critical step since lipofuscin impairs lysosomal enzyme activation such as that of cathepsin D (Nociari et al., 2017). The formation of a 2:1 cyclodextrin–A2E complex has been predicted by in silico models, suggesting that each cyclodextrin can accommodate an arm of the A2E molecule, thereby reducing lipofuscin toxicity (Nociari et al., 2017).  

2. Cholesterol Depletion and Modulation of Lysosomal Lipid Homeostasis:  
HPβCD is well known for its ability to extract free and esterified cholesterol from cellular membranes. In the context of dry AMD, cholesterol accumulation contributes to lysosomal dysfunction by perturbing the activity of the vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), leading to lysosomal alkalinization which in turn reduces cathepsin D activity. By depleting excess cholesterol from the POS and RPE, HPβCD can facilitate the restoration of lysosomal acidity. This cholesterol depletion has been documented in several animal models in which HPβCD treatment led to significant reductions in retinal cholesterol levels and improved ultrastructural characteristics of the RPE (El-Darzi et al., 2021). Additionally, this depletion is likely to relieve the inhibition of v-ATPase activity and promote effective autophagosome–lysosome fusion, thereby enhancing overall lysosomal function (Hata et al., 2018; Gaspar et al., 2017).

3. Activation of Autophagy and TFEB-Mediated Lysosomal Biogenesis:  
In many contexts of lysosomal storage and lipid overload, cellular homeostasis can be restored by triggering autophagy. HPβCD has been shown to induce autophagy by upregulating TFEB, a master transcriptional regulator that governs lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic pathways. Activation of TFEB leads to increased expression of genes involved in lysosome formation, acidification, and function. In experimental models, HPβCD has been reported to promote TFEB translocation to the nucleus, thereby enhancing lysosome-mediated degradation of accumulated substrates such as lipofuscin components (Moruno-Manchon et al., 2016; Nociari et al., 2017). It should be noted that not all studies find TFEB upregulation in all cell types; for instance, some human fibroblast studies have highlighted a cholesterol-mediated mechanism with no direct evidence of TFEB activation (Gaspar et al., 2017). Thus, the net effect of HPβCD may stem from a combination of direct removal of toxic aggregates and improvements in autophagic flux via restored lysosomal pH, rather than relying solely on TFEB-mediated biogenesis.

4. Enhancement of Lysosomal Exocytosis:  
A less widely discussed but complementary mechanism involves the induction of calcium-dependent lysosomal exocytosis. HPβCD has been shown in some studies to promote the exocytosis of lysosomal contents, thereby facilitating the clearance of undegraded material from the cell. This process may help eliminate toxic lipofuscin and other aggregated compounds that accumulate in RPE cells over time (Nociari et al., 2017).  

5. Restoration of Cathepsin D Activity and POS Degradation:  
Cathepsin D is a critical lysosomal protease involved in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) material within RPE cells. Accumulated lipofuscin and cholesterol can raise lysosomal pH and directly interfere with cathepsin D maturation and activity. By extracting excess cholesterol and lipofuscin precursors, HPβCD is expected to normalize lysosomal pH and thereby restore cathepsin D function. This restoration is key to improving POS degradation efficiency, which is compromised in dry AMD and contributes to the progressive degeneration of RPE cells (Gaspar et al., 2017; Nixon, 2016). Although direct measurements of enhanced cathepsin D activity following HPβCD treatment in AMD models are not extensively reported in the current literature, the underlying biochemical interactions support the hypothesis that a more acidic lysosomal environment will favor proper cathepsin D activation (El-Darzi et al., 2023; Nociari et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the integrated mechanisms described above, the expected therapeutic effect of HPβCD in dry AMD models is multifold. First, by forming inclusion complexes with A2E and related lipofuscin precursors, HPβCD is expected to lower the intracellular burden of these toxic compounds in RPE lysosomes. This direct extraction would lead to a decrease in the accumulation of lipofuscin, which is known to exacerbate oxidative stress and inflammation in the RPE (Nociari et al., 2017). Second, through its cholesterol-extracting properties, HPβCD should mitigate lipid overload within the RPE cell membranes and lysosomes. This reduction in cholesterol content is predicted to relieve the inhibition on the lysosomal v-ATPase, thereby restoring the acidic pH necessary for optimal lysosomal enzyme function. Consequently, cathepsin D activity should be reinstated, enhancing the capacity of RPE cells to degrade phagocytosed POS material (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Hata et al., 2018). Third, if HPβCD additionally promotes autophagy via TFEB nuclear translocation and increased lysosome biogenesis, there would be an overall improvement in the turnover of cellular debris and a reinforcement of the cell’s degradative machinery. In turn, these improvements should lead to enhanced clearance of damaged proteins, lipids, and photoreceptor debris, thereby reducing RPE cell stress and dysfunction—a primary drive behind dry AMD pathology (Moruno-Manchon et al., 2016; Nociari et al., 2017).  
Furthermore, because lipofuscin accumulation is directly linked to impaired clearance of POS and chronic inflammation, reducing its burden should indirectly improve the visual cycle. Improvements in RPE function would likely translate to better photoreceptor support and potentially slow the progression of macular degeneration, which is critically important in managing dry AMD. In sum, the expected effect of HPβCD is a synergistic improvement in lysosomal function mediated by both direct chemical extraction of toxic substances and indirect enhancement of cellular clearance pathways (Gaspar et al., 2017; Hata et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
Hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin presents several compelling strengths as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its well-documented ability to extract cholesterol and lipophilic toxins from cells has been validated in several preclinical models, and its potential for restoring lysosomal pH and, consequently, lysosomal enzyme activity is particularly attractive in the context of AMD’s impairment of RPE degradative functions (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Nociari et al., 2017). The multifaceted mechanism of action—ranging from direct complexation with A2E to cholesterol depletion and potential activation of autophagy via TFEB—addresses several interconnected pathological processes that drive dry AMD progression. Moreover, cyclodextrins’ extensive history of use in other lipid storage disorders provides a valuable precedent for their clinical repurposing and supports the feasibility of translating these findings into an ocular application (Hata et al., 2018).  

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. There is some inconsistency in the literature regarding the ability of HPβCD to activate TFEB, with certain studies reporting a predominantly cholesterol-mediated mechanism without marked transcriptional upregulation of lysosomal biogenesis (Gaspar et al., 2017). This indicates that the beneficial effects may depend on the specific cellular context and disease model. Additionally, while preclinical evidence in models of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis and lipofuscin accumulation is promising (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023), there remains a need for more direct studies in AMD models—preferably in vitro studies using primary RPE cells or in vivo studies in well-established dry AMD animal models such as the Abca4−/− or other relevant transgenic lines. The dosing issue is also a consideration; in some studies, effective lipofuscin clearance required higher concentrations of HPβCD, which in turn may introduce off-target effects or toxicity concerns that have been noted in other cyclodextrin applications, such as ototoxicity in systemic administration (Gaspar et al., 2017). Moreover, while its ability to cross blood–retina barriers has been demonstrated in some contexts (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023), ensuring sufficient local concentration in the RPE to achieve the desired lysosomal effects without eliciting adverse systemic effects remains an important translational challenge.

In conclusion, the cumulative evidence from biochemical, cellular, and preclinical studies supports the hypothesis that HPβCD has considerable potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its dual action in directly binding and extracting toxic lipofuscin precursors and in correcting cholesterol-mediated lysosomal dysfunction addresses two key pathogenic pathways in dry AMD. While additional research is needed to optimize dosing, verify the mechanism in AMD-specific models, and fully assess safety profiles in the ocular context, the strengths of HPβCD—derived from its proven track record in modulating lipid metabolism and lysosomal function—make it a promising candidate for further development (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Gaspar et al., 2017). The proposed clinical strategy aiming to lower A2E levels, restore lysosomal pH and cathepsin D activity, and enhance POS degradation is well supported by the current literature, and thus HPβCD merits strong consideration for inclusion in the dry AMD therapeutic pipeline.

Overall, while some mechanistic nuances remain to be elucidated, particularly regarding the relative contributions of TFEB activation versus cholesterol extraction, the convergence of preclinical findings and the candidate’s established utility in lysosomal storage disorders provide a solid foundation for advancing HPβCD toward clinical evaluation in dry AMD. Continued investigation into its pharmacokinetics, local retinal bioavailability, and long-term effects on RPE function, along with careful dose optimization in relevant AMD animal models, will be essential next steps in validating its therapeutic value (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Gaspar et al., 2017).

This comprehensive review indicates that HPβCD stands as a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD with several strengths that are directly aligned with the pathophysiological challenges of the disease, while also highlighting areas that require further investigation to ensure a safe and effective translation from preclinical models to clinical application (Hata et al., 2018; Nociari et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ceapin-A7 is a small molecule inhibitor that belongs to the pyrazole amide class of compounds. It was originally discovered through high‐throughput cell‐based screening assays designed to identify modulators of the unfolded protein response (UPR), with an emphasis on selectively targeting the ATF6α signaling branch (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Hetz et al., 2019). Structural optimization through structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies led to the development of Ceapin-A7 as a potent derivative with submicromolar inhibitory activity against ATF6α (Hetz et al., 2019). The molecule’s chemical origins are purely synthetic; its pyrazole amide core is complemented by additional substituents that optimize its binding affinity and selectivity. Traditionally, compounds in this chemical class have been explored as research tools to dissect the UPR pathways and have shown promise in modulating ER stress signaling in various cellular contexts (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). The compound’s design exploits the unique structure–function relationships of ATF6α, aiming to interfere with its normal intracellular trafficking rather than block downstream proteolysis directly, which marks a novel approach compared with many enzyme inhibitors developed for other targets.

Therapeutic History:  
To date, Ceapin-A7 has been mainly used as an investigative tool in cellular models to study mechanisms underlying ER stress and the UPR. Its ability to selectively inhibit ATF6α activation has been characterized in multiple cell lines, including human osteosarcoma U2-OS cells and HEK293 cells engineered to express tagged ATF6α constructs (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Hetz et al., 2019). Although there is extensive preclinical evidence supporting its utility in modulating UPR signaling—all of which has been generated in the context of studies on cancer cells, neurodegeneration, and endothelial dysfunction—there is no historically established clinical or veterinary usage for Ceapin-A7 specifically in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal degenerative diseases. However, the mechanistic insights gained from its application in other cell types have spurred investigations into repurposing Ceapin-A7 as a potential therapeutic candidate for correcting maladaptive ER stress responses in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which plays a pivotal role in diseases such as dry AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Torres et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
Ceapin-A7 exerts its pharmacological action by selectively inhibiting the ATF6α branch of the UPR. Under normal ER stress conditions, ATF6α, a 90-kDa transmembrane protein located in the endoplasmic reticulum, undergoes a stress-induced conformational change that facilitates its packaging into COPII vesicles and subsequent trafficking to the Golgi apparatus. Once in the Golgi, ATF6α is cleaved sequentially by site-1 (S1P) and site-2 (S2P) proteases to release its N-terminal transcription factor domain, which then translocates to the nucleus to upregulate several chaperone and ER stress-related genes (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Ceapin-A7 intervenes at this critical transport step. Rather than inhibiting the proteolytic machinery directly, Ceapin-A7 selectively prevents the ER-to-Golgi trafficking of ATF6α. Mechanistic studies have demonstrated that upon treatment with Ceapin-A7, ATF6α is sequestered within the ER where it accumulates in discrete foci. Fluorescence microscopy analyses have shown that these foci do not colocalize with ER exit site markers such as SEC16 or SEC31A, indicating that the compound disrupts the selection of ATF6α into COPII vesicles (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

One particularly novel aspect of Ceapin-A7’s mechanism is its induction of a neomorphic inter-organelle tether. Detailed proteomic and genome-wide CRISPR interference screening studies have revealed that Ceapin-A7 induces a physical interaction between the cytosolic domain of ATF6α and the peroxisomal transporter protein ABCD3 (Torres et al., 2019). This newly formed tether effectively anchors ATF6α within the ER and precludes its normal traffic to the Golgi. In addition, Ceapin-A7 appears to stabilize ATF6α in its oligomeric state, rather than allowing it to convert to the transport-competent monomeric form (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). The fact that these mechanistic events are reversible upon compound washout further indicates that Ceapin-A7 provides a transient yet highly specific method for modulating ATF6α activity without causing permanent alterations to the protein structure or its eventual capacity to function when the inhibitor is removed (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Such high selectivity distinguishes Ceapin-A7 from broader ER stress inhibitors that often affect multiple UPR signaling branches.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the hypothesized role of Ceapin-A7 is to inhibit chronic ATF6α overactivation in RPE cells, thereby rebalancing the UPR toward adaptive rather than pro-apoptotic responses. Chronic or overwhelming ER stress in RPE cells, as observed in AMD, is associated with decreased expression of genes critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis, including those linked to autophagy, lysosomal function, and the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Because RPE cells are responsible for daily phagocytosis of POS, maintaining efficient lysosomal clearance is crucial for retinal health. In dry AMD, impaired phagocytosis leads to the buildup of toxic byproducts such as lipofuscin, which further exacerbates cellular dysfunction (Kubra et al., 2022; Benedetti et al., 2024).

The therapeutic hypothesis for Ceapin-A7 centers on its capacity to inhibit ATF6α at an IC₅₀ in the low micromolar range (approximately 2 µM, as proposed), thus reducing maladaptive UPR signaling. By preventing ATF6α from trafficking and undergoing proteolytic activation, Ceapin-A7 is expected to alleviate the chronic ER stress that drives RPE dysfunction. In a proposed assay—using ARPE-19 cells in conditions of induced ER stress (for instance, via tunicamycin treatment)—Ceapin-A7 should reduce the levels of cleaved, active ATF6α. This in turn is expected to restore the gene expression patterns associated with lysosomal enzyme production and phagocytic receptor synthesis, thereby enhancing the clearance of POS components (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Furthermore, because the ATF6 branch of the UPR is associated with the upregulation of chaperones like BiP/Grp78, persistent activation can lead to resource exhaustion and an imbalance that favors apoptotic signaling under chronic ER stress conditions (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). By selectively inhibiting this pathway, Ceapin-A7 might reduce excessive chaperone induction and allow cellular systems to shift toward a more balanced, adaptive stress response that promotes autophagy and lysosomal function. Importantly, RPE cells express ATF6, as evidenced by studies utilizing ARPE-19 and primary RPE cultures, making these cells appropriate targets for ATF6 modulation (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Thus, the expected effect is a reestablishment of normal proteostasis in RPE cells via the restoration of adaptive autophagy, improved lysosomal enzyme activity, and enhanced phagocytic receptor expression, all of which are critical for the sustained clearance of photoreceptor outer segment debris and prevention of cytotoxic accumulation in dry AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
Ceapin-A7 represents an innovative therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration due to its unique and selective mechanism of action targeting the ATF6α branch of the UPR. One of the main strengths of this compound is its ability to modulate a very specific aspect of cellular stress signaling. By preventing the ER-to-Golgi trafficking of ATF6α and thereby inhibiting its proteolytic activation, Ceapin-A7 offers a promising strategy for shifting the balance of UPR signaling toward adaptive autophagy instead of chronic, detrimental ER stress (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). This is particularly relevant in the context of RPE cells, which require efficient protein quality control and robust lysosomal function to maintain photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance and overall retinal integrity.

In vitro studies have validated the mechanism of Ceapin-A7, with data showing that the compound induces the formation of discrete ATF6α-positive foci in the ER (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Moreover, the reversible nature of its action implies that Ceapin-A7 may offer a controllable therapeutic window, enabling fine-tuning of UPR modulation in a clinical setting (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). The involvement of peroxisomal protein ABCD3 in a neomorphic tethering mechanism further differentiates Ceapin-A7 from other UPR modulators by introducing a novel means of sequestering ATF6α (Torres et al., 2019). Such specificity is particularly compelling because it suggests that Ceapin-A7 can mitigate the chronic ER stress observed in dry AMD without interfering with other UPR branches (such as IRE1 or PERK), which are essential for normal cellular adaptation to transient stress.

However, there are notable limitations and challenges that warrant careful evaluation. First, despite the extensive preclinical work in cell lines and non-retinal systems, Ceapin-A7 has yet to be thoroughly evaluated in RPE-specific models or in vivo systems relevant to AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Second, the full spectrum of off-target effects is not yet fully characterized. While Ceapin-A7 shows selectivity for ATF6α, the influence of its induced neomorphic tether between ATF6α and ABCD3 on peroxisome function remains to be fully elucidated. Although available evidence suggests that Ceapin-A7 does not interfere significantly with ABCD3’s normal transporter function (Torres et al., 2019), the robustness of these findings in the retinal context remains an open question.

Another potential caveat is the dual role that ATF6α may play in various tissues. Although chronic activation of ATF6α is thought to contribute to maladaptive ER stress and consequent cellular dysfunction in AMD, ATF6α also participates in adaptive responses by upregulating crucial ER chaperones that preserve proteostasis (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Therefore, complete inhibition of ATF6α activity might have unintended consequences if not properly dosed or if the timing of inhibition is not carefully managed. An optimal therapeutic strategy might require a fine balance between sufficient ATF6α inhibition to restore lysosomal and phagocytic function in RPE cells and preserving enough ATF6α activity to maintain overall cellular homeostasis, particularly in tissues under variable stress dynamics.

Moreover, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of Ceapin-A7 in the ocular environment have not been established. For a drug candidate to be viable in treating dry AMD, it must be effectively delivered to the RPE with minimal systemic exposure, maintain a stable concentration over time, and be cleared without inducing local toxicity. The formulation challenges of ocular drug delivery, including crossing the blood-retinal barrier and achieving sustained release in the subretinal space, remain critical hurdles that must be addressed in future studies (Hetz et al., 2019; Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Finally, long-term safety studies are essential. The reversible nature of Ceapin-A7’s effects is promising; however, chronic treatment in a degenerative condition like dry AMD necessitates an in-depth understanding of the potential cumulative effects or chronic alterations in ER stress responses over time. Safety profiles in animal models, particularly those that recapitulate the chronic oxidative stress and proteostasis defects seen in AMD, will be crucial for advancing Ceapin-A7 into clinical trials.

In summary, Ceapin-A7 holds significant promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its precise mechanism—selectively inhibiting ATF6α activation by preventing its ER-to-Golgi trafficking and inducing a novel tether with ABCD3—positions it as a unique tool for rebalancing maladaptive UPR signaling (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Torres et al., 2019). The expected therapeutic benefit in RPE cells is the restoration of adaptive autophagy, maintenance of lysosomal function, and enhanced phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, all of which are critical to slowing or halting the progression of dry AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Nevertheless, the lack of extensive in vivo data in retinal models and the potential for off-target effects or unintended suppression of adaptive ER stress responses are significant concerns that must be addressed before clinical translation (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Rigorous investigation in RPE-specific systems, careful dose–response studies, pharmacokinetic profiling, and long-term safety evaluations are essential next steps. Overall, Ceapin-A7 is a mechanistically innovative candidate that merits further preclinical development as a novel intervention for dry AMD, provided that its complex interplay with ER stress, autophagy, and lysosomal function is thoroughly characterized in ocular tissues (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).
