Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab is a recombinant, humanized monoclonal IgG kappa antibody that specifically binds complement component C5 and prevents its proteolytic activation into C5a and C5b, thereby blocking terminal pathway activity and membrane attack complex (MAC; C5b-9) assembly while leaving upstream C3-dependent functions largely intact (for example, opsonization and immune-complex handling) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; West et al., 2024). It was discovered by screening large panels of murine anti-human C5 monoclonals for potent inhibition of C5 activation and terminal complement–mediated hemolysis; the parental murine antibody (5G1.1) was then humanized by CDR grafting into human germline frameworks and engineered to use a hybrid IgG2/IgG4 heavy-chain constant region to minimize Fcγ receptor binding and classical-pathway activation (reducing effector functions that could confound terminal pathway blockade) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009). Eculizumab binds human C5 with very high affinity (Kd approximately 120 pM) and sterically prevents convertase engagement with the MG7 domain of C5; epitope mapping identifies residues in the MG7 domain (including the KSSKC motif around Arg885) critical for binding, and Arg885His/Cys polymorphisms have been linked to clinical non-responsiveness in some patients, consistent with the structural epitope (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

As a drug class, complement inhibitors have been deployed to treat diseases driven by complement dysregulation, with C5 blockade representing a terminal-pathway strategy that ablates C5a signaling and MAC-mediated cytolysis while preserving many proximal complement functions; eculizumab was the first complement inhibitor approved for clinical use and catalyzed broad clinical development of C5, C3, and alternative pathway–targeted agents across hematology, nephrology, neurology, and, more recently, ophthalmology (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Eculizumab is administered intravenously, exhibits a long serum half-life (~272 ± 82 hours), a limited volume of distribution consistent with an intravascularly confined antibody, and shows pharmacodynamic correlation between serum trough concentrations and blockade of hemolytic activity; vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis is required due to increased susceptibility when terminal complement is inhibited (Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Within ophthalmology, complement activation products and MAC deposition have been implicated in AMD pathogenesis, motivating clinical trials of complement inhibitors including C5-directed agents; eculizumab has been formally evaluated in a randomized phase 2 setting for non-exudative AMD (geographic atrophy and drusen cohorts) via systemic administration (Kassa et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Halawa et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
Eculizumab has an extensive clinical record in systemic complement-mediated disorders. It revolutionized therapy for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), where it reduces intravascular hemolysis, decreases transfusion requirements, and improves quality of life; it is also approved for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and for neurologic autoimmune indications including anti–acetylcholine receptor–positive generalized myasthenia gravis and aquaporin-4–positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Early clinical pharmacology in PNH demonstrated that an induction regimen of 600 mg weekly for four weeks followed by 900 mg every other week maintained near-complete terminal pathway blockade and significantly reduced hemolysis and transfusion needs; these dosing principles align with its long half-life and the concentration dependence of hemolytic inhibition (Hillmen et al., 2004; Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012). Despite robust control of intravascular hemolysis, residual extravascular hemolysis can persist because C3 opsonization is not prevented by C5 inhibition, illustrating an important mechanistic limitation of terminal-pathway agents (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; West et al., 2024).

The drug’s safety profile is dominated by infection risk with encapsulated organisms—particularly meningococcal disease—necessitating vaccination; otherwise, eculizumab has shown acceptable tolerability across long-term use, with clinical programs incorporating monitoring of functional complement activity (CH50) to confirm pharmacodynamic blockade and dose adequacy (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009; Eskandary et al., 2016). Mechanistically relevant sources also report pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic complexities: high-affinity binding at acidic endosomal pH encourages recycling of eculizumab:C5 complexes by FcRn, leading to accumulation of total C5 bound to the drug in circulation; next-generation engineering in ravulizumab introduced pH-dependent release to minimize cargo recycling and extend dosing intervals (Schmidt & Smith, 2023).

In ophthalmology, eculizumab has been investigated as a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD. The COMPLETE study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), a single-center, randomized, double-masked phase 2 trial, evaluated intravenous eculizumab in two cohorts: geographic atrophy (GA) and intermediate AMD with high-risk drusen; patients were randomized 2:1 to eculizumab or saline over 24 weeks with follow-up to 52 weeks (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the GA cohort (n = 30 study eyes), eculizumab did not reduce GA enlargement versus placebo at 26 or 52 weeks (square-root–transformed growth 0.19 ± 0.12 mm vs. 0.18 ± 0.15 mm at 26 weeks, P = 0.96; 0.37 ± 0.22 mm vs. 0.37 ± 0.21 mm at 52 weeks, P = 0.93), and no drug-related adverse events were reported (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the drusen cohort (n = 30 total participants; 20 active, 10 placebo), eculizumab failed to meet the prespecified primary endpoint of a ≥ 50% reduction in drusen cube-root volume at 26 weeks; none of 18 treated eyes achieved this threshold, while one placebo eye did (10%; P = 0.36), and there was no detectable difference in mean drusen growth between arms through 26–52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014). Trial conduct included meningococcal vaccination and careful multimodal imaging; retention was high with 28/30 completing 52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). Independent evidence syntheses judged the certainty of evidence as low to very low due to small sample size, imprecision, and some risk of bias; overall, systemic eculizumab “may have made little to no difference” in BCVA and GA lesion growth in the available cohort (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistically similar C5-directed agents have not shown positive phase 2 outcomes in GA when administered systemically or intravitreally (e.g., LFG316 failed in phase 2), whereas intravitreal C5 inhibition with avacincaptad pegol progressed to later-phase testing and regulatory review, suggesting that drug, route, and pharmacology may be important determinants of outcome; by contrast, intravitreal C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) demonstrated efficacy and has been approved for GA, underscoring the translational relevance of target selection and ocular delivery (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024). Multiple reviews conclude that systemic eculizumab is no longer in development for AMD and highlight delivery and mechanistic concerns as likely contributors to the negative results (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, eculizumab targets the MG7 domain of C5 and sterically prevents formation of the C5 convertase–substrate complex, thereby inhibiting the cleavage of C5 into the potent anaphylatoxin C5a and C5b, which nucleates membrane attack complex assembly with C6–C9 (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Rother et al., 2007). Structural analysis of an eculizumab Fab bound to C5 resolved at 4.2 Å shows that five CDRs form the principal interface with MG7; mutational scanning of CDR residues identifies a network of contacts necessary for high-affinity binding, and kinetic assays confirm that these interactions prevent complement-mediated hemolysis in vitro (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016). The epitope includes residues near Arg885, and clinical resistance due to Arg885His/Cys substitutions in C5 provides orthogonal validation of the binding site (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

Pharmacodynamically, eculizumab ablates terminal pathway function: it suppresses CH50 to near zero when trough serum concentrations exceed ~35 μg/mL; however, because proximal C3 activation continues, C3b deposition and downstream opsonins accumulate on surfaces, which can drive extravascular clearance and generate residual pathology even under complete C5 blockade in appropriate disease contexts (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). Additional mechanisms can undermine complete terminal pathway control: (1) during intense proximal activation, densely opsonized surfaces can support C5 activation by convertases in ways that partially bypass classical C5 convertase assembly or even promote conformational C5 activation on surface C3b clusters; such context-dependent activation can manifest as “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” despite apparently adequate free drug levels, and has been reported in clinical settings as residual terminal-pathway activity and elevated sC5b-9 in some patients (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). (2) Eculizumab binds C5 with high affinity at both neutral and mildly acidic pH, allowing FcRn to recycle eculizumab:C5 complexes and potentially alter antigen disposition; ravulizumab’s pH-dependent binding was engineered to release C5 in endosomes and improve pharmacokinetics by avoiding cargo recycling (Schmidt & Smith, 2023). These features are germane to dose selection, monitoring, and potential resistance or escape during strong complement activation.

Rationale for C5 inhibition in AMD rests on abundant mechanistic and histopathological evidence that C5-derived effectors and MAC participate in retinal/choroidal injury. C5a is detected in drusen and acts as a chemotactic and proinflammatory mediator capable of inducing VEGF expression from retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, while C5b initiates MAC assembly; MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris increases with aging and is elevated in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019). Sub-lytic and lytic MAC on choroidal endothelium causes cell injury and can trigger surviving endothelial cells to upregulate VEGF and matrix metalloproteinases, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic injury and pro-angiogenic remodeling; complement regulatory proteins such as CD59 are natural inhibitors of MAC formation and their dysfunction or insufficiency can predispose to damage (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2021). Complement dysregulation in AMD further includes genetic risk (e.g., CFH variants) and evidence of alternative pathway activation in ocular tissues, suggesting both proximal and terminal effector involvement in disease biology (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Importantly, proximal inhibition at C3 has shown the capacity to restore lysosomal function and reduce sub-RPE drusen-like deposits in human iPSC-derived RPE models carrying the high-risk CFH Y402H variant by reducing C3 turnover and lowering downstream MAC (C5b-9) localization at lysosomes; in this system, a compstatin analogue (Cp40) suppressed C3b and MAC deposition and reversed lysosomal abnormalities, whereas direct C5 inhibition has not been shown in this model to rescue lysosomal function, and clinical C5 blockade has failed in GA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). These data reinforce that while terminal pathway effectors are present and likely pathogenic in AMD, distal blockade at C5 does not necessarily address upstream complement turnover that drives intracellular lysosomal stress in RPE, and proximal intervention may be required to normalize cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
The hypothesis proposes that high-affinity C5 blockade with eculizumab will prevent MAC assembly on RPE, thereby reducing sub-RPE deposit–driven lysosomal stress and indirectly supporting photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis in dry AMD. Mechanistically, preventing C5 cleavage would abrogate both C5a signaling and C5b-dependent MAC formation; given the documented presence of C5a in drusen and increased MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane/choriocapillaris with age and AMD, terminal pathway inhibition is expected to reduce MAC-mediated endothelial and RPE injury, dampen MAC-induced VEGF/MMP signaling, and potentially mitigate inflammation (Kassa et al., 2019). In principle, if MAC-driven lysosomal injury contributes to RPE dysfunction, C5 inhibition could reduce new MAC deposition at the RPE surface and limit subsequent endocytosis of MAC into lysosomes, thereby lowering lysosomal burden (Park et al., 2021).

However, two key bodies of evidence temper this expectation. First, clinical testing of systemic eculizumab in GA and intermediate AMD failed to show benefit on primary anatomical endpoints (GA growth and OCT drusen volume) through 26–52 weeks, despite established systemic pharmacodynamic blockade; these negative outcomes argue that either (a) terminal pathway activity at C5 is not the principal driver of lesion growth/drusen regression during the studied disease stages/time horizon, or (b) pharmacokinetic compartmentalization limited ocular target engagement after intravenous dosing (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Filho et al., 2014). Reviews explicitly highlight the compartment barrier problem—systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina or sub-RPE space due to the blood–retina/Bruch’s membrane barriers and large molecular size—and note that eculizumab exposure shorter than six months is unlikely to show benefit in slowly progressive GA, compounding interpretation (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Second, cellular models directly linking complement dysregulation to lysosomal failure in high-risk AMD RPE show that upstream C3 inhibition, not terminal C5 blockade, restores lysosomal function and reduces deposit formation; this suggests that intralysosomal stress is driven by continuous C3 turnover and opsonization rather than MAC alone, and that distal C5 blockade may be insufficient to normalize these processes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Consequently, POS phagocytosis metrics may improve only marginally or not at all if the dominant insult is proximal complement turnover rather than MAC-mediated damage. The clinical failure to slow GA growth or reduce drusen volume with systemic eculizumab supports the inference that target engagement at C5, via the tested route and schedule, did not translate into macroscopic anatomical benefit in human AMD eyes within one year (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).

If eculizumab were to be tested in vitro on human RPE, appropriate readouts would include: surface and intracellular MAC (C5b-9) quantification, lysosomal number/size and membrane integrity (e.g., LAMP2, Galectin-8), Cathepsin D activity, autophagic flux, and POS degradation kinetics; concomitant measurement of upstream C3b/iC3b/C3d deposition would be essential to interpret whether C5 inhibition is affecting the dominant pathogenic pathway in the assay (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In vivo, ocular pharmacokinetic considerations dominate: intravitreal administration delivers drug to the retina and sub-RPE space but is not reported for eculizumab in the provided context and would carry different safety and dosing constraints; systemic dosing faces blood–retina barrier limitations that likely constrained ocular target engagement in COMPLETE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Notably, nearly all complement inhibitors that have shown anatomical effects in GA have been delivered intravitreally, underscoring the importance of route of administration for ocular diseases (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic rationale: C5a and MAC are present in AMD-relevant tissues; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD and can drive endothelial injury, VEGF/MMP upregulation, and potentially RPE dysfunction; blocking C5 should diminish these terminal effector signals (Kassa et al., 2019; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Potent, well-characterized biologic: Eculizumab binds human C5 with picomolar affinity, has a well-defined structural epitope in the MG7 domain, and reliably ablates terminal pathway function systemically with a large clinical safety database outside ophthalmology (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
- Clinical feasibility and tolerability: In AMD trials, intravenous eculizumab was well tolerated without drug-related adverse events and with no clear signal for increased neovascular conversion or ocular infection within one year, supporting general safety of systemic C5 blockade in this population under vaccination protocols (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Negative clinical efficacy in AMD: The randomized phase 2 COMPLETE trial showed no reduction in GA growth and no meaningful reduction in drusen volume through 26–52 weeks; certainty is limited by small sample size but confidence intervals and replication across endpoints argue against a large treatment effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).  
- Compartmentalization barriers for systemic dosing: Blood–retina and Bruch’s membrane barriers likely limit ocular exposure to intravenously administered eculizumab; multiple reviews cite inadequate ocular penetration as a plausible reason for failure, and systemic eculizumab is no longer being pursued in AMD (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
- Target selection may be too distal for RPE lysosomal rescue: Human iPSC-RPE data indicate that complement-driven lysosomal pathology and drusen-like deposits are reversed by C3 inhibition, with concomitant reduction of downstream MAC, while C5 blockade alone has not been shown to restore lysosomal metrics and did not slow GA clinically; this suggests that proximal complement turnover is the dominant driver of RPE lysosomal stress (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Mechanistic escape and incomplete terminal control: Under strong activation, C5 can be activated on dense C3b clusters with features of convertase bypass or conformational priming; stoichiometric C5 inhibitors can form long-lived C5:antibody complexes on surfaces, potentially allowing residual terminal activity, and clinical “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” has been documented (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
- Genetic and biochemical determinants of response: C5 polymorphisms (e.g., R885H/C) can abolish binding and confer resistance; while prevalence in AMD populations is unknown here, such variants are important risk factors for nonresponse (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).  
- Safety/logistics: Terminal complement blockade mandates meningococcal vaccination and vigilance for invasive infections; while acceptable systemically in selected diseases, risk–benefit in a chronic, slowly progressive ocular disorder is less favorable, and the cost and infusion burden are high (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Contextualization with alternative complement strategies  
- C5 vs C3: Clinical success in GA has emerged at the level of C3 (pegcetacoplan), consistent with cellular data showing rescue of lysosomal function by upstream blockade; by contrast, systemic C5 inhibition with eculizumab and other C5-directed agents failed to meet GA endpoints in early trials, and LFG316 also did not demonstrate efficacy in GA (West et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Route of administration: Most agents demonstrating anatomical effects in GA are delivered intravitreally; eculizumab’s large size and systemic administration likely limited ocular penetration in COMPLETE, and no intravitreal eculizumab data are provided here to support local delivery (Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
- Risk of adverse ocular remodeling: Complement modulation has complex, context-dependent effects; in some models, complement inhibition or modulation can alter macrophage polarization and influence CNV formation, underscoring that indiscriminate or poorly targeted complement blockade could have unintended consequences; while the eculizumab AMD trials did not show a neovascular signal, vigilance is warranted when selecting targets and doses (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2021).

Decision Implications  
- As a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD, eculizumab has a low probability of success based on randomized clinical evidence, pharmacokinetic compartment limitations, and mechanistic considerations indicating that distal C5 blockade may not correct the proximal complement turnover driving RPE lysosomal pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- If C5 remains a target of interest, local ocular delivery and alternative molecular formats designed for intravitreal pharmacokinetics (e.g., smaller C5-binding entities, RNAi to intraocular C5 production, or intravitreal C5 inhibitors such as avacincaptad pegol) are more plausible routes; indeed, avacincaptad has advanced in GA, while systemic eculizumab has been discontinued in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019; Nadeem et al., 2023; West et al., 2024).  
- For assays aimed at lysosomal stress and POS phagocytosis, prioritizing proximal complement inhibitors (e.g., C3-targeting) is more aligned with human RPE data and recent clinical experience, whereas C5 inhibition alone is unlikely to fully normalize lysosomal function or confer robust structural benefit (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; West et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
Eculizumab provides a clear mechanistic means to extinguish terminal complement effectors implicated in AMD biology, but the totality of evidence—negative randomized clinical data in GA and drusen, route-of-administration barriers to ocular exposure, mechanistic escape during high activation, and cellular evidence favoring proximal over distal inhibition for lysosomal rescue—argues against further development of systemic eculizumab for dry AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The program should be deprioritized in favor of intraocularly suited agents and proximal complement targets, unless a compelling, testable strategy emerges to achieve effective intraocular C5 blockade with eculizumab (which is not supported by the present context) (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistic Appendix: Biochemical and Pathobiologic Evidence Relevant to the Hypothesis  
- Complement activation and terminal effectors in AMD:  
  - C5a is present in drusen and induces VEGF from RPE; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD; MAC induces endothelial lysis and sub-lytic survival signaling that upregulates VEGF and MMPs (Kassa et al., 2019).  
  - Alternative pathway dysregulation is central in AMD; genetic and experimental data implicate factor H and alternative pathway components in AMD and CNV models; inhibition of C3a, C5a, CFB, MAC or supplementation with CD59/CFH blocks CNV in animals (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Eculizumab structure–function:  
  - Epitope on MG7 with steric convertase blockade; high-affinity binding and resistance polymorphisms at Arg885; CDR function validated by mutational scans (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
  - PK/PD: long half-life, vascular distribution, CH50 suppression threshold, FcRn recycling of C5:eculizumab complexes; ravulizumab engineering to improve recycling and dosing (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
  - Breakthrough mechanisms: convertase bypass and surface-induced conformational activation on dense C3b clusters; residual TP activity despite inhibitors under strong activation (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; Mannes et al., 2021).  
- Clinical AMD trials:  
  - COMPLETE GA cohort: no slowing of GA growth at 26 or 52 weeks; well tolerated (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021).  
  - COMPLETE drusen cohort: no ≥ 50% reduction in drusen volume in treated eyes at 26 weeks; no significant change in drusen growth vs placebo (Filho et al., 2014).  
  - Critical appraisals: small sample, imprecision, risk of bias; systemic delivery may not achieve retinal levels; eculizumab no longer in AMD development (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023).  
- RPE lysosomal biology:  
  - In high-risk Y402H iPSC-RPE, excessive C3 turnover increases MAC internalization and overloads lysosomes; C3 inhibition with Cp40 reduces both C3b and MAC, reverses lysosomal defects, and reduces drusen-like deposits; direct C5 inhibition is not shown to restore lysosomal function in this model (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Operational Recommendation  
- Do not advance systemic eculizumab for dry AMD. If C5 remains a strategic target, consider intravitreal agents designed for ocular PK and evaluate them head-to-head against proximal inhibitors in RPE lysosomal-function assays that quantify both MAC and C3 fragment deposition, with translational go/no-go predicated on alignment with known clinical signals in GA (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
NT-219 is a small-molecule inhibitor originally characterized as a novel attenuator of insulin/IGF signaling (IIS) that blocks the IGF1R→AKT axis via a dual mechanism: rapid reduction of IGF1 receptor autophosphorylation to prevent downstream AKT activation, and promotion of inhibitory Ser phosphorylation and degradation of IRS1 and IRS2 to sustain IIS suppression in cells (dual-step mechanism) (El-Ami et al., 2014). In the earliest in vitro characterizations, NT-219 inhibited IGF1-induced AKT phosphorylation, induced IRS1/2 Ser phosphorylation and degradation, and elevated expression of FOXO target genes such as p27 and MnSOD in human A375 and N2a cells, thereby functionally mimicking reduced IIS in mammalian cells (El-Ami et al., 2014). In vivo, NT-219 increased stress resistance and protected Caenorhabditis elegans from proteotoxic stress induced by human Aβ or polyQ models, without extending lifespan, consistent with partial IIS attenuation and downstream activation of DAF-16/FOXO and HSF-1 programs (El-Ami et al., 2014).

Beyond IIS, several oncology reports and abstracts describe NT-219 as suppressing IRS1/2 and phosphorylated STAT3, framing the compound as a dual inhibitor of IRS and STAT3 signaling with activity in murine melanoma and colorectal cancer (CRC) systems (e.g., B16 melanoma variants, CRC brain metastasis models) (Azevedo et al., 2023). In CRC work, NT-219 is presented as a first-in-class IRS2-targeting agent that triggers IRS2 Ser phosphorylation and degradation, reducing oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) gene expression and mitochondrial respiration in IRS2-expressing CRC cells, with antitumor synergy when combined with 5-FU in intracranial CRC brain metastasis mouse models (Greenberg et al., 2022a, 2022b).

With respect to provenance, author affiliations and disclosures indicate NT-219’s development by NovoTyr/TyrNovo; one source states that a company developing NT-219 positions it as a novel IRS1/2 inhibitor, noting it is “already being tested in clinical trials,” although details of those trials are not provided in the excerpt (El-Ami et al., 2014; Greenberg et al., 2022a). Available reports do not supply chemical synthesis routes, structural class information, formulation beyond use of 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin for solubilization in some experiments, or pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic details (El-Ami et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History  
The preclinical history of NT-219 spans two principal areas: (1) aging/neurodegeneration model systems in C. elegans and cell culture; and (2) oncology models in mice and human cancer cell lines. In nematodes, NT-219 reduced late-onset proteotoxicity in Aβ and polyQ models, increased stress resistance (heat shock, UV), induced DAF-16 nuclear translocation, and required DAF-16 and HSF-1 for its protective effects; the compound did not extend lifespan under the reported paradigms, distinguishing stress/proteostasis benefits from longevity effects (El-Ami et al., 2014). The authors explicitly called for testing NT-219 in vertebrate Alzheimer’s or Huntington’s disease models, emphasizing that efficient administration routes would need to be developed; the excerpt provides no evidence that such mammalian neurodegeneration studies were completed (El-Ami et al., 2014).

In oncology, multiple independent preclinical lines report NT-219’s ability to destabilize IRS2 protein, suppress OXPHOS genes, reduce mitochondrial respiration in IRS2-positive CRC cells, and synergize with 5-FU to inhibit CRC brain metastasis growth and extend survival in mice (Greenberg et al., 2022a, 2022b). Additional immuno-oncology abstracts describe NT-219 as a dual IRS/STAT3 inhibitor that increases tumor PD-L1 and improves the efficacy of anti–PD-1 or anti–CTLA-4 by reprogramming the tumor microenvironment toward higher CD8+ T-cell activation and reduced myeloid suppressor populations in murine melanoma models (Azevedo et al., 2023). One CRC preprint notes TyrNovo develops NT-219 and states it is “already being tested in clinical trials,” but the materials provided do not contain peer-reviewed clinical data, detailed safety/tolerability, or ocular exposure information (El-Ami et al., 2014; Greenberg et al., 2022a).

Critically, there is no report in the provided literature of NT-219 being used to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinal degenerations, or any ocular disease; likewise, there is no published application to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, MerTK signaling, or photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis (El-Ami et al., 2014; Greenberg et al., 2022a; Azevedo et al., 2023). Within the RPE field, the candidate is untested, and the extrapolation from cancer and nematode proteostasis contexts to RPE phagocytosis is speculative in the absence of ocular data.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary mechanistic characterization places NT-219 as an IIS/IGF1R pathway inhibitor acting through a dual-step process: early partial inhibition of IGF1R autophosphorylation that prevents AKT phosphorylation (Thr308, Ser473), followed by induction of inhibitory Ser phosphorylation of IRS1/2 and their proteasomal degradation, which produces a sustained IIS blockade (El-Ami et al., 2014). In human cells, this culminates in reduced AKT activity and a shift toward FOXO-dependent transcription (e.g., increased p27, MnSOD), indicative of stress-responsive and anti-proliferative programs typical of IIS attenuation (El-Ami et al., 2014). In C. elegans, IIS attenuation by NT-219 triggers DAF-16/FOXO nuclear translocation and HSF-1 activation to enhance proteostasis and stress resistance; protection from proteotoxicity requires these effectors, as daf-16 or hsf-1 RNAi abrogates benefits (El-Ami et al., 2014).

Mechanistic distinctions versus canonical IIS genetic knockdown are noted. For Aβ models, NT-219 promotes accumulation of higher molecular weight Abeta species (hyperaggregation) similar to IIS reduction by daf-2 RNAi, consistent with detoxification by sequestration of oligomers; for polyQ models, NT-219 reduces SDS-resistant aggregates but does not increase high-MW species to the same extent as daf-2 RNAi, implying compound-specific modulation of protein aggregation dynamics (El-Ami et al., 2014). Collectively, NT-219 acts upstream (IGF1R and IRS1/2) to suppress AKT and activate FOXO/HSF-1/NRF-like programs, with context-dependent modulation of aggregation states.

Oncology abstracts expand NT-219’s mechanism to include suppression of phosphorylated STAT3 and dual targeting of IRS1/2 and STAT3, which increases PD-L1, reduces suppressive myeloid cells, and synergizes with checkpoint inhibitors in melanoma models, and also anchors the agent’s proximal action to IRS2 degradation with downstream suppression of OXPHOS and β-catenin in CRC brain metastasis models (Azevedo et al., 2023; Greenberg et al., 2022a, 2022b). These oncology data reinforce IRS1/2 as validated proximal targets of NT-219 and suggest broader transcriptional/immunologic impacts via STAT3 in tumor contexts (Azevedo et al., 2023).

No evidence in the provided literature indicates that NT-219 directly inhibits SHP2 phosphatase activity; the compound is repeatedly characterized by its actions on IGF1R autophosphorylation and IRS1/2 degradation, with some reports adding STAT3 inhibition, but there is no description of direct SHP2 binding or enzymatic inhibition (El-Ami et al., 2014; Azevedo et al., 2023). Likewise, there is no evidence presented that NT-219 modulates MerTK phosphorylation or its dephosphorylation by any phosphatase.

Disease Biology Context and Relevance to Hypothesized Mechanism in RPE  
RPE clearance phagocytosis of POS is a receptor-integrated, actomyosin-driven process requiring both αvβ5 integrin and MerTK, with a choreography that separates POS recognition/binding from internalization and processing (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Müller & Finnemann, 2020). MFG-E8 bridges phosphatidylserine on POS to αvβ5 integrin, triggering FAK activation, which in turn promotes MerTK phosphorylation at light onset in vivo; RPE lacking αvβ5 fail to exhibit the coordinated FAK/MerTK phosphorylation cycle and display desynchronized phagocytosis (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Müller & Finnemann, 2020). MerTK activation then drives essential engulfment signaling toward the actin cytoskeleton, with protrusive actin assembly and myosin-II–based contractility required to form and close the phagocytic cup (Zihni, 2025).

Downstream of MerTK, multiple mechanistic routes engage the Rho family GTPases and PI3K signaling. Mer recruits PI3K and PLC-γ to generate PIP2/PIP3 and activate PKCs, while PIP3 species bind DOCK180 family GEFs (as complexes with ELMO) to activate Rac1 at the membrane; independently, Gas6–Mer signaling can phosphorylate Vav1 (a Dbl-family GEF), further promoting Rac1 activation (Wu et al., 2006). In parallel to this Mer-dependent axis, POS–MFG-E8–αvβ5 engagement activates Rac1 via a pathway that is independent of FAK and MerTK, indicating that Rac1 activation is integrin-driven and converges with MerTK-dependent cytoskeletal programs during cup formation (Lieffrig et al., 2023). Functional studies demonstrate that Rac1 activation is necessary, and that a coordinated increase of Rac1 activity with suppression of RhoA/ROCK signaling is independently required to assemble the F-actin phagocytic cup; perturbing either node (e.g., sema4D/plexin-B1 reducing Rac1, RhoA activation) impairs internalization (Lieffrig et al., 2023). Notably, in MERTK-deficient RPE, Rac1 activation upon POS challenge persists but F-actin phagocytic cups fail to form due to failure to downregulate the RhoA–ROCK pathway; pharmacological ROCK inhibition is sufficient to restore engulfment, acidification, and digestion in MERTK-lacking RPE, highlighting the primacy of the Rac1/RhoA balance for internalization and processing (Lieffrig et al., 2023).

PI3K–AKT signaling participates in RPE cytoskeletal regulation, but with nuance: AKT1/2 are expressed and activated in RPE by POS challenge; AKT inhibition increases POS binding while leaving internalization largely unaffected, and AKT controls F-actin recruitment by regulating myosin-II localization to phagocytic cups—myosin-II activity is required for internalization (Lieffrig et al., 2023). This suggests that complete blockade of AKT can alter cortical cytoskeletal dynamics in ways that may not improve (and might complicate) internalization, even if binding is increased (Lieffrig et al., 2023). More broadly in the retina and RPE, IGF-1/insulin receptors activate PI3K/AKT and are linked to cytoprotection; IGF-1R is tyrosine-phosphorylated by light stress in ROS membranes with associated PI3K binding, and PI3K–AKT activation protects RPE from oxidative injury, a key pathogenic driver in AMD (Rajala, 2010). Thus, systemically blocking IGF1R→AKT may deprive RPE of a cytoprotective pathway critical under oxidative stress conditions relevant to dry AMD (Rajala, 2010).

The hypothesis under consideration asserts that IGF1R activation recruits SHP2 to dephosphorylate MerTK, and that dual IGF1R/SHP2 inhibition by NT-219 would sustain MerTK phosphorylation and enhance PI3K/Rac1 signaling to improve POS internalization. The provided literature does not support this cross-talk model. While MerTK possesses domains that can recruit SH2-containing adapters and there is a plausible framework for SH2-mediated anti-inflammatory signaling, the specific involvement of SHP2 in dephosphorylation/regulation of MerTK in RPE is not demonstrated in the provided sources; indeed, multiple reviews explicitly note the absence of direct evidence for MerTK dephosphorylation or SHP2 activity in RPE/retina controlling phagocytosis or AMD-relevant outcomes (Ghosh et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015; Ghosh et al., 2024; Lieffrig et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Furthermore, none of the NT-219 sources implicate SHP2 as a target; rather, they define the compound’s proximal activity against IGF1R autophosphorylation and IRS1/2 degradation (and STAT3 in oncology abstracts), with no SHP2 pharmacology reported (El-Ami et al., 2014; Azevedo et al., 2023). Absent evidence that IGF1R activation suppresses MerTK via SHP2 in RPE, or that NT-219 inhibits SHP2, the central premise—to sustain MERTK phosphorylation by dual IGF1R/SHP2 inhibition—remains unsubstantiated in the current literature set.

Expected Effect  
Proposed assay: ARPE-19 (or primary human RPE) POS clearance phagocytosis with readouts for binding, internalization, Rac1-GTP, RhoA activity, F-actin cup formation, MERTK phosphorylation status, and myosin-II localization.

Mechanistic expectation from the literature:
- NT-219 will inhibit IGF1R autophosphorylation and reduce AKT phosphorylation; it will also induce IRS1/2 Ser phosphorylation and degradation, producing a sustained IIS blockade in RPE if the compound engages its canonical targets in this cell type (El-Ami et al., 2014).
- In RPE phagocytosis, AKT inhibition increases POS binding while leaving internalization largely unaffected; AKT controls myosin-II localization to cups and myosin-II activity is required for internalization; therefore, IIS blockade by NT-219 could alter binding and myosin-II dynamics without enhancing internalization, and might even risk impairing the coordinated contractility required for cup closure depending on the extent and timing of AKT suppression (Lieffrig et al., 2023).
- There is no evidence that NT-219 directly increases MERTK phosphorylation or sustains it by inhibiting a MerTK-directed phosphatase; FAK is the upstream effector known to promote MERTK activation after αvβ5 engagement, and Mer-driven PI3K/PIP3 production recruits DOCK180/ELMO to activate Rac1, while Vav1 provides a parallel route to Rac activation (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2006).
- Rac1 activation required for cup formation is driven by αvβ5 ligation via a pathway independent of FAK and MerTK and is modulated by semaphorin/plexin signaling; there is no indication that IGF1R/IIS inhibition increases Rac1 activation or overrides antagonistic RhoA/ROCK signaling (Lieffrig et al., 2023). Indeed, cup formation requires both increased Rac1 and decreased RhoA activity; manipulating only IIS/AKT is unlikely to rebalance this axis favorably (Lieffrig et al., 2023).
- In MERTK-deficient RPE, failure to suppress RhoA/ROCK—not failure to activate Rac1—explains defective cup formation; pharmacological ROCK inhibition rescues engulfment and downstream maturation, underscoring that targeting ROCK can bypass some MerTK-dependent defects (Lieffrig et al., 2023).

Taken together, the most defensible expectation is that NT-219 will reduce IIS/AKT signaling in ARPE-19, potentially increase POS binding, and alter myosin-II localization to cups, without a clear mechanism to enhance internalization; effects on Rac1-GTP are unlikely to be directly augmented, and there is no sound mechanistic basis in the provided literature to expect sustained MerTK phosphorylation through SHP2 inhibition by NT-219 (El-Ami et al., 2014; Lieffrig et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2006). Given evidence that PI3K–AKT activation protects RPE from oxidative damage—a central feature of dry AMD pathophysiology—sustained IIS blockade could be deleterious outside of a narrow, carefully controlled window (Rajala, 2010).

Contextualizing with dry AMD biology and MerTK function:
- MerTK is essential for RPE internalization of POS; genetic loss causes failure to engulf POS and retinal degeneration in RCS rats and some mouse models, and MERTK/TYRO3 signaling redundantly maintains an anti-inflammatory RPE gene expression program that influences retinal viability (Müller & Finnemann, 2020; Albert et al., 2015; Ghosh et al., 2024).
- After ingestion, internalized POS phagosomes enter LC3-associated phagocytosis (LAP) and autophagy pathways required for efficient degradation; MerTK promotes autophagy and inhibits NLRP3 inflammasomes, constraining retinal inflammation (Ghosh et al., 2024). These functions are distinct from IIS modulation and point to MerTK-proximal strategies (e.g., enhancing MerTK activation, targeting RhoA/ROCK to restore cup formation) as more rational levers to improve phagocytosis than IGF1R inhibition (Lieffrig et al., 2023).
- In RPE lacking MerTK ligation, phagocytic cup formation is impaired even when Rac1 activation is intact, and ROCK inhibition restores engulfment and maturation—an actionable, pathway-proximal intervention that has empirical support in RPE systems (Lieffrig et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Pharmacologic definition and tractability: NT-219’s mechanism is well supported in mammalian cells by decreased IGF1R autophosphorylation, suppressed AKT phosphorylation, and sustained IIS blockade via IRS1/2 Ser phosphorylation and degradation, with downstream activation of FOXO-regulated gene expression (El-Ami et al., 2014).
- In vivo activity in worms and robust oncology preclinical signals indicate that NT-219 is bioactive and can produce meaningful phenotypes via IIS attenuation and IRS1/2 suppression; preclinical efficacy includes synergy with 5-FU in CRC brain metastasis and potentiation of checkpoint blockade in melanoma (El-Ami et al., 2014; Greenberg et al., 2022a; Azevedo et al., 2023).
- The compound’s formulation has precedent (2-HP-β-cyclodextrin) and dose ranges have been explored in cell and worm systems, offering starting points for exploratory dosing in vitro (El-Ami et al., 2014; Greenberg et al., 2022b).

Weaknesses and key risks for dry AMD  
- Mechanistic disconnect with the hypothesis: There is no evidence in the provided literature that IGF1R activation recruits SHP2 to dephosphorylate MerTK in RPE, nor that NT-219 inhibits SHP2; MerTK’s downstream anti-inflammatory signaling may involve SH2-adapter recruitment, but SHP2-mediated dephosphorylation of MerTK in RPE has not been demonstrated (Ghosh et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2006; El-Ami et al., 2014; Ghosh et al., 2024). The central premise—that dual IGF1R/SHP2 inhibition by NT-219 will sustain MerTK phosphorylation—is unsupported by current evidence (El-Ami et al., 2014; Ghosh et al., 2024).
- Risk of antagonizing protective signaling: IGF1R/IR→PI3K/AKT signaling protects RPE from oxidative stress, a driver of dry AMD; broad IIS/AKT inhibition could be cytotoxic or reduce resilience to oxidative injury in RPE (Rajala, 2010).
- RPE phagocytosis data argue against the expected pro-internalization effect: In RPE, AKT inhibition increases binding but leaves internalization largely unaffected, and AKT controls myosin-II localization required for internalization; sustained IIS/AKT blockade is not a rationale to boost internalization and may perturb the force-generation needed for cup closure (Lieffrig et al., 2023).
- Lack of ocular/RPE data: There are no reports of NT-219 in ocular tissues, RPE cells, or phagocytosis assays; the compound’s tolerability, pharmacology, and target engagement in RPE are unknown (El-Ami et al., 2014).
- More mechanistically proximal and validated levers exist: Cup formation requires increased Rac1 and decreased RhoA/ROCK; in MERTK deficiency, ROCK inhibition rescues engulfment and downstream events, whereas Rac1 activation cannot overcome high RhoA activity; targeting ROCK or MerTK activation itself is more directly supported to enhance POS internalization (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2006).
- The candidate’s oncology-specific mechanistic breadth (IRS/STAT3 dual inhibition, β-catenin/OXPHOS modulation) introduces off-target immunologic and metabolic effects that could be undesirable in retina and RPE, where mitochondrial function and immune quiescence are tightly regulated (Greenberg et al., 2022a, 2022b; Azevedo et al., 2023).

Assessment of the specific mechanistic claims in the proposal:  
- “IGF1R activation recruits SHP2 to dephosphorylate MerTK”: The provided literature does not support this assertion. While MerTK contains domains that can engage SH2-containing proteins and may suppress NF-κB through SHP-related mechanisms in other phagocytes, specific demonstration of SHP2-mediated MerTK dephosphorylation or suppression in RPE is absent (Wu et al., 2006; Ghosh et al., 2024). No source shows that IGF1R recruits SHP2 to target MerTK in RPE.  
- “NT-219 is a dual IGF1R/SHP2 inhibitor”: None of the documents identify NT-219 as a SHP2 inhibitor. The compound acts on IGF1R autophosphorylation and IRS1/2 degradation, and some oncology abstracts add STAT3 inhibition; SHP2 is not listed among NT-219’s targets (El-Ami et al., 2014; Azevedo et al., 2023).  
- “Sustained MerTK phosphorylation and Rac1-GTP by NT-219”: MerTK activation is promoted by the αvβ5→FAK axis and by its ligation through GAS6/PROS1; downstream, Mer activates PI3K, DOCK180/ELMO, and Vav1 to elevate Rac1. IIS suppression by NT-219 does not obviously reinforce this cascade and, importantly, Rac1 activation required for cup formation is driven by αvβ5 signaling independent of FAK/MerTK, and inadequate suppression of RhoA/ROCK—not Rac1 deficiency—limits cup formation in MERTK-deficient settings (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2006).

Recommendation  
Given the absence of supporting evidence for the proposal’s key mechanistic link (IGF1R/SHP2→MerTK dephosphorylation) and potential risks of IIS/AKT suppression in RPE cells under oxidative stress, NT-219 should not be prioritized as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD to enhance RPE phagocytosis. If the team wishes to explore this axis despite these concerns, initial work should be stringently gated to low-risk, mechanistically focused in vitro experiments in human RPE with explicit go/no-go criteria:

- Biochemical target engagement in RPE: confirm IGF1R autophosphorylation and AKT suppression, and assess IRS1/2 degradation at NT-219 exposures spanning reported active ranges in human cells, with parallel viability and oxidative stress-challenge assays (El-Ami et al., 2014; Rajala, 2010).  
- MerTK signaling: test whether NT-219 alters MerTK tyrosine phosphorylation after POS challenge or GAS6/PROS1 addition, with FAK-dependent activation as positive control; due to the lack of any SHP2 data for NT-219, include SHP2 activity readouts only as exploratory corollaries, not as assumed mechanisms (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Müller & Finnemann, 2020; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
- Phagocytosis function: quantify POS binding versus internalization; F-actin cup counts; myosin-II localization; Rac1-GTP and RhoA-GTP; include ROCK inhibition as a positive internalization control and sema4D as a Rac1-downregulating negative control (Lieffrig et al., 2023).  
- Autophagy/LAP and inflammatory readouts: measure LC3-II, p62, and NLRP3-related markers following POS feeding with/without NT-219 to detect adverse effects on LAP or pro-inflammatory signaling, as MERTK’s anti-inflammatory function via autophagy is integral to retinal homeostasis (Ghosh et al., 2024).

Absent clear, positive results across these mechanistic checkpoints, further development should be halted. Parallel investment is better directed toward pathway-proximal strategies with published efficacy signals in RPE:

- Rho kinase inhibition to restore cup formation and downstream processing in MerTK-compromised contexts (Lieffrig et al., 2023).  
- Direct MerTK pathway activation (optimized GAS6/PROS1 engagement, integrin→FAK reinforcement), guided by the well-defined αvβ5→FAK→MerTK signaling axis (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Müller & Finnemann, 2020).  
- Modulators that enhance LAP/autophagy to promote POS digestion and inhibit NLRP3, aligning with MERTK’s anti-inflammatory role (Ghosh et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
On balance, NT-219’s pharmacology is incompatible with the proposal’s mechanistic rationale and presents non-trivial risks in the RPE context. The evidence base does not support SHP2 involvement in MerTK dephosphorylation in RPE or NT-219 activity at SHP2, and IIS/AKT inhibition is unlikely to enhance POS internalization while potentially undermining RPE resilience to oxidative stress relevant to dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015; Ghosh et al., 2024; El-Ami et al., 2014; Rajala, 2010). The candidate lacks ocular data, and superior, pathway-proximal approaches exist with direct evidence for improving phagocytosis or downstream processing. Deprioritize NT-219 for dry AMD and redirect efforts to ROCK pathway modulation, MerTK pathway agonism, and LAP/autophagy enhancement strategies that align with established RPE phagocytosis biology (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Müller & Finnemann, 2020; Ghosh et al., 2024).

Analysis: Candidate 1 (Brefeldin A) is a well-characterized Golgi transport inhibitor with a clear molecular mechanism and extensive biochemical literature. However, its non-selective blockade of ER-to-Golgi trafficking poses a high risk of disrupting essential RPE functions (e.g., secretion of survival factors, phagosome maturation) and inducing ER stress. Poor bioavailability, systemic toxicity, and the need for highly controlled dosing or novel ocular delivery render its translational path extraordinarily challenging. There is no direct evidence of beneficial effects in dry AMD models; the rationale rests on indirect complement modulation analogies, with substantial safety and off-target liabilities. Candidate 2 (CD82 agonist peptide) targets a core AMD pathology—impaired RPE phagocytosis—by enhancing αvβ5 integrin clustering via tetraspanin CD82 activation. Integrin-mediated POS clearance is directly linked to AMD progression, and the peptide’s mechanism is both specific and disease-relevant. Although direct preclinical AMD data are lacking, the peptide class has favorable safety profiles for ocular delivery, lower systemic toxicity, and existing assays for phagocytosis. Feasibility of intravitreal injection or controlled-release implants is well established for peptides. The main gaps are validating CD82 expression/function in AMD RPE and demonstrating direct agonist activity on integrin clustering. Overall, Candidate 2 combines a disease-centric MoA, reasonable safety and delivery prospects, and manageable preclinical requirements, whereas Candidate 1’s broad toxicity and delivery hurdles outweigh its mechanistic intrigue.
Reasoning: Between these two repurposing strategies, Candidate 2 is superior because it addresses a central, upstream RPE dysfunction—POS phagocytosis—via a defined receptor-integrin interaction with a peptide that can be locally delivered to the retina. Its target biology is directly implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis, and the safety/tolerability profile of ocular peptides is far more favorable than systemic Golgi disruption by Brefeldin A. Brefeldin A’s high toxicity, non-selectivity, poor ocular targeting, and lack of direct AMD evidence make it a poor translational candidate despite its well-characterized MoA. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Brefeldin A (BFA) is a natural product originally isolated in 1958 from Penicillium decumbens, and its discovery marked the beginning of intensive studies on its unique ability to disrupt intracellular protein trafficking (Hung, 2020). Structurally, BFA is a macrolide characterized by a complex fused system comprising a cyclopentane moiety linked to a 13-membered lactone, and this distinctive architecture has spurred extensive synthetic and medicinal chemistry efforts over the past decades (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015). By targeting the secretory pathway, BFA acts as a Golgi transport inhibitor, primarily through its binding to a protein complex involving a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) and the small G protein Arf1. This binding event results in the rapid disassembly of the Golgi apparatus and redistribution of its components back into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Hung, 2020). BFA is therefore classified among natural product inhibitors of intracellular trafficking, a group that has long served as invaluable research tools in cell biology to dissect the mechanisms of vesicular transport and Golgi-ER dynamics. Its broad bioactivities—as an antiviral, antifungal, and antimitotic agent—have principally been exploited in preclinical research rather than clinical therapeutics (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, BFA has been employed almost exclusively as a biochemical probe to investigate protein processing, secretion, and Golgi morphology in diverse eukaryotic cells. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that BFA’s ability to stall ER-to-Golgi trafficking can modulate various cellular processes including secretion of cytokines, hormones, and growth factors (Hung, 2020). Its documented effects on blocking transport have been leveraged in cancer cell studies where BFA-induced apoptosis and cell cycle arrest were observed, owing to mislocalization of key signaling molecules (Stierle & Stierle, 2015). Despite these promising cellular effects, the clinical development of BFA as a conventional therapeutic agent has been hindered by issues such as poor bioavailability and significant toxicity with prolonged exposure (Seehafer et al., 2013). Importantly, while BFA has not been directly applied in clinical studies for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or any similar degenerative retinal diseases, its mechanistic action on intracellular trafficking, ER stress, and protein secretion renders it an intriguing candidate for repurposing. In the context of AMD, where complement dysregulation and lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells play a critical pathogenic role, BFA could potentially offer a novel means of attenuating the buildup of complement components and misfolded proteins (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). While none of the published literature explicitly documents the use of BFA for AMD therapy, related studies in RPE cellular models have highlighted the importance of complement modulation and lysosomal restoration, establishing a rationale for investigating trafficking inhibitors such as BFA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
On a molecular level, the mechanism of action for Brefeldin A is well characterized. BFA binds to the complex comprising a catalytic GEF and the small GTPase Arf1, inhibiting the exchange of GDP for GTP on Arf1. This inhibition precludes proper recruitment and coat assembly for vesicle budding at the Golgi membranes, leading to a collapse of the Golgi structure and the retrograde redistribution of Golgi proteins to the ER (Hung, 2020). The immediate consequence of this inhibition is a profound disruption in the secretory pathway, which not only halts the export of proteins but also results in an accumulation of proteins within the ER. In cell types where the regulated secretion of proteins is critical for homeostasis, such as in RPE cells, this effect can have dual ramifications. On the one hand, it may help prevent the secretion of misfolded or aberrantly processed proteins, including complement components that are implicated in local inflammation and lysosomal deposition (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). On the other hand, the blockade of Golgi trafficking may transiently lower the secretion of proteins that otherwise contribute to the local pool of complement proteins which, if misfolded or overproduced, could lead to an increase in intracellular complement activation and subsequent deposition of the membrane attack complex (MAC, particularly C5b-9) within lysosomes (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In RPE cells, where robust daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) is essential, the maintenance of lysosomal function is critical; overburdening of lysosomes with complement-derived debris has been implicated in the formation of drusen and lipofuscin accumulation, both of which underlie AMD pathology (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The proposed intervention using BFA therefore leverages its well-established ability to modulate protein trafficking to indirectly reduce the burden of misfolded or overabundant complement proteins on the lysosomal system, thereby potentially restoring cathepsin activity and overall lysosomal function in RPE cells.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing BFA in dry AMD is that brief pulses of BFA administration will selectively inhibit the ER-to-Golgi trafficking route in RPE cells, thereby reducing the processing and secretion of misfolded complement proteins. RPE cells are known to contribute to local complement activation through the production and turnover of various complement components; in AMD, aberrant complement regulation leads to increased turnover, formation of complement split products, and the deposition of terminal complement complexes (C5b-9) in the lysosomes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The expected outcome of BFA treatment would be a reduction in the export of these misfolded or excessively generated complement proteins, ultimately leading to decreased local complement activation and a reduction in lysosomal overload by MAC proteins. Experimental evidence from studies using compstatin analogues (e.g., Cp40) in Y402H-RPE cell models has shown that complement inhibition can restore lysosomal function and cathepsin activity, thereby reducing lysosome size, diminishing drusen-like deposits, and improving the overall cellular phenotype (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015). By analogy, transient BFA treatment is anticipated to produce similar beneficial effects on lysosomal physiology in RPE cells, provided that the inhibition is carefully timed to avoid prolonged exposure which could be deleterious (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Furthermore, because RPE cells are responsible for the daily clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, maintaining an unencumbered lysosomal system is crucial for long-term retinal health. The expected biochemical cascade following BFA administration would therefore include a reduction in ER stress due to diminished protein export, lower secretion of misfolded complement proteins, and a subsequent decrease in complement-mediated lysosomal damage. This in turn should lead to a stabilization or even an improvement in cathepsin levels and activity, promoting a more efficient degradation of cellular debris and restoration of POS clearance (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential repurposing of Brefeldin A as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD is innovative and grounded in a detailed understanding of both its mechanism of action and the pathophysiology of AMD. Several strengths underlie this approach. First, BFA has a well-characterized molecular mechanism that directly affects the secretory pathway by inhibiting ER-to-Golgi trafficking. This offers a mechanistic basis for reducing the secretion of misfolded or aberrantly processed complement proteins—the accumulation of which is a central driver of lysosomal dysfunction and local complement activation in RPE cells (Hung, 2020). Second, preclinical research in AMD models has demonstrated that modulating complement activity, whether through direct inhibition of complement components or by enhancing lysosomal function, can reverse pathological phenotypes associated with the disease (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015). This suggests that a strategy aimed at indirectly reducing complement deposition via interference with protein trafficking holds considerable promise. Third, the idea of using brief pulses of BFA rather than continuous dosing could allow for a transient therapeutic effect that minimizes the known toxicities associated with prolonged BFA exposure—thus potentially overcoming one of the key limitations that has prevented its clinical development in other contexts (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015).

Nonetheless, there are significant challenges and weaknesses that must be addressed before this approach can be advanced. One of the primary concerns relates to the non-selectivity of BFA’s action. Because BFA disrupts a fundamental cellular process, its effects are not confined solely to the trafficking of misfolded complement proteins. It is likely to inhibit the normal secretion of multiple proteins that are essential for RPE cell function, which could inadvertently impair the phagocytosis and processing of photoreceptor outer segments (Hung, 2020; Seehafer et al., 2013). Such disruption could paradoxically exacerbate the very lysosomal dysfunction it is intended to ameliorate, particularly if dosing is not carefully titrated. Furthermore, while transient inhibition may mitigate toxicity, achieving the precise balance between therapeutic efficacy and cellular viability will require rigorous optimization in both in vitro and in vivo models. Another potential drawback is related to pharmacokinetics and delivery. BFA’s poor bioavailability and potential systemic toxicity have long been recognized as obstacles for its use beyond experimental settings (Seehafer et al., 2013). Delivering BFA specifically to the RPE while avoiding off-target effects in other ocular or systemic tissues will demand innovative formulation strategies, such as localized drug delivery systems, which inherently add another layer of complexity to the drug development process. Additionally, while the hypothesis is supported by analogous studies demonstrating that complement modulation can restore lysosomal function in AMD models (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015), there is currently no direct evidence that BFA’s inhibition of ER-to-Golgi trafficking will reproduce these beneficial effects in the delicate environment of the retina. The potential for unforeseen interactions with other components of the RPE’s protein processing machinery or compensatory cellular responses further complicates the translational prospects of this approach.

In summary, as an expert drug development team leader tasked with evaluating promising repurposed drugs for dry AMD, I find the proposal to repurpose Brefeldin A to be both innovative and mechanistically intriguing. The strengths of this candidate lie in its well-characterized molecular target—namely, the inhibition of Arf1-mediated vesicle budding at the Golgi—and its potential to modulate a key pathological feature of AMD, namely the dysregulated secretion and accumulation of complement proteins that leads to lysosomal impairment and MAC deposition (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). However, the inherent risks associated with disrupting a central cellular process cannot be overstated. The lack of selectivity in BFA’s action, potential toxicity from even brief exposures, and challenges in targeting the RPE specifically are serious obstacles that must be systematically addressed. Further preclinical studies are required to delineate the dose-response relationship in RPE cell models, to examine the long-term effects of transient BFA-induced trafficking inhibition on cellular health, and to validate the hypothesis that such intervention can indeed reduce lysosomal MAC deposition and rescue cathepsin activity. Only with convincing evidence from rigorous in vitro and in vivo experiments would it be justified to consider advancing BFA as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. In conclusion, while the proposed use of BFA presents a compelling mechanistic rationale with some supportive preclinical analogies from the literature (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020), significant challenges regarding specificity, delivery, and safety need to be overcome before this approach can be deemed a viable therapeutic option for dry AMD.
