Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Axitinib is a synthetic, indazole-based, small-molecule receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor originally discovered via medicinal chemistry optimization for anti-angiogenic oncology indications and subsequently approved as an oral therapy (Inlyta) for advanced renal cell carcinoma, reflecting high potency and selectivity for vascular endothelial growth factor receptors (VEGFR1–3) with additional activity against PDGFR-β and c-KIT (Fei et al., 2024; Tosi et al., 2017). In biochemical and cellular assays relevant to ocular angiogenesis, axitinib demonstrates pan-VEGFR inhibition with substantially greater sensitivity than anti-VEGF monoclonal antibodies in endothelial cells, and it also inhibits PDGFR-β–mediated signaling in pericytes at low nanomolar concentrations, consistent with dual-pathway blockade within the VEGF/PDGF axis (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Pharmacologically, oral axitinib exhibits a short plasma half-life (~2.5–6.1 h) requiring twice-daily systemic dosing in oncology, and class-typical adverse events are dominated by hypertension; these PK/AE features motivated ocular delivery strategies to achieve high intraocular exposure with minimal systemic spillover (Siedlecki et al., 2017). As a class, multi-targeted VEGFR/PDGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have long been deployed systemically for cancer and are being repurposed for ocular neovascular diseases with the goals of broader VEGF-pathway suppression and reduced injection burden via sustained intraocular delivery platforms (suprachoroidal suspensions, intravitreal depot implants, and bioresorbable hydrogel systems) (Fabre et al., 2022; Fei et al., 2024). Axitinib is notable among TKIs for very high VEGFR affinity and measurable inhibition of other angiogenesis-related kinases, including TIE2, which has implications for both efficacy breadth and potential effects on vascular stability in the retina and choroid (Leitch et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical ocular data consistently show axitinib suppresses choroidal and retinal neovascularization across models, with oral dosing at 5 mg/kg reducing laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (L-CNV) in mice, and continuous low-dose systemic infusion (0.875 mg/day for 7 days) decreasing fluorescein leakage and CNV lesion area in rats; in vitro, axitinib suppresses 3D sprouting and inhibits both endothelial and pericyte proliferation/migration at non-toxic concentrations, aligning with dual VEGFR/PDGFR blockade (Fei et al., 2024; Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In a rat L-CNV model, axitinib reduced FA leakage scores and CNV lesion area by approximately one-third versus vehicle, and in co-culture sprouting assays axitinib alone outperformed anti-VEGF and anti-PDGF combinations, reinforcing the mechanistic rationale for dual-pathway inhibition in pathological ocular angiogenesis (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Combinatorial approaches show synergy: co-administration with anti-VEGF antibodies enhanced anti-angiogenic effects in nonclinical studies, consistent with the broader concept that inhibiting pericyte/PDGFR-β support can potentiate VEGF-directed therapy (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Siedlecki et al., 2017).

Multiple ocular delivery strategies for axitinib have entered human investigation in neovascular AMD (nAMD) to address the treatment burden and durability limitations of intravitreal biologics, including a suprachoroidal injectable suspension (CLS-AX) and an intravitreal bioresorbable hydrogel implant (OTX-TKI) designed for 6–9 months of sustained release (Fei et al., 2024). Early clinical and translational signals indicate that suprachoroidal delivery achieves high posterior segment exposure with minimal systemic levels, and initial phase 1/2a experience with CLS-AX in nAMD reported acceptable tolerability and pharmacologic activity at low doses, while OTX-TKI demonstrated favorable safety and durability in early cohorts (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020). Across the TKI class, parallel depot strategies (e.g., vorolanib in Durasert, sunitinib depots) have shown biologic activity and reduced treatment burden in nAMD, although some programs reported visual acuity tradeoffs or required rescue therapy at non-negligible rates, highlighting the need for careful dose, exposure, and target-selectivity optimization (Fei et al., 2024; Leitch et al., 2024).

Topical/eye-drop TKI programs (pazopanib, regorafenib, PAN-90806, acrizanib) underscore translational challenges: although preclinical topical dosing can reduce leakage and CNV thickness, multiple phase II programs failed to meet efficacy endpoints or were terminated due to insufficient posterior segment exposure and ocular safety issues such as reversible corneal haze with acrizanib, indicating that noninvasive delivery often cannot reproducibly attain therapeutic concentrations at the choroid/RPE in humans (Fei et al., 2024). Importantly, the available literature contains no reports of axitinib being tested clinically for dry AMD (geographic atrophy) or for enhancing RPE phagocytosis; the development history for axitinib and related VEGFR/PDGFR TKIs is focused on nAMD and other retinal vascular diseases, and reviews repeatedly note a lack of evidence for dry-AMD applications in this drug class to date (Fei et al., 2024). Furthermore, while localized ocular delivery is being pursued to mitigate systemic exposure, case reports of retinal adverse events during systemic axitinib therapy—including impaired retinal circulation, reversible retinal toxicity, and central retinal vein occlusion—require vigilance and thoughtful PK/PD design in ocular programs (Bakri et al., 2024). More broadly, despite active investigation of small molecules for AMD, reviews emphasize that no clinical success stories for small-molecule drugs in AMD (outside recently approved complement inhibitors for GA) have been established, underscoring translational risk for new mechanisms and reformulations (Fei et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Axitinib is a potent ATP-competitive inhibitor of VEGFR1 (FLT1), VEGFR2 (KDR), and VEGFR3 (FLT4), with additional inhibitory activity against PDGFR-β and c-KIT, thereby interrupting intracellular tyrosine kinase signaling downstream of multiple pro-angiogenic ligands, including VEGF-A/B/C/D and PDGF-B (Tosi et al., 2017; Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In relevant ocular cell types, axitinib inhibits VEGF-driven endothelial proliferation with markedly greater potency than anti-VEGF antibodies and exerts nanomolar inhibition of PDGF-driven pericyte proliferation, supporting the mechanistic premise that simultaneous disruption of endothelial and pericyte signaling can destabilize nascent pathological vessels and reduce neovascular growth (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). In 3D co-culture sprouting models that recapitulate endothelial–pericyte interactions, axitinib alone achieves robust inhibition of sprout number and length across low-nanomolar concentrations, matching or exceeding the effect of anti-VEGF plus anti-PDGF combinations, a pattern consistent with multi-receptor inhibition at the level of VEGFR/PDGFR RTKs (Giddabasappa et al., 2016). Preclinical studies in retinal endothelial cells further demonstrate axitinib suppression of downstream MAPK/ERK signaling and oxidative stress markers, aligning with direct VEGFR pathway inhibition; limited in vitro reports also suggest reduction of VEGFR1/VEGFR2 and PDGFR-β phosphorylation in RPE or mixed cell models, though these do not extend to functional phagocytosis endpoints (Lazzara et al., 2024).

Mechanistically, axitinib’s kinase profile extends beyond VEGFR/PDGFR to other angiogenesis-modulating targets; notably, among three pan-VEGFR TKIs profiled preclinically (vorolanib, sunitinib, axitinib), only axitinib exhibited strong TIE2 inhibition, a pathway essential for vascular quiescence and stability that could influence choroidal and retinal vascular homeostasis under chronic intraocular exposure (Bakri et al., 2024). In comparative kinase panels and endothelial functional assays, all three TKIs displayed robust pan-VEGFR inhibition and abolished endothelial sprouting at high concentrations, but the TIE2-inhibitory signal was disproportionately strong for axitinib, suggesting type-specific off-target consequences that warrant consideration during dose selection for chronic ocular use (Bakri et al., 2024). While intravitreal biologics neutralize extracellular VEGF ligands, axitinib acts intracellularly to block receptor signaling, potentially addressing compensatory upregulation of VEGF-C/D observed with VEGF-A-only inhibition; however, the breadth of intracellular TKI targeting can also propagate off-target effects in non-endothelial cells if exposures are not carefully controlled (Leitch et al., 2024).

Delivery-route pharmacology is central to ocular mechanism realization: suprachoroidal injection of axitinib has demonstrated posterior-segment targeting with markedly elevated drug levels in the posterior eye cup versus intravitreal injection in rabbits and sustained RPE/choroid exposure with minimal systemic levels, thereby achieving compartmentalized receptor inhibition where angiogenic lesions and the RPE reside (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020). Complementary intravitreal hydrogel implant strategies (OTX-TKI) provide long-acting axitinib delivery (6–9 months), maintaining pharmacologically relevant intraocular concentrations to chronically suppress VEGFR/PDGFR signaling in nAMD; these platforms are designed to mitigate systemic adverse events while sustaining on-target ocular pharmacodynamics (Fei et al., 2024). Importantly, chronic VEGF pathway suppression carries theoretical risks for neurosensory retina and RPE health, and reviews emphasize the need to balance durable angiogenic control with potential adverse effects of continuous VEGF blockade in ocular tissues, particularly for non-neovascular indications (Wolf et al., 2022).

Therapeutic targets in the RPE relevant to the present hypothesis—MerTK and αvβ5 integrin—are core components of the photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytic machinery, with αvβ5 required for synchronized diurnal phagocytosis and MerTK essential for engulfment and internalization; however, the provided literature contains no direct experimental evidence that axitinib upregulates MerTK or αvβ5 expression or function in RPE, nor that PDGFR-β signaling tonically suppresses RPE phagocytic differentiation in vivo (Tosi et al., 2017). Reviews and experimental summaries repeatedly state that available axitinib data focus on endothelial/pericyte targets and CNV models, and that no studies directly link axitinib to enhanced RPE POS uptake, MerTK activation, or αvβ5 integrin upregulation in dry AMD models or RPE cell assays (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). Therefore, while axitinib’s biochemical capacity to inhibit PDGFR-β could, in principle, modulate RPE phenotypes if PDGFR-β were a suppressive node in RPE phagocytic signaling, this mechanistic leap is not supported by direct evidence in the provided literature (Bakri et al., 2024; Fei et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The proposed assay hypothesis is that low-dose axitinib will modulate PDGFR-β signaling in RPE to promote a pro-phagocytic differentiation state, enhancing MerTK and αvβ5 expression and POS uptake; however, the body of evidence provided does not include direct demonstrations of axitinib increasing RPE phagocytosis, MerTK activation, or αvβ5 expression in vitro, ex vivo, or in vivo (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). Available data show that axitinib reduces VEGFR1/VEGFR2 and PDGFR-β phosphorylation in retinal endothelial systems and in limited contexts citing RPE/HUVEC cells, but these findings stop short of connecting PDGFR-β inhibition to increased RPE phagocytic function, and no POS ingestion assays, MerTK phosphorylation readouts, or αvβ5 functional binding assays are reported for axitinib in RPE (Lazzara et al., 2024). By contrast, the canonical RPE phagocytic apparatus depends on αvβ5-mediated POS binding and MerTK-mediated engulfment, with genetic ablation models establishing necessity; the literature here confirms this machinery but does not implicate PDGFR-β overactivation as a hindrance to RPE phagocytic differentiation nor demonstrate that TKIs restore phagocytosis in RPE (Tosi et al., 2017).

If the assay system relies on differentiating human RPE and measures POS uptake alongside MerTK and αvβ5 expression, axitinib’s expected on-target effects would be limited to PDGFR-β kinase inhibition in RPE if PDGFR-β is expressed and active under the assay conditions; nevertheless, there is no provided evidence that such inhibition increases MerTK or αvβ5 levels or POS ingestion, and the hypothesis that PDGFR-β tone suppresses RPE phagocytosis remains unsubstantiated here (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017). It is conceivable that low-dose axitinib could indirectly affect RPE phenotype via modulation of growth-factor signaling crosstalk, extracellular matrix deposition, or oxidative stress pathways observed in retinal endothelial cells; however, the provided literature does not extend these effects to RPE phagocytic function, and any expectation of enhanced MerTK/αvβ5 expression is speculative in the absence of direct data (Siedlecki et al., 2017; Lazzara et al., 2024).

Translational pharmacology considerations highlight both opportunity and risk: suprachoroidal axitinib enriches drug at the choroid/RPE with minimal systemic exposure, offering a delivery solution for RPE-targeted modulation if the mechanism were validated; at the same time, axitinib’s TIE2 inhibition and class-level concerns about chronic VEGF pathway suppression in the neurosensory retina argue for caution in non-neovascular indications such as dry AMD (Kaiser et al., 2020; Bakri et al., 2024). Moreover, systemic axitinib has been associated with retinal vascular adverse events in case reports, indicating that even low systemic exposures can affect retinal physiology, so RPE-targeted development would necessitate rigorous intraocular PK/PD mapping and safety margins that preserve vascular stability while testing RPE functional endpoints (Bakri et al., 2024). Given these constraints, the expected effect in an RPE phagocytosis assay is, at present, not evidence-based in the provided materials and should be framed as a hypothesis requiring first-principles validation rather than an anticipated outcome derived from prior literature (Fei et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
- Pharmacologic potency and dual-pathway coverage: Axitinib’s high-affinity pan-VEGFR inhibition with demonstrated PDGFR-β activity enables simultaneous suppression of endothelial and pericyte signaling, a combination that underpins robust anti-angiogenic efficacy in CNV models and may reduce fibrosis-linked extracellular matrix deposition in neovascular settings (Giddabasappa et al., 2016).  
- Validated ocular delivery options: Suprachoroidal suspension (CLS-AX) and intravitreal hydrogel implant (OTX-TKI) platforms have progressed into clinical testing for nAMD with encouraging ocular safety/PK signals, providing translationally relevant routes to expose the RPE/choroid compartment while minimizing systemic exposure (Wolf et al., 2022; Fei et al., 2024).  
- Clinical-stage experience in nAMD: Early-phase trials indicate biological activity and tolerability of axitinib-based intraocular approaches, suggesting a viable path to long-acting ocular therapy development if a new indication such as RPE phagocytosis enhancement is supported by mechanistic data (Leitch et al., 2024).  
- Class learnings and comparator programs: The broader TKI field in nAMD (vorolanib, sunitinib derivatives) offers benchmarks for durability, rescue-free rates, and safety considerations, facilitating rational dose and exposure setting for axitinib formulations (Fei et al., 2024; Leitch et al., 2024).  

Limitations and Critical Gaps  
- No direct evidence for RPE phagocytosis enhancement: Across the provided literature, there are no RPE-specific data showing axitinib increases MerTK or αvβ5 expression, augments POS binding or internalization, or improves phagocytic capacity in differentiating RPE; multiple summaries explicitly state the absence of such evidence and confine axitinib’s demonstrated actions to anti-angiogenic endpoints (Fei et al., 2024; Siedlecki et al., 2017).  
- Unvalidated mechanistic premise in RPE: While PDGFR-β is central to pericyte biology and vessel stabilization, the assertion that PDGFR-β overactivation hinders RPE differentiation and that its inhibition promotes a pro-phagocytic state is not supported in the provided texts, and the core RPE phagocytic machinery (MerTK, αvβ5) is not linked here to PDGFR-β modulation by TKIs (Tosi et al., 2017; Bakri et al., 2024).  
- Safety liabilities and target selectivity: Axitinib’s strong TIE2 inhibition could perturb vascular stability with chronic intraocular exposure, and class-level concerns exist for continuous VEGF pathway suppression affecting neurosensory retina and RPE; rare but notable retinal vascular AEs reported with systemic axitinib further mandate conservative exposure design and careful safety pharmacology tailored to non-neovascular indications (Bakri et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022).  
- Delivery constraints for non-neovascular endpoints: Topical TKI programs frequently failed due to inadequate posterior segment exposure and/or ocular surface safety findings, suggesting that any RPE-targeted application of axitinib would require invasive delivery (suprachoroidal/IVT depot) with chronic exposure, elevating the bar for safety and benefit-risk justification in a dry AMD population (Fei et al., 2024).  
- Field precedent: Reviews underscore that, to date, small-molecule success in AMD has been limited, and there are no approved ocular TKIs for either wet or dry AMD, reinforcing translational uncertainty for new mechanism-of-use proposals lacking direct preclinical support (Fei et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).  

Development Recommendations and Go/No-Go Criteria  
- Mechanistic validation in RPE: Before proceeding, perform a staged in vitro program in human iPSC-RPE and primary RPE to test whether axitinib modulates PDGFR-β phosphorylation and secondarily increases MerTK expression, MerTK phosphorylation upon POS challenge, αvβ5 expression/localization, and POS binding/internalization; include dose-response spanning sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar exposures aligned with ocular PK projections from suprachoroidal or depot IVT delivery (Wolf et al., 2022; Kaiser et al., 2020).  
- Specificity controls and orthogonal readouts: Use chemical and genetic controls to isolate PDGFR-β dependence (e.g., PDGFR-β ligand titrations, selective PDGFR-β inhibitors distinct from axitinib, and PDGFR-β knockdown), and include neutralizing antibodies and MerTK/αvβ5 functional blocking to map pathway causality for any observed phagocytosis changes (Tosi et al., 2017; Siedlecki et al., 2017).  
- Safety pharmacology in pigmented models: Given potential TIE2-related and VEGF-suppression liabilities, include long-term RPE morphology, barrier function (TEER), transcriptomic stress signatures, and photoreceptor/RPE co-culture viability endpoints at projected clinical exposures; extend to pigmented rabbit or NHP pharmacology to define posterior-segment exposure, ocular distribution (RPE/sclera/choroid), and a NOAEL for chronic dosing (Bakri et al., 2024; Kaiser et al., 2020).  
- Translational gating: Advance only if axitinib reproducibly increases POS uptake and MerTK/αvβ5 functional markers in RPE with a therapeutic window that avoids endothelial destabilization signals and preserves neuronal/RPE integrity in chronic exposure models; otherwise, deprioritize axitinib for RPE-targeted dry AMD and refocus efforts on mechanisms directly validated to enhance RPE phagocytosis or survival (Fei et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022).  

Conclusion  
On the strength of available evidence, axitinib is a validated, potent anti-angiogenic TKI with multiple ocular delivery platforms in clinical development for nAMD and robust preclinical efficacy in CNV models; however, the central hypothesis that low-dose axitinib enhances RPE phagocytosis via PDGFR-β modulation and upregulates MerTK/αvβ5 lacks direct support in the provided literature, and multiple sources explicitly state that no such RPE-centric data exist for axitinib at present (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Fei et al., 2024). The translational and safety profiles suggest that invasive ocular delivery could achieve RPE-adjacent exposure, but off-target TIE2 inhibition and class-level VEGF-suppression risks must be weighed carefully in a non-neovascular indication, particularly absent clear preclinical efficacy on RPE phagocytic endpoints (Bakri et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2022). Accordingly, while axitinib remains attractive for anti-angiogenic applications, it should not be advanced for dry AMD on a phagocytosis-enhancement rationale without first producing compelling, direct RPE mechanistic data; in the absence of such data, development resources would be better allocated to candidates with demonstrated effects on MerTK/αvβ5 function or on complement-mediated RPE pathology more proximal to dry AMD pathophysiology (Giddabasappa et al., 2016; Fei et al., 2024). Pending rigorous in vitro and ex vivo validation as outlined, the current evidence base supports a cautious “mechanism validation required” stance rather than progression to in vivo dry AMD studies or clinical translation for this proposed use (Fei et al., 2024; Bakri et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
VU0155072 is a synthetic small‐molecule agonist that selectively targets the sphingosine‐1‐phosphate receptor 5 (S1PR5). Similar to the structurally characterized S1PR5 agonist A-971432—synthesized via a two‐step process employing reductive amination with azetidine-3-carboxylic acid derivatives (Hobson et al., 2015)—VU0155072 is assumed to incorporate a pharmacophore that confers both high potency and selectivity within the sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor family. Compounds in this class have generally exploited the azetidine or related amino acid framework as a bioisostere to mimic the native lipid ligand, sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), while avoiding the metabolic liabilities of phosphorylated amino alcohols (Hobson et al., 2015). S1P receptor modulators as a group have been widely evaluated in a range of therapeutic areas—from multiple sclerosis and other neurodegenerative disorders to ocular pathologies—due to their ability to modulate immune cell trafficking and endothelial barrier function (Birgbauer, 2024; Hobson et al., 2015). In this context, VU0155072 marks a potential reagent that could be repurposed for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by leveraging its selective activation of S1PR5 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells.

Therapeutic History:  
The broader class of S1P receptor modulators has an extensive therapeutic history, with agents like fingolimod having been approved for multiple sclerosis owing to their immunomodulatory effects; however, these agents generally lack receptor subtype selectivity and consequently trigger side effects related to non-selective S1P receptor engagement (Birgbauer, 2024; Nakamura et al., 2024). More recent efforts have focused on enhancing receptor selectivity, as exemplified by A-971432—which is a selective S1PR5 agonist developed for neurodegenerative conditions—and ASP4058, an S1P1/5-selective agonist that has demonstrated efficacy in ocular vascular pathology models relevant to wet age-related macular degeneration (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024). Despite these advances, none of the compounds described to date have been definitively applied to dry AMD. In contrast to wet AMD therapies, which predominantly target abnormal neovascularization through modulation of VEGF pathways (Nakamura et al., 2024), the potential therapeutic application of S1PR5 agonists in dry AMD lies in their capacity to restore or enhance the phagocytic function of RPE cells. Preliminary evidence suggests that RPE phagocytosis—a critical process for the daily removal of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—may be modulated via S1P receptor signaling. Notably, a human RPE-based screening platform identified compounds capable of enhancing POS phagocytosis, with subsequent transcriptomic analyses revealing that S1PR5 was among the top upregulated genes associated with the enhanced phagocytic response (Schreiter et al., 2020). Moreover, while most of the literature on S1P receptor agonists has focused on neurodegenerative or ocular vascular indications, there is a growing rationale for repurposing these agents for dry AMD, given that RPE dysfunction—including impaired phagosome-lysosome fusion and subsequent accumulation of cellular debris—is a hallmark of the disease (Hobson et al., 2015; Schreiter et al., 2020). Thus, VU0155072, though primarily a research reagent at this stage, stands as a candidate with potential utility for dry AMD based on its receptor selectivity and the emerging role of S1PR5 in RPE phagocytic trafficking.

Mechanism of Action:  
S1PR5 is a member of the G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) family activated by the endogenous ligand sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P). Its activation typically engages downstream signaling cascades that include the modulation of Rho family GTPases, regulation of the actin cytoskeleton, and activation of kinases such as AKT, all of which are crucial for vesicle transport and membrane fusion events (Hobson et al., 2015). In the context of RPE cells, the mechanistic hypothesis for VU0155072 centers on its ability to enhance phagosome-lysosome fusion and the degradation of POS. This is predicated on the observation that modulation of S1P receptor signaling impacts intracellular trafficking pathways. For instance, activation of S1PR5 has been linked to changes in cytoskeletal dynamics that favor efficient vesicular movement and fusion events—a process essential for the clearance of phagosomes containing photoreceptor debris (Schreiter et al., 2020). Additionally, the receptor’s downstream signaling may stimulate pathways involving Rho-associated kinases (ROCK) or PI3K/AKT, both of which facilitate the reorganization of actin filaments and promote the maturation and fusion of phagosomes with lysosomes (Hobson et al., 2015). Importantly, data from a study using a human RPE-based screening platform indicated that pharmacological inhibition of S1PR5 impaired the phagocytic uptake and processing of POS, implying that its activation could restore this cellular function (Schreiter et al., 2020). However, it is noteworthy that several studies examining receptor distribution in RPE cells (using the ARPE-19 cell line as a model) have reported that S1PR5 mRNA expression is very low compared with other S1P receptors such as S1PR3 (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022). This observation raises questions about the sufficiency of endogenous S1PR5 expression in mediating phagocytic processes and whether exogenous activation by a potent agonist like VU0155072 can override such limitations. Nonetheless, the proposed mechanism is coherent with the hypothesis that selective S1PR5 activation leads to enhanced phagosome-lysosome fusion—an effect that would be indirectly mediated by the receptor’s influence on cytoskeletal remodeling and vesicular trafficking proteins.

Expected Effect:  
The primary therapeutic expectation for VU0155072 in dry AMD is that selective activation of S1PR5 in RPE cells will augment the rate and efficiency of phagocytosis, specifically by promoting the fusion of phagosomes with lysosomes and thereby ensuring effective degradation of POS. In dry AMD, one of the pathogenic factors is the defective clearance and subsequent accumulation of photoreceptor debris, which contributes to RPE dysfunction and the formation of drusen. By facilitating robust phagocytic processing, VU0155072 is anticipated to alleviate the cellular stress associated with toxic accumulation, restore RPE homeostasis, and ultimately preserve retinal function (Schreiter et al., 2020). In vitro assays using human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or iPSC-derived RPE) could be employed to assess the efficacy of VU0155072. These assays might measure parameters such as the rate of POS uptake, the kinetics of phagosome-lysosome fusion (potentially using co-localization markers of lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1), and levels of residual POS components after treatment. Given the reported effective concentration (EC₅₀) in the vicinity of 150 nM, one would expect that treatment with VU0155072 at or near this concentration would lead to measurable improvements in phagocytic flux. Moreover, its selectivity may allow the compound to act in a highly targeted fashion, reducing the potential for adverse effects associated with off-target activation of other S1P receptor subtypes—a significant benefit given the pleiotropic roles of other S1P receptors in immune modulation and vascular homeostasis (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024). An additional facet of the expected effect is the possibility that S1PR5 activation may engage MERTK-independent signaling pathways. MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase critical for POS phagocytosis, is often implicated in inherited forms of retinal degeneration when mutated. Should VU0155072 provide an alternate route to stimulate phagosome maturation and clearance, it could be particularly beneficial in cases where MERTK function is compromised (Schreiter et al., 2020). Nonetheless, the low endogenous expression of S1PR5 in commonly used RPE cell lines (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022) may necessitate the use of primary or stem cell-derived RPE models in order to fully capture the therapeutic potential of this approach.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, VU0155072 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD due to its high selectivity for S1PR5 and the compelling hypothesis that S1PR5 activation can restore phagocytic flux in RPE cells. One of the key strengths of this approach is the mechanistic precision: by specifically targeting S1PR5, VU0155072 is expected to modulate intracellular trafficking pathways that are critical for the maintenance and renewal of the RPE’s phagocytic machinery. This stands in contrast to previous S1P receptor modulators that, due to their nonselective binding profiles (such as fingolimod), have demonstrated a range of off-target effects including unwanted immune modulation and vascular dysfunction (Birgbauer, 2024; Nakamura et al., 2024). Moreover, studies on similar S1PR5 agonists like A-971432 have established that selective receptor activation can be achieved with favorable pharmacokinetic profiles, and the precedent set by ASP4058 in addressing ocular pathologies suggests that S1P receptor modulation can be therapeutically beneficial in the retinal context (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024).  

However, the candidate also faces several challenges. A significant potential weakness is the reported low endogenous expression of S1PR5 in RPE cell lines, such as ARPE-19, where expression levels are markedly lower than those of other S1P receptors (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022). This observation raises the question of whether exogenous activation by VU0155072 will be sufficient to elicit a robust phagocytic response in the RPE, or whether receptor upregulation might already be a prerequisite for therapeutic efficacy. Furthermore, while there is evidence that S1PR5 signaling can influence phagocytic processes (Schreiter et al., 2020), most of the existing research has focused on its roles in CNS function and vascular stability rather than in the specific context of RPE-mediated POS degradation. Hence, the proposed mechanism—restoration of phagosome-lysosome fusion and enhancement of POS degradation via S1PR5 activation—remains largely inferential and will require rigorous experimental validation in appropriate in vitro and in vivo models of dry AMD.  

Another consideration is the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic profile of VU0155072, which are described as being favorable in rodents. In theory, such data support its potential translation into clinical settings; however, the degree to which rodent PK accurately predicts human ocular tissue exposure remains uncertain, particularly given the unique microenvironment and barrier properties of the human retina. Additionally, it will be imperative to assess whether VU0155072 exerts any off-target effects on other S1P receptor subtypes, despite its purported selectivity. Off-target binding could complicate the interpretation of preclinical results or introduce safety concerns that have been observed with less selective S1P receptor modulators (Birgbauer, 2024; Nakamura et al., 2024).

From a disease-modifying perspective, the hypothesis that enhancement of phagocytic flux in RPE cells can ameliorate the progression of dry AMD is attractive because it targets a central pathogenic mechanism—namely, the chronic failure of POS clearance that leads to lipofuscin accumulation, drusen formation, and subsequent RPE atrophy. If VU0155072 can indeed stimulate the phagocytic machinery through S1PR5 activation in a meaningful way, it could potentially slow or even reverse some of the degenerative changes associated with dry AMD. This mechanism-driven approach represents a departure from merely symptomatic treatments, addressing the underlying cellular dysfunction that characterizes the disease (Hobson et al., 2015; Schreiter et al., 2020).

In conclusion, while VU0155072 is supported by a mechanistic rationale rooted in S1PR5-mediated regulation of intracellular trafficking and phagocytosis in RPE cells, several factors must be carefully considered before committing to this candidate as a viable therapeutic for dry AMD. The strengths of VU0155072 lie in its receptor specificity, favorable PK in rodent models, and the emerging evidence linking S1PR5 activation with improved phagocytic function in RPE—a critical process compromised in dry AMD. In contrast, the limited endogenous expression of S1PR5 in commonly used RPE models (Qiao et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022) and the scarce direct evidence of S1PR5 agonism ameliorating dry AMD pathology represent significant challenges. These weaknesses highlight the necessity for further basic research to quantify S1PR5 expression in relevant human RPE cells, to confirm the downstream signaling events triggered by VU0155072, and to validate the beneficial effects of enhanced phagosome-lysosome fusion using both in vitro and in vivo models of dry AMD. Ultimately, while VU0155072 shows promise as a mechanistically precise candidate for restoring phagocytic flux and addressing a key pathological feature of dry AMD, the current literature underscores the need for additional studies to fully establish its therapeutic potential in this context (Hobson et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2024; Qiao et al., 2012; Schreiter et al., 2020; Sorenson et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ibrutinib is a fully synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally developed as an irreversible inhibitor of Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK). It achieves inhibition by covalently binding to the conserved Cys481 residue located within the ATP‐binding pocket of BTK, a key member of the TEC family of kinases. This irreversible binding results in permanent inactivation of BTK, thereby interrupting B‐cell receptor signaling as well as other downstream pathways that are critical for cell survival and proliferation (Xie et al., 2021). As a member of the broader class of tyrosine kinase inhibitors, ibrutinib is designed through refined organic synthesis strategies that optimize its selectivity and potency. Compounds of this chemical class have been extensively utilized in oncology, particularly for the treatment of B‐cell malignancies, where they serve to disrupt aberrant oncogenic signaling pathways. Ibrutinib is available commercially (e.g., SelleckChem Cat. No. S2680) and has been subject to rigorous clinical evaluation, ensuring that its chemical properties, including its irreversible binding mechanism and cell penetration capabilities, are well established in the literature (Xie et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, ibrutinib was developed and advanced clinically for hematologic cancers such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia (WM), and other B‐cell malignancies. Its success in these domains is attributed to its effective inhibition of BTK, a kinase that is critical for B‐cell receptor signaling and survival (Xie et al., 2021). Once approved by the U.S. FDA in 2013, it rapidly became a standard of care in oncology. Outside of its oncologic use, ibrutinib has been recognized for its immunomodulatory effects that extend to innate immune cells such as macrophages, dendritic cells, and, notably, microglia. Although the primary application of ibrutinib is in cancer therapy, there is emerging evidence and growing scientific interest suggesting that BTK plays a role in innate immune signaling pathways that contribute to chronic inflammatory states, including those implicated in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Brandli et al., 2024). In pharmacovigilance studies, ocular adverse events—including uveitis, cataracts, and retinal disorders—have been identified among patients treated with ibrutinib, which indicates that the molecule penetrates ocular compartments and exerts biological effects there (Allouchery et al., 2021). However, despite these observations, ibrutinib has not been previously developed or marketed for the treatment of dry AMD or similar degenerative retinal diseases. Instead, its potential repurposing arises from the hypothesis that by modulating BTK-dependent inflammatory pathways in microglia and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, ibrutinib might reduce deleterious inflammasome priming and cytokine production that contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ibrutinib exerts its primary action by binding irreversibly to BTK, thereby preventing autophosphorylation and subsequent transmission of intracellular signals that lead to inflammation and cell survival. BTK is not only a critical mediator of B‐cell receptor signaling but is also expressed in cells of the innate immune system including microglia and RPE cells. Its activation is linked to the regulation of the NLRP3 inflammasome—a multiprotein complex that senses cellular stress, leading to the activation of caspase-1 and the maturation and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Brandli et al., 2024). There is accumulating evidence that BTK facilitates the priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome in response to various stimuli, including oxidative stress and the accumulation of deleterious protein aggregates, both of which are implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis. Experimental data suggest that inhibition of BTK by ibrutinib can lead to a reduction in IL-1β release, which in turn may lower downstream pro-inflammatory signals such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) (Far et al., 2022; Allouchery et al., 2021). Moreover, the preservation of lysosomal cathepsin activity observed in ARPE-19 cells under inflammasome-stimulating conditions implies that BTK inhibition may also support the maintenance of RPE lysosomal integrity and phagocytic function. Such actions are critical for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and prevention of drusen accumulation—a hallmark of dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). In summary, by covalently binding to BTK, ibrutinib not only halts aberrant immune cell signaling but also indirectly modulates inflammasome activity and associated inflammatory cytokine release in retinal cells (Xie et al., 2021; Brandli et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for the repurposing of ibrutinib in dry AMD revolves around its ability to inhibit BTK activity within microglia and RPE cells, thereby suppressing inflammasome priming and limiting the production of inflammatory mediators such as IL-1β and TNFα. In the context of an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells, it is anticipated that the application of ibrutinib (IC₅₀ ~0.5 nM) will result in a marked attenuation of inflammasome activation, as evidenced by reduced secretion of IL-1β and preserved lysosomal cathepsin activity (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). The proposed mechanism by which ibrutinib exerts its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD is multifaceted. First, by inhibiting BTK, the compound is expected to downregulate the overactive NLRP3 inflammasome that plays a central role in the inflammatory cascade within the retinal pigment epithelium (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024). Second, by reducing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines—especially TNFα—which have been shown to negatively impact the phagocytic ability of RPE cells, ibrutinib may help to maintain the clearance of photoreceptor outer segment debris. This is particularly important because impaired clearance mechanisms contribute to the accumulation of drusen and subsequent RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024). Moreover, animal and clinical pharmacovigilance studies have provided evidence that ibrutinib is capable of crossing the blood-brain and blood-retinal barriers, suggesting that it can reach retinal tissues at therapeutically relevant concentrations. Although there is documented evidence of ocular adverse events in patients treated with ibrutinib for hematologic malignancies—including instances of uveitis and cystoid macular edema—such effects have been largely reported as unintended consequences rather than engineered therapeutic outcomes. In the current repurposing framework, the premise is that controlled intravitreal or local administration, possibly as a modified formulation, could harness the anti-inflammatory properties of ibrutinib while minimizing systemic exposure and the risk of ocular adverse events (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022). Ultimately, the expected effect is a preserved RPE function with enhanced ability to clear POS debris, thereby mitigating the degenerative progression typically observed in dry AMD (Korhonen, 2024; Brandli et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
Ibrutinib presents as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to its well-characterized molecular mechanism and its established clinical profile in oncology. One of the major strengths of ibrutinib lies in its potent and selective irreversible inhibition of BTK, a kinase implicated not only in B-cell malignancies but also in the pathogenesis of inflammatory retinal diseases through its role in NLRP3 inflammasome priming (Xie et al., 2021). The scientific rationale for its repurposing is supported by preclinical observations indicating that BTK inhibition leads to reduced IL-1β secretion and preservation of lysosomal function in RPE cells, which are essential for maintaining photoreceptor homeostasis and preventing drusen accumulation in dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). Furthermore, the demonstration that ibrutinib crosses the blood-retinal barrier underscores its potential utility in directly targeting retinal tissues, especially when administered via routes that ensure localized high concentrations with limited systemic exposure (Xie et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022).

However, there are several challenges and weaknesses associated with this therapeutic candidate. First, the ocular safety profile of ibrutinib is a matter of concern, as pharmacovigilance data have linked ibrutinib to a spectrum of adverse ocular events including cataracts, uveitis, and retinal disorders (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022). While these effects have so far been observed in the context of systemic cancer therapy, they raise important safety questions when considering chronic administration for a disease such as dry AMD that often requires long-term treatment. Second, the dosages and formulation required to achieve an anti-inflammatory effect in the retina, while concurrently minimizing cytotoxicity and other off-target effects, remain uncertain. Ibrutinib’s off-target inhibitory effects, such as its activity against VEGFR2, may impart vascular side effects that could further complicate its use in the delicate retinal environment (Allouchery et al., 2021). Third, the repurposing strategy relies heavily on the extrapolation of cellular and animal model data—such as the observed reduction of inflammasome activation and preservation of cathepsin activity in ARPE-19 cells—to the complex pathophysiology of human dry AMD. The heterogeneity of dry AMD pathogenesis, driven by a confluence of genetic, environmental, and age-related factors, means that successful translation from preclinical models to effective clinical outcomes is not guaranteed (Korhonen, 2024; Brandli et al., 2024). Additionally, while there is a robust theoretical framework underpinning BTK’s involvement in inflamed retinal microenvironments, direct evidence of ibrutinib’s efficacy in modulating microglial or RPE function specifically in the setting of dry AMD remains limited.

Despite these challenges, the mechanistic rationale for using a BTK inhibitor in dry AMD is compelling. The interplay between NLRP3 inflammasome activation, chronic low-grade inflammation, and RPE dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a pivotal driver of dry AMD progression (Brandli et al., 2024). If ibrutinib can effectively attenuate these inflammatory processes without incurring prohibitive adverse events, it may offer a novel therapeutic avenue for a disease area currently lacking effective treatment options. However, this necessitates a series of rigorous preclinical studies to characterize the dose-response relationship, evaluate retinal safety, and define the pharmacokinetic profile of ibrutinib when delivered via ocular routes. Moreover, any proposed clinical trial must incorporate comprehensive ophthalmologic monitoring given the known spectrum of ibrutinib-induced ocular side effects (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022).

In summary, while ibrutinib is primarily an approved oncologic agent, its underlying mechanism of inhibiting BTK—the kinase that modulates inflammasome priming in microglia and RPE cells—provides a strong scientific basis for its repurposing in dry AMD. The expected effects of reduced IL-1β and TNFα production, coupled with preserved lysosomal cathepsin activity and improved phagocytic function, align well with the therapeutic goals of mitigating chronic inflammation and preserving retinal integrity in dry AMD. Nevertheless, the potential ocular adverse effects and the challenges related to achieving a favorable therapeutic index in the retinal environment are significant concerns that must be addressed through further rigorous preclinical and clinical evaluations (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). Overall, ibrutinib represents an intriguing candidate with a solid mechanistic rationale for dry AMD treatment; however, careful attention to formulation, dosing, and safety testing is warranted before advancing this repurposing strategy to later-stage clinical trials (Xie et al., 2021; Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Auranofin is an orally bioavailable gold(I) complex that was first synthesized as a candidate to treat rheumatoid arthritis and is historically considered the first orally administered gold drug. Chemically, it is composed of a water‐soluble aurothioglucose moiety linked to a lipophilic triethylphosphine ligand, and, upon metabolism, it yields active gold species such as a triethylphosphine–gold(I) cation and gold–thioglucose derivatives (Abdalbari, 2025). Auranofin belongs to the class of organogold compounds, which have long been recognized for their anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties. In general, this class of compounds has been used primarily in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis due to their ability to modulate immune cell activity, interfere with inflammatory cytokine production, and target redox-sensitive enzymes. Although originally developed and clinically validated for rheumatic diseases, research over the past decades has repurposed auranofin for anticancer, antiparasitic, antimicrobial, and more recently, for potential neuroprotective indications (Madeira, 2012; Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a).  

Therapeutic History:  
Auranofin has an established therapeutic history as an anti-rheumatic agent with a clinical safety profile characterized over several decades of use. In the 1980s it was approved by regulatory agencies for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis where it demonstrated comparable efficacy with fewer severe side effects relative to parenteral gold salts, while its oral delivery provided a significant improvement in patient compliance (Abdalbari, 2025). In addition to its use in rheumatology, auranofin has been studied for its anticancer properties, with investigations demonstrating its ability to induce reactive oxygen species (ROS), inhibit cell proliferation, and trigger apoptosis in various cancer models including ovarian, lung, and mesothelioma cells (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a; Mertens et al., 2023). Despite its broad repurposing interest in oncology and infectious diseases, auranofin has not been directly used for treating dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, the cellular mechanisms implicated in its pharmacological actions—particularly its effects on redox homeostasis and anti-inflammatory pathways—provide a compelling rationale for exploring its potential in dry AMD, a disease known to involve chronic oxidative stress, lysosomal dysfunction, and inflammation in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021b; Chen et al., 2023).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary molecular target of auranofin is thioredoxin reductase (TrxR), a critical selenoenzyme involved in maintaining cellular redox balance. Auranofin interacts with TrxR by binding preferentially to its redox-active selenocysteine residue, thereby irreversibly inhibiting its NADPH-dependent catalytic activity (Abdalbari, 2025). Inhibition of TrxR disrupts the thioredoxin (Trx) system leading to an accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and oxidative stress within the cell. This increase in ROS, while potentially cytotoxic at high levels, can also serve as a signal to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, a master regulator of antioxidant responses. Under conditions of elevated oxidative stress, Nrf2 translocates to the nucleus and binds to antioxidant response elements (ARE) in the regulatory regions of target genes, inducing the expression of several cytoprotective enzymes, including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) and enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis and regeneration (Chen et al., 2016; Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a).  

In addition to its redox-modulatory function, auranofin has been reported to affect lysosomal pathways. Preclinical studies in RPE-derived cells (ARPE-19) have shown that auranofin can attenuate lysosomal alkalinization and thereby improve lysosomal function, an effect that may translate into enhanced degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) under oxidative stress conditions (Chen et al., 2016). Auranofin’s dual impact—disrupting redox homeostasis via TrxR inhibition while simultaneously triggering a compensatory Nrf2-mediated antioxidant response and preserving lysosomal function—constitutes an attractive mechanistic rationale for its repurposing into ocular indications (Abdalbari, 2025).  

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesized mechanism, when applied to RPE cells, auranofin is expected to inhibit TrxR activity, thus initially promoting an increase in ROS production. This controlled elevation in ROS is anticipated to serve as a secondary signal for the activation of Nrf2, which in turn drives the transcription of antioxidant genes such as HO-1 and genes involved in glutathione synthesis, thereby restoring intracellular redox balance (Madeira, 2012; Abdalbari, 2025). In ARPE-19 cell assays, this cascade should lead to a measurable increase in cellular antioxidant capacity, as well as a reduction in oxidative damage markers. Furthermore, by preserving or even restoring lysosomal acidity and function, auranofin is expected to boost the degradation of POS, particularly in cells challenged with lipofuscin components such as A2E that are known to disrupt lysosomal function (Chen et al., 2016). The enhanced clearance of POS should, in theory, mitigate the accumulation of toxic byproducts that contribute to RPE senescence and the progression of dry AMD (Chen et al., 2023; Brodzka et al., 2024). Moreover, the improvement in lysosomal function may also translate into better maintenance of the RPE’s barrier function and phagocytic capacity, both of which are vital for retinal homeostasis. The oral safety profile established in rheumatoid arthritis supports the notion that, with proper dosing and perhaps targeted ocular delivery strategies, auranofin could be repurposed safely for ocular use, though detailed pharmacokinetic studies in ocular tissues would be required to confirm this (Abdalbari, 2025).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Auranofin presents several compelling strengths as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its well-documented history as an orally administered anti-rheumatic agent with an established human safety profile allows for rapid progression into clinical testing if preliminary ocular efficacy is demonstrated. The mechanistic rationale is robust: by inhibiting TrxR, auranofin triggers an increase in ROS that activates the Nrf2 pathway, culminating in the upregulation of cytoprotective antioxidant genes, restoration of glutathione levels, and the preservation of lysosomal function—all of which are key factors in countering the pathogenic processes in dry AMD (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a; Mertens et al., 2023). In addition, preclinical evidence in RPE models indicates that auranofin can modulate signaling pathways such as EGFR/MAPK and that its effects are ROS-dependent, as demonstrated by the mitigation of toxicity with the antioxidant N-acetyl cysteine (Chen et al., 2016).  

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges remain. Although the mechanistic data derived from cancer and non-ocular studies are promising, direct in vivo evidence of auranofin’s efficacy in AMD or related RPE dysfunction models is currently lacking. The cytotoxic nature of auranofin at higher concentrations observed in ARPE-19 cells necessitates careful determination of a dosing window that maximizes the beneficial activation of Nrf2 and lysosomal preservation without exacerbating oxidative damage or inducing cell death (Chen et al., 2016; Madeira, 2012). Furthermore, while the systemic safety of auranofin in rheumatic diseases is relatively well established, the specific requirements for ocular drug delivery—such as achieving sufficient retinal bioavailability while minimizing off-target effects—pose additional challenges that must be addressed through formulation innovation and rigorous preclinical testing (Abdalbari, 2025). Finally, because the pathogenesis of dry AMD is multifactorial, involving not only oxidative stress and lysosomal dysfunction but also inflammatory and complement-mediated processes, it is possible that auranofin alone may not be sufficiently efficacious in a clinical setting without combination with other therapeutic modalities designed to address these complementary pathways (Abdalbari & Telleria, 2021a; Chen et al., 2016).  

In summary, auranofin holds potential as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD due to its ability to modulate critical redox pathways via TrxR inhibition and subsequent Nrf2 activation, along with its potential to restore lysosomal function and improve the clearance of POS-related debris. Its established safety record in rheumatoid arthritis, combined with promising mechanistic underpinnings observed in both non-ocular and limited ocular cell models, supports further investigation into its use for dry AMD. However, given the current gaps in direct ocular evidence and the challenges of ocular drug delivery, additional preclinical studies specifically in AMD-relevant models (including detailed ARPE-19 studies, in vivo AMD models, and pharmacokinetic assessments in retinal tissue) are warranted to fully validate its therapeutic potential and safety for eventual clinical application (Chen et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2016; Madeira, 2012; Abdalbari, 2025).

Its primary biological function is to act as a cofactor for the serine protease factor I, thereby mediating the proteolytic cleavage of complement components C3b and C4b that are deposited on host cell surfaces. Previous recombinant production approaches for CD46 have employed adenoviral or adeno-associated viral vector technology, where the CD46 gene is inserted into an appropriate vector and delivered to target cells; however, the candidate in discussion is a purified recombinant protein intended for exogenously controlled dosing (Sweigard et al., 2011).  

As a member of the biologic class of complement regulatory proteins, recombinant CD46 belongs alongside other therapeutic proteins that target dysregulated complement activation, an approach that has gained prominence in treating complement-mediated diseases. The concept behind these therapeutics is to harness or augment natural regulatory mechanisms; in this instance, restoring or increasing the activity of CD46 on RPE cells may correct complement dysregulation implicated in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Leaderer et al., 2015; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021). The therapeutic rationale for targeting complement dysregulation in AMD has been borne out by extensive biochemical and clinical investigations. In several preclinical studies, researchers have explored approaches to mitigate complement-mediated damage in ocular diseases by increasing CD46 expression or activity. Such studies have shown that increased CD46 expression in RPE not only reduced complement deposition as measured by decreased membrane attack complex (MAC) formation but also provided significant protection against complement-mediated cell damage (Sweigard et al., 2011). Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, CD46 functions as a regulatory checkpoint in the complement system by facilitating the inactivation of complement components that have been deposited on host cell surfaces. Its mechanism of action centers on its ability to serve as a cofactor for factor I, a plasma serine protease responsible for cleaving and inactivating C3b and C4b (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011). The protein comprises four contiguous short consensus repeat (SCR) domains or complement control protein (CCP) domains, and these are arranged in a manner that creates high-affinity binding sites for the C3b and C4b fragments (Leaderer et al., 2015; Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021; Parsons et al., 2023).

Under physiological conditions, when C3b and C4b are deposited on the cell surface as a result of complement pathway activation, CD46 binds to these fragments through its CCP domains. This binding positions factor I in an optimal orientation to cleave C3b and C4b into their inactive forms, iC3b and iC4b, respectively, thereby halting further progression of the complement cascade (Leaderer et al., 2015; Sweigard et al., 2011). By preventing the formation of the C3 and C5 convertases, CD46 effectively stops the downstream assembly of the MAC—a multi-protein complex that, if formed in excess, can lead to cell lysis and tissue injury.

The correct spatial arrangement of these domains is critical for both high-affinity binding and subsequent catalytic efficiency with factor I (Liszewski & Atkinson, 2021; Sweigard et al., 2011). In the experimental paradigm under consideration, the central hypothesis posits that exogenous CD46 will “increase membrane cofactor activity on RPE, enhancing inactivation of C3b and reducing complement-mediated lysosomal stress, indirectly improving the phagocytic function of RPE.” On a cellular level, the expected effect following administration of recombinant human CD46 is a measurable reduction in complement deposition on RPE cell membranes, particularly the MAC, which is the terminal effector of the complement cascade. The candidate’s chemical structure and mechanism of enzyme inhibition suggest that it may increase levels of activating histone marks such as H3K4me3 at key gene promoters, ultimately facilitating a transcriptionally active chromatin state in RPE cells.

In rodent models, preliminary ocular safety data suggest tolerability, providing an impetus to explore its potential application in diseases such as dry AMD (Campello et al., 2021; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). By virtue of its synthetic origin and the ability to fine-tune its dosage and delivery, Methylstat offers a strategic advantage over compounds that require extensive de novo safety profiling. It aims to extend the paradigm of epigenetic therapy to a class of enzymes that has not been rigorously evaluated in the context of AMD, thereby potentially uncovering new biological insights and therapeutic windows (Campello et al., 2021).

IV. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, Methylstat functions by inhibiting the catalytic activity of JmjC domain-containing histone demethylases. These enzymes are responsible for demethylating lysine residues on histone tails—a modification that can either activate or repress gene transcription depending on the residue involved and the degree of methylation. For instance, trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4me3) is generally associated with open chromatin and active transcription, particularly at gene promoter regions. Under normal physiological conditions, a dynamic equilibrium between methylation and demethylation controls chromatin accessibility and the transcriptional potential of a cell (Campello et al., 2021).

Methylstat’s inhibition of these enzymes is expected to lead to an accumulation of methylation marks such as H3K4me3. This buildup can render the chromatin more accessible to transcription factors and the transcriptional machinery, thereby upregulating the expression of genes involved in cellular homeostasis. Specifically, the hypothesis driving the use of Methylstat in dry AMD is that this drug will increase H3K4me3 levels at the promoters of key regulatory genes involved in autophagy and phagocytosis—most notably transcription factor EB (TFEB) and MER tyrosine kinase (MERTK) (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. When its expression is upregulated, there is an increased transcription of a suite of genes that coordinate the formation of autophagosomes, lysosomal fusion, and the processing of intracellular debris (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). In parallel, MERTK is critically involved in the phagocytic function of RPE cells, particularly in the uptake and clearance of POS, which are regularly shed by photoreceptors as part of their normal renewal process. By enhancing the transcription of such genes, Methylstat may ultimately promote more efficient autophagic flux and phagocytic clearance, mitigating the accumulation of damaged proteins and debris that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Sinha et al., 2016).

At a biochemical level, the inhibition mechanism most likely involves Methylstat binding to the active site of the demethylase where essential cofactors such as Fe(II) and α-ketoglutarate are coordinated. By chelating or otherwise interfering with these cofactors, Methylstat prevents the oxidative demethylation reaction that would normally remove methyl groups from histone substrates. The net consequence is an epigenetic shift toward transcriptional activation of autophagy and phagocytosis genes (Grigoryan & Markitantova, 2025). Moreover, in the oxidative environment typical of stressed RPE cells, maintaining an active autophagic response is critical to counterbalancing the accumulation of cellular damage. The literature underscores that impaired autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are pivotal to the progression of AMD, as these pathways are central to the degradation of oxidized proteins and other cellular waste products (Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

An additional layer of complexity in this mechanism is the interplay between histone methylation and the broader network of epigenetic modifications. Dysregulation of histone deacetylases (HDACs) in AMD has been well documented (Campello et al., 2021; Kaštelan et al., 2024), and it often results in a transcriptionally repressive chromatin state. By contrast, Methylstat’s action is aimed at promoting a transcriptionally permissive configuration through the sustained presence of methyl marks. Thus, combining Methylstat’s mechanism with insights into HDAC regulation could eventually lead to combination therapies that more comprehensively restore the epigenetic balance in damaged RPE cells (Zibetti, 2025).

V. Expected Effect  
In vitro assays utilizing cultured RPE cells exposed to oxidative stress are expected to provide the first line of evidence regarding the efficacy of Methylstat. Under conditions that mimic the stress encountered in the aging retina, RPE cells experience an overload of damaged proteins and dysfunctional organelles. This is typically exacerbated by impaired autophagy—a process that is essential not only for recycling cellular components but also for mitigating apoptotic signals and inflammatory responses associated with chronic stress (Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

It is anticipated that treatment with Methylstat will yield several measurable outcomes in these assays. First, there should be an observable increase in global levels of H3K4me3, particularly at promoters of autophagy- and phagocytosis-related genes. Chromatin immunoprecipitation studies could verify this epigenetic shift, providing direct evidence that the histone demethylase activity is being successfully inhibited (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Second, such an epigenetic change should correspond to upregulated transcription of TFEB, MERTK, and potentially other downstream effectors vital for lysosomal function and autophagosome formation (Sinha et al., 2016). Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and RNA sequencing approaches would likely reveal increased messenger RNA levels for these genes, reinforcing the expected mechanism of action.

Functionally, RPE cells exposed to Methylstat may exhibit enhanced clearance of photoreceptor outer segments. In the healthy eye, efficient phagocytosis of these outer segments by RPE cells is essential to maintain photoreceptor function and overall retinal integrity. Under oxidative stress conditions, compromised phagocytosis leads to the accumulation of debris, formation of lipofuscin, and subsequent cellular senescence (Campello et al., 2021; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). By promoting the expression of genes directly involved in phagocytic uptake and lysosomal degradation, Methylstat is hypothesized to boost the cells’ capacity to remove POS cargo effectively. This enhanced clearance could not only improve retinal function but also potentially slow or reverse the progression of dry AMD.

Furthermore, the expected increase in TFEB activity would likely lead to improved lysosomal biogenesis and function. Given that lysosomal fusion and clearance are critical to mitigating cellular damage within the RPE, enhanced TFEB-driven gene expression offers a compelling mechanistic rationale. In fact, several studies have indicated that restoration of autophagic processes and lysosomal function represents a promising therapeutic strategy to counteract the accumulation of cellular waste and the ensuing inflammatory cascade seen in AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). The net result of these effects would be the preservation of cellular homeostasis and prevention of premature senescence in RPE cells, which is a critical upstream event in the development of AMD pathology (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Campello et al., 2021).

In summary, the expected effect of Methylstat in cell-based assays is twofold: (1) an epigenetic reprogramming event characterized by increased H3K4me3 levels and upregulation of key autophagy and phagocytosis genes, and (2) a physiological enhancement of POS uptake and lysosomal degradation processes, thereby potentially mitigating the deleterious sequelae of oxidative stress in the aging retina (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

VI. Overall Evaluation  
The assessment of Methylstat as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD involves a careful weighing of the theoretical strengths against practical challenges and gaps in current evidence. On the strength side, the concept of epigenetic modulation in restoring retinal cellular homeostasis is supported by a growing body of evidence. Studies have demonstrated that targeting chromatin modifiers—such as HDACs and acetylases—can confer therapeutic benefits in models of retinal degeneration (Campello et al., 2021). Methylstat extends this approach by specifically targeting JmjC histone demethylases, thereby offering a novel mechanism that could upregulate genes crucial for autophagy and phagocytosis. The proposed increase in H3K4me3 levels at promoters of TFEB and MERTK is especially attractive because these genes are central to maintaining the lysosomal integrity and phagocytic function of RPE cells, functions that are critically compromised in AMD (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Another significant strength lies in the practical aspects of drug development. Methylstat has already been characterized in other contexts, and preliminary rodent ocular safety data add a level of confidence regarding its tolerability (Campello et al., 2021; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Given that drug repurposing can greatly accelerate the timeline from preclinical validation to clinical application, Methylstat represents an appealing candidate from a strategic standpoint. Additionally, its small molecular size and synthetic origins provide opportunities for chemical optimization that may improve its specificity for retinal targets while minimizing systemic toxicity (Campello et al., 2021).

However, there are notable weaknesses and challenges associated with this therapeutic strategy. Foremost among these is the limited evidence linking JmjC histone demethylases—specifically the ones targeted by Methylstat—with AMD pathology. The Open Targets data indicate that potential targets such as KDM4A and KDM4C have low association scores with AMD, and there is scant evidence of their expression changes or pathogenic involvement in the retinal pigment epithelium during disease progression (Buniello et al., 2025). This suggests that while the theoretical underpinning is sound, the direct relevance of these enzymes to the disease phenotype remains to be conclusively demonstrated. As such, there is a significant risk that inhibition of these targets may not yield the expected therapeutic benefits.

Furthermore, the complexity of epigenetic regulation in the retina cannot be understated. RPE cells are subject to a tightly coordinated network of epigenetic modifications that interact dynamically. Whereas histone demethylation plays an important role, it is but one component of a broader regulatory milieu that includes histone acetylation, methylation at different residues, and DNA methylation. Consequently, the inhibition of one enzyme class may lead to compensatory changes in others, potentially diluting or even reversing the intended outcome. For instance, while Methylstat may increase H3K4 trimethylation, other repressive histone marks might persist or even become upregulated in response, thereby limiting the net transcriptional activation of autophagy and phagocytosis genes (Kaštelan et al., 2024; Zibetti, 2025; Sinha et al., 2016).

There is also the challenge of off-target effects. Histone demethylases are broadly expressed and are involved in numerous cellular processes beyond autophagy and phagocytosis. Inhibition of these enzymes in non-target cells could lead to unforeseen side effects, potentially compromising tissue integrity or inducing aberrant gene expression profiles that might exacerbate inflammation or other deleterious processes. Given that the retina is a highly specialized tissue with a fine balance of metabolic and oxidative stresses, any off-target effects resulting from systemic exposure to Methylstat will need to be carefully evaluated in preclinical studies (Buniello et al., 2025).

Another practical consideration is whether the epigenetic modulation achieved by Methylstat will be of sufficient magnitude and duration to effect functional improvements in RPE cells. Upregulation of TFEB and MERTK is an attractive proposition; however, the transcriptional responses in cells under chronic oxidative stress may differ from those in controlled in vitro environments. Additionally, the kinetics of chromatin modifications can be highly cell context-dependent, and there remains uncertainty regarding how quickly and sustainably Methylstat-mediated chromatin changes will translate into improved autophagic flux. This is particularly relevant given that AMD is a chronic disease and any therapeutic intervention must yield long-term benefits to justify clinical use (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

In light of these considerations, a phased and incremental research strategy is advisable. Initial studies should focus on establishing robust links between histone demethylase activity, H3K4me3 levels, and the transcriptional status of autophagy and phagocytosis genes in RPE cells. Advanced genomic techniques, such as ChIP-seq and RNA-seq, should be employed to detail the chromatin landscape before and after Methylstat treatment. Such studies will help to determine whether the predicted epigenetic changes are indeed occurring at the necessary target loci, and whether these changes correlate with improved cellular function.

Additionally, in vivo models of dry AMD should be used to validate the therapeutic effect of Methylstat in a physiologically relevant context. Rodent models that recapitulate key features of RPE dysfunction and oxidative stress are particularly valuable in this regard. Evaluations should include histological assessments of RPE integrity, measurements of lysosomal enzyme activity, and functional assays of photoreceptor viability. It will also be important to monitor potential systemic effects, given the widespread expression of histone demethylases throughout the body (Campello et al., 2021; Sinha et al., 2016).

Finally, combination therapies that target multiple aspects of the epigenetic network may be warranted. Given that other chromatin modifiers, such as histone deacetylases, have already shown therapeutic potential in AMD (Campello et al., 2021; Kaštelan et al., 2024), a synergistic approach that includes Methylstat along with HDAC inhibitors or mTOR modulators might provide a broader restoration of the epigenetic landscape in RPE cells. Such combinations would need to be carefully optimized to balance efficacy with safety, but they could ultimately offer a more comprehensive strategy to counteract the multifactorial etiology of AMD (Zibetti, 2025; Sinha et al., 2016).

VII. Conclusion  
In summary, Methylstat presents an intriguing candidate for repurposing as a therapy for dry age-related macular degeneration. The theoretical basis for its use rests on its ability to inhibit JmjC histone demethylases, leading to an accumulation of activating histone marks such as H3K4me3. This epigenetic reprogramming is hypothesized to enhance the expression of critical autophagy and phagocytosis genes—including TFEB and MERTK—in RPE cells, thereby improving the uptake and lysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments. Should these cellular processes be successfully augmented, the downstream effect would be a reduction in oxidative stress–induced damage, preservation of RPE function, and ultimately a slowdown or reversal of AMD progression (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

The strengths of this approach include its innovative mechanism that builds on the established relevance of epigenetic dysregulation in retinal degeneration, as well as the practical advantages associated with drug repurposing. Methylstat’s synthetic nature, existing preclinical safety data, and capacity for chemical modification all contribute to its potential as a versatile therapeutic tool. Moreover, the focus on restoring autophagic and phagocytic pathways aligns well with current insights into AMD pathophysiology, which repeatedly highlight the importance of efficient waste clearance in maintaining retinal cell homeostasis (Campello et al., 2021; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Nevertheless, challenges remain. The current evidence directly linking JmjC histone demethylases to AMD pathogenesis is limited. Open Targets analyses indicate a low association of enzymes such as KDM4A and KDM4C with the disease phenotype, raising concerns about whether their inhibition will yield significant clinical benefits (Buniello et al., 2025). Moreover, the complexity of epigenetic regulation—and the potential for compensatory mechanisms among various chromatin modifiers—necessitates a cautious approach. Off-target effects, the kinetics of transcriptional changes, and the chronic nature of AMD all underscore the need for comprehensive preclinical evaluation before advancing Methylstat into clinical trials.

In conclusion, while Methylstat exhibits several compelling features that justify its further investigation as a therapy for dry AMD, it is clear that significant gaps in our understanding of the role of histone demethylases in retinal aging must be addressed. Rigorous in vitro studies, supported by in vivo animal model data, are essential to validate the proposed mechanism of action and to optimize dosage and delivery strategies. Only through such a multifaceted approach can the full therapeutic potential of Methylstat be properly ascertained. If these initial studies demonstrate robust, reproducible benefits in restoring autophagic, phagocytic, and lysosomal functions in RPE cells, then Methylstat may emerge as a valuable addition to the currently limited therapeutic arsenal for dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Overall, the proposal to repurpose Methylstat for dry AMD treatment is scientifically intriguing and mechanistically plausible. However, the journey from hypothesis to clinical efficacy will require careful validation of the compound’s epigenetic impact in the pathological context of AMD. With concerted efforts combined with stratified preclinical studies, this candidate may open new avenues for precision pharmacotherapy in age-related retinal diseases (Campello et al., 2021).
