Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is a fully synthetic small molecule in the 4-aminoquinoline (4AQ) class, developed in the mid-20th century as a hydroxylated analogue of chloroquine (CQ) to improve tolerability; HCQ differs from CQ by a terminal hydroxyl group on the side chain (HCQ: C18H26ClN3O, 336 g/mol; CQ: C18H26ClN3, 320 g/mol) (Browning, 2014a, 2014b). Industrially, HCQ can be prepared by condensing N1-N-ethyl-N1-β-hydroxyethyl-1,4-pentanediamine with 4,7-dichloroquinoline, paralleling the CQ route from the same quinoline core with an altered aminoalkyl side chain (Rainsford et al., 2015). As a class, HCQ/CQ are alkylated 4-aminoquinolines: weak, amphiphilic bases bearing a flat quinoline nucleus and a basic side chain that traverse membranes in unprotonated form and undergo protonation-dependent sequestration in acidic intracellular compartments (lysosomes, endosomes, Golgi) — a defining pharmacologic property (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Chloroquine’s two basic centers (pKa ≈ 10.2 and 8.1) illustrate the protonation behavior that drives lysosomal trapping; at lysosomal pH (≈ 4–5) these agents become diprotonated and accumulate, with lysosome:plasma distribution ratios measured on the order of ≈ 160 000 and intralysosomal concentrations up to ≈ 2 × 10⁻² M reported for CQ, elevating lysosomal pH toward ≈ 6 (Browning, 2014b, 2014a). Pharmacokinetically, HCQ exhibits high oral bioavailability (≈ 0.7–0.8), an extremely large apparent volume of distribution (> 40 000 L), and a long terminal elimination half-life (≈ 40–60 days), with blood concentrations exceeding plasma due to extensive intracellular partitioning and tissue sequestration (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Melanin-containing ocular tissues are prominent depots; with chronic ingestion, uveal and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) concentrations can reach up to ≈ 10 000× plasma, reflecting lysosomal trapping and melanin binding (Browning, 2014a). Enantiomer-specific disposition has been observed for HCQ, with stereoselective accumulation noted in blood compartments, underscoring complex distribution kinetics (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). Clinically, HCQ is commonly administered as the sulfate salt, and CQ as the phosphate salt (Neto et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
HCQ and CQ were developed as antimalarials and subsequently repurposed as disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), with additional uses across dermatology and other immune-mediated conditions; HCQ is generally preferred over CQ for chronic therapy due to a better safety profile while maintaining comparable immunomodulatory efficacy (Rainsford et al., 2015; Neto et al., 2020). Broad clinical applications documented for HCQ/CQ include SLE, RA, primary Sjögren’s syndrome, discoid/cutaneous lupus erythematosus, polymorphous light eruption, solar urticaria, porphyria cutanea tarda, and other inflammatory dermatoses, reflecting lysosomotropic and immune-modulating actions (Rainsford et al., 2015; Rapparini et al., 2025). Mechanistically motivated repurposing has extended to autophagy inhibition in oncology trials, typically at daily doses far exceeding rheumatologic regimens, although HCQ is not approved as an anticancer adjuvant (Yusuf et al., 2023). Over recent decades HCQ prescriptions have increased substantially due to its relative affordability and systemic safety advantages, expanding the exposed population and the need for ocular safety surveillance (Yusuf et al., 2023).

With respect to retinal disease, the literature emphasizes retinotoxic risk and mechanistic links to RPE lysosomal dysfunction rather than therapeutic benefit in degenerative macular disease; authoritative pharmacology and ophthalmology sources do not provide evidence that HCQ/CQ have been used as treatments for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and instead catalogue retinal toxicity mechanisms and monitoring practices associated with long-term systemic use (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). Multiple summaries note that available data do not support therapeutic use of 4AQs for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerations, while documenting ocular accumulation, lysosomal alkalinization, and RPE stress as central safety concerns (Browning, 2014a). Retinopathy, although uncommon at recommended doses, is a recognized dose- and duration-related adverse effect that can be irreversible and may progress after drug cessation, motivating dose caps and structured ophthalmic screening (Rainsford et al., 2015; Ding et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action  
Lysosomotropism and lysosomal alkalinization  
HCQ/CQ are canonical lysosomotropic weak bases that accumulate massively within acidic intracellular organelles and elevate their pH, directly impairing acidity-dependent lysosomal hydrolases, receptor recycling, and degradative pathways including autophagy (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b). In vitro and cell-system studies report that chloroquine exposure increases lysosomal pH from ≈ 4–5 toward ≈ 6, a change sufficient to inhibit cathepsin activities and other acid hydrolases; pharmacologic blockade of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase with bafilomycin A₁ abrogates CQ’s lysosomotropism and toxicity, pinpointing disruption of lysosomal acidification as the proximal driver (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b). In RPE cells specifically, the lysosomotropic alkalinization by 4AQs inhibits lysosomal enzyme activity and autophagic flux, leading to accumulation of undegraded material; experimental inhibition of vacuolar acidification with bafilomycin phenocopies these degradative defects, indicating that pH elevation per se is sufficient to impair RPE lysosomal function (Guha et al., 2014).

Immune modulation and nucleic acid sensing  
Elevation of endolysosomal pH by 4AQs inhibits MHC class II antigen processing and presentation and blocks activation of endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR-3/7/9), thereby reducing MyD88-dependent interferon production and dampening pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion from mononuclear cells and dendritic cells (IL-1, IL-6, TNF, IFN-α/γ, CCL4) (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020). The class also interferes with cGAS–STING pathway activation through inhibition of cGAMP synthase and reduces T-cell co-stimulatory signaling (e.g., CD154), a mechanistic constellation that explains DMARD efficacy without significant increases in opportunistic infections (Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020; Browning, 2014b). Additional molecular interactions reported for 4AQs include DNA binding/intercalation, kinase pathway modulation (e.g., ERK/MAPK), and diverse enzyme interactions (e.g., cholinesterase), reflecting broad pleiotropy at pharmacologic and suprapharmacologic exposures (Browning, 2014a).

RPE-relevant degradative biology: cathepsins and POS processing  
The RPE depends critically on acidic lysosomes and cathepsin activity to clear the daily phagocytic load of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and maintain autophagic flux; failure of this system yields lipofuscin accumulation and contributes to AMD pathogenesis (Sharif, 2015). Multiple lysosomal proteases are expressed by RPE, including cysteine cathepsins B, L, and S as well as aspartyl cathepsin D; cathepsins are synthesized as pre-proenzymes, processed via the secretory pathway, and activated in the acidic lumen of late endosomes/lysosomes (Sharif, 2015). In human RPE/choroid and RPE cell lines, both inactive and active forms of cathepsin B, L, and S have been detected; functional studies show that broad cysteine protease inhibition or cathepsin S knockdown impairs POS degradation and increases lipofuscin-like inclusions, underscoring their role in RPE proteostasis (Sharif, 2015). Cathepsin D, a major lysosomal aspartyl protease in RPE, is essential for POS processing; its maturation and catalytic efficiency are strongly pH-dependent and occur within the acidic lysosomal lumen (Cardoso et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).

CQ/HCQ disrupt lysosomal proteolysis and lysosome dynamics in RPE  
In RPE models, CQ induces a rapid lysosomal pH increase followed by partial pH recovery, yet produces persistent lysosomal enlargement, accumulation of undegraded endocytic, phagocytic, and autophagic cargos, and a progressive reduction in accessibility of enlarged lysosomes to the endocytic pathway — a phenotype consistent with impaired autolysosome reformation and failure to regenerate a pool of degradatively competent lysosomes (Cardoso et al., 2023). A salient molecular signature of CQ exposure is accumulation of pro-cathepsin D and the lysosomal membrane protein LAMP1 without corresponding mRNA increases, indicating impaired processing/turnover rather than transcriptional upregulation; protease inhibitor treatment phenocopies this pro-cathepsin D accumulation, linking CQ’s effect to reduced proteolytic capacity (Cardoso et al., 2023). Although lysosomotropic agents can activate TFEB-dependent lysosomal gene transcription at high concentrations, the inhibitory effects on cathepsin maturation and lysosome reformation dominate in RPE models at low doses and precede any compensatory changes in gene expression (Cardoso et al., 2023).

HCQ further impairs RPE lysosomes by perturbing cholesterol homeostasis and promoting lysosomal membrane permeability (LMP), with cytosolic release of cathepsin B  
Beyond general autophagy/lysosome inhibition, HCQ suppresses mTORC1-dependent cholesterol biosynthesis, a change that increases lysosomal membrane permeability and allows lysosomal cathepsin B to translocate into the cytosol, where it can activate caspase-dependent apoptosis and drive caspase-independent phosphatidylserine externalization; these effects are mitigated by neutral pH-selective cathepsin B inhibition and exacerbated by pharmacologic cholesterol lowering (simvastatin) or depletion (methyl-β-cyclodextrin) (Wicks et al., 2022). These data in ARPE-19 RPE cells indicate that HCQ-induced lysosomal dysfunction and LMP sensitize RPE to additional stressors (e.g., UV), compounding vulnerability in aging retinal tissue (Wicks et al., 2022).

RPE/retinal stress signatures and storage phenotypes with 4AQ exposure  
Cell and animal studies document that 4AQ exposure produces RPE and retinal stress consistent with impaired lysosomal degradation: multilamellar myeloid bodies in RPE, photoreceptors, and ganglion cells; inhibition of oxidative enzymes in photoreceptors; decreased retinal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and glutathione with increased lipid peroxidation; disruption of the blood–retina barrier; and inhibition of protein synthesis in RPE culture (Browning, 2014a). In RPE cell culture, high concentrations of CQ perturb fusion of autophagic vesicles, increase LC3-II and p62, and can drive cell death, while intravitreal bafilomycin reproduces opsin-loaded phagolysosome accumulation, affirming that alkalinization is sufficient to cause degradative backlog (Guha et al., 2014). Chronic CQ treatment in mice increases mRNA expression of v-H⁺-ATPase and TFEB, consistent with compensatory attempts to reacidify lysosomes and enhance biogenesis, but does not normalize degradative function during exposure (Guha et al., 2014).

Absence of evidence for “low-dose stabilization” of lysosomal pH in RPE  
Across mechanistic summaries and primary RPE studies, there is no evidence that low-dose HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH at an “optimal” value, preserves cathepsin activity, or enhances POS degradation; rather, the consistent effect is lysosomal alkalinization with inhibition of lysosomal enzymes (including cathepsin B) and blockade of autophagic/lysosomal degradation (Browning, 2014a). In fact, low-dose CQ already yields accumulation of pro-cathepsin D and cargo buildup in RPE, indicating that even modest lysosomotropic perturbation degrades proteolytic competence, counter to the hypothesis (Cardoso et al., 2023).

Pharmacokinetic and ocular deposition constraints  
The extreme tissue distribution and ocular melanin binding of 4AQs undermine precise intraocular dose control: uveal/RPE drug levels can markedly exceed plasma during chronic dosing, and the terminal half-life is long, with months-long detectability after discontinuation due to depot release (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). These properties make “titration” to a narrow, hypothetical lysosomal pH window impractical and raise the risk of sustained lysosomal alkalinization even with ostensibly low systemic doses (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis proposes that submicromolar HCQ will “fine-tune” lysosomal pH in RPE to an optimal range for cathepsin activity, thereby preserving cathepsin function and enhancing POS degradation without blocking autophagy. The aggregate evidence contradicts this at mechanistic, cellular, and pharmacokinetic levels.

- Cathepsins in RPE require an acidic lumen for zymogen processing and catalytic function, and multiple cathepsins (B, L, S, D) are expressed and active in RPE lysosomes where they regulate POS degradation and autophagy; broad cysteine protease inhibition or specific cathepsin S knockdown impairs POS clearance and increases lipofuscin-like inclusions, demonstrating the acid-dependent protease requirement (Sharif, 2015). In this context, 4AQs act as lysosomal alkalinizers that inhibit acid hydrolases; CQ/HCQ inhibit cathepsin B and disrupt cathepsin D processing, with CQ causing pro-cathepsin D accumulation and reduced maturation into the active enzyme, a phenotype directly linked to impaired lysosomal proteolysis and cargo clearance (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). Therefore, the expected effect of submicromolar HCQ is not preservation but reduction of cathepsin function in RPE lysosomes, with consequent impairment of POS proteolysis (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023).

- In RPE cells, CQ/HCQ exposure impairs autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, producing enlarged, cargo-laden lysosomes that are progressively less accessible to endocytic inputs; these dynamics deplete the pool of degradatively competent lysosomes needed for daily POS processing, an effect observed even at “low-dose” CQ and preceding transcriptional responses (Cardoso et al., 2023). Thus, in assays measuring POS degradation and lysosomal flux, HCQ is predicted to slow, not enhance, turnover (Cardoso et al., 2023).

- HCQ further increases lysosomal membrane permeability and releases cathepsin B into the cytosol by impairing mTORC1-dependent cholesterol biosynthesis, activating pro-death signaling and phosphatidylserine externalization; pharmacologic cholesterol lowering/depletion magnify these effects, suggesting that HCQ’s action sensitizes RPE to metabolic and environmental stress rather than stabilizing proteolysis (Wicks et al., 2022).

- Beyond lysosomal pH, 4AQs disrupt other RPE functions essential for photoreceptor support: CQ inhibits rod outer segment phagocytosis in human/pig RPE cell lines, and HCQ/CQ inhibit OATP1A2 in human RPE, potentially perturbing all-trans-retinol uptake and the visual cycle — liabilities expected to worsen POS handling and photoreceptor maintenance in AMD models (Yusuf et al., 2023).

- The claim that “over-acidification” in RPE lysosomes needs moderation lacks evidentiary support in this literature corpus; the dominant pathologic signal in RPE aging and AMD models is lysosomal under-acidification/alkalinization and degradative impairment, which 4AQs exacerbate rather than correct (Guha et al., 2014).

- Pharmacokinetically, due to massive ocular accumulation and prolonged tissue persistence, “low systemic dose” does not guarantee low intra-RPE exposure; achieving and maintaining a narrow “optimal pH” window is improbable and unsafe for chronic indications with slowly reversible tissue exposure (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

In sum, in assays of RPE lysosomal function and POS degradation, the most probable outcomes of HCQ at submicromolar concentrations are lysosomal pH elevation, inhibited cathepsin activity/maturation (including cathepsin B inhibition and pro-cathepsin D accumulation), impaired autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, increased LMP with cytosolic cathepsin B release, inhibition of POS phagocytosis, and potential disruption of retinoid transport — all expected to reduce, not enhance, POS degradation (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023; Wicks et al., 2022; Yusuf et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths for development feasibility  
- Extensive clinical pharmacology and systemic experience: HCQ has well-characterized oral pharmacokinetics, metabolism, and drug–drug interactions, with validated immunomodulatory mechanisms (endolysosomal pH elevation, TLR/cGAS–STING inhibition, cytokine suppression) across rheumatology and dermatology; supply chains and clinical dosing paradigms are established, enabling rapid translational work if warranted (Browning, 2014b; Schrezenmeier & Dörner, 2020; Rainsford et al., 2015). The compound’s canonical lysosomotropic action makes it a useful positive control for modeling lysosomal alkalinization and degradative impairment in RPE assays benchmarking alternative, mechanistically restorative strategies (Browning, 2014b).

- Lower ocular toxicity relative to CQ at equipotency: HCQ is generally less retinotoxic than CQ, a difference attributed in part to greater polarity and lower lipophilicity; however, the class risk remains dose- and duration-dependent and clinically significant (Browning, 2014a; Rainsford et al., 2015).

Critical weaknesses for dry AMD  
- Mechanistic conflict with therapeutic goal: RPE catabolism of POS requires acidic lysosomes and intact cathepsin maturation/activity; 4AQs elevate lysosomal pH, inhibit cathepsin activity (including cathepsin B) and maturation (cathepsin D), impair autophagic flux and lysosome reformation, and induce cargo accumulation — a set of changes that predict impaired POS processing and enhanced lipofuscin burden rather than restoration of lysosomal proteolysis (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). No evidence in RPE/AMD models supports the hypothesis that “low-dose” HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH to optimize cathepsin function; the reported outcomes consistently indicate degradative inhibition (Browning, 2014a).

- Ocular tropism and prolonged tissue persistence: The combination of melanin binding and lysosomal trapping produces extreme ocular accumulation and very slow washout, making precise intraocular dose control infeasible and raising the risk of prolonged lysosomal alkalinization even after dose reduction or cessation (Browning, 2014a; Browning, 2014b).

- Added liabilities in RPE and retina: HCQ promotes lysosomal membrane permeability and cytosolic cathepsin B release in RPE, sensitizing cells to UV and cholesterol-lowering stresses; CQ/HCQ also inhibit POS phagocytosis and OATP1A2 in RPE, potentially disrupting retinoid uptake and the visual cycle, and they induce retinal stress signatures (oxidative enzyme inhibition, antioxidant depletion, barrier disruption) — all detrimental in the aging macula (Wicks et al., 2022; Yusuf et al., 2023; Browning, 2014a).

- Absence of supportive precedent in AMD: Comprehensive pharmacologic and ophthalmic reviews provide no evidence that HCQ/CQ have been successfully used to treat dry AMD or analogous retinal degenerations; rather, they underscore retinotoxic risk and mechanisms consistent with RPE lysosomal dysfunction (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a).

Strategic implications and recommendation  
The central hypothesis — that low-dose HCQ can fine-tune RPE lysosomal pH to preserve cathepsin activity and enhance POS degradation — is at odds with the mechanistic canon and RPE-focused data for 4AQs, which consistently demonstrate lysosomal alkalinization, cathepsin inhibition or maturation block, impaired lysosome reformation and autophagic flux, and accumulation of undegraded cargo (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023). No cited evidence shows that HCQ stabilizes lysosomal pH or improves POS degradation in RPE or AMD models; on the contrary, RPE studies with CQ/HCQ and mechanistic summaries emphasize inhibited lysosomal enzymes and autophagy as core actions (Browning, 2014a; Guha et al., 2014). Given extreme ocular accumulation and prolonged tissue retention, exploratory dosing aimed at a narrow “optimal” intralysosomal pH is neither controllable nor safe in a chronic neurodegenerative indication; adverse lysosomal effects could persist despite dose adjustments due to depot release (Browning, 2014b; Browning, 2014a). If the program goal is to restore RPE lysosomal proteolysis and POS turnover in dry AMD, agents that acidify lysosomes, facilitate cathepsin maturation/activity, or pharmacologically promote lysosome reformation (as suggested by pathways implicated in CQ-induced defects) align mechanistically, whereas HCQ/CQ, as archetypal alkalinizers and autophagy inhibitors, do not (Cardoso et al., 2023).

Conclusion: HCQ (Sigma-Aldrich H0915) is not a suitable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD under the proposed mechanism. The weight of biochemical, cellular, and pharmacokinetic evidence indicates HCQ will alkalinize RPE lysosomes, inhibit cathepsin function and maturation, impair autophagic flux and POS processing, and increase RPE vulnerability to stress, while ocular accumulation and long half-life amplify risk; no supportive evidence exists for benefit in dry AMD (Browning, 2014a; Cardoso et al., 2023; Wicks et al., 2022; Browning, 2014b). I recommend against advancing HCQ for AMD and suggest redirecting efforts toward mechanisms that restore lysosomal acidity, cathepsin activity, and lysosome reformation in RPE (Cardoso et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Adalimumab (marketed as Humira) is a fully humanized recombinant IgG1 monoclonal antibody developed using recombinant DNA technology that targets tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNFα). As a member of the anti‐TNFα class of biologics, adalimumab is designed to bind both soluble and membrane‐bound TNFα with high affinity, thereby preventing its interaction with the TNF receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2) on target cells. This antibody was originally discovered and engineered to address systemic inflammatory diseases, and its fully human composition is intended to lower immunogenicity compared to earlier chimeric molecules such as infliximab. In its development, molecular engineering efforts focused on isolating the relevant antibody variable regions that exhibit specificity for TNFα, followed by the construction of a recombinant molecule with human constant regions to improve tolerability and clinical efficacy. Anti‐TNFα antibodies belong to a broader class of therapeutic compounds that have dramatically changed the treatment landscape for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. They have been widely applied in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn’s disease, and ulcerative colitis, and over the past two decades, their use has been extended into ocular inflammatory diseases such as non‐infectious uveitis. Such applications underscore the versatility and translational potential of TNFα inhibition in modulating inflammatory cascades (Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History:  
Adalimumab’s clinical journey began with its approval for systemic autoimmune diseases where TNFα plays a fundamental role in mediating inflammation and tissue damage. Its robust performance in rheumatoid arthritis and related conditions has been well documented in numerous large-scale randomized controlled trials, which demonstrated significant improvement in clinical outcomes and inflammatory markers. These successes provided the foundation for exploring its application in other diseases characterized by inflammatory dysregulation. In recent years, growing evidence from both biochemical studies and clinical observations has highlighted the role of chronic inflammation in the pathogenesis of several retinal degenerative disorders. In particular, studies have shown that TNFα is upregulated in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and may contribute to the degeneration seen in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). For example, preclinical work has demonstrated that inflammation mediated by TNFα can impair the integrity of RPE cells, reduce the expression of proteins critical for RPE function (including visual cycle proteins and complement regulators) and disrupt phagocytic clearance mechanisms; these findings form the basis for hypothesizing that TNFα blockade may preserve RPE function in dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

While the majority of clinical uses of adalimumab have been in the realm of systemic and ocular inflammatory conditions such as non‐infectious uveitis, there has been emerging interest in repurposing anti‐TNFα therapies for retinal degenerations. In the context of ocular disease, several investigators have explored both systemic and local (intravitreal or subconjunctival) routes of administration to modulate intraocular inflammation. Pilot clinical trials and case reports have assessed intravitreal adalimumab in patients with uveitis and even in those with neovascular (“wet”) AMD refractory to anti‐VEGF therapies; these studies reported varying degrees of efficacy and underscored an acceptable local safety profile, though in some instances, higher dosages have been associated with ocular toxicity. In animal studies, intravitreal or subconjunctival administration of adalimumab has been shown to reduce inflammation and offer neuroprotection in models of retinal degeneration, such as in the rd10 mouse model for retinitis pigmentosa, establishing a precedent for local administration to achieve high ocular levels with minimal systemic exposure. Despite these advancements, use of adalimumab specifically for dry AMD has not been established in clinical practice. The proposed approach builds on the mechanistic insights from studies demonstrating that elevated TNFα levels can lead to downregulation of phagocytic receptors and lysosomal enzymes in RPE cells—processes central to dry AMD pathology—and posits that reversing these effects via TNFα neutralization may preserve RPE function (Nashine et al., 2022; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of adalimumab centers on its targeted neutralization of TNFα. TNFα is a proinflammatory cytokine produced by a variety of cell types that include activated T lymphocytes, macrophages, and, importantly, resident cells in the eye such as RPE and Müller glia. When secreted into the extracellular milieu, TNFα binds to its receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2), triggering intracellular signaling cascades that lead to the activation of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and other pathways that promote the expression of additional inflammatory cytokines, adhesion molecules, and matrix metalloproteinases. These processes collectively contribute to a sustained inflammatory response that can result in cellular dysfunction and death. Adalimumab, by virtue of its high affinity binding, sequesters TNFα and prevents receptor engagement. In doing so, it effectively interrupts these downstream proinflammatory signals and halts the amplification of the inflammatory cascade (Wang et al., 2011; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium cells, TNFα-mediated signaling has been implicated in the suppression of genes critical to the maintenance of RPE functions. Specifically, experimental studies have suggested that exposure to TNFα leads to a reduction in the expression of MERTK—a receptor tyrosine kinase essential for the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—as well as cathepsin D, a lysosomal enzyme crucial for the degradation of engulfed material. The decrease in MERTK expression compromises the ability of RPE cells to efficiently phagocytose POS, thereby potentially contributing to the accumulation of cellular debris, drusen formation, and further RPE stress that are characteristic of dry AMD. In parallel, a reduction in cathepsin D would impair lysosomal degradation, exacerbating the intracellular buildup of waste products and further undermining cellular homeostasis in the RPE. By neutralizing TNFα, adalimumab is hypothesized to prevent these detrimental changes, preserving the expression levels of MERTK and cathepsin D and thereby maintaining robust phagocytic and degradative capacity in RPE cells (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021).

At the molecular level, the binding of adalimumab to TNFα is mediated via its antigen-binding (Fab) region, which recognizes specific epitopes on the cytokine. This interaction is characterized by high affinity and specificity, ensuring that even low concentrations of the antibody can effectively neutralize TNFα activity. The blockade prevents TNFα from initiating receptor-mediated signaling that would otherwise promote inflammation and cellular stress. Moreover, because TNFα is known to regulate not only inflammatory cytokine production but also apoptotic processes, its inhibition may confer additional neuroprotective effects in the retina by reducing signals that lead to programmed cell death. The comprehensive inhibition of TNFα by adalimumab therefore stands as a multifaceted intervention, addressing both the inflammatory insult and its secondary effects on critical cellular functions in the RPE (Wang et al., 2011; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Nashine et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for leveraging adalimumab in dry AMD rests on its potential to neutralize elevated TNFα levels in the subretinal microenvironment. Elevated TNFα has been implicated in the pathological downregulation of key proteins involved in RPE function, notably MERTK and cathepsin D. MERTK is a receptor that plays an essential role in the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, a process that is critical for the renewal of photoreceptors and the overall maintenance of retinal health. Cathepsin D, on the other hand, is involved in the lysosomal degradation of the ingested material; together, these proteins ensure that the RPE can effectively clear and recycle photoreceptor debris. In dry AMD, this phagocytic process is compromised, leading to the accumulation of cellular waste products and drusen formation, which further fuels inflammation and RPE degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Administration of adalimumab is expected to interrupt this cascade by neutralizing TNFα, thereby preventing its signaling that leads to the downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D. With TNFα effectively neutralized, RPE cells should experience a more favorable molecular milieu in which the expression of these critical proteins is maintained at functional levels. This preservation would, in turn, support the RPE’s capacity to phagocytose and degrade photoreceptor outer segments, thereby averting the buildup of toxic waste products. Furthermore, since TNFα signaling also contributes to other aspects of cellular stress and inflammation—such as the upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines and the induction of apoptotic pathways—the neutralization of TNFα by adalimumab may also reduce overall cellular stress and promote RPE cell survival and function (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022).

In vitro assays using cultured human RPE cells exposed to TNFα could be employed to test this hypothesis. In these experiments, treatment with adalimumab should result in the normalization or preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression levels when compared to TNFα-treated controls. In addition, functional assays measuring the uptake and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (or surrogate fluorescent particles) would be expected to show improved phagocytic efficiency in RPE cells treated with adalimumab. Such findings would provide robust mechanistic support for the proposed therapeutic strategy. Moreover, preliminary in vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD or models of induced RPE dysfunction could further validate that TNFα blockade leads to preservation of RPE integrity, improved photoreceptor survival, and retardation of retinal degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Considering that the expression of MERTK is well documented in RPE cells and that its function is critical for POS phagocytosis—a process that declines with aging and in the presence of inflammatory mediators—the ability of adalimumab to maintain or restore MERTK expression would be highly relevant in the context of dry AMD. In the proposed strategy, adalimumab may also help to stabilize other RPE functions, such as the regulation of the complement cascade and the visual cycle, both of which have been shown to be adversely affected by TNFα exposure. Thus, the anticipated effect of adalimumab is not limited solely to the preservation of phagocytic machinery; it may also contribute to a broader stabilization of RPE cell health in the face of chronic low-grade inflammation that characterizes dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of adalimumab as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a compelling yet cautiously optimistic perspective. One of the principal strengths of adalimumab lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action; by neutralizing TNFα, it directly addresses a central mediator of inflammation that has been implicated in the dysregulation of RPE functions. The experimental evidence indicating that TNFα exposure can lead to the downregulation of essential proteins such as MERTK and cathepsin D provides a strong rationale for the hypothesis that TNFα inhibition might preserve the RPE’s ability to maintain photoreceptor homeostasis. This mechanistic insight is particularly attractive because it targets one of the fundamental dysfunctions in dry AMD—namely, the failure of the RPE to clear photoreceptor outer segments effectively, which leads to the accumulation of drusen and progressive retinal degeneration (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the extensive clinical experience with adalimumab in systemic and ocular inflammatory diseases supports its safety profile. The fact that adalimumab is already approved by regulatory agencies, coupled with several clinical studies demonstrating its localized safety when administered intravitreally or via related routes in ocular conditions such as uveitis, adds to its attractiveness as a candidate for repurposing (Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010; Leal et al., 2018; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. To date, most studies involving adalimumab in the ocular context have focused on inflammatory conditions such as uveitis and neovascular AMD rather than dry AMD specifically. As a result, direct clinical evidence supporting its efficacy in preserving RPE phagocytic function in dry AMD is currently limited. The hypothesis that adalimumab can prevent the TNFα-induced downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D is primarily based on preclinical observations, and further mechanistic studies, both in vitro and in relevant animal models, are necessary to validate this pathway in the context of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Nashine et al., 2022; García-Layana et al., 2021).

Another potential challenge with using adalimumab for dry AMD is related to drug delivery and dosing. While intravitreal administration has shown promise in limited studies, determining the optimal dose that achieves effective TNFα blockade without incurring retinal toxicity remains an unresolved issue. Some animal studies have indicated that higher doses of intravitreal adalimumab can lead to retinal inflammation, reduced electroretinogram responses, or histopathological evidence of toxicity. Given that dry AMD is a chronic condition and would likely require repeated dosing or sustained drug delivery systems, the long-term safety of local TNFα blockade needs to be rigorously evaluated (Manzano et al., 2008; Pascual-Camps et al., 2014).

Moreover, because TNFα plays roles in normal immune surveillance and tissue repair, its complete inhibition—especially in an aged population that may have impaired immune responses—could theoretically predispose patients to infections or other adverse effects. Although the systemic safety profile of adalimumab is well established, the ocular microenvironment has distinct immunological characteristics, and the long-term effects of TNFα inhibition on retinal homeostasis, particularly regarding complement activation and maintenance of the blood–retinal barrier, require further study. There is also the possibility that compensatory inflammatory pathways may become activated in response to TNFα blockade, potentially diminishing the efficacy of the intervention over time (García-Layana et al., 2021; Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Sharma et al., 2009).

Additionally, the magnitude of the contribution of TNFα to the pathogenesis of dry AMD relative to other factors—such as oxidative stress, genetic predispositions (including polymorphisms in complement factors), and lipid metabolism abnormalities—remains to be fully delineated. It is possible that TNFα is one of several drivers of RPE dysfunction, and that its inhibition may need to be combined with other therapeutic strategies (for example, antioxidant supplementation or complement inhibitors) to achieve a meaningful clinical benefit. Therefore, while the rationale for adalimumab is compelling, a monotherapy approach may not be sufficient to halt the multifactorial progression of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nussenblatt et al., 2010).

In summary, adalimumab presents a promising repurposed candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on its potent and specific inhibition of TNFα—a cytokine implicated in the downregulation of crucial RPE proteins such as MERTK and cathepsin D. The drug’s extensive use in other inflammatory settings, along with preliminary evidence supporting its ocular safety, lend credibility to the hypothesis that TNFα blockade can preserve the phagocytic machinery of RPE cells and potentially slow the degenerative process characteristic of dry AMD. Nevertheless, significant challenges remain, including the need for robust preclinical validation in dry AMD models, optimization of ocular dosing regimens, and long-term safety assessments in an elderly population. A carefully designed series of in vitro experiments using human RPE cells—followed by well-controlled animal studies—should be undertaken to establish proof of concept regarding the preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression and function. If these studies yield positive results, subsequent early-phase clinical trials could be justified to evaluate the efficacy of intravitreal adalimumab in patients with dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010).

In light of these considerations, our recommendation is to advance adalimumab into a rigorous preclinical testing pipeline aimed specifically at dry AMD models. This should include studies that measure the expression levels and activity of MERTK and cathepsin D in RPE cells under conditions of TNFα stimulation, both in the presence and absence of adalimumab treatment. Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiling in ocular tissues, along with assessments of retinal structure and function via in vivo imaging and electrophysiological testing, will be critical to determining an appropriate dosing strategy. Finally, integration with complementary therapeutic approaches may be considered to address other facets of dry AMD pathogenesis. While the path to clinical application is fraught with challenges, the potential benefit of preserving RPE phagocytic function—and by extension, photoreceptor survival—in a disease with very limited current treatment options provides a strong impetus for further development of this candidate (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022).

In conclusion, adalimumab’s established molecular profile as a potent TNFα inhibitor, its extensive clinical track record in systemic and ocular inflammatory diseases, and the emerging data linking TNFα to RPE dysfunction collectively support the rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD. Nevertheless, given the complexity of AMD pathogenesis and the potential risks associated with chronic intraocular immunomodulation, a thorough and methodical approach to preclinical investigation is warranted before embarking on large-scale clinical trials. The ultimate goal is to validate that neutralization of TNFα can indeed preserve the phagocytic capabilities of the RPE, thereby maintaining retinal health and preventing the progression of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Strengths of this candidate include its potent and specific inhibition of TNFα, which is a key mediator in inflammatory cascades, its favorable immunogenicity profile stemming from its fully human composition, and its prior demonstration of safety in ocular applications such as uveitis. In addition, the biological rationale is supported by evidence that TNFα negatively impacts the expression of proteins critical for RPE phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation—a process that, when impaired, underlies the pathology of dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021).

On the other hand, weaknesses center on the limited direct evidence for efficacy in dry AMD, potential challenges in achieving precise intraocular dosing without inducing retinal toxicity, and uncertain long-term consequences of sustained TNFα inhibition in the delicate immune environment of the eye. Moreover, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD suggests that a singular focus on TNFα may not fully address the disease’s complex pathophysiology, raising the possibility that combination therapies might eventually be necessary for optimal outcomes (Manzano et al., 2008; Sharma et al., 2009; Nussenblatt et al., 2010).

Given these observations, our evaluation concludes that adalimumab represents a promising and scientifically sound candidate for repurposing to treat dry AMD. Its mechanistic profile aligns well with the goal of preserving RPE phagocytic function by preventing TNFα-mediated downregulation of key proteins like MERTK and cathepsin D. However, to move forward with this candidate, research efforts must focus on resolving the outstanding questions through rigorous preclinical studies, optimization of the drug delivery method, and detailed long-term safety assessments. If successful, these steps could pave the way for early-phase clinical trials designed to test the efficacy of intravitreal adalimumab in stabilizing or improving RPE function in patients with dry AMD (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; García-Layana et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2022; Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, 2010).

In summary, while the current body of literature on adalimumab has primarily focused on its role in systemic inflammatory diseases and ocular inflammatory conditions such as uveitis and neovascular AMD, the underlying mechanistic data provide a persuasive rationale for extending its application to dry AMD. The hypothesis that adalimumab can preserve RPE phagocytic function by neutralizing TNFα—thereby preventing the deleterious downregulation of MERTK and cathepsin D—is scientifically plausible and merits further systematic investigation. The potential benefits of repurposing a well-characterized agent with an established safety profile are substantial, especially in a disease area where effective treatments remain elusive (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007).

Overall, our recommendation for the drug development team is to prioritize a series of detailed preclinical studies that examine the effects of adalimumab on RPE cells under TNFα-induced stress conditions, with particular emphasis on the regulation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression and subsequent phagocytic activity. These studies should involve both conventional cell culture models and in vivo models that mimic the chronic inflammatory environment observed in dry AMD. Should these studies yield positive results, a phase I/II clinical trial focusing on safety and early efficacy in patients with dry AMD would be justified. This stepwise approach will ensure that the promising mechanistic rationale is thoroughly vetted before large-scale clinical application (Dörschmann et al., 2023; García-Layana et al., 2021; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

In conclusion, the convergence of molecular, biochemical, and clinical evidence supports the further exploration of adalimumab as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to mitigate TNFα-mediated inflammatory cascades could play a critical role in preserving RPE function, maintaining photoreceptor health, and ultimately slowing the progression of a disease that currently lacks effective treatments. Nonetheless, rigorous preclinical validation and careful consideration of dosing and long-term safety will be essential to realize its potential in this new indication (Dörschmann et al., 2023; Levy-Clarke et al., 2014; Theodossiadis et al., 2007; Olivares-González et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB202190 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor belonging to the pyridinyl imidazole class of compounds. Originally discovered through rigorous cell‐based phenotypic screens aimed at identifying agents with anti‐inflammatory properties, SB202190 was developed to selectively inhibit p38 mitogen‐activated protein kinase (MAPK), particularly the α and β isoforms. The molecule was first characterized using radiolabeled ligand binding studies, which confirmed its ability to bind the ATP‐binding pocket of p38 MAPK and suppress its catalytic function (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). Being available commercially (e.g., Sigma‐Aldrich Cat. No. SML0687), SB202190 has been widely used as a biochemical tool to dissect the role of p38 in cellular stress and inflammatory responses. This class of compounds, including SB203580 as a closely related analogue, is recognized for its ability to modulate intracellular signaling cascades under various stress conditions. They have been broadly used in research settings to probe the molecular basis of cytokine production, cell differentiation, apoptosis, and cytoskeletal regulation (Young, 2013; Maugeri et al., 2021). The candidate under discussion is being repurposed with the hypothesis that its high potency against p38α/β—exhibiting an IC₅₀ of approximately 40 nM—can be leveraged to correct stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling defects and improve the phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative stress conditions that mimic the pathophysiology of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Liu et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, SB202190 has been predominantly employed as a research reagent to interrogate the role of p38 MAPK signaling in various cell types and disease models. In the context of ocular studies, SB202190, similar to its analogue SB203580, has been used to examine fibrotic responses, cell migration, and cytokine production in RPE cells. For instance, several in vitro studies have demonstrated that inhibition of p38 MAPK by SB202190 effectively reduces TGF‐β2–induced extracellular matrix (ECM) production (specifically collagen type I and fibronectin synthesis), which serves as an experimental surrogate for fibrotic remodeling observed in retinal degenerative conditions (Saika et al., 2005). Moreover, experiments using ARPE‐19 human RPE cells have revealed that SB202190 can reverse abnormal cell migration and reduce the transformation of RPE cells into fibroblast‐like cells in models of proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) (Saika et al., 2005). Although these models do not directly replicate dry AMD, they capture key aspects of RPE dysfunction, such as cytoskeletal disorganization and aberrant ECM deposition, which are also implicated in the progression of AMD. Beyond ocular research, p38 MAPK inhibitors have been investigated in other pathologies characterized by chronic inflammation and stress‐induced cellular dysfunction, including rheumatoid arthritis and muscular dystrophies (Brennan et al., 2021; Hirosawa et al., 2009). However, to date, clinical applications of SB202190 itself have not been pursued, and its use has remained restricted to preclinical experimental studies, thereby providing both a strong mechanistic rationale and a cautionary note regarding its translational potential (Federspiel et al., 2023; Young, 2013). Importantly, while numerous studies have elucidated p38 MAPK’s involvement in retinal injury and oxidative stress responses, there is limited direct clinical evidence supporting the use of SB202190 for treating dry AMD, and its application in this indication remains strictly hypothetical at this stage (Moustardas et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB202190 is known to selectively target the ATP‐binding pocket of p38 MAPK, thereby inhibiting its enzymatic activity and preventing the phosphorylation of downstream substrates that are pivotal to stress‐induced signaling cascades. Under normal conditions, p38 MAPK becomes activated through dual phosphorylation on specific threonine and tyrosine residues within its activation loop. Once activated, p38 MAPK stimulates various substrates, including transcription factors (e.g., cFos) and regulatory proteins involved in the control of cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and inflammatory mediator production (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). In RPE cells, activation of p38 MAPK has been linked to cytoskeletal rearrangements that lead to stress‐induced cellular defects; these include formation of abnormal actin structures and impaired formation of phagocytic cups necessary for the internalization of POS (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). In the experimental setting, SB202190 has been shown to effectively block the TGF‐β2 mediated phosphorylation of p38, thereby reducing the transcriptional activity of Smad3/4 complexes without impacting the initial receptor‐mediated phosphorylation events of Smads2/3. This mechanism suggests that SB202190 acts downstream of TGF‐β receptor activation, interfering with p38‐dependent enhancement of transcription factor complex formation and nuclear translocation, which in turn can dampen pathological ECM production and abnormal cell migration (Saika et al., 2005). Additionally, literature indicates that stress‐activated p38 signaling contributes to the senescence of RPE cells by regulating the senescence‐associated secretory phenotype (SASP) through modulation of p53 and NF‐κB pathways (Liu et al., 2025). By inhibiting p38 MAPK, SB202190 is hypothesized to replicate the protective effects of endogenous negative regulators such as DUSP4, which dephosphorylate and inactivate p38 MAPK, ultimately reducing RPE cell senescence and maintaining cellular homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025). It is noteworthy that p38 MAPK signaling is intricately intertwined with other MAPK family members, and some studies have reported that SB202190, particularly at higher doses, exhibits a biphasic response where alternative signaling pathways (such as MEK/ERK) may become upregulated, emphasizing the importance of careful dose optimization in any therapeutic application (Wang et al., 2024; Hirosawa et al., 2009). Thus, the mechanism of action of SB202190 involves a highly specific inhibition of p38α/β kinase activity, which is expected to restore normal actin dynamics and cytoskeletal organization in RPE cells, thereby facilitating proper phagosome formation and efficient POS uptake under oxidative stress conditions akin to those found in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The primary hypothesis driving the repurposing of SB202190 for dry AMD is that inhibition of p38α/β in RPE cells will reduce stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling defects and thereby improve the phagocytic internalization of photoreceptor outer segments. Under oxidative stress conditions, such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) in in vitro models using ARPE‐19 cells, activation of p38 MAPK is known to mediate cytoskeletal disorganization and promote aberrant cell migration, processes that are deleterious to the RPE’s phagocytic function (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). By inhibiting p38 MAPK with SB202190 at a low nanomolar concentration (approximately 40 nM), it is anticipated that the compound will reduce the phosphorylation of p38, thereby preventing the downstream activation of stress‐responsive transcription factors and proteins responsible for actin remodeling (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). In doing so, SB202190 is expected to “normalize” the actin cytoskeletal dynamics in H₂O₂‐treated ARPE‐19 cells, thus facilitating the re‐establishment of properly organized phagocytic cups required for POS ingestion—a process critical for photoreceptor maintenance and overall retinal homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025; Saika et al., 2005). In parallel, inhibition of p38 MAPK may downregulate pro‐fibrotic and pro‐senescent signaling pathways (e.g., those mediated by TGF‐β2, p53, and NF‐κB), therefore limiting the aberrant deposition of ECM components and improving the overall cellular microenvironment (Liu et al., 2025; Saika et al., 2005). As a result, the expected effect of SB202190 in the assay proposed would be a significant improvement in phagosome internalization of POS under oxidative conditions, combined with a reduction in the markers of cytoskeletal stress and cell senescence. Moreover, enhanced phagocytic activity by RPE cells could mitigate pathological features of dry AMD, such as drusen formation and eventual RPE degeneration, thereby potentially slowing disease progression (Moustardas et al., 2023; Du et al., 2010). The compound’s effect is further anticipated to extend to modulation of inflammatory cytokine release, given the well‐established role of p38 MAPK in regulating cytokine production, thus providing a dual benefit by both preserving cytoskeletal integrity and reducing chronic, low‐grade inflammation in the retina (Liu et al., 2025; Kyosseva, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
Evaluating the potential of SB202190 as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD involves weighing both the strengths and the inherent challenges associated with targeting the p38 MAPK pathway in the RPE. One of the major strengths of SB202190 is its well‐characterized mechanism of action as a selective inhibitor of p38α/β, which is pivotal in mediating stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling, inflammation, and cellular senescence in RPE cells. The compound has demonstrated robust in vitro anti‐fibrotic and anti‐migratory effects in ARPE‐19 cell models that mirror key features of RPE dysfunction observed in dry AMD (Saika et al., 2005). Furthermore, the concept of normalizing actin dynamics to enhance phagocytic cup formation and subsequent POS uptake is highly attractive, given that impaired phagocytosis is a core feature driving the degeneration observed in dry AMD (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). The protective role played by endogenous regulators like DUSP4, which deactivates p38 MAPK and preserves RPE integrity, supports the rationale for a pharmacological approach that mimics this effect (Liu et al., 2025). Additionally, numerous studies have shown that p38 MAPK inhibitors can modulate inflammatory responses and reduce ECM deposition; such effects are promising in the context of retinal diseases where chronic inflammation and fibrosis exacerbate degenerative processes (Moustardas et al., 2023; Saika et al., 2005).

However, several weaknesses and potential caveats must be thoroughly considered. First, the p38 MAPK pathway exhibits complex, context‐dependent behavior in RPE cells. There is evidence suggesting that, under certain circumstances, p38 MAPK activation can be cytoprotective by facilitating adaptive stress responses, such as the upregulation of antioxidant defenses (Pocrnich et al., 2009). This duality indicates that complete or prolonged inhibition of p38 MAPK may inadvertently dampen protective signaling, potentially leading to adverse outcomes. Additionally, published studies have documented that SB202190, when used at higher concentrations, can show biphasic responses or off‐target effects that might include the unintended activation of alternative MAPK pathways (Wang et al., 2024; Hirosawa et al., 2009). This underscores the critical need for precise dose optimization and comprehensive pharmacodynamic studies to define a therapeutic window where the beneficial effects on cytoskeletal remodeling and phagocytosis are maximized while the risks of impairing physiological stress responses are minimized.

Furthermore, while the preclinical literature provides substantial mechanistic insights and supportive data from retinal injury models—particularly in contexts such as PVR—the clinical translation of these findings to dry AMD remains unproven. SB202190 has not been advanced into clinical trials for retinal degenerative diseases, and its application has thus far been confined to experimental paradigms (Kim et al., 2021; Kyosseva, 2016). Therefore, any proposal to repurpose SB202190 for dry AMD must be accompanied by robust in vivo efficacy studies using animal models that faithfully recapitulate the chronic, multifactorial nature of the disease. Moreover, the impact of SB202190 on other critical RPE functions, such as phagocytosis of POS under normal conditions and cytoskeletal dynamics related to cell adhesion and migration, needs to be extensively characterized to avoid unintended disruption of essential homeostatic processes (Kim et al., 2021; Kyosseva, 2016).

Another consideration is the limitation inherent to the use of SB202190 as a research tool rather than a clinical‐grade pharmaceutical compound. Its pharmacokinetic and safety profiles have been characterized in experimental contexts, but there is a lack of clinical data regarding potential ocular toxicity, bioavailability, and long‐term impact on retinal structure and function (Federspiel et al., 2023; Young, 2013). The multifaceted role of p38 MAPK in the retina—spanning inflammatory cytokine production, regulation of apoptosis, and cytoskeletal dynamics—means that a fine balance must be maintained; excessive suppression could lead to undesired consequences such as impaired wound healing or compromised cell survival under stress. As such, a detailed understanding of the dose‐response relationship and the temporal dynamics of p38 inhibition in specific RPE subpopulations will be essential.

In summary, SB202190 presents as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on strong mechanistic rationale and preclinical evidence supporting its ability to modulate pathological pathways implicated in RPE dysfunction. Its capacity to inhibit p38α/β with high potency, restore actin dynamics under oxidative conditions, and improve phagocytic function aligns well with the therapeutic goals of preserving RPE integrity and retinal homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the dualistic nature of p38 MAPK signaling—with its capacity to mediate both deleterious and protective responses—poses a significant challenge that mandates careful and comprehensive preclinical evaluation. The candidate’s strengths reside in its well‐characterized inhibitory activity, established use in modulating fibrotic and inflammatory responses in ocular models, and its potential to replicate the endogenous protective functions mediated by regulators such as DUSP4 (Liu et al., 2025). Conversely, the weaknesses center on potential off‐target effects, the risk of inadvertently suppressing adaptive stress responses, and the absence of clinical studies directly addressing dry AMD.

Overall, while SB202190 holds promise based on its molecular mode of action and supportive in vitro data regarding cytoskeletal normalization and phagocytosis, the translational viability for dry AMD will ultimately depend on rigorous dosing studies, long‐term safety assessments, and demonstration of efficacy in animal models that capture the chronic oxidative and inflammatory milieu of the human retina (Moustardas et al., 2023; Saika et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2024). Only through such comprehensive studies can we adequately determine whether SB202190’s benefits outweigh its potential risks and if it can be successfully repurposed as a therapeutic intervention to mitigate the progression of dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Geldanamycin is a small-molecule inhibitor of heat shock protein 90 (HSP90) that originally garnered attention as a naturally derived product from Streptomyces species, and it belongs to the benzoquinone ansamycin class of compounds. As a natural product, geldanamycin was first isolated for its antibiotic properties and later found to exert potent effects on cellular protein homeostasis by binding the N-terminal ATP-binding pocket of HSP90. This mode of binding disrupts the chaperone function of HSP90, which is responsible for assisting in the stabilization and maturation of numerous client proteins, including signaling regulators and enzymes. Compounds of this chemical class have historically been investigated for their anticancer potential, given that HSP90 plays a central role in sustaining oncogenic signaling by stabilizing mutated or overexpressed proteins. In the context of ocular research, geldanamycin’s ability to modulate proteostasis and inflammatory cascades has prompted its investigation as a potential therapy for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), where dysregulated protein aggregation, impaired autophagy, and chronic inflammation are key pathological features (Piippo et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, geldanamycin and related HSP90 inhibitors have been used primarily as research tools to interrogate the role of molecular chaperones in cancer, neurodegeneration, and cellular stress responses. In preclinical studies, geldanamycin demonstrated the capacity to induce a robust heat shock response characterized by the upregulation of HSP70 and concomitant modulation of client proteins that depend on HSP90. Its inhibition of HSP90 has been extensively explored in models of protein aggregation diseases and in studies of inflammasome regulation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. For example, several reports have provided direct experimental evidence that HSP90 inhibition by geldanamycin prevents the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in human RPE models—specifically in ARPE-19 cells, human embryonic stem cell-derived RPE, and primary human RPE—by disrupting the protective HSP90–SGT1 complex that stabilizes NLRP3, thereby triggering autophagy-mediated clearance of the receptor (Piippo et al., 2018). In related studies, geldanamycin was also shown to induce an HSP70 response that can modulate proteostasis and reduce cellular inflammatory stress, although its high toxicity has consistently been reported as a barrier to clinical application in humans (Chen et al., 2021). While geldanamycin itself has not been approved for clinical use in dry AMD, its mechanistic insights have spurred research into repurposing HSP90 inhibitors for ocular indications, albeit with a need for derivatives or alternative candidates (Chen et al., 2021; Piippo et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, HSP90 functions as an ATP-dependent molecular chaperone that is critical for the correct folding, stabilization, and activation of a wide range of client proteins, including kinases, transcription factors, and components of the inflammasome complex such as NLRP3. Under basal conditions, HSP90, together with its co-chaperone SGT1, forms a complex with NLRP3 that maintains the receptor in an inactive yet activation-competent state. Geldanamycin binds to the N-terminal ATP-binding pocket of HSP90, thereby competitively inhibiting its ATPase activity and disrupting its chaperone cycle. This inhibition leads to the dissociation of the HSP90–SGT1 complex, releasing NLRP3. Once liberated from the protective chaperone complex, NLRP3 is highly unstable and becomes a substrate for intracellular degradation mechanisms. In the specific context of human RPE cells, experimental evidence has shown that geldanamycin preferentially promotes the autophagic clearance of NLRP3 rather than its proteasomal degradation. Mechanistic experiments that used proteasome inhibition with MG-132 and lysosomal/autophagy inhibition with bafilomycin A₁ or chloroquine revealed that when autophagy is intact, geldanamycin drives the degradation of NLRP3 via the autophagy pathway, resulting in a robust reduction in caspase-1 activity and IL-1β secretion (Piippo et al., 2018). This HSP90-dependent regulation of NLRP3 is particularly significant because inflammasome activation in RPE cells is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In addition, geldanamycin induces the expression of HSP70, a cytoprotective chaperone that further contributes to maintaining proteostasis under stress conditions; however, the increase in HSP70 is a double-edged sword, as it reflects cellular stress responses that could have both beneficial and deleterious effects if dysregulated (Chen et al., 2021; Ryhänen, 2011). Notably, the timing of geldanamycin administration is critical: its inhibitory effect on IL-1β secretion is maximal when added immediately prior to the induction of proteasome or autophagy inhibition, indicating that the HSP90 inhibition must occur before the onset of overwhelming proteostatic stress to be effective (Piippo et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic findings, the expected therapeutic effect of geldanamycin in a dry AMD model is multi-pronged. First, by binding to HSP90 and disrupting its stabilization of NLRP3, geldanamycin is anticipated to accelerate the autophagic clearance of NLRP3 complexes. This clearance is expected to blunt the assembly and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, thereby reducing the cleavage of pro-caspase-1 and ultimately diminishing the production and secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β. In the context of dry AMD, where low-grade chronic inflammation and impaired clearance of damaged cellular proteins contribute to disease progression, the suppression of inflammasome activation is a desirable outcome that could help mitigate retinal inflammation and cell death (Piippo et al., 2018). Second, by reducing the persistent activation of the inflammasome, geldanamycin may help preserve lysosomal function, which is critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE. Lysosomal dysfunction and the resultant accumulation of lipofuscin are hallmark features in the pathogenesis of dry AMD; therefore, maintaining efficient lysosomal degradation is key to restoring RPE homeostasis. Although direct evidence linking geldanamycin to enhanced POS digestion is not comprehensively detailed in the current literature excerpts, there is reasonable mechanistic rationale to suggest that improved autophagic flux and decreased inflammatory burden could promote better phagocytic competence in RPE cells (Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025; Piippo et al., 2018). Finally, given that HSP90 inhibition via geldanamycin has been shown to reduce proteostasis stress and modulate key inflammatory pathways, its application in RPE models of dry AMD could result in improved cellular survival and function, potentially slowing or reversing aspects of the degenerative process. It is important to note that the hypothesized effective concentration (EC₅₀ around 500 nM) is based on in vitro studies in RPE cells, and achieving this efficacy in an in vivo ocular setting via intravitreal administration would require careful dosing and pharmacokinetic optimization to mitigate systemic toxicity (Piippo et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
Geldanamycin represents a promising candidate from a mechanistic perspective for treating dry AMD due to its unique mode of action as an HSP90 inhibitor. The strengths of this therapeutic approach include its ability to directly target a key regulatory protein that stabilizes the NLRP3 inflammasome, leading to downregulation of a major pro-inflammatory pathway implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis. Preclinical research in RPE models, including ARPE-19, hESC-derived RPE, and primary human RPE, has consistently demonstrated that geldanamycin can reduce caspase-1 activity and IL-1β secretion by promoting autophagic degradation of NLRP3, which is central to halting the vicious cycle of chronic inflammation (Piippo et al., 2018). This is further supported by studies indicating that proper timing of HSP90 inhibition is crucial to maximize the clearance of NLRP3 and achieve therapeutic benefits before proteostatic stress overwhelms the cellular degradation machinery (Piippo et al., 2018). Additionally, the induction of HSP70 following geldanamycin treatment may confer additional cytoprotective effects by promoting proper protein folding and assisting in the clearance of misfolded proteins, thus helping preserve lysosomal function and potentially improving photoreceptor outer segment (POS) digestion—a process that is compromised in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2021; Ryhänen, 2011).

However, significant challenges limit the clinical translation of geldanamycin. One of the major weaknesses of this therapeutic candidate is its well-documented toxicity profile. Numerous studies have reported that while geldanamycin is effective in modulating HSP90 and reducing inflammasome activation at low nanomolar doses, its inherent cytotoxicity and off-target effects make it unsuitable for direct clinical application. In several experimental settings, geldanamycin has been described as “too toxic for human administration,” with adverse effects observed in both in vitro and in vivo models (Piippo et al., 2018). Such toxicity is believed to arise in part from the quinone moiety of the molecule, which can engage in redox cycling and generate reactive oxygen species, thereby exacerbating cellular stress and impairing normal proteostasis. Furthermore, while the small-molecule nature of geldanamycin is an advantage in terms of drug delivery—especially for routes such as intravitreal injection—the narrow therapeutic window means that fine-tuning the dose to achieve the desired biological effect without incurring toxicity remains a significant hurdle. There is also the possibility that global inhibition of HSP90 could destabilize multiple client proteins beyond NLRP3, leading to unintended perturbations in vital signaling pathways and cellular homeostasis (Chen et al., 2021).

In addition, despite the promising preclinical data supporting the use of geldanamycin for reducing inflammasome activation in RPE cells, there is a noticeable gap in the literature concerning its impact on other critical aspects of dry AMD pathology—specifically, the direct enhancement of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) digestion. Although it is hypothesized that preserving lysosomal function via inhibition of chronic inflammasome activity should translate into improved phagocytosis of POS by RPE cells, definitive experimental evidence demonstrating that geldanamycin treatment leads to enhanced POS clearance in AMD models is lacking (Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025; Piippo et al., 2018). This represents an area where further targeted studies are required.

Overall, geldanamycin’s mechanism of action is compelling from a proof-of-concept perspective; it elucidates how HSP90 inhibition can modulate the stability of key inflammatory mediators such as NLRP3 and thereby attenuate detrimental inflammatory cascades in RPE cells. The detailed biochemical insights provided by studies using geldanamycin have been invaluable for understanding the interplay between proteostasis, autophagy, and inflammation in the context of dry AMD. However, the clinical translation of geldanamycin as a therapeutic candidate is considerably hampered by its toxicity profile and the potential for off-target effects. Consequently, while geldanamycin offers important mechanistic validation for targeting HSP90 as a strategy to modulate NLRP3 inflammasome activity, repurposing efforts for dry AMD would likely need to focus on less toxic analogues or more selective HSP90 inhibitors (such as TAS-116) that preserve the beneficial effects on proteostasis without incurring significant cytotoxicity (Piippo et al., 2018). In summary, geldanamycin is a scientifically sound candidate from the perspective of modulating key pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD, yet its translational potential is limited by safety concerns that must be addressed either through structural modifications or by identifying alternative inhibitors within the HSP90 inhibitor class that demonstrate improved ocular and systemic tolerability.
