Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Cerulenin is a natural product originally isolated from the filamentous fungus Cephalosporium caerulens and was the first discovered fatty acid synthase (FAS) inhibitor (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; López & Diéguez, 2007). Chemically, this compound is classified as an epoxy-keto fatty acid analogue; it contains a reactive epoxide ring conjugated to a diene/amidic structure that mimics fatty acid substrates. This reactive epoxide is key to its mechanism because it enables cerulenin to irreversibly bind to its target enzyme via covalent modification. As such, cerulenin belongs to the class of FAS inhibitors that historically have been used as biochemical probes to investigate lipid metabolism and, subsequently, as lead compounds in the development of antineoplastic agents, given the upregulation of de novo lipogenesis in many cancers (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; López & Diéguez, 2007; Abramson, 2011). The molecule’s natural origin, combined with its potent inhibitory activity, has made it a valuable tool in studies of metabolic regulation and lipogenesis over several decades.

Therapeutic History:  
In the past, cerulenin was primarily developed and investigated as an antimicrobial and antifungal antibiotic due to its capacity to irreversibly inhibit fatty acid synthesis in both bacterial and eukaryotic systems (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Subsequent research in the fields of oncology and metabolic regulation revealed that several tumor types exhibit elevated expression of FAS, making FAS inhibitors promising candidates for anticancer therapy. Preclinical studies demonstrated that cerulenin could induce apoptosis in tumor cells, delay disease progression in xenograft models, and even affect systemic metabolic parameters such as food intake and body weight in rodent models (López & Diéguez, 2007; Heath, White, & Rock, 2002; Goodman & McFadden, 2007). Despite these promising results, its clinical utility has been constrained by poor chemical stability—primarily due to its reactive epoxide moiety—and significant toxicity stemming from irreversibility and off-target interactions with other cysteine-containing proteins (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Furthermore, while modifications have led to second-generation analogues like C75, designed to improve stability and selectivity, there are no records of cerulenin being specifically applied to ophthalmologic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal lipotoxicity diseases (Menendez & Lupu, 2017; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999). Although cerulenin has been explored in other in vivo models (for example, for retinitis pigmentosa in preclinical studies), no clinical trials have been registered for its use in AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, cerulenin exerts its biological effects by targeting the fatty acid synthase complex. Its mechanism involves the formation of an irreversible covalent adduct with an active-site cysteine residue (specifically, Cys1305) within the ketosynthase (KS) domain of type I FAS. This is achieved by an epoxide ring-opening reaction at the C-2 position of cerulenin, leading to the nucleophilic attack by the thiol (-SH) group of the catalytic cysteine residue (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008). Crystallographic studies have provided precise structural insights into this interaction, showing that such covalent modification not only blocks the initial acyl-transfer step but also induces conformational changes—such as the flipping of key residues like F1646 and the rotation of M1251—that ultimately disrupt the hydrophobic acyl-binding tunnel required for fatty acid chain elongation (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008; Fhu & Ali, 2020). In addition to inhibiting FAS directly, cerulenin has also been shown to impair protein palmitoylation, a post-translational modification that plays an important role in regulating membrane association and signaling functions of numerous proteins including Ras oncoproteins (Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999). This dual mechanism—targeting both de novo fatty acid synthesis and protein acylation—underscores the broad-spectrum bioactivity of cerulenin and its potential impact on multiple cellular pathways that are dysregulated in disease states (Menendez & Lupu, 2017; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis underpinning the proposed repurposing of cerulenin for dry AMD centers on its ability to attenuate de novo lipogenesis in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. In the context of dry AMD, pathologic accumulation of lipofuscin and toxic bisretinoid compounds such as A2E is thought to result from excessive lipid synthesis and impaired degradation of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) material. Excess levels of intracellular fatty acids, often derived from hyperactive FAS, contribute to the generation of these lipofuscin precursors—ultimately impairing lysosomal function and leading to RPE dysfunction (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020). By inhibiting FAS activity in the RPE, cerulenin is expected to reduce the synthesis of fatty acids that serve as precursors for lipofuscin components. This reduced lipogenesis should, in theory, alleviate the accumulation of lipofuscin, restore optimal levels of lysosomal pH, and enhance the activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D—thereby improving the degradation and turnover of POS material (Radka & Rock, 2022; Troudi, Pagès, & Brunel, 2021). Furthermore, since oxidative stress is a key driver of abnormal lipid metabolism in RPE cells, the ability of cerulenin to lower fatty acid synthesis may concurrently reduce the burden of oxidative damage and improve cellular homeostasis (Vázquez et al., 2008; Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007). It is also noteworthy that FAS expression has been detected and functionally characterized in various extrahepatic tissues; while direct evidence of its expression in RPE cells is less extensively documented in the provided citations, the extrapolation from other cellular models supports the likelihood that modulating FAS activity in RPE would confer benefits in lipid turnover and lysosomal efficiency (Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999; Johansson et al., 2008). Thus, within the proposed assay—where RPE cells are subjected to oxidative stress that mimics the environment of dry AMD—cerulenin is anticipated to lower intracellular lipid levels, minimize the generation of lipofuscin precursors, and ultimately restore RPE functional capacity.

Overall Evaluation:  
Cerulenin presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD owing to its well-documented ability to inhibit fatty acid synthase through a unique irreversible, covalent mechanism. Its molecular footprint, characterized by a reactive epoxide ring, has been exploited in multiple studies to evaluate cellular lipid synthesis and, by extension, to modulate metabolic pathways that underpin several disease processes (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Abramson, 2011). Mechanistically, its capacity to bind to a crucial cysteine residue in the FAS enzyme and to interfere with lipid assembly positions it as a potentially valuable agent to counter the lipid-driven pathogenesis implicated in RPE dysfunction and lipofuscin accumulation in dry AMD (Abramson, 2011; Johansson et al., 2008).

The strengths of cerulenin as a candidate include its small-molecule profile, which facilitates cellular entry; its established use as a research tool in in vitro and in vivo models; and its dual activity profile that not only curtails de novo lipogenesis but may also impede aberrant protein palmitoylation. Such multifaceted activity could be beneficial in a complex tissue environment like the retina, where multiple overlapping metabolic dysfunctions contribute to disease progression (Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007; Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999). In particular, by reducing the synthesis of fatty acids in RPE cells, cerulenin could deplete one of the key substrates for the formation of lipofuscin precursors such as A2E, thereby potentially improving lysosomal degradation of shed POS and arresting a vicious cycle of intracellular lipid accumulation and oxidative stress (Radka & Rock, 2022; Troudi, Pagès, & Brunel, 2021).

However, several weaknesses must be carefully considered. Cerulenin’s inherent chemical instability, attributed to its reactive epoxide ring, raises significant concerns regarding its pharmacokinetic profile and overall toxicity, especially in a sensitive tissue like the retina where off-target effects may exacerbate cellular stress rather than alleviate it (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Heath, White, & Rock, 2002). The irreversible nature of its enzyme inhibition—while beneficial for ensuring sustained suppression of FAS—may lead to collateral damage in non-target tissues, and the narrow therapeutic window observed in other preclinical studies suggests that dose optimization could be challenging (Fhu & Ali, 2020; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Moreover, although the hypothesis posits that inhibition of de novo lipogenesis in the RPE will mitigate lipid accumulation and improve lysosomal function, there is a paucity of direct evidence linking cerulenin or similar FAS inhibitors to improved outcomes in dry AMD models specifically. The documented applications of cerulenin are primarily in the realms of oncology and metabolic regulation, with little precedent for its use in ocular conditions (Lawrence, Zilfou, & Smith, 1999; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). This suggests that while the mechanistic rationale is sound, the translational leap to an ocular indication will require additional supportive data both from in vitro RPE assays and from appropriate animal models of AMD.

Another point of concern is that cerulenin’s nonselective inhibition of fatty acid synthase may also impair essential lipid synthesis in cells that require robust regenerative capacity, potentially leading to unintended cytotoxicity or impaired cell membrane maintenance. In the context of the RPE, where cellular health is paramount for photoreceptor support, any off-target lipid synthesis inhibition must be tightly controlled (Goodman & McFadden, 2007; Fhu & Ali, 2020). Furthermore, its use in vivo has been historically hampered by issues such as poor aqueous solubility—it often requires solvents like DMSO for administration—and its propensity for rapid degradation in protic environments, all of which represent substantial formulation challenges that must be overcome for ocular delivery (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Vázquez et al., 2008).

Given these considerations, while cerulenin offers a compelling proof-of-concept relating to the modulation of lipogenesis and lysosomal function, its practical development as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD would likely necessitate further chemical modifications. The precedent set by the development of derivatives such as C75—which were specifically engineered to overcome the limitations of cerulenin by removing the problematic epoxide group and enhancing stability—suggests that optimization is both possible and necessary (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Optimized analogues with improved pharmacokinetic and safety profiles may hold greater promise in the ocular setting than the parent compound.

In summary, cerulenin’s capacity to inhibit fatty acid synthase at the molecular level through irreversible covalent binding is well-established and aligns with the proposed therapeutic mechanism of reducing RPE lipid accumulation and lipofuscin precursor formation. However, its historical limitations in terms of chemical stability, toxicity, and nonselectivity present significant hurdles for its repurposing in dry AMD. The compound’s extensive use in metabolic and oncologic research provides a strong foundation for understanding its biochemical actions, but the absence of direct evidence in retinal models and the challenges associated with its delivery to ocular tissues temper enthusiasm for immediate clinical translation (Angeles & Hudkins, 2016; Fhu & Ali, 2020; Menendez & Lupu, 2017). Therefore, while there is sufficient mechanistic rationale to pursue further preclinical investigations—potentially in parallel with the development of more stable derivatives—the current state of evidence suggests that cerulenin itself may not be ideal as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD without significant further optimization. More comprehensive in vitro studies using RPE cell models and targeted in vivo studies in AMD-relevant animal models are needed to validate whether the inhibition of de novo lipogenesis by cerulenin can indeed translate into restored lysosomal function and improved photoreceptor outer segment degradation in this disease context (Lee, Stephens, & Englund, 2007; Radka & Rock, 2022).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of MitoQ as a therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD) based on its chemical origins, therapeutic history, mechanism of action, expected effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and an overall assessment of its potential.

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

MitoQ is a synthetically derived mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant that was developed by chemically conjugating a redox‐active ubiquinone (a structural analogue of the endogenous coenzyme Q10) to a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation via a decyl (approximately 10‐carbon) alkyl linker (Gueven et al., 2017; Rocha et al., 2014). The TPP⁺ moiety is chosen because its positive charge and high lipophilicity enable it to readily traverse biological membranes and to exploit the large, negative mitochondrial membrane potential for selective accumulation in the mitochondrial matrix (Lukashev et al., 2014; Kim & Han, 2017). The synthesis of MitoQ involves standard organic conjugation chemistry where the ubiquinone scaffold is covalently linked to the TPP⁺ unit, thereby converting a relatively non–mitochondria‐selective antioxidant into a compound that is “targeted” to mitochondria in a membrane‐potential–dependent manner (Gueven et al., 2017).

MitoQ belongs to a broader class of compounds known as mitochondria‐targeted antioxidants (MTAs). These compounds are designed to overcome the limitations of conventional antioxidants whose systemic distribution rarely leads to sufficient concentrations in mitochondria—the primary site of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Over the past decades, TPP⁺–conjugated antioxidants (including MitoQ, MitoVit E, SkQ1, and MitoTEMPO) have been actively developed and studied in various preclinical and clinical contexts with the aim of mitigating oxidative stress in a range of disorders (Gueven et al., 2017; Fields et al., 2023). Unlike natural antioxidants that occur endogenously (e.g., coenzyme Q10 in the mitochondrial inner membrane), MitoQ is a synthetic molecule whose design is entirely based on medicinal-chemistry principles that link a potent antioxidant moiety with a mitochondrial targeting domain. This chemical class of compounds has been used in multiple experimental paradigms—including cardiovascular, metabolic, neurodegenerative, hepatic, and inflammatory diseases—where oxidative damage is key to the pathological process (Lukashev et al., 2014; Apostolova & Victor, 2015). In summary, MitoQ’s design confers it high mitochondrial uptake and a redox-cycling ability that is central to its biochemical activities.

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

MitoQ has been extensively evaluated in numerous preclinical disease models because of its capacity to concentrate in mitochondria and scavenge ROS. Numerous animal studies have demonstrated its protective effects in models of neurodegeneration, cardiovascular injury (e.g., ischemia–reperfusion injury), metabolic syndrome, and hepatic toxicity (Gueven et al., 2017; Apostolova & Victor, 2015). For example, preclinical animal models have shown that oral administration of MitoQ can reduce lipid peroxidation, improve mitochondrial respiration, and restore ATP production in tissues compromised by oxidative stress (Kim & Han, 2017; Apostolova & Victor, 2015). Moreover, MitoQ has reached the clinical arena; double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials have been conducted in conditions such as Parkinson’s disease and chronic hepatitis C to assess its efficacy and safety in humans (Gueven et al., 2017; Apostolova & Victor, 2015). In these studies, MitoQ exhibited a favorable pharmacokinetic profile with evidence of oral bioavailability and rapid tissue uptake driven by mitochondrial membrane potential (Gueven et al., 2017; Forini et al., 2020).

Notably, while the broader class of mitochondria-targeted antioxidants has been extensively investigated, the evidence for MitoQ’s use specifically in ocular contexts such as dry age–related macular degeneration is limited. In one animal study of inherited photoreceptor degeneration related to elevated ROS, MitoQ failed to restore retinal complex I activity, glutathione (GSH) levels, or prevent photoreceptor degeneration (Gueven et al., 2017). This result suggests that MitoQ’s efficacy in ocular settings, particularly for retinal degenerative processes, might not be as robust as observed in systemic or neurological diseases. In contrast, other mitochondria-targeted compounds such as SkQ1 have shown promising preclinical outcomes in ocular and age-related conditions (Lukashev et al., 2014; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). Thus, while the therapeutic history of MitoQ in general oxidative stress–related conditions is well documented—with several positive outcomes in cardiometabolic and neurodegenerative models—the evidence supporting its repurposing for dry AMD remains mixed and requires further investigation.

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

MitoQ’s mechanism of action is intricately tied to its structural design and mitochondrial targeting capabilities. Once administered, the TPP⁺ moiety propels MitoQ across biological membranes and into the mitochondrial matrix, where the large negative membrane potential (approximately –150 to –180 mV) ensures that MitoQ accumulates up to several hundred times above cytosolic concentrations (Gueven et al., 2017; Rocha et al., 2014). After mitochondrial entry, the ubiquinone moiety of MitoQ is enzymatically reduced—primarily by Complex II (and potentially by Complex I in some contexts)—to generate its active antioxidant form, mitoquinol (MitoQH₂) (Lukashev et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2014). This reduction is a key step because only the reduced form is effective in scavenging harmful free radicals.

The active mitoquinol acts as an electron donor, neutralizing reactive oxygen species such as superoxide (O₂⁻·) and peroxynitrite (ONOO⁻) (Kim & Han, 2017; Subramanian et al., 2010). In doing so, it interrupts lipid peroxidation chains within the mitochondrial inner membrane—a process that can lead to damage of critical mitochondrial proteins, lipids, and enzymes essential for ATP production. The antioxidant action of MitoQ is not a one-off event; rather, mitoquinol, upon donating an electron, is oxidized back to its quinone form, where it can then be re-reduced by the mitochondrial respiratory chain to continue the cycle (Gueven et al., 2017; Rocha et al., 2014). This rechargeable, redox-cycling behavior is what underpins its classification as a “rechargeable mitochondria-targeted antioxidant.”

At the molecular level, MitoQ is thought to provide protection by directly intercepting lipid peroxyl radicals before they can propagate membrane damage. The proximity of MitoQ’s quinone moiety to the phospholipid bilayer of the inner mitochondrial membrane, thanks to its hydrophobic decyl chain, is critical to its function (Gueven et al., 2017). The compound’s localization is highly dependent on mitochondrial membrane potential; experimental studies have demonstrated that dissipating the membrane potential with uncouplers such as FCCP significantly reduces MitoQ uptake and thereby its subsequent antioxidant effects (Gueven et al., 2017; Kim & Han, 2017).

Beyond its direct ROS-scavenging activity, MitoQ has been shown in several studies to contribute to the preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics. By preventing oxidative damage to components of the electron transport chain, it aids in maintaining mitochondrial ATP production, which is crucial for cellular functions including the energy-intensive process of phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation in RPE cells (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). In addition, there is emerging evidence that targeting mitochondrial ROS not only mitigates damage at the level of the membrane but may also normalize the expression of autophagy markers and improve the overall turnover of damaged organelles (Gueven et al., 2017; Kim & Han, 2017). Such cellular housekeeping functions are intimately linked to the health and function of retinal pigment epithelium, particularly in the context of age-related degeneration where mitochondrial dysfunction and lysosomal impairment have been implicated.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Models

Dry AMD is characterized by the progressive dysfunction of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which is essential for the phagocytosis, degradation, and recycling of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Oxidative stress, particularly to the mitochondria within RPE cells, has been implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Accumulating evidence suggests that mitochondrial ROS can impair cytoskeletal remodeling, disrupt lysosomal function, and lead to the accumulation of toxic waste products—all contributing to RPE dysfunction (Gueven et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014).

Based on its mechanism of action, the hypothesis is that MitoQ will concentrate within the mitochondria of RPE cells, where its redox-cycling and ROS-scavenging properties will help to mitigate the deleterious effects of oxidative stress. Specifically, by reducing mitochondrial ROS, MitoQ is expected to prevent oxidative damage to the phagosome–lysosome system. This, in turn, should preserve the efficient uptake and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments, a process that is intimately related to the maintenance of RPE health and function (Gueven et al., 2017; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Experimental assays designed to test this hypothesis would likely involve subjecting cultured RPE cells to oxidative stress (using agents such as H₂O₂ or cigarette smoke extract) and assessing the impact of MitoQ on several key parameters. These parameters include:

1. Mitochondrial ROS levels, as measured by specific fluorescent indicators. A decrease following MitoQ treatment would confirm its ROS scavenging activity (Kim & Han, 2017; Gueven et al., 2017).

2. ATP production within RPE cells, restoring normal energy levels essential for phagocytosis. Effective MitoQ treatment should help normalize ATP levels that are typically depressed under oxidative stress conditions (Gueven et al., 2017; Fields et al., 2023).

3. Lysosomal function and autophagy markers, such as LC3-II, p62, and cathepsin activity, which serve as proxies for the proper degradation and turnover of cellular components. Normalization of these markers in the presence of MitoQ would suggest that its protective actions extend to maintaining phagosome–lysosome integrity (Gueven et al., 2017; Kim & Han, 2017).

4. Photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake and degradation assays in RPE cells. Improved efficiency in these assays following MitoQ treatment would support the hypothesis that MitoQ helps preserve RPE function in the face of oxidative stress (Gueven et al., 2017; Rocha et al., 2014). Although direct published studies of MitoQ in this context are not abundant, analogies can be drawn from its ability to restore autophagic flux in other disease models (Amorim et al., 2018; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Moreover, because mitochondrial ROS has been implicated in impairing cytoskeletal remodeling—a process crucial for the proper formation and movement of phagosomes—the normalization of such cellular dynamics through MitoQ may further contribute to the restoration of POS phagocytosis (Lukashev et al., 2014; Gueven et al., 2017). Given the favorable pharmacokinetic profile of MitoQ already demonstrated in human studies (including rapid tissue uptake and oral bioavailability) (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Forini et al., 2020), it is reasonable to expect that, upon targeted delivery in preclinical models of oxidative-stress–induced dry AMD, MitoQ would attenuate mitochondrial oxidative damage and consequently preserve RPE functional capacity.

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

In summary, MitoQ exemplifies a highly engineered mitochondria-targeted antioxidant with a well-understood chemical structure and mechanism of action. The strength of MitoQ lies in its design: by conjugating a potent antioxidant moiety to a TPP⁺ carrier, it achieves selective accumulation in mitochondria where oxidative stress is most deleterious. This design has been validated in numerous preclinical studies across a broad spectrum of diseases, with several reports of improved mitochondrial bioenergetics, reduced lipid peroxidation, and restoration of redox balance in tissues under oxidative pressure (Gueven et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014; Rocha et al., 2014). Its favorable pharmacokinetic and safety profiles in human trials for other indications further support its potential as a drug candidate (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Forini et al., 2020).

For the treatment of dry AMD, the proposed hypothesis that MitoQ will accumulate in RPE mitochondria and thereby preserve the phagosome–lysosome machinery is mechanistically sound. There is ample biochemical rationale suggesting that mitigating mitochondrial ROS can restore cellular functions such as ATP production and autophagy, both of which are critical in the RPE’s handling of photoreceptor outer segments (Gueven et al., 2017; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). Moreover, the overall reduction in oxidative damage could conceivably stabilize the cytoskeletal dynamics necessary for efficient phagocytosis (Lukashev et al., 2014).

However, several important challenges and weaknesses remain. First, although MitoQ has demonstrated robust effects in many systemic and neuronal models, its efficacy in ocular models, particularly those relevant to dry AMD, remains underexplored. In fact, some preclinical studies have shown that MitoQ failed to restore mitochondrial complex I activity or prevent photoreceptor degeneration in mouse models with elevated ROS (Gueven et al., 2017). In contrast, other mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (such as SkQ1) have shown more promising ophthalmic outcomes, including in phase II clinical trials for ocular surface disease (Lukashev et al., 2014; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). This mixed evidence raises concerns about whether MitoQ’s pharmacodynamics in the retina will meet the requisite therapeutic thresholds needed to prevent or slow dry AMD progression.

A second potential weakness is related to tissue-specific biodistribution. Although MitoQ is designed to concentrate in mitochondria via the TPP⁺ mechanism, the specificity with which it targets RPE cells versus other retinal cell types or non-ocular tissues is not well established. There is a concern that the compound’s systemic administration might lead to underdosing in the RPE, which is critical for its hypothesized mechanism in dry AMD. Furthermore, in neurodegenerative trials—such as those for Parkinson’s disease—MitoQ did not show clinical efficacy, possibly due to limitations in crossing the blood–brain barrier or other tissue-specific factors (Gueven et al., 2017).

Moreover, while MitoQ is effective at scavenging certain ROS, its antioxidant efficacy may also be limited by its own redox cycling; at high concentrations, some studies have suggested that TPP⁺–linked antioxidants might act as pro-oxidants, potentially causing additional mitochondrial stress (Gueven et al., 2017; Kim & Han, 2017). Therefore, determining the optimal therapeutic window will be critical to avoid potential off-target toxicity, especially in a delicate tissue like the retina.

Another consideration is the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD. Beyond mitochondrial oxidative stress, factors such as inflammation, complement dysregulation, and genetic predispositions (e.g., in complement factor H) contribute to its development. While MitoQ’s targeted action on mitochondria may address only one facet of this complex disease, combination therapies might ultimately be required to achieve meaningful clinical benefit.

Strengths of MitoQ include its well-documented mechanism of action, the robust body of preclinical work supporting its ability to restore mitochondrial bioenergetics and reduce oxidative damage in a variety of cell types, and its relatively safe profile in earlier human trials. The synthetic nature of MitoQ allows for reproducible manufacturing and potential chemical modifications to optimize its ocular delivery. Additionally, the concept of directly mitigating mitochondrial ROS is highly relevant in the context of the RPE, where oxidative damage is recognized as a key event in the progression of dry AMD (Gueven et al., 2017; Rocha et al., 2014).

In conclusion, while MitoQ is a promising candidate from the standpoint of its chemical design and systemic antioxidant efficacy, its translation to the treatment of dry AMD remains an area that requires careful and focused investigation. The hypothesis that MitoQ can ameliorate RPE dysfunction via preservation of mitochondrial and lysosomal integrity is plausible, yet the preclinical evidence in ocular models is limited and in some cases mixed. Future studies should involve dedicated ocular pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic assessments, evaluation in relevant RPE cell culture models and animal models of oxidative-stress–induced dry AMD, and careful titration of dosing to avoid potential pro-oxidant effects.

Overall, the candidate exhibits significant promise due to its targeted antioxidant mechanism and favorable safety profile; however, the lack of robust ocular-specific evidence represents a notable weakness. Continued research into its retinal uptake, the effect on phagosome–lysosome dynamics in RPE cells, and comparison with other ophthalmic mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (such as SkQ1 or peptide-based approaches) will be critical for validating its potential in dry AMD. This evaluation suggests that MitoQ is a viable candidate meriting further preclinical investigation, though alternative mitochondria-targeted compounds with more directly demonstrable ocular benefits may also need to be considered in parallel (Gueven et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014; Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Rocha et al., 2014; Kim & Han, 2017; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2014; Sheu et al., 2006).

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
Final Remarks

In summary, MitoQ represents a sophisticated example of mitochondria-targeted drug development with an established scientific rationale and a strong background in combating oxidative stress. Its structural design as a TPP⁺-conjugated ubiquinone analogue makes it particularly suited to accumulate within mitochondria and neutralize ROS—a mechanism that is highly relevant to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. Although preclinical and clinical studies outside the eye have shown promise, evidence specific to retinal diseases is either lacking or inconclusive. Therefore, while the candidate is scientifically sound, further focused research involving ocular-specific models and functional assessments in RPE cells is imperative before advancing to clinical trials for dry AMD. The strengths lie in its well-established mitochondrial targeting strategy, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and systemic safety data, whereas the primary weaknesses involve insufficient ocular efficacy data, potential dosing challenges, and the need to address the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. Based on the literature, MitoQ remains a promising repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD—but further preclinical studies focusing directly on RPE function under oxidative stress and assessing the preservation of phagosome–lysosome integrity are warranted to definitively validate its efficacy.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Oncostatin M (OSM) is a cytokine originally identified as a member of the interleukin‐6 (IL-6) family and is naturally produced by various immune cells. Recombinant OSM, as provided by R&D Systems (Cat. No. 287-OM), is synthesized using recombinant DNA technology and purified to ensure bioactivity. As a protein therapeutic, OSM belongs to the class of cytokine-based drugs, which have historically been harnessed for their abilities to modulate inflammatory responses, regulate cell differentiation, and promote tissue repair. The recombinant formulation offers high purity and biological consistency, which makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing in ocular diseases. Prior studies have shown that cytokines from the IL-6 family, including OSM, CNTF, and LIF, are capable of inducing cellular protective mechanisms in the retina and may influence inflammatory and repair pathways (Brown, 2015; Pacione, 2004).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, OSM has been investigated in various models of retinal degeneration where its administration was correlated with protection of retinal ganglion cells and photoreceptors. In a rat model of retinal degeneration, OSM injection led to a reduction in photoreceptor loss, suggesting its neuroprotective potential in ocular pathologies (Brown, 2015; Xia et al., 2011). Beyond the retina, evidence indicates that OSM can influence epithelial repair and barrier integrity in tissues affected by inflammation, as seen in studies of airway epithelial cells in diseases such as asthma and allergic rhinitis (Pothoven & Schleimer, 2017). In terms of specific use against dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), there is no direct clinical history of OSM application; however, the body of work on cytokine-based interventions in ocular diseases is promising and supports repurposing efforts. Notably, the success in using CNTF—a cytokine with mechanistic similarities to OSM—in clinical studies to preserve photoreceptors and improve retinal function underscores the potential of this class of agents for treating degenerative retinal disorders (Xia et al., 2011).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of OSM is initiated by its binding to the OSM receptor (OSMR), which forms a heterodimeric complex with the signal-transducing receptor subunit gp130. This receptor engagement prompts the recruitment of Janus kinases (JAKs), including Jak2 and Tyk2, leading to the phosphorylation of specific tyrosine residues on the receptor and subsequent activation of the Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription 3 (STAT3) (Pacione, 2004; Richards, 2013). Once phosphorylated, STAT3 forms homodimers that translocate to the nucleus and bind to STAT-responsive elements in the promoter regions of target genes. Among the genes regulated by STAT3 are those implicated in the acute phase response, such as A2m, as well as genes like Cebpd, which are involved in immune and pro-inflammatory responses (Pacione, 2004).

In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—critical for maintaining photoreceptor health—the activation of STAT3 may have multiple beneficial effects. Studies have shown that OSM not only induces STAT3 phosphorylation in RPE cells, but also phosphorylates ERK1/2 MAP kinase, indicating a broad spectrum of signal transduction modulation that influences cell survival, differentiation, and cytoskeletal organization (Li et al., 2011). Given that cytoskeletal reorganization is essential for the formation of phagocytic cups and subsequent photoreceptor outer segment (POS) internalization, OSM-mediated STAT3 activation is hypothesized to contribute directly to these processes. It is important to note that similar effects have been observed with related IL-6 family cytokines in various epithelial models, supporting the notion that STAT3 signaling plays a pivotal role in establishing and maintaining epithelial barrier integrity (Richards, 2013; Pacione, 2004; Tiffen et al., 2008).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis proposed for repurposing OSM in dry AMD is that when administered at concentrations around the EC₅₀ (~0.1 nM), OSM will robustly activate STAT3 in RPE cells. This activation is expected to drive the transcription of genes that encode tight junction proteins and cytoskeletal elements critical for the morphological and functional integrity of the RPE layer. Enhanced expression of these genes would, in theory, facilitate reorganization of the cytoskeleton, thereby enabling the efficient formation of phagocytic cups. As phagocytosis of shed POS is a central function of the RPE—ensuring the renewal of the photoreceptor layer—improvements in this process may directly translate into enhanced retinal health and slow disease progression in dry AMD (Li et al., 2011; Richards, 2013).

Evidence from the literature suggests that STAT3 activation plays a role in cytoskeletal dynamics and barrier function. For example, in studies with human fetal RPE cells, OSM stimulation led to phosphorylated STAT3 accumulation, which is correlated with modifications in cell shape, inhibition of uncontrolled proliferation, and potentially enhanced phagocytosis (Li et al., 2011). Moreover, the beneficial effects witnessed in similar cytokine treatments, such as with CNTF, reinforce the notion that a shared signaling cascade involving STAT3 not only supports neuroprotection but also augments cellular processes essential for maintaining the RPE’s barrier functions and phagocytic competence (Xia et al., 2011; Mori et al., 2024). However, while the expected induction of tight junction and cytoskeletal gene expression is mechanistically plausible based on the STAT3 pathway, direct evidence linking OSM-induced gene expression specifically to enhanced phagocytic cup formation in RPE cells remains to be conclusively established and would benefit from further in vitro and in vivo validation (Pothoven & Schleimer, 2017; Pacione, 2004).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of Oncostatin M for the treatment of dry AMD is supported by a mechanistic rationale that draws on its established role in STAT3-mediated cellular signaling and its previous demonstrations of neuroprotective effects in retinal degeneration models. One of the key strengths of OSM as a candidate lies in its ability to activate STAT3—a transcription factor that governs a spectrum of genes involved in cell survival, cytoskeletal reorganization, and barrier integrity. This is highly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments contribute to disease progression (Brown, 2015; Pacione, 2004). Additionally, the availability of a high-quality recombinant form, combined with prior research in ocular models showing evidence of photoreceptor protection and potential enhancement of retinal function, renders OSM an attractive prospect for repurposing (Xia et al., 2011; Mori et al., 2024).

Despite these strengths, several challenges and potential weaknesses warrant consideration. First, although OSM-induced STAT3 activation is well documented, its downstream effects on tight junction proteins and the cytoskeletal apparatus within RPE cells have not been conclusively demonstrated in the context of dry AMD. This dual nature of OSM’s action necessitates careful dosing and thorough characterization of its effects on RPE function to avoid adverse outcomes such as enhanced inflammation or unwanted EMT that could exacerbate retinal degeneration.

Detailed dose-response studies and time-course experiments will be imperative to delineate the precise window in which OSM functions as a promoter of barrier integrity and efficient phagocytosis, rather than triggering pathological changes detrimental to RPE function (Li et al., 2011; Tiffen et al., 2008).

In terms of translational potential, the strategy of repurposing an existing recombinant cytokine such as OSM offers significant advantages, including the possibility of leveraging existing manufacturing, formulation, and regulatory data. This could expedite the transition from preclinical studies to early-phase clinical trials in patients with dry AMD. Nonetheless, the preclinical evidence specific to dry AMD remains preliminary, and further research is needed to systematically assess OSM’s effects on RPE cell morphology, tight junction formation, cytoskeletal organization, and phagocytic efficiency. It would be beneficial to conduct detailed in vitro experiments using human RPE cell lines or primary RPE cultures, evaluating not only short-term signaling events (e.g., STAT3 phosphorylation kinetics) but also long-term outcomes such as maintenance of the barrier phenotype and resistance to oxidative or inflammatory stress. Such studies could be complemented by in vivo investigations in animal models that mimic the key features of dry AMD, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the balance between beneficial and potentially harmful effects of OSM in the ocular environment (Li et al., 2011; Pacione, 2004).

Overall, Oncostatin M presents as an innovative and mechanistically plausible candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. Its ability to activate STAT3 is intrinsically linked to cytoskeletal reorganization and epithelial barrier maintenance, processes that are critical for proper RPE function and the clearance of shed POS. The preclinical data from retinal degeneration models, along with evidence from related cytokines, lend credence to the hypothesis that OSM could enhance POS internalization and overall retinal health when applied at carefully optimized concentrations (Brown, 2015; Xia et al., 2011). However, the candidate’s dualistic role in modulating epithelial barrier function—including the risk of inducing EMT and compromising cellular integrity at inappropriate doses—necessitates a cautious and methodical approach to further development (Pothoven & Schleimer, 2017).

Detailed investigations into the optimal dosing regimen, the kinetics of STAT3 activation, and the downstream transcriptional events governing tight junction and cytoskeletal gene expression are crucial. Only through rigorous preclinical evaluation—encompassing both in vitro mechanism-based assays and in vivo efficacy studies—can we validate whether OSM truly possesses the capacity to enhance phagocytic cup formation and POS internalization as hypothesized. The balance between therapeutic benefit and potential adverse effects must be carefully managed to harness the full potential of OSM as a treatment for dry age-related macular degeneration (Pacione, 2004; Li et al., 2011; Richards, 2013).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nintedanib is a synthetic small‐molecule drug originally discovered and developed by Boehringer Ingelheim through an extensive lead optimization program that began in the late 1990s. Its design emerged during early cancer drug discovery efforts focused on angiogenesis inhibition, inspired in part by Judah Folkman’s pioneering work. The compound belongs to the indolinone chemical class – more precisely, it is a 6‐methoxycarbonyl‐substituted indolinone derivative – and was identified after systematic structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies that evaluated numerous six‐substituted indolinone analogues. In particular, modifications such as moving an amido group on the oxindole scaffold were shown to eliminate unwanted CDK4 inhibition while retaining potent VEGFR inhibition, and these insights eventually led to the convergence on the lead compound now known as nintedanib (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 1–8). The synthetic strategy employed a convergent approach that involved classical malonic ester addition reactions, followed by hydrogenation under acidic conditions that induced decarboxylative cyclization, and concluded with condensation steps and salt formation (resulting in the monoethanesulfonate form) to yield a highly crystalline final product (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 5–10, 39–43). As an indolinone derivative, nintedanib exemplifies a well‐studied class of therapeutic compounds that modulate receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs). Similar compounds in this class have been widely used in antiangiogenic and antifibrotic therapies in oncology and pulmonary medicine, and their ability to simultaneously inhibit multiple RTK pathways has been key to overcoming resistance mechanisms frequently encountered with single‐target inhibitors (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 1–5; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 22–25).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, nintedanib was developed with an emphasis on its anticancer potential. Its original targeting of the vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR) and subsequent demonstration of triple angiokinase inhibition – simultaneously inhibiting VEGFR, platelet‐derived growth factor receptors (PDGFR), and fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFR) – made it a candidate for addressing tumor angiogenesis. Early preclinical studies confirmed that nintedanib potently inhibited endothelial cell proliferation and in vivo tumor growth, leading to its progression into numerous Phase I through III clinical trials for non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), ovarian cancer, and other malignancies (Azuma et al., 2015, pp. 3–5; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 20–22). In addition, the compound’s remarkable specificity, as evidenced by low nanomolar inhibition of PDGFR and VEGFR family members (with IC₅₀ values in the range of 13–65 nM for different targets), underscored its potential as a broad‐spectrum antiangiogenic agent (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 10–15; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 12–14).  

Beyond its oncology applications, accumulating clinical evidence revealed that nintedanib also exhibits strong antifibrotic properties. Its efficacy in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) – with demonstrated improvements in forced vital capacity decline and overall clinical outcomes – led to its regulatory approval for IPF treatment in regions such as Europe and the United States (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 36–39; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 20–22). These diverse therapeutic indications illustrate that while nintedanib was originally intended as an anticancer agent, its mechanism of inhibiting multiple RTK‐mediated pathways allowed its repurposing for fibrotic diseases. Although nintedanib has not yet been extensively used in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), recent preclinical evidence in ocular models has suggested that its kinase inhibition profile could be exploited to modulate dysfunctional signaling in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17). Notably, studies in retinal models have demonstrated that nintedanib can suppress VEGF secretion and reduce neovascularization, both of which provide indirect evidence supporting its ocular tolerability and hint at potential utility in diseases such as dry AMD.  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, nintedanib exerts its pharmacological effect by acting as a competitive inhibitor of the ATP‐binding site located within the catalytic domain of receptor tyrosine kinases. Structural studies, including co‐crystallization and high‐resolution X‐ray diffraction analyses, have revealed that its indolinone core is critical for binding; the molecule forms two canonical hydrogen bonds with key residues within the kinase “hinge” region – for example, interactions with the nitrogen of a conserved cysteine residue (such as Cys919 in VEGFR2) and with a carbonyl oxygen (such as Glu917) – thereby stabilizing its association with the enzyme (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12). The presence of a methyl carboxylate substituent on the indolinone core further extends into the kinase specificity pocket to reinforce binding, and a methyl piperazinyl side chain interacts with solvent‐exposed portions of the protein, contributing both to the agent’s selectivity and to its sustained inhibitory profile (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 39–43; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12).  

Functionally, nintedanib displays potent inhibition of multiple RTKs. Its IC₅₀ values have been reported to be in the low nanomolar range for VEGFR subtypes (e.g., approximately 21 nM for VEGFR2 and 13 nM for VEGFR3), as well as for PDGFR isoforms (roughly 41–58 nM) and FGFR family members (with values ranging from 37 nM for FGFR2 to higher values for other FGFRs) (Azuma et al., 2015, pp. 3–5; Roth et al., 2015, pp. 10–15; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 12–14). By competitively occupying the ATP‐binding pocket, nintedanib prevents receptor autophosphorylation, thereby blocking subsequent activation of downstream signaling cascades, including the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and protein kinase B (Akt) pathways (Reck, 2015, pp. 2–3; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12). This broad inhibition interrupts not only angiogenic signaling in endothelial cells and pericytes but also fibrotic signaling in fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. An additional key feature of nintedanib’s mode of action is the sustained duration of receptor blockade; experimental studies have shown that even after a short 1-hour exposure, inhibition of VEGFR2 phosphorylation can persist for at least 32 hours, suggesting a relatively slow dissociation rate from the kinase active site (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 10–15; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12).  

In the specific context of retinal pigment epithelial cells, PDGFRβ and FGFR1 are among the RTKs implicated in maintaining cellular differentiation, regulating cytoskeletal organization, and modulating phagocytic activity. Dysregulation of these signaling pathways in RPE cells may lead to a decrease in the effective expression of key phagocytic receptors such as integrin αvβ5 and MERTK – receptors that are vital for the ingestion and clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Although much of the detailed mechanistic work in RPE cells remains in the early stages, the existing experimental evidence supports the notion that balanced RTK signaling is necessary for optimal RPE function. By inhibiting overactive signaling through PDGFRβ and FGFR1, nintedanib could restore a more physiologic phosphorylation state that permits proper receptor recycling and expression at the cell surface, thereby supporting phagocytosis and maintaining cellular integrity (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17). Additionally, by modulating these upstream kinases, downstream events that regulate cytoskeletal dynamics – potentially including reorganization of actin filaments and stabilization of focal adhesions – could be favorably altered. Although direct evidence in RPE cells is still emerging, analogous effects in other cell types have been observed when RTK signaling is normalized by multi-target inhibitors such as nintedanib (Hilberg et al., 2018, pp. 14–15, 19–20).  

Expected Effect:  
Within the RPE, efficient phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments is fundamental to retinal homeostasis, and failure of this process is believed to contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. The hypothesis proposes that dysregulated PDGFRβ and FGFR1 signaling in RPE cells impairs the expression and functional activity of phagocytic receptors, notably integrin αvβ5 and MERTK, which are responsible for recognizing and internalizing shed POS. Under normal conditions, these receptors are tightly regulated by extracellular signals, many of which are modulated by RTK activity. In the diseased state, abnormal RTK phosphorylation – perhaps via overactivation of PDGFR and FGFR pathways – could lead to a decrease in phagocytic receptor levels and result in defective POS clearance, contributing to the accumulation of cellular debris, chronic inflammation, and eventual geographic atrophy observed in dry AMD.  

By virtue of its potent inhibitory properties, nintedanib is expected to act by normalizing the aberrantly high RTK signaling in RPE cells. Its inhibition of PDGFRβ, in particular, would be anticipated to reduce excessive downstream signaling that might otherwise lead to a suppression of phagocytic receptor synthesis or recycling. In parallel, FGFR1 inhibition could correct imbalances in signaling that contribute to impaired cytoskeletal remodeling. The cytoskeleton is intimately involved in the process of phagocytosis, not only by providing the structural basis for membrane extension during engulfment but also by facilitating receptor clustering and the formation of phagocytic cups. Therefore, it is plausible to expect that the use of nintedanib would lead to enhanced expression of integrin αvβ5 and MERTK at the RPE cell surface as normal feedback loops are reinstated, thereby promoting increased rates of POS ingestion in assays of RPE differentiation (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17).  

Furthermore, preclinical studies have shown that in settings where RPE cells are exposed to pathological stimuli (such as necrotic cell lysates, which serve as a surrogate for sterile inflammatory conditions seen in retinal diseases), treatment with nintedanib results in a concentration-dependent suppression of aberrant VEGF secretion. This observation suggests that nintedanib is not only capable of regulating angiogenic processes in the retina but may also normalize other aspects of RPE cell function that rely on balanced RTK signaling (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13). In the context of the proposed assays, one would expect that treatment with nintedanib will restore proper receptor tyrosine kinase activity, result in the upregulation of phagocytic receptor expression, and enhance the mechanical and structural reorganization required for efficient POS uptake. These outcomes could be measured both biochemically – through assays of receptor expression and phosphorylation levels – and functionally, via quantification of POS ingestion in differentiated RPE cultures (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12; Rashdan & Hanna, 2014, pp. 2–3).  

In addition to its direct impact on RTK signaling, nintedanib’s inhibition is anticipated to indirectly influence other cytoskeleton-regulating pathways that are governed by MAPK and Akt cascades. These pathways have been associated with the regulation of actin dynamics and the assembly of focal adhesions, both of which are essential for robust phagocytic activity. Thus, normalization of these signaling pathways may foster an environment in RPE cells where cytoskeletal remodeling is optimized, ultimately leading to improved structural integrity and function—key factors in maintaining retinal health in the face of degenerative processes (Reck, 2015, pp. 2–3; Hilberg et al., 2018, pp. 19–20).  

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, nintedanib presents a compelling profile as a therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration. One of its primary strengths is its well‐documented ability to inhibit multiple receptor tyrosine kinases simultaneously. This triple angiokinase inhibition—encompassing VEGFR, PDGFR, and FGFR—has been extensively characterized in both in vitro and in vivo models, resulting in robust antitumor and antifibrotic effects in clinical studies for cancer and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 36–39; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 20–22). The compound’s chemical structure, based on its indolinone core, not only permits tight binding and competitive inhibition at the ATP‐binding site but also provides the necessary selectivity that minimizes off-target effects, a critical feature when considering repurposing for a delicate tissue such as the retina (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12; Roth et al., 2015, pp. 39–43).  

From a therapeutic history perspective, the extensive clinical experience with nintedanib in non‐small cell lung cancer and IPF engenders a level of confidence in its pharmacokinetic profile and tolerability when administered systemically. Although its use in ocular applications remains experimental, preliminary preclinical findings provide encouraging data. For instance, studies have demonstrated that nintedanib can inhibit VEGF secretion from retinal pigment epithelial cells exposed to pathological stimuli and can reduce retinal and choroidal neovascularization in animal models. These findings support the notion that, with appropriate reformulation or local delivery (e.g., intravitreal injection), nintedanib could achieve therapeutic levels in the retina without incurring unacceptable toxicity (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17).  

The mechanistic basis for considering nintedanib in dry AMD is particularly appealing. Dry AMD is characterized in part by the dysfunction of RPE cells, including impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments—a process tightly regulated by surface receptors such as integrin αvβ5 and MERTK. Dysregulation of upstream receptor tyrosine kinases, notably PDGFRβ and FGFR1, is hypothesized to contribute to the diminished expression or function of these phagocytic receptors. Nintedanib, by virtue of its potent inhibition of these kinases, holds the potential to recalibrate RTK signaling networks toward a more balanced state. This recalibration may not only restore proper levels of phagocytic receptors on RPE cells but also promote cytoskeletal remodeling necessary for the engulfment and processing of POS (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17). The downstream effects of such restoration could conceivably slow or even reverse aspects of RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration in dry AMD.  

Nonetheless, there are important considerations and potential weaknesses. One significant challenge lies in the delivery of nintedanib to the retina at therapeutic concentrations. Systemic administration of nintedanib is associated with low oral bioavailability and extensive first-pass metabolism (as observed in its use for IPF), which implies that direct ocular administration, likely via intravitreal injection, would be necessary for effective treatment of dry AMD. Although preclinical studies have demonstrated tolerability in ocular models, comprehensive toxicology studies specific to the retinal environment are required to ensure that the compound does not adversely affect other critical retinal cell types, including photoreceptors and inner retinal neurons (Roth et al., 2015, pp. 15–19; Roth et al., 2016, pp. 12–14).  

Another potential limitation is the broad scope of kinase inhibition exerted by nintedanib. While its ability to simultaneously target VEGFR, PDGFR, and FGFR is a strength in terms of overcoming compensatory mechanisms, it also raises the possibility of off-target effects that may disrupt other cellular processes in the retina. The retina is a highly specialized and tightly regulated tissue, and even subtle perturbations in signaling networks can lead to unintended consequences. Therefore, it will be critical to establish that nintedanib’s inhibition of RTKs in RPE cells does not interfere with other essential pathways—especially those involved in retinal development and neuroprotection (Hilberg et al., 2018, pp. 14–15; Hilberg et al., 2018, pp. 19–20).  

In addition, while the hypothesis that nintedanib can enhance phagocytic receptor expression (e.g., upregulating integrin αvβ5 and MERTK) is supported by the general principle that RTK signaling modulates these receptors, direct evidence linking nintedanib treatment to increased phagocytosis in RPE cells is still at an early, hypothesis‐driven stage. Rigorous experimental validation will be needed, potentially involving detailed biochemical assays to measure receptor expression and functional assays to assess POS ingestion rates in differentiated RPE cultures as well as in relevant animal models of dry AMD (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12; Rashdan & Hanna, 2014, pp. 2–3).  

Furthermore, while the ocular tolerability of nintedanib has been indirectly inferred from its use in non‐small cell lung cancer and preclinical models of choroidal neovascularization, comprehensive studies specifically designed to evaluate its safety profile in the context of dry AMD are lacking. Given that dry AMD is a chronic condition that would likely require long‐term treatment, issues of sustained drug exposure, potential cumulative toxicity, and the risk of eliciting off‐target effects must be thoroughly investigated (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13; Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 16–17).  

Overall, nintedanib’s established preclinical and clinical data in oncology and fibrosis, combined with its potent multi-targeted inhibition of key receptor tyrosine kinases, provides a strong foundation for its consideration as a repurposed therapeutic candidate in dry AMD. The molecular rationale—that abnormal PDGFRβ and FGFR1 signaling impair the expression and function of essential phagocytic receptors in RPE cells—is both biologically plausible and supported by insights from related pathologies. The anticipated restoration of phagocytic capacity via improved expression of integrin αvβ5 and MERTK, along with enhanced cytoskeletal remodeling conducive to POS uptake, represents an attractive therapeutic mechanism that could address a central defect in dry AMD pathogenesis (Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17).  

In conclusion, while the repurposing of nintedanib for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic framework and encouraging early preclinical findings, significant gaps remain that must be addressed before further clinical development is warranted. Critical next steps include:  
1. Detailed in vitro studies using differentiated human RPE cells to measure the impact of nintedanib on PDGFRβ and FGFR1 phosphorylation status, the expression levels of integrin αvβ5 and MERTK, and functional phagocytic assays assessing POS uptake.  
2. In vivo investigations in relevant animal models of dry AMD to evaluate retinal pharmacokinetics, tissue distribution, and the long-term safety profile following local ocular administration.  
3. Exploration of optimal delivery strategies to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic absorption and potential off-target effects.  
4. Further mechanistic studies to elucidate the downstream signaling pathways – including MAPK and Akt cascades – that may be modulated by nintedanib in the RPE and contribute to cytoskeletal remodeling.  

By addressing these areas, it should be possible to rigorously validate whether nintedanib can indeed “normalize” RTK signaling in the RPE and restore the phagocytic function that is compromised in dry AMD. The strengths of nintedanib lie in its potent, well-characterized kinase inhibition and its established clinical safety record in other disease indications. However, challenges remain in adapting its pharmacologic profile to the unique requirements of retinal therapy and ensuring that its broad RTK profile does not inadvertently disrupt other critical ocular functions. If these challenges can be overcome through careful preclinical and translational research, nintedanib may represent a transformative therapeutic option for addressing an unmet need in dry AMD (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 1–5, 20–22; Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13).  

Overall, our evaluation suggests that while caution must be exercised due to potential pharmacokinetic and off-target concerns, the available biochemical and clinical evidence provides sufficient justification for further investigation. The detailed molecular insights into nintedanib’s action, its demonstrated efficacy in modulating kinase pathways central to angiogenesis and fibrosis, and preliminary data in ocular models collectively support its candidacy for repurposing in dry AMD. Rigorous further studies will determine its ultimate utility, but current data indicate that nintedanib is a promising candidate worthy of additional mechanistic and translational evaluation (Roth et al., 2016, pp. 8–12; Reck, 2015, pp. 2–3; Hatano et al., 2019, pp. 10–13, 16–17).

FX-68 is a synthetic small‐molecule agonist developed from a chemical library (ChemBridge Cat. This compound is designed to mimic the natural ligand, fractalkine (CX3CL1), and has been optimized for potency with an EC₅₀ of approximately 100 nM, which suggests that it is capable of activating CX3CR1 at pharmacologically achievable concentrations (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–5, 6–7). The candidate belongs to the broader category of small-molecule GPCR agonists, a class that has been successfully employed in various inflammatory and neurodegenerative indications because of their favorable oral bioavailability and capacity to cross biological barriers; such compounds have a long history in modulating immune cell behavior and attenuating aberrant inflammation (Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 2–4; Chinnery et al., 2012, pp. 7–8). In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), FX-68 is proposed to restore appropriate signaling in the CX3CL1–CX3CR1 axis—a pathway that is critically involved in the regulation of microglial migration, phagocytosis and, indirectly, the trophic support provided to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6). The link between CX3CR1 function and retinal health was established through extensive genetic and preclinical studies, in which loss-of-function mutations or deficiencies in CX3CR1 were found to produce a constellation of AMD-like features, including the accumulation of subretinal microglia, formation of drusen-like deposits, and secondary photoreceptor degeneration (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7; Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 4–5). Historically, research in this area has focused on genetic knock-out models and human polymorphism analyses rather than on the administration of direct pharmacologic agonists; for example, CX3CR1-deficient mice consistently exhibit abnormal subretinal microglial behavior and accompanying retinal pathology, which has been used as a rationale for targeting this signaling pathway therapeutically (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–6). Although exogenous delivery of CX3CL1 has been explored in certain experimental paradigms, no small-molecule CX3CR1 agonist has yet been advanced in clinical or veterinary practice for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerations (Chinnery et al., 2012, pp. 7–8; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3). Instead, the therapeutic potential in this space has largely emerged indirectly from studies that demonstrate that disrupted CX3CR1 signaling is deleterious to retinal homeostasis, thereby suggesting that its appropriate stimulation could restore normal microglial behavior (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7). As a repurposed candidate, FX-68 aims to fill this translational gap by reactivating a pathway that is both genetically implicated in AMD and mechanistically understood in other contexts of neuroinflammation (Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 2–5).
