Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Cp40‐Peg is a PEGylated analog derived from the original compstatin peptide, a cyclic peptide identified through phage display technology and subsequently optimized for high‐affinity binding to complement component C3. The parent molecule, Cp40, binds specifically to C3 with nanomolar potency (IC₅₀ ~ 1 nM) and was engineered to interrupt the complement cascade by preventing the cleavage of C3 into its active fragments. To improve upon the pharmacokinetic limitations of unmodified compstatin peptides, Cp40 was chemically modified by conjugation with polyethylene glycol (PEG), a strategy known as PEGylation, which is designed to substantially extend systemic and, in this case, intraocular half‐life. This molecular modification confers several advantages, including enhanced aqueous solubility, reduced proteolytic degradation, and diminished renal clearance, all of which contribute to sustaining therapeutic concentrations for extended durations within ocular tissues. As a member of the compstatin class of complement inhibitors, Cp40‐Peg belongs to a novel class of therapeutics that have been explored for their capacity to modulate complement activation in various inflammatory and degenerative conditions, including ocular diseases. The design of Cp40‐Peg is grounded in decades of biochemical research that have progressively refined the structure–activity relationship (SAR) of compstatin peptides to achieve not only improved potency but also desirable pharmacokinetic properties for chronic indications such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
The evolution of compstatin-based therapies can be traced back to initial studies that harnessed the cyclic peptide’s ability to inhibit complement activation, a finding that spurred interest in targeting complement-mediated pathology. Early compstatin analogs were investigated in the context of systemic complement dysregulation disorders such as paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and sepsis, with subsequent research extending these findings to ocular indications where complement-mediated inflammation plays a critical role in disease progression. Multiple compstatin derivatives have undergone rigorous preclinical testing in animal models, including cynomolgus monkeys, where the peptides demonstrated significant efficacy in suppressing drusen formation and restoring retinal health by mitigating complement overactivation (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2015). More recently, compounds in this class have been repurposed for the treatment of dry AMD. For example, pegcetacoplan, a PEGylated compstatin analog distinct from Cp40‐Peg but conceptually similar, has been advanced into Phase III clinical trials and has shown promising results in reducing geographic atrophy (GA) lesion growth in dry AMD patients (Ong et al., 2024; Patel et al., 2022). Cp40‐Peg, the candidate under review, builds upon this established therapeutic framework by combining the potent and selective C3 inhibition of Cp40 with a PEGylation strategy designed to extend the intraocular residence time to greater than three months, as demonstrated in non‐human primate studies (Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). Although Cp40‐Peg is in earlier stages of development relative to some other compounds in the class, its preclinical profile—marked by sustained C3-saturating levels and restoration of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function—is highly encouraging for further advancement in dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of Cp40‐Peg is centered on its targeted inhibition of the complement cascade at the level of C3, an essential component that converges all three complement activation pathways (classical, lectin, and alternative). Cp40, a cyclic peptide with a refined amino acid sequence, binds to a critical region on the C3 molecule—specifically, the MG4/MG5 domains—thereby sterically hindering the formation of the C3 convertase enzyme complexes (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2015). This targeted binding effectively prevents the cleavage of native C3 into its active fragments including C3a, a potent anaphylatoxin, and C3b, which participates in opsonization and subsequent formation of the C5 convertase. Through this inhibition, Cp40‐Peg interrupts the propagation of the cascade that ordinarily leads to the formation of pro-inflammatory mediators and the assembly of the membrane attack complex. Importantly, the PEGylation of the Cp40 moiety does not compromise its binding affinity; rather, it stabilizes the molecule in the vitreous humor and ensures that sustained levels of the inhibitor are maintained over a prolonged period. This combination of high affinity (IC₅₀ ~ 1 nM) with extended residence time means that Cp40‐Peg is capable of providing continuous complement suppression on the RPE surface. Consequently, by averting chronic complement activation, the compound mitigates the inflammatory damage that contributes to the degeneration of photoreceptor cells and RPE dysfunction, an aspect that is further linked to impaired lysosomal and autophagic processing in dry AMD (Lamers et al., 2022; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The detailed structural interactions—illustrated by compstatin’s binding to critical loops on C3—help ensure that while complement is inhibited in a pathological context, essential immune functions that rely on regulated complement activity are preserved to some extent, highlighting the therapeutic precision achieved with this class of inhibitors (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2015; Hughes et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Dry AMD is characterized by the progressive degeneration of the macula due in part to chronic inflammation, drusen accumulation, and impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE. The hypothesis underlying the use of Cp40‐Peg in dry AMD is that sustained blockade of C3 will result in significant reductions in local complement-mediated inflammation that drive RPE dysfunction. By preventing the cleavage of C3, Cp40‐Peg is expected to reduce the production of complement activation fragments that contribute to an inflammatory microenvironment, thereby alleviating the deposition of complement components on RPE cells. This continuous inhibition of complement activity is projected to restore lysosomal and autophagic functionality within the RPE, improving the cells’ ability to process and clear POS debris—a process that is critically impaired in dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The expected pharmacodynamic effect is a decrease in the accumulation of drusen-like deposits and a concomitant improvement in the structural and functional integrity of the RPE. Preclinical studies in non-human primate models have demonstrated that prolonged intraocular exposure to Cp40-based inhibitors leads to a reduction in complement deposition and an improvement in lysosomal clearance markers, supporting the proposed mechanism by which Cp40‐Peg may exert its therapeutic benefits (Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). Moreover, the high target specificity and sustained inhibition translate into a pharmacological profile that could potentially reduce treatment frequency and improve patient compliance. Data from in vitro assays using high-risk RPE cells have shown that treatment with Cp40 analogs not only curtails complement activation but also promotes morphological and functional recovery of lysosomal compartments, thereby enhancing autophagy—a process critical for the clearance of photoreceptor debris and overall cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). This dual action of dampening inflammation and restoring RPE phagocytic function is expected to slow or even halt the progressive degenerative changes seen in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
In assessing the potential of Cp40‐Peg as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several critical strengths and potential limitations emerge. One of the major strengths of Cp40‐Peg is its potent and selective inhibition of C3 at extremely low nanomolar concentrations, which has been well established in biochemical studies. This high degree of potency ensures that even low concentrations of the inhibitor can achieve significant blockade of the complement cascade, a feature that is particularly important in the context of chronic diseases where sustained inhibition is required (Lamers et al., 2022; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Another key advantage is the PEGylation strategy that confers an extended intraocular residence time, with preclinical studies suggesting that a single intravitreal injection may maintain C3-saturating levels for more than three months. This long-acting pharmacokinetic profile is highly advantageous in reducing the treatment burden on patients and improving adherence in a chronic condition like AMD (Mastellos et al., 2015; Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

From a mechanistic perspective, Cp40‐Peg directly addresses the core pathogenic processes underlying dry AMD by targeting an essential mediator of inflammation. By inhibiting C3 activation, the drug not only blocks the generation of inflammatory anaphylatoxins and opsonins but also facilitates the restoration of critical RPE functions, including lysosomal degradation and autophagic processing vital for POS clearance. Such restoration is fundamental to re-establishing cellular homeostasis and mitigating the degenerative progression seen in dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Furthermore, the specificity of the compstatin-based approach minimizes the risk of widespread immune suppression, as it selectively targets one pivotal node in the complement cascade rather than broadly inhibiting immune function. This precision could potentially translate into a favorable safety profile, although vigilance regarding complement inhibition–related adverse effects must be maintained.

Despite these significant strengths, there are important challenges and potential weaknesses associated with Cp40‐Peg that must be considered. Long-term inhibition of the complement system, even if targeted and partial, can theoretically predispose patients to an increased risk of infections, particularly in the context of ocular immunity where defense against pathogens is crucial. Clinical trials of related agents, such as pegcetacoplan, have reported adverse events including increased incidences of neovascular complications, which underscore the need for careful safety evaluation in future studies (Ong et al., 2024; Mastellos et al., 2015). Moreover, while PEGylation offers extended residence time, it also introduces potential complications such as the development of anti-PEG antibodies. Such immunogenic responses could potentially alter the pharmacokinetics and efficacy of the drug over time, necessitating dose adjustments or alternative strategies in the long-term management of dry AMD (Mastellos et al., 2015; Park et al., 2019). Another consideration is the challenge of translating preclinical efficacy into clinical success. Although non-human primate models have provided promising data on the restoration of RPE homeostasis and prolonged complement suppression, the complexity of human AMD pathobiology demands rigorous clinical investigations to confirm these effects in patients with diverse genetic and environmental backgrounds (Lamers et al., 2022; Yu & Wykoff, 2021).

When comparing Cp40‐Peg with other therapeutic candidates within the compstatin family, its prolonged intraocular residence and potent C3 inhibition distinguish it as a particularly attractive candidate for dry AMD. However, the balance between achieving sufficient complement inhibition to confer therapeutic benefit and avoiding excessive blockade that could compromise host defense mechanisms remains a critical aspect of its clinical development. The continued progression of related agents into advanced clinical trial phases lends credence to the overall strategy, yet also highlights the necessity for comprehensive long-term safety and efficacy studies specifically tailored to the dry AMD patient population (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2022).

In summary, Cp40‐Peg exhibits a compelling combination of molecular potency, extended pharmacokinetic properties, and a mechanistically sound approach to addressing the pathological features of dry AMD—namely, chronic complement-mediated inflammation and RPE dysfunction. Its ability to sustain C3 inhibition over extended periods holds promise for improved dosing regimens and better patient adherence. Nonetheless, the risk of complement inhibition–related adverse effects, challenges associated with PEGylation such as immunogenicity, and the inherent complexities of translating preclinical findings to clinical efficacy represent important hurdles that will need to be overcome in future studies. Overall, while further detailed preclinical and early-phase clinical trials are warranted, the current evidence supports the continued development of Cp40‐Peg as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, with the potential to significantly restore RPE function and retard disease progression by re-establishing lysosomal and autophagic balance (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2015; Hughes et al., 2020; Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Ong et al., 2024).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of 2‐hydroxypropyl‐β‐cyclodextrin (HPβCD; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. C0926) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
HPβCD is a chemically modified cyclic oligosaccharide belonging to the cyclodextrin drug class, which consists of cyclic arrangements of glucopyranose units. In the case of HPβCD, hydroxypropyl groups are substituted on the β-cyclodextrin ring, thereby increasing its water solubility and overall biocompatibility while maintaining the inherent toroidal structure with a hydrophobic inner cavity and hydrophilic exterior. This unique architecture allows HPβCD to encapsulate lipophilic compounds such as cholesterol, forming stable inclusion complexes that enhance the solubilization, mobilization, or extraction of these molecules from biological membranes or intracellular compartments (Braga, 2023; Davidson et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020). Originally discovered and adapted as an excipient to improve the solubility and delivery of hydrophobic drugs, cyclodextrins have more recently gained attention as active pharmaceutical ingredients due to their capacity to modulate lipid metabolism. In particular, HPβCD is being repurposed as a therapeutic candidate because of its established ability to reduce cholesterol accumulation in tissues—an effect that is central to its potential role in addressing dry AMD pathology (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, HPβCD has been widely utilized as a pharmaceutical excipient and delivery system with a strong safety record, as evidenced by its FDA-approved use in various formulations. More notably, its cholesterol-binding and mobilizing activity has driven its repurposing for treatment of cholesterol storage disorders, most prominently Niemann–Pick Type C (NPC) disease. In NPC, HPβCD has been administered by various routes—including systemic, intrathecal, and subcutaneous injections—to solubilize and extract unesterified cholesterol from lysosomal compartments, thereby ameliorating the pathological accumulation of lipids in neuronal and peripheral tissues (Davidson et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Kfoury et al., 2025; Rao & Fliesler, 2021). Preclinical studies in NPC models have consistently demonstrated that HPβCD can normalize cholesterol trafficking and extend lifespan in affected animals. Additional biochemical and clinical studies in related fields such as atherosclerosis further underscore the compound’s potency as a cholesterol-mobilizing agent (Braga, 2023; Coisne et al., 2016; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020). Although HPβCD has not been used explicitly in clinical trials for dry AMD to date, the mechanistic rationale for its application is compelling since retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells in dry AMD exhibit lysosomal cholesterol accumulation and associated dysfunction similar to the cellular defects observed in NPC and atherosclerotic conditions (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023). Moreover, retinal studies in mouse models have shown that HPβCD can reduce cholesterol levels in the retina and restore aspects of cellular homeostasis, thereby laying the groundwork for the proposed repurposing in dry AMD (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, HPβCD functions primarily by exploiting its unique cyclic structure, which provides a hydrophobic cavity designed to accommodate cholesterol molecules. The hydrophobic interactions between the cyclodextrin cavity and the sterol ring system of cholesterol enable HPβCD to form a reversible inclusion complex with both free and esterified cholesterol. This process shifts the equilibrium of intracellular cholesterol pools and promotes a net efflux of cholesterol from cellular membranes and lysosomal compartments (El-Darzi et al., 2023; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020).

In cells burdened by cholesterol accumulation—such as RPE cells in the context of drusen formation—the excess cholesterol impairs the fluidity of membranes and disrupts the acidification and enzymatic activity within lysosomes. HPβCD is hypothesized to extract this excess cholesterol from the lysosomal membrane, thereby restoring proper membrane fluidity and normalizing the pH within the lysosome. This in turn is expected to reactivate lysosomal enzymes, such as cathepsins, and restore proper autophagic flux and phagocytic turnover of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Coisne et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

On a biochemical level, studies have shown that HPβCD can upregulate proteins related to cholesterol efflux. For instance, the compound has been observed to modulate the expression of ATP-binding cassette transporters, such as ABCA1 and ABCG1, via liver X receptor (LXR)-dependent pathways. Additionally, HPβCD treatment can alter the cellular distribution of cholesterol by promoting trafficking from the lysosome to other cellular compartments such as the endoplasmic reticulum, where it is enzymatically esterified and eventually excreted (Cougnoux et al., 2023; El-Darzi et al., 2021; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020).

Another important mechanistic aspect is the compound’s influence on lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. HPβCD has been shown to increase the abundance of lysosome-associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) and to activate the transcription factor EB (TFEB), which is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic processes. Such activation contributes to maintaining cellular clearance pathways that are essential for RPE cell health, especially in the face of chronic insult from photoreceptor outer segments and accumulated lipofuscin bisretinoids (Braga, 2023; Brown et al., 2016). Through these molecular interactions, HPβCD may counteract the cellular stress induced by disrupted cholesterol homeostasis, thereby mitigating the dual impact of both lipid accumulation and impaired lysosomal degradation that is central to dry AMD pathogenesis. However, it is noteworthy that some studies have reported that prolonged exposure to HPβCD can induce pro-inflammatory responses and even ototoxicity in animal models, underscoring the importance of optimizing dosing regimens (Houben et al., 2021a, 2021b; Yamada et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis driving the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is that by extracting the excess cholesterol accumulated in the lysosomes of RPE cells, the compound will restore normal cellular functions. The primary expected effect is multifold. First, the removal of cholesterol is anticipated to restore lysosomal pH to its optimal acidic range. An appropriate pH is crucial for the full activation of lysosomal hydrolases, such as cathepsins, which are necessary for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments that normally enter the RPE through phagocytosis (Braga, 2023; El-Darzi et al., 2023). Second, by normalizing membrane fluidity, HPβCD would improve the trafficking and fusion of lysosomes, thus enhancing the clearance of cellular waste. This improved clearance capacity may help resolve drusen-like deposits and prevent inflammatory activation of retinal microglia and macrophages—a process that has been implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Brown et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Houben et al., 2021b).

From a molecular perspective, RPE cells express key proteins involved in cholesterol handling, including NPC1, ABCA1, and LXR. The activation of these pathways after HPβCD application could lead to improved reverse cholesterol transport, where the excess cholesterol is removed from RPE cells and delivered to extracellular acceptors for clearance (Davidson et al., 2016; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020). This facilitated removal is expected to lower intracellular levels of unesterified cholesterol, reduce cholesterol crystal formation, and subsequently attenuate the pro-inflammatory milieu that contributes to RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Braga, 2023; Houben et al., 2021b).

In experimental assays, one might expect to observe a decrease in the levels of cholesterol and cholesterol crystals by biochemical analyses or imaging of RPE cells treated with HPβCD, alongside a normalization of lysosomal pH values measured via pH-sensitive dyes. Enzyme assays should reveal a restoration of cathepsin activity, and phagocytosis assays would ideally demonstrate an increased turnover of POS. Taken together, these effects would not only preserve RPE cell function but also potentially slow the progression of the disease and improve retinal structure and function (Coisne et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, HPβCD represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its well-documented ability to modulate cholesterol homeostasis and improve lysosomal function. The compound’s favorable physicochemical properties—stemming from its cyclic oligosaccharide structure and enhanced solubility due to hydroxypropylation—make it an attractive candidate for drug repurposing. The extensive preclinical evidence in lysosomal cholesterol storage disorders, including NPC disease and atherosclerosis models, provides a solid foundation that supports its potential efficacy in conditions characterized by intracellular cholesterol dysregulation, such as dry AMD (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

One of the major strengths of HPβCD is its multifaceted mechanism of action. It not only physically extracts cholesterol by forming inclusion complexes but also appears to modulate key cellular pathways that govern cholesterol efflux, lysosomal biogenesis, and autophagic clearance. This combined activity has the potential to address several pathological features of dry AMD simultaneously: restoring lysosomal pH, normalizing the activity of pH-dependent enzymes like cathepsins, and enhancing the degradation of deposited photoreceptor outer segments. Additionally, the evidence that HPβCD can reduce inflammatory activation by preventing cholesterol crystal formation and macrophage recruitment further supports its application in a disease state where chronic inflammation is a well-known driver of progression (Brown et al., 2016; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020).

However, there are also notable weaknesses and concerns that must be carefully considered. First, while HPβCD’s safety profile is well-established for its role as an excipient and, to some extent, in NPC clinical trials, significant safety issues have been reported in the context of systemic and even local administration. Ototoxicity has emerged as a recurrent concern in multiple preclinical studies and some clinical observations, which could be particularly problematic if similar toxicities are encountered when used in the delicate tissues of the eye (Braga, 2023; Calias, 2018; Yamada et al., 2021). Moreover, some studies have reported dose-dependent pro-inflammatory effects upon chronic exposure to HPβCD, underscoring the necessity for optimizing dosing regimens and careful monitoring of inflammatory markers (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Hoque et al., 2020).

Another potential challenge is the delivery route. Given that the eye is a compartment with unique barriers and an immunoprivileged status, determining the optimal method of administration (e.g., intravitreal injection, topical eye drops, or systemic administration with targeted delivery) will be critical. The compound’s ability to cross the blood-retina barrier has been demonstrated in preclinical models, but achieving sufficient retinal concentration without systemic toxicity may require advanced formulation strategies, such as encapsulation in polymer-based nanoparticles or the development of polyrotaxane-based delivery systems (Coisne et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

The overall evaluation is therefore cautiously optimistic. On the one hand, the strong mechanistic rationale for using HPβCD to address the underlying cholesterol dysregulation and lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD is supported by a robust body of literature from related fields (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020). The compound benefits from established use in other cholesterol accumulation disorders and has clearly defined biochemical activities that could be translated into therapeutic benefits in the context of AMD. On the other hand, significant challenges remain in terms of safety—especially related to ototoxicity and potential inflammatory side effects—and in the optimization of delivery methods that can achieve effective retinal concentrations without off-target toxicity (Braga, 2023; Houben et al., 2021a; Yamada et al., 2021).

Given these considerations, it is recommended that the next phases of drug development focus on detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicity studies specific to ocular tissues, along with the exploration of novel delivery formulations that may mitigate systemic and local adverse effects. Further preclinical validation using AMD-relevant models is warranted to assess functional outcomes such as restoration of lysosomal pH, increased cathepsin activity, improved phagocytic efficiency of POS, and ultimately, preservation of retinal structure and function (Coisne et al., 2016; El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).

In conclusion, while HPβCD demonstrates considerable potential as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its cholesterol-extracting capabilities and beneficial effects on lysosomal function, the balance between efficacy and safety remains a critical area for further investigation. The strengths—mechanistic depth, prior clinical use in related disorders, and robust preclinical data—are compelling; however, the weaknesses, notably regarding ototoxicity and the need for optimized delivery, must be addressed before moving to clinical trials in AMD patients (Braga, 2023; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Mahjoubin-Tehran et al., 2020; Yamada et al., 2021). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ibrutinib is a fully synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally developed as an irreversible inhibitor of Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK). It achieves inhibition by covalently binding to the conserved Cys481 residue located within the ATP‐binding pocket of BTK, a key member of the TEC family of kinases. This irreversible binding results in permanent inactivation of BTK, thereby interrupting B‐cell receptor signaling as well as other downstream pathways that are critical for cell survival and proliferation (Xie et al., 2021). As a member of the broader class of tyrosine kinase inhibitors, ibrutinib is designed through refined organic synthesis strategies that optimize its selectivity and potency. Compounds of this chemical class have been extensively utilized in oncology, particularly for the treatment of B‐cell malignancies, where they serve to disrupt aberrant oncogenic signaling pathways. Ibrutinib is available commercially (e.g., SelleckChem Cat. No. S2680) and has been subject to rigorous clinical evaluation, ensuring that its chemical properties, including its irreversible binding mechanism and cell penetration capabilities, are well established in the literature (Xie et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, ibrutinib was developed and advanced clinically for hematologic cancers such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia (WM), and other B‐cell malignancies. Its success in these domains is attributed to its effective inhibition of BTK, a kinase that is critical for B‐cell receptor signaling and survival (Xie et al., 2021). Once approved by the U.S. FDA in 2013, it rapidly became a standard of care in oncology. Outside of its oncologic use, ibrutinib has been recognized for its immunomodulatory effects that extend to innate immune cells such as macrophages, dendritic cells, and, notably, microglia. Although the primary application of ibrutinib is in cancer therapy, there is emerging evidence and growing scientific interest suggesting that BTK plays a role in innate immune signaling pathways that contribute to chronic inflammatory states, including those implicated in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Brandli et al., 2024). In pharmacovigilance studies, ocular adverse events—including uveitis, cataracts, and retinal disorders—have been identified among patients treated with ibrutinib, which indicates that the molecule penetrates ocular compartments and exerts biological effects there (Allouchery et al., 2021). However, despite these observations, ibrutinib has not been previously developed or marketed for the treatment of dry AMD or similar degenerative retinal diseases. Instead, its potential repurposing arises from the hypothesis that by modulating BTK-dependent inflammatory pathways in microglia and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, ibrutinib might reduce deleterious inflammasome priming and cytokine production that contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ibrutinib exerts its primary action by binding irreversibly to BTK, thereby preventing autophosphorylation and subsequent transmission of intracellular signals that lead to inflammation and cell survival. BTK is not only a critical mediator of B‐cell receptor signaling but is also expressed in cells of the innate immune system including microglia and RPE cells. Its activation is linked to the regulation of the NLRP3 inflammasome—a multiprotein complex that senses cellular stress, leading to the activation of caspase-1 and the maturation and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Brandli et al., 2024). There is accumulating evidence that BTK facilitates the priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome in response to various stimuli, including oxidative stress and the accumulation of deleterious protein aggregates, both of which are implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis. Experimental data suggest that inhibition of BTK by ibrutinib can lead to a reduction in IL-1β release, which in turn may lower downstream pro-inflammatory signals such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) (Far et al., 2022; Allouchery et al., 2021). Moreover, the preservation of lysosomal cathepsin activity observed in ARPE-19 cells under inflammasome-stimulating conditions implies that BTK inhibition may also support the maintenance of RPE lysosomal integrity and phagocytic function. Such actions are critical for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and prevention of drusen accumulation—a hallmark of dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). In summary, by covalently binding to BTK, ibrutinib not only halts aberrant immune cell signaling but also indirectly modulates inflammasome activity and associated inflammatory cytokine release in retinal cells (Xie et al., 2021; Brandli et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for the repurposing of ibrutinib in dry AMD revolves around its ability to inhibit BTK activity within microglia and RPE cells, thereby suppressing inflammasome priming and limiting the production of inflammatory mediators such as IL-1β and TNFα. In the context of an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells, it is anticipated that the application of ibrutinib (IC₅₀ ~0.5 nM) will result in a marked attenuation of inflammasome activation, as evidenced by reduced secretion of IL-1β and preserved lysosomal cathepsin activity (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). The proposed mechanism by which ibrutinib exerts its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD is multifaceted. First, by inhibiting BTK, the compound is expected to downregulate the overactive NLRP3 inflammasome that plays a central role in the inflammatory cascade within the retinal pigment epithelium (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024). Second, by reducing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines—especially TNFα—which have been shown to negatively impact the phagocytic ability of RPE cells, ibrutinib may help to maintain the clearance of photoreceptor outer segment debris. This is particularly important because impaired clearance mechanisms contribute to the accumulation of drusen and subsequent RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024). Moreover, animal and clinical pharmacovigilance studies have provided evidence that ibrutinib is capable of crossing the blood-brain and blood-retinal barriers, suggesting that it can reach retinal tissues at therapeutically relevant concentrations. Although there is documented evidence of ocular adverse events in patients treated with ibrutinib for hematologic malignancies—including instances of uveitis and cystoid macular edema—such effects have been largely reported as unintended consequences rather than engineered therapeutic outcomes. In the current repurposing framework, the premise is that controlled intravitreal or local administration, possibly as a modified formulation, could harness the anti-inflammatory properties of ibrutinib while minimizing systemic exposure and the risk of ocular adverse events (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022). Ultimately, the expected effect is a preserved RPE function with enhanced ability to clear POS debris, thereby mitigating the degenerative progression typically observed in dry AMD (Korhonen, 2024; Brandli et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
Ibrutinib presents as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to its well-characterized molecular mechanism and its established clinical profile in oncology. One of the major strengths of ibrutinib lies in its potent and selective irreversible inhibition of BTK, a kinase implicated not only in B-cell malignancies but also in the pathogenesis of inflammatory retinal diseases through its role in NLRP3 inflammasome priming (Xie et al., 2021). The scientific rationale for its repurposing is supported by preclinical observations indicating that BTK inhibition leads to reduced IL-1β secretion and preservation of lysosomal function in RPE cells, which are essential for maintaining photoreceptor homeostasis and preventing drusen accumulation in dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). Furthermore, the demonstration that ibrutinib crosses the blood-retinal barrier underscores its potential utility in directly targeting retinal tissues, especially when administered via routes that ensure localized high concentrations with limited systemic exposure (Xie et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022).

However, there are several challenges and weaknesses associated with this therapeutic candidate. First, the ocular safety profile of ibrutinib is a matter of concern, as pharmacovigilance data have linked ibrutinib to a spectrum of adverse ocular events including cataracts, uveitis, and retinal disorders (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022). While these effects have so far been observed in the context of systemic cancer therapy, they raise important safety questions when considering chronic administration for a disease such as dry AMD that often requires long-term treatment. Second, the dosages and formulation required to achieve an anti-inflammatory effect in the retina, while concurrently minimizing cytotoxicity and other off-target effects, remain uncertain. Ibrutinib’s off-target inhibitory effects, such as its activity against VEGFR2, may impart vascular side effects that could further complicate its use in the delicate retinal environment (Allouchery et al., 2021). Third, the repurposing strategy relies heavily on the extrapolation of cellular and animal model data—such as the observed reduction of inflammasome activation and preservation of cathepsin activity in ARPE-19 cells—to the complex pathophysiology of human dry AMD. The heterogeneity of dry AMD pathogenesis, driven by a confluence of genetic, environmental, and age-related factors, means that successful translation from preclinical models to effective clinical outcomes is not guaranteed (Korhonen, 2024; Brandli et al., 2024). Additionally, while there is a robust theoretical framework underpinning BTK’s involvement in inflamed retinal microenvironments, direct evidence of ibrutinib’s efficacy in modulating microglial or RPE function specifically in the setting of dry AMD remains limited.

Despite these challenges, the mechanistic rationale for using a BTK inhibitor in dry AMD is compelling. The interplay between NLRP3 inflammasome activation, chronic low-grade inflammation, and RPE dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a pivotal driver of dry AMD progression (Brandli et al., 2024). If ibrutinib can effectively attenuate these inflammatory processes without incurring prohibitive adverse events, it may offer a novel therapeutic avenue for a disease area currently lacking effective treatment options. However, this necessitates a series of rigorous preclinical studies to characterize the dose-response relationship, evaluate retinal safety, and define the pharmacokinetic profile of ibrutinib when delivered via ocular routes. Moreover, any proposed clinical trial must incorporate comprehensive ophthalmologic monitoring given the known spectrum of ibrutinib-induced ocular side effects (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022).

In summary, while ibrutinib is primarily an approved oncologic agent, its underlying mechanism of inhibiting BTK—the kinase that modulates inflammasome priming in microglia and RPE cells—provides a strong scientific basis for its repurposing in dry AMD. The expected effects of reduced IL-1β and TNFα production, coupled with preserved lysosomal cathepsin activity and improved phagocytic function, align well with the therapeutic goals of mitigating chronic inflammation and preserving retinal integrity in dry AMD. Nevertheless, the potential ocular adverse effects and the challenges related to achieving a favorable therapeutic index in the retinal environment are significant concerns that must be addressed through further rigorous preclinical and clinical evaluations (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). Overall, ibrutinib represents an intriguing candidate with a solid mechanistic rationale for dry AMD treatment; however, careful attention to formulation, dosing, and safety testing is warranted before advancing this repurposing strategy to later-stage clinical trials (Xie et al., 2021; Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mini‐FH is a rationally engineered, recombinant protein therapeutic derived from human complement factor H (FH) by selectively fusing its N-terminal complement control protein (CCP) modules 1–4 with its C-terminal CCP modules 19–20 (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). This minimal construct is synthesized through recombinant DNA methodologies that allow for expression in suitable heterologous systems such as yeast, insect cells, or mammalian cell lines; its design takes full advantage of recent advances in protein engineering guided by high‐resolution structural data (Dobo et al., 2018; Makou et al., 2013). Belonging to the class of engineered biologics—or “modular complement regulators”—Mini‐FH represents a more manufacturable, compact alternative to full‐length FH (≈155 kDa), reducing the molecular weight to roughly 40–45 kDa, which is expected to facilitate improved tissue and cellular penetration (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). This therapeutic candidate is designed to recapitulate the dual functionality of native FH: the CCP1–4 region provides regulatory activity through decay‐accelerating and cofactor functions against the alternative pathway (AP) C3 convertase, while the CCP19–20 region confers selective binding to surface‐associated ligands, including C3b/C3d and glycosaminoglycans, thereby anchoring the inhibitor to host membranes (Merle et al., 2015; Biggs et al., 2022). In essence, Mini‐FH is synthesized as a fusion protein that retains critical complement regulatory activities in a smaller, more agile molecule; this design underscores a broader trend in drug development toward developing “miniaturized,” high‐potency biologics that can overcome limitations of full‐length proteins in terms of tissue distribution and immunogenicity (Dobo et al., 2018; Makou et al., 2013).

Therapeutic History:  
The use of complement regulators as therapeutic agents has a long history in clinical research, particularly for diseases driven by dysregulation of the AP of complement. Engineered FH fragments like Mini‐FH have been the subject of extensive biochemical and preclinical evaluation, with studies demonstrating that constructs consisting of CCP1–4/19–20 exhibit enhanced binding to C3 fragments and improved decay‐accelerating activity compared to native FH on a per‐molecule basis (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). Preclinical in vitro assays, such as surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and hemolytic assays, have confirmed that Mini‐FH binds C3b with high affinity and competitively inhibits AP convertase formation by both displacing factor B and accelerating convertase decay (Dobo et al., 2018; Biggs et al., 2022). Moreover, animal studies, including those involving FH‐deficient mice, have provided compelling evidence for the in vivo activity of such engineered constructs, wherein administration of Mini‐FH or homodimeric variants (e.g., HDM-FH) reduced complement deposition and ameliorated tissue pathology in models of complement‐mediated kidney disease (de Boer et al., 2020; Kamala et al., 2021). Although direct clinical trials of Mini‐FH specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) have not yet been reported, related compounds such as full‐length recombinant FH (GEM103) have entered phase-2 clinical testing for AMD, thereby validating the concept of using FH‐based molecules to restore complement homeostasis in ocular diseases (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Additionally, engineered versions of FH, including dimerized variants designed to enhance serum half-life and tissue binding, have shown promising preclinical efficacy in non-ocular models such as paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and C3 glomerulopathy, further suggesting that the underlying mechanism is broadly applicable to complement‐mediated disorders (de Boer et al., 2020; Biggs et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of Mini‐FH relies on its ability to simultaneously exploit the dual functionalities of FH through its modular design. The N-terminal CCP1–4 domain comprises the core regulatory region that mediates AP control by binding directly to C3b. This interaction competitively prevents the binding of factor B (FB), thereby inhibiting the formation of the pro-convertase C3bB complex and effectively blocking the assembly of the C3 convertase (C3bBb) (Merle et al., 2015; Kamala et al., 2021). In addition, CCP1–4 exerts decay-accelerating activity by accelerating the dissociation of Bb from the C3bBb complex; it also provides a binding platform for factor I (FI), thereby functioning as a cofactor that promotes the proteolytic cleavage of C3b to inactive iC3b (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). Complementing this, the C-terminal CCP19–20 domains of Mini‐FH are involved in high-affinity ligand recognition. These domains bind to the thioester-containing domain (TED) of C3b as well as to C3d fragments, which are present at sites of previous complement activation, and they interact with glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) and sialic acid residues on host cell surfaces (Merle et al., 2015; Biggs et al., 2022). This binding not only increases the overall avidity of the interaction by engaging multiple sites on a single C3b molecule but also serves to target the regulatory activity specifically to host surfaces that are decorated with complement activation products—a critical factor in distinguishing self from non-self (Dobo et al., 2018; Makou et al., 2013). Furthermore, by engaging in a dual binding mode, Mini‐FH effectively “bridges” the regulatory and recognition functions that in full-length FH are partially masked by the intervening CCP modules, thus resulting in a higher potency per molecule (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Structural studies, including crystallographic analysis of complexes such as C3b:Mini-FH:FI, substantiate that Mini-FH engages two spatially distinct sites on C3b and even recruits FI through additional contacts involving CCP2–3, which further enhances its complement inhibitory function (Biggs et al., 2022). The overall consequence of these molecular interactions is the efficient disruption of the AP amplification loop, thereby reducing the cascade of complement activation products and ultimately limiting tissue damage driven by uncontrolled complement activity (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the hypothesis posits that Mini-FH will competitively bind to C3b deposited on the surfaces of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and within Bruch’s membrane, specifically restoring local complement regulation by the alternative pathway (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). The expected mechanism is that, upon intravitreal administration, Mini-FH will localize to the subretinal space where excessive complement activation is known to occur as a result of FH deficiency or dysfunction associated with the Y402H polymorphism. Once there, the CCP1–4 segment of Mini-FH is anticipated to exert decay-accelerating and cofactor activities that promote the inactivation of C3b—inhibiting the formation and persistence of the C3 convertase (C3bBb) and thereby interrupting the amplification of the cascade (de Boer et al., 2020; Dobo et al., 2018). This biochemical activity is expected to result in a reduction of downstream complement components such as C5b–9 (the membrane attack complex) and inflammatory mediators like C3a and C5a, which are implicated in the chronic inflammation observed in dry AMD (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

From a cellular perspective, by limiting complement activation on RPE surfaces, Mini-FH is expected to reduce the formation and accumulation of drusen-like deposits—extracellular aggregates that have been associated with inappropriate complement activity and are a hallmark of AMD pathology (Dobo et al., 2018; Makou et al., 2013). In addition, the engagement of CCP19–20 with surface-bound C3b/C3d and GAGs should enhance the targeted accumulation of Mini-FH on the RPE and in Bruch’s membrane, areas that are known hotspots for complement dysregulation in AMD (Merle et al., 2015; Biggs et al., 2022). This targeted binding not only localizes the regulatory function where it is most needed but may also facilitate secondary beneficial effects; for example, by mitigating complement-mediated cytotoxicity, Mini-FH may indirectly improve the phagocytic function of the RPE. Efficient post-phagocytosis is critical for the daily clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and disruption of this process is a contributing factor in the progression of AMD (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Preclinical experiments in RPE explant models or murine AMD models that have been exposed to Mini-FH are thus expected to demonstrate a decrease in C3 deposition and complement activation markers, accompanied by restoration of normal RPE phagocytic capacity (de Boer et al., 2020; Dobo et al., 2018). Moreover, due to its relatively small size when compared to full-length FH, Mini-FH is predicted to have superior tissue penetration, which is essential for reaching the deeper layers of Bruch’s membrane and the subretinal space, where the pathological complement activation predominantly occurs (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating the potential of Mini-FH (Recombinant FH CCP1–4/19–20) as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key strengths and challenges emerge. One of the primary strengths of Mini-FH is its rational design based on a deep understanding of FH architecture and function. By incorporating the most critical regulatory and recognition domains into a single, compact molecule, Mini-FH offers enhanced potency on a per-molecule basis and efficient competitive binding to C3b. The enhanced decay-accelerating activity and ability to serve as a cofactor for FI-mediated C3b inactivation have been well documented in preclinical assays, including SPR and hemolysis studies (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). These features are especially promising given that dysregulated complement activation is a central element of AMD pathogenesis. Furthermore, Mini-FH’s smaller size relative to full-length FH suggests improved penetration into ocular tissues such as Bruch’s membrane and the subretinal space, where therapeutic intervention is most needed (Dobo et al., 2018; de Boer et al., 2020).

Another significant strength is the translational rationale supported by biochemical and preclinical animal studies. Engineered FH fragments, including Mini-FH variants, have demonstrated efficacy in reducing complement activity in murine models of complement dysregulation, such as C3 glomerulopathy and PNH, which supports the concept that restoring control over the AP can ameliorate tissue damage (Kamala et al., 2021; Biggs et al., 2022). The fact that full-length recombinant FH (GEM103) is already being evaluated clinically for AMD further bolsters the therapeutic validity of targeting the complement cascade in ocular diseases (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Moreover, the diverse strategies employed in the development of similar biologics (e.g., dimerized forms of Mini-FH or fusion constructs with additional targeting domains) point to an active area of research and innovation that is likely to yield clinically effective solutions (Makou et al., 2013; Dobo et al., 2018).

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges warrant careful consideration. Although Mini-FH has demonstrated robust in vitro complement regulatory activity, its reduced size relative to the full-length molecule may also come with a trade-off, such as a potential reduction in FI cofactor activity under certain conditions (de Boer et al., 2020; Kamala et al., 2021). This diminished cofactor activity might necessitate higher dosing to achieve complete complement inhibition, which in turn could impact the safety profile and overall therapeutic index in the delicate ocular environment. Immunogenicity remains another concern; engineered proteins can sometimes elicit anti-drug antibodies (ADAs), and although intravitreal delivery benefits from the eye’s relative immune privilege, long-term administration in a chronic disease like AMD may eventually overcome this barrier (Kamala et al., 2021; Biggs et al., 2022). In addition, while animal model data in non-ocular systems are promising, the unique anatomy and microenvironment of the retina—especially the dynamics of RPE function, Bruch’s membrane characteristics, and POS phagocytosis—present additional layers of complexity that have not yet been fully addressed by preclinical studies specific to this application (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

There is also the challenge of ensuring consistent manufacturing and high-yield recombinant production of a complex, multi-domain protein like Mini-FH. Although advances in recombinant expression systems have made it feasible to produce such proteins at scale, the retention of full activity, appropriate post-translational modifications, and proper folding is critical for therapeutic efficacy and must be established within a robust quality control framework (Makou et al., 2013). Furthermore, the pharmacokinetic profile of Mini-FH, including its half-life on ocular tissues and systemic clearance if any, requires detailed investigation; alterations in inter-domain linker length or structural flexibility could impact tissue distribution and drug retention at the target site (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

From a mechanistic standpoint, while Mini-FH is designed to restore regulation by competitively binding to C3b and facilitating its inactivation, the downstream consequences of complement repression in the retina are multifaceted. In dry AMD, chronic complement dysregulation not only drives inflammation but also contributes to impaired phagocytosis of POS by the RPE. Although preclinical evidence suggests that restoring complementary control can indirectly improve RPE function (Kamala et al., 2021), the exact molecular pathways linking complement inhibition to improved POS clearance have not been fully elucidated, necessitating further mechanistic studies in retinal model systems (Dobo et al., 2018).

In summary, Mini‐FH represents a highly promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its engineered dual functionality—providing both potent AP convertase regulatory activity and targeted binding to complement‐deposited surfaces—as well as its potential for superior tissue penetration given its compact molecular size (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). Its mechanism of action is well supported by structural, biochemical, and preclinical data, and the conceptual framework is further validated by ongoing clinical evaluations of full‐length recombinant FH in AMD. However, while the biochemical rationale and preclinical models lend strong support to the therapeutic strategy, challenges remain in translating these findings to the complex ocular environment; these include ensuring sufficient FI cofactor activity, managing potential immunogenicity, optimizing intravitreal delivery parameters, and confirming that the beneficial effects observed in kidney or systemic models are recapitulated in retinal tissues (de Boer et al., 2020; Dobo et al., 2018).

However, several critical issues must be addressed before advancing Mini‐FH as a clinical candidate for dry AMD. First, direct evidence from retinal model systems is required to confirm that the biochemical potency of Mini‐FH translates into meaningful therapeutic outcomes in the context of RPE integrity, Bruch’s membrane function, and POS phagocytosis (de Boer et al., 2020; Dobo et al., 2018). Second, while the immune privileged status of the eye may mitigate ADA risk, long-term intravitreal delivery studies need to be conducted to establish both safety and sustained efficacy over the chronic course of AMD (Kamala et al., 2021; Biggs et al., 2022). Third, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles in the ocular milieu must be rigorously characterized to determine the optimal dosing regimen, ensuring that Mini‐FH reaches and remains active at the target site without eliciting off-target effects (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Finally, manufacturing consistency and scalability remain practical challenges for any complex recombinant protein therapeutic, and these aspects must be optimized early in the development process to facilitate clinical translation (Makou et al., 2013).

In conclusion, Mini‐FH (Recombinant FH CCP1–4/19–20) is a state-of-the-art, mechanistically driven therapeutic candidate that harnesses the targeted complement inhibitory potential of engineered FH fragments for the treatment of dry AMD. Its design leverages the strengths of both the N-terminal regulatory and C-terminal recognition domains, offering a potent means to counteract the dysregulated complement activation underlying AMD pathology. While the preclinical data from non-ocular models are very promising, targeted studies in retinal systems are necessary to confirm its efficacy and safety in the context of dry AMD. Based on the comprehensive literature review, Mini‐FH represents a compelling candidate with strong scientific rationale and significant translational potential, but further preclinical work specifically focused on retinal endpoints is essential before progressing to clinical trials. The balance between enhanced C3b binding and potential trade-offs in FI cofactor activity, along with considerations of immunogenicity and optimal delivery strategies, will be critical determinants of its ultimate clinical success in alleviating the burden of dry AMD (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018; de Boer et al., 2020; Biggs et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Brexpiprazole is a synthetic, orally available fifth‐generation antipsychotic developed by Otsuka Pharmaceutical that belongs to the class of serotonin–dopamine activity modulators (SDAMs). It was discovered and developed as an improvement over earlier dopamine partial agonists in order to achieve balanced modulation of neurotransmission. Chemically, brexpiprazole was designed as a dihydrocarbostyril derivative that retains partial agonistic properties at dopamine D₂ receptors while simultaneously exhibiting potent partial agonism at serotonin 5-HT₁A receptors and antagonism at serotonin 5-HT₂A receptors (Das et al., 2016). This balanced receptor profile has been exploited primarily for psychiatric indications, but the receptor distribution of serotonin receptors is not limited to neuronal tissues. In particular, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) expresses several serotonin receptor subtypes, and there is compelling biochemical evidence that serotonergic signaling influences inflammatory gene expression and cellular homeostasis in these cells (Biswal et al., 2015). As such, brexpiprazole’s well‐defined receptor interactions position it as a promising candidate to modulate pathological pathways in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
Brexpiprazole has an established history for its use in central nervous system disorders. It has been approved for the treatment of schizophrenia and as an adjunct therapy in major depressive disorder owing to its favorable safety and tolerability profiles, which include a low risk of extrapyramidal side effects and modest metabolic liabilities (Das et al., 2016; Fabre et al., 2022). To date, however, no clinical trials or preclinical studies have directly examined brexpiprazole for the treatment of retinal degenerative conditions such as dry AMD. Nevertheless, multiple studies have investigated the therapeutic potential of 5-HT₁A receptor agonists in retinal models. For example, research utilizing 8-OH-DPAT—a prototypical 5-HT₁A agonist—demonstrated significant antioxidant protection in RPE cells, reduction in oxidative stress markers, and preservation of retinal architecture under conditions of mitochondrial oxidative stress (Biswal et al., 2015). Other compounds with selective 5-HT₁A agonist properties, such as tandospirone, have been evaluated in retinal models, albeit with mixed clinical outcomes (Buschini et al., 2015). This preclinical precedence establishes an indirect rationale for repurposing brexpiprazole in dry AMD even if direct ocular applications have not been previously explored.

Mechanism of Action:  
Brexpiprazole exerts its pharmacological effects primarily through dual modulation of serotonergic receptors. Its partial agonism at 5-HT₁A receptors, with reported potency in the low nanomolar range (EC₅₀ ~ 5 nM as hypothesized), is thought to trigger intracellular cascades that promote cellular survival and antioxidant defenses. Activation of the 5-HT₁A receptor in other tissues has been associated with upregulation of key antioxidant enzymes—including metallothionein-1 (MT-1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NADPH quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NqO1), catalase, and superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1)—thereby mitigating oxidative stress and reducing mitochondrial damage (Biswal et al., 2015). In RPE cells—the cell type critical for photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance—the 5-HT₁A receptor is endogenously expressed, and its activation has been linked to attenuation of inflammatory signaling. Preclinical studies using other 5-HT₁A agonists in ARPE-19 cells have shown reductions in oxidative stress markers and inflammatory mediators, as well as preservation of tight junction proteins (Biswal et al., 2015).

Simultaneously, brexpiprazole’s antagonism at 5-HT₂A receptors may complement these effects by further modulating inflammatory responses. Blockade of 5-HT₂A receptors has been associated with reduced microglial activation and decreased complement deposition in the outer retina, contributing to neuroprotection in models of retinal degeneration (Biswal et al., 2015; Das et al., 2016). This dual receptor effect is proposed to result in an overall anti-inflammatory microenvironment in the RPE, which is crucial because chronic inflammation is a key pathological feature in dry AMD. Moreover, the compound’s modulation of serotonergic signaling may indirectly support the maintenance of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, which are essential for the normal clearance of POS (Biswal et al., 2015). Although direct studies with brexpiprazole in RPE cells are lacking, these mechanistic insights derived from similar 5-HT₁A agonists underpin the hypothesis that brexpiprazole could reduce production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6 and TNF-α) and restore normal phagocytic and lysosomal function (Biswal et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
In an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells or isolated RPE cells under conditions of complement-induced stress, brexpiprazole is expected to act by modulating serotonergic receptor signaling to yield a multi-faceted protective effect. Specifically, its 5-HT₁A agonism should trigger intracellular survival pathways that result in the upregulation of antioxidant defenses analogous to the responses observed with 8-OH-DPAT in similar models (Biswal et al., 2015). This effect is anticipated to lead to a reduction in oxidative stress markers, such as 8-OH-deoxyguanosine or nitrotyrosine adducts, which are typically elevated in conditions of mitochondrial oxidative injury (Biswal et al., 2015).

Additionally, brexpiprazole is hypothesized to reduce the expression of key pro-inflammatory cytokines—specifically IL-6 and TNF-α—through receptor-mediated modulation of inflammatory signaling cascades. In a cell culture model where RPE cells are exposed to oxidative and complement-mediated insults, a drop in these cytokine levels would be indicative of an amelioration of stress-induced inflammatory responses (Biswal et al., 2015; Wright & Ambati, 2016). This anti-inflammatory effect is critical because uncontrolled inflammation not only perpetuates oxidative damage but also disrupts the barrier and phagocytic functions of the RPE.

Furthermore, the candidate is expected to preserve or restore the expression of MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase crucial for the phagocytosis of POS, as well as cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease necessary for the degradation of internalized material (Biswal et al., 2015; Fischer, 2016). Successful maintenance of these proteins would directly support the clearance functions of RPE cells, an essential element for retinal homeostasis that is compromised in dry AMD. This improved phagocytic capacity, coupled with reduced cytokine production, would likely result in overall preservation of RPE structure and function, as reflected in enhanced visual function in preclinical models (Biswal et al., 2015).

Moreover, although the clinical studies of other serotonergic compounds such as tandospirone have yielded mixed results—with at least one phase III trial for geographic atrophy being discontinued due to lack of efficacy (Buschini et al., 2015)—the favorable pharmacokinetic properties and established safety profile of brexpiprazole in other indications provide a strong rationale for its repurposing, particularly if its ocular penetration can be demonstrated in relevant preclinical models (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation:  
Brexpiprazole offers several attractive strengths as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its dual mechanism—partial agonism at 5-HT₁A receptors paired with antagonism at 5-HT₂A receptors—is well aligned with the emerging understanding of how serotonergic signaling influences retinal cell survival, oxidative stress, and inflammation (Biswal et al., 2015). The wealth of preclinical evidence supporting the role of 5-HT₁A receptor activation in reducing oxidative damage and preserving RPE function under stress conditions provides a sound mechanistic basis for expecting similar protective effects from brexpiprazole. In addition, the targeting of phagocytic receptor expression (i.e., MERTK) and lysosomal enzymes (i.e., cathepsin D) represents a novel strategy to address one of the fundamental dysfunctions in dry AMD: impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (Biswal et al., 2015).

Brexpiprazole’s established safety profile and pharmacokinetics in psychiatric populations further underscore its potential for repurposing. Its high oral bioavailability and documented tolerability in long-term studies, along with evidence that similar compounds can penetrate ocular tissues when administered systemically, add to the candidate’s appeal (Das et al., 2016; Fabre et al., 2022). This is particularly relevant given the chronic nature of dry AMD and the need for therapies that can be safely administered over extended periods.

However, several significant weaknesses and gaps warrant cautious consideration. First, direct evidence linking brexpiprazole to improved RPE function—specifically, its effects on inflammatory signaling markers IL-6 and TNF-α, and on the preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression—remains theoretical and extrapolated from studies using other 5-HT₁A agonists like 8-OH-DPAT (Biswal et al., 2015). This means that while the underlying mechanistic hypothesis is plausible, there is a pressing need for targeted in vitro and in vivo studies focused on brexpiprazole in ocular models. In particular, experiments using ARPE-19 cells under conditions of oxidative or complement-induced stress must be conducted to confirm that brexpiprazole can indeed modulate cytokine levels and restore phagocytic function in these cells.

Another shortcoming is the uncertainty regarding ocular penetration. Although the systemic administration of 5-HT₁A agonists in animal models has led to beneficial retinal outcomes (Biswal et al., 2015), brexpiprazole’s distribution into ocular tissues has not been directly evaluated. It is essential to ascertain the extent to which brexpiprazole reaches the RPE at therapeutically relevant concentrations, particularly given that dosage regimens for psychiatric conditions may not be directly translatable to ocular therapy (Biswal et al., 2015).

Furthermore, while the anti-inflammatory hypothesis is supported by the general role of serotonergic signaling in RPE cells, the direct measurement of inflammatory cytokines and downstream phagocytic markers in response to brexpiprazole treatment remains to be demonstrated. Given that earlier clinical attempts using tandospirone for AMD were unsuccessful (Buschini et al., 2015), there is a need to critically assess whether brexpiprazole’s receptor profile confers advantages that overcome the limitations observed with other 5-HT₁A agonists. Additionally, potential off-target effects in the ocular environment—such as those arising from modulation of other receptor systems—must be thoroughly evaluated.

In summary, brexpiprazole presents a scientifically sound and innovative approach to the treatment of dry AMD by virtue of its serotonergic receptor modulation. Its dual action on 5-HT₁A and 5-HT₂A receptors is supported by a robust body of preclinical evidence indicating that 5-HT₁A receptor activation can reduce oxidative stress and inflammation in RPE cells, while also preserving essential functions like POS clearance (Biswal et al., 2015). The candidate’s excellent safety profile in psychiatric applications and potential for systemic administration further enhance its appeal. Nevertheless, the absence of direct experimental data linking brexpiprazole to improved phagocytosis, reduced IL-6 and TNF-α production, and maintained lysosomal enzyme expression in RPE cells represents a critical gap that must be addressed. As such, while the repurposing of brexpiprazole for dry AMD holds promise, a series of preclinical experiments—encompassing in vitro ARPE-19 cell assays, in vivo ocular pharmacokinetic studies, and efficacy models of retinal degeneration—are required before progressing to clinical trials. Overall, given the mechanistic rationale and the encouraging safety and pharmacological characteristics of brexpiprazole, further research is justified to validate its application in dry AMD, provided that the aforementioned knowledge gaps are systematically addressed (Das et al., 2016; Biswal et al., 2015).
