Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The candidate under review is an AAV2-hTLR4 decoy gene therapy vector engineered to express a soluble form of the Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) decoy peptide. This gene therapy approach is synthetically designed by leveraging the adeno-associated virus serotype 2 (AAV2) as a delivery vector to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). The decoy peptide is derived from the extracellular domain of TLR4 and is modified to be secreted into the subretinal space. Its design intends to bind and sequester danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that would normally interact with endogenous TLR4 receptors on RPE cells. In doing so, the decoy receptor limits the activation of proinflammatory cascades that are implicated in the pathogenesis of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). The therapeutic falls within the class of gene therapy compounds designed to modulate innate inflammatory signaling. Gene therapy for ocular diseases has a history of success given the immune-privileged nature of the eye and the precise targeting achievable using AAV2 vectors, as evidenced by previously approved treatments for inherited retinal dystrophies. This candidate leverages a similar platform but repurposes it to attenuate chronic sterile inflammation by acting as a molecular sink for DAMPs, thus aiming to preserve RPE homeostasis and its critical phagocytic functions (Klettner & Roider, 2021; Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, modulation of TLR signaling has been extensively studied in the context of inflammatory and degenerative diseases. Multiple preclinical studies have emphasized the role of TLR4 in mediating retinal inflammation and degeneration in AMD. Experimental evidence has demonstrated that activation of TLR4 in RPE cells leads to the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-1β, and that the chronic engagement of TLR4 by DAMPs present in drusen contributes to RPE dysfunction and photoreceptor loss (Klettner & Roider, 2021; Titi-Lartey, Mohammed, & Amoaku, 2022). Moreover, genetic association studies have identified specific TLR4 variants as risk factors for AMD, thereby underpinning its significance as a therapeutic target (Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024). Although direct clinical evidence using a TLR4 decoy has not yet been reported specifically for dry AMD, analogous strategies using decoy receptors have been applied in other inflammatory contexts to attenuate signaling by competitively inhibiting ligand-receptor interactions. Additionally, the use of AAV2 as a gene delivery vehicle has been validated by successful clinical trials in ocular gene therapy, including previous applications such as AAV2-mediated delivery of RPE65 for Leber congenital amaurosis and AAV2-VMD2-hMERTK for MERTK-associated retinitis pigmentosa; these precedents illustrate both safety and efficacy in targeting retinal cells (Inana et al., 2018; Ramlogan-Steel et al., 2019). Thus, while the AAV2-hTLR4 decoy candidate is novel with respect to its direct application for dry AMD, it builds on a substantial body of preclinical evidence implicating TLR4 in AMD as well as on the proven track record of AAV2-based ocular gene therapies.

Mechanism of Action:  
The fundamental mechanism of the AAV2-hTLR4 decoy therapy entails the intracellular delivery of a transgene encoding a soluble form of TLR4 that is secreted by transduced RPE cells. Under normal pathological conditions, various DAMPs—including but not limited to 7-ketocholesterol, oxidized lipids, amyloid-β peptides, and HMGB1—accumulate in the subretinal space as a result of chronic cellular stress and drusen formation, triggering TLR4-mediated inflammatory responses (Klettner & Roider, 2021; Titi-Lartey, Mohammed, & Amoaku, 2022). Endogenous TLR4 on RPE cells, upon binding these DAMPs, initiates downstream signaling cascades via both the MyD88-dependent and TRIF-dependent pathways. This leads to activation of transcription factors such as NF-κB and IRF3, which in turn stimulate the production of proinflammatory cytokines including TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-8, all of which have been implicated in the inflammatory milieu of AMD (Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018; Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024).  

By expressing a soluble decoy form of TLR4, the candidate therapy competitively binds the available DAMPs in the subretinal space before they engage the membrane-bound receptors on RPE cells. This sequestration of DAMP ligands reduces the activation of the endogenous TLR4 signaling cascade. Notably, several experimental studies have suggested that chronic TLR4 activation in the RPE is associated not only with increased inflammatory cytokine production, but also with the downregulation of essential receptors involved in phagocytosis, namely MERTK and αvβ5 integrin. These receptors are crucial for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) from the RPE, and their reduced expression contributes to impaired phagocytosis and further retinal degeneration (Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024). Therefore, the decoy is expected to provide a dual benefit: it dampens pathological inflammation mediated by cytokine overproduction and helps maintain the levels of phagocytic receptors essential for RPE function.  

At the molecular level, the decoy receptor binds DAMPs through its extracellular ligand-binding domains, effectively neutralizing these molecules by preventing them from binding to the transmembrane TLR4 that would trigger inflammatory signal transduction. The transgene is delivered using an AAV2 vector, which is known for its high tropism for RPE cells and its capacity to achieve long-term transgene expression with minimal immunogenicity. Studies using AAV2 vectors in retinal tissues have confirmed robust gene expression with a favorable safety profile, making this vector a suitable choice for chronic diseases such as dry AMD (Ramlogan-Steel et al., 2019; Inana et al., 2018).  

Furthermore, preserving normal RPE phagocytic functions by preventing the downregulation of receptors like MERTK is critical, as there is evidence that TLR4-mediated inflammation interferes with these functions, potentially creating a detrimental feedback loop that exacerbates degeneration (Klettner & Roider, 2021; Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018). Consequently, the blockade of TLR4 activation via the decoy molecule should lead to a more balanced inflammatory response and maintain proper RPE functionality in clearing POS, thereby slowing the progression of AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The primary expected outcome of administering the AAV2-hTLR4 decoy gene therapy is a marked reduction in the chronic inflammatory state observed in dry AMD. In experimental settings such as RPE explant cultures, expression of the soluble TLR4 decoy is anticipated to lead to a significant reduction in the levels of key proinflammatory cytokines, particularly TNF-α and IL-1β, which are known mediators of retinal inflammation and degeneration (Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024; Klettner & Roider, 2021). By limiting the availability of DAMPs that would otherwise activate endogenous TLR4, the therapy is expected to attenuate the downstream NF-κB activation and the resultant cytokine cascade. This reduction in inflammation should, in turn, preserve or even restore the expression of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and αvβ5 integrin on the RPE (Inana et al., 2018; Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024).  

The maintenance of these receptors is critical because they mediate the phagocytosis of POS, a process essential for retinal homeostasis and visual function. In the context of AMD, compromised phagocytosis leads to an accumulation of debris and further cellular stress, thereby perpetuating a cycle of inflammation and degeneration. Therefore, through the preservation of MERTK and integrin αvβ5 expression, the decoy therapy is hypothesized to support normal POS clearance, thereby improving RPE cell health and reducing the progression of retinal degeneration (Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018; Titi-Lartey, Mohammed, & Amoaku, 2022).  

In addition to the biochemical assays and ex vivo RPE explant studies that are likely to show a decrease in inflammatory mediator levels, in vivo models of retinal degeneration may demonstrate improved structural and functional outcomes following treatment. This might include reduced RPE atrophy, diminished formation of drusen-like deposits, and stabilization or improvement in retinal morphology on imaging studies. Functional assessments could show attenuation of visual decline over time in animal models, mirroring the clinical goal of preserving vision in dry AMD patients. The broad immunomodulatory effect of the decoy is therefore expected not only to dampen the deleterious inflammatory response but also to contribute to the long-term maintenance of retinal tissue integrity and function (Klettner & Roider, 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the AAV2-hTLR4 decoy gene therapy candidate represents a promising therapeutic approach for dry AMD owing to its targeted mechanism to modulate innate inflammatory signaling. Among the key strengths of this candidate is its strong mechanistic rationale. A wealth of preclinical evidence highlights TLR4’s central role in AMD pathogenesis, where DAMP-induced TLR4 activation contributes to chronic inflammation and the detrimental downregulation of phagocytic receptors (Klettner & Roider, 2021; Titi-Lartey, Mohammed, & Amoaku, 2022). By employing a soluble decoy receptor to intercept DAMPs, this approach offers a targeted method to mitigate the adverse inflammatory cascade while simultaneously preserving critical RPE functions necessary for photoreceptor outer segment clearance (Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024).  

Another significant strength is the use of an AAV2 vector for gene delivery. AAV2 is one of the most extensively studied and clinically validated gene therapy vectors for ocular applications, with a proven record of safety and efficacy in several retinal disorders (Ramlogan-Steel et al., 2019; Inana et al., 2018). The subretinal delivery of AAV2-based therapies has been demonstrated to produce sustained transgene expression with minimal immunogenicity, a feature particularly advantageous in treating chronic conditions such as dry AMD. This platform further benefits from its ability to transduce non-dividing cells, such as RPE, and achieve long-term expression, which is critical for a disease that requires prolonged therapeutic intervention.  

On the other hand, there are several challenges and potential weaknesses that warrant careful consideration. One notable concern is the inherent redundancy in Toll-like receptor signaling. Although TLR4 is a critical mediator of inflammatory responses in the retina, other TLRs such as TLR2 and TLR3 have also been implicated in AMD pathogenesis (Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018; Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024). As such, an approach that solely targets TLR4 may not address the entire spectrum of innate immune activation in the diseased retina. This redundancy might diminish the overall efficacy of the decoy if compensatory mechanisms via other receptors persist.  

Additionally, TLR4 is known to play a dual role in RPE physiology. While its activation under pathological conditions exacerbates inflammation and cellular dysfunction, TLR4 is also involved in the normal phagocytic clearance of POS (Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024). Consequently, complete inhibition of TLR4 signaling could unintentionally compromise physiological processes, leading to adverse effects on retinal homeostasis. Achieving the appropriate balance between inhibiting pathological inflammation and preserving essential immune functions will be a central challenge in the optimization of this therapeutic candidate.  

Another potential weakness relates to the immunological response elicited by the AAV2 vector itself. Although AAV2 has been shown to be relatively non-immunogenic in the ocular environment, there remains a risk of dose-dependent immune reactions, particularly if high levels of transgene expression occur. Pre-existing neutralizing antibodies to AAV2 in some patient populations could also limit the efficacy of the therapy (Ramlogan-Steel et al., 2019). Moreover, while early-phase clinical trials with other AAV2-based treatments have demonstrated favorable safety profiles, long-term data will be necessary to fully evaluate the risk of inflammatory complications or vector-related toxicity in the context of a decoy receptor that is intended to modulate immune signaling.  

From a mechanistic perspective, while the therapeutic hypothesis is compelling, the direct experimental evidence supporting a reduction in TNF-α and IL-1β levels in RPE explants using a TLR4 decoy is still limited. Most of the current evidence is derived from mechanistic studies that have established a correlation between TLR4 activation and proinflammatory cytokine production in AMD (Klettner & Roider, 2021; Titi-Lartey, Mohammed, & Amoaku, 2022; Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024). As such, further in vitro and in vivo studies will be necessary to confirm that the AAV2-mediated delivery of the TLR4 decoy convincingly modulates these inflammatory pathways without adversely affecting normal RPE functions.  

Overall, the AAV2-hTLR4 decoy gene therapy candidate offers a novel and rational approach to treating dry AMD by directly targeting a central component in the inflammatory cascade. Its strengths lie in its targeted sequestration of DAMPs, the potential to preserve RPE phagocytic receptor expression, and the well-established safety of AAV2 vector delivery in the eye (Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018; Klettner & Roider, 2021). However, issues such as potential compensatory mechanisms by other TLRs, the dual role of TLR4 in both pathological and physiological contexts, and possible vector immunogenicity underscore the need for comprehensive preclinical validation. The candidate is promising, but further investigation into dosing, delivery route, and long-term expression is essential to ensure that the therapeutic benefits outweigh any risks in the clinical setting of dry AMD (Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018; Klettner & Roider, 2021).  

In conclusion, while the AAV2-hTLR4 decoy represents a highly innovative approach to modulating innate immunity in dry AMD, its future success will depend on rigorous preclinical studies that confirm its ability to selectively dampen pathological inflammation without disrupting normal RPE functions. The convergence of mechanistic insights on TLR4 signaling in AMD pathogenesis and the proven capabilities of AAV2 gene therapy creates a strong rationale for further development of this candidate. Continued evaluation through biochemical assays, RPE explant studies, and animal models of retinal degeneration is recommended to refine dosing strategies and assess long-term safety and efficacy prior to advancing into clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human MCP-1 (monocyte chemoattractant protein-1), also known as CCL2, is a biologically active recombinant cytokine derived using modern recombinant protein production techniques under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) conditions (Ramkumar et al., 2010). This molecule belongs to the CC chemokine family and is naturally secreted in response to tissue injury and inflammatory stimuli, where it functions primarily to recruit monocytes, memory T cells, and dendritic cells via binding to its cognate receptor CCR2 (Chen & Xu, 2015). Its synthesis involves expression in appropriate host cells (commonly mammalian or bacterial expression systems) followed by purification and rigorous quality control measures, such that its physicochemical properties and pharmacokinetics are well characterized for ocular administration (Tolentino et al., 2023; Wong et al., 2022). As a therapeutic candidate, recombinant human MCP-1 represents a protein biologic aiming to restore a natural homeostatic mechanism that appears to be compromised in age-related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly in models where a deficiency in CCL2 drives drusen-like lesions through impaired recruitment and function of phagocytic cells (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the biological role of MCP-1 has been extensively characterized in both experimental and genetic models of inflammatory and degenerative diseases. In murine models of AMD, genetic knockout studies have demonstrated that deficiency in Ccl2 (the murine homolog) results in the development of AMD-like retinal changes including drusen-like deposits, thickening and fragmentation of Bruch’s membrane, disrupted collagen and elastin layers, and eventual retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009). These findings have provided substantial preclinical evidence that the CCL2/CCR2 axis is critical for the recruitment of monocytes to the subretinal space, thus facilitating debris clearance and maintenance of retinal homeostasis (Chen & Xu, 2015; DaCosta, 2015). In contrast, some studies have also indicated that improper or excessive recruitment of CCR2⁺ cells may lead to pathological states, including amplified inflammatory cytokine production (Chen & Xu, 2015) and even contribute to angiogenic responses under certain conditions (Hu et al., 2016; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). While recombinant MCP-1 has been used in basic research to probe the role of chemokine signaling in immune cell trafficking and inflammation in various diseases, its direct therapeutic application for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative conditions has not been previously established in clinical or formal veterinary studies (Marin-Castaño, 2013). The unique proposition in the current candidate is to administer low doses of recombinant MCP-1 directly into the subretinal space in order to restore the regulated recruitment of monocytes and thereby improve clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris—a strategy that has been hypothesized based on earlier experimental findings (Luhmann et al., 2009; Chen & Xu, 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
MCP-1 functions as a chemoattractant by binding with high affinity to the CCR2 receptor expressed on inflammatory monocytes and certain subsets of macrophages. Once the ligand binds, it initiates a cascade of intracellular signaling events mediated by G-proteins that result in actin cytoskeleton reorganization, cell polarization, and directed migration towards higher concentrations of MCP-1 (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Chen & Xu, 2015). In the context of ocular physiology, RPE cells under stress conditions or oxidative insult have been shown to secrete MCP-1 as part of an endogenous mechanism intended to attract CCR2⁺ monocytes to areas of debris accumulation (Marin-Castaño, 2013). These recruited monocytes are expected to differentiate into macrophages capable of phagocytosing shed POS debris and other cellular waste products that accumulate with aging and contribute to drusen formation (Luhmann et al., 2009). At the molecular level, binding of MCP-1 to CCR2 results in receptor dimerization and the activation of downstream effectors such as phospholipase C, MAP kinases, and small GTPases that collectively drive cytoskeletal changes and cell motility (Chen & Xu, 2015). It is important to note that the MCP-1/CCR2 axis is tightly regulated, and its function is context dependent; in some models, an overactive response can lead to exacerbated inflammation, while in others the signaling is critical for normal tissue repair and debris clearance (Luhmann et al., 2009; DaCosta, 2015). The hypothesis under evaluation contends that a carefully titrated, low-dose supplementation of recombinant MCP-1 in a dry AMD setting—characterized by Ccl2 deficiency—is capable of reinstating physiologic levels of monocyte recruitment to the subretinal space, thereby bolstering the phagocytic capacity of these cells and normalizing RPE function in terms of outer segment processing (Tolentino et al., 2023; Luhmann et al., 2009).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed mechanism, the expected outcome of administering low-dose recombinant human MCP-1 is an enhancement in the homing behavior of CCR2⁺ monocytes toward the subretinal space. In experimental models where Ccl2 deficiency leads to an accumulation of drusen-like deposits, the rationale is that MCP-1 supplementation will counter the defect in chemotactic signaling, allowing monocytes to effectively transmigrate through the choriocapillaris and accumulate at sites in the retina where depot of POS debris occurs (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009). In these settings, recruited monocytes are anticipated to engage in active phagocytosis of lipofuscin-laden debris, thus alleviating the burden on the RPE cells which are responsible for digesting and recycling photoreceptor outer segments (Chen & Xu, 2015; Marin-Castaño, 2013). Improvement in the RPE’s phagocytic index is hypothesized to lead to several beneficial downstream effects; these include reduced drusen formation, preservation of the structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane, and ultimately a deceleration in the progression of dry AMD pathology (Luhmann et al., 2009). Furthermore, because recombinant MCP-1 is provided in a controlled low-dose fashion, the intended effect is to mimic the physiological signaling observed in the nonpathological state, thereby avoiding overactivation of inflammatory pathways that could otherwise potentiate a deleterious chronic inflammatory milieu (Marin-Castaño, 2013). It should be emphasized that while the concept is theoretically sound, there remains an inherent risk that the recruited monocytes, if not adequately polarized into a reparative (or M2) phenotype, might adopt a pro-inflammatory (or M1) profile that could exacerbate local tissue damage (Chen & Xu, 2015; Elbaz-Hayoun et al., 2023). Thus, the assay’s success will hinge on demonstrating that low-dose MCP-1 can selectively enhance beneficial debris clearance while avoiding unintended inflammatory side effects—a balance that must be meticulously evaluated in preclinical models before any translation to clinical settings (DaCosta, 2015; Tolentino et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
A comprehensive evaluation of recombinant human MCP-1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a candidate with a strong biological rationale based on its central role in monocyte recruitment and tissue repair. The primary strength of this candidate lies in its capacity to restore a key homeostatic function that is compromised in Ccl2 deficiency models of AMD, as evidenced by robust preclinical data showing that diminished MCP-1 signaling correlates with drusen accumulation and RPE dysfunction (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009). Moreover, the fact that recombinant MCP-1 is available as GMP-grade material with known ocular pharmacokinetic properties lends a degree of translational feasibility to the proposed studies (Wong et al., 2022; Tolentino et al., 2023). The hypothesis that subretinal injection of low-dose MCP-1 can ameliorate debris accumulation by recruiting CCR2⁺ monocytes is supported by the well-established molecular interactions between MCP-1 and CCR2, which have been validated in several inflammatory and degenerative models (Chen & Xu, 2015; Marin-Castaño, 2013).

However, several critical weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, the literature presents conflicting roles for the MCP-1/CCR2 axis in AMD pathogenesis. While genetic deficiencies in CCL2 lead to drusen-like lesions, other studies have shown that blocking MCP-1/CCR2 signaling can yield protective effects by reducing inflammatory monocyte recruitment and subsequent tissue damage (Hu et al., 2016; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Elbaz-Hayoun et al., 2023). This dichotomy underscores the delicate balance between debris clearance and inflammation; excessive or misdirected monocyte recruitment may inadvertently exacerbate retinal degeneration rather than ameliorate it (Marin-Castaño, 2013; Tolentino et al., 2023). Second, there is a substantial risk that exogenously administered MCP-1—even at low doses—could stimulate an overzealous inflammatory response if it fails to promote the desired anti-inflammatory, reparative monocyte phenotype. Given that monocyte polarization is highly context dependent, additional studies would be required to ensure that the recruited cells adopt a phenotype conducive to tissue repair rather than one that contributes to chronic inflammation or neovascular complications (Chen & Xu, 2015; Elbaz-Hayoun et al., 2023). Third, while the candidate hypothesis is partly based on observations from knockout models, these models have inherent limitations; some studies indicate that the majority of AMD-related morphological changes in Ccl2- and Ccr2-deficient mice may actually represent accelerated aging rather than true disease pathology (Luhmann et al., 2009; Tolentino et al., 2023). Thus, extrapolating these findings to a therapeutic scenario in human dry AMD requires careful validation in models that more accurately recapitulate the human disease phenotype.

In summary, recombinant human MCP-1 holds promise as a novel therapeutic strategy for dry AMD by potentially restoring a physiologic mechanism for debris clearance through the recruitment of CCR2⁺ monocytes. Its strengths include its well-characterized molecular mechanism, availability as a GMP-grade product with defined ocular pharmacokinetics, and a solid preclinical rationale based on studies showing that CCL2 deficiency leads to AMD-like pathology (Ramkumar et al., 2010; Luhmann et al., 2009). Conversely, its weaknesses stem from the complex and sometimes contradictory roles of the MCP-1/CCR2 axis in retinal inflammation and degeneration, the risk of inadvertently triggering detrimental inflammatory responses, and the challenge of translating findings from knockout models to a clinical setting (Hu et al., 2016; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Elbaz-Hayoun et al., 2023). Given these considerations, while the candidate is scientifically intriguing, further rigorous preclinical research is essential to define the appropriate dosing regimen, confirm the beneficial polarization of recruited monocytes, and rule out any potential exacerbation of inflammatory pathology before advancing to clinical trials. This balanced approach will ultimately determine whether recombinant MCP-1 can be viably repurposed as a therapeutic agent to mitigate the progression of dry AMD by enhancing RPE function and debris clearance (Marin-Castaño, 2013; DaCosta, 2015).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
FX-68 is a synthetic small‐molecule agonist developed from a chemical library (ChemBridge Cat. No. 6789012) and represents an emerging member of a class of chemokine receptor modulators that selectively target CX3CR1. This compound is designed to mimic the natural ligand, fractalkine (CX3CL1), and has been optimized for potency with an EC₅₀ of approximately 100 nM, which suggests that it is capable of activating CX3CR1 at pharmacologically achievable concentrations (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–5, 6–7). The candidate belongs to the broader category of small-molecule GPCR agonists, a class that has been successfully employed in various inflammatory and neurodegenerative indications because of their favorable oral bioavailability and capacity to cross biological barriers; such compounds have a long history in modulating immune cell behavior and attenuating aberrant inflammation (Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 2–4; Chinnery et al., 2012, pp. 7–8). In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), FX-68 is proposed to restore appropriate signaling in the CX3CL1–CX3CR1 axis—a pathway that is critically involved in the regulation of microglial migration, phagocytosis and, indirectly, the trophic support provided to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6). Its synthetic origin coupled with repurposing potential makes FX-68 an attractive candidate for conditions in which deficient microglial clearance and disrupted RPE–microglia crosstalk contribute to disease progression (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3, 4–5).

Therapeutic History:  
The link between CX3CR1 function and retinal health was established through extensive genetic and preclinical studies, in which loss-of-function mutations or deficiencies in CX3CR1 were found to produce a constellation of AMD-like features, including the accumulation of subretinal microglia, formation of drusen-like deposits, and secondary photoreceptor degeneration (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7; Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 4–5). Historically, research in this area has focused on genetic knock-out models and human polymorphism analyses rather than on the administration of direct pharmacologic agonists; for example, CX3CR1-deficient mice consistently exhibit abnormal subretinal microglial behavior and accompanying retinal pathology, which has been used as a rationale for targeting this signaling pathway therapeutically (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–6). Although exogenous delivery of CX3CL1 has been explored in certain experimental paradigms, no small-molecule CX3CR1 agonist has yet been advanced in clinical or veterinary practice for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerations (Chinnery et al., 2012, pp. 7–8; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3). Instead, the therapeutic potential in this space has largely emerged indirectly from studies that demonstrate that disrupted CX3CR1 signaling is deleterious to retinal homeostasis, thereby suggesting that its appropriate stimulation could restore normal microglial behavior (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7). As a repurposed candidate, FX-68 aims to fill this translational gap by reactivating a pathway that is both genetically implicated in AMD and mechanistically understood in other contexts of neuroinflammation (Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 2–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
The CX3CL1–CX3CR1 axis is a pivotal mediator of neuron–microglia communication in the retina and broader central nervous system, where fractalkine (CX3CL1) exists in both membrane-bound and soluble forms and interacts exclusively with CX3CR1, a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) expressed predominantly by microglia (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–5, 6–7). Under physiological conditions, tonic signaling through CX3CR1 serves to restrain microglial activation, regulate their migratory behavior, and facilitate their efficient surveillance and debris clearance functions (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6). In the diseased retina—such as in dry AMD—loss or dysfunction of CX3CR1 impairs these regulatory mechanisms, leading to chronic accumulation of lipid-laden microglia in the subretinal space, excessive phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and subsequent RPE stress and degeneration, a sequence that contributes to the formation of drusen-like deposits and ultimately to photoreceptor cell death (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3, 6–7).

FX-68 is designed as a CX3CR1 agonist that binds to and activates this receptor, mimicking the natural action of CX3CL1. Upon binding, it is expected to trigger downstream signaling cascades typical of GPCR activation, including modulation of adenylate cyclase activity and activation of MAP kinase pathways, which in turn alter cytoskeletal dynamics essential for microglial migration and phagocytosis (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–6). At a molecular level, proper CX3CR1 activation is theorized to correct the aberrant microglial behavior seen in CX3CR1 deficiency: it should promote the egression or apoptotic clearance of subretinal microglia that have phagocytosed excessive amounts of POS debris and prevent their transformation into foam cells laden with intracellular lipids (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7; Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4). Moreover, by reestablishing a functional microglia–RPE communication axis, FX-68 may help restore the RPE’s inherent phagocytic capacity to clear POS effectively, ultimately leading to improved outer retinal homeostasis (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). With CX3CR1 activation, signaling may also suppress the production of proangiogenic factors such as VEGF, thereby limiting pathological neovascularization—a secondary complication sometimes observed in the context of AMD (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). This mechanism is further supported by studies in which exogenous CX3CL1 reduced microglial phagocytosis and inflammatory activation in models of retinal degeneration, albeit in genetic loss-of-function contexts rather than using a pharmacologic agonist (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Zabel et al., 2016, pp. 10–12). The overall molecular interaction profile of FX-68, therefore, hinges on reinstating the anti-inflammatory, pro-homeostatic functions of CX3CR1 in retinal microglia, with the intended effect of reducing deleterious phagocytosis and enhancing trophic support for the RPE (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assays and in preclinical models—particularly in the challenging Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mouse model, which recapitulates many aspects of dry AMD—the expected effect of FX-68 is multifaceted. First, by binding and activating CX3CR1 on retinal microglia, FX-68 is anticipated to restore regulated cell migration and proper phagocytic clearance, thereby reducing the abnormal accumulation of subretinal microglia that is observed in CX3CR1-deficient models (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). Such restoration is expected to lead to a normalization of the phagocytic process, where instead of over-ingesting POS debris and becoming lipid-laden foam cells, microglia will clear debris efficiently and then either return to a surveillant state or undergo timely apoptosis or emigration away from the subretinal space (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6).

Second, FX-68 is proposed to facilitate enhanced trophic support for RPE cells. Evidence suggests that proper microglial signaling is critically involved in modulating RPE phagocytosis of POS, partly through the secretion of growth factors and early inflammatory mediators that prime RPE cells for efficient clearance functions (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). In co-culture assays involving microglia and RPE cells, treatment with FX-68 is expected to lead to an increase in the efficiency of POS turnover, as microglial activation is reined in and redirected toward beneficial debris clearance rather than deleterious inflammatory activation (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). This effect, in theory, would reduce the buildup of toxic debris in the subretinal region, limit the formation of drusen-like deposits and diminish secondary inflammatory and proangiogenic signaling, such as excessive VEGF release, that further compromise retinal integrity (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3; Rashid et al., 2019, p. 14).

Moreover, in animal models like the Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mice—where the dual deficiency exacerbates retinal degeneration and drusen-like pathology—FX-68 is expected to mitigate these phenotypes by reactivating the CX3CR1 pathway. The hypothesis posits that restoration of CX3CR1 signaling will not only lower subretinal microglial accumulation but also re-establish a crosstalk with the RPE that is essential for maintaining the delicate balance between debris clearance and inflammation (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). In this way, the compound may indirectly improve photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance, thereby preserving overall photoreceptor function and slowing the progression of dry AMD (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6; Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4).

An important aspect of the expected effect is the modulation of microglial cytokine production. CX3CR1 signaling has been linked to the suppression of proinflammatory pathways—in particular, the reduction of IL-1β and VEGF expression, which are key mediators of chronic inflammation and pathological angiogenesis (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–7). FX-68, by serving as a CX3CR1 agonist, would clarify whether the attenuation of these proinflammatory signals could indeed translate to structural and functional retinal preservation in vivo. This result would be highly significant given that chronic inflammation is a critical driver of dry AMD progression (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 2–3; Rashid et al., 2019, p. 14).

Furthermore, the expected effect extends to the normalization of microglial morphology and dispersal. In healthy retinas, microglia are characterized by a ramified morphology that is conducive to efficient surveillance, whereas in CX3CR1-deficient retinas, microglia become amoeboid, exhibit excessive adhesion, and accumulate in the subretinal space (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). FX-68 is anticipated to promote a return to the ramified, homeostatic phenotype, thereby reducing the deleterious impact of microglial hyperactivation and aberrant phagocytosis on both photoreceptors and RPE cells (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6). Altogether, these expected effects form the basis of the hypothesis that FX-68 may improve outer retinal homeostasis by enhancing POS turnover and supporting the RPE via finely tuned microglial regulation (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 6–7; Rashid et al., 2019, p. 14).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of FX-68 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD must balance a compelling mechanistic rationale against significant preclinical gaps and potential safety concerns. On the one hand, there is robust and convergent evidence from genetic and experimental studies that impaired CX3CR1 signaling leads to pathological subretinal microglial accumulation, excessive phagocytosis of photoreceptor debris, and subsequent RPE and photoreceptor damage—as seen in various mouse models and human genetic association studies (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7; Raoul et al., 2010, pp. 4–5; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–5). This evidence strongly supports the notion that reactivating CX3CR1 signaling could normalize microglial behavior, improve debris clearance, limit drusen formation, and ultimately slow the progression of retinal degeneration (Fletcher, 2020, pp. 2–4; Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 5–6).

A key strength of FX-68 is its small-molecule nature, which provides advantages in terms of potential administration routes (oral or topical), manufacturability, and the possibility for fine-tuning its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties. With an EC₅₀ of approximately 100 nM, FX-68 appears to be a potent agonist, meaning that it could achieve therapeutic concentrations without off-target effects if the dosing regimen is carefully optimized (Combadière et al., 2007, pp. 4–7). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Anacetrapib is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor of cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) originally developed by Merck as part of a class of compounds aimed at modulating lipid metabolism. This compound was identified and refined through extensive medicinal chemistry programs designed to target CETP’s lipid transfer function. As a member of the CETP inhibitor class, anacetrapib has been developed primarily for cardiovascular risk reduction by increasing high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL‐C) and lowering low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C), and its chemical structure and binding properties have been designed to disrupt the lipid‐transfer tunnel of the CETP enzyme (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Tall & Rader, 2018). The proposed repurposing for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on the rationale that by inhibiting CETP, the agent could raise local HDL levels in Bruch’s membrane (BrM) and improve reverse cholesterol transport, thereby reducing drusen‐like lipid accumulation and indirectly supporting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) phagocytic capacity—a hypothesis derived from observed associations between CETP activity, local retinal lipid metabolism, and AMD pathogenesis (Betzler et al., 2020; Shughoury et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, CETP inhibitors have been evaluated extensively for their potential to address dyslipidemia and reduce atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Anacetrapib, in particular, has undergone large clinical trials such as the DEFINE and REVEAL studies, where its efficacy in raising HDL‐C by approximately 138% and reducing LDL‐C by 37–40% compared to placebo was demonstrated (Cheung et al., 2017; Tall & Rader, 2018). The class of CETP inhibitors also includes compounds such as torcetrapib, dalcetrapib, and evacetrapib—with torcetrapib’s development being terminated due to off‐target effects including blood pressure elevations, while anacetrapib and evacetrapib showed more favorable profiles in subsequent trials (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Sirtori, 2011). Although these compounds were developed to address cardiovascular pathologies, genetic and mechanistic studies have implicated CETP and HDL metabolism in the ocular environment as well. Several genome‐wide association studies and Mendelian randomization studies have demonstrated a relationship between CETP gene variants, HDL levels, and AMD risk (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020). Despite this, no CETP inhibitor has previously been used in a clinical setting for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular diseases, and the repurposing of anacetrapib for dry AMD represents a novel therapeutic direction inspired by preclinical studies in murine models that suggest potential benefits in the retinal context (Cheung et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
Anacetrapib functions by binding to CETP, thereby preventing the transfer of cholesteryl esters from HDL to apolipoprotein B‐containing lipoproteins (i.e., LDL, very‐low‐density lipoprotein [VLDL]) and the subsequent exchange of triglycerides in the opposite direction. At the molecular level, CETP normally operates via a tunnel‐mechanism or shuttle mechanism to facilitate the bidirectional lipid transfer between lipoproteins. Inhibition of CETP by anacetrapib results in the accumulation of cholesterol-rich, enlarged HDL particles and a concomitant reduction in the levels of atherogenic LDL particles (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Sirtori, 2011). In the context of the retina, emerging evidence suggests that CETP is expressed not only systemically but also locally—in the retinal pigment epithelium, photoreceptor outer segments, and interphotoreceptor matrix (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). The rationale is that CETP activity in Bruch’s membrane may normally lower HDL levels, thereby impairing the capacity for reverse cholesterol transport in this specialized extracellular matrix, which can lead to the accumulation of lipids and the formation of drusen. By inhibiting CETP, anacetrapib may restore or increase local HDL levels, improving the efflux of accumulated cholesterol and other lipids from the RPE and neighboring structures (Fan et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2022). Moreover, the resulting HDL particles may gain enhanced cholesterol efflux capacity, as evidenced by preclinical studies that show increased cholesterol removal from macrophages via ABCA1- and ABCG1-mediated pathways (Sirtori, 2011; Page et al., 2016). In addition, proper HDL particle composition under CETP inhibition could influence key inflammatory regulatory mechanisms through the carriage of complement factors, which are linked to AMD pathogenesis (Tricorache et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assay, treatment with anacetrapib is expected to increase HDL levels locally in Bruch’s membrane, thereby enhancing reverse cholesterol transport across the retinal layers. The improved cholesterol efflux from the RPE is postulated to mitigate the accumulation of drusen-like lipid deposits—a hallmark of dry AMD—and potentially restore critical cellular functions such as integrin localization and associated phagocytic receptor activity (Cheung et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020). This restoration of lipid homeostasis is anticipated to reduce the build-up of oxidized lipids and other debris beneath the RPE, ultimately alleviating RPE dysfunction—a central component in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). The mechanism relies on the observation that HDL not only serves as a cholesterol acceptor but also carries important complement regulatory proteins and inflammatory mediators; thus, its normalization in Bruch’s membrane could indirectly support the phagocytic activity of RPE cells and improve tissue homeostasis (Lin et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). Gene expression studies have identified CETP expression in ocular tissues, reinforcing the notion that local CETP inhibition may directly influence lipid handling in the retina (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). Ultimately, the expected outcomes in preclinical models—and, by extension, in clinical trials—are a measurable reduction in drusen burden, improvement in RPE functionality, and a potential delay or attenuation in the progression of dry AMD (Schmidt et al., 2020; Cheung et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of anacetrapib for the treatment of dry AMD presents a compelling opportunity, supported by a solid mechanistic hypothesis and a favorable human safety profile established in cardiovascular trials. Among the clear strengths is the extensive biochemical and clinical data on CETP inhibitors in the context of dyslipidemia; anacetrapib has demonstrated robust HDL‐C raising and LDL‐C lowering effects, with a tolerability profile superior to earlier CETP inhibitors such as torcetrapib (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Tall & Rader, 2018). Furthermore, emerging evidence of CETP expression in ocular tissues and its potential role in modulating local lipid metabolism—combined with findings that suggest dysfunctional HDL composition may contribute to drusen formation—lends strong support to the therapeutic rationale (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017).

However, there are important weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed. First, the genetic and epidemiological data linking HDL cholesterol and AMD have been paradoxical; several Mendelian randomization studies have implicated HDL‐raising alleles, particularly those related to CETP modulation, with an increased risk for AMD (Betzler et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2017). This counterintuitive observation raises concerns that simply increasing HDL levels may not guarantee improved RPE function unless the quality and functionality of HDL particles are also enhanced (Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022). Second, while the cardiovascular applications of anacetrapib provide a strong safety signal, the ocular-specific pharmacodynamics and tissue distribution of the drug remain largely unexplored. It is conceivable that the systemic modulation of HDL might not translate into the desired local changes in Bruch’s membrane, particularly given the unique lipid microenvironment of the retina (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Third, preclinical data demonstrating that anacetrapib can reduce BrM lipid burden and restore integrin localization in murine models, although promising, have yet to be validated extensively, and species differences in CETP expression and lipid metabolism could limit translatability to human patients (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Lastly, the long-term consequences of altering CETP activity in the retina are unknown, and there exists a potential risk that chronic CETP inhibition could inadvertently disrupt local complement regulation or other aspects of retinal homeostasis, given the tight interplay between lipid metabolism and inflammation in AMD pathogenesis (Tricorache et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2015).

Overall, while the conceptual framework underlying the repurposing of anacetrapib for dry AMD is scientifically intriguing and supported by a convergence of genetic, biochemical, and preclinical mechanistic data, further investigation is needed to reconcile the paradoxical relationships observed in human genetic studies, to precisely characterize the local retinal pharmacokinetics of the drug, and to validate its effects on reverse cholesterol transport in the specific context of the retina. In summary, anacetrapib holds potential as a novel therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but its ultimate success will depend on carefully designed preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials that specifically address its ocular efficacy and safety profile (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide, a water‐soluble form of vitamin B3, is a naturally occurring compound that plays a critical role in cellular metabolism by serving as a precursor for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺) synthesis. It is available both through dietary sources and chemical synthesis and has been produced at high purity for research purposes (Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. N4126). Nicotinamide belongs to the vitamin B3 class of compounds, which have been extensively used as nutritional supplements and metabolic regulators; these compounds are well recognized for their role in the salvage pathway that replenishes NAD⁺ levels in cells. The therapeutic candidate under consideration is repurposed with the hypothesis that at a concentration of 10 mM, nicotinamide will boost intracellular NAD⁺ pools and enhance the activity of NAD⁺‐dependent enzymes, such as sirtuins, leading to improved mitochondrial function and increased deacetylation of autophagy regulators. Such effects are expected to restore phagocytic function, specifically the photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation, in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cultures pertinent to dry age‐related macular degeneration (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, nicotinamide has been investigated in various preclinical and clinical settings for its potential neuroprotective effects and its capacity to modulate cellular metabolism. In the context of ocular health, several studies have demonstrated that nicotinamide supplementation can enhance NAD⁺ levels and improve mitochondrial function in retinal cells. Preclinical studies have reported that this vitamin not only supports retinal ganglion cell health in glaucoma models but also shows promise in improving photoreceptor and RPE function in models of age-related macular degeneration (Gemae et al., 2024). Although there remains limited direct clinical experience with nicotinamide in dry AMD, the compound has been a subject of interest in related ocular conditions due to its favorable safety profile and widespread use in other age-related and mitochondrial dysfunction settings (Gemae et al., 2024). More recent investigations have focused on its ability to rescue mitochondrial deficits and restore autophagic flux in RPE cells, with data indicating that in models of CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE, nicotinamide can ameliorate lysosomal processing and POS degradation problems (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). This body of evidence, compounded with its extensive historical use as a nutritional supplement, supports the rationale for repurposing nicotinamide as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, nicotinamide exerts its effects primarily through its role as a key precursor in the NAD⁺ salvage pathway. In this pathway, nicotinamide is converted to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) via the enzyme nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), and subsequently to NAD⁺ by NMN adenylyltransferase. NAD⁺, in turn, is an essential co-factor for numerous enzymes involved in energy metabolism and cellular homeostasis, most notably the sirtuin family of NAD⁺-dependent deacetylases (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Sirtuins, such as SIRT1 and SIRT3, play a pivotal role in mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and regulation of autophagy by deacetylating key transcription factors and enzymes that control metabolic stress responses (Gemae et al., 2024). In RPE cells, increased NAD⁺ levels facilitate the activation of these sirtuins, which then deacetylate a range of targets including histones and autophagy regulators, leading to improved mitochondrial structure and function, enhanced energy production, and the promotion of efficient autophagic and lysosomal degradation pathways (Gemae et al., 2024). Furthermore, the improved mitochondrial function translates into a better cellular energy state, providing the necessary ATP required for high-energy processes such as POS phagocytosis. Experimentally, administration of nicotinamide has been shown to yield a two-fold increase in NAD⁺ levels in ARPE-19 cells, thereby confirming its ability to augment the cellular bioenergetic capacity (Hazim et al., 2022). This mechanism also intersects with the regulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, as enhanced mitochondrial function and sirtuin activity contribute to lower oxidative stress, a known contributor to cellular senescence and dysfunction in the aging retina (Gemae et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the current proposal is that nicotinamide, administered at a concentration of 10 mM in vitro, will significantly increase NAD⁺ levels in RPE cells, thereby enhancing sirtuin activity and downstream mitochondrial function. This boost in NAD⁺ is expected to promote deacetylation of autophagy regulators, which will, in turn, normalize the autophagic flux and facilitate the effective degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE. In models of dry AMD, where phagocytosis deficits and impaired proteostasis are key pathological features, the restoration of autophagy and mitochondrial activity is anticipated to ameliorate cellular senescence and maintain retinal homeostasis (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Data from previous studies suggest that in aging RPE, reduced NAMPT expression is linked to decreased NAD⁺ levels and compromised SIRT1 function, leading to cellular senescence and defective mitochondrial dynamics (Jadeja et al., 2018). By contrast, nicotinamide supplementation helps to reverse these effects, as evidenced by restored NAD⁺ content and reactivation of sirtuins that enable degradation of accumulated defective cellular components, thereby improving lysosomal enzyme processing and phagocytosis (Jadeja et al., 2018). Moreover, enhanced mitochondrial metabolism has been correlated with improved RPE differentiation and the maintenance of a polarized epithelial phenotype, critical factors in ensuring effective POS phagocytosis and overall retinal health (Hazim et al., 2022). Thus, the expected outcome is that nicotinamide treatment will correct metabolic impairments, reduce oxidative stress, and restore phagocytic efficiency in dry AMD cultures, which are all essential for halting or even reversing disease progression (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
Nicotinamide emerges as a highly promising therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on its multi-faceted mechanism of action and extensive preclinical evidence supporting its role in maintaining retinal health. One of the primary strengths of nicotinamide is its excellent safety profile and widespread historical use as a nutritional supplement, which significantly lowers the risk associated with its repurposing (Gemae et al., 2024). Its ability to augment NAD⁺ levels and activate sirtuins directly addresses several key pathological processes in dry AMD, including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and impaired autophagy. Experimental findings have consistently shown that increased NAD⁺ levels, mediated by nicotinamide or its analogues such as NMN, correlate with reduced cellular senescence and improved lysosomal and mitochondrial function in RPE cells (Jadeja et al., 2018).

Moreover, the convergence of multiple lines of evidence—from studies detailing NAMPT decline in aging RPE, to those demonstrating the restoration of NAD⁺ and sirtuin activity by nicotinamide—provides a robust biochemical rationale for its use in combating dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024). The ability of nicotinamide to enhance mitochondrial respiration in ARPE-19 cells and primary human fetal RPE cells further underscores its potential in promoting a healthy, polarized RPE phenotype capable of efficient POS phagocytosis (Hazim et al., 2022). These studies also suggest that improved mitochondrial metabolism is closely linked to enhanced proteostasis and autophagic clearance of damaged cellular components—an outcome that is particularly relevant given the known deficits in autophagy and lysosomal processing observed in dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024).

However, while the preclinical data are encouraging, several challenges must be acknowledged. One potential weakness lies in the translation of in vitro findings to in vivo therapeutic efficacy. The concentration of 10 mM nicotinamide used in cell culture experiments may not directly correspond to achievable or sustainable therapeutic levels in the human retina. Moreover, while nicotinamide is known to boost NAD⁺ synthesis, there is a nuanced balance in its effects on sirtuin activity; in certain contexts, excessive nicotinamide has been reported to inhibit sirtuins, suggesting that dosing and timing will be critical parameters that require careful optimization (Will-Orrego, 2020). There is also the inherent challenge of the multifactorial nature of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired autophagy are only parts of a complex network of pathological events that include inflammatory signaling, extracellular matrix alterations, and genetic predispositions. Thus, while nicotinamide addresses several of these pathways, it may need to be combined with other therapeutic agents to achieve a comprehensive treatment effect (Gemae et al., 2024; Will-Orrego, 2020).

Another important consideration is the need for more extensive clinical studies. Although nicotinamide’s safety profile is well established in the context of dietary supplementation and its use in other neurological and ocular conditions, robust clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD are lacking (Gemae et al., 2024; Lin, 2020). Future research will need to focus not only on the pharmacokinetics and optimal dosing strategies in human subjects but also on precise biomarkers indicating the restoration of NAD⁺ metabolism, mitochondrial function, and POS phagocytosis. Furthermore, mechanistic studies that dissect the interactions between nicotinamide-driven NAD⁺ elevation and the downstream modulation of autophagy regulators will be essential to confirm the proposed mode of action and to identify any potential off-target effects.

Overall, the repurposing of nicotinamide for dry AMD presents several compelling advantages. Its established safety, low cost, and known biochemical mechanisms strongly support its potential as a therapeutic candidate. Preclinical evidence indicates that nicotinamide not only restores NAD⁺ levels but also reactivates sirtuin pathways, thereby mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction and defective autophagy that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. These effects could translate into improved cellular proteostasis and enhanced POS phagocytosis, ultimately preserving retinal integrity and visual function (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Nevertheless, the path forward will require careful dose optimization and rigorous clinical validation to ensure that the in vitro benefits observed translate into meaningful clinical outcomes. In summary, despite the challenges associated with translating cell-based results into human therapy, nicotinamide remains an attractive candidate whose mechanism, historical use, and preclinical successes justify further investigation as a potential treatment for dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Lin, 2020).
