I. OVERVIEW OF THERAPEUTIC CANDIDATE

SKF96365 (1-{[3-(4-methoxyphenyl)propoxy]-4-methoxyphenethyl}-1H-imidazole hydrochloride) is a fully synthetic small molecule discovered by medicinal chemists interested in modulating receptor-mediated calcium entry pathways. Originally introduced as an inhibitor of receptor-induced Ca²⁺ influx in non‐excitable cells such as platelets and neutrophils (Singh et al., 2010), the compound later gained attention as a modulator of transient receptor potential (TRP) channels. As a member of the imidazole derivative class, SKF96365 shares structural features with phenylalkylamine compounds and is characterized by its alkylated imidazole core embellished with substituted methoxyphenyl moieties; these structural modifications were purposefully introduced to confer the molecule with broad activity on Ca²⁺ permeation mechanisms (Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011; Singh et al., 2010; Harteneck, Klose, & Krautwurst, 2011).

The chemical synthesis of SKF96365 involves multi-step organic transformations, whereby the imidazole ring is first derivatized and subsequently appended with both aliphatic and aromatic substituents. These modifications are believed to be critical in endowing SKF96365 with the ability to interact with various ion channel proteins across the plasma membrane. Although initially developed for its capacity to block receptor-mediated Ca²⁺ entry, further pharmacological investigations revealed that SKF96365 exhibits broad-spectrum activity by inhibiting not only store-operated channels (SOCE) and receptor-operated channels (ROC) but also interfering with key subtypes of the transient receptor potential canonical (TRPC) family (Singh et al., 2010).

The compound’s broad inhibitory spectrum, however, comes at the cost of selectivity. While low micromolar concentrations (typically in the range of 2–30 μM) are required to inhibit TRPC channels, SKF96365 has also been shown to block other calcium channels such as low‐voltage‐activated T‐type channels at submicromolar concentrations (IC₅₀ ~560 nM) (Singh et al., 2010). This dual and even overlapping activity pattern reflects its classification as a non‐selective TRP channel blocker and places it within the larger group of broad-spectrum calcium channel modulators. Its widespread use across a multitude of experimental systems—from studies of cellular Ca²⁺ entry in endothelial cells to investigations in neuronal and glial systems—further underscores its utility as a pharmacological tool, despite the inherent drawbacks associated with low target selectivity (Singh et al., 2010; Harteneck, Klose, & Krautwurst, 2011; Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011).

In summary, SKF96365 is a synthetic compound belonging to the imidazole derivative family, originally designed to inhibit receptor‐mediated Ca²⁺ influx. It has been repurposed as a TRPC channel inhibitor, although its inhibitory profile extends well beyond TRPC channels to include several classes of voltage‐gated and store-operated channels. This broad mechanism of action, while advantageous for experimental dissection of Ca²⁺ signaling pathways, poses potential challenges for its development as a selective therapeutic agent for dry AMD (Singh et al., 2010).

─────────────────────────────  
II. THERAPEUTIC HISTORY

The therapeutic history of SKF96365 reflects its evolution from a research tool into a potential candidate for repurposing in diverse pathological states. Initially, SKF96365 was introduced in the early 1990s as an inhibitor of receptor-mediated calcium entry. Early studies demonstrated that it could effectively block Ca²⁺ influx in non‐excitable cells such as platelets, neutrophils, and endothelial cells, with reported half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC₅₀’s) of approximately 10 μM (Singh et al., 2010; Harteneck, Klose, & Krautwurst, 2011). These early findings spurred interest in its utility as a diagnostic blocker for various Ca²⁺ entry mechanisms, particularly before the molecular identification of TRP channels.

Following the molecular cloning of TRPC family members, SKF96365 was quickly repurposed to study these channels in both heterologous expression systems and native tissues. Its ability to inhibit TRPC channels in multiple cell types solidified its reputation as a key pharmacological tool. For example, studies in cultured cells such as PC-12 and HL-60 cells provided evidence for its capacity to differentiate between ATP- and bradykinin-induced Ca²⁺ entry and offered insights into receptor-regulated calcium entry pathways (Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011). In addition to non-ocular systems, SKF96365 has been widely used in research involving the cardiovascular and nervous systems, highlighting its diverse biological applications.

In the context relevant to ocular research, several investigations have applied SKF96365 to retinal models. For instance, studies in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells indicated that basal calcium entry in these cells is mediated, at least in part, by TRPC channels. One particular study demonstrated that in both cultured RPE cells and primary human RPE cells, SKF96365 reduced intracellular Ca²⁺ concentration in a dose-dependent fashion, implicating TRPC channels in the maintenance of basal Ca²⁺ levels necessary for proper RPE function (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007). Moreover, ocular safety data from experiments using SKF96365 in lamina cribrosa cells—cells that contribute to the optic nerve head microenvironment implicated in glaucoma—have shown that at concentrations around 10 μM to 100 μM, the compound can modulate Ca²⁺-dependent signaling without overt cytotoxicity (Irnaten et al., 2020).

Additional preclinical studies have not only examined SKF96365 in the context of RPE cellular physiology but also explored its potential in anti-proliferative and anti-fibrotic applications. In malignant glioma cells, for example, concentrations in the 25 μM range were shown to suppress proliferation, an effect that was attributed to its combined blockade of TRPC channels and low‐voltage‐activated T‐type channels (Singh et al., 2010). Despite these encouraging preclinical findings, to date there have been no clinical or veterinary applications of SKF96365 specifically for the treatment of dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative conditions.

Collectively, the therapeutic history of SKF96365 demonstrates that while it has been a valuable experimental tool for elucidating Ca²⁺ dynamics in a wide array of tissues—including ocular cells—it has not yet been translated into a clinical therapeutic for conditions such as dry AMD. Its continued use in preclinical studies helps to support the strategy of targeting calcium dysregulation; however, concerns over its off-target activity underline the challenges inherent in repurposing a broadly acting ion channel modulator for chronic degenerative diseases (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Irnaten et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
III. MECHANISM OF ACTION

A detailed understanding of the mechanism of action of SKF96365 provides important insights into both its potential utility and its limitations as a therapeutic candidate. SKF96365 was originally characterized as an inhibitor of receptor-mediated calcium entry, a function that was later expanded upon with the identification of TRP channels. Mechanistically, SKF96365 has been shown to inhibit receptor-operated and store-operated calcium entry pathways, acting as a noncompetitive, state-independent, and voltage-insensitive blocker—that is, it interferes with Ca²⁺ entry regardless of whether channels are in the closed, open, or inactivated state (Singh et al., 2010; Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011).

Electrophysiological studies in heterologous systems reveal that SKF96365 inhibits recombinant TRPC channel currents at IC₅₀ values generally in the low micromolar range (approximately 5–30 μM). However, a striking aspect of its pharmacological profile is its potent inhibition of low‐voltage‐activated T‐type calcium channels. For example, investigations using human CaV3.1 channels have determined an IC₅₀ of approximately 560 nM for SKF96365—a potency that is nearly an order of magnitude higher than that observed for TRPC channels (Singh et al., 2010). This inhibitory action on T‐type channels is consistent with findings in native tissue models such as rat cerebellar Purkinje cells, where SKF96365 produced profound and rapid blockade of T-type Ca²⁺ currents.

The molecular basis for SKF96365’s broad channel blockade likely involves a direct interaction with the ion permeation pores of these channels. While the detailed binding site has not been unequivocally defined, evidence suggests that SKF96365 interacts allosterically with channel structures, leading to pore block without significantly altering the kinetics of channel activation or inactivation. This mode of inhibition appears to be state-independent, meaning that channel blockade occurs irrespective of the channel’s conformational state (Singh et al., 2010). In addition to its effects on TRPC and T-type channels, SKF96365 also impairs the function of high‐voltage‐activated calcium channels (including L‐type, P/Q‐type, and N‐type channels) when used at typical concentrations employed in TRPC channel studies (Singh et al., 2010).

Beyond calcium channels, the compound has been reported to exhibit off-target activities against other ion channels and cellular components. For instance, it has been shown to inhibit certain potassium channels, interfere with sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase activity, and even affect nicotinic receptor function in some cellular contexts (Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011; Singh et al., 2010). This promiscuity in channel blockade is a double-edged sword: on one hand, it increases the overall capacity of SKF96365 to alter intracellular Ca²⁺ dynamics; on the other hand, it complicates the attribution of specific physiological or pathological outcomes solely to TRPC inhibition.

From a molecular perspective, TRPC channels in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) are thought to contribute to the maintenance of basal calcium levels that are requisite for key cellular processes such as phagocytosis and endolysosomal trafficking. Although SKF96365 was not originally designed with ocular applications in mind, its ability to inhibit these channels makes it a candidate for modulating disrupted Ca²⁺ signaling in RPE cells—a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Zhao et al., 2015). However, the breadth of SKF96365’s mechanism of action means that at concentrations required to modulate TRPC channel activity within the RPE, the compound is very likely to concurrently block other calcium channel subtypes. This scenario is corroborated by data demonstrating that at 10 μM, SKF96365 can block recombinant channels from all three major voltage-gated calcium channel classes, including CaV1 (L-type), CaV2 (P/Q-, N-type), and CaV3 (T-type) channels (Singh et al., 2010).

The molecular consequences of such broad calcium blockade include an overall reduction in Ca²⁺ influx, which could normalize cytosolic Ca²⁺ transients if they are aberrantly elevated but might also disrupt other calcium-dependent signaling cascades necessary for healthy cellular function. In the context of RPE cells, where tightly regulated Ca²⁺ oscillations are critical for proper phagosome–lysosome fusion and photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation, this balance is particularly delicate. The potential therapeutic benefit of SKF96365 in dry AMD thus hinges on its ability to recalibrate Ca²⁺ homeostasis without triggering deleterious off-target effects (Singh et al., 2010).

─────────────────────────────  
IV. EXPECTED EFFECT IN DRY AMD

Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by progressive RPE dysfunction, abnormal calcium signaling, impaired phagocytosis of POS, and subsequent accumulation of toxic deposits such as lipofuscin. In healthy RPE cells, calcium regulation is essential for several cellular processes, including the fusion of phagosomes with lysosomes—a step that is critical for the degradation of shed photoreceptor outer segments. Dysfunction in these calcium-dependent events is believed to contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2015; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

The central hypothesis under consideration is that SKF96365 will modulate Ca²⁺ influx through TRPC channels in RPE cells, with an approximate IC₅₀ near 5 μM, thereby normalizing cytosolic Ca²⁺ transients. This normalization is expected to restore proper Ca²⁺ dynamics that drive efficient phagosome trafficking and lysosome fusion. In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells—the human cell line commonly employed as a model for RPE physiology—demonstrate that disrupting abnormal Ca²⁺ entry can lead to improved co-localization of lysosomal markers such as LAMP1 with intracellular phagosomes. The increased co-localization is taken as an indicator of enhanced phagosome–lysosome fusion and, consequently, more effective degradation of POS (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

In practical terms, if SKF96365 is able to restore near-physiological Ca²⁺ transients in the RPE, the process of phagosome maturation would likely proceed more efficiently. Under normal conditions, following the ingestion of photoreceptor outer segments, phagosomes are trafficked through a maturation process involving early endosomal (e.g., Rab5-positive) and late endosomal/lysosomal (e.g., Rab7-, LAMP1-positive) steps before complete degradation occurs (Zhao et al., 2015; Keeling et al., 2018). By counteracting the dysregulation in Ca²⁺ entry, SKF96365 could theoretically help re-establish the kinetics of phagosome–lysosome fusion and POS clearance, which might slow or prevent the accumulation of deleterious deposits in RPE cells—a hallmark of dry AMD progression.

Moreover, evidence from ocular research suggests that SKF96365 has been applied in experimental settings beyond RPE studies. For instance, in lamina cribrosa cells—a cell type implicated in glaucomatous pathology—SKF96365 at concentrations around 10 μM was able to mitigate oxidative stress–induced profibrotic gene expression. While this study was not focused on AMD, the fact that the compound could safely modulate Ca²⁺-dependent signaling pathways in an ocular context lends indirect support to the idea that similar mechanisms might be harnessed in RPE cells (Irnaten et al., 2020).

However, a critical aspect of the expected effect is the balance between beneficial TRPC channel inhibition and detrimental off-target blockade. Because SKF96365 potently blocks T-type calcium channels (with an IC₅₀ near 560 nM) and also affects high-voltage-activated channels, there is a substantial risk that, at concentrations effective for TRPC modulation, the compound will inhibit additional calcium channels necessary for other vital RPE functions. As a result, while the anticipated normalization of Ca²⁺ transients may promote phagosome maturation and enhance LAMP1 co-localization with phagosomes, the broad inhibitory profile could also lead to unintended suppression of other calcium-dependent processes that maintain RPE cell homeostasis (Singh et al., 2010).

In summary, the expected effect of SKF96365 in dry AMD is twofold. First, it is anticipated to reduce pathological Ca²⁺ overload in RPE cells by inhibiting aberrant TRPC channel activity, thereby restoring the intracellular Ca²⁺ signaling required for phagosome–lysosome fusion. Second, this normalization is expected to improve the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments, which, in turn, would reduce the accumulation of cellular debris that contributes to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. Nonetheless, these effects must be interpreted with caution given the compound’s propensity for off-target interactions, which may complicate its overall benefit-risk profile (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Singh et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2015).

─────────────────────────────  
V. OVERALL EVALUATION

Evaluating SKF96365 for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD requires a careful weighing of its mechanistic rationale against the limitations imposed by its pharmacological profile. On the strength side, SKF96365 offers a compelling mechanism based on decades of research linking Ca²⁺ dysregulation to RPE dysfunction. Its ability to inhibit TRPC channels—a family of ion channels that contribute to the maintenance of basal Ca²⁺ levels and are critical for processes such as phagosome trafficking and lysosome fusion in RPE cells—directly addresses a known pathological mechanism in dry AMD (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007). The hypothesis that normalization of aberrant Ca²⁺ transients can enhance the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments is well supported by experimental evidence demonstrating improved lysosomal marker co-localization in cultured RPE cells when Ca²⁺ entry is moderated (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

Additionally, SKF96365 has an established track record as an ocular research tool. Studies in lamina cribrosa cells in glaucoma models have shown that the compound can be administered at ocularly relevant concentrations with observable functional effects on Ca²⁺-dependent gene expression without immediate cytotoxicity (Irnaten et al., 2020). This observed ocular safety in short-term studies lends some support to its potential translation into an ocular therapeutic context. Moreover, the broader utility of SKF96365 in modulating intracellular Ca²⁺ has been confirmed in a variety of preclinical models, ranging from glioma cell lines to endothelial cells, highlighting its robustness as a Ca²⁺ channel inhibitor (Singh et al., 2010).

However, several significant weaknesses temper the overall enthusiasm for direct repurposing of SKF96365 as a treatment for dry AMD. The foremost limitation is its lack of selectivity. Although SKF96365 inhibits TRPC channels in the micromolar range, it concurrently blocks other calcium channels—most notably T-type channels—with a potency that is approximately ninefold greater than that for TRPC channels (Singh et al., 2010). Such potent off-target blockade is problematic because T-type calcium channels, along with L-type and other voltage-gated channels, are essential for a multitude of cellular functions within the retina and the central nervous system. Their inadvertent inhibition could lead to compromised cellular viability and dysregulation of signaling cascades that extend beyond phagosome clearance in the RPE (Singh et al., 2010).

Another critical concern is the compound’s broad spectrum of activity. In addition to its effects on TRPC and T-type channels, SKF96365 has been shown to inhibit high-voltage-activated calcium channels, interfere with potassium channel conductance, inhibit sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase activity, and even modulate nicotinic receptor function (Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011; Pena & Ordaz, 2008). The concomitant blockade of these various ion channel systems increases the risk that systemic or even localized ocular administration of the compound will produce off-target adverse effects that may compromise both retinal and extra-retinal cell functions. In the context of dry AMD—a chronic degenerative condition that would likely require long-term therapy—the risk of cumulative toxicity or dysregulation of fundamental Ca²⁺-dependent processes is particularly concerning.

Moreover, while mechanistic studies in cell culture models (such as ARPE-19 cells) have provided valuable insights into SKF96365’s role in modulating Ca²⁺ signaling, there is a distinct lack of in vivo data demonstrating its efficacy in models of dry AMD. The retinal environment in vivo is complex, with contributions from multiple cell types—including RPE, photoreceptors, microglia, and vascular endothelial cells—and is subject to intricate immune and inflammatory interactions. The translation of in vitro findings to in vivo efficacy, especially for a compound with a narrow therapeutic index resulting from overlapping inhibitory concentrations for TRPC versus T-type channels, remains a formidable challenge (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Irnaten et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2010).

A further limitation is that the expected benefit—namely, the normalization of Ca²⁺ transients to restore phagolysosomal fusion—relies on a very specific modulation of intracellular signals. RPE cells exhibit highly regulated calcium oscillations that are critical not only for phagocytosis but also for maintaining cellular metabolism, gene expression, and autophagic processes. Given that SKF96365 is a nonselective inhibitor, it is likely to perturb these tightly controlled Ca²⁺ signaling networks in ways that are not entirely predictable. Such disturbances might lead to unintended alterations in RPE function, potentially exacerbating rather than ameliorating the compromised homeostasis seen in dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2010).

Finally, while there is some evidence in ocular contexts from glaucoma models, the chronic administration required for a degenerative disease such as dry AMD has not been explored. Long-term safety studies in animal models, coupled with detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic analyses, are necessary to fully assess whether SKF96365 could be safely repurposed for ocular use. The risk of systemic absorption and off-target effects in the central nervous system or cardiovascular tissues cannot be ignored, given the compound’s known actions on multiple ion channel types (Irnaten et al., 2020; Maier et al., 2015).

In weighing these strengths and weaknesses, SKF96365 appears to offer valuable proof-of-concept evidence that modulating Ca²⁺ influx through TRPC channels can impact processes relevant to RPE phagosome trafficking and POS clearance. However, the compound’s broad-spectrum inhibition, particularly its potent T-type calcium channel blockade, undermines its candidacy as a safe, selective, and effective therapeutic agent for dry AMD. Consequently, while SKF96365 remains an important pharmacological tool in dissecting the role of Ca²⁺ signaling in RPE physiology, its direct repurposing for clinical treatment of dry AMD would require significant chemical refinement—or the development of derivative compounds with improved selectivity—to narrow its inhibitory spectrum and thus enhance its therapeutic index (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

─────────────────────────────  
VI. CONCLUSION

In conclusion, the comprehensive literature review indicates that SKF96365, a synthetic imidazole derivative initially developed as an inhibitor of receptor-mediated calcium entry, demonstrates robust activity against a variety of calcium channels—including TRPC channels that contribute to basal Ca²⁺ influx in retinal pigment epithelial cells. Its ability to modulate Ca²⁺ transients provides a mechanistically attractive hypothesis for restoring proper phagosome–lysosome fusion and enhancing photoreceptor outer segment clearance—which are central to the pathogenesis of dry age-related macular degeneration (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

Nonetheless, significant challenges temper its clinical potential. The compound’s nonselectivity, evidenced by its potent blockade of low-voltage-activated T-type channels (IC₅₀ ~560 nM) and its concurrent inhibition of high-voltage-activated calcium channels and other ion channel systems, severely narrows the feasible therapeutic window (Singh et al., 2010; Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011). The risk that, at effective doses intended to normalize RPE Ca²⁺ signaling, SKF96365 might inadvertently suppress essential calcium-dependent processes is nontrivial, especially given the delicate balance of Ca²⁺ homeostasis required in the RPE for photoreceptor maintenance and survival (Singh et al., 2010; Maier et al., 2015).

Furthermore, although preclinical in vitro evidence in ARPE-19 cells and similar models is promising, there remains a critical gap in in vivo data specific to dry AMD. The complex interplay of cellular, molecular, and environmental factors in the human retina poses considerable hurdles for the translation of cell culture findings to clinically relevant outcomes. In addition, the chronic nature of AMD necessitates long-term safety and efficacy data—information that is currently lacking for SKF96365 in the context of ocular therapeutics (Irnaten et al., 2020; Maier et al., 2015).

Given these considerations, SKF96365 may best be regarded at this stage not as a final drug candidate for dry AMD therapy, but rather as a lead compound that validates the strategy of targeting aberrant Ca²⁺ signaling within RPE cells. Future research should focus on chemically optimizing SKF96365 to enhance its selectivity for TRPC channels while minimizing off-target interactions with T-type, L-type, and other voltage-gated channels. Parallel investigations into alternative TRPC modulators with a narrower pharmacological profile may also prove fruitful. In any case, rigorous preclinical studies—including in vivo models of dry AMD—are imperative before clinical translation can be contemplated (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

Ultimately, the therapeutic strategy of modulating Ca²⁺ influx to restore phagosome–lysosome fusion and improve POS clearance in RPE cells remains a compelling avenue for treating dry AMD. SKF96365 offers a valuable starting point and proof-of-concept, but its broad-spectrum ion channel inhibition necessitates careful re-engineering to achieve the necessary balance between efficacy and safety. Only with further chemical refinement, targeted in vivo validation, and comprehensive toxicity evaluation can such a compound be advanced toward clinical trials for dry AMD (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Zhao et al., 2015).

─────────────────────────────  
OVERALL EVALUATION SUMMARY

• Overview of the Candidate:  
SKF96365 is a synthetic imidazole derivative belonging to the broad-spectrum TRP channel blockers, originally developed to inhibit receptor-mediated Ca²⁺ entry. Its chemical structure and modifications enable it to interact with multiple Ca²⁺ channels, making it a useful tool in experimental Ca²⁺ signaling studies (Singh et al., 2010; Harteneck, Klose, & Krautwurst, 2011).

• Therapeutic History:  
While extensively used in preclinical studies—including in retinal pigment epithelial cells and ocular models such as lamina cribrosa cells—SKF96365 has not yet been applied in clinical or veterinary settings for dry AMD. Its application has primarily been limited to research investigations aimed at deciphering Ca²⁺-dependent cellular mechanisms (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Irnaten et al., 2020).

• Mechanism of Action:  
The compound functions as a nonselective inhibitor of Ca²⁺ entry. It shows moderate potency against TRPC channels (IC₅₀ ~5–30 μM) but exhibits much greater potency against T-type Ca²⁺ channels (IC₅₀ ~560 nM). Its inhibition is non-competitive, state-independent, and voltage-insensitive, indicating a broad and allosteric pore-blocking mechanism (Singh et al., 2010).

• Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, SKF96365 is hypothesized to restore calcium homeostasis in RPE cells by modulating aberrant TRPC-mediated Ca²⁺ entry. This, in turn, is expected to enhance phagosome–lysosome fusion and improve the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments—a process critical for preventing the toxic accumulation of cellular debris that characterizes dry AMD (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Zhao et al., 2015).

• Overall Evaluation:  
Despite a strong mechanistic rationale and promising in vitro data indicating that modulation of Ca²⁺ signaling can improve RPE function, the broad off-target effects of SKF96365 represent a significant challenge. Its potent inhibition of T-type and high-voltage-activated calcium channels, along with other ion channels, undermines its potential as a therapeutic agent. The lack of in vivo data in AMD models and concerns over long-term ocular safety further limit its immediate clinical applicability. Therefore, while SKF96365 remains an invaluable research tool, it appears better suited as a lead compound for further optimization rather than as a final candidate for dry AMD therapy (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

─────────────────────────────  
FINAL RECOMMENDATION

Based on the detailed literature review, SKF96365 offers a proof-of-concept for the modulation of disrupted Ca²⁺ signaling—a pathway critically implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. However, its inherent nonselectivity, especially the potent blockade of T-type Ca²⁺ channels at concentrations that overlap with those required for TRPC channel inhibition, poses significant concerns regarding both efficacy and safety in the RPE in vivo. The compound’s reported ocular safety in acute glaucoma models is encouraging but insufficient to guarantee tolerability during chronic administration required in dry AMD. Therefore, while SKF96365 validates the general approach of normalizing Ca²⁺ transients to enhance phagosome–lysosome fusion, further chemical optimization to improve selectivity for TRPC channels is essential before advancing toward clinical evaluation for dry AMD. Future studies should pivot toward either developing derivatives with a narrower spectrum of activity or employing combination strategies that mitigate its off-target effects, while concurrently establishing robust preclinical models to evaluate long-term outcomes in the retina (Singh et al., 2010; Irnaten et al., 2020).

In conclusion, SKF96365 represents a scientifically intriguing candidate as a modulator of Ca²⁺ dynamics with potential implications for the treatment of dry AMD. However, its nonselective mode of action underscores the need for further research and chemical refinement. Until these issues are addressed, SKF96365 should be regarded primarily as an experimental tool for validating the role of Ca²⁺ signaling in RPE dysfunction rather than as a direct therapeutic option for dry AMD.

Zinc sulfate (ZnSO₄; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. Z0251) is an inorganic salt that dissociates readily in aqueous solutions to yield zinc ions (Zn²⁺) and sulfate anions. Zinc sulfate is a well‐characterized compound produced via chemical synthesis and has been used for decades as a nutritional supplement to treat zinc deficiency. Historically, the use of zinc in medical treatments dates back to its role as an essential trace element in numerous biological systems. In the context of ocular diseases, mounting evidence has implicated zinc deficiency in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Although many of these reports have employed zinc ionophores (e.g., ClioQ, 1H10) to facilitate zinc delivery into cells, they highlight a fundamental therapeutic rationale: zinc is an essential cofactor for proper lysosomal enzyme function, and its supplementation can reverse key features of cellular dysfunction associated with dry AMD (Choi et al., 2024). Clinical approaches, particularly those emerging from the AREDS trials, have also shown that high-dose zinc supplementation (typically delivered as zinc oxide or zinc sulfate) can slow the progression of AMD (Qin, 2007). While these formulations primarily aimed to address generalized zinc deficiency and oxidative stress, they establish a precedent for the repurposing of zinc salts—specifically zinc sulfate—in ocular disorders such as dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, zinc acts as an indispensable cofactor for a multitude of enzymes, including the zinc-dependent cathepsins B and L. Cathepsins are lysosomal proteases critical for the degradation of phagocytosed POS, autophagic cargo, and other intracellular substrates that accumulate over time. In the RPE, the efficient clearance of POS is a daily and metabolically demanding process; thus, any impairment in cathepsin activity can lead to the accumulation of undegraded material, contributing to the formation of lipofuscin and subsequent cellular toxicity (Julien et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2024). Zinc ions contribute structurally and catalytically to the proper folding and activity of these cathepsins. Under conditions of zinc deficiency or altered intracellular zinc distribution—as has been observed in aged RPE and AMD patients—the activity of cathepsin B and L becomes suboptimal, leading to lysosomal dysfunction (Julien et al., 2011; Rajapakse et al., 2017).

Several reports have demonstrated that exposure to bisretinoids such as A2E leads to dose-dependent cell death and lysosomal alkalinization in ARPE-19 cells; this in turn impairs the activity of lysosomal hydrolases that require an acidic environment for optimal function (Choi et al., 2024). Zinc supplementation, when delivered intracellularly via ionophores in these models, restored lysosomal acidification and enabled the reactivation of the degradative machinery, including zinc-dependent enzymes (Choi et al., 2024). This reacidification is crucial because lysosomal proteases, including cathepsin B/L, demonstrate maximal catalytic activity at a pH of approximately 4.5–5.0—a condition that is disrupted in diseased RPE cells (Choi et al., 2024). Moreover, zinc has been shown to influence autophagy dynamics: in models where A2E treatment led to an arrest in autophagic flux (evidenced by increased p62 and LC3-II levels), zinc supplementation was able to reduce p62 levels and partially restore proper autophagic turnover (Choi et al., 2024). These observations suggest that zinc not only acts as a structural cofactor for lysosomal enzymes but also indirectly supports the maintenance of lysosomal pH homeostasis and autophagic function. The proposal under evaluation extends this line of reasoning by hypothesizing that direct supplementation with Zn²⁺—provided in the form of zinc sulfate—could similarly restore cathepsin B/L activity in RPE cells, thereby improving phagolysosomal enzyme function and photoreceptor outer segment degradation in dry AMD models (Choi et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Based on the aforementioned mechanistic rationale, the expectation is that ZnSO₄ supplementation will elevate intracellular Zn²⁺ concentrations in RPE cells, thereby reconstituting the proper activity of zinc-dependent enzymes. In the context of dry AMD, where lysosomal dysfunction is a key pathological feature, the restoration of cathepsin function is anticipated to improve the degradation of POS. Successful clearance of POS is critical to prevent the buildup of lipofuscin and other deleterious aggregates that contribute to RPE degeneration (Rajapakse et al., 2017). In cell-based assays—such as those using ARPE-19 cells exposed to A2E—the addition of zinc sulfate is hypothesized to act by increasing the bioavailability of Zn²⁺, which in turn would lead to several interrelated outcomes: (1) reacidification of lysosomes as zinc supports proton pump function and stabilizes lysosomal membranes, (2) enhanced enzymatic activity of cathepsins B and L, leading to improved proteolytic clearance, and (3) restoration of autophagic flux as evidenced by decreased p62 accumulation and normalized LC3-II turnover (Choi et al., 2024; Rajapakse et al., 2017). Furthermore, improved phagolysosomal function would likely reduce the intracellular accumulation of A2E and other toxic by-products, ultimately leading to increased cell viability and better overall RPE function. It is important to note that although many of the existing studies have utilized zinc ionophores to deliver Zn²⁺ into cells, the existing ocular safety profile for zinc sulfate formulations (as evidenced by previous clinical studies using zinc sulfate eye drops) supports the feasibility of adapting ZnSO₄ for this application (Qin, 2007). Moreover, gene expression studies confirm that RPE cells express high levels of cathepsin B and L, and their dysfunction correlates with AMD pathogenesis; thus, elevating Zn²⁺ levels may have a directly beneficial impact on these key enzymatic pathways (Julien et al., 2011).

Overall Evaluation  
The repurposing of zinc sulfate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on several well-founded observations. First, there is a robust body of preclinical evidence indicating that zinc supplementation can restore lysosomal function in RPE cells challenged with A2E-induced toxicity, which is a well-characterized in vitro model of dry AMD (Choi et al., 2024). This evidence includes improvements in lysosomal pH, reductions in A2E accumulation, and restored autophagic flux. Second, clinical data from large-scale studies such as AREDS have established that zinc supplementation—albeit delivered in a different form than zinc sulfate—confers a statistically significant reduction in the progression risk of AMD (Qin, 2007). Third, mechanistic studies have underlined the pivotal role of zinc as a cofactor for cathepsin B and L, enzymes that are crucial for the phagolysosomal degradation of POS. In the diseased state, reductions in zinc availability or disruptions in zinc homeostasis result in diminished cathepsin activity, impaired clearance of cellular debris, and subsequent lipofuscin accumulation (Julien et al., 2011; Rajapakse et al., 2017).

Despite these strengths, the candidate does have notable limitations. A significant concern is that most of the supportive in vitro studies have used zinc ionophores (such as ClioQ or 1H10) to ensure efficient intracellular delivery of zinc (Choi et al., 2024). Zinc sulfate, being a simple salt, does not possess intrinsic ionophore properties, which may limit its immediate cellular uptake and availability to lysosomal compartments. This suggests that while ZnSO₄ has a favorable safety profile and is easily formulated, its efficacy in rescuing intracellular cathepsin activity may be contingent on formulation strategies that enhance cellular uptake, such as combining it with a permeation enhancer or designing specialized delivery vehicles. Additionally, direct evidence linking zinc sulfate supplementation to the restoration of cathepsin B/L activity in RPE cells is currently inferred from studies using alternative zinc delivery methods rather than from studies employing ZnSO₄ directly (Rajapakse et al., 2017). Therefore, while the hypothesis is strongly supported by mechanistic reasoning and parallel evidence from related studies, targeted experiments specifically using ZnSO₄ in models of dry AMD are necessary to confirm its therapeutic potential.

Another consideration is the multifactorial nature of AMD pathogenesis. While lysosomal dysfunction and cathepsin impairment are certainly central features, AMD is also driven by oxidative stress, inflammation, and complement dysregulation. Zinc exerts broader antioxidant effects partly through its involvement in metallothionein systems and by modulating the activity of antioxidant enzymes (Rajapakse et al., 2017). Thus, while restoring cathepsin activity represents a compelling mechanistic target, zinc sulfate supplementation might also confer additional benefits that go beyond enzyme cofactor replacement. However, these pleiotropic effects may complicate the interpretation of the therapeutic outcomes, making it challenging to ascribe clinical benefits solely to the restoration of cathepsin activity.

In summary, zinc sulfate represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD on several fronts. Its inherent ability to donate Zn²⁺, a cofactor crucial for the activity of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsins B and L, forms the basis of its proposed mechanism of action. Preclinical evidence indicates that zinc supplementation can restore lysosomal pH, reduce A2E accumulation, and enhance autophagic flux in RPE cells—key elements that underpin the pathological cascade of dry AMD (Choi et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical trial data from studies using zinc compounds, including those with zinc sulfate formulations as ocular drops, further underscore the potential efficacy and safety of zinc-based therapies in AMD (Qin, 2007). Nevertheless, the translational success of ZnSO₄ hinges on addressing the challenge of effective cellular uptake. Without the use of an ionophore or an advanced delivery system, there is a risk that ZnSO₄ may not achieve the intracellular zinc concentrations required to modulate cathepsin activity and, by extension, lysosomal function in a robust manner. Additionally, while mechanistic studies have provided indirect evidence linking zinc levels to cathepsin function in RPE cells (Julien et al., 2011), direct validation of the therapeutic hypothesis with ZnSO₄ remains limited.  

Strengths of the candidate include its well-established production, favorable safety profile in ocular applications, and substantial supporting evidence from both preclinical and clinical studies that underscore the importance of zinc in maintaining lysosomal integrity and protease function (Choi et al., 2024; Rajapakse et al., 2017). The repurposing strategy is bolstered by a strong theoretical rationale: correction of zinc deficiency in the RPE should restore cathepsin effectiveness and thereby improve the degradation of POS, a function known to be compromised in dry AMD (Choi et al., 2024).

Conversely, weaknesses include the fact that most experimental paradigms demonstrating zinc’s benefits have relied on assisted delivery mechanisms (ionophores) and have not been directly replicated with zinc sulfate alone. This introduces uncertainty regarding the bioavailability of zinc ions when administered as ZnSO₄ in the intended therapeutic context. Furthermore, AMD is a complex, multifactorial disease, and while addressing lysosomal enzyme dysfunction is promising, it remains only one aspect of the overall pathology. Without addressing complementary pathological mechanisms such as chronic oxidative stress and inflammation, zinc sulfate alone may not suffice as a standalone therapy. Finally, the lack of direct evidence from ZnSO₄-specific studies in relevant dry AMD models (as opposed to studies using zinc ionophores) highlights the need for further targeted research before progressing to clinical trials.

Overall, the evaluation of zinc sulfate as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a strong theoretical foundation conditioned on its role as a zinc donor to rescue Zn-dependent cathepsin activity in the RPE. The candidate leverages a well-known mechanism where zinc acts both structurally and catalytically within lysosomal proteases, and clinical data from related zinc supplementation studies provide an encouraging backdrop. However, the translational challenges concerning the effective delivery of Zn²⁺—particularly in the absence of an ionophore—must be carefully addressed. In conclusion, zinc sulfate exhibits considerable potential as part of a multifaceted therapeutic strategy targeting lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD, with the caveat that further studies are needed to optimize its delivery, validate its mechanism in precise AMD models, and integrate it effectively within a broader therapeutic regimen that tackles the multifactorial nature of the disease (Choi et al., 2024; Qin, 2007).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO‐Me) is a fully synthetic derivative of the naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid oleanolic acid. The parent molecule, oleanolic acid, is widely found in many plants and has been used for centuries in traditional medicine owing to its modest anti‐inflammatory and hepatoprotective properties. However, to overcome its relatively low intrinsic potency and poor pharmacokinetics, medicinal chemists modified oleanolic acid by introducing key structural changes. In particular, the synthesis of CDDO (2-cyano-3,12-dioxoolean-1,9-dien-28-oic acid) involved the installation of a cyano group at the C2 position and oxidation at positions C3 and C12, generating an electrophilic cyanoenone moiety; subsequent esterification at the C28 carboxyl group yielded bardoxolone methyl as the C28 methyl ester. These chemical modifications resulted in a molecule with two electrophilic Michael acceptor sites that are essential for its biological action, notably its ability to react reversibly with cysteine thiols in target proteins. Being part of the synthetic oleanane triterpenoids family, bardoxolone methyl falls into a class of compounds that has been extensively explored for their anti‐inflammatory, antioxidant, anticancer, and cytoprotective activities in various disease models (Borella et al., 2019).

This class of synthetic triterpenoids has historically been pursued to potentiate the natural but modest bioactivities of plant‐derived triterpenes such as oleanolic and ursolic acids. Early research aimed at enhancing anti‐inflammatory activity led to the discovery of potent derivatives such as CDDO, CDDO‐Im (the imidazolide derivative), and ultimately bardoxolone methyl. Their design was motivated by the need to generate highly potent, orally bioavailable agents capable of activating key cytoprotective pathways. The robust preclinical efficacy observed with these compounds in various models of oxidative stress, inflammation, and even tumorigenesis provided proof‐of‐concept for their use as drug candidates (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021). Consequently, bardoxolone methyl has emerged as a leading representative of this chemical class, notable for its finely tuned electrophilic reactivity and its ability to induce a broad spectrum of protective gene products.

Therapeutic History:  
Bardoxolone methyl has a well‐documented history of investigation in both preclinical and clinical settings across various therapeutic indications. Originally developed for its potent anti‐inflammatory and antioxidant properties, it was first investigated in oncology where its pro‐apoptotic and antiproliferative effects were characterized in multiple cancer cell types such as pancreatic, colorectal, ovarian, and breast cancer. Early preclinical studies demonstrated that at nanomolar and low micromolar concentrations, CDDO and its derivatives could exert robust cytoprotective effects via the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2‐related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, as well as induce cell cycle arrest and trigger apoptosis in cancer cells (Borella et al., 2019; Tanase et al., 2022).

Following its anticancer exploration, a serendipitous clinical observation during early oncology trials revealed that patients treated with bardoxolone methyl experienced improved renal function, as measured by an elevation in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). This finding prompted a pivot in therapeutic focus toward kidney diseases, particularly chronic kidney disease (CKD) associated with type 2 diabetes. The promising renoprotective data initially generated in Phase I oncology studies led to Phase II trials (such as the BEAM trial) where bardoxolone methyl displayed remarkable efficacy in increasing eGFR in CKD patients. However, in a subsequent Phase III study (the BEACON trial), concerns were raised after an unexpected increase in cardiovascular events, particularly heart failure, halted the trial. These mixed clinical outcomes have since spurred ongoing efforts to better understand and optimize the safety profile of bardoxolone methyl while leveraging its strong cytoprotective properties (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Sakashita et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).

Notably, while bardoxolone methyl has been extensively investigated in oncology and renal diseases, there is currently no record or published clinical trial data indicating that this compound has been used for treating dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or similar ocular conditions. Nonetheless, its underlying mechanism—primarily Nrf2 activation—is highly relevant to the pathobiology of dry AMD, given that oxidative stress and proteostasis imbalance are central to RPE cell dysfunction. Thus, while previous therapeutic applications have focused on systemic diseases, the repositioning of bardoxolone methyl to an ocular indication represents a scientifically plausible and innovative strategy that builds on its earlier demonstrated biochemical activities in other organ systems (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Bardoxolone methyl’s primary mode of action is its potent and selective activation of the Keap1/Nrf2/ARE (antioxidant response element) pathway. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytoplasm by its inhibitory binding partner Keap1, which targets Nrf2 for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl, owing to its electrophilic cyanoenone structure, covalently modifies reactive cysteine residues on Keap1 (including key sensors such as Cys151), thereby inhibiting its E3 ligase activity. This modification prevents the degradation of Nrf2, allowing it to accumulate and translocate into the nucleus (Hong et al., 2012; Mathis & Cui, 2016).

Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 dimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to ARE sequences in the promoter regions of various cytoprotective genes. This leads to the transcriptional induction of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxification enzymes, including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), glutathione S-transferases, and several molecular chaperones involved in protein folding and proteostasis. Through these gene products, bardoxolone methyl exerts robust antioxidant, anti‐inflammatory, and cytoprotective effects that help mitigate oxidative stress and repair cellular damage (Mathis & Cui, 2020; Tanase et al., 2022).

In addition to Nrf2‐mediated gene induction, bardoxolone methyl has been shown to modulate other signaling pathways that contribute to its anti‐inflammatory profile. For instance, it can inhibit NF-κB signaling, which reduces the transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines, and also affect pathways involving JAK/STAT and PI3K/Akt/mTOR, all of which have been implicated in the control of cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival (Sporn et al., 2011). The dual capacity to both upregulate protective gene networks and downregulate inflammatory signaling is central to the pharmacological action of bardoxolone methyl and underscores its potential to modulate cellular processes that are dysregulated in conditions characterized by oxidative and proteostatic stress (Cores et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014).

Furthermore, crystallographic and proteomic studies have provided molecular‐level evidence for the reversible Michael‐addition interaction between bardoxolone methyl and target cysteine residues on Keap1. This “dock and lock” mechanism ensures that the electrophilic reactivity of the compound is directed preferentially toward specific regulatory cysteines, thereby limiting non‐specific alkylation and supporting its relatively high potency as an Nrf2 activator (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
The hypothesis for repurposing bardoxolone methyl in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is grounded firmly in its ability to activate Nrf2 and thereby bolster the endogenous antioxidant defenses of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). In the RPE, oxidative damage is a pivotal pathomechanism that contributes to the accumulation of lipofuscin, impairment of autophagic flux, and ultimately, decreased phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). As Nrf2 plays a critical role in maintaining redox homeostasis within the RPE, its activation is expected to alleviate oxidative and proteostatic stress, thereby protecting critical functions such as phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation.

At an effective concentration in the submicromolar range (with an EC₅₀ estimated around 0.1 µM), bardoxolone methyl is anticipated to induce the transcription of genes such as HO-1 and NQO1 as well as chaperone proteins that ensure proper protein folding and degradation. The upregulation of these cytoprotective proteins may protect phagocytic receptors from oxidative modifications and preserve lysosomal enzymatic activity, which is essential for the degradation of ingested POS. This action is particularly crucial because impaired phagocytic function contributes to the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin and other debris in RPE cells—a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021).

Moreover, the robust activation of Nrf2 by bardoxolone methyl can help counterbalance the deficit in endogenous antioxidant capacity observed in the RPE of patients with dry AMD, as Nrf2 deficiency has been shown experimentally to exacerbate lipofuscin accumulation and autophagy blockade. Preclinical studies in non‐ocular systems have consistently demonstrated that treatment with CDDO‐Me leads to a marked increase in the expression of antioxidant genes and proteins that are implicated in both oxidative stress management and the maintenance of proteostasis (Hong et al., 2012; Sporn et al., 2011). Extrapolating from these findings, it is reasonable to expect that treatment with bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD cultures would result in a more effective clearance of POS by correcting the underlying oxidative imbalance and restoring lysosomal function. It is also plausible that enhanced expression of chaperones and stress‐response proteins would contribute to improved recycling of degraded photoreceptor material, thereby reducing the burden of intracellular debris (Cores et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014).

In addition, the effects of bardoxolone methyl on other signaling cascades—such as its inhibitory impact on NF-κB—could further reduce inflammatory responses within the RPE. Chronic inflammation is increasingly recognized as a contributing factor to AMD progression, and the suppression of pro‐inflammatory mediators would be expected to create a more favorable cellular environment for tissue repair and maintenance of RPE function (Sporn et al., 2011). Collectively, by activating Nrf2 and modulating inflammatory signaling pathways, bardoxolone methyl is expected to restore the cellular homeostasis of RPE cells, leading to enhanced phagocytosis of POS and potentially slowing or even reversing the degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Bardoxolone methyl represents an innovative and promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration, particularly given its well‐characterized ability to activate the Nrf2 pathway and trigger a potent antioxidant and proteostatic response. One clear strength of this compound is its robust preclinical and clinical profile in other indications; extensive studies in oncology and chronic kidney disease have established its capability to induce protective gene networks, coupled with a well‐defined mechanism of action that is directly applicable to combating oxidative stress—one of the central features of dry AMD pathogenesis (Borella et al., 2019).

From a mechanistic standpoint, bardoxolone methyl’s electrophilic structure enables it to interact in a highly regulated manner with the Keap1 protein. This interaction leads to the stabilization and nuclear translocation of Nrf2, culminating in the transcriptional activation of a spectrum of cytoprotective genes, including HO-1, NQO1, and various chaperones. These genes are known to be expressed in RPE cells and are essential for maintaining the integrity of phagocytic receptors and lysosomal enzymes that mediate POS clearance. Thus, the molecular rationale for its use in dry AMD is strong, as it addresses a fundamental aspect of RPE cell dysfunction (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Hong et al., 2012).

In terms of therapeutic history, while bardoxolone methyl has not previously been applied to ocular indications, its repositioning for dry AMD is scientifically warranted by the extensive evidence linking Nrf2 deficiency to the progression of RPE degeneration and lipofuscin accumulation. The previously observed benefits in non‐ocular systems, such as improvements in renal function via Nrf2 activation, support the idea that similar cytoprotective processes could be beneficial in the eye, particularly if local delivery or ocular formulation approaches can be developed to maximize efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure (Sakashita et al., 2021; Tanase et al., 2022).

Nevertheless, there are several challenges and weaknesses that must be carefully considered. First, the systemic use of bardoxolone methyl has been marred by significant cardiovascular safety concerns, as evidenced by the terminated BEACON trial in CKD patients. Although these adverse events were observed in a systemic context and might be mitigated by localized (for example, intravitreal) administration in the eye, they nonetheless raise caution regarding the compound’s off‐target effects and overall safety profile. The intrinsic electrophilicity that underlies its mechanism also bears the potential risk of non‐specific protein modification and cytotoxicity if not carefully controlled, particularly in a delicate tissue such as the retina (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014).

Second, while preclinical ocular safety data are being cited as supportive evidence for repositioning, robust and comprehensive studies specific to retinal tissues and RPE cell models must be undertaken to confirm that the drug does not induce unintended damage or disrupt other vital functions of the retina. Pharmacokinetic challenges—such as achieving and maintaining an effective therapeutic concentration in the RPE without eliciting systemic exposure—will also need to be addressed. The EC₅₀ for Nrf2 activation in RPE is hypothesized to be approximately 0.1 µM, and this level must be reliably achieved in an ocular setting, ideally through controlled‐release formulations or targeted delivery systems (Cores et al., 2020).

An additional consideration is the complexity of dry AMD itself, which is influenced not only by oxidative stress and impaired autophagy but also by chronic low‐grade inflammation, complement dysregulation, and extracellular matrix alterations in Bruch’s membrane. Although bardoxolone methyl’s anti‐inflammatory effects via NF-κB inhibition are a potential asset, it remains to be determined how these multiple pathways will interact within the unique microenvironment of the retina. Tailored preclinical studies that specifically evaluate the compound’s impact on POS clearance, RPE phagocytosis, and lysosomal function in models of dry AMD are essential to validate the underlying hypothesis (Sporn et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2014).

On the strength side, the repositioning of bardoxolone methyl is supported by its extensive clinical investigation in other indications. The existence of Phase I and II human data provides a valuable foundation regarding dosing, pharmacokinetics, and some aspects of safety, which can significantly de‐risk early translational studies in the ocular domain. The compound’s well‐documented capacity to activate Nrf2—a pathway known to be highly relevant in the aging RPE and in the pathogenesis of dry AMD—further underscores its potential utility. Moreover, the synthetic nature of bardoxolone methyl facilitates the possibility of further chemical optimization and the development of novel formulations (such as nanoparticle‐ or liposome‐based ocular delivery systems) that may enhance its safety and efficacy profile when administered locally (Borella et al., 2019; Borella et al., 2019; Sporn et al., 2011).

In summary, bardoxolone methyl appears to be a promising candidate for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration based on its potent Nrf2‐activating properties and its capacity to upregulate antioxidant and proteostasis genes. These effects could theoretically restore and enhance the phagocytic function of RPE cells, thereby improving the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and reducing lipofuscin accumulation—a central pathogenic feature of dry AMD. While the repurposing hypothesis is scientifically sound and mechanistically compelling, the unique challenges of ocular drug development must be navigated cautiously (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2014; Thomas, 2012; Dao et al., 2015).

Bardoxolone methyl’s robust mechanistic action as an Nrf2 activator—coupled with its documented preclinical and early clinical efficacy in other indications—positions it as a highly attractive repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its molecular design, derived from oleanolic acid and enhanced through strategic electrophilic modifications, underpins a powerful ability to upregulate antioxidant defenses and restore proteostasis. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB202190 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor belonging to the pyridinyl imidazole class of compounds. Originally discovered through rigorous cell‐based phenotypic screens aimed at identifying agents with anti‐inflammatory properties, SB202190 was developed to selectively inhibit p38 mitogen‐activated protein kinase (MAPK), particularly the α and β isoforms. The molecule was first characterized using radiolabeled ligand binding studies, which confirmed its ability to bind the ATP‐binding pocket of p38 MAPK and suppress its catalytic function (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). Being available commercially (e.g., Sigma‐Aldrich Cat. No. SML0687), SB202190 has been widely used as a biochemical tool to dissect the role of p38 in cellular stress and inflammatory responses. This class of compounds, including SB203580 as a closely related analogue, is recognized for its ability to modulate intracellular signaling cascades under various stress conditions. They have been broadly used in research settings to probe the molecular basis of cytokine production, cell differentiation, apoptosis, and cytoskeletal regulation (Young, 2013; Maugeri et al., 2021). The candidate under discussion is being repurposed with the hypothesis that its high potency against p38α/β—exhibiting an IC₅₀ of approximately 40 nM—can be leveraged to correct stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling defects and improve the phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative stress conditions that mimic the pathophysiology of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Liu et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, SB202190 has been predominantly employed as a research reagent to interrogate the role of p38 MAPK signaling in various cell types and disease models. In the context of ocular studies, SB202190, similar to its analogue SB203580, has been used to examine fibrotic responses, cell migration, and cytokine production in RPE cells. For instance, several in vitro studies have demonstrated that inhibition of p38 MAPK by SB202190 effectively reduces TGF‐β2–induced extracellular matrix (ECM) production (specifically collagen type I and fibronectin synthesis), which serves as an experimental surrogate for fibrotic remodeling observed in retinal degenerative conditions (Saika et al., 2005). Moreover, experiments using ARPE‐19 human RPE cells have revealed that SB202190 can reverse abnormal cell migration and reduce the transformation of RPE cells into fibroblast‐like cells in models of proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) (Saika et al., 2005). Although these models do not directly replicate dry AMD, they capture key aspects of RPE dysfunction, such as cytoskeletal disorganization and aberrant ECM deposition, which are also implicated in the progression of AMD. Beyond ocular research, p38 MAPK inhibitors have been investigated in other pathologies characterized by chronic inflammation and stress‐induced cellular dysfunction, including rheumatoid arthritis and muscular dystrophies (Brennan et al., 2021; Hirosawa et al., 2009). However, to date, clinical applications of SB202190 itself have not been pursued, and its use has remained restricted to preclinical experimental studies, thereby providing both a strong mechanistic rationale and a cautionary note regarding its translational potential (Federspiel et al., 2023; Young, 2013). Importantly, while numerous studies have elucidated p38 MAPK’s involvement in retinal injury and oxidative stress responses, there is limited direct clinical evidence supporting the use of SB202190 for treating dry AMD, and its application in this indication remains strictly hypothetical at this stage (Moustardas et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB202190 is known to selectively target the ATP‐binding pocket of p38 MAPK, thereby inhibiting its enzymatic activity and preventing the phosphorylation of downstream substrates that are pivotal to stress‐induced signaling cascades. Under normal conditions, p38 MAPK becomes activated through dual phosphorylation on specific threonine and tyrosine residues within its activation loop. Once activated, p38 MAPK stimulates various substrates, including transcription factors (e.g., cFos) and regulatory proteins involved in the control of cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and inflammatory mediator production (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). In RPE cells, activation of p38 MAPK has been linked to cytoskeletal rearrangements that lead to stress‐induced cellular defects; these include formation of abnormal actin structures and impaired formation of phagocytic cups necessary for the internalization of POS (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). In the experimental setting, SB202190 has been shown to effectively block the TGF‐β2 mediated phosphorylation of p38, thereby reducing the transcriptional activity of Smad3/4 complexes without impacting the initial receptor‐mediated phosphorylation events of Smads2/3. This mechanism suggests that SB202190 acts downstream of TGF‐β receptor activation, interfering with p38‐dependent enhancement of transcription factor complex formation and nuclear translocation, which in turn can dampen pathological ECM production and abnormal cell migration (Saika et al., 2005). Additionally, literature indicates that stress‐activated p38 signaling contributes to the senescence of RPE cells by regulating the senescence‐associated secretory phenotype (SASP) through modulation of p53 and NF‐κB pathways (Liu et al., 2025). By inhibiting p38 MAPK, SB202190 is hypothesized to replicate the protective effects of endogenous negative regulators such as DUSP4, which dephosphorylate and inactivate p38 MAPK, ultimately reducing RPE cell senescence and maintaining cellular homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025). It is noteworthy that p38 MAPK signaling is intricately intertwined with other MAPK family members, and some studies have reported that SB202190, particularly at higher doses, exhibits a biphasic response where alternative signaling pathways (such as MEK/ERK) may become upregulated, emphasizing the importance of careful dose optimization in any therapeutic application (Wang et al., 2024; Hirosawa et al., 2009). Thus, the mechanism of action of SB202190 involves a highly specific inhibition of p38α/β kinase activity, which is expected to restore normal actin dynamics and cytoskeletal organization in RPE cells, thereby facilitating proper phagosome formation and efficient POS uptake under oxidative stress conditions akin to those found in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The primary hypothesis driving the repurposing of SB202190 for dry AMD is that inhibition of p38α/β in RPE cells will reduce stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling defects and thereby improve the phagocytic internalization of photoreceptor outer segments. Under oxidative stress conditions, such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) in in vitro models using ARPE‐19 cells, activation of p38 MAPK is known to mediate cytoskeletal disorganization and promote aberrant cell migration, processes that are deleterious to the RPE’s phagocytic function (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). By inhibiting p38 MAPK with SB202190 at a low nanomolar concentration (approximately 40 nM), it is anticipated that the compound will reduce the phosphorylation of p38, thereby preventing the downstream activation of stress‐responsive transcription factors and proteins responsible for actin remodeling (Young, 2013; Hirosawa et al., 2009). In doing so, SB202190 is expected to “normalize” the actin cytoskeletal dynamics in H₂O₂‐treated ARPE‐19 cells, thus facilitating the re‐establishment of properly organized phagocytic cups required for POS ingestion—a process critical for photoreceptor maintenance and overall retinal homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025; Saika et al., 2005). In parallel, inhibition of p38 MAPK may downregulate pro‐fibrotic and pro‐senescent signaling pathways (e.g., those mediated by TGF‐β2, p53, and NF‐κB), therefore limiting the aberrant deposition of ECM components and improving the overall cellular microenvironment (Liu et al., 2025; Saika et al., 2005). As a result, the expected effect of SB202190 in the assay proposed would be a significant improvement in phagosome internalization of POS under oxidative conditions, combined with a reduction in the markers of cytoskeletal stress and cell senescence. Moreover, enhanced phagocytic activity by RPE cells could mitigate pathological features of dry AMD, such as drusen formation and eventual RPE degeneration, thereby potentially slowing disease progression (Moustardas et al., 2023; Du et al., 2010). The compound’s effect is further anticipated to extend to modulation of inflammatory cytokine release, given the well‐established role of p38 MAPK in regulating cytokine production, thus providing a dual benefit by both preserving cytoskeletal integrity and reducing chronic, low‐grade inflammation in the retina (Liu et al., 2025; Kyosseva, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
Evaluating the potential of SB202190 as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD involves weighing both the strengths and the inherent challenges associated with targeting the p38 MAPK pathway in the RPE. One of the major strengths of SB202190 is its well‐characterized mechanism of action as a selective inhibitor of p38α/β, which is pivotal in mediating stress‐induced cytoskeletal remodeling, inflammation, and cellular senescence in RPE cells. The compound has demonstrated robust in vitro anti‐fibrotic and anti‐migratory effects in ARPE‐19 cell models that mirror key features of RPE dysfunction observed in dry AMD (Saika et al., 2005). Furthermore, the concept of normalizing actin dynamics to enhance phagocytic cup formation and subsequent POS uptake is highly attractive, given that impaired phagocytosis is a core feature driving the degeneration observed in dry AMD (Pocrnich et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024). The protective role played by endogenous regulators like DUSP4, which deactivates p38 MAPK and preserves RPE integrity, supports the rationale for a pharmacological approach that mimics this effect (Liu et al., 2025). Additionally, numerous studies have shown that p38 MAPK inhibitors can modulate inflammatory responses and reduce ECM deposition; such effects are promising in the context of retinal diseases where chronic inflammation and fibrosis exacerbate degenerative processes (Moustardas et al., 2023; Saika et al., 2005).

However, several weaknesses and potential caveats must be thoroughly considered. First, the p38 MAPK pathway exhibits complex, context‐dependent behavior in RPE cells. There is evidence suggesting that, under certain circumstances, p38 MAPK activation can be cytoprotective by facilitating adaptive stress responses, such as the upregulation of antioxidant defenses (Pocrnich et al., 2009). This duality indicates that complete or prolonged inhibition of p38 MAPK may inadvertently dampen protective signaling, potentially leading to adverse outcomes. Additionally, published studies have documented that SB202190, when used at higher concentrations, can show biphasic responses or off‐target effects that might include the unintended activation of alternative MAPK pathways (Wang et al., 2024; Hirosawa et al., 2009). This underscores the critical need for precise dose optimization and comprehensive pharmacodynamic studies to define a therapeutic window where the beneficial effects on cytoskeletal remodeling and phagocytosis are maximized while the risks of impairing physiological stress responses are minimized.

Furthermore, while the preclinical literature provides substantial mechanistic insights and supportive data from retinal injury models—particularly in contexts such as PVR—the clinical translation of these findings to dry AMD remains unproven. SB202190 has not been advanced into clinical trials for retinal degenerative diseases, and its application has thus far been confined to experimental paradigms (Kim et al., 2021; Kyosseva, 2016). Therefore, any proposal to repurpose SB202190 for dry AMD must be accompanied by robust in vivo efficacy studies using animal models that faithfully recapitulate the chronic, multifactorial nature of the disease. Moreover, the impact of SB202190 on other critical RPE functions, such as phagocytosis of POS under normal conditions and cytoskeletal dynamics related to cell adhesion and migration, needs to be extensively characterized to avoid unintended disruption of essential homeostatic processes (Kim et al., 2021; Kyosseva, 2016).

Another consideration is the limitation inherent to the use of SB202190 as a research tool rather than a clinical‐grade pharmaceutical compound. Its pharmacokinetic and safety profiles have been characterized in experimental contexts, but there is a lack of clinical data regarding potential ocular toxicity, bioavailability, and long‐term impact on retinal structure and function (Federspiel et al., 2023; Young, 2013). The multifaceted role of p38 MAPK in the retina—spanning inflammatory cytokine production, regulation of apoptosis, and cytoskeletal dynamics—means that a fine balance must be maintained; excessive suppression could lead to undesired consequences such as impaired wound healing or compromised cell survival under stress. As such, a detailed understanding of the dose‐response relationship and the temporal dynamics of p38 inhibition in specific RPE subpopulations will be essential.

In summary, SB202190 presents as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on strong mechanistic rationale and preclinical evidence supporting its ability to modulate pathological pathways implicated in RPE dysfunction. Its capacity to inhibit p38α/β with high potency, restore actin dynamics under oxidative conditions, and improve phagocytic function aligns well with the therapeutic goals of preserving RPE integrity and retinal homeostasis (Liu et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the dualistic nature of p38 MAPK signaling—with its capacity to mediate both deleterious and protective responses—poses a significant challenge that mandates careful and comprehensive preclinical evaluation. The candidate’s strengths reside in its well‐characterized inhibitory activity, established use in modulating fibrotic and inflammatory responses in ocular models, and its potential to replicate the endogenous protective functions mediated by regulators such as DUSP4 (Liu et al., 2025). Conversely, the weaknesses center on potential off‐target effects, the risk of inadvertently suppressing adaptive stress responses, and the absence of clinical studies directly addressing dry AMD.

Overall, while SB202190 holds promise based on its molecular mode of action and supportive in vitro data regarding cytoskeletal normalization and phagocytosis, the translational viability for dry AMD will ultimately depend on rigorous dosing studies, long‐term safety assessments, and demonstration of efficacy in animal models that capture the chronic oxidative and inflammatory milieu of the human retina (Moustardas et al., 2023; Saika et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2024). Only through such comprehensive studies can we adequately determine whether SB202190’s benefits outweigh its potential risks and if it can be successfully repurposed as a therapeutic intervention to mitigate the progression of dry AMD.
