Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
AMY-101 is a third-generation compstatin analogue built on the Cp40 scaffold, a cyclic, disulfide-constrained peptide discovered through iterative structure–activity optimization of the original compstatin hit identified by phage display against C3/C3b in 1996 (initial macrocycle I[CVVQDWGHHRC]T) (Lamers et al., 2022). Key potency-improving modifications en route to Cp40 include N-methylation of Trp and insertion of sarcosine, which rigidify the backbone and substantially increase binding affinity to C3; Cp40 (y-I[CV(1Me)WQDWSarAHRC]mI) binds a defined pocket between MG4/MG5 on the β-chain of C3/C3b with subnanomolar affinity and high selectivity for human and nonhuman primate (NHP) C3, while sparing other species, thereby necessitating NHP for translational in vivo work (Lamers et al., 2022). Mechanistically, compstatins are protein–protein interaction inhibitors: they occupy a substrate-binding site on C3 that prevents association with the C3 convertases, blocking convertase-mediated cleavage of native C3, and thereby interrupting the amplification loop and downstream effector generation (C3a, C3b, C5a, and membrane attack complex) independent of the initiating pathway (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Compstatin analogues comprise a class of synthetic macrocyclic peptides that target the central node of complement activation at C3, distinguishing them from terminal-pathway blockers (e.g., C5 antibodies) and alternative-pathway–restricted inhibitors (e.g., factor D), which have shown mixed outcomes in complex complement-driven diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Mastellos et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Clinically, the compstatin platform has matured to produce both a PEGylated bivalent C3 inhibitor (pegcetacoplan/APL-2) approved for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and non-PEGylated Cp40-derived candidates such as AMY-101 in human trials, establishing class translatability and safety management paradigms for chronic C3 inhibition (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

For ophthalmic translation, medicinal chemistry on Cp40 has produced fourth-generation, non-PEGylated lysine-extended derivatives (Cp40-KK, Cp40-KKK) with markedly improved solubility and favorable intraocular retention after intravitreal (IVT) administration in NHPs; these scaffolds maintain subnanomolar C3 affinity and exhibit retinal tissue engagement and co-localization with C3, suggesting target-driven distribution in ocular compartments (Hughes et al., 2020). Within the compstatin clinical lineage, earlier intravitreal compstatin (POT-4) and the PEGylated derivative APL-2/pegcetacoplan provided clinical benchmarks in geographic atrophy (GA), albeit with formulation-dependent considerations (e.g., PEG-associated risks) that motivate PEG-free ocular candidates such as AMY-101 or next-generation Cp40 analogues tailored for ocular delivery (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Compstatin peptides have undergone extensive preclinical characterization and early clinical translation across complement-driven indications. Systemically, Cp40/AMY-101 blocked intravascular hemolysis and C3b opsonization in primate models and attenuated alloimmune responses and downstream B/T cell activation in transplantation models, demonstrating potent complement control and immunomodulatory ripple effects in vivo (Lamers et al., 2022). AMY-101 progressed through a first-in-human phase 1 trial (single and multiple ascending doses; subcutaneous and intravenous) with acceptable safety, no serious adverse events, and pharmacodynamic evidence of complement pathway modulation in healthy volunteers (Amyndas Pharmaceuticals S.A., 2017), and subsequently achieved local-delivery efficacy in a randomized, double-blind, split-mouth Phase IIa study for gingival inflammation with durable anti-inflammatory responses and no drug-induced immunogenicity detected (Hasturk et al., 2021). In the periodontal trial, AMY-101 reduced clinical indices (modified gingival index, bleeding on probing) and decreased matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-8, MMP-9) in gingival crevicular fluid, with effects persisting up to 90 days after the three weekly local injections, supporting local tolerability, biomarker responsiveness, and sustained pharmacodynamic action (Hasturk et al., 2021).

Within ophthalmology and AMD, multiple lines of evidence support the clinical plausibility of C3-directed strategies. Early intravitreal compstatin (POT-4) dosing in a primate model was associated with disappearance of drusen deposits, and PEGylated C3 inhibition (APL-2/pegcetacoplan) reduced GA lesion growth in Phase II and has achieved efficacy signals in Phase III, representing the first successful complement intervention in GA and validating the target class for dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). Conversely, downstream or pathway-restricted modulation disappointed: anti-C5 agents (eculizumab, LFG316) and alternative pathway blockade at factor D (lampalizumab) failed to deliver clinical benefit in GA, bolstering the rationale for upstream C3 control that addresses both opsonization and effector generation (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Although AMY-101 itself has not yet been reported in human ocular trials in the provided context, Cp40-class derivatives have been tailored for ocular use and evaluated in NHPs after single IVT injections, achieving prolonged C3-saturating vitreous concentrations and retinal/choroidal target engagement for over three months—exposure metrics compatible with infrequent intravitreal maintenance regimens (Hughes et al., 2020).

Critically, human iPSC-derived RPE models carrying the common CFH Y402H high-risk variant establish a mechanistic and phenotypic bridge to AMD and provide in vitro evidence that Cp40 reverses disease-relevant pathology, particularly lysosome/autophagy defects and complement-driven lysosomal overburden, thereby directly supporting the translational concept for dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The RPE findings are reinforced by the broader AMD complement literature: complement activation on photoreceptor outer segments drives monocyte-dependent retinal atrophy, factor H genetics (including Y402H) modulates ocular alternative pathway activity, and complement deposition in Bruch’s membrane/sub-RPE space contributes to drusen biogenesis and RPE stress—elements that are mechanistically addressable by C3 blockade (Mastellos et al., 2019).

In sum, compstatin-class agents have an extensive preclinical pedigree and emergent clinical validation. For AMD specifically, the class has ocular proof-of-concept (POT-4) and clinical validation of C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan), and Cp40 analogues demonstrate prolonged ocular PK in NHP; AMY-101 contributes human safety and local-delivery experience that supports translational risk management but requires dedicated ocular development for dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
C3 sits at the convergence of the classical, lectin, and alternative complement pathways; its cleavage by C3 convertases (C4b2b for CP/LP and C3bBb for AP) produces the anaphylatoxin C3a and the opsonin C3b, which seeds an amplification loop by forming additional alternative pathway convertases on activating surfaces (Mastellos et al., 2019). Persistent generation and deposition of C3b (and downstream C5b-9) under dysregulated conditions fuels inflammatory tissue damage and membrane injury; thus, targeting C3 offers initiation-independent suppression of both opsonization and effector generation (C3a, C5a, MAC), addressing multiple pathogenic modalities concurrently (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Compstatins, including Cp40/AMY-101, are substrate-protecting inhibitors that bind to a defined site on C3/C3b (between MG4 and MG5 of the β-chain) and prevent the binding of native C3 to the active convertase, thereby blocking C3 turnover and the AP amplification cycle regardless of initiating pathway (Lamers et al., 2022). This binding mode is supported by co-crystallographic and kinetic analyses, and SAR has established critical roles for N-methylated Trp and charged residues (Asp7, Arg12) in affinity and solubility (Lamers et al., 2022). Unlike some PEGylated bivalent constructs that display altered target preference and weaker affinity to soluble C3, monovalent PEG-free Cp40 binds strongly to both soluble and surface-bound C3/C3b, preserving potency where soluble target is abundant (e.g., in plasma and vitreous), a beneficial profile for local ocular delivery (Lamers et al., 2022).

In human iPSC-RPE carrying CFH Y402H, C3 overactivation and increased C3 turnover correlate with multiple autophagy–lysosome abnormalities: increased expression of autophagosome markers (LC3-II, p62, ATG12–ATG5), expansion and activation of late endosomal/lysosomal/exosomal compartments (LAMP1, CD63; increased Lysotracker), reduced lysosomal functional readouts (decreased Cathepsin D expression/activity), swollen lysosome-like vesicles, lysosomal membrane fragility (elevated galectin-8 recruitment), and extracellular deposition of Cathepsin D in ApoE-positive drusen-like material (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Mechanistic links are twofold: (1) excessive extracellular C3 activation increases surface C5b-9 (MAC) formation, which is internalized to lysosomes and triggers lysosomal membrane permeabilization with cathepsin leakage; (2) intracellular C3–autophagy crosstalk via ATG16L1 and cathepsin-mediated C3 activation may perturb autophagy flux, compounding lysosomal stress (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In this model, Cp40 reduces C3 turnover (biochemical ELISA/MSD readouts) and diminishes C3b and C5b-9 deposition on and within RPE, leading to restoration of lysosomal pH/function and autophagic flux (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Specifically, Cp40 treatment increases Cathepsin D expression/activity, reduces lysosome size and swelling, stabilizes lysosomal membranes (reduced galectin-8/LAMP co-localization), normalizes melanosome content (increased mature type 4 melanosomes), and decreases the volume of drusen-like deposits on transwells—collectively, a reversal of RPE disease phenotypes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Importantly, the RPE data underscore that “tuning” C3 is necessary: stable shRNA knockdown of C3 (~85% reduction) did not restore melanosome/lysosome number and increased stress vacuoles indicative of a detrimental effect, whereas pharmacologic Cp40-mediated control of C3 turnover (not wholesale depletion) was beneficial—consistent with C3’s homeostatic roles in tissue clearance and immune surveillance (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Rapamycin-driven autophagy activation failed to correct lysosomal deficits in the same AMD-RPE model, underscoring that upstream removal of complement burden may be required to re-enable autophagic clearance in complement-dysregulated RPE (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

For ophthalmic PK/PD, next-generation Cp40 derivatives (Cp40-KK, Cp40-KKK) demonstrate prolonged vitreous residence and target engagement after single IVT injection in cynomolgus NHPs, measured by a sensitive SPR-based competition assay that recovers peptide from C3 complexes by heat dissociation and quantifies active inhibitor; ocular C3 levels were assayed in parallel (Hughes et al., 2020). Following a 0.5 mg IVT dose, Cp40-KKK maintained C3-saturating vitreous concentrations over three months (~200 nM during month 1; ~100–120 nM by month 3) and co-localized with C3 in retinal/choroidal tissue, suggesting target-driven retention and possible depot release; intraocular C3 concentrations measured were ~0.1–2 nM, implying inhibitor:target ratios sufficient for sustained pharmacodynamic coverage (Hughes et al., 2020). Only ~0.2% of the initial dose remained unbound in vitreous by day 14, consistent with rapid clearance of free peptide and prolonged persistence of target-bound pools (Hughes et al., 2020). These PK relationships, combined with AMY-101’s subnanomolar C3 affinity and prolonged plasma half-life (>60 h), support the feasibility of durable local complement control via IVT compstatin analogues without PEGylation (Lamers et al., 2022; Hasturk et al., 2021; Lamers et al., 2022).

Expected Effect  
In the proposed iPSC-RPE assay, AMY-101/Cp40 is expected to bind native C3 in the extracellular milieu and block its convertase-mediated cleavage, thereby suppressing both C3a/C3b generation and downstream terminal-pathway activation, including formation and lysosomal internalization of C5b-9 complexes that exacerbate lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cathepsin leakage in complement-dysregulated RPE (Lamers et al., 2022; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The RPE model provides direct biochemical and cell-biological readouts that respond to C3 inhibition: Cp40 reduced C3 turnover (C3b/iC3b/C3c in supernatants), decreased surface and lysosomal C3b and C5b-9, and restored lysosomal functional markers (Cathepsin D expression and activity), organelle morphology (reduced lysosomal swelling; increased mature melanosomes), and membrane integrity (decreased galectin-8 recruitment), with associated reductions in drusen-like deposit burden—outcomes that would be expected for AMY-101 under similar conditions (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Given the measured RPE complement activity and the presence of C3 in ocular compartments, PD monitoring can include extracellular C3 fragment profiling (e.g., MSD capture for C3a domain detecting C3b; ELISA for C3b/iC3b/C3c), surface and lysosomal C5b-9 immunostaining (e.g., co-localization with LAMP markers), and lysosomal/autophagy endpoints such as LAMP1/CD63 expression, LysoTracker signal, LC3-II and p62 accumulation, Cathepsin D protein/activity, and galectin-8–based lysosomal damage assays (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In the referenced RPE studies, effective Cp40 exposure used 6 µM for seven days with media change mid-course—a regimen that achieved robust biochemical and morphological rescue; potency in cellular systems is governed by high target abundance and convertase dynamics and may not mirror biochemical IC₅₀ values, but AMY-101’s subnanomolar C3 affinity and the low-nanomolar ocular C3 concentrations measured in NHP vitreous suggest that pharmacologically relevant free drug levels in the assay will saturate target (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). We note that no direct IC₅₀ for Cp40/AMY-101 in RPE culture is provided in the cited work; therefore, the proposed IC₅₀ value (~0.5 µM) cannot be confirmed from the current context and dosing should be guided empirically by the established 6 µM exposure used to reverse phenotypes in the Y402H model (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Regarding photoreceptor outer segment (POS) processing, impaired lysosomal function in RPE is causally linked to defective POS degradation; complement activation on POS can drive monocyte-dependent retinal atrophy, providing disease-relevant context for expecting that restoration of lysosomal flux via C3 inhibition would secondarily improve POS handling (Mastellos et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). However, the provided RPE studies did not explicitly report POS uptake/degradation assays in Cp40-treated cells, so POS-specific rescue should be treated as a testable hypothesis rather than an established outcome; lysosomal/autophagy restoration and reduced complement burden provide a mechanistic basis for such improvement (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

For translational extrapolation to IVT dosing paradigms, ocular PK from Cp40-KK/KKK in NHP indicates that non-PEGylated Cp40 analogues can achieve multi-month C3-saturating exposure (retinal/choroidal co-localization with C3), which, combined with AMY-101’s high-affinity binding and absence of PEG (avoiding anti-PEG immunogenicity and PEG-related tissue effects), supports feasibility of infrequent dosing with a favorable mechanistic risk–benefit profile (Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
– Mechanistic centrality and breadth of action at C3: AMY-101 directly blocks the C3 convertase–substrate interaction, upstream of opsonization and effector generation, thereby intercepting multiple pathogenic drivers operative in dry AMD (C3b deposition, C3a/C5a-mediated inflammation, and MAC-mediated membrane injury), in contrast to pathway-restricted or terminal-pathway agents that have underperformed in GA (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). By protecting C3 from cleavage rather than inhibiting a specific convertase assembly, AMY-101 exerts initiation-independent control, appropriate for the complex and mixed complement activation modes present in AMD (Hasturk et al., 2021).  
– Direct human RPE disease-model evidence: In Y402H iPSC-RPE, Cp40 suppressed C3 turnover and downstream C5b-9 deposition, relieved lysosomal overburden and membrane fragility, restored Cathepsin D expression/activity and melanosome maturation, and reduced drusen-like deposits—an unusually comprehensive, mechanistically coherent rescue of AMD-relevant cellular pathology that maps directly onto the hypothesized mode of action for AMY-101 (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Ocular PK/translational feasibility: Single IVT dosing of Cp40 lysine-extended derivatives in NHPs yielded >90 days of C3-saturating intraocular exposure with retinal/choroidal target engagement and co-localization, supporting achievable, infrequent dosing intervals for a PEG-free compstatin platform; methods to quantify ocular drug and C3 (SPR competition; ELISA) and retinal localization are validated and can be deployed for PD monitoring (Hughes et al., 2020).  
– Clinical precedent for the target class in GA and systemic safety: Pegcetacoplan’s efficacy in reducing GA growth validates C3 inhibition in dry AMD; prolonged systemic C3 inhibition has an acceptable safety profile with appropriate vaccination and monitoring, and AMY-101 itself showed favorable safety, lack of anti-drug antibodies, and durable local efficacy in a human local-delivery setting (periodontal disease) (Lamers et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2020; Hasturk et al., 2021).  
– PEG-free design: Non-PEGylated Cp40 analogues avoid PEG-associated liabilities (anti-PEG antibodies, tissue vacuolation, and potential association with CNV conversion observed in a subset of GA patients on PEGylated C3 inhibitors), while maintaining strong affinity for soluble C3—attributes favorable for chronic ocular use (Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

– No human ocular clinical data for AMY-101: Despite compelling RPE in vitro data and NHP ocular PK for related derivatives, AMY-101 lacks reported human ocular PK/safety and clinical efficacy data in AMD in the provided context; bridging studies will be required to confirm ocular tolerability, immunogenicity, and dosing intervals specific to AMY-101 (Lamers et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2020).  
– Species specificity constrains preclinical breadth: Compstatins bind human/NHP C3 with high specificity, precluding meaningful small-animal efficacy studies beyond surrogate approaches; this increases reliance on NHP for ocular PK/PD and toxicity packages and complicates broader in vivo AMD model validation (Lamers et al., 2022).  
– POS degradation not yet demonstrated under Cp40 in RPE: Although lysosomal/autophagy restoration strongly predicts improved POS clearance, the provided RPE studies did not report POS uptake/degradation assays post-Cp40; this is an essential disease-relevant endpoint to include in the next-stage validation (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Need to balance complement suppression: Stable C3 knockdown in the RPE model exacerbated stress phenotypes, underscoring the necessity for controlled pharmacologic inhibition rather than depletion; clinical protocols must monitor for under/over-suppression and preserve homeostatic complement roles in the immunoprivileged ocular environment (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Potential safety/biology caveats with C3 blockade in the eye: Theoretical risks include modulation of macrophage polarization that might favor neovascularization and the necessity to maintain anti-infective surveillance locally; although systemic experience with vaccination mitigates infectious risk, ocular-specific risks and CNV conversion propensity must be assessed prospectively for PEG-free C3 inhibitors (Mastellos et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2020). Patient stratification (“complotype”) and baseline complement activity vary with age/sex and genetics (e.g., CFH), necessitating biomarker-driven inclusion and response frameworks in trials (Mastellos et al., 2019).

Decision-grade Assessment and Development Plan  
– Scientific validity: Strong. The AMD-RPE disease biology is directly addressed by AMY-101’s mechanism, with robust iPSC-RPE rescue data for Cp40 spanning biochemical, organellar, and deposit readouts; the mechanism integrates with known complement–lysosome–autophagy crosstalk and MAC-induced lysosomal permeabilization (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Translational feasibility: Good, with defined tasks. Ocular PK/PD in NHPs for Cp40 derivatives is compelling and suggests IVT dosing intervals of 2–3 months; AMY-101 has favorable systemic/local safety credentials and is PEG-free (Hughes et al., 2020; Hasturk et al., 2021). The absence of human ocular data for AMY-101 is a remediable gap.  
– Comparative landscape: Favorable. Factor D and C5 failures in GA argue for upstream intervention; C3 inhibition has shown clinical benefit (pegcetacoplan), placing AMY-101 in a validated mechanistic class, with potential safety advantages from PEG-free design and strong affinity to soluble C3 (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).  
– Key risks: Ocular safety (immunogenicity, inflammation, CNV conversion), pharmacodynamic over-suppression, and unknowns around long-term retinal tissue distribution with AMY-101 (as distinct from Cp40-KKK). These will be addressed with staged NHP toxicology/PK, dosing optimization, and clinical biomarker surveillance (Hughes et al., 2020; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Recommended studies before IND for dry AMD  
1) In vitro translational package in human iPSC-RPE (Y402H and non-risk): reproduce Cp40 rescue with AMY-101 under identical conditions (6 µM; 7-day dosing), including biochemical C3 turnover (C3b/iC3b/C3c), surface/lysosomal C5b-9, LAMP1/CD63, LysoTracker, LC3-II, p62, galectin-8, Cathepsin D expression and activity, melanosome quantitation, and drusen-like deposit volume (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Add POS feeding assays (pulse–chase of isolated POS) to quantify phagosome–lysosome fusion kinetics and rhodopsin degradation as POS-specific endpoints (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
2) Ocular PK and PD in cynomolgus NHPs with AMY-101: single- and multiple-dose IVT, vitreous/tissue levels by SPR competition assay, vitreous C3 fragments and C3:drug ratios, retinal/choroidal co-localization, and depot behavior versus Cp40-KKK; include dose ranging (≥0.5 mg) and extended sampling to ≥90 days (Hughes et al., 2020).  
3) Ocular safety/toxicology: GLP IVT studies (single and repeat-dose) evaluating inflammation, IOP, ERG, OCT/FAF, histopathology (RPE, choroid, retina), and immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies intraocular/systemic) with correlation to drug levels and C3 suppression; monitor for CNV risk signals (Mastellos et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2020).  
4) Biomarker strategy: translate RPE/animal biomarkers to clinical sampling—aqueous/vitreous C3 fragments, C5a, sC5b-9; imaging biomarkers (FAF for lipofuscin; OCT for outer retinal integrity; autofluorescent deposit quantification) to track pharmacodynamic effects on deposit burden and RPE health (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2020).  
5) Patient stratification plan: incorporate CFH Y402H and broader complotype profiling in trial design, with baseline complement activity and demographic modifiers (age, sex) to enrich for responders and appropriately power efficacy analyses (Mastellos et al., 2019).

Conclusion  
AMY-101 (Cp40) is a mechanistically precise, high-affinity C3 inhibitor whose action is well matched to the complement-driven lysosomal/autophagy pathology observed in dry AMD RPE biology; Cp40 has already demonstrated reversal of Y402H RPE disease phenotypes across orthogonal readouts, and Cp40-class ocular PK in NHPs supports infrequent IVT dosing without PEG, addressing practical treatment constraints (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The class has clinical validation in GA (pegcetacoplan) and an increasingly reassuring safety dossier for chronic C3 inhibition, while AMY-101 itself exhibits favorable human safety and local-delivery performance in non-ocular indications (Lamers et al., 2022; Hasturk et al., 2021). The principal development gaps—human ocular PK/safety for AMY-101 and POS-specific efficacy readouts—are tractable with focused preclinical and early clinical work. Taken together, the weight of mechanistic, cellular, and translational evidence supports advancing AMY-101 into an ophthalmic development path for dry AMD with a high likelihood of mechanistic efficacy and a manageable risk profile under a biomarker-driven, stratified clinical strategy (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB415286 is a synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK-3β) that belongs to the class of anilinomaleimide derivatives. It was discovered through high-throughput screening approaches using compound libraries such as that of SmithKline Beecham, where its ability to inhibit GSK-3β activity was identified in vitro with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range (approximately 20 nM) (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). As a representative of GSK-3β inhibitors, SB415286 has been widely used as a research tool to interrogate the role of GSK-3β in multiple biological processes including Wnt/β-catenin signaling, apoptosis, oxidative stress regulation, and autophagy. The chemical optimization of these compounds was driven by the need for greater potency and specificity in modulating complex kinase networks associated with neurodegenerative and ocular pathologies. SB415286 is commercially available (Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. SML0787) and exhibits properties that make it suitable for cell-based assays as well as animal studies targeting retinal cell functions (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In general, compounds in this class have been used in preclinical models to activate Wnt signaling by preventing β-catenin degradation, thereby enhancing transcription of genes involved in cell survival, differentiation, and tissue regeneration. This approach has been applied primarily in neurological research as well as in studies focusing on retinal degeneration, making SB415286 a candidate of interest for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
GSK-3β inhibitors as a class have a long history of preclinical exploration in various disease models, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and other neurodegenerative disorders where excessive kinase activity contributes to neuronal cell death. SB415286, in particular, has been used in primary neuronal cultures to elucidate the role of GSK-3β in mediating apoptotic pathways. Early studies demonstrated that inhibition of GSK-3β with compounds like SB415286 could protect neurons from intracellular stresses by moderately suppressing pro-apoptotic signals (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In the ocular field, GSK-3β inhibitors have been explored in the context of diabetic retinopathy, where their use was associated with improved retinal ganglion cell survival and mitigation of neurodegenerative processes induced by oxidative stress (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20). Furthermore, related compounds such as SB216763—sharing similar mechanisms—with evidence of restoring Nrf2 levels in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) under oxidative stress supports the hypothesis that GSK-3β inhibition is beneficial in ocular settings (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6; Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 10–12). Despite these promising findings, the clinical evidence directly linking GSK-3β inhibition to the treatment of dry AMD remains sparse. In fact, comprehensive analyses such as those performed using the Open Targets Platform have revealed only a very weak association between GSK3B and AMD with minimal literature evidence, suggesting that while the concept is scientifically sound and mechanistically plausible, direct translational studies in dry AMD are still in an early stage (Buniello et al., 2025). Nevertheless, the preclinical use of SB415286 in retinal models of diabetic retinopathy and its documented capacity to modulate pathways relevant to oxidative stress and autophagy imply that repurposing this candidate for dry AMD merits further investigation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, GSK-3β is a serine/threonine kinase that is constitutively active in many cells and functions as a pivotal regulator of several intracellular signaling cascades. Under basal conditions, GSK-3β phosphorylates its substrates—including β-catenin—thereby marking them for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. In the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, the inhibition of GSK-3β (either through upstream signals such as Wnt ligand binding or via pharmacological inhibitors like SB415286) prevents the phosphorylation of β-catenin, allowing it to accumulate in the cytoplasm and eventually translocate into the nucleus (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Once in the nucleus, β-catenin forms complexes with TCF/LEF transcription factors to drive the transcription of genes involved in cell proliferation, differentiation, and cytoskeletal remodeling. In the context of RPE cells, this activation is critical because it is believed to upregulate lysosomal proteins, such as LAMP1, and phagocytic receptors, like MERTK, that are essential for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17; Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).  

Moreover, GSK-3β also exerts a negative regulatory influence on the Nrf2/NRF2 antioxidant pathway. Under oxidative stress, Nrf2 typically transactivates a battery of cytoprotective genes; however, GSK-3β phosphorylates Nrf2 at specific motifs within its Neh6 domain, facilitating recognition by the β-TrCP E3 ubiquitin ligase and leading to its degradation (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6). Hence, inhibition of GSK-3β with SB415286 can stabilize Nrf2, thereby reinforcing the cellular antioxidant capacity—a particularly attractive mechanism given the elevated oxidative stress encountered in aging RPE cells in dry AMD.  

In addition to these signaling events, inhibition of GSK-3β modulates autophagy. Research indicates that proper autophagic flux is necessary for the turnover of damaged cellular components, including the disposal of POS debris, and that impaired autophagy is a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 10–12, 32–34). By inhibiting GSK-3β, SB415286 is hypothesized to promote the autophagy/Nrf2 axis, thereby enhancing lysosomal function and improving the clearance of accumulated waste products in RPE cells. It is also important to note that GSK-3β is implicated in the regulation of the cytoskeletal machinery; its inhibition may lead to reorganization of actin and other cytoskeletal elements, which is critical for the phagocytic process in RPE cells (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). However, caution is warranted because GSK-3β not only modulates beneficial pathways but also participates in processes such as epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), where excessive or inappropriate inhibition has been associated with fibrotic changes in the RPE (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 14–18). Thus, while the inhibition of GSK-3β by SB415286 is expected to elevate β-catenin levels and trigger downstream transcription of lysosomal and cytoskeletal genes, the balance of these signaling events must be carefully modulated to avoid adverse outcomes.

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis proposes that SB415286 will act directly on RPE cells by inhibiting GSK-3β, thereby releasing the inhibition on β-catenin. The resultant accumulation and nuclear translocation of β-catenin are expected to drive the transcription of a subset of genes critical for maintaining RPE function, including those involved in lysosome biogenesis (e.g., LAMP1) and the phagocytic machinery (e.g., MERTK). In dry AMD, a deficiency in the clearance of POS is a contributing factor to RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration, so enhancing gene expression that supports these processes is of significant therapeutic interest (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17).  

In cell-based assays—particularly flow cytometry-based phagocytosis assays—it is anticipated that treatment with SB415286 will result in an increased rate of POS uptake by RPE cells. This improvement in phagocytic efficiency is thought to arise from the upregulation of cytoskeletal genes that govern actin dynamics, which in turn facilitate the formation of phagocytic cups and subsequent internalization of photoreceptor debris (Bonnet et al., 2021, pp. 4–5; Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 32–34). Additionally, by relieving the negative regulation on Nrf2, SB415286 is expected to bolster the antioxidant defense mechanisms in RPE cells. The stabilization of Nrf2 not only aids in the upregulation of detoxification and radical-scavenging enzymes but also indirectly supports autophagy—a process crucial for the degradation of cellular waste and maintenance of cellular homeostasis in the aging RPE (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6).  

Furthermore, emerging data from ocular models of diabetic retinopathy provide supporting evidence that GSK-3β inhibitors can improve retinal cell survival and function. Although diabetic retinopathy and dry AMD are distinct conditions, both involve significant oxidative stress, inflammation, and RPE dysfunction. The translational potential observed in these models suggests that SB415286 may similarly ameliorate pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD by enhancing the phagocytic and lysosomal capacity of RPE cells (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20). Nevertheless, the dualistic nature of GSK-3β’s roles necessitates a cautious interpretation; while promoting β-catenin signaling is advantageous for lysosomal and cytoskeletal gene expression, overactivation of Wnt signaling has been implicated in unwanted cellular phenotypes such as EMT, which could potentiate fibrotic responses if not carefully controlled (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 14–18). Therefore, the expected beneficial effects of SB415286 on POS clearance must be weighed against the risk of activating other deleterious pathways.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating SB415286 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key aspects emerge from the literature review. On one hand, the compound’s potent inhibition of GSK-3β, a kinase centrally involved in multiple signaling pathways, offers a mechanistically coherent strategy for addressing several pathological features of dry AMD. By targeting GSK-3β, SB415286 is designed to simultaneously activate Wnt/β-catenin signaling and stabilize Nrf2, thereby promoting the transcription of genes such as LAMP1 and MERTK that are essential for effective lysosomal function and phagocytosis in RPE cells (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17). The induction of lysosomal and cytoskeletal genes is expected to enhance the phagocytic clearance of POS, a critical function that is often compromised in the diseased RPE, ultimately helping to mitigate the progression of dry AMD. Additionally, supportive evidence from diabetic retinopathy models and other retinal degeneration studies suggests that modulating GSK-3β activity can exert beneficial effects in ocular tissues (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20).  

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be considered. First, GSK-3β is a multifunctional kinase that plays roles in a wide array of cellular processes; it is involved not only in the regulation of the Wnt/β-catenin and Nrf2 pathways but also in the control of apoptosis, glucose homeostasis, and even inflammatory responses. The broad distribution and pleiotropic functions of GSK-3β raise concerns about off-target effects and unwanted side effects when its activity is pharmacologically inhibited. For instance, unchecked activation of β-catenin signaling could inadvertently promote epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in RPE cells—a process that has been linked to fibrotic changes and worsening of retinal pathology (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 14–18). The risk of such adverse outcomes underscores the importance of fine-tuning the dosage and exposure duration of SB415286 to achieve a therapeutic window that maximizes benefits while minimizing collateral activation of harmful signaling cascades.  

Another notable limitation is the relatively weak overall association between GSK3B and AMD as evidenced by integrative platforms, which point to only a minimal body of literature linking GSK-3β directly to the pathogenesis of AMD (Buniello et al., 2025). This weak association suggests that, although the mechanistic rationale for employing GSK-3β inhibitors is compelling at a biochemical level, direct evidence from AMD models remains limited. Consequently, while preclinical data in related retinal conditions are encouraging, additional research using dry AMD-specific models is required to establish the efficacy, safety, and dosing regimens for SB415286 in this context.  

Furthermore, the dual role of GSK-3β in both apoptosis and survival presents another layer of complexity. On one hand, inhibition of GSK-3β may protect RPE cells from intrinsic apoptotic stimuli by preventing the activation of mitochondrial death pathways; on the other hand, it may also inadvertently increase sensitivity to extrinsic apoptotic signals, thereby complicating the overall cellular response (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 2–5). This paradoxical effect, combined with the potential for overlap with other kinases given the structural similarity among kinase domains, necessitates rigorous pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic investigations to ensure that SB415286 can be administered safely without compromising RPE cell viability or function.  

In summary, SB415286 stands out as a promising repurposed drug candidate with a strong mechanistic foundation for the treatment of dry AMD. Its targeted inhibition of GSK-3β is expected to unleash β-catenin–driven transcriptional programs that upregulate lysosomal, cytoskeletal, and phagocytic genes, thereby enhancing the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments—a critical deficit in dry AMD pathology (Hyttinen et al., 2019, pp. 9–10; Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 16–17). The compound’s track record in preclinical ocular models, particularly in contexts where oxidative stress and autophagic impairment are prominent, supports its potential translational value (Hottin et al., 2022, pp. 5–6, 19–20). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ezetimibe (SCH-58235) is a synthetic small molecule developed as a specific inhibitor of intestinal sterol absorption and clinically positioned as an LDL-cholesterol–lowering agent and as therapy for rare sterol storage disorders such as sitosterolemia (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, 2001). Ezetimibe’s pharmacological class is “cholesterol absorption inhibitor,” a class characterized by selective action at the intestinal epithelium to reduce uptake of dietary and biliary cholesterol, thereby decreasing hepatic delivery of chylomicron-derived cholesterol, upregulating LDL receptor–mediated clearance, and lowering plasma LDL-C; in human and animal studies, agents in this class also increase fecal neutral sterol excretion and augment reverse cholesterol transport (RCT) from plasma to feces (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, 2001; Radiant Research, 2008; Ostlund, 2014; Bujold, 2012). Mechanistically, this class targets the Niemann–Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) protein at the apical surface of intestinal enterocytes, the principal protein-mediated pathway for sterol influx from mixed micelles; inhibition of NPC1L1 decreases absorption efficiency and increases fecal sterol output (Guo et al., 2024; Murillo, 2016; Bujold, 2012). Within ophthalmology, ezetimibe has been proposed in preclinical AMD literature as a systemic modulator of cholesterol handling that could mitigate diet-induced lipoprotein stress and downstream retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/Bruch’s membrane (BrM) pathology, but published ocular outcome data are not yet available (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). In short, ezetimibe is a clinically established synthetic NPC1L1 inhibitor designed to reduce intestinal sterol uptake and circulating atherogenic lipoproteins; its repurposing to dry AMD rests on the hypothesis that systemic lipid lowering will secondarily ameliorate RPE lipid burden and associated lysosomal/autophagy dysfunction (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Clinical use and systemic metabolic effects. Ezetimibe is an approved LDL-lowering therapy for hypercholesterolemia and sitosterolemia, typically dosed at 10 mg daily, and is widely used in combination with statins to achieve LDL targets with improved tolerability compared with high-intensity statin monotherapy in cardiovascular populations (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, 2001; Cho, 2023). Human metabolic studies using stable isotope tracers demonstrate that ezetimibe increases endogenous fecal neutral sterol excretion and reduces intestinal cholesterol absorption as expected for an NPC1L1 inhibitor; crossover and parallel-arm trials confirm effects on absorption efficiency and synthesis compensation, particularly when combined with statins (Radiant Research, 2008; Ostlund, 2014; Organon and Co., 2003). In randomized human feeding studies, ezetimibe reduces cholesterol absorption and lowers LDL-C; combined with phytosterols, effects on fecal sterols and LDL are additive, consistent with distinct yet complementary intestinal mechanisms (Washington University School of Medicine, 2009). In atherosclerosis-prone mice, ezetimibe reduces plaque burden; genetic deficiency of NPC1L1 similarly prevents atherosclerosis, and these intestinal manipulations enhance macrophage-to-feces RCT, implicating transintestinal cholesterol efflux (TICE) as a significant route for whole-body cholesterol disposal (Bujold, 2012).

Non-ocular lipid disease contexts. Beyond hypercholesterolemia, ezetimibe has been clinically evaluated in sitosterolemia (inherited sterol transport disorder), producing reductions in plasma plant sterols and LDL-C consistent with intestinal absorption blockade; protocols emphasize its role as a specific cholesterol absorption inhibitor in these patients (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, 2001). Multiple cardiovascular trials have examined ezetimibe’s LDL-lowering efficacy alone and in combination, and protocol summaries and meta-trials reiterate its intestinal mechanism and complementarity with statins (Organon and Co., 2003; Cho, 2023).

Ophthalmic/retinal disease history. The AMD preclinical literature reviewed by Landowski and Bowes Rickman identifies dietary cholesterol as a modifiable driver of AMD-like pathology in aged complement factor H (CFH) transgenic mice: high-fat, cholesterol-enriched (HFC) diets increase circulating lipoproteins, and aged CFH-H/H mice on HFC or high-cholesterol diets exhibit decreased scotopic ERG b-wave amplitudes; based on these observations, the authors propose that therapeutics reducing intestinal cholesterol uptake (citing ezetimibe) “may prevent visual loss in aged CFH-H/H HFC mice,” with ongoing studies to test whether ezetimibe can mimic dietary modulation and influence eyecup ApoB48 and ApoA-1 (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). However, those reports explicitly note that these are investigational questions; no completed preclinical data on retinal function, RPE lipid endpoints, autophagy, or lysosomal indices under ezetimibe treatment are presented in the cited excerpts (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). Reviews of lipid-lowering therapies in diabetic retinopathy (DR) list ezetimibe among LDL-lowering agents of interest but underscore the absence of large randomized controlled trials with DR endpoints and provide no ocular pharmacokinetic or safety data for ezetimibe; the text highlights that intraocular delivery can dramatically alter retinal exposure relative to systemic administration, underscoring a translational gap for systemically delivered LDL-modifying agents in ocular disease (Jenkins et al., 2022). Across the provided literature, there are no reports of ezetimibe being used to treat dry AMD or direct analogs (e.g., Stargardt disease) in humans, and no completed preclinical animal studies demonstrating ezetimibe-induced improvements in RPE lipofuscin, lysosome/autophagy function, photoreceptor survival, or drusen-like deposits (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary molecular target and tissue of action. The canonical molecular target for ezetimibe is NPC1L1, a sterol influx transporter localized to the apical membrane of small-intestinal enterocytes, which mediates uptake of dietary and biliary cholesterol from mixed micelles; blocking NPC1L1 reduces intestinal absorption and lowers delivery of cholesterol to the liver via chylomicrons, thus decreasing hepatic VLDL production and circulating LDL levels (Guo et al., 2024; Murillo, 2016). The LDL-lowering and fecal sterol-raising effects of ezetimibe in humans and mice, together with similar outcomes observed in NPC1L1 deficiency, support on-target action at the intestinal epithelium (Bujold, 2012; Radiant Research, 2008; Ostlund, 2014; Organon and Co., 2003). Ezetimibe’s systemic metabolic effects—reduced LDL-C and enhanced RCT/TICE—are therefore downstream consequences of intestinal NPC1L1 inhibition rather than direct hepatic or peripheral tissue binding (Bujold, 2012; Radiant Research, 2008).

Systemic lipid fluxes relevant to the eye. After intestinal absorption, cholesterol is packaged into chylomicrons (ApoB48-containing) that deliver dietary lipid to the liver; hepatic secretion of VLDL (ApoB100-containing) and intravascular remodeling generate LDL, which distributes cholesterol systemically, including to the eye; cellular uptake of LDL occurs via the LDL receptor (LDLR) on peripheral cells (including RPE), while HDL mediates reverse cholesterol transport from tissues back to the liver through ABCA1/ABCG1-dependent efflux (Unknown Reference). The RPE has LDL and scavenger receptor activity and participates in receptor-mediated uptake of lipoprotein-bound cholesterol; this receptor-mediated uptake is proposed to be a major route for retinal cholesterol acquisition from systemic circulation, complementing local synthesis (Zekavat et al., 2017). Thus, ezetimibe can plausibly modulate ocular lipid influx indirectly by lowering plasma LDL and chylomicron-remnant delivery to the outer retina, which may reduce lipoprotein deposition in Bruch’s membrane and sub-RPE basal deposits in models where circulating lipoproteins contribute materially to the ocular lipid burden (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Retinal cholesterol homeostasis and AMD-relevant pathobiology. Retina and RPE cholesterol derive largely from in situ synthesis behind the blood–retinal barrier, stringently controlled by transcriptional networks (SREBP2, LXR/RXR) and efflux transporters (ABCA1/ABCG1); age-related dysfunction in these pathways, along with mitochondrial decline, is implicated in AMD (Guo et al., 2024; Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). Lipids constitute a large fraction of drusen volume (~40%), and oxidized cholesterol species—notably 7-ketocholesterol (7KCh)—accumulate in the outer retina and RPE, where they inhibit autophagic flux (elevated p62), promote lipofuscin accumulation within lysosomes, activate NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasomes, and trigger apoptosis, collectively linking cholesterol dysregulation to lysosomal dysfunction and inflammation in AMD (Guo et al., 2024). These pathogenic cascades are exacerbated by inefficiencies in photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis and degradation by the RPE, processes that can be impaired by lipofuscin bisretinoids such as A2E and cholesterol crystal-driven inflammasome activation (Nociari et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2024). Independent preclinical work shows that enhancing cholesterol efflux (e.g., via LXR agonism) and inducing autophagy can normalize endosomal/lysosomal morphology and reduce RPE lipid accumulation in disease models such as Abca4-/-, and that RPE-specific ablation of ABCA1/ABCG1 produces lipid accumulation, RPE/photoreceptor degeneration, and vision loss—highlighting the centrality of cholesterol handling to retinal health (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). These data provide a mechanistic framework in which interventions that reduce retinal lipid influx, promote efflux, or restore lysosomal/autophagic capacity could beneficially modulate AMD-relevant endpoints.

Distinguishing NPC1L1 (intestinal) from NPC1 (lysosomal). It is important to differentiate the intestinal sterol influx transporter NPC1L1 (targeted by ezetimibe) from the lysosomal cholesterol egress protein NPC1; loss or inhibition of NPC1 traps cholesterol in late endosomes/lysosomes, whereas modulation of NPC1L1 affects apical enterocyte uptake (Schmiedt, 2012). In human RPE, palmitoylation of NPC1 governs cholesterol export from late endosomes; mutation of key cysteines increases lysosomal cholesterol accumulation without altering gross NPC1 localization, underscoring that RPE cholesterol trafficking depends on NPC1 and intracellular sorting mechanisms, not on NPC1L1 (Li et al., 2022). The provided literature does not demonstrate expression or functional roles for NPC1L1 in RPE, and no direct ocular actions of ezetimibe on RPE cholesterol uptake or lysosomal function are reported (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024).

AMD-relevant systemic–ocular linkage in CFH models. In aged CFH-transgenic mice, high-fat/high-cholesterol diets increase circulating chylomicron/VLDL/LDL and are associated with decreased scotopic ERG responses and sub-RPE deposit phenotypes; these findings motivate testing whether decreasing intestinal cholesterol absorption (e.g., ezetimibe) can mimic dietary cholesterol restriction and preserve visual function (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). The same review emphasizes RPE-derived lipoprotein accumulation in BrM and proposes that reducing intestinal cholesterol could reduce ocular ApoB48/ApoA-1 signals in the eyecup, consistent with lower lipoprotein flux to or from RPE/BrM (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). However, these are prospective hypotheses; experimental results were not reported in the excerpts (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Proposed hypothesis and assay context. The working hypothesis asserts that ezetimibe will “block cholesterol uptake in RPE (IC50 ~0.5 µM), reducing cholesterol-driven lysosomal dysfunction and lipofuscin, thereby improving POS degradation in dry AMD models,” and claims that ezetimibe “reduces cholesterol content in RPE, normalizes lysosomal pH, and enhances POS clearance in high-cholesterol culture,” with supportive statements about oral safety and ocular penetration in animals. The provided literature does not support these specific assertions: there are no data in the excerpts demonstrating NPC1L1 expression in RPE, ezetimibe binding or potency against an RPE target, direct effects on RPE cholesterol content, lysosomal pH normalization, lipofuscin reduction, or POS degradation, and no ocular penetration measurements are reported (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024; Jenkins et al., 2022). Therefore, a direct RPE-cell autonomous mechanism for ezetimibe is currently unsubstantiated by the cited literature.

Mechanistically grounded expectations in vitro (RPE systems). Given the lack of evidence that RPE expresses NPC1L1, the expected direct effect of ezetimibe in RPE culture under high-cholesterol conditions is uncertain. RPE cholesterol uptake from the extracellular milieu is thought to be mediated predominantly by LDLR and scavenger receptors acting on lipoprotein particles, not by NPC1L1-mediated micellar uptake as in enterocytes (Zekavat et al., 2017). Moreover, intracellular lysosomal cholesterol egress in RPE depends on NPC1/NPC2 and is modulated by protein palmitoylation and other lysosomal trafficking determinants, not by NPC1L1 (Li et al., 2022; Schmiedt, 2012). Consequently, unless ezetimibe has unidentified off-target activity relevant to RPE cholesterol uptake or lysosomal function, one would not anticipate robust correction of lysosomal cholesterol storage, lysosomal pH, autophagic flux, lipofuscin accumulation, or POS digestion kinetics in RPE culture solely from ezetimibe exposure; the provided literature does not document such off-target activities (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024). In contrast, other interventions have demonstrated RPE-directed effects in vitro and in vivo: autophagy inducers reduce intracellular RPE lipid burden, and LXR agonism can normalize endosomal size and reduce complement activation in Abca4-/- RPE—establishing precedents for lipid/autophagy-targeted corrections in RPE models (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). Additionally, β-cyclodextrins directly deplete lysosomal cholesterol and reduce lipofuscin bisretinoids in RPE models, highlighting an approach that directly targets the lysosome rather than systemic lipid flux (Nociari et al., 2017).

Mechanistically grounded expectations in vivo (mouse AMD-relevant models). In systems where circulating lipoproteins contribute substantially to outer-retinal lipid burden—e.g., aged CFH-transgenic mice exposed to HFC diets—reducing intestinal cholesterol absorption with ezetimibe should lower plasma chylomicron remnants/VLDL/LDL, reduce delivery of cholesterol to the outer retina via lipoprotein receptors, and potentially decrease RPE/BrM lipoprotein deposition and sequelae such as ERG attenuation and sub-RPE basal deposit accumulation; the CFH literature explicitly proposes this test and notes ongoing studies (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). Mechanistically, this would be a systemic route: ezetimibe acts in the intestine, lowers circulating atherogenic lipoproteins, and thereby diminishes receptor-mediated uptake into RPE; it would not require NPC1L1 expression in the eye (Guo et al., 2024; Zekavat et al., 2017). If successful, ancillary effects could include downstream reductions in oxidized cholesterol species such as 7KCh in the outer retina, potentially normalizing autophagic flux and reducing inflammasome activation driven by lipid peroxidation, although such cascading benefits remain hypothetical in the absence of reported in vivo data (Guo et al., 2024). It should be noted that mice differ from humans in plasma lipoprotein distribution due to the absence of CETP (mouse plasma is HDL-dominant), which can alter the plasma lipid response to intestinal absorption blockade and complicate extrapolation of systemic lipid changes to ocular endpoints; diet manipulations can partially humanize lipoprotein profiles but introduce other confounders (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). These interspecies differences emphasize the need for careful readouts of ocular lipid and function rather than reliance on plasma LDL changes alone.

Target expression and pathway linkage. The hypothesis’s protein target for direct ocular action is NPC1L1; however, the provided literature does not demonstrate NPC1L1 expression in human or mouse RPE, nor does it provide functional evidence for an NPC1L1-dependent uptake pathway in RPE cells (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024). In contrast, multiple sources document LDLR/scavenger receptor–mediated lipoprotein uptake in RPE and predominant local retinal cholesterol synthesis behind the blood–retinal barrier, suggesting that systemic LDL flux and local biosynthesis/efflux determine RPE lipid load (Zekavat et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2024). Within lysosomes, cholesterol egress uses NPC1/NPC2, and manipulation of these pathways (e.g., via palmitoylation state) alters lysosomal cholesterol burden in RPE (Li et al., 2022). Therefore, if ezetimibe were to produce benefits in AMD models, the most parsimonious mechanism would be indirect and systemic (reducing lipoprotein delivery to the eye) rather than a direct RPE NPC1L1-dependent effect (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Safety and ocular exposure considerations. The clinical literature presented confirms extensive systemic use of ezetimibe, including long-duration combination therapy trials, supporting a favorable systemic safety profile; however, the provided excerpts contain no eye-specific pharmacokinetic or safety data and emphasize that systemic LDL-lowering agents generally lack large ocular endpoint trials and that ocular delivery can alter tissue exposure relative to systemic administration (Cho, 2023; Jenkins et al., 2022). Consequently, the assumption that orally dosed ezetimibe achieves pharmacologically relevant concentrations in ocular tissues is not substantiated by the cited material (Jenkins et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong systemic pharmacology and safety foundation. Ezetimibe is a clinically validated oral NPC1L1 inhibitor with robust human and animal data demonstrating reduced intestinal cholesterol absorption, increased fecal neutral sterol excretion, augmented reverse cholesterol transport, and lowered circulating LDL-C; these systemic effects are precisely the inputs one would manipulate to test lipid-driven outer-retinal pathology in diet-sensitive AMD models (Radiant Research, 2008; Ostlund, 2014; Organon and Co., 2003; Bujold, 2012).  
- Mechanistic plausibility via systemic–ocular linkage in selected models. Aged CFH-transgenic mice demonstrate diet-induced increases in circulating chylomicron/VLDL/LDL, sub-RPE lipid deposition, and ERG decrements; authors of a leading AMD lipid review specifically propose ezetimibe as a test agent to mimic dietary cholesterol restriction and potentially prevent visual loss in these mice, with ongoing studies to evaluate effects on ocular lipoprotein markers (ApoB48, ApoA-1) (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
- Meaningful disease biology linkage. Independent lines of evidence implicate cholesterol and its oxidized derivatives (7KCh) in autophagy blockade, lysosomal lipofuscin accumulation, inflammasome activation, and RPE/photoreceptor cell death—key pathologies in dry AMD—supporting the concept that reducing retinal lipid influx or burden could yield functional benefit (Guo et al., 2024). Preclinical manipulations that increase efflux (LXR agonism) or induce autophagy normalize endosome/lysosome phenotypes in RPE models, further strengthening the causal pathway between lipid load and degradative capacity (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
- Practical development advantages. Ezetimibe is already formulated for oral use, with known human dosing, tolerability, and pharmacodynamic biomarkers (fecal sterols, cholesterol absorption efficiency), enabling rapid, biomarker-driven translational studies if ocular efficacy can be shown in animals (Radiant Research, 2008; Organon and Co., 2003).

Weaknesses and key gaps  
- No evidence for direct RPE NPC1L1 expression or action. The provided literature does not document NPC1L1 expression in RPE or other ocular tissues, nor any cellular data showing ezetimibe reduces RPE cholesterol content, normalizes lysosomal pH, augments autophagic flux, lowers lipofuscin, or improves POS degradation; the specific potency claim (IC50 ~0.5 µM in RPE) is unsupported by the cited sources (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024). This undermines the core in vitro arm of the proposed hypothesis.  
- Retinal cholesterol is primarily locally synthesized. Due to the blood–retinal barrier, retinal cholesterol pools arise chiefly from in situ synthesis; modulating intestinal absorption may have limited impact on retinal cholesterol content unless circulating lipoproteins contribute substantially to outer-retinal lipid influx in the specific model under study (Guo et al., 2024). While RPE does possess LDL/scavenger receptor activity and can take up systemic lipoproteins, the quantitative contribution relative to local synthesis remains uncertain and likely context-dependent (Zekavat et al., 2017).  
- Lack of ocular pharmacokinetic and clinical endpoint data. There are no reported data on ezetimibe ocular penetration or exposure in animals or humans, and reviews emphasize the absence of large randomized retinal endpoint trials for LDL-lowering drugs, including ezetimibe; ocular efficacy with systemic dosing therefore remains speculative (Jenkins et al., 2022).  
- Species and model translation caveats. Mice lack CETP and are HDL-dominant, which affects systemic lipid responses to intestinal absorption inhibition and complicates extrapolation to human lipoprotein physiology; diet manipulations can humanize lipoproteins but introduce confounding metabolic changes that could independently influence RPE lysosomal/autophagy function (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). In addition, anatomical differences between mouse and human retinas (rod-dominance, RPE density, POS phagocytic load) can alter lysosomal stress and degradative capacity, further complicating translation (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
- Comparative mechanistic alternatives are more direct. Other interventions with demonstrated RPE-centric mechanisms—LXR agonists to increase ABCA1/ABCG1-mediated efflux, autophagy inducers, and β-cyclodextrins that directly solubilize lysosomal cholesterol and bind bisretinoids—have shown positive effects on RPE endosomal/lysosomal phenotypes or lipofuscin burden in preclinical models, suggesting more direct levers on the implicated pathogenic nodes than systemic intestinal absorption blockade (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Nociari et al., 2017).

Decision-oriented recommendations  
- Do not proceed on the assumption of a direct RPE target for ezetimibe. Before committing to RPE-centric in vitro efficacy claims, establish whether NPC1L1 is expressed in primary human RPE/iPSC-RPE and at what level; the provided literature indicates this is unknown, and NPC1L1 is classically enterocyte-restricted (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024; Murillo, 2016). In parallel, verify that ezetimibe has no off-target effects on LDLR- or scavenger receptor-mediated lipoprotein uptake in RPE and no direct impact on NPC1-dependent lysosomal cholesterol egress; current RPE mechanistic data implicate NPC1 palmitoylation in lysosomal cholesterol egress, not NPC1L1 activity (Li et al., 2022; Schmiedt, 2012).  
- Prioritize an in vivo, systemic-mechanism proof-of-concept study in a diet-sensitized AMD model. The strongest rationale for ezetimibe in AMD resides in aged CFH-transgenic mice where HFC diet increases circulating lipoproteins and impairs retinal function; test whether ezetimibe prevents ERG decline and reduces ocular ApoB48/ApoA-1 and sub-RPE lipid deposition under HFC challenge, as proposed in ongoing preclinical work (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). Include endpoints that index RPE lysosome/autophagy status and lipid oxidation (e.g., p62/LC3 flux, lysosomal pH, A2E/7KCh, NLRP3 activation) to probe whether systemic lipid lowering secondarily normalizes degradative pathways (Guo et al., 2024; Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
- Incorporate lipid handling comparators that act directly at the RPE. To de-risk mechanism, include a positive-control arm with an LXR agonist (to increase ABCA1/ABCG1) or an autophagy inducer known to reduce RPE lipid burdens, and consider a β-cyclodextrin arm to directly test whether lowering lysosomal cholesterol and bisretinoids rescues degradative function; these comparators will benchmark the magnitude of effect achievable with RPE-centric strategies (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Nociari et al., 2017).  
- Use plasma and fecal sterol biomarkers to confirm on-target intestinal action. Quantify fecal neutral sterol excretion and cholesterol absorption efficiency to verify effective NPC1L1 inhibition in vivo; these human-validated biomarkers have a mechanistic link to ezetimibe action and can anchor ocular outcome interpretations to on-target pharmacodynamics (Radiant Research, 2008; Ostlund, 2014; Organon and Co., 2003).  
- Plan for translational risks tied to retinal cholesterol sources. Given the primacy of local retinal cholesterol synthesis, negative results in models with minor circulating lipoprotein contributions to RPE lipid load would not falsify all systemic lipid-lowering hypotheses but would argue against ezetimibe’s utility except in specific lipid-sensitized genetic/dietary contexts (Guo et al., 2024; Zekavat et al., 2017). Selection of models should therefore be driven by evidence of systemic lipid influx effects on RPE/BrM biology (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Bottom line. On current evidence, ezetimibe has credible potential to test the systemic lipid-influx axis of AMD pathogenesis in select diet-sensitized genetic models (e.g., aged CFH-H/H on HFC diets), with a plausible mechanism to reduce plasma lipoproteins and secondarily lower RPE/BrM lipid deposition; however, there is no substantiation for direct RPE action via NPC1L1, no reported ocular pharmacokinetics, and no preclinical efficacy data published on RPE lysosome/autophagy endpoints or lipofuscin under ezetimibe treatment. For dry AMD, ezetimibe should be considered a hypothesis-generating, low-to-moderate probability repurposing candidate with high translational uncertainty; it merits a focused, biomarker-anchored in vivo proof-of-concept in an appropriate model, but should not displace more direct RPE-targeting lipid/autophagy strategies in the near-term pipeline (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Nociari et al., 2017; Jenkins et al., 2022).

Detailed appraisal of disease biology and how ezetimibe might intersect  
- Cholesterol exposure and RPE degradative failure. Excess cholesterol in the outer retina oxidizes to 7KCh and other oxysterols that directly inhibit autophagic flux (p62 accumulation), acidify/injure mitochondria, and promote polymerization of oxidation products that become lipofuscin within lysosomes; lipofuscin accumulation impairs lysosomal phagocytosis and autophagy, reducing POS clearance—a core function of RPE (Guo et al., 2024). These processes activate NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling and lead to RPE and photoreceptor apoptosis in rodent models, reproducing elements of dry AMD pathophysiology (Guo et al., 2024). Although ezetimibe does not directly target RPE degradative machinery, a systemic reduction in lipoprotein-delivered cholesterol could attenuate upstream substrate pressure for these oxidative and degradative stress pathways in models where systemic influx is important (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
- RPE lipid handling machinery points to more proximal targets. ABCA1/ABCG1 are critical for RPE cholesterol efflux; their loss in RPE leads to lipid accumulation, degeneration, and vision loss, while pharmacologic LXR activation mimics endosomal normalization seen with acid sphingomyelinase inhibition in Abca4-/- RPE, illustrating the benefit of directly boosting efflux pathways (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022). Such direct manipulation of RPE lipid handling may offer a higher likelihood of efficacy than systemic manipulations in models where local synthesis dominates retinal cholesterol pools (Guo et al., 2024).  
- Lipoprotein biology and CFH genetic risk. CFH variants modulate RPE-derived lipoprotein accumulation in BrM, and HFC diets exacerbate ocular phenotypes in CFH-transgenic mice, positioning systemic lipoprotein burden as a modifiable driver in these contexts; ezetimibe is explicitly proposed in this literature as a candidate to reduce intestinal cholesterol uptake and test whether lowering circulating lipoproteins rescues visual function (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Programmatic risk–benefit and go/no-go criteria  
- Go criteria for advancing to animal efficacy testing:  
  • Demonstration of on-target intestinal pharmacodynamics in the chosen species/diet (increased fecal neutral sterols; reduced fractional cholesterol absorption) at a clinically relevant dose (Radiant Research, 2008; Organon and Co., 2003).  
  • Aged CFH-transgenic mice on HFC diet with documented elevation of plasma chylomicron/VLDL/LDL and ERG decrements at baseline, to ensure model sensitivity to circulating lipoprotein changes (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
  • Predefined ocular endpoints that read out RPE lipid and degradative status (ApoB48/ApoA-1 eyecup content, RPE/BrM lipid histology, LC3/p62 flux, lysosomal pH, A2E/7KCh levels, complement activation, ERG b-wave amplitude) (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024).  

- No-go criteria prior to significant resource commitment:  
  • Failure to demonstrate on-target intestinal pharmacodynamics at tolerated doses in the selected model (Radiant Research, 2008).  
  • Lack of effect on ocular lipoprotein readouts (ApoB48/ApoA-1) or ERG despite robust plasma LDL lowering and fecal sterol increase, suggesting that circulating lipoprotein flux is not rate-limiting for the ocular phenotypes in that model (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
  • Evidence from expression analyses that NPC1L1 is not expressed in RPE (which would deprioritize direct cellular assays) and that systemic LDL reductions do not translate to reduced RPE lipid load (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Zekavat et al., 2017).

Summary conclusions  
- The overarching mechanistic thesis that cholesterol-driven lysosomal/autophagy dysfunction underlies key dry AMD phenotypes is well supported by preclinical data (7KCh-driven autophagy inhibition, lipofuscin accumulation, inflammasome activation, and apoptosis), and interventions that improve RPE lipid handling and degradative capacity show benefit in relevant models (Guo et al., 2024).  
- Ezetimibe’s capacity to reduce intestinal cholesterol absorption and lower circulating atherogenic lipoproteins is firmly established; translationally, this provides a credible lever to test whether systemic lipoprotein pressure influences RPE/BrM lipid deposition and function in susceptible genotypes/diets (Bujold, 2012; Radiant Research, 2008; Ostlund, 2014; Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).  
- However, the specific claim that ezetimibe directly blocks RPE cholesterol uptake with sub-micromolar potency, normalizes lysosomal pH, reduces lipofuscin, and enhances POS degradation lacks support in the provided literature; moreover, NPC1L1 expression in RPE has not been demonstrated in these sources, and the intestine-restricted action of ezetimibe argues that any ocular benefits would be indirect via systemic lipid lowering (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Guo et al., 2024).  
- Given the lack of ocular PK data and the primacy of local retinal cholesterol synthesis, the prior probability of large clinical benefit in unselected dry AMD populations is modest; nonetheless, in CFH-sensitized, diet-exacerbated models the hypothesis is testable and may yield meaningful insights about the contribution of systemic lipoproteins to outer-retinal pathology (Guo et al., 2024; Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

Recommendation: Advance ezetimibe to a focused, biomarker-rich preclinical proof-of-concept in aged CFH-H/H mice under HFC diet, with stringent ocular endpoints and on-target intestinal PD confirmation. In parallel, deprioritize RPE-centric in vitro efficacy claims pending demonstration of NPC1L1 expression in RPE and direct cellular activity; maintain higher prioritization for agents with demonstrated RPE-direct mechanisms (LXR agonists, autophagy inducers, β-cyclodextrins) as nearer-term AMD therapeutics (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022; Nociari et al., 2017).
