Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MCC950 is a synthetic diarylsulfonylurea small molecule originally identified from an IL-1β processing inhibitor chemotype and later defined as a highly potent and selective inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome complex (Coll et al., 2015). Within the inflammasome‐inhibitor landscape, MCC950 is representative of sulfonylurea‐based NLRP3 inhibitors that block canonical and noncanonical NLRP3 activation while sparing other inflammasomes (AIM2, NLRC4, NLRP1) and upstream innate pathways (e.g., TLR-NF-κB priming) (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Mechanistically, MCC950 acts directly on NLRP3 to prevent assembly of the adaptor ASC (apoptosis‐associated speck-like protein containing a CARD) into oligomeric “specks,” thereby preventing caspase-1 activation and maturation of IL-1β and IL-18 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Follow-on mechanistic analyses indicate MCC950 binds the NLRP3 NACHT domain to inhibit its ATPase function and thereby prevent NLRP3 activation; mechanistic models include prevention of ASC oligomerization and disruption of required conformations for NEK7–NLRP3 cooperation during sensor activation (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2023).

This class (selective NLRP3 inhibitors) has been broadly leveraged in preclinical inflammatory disease models to selectively blunt inflammasome‐driven IL-1 family cytokine maturation and pyroptosis without pan‐suppressing innate immune sensing, with documented in vivo efficacy in autoimmune encephalomyelitis, CAPS (NLRP3 gain‐of‐function), spontaneous colitis, atherosclerosis, and myocardial infarction models (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021; Wooff et al., 2020). In ocular biology, several sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950 and chemically related CRID3/IFM compounds—reduce IL-1β secretion and cell lysis in human RPE models and ex vivo mouse RPE/choroid eye cups under diverse AMD‐relevant triggers (lysosomal membrane permeabilization, oxidative/photooxidative stress, and P2X7 activation) (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic and non‐ocular indications. MCC950 has repeatedly shown robust pharmacodynamic suppression of inflammasome outputs and disease modification in vivo. Oral dosing in a spontaneous colitis model suppressed IL-1β/IL-18 production ex vivo and improved clinical/histopathologic indices (Perera et al., 2018). In APC‐driven autoimmune encephalomyelitis and in CAPS, MCC950 reduced IL-1β production and ameliorated disease; in CAPS it rescued neonatal lethality (Coll et al., 2015). In ApoE-deficient mice, MCC950 reduced atherosclerotic plaque burden, intraplaque macrophages, and systemic TNF-α/IL-1β/IL-6/IL-18 (Zeng et al., 2021). Across these studies MCC950 demonstrates in vivo target engagement, cytokine suppression, and disease modification with high selectivity for NLRP3 (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021). However, translational reviews emphasize that many NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950‐class agents—face liabilities for organ penetration (including eye/brain) and potential liver toxicity, underscoring formulation/delivery and safety risks that must be addressed for ocular use (Ortega et al., 2024).

Ocular and retinal contexts. In the ischemic OIR model, MCC950 lowered retinal neovascularization and vascular leakage and shifted an aberrant cytokine balance (decreased IL-1β activity with increased IL-18 activity), with accompanying reductions in angiogenesis‐ and pericyte‐associated signaling molecules (VEGF, VEGFR1/2, MMP2/9, PDGFR-β, Ang2) and evidence of inflammasome activation localized predominantly to macrophages (F4/80+) over endothelium (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Sui et al., 2020c). In a glaucoma model (DBA/2J), MCC950 reduced NLRP3 and cleaved caspase-1 in retina and mitigated retinal ganglion cell loss independently of intraocular pressure, indicating on‐target retinal neuroinflammation suppression (Li, 2020).

By contrast, in a laser‐induced CNV model (wet AMD), short‐course MCC950 lowered IL-1β transcript/protein but paradoxically increased total CNV lesion volume and recruitment of microglia and monocyte‐derived macrophages; ERG a- and b-waves were unchanged, suggesting no gross electrophysiological toxicity under those conditions (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b). This aligns with genetic evidence that inflammasome–IL-1β signaling promotes CNV largely through macrophages/microglia and that non‐NLRP3 inflammasomes also contribute, implying that selectively inhibiting NLRP3 may have complex, context‐dependent effects in neovascular disease (Marneros, 2023a; Marneros, 2023b).

In dry‐AMD–relevant photo‐oxidative damage (PD), intravitreal MCC950 failed to rescue function/structure and high‐dose MCC950 worsened ERG amplitudes: 20 µM showed no functional change versus PBS and did not alter photoreceptor death or IBA-1+ microglia counts; 100 µM significantly reduced ERG function (Wooff et al., 2020b). In the same study, Casp1/11−/− mice exhibited strong protection, whereas Nlrp3−/− mice showed only partial functional preservation, and pharmacologic NLRP3 inhibition or Nlrp3 siRNA provided no benefit (and in some readouts reduced function), leading to the conclusion that downstream caspase-1 is a dominant driver whereas NLRP3 may be neither necessary nor sufficient in this model (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). The authors also highlighted uncertainties about NLRP3 localization (predominantly INL/GCL rather than RPE), protein detection sensitivity, and the absence of ocular pharmacokinetic data for MCC950 (Wooff et al., 2020b).

RPE cell and ex vivo ocular models. In IL-1α–primed ARPE-19 and primary human RPE (pRPE), sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors reduced inflammasome activation and cell injury across diverse triggers relevant to GA, including LMP (Leu-Leu-OMe), oxidative stress (H₂O₂), lipofuscin/photooxidative insult (HNE-POS + blue light), and P2X7 activation (BzATP); in Abca4−/− eye cups, selective NLRP3 inhibitors suppressed IL-1β and LDH release and preserved RPE morphology after blue‐light irradiation (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024). A 2024 synthesis that included MCC950 reports that MCC950, IFM-632, and IFM-514 each decreased IL-1α-primed RPE inflammasome activation independent of the activation trigger, consistent with target class effects in RPE models (Korhonen, 2024). These in vitro/ex vivo data strongly support that NLRP3 activity can be engaged in RPE and that selective, small‐molecule inhibition suppresses canonical outputs (IL-1β, LDH) under multiple AMD‐relevant insults. However, detailed analyses of autophagic flux restoration or lysosomal integrity rescue after MCC950 are not reported in these excerpts (Wang et al., 2019).

Emerging genetics for AMD‐relevant deposits. In a monogenic EFEMP1 R345W knockin model (ML/DHRD) that recapitulates basal laminar deposits (BLamDs), as well as in aged WT mice, whole‐animal deletion of Nlrp3 or Casp1 significantly reduced BLamD size/coverage, normalized proinflammatory retinal cytokine profiles, and reduced microglial activation; these data provide genetic causality linking NLRP3–caspase-1 activity to deposit formation and inflammatory milieu (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). The same preprint cautions that NLRP3 inhibitors frequently suffer inadequate ocular penetration and potential liver toxicity, and emphasizes the need to determine whether ocular‐local versus systemic NLRP3 suppression is required (Ortega et al., 2024b).

Mechanism of Action  
Molecular target and binding mechanism. NLRP3 is a tripartite sensor (PYD–NACHT–LRR) that oligomerizes upon priming and activation to recruit ASC via PYD–PYD interactions, which in turn polymerizes and recruits pro-caspase-1 via CARD–CARD interactions to form an active inflammasome; active caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 and the pore‐forming effector gasdermin D (GSDMD) to elicit cytokine secretion and pyroptosis (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). MCC950 binds NLRP3 and prevents its ATPase activity (NACHT domain), disrupting a conformational step required for oligomerization and ASC speck assembly; in cellular systems, MCC950 suppresses both canonical (e.g., K⁺ efflux, lysosomal rupture, mitochondrial ROS) and noncanonical (caspase-11–triggered) activation pathways (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Notably, MCC950 does not broadly interfere with upstream priming (NF-κB–dependent transcription of NLRP3 and cytokine precursors), K⁺ or Ca²⁺ flux, or NLRP3–ASC direct binding in simple biochemical assays; rather, it functionally prevents ASC oligomerization and caspase-1 processing, reflecting target engagement at the level of sensor activation/oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Selectivity is strong: activity against AIM2, NLRC4, and NLRP1 inflammasomes is not observed, and broad target screening reveals only weak off-target activity (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018).

Cell-context specificity in the retina and RPE. Expression of NLRP3 and caspase-1 in the retina is cell-type and stimulus dependent. In vitro, microglia robustly upregulate Nlrp3, Casp1, and Il1b upon stimulation; Müller cells can increase Nlrp3 and Il1b without matching Casp1 elevation; photoreceptor‐line cells upregulate Nlrp3 while reducing Casp1; ARPE-19 cells often show undetectable NLRP3 protein and variable inflammasome readouts under some conditions (Wooff et al., 2020a). In situ, NLRP3 labeling is minimal in dim-reared mouse retinas but becomes detectable in the INL/GCL after PD, and AMD donor tissue shows NLRP3 in INL/GCL, suggesting inner-retina/microglial inflammasome contributions that complicate direct linkage to outer retina/RPE degeneration (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). Conversely, multiple human and preclinical reports demonstrate NLRP3 upregulation in macular RPE of AMD eyes with strong increases in pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 transcripts, co-localization of NLRP3 with autophagosome-like structures, and mitochondrial damage/autophagy signatures—though the literature is conflicted by antibody specificity and cell line variability (Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b; Marneros, 2023b). Taken together, these data imply that in AMD-relevant contexts, NLRP3 activation can occur in RPE and in inner-retinal microglia/Müller/immune cells; drug effects will be inherently cell-type dependent.

Pathway-level effects in retinal models. In ischemic retinopathy (OIR), NLRP3 activation (NLRP3/ASC/CASP1 upregulation and ASC specks) is observed primarily in macrophages and endothelium, and MCC950 reversal of an increased IL-1β/decreased IL-18 pattern is associated with reduced neovascularization and leakage, implicating vascular-cell responses to inflammasome cytokines as drivers of pathology (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b). In wet AMD CNV, inflammasome activation is localized mainly to infiltrating macrophages and microglia, and IL-1β is a principal driver of lesion growth; however, pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition increased lesion size in one study despite reduced IL-1β, suggesting additional non-NLRP3 inflammasomes and compensatory mechanisms (or cell-intrinsic NLRP3 roles) shape outcomes (Marneros, 2023a; Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b).

Expected Effect  
Proposed assay and mechanism. The proposal posits that MCC950 will specifically inhibit NLRP3 assembly in RPE (IC₅₀ ~7.5 nM), reducing IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, preventing inflammasome-induced lysosomal damage, preserving autophagic flux, and thereby enhancing photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance. Mechanistic underpinnings exist for the first components of this cascade: (i) MCC950 demonstrates nanomolar potency and high selectivity for NLRP3 and suppresses downstream IL-1β/IL-18 (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018); (ii) in IL-1α–primed RPE models (ARPE-19 and pRPE), sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950 in compiled data—suppress IL-1β and LDH release across LMP, oxidative stress, lipofuscin/photooxidative, and P2X7 activation paradigms, and preserve ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology under blue-light irradiation (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024). These findings support the expected reduction of canonical inflammasome outputs in RPE assays under multiple AMD-like stimuli.

Lysosome/autophagy preservation and POS clearance. Autophagy is a key negative regulator of NLRP3 activation: it limits ROS and damaged mitochondria, targets assembled inflammasomes for degradation, and suppresses IL-1β responses; conversely, autophagy suppression increases inflammasome activation and pyroptosis in RPE (Celkova et al., 2015). AMD-relevant triggers—including lipofuscin bisretinoids (e.g., A2E) and oxidative stress—cause lysosomal stress/LMP and NLRP3 activation in RPE, and caspase-1 inhibition can prevent RPE death in LMP contexts (Ildefonso et al., 2016). However, direct evidence that MCC950 restores autophagic flux or lysosomal integrity in RPE is not reported in the cited primary RPE inhibitor studies; the RPE evidence centers on IL-1β and LDH suppression and morphological preservation in ex vivo tissue but does not include autophagy- or lysosome-specific readouts or POS phagocytosis assays (Wang et al., 2019). Therefore, while it is plausible that NLRP3 suppression will indirectly favor autophagy homeostasis in stressed RPE by damping inflammasome-driven pyroptotic signaling (and thereby reduce further lysosomal damage), the proposed “preservation of autophagy and enhanced POS clearance” remains unproven for MCC950 and should be tested explicitly (Celkova et al., 2015).

Disease- and cell-type context expectations. In dry AMD models that feature outer-retinal/RPE degeneration, the translation of RPE in vitro suppression of NLRP3 to in vivo benefit is uncertain. In PD (a dry-AMD–relevant model), intravitreal MCC950 failed to confer protection and at higher dose impaired retinal function; Nlrp3−/− mice showed only partial protection while Casp1/11−/− mice were strongly protected, arguing that downstream caspase-1 and/or other inflammasomes may be the dominant drivers in photoreceptor death (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). In EFEMP1 R345W and aged WT models, genetic inactivation of Nlrp3 or Casp1 reduced basal laminar deposit burden and inflammatory signatures, supporting target pathway relevance for drusen/BLamD biology, but pharmacological MCC950 efficacy in these genetic models has not been reported (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). Importantly, if inflammasome activation in vivo is dominated by subretinal macrophages/microglia in some contexts (e.g., autophagy-impaired RPE signals that activate macrophage inflammasomes), the expected pharmacologic effect of MCC950 may depend more on drug exposure to myeloid cells in the subretinal/choroidal space than on direct RPE engagement (Liu et al., 2016).

Finally, IL-18 biology is context-dependent: while IL-1β is broadly pro-angiogenic and disruptive, IL-18 can be protective/anti-angiogenic in neovascular settings, and AMD-relevant studies have reported discordant roles for IL-18 across disease phenotypes (Celkova et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). Given that NLRP3 blockade reduces both IL-1β and IL-18, net effects on tissue outcomes may vary by disease stage and cell-type source; in OIR, MCC950 “normalized” an inverted IL-1β/IL-18 pattern and improved pathology (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020c), whereas in CNV, MCC950 increased lesion volume—implicating competing effects and non-NLRP3 inflammasomes (Dieckmann et al., 2024a).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- On-target potency/selectivity. MCC950 is among the most potent and selective NLRP3 inhibitors described, blocking canonical and noncanonical activation at nanomolar concentrations and sparing other inflammasomes and upstream pathways; it consistently suppresses IL-1β/IL-18 maturation and caspase-1 activation in primary macrophages and multiple in vivo models (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Perera et al., 2018).  
- RPE-target class activity under AMD-relevant stimuli. Sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors, including MCC950 in compiled datasets, reproducibly suppress IL-1β and LDH in IL-1α–primed ARPE-19 and primary human RPE triggered by LMP, oxidative/photooxidative stress, and P2X7 activation; ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology is preserved by an NLRP3 inhibitor during photooxidative stress (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024).  
- Genetic target validation in AMD-relevant deposit biology. Whole‐body Nlrp3 or Casp1 deletion reduces BLamDs and normalizes inflammatory signatures in EFEMP1 R345W mice and even prevents spontaneous deposits in aged WT, indicating the inflammasome pathway contributes causally to deposit formation and retinal inflammation (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c).  
- Demonstrated retinal efficacy in ischemic models and neuroinflammation. MCC950 improves vascular pathology in OIR (reduced neovascularization and leakage with cytokine-pattern reversal) and rescues retinal ganglion cells in glaucoma, supporting retinal target engagement and functional protection in relevant pathologies (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Li, 2020).

Liabilities and gaps  
- Lack of efficacy and potential toxicity in dry-AMD–relevant PD. Intravitreal MCC950 did not improve functional or structural outcomes in PD and at 100 µM worsened ERG amplitudes; Nlrp3 siRNA similarly failed to protect despite gene knockdown; Casp1/11 deletion was robustly protective while Nlrp3 deletion was only partially protective, arguing sensor-specific inhibition may be insufficient in photoreceptor death contexts (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- Mixed effects in neovascular disease. MCC950 increased CNV lesion volume in LCNV despite lowering IL-1β, and Nlrp3−/− mice displayed larger lesions, raising concern that NLRP3 blockade may remove protective constraints in some inflammatory/angiogenic contexts; non-NLRP3 inflammasomes likely contribute, further complicating pharmacodynamics (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).  
- Uncertain ocular delivery, exposure, and safety margin. Ocular PK for MCC950 is not defined; the PD study underscores unknown intravitreal bioavailability and clearance, and preclinical reviews warn of poor eye penetration and potential liver toxicity with many NLRP3 inhibitors; high intravitreal dose impaired ERG function in PD (Wooff et al., 2020b; Ortega et al., 2024b). While ERGs were unchanged in one CNV study, that does not establish comprehensive ocular safety (Dieckmann et al., 2024a).  
- RPE biology heterogeneity and expression uncertainty. In vivo NLRP3 induction localizes largely to inner retina/microglia rather than RPE in PD; ARPE-19 NLRP3 expression is variable in the literature and some human studies report low/undetectable NLRP3 in RPE, with concerns about antibody specificity, suggesting that direct RPE targeting may not be universally relevant across models or donors (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b; Marneros, 2023b).  
- Unproven restoration of autophagy/lysosomal function by MCC950. Although autophagy restrains inflammasome activation and lysosomal damage is a key trigger in RPE, direct evidence that MCC950 preserves autophagic flux, lysosomal integrity, or POS processing in RPE is absent in the cited studies; current RPE data document IL-1β/LDH suppression and morphology preservation but not autophagy or phagolysosomal kinetics (Celkova et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019).  
- Pathway redundancy suggests downstream targeting may be superior. Strong protection in Casp1/11−/− mice versus weak/absent benefits from NLRP3 inhibition in PD argue for targeting the shared downstream protease (caspase-1) or gasdermin D rather than individual sensors in retinal degeneration (Wooff et al., 2020a).

Risk-adjusted development path and decision inflection points  
- Go/no-go evidence needed in dry-AMD–relevant RPE assays. Establish whether MCC950 preserves lysosomal integrity and autophagic flux in RPE under LMP/photooxidative/P2X7 triggers and whether it restores POS digestion. Required readouts: LC3-II/I and p62 kinetics with and without bafilomycin, lysosomal pH and cathepsin activity, galectin-3 puncta for LMP, ASC speck formation, caspase-1 activity (FLICA), GSDMD cleavage, IL-1β/IL-18 maturation, and POS ingestion/digestion assays in ARPE-19 and pRPE (Celkova et al., 2015; Ranta-aho et al., 2021).  
- Ocular PK/PD and safety. Quantify intravitreal half-life, retinal/RPE/choroid distribution, and exposure–response for inflammasome suppression with MCC950; determine maximum non-toxic intravitreal dose across species. Include ERG, OCT, histopathology, IBA-1/microglial activation, and cytokine profiling. Investigate sustained intravitreal delivery strategies (e.g., silica-based nanoparticles) that have shown extended ocular release and improved anti-inflammatory efficacy for MCC950 in non-AMD contexts, while generating ocular PK and biodegradation data (Sun et al., 2023).  
- Efficacy in chronic dry-AMD models. Test MCC950 in EFEMP1 R345W mice (BLamD) and aging WT (spontaneous BLamD) with local ocular delivery; endpoints: BLamD size and coverage, RPE/Bruch’s integrity, microglial recruitment (Iba1), and cytokine panels. Given PD negative findings, prioritize deposit/atrophy models where genetic Nlrp3/Casp1 loss is protective (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c; Wooff et al., 2020b).  
- Cell-type–specific targeting and biomarkers. Because inflammasome activation is often myeloid-dominant in vivo, delineate whether MCC950’s ocular benefits, if any, require exposure to subretinal macrophages/microglia versus RPE. Use cell-specific pharmacodynamic markers (ASC specks in Iba1+ cells vs RPE65+ cells; IL-1β/IL-18 localization) to define pharmacologic engagement (Liu et al., 2016; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- Comparative strategy. In parallel, benchmark a caspase-1 inhibitor (or GSDMD inhibitor) against MCC950 in the same models, given the superior genetic protection with Casp1/11 deletion and the possibility of non-NLRP3 inflammasome contribution (Wooff et al., 2020a; Marneros, 2023a).

Bottom line  
MCC950 has strong mechanistic rationale, exquisite target selectivity, and reproducible suppression of inflammasome outputs in RPE assays across diverse AMD-like triggers. Genetic data incriminating NLRP3–caspase-1 in deposit biology strengthen the target hypothesis in a subset of dry-AMD phenotypes. However, the most AMD-relevant in vivo pharmacology with MCC950 to date is not supportive: no benefit and possible functional toxicity in PD, and mixed signals in neovascular settings (benefit in OIR, harm in LCNV). The translational path is further complicated by variable NLRP3 expression in RPE in vivo, dominance of myeloid inflammasomes in many retinal contexts, uncertain ocular PK/penetration, and the untested premise that MCC950 restores RPE autophagy/lysosomal function and POS clearance.

Given these data, MCC950 should not advance directly to costly IND-enabling studies for dry AMD without targeted de-risking experiments. The highest-value next steps are (i) mechanistic RPE assays that test autophagy/lysosome rescue and POS processing, (ii) rigorous ocular PK/safety to define a therapeutic index and viable delivery modality, and (iii) efficacy in deposit/atrophy models where the genetic target is validated (EFEMP1 R345W, aged WT). If these studies confirm robust ocular exposure, a favorable safety margin, and disease modification, MCC950—or a chemically optimized ocular NLRP3 inhibitor—could warrant advancement for specific dry-AMD endophenotypes. If not, downstream inflammasome targeting (caspase-1/GSDMD) may represent a more effective and generalizable strategy for retinal degeneration.

Mechanism of Action (detailed)  
NLRP3 activation requires priming (e.g., NF-κB upregulation of NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β/IL-18) and a second signal (e.g., K⁺ efflux via P2X7, lysosomal rupture with cathepsin release, mitochondrial ROS) that promotes sensor oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). NLRP3’s NACHT domain cycles ATP and orchestrates a conformational change enabling PYD-driven nucleation of ASC, which polymerizes into higher-order filaments/specks that template pro-caspase-1 recruitment and activation; activated caspase-1 cleaves GSDMD to induce pyroptotic pore formation and processes IL-1β/IL-18 for secretion (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). MCC950 binds NLRP3 to suppress its ATPase activity (NACHT), preventing the conformational activation needed for ASC oligomerization and caspase-1 activation; in functional assays MCC950 suppresses both canonical and noncanonical pathways and decreases processed caspase-1 p10/p20 in supernatants without altering upstream TNF-α secretion after TLR priming (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Evidence from retinal disease states aligns with these mechanisms: MCC950 reduces NLRP3 and cleaved caspase-1 in glaucomatous retina (DBA/2J), and in OIR normalizes IL-1β/IL-18 signaling and reduces pathologic neovascularization and leakage (Li, 2020; Sui et al., 2020a).

Inflammasome biology in RPE and AMD is multifactorial. AMD-associated triggers—lipofuscin photooxidation, A2E/oxidative stress, drusen lipid adducts (CEP), Alu RNA accumulation from DICER1 deficiency, and lysosomal destabilization—induce NLRP3 activation in RPE or in recruited subretinal macrophages (Ildefonso et al., 2016; Celkova et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016). Autophagy limits NLRP3 activation by removing damaged mitochondria and targeting assembled inflammasomes for autophagosomal degradation; autophagy blockade increases IL-1β production and pyroptotic susceptibility (Celkova et al., 2015). Pharmacologic NLRP3 blockade in RPE reduces IL-1β and LDH release under LMP, oxidative, photooxidative, and P2X7 activation, consistent with suppression of caspase-1 activation and pyroptotic lysis (Wang et al., 2019). Whether these biochemical effects in RPE suffice to modify chronic, multicellular retinal degeneration in vivo depends on drug delivery to relevant compartments (RPE, subretinal macrophages/microglia), on the relative contributions of non-NLRP3 inflammasomes, and on downstream cytokine biology (e.g., IL-18’s context-dependent effects).

Therapeutic History (detailed)  
- Preclinical systemic efficacy and selectivity: MCC950 exhibits nanomolar potency for NLRP3 in human/mouse macrophages, sparing AIM2, NLRC4, NLRP1; suppresses caspase-1 p10 and IL-1β secretion; improves disease in EAE and CAPS; PK characterized; off-targets largely excluded (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018). In atherosclerosis, MCC950 decreased plaques, macrophage content, and circulating cytokines without overt systemic organ toxicity, though cross-indication reviews caution about liver toxicity risk for the class (Zeng et al., 2021; Ortega et al., 2024b).  
- Ocular ischemic/neovascular settings: In OIR, MCC950 reversed an increased IL-1β/decreased IL-18 pattern, reduced neovascularization and leakage, and modulated endothelial/pericyte signaling; inflammasome activity localized more to macrophages than endothelium (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Sui et al., 2020c). In LCNV, MCC950 lowered IL-1β but increased lesion volume; ERG unchanged; genetic Nlrp3 loss also increased lesion size—collectively indicating a complex, possibly protective role of NLRP3 in CNV or compensation by other inflammasomes (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).  
- Dry-AMD–relevant PD and NLRP3 targeting: Intravitreal MCC950 did not protect PD retina; 100 µM reduced ERG amplitudes. Nlrp3 siRNA reduced transcript but not pathology; Nlrp3−/− protected partially; Casp1/11−/− protected robustly, pointing to caspase-1 as the better target (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- RPE in vitro/ex vivo: CRID3/IFM inhibitors (sulfonylureas, same target class as MCC950) reduced IL-1β and LDH across LMP, H₂O₂, lipofuscin/photooxidation, and P2X7 triggers in ARPE-19/pRPE and preserved ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology under photooxidation (Wang et al., 2019). Compiled 2024 data list MCC950 alongside IFM analogs as effective in IL-1α–primed RPE independent of trigger (Korhonen, 2024).  
- Genetic validations in chronic deposit models: Nlrp3 or Casp1 deletion reduces BLamD in EFEMP1 R345W mice and in aged WT, with reduced microglial activation and normalization of cytokine profiles (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). These models offer strong causal support for inflammasome targeting in GA-relevant pathology, albeit via genetic ablation rather than pharmacologic inhibition.

Expected Effect (detailed)  
In ARPE-19/pRPE assays primed with IL-1α, MCC950 should suppress NLRP3 activation triggered by:  
– LMP (Leu-Leu-OMe), where caspase-1 inhibition prevents RPE death and NLRP3 inhibitors reduce IL-1β and LDH release (Ildefonso et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019).  
– Oxidative and lipofuscin/photooxidative stress (H₂O₂, HNE-POS + blue light), where NLRP3 inhibitors significantly lower IL-1β and LDH and preserve RPE morphology ex vivo (Wang et al., 2019).  
– P2X7 activation (BzATP), a canonical AMD-relevant danger signal leading to K⁺ efflux and inflammasome assembly; selective NLRP3 inhibitors attenuate IL-1β and LDH in Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺-free conditions (Wang et al., 2019).

Because autophagy restrains inflammasome activation and removes inflammasome complexes, a reduction in NLRP3 activity may secondarily stabilize autophagic flux under stress. Yet, this remains hypothetical for MCC950 in RPE; explicit autophagy and lysosomal readouts (LC3 flux, p62, LAMP1/2, cathepsin B/D activities, lysosomal pH, galectin-3 LMP puncta) have not been detailed in the RPE inhibitor studies referenced (Celkova et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019). Therefore, while reduction of IL-1β/LDH and preservation of morphology are expected and supported, the proposed enhancement of POS clearance should be considered an untested hypothesis requiring targeted experimentation.

In vivo, efficacy expectations diverge by model:  
– Deposit/atrophy (EFEMP1 R345W, aged WT) are rational choices: genetic deletion of Nlrp3/Casp1 is protective, so MCC950 might reduce BLamD burden and retinal inflammation if adequate ocular exposure is achieved (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c).  
– Photoreceptor acute degeneration (PD) may not respond to NLRP3 inhibition and may be sensitive to dose-related toxicity, favoring downstream caspase-1 inhibition or broader inflammasome suppression (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
– Neovascular models diverge: OIR improved with MCC950; CNV worsened. Dry-AMD-focused development should avoid neovascular endpoints initially, or stratify hypotheses based on IL-1β/IL-18 balance and myeloid contribution (Sui et al., 2020a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).

Overall Evaluation  
MCC950 is a mechanistically compelling, best-in-class NLRP3 inhibitor with credible RPE-target class activity in vitro and strong genetic support for inflammasome involvement in deposit biology. However, the in vivo ocular pharmacology to date is mixed and generally unsupportive for broad dry-AMD application without further de-risking: failure and potential toxicity in PD, context-dependent effects in neovascular models, uncertain RPE expression/engagement in vivo, lack of ocular PK, and unproven restoration of autophagy/lysosomal function in RPE.

On balance, MCC950 merits continued investigation as a mechanistic probe and potential therapeutic lead for specific dry-AMD endophenotypes linked to deposit pathology and chronic inflammasome signaling—provided that the next tranche of studies addresses ocular PK/safety, cell-type exposure, and autophagy/lysosome outcomes. In parallel, downstream targeting (caspase-1) should be benchmarked given superior genetic protection and potential coverage of multiple inflammasome sensors. If MCC950 cannot meet ocular exposure and safety requirements, alternative delivery (e.g., sustained-release nanoparticles) or next-generation NLRP3 inhibitors with better ocular PK and safety profiles may be required (Sun et al., 2023; Ortega et al., 2024b).

In summary, MCC950 has plausible potential for dry AMD if—and only if— its ocular pharmacology can be tuned to the appropriate disease biology: chronic deposit/atrophy with documented inflammasome involvement, sufficient drug exposure at RPE/subretinal myeloid compartments, and a safety margin that avoids the functional liabilities observed at higher intravitreal doses in PD. Without these, the probability of technical success remains low relative to downstream inflammasome targets.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The therapeutic candidate under evaluation is a CD59-Fc fusion protein, a recombinant biologic that combines the extracellular functional domain of CD59—a naturally occurring complement regulatory protein—with the Fc portion of an immunoglobulin (typically IgG1) to extend its ocular half‐life and improve tissue penetration. This fusion protein is synthesized using recombinant DNA technology in mammalian cell expression systems to ensure proper post‐translational modifications and folding, which are critical for retaining high binding affinity (with a reported dissociation constant, Kd, of <1 nM) toward its targets, the complement components C8 and C9, on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) surfaces (Qin et al., 2021; Tan, 2018). The compound belongs to the class of complement inhibitors—a group of therapeutic agents that have been developed to modulate the immune complement cascade, thereby mitigating complement-mediated tissue damage; historically, this class has been primarily investigated for inflammatory and degenerative conditions, including paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, and more recently age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The rationale behind harnessing a CD59-based approach is based on the well-established physiological role of native CD59 in inhibiting the terminal pathway of complement activation by blocking the incorporation of C9 into the C5b-8 complex to form the membrane attack complex (MAC), thus preventing cell lysis and downstream inflammatory cascades (Tan et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
CD59, as a natural complement regulatory protein, has been a focus of research for several years due to its intrinsic ability to safeguard host tissues from complement-mediated injury; multiple studies have demonstrated that impaired CD59 recycling or decreased CD59 surface expression is associated with increased MAC deposition on RPE cells in AMD models, ultimately leading to lysosomal dysfunction and cellular injury (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Although the CD59-Fc fusion protein itself has not been extensively tested in clinical settings, analogous therapeutic approaches—including gene therapy strategies such as AAVCAGsCD59, which deliver soluble forms of CD59 to the retina—have been evaluated preclinically and in early-phase clinical trials, with evidence suggesting that enhancement of CD59 function can reduce complement-mediated damage in the eye (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2021). In addition, complementary studies using other classes of complement inhibitors (for example, compstatin analogs like Cp40 that act upstream at the C3 convertase level) have demonstrated reversal of pathological phenotypes in AMD models by protecting lysosomal integrity and restoring RPE cellular function (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). While most of the clinical research in dry AMD has focused on C3- and C5-targeting agents (such as pegcetacoplan and avacincaptad pegol, respectively) with mixed outcomes, these data collectively support the strategy of terminal pathway inhibition as a viable approach; however, the CD59-Fc candidate distinguishes itself by directly recapitulating the naturally evolved mechanism of MAC inhibition (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022). Notably, while the clinical history of CD59-based therapies in AMD is still in its early stages, preclinical models strongly implicate the loss of CD59 function in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, thereby making CD59 enhancement a rational repurposing strategy in this context (Tan et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the CD59-Fc fusion protein acts by binding specifically to the complement components C8 and/or C9, which is critical during the final assembly phase of the MAC; normally, native CD59 prevents the recruitment of C9 to the C5b-8 complex, thereby effectively halting pore formation on the target cell membrane, which would otherwise lead to uncontrolled ion fluxes, cell lysis, or sub-lytic MAC deposition that can trigger pro-inflammatory and pro-apoptotic signaling cascades (Tan et al., 2016). The high affinity binding (Kd < 1 nM) is expected to allow the fusion protein to effectively compete with endogenous CD59, thereby providing robust inhibition even in the milieu of heightened complement activation as observed in AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In addition to its direct inhibition of MAC assembly, the Fc fragment confers several pharmacokinetic advantages: it enhances the protein’s stability, increases its half-life through neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)-mediated recycling, and may facilitate localized retention within the ocular environment upon intravitreal injection, ensuring sustained therapeutic levels over prolonged treatment intervals (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2021). Moreover, by preventing MAC deposition on RPE cells, the candidate is anticipated to safeguard the integrity of lysosomal membranes—a process crucial for proper autophagic function and the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS); lysosomal damage through MAC-induced membrane permeabilization has been implicated in RPE dysfunction and the subsequent progression of dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). On a cellular level, experimental models have shown that complement attack leads to lysosomal swelling, membrane fragility, and eventual mitochondrial dysfunction due to leakage of lysosomal enzymes (such as Cathepsin D) into the cytosol or drusen-like deposits; by mitigating MAC formation, CD59-Fc is expected to interrupt this deleterious cascade and restore cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
The expected pharmacodynamic effect of the CD59-Fc fusion protein centers on its capacity to prevent MAC deposition on the cell surface of RPE cells; this is hypothesized to occur through the high-affinity binding of the fusion protein to complement components C8 and C9, thereby precluding the insertion of the complete MAC pore into the plasma or lysosomal membranes of these cells (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). By averting MAC formation, the candidate helps maintain lysosomal membrane integrity, which in turn supports normal autophagic degradation and proper phagocytic processing of POS—a process that is critically impaired in AMD and is associated with lipofuscin accumulation and further complement activation (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In functional assays, treatment with CD59-Fc is expected to result in a significant reduction of intracellular MAC deposition, as evidenced by decreased staining of markers associated with complement activation, and to preserve lysosomal structure, as reflected by normalized lysosome size and reduced markers of lysosomal membrane permeability (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). This preservation of lysosomal function is central to ensuring that the RPE retains its ability to efficiently phagocytose and degrade POS, thereby sustaining the retinal microenvironment and potentially slowing or reversing the progression of geographic atrophy—the late stage of dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Moreover, by protecting mitochondrial integrity indirectly through the maintenance of lysosomal function, CD59-Fc may also reduce oxidative stress and apoptotic signaling within RPE cells, contributing further to cell survival and retinal health (Tan et al., 2016). The candidate’s mechanism is supported by data from ex vivo experiments in complement-challenged explants, where application of complement inhibitors similar to CD59-based agents reduced MAC deposition and preserved lysosomal morphology (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2021). Additionally, studies where cholesterol accumulation or the presence of oxidized lipoproteins disrupts CD59 recycling correlate with enhanced MAC deposition and lysosomal dysfunction, reinforcing the notion that restoring CD59 activity through a fusion protein could have broad protective effects on the RPE (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
In assessing the potential of the CD59-Fc fusion protein as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses become apparent. On the positive side, the candidate leverages the body’s natural defense mechanism against complement-mediated injury by directly targeting a key step in the formation of the membrane attack complex, a process that has been strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of AMD. Numerous preclinical studies have established that excessive MAC deposition on RPE cells leads to lysosomal dysfunction, impaired autophagy, and subsequent RPE cell death, all of which are critical factors in the progression of geographic atrophy (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The CD59-Fc fusion protein is therefore expected to interrupt this pathological cascade by preserving lysosomal integrity and promoting the maintenance of cellular homeostasis, with potential downstream benefits including the restoration of normal POS phagocytosis and improved metabolic health of RPE cells (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Another strength is the inclusion of the Fc moiety, which not only extends the protein’s half-life, ensuring sustained therapeutic exposure in the eye, but may also aid in achieving effective localized concentrations following intravitreal administration (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2021). This pharmacokinetic advantage is particularly significant in ocular therapies, where frequent dosing and short half-life of drugs have historically challenged the long-term management of chronic conditions such as dry AMD. Moreover, the concept of using a recombinant fusion protein to mimic or enhance endogenous regulatory mechanisms has precedence in other therapeutic areas, providing a solid scientific foundation for this approach (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Tan et al., 2016).

However, there are also notable challenges and potential weaknesses that warrant careful consideration. One primary concern is that, while preclinical models and ex vivo explant studies provide promising evidence for the efficacy of complement inhibitors in halting or reversing complement-mediated damage, the translation of these findings into clinical success in dry AMD has been fraught with mixed results. Several complement inhibitors, particularly those targeting upstream components like C3 and C5 (e.g., pegcetacoplan, avacincaptad pegol), have shown significant anatomical benefits such as reduced geographic atrophy lesion growth but have failed to reliably improve visual acuity, and in some instances have been associated with adverse events such as conversion to neovascular AMD (Tzoumas et al., 2023). Although CD59-Fc acts at a different point in the complement cascade, the complexity of the complement system in the ocular microenvironment and the possibility of compensatory mechanisms remain a potential hurdle that could limit therapeutic efficacy (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Another consideration is that the CD59-Fc fusion protein has yet to be tested extensively in in vivo models of AMD, and its pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics in the human eye are largely unknown. Challenges such as achieving sufficient tissue penetration, avoiding systemic immune activation, and mitigating any unforeseen off-target effects will need to be addressed in rigorous preclinical studies before any clinical trial can be contemplated (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022). Additionally, there is always the risk associated with biologics that their large molecular size or Fc-mediated effector functions might lead to immunogenicity or unexpected interactions with other components of the immune system, potentially triggering inflammatory responses—this is particularly critical in the immune-privileged ocular environment where preserving immune homeostasis is essential (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Finally, while the hypothesis postulates that by protecting lysosomal membranes CD59-Fc will indirectly improve POS phagocytic and degradative function, the relationship between complement suppression and restoration of complex RPE cell functions remains to be conclusively established in AMD pathology. Although there is compelling evidence that complement-mediated MAC deposition is deleterious to lysosomal function and that complement inhibition can restore cellular homeostasis, the multifactorial nature of AMD pathogenesis—which includes oxidative stress, lipid dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and genetic predispositions—means that CD59-Fc may need to be used in combination with other therapeutic strategies to achieve clinically meaningful outcomes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2016).

In summary, the CD59-Fc fusion protein represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its profound mechanistic rationale, which is anchored in the prevention of MAC formation and the subsequent protection of lysosomal membranes in RPE cells. Its design to mimic and potentiate a natural protective pathway, combined with the pharmacokinetic benefits conferred by the Fc fusion, positions it favorably among complement-based therapeutic strategies. However, the challenges of translating preclinical successes into reliable clinical outcomes in the heterogeneous and multifactorial landscape of AMD cannot be understated. A focused program of further preclinical studies—including detailed pharmacodynamic assessments, tissue distribution, efficacy in robust in vivo models of dry AMD, and safety evaluations—will be essential to validate the therapeutic potential of CD59-Fc prior to embarking on human clinical trials. Overall, while the strengths of the candidate are compelling, its ultimate success will depend on resolving the inherent complexities of complement regulation in the retinal microenvironment and ensuring that the beneficial effects on lysosomal preservation translate into meaningful improvements in visual function and disease progression in patients with dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2016; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Brefeldin A (BFA) is a natural product originally isolated in 1958 from Penicillium decumbens, and its discovery marked the beginning of intensive studies on its unique ability to disrupt intracellular protein trafficking (Hung, 2020). Structurally, BFA is a macrolide characterized by a complex fused system comprising a cyclopentane moiety linked to a 13-membered lactone, and this distinctive architecture has spurred extensive synthetic and medicinal chemistry efforts over the past decades (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015). By targeting the secretory pathway, BFA acts as a Golgi transport inhibitor, primarily through its binding to a protein complex involving a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) and the small G protein Arf1. This binding event results in the rapid disassembly of the Golgi apparatus and redistribution of its components back into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Hung, 2020). BFA is therefore classified among natural product inhibitors of intracellular trafficking, a group that has long served as invaluable research tools in cell biology to dissect the mechanisms of vesicular transport and Golgi-ER dynamics. Its broad bioactivities—as an antiviral, antifungal, and antimitotic agent—have principally been exploited in preclinical research rather than clinical therapeutics (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, BFA has been employed almost exclusively as a biochemical probe to investigate protein processing, secretion, and Golgi morphology in diverse eukaryotic cells. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that BFA’s ability to stall ER-to-Golgi trafficking can modulate various cellular processes including secretion of cytokines, hormones, and growth factors (Hung, 2020). Its documented effects on blocking transport have been leveraged in cancer cell studies where BFA-induced apoptosis and cell cycle arrest were observed, owing to mislocalization of key signaling molecules (Stierle & Stierle, 2015). Despite these promising cellular effects, the clinical development of BFA as a conventional therapeutic agent has been hindered by issues such as poor bioavailability and significant toxicity with prolonged exposure (Seehafer et al., 2013). Importantly, while BFA has not been directly applied in clinical studies for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or any similar degenerative retinal diseases, its mechanistic action on intracellular trafficking, ER stress, and protein secretion renders it an intriguing candidate for repurposing. In the context of AMD, where complement dysregulation and lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells play a critical pathogenic role, BFA could potentially offer a novel means of attenuating the buildup of complement components and misfolded proteins (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). While none of the published literature explicitly documents the use of BFA for AMD therapy, related studies in RPE cellular models have highlighted the importance of complement modulation and lysosomal restoration, establishing a rationale for investigating trafficking inhibitors such as BFA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
On a molecular level, the mechanism of action for Brefeldin A is well characterized. BFA binds to the complex comprising a catalytic GEF and the small GTPase Arf1, inhibiting the exchange of GDP for GTP on Arf1. This inhibition precludes proper recruitment and coat assembly for vesicle budding at the Golgi membranes, leading to a collapse of the Golgi structure and the retrograde redistribution of Golgi proteins to the ER (Hung, 2020). The immediate consequence of this inhibition is a profound disruption in the secretory pathway, which not only halts the export of proteins but also results in an accumulation of proteins within the ER. In cell types where the regulated secretion of proteins is critical for homeostasis, such as in RPE cells, this effect can have dual ramifications. On the one hand, it may help prevent the secretion of misfolded or aberrantly processed proteins, including complement components that are implicated in local inflammation and lysosomal deposition (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). On the other hand, the blockade of Golgi trafficking may transiently lower the secretion of proteins that otherwise contribute to the local pool of complement proteins which, if misfolded or overproduced, could lead to an increase in intracellular complement activation and subsequent deposition of the membrane attack complex (MAC, particularly C5b-9) within lysosomes (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In RPE cells, where robust daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) is essential, the maintenance of lysosomal function is critical; overburdening of lysosomes with complement-derived debris has been implicated in the formation of drusen and lipofuscin accumulation, both of which underlie AMD pathology (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The proposed intervention using BFA therefore leverages its well-established ability to modulate protein trafficking to indirectly reduce the burden of misfolded or overabundant complement proteins on the lysosomal system, thereby potentially restoring cathepsin activity and overall lysosomal function in RPE cells.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing BFA in dry AMD is that brief pulses of BFA administration will selectively inhibit the ER-to-Golgi trafficking route in RPE cells, thereby reducing the processing and secretion of misfolded complement proteins. RPE cells are known to contribute to local complement activation through the production and turnover of various complement components; in AMD, aberrant complement regulation leads to increased turnover, formation of complement split products, and the deposition of terminal complement complexes (C5b-9) in the lysosomes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The expected outcome of BFA treatment would be a reduction in the export of these misfolded or excessively generated complement proteins, ultimately leading to decreased local complement activation and a reduction in lysosomal overload by MAC proteins. Experimental evidence from studies using compstatin analogues (e.g., Cp40) in Y402H-RPE cell models has shown that complement inhibition can restore lysosomal function and cathepsin activity, thereby reducing lysosome size, diminishing drusen-like deposits, and improving the overall cellular phenotype (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015). By analogy, transient BFA treatment is anticipated to produce similar beneficial effects on lysosomal physiology in RPE cells, provided that the inhibition is carefully timed to avoid prolonged exposure which could be deleterious (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Furthermore, because RPE cells are responsible for the daily clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, maintaining an unencumbered lysosomal system is crucial for long-term retinal health. The expected biochemical cascade following BFA administration would therefore include a reduction in ER stress due to diminished protein export, lower secretion of misfolded complement proteins, and a subsequent decrease in complement-mediated lysosomal damage. This in turn should lead to a stabilization or even an improvement in cathepsin levels and activity, promoting a more efficient degradation of cellular debris and restoration of POS clearance (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential repurposing of Brefeldin A as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD is innovative and grounded in a detailed understanding of both its mechanism of action and the pathophysiology of AMD. Several strengths underlie this approach. First, BFA has a well-characterized molecular mechanism that directly affects the secretory pathway by inhibiting ER-to-Golgi trafficking. This offers a mechanistic basis for reducing the secretion of misfolded or aberrantly processed complement proteins—the accumulation of which is a central driver of lysosomal dysfunction and local complement activation in RPE cells (Hung, 2020). Second, preclinical research in AMD models has demonstrated that modulating complement activity, whether through direct inhibition of complement components or by enhancing lysosomal function, can reverse pathological phenotypes associated with the disease (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015). This suggests that a strategy aimed at indirectly reducing complement deposition via interference with protein trafficking holds considerable promise. Third, the idea of using brief pulses of BFA rather than continuous dosing could allow for a transient therapeutic effect that minimizes the known toxicities associated with prolonged BFA exposure—thus potentially overcoming one of the key limitations that has prevented its clinical development in other contexts (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015).

Nonetheless, there are significant challenges and weaknesses that must be addressed before this approach can be advanced. One of the primary concerns relates to the non-selectivity of BFA’s action. Because BFA disrupts a fundamental cellular process, its effects are not confined solely to the trafficking of misfolded complement proteins. It is likely to inhibit the normal secretion of multiple proteins that are essential for RPE cell function, which could inadvertently impair the phagocytosis and processing of photoreceptor outer segments (Hung, 2020; Seehafer et al., 2013). Such disruption could paradoxically exacerbate the very lysosomal dysfunction it is intended to ameliorate, particularly if dosing is not carefully titrated. Furthermore, while transient inhibition may mitigate toxicity, achieving the precise balance between therapeutic efficacy and cellular viability will require rigorous optimization in both in vitro and in vivo models. Another potential drawback is related to pharmacokinetics and delivery. BFA’s poor bioavailability and potential systemic toxicity have long been recognized as obstacles for its use beyond experimental settings (Seehafer et al., 2013). Delivering BFA specifically to the RPE while avoiding off-target effects in other ocular or systemic tissues will demand innovative formulation strategies, such as localized drug delivery systems, which inherently add another layer of complexity to the drug development process. Additionally, while the hypothesis is supported by analogous studies demonstrating that complement modulation can restore lysosomal function in AMD models (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015), there is currently no direct evidence that BFA’s inhibition of ER-to-Golgi trafficking will reproduce these beneficial effects in the delicate environment of the retina. The potential for unforeseen interactions with other components of the RPE’s protein processing machinery or compensatory cellular responses further complicates the translational prospects of this approach.

In summary, as an expert drug development team leader tasked with evaluating promising repurposed drugs for dry AMD, I find the proposal to repurpose Brefeldin A to be both innovative and mechanistically intriguing. The strengths of this candidate lie in its well-characterized molecular target—namely, the inhibition of Arf1-mediated vesicle budding at the Golgi—and its potential to modulate a key pathological feature of AMD, namely the dysregulated secretion and accumulation of complement proteins that leads to lysosomal impairment and MAC deposition (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). However, the inherent risks associated with disrupting a central cellular process cannot be overstated. The lack of selectivity in BFA’s action, potential toxicity from even brief exposures, and challenges in targeting the RPE specifically are serious obstacles that must be systematically addressed. Further preclinical studies are required to delineate the dose-response relationship in RPE cell models, to examine the long-term effects of transient BFA-induced trafficking inhibition on cellular health, and to validate the hypothesis that such intervention can indeed reduce lysosomal MAC deposition and rescue cathepsin activity. Only with convincing evidence from rigorous in vitro and in vivo experiments would it be justified to consider advancing BFA as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. In conclusion, while the proposed use of BFA presents a compelling mechanistic rationale with some supportive preclinical analogies from the literature (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020), significant challenges regarding specificity, delivery, and safety need to be overcome before this approach can be deemed a viable therapeutic option for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ceapin-A7 is a small molecule inhibitor that belongs to the pyrazole amide class of compounds. It was originally discovered through high‐throughput cell‐based screening assays designed to identify modulators of the unfolded protein response (UPR), with an emphasis on selectively targeting the ATF6α signaling branch (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Hetz et al., 2019). Structural optimization through structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies led to the development of Ceapin-A7 as a potent derivative with submicromolar inhibitory activity against ATF6α (Hetz et al., 2019). The molecule’s chemical origins are purely synthetic; its pyrazole amide core is complemented by additional substituents that optimize its binding affinity and selectivity. Traditionally, compounds in this chemical class have been explored as research tools to dissect the UPR pathways and have shown promise in modulating ER stress signaling in various cellular contexts (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). The compound’s design exploits the unique structure–function relationships of ATF6α, aiming to interfere with its normal intracellular trafficking rather than block downstream proteolysis directly, which marks a novel approach compared with many enzyme inhibitors developed for other targets.

Therapeutic History:  
To date, Ceapin-A7 has been mainly used as an investigative tool in cellular models to study mechanisms underlying ER stress and the UPR. Its ability to selectively inhibit ATF6α activation has been characterized in multiple cell lines, including human osteosarcoma U2-OS cells and HEK293 cells engineered to express tagged ATF6α constructs (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Hetz et al., 2019). Although there is extensive preclinical evidence supporting its utility in modulating UPR signaling—all of which has been generated in the context of studies on cancer cells, neurodegeneration, and endothelial dysfunction—there is no historically established clinical or veterinary usage for Ceapin-A7 specifically in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal degenerative diseases. However, the mechanistic insights gained from its application in other cell types have spurred investigations into repurposing Ceapin-A7 as a potential therapeutic candidate for correcting maladaptive ER stress responses in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which plays a pivotal role in diseases such as dry AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Torres et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
Ceapin-A7 exerts its pharmacological action by selectively inhibiting the ATF6α branch of the UPR. Under normal ER stress conditions, ATF6α, a 90-kDa transmembrane protein located in the endoplasmic reticulum, undergoes a stress-induced conformational change that facilitates its packaging into COPII vesicles and subsequent trafficking to the Golgi apparatus. Once in the Golgi, ATF6α is cleaved sequentially by site-1 (S1P) and site-2 (S2P) proteases to release its N-terminal transcription factor domain, which then translocates to the nucleus to upregulate several chaperone and ER stress-related genes (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Ceapin-A7 intervenes at this critical transport step. Rather than inhibiting the proteolytic machinery directly, Ceapin-A7 selectively prevents the ER-to-Golgi trafficking of ATF6α. Mechanistic studies have demonstrated that upon treatment with Ceapin-A7, ATF6α is sequestered within the ER where it accumulates in discrete foci. Fluorescence microscopy analyses have shown that these foci do not colocalize with ER exit site markers such as SEC16 or SEC31A, indicating that the compound disrupts the selection of ATF6α into COPII vesicles (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

One particularly novel aspect of Ceapin-A7’s mechanism is its induction of a neomorphic inter-organelle tether. Detailed proteomic and genome-wide CRISPR interference screening studies have revealed that Ceapin-A7 induces a physical interaction between the cytosolic domain of ATF6α and the peroxisomal transporter protein ABCD3 (Torres et al., 2019). This newly formed tether effectively anchors ATF6α within the ER and precludes its normal traffic to the Golgi. In addition, Ceapin-A7 appears to stabilize ATF6α in its oligomeric state, rather than allowing it to convert to the transport-competent monomeric form (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). The fact that these mechanistic events are reversible upon compound washout further indicates that Ceapin-A7 provides a transient yet highly specific method for modulating ATF6α activity without causing permanent alterations to the protein structure or its eventual capacity to function when the inhibitor is removed (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Such high selectivity distinguishes Ceapin-A7 from broader ER stress inhibitors that often affect multiple UPR signaling branches.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the hypothesized role of Ceapin-A7 is to inhibit chronic ATF6α overactivation in RPE cells, thereby rebalancing the UPR toward adaptive rather than pro-apoptotic responses. Chronic or overwhelming ER stress in RPE cells, as observed in AMD, is associated with decreased expression of genes critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis, including those linked to autophagy, lysosomal function, and the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Because RPE cells are responsible for daily phagocytosis of POS, maintaining efficient lysosomal clearance is crucial for retinal health. In dry AMD, impaired phagocytosis leads to the buildup of toxic byproducts such as lipofuscin, which further exacerbates cellular dysfunction (Kubra et al., 2022; Benedetti et al., 2024).

The therapeutic hypothesis for Ceapin-A7 centers on its capacity to inhibit ATF6α at an IC₅₀ in the low micromolar range (approximately 2 µM, as proposed), thus reducing maladaptive UPR signaling. By preventing ATF6α from trafficking and undergoing proteolytic activation, Ceapin-A7 is expected to alleviate the chronic ER stress that drives RPE dysfunction. In a proposed assay—using ARPE-19 cells in conditions of induced ER stress (for instance, via tunicamycin treatment)—Ceapin-A7 should reduce the levels of cleaved, active ATF6α. This in turn is expected to restore the gene expression patterns associated with lysosomal enzyme production and phagocytic receptor synthesis, thereby enhancing the clearance of POS components (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Furthermore, because the ATF6 branch of the UPR is associated with the upregulation of chaperones like BiP/Grp78, persistent activation can lead to resource exhaustion and an imbalance that favors apoptotic signaling under chronic ER stress conditions (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). By selectively inhibiting this pathway, Ceapin-A7 might reduce excessive chaperone induction and allow cellular systems to shift toward a more balanced, adaptive stress response that promotes autophagy and lysosomal function. Importantly, RPE cells express ATF6, as evidenced by studies utilizing ARPE-19 and primary RPE cultures, making these cells appropriate targets for ATF6 modulation (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Thus, the expected effect is a reestablishment of normal proteostasis in RPE cells via the restoration of adaptive autophagy, improved lysosomal enzyme activity, and enhanced phagocytic receptor expression, all of which are critical for the sustained clearance of photoreceptor outer segment debris and prevention of cytotoxic accumulation in dry AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
Ceapin-A7 represents an innovative therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration due to its unique and selective mechanism of action targeting the ATF6α branch of the UPR. One of the main strengths of this compound is its ability to modulate a very specific aspect of cellular stress signaling. By preventing the ER-to-Golgi trafficking of ATF6α and thereby inhibiting its proteolytic activation, Ceapin-A7 offers a promising strategy for shifting the balance of UPR signaling toward adaptive autophagy instead of chronic, detrimental ER stress (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). This is particularly relevant in the context of RPE cells, which require efficient protein quality control and robust lysosomal function to maintain photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance and overall retinal integrity.

In vitro studies have validated the mechanism of Ceapin-A7, with data showing that the compound induces the formation of discrete ATF6α-positive foci in the ER (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Moreover, the reversible nature of its action implies that Ceapin-A7 may offer a controllable therapeutic window, enabling fine-tuning of UPR modulation in a clinical setting (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). The involvement of peroxisomal protein ABCD3 in a neomorphic tethering mechanism further differentiates Ceapin-A7 from other UPR modulators by introducing a novel means of sequestering ATF6α (Torres et al., 2019). Such specificity is particularly compelling because it suggests that Ceapin-A7 can mitigate the chronic ER stress observed in dry AMD without interfering with other UPR branches (such as IRE1 or PERK), which are essential for normal cellular adaptation to transient stress.

However, there are notable limitations and challenges that warrant careful evaluation. First, despite the extensive preclinical work in cell lines and non-retinal systems, Ceapin-A7 has yet to be thoroughly evaluated in RPE-specific models or in vivo systems relevant to AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Second, the full spectrum of off-target effects is not yet fully characterized. While Ceapin-A7 shows selectivity for ATF6α, the influence of its induced neomorphic tether between ATF6α and ABCD3 on peroxisome function remains to be fully elucidated. Although available evidence suggests that Ceapin-A7 does not interfere significantly with ABCD3’s normal transporter function (Torres et al., 2019), the robustness of these findings in the retinal context remains an open question.

Another potential caveat is the dual role that ATF6α may play in various tissues. Although chronic activation of ATF6α is thought to contribute to maladaptive ER stress and consequent cellular dysfunction in AMD, ATF6α also participates in adaptive responses by upregulating crucial ER chaperones that preserve proteostasis (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Therefore, complete inhibition of ATF6α activity might have unintended consequences if not properly dosed or if the timing of inhibition is not carefully managed. An optimal therapeutic strategy might require a fine balance between sufficient ATF6α inhibition to restore lysosomal and phagocytic function in RPE cells and preserving enough ATF6α activity to maintain overall cellular homeostasis, particularly in tissues under variable stress dynamics.

Moreover, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of Ceapin-A7 in the ocular environment have not been established. For a drug candidate to be viable in treating dry AMD, it must be effectively delivered to the RPE with minimal systemic exposure, maintain a stable concentration over time, and be cleared without inducing local toxicity. The formulation challenges of ocular drug delivery, including crossing the blood-retinal barrier and achieving sustained release in the subretinal space, remain critical hurdles that must be addressed in future studies (Hetz et al., 2019; Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Finally, long-term safety studies are essential. The reversible nature of Ceapin-A7’s effects is promising; however, chronic treatment in a degenerative condition like dry AMD necessitates an in-depth understanding of the potential cumulative effects or chronic alterations in ER stress responses over time. Safety profiles in animal models, particularly those that recapitulate the chronic oxidative stress and proteostasis defects seen in AMD, will be crucial for advancing Ceapin-A7 into clinical trials.

In summary, Ceapin-A7 holds significant promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its precise mechanism—selectively inhibiting ATF6α activation by preventing its ER-to-Golgi trafficking and inducing a novel tether with ABCD3—positions it as a unique tool for rebalancing maladaptive UPR signaling (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Torres et al., 2019). The expected therapeutic benefit in RPE cells is the restoration of adaptive autophagy, maintenance of lysosomal function, and enhanced phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, all of which are critical to slowing or halting the progression of dry AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Nevertheless, the lack of extensive in vivo data in retinal models and the potential for off-target effects or unintended suppression of adaptive ER stress responses are significant concerns that must be addressed before clinical translation (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Rigorous investigation in RPE-specific systems, careful dose–response studies, pharmacokinetic profiling, and long-term safety evaluations are essential next steps. Overall, Ceapin-A7 is a mechanistically innovative candidate that merits further preclinical development as a novel intervention for dry AMD, provided that its complex interplay with ER stress, autophagy, and lysosomal function is thoroughly characterized in ocular tissues (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).
