Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MCC950 is a synthetic diarylsulfonylurea small molecule originally identified from an IL-1β processing inhibitor chemotype and later defined as a highly potent and selective inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome complex (Coll et al., 2015). Within the inflammasome‐inhibitor landscape, MCC950 is representative of sulfonylurea‐based NLRP3 inhibitors that block canonical and noncanonical NLRP3 activation while sparing other inflammasomes (AIM2, NLRC4, NLRP1) and upstream innate pathways (e.g., TLR-NF-κB priming) (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Mechanistically, MCC950 acts directly on NLRP3 to prevent assembly of the adaptor ASC (apoptosis‐associated speck-like protein containing a CARD) into oligomeric “specks,” thereby preventing caspase-1 activation and maturation of IL-1β and IL-18 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Follow-on mechanistic analyses indicate MCC950 binds the NLRP3 NACHT domain to inhibit its ATPase function and thereby prevent NLRP3 activation; mechanistic models include prevention of ASC oligomerization and disruption of required conformations for NEK7–NLRP3 cooperation during sensor activation (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2023).

This class (selective NLRP3 inhibitors) has been broadly leveraged in preclinical inflammatory disease models to selectively blunt inflammasome‐driven IL-1 family cytokine maturation and pyroptosis without pan‐suppressing innate immune sensing, with documented in vivo efficacy in autoimmune encephalomyelitis, CAPS (NLRP3 gain‐of‐function), spontaneous colitis, atherosclerosis, and myocardial infarction models (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021; Wooff et al., 2020). In ocular biology, several sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950 and chemically related CRID3/IFM compounds—reduce IL-1β secretion and cell lysis in human RPE models and ex vivo mouse RPE/choroid eye cups under diverse AMD‐relevant triggers (lysosomal membrane permeabilization, oxidative/photooxidative stress, and P2X7 activation) (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic and non‐ocular indications. MCC950 has repeatedly shown robust pharmacodynamic suppression of inflammasome outputs and disease modification in vivo. Oral dosing in a spontaneous colitis model suppressed IL-1β/IL-18 production ex vivo and improved clinical/histopathologic indices (Perera et al., 2018). In APC‐driven autoimmune encephalomyelitis and in CAPS, MCC950 reduced IL-1β production and ameliorated disease; in CAPS it rescued neonatal lethality (Coll et al., 2015). In ApoE-deficient mice, MCC950 reduced atherosclerotic plaque burden, intraplaque macrophages, and systemic TNF-α/IL-1β/IL-6/IL-18 (Zeng et al., 2021). Across these studies MCC950 demonstrates in vivo target engagement, cytokine suppression, and disease modification with high selectivity for NLRP3 (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021). However, translational reviews emphasize that many NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950‐class agents—face liabilities for organ penetration (including eye/brain) and potential liver toxicity, underscoring formulation/delivery and safety risks that must be addressed for ocular use (Ortega et al., 2024).

Ocular and retinal contexts. In the ischemic OIR model, MCC950 lowered retinal neovascularization and vascular leakage and shifted an aberrant cytokine balance (decreased IL-1β activity with increased IL-18 activity), with accompanying reductions in angiogenesis‐ and pericyte‐associated signaling molecules (VEGF, VEGFR1/2, MMP2/9, PDGFR-β, Ang2) and evidence of inflammasome activation localized predominantly to macrophages (F4/80+) over endothelium (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Sui et al., 2020c). In a glaucoma model (DBA/2J), MCC950 reduced NLRP3 and cleaved caspase-1 in retina and mitigated retinal ganglion cell loss independently of intraocular pressure, indicating on‐target retinal neuroinflammation suppression (Li, 2020).

By contrast, in a laser‐induced CNV model (wet AMD), short‐course MCC950 lowered IL-1β transcript/protein but paradoxically increased total CNV lesion volume and recruitment of microglia and monocyte‐derived macrophages; ERG a- and b-waves were unchanged, suggesting no gross electrophysiological toxicity under those conditions (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b). This aligns with genetic evidence that inflammasome–IL-1β signaling promotes CNV largely through macrophages/microglia and that non‐NLRP3 inflammasomes also contribute, implying that selectively inhibiting NLRP3 may have complex, context‐dependent effects in neovascular disease (Marneros, 2023a; Marneros, 2023b).

In dry‐AMD–relevant photo‐oxidative damage (PD), intravitreal MCC950 failed to rescue function/structure and high‐dose MCC950 worsened ERG amplitudes: 20 µM showed no functional change versus PBS and did not alter photoreceptor death or IBA-1+ microglia counts; 100 µM significantly reduced ERG function (Wooff et al., 2020b). In the same study, Casp1/11−/− mice exhibited strong protection, whereas Nlrp3−/− mice showed only partial functional preservation, and pharmacologic NLRP3 inhibition or Nlrp3 siRNA provided no benefit (and in some readouts reduced function), leading to the conclusion that downstream caspase-1 is a dominant driver whereas NLRP3 may be neither necessary nor sufficient in this model (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). The authors also highlighted uncertainties about NLRP3 localization (predominantly INL/GCL rather than RPE), protein detection sensitivity, and the absence of ocular pharmacokinetic data for MCC950 (Wooff et al., 2020b).

RPE cell and ex vivo ocular models. In IL-1α–primed ARPE-19 and primary human RPE (pRPE), sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors reduced inflammasome activation and cell injury across diverse triggers relevant to GA, including LMP (Leu-Leu-OMe), oxidative stress (H₂O₂), lipofuscin/photooxidative insult (HNE-POS + blue light), and P2X7 activation (BzATP); in Abca4−/− eye cups, selective NLRP3 inhibitors suppressed IL-1β and LDH release and preserved RPE morphology after blue‐light irradiation (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024). A 2024 synthesis that included MCC950 reports that MCC950, IFM-632, and IFM-514 each decreased IL-1α-primed RPE inflammasome activation independent of the activation trigger, consistent with target class effects in RPE models (Korhonen, 2024). These in vitro/ex vivo data strongly support that NLRP3 activity can be engaged in RPE and that selective, small‐molecule inhibition suppresses canonical outputs (IL-1β, LDH) under multiple AMD‐relevant insults. However, detailed analyses of autophagic flux restoration or lysosomal integrity rescue after MCC950 are not reported in these excerpts (Wang et al., 2019).

Emerging genetics for AMD‐relevant deposits. In a monogenic EFEMP1 R345W knockin model (ML/DHRD) that recapitulates basal laminar deposits (BLamDs), as well as in aged WT mice, whole‐animal deletion of Nlrp3 or Casp1 significantly reduced BLamD size/coverage, normalized proinflammatory retinal cytokine profiles, and reduced microglial activation; these data provide genetic causality linking NLRP3–caspase-1 activity to deposit formation and inflammatory milieu (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). The same preprint cautions that NLRP3 inhibitors frequently suffer inadequate ocular penetration and potential liver toxicity, and emphasizes the need to determine whether ocular‐local versus systemic NLRP3 suppression is required (Ortega et al., 2024b).

Mechanism of Action  
Molecular target and binding mechanism. NLRP3 is a tripartite sensor (PYD–NACHT–LRR) that oligomerizes upon priming and activation to recruit ASC via PYD–PYD interactions, which in turn polymerizes and recruits pro-caspase-1 via CARD–CARD interactions to form an active inflammasome; active caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 and the pore‐forming effector gasdermin D (GSDMD) to elicit cytokine secretion and pyroptosis (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). MCC950 binds NLRP3 and prevents its ATPase activity (NACHT domain), disrupting a conformational step required for oligomerization and ASC speck assembly; in cellular systems, MCC950 suppresses both canonical (e.g., K⁺ efflux, lysosomal rupture, mitochondrial ROS) and noncanonical (caspase-11–triggered) activation pathways (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Notably, MCC950 does not broadly interfere with upstream priming (NF-κB–dependent transcription of NLRP3 and cytokine precursors), K⁺ or Ca²⁺ flux, or NLRP3–ASC direct binding in simple biochemical assays; rather, it functionally prevents ASC oligomerization and caspase-1 processing, reflecting target engagement at the level of sensor activation/oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Selectivity is strong: activity against AIM2, NLRC4, and NLRP1 inflammasomes is not observed, and broad target screening reveals only weak off-target activity (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018).

Cell-context specificity in the retina and RPE. Expression of NLRP3 and caspase-1 in the retina is cell-type and stimulus dependent. In vitro, microglia robustly upregulate Nlrp3, Casp1, and Il1b upon stimulation; Müller cells can increase Nlrp3 and Il1b without matching Casp1 elevation; photoreceptor‐line cells upregulate Nlrp3 while reducing Casp1; ARPE-19 cells often show undetectable NLRP3 protein and variable inflammasome readouts under some conditions (Wooff et al., 2020a). In situ, NLRP3 labeling is minimal in dim-reared mouse retinas but becomes detectable in the INL/GCL after PD, and AMD donor tissue shows NLRP3 in INL/GCL, suggesting inner-retina/microglial inflammasome contributions that complicate direct linkage to outer retina/RPE degeneration (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). Conversely, multiple human and preclinical reports demonstrate NLRP3 upregulation in macular RPE of AMD eyes with strong increases in pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 transcripts, co-localization of NLRP3 with autophagosome-like structures, and mitochondrial damage/autophagy signatures—though the literature is conflicted by antibody specificity and cell line variability (Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b; Marneros, 2023b). Taken together, these data imply that in AMD-relevant contexts, NLRP3 activation can occur in RPE and in inner-retinal microglia/Müller/immune cells; drug effects will be inherently cell-type dependent.

Pathway-level effects in retinal models. In ischemic retinopathy (OIR), NLRP3 activation (NLRP3/ASC/CASP1 upregulation and ASC specks) is observed primarily in macrophages and endothelium, and MCC950 reversal of an increased IL-1β/decreased IL-18 pattern is associated with reduced neovascularization and leakage, implicating vascular-cell responses to inflammasome cytokines as drivers of pathology (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b). In wet AMD CNV, inflammasome activation is localized mainly to infiltrating macrophages and microglia, and IL-1β is a principal driver of lesion growth; however, pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition increased lesion size in one study despite reduced IL-1β, suggesting additional non-NLRP3 inflammasomes and compensatory mechanisms (or cell-intrinsic NLRP3 roles) shape outcomes (Marneros, 2023a; Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b).

Expected Effect  
Proposed assay and mechanism. The proposal posits that MCC950 will specifically inhibit NLRP3 assembly in RPE (IC₅₀ ~7.5 nM), reducing IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, preventing inflammasome-induced lysosomal damage, preserving autophagic flux, and thereby enhancing photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance. Mechanistic underpinnings exist for the first components of this cascade: (i) MCC950 demonstrates nanomolar potency and high selectivity for NLRP3 and suppresses downstream IL-1β/IL-18 (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018); (ii) in IL-1α–primed RPE models (ARPE-19 and pRPE), sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950 in compiled data—suppress IL-1β and LDH release across LMP, oxidative stress, lipofuscin/photooxidative, and P2X7 activation paradigms, and preserve ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology under blue-light irradiation (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024). These findings support the expected reduction of canonical inflammasome outputs in RPE assays under multiple AMD-like stimuli.

Lysosome/autophagy preservation and POS clearance. Autophagy is a key negative regulator of NLRP3 activation: it limits ROS and damaged mitochondria, targets assembled inflammasomes for degradation, and suppresses IL-1β responses; conversely, autophagy suppression increases inflammasome activation and pyroptosis in RPE (Celkova et al., 2015). AMD-relevant triggers—including lipofuscin bisretinoids (e.g., A2E) and oxidative stress—cause lysosomal stress/LMP and NLRP3 activation in RPE, and caspase-1 inhibition can prevent RPE death in LMP contexts (Ildefonso et al., 2016). However, direct evidence that MCC950 restores autophagic flux or lysosomal integrity in RPE is not reported in the cited primary RPE inhibitor studies; the RPE evidence centers on IL-1β and LDH suppression and morphological preservation in ex vivo tissue but does not include autophagy- or lysosome-specific readouts or POS phagocytosis assays (Wang et al., 2019). Therefore, while it is plausible that NLRP3 suppression will indirectly favor autophagy homeostasis in stressed RPE by damping inflammasome-driven pyroptotic signaling (and thereby reduce further lysosomal damage), the proposed “preservation of autophagy and enhanced POS clearance” remains unproven for MCC950 and should be tested explicitly (Celkova et al., 2015).

Disease- and cell-type context expectations. In dry AMD models that feature outer-retinal/RPE degeneration, the translation of RPE in vitro suppression of NLRP3 to in vivo benefit is uncertain. In PD (a dry-AMD–relevant model), intravitreal MCC950 failed to confer protection and at higher dose impaired retinal function; Nlrp3−/− mice showed only partial protection while Casp1/11−/− mice were strongly protected, arguing that downstream caspase-1 and/or other inflammasomes may be the dominant drivers in photoreceptor death (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). In EFEMP1 R345W and aged WT models, genetic inactivation of Nlrp3 or Casp1 reduced basal laminar deposit burden and inflammatory signatures, supporting target pathway relevance for drusen/BLamD biology, but pharmacological MCC950 efficacy in these genetic models has not been reported (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). Importantly, if inflammasome activation in vivo is dominated by subretinal macrophages/microglia in some contexts (e.g., autophagy-impaired RPE signals that activate macrophage inflammasomes), the expected pharmacologic effect of MCC950 may depend more on drug exposure to myeloid cells in the subretinal/choroidal space than on direct RPE engagement (Liu et al., 2016).

Finally, IL-18 biology is context-dependent: while IL-1β is broadly pro-angiogenic and disruptive, IL-18 can be protective/anti-angiogenic in neovascular settings, and AMD-relevant studies have reported discordant roles for IL-18 across disease phenotypes (Celkova et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). Given that NLRP3 blockade reduces both IL-1β and IL-18, net effects on tissue outcomes may vary by disease stage and cell-type source; in OIR, MCC950 “normalized” an inverted IL-1β/IL-18 pattern and improved pathology (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020c), whereas in CNV, MCC950 increased lesion volume—implicating competing effects and non-NLRP3 inflammasomes (Dieckmann et al., 2024a).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- On-target potency/selectivity. MCC950 is among the most potent and selective NLRP3 inhibitors described, blocking canonical and noncanonical activation at nanomolar concentrations and sparing other inflammasomes and upstream pathways; it consistently suppresses IL-1β/IL-18 maturation and caspase-1 activation in primary macrophages and multiple in vivo models (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Perera et al., 2018).  
- RPE-target class activity under AMD-relevant stimuli. Sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors, including MCC950 in compiled datasets, reproducibly suppress IL-1β and LDH in IL-1α–primed ARPE-19 and primary human RPE triggered by LMP, oxidative/photooxidative stress, and P2X7 activation; ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology is preserved by an NLRP3 inhibitor during photooxidative stress (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024).  
- Genetic target validation in AMD-relevant deposit biology. Whole‐body Nlrp3 or Casp1 deletion reduces BLamDs and normalizes inflammatory signatures in EFEMP1 R345W mice and even prevents spontaneous deposits in aged WT, indicating the inflammasome pathway contributes causally to deposit formation and retinal inflammation (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c).  
- Demonstrated retinal efficacy in ischemic models and neuroinflammation. MCC950 improves vascular pathology in OIR (reduced neovascularization and leakage with cytokine-pattern reversal) and rescues retinal ganglion cells in glaucoma, supporting retinal target engagement and functional protection in relevant pathologies (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Li, 2020).

Liabilities and gaps  
- Lack of efficacy and potential toxicity in dry-AMD–relevant PD. Intravitreal MCC950 did not improve functional or structural outcomes in PD and at 100 µM worsened ERG amplitudes; Nlrp3 siRNA similarly failed to protect despite gene knockdown; Casp1/11 deletion was robustly protective while Nlrp3 deletion was only partially protective, arguing sensor-specific inhibition may be insufficient in photoreceptor death contexts (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- Mixed effects in neovascular disease. MCC950 increased CNV lesion volume in LCNV despite lowering IL-1β, and Nlrp3−/− mice displayed larger lesions, raising concern that NLRP3 blockade may remove protective constraints in some inflammatory/angiogenic contexts; non-NLRP3 inflammasomes likely contribute, further complicating pharmacodynamics (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).  
- Uncertain ocular delivery, exposure, and safety margin. Ocular PK for MCC950 is not defined; the PD study underscores unknown intravitreal bioavailability and clearance, and preclinical reviews warn of poor eye penetration and potential liver toxicity with many NLRP3 inhibitors; high intravitreal dose impaired ERG function in PD (Wooff et al., 2020b; Ortega et al., 2024b). While ERGs were unchanged in one CNV study, that does not establish comprehensive ocular safety (Dieckmann et al., 2024a).  
- RPE biology heterogeneity and expression uncertainty. In vivo NLRP3 induction localizes largely to inner retina/microglia rather than RPE in PD; ARPE-19 NLRP3 expression is variable in the literature and some human studies report low/undetectable NLRP3 in RPE, with concerns about antibody specificity, suggesting that direct RPE targeting may not be universally relevant across models or donors (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b; Marneros, 2023b).  
- Unproven restoration of autophagy/lysosomal function by MCC950. Although autophagy restrains inflammasome activation and lysosomal damage is a key trigger in RPE, direct evidence that MCC950 preserves autophagic flux, lysosomal integrity, or POS processing in RPE is absent in the cited studies; current RPE data document IL-1β/LDH suppression and morphology preservation but not autophagy or phagolysosomal kinetics (Celkova et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019).  
- Pathway redundancy suggests downstream targeting may be superior. Strong protection in Casp1/11−/− mice versus weak/absent benefits from NLRP3 inhibition in PD argue for targeting the shared downstream protease (caspase-1) or gasdermin D rather than individual sensors in retinal degeneration (Wooff et al., 2020a).

Risk-adjusted development path and decision inflection points  
- Go/no-go evidence needed in dry-AMD–relevant RPE assays. Establish whether MCC950 preserves lysosomal integrity and autophagic flux in RPE under LMP/photooxidative/P2X7 triggers and whether it restores POS digestion. Required readouts: LC3-II/I and p62 kinetics with and without bafilomycin, lysosomal pH and cathepsin activity, galectin-3 puncta for LMP, ASC speck formation, caspase-1 activity (FLICA), GSDMD cleavage, IL-1β/IL-18 maturation, and POS ingestion/digestion assays in ARPE-19 and pRPE (Celkova et al., 2015; Ranta-aho et al., 2021).  
- Ocular PK/PD and safety. Quantify intravitreal half-life, retinal/RPE/choroid distribution, and exposure–response for inflammasome suppression with MCC950; determine maximum non-toxic intravitreal dose across species. Include ERG, OCT, histopathology, IBA-1/microglial activation, and cytokine profiling. Investigate sustained intravitreal delivery strategies (e.g., silica-based nanoparticles) that have shown extended ocular release and improved anti-inflammatory efficacy for MCC950 in non-AMD contexts, while generating ocular PK and biodegradation data (Sun et al., 2023).  
- Efficacy in chronic dry-AMD models. Test MCC950 in EFEMP1 R345W mice (BLamD) and aging WT (spontaneous BLamD) with local ocular delivery; endpoints: BLamD size and coverage, RPE/Bruch’s integrity, microglial recruitment (Iba1), and cytokine panels. Given PD negative findings, prioritize deposit/atrophy models where genetic Nlrp3/Casp1 loss is protective (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c; Wooff et al., 2020b).  
- Cell-type–specific targeting and biomarkers. Because inflammasome activation is often myeloid-dominant in vivo, delineate whether MCC950’s ocular benefits, if any, require exposure to subretinal macrophages/microglia versus RPE. Use cell-specific pharmacodynamic markers (ASC specks in Iba1+ cells vs RPE65+ cells; IL-1β/IL-18 localization) to define pharmacologic engagement (Liu et al., 2016; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- Comparative strategy. In parallel, benchmark a caspase-1 inhibitor (or GSDMD inhibitor) against MCC950 in the same models, given the superior genetic protection with Casp1/11 deletion and the possibility of non-NLRP3 inflammasome contribution (Wooff et al., 2020a; Marneros, 2023a).

Bottom line  
MCC950 has strong mechanistic rationale, exquisite target selectivity, and reproducible suppression of inflammasome outputs in RPE assays across diverse AMD-like triggers. Genetic data incriminating NLRP3–caspase-1 in deposit biology strengthen the target hypothesis in a subset of dry-AMD phenotypes. However, the most AMD-relevant in vivo pharmacology with MCC950 to date is not supportive: no benefit and possible functional toxicity in PD, and mixed signals in neovascular settings (benefit in OIR, harm in LCNV). The translational path is further complicated by variable NLRP3 expression in RPE in vivo, dominance of myeloid inflammasomes in many retinal contexts, uncertain ocular PK/penetration, and the untested premise that MCC950 restores RPE autophagy/lysosomal function and POS clearance.

Given these data, MCC950 should not advance directly to costly IND-enabling studies for dry AMD without targeted de-risking experiments. The highest-value next steps are (i) mechanistic RPE assays that test autophagy/lysosome rescue and POS processing, (ii) rigorous ocular PK/safety to define a therapeutic index and viable delivery modality, and (iii) efficacy in deposit/atrophy models where the genetic target is validated (EFEMP1 R345W, aged WT). If these studies confirm robust ocular exposure, a favorable safety margin, and disease modification, MCC950—or a chemically optimized ocular NLRP3 inhibitor—could warrant advancement for specific dry-AMD endophenotypes. If not, downstream inflammasome targeting (caspase-1/GSDMD) may represent a more effective and generalizable strategy for retinal degeneration.

Mechanism of Action (detailed)  
NLRP3 activation requires priming (e.g., NF-κB upregulation of NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β/IL-18) and a second signal (e.g., K⁺ efflux via P2X7, lysosomal rupture with cathepsin release, mitochondrial ROS) that promotes sensor oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). NLRP3’s NACHT domain cycles ATP and orchestrates a conformational change enabling PYD-driven nucleation of ASC, which polymerizes into higher-order filaments/specks that template pro-caspase-1 recruitment and activation; activated caspase-1 cleaves GSDMD to induce pyroptotic pore formation and processes IL-1β/IL-18 for secretion (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). MCC950 binds NLRP3 to suppress its ATPase activity (NACHT), preventing the conformational activation needed for ASC oligomerization and caspase-1 activation; in functional assays MCC950 suppresses both canonical and noncanonical pathways and decreases processed caspase-1 p10/p20 in supernatants without altering upstream TNF-α secretion after TLR priming (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Evidence from retinal disease states aligns with these mechanisms: MCC950 reduces NLRP3 and cleaved caspase-1 in glaucomatous retina (DBA/2J), and in OIR normalizes IL-1β/IL-18 signaling and reduces pathologic neovascularization and leakage (Li, 2020; Sui et al., 2020a).

Inflammasome biology in RPE and AMD is multifactorial. AMD-associated triggers—lipofuscin photooxidation, A2E/oxidative stress, drusen lipid adducts (CEP), Alu RNA accumulation from DICER1 deficiency, and lysosomal destabilization—induce NLRP3 activation in RPE or in recruited subretinal macrophages (Ildefonso et al., 2016; Celkova et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016). Autophagy limits NLRP3 activation by removing damaged mitochondria and targeting assembled inflammasomes for autophagosomal degradation; autophagy blockade increases IL-1β production and pyroptotic susceptibility (Celkova et al., 2015). Pharmacologic NLRP3 blockade in RPE reduces IL-1β and LDH release under LMP, oxidative, photooxidative, and P2X7 activation, consistent with suppression of caspase-1 activation and pyroptotic lysis (Wang et al., 2019). Whether these biochemical effects in RPE suffice to modify chronic, multicellular retinal degeneration in vivo depends on drug delivery to relevant compartments (RPE, subretinal macrophages/microglia), on the relative contributions of non-NLRP3 inflammasomes, and on downstream cytokine biology (e.g., IL-18’s context-dependent effects).

Therapeutic History (detailed)  
- Preclinical systemic efficacy and selectivity: MCC950 exhibits nanomolar potency for NLRP3 in human/mouse macrophages, sparing AIM2, NLRC4, NLRP1; suppresses caspase-1 p10 and IL-1β secretion; improves disease in EAE and CAPS; PK characterized; off-targets largely excluded (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018). In atherosclerosis, MCC950 decreased plaques, macrophage content, and circulating cytokines without overt systemic organ toxicity, though cross-indication reviews caution about liver toxicity risk for the class (Zeng et al., 2021; Ortega et al., 2024b).  
- Ocular ischemic/neovascular settings: In OIR, MCC950 reversed an increased IL-1β/decreased IL-18 pattern, reduced neovascularization and leakage, and modulated endothelial/pericyte signaling; inflammasome activity localized more to macrophages than endothelium (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Sui et al., 2020c). In LCNV, MCC950 lowered IL-1β but increased lesion volume; ERG unchanged; genetic Nlrp3 loss also increased lesion size—collectively indicating a complex, possibly protective role of NLRP3 in CNV or compensation by other inflammasomes (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).  
- Dry-AMD–relevant PD and NLRP3 targeting: Intravitreal MCC950 did not protect PD retina; 100 µM reduced ERG amplitudes. Nlrp3 siRNA reduced transcript but not pathology; Nlrp3−/− protected partially; Casp1/11−/− protected robustly, pointing to caspase-1 as the better target (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- RPE in vitro/ex vivo: CRID3/IFM inhibitors (sulfonylureas, same target class as MCC950) reduced IL-1β and LDH across LMP, H₂O₂, lipofuscin/photooxidation, and P2X7 triggers in ARPE-19/pRPE and preserved ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology under photooxidation (Wang et al., 2019). Compiled 2024 data list MCC950 alongside IFM analogs as effective in IL-1α–primed RPE independent of trigger (Korhonen, 2024).  
- Genetic validations in chronic deposit models: Nlrp3 or Casp1 deletion reduces BLamD in EFEMP1 R345W mice and in aged WT, with reduced microglial activation and normalization of cytokine profiles (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). These models offer strong causal support for inflammasome targeting in GA-relevant pathology, albeit via genetic ablation rather than pharmacologic inhibition.

Expected Effect (detailed)  
In ARPE-19/pRPE assays primed with IL-1α, MCC950 should suppress NLRP3 activation triggered by:  
– LMP (Leu-Leu-OMe), where caspase-1 inhibition prevents RPE death and NLRP3 inhibitors reduce IL-1β and LDH release (Ildefonso et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019).  
– Oxidative and lipofuscin/photooxidative stress (H₂O₂, HNE-POS + blue light), where NLRP3 inhibitors significantly lower IL-1β and LDH and preserve RPE morphology ex vivo (Wang et al., 2019).  
– P2X7 activation (BzATP), a canonical AMD-relevant danger signal leading to K⁺ efflux and inflammasome assembly; selective NLRP3 inhibitors attenuate IL-1β and LDH in Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺-free conditions (Wang et al., 2019).

Because autophagy restrains inflammasome activation and removes inflammasome complexes, a reduction in NLRP3 activity may secondarily stabilize autophagic flux under stress. Yet, this remains hypothetical for MCC950 in RPE; explicit autophagy and lysosomal readouts (LC3 flux, p62, LAMP1/2, cathepsin B/D activities, lysosomal pH, galectin-3 LMP puncta) have not been detailed in the RPE inhibitor studies referenced (Celkova et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019). Therefore, while reduction of IL-1β/LDH and preservation of morphology are expected and supported, the proposed enhancement of POS clearance should be considered an untested hypothesis requiring targeted experimentation.

In vivo, efficacy expectations diverge by model:  
– Deposit/atrophy (EFEMP1 R345W, aged WT) are rational choices: genetic deletion of Nlrp3/Casp1 is protective, so MCC950 might reduce BLamD burden and retinal inflammation if adequate ocular exposure is achieved (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c).  
– Photoreceptor acute degeneration (PD) may not respond to NLRP3 inhibition and may be sensitive to dose-related toxicity, favoring downstream caspase-1 inhibition or broader inflammasome suppression (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
– Neovascular models diverge: OIR improved with MCC950; CNV worsened. Dry-AMD-focused development should avoid neovascular endpoints initially, or stratify hypotheses based on IL-1β/IL-18 balance and myeloid contribution (Sui et al., 2020a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).

Overall Evaluation  
MCC950 is a mechanistically compelling, best-in-class NLRP3 inhibitor with credible RPE-target class activity in vitro and strong genetic support for inflammasome involvement in deposit biology. However, the in vivo ocular pharmacology to date is mixed and generally unsupportive for broad dry-AMD application without further de-risking: failure and potential toxicity in PD, context-dependent effects in neovascular models, uncertain RPE expression/engagement in vivo, lack of ocular PK, and unproven restoration of autophagy/lysosomal function in RPE.

On balance, MCC950 merits continued investigation as a mechanistic probe and potential therapeutic lead for specific dry-AMD endophenotypes linked to deposit pathology and chronic inflammasome signaling—provided that the next tranche of studies addresses ocular PK/safety, cell-type exposure, and autophagy/lysosome outcomes. In parallel, downstream targeting (caspase-1) should be benchmarked given superior genetic protection and potential coverage of multiple inflammasome sensors. If MCC950 cannot meet ocular exposure and safety requirements, alternative delivery (e.g., sustained-release nanoparticles) or next-generation NLRP3 inhibitors with better ocular PK and safety profiles may be required (Sun et al., 2023; Ortega et al., 2024b).

In summary, MCC950 has plausible potential for dry AMD if—and only if— its ocular pharmacology can be tuned to the appropriate disease biology: chronic deposit/atrophy with documented inflammasome involvement, sufficient drug exposure at RPE/subretinal myeloid compartments, and a safety margin that avoids the functional liabilities observed at higher intravitreal doses in PD. Without these, the probability of technical success remains low relative to downstream inflammasome targets.

Analysis: Both candidates target key pathogenic processes in dry AMD—SB415286 via GSK-3β inhibition to activate Wnt/β-catenin, stabilize Nrf2, and enhance autophagy/lysosomal function in RPE cells; TTP-488 via RAGE antagonism to block AGE-RAGE mediated inflammation, oxidative stress, lysosomal alkalinization, and fibrotic signaling. SB415286 has high in vitro potency (IC₅₀ ~20 nM) and preclinical use in neuronal and diabetic retinopathy models, but direct evidence in dry AMD models is sparse; integrative databases show only weak GSK3B-AMD association. TTP-488, also known as Azeliragon, is a small-molecule synthetic RAGE antagonist originally discovered in the context of Alzheimer’s disease research. It belongs to the class of compounds designed to block the receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) by preventing the interaction between RAGE and its ligands – such as advanced glycation end products (AGEs), amyloid-β peptides, and S100 proteins – that trigger downstream inflammatory signaling cascades. The synthetic origin of TTP-488 stems from medicinal chemistry efforts targeting neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress pathways, and members of this compound class have been investigated for their anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative, and anti-fibrotic properties in multiple disease settings. Historically, TTP-488 has been evaluated in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease, where its ability to block RAGE-mediated amyloid-β interactions provided a sound mechanistic rationale for attenuating neuroinflammation and oxidative damage. In these trials, TTP-488 demonstrated an acceptable oral safety profile and favorable pharmacokinetics that make systemic administration feasible—a key consideration when repurposing drugs for alternative indications. While the use of TTP-488 specifically for dry AMD has not been clinically evaluated, a growing body of preclinical evidence has implicated RAGE signaling as a central mediator in AMD pathogenesis. For instance, studies have reported that RAGE expression is significantly upregulated in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells in AMD and that advanced glycation end products accumulate in the drusen deposits characteristic of the disease (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2, 7–8). Moreover, animal models using RAGE-deficient mice have shown reduced choroidal neovascularization and attenuated retinal fibrosis, suggesting that RAGE inhibition could also be beneficial in conditions with similar underlying pathology such as dry AMD (Park, 2017, pp. 157–163, 163–168). At the molecular level, TTP-488 functions by competitively inhibiting the binding of multiple pathological ligands to the RAGE receptor. Under normal or stressed conditions, AGEs accumulate on extracellular matrices and within drusen deposits, where they interact with RAGE on RPE cells to trigger the activation of several downstream signaling cascades. Activation of RAGE results in the induction of nuclear factor-kappaB (NF-κB), p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), and TGF-β/Smad2 signaling pathways, which collectively contribute to increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, chronic inflammation, and the promotion of fibrotic responses (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2; Barile & Schmidt, 2007, pp. 3–4). TTP-488, by binding to RAGE with high affinity, prevents AGE-RAGE interactions and thereby interrupts this cycle. Moreover, preclinical studies have demonstrated that the inhibition of RAGE through agents such as TTP-488 can attenuate TGF-β2-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in RPE cells, reduce mitochondrial ROS production, and diminish the expression of fibrotic markers like α-smooth muscle actin (αSMA) and collagen I (Sreekumar et al., 2025, pp. 7–10). Blocking these signaling cascades is anticipated to lead to a normalization of lysosomal pH, enhanced clearance of extracellular debris, and ultimately improved phagocytosis of POS, thereby supporting retinal homeostasis (Barile & Schmidt, 2007, pp. 3–4; Park, 2017, pp. 163–168).

The expected therapeutic effect of TTP-488 in the context of dry AMD is based on its ability to restore normal RPE function by mitigating the harmful consequences of AGE-induced RAGE activation. In a typical assay, when cultured RPE cells are exposed to excessive AGEs, the interaction with RAGE triggers oxidative stress and lysosomal dysfunction, leading to impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments—a critical physiological process required for retinal renewal. This class of compounds has been widely explored for neuroprotective purposes and has been utilized in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease, where an acceptable safety profile was established. The fact that homotaurine has progressed to advanced clinical stages in Alzheimer’s research supports its tolerability and widespread bioactivity, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in ocular diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Carullo et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, homotaurine has been primarily evaluated in the context of Alzheimer’s disease, where its anti-aggregation properties and potential to interfere with amyloid-β deposition were of paramount interest. Its prior clinical examination, which concluded with a favorable safety record, provides a solid foundation for its repurposing in other neurodegenerative conditions. Although there is no direct record of homotaurine being used to treat dry AMD, other compounds that modulate GABAergic signaling have been investigated in retinal degenerative models. For example, several studies have documented the expression of GABA receptor subunits, including those of the GABAA family, in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, suggesting that pharmacological targeting of these receptors may have therapeutic implications in diseases associated with retinal dysfunction (Arellano et al., 2025). Furthermore, inhibitory neurotransmitters such as GABA have been implicated in maintaining proper cellular excitability and synaptic balance in the retina; alterations in their regulation are associated with excitotoxicity and neurodegeneration in retinal conditions including macular degeneration (Pavan & Dalpiaz, 2018; Schur et al., 2018). In a similar vein, preclinical studies have used GABA modulators to rescue or protect RPE and photoreceptor function in models of retinal degeneration and light-induced injury (Schur et al., 2018). Thus, while direct clinical evidence for homotaurine in dry AMD is lacking, its antecedents in the GABAergic drug class and the known vulnerability of RPE cells to excitotoxic calcium overload position it as a promising candidate for therapeutic repurposing.

Mechanism of Action:  
The hypothesized mechanism of action of homotaurine in dry AMD rests on its ability to activate GABAA receptors expressed on RPE cells. Under physiological conditions, GABAA receptors are heteropentameric chloride channels that, upon binding GABA, permit chloride influx and hyperpolarize the cell membrane. This hyperpolarization ordinarily serves to counteract excessive excitation and limit voltage-gated calcium channel opening. In the context of RPE function, maintaining a tight regulation of intracellular calcium is paramount because calcium levels directly influence cytoskeletal reorganization, phagosome trafficking, and lysosomal fusion events necessary for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Nagymihaly et al., 2021). Several studies have documented that RPE cells not only express GABAA receptor subunits, such as GABAAα1, but that receptor activation in these cells can modify intracellular calcium concentrations, thereby modulating a host of calcium-dependent cellular processes—including phagocytosis (Arellano et al., 2025).

In dry AMD, the RPE’s phagocytic capacity is compromised, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and other toxic by-products, which in turn further disrupt cellular function and promote oxidative stress (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018). Homotaurine’s binding to GABAA receptors is expected to stabilize the membrane potential and reduce the abnormal Ca²⁺ influx that occurs during excitotoxic stress. This reduction in calcium entry is anticipated to alleviate downstream effects such as dysregulated cytoskeletal dynamics and impaired lysosomal trafficking. Cytoskeletal reorganization is essential for phagosome motility; proper F-actin dynamics direct the trafficking of phagosomes toward lysosomal compartments where degradation occurs (Inana et al., 2018; Nagymihaly et al., 2021). Moreover, studies have demonstrated that inflammatory mediators present in AMD, including TNF-α and interleukin-1β, modulate GABAA receptor expression and function, suggesting that modulation of these receptors could be a viable strategy to counteract inflammation-driven excitotoxicity (Arellano et al., 2025). In addition, the excitotoxic environment generated by imbalanced glutamate/GABA signaling in the retina can be mitigated by restoring the inhibitory tone through GABAA receptor activation. The specific EC₅₀ of approximately 10 µM for homotaurine indicates that it has the potential to achieve receptor activation within a therapeutic window that is plausible in an ocular formulation (Carullo et al., 2020; Arellano et al., 2025). Taken together, the combined modulation of calcium influx, along with the stabilization of cytoskeletal and lysosomal pathways, constitutes a comprehensive molecular strategy that homotaurine may employ to rescue impaired POS degradation in dry AMD.

The proposed assay in ARPE-19 cells—a well-established in vitro model for RPE function—aims to evaluate whether homotaurine, via activation of GABAA receptors, can restore impaired photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis under conditions of glutamate-induced stress. RPE cell dysfunction in dry AMD is characterized by diminished phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation of POS, leading to the pathological accumulation of lipofuscin, which further impedes cellular function (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018). Experimental evidence in related studies supports that compounds with similar mechanisms (i.e., GABA modulators and taurine-related molecules) are capable of influencing intracellular calcium signaling and can enhance the uptake and processing of POS in RPE cells (Arellano et al., 2025; López-Colomé et al., 1994). In a stress state, glutamate excess drives excitotoxic Ca²⁺ entry that may dysregulate these processes. By antagonizing this excitotoxic cascade, homotaurine is anticipated to reduce the aberrant Ca²⁺ load, thereby restoring the dynamic equilibrium that supports both cytoskeletal integrity and lysosomal trafficking. This mechanism is supported by studies showing that dysregulation of Ca²⁺ not only impairs phagosome motility but also has deleterious effects on downstream lysosomal fusion and degradation, ultimately impacting cellular clearance mechanisms (Si et al., 2023; Nowak et al., 2025). Thus, the expected effect is a measurable enhancement in POS uptake as well as improved degradation kinetics in RPE cells subjected to glutamate-induced stress, which would correlate with potential therapeutic efficacy in dry AMD. Furthermore, since the underlying pathology of dry AMD involves chronic oxidative stress and accumulation of metabolic by-products, a pharmacological intervention that can restore intracellular homeostasis has far-reaching implications for halting or even reversing disease progression (Arellano et al., 2025).

In evaluating homotaurine for dry age-related macular degeneration, several critical observations emerge. One of the key strengths of homotaurine is its well-documented safety profile from Alzheimer’s clinical trials, which lowers the translational hurdles when repurposing the compound for ocular administration. The fact that homotaurine is a GABA analogue that activates GABAA receptors—a receptor class that is expressed on RPE cells and critically involved in regulating intracellular Ca²⁺—provides a strong mechanistic rationale for its application in dry AMD (Arellano et al., 2025). By potentially mitigating excitotoxic Ca²⁺ influx, homotaurine could restore normal cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal trafficking, both of which are indispensable for the effective degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).

Among the strengths, the following points are notable:  
1. The candidate’s mechanism directly addresses a central pathology of dry AMD—namely, impaired RPE phagocytosis and lysosomal dysfunction—which leads to toxic lipofuscin accumulation (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018).  
2. Activation of GABAA receptors by homotaurine could normalize Ca²⁺ handling within RPE cells, thereby alleviating the excitotoxic stress that is linked to altered cytoskeletal assembly and defective phagosome trafficking (Arellano et al., 2025; Inana et al., 2018).  
3. The compound’s history in Alzheimer’s trials suggests a favorable safety margin and known pharmacokinetic properties that may be adapted for ocular use, thus enhancing its potential for rapid clinical translation (Carullo et al., 2020).  
4. Preclinical evidence from other studies involving GABA modulators and related compounds shows that interfering with aberrant neurotransmitter signaling in the retina can elicit neuroprotective and phagocytosis-enhancing effects (Schur et al., 2018).

Conversely, some weaknesses and uncertainties remain that necessitate further investigation:  
1. Although the proposed EC₅₀ of approximately 10 µM for homotaurine is within a plausible therapeutic window for GABAA receptor activation, the actual pharmacodynamic response in RPE cells—especially in the diseased microenvironment of dry AMD—remains to be rigorously quantified (Arellano et al., 2025).  
2. The retinal microenvironment in dry AMD is complex, characterized not only by excitotoxic stress but also by chronic oxidative stress, inflammation, and altered expression of multiple receptor types. In such a context, GABAA receptor activation could be affected by altered ionic gradients, potentially leading to reversed or atypical receptor responses as has been documented in other retinal degenerations (Arellano et al., 2025; Telegina et al., 2022).  
3. While indirect evidence supports the role of GABAergic modulation in restoring phagocytic function, there is a paucity of direct data demonstrating that homotaurine can specifically enhance POS uptake in ARPE-19 cells under injurious conditions. This gap necessitates additional in vitro studies to detail its effects on cytoskeletal reorganization, vesicular trafficking, and lysosomal fusion dynamics (Si et al., 2023; Nagymihaly et al., 2021).  
4. The exact downstream signaling pathways that link GABAA receptor activation to the observed improvements in phagocytic function must be delineated further. For example, the interplay between calcium channel deactivation, actin cytoskeleton stabilization, and the regulation of key phagocytic receptors (e.g., MerTK, αvβ5 integrin) remains incompletely characterized in the context of GABAergic modulation (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).  
5. Finally, the translational leap from in vitro findings in ARPE-19 cells to a robust therapeutic effect in human dry AMD patients is non-trivial. Aging RPE cells in vivo exhibit additional layers of complexity, including altered gene expression profiles, metabolic imbalances, and possible shifts in receptor isoforms, all of which might influence the responsiveness to homotaurine (Nowak et al., 2025; Si et al., 2023).

Overall, homotaurine represents a scientifically sound and mechanistically plausible candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its potential to activate GABAA receptors on RPE cells, thereby reducing excitotoxic calcium influx and normalizing the intracellular processes that govern cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal trafficking, aligns well with the pathophysiological underpinnings of AMD (Arellano et al., 2025). Given the favorable safety data from Alzheimer’s trials and the breadth of preclinical evidence supporting the neuroprotective effects of GABAergic modulation in retinal contexts, homotaurine merits further exploration. Prior to clinical application, however, detailed mechanistic studies using ARPE-19 cells and appropriate animal models of dry AMD must be conducted. These studies should focus on quantifying calcium flux, cytoskeletal dynamics, phagosome motility, and lysosomal fusion efficiency upon homotaurine treatment under pathologically relevant conditions. Additionally, it will be important to investigate potential off-target effects and to determine whether combinatorial therapies that address oxidative stress and inflammation might synergize with homotaurine’s mechanism. In summary, while challenges remain, the repurposing of homotaurine for dry AMD offers a promising therapeutic avenue worthy of investment and further preclinical validation (Arellano et al., 2025; Si et al., 2023; Carullo et al., 2020).

────────────────────────────────────────  
I. OVERVIEW OF THE THERAPEUTIC CANDIDATE  

GSK0660 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor that gained prominence as the very first PPARβ/δ (peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor beta/delta)–selective inhibitory ligand reported in the scientific literature (Toth et al., 2012). Its design represents a significant breakthrough in the field of nuclear receptor modulation by demonstrating that subtype selectivity within the PPAR family can indeed be achieved with a low molecular weight organic compound. Structurally, GSK0660 belongs to the thiophenecarboxylate chemical class and features a uniquely tailored molecular architecture that includes several key pharmacophores: a methoxy‐substituted 1,4‐diaminobenzene core thought to be essential for receptor binding; a 4′‐aminophenyl substituent that not only contributes to high‐affinity interactions with the receptor’s ligand‐binding domain but also offers a promising site for subsequent chemical modification; and a methyl thiophene carboxylate moiety that helps orient the molecule within the hydrophobic pocket of PPARβ/δ (Toth et al., 2012). Extensive structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies have demonstrated that modifications to portions of the molecule—particularly the 4′‐aminophenyl substituent by introduction of medium‐length n‐alkyl chains—can enhance binding affinity by up to tenfold compared to the original structure (Toth et al., 2012).

GSK0660 was originally synthesized through a multistep organic process that began with commercially available precursors, followed by key transformation steps such as nucleophilic aromatic substitution to install appropriate groups on a benzene ring, catalytic reduction to generate the requisite amine functions, and finally sulfonamidation reactions to yield the final compound (Toth et al., 2012). In essence, this compound was developed primarily as a research tool to dissect the specific biological roles of PPARβ/δ and does not itself originate from a natural product or traditional antibiotic source. Instead, its design and synthesis reflect a targeted medicinal chemistry strategy aimed at obtaining a high degree of receptor selectivity.

Belonging to the broader class of PPAR modulators, GSK0660 occupies a niche that is distinct from the more commonly encountered PPAR agonists. Whereas most efforts historically have focused on the development of agonists for metabolic disorders and anti‐inflammatory indications, GSK0660 and its close analogs are used primarily to achieve receptor inhibition. This selective antagonism is critical for experimental setups in which the contribution of PPARβ/δ to downstream gene regulation and cellular homeostasis is being evaluated (Toth et al., 2012). Furthermore, the structure of GSK0660 aligns with the more general trends in nuclear receptor ligand development, capturing several “drug‐like” properties that, despite known limitations in bioavailability, maintain its status as a high‐quality research compound in proof‐of‐concept investigations.

────────────────────────────────────────  
II. THERAPEUTIC HISTORY  

GSK0660 has been widely used as a chemical probe to examine the biological functions of PPARβ/δ in various preclinical models. In early studies, it served as the first selective antagonist for this receptor subtype and was instrumental in clarifying the roles of PPARβ/δ in lipid metabolism, cell proliferation, and inflammation (Toth et al., 2012). Its experimental applications have spanned a number of research areas. For instance, several investigations in models of neurodegeneration—particularly in Parkinson’s disease—have utilized GSK0660 in both in vitro experiments (using human neuroblastoma cell lines such as SH‐SY5Y) and in vivo rodent models. In these studies, GSK0660 was able to negate the neuroprotective effects of PPARβ/δ agonists by blocking the receptor’s activity, thereby providing compelling evidence for a detrimental role of PPARβ/δ activation under neurodegenerative stress conditions (Antonosante et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023). Such data have contributed to a nuanced understanding of PPAR signaling in the brain, implying that under certain conditions receptor inhibition may be more desirable than activation.

Moreover, GSK0660 has also been evaluated in dermatological applications. In recent studies focusing on psoriasis‐like skin disease, GSK0660—when formulated topically—was shown to mitigate epidermal hyperplasia and reduce inflammatory markers without systemic drug accumulation, thus proving useful for localized treatment strategies (Hack et al., 2012). These dermatological studies not only underscored the compound’s ability to counteract PPARβ/δ‐mediated signaling in inflamed tissues but also highlighted practical challenges associated with its formulation. For example, its inherent chemical instability, manifesting as a tendency to undergo oxidation (where solutions of GSK0660 may turn green upon light exposure at room temperature), underscores issues related to its shelf‐life and stability in clinical formulations (Hack et al., 2012; Lieber, 2015).

Despite its usefulness in these diverse experimental models—ranging from neurodegenerative to inflammatory skin diseases—the therapeutic history of GSK0660 reveals a critical gap: there is no record within the available literature of its application in ocular diseases or in the treatment of dry AMD. A systematic search of clinical trial databases has confirmed that no human clinical investigations have been registered evaluating GSK0660 for indications such as retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, macular degeneration, or related ocular conditions (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). In other words, while the compound has been validated as a tool in non‐ocular systems, its repurposing for dry AMD is entirely uncharted territory. This lack of ocular‐specific data is a limitation that must be considered when assessing its potential for enhancing lysosomal function in RPE cells.

Furthermore, limitations inherent to GSK0660—most notably its poor systemic bioavailability and the requirement for relatively high concentrations to achieve effective antagonism—are recurring themes in its therapeutic history (Toth et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016; Lieber, 2015). Such pharmacokinetic drawbacks have spurred efforts to develop improved derivatives that possess enhanced potency and bioavailability. For instance, SAR studies have evaluated modifications to the 4′‐aminophenyl substituent, yielding analogs with substantially higher binding affinities (Toth et al., 2012). Nonetheless, all available records indicate that GSK0660 itself has remained primarily as a research tool rather than advancing to clinical or even advanced developmental stages in any therapeutic domain beyond the proof‐of‐concept experimental setting.

────────────────────────────────────────  
III. MECHANISM OF ACTION  

At the molecular level, GSK0660 exerts its action by binding selectively to the ligand‐binding domain (LBD) of PPARβ/δ, thereby inhibiting receptor activation. This interaction is competitive in nature; GSK0660 occupies the receptor pocket, effectively blocking binding of endogenous ligands or synthetic agonists (Toth et al., 2012). The molecular determinants of this selective interaction have been elucidated through SAR studies. The methoxy‐substituted 1,4‐diaminobenzene core forms critical hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts with specific residues within the LBD, while the 4′‐aminophenyl group and the methyl thiophene carboxylate moiety contribute additional electrostatic and van der Waals interactions that stabilize the binding complex (Toth et al., 2012).

A notable aspect of GSK0660’s pharmacology is its dual mode of action. In addition to functioning as a competitive antagonist, GSK0660 has been reported in some experimental contexts to act as an inverse agonist. Under basal conditions—where PPARβ/δ exhibits a low level of constitutive transcriptional activity—GSK0660 can further suppress receptor activity beyond mere inhibition by promoting the recruitment of transcriptional corepressors. These corepressors (including members of the NCoR/SMRT family and class I histone deacetylases) bind to the receptor‐corepressor complex, modifying chromatin structure and decreasing transcription of PPARβ/δ target genes (Lieber, 2015; Monsalve et al., 2013). Through these mechanisms, GSK0660 effectively shifts the balance away from gene activation toward transcriptional repression.

The detailed molecular interactions responsible for these phenomena have been characterized using a variety of biochemical assays, including competitive TR‐FRET binding studies and reporter assays in cell‐based systems (Toth et al., 2012). The ability of GSK0660 to inhibit transcriptional activation in response to exogenous agonists has been well demonstrated in several cell models—including skeletal muscle myoblasts where PPARβ/δ activates genes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase‐1A or pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase‐4 (Monsalve et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016). This cellular pharmacology underpins its potential to serve as an experimental “off‐switch” for PPARβ/δ‐mediated transcription.

In the context of the proposed repurposing hypothesis for dry AMD, the mechanistic emphasis shifts toward the regulation of lysosomal biogenesis through transcription factor EB (TFEB). Although direct evidence linking PPARβ/δ antagonism with the modulation of TFEB activity in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells is not yet established, the working hypothesis posits that PPARβ/δ normally exerts a repressive influence on a suite of genes involved in lysosomal function—the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. TFEB is recognized as the master regulator of lysosomal and autophagic gene expression and, upon activation, translocates to the nucleus to drive expression of critical lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1 and proteases such as Cathepsin D (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). By antagonizing PPARβ/δ, GSK0660 is hypothesized to relieve this repressive effect, thereby “releasing the brake” on TFEB activity. This would allow for enhanced transcription of lysosomal genes that are vital for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and the clearance of toxic lipofuscin constituents like A2E.

It is important to note that while the biochemical rationale is compelling, the specific molecular details linking PPARβ/δ inhibition to enhanced TFEB function have yet to be firmly established in ocular models. Nonetheless, the ability of GSK0660 to modulate receptor conformation and corepressor recruitment provides a credible mechanistic basis for the hypothesis, even as further studies must elucidate the crosstalk between PPARβ/δ signaling and the lysosomal gene network in RPE cells (Toth et al., 2012; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Lieber, 2015).

────────────────────────────────────────  
IV. EXPECTED EFFECT IN RPE MODELS  

Dry AMD is characterized by gradual dysfunction and atrophy of the RPE, which plays an essential role in the daily phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). A central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD is the accumulation of undigested POS material and the toxic byproduct A2E, which, in turn, leads to lipofuscin deposition, oxidative stress, and eventual RPE cell death. Critical to the maintenance of RPE homeostasis is the proper function of the lysosomal machinery responsible for cellular clearance. Lysosomal biogenesis, autophagic flux, and the efficient degradation of internalized debris are centrally regulated by transcription factor EB (TFEB), which activates the CLEAR network of genes encoding proteins such as LAMP1 (a lysosomal‐associated membrane protein) and Cathepsin D (a key lysosomal protease) (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Under normal conditions, PPARβ/δ appears to play a role in regulating gene expression through the recruitment of coactivators and corepressors. The hypothesis driving the repurposing of GSK0660 for dry AMD is that activated PPARβ/δ imposes a repressive signal on the CLEAR network genes, thereby limiting TFEB‐mediated lysosomal biogenesis in RPE cells. In an experimental paradigm based on A2E‐loaded RPE cell cultures—a standard in vitro model that mimics the cellular environment of dry AMD—it is anticipated that treatment with GSK0660 at concentrations approximating its receptor inhibition IC₅₀ (~200 nM) will alleviate PPARβ/δ‐mediated repression. This derepression is expected to promote the nuclear translocation of TFEB and upregulate its target genes, culminating in an enhanced lysosomal degradative capacity (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

The expected cellular responses following GSK0660 treatment in RPE models can be summarized as follows. First, by interrupting the ligand‐induced activation of PPARβ/δ, GSK0660 should shift the balance between transcriptional coactivators and corepressors in favor of a transcriptional environment that supports lysosomal gene expression. This would lead to a measurable increase in the mRNA and protein levels of LAMP1 and Cathepsin D, both of which are critical for lysosomal function and for the degradation of POS components (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Second, the enhanced expression of these proteins should translate into an improved capacity for POS degradation—a phenotype that can be monitored using assays that track the clearance of fluorescently labeled POS or the reduction in A2E accumulation. Third, improved lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic clearance are expected to reduce the chronic accumulation of lipofuscin, thereby mitigating oxidative stress and preserving RPE function over time.

In addition to these molecular and cellular endpoints, there is also the expectation that successful derepression of TFEB activity will indirectly contribute to improved cell viability and resistance to stress. The RPE, being highly active in terms of metabolic turnover and phagocytic activity, is particularly vulnerable to the detrimental effects of lysosomal dysfunction. Thus, a treatment that effectively restores lysosomal function is likely to bolster the RPE’s ability to manage accumulated debris and maintain metabolic homeostasis.

It should be acknowledged that one of the primary challenges will be the optimization of the effective dose of GSK0660 in the context of ocular cells. While the compound exhibits potent receptor inhibition in vitro, previous studies have identified limitations with its bioavailability and chemical stability (Toth et al., 2012; Strosznajder et al., 2021). These issues necessitate careful attention to formulation and drug delivery strategies tailored to the ocular environment. For example, controlled‐release formulations or nanoparticle‐based delivery systems might be required to ensure that effective local concentrations of GSK0660 can be maintained in the retina while avoiding systemic exposure and off‐target effects.

Moreover, despite the attractive theoretical framework linking PPARβ/δ antagonism to TFEB activation, direct experimental evidence in RPE cells is currently lacking. As such, the expected effect remains a hypothesis that must be rigorously validated through a series of in vitro assays—including quantitative PCR for lysosomal gene expression, immunoblotting for protein markers, and functional assays to assess the clearance of photoreceptor debris. Additional studies might also involve monitoring autophagic flux using established markers such as LC3-II and p62 to provide a more comprehensive picture of the compound’s impact on RPE cell homeostasis.

────────────────────────────────────────  
V. OVERALL EVALUATION  

GSK0660 stands out as a highly characterized PPARβ/δ antagonist with a well‐documented profile in non‐ocular applications. The compound’s discovery as the first selective ligand for PPARβ/δ established a benchmark in the field and has since made it a prominent research tool in studies of neurodegeneration, inflammation, and even dermatological applications such as psoriasis (Toth et al., 2012; Antonosante et al., 2023; Hack et al., 2012). From a medicinal chemistry perspective, the structural features of GSK0660—the methoxy‐substituted 1,4‐diaminobenzene core, the 4′‐aminophenyl substituent, and the methyl thiophene carboxylate moiety—endow the molecule with high selectivity for the receptor. SAR studies have demonstrated that modifications to these groups can further enhance binding affinity, offering prospects for optimization if needed (Toth et al., 2012).

The principal strength of the compound lies in its receptor selectivity and in its demonstrated capacity to function as both a competitive antagonist and an inverse agonist. This duality is central to the proposed mechanism for reversing PPARβ/δ‐mediated repression of TFEB, which in turn may enhance lysosomal biogenesis and improve the degradative capacity of RPE cells. Considering that lysosomal dysfunction and the resultant accumulation of undegraded POS and toxic byproducts such as A2E are recognized pathological features of dry AMD, the hypothesis that GSK0660 can restore a more robust lysosomal function is innovative and scientifically compelling (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

However, significant caveats temper this optimism. One major limitation is that, to date, GSK0660 has not been studied in the context of retinal diseases or any ocular applications. Although extensive preclinical research has been undertaken in models of Parkinson’s disease and psoriasis, no direct evidence supports its efficacy in modulating RPE cell lysosomal function or in mitigating dry AMD pathology (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Lieber, 2015). This represents a considerable translational gap that would require substantial preclinical work to bridge.

Another critical challenge is the compound’s pharmacokinetic profile. GSK0660 is known to suffer from poor bioavailability, and it frequently requires relatively high concentrations to achieve its intended effects in vitro. Furthermore, the chemical instability of GSK0660—demonstrated by its tendency to oxidize and change color under conditions of light exposure and room temperature storage—poses additional obstacles for formulation development, especially in a sensitive environment such as the eye where prolonged stability and controlled drug release are paramount (Toth et al., 2012; Hack et al., 2012; Strosznajder et al., 2021).

The translation of these findings to an application in dry AMD would also necessitate a careful reexamination of dosing strategies and delivery mechanisms. For instance, while topical formulations have been effective in dermatological models (Hack et al., 2012), the ocular setting will require alternative approaches to bypass obstacles such as the blood‐retinal barrier and to achieve sustained local drug concentrations without systemic spillover. Innovative drug delivery platforms—perhaps involving biodegradable implants, nanoparticles, or hydrogels—will likely need to be developed to turn the promising molecular mechanism of GSK0660 into a clinically viable treatment option.

Furthermore, although the mechanistic rationale linking PPARβ/δ antagonism with the activation of TFEB is theoretically sound, the direct evidence supporting this specific link in RPE cells is limited. Existing literature on TFEB clearly demonstrates its role as a master regulator of lysosomal genes in retinal cells (Abokyi & Tse, 2025), yet none of the studies directly establish that PPARβ/δ provides a repressive signal to TFEB in this context. Thus, the entire repurposing hypothesis, while attractive, remains speculative until dedicated studies in RPE models confirm that inhibition of PPARβ/δ by GSK0660 indeed results in derepression of TFEB and a subsequent upregulation of lysosomal markers such as LAMP1 and Cathepsin D.

Lastly, while GSK0660 has garnered a robust reputation as a research tool, its historical use in non‐ocular tissues suggests that extensive medicinal chemistry optimization may be required to enhance its physicochemical properties for ocular therapy. In essence, the compound may serve as an excellent lead structure, but modifications that improve its bioavailability, chemical stability, and potency in the ocular microenvironment will be essential steps before considering any clinical translation.

At the molecular level, GSK-3β is a serine/threonine kinase that is constitutively active in many cells and functions as a pivotal regulator of several intracellular signaling cascades.
