Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SHP099 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule allosteric inhibitor of the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP2 (PTPN11) discovered by Novartis through a target-biased screening paradigm that enriched for modulators of full-length, autoinhibited SHP2 and counter-selected catalytic-site binders, followed by structure-based medicinal chemistry optimization to stabilize the closed SHP2 conformation rather than engage the conserved active site (chemical identity: 6-(4-amino-4-methylpiperidin-1-yl)-3-(2,3-dichlorophenyl)pyrazin-2-amine) (PDB: 5EHR) (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kong & Long, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). In the 1.7 Å co-crystal, SHP099 occupies a central “tunnel” at the interface of the N-SH2, C-SH2, and PTP domains present only in the autoinhibited state; its aminopyrazine/amine motif forms hydrogen bonds to Arg111 and Phe113 in the SH2 linker and to Glu250 in the PTP domain, while a 2,3-dichlorophenyl moiety engages hydrophobic residues (Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, Gln495), thereby clamping the interdomain interface and disfavoring opening/activation (ligand volume ~262 Å3; tunnel ~464 Å3) (Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Biochemically, SHP099 is potent and selective (SHP2 enzymatic IC50 ≈ 0.070–0.071 µM; no detectable activity across panels of 21 phosphatases and 66 kinases, including SHP1) and translates to cellular pathway inhibition (p-ERK IC50 ≈ 0.250 µM), with high aqueous solubility, high permeability without efflux, and acceptable mouse oral exposure/bioavailability (~46%) (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kong & Long, 2022). Mechanistically, SHP099 functions as a “molecular glue” that stabilizes the closed, autoinhibited SHP2 conformation via a conformational selection mechanism; affinity is reduced for strongly activating SHP2 mutants (for example, E76K) that bias the open state, although high concentrations can re-close some mutants in vitro and in cells (Meem, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).

SHP099 belongs to the class of SHP2 “tunnel-site” (site 1) allosteric inhibitors that stabilize the autoinhibited state by engaging the N-SH2/C-SH2/PTP interdomain pocket; dual allosteric occupancy (site 1 plus a distal latch, site 2) is structurally and biochemically validated and produces cooperative inhibition when SHP099 is combined with a site-2 ligand (for example SHP244 analogs), underscoring the druggability of multiple noncatalytic surfaces on SHP2 (Fodor et al., 2018; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Discovery and SAR established that the aminopyrazine ring amine is essential (Glu250 H-bond), the 4-amino-4-methylpiperidine motif is favored over piperazines for potency, and an ortho-chlorine on the phenyl ring is critical; a representative synthesis employs Suzuki–Miyaura coupling to install the dichlorophenyl substituent on a pyrazinamine core, followed by SNAr to append the Boc-protected 4-methylpiperidin-4-amine and final acid deprotection to the free base (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-level development moved the SHP099 pharmacophore into diverse chemotypes (for example, pyrimidinones and fused bicyclic pyrazolopyrimidinones) and into clinical candidates (for example, TNO155, RMC-4630, BBP-398), reflecting translational momentum for SHP2 allosteric inhibition (Kerr et al., 2021; Tojjari et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
SHP099 established in vivo proof-of-concept for allosteric SHP2 inhibition in oncology. In an EGFR-amplified esophageal squamous carcinoma xenograft (KYSE-520), oral SHP099 produced dose-dependent pathway suppression (tumor p-ERK), antiproliferative effects, and tumor growth inhibition up to stasis at 100 mg/kg, supported by measurable exposure and oral bioavailability (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Additional preclinical efficacy includes activity in EGFR-driven xenografts and reduction of leukemic burden in FLT3-ITD–positive AML models after oral dosing, with no overt toxicity noted in those studies (Dempke et al., 2018). In glioblastoma models, SHP099 achieved brain exposure after 100 mg/kg oral dosing, reduced tumor growth and vascularity in orthotopic xenografts, and showed activity both as monotherapy and combined with temozolomide, demonstrating CNS penetration and antitumor pharmacology in mice (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-wide, SHP2 allosteric inhibitors have shown single-agent and combination efficacy in RTK/RAS/MAPK-driven tumors, have been advanced into clinical studies across multiple solid tumors, and display mechanism-consistent biomarker modulation (for example, decreased p-ERK) in preclinical models (Kerr et al., 2021; Stanford & Bottini, 2023; Tojjari et al., 2023).

Within the materials provided here, there are no reports of SHP099 (or any SHP2 allosteric inhibitor) being used in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis models, or any ocular indication; multiple reviews focus on oncology/immuno-oncology and either enumerate preclinical tumor evidence or clinical oncology programs, without ocular/retinal data (Kerr et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2020). Consequently, repurposing SHP099 for dry AMD would be a first-in-class application with no precedent in the supplied literature (Yuan et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
SHP2 is maintained in an autoinhibited state by intramolecular engagement of the N-SH2 domain with the PTP catalytic domain; engagement of SH2 domains by bis-phosphotyrosyl motifs on receptors/adaptors relieves autoinhibition, allowing both catalytic and scaffolding functions that couple receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) to RAS activation and downstream MAPK/PI3K signaling (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). SHP099 binds in a tunnel formed by the N-SH2, C-SH2, and PTP domains of autoinhibited SHP2 and locks this closed conformation: crystallography defines hydrogen bonds to Arg111 and Phe113 (SH2 linker) and Glu250 (PTP domain), and hydrophobic contacts to Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, and Gln495 that together stabilize the interface and preclude opening; pre-organization of Arg111 additionally supports a cationic–π interaction with SHP099’s dichlorophenyl ring (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Selectivity over SHP1 is rationalized structurally by differences in SH2-linker/tunnel geometry that preclude analogous Arg/Phe contacts, consistent with lack of SHP1 inhibition in broad profiling (Diop et al., 2022). Binding follows conformational selection, with lowered potency against mutants that favor the open state (for example, E76K, D61Y), though high concentrations or dual-site allosteric occupancy can re-close certain mutants and enhance inhibition (Fodor et al., 2018; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-level medicinal chemistry around SHP099 uncovered both optimization paths (for example, pyrimidinones, fused bicyclic scaffolds) and liabilities such as unexpected hERG inhibition in some derivatives and combination-dosing tolerability issues in mice, underscoring the need for careful safety pharmacology (Meem, 2022).

RPE POS phagocytosis is a ligand-directed, RTK-driven process with defined signaling architecture. Externalized phosphatidylserine on shed POS tips is opsonized (for example, by MFG-E8), engages apical αvβ5 integrin, and triggers a pathway in which MerTK (activated by Gas6 or Protein S) is essential for physiological engulfment in vivo; loss-of-function MERTK mutations in RCS rats or humans abolish POS internalization and cause rapid photoreceptor degeneration (Ghosh et al., 2024; Moran et al., 2022). At the cytoskeletal level, formation of the F-actin phagocytic cup beneath bound POS requires Rac1 activation and a concurrent decrease in RhoA/ROCK-mediated contractility; RhoA elevation blocks cup formation even when Rac1 is active, whereas ROCK inhibition is both necessary and sufficient to enable cup formation and POS internalization and can rescue engulfment and acidification in MerTK-deficient RPE ex vivo (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Mao & Finnemann, 2021). Mechanistically downstream of MerTK, Src is activated and (i) phosphorylates and activates focal adhesion kinase (FAK), recruiting the p130CAS/CRKII/DOCK180 module that activates Rac1, and (ii) phosphorylates GDP-dissociation inhibitor GDI1, promoting dissociation from Rab5 to facilitate Rab cycling needed for cup formation and early phagosome dynamics (Shelby et al., 2015). These pathways define measurable biochemical checkpoints (MerTK/Src/FAK phosphorylation, Rac1-GTP, RhoA/ROCK activity) and functional readouts (cup formation, internalization, phagolysosomal acidification) relevant to any attempt to modulate RPE phagocytosis pharmacologically (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Moran et al., 2022).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis is that SHP099 will inhibit SHP2 in RPE (biochemical IC50 ~70–75 nM), sustain MerTK phosphorylation, maintain Rac1-GTP, and thereby increase POS internalization. The supplied literature confirms that SHP099 potently and selectively inhibits SHP2 by stabilizing the autoinhibited state and blocks RTK→RAS/MAPK signaling in cells, but it does not demonstrate that SHP2 directly dephosphorylates MerTK in RPE or that SHP2 inhibition prolongs MerTK phosphorylation or increases RPE POS uptake (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). Across systems, SHP2 acts as a positive transducer linking activated RTKs to RAS/ERK signaling; SHP2 allosteric inhibition decouples upstream RTKs from RAS activation, lowering RAS-GTP and p-ERK, which is consistent with a broad attenuation of RTK-driven outputs rather than prolonged receptor phosphorylation per se (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). Within the provided ocular literature, the only experimentally demonstrated pharmacologic rescue of RPE POS uptake is acute ROCK inhibition, which operates downstream of MerTK to reduce actomyosin contractility and enable cup formation and internalization—even rescuing MerTK-deficient RPE ex vivo—whereas elevating RhoA blocks phagocytosis despite Rac1 activation (Mao & Finnemann, 2021). Thus, while SHP099 will almost certainly inhibit SHP2 in RPE if exposure is achieved, the predicted increase in POS internalization via prolonged MerTK phosphorylation and sustained Rac1-GTP is speculative and not supported by direct evidence in the materials provided here (Kerr et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2020).

If the assay readout is POS phagocytosis in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE, the mechanistic checkpoints most directly supported by the literature are: phosphorylation kinetics of MerTK and Src/FAK; Rac1-GTP elevation coincident with cup formation; RhoA/ROCK suppression; and functional measures of cup assembly, POS internalization, and phagolysosomal acidification, with a ROCK inhibitor as a validated positive control (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Mao & Finnemann, 2021; Moran et al., 2022). Ocular pharmacokinetics for SHP099 are unknown in the provided corpus; although brain exposure has been documented after oral dosing in mice, retinal/RPE exposure should not be inferred and would need to be measured for systemic or local (for example, intravitreal) dosing paradigms (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths for repurposing consideration  
- Potent, selective, and structurally validated target engagement. SHP099 is characterized at atomic resolution (PDB 5EHR) with a coherent interaction network (Arg111, Phe113, Glu250; Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, Gln495) that rationalizes potency, selectivity versus SHP1, and conformational bias, increasing confidence that SHP2 inhibition will translate biochemically in RPE if drug exposure is achieved (Diop et al., 2022; Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Drug-like properties and in vivo activity. SHP099 exhibits favorable physicochemical properties (high solubility; Caco-2 permeability without efflux), oral bioavailability (~46% in mice), dose-dependent pathway modulation in tumors, and robust xenograft efficacy; CNS exposure after oral dosing has been demonstrated in mice, indicating trans-barrier distribution is feasible with adequate exposure (Fortanet et al., 2016; Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Class-level translational experience. Multiple SHP2 allosteric inhibitors derived from the SHP099 tunnel pharmacophore have entered clinical testing across solid tumors, enabling leverage of class pharmacology, safety learning, and combination strategies if ocular repurposing proceeds (Kerr et al., 2021; Stanford & Bottini, 2023; Tojjari et al., 2023).

Key weaknesses and risks specific to dry AMD/RPE phagocytosis  
- Mechanistic gap in RPE. The premise that SHP2 dephosphorylates MerTK to terminate phagocytic signaling in RPE, and that SHP2 inhibition will prolong MerTK phosphorylation and sustain Rac1 activation, is not supported by the supplied literature; no direct data link SHP2 to MerTK regulation in RPE or demonstrate SHP099-induced increases in POS uptake (Kerr et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2020). In contrast, RhoA/ROCK suppression is a validated, decisive permissive event for cup formation/internalization and can rescue MerTK deficiency, suggesting that targeting ROCK remains a higher-confidence pharmacological route to enhance POS uptake (Mao & Finnemann, 2021).  
- Potential on-target countereffects on trophic RTK signaling. SHP2 broadly transduces RTK signals to RAS/ERK; allosteric SHP2 inhibition reduces RAS-GTP/p-ERK by disconnecting RTKs from downstream pathways, which could dampen beneficial RTK-mediated homeostatic signaling in RPE and choroid (for example, PDGFR, c-MET, IGF1R) even if MerTK phosphorylation were transiently increased, necessitating careful evaluation of RPE viability and stress responses in addition to phagocytosis endpoints (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021).  
- Ocular PK/tissue exposure unknown. There is no reported ocular distribution for SHP099 in the materials provided; CNS penetration does not ensure retinal/RPE exposure, and systemic dosing to achieve ocular levels may be limited by plasma protein binding, efflux, or tolerability, while intravitreal dosing introduces local safety and formulation challenges that would require de novo assessment (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Class liabilities and context-dependent potency. Medicinal chemistry around SHP099 identified derivatives with unexpected hERG activity and tolerability issues in some combination regimens; while not demonstrated specifically for SHP099 here, this flags a class risk requiring prospective cardiac and ocular safety pharmacology. Conformational-selection binding also means potency varies with SHP2 activation state, which is undefined in aging human RPE and could shift under inflammatory or oxidative stress present in dry AMD (Meem, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Lack of precedent in ocular models. No ocular, retinal, or RPE data for SHP099 or related allosteric SHP2 inhibitors are available in the supplied literature, increasing translational uncertainty for this repurposing (Yuan et al., 2020).

Program decision and de-risking experiments  
On the basis of the information provided, SHP099 is not yet a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD without foundational mechanistic validation in RPE. The central claim—that SHP2 inhibition prolongs MerTK phosphorylation and increases POS internalization—remains speculative in the absence of RPE data (Yuan et al., 2020). If the team elects to explore this hypothesis, a gated, mechanism-first workplan is advised:

- Define pathway engagement in RPE. Confirm SHP2 expression and activation state during phagocytosis in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE; assess whether SHP2 associates with MerTK/Src/FAK complexes upon POS challenge by co-immunoprecipitation or proximity assays (Shelby et al., 2015).  
- Biochemical time-courses ± SHP099. Quantify MerTK phosphorylation kinetics, Src and FAK activation, Rac1-GTP, and RhoA/ROCK activity after POS addition with a SHP099 concentration range bracketing its biochemical potency in enzyme assays; benchmark effect sizes against a ROCK inhibitor positive control, which is validated to rescue phagocytosis even in MerTK-deficient contexts (Mao & Finnemann, 2021).  
- Functional phagocytosis assays. Measure POS binding, F-actin cup formation, internalization, and phagolysosomal acidification under the same conditions, using established assays and timepoints aligned to the diurnal phagocytic peak where applicable (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Moran et al., 2022).  
- Ocular PK and safety. Establish retinal/RPE exposure after systemic and (if considered) intravitreal dosing, and perform ocular tolerability assessments (inflammation, ERG, histopathology) to identify potential on- or off-target liabilities early, mindful of class risks noted in optimization campaigns (Meem, 2022; Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).

In summary, SHP099 is a potent, selective, and well-characterized SHP2 allosteric inhibitor with robust oncology pharmacology and drug-like properties, but the case for repurposing to dry AMD by enhancing RPE POS phagocytosis is unsubstantiated in the provided literature and carries meaningful mechanistic and translational risks. Prioritizing direct RPE mechanistic studies and ocular PK/tolerability before any disease-model investment is the appropriate next step; in parallel, ROCK pathway modulation remains the most evidence-backed pharmacologic lever to augment phagocytosis in this system and should serve as a positive control and a benchmark for effect size (Fortanet et al., 2016; Mao & Finnemann, 2021; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Metformin is a well‐established biguanide originally derived from the natural compound galegine found in Galega officinalis. Over decades of development, it has been chemically optimized and synthesized into its modern, orally administrable form. Today, metformin is classified within the antidiabetic drug class and is routinely used to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus. Its discovery as an antihyperglycemic agent was serendipitous, and subsequent structural modifications have resulted in a drug with an excellent safety profile and pleiotropic effects beyond blood glucose regulation. As a small synthetic molecule available from reputable suppliers such as Sigma‐Aldrich (Cat. No. D150959), metformin has been repurposed in recent years for potential applications outside of metabolic diseases, including neurodegeneration and retinal degenerative disorders. This candidate belongs to a class of compounds that have historically been used for systemic metabolic control, but emerging evidence also suggests that their ability to activate AMPK—a critical cellular energy sensor—can be exploited to modulate autophagy and mitochondrial function in non‐metabolic tissues, including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhao et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, metformin has long been the first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes due to its robust glucose-lowering capability and favorable long-term risk profile. The extensive clinical use of metformin in diabetic populations has allowed researchers to retrospectively observe its pleiotropic effects on other organ systems. Notably, retrospective epidemiological studies have demonstrated that diabetic patients treated with metformin exhibit a lower incidence of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) compared to non-users, suggesting potential protective effects in the retina (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Huang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Furthermore, preclinical studies investigating metformin in vitro have shown that it protects human RPE cells against oxidative stress-induced damage, largely mediated by stimulation of the AMPK pathway (Zhao et al., 2020). In addition, in vivo models employing metformin have provided evidence of its ability to mitigate light-induced photoreceptor loss and retinal degeneration, supporting the hypothesis that its molecular targets in the RPE could be leveraged against dry AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Miyagishima et al., 2021). Although metformin has not been established as a conventional treatment for AMD, its proven use in modulating metabolic pathways, along with demonstrable effects on autophagy, mitochondrial function, and inflammation in retinal cells, provides the rationale for repurposing it in the context of dry AMD (Vessey et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, metformin exerts its primary pharmacological effects by inhibiting mitochondrial electron transport chain complex I, which leads to a reduction in ATP production and a concomitant increase in the AMP/ATP ratio. This energetic shift results in the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a master regulator of cellular metabolism and autophagy (Zhao et al., 2020). Activated AMPK phosphorylates several downstream targets that collectively restore energy homeostasis; among these targets are key regulators of autophagy, including the inhibition of mTOR and the direct phosphorylation of ULK1, which initiates autophagosome formation (Zhao et al., 2020; Dang et al., 2021). One important biochemical hallmark of this autophagy induction is the conversion of cytosolic LC3-I to its lipidated, membrane-bound form LC3-II, which has been used extensively as a marker to assess autophagy flux in RPE cell studies (Zhao et al., 2020). Additionally, metformin’s activation of AMPK influences mitochondrial biogenesis through upregulation of transcription co-activators such as PGC-1α, thereby promoting the generation of new, functionally active mitochondria (Dang et al., 2021; Sekar et al., 2023). These mechanisms are particularly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where RPE metabolic dysfunction is a key pathological feature. Moreover, metformin has been shown to modulate lipid metabolism, notably by enhancing cholesterol efflux via the AMPK/LXR pathway, which can reduce intracellular lipid accumulation—a contributor to drusen formation in AMD (Dang et al., 2021). Additional anti-inflammatory effects are mediated through suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation and modulation of VEGF signaling, further contributing to the overall cytoprotective profile of metformin in the retina (Dang et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed hypothesis and existing evidence, it is expected that metformin will activate AMPK in RPE cells, thereby promoting autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis. In practical terms, treatment with metformin is anticipated to lead to a measurable increase in LC3-II formation, a reduction in intracellular lipid accumulation, and restoration of ATP levels in RPE cells—specifically in models employing CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE cells, which serve as a relevant in vitro model of AMD (Zhao et al., 2020). The enhanced autophagic flux, as indicated by increased LC3-II levels and decreased p62 levels, will facilitate the clearance of damaged organelles, including dysfunctional mitochondria. This process of mitophagy is expected to improve overall mitochondrial homeostasis, thereby restoring the energetic capacity required for efficient phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Given that efficient POS degradation by RPE cells is critical for photoreceptor renewal and retinal health, the metformin-induced restoration of energy balance and autophagic function could lead to improved visual function. Importantly, AMPK is expressed in RPE cells and has been shown to be a crucial mediator of autophagy and mitochondrial quality control in these cells, ensuring that metformin’s mechanism of action is well-targeted to the cellular environment affected in dry AMD (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Furthermore, several in vivo studies support the notion that metformin can rescue mitochondrial function and enhance cellular clearance mechanisms, which are expected outcomes of its use in dry AMD models (Sekar et al., 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating metformin as a drug candidate for treating dry age-related macular degeneration, there are several notable strengths. First, metformin’s well-established safety profile from decades of clinical use for type 2 diabetes offers an advantageous starting point for repurposing—its known pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties facilitate its potential translation to ophthalmic indications (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Second, robust preclinical data support metformin’s ability to activate AMPK and promote autophagy, two pathways intimately involved in the maintenance of RPE health. Activation of AMPK has been repeatedly shown to enhance LC3-II formation, reduce oxidative stress, restore mitochondrial membrane potential, and upregulate mitochondrial biogenesis, all of which are critical to counteracting the metabolic deficits seen in AMD (Zhao et al., 2020; Dang et al., 2021; Sekar et al., 2023). Third, epidemiological studies have suggested that metformin use correlates with a reduced incidence of AMD, lending clinical relevance to its potential protective effects in the retina (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Huang et al., 2023). Fourth, the ability of metformin to modulate lipid metabolism, particularly by promoting cholesterol efflux and thereby reducing drusen-associated lipid accumulation, represents another beneficial mechanism targeting a fundamental aspect of AMD pathology (Dang et al., 2021).

However, several weaknesses and challenges must also be considered. Although many preclinical and retrospective clinical studies point toward a beneficial role of metformin in retinal health, direct prospective evidence in dry AMD patients remains limited. Some of the data originate from studies published in journals of variable quality, and there exists heterogeneity in the responses observed across different model systems, including patient-derived RPE cells where metformin’s effects may vary (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Moreover, while metformin is effective in activating AMPK systemically at standard doses used for diabetes, the optimal dosing regimen, route of administration, and tissue-targeting strategies necessary to achieve effective concentrations in the retinal tissue remain to be determined. The possibility that metformin’s efficacy may depend on specific genetic or metabolic backgrounds of patients—such as differences in CFH status or other AMD-related risk factors—also raises concerns about patient heterogeneity in clinical trials (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Additionally, while the expected restoration of autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis is promising, the precise quantitative changes in LC3-II, ATP levels, lipid accumulation, and POS degradation need rigorous validation under controlled experimental conditions before definitive conclusions can be drawn (Zhao et al., 2020; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Finally, potential systemic side effects such as gastrointestinal disturbances, rare occurrences of lactic acidosis, and vitamin B12 deficiency, albeit infrequent, may need consideration when repurposing metformin for chronic ocular use, especially in non-diabetic populations (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Brown et al., 2019).

Overall, metformin represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its multifaceted effects on enhancing autophagy, improving mitochondrial biogenesis, and restoring cellular energy metabolism in RPE cells. Its safety profile and broad availability further support its potential for rapid clinical translation. Nonetheless, the candidate’s ultimate success will depend on careful dose optimization, robust clinical trial designs that account for inter-patient variability, and further mechanistic studies to precisely delineate the quantitative biochemical improvements—such as LC3-II increase, lipid clearance, ATP restoration, and enhanced POS degradation—in preclinical AMD models (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhao et al., 2020). The convergence of epidemiological, biochemical, and preclinical data thus supports proceeding with further validation studies, while also highlighting the need to address remaining uncertainties regarding tissue-specific drug delivery and long-term outcomes in the context of dry AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Vessey et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Metoprolol is a second-generation, β1-selective adrenergic receptor antagonist developed within the broader historical evolution of β-blockers that began with Sir James Black’s introduction of β-adrenergic blockade for angina and expanded into major cardiovascular indications over subsequent decades (Opie, 2013; Mandiricha & Rochmanti, 2020). Within this class, β1-selective antagonists such as metoprolol competitively inhibit catecholamine binding at β1-adrenergic receptors, attenuating Gs–adenylyl cyclase–cAMP signaling and downstream protein kinase A (PKA) effects in tissues where β1-ARs are functionally expressed, most prominently the heart (Böhm et al., 2023; Mandiricha & Rochmanti, 2020). β-blockers as a class are synthetic small molecules with heterogeneous structures and pharmacokinetic properties (lipophilicity, bioavailability, hepatic versus renal clearance, intrinsic sympathomimetic activity), which shape their tissue penetration and side-effect profiles; metoprolol is moderately lipophilic and is predominantly cleared via hepatic CYP2D6-mediated metabolism (Panjrath & Messerli, 2006; Opie, 2013).

Therapeutically, β-blockers (including metoprolol) are widely used for hypertension (historically), angina pectoris, arrhythmia rate control, post–myocardial infarction secondary prevention, and chronic heart failure, with robust evidence for mortality and morbidity reduction in selected cardiovascular settings (Opie, 2013). In ophthalmology, β-adrenergic antagonists became a major class for open-angle glaucoma due to their ability to lower intraocular pressure (IOP) by reducing aqueous humor production via ciliary body β-adrenergic receptors; the archetypal agent is the nonselective β-blocker timolol, whereas the β1-selective agent betaxolol was developed to mitigate β2-mediated respiratory adverse effects (Nartey et al., 2021; Nocentini & Supuran, 2019). Importantly for posterior-segment drug delivery, early clinical work has evaluated intravitreal metoprolol tartrate at low dose with safety-focused endpoints, establishing preliminary tolerability and paving the way for hypothesis-driven ocular repurposing studies (Chaves et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic cardiovascular use  
Metoprolol has long-standing use as a β1-selective blocker for ischemic heart disease and heart failure; it is among the best-studied β-blockers for postinfarct protection and chronic heart failure alongside carvedilol and bisoprolol, reducing arrhythmic deaths and improving survival when properly titrated in stable systolic heart failure cohorts (Opie, 2013). Post–myocardial infarction, guideline-supported β-blockade with agents such as metoprolol succinate reduces long-term mortality by approximately a quarter in aggregate analyses, with additive benefit when combined with renin–angiotensin blockade (Opie, 2013). In hypertension, β-blockers have lost primacy as first-line therapy in uncomplicated disease due to inferior stroke prevention and metabolic adverse profiles compared with alternative classes, although β1-selective agents remain integral in specific comorbid contexts (e.g., ischemic heart disease, tachyarrhythmias) (Panjrath & Messerli, 2006; Opie, 2013). Pharmacologically, metoprolol’s hepatic metabolism via CYP2D6 yields clinically relevant drug–drug interaction risk (e.g., with paroxetine/fluoxetine), with interindividual variability in exposure that has been documented in pharmacogenetic studies and long-term PK observations (Ali et al., 2019; Nieminen et al., 2005; Opie, 2013).

Ophthalmic class use and metoprolol-specific ocular experience  
In ophthalmology, topical β-adrenergic antagonists are established agents to lower IOP, reducing aqueous humor production via antagonism of β-receptors in the ciliary body and iris/ciliary processes; timolol has been the archetype since 1978, and betaxolol (β1-selective) was introduced to minimize β2-related bronchospasm risks, albeit with somewhat reduced IOP-lowering efficacy relative to timolol (Nartey et al., 2021; Nocentini & Supuran, 2019). Betaxolol is repeatedly cited for neuroprotective actions in ocular models (e.g., slowing retinal changes after ischemia/reperfusion), underscoring that some β-blockers possess non-IOP biological effects on retinal cells (Nartey et al., 2021). Multiple sources list metoprolol among β1-selective agents and, in some reports, among β-blockers available for topical ophthalmic use; however, detailed clinical IOP-lowering data, efficacy comparisons, or neuroprotective endpoints specific to metoprolol in glaucoma are not provided in the materials at hand (Nartey et al., 2021). Topical β-blockers can cause systemic adverse effects because of nasolacrimal absorption without first-pass metabolism, including bronchospasm and bradyarrhythmias, necessitating caution in patients with reactive airway disease or conduction disorders and motivation for strategies to reduce systemic exposure (Vander Zanden et al., 2001; Nocentini & Supuran, 2019).

Of particular relevance to posterior-segment indications, a small phase I clinical study delivered off-label intravitreal metoprolol tartrate (50 μg/0.05 mL) in five eyes with circumscribed choroidal hemangioma, with safety assessments including full-field ERG (ISCEV protocol), OCT-based retinal thickness and choroidal thickness, anterior segment/vitreous inflammation, BCVA, and systemic blood pressure; the investigators reported no ERG evidence of toxicity, no clinical inflammation, stable IOP, stable choroidal thickness, no visual acuity deterioration, and modest reductions in retinal thickness or intra/subretinal fluid in a subset at four weeks (Chaves et al., 2021). Parallel rabbit studies did not show acute retinal toxicity at 50–100 μg intravitreal doses, supporting the human dose selection as biologically tolerable; nevertheless, limitations include very small sample size, single-dose exposure, short follow-up, and lack of dose–response or repeated-administration data (Chaves et al., 2021). The same group and others frame β-adrenergic blockade as an emerging target for neovascular or vascular ocular lesions, with propranolol providing historical precedent (infantile hemangiomas systemically; anecdotal ocular cases), while β1-selective metoprolol is explored for intraocular use owing to physicochemical compatibility and safety signals (Böhm et al., 2023; Chaves et al., 2021).

History in retinal/degenerative disease models  
Outside of pressure lowering and ocular vascular lesions, the provided sources report that metoprolol demonstrated neuroprotective effects in a rat model of retinal degeneration when given intraperitoneally or orally, and that metoprolol was not toxic to cultured retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells in vitro, implying a tolerable profile at the RPE level (Chaves et al., 2021). While this signals potential relevance to retinal cell survival, the evidence is preliminary, systemic rather than local in the degeneration model, and not specific to age-related macular degeneration subtypes; no clinical data in dry AMD were identified in the supplied materials (Chaves et al., 2021). The literature here does not document trials or case series of β1-selective antagonists for dry AMD, geographic atrophy, or RPE phagocytic dysfunction endpoints, so any linkage is inferential based on class mechanisms and exploratory safety/biology rather than disease-directed outcomes (Chaves et al., 2021; Nartey et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary pharmacology and signaling  
β1-adrenergic receptors are G-protein–coupled receptors classically coupled to Gαs, stimulating adenylyl cyclase, increasing intracellular cAMP, and activating PKA with broad downstream effects on ion channels, contractile machinery, and metabolism; antagonists such as metoprolol prevent catecholamine binding and blunt these signaling cascades in β1-expressing tissues (Böhm et al., 2023). β1-ARs are predominantly expressed in the heart, congruent with the robust chronotropic and inotropic effects of catecholamines and the established therapeutic actions of β1-selective blockade in cardiovascular disease; classically, blockade reduces cardiac output and renin release, lowering myocardial oxygen demand and ameliorating ischemic symptoms (Mandiricha & Rochmanti, 2020). Lipophilicity governs CNS penetration and neuropsychiatric side effects across the class, with more lipophilic agents crossing the blood–brain barrier more readily and potentially engaging central β-AR or other targets; metoprolol exhibits moderate lipid solubility, implying some CNS penetration and reinforcing that β-adrenergic mechanisms relevant to neurobiology are plausible with this agent (Opie, 2013; Panjrath & Messerli, 2006).

Ocular mechanisms and β-adrenergic pharmacology  
In the eye, β-adrenergic receptors in the ciliary body and related anterior segment tissues regulate aqueous humor production, and β-adrenergic antagonists reduce IOP by suppressing aqueous humor secretion; timolol’s nonselective β1/β2 blockade is highly effective for IOP lowering, while β1-selective betaxolol is generally less potent in IOP reduction but carries a reduced risk of β2-mediated respiratory adverse events (Nocentini & Supuran, 2019; Nartey et al., 2021). Beyond IOP, betaxolol displays neuroprotective properties in ocular models, including slowing of retinal changes after ischemia/reperfusion injury—a finding that suggests at least some β-blockers can confer direct retinal cell benefits independent of aqueous suppression, potentially via calcium channel modulation or other non-adrenergic mechanisms (Grieshaber & Flammer, 2010; Nartey et al., 2021). In posterior segment disease, β-adrenergic modulation has been hypothesized to affect angiogenesis and neural damage processes, with propranolol historically associated with ocular vascular lesion regression and preliminary trials pivoting toward exploring β1-selective metoprolol intravitreally due to formulation advantages; within this frame, β-ARs constitute a therapeutic target space extending beyond anterior segment fluid dynamics (Chaves et al., 2021).

Pharmacokinetic and safety considerations  
Metoprolol is extensively metabolized by CYP2D6, with genotype and drug–drug interactions modulating exposure; while these features are central to systemic administration, intravitreal delivery aims to limit systemic exposure, and early phase I data reported no significant changes in systemic blood pressure, suggesting minimal hemodynamic spillover at the tested ocular dose (Chaves et al., 2021; Opie, 2013). Importantly, an animal study with intravitreal propranolol (not metoprolol) detected photopic ERG amplitude reductions in rabbits at 28 days, emphasizing the necessity of agent- and dose-specific retinal electrophysiologic safety evaluation for β-blockers administered intraocularly; metoprolol at 50 μg intravitreally did not demonstrate ERG toxicity in small human series and rabbits, but long-term and repeated-dose safety remain untested (Chaves et al., 2021).

Relevance to RPE biology and dry AMD  
The supplied literature confirms that metoprolol is not toxic to RPE cells in vitro and that systemic metoprolol has neuroprotective effects in a rat retinal degeneration model; however, the materials do not document β1-AR expression in RPE, metoprolol’s modulation of RPE cAMP/PKA signaling, or effects on actin cytoskeleton dynamics, phagocytic cup formation, or photoreceptor outer segment (POS) internalization in RPE (Chaves et al., 2021). Likewise, while β-adrenergic pharmacology is invoked as a potential target in retinal vascular disease and ocular tumors, no evidence is provided here linking β1-selective antagonism to enhanced RPE phagocytic function, reduced cytoskeletal stiffness, or amelioration of dry AMD pathology, and no clinical evaluations in dry AMD are presented in the supplied texts (Böhm et al., 2023; Chaves et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectation under the proposed hypothesis  
The proposal hypothesizes that metoprolol, via β1-AR blockade in RPE, will reduce cAMP levels, alleviate cAMP-driven cytoskeletal stiffness, enhance actin remodeling, and thereby improve POS phagocytosis under stress conditions (e.g., in ARPE-19 assays), with an IC50 in the tens of nanomolar range; the supplied literature does not include data validating β1-AR expression in RPE, metoprolol’s potency at RPE β1-AR, or its effects on RPE actin dynamics or phagocytic cup formation (Chaves et al., 2021). The available ocular evidence base for metoprolol consists of safety-oriented intravitreal studies in choroidal hemangioma, in vitro RPE non-toxicity, and class-level ocular pharmacology centered on aqueous humor production and neuroprotective properties of betaxolol rather than RPE phagocytosis (Chaves et al., 2021; Nartey et al., 2021). Therefore, while β-adrenergic GPCR blockade would be expected to reduce cAMP in β1-expressing cells, the downstream link from cAMP reduction to RPE cytoskeletal remodeling and increased phagocytosis is not substantiated by the provided materials; accordingly, the expected effect in a phagocytosis assay remains speculative given the evidence presented here (Böhm et al., 2023).

Cellular expression and disease relevance  
The hypothesis requires that β1-AR is expressed and functionally coupled in the RPE, which is not documented in the present set of sources; instead, the ocular β-AR literature provided focuses on ciliary body (aqueous secretion) and, more broadly, retinal neuroprotection and vascular modulation at the tissue level (Grieshaber & Flammer, 2010; Nocentini & Supuran, 2019). Although metoprolol’s lack of RPE cytotoxicity supports feasibility for RPE-directed assays, translation to dry AMD hinges on improving RPE-mediated processes relevant to disease (e.g., POS clearance), which are not addressed in the current citations; moreover, no dry AMD or geographic atrophy outcomes have been studied with metoprolol in clinical or preclinical AMD models in the provided context (Chaves et al., 2021).

Delivery and dosing  
Given the anterior segment systemic absorption risks of topical β-blockers and the desire to target posterior RPE, intravitreal delivery is mechanistically attractive; the phase I trial indicates that a 50 μg/0.05 mL intravitreal dose is acutely tolerable with no ERG toxicity at four weeks, slight reductions in retinal thickness in chronic choroidal hemangioma, and no meaningful systemic blood pressure changes, which collectively support feasibility of posterior-segment dosing for exploratory mechanistic studies (Chaves et al., 2021). However, dose–response, repeat-dose safety, and long-term retinal electrophysiological effects remain unresolved and are particularly important given the ERG effects observed with intravitreal propranolol in animals, underscoring the necessity of cautious, stepwise dose escalation and comprehensive functional readouts if proceeding (Chaves et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Known pharmacology and druggability: Metoprolol is a well-characterized β1-selective antagonist with decades of systemic clinical experience and a clear molecular mechanism of action centered on β1-AR antagonism of Gs–AC–cAMP signaling; its class has demonstrable ocular pharmacology, establishing druggability of ocular β-adrenergic targets (Böhm et al., 2023; Nocentini & Supuran, 2019).  
- Ocular feasibility and early safety: Intravitreal metoprolol tartrate at 50 μg/0.05 mL has early human safety signals (no ERG toxicity, no inflammation, no VA deterioration at four weeks) and parallel animal data without acute retinal toxicity at 50–100 μg, supporting the feasibility of posterior-segment delivery for mechanistic or efficacy studies (Chaves et al., 2021).  
- RPE tolerability and retinal neuroprotection signals: In vitro, metoprolol did not exhibit toxicity to RPE cells, and in vivo systemic dosing showed neuroprotective effects in a rat retinal degeneration model, suggesting a favorable biological profile in retinal cell contexts, albeit not AMD-specific (Chaves et al., 2021).  
- Ocular β-blocker precedent with neuroprotective actions: Betaxolol (β1-selective) exhibits neuroprotective effects in ocular models beyond IOP lowering, indicating that at least some β1 blockers can confer retinal cell protection via mechanisms that may be independent of aqueous suppression, a conceptual precedent for exploring β1-targeted biology in posterior ocular tissues (Grieshaber & Flammer, 2010; Nartey et al., 2021).

Weaknesses and key evidence gaps for dry AMD  
- Absence of RPE β1-AR functional data: The central hypothesis requires β1-AR expression and functional coupling in RPE regulating cAMP-dependent actin dynamics and phagocytosis; the provided literature does not document β1-AR expression in RPE, nor metoprolol effects on RPE actin remodeling, phagocytic cup formation, or POS internalization, making the mechanistic premise unsubstantiated by the present citations (Chaves et al., 2021).  
- No dry AMD–specific preclinical or clinical data: There are no dry AMD or geographic atrophy studies—preclinical or clinical—using metoprolol in the provided materials; consequently, disease relevance and translational signal are absent (Chaves et al., 2021; Nartey et al., 2021).  
- Limited intravitreal safety characterization: Human intravitreal data are phase I, single-dose, and short-term; repeated dosing, long-term ERG stability, and dose–response safety are not assessed, and animal data with intravitreal propranolol reveal potential electrophysiologic risks, necessitating cautious development (Chaves et al., 2021).  
- Class heterogeneity and target specificity: Ocular β-blocker data demonstrating neuroprotection are centered on betaxolol; translating these effects to metoprolol without mechanistic support may be nontrivial given potential off-target (e.g., calcium channel) contributions unique to specific molecules (Grieshaber & Flammer, 2010; Nartey et al., 2021).  
- Systemic exposure considerations in non-intravitreal routes: Topical β-blockers can produce clinically significant systemic adverse effects via nasolacrimal absorption; while intravitreal dosing mitigates this risk, any exploration of topical delivery to RPE would require careful systemic safety mitigation (Vander Zanden et al., 2001; Nocentini & Supuran, 2019).

Risk–benefit and development implications  
On balance, metoprolol has an encouraging early ocular safety profile by intravitreal administration at low dose and a favorable RPE tolerability signal, but the mechanistic and disease-relevant evidence for dry AMD is currently insufficient to justify efficacy-focused clinical development; instead, a staged preclinical program to test the RPE phagocytosis hypothesis is warranted before advancing (Chaves et al., 2021). Specifically:  
- Mechanism validation: Confirm β1-AR expression and signaling in human RPE (primary RPE and ARPE-19), quantify cAMP responses to β-agonists and metoprolol antagonism, and interrogate actin dynamics and phagocytic cup formation using live-cell imaging and POS uptake assays under stress paradigms relevant to RPE dysfunction; no such evidence is provided in the current literature set (Chaves et al., 2021).  
- Safety pharmacology: Extend intravitreal safety to repeated dosing and longer follow-up with ERG, OCT, microperimetry, and visual function endpoints, including dose-ranging to define a minimal biologically active and maximal tolerated intravitreal exposure; the phase I trial highlights these gaps explicitly (Chaves et al., 2021).  
- Disease-model relevance: In the absence of dry AMD data, test efficacy in retinal degeneration or RPE stress models that recapitulate phagocytic impairment and RPE atrophy features, while monitoring for neuroprotective or anti-inflammatory readouts suggested by class literature; the existing animal work with systemic metoprolol in retinal degeneration supports feasibility but is not disease-specific (Chaves et al., 2021).

Given the present evidence, metoprolol should be considered a plausible exploratory tool compound for posterior-segment β1-AR biology in the retina/RPE with a preliminary intravitreal safety margin at low doses, but not yet a validated therapeutic candidate for dry AMD; only if RPE β1-AR signaling is shown to regulate phagocytosis and actin remodeling in a way that metoprolol favorably modulates and if such effects translate to structural/functional benefit in relevant models should a dry AMD program proceed (Chaves et al., 2021; Nartey et al., 2021). Until then, the proposed mechanism—cAMP-driven cytoskeletal modulation to enhance POS internalization by RPE via β1 blockade—remains hypothetical in the context of the supplied literature, and the development path should prioritize rigorous mechanistic and safety groundwork before considering clinical translation (Böhm et al., 2023; Chaves et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Divanillin is a naturally occurring oxidative dimer of vanillin that belongs to the class of phenolic dimers. Its synthesis is based on the oxidative coupling of monomeric vanillin—a well‐known flavor and fragrance molecule—using either chemical oxidants or, more efficiently, enzymatic methods. For instance, studies have demonstrated that fungal laccases, in particular, those derived from white-rot fungi such as Funalia trogii, can oxidize vanillin to form divanillin with near-quantitative yields under controlled reaction conditions (Esparan, 2015; Tai et al., 2011). Historically, divanillin was first noted for its presence in cured vanilla beans and has subsequently been developed for applications in the flavor and fragrance industries owing to its potent taste-enhancing properties, including its well-documented bitterness masking effects and its very low sensory threshold (Esparan, 2015; Krings et al., 2015; Torres-Zamudio et al., 2025). Its chemical profile, with lower water solubility compared to vanillin, also sets it apart as a candidate in formulations where controlled bioavailability is desired. As a low-molecular-weight compound, divanillin is amenable to formulation for ocular applications, and its repurposing as a modulator of intracellular signaling pathways, specifically in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), is a novel extension of its traditional roles.  

Therapeutic History:  
Divanillin’s historical usage has been largely in the realm of food and cosmetic applications. It has been known since the late 19th century and has been subject to extensive chemical characterization and synthesis studies through the early to mid-20th century (Esparan, 2015; Krings et al., 2015). In these fields, it is typically employed as a taste enhancer and bitterness masking agent, with its generation via enzymatic oxidation contributing to its characterization as a stable, bioactive phenolic dimer (Esparan, 2015; Torres-Zamudio et al., 2025). Over the years, the antioxidant properties of vanillin and its derivatives have been a major focus, with research demonstrating that multi-vanillin moieties can yield compounds with dramatically enhanced antioxidant activity compared to vanillin alone (Scipioni et al., 2018). Although these studies have primarily concentrated on neuroprotection, DNA damage protection, and cellular antioxidant capacities—such as those observed in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells—the literature does not currently report any direct clinical or preclinical application of divanillin for retinal diseases, including dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Scipioni et al., 2018; Tai et al., 2011). In parallel, a number of small-molecule SIRT1 activators, such as resveratrol and other natural polyphenols, have been explored in various ocular models and have shown promise in protecting RPE cells from oxidative damage and in modulating inflammatory pathways (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Ishida et al., 2017; Taurone et al., 2022). Thus, while divanillin itself has not been previously used for treating dry AMD or similar retinal conditions, its structural relationship to vanillin combined with emerging evidence regarding the benefits of vanillin derivatives suggests that repurposing divanillin for ocular use is a feasible and promising strategy.

Mechanism of Action:  
The central hypothesis proposed for divanillin is that it can function as a small molecule activator of SIRT1 in retinal pigment epithelial cells by achieving an effective concentration (EC₅₀) of approximately 1 µM. SIRT1 is a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)-dependent deacetylase that has critical roles in cellular metabolism, stress responses, and longevity. One of its well-established functions is the deacetylation of key cytoskeletal regulatory proteins, including cortactin and cofilin, which govern actin assembly and remodeling (Shentu et al., 2016). Cortactin, for instance, is a scaffold protein that binds to filamentous actin (F-actin) and the Arp2/3 complex and is involved in the formation of cell protrusions and phagocytic cups, whereas cofilin facilitates actin filament severing and turnover. In endothelial cells, it has been shown that AMPK phosphorylates cortactin at a critical threonine residue, priming it for SIRT1-mediated deacetylation; this sequential modification is essential for cortactin’s proper localization at the cell periphery and for dynamic actin remodeling (Shentu et al., 2016). Although this mechanism has been elucidated mainly in endothelial and other cell types, it is highly plausible that a similar pathway operates in RPE cells, where robust cytoskeletal dynamics are needed to support the daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Tarau et al., 2019; Cabrera, 2018).  

In RPE cells, phagocytosis is not a mere housekeeping task but a highly regulated process that demands rapid and targeted rearrangement of the actin cytoskeleton to form phagocytic cups that engulf the shed POS. Emerging studies have demonstrated that oxidative stress—a feature central to dry AMD pathology—can cause significant disruptions in the actin cytoskeleton, which contribute to impaired POS uptake and cellular degeneration (Tarau et al., 2019). SIRT1 activation, by deacetylating substrates such as cortactin and possibly cofilin, may restore or enhance the dynamic assembly of F-actin, thereby promoting more efficient phagocytic cup formation and POS internalization. In parallel, activation of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis in RPE cells has been linked with improved mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant responses, offering a dual mode of cytoprotection—a mechanism that is particularly attractive in the context of chronic oxidative stress typical of dry AMD (Ishida et al., 2017; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Furthermore, other small-molecule SIRT1 activators have already demonstrated the capacity to modulate oxidative stress and confer cellular protection in ocular models (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Taurone et al., 2022), lending additional credence to the hypothesis that divanillin may exert similar beneficial effects. In summary, the proposed mechanism of action for divanillin involves its SIRT1 activation properties leading to enhanced deacetylation of cytoskeletal regulatory proteins, which in turn promotes actin reorganization necessary for efficient phagocytosis by RPE cells under conditions of oxidative stress.

Expected Effect:  
Under the experimental conditions outlined in the proposal, treatment of RPE cells with divanillin at concentrations around its EC₅₀ of 1 µM is expected to result in the activation of SIRT1, a response that could be measured using biochemical assays indicative of its deacetylase activity. This SIRT1 activation is anticipated to lead to the deacetylation of its substrates, notably cortactin and cofilin, which are critical to the regulation of F-actin polymerization and reorganization (Shentu et al., 2016). At the molecular level, enhanced deacetylation of cortactin should facilitate its translocation to the cell periphery, where it can interact more effectively with the actin cytoskeleton, thereby promoting the formation of phagocytic cups, structures that are essential for the ingestion of POS (Tarau et al., 2019; Cabrera, 2018). The resulting improvement in cytoskeletal dynamics is projected to augment the ability of RPE cells to internalize shed photoreceptor outer segments—a process that is compromised in dry AMD due to cumulative oxidative damage and cytoskeletal disruption (Scipioni et al., 2018; Tarau et al., 2019).

Furthermore, activation of SIRT1 is expected to simultaneously confer additional cytoprotective benefits, including the enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis and function through the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis. This effect is highly relevant in RPE cells because their high metabolic demand and constant exposure to oxidative stress make them particularly vulnerable to mitochondrial dysfunction (Ishida et al., 2017; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). The improved mitochondrial function coupled with enhanced phagocytic efficiency would likely reduce the accumulation of oxidative damage and cellular debris, thereby mitigating key pathological features of dry AMD. Based on analogous studies employing other SIRT1 activators—such as resveratrol, which has been shown to protect RPE cells from oxidative stress and improve their phagocytic capability—the anticipated outcomes with divanillin include a measurable increase in POS uptake and improved cellular resilience under stress conditions (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Taurone et al., 2022). Consequently, these translational effects would be expected to translate into overall improved cellular homeostasis and a potential retardation of the degenerative processes observed in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
In assessing divanillin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several compelling strengths emerge. First and foremost, divanillin is a small-molecule agent that can be synthesized via well-established enzymatic processes from vanillin, a compound with a long history of safe use in food and cosmetic applications (Esparan, 2015). This favorable tolerability profile, combined with its robust antioxidant properties, provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in the ocular setting. The preclinical literature on vanillin derivatives indicates that incorporating multiple vanillin moieties into a single molecule can lead to a dramatic increase in antioxidant and cytoprotective activities (Scipioni et al., 2018), suggesting that divanillin may confer similar benefits in the context of retinal degeneration.  

Moreover, the innovative hypothesis that divanillin can activate SIRT1 in RPE cells is supported by a broader body of work demonstrating that SIRT1 plays a critical role in modulating oxidative stress, mitochondrial biogenesis, and cytoskeletal dynamics. There is substantial literature illustrating that SIRT1 activation leads to the deacetylation of key regulatory proteins such as cortactin, thereby promoting actin cytoskeleton remodeling—a process essential for phagocytic cup formation and efficient photoreceptor outer segment internalization (Shentu et al., 2016; Tarau et al., 2019). In this regard, targeting the SIRT1 pathway is a sound strategy, given that other natural SIRT1 activators, including resveratrol, have exhibited beneficial effects in RPE models under oxidative stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Taurone et al., 2022). This dual action—not only providing antioxidant protection but also enhancing the structural functionality of RPE cells—addresses two critical components of dry AMD pathogenesis: oxidative damage and impaired phagocytosis.

Despite these promising attributes, several weaknesses and uncertainties remain. Foremost among these is the lack of direct experimental evidence linking divanillin with SIRT1 activation in RPE cells. The proposed effective concentration (EC₅₀ ~ 1 µM) is based on extrapolations from studies with other vanillin derivatives and SIRT1 activators; however, no published data currently validate this specific potency for divanillin in ocular cells. In addition, while the mechanism by which SIRT1 deacetylates cortactin and potentially cofilin is well established in endothelial cells and other models (Shentu et al., 2016), it remains an assumption that RPE cells will respond identically, given their unique metabolic demands and specialized phagocytic functions (Tarau et al., 2019; Cabrera, 2018).  

There is also a significant gap concerning the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of divanillin in the context of ocular delivery. Although its small-molecule status and prior applications in non-ocular formulations suggest that it may have acceptable ocular tolerability and penetration, dedicated studies in retinal models or in vivo eye preparations are necessary to confirm its bioavailability and efficacy at the site of action. Furthermore, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD—with contributions from chronic inflammation, complement system dysregulation, and extracellular deposit formation—means that targeting SIRT1 and cytoskeletal dynamics may represent only one aspect of a comprehensive therapeutic approach (Crooke et al., 2017; Taurone et al., 2022). It will be important to consider whether divanillin’s purported mechanism can effectively address these other pathogenic mechanisms either alone or in combination with other treatments.

Another limitation is that, while divanillin’s antioxidant and cytoprotective properties have been indirectly demonstrated in studies examining vanillin and its derivatives (Scipioni et al., 2018; Tai et al., 2011), the direct link between these properties and improved phagocytic performance in RPE cells is yet to be established. Given that RPE phagocytosis is a highly specialized function that relies on precise spatial and temporal coordination of cytoskeletal activity (Tarau et al., 2019; Cabrera, 2018), even modest discrepancies in the modulation of actin dynamics could have substantial downstream effects on cellular homeostasis.  

Taken together, the overall evaluation of divanillin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. On the strength side, divanillin’s natural origin, ease of synthesis, and demonstrated antioxidant activity support its potential repurposing as a SIRT1 activator in the RPE. Its ability to modulate SIRT1—if validated experimentally—could translate into improved deacetylation of cytoskeletal regulatory proteins, enhanced F-actin remodeling, and more efficient phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments. These effects, in turn, could mitigate key aspects of dry AMD pathology, including the accumulation of oxidative damage and the gradual loss of RPE function. Such a dual mechanism of action—combining antioxidant protection with improved cellular architecture—is particularly attractive given the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD (Scipioni et al., 2018; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Shentu et al., 2016).  

However, the proposal is not without its challenges. The absence of direct evidence for divanillin’s SIRT1 activation in RPE cells, an unvalidated EC₅₀, and potential differences in the response of RPE cells compared to other cell types mean that significant preclinical work remains to be done. Rigorous in vitro studies using primary RPE cultures or established RPE cell lines will be necessary to confirm that divanillin can indeed enhance SIRT1 activity, deacetylate key substrates like cortactin and cofilin, and ultimately improve phagocytic cup formation and POS uptake. Additionally, in vivo studies using animal models of dry AMD will be critical to evaluate the compound’s pharmacokinetics, ocular bioavailability, and long-term safety and efficacy.  

In conclusion, divanillin represents a promising novel candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its potential to activate SIRT1 and thereby enhance actin cytoskeleton remodeling and phagocytosis addresses two critical pathological aspects of dry AMD—oxidative stress and impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments. Nonetheless, the current body of literature provides only indirect support for this mechanism, and several key areas require further investigation. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SR1078 is a synthetic ligand originally discovered as the first reported small‐molecule agonist for the orphan nuclear receptors RORα and RORγ. It was developed on a benzenesulfonamide scaffold and is marketed commercially (Tocris Cat. No. 3491) as a tool compound for probing ROR biology in vitro and in vivo (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016). As a RORα agonist, SR1078 belongs to the nuclear receptor modulator class of compounds, a family of therapeutics that have historically been used to orchestrate transcriptional programs related to metabolism, inflammation, and circadian regulation across various tissues (Solt & Burris, 2012). The synthetic origins of SR1078 trace back to programs that sought to optimize ligand interactions within the ROR ligand binding domain; detailed chemical characterization studies have shown that SR1078 binds and stabilizes the receptor’s active conformation, particularly by engaging critical residues that allow proper positioning of helix 12 for subsequent coactivator recruitment (Wang et al., 2010). This class of compounds has previously been employed primarily as a chemical biology probe in preclinical research, addressing metabolic dysregulation in liver and immunomodulatory effects in macrophages, and sometimes even in contexts such as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and autoimmune models (Matsuoka & Michihara, 2021; Wang et al., 2010).

Therapeutic History:  
SR1078 has been extensively exploited as a research tool rather than a clinical therapeutic; its major preclinical applications include the characterization of RORα-dependent transcriptional regulation in cell-based systems as well as demonstrating in vivo efficacy by modulating metabolic target genes such as FGF21 and G6Pase in liver tissue (Wang et al., 2010). In multiple studies, a single 10 mg/kg intraperitoneal (i.p.) dose of SR1078 in mice produced measurable plasma exposures in the low micromolar range—specifically approximately 3.6 μM at 1 hour post-dose—indicating that the compound has appreciable systemic bioavailability when administered in vivo (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016; Wang et al., 2010). Despite these promising pharmacokinetic data in non-ocular models, there are no registered clinical trials or preclinical studies in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal degenerative diseases on public repositories such as ClinicalTrials.gov (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.); indeed, the literature does not document any previous therapeutic use of SR1078 for treating dry AMD or analogous retinal conditions (Wang et al., 2010). Moreover, while several studies have harnessed SR1078 to explore ROR-dependent transcriptional mechanisms in liver and immune cells, the compound’s utility in ocular pathologies has not been established, which means that its repurposing for AMD remains a novel and uncharted application at this time (Solt & Burris, 2012; Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SR1078 exerts its pharmacological effects by binding directly to the ligand binding domains (LBDs) of the retinoic acid receptor–related orphan receptors, with particular emphasis on RORα. Binding of SR1078 induces a conformational change in the receptor that leads to stabilization of helix 12 (H12), a structural event that is critical for the recruitment of LXXLL-containing coactivator proteins (Wang et al., 2010). This ligand-dependent stabilization promotes enhanced transcription of canonical ROR target genes including metabolic regulators such as fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) and glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase), as demonstrated in liver-based assays in HepG2 cells and in vivo in murine models (Wang et al., 2010). Additionally, in immunological contexts, RORα activation by SR1078 has been associated with shifts in macrophage polarization toward an M2 phenotype via upregulation of the Krüppel-like factor 4 (KLF4) gene, showcasing the versatility of RORα signaling in modulating inflammatory states (Matsuoka & Michihara, 2021). Despite these well-characterized mechanisms, it must be noted that the current literature does not provide any direct evidence that SR1078 modulates the transcription of phagocytic receptors—particularly S1PR5—in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) or that it enhances the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016; Solt & Burris, 2012). The hypothesis under consideration extends the established mechanism of SR1078’s action into a novel pathway linked to RPE physiology by proposing that SR1078 activation of RORα will lead to upregulation of S1PR5, a receptor that is implicated in phagosome maturation and may offer MERTK-independent enhancement of POS uptake and trafficking (Buniello et al., 2025). However, while SR1078 is well characterized for its ROR-dependent transcriptional effects in other cell types, detailed biochemical data connecting its activity to the expression of S1PR5 in RPE remain absent in the current literature corpus (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016; Solt & Burris, 2012). Furthermore, studies investigating RORα in retinal contexts have primarily focused on inflammatory and angiogenic processes, with limited discussion of phagocytic receptor dynamics and POS handling (Buniello et al., 2025; Lew, Mazzoni, & Finnemann, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing SR1078 for dry AMD is that activation of RORα in RPE cells by SR1078 will drive transcriptional upregulation of S1PR5, thereby enhancing the availability or function of phagocytic receptors required for the efficient uptake, trafficking, and eventual degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). This is especially relevant for MERTK-mutant iPSC-RPE models, where defective MERTK-dependent phagocytosis has been well-documented as a key pathological mechanism leading to accumulations of POS debris and subsequent retinal degeneration (Ramsden et al., 2017; Lukovic et al., 2015). In these models, MERTK deficiency abolishes the normal internalization of POS, leading to functional deficits in the RPE (Ramsden et al., 2017). The expected therapeutic effect of SR1078, as posited, would be the restoration of phagocytic capacity through a bypass mechanism; by activating RORα, it is anticipated that SR1078 may upregulate S1PR5 expression, which in turn is hypothesized to support phagosome maturation and a pathway of POS uptake that does not solely rely on MERTK signaling (Buniello et al., 2025). This effect is bolstered by mechanistic reasoning suggesting that S1P receptor signaling plays a role in phagosome dynamics, as demonstrated in studies highlighting sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) mediated regulatory pathways in the RPE (Lee et al., 2025); however, it is important to emphasize that these studies have primarily implicated S1PR3 rather than S1PR5, and the evidence for S1PR5’s involvement in RPE phagocytosis is comparatively limited (Buniello et al., 2025). Additionally, a follow-up reference (Unknown Reference) has been mentioned in internal discussions to indicate that SR1078 induces S1PR5 transcription in RPE, although this publication is not directly available in the current context. Therefore, if the hypothesis holds true, treatment with SR1078 would be expected to mitigate the phagocytic deficits observed in MERTK-mutant iPSC-RPE by increasing the transcriptional output of S1PR5 and possibly other RORα-dependent genes linked to membrane trafficking and lipid handling, thereby normalizing POS processing and ultimately slowing the progression of dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025). However, any such expected effect remains largely hypothetical at this stage, given the absence of direct experimental data linking SR1078-mediated RORα activation to enhanced POS uptake in RPE cells (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016; Solt & Burris, 2012).

In evaluating SR1078 as a therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses need to be considered. One of the major strengths is that SR1078 is a well-characterized synthetic agonist with robust biochemical evidence supporting its ability to modulate RORα activity. Its pharmacological profile includes demonstrable in vivo exposure, with measurable plasma concentrations following i.p. dosing, and it has been shown to activate canonical ROR target genes in hepatic and immune cell contexts (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016; Wang et al., 2010). Its established use as a chemical biology tool provides a solid foundation regarding its mechanism of action, including the ligand-induced stabilization of helix 12 within the receptor’s ligand binding domain, a critical determinant for coactivator recruitment and transcriptional activation (Wang et al., 2010). Moreover, SR1078’s potential brain penetrance is cited in internal discussions, which could be advantageous for targeting tissues behind biological barriers such as the blood–retina barrier, although detailed ocular pharmacokinetic data are not available in the current literature (Wang et al., 2010). This systemic exposure and preclinical PK profile may allow for eventual ocular delivery if its safety and efficacy in retinal cells can be established.

Despite these strengths, there are notable weaknesses and gaps in the evidence supporting the repurposing of SR1078 for dry AMD. First, while SR1078 is a proven RORα agonist in other tissue systems, there is no direct experimental data demonstrating that RORα activation by SR1078 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) leads to upregulation of S1PR5 or enhancement of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake. The proposed mechanism—that RORα activation will upregulate S1PR5, which in turn supports phagosome maturation and MERTK-independent POS uptake—is conceptually plausible, but it remains speculative in the absence of specific studies connecting these dots (Cyr, Bronner, & Crawford, 2016; Solt & Burris, 2012). In fact, available open-target data suggest that while RORA (and by extension, its modulators) has some animal-model support in retinal diseases, both RORA and S1PR5 display minimal recorded evidence linking them directly to age-related macular degeneration (Buniello et al., 2025).

Another concern is the potential for adverse effects. One excerpt has indicated that activation of RORα by SR1078 in certain cellular contexts can result in elevated p53 levels and apoptosis (Solt & Burris, 2012). Such pro-apoptotic effects in RPE cells would be counterproductive in any therapy aimed at rescuing or preserving photoreceptor function, since the health of the RPE is critical for maintaining retinal integrity (Solt & Burris, 2012).

Furthermore, while several preclinical studies document the efficacy of SR1078 in modulating metabolic and immune pathways in liver and macrophage models (Wang et al., 2010; Matsuoka & Michihara, 2021), none of these studies have extended their investigations into RPE cell biology or directly measured outcomes such as POS phagocytosis. At present, the literature does not provide such evidence; thus, the anticipated beneficial effect in the RPE remains hypothetical.
