Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Huperzine A is a naturally occurring alkaloid that was first isolated in the early 1980s from the Chinese medicinal plant Huperzia serrata, commonly referred to as Qian Ceng Ta (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000). As a member of the lycopodium alkaloids, Huperzine A exhibits a unique chemical structure characterized by a rigid bicyclic framework that contributes to its high affinity for acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition (Ferreira et al., 2016; Bai et al., 2000). Originally discovered through biodirected research into traditional Chinese medicines, Huperzine A was soon recognized for its ability to reverse cognitive deficits by elevating acetylcholine (ACh) levels in the central nervous system (Ferreira et al., 2016). Over subsequent decades, the compound has been synthesized and investigated extensively via both natural extraction and chemical synthesis to overcome issues related to its low natural yield (Ferreira et al., 2016). Huperzine A belongs to a therapeutic class of compounds known as AChE inhibitors, which have traditionally been used to treat conditions associated with cholinergic deficits, most notably Alzheimer’s disease. Its well-documented pharmacokinetic profile—including rapid absorption, wide body distribution, and effective penetration of the blood–brain barrier—has made it an attractive candidate not only for neurodegenerative disorders but, as emerging data suggest, for other diseases where cholinergic modulation may be beneficial (Filho et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Huperzine A has been used in traditional Chinese medicine for a variety of indications including the treatment of contusions, swelling, and memory impairments (Bai et al., 2000; Ferreira et al., 2016). Its modern therapeutic development began when its potent, reversible, and selective AChE inhibitory properties were identified, leading to its approval in China as a palliative treatment for Alzheimer’s disease (Ferreira et al., 2016; Filho et al., 2006). Preclinical studies and clinical trials have demonstrated that Huperzine A increases synaptic acetylcholine levels by blocking the enzyme that degrades it; this effect on cholinergic neurotransmission has validated its use in patients with Alzheimer’s and age-associated cognitive decline (Bai et al., 2000; Muñoz-Torrero & Camps, 2008). In the United States, its limited regulatory status as a dietary supplement marketed for memory enhancement further reinforces its established record in modulating cholinergic function (Ferreira et al., 2016). Although its primary clinical application has been neurological—especially in the domain of Alzheimer’s disease—recent preclinical models in ophthalmology have assessed the ocular tolerability of Huperzine A in animal models of age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a finding that presents a compelling case for its repurposing. However, as of now, there is no direct clinical evidence supporting its use in treating dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative diseases; rather, the therapeutic rationale is built on its biochemical actions and benefits observed in nonocular systems (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2006).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Huperzine A exerts its primary effect by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme responsible for catalyzing the breakdown of acetylcholine (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000). This inhibition is both reversible and selective, allowing for a sustained elevation of acetylcholine levels in synaptic clefts without causing the overstimulation typically associated with nonselective cholinergic agents (Filho et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016). The compound binds within the active gorge of AChE, interacting with critical amino acid residues such as tryptophans and tyrosines, thereby preventing the hydrolysis of acetylcholine and enhancing cholinergic neurotransmission (Ferreira et al., 2016; Muñoz-Torrero & Camps, 2008). In addition to its cholinesterase inhibitory activity, Huperzine A has been found to exhibit NMDA receptor antagonism at cerebral synapses, suggesting an additional neuroprotective dimension to its pharmacology (Orhan et al., 2009; Ferreira et al., 2016). This multifaceted pharmacological profile—combining AChE inhibition, NMDA receptor antagonism, and enhancements in neuroprotection—has contributed to its reputation as a “nootropic” agent in both traditional and modern medicine (Bai et al., 2000; Tumiatti et al., 2008).

For the present hypothesis targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), the mechanism of action is being reexamined from a different angle. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, it is hypothesized that Huperzine A, by inhibiting AChE, will increase the local concentration of acetylcholine. Elevated acetylcholine can engage muscarinic receptors, which have been reported to have an EC₅₀ value of approximately 10 nM in similar cellular contexts (Zaki et al., 2020). Muscarinic receptor activation in RPE cells is proposed to stimulate downstream signaling pathways including PI3K/Akt and the small GTPase Rac1. PI3K/Akt signaling is a well-characterized pro-survival pathway that also mediates cytoskeletal rearrangements necessary for phagocytic cup formation—a prerequisite for the efficient ingestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Froestl et al., 2013; Zaki et al., 2020). Additionally, Rac1 activation is known to modulate actin dynamics within cells, facilitating the necessary structural changes for phagocytosis. Although this specific signaling cascade in RPE cells has not been extensively detailed in the existing literature on Huperzine A, the groundwork laid by studies in cholinergic modulation of cytoskeletal dynamics in other cell types, such as macrophages, provides a plausible biochemical rationale (Orhan et al., 2009; Shah et al., 2023). The combination of AChE inhibition with enhanced muscarinic receptor signaling is, therefore, proposed to improve RPE phagocytic function—a critical process in maintaining retinal health and potentially mitigating the pathogenic accumulation of debris that characterizes dry AMD (Qian & Ke, 2014; Tumiatti et al., 2008).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of Huperzine A for dry AMD is that its cholinesterase inhibitory action will lead to a localized increase in acetylcholine within the RPE. In turn, this elevation is expected to activate muscarinic receptors expressed on the surface of RPE cells—a hypothesis that is supported by the known high sensitivity of these receptors to acetylcholine, with effective concentrations in the nanomolar range (Zhu et al., 2006). Activation of these receptors is anticipated to trigger the PI3K/Akt signaling cascade, a pathway critical for cell survival and the regulation of cytoskeletal dynamics, and to induce Rac1 activation. Rac1 is a central regulator of actin polymerization and is essential for the formation of the phagocytic cup that facilitates the ingestion and clearance of POS from the subretinal space.

Experimental evidence from preliminary studies using ARPE-19 cells—the commonly used human retinal pigment epithelial cell line—indicates that treatment with Huperzine A enhances POS uptake via Rac1 activation (Ferreira et al., 2016). This finding is particularly significant because the failure of RPE cells to phagocytose POS efficiently is a key pathological feature in dry AMD, leading to the accumulation of debris and subsequent retinal degeneration. Thus, by augmenting the phagocytic activity of RPE cells through muscarinic receptor-mediated signaling, Huperzine A may help restore or maintain the integrity of the outer retina. The expected outcome of such treatment would be an improvement in the clearance of photoreceptor debris, which could in theory reduce the progression of dry AMD or at least slow its degenerative course.

Moreover, given that cholinergic pathways are known to modulate cytoskeletal rearrangements in multiple cell types, the repurposing of Huperzine A for ocular applications builds upon the concept of leveraging well-understood neurological mechanisms in a novel tissue context (Bai et al., 2000; Zaki et al., 2020). The enhanced phagocytosis of POS in ARPE-19 cells, coupled with previously demonstrated ocular tolerability in preclinical models of AMD, provides supportive evidence for the clinical evaluation of Huperzine A as an innovative treatment strategy for dry AMD (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating Huperzine A as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key strengths are apparent. First, its well-established safety profile, particularly in the context of neurological applications, is encouraging; clinical trials in Alzheimer’s disease have consistently demonstrated its tolerability even at doses that elicit significant cholinergic effects (Filho et al., 2006; Bai et al., 2000). The compound’s rapid absorption and favorable pharmacokinetics, including its ability to permeate the blood–brain barrier, suggest that similar pharmacodynamic properties may be achievable in ocular tissues following appropriate formulation adjustments (Ferreira et al., 2016; Ferreira et al., 2016). Second, its dual mechanism of action—as a robust acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and as an agent with additional neuroprotective properties via NMDA receptor antagonism and other pathways—provides a multifaceted approach to ameliorating cellular dysfunction (Orhan et al., 2009; Tumiatti et al., 2008). This multifactorial pharmacology is particularly relevant in complex diseases such as dry AMD, where a single pathogenic mechanism is rarely responsible for disease progression.

The proposed mechanism of repurposing Huperzine A for dry AMD is innovative in that it leverages cholinergic modulation in a new compartment—the retinal pigment epithelium. By increasing extracellular acetylcholine, Huperzine A is expected to stimulate muscarinic receptors that, in turn, activate signaling pathways (PI3K/Akt and Rac1) involved in cytoskeletal rearrangement and phagocytic cup formation (Zaki et al., 2020; Orhan et al., 2009). This hypothesis is supported by preliminary in vitro findings in ARPE-19 cells, where enhanced uptake of POS has been observed upon treatment with Huperzine A (Qian & Ke, 2014; Ferreira et al., 2016). Considering that impaired POS clearance is a central contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the potential to restore RPE phagocytic function represents a promising therapeutic strategy.

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. Despite the compelling mechanistic rationale, direct evidence supporting the effectiveness of Huperzine A in animal models of dry AMD remains limited. Most of the existing literature is focused on its use in Alzheimer’s disease and cognitive enhancement, so there is a translational gap that needs to be addressed through robust preclinical studies specifically designed to assess retinal health and function (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2006). Moreover, while the modulation of muscarinic receptors and downstream PI3K/Akt and Rac1 signaling is plausible, the expression profile and sensitivity of these receptors in RPE cells relative to other cell types have not been fully elucidated in the context of AMD. Additional investigation is required to verify that the EC₅₀ value of approximately 10 nM for muscarinic receptor activation, which has been derived largely from studies in other systems, holds true in retinal tissue (Zhu et al., 2006; Zaki et al., 2020).

There is also the issue of drug delivery. Huperzine A’s systemic administration is well documented, but its formulation for ocular delivery presents unique challenges. The blood–retinal barrier is distinct from the blood–brain barrier, and achieving optimal drug concentration in the retina without off-target effects remains a major hurdle in ophthalmic drug development (Ferreira et al., 2016; Ferreira et al., 2016). It is essential to determine whether topical, intravitreal, or systemic administration would be most effective while maintaining a safe profile. The current evidence of ocular tolerability in AMD preclinical models is encouraging but must be confirmed in studies that specifically evaluate pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic factors in the eye (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Another potential weakness concerns the specificity of the proposed mechanism. While increasing acetylcholine levels in RPE cells may indeed enhance phagocytosis, there is a risk that such a generalized enhancement of cholinergic signaling could have unintended consequences on other retinal cell types or could lead to dysregulation of the delicate balance of neurotransmission in the retina. Off-target effects might manifest as alterations in retinal cell function, vascular regulation, or even inflammatory responses. These possibilities underscore the importance of carefully titrating the dose and thoroughly evaluating the long-term effects of Huperzine A in retinal tissue (Tumiatti et al., 2008).

From the standpoint of drug development, repurposing a compound like Huperzine A offers several advantages. Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in neurological applications provides a robust safety database that may help streamline regulatory approval processes for new indications. Furthermore, its natural origin and the availability of synthetic production methods help mitigate supply concerns associated with its low natural yield—an issue that has historically plagued natural product drug development (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2009). However, the challenges associated with scaling up production, ensuring batch-to-batch consistency, and adapting formulation technologies for ocular use must be addressed through targeted research initiatives (Froestl et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2006).

The multifaceted pharmacology of Huperzine A also suggests that it may confer additional benefits beyond enhanced phagocytosis. Its neuroprotective effects, possibly mediated through NMDA receptor antagonism and antioxidant properties, could provide a dual therapeutic advantage in the context of dry AMD—a disease characterized not only by defective phagocytosis but also by oxidative stress, inflammation, and subsequent retinal degeneration (Orhan et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2020). If Huperzine A can be shown to protect retinal cells from oxidative damage while simultaneously restoring phagocytic function, it may serve as a disease-modifying agent rather than merely a symptomatic treatment.

In summary, Huperzine A presents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well-established mechanism as an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, favorable safety profile in neurological applications, and potential to stimulate muscarinic receptor signaling pathways in RPE cells—a process that is critical for the maintenance of photoreceptor outer segment turnover (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000; Ferreira et al., 2016). From a strategic perspective in drug development, repurposing Huperzine A for dry AMD is an attractive approach due to its existing body of research, established safety profile, and potential multifaceted mechanisms that extend beyond simple cholinesterase inhibition. The weaknesses, by contrast, lie primarily in the current lack of direct experimental data linking its pharmacology to RPE-specific outcomes in dry AMD, and potential difficulties in achieving effective and localized delivery to the retina without eliciting off-target effects (Zhu et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016). In conclusion, based on a comprehensive review of the literature and the available biochemical, clinical, and pharmacological data, Huperzine A emerges as a compelling candidate for further investigation as a repurposed drug for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its multifaceted pharmacodynamic profile, combined with promising preliminary data on enhanced POS uptake in ARPE-19 cells, supports continued exploration of its potential to restore RPE function through muscarinic receptor-mediated and Rac1-dependent signaling pathways. Moving forward, the research team should concentrate on validating the expression of relevant muscarinic receptors in RPE cells, characterizing the downstream activation of PI3K/Akt and Rac1 in response to Huperzine A treatment, and developing a targeted ocular delivery system that achieves sufficient retinal bioavailability while preserving the compound’s safety profile. These steps, together with rigorous in vivo efficacy studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD, will be critical in determining whether Huperzine A can be effectively repurposed for this challenging indication (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Ferreira et al., 2016; Qian & Ke, 2014; Zaki et al., 2020).

Such an approach would not only provide a novel therapeutic option for patients with dry AMD—a condition for which effective treatments are currently limited—but also exemplify the translational potential of natural product-based drug discovery, bridging time-honored traditional medicine with modern biomedical innovation (Bai et al., 2000; Filho et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2020). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Brefeldin A (BFA) is a natural product originally isolated in 1958 from Penicillium decumbens, and its discovery marked the beginning of intensive studies on its unique ability to disrupt intracellular protein trafficking (Hung, 2020). Structurally, BFA is a macrolide characterized by a complex fused system comprising a cyclopentane moiety linked to a 13-membered lactone, and this distinctive architecture has spurred extensive synthetic and medicinal chemistry efforts over the past decades (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015). By targeting the secretory pathway, BFA acts as a Golgi transport inhibitor, primarily through its binding to a protein complex involving a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) and the small G protein Arf1. This binding event results in the rapid disassembly of the Golgi apparatus and redistribution of its components back into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Hung, 2020). BFA is therefore classified among natural product inhibitors of intracellular trafficking, a group that has long served as invaluable research tools in cell biology to dissect the mechanisms of vesicular transport and Golgi-ER dynamics. Its broad bioactivities—as an antiviral, antifungal, and antimitotic agent—have principally been exploited in preclinical research rather than clinical therapeutics (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, BFA has been employed almost exclusively as a biochemical probe to investigate protein processing, secretion, and Golgi morphology in diverse eukaryotic cells. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that BFA’s ability to stall ER-to-Golgi trafficking can modulate various cellular processes including secretion of cytokines, hormones, and growth factors (Hung, 2020). Its documented effects on blocking transport have been leveraged in cancer cell studies where BFA-induced apoptosis and cell cycle arrest were observed, owing to mislocalization of key signaling molecules (Stierle & Stierle, 2015). Despite these promising cellular effects, the clinical development of BFA as a conventional therapeutic agent has been hindered by issues such as poor bioavailability and significant toxicity with prolonged exposure (Seehafer et al., 2013). Importantly, while BFA has not been directly applied in clinical studies for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or any similar degenerative retinal diseases, its mechanistic action on intracellular trafficking, ER stress, and protein secretion renders it an intriguing candidate for repurposing. In the context of AMD, where complement dysregulation and lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells play a critical pathogenic role, BFA could potentially offer a novel means of attenuating the buildup of complement components and misfolded proteins (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). While none of the published literature explicitly documents the use of BFA for AMD therapy, related studies in RPE cellular models have highlighted the importance of complement modulation and lysosomal restoration, establishing a rationale for investigating trafficking inhibitors such as BFA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
On a molecular level, the mechanism of action for Brefeldin A is well characterized. BFA binds to the complex comprising a catalytic GEF and the small GTPase Arf1, inhibiting the exchange of GDP for GTP on Arf1. This inhibition precludes proper recruitment and coat assembly for vesicle budding at the Golgi membranes, leading to a collapse of the Golgi structure and the retrograde redistribution of Golgi proteins to the ER (Hung, 2020). The immediate consequence of this inhibition is a profound disruption in the secretory pathway, which not only halts the export of proteins but also results in an accumulation of proteins within the ER. In cell types where the regulated secretion of proteins is critical for homeostasis, such as in RPE cells, this effect can have dual ramifications. On the one hand, it may help prevent the secretion of misfolded or aberrantly processed proteins, including complement components that are implicated in local inflammation and lysosomal deposition (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). On the other hand, the blockade of Golgi trafficking may transiently lower the secretion of proteins that otherwise contribute to the local pool of complement proteins which, if misfolded or overproduced, could lead to an increase in intracellular complement activation and subsequent deposition of the membrane attack complex (MAC, particularly C5b-9) within lysosomes (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In RPE cells, where robust daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) is essential, the maintenance of lysosomal function is critical; overburdening of lysosomes with complement-derived debris has been implicated in the formation of drusen and lipofuscin accumulation, both of which underlie AMD pathology (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The proposed intervention using BFA therefore leverages its well-established ability to modulate protein trafficking to indirectly reduce the burden of misfolded or overabundant complement proteins on the lysosomal system, thereby potentially restoring cathepsin activity and overall lysosomal function in RPE cells.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing BFA in dry AMD is that brief pulses of BFA administration will selectively inhibit the ER-to-Golgi trafficking route in RPE cells, thereby reducing the processing and secretion of misfolded complement proteins. RPE cells are known to contribute to local complement activation through the production and turnover of various complement components; in AMD, aberrant complement regulation leads to increased turnover, formation of complement split products, and the deposition of terminal complement complexes (C5b-9) in the lysosomes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The expected outcome of BFA treatment would be a reduction in the export of these misfolded or excessively generated complement proteins, ultimately leading to decreased local complement activation and a reduction in lysosomal overload by MAC proteins. Experimental evidence from studies using compstatin analogues (e.g., Cp40) in Y402H-RPE cell models has shown that complement inhibition can restore lysosomal function and cathepsin activity, thereby reducing lysosome size, diminishing drusen-like deposits, and improving the overall cellular phenotype (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015). By analogy, transient BFA treatment is anticipated to produce similar beneficial effects on lysosomal physiology in RPE cells, provided that the inhibition is carefully timed to avoid prolonged exposure which could be deleterious (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Furthermore, because RPE cells are responsible for the daily clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, maintaining an unencumbered lysosomal system is crucial for long-term retinal health. The expected biochemical cascade following BFA administration would therefore include a reduction in ER stress due to diminished protein export, lower secretion of misfolded complement proteins, and a subsequent decrease in complement-mediated lysosomal damage. This in turn should lead to a stabilization or even an improvement in cathepsin levels and activity, promoting a more efficient degradation of cellular debris and restoration of POS clearance (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential repurposing of Brefeldin A as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD is innovative and grounded in a detailed understanding of both its mechanism of action and the pathophysiology of AMD. Several strengths underlie this approach. First, BFA has a well-characterized molecular mechanism that directly affects the secretory pathway by inhibiting ER-to-Golgi trafficking. This offers a mechanistic basis for reducing the secretion of misfolded or aberrantly processed complement proteins—the accumulation of which is a central driver of lysosomal dysfunction and local complement activation in RPE cells (Hung, 2020). Second, preclinical research in AMD models has demonstrated that modulating complement activity, whether through direct inhibition of complement components or by enhancing lysosomal function, can reverse pathological phenotypes associated with the disease (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015). This suggests that a strategy aimed at indirectly reducing complement deposition via interference with protein trafficking holds considerable promise. Third, the idea of using brief pulses of BFA rather than continuous dosing could allow for a transient therapeutic effect that minimizes the known toxicities associated with prolonged BFA exposure—thus potentially overcoming one of the key limitations that has prevented its clinical development in other contexts (Seehafer et al., 2013; Stierle & Stierle, 2015).

Nonetheless, there are significant challenges and weaknesses that must be addressed before this approach can be advanced. One of the primary concerns relates to the non-selectivity of BFA’s action. Because BFA disrupts a fundamental cellular process, its effects are not confined solely to the trafficking of misfolded complement proteins. It is likely to inhibit the normal secretion of multiple proteins that are essential for RPE cell function, which could inadvertently impair the phagocytosis and processing of photoreceptor outer segments (Hung, 2020; Seehafer et al., 2013). Such disruption could paradoxically exacerbate the very lysosomal dysfunction it is intended to ameliorate, particularly if dosing is not carefully titrated. Furthermore, while transient inhibition may mitigate toxicity, achieving the precise balance between therapeutic efficacy and cellular viability will require rigorous optimization in both in vitro and in vivo models. Another potential drawback is related to pharmacokinetics and delivery. BFA’s poor bioavailability and potential systemic toxicity have long been recognized as obstacles for its use beyond experimental settings (Seehafer et al., 2013). Delivering BFA specifically to the RPE while avoiding off-target effects in other ocular or systemic tissues will demand innovative formulation strategies, such as localized drug delivery systems, which inherently add another layer of complexity to the drug development process. Additionally, while the hypothesis is supported by analogous studies demonstrating that complement modulation can restore lysosomal function in AMD models (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Georgiannakis et al., 2015), there is currently no direct evidence that BFA’s inhibition of ER-to-Golgi trafficking will reproduce these beneficial effects in the delicate environment of the retina. The potential for unforeseen interactions with other components of the RPE’s protein processing machinery or compensatory cellular responses further complicates the translational prospects of this approach.

In summary, as an expert drug development team leader tasked with evaluating promising repurposed drugs for dry AMD, I find the proposal to repurpose Brefeldin A to be both innovative and mechanistically intriguing. The strengths of this candidate lie in its well-characterized molecular target—namely, the inhibition of Arf1-mediated vesicle budding at the Golgi—and its potential to modulate a key pathological feature of AMD, namely the dysregulated secretion and accumulation of complement proteins that leads to lysosomal impairment and MAC deposition (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). However, the inherent risks associated with disrupting a central cellular process cannot be overstated. The lack of selectivity in BFA’s action, potential toxicity from even brief exposures, and challenges in targeting the RPE specifically are serious obstacles that must be systematically addressed. Further preclinical studies are required to delineate the dose-response relationship in RPE cell models, to examine the long-term effects of transient BFA-induced trafficking inhibition on cellular health, and to validate the hypothesis that such intervention can indeed reduce lysosomal MAC deposition and rescue cathepsin activity. Only with convincing evidence from rigorous in vitro and in vivo experiments would it be justified to consider advancing BFA as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. In conclusion, while the proposed use of BFA presents a compelling mechanistic rationale with some supportive preclinical analogies from the literature (Georgiannakis et al., 2015; Cerniauskas et al., 2020), significant challenges regarding specificity, delivery, and safety need to be overcome before this approach can be deemed a viable therapeutic option for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide, a water‐soluble form of vitamin B3, is a naturally occurring compound that plays a critical role in cellular metabolism by serving as a precursor for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺) synthesis. It is available both through dietary sources and chemical synthesis and has been produced at high purity for research purposes (Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. N4126). Nicotinamide belongs to the vitamin B3 class of compounds, which have been extensively used as nutritional supplements and metabolic regulators; these compounds are well recognized for their role in the salvage pathway that replenishes NAD⁺ levels in cells. The therapeutic candidate under consideration is repurposed with the hypothesis that at a concentration of 10 mM, nicotinamide will boost intracellular NAD⁺ pools and enhance the activity of NAD⁺‐dependent enzymes, such as sirtuins, leading to improved mitochondrial function and increased deacetylation of autophagy regulators. Such effects are expected to restore phagocytic function, specifically the photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation, in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cultures pertinent to dry age‐related macular degeneration (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, nicotinamide has been investigated in various preclinical and clinical settings for its potential neuroprotective effects and its capacity to modulate cellular metabolism. In the context of ocular health, several studies have demonstrated that nicotinamide supplementation can enhance NAD⁺ levels and improve mitochondrial function in retinal cells. Preclinical studies have reported that this vitamin not only supports retinal ganglion cell health in glaucoma models but also shows promise in improving photoreceptor and RPE function in models of age-related macular degeneration (Gemae et al., 2024). Although there remains limited direct clinical experience with nicotinamide in dry AMD, the compound has been a subject of interest in related ocular conditions due to its favorable safety profile and widespread use in other age-related and mitochondrial dysfunction settings (Gemae et al., 2024). More recent investigations have focused on its ability to rescue mitochondrial deficits and restore autophagic flux in RPE cells, with data indicating that in models of CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE, nicotinamide can ameliorate lysosomal processing and POS degradation problems (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). This body of evidence, compounded with its extensive historical use as a nutritional supplement, supports the rationale for repurposing nicotinamide as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, nicotinamide exerts its effects primarily through its role as a key precursor in the NAD⁺ salvage pathway. In this pathway, nicotinamide is converted to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) via the enzyme nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), and subsequently to NAD⁺ by NMN adenylyltransferase. NAD⁺, in turn, is an essential co-factor for numerous enzymes involved in energy metabolism and cellular homeostasis, most notably the sirtuin family of NAD⁺-dependent deacetylases (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Sirtuins, such as SIRT1 and SIRT3, play a pivotal role in mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and regulation of autophagy by deacetylating key transcription factors and enzymes that control metabolic stress responses (Gemae et al., 2024). In RPE cells, increased NAD⁺ levels facilitate the activation of these sirtuins, which then deacetylate a range of targets including histones and autophagy regulators, leading to improved mitochondrial structure and function, enhanced energy production, and the promotion of efficient autophagic and lysosomal degradation pathways (Gemae et al., 2024). Furthermore, the improved mitochondrial function translates into a better cellular energy state, providing the necessary ATP required for high-energy processes such as POS phagocytosis. Experimentally, administration of nicotinamide has been shown to yield a two-fold increase in NAD⁺ levels in ARPE-19 cells, thereby confirming its ability to augment the cellular bioenergetic capacity (Hazim et al., 2022). This mechanism also intersects with the regulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, as enhanced mitochondrial function and sirtuin activity contribute to lower oxidative stress, a known contributor to cellular senescence and dysfunction in the aging retina (Gemae et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the current proposal is that nicotinamide, administered at a concentration of 10 mM in vitro, will significantly increase NAD⁺ levels in RPE cells, thereby enhancing sirtuin activity and downstream mitochondrial function. This boost in NAD⁺ is expected to promote deacetylation of autophagy regulators, which will, in turn, normalize the autophagic flux and facilitate the effective degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE. In models of dry AMD, where phagocytosis deficits and impaired proteostasis are key pathological features, the restoration of autophagy and mitochondrial activity is anticipated to ameliorate cellular senescence and maintain retinal homeostasis (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Data from previous studies suggest that in aging RPE, reduced NAMPT expression is linked to decreased NAD⁺ levels and compromised SIRT1 function, leading to cellular senescence and defective mitochondrial dynamics (Jadeja et al., 2018). By contrast, nicotinamide supplementation helps to reverse these effects, as evidenced by restored NAD⁺ content and reactivation of sirtuins that enable degradation of accumulated defective cellular components, thereby improving lysosomal enzyme processing and phagocytosis (Jadeja et al., 2018). Moreover, enhanced mitochondrial metabolism has been correlated with improved RPE differentiation and the maintenance of a polarized epithelial phenotype, critical factors in ensuring effective POS phagocytosis and overall retinal health (Hazim et al., 2022). Thus, the expected outcome is that nicotinamide treatment will correct metabolic impairments, reduce oxidative stress, and restore phagocytic efficiency in dry AMD cultures, which are all essential for halting or even reversing disease progression (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
Nicotinamide emerges as a highly promising therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on its multi-faceted mechanism of action and extensive preclinical evidence supporting its role in maintaining retinal health. One of the primary strengths of nicotinamide is its excellent safety profile and widespread historical use as a nutritional supplement, which significantly lowers the risk associated with its repurposing (Gemae et al., 2024). Its ability to augment NAD⁺ levels and activate sirtuins directly addresses several key pathological processes in dry AMD, including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and impaired autophagy. Experimental findings have consistently shown that increased NAD⁺ levels, mediated by nicotinamide or its analogues such as NMN, correlate with reduced cellular senescence and improved lysosomal and mitochondrial function in RPE cells (Jadeja et al., 2018).

Moreover, the convergence of multiple lines of evidence—from studies detailing NAMPT decline in aging RPE, to those demonstrating the restoration of NAD⁺ and sirtuin activity by nicotinamide—provides a robust biochemical rationale for its use in combating dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024). The ability of nicotinamide to enhance mitochondrial respiration in ARPE-19 cells and primary human fetal RPE cells further underscores its potential in promoting a healthy, polarized RPE phenotype capable of efficient POS phagocytosis (Hazim et al., 2022). These studies also suggest that improved mitochondrial metabolism is closely linked to enhanced proteostasis and autophagic clearance of damaged cellular components—an outcome that is particularly relevant given the known deficits in autophagy and lysosomal processing observed in dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024).

However, while the preclinical data are encouraging, several challenges must be acknowledged. One potential weakness lies in the translation of in vitro findings to in vivo therapeutic efficacy. The concentration of 10 mM nicotinamide used in cell culture experiments may not directly correspond to achievable or sustainable therapeutic levels in the human retina. Moreover, while nicotinamide is known to boost NAD⁺ synthesis, there is a nuanced balance in its effects on sirtuin activity; in certain contexts, excessive nicotinamide has been reported to inhibit sirtuins, suggesting that dosing and timing will be critical parameters that require careful optimization (Will-Orrego, 2020). Overall, the repurposing of nicotinamide for dry AMD presents several compelling advantages. Its established safety, low cost, and known biochemical mechanisms strongly support its potential as a therapeutic candidate. Preclinical evidence indicates that nicotinamide not only restores NAD⁺ levels but also reactivates sirtuin pathways, thereby mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction and defective autophagy that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. These effects could translate into improved cellular proteostasis and enhanced POS phagocytosis, ultimately preserving retinal integrity and visual function (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Nevertheless, the path forward will require careful dose optimization and rigorous clinical validation to ensure that the in vitro benefits observed translate into meaningful clinical outcomes. In summary, despite the challenges associated with translating cell-based results into human therapy, nicotinamide remains an attractive candidate whose mechanism, historical use, and preclinical successes justify further investigation as a potential treatment for dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Lin, 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB431542 is a well‐characterized, synthetic small molecule inhibitor originally developed through medicinal chemistry efforts by researchers at GlaxoSmithKline. Its chemical structure, formally denoted as 4-(5-benzo[1,3]dioxol-5-yl-4-pyridin-2-yl-1H-imidazol-2-yl)-benzamide, incorporates a benzodioxole moiety linked to a pyridyl-imidazol core and terminated by a benzamide group, placing it within the imidazole class of compounds (Laping et al., 2002). SB431542 belongs to the class of transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) type I receptor kinase inhibitors (commonly referred to as ALK5 inhibitors) that inhibit ATP-dependent receptor activation. Initially designed as an improvement over less-selective kinase inhibitors—such as early p38 MAPK inhibitors that exhibited off-target ALK5 inhibition—SB431542 emerged from a rational structure–activity relationship (SAR) campaign aimed at optimizing both potency and selectivity (Laping et al., 2002). Its discovery has been pivotal in establishing a molecular tool for dissecting TGFβ signaling, and its chemical synthesis reflects a focused effort on achieving high-affinity, ATP-competitive inhibition of the TGFβ receptor. This compound has been extensively used in preclinical research to study fibrotic mechanisms and cellular differentiation, thereby marking its reputation as a “gold standard” in TGFβ pathway inhibition (Laping et al., 2002).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SB431542 is primarily rooted in its application as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. In numerous preclinical studies, SB431542 has been consistently used to inhibit TGFβ-induced processes such as extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis, Smad protein activation, and the induction of a fibrotic phenotype in various cell types including renal epithelial cells, fibroblasts, and even certain cancer cell models (Laping et al., 2002). Biochemical studies have shown that SB431542 effectively blocks the phosphorylation of Smad3 with an IC50 of approximately 94 nM, thereby preventing the downstream transcriptional activation of cytokines and matrix proteins (Laping et al., 2002). Its anti-fibrotic effects have been extensively characterized in in vitro assays, where it reduced the expression of collagen I α1, fibronectin, and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) mRNA, thus providing compelling evidence that the compound modulates TGFβ-induced ECM remodeling (Laping et al., 2002).

While SB431542 has been applied in many experimental models to study pathways implicated in fibrotic diseases such as glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, liver cirrhosis, and pulmonary fibrosis, there is scant direct evidence of its historical use in ocular pathologies, particularly dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Akhund et al., 2023; Nyati et al., 2011). However, TGFβ signaling has been implicated in retinal pathologies and in the mesenchymal transition of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells from which some studies have emerged using general TGFβ inhibitors to reverse such pathological changes (Radeke et al., 2015). Although SB431542 itself has not been used in clinical trials for AMD, its mechanistic profile and reported efficacies in other fibrotic and ECM remodeling contexts make it a promising candidate for repurposing to address the abnormal matrix remodeling observed in dry AMD. Preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues have established that targeted inhibition of TGFβ signaling leads to substantial reductions in fibrotic markers, suggesting that similar approaches could mitigate Bruch membrane (BrM) alterations in AMD (Laping et al., 2002).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB431542 functions as an ATP-competitive inhibitor selectively targeting the kinase domain of the TGFβ type I receptor (TGFβRI, also known as ALK5). Its mechanism of action centers on binding to the ATP-binding pocket of TGFβRI, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of key intracellular effectors, primarily the Smad2 and Smad3 proteins (Laping et al., 2002). In normal TGFβ signaling, binding of the ligand (e.g., TGFβ1) to its receptors induces the formation of a heteromeric complex consisting of TGFβRI and TGFβRII, leading to the phosphorylation and activation of Smad2/3. These phosphorylated Smad proteins then form a complex with Smad4, translocate to the nucleus, and activate the transcription of pro-fibrotic genes, including those involved in ECM protein synthesis such as collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002).

Detailed molecular interaction studies have revealed that SB431542 makes critical hydrogen bonding contacts within the ATP-binding site of TGFβRI. For example, the benzodioxol moiety is reported to form a hydrogen bond with the amide nitrogen of His283, while additional interactions with Lys232 and other hydrophobic residues stabilize the inhibitor within the binding pocket (Leonardo-Sousa et al., 2025). This precise molecular engagement confers its high selectivity, as even minor substitutions in the binding region—such as mutations at the gatekeeper residue—can significantly alter inhibitor efficacy (Laping et al., 2002; Leonardo-Sousa et al., 2025). Furthermore, while SB431542 shows potent inhibition against ALK5, it also inhibits closely related receptors such as ALK4 and ALK7 with only modest differences in potency (IC50 for ALK4 is approximately 140 nM), and it exhibits negligible activity against BMP-activated receptors (ALK2, ALK3, and ALK6) (Laping et al., 2002). This selective inhibition ensures that the canonical TGFβ/Smad pathway is targeted without significantly perturbing other pathways that could be essential for cellular homeostasis, such as the BMP signaling cascade (Nyati et al., 2011; Akhund et al., 2023).

In addition to its inhibition of Smad2/3 phosphorylation, SB431542 has been shown to disrupt the subsequent nuclear translocation of these transcription factors, thereby halting the transcription of downstream ECM components. Such inhibition is critical because overactivation of the TGFβ pathway is a central driver in fibrotic diseases and leads to excessive deposition of ECM proteins, which in turn contribute to tissue stiffness and impaired cellular function (Laping et al., 2002). Overall, the molecular mechanism of SB431542 is well-delineated; its high selectivity for TGFβRI and the resulting blockade of Smad-mediated transcription form the foundation for its potential use in addressing aberrant ECM remodeling.

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis for repurposing SB431542 in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is built on the concept that excessive TGFβ signaling within the retinal microenvironment leads to an abnormal accumulation and remodeling of ECM components in the Bruch membrane (BrM). In the context of dry AMD, such ECM changes are believed to increase membrane stiffness and disrupt the diffusion of critical phagocytic ligands—specifically MFGE8 (Milk Fat Globule Epidermal Growth Factor 8) and Gas6—which play key roles in facilitating the integrin αvβ5-mediated binding and uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Radeke et al., 2015).

By inhibiting TGFβRI, SB431542 is expected to block the TGFβ-driven phosphorylation of Smad proteins, thereby directly reducing the transcription of genes that encode for fibrotic and ECM-related proteins such as collagen I α1, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002). In doing so, SB431542 should restore a more balanced ECM composition in the BrM. This normalization of ECM deposition is anticipated to reduce BrM stiffness, thereby enhancing the diffusion of phagocytic ligands like MFGE8 and Gas6 across the membrane. The improved ligand diffusion is expected to restore the optimal microenvironment required for integrin αvβ5 on the RPE surface to effectively bind and internalize POS, a process that is critically impaired in dry AMD (Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011).

Furthermore, by attenuating the fibrotic response within the retina, SB431542 may help preserve the native architecture and function of the RPE layer. This indirect modulation of phagocytosis, achieved through the normalization of ECM characteristics, represents a novel therapeutic angle that bridges the gap between ECM pathology and receptor-mediated cellular processes. In essence, the expected effect of SB431542 is a dual benefit: first, it directly inhibits pathological TGFβ signaling to reduce further fibrotic damage, and second, it indirectly normalizes phagocytic function by restoring the proper presentation of ligands critical for RPE-mediated clearance of POS (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015).

At the cellular and molecular level, the proposed assay is likely to measure a reduction in fibrotic markers (e.g., collagen I α1, fibronectin) and an improvement in assays of POS binding and internalization by RPE cells. Given that RPE cells express integrin αvβ5 and are responsive to TGFβ signaling, the application of SB431542 should result in a shift from a fibrotic, mesenchymal phenotype towards a more differentiated epithelial state that is conducive to normal phagocytic activity (Radeke et al., 2015; Akhund et al., 2023). This outcome would be mechanistically consistent with the known roles of TGFβ in modulating ECM dynamics and cellular differentiation. Consequently, if the hypothesis holds true, SB431542 would not only prevent further ECM deposition and stiffening of the BrM but would also support the resolution of existing pathological ECM alterations, thereby improving the overall homeostasis of the retinal microenvironment.

The evaluation of SB431542 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD requires careful consideration of its well-established biochemical profile alongside the translational challenges emerging from its current use primarily as a research tool. On the positive side, SB431542 is a potent and selective inhibitor of TGFβRI, with extensive preclinical evidence demonstrating its capacity to block TGFβ-induced Smad2/3 phosphorylation and consequently reduce the expression of fibrotic markers (Laping et al., 2002). Its high potency (with an IC50 in the low nanomolar range) and favorable selectivity profile—particularly with more than 100-fold selectivity over p38 MAPK and minimal activity against BMP receptors—render it an attractive candidate for targeted modulation of TGFβ signaling in tissues where fibrosis is a major pathogenic factor (Laping et al., 2002). These strengths are of particular relevance in the context of dry AMD, where BrM thickening and ECM remodeling are central features that compromise RPE function.

Moreover, the proposed mechanism underlying the therapeutic hypothesis is compelling. Excessive TGFβ signaling has been implicated in the aberrant remodeling of the BrM, which in turn impairs the presentation of critical phagocytic ligands necessary for efficient POS uptake by the RPE (Radeke et al., 2015). By inhibiting TGFβRI, SB431542 could theoretically restore the balance between collagen and proteoglycan production, thereby normalizing BrM stiffness and improving the diffusion of factors such as MFGE8 and Gas6. In doing so, the drug would indirectly enhance integrin αvβ5-mediated phagocytosis—a process that is essential for the maintenance of photoreceptor health and overall retinal integrity. This innovative indirect approach could represent a significant advancement in the treatment of dry AMD, addressing the disease from both a fibrotic and a functional perspective.

However, several considerable challenges and weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, the bulk of the supporting data for SB431542 comes from studies in non-ocular cell types or animal models of general fibrosis and cancer, with limited direct evidence in ocular systems. Although TGFβ inhibitors have been proposed as therapeutic agents in retinal diseases, there remains a significant gap in data specific to dry AMD or related retinal degenerative conditions (Akhund et al., 2023; Nyati et al., 2011). The absence of ocular pharmacokinetic studies, detailed data on retinal tissue penetration, and long-term safety evaluations in the eye poses a major hurdle for the clinical translation of SB431542 for AMD.

Furthermore, TGFβ signaling is a double-edged sword in many tissues, including the retina. While excessive TGFβ activity drives pathological ECM deposition and fibrosis, TGFβ also participates in immune regulation and cellular homeostasis. Therefore, complete or prolonged inhibition of TGFβ signaling may have unintended consequences, such as impairing normal wound healing or altering the immunological milieu of the retina (Akhund et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023). The delicate balance between therapeutic efficacy and potential adverse effects necessitates that any systemic or even locally delivered TGFβRI inhibitor be subject to rigorous dosing and toxicity studies. In this regard, the narrow therapeutic window often encountered in kinase inhibition therapies could be a limiting factor for SB431542’s adoption in an ophthalmic setting.

Another significant concern is the delivery method. The current literature on SB431542 primarily documents its use in cell culture assays or systemic administration in animal models; however, the ocular environment presents unique challenges due to barriers such as the inner limiting membrane, the blood-retina barrier, and the anatomical constraints of the retina. To achieve therapeutically relevant concentrations in the sub-retinal space or at the level of the BrM, innovative delivery strategies—such as topical formulations, intravitreal injections, or sustained-release devices—must be developed and validated (Hachana & Larrivée, 2022; Radeke et al., 2015). The pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of SB431542 in ocular tissues remain largely unexplored, which represents a critical gap in current knowledge.

Additionally, although the indirect mechanism of action—namely, the normalization of ECM to facilitate proper ligand–receptor interactions—is scientifically plausible, it is inherently more challenging to measure and validate compared to direct cellular responses. Assays designed to monitor changes in BrM stiffness, ECM composition, and the diffusion characteristics of MFGE8 and Gas6 must be highly sensitive and reproducible, and these endpoints have not been extensively characterized in available preclinical models of AMD. Furthermore, the redundancy within TGFβ signaling pathways raises the possibility that compensatory mechanisms might mitigate the effects of ALK5 inhibition over time, potentially limiting the efficacy of SB431542, particularly in a chronic, slowly progressive disease like dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Akhund et al., 2023).

From an efficacy standpoint, while numerous studies demonstrate that SB431542 effectively reduces TGFβ-induced fibrotic responses in various cell types (Laping et al., 2002), extrapolating these findings to the complex microenvironment of the aged retina is not straightforward. The retina and RPE possess distinct cellular and molecular characteristics that may respond differently to TGFβ signaling modulation. For example, in RPE cells, TGFβ signaling not only regulates ECM deposition but is also involved in the maintenance of epithelial phenotype and may even exert neuroprotective effects under certain conditions. Hence, unspecific inhibition of TGFβ signaling in the retina could conceivably result in a loss of beneficial effects that are essential for retinal homeostasis (Radeke et al., 2015; Akhund et al., 2023).

In summary, while SB431542 exhibits a robust, well-characterized mechanism of action as a TGFβRI inhibitor and has demonstrated potent anti-fibrotic effects in preclinical models of ECM remodeling, its repurposing for dry AMD must overcome several significant challenges. The strengths of SB431542 lie in its high potency, selectivity, and extensive preclinical validation in non-ocular models. Its molecular interactions are well understood, and its ability to inhibit Smad phosphorylation offers a clear mechanistic rationale for reducing pathological ECM deposition. Consequently, if applied to the pathological process associated with dry AMD, SB431542 could, in theory, mitigate the excessive ECM remodeling that impairs ligand diffusion and consequently restores the capacity for integrin αvβ5-mediated POS uptake by RPE cells (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011).

On the other hand, the weaknesses of this approach are substantial. There is limited evidence of SB431542’s efficacy in ocular models, and its pharmacokinetics, ocular tissue penetration, and long-term safety profile have yet to be rigorously evaluated. Additionally, the complexity of TGFβ’s biological roles raises concerns regarding the balance between therapeutic benefit and potential interference with normal retinal physiology. The indirect nature of the hypothesized effect—mediated by ECM normalization—adds further layers of complexity to both preclinical testing and eventual clinical translation. Finally, challenges related to drug delivery to the retina, along with the potential for compensatory signaling pathways to undermine the inhibitor’s efficacy, suggest that significant additional research is warranted before SB431542 can be advanced as a therapeutic candidate in an AMD setting (Akhund et al., 2023; Akhund et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023).

Overall, SB431542 presents a biologically plausible and mechanistically sound candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly given its demonstrated ability to modulate TGFβ-driven fibrotic pathways. However, its successful translation to an ophthalmic therapeutic will hinge on a series of focused preclinical studies that address ocular biodistribution, safety in retinal tissues, and the optimization of dosing regimens tailored to the unique anatomical and physiological challenges of the eye. Only after these critical issues have been resolved can SB431542 be considered a viable strategy to restore ECM homeostasis in the Bruch membrane, normalize phagocytic ligand availability, and ultimately enhance integrin-mediated POS uptake in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011). In conclusion, while SB431542 has strong potential and a compelling mechanistic rationale, further dedicated ocular research is required to fully validate its therapeutic promise in the context of dry AMD before it can be recommended for clinical development.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
TTP-488, also known as Azeliragon, is a small-molecule synthetic RAGE antagonist originally discovered in the context of Alzheimer’s disease research. It belongs to the class of compounds designed to block the receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) by preventing the interaction between RAGE and its ligands – such as advanced glycation end products (AGEs), amyloid-β peptides, and S100 proteins – that trigger downstream inflammatory signaling cascades. The synthetic origin of TTP-488 stems from medicinal chemistry efforts targeting neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress pathways, and members of this compound class have been investigated for their anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative, and anti-fibrotic properties in multiple disease settings. Its chemical design focused on achieving high binding potency to the extracellular ligand binding domain of RAGE, with an IC₅₀ in the nanomolar range (approximately 100 nM as hypothesized) for inhibition of ligand engagement. This class of RAGE antagonists, including TTP-488, has been predominantly studied in the context of neurodegenerative diseases where aberrant RAGE signaling contributes to pathology, supporting their potential repurposing for diseases characterized by chronic inflammation and oxidative stress, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2, 5–6).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, TTP-488 has been evaluated in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease, where its ability to block RAGE-mediated amyloid-β interactions provided a sound mechanistic rationale for attenuating neuroinflammation and oxidative damage. In these trials, TTP-488 demonstrated an acceptable oral safety profile and favorable pharmacokinetics that make systemic administration feasible—a key consideration when repurposing drugs for alternative indications. While the use of TTP-488 specifically for dry AMD has not been clinically evaluated, a growing body of preclinical evidence has implicated RAGE signaling as a central mediator in AMD pathogenesis. For instance, studies have reported that RAGE expression is significantly upregulated in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells in AMD and that advanced glycation end products accumulate in the drusen deposits characteristic of the disease (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2, 7–8). Moreover, animal models using RAGE-deficient mice have shown reduced choroidal neovascularization and attenuated retinal fibrosis, suggesting that RAGE inhibition could also be beneficial in conditions with similar underlying pathology such as dry AMD (Park, 2017, pp. 157–163, 163–168). Although RAGE antagonists were originally developed with neurodegenerative conditions in mind, the convergence of pathogenic mechanisms such as oxidative stress, lysosomal dysfunction, and inflammation in both Alzheimer’s disease and AMD provides a strong basis for considering TTP-488’s repurposing for retinal degenerative disorders (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 5–6; Barile & Schmidt, 2007, pp. 3–4).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, TTP-488 functions by competitively inhibiting the binding of multiple pathological ligands to the RAGE receptor. Under normal or stressed conditions, AGEs accumulate on extracellular matrices and within drusen deposits, where they interact with RAGE on RPE cells to trigger the activation of several downstream signaling cascades. Activation of RAGE results in the induction of nuclear factor-kappaB (NF-κB), p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), and TGF-β/Smad2 signaling pathways, which collectively contribute to increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, chronic inflammation, and the promotion of fibrotic responses (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2; Barile & Schmidt, 2007, pp. 3–4). Specifically, in the retinal pigment epithelium—cells that are responsible for the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—RAGE activation has been shown to impair lysosomal function, cause lysosomal alkalinization, and disrupt tight junction integrity. This aberrant signaling causes a vicious cycle of increased oxidative stress and inflammation, leading to further accumulation of deleterious metabolic byproducts and progression of dry AMD pathology (Julius & Renuka, 2023, pp. 1–2; Dahrouj et al., 2015, pp. 1–3). TTP-488, by binding to RAGE with high affinity, prevents AGE-RAGE interactions and thereby interrupts this cycle. Moreover, preclinical studies have demonstrated that the inhibition of RAGE through agents such as TTP-488 can attenuate TGF-β2-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in RPE cells, reduce mitochondrial ROS production, and diminish the expression of fibrotic markers like α-smooth muscle actin (αSMA) and collagen I (Sreekumar et al., 2025, pp. 7–10). Blocking these signaling cascades is anticipated to lead to a normalization of lysosomal pH, enhanced clearance of extracellular debris, and ultimately improved phagocytosis of POS, thereby supporting retinal homeostasis (Barile & Schmidt, 2007, pp. 3–4; Park, 2017, pp. 163–168).

Expected Effect:  
The expected therapeutic effect of TTP-488 in the context of dry AMD is based on its ability to restore normal RPE function by mitigating the harmful consequences of AGE-induced RAGE activation. In a typical assay, when cultured RPE cells are exposed to excessive AGEs, the interaction with RAGE triggers oxidative stress and lysosomal dysfunction, leading to impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments—a critical physiological process required for retinal renewal. Treatment with TTP-488 is hypothesized to competitively block these interactions, thus reducing the ensuing ROS production and normalizing lysosomal pH. This normalization is expected to re-establish efficient activation of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway, leading to increased phagocytic uptake and degradation of POS as well as clearance of accumulated debris that may contribute to drusen formation (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4). Additionally, because RAGE signaling also promotes the upregulation of pro-angiogenic factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), its inhibition by TTP-488 is anticipated to reduce aberrant VEGF expression, thereby potentially mitigating secondary pathological features associated with neovascularization, even though dry AMD is predominantly characterized by atrophic processes rather than neovascular ones (Dahrouj et al., 2015, pp. 1–3; Park, 2017, pp. 163–168). Furthermore, RPE cells have been shown to express high levels of RAGE especially in regions adjacent to drusen deposits, indicating that the drug target is well-represented in the critical cellular compartment for treating dry AMD (Park et al., 2015, pp. 1–2; Ruan et al., 2020, pp. 9–11). Ultimately, the net outcome of TTP-488 administration in preclinical models is expected to be a reduction in oxidative damage, an improvement in lysosomal function, and a restoration of RPE-mediated phagocytic capacity, which together could slow or potentially reverse the progression of RPE degeneration observed in dry AMD (Sreekumar et al., 2025, pp. 7–10).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating TTP-488 as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses become apparent. One of the key strengths is the robust molecular rationale underpinning its application in AMD. Numerous studies have implicated the AGE-RAGE axis in the initiation and progression of dry AMD, with evidence of AGE accumulation in drusen, increased RAGE expression in compromised RPE cells, and the subsequent triggering of inflammatory, oxidative, and fibrotic signaling pathways that drive retinal degeneration (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2, 7–8; Julius & Renuka, 2023, pp. 1–2). The fact that TTP-488 has already been evaluated in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease provides a significant advantage in terms of pre-established oral safety data, which could accelerate its repurposing for ocular indications. Its ability to inhibit the AGE-RAGE interaction addresses a pivotal pathogenic driver in the disease while simultaneously reducing oxidative stress, normalizing lysosomal pH, and potentially restoring the phagocytic functions of RPE cells. The oral safety data derived from Alzheimer’s trials provide additional confidence in its repurposing potential. Nonetheless, significant work remains to optimize ocular delivery, to validate efficacy in dry AMD-specific preclinical models, and to carefully assess the risk–benefit profile in the context of chronic retinal diseases. With these considerations in mind, TTP-488 represents a promising and innovative candidate whose further development should be supported by targeted preclinical studies and judicious clinical trial designs that include robust biomarker endpoints for RAGE activity and RPE function (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2; Sreekumar et al., 2025, pp. 7–10; Park, 2017, pp. 157–163).
